It immediately refreshes and scrubs r+-1..+-4 using the physical adjacency map. If more cases appear, it raises local refresh and asks the OS to quarantine (remap) the hot aggressor pages.
why: Free ECC events become hammer and weak-cell sensors (facts 3 and 9), and stop cascades before they reach uncorrectable errors. It needs firmware and a kernel hook only.

title: Solar PVEL-style bankability scorecard for memory reliability
idea: Like the independent PV module scorecard that made new panel makers financeable, an independent lab buys parts off the line and publishes 125 C/10-year HTOL, retention and electromigration scores for every supplier, which lenders use as covenants.
why: Turns reliability into a public, bankable metric, cutting cost of capital for new fabs that score well and widening the supplier base.

title: 1980s DNQ-novolac i-line strategy for PFAS-free domestic interposers
idea: Standardize HBM interposers and RDL at >=1.5-2 um lines on non-chemically-amplified DNQ-novolac resist and i-line steppers, 1980s tooling that is cheap, available used and buildable in the U.S., and design memory interfaces wide and slow enough to fit those rules.
why: Constraint and US manufacturability: DNQ resists contain no PFAS PAGs; i-line steppers cost ~$3-5M versus $20M+ for ArF, enabling domestic interposer capacity under a shared open standard.
note: Coarse RDL on i-line is routine; PFAS-free angle is new but costs bandwidth density.

title: Metronome refresh locked to AI all-reduce phases
idea: Random stimulus 'metronome': everything happens on the beat. The accelerator tells HBM the beat of its training step, and the memory controller bunches all refresh into the predictable windows when HBM is idle (network all-reduce, optimizer step on cached data) instead of spreading it uniformly.
why: Hides most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth tax (fact 3) without changing the cell; needs only system firmware plus a small refresh-postpone extension.

title: Rescue rejected DRAM dies behind a strong-ECC buffer controller
idea: Box: existing dies x existing access x existing SA x ECC buffer chip on module x existing substrate x existing fabs. Buy dies that fail JEDEC bins with <=1% bad bits at scrap prices and package them on modules or CXL cards whose buffer chip runs LDPC plus remapping, sold as a new grade.
why: Usable supply rises right away (recapturing yield loss of a few to 10%) with zero new fabs; cost per bit down.

title: Grade-B DRAM exchange selling dies with certified error maps
idea: Box [medium: any | access: any | sense: standard | integration: DIMM or CXL | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. A broker buys dies that fail JEDEC retention or hammer limits, tests each to a signed per-die error map, and sells them to hyperscalers whose controllers load the map to retire rows and set per-bank refresh.
why: Supply: unlocks the 5-15% of output that is scrapped or downbinned today, at ~40% discount.

title: Retention-binned dies shipped with mandated fine-granularity refresh
idea: Box[Source=dies failing 32 ms retention test x Transform=bin and mark as short-retention SKU x Integration=standard DIMM, SPD flags 2x refresh x Owner=DRAM maker]: dies that miss retention spec but pass at doubled refresh are sold as a discounted SKU, and BIOS reads the SPD flag and enables DDR5's 2x refresh rate.
why: Turns retention-tail scrap into supply (~1-3% more good bits per wafer) at ~1-3% bandwidth cost; no interface change.

title: On-die memory passport logs wear, faults and material content
idea: Worsen: give every chip no history, so recyclers must assume it is junk. Flip: reserve a small OTP/eFuse region where the chip logs total activations, ECC corrections, repairs and a bill-of-materials hash, readable by a standard command, so graders can price and route reuse in seconds.
why: Makes reuse and material recovery pay: grading cost falls ~10x and the reuse rate rises.

title: NAND-style bad-block maps let partially-good DRAM dies ship
idea: Worse: scrap or down-bin any die whose repair fuses run out. Flip: ship DRAM with a host-visible bad-mat table, like NAND bad blocks, and sell a nominal 32 Gb die as 30 Gb usable, with the OS or CXL controller simply never mapping dead mats.
why: Yield at leading nodes and in HBM (fact 6, 20-30% yield loss): recovering dies that fail on only a few mats can add 10-20% more sellable bits per wafer without new fabs.
note: Partial-good DRAM sales are old; CXL-mapped bad mats is a modern twist.

title: Non-power-of-two partial-good DRAM dies with OS bad-bank maps
idea: Worse: scrap every die with a failed bank or sub-array beyond the repair fuses. Flip: sell 12/20/28 Gb harvested dies with whole banks fused off, publishing a bad-bank map in SPD that memory controllers and the OS honor, the way CPU vendors harvest cores.
why: Recovers dies that are scrap today: usable bits per wafer up ~3-8% at zero capex.

title: Open DRAM periphery compiler on a shared U.S. pilot PDK
idea: Worse: make every memory startup re-invent sense amps, decoders and PHYs under NDA. Flip: fund an open-source generator, OpenRAM-style but for 1T1C, gain-cell and novel cells, that emits sense amps, row decoders, charge pumps and DDR/CXL PHYs for a shared U.S. pilot-line PDK.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; reusable open periphery could cut new-cell design cost and time ~70%, widening the supplier base.

title: Inference model cartridges in via-programmed mask ROM
idea: Worse: hold frozen model weights in refreshing DRAM. Flip: ship weights of stable production models as via-programmed ROM cartridges built on 28-40 nm lines, one custom via mask per model, with 20-50 ns random reads.
why: Read-only weights need zero refresh; dense ROM cells on mature nodes free DRAM for truly dynamic data.

title: Open CXL reference controller for static and nonvolatile memories
idea: Worse: make each new memory maker build its own controller and survive hyperscaler qualification alone. Flip: an OCP-style consortium publishes open RTL and firmware for a CXL Type-3 controller with no refresh engine, persistence and wear hooks, and a shared qualification suite.
why: Cuts time-to-market for refresh-free memories by ~2 years and lowers entry cost.

title: Gleaner's cool tier: sense-marginal dies for liquid-cooled racks
idea: Farmers glean the field after harvest. Dies that fail sense margin only above ~75 C are binned as cool-tier DDR5/HBM, sold at standard JEDEC timings into liquid- and immersion-cooled racks that hold devices under 60 C.
why: Turns marginal yield loss into salable bits (+3-8% supply), exploiting how leakage and offset tighten when cool (fact 3).

title: Child's rubber stamp: micro-transfer printing memory dielets onto logic
idea: A child stamps hundreds of stickers at once. Release 50x50 um memory dielets from their source wafer on undercut tethers, then pick thousands at a time with a PDMS stamp and print them onto a logic wafer at +/-1.5 um placement.
why: Memory from any small fab can be printed millimetres from compute with no interposer or TSVs (Facts 5, 6). A uTP tool costs ~$1-2M.
note: uTP is commercial; tiny dielets limit capacity per placement and I/O density.

title: Smelter manager turns dead aluminum plants into memory fabs
idea: Persona: an aluminum smelter manager who knows where cheap firm power already lands. Site new DRAM fabs on shuttered U.S. smelter sites in the Pacific Northwest, Ohio Valley and Kentucky. These sites already have 300-600 MW grid interconnects, water rights, rail and industrial zoning.
why: Energy, water and time inputs: saves 1-2 years in the grid queue and ~$0.5-1B of infrastructure per fab.

title: Migratory birds follow the sun: shift memory-heavy services across time zones
idea: Birds don't winter where food is scarce. A global scheduler moves memory-hungry, latency-tolerant work (batch inference, embedding refreshes, index builds, prefix-KV warmups) each day to the regions at their nightly trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for its own interactive peak rather than the sum of all peaks.
why: Diurnal swings of 30-50% mean pooling in time cuts total provisioned DRAM 15-25% with no new hardware.

title: Insurance actuary prices risk: discounted VMs with memory-pressure insurance
idea: Actuaries price rare events. A cloud or colo sells VMs 25% cheaper whose guests agree that during rare host pressure events up to 30% of their pages may be served from a compressed tier. Credits ('claims') are paid automatically per minute of measured degradation. Billing and telemetry software fits in the budget.
why: Pricing overcommit turns a hidden risk into a product, so providers can safely run 1.3-1.5x memory overcommit.

title: Ephemeral-grade DRAM: sell retention rejects to frame-buffer users
idea: Camera, display and network ring buffers overwrite every byte within ~16 ms. Create a product grade for dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16-32 ms, sold to customers whose controllers guarantee a rewrite cadence and issue no refresh at all.
why: Scarce supply: turns retention-fail scrap and downbins (a few % of output) into usable bits, and these buyers spend zero refresh energy; adds supply without a new fab.

title: Token-ring wordline sequencer for append-only KV-cache mats
idea: KV-caches append and stream tokens in order, so dedicated mats replace the row decoder with a token passed along a chain of shift-register stages (one per 8 wordlines plus a 3-bit local predecoder), allowing random access only at block granularity. Everything is drawn at DUV pitch.
why: Row-decoder area -60% in AI-tier mats with no EUV-pitch decoders, matched to KV-cache access patterns.

title: Wired-NOR zero-detect lines suppress all-zero bursts at sense stripes
idea: Satellites downlink only non-trivial data: each SA group pulls down a wired-NOR line if any latched bit is 1, so all-zero 64-byte sectors return a 1-bit flag instead of a full burst over global I/O and pins. Sparse AI activations and zero-padded KV pages benefit most.
why: I/O energy (fact 5) down 20-50% on sparse data with trivial DUV circuitry.

title: Data-parallel training: model replicas become each other's ECC
idea: In a 10,000-GPU job, every data-parallel rank holds identical weights. Periodically checksum each 2 MB weight shard, compare checksums across replicas over NVLink or InfiniBand, and repair any mismatched shard by copying it from a majority peer. Local HBM errors are then corrected by replication that already exists.
why: Weights are ~30-50% of training HBM. Cross-replica voting gives TMR-like protection for free and lets weight regions run on weaker dies or relaxed refresh (facts 3, 6).

title: Cold-grade bins: sell retention-reject dies to cryo and immersion racks
idea: Extreme user: 4 K quantum-control racks and LN2- or oil-immersed AI pods, where DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude. Fabs create a priced 'cold-grade' SKU from dies that fail 64 ms retention at 85 C but pass at 45 C or below, sold with a contractual maximum case temperature to immersion-cooled racks that hold DIMMs at 30-40 C.
why: Retention-tail fallout (fact 3) is scrapped or downbinned today; reclaiming 2-5% of wafer output as a priced bin adds bit supply with zero new capex.

title: Classified-grade DRAM sanitization so secure fleets stop shredding
idea: Classified and financial systems shred all memory. A 10-person lab offers NIST 800-88-style DRAM sanitization (powered-off hold, verified all-zero readback, SPD wipe) with chain-of-custody video and a certificate, so secure fleets resell modules instead of destroying them.
why: Unlocks memory destroyed by policy today, plausibly a double-digit share of enterprise retirements.
note: DRAM loses data on power-off; barrier is policy acceptance, not physics.

title: Short-retention grade: sell dies that fail 64 ms but pass 16 ms
idea: Time shift of the retention spec: dies that miss the 64 ms refresh window but pass at 16 ms are binned as a new 'short-retention' SKU, shipped with controller firmware that refreshes 4x faster, and placed where data lives under a second (AI activations, caches, scratch tiers).
why: Turns yield-loss dies on wafers already processed into sellable bits; claimed +3-8% bit output with zero new capex. Costs some refresh energy only in tiers that tolerate it.
note: Characterizable with SoftMC-style FPGA testers.

title: Stranded-memory buyback: telemetry finds surplus DIMMs in enterprises
idea: Months-long observation: an agent records each enterprise server's 90-day peak working set, and a buyback service pulls DIMMs above the 99th-percentile need and resells them to cloud and AI buyers.
why: Enterprises typically overprovision RAM by 30-50%. Releasing it is new usable supply at near-zero cost, with no fab and no gases.

title: HP hot-plug RAID memory revived as a parity tier in 3D stacks
idea: HP's hot-plug RAID memory was dropped because it gave up 20-25% of capacity to redundancy. Inside a 3D DRAM or HBM stack, add one XOR parity tier per 16 data tiers plus a spare. When a tier fails, its data is rebuilt onto the spare in the background and the stack stays in service.
why: About 6% overhead to survive a whole-tier failure, raising 3D stack yield and life (facts 2, 6) with repair built in.

title: Relabel scandal fixed: certified, graded reclaimed DRAM chips
idea: Harvested DRAM from e-waste got a bad name because chips were sanded, remarked and sold as new. Fix: a certified reclamation line desolders and reballs each chip, runs full retention, speed and row-hammer characterization, writes a tamper-evident provenance record (original lot ID read from the die's fuses plus test results), and sells the chips openly in graded tiers with warranty.
why: Supply: turns millions of discarded DIMMs into trusted bits at a fraction of new cost; recovering even ~5% of annual bit demand matters when prices are 4x.

title: Ink-saver encoding keeps fewest cells in leaky charged state
idea: Like ink-saving fonts that print letters with holes, encode each burst with a low-weight code (e.g., 16b to 18b with per-group inversion) chosen using the die's true-cell/anti-cell map, so as few cells as possible sit in the charged state that leaks; retention failures are nearly all charged-to-discharged.
why: Cuts the population of retention-vulnerable cells by ~30-40%, so the same leakage tail (fact 3) yields fewer failures and refresh can stretch ~1.5x; restore energy drops slightly (fact 10) for ~6-12% capacity cost.

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.
why: Rescues dies that exceed on-die redundancy (several yield points) and makes cross-die repair nearly free because overlaps are engineered to near zero.

title: Grade-mixed ranks: Reed-Solomon makes one cheap die harmless
idea: Ideal: any die can be used. Closest: a rank uses symbol-level Reed-Solomon over 10 chips with 2 check chips, which lets one chip per rank be a cheap C-grade die with raw BER ~1e-5 (treated as a known-unreliable symbol) while the module still meets server RAS targets.
why: Supply and cost: absorbs down-binned dies into server modules, lowering module cost ~10-15%.
note: Symbol RS tolerating one C-grade die is straightforward; moderate cost win.

title: Telemetry-backed warranties that make used DRAM bankable
idea: Ideal: used memory is trusted as much as new. Closest achievable with no new fab: an insurer underwrites 3-year warranties on second-life DIMMs, priced from each module's logged correctable-error history and burn-in screen, so clouds accept refurbished DRAM in production.
why: Reuse demand unlock: lets 20-30% of retired server DRAM re-enter service.

title: Let the model refresh itself: compiler sweeps every weight row per window
idea: 10-person constraint: a compiler pass instead of hardware. For inference, place and stream the weights so every DRAM row holding weights is activated at least once per 32 ms; each read restores its row. The controller disables explicit refresh for those banks and falls back to REF only if a token stall exceeds the window.
why: Fact 3: weights are the majority of inference DRAM bytes, so their refresh energy and bandwidth drop to ~zero with only a compiler change and a controller flag.

title: Million-dollar bounty for a chokepoint-free capacitor module
idea: Within $1M/24 months: put the whole budget into staged prizes ($100k milestones, $500k grand prize) for any team that shows a DRAM capacitor module of >=5 fF at <=40 nm pitch using no He, W, Hf/Zr, PFAS or HPQ-dependent steps, verified by an independent university fab.
why: Prizes often draw 10-40x their value in outside effort, turning a tiny budget into dozens of parallel material searches aimed at the capacitor charge wall.

title: Die passport: on-die ledger makes recycled DRAM cheap to re-bin
idea: Rule: every die must be recyclable without full re-test. Each die carries a few-kB OTP or MRAM ledger recording its retention map, measured hammer threshold, PPR repairs, temperature history and error counts. Refurbishers read the ledger in seconds to re-bin and re-sell the die.
why: Re-test cost (the main barrier to DRAM reuse) drops ~80%, making second-life dies economical and raising usable supply.
note: Cheap re-binning for reuse.

title: Substitute explicit refresh with weight-streaming reads that restore rows
idea: Substitute refresh commands for LLM weight regions with read-restore. During decode every weight row is activated once per token (~20-50 ms), and each activation fully restores its charge, so the controller tracks how often each row is read and suppresses refresh while serving. This is controller logic only, with no fab step.
why: Weights fill most HBM capacity in inference, so refresh there is pure waste: ~10% of bandwidth and refresh energy recovered.

title: FPGA retimer that compresses cache lines in flight
idea: Substitute raw transfers on a CXL memory link with an inline FPGA stage doing base-delta-immediate plus zero-run coding of 64 B lines, packing 2-3 compressed lines into each flit in both directions.
why: Fact 5: effective link bandwidth +1.5-2x and expander capacity +1.3-1.8x for typical data, delivered as pure logic design.
note: Inline cache-line link compression is published art.

title: XOR-delta page migration between memory tiers
idea: Substitute full-page copies when a hypervisor moves pages between HBM, DDR and CXL tiers with XOR deltas against the stale copy kept in the far tier, sending only cache lines flagged dirty since the last migration.
why: Fact 5: tiering traffic down 60-90% for read-mostly pages, making cheap far memory usable so less HBM is needed.

title: Substitute DIMM-level ECC with algorithm-based fault tolerance in GEMMs
idea: Store AI weights in ECC-less cheap memory and append row/column checksums to each matrix; matmul kernels verify checksums on the fly and correct single errors or reload the tile on mismatch.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC bit overhead and lets inference run on high-BER bins, raising usable supply ~10-15%.
note: Huang-Abraham ABFT is decades old; mature and easy to demo.

title: Substitute stored KV caches with NV lineage tokens and deterministic recompute
idea: Instead of persisting huge DRAM states (e.g., LLM KV caches), persist only the small inputs, seeds and checkpoints in NV, and regenerate the DRAM contents deterministically after power returns.
why: Persistence cost drops by 100-1000x per session since only the generator survives; uses existing DRAM.
note: Recompute-vs-store for KV caches is standard practice in serving systems.

title: EEPROM high-voltage module builds a thick-oxide, high-Vt access transistor
idea: Use the 1990s EEPROM HV process: 12-15 nm gate oxide, Vt ~1.3 V and channels of 0.5 um or more. EEPROM charge pumps boost the wordline to 5-6 V.
why: Off-leakage of ~1e-18 A gives minute-scale retention, so refresh is negligible. It trades density for a refresh-free tier made in any legacy fab.

title: Datacenter DIMM salvage reborn as tested CXL memory pools
idea: Combine server decommissioning with CXL memory expansion: desolder DRAM packages from retired DDR4/DDR5 modules, retest and speed-bin them, and mount them on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller hides mixed timing and maps weak rows out.
why: Every reused retired bit displaces a new wafer start; at 4x prices, recovering even 5% of supply needs zero fab capital, zero helium and zero quartz.

title: Mobile-OS saved-instance-state: kernel discards rebuildable caches by cost
idea: Borrowed from Android, which kills background apps after they save compact state bundles: applications tag regions with a rebuild cost (ns/byte to recompute or re-fetch), and the kernel reclaims the lowest cost-per-byte regions first, signalling the app to rebuild lazily instead of swapping.
why: Caches (memoization, decompressed assets, JIT code) are 20-40% of server RAM; cost-aware discard can shrink provisioned DRAM 15-25% with predictable tails.

title: Fax-machine run-length coding compresses sparse traffic on memory bus
idea: Adapted from Group 3 fax Modified Huffman/RLE: a 180 nm codec on the memory buffer encodes zero runs and repeated values in activations, sparse weights and KV-cache before they cross the bus and land in DRAM.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and effective capacity: ReLU and sparse tensors are often 50-90% zeros, so 2-5x fewer bits are moved and stored.
note: Zero/RLE memory compression is established art.

title: Long-channel thick-oxide gain cell in open-source 130 nm
idea: MAGNIFY channel length ~10x and oxide thickness ~3x on the write device: a 3T gain cell in the open SKY130/GF180 PDKs uses the 5 V thick-oxide transistor as write switch (aA subthreshold leakage) and stores on the read transistor's gate; free or cheap shuttles allow monthly iterations.
why: Retention ~1-10 s vs 64 ms (fact 3) in U.S.-fabbed nodes with near-zero capital; niche embedded DRAM for chiplets.
note: Gain-cell eDRAM in open PDKs already explored; niche.

title: Harvest and re-bin DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Magnify each die's service life: retired hyperscaler DIMMs are retested at speed, re-binned by retention, and rebuilt into CXL expansion cards for cold tiers, with laser die-debond to rescue good dies from failed modules.
why: Each reused GB avoids ~1 GB of new wafer, EUV, helium and water. Millions of DIMMs retire every year while prices are up 4x.
note: Retired-DIMM reuse behind CXL already piloted by hyperscalers; die-level debond adds little.

title: Magnify entropy coding to lossless BF16 exponent compression
idea: Magnify the encoder in the DMA/memory controller to an inline lossless entropy coder for floating-point exponents. BF16/FP8 exponents carry only ~2.5-3 bits of entropy, so they are Huffman/ANS-coded per 4 KB block, and mantissas and sign pass through raw.
why: A ~1.4-1.5x lossless shrink of all weights, activations and optimizer tensors, with no accuracy cost, cuts both HBM capacity and pJ/bit moved.

title: Eliminate explicit refresh for weights re-read every inference pass
idea: The controller keeps a per-row touched-this-window bit; in LLM serving, where weight rows are streamed every token (<20-50 ms), rows proven read within tREFW get REF suppressed because each activation already restores the cells. A watchdog issues REF only to rows the access pattern missed.
why: Weight-streaming inference touches most of HBM per token; suppressing redundant refresh recovers ~10-20% bandwidth and ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy across the weight footprint.

title: Eliminate stored zeros: zero-line bitmaps keep sparse tensors off DRAM
idea: The controller keeps a 1-bit-per-64-byte zero map in on-die SRAM; all-zero lines and zero-dominant lines (run-length encoded) are never written to or read from the DRAM array.
why: ReLU-sparse activations, pruned weights and optimizer states with 50-90% zero lines see 2-10x fewer accesses, >10x on the sparsest tensors, and freed capacity.

title: Eliminate the OS page cache: storage DMAs straight into app buffers
idea: Remove the kernel page cache entirely: file reads DMA directly from NVMe into application-owned buffers (io_uring fixed buffers), and any read caching moves into the SSD's own SLC region or a CXL-attached flash tier with a small SRAM line cache.
why: Page cache commonly holds 20-40% of server DRAM; eliminating it as a DRAM consumer frees that capacity at near-zero cost per bit.

title: Eliminate fork's 2x memory peak with userfaultfd write-protect snapshots
idea: A 10-person team ships a library that replaces fork-based snapshots (Redis BGSAVE, Postgres-style checkpoints) with userfaultfd write-protection: the snapshotter streams pages to disk and copies only pages written mid-snapshot.
why: In-memory stores are provisioned at about 2x their data to survive fork copy-on-write storms; removing that cuts their DRAM by up to 45%.
note: userfaultfd-WP snapshots already ship in QEMU and Dragonfly.

title: Eliminate hash-table overhead with succinct minimal-perfect-hash cache modules
idea: A Redis module rebuilds read-mostly keyspaces into a minimal perfect hash (about 2 bits/key) plus Elias-Fano-packed values, with a small mutable delta table merged incrementally.
why: Pointer-rich hash tables cost 50-80 B/key of overhead; density improves 3-5x.
note: Succinct/MPH packing is well known; Redis module is a straightforward application limited to read-mostly keyspaces.

title: Eliminate background app residency with compressed heap hibernation on clients
idea: A desktop OS service serializes the JS/V8 heaps of background browser tabs and Electron apps into zstd blobs on SSD and restores them lazily on focus, with sub-second resume.
why: Electron apps and tabs consume 300 MB-1 GB each; laptops could ship 8 GB instead of 16 GB and cut client DRAM demand.

title: Eliminate stranded DIMMs: fleet profiling plus physical DIMM redistribution
idea: A 10-person service profiles fleet memory use with eBPF, finds hosts with chronically idle DIMMs, and sends technicians to move modules into memory-starved hosts during maintenance windows.
why: Fleets typically strand 20-30% of installed DRAM; reallocating it defers new purchases by a year or more.
note: Simple ops play; channel population rules and labor limit gains.

title: Eliminate forced DDR5 migration: new DDR4 boards for dual-support CPUs
idea: Eliminate the platform change that strands DDR4: contract an ODM to build new DDR4 boards for CPUs and embedded SoCs whose controllers support both DDR4 and DDR5, aimed at the reclaimed-DDR4 pool; ~$800k NRE and first batch.
why: Gives used DDR4 a large new home and moves buyers off scarce DDR5.

title: Compact free memory into refresh-off segments
idea: Reverse the OS goal from spreading pages to packing them: a kernel compaction daemon migrates live pages out of the top DRAM segments whenever utilization falls, then switches those segments' refresh off using partial-array self-refresh or segment masking that LPDDR5/DDR5 already support.
why: Servers average ~40-60% DRAM utilization and phones idle with free memory; refresh-off empty segments cut refresh/idle power ~30-50% (fact 3); software only.
note: PASR-based compaction proposed in literature and kernels; pure software demo.

title: Reverse the e-waste flow: profile and redeploy retired server DRAM
idea: Flip decommissioned DIMMs from shredder back to rack: test pulled DDR4/DDR5 modules on existing ATE for per-row retention and error history, sort them into retention grades, and redeploy them in CXL memory-expander pools whose controller applies per-row multi-rate refresh and assigns weak rows to spare or short-lived buffer duty.
why: Raises usable memory supply with zero fab capacity (hyperscalers retire many PB per year) while retention-graded refresh keeps energy per bit acceptable (fact 3).

title: Erasure-coded in-memory shards replace triple DRAM replicas
idea: Instead of keeping 2-3 full DRAM replicas of hot data in in-memory databases and caches, split each object into k data plus m parity shards across nodes (e.g. 10+4 Reed-Solomon) and rebuild over RDMA when a node fails.
why: Resilience overhead drops from 2-3x to ~1.4x of the dataset: 40-55% less DRAM for replicated in-memory tiers.

title: HBM stealing: idle neighbor GPUs host overflow KV blocks
idea: Reverse the swap direction from down-to-host to sideways-to-peers: a cluster daemon tracks free HBM on each GPU and pages KV blocks into idle neighbors over NVLink/ICI, ~10x faster than host DDR, before any new memory is bought.
why: GPU fleets often leave 20-40% of HBM unused on some devices; pooling it raises usable capacity by that margin in software alone, with no gas-consuming fabrication.

title: Delay-and-cluster scheduler groups requests by shared prefix
idea: Rearrange time: the router holds incoming requests for up to ~150 ms on purpose and releases them in batches grouped by system-prompt or document prefix to the same replica, so one prefix KV copy serves dozens of concurrent requests.
why: Prefix KV duplication across replicas disappears; KV memory per request falls 2-5x for templated workloads, using only scheduling software on installed GPUs.

title: Admit LLM requests by predicted KV-seconds, not arrival order
idea: Reverse the scheduler's input: a small regressor predicts each request's output length and context so the scheduler admits and orders work by predicted KV-byte-seconds (shortest-KV-first, with preemption) instead of FIFO, bounding peak KV rather than provisioning for it.
why: Peak KV memory falls ~1.5-2x at equal throughput, delivered as a software update on installed accelerators.

title: Shared inverted page tables end per-process mapping copies
idea: Reverse the page-table direction for shared memory: one table per shared physical region (indexed by frame, or a kernel-shared upper-level table) is linked into every process that maps it, instead of each of hundreds of database worker processes building its own copy.
why: Databases with large shared buffers can burn tens of GB on duplicate page tables; sharing them recovers that DRAM with a kernel change alone.

title: Fleet DIMM gleaning: telemetry-guided physical rebalancing of installed memory
idea: Rearrange the DIMMs already installed across a fleet: per-server memory telemetry finds hosts whose peak use never exceeds half their DRAM, and technicians pull those modules during routine maintenance and install them in memory-starved hosts of the same generation.
why: Fleets often have 20-30% of DRAM never touched; moving it costs far less than buying new bits at 4x prices and needs no rare gases.
note: Operational practice, modest gain.

title: PCI-class hardware RAM Doubler card for cold pages
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: take compression out of the latency path entirely; a 180 nm bus-master card (PCI-X/PCIe gen1 class, ~1 GB/s) compresses only pages idle >1 s with an LZ-class engine and packs them into a compressed DRAM pool, which the OS uses like zswap with hardware offload, echoing 1996's RAM Doubler.
why: Cold-page churn is ~10-100 MB/s per server, well within 1990s bandwidth; 20-40% more effective DRAM with no CPU cycles spent.

title: Hash-consing allocator merges identical immutable objects at birth
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: the language runtime interns every immutable object (strings, tuples, small records, JSON subtrees) through a hash table at allocation, so identical values become one physical object, as 1990s Lisp and ML systems did; it runs on any CPU.
why: Duplicate objects are 10-40% of heaps in data-processing services, and object-level dedup is far finer than page dedup.
note: Hash-consing and JVM string dedup are old art.

title: Feedback: self-tuning shared dictionaries compress traffic on both link ends
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: the memory base die and the accelerator each keep matched 256-entry value dictionaries. Repeated words (zeros, common weight and activation values) travel as 8-bit indices, and both sides update their dictionaries in lockstep each epoch using hit-rate feedback.
why: Data movement (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer link bits per useful bit for AI tensors, cutting pJ per useful bit and bandwidth demand.
note: Frequent-value/dictionary link compression is prior art.

title: Merging: content-addressed CXL appliance deduplicates shared KV prefixes
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging identical objects: a 28 nm CXL memory appliance hashes every 4 KB page written by many inference sessions (shared system prompts, common prefixes, replicated weights). It stores each distinct page once in commodity DDR4 and uses copy-on-write when a page diverges. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: 2-5x effective capacity for multi-tenant LLM serving with shared prompts, built entirely from trailing-node logic and legacy DRAM.
note: KSM and vLLM prefix sharing already capture this.

title: Prior action: weights stored entropy-coded, decoded by 28 nm ingress engines
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: compress model weights offline with per-tensor entropy coding (Huffman/ANS on quantized values) and keep them compressed in DRAM. A 28 nm decoder chiplet at the accelerator's memory ingress expands them at line rate. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity and data movement (fact 5): 1.4-2x fewer DRAM bits and link bits per weight, with the decode logic built in trailing fabs.
note: Weight entropy coding known (e.g. DFloat11); gains shrink after quantization.

title: Predictive-coding memory link transmitting only prediction errors
idea: The visual cortex sends mostly prediction errors, not raw images. Identical lightweight predictors (last-value, stride, zero-run) sit at both ends of a CXL/DIMM link on FPGA, and only the entropy-coded XOR residual crosses the wire. FPGA prototype, ~$600k in 18 months.
why: Fact 5: residuals are mostly zeros, so ~1.5-2x fewer bits cross a 10-20 pJ/bit link. That buys effective bandwidth and energy and lets fewer channels feed the same compute.

title: Mayfly memory: refresh-free banks for data that dies young
idea: Adult mayflies live a day and have no working gut, so no maintenance organs for a short life. An allocator flag marks 'ephemeral' pages (AI activations, KV scratch, network buffers) that are rewritten within the 64 ms guaranteed retention. The controller skips refresh, or uses partial-array refresh, for banks holding only such data. Linux patch, controller firmware and FPGA demo, ~$600k in 24 months.
why: Fact 3: recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and refresh energy on the large share of AI memory that is short-lived.

title: Hummingbird torpor mode for fab tool gas purges
idea: Hummingbirds drop their metabolism ~95% at night. Give every etch, CVD and implant tool a predictive torpor state, keyed to the MES dispatch queue, that cuts helium backside and carrier purges to a trickle seal flow when no wafer is due for N minutes and restores full flow seconds before the next lot arrives.
why: Tools idle 20-40% of the time, often with purges still flowing; could cut fab helium and specialty-gas use 15-30% with software and valves alone while Qatar is offline.

title: Lichen pairing turns retired servers into RDMA memory donors
idea: Lichen fuses a fungus and an alga into a new organism; a stripped retired server (old CPU, full DRAM) runs a tiny memory-server OS and lends its DRAM over RDMA as remote swap to new servers, its only job being memory.
why: Supply: retiring servers' DRAM gets a second 3-5-year life; 25-40% less new DRAM per new server.

title: Postsynaptic-register signaling: wires toggle only on surprise
idea: Each HBM data lane keeps a 'postsynaptic' predictor latch at the receiver mirrored at the sender (last value per lane per burst position, updated identically at both ends like a Hebbian trace). The sender fires a release pulse only when the real bit differs from the prediction, so steady bit positions such as exponents, sign bits and zero-padding never toggle the wire.
why: Interface pJ/bit (fact 5): ML tensors have strong per-bit-position redundancy; claim 30-50% fewer wire transitions on HBM/DDR links, i.e. 30-50% I/O energy cut with no change to DRAM cells.
note: Variant of bus-invert and transition coding, which are widely known.

title: Synaptic-spine gain cells: every mature logic fab becomes memory fab
idea: Synapses store weight as charge on a dendritic spine with no dedicated capacitor. A 3-transistor silicon gain cell stores charge on the read transistor's gate and ships as an open memory compiler for 28-65 nm logic processes, so U.S. mature logic fabs can make DRAM-class chips with no high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch.
why: Removes the hardest capacitor steps and EUV; widens DRAM-capable U.S. sites from ~1 to >10, at lower density per die.

title: Certified pre-owned DRAM: re-profiled hyperscaler memory with warranty
idea: Borrowed from certified pre-owned cars: a 10-person shop buys DIMMs from retired cloud servers by the ton, runs 48-hour retention, row-hammer and temperature profiling on FPGA test rigs, rewrites each DIMM's SPD with measured timing and refresh bins, swaps weak chips and sells warrantied modules for CXL memory expanders.
why: Supply: millions of DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply with zero wafer capacity at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Linux-style open DRAM compiler on U.S. open PDKs
idea: Borrowed from open-source software turning OS kernels into a commons: a 10-person team builds an OpenRAM-like generator for gain-cell and 1T1C eDRAM macros on the SkyWater 130 nm and GlobalFoundries 180 nm open PDKs, emitting layout, sense amps, refresh controller and characterization so any ASIC team embeds MBs of dense memory instead of buying discrete DRAM.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: moves some IoT, edge and defense demand off commodity DRAM onto memory made in U.S. foundries, at ~2-3x SRAM density.

title: Nespresso pods: sealed precursor cartridges for micro-fab ALD
idea: Borrowed from coffee pods that made espresso possible without a barista: package each ALD precursor (TEMAZ, TMA, TiCl4) in sealed, barcoded, heated single-use cartridges with built-in vapor regulation that click into a tool manifold, so a small fab skips bulk chemical delivery, gas cabinets and abatement plumbing.
why: Capital: bulk specialty-chemical systems are ~10% of fab capex and months of build; cartridges let small U.S. pilot fabs start in weeks.
note: Ampoule-based ALD delivery already standard.

title: RAID for RAM: erasure-coded stripes replace triple-copy replicas
idea: Distributed in-memory stores (Redis replicas, parameter servers, failover KV-cache copies) keep 2-3 full copies; instead stripe data with Reed-Solomon (e.g. 8+2) across nodes' DRAM over RDMA/CXL and reconstruct on node loss as RAID-6 does for disks.
why: Cuts redundancy overhead from 200% to 25%, ~2.4x less DRAM for fault-tolerant in-memory tiers.
note: EC-Cache, Hydra and Carbink already do this.

title: Leitner boxes: spaced-repetition promotion from NV into DRAM
idea: Like flashcards moving up Leitner boxes only after recalls at spaced intervals, pages live in persistent memory by default and are promoted one box at a time (NV -> compressed DRAM -> plain DRAM) only after accesses at increasing intervals, filtering one-off scans.
why: Prevents scan pollution from bloating DRAM tiers; keeps DRAM to the truly recurrent working set, ~20-30% smaller for the same hit rate.

title: Urban-mining refurbishment line for retired server DIMMs
idea: Urban mining pulls metals out of e-waste; this recovers the bits instead. A semi-automated line tests decommissioned DDR4 from retired fleets, maps weak rows, rewrites SPD, and deploys the modules behind FPGA CXL-DDR4 adapters that hide the weak-row map through page retirement. Test racks, adapters and 3 staff fit within $1M.
why: Millions of retired DIMMs a year become supply at near-zero fab capital (fact 4), and recycling also works around the resource chokepoints.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL.

title: Intel 1103 three-transistor cell rebuilt on 22-nm FD-SOI back gates
idea: The first commercial DRAM (1103, 1970) was a 3T gain cell. Rebuild it on existing 22/28-nm FD-SOI lines with a thick-oxide write transistor held under reverse back-bias for sub-aA leakage and a thin-oxide read transistor whose back gate is pulsed only during reads for ~5x read current.
why: No capacitor (Fact 1); back-bias pushes retention to ~1 s (Fact 3: refresh energy down ~10-15x); non-destructive read removes write-back (Fact 8); existing non-EUV capacity.
note: 3T gain cell on FD-SOI is well-trodden eDRAM; easy MPW demo, lower density than 1T1C.

title: Morse-code revival: frequency-weighted transition-minimal codes on memory links
idea: As Morse gave frequent letters the shortest codes, profile tensor statistics (BF16/FP8 exponent clusters, zero runs) and assign link codewords so the commonest symbols cause the fewest wire toggles and terminated ones, with codebooks swapped per tensor in the PHY.
why: Fact 5: I/O energy tracks toggles and terminated ones; skewed AI tensors allow 30-50% fewer transitions (30-50% lower link energy) plus ~1.3x effective bandwidth from compression.

title: Sell imperfect dies: fractional-capacity DRAM with OS bad-page maps
idea: Inverts 'every die must be perfect': ship dies with up to 10-30% failing rows or subarrays as non-power-of-two capacity parts, with a signed bad-page map in an on-module EEPROM that firmware or the CXL controller reads at boot and never allocates.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by recovering scrapped or downbinned dies (HBM yield is down 20-30%); every recovered die saves its full share of quartz, helium, energy and water.

title: Turn spare 28-65 nm logic fabs into memory fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must come from DRAM fabs'. Standardize a pure-logic-process 3T gain-cell macro (no capacitor module) with on-die short-interval refresh, sold as CXL/UCIe memory chiplets that any mature-node logic fab can run on its existing flow.
why: Unlocks depreciated capacity in months, not 3-5 years; ~0.1-0.15 Gb/mm2 at 28 nm (~3x less dense) on wafers costing ~1/3, near parity cost per bit for cache/near-memory roles.

title: Whole-block dataflow fusion keeps intermediates only in SRAM
idea: Inverts 'every operator writes its output to memory': a compiler fuses an entire transformer block (norm, QKV, attention, MLP) into one persistent streaming kernel that passes tiles core-to-core through on-chip SRAM, so intermediate activations never touch DRAM/HBM during inference.
why: Removes activation buffers and workspace (often 10-30% of inference memory) and the traffic they generate.

title: Zygote fork: preinitialize runtimes once, copy-on-write everywhere
idea: Inverts 'each container boots its own runtime': as with Android's zygote, each node keeps a pre-warmed Python/JVM/ML-framework process with libraries and shared weights loaded, and every new container forks from it and shares pages copy-on-write. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Per-instance memory for interpreter, libraries and shared weights (often 200 MB-2 GB) is paid once per node, cutting container fleet DRAM 2-4x.
note: Zygote and forkserver patterns are established.

title: Recompute beats retain: drop KV between turns, then re-prefill
idea: Inverts 'prefill is expensive and KV is cheap': at 4x DRAM prices, holding a user's KV through human think time costs more per GB-hour than the prefill FLOPs to rebuild it. The server keeps only token text between turns, re-prefills on existing GPUs, and a cost model picks keep, spill or recompute per session.
why: Idle sessions are typically >90% of open sessions, so resident KV drops several-fold for chat fleets, in software only.
note: Dropping or spilling KV between turns with a cost model is common serving practice.

title: Per-application trained zstd dictionaries in kernel memory compression
idea: Inverts 'one generic compressor fits all memory': zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per workload class (Java heap, Python objects, protobufs) from sampled cold pages and recompresses cold pages with it on idle cores. Software on existing servers.
why: Dictionaries lift compression on small pages from ~2.5x to ~4x, freeing another 10-20% of DRAM fleet-wide.

title: Cold-byte reaper right-sizes heaps using idle-page tracking
idea: Inverts 'allocated means needed': page-idle tracking (DAMON or the idle bitmap) finds heap regions untouched for minutes, and an agent then lowers JVM -Xmx, Go GOMEMLIMIT and cache sizes per service, rolling back on latency regressions. Software only.
why: Fleet audits typically find 20-40% of resident memory cold; right-sizing frees that DRAM in servers already installed.
note: Close to TMO/Senpai/DAMON-based proactive reclaim.

title: Expiry-dated memory: allocations carry leases that must be renewed
idea: Inverts 'an allocation lives until someone frees it': the allocator gives every long-lived block a lease renewed by access. Unrenewed blocks are compressed first, then paged out to flash and reported as suspected leaks with their allocation stack. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Long-running services leak or bloat 10-30% over their uptime; leases cap that growth with no hardware.

title: Power-gate idle ranks once idle time beats the break-even
idea: Compute the break-even from first principles. A 64 GB DDR5 RDIMM in self-refresh burns ~0.5 W, while spilling and restoring 64 GB to NVMe costs ~2 nJ/B each way (~250 J), so any idle stretch beyond ~8 minutes is cheaper with the rank powered off. Add a hypervisor policy that compacts cold pages, spills them to NVMe or compresses them into active ranks, and cuts the rank's rails through the DIMM PMIC. Software and firmware, <$500k.
why: This removes retention energy entirely for idle capacity (overnight and diurnal troughs), attacking refresh's 16-33% share of idle power across the data center (fact 3).

title: 22FDX eDRAM with back-gate retention bias on a U.S. line
idea: Fully depleted SOI gives every transistor an independent back gate with a ~80 mV/V body factor. Tape out a 1T1C (MIM-capacitor) eDRAM macro on GlobalFoundries 22FDX in Malta, NY via MPW. The array's back-gate well swings to -2 V during retention, raising access Vt ~160 mV, and returns to 0 V during access. MPW, design and test fit ~$700k over 20 months.
why: +160 mV of Vt at ~70 mV/dec cuts hold-state subthreshold leakage ~200x while keeping access current. It demonstrates refresh-light, DRAM-class embedded memory on a U.S. fab (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Second-life DDR4 behind CXL controllers with per-row refresh
idea: Hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 RDIMMs that still work but whose retention tails have aged. Build a CXL Type-3 FPGA card that hosts eight retired DIMMs, profiles every row at intake, and runs per-row refresh plus strong ECC. Sell it as a far-memory tier; the prototype and pilot run fit within $1M and 24 months.
why: Adds usable capacity without new wafers (supply, capital and scarce-resource axes), with refresh tuned to measured retention rather than spec (fact 3).
note: Azure-style CXL reuse of DDR4 already announced.

title: Joule-and-dollar ledger deciding store versus recompute per tensor
idea: Price every resident object by its physical rent: capacity amortization ($/GB-s) plus refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit per 64 ms), against the energy and time to rebuild it from its inputs (FLOPs x ~0.5 pJ). A runtime keeps a lineage graph, like Spark or autograd, and drops any tensor, query intermediate or memo entry whose rebuild cost is below its rent, extending activation checkpointing to all data.
why: 30-60% smaller footprint for training activations, analytics intermediates and memo caches, because energy per FLOP has fallen ~10x faster than DRAM cost per bit.
note: Generalizes DTR/Checkmate rematerialization.

title: Dandelion seeds: erasure-coded in-memory data replaces triple replicas
idea: Dandelions scatter many small seeds rather than three big ones: in-memory caches and stores (Redis, parameter servers, checkpoint shards) replace 3x DRAM replication with Reed-Solomon 10+4 striping across nodes, rebuilding lost shards from peers over RDMA. Software only.
why: Redundancy overhead drops from 200% to 40%, freeing ~50% of DRAM in replicated memory tiers.

title: Vending machine: per-GB-hour marketplace for idle cluster DRAM
idea: Like a vending machine for memory: a software agent on each server advertises idle DRAM, and a broker rents it to memory-starved jobs as RDMA-backed far memory (swap/tier) at per-GB-hour prices, built on stock Linux and RDMA NICs. $1M covers a 4-person team for 24 months.
why: Stranded memory (often 25-40% idle) becomes usable supply with no fab; effective DRAM supply grows 10-20% per adopting cluster.

title: Jigsaw puzzle: compiler packs tensor tiles to DRAM row boundaries
idea: Like fitting jigsaw pieces: a compiler pass lays out weights and KV-cache tiles so that each row activation delivers a whole tile of useful data and every opened page is read fully, guided by the DRAM's address-mapping function.
why: Destructive read and 128x page overfetch (fact 8); cuts activation energy per useful bit 3-10x on supported workloads.
note: DRAM-aware layout is standard; AI streams already have good row locality.

title: Mailbox: CXL FPGA card does gather and filter near memory
idea: Like dropping a letter in a mailbox: the host writes a command descriptor to a mailbox region on an FPGA CXL memory card, the card gathers, filters or sparse-indexes rows locally, and only result lines return across the link. Built on an off-the-shelf FPGA CXL board.
why: Data movement: 5-20x fewer bytes over the link for embedding and graph lookups.
note: Widely pursued (CXL-PNM, SmartSSD); easy FPGA demo but incremental.

title: Tetris: 32-byte sector fetch via burst-chop and sector-valid caches
idea: Like Tetris filling only the gaps: last-level caches track 32B sector-valid bits, and the controller issues DDR5 burst-chop or LPDDR short bursts so sparse accesses fetch half lines. Implemented in open-source controller RTL.
why: Overfetch (fact 8); 20-40% less data moved on irregular workloads.

title: Derivable pages: kernel drops memory it can recompute from recipes
idea: Box: recompute × OS kernel × page × memory pressure × registered recipe handle. Applications mark pages as derived (decompressed libraries, parsed configs, dequantized weights, JIT code) with a callback; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and re-runs the recipe on fault instead of swapping.
why: A large share of anonymous memory is a cache of cheap computation; making it reclaimable cuts provisioned DRAM 10–30% with no swap I/O.

title: Reed–Solomon striping replaces triple replication in in-memory stores
idea: Box: redundancy reduction × distributed key-value tier × object stripe × on write × RS(6,3) with NIC offload. Objects are striped across nodes with parity encoded by the NIC; reads gather data fragments in parallel over RDMA, with decode only on failure.
why: Durability overhead drops from 3× to 1.5×, halving DRAM for replicated caches and session stores fleetwide.

title: Per-feature byte budgets enforced in CI at contract DRAM price
idea: Box: governance × software process × service feature × every merge × bytes-per-request metric. Each service declares resident-set and bytes-per-request budgets; CI profiles memory, blocks merges over budget, and dashboards price each MB at the current DRAM contract price.
why: Software memory bloat grows ~10–20% a year; priced budgets bend demand 10–30% when DRAM costs 4× more.

title: Frozen shared interpreter heaps mapped by every worker process
idea: Box: share × language runtime × immutable object arena × interpreter startup × mmap-shared snapshot. Python/Node/Ruby servers freeze imported modules, bytecode, constants and read-only model data into a snapshot arena mapped read-only by all workers, with immortal objects so refcount writes no longer un-share pages.
why: Multi-worker servers duplicate hundreds of MB per worker; sharing frozen arenas cuts their RSS 30–60% with a pure software change and no fluorinated inputs.
note: PEP 683 immortal objects and prefork sharing known.

title: Allocation-time hash-consing of immutable values in managed runtimes
idea: Box: dedup × runtime allocator × immutable object × at allocation × concurrent table of canonical instances. Strings, tuples, boxed numbers, decoded JSON subtrees and records marked immutable are looked up on allocation and replaced by a canonical shared instance.
why: Data-heavy services carry 20–40% duplicate immutable objects; canonicalization reclaims most of it in software, with no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Zygote fleets: every microVM is a copy-on-write clone
idea: Po: every program is a clone of one ancestor. Serverless and microservice fleets on U.S.-built servers boot one golden, fully warmed microVM per runtime and fork every instance from it copy-on-write, Android-zygote style at VM scale, so warm pools share runtime, JIT code and heap prefixes.
why: Warm-pool memory is mostly identical runtime state; CoW forking cuts per-instance resident memory 3-10x, stretching scarce domestic DRAM.

title: One cache only: merge the database buffer pool with page cache
idea: Po: there is only one cache in the machine. A kernel interface lets databases and storage engines adopt the OS page cache as their buffer pool, with app-controlled eviction hints and pinning, eliminating the second copy of every hot page on U.S.-made servers.
why: Double caching wastes up to 2x on hot data; unifying recovers 20-40% of DRAM in storage-heavy servers.

title: Retired-server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory expanders
idea: Worsen: shred millions of working DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs whenever hyperscalers refresh servers every 4-5 years. Flip: run a take-back line that retests modules, maps weak rows and mounts the modules behind CXL controllers with stronger ECC and adaptive refresh as a far-memory tier.
why: Raises usable supply immediately with zero new wafers: each reused GB avoids nearly the full fab cost and could add several % to annual server DRAM supply.
note: Same retired-DIMM CXL reuse as I-01583.

title: Internal GB-second futures market in the cluster scheduler
idea: Worsen: give every job free, fixed memory reservations sized for peak. Flip: jobs bid for memory in GB-second futures with a surge price at saturation; under-used reservations are resold as spot memory with a 1-second reclaim contract backed by compressed swap.
why: Capacity and capital: turns the 20-30% of datacenter DRAM that is stranded into sellable capacity, so 1.25-1.4x more work per installed GB.
note: Market-based reclamation and spot memory resemble Borg reclamation and Memtrade.

title: Bytes-per-feature regression gate in CI
idea: Worsen: hide memory cost from developers so bloat compounds every release. Flip: CI measures resident bytes per feature on reference workloads, prices them at live DRAM cost, and blocks merges that add memory without a signed budget increase.
why: Capacity: cultural and tooling lever that historically recovers 20-50% of footprint over a few release cycles.

title: Child's LEGO staircase: shingled die stack with printed edge wires
idea: A child stacks bricks in a staircase. Shingle-stack 16 thinned DRAM dies with an offset, then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the stair edges to connect the stack. The tools are a ~$1M printer and die bonder a 10-person team can run.
why: Removes TSV keep-out area and the 20-30% HBM yield loss (Fact 6) for a mid-bandwidth stack of ~500 IO from two staircase edges.

title: Open-source hacker's memory compiler for a U.S. open-PDK fab
idea: In the Linux spirit, a 10-person team publishes an open-source generator for 3T gain-cell macros boosted with stacked metal-oxide-metal capacitors on SkyWater 130/90 nm and GF 22FDX, with layout, refresh controller and characterization.
why: ~2-3x denser than SRAM and made in a U.S. fab. Moves embedded buffers off commodity DRAM and SRAM supply, and is a U.S. manufacturability win.

title: Linguist's Zipf law: precision proportional to word frequency
idea: Linguists know a few words carry most usage. Embedding and output-projection rows are sorted by token or ID frequency and quantized on a log-frequency schedule: 8-bit for the top 1%, 4-bit for the next 10%, and 2-bit codebooks for the long tail, with a learned scale per tier.
why: Rare rows contribute little loss, so vocabulary and embedding tables shrink 3-5x with negligible quality impact. This matters for 256k-vocabulary LLMs and recsys.
note: Frequency-based mixed-precision embeddings are known in recsys.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer: 32-bit compressed pointers everywhere via cage allocator
idea: Under embargo you rewrite the software to fit the machine you have. Compilers and allocators place each heap in a 4-32 GB 'cage' and store all heap pointers as shifted 32-bit offsets. The JVM and V8 already do this; a compiler flag plus ABI shim extends it to C++, Rust and Go.
why: Pointers are 20-40% of the heap in pointer-heavy services (graphs, trees, ORMs). Halving them cuts DRAM 10-25% fleet-wide with no new hardware.

title: Child says share your toys: one host copy of weights
idea: A child asks why ten pods load the same model ten times. An open-source daemon pins each model file once per host in hugepage-backed shared memory, and patched vLLM, TGI and PyTorch loaders mmap it read-only instead of keeping private host-RAM copies for staging, CPU offload and fast restart. Two engineers, ~9 months, ~$400k.
why: Inference hosts hold 4-8 duplicate host-RAM copies of the same weights. Dedup frees hundreds of GB per node, so cheaper host SKUs can be bought.
note: Shared mmap of weights; straightforward.

title: Farmer's almanac: seasonal working-set forecasts drive safe memory overcommit
idea: Farmers plant by the almanac. A controller learns each VM or pod's daily and weekly working-set seasonality from sampled PTE access bits and overcommits hosts to the forecast plus a margin. A zswap/CXL compressed tier acts as the 'frost guard' that absorbs mispredictions. It ships as open-source KVM and Kubernetes plugins with a 3-person team within $1M.
why: Allocated memory averages 40-60% utilization. Forecast-based overcommit reaches 1.3-1.6x effective capacity per DIMM.
note: Forecast-based overcommit is established hyperscaler practice.

title: Accountant's shadow price: bill every team DRAM at 2026 spot
idea: An accountant makes hidden costs visible. A chargeback tool reads each service's resident GB-hours from cgroup stats and bills them at the current 4x contract price in dashboards, PR comments and quarterly budgets, with a savings leaderboard. The tool costs under $300k; the rest of the budget funds pilots at three companies.
why: Once memory is a visible line item, teams typically cut 15-30% within a year through heap caps, cache sizing and replica trimming. It is a policy lever with near-zero capital.
note: Standard FinOps practice applied to memory.

title: Air traffic controller assigns landing slots by predicted output length
idea: Controllers schedule landings so the runway is never overbooked. A small classifier predicts each request's output length from the prompt. The scheduler reserves KV pages for the predicted trajectory and packs requests to ~95% peak occupancy instead of sizing for the worst case, preempting by swap only on mispredictions. Software only.
why: Conservative KV reservation wastes 30-60% of HBM. Predicted landing slots raise concurrency per GB 1.5-2x.
note: PagedAttention already removed most reservation waste; length prediction is published.

title: Kintsugi potter repairs cracks: reuse DIMMs with known-bad rows
idea: Kintsugi makes cracked pottery whole and valuable. A ~$50k automated tester maps the failing rows of scrapped or factory-reject DIMMs and writes the bad-row map into a small SPD/EEPROM sidecar. A Linux boot-time driver reads the map and permanently retires those pages, so each DIMM serves ~99.9% of its capacity.
why: Many field returns and test rejects fail in only a handful of rows. Reclaiming them adds usable supply at ~zero silicon cost and also cuts e-waste.
note: badram/PPR exist; supply impact small.

title: Basking lizard: thermal-aware data migration between memory stacks
idea: A lizard shuttles between sun and shade: the memory controller watches each stack's temperature and moves hot, frequently refreshed pages from the warmest stack to cooler stacks or banks over the interposer, keeping all stacks under their retention limit.
why: At 125 C ambient, hotspots force refresh to double for every ~10 C rise; evening out heat across stacks claims about 2x less refresh overhead.

title: LLM decode sweeps counted as refresh: implicit-refresh accounting
idea: In AI inference each decode token reads the whole live KV cache every ~20-60 ms, and every activation restores its row. A per-row last-activated timestamp in the controller marks rows a sweep recently touched and drops them from the refresh schedule, so only cold rows get explicit refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: for KV-cache-dominated HBM most explicit refresh disappears, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth refresh takes at 32-64 Gb, with no device change.

title: Remanufacture retired hyperscaler DIMMs for 30-year industrial spares
idea: Extreme user: industrial plants that need DDR4 spares decades after launch. Run a line that strips DRAM packages from 5-6-year-old retired server DIMMs (DRAM barely wears out), retests and bins them, then rebuilds them onto new PCBs with fresh PMICs and SPD data.
why: Supply with no fab capital: millions of GB per year return to use at a fraction of new-bit cost and energy.

title: Flight-recorder templates: logs stored as template IDs plus variables
idea: From flight data recorders that encode events compactly: logging libraries and memory-resident log stores split each line into a static template (stored once, given an ID at compile time) and typed variable fields packed columnar in binary, never materializing text.
why: Log text is 10-50x redundant; template encoding cuts in-memory log and trace buffers 10x+, with matching fab-water savings.
note: Already done by NanoLog/CLP-style systems; small DRAM segment.

title: Ad-tech cardinality extreme: sketch-first databases that answer approximately
idea: From ad platforms counting billions of distinct users: in-memory analytics keep HyperLogLog, KLL quantile and count-min sketches as the primary resident structures and push exact rows to flash, answering dashboards from sketches and touching rows only for audits.
why: Sketches are 100-1000x smaller than raw rows for aggregate queries; resident DRAM falls 10x+ with a matching water cut.

title: Industrial-longevity harvest-and-rebin of retired server DRAM
idea: Factories keep 30-year-old controllers alive by harvesting parts. Build automated lines that pull DIMMs from retired servers, burn-in and speed-bin them, and repackage the dies into CXL memory expanders for cold/warm tiers sold with a supply guarantee.
why: Hyperscalers retire servers every 4-6 years with DRAM good for 10+; recovering even 30% adds several percent to annual usable supply at a fraction of new-bit cost.

title: Exascale ABFT: checksum rows riding inside weight matrices
idea: Million-core supercomputers use Huang-Abraham algorithm-based fault tolerance. Append a checksum row and column to every weight and activation tile, so each GEMM on the accelerator detects and corrects single corrupted elements in the operands it just read from HBM, for ~1-3% extra FLOPs. HBM devices and protocol are untouched.
why: End-to-end correction covers weak on-die ECC, so accelerators can use lower-grade HBM dies or switch off sideband ECC and reclaim its ~3-12% of capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6).

title: Mars-rover discipline: ultra-lean runtime halves edge RAM
idea: Rovers run for years on 256 MB. A 10-person team maintains a flight-software-style lean Linux and inference runtime (static allocation, execute-in-place, flash-mapped weights, no GC) for edge AI boxes and appliances, certified against a RAM budget.
why: Cuts DRAM per edge device 40-60%; demand relief that scales through distribution.
note: Executable; edge DRAM demand is a modest segment.

title: Burn built-in post-package repair fuses during refurbishment
idea: Spacecraft reconfigure around failures in orbit. DDR4/DDR5 dies already carry hPPR spare rows, so a 10-person refurb line runs targeted weak-row tests on harvested modules and burns permanent repairs before resale, restoring failing modules to full spec.
why: Rescues modules that fail on only a few rows, which is common in aged DRAM, at near-zero cost.

title: Geological-strata scheduling: map data lifetime to each tier's measured retention
idea: Treat a 3D stack like sediment strata, each tier with its own retention from process variation: measure every tier's retention at test and expose it to the memory controller. The controller puts short-lived data (activations, KV-cache that dies within 50 ms) in leaky tiers that never need refresh and long-lived data in strong tiers.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and 3D yield: tiers that would fail retention binning become usable, and refresh drops ~2-5x.

title: Sleep-consolidation pass re-encoding memory during idle troughs
idea: This borrows from how sleep consolidates memory. In nightly or between-batch idle windows, a host daemon re-encodes cold resident data with slow, strong codecs that are too expensive online: zstd-19, learned dictionaries, global dedup and struct-of-arrays relayout. Online paths only ever decompress with cheap decoders.
why: Asymmetric codecs reach 3-4x where online-speed codecs get about 2x. Spending off-peak compute shrinks daytime DRAM for cold data by 30-50%.
note: zram recompression already does this.

title: Ramtron imprint beaten by periodic data-polarity inversion
idea: PZT FeRAM lost margin at high temperature because a polarization held one way for years imprints: defect dipoles align and the loop shifts. Every few days at 125 C, a background engine rewrites each row inverted and toggles a per-row polarity flag, so no domain spends more than about half its life in one direction and imprint averages out.
why: Removes the dominant 125 C/10 y FeRAM failure mode at ~1e-6 duty-cycle energy; works with any ferroelectric (HZO, AlScN, PZT).
note: Polarity inversion for imprint likely in prior patents; simple controller demo.

title: Sinclair's audio RAM revived: sell partially good DRAM with defect maps
idea: 1980s ZX Spectrums used half-defective 64k DRAM ('ARAM'), a market that vanished as yields rose. With HBM yields down 20-30%, sort dies with failed banks, burn a signed defect map into an eFuse page, and let accelerator memory controllers or CXL expanders skip dead banks for KV cache and activations.
why: Every scrapped die is sunk helium, quartz, tungsten, water and energy; recovering half the fallout lifts usable supply ~10-15% with zero new materials or capex.

title: Nitrogen triple bond broken: erasure-coded RAM replaces 3x replication
idea: N2's triple bond is strength bought with waste; in-memory databases and caches that keep three full replicas instead stripe objects as (k=10, m=2) Reed-Solomon fragments across 12 servers' DRAM over RDMA/CXL, with reconstruction on failure done by a NIC-offloaded decoder.
why: Replication overhead drops from 3.0x to 1.2x, so replicated in-memory tiers need ~2.5x less DRAM at the cost of ~5-20 us degraded-read latency (cost/bit, capital).

title: Bismuth hopper crystals: arrays stored as wavelet pyramids, read coarse first
idea: Bismuth grows as nested stair-step hopper crystals; simulation fields, images, video frames and analytics cubes are stored as integer wavelet pyramids with each level in its own pages, so previews, renders and approximate queries read only coarse levels and fetch finer levels by region on demand, while cold fine levels are dropped or sent to flash.
why: Coarse reads touch 1/16-1/64 of the bits, a >10x cut in energy per access, and dropping fine levels of cold data saves 2-4x DRAM (energy, density).

title: Cu: copper cold-plate DIMM sleeves buy 4x longer refresh
idea: A machined, brazed copper sleeve plumbed into the server's existing liquid loop holds DRAM packages below 45 C; after a per-module retention screen, BIOS tables set tREFI 2-4x longer. CNC and brazing fit a 10-person shop.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C; recovers much of the 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: U: enrichment-cascade grading of secondhand DRAM for matched workloads
idea: Like centrifuge cascades enriching U-235, a line of FPGA testers in series progressively sorts used DIMMs by retention, hammer threshold and error history into grades, each sold with a workload certificate (error-tolerant AI cache, general compute, critical).
why: Recovers decommissioned modules into usable supply during the 4x price spike with minimal capital.
note: Used-DIMM test-and-grade is a known refurbishment business; workload certificates a twist.

title: Sourdough starter: cultured dictionaries recompress cold pages
idea: Like a sourdough culture that is kept alive and fed, idle cores keep a per-workload compression dictionary that is trained continuously on sampled cold pages (zstd-style dictionary learning, refreshed hourly). Cold pages are 'fermented' by re-encoding them with the current culture. Old culture versions are kept so older pages stay decodable.
why: Dictionary-primed compression of 4 KB pages achieves a 1.5-2x better ratio than plain LZ on small blocks, turning a 2x compressed tier into about 3x with no new hardware.

title: Kanban buffers: memory scales with throughput, not connection count
idea: Toyota kanban caps work in process with physical cards. Per-connection pinned send and receive buffers (RDMA queue pairs, TCP socket buffers, gRPC channels) are replaced by a fixed pool of buffer 'cards' sized by Little's law: throughput times latency times a safety factor. A sender must hold a card (a credit) to transmit, and cards return to the pool when the data is consumed.
why: Servers with 10k-100k connections pin tens of GB in mostly idle buffers; kanban sizing cuts network and IO buffer memory 10-100x at the same throughput.

title: Value-stream map: classify every resident byte into the seven wastes
idea: Lean value-stream mapping, applied to memory. An always-on profiler (page access bits, allocator tags, PEBS sampling) assigns every resident byte to one of Toyota's wastes: overproduction (prefetched, never used), inventory (cold for over 10 min), defects (leaked), overprocessing (duplicate copies or serializations) and waiting (pinned buffers). It then outputs a ranked kaizen list with automatic fixes such as madvise, compression, dedup and buffer shrinking.
why: Fleet studies often find 20-50% of DRAM cold or wasted; systematic waste accounting can recover about 25% of capacity without hardware changes.

title: Second-life re-binning retunes sensing on retired server DIMMs
idea: Ideal result: no DIMM ever goes to the shredder. A depot tester sweeps each retired module's per-bank tRCD, tWR and refresh margins, writes a custom timing and refresh profile into its SPD, and resells it into edge, client and cache tiers.
why: Usable supply: extends module life 3-5 years, adding supply during a 4x price spike at near-zero capital.

title: Price-indexed scheduler decides park versus re-prefill for idle sessions
idea: IFR: idle conversations hold no memory yet resume instantly. Closest: the serving scheduler compares each parked session's KV cost (GB x expected idle seconds x spot DRAM $/GB-s) with the FLOP cost of re-prefilling from text, using a learned per-user think-time distribution, and evicts to text or flash whenever re-prefill is cheaper.
why: 30-60% of inference KV belongs to sessions idle between turns; with DRAM at 4x price this cuts provisioned KV DRAM ~2x by turning abundant compute into memory.

title: Scheduler pairs jobs with anticorrelated memory peaks on shared slabs
idea: IFR: memory sized for total use, not for the sum of peaks. Closest: a cluster scheduler profiles each job's memory time series and co-locates anticorrelated pairs (checkpointing training vs diurnal inference, ETL vs serving) on one pooled DRAM slab with priority preemption to compressed swap.
why: Cuts provisioned DRAM 20-35% versus peak-sized allocation.

title: Use the dormant knob: PASR plus nightly memory compaction
idea: 10-person constraint: no new silicon, so use what LPDDR already ships. An OS patch compacts movable pages out of whole LPDDR5X segments when load is low, then sets the mode-register partial-array self-refresh (PASR) bits so the empty segments stop refreshing. A watermark policy re-enables them before they are allocated.
why: Fact 3: idle servers and phones often hold 30-60% free memory, and self-refresh energy falls in proportion when it stops being refreshed. It is a kernel patch a small team can upstream.

title: Metadata replaces refresh: zero-row skip in the memory controller
idea: 10-person constraint: controller logic only. Keep a 1-bit-per-row all-zero bitmap, set by zeroing writes, OS page frees or detected zero rows. Rows marked zero leave the targeted-refresh schedule, and reads to them return zeros from the controller without activating the DRAM.
why: Fact 3: sparse tensors, padding and freshly zeroed pages often leave 10-30% of rows all-zero, and those rows stop costing refresh and activation energy.

title: Point-of-use helium micro-recovery skid on tool exhaust
idea: Within $1M/24 months: build a refrigerator-sized skid that taps the foreline of He-backside etch and CVD tools, separates He from the N2 purge with a hollow-fiber membrane plus a small PSA stage, and returns 99.99% He to the chuck supply; pilot it on 3 tools.
why: Captures ~60-80% of per-tool helium while Qatar's ~30% is offline, with payback in months at shortage prices and no fab-wide liquefier.
note: Point-of-use He recovery is engineering only; a 3-tool pilot fits budget.

title: No per-word ECC: ABFT tile checksums guard weight matrices
idea: Imposed limit: no per-word ECC for weights. Each 128x128 weight tile carries one checksum row and one checksum column, verified for free inside the matmul (Huang-Abraham ABFT). A flipped element is located at the intersection of the failing row and column and corrected from the checksums.
why: Protection overhead falls from 12.5% to ~1.6%, and the checking rides on compute already being done. Weight memory can use non-ECC or raw-BER DRAM.
note: Huang-Abraham ABFT for DNN GEMM is established.

title: Never discard: modules shrink capacity gracefully as spares run out
idea: Rule: no module is ever thrown away for errors. Firmware consumes spare rows via soft PPR. When spares are exhausted, it offlines failing 2 MB regions and advertises reduced capacity through CXL dynamic capacity, and the OS migrates pages away. End-of-life modules are resold at their measured remaining capacity.
why: Extends module life ~2x and keeps ~95% of a module's bits in service instead of discarding 100% at the first uncorrectable error.
note: Page offlining exists; CXL dynamic capacity resale framing incremental.

title: Octopus arm ganglia: in-tier decoders built in the same channel film
idea: Octopus arms carry their own ganglia; in a 3D stack, form a small oxide-TFT decoder in each tier from the same channel film and the same slit/hole patterning as the cells, so each tier needs only ~log2(N) shared address lines instead of N individually contacted wordlines.
why: Per-tier contacts, staircases and CMOS drivers stop growing with tier count, so 120+ tiers (~10x bits/mm2) can be built without the periphery (49% of the die) and contact cost scaling up (facts 2, 7).
note: Shared-film decoders per tier cut wordline contacts to log2(N); doubt: decoder TFT quality from lateral cell patterning.

title: Substitute global bitline sensing with local gain transistors from same VCT step
idea: Split each bitline into 16-cell segments; each segment's charge drives the gate of a local gain transistor made in the same vertical-channel-transistor step as the cells (no extra mask), which pulls a ~50 mV current-mode signal onto the global bitline. With a ~1 fF local line, the cell needs only ~1 fF, so the capacitor can be shallow.
why: Constraint: 50 mV global swing instead of ~0.5 V plus 5x smaller cell charge gives ~10-20x less bitline energy per access; facet: capacitor AR from ~70:1 to ~15:1 (fact 1).
note: Segment-local gain lets ~1 fF cells and shallow capacitors; doubt: gain-transistor Vt mismatch vs 50 mV signal.

title: PAM-8 telecom signaling in stacked gain cells with pilot cells
idea: Borrow PAM/QAM with training symbols: hold 8 voltage levels on each oxide-semiconductor gain-cell node, write pilot cells with known levels in every row so the sense ADC tracks leakage drift, and stack 4 deposited tiers in the BEOL.
why: 10x at same cost: 3 bits/cell x 4 tiers is ~12x bits per footprint; tiers are deposited oxide layers (no EUV) and pilot-tracked thresholds tolerate drift.
note: MLC times BEOL tiers multiplies bits per footprint; doubt: 8-level margins on leaky nodes and ADC read latency.

title: Magnify thread count 1000x so flash serves as main memory
idea: Magnify hardware contexts to thousands per core (barrel processor) so the core tolerates ~2-5 us line reads from low-latency NAND used as load/store main memory. DRAM shrinks to a 1/10-size line buffer.
why: Throughput workloads (graph, analytics, serving) get 10-20x capacity per dollar, because flash costs ~1/10-1/20 of DRAM per bit.
note: Key doubt: 64B loads from 4KB+ flash pages cause huge read amplification, IOPS ceilings and write wear.

title: Magnify periodicity: mask-free interference lithography for memory arrays
idea: Memory arrays are perfect gratings, so print them with a ~$300k four-beam 193 nm laser interference exposure in one flash per wafer, pitch-split by self-aligned quadruple patterning, repeated for 4 array tiers; all irregular periphery goes on a cheap CMOS chiplet hybrid-bonded on top.
why: Removes EUV scanners and masks from the array (litho ~30-40% of wafer cost and most capex); ~10x cheaper array processing times 4 stacked tiers targets ~100x lower cost per GB.
note: Arrays are gratings so IL is apt; overlay/registration across layers and trims is the key doubt; 100x overclaimed.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K: capacitorless cryogenic memory vaults
idea: At 77 K junction and subthreshold leakage collapse by orders of magnitude, so a deposited poly-Si 1T0C cell (no capacitor, no EUV) holds data for hours; stack ~100 such layers and run racks in liquid-nitrogen baths costing cents per liter.
why: Removes the capacitor charge wall and refresh; cheap stacked poly-Si layers target ~$0.1/GB (~100x), trading cooling energy and system complexity.
note: 77 K collapses leakage enabling capacitorless stacked poly-Si; cooling overhead and system adoption are the doubts.

title: Eliminate per-accelerator weight replicas via optical multicast weight broadcast
