idea: Keep one copy of model weights in a pooled memory appliance and broadcast each layer's weights over a passive optical splitter to 8-64 accelerators that consume them in lockstep; local HBM holds only KV and activations.
why: Removes 8-64x duplication of weights across a serving pod; HBM per accelerator could drop 50-70%, easing the HBM TSV-tax bottleneck.
note: Passive splitter broadcast to lockstep accelerators; same mechanism as I-00277, same bandwidth and sync doubts.

title: Lotus-seed dormancy: ultra-wide-bandgap gain cell that holds charge for years
idea: Sacred lotus seeds stay viable for ~1,300 years by sealing a dormant embryo in an impermeable coat. Build a 2T gain cell whose access transistor has an ultra-wide-bandgap channel (Ga2O3 or AlGaN, Eg 4.8-6 eV) and a ferroelectric back gate that stays polarized to deep depletion when power drops. Storage-node leakage falls below ~10^-24 A, so a 1 fF node keeps its level for years.
why: Makes a DRAM-structure cell non-volatile with no exotic storage physics: DRAM-like write and read speed, unlimited endurance (charge on a node, no wear) and no refresh. BEOL-compatible.
note: Extends IGZO-style gain cells to Ga2O3/AlGaN; doubt: 1e-24 A total node leakage incl. read-gate dielectric for years retention.

title: Darkroom development: pillar-foot gain transistor reads a 0.5 fF cell
idea: Like a latent photographic image amplified by development, store only ~0.5 fF per 3D cell and put one thin-film gain transistor at the foot of every 16-cell vertical local bitline; the cell perturbs only ~1 fF of local line and the gain device converts it into current on a 100 mV-swing global line.
why: Energy per access and capacitor wall (facts 1, 8, 10): switched capacitance per read falls from ~85 fF at 1 V to a few fF plus a low-swing global line; claims ~10x lower read energy.
note: Gain transistor per 16-cell local bitline lets ~0.5 fF cells sense, easing the capacitor wall; doubts are TFT Vt mismatch and write-back.

title: Gateless rectifier access: ultra-wide-bandgap Schottky diode replaces the transistor
idea: Inverts 'the access device needs a gate': each capacitor reaches its bitline through a vertical Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) Schottky diode and the wordline is the cell plate; to write, raise the plate so the node clamps to the bitline level plus Vf, then drop it ('clamp-and-drop' sets any level), and to read, raise the plate and sense the dumped charge. Reverse leakage in a 4.8 eV material is orders of magnitude below silicon generation current.
why: Removes the 3-terminal transistor, its leakage tail (fact 3) and the 3 V boosted wordline (fact 10); a 2-terminal 4F2 cell stacks without a lateral transistor (fact 2).
note: Two-terminal wide-gap Schottky access could stack 4F2 cells; doubts: half-select disturb, Vf-set levels, destructive plate read.

title: Drown it in nitrogen: capacitorless tiers holding data for hours
idea: Inverts 'memory must work at room temperature': immerse memory sleds in liquid nitrogen, where subthreshold and generation leakage fall by many decades, so a bare gate-node or floating-body cell in many-tier poly-Si stacks with no capacitor at all retains for minutes to hours; LN2 at ~$0.1/L and cryo-rack designs carry the heat.
why: Deletes the capacitor module (fact 1) and allows cheap many-tier poly stacks with near-zero refresh, claimed ~100x cost/GB at NAND-like layer cost; trade-off is cryo plant energy and logistics.
note: LN2 lets capacitorless poly-Si cells retain long enough for NAND-like stacking; doubt: cryo plant energy and logistics at scale.

title: Vertical CCD charge-packet strings replacing per-bit access transistors
idea: Store bits as charge packets in potential wells under 64 stacked gate electrodes along one vertical channel, reviving 1970s CCD memory in 3D. Packets clock to an end-of-string sense amp at ~1 ns per transfer with CTE >0.99999, and a page cache hides the shift latency.
why: With no capacitor and no access transistor per bit, both 3D-DRAM blockers (fact 2) vanish. One sense node serves 64 bits, cutting periphery share (fact 7), and each bit costs one deposited gate layer.
note: No capacitor or transistor per bit, 3D-NAND cost structure; doubts are poly-channel CTE, dark-current retention, serial latency.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods use capacitorless 4F2 cells stacked eight high
idea: At 77 K subthreshold swing falls to ~15 mV/decade and thermally activated leakage drops >1e10, so a bare ~0.05 fF transistor gate holds charge for hours and needs no capacitor, while Cu/Mo wire resistivity drops ~6x. Build 4F2 vertical gain cells in 8 decks and run memory sleds immersed in LN2 made from air (no helium).
why: No capacitor + 8 decks = ~10x density at similar wafer cost; refresh vanishes and ~0.4 V operation cuts CV2 ~6x, offsetting cooling power at system level.
note: 77 K makes bare-gate gain cells retain for hours; doubt: ~10x cryocooler overhead and 8-deck density claim not cryo-specific.

title: Rack-level weight broadcast: one copy of model weights, many accelerators
idea: Information theory says N identical copies carry the information of one, yet inference clusters replicate the same weights in every accelerator's HBM. Put a single weight copy in a CXL/optical multicast memory appliance per rack and stream tiles with deterministic prefetch, keeping only working tiles and KV-cache in local HBM.
why: Do DRAM's job with less: for 8-64-way replicated serving, cuts weight-holding HBM 4-30x, freeing HBM wafer capacity (3x area/bit tax) at the cost of a few extra pJ/bit of streaming.
note: One weight copy per rack frees replicated HBM; doubt: decode needs full-weight bandwidth per token, requiring lockstep multi-TB/s multicast.

title: Hole-confining SiGe quantum-well body for capacitorless 3D tiers
idea: Box = {medium: holes trapped in a compressively strained Si0.6Ge0.4 quantum well | access: lateral gate-all-around Si nanosheet | sense: threshold-shift read current (1T0C) | integration: 30-60 tier epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattice | substrate: Si | fab: one epitaxy run + staircase etch}. The ~0.35 eV valence-band offset forms a pocket under each nanosheet that holds holes written by impact ionization or GIDL, aiming for 100-1000x the retention of a homogeneous-Si floating body with no capacitor at all.
why: Fact 2: removes the capacitor that blocks 3D DRAM, so tier count rather than lithography sets density; target 4-8x bits/mm2 at 32+ tiers, built mostly with deposition and etch.
note: Capacitorless 3D tiers via valence-band hole well; doubt: retention gain vs GIDL/junction leakage in thin nanosheets.

title: Po: flash that forgets on purpose — direct-tunnel volatile charge-trap tier
idea: Po: flash memory that forgets on purpose. Extracted: change the 3D NAND recipe to a 1.5-2.5 nm tunnel oxide so writes use low-field direct tunnelling (no Fowler-Nordheim damage, endurance >1e12) and accept 1-10 s retention; run idle NAND fab capacity in a down-cycle as a second-tier DRAM refreshed every second.
why: NAND-like ~$0.05-0.1/GB (about 100x below DRAM contract) from existing fabs with no new tools. Trade-offs: 100s of ns to us reads and background refresh every few seconds.
note: Idle NAND lines as refreshed cheap tier; doubts: trap endurance and microsecond reads.

title: Row-as-codeword: in-DRAM LDPC turns overfetch into redundancy
idea: Po: the 128x overfetch is a gift. Each 8 Kb row is one LDPC codeword (~10% parity) decoded by a parallel bit-flipping decoder at the row buffer on every activation, fixing the ~80 raw errors per row at 1% BER; the same decoder writes corrected data back during refresh so errors never accumulate.
why: Makes 1%-BER cells usable at ~10% overhead (Shannon floor at p=0.01 is ~8%) with ~10-15 ns decode added to tRCD; overfetch (fact 8) becomes useful work.
note: Row-scale LDPC makes 1%-BER cells usable; doubt: parallel decoder area/latency in sense-amp stripe on DRAM process.

title: Drip-irrigation farmer: 0.5 fF planar cells with virtual-ground sensing
idea: Drip irrigation delivers a few drops where needed instead of flooding the field. An ultra-low-leakage wide-gap access device (off <1e-21 A) lets the capacitor shrink to a planar 0.5 fF, 10x below today's 5 fF pillar, and the bitline is clamped by a virtual-ground charge integrator so the tiny packet lands on a small feedback capacitor without swinging the bitline.
why: Retention stays >1 s with 10x less charge, so charge moved per access falls ~10x and the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and its HAR-etch capital disappear.
note: Ultra-low-leak wide-gap access lets a planar 0.5 fF cap replace the 60:1 pillar; doubt: sensing ~3k electrons at DRAM speed and noise.

title: Pacemaker nanowatt array: 8-tier vertical bitlines with local gain
idea: A pacemaker budget means tiny bitline swings; give each vertical bitline only 8 tiers of cells and a one-transistor gain stage at its base, so local bitline capacitance is ~0.1 fF and a 1 fF capacitor still develops ~450 mV. The gain stage alone drives the long global bitline.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): Cs can drop ~5x to ~1 fF, a shallow capacitor that fits lateral 3D tiers (fact 2); bitline energy down ~10x (fact 10).
note: 8-cell vertical bitline with local gain lets 1 fF caps sense; doubt: gain-transistor Vt mismatch and area under array.

title: Rack-wide lockstep layer broadcast replaces per-server weight copies
idea: One memory sled per rack holds the model weights once. It broadcasts each layer over a multicast optical fabric while all 64 servers execute that same layer in lockstep. Each GPU keeps only a two-layer double buffer of weights. Spatial replication becomes a synchronized schedule in time.
why: Weights are replicated N times today; this makes it one copy per rack. That frees 40-80% of each GPU's HBM for KV, or allows proportionally less HBM per accelerator.
note: Same as rack-scale lockstep broadcast; HBM freed for KV, but per-GPU optical bandwidth must match weight read rate.

title: NRAM revived with chlorine-purified methane nanotubes: a metal-free carbon cell
idea: Nantero NRAM stalled largely because CNT fabrics carried Fe/Co/Ni catalyst residue that DRAM fabs refused, and supply was boutique. Grow nanotubes by methane pyrolysis on a floating catalyst (co-producing hydrogen), strip metals to sub-ppb by ~2,500 C chlorine-gas purification as used for nuclear graphite, then spin the fabric as a two-terminal van der Waals switch between TiN electrodes in a crosspoint.
why: Switching element is pure carbon from natural gas (no Hf, Ge, Te, Pt), and the by-product H2 offsets fab energy; NRAM's ns-class switching, >1e11 cycles and nonvolatility remove capacitor and refresh; 4F2 crosspoint per deck.
note: Purification fixes NRAM's fab-contamination blocker; doubt: NRAM speed/endurance at DRAM duty never shown at scale.

title: Quantum-confined 2 nm channels widen bandgap and kill generation leakage
idea: Effect: quantum confinement. Access transistors of stacked lateral cells are ~2 nm-thick Si nanosheets in a Si/SiGe superlattice stack; confinement raises the effective bandgap ~0.3-0.4 eV, and because generation leakage scales ~exp(-Eg/2kT), off-state tails fall ~100-1000x, so ~0.5 fF suffices for 64 ms.
why: 10x density: no AR-75 capacitor and a 40-tier epitaxial superlattice stack (3D-NAND-style staircase) gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: one deep-etch module and epi replace the EUV-heavy capacitor and cell layers.
note: Generation leakage falls ~exp(-dEg/2kT), but GIDL, traps and thickness-driven Vth spread may dominate at 2 nm.

title: Nanoimprint-printed oxide-TFT access tiers replace EUV economics
idea: IFR: patterning the switch costs nothing. Pattern the access-transistor and wordline levels of BEOL oxide-TFT 1T1C tiers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (sub-15 nm half-pitch, ~1/10 the per-layer cost, no EUV), using self-aligned double imprint for the densest level, and stack ten tiers.
why: Constraint: EUV and depreciation are ~55% of cost (fact 4); if a tier costs ~1/10 of an EUV front-end layer set, ten tiers fit in today's wafer cost for 10x bits, and the single EUV supplier chokepoint is avoided.
note: Cheap NIL-patterned IGZO tiers could multiply bits/wafer; doubt: per-tier capacitor, NIL defectivity and overlay.

title: Main memory inside the logic die's own metal stack (monolithic BEOL oxide gain cells)
idea: After the logic metal stack is complete (TSMC has already embedded an oxide-semiconductor-selector memory fully in BEOL above advanced logic), deposit 8-16 tiers of vertical IGZO/ZTO 2T0C cells with 3 bits/cell write-verify, local complementary-oxide sensing (B2-08) and short vias down to SRAM-buffered memory controllers. Oxide cells retain >200 s at 95 C, so they tolerate sitting on hot logic. On backside-power logic, the frontside BEOL is less congested. Capacity is the target, not cache: an 800 mm2 die area carries 76-152 GB.
why: 76-152 GB over an 800 mm2 die (3 b x 8-16 tiers at F=40 nm, no EUV); interface energy 3.5 -> ~0.2 pJ/bit, saving 211-422 W per accelerator at 8-16 TB/s; zero extra wafers; added cost ~$0.87/GB at $500 per tier per wafer and 80% yield.
note: Capacity-class (76-152 GB) memory in logic BEOL at ~0.2 pJ/bit; doubt: 3-bit oxide MLC stability on hot logic and BEOL yield.

title: Minify parameters, magnify retrieval from a flash corpus
idea: Minify the parametric model ~10-25x and magnify non-parametric memory: knowledge sits in a NAND-resident retrieval corpus that the model queries per chunk, RETRO-style, so DRAM holds only the small model and a hot shard.
why: Weight DRAM falls >=10x for equal quality, with facts moved to bits that cost ~1/15 as much.
note: Shifting knowledge from weights to flash corpus could cut weight DRAM 10x; RETRO prior art, doubt is reasoning-quality parity.

title: Million-token agents: 1-bit key sketches in DRAM, KV on flash
idea: From the extreme user of million-token AI contexts: keep a 1-bit SimHash sketch of every attention key in DRAM, use it to estimate attention scores, and fetch only the top-scoring full-precision KV blocks from CXL-attached flash through a prefetcher driven by the sketch scores.
why: Holds roughly 1/128-1/256 of the KV-cache in DRAM/HBM, turning KV capacity into a flash problem and dodging the HBM area tax (fact 6).
note: LSH-sketch sparse attention is known (MagicPIG, InfiniGen); flash bandwidth per decode step is the key doubt.

title: Shallow-trap nitride liner turns the access transistor into the cell
idea: Scarcity rule: one transistor, no capacitor, no new material. Engineer the gate-stack SiN liner with shallow 0.6-0.8 eV traps that a 1.5 V pulse loads in ns by direct tunneling through 1.5 nm SiO2, shifting threshold for seconds; the shallow depth allows low-field cycling that avoids NAND-style oxide wear.
why: A ~4F2 1T cell from standard materials removes the capacitor (facts 1, 2) and its EUV layers (fact 4) while seconds of retention cut refresh; 1e15-cycle endurance is the risk.
note: Volatile SONOS/1T trap DRAM known; doubt: 1e15-cycle endurance and Vt margin with shallow traps.

title: Pay per gigabyte made: production tax credit instead of grants
idea: Reverse when the subsidy is paid: replace upfront grants with a 10-year production tax credit per good GB made in the U.S. (like the wind PTC). The credit tapers over time and gets a bonus for low-capex processes.
why: Rewards bits shipped rather than buildings built. Draws entrants with lean processes and helps lift the U.S. share above 1-2%.
note: Same per-Gb production tax credit as I-00436.

title: Per-gigabit production tax credit rewards output, not buildings
idea: What the economy needs is good bits, so pay for bits: a $0.05-0.20/Gb credit for known-good DRAM made in the U.S., declining over 10 years, modeled on the wind production tax credit. Unlike capex grants it pays only for yield and utilization, forcing efficient operation.
why: U.S. manufacturability and cost: closes the ~25-40% U.S. cost gap at the margin and rewards yield, which capex grants ignore.
note: Same per-Gb production tax credit as I-00436.

title: Substitute helium cryogenics with liquid-nitrogen-immersed DRAM tier
idea: Substitute any helium cryostat with 77 K liquid-nitrogen immersion for a pooled-memory sled; the nitrogen comes from air separation, with no helium or neon. At 77 K subthreshold and junction leakage fall more than 1e6x and retention reaches hours, so the access transistor can use a lower Vt and a ~1.5 V wordline.
why: Refresh essentially disappears, wordline energy drops ~4x and wire resistance ~5x; cryocooler energy is traded for density and refresh savings in a disaggregated pool.
note: Cryogenic DRAM studied (CryoRAM, CLL-DRAM); cooling overhead decides net gain.

title: Substitute hot DRAM capacity with hybrid-bonded stacks of depreciated 28 nm SRAM
idea: Stack 8-16 dies of high-density 28 nm SRAM from fully depreciated, non-EUV foundry lines directly on the accelerator by hybrid bonding as its hottest working-set tier, exploiting SRAM's non-destructive read and zero refresh.
why: Constraint: ~0.05-0.2 pJ/bit at um distance versus 3-15 pJ/bit for HBM/DDR5 (>10x); capital: no DRAM fab, no EUV. Cost per bit is ~10-20x worse, so it suits only the hottest few GB.

title: Magnify usable capacity: compression engines in every CXL controller
idea: Put line-rate LZ4/zstd-class compression engines in CXL memory controllers, back them with an OCP procurement spec and OS policy (compressed tiers on by default), and expose compressed capacity as plain addressable memory.
why: Server memory typically compresses 2-3x; effective usable supply grows ~1.5-2x on warm pages without a single new wafer.

title: Planarian neoblast spare tiers adopt any failed tier's identity
idea: Build 4 'neoblast' spare tiers per 64-tier stack whose staircase is wired through an antifuse-programmable tier-address decoder; after test, any defective tier is disabled and a spare assumes its address, giving tier-level regeneration instead of only row/column repair.
why: 3D yield compounding: at 99% per-tier yield a 64-tier stack yields ~53%, with 4 spares >99%, roughly 1.8x lower effective cost per bit.

title: IBM Lease-and-Reclaim: DRAM-as-a-Service With Guaranteed Return
idea: Revive IBM's mainframe-era model in which IBM owned and recovered every core-memory box: memory makers lease modules to data centers with mandatory return at end of term, then retest, rebin and re-lease them into lower tiers (inference, CXL cold pools, edge).
why: Supply: extends each bit's productive life from ~5 to 10+ years, cutting new-bit demand, while makers capture the refurbishment margin.
note: Extends bit-years; hardware-as-a-service precedent.

title: Cascade leasing moves each DRAM module through three owners
idea: Copy aircraft leasing. A lessor owns DIMMs and moves them from hyperscale AI (years 0-4) to enterprise and education (4-8) to industrial and IoT gateways (8-15), with price-indexed leases, mandatory return, and retest and regrade at each handoff.
why: Delivers 2-3x more bit-years per manufactured bit; DRAM wears out far later than its first owner retires it.

title: Memory futures: decade offtake contracts pre-fund new DRAM fabs
idea: Shift capital timing: hyperscalers buy 10-year capacity futures with upfront pre-delivery payments (as airlines do for aircraft), which collateralize fab construction loans and set a price band.
why: Moves capital intensity off the memory maker's balance sheet; ~30% of fab capex pre-funded lowers the cost of capital by several points.

title: Po old DRAM is an ore body: urban-mined DIMM reclamation lines
idea: Po: 'the richest DRAM mine is a landfill.' Extracted: build automated lines that strip DRAM packages from DIMMs in decommissioned servers, retest each package at speed and temperature, re-bin, and re-mount them on CXL memory-expander cards whose controller maps out weak rows.
why: Effective supply: servers retire on 4-6-year cycles with healthy DRAM; reclaimed bits add supply with zero wafer starts, helium, quartz or EUV.

title: Spatial pipelining: activations ride chip-to-chip links, never parking
idea: Ideal: data is always moving and never at rest, so nothing has to be retained. Closest achievable: map a model layer-per-chiplet across a wafer or board so activations stream over short die-to-die links from one tile's SRAM buffer to the next, with weights pinned in each tile's local static storage and no DRAM holding activations.
why: Zero refresh power and fact 5: ~0.1 pJ/bit per hop vs 3-4 pJ/bit for an HBM round trip; DRAM demand for activations falls to zero.
note: Already done by wafer-scale and dataflow accelerators.

title: Cargo load-planning: per-row data masks keep weak cells discharged
idea: Adapted from ship load planning, which puts heavy cargo where the hull is strongest: using a factory map of weak-retention cells, every write picks one of four XOR scrambling masks (2 tag bits per row) so known weak cells hold the value their leakage pulls them toward. A cell already at its leakage endpoint cannot lose data.
why: Retention failures only hit cells holding the 'uphill' value; steering weak cells to safe values lets each row refresh at the rate of its strong cells, removing the tail from the refresh budget and cutting refresh 4x or more (fact 3) for ~0.4% tag overhead.
note: Sparse weak cells let a 2-bit mask per segment park them at their leakage endpoint.

title: Antivirus signature updates for fleet-learned hammer patterns
idea: Adapted from antivirus engines and immune memory, where a threat seen once anywhere becomes a signature everywhere: hyperscalers stream correctable-error locations and controller activation histograms to a central service that learns new hammer shapes (many-sided, half-double), compiles them into small finite-state detectors and pushes them fleet-wide as memory-controller microcode updates.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): mitigations frozen in silicon are bypassed within a year; patchable detection lets vendors ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation and keeps cheaper, more hammer-prone dies usable.
note: Patchable controller detectors from fleet telemetry; needs programmable MC hooks.

title: Library LOCKSS: peer GPU replicas serve as ECC for weights
idea: Adapted from digital-preservation networks ('Lots Of Copies Keep Stuff Safe') that repair a corrupted copy from peers: in data-parallel inference and training, weights are already replicated on many GPUs, so HBM weight regions run detection-only parity with ECC disabled, and a detected error triggers a 64 B fetch of the same address from a peer GPU's replica over NVLink or Ethernet.
why: HBM capacity and cost (facts 5, 6): reclaims ~12.5% ECC capacity and sideband bandwidth for weight regions and lets lower-grade HBM stacks be used, with firmware and runtime changes only.

title: Eliminate the 5-year refresh: DIMM life-extension insurance
idea: Eliminate refresh-driven DIMM retirement: a managing general agent prices a policy from fleet correctable-error telemetry covering failures of DIMMs kept in service in years 6-9; $1M builds the actuarial model, a carrier partnership and two pilots.
why: Keeping DRAM 2-3 years longer cuts replacement demand ~25-40% in that segment.
note: Telemetry-priced warranty is a novel reuse enabler.

title: Negabytes: pay customers to release memory during shortages
idea: Reverse supply and demand, as electricity demand-response does: clouds and memory makers auction credits per GB-month that customers give up through compression, tiering or shorter model contexts. They resell the freed capacity during shortage periods.
why: Usable supply at zero capex: trimming 5-15% of demand in a tight market moves prices more than the same amount of new fab capacity.
note: Demand-response applied to DRAM capacity; software/market pilot with one cloud is feasible.

title: Quorum-sensing analog bus for collective link width scaling
idea: Every memory chiplet leaks a current proportional to its queued demand onto one shared analog 'autoinducer' wire. The summed voltage acts like a bacterial quorum concentration: when it crosses thresholds, all PHYs together wake extra lanes or drop to narrow mode within nanoseconds, with no packet-based negotiation.
why: Idle I/O power: memory PHYs burn much of their power at low utilization; collective, instant width scaling could cut PHY idle energy 40-60%.
note: Clever shared analog wire for collective lane gating; niche idle-power gain.

title: Codon-degeneracy encoding: likely bit-flips map to near-identical values
idea: The genetic code is arranged so most point mutations yield the same or a similar amino acid; encode AI weights and activations in a learned number format whose least-significant code bits are placed in each row's measured weakest cell positions and whose code assignment is Gray-like, so the most probable flips cause the smallest numerical change.
why: ECC and refresh cost for tolerant data (most AI memory): such regions can drop the 12.5% ECC overhead and run ~10x longer refresh with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Drum optimum-programming compiler for in-flight delay-line memories
idea: 1950s drum programmers (SOAP for the IBM 650) placed each word where it would pass under the head just in time. Build a compiler and runtime that schedules AI tensor tiles into recirculating loops (acoustic, photonic, spin-wave) so each tile reaches its tap exactly when the accelerator needs it.
why: Turns circulation delay into near-zero effective latency for predictable AI dataflows (weights, KV streams), so cheap delay storage displaces DRAM capacity with no fab at all.
note: Clever drum-style scheduling, but value hinges on delay-line media whose density is orders below DRAM.

title: Fairchild CCD serial memory revived as sequential weight streamer
idea: Revive 1975 CCD serial memories (serial-parallel-serial organization): a double-poly CCD chip built at 0.5-1 um in a university nanofab holds weights as charge packets that shift past one output amplifier per register in exactly the order inference reads them every token. Circulation regenerates charge, so there is no refresh controller, row decoder or storage capacitor.
why: Weights are read strictly sequentially, so random access is wasted; CCD needs ~2-4F^2 and no capacitor or contact per bit, a periphery-free (fact 7) weight tier that takes weights out of DRAM, demonstrated in a university fab and then moved to any image-sensor fab.
note: Novel use of CCD shift registers; density at mature node loses to DRAM.

title: Tape-library robots shuttle preloaded CXL memory sleds between racks
idea: Treat DRAM like 1960s tape reels: a robotic library moves hot-pluggable 1-4 TB CXL memory sleds, preloaded with model weights or KV caches, to whichever rack needs them and inserts them into blind-mate CXL backplane slots in seconds.
why: Scarce-resource strategy: fleet DRAM utilization is often <50%; migrating physical capacity on minute timescales instead of over-provisioning every server could cut fleet DRAM 20-30%, and preloaded sleds avoid pushing TBs over the network.

title: Poppelbaum stochastic counts store KV-cache LSBs in unrefreshed rows
idea: 1960s stochastic computers (Gaines, Poppelbaum) coded numbers as a count of 1s, so one flipped bit moves the value by one quantum instead of wrecking it. Each 8-bit KV-cache value keeps its 5 MSBs in normally refreshed rows and its 3 LSBs as a 7-cell count code in rows refreshed 10x less often; a decay flip there shifts the value by exactly 1 LSB, which attention tolerates.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): over half the cells of the fastest-growing AI tier skip ~90% of refresh at a bounded accuracy cost; density cost ~1.5x on those values, so it pays only for hot, short-lived tensors.
note: Unary count code bounds flip error; 1.5x density cost limits payoff.

title: Latch-resolution time flags convert errors into cheap erasures
idea: A weak (hot, leaky) cell produces a small signal and the latch resolves slowly; a timing comparator per SA group marks bits that resolved late as erasures. Reed-Solomon/BCH corrects 2 erasures for the cost of 1 error, so soft information is free.
why: ~2x stronger correction at the same parity, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C or smaller Cs (facts 1, 3).

title: Hourglass: unseparated zircon hafnium-zirconium precursors for capacitor dielectrics
idea: Stimulus 'hourglass' (zircon sand runs through unsorted) -> DRAM dielectrics and ferroelectric HZO do not need Hf and Zr separated; HZO even wants them mixed. A 10-person team makes metal-amide precursors directly from crude ZrCl4/HfCl4 (natural ~2% Hf), blended to target ratio, skipping nuclear-grade solvent-extraction separation.
why: Hf/Zr separation is a few-plant chokepoint; skipping it cuts precursor metal cost and dependence while using U.S. mineral-sand zircon.
note: Non-obvious: dielectrics tolerate natural Hf in Zr, so skipping nuclear-grade separation is free.

title: Recompute-on-decay replaces refresh for training activation stashes
idea: Jump from the cell timescale to the training-job timescale: activations stashed for the backward pass get no refresh; each 64 B block carries parity plus a weak-sense flag, and any flagged block is regenerated by re-running its forward segment from the nearest checkpoint, as gradient checkpointing already does.
why: Activation stashes are ~30-60% of training memory; zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for <1% recompute, since most stashes live <1 s.

title: Refresh-by-migration: refresh rows by moving them to their next tier
idea: Fuse the 64 ms refresh timescale with the tiering timescale: instead of activating rows only to rewrite them in place, the controller reads rows due for refresh out over the link and writes them to their new home (hot rows up toward on-package, cold rows down to pooled memory). Mandated refresh activations become free migration bandwidth.
why: Converts ~46 fJ/bit refresh spend (fact 3) into useful placement work and cuts separate migration traffic by ~30-50% in tiered memory systems.

title: Graveyard harvest fund for dead storage-element IP and engineers
idea: Systematically acquire lapsed or abandoned storage-element patent families (Z-RAM, T-RAM/VLT, Unity CMOx, Spin Memory PSC, Qimonda trench) and rehire their device engineers. Run each through a 'name the killer, fix only the killer' gate with a 90-day test-chip budget.
why: Starts on a decade of sunk R&D at pennies on the dollar, cutting time to first silicon by an estimated 2-4 years (capital and time axis).

title: Cyclos resonant clocking dropped over DVFS; memory strobes run fixed frequency
idea: Cyclos' resonant clock mesh shipped in AMD Piledriver and then vanished because on-die inductors cost area and resonance broke across wide DVFS frequency ranges. Memory interfaces run a fixed frequency per speed bin on heavily loaded clock/strobe (WCK/DQS) networks, so resonate those networks with air-core Cu inductors in the package RDL or interposer (no Co/Fe magnetics, no die area), recovering ~50-70% of their CV2 energy each cycle.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): clock/strobe toggling is ~20-30% of memory PHY power, so a claimed 10-20% total PHY energy cut using only Cu and dielectric.

title: Memory retention energy metric in data-center efficiency codes
idea: Ideal: refresh waste is visible and priced. Closest achievable: add a standardized 'retention energy per stored GB-hour' metric, read from DRAM REF counters, to federal data-center efficiency reporting and procurement alongside PUE, with procurement preference for systems that reach zero refresh on declared workloads.
why: Creates market pull for zero-refresh architectures, since refresh is 16-33% of idle DRAM power and roughly 1-3% of IT energy; a cheap policy lever.

title: Check bits capped at 3%: Z-channel codes for one-way leakage
idea: Limit: no more ECC overhead than today. Retention errors are unidirectional: charged cells decay, empty cells do not, and polarity is fixed per true or anti cell. Map logical bits to physical polarity, then encode each 512-bit row segment with asymmetric (Z-channel, Varshamov-Tenengolts-style) codes. These correct t one-way errors with far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Fact 3: correcting ~2-3x more retention errors at equal overhead permits ~4-8x longer refresh intervals in the exponential-tail regime, a direct cut to refresh energy and bandwidth loss.
note: Unidirectional retention errors suit Z-channel codes; gain over BCH at equal overhead is modest.

title: Swap generic LZ4 page compression for per-app trained dictionaries
idea: Substitute a one-size codec with app-specific dictionaries. zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per cgroup from sampled pages (repeated object headers, layouts, strings), compresses that app's cold pages with it, and retrains nightly. It is a kernel-only change.
why: Raises cold anonymous-memory compression from ~2.5x to ~4-5x, so the same DIMMs hold 30-50% more working set.
note: Per-cgroup zstd dictionaries for zswap; a 4-5x ratio is optimistic.

title: TCP congestion control applied to the refresh interval
idea: Adapted from TCP's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease loop: each bank's refresh interval grows a step every epoch while patrol scrubs see zero ECC-corrected retention errors, and halves as soon as one appears, with a hard floor at JEDEC timing. Corrected errors play the role of packet loss.
why: Finds each part's real retention limit at its real temperature and age instead of the worst-case spec, typically 4-8x longer intervals in cool, lightly loaded systems (fact 3), with no new cell physics.

title: MIDI-style memory: ship generator seeds, regenerate data beside DRAM
idea: Adapted from MIDI, which sends notes rather than audio: regenerable tensor parts (random projections, low-rank bases, positional tables) are stored as seeds plus generator code. A 180 nm PRNG/LFSR engine on the memory buffer recreates them on the fly instead of reading them.
why: Data movement and capacity: regenerable tensors are neither stored nor moved; ~10-30% capacity and bandwidth savings for suitable models.

title: Video error concealment for KV-cache and activation memory
idea: Adapted from video decoders that conceal lost macroblocks by interpolating from neighbors instead of stopping playback: KV-cache and activation buffers get one parity bit per 32-bit word, and when parity fails the runtime replaces the corrupted element with the mean of the same head's adjacent tokens (or zeroes it and renormalizes attention) instead of raising a machine check.
why: ECC overhead and refresh (facts 3, 8): detect-only parity costs ~3% instead of 12.5% and lets the cache run longer refresh at higher BER; transformers are robust to sparse token corruption, so the largest inference memory consumer moves to cheaper bits.

title: Vinyl pre-emphasis: controller-boosted restore for flagged weak rows
idea: Adapted from vinyl recording's RIAA pre-emphasis, which boosts fragile high frequencies at cutting time so they survive playback: the controller keeps a small table of rows identified as weak and issues their writes and refreshes with extended tRAS/tWR (or back-to-back double activation) so their cells are fully restored to VARY instead of being truncated by tight default timings.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): many weak cells are under-restored rather than truly leaky; full restore on the ~0.1% flagged rows recovers ~10-20% charge and lets the whole device run a longer refresh interval, in controller firmware on existing chips.

title: Eliminate parity bits: flip-bounded number encodings for weights in cheap tiers
idea: Store weights in high-BER <=400 C memory using a number format built so that any single bit flip moves the value only a small, bounded amount: Gray-coded exponents, redundant thermometer-coded top bits and a saturating decode. No parity is needed.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC overhead and decoder energy for weight storage, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 with <0.5% accuracy loss.
note: Software-demoable robust encoding for weights.

title: Eliminate the R&D lab: $1M prize for open gain-cell macro
idea: Eliminate hiring a research team: a $750k inducement prize plus $250k shuttle credits rewards the first open-source gain-cell DRAM macro on US open PDKs reaching >=10 ms retention and <=20 ns access, judged on silicon within 24 months.
why: Prizes typically pull 5-10x the purse in outside effort and yield a free, US-fabricable embedded DRAM block.
note: Fits $1M exactly; output is an embedded block, not commodity bits.

title: Upcycle commodity DRAM dies with pad-rearranging RDL
idea: Rearrange the pads, not the die: buy known-good LPDDR bare dies, and in a university nanofab add a polyimide plus electroplated-Cu redistribution layer (contact aligner, 5 um lines) that fans the edge pad row into an area array matched to a logic test chip, then flip-chip the two face-to-face.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: wide-I/O-like short links from commodity dies with ~$1M of tools, showing ~1 pJ/bit without a TSV line (facts 5, 6).

title: Fine-tune each model to its own DRAM's fault map
idea: Reverse adaptation: instead of repairing memory to fit the model, each deployed model is briefly fine-tuned with weights forced to zero at the exact stuck or weak bit positions of the DRAM it occupies, absorbing the higher defect density of a fluorine-free fab.
why: Ships dies with ~1e-5 hard-fault density for inference at <0.1% accuracy loss and no repair area.

title: CRISPR spacer library of row-hammer attack signatures
idea: Bacteria keep snippets of past viral DNA as spacers to recognize reinfection. The controller keeps a compact CAM of hashed aggressor-pattern signatures (address deltas, cadence relative to refresh), shared fleet-wide by firmware update, and triggers targeted refresh only on matches, over a cheap probabilistic baseline. Firmware, FPGA and attack corpus, ~$500k in 18 months.
why: Fact 9: learns new many-sided patterns after first sighting while issuing ~5x fewer mitigation refreshes than blanket probabilistic schemes.

title: Cicada prime-period refresh jitter defeating hammer synchronization
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime cycles (13, 17 years) so predators cannot sync with them. Controller firmware schedules REF commands per bank at co-prime, jittered intervals within DDR5's postpone/pull-in allowance (mean stays tREFI). Neither workloads nor attackers can then phase-lock activations to in-DRAM TRR sampling windows. Firmware plus FPGA tests, ~$250k in 12 months.
why: Fact 9: synchronization-based patterns defeat TRR. Desynchronizing restores TRR effectiveness with zero die area.
note: Jittered REF timing within tREFI allowance to break attacker sync with TRR; cheap FPGA test.

title: Overlapping reading frames share MSB bit-planes between correlated tensors
idea: Viruses read one RNA in shifted frames to make different proteins; a base model and its fine-tunes (or strongly correlated projections) store a shared most-significant bit-plane once, each variant keeping only its own low-order planes, read through frame-specific offsets.
why: Capacity: 30-50% savings for families of correlated weights.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes matched to true-cell and anti-cell leakage
idea: Optical on-off links lose photons but never create them (the Z-channel). DRAM retention errors are one-way per cell type: true cells go 1->0, anti-cells 0->1. A quick test maps each part's true/anti layout. The FPGA controller then uses asymmetric-error-correcting codes (Varshamov/constant-weight style) that correct t one-way errors with about half the parity symmetric BCH needs.
why: The same parity budget corrects ~2x the retention errors, so refresh intervals can stretch 2-4x (fact 3). It is pure coding plus firmware, which fits the budget.
note: Pure coding plus FPGA DRAM testing; half-parity claim likely optimistic.

title: Holographic spreading: Walsh-Hadamard encoding of tolerant data before storage
idea: Every fragment of a hologram holds a blurred copy of the whole image. The accelerator or controller applies a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to each 64-value block before writing and clips on the inverse. A flipped bit then becomes small noise spread over 64 values instead of one catastrophic exponent error. It runs on existing hardware in firmware or kernels.
why: Error-tolerant data (activations, images) degrade gracefully in weak or rarely refreshed memory, giving refresh and ECC savings on 30-60% of AI capacity (fact 3).

title: Delta-modulation encoding for AI tensors in error-prone 3D strings
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1946 delta modulation: store KV-cache and activation sequences as 1-bit delta streams along the token axis across vertical tiers, so each cell's bit is worth one small step and a 1% cell BER adds only ~1% amplitude noise; the controller integrates on read.
why: Facts 1 and 5: lets marginal ~2 fF cells hold AI working sets; ~3x denser cells outweigh the ~1.5-2x bit overhead of delta coding for correlated tensors.
note: KV tensors weakly correlated along tokens; net gain doubtful.

title: No. 1 ESS audit programs scan for silent DRAM corruption
idea: Bell's No. 1 ESS ran continuous audit programs that walked switching tables, checked structural invariants and repaired corrupted records. Runtimes run a low-priority auditor that checks invariants of live data (pointer ranges, allocator headers, type tags, per-block hashes of model weights) at ~1% CPU and repairs from replicas or recomputes, catching silent corruption that slips past ECC.
why: Bounding silent data corruption lets operators relax refresh and ECC strength on bulk memory (refresh energy -30-50%) while keeping corruption risk at today's level.

title: Holographic page spreading: Hadamard-encode weights so failures become noise
idea: 1970s holographic memories spread every bit across the whole plate, so a scratch only added noise. Before writing neural-network weight pages, a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform is applied across each 2 KB block; dead bitlines, hammered regions or retention clusters then come back after the inverse transform as low-amplitude noise spread over all weights, which models tolerate without ECC.
why: Error tolerance for the largest AI capacity tier: removes 12.5% ECC overhead and repair for weight memory and tolerates clustered faults, for ~log2(N) adds per value in the base die.

title: Chokepoint-aware process kit: element budgets as design rules
idea: Inverts 'choose materials for performance, then source them': annotate every process module with grams of W, Hf, Ru, He, PFAS, quartz and water per wafer plus a supplier-concentration (HHI) index, and run a flow optimizer that picks the recipe meeting electrical targets at minimum chokepoint exposure.
why: Makes scarce-resource intensity a first-class metric; expected 30-60% cut in chokepoint-weighted inputs per bit by surfacing substitutions (Al for W, Mo for Ru, H2 for He).

title: Chaos-engineering controller that probes margins with shadow writes
idea: Inverts 'operate safely inside a fixed guardband': the controller continuously writes shadow copies of live lines into a scratch row using aggressive timings and refresh, compares them with the protected original, and learns per-bank safe tRCD/tRAS/refresh envelopes that track temperature and aging.
why: Recovers the 20-40% timing and refresh guardband sized for worst-case cells (facts 3, 10), raising usable bandwidth and lowering energy.

title: Post-package repair as a scalpel for the retention tail
idea: DDR4 and DDR5 already expose soft and hard post-package repair for hard faults. Repurpose it: profile in the field, remap the few rows per bank whose retention is below 256 ms onto spare rows, and run the module at 2-4x tREFI with ECC and patrol scrub as a safety net. Needs BIOS/BMC firmware and a validation lab, ~$400k over 18 months.
why: The refresh interval is dictated by a ~1e-6 fraction of cells. Removing that fraction moves the interval toward median retention (seconds) on existing parts (fact 3); the spare-row count caps how far this goes.
note: Few spare rows per bank and VRT cap the gain, but a firmware-only fleet pilot is cheap.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes match one-directional decay errors
idea: Physics says retention errors go only one way: charged cells lose charge and never gain it. After true/anti-cell mapping, every decay error is therefore a charged-to-empty flip. Implement an asymmetric (Z-channel) error-correcting code, such as Varshamov-Tenengolts or a constant-weight-augmented BCH, in an FPGA controller; it needs about half the parity of a symmetric code. Extend refresh until the decay BER reaches the code's budget. Fits $1M and 24 months.
why: Running at 4-8x longer refresh with ~3-6% parity overhead cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss in proportion (fact 3).

title: Bit-plane split refresh: exponents guarded, low mantissa bits relaxed
idea: Bits do not carry equal information: a flipped low mantissa bit in bfloat16 perturbs a value by <2^-4 relative, while an exponent flip can be catastrophic. Transpose KV-cache and activation tensors into bit-planes. Sign, exponent and the top 3 mantissa bits go in normally refreshed banks; the low 4 mantissa bits go in banks refreshed 8-16x less. Validate on open LLMs with a ~$150k software and FPGA effort.
why: Relaxing refresh 8x on a quarter of KV-cache bits trims ~20% of its refresh energy with <6% error per value (fact 3).

title: Access-is-refresh mapping puts hot pages on weak rows
idea: Every activation restores a row. The controller maps the most frequently accessed pages onto rows binned as weakest-retention at a 125 C test, so natural traffic refreshes them, while strong rows hold cold data with long refresh.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) at hot cut ~30-60% with no hardware cost beyond a retention bin table.

title: Unidirectional error codes matched to one-way charge leakage
idea: Retention physics is one-way: a charged node can only lose electrons, so true-cells fail 1->0 and anti-cells fail 0->1, never the reverse. After de-scrambling cell polarity, apply Bose-Lin/Borden t-unidirectional-error-correcting codes. They need far fewer check bits than symmetric BCH for the same t.
why: Retention tail/ECC overhead: parity drops from 6.25% to ~3%, or 2x the correction at equal overhead, which allows longer refresh.

title: Hadamard-spread weight storage turns bit flips into tiny noise
idea: One exponent or MSB flip in BF16/INT8 weights can wreck a model, which forces DRAM-grade BER. Store each block of 64 weights after a 64-point Walsh-Hadamard transform, invertible in the accelerator for <1% compute. A single stored-bit flip then spreads as +/-delta/8 across 64 weights, below model noise.
why: Error tolerance: inference weights can live at raw BER ~1e-6, i.e., ~10x slower refresh or weak dies, for most AI memory footprint.

title: Spare tire: repurpose ECC lanes as data for hash-verified weights
idea: The 'spare tire' is the ECC chip on every server DIMM. For read-only model weights protected by per-block cryptographic hashes at load time plus periodic scrubbing, the controller uses the ECC lanes as extra data width.
why: Bandwidth and capacity: +25% on existing DIMMs, and ~11% of installed bits are reclaimed for AI weights.

title: Tattoo: aerosol-jet printed die-to-die bridges across chiplet gaps
idea: Forced 'tattoo ink': an aerosol-jet printer writes 20 um-pitch silver/copper traces over a printed dielectric ramp directly across the gap between a memory die and a logic die placed on a plain substrate, replacing silicon bridges. Tool rental or a ~$500k tool fits the budget.
why: Capital intensity: maskless chiplet interconnect at a fraction of bridge or interposer cost, buildable in any U.S. lab.

title: Garbage collector compresses cold object subgraphs behind forwarding stubs
idea: Box: compression × managed-runtime GC × object subgraph × untouched for N cycles × read-barrier inflate. During marking the runtime serializes cold subgraphs into compressed blobs and installs stubs; a read barrier inflates them on first touch.
why: Managed heaps run 2–5× larger than live data and much of it is cold; cold-object compression cuts heap 30–50%.

title: Page-aligned content-defined packaging so kernel dedup actually hits
idea: Box: dedup enablement × build and packaging toolchain × 4 KB/2 MB chunk × build time × content-defined chunking with alignment padding. Binaries, container layers and model files are laid out so identical content lands on identical page boundaries across versions and tenants, letting existing same-page merging match it.
why: Small offsets defeat page dedup today; alignment lifts merge rates from a few percent to 20–40% on dense hosts, a pure toolchain change free of fluorinated chemistry.

title: GPU texture units decode block-compressed weights at zero ALU cost
idea: Box: decompress × existing GPU texture-sampling hardware × 4×4 block × every fetch × BC4/BC5 (ASTC on mobile) endpoint-plus-index format. Weights are encoded as single- or dual-channel block-compressed textures by an encoder that minimizes matmul output error, and kernels fetch them through the texture path, which decompresses in fixed-function hardware.
why: ~4 bits per weight (4× smaller than FP16) with free random-access decode on silicon already shipped in every GPU, so no new chips and no fluorinated chemistry.
note: Free fixed-function decode, but BC formats offer ~4b like existing quantization; accuracy unclear.

title: Librarian's closed stacks: garbage collector exiles cold objects to NVMe
idea: Libraries keep rarely requested books in closed stacks. A modified generational GC (OpenJDK or Go) samples object reads with 1% read barriers. Objects untouched for N collections are compacted into closed-stack regions and madvised out to NVMe, with forwarding pointers so a touch faults back the whole batch. Fundable as a 24-month, 3-person project.
why: Managed heaps are sized 2-3x their live data and hold large cold populations. Object-granular exile cuts heap DRAM 25-50% and beats page-level swap on mixed hot/cold pages.

title: Scrap-metal dealer: memory-recovery contractor paid in reclaimed gigabytes
idea: Scrap dealers profit from what others throw away. A 6-person firm audits client fleets (heap dumps, page census, configs), applies the fixes, and keeps 30% of the first year's avoided DRAM purchases, verified by telemetry. The $1M covers runway until the first two contracts pay.
why: Most enterprises have 20-40% reclaimable memory but no team to get it. At 4x prices, gain-sharing makes adoption risk-free and unlocks supply without fabs.

title: Battle-short mode: zero out uncorrectable AI weights and keep running
idea: A military 'battle short' bypasses protective trips during combat. In AI inference, when the controller reports a poisoned (uncorrectable) line from a weight region, the runtime substitutes zeros or the per-channel mean for those 32 FP16 values and keeps going instead of raising a machine check. It logs the address so the page can be reloaded later.
why: Neural nets tolerate dropout-like loss of a few weights. Removing the crash penalty lets weight memory run on cheaper dies at higher uncorrectable-error rates (facts 3, 6).
note: Zero-substitution on poison; software.

title: Lateral-BJT sense amplifier on open 130 nm PDK gain-cell macro
idea: Effect: Boltzmann-diffusion matching of bipolar Vbe. A small team designs a gain-cell memory macro on a SkyWater/GF open-PDK MPW whose sense amp is a differential pair of parasitic vertical/lateral BJTs. Vbe mismatch is ~0.5-1 mV versus ~10-20 mV for small MOSFETs, so tiny 2T/3T gain-cell read currents are resolved by a small, untrimmed stage.
why: Sense margin and U.S. manufacturability: 512+ cells per SA and lower read currents (longer retention) in a U.S. 130 nm fab, designed fabless.
note: BJT pair for low-offset gain-cell sensing on open 130 nm PDK; easy MPW demo, mature-node niche.

title: Fluorine vapor XeF2 carves lateral capacitor cavities in poly-Si stacks
idea: Deposit an LPCVD poly-Si/SiO2 multilayer, etch a vertical slit, and expose it to XeF2 vapor, which isotropically recesses only the poly-Si (>1000:1 to SiO2) by a timed 100-200 nm; ALD then lines the horizontal cavities with TiN/ZrO2/TiN as lateral capacitors for 8-16 tiers.
why: Demonstrates lateral 3D-DRAM capacitor formation (fact 2) with a plasma-free, stiction-free etch present in most university MEMS labs, avoiding SiGe epi entirely.
note: Cheap, demo-ready lateral capacitor cavity test vehicle; loading-dependent timed recess is the only issue.

title: Lithium intercalation allocator: tiny objects packed into size-class slack
idea: As Li+ ions slot into the gaps between graphite layers, the allocator intercalates sub-64 B objects into the unused tail slack of larger size-class slots (a 300 B object in a 384 B slot leaves 84 B), tracking them with a per-slab slack bitmap and CHERI-style bounded pointers so overflows trap instead of corrupting neighbors.
why: Size-class internal fragmentation wastes ~10-20% of heap in jemalloc/tcmalloc fleets; reclaiming the slack gives ~8-15% less DRAM with no new memory hardware (cost/bit, density).

title: Flour sifter: multi-sieve sketches replace exact tables, median rejects flips
idea: Millers sift flour through a stack of sieves. Exact counting and lookup tables (flow tables, feature-frequency counters, dedup indices, recommendation counts) are replaced by count-median sketches with 5 'sieves' of saturating 8-bit log counters. Taking the median across sieves rejects a counter that a flip pushed up or down, so 1% BER barely moves the estimate.
why: Sketches use 10-100x less memory than exact hash tables at bounded error, and the median turns 1% cell BER into a negligible error.
note: Median across sketch rows absorbs cell flips; enables cheap high-BER cells for sketch workloads.

title: Halftone dithered weight storage spreads cell failures like printer dots
idea: Borrow halftone/error-diffusion printing: keep the sign and top bits of each AI weight in protected cells, but store the low-order magnitude as a thermometer (dot-density) code across 3 unprotected, refresh-relaxed cells, with error diffusion pushing each weight's rounding residual into its tile neighbours. A failed cell then moves a weight by one fine step that averages out across the tile, instead of flipping a binary bit.
why: Lets ~70% of weight-memory cells run at raw BER ~1e-3 with 4-8x longer refresh and no ECC parity (fact 3 refresh energy, ECC area); trades a little density on low-order bits for large refresh and ECC savings on inference memory.
note: Thermometer code costs density; software demo easy.

title: Egg-free baking: helium-free etch and anneal recipes qualified academically
idea: Bakers swap eggs for aquafaba and requalify the recipe. Use nanofab etchers and furnaces to requalify DRAM-relevant steps without helium: hydrogen-argon backside chuck cooling with retuned clamp pressure, and N2/Ar carrier, dilution and anneal cooling gases. Publish the transfer data openly.
why: Helium chokepoint: removes the need rather than recycling it, giving cheap cross-fab de-risking.
note: H2/Ar backside cooling requalification is cheap nanofab work; H2 safety and cooling parity are the unknowns.

title: Error concealment: interpolate uncorrectable words from neighbors
idea: Ideal: errors that are invisible. Closest: a 180 nm memory-side controller tags image, audio and tensor regions; when a word there is uncorrectable it substitutes the average of neighboring elements, as video decoders conceal lost macroblocks, instead of raising a machine check.
why: Fact 3: tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER on media and AI tensors, enabling relaxed refresh and weaker cells for those regions.

title: BF16 split across refresh tiers: sign and exponent guarded, mantissa relaxed
idea: 10-person constraint: only data layout is ours. A custom allocator puts the sign-and-exponent byte planes of BF16/FP8 tensors in normally refreshed rows and the low mantissa bit-planes in rows refreshed every 1-2 s. It accepts rare low-order flips, which training and inference tolerate.
why: Fact 3: about half of tensor bits move to a ~20x slower refresh tier, cutting refresh energy ~45% for model memory with only an allocator and controller configuration.

title: University cleanroom only: indium-free ALD zinc-tin-oxide access TFTs on MPW CMOS
idea: 10-person constraint: no fab, only a shared university cleanroom. Buy periphery-only CMOS wafers from a 130/180 nm MPW shuttle and post-process the BEOL at <=350 C: ALD ZnSnO channels (no indium or other scarce elements), ALD Al2O3 gates and planar MIM capacitors. This gives access devices with ~1e-20 A/um-class off-current stacked over the logic.
why: Facts 3 and 4 plus resources: demonstrates a refresh-free BEOL memory tile (hours of retention) with no EUV, no indium and no DRAM fab, buildable by ~10 people in ~18 months for niche low-density parts and as a pilot route.

title: PMIC firmware only: undervolt DRAM rails during self-refresh to measured margin
idea: 10-person constraint: we can design only the DIMM's power path. DDR5 DIMMs carry their own PMIC, so custom PMIC firmware or a custom board steps VDD and VPP down during self-refresh to each module's minimum, found by a boot-time margin sweep, plus a 50 mV guard. Rails return to nominal on exit.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy scales roughly as V2, so 10-15% lower rails cut self-refresh energy ~20-28% per DIMM with board and firmware work only.

title: Post-package-repair rescue line for returned DIMMs
idea: Within $1M/24 months: write open firmware that runs exhaustive row-retention and hammer tests on returned and failing DDR4/DDR5 modules, then permanently remaps bad rows through JEDEC hard post-package-repair fuses and re-certifies modules that would otherwise be shredded.
why: A few failing rows now scrap whole modules; rescuing ~50-70% of returns adds supply with zero materials and yields field data on retention tails.
note: hPPR spare rows are few per bank group, limiting rescue rate.

title: Nested-precision bit-plane memory + self-speculative decoding
idea: INT8/FP8 weights are quantised in a nested (Matryoshka-style) way, so the top 2 or 4 bit planes are themselves a usable low-precision model. The memory controller stores the planes in separate address ranges and streams 'planes 0-1', 'planes 0-3' or all of them, in 512 B-2 KB chunks that match DRAM bursts and pages. Decode is self-speculative: draft k tokens with the top planes only (25-50% of the weight bytes), then verify all k in one batched pass with every plane. No second model is stored.
why: 1.1-1.8x effective decode bandwidth (weight reads per accepted token 0.89-0.55), with zero extra capacity.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers as one-dimensional memory substrates
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: replace the 2D wafer with a 1D substrate. A macroscopic preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and metal electrodes is thermally drawn into kilometres of fiber whose cross-section is one memory column (bitline, storage electrodes, access channel); fibers are then woven or laminated with orthogonal wordline fibers into 3D blocks.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): draw towers make kilometres per hour with no lithography, and wide-gap chalcogenides give low leakage (Fact 3); density and speed are highly speculative.
note: Litho-free km-scale drawn fiber columns woven into 3D blocks; doubt: fiber feature sizes and chalcogenide speed far from DRAM density.

title: Swap layer-by-layer 3D stacking for rolling one patterned membrane
idea: Pattern one planar layer of thin-film gain cells with DUV on a strained SiNx bilayer, release it, and let the built-in strain roll it into a 20-winding tube. Each winding becomes a memory tier, and the tiers connect through edge contacts along the roll axis.
why: Gives 20 tiers from one deposition and patterning sequence (fact 2), so cost does not grow with the tier count, and no EUV is used (fact 4).
note: 20 tiers from one patterning would collapse 3D cost; dense edge interconnect across windings and alignment are the doubt.

title: Multilayer optical-disc focus addressing via threshold-coded tiers
idea: Like BD-XL picking a layer by focus depth, give each of 32 storage tiers on one shared vertical wordline a distinct access threshold set by deposited channel thickness; address tier k by stepping wordline voltage and differencing successive bitline reads, and write each column in descending-threshold order.
why: 10x at same cost: removes per-tier bitline staircases and select lines, so 32 tiers cost about one hole etch plus depositions; ~15x bits per footprint.
note: Addresses 32 tiers by Vt stepping, no staircases; doubt: Vt variation and read margin across 32 levels on one wordline.

title: Snack-bag web metallizers vacuum-coat 128-tier stacks by the kilometer
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll metallizers that coat packaging film at ~1,000 m/min: deposit 128 alternating Mo/SiOx wordline/insulator layers on a heat-tolerant web in multi-drum passes, laminate the stack onto a CMOS wafer, then one hole etch plus ALD finishes vertical-channel gain cells.
why: Tier-stack deposition is a dominant 3D cost; web coating is ~100x cheaper per m2, and with one mask for all tiers the path reaches ~$0.1/GB; trade-offs: lamination voids, lower tier quality, refresh-heavy cells.
note: Web-coated tier stacks could slash deposition cost; pinholes, lamination voids and etching through a web are the doubts.

title: Fifty-electron bit read by repeated non-destructive skipper sampling
idea: MINIFY the stored charge ~600x (from ~30,000 e- to ~50 e-): the storage node is a ~0.01 fF floating diffusion with no capacitor, and a per-subarray skipper-CCD-style floating-gate amplifier shuttles the packet under its sense gate N=16 times, averaging read noise below 1 e- rms before write-back.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the AR 60-75:1 etch; cell heads toward 4F2 and write CV2 energy falls ~100x. Only viable if node leakage is pushed to ~1e-21 A (pair with a wide-gap or pinned node).
note: ~600x less charge kills the capacitor wall; doubts: 1e-21 A node leakage and 16 skipper samples within DRAM latency.

title: Magnify the draw ratio: fiber-drawn lithography-free memory arrays
idea: Build a centimeter-scale preform holding thousands of channels of semiconductor glass, metal and insulator, thermally draw it 10,000:1 into km fibers so features shrink to sub-micron, then fuse and slice fiber bundles into faceplates where each core is a vertical transistor-capacitor cell addressed by one coarse metallization.
why: Drawing replaces lithography: one draw tower outputs km/hour, so array cost falls to ~cents/cm2, targeting ~100x lower $/GB for slow first-generation DRAM-like tiers.
note: Thermal drawing replaces litho cheaply; doubt: drawn semiconductors make poor transistors and per-bit density may lag badly.

title: Magnify throughput 100x: solar-style inline memory lines
idea: Borrow photovoltaic manufacturing (belt-fed inline PECVD, laser scribing, screen-print metallization at ~8,000 wafers/hour per line) to make vertical thin-film transistor-capacitor cells whose critical dimensions are set by film thickness and laser scribe, not lithography.
why: PV processes a wafer for ~$0.2 vs ~$5,000+ for DRAM; even holding ~1/500 of the bits, cost per GB drops ~100x+, accepting low density, big modules and slower first versions.
note: Key doubt: ~500x lower density makes modules huge; periphery and RC still need fine litho.

title: Minify reliability to 1e-3 BER: junk-tolerant stacked memory
idea: Sell memory for noise-tolerant AI tensors at a raw 1e-3 bit error rate: skip sort, burn-in, repair and final test, let each die self-map defects via boot-time BIST, and absorb errors with stochastic rounding and error-resilient training.
why: Dropping the yield gate lets fabs stack 64 cheap thin-film cell layers whose compound yield would otherwise be near zero, and removes ~25-40% test/repair cost; together these target ~100x lower $/GB.
note: Error tolerance unlocks low-yield 64-tier stacks; doubt: 1e-3 raw BER corrupts exponent bits unless critical bits get protection.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoint: display-fab capex per m2 is ~50-100x lower than a DRAM fab, with no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible or EUV; targets ~$1-3/GB for a slower (~100 ns) tier that frees real DRAM for hot data.
note: Idle Gen-8.5 LCD fabs as capacity-tier memory; doubt: 12-16 tier panel yield and defect density at panel scale.

title: Vacuum as the insulator: field-emission two-terminal crossbar storage cell
idea: Reverse insulator and conductor: each storage node is a metal island over a sealed 3-5 nm vacuum gap to a sharp emitter at a wordline/bitline crossing; below the Fowler-Nordheim threshold the gap passes essentially nothing, while ~2x the field drives uA emission to charge or discharge it in ns.
why: Leakage tail and 3D blocker (facts 2,3): super-exponential I-V gives >1e12 on/off with no transistor, so 4F2 crossbar tiers can stack with no lateral transistor at all.
note: Super-exponential FN I-V as built-in selector; doubt: sealed 3-5 nm gaps, emitter wear, and tiny island charge readout.

title: Roll a 2D array film into a multi-turn scroll
idea: Turn area into tiers by rolling instead of stacking: fabricate a thin-film oxide DRAM array on a strained bilayer membrane with the existing mask set, then use one added release mask so the film self-rolls into a 10-30 turn Swiss roll, with turns connected through contacts at the scroll edge.
why: Density and 3D cost (facts 2,4): 10-30x bits per footprint without per-tier processing; rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors already exist.
note: 10-30 tiers from one patterned film; doubt: connecting inner turns and yield of rolled arrays.

title: Another dimension: 512-tier vertical charge-coupled strings with one sense node
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bits are charge packets in potential wells along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel gated by 512 stacked wordline plates, a one-hole 3D-NAND-like process with no capacitor and no per-bit transistor. Reads clock the packets CCD-style down the pillar into one floating-diffusion sense node under the array, which regenerates them and re-injects them at the top, so refresh is just recirculation.
why: 100x path: NAND-like cost (~$0.05-0.15/GB) because periphery is one sense node per 512 bits, no EUV and few masks per tier; trade-offs: serial 10-50 us page access, and charge-transfer inefficiency and dark current cap string length, so a small DRAM cache must front it. Attacks Facts 1, 2, 4 and 7.
note: NAND-like cost for refresh-by-recirculation memory; but 10-50 us serial access is not DRAM-class, and CTI over 512 transfers is doubtful.

title: Blessing in disguise: Geiger-mode avalanche bitline sensing of 100-electron cells
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise turns breakdown, normally a failure, into gain: each bitline segment ends in a SPAD-like junction biased just above avalanche breakdown, which a stored packet of ~100 electrons triggers into a full-swing self-quenched pulse, so storage nodes need only ~0.02 fF and can be plain planar diffusions.
why: 100x path: deletes the capacitor module (Fact 1) and allows near-4F2 planar or stacked cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: dark counts and afterpulsing need repeat reads and strong ECC, ~10-100 ns quench recovery and higher sense voltage. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 4.
note: Avalanche gain could delete the capacitor module; doubts are dark counts, afterpulsing, high bias at DRAM pitch, junction leakage swamping 100-electron packets.

title: Coaxial gallium-oxide 2T0C cell grown inside one vertical hole
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: in a 3D-NAND-like stack of word planes, one DUV-printed hole receives nested ALD shells at each tier recess - an outer amorphous Ga2O3 write channel gated by the plane, a metal storage-node ring, a thin dielectric, and an inner Ga2O3 read channel gated by that ring.
why: Ga2O3's 4.8 eV gap gives off-current below ~1e-21 A, so retention exceeds years and refresh is zero with no capacitor module; one hole mask serves 32-64 tiers, raising density without EUV (facts 2, 3, 4).
note: Refresh-free multi-tier gain cell from one hole; ALD amorphous Ga2O3 mobility and nested-shell control are the doubt.

title: Pollen-tube confined epitaxy grows monocrystalline channels in every tier
idea: A pollen tube grows only inside the style's channel; deposit a cheap 120-pair PECVD oxide/nitride stack as in 3D NAND, strip the nitride through slits to leave tunnels, then grow single-crystal Si into all tunnels at once by template-confined lateral epitaxy seeded from the substrate at each slit base.
why: Replaces slow, strain-limited Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattices (capped near 30-60 layers) with 3D-NAND-cost stacks, making 120 tiers (~10x bits/mm2) affordable at near-flat wafer cost (fact 2).
note: Single-crystal Si grown into NAND-style nitride-strip tunnels; lateral confined-epi distance and defects are the doubt.

title: Apical-meristem nanowires grow stacked transistors along their own axis
idea: Shoots add segments at the tip; grow vertical Si nanowires by catalyst-tip (VLS) growth from the pad lattice while switching dopant and Ge gases every ~25 nm, so each wire holds 16 axial n+/p/n+ transistor segments, then fill around the forest with alternating spin-on dielectric and conductor layers that become wordline tiers timed to the segments.
why: Channels for all 16 tiers come from one growth run instead of patterning; at ~40 nm wire pitch that is ~100 nm2 per bit, ~8-10x bits/mm2 at roughly flat cost (fact 2).
note: All tiers' channels from one VLS growth; aligning wordline tiers to dopant segments and catalyst contamination are the doubt.

title: Myelin multilamellar self-assembly lays down twenty tiers in one coat
idea: Schwann cells wrap axons in dozens of uniform lamellae; spin a high-chi lamellar block copolymer that orders parallel to the substrate into 20+ layers (~12 nm period), then use sequential infiltration synthesis to turn one block into AlOx insulator and the other into In2O3 channel, creating a whole tier stack in one coat-anneal-infiltrate sequence below 200 C.
why: Tier-stack cost drops from ~100 depositions to one coat plus a few infiltration cycles; 40+ BEOL-compatible tiers with a single hole/slit patterning give ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat cost (facts 2, 4).
note: 40 tiers from one coat; SIS oxides are device-poor, and 12 nm period leaves no room for wordlines.

title: Cochlear amplifier: Hopf-poised sense amp hears sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Cochlear hair cells sit at a Hopf bifurcation, giving huge gain for faint sounds; bias each sense amplifier at the edge of oscillation with a calibrated negative-resistance loop so the tiny bitline perturbation of a ~1 fF cell tips it decisively, with per-amp calibration of the bifurcation point.
why: Capacitor charge wall: if 1-2 fF cells become readable, pillar AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~15-20:1, cutting deposition/etch cost and opening lateral 3D capacitors.
note: Latches already regenerate from instability; Hopf poise does not beat kT/C noise or offset.

title: Airport baggage conveyor: vertical charge-coupled bit strings in 3D stacks
idea: Like bags riding a conveyor to one scanner, deposit a 3D-NAND-style stack of 64-128 gate layers around a vertical wide-gap channel (e.g., Ga2O3 or ZnSnO) and clock charge packets up and down it CCD-style; a single sense/restore node at the top of each string reads and rewrites packets as they pass. A bit is a potential well under a gate, so each tier costs one deposition, not a transistor plus capacitor.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 3D density without a 3D capacitor or lateral transistor; ~100 tiers at 3 gates/bit gives ~30 bits per hole, ~5-10x density with no added EUV; serial shift (~1 ns/stage) keeps average latency ~20-30 ns only if strings stay short.
note: Key doubt: charge-transfer efficiency in oxide channels over 100+ shifts; serial latency limits string length.

title: Photomultiplier read: avalanche gain junction under each pillar
idea: Like a photomultiplier or SPAD turning one photon into a pulse, place a quenched avalanche junction at the foot of each vertical bitline biased just below breakdown; a 0.1 fF cell's few hundred electrons trigger ~100x multiplication, then a passive quench resets it, so cells and lines stay tiny.
why: Capacitor wall and access energy (facts 1, 8): Cs drops ~50x and the local line stays a few fF; claims >10x lower energy per read if avalanche statistics and dark counts are tamed.
note: Avalanche gain lets Cs shrink ~50x; dark counts, gain noise and high bias fight the voltage floor.

title: Plated-wire memory rebuilt as vertical plated vias in 3D stacks
idea: Plated-wire memory (Voyager era) stored bits in the circumferential magnetization of permalloy plated on a wire and read them non-destructively by tilting it with a word strap. Make the wire a vertical copper pillar in a 3D-NAND-style hole lined with circumferentially anisotropic CoFeB, use the stacked tier planes as word straps, write by coincident pillar plus strap current, and read by a small strap pulse that tilts the film and induces a pillar voltage.
why: 100+ tiers from one hole etch with no lateral transistor or capacitor (Fact 2), non-destructive read (Fact 8), non-volatile (Fact 3); ~1/5 the cost per bit of 2D DRAM if signal suffices.
note: 100+ tiers from one hole etch; doubt: inductive read signal scales with flux area and is uV at nm scale.

title: Threshold-switch crossbar capacitors: 64 decks, refreshed constantly
idea: Inverts 'an access device must hold the bit for 64 ms': put a chalcogenide ovonic threshold switch in series with a tiny MIM capacitor at every crossbar node, stack 64 self-aligned decks with two KrF masks each, accept us-to-ms retention set by OTS leakage, and refresh whole decks in parallel from base CMOS.
why: 4F2 per deck with no transistor or EUV, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off is refresh power (~20-40% of total), half-select disturb and OTS drift.
note: us retention means ~1000x refresh rate; refresh power likely dominates, not 20-40%.

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.
why: Roll-to-roll layers cost ~$1-5/m2 versus ~$10,000/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so even at ~30x lower density it is ~100x cheaper per GB for transient data; trade-off: no long-term storage, ~100 ns-1 us access.
note: Ultra-cheap R2R layers for transient data; doubts: 100 nm R2R overlay, inter-foil interconnect, sub-µs access.

title: Self-assembled diode dots: block copolymers replace EUV for every cell
idea: Inverts 'lithography must define each access device': coat a PS-b-PDMS block copolymer guided by coarse 193 nm trenches into 10 nm-pitch dot arrays, then convert each dot by sequential infiltration synthesis into a vertical oxide Schottky diode atop a MIM nanocapacitor, mapping out defective dots at test.
why: Zero EUV layers (fact 4) and ~1 mask per tier at 10 nm pitch; with 8 tiers, ~100x lower cost per GB; trade-off is diode leakage forcing ms refresh and DSA defect remapping.
note: EUV-free 10 nm-pitch stacked tiers; doubts: DSA defectivity, SIS diode rectification, diode-access leakage.

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.
why: Two-terminal low-mask crossbar with refresh-free retention, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: heater energy per row access, thermal crosstalk, ~100 ns cycle.
note: 1.5 eV activation gives ~1e14 on/off between 25 and 400 C; doubts: heater energy, thermal crosstalk, dielectric leakage when hot.

title: One global clock restores every cell: gated-diode charge-pump bistables
idea: Inverts 'refresh is done row by row by sense amps': each cell is a gated diode (large capacitance when inverted, small when depleted) tied to a shared plate clock and a diode to the supply; a stored '1' couples the clock strongly and is topped up each cycle while a '0' couples weakly and stays below the diode threshold, so one global clock refreshes billions of cells at once.
why: Lets cheap leaky TFT or poly cells work with no row refresh, sense-amp refresh path or refresh controller (fact 7), ~2 devices per cell in low-mask tiers, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: continuous clock power and margin between stable points.
note: Global clock tops up only stored 1s, letting leaky TFT cells skip row refresh; doubt: continuous clock power and bistable margins across billions of cells.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche read of a hundred-electron storage node
idea: Shrink the storage node to ~20 aF holding ~100 electrons and wire it as the bias of a SPAD-like junction. At read the junction is armed above breakdown for ~2 ns: a stored '1' tips it into avalanche (gain ~1e5) and a '0' does not, then an active quench resets it.
why: Poisson statistics need only N >= 36 electrons for 6-sigma discrimination, and kT/C noise on 20 aF is ~2 electrons rms. Storing 31,000 electrons is an artifact of bitline charge sharing, so the capacitor shrinks ~50x, deleting the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and 1-2 patterning layers (fact 4).
note: Shrinks storage node ~50x, but retention scales with C and avalanche dark counts/variability threaten read fidelity.

title: Partial-charge sip read makes DRAM sensing non-destructive
idea: A tightly controlled subthreshold wordline pulse lets only ~3% of the cell charge (~450 e-) leak into a 0.2 fF local sense node; kT/C charge noise there is ~6 e-, so 450 e- is a >20 sigma signal (~0.36 V). The cell keeps 97% of its charge, so nothing is restored and only the addressed 64 B is sensed; normal refresh tops cells up.
why: Kills destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): per-useful-bit read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also removes row-activation hammer stress.
note: Subthreshold partial read gives non-destructive 64B access; needs ~0.2 fF local sense nodes and precise sip control across Vt spread.

title: Vertical charge-coupled columns store packets without access transistors
idea: Deposit a 3D-NAND-like gate stack around a single-crystal or recrystallized channel and clock the gate tiers in three phases to shift charge packets up the column to one sense node at the top, so 128 bits share one transistor and no capacitor.
