why: Leakage physics: a buried potential well loses charge only by thermal generation, far below a transistor off-state tail (fact 3), and removing the per-cell capacitor sidesteps the charge wall (fact 1); a 128-deep shift at ~1 ns per step keeps access near DRAM class while density follows tier count.
note: 128 bits per sense node with no capacitor; doubts: transfer inefficiency in poly channels, shift energy and serial latency.

title: Vertical charge-coupled strings store 64 bits per pillar without capacitors
idea: A bit is just a charge packet and needs only a potential well, not a capacitor plus transistor. Use NAND-like vertical pillars whose tiered gates clock 3-phase wells that shift packets to one sense amplifier at the pillar top: 192 tiers give 64 bits per pillar at 60 nm pitch.
why: ~56 nm2/bit (~15x today) with one contact per 64 bits; deletes per-cell capacitor dielectric (Zr/Hf), tungsten contacts and EUV. Transfer inefficiency and serial latency are the risks.
note: Capacitorless vertical CCD shift strings give ~15x density; poly-channel leakage, transfer loss over 64 shifts and serial latency are doubts.

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.
why: 8-16 stacked BEOL crossbar layers at 4F^2 with 2-3 masks each could approach ~100x cheaper per GB; trades latency (us tile decode), energy and endurance.
note: Decoding summed currents needs high ADC precision against IR drop; resistive endurance not DRAM-class.

title: Vertical 3D charge-coupled shift-register memory with one regenerator per string
idea: Po: the bit is a rumor passed down a line. Store charge packets in potential wells along a tall vertical channel with dozens of stacked gate layers (3D NAND-like tiers clocked as a CCD); packets shift up and down and only the end-of-string regenerating sense amp restores them, so refresh is the shifting itself, with no per-bit capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: reuses 3D NAND tier deposition (no EUV per tier, density scales with tier count); access becomes 100 ns-1 us block access, suited to tensor streams.
note: 3D NAND tiers clocked as a CCD avoid per-bit transistors; poly-Si transfer efficiency, dark current and serial access are doubts.

title: Origami artist: roll one flat DRAM membrane into twenty tiers
idea: An origami artist turns a flat sheet into volume. Pattern one 2D cell array on a strained bilayer nanomembrane (e.g., SiN/SiGe) over a sacrificial layer; on release, built-in strain rolls it into a tight Swiss roll of ~20 turns, so one 2D lithography pass yields 20 tiers, with wordlines running along the roll and contacted at its edge.
why: Gets 3D density (fact 2) from 2D lithography, avoiding 26-tier stack deposition and deep etch; litho cost per bit falls ~1/N with N turns. Speculative: turn-to-turn registration, heat removal, edge contacts.
note: 20 tiers from one 2D pass; turn registration, edge contacts and heat removal are unsolved.

title: Swiss-roll DRAM: self-rolling nanomembrane turns one planar array into 50 tiers
idea: Scale jump from meter-scale battery jelly-rolls down to microns: fabricate a planar oxide-semiconductor 1T1C array on a pre-strained SiNx/SiNx bilayer, undercut it, and let the strain roll it into a ~10-um tube of ~50 windings; radial vias are electroplated afterwards through windows that line up after rolling. One lithography pass yields ~50 stacked tiers.
why: Attacks 3D's need for 26+ tiers and the litho cost of each tier (facts 2, 4): tier count comes from mechanics rather than deposition and etch loops, claiming ~20-50x bits per litho layer.
note: Tiers from strain rolling, one litho pass; doubt: inter-winding vias and array yield after rolling.

title: Optane's crosspoint kept, PCM swapped for selector-gated capacitor
idea: Optane died largely on cost and PCM endurance, but its stacked crosspoint and OTS selector worked. Place a tiny MIM capacitor in series with the OTS at each crosspoint: the selector's threshold snap acts as a transistor-free access device, turning the array into a refreshed 4F2 multi-deck DRAM.
why: 4F2 per deck with stackable decks and no lateral transistor (Fact 2); reuses idle chalcogenide PVD tooling. Risk: OTS sub-threshold leakage must reach ~fA.
note: Transistor-free multi-deck DRAM; OTS off-leakage needs fA-level, orders below demonstrated, and holding-current behavior complicates writes.

title: Fairchild CCD memory reborn as vertical IGZO buried-channel CCD
idea: 1970s CCD memories died from serial access and silicon dark current that filled potential wells within ms when hot. Stack 64-128 gate tiers 3D-NAND-style around a vertical IGZO channel, store electron packets under alternate gates and shift a few stages to a top sense node. IGZO has no holes to invert the channel and a ~3.1 eV gap, so thermal generation stays negligible at 125 C and packets last seconds or more.
why: 3D DRAM with no capacitor and no per-tier transistor (Fact 2), ~10x bits per litho layer; retention far beyond 64 ms even at 125 C.
note: Capacitorless 3D DRAM: packets shift along tiers; doubt is IGZO charge-transfer efficiency with traps and serial latency.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.
why: Transistor-free, stackable 4F2 crosspoint DRAM (attacks the 3D DRAM blocker and litho cost). Because drift makes leakage fall over time instead of sitting at a fixed tail, refresh is claimed to be ~10x longer than in half-select-limited crosspoint designs.
note: Drift-as-feature is clever, but OTS off-leakage sits ~1e6x above fA retention needs; stackable transistorless DRAM if solved.

title: Snapback counting reads N stacked threshold cells per crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: Optane died partly because each extra deck needed its own lithography and decoders, so cost never scaled past two decks. Fix: deposit 8 chalcogenide threshold-switching memory layers in series at every crosspoint, pattern them with one etch, and engineer a different threshold window for each layer. One voltage ramp per pillar is read by counting and timing the snapback current spikes, whose pattern encodes all 8 states.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 bits per 4F^2 crosspoint vs 1 bit per 6F^2 is ~12x density, with one patterning step and one decoder set shared by all 8 layers, so decks no longer multiply masks.
note: 8 OTS layers per crosspoint with one etch could give ~12x density; doubt: Vth variability across 8 windows, read disturb, endurance.

title: Zettacore redox molecules: eight built-in reference levels per cell
idea: Failure mined: Zettacore's porphyrin molecular memory stored charge in discrete oxidation states but died on CMOS process heat and slow voltammetric reads. Fix: after the 400 C steps, graft thermally robust ferrocene/porphyrin mixtures with 7 redox couples onto a nanoporous TiN electrode. The sense amp's reference ladder is a reference electrode coated with the same molecules, so the potential plateaus self-calibrate and each cell stores 3 bits.
why: 10x at the same cost: 3 bits per cell x a crosspoint-compatible 4F^2 footprint (the porous electrode supplies ~50 fF-equivalent charge) x fewer reference generators = ~9-12x vs 1 bit per 6F^2. The molecules cost pennies per wafer.
note: Multi-redox molecules self-calibrate 3-bit levels; thermal budget, kinetics and endurance are major doubts.

title: Plasma-display memory effect: global sustain waveform replaces refresh and transistors
idea: Failure mined: plasma displays held each pixel's state as wall charge under a global AC sustain waveform, with only row and column drivers and no per-pixel transistor, and lost to LCD and OLED on power. Fix: each crosspoint cell pairs a thin threshold switch with a small capacitor in a hysteresis loop. A global sustain clock re-pumps every 1 cell while 0 cells never fire, and coincident row/column pulses set or clear individual cells.
why: 10x at the same cost: no access transistor, refresh controller or refresh bandwidth. 4F^2 cells in 4 self-aligned decks sharing lines (~6x) x periphery shrinking to ~20% (~1.6x) = ~10x.
note: Plasma-style global sustain removes access transistor and refresh; selector endurance under constant sustain firing and read path are the doubts.

title: Charge-injection-device cells: two-gate X-Y charge storage with non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: GE's charge-injection device (CID) imager lost to CCDs, yet it had an X-Y addressed, transistor-free pixel of two coupled MOS gates, read non-destructively by moving charge between the gates and sensing the column. Fix: use CID pairs as memory cells, with the row gate and column gate overlapping one storage well. A write injects charge; a read shifts it under the column gate and back, so the charge never leaves the well and can be re-read for multi-level sensing.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistor-free ~4F^2 cell (1.5x) x 3 bits per well from averaged non-destructive re-reads (3x) x no restore and much less periphery (~2x) = ~9-10x, using planar CMOS-image-sensor processing.
note: Transistor-free X-Y well with nondestructive re-reads; doubt: thermal generation fills wells fast and column signal is tiny.

title: ZettaCore's molecular redox storage repurposed as a charge-multiplying capacitor coating
idea: ZettaCore stored charge in porphyrin redox molecules on silicon but died on the 400C BEOL thermal budget. Graft thermally stable inorganic redox clusters (polyoxometalates) inside each 3D DRAM capacitor. Each cluster stores several electrons at a fixed potential, adding pseudocapacitance on top of the dielectric's.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-10x charge per um2 lets 3D tiers use short, low-AR capacitors (fact 2).
note: Redox clusters multiply charge per area; doubt: ns-scale Faradaic kinetics, retention, and endurance.

title: Josephson-era missing memory: 77 K thin-oxide 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: IBM's Josephson program (cancelled 1983) and later cryogenic computing stalled for lack of dense, cheap cold memory. At 77 K leakage collapses, so a 3D NAND-style vertical string with a 1.5-2 nm direct-tunneling oxide instead of ~7 nm Fowler-Nordheim oxide programs at ~3-5 V in tens of ns, suffers little hot-carrier wear and holds charge for hours.
why: Meets 100x: NAND cost structure (~$0.03-0.08/GB) with near-DRAM write speed, refresh-free hours retention and ~1e12-class endurance. Trade: liquid-nitrogen cooling (~10-15% facility overhead).
note: NAND cost with near-DRAM writes; doubt: direct tunneling through 2 nm oxide is temperature-insensitive, so hours retention is unlikely.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D antifuse stack made rewritable with selector-charged capacitors
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D poly-diode antifuse memory (bought by SanDisk in 2005) stacked cheaply at ~4 masks per layer but died for being write-once. Keep the stacked poly pillar process and swap the antifuse for a small planar MIM capacitor charged through a bidirectional punch-through n-p-n selector, giving 1S1C dynamic cells with unlimited endurance, refreshed like DRAM.
why: Meets 100x: no access transistor, no high-AR capacitor, 8-16 DUV decks; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: selector leakage forces ms-scale refresh, higher refresh power, thin sense margin.
note: No transistor per bit, ~$0.1/GB; poly punch-through selector leakage and half-select disturb likely kill retention.

title: Kovio's liquid-silicon ink printed into 32 cheap gain-cell tiers
idea: Kovio printed silicon RFID from liquid cyclopentasilane and folded in 2014 on a tiny market and hard-to-handle pyrophoric ink. Inside a sealed inert coater module, spin 20 nm silicon films from ink, crystallize only the top film with a nanosecond laser, and stack 32 tiers of poly-Si 2T gain cells, each tier patterned by one imprint.
why: Meets 100x: each tier costs a spin, a laser scan and one imprint (~$5-10/wafer) instead of epitaxy or transfer; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: grain-boundary leakage forces ms refresh and defect mapping.
note: Spin-on Si tiers at ~$5-10/wafer each; grain-boundary leakage and ms refresh likely erode DRAM-class value.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.
why: Meets 100x: tiers are just thin depositions, writes are fast direct tunneling (~10s of ns), retention minutes to hours; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: 3x cell redundancy, calibration time, variability.
note: Thin-film tiers with no capacitor could hit ~$0.1/GB; doubt: grain threshold scatter despite write-verify and 3x redundancy.

title: Redox pseudocapacitor nanocell replaces 70:1 pillar with planar charge sponge
idea: Effect walk: Faradaic surface redox (pseudocapacitance). Replace the dielectric capacitor with a 5-nm hydrous RuO2 or Ti3C2 MXene film against a nanometre solid proton conductor; fast surface redox stores ~100-1000 uF/cm2 versus ~7 uF/cm2 for ZrO2, so a flat 30x30 nm pad holds ~4-5 fF at 0.5 V.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) with no AR 60-75 etch, removing the deep-etch/deposition module (~30-50% of capacitor cost); risks are self-discharge and whether surface redox keeps up at ns timescales.
note: Planar 4-5 fF pad removes the pillar; pseudocap kinetics are ms-scale and self-discharge is high.

title: Room-temperature single-electron electrometer at every vertical bitline foot
idea: Coulomb blockade: a sub-3 nm silicon island single-electron transistor, formed by self-limiting fin oxidation, sits at the base of each vertical bitline as a charge electrometer that can resolve ~10 electrons. Lateral 3D tier capacitors can then hold 0.2 fF instead of 5 fF, because the read no longer depends on charge-sharing against a large bitline capacitance.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) that blocks thin 3D tiers (fact 2); claim 20x smaller Cs, so planar tier capacitors become viable.
note: RT Coulomb-blockade readout could cut Cs 20x; doubt: sub-3 nm island variability and offset charge across billions of bitlines.

title: Accordion-folded single membrane becomes 26 tiers of crystalline cells
idea: Process one planar single-crystal membrane (SOI device layer) with lateral access transistors in a strip pattern, release it, then fold it accordion-style like a road map using prestressed hinge lines. N folds yield N tiers that all came from one high-quality planar process.
why: Fact 2: gives 3D DRAM single-crystal lateral transistors for every tier while using only planar processing once. Folding replaces 26x deposition/etch loops.
note: Folding gives tiers but no dense inter-tier contacts or nm alignment; micron tier pitch caps density.

title: Gen-10.5 display-glass panels stacked with twenty tiers of oxide-TFT DRAM
idea: Ideal: memory sold like window glass. Closest: use Gen-10.5 display lines (~9.9 m2 panels) to build 2T0C/1T1C tiers from In-free ZnSnO TFTs, Mo/Al lines and planar Al2O3/TiO2 caps (TFT off-current ~1e-21 A/um makes small caps adequate), 4-5 masks per tier with panel nanoimprint at F~0.25 um, 20 tiers stacked at <=350 C.
why: 100x: panel processing ~$25/m2 per tier vs ~$150k/m2 for leading DRAM wafers; at ~0.5 um2/bit (~250 GB/m2/tier) x 20 tiers = 5 TB/m2 for ~$500 -> ~$0.1/GB vs ~$10/GB today. Trades latency (100-300 ns), volume and power; zero EUV, W, Hf, He.
note: Display-line tiers could cut slow-tier $/GB ~10x; doubts: 20-tier yield, panel nanoimprint overlay, 100-300 ns latency.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift strings: memory without per-bit transistors
idea: Ideal: memory with no transistor, capacitor or contact per bit. Closest: in a 3D-NAND-like stack, clock tier wordlines three-phase so charge packets move along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel like a CCD; each string is a shift register read by one sense amp at its foot, with a regeneration stage every ~32 tiers to cancel transfer loss.
why: 100x: deletes the cell capacitor, contacts and leakage tail (Facts 1-3), uses only Si/O/N/Mo, and scales density with tier count at ~3D-NAND cost (~$0.05/GB). Trades serial access (~100-300 ns per 64-stage shift, hidden by bank interleaving) and charge-transfer efficiency.
note: Charge-transfer efficiency in trap-rich amorphous oxide channels is the killer doubt.

title: Ion-beam ripple self-patterning writes wafer-wide nanoline arrays without masks
idea: Ideal: line arrays that appear by themselves under a flood beam. Closest: off-normal low-energy Ar+ sputtering of an a-Si or metal hard-mask film spontaneously forms Bradley-Harper ripples at 20-40 nm wavelength, phase-locked by a coarse pre-pattern; transfer them as wordline/bitline gratings and repeat rotated 90 degrees for the crossing grid.
why: 100x: pattern formation costs one broad-beam ion-source step (tens of $k tooling) instead of SAQP/EUV, cutting array patterning per layer >50x and enabling ~$0.1/GB in multi-tier stacks; trades long-range order and line-edge roughness.
note: Maskless self-organized gratings could slash patterning cost; long-range order and LER are far from DRAM specs.

title: Vertical oxide CCD string: transistor-less 3D charge-shift memory
idea: Etch one high-aspect-ratio hole through 128-256 alternating W/Mo and SiO2 word planes (the same module as 3D NAND), and line it with a thin gate oxide and an ALD IGZO/IGO channel. Clock planes in 4 phases (2 gates per bit): each bit is a packet of ~1,000-5,000 electrons in an accumulation well. Si CCDs lose stored charge to thermal generation (dark current); wide-gap IGZO generates essentially no carriers, so packets hold, limited only by inter-well barriers and gate leakage. Reading shifts packets out of the top of the string into a charge-transfer sense amp (B1-04) on bonded periphery, and data recirculates to the bottom: a delay-line memory with 32-64-bit strings and thousands of parallel holes per line access. Planes are segmented into small blocks to keep plane RC at ~1 ns per phase.
why: 4.2-8.3x 1b density (1.85-3.7 Gb/mm2 at 128-256 planes) with zero per-bit devices; streaming read energy 17-67 fJ/bit; but access is serial (32-128 ns worst-case to a given bit).
note: Transistor-less charge-shift strings on NAND tooling; doubts: IGZO trap states hurting transfer efficiency, and serial access latency.

title: Nanogap (vacuum/air) tunnel-barrier floating node: flash-like retention without oxide wear
idea: The floating metal node (TiN or W, anchored on dielectric on one side) faces a write electrode across a 2.5-4 nm gap. The gap is made by removing an ALD sacrificial layer (carbon or Al2O3) and then sealed, like BEOL air-gaps or NASA's nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors, which work in air because the gap is far below the ~70 nm mean free path. The node is the gate of an IGZO or Si read transistor (2T-like gain cell), so the read is non-destructive. Writing uses field emission at a few V/nm (field enhancement 2-3 at edges); holding relies on the exponential non-linearity of tunnelling. Charge never passes through a solid dielectric, so there are no trap generation, SILC or charge-to-breakdown limits, the mechanisms that cap flash endurance at ~1e5. Low-work-function coatings (LaB6-class, 2.7 eV) cut write voltage, but even plain TiN (4.5 eV) works at 8 V.
why: [SPECULATIVE] A non-volatile, refresh-free DRAM-class gain cell: retention 3.7e4 s (2.5 nm gap, 2.7 eV) to >1e8 s (3 nm), writes in 0.4-40 ns. Endurance is not set by oxide damage, with a target of >=1e12.
note: Charge never crosses a solid dielectric, removing oxide-wear endurance limits; doubt: sealing reproducible 2.5-4 nm gaps given exponential gap sensitivity.

title: Eliminate linear KV growth with holographic superposed token memory
idea: Bind each old token's key/value pair to a random unit-phase vector and add it into a fixed-size complex matrix (holographic reduced representation); the newest N tokens stay exact and older ones are retrieved approximately by unbinding.
why: KV memory becomes O(1) in context length beyond a window: 10-100x savings for million-token contexts.
note: Effectively fast-weight/linear-attention memory; HRR capacity scales with dimension, so exact recall of millions of tokens is doubtful.

title: Transformer page-fault oracle prefetches from NVMe
idea: Worsen: let pages fault in one at a time from storage. Flip: a small sequence model trained on each application's fault traces predicts the next 1,000 pages about 200 us ahead and streams them from NVMe into a DRAM cache sized at 1% of the dataset.
why: Cost: 100x smaller DRAM for a given dataset when the learned predictor hits over 99%; trades misprediction stalls.
note: If >99% hit 200 us ahead held, DRAM could be ~1% of dataset; doubt: irregular workloads rarely predictable at that accuracy.

title: Idle tensor cores regenerate old-context KV from token IDs
idea: This adds zero masks. Decode is memory-bound, with tensor cores ~70% idle. For context older than a horizon, the server keeps only 4-byte token IDs plus a mid-layer checkpoint every N layers, and recomputes K/V in the idle compute slots of each decode step. Nanosecond-scale compute replaces seconds-scale storage.
why: Old-context KV bytes drop 50-500x for long contexts, paid for by compute that was otherwise idle.
note: Recomputing old-context K/V every decode step far exceeds idle compute; hidden-state checkpoints can exceed GQA KV size.

title: Zn: MgZnO/ZnO quantum-well charge bucket under a sense channel
idea: Deposit a ZnO quantum well clad by Mg0.3Zn0.7O barriers (conduction-band offset ~0.4-0.6 eV) beneath a thin oxide read channel; electrons parked in the well screen the channel and shift its threshold, so retention comes from a band offset rather than a thick capacitor dielectric.
why: Replaces the capacitor (facts 1, 2) with a low-temperature, BEOL-stackable heterostructure of abundant Zn and Mg for many 3D tiers; defect-assisted leakage out of the well is the risk.
note: BEOL-stackable capacitorless tiers would multiply density, but a 0.5 eV offset gives only ~ms thermionic retention.

title: Seashell spiral: logarithmically spaced KV retention with merged summaries
idea: Nautilus chambers grow geometrically: keep every token of the last 256, every 2nd from 256-1k, every 4th from 1k-4k and so on, folding dropped tokens' KV into their surviving neighbour by attention-weighted averaging, so KV grows O(log n). Pure software, nothing fabricated.
why: Long-context KV becomes O(log n) instead of O(n): a 1M-token context fits in roughly 20k tokens of KV.
note: O(log n) KV would shrink 1M contexts ~50x; doubt: merging old tokens badly hurts retrieval and needle tasks.

title: Vaccine advance market commitment for first manufacturable 3D DRAM
idea: Adapted from Gavi's pneumococcal vaccine AMC: buyers jointly pledge to purchase a set volume (e.g., 2 EB) at a premium price from whichever supplier first ships 3D DRAM that meets density, endurance and 10-100 ns specs. The premium tapers as volume grows.
why: Guarantees a market for the risky first 3D fab and pulls forward the 26+ tier cell (Fact 2), steering private R&D at a density step change (density, cost per bit).
note: AMC shifts first-mover risk for 3D DRAM; effect on timing depends on pledge size.

title: Game-cartridge model distribution: sealed ROM weight modules sold per version
idea: Copy the NES/Game Boy cartridge business: model vendors ship each release as a sealed, keyed module of wide-parallel mask-ROM dies that plugs into a standard high-bandwidth slot on inference servers. Upgrades are cartridge swaps, the weight license rides with the hardware, and retired cartridges flow to a secondary market for edge and enterprise boxes.
why: Moves static-weight storage, 40-70% of DRAM bought for inference fleets, out of the scarce DRAM market into mask-ROM made on depreciated fabs; also keeps plaintext weights out of DRAM.
note: Swappable sealed mask-ROM weight modules; model churn and ROM bandwidth are doubts.

title: Trilogy wafer-scale fixed with bondable patch-tile repair sites
idea: Gene Amdahl's Trilogy failed because wafer-scale defects could not be fixed after the wafer was built. Lay out a wafer-scale DRAM slab with a grid of empty landing sites over each region. After test, or later in a service depot, a known-good DRAM tile is bonded over any dead region and the router remaps it.
why: Wafer-scale economics for packaging and I/O energy (facts 5, 6) without the yield risk. The slab stays repairable over a 10-year life.

title: Tier-RAID for 3D DRAM tolerates weak lateral transistors
idea: Ideal: 3D DRAM where bad tiers do not matter. Closest: stack 36 tiers of which 4 are parity tiers, stripe each logical row across tiers under an erasure code, and let tiers whose lateral transistors show 100x worse leakage tails be declared erased between refreshes rather than refreshed faster.
why: Fact 2: relaxes the lateral-transistor specs that block 3D manufacturability and may pull 3D break-even earlier at ~11% overhead.
note: Erasure-coded tiers relax lateral-transistor tail specs; needs 3D DRAM to prove beyond simulation.

title: Gain-cell shadow-row tier replaces the sense-amp latch as row buffer
idea: Substitute the single sense-amp row buffer per bank with an extra top tier of nondestructive 3T oxide-semiconductor gain cells over each sub-array holding 8-16 'shadow rows'; an activated row is copied once into a shadow, and later hits and re-opens read the shadow without re-activating or re-restoring the DRAM row.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): est. 3-5x fewer activations on server traces, cutting ACT energy and aggressor counts; the tier is stacked, not added to footprint (~5% cost).

title: Substitute investor capital with customer-prepaid ten-year bit-supply notes
idea: Hyperscalers prepay for guaranteed exabits per year through a tradable 'bit-supply note' tied to one specific fab line, priced cost-plus with an index; the fab's capital comes from those who most fear the shortage.
why: Capital intensity: moves $15B+ of risk off the memory maker's balance sheet, shortens time-to-decision, and damps the boom-bust underinvestment behind the 4x price spike.

title: Substitute interposer wiring with glass-core millimetre unterminated memory links
idea: Place LPDDR-class dies within 1 mm of the processor on a glass-core panel substrate with 2 um lines, and replace terminated DDR signaling with unterminated 0.2 V-swing CMOS links that behave like on-die wires; panel glass replaces silicon interposers.
why: Constraint: I/O energy falls from ~5-10 to ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit (>=10x on the I/O share); capital: 510x515 mm glass panels cost a fraction of silicon interposers and need no TSVs.

title: Swap local phone LPDDR for pooled edge DRAM for background apps
idea: Substitute on-device RAM with a shared edge pool. Phones freeze background apps and stream their compressed process images to edge-cloud DRAM over 5G and Wi-Fi, then restore them lazily through page-fault streaming. Statistical multiplexing lets one edge GB serve many phones.
why: Phones are roughly a third of DRAM bits and carry 8-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm. Phones could ship with 30-50% less LPDDR, with a much smaller pooled amount at the edge.
note: Phones big bit share; restore latency over radio is the doubt.

title: Swap DRAM-resident frozen weights for via-programmed 3D ROM chiplets
idea: Substitute rewritable DRAM with mask-programmed vertical ROM strings, NAND-like stacks whose bits are set by via or implant and never written, for open-weight models that stay frozen for a year. The chiplets are built on a mature U.S. line and swapped like cartridges when the model is upgraded.
why: No capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, made on domestic mature-node capital. Frees HBM for KV cache. The main risk is the model becoming obsolete, not physics.

title: Bonded SRAM sector buffers fused with segmented wordlines
idea: Hybrid-bond a thin SRAM/logic layer so each 1 Kb wordline segment has its own SRAM sector buffer at the bond site; an activate opens only one 64-bit segment and the buffer serves column hits, merging row buffer, cache and wordline segmentation.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): activation energy per useful bit drops ~8-10x (about 5.9 to ~0.7 pJ); fewer full-row activations also lowers hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Error-bounded scientific compression built into the memory controller
idea: Combine ZFP/SZ-style transform coding with the memory controller: pages tagged approximate-OK (simulation fields, activations, gradients) are stored at fixed rates of 8-16 bits per float with guaranteed absolute error bounds, using fixed-rate blocks so random access stays O(1).
why: 2-4x capacity for floating-point working sets that tolerate bounded error.
note: ZFP fixed-rate in controller; gains limited to error-tolerant FP data.

title: LED-lithography coarse wiring paired with ultra-wide slow low-swing bus
idea: Combine 365 nm UV-LED array exposure (solid-state: no Hg-Ar/Xe lamp, no neon excimer), which only patterns ~2-5 um lines, with an interface designed for that limit: 8-16k parallel interposer wires at 0.5-1 Gb/s, 100-150 mV swing, no SerDes or DLL, delivering TB/s from coarse wiring.
why: Data movement and capital: ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, with interposers made in PCB-class fabs; the constraint becomes the design driver.
note: Design the interface to 2-5 um LED-litho rules; wide-slow is known but the constraint pairing is sensible.

title: Combinatorial coupon line for 100x faster process learning
idea: Minify experiments to 25 mm coupons with gradient deposition and run 1000 process splits per week on a high-throughput pilot line, so new-cell development needs a $50M line, not a full fab.
why: Development time and capital: compresses 3-5 year node learning toward 1 year and lowers entry cost for US newcomers.

title: Open replaceable memory chiplet standard tied to procurement
idea: MAGNIFY interchangeability: an open mechanical and electrical spec for socketed memory chiplets (UCIe-style), required in federally funded AI clusters, so any vendor's memory can be swapped.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply resilience: new domestic memory makers can sell into installed systems; repair beats scrap.
note: Procurement-backed open socket spec; adoption and performance cost of sockets.

title: Eliminate retention requirements: refresh-free banks for short-lived AI tensors
idea: The compiler tags tensors that live <1 ms (activations, pipeline gradients, short-request KV) into ephemeral banks built with ~1 fF low-aspect capacitors on 4x shorter bitlines at 0.6 V, never refreshed; the controller tracks age and copies out anything nearing its retention limit.
why: Removes the high-AR capacitor (PFAS etch, Zr) and refresh for those banks; ~5x lower bitline C times ~2.8x lower V2 gives >10x lower energy per access.

title: Eliminate energy-blind memory buying: pJ-per-bit indexed offtake contracts
idea: A hyperscaler and DOE consortium guarantees 7-year premium offtake for memory measured at <=0.5 pJ per useful bit under a public JEDEC-style energy test, with CHIPS grants for converting U.S. lines to such products.
why: Makes 10x-energy designs bankable; each 10x cut trims data-center power, grid build-out and cooling water.

title: Eliminate per-tier perfection: vertical RAID parity tier in monolithic stacks
idea: In a monolithic stack of N memory tiers built at <=400 C, one tier in every 8 holds XOR parity for the vertical column of cells. A tier region lost to a deposition defect, crack or later failure is rebuilt from the other tiers on read, so stack yield no longer falls as Y^N.
why: Breaks the compound-yield barrier that makes 26+ tier stacks uneconomic (fact 2); 12.5% overhead buys tolerance of whole-tier defect regions.
note: Directly attacks the Y^N compound-yield wall for monolithic 3D DRAM.

title: Micro-sense: one local amplifier per 16 cells
idea: Reverse the cell-to-amplifier ratio: instead of ~500 cells on a long bitline per sense amp, place a 3-4 transistor local preamp (CMOS under array) under every 16-cell local bitline, so bitline capacitance drops from ~50 fF to ~3 fF. The transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) rises from ~0.1 to ~0.6, so a cell stays readable after losing far more of its charge.
why: Retention margin (facts 1, 3): tolerating 3-5x more charge loss lengthens refresh 3-5x at the same leakage, or permits a ~2 fF capacitor instead of chasing AR 115.
note: Area and offset of tiny preamps per 16 cells under array.

title: Customer-owned tool fleet leased to the memory fab
idea: Reverse capital ownership: hyperscalers buy and own the scanners, etchers and deposition tools as a securitized asset pool and lease them to a fab operator under take-or-pay output contracts.
why: Capital intensity: moves ~55% depreciation off the memory maker's books, cuts its cost of capital and lets new U.S. entrants start with near-zero tool capex.

title: Carousel DRAM: memory broadcasts everything, consumers just listen
idea: Reverse request/response: in carousel mode the DRAM runs a fixed scan that reads every row in order and broadcasts it on a wide unidirectional bus, and consumers (e.g. LLM decode cores that read the same weights in the same order every token) latch what they need. The scan read restores each row, so separate refresh disappears, and there is no command/address bus or random activation; a small conventional port handles writes.
why: Attacks overfetch and refresh (facts 3, 5, 8): 100% row utilisation instead of ~1/128, refresh energy and bandwidth folded into useful reads, CA pins and controller removed; estimated 3-5x lower pJ per useful bit for weight streaming.
note: Echoes the VRAM serial-access port; fixed order breaks for MoE and multi-model.

title: Memory-centric motherboard: compute cartridges plug into memory
idea: Reverse socket roles: the board is a mesh of DRAM modules and CXL/optical switches, and CPUs and accelerators are pluggable cartridges that attach to the memory regions they need. Memory stays installed for 8-10 years while compute is refreshed every 2.
why: Raises usable supply by ending DRAM disposal at each server refresh and recovering ~25-40% stranded DRAM, effectively 1.5-2x more usable bits from the same production.

title: Double-sided glass interposer: memory below, compute above
idea: Flip the interposer into a sandwich: make through-glass vias in photostructurable glass by UV exposure, bake and HF etch, bond DRAM dies to the underside and compute to the top directly above them, so the memory path is a 100-200 um vertical via instead of millimetres of lateral wire.
why: Facts 5 and 6: lateral interposer wires become short verticals (~0.2 pJ/bit), and glass is cheaper than a silicon interposer and needs only basic litho and wet etch.

title: Discarding and recovering: JEDEC managed-DRAM class without on-die repair
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: a new JEDEC 'managed DRAM' class removes laser/e-fuse repair banks, redundancy muxes and most wafer-sort retention testing from the die; the host discovers bad rows and columns at boot with a BIST march, discards them and recovers capacity from 5-10% over-provisioning, as NAND does with bad blocks.
why: 100x enabler: repair periphery (~5% of die) and test (~10-15% of cost) go away, and arrays can be built in low-cost, defect-tolerant processes that are unshippable today; trade-offs: capacity varies per part and boot-time mapping is required.

title: Liquid-nitrogen floating-body tiers for a pooled cryogenic memory
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter changes: run a stacked 1T floating-body array at 77 K inside an LN2-immersed rack-level memory pool, where SRH generation and GIDL fall by ~10^6-10^8. Stored hole states then persist for minutes and steeper subthreshold slopes allow ~0.5 V operation.
why: Fact 3 and 10: refresh effectively disappears and CV2 energy falls ~4x; capacitorless ~4F2 cells, provided cooling overhead stays below the energy saved.

title: Refresh doubles as scrub via per-subarray syndrome engines
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a small shared syndrome/correct engine on each subarray sense-amp stripe checks every row while it sits in the sense amps during its refresh activation and writes corrected bits back before precharge.
why: Every row is scrubbed every refresh window (vs DDR5 ECS ~once per 24 h, >1000x more often), so single-bit errors never accumulate into uncorrectable doubles; tolerates ~100x weaker cells for ~2-3% area.

title: Composite: new-die cache fronts reclaimed DDR4 dies on CXL modules
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: a CXL module pairs one new DDR5 die as a write-back cache with seven reclaimed DDR4 dies, run by an existing controller re-spun with one changed metal mask to add the caching and wear map.
why: Supply: converts recycled dies into near-new performance capacity, cutting fresh-bit demand ~85% per module.

title: ISO-container memory tile: an open hybrid-bond array standard
idea: Standardize a memory container: a 1 Gb array tile with fixed footprint, fixed hybrid-bond pad map (sense-amp interface, power, test) and fixed timing protocol, so any maker's array tile bonds onto any vendor's base die, as ISO containers did for shipping.
why: Capital intensity and supply diversity (facts 4, 6): new array makers (oxide, 3D, legacy fabs) can enter without building periphery and I/O; claims faster capacity ramp and commodity tile pricing.
note: UCIe-like standard for bonded array tiles; adoption by incumbents is the hurdle.

title: Post-it tier: tiny 1 ms-retention cells for transient data
idea: A Post-it is cheap because it need not last; dedicate a 3D tier to 0.5 fF cells with ~1 ms retention on short bitlines for data whose lifetime is shorter than that (activations, in-flight KV, gradients), placed there by the compiler and never refreshed.
why: Capacitor wall, refresh and access energy (facts 1, 3, 8): ~10x smaller Cs and shorter lines cut switched charge ~10x with zero refresh; claims ~10x lower energy per access for transient traffic.
note: Compiler-placed refresh-free short-lived data is sound; related to approximate/eDRAM activation buffers.

title: LCD-fab panel interposers on Gen-8 display glass
idea: Display backplanes are made on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass at ≤350 C. Convert idle LCD/TFT lines to pattern multi-layer Cu RDL (2 um L/S) and through-glass vias on full panels, then cut the panels into HBM interposers. Every step stays ≤350 C.
why: A panel has ~70x the area of a 300 mm wafer. Interposer cost per mm² could fall 5-10x, and CoWoS-class capacity could be added in existing display lines, including U.S. conversions.
note: Glass interposers widely pursued; LCD-line reuse is the twist.

title: Revival tournament: twelve forgotten storage elements on one common test chip
idea: Fund 12 revived storage elements (core, plated wire, bubble, parametron, CCD, Selectron and others) to a shared 1-Mb test vehicle with identical sense/IO periphery and one scorecard (fJ/bit, ns, F2, retention, endurance) on shared shuttle wafers, with kill-or-scale gates at 6 and 12 months and prize money for crossing DRAM-class thresholds.
why: Compares physics fairly at ~$2M per element instead of $100M+ per startup and compresses discovery time; attacks the capital and time chokepoints.
note: Common 1-Mb vehicle and scorecard for revived elements; $24M total exceeds demo budget.

title: Core-plane separation: universal 28-nm periphery die bonded to revived arrays
idea: Core memories separated the passive core plane from shared drive and sense electronics. Split every revived storage array (magnetic, mechanical, charge) from a standard 28-nm sense/IO die hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer on existing CIS-fab bonding lines, with a programmable sense front end (current, voltage, inductive, phase).
why: Periphery is ~49% of DRAM die (Fact 7); moving it to a cheap mature-node die makes arrays ~100% array and lets any exotic element reach a DDR/CXL interface without its own PHY.

title: Diode-matrix ROM reborn as hybrid-bonded via-programmed weight layer
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-matrix ROM: frozen base-model weights are encoded by the presence and size of vias (2-3 bits per via resistance class) in a mature-node ROM wafer hybrid-bonded under the accelerator, with one programmable via mask per model. Bitlines feed straight up into the MAC arrays.
why: Capacity/cost: weights (50-80% of inference memory) leave HBM, which is then sized for KV only; via-ROM at ~2F^2 per 2-3 bits on a 28 nm wafer has no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, roughly 5-10x lower cost per bit than DRAM.

title: Goodyear STARAN Associative Search for KV-Cache Recall In DRAM
idea: Revive the 1972 STARAN bit-serial associative array processor: add a 1-bit comparator and match latch to each DRAM sense amplifier so a query key is compared against every stored key in an open row in parallel, and only matching token addresses leave the chip.
why: Energy per useful access: attention retrieval moves only matched KV entries, 10-30x fewer bits off-chip; implemented as a small sense-amp addition on existing DRAM lines.
note: Sense-amp match logic is known PIM; attention needs similarity top-k, not exact key match.

title: Lease bits not chips: vendor-owned memory with cascade redeployment
idea: Inverts 'the buyer owns the DRAM': vendors keep title and rent capacity per GB-month, then pull returned modules down a cascade (AI training -> inference -> enterprise -> edge -> consumer), re-binning at each step.
why: Each die serves 2-3 lifetimes instead of one, raising usable supply ~1.5-2x over a decade from the same wafers and smoothing the vendor revenue cycle that drives under-investment.

title: JEDEC 'one-second class' standard unlocking low-barrier memory elements
idea: Standardize a memory class with 1 s retention at 85 C, >=1e16 endurance and mandatory on-die ECC scrub. Barrier height = ln(retention/attempt time) kT, so emerging elements (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM) can be designed at ~28 kT instead of 60 kT, trading unneeded retention for write energy and endurance.
why: Write energy and wear scale with barrier height, so halving it gives new storage physics a qualified path to fill DRAM sockets now, raising usable supply.

title: Fab-reject partial-good DRAM dies stitched by remapping base die
idea: Dies that fail one bank, speed bin or retention test are scrapped even though >90% of their cells work. Buy them at scrap price, stack 8-16 on a cheap logic base die that self-tests at boot and remaps at 1 KB granularity around bad regions, and sell the result as a slower seconds-grade memory tier.
why: Die cost near zero, package plus base die ~$0.1-0.3/GB, ~30-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades speed and density; supply ~5-10% of output.
note: Cheap slow tier; supply bounded at 5-10% of output.

title: Memory-as-a-lease with mandatory take-back keeps bits circulating
idea: Because DRAM bits do not wear out, transfer of ownership is the real waste mechanism. Manufacturers lease modules by GB-month with RFID-tracked serials and contractual take-back, then redeploy returned modules down a tier ladder (training to inference to enterprise to edge) over ~15 years.
why: Usable supply: triples service life per manufactured bit, multiplying cumulative supply ~2-3x for the same wafer starts.
note: Interface generation changes (DDR4 to DDR5) limit downstream redeployment.

title: Lego studs: open standard for array-to-periphery bonded interfaces
idea: Lego bricks from any box snap together because the stud is standardized. Publish an open, royalty-free 'memory stud' spec covering bond pitch, per-bitline-group pad maps, voltage domains, test hooks and known-good-die protocol, so array-only wafers from any fab can bond to periphery wafers from any foundry; tie CHIPS-style funding to compliance.
why: Capital and supply diversity: breaks the 3-vendor vertical integration, letting U.S. logic foundries and new array specialists each enter with roughly half the capex of a full DRAM fab.

title: Vending machine: tool vendors own tools, fab pays per wafer pass
idea: Random stimulus 'vending machine' (owner stocks it, you pay per item) -> lithography, etch and deposition OEMs own and maintain tools inside a new DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass, with uptime guarantees, backed by a federal loan guarantee pool.
why: Capital intensity (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) turns into variable cost. A U.S. entrant's upfront capex could fall ~50-60%, and OEMs gain recurring revenue.

title: Telephone switchboard: optical circuit switch re-patches memory sleds
idea: An operator plugging cords: a MEMS optical circuit switch at rack level connects any socket's CXL links to any memory sled, re-patched every few minutes by a scheduler, so stranded memory on one server becomes another's without packet-switch latency or buffering.
why: About 25% of datacenter DRAM is stranded; circuit-switched pooling recovers most of it at near direct-attach latency.
note: MEMS OCS re-patching CXL links recovers stranded DRAM without packet-switch latency; CXL-over-optics PHY and reconfiguration pauses are the doubt.

title: Morphological-box test chip: 10,000 storage-element combinations per wafer
idea: Box = {all six axes varied on purpose}: a standard periphery wafer carries 10,000 1-kbit tiles, and gradient sputtering, area-selective ALD and maskless e-beam give each tile its own medium, electrode, access device and anneal. On-chip BIST logs retention tails, endurance and disturb automatically, so the morphological box becomes a physical experiment that outputs a ranked Pareto map of combinations every month.
why: Cuts the learning cycle for new storage elements by ~100x and finds non-obvious medium/electrode pairs that single-material programs miss.
note: Combinatorial materials plus BIST is known art; per-tile processing on a periphery wafer strains a $1M budget.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells let dies refresh at true retention
idea: Box: standard cell x canary cells with a leakier access transistor made by one extra Vt-lowering implant mask x on-die canary sensing x per bank x Si x one mask. Canaries fail at ~1/4 of the weakest real cell's retention, so the die stretches its interval until canaries start failing, tracking temperature, voltage and aging live.
why: Replacing worst-case spec with live tracking typically allows 2-4x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) 50-75%.
note: Canary retention monitors known; tracking VRT tail cells is the doubt.

title: HBM stack RAID with a parity die and live rebuild
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: 12-high HBM stack | substrate: bulk | fab: standard]. One die of a 12-high stack holds XOR/RS parity across the other 11, so a die with dead TSVs, a failed bank or a hammer-corrupted row is reconstructed on the fly instead of scrapping the whole stack.
why: Fact 6: converts 20-30% stack yield loss into ~8% capacity overhead and ships stacks that fail today.

title: Segment-aligned ECC codewords enable 64-bit micro-activations
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: segmented local wordline | sense: local sense per 72-cell segment | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Only one 64+8-bit segment of a row is raised and the whole ECC codeword lives inside that segment, so small accesses keep full SECDED protection and hammer disturbance and counters are confined to segment neighbours.
why: Constraint/Fact 8: removes the ~128x page overfetch, ~10-30x lower activation energy per useful bit, and shrinks hammer exposure per access.

title: Advance market commitment for non-DRAM byte-addressable tiers
idea: Box[Owner=hyperscaler consortium x Finance=advance market commitment x Medium=any byte-addressable memory meeting latency and endurance specs x Channel=guaranteed purchase volume]: buyers commit a fixed purchase volume at a set price to any supplier that hits ~100 ns access and 10^15 endurance, like vaccine AMCs.
why: Pulls new memory technologies to volume; de-risks entrant fabs and diversifies supply away from DRAM.

title: Compiler-proven tensor lifetimes shorter than retention need zero refresh
idea: Po: data dies before it decays. In AI training, activations and gradients live ~1-10 ms between write and last read; the compiler proves each tensor's lifetime and places it in capacitorless floating-body memory with ~10 ms retention that is never refreshed, while long-lived weights go elsewhere.
why: Facts 1 and 3: lets a cheap, poor-retention capacitorless cell serve 40-60% of training memory with zero refresh energy.

title: Milestone prize for capacitorless 4F^2 cell meeting DRAM spec
idea: Po: the government bans capacitors. Fund a U.S. prize with staged payouts: $50M for a capacitorless 4F^2 cell holding 64 ms at 85 C on 300 mm wafers, $200M for a 1 Gb array at 1e15 endurance made in a domestic fab, with IP licensed to all U.S. makers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: pulls many capacitorless paths forward in parallel for a few hundred million dollars instead of a $15B fab.

title: Advance market commitment paying only for 10x-density, cost-parity DRAM
idea: Worse: subsidize fab floor space that just replicates 6F2 DRAM. Flip: a U.S. government plus hyperscaler buyers' club pre-commits to buy a fixed volume (e.g., 10 EB) at today's $/wafer-equivalent only from parts with >=10x bits/mm2 versus 1-gamma DRAM, paying milestone premiums for tier-yield results and nothing for raw capacity.
why: A pull incentive aimed exactly at the 10x-density, same-cost target that de-risks the 3-5 year, $15B bet (fact 4) for whichever 3D architecture wins, and anchors the output in U.S. fabs.

title: Right-to-reuse mandate: socketed memory plus module deposit refund
idea: Worse: solder all LPDDR to the board so the memory dies with the laptop or phone. Flip: require socketed CAMM2/LPCAMM-class modules in PCs and servers above a price threshold, plus a $2-5 per-module deposit refunded when modules reach certified refurbishers.
why: Moves recovered consumer memory from near zero to a majority of units, roughly doubling DRAM bit-life and cutting new-wafer demand; lowers capital and scarce-resource intensity per useful bit-year.

title: Advance market commitment buyers' club for refresh-free memory
idea: Worse: buy only today's DRAM so no one funds alternatives. Flip: hyperscalers and governments commit, vaccine-style, to buy a fixed volume (e.g. 1 EB) of DRAM-class memory with zero refresh power at a guaranteed price if delivered at spec by 2030.
why: Pulls private capital into refresh-free cells and de-risks entrants.

title: Biologist's DNA proofreading: early-warning margin reads before cells fail
idea: Cells repair DNA lesions before they become mutations. A background scrubber reads each row with the sense-amp reference deliberately shifted ~30% of signal toward the decayed level; rows whose ECC syndrome changes under the shifted read are flagged 'damaged' and refreshed now, while rows that stay clean have their own refresh period doubled step by step, up to 1 s.
why: Refresh is set by the worst row at the worst temperature; evidence-based per-row periods cut refresh operations 4-10x and catch variable-retention cells as they shift.

title: Lego standard: open array-to-periphery hybrid-bond interface
idea: A child snaps any brick onto any brick. Publish an open, royalty-free standard for the bonded interface between DRAM array wafers and CMOS periphery wafers (pad pitch, bitline mux ratio, sense-node electrical spec, test hooks) so array makers and logic fabs can mix and match.
why: Lets U.S. logic fabs supply periphery wafers and new array startups skip the 49% periphery design burden, lowering capital and entry barriers (facts 4, 7).

title: Biologist's mitochondrial cristae: internally folded lateral capacitor
idea: Mitochondria fold their membranes to multiply area. Make each 3D DRAM tier a stack of 4 SiGe sub-layers with alternating Ge content, then use a Ge-selective lateral recess to corrugate the capacitor cavity walls before depositing the electrode and dielectric.
why: ~3x capacitor area for the same lateral length, so the horizontal capacitor shrinks and tier pitch tightens (Facts 1, 2).

title: Accountant's frozen node: stop shrinking, depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: An accountant sees depreciation at ~55% of wafer cost while each shrink buys only 10-20%. Freeze lithography at today's node and win bits only by stacking (tiers, bonding) and design (refresh, periphery), running a paid-off copy-exact tool set for 15 years instead of 5 and financing fabs like toll roads.
why: Halving the depreciation share cuts wafer cost ~25-30%, more than a node shrink buys; copy-exact capacity with a fixed tool list builds faster (~2 years) and cheaper. Risk: rivals that keep shrinking; density must come from stacking.

title: Embargo engineer: BEOL-only memory tiers on existing U.S. logic lines
idea: With no front-end DRAM fab available, use only back-end tools that every mature logic fab already owns (PVD, PECVD, Cu damascene, <=400 C forming-gas anneal) to add 4-8 tiers of oxide-semiconductor 3T gain cells over finished 28-65 nm U.S. logic wafers, whose logic doubles as the periphery.
why: Converts underused U.S. mature-node BEOL capacity into memory with a ~$100-300M retrofit instead of a $15B fab, lifting U.S. manufacturability from 1-2% share. Risk: density and retention trail 1c DRAM, which is acceptable for embedded and near memory.

title: Commodities trader's DRAM bit futures to pre-sell fab output
idea: List an exchange-traded DRAM futures and options contract, settled on a standardized 16 Gb DDR5-equivalent bit index. New entrants can then sell 3-5 years of output forward and hedge it, and lenders can underwrite fabs on hedged revenue the way they underwrite LNG terminals.
why: Capital intensity: hedged revenue could cut the equity a $15B fab needs by ~30-40% and draw in infrastructure investors who avoid commodity price risk.
note: Liquidity and contract standardization are the doubts.

title: LN2-immersed memory pods with planar 0.5 fF capacitors, 100 tiers
idea: Design for a 77 K cryogenic computer: access-transistor leakage falls ~10^6x, so retention stops sizing the capacitor and, with 64-cell short bitlines, a flat 0.5 fF planar MIM capacitor suffices, making each tier a thin planar layer and 100-tier monolithic stacks practical. Ship the memory as liquid-nitrogen-immersed CXL pods beside the accelerator (nitrogen is abundant and cheap).
why: Removes the AR 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3) and clears the 26+ tier break-even for 3D (fact 2) with planar tiers; claim 5-10x bits per mm2, with cooling overhead paid only on low-dissipation memory pods.

title: PON burst-mode PHY: memory links that sleep between bursts
idea: Fiber-to-the-home ONUs transmit in bursts with receivers that lock in tens of ns. Give memory PHYs burst-mode clock-data recovery with short preambles and ~1-5 ns wake, so termination, clocks and CDR are fully off between transactions instead of idling.
why: Memory links average 20-40% utilization yet burn much of their power idle; burst mode makes link energy proportional to accesses, ~5-10x lower energy per access at low utilization.

title: Satellite scrub-per-refresh: ECC engines inside every sense-amp stripe
idea: Satellites crossing the South Atlantic Anomaly scrub memory faster than upsets can accumulate. Put a small SEC-DED engine in each subarray's sense-amp stripe, so every refresh of a row reads, corrects and writes back corrected data instead of re-amplifying whatever is there. Single flips are cleared every 64 ms, so two independent errors never pile up in one codeword.
why: Double errors from accumulation are what force worst-case cell specs. Correcting at every refresh allows ~10x higher raw single-bit error rates for the same uncorrectable rate, which accepts weaker capacitors and leakier tails at a few percent extra periphery (facts 1, 3).
note: Correct at every refresh to stop error accumulation; periphery area cost.

title: Tick-to-trade speculation: use data before strong ECC finishes
idea: High-frequency trading systems act on market data before full validation and unwind on the rare error. Inside the host memory controller, forward the raw 64 B line at normal latency while a heavier decoder (two-symbol-correcting Reed-Solomon over a burst pair) runs in the background. If it disagrees, the core replays dependent instructions through its existing branch-mispredict machinery. Standard DDR5/HBM bursts carry exactly the same bits.
why: Strong ECC normally adds 5-10 ns of latency, so vendors lean on stronger cells instead. Hiding decode latency enables chipkill-class correction on every access and tolerates ~10x weaker raw cell populations at no latency cost (facts 1, 3).

title: CCD-style serial charge memory for streamed model weights
idea: Time-shift insight: inference reads weights in the same order every token, so random access is unnecessary. Store weights as charge packets clocked through buried-channel CCD shift registers (no per-bit access transistor, no bitline contact), tapped at the end by a single sense amp per 4k-bit chain.
why: Periphery and cell area: ~2-3F2 per bit and ~80% fewer sense amps; data movement drops because packets flow toward compute; targets 2-3x density for weight storage.
note: Sequential weight streaming suits CCD shift registers; CCD-in-CMOS shuttles exist.

title: Model-ROM DIMMs hold frozen weights with DRAM interfaces
idea: Time jump to model-release cadence: inference weights frozen for months are written once into via- or antifuse-programmed ROM mats that reuse DRAM-style sense amps and the DDR/LPDDR interface, and modules are recycled when the model retires.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; capacitor-free ~4F2 ROM cells need zero refresh (fact 3), give ~3x density (fact 1) and skip capacitor EUV/HAR steps (fact 4).

title: Cryogenic memory racks let capacitors shrink with abundant dielectrics
idea: Time-and-temperature shift: access-transistor and junction leakage falls roughly 2x for every 10 C, so a rack held at 100-120 K stretches retention from 64 ms to minutes. That slack lets the cell use a 1-2 fF capacitor with plain Al2O3/SiN at ~20:1 aspect ratio instead of ZrO2/HfO2 stacks at 60-75:1.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall and the Hf/Zr and fluorocarbon-etch intensity: ~3x lower AR, no high-k precursors, refresh near zero. Cooling overhead means net energy wins only for dense cold memory pools.
note: Cooling overhead limits to dense cold pools.

title: Single MIM-capacitor mask giving SoCs a compression-metadata eDRAM
idea: One BEOL MIM-capacitor mask added to the CPU/GPU logic process yields dense 1T1C eDRAM at about 3x SRAM density. It is used only for compressed-memory metadata and translation (sector sizes, line pointers) for all of main memory. Metadata misses, the main reason compressed DRAM is slow, disappear, so 32-64 MB of on-die storage governs a TB-scale tier.
why: It makes 2-3x main-memory compression latency-neutral, so servers can install proportionally less DRAM.

title: Vendor-owned memory leasing with socketed, design-for-disassembly packages
idea: Ownership time shift: vendors lease DRAM by GB-year rather than selling it, and ship socketed, solder-free packages so they can recall, retest and re-lease the same die over 10-15 years across 3 server generations.
why: Vendors earn on lifetime use rather than one sale, so durability becomes an incentive. The installed die base works 2-3x longer, which multiplies effective supply.

title: Royalty-free JEDEC array-to-periphery bonding standard
idea: Failures mined: RDRAM died in a royalty war and Gen-Z in consortium fragmentation. Fix: a JEDEC standard for the hybrid-bond interface between DRAM array wafers and periphery wafers (bond map, preamp electricals, test hooks), backed by a royalty-free patent pool. Any U.S. logic fab can then sell periphery wafers to any array maker.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: periphery (~49% of the die) moves to commodity logic fabs, cutting the capital needed to enter DRAM by ~30-40%.

title: Write-once AI weights move to a 3D antifuse ROM tier
idea: Failure mined: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D one-time-programmable diode/antifuse memory was dense and cheap but found no market for write-once bits. Fix: frozen inference weights are exactly that market. Program them into 8-deck 3D antifuse crosspoints with a DRAM-class read path (short bitlines, 40 ns random read), freeing HBM and DRAM for KV cache and activations.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 decks x 4F^2 = ~12x DRAM bits/mm^2 with no capacitor, refresh or write path. Weights are 50-80% of inference DRAM demand, so the DRAM bought per deployed model falls 2-5x.
note: 3D antifuse ROM for frozen weights; model churn strands write-once chips, HBF competes.

title: Nantero lesson: quarantine exotic memory films on a bonded wafer
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled partly because fabs would not let CNT material into front-end lines for fear of contamination. Make the exotic memory film (CNT, chalcogenide or any new material) on a separate carrier wafer in a small dedicated US line, then hybrid-bond it onto the finished CMOS periphery wafer, so the CMOS fab never touches the material.
why: Breaks the fab-acceptance barrier that kills new cells (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability): new memory layers in a $200-500M line instead of a $15B fab.

title: Rambus micro-threading revived as tier-granular activation in 3D DRAM
idea: Rambus micro-threading (rows split into small, independently activated pieces) was never adopted in planar DRAM because of decoder area and pin cost. In 3D DRAM, give each tier its own local wordline driver, so an activate opens one tier of one mat (~1 Kb) instead of an 8 Kb page.
why: Cuts the 128x overfetch and ~5.9 pJ per useful bit of random reads (fact 8) by ~8x, and shrinks the row-hammer blast radius (fact 9).

title: ArchShield fault maps replaced by in-row stuck-aware scrambler masks
idea: ArchShield-style weak-cell fault maps died on lookup latency and OS-reserved memory. Fix: leaky cells only lose the charged state, so treat them as 'partially stuck at 0' (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov defect coding); each row stores its weak-cell positions in a few spare cells that are read for free when the row opens, and on-die logic picks one of 4-8 scrambler masks that leaves those cells discharged, saving the mask ID with the line.
why: Retention-weak cells stop causing errors at ~0.5% overhead, so smaller-Cs or leakier cells become acceptable (charge wall fact 1, leakage tail fact 3).

title: Liquid-nitrogen-only 3D DRAM with tenfold smaller lateral capacitors
idea: Design a 3D DRAM exclusively for 77 K immersion pods (LN2 is cheap, abundant and US-made): subthreshold leakage falls >10^6x, so a lateral cell with a ~0.5 fF capacitor that fits inside a 25 nm tier, paired with very short local bitlines, retains data for seconds.
why: Dissolves the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the 3D capacitor blocker (fact 2); refresh approaches zero (fact 3) and tier pitch roughly halves, ~2x tiers per stack height, with cooling cost offset by lower wire resistance and no refresh.

title: Chromium palette: weights as indices into base-die SRAM codebooks
idea: Chromium means color; like an indexed-color GIF, each 8-weight vector is stored in DRAM as a 16-bit index into per-layer codebooks held in SRAM on the HBM base die, which expands indices next to the TSVs so DRAM bursts and TSVs carry only indices.
why: About 2 bits per weight moved instead of 16 for bf16 gives ~8x fewer DRAM bits, and with no overfetch of unused precision ~10x lower energy per weight fetched, while weight DRAM shrinks ~8x (energy, density).

title: W: tungsten-free contactless probing raises known-good-die for HBM
idea: Replace W/Re needle probe cards (China ~80% of tungsten) with inductive/capacitive coupling coils placed in the scribe line and die I/O, so DRAM core wafers are tested at full speed without touching pads, enabling at-speed known-good-die screening before stacking.
why: HBM yield (fact 6) and scarce resources: at-speed KGD could halve the 20-30% stack yield loss and removes a tungsten dependency plus pad damage that hurts hybrid bonding.
note: Inductive/capacitive probing known (Scanimetrics); power still needs contact.

title: Dairy cold-chain milk-run delivers LN2 to cryogenic memory pods
idea: Put capacity-memory sleds in sealed 77 K dewar pods topped up by scheduled liquid-nitrogen deliveries, like a dairy milk-run. Industrial LN2 is a by-product of oxygen plants, so no on-site compressor is needed.
why: Zero refresh power: at 77 K, access-transistor leakage falls by >10 orders of magnitude and retention runs from hours to days, so refresh is disabled. CV^2 energy and wire resistance also drop.

title: USDA-style retention grade stamp and JEDEC refresh-optional mode
idea: Like USDA grading stamps on meat and eggs, require every DRAM die to carry a tested retention grade (e.g., R1 >= 250 ms, R2 >= 2 s at 85 C) and standardize a JEDEC mode that disables refresh per bank. Software can then target refresh-free placement.
why: Zero refresh power deployable at scale: makes refresh-disabled operation a standard, verifiable product attribute instead of a lab trick.

title: Corrugated cardboard flutes: sub-layer recess multiplies tier capacitor area
idea: Deposit each tier's capacitor slab as a fluted superlattice of thin alternating sublayers; after the single added mask opens the capacitor slot, a selective lateral recess etches alternate sublayers to corrugate the slot walls like cardboard flutes, and ALD electrode/high-k/electrode lines the corrugations.
why: Facts 1 and 2: 2-3x capacitor area per lateral 3D cell with no per-tier masks, reaching ~5 fF at shorter lateral length and tighter pitch.

title: Plywood cross-grain tier rotation turns 3D line faults into single bits
idea: Plywood alternates grain 90 degrees so a split cannot run through the panel; in monolithic 3D DRAM, rotate each tier's wordline direction (or its logical bit-to-codeword map) relative to its neighbours and assemble codewords vertically across tiers, so one broken wordline in tier k becomes one bit in each of many codewords.
why: Tier-level line defects are the expected killer of 26+-tier 3D DRAM (fact 2); converting them into correctable single-bit errors could tolerate ~10x higher line-defect density per tier.

title: Gang-run press sheets: multi-project shuttles on a real DRAM line
idea: Commercial printers gang many small jobs onto one press sheet. A DRAM maker reserves a few wafers each month on which startups' and universities' novel cells, capacitors and periphery share one reticle field and run through the production capacitor module. Cost is split pro rata, as MOSIS/Europractice do for logic.
why: Innovation throughput and new entrants: cuts the cost of a real-process memory-cell trial from ~$20-50M (owning a line) to ~$0.2-0.5M, multiplying the number of credible new memory entrants.

title: Storage-element prize judged on a common 300 mm test vehicle
idea: IFR: the perfect bit shows up because everyone tries. Closest achievable: a $50M tiered prize (<=4F^2, >=1 s retention, <=10 ns, >=1e15 cycles) where finalists integrate their storage element on a shared U.S. 300 mm wafer that already carries real sense amps and periphery.
why: Speeds storage-element discovery and U.S. manufacturability; the shared periphery wafer cuts each team's capital need ~100x.

title: Micro-mat activation with sub-wordline drivers built into each tier
idea: IFR: 'an activate opens only the bytes requested.' Backward: tile each 3D tier into 4 kb micro-mats and build an oxide-semiconductor sub-wordline driver inside the tier at each mat edge, so the global wordline only steers a local driver and one ACT energizes 512 bits instead of 8 kB.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~16x less activate energy, taking random reads from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.5-1 pJ per useful bit.

title: Contactless e-beam test of each tier before burial
idea: IFR: 'every tier is known-good before it is buried.' Backward: after each monolithic tier, run multi-beam e-beam voltage-contrast inspection to find open or shorted cell strings, and write the defect map into a per-tier repair ROM so later tiers and the controller route around dead strings.
why: 3D yield (fact 2): 0.5% loss per tier compounds to ~40% at 100 tiers; per-tier mapping recovers most of it.

title: LTPO memory panel: polysilicon sense amps, oxide cells, one glass sheet
idea: IFR: 'periphery and array each get their perfect transistor.' Backward: copy the LTPO OLED backplane flow: laser-crystallized polysilicon (~100 cm2/Vs) on glass for sense amps, decoders and I/O, with low-leakage IGZO 2T gain cells stacked above, so one glass die holds fast periphery and long-retention cells.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and capital: periphery-under-array on the same sheet in existing display LTPO lines; seconds of retention cut refresh ~100x.

title: Via-ROM weight stacks written by maskless direct-write
idea: Ideal: frozen model weights stored with zero energy and zero masks. Closest achievable: build via-programmed ROM arrays at 28 nm whose single programming via layer is written per model by multi-beam e-beam direct-write, stack 8-16 dies in an HBM footprint and hybrid-bond them to the accelerator so weights stream with no refresh and no write path.
why: Zero refresh, no capacitor (fact 1), no EUV (fact 4) and ~2-4x cheaper per bit than DRAM on depreciated 28 nm lines; frees HBM for KV cache.
note: Hardwired-weight startups exist; e-beam write throughput and model churn are doubts.

title: TSV erasure coding replaces HBM spare TSVs and repair
idea: Ideal: TSV defects do not matter. Closest: data across the 1024-bit HBM interface is Reed-Solomon coded in lane groups (e.g., 8 parity lanes per 128), so open or resistive TSVs are corrected on the fly as erasures instead of being repaired with spares and fuses at test.
why: Fact 6: recovers part of the 20-30% stack yield loss and permits finer TSV pitch with higher defect rates for ~6% lane overhead.
note: Turns TSV repair into RS erasure decoding; lane-group parity is a twist on spare-TSV schemes.

title: Exchange-traded DRAM bit futures for price discovery and hedging
idea: Ideal: memory prices known years ahead. Closest achievable: standardized cash-settled quarterly futures per Gb of DDR5-equivalent on an exchange (CME/LME style), letting buyers hedge and new fabs pre-sell output as collateral for lenders.
why: Capital cost: hedged revenue lowers WACC by several points and makes entrant fabs financeable.

title: Dual-mode HZO capacitor snapshots to polarization on self-refresh entry
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): power states are only those DDR defines. Run an HZO capacitor below its coercive field as a plain DRAM capacitor in normal operation; on Self-Refresh Entry the die sweeps rows above coercive field to store data as polarization and powers the array off, and after Self-Refresh Exit each row's first ACT performs the destructive ferroelectric read and restores it as charge within tRCD.
why: Self-refresh power falls to ~0 (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) while ferroelectric switching happens only per power-down, so ~1e11 FE endurance is ample; lazy restore fits within tXS.
note: Ferroelectric used only at power-down; HZO imprint, wake-up and low linear k are the risks.

title: JEDEC cell-agnostic conformance badge for non-capacitor DDR5 dies
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged) turned into policy: fund a JEDEC/CHIPS conformance suite that certifies any DDR5/HBM3 die by behavior alone (timings, refresh tolerance, 1e16-write endurance stress, hammer tests) rather than by cell type, and pair it with federal procurement preference for certified second-source dies built on new storage elements.
why: Cuts the adoption barrier for new storage elements to zero controller changes and shortens qualification by years, widening supply and U.S. manufacturability.
note: Lowers adoption barrier for new cells; JEDEC already behavior-based, procurement lever is the twist.

title: Micro-mat 3D array with 64-byte pages via bonded local drivers
idea: Limit: a page may not exceed 64 bytes. Cut wordlines into 512-bit segments, each driven by its own local wordline driver placed on a hybrid-bonded logic layer directly beneath that mat, so the extra drivers cost no array area.
why: Fact 8: removing 128x overfetch takes random-access energy from about 5.9 pJ per useful bit toward about 1 pJ.

title: Spare-tier redundancy with per-column remap fuses in bonded logic
idea: Limit: a 128-tier stack must still yield at least 95%. Build 136 tiers, test each column, and map up to eight defective tiers per column to spares through a remap table held in the bonded logic layer, replacing classic row/column sparing.
why: Fact 2: turns compound tier yield (0.995^128 = 53%) into high stack yield, making high tier counts economic.

title: Bit-plane sliced stacks make data movement proportional to precision
idea: Scarcity: no reading bits the model will not use. Each die in a 16-high stack holds one bit-plane (die 0 = sign/MSB) and the base die reassembles words, so an FP4 inference read activates only the top 4 dies while FP16 training reads all 16.
why: Data movement and activation energy (facts 5, 8): low-precision reads cost ~4x less energy and bandwidth with no reformatting of stored weights.
note: Precision-proportional reads; bit-plane layouts studied but per-die slicing is neat.

title: Coolant-backed memory wafer: microchannels in the memory layer of a memory-on-logic stack
idea: In a face-to-face memory-on-logic stack (B3-02, or any bonded DRAM-over-logic), etch 100-200 um deep microchannels into the back of the thick memory wafer, away from its devices, and run warm water through them. The memory devices then sit only ~50 um of silicon plus their own BEOL from the coolant, while the logic's heat crosses the memory on its way out. With in-silicon microchannels of the kind Microsoft and Corintis demonstrated in 2025, the memory layer runs ~9-28 K above coolant instead of at the 70-105 C of a cold-plate GPU junction. DRAM retention roughly doubles for every 10 C drop, so a Si 1T1C array at ~45 C holds a 64 ms tail cell for ~1 s.
why: Refresh energy and refresh busy-time 8-16x lower for ordinary Si DRAM (64 ms -> 0.5-1 s; 7.6% -> 0.5-0.9% of time), and standard DRAM becomes viable directly on 1 kW logic without switching to oxide cells.

title: Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder: kill the staircase so 3D DRAM lines can be short
idea: 3D NAND reaches each tier's horizontal line through a staircase whose length grows with tier count; DRAM wants short lines (sub-page activation, low RC), and at 64 tiers a ~32 um staircase is longer than a 512-cell line. Instead, route every tier's horizontal line under 2*log2(N) vertical select-gate pillars before it merges into one common vertical contact. In each tier, each select region is permanently depletion-mode (always on) or enhancement-mode according to that tier's binary address, so driving the pillars with an address and its complement opens exactly one tier's path. The code is written per tier during deposition with one coarse (um-scale, i-line) block mask, or, as in Macronix-style LSM for 3D NAND, by programming charge-trap select gates once at test.
why: Line-termination area 12x smaller at 64 tiers (32 um staircase -> 2.7 um) and 21x at 128; line-end overhead for a 128-cell line 83% -> 30%, enabling 4x shorter wordlines and correspondingly less activation overfetch.

title: Yield firewall: spare tiers per block plus pre-tested tier groups
idea: Build 64 + s tiers per block and fuse out up to s defective tiers per block through the tier decoder (B3-08 makes tier selection programmable), so one killer defect in one tier no longer kills a block. For very tall stacks, build tiers in groups of 8 on separate carriers, run parametric tests on each group (vertical-bitline continuity, leakage, Vt maps from built-in test structures), and stack only good groups by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. That turns a multiplicative 64-tier yield into a sum of 8-tier yields plus bond yields.
why: Required per-block-tier killer-defect rate relaxed 2.5x (0.2% -> 0.5%) for 6% area overhead at 97.5% die yield; pre-tested groups lift 64-tier stack yield from 53% to ~97% at 0.99 per tier.

title: GRS-linked LPDDR 'HBM-lite' on an organic substrate
idea: Stacks of standard LPDDR5X/6 dies (wire-bonded or face-to-face pairs) sit on an organic package beside a small logic buffer die. The LPDDR dies talk to the buffer over ~1-2 mm unterminated traces. The buffer talks to the accelerator over ground-referenced signalling (GRS: single-ended, a charge-pump negative rail, forwarded clock) at 20-25 Gb/s per pin across 5-30 mm of organic substrate. There is no silicon interposer and no TSV in the DRAM. Ten to sixteen such packages around an accelerator give HBM-class aggregate bandwidth.
why: ~3x fewer DRAM wafers per bit than HBM at 2.7-3.4 pJ/bit (HBM3E: 3.44), with no silicon interposer.

title: Swap room temperature for 77 K to freeze leakage, planar caps
idea: Run 1T1C cells made on a 28-nm DUV logic process in liquid-nitrogen-immersed memory sleds. At 77 K, junction and GIDL leakage fall by >10^6 and Cu wiring resistance falls ~5x, so a ~1 fF planar MIM cap keeps data for hours and is sensed on short, low-capacitance bitlines.
why: Turns any mature DUV logic fab into a DRAM source with no pillar etch and no EUV (facts 1, 4), and refresh all but disappears (fact 3). LN2 cooling costs ~10 W per watt removed.
note: Same LN2 cryo-DRAM idea.

title: Top-metal inductive coils over arrays replace HBM TSVs
idea: Substitute through-silicon vias with near-field inductive coil pairs drawn in top metal directly above the cell arrays, which use no silicon area. Stacked dies talk through face-to-back magnetic coupling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV-related yield loss (20-30%), cutting area per bit and stacking cost.
note: ThruChip-style coupling already demonstrated, including on DRAM stacks.

title: Substitute room temperature with 77 K so shallow capacitors suffice
idea: Operate DRAM in liquid nitrogen, where access-transistor leakage drops >10^6, so a 0.5-1 fF capacitor with AR ~10:1 holds data for minutes; subthreshold slope steepens to ~20 mV/dec, letting array voltages fall to ~0.5 V while bitline resistance drops ~5x.
