why: Constraint: 5x smaller C and 2x lower V give ~20x lower array energy per access (net ~10x after large-plant LN2 cooling overhead); facet: eliminates HAR capacitor etch and support meshes (facts 1 and 4).

title: Swap SSD DRAM mapping tables for learned piecewise-linear FTL in SRAM
idea: Substitute the SSD's DRAM logical-to-physical map (~1 GB per TB) with a learned index of piecewise-linear segments held in controller SRAM. The FTL lays out writes in a log-structured way to keep segments long, and a small exact table catches outliers.
why: Enterprise SSDs use a noticeable share of DRAM bit shipments (exabytes of flash at 1 GB/TB). A 50-200x smaller map removes nearly all SSD DRAM and returns that supply to servers.

title: Swap full KV heads for a shared low-rank latent via SVD retrofit
idea: Substitute full K and V with one latent per token: an existing model's K and V projections are factored jointly by SVD into a rank-r down-projection, the up-projections are absorbed into the query and output matrices, and a brief fine-tune follows (an MLA-style retrofit). This runs on today's GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Cuts KV 4-8x for models already deployed, without pretraining from scratch.
note: MHA2MLA/TransMLA known.

title: Swap block-compressed game textures for neural latent textures
idea: Substitute BC7 textures (8 bits per texel) with small neural latent grids plus a per-material MLP, decoded by pixel shaders on existing tensor cores at ~1-2 bits per texel in the same GDDR/HBM.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game VRAM. 4-6x compression lets GPUs ship with half the memory at equal fidelity on today's hardware.

title: Water-droplet self-assembly replaces precision pick-and-place
idea: Substitute the $1-3M precision die bonder with capillary self-alignment: hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surroundings are patterned on interposer and dies, and a dispensed water droplet pulls each roughly placed die into sub-micron alignment as it evaporates before direct bonding.
why: Capital intensity: alignment tooling ~100x cheaper; coarse, parallel placement raises throughput for a small line.

title: Substitute TiN electrodes with conductive-oxide electrodes for fatigue-free HZO
idea: Replace TiN electrodes on HfZrO ferroelectric capacitors with oxide electrodes (RuO2, IrO2 or indium-free LaNiO3) that act as oxygen-vacancy sinks, the same fix that removed fatigue in PZT FeRAM.
why: Endurance from ~1e11 toward >1e14 cycles makes FeRAM close to DRAM-class endurance; LaNiO3 avoids platinum-group scarcity.
note: Oxide electrodes with HZO studied; even 1e14 cycles falls short of DRAM-class endurance.

title: Weak-row CAM companion die on the DIMM buffer
idea: A 180 nm CAM-plus-timer die, or a block in the RCD buffer, holds the addresses of the ~0.1% weak rows found at test. It issues targeted extra refreshes for them while the DRAM runs at a 4-8x lower base refresh rate.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth fall 75-85%, and a legacy node is enough for a ~10k-entry CAM.
note: RAIDR-like; VRT cells undermine static weak-row lists.

title: Capillary self-alignment fused with hybrid die-to-wafer bonding
idea: Pattern hydrophilic bond-pad fields and hydrophobic die rims so a thin water film self-centers each DRAM die to <0.5 um by surface tension before Cu-Cu bonding, letting fast, simple US-built pick-and-place replace imported precision hybrid bonders.
why: HBM stacking (fact 6) and US manufacturability: ~10x throughput and ~5x lower tool cost than precision die-to-wafer bonders made abroad; supports 16-24-high domestic stacks.

title: Router lookahead predicts MoE experts for just-in-time paging
idea: Combine the mixture-of-experts gating network with a prefetcher: a cheap distilled copy of layer L+2's router runs on layer L's hidden state to predict which experts will fire, and those experts are paged from flash/CXL into HBM two layers ahead, so only ~10-20% of experts are resident.
why: MoE models leave 80-95% of weights inactive per token; DRAM for weights shrinks 5-10x.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM stores frozen foundation-model weights
idea: Combine core-rope / mask-ROM hard-wiring with LLM deployment: a frozen base model's quantized weights are encoded in one via layer of a 40-65 nm DUV logic process (one transistor or less per bit, multi-level via codes) next to the compute array, while only LoRA adapters and KV use writable DRAM.
why: Removes weights from DRAM entirely for stable models using only mature DUV processes; only the via mask changes per model, so NRE stays low.

title: Diffraction-grating interference lithography patterns periodic arrays maskless
idea: Adapted from holographic diffraction-grating production: since cell arrays are periodic, expose the whole array with two- or three-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~40 nm half-pitch, no mask, no EUV) and use cheap conventional litho only for array edges and periphery.
why: Interference tools cost ~1/20 of a scanner and expose a wafer in seconds; combined with 3D tiers, patterning cost per bit ~-95% (fact 4) toward 100x per GB.

title: Library card catalogs: SRAM filters front non-volatile records
idea: Borrowed from libraries that keep a compact card catalog by the door and books in the stacks: large DRAM hash tables (dedup indexes, key-value stores, routing tables) are replaced by SRAM-resident ribbon/cuckoo filters plus learned position models that point to the exact NVM block, so each lookup costs one NVM read.
why: Index structures often dominate server DRAM; filters need ~1-2 bytes per key versus 30-100 in DRAM tables, a 20-50x reduction with no refresh.
note: SILT/learned-index style; one NVM read per lookup is known art.

title: Weak-cell exile: banish leakage-tail cells to a tiny SRAM
idea: Profile per-cell retention at test and periodically in the field, remap the ~0.01-0.1% of cells with retention <1 s into an on-die SRAM/CAM patch table keyed by address, and refresh the remaining 99.9% at 1 s instead of 64 ms. Online re-profiling catches variable-retention-time cells.
why: Minifying who sets the refresh rate magnifies the interval ~16x: refresh energy and bandwidth tax down ~16x for <0.5% die area.

title: Inductive coupling coils replace TSVs between stacked dies
idea: MINIFY TSVs to zero for data: copper coils in each die's top BEOL (<=250 C) couple signals inductively to the dies above and below (ThruChip-style), so stacks need no TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones for data.
why: Fact 6: removes much of the TSV area tax and stack yield loss; power still needs a few TSVs or edge delivery.

title: Minify bitline to 16 cells with 2-transistor local preamp
idea: Cut each bitline into 16-cell segments. Each segment drives a global bitline through a 2-transistor local preamplifier, so the bitline capacitance seen by a cell falls from about 80 fF to about 3 fF. With that ratio, Cs can shrink from 5 fF to about 0.5 fF, and the capacitor becomes a shallow planar or low-AR cup instead of a 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Cs needed drops by 10x, removing the need for AR 115 or k 70. Area overhead is about 12%, against much cheaper capacitor process steps.

title: Minify litho capex: nanoimprint a 4F2 hex array
idea: Commission one $100k nanoimprint master of a hexagonal 4F2 pillar array at about 20 nm pitch and replicate it on coupons with a rented NIL tool, proving pattern fidelity and overlay for the cell layer.
why: Litho capital: one stamp could replace multiple EUV exposures for the regular cell array, about 5-10x cheaper per layer.
note: NIL pursued for NAND by Canon/Kioxia; defectivity and overlay are the doubts; cheap to test.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in every wafer chuck
idea: Minify helium to zero: swap the He backside gas in etch and CVD electrostatic chucks for on-site electrolytic H2 at 5-15 Torr, which conducts heat about 20% better than He. Per-chuck flows are under 0.1 slm and are N2-diluted in the vacuum exhaust, so they stay far below flammability limits.
why: Backside cooling is the largest single helium use in a DRAM fab. Removing it cuts fab He demand ~60-70% and the exposure to the Qatar outage (~30% of supply), using an abundant, US-producible gas.

title: DIMM buffer deduplication magnifies effective capacity two to three times
idea: Magnify each physical bit's reach: a CXL/DIMM buffer chip hashes 64 B lines, stores identical and zero lines once in a content-addressed table, and compresses the rest with a ~4 ns LZ-lite engine.
why: Datacenter memory holds 20-60% duplicate or zero content. 2-3x effective GB per wafer means 2-3x less silicon, tungsten and hafnium per job.

title: DRAM in the metal layers of any logic wafer
idea: Magnify where memory can be made: build a low-temperature (<400 C) gain-cell DRAM inside the BEOL interconnect stack of foundry logic wafers as two extra metal levels, so no dedicated DRAM fab is needed.
why: Capital intensity: piggybacks on existing logic fab capacity worldwide, including US foundries; incremental cost is a few masks rather than a new $15B fab.

title: Minify precision to ternary: 5-trits-per-byte packing in controller
idea: Minify weights to native ternary (1.58-bit) models. The memory controller packs 5 trits per byte (3^5=243) and unpacks into add/subtract-only matmul units, with no multipliers.
why: ~10x fewer weight bits than FP16 and lower data-movement energy, on the same DRAM parts.
note: BitNet b1.58 kernels already pack trits.

title: Minify scientific arrays with in-line error-bounded lossy compression
idea: Minify smooth numeric data (simulation grids, time series, climate fields) using an SZ/ZFP-class error-bounded predictive compressor in the memory controller. Users set an absolute error bound per allocation.
why: 10-50x for scientific and HPC arrays at guaranteed error, so the same nodes run 10x larger problems.

title: Charge-recycling stacked I/O drivers
idea: MINIFY I/O energy by stacking four driver domains in series between VDD and ground, so the charge spent toggling one lane's wire flows on to drive the next, with level-shifted receivers.
why: Interface energy per bit: ideal ~4x lower supply current for the I/O; claims ~2.5x in practice.
note: Stacked charge-recycling drivers are published art; ~2.5x I/O energy.

title: Eliminate refresh with liquid-nitrogen cooling instead of helium cryogenics
idea: Eliminate refresh and the tall capacitor by running DRAM at 77 K, cooled with liquid nitrogen (an air-separation product, not helium): junction and GIDL leakage fall by >1e6, retention goes from 64 ms to hours, and Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~1-2 fF, a planar or AR-15 capacitor. Rack-level LN2 immersion loops use no rare gas at any step.
why: Removes refresh power (16-33% of idle, fact 3), wire resistance falls ~5x (fact 5), and the smaller capacitor drops the AR-75 etch (fact 1); the helium ban pushes cooling to N2, the cheapest cryogen; cooling overhead is offset by lower power.
note: Cryo DRAM studied (CryoRAM, IBM); cooling overhead offsets refresh savings.

title: Eliminate helium backside cooling: closed-loop hydrogen chuck gas
idea: Etch and implant chucks flow He at 5-20 Torr behind the wafer; swap it for H2 (thermal conductivity 0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K), confined by a sealed ceramic land, recaptured through a Pd-membrane purifier and recirculated, with chamber H2 sensors interlocked well below the lower explosive limit.
why: Backside cooling is a top fab helium use while Qatar's ~30% of supply is offline; cuts fab He draw 50-80% with equal or better wafer temperature control.

title: Eliminate helium and leakage: liquid-nitrogen-cooled DRAM at 0.4 V
idea: Immerse DRAM stacks in LN2 made on site from air (no helium), retarget access-transistor thresholds for 77 K, and run the array at 0.4-0.5 V, where copper resistance is ~6x lower and the leakage tail vanishes so refresh is dropped.
why: ~6x from V2, refresh removed and smaller drivers give ~10x at the memory; the 77 K plant overhead only pays off when shared with cryo-cooled logic pods.

title: Eliminate TSVs and solder: inductive-coupling links between thinned dies
idea: Stack ~20 um thinned DRAM dies with vertically aligned on-chip spiral coils, passing data by near-field inductive coupling and delivering power through a few large vias or edge rails.
why: Removes most copper TSVs, Sn-Ag microbumps and keep-out zones behind HBM's ~3x area tax (fact 6); ~0.1 pJ/bit versus 3-4 pJ/bit.
note: Inductive-coupling DRAM stacks already demonstrated; power delivery still needs TSVs.

title: Eliminate the clock: asynchronous self-timed DRAM without DLLs or ODT
idea: Replace DDR's DLL, clock tree and on-die termination with a four-phase bundled-data handshake over short in-package links; each bank signals completion, so an idle interface burns nothing.
why: DLL, clocking and termination are a large share of DRAM I/O power even when idle; I/O energy falls from ~5 to <0.5 pJ/bit on short channels.

title: Eliminate signal TSVs between HBM core dies: inductive-coupling vertical links
idea: Replace the thousands of signal TSVs in core dies with on-chip coil pairs that couple data and clock between neighboring thinned dies, keeping only a few large power vias; the base die still presents a standard HBM3E/HBM4 PHY to the GPU.
why: Fact 6: removes most deep-via etch, liner, Cu fill, reveal and micro-bumps, recovering part of the ~3x area-per-bit tax and the 20-30% stack yield loss.
note: Keio ThruChip inductive coupling already demonstrated with DRAM stacks.

title: Eliminate idle-expert residency with one-layer-ahead MoE expert prefetch
idea: An open-source MoE runtime runs the next layer's router on the current hidden state to predict its experts one layer early and streams them over PCIe from host or NVMe, so HBM holds only about 25% of experts plus a hot cache.
why: MoE models need 3-4x less accelerator memory, which directly reduces HBM, the scarcest DRAM product.

title: Eliminate idle refresh: let data decay, repair at wake
idea: When a device enters deep idle, the controller encodes each page with a strong long-codeword BCH/LDPC and stops refresh for seconds to minutes. At wake it decodes every page, correcting the raw BER of ~1e-5 to 1e-4 that accumulated meanwhile.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and phones and laptops idle most of the time, so DRAM standby power drops ~50-80%.
note: Close to Morphable ECC; strong-code idle refresh skipping is known.

title: Eliminate decommissioning: memory sleds outlive three CPU generations
idea: Eliminate the assumption that DRAM retires with its server: hyperscalers move bulk DDR into CXL-attached memory sleds on a 10-year depreciation schedule and swap only CPU/accelerator sleds every 3-4 years, inserting a retimer/protocol-bridge card at each refresh.
why: Fleet refresh scraps DIMMs at year 4-5 although bits last >10 years; decoupling cuts new-DRAM demand per refresh cycle ~30-50% with zero new wafers.

title: Latch-up as a feature: gated vertical thyristor bit
idea: Turn CMOS's classic failure into the storage mechanism: a vertical p-n-p-n stack in 1990s bulk silicon, 180 nm litho, with a capacitively coupled gate on its p-base latches into high-current on (1) or stays blocking (0); gate pulses set and reset it, and the read current is uA-scale with no capacitor.
why: Charge wall and sense signal (facts 1,8): no capacitor, read signal ~100x a DRAM cell, ~8F2 footprint; standby holding current or periodic refresh is the trade.
note: Essentially TCCT/T-RAM; known physics, standby current and variability killed it before.

title: Ferroelectric as backup, not primary: dual-mode DRAM/FeRAM capacitor
idea: Reverse the ferroelectric's role: run a PZT or SBT capacitor (1990s FeRAM process, 0.35-0.18 um) as a plain DRAM cell below its coercive voltage during active use, and switch polarization only to park a row when it goes idle, so idle rows need no refresh at all.
why: Refresh power (fact 3): idle rows draw zero refresh while active rows keep DRAM endurance; polarization switches only once per idle event (~1e9 lifetime); ready for old-node fabs.
note: Close to Micron NVDRAM and 1990s nonvolatile-DRAM dual-mode schemes.

title: TSV-free HBM: stack dies that talk by inductive coupling
idea: Reverse wires to fields: replace through-silicon vias with on-die inductive coil transceivers between thinned stacked dies, with power carried by a few large edge vias or the backside.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes TSV etch, liner, fill and CMP and their 20-30% yield loss, and could cut HBM area per bit toward DDR5 levels.
note: Kuroda's ThruChip Interface is known; power delivery and bandwidth density are the limits.

title: Layer-major batching: one layer resident across thousands of requests
idea: Swap the serving loop nest from token-outer/layer-inner to layer-outer/request-inner: run layer L for a whole queue of thousands of requests, then evict it and load L+1 from flash or far memory, so DRAM holds only one layer's weights plus that layer's KV slice at a time.
why: For throughput-oriented offline inference, resident weights drop by the depth factor (~60-120x) and total DRAM need falls 5-20x, at the cost of latency.
note: FlexGen-style layer-major batching.

title: Return addresses, not data: similarity search inside the stack
idea: Reverse the query direction: the host sends a query vector, a dot-product/top-k engine in the base die scans stored keys at internal bandwidth, and it returns only the k indices and scores; the host then fetches just those k values.
why: Long-context KV caches and vector databases (facts 5, 8): link traffic drops 10-100x because keys never leave the stack.
note: Near-memory ANN / top-k engines widely studied (RecNMP, UPMEM, Samsung PIM).

title: Inductive broadcast stack: one coil talks to all tiers
idea: Replace through-vias with through-fields: plate 2-turn spiral coils in the RDL of thinned (<=25 um) dies stacked with adhesive; a base-die transmitter coil couples to aligned coils on every tier at once, so commands broadcast to all dies and each die replies in its own time slot.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV etch or Cu fill, ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit inductive links, made with plating and adhesive bonding only.

title: Flip the hierarchy: 3D NAND as main memory, DRAM as cache
idea: Reverse DRAM's place in the hierarchy: capacity-bound workloads (embedding tables, KV-cache spill, vector databases) run on memory-semantic SLC 3D NAND behind a CXL controller. A small DRAM cache sits in front, so bulk capacity comes from 200+ layer NAND.
why: 3D NAND gives roughly 10x+ more bits per wafer than DRAM, so water and capex per GB of capacity fall ~10x. DRAM wafers are saved for latency-critical use.

title: Tail-bit eviction table lets the bulk array refresh 16x slower
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: extract the few harmful cells instead of running the whole array at their pace. At final test each die is screened against a 1 s / 85 C retention target; the ~1e-5 of bits that fail are fuse-mapped into a per-bank CAM + SRAM 'tail cache' (~32 kb) that transparently intercepts their reads and writes, with on-die ECC covering variable-retention escapees.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (Fact 3): refresh is set by the 99.999th percentile, not the worst cell, giving 8-16x fewer refresh operations for ~0.3-0.5% die area; idle refresh power drops from 16-33% to a few percent.
note: Tail-bit remapping resembles ArchShield/RAIDR; VRT escapees are the doubt.

title: Capillary self-alignment for mass-parallel die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: dispense a sub-uL water film on hydrophilic bond sites ringed by hydrophobic borders, drop DRAM dies with a fast coarse pick-and-place, and let surface tension pull each die to <200 nm alignment. Hybrid bonds form as the film evaporates, placing thousands of dies per minute.
why: Fact 6: cuts HBM stacking cost and time, enables finer bond pitch (cheaper TSVs) and known-good-die everywhere; could lift HBM stack yield 10-20 points.

title: Near-DIMM dequantize-and-pool engine for embedding tables
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge the gather, dequantize and sum-pool steps of recommendation embedding lookups into a 180 nm logic chip on the module buffer; rows are stored as 4-bit codes with a per-row scale, and the chip expands and pools them locally, returning one FP16 vector per lookup bag.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale and dominate recommender DRAM; in-place dequant makes 4-bit storage practical (~4x capacity) and cuts channel traffic 10-50x.

title: Lisp-machine-style hardware GC tracer beside the memory controller
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: burn garbage faster with a 180 nm tracing coprocessor next to memory (like the Symbolics and TI Explorer GC assists) that marks reachable objects in parallel at memory bandwidth using tag bits, so managed runtimes collect continuously and run heaps at ~1.2x live size instead of the usual 2-3x.
why: Java/Go/JS/Python fleets spend 40-60% of heap DRAM on GC headroom; tracing is memory-bound, so old-node logic is fast enough.

title: The other way round: 28 nm attention engines beside DDR4 do decode
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of moving the KV cache to the GPU, move the low-arithmetic-intensity attention step to the memory. Memory-rich nodes pair many DDR4 channels with 28 nm attention ASICs that run decode attention in place and return only small output vectors, while the GPU keeps the dense matmuls. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement and HBM demand (facts 5, 6): the KV cache leaves HBM entirely, and only ~1/1000 of the KV bytes cross the network per token.
note: Close to AttAcc/NeuPIMs/attention-offloading work.

title: Thymic negative-selection screening catches variable-retention cells continuously
idea: Like the thymus, which deletes T cells that react to self-antigens under stress, the controller uses idle time to test a rotating slice of rows under stress (doubled refresh interval, worst-case coupling patterns), flags rows whose cells flip in a small on-die 'antibody' table, and runs every unflagged row at 4x relaxed refresh.
why: Continuous screening makes retention-aware refresh safe against variable-retention-time cells that change over life, giving ~70-75% fewer refreshes plus the matching energy and bandwidth gain.
note: AVATAR/REAPER-style prior art.

title: Vinyl record pressing: nanoimprint-stamped storage-node arrays, no EUV
idea: Records are pressed from one nickel master: e-beam-write a single master of the storage-node hole array once, electroform nickel or Si daughter stamps, and replicate it on every wafer by UV nanoimprint followed by RIE and ALD fill; perfectly periodic cell arrays tolerate imprint defects far better than logic.
why: Fact 4 capital: replaces 1-3 EUV exposures (~$150M+ tool) for the storage-node layer with a ~$5M imprinter, cutting that layer's patterning capex 10-30x and easing a U.S. fab; a university e-beam writer plus imprinter can demonstrate 20-nm half-pitch arrays.
note: NIL for memory pursued (Canon/Kioxia); overlay and defectivity decide.

title: Freight consolidation hub: base die sorts requests by row
idea: Like a cross-dock that fills containers before shipping, a 32 MB SRAM queue in the HBM/3D base die holds ~50k pending requests, radix-sorts them by row in hardware and fires an activation only when 32+ lines for that row are waiting or a deadline expires.
why: Activation amortization (fact 8): each activation serves 32-64 useful lines instead of 1-2 for random traffic; claims ~10x lower energy per access on latency-tolerant AI and graph workloads.
note: Row-locality batching known in controllers; base-die 32 MB queue raises latency/area.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane tiers: fetch only the precision needed
idea: Progressive JPEG sends coarse bits first; store each tensor element's bits across separate 3D tiers (MSB plane, next plane, and so on) so a pass needing 4-bit precision activates 4 of 16 bit-plane rows, and MSB-plane zeros mask whole lower-plane fetches.
why: Precision overfetch (facts 5, 8): bits activated and moved per useful value drop 4x, toward ~10x with MSB-gated skipping; claims ~10x lower energy per AI access.

title: Git-style Merkle heap: forked agent sessions share unchanged memory
idea: Represent a process's heap and KV state as a content-addressed Merkle tree of 4 KB chunks with hardware-assisted hashing; forking an agent (tree search, best-of-N, multi-agent branches) copies only the root and the diverging chunks, like git branches.
why: Agentic workloads fork state constantly; N branches cost ~1x plus deltas instead of Nx, a 5-20x DRAM saving for tree-search inference.
note: Close to fork() CoW plus radix/prefix KV sharing already in serving engines.

title: Kanban cards for layer streaming from SSD to GPU
idea: Toyota-style kanban: a hardware credit counter between the GPU and an NVMe controller releases the next layer's weights or KV pages only when a consumer slot frees, so DRAM/HBM holds exactly pipeline-depth (2-3 layers) of inventory, never the whole model.
why: Runs models 5-10x larger than HBM at near-full batch throughput; substitutes cheap flash bandwidth for DRAM capacity.

title: Table-side hot pot: attention cooked inside the memory module
idea: Like hot pot where diners cook at the table instead of the kitchen, put decode-attention units inside commodity LPDDR CXL modules so the KV cache never leaves them; the GPU sends the query vector and receives the attention output.
why: Moves the largest inference memory consumer out of scarce HBM (~3x wafer per bit) into commodity DRAM and cuts decode data-movement energy ~5-10x.

title: Pupation: cold pointer structures metamorphose into succinct NV forms
idea: Like a caterpillar reorganizing into a compact pupa, cold pointer-rich structures (tries, graphs, inverted indexes) are rebuilt into succinct rank/select encodings (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees) stored in byte-addressable NV and queried in place without decompression.
why: Succinct forms approach entropy and are 5-20x smaller than pointer forms; data stays durable and off DRAM.
note: Succinct encodings placed in NV; same core as I-02147.

title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory with early-stop streaming
idea: Progressive JPEG sends coarse detail first, then fine. Store tensors bit-plane-transposed so a burst returns the MSBs of many values first. The consumer (attention scoring, vector search) ends the stream once it has enough precision, and fetches low bit-planes only for the top-k survivors.
why: Attention and similarity search need full precision on only a few entries. MSB-first fetch could cut bits moved for KV-cache and embedding reads 2-4x.

title: EV-battery second-life cascade for retired hyperscaler DIMMs
idea: Borrowing the EV-battery second-life playbook (car pack -> grid storage), retired server DIMMs are run through an automated rig that measures each rank's retention time and row-hammer flip threshold, then re-labelled into tiers (A: production CXL pool, B: cache/scratch, C: read-mostly). An SPD-written 'state of health' field tells the host controller what refresh interval and activation limit to use for that module.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers: hyperscalers retire hundreds of PB of DRAM every 4-5 years; reusing even 30% for 3 more years adds ~5-8% to annual effective bit supply at <20% of new cost per bit.

title: Airbnb for stranded server DRAM across a CXL fabric
idea: Modeled on Airbnb renting empty rooms, every server in a hall exposes its unallocated DRAM pages to a CXL switch; a broker lists free capacity, tenants rent GB-minutes, and hardware page-ownership tags plus memory encryption keep tenants isolated while the host can evict with notice.
why: Data-center DRAM is typically 40-60% allocated but idle; renting the stranded half raises effective fleet supply 20-30% without new chips.
note: Stranded-memory pooling (e.g., Pond) is known; brokered GB-minute market is the twist.

title: T-RAM thyristor latch revived on existing SOI production lines
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor's thin capacitively-coupled thyristor (abandoned around 2010) held bits as the latched state of a gate-coupled pnpn device. Re-target it to existing 22FDX and 45-nm PD-SOI flows, using modern back-bias to cut standby current and ALD gate dielectric to tighten the coupled gate.
why: Regenerative bistable storage in ~10F2 with ~1 ns reads and large read current, no capacitor (Fact 1), and only pulse-refresh every few seconds (Fact 3); entirely existing SOI capacity.
note: Same thyristor latch, on FD-SOI.

title: Charge-transfer preamplifier revived with one low-Vt implant
idea: The charge-transfer sense schemes of 1970s DRAMs moved bitline charge through a near-threshold transistor onto a tiny node. One added low-Vt implant mask makes pitch-matched transfer gates that, biased at threshold, pass the cell's signal charge from a ~60 fF bitline onto a ~4 fF node, multiplying voltage swing ~5-10x before the latch.
why: Large signal gain (fact 1) permits 3D DRAM tiers with ~1-2 fF capacitors (fact 2) or 2-4x longer bitlines with fewer sense amps (fact 7).
note: 1970s charge-transfer preamp revived; Vt mismatch of transfer gate limits gain but enables smaller Cs.

title: Ershov hash-consing of tensor blocks across fine-tunes and agent forks
idea: Revive Ershov's 1958 hash-consing in the memory controller: every 4 KB weight or KV block is content-hashed on write and interned in a global table, so identical blocks across fine-tuned variants, unmerged adapters, forked agent contexts and replicas are stored once, and near-identical blocks are stored as base pointer plus XOR-compressed residual. Divergence triggers copy-on-write.
why: Capacity: multi-tenant pools of hundreds of partial fine-tunes and agent trees are mostly duplicate blocks; 5-50x reduction for those pools.
note: Exact plus XOR-residual dedup of blocks overlaps I-01197; full fine-tunes rarely share identical blocks.

title: No.1 ESS program-store/call-store split by page write rate
idea: The 1965 No.1 ESS kept programs in a read-mostly twistor 'program store' and live call data in a small writable ferrite 'call store'. Revive the split: the hypervisor classifies pages by measured write rate, placing read-mostly pages (weights, code, static tables) on denser memories with slow or endurance-limited writes (NOR-like, ReRAM, PCM) and only write-hot pages in DRAM.
why: Read-mostly data is 50-70% of AI server bytes; memories that fail as DRAM replacements on endurance become DRAM capacity substitutes, cutting DRAM per server 40-60%.

title: IBM MXT Revival: Hardware Memory Compression Inside CXL Expanders
idea: Revive IBM's 2000 Memory eXpansion Technology (the Pinnacle controller: parallel LZ compression of 1 KB blocks into sectored storage with a decompressed-line cache) inside CXL Type-3 expander controllers, with a per-page translation table and an on-controller SRAM line cache so the OS simply sees about twice the capacity.
why: Usable supply: MXT measured ~2x on real server data; a 1.8-2.5x effective capacity on the pooled tier is equivalent to doubling DRAM output for that tier with zero new fab capacity.

title: ETA-10 Revival: Liquid-Nitrogen Pods for Commodity DRAM at 77 K
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 liquid-nitrogen-immersed CMOS supercomputer: immerse standard DRAM in LN2 pods (nitrogen is abundant, unlike helium), where leakage collapses so retention reaches minutes and refresh is switched off, the steeper subthreshold slope lets VARY and wordline drop to ~0.4/1.2 V, and copper resistance falls ~7x.
why: Energy per access: V2 cut ~6-8x, wire RC ~7x lower, refresh gone, net ~10x lower energy per access; also returns the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh, using existing chips and a new packaging business.
note: Cryo-DRAM studied widely; cooling overhead at 77 K erodes the claimed ~10x net energy gain.

title: IBM System/360 Channel Programs Run Inside the Memory Module
idea: Revive the 1964 S/360 I/O channel, which executed its own channel-command-word programs: CXL memory modules accept CCW-style scatter, gather, filter and top-k programs, walk pointers locally, and return only result bytes to the host.
why: Data movement and overfetch: for pointer chasing, KV lookups and embeddings, 10-100x fewer bits cross the link, >=10x lower energy per useful access, and one module serves more hosts.

title: Second life for leaky silicon: refresh-tuned salvage of retention rejects
idea: Inverts 'a die that fails 64 ms retention is scrap': buy fab retention-reject dies and decommissioned server and phone DRAM at scrap prices, profile each chip's retention map on high-throughput testers, and mount them on CXL boards whose controller refreshes at the measured interval (4-8 ms) and remaps the worst rows.
why: Marginal cost is scrap value plus test (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x cheaper per GB, adding supply with no fab and U.S.-sited refurbishment; trade-off is higher refresh energy, ~10-20% bandwidth loss and heterogeneous parts.

title: TSV-free inductive-coil stack of headless DRAM dies
idea: Inverting 'stacked dies must be wired with TSVs': thinned dies talk through top-metal coil pairs (near-field inductive links, ~1 Gb/s per coil), power arrives by edge wire bonds, and only the bottom master die carries I/O, DLL and regulators while upper dies are headless arrays.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area per bit vs DDR5) and its 20-30% stacking yield loss while keeping wide internal bandwidth.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in every chuck
idea: Inverts 'helium is the only safe backside heat-transfer gas': feed electrostatic chucks in etch/CVD/implant with 5-20 Torr hydrogen (thermal conductivity higher than He) from an on-site electrolyzer, recirculated through a palladium-membrane loop with sub-LEL leak sensing; the backside gas never touches plasma.
why: Backside cooling is one of the largest fab helium uses; removes dependence on Qatar (~30%, offline since March 2026) for that load; H2 is made from water and power on site.

title: Read-mostly tier on legacy SLC NAND for weights and code
idea: Inverts 'working memory needs unlimited endurance': weights, shared libraries and embedding tables are rarely written, so they are mapped byte-addressably onto pSLC NAND from depreciated 2D and early-3D NAND lines. A DRAM read cache sits in front, and a write-rate limiter enforces the endurance budget.
why: Read-mostly bytes are 30-60% of inference memory; moving them to existing NAND frees DRAM at ~1/10 the cost per bit.

title: Model-on-ROM: frozen weights etched in 40 nm mask ROM
idea: Inverts 'weights must live in rewritable memory': a frozen foundation model's INT4 weights are etched as mask ROM on existing 40 nm logic lines (~0.01 um2 per bit, so a 7B model needs ~280 mm2 of bitcells across a few dies) next to small accelerators, leaving all DRAM for KV and activations.
why: Removes weight DRAM entirely for long-lived deployed models, using mature, plentiful capacity and no DRAM wafers.

title: Looped transformers reuse one block's weights many times
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own weights': models are retrained or distilled into a few shared blocks that execute repeatedly, with tiny per-iteration adapters, so depth costs FLOPs on existing GPUs instead of weight bytes.
why: Weight memory drops 4-12x for the same effective depth, freeing DRAM/HBM for KV and larger batches.

title: Kinetic-inductance nanowire loops storing single flux quanta at 4 K
idea: Store each bit as the presence or absence of one flux quantum (Phi0 = 2.07e-15 Wb) in a loop of 20 nm NbN nanowire. Huge kinetic inductance keeps beta_L = 2*pi*L*Ic/Phi0 > 1 in a ~100 nm loop, the persistent current never decays, and a nanocryotron reads it.
why: Zero leakage and write energy ~Ic*Phi0 ~ 1e-19 J, ~1000x below DRAM. Aimed at cryogenic AI and quantum-control racks; density is set by loop inductance, not capacitor charge (facts 1, 3, 10).
note: MIT nanowire flux-loop memory exists; cryo niche.

title: Expiring memory: retention sized to the data's lifetime, never refreshed
idea: AI activations, KV-cache blocks and gradients live 1-500 ms. The allocator tags each buffer with its lifetime and places it in banks whose measured cell retention exceeds that lifetime, and those banks never refresh because the data is dead before it decays.
why: Removes refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss (fact 3) for most AI traffic. Cells that only need ~100 ms retention can also use smaller capacitors (fact 1).
note: Close to RANA/Flikker retention-aware placement prior art; needs controller-level refresh disable.

title: Built-in-bias antiferroelectric ZrO2 minor-loop dynamic polarization cell
idea: ALD ZrO2 crystallizes antiferroelectric at <=350 C. Asymmetric TiN/RuO2 electrodes (~0.5 eV work-function offset) shift the double loop so zero bias sits inside one lobe, and the field-induced ferroelectric state stores the '1', relaxing over a designed ~1 s with no wake-up or imprint fatigue.
why: 2-3x the charge per area of a linear dielectric (fact 1) with antiferroelectric endurance >1e12. A refreshable volatile ferroic store at BEOL temperature.
note: NaMLab (Pesic 2016) already showed work-function-biased AFE ZrO2 memory.

title: Spare-die HBM stacks with base-die crossbar remapping
idea: Stack yield compounds as y^N, so 12 dies at 98% bond yield gives ~78%. Build 13-high stacks whose base die holds a channel crossbar that remaps any failed die to the spare, plus spare TSV lanes rerouted at runtime without fuses.
why: Turns compounding yield into binomial 12-of-13 yield, recovering most of HBM's 20-30% yield loss for ~8% extra silicon (fact 6).

title: Content-addressed memory fabric stores each identical page once
idea: Across a datacenter, KV-cache prefixes, system prompts, libraries and weights repeat thousands of times. A CXL switch hashes 4 KB pages on write, keeps each unique page once in a pooled DRAM/NAND backend, and hands hosts copy-on-write pointers, with a prefix-trie index for KV caches.
why: Shared-prefix chat serving can dedup 10-100x, so effective cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades write latency and isolation complexity.

title: Address-event storage keeps only coordinates of nonzero values
idea: When activations are >99% zero (ReLU-fied LLMs, spiking nets, event sensors), storing the zeros wastes ~99% of bits. Store tensors as address-event streams (index plus small value) in the interface die, expand them only inside SRAM next to the MAC arrays, and train with sparsity regularizers targeting 99%+.
why: Bytes stored and moved fall 30-100x for sparse tensors; trades model architecture freedom.

title: Canary replica cells at 60% Cs set local refresh
idea: Each subarray carries 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (60% of nominal Cs, written '1'). They see the same temperature, voltage, VRT and aging as the array but fail first. Background logic polls them, and the subarray's refresh rate relaxes until a canary fails, then steps up.
why: Refresh guardband (fact 3): physical tracking replaces worst-case margins, for 2-4x fewer refreshes.
note: Replica/monitor cells for adaptive refresh are long patented; VRT cells are not tracked by canaries.

title: Write-coalescing plus start-gap rotation qualifies 1e11-endurance cells
idea: First-principles budget: a hot line can take ~2e11 writes in 5 years. An on-die 1 MB write-combining SRAM absorbs >95% of hot rewrites, and start-gap row rotation spreads the rest, so per-cell writes fall below 1e10.
why: Widens the capacitorless menu: charge-trap, volatile MRAM and ferroelectric cells with 1e11-1e12 endurance can serve as DRAM.

title: Fridge magnets: inductive coupling links replace TSVs in stacks
idea: Stick dies together like fridge magnets: replace HBM TSVs with on-die coils that couple data inductively between thinned stacked dies at ~1 Gb/s per coil and ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit, so no TSV keep-out zones or through-silicon etch are needed.
why: Die-to-die energy ~10x below today's TSV plus PHY paths, and removes the TSV area/yield tax (fact 6: ~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss).

title: Lotus-leaf droplets: capillary self-assembly bonds memory tiles onto logic
idea: Water beads align on a lotus leaf: put a droplet on each hydrophilic bond site of a logic wafer, release thousands of small (1-2 mm2) known-good DRAM tiles in fluid, and let surface tension pull each tile to <0.5 um alignment before it direct-bonds as the water evaporates. No fine-alignment die-to-wafer bonder is needed.
why: 3D integration capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): batch fluidic placement at >10k tiles/hour replaces $10M+ D2W bonders, making memory-on-logic cheap.

title: Party balloon: per-pump helium harvest-and-repurify loop
idea: Random stimulus 'party balloon' (helium that silently leaks away) -> treat every dry-pump exhaust as a leaking balloon. A compact hollow-fiber membrane stage plus cold-trap/getter polisher on each etch and implant pump exhaust pulls backside-cooling helium out of the N2 ballast at >90% recovery, repurifies it to 6N and feeds it back to the chucks.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% of supply offline): cuts fab helium purchases ~70-85% and buffers supply shocks at minor energy cost.
note: Fab helium recovery systems are commercial; per-pump membranes are an incremental twist.

title: Welding torch: bolt-on hydrogen backside-cooling kit for etch chucks
idea: Stimulus 'welding torch' (hydrogen handled safely every day) -> a 10-person team assembles a bolt-on kit (small PEM electrolyzer, palladium purifier, mass-flow controller, H2 sensors and interlocks) that swaps 5-20 Torr helium backside gas for hydrogen (0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K) on existing electrostatic chucks.
why: Eliminates helium from its largest fab use; H2 is made on demand from water and power, and the kit is built from catalog parts.

title: Magnifying glass: foveated KV precision around attention focus
idea: Like foveated rendering, the KV manager keeps recent tokens and retrieval anchors at FP8, mid-distance tokens at 3-bit and far tokens merged into learned gist tokens, re-sharpening a region from a flash copy when attention mass returns to it.
why: 4-10x KV footprint reduction on long contexts with bounded quality loss.

title: Mosaic tiles: embedding tables assembled from shared tile codebooks
idea: A mosaic renders any image from a few tile colours: store recommendation embedding rows as product-quantized codes into a few shared codebooks, decoded by a memory-side gather engine on a CXL device so the host still sees full-precision rows.
why: Recsys embedding tables reach TBs and are the largest DRAM consumer in ad datacenters; 8-16x compression.

title: Jacquard punch cards: via-programmed ROM stores frozen base model
idea: A loom's pattern is punched holes: freeze a foundation model's weights into mask-ROM where one cheap via mask (no EUV, back-end only, <=400 C) programs every bit, stacked in 2-4 back-end crosspoint layers on a logic chip; fine-tunes and LoRA deltas stay in DRAM.
why: ROM is denser, refresh-free and capex-light versus DRAM; for million-unit edge/inference SKUs base-weight DRAM goes to zero.

title: MoO2-templated rutile TiO2 capacitor: k of 90 without ruthenium
idea: Box = {medium: charge in rutile-phase TiO2 (k~80-100) | access: Si FET | sense: charge share | integration: 1T1C pillar at AR ~30:1 | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: ALD from TiCl4 made in the U.S. from Florida/Georgia ilmenite, on a rutile-structured MoO2 bottom electrode from Colorado molybdenum}. MoO2 shares the rutile lattice, so it templates rutile TiO2 at low temperature the way RuO2 does, and light Al doping holds leakage down.
why: Fact 1 calls for k~70: this delivers it with domestic elements, removes Ru (South Africa) from the stack and cuts AR ~2x.
note: Rutile templating on RuO2/MoO2 explored; small TiO2 bandgap leakage is the persistent issue.

title: Liquid-nitrogen planar DRAM: helium-free cold shrinks the capacitor tenfold
idea: Box = {medium: charge on a planar 0.5 fF ZrO2 MIM with no pillar | access: Si FET at 77 K | sense: low-noise cryogenic SA | integration: memory sleds immersed in LN2 from U.S. air-separation plants | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: relaxed-pitch patterning with a U.S. multibeam e-beam writer}. At 77 K subthreshold and junction leakage drop by more than 1e6, so retention reaches minutes even with a tiny planar capacitor, and nitrogen cooling avoids the helium chokepoint entirely.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: no high-AR capacitor, essentially no refresh, no EUV; LN2 is cheap and made domestically.
note: Cryo-DRAM studied (Rambus, CryoRAM); LN2 ~10 W/W overhead caps system gain.

title: Shadow router prefetches next-layer MoE experts from CXL flash
idea: Box: tiering × MoE inference runtime × expert × predicted one layer early × CXL-attached low-latency NAND. A tiny predictor maps the current hidden state to the next layer's likely experts, which stream into a small HBM expert cache while the current layer computes.
why: MoE models leave >90% of parameters idle per token; holding only active plus predicted experts shrinks resident weights 4–8×.
note: Pre-gated MoE / MoE-Infinity already pursue this.

title: Sense amplifiers double as 100 mV interposer link receivers
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x cross-coupled latch receiver x 100 mV-swing interposer wires treated as long bitlines x Si interposer x standard fab. The interface reuses the DRAM's own sense-amp latch topology as a clocked receiver, so the transmitter only dumps a small charge on the wire, like a cell sharing charge with a bitline.
why: Interface energy (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): CV2 at ~0.1 V swing gives ~10x less link energy, HBM I/O from ~1 pJ toward 0.1-0.2 pJ/bit.
note: StrongARM latch receivers and ground-referenced low-swing links are established.

title: Flash-resident KV cache with attention-guided prefetch over CXL
idea: Box: dense 3D NAND x standard x standard x CXL/optical link with predictive prefetch engine x SSD x standard. The LLM KV cache lives on flash; a small predictor in the controller uses top-k attention scores to prefetch the token blocks the next step needs into a 10x smaller DRAM buffer.
why: Water and DRAM demand: ~10x less DRAM per served session; NAND needs far less fab water per bit, so memory water per session falls ~10x.
note: Close to InfiniGen/ShadowKV-style attention-guided KV offload.

title: Second-life CXL memory bricks from retired server DIMM dies
idea: Box[Source=retired DIMMs x Transform=laser debond+KGD retest x Integration=CXL Type-3 x Owner=recycler-OEM JV x Finance=EPR take-back credits x Scale=regional centers]: retired DDR4/DDR5 packages are desoldered, retested at temperature and re-mounted 32-64 per card behind a CXL controller as a far-memory tier, with the recycler paid by extended-producer-responsibility credits.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers; recapturing ~30% of retired server DRAM as far memory adds an estimated 5-10% effective capacity at ~20-30% of new cost per bit.

title: Rack-pool memory-as-a-service metered in GB-hours
idea: Box[Integration=CXL switch-attached memory pool x Owner=colo operator x Finance=GB-hour subscription x Scale=rack]: colocation providers pool DRAM per rack, lease it to servers on demand, and bill GB-hours, so servers ship with minimal local DRAM and borrow the rest.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: raising fleet DRAM utilization from ~50% to ~75% cuts DRAM purchases ~30% for the same work.

title: Controller-side line compression licensed per gigabyte saved
idea: Box[Transform=CPU memory-controller LZ-class cache-line compression x Integration=unchanged DDR5 channel x Owner=IP licensor x Finance=royalty per effective GB]: the controller compresses lines into packed physical pages (IBM MXT style) with metadata cache, and the licensor is paid per effective GB delivered.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: ~1.5-2x effective capacity on typical data; same DIMMs.

title: OS compacts live pages into best-retention rows before self-refresh
idea: Po: the best cells do all the work. On entering idle, the OS migrates live pages into rows profiled as the top-decile retention class and powers the rest down with partial-array self-refresh, so the self-refresh interval is set by the best rows, not the worst.
why: Fact 3 idle power: best-decile rows retain ~10x longer than the worst, so standby refresh power in phones and edge boxes drops up to ~10x.
note: Commodity self-refresh interval is internal; needs extended-interval self-refresh support.

title: Fading KV: tokens lose bits as attention ignores them
idea: Po: memory that shrinks when you look away. Each KV entry carries an attention-usage counter and steps down 16 to 8 to 4 to 2 bits, then merges into a pooled summary vector, as its cumulative attention mass decays, mimicking human memory consolidation.
why: Most long-context tokens get negligible attention; graded decay gives 4-8x KV reduction with smoother quality loss than hard eviction.
note: MiKV/ZipCache-style mixed-precision KV known.

title: One copy of each AI model per rack via content-addressed pooling
idea: Po: there is only one copy of every model. Inference hosts serving the same open-weight model map its weights read-only from a content-addressed (hash per 2 MB page) CXL memory pool shared across tenants and GPUs, instead of each VM loading its own copy into host DRAM.
why: Popular models are replicated dozens of times per rack in host memory; dedup frees ~30-60% of host DRAM on inference fleets; attacks usable capacity per installed bit.

title: RAID across tiers: one parity tier per sixteen
idea: Worse: let one defective tier among 200 kill or degrade the die. Flip: write each 16-tier group with an XOR parity tier computed in the base die and reconstruct a failed tier's bits on read, so random tier defects become correctable instead of becoming yield loss.
why: At 200 tiers, tier-defect yield^N would wreck cost per good bit; ~6% parity overhead holds die yield near 2D levels, so 10x density survives at the same cost (facts 2, 6).

title: Scatter-gather descriptor port returns only the useful bytes
idea: Worsen: open a whole 1-8 KB row to deliver one 4-byte embedding element. Flip: give the HBM base die a descriptor port where the host posts index lists; the base die activates sub-rows, gathers only the requested sectors into dense packets and ships those, so the bus carries only useful bytes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 4-16x fewer bits moved per useful bit for sparse embedding, graph and MoE routing workloads.

title: Grade-B DRAM: rebinned decommissioned DIMMs behind CXL expanders
idea: Worse: shred DDR4/DDR5 when servers retire after 4-5 years. Flip: route retired DIMMs through a high-throughput retest line (retention, row-hammer threshold, speed bin) and redeploy them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate old DDR generations to any new host, with ECC strength set by each module's measured bin.
why: Reuse: retired fleet memory is exabyte-scale; redeploying ~30% of it adds roughly 10-15% to annual usable bit supply with no wafers, helium, EUV or fab capital.

title: Rack memory spot exchange auctioning stranded GB-hours over CXL
idea: Worse: let every server own its memory so 25-50% sits stranded while neighbors swap to disk. Flip: a rack-level CXL switch pools DRAM and a scheduler runs a sub-second auction in which tenants bid for GB-hours, publishing the clearing price as an internal scarcity signal.
why: Cuts cluster DRAM provisioning ~20-30% for the same workloads, equivalent to new supply with no fab.

title: Plumber's capillary self-alignment: water-droplet HBM die stacking
idea: A plumber knows water finds its level. Drop HBM dies coarsely (+/-20 um) onto hydrophilic bond sites carrying a water microdroplet; surface tension pulls each die into <1 um alignment within milliseconds, then evaporation and one collective hybrid-bond anneal fix every die at once.
why: Replaces slow precision thermocompression/pick-and-place bonders (~1-2k UPH, ~$3M each) with fast coarse placement (>10k UPH) and a batch anneal, attacking the HBM stacking tax (fact 6). Risks: particles, water residue and bond voids.

title: Alien who sees only entropy: entropy-sized frames in CXL expander
idea: An alien observer sees information content, not 4 KB pages. A CXL Type-3 controller measures each incoming page's compressibility inline and stores it in a 512 B, 1 KB, 2 KB or 4 KB slot. A sub-page indirection table and per-class free lists track the slots, so the host sees full nominal capacity while the media holds only the entropy.
why: Server memory typically compresses 2-3x. Transparent entropy-sized storage gives 1.8-2.5x effective capacity per DRAM chip with zero OS changes, attacking cost per bit.

title: Octopus arms think locally: filtering engines inside CXL memory modules
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms. Each CXL memory module gets a small engine for scan, filter, hash-probe and gather, so analytics and database operators run where the data sits and return only results. That eliminates the host-side staging buffers, decoded copies and hash tables that currently mirror the data in local DRAM.
why: Analytics nodes often hold 2-3 copies of hot data (raw, decoded and intermediate). Near-data operators cut host DRAM 30-60% and also cut data-movement energy.
note: Computational CXL memory widely pursued.

title: Mole lives underground: vector search fully inside SSD controllers
idea: A mole never needs the surface. Billion-scale vector indexes (a graph ANN plus PQ codes, normally hundreds of GB of DRAM) live entirely on SSDs whose controllers walk the graph and compute PQ distances internally. The host keeps only a tiny entry-point table and receives top-k IDs.
why: This removes 90%+ of the DRAM in RAG and vector-database servers, where DRAM now costs ~20-40x flash per byte, at retrieval-acceptable millisecond latency.

title: Child asks why servers don't share: per-second rack memory market
idea: A child sees half of each server's RAM sitting idle and asks why they don't share. A CXL 3.x rack pool lends each host's stranded DRAM in 256 MB slices through a per-second internal auction run by the fabric manager, and reclaims a slice in under 100 ms by migrating its pages to a compressed tier.
why: Usable supply: hyperscaler DRAM utilization is ~50-60%; pooling plus a price signal could cut fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%, at ~200 ns extra latency on borrowed pages.

title: Hotel concierge: on-module DRAM front desk over flash storage
idea: A concierge keeps tonight's keys at the desk and everything else in storage. An on-module 'memory hotel' pairs 16 GB of DRAM with 256 GB of low-latency SLC flash behind a controller that predicts and prefetches hot 4 KB pages, presenting 272 GB to the host as byte-addressable CXL memory.
why: Meets the 10x constraint in capacity per module: ~10x for about the same module cost, since SLC flash is ~1/10 of DRAM's $/bit. A hot-set hit rate above 99% keeps average latency DRAM-class, but misses cost ~5-10 us and flash endurance limits write-heavy use.

title: Work-function-offset antiferroelectric gives two zero-bias states for pacemakers
idea: Pacemakers need memory that idles at zero power for ten years; one added mask patterns a high-work-function RuO2 top electrode (vs TiN) over ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric capacitors, shifting one double-hysteresis loop so two polarization states coexist at 0 V. Antiferroelectric switching avoids HZO wake-up and offers 1e12+ endurance.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free capacitor in the existing cell geometry for one mask (fact 3); read remains destructive but refresh energy and standby power vanish.

title: Automotive tier-RAID: erasure code striped across stacked array tiers
idea: Automotive ASIL-D allows no silent bit loss at 150 C; stripe each 64-byte line across 9 tiers of a 3D array (8 data + 1 parity) read in parallel, so any single tier with weak or hammered cells is rebuilt on the fly. Refresh can then be set by the typical tier rather than the worst cell anywhere in the stack.
why: The leakage tail sets refresh (fact 3): ~4x longer refresh interval because single-tier tail failures are corrected; tier yield (fact 2) improves at ~12% parity overhead.
note: Chipkill-style parity ported to 3D tiers; parallel 9-tier activation costs power.

title: Dilution-fridge-grade helium recapture ring on every etch chuck
idea: Quantum-computing labs recover >95% of helium boil-off; copy them by adding an edge-scavenging vacuum ring around each electrostatic chuck that captures backside-cooling helium leakage and feeds a tool-side membrane purifier and compressor returning 99.999% He to the chuck line. A fab helium 'bank' meters per-tool recovery the way a cryo lab does.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline since March 2026): cuts fab He purchases ~80-90% with small capex and protects etch/CVD uptime.

title: Rocket-test-stand hydrogen as backside wafer coolant instead of helium
idea: Rocket engine test stands handle hydrogen routinely, and H2 conducts heat better than He (0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K). Run chuck backside cooling on 5-20 Torr electrolytic H2 (or H2/Ar) with leak-tight seals, H2 sensors and dilution exhaust, qualifying each etch chemistry for H-radical side effects.
why: Removes the largest fab helium use in etch and deposition; H2 is made domestically on site from water and power, with equal or better wafer temperature control.

title: Recommender long tail: synthesize rare-ID embeddings from features
idea: From the largest single DRAM user, ad recommenders with TB-scale embedding tables: only IDs seen more than N times get a stored row, and every tail ID's embedding is computed on the fly by a small feature tower from side attributes (category, text, graph neighbors) trained jointly with the model.
why: 90%+ of embedding rows are long-tail IDs touched rarely; synthesizing them cuts embedding DRAM 5-10x.

title: Digital-hoarder edge case: object-level access sampling exiles untouched objects
idea: From the user who opens everything and touches nothing: the memory controller samples access bits per object rather than per page via allocator-tagged address ranges, and objects untouched for a window are compacted together and exiled to compressed CXL flash with a fault-driven return path.
why: In hoarding workloads 80-95% of resident bytes are cold; object-level exile lets DRAM shrink ~10x with fab water following.
note: Object-granular far memory (AIFM, Carbink) is known; 80-95% cold claim is optimistic.

title: Fraud-graph pointer chasing executed inside the memory stack
idea: Fraud-detection and social graphs are extreme pointer chasers with one useful word per hop. Put a tiny walker engine in the base die that follows pointer chains and returns only the final result, keeping every intermediate hop inside the stack.
why: Each hop otherwise crosses the PHY twice with a full burst; internal hops cost far less, ~10x lower energy per logical graph access and lower latency.
note: IMPICA/Tesseract-class pointer-chasing PIM is known.

title: Prompt-prefix commons: one shared KV cache per data center
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache, where thousands of tenants send identical system prompts and documents. Providers agree on canonical tokenization and keep shared read-only KV pages for common prefixes in a pooled CXL tier, stored once with copy-on-write.
why: Cuts inference DRAM demand 20-50% for chat workloads; usable supply rises with no new bits.

title: 77 K immersion pods let storage capacitors shrink tenfold
idea: Jump from cell to datacenter scale: put memory sleds in liquid-nitrogen immersion pods where access-transistor leakage falls by ~6 orders, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the capacitor only needs to beat sense-amp offset, not leakage (~0.5 fF instead of 5 fF).
why: Capacitor wall and refresh: 10x smaller Cs, refresh eliminated, enabling short planar or 3D cells; cooling overhead amortized at rack scale.
note: Same LN2 cryo-DRAM idea.

title: Tail rows exiled to an on-die SRAM jail
idea: Scale shift: the ppm-scale retention tail is served by a tiny memory with a different timescale; rows or 64 B segments failing a 1 s retention test at sort or in the field are remapped through a CAM into a few hundred KB of on-die SRAM or fast-refresh eDRAM, letting the rest of the array run at 1 s refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~16x fewer refresh ops for <0.5% die area, because the long tail sits in ~1e-5 of rows.
note: RAIDR/ArchShield-style prior art; VRT cells escaping profiling are the key risk.

title: Depth-recurrent models reuse one block's weights across time steps
idea: This adds zero masks. Model labs train looped or depth-recurrent transformers that apply a few weight blocks repeatedly across depth, with tiny per-iteration adapters. Space (unique layers) is traded for time (iterations), paid for with compute that decode leaves idle anyway.
why: 4-8x fewer resident weight bytes at similar quality on many tasks, freeing HBM for KV.

title: Capillary droplet self-alignment for sub-micron chiplet-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Shift alignment from a multi-million-dollar robot to molecular-scale surface tension: hydrophilic pad patterns plus a water droplet pull each DRAM chiplet into register to <200 nm as the droplet evaporates, then Cu/oxide direct bonding locks it. A coarse +/-10 um pick-and-place is enough because the liquid does the last mile.
why: Cuts hybrid-bonding tool capital ~5-10x and raises throughput ~10x, making 1-2 um pitch DRAM-on-logic affordable for U.S. OSATs (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability, pJ/bit).
note: Capillary self-assembly is demonstrated (Tohoku, Leti); cheap tool demo feasible.

title: Function-shipping packets: memory requests carry bytecode run at the hub
idea: Invert the scale of what moves: instead of hauling gigabytes to the CPU, each CXL request carries a ~64-byte verified bytecode (filter, gather, reduce) that a tiny core on the memory hub executes, returning only the result. The fabric moves kernels, not data.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) drops 10-100x for gather and scan-heavy work, and fewer bits in flight shrink the DRAM needed for staging buffers.

title: Robotic second-life harvest of retired DRAM into CXL memory shelves
idea: DRAM reclaim from retired servers and phones has failed on manual handling, mixed generations and test cost. Decommissioning lines at hyperscalers use robots to pull DIMMs and reflow-desolder LPDDR packages, run a 10-minute BIST sort, and mount mixed DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR parts behind CXL controllers that hide generation differences in pooled second-life shelves.
why: Meets 100x: the bits are already paid for; harvest plus test ~$0.05-0.1/GB vs ~$5-10/GB new, with zero fab capex. Trades: older speeds, higher power per bit, supply tied to retirement cycles.

title: AMD HBCC, fixed: hardware-paged HBM cache with attention-aware prefetch
idea: Vega's High-Bandwidth Cache Controller paged system memory into VRAM in hardware but died because games fit in VRAM anyway. Revive it for LLM serving: HBM becomes a hardware-managed page cache over host LPDDR/CXL, and the prefetcher uses the previous decode step's attention-score sparsity to fetch only KV pages likely to be attended next.
why: HBM per GPU can drop 2-4x for long-context serving (HBM costs ~3x wafer area per bit); decode access is predictable enough to hide the far-tier latency.
note: InfiniGen-style speculative KV prefetch over unified memory exists.

title: eASIC structured ASIC, fixed: via-programmed ROM holding frozen weights
idea: Mask ROM died because every code change needed a full mask set, and eASIC's single-via customization never found volume. Store a frozen production model's weights in a via-programmable ROM fabric where one cheap non-EUV via mask encodes the bits, so a model update costs one mask and a two-week spin, not a new chip.
why: Weights at ~1 via per bit with no capacitor, refresh or DRAM; capital and energy per bit fall sharply for long-lived models.

title: Optane latency, fixed: look-ahead MoE router hides flash fetch
idea: Optane failed partly because software could not hide its latency on unpredictable accesses. Co-design the model instead: train each MoE router to choose experts for layer L+2 from layer L's hidden state, giving two layers of warning to fetch expert weights from flash into SRAM before they are needed.
why: MoE models with hundreds of GB of experts serve from flash plus SRAM, driving weight DRAM toward zero.

title: IBM MXT rebuilt at 180 nm: cold-page compressing module buffer
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled server memory with hardware compression but was dropped for its added latency once DRAM became cheap. Fix: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module compresses only cold pages during idle cycles (base-delta and zero-page codecs small enough for 1990s gate budgets), while hot pages stay uncompressed, so most accesses pay no penalty.
why: ~1.5-2x effective capacity on existing DIMMs; at 4x bit prices, a few-dollar 180 nm chip is cheaper than buying the bits.

title: Barrier-trimmed MTJ trades ten-year retention for tenfold cheaper writes
idea: Effect walk: Neel-Arrhenius thermal activation. Design the MTJ free layer for thermal stability ~25-30 (seconds of retention at 85 C) instead of ~60 (ten years); critical current scales with the barrier, so writes need ~2-2.5x less current and, with shorter pulses, ~5-10x less energy, while a refresh every ~100 ms costs ~1% duty.
why: Turns MRAM's over-engineered retention into energy: a DRAM-class volatile cell from a mature MTJ stack at ~10x lower write energy than NVM-grade STT, with non-destructive read and no capacitor (fact 1).
note: Known relaxed-retention STT-MRAM concept (Smullen 2011); straightforward to execute.

title: Flux quanta in kinetic-inductance nanowire loops for cryogenic AI memory
idea: Effect walk: flux quantization in superconductors. Each bit is the presence or absence of one flux quantum in a loop of 10-nm-wide NbN or NbTiN nanowire whose large kinetic inductance shrinks the loop to ~0.1 um2; writes and reads use nanocryotron (nTron) switches instead of Josephson junctions, costing ~10^-18 J per access.
why: Access energy ~10^-18 J vs ~10^-14 J for DRAM cell+bitline: even after a ~500x 4-K cooling penalty it remains ~20x lower, giving cryogenic accelerators and quantum-control stacks a missing dense memory.

title: Conducting ferroelectric domain walls as switchable nanoscale wires
idea: Effect walk: domain-wall conduction. In a thin-film LiNbO3 or ErMnO3 cell, a written charged domain wall bridging two electrodes conducts ~10^4x better than the bulk; short pulses inject or erase the wall to store the bit, and a 0.1-V read through the wall leaves polarization untouched.
why: A non-destructive 0.1-V read with large margin removes the restore cycle and full-rail bitline charging (facts 8, 10), cutting read energy >10x; the wall is ~1 nm wide, so density is set by lithography, not physics.
note: LiNbO3 domain-wall memory demonstrated (Fudan); Si integration needs bonding.

title: Capillary self-alignment for cheap high-throughput die-to-wafer stacking
idea: Surface tension: hydrophilic bond pads with hydrophobic surroundings, plus a water microdroplet, pull each roughly placed die to <200 nm alignment as the water evaporates, before direct hybrid bonding. Fast, coarse pick-and-place replaces slow precision bonders.
why: Cuts capital and throughput limits of HBM and 3D die stacking (facts 4 and 6); claim 5-10x die-to-wafer throughput per tool, which suits US assembly lines.

title: Water-droplet capillary self-alignment stacks DRAM dies without thermocompression bonders
idea: Effect: surface-tension energy minimization. Pattern hydrophilic pads inside hydrophobic surrounds on the dies; a coarse, ~$150k used pick-and-place drops each die onto a water film, and capillary force pulls it to <1 um alignment within ~100 ms before direct bonding. A 24-month, $1M program demonstrates 4-high wide-I/O stacks.
why: Fact 6: HBM stacking uses $3-5M TCB or hybrid bonders with slow per-die alignment; parallel capillary alignment could cut stacking capex per unit ~5-10x.

title: Cu: electroplated copper coils link stacked dies without TSVs
idea: Replace HBM TSVs with inductive-coupling transceivers: spiral Cu coils, electroless-seeded and electroplated with no argon-sputtered barrier or seed, in each die's top metal pass data magnetically through 20-50 um of thinned silicon.
why: Eliminates TSV area, keep-out zones and TSV yield loss (fact 6, ~3x area per bit) at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit links.

title: Platinum catalyst banks: analytics filters run at the bank surface
idea: Like a catalytic converter reacting gas on the platinum surface without moving it elsewhere, each DRAM bank group gets a small predicate unit beside its sense amplifiers that decodes dictionary-compressed columns and evaluates WHERE clauses and aggregates in place; only matching row IDs or partial sums cross the I/O.
why: Off-chip I/O dominates the 10-20 pJ/bit DDR cost; scans at 1-5% selectivity move 20-100x fewer bits (>10x lower energy per useful access), and columns can stay 3-5x compressed in DRAM because decoding happens at the bank (energy, density).

title: Lanthanide contraction ordering: shrink graph gaps, then stream compressed
idea: Atoms contract steadily across the lanthanides; a reordering pass (community detection plus Gorder) renumbers graph vertices so neighbors get nearby IDs, then adjacency lists are stored as gap-coded Elias-gamma/varint streams decoded by a near-memory unit, turning random neighbor reads into sequential compressed streams.
why: Graph DRAM shrinks 4-10x, and sequential compressed streaming replaces random 64 B reads at ~5.9 pJ per useful bit with ~0.3-0.5 pJ, >10x lower energy per access (energy, density).

title: Retread memory: remanufacture retired server DRAM inside ECC shells
idea: Like tyre retreading, harvest DDR4/DDR5 from retired servers, re-test and re-bin at die or package level, and remount it on CXL expanders whose buffer chip adds strong symbol ECC, scrubbing and page retirement to absorb ageing errors.
why: Hyperscalers retire exabytes of DRAM every 4-6 years; recovering even 30% adds supply with near-zero new wafers, helium or EUV (scarcity, cost).
note: Retired-DRAM reuse behind CXL buffers already done (Azure GreenSKU/Pond); ECC-shell remount adds little new.

title: Erasure-coded decay: refresh only when information is at risk
idea: IFR: refresh happens only when information, not charge, is about to be lost. Store each page with a strong cross-row LDPC/erasure code and let cells decay; a background reader samples syndrome weight per page and re-encodes only pages nearing the correction limit.
why: Fact 3: the refresh interval is set by code tolerance instead of the worst cell, plausibly 10x fewer refreshes for ~6-12% parity overhead.
note: Strong-ECC refresh relaxation known; parity and latency cost.

title: Two-layer DRAM window streams weights from parallel flash channels
idea: IFR: weights need no DRAM residency. Closest: weights live across 16-64 NVMe/low-latency flash channels and stream layer by layer into a double buffer holding exactly two layers; the batch grows until per-layer compute hides the flash read time.
why: Weight DRAM falls by L/2 (40-60x for 80-120-layer models) for offline inference and fine-tuning; flash costs ~1/20 per bit.

title: Weight carousel rotates model shards around an accelerator ring
idea: IFR: one copy of the weights serves every chip at once. Closest: N accelerators each hold 1/N of the weights and continuously pass shards around the ring over chip-to-chip links; each chip applies the passing shard to its own batch, so the ring stores weights once instead of N times.
why: N-fold cut in replicated weight memory for data-parallel serving (8x on an 8-chip ring), paid for with link bandwidth that consumes no DRAM wafers.

title: Frozen foundation models burned into via-programmed ROM
idea: IFR: weights use no DRAM because they are the hardware. Closest: for models frozen for years (speech, embedding, vision encoders) weights are encoded by one custom via mask as ROM beside the MACs at ~0.1 um2/bit, with LoRA adapters in SRAM for updates.
why: Removes 70-90% of inference DRAM for frozen models; ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and only one non-EUV custom mask.

title: KV cache as inverted-file vector index with DRAM-resident centroids
idea: IFR: context length is free. Closest: KV blocks are clustered online into an IVF index stored in flash; DRAM holds only the centroids and a recent window, and each decode query fetches its top-k clusters for sparse attention.
why: DRAM per million-token context falls 20-50x with ~1% quality loss on retrieval-heavy tasks.
note: RetrievalAttention/ClusterKV-class prior art.

title: SONOS NOR arrays compute dense layers where the weights sit
idea: IFR: weights never move and never occupy DRAM. Closest within Si/O/N: poly-Si/SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2 charge-trap NOR arrays (no Hf, W or Ta; Ti-silicide contacts) store 4-bit weights as trapped charge and do analog multiply-accumulate by summing bitline currents; only activations and KV use DRAM.
why: Removes weight DRAM (50-80% of inference memory) with a three-element memory stack mature U.S. fabs already run.

title: Hybrid state-space retrofit replaces most attention layers' KV
idea: IFR: context costs constant memory. Closest with no new hardware: replace 7 of every 8 attention layers in a trained model with linear-recurrent state-space layers (fixed-size state) distilled from the originals, keeping one attention layer in eight for exact recall.
why: ~8x KV reduction for long contexts at modest quality cost.
note: Mamba-in-Llama distillation retrofits known.

title: Canary cells that decay first and call for refresh
idea: Ideal: memory that knows the instant it starts forgetting. Closest: every subarray carries a few deliberately weakened canary cells (narrower access FET, ~30% smaller Cs, written to '1'); a tiny comparator polls them and the subarray is refreshed only when its canaries droop past a guard threshold, so refresh follows real temperature, voltage and aging per subarray instead of the worst-case corner.
why: Fact 3: removes the 4-8x worst-case guard band in refresh rate; ~50-75% refresh energy cut in typical conditions.

title: CCD-loop memory: charge packets circulate, no per-bit contact
idea: Scarcity rule: no transistor or contact per bit. Bits ride as charge packets in buried-channel CCD loops of 64 cells clocked by 2-phase gates, and one sense-and-regenerate stage per loop reads and restores each packet as it passes, so a bit costs only ~2F2 of gate pitch.
why: Removes per-bit transistors and contacts (fact 4) for ~3x density at the same F; buried-channel dark current gives seconds of retention; the ~32-clock average wait adds latency.
note: 1970s CCD memory revival; latency penalty.

title: Indium- and gallium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cells
idea: Imposed scarcity: zero indium and gallium (China-dominated). Build a 2T0C gain cell whose write transistor is amorphous Zn-Sn-O made by ALD below 300 C, Si-doped to suppress oxygen-vacancy leakage, with charge stored on the read transistor's gate.
why: Off-current near 1e-19 A/um stretches retention from 64 ms to minutes, removing most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh; uses earth-abundant Zn and little Sn instead of IGZO's critical metals.

title: Combinatorial abundant-element dielectric library for capacitors
idea: Within $1M/24 months: co-sputter graded Ti-Al-Si-Mg-Ca-O-N thin-film libraries (crustal-abundant elements only) on probe-array wafers, auto-measure k, leakage and breakdown across ~10,000 compositions, and hand the top 10 to ALD recipe development.
why: Searches for a k>=60, low-leakage capacitor dielectric with no Hf, Zr, Sr or rare earths, aimed straight at the capacitor charge wall, at lab cost.

title: Droplet self-alignment bonds dies at 10,000 per hour
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: water droplets on hydrophilic pads pull dies into sub-0.5 um alignment by capillary force, then oxide-oxide and Cu-Cu direct bonds form in a ~250 C anneal, with no polymer and no solder to age at 125 C.
why: Facts 6 and 4: ~10x die-to-wafer throughput vs ~$5M precision pick-and-place bonders; stacked-memory back-end capex down several-fold.

title: Ship each binary with its own memory-compression dictionary
idea: Imposed limit: each GB of DRAM must hold 4 GB of apparent data. At build time the toolchain profiles heap snapshots and trains a 64 KB dictionary per object type; the binary carries it, the OS loads it into the memory controller, and each page is compressed against its app's dictionary, tagged with a per-page dictionary ID.
why: Generic hardware memory compression reaches ~1.5-2x; dictionaries trained per app could reach 3-4x on structured heaps (JSON, protobuf, JVM objects), multiplying effective capacity.

title: NAND-style zig-zag wire-bond stacks put 64 DRAM dies in one package
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Borrow mobile NAND packaging, where 16-32 dies stack in a zig-zag staircase with wire bonds for cents, and apply it to DRAM as a capacity tier: 64 dies per package on 8 wire-bonded channels at modest bandwidth.
why: Wire bonding is depreciated, U.S.-available and ~10x cheaper per die than TSV stacking; 64 dies per package is ~10x+ capacity per footprint vs 4-8-die DDR packages.

title: Scrub-as-refresh: 1-second refresh, page-level code, lazy scrub
idea: Each 1 KB DRAM page gets ~2% spare columns holding a BCH code (t=12 over GF(2^14)). The refresh engine restores rows about every second with a plain activate-precharge; the array itself is unchanged. A background scrubber decodes and rewrites each row about once a minute, so errors from weak and VRT cells can accumulate for at most one scrub period. Decoding at every refresh would eat most of the savings, so the scrub is lazy. Three add-ons stretch the interval further. (a) Per-subarray canary rows with undersized caps set the interval from measured leakage at the actual temperature, not from the 85 C 6.4-sigma worst case. (b) Retention errors only go one way (charged -> discharged, polarity known per true/anti cell), so an asymmetric (Z-channel) code needs fewer parity bits. (c) A write encoder flips 64-bit words to minimise how many cells sit charged. Fast-path reads use the existing on-die SEC; the page code is consulted only when an error is detected.
why: ~15x less refresh energy, scrub included. Refresh busy time drops from 7.6% to 0.5% at 16 Gb, or from 20.5% to 1.3% at 64 Gb. All on today's Si 1T1C cell, for ~2% parity.

title: Minify optimizer state from 16 bytes to ~2.5 bytes/param
idea: Minify training memory: FP8 weights with stochastic rounding (no FP32 master copy), 4-bit block-quantized first moments and factored (row/column) second moments, fused into the optimizer kernel.
why: Optimizer and master-weight state dominates training DRAM/HBM. Per-parameter bytes drop ~6x, so the same model trains on far fewer HBM stacks.

title: Eliminate Adam optimizer state with moment-free sign updates
idea: Train with a sign-based optimizer whose only per-parameter state is a 1-bit error-feedback residual, removing the two fp32 moment tensors that Adam keeps for every weight.
why: Optimizer state is about 2/3 of mixed-precision training memory beyond weights; removing it cuts total training memory 40-60%.

title: Eliminate backprop activation storage via forward-only perturbation training
