idea: Ideal: a dielectric with infinite k so the capacitor needs no height. Closest: an antiferroelectric ZrO2-rich HfZrO film whose field-induced AFE-to-FE transition is centered at the plate bias, so the small storage-voltage swing rides the steep part of the P-E curve for k_eff ~100-150.
why: Fact 1: k ~70 is the stated requirement; at k_eff ~100 pillar AR drops from ~70:1 to ~30:1, deleting the hardest etch/deposition loops and the anti-collapse support layers.
note: Hysteresis and fatigue at the AFE-FE transition versus 1e15 cycles.

title: Four-level gain cells double bits without a lithography node
idea: Ideal: more bits from the same pattern. Closest: store four charge levels on the read-transistor gate of a capacitorless gain cell, exploiting its non-destructive current read with a time-to-threshold sensing ADC per sub-array, and refresh only the inner levels that drift first.
why: Fact 4: 2 bits/cell equals several 10-20% node shrinks with zero new tools or masks.

title: In/Ga-free zinc-silicon-oxide gain cells stacked over accelerator logic
idea: IFR: the KV cache lives on the compute die for free. The constraint bans IGZO, so use amorphous Zn-Si-O channels: 2T0C gain cells deposited below 400 C in the BEOL above the attention units, with TiN electrodes and Al2O3 gate dielectric, holding transient KV and activations for milliseconds with occasional refresh.
why: Moves the hot KV set off external HBM; if ZSO leakage approaches IGZO's, refresh becomes negligible and several GB sit on-die.

title: Vector-quantized KV cache sized to fit base-die SRAM
idea: Ideal: the working set shrinks until static memory can hold it. Closest achievable: the base die encodes each KV vector as 2-4 indices into learned per-head codebooks (product quantization), shrinking the KV cache 8-16x so the hot cache fits in base-die SRAM, and computes attention scores directly on the codes.
why: Zero refresh power for the KV tier and 8-16x less KV traffic (fact 5); KV cache is the fastest-growing DRAM consumer in long-context inference.
note: Even 16x-compressed KV caches exceed base-die SRAM; PQ KV caches already published.

title: Capacitive-read crosspoint: hysteretic MFS stack, no access transistor
idea: Scarcity rule: no transistor at the cell. Each crosspoint is a metal/ferroelectric/semiconductor stack whose polarization leaves the semiconductor in accumulation or depletion, and a sub-coercive AC read pulse senses the 3-5x small-signal capacitance difference, drawing no DC sneak current and never disturbing the state. Only writes switch polarization.
why: Stackable 4F2 crosspoint without selectors (facts 2, 4, 7) with nondestructive read removing restore (fact 8); ferroelectric write endurance (~1e11) needs write-sparing.
note: Nondestructive capacitive FE read studied; write half-select disturb and 1e11 endurance limit.

title: Normally-on wordline clamps turn IGZO DRAM non-volatile for months
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, using a capacitor cell. Oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) access transistors leak ~1e-20 A, so the only threat when power drops is wordlines floating up. Each wordline gets a depletion-mode IGZO pull-down held off by the live supply; when power vanishes it turns on by itself and clamps every wordline to ground, giving months of unpowered retention.
why: NV with DRAM endurance and speed, no ferroelectric wear, and a periphery cost of one tiny device per wordline driver; refresh shrinks to a power-up scrub (fact 3).
note: Months need ~1e-21 A leakage; close to SEL oxide-semiconductor memory work.

title: Catalytic wet-etched silicon molds for 115:1 capacitors
idea: Imposed scarcity: no fluorocarbon plasma and no high-aspect-ratio etch tool. Deposit a sacrificial silicon mold above a nitride barrier, pattern a graphene or Pt catalyst mesh, and let catalyst-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2 sink vertical holes beyond 100:1; line them with TiN/ZAZ, then dissolve the silicon mold in TMAH.
why: Reaches the AR~115 capacitor charge wall with no PFC gases (high GWP, PFAS rules) and no $5M+ etcher; holes stay straight because the catalyst sinks chemically rather than relying on ion flux.
note: Catalyst-assisted etch avoids PFC plasma; catalyst wandering at ~20 nm holes and 100:1 is the key doubt.

title: Layer-lockstep weight broadcast: each server holds one-sixteenth of model
idea: Imposed limit: no server may store more than 1/16 of a model's weights. Sixteen inference servers each keep one shard in DRAM and take turns multicasting their layers over an optical broadcast bus; every server runs its own batch in lockstep, using each layer as it streams past and then discarding it, like a choir reading from one shared score.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference DRAM; cluster-wide weight DRAM falls ~16x in exchange for multicast bandwidth (a few hundred GB/s), cutting how much DRAM each server needs.
note: Decode-rate broadcast bandwidth is likely >1 TB/s, not a few hundred GB/s.

title: Urban-mined DRAM dies from retired servers restacked into dense modules
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Chemically decap DDR4 packages from decommissioned servers, retest the harvested dies, thin them and restack 16-32 high with wire-bond or sidewall interconnect into high-capacity modules for a capacity-tier memory product.
why: The dies are already paid for: near-zero die cost lets a module carry 10x the dies at the same price, made domestically from e-waste.

title: Base-die KV-cache codec stores ten contexts in one's space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. The HBM base die compresses KV-cache blocks on write (per-channel 2-bit quantization, residual low-rank sketch, entropy-coded outliers) and decompresses on read at line rate, transparent to the GPU kernels.
why: KV cache dominates LLM serving memory; ~8-10x compression inside the module raises effective bits per purchased bit about 10x.

title: Zero added read latency: optimistic CRC read, lazy LDPC correction
idea: Imposed limit: ECC may add zero read latency. Data returns immediately with a 1-cycle CRC check, and the core speculates on it. On a CRC failure the pipeline squashes, and a strong flash-style LDPC decoder (~200 ns) corrects the line from a long codeword spanning 4 lines.
why: Flash-class codes become usable in DRAM, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 cells (cheaper, denser, lower voltage) with no average latency penalty.
note: At 1e-4 raw BER ~5% of lines fail CRC; squash and 4-line decode cost may erase the win.

title: AAO-Cap: self-ordered anodic-alumina capacitor mold
idea: Sputter a 2.5-3 um Al film over the access-transistor array and its TiN/W landing pads. Nanoimprint shallow pits registered to the pads (Masuda pretexturing), then anodize at ~15-20 V in sulfuric/oxalic acid: pores nucleate at the pits and grow straight down at aspect ratio >=100, stopping at the pad metal; the alumina barrier at each pore bottom is thinned by a voltage ramp-down and removed by a short wet or atomic-layer etch. An ALD Al2O3 liner seals the anion-contaminated pore walls, then TiN / ZrO2-Al2O3-ZrO2 (or the B2-02/B2-03 dielectric) / TiN cup capacitors are ALD-coated inside the pores. The rigid alumina honeycomb stays in place as the mechanical support lattice, so there is no pillar leaning and no SiN support-lattice masks. The bit is stored and sensed exactly as in a 1T1C cell (Si BCAT or IGZO 4F2 VCT access device).
why: Capacitor 2.5-3 um tall (pore AR ~100-115) with no plasma HAR etch: Cs 7.4-8.9 fF at a 4F2 40 nm-pitch cell (+37-64% vs 1-beta's 5.4 fF) at ~1-beta-parity density with periphery under cell; capacitor-hole module goes from ~3 masks + fluorocarbon HAR etch + SiN lattice to 1 imprint + wet anodization (~8 Wh/wafer).
note: Pore registration to pads at 40 nm pitch and pore-bottom opening are the doubts.

title: Stream seeds, not weights: on-die regeneration of model tensors
idea: Substitute dense weight transfers from HBM with PRNG seeds plus small low-rank/sparse residuals; an LFSR engine on the compute die regenerates the pseudo-random basis and the residual corrects it, so each 64 B of weights crosses the link as ~8-16 B.
why: Fact 5: bytes moved per token and weight capacity both drop ~4-8x for compressible layers.
note: SeedLM-style PRNG weight compression already published; trained weights compress poorly this way.

title: Halftone error diffusion: 2-3-bit stored activations preserving dot products
idea: Borrowed from Floyd-Steinberg print halftoning: when activations or KV are written to memory at 2-3 bits, each element's rounding error is diffused into its not-yet-quantized neighbors along the reduction dimension, so downstream dot products stay nearly unbiased. A small write-path unit performs the diffusion in the store stream.
why: 5-8x fewer bits than FP16 for stored intermediates with accuracy closer to naive 4-6-bit quantization; direct capacity and bandwidth gain.

title: CERN two-level trigger decides which KV entries survive
idea: Borrowed from LHC trigger systems that keep ~1 event in 100,000: new KV entries wait in a fixed-latency level-1 SRAM ring while on-die accumulators sum the attention mass each token receives over the next K steps; only tokens passing the L1 threshold are promoted to DRAM, and a slower software 'high-level trigger' periodically re-scores and drops survivors.
why: Long-context KV grows linearly with tokens; physics-style triggering can keep 5-20% of tokens at small accuracy loss, a 5-20x KV reduction.

title: Minify context to gist tokens: 30x learned compression
idea: Minify a long prompt or document context into 32-64 learned 'gist' soft tokens, produced by a small compressor model. Only the gist KV is stored and reused across turns and users.
why: 16-30x less KV per cached document, so prefix caches hold 10x+ more context in the same DRAM.

title: Compile long shared contexts into adapters instead of KV
idea: Reverse context->weights: documents reused across many requests (codebases, manuals, policies) are distilled offline into a small LoRA or a trained KV 'cartridge' of a few MB, so requests stop holding a 100k-token KV cache for the same text.
why: KV for repeated long contexts drops 10-100x: a few MB of cartridge instead of GBs of KV per concurrent request.
note: Matches Stanford Cartridges work.

title: Resident key sketches, full KV parked in flash
idea: Flip which part of attention lives in DRAM: only 1-bit sign sketches of the keys plus a graph ANN index stay resident, while full-precision K/V blocks live on NVMe; each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks the sketch picks.
why: Million-token contexts fit in ~1/16-1/32 of the KV DRAM, with the bulk on flash at ~10x lower cost per bit.

title: Synaptic tag-and-capture promotes only reinforced KV entries
idea: New KV entries are written provisionally at 2-4 bit into a small scratch ring carrying a decaying 'tag'; only entries that receive above-threshold attention mass while tagged 'capture' promotion to full-precision storage, mirroring synaptic tagging and capture in long-term potentiation. Untagged entries expire or remain as 2-bit sketches.
why: KV capacity: most tokens never receive meaningful attention; 3-6x KV footprint reduction with bounded accuracy loss.

title: CDMA embedding tables: superposed rows with orthogonal spreading codes
idea: Like CDMA letting many phones share one channel, rarely accessed embedding rows of different IDs are summed into the same physical row after multiplying by pseudo-random +/-1 codes; a lookup multiplies by the ID's code to despread, leaving the others as low-level noise.
why: Recommender embedding tables are TB-scale with a long tail; 4-16x compression of tail rows with graceful noise instead of hard hash collisions.

title: Gist tokens compress idle conversation context into learned summaries
idea: Inverts 'context must be kept as raw per-token KV': when a session goes idle, a small trained compressor squeezes its KV into a few dozen 'gist' states that condition the model almost equivalently when the user returns. It is software only and runs on GPUs already installed.
why: Resident KV for idle multi-turn sessions drops 10-50x, so existing hardware can hold far more concurrent users.

title: Experts stored as shared base plus low-rank deltas
idea: MoE experts and per-tenant fine-tunes are highly correlated, so their joint information is far less than N full matrices. Factor each expert as W_base + A_i B_i (rank 32-128) and compute x.W_base + (x.A_i).B_i on the fly, so memory holds one base and N small deltas.
why: 5-10x smaller expert and multi-tenant fine-tune memory, for a few percent extra FLOPs.

title: Seeded procedural weights regenerated beside the multiply units
idea: A tensor's true storage cost is its Kolmogorov complexity, not its size. Train models whose matrices are W = PRNG(seed per block) times a few learned coefficients, and place LFSR/hash generators next to the MAC arrays to regenerate weights on the fly, so memory holds seeds and coefficients only.
why: 10-100x fewer stored and moved bytes, so cost per effective GB ~100x lower; trades training effort and some accuracy.
note: SeedLM already does LFSR-seed weight compression at ~3-4 bits; 10-100x unproven.

title: Speculative decoding lets big models live in host DRAM, not HBM
idea: Box: amortize × decode algorithm × k-token draft window × per step × target weights in installed host DDR. A small draft model in HBM proposes k tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, so each large-model weight read is amortized over k×batch tokens and its weights can sit in slower, already-installed host memory.
why: Cuts HBM needed per served model 3–5× by tolerating lower weight bandwidth; algorithm-only on existing servers, so no new fluorinated chemistry.
note: SpecExec-style offloading exists; host DDR/PCIe bandwidth caps throughput.

title: Pruned-to-customer MoE: deploy only the experts real traffic wakes
idea: Po: a customer only needs the experts they actually use. Each domestic deployment profiles a week of its own traffic, drops experts with negligible routing mass, patches the router with a small distilled fix-up for residual tokens, and serves the slimmed MoE on U.S.-made hardware.
why: Domain traffic typically activates a minority of experts; pruning 50-70% of them shrinks weight memory in proportion with small task-quality loss.

title: Gist tokens compress old context 100x
idea: Worsen: keep KV for every raw token of a long conversation. Flip: periodically have the model compress each 1,000-token span into about 10 learned gist tokens whose KV replaces the span, with the raw text archived on cheap storage for exact re-reads.
why: Cost: 100x less KV per archived span; trades lossy recall of fine detail.

title: Developmental biologist: thousands of fine-tunes as epigenetic bit-masks
idea: Every cell shares one genome and differs only in which genes are switched on. Thousands of fine-tuned variants are served from one base copy in HBM. Each variant is stored as a run-length-coded sparse sign-flip/zero mask of about 0.1 bit per parameter or less, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel.
why: This replaces per-tenant full copies or large adapters. 1,000 variants of a 70B model fit in roughly the memory of 1.1 copies, a 100x+ saving for multi-tenant serving.

title: Eliminate per-company reliability qualification: national BEOL-memory test vehicle program
idea: Fund a shared public test chip and accelerated-aging method (drift, hydrogen, PBTI, disturb) for <=400 C memory devices, with open data and a JEDEC-track spec. Each startup then qualifies against a common model instead of spending 18-24 months on bespoke reliability work.
why: Qualification time and risk are the main barriers for new BEOL memory entrants; a shared vehicle could halve time-to-market and widen the supplier base.

title: Fab load-shifting using UPW and liquid nitrogen as energy storage
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: run the power-hungry subsystems that can be buffered (ASU liquefaction, UPW reverse osmosis, chiller ice making) in pulses during cheap renewable or nuclear hours. Their output is stored in LN2 dewars, UPW tanks and ice banks, so grid draw is periodic while the process tools run continuously.
why: Energy intensity: ~15-25% of fab load becomes flexible, for ~10% lower energy cost and access to U.S. sites with weaker grids.

title: Ecological niche partitioning: retention-binned memory SKUs for matching workloads
idea: Species partition niches instead of competing for one; test-sort dies by measured retention tail into 'arctic' (certified 256 ms tREFI, premium for inference/HBM), standard, and 'ephemeral' (short retention, cheap, sold for TTL activation buffers), with the certified tREFI exposed in a JEDEC mode register.
why: Monetizes the retention distribution instead of designing to the worst tail, and turns dies now downgraded into sellable ephemeral bits (+3-8% yield-equivalent supply).

title: Bubble-memory bootloop maps let partial-capacity HBM stacks ship
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with a bootloop PROM listing bad minor loops, which controllers simply skipped. Apply it to HBM/DDR: instead of scrapping stacks with dead pseudo-channels or subarrays, burn a bootloop map into the base die, sell 20/24/28 GB SKUs, and have the controller and OS remap around dead regions at subarray granularity.
why: Fact 6 (HBM yield down 20-30%): recovering most failing stacks as lower-capacity SKUs raises usable HBM bits per wafer 10-25%.

title: Spare-tier HBM: thirteen dies for twelve, fused at test
idea: First principle: with die yield y = 0.98, a 12-high stack yields 0.98^12 = ~79%, but one spare die plus a TSV crossbar remap programmed by e-fuse after stack test gives P(at most 1 failure in 13) = ~97%. Add one redundant die per stack and steer around any bad die at test, and again in the field.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): 21% stack loss becomes ~3% for 8% extra silicon; repairable by design.
note: Sound yield math; stack loss is partly bonding, not die.

title: Memory consortium take-or-pay contracts open small U.S. helium fields
idea: Scale jump from the chamber to geology, and from monthly purchases to 15-year contracts. A U.S. memory consortium signs take-or-pay offtake from small Montana, Saskatchewan and Kansas helium fields equipped with modular membrane-plus-PSA wellhead units, with delivery as liquid helium in ISO containers.
why: Hedges the Qatar ~30% outage and stabilizes fab helium cost. These small fields are uneconomic without an anchor buyer.

title: Retention-signature die matching when assembling stacks
idea: No EUV: mature DUV dies have wider retention spread. Scale shift (die test data -> package assembly): sort known-good dies into retention-signature bins and stack only matched dies, so each stack runs at its own refresh rate instead of the worst die's in a random mix; outlier dies go to high-refresh SKUs.
why: Cuts stack refresh overhead ~2x and raises usable yield of wide-spread DUV dies.

title: Lead-free's chaotic transition fixed: shared qualification bank for abundant materials
idea: The 2006 RoHS lead-free switch went badly (tin whiskers, brittle joints) because each OEM repeated years of reliability testing alone. Fund a pre-competitive U.S. qualification bank, CHIPS-funded and governed by OSATs and hyperscalers, that runs JEDEC thermal-cycle, electromigration and HAST tests once on Earth-abundant packaging materials (Zn-Al joints, Cu-Mn barriers, Cu sinter, AlN dielectrics, ferrite magnetics) and publishes shared data and design rules.
why: Cuts 2-3 years and per-firm cost from qualification, making substitution away from Sn, Ag, In, Ta, W and Co practical for U.S. memory packaging and resilient to chokepoints.

title: Fab fire-sales stopped: strategic bank for 180 nm-plus tools
idea: When Qimonda and other fabs closed, their mature tools went abroad for cents on the dollar, and most retiring 200 mm tools are still exported. Fix: a federal strategic tool bank buys retiring steppers, etchers, furnaces and implanters (180 nm and above), refurbishes them, and leases them cheaply to domestic micro-fabs making memory companion chips, interposers and test hardware.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: 1990s-class tools cost ~1-5% of new, and a standing pool can equip dozens of small U.S. lines.
note: Executable; impact limited to companion chips.

title: Substitute 85 C air-cooled DIMMs with 35 C cold plates
idea: Substitute air cooling with direct liquid cold plates holding DIMMs and HBM at ~35 C, plus a new JEDEC 'cool-tier' mode register that certifies temperature-scaled refresh (leakage halves every ~8-10 C).
why: Running 50 C cooler gives ~16-32x retention; refresh drops at least 8x, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth and the 16-33% idle-power share of refresh.

title: Substitute scrapping retention-fail dies with retention-binned memory SKUs
idea: Substitute pass/fail retention screening with binning. Dies that fail 64 ms at 85 C are sold with an SPD flag for 32 ms refresh or for cooled racks; long-retention dies sell at a premium into low-power edge and mobile.
why: Raises usable bit supply 3-8% from existing wafers with zero capital, and turns retention into a priced feature.
note: Downgraded parts already sold; few-% supply gain.

title: Substitute blanket refresh with compiler-declared short-lifetime no-refresh zones
idea: Substitute uniform refresh with lifetime-aware refresh. An AI compiler places activations, gradients and KV-cache blocks that live shorter than the guaranteed retention window in banks flagged 'no-refresh', and the controller refreshes a bank only when its oldest live write exceeds that window. No new process or tool is needed, so no gases.
why: Much of accelerator DRAM holds data that lives under 10 ms; skipping its refresh cuts refresh energy ~50-80% in those banks and recovers bandwidth.

title: Token-passing shift-chain wordline sequencer for streaming weight memory
idea: Substitute the random-access row decoder with a one-flop-per-wordline token chain that steps to the next row on each activate, plus a coarse jump decoder every 64 rows. This targets AI weight and KV streaming, where row order is known.
why: Periphery area: row decode logic shrinks ~60% and wordline select energy drops to one flop toggle; fits HBM-class AI memory, where streaming dominates.

title: Column-periphery zero-skip compression replaces raw data serialization
idea: Substitute raw serialization of the row buffer with zero-run and base-delta compression units in the column periphery that send only non-zero bytes plus a bitmask over the interface. This exploits sparse AI activations and KV caches.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer bits on the wire for sparse tensors, cutting I/O energy and raising effective bandwidth and capacity.

title: Swap 64-bit pointers for region-relative 32-bit pointer instructions
idea: Substitute absolute 64-bit pointers with hardware base-plus-offset addressing. New load and store instructions take a 32-bit offset from a per-region base register with a hardware bounds check, so C/C++ compilers can emit 32-bit pointers in heaps above 4 GB without software decode overhead.
why: Pointer-dense heaps (graphs, trees, object stores, databases) shrink 25-40%. Compressed oops already proves this in software, and the hardware path brings it to native code.

title: Swap ECC-chip overhead for end-to-end checksums on reloadable data
idea: Substitute hardware ECC with software integrity for data that can be reloaded. Model weights, container images and page-cache copies of files sit on non-ECC DIMMs, guarded by per-block hashes that a background scrubber checks; a mismatched block is simply re-read from SSD. ECC DIMMs keep only mutable state.
why: DDR5 ECC RDIMMs spend 20% of their chips (8 of 40 bits per subchannel) on ECC, and this reclaims those bits for the reloadable data class. Standard DIMMs and interfaces throughout.

title: Flyover twinax cables replace motherboard memory traces
idea: Substitute long PCB memory traces with ultra-low-loss twinax cables terminated right beside the CPU socket, so memory modules sit in a separate sled and each channel supports more DIMMs or longer reach without retimers.
why: Capacity per socket: ~2x DIMMs per channel or memory moved to cooler zones; a small team builds the harness and adapter boards.
note: Flyover cables already ship.

title: Graded-speed DRAM bins packaged into wide slow modules
idea: Substitute prime-only DRAM sourcing with fab speed-reject and down-bin dies, graded on an open-source FPGA DRAM tester and packaged into wide, slow modules where 2x more chips at lower clock deliver the same bandwidth.
why: Supply and cost per bit: dies otherwise scrapped or discounted become usable supply; +5-10% bits at 30-50% lower cost per bit.

title: Substitute room-temperature DIMMs with sub-zero cold-plate memory loops
idea: Swap air cooling of DRAM for a dedicated dew-point-controlled liquid loop holding modules at about -10 C; leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, so retention rises ~8-10x and refresh intervals stretch, and tail-limited cells pass.
why: Refresh power (fact 3) drops ~80-90% and weak bins become usable; needs no change to the die.
note: Cold/cryo DRAM well studied; chiller energy and condensation offset refresh savings.

title: Substitute blind refresh with compiler-proven refresh-by-use schedules
idea: A compiler/runtime for AI training proves that every row of a tensor region is read or written within its retention time each iteration, and marks those regions refresh-exempt in a controller table.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3): for training memory that turns over every few ms, ~70-90% of refresh can be skipped.
note: Refresh-by-access (Smart Refresh) known; compiler proof is the twist.

title: Substitute stuck-cell loss with coset coding that writes on dirty paper
idea: When NV cells wear to stuck-at values, the encoder picks among 2^k coset representatives of each data word the one that agrees with known stuck cells (Gelfand-Pinsker 'dirty paper' coding), so dead cells still store bits correctly.
why: Endurance (DRAM-class needs effectively unlimited): extends usable life of ReRAM/PCM arrays ~10-100x past first stuck cell at a few % overhead.

title: Substitute landfill for CXL afterlife pools of retired DDR4 DIMMs
idea: Swap scrapping old DIMMs for CXL memory appliances whose controllers host 16-32 harvested DDR4 DIMMs each as a far-memory tier, with the controller absorbing timing and retention quirks.
why: Extends useful life of existing bits by 3-5 years, cutting new-DRAM demand per server by ~20-30% in cloud fleets.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL.

title: Substitute lone mid-size buyers with a memory purchasing cooperative
idea: Swap thousands of small spot-market buyers for a member-owned cooperative (like rural electric co-ops) that pools demand from universities, SMB clouds and OEMs to sign multi-year allocations and run a shared buffer inventory.
why: Gives small buyers hyperscaler-class allocation; pooled forecasting cuts spot exposure and bullwhip over-ordering that inflates apparent shortage by ~10-20%.
note: Purchasing co-ops are established practice.

title: Share the accelerator cold-plate loop with HBM and DIMMs
idea: Extend the GPU liquid-cooling cold plates over HBM stacks and DIMMs to hold the arrays at 30-40 C instead of 85-95 C. Thermal sensors then step the refresh multiplier down from 2x to 0.25x.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C, so 16-20x more retention headroom. The 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss falls below 1% and refresh energy drops ~90%.
note: Liquid-cooled DIMMs/HBM already deployed; refresh gain bounded by refresh share.

title: Retention-certified DRAM grades sold at a premium
idea: Use legacy test flows to bin dies by measured retention (256 ms, 1 s at 45 C) and program the refresh setting into SPD. Long-retention bins go to battery devices; leaky bins go to cooled data centers.
why: Monetizes the existing retention spread with zero capex, cutting refresh energy ~75% in the premium segment.

title: Legacy DDR4 dies aggregated by a 28nm CXL base
idea: Co-package 8-16 dies from mature DDR4 lines on a 28 nm logic base that runs the DDR4 cores slowly but wide in parallel and exposes a CXL memory interface, taking over refresh management, ECC and hammer mitigation in the base.
why: Supply and capital (fact 4): turns trailing DDR4 capacity into a usable server memory tier at near-zero capex; base dies can be made in U.S. trailing fabs.

title: Cross-die shared redundancy pool for stacked memory
idea: Combine stack interconnect with repair: rather than each die carrying its own spare rows and columns, pool spares on one die (or spread across the stack) and remap failing rows of any die through the base die's TSV/bond network with a content-addressable remap table.
why: HBM yield (fact 6, 20-30% loss): stack-level sparing rescues dies that fail per-die repair, raising stack yield ~10-15 points and trimming per-die spare area 2-3%.

title: Segment-base hardware makes 32-bit compressed pointers universal
idea: Combine x86-style segment base registers with pointer compression: the load/store unit adds a per-region base plus a 3-bit shift to 32-bit references in a single cycle, so C/C++/Rust allocators and runtimes can use compressed pointers in any heap, not only JVM/V8-style ones.
why: Pointer-heavy structures (graphs, trees, ASTs, indexes) shrink 30-40%.

title: Retired DDR4 DIMMs pooled behind a compressing CXL controller
idea: Combine decommissioned DDR4 modules (built on pre-EUV nodes) with a 28 nm CXL pooling controller that adds inline compression and per-DIMM health remapping, deployed as the far-memory tier of new servers instead of being shredded.
why: Adds usable supply from bits that already exist with no fab; compression offsets lower density, and recyclers or OEMs can run it as a takeback business.

title: SmartNIC fuses page compression with far-memory transport
idea: Combine a 28 nm FPGA SmartNIC's packet pipeline with a page compressor: pages evicted to remote memory are compressed, encrypted and RDMA-sent in one pass, and on fault the NIC decompresses directly into the host page, so far memory costs no CPU and stores 2-3x more per remote GB.
why: Makes rack-level far memory over commodity Ethernet practical, so each server needs less local DRAM.
note: Combination of known far-memory and NIC offload.

title: Erasure-coded TSV lanes replace spare TSVs and repair fuses
idea: Combine network forward-error-correction with the TSV interface: data crosses the stack as Reed-Solomon codewords spread over all TSV lanes, so open or resistive TSVs are decoded as erasures in the base die instead of being steered to spare TSVs by fuses after test.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): removes spare-TSV area and repair-fuse test steps and tolerates in-field TSV failures; targets several points of stack yield and lower test cost.

title: Bank-fused salvage dies sold as partial-capacity SKUs
idea: Combine DRAM yield binning with CPU-style core harvesting. Dies whose failures exceed the redundancy budget have whole banks or bank groups e-fused off and are sold as 12 Gb, or as 3/4-capacity parts, with an SPD-declared address map that controllers already support.
why: Turns 3-8% of scrapped die per wafer into sellable bits, which lifts effective wafer output a few percent with no extra capex.

title: Pharma cold chain: a refrigerated memory tier near minus 30 C
idea: Adapted from the pharmaceutical cold chain: capacity DIMMs sit in sealed, dry-nitrogen-purged sleds on a separate glycol loop chilled to about -30 C by a shared rack chiller, and the controller scales the refresh interval with measured die temperature.
why: Junction leakage roughly halves every 8-10 C, so going from 85 C to -30 C stretches retention 100-1000x and nearly removes refresh (fact 3); chiller energy is shared across a rack, and wires and transistors also speed up.

title: SSD pSLC trick: aging regions downgrade to twin-cell differential mode
idea: Adapted from SSDs that run worn TLC blocks in pseudo-SLC mode: when telemetry shows a region's retention degrading, the controller reformats it so each bit uses two adjacent cells storing complementary charge, sensed differentially. The region loses half its capacity but gains ~4x retention and stays in service.
why: Graceful degradation instead of replacement: aging access devices (fact 3) no longer force faster refresh chip-wide or scrapping; capacity sheds in small steps and module life extends by years.
note: Twin-cell and CLR-DRAM prior art.

title: Particle-detector zero suppression for sparse data bursts
idea: Borrowed from LHC detector readout zero suppression: each column group computes a wired-OR nonzero flag during sensing, and bytes that are all zero are sent as a 1-bit tag instead of toggling global data lines and I/O drivers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): AI activations and KV caches are 30-60% zero bytes, so global-bus and I/O energy drop ~25-45% for <1% area.
note: Zero-value compression and DBI are known.

title: Caterpillar-style remanufacturing harvests DRAM from retired servers
idea: Adapted from Caterpillar Reman's core-deposit model. Hyperscalers return DIMMs from 4-6-year-old servers for a credit; a reman line desolders DRAM packages, burns them in, screens them at derated timings and rebuilds them into modules for edge, PC and CXL-pooled capacity tiers.
why: Retired servers hold enormous DRAM volume. Recovering even 30% adds supply with zero new wafers, helium, quartz or tungsten, at perhaps 30-50% of new cost per bit.

title: Ugly-produce partial-good DRAM dies with fused-out banks
idea: Adapted from grocers selling cosmetically imperfect produce. Bin DRAM dies that have dead banks or subarrays, which are normally scrapped, as partial-good parts: on-die fuses remap the address space, an SPD field reports usable capacity, and OS/CXL memory managers consume the odd-sized capacities.
why: Recovers ~3-8% of wafer output at advanced nodes. Each recovered bit already carries its full embedded helium, quartz, tungsten and energy, so it comes at zero extra resource.

title: Egg-grading economics: retention-graded dies sold with refresh maps
idea: Food grading sells every egg by grade; test each DRAM die's retention tail and sell weaker dies as a managed-refresh grade with a per-die weak-row map stored on the module, so the controller refreshes only those rows faster instead of the die being repaired or scrapped.
why: Effective fab output: recovers ~5-10% of dies lost to retention fails or repair limits and needs fewer redundant rows and fuses (fact 7); each yield point is ~1% cost per bit.

title: Postal ZIP codes: region-relative 32-bit pointers in hardware
idea: Borrowed from postal routing (zone plus local address): an ISA extension where pointers are 32-bit 'ZIP + offset' values resolved through a region register file in the load unit, letting native data structures use half-size pointers, not just JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; 20-35% footprint reduction across native code.

title: Satellite downlink budgets: storage-side filtering before data reaches DRAM
idea: Borrowed from Earth-observation satellites that process onboard because downlink is scarce: each query gets a 'downlink budget' in host DRAM bytes, and the planner pushes filters, projections and pre-aggregation into computational SSDs until the result fits, so raw scans never land in DRAM.
why: Analytics engines buffer raw columnar data in DRAM; pushing selection into storage cuts working-set DRAM 5-20x for selective queries.

title: Toyota kanban: WIP tokens keep fused-operator intermediates on-chip
idea: Borrowed from kanban cards that cap work-in-progress between stations: a dataflow accelerator passes hardware kanban tokens between fused operator stages, and a producer may emit a tile only when its consumer returns a token, bounding every intermediate tensor to a fixed SRAM budget so activations never touch DRAM.
why: Intermediates (often 30-60% of inference/training DRAM capacity and traffic) stay in SRAM with zero refresh; DRAM need shrinks to weights and checkpoints.

title: 1990s VCSEL ribbon optics disaggregate memory onto rack shelves
idea: Adapted from 1990s 12-channel 850 nm VCSEL parallel-optics datacom modules on multimode ribbon: memory moves to dedicated shelves linked to compute by many slow parallel VCSEL lanes, with driver and receiver chips at 180 nm or larger.
why: Raises usable supply through pooling and moves DRAM away from hot accelerators; mature GaAs VCSEL lines give ~5-10 pJ/bit at 2.5 Gb/s lanes, fine for capacity tiers.

title: Prestressed-concrete trick: stress films flatten ultra-thin memory stacks
idea: Adapted from prestressed concrete: calibrated PECVD nitride/oxide films are deposited on the back of each thinned DRAM die so their built-in stress cancels the warpage that appears at bonding temperature. 30 um dies then stack flat with simple thermocompression.
why: Warpage limits HBM yield and stack height (fact 6); targets both using 1990s deposition tools.
note: Backside stress films for warpage are routine practice.

title: Automotive remanufacturing: reclaimed server DRAM recertified with defect maps
idea: Adapted from remanufactured auto parts that are torn down, tested and resold with a warranty: retired DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs from hyperscaler decommissions run through a retention-and-hammer characterization rack built from off-the-shelf FPGA testers, weak rows are written into an SPD-extension defect map, and modules ship with firmware that makes the OS retire those pages at boot.
why: Supply and scarce resources: at ~4x prices, a recertified channel adds bits with zero wafers, helium, quartz or EUV; recovering even 10% of decommissioned modules is a meaningful share of annual bit supply.
note: Already done (Azure CXL DDR4 reuse, refurb resellers).

title: Outlet-store triage: route reject dies by failure type
idea: Adapted from garment outlets that sort irregulars by flaw type and sell each to a buyer who does not care about that flaw: dies that fail final test are classified on existing testers by signature (retention-weak, speed-weak, hammer-weak, stuck-bit) and packaged into matched products: retention-weak into high-refresh CXL tiers, speed-weak into low-clock edge devices, hammer-weak into read-mostly AI weight stores with low activation rates.
why: Yield and cost per bit (fact 4): each failure type is harmless in some workload; recovering 3-5% of currently scrapped dies adds bits from existing trailing and current lines with no new capacity.
note: Downgrade binning and second-tier resale already exist.

title: Airline fare classes: reliability-tiered cloud memory pricing
idea: Adapted from airline fare classes that sell the same seat at different prices with different guarantees: cloud providers offer VM memory in three tiers (full Chipkill ECC, single-error correction on relaxed refresh, detect-only on salvaged DRAM) at stepped prices, backed by separate physical pools and SLA terms stating error rates.
why: Supply and cost per bit: monetizes lower-reliability bits that would otherwise be scrapped and shifts tolerant workloads (batch analytics, caches, inference) off premium DRAM, stretching scarce supply.
note: Heterogeneous-reliability memory proposed (Luo et al. 2014); pricing tiers incremental.

title: Toyota RESCUE-style multi-tier chokepoint map with prequalified alternates
idea: Adapted from Toyota's post-2011 supplier database tracing parts to tier-N: map every DRAM input down to the mine or plant (quartz, tungsten, neon, resist monomers, helium), flag single-site nodes, and pay to dual-qualify alternates before a crisis.
why: Turns months-long disruptions (helium outage, Spruce Pine hurricane) into weeks; protects the ~5-15% of yearly output exposed to single-node events (scarce resources, supply).

title: Nuclear Navy pipeline: veteran reactor techs retrained as fab technicians
idea: Adapted from the U.S. Navy nuclear training model (rigid procedures, contamination control, shift discipline): a 6-month accelerated fab-technician program for transitioning nuclear and aviation-maintenance veterans, with signing bonuses and guaranteed fab placements.
why: The shortage of tens of thousands of technicians gates U.S. fab ramps; a disciplined, ready pool shortens ramp time and cuts labor-driven yield loss (U.S. manufacturability, time).
note: Fab veteran-hiring programs already exist.

title: Magnify the retention tail into a product: long-retention premium bin
idea: Measure each die's retention distribution at wafer sort and sell the top-quartile dies as 'LR' parts with a guaranteed 256 ms-1 s refresh spec at a premium to hyperscalers; controllers read the bin and lengthen tREFI accordingly.
why: Monetizes existing variation: 4-16x less refresh on LR parts, more effective bandwidth and lower power without new fabs.

title: Minify refresh by die position: per-die refresh in HBM stacks
idea: On an FPGA-with-HBM board, measure how retention varies with each die's position in the stack, then have a custom controller issue per-channel refresh at rates matched to each die's measured temperature and retention rather than the hottest die.
why: Refresh in 3D stacks: could cut refresh by about 30-40% on cooler dies, using firmware and controller IP that cost about $300k.
note: Temperature/retention-aware refresh well known; modest overall energy gain.

title: XOR-delta writes: send only the changed bytes
idea: MINIFY write traffic: the base die keeps the old cache line, the host sends only the nonzero bytes of new XOR old plus a bitmask, and the base die patches the row with a masked write.
why: Data-movement energy and write bandwidth: optimizer, gradient and KV updates are often sparse in bytes; claims 2-4x less write traffic.

title: Self-healing links with spare lanes and field remap
idea: MAGNIFY lane redundancy to ~10% spares with a base-die crossbar that keeps checking bump and TSV margins in service and retires links degraded by electromigration on the fly.
why: Lifetime and yield: packages repair their own wires instead of failing; claims 2x interconnect lifetime.

title: Memory leasing with guaranteed take-back and refurbishment
idea: MINIFY ownership: vendors lease HBM and CXL modules, take them back at end of term, refurbish and redeploy them, which gives them a financial reason to design for disassembly.
why: Effective supply and capital: each module serves 2-3 lifecycles; cuts buyer capex at a time when prices have risen 4x.

title: Magnify tolerated defects: Swiss-cheese DIMMs ship bad-page maps
idea: Sell DIMMs certified to contain up to 2% bad 4 KB pages, with the bad-page list in SPD. Firmware and the OS/hypervisor exclude those pages at boot, like NAND bad-block tables.
why: Fact 4: dies with clustered defects become sellable capacity instead of scrap, adding +5-15% sellable bits per wafer at ~2% capacity cost.

title: Magnify bit-significance split: unrefreshed, under-volted mantissa-LSB chips
idea: Bit-transpose bf16/fp8 tensors so low-order mantissa bits land on dedicated chips or banks that run with 4x longer refresh and lower VARY. Sign and exponent bits keep full ECC and nominal refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 10: about half of model-weight bits tolerate 1e-4 BER, so refresh and array energy on those chips drop ~50-75% for <0.1% accuracy loss.
note: Sparkk/EDEN already explored per-bit-significance refresh for approximate data.

title: Minify the quality bar: sell grade-B dies with defect maps
idea: Ship dies and HBM stacks that fail full spec with an on-module defect map (bad rows, columns, banks) that the controller or OS maps out badram-style, into AI KV caches, analytics and test tiers.
why: Monetizes the 10-30% yield loss, raising sellable bits per wafer ~10-20% at zero fab cost.

title: Eliminate refresh for ephemeral data: lifetime-tagged no-refresh DRAM regions
idea: Software tags allocations with a maximum lifetime (activations, gradients, KV-cache blocks consumed within milliseconds); the controller maps them to banks with refresh disabled, and a per-region epoch timer faults if data outlives the guaranteed retention bin. Data that dies before it decays is never refreshed.
why: AI activation traffic often lives <10-50 ms; removing refresh for 30-60% of HBM capacity eliminates the 16-33% idle-power refresh share and 10-20% bandwidth loss on those banks with no cell change.
note: Similar to RANA and partial-array refresh; low-risk, modest gain.

title: Eliminate charged cells: inversion encoding plus refresh skip for discharged rows
idea: Each row stores a 1-bit inversion flag chosen at write time so most cells sit in the discharged, non-leaking state; rows whose cells are all discharged (zero pages, sparse activations, quantized weights' high bits) are flagged and skipped by refresh.
why: AI tensors are 30-70% zero or sparse; skipping such rows and halving charged cells elsewhere cuts refresh count 30-50% and lowers row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Eliminate row decoders: token-passing wordlines for streaming memory tiers
idea: For sequential tiers (AI weights, KV-cache streams, checkpoints), remove the row decoder tree. Each wordline driver holds a one-bit token in a 2-transistor dynamic stage and passes it to the next row on every activate clock, so rows open in a fixed order. A 'jump' tap every 512 rows allows coarse seeks.
why: Removes the row decoder and predecoder (~4-6% of die) and ~15 address wires per mat. Random access is lost but streaming traffic (~80% of weight reads) keeps full bandwidth.

title: Eliminate the guest OS inside every VM with unikernel images
idea: Compile cloud services as unikernels or library OSes that link only the kernel functions they use, removing the 200 MB-1 GB guest kernel, init system and page cache that each VM duplicates.
why: Dense VM hosts carrying hundreds of guests recover 10-30% of host DRAM.

title: Eliminate host DRAM staging: GPU servers spec'd with quarter memory
idea: Use GPUDirect Storage loaders so weights and datasets go NVMe-to-HBM directly, and publish an open reference server spec with 256 GB host DRAM instead of 1-2 TB; it is a software plus integration business.
why: Host DRAM in AI servers, much of it staging buffers, is a large and growing DRAM sink; cuts of 4-8x per server are possible.

title: Die passport: on-die non-volatile test history ends retesting
idea: Eliminate repeated testing at every packaging step: each memory die carries a small OTP/ReRAM log written at wafer sort, burn-in and post-bond test (bin, repair map, timing margins, weak rows), read by the stacker and later by the system.
why: Test is ~10-20% of memory cost and HBM retests dies several times; passports cut test time ~30-50%, and systems use the weak-row map to avoid extra refresh.

title: Eliminate refresh for compiler-proven short-lived tensor pages
idea: Stop treating refresh as a service every page gets. The ML compiler/runtime proves that each activation or KV buffer is rewritten or freed within T_live (typically under 5 ms) and tags its pages with a page-table 'lifetime' bit. The controller's refresh engine then skips any row whose last write is younger than the measured worst-case retention minus a margin.
why: Refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth, fact 3): 60-80% of AI DRAM traffic is short-lived, so refresh operations drop ~3-5x, and weaker-retention cells become acceptable for those pages.
note: Smart Refresh/RANA-style skipping is known.

title: Eliminate scrap: sell out-of-spec dies as BER-certified AI memory
idea: Dies that fail retention or refresh specs are not discarded. Each is graded by measured raw BER and retention, then sold as a discounted 'AI-grade' module whose controller applies stronger ECC and shorter refresh. Inference clusters buy the cheaper GB.
why: Turns yield loss (often 5-15% on leading nodes) into sellable supply with no new wafers; a fast capacity lever during the shortage.
note: Binning and salvage of sub-spec dies already practiced (e.g., SpecTek).

title: Eliminate spare rows and fuses: base-die CAM remaps failing blocks
idea: Remove redundant rows and columns and the laser/e-fuse blocks from the DRAM core. An HBM/CXL logic die holds a CAM plus a spare SRAM/DRAM pool that remaps any failing 64 B block at any point in life. The CAM is filled from test results and field ECC events.
why: Redundancy plus fuses take ~3-6% of the die, and repair is one-shot; lifelong, fine-grained remap recovers that area and saves dies with clustered defects.

title: Eliminate the end-of-life cliff: ECC rate that grows with age
idea: Partition memory into regions whose code rate the controller can reprogram, e.g. from 64/72 up to 64/80. When scrubbing reports rising error rates from aging, VRT or hammer damage, a region trades capacity for a stronger code and the OS shrinks its advertised size.
why: Allows shipping lower-margin dies and extends fleet module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand during the shortage.

title: Eliminate retention-fail scrap: sell weak dies as fast-refresh grade
idea: Eliminate the 64 ms retention gate: dies that fail 64 ms but pass 16-32 ms are bought, binned and sold with an SPD flag that forces the controller's existing 2x/4x refresh mode; ~$400k for binning and qualification.
why: Converts retention-tail rejects into usable bits for bandwidth-insensitive capacity tiers at a small refresh-energy penalty.

title: Fuse-less DRAM: host controller holds the repair map
idea: Reverse who repairs: the die ships without fuse/antifuse banks or address-compare redundancy logic; failing rows and columns are recorded in a signed on-module SPD map at test, and the memory controller or OS remaps them to spare rows at boot.
why: Fact 7: removes fuse banks, redundancy comparators and post-package-repair circuits (~3-5% die); spare rows become ordinary capacity when unused.

title: Reverse logistics: remanufacture retired server DRAM
idea: Reverse the supply flow: build industrial lines that harvest DRAM packages from decommissioned servers, re-ball them, run a burn-in and binning test, and re-module them into certified 'second-life' DIMMs for less demanding tiers.
why: Adds supply with ~1% of fab capex per bit; hyperscalers retire many exabytes-years of working DRAM every year.
note: Refurb DIMM market already exists; supply adds at low capex.

title: 32-bit relative pointers ABI shrinks C/C++ heaps
idea: Reverse the 64-bit default: an allocator ABI puts each process's heap in 4 GB regions and the compiler stores pointers as 32-bit offsets from a region base register (as Java compressed oops and V8 already do), using fat pointers only where regions are crossed.
why: Pointer-heavy data structures shrink 25-40%, recovering DRAM through a recompile of software on existing CPUs.

title: Quarantine hot aggressor rows inside a moat subarray
idea: Flip mitigation from victims to aggressors: a row exceeding the hammer threshold is migrated into a small quarantine subarray where every occupied row is flanked by two never-used guard rows, so further hammering finds no victims; it migrates back when it cools.
why: Row hammer: replaces repeated victim refreshes (bandwidth tax) with one migration; costs ~0.5% capacity for the moat.
note: Essentially AQUA.

title: Nonvolatile fault-map sidecar remembers weak cells across power cycles
idea: Rearrange where reliability knowledge lives: a small MRAM chiplet patterned by argon ion-beam etching (no fluorinated chemistry) is co-packaged with each DRAM stack and stores per-row retention classes, hammer thresholds and patch lists, so profiling survives power-off and travels with the module.
why: Makes field profiling, per-row refresh and host-owned repair practical without re-profiling at every boot.
note: Storing retention/weak-row profiles in SPD-like NV storage is close to existing practice.

title: Excessive action: multi-row activation sums redundant copies in weak mats
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: in mats with weak cells or high temperature the controller writes each bit into 2-4 rows sharing the same bitlines and later opens them together so their charges sum on the bitline, trading capacity for 2-4x signal instead of scrapping the die or raising refresh.
why: Facts 1 and 3: dies with weak tails sell at reduced capacity instead of being scrapped (yield ~+5-15%), and refresh in redundant mode can drop ~4x.

title: Retired server DIMMs reharvested into pooled CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round, memory flowing back up the supply chain: hyperscalers return DDR4/DDR5 from decommissioned servers to a qualification line. The line desolders the DRAM, retests it at speed and temperature, bins it by retention class, and rebuilds it onto CXL Type-3 expander cards for capacity tiers.
why: Adds usable DRAM supply with zero wafers, at ~30-50% of the cost per bit of new parts. A large share of retired server DRAM is still functional.

title: Per-recipe scarcity ledger that feeds back into process engineering
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: meter each tool's use per wafer of He, ALD precursors, fluorinated gases, UPW and kWh. Price each at a shadow scarcity cost (e.g., helium at its outage price) inside the fab's cost-per-bit model, so recipe changes are scored and rewarded on scarce-resource reduction.
why: Sustained sub-metering feedback has delivered 20-40% resource cuts in energy programs. This applies the same loop to every chokepoint input at once.
note: Shadow-priced sub-metering is sound management practice; incremental.

title: Follow-the-moon placement of memory-hungry jobs across regions
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: route memory-heavy batch work (long-context KV-heavy jobs, analytics, fine-tuning) to whichever regions are in their nightly interactive trough, so each region's DRAM is sized for the global average instead of its own daytime peak plus batch.
why: Diurnal peak-to-trough ratios of 2-3x mean 20-35% less global DRAM; needs only schedulers and existing networks.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM freezes model weights into old-node silicon
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: freeze 'liquid' read-only weights into 'solid' via-programmed NOR/NAND mask ROM on 180 nm lines, where only one via mask changes per model, so frozen weights and vocabulary tables leave DRAM for cheap, refresh-free, one-transistor-per-bit storage.
why: Removes read-only data from DRAM for edge and embedded inference with zero refresh and cheap masks (~$20-50k); density of ~0.1-0.2 GB/cm2 limits it to small models.

title: Factory weak-cell dictionary turns errors into cheap erasures
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: each die's weak-cell addresses found at sort are compressed into on-package antifuse/NOR storage and loaded into the decoder at boot, which treats those positions as erasures (one check symbol each instead of two for an unknown error).
why: About 2x correction capability from the same parity, so dies failing today's retention bins pass; a few % yield plus longer refresh at no area cost.
note: Known-defect erasure decoding is classic (ArchShield-like fault maps).

title: Parameter change: chilled-grade DRAM with one-mask on-die thermistor guarantee
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: dies failing retention at 85 C but passing at 45 C ship as 'chilled grade' for liquid-cooled racks; one added mask adds a thin-film thermistor so the controller enforces the operating window and doubles refresh if exceeded.
why: Retention yield: leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, recovering a slice of dies scrapped today.

title: Lizard basking: per-tier refresh follows the stack's thermal gradient
idea: Lizards shuttle between sun and shade; in a 3D stack over logic, top tiers near the spreader run ~10-15 C cooler than bottom tiers, so embed a thermistor per tier group, refresh each tier at its own temperature-derived rate, and place refresh-sensitive or rarely touched data in the coolest tiers.
why: Uniform worst-case refresh at 125 C wastes ~2x on cooler tiers; tier-specific refresh recovers 30-50% of refresh energy and bandwidth at grade-1 temperatures.

title: Pit-viper pit organs: canary cells time refresh per mat at 125 C
idea: Pit vipers sense heat with dedicated ultra-sensitive organs; put deliberately weakened canary cells (smaller capacitor, wider access device) in every 3D mat, check them each refresh tick, and refresh a mat only when its canaries start to fail, measuring real leakage at the actual local temperature and age.
why: Grade-1 parts otherwise refresh at worst-case 125 C end-of-life rates; canary-timed refresh cuts refresh 2-4x in typical conditions while staying safe as devices age over 10 years.

title: Hermit-crab re-shelling: retired DDR4 rehoused in CXL expanders
idea: Hermit crabs move into shells that others discard. Buy DDR4 DIMMs from server decommissioning, screen them with a 24-hour retention and row-hammer test, and resell them inside CXL Type-3 expander cards with DDR4 controllers as a warm memory tier.
why: Recovers exabytes of working DRAM that would otherwise be shredded, adding supply in weeks with no wafers, helium or quartz at perhaps 20-30% of new DDR5 cost per GB.

title: Immune self-tolerance binning keeps dies with weak cells
idea: The immune system learns to tolerate self after thymic screening instead of destroying every odd cell. At wafer sort, write each die's weak-retention rows into an on-die fuse self-map and ship the die with per-row adaptive refresh and remapping, instead of scrapping dies that fail a uniform 64 ms test.
why: Raises good-die yield 5-15% at 1-beta/1-gamma nodes, so fewer wafers (and less quartz, helium and energy) go into each GB sold.

title: Apoptotic eat-me telemetry retires memory packages before they fail
idea: Like cells displaying phosphatidylserine before apoptosis, each DRAM package exports correctable-error rate, retention drift and hammer-count signals; crossing a threshold triggers live migration of its pages and schedules a tool-less swap of just that unit, so failures never crash jobs or force whole-board scrap.
why: Repairability: removes ~10% just-in-case DRAM headroom and extends module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand.

title: Salamander regeneration: rewritable row remapping that never runs out
idea: One-time fuse-based post-package repair is replaced by a rewritable on-module remap SRAM plus spare rows reserved per bank, so as cells weaken with age the module regrows healthy rows indefinitely and recycled chips are re-repaired at every life cycle.
why: Lifetime and reuse yield: second-life DRAM usable at 95%+ capacity instead of being binned out.
note: Soft PPR and controller remapping already exist.

title: Datacenter spleen grades and recirculates aging memory modules
idea: The spleen filters old red blood cells and recycles their iron; a campus test station receives every pulled module, characterizes retention, hammer threshold and speed, and re-dispatches it to the tier it can still serve (hot, warm, approximate, scrap), feeding results back to procurement.
why: Supply: longer useful life for every purchased bit; 20-30% less new DRAM procured per year.
note: Grading and redeploying pulled modules; same reuse core as I-04900.

title: Hermit-crab reuse: re-home DRAM from retired modules into CXL expanders
idea: Hermit crabs move into shells others have left. A U.S. reverse-logistics business does the same for retired server DIMMs and boards: robots desolder the DRAM packages, which are retested, speed-binned and graded for warranty, then re-mounted in high-capacity CXL memory expanders that hide their slower speed behind tiering.
why: Usable supply and U.S. manufacturability: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4/DDR5 modules a year; re-homing even 10% of that adds several % effective supply with near-zero wafer capital.
note: Same retired-DRAM-to-CXL reuse mechanism.

title: Apoptotic cascade: retire a failing page's predicted spatial accomplices
idea: Apoptotic cells signal their neighbours; when the OS retires a page for a hard error, a learned fault-cluster model of the die (shared wordline, bitline, sub-wordline driver, TSV column) pre-emptively migrates and retires the physically co-located pages most likely to fail next, before they produce uncorrectable errors.
why: Field reliability of weaker, cheaper bins: most uncorrectable errors come from spatially clustered faults; pre-emptive retirement could cut UE rates ~5-10x for <0.1% capacity, letting marginal dies ship.

title: Tardigrade tun state: idle pages dehydrate into strong code, slow refresh
idea: Tardigrades survive by shutting down into a protective tun; pages untouched for N seconds are compressed and rewritten with a heavy BCH/LDPC code in the space freed, and their rows move to a 10-30x slower refresh tier, rehydrating on first access.
why: Refresh at 32-64 Gb (16-33% of idle power): most memory is idle at any instant; strong coding absorbs the higher raw BER of seconds-long refresh, cutting idle refresh energy ~10x.
note: Close to Morphable ECC (idle strong code plus slow refresh).

title: Evaporating pheromone memory: never refresh data born to expire
idea: Ant pheromone trails are useful because they evaporate; an allocator API lets software tag buffers (activations, KV-cache spills, packets, shuffle data) with a time-to-live shorter than the region's measured retention, and the controller never refreshes those rows, simply reclaiming them at expiry.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth: transient buffers are a large share of AI traffic and live microseconds to milliseconds; zero refresh for them saves their share of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.
note: Dead-data refresh skipping is published art (semantic/ESKIMO-style refresh).

title: Detritivore economy: reclaim rejected and partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Decomposers turn waste into food; buy the 10-25% of DRAM dies and HBM stacks that fail bin (retention, speed, partial array) at near-scrap prices, package them on CXL expanders whose controller maps around dead regions and runs them at 4x refresh and relaxed timing, and sell them as capacity-tier memory.
why: Supply and cost: fab yield loss is a large pool of nearly free bits; marginal cost ~1/100 of good parts, adding a few % of global bit supply with zero new fab capex.

title: Mycorrhizal memory commons: cross-tenant DRAM lending over CXL fabric
idea: Like fungal networks shuttling carbon from sun-rich trees to shaded ones, rack-scale CXL 3.x switches let servers with idle DRAM lend pages to memory-starved neighbours. A broker reads per-host free-memory telemetry, rebalances continuously, and pays lenders per GB-hour from a 'carbon credit' ledger.
why: Clouds strand ~20-30% of installed DRAM; recovering half of it raises usable supply ~10-15% with zero new wafers (supply, cost per bit).

title: Pando clonal SRAM chiplets from oversupplied 28 nm logic
idea: Pando is one aspen organism expressed as thousands of identical stems on shared roots. A standard UCIe SRAM chiplet, identical across foundries and traded as a commodity like DDR, is made in oversupplied 28-40 nm fabs and stacked under accelerators as last-level memory.
why: Moves a slice of HBM demand (10-20% of working-set hits) to idle mature capacity; latch cells have unlimited endurance and no capacitor.

title: Airline departure board: compiler-published buffer lifetimes elide refresh entirely
idea: Airlines know every departure in advance and staff gates accordingly. AI accelerator compilers know statically when each activation or gradient buffer is next rewritten; they publish per-region lifetimes to the memory controller, which skips refresh for any row guaranteed to be rewritten or freed within tREFW.
why: Training activations live milliseconds, so 40-70% of HBM rows may never need refresh in such workloads, recovering much of the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: Camel-nose countercurrent cascade rinses for periphery wet benches
idea: A camel's nasal turbinates recover exhaled water by countercurrent exchange. Plumb periphery wet benches as 4-stage countercurrent cascades: fresh UPW enters only the final rinse and its overflow feeds the stage before, with inline resistivity/TOC sensors advancing wafers instead of timed overflow; periphery's relaxed contamination spec permits it.
why: Water: rinse water per periphery clean falls ~8-12x (efficiency compounds with stage count) with no new chemistry.

title: Radio broadcast reads: one activation multicast to many consumers
idea: One transmitter serves a whole city; in a 3D DRAM-on-logic stack, activate a row of shared weights once and multicast it over a base-die broadcast bus to all 16-64 compute tiles subscribed to that row address in the same step (batched or tensor-parallel inference).
why: Activation and movement energy (facts 5, 8): one access serves N consumers; claims 10-60x lower energy per delivered weight in batched inference.
note: Batched inference already amortizes weight reads via on-chip buffers.

title: MRI zero-boil-off logic: per-tool helium recapture and reliquefaction
idea: Borrowing from MRI magnets that went 'zero boil-off' with cold-head recondensers: fit every etch/deposition cluster with a helium recapture manifold on electrostatic-chuck backside-gas leak paths, load-lock purges and leak-check exhaust, feeding a small cryocooler purifier that recompresses or reliquefies He for reuse. Fab helium becomes a closed inventory topped up a few percent per month instead of a consumable.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium supply has been offline since March 2026; recapture cuts purchased helium per wafer by ~80-90% and decouples DRAM output from the helium chokepoint.
note: Same per-tool He recapture as I-11246.

title: MRI zero-boil-off approach: helium recapture skids for fab tools
idea: Borrowed from modern MRI magnets, which lose almost no helium because a cryocooler recondenses boil-off: a small team builds bolt-on skids that collect helium from chuck backside, leak-check and purge exhausts, run it through a membrane separator, pressure-swing adsorber and cryo-purifier, and return 6N helium to the tool manifold.
why: Scarce resource: recapturing 70-90% of fab helium shields DRAM output from the Qatar outage for roughly $1M per fab.

title: Actuarial adaptive test: warranty-priced risk replaces blanket burn-in
idea: Borrowed from insurers, who price risk statistically instead of inspecting every customer: a small team builds a model using each die's inline and probe parametrics to predict field-failure probability, skips long burn-in and retention screens for the low-risk ~80%, and backs the shipped population with a priced warranty reserve.
why: Capital: DRAM test and burn-in is ~10-15% of back-end capex and a throughput bottleneck; adaptive test can cut tester-hours 30-50%.

title: Airline overbooking for RAM: overcommit by measured no-show rate
idea: Hypervisors record, per application class, the fraction of allocated memory never touched ('no-shows') and overbook physical DRAM by that rate, with a pre-agreed bump protocol (compress, then demote to CXL flash) for rare oversubscription and a yield-managed premium for guaranteed seats.
why: Cloud VMs often touch only 40-60% of allocated RAM; statistical overbooking could cut provisioned DRAM per VM 25-40%.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired DDR4 reborn in CXL cold tiers
idea: Like EV batteries repurposed for grid storage, harvest DDR4 DIMMs from decommissioned servers, bin them with a test robot, and mount them in CXL expansion boxes acting as a compressed cold tier behind new DDR5.
why: Avoids buying new bits for the coldest 30-50% of memory; supply relief at near-zero marginal cost and zero new wafers.

title: Shared parking for memory: co-locate day and night workloads
idea: Like office parking reused by residents at night, pair anti-correlated workloads (daytime inference, night batch training/ETL) on one DRAM pool and swap working sets via fast NVMe snapshots at shift change, sizing DRAM to the peak of the sum rather than the sum of peaks.
why: Peak-of-sum vs sum-of-peaks can save 30-45% of fleet DRAM where diurnal patterns are strong.
note: Diurnal colocation and harvest VMs are known practice.

title: Fractional-reserve memory banking with a CXL reserve pool
idea: A bank keeps only part of its deposits as cash. Servers likewise promise more DRAM than they hold, and a rack CXL pool acts as the reserve. A telemetry-driven 'reserve ratio' sets how much local DRAM backs promised capacity. When a run starts, a 'lender of last resort' compresses cold pages to a swap tier.
why: Cloud DRAM is often 40-60% stranded or idle. Overcommit backed by a pooled reserve could cut DRAM bought per server by 20-35% at the same SLA.
note: Close to Microsoft Pond pooling and overcommit.

title: Noise-shaped bit-plane placement of AI tensors in weak rows
idea: Audio noise shaping pushes quantization noise into bands nobody hears. Weights and KV-cache are stored bit-plane transposed. Sign, exponent and high mantissa planes go to profiled strong rows with ECC. Low mantissa planes go to weak rows at relaxed refresh (about 1 s) with no ECC, where any flips land as tiny numeric noise. The software allocator and profiler fit within $1M.
why: Refresh on 50-70% of AI memory could drop 10x, the ECC overhead goes away for those planes, and accuracy loss stays below ~0.1% (facts 3 and 5).

title: HARQ incremental redundancy: strong parity fetched only on decode failure
idea: LTE's HARQ sends extra redundancy only when the first decode fails. Light SEC-DED is stored inline, and strong BCH/RS incremental parity lives in a separate parity region in another bank. The controller fetches the strong parity only when the inline decode flags an uncorrectable error. Writes to the parity region are coalesced.
why: Strong correction (tolerating 10-100x more weak cells, so refresh can run 2-4x longer) at near-zero read-bandwidth cost (facts 3 and 5). FPGA demo on DDR5.

title: Five-star tube grading reborn: retention-graded DRAM for relaxed refresh
idea: Revive the military practice of hand-selecting premium 'five-star' vacuum tubes: test every U.S.-made DRAM die for retention on U.S. testers, bin the tail-free fraction as long-retention parts certified for a 4-8x refresh interval, and sell them at a premium to U.S. hyperscalers whose controllers apply the certified interval.
why: Monetizes the natural retention distribution (fact 3): 4-8x less refresh energy and bandwidth on graded parts with no process change, and a business case for domestic fabs.
note: Vendors already bin; retention-graded parts studied in RAIDR/AVATAR; VRT undermines static grading.

title: Audio-RAM revival: sell partially defective DRAM for tolerant AI workloads
idea: Revive 1980s ARAM, defective DRAM sold for answering machines: bin HBM/DDR dies that fail full spec, burn their bad-row maps into on-die fuses/SPD, and sell them for error-tolerant KV cache and low-precision activation storage, with the OS/runtime retiring the mapped rows.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: HBM yield loss is 20-30%, and recovering half of it raises usable bits per wafer 10-15% with no new capacity.

title: Wartime salvage drive for DRAM: harvest chips from retired servers
idea: Revive WWII scrap-salvage logistics for memory: collect DDR4/DDR5 modules from decommissioned servers, robotically desolder and re-ball the packages, burn-in and retest them, and rebuild them onto CXL memory-expander cards pooled as a slower tier.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: millions of server DIMMs are shredded every year, and reuse adds supply with zero wafers, helium or quartz; claims several percent of annual bit demand.

title: Erlang-B trunk dimensioning for rack-pooled CXL memory
idea: Treat servers' memory peaks like telephone call traffic: the rack shares a CXL memory 'trunk' sized with Erlang-B for a 0.1% blocking target, and blocked requests overflow to compressed swap the way blocked calls overflowed to alternate routes. Each server keeps only its base load locally.
why: Per-server peak provisioning wastes the peak-to-mean gap; statistical multiplexing over 32-64 servers cuts rack DRAM 30-45%.

title: Cray-2 Fluorinert revival: boiling-pinned memory retunes refresh without water
idea: The Cray-2 (1985) ran its stacked boards submerged in circulating Fluorinert. Immerse DIMMs and HBM in a low-GWP two-phase fluid boiling at ~50 C, which pins every die at that temperature, then calibrate refresh interval, sense trims and ECC strength once for 50 C instead of the 85-95 C worst case; vapour is condensed by dry coolers.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): dry condensers need no evaporative towers (WUE ~1.8 to <0.1 L/kWh, >10x), and a pinned 50 C die leaks ~8x less than at 85 C, so refresh falls ~4-8x and the retention tail stops limiting weaker cells.

title: Staktek-Style Package Stacking to Bypass the TSV Bottleneck
idea: Revive the 1990s Staktek/Dense-Pac technique of stacking finished, fully tested packages with flex-frame rails: towers of 4-8 conventional wire-bonded DDR5 packages per site build 256-512 GB capacity RDIMMs on ordinary OSAT lines instead of TSV lines.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV stacks use ~3x the wafer area per bit and lose 20-30% yield; package stacking uses standard dies, known-good packages and idle OSAT capacity for the capacity tier, freeing TSV capacity for HBM.

title: Data that dies young: refresh-free banks for transient tensors
idea: Inverts 'every byte must be retained until overwritten': the compiler tags each AI tensor with its lifetime (activations and KV segments often live <10 ms), and the memory controller places them in banks whose refresh is masked off, guaranteeing reuse or overwrite within the profiled retention window; only weights and long-lived state sit in refreshed banks.
why: Removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) for most accelerator traffic (worth ~10-20% bandwidth and much of idle power) with only a per-bank refresh-mask command.

title: No fuses, no spare rows: ship DRAM with a signed defect map
idea: Inverting 'every die must look perfect': delete redundant rows/columns, fuse banks and repair logic; at test, write each die's failing 4 KB pages into a signed SPD defect map and have the memory controller or OS allocator skip them like NAND bad blocks.
why: Recovers ~5-8% die area plus repair test time and raises sellable yield, for ~6-10% lower cost per bit with low technical risk; needs controller/OS support.

title: Follow-the-moon: shift memory-heavy batch to regions with idle DRAM
idea: Inverts 'memory demand is local in time': a global scheduler moves memory-bound batch work (index builds, embedding generation, training-data prep) to datacenters in their night trough, where DRAM sits idle after interactive demand falls.
why: Interactive fleets are sized for diurnal peaks and leave 30-50% of DRAM idle off-peak; time-shifting avoids buying new DRAM for batch growth.

title: Read-mostly asymmetric links: fat downstream lanes, thin upstream lane
idea: Invert 'memory links are symmetric and bidirectional': inference reads 20-100x more than it writes, so build PHYs with unidirectional memory-to-host lanes (no turnaround, simpler drivers and termination) plus a narrow write lane.
why: Removes turnaround penalty and halves transceiver complexity per lane; ~20-30% more usable bandwidth per pin and smaller PHY area.

title: Recruit Elpida and Qimonda diaspora engineers to seed U.S. fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM talent only exists inside incumbent vendors': a fellowship pays retired or displaced engineers from Elpida, Qimonda and closed DRAM lines to transfer process know-how and train U.S. technicians at new fabs and community-college programs.
why: U.S. manufacturability: talent is a hidden chokepoint; shortens new-entrant ramp learning curves by years.
note: Already how CXMT and others ramped.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal at 400 C erasing the leakage tail
idea: The <=13 fA retention-tail cells come from trap-assisted tunneling through a few interface and junction dangling bonds. A 20 atm D2 anneal at 400 C passivates them, and the Si-D bond resists hot-carrier and field depassivation several times better than Si-H, cutting the tail at its physical source.
why: Pushing the tail out 10x stretches refresh intervals 2-4x, saving ~50-75% of refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) with one anneal step that fits existing fabs.
note: High-pressure D2 anneal already used commercially.

title: Controller-held repair map deletes on-die fuses and compare logic
idea: Repair information is only (#faulty rows x log2 N) bits, a few kbit, yet fuse banks and address comparators cost percent-level die area. Ship dies with no redundancy steering; the bad-row/column map measured at test is stored in the module SPD and the host controller remaps physical addresses.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~3-5% die area recovered; repairs become updatable in field.

title: Harvest DRAM dies from retired servers into CXL memory pools
idea: Charge storage causes no atomic change, so DRAM has no wear-out and a retired DIMM's dies still embody every scarce input. Desolder and retest dies at scale, rebin by speed and retention, and repackage them into CXL Type-3 expanders with stronger ECC and patrol scrub as tier-2 memory.
why: Adds ~10-20% of annual DRAM bit supply with zero new wafers, helium, quartz or tungsten, as a US remanufacturing business.
note: Same retired-die harvest into CXL as I-01583.

title: Exponent-dictionary storage for BF16 and FP8 tensors
idea: Measured from the data, the 8-bit exponent field of trained BF16 weights and activations holds only ~2.5-3 bits of entropy because values cluster within a few octaves. Logic on the HBM/CXL base die stores each 128-value block as 3-bit codes into a per-block 8-entry exponent palette plus raw sign and mantissa, with a raw fallback for outlier blocks.
why: Lossless ~1.4x smaller tensors (16 bits to ~11.4 bits per value) with bit-exact results, so a model that needed 8 HBM stacks fits in 6.
note: DFloat11/ZipNN known; ~1.4x.

title: Stack-distance profiler sizing each VM's DRAM to its miss-curve knee
idea: The minimum DRAM a workload needs is set by its reuse-distance distribution, not its allocation. A hardware Mattson stack-distance sampler in the memory controller (hashed address sampling with a small SHARDS-style tree) builds each VM's miss-ratio curve in real time; the hypervisor grants local DRAM up to the knee and backs the tail with compressed or CXL memory.
why: Servers carry 25-40% more DRAM than the measured knee; sizing to it cuts purchases ~20-30% at <2% slowdown.
note: SHARDS/MRC-based memory sizing is known; hardware sampler is incremental.

title: Phase-shifting jobs to anticorrelate memory peaks in a pool
idea: Provisioning for the sum of peaks instead of the peak of the sum wastes capacity. A scheduler fingerprints each job's memory-over-time curve (batch ETL, training checkpoints, nightly builds) and offsets start times so that peaks interleave, then sizes the shared pool to the measured peak of the sum plus a margin.
why: In mixed fleets the peak of the sum is typically 30-50% below the sum of peaks, and pool DRAM falls by about as much.

title: Sub-ambient coolant loop priced against Arrhenius refresh savings
idea: Tail leakage has Ea ~0.6-0.9 eV, so retention doubles every ~8-10 C, and dropping junctions from 85 C to 25 C buys ~60-100x retention. Route 10 C facility water to the memory cold plates first, and let on-die sensors stretch refresh to 1-4 s.
