why: Row hammer (fact 9): guard rows normally waste up to ~50% capacity; storing parity in them turns wasted space into correction capability on existing DRAM with software only.

title: Chaos engineering certifies software so memory specs can relax
idea: Adapted from Netflix-style chaos engineering, which injects failures in production until systems tolerate them: a hypervisor-level injector flips random bits in tagged memory regions at controlled rates, and applications that pass sustained injection at BER ~1e-7 are certified to run on relaxed memory pools with weaker ECC, longer refresh and lower-bin dies.
why: Cost per bit and supply: creates demand for lower-reliability bits that existing fabs can produce with relaxed test and repair, raising sellable yield without new capacity.

title: Telecom line coding: hammer-aware coset scrambling chosen per row
idea: Adapted from line codes (8b/10b, DC-balanced scramblers) that avoid patterns a channel handles badly: the memory controller tries 4 scrambler seeds on each row write and picks the one that minimizes known worst-case victim-aggressor stripe patterns (alternating data opposite to neighbors), storing the 2-bit seed index in spare ECC bits.
why: Row hammer and pattern-dependent retention (facts 3, 9): flip probability depends strongly on data pattern; avoiding worst patterns could raise the effective hammer threshold ~2-5x on existing chips with controller logic only.

title: Blood-bank cross-matching of DRAM dies to workload retention needs
idea: Adapted from blood typing and cross-matching: each die's retention tail, row-hammer threshold and timing margin are encoded as a 'blood type' in SPD. The memory scheduler cross-matches dies that fail the 64 ms JEDEC retention spec to workloads that rewrite data constantly (KV caches, activations, stream buffers), where natural rewrites stand in for refresh.
why: Recovers dies now scrapped or downbinned (a few % of output) at full value and cuts refresh energy on matched workloads (Facts 3 and 9; cost per bit).

title: Five-minute electricity-style spot market for pooled CXL memory
idea: Adapted from grid operators' 5-minute real-time dispatch: rack-level CXL memory pools post free GB every 5 minutes into an internal auction. Tenants bid by latency tier, and the hypervisor migrates pages to the winners, with locational prices for near and far pools.
why: Clouds strand ~25-50% of provisioned DRAM; marginal pricing pushes utilization toward ~80% and cuts DRAM bought per workload ~20-30% (usable supply).

title: Kidney paired-exchange matching for surplus memory inventories
idea: Adapted from kidney paired-donation chains: a clearinghouse runs a matching algorithm over firms' surplus and needed memory SKUs (DDR4 vs DDR5, LPDDR vs GDDR, dies vs modules) to form multi-party swap chains, with escrow and standardized incoming test.
why: In shortages, billions of dollars of wrong-type inventory sit idle; matching could free several % of effective supply within weeks (usable supply).

title: Minify charged cells: discharge-biased coding skips empty-row refresh
idea: The controller encodes each line (XOR with a learned base plus bus-invert, polarity flipped for true/anti-cell subarrays) so >90% of cells sit in the discharged, non-leaking state, and a per-row flag marks rows with no charged cells, which are never refreshed.
why: Only charged cells need refresh; zero-heavy and sparse tensor data yields 2-5x fewer refreshed rows.

title: Shift-register row sequencer replaces decoders in streaming banks
idea: MINIFY the row decoder in designated stream banks to a circular shift register that advances one wordline per ACT plus a coarse 1-of-16 jump decoder, since AI weight and KV streams open rows in order; random traffic is steered to normal banks.
why: Fact 7: decoder area -80% and decode energy -70% in stream banks; ~5-8% die saved if half the banks stream.

title: Skip restore for read-once data like KV-cache streams
idea: MINIFY restore work: a read-and-forget command lets the SA latch the row without driving restore current back into the cells, and the controller marks the row invalid, for data consumed once (streamed activations, KV pages being evicted).
why: Fact 8: restore is ~40-50% of activation energy and time; skipping it raises effective bandwidth and reduces disturbance to neighbors.

title: Back-gate-pulsed dual-gate IGZO sense amplifiers
idea: Dual-gate IGZO SA transistors (<=350 C) get their back gate pulsed to +2 V only during the ~2-3 ns sense window, MAGNIFYING drive current ~3x, and parked at -1 V otherwise, MINIFYING leakage.
why: Facts 3 and 10: closes most of the oxide-versus-Si speed gap for over-array SAs while keeping periphery standby leakage near zero.

title: Magnify yield: stitch rejected DRAM dies into good ones
idea: Buy partially failing or downbinned DRAM dies at scrap prices, then pair three partial dies under a small remap and sparing logic die (FPGA first, then a $100k MPW ASIC) that presents one fully good logical die in a stacked package.
why: Scarce supply: turns DRAM yield fallout (a few % of output) into sellable capacity at about 30-50% of contract price, with no fab.
note: Vendors already sell off-spec dies; bare-die supply access and assembly cost are the risks.

title: Minify TSV count 4x with PAM-4 and time-multiplexed vias
idea: Design TSV transceivers that send PAM-4 at 2x the symbol rate, with 2:1 time-multiplexing, so a quarter of the TSVs carry the same bandwidth. Validate on a TSV interposer MPW and license to stack makers.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV keep-out area and drilling yield loss could fall about 4x. The test vehicle costs about $500k.

title: Minify precision on demand with bit-plane sliced storage
idea: Minify what stays resident by storing tensors, images and sensor arrays transposed into bit planes. The top planes live in DRAM and the low-order planes in CXL flash, which are fetched only when a consumer asks for full precision.
why: Many readers (previews, early training epochs, approximate queries) need only the top 4-8 bits, which gives ~1.5-3x less DRAM plus lower bandwidth.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive memory interface
idea: MINIFY clocking to zero: replace the DDR clock, DLLs and training with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive handshake coding between DRAM and host, so the I/O idles at zero dynamic power.
why: Interface idle power (DLL/PLL is a large share of DRAM standby I/O): claims 30-50% lower interface power and no training time.

title: Pluggable memory modules in an optical transceiver form factor
idea: MINIFY the replacement unit to a faceplate-pluggable module in an OSFP-like case holding DRAM plus a photonic link, hot-swapped like a network transceiver.
why: Memory pooled and serviceable at the rack edge; GPU packages no longer lock in memory; better utilization and repair.
note: Optical CXL memory pooling exists; OSFP form factor is a packaging twist.

title: Minify hammer-counter updates with 4-bit probabilistic Morris counters
idea: Keep a 4-bit Morris-style approximate counter per row in spare cells. On each activation an on-die LFSR increments it only with probability base^-c, so 4 bits span ~1k-30k activations and the counter is rewritten on only a few percent of activations. Victim refresh fires at a threshold set with a safety margin.
why: Fact 9: per-row activation tracking (PRAC-style) with 4x fewer counter bits and ~10-50x fewer read-modify-write updates, shrinking the tRC penalty of hammer defense.

title: Minify refresh to data lifetime with compiler-tagged ephemeral regions
idea: Allocators and AI runtimes tag buffers with their expected lifetime (activations, gradients and temporary KV pages live <50 ms). The DRAM exposes per-region no-refresh mode registers, and the controller refreshes only rows whose last write is older than their retention bin.
why: Fact 3: most HBM bytes in training and inference are rewritten faster than they leak, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss in those regions fall ~60-80%.

title: Minify protection for regenerable data: CRC-detect, then recompute
idea: Classify data as regenerable (activations, KV cache, decompressed copies, file cache) and store it with only an 8-bit CRC per 512 bits. On a mismatch the runtime recomputes or re-fetches it from the source instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 4: frees most side-band ECC bits for capacity (+~10%) and lets regenerable data sit in weaker or slower-refreshed bins.

title: Magnify off-resistance with two series oxide TFTs per cell
idea: Each cell uses two oxide TFTs in series on the same wordline, since glass area is cheap. The stack effect lowers off-state leakage, and one leaky transistor can no longer drain the cell.
why: Fact 3: both independent devices must be leaky for a cell to fail, which squares the tail probability (1e-6 to 1e-12), so refresh can be set by the median.

title: Eliminate the one-size retention spec: per-die retention descriptor standard
idea: Propose a JEDEC extension in which each die stores its measured retention distribution (per bank, per temperature) in an on-die fuse table and the host sets tREFI per bank from it; validated dies advertise 128-512 ms classes. The single worst-case 64 ms contract disappears.
why: Most dies retain far longer than spec; per-die refresh rates cut refresh power and bandwidth loss 2-8x industry-wide with zero fab capital.

title: Eliminate refresh of read-only copies: re-fetch from durable backing store
idea: Read-only data (weights, embeddings) is mapped to never-refreshed banks with strong per-line ECC; when ECC flags drift the line is re-fetched from a NAND or CXL pool that holds the master copy, and a scrubber rewrites lines nearing their measured retention age. Refresh becomes on-demand repair.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth fall to near zero for the read-only majority of inference memory, trading rare microsecond re-fetches for constant refresh.
note: Refetch from backing store instead of recompute; same skip-refresh-and-regenerate core.

title: Eliminate the restore phase: consume-on-read memory for single-use data
idea: Add a destructive-read command and 'read-once' regions whose sense amps never write back. Activations, gradient buffers, evicted KV entries and packets are read once, then the row is marked free, so the SA fires at low swing and the row closes right after the burst.
why: Restore is ~40-50% of row-cycle energy and tRAS (fact 8). For read-once traffic (~30-50% of accelerator traffic), row energy falls ~40% and bank occupancy ~35%, so fewer bits are needed per unit of throughput.
note: Destructive-read regions for read-once traffic; related to restore truncation and IBM destructive-read eDRAM.

title: Eliminate fluorinated test fluids: self-heating hammer-pattern thermal screening
idea: Hot test and burn-in normally rely on PFPE (Galden/Fluorinert) chillers and baths. Instead each die heats itself to 95-125 C with an all-bank activate pattern (~1-2 W), closed-loop on an on-die ring-oscillator thermometer, so handlers need only air-cooled chucks and retention screens run at true temperature.
why: Removes PFAS heat-transfer fluids from test floors and cuts handler capex ~30%; the pattern also screens hammer-weak rows (fact 9).
note: Self-heating test removes PFAS fluids; temperature uniformity is the question.

title: Eliminate helium from the fab: hydrogen backside cooling and tracer leak checks
idea: Replace helium backside gas on etch and CVD electrostatic chucks with low-pressure hydrogen or forming gas (higher thermal conductivity, sealed with flow monitoring), and replace helium mass-spec leak checks with 5% hydrogen tracer detection.
why: Scarce resource: Qatar's ~30% helium share is offline; fab helium use could drop >80%, removing a supply shock that can idle etch fleets.

title: Eliminate sideband ECC bits for AI tensors using algorithmic checksums
idea: Put recomputable AI data on non-ECC channels and protect it with algorithm-based fault tolerance: row and column checksums on each matmul, with recompute on mismatch, so no memory ECC is needed for those regions.
why: Reclaims the 20-25% of RDIMM bits spent on ECC chips for the biggest DRAM consumer class.

title: Eliminate unneeded mantissa bits with bit-plane tensor storage
idea: Tensors are laid out as separate bit planes; a profiler sets per-tensor error budgets and the planes below them are never written, while the memory controller fetches only the planes a kernel asks for.
why: Mixed workloads hold 1.5-3x more tensors per GB, with matching cuts in fetch energy.

title: Orthogonal-access memory reads rows or columns, killing transposes
idea: Eliminate transpose and relayout copies: each cell in a dedicated tile gets two access devices on orthogonal wordline/bitline pairs (dual-port 2T gain cell), so a weight tile is read row-major in the forward pass and column-major in the backward pass without being moved.
why: Transposes and layout shuffles cost an extra read+write of tensors (~10-20% of training traffic); a small dual-port region at ~1.5x cell area removes that traffic.

title: Controller-less DRAM: compiler emits cycle-exact raw memory commands
idea: Eliminate the memory controller's queues, reorder logic and refresh scheduler: for static AI graphs the compiler schedules every ACT/RD/WR/REF at cycle level with temperature-guarded margins, and the PHY simply replays the command stream.
why: Controllers cost SoC area/power and add 20-40 ns latency plus variance; deterministic schedules reach >90% bus utilization and return the area to compute or SRAM.

title: One shared non-volatile weight copy mapped by sixteen hosts
idea: Eliminate per-server weight copies: a CXL 3.x multi-headed NV memory device holds a model once and 16 hosts map it read-only; hosts keep only KV caches and activations in local DRAM.
why: Inference fleets replicate 100s of GB of identical weights on every node; one copy per 16 hosts cuts weight DRAM up to ~16x, and NV means no reload after maintenance or outages.
note: Per-token weight bandwidth through one shared device is the bottleneck.

title: Eliminate in-DRAM parity: keep strong parity on flash, CRC in DRAM
idea: For read-mostly pages (weights, code, embeddings), DRAM stores only a 16-bit CRC per 512 B, and a strong Reed-Solomon parity block lives on CXL-attached flash or the SSD. A CRC miss triggers a parity fetch and reconstruction.
why: Frees most of the ~12.5% ECC overhead on the largest data class and tolerates weaker cells; ~10% more usable capacity at near-zero cost.

title: Eliminate weak-cell errors by storing safe states: data inversion masks
idea: True cells fail only from charged to discharged, and anti-cells only the reverse. The controller keeps a weak-cell map and, for each 64-bit word, picks one of 4 XOR masks so every known weak cell stores its non-decaying state. The 2-bit mask index replaces some ECC bits.
why: Eliminates most retention-tail failures without shortening refresh; could double the refresh interval at <3% overhead.

title: Eliminate discard-on-error policy: re-harvest retired fleet DIMMs die-by-die
idea: An e-waste and procurement rule requires that DIMMs hyperscalers retire at correctable-error thresholds be offered to a re-test line before shredding. The line re-characterizes each die, maps its faults and repackages the healthy dies (the majority) into remapped modules for tolerant workloads.
why: Turns part of the millions of DIMMs retired each year into new supply with no wafer starts; immediate shortage relief.

title: Eliminate single-device leakage tails: two series oxide TFTs per cell
idea: Stack a second access TFT vertically over the first (no extra area in BEOL) with an independently formed gate stack. A cell leaks only if both devices are tail outliers, so the tail probability is squared (1e-6 becomes 1e-12).
why: Turns the worst-cell retention problem (fact 3) from a statistical tail into a near-impossible coincidence, so refresh intervals can be set by median cells, 10-100x longer.

title: Eliminate the 85C margin: cold-only DRAM grade for liquid racks
idea: Eliminate the worst-case temperature spec: dies failing at 85-95C but passing at 45C are certified Cold-Grade for direct-liquid-cooled racks with guaranteed coolant temperature and on-DIMM thermal shutdown; $1M funds binning, sensors and one data-center pilot.
why: Retention roughly doubles per ~10C cooler, so thermal-screen rejects become usable bits as liquid cooling spreads.

title: Eliminate perfect-bit requirement: Grade-C DRAM for error-tolerant workloads
idea: Eliminate the near-zero-error spec where it does not matter: modules with measured raw BER ~1e-12 to 1e-9 are sold for CDN video caches and checkpoint staging protected by software CRC and re-fetch; ~$500k pilot with one CDN.
why: Widens usable bin yield; cache workloads simply re-fetch on a CRC miss.
note: Approximate-DRAM idea with a concrete CDN pilot; yield gain is small.

title: Eliminate repeat qualification: shared reliability dataset for substitute DRAM
idea: Eliminate 12-24-month per-OEM requalification when switching DRAM sources: a consortium runs one automotive-grade stress dataset per part (HTOL, temperature cycling, ESD) and shares it under a common audit, so members switch to available parts in weeks; $1M funds lab time for ~40 parts.
why: Makes existing alternative supply usable quickly instead of waiting for a qualified part.

title: Eliminate the cleanroom for R&D: glovebox micro-line for oxide-TFT memory
idea: Eliminate the cleanroom for prototyping: a ~$700k line of nitrogen gloveboxes with sputter, ALD and maskless laser direct-write on 100mm glass builds low-temperature oxide-TFT 2T0C arrays to prove yield per dollar within 24 months.
why: Proves capital-light memory manufacturing at ~1/1000 of fab capex before scaling.

title: Lay the capacitor down: MLCC-style 30-electrode stacks inside each cell
idea: Rearrange from tall-and-thin to flat-and-many: deposit 30 alternating TiN/Nb2O5 layers, pattern 180 nm cells with two offset staircase edge contacts so odd and even electrodes interleave like a ceramic MLCC; capacitance comes from layer count, not etch depth or litho.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) at 180 nm: 0.2 um2 x 30 layers x ~40 fF/um2 ~ 240 fF per cell, enough for 4-bit multilevel storage, EUV-free (fact 4); risk is film stress and staircase contact yield.

title: Run the image-sensor pixel backward: pinned-photodiode memory lines
idea: Convert depreciated 180-110 nm CMOS image-sensor lines into memory by reversing the pixel: inject charge into each pinned photodiode from the floating diffusion (fill-and-spill), hold it in the pinned well (dark current ~1-10 e-/s), then transfer forward and read by correlated double sampling with column ADCs; 3000 e- full well and 2 e- noise allow ~6 bits per cell.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capital: retention of seconds instead of 64 ms, capacity from existing paid-off fabs; ~0.2 um2/bit effective, so a refresh-light warm tier sold on fab-conversion economics.
note: Pinned well gives seconds retention but ~0.2 um2/bit and slow CDS read limit to warm tier.

title: Steer data into the discharged state on unmodified DRAM
idea: Flip data polarity from outside the chip: commodity DRAM mixes true-cell and anti-cell subarrays. Map them once per part number with retention tests, then have the controller XOR-invert data per address so zeros, the most common value, land as discharged charge in both cell types, replacing today's random scrambling with a polarity-aware mask.
why: Fewer charged cells means fewer cells that can fail, so ECC-protected refresh relaxes ~2x (fact 3); controller logic only, on existing chips.

title: Tail bounty: pay for decades of worst-cell leakage cut
idea: Reverse the research metric from median to tail: a CHIPS-funded open prize pays per decade of 1-ppm-tail off-current reduction, measured on standard 1 Mb access-transistor test arrays built on shared 130/65 nm multi-project-wafer shuttles at existing U.S. foundries. Winning device recipes are licensed to DRAM makers.
why: Targets the ~13 fA tail that sets refresh (fact 3) with many cheap university and startup experiments on existing trailing-node shuttles instead of new fabs.

title: Token-passing row sequencer replaces the random-access row decoder
idea: Reverse random access into order: for AI-weight and KV-cache streaming parts, rows open as a token shifts one wordline per step through a shift-register chain with a small jump table, deleting the NAND-tree row decoder and its pitch-limited predecode buses.
why: Fact 7: row decoders ~8-10% of die -> ~1-2%; activations pipeline back-to-back and decode power drops ~90%; random access survives at bank granularity.

title: Periphery first, indium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cells last
idea: Reverse front-end order: finish CMOS periphery, then build a 2T gain-cell array in BEOL from sputtered zinc-tin-oxide (no indium, no gallium) at <400 C on top of the logic.
why: IGZO depends on indium and gallium (China ~98% of gallium); ZTO uses abundant Zn/Sn and keeps the BEOL-stacking density gain without the chokepoint metals.

title: Test in the field, not on the tester: self-learned error maps
idea: Reverse when testing happens: ship dies after minimal wafer sort, and let on-die BIST plus ECC syndrome logging build and update the bad-cell map during normal use, within the 1% BER budget.
why: ATE capital and test energy are a large back-end cost; cuts test time per die ~5-10x and removes burn-in ovens.

title: Speculative pre-free with lineage recompute on surprise reuse
idea: Invert keep-until-proven-dead: the runtime predicts each large object's last use, frees it at once, and keeps only its lineage (the operator and inputs that made it); a mispredicted later read triggers recomputation instead of a fault.
why: Peak memory of dataflow, ML and analytics pipelines drops 20-40% at a bounded recompute cost.

title: Tenants rent idle DRAM back to the provider every second
idea: Reverse ownership inside each server: VMs and containers hold memory as one-second leases priced by an auction in the hypervisor; tenants earn credits for memory they release, and the host hands it to memory-hungry neighbors through free-page reporting.
why: Cloud servers strand ~25% of DRAM; a market that pays tenants to release it can recover most of that, cutting fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%.

title: Reject-bin DRAM becomes the approximate-data memory tier
idea: Reverse the quality order: dies and DIMMs that fail retention or weak-cell binning (already made, normally scrapped) are packaged into an 'approximate' CXL tier with masked-error semantics, holding error-tolerant data such as video frames, NN activations and low-attention KV.
why: Adds usable bits from yield loss with zero new wafer starts, so no neon excimer litho or helium-cooled etch is used; recovering 3-5% of industry yield loss adds supply on the order of a mid-size fab line.
note: Approximate tier from reject-bin dies; same salvage core as I-05808; approximate DRAM (Flikker) is known.

title: Certify crypto-erase so retired DIMMs are resold, not shredded
idea: Reverse the security default: a NIST/ISO-certified power-off and pattern-overwrite attestation for volatile DRAM, with signed logs from the server BMC, replaces mandatory physical shredding of memory modules in government and enterprise disposal rules.
why: DRAM is volatile, yet shredding destroys working capacity that could supply the secondary market; every reused GB replaces new fab output that would need neon litho and helium-cooled tools.

title: Harvest laptop and console DRAM from e-waste into CXL sleds
idea: Reverse the supply chain: automated desolder, reball and burn-in lines pull DDR4/DDR5 BGA packages from recycled laptops, consoles and SO-DIMMs, bin them by speed and retention, and remount them on CXL far-memory cards behind a compression controller.
why: E-waste holds large amounts of DRAM that is already made; reclaiming it adds U.S.-processed memory supply with no neon litho or helium use.
note: Reballed reclaimed DRAM reliability and volume limited.

title: Lane-direction-reconfigurable PHY for read-heavy phases
idea: Reverse fixed DQ symmetry: each lane has a transmitter and a receiver at both ends and can be reassigned in microseconds, so during LLM decode ~90% of lanes point memory-to-host and they flip back for checkpoint writes; per-burst bus turnaround disappears.
why: Recovers the ~10-15% bandwidth lost to read/write turnarounds and gives up to ~1.8x effective read bandwidth in read-dominated phases (fact 5).

title: Memory as master: the stack pushes tensors to compute
idea: Reverse who initiates: the host writes a descriptor program (tensor shapes, strides, schedule) once, and a DMA engine in the DRAM base die pushes data on its own schedule into the accelerator's SRAM over a write-only link; the host never issues per-line reads.
why: Removes request traffic and round-trip latency, and memory can order row activations optimally (fewer activations, less energy and row-hammer exposure); ~20% more effective bandwidth (facts 5, 8, 9).
note: Descriptor-driven push resembles decoupled access and DMA streaming.

title: Charge-sparse constant-weight encoding so most cells hold zero
idea: Reverse which state carries information: each 64 b word is encoded into an 80-cell constant-weight codeword with only ~25% charged cells, so ~75% of cells sit in the discharged state that cannot leak or be hammered; any 1->0 flip changes the weight, giving free detection.
why: Retention-vulnerable cells and hammer exposure drop ~2-3x and write energy falls; the ~25% capacity cost is repaid by permitting cheaper, weaker cells and longer refresh.

title: Lifetime-matched retention: data expires before the cell forgets
idea: Flip refresh to follow the data's lifespan instead of the cell's: AI activations, KV-cache blocks and network buffers declare a time-to-live at allocation and land in a refresh-free region whose cells only guarantee ~5 ms retention; the controller refreshes only lines whose TTL outlives that window.
why: Refresh (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) eliminated for short-lived data, and that region can use low-AR capacitors with ~3x less charge.

title: Weak cells hold only clean pages, re-fetched on error
idea: Rearrange placement by dirtiness: pages with an intact copy in flash or CXL far memory (weights, code, read-mostly caches) go to cheap weak-retention DRAM protected only by a 16-bit CRC, and a CRC failure triggers a re-fetch instead of correction; a line is migrated to strong ECC banks on its first write.
why: Lets ~60-80% of inference-server capacity use reject-grade or long-refresh cells; ECC overhead on that share drops from 12.5% to ~3%.

title: Memory that trades capacity for parity as it ages
idea: Rearrange the parity/data split over the product lifetime: modules start with ~2% parity, and as the error log shows a region degrading, the controller re-encodes it with a stronger code and hot-unplugs the freed pages from the OS, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: Extends module service life ~2x and lets fabs ship cells that are weaker at end of life; fewer replacements raise usable supply.

title: Corrected-error patterns detect hammer instead of activation counting
idea: Reverse cause and effect: rather than counting activations, the controller spatially correlates corrected-error syndromes from scrubs and reads, using planted canary rows holding worst-case patterns; correctable flips clustering in rows R+1/R-1 identify R as an aggressor to throttle.
why: Row hammer: near-zero-area mitigation tuned to real chip vulnerability, suited to low-cost parts or as a backstop to counters.

title: Phones feed servers: robotic LPDDR harvesting from e-waste
idea: Reverse the e-waste flow: robots desolder LPDDR packages from recycled phones and laptops with hot gas. The packages are re-balled with dry flux, tested and mounted on CAMM/SOCAMM-style CXL or edge-inference boards.
why: Huge numbers of GB sit in discarded devices. Harvested capacity uses no fab water and only dry rework, so water per usable GB is >100x lower than for new bits.

title: Memory passports: certified pre-owned DRAM exchange with telemetry
idea: Rearrange the market: every module logs ECC corrections, temperature and activation counts to a 'passport' kept in its SPD. A clearinghouse grades and warrants used memory from that history, so it trades like a certified pre-owned car.
why: Lack of trust blocks reuse. Warrantied second-life memory adds capacity with >10x less water per GB than new fab output.

title: Memory leasing with depot rejuvenation and retention re-binning
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: makers lease socketed DDR/CXL modules to hyperscalers and take them back every ~3 years; depots map retention, bulk-anneal to heal dielectric traps, re-bin by retention class and re-lease to less demanding tiers.
why: Usable supply: ~1.5-2x more service-years per wafer start during the 4x price spike; better capital efficiency.
note: Leasing executable; anneal-based rejuvenation of retention traps is unproven.

title: Bootstrapped guard node gives the inner switch zero voltage to leak
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality (the electrometer guard trick): put two access transistors in series and drive their middle node from a source follower whose gate is the storage node. In retention the inner transistor sees ~0 V across it and leaks almost nothing, while all leakage from the bitline is absorbed by the actively driven guard node.
why: Subthreshold current scales as (1 - exp(-Vds/kT)), so holding Vds ~ 0 gives ~100x lower leakage (Fact 3): seconds-scale retention for a 3T cell, trading some density for refresh-free cache/HBM tiers.
note: Density trade confines it to cache/eDRAM tiers.

title: Compiler-tagged ephemeral memory that is never refreshed
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: let data that will die anyway go unrefreshed. Compilers and AI runtimes place allocations whose lifetime is shorter than guaranteed retention (activations, KV-cache blocks overwritten each step, staging buffers) in an 'ephemeral' region whose rows the controller never refreshes, with a hardware write-timestamp that faults reads of expired data.
why: Much of AI memory traffic is short-lived (Facts 3, 5): claim 30-70% fewer refreshes in accelerator memory and recovered bandwidth, with no device change.

title: Curvature: ring-gate annular transistors make edge-free matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: the cross-coupled sense-amp transistors are drawn as annular (ring-gate) devices with the drain in the centre, so there is no STI channel edge; edge-related threshold mismatch and narrow-width effects, a major part of sense-amp offset, disappear, and curvilinear masks from multi-beam writers make the rings printable.
why: Facts 1 and 7: sense-amp offset sigma ~-30-40%, so the latch can be ~30% smaller or the cell signal requirement can drop by ~10 mV.

title: Continuity: rolling-scan drum memory needs only a shift-register row scanner
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: like a display gate driver, a shift register sweeps every row in order, sensing and restoring each (so refresh is the scan itself) and presenting each row to a page buffer as it passes; requests wait for their row to come around, removing row address decoders, refresh logic and most control.
why: 100x path: row periphery shrinks to a TFT gate-driver-on-array strip (~1-2% of area) buildable on glass or BEOL lines and repeatable in stacked tiers; trade-offs: average latency is half a scan (~5-30 us), so it suits streaming and batched AI tensors. Attacks Facts 3 and 7.

title: Plateless bridge capacitor stores one bit between twin nodes
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge the two capacitors of a twin cell into one capacitor whose two electrodes are both storage nodes, each reached by its own access transistor on complementary bitlines, with no common plate. Writing puts +V/-V across the single capacitor and the sense amp sees the full differential charge.
why: Fact 1 and 10: ~2x signal per fF lets Cs halve or VARY drop ~30%; deleting the plate layer saves a deposition and contact module.

title: Read-restore 3T gain cell: every read is a refresh
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: add a p-type third transistor whose gate is the precharged read bitline and whose channel links the storage gate to a restore rail. When a stored 1 pulls the read bitline low, the feedback device turns on and tops the storage node back up; a stored 0 leaves the bitline high and the device off.
why: Fact 3: accessed rows refresh themselves, so explicit refresh covers only cold rows (~50-90% fewer refresh operations for typical access patterns); no capacitor.

title: Thermal-expansion valves cut idle purge-gas flows automatically
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: fit tool gas lines with passive bimetal or shape-memory valves keyed to chamber-wall or heater temperature. When a chamber idles and cools, the valve throttles He, N2 and H2 purge to a trickle, and it reopens as the heaters ramp, with no software change or recipe requalification.
why: Idle purge is often 20-40% of process-gas use, so this cuts He and N2 consumption and the ASU energy behind it by a similar share.

title: Photopatternable hafnium-oxo resist that becomes the functional film
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes (change a substance's properties): use a Hf/Zr oxo-cluster resist that, after exposure and development, is annealed straight into dense HfO2/ZrO2 that stays as a hardmask, spacer or isolation layer, so the patterned film is never etched.
why: Collapses deposit-coat-expose-etch-strip into coat-expose-develop-anneal, saving ~3-4 steps per use and some etch chambers (process steps, tool cost).

title: Ephemeral-grade dies: retention-failing DRAM sold for TTL-bounded data
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but hold data for 4-8 ms are sold as E-grade parts with refresh logic fused off, and the runtime places only data with a hard time-to-live below the rated window (collective-communication buffers, prefetch staging, pipeline handoffs), invalidating pages at expiry.
why: Zero refresh power; recovers the ~3-8% retention yield loss and skips the long hot retention-pause tests that dominate DRAM test time (~20-30% test-cost and tester-capex cut) (facts 3, 4).
note: Data-lifetime-aware refresh skipping is known (e.g., accelerator eDRAM); new as a binning SKU.

title: Silicon-carbide refresh-free memory in idle EV power-device fabs
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the same 150/200 mm 4H-SiC lines that make EV MOSFETs (overbuilt in the U.S. as EV demand slowed) produce 1T1C memory, since SiC's 3.26 eV gap suppresses thermal generation so strongly that SiC MOS storage cells have shown retention extrapolating to years at room temperature.
why: Zero refresh, built on existing U.S. i-line/DUV tools with near-zero new capex; density is ~50-100x below DRAM, so it serves persistent, edge and high-temperature tiers and frees mainstream DRAM for hot data (U.S. manufacturability, capital).
note: SiC DRAM retention was shown in the 1990s; density 50-100x below DRAM limits it to niche tiers.

title: Floating-body 1T cells revived for millisecond-lived pipeline buffers
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: rather than fight floating-body retention (why 1T-DRAM failed), embrace it - build SOI or stacked-Si floating-body cells with ~10-100 ms retention and use them only for data overwritten every few ms (pipeline-parallel handoff buffers, double-buffered GEMM tiles, network rings), with refresh logic removed.
why: Zero refresh; the cell is a single transistor with no capacitor module (~25% fewer array steps, no HAR etch) and stacks readily into 3D (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Controller-side pointer high-bit extraction into per-page region tags
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: the memory controller detects 64-bit words whose upper 24 bits equal a per-page 'region tag' (pointers into the same heap region), strips those bits and packs eight 40-bit pointers into a 40-byte slot, restoring them on read with one mux stage. It is hardware compressed-oops for every language, not just the JVM.
why: Pointer-heavy heaps (graph DBs, Go/Java, kernels, B-trees) are 30-60% pointers; 20-35% capacity gain on those pages at ~1-cycle decode.

title: Encode-heavy, decode-cheap memory codec trained by idle cores
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: reads outnumber writes ~3-10x, so use an asymmetric codec: pages are written raw, then idle cores or a background engine re-encode warm pages with expensive search (optimal parsing plus per-page tANS tables), while the read path is a fixed two-stage table-lookup decoder with deterministic ~10 ns latency.
why: Gets entropy-coder ratios (2.5-3.5x) at BDI-class read latency on warm data; 1.5-2x effective DRAM on read-mostly working sets.

title: Live-morphing data structures between dense and succinct forms
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: runtime libraries let every hash map, vector and index switch representation online, morphing cold instances into succinct forms (Elias-Fano, rank/select bitvectors, minimal perfect hashes) and expanding hot ones back to pointer-rich forms, driven by sampled access counts.
why: Much in-memory data is cold but must stay in DRAM; succinct forms are 3-10x smaller, giving 1.5-2.5x heap reduction in data-heavy services.
note: Online dense/succinct morphing; switching cost and pointer stability are issues.

title: Precision-transcoding DIMM buffer for tagged ML address ranges
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: a 180 nm buffer chip on the module holds a small range table; writes to tagged ranges are converted FP32 to BF16 or FP16 to FP8 with stochastic rounding and stored packed into a half- or quarter-size physical region, and reads are expanded back, so precision varies by region with no software changes.
why: CPU-side ML data (embeddings, optimizer state, feature stores) is often FP32; 2-4x capacity on those ranges using simple 180 nm arithmetic.

title: The other way round: DRAM pushes a precompiled tensor schedule
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the GPU requesting every line, the compiler loads a tensor-streaming schedule into the HBM base die. The base die opens rows in a fixed order and pushes data to the accelerator, so the command/address bus becomes a rarely used control channel.
why: Data movement (fact 5), overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): no request traffic, no row misses, and each row opens once per pass, for ~20-30% more effective bandwidth and fewer activates.

title: Spheroidality: ring of compute chiplets with memory inside and outside
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality (curves instead of lines): place compute chiplets in a ring on a large panel substrate, giving the ring both an inner and an outer shoreline. Memory stacks sit inside the hole and around the outside.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~1.6x more memory beachfront per unit of compute area at the same short wire length, avoiding longer links with higher pJ/bit.

title: Spheroidality: radial server board with memory cards as equal spokes
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: lay out a round motherboard with the CPU or accelerator at the center and memory cards plugged in radially like spokes. Every channel gets the same short trace length, so more DIMMs fit per channel at full speed. Built with existing PCB and connector lines. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity per socket and signal integrity (fact 5): ~1.5-2x more DIMMs per socket at DDR5 speed (2 DIMMs per channel without derating), using cheap commodity DIMMs.

title: Z-channel asymmetric code with minority-charge data inversion
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: retention failures are almost only charged-to-discharged, so each word stores an inversion flag that minimizes charged cells (using the known true/anti-cell polarity of each row) and is protected by a Z-channel asymmetric code that corrects only charge-loss flips.
why: Asymmetric codes need ~30-40% fewer check bits for equal correction, and at most half the cells are ever charged, halving leakage exposure; relaxes the retention-tail spec ~2-4x.

title: Continuous stressed-read margin probing predicts failing cells
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: idle bank cycles run nonstop stressed reads with a shortened sensing delay and an offset reference, the DRAM analog of flash read-retry, so cells drifting toward failure are found and migrated weeks before they flip.
why: Turns idle time into predictive reliability: ~10x fewer uncorrectable events and less shipped margin, needing only a reference trim beyond existing circuits.
note: Reduced-timing margin probing doable on FPGA DRAM testers today.

title: Local quality: lifetime-matched retention binning for short-lived AI data
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of one 64 ms retention spec, bin dies by measured retention (8/16/32/64 ms) and sell fast-leaking dies into streaming buffers, activation scratchpads and NIC queues where data is overwritten before it decays; the controller refresh rate is read from the die's bin fuse.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) currently scraps or downgrades dies; matching data lifetime to retention adds ~3-6% sellable output.

title: Flytrap two-touch counter: analog leaky-integrator row-hammer sentinel
idea: The Venus flytrap counts touches with a decaying calcium signal and closes only after two touches within ~30 s. Give each row one extra storage capacitor that gets a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks through a calibrated transistor. When its voltage crosses a threshold, a comparator fires a targeted refresh of the neighbours, so per-row activation counting costs one cell's area instead of SRAM counters.
why: Row hammer (fact 9, flips at ~1k activations): per-row tracking at ~0.1% area, versus 1-3% for counter tables. The decay forgets benign accesses automatically.
note: Analog leaky per-row counter is cheap; calibration across PVT is the doubt.

title: Deciduous shedding: let clean backed pages decay unrefreshed
idea: Trees drop leaves in winter rather than pay to maintain them; the OS marks rows holding clean page-cache or model-weight copies that also live on SSD with a per-row 'deciduous' bit, refresh is disabled on them during idle, and a canary/ECC check on first access triggers refetch from storage if they have decayed.
why: In servers 30-50% of DRAM is clean cache; dropping its refresh cuts idle refresh energy roughly proportionally and frees refresh bandwidth.

title: Penguin-huddle thermal rotation of long-lived data in HBM stacks
idea: Emperor penguins rotate so no bird stays on the cold edge too long; the HBM controller maps long-lived data (weights, KV cache) to the coolest dies far from the logic base and short-lived activations to the hottest dies, and runs a separate temperature-graded refresh rate per die.
why: Stacks have 10-20 C gradients; refreshing cool dies at half rate and hot dies only for data that outlives retention cuts stack refresh energy ~30-50% without new devices.

title: Photoreceptor light adaptation: reference voltage tracking time since refresh
idea: Like a photoreceptor shifting its operating point with ambient light, a per-bank reference generator walks the sense reference down the expected charge-loss curve since that row group's last refresh. A drooped '1' is then still compared against a threshold midway between the decayed '1' and the '0'.
why: Fact 3: a fixed mid-rail reference fails a '1' at VDD/2. A tracking reference roughly doubles the allowable droop, extending tREFW 1.5-2.5x and cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% bandwidth tax in proportion.
note: Reference following average decay helps little for tail cells.

title: Polyploid bits: three tier copies charge-summed onto one bitline
idea: Heat-stressed plants often become polyploid, carrying extra genome copies; write each bit into three cells in three tiers on the same vertical bitline and activate all three together on read so their charges sum, letting one hot leaky tail cell be outvoted by the other two.
why: 125 C leakage tail: 3x summed signal that is statistically immune to single tail cells permits near-room-temperature refresh intervals in a dense 3D stack where tiers are cheap.
note: 3x area for retention margin; poor density trade.

title: Mangrove salt glands: hydrogen-getter wells drain each oxide tier
idea: Mangroves excrete salt through dedicated leaf glands; place Ti/Pd-capped getter 'glands' (small trenches of hydrogen-absorbing metal) every few microns in each tier of an oxide-semiconductor 3D array so hydrogen diffusing at 125 C flows into sinks instead of donor-doping the channels.
why: Hydrogen-driven Vt shift is the main 10-yr high-temperature failure of oxide channels; getter wells could hold drift <50 mV over 10 yrs at 125 C, making low-leakage oxide 3D tiers automotive-grade.

title: Clonal-selection antibody codebook compresses frequent cache-line patterns
idea: The memory controller keeps a 4K-entry 'antibody repertoire' of 64-byte line patterns; a line matching an antibody within a few bit flips is stored as a 12-bit pointer plus a sparse mutation mask. Antibodies that match often are cloned and hypermutated into variants and unused ones die, so the codebook evolves per workload like adaptive immunity.
why: Effective capacity: adaptive line-level compression, 1.5-3x on weights, page tables and zero-heavy activations, no software changes.

title: Physarum tube-reinforcement solver places pages across pooled CXL memory
idea: Each host-to-memory-node path is modeled as a slime-mould tube whose conductance grows with page traffic and decays otherwise; pages migrate along thickening tubes, so the pool converges on a minimal network where a shared page lives once, near its heaviest consumers, instead of being replicated per host.
why: Stranded and replicated DRAM in racks: 20-35% less total DRAM at near-local latency.

title: Seed dormancy with cue-triggered germination for cold pages
idea: Cold pages are dried into compact 'seeds' (compressed to ~25%) in a far tier; a tiny learned cue detector watches request streams for germination cues (user login, job phase markers, specific syscalls) and rehydrates exactly those seeds ahead of use, as seeds sprout on temperature and moisture cues rather than on demand.
why: Tiering: lets 40-60% of resident data leave DRAM with fewer demand-miss stalls than recency-based tiering.

title: Age polyethism assigns leaky aged chips to error-tolerant data
idea: Older worker ants take on riskier foraging jobs; recycled modules with weaker retention tails host data that tolerate rare flips (low-priority KV, activations, recomputable caches) under light ECC, while young chips hold critical state.
why: Reuse yield: turns marginal chips into useful capacity, adding 10-20% second-life supply.

title: Starfish regrowth: compression slack pays for erasure-coded memory
idea: A starfish regrows from one arm; pages are compressed and the freed space holds erasure-code parity striped across modules, so any single module can be hot-pulled for repair and rebuilt from the rest with no net capacity cost.
why: Repair without downtime or overprovisioning; makes cheaper, less reliable recycled modules safe to deploy.

title: Antibody tags: send a fingerprint instead of an already-known line
idea: The HBM base die and the host controller each keep an 'immune memory' of hashes of recently transferred 64 B lines. When a requested line matches a hash the host already holds, the stack sends a 16-bit antibody tag and the host rebuilds the line from its own scratchpad, with a full-transfer fallback on mismatch. Zero lines, duplicated KV-cache blocks and repeated weight tiles become near-free transfers.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and effective bandwidth: in dedup-heavy AI and VM workloads, 15-40% of transfers could collapse to tags, cutting link energy and freeing bandwidth.
note: Hash-tag dedup across the link; gains depend on duplicate-heavy traffic and synchronized dictionaries.

title: Sleep-replay consolidation: idle-time co-location of co-accessed lines
idea: During idle windows the HBM base die replays a log of recent accesses, as the hippocampus replays sequences during sleep, and physically migrates lines that were used together into the same DRAM row (with a small remap table). Later bursts become open-page hits, so one row activation serves many useful lines.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): could cut the ~5.9 pJ per useful random bit by 2-4x for recurring access patterns and lower activation counts that drive row hammer.

title: Leaf-venation coolant network inside a glass-core interposer
idea: A glass panel replaces the silicon interposer and is laser-modified and etched with hierarchical, loop-rich vein channels modeled on dicot leaves: a midrib feeds secondary veins that feed reticulate loops under each DRAM stack and the GPU. The loops let coolant route around a blocked channel, as leaves survive insect damage.
why: Thermal limit on stack height and refresh (fact 3): glass panels cost ~2-3x less per area than silicon interposers, and embedded cooling allows taller, cooler stacks with less refresh overhead.

title: Bouligand helicoidal fiber core for warp-free organic memory substrates
idea: Mantis-shrimp clubs and beetle cuticle stack fiber plies in a slow helix, which gives isotropic stiffness and deflects cracks. Organic package cores are laid up the same way, with glass-fiber plies rotated ~15 degrees per layer instead of a 0/90 weave, giving quasi-isotropic in-plane CTE and low warpage in thin, large panels that carry many memory chiplets.
why: Lets organic substrates replace silicon interposers by staying flat enough for 10-20 um-pitch chiplet bonding; panel-level cost with no wafer-scale tools.

title: Axon-tract optical bundles written in 3D inside glass interposers
idea: Brain white matter routes millions of axons through 3D tracts. A femtosecond laser writes buried 3D waveguides inside a glass interposer that cross over and under each other without crosstalk, linking GPU optical engines to many memory stacks spread across the panel.
why: Data movement and shoreline: 3D routing breaks the 2D edge limit on attached stacks; ~0.1-0.3 dB/cm loss lets memory sit several cm away at near-constant pJ/bit.

title: Uracil-glycosylase coding: make every charge-leak an illegal symbol
idea: DNA spots cytosine deamination because uracil does not belong in DNA; since DRAM retention errors are unidirectional (true-cells leak 1->0, anti-cells 0->1), store words in constant-weight/Berger-style codes polarized per cell orientation so every leak lowers the weight, becomes an illegal codeword, and is located by direction and fixed with a cheap asymmetric (Z-channel) decoder.
why: Retention tail (<=13 fA leakers) and refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% idle power): asymmetric codes correct leak errors with roughly half the check bits of symmetric BCH at equal strength, enabling ~4-8x longer refresh intervals.

title: Physarum tube-thickening: refresh flux follows observed error flow
idea: Slime mould thickens tubes that carry flow and lets idle ones wither; each subarray holds a refresh 'conductance' that increments whenever on-die ECC corrects an error there and decays geometrically otherwise, and the refresh scheduler splits its budget in proportion, so refresh converges onto where leakage actually lives.
why: Refresh overhead: most rows retain for seconds; concentrating the budget on the ~0.1% weak regions and tracking VRT/temperature drift automatically cuts refresh energy ~5-10x.

title: Cicada prime-period sampling so hammer patterns cannot phase-lock
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on 13- or 17-year cycles so predators cannot synchronize; run TRR sampling windows and victim-refresh slots on mutually prime, per-bank randomly reseeded periods (13/17/19/23 tREFI), so many-sided and half-double patterns that exploit fixed sampler cadence never phase-lock with all banks.
why: Row hammer: TRRespass-style bypasses exploit periodic samplers; prime-period scheduling restores probabilistic guarantees using only small LFSR state, avoiding the 2-5% area of growing trackers.

title: Grid-cell residue codes: each modulus lives on a separate cheap die
idea: Entorhinal grid cells encode position with several periodic modules, a residue number system with built-in error correction; store integers and weights as residues modulo coprime moduli plus two redundant moduli, each residue on a different ultra-cheap low-yield die, so one or two dead dies are corrected and add/multiply run per residue near memory.
why: Lets 70-80% die yields and high raw error rates pass at system level with no known-good-die sort or repair, plus carry-free near-memory compute; a pathway to ~100x cheaper per GB.
note: Residues on separate dies is erasure coding with compute; 100x claim unsupported.

title: Mycorrhizal parity pool: zero-ECC cheap modules share a common fungus
idea: Trees share nutrients through mycorrhizal networks; strip ECC chips and per-module repair from ultra-cheap memory modules and keep one shared erasure-parity pool on a CXL switch protecting hundreds of modules, rebuilding any module's failed lines on demand.
why: Amortizes protection (12.5-25% per module down to ~2-5% pool-wide) and tolerates high module failure rates, so the cheapest media classes become deployable; contributes to ~100x effective cost per GB.

title: PERC solar back side: negative-charge Al2O3 fences carriers from storage node
idea: PERC solar cells use ALD Al2O3 carrying ~1e13 cm-2 negative fixed charge to repel minority carriers from surfaces; wrap storage-node junction sidewalls and isolation liners in 5-nm ALD Al2O3 so the field pushes the generation-active depletion edge away from defective interfaces, followed by forming-gas hydrogenation, demonstrated on university test diodes and gated capacitors.
why: Fact 3: perimeter interface generation dominates the leakage tail, so ~10x lower perimeter generation gives ~3-10x longer worst-cell retention using only ALD and a furnace.

title: PERC solar trick: negative-charge alumina liners silence storage-junction surface leakage
idea: PERC solar cells keep minority carriers off the rear surface with ALD Al2O3 carrying ~10^13 cm^-2 negative fixed charge. Line the storage-node contact sidewall and STI edge, where the n+ junction meets a surface, with the same charged Al2O3 so holes accumulate in the p-well surface and the depletion region (and its interface-trap generation) is pushed off the surface.
why: Perimeter/surface generation is a large part of the junction-leakage tail (fact 3); field-effect passivation cut solar surface recombination ~10x, so 3-5x lower tail leakage and 2-4x longer refresh interval is plausible.

title: Fractional-reserve banking: row-parity reserve absorbs fluorine-free process's wider tail
idea: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits on hand because withdrawals rarely coincide. Accept the wider retention tail of a hydrogen-passivated, fluorine-free process by adding one XOR parity row per 32-row group inside each subarray; refresh at an interval where at most one row per group is likely to hold a decayed cell, and rebuild that row from parity when ECC flags it.
why: Sets refresh near the 99.99th-percentile cell instead of the 6-sigma tail: 2-4x fewer refreshes (fact 3) for ~3% area, turning the constraint's yield penalty into design margin.

title: Regenerative braking for wordlines via stepwise energy recovery
idea: Like an EV recovering energy while braking, discharge each 3 V wordline down a 5-step on-die capacitor ladder (stepwise adiabatic charging) instead of to ground, and charge the next wordline back up the same ladder.
why: Voltage floor/energy: wordline CV2 loss at ~3 V falls ~60-70% (N-step charging dissipates ~1/N), with less charge-pump load.

title: Record-pressing father-mother-son electroforming multiplies nanoimprint stamps
idea: Borrowed from vinyl pressing, which electroforms a nickel 'father' from the lacquer master, then 'mothers', then hundreds of 'son' stampers: a 10-person shop takes one e-beam quartz master per DRAM array layer, electroforms nickel generations and casts UV-cured hybrid-polymer working stamps, selling cheap daughter templates to NIL fabs.
why: Fact 4: NIL cost is dominated by template price and wear; daughter replication can cut template cost per wafer 10-100x. Defect amplification across generations is the risk.

title: Weather-balloon swap: hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in chucks
idea: Borrowed from weather services that fly hydrogen instead of scarce helium: H2 conducts heat about as well as or better than He, so a small team builds a retrofit gas panel feeding 5-20 Torr electrolytic H2 to electrostatic-chuck backside cooling, with N2 sheath, ppm leak sensing and interlocks, qualifying tool by tool.
why: Scarce resource: backside cooling is a top fab helium use and ~30% of helium supply is offline since March 2026; H2 diffusion into devices and safety qualification are the risks.

title: Memory futures market inside the cluster scheduler
idea: Borrow commodity futures: jobs buy forward contracts for GB-hours at submission, the scheduler clears the market every minute, and spot-price spikes automatically switch jobs into pre-registered compressed or recompute modes or let them sell capacity back.
why: Price signals reveal which jobs can shrink cheaply; claims 15-25% lower peak DRAM provisioning in shared AI clusters by flattening demand.

title: Train-timetable DRAM: compiler-scheduled interface without command bus
idea: Railways run on timetables, not per-trip dispatch. The AI compiler pre-loads a deterministic access schedule (row, bank, cycle) into a small sequencer on the HBM base die. The sequencer opens rows just in time and streams data in fixed slots. The host sends only a start token and occasional amendments.
why: Drops command/address pins and most controller handshakes. That frees bumps for data (~10-15% more bandwidth per stack) and wastes fewer activations, because each row opens exactly when it is needed.

title: Coral-reef plating: electroless-grown pillars fuse stacked dies
idea: Stalactites and stalagmites grow until they join into a column. Align stacked dies with a small gap and flow electroless Cu/Ni bath between them. Facing pads grow until they merge into solid joints below 80 C, with no reflow or anneal.
why: Room-temperature vertical joints at <10 um pitch avoid the thermal budget and warpage, enabling many-tier stacks and denser die-to-die interfaces.

title: Synonymous-codon encoding that hides known weak cells
idea: Synonymous codons let DNA tolerate mutations without changing the protein. Each 8-bit symbol is written into 9 cells. Using the row's known weak-cell map, and the fact that a true cell leaks only 1->0, the encoder picks the synonymous codeword that places a discharged '0' in every known leaky cell (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memory with defects). Weak cells then never hold charge that can leak.
why: With ~12% overhead, cells with poor retention (fact 3) stay in service and refresh is no longer set by the tail. Refresh could stretch 4-8x for rows with mapped defects.
note: Stuck-at coding known from PCM (SAFER/Aegis); DRAM retention application is a twist.

title: Bridge load-posting: measured per-module hammer limits written to SPD
idea: Bridges post weight limits from inspection rather than from design worst case. An open FPGA tester for commodity DDR5 (5 rigs at about $50k each) measures each module's minimum hammer threshold and retention tail in about 20 minutes and writes them to SPD vendor bytes. A BIOS patch then sets RFM/PRAC thresholds and refresh per module.
why: Most modules are far stronger than the worst case. Per-module settings cut mitigation bandwidth and refresh 30-60% (facts 3 and 9) with no new silicon.
note: Hammer thresholds vary with pattern and temperature; a 20-minute test may miss worst case.

title: Actuarially insured B-grade DRAM on FPGA-CXL cards
idea: Outlets sell factory 'seconds' with a warranty attached. Buy retention-rejected or down-binned dies and modules (fail at 64 ms, pass at 32 ms; sold 10-30% cheaper or scrapped). Mount them behind an FPGA CXL controller that refreshes at 2x and applies strong symbol ECC, and price the warranty from logged error data. Pilot 1,000 cards within the $1M budget.
why: Turns a scrap stream into usable capacity during the 4x shortage, at an estimated 30-50% lower cost per bit and no new wafer capital (fact 4).

title: Mercury delay line reborn in RF SAW-filter fabs on lithium tantalate
idea: The UNIVAC mercury tank stored bits as acoustic pulses circulating between transducers. Existing RF front-end filter fabs (LiTaO3/LiNbO3, 0.25-0.5 um litho, billions of units per year, some in the U.S.) can make folded SAW delay loops with interdigital transducers, paired with a CMOS regenerator die.
why: No cell structure; ~4 km/s acoustic velocity gives 50,000x more delay per mm than light, so 2 GHz x 1 us loops hold 2 kb each as a refresh-free streaming tier that offloads sequential DRAM traffic; value is capex and supply chain, not density.
note: Reuses SAW filter fabs for a streaming tier; low density, ~us latency.

title: Z80 R-register reborn: inference weight sweeps certified as refresh
idea: Revive the Zilog Z80's trick of refreshing DRAM during opcode fetch: the memory controller tracks which rows were read within the retention window and suppresses explicit refresh for them. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token (~20-50 ms), so the scheduler orders weight reads to touch every row within tREFW and weight regions in HBM become self-refreshing.
why: Removes most explicit refresh for weight-resident HBM (facts 3, 5); weights often fill 50-80% of capacity, so refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax fall roughly in proportion.
note: Access-implied refresh skipping (Smart Refresh) known; LLM weight sweep within tREFW is a neat new application.

title: Keithley driven-guard cell: a follower nulls access-transistor Vds
idea: Revive the electrometer's driven guard, which kills leakage by holding a node's surroundings at the node's own voltage: split the access path into two series transistors with a tiny cell-local node between them. A zero-Vt native source follower from the storage node drives that local node, so the inner transistor sees Vds near 0 in hold and its subthreshold leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Directly attacks the subthreshold part of the tail (fact 3): 10-100x longer retention for 1.5-2x cell area, which is worth it in a refresh-free tier.
note: Bootstrapped/guarded leakage-cancel switches exist in gain-cell eDRAM and S/H circuits; area penalty limits density.

title: Atlas one-level store: lifetime-tagged pages that never get refreshed
idea: Revive the 1962 Manchester Atlas one-level store, whose hardware page tables tracked residency: add a lifetime-class bit to page-table entries and to the memory controller. Tensors rewritten faster than the retention time (activations, gradient buffers, ring buffers) go into rows marked no-refresh, and the OS guarantees each is rewritten within the certified retention time.
why: Short-lived AI data can be a large share of training memory; skipping refresh for it cuts refresh energy and the bandwidth tax roughly in proportion (fact 3), with no device change.

title: Energy Star for memory: label DIMMs by idle refresh watts
idea: Revive the EPA's 1992 Energy Star program, which pushed PCs into sleep modes: create an Energy Star memory tier based on measured self-refresh watts per GB at 45 C, and require the top tier in federal procurement, rewarding low-leakage access devices from U.S. fabs.
why: Creates market pull for cutting refresh energy (fact 3), which is 16-33% of idle memory power, and steers U.S. data-center buying.

title: Equivalent-time sampling scope built into each sense stripe
idea: 1960s sampling oscilloscopes captured GHz waveforms by sampling repeated events at slipping delays. Add one sampling switch and comparator per sense stripe; across repeated activations it reconstructs the real bitline charge-sharing waveform, and boot firmware sets each mat's tRCD and sense-enable timing from it.
why: Removes worst-case timing guardbands: ~15-25% lower tRCD/tRAS and better yield of slow mats (facts 1, 4).
note: On-die equivalent-time sampling to set per-mat timings; AL-DRAM-like gains.

title: Two-out-of-five constant-weight codes enable reference-free ranked sensing
idea: Revive the IBM 650 / Bell relay 2-out-of-5 code: each group of n cells is written as a constant-weight word and sensed by picking the k strongest cells with a winner-take-all comparator instead of a fixed reference, so tier-to-tier Vt shifts and common leakage cancel. Residual ~1% rank flips are fixed by an outer code.
why: Facts 2 and 3: no dummy/reference bitlines and ~4x longer retention because drift becomes common-mode; tolerates poorly matched 3D tiers.
note: Reference-free ranked sensing echoes rank modulation for flash; new to DRAM.

title: Complementary twin cells on adjacent tiers cancel stack variation
idea: Revive IBM's balanced-capacitor read-only store and early twin-cell DRAM: store each bit as opposite charges in vertically adjacent tiers on the same pillar and sense differentially, so tier-correlated etch and doping variation cancels and a ~1% single-ended raw BER becomes ~1e-6 at the pair.
why: Facts 1 and 2: Cs can drop ~2x and tiers can thin, since differential sensing doubles signal; relaxes the 3D capacitor requirement.
note: Twin cell halves density; BER improvement claim optimistic.

title: Dolan-bridge angled evaporation forms self-aligned sub-litho features
idea: Revive Dolan's 1977 suspended-resist-bridge shadow evaporation, used to make Josephson junctions: one coarse imprint forms a resist bridge, and two evaporations at opposite angles in high vacuum (oxidation in O2, no argon milling) deposit overlapping strips whose overlap width is set by angle and bridge height rather than litho. Use it for ~10 nm gate-to-contact overlaps and narrow metal strips.
why: Fact 4: turns a high-resolution litho layer into a coarse layer plus geometry, removing EUV or immersion passes on self-aligned structures; e-beam evaporators cost ~$1-2M and need no rare gas. Risks are throughput and step coverage.

title: Lisp-machine CDR-coding deletes adjacent pointers from managed heaps
idea: Generalize MIT/Symbolics Lisp-machine cdr-coding: the garbage collector lays objects out in traversal order and a 2-bit tag per word says 'next reference is the adjacent object', so the load unit synthesizes that address and the 8-byte pointer is never stored. Applies to Java/Go/Python heaps, graph databases and B-trees.
why: Pointers are 30-50% of bytes in managed heaps and graph stores, a large share of datacenter DRAM; eliding adjacent-object pointers recovers 15-30% of that capacity at near-zero CPU cost.

title: ICL DAP bit-plane storage with early-terminating dot products
idea: Store weights and keys as bit planes like the ICL Distributed Array Processor, MSB plane first, and compute dot products plane by plane, stopping as soon as the running bound proves an output's sign or top-k membership. Low-order planes are fetched only for close calls and live in a cheap slow tier.
why: On average 3-4 of 8 planes are needed, so 2-4x less HBM traffic, and only high planes need premium DRAM.

title: Drum-memory revival: command-free rotational streaming mode for HBM stacks
idea: Add a 'drum mode' in which each bank activates rows in a fixed cyclic order and streams them past the PHY like drum tracks past fixed heads, with no command/address traffic; a compiler places tensors at rotational offsets (IBM 650 SOAP-style optimum programming) so data arrives exactly when compute needs it.
why: Facts 3/7/8: drops C/A pins and scheduler logic (~15-20% of PHY area/power), every opened row is fully consumed (no 128x overfetch) for streaming AI loads, and refresh becomes implicit because every row is read once per rotation inside the retention window.

title: Telephone-hybrid revival: simultaneous bidirectional signaling doubles every TSV
idea: Revive the telephone 2-wire/4-wire hybrid and Edison's quadruplex telegraph: each TSV and microbump carries read and write data at once, and an on-die replica-driver hybrid subtracts the local transmit waveform from the received sum.
why: Fact 6: halves TSV/bump count per unit bandwidth (or doubles stack bandwidth), shrinking the TSV area tax that makes HBM ~3x the wafer area per bit; ~10-15% die area back.

title: Phantom-circuit revival: center-tapped third channel rides two differential pairs
idea: Like 1880s telephone phantom circuits, encode a third data stream as the common-mode difference between two differential pairs, injected and recovered through center-tapped terminations, on memory SerDes and package traces.
why: 1.5x bandwidth per wire on differential memory links (CXL/SerDes), so fewer package pins and substrate layers per TB/s; modest energy overhead, common-mode noise is the risk.

title: 1968 ECDM revival: spark-drilled glass interposer vias in caustic, no HF
idea: Revive Kurafuji's electrochemical discharge machining: tool electrodes in NaOH/KOH electrolyte create gas-film sparks that thermally and chemically drill 20-50 um vias through glass interposer panels, with arrays of parallel electrodes for throughput.
why: Constraint: removes hydrofluoric acid (laser-induced deep etching) and SF6 plasma from glass via formation, unlocking large, cheap, low-loss glass panels that host many HBM stacks.

title: Masoretic letter counts as Berger tags catch every one-way decay
idea: Masoretic scribes verified scrolls by counting letters, which exposes any omission. DRAM retention loss is one-way (charged to discharged, per physical cell polarity), so each 64-bit word carries a 7-bit complemented count of physically charged cells (a Berger code): any number of leakage flips lowers the data count and raises the tag, so detection is guaranteed, and on mismatch the controller re-reads with a lowered reference to locate the faded cells.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): guaranteed detection of all leakage errors for 7 bits per 64 lets refresh be relaxed 2-4x safely with a repair fallback, roughly halving refresh's 16-33% share of idle power.
note: Unidirectional retention errors detected; detect-only.

title: Reed's 1954 majority-logic decoder built into the sense-amp stripe
idea: Irving Reed decoded Reed-Muller codes with one layer of parity checks feeding majority gates, with no iterative algebra. Weak subarrays use a one-step majority-logic-decodable (273,191) difference-set code whose XOR checks and majority votes form a single gate layer beside the column multiplexer, correcting 8 random errors per access in ~1 ns with no syndrome tables.
why: Weaker cells acceptable (facts 1, 3): tolerates raw BER ~1e-4 instead of ~1e-9 without a latency penalty, so Cs can drop ~30% or refresh stretch ~8x in those subarrays; ~40% parity there, applied only where cells are weak.

title: Mitsubishi cached DRAM revival: SRAM row cache absorbs hammering
idea: Mitsubishi's 1990s Cached DRAM and Ramtron's Enhanced DRAM put a small SRAM row cache on the die. Revive it as a hammer absorber: a 16-entry SRAM row cache per bank inserts a row on its second activation within a window, so repeat activations of hot rows are served from SRAM while the physical wordline stays closed, with an eviction counter that triggers neighbour restore if an attacker thrashes the cache.
why: Row hammer and activation energy (facts 8, 9): bounds physical ACTs per row below the ~1k flip threshold without per-row counters and cuts activation energy for hot rows ~90%; die area +2-3%.
note: Row cache bounds ACTs; thrash path still needs counters.

title: Delay-line mode: streamed weight reads double as refresh at 115 C
idea: In mercury delay lines, data were refreshed simply by circulating. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token batch (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight reads to touch every row within its hot retention window and marks those banks refresh-exempt, with a watchdog that issues real refresh whenever traffic pauses.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): weight banks stay correct at 105-115 C, where refresh would otherwise quadruple, so memory no longer forces chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers); weight-memory refresh energy drops to ~0.

title: IBM 650 SOAP-style placement puts tolerant tensors in the hottest dies
idea: The IBM 650's SOAP assembler placed each instruction where the rotating drum would deliver it soonest. A placement compiler does the same with heat: from a thermal map of the HBM stack (top and centre dies run hottest) it places error-tolerant data (KV cache, activations, gradients) in the hottest banks with relaxed refresh and critical data (optimizer state, page tables) in the coolest, most protected banks.
why: Water: the stack's allowed average temperature rises ~10-15 C because only tolerant data sit in hot spots, enabling warm-water dry cooling without evaporation (>10x less facility water); refresh energy -30%.

title: VCR dropout compensator revival: conceal faulty words in AI tensors
idea: VCRs hid tape dropouts by substituting the previous scan line from a delay line. The accelerator's memory controller keeps a map of known-bad or uncorrectable words in tensor memory and on access substitutes a predicted value (neighbouring element, channel mean, or zero for activations) instead of trapping or retrying, logging each event.
why: Water: lets AI-tensor DRAM from an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water fab ship without repair fuses or spare rows, because scattered point defects are concealed instead of repaired; ~10% less capacity and ECC overhead.

title: ARAM Revival: Retention-Weak DRAM Grade for Error-Tolerant AI Tensors
idea: Revive 1980s 'audio RAM' (known-defective DRAM sold cheaply for answering machines) as a T-grade tier: dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass at 8-16 ms, or have clustered stuck bits, ship with a defect bitmap in SPD; the memory controller refreshes them faster and the scheduler places only error-tolerant data (activations, KV caches, gradient buffers) there while masking mapped bits.
why: Supply: the retention tail is a major test-reject category; converting it into usable capacity adds ~2-5% bits and a ~50%-price tier without new wafers.
note: Monetizes retention rejects for tolerant AI data; needs controller/OS support for mapped refresh.

title: Bucket-brigade row shifting replaces column decoders
idea: Inverting 'columns are picked by a decoder and mux': after sensing, the row buffer is shifted toward the I/O edge through a latch chain like a CCD image sensor, so data streams out in order without column-select lines or decoders; random columns use 16-position skip taps.
why: Removes column decoders and CSL wiring (~8-12% of periphery) and suits streaming AI tensor reads, at some random-access latency cost.

title: Hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in cryo-etch of 3D stacks
idea: Inverts 'wafer chucks need helium backside cooling.' Use low-pressure H2 (higher thermal conductivity than He) as the backside heat-transfer gas for cryogenic high-aspect-ratio etch of 100+ tier stacks, with leak-tight chucks and point-of-use electrolytic H2.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps 3D-stack etch running with no He; cryo etch is what makes 100+ tiers etchable.

title: Reject wafers reborn as passive interposers, bypassing ABF substrates
idea: Inverts 'HBM needs prime silicon interposers or organic ABF laminates': regrind test and yield-reject wafers into passive redistribution interposers with 2-3 copper layers patterned on mature i-line steppers, then hybrid-bond DRAM stacks and logic directly onto them.
why: Interposer silicon and single-supplier ABF film are CoWoS/HBM chokepoints; reclaimed wafers cost ~10% of prime and consume no new crucible quartz.
note: Reject wafers as passive interposers is plausible; fine RDL on i-line is the limit.

title: Token-loop restoration: inference reads restore weights before they fade
idea: Inverts 'refresh must be a separate maintenance operation': lay out inference weights so every row is activated (and thus restored by its sense amplifier) once per decoding step (<20 ms) and remove refresh from those banks; if the token loop stalls, the read-only weights are dropped and re-streamed from flash.
why: Zero refresh power and ~10% bandwidth back in weight banks; the 20 ms retention target allows shorter capacitors with less mold and fluorocarbon etch per bit.
note: Refresh skipping for recently activated rows (Smart Refresh) applied to LLM decode weights; modest gain.

title: Lineage paging: drop recomputable pages, rebuild them on fault
idea: Inverts 'data must be stored to be kept': the kernel records a lineage (source file + offset + transform such as decompress, JIT, parse or decode) for derived pages. Under pressure it evicts them without writing them anywhere, and on a fault it rebuilds them by replaying the transform on a spare core, like Spark lineage applied to the page cache and runtime heaps.
why: Derived data (decompressed caches, JIT code, parsed configs, decoded media) is often 15-30% of resident memory; reclaiming it with no swap I/O cuts DRAM need by that share.
note: Spark-style lineage for derived pages; clean file pages already drop free.

title: DIMM leasing: pull idle DRAM out of enterprise servers
idea: Inverts 'installed DRAM stays where it was first installed': a telemetry agent shows that enterprise servers use only ~40% of their installed memory. A broker buys or leases the surplus DIMMs, pulls them during maintenance windows and redeploys them to clouds and AI builders.
why: Hundreds of PB of DRAM sit underused in enterprise datacenters; recirculating 10-20% of it equals months of global output.

title: Push-streaming DRAM: memory runs the schedule, host stops asking
idea: Invert 'memory is a passive slave waiting for commands': the compiler uploads a static access program (tensor walk, bank interleave, refresh slots) into a tiny sequencer on the HBM base die, which activates banks and pushes data down a unidirectional link in fixed slots; the host keeps only a credit/abort lane, no command/address bus.
why: Removes CA pins and host scheduling logic (~15-25% of PHY pins/power), kills turnaround bubbles and lets the base die slot refresh and row-hammer mitigation into idle windows; ~1.3x effective bandwidth for static AI graphs.
note: Static-graph push streaming; ~1.3x bandwidth, related to decoupled access/execute art.

title: Significance-aware lanes: MSBs robust, LSBs cheap and noisy
idea: Invert 'all bits deserve the same wire': route sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits over full-swing terminated lanes and low-mantissa bits over ultra-low-swing unterminated lanes run at a bit-error rate AI numerics tolerate.
why: Half or more of tensor bits ride at 3-5x lower energy; ~40% lower interface energy for AI traffic.

title: Imperfect-by-contract DRAM tier for noise-trained AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must be perfect': a DRAM tier runs with refresh stretched 8x (~512 ms) and a published raw BER (1e-7 to 1e-5); training frameworks inject bit-flip noise matched to that datasheet BER in the final epochs so models are certified robust, and the runtime places weights and KV-cache only on this tier.
