why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) cut ~85% on the tier; dies failing standard retention bins become sellable, raising effective supply ~10-15%.

title: Write data so weak cells hold their leak-to value
idea: Inverts 'data is stored as-is': each 64-bit word carries 2 coset bits selecting one of four XOR masks; the write encoder picks the mask that leaves the word's known weak cells (true-cells leak to 0, anti-cells to 1) already in their discharged state, so leakage cannot corrupt them.
why: Neutralizes most retention-tail cells (fact 3) for 3% overhead; with 1-2 weak cells per word the refresh interval can rise ~4-8x.
note: Stuck-at coset coding applied to retention; VRT cells break the static map.

title: Store the recipe, not the parity: lineage recompute on error
idea: Inverts 'memory must correct its own errors': for recomputable tensors (activations, decompressed weights, caches) the runtime replaces SECDED with a 4-bit detection CRC plus a pointer to the producing kernel; on a detected error it recomputes only the affected tile from its inputs.
why: Halves ECC overhead for recomputable data and tolerates ~100x higher BER, permitting much longer refresh; recompute cost is negligible at realistic error rates.

title: Constrained codes that never write the worst coupling pattern
idea: Inverts 'any data pattern must be storable': a 64b/66b-style constrained code forbids the stripe and checkerboard patterns that maximize bitline-to-bitline and cell-to-cell coupling, so the array only ever stores mild patterns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent failures, a large share of the retention and hammer tail, drop ~3-10x for 3% capacity.
note: Needs in-DRAM encoding since host does not know physical layout.

title: Matrix checksums replace DRAM ECC for AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must protect itself': weight matrices carry row and column checksum vectors (algorithm-based fault tolerance); the GEMM kernel verifies output checksums and corrects single weight-tile errors, so HBM holding weights runs without on-die ECC or with relaxed refresh.
why: Reclaims the ~12% ECC area and bandwidth in HBM (fact 6) and tolerates higher raw BER for <2% compute overhead.

title: Triple-row activation gives free analog majority voting
idea: Inverts 'only one row opens at a time': critical data (page tables, kernel, model metadata) is written into three rows of one subarray; a read opens all three at once so charge sharing makes the sense amp resolve the majority, giving TMR voting in a single access with no logic.
why: Hammer- and retention-proof storage (facts 3, 9) for the ~1% of data whose corruption is catastrophic, with no added latency.

title: RAID-5 across HBM stacks accepts one dead die
idea: Inverts 'every die in a stack must work': the accelerator controller stripes each line across 8 HBM stacks with one parity channel, so a stack with one failed core die or channel ships and runs degraded instead of being scrapped.
why: HBM stacked-yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) could fall by more than half; parity costs ~12% capacity but saves whole stacks.

title: Retired GPUs repurposed as HBM memory appliances for newer accelerators
idea: Inverts 'an accelerator is worthless once its compute is obsolete': older GPUs stay in racks as 80-141 GB HBM memory servers, reached by newer accelerators over NVLink/CXL fabrics for KV-cache and parameter offload, their compute used only for copy and compression.
why: HBM scarcity: reuses HBM stacks that cannot be desoldered, adding terabytes of high-bandwidth far memory per rack without new HBM wafers.
note: Remote HBM is throttled to link bandwidth, so it acts like ordinary CXL far memory.

title: Stripe codewords across many die to pool error budgets
idea: Inverts 'each DRAM die must stand on its own quality': a CXL controller interleaves every codeword across 8-16 die from mixed sources (harvested, reject, new), so a die near 1% raw BER is averaged with clean die and the code works at the pooled rate.
why: Reuse and yield: lets heterogeneous, imperfect die be pooled into reliable memory, widening what is sellable from every supply stream.
note: Chipkill/RAID-style striping extended to mixed-quality die.

title: Compiler-certified weight re-reads replace refresh during LLM decoding
idea: Every activation is a full restore, and an LLM decode step streams all weights every ~10-50 ms. Add a pass to an open compiler (TVM, Triton or XLA) that proves each weight row is re-read within 32 ms, reordering layer streams if needed. It hands the memory controller a manifest to drop REF for those banks. A small team can demonstrate it on an FPGA accelerator testbed for under $1M in 18 months.
why: Weights fill 60-80% of inference memory, so suppressing their refresh removes most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss and its energy (fact 3).

title: Arrhenius leakage odometer schedules refresh by integrated charge loss
idea: Leakage scales as exp(-Ea/kT), so integrate a per-module charge-loss budget, the integral of exp(-Ea/kT(t)) dt, from DIMM thermal-sensor samples. Measure each module's Ea at boot by timing first failures at two temperatures. Refresh when the integral reaches the equivalent of 64 ms at 85 C. Controller firmware plus validation costs well under $1M and 12 months.
why: With Ea ~0.6 eV, a DIMM at 50 C leaks ~8x less, and at 40 C ~16x less, than in the 85 C case the spec assumes. Refresh energy and bandwidth fall 5-10x in typical fleets (fact 3).
note: Arrhenius-integrated refresh budget; temperature-compensated self-refresh already exists.

title: Decay-tolerant page cache re-faults from flash instead of refreshing
idea: Clean pages (file cache, model weights loaded from NVMe, read-only container layers) have an authoritative copy on storage, so they need probable, not guaranteed, retention. Keep them in banks at 8x relaxed refresh with a per-line CRC. On a mismatch the kernel drops the page and re-faults it from storage. A kernel patch plus controller CRC fits easily within $1M and 18 months.
why: Clean pages often fill 30-60% of server DRAM; cutting their refresh 8x removes a large share of refresh energy (fact 3) at no capacity cost.

title: Open BMC retention telemetry builds per-part-number refresh tables
idea: Ship an open-source BMC agent that logs corrected-error addresses, DIMM temperatures and part/lot numbers, and runs a 2-minute monthly retention probe on one drained rank. Pool anonymized data across operators into a public per-lot retention model that publishes safe tREFI tables with quantified risk. Software plus a small data team, <$700k over 24 months.
why: Spec refresh is set by the worst lot of the worst vendor; statistics over 100k+ DIMMs justify 2-4x relaxation for most lots (fact 3).

title: Best-effort memory cloud instances priced like spot capacity
idea: Offer a cloud instance class whose memory runs at 4-8x relaxed refresh, optionally on salvaged or second-life DRAM, at ~40% lower price. Guests see it as 'best-effort RAM' with a poison-page signal. Target workloads that checkpoint or recompute, such as ML training with frequent checkpoints, caches and batch analytics. A neocloud can pilot it on a few racks for <$1M within 24 months.
why: Turns the retention guardband into a priced product tier, lowering the effective cost per usable bit and stretching scarce DRAM supply (fact 3, cost per bit).

title: Canary columns detect row hammer and hot retention together
idea: Reserve ~8 columns per row holding a known pattern written at a deliberately weaker level; whenever the row is opened (access or refresh) the SAs check the canaries for free. A flipped canary means the row's neighbors are hammered or leakage at 125 C is outrunning refresh, triggering targeted refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and retention (fact 3) monitored with ~0.1% area and no counters; physics-tracking at any temperature.
note: Weak canaries as in-situ hammer/retention sensors.

title: Chlorinated carborane photoacids replace perfluorinated sulfonates in DRAM resists
idea: A photoacid only needs a weakly coordinating conjugate base; the icosahedral carborane anion CB11H6Cl6- spreads its charge over 12 cage atoms, giving acid strength beyond triflic acid with zero C-F bonds. Pair it with triphenylsulfonium cations; the bulky cage also shortens acid diffusion for lower line-edge roughness.
why: Removes PFAS photoacid generators facing EU/US restriction from every ArF/EUV resist; boron is US-mined.

title: Regenerable release coating extends imprint template life tenfold
idea: First principle: template wear happens in the top few nm where contact occurs, so the template body never needs replacing if its surface can be renewed. Coat imprint templates with a ~2 nm ALD sacrificial layer (Al2O3 plus fluorinated SAM) that is stripped and redeposited every ~1,000 imprints to restore the exact CD.
why: Mask/template cost for EUV-free imprint (fact 4): ~10x lower template cost per wafer.

title: Rack-level spot market for gigabyte-seconds of pooled memory
idea: Treat DRAM as a perishable flow (GB-s), not a stock. Each rack's CXL memory pool runs a second-by-second auction in which jobs bid for leases that carry an eviction penalty, and the scheduler packs the bids so pooled DRAM runs at 85-90% utilization instead of the 50-60% of statically provisioned servers.
why: Recovers most of the 25-40% stranded memory in clouds, for ~15-25% fewer DRAM bits per unit of work; pool operators get a business model.

title: Charge-minimizing inversion coding keeps bits in non-leaking state
idea: Only the charged state decays, so the error rate scales with the fraction of charged cells. A per-32-bit codebook flag (bus-invert style, aware of true/anti polarity) stores each chunk so that >=65% of cells sit in the discharged state.
why: Retention errors/refresh: exposure to tail failures roughly halved, which permits ~2x longer refresh with the same ECC, plus lower write energy.

title: Per-row variable-rate codes from factory cell-quality map
idea: Capacitorless cells spread widely in quality (read-transistor Vt, hole retention). At test, measure each row's raw BER and assign one of 4 code rates (none/SEC/DEC/t=4), stored as a 2-bit map in the controller. Good rows keep full capacity, and bad rows pay parity instead of being scrapped.
why: Yield/usable bits: +10-20% vs fixed worst-case ECC for capacitorless arrays.

title: Per-row retention maps let controllers sell today's scrapped weak dies
idea: Leakage is a per-cell tail (<=13 fA), not a per-die property, yet dies that fail 64 ms retention in a few rows are fused down or scrapped. Ship such dies with an on-die retention map that a CXL/HBM controller reads to refresh only the weak rows at 8-16 ms, turning reject bins into saleable capacity.
why: Yield and cost per bit: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output that is now discarded; the extra refresh is confined to <1% of rows, so the energy penalty is negligible.
note: Per-row variant of retention-graded salvage in I-00435; RAIDR-like.

title: Milk-carton expiry dates let dying data skip refresh
idea: Random stimulus 'milk carton expiry date': some contents are gone before they spoil. The compiler/runtime tags allocations (activations, KV-cache tiles, gradient buffers) with a deadline; a per-row expiry register in the DRAM refresh engine skips refresh for any row whose data is guaranteed overwritten or freed before its retention window ends.
why: In AI training most HBM rows are rewritten within 10-60 ms; skipping them cuts refresh operations 50-80% and recovers much of the 10-20% bandwidth tax (fact 3).

title: Strowger stepper: token-passing wordline drivers replace local row decoders
idea: A Strowger telephone switch steps one contact per pulse instead of decoding a full number. For streaming and AI traffic that walks rows in order, make each wordline driver a bootstrapped 4-transistor dynamic shift stage (as in LCD gate-on-array drivers) passing a single token, and keep a coarse random-access decoder only every 32 rows to jump the token.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): removes the row-address bus and per-row NAND decode from the local driver strip, perhaps 20-30% of decoder area; random jumps cost up to 31 extra clock steps, acceptable for sequential tiers.
note: Token-passing wordline drivers, same mechanism.

title: Egg grading: on-die margin sweep sells refresh-grade memory tiers
idea: Grade dies like eggs (AA, A, B): every die runs an on-die sweep of SA reference offset steps and retention waits, then is sold as a 'cool-datacenter' grade (256 ms refresh at <=60 C), a standard grade or a 'hot' grade; operators who run cold buy parts needing 4x less refresh.
why: Usable supply and refresh tax (fact 3): turns retention spread into priced tiers, recovering 10-20% bandwidth on graded parts and monetizing margin now wasted on worst-case design.

title: Drill bit: carbide-scrap microrefinery makes fluorine-free tungsten chloride precursor
idea: Stimulus 'drill bit' (worn cemented carbide) -> a 10-person microrefinery oxidizes and chlorinates scrap WC tool inserts and spent W targets into sublimation-purified WCl5/WCl6 for fluorine-free ALD/CVD tungsten.
why: Domestic recycled tungsten sidesteps China's ~80% share and removes WF6 handling; recycling already supplies ~30% of world tungsten.

title: Sourdough starter: pages kept as regenerable seed-plus-recipe stubs
idea: Forced connection: a baker keeps a pinch of starter, not the bread. Add an MMU/OS page class 'regenerable' whose PTE points to a 64-byte recipe (PRNG seed, generator kernel ID, parameters); on fault a near-memory engine re-materialises the 4 KB page in ~1 us and under pressure the page is simply dropped instead of swapped. Targets init weights, RoPE/sin tables, lookup tables, decompressed assets, pattern pages and deterministic intermediates.
why: Cost per bit / capacity: 5-25% of resident footprint in AI and HPC jobs is derivable; dropping instead of storing it gives 1.05-1.3x effective capacity with no new DRAM.

title: Origami: address unit stores structured matrices as their generators
idea: Fold rather than cut more paper: an address-transform unit in the memory controller treats tagged regions as symmetric, Toeplitz, circulant, banded or block-repeated, storing only the generating vector or triangle and computing (i,j) to generator offset on every access, so software still sees a dense matrix.
why: n^2 to n (or 2x for symmetric) storage for covariance, Hessian, convolution, positional-bias and kernel matrices in HPC and science codes, with no code rewrite.

title: Kaleidoscope: one tensor copy, many layouts via controller remapping
idea: A kaleidoscope shows many patterns from one set of beads: the memory controller exposes row-major, column-major and tiled 'views' of a single physical tensor through programmable address swizzles, so training no longer keeps transposed weight copies, layout-converted buffers or im2col expansions.
why: Duplicate layouts and expansions take 10-30% of training memory; removing them is 1.1-1.4x capacity.

title: Stained glass from shards: salvaged DRAM dies become CXL expanders
idea: Artists turn shards into windows: desolder DRAM packages from decommissioned servers (reflow <260 C), retest and bin them, and remount them on low-temperature panel-level substrates behind a compressing CXL controller, producing new capacity-tier modules from e-waste.
why: Millions of DDR4 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply at near-zero wafer cost and no high-temperature step, and compression makes old density competitive (~2x effective).

title: Sponge: porous-silicon low-k trenches under long interposer wires
idea: Like a sponge: regions of the silicon interposer under long RDL lines are electrochemically etched into porous silicon (k about 2 vs 3.9). This cuts line capacitance roughly 40%, and the CV-squared energy of cm-long chiplet links falls with it.
why: pJ/bit on 2.5D links (fact 5): roughly 30-40% lower link energy at the same swing.

title: Typewriter ribbon: revive tape-automated bonding for fine-pitch memory links
idea: Inspired by the typewriter ribbon: use modern 20 um-pitch polyimide flex tape (TAB, a 1970s technology) gang-bonded to memory and processor pads, giving wide, short memory buses between separate packages without an interposer.
why: Interposer cost and capacity; wide-bus links at ~1 pJ/bit from existing flex makers.

title: Toothpaste: stencil-printed silver-sinter micro-bumps for chiplet assembly
idea: Squeezed like toothpaste: nano-silver sinter paste is stencil-printed into 40 um-pitch bumps and sintered at about 200 C without thermocompression bonders, on equipment that SMT lines already own.
why: Capital intensity and thermal budget; low-temperature joints protect DRAM retention, and assembly needs about 1/10 the tool cost.

title: Library late fees: refresh debt budgeted against ECC correction margin
idea: Rows accrue a 'fine' equal to predicted bit-error probability (temperature, elapsed time, profiled retention class); the controller refreshes a row only when expected errors in its codewords approach a set fraction of the code's correction capacity, so healthy rows run overdue for seconds.
why: Fact 3: converts idle ECC slack into skipped refreshes, ~50-80% refresh reduction at <=1e-15 uncorrectable rate.

title: Tetris placement: compressed payload shifted so slack lands on weak bits
idea: Lines are compressed (BDI/FPC); the controller keeps a per-row weak-bit mask and rotates/offsets the compressed payload inside the 64 B line so known-weak or stuck positions fall into padding, recorded by a 3-6 bit shift field - PCM stuck-at masking ported to DRAM retention tails.
why: ~40% of lines become immune to known weak cells with no extra parity, permitting longer refresh or acceptance of cheaper, leakier dies.

title: One-way street: Z-channel asymmetric codes for unidirectional hot retention errors
idea: At 125 C nearly all errors are charged-to-discharged; mapping every cell to logical polarity (true/anti cells) makes the channel a one-way Z-channel, and asymmetric codes correct t unidirectional errors with ~30-40% fewer parity bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Same ~6% overhead corrects ~2x more hot retention errors, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C over the 10-year life.

title: Blood bank: type-matched inference-grade DRAM from ECC-failing die
idea: Random stimulus 'blood bank' -> type-match donors to recipients. Die with raw BER of 1e-9 to 1e-6 (rejected today) are typed and sold as 'inference grade' for quantized weights and KV caches, with the controller placing sensitive metadata in the die's strong rows and bulk tensors in weak rows.
why: Turns yield loss into supply: est. +3-6% sellable bits/wafer, cost per usable bit down proportionally, for workloads that already tolerate approximate data.

title: Decay-tracking reference voltage widens aged-cell sense margin
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA whose reference comes from a replica cell pair written at the last refresh and leaking in parallel x in-mat x Si x design only. Because true-cell 1s decay while 0s stay, the reference drifts down with the average 1, keeping the decision point midway between a decayed 1 and a 0.
why: Usable signal for aged cells roughly doubles, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh interval (fact 3) with no process change.

title: Buy retention-reject dies and run them in fast-refresh CXL pools
idea: Box: commodity dies that failed 64 ms retention x standard access x standard sense x CXL expander controller with 8-16 ms refresh and per-row remap x system x Si x zero masks. A company buys downgraded dies at scrap prices, profiles them, and sells pooled CXL capacity where extra refresh is hidden by bank parallelism.
why: Raises usable supply by reclaiming a few % of output now scrapped or downgraded, with zero fab capital (capital intensity, supply).
note: Salvage downbinned dies in CXL pools; supply gain only a few percent.

title: Token-ring wordline selection for streaming-mode DRAM banks
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x standard SA x shift-register wordline selection x bulk Si x standard flow. In AI-weight and KV-cache streaming banks, a one-hot token passed along a shift register selects successive rows, with only coarse 64-row-block decoding for random jumps, replacing full in-pitch row decoders.
why: Row decoder area -70-80% in streaming banks; lower activation energy for sequential reads.
note: LCD gate-driver style token rows for streaming banks; per-row shift stage may not beat decoder area.

title: Stack-level erasure coding rescues HBM stacks with one weak die
idea: Box: standard cells x Si access x per-die soft SA x cross-die erasure code in base die x Si x TSV stacking. Each codeword is spread across all 12-16 dies of an HBM stack, so a die with ~1% bad cells or a weak TSV group counts as a partial erasure instead of scrapping the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax: most of the 20-30% stack yield loss recovered; effective HBM supply +15-25%.

title: Asymmetric-pitch pillars let conformal gates self-merge into wordlines
idea: Box: MIM charge x vertical GAA pillar x voltage sense amp x 2D x Si x one dot mask with pitch_x below twice the gate thickness and pitch_y above it. Conformal ALD TiN merges between pillars along x into continuous wordlines but stays split along y, and an anisotropic spacer etch isolates rows, giving wordlines with no wordline mask and ~3 masks for the cell.
why: Mask count and overlay (fact 4) with a 4F2-like vertical cell from ALD and RIE; risk is wordline resistance of thin merged TiN and pillar CD variation.

title: National nanofab DRAM shuttle with an open cell PDK
idea: Box: business/policy axis set to distributed prototyping. Fund an NNCI-style shuttle where a standardized 150 mm open DRAM cell flow (contact litho, EBL, ALD, sputter only) runs quarterly in ten university nanofabs with shared test chips, open PDK and characterization, so startups test new cells for ~$50k in months instead of $5-10M.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time-to-innovation: widens the funnel of new cell concepts using fabs that already exist; risk is translation from 150 mm university flows to 300 mm production.

title: Profile-guided compiler narrows over-wide fields with overflow traps
idea: Box: representation shrink × compiler × struct field × profile-guided × narrow + reorder + trap. Fields whose observed ranges fit fewer bits (int64 counters under 2^20, enums, flags) are narrowed and packed, with cheap overflow traps that re-widen via deoptimization.
why: Padding and over-wide fields waste 20–40% of in-memory object bytes.
note: Speculative narrowing with deopt traps.

title: Layer recompute replaces ECC for AI training activations
idea: Box [medium: ECC-free cheap DRAM | access: standard | sense: 32-bit CRC per tile | integration: accelerator HBM | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Activations saved for the backward pass go into ECC-less, relaxed-refresh memory with a CRC per tile; a mismatch triggers recomputation of that layer from the last checkpoint, which costs <1% compute at observed error rates.
why: Reliability tax: drops 12.5% ECC overhead and lets ~2x weaker memory hold 40-60% of the training footprint.

title: Open-source eDRAM macro compiler for 22/28 nm foundries
idea: Box[Medium=MIM/trench eDRAM x Access=logic FET x Sensing=open sense-amp IP x Fab=mature foundry node x Owner=open consortium x Finance=membership dues]: publish a silicon-proven, permissively licensed eDRAM macro generator (array, refresh controller, sense amps, BIST) so any 22/28 nm foundry customer can build on-die working memory without buying discrete DRAM.
why: Moves some DRAM demand onto abundant mature-node logic capacity, which has ~3x more global wafer starts than DRAM; cuts discrete-DRAM demand for edge and accelerator SRAM-adjacent buffers.
note: OpenRAM-style for eDRAM; MIM/trench availability at 22/28 nm limits; gain-cell variant easier.

title: Mixed-vendor DIMMs harmonized via per-DRAM addressability trims
idea: Box[Source=qualified dies from any vendor x Transform=per-die timing and Vref trims via DDR5 PDA mode registers set by the RCD at boot x Integration=standard RDIMM x Owner=module maker]: build modules from whichever qualified dies are available and let the buffer program each die's offsets.
why: Supply fungibility: modules need not wait for one vendor's dies, smoothing allocation shortages; interface unchanged.

title: Refresh-off KV-cache zones with recompute-on-ECC-fail
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. LLM serving runtimes tag KV-cache and activation pages as decay-tolerant; the controller places those banks in a ~1 s refresh mode, and when on-die ECC flags an uncorrectable block the runtime recomputes that token's keys and values from the prompt instead of faulting.
why: Fact 3: KV cache is often 30-60% of inference DRAM; cutting its refresh 16x removes most refresh energy there and returns bandwidth to compute.
note: Recompute-on-ECC-fail for KV cache; refresh is modest share of inference energy.

title: Capacitorless gain-cell memory tiles from mature U.S. logic fabs
idea: Po: memory made in a factory that has never made a capacitor. License a 3T silicon gain cell on 22-28 nm logic processes at existing U.S. foundries and sell it as memory tiles hybrid-bonded under accelerators, hiding its ~1 ms retention with retention-aware refresh, with no capacitor module, EUV or DRAM fab needed.
why: Fact 4 and capital: uses depreciated U.S. logic capacity (near-zero new capex) for near-compute buffers, offloading 10-20% of HBM demand.

title: Sell retention-failed dies as never-refreshed ephemeral memory
idea: Po: the rejects are the product. Bin dies that fail the 64 ms retention spec but pass 4-8 ms and sell them as 'ephemeral memory' stacks for streaming workloads that must rewrite every buffer within a contractual window, enforced by a controller watchdog; refresh is never issued.
why: Supply: turns a top reject category into sellable bits (a few % more supply) at zero refresh power.

title: Aging KV cache in never-refreshed tiers, models trained to forget
idea: Po: let memory forget like a brain. Store KV-cache and activation low-order bit-slices in never-refreshed tiers and sign/high bits in protected tiers, and train models with the measured 1-to-0 decay statistics so old entries gracefully lose precision (8b toward 4b) as they age, matching how attention importance decays.
why: Refresh zero for ~half of AI working capacity; accuracy loss targeted <0.5% through decay-aware training.

title: Po the array is a hologram: interference-lithography cell arrays
idea: Po: 'the memory array is a hologram.' Extracted: expose the periodic array layers (active lines, wordlines, bitlines) by two- and four-beam interference of a 1990s frequency-quadrupled 266 nm laser, printing ~150 nm-pitch gratings over a whole 200 mm wafer at once; a KrF stepper then trims at mat edges and patterns the periphery.
why: Litho capital and masks: array layers need no reticle and no scanner time, at roughly 2x finer pitch than the stepper alone, with U.S.-buildable optics.
note: 150 nm pitch helps only legacy lines; overlay to other layers is the hard part.

title: Open DRAM PDK portable across any 28-65 nm foundry
idea: Po: DRAM is open source. Publish an open, foundry-portable gain-cell/1T1C memory process design kit using only steps every 28-65 nm logic fab already runs (MIM capacitors, standard high-k, existing implants), so dozens of mature fabs can fill idle capacity with interchangeable memory dies.
why: Supply concentration and idle capacity: converts surplus mature wafer starts into multi-source memory with zero new fab.
note: Mature-node memory density far below DRAM; cost per bit uncompetitive.

title: Expiring allocations: memory pages with a built-in death date
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Every allocation carries a TTL set by the programmer or inferred by the runtime (caches, session state, speculative buffers); the OS and memory controller reclaim expired pages without any free() call and stop refreshing those rows the moment they expire.
why: Cloud heaps carry 20-40% stale cache/session data nobody frees; TTL reclamation cuts resident footprint ~20-30% and drops refresh energy on dead rows (fact 3).
note: TTL semantics to stop refresh on dead rows; programmer adoption limits gains.

title: Byte-rent compiler: auto-narrow every field to its observed range
idea: Po: programs pay rent for every byte per second. A profile-guided compiler pass records production value ranges and cardinalities, then recompiles structs with the narrowest integer widths, enums as bitfields and packed booleans, with guarded widening on overflow.
why: Typical business objects store 8-16-bit values in 64-bit fields; auto-narrowing cuts object footprint 30-50%.

title: Fuzzy structures: compiler swaps exact maps for sketches when allowed
idea: Po: memory is approximate by default. Developers annotate tolerances (e.g., count within 1%), and the compiler/runtime substitutes count-min sketches, HyperLogLog, quotient or Bloom filters for exact hash maps and sets in telemetry, dedup and analytics code.
why: Replaces GB-scale exact counters with MB-scale sketches: 100-1000x memory reduction for those structures.

title: Mirrored predictors so only residuals cross the memory bus
idea: Po: memory sends guesses, not data. The HBM base die and the GPU memory controller run identical tiny value predictors (last-value, stride and delta per cacheline region) in lockstep; on each read only the entropy-coded residual against the shared prediction crosses the link.
why: Attacks 3-4 pJ/bit data-movement energy; structured tensors and pointers compress 1.5-3x, raising effective bandwidth and cutting link energy by the same factor.

title: Reel-to-reel DRAM tape wrapped around a cooling pipe
idea: Po: memory is sold by the metre. Mount bare DRAM dies on a continuous copper-on-polyimide tape (tape-automated bonding style) with fine-line flex wiring, then wrap the tape helically around a liquid-cooled tube to form a cylindrical module plugged in at one end.
why: Low-capex reel-to-reel assembly that U.S. flex-circuit makers can run, with no interposer and excellent cooling.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive links inside the HBM stack
idea: Po: time is abolished. Replace the stack's source-synchronous DDR interface with 1-of-4 delay-insensitive asynchronous encoding on TSVs and microbumps, deleting DLLs, PLLs and link training so lanes idle at zero power and run as fast as voltage and temperature allow.
why: Shrinks PHY periphery and idle power and enables deep voltage scaling; ~30% interface energy cut.

title: Cloud billing per byte crossing the HBM interface
idea: Po: moving data costs money, storing it is free. Cloud providers meter and price bytes crossing each accelerator's memory interface and refund locality-friendly jobs, steering frameworks toward fusion and on-chip reuse so fleets need fewer HBM stacks.
why: Software-driven traffic cuts of 20-40% let the same DRAM supply serve more workloads; a market fix for a supply squeeze.

title: Coset scrambling picks the least-coupled data pattern per row
idea: Po: memory that lies, but chooses its lie. On write, the controller tries four fixed scramble masks per row segment and stores the one minimizing charged-next-to-discharged adjacencies along bitline and passing-gate directions, recording the 2-bit mask ID in spare columns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling: the worst-case patterns that set the retention spec become rare, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~0.4% capacity overhead.

title: Pointer high-bit checksums catch flips without ECC chips
idea: Po: pointers that know where they should point. The compiler and runtime store a 12-16-bit checksum of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits, checked on dereference by a cheap instruction; corrupted pointers trap and are reloaded from a replica.
why: Most catastrophic memory-error crashes are corrupted pointers; lets cheaper non-ECC DRAM serve more servers with crash rates closer to ECC parts.

title: Unidirectional codes exploit retention's one-way error direction
idea: Po: errors only fall downhill. Leakage only discharges cells (1->0 for true cells, 0->1 for anti cells), so the controller uses asymmetric Z-channel codes (a Berger-style count check plus a t-asymmetric BCH) laid out by cell polarity, correcting retention errors with fewer check bits than symmetric ECC.
why: Retention (fact 3): ~40% fewer check bits for the same retention coverage, or stronger correction that allows longer refresh.

title: Iterative product codes with tiny hard-decision decoders
idea: Po: the code is a crossword puzzle. A 4 KB page is laid out as a 2D array protected by short BCH row and column component codes (like optical-transport staircase codes); a few rounds of iterative hard-decision decoding fix 1% BER at ~12-15% overhead.
why: Keeps 1%-BER memory affordable in power: ~10x less decoder energy than soft LDPC, well under 0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Flip-bounded number formats make weight memory ECC-free
idea: Po: numbers that can't be badly wrong. Weights use a redundant signed-digit encoding in which no single bit carries more than ~1/16 of the value range (e.g., 10 bits for 8-bit precision), so 1% raw flips act as small additive noise that noise-aware training absorbs with no decoder.
why: Zero decode latency and ~25% encoding overhead (vs ECC plus refresh) for the weight-streaming bulk of inference memory, run on cheap 1%-BER cells with minimal refresh.

title: Incremental-redundancy reads fetch extra parity only on failure
idea: Po: memory that talks like a cellular radio. Each line carries a short fast-path BCH; extra parity for a much stronger code sits in a separate row and is fetched HARQ-style only when the short decoder fails (a few % of reads at 1% BER).
why: Holds average access latency near the 10-100 ns DRAM class while guaranteeing 1%-BER correction; average latency penalty ~5-8%.

title: Chill commodity DDR5 to minus 40 C and stretch refresh
idea: Worsen: run memory hot beside 1 kW accelerators, where leakage doubles every ~10 C. Flip: build a $1M pilot of sealed two-phase-cooled DDR5 RDIMMs held at -40 C, where storage-node junction leakage drops ~100x, program the controller for 16x longer refresh intervals, and qualify within 24 months.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth on existing chips right away (fact 3: recovers most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax).
note: Cooling energy and condensation offset refresh savings; refresh is a modest share.

title: Deep-trench storage caps from US trench-power MOSFET fabs
idea: Worsen: claim only DRAM fabs can etch high-AR capacitors. Flip: trench-MOSFET power fabs (mature 200 mm, US-based) already etch deep silicon trenches daily; fund ~$700k of engineering lots to make 40:1 trench capacitors at 200 nm pitch as the storage layer of a 3D-bonded memory die.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: depreciated 200 mm tools, and IBM eDRAM already proved trench storage caps.

title: One-million-dollar Bit Prize judged on a standard test chip
idea: Worsen: let only incumbents with billion-dollar fabs propose storage elements. Flip: put the full $1M into a 24-month open prize: any storage element that hits 20 ns write, 1e15 cycles and 1 s retention on a supplied standard probe-card test vehicle wins, judged on measured data.
why: Leverages ~10-100x the budget in outside R&D effort and surfaces new storage physics fast.
note: $1M prize with steep spec may draw few serious entrants.

title: Ephemeral DRAM tier sold from retention-failing dies
idea: Worse: scrap every die that misses 64 ms retention. Flip: bin 4-16 ms dies as refresh-free 'ephemeral memory' for AI activations and KV tiles overwritten every few ms, with the controller guaranteeing rewrite-before-expiry or recompute.
why: Raises usable bit supply 5-15% from existing wafers and removes refresh for that tier (scarcity, fact 3).

title: Temperature-adaptive ECC turns spare bits into stronger code when hot
idea: Worse at 125 C: double the refresh rate the moment the die gets hot. Flip: above 95 C the on-die ECC engine regroups codewords from SEC to a 3-bit-correcting BCH using reserved parity columns, and refresh stays at 1x because weak-cell errors get corrected and scrubbed instead.
why: Avoids the 2x hot-refresh penalty in energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for ~3% capacity reserved.

title: Open-source DRAM periphery IP library on a U.S. foundry
idea: Worse: keep sense-amp, decoder and pump know-how locked inside three companies. Flip: a federally funded consortium publishes silicon-proven sense amps, wordline drivers, charge pumps and test macros on a U.S. mature node, so startups pairing novel cells with standard periphery need not reinvent it.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: removes years of periphery design time and cost for new entrants.
note: Federally funded open DRAM periphery library on a U.S. mature node; pilot macros fit SKY130 shuttles.

title: Hydrogen backside wafer cooling replaces helium in etch chucks
idea: Worsen: make every etch and deposition chuck bleed Qatari helium as backside coolant and use helium mass-spec for every leak check. Flip: run backside cooling on low-pressure (~10 Torr) pure H2, whose thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/mK) beats He (~0.15), in a sealed, interlocked chuck loop with a Pd-membrane purifier, and switch leak checks to H2/N2 forming-gas sensors.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% of supply offline): removes the largest helium use in a DRAM fab, cutting fab He demand ~70-90% with no change to thermal control.

title: Fab waste heat drives membrane distillation for ultrapure water
idea: Worsen: dump abatement, chiller and compressor heat to cooling towers that evaporate millions of gallons. Flip: route 40-70 C process-cooling water through vacuum membrane distillation modules that produce the high-purity feed for the UPW plant, so heat that would evaporate water purifies it instead.
why: Water and energy together: could supply ~30-50% of UPW makeup with almost no added energy and cuts cooling-tower evaporation.

title: Solderless compression-attach DRAM packages movable between board generations
idea: Worsen: solder LPDDR and DDR chips permanently to boards, so one dead CPU scraps all of its memory. Flip: seat each DRAM package in a spring-pin elastomer socket with a clamp frame (a chip-level CAMM), so packages can be lifted out, retested and re-seated in the next server generation.
why: Raises usable supply by extending DRAM service life 2-3x with no desolder or reball damage: scarce-resource intensity per bit-year falls ~50%.
note: Chip-level CAMM; LPDDR signal integrity through elastomer sockets is the risk.

title: Allocation leases that auto-demote unrenewed objects
idea: Worsen: let leaked and forgotten allocations live in DRAM forever. Flip: allocations carry a lease; the runtime renews leases on touch through access bits, and objects whose lease expires are migrated to a compressed far tier, with a fault bringing them back if ever touched.
why: Capacity: recovers the 10-25% of long-running service memory that is leaked or logically dead.

title: Command-less DRAM running a compiler-loaded access microprogram
idea: Worsen: let a controller guess access order at runtime, causing row conflicts and command-bus congestion. Flip: AI compilers know the whole dataflow, so they emit a time-triggered row/column schedule loaded into a sequencer in the memory base die; command/address pins are deleted and reused as data lanes.
why: Interface efficiency: ~20-30% more data pins, near-100% row-buffer hit rate, controller area removed from the logic die, lower energy per useful bit.

title: Z-channel asymmetric ECC matched to one-way charge loss
idea: Worse: use symmetric codes that spend parity guarding against discharged-to-charged flips that almost never happen. Flip: since leakage and hammering mostly drain charge, use asymmetric (Z-channel, Varshamov-type) codes with true/anti-cell-aware mapping, which correct t unidirectional errors with fewer check bits than symmetric BCH.
why: ECC overhead and weak-cell tolerance: ~30-40% fewer parity bits for the same protection, or ~2x correction at the same overhead, enabling relaxed refresh.

title: Federated yield-learning commons on anonymized wafer maps
idea: Worse: let every fab relearn the same defect signatures in secret. Flip: fabs train shared defect-classification models by federated learning on local wafer maps and inspection images so only weights leave each site, and new entrants receive the pre-trained model free.
why: Pulls new-line yield ramps in by months; yield-limited supply rises.

title: Self-expiring cache on retention-reject dies with write-time tags
idea: Worse: keep refreshing cache lines that will never be read again. Flip: each row carries a coarse write timestamp, and rows older than the die's measured retention count as cache misses refilled from flash or pooled memory, so weak-retention dies run with refresh off.
why: Zero refresh power, and dies that fail retention binning become usable supply.

title: Innkeeper's rule: house the restless guests in the weak rows
idea: An innkeeper puts the up-all-night guests in the rooms by the noisy street. The controller profiles weak rows and remaps the hottest pages (touched more often than every 16 ms) into them, since every activation restores charge; strong rows hold cold data, and the global refresh period is set by strong rows only.
why: Turns natural activations into free refresh: the global interval can stretch 2-4x, with a fallback refresh only when a weak row goes quiet.

title: Postal routing: packet-switched mats replace global decoders
idea: A postal worker sorts by zip code at each hub instead of reading one master list. Replace global row/column decoders and wide global I/O buses with a small on-die mesh: address and data packets hop to mats, each mat decodes locally, and replies return as packets.
why: Shrinks global wiring and decoders (part of fact 7's 49%) and lets many small sub-mat accesses run concurrently, cutting overfetch (fact 8).
note: Packet-routed mats replace global decode/buses; router latency and area overhead are the question.

title: Alien's 'not sure' bit: confidence-tagged sensing feeds erasure ECC
idea: An alien answers yes, no or not sure. Each SA group gets a resolution-time detector: a latch slower than a threshold to resolve flags its bit as an erasure, and the on-die ECC decoder switches to erasure decoding, which fixes about twice as many flagged errors as blind ones.
why: Doubles the effective error budget of the existing on-die ECC, buying ~30% less cell charge or longer bitlines (facts 1, 7) with no interface change.
note: Resolution-time erasure flags, same soft-sensing core.

title: Hydro cascade: voltage-stacked global I/O lanes reuse current
idea: A river turns two mill wheels in series. Two internal global data-line domains are stacked between VDD and ground, one swinging VDD to VDD/2 and the other VDD/2 to ground, so the same charge drives both before reaching ground; a small balancer absorbs mismatch.
why: Halves internal global I/O energy, a big share of DRAM's 10-20 pJ/bit (fact 5), with external DQ unchanged.
note: Voltage-stacked global data lines reuse charge; known logic technique newly applied to DRAM internal I/O.

title: Islamic-tiling artist's 60-degree lattice packs cells at 3.46F2
idea: A geometric-pattern artist would never use a square grid. Put vertical-channel cells on a triangular lattice, run wordlines along one 60-degree lattice direction and bitlines along a second, and pattern both with the periodic interference or spacer flows.
why: Hexagonal packing gives sqrt(3)/2 x 4F2 = 3.46F2, ~13% more bits per area beyond 4F2 with no node shrink (Facts 4, 7).

title: Embargo engineer swaps helium backside cooling for hydrogen
idea: Persona: a Soviet engineer under embargo, with no helium. Run the electrostatic-chuck backside gas on dry H2 at 5-15 Torr through flow-limited orifices, with H2 detectors. H2 conducts heat at ~0.18 W/m-K versus 0.15 for He. Requalify recipes, because the few sccm that leak into the chamber act like the H2 additions many etch and CVD recipes already use.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline): removes the largest recurring He use in DRAM etch and deposition fleets. Per-wafer He use could fall >80% at near-zero capex.
note: H2 conductivity matches He; flammability safety and chamber requalification are the main costs.

title: Arctic pipeline engineer cools etch chucks without PFAS fluids
idea: Persona: an Arctic engineer who keeps pipelines flowing with CO2 and hydrocarbons. Replace Novec/Fluorinert chiller fluids, discontinued in 3M's PFAS exit, with direct-expansion CO2 (R744) evaporators in the chuck for -60 C to +20 C. Use synthetic isoparaffin loops for warmer stages.
why: Removes PFAS heat-transfer fluids, which carry high GWP and ban risk, from the cryo-etch fleet that cuts DRAM capacitor holes.

title: Child asks why photoresist needs Teflon chemistry: carborane acid generators
idea: Persona: a child asks why the 'ink' needs the same stuff as non-stick pans. Replace perfluoroalkyl-sulfonate photo-acid generators with sulfonium salts of closo-carborane anions (CB11H12-). These superweak, non-coordinating boron-carbon anions give strong photo-acids with zero fluorine.
why: PAGs are a hard PFAS use in DUV and EUV resists that faces EU bans. Carborane anions keep the acid strength and low diffusion that 12 nm patterning needs.

title: Child asks 'why remember?': forget-by memory leases with recompute recipes
idea: A child asks why you'd keep every toy out forever. So each allocation carries a forget-by lease and a lineage recipe: the function and input handles that produced it. On expiry or memory pressure the OS drops the page and keeps only the recipe, and a later touch faults and recomputes it. This is Spark-RDD lineage moved down into virtual memory, aimed at caches, memo tables, decoded assets and derived indexes.
why: Derived data is often 30-50% of resident memory. Making it recompute-on-demand cuts resident DRAM 20-40% for cache-heavy services, paid for with spare CPU cycles.
note: Spark lineage pushed into VM; gain bounded by share of derived data and recompute cost.

title: Neuroscientist's predictive brain: store only prediction residuals in memory controller
idea: The cortex mostly transmits prediction errors. The memory controller runs cheap per-line predictors (stride, delta from the neighboring line, or the previous version of the line) and stores just the residual plus a 2-bit predictor tag. This is video motion compensation applied to arrays, page tables, counters and timestamps.
why: Numeric arrays and pointers are highly predictable. Residual coding gets 2-4x on exactly the data where dictionary and LZ methods fail, raising effective capacity per bit.

title: Artist's negative space: asymmetric Z-channel ECC for one-way charge leakage
idea: An artist reads the empty space as much as the ink: retention errors almost always go from charged to discharged, so the controller tracks true-cell/anti-cell polarity per row, maps data so every retention error is a one-way flip, and uses asymmetric (Z-channel) error-correcting codes that need far fewer parity bits than symmetric BCH for the same correction.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~40% less parity for equal protection, or about twice the retention errors corrected for equal overhead, which lets cells run on thinner margins.

title: Immunologist's fever: ECC strength rises with temperature, not refresh rate
idea: The body runs a fever to fight infection instead of working harder everywhere: above 85 C the controller switches marked regions from SECDED to a stronger BCH code, using adjacent capacity the OS reserved in advance, instead of doubling refresh across the whole device.
why: Fact 3: avoids 2x-refresh mode (10-20% bandwidth at high density), and only cold-tolerant capacity is borrowed.

title: Actuary's bronze tier: discounted relaxed-refresh memory for checkpointed jobs
idea: An actuary prices risk instead of eliminating it: cloud providers sell a 'bronze memory' NUMA node with relaxed refresh and lighter ECC at a 30-40% discount for jobs that checkpoint (ML training, batch analytics), opted in through an madvise-style flag, so lower-bin dies get a paying home.
why: Frees refresh bandwidth and lets the market absorb weaker cells, raising usable supply.

title: Embargo engineer's reballing brigade for e-waste phone LPDDR
idea: Like a Soviet engineer under embargo salvaging chips from Western hardware, automated lines pull LPDDR4X/LPDDR5 packages off scrapped phones and laptops (IR desolder, X-ray inspection, reball). Packages pass 48-hour march and retention screens and are mounted, graded, on CXL Type-3 carrier cards whose controller maps around weak banks.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2B phones a year retire with 4-12 GB each; recovering 10% gives ~1 EB/yr of DRAM-class capacity (a few % of world bit supply) with almost no fab capital.
note: Many phone LPDDR packages are PoP or uMCP with NAND; old LPDDR4X has limited value.

title: Prospector reworks tailings: tungsten from fab waste and boards
idea: Like prospectors reworking old tailings, recover tungsten from WF6 exhaust scrubbers, W-CMP slurry and scrapped memory boards by electrochemical leaching and solvent extraction. The output is domestic fab-grade WF6 feedstock.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint (China ~80% of tungsten): well under half of the WF6 fed into a chamber ends up as film, so a closed loop could cover a large share of a U.S. DRAM fab's tungsten demand.

title: KV-cache significance split: mantissa tails in unrefreshed rows
idea: LLM KV caches tolerate noise in low-order mantissa bits. Keep sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in normally refreshed ECC rows, and put the low 4-5 mantissa bits of each BF16/FP8 value in rows refreshed only at their 1%-BER age with no ECC, so softmax sees those flips as tiny noise.
why: Facts 3 and 5: ~30-40% of KV bits drop most refresh and all parity, cutting HBM refresh energy and ECC overhead; expected perplexity change <0.1%.

title: Downhole adaptive code rate: parity grows as the die heats
idea: Oil-well tools swing 25-200 C and cannot afford refresh that doubles every ~10 C. Keep refresh fixed and let raw BER float from 0.01% up to 1%; an on-die thermometer steps each page's code rate from 0.97 down to 0.85, borrowing spare capacity from a reserved pool when hot.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy stays flat across temperature instead of rising 4-8x when hot; capacity rather than energy absorbs heat, which suits AI servers running memory at 85-95 C.

title: $1 IoT sensor log repaired by signal smoothness, not ECC
idea: Cheap sensor nodes log slow physical signals (temperature, vibration, ECG). Their embedded 1T1C macro has no ECC and refreshes only at its 1%-BER age (seconds); firmware delta-encodes samples and a Hampel/median filter at read removes physically impossible isolated jumps, using the signal's physics as the code.
why: Cost and fact 3: an ECC-free, rarely refreshed embedded DRAM replaces SRAM at ~5x density in low-cost MCUs, and refresh, often the sleep-power floor, nearly vanishes.

title: Probe-style closed-loop power control applied to refresh pacing
idea: Space probes tune transmit power from receiver feedback to sit just above the error target. Make each row group's refresh period a control loop: the decoder reports corrected-bit counts per page, and the controller lengthens or shortens that group's period to hold raw BER near a 0.5-1% setpoint, following temperature, aging and VRT without profiling.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows each group's real decay instead of the global worst case, about 2x below a fixed 1%-quantile schedule, with built-in safety.

title: CD-player C2 flags: sense amps that mark uncertain bits as erasures
idea: CD players mark scratched symbols as erasures so the decoder can fix twice as many. Give the bitline sense amplifier a third 'uncertain' output (a window comparator about +/-20 mV around the reference) so weakly decayed cells reach the decoder as erasures rather than silent errors, doubling correctable bits per parity bit.
why: Fact 3: at fixed parity, refresh can stretch further, or the same 1% cell BER needs about half the parity; costs a few transistors per sense amp.

title: Spacecraft execute-in-place: run code straight from CXL flash
idea: From spacecraft that execute directly from radiation-tolerant NOR to spare scarce RAM: servers map binaries, shared libraries and read-only model files execute-in-place from CXL-attached flash modules with an on-module SRAM/DRAM line cache, so no page-cache copy is made in host DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 10-25% of server DRAM and are duplicated per container; XIP shrinks that to a small module cache.

title: Mars-rover precision on demand: bit-plane memory layout and tiering
idea: From rovers that downlink images progressively, most significant bits first: store tensors and images bit-plane-major, keep the top planes in DRAM and the low planes in flash or nowhere, and let each reader request only the planes its precision needs.
why: Many consumers (inference, previews, analytics) need 4-8 of 16-32 bits; plane tiering cuts DRAM 2-4x without fixing precision at write time.
note: Bit-plane layout breaks locality; most inference needs full precision.

title: Sealed-submarine contract: applications negotiate memory like video bitrate
idea: From submarines that must keep running as hardware fails during months sealed: an OS API (memory.qos) lets apps register quality-versus-footprint ladders (cache size, model precision, index granularity), and the kernel steps each app down or up the ladder under pressure instead of swapping or OOM-killing.
why: Lets fleets provision for typical rather than peak memory: 20-40% fewer DIMMs with graceful quality loss.

title: Desert water discipline: cgroup quotas in liters per GB-hour
idea: From desert nomads who budget every liter: the kernel gains a water.max cgroup controller that converts each container's resident GB-hours into liters (amortized fab UPW per bit plus site WUE times memory power); over-budget pages are compressed or tiered to flash automatically, and budgets ratchet down 10x on a published schedule.
why: Makes water the binding resource, forcing compression and tiering that drive resident DRAM, and thus embedded fab and cooling water, down an order of magnitude per workload.
note: Essentially memory quotas with a water proxy; 10x ratchet is aspirational, not physical.

title: Exchange matching engines: keep the input log, replay state on demand
idea: From exchanges that can rebuild any order book from a deterministic input journal: rarely read service state (sessions, carts, per-user caches) is not kept resident; only an append-only input log on flash plus periodic snapshots exist, and state is rebuilt by deterministic replay when a request arrives.
why: For long-tail state touched once every few hours, replay replaces resident bytes, cutting DRAM for that state 10-100x and the water to make it.

title: Append-only log port built for KV-cache streaming
idea: The long-context KV cache is an extreme user: written once per token, appended sequentially, read whole every step. Add a port mode with a hardware append pointer (writes carry no address) and descriptor-driven sequential read streams, so command/address traffic, row-conflict scheduling and refresh collisions largely vanish for that region.
why: Cuts CA pins ~60% and lifts bus efficiency from ~70% to ~95% for KV traffic; ~30% more bandwidth per pin without new cells.

title: Radio-telescope corner-turn base die gives free transposes
idea: Radio correlators (SKA, ALMA) spend much of their memory budget on the 'corner turn' that transposes time-major data to frequency-major. Store tiles diagonally skewed across banks and add a butterfly transpose network in the HBM base die, so a matrix written row-major streams out column-major at full burst efficiency.
why: Strided/transposed reads waste 50-90% of fetched bytes (page overfetch); attention, FFT and weight-gradient transposes run at full efficiency, ~2-5x effective bandwidth in those phases.

title: Genlock-synchronized command-free memory interface
idea: Broadcast studios genlock every device to one reference so nothing negotiates timing. The compiler emits a static access schedule for a training step; host and memory base die run identical cycle-accurate sequencers locked to a shared clock, so no commands or addresses cross the interface, only data and a rare resync word.
why: Repurposes CA pins as data (+20-30% bandwidth per pin), removes controller complexity and makes row-hammer-safe schedules provable at compile time.

title: Fly-by-wire redundancy: erasure-code across stacks to accept defective dies
idea: Flight controls tolerate failed channels by redundancy. Stripe each cache line with a Reed-Solomon code across 8+2 stacks/channels, so stacks with dead channels or weak dies can ship and run; the controller remaps on the fly.
why: Turns part of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss into usable supply; worthwhile when yield loss exceeds the ~20% parity overhead.

title: Neural-implant address-event bus for sparse tensors
idea: Neural implants with 1,000+ electrodes send spikes as address events, not frames, to stay within milliwatts. Store activations and KV in a sparse layout and run the link in address-event representation: only nonzero values with compressed coordinates cross the PHY, each event gating its own lane.
why: At 70-95% activation sparsity (ReLU, MoE, pruned models) bits moved per logical access fall ~3-10x; energy tracks information rather than tensor size.

title: Laptop panel-self-refresh: mirrored dictionaries deduplicate memory link traffic
idea: Laptop eDP panels self-refresh so the GPU stops resending unchanged frames. Keep synchronized small dictionaries of recent 64 B lines at both ends of the memory link; when a line or near-match is already in the far dictionary, send a 10-bit index plus a sparse diff instead of 512 bits.
why: Repeated lines (zero pages, shared prefixes, embeddings) are common; at 50-90% hit rates link energy per access falls ~3-10x without touching cells.

title: Intermittent-IoT rebuild: refresh-free weights refetched from flash on CRC fail
idea: Energy-harvesting IoT nodes let volatile state die and rebuild it from nonvolatile checkpoints. Apply that to immutable LLM weights: refresh the weight region only every 1-4 s (most cells retain seconds), give each 4 KB page a CRC-32 checked on read, and silently re-DMA any failing page from the golden copy on SSD or flash. This needs a per-region refresh-interval register.
why: Weights are ~50-80% of inference memory. Cutting their refresh 16-64x removes most refresh power and bandwidth for that footprint, and lets weight memory use retention-reject dies (fact 3).
note: Inference reads weights every token, which already restores rows; savings may be smaller than claimed.

title: Long-context KV triage: low-attention tokens live on relaxed-refresh ranks
idea: Million-token KV caches are among the most extreme memory users. Track each token's cumulative attention score and migrate the bottom ~70% of tokens' K/V blocks onto ranks the controller runs at 4x longer tREFI, or onto retention-weak binned DIMMs. High-attention tokens stay on standard ranks, and errors in rarely attended tokens barely move outputs.
why: The KV cache dominates long-context serving memory. Relaxing refresh on most of it saves refresh power and bandwidth and creates demand for weak bins (fact 3).

title: Genome-coverage redundancy: reclaim ECC lanes as data for self-protected pages
idea: Sequencers keep 30x-redundant reads, so single flips do not matter. On ECC DIMMs and HBM, the OS marks pages that are already protected end-to-end (erasure-coded objects, checksummed caches, FEC'd media, replicated weights), and the controller uses the 8 ECC bits per beat on those pages as data, exposing 12.5% more capacity.
why: Turns up to 12.5% of installed ECC capacity into usable bits on eligible pages. At fleet scale that is new supply without new wafers.
note: Up to 12.5% capacity on end-to-end-protected pages.

title: NICU-style first days: field burn-in under mirroring replaces burn-in ovens
idea: Neonatal ICUs watch newborns most closely in the first days, because that is when failures cluster. Ship DRAM without the multi-hour burn-in step. Server BIOS runs new DIMMs in standard memory-mirroring mode with aggressive patrol scrub for the first ~72 hours, retires any infant-mortality failures, then releases full capacity.
why: Burn-in ovens and test time are a real slice of DRAM back-end capital. Moving infant screening into the field cuts test capex and cycle time by ~10-20% (fact 4).
note: Moves infant screening to field mirroring; modest test capex saving.

title: Recompute-grade DRAM SKU priced by verified raw bit-error rate
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache and activations are recomputable, so a bit flip costs a recompute, not a crash. Fabs ship dies that fail strict screens at a guaranteed raw BER (e.g., 1e-10 per bit-hour); inference stacks add per-block checksums and recompute on mismatch, and buyers pay per verified-good GB-hour.
why: Turns statistical-screen fallout into supply and lets buyers drop ECC overhead; perhaps 3-8% more sellable bits per wafer.

title: Certified remanufactured DRAM: package harvest, reball and warranty standard
idea: Shenzhen rework shops, an extreme informal user, already desolder and reball DRAM from scrap. Formalize it with a UL-style certification covering test protocol, burn-in, traceability and a 3-year warranty, under which retired hyperscaler DIMM packages are harvested, reballed and rebuilt onto new module and CXL PCBs.
why: Tens of millions of DIMMs retire each year; 30% recovery adds several % of global bit supply at ~10-20% of new cost with no fab capex.
note: Certification standard twist on the package-harvest mechanism.

title: DRAM-lean label: certification that weans devices off unneeded DRAM
idea: Modeled on Energy Star, a 'DRAM-lean' label for TVs, set-top boxes, routers and car head units certifies firmware that meets a RAM budget (zram, execute-in-place from NOR, pruned services), backed by procurement preferences, returning gigabytes per device to the market.
why: Embedded consumer devices absorb many bits at low utilization; a 30% trim frees meaningful supply.

title: Hourly memory-capacity marketplace in colocation CXL pools
idea: Render farms, tax-season and quarter-close workloads are extreme users with offset peaks. Colos install CXL-switched DRAM pools and auction terabyte-hours to tenants, moving capacity between hosts in seconds.
why: Average DRAM utilization is ~40-60%; cross-tenant pooling toward 80% raises usable supply 1.3-1.6x.

title: Triple-vote modules built from reject dies, cubesat-style
idea: Cubesat builders fly three COTS memories with majority voting instead of rad-hard parts. A 10-person shop builds modules where three near-free reject-grade dies hold each word and a small FPGA votes bitwise and scrubs, giving industrial-grade reliability from scrap.
why: Turns zero-value fallout into high-reliability supply: 3x silicon at ~0.1x die cost.

title: Retention-fingerprint registry that authenticates resold DRAM chips
idea: Copying sneaker-resale authentication, a 10-person service records each chip's random weak-cell retention map, a natural PUF, at first sale. Any later reseller re-reads the map in minutes to prove the chip is genuine and not relabeled.
why: Counterfeits poison grey-market supply; authentication lets secondary DRAM reach defense and enterprise buyers.

title: Package-on-package de-stacking line for phone LPDDR
idea: Extreme user: over a billion phones a year, many with LPDDR stacked package-on-package on the SoC. A 10-person line uses gradient heating and a shear fixture to split the stack without reflowing the lower joints, recovering 4-12 GB LPDDR4X/5 packages per phone for retest.
why: Phones are the largest untapped pool of modern DRAM scrap; even 5% recovery is hundreds of PB a year.

title: Ephemeral DRAM sized for millisecond data lifetimes
idea: Time-shift the retention spec from 64 ms to the real lifetime of AI activations and KV-cache tiles (often <2 ms between write and last read): build arrays with capacitors 4-5x smaller and short-pillar cells, tagged in the address map as 'ephemeral', and never refresh them; the runtime guarantees consume-before-expire.
why: Capacitor wall and refresh energy: ~4x smaller Cs, no refresh for that tier, roughly 30-40% lower cost per bit for activation memory.
note: Software-guaranteed expiry is easy to demo; cost gain limited to activation memory.

title: Significance-graded cell sizes for MSB and LSB bits
idea: Time-shift by bit importance: lay out arrays with large-capacitor cells for exponent and high bits and small, unrefreshed cells for low mantissa bits of AI weights and activations, which may decay gracefully between writes.
why: Cost per bit and refresh: ~25-35% area saving and half the refresh energy for FP16/BF16 tensors with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Fleet-learned per-row retention atlas built over years
idea: Scale jump from one DIMM to a million-server fleet and time jump from a 64 ms spec to multi-year observation: every server runs low-priority retention probes (write pattern, pause 0.25-4 s, read) in idle banks and uploads per-row results with temperature; a fleet model keyed by die lot, wafer position and age assigns each row a refresh bin loaded at boot, and repeated sightings flag variable-retention cells.
why: Refresh (fact 3): >99.9% of rows retain >1 s, so binning most rows to 256 ms-1 s cuts refresh ops ~4-8x, while fleet statistics catch rare VRT behaviour that a single factory test cannot see.

title: Fleet-learned per-bank sense timing pushed by firmware
idea: Scale jump to the datacenter and to years: every module reports per-bank minimum passing tRCD/tRAS from periodic margin sweeps, the fleet models them by vendor lot, temperature and age, and firmware pushes per-bank timing tables back, re-tightening or relaxing as drift appears.
why: Typical banks carry 30-50% timing slack, so ~20-30% lower latency and activation energy fleet-wide with no new silicon (facts 7, 10).

title: Log-domain time-to-threshold sensing keeps decayed gain cells readable
idea: Time-domain sensing: gain cells are read by timing how long the read current takes to discharge a sense node, decided on a log-time scale; since subthreshold read current is exponential in stored voltage, a '1' that has lost 0.6 V still discharges ~10^3x faster than a '0', so cells stay readable 3-10x longer, reaching minutes, and session KV caches need no refresh.
why: Stretches gain-cell retention past session idle times, deleting refresh (fact 3); the log scale also absorbs temperature drift.

title: Cryo-trapping unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust for on-site reuse
idea: Tungsten CVD consumes only ~20-30% of the WF6 it is fed. Condense the remainder from the foreline at -80 C (WF6 boils at 17 C) before the abatement burner, distill it free of HF and byproducts, and return it to the gas loop weekly, closing a minute-scale waste into a week-scale cycle.
why: Cuts tungsten (China ~80%) and fluorine consumption for W layers 2-4x and reduces abatement fuel energy.

title: Bit-year embodied-resource labels reward memory that lives longer
idea: Time-scale shift from purchase to service life: require DIMM and HBM vendors to publish helium, tungsten, water and energy per bit-year of rated service. Tie procurement and tax credits to the lowest per-bit-year figure, rewarding 10-year-rated modules and take-back programs.
why: Most DRAM retires at 3-5 years while the silicon is good for 15+. Doubling service life halves chokepoint-material intensity per delivered bit-year.

title: Partial-good HBM stacks resold as shorter-height stacks
idea: Scale shift from die to stack: instead of scrapping 12-high HBM stacks with one or two failed core dies, fuse off those dies through base-die stack-ID remapping. The stacks ship as 8- or 10-high capacity parts for inference cards.
why: Recovers much of the 20-30% HBM yield loss as usable bits, with no extra wafer starts.

title: MEMS-fab vapor HF releases capacitor molds with no rinse water
idea: Phase shift from liquid to vapor: run the anhydrous HF/alcohol vapor release tools that are standard in existing 200 mm MEMS fabs to strip sacrificial oxide molds around capacitor pillars. There is no liquid, no rinse, no capillary collapse and no UPW.
why: Saves tens to hundreds of liters of UPW per wafer at that step, allows taller pillars and puts idle MEMS capacity to work on capacitor modules.

title: Byte-second pricing for compilers, runtimes and schedulers
idea: Allocators, ML compilers and cluster schedulers optimize byte-seconds (capacity x residency time) instead of peak bytes. The compiler rematerializes or streams any tensor whose recompute energy is lower than the cost of holding it in DRAM for that many byte-seconds, and clusters bill tenants per GB-microsecond actually resident.
why: Moving the metric from space to space x time makes short-lived data cheap and idle long-held data expensive. That gives 2-5x less activation footprint in training and 20-30% at cluster level.

title: Cache-line-granular hot packing across cold pages
idea: A CXL controller tracks access bits per 64 B line within hot pages. It migrates the cold lines of hot pages to a compressed far tier and packs hot lines from many pages into dense hot frames through an indirection table. Tiering shifts from the 4 KB page scale to the 64 B line scale.
why: Only 20-40% of the lines in a typical hot page are hot. This needs 1.5-2x less fast DRAM for the same miss rate.

title: Staggered garbage-collection cycles sharing one pooled heap headroom
idea: Co-located JVM, Go and .NET processes each reserve 1.5-3x their live heap as headroom. A node-level coordinator staggers their GC cycles in time and lends a single shared headroom region (memfd plus ballooning) to whichever process is about to collect.
why: Headroom is multiplexed in time instead of replicated per process, for 20-40% less DRAM on managed-language fleets.
note: Time-multiplexed GC headroom across processes.

title: Fleet-trained static dictionaries burned into memory-controller firmware
idea: This adds zero masks. A dictionary of the most frequent 64 B patterns (pointers, zero runs, float templates, ELF and JIT idioms) is trained on years of fleet memory dumps and shipped yearly into controller SRAM through firmware. Every line then compresses against fleet-scale statistics instead of local history.
why: 1.3-1.6x extra compression on small lines, where local adaptive codecs fail, so hosts need less installed DRAM.

title: Address-free scheduled-stream DRAM programmed at compile time
idea: Shift address generation from runtime nanoseconds to compile time: for AI graphs the whole access sequence is known, so the compiler loads a compact access program into the stack's base die, which streams rows in order with no command/address traffic. The host simply consumes a tape.
why: Eliminates command/address bus pins and energy and lets each row be activated once and fully consumed, attacking 128x overfetch (fact 8) and bus energy (fact 5): ~20-30% interface energy saved.

title: Graceful capacity decay: code rate grows as modules age
idea: Stretch the memory's timescale to a decade: the base die tracks raw BER as cells wear and leak (up to 1% and beyond), automatically raising parity and announcing a slightly lower capacity through a hot-capacity-change event the OS honors. Modules retire only when ~15% capacity is gone.
why: Roughly doubles service life of deployed DRAM/HBM, effectively adding supply, and lets new parts ship with thinner margins.
note: Page retirement plus adaptive ECC; DRAM rarely retires from wear, so supply gain is small.

title: TTL-tagged writes: rows holding short-lived data skip refresh
idea: Match data lifetime to retention time: every write over the interface carries a time-to-live hint (activations microseconds, KV cache seconds), and rows whose data dies before 1% of cells decay are never refreshed. At 1% tolerance that unrefreshed window stretches from 64 ms to roughly 1 s.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) ~70-90% for AI working sets.
note: Related to Flikker/refresh-skipping art; needs error tolerance at 1 s windows.

title: lossy_malloc: cloud memory tier priced by tolerated bit error rate
idea: Create a datacenter-scale market: the allocator exposes lossy_malloc(ber=1e-2), mapping those pages onto pools with 1%-BER cells, B-grade dies or relaxed refresh at ~1/3 the price, and frameworks place embeddings, KV caches and media buffers there by default.
why: Creates demand for cheap error-tolerant capacity, multiplying usable supply for AI and media without new fabs.
note: Approximate-memory allocator as a market tier; framework adoption and 1/3 price are the doubts.

title: Z-channel coding exploits one-way charge leakage at the interface encoder
idea: Use the physics timescale of leakage: retention errors almost only turn stored charge to no-charge, so the interface encoder maps data to true/anti-cell polarity to minimize charged cells and applies an asymmetric (Z-channel) code. At 1% one-directional error, capacity rises from 0.92 to ~0.95 and parity needs fall ~40%.
why: Cuts ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells and reduces charged-cell count (refresh and CV2 energy, facts 3, 10) by ~20-30%.
note: Exploits unidirectional retention errors; unidirectional codes known.

title: Exponential-decay bloom filter tracks hours-long VRT toggling
idea: Timescale shift (64 ms refresh -> hours-long trap dwell): variable-retention-time cells flip between leaky and good trap states with hours-scale dwell. The controller keeps a time-decaying counting bloom filter of rows that recently showed corrected errors and refreshes only those fast, letting entries fade as the dwell statistics expire.
why: Handles the VRT tail that static retention profiling misses, enabling relaxed baseline refresh (e.g. 256 ms) with near-zero escapes.

title: SAQP pitch-walk classes get their own refresh and ECC
idea: No EUV: self-aligned quadruple patterning on DUV produces systematic alpha/beta/gamma line-width classes. Scale shift (litho systematics -> refresh scheduling): tag each row by its spacer class at design time and run separate refresh intervals and ECC strengths per class rather than guard-banding all rows to the worst class.
why: Recovers ~20-40% of refresh energy and lets multi-patterning replace EUV despite its CD variation.
note: Testable on commodity DRAM via retention vs row index mod 4; systematic class effect may be swamped by random tail.

title: First-week in-field self-profiling replaces factory retention bakes
idea: No EUV: skip the hours-long high-temperature retention test at the factory. Time/scale shift (factory hours -> field week): the module ships with conservative refresh, self-profiles each row's retention during its first week in a server, then relaxes refresh row by row.
why: Cuts test capex and floor time (a major cost for mature-node fabs) and finds VRT/temperature-specific tails in their real environment.

title: Follow-the-sun GB-hour exchange that moves memory-hungry jobs, not memory
idea: Planet-scale, hourly time shift: a spot market prices idle DRAM in GB-hours per datacenter region. Schedulers migrate batch jobs that need lots of memory (ETL, graph analytics, fine-tuning) to regions whose interactive load is at its nightly low, so installed DIMMs stay busy around the clock.
why: Fleet DRAM utilization is often ~40%. Lifting it to ~65% adds ~50% usable supply without any new bits.

title: Purdue SiC DRAM revived by the EV silicon-carbide wafer glut
idea: Purdue's 1990s 4H-SiC DRAM cells held charge for years at room temperature, because the 3.26 eV gap suppresses thermal generation, but the work stalled on expensive, defect-ridden SiC wafers. EV power electronics have since made 200 mm SiC cheap. Build a planar 1T1C SiC cell with a nitrided gate oxide on U.S.-grown SiC, using spare power-device line capacity, as a refresh-free DRAM-class tier.
why: Near-nonvolatile DRAM that needs essentially no refresh, made on existing U.S. SiC capacity. Density is lower than silicon DRAM, so the gains are energy per bit and supply security, not cost per bit.
note: Purdue SiC DRAM physics proven; cheap EV SiC wafers revive it as low-density nonvolatile tier.

title: Nextreme thin-film thermoelectrics revived to dodge 85C refresh doubling
idea: Nextreme's thin-film thermoelectric coolers faded because of poor efficiency. Refresh doubles above 85 C, so even a low-COP cooler pays off if it shaves the last 5-10 C. Screen-print Bi2Te3-based thermoelectric films onto DIMM and HBM heat spreaders and turn them on only when the die sensors approach 80 C.
why: Keeps hot accelerator memory in 1x refresh, avoiding the extra ~46 fJ/bit of refresh and ~10% of bandwidth that 2x refresh costs. Printable and cheap.

title: Thinfilm's yield problem solved by self-clearing printed electrodes
idea: Thinfilm's printed memories struggled with yield because of pinholes and leaky spots. Borrow the self-healing of metallized-film capacitors: print 20 nm aluminium top electrodes, so that during a burn-in pulse any leakage hot spot heats up and vaporizes the electrode around it. That disconnects the leaky cell, which is then mapped out instead of setting the retention time.
why: Physically clips the leakage tail of printed arrays, so refresh is set by intrinsic leakage rather than defects. Printable.

title: Project Ara lesson: optically coupled hot-swap memory tiles
idea: Google's Project Ara modular phone failed partly because its electro-permanent-magnet connectors could not carry enough bandwidth reliably. Couple swappable DRAM tiles to the host through short free-space optical links (VCSEL and photodiode arrays through a glass window), held by a mechanical latch. Tiles hot-swap with no wear-prone electrical connector.
why: Dense bandwidth with no contacts to wear (fact 5), plus field-replaceable, recyclable memory capacity.

title: Staktek package stacking reborn as blade-stacked, edge-contact DRAM dies
idea: Staktek's stacked packages lost to TSVs because their flex leads were coarse. Mount each thinned DRAM die on a thin carrier blade with fine edge contacts, and slide the blades into a compression-contact backplane next to the processor. Any blade can be pulled and replaced.
why: Replaces TSVs (fact 6) with edge contacts and makes each die serviceable and recyclable, at density near HBM with no TSV yield loss.

title: Indium-free zinc-tin-oxide tiers revived for recyclable 3D DRAM
idea: Zinc tin oxide (ZTO) transistors lost to IGZO on mobility and etch control. 3D DRAM access devices need low leakage more than mobility, so use ZTO channels for the stacked tiers, with an all-oxide stack chosen so zinc and tin are recovered by a simple acid leach.
why: Avoids indium (China-dominated, scarce) in oxide-channel 3D DRAM (facts 2, 3), with a recycling route designed in.

title: Adiabatic charge-recovery wordline drivers borrowed from failed reversible computing
