idea: Adiabatic logic died in CPUs because multiphase power clocks and slow ramps cost speed. DRAM wordlines are big, slow (5-10 ns), ~3 V capacitive lines, ideal for it: ramp each subarray's wordline to VPP through a 4-8 step tank-capacitor ladder and return the charge to the tanks on precharge.
why: Wordline CV2 at ~3 V is stuck (voltage floor); N-step charging cuts dissipation ~1/N (>60% at 4 steps) and shrinks VPP charge pumps in the periphery; energy is the resource saved.
note: Stepwise charging is known adiabatic art; wordline energy is a minor slice of DRAM energy.

title: Holtronic's lesson: Talbot self-imaging prints sub-micron memory arrays on panels
idea: Holtronic's total-internal-reflection holographic lithography died needing perfectly flat substrates and costly holograms for arbitrary patterns. Memory arrays are periodic: displacement Talbot lithography (a grating mask lit by collimated i-line light while the gap scans one Talbot period) prints focus-insensitive 200-400 nm hole and line arrays across warped Gen-8 glass, with ordinary panel steppers only for periphery.
why: Raises glass-panel memory density ~10-30x over 1.2 um panel steppers with no EUV or projection optics; the mask is a cheap grating; lamp energy only; fluorine-free i-line resists.

title: No working p-type oxide? Build glass memory periphery from n-only circuits
idea: Two decades of p-type oxide TFTs (SnO, Cu2O, NiO) failed to match n-type oxides in mobility or stability, blocking CMOS periphery on glass. Stop chasing p-type: design decoders, wordline drivers and sense amps in n-only pseudo-CMOS with capacitive bootstrapping and precharge-evaluate dynamic logic in the same ZTO layer as the array, sharing 3-4 masks.
why: Periphery is ~49% of a DRAM die; sharing the array's single oxide stack roughly halves mask count on glass and removes the per-tier silicon CMOS chiplet; dynamic-logic power is acceptable at memory duty cycles.

title: Audio-RAM trick revived: sell fail-bin DRAM behind remapping controllers
idea: In the 1980s, partially defective DRAMs were sold cheaply as 'audio RAM' until digital systems demanded perfect parts. Revive it for computing: fail-bin dies (bad rows, weak-retention cells, HBM stacks with one dead die) ship with a full fault map in SPD flash, a CXL controller remaps bad rows per page, and retention-weak parts run chilled to 0 C or at 32 ms refresh.
why: Meets 100x for its slice: dies otherwise scrapped (~10-20% of DRAM output, 20-30% of HBM) sell near scrap value, ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: supply limited to a few % of bits, controller complexity, slightly higher refresh power.

title: Transcendent memory, fixed: rack-pooled ephemeral page cache over CXL switch
idea: Linux cleancache/frontswap were deleted because only Xen used them and copies were synchronous per hypervisor. Rebuild tmem's put/get-may-fail semantics on a CXL 3 switch-attached rack pool with async DMA: hosts push clean page-cache pages to the pool and drop them locally, and the pool may discard anything anytime, so no coherence or durability is needed.
why: Hosts stop overprovisioning page cache; ~20-30% less DRAM per server since clean data is held once per rack and can be dropped safely.

title: HICAMP, fixed: content-addressed dedup hidden inside a CXL memory device
idea: Stanford's HICAMP stored memory as deduplicated immutable 64 B lines linked in DAGs but died because it needed a new CPU and programming model. Implement it inside a CXL expander that presents a flat address space: writes hash each line, a line-ID table maps addresses to unique content, and reference counts free lines, so VM images, checkpoints and string-heavy heaps dedup with zero software change.
why: Dedup ratios of 1.5-4x on VM/container fleets and multi-model serving cut physical DRAM per workload with no ISA change.

title: Micron Automata Processor reborn as CXL-side predicate filter
idea: Micron's in-DRAM NFA Automata Processor died as a standalone PCIe card with proprietary tooling and no killer app. Embed the NFA/predicate fabric inside a CXL memory expander and compile it from standard SQL WHERE clauses and regexes (DuckDB/Postgres plugin), so scans run where cold tables live and only matching rows enter host DRAM.
why: Host DRAM working set for analytics shrinks by the filter selectivity (often 10-100x); cold tables stay on cheaper far memory.

title: Lisp-machine cdr-coding revived as hardware next-pointer elision
idea: Symbolics/LMI cdr-coding replaced next-pointers with 2-bit tags when list cells were contiguous, and died with Lisp machines. Add a memory-side 'implicit successor' bit per 16 B chunk: allocators place linked nodes contiguously, the controller drops the 8 B pointer whenever next == this+size, and reconstructs it on load.
why: Linked lists, trees and graph adjacency structures lose 25-50% of their bytes, shrinking DRAM for pointer-chasing workloads.

title: IBM expanded storage, fixed: synchronous page-move to a cheap tier
idea: IBM mainframe Expanded Storage (1985-2000s) was a cheaper DRAM tier reached by a synchronous page-move instruction, retired when 64-bit addressing made it look unnecessary. Revive it as an ISA/CXL instruction that moves a 4 KB page between near DRAM and a compressed or LPDDR far tier in ~1 us with no page fault or I/O stack.
why: Swap-in at ~1 us instead of 10-100 us lets OSes run with 30-50% smaller near DRAM and negligible stalls.

title: EIE sparse engine, fixed: fixed-rate tANS weights decoded at MACs
idea: EIE/Deep Compression's Huffman-coded sparse weights never took off because variable-length decode stalled lockstep hardware. Use block-fixed-rate tANS: each 256-weight block is coded to an exact bit budget with per-block tables, so parallel decoders at every MAC column run in lockstep straight from compressed SRAM.
why: Weights held at ~2.5-3 bits on SRAM-only chips: ~1.5-2x more model per mm^2 with no DRAM.

title: Optane wear tail decoded as erasures to double Reed-Solomon power
idea: 3D XPoint carried heavy ECC and indirection latency to cover its wear-out tail. Fix: per-line write counters in out-of-band metadata plus a per-cell wear model flag near-dead bits, which are passed to the Reed-Solomon decoder as erasures, since an erasure costs one parity symbol instead of two.
why: Same parity covers ~2x more worn bits, giving 3-5x longer life or half the ECC overhead for any wear-limited DRAM substitute (cost per bit, endurance).

title: Smart Refresh counters replaced by streaming sweep-coverage proofs
idea: Smart Refresh (skipping refresh for recently accessed rows) died because per-row timestamp counters cost area and gave no coverage guarantee. Fix: accelerators that stream every weight row each iteration order reads as a strict per-bank address sweep, so one sweep pointer plus a deadline timer proves every row was activated within tREFW; the refresh engine is disabled, and if the workload stalls past the deadline the region is marked stale and reloaded from its persistent copy.
why: Zero refresh power and zero refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) for weight-resident HBM.

title: LPDDR PASR's failure fixed by expiring, poisonable no-refresh memory zones
idea: LPDDR's partial-array self-refresh was rarely used because operating systems could not guarantee which data was disposable. Fix: OS 'ephemeral zones' are never refreshed; allocations there carry a deadline (KV-cache blocks, activations, network buffers), the memory controller poisons any line past its deadline, and the runtime recomputes it (e.g., re-prefill the KV block) on a poisoned read.
why: Zero refresh power for an estimated 30-60% of AI-server memory, with correctness guaranteed by poison semantics instead of stored charge.

title: Audio-RAM for AI: approximate grade from row-failed dies
idea: In the 1990s partly defective DRAMs were sold as audio RAM for answering machines, until flash ended that market. Fix: create a formal approximate grade whose bad-row maps ship in the module's SPD, and use these dies for error-tolerant AI data (activations, low-order KV-cache bits, embeddings), with the framework placing critical data only on clean rows.
why: Yield: recovers perhaps 3-8% of wafer output that is now scrapped or deeply discounted, a large number of bits in a shortage.

title: ESDRAM's chipset snub fixed: SRAM row-cache companion die
idea: Enhanced Memory Systems' ESDRAM and Mitsubishi's cached DRAM put SRAM row caches on DRAM in the 1990s but died because Intel chipsets would not support them. Fix without host changes: a separate 180 nm SRAM die on a CXL-buffered module latches each opened row and serves repeated hits itself, so older reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 dies behave like faster parts and open rows far less often.
why: Reuse and energy: makes aged dies usable in latency-sensitive slots and cuts row activations (row-hammer exposure and ~5.9 pJ/useful-bit overfetch) by ~30-50% on workloads with locality.
note: FPGA-provable; benefit bounded by locality already captured by row buffers.

title: Cold-grade bin: immersion racks run retention-reject DRAM dies
idea: Effect: Arrhenius thermally activated junction leakage (~0.6 eV). A 10-person firm buys dies that fail the 85 C/64 ms retention test at scrap prices, has an OSAT package them, and deploys them only in single-phase immersion racks held at 30-40 C, where retention is ~8-16x longer and the dies pass with margin. An off-the-shelf FPGA/CXL controller checks retention at operating temperature.
why: Usable supply: reject bins (an estimated 2-5% of output) become sellable memory with zero fab capex.

title: FD-SOI back-gate voltages null sense-amp offset on a 22FDX shuttle
idea: Effect: body effect through the buried oxide. On an FD-SOI MPW, each SA pair's back gate is tied to a small hold capacitor that an auto-zero loop charges during a calibration slot; the ~80 mV/V body coefficient nulls offset and re-calibrates every refresh period, tracking aging and temperature.
why: SA area (fact 7): minimum-size SA devices (4-8x smaller) become usable; GF 22FDX in New York gives a U.S. path for a fabless team.

title: Mandate hammer-threshold grading so retired DIMMs re-enter service
idea: Effect: wordline-coupling disturbance (row-hammer first-flip count, HCfirst). Policy plus small lab: before hyperscaler DIMMs are shredded, a standard FPGA test measures each module's HCfirst and retention spread; modules get grades (e.g., hammer-tolerant, read-mostly cache tier) under an OCP spec and are resold, with reuse tax credits.
why: Usable supply: datacenters retire DRAM after 4-6 years while most cells are healthy; recovering 20% of retired DDR4/DDR5 adds supply with zero fab capex.

title: Polarity-swapping sense amps balance BTI aging to shrink offset margins
idea: Effect: bias-temperature instability (NBTI/PBTI) threshold drift. Every refresh epoch, a swap network flips which half of each SA pair connects to the true versus complement bitline (data stored inverted, one flag per mat), so BTI shifts build up equally on both transistors and cancel instead of growing into offset.
why: SA area (fact 7): reclaims the end-of-life offset margin (often ~30% of the budget), allowing smaller SA devices or longer bitlines; a pure design change on MPW.
note: Periodic SA polarity swap equalizes BTI drift; known from SRAM aging mitigation, cheap to prove.

title: Bond-wire inductive boost converter generates wordline voltage without charge pump
idea: Effect: inductive flyback (L di/dt). Use the package's existing bond-wire inductance (~1-2 nH per wire, several in parallel) as the inductor of an on-die switched boost converter at ~0.5-1 GHz, generating VPP at ~70% efficiency instead of a ~30%-efficient multi-stage capacitive pump.
why: Periphery area/energy (facts 7, 10): VPP generator area ~-60% and energy ~-50%, using only standard wire bonding and MPW CMOS.

title: Accommodation-engineered argon backside cooling replaces helium wafer chucks
idea: Effect: free-molecular (Knudsen) gas conduction scales with alpha/(2-alpha)*P/sqrt(M), and helium's accommodation coefficient on smooth ceramic is only ~0.3 while argon's is ~0.8-0.9. Redesign electrostatic chucks with a 3-5 um gap, nano-textured Al2O3 mesas and stronger sealing bands so Ar/N2 runs at 2-3x the pressure while staying free-molecular, matching helium heat-transfer coefficients.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): backside cooling is one of the largest fab helium uses; target ~100% He removal on etch/deposition chucks with <15% throughput penalty.
note: Higher Ar accommodation can offset mass penalty in free-molecular regime; worth a quick chuck test.

title: Unseparated zirconium-hafnium precursors exploit lanthanide-contraction chemical twins
idea: Effect: lanthanide contraction gives Zr4+ and Hf4+ nearly identical radii and dielectric chemistry, so ZrO2 capacitor layers and HfO2 gate layers tolerate natural 1-3% cross-content. Write a SEMI/JEDEC spec for separation-free Zr(Hf) precursors made directly from zircon sand, skipping the nuclear-grade solvent-extraction plants where hafnium supply is concentrated.
why: Hafnium (~70 t/yr from a few refiners): supply opens to all zircon miners (Australia, South Africa, U.S.) and precursor cost falls.
note: Zr/Hf intermixing tolerable; savings small vs precursor purification.

title: Used Blu-ray mastering lasers write 40 nm imprint masters by heat-mode
idea: Effect: thermal-threshold nonlinearity. Buy two retired 405 nm Blu-ray mastering rigs (~$150k each), swap the spindle for a used XY air-bearing stage, and coat masters with a phase-change resist (AgInSbTe or Ge-Sb-Te): only the center of the Gaussian spot passes the crystallization threshold, so ~40 nm marks are written and then wet-etched selectively. The rest of the $1M funds 24 months of DRAM-array NIL master demos.
why: Masks and capital: e-beam-written NIL masters cost $0.5-1M+ each; a ~$400k heat-mode writer cuts master cost >10x and gives the U.S. its own master supply.

title: Arrhenius rebinning sells retention-reject DRAM into temperature-guaranteed liquid-cooled racks
idea: Effect: thermally activated (Arrhenius) junction leakage, with retention roughly doubling every ~10 C cooler. Buy retention-downgraded DRAM parts at scrap prices, screen them on a ~$250k rig at 45 C and 64 ms refresh, and ship them only on liquid-cooled CXL memory modules whose controller firmware enforces a hard 50 C ceiling and throttles above it. $1M covers the rig, firmware and qualification within 24 months.
why: Raises usable supply with zero fab capital: if even 1-2% of world output is downbinned for retention, recovering it equals the output of part of a multi-billion-dollar fab.
note: Zero-capex supply recovery; depends on vendors selling retention rejects.

title: Light-addressed electrodeposition prints periphery metal from a DMD projector
idea: Effect: photoconductivity. In a plating bath, a DMD projector lights a photoconductive a-Si:H or TiO2 seed layer, making only the lit pixels conductive, so copper deposits in the projected pattern with no mask or resist. $150k of optics plus ~$700k of development reaches 1-2 um lines for periphery and redistribution layers in 24 months.
why: Facts 6 and 7 and masks: maskless metal for periphery and packaging RDL cuts mask and litho cost for low-volume U.S. DRAM and fast design spins.

title: Capillary condensation fills only narrow array gaps, eliminating block masks
idea: Effect: capillary condensation (Kelvin equation). Below saturation, a precursor vapor such as a silazane condenses only in gaps narrower than the Kelvin radius (~10-20 nm), so dense array trenches fill while wide periphery stays open; a cure turns the liquid into oxide. $1M tests the effect on test arrays at university fabs within 24 months.
why: Fact 4: each array/periphery block mask removed saves a litho plus etch pass; Kelvin-selective fill could drop 1-3 block masks per flow.

title: Compiler lifetime typing parks short-lived buffers in refresh-free banks
idea: Arrhenius scaling puts DRAM tail retention at 125 C around 8-16 ms. The compiler tags every buffer with its lifetime (activations, per-step KV, DMA staging). Buffers whose producer-consumer gap is under 2 ms go to banks with refresh disabled, and long-lived data goes to robust NVM. On-die canary cells re-check the retention model at every boot over the 10-year life.
why: At 125 C, refresh would eat 20-40% of bandwidth. Turning it off for ~70% of banks recovers that bandwidth, so a smaller DRAM serves the same workload.

title: Leak-toward-zero encoding turns thermal retention loss into harmless pruning
idea: DRAM charge leaks only one way (true cells go 1 to 0). Store neural weights in sign-magnitude with magnitude bits in true cells and the sign bit in robust NVM, so any leakage flip at 125 C can only shrink a weight's magnitude, which acts like gentle pruning. Error-tolerant tensors then live in banks with 4-8x relaxed refresh.
why: Recovers refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3) and removes the guard-band overprovisioning hot designs carry. Expect ~20-30% less DRAM for the same delivered bandwidth.

title: Acoustoplasticity: room-temperature ultrasonic bonding of DRAM chiplets on moving webs
idea: Use the Blaha acoustic-softening effect: 40-60 kHz ultrasound softens copper bumps so DRAM chiplets bond to printed Cu-on-polyimide in ~100 ms at room temperature, synchronized with web motion like RFID strap bonding.
why: Assembly capex and thermal budget (fact 6): no reflow ovens or thermocompression bonders; heat-free bonding avoids retention damage; pitch limited to ~30-40 um.
note: 30-40 um pitch is coarse for memory bandwidth.

title: Telegraph-noise fingerprinting quarantines variable-retention cells
idea: Effect: random telegraph noise from single-trap capture and emission. A background test mode measures a suspected cell's retention repeatedly at several pause times; a VRT cell shows bimodal pass/fail statistics with characteristic dwell times, while a merely weak cell shows a single threshold. Only bimodal cells are remapped to a small per-bank spare-cell CAM.
why: VRT is why refresh cannot follow measured retention (fact 3): isolating the ~1e-6 VRT population makes profiled multi-rate refresh safe, cutting refresh operations ~70%.

title: Z-channel codes exploit leakage that only drains ones
idea: Effect: thermodynamic relaxation asymmetry, where leakage only moves a cell toward equilibrium. Data is mapped per subarray (true/anti-cell aware) so the charged state is always logical 1, making retention errors strictly 1->0; asymmetric-error codes (Varshamov-Tenengolts, Z-channel LDPC) then correct t errors with ~half the parity of symmetric codes, and write-side sparse coding (<=40% ones) shrinks the vulnerable population.
why: 10x density: ~100x more raw retention BER tolerated at the same ~8% parity lets poor-retention 0.3 fF thin-film cells stack 24 tiers (~10x) at the same cost.
note: Z-channel gain ~2x, not 100x claimed.

title: Arrhenius cold-grade bin turns retention fallout into sellable memory
idea: Junction leakage roughly doubles every ~10 C, so a die that fails 64 ms retention at 85 C has ~16x margin at 45 C. Create a JEDEC 'cold-grade' bin and SPD flag for dies that pass only below 50 C, sold exclusively into liquid- and immersion-cooled AI racks that guarantee die temperature.
why: Recovers the 3-8% of wafer output scrapped or down-binned for retention, raising bit supply with zero new fab capital; refresh energy also drops in those racks.

title: Acoustic-streaming megasonic rinses cut ultrapure water for drought-sited fabs
idea: MHz piezo nozzles drive acoustic streaming that thins the diffusion boundary layer, so a thin film of recycled UPW replaces multi-tank rinse cascades. In-line conductivity endpointing stops each rinse once it is clean.
why: DRAM fabs use ~10-20 ML/day; a 50-70% rinse-water cut makes water-capped Arizona and Texas sites viable.

title: Molten-salt electrorefining reclaims tungsten and ruthenium from spent sputter targets
idea: Planar targets are scrapped at ~30-40% utilization and chamber shields collect metal. A regional refinery anodically dissolves W/Ru/Ta in a fluoride-chloride melt where ions migrate and plate as 5N metal, sold back to target makers under buy-back contracts.
why: Creates domestic secondary tungsten supply from the ~60% of target metal now wasted.

title: Shape-memory clamps replace solder for swappable memory packages
idea: LGA DRAM packages are held to boards by NiTi clips that grip in the austenite phase at room temperature and relax when chilled below their martensite finish with a cold-spray tool (thermal hysteresis). A technician swaps a failed package in seconds, and good ones are reused.
why: Soldered LPDDR is the main barrier to memory repair and reuse; this makes boards serviceable.
note: CAMM2 already addresses serviceability.

title: Tunneling-clock deposit-refund system pays owners to return memory
idea: Each module carries a floating-gate cell whose tunneling charge loss acts as a powerless chronometer. A deposit charged at sale is refunded on return, scaled by measured age and wear, which funds take-back and guarantees recyclers a supply stream.
why: Non-hyperscaler server memory take-back is low; a deposit-refund like bottle bills could lift returns above 80%.

title: KOH-etched {111} sidewall channels: crystal planes replace EUV critical dimensions
idea: K: on (110) silicon, KOH etches {111} planes ~100x slower than others, so DUV-defined trenches self-terminate on atomically flat vertical {111} walls; fins between two such walls are thinned by timed lateral undercut, giving sub-20 nm access channels whose width comes from crystal geometry and etch time, not litho.
why: Atomically smooth {111} interfaces cut interface-trap density and edge-roughness Vt scatter, tightening the leakage tail (fact 3) without EUV (fact 4).

title: Hydrogen anneal reshapes hole arrays into stacked silicon-on-nothing tiers
idea: Etch rows of deep holes with periodically modulated diameter by cycled DRIE, then anneal at ~1100 C in H2 in a hydrogen-capable university furnace: Si surface migration closes each row into a stack of flat buried voids, leaving thin single-crystal Si membranes between them as device tiers and the voids as capacitor or isolation cavities.
why: Multiple crystalline lateral-transistor tiers from a bulk wafer using only i-line litho, DRIE and a furnace (fact 2), no epi reactor or bonder; an ideal 4-8-tier lateral-cell testbed.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling in electrostatic chucks replaces helium
idea: Periodic-table walk, H (1): feed H2 (thermal conductivity 0.18 W/mK, above He's 0.15) at 5-20 Torr behind wafers in etch/CVD chucks; sccm flows stay below the flammability limit with N2-diluted exhaust, and supply comes from on-site electrolysis.
why: Removes one of the largest fab helium uses during the Qatar outage; H2 comes from water.

title: Magnesium-light pointers: hardware-compressed 64-bit pointers in memory
idea: Magnesium cuts vehicle weight without losing strength; a load/store extension keeps 64-bit pointers in memory as 32-bit offsets from one of 16 region-base registers selected by 4 tag bits, expanding on load and compressing on store, which generalizes JVM compressed oops to C/C++/Rust heaps transparently.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, JS/Python objects) is 30-60% pointers; halving them saves ~15-30% DRAM for those workloads (density).

title: Si: anodized porous-silicon interposer cuts HBM link capacitance
idea: Electrochemically anodize the top 50-100 um of the silicon interposer into mesoporous Si (~60% porosity, k~2-3, very high effective resistivity) before building the RDL, so HBM-to-logic traces sit on a near-air dielectric instead of SiO2 over lossy doped Si. Anodization is a maskless wet bath step that fits existing 65 nm-class interposer lines.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~30-40% lower line capacitance and substrate loss, interposer I/O ~0.5 -> ~0.3 pJ/bit and ~2x reach so 12+ HBM stacks can ring one accelerator.

title: Li: beta-eucryptite negative-expansion filler stops HBM package warpage
idea: Replace part of the fused-silica filler in mold compound and underfill with beta-eucryptite (LiAlSiO4, CTE ~ -6 ppm/K, from abundant Li, Al, Si) to bring composite CTE to ~3 ppm/K matching silicon, eliminating warpage of 8-12-stack HBM packages.
why: HBM packaging yield and size: warpage limits interposer size and causes bump opens; CTE matching allows more stacks per package and reduces high-purity fused-quartz filler demand.

title: Si: mature-node hammer-guard buffer chip for commodity DIMMs
idea: A 10-person fabless team tapes out a small 28-40 nm companion chip on a multi-project wafer that sits beside the RCD, snoops ACT commands, keeps Misra-Gries hot-row counters and issues targeted refresh-management commands to any vendor's DRAM.
why: Retrofits strong row hammer protection (fact 9) onto cheaper DRAM using U.S.-manufacturable mature-node silicon.

title: N: Cryo-binning resurrects retention-rejected DRAM dies in liquid nitrogen
idea: Dies and aging modules that fail 64 ms retention at 85 C because of the junction-leakage tail retain for seconds at 77 K; grade them by cold retention and sell them into LN2-cooled cold-memory sleds where refresh is nearly turned off.
why: Converts several percent of yield loss and retired modules into usable supply and cuts refresh energy >90% in that tier.

title: Retread DRAM: remanufactured modules sold with per-row retention maps
idea: Like tire retreading, take DRAM from decommissioned servers, re-characterize each row's retention at temperature, and write the map into the SPD. Resell the modules for tiers whose controllers apply per-row refresh rates.
why: Raises usable supply during shortage. Per-row refresh on mapped modules cuts refresh energy 2-4x versus blanket rates.

title: Day-old bread pricing: discounted refresh-disabled perishable-memory cloud SKU
idea: Cloud providers sell refresh-disabled DRAM capacity at a discount, the way bakeries sell day-old bread. It comes with a retention SLA (e.g., data valid for 200 ms after its last write) for batch shuffles, caches and inference scratch. Hypervisors map it to unrefreshed banks.
why: Zero refresh power on that capacity. It creates a market price signal that turns refresh-free operation into extra usable supply during the shortage.

title: Sand-mold disposable cache: DRAM copies decay, nonvolatile pattern persists
idea: Like sand-casting molds broken after each pour while the pattern is kept, treat DRAM as a cache of clean lines backed by a dense nonvolatile master. Each line carries a restore timestamp. Lines past their certified retention are silently invalidated as misses instead of refreshed.
why: Zero refresh power. Capacity is spent only on lines being used, so DRAM needed per workload falls and the cost is an occasional refill from backing storage.

title: Cold forging: 77 K-operated 180 nm DRAM with planar capacitors
idea: Like cold forging, which gains strength by working metal cold, run a 180 nm planar-capacitor DRAM in liquid nitrogen. Junction and subthreshold leakage fall by >10^6 and SA transistors gain ~2x transconductance with lower noise, so small ~2-3 fF planar caps sense reliably and refresh nearly disappears.
why: No tall capacitors, EUV or refresh for a datacenter memory tier on cheap U.S. 180 nm wafers; this offsets part of the ~10x density penalty and cooling cost, and SA area shrinks from better gm and matching.
note: Density penalty of 180 nm planar cells outweighs refresh savings.

title: Tree-ring staircase: CMP a trench-filled stack to expose every tier
idea: Like grinding Damascus steel or turning a log to reveal growth rings, deposit the tier stack conformally into a wide sloped trench and CMP flat, so every tier surfaces as its own band and wordline contacts land with one lithography step instead of 10-30 resist-trim and etch cycles.
why: Staircase formation costs area and many litho/etch loops as tiers grow (facts 2, 4); one CMP plus one contact mask could cut staircase cost >5x and area ~2x.
note: Conformal stack in sloped trench then CMP is plausible and demoable; staircase is a small area share.

title: Co-fired tiers: deposit all oxide channels amorphous, activate once
idea: Like co-firing green ceramic tapes in one kiln pass, deposit every tier's oxide-semiconductor channel and high-k amorphous at room temperature, then run one final anneal for the whole stack instead of annealing each tier and re-baking the lower tiers N times.
why: Accumulated thermal budget drifts lower-tier threshold voltage and leakage (facts 2, 3); one co-fire makes tier N match tier 1 and removes N-1 anneals (~20-30% cycle time).

title: Plate-less holographic print plus one cookie-cutter trim mask
idea: Expose the hexagonal storage-node array by three-beam immersion interference (no mask, perfect periodicity, one spacer pitch split), then use exactly one cheap DUV cookie-cutter mask to blank the pattern outside mats and at mat edges.
why: Fact 4: removes the EUV array-hole layer; interference exposure tools cost roughly a tenth of EUV, with lower roughness and no reticle defects in the array.

title: G-code memory: store the toolpath, regenerate the part
idea: A 3D printer stores G-code, not the finished object. In the same way, deterministic data (positional-encoding tables, attention and dropout masks, index arrays, hashed embeddings, PRNG-initialized weights, procedural textures) is replaced by a 'toolpath' descriptor: kernel ID, seed and parameters. A tiny micro-sequencer on the CXL or DIMM buffer regenerates any line on load, and a page-table bit marks procedural pages.
why: Removes the 5-20% of AI and graphics footprint that is regenerable data stored for no reason; regenerating a line costs a few ns instead of DRAM bits.
note: Regenerable data share likely small.

title: Miura-fold addressing: store mirrored structures once, unfold in hardware
idea: Origami packs a large sheet into a small footprint using a fold map. An address-fold unit in the memory controller recognizes registered fold regions (symmetric, Toeplitz, circulant, block-repeated, palindromic) and maps each virtual access through a fold function, for example (i,j)->(min,max) for symmetric or (i-j) for Toeplitz. Only the fundamental domain is stored physically, and writes stay consistent automatically.
why: Saves 2x on symmetric matrices (covariance, Hessians, undirected graphs, distance matrices) and N-fold on Toeplitz and relative-position-bias tables, with no change to software that indexes the full array.

title: Zone refining: sweep high-entropy lines to one end of memory
idea: Zone refining drives impurities to one end of a silicon ingot. Likewise a background sweeper scans memory, measures the entropy of each line, and moves incompressible lines (encrypted, already compressed, random) into a dedicated 'impurity' region. The remaining pages become pure, zero-rich and low-entropy, so a cheap fixed-function line compressor gets 2-4x on them without a heavyweight per-page algorithm.
why: Page compression averages only about 1.5x mainly because a few random lines spoil each page; segregating them raises the gain on memory-expansion tiers toward 2-3x.
note: LCP's exception region is related; line relocation adds metadata overhead.

title: Shift work: co-schedule jobs whose memory peaks are anti-phase
idea: Factories run shifts so machines never sit idle. The scheduler profiles each job's memory-versus-time curve (training forward/backward peaks, batch ETL, diurnal inference load) and pairs jobs with anti-correlated peaks on a shared HBM/DRAM pool, quickly swapping out the working set of whichever partner is in its trough. Pairing is solved like a shift roster.
why: Pools sized for the sum of peaks become pools sized for the peak of the sum, using 1.3-2x fewer GB per job across a cluster.

title: Lumber grading: bit-planes sorted into clear-grade and framing-grade memory
idea: Sawmills grade boards: clear wood for visible faces, knotty #3 for hidden studs. Tensors are stored as bit-planes. The sign and top two magnitude planes go to strongly coded memory, and the lower planes go raw into 1%-BER cells. The plane boundary is chosen per tensor so that the expected flip error (2^k x 1%) stays below the quantization noise.
why: 60-75% of each number's bits are low-significance planes where 1% flips add noise below the quantization floor, so high-grade memory demand falls 3-4x.

title: Jacquard-woven passive optical shuffle backplane for memory pooling
idea: Weave 4,096 fibers on a loom into a fixed perfect-shuffle pattern so 64 CPUs reach 64 memory sleds all-to-all with no switches. The topology is set by the weave, like a textile pattern.
why: Pooling recovers the ~20-30% of DRAM stranded in servers, raising usable supply without new wafers; passive optics add no switch energy.

title: Solera placement: weak rows host hot data refreshed by use
idea: In a solera the youngest wine sits in the most-handled barrels; map frequently activated pages onto rows with the worst measured retention, since each activation restores their charge more often than refresh would, and put cold pages on the strongest rows, which then get 4-8x longer refresh intervals.
why: Uses retention-tail rows (fact 3) instead of sparing them and cuts refresh on the cold majority; ~2-4x refresh reduction with no added cells.

title: RepRap for nanofabs: open-hardware, self-replicating memory process tools
idea: RepRap 3D printers print their own parts. Publish open designs for a memory micro-fab's core tools (ALD reactor, sputter, mask aligner, RTA, wet benches) that a university nanofab and machine shop can build and copy, including fixtures each tool makes for the next.
why: Capital and time: drops a pilot memory line's tool bill from ~$50M to ~$3-5M, so dozens of regional micro-fabs can prototype and make niche memory.

title: Open printed-memory PDK and ink library for distributed iteration
idea: IFR: thousands of labs test a new storage element every week at near-zero cost. Closest achievable: publish an open R2R process kit (standard printed electrode and access layers, test-structure layouts, characterization scripts) plus a shared ink bank so any lab can drop a new storage ink into a known stack.
why: Speeds discovery and grows the U.S. talent base; cost per experiment drops from ~$100k fab shuttle to ~$100 print run.
note: Printed devices are far from DRAM-class density and speed; mainly a discovery and talent lever.

title: Two-phase CO2 chuck cooling replaces perfluorinated heat-transfer fluids
idea: Ideal: chillers with no exotic fluids. Closest: cool cryogenic etch chucks and chamber walls with pumped two-phase CO2 (R744) evaporating inside chuck channels (-50 C reachable), replacing Galden/Novec perfluoropolyether coolants after 3M's Novec exit.
why: Eliminates a PFAS supply chokepoint in every etch/deposition chiller; CO2 latent heat improves chuck temperature uniformity; GWP ~10,000 -> 1.

title: Predictive link coding: both ends guess, only residuals travel
idea: Ideal: send nothing because the receiver already knows. Closest achievable: run an identical tiny predictor (per-stream stride/delta or last-value) in the base die and the GPU PHY, transmit only XOR residuals with run-length coding, and resync on mismatch, like a video codec for memory traffic.
why: Fact 5: for smooth activations, KV cache and pointer-heavy data 30-60% of transferred bits are predictable, cutting link toggles and I/O energy by a similar fraction.

title: Read-as-refresh: scheduler guarantees every live row is touched
idea: Ideal: memory that never needs refreshing because it is always in use. Closest achievable: in LLM decode every weight and resident KV entry is read once per token, so the serving scheduler caps step time below 32 ms, lays tensors so each step activates every occupied row, and the base die verifies row coverage and issues no REF; sequences that go idle are evicted rather than kept.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) and the 10-20% bandwidth loss go to zero for decode-dominated serving because ordinary activate-restore does the job for free.

title: TTL-tagged allocations: data declared dead before it can decay
idea: Ideal: data lives exactly as long as it is needed. Closest achievable: add a time-to-live field to the memory allocation interface; regions tagged TTL < retention (activations, gradient buckets, collective-comm buffers, scratch) go to banks whose refresh circuits are disabled, and the base die faults any access arriving after expiry.
why: Fact 3: in training a majority of HBM traffic and much capacity is transient data with microsecond-to-millisecond lifetimes; those bits never pay refresh energy or bandwidth.

title: Let it rot: detect decayed lines and recompute instead
idea: Ideal: never spend energy keeping data you could regenerate. Closest achievable: KV cache and activation checkpoints sit in unrefreshed DRAM with a strong per-line checksum; when a line decays the base die flags it and the runtime recomputes it from upstream tokens or inputs instead of ever rewriting it.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power for regenerable data, trading occasional recompute FLOPs (abundant) for retention energy and bandwidth (scarce); the leakage tail becomes a performance statistic, not a reliability wall.
note: Unrefreshed KV with checksums and recompute; refresh is ~10-20% of DRAM power, so gain is bounded.

title: Significance split: MSBs in static cells, LSBs allowed to fade
idea: Ideal: protect only the bits that matter. Closest achievable: the base die bit-slices each fp8/bf16 word so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits go to on-logic SRAM while low mantissa bits go to never-refreshed DRAM, where decay toward zero acts as graceful rounding noise for neural-network tensors.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power with bounded numerical error (<0.5% relative per decayed value); ~50-60% of bits live in cheap DRAM and the rest in SRAM already present on the base die.

title: Age-out tiering: base die evicts rows before retention, never refreshes
idea: Ideal: every row is either fresh or gone. Closest achievable: the HBM base die keeps a per-row age counter; rows nearing ~50 ms without natural access are compressed and written once to a dense non-volatile tier (stacked NAND or a remote pool) and the DRAM row is freed, making DRAM a pure write-back cache of recent data with no REF command.
why: Fact 3: refresh power goes to zero and idle DRAM can be fully powered off; long-lived cold data costs one write instead of ~16 refreshes per second forever.

title: Lifetime-tagged allocation skips refresh for short-lived data
idea: Ideal: no refresh because data dies before it decays. Closest: allocators tag buffers with expected lifetime (activations, packets, frame buffers); rows holding only data due to be overwritten within the retention guarantee are excluded from refresh by a per-row skip bit set by the controller.
why: Fact 3: in AI and streaming workloads ~50% of rows hold data living <64 ms, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50%.

title: Decay-direction coding: store mostly safe bits, detect with Berger
idea: Ideal: data that cannot decay. Closest: each word is stored inverted (with a flag bit) whenever that leaves fewer cells in the leaky charged state; rows that end up fully discharged skip refresh, and because the remaining errors are unidirectional (charged to discharged only) a cheap Berger count code detects every one of them.
why: Fact 3: halves worst-case leaky bits, skips refresh on sparse rows and swaps SECDED for ~log2(n) check bits.

title: Triple-row activation turns charge sharing into majority vote
idea: Ideal: redundancy computed for free by physics. Closest: in a 180 nm array each critical bit is written to three rows on the same bitlines; a read opens all three wordlines at once so charge sharing settles the bitline to the analog majority, masking any one decayed or flipped cell with no logic.
why: Fact 3: a 2-of-3 tolerant tier whose refresh can run ~10x slower; 3x area but zero ECC logic.

title: Defect-aware coset coding makes weak cells store their safe value
idea: Ideal: defects that happen to store the right value. Closest: the encoder knows each row's weak-cell positions from a BIST map and, using Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memories with defects, picks one of several coset encodings so every weak cell holds the value it decays toward; a few index bits per block replace remapping.
why: Fact 3: neutralizes known tail cells with ~2-4% overhead and no spare rows, using simple 180 nm logic.
note: Stuck-at coset coding ported from PCM; VRT cells not in BIST map limit gains.

title: Controller-only polarity steering: weak cells always store their discharged state
idea: 10-person constraint: with no process access, we exploit what we can learn about the cells. After profiling each row's true/anti-cell layout and weak cells, the controller picks one of a few per-row XOR masks (kept in a side table) so the row's weak cells always hold their discharged, non-leaking value. Rows whose weak cells are all parked empty drop to the slow refresh tier.
why: Fact 3: weak cells fail only when charged. Steering them to the empty state removes them from the refresh-setting tail and moves ~80%+ of weak rows to an interval of 1 s or more.

title: Recompute instead of refresh: checksummed recomputable activations
idea: 10-person constraint: a software library. Mark tensors that are cheap to recompute (activations saved for the backward pass, KV-cache prefixes) as recompute-on-loss and store them in relaxed-refresh regions (e.g. 1 s), with a 32-bit checksum per tile. On a mismatch, recompute the tile from its checkpointed inputs instead of paying refresh to protect it.
why: Fact 3: trades rare recomputation (<0.1% of FLOPs) for near-zero refresh on a large share of training memory.

title: Foundry SONOS as a trim knob: per-cell one-time Vt tuning
idea: 10-person constraint: only foundry-standard options are available to us. Design an eDRAM macro on a mature MPW process that offers SONOS charge-trap transistors, and use the SONOS device itself as the access transistor. At test, measure each cell's leakage and give leaky cells a single program pulse that raises their Vt 0.3-0.5 V for life, deleting the tail cell by cell.
why: Fact 3: the refresh interval is set by the worst cell. Trimming the tail to the median could lengthen refresh ~10x using standard foundry eNVM devices and a test program.

title: Certify, don't fabricate: an R4 retention-grade standard and test lab
idea: 10-person constraint: create a market signal instead of a device. Define an open 'R4' grade (passes 256 ms at 85 C with ECC, VRT-screened over 3 thermal cycles) and run a small certification lab with FPGA testers. Hyperscalers and BIOS vendors auto-enable 4x tREFI for R4-labelled modules, so suppliers compete on their retention tail.
why: Fact 3: creates commercial pull for tail reduction and unlocks ~75% refresh savings fleet-wide through policy and a 10-person lab.
note: VRT screening over three thermal cycles unlikely to be trusted for 4x tREFI.

title: Compression pays for ECC: freed bits buy stronger codes
idea: 10-person constraint: controller logic only. Compress each 64 B line (base-delta or FP-exponent compression). When a line shrinks by at least 12.5%, store a stronger BCH or Reed-Solomon code in-line in the freed bits so the line can sit in a 4-8x slower refresh tier. Incompressible lines keep normal refresh.
why: Fact 3: with ~60-70% of AI and server lines compressible, most memory moves to a slow refresh tier at no capacity cost.
note: Compression-for-ECC known (COP); using freed bits to qualify slow refresh tier is a fair twist.

title: Dirty-row trickle persistence bounds the power-fail energy budget
idea: Constraint: survive sudden power loss with only a tiny hold-up capacitor. Periphery keeps one dirty bit per row and an in-die copy engine uses idle refresh slots to copy dirty rows into an on-die NV bank, capping outstanding dirty rows at N (e.g., 4k), so hold-up energy covers just N rows.
why: Backup energy and capacitor size drop 100-1000x compared with a full-die dump; the copy reuses refresh bandwidth that is spent anyway (fact 3).

title: Hydrogen backside cooling retrofit for etch chucks
idea: Within $1M/24 months: in a university fab, retrofit a used 300 mm etcher's electrostatic chuck to run H2 backside gas at ~10 Torr (no O2 present, so no ignition path), with Pd-getter cleanup and leak interlocks, and map wafer temperature against He.
why: H2's thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/m-K) exceeds He's (~0.15), so cooling is equal or better while removing the largest per-wafer helium use; H2 can be made anywhere.

title: Defense Production Act priority rating for semiconductor helium
idea: Within $1M/24 months: fund analysis and a coalition petition for DPA Title I priority ratings (DO/DX) on U.S.-produced helium, NF3 and WF6 deliveries to domestic memory fabs during declared shortages, with a fab-usage reporting template.
why: Shortage allocation is now first-come or contract-based; rated-order priority keeps U.S. DRAM lines running at negligible public cost.
note: DPA rated orders exist; extending to fab gases is executable policy work, modest impact.

title: Acoustic and infrared watch lets crucibles survive extra pulls
idea: Within $1M/24 months: retrofit crystal pullers with acoustic-emission sensors and IR wall imaging that detect bubble growth and cristobalite spalling in the quartz crucible, so operators safely add one more recharge pull per crucible instead of retiring it on a fixed schedule.
why: One extra pull per crucible means ~20-50% fewer crucibles per kg of ingot, directly stretching Spruce Pine supply.

title: Crystal planes, not lithography, define atomically flat vertical channels
idea: Constraint: nothing finer than 80 nm may be printed for the active area. On (110) wafers, anisotropic TMAH etching exposes vertical {111} walls, so coarse 80 nm lines are wet-thinned to 8-10 nm fins whose sidewalls are crystal planes, then cut into pillars for vertical-channel access transistors.
why: Facts 3 and 4: removes EUV/SAQP from active definition; near-zero line-edge roughness tightens the leakage tail ~2x; the wet etch costs a few dollars per wafer.

title: In-die reliability sensors finish qualification in weeks, not quarters
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: embed TDDB, BTI, EM and retention monitor arrays in every die and calibrate a physics-of-failure model at 175 C, replacing lot-by-lot 1000-hour high-temperature operating life tests with continuous, data-driven qualification.
why: Capital and time: cuts 4-6 months from each new fab or node ramp, so capital earns revenue sooner while proving the 10-year life.

title: Follow-the-moon: migrate memory-hungry batch jobs to night regions
idea: Imposed limit: no region may buy DRAM for its own daytime peak. Fleet schedulers move memory-heavy batch work (index builds, preemptible training, analytics) to regions whose interactive load is at its nightly low, and each region is sized for the global average instead of its local peak.
why: Daily swings in DRAM utilization run 30-50%; shifting work across time zones can cut fleet-installed DRAM ~15-25%.

title: Runtimes pay per-byte rent and shrink caches automatically
idea: Imposed limit: every resident byte pays rent each second. The OS publishes a live DRAM price per GB-second; language runtimes (JVM, CPython, V8) and app caches expose value-per-byte curves and shrink memo tables, JIT code caches and object pools until the marginal hit value falls below the rent.
why: Software caches grow to fill whatever memory exists; price-driven shrinking can recover 10-30% of host DRAM without hard limits.
note: Marginal-value cache shrinking via OS price signal; runtimes must expose value curves.

title: Printed RFID logbooks unlock a second life for retired DIMMs
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a printed RFID tag with a printed temperature-integrating sensor goes on every DIMM and logs hours, thermal history and correctable-error counts. When servers retire, modules are graded instantly without bench testing and redeployed into lower-tier pools or memory-expansion boxes instead of being shredded.
why: Hyperscalers retire servers after 4-6 years with working DRAM; trustworthy grading could return several percent of annual bit demand to service from existing modules.

title: Publish-subscribe row broadcast turns overfetch into delivered prefetch
idea: Scarcity: no fetched bit may be wasted. When a row opens, the base die multicasts the row's other lines on a low-priority channel to every last-level-cache slice that registered interest in that address region (a subscription table in the base die) instead of discarding them at precharge.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): converting even 10-20% of overfetched lines into hits cuts energy per useful bit ~2x on irregular workloads.
note: Extra pushed lines consume link bandwidth, the scarce resource in HBM.

title: Helium-free laser-etched vias for memory stacks
idea: Scarcity: no helium (Qatar offline), so no He backside-cooled DRIE chucks and no He leak tests. Form through-vias by femtosecond laser modification plus selective wet etching (laser-induced deep etching) in glass or silicon carriers, and check hermeticity with a hydrogen/forming-gas tracer.
why: Helium chokepoint and via cost: batch wet etch handles many wafers per bath with no plasma tool, removing helium from via formation.

title: Approximate tensor lanes run 50 mV swing with no retries
idea: Scarcity: zero error-correction budget on the link. Tag activation and gradient traffic as approximate and run those lanes at ~50 mV swing and BER ~1e-6 with no ECC or retransmission, while pointers and metadata use standard robust lanes.
why: Interface energy and voltage floor (facts 5, 10): CV2 falls with swing, giving 3-5x lower I/O energy on most AI traffic.
note: Exponent and sign flips are catastrophic, so lanes need selective protection.

title: Two-phase immersion memory bricks drop DIMM spacing to millimetres
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount dies on 0.2 mm boards at 1.5 mm pitch with boiling-channel gaps and submerge them in dielectric fluid; nucleate boiling removes ~100 W/cm2, so heat spreaders and airflow spacing disappear.
why: Volumetric density: air-cooled DIMM pitch is ~10 mm; 1.5 mm pitch gives ~6-10x bits per liter while dropping spreaders and fans offsets the fluid cost.

title: Zero refresh budget: rewrites of training tensors serve as refresh
idea: Imposed limit: the DRAM may spend zero cycles on refresh. The controller keeps a 2-bit last-written epoch per row, and the training runtime guarantees every activation, gradient and KV buffer is rewritten each step (<20 ms). Rows written within tRET are never refreshed; only a small long-lived bank group holding weights and optimizer state keeps conventional refresh.
why: Fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth. In training, 70-90% of rows are short-lived, so most refresh energy and bandwidth loss disappear.

title: No ECC chip: exponent-only parity carved from mantissa LSBs
idea: Imposed limit: no x72 ECC devices allowed. For bf16/fp8 tensors, the controller reorders bits so the sign and exponent fields of 8 values share one SEC-DED codeword whose check bits are stored in the stolen mantissa LSB of each value. A mantissa flip causes a bounded relative error of under 1%; a catastrophic exponent flip is corrected.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC device overhead (x72 to x64) and tolerates raw BER ~1e-6 cells, so cheaper or weaker DRAM is usable for AI weights and activations.
note: Exponent-protecting codes for bf16 weights; easy software/FPGA demo, niche to AI tensors.

title: Zero ECC storage: recompute-from-lineage repairs transient tensors
idea: Imposed limit: no correction bits for transient data. Only a 32-bit CRC per 4 KB is stored, for detection. On a mismatch the runtime re-executes the producing op from its upstream inputs (the op lineage, as in Spark RDDs) within the same step, so recomputation becomes the correction mechanism.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC storage over 60-80% of an AI job's footprint and lets transient tensors live in cheaper, higher-BER DRAM.

title: 4 ms cells allowed: compressed lines packed around weak bits
idea: Imposed limit: some cells may retain only 4 ms. Each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or FPC), and the compressed payload is laid out so that the known weak bit positions in that physical line are skipped as don't-care holes. The weak-bit mask comes from a per-row fault map.
why: Rows with dozens of weak cells stay usable at normal refresh rates, so retention-tail binning loss (5-10% of rows) becomes near zero.

title: KV cache at one-third cost: range-clamp decoding in gray memory
idea: Imposed limit: KV-cache memory must cost a third as much. The KV cache is stored in gray memory, meaning DRAM run at a 4x refresh interval and low VARY. Instead of parity, per-head statistics (min/max norms) are stored, and any value read outside its head's range is clamped. Attention softmax is robust to sparse bounded flips.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh and array energy for the KV cache drop 3-4x, and higher-BER binned dies can serve LLM inference.

title: Each GB serves three owners: content-addressed shared weight memory
idea: Self-imposed limit: every byte must have at least three readers. Model weights are hashed and stored once in a read-only CXL shared-memory segment that dozens of inference hosts map at the same time, instead of each host keeping its own copy in local DRAM.
why: Host DRAM in inference fleets is dominated by duplicate weights; deduplication cuts that footprint 3-10x.

title: Hf-free MPB zirconia with work-function-biased operating point
idea: Today's DRAM uses Al-doped ZrO2 (k ~40, EOT ~0.6-0.7 nm). The highest reported hafnia-zirconia k values (56-64) sit at the morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) between ferroelectric-orthorhombic and tetragonal phases, using HZO superlattices that contain Hf. Here the stack is Zr-only ZrO2 (5.5-6 nm) whose phase balance is set by dopant (Al, Si, Y), thickness and electrode strain. An antiferroelectric-like ZrO2 has its highest small-signal permittivity near its field-induced transition; a built-in bias from work-function-asymmetric electrodes (TiN bottom, doped-SnO2 or MoO2 top) shifts that peak into the 0-0.5 V storage window. The capacitor is otherwise a standard pillar or stub.
why: EOT 0.55 -> ~0.41 nm (k 40 -> 56): the same 5.4 fF from a 0.97 um pillar instead of 1.29 um (AR 62 -> 46), or +34% Cs at the same height, Hf-free. A modest step on its own; it compounds with B2-01 (taller AAO cups) or B2-08 (shorter bitlines).

title: Fluorine-free carbon mold for capacitor holes and sacrificial 3D tiers
idea: Replace the SiO2 capacitor mold with a 1.3-2.5 um PECVD amorphous-carbon film (the 3D-NAND hardmask material) capped by a thin SiN or Al2O3 support lattice. Holes are etched anisotropically in O2/COS or H2/N2 plasma (sulfur or nitrogen sidewall passivation, no fluorine). ALD electrode and dielectric (or oxide channel) fill the holes; the carbon is then burned out by O2 or removed by H2 plasma, leaving free-standing, lattice-supported structures. In 3D stacks, carbon replaces SiN as the sacrificial tier: a low-pressure thermal O2 burn is reaction-limited, so the lateral recess is uniform from top to bottom of the stack, and the product is CO2.
why: Eliminates fluorocarbon gas from the capacitor/channel-hole modules (~5.6e13 HAR holes per wafer at 1-beta) and makes 3D lateral recess a thermal, reaction-limited step; the mold leaves ~0.6 g CO2/wafer instead of PFAS-class by-products.

title: Significance-split memory: gold-grade sign/exponent, sand-grade mantissa
idea: The memory controller (GPU or HBM base die) splits tagged tensors (weights, KV, activations) into bit-plane groups placed in different banks, so both are fetched in parallel. Sign and exponent are Huffman-coded to ~3 b (entropy ~2.6 b of 8) and stored in normal rows with ECC and standard refresh. The 7 mantissa planes go to 'approximate' banks with four relaxations: no ECC parity, refresh at ~1 s (raw BER ~1e-5), an optional separate lower VARY rail (~0.75 V), and lower-swing I/O lanes run at BER ~1e-6. Dies or subarrays that fail exact screening (weak cells, high-offset SAs) are binned for mantissa duty instead of scrapped. Ordinary data stays exact; a page-attribute bit selects the mode.
why: For BF16 tensors: x1.58 capacity per DRAM bit (18 -> 11.4 cells per value incl. ECC), x3.7 less refresh energy per value, ~x2 less array energy and ~x2.8 less I/O driver energy on mantissa planes. FP8 x1.41; FP4 x1.18: the lever shrinks as formats narrow.

title: Swap fixed model size for nested sub-models that shrink with memory
idea: Substitute a fixed footprint with an elastic one. Matryoshka-style transformers are trained so that narrower sub-models are prefixes of the full weight matrices (the first k heads and MLP columns); when memory is scarce the server unmaps the tail columns and serves the nested model, then re-expands when memory frees up.
why: Memory becomes a dial, not a hard requirement: 2-4x less resident weight memory at peak scarcity, so fleets can be provisioned for average rather than peak load.

title: Swap per-parameter Adam moments for count-sketch shared moment tables
idea: Substitute one moment slot per parameter with a hashed count-sketch about 1/10 the size: each parameter maps to several buckets, the median is taken on read, and exact moments are kept only for heavily updated embedding rows. Optimizer code only.
why: Adam state is 2x fp32 per parameter, often larger than the weights themselves. A sketch cuts optimizer HBM/DRAM 5-10x, so a model trains on fewer GPUs' worth of memory.

title: Electrometer guard bootstrap shields the write transistor
idea: A 4T gain cell has two series write transistors. The source-follower read transistor drives their middle node to track the storage voltage, as a guarded electrometer input does, so the inner device sees Vds~0. This fits a 250-180 nm logic process.
why: Subthreshold current, proportional to 1-exp(-Vds/kT), falls ~100x, giving long retention without a special material.
note: Bootstrapped/feedback 4T gain cells exist in eDRAM literature; cheap 180 nm MPW demo, niche gain.

title: Token-cadence weight reads replace auto-refresh
idea: In LLM decode every weight row is activated each token (20-50 ms). A 180 nm controller or FPGA marks weight banks as refreshed by access, suppresses auto-refresh while cadence stays inside the retention window, and falls back to auto-refresh when traffic stalls.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth for the weight region drop to zero, recovering the 10-20% bandwidth tax at 32-64 Gb with no new silicon.
note: Smart Refresh (2007) skips recently accessed rows; LLM cadence application is the twist.

title: JIT profiler narrows object fields with deoptimizing guards
idea: Combine JIT profiling with value-range compression: the runtime observes that fields only hold small ranges (counters under 65k, few enum values, pointers within one region) and rewrites class layouts to 16-, 8- or 2-bit fields, falling back to wide layouts when a guard catches an overflow.
why: Object-heavy services could shrink heaps 30-50% with no source changes.

title: Vision token-merging applied to KV cache compaction
idea: Combine ViT bipartite token merging with KV eviction: adjacent tokens whose keys are highly similar merge into a weighted centroid K/V with a stored count, and attention adds log(count) to the logit so merged entries keep their probability mass.
why: 2-4x KV reduction with lower quality loss than hard eviction.

title: Midpoint-bootstrapped stacked switch nulls storage-node leakage
idea: MINIFY the voltage across the leakage path to millivolts: the write switch is split into two series transistors and their midpoint is driven by a small feedback transistor from the read device that mirrors the stored level, so the inner switch sees ~0 V drain-source during hold (a sample-and-hold trick applied per cell).
why: Leakage 100-1000x lower so retention reaches seconds (fact 3) in any foundry node; a 4T cell designable by a small team.
note: Bootstrap leakage nulling is known in eDRAM gain cells; 4T area confines it to embedded niches.

title: Minify TSVs to zero: print staircase stack interconnects
idea: Offset 16 commodity bare LPDDR dies into a staircase and aerosol-jet print fine sidewall traces down each step to a substrate, giving a tall, TSV-free stack built in a packaging lab for about $300k.
why: HBM TSV tax: more capacity per package without the 3x wafer area or the 20-30% TSV yield hit, using dies that can be bought today.

title: Magnify threshold during hold with FD-SOI back-gate bias
idea: Design a 1T1C or 2T cell on a 22 nm FD-SOI MPW in which the back gate swings to about -2 V during hold to raise the access transistor's Vt and cut leakage about 1000x, then returns to 0 V for fast access.
why: Refresh: retention moves from ms toward seconds on a commercial process with no new materials. Test chip and characterization cost about $400k.

title: Eliminate system-prompt KV by baking fixed prompts into adapters
idea: Distill each tenant's long fixed system prompt or reference document into a tiny LoRA adapter through context distillation, so sessions carry no prefix KV at all; it ships as a software tool by a small team.
why: Prefix KV can be 10-50% of per-session memory in agent workloads; after baking, it is a few MB shared per tenant.

title: Eliminate per-pod JVM headroom with a node-level elastic heap broker
idea: A sidecar daemon watches GC pressure across all JVMs on a node and, through GC tuning hooks and madvise, shrinks idle heaps and lends the freed pages to busy ones in real time, instead of each pod reserving its own peak.
why: Kubernetes Java fleets overprovision heap 1.5-3x; pooling headroom per node saves 25-40% of DRAM.
note: Similar to existing elastic-heap JVM features.

title: Eliminate the separate swap tier: spare GPU HBM as host swap
idea: A daemon exposes the unused HBM of under-loaded inference GPUs as a compressed swap device for the host over PCIe peer-to-peer, and evicts it instantly when the GPU needs memory back.
why: Inference fleets average 30-50% unused HBM; turning that into host memory delays CPU DRAM purchases.

title: Eliminate memory ECC for tensors: algorithm-based checksums ride along
idea: Append Huang-Abraham row and column checksum vectors to every weight and activation matrix stored in DRAM. The GEMM computes its output checksums as a byproduct, so a mismatch locates and corrects a corrupted element in place, and the DRAM itself carries no ECC.
why: Recovers ECC capacity and controller energy for >80% of AI memory traffic; ~1-3% checksum overhead vs 12.5% parity, allowing cheaper ECC-free dies.

title: Let the workload refresh: skip REF when activations cover every row
idea: Reverse who refreshes: in LLM inference every weight row is activated each token (~10-50 ms), and every ACT/PRE already restores its row. The memory controller keeps a per-bank activation-coverage bitmap over the refresh window and withholds REF for banks that were fully covered, falling back to normal REF the moment coverage lapses, while still issuing row-hammer RFM commands; firmware only, on unmodified DDR5/HBM.
why: Removes most refresh energy and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss (fact 3) for weight-streaming AI memory; no fab, firmware on existing controllers.

title: Seed-generated tensors regenerate on read instead of being stored
idea: Replace stored pseudo-random structures (random projections, LoRA bases, hashed embedding tables, init-derived weight parts) with a PRNG seed plus a few learned coefficients; an on-chip counter-based generator (Philox-style) recreates each tile at read time.
why: Storage turns into compute: 10-100x smaller footprint for the parts of models and recommenders that can be regenerated, and no DRAM traffic for them.

title: Idle consumer PCs and consoles run offline batch AI jobs
idea: Reverse where batch AI lives: embedding generation, evaluation sweeps and synthetic-data jobs are split into small-model shards and dispatched (Folding@home-style, for paid credits) to idle gaming PCs and consoles whose 16-32 GB of DRAM and GPUs sit unused most hours.
why: Shifts latency-tolerant memory demand off datacenter DRAM onto hundreds of millions of GB already built; no new fab output, so no neon or helium.

title: Trust-domain-salted dedup with constant-time copy-on-write
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of fleet-wide page dedup (switched off after Flip-Feng-Shui and timing side channels), salt dedup fingerprints per trust domain so pages merge only inside one tenant, and route every write to a mergeable page through the same constant-latency CoW path whether shared or not. Each region gets its own dedup policy instead of one global on/off switch.
why: Resolves 'dedup saves memory vs dedup leaks information'; recovers 10-30% capacity on VM/container hosts where dedup is disabled today.

title: Key-only residency: values fetched from flash for top-k tokens
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: keep only the quantized keys of long contexts in HBM, because keys decide where attention goes, and leave values on NVMe/CXL; after scoring, fetch values only for the top-k attended tokens (typically 1-5%) with batched reads.
why: Values are half the KV footprint and sparse attention touches few of them; ~2x KV HBM reduction with bounded flash bandwidth.
note: ShadowKV/InfiniGen-style prior art.

title: Chemotaxis run-and-tumble firmware harvesting per-bank timing guardband
idea: E. coli keeps running while conditions improve and tumbles when they worsen. Controller firmware nudges a bank's tRCD/tRP/tRAS down one clock at random and keeps the change while ECC scrubs and canary rows stay clean (run). It reverts and re-randomizes on any corrected error (tumble), tracking temperature and aging. About $500k of firmware and FPGA validation over 18 months.
why: Commodity timings carry 20-40% guardband. Harvesting ~20% lower latency adaptively raises useful bandwidth per DIMM, so fewer DIMMs serve a workload.

title: Synaptic-scaling refresh loop holding corrected errors at a set point
idea: Neurons scale synapses to keep firing near a homeostatic set point. A controller loop stretches each rank's refresh interval additively until host/on-die ECC corrected-error counts reach a tiny target (e.g., 1 per 10^14 bit-hours). It shrinks the interval multiplicatively on any rise and snaps to the JEDEC rate when errors cluster. Firmware plus a 12-month soak on 200 DIMMs, ~$700k.
why: Fact 3: cool datacenter DIMMs could safely run 2-3x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth ~50% with zero hardware change.
note: Close to AVATAR/REAPER; VRT is the risk.

title: Foveated KV precision falls off with attention eccentricity
idea: Like the retina's dense fovea and sparse periphery, each attention head stores KV at 8-bit for the top-attended 5% of tokens, 4-bit for the next band and 1-2-bit sketches for the periphery; a 'saccade' (attention shift onto a peripheral token) re-fetches its full-precision copy from a compressed backing tier.
why: KV capacity and bandwidth: 3-5x fewer bits per token at near-baseline quality.
note: Importance-based mixed-precision KV is known (MiKV, ZipCache).

title: Capsule wardrobe weights: one global codebook for every layer
idea: A capsule wardrobe mixes a few garments into many outfits; store one model-wide codebook of 64K 8-dim weight vectors in on-chip SRAM and represent every layer as 16-bit indices into it (2 bits/weight), trained with codebook-aware fine-tuning.
why: 2 bits/weight with a shared on-chip codebook avoids per-layer codebook overhead; ~8x smaller weights in DRAM vs FP16.
note: VQ quantizers (AQLM/QuIP#) are prior art; gain over 4-bit is modest.

title: Card catalog: tiny learned index in DRAM, records in NV
idea: Like a library card catalog pointing into the stacks, keep a piecewise-linear learned index of a few MB in DRAM that predicts the exact NV page holding any key, so each lookup costs one byte-addressable NV read and records never need DRAM residency.
why: Key-value index memory shrinks 10-100x vs DRAM B-trees and data stays durable on CXL-NAND or MRAM.

title: Morse-code exponent coding on the memory link
idea: Morse gives frequent letters short codes. A tiny per-channel encoder in the HBM base die and the host PHY maps the highly skewed BF16/FP8 exponent fields to variable-length codes from a per-tensor table. Mantissas are sent raw.
why: Exponents hold only ~2-3 bits of entropy in 8 bits. Lossless coding cuts weight and activation traffic ~15-25%, with the same share of link energy saved.
note: Lossless exponent coding of BF16 already published; link-side variable length adds latency.

title: Context decoding: data-type priors resolve uncorrectable memory errors
idea: Readers fix typos from context. On a detected-uncorrectable error, the kernel lists the candidate codewords at minimum distance that fit the syndrome. It picks the one plausible for the data type: a pointer that is aligned and inside a valid VA range, a float exponent within the tensor's range, valid UTF-8, legal page-table bits. Type tags come from the compiler or the allocator, and the Linux patch plus evaluation fit within $1M.
why: Turning ~50-80% of DUEs into corrections allows cheaper ECC or relaxed refresh on weaker DRAM (facts 3 and 8).
note: Essentially SDECC (Gottscho 2016).

title: Radar MTI cancellers: store only frame-to-frame activation changes
idea: Copy radar moving-target-indicator cancellers, which stored one sweep in a delay line and subtracted the next: video and streaming-sensor models keep a reference activation map and store and propagate only entries whose change exceeds a threshold, as sparse deltas, refreshing the reference every N frames.
why: Static-camera and robot streams change <10% of activations per frame; activation memory and bandwidth drop 5-20x for video-analytics fleets.

title: Matryoshka weights that shrink themselves under memory pressure
idea: Inverts 'a deployed model has a fixed size': nested-width training lets a serving node evict the trailing slices of every weight matrix when DRAM is tight and reload them when it is not, trading a few points of quality for 2-4x less weight memory in real time.
why: An elastic footprint lets fleets size DRAM for average demand instead of peak.
note: MatFormer/Flextron-style nesting already published.

title: Hibernate idle functions to flash between requests in under 1 ms
idea: Inverts 'a warm service must stay resident': after ~50 ms idle, an idle container's dirty pages are compressed and snapshotted to a CXL-attached flash tier, and the next request restores them lazily through userfaultfd prefetch of the recorded working set.
why: Serverless and microservice instances are idle >90% of the time; DRAM per hosted function drops 5-10x.

title: Optimizer states superposed inside count-sketch arrays
idea: Inverts 'each memory cell stores exactly one value': Adam moments for huge embedding and expert tables live in a few count-sketch arrays where many parameters share cells through signed hashes, and the median of the hashed reads recovers each parameter's moment.
why: Optimizer state, normally 2-3x the weight size, shrinks 5-20x for sparse or embedding-heavy models.

title: Value-range narrowing: JIT shrinks fields to the bits actually used
idea: Inverts 'a field's width is fixed by its declared type': a profiling JIT sees that int64/double fields hold small ranges (counters, enums, timestamps near now) and re-lays objects into bit-packed struct-of-arrays, with guard deoptimization if a value ever overflows.
why: Java, JS and Python heaps carry 40-70% unused high-order and padding bits; heaps shrink 1.5-2.5x with no programmer change.

title: Refresh-off banks for tensors that die before they decay
idea: First principle: if data lives for less than the guaranteed retention (64 ms, with a median of seconds), refreshing it is pure waste. Patch an open accelerator runtime and an FPGA HBM/DDR5 controller so activations, in-flight gradients and per-step scratch go to banks that get no per-bank REF commands. A hardware 32 ms age watchdog turns refresh back on if any page outlives its lease. About $600k and 18 months of engineering.
why: AI working sets are dominated by short-lived tensors. Suppressing refresh on half the banks returns ~5-10% bandwidth and half the refresh energy at 32-64 Gb densities (fact 3), with zero fab changes.

title: Allocator-driven row refresh: never refresh empty memory
idea: Disable auto-refresh on an FPGA/CXL memory controller and issue targeted ACT-PRE refreshes only for rows backing allocated pages. The kernel's buddy allocator updates the bitmap of allocated rows through a doorbell register. Freed pages are simply abandoned and zeroed on reallocation. Kernel plus controller code costs ~$300k over 12 months.
why: Refresh energy scales with rows refreshed, and fleet memory is often 30-50% free or reclaimable, so about that fraction of refresh energy and REF bandwidth comes back (fact 3).

title: Capacitorless gain-cell memory on idle U.S. 22-28 nm logic lines
idea: The charge wall is a capacitor problem; a 3T gain cell stores charge on a transistor gate and amplifies it locally, needing no special capacitor process. Run gain-cell memory dies on underused U.S. 22-28 nm FD-SOI logic lines, using reverse back-bias to push leakage down for ms-class retention, accepting ~3-4x DRAM cell area.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: zero new fab capex and immediate capacity for buffer and cache-tier memory from existing domestic lines.

title: Tin can: indium- and gallium-free zinc-tin-oxide targets for gain cells
idea: Stimulus 'tin can' -> a 10-person team hot-presses Si-doped zinc-tin-oxide sputter targets from commodity ZnO and SnO2, tuned for BEOL oxide-semiconductor gain-cell transistors, so memory makers can skip IGZO's indium and gallium.
why: Gallium (~98% China, export-controlled) and indium (~60% China) become unnecessary for oxide-channel memory; target pressing is small-shop scale.

title: Ant pheromone: hot pages migrate autonomously toward requesting chiplet
idea: Like ants following pheromone trails: each memory chiplet keeps per-page counters tagged by requester, and pages whose trail strength crosses a threshold migrate across the chiplet mesh toward the heaviest user in the background.
why: Data-movement energy: 30-40% fewer mesh hops on average for multi-chiplet accelerators.

title: Bit-flip-aware training lets LLM caches run with zero ECC
idea: Box: cheapest cell x Si access x minimal SA x no ECC x bulk Si x standard. Models are trained and quantized with 1% random bit-flip injection on weights and KV-cache (bit-flip dropout, clamped exponent bits), then stored in uncoded relaxed DRAM where 1% flips act as regularization noise.
why: Removes all ECC parity and decode logic for AI tiers: +12% capacity and lower latency on top of relaxed-cell savings.
note: Close to EDEN-style approximate DRAM for DNNs.

title: Park idle chat sessions as token IDs, re-prefill in FLOP valleys
idea: Box: recompute × inference runtime × whole-session KV × idle >30 s × backing = 2-byte token IDs. Idle sessions drop their KV cache (~100–300 KB per token for large models) and keep only token IDs; when the user returns, a scheduler re-prefills the context in bursts on compute left idle between decode steps.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes at ~10^5:1 compression of parked state; cuts resident KV in multi-tenant chat serving 3–10× because most sessions are idle most of the time.
note: Evict-and-recompute already standard in vLLM preemption.

title: Bit-plane weight layout: one stored copy serves every precision tier
idea: Box: progressive precision × memory layout × bit-plane × per-request policy × MSB-first planes. Weights are stored as bit-planes so a request tier or insensitive layer fetches only the top k planes, replacing separate 8-, 4- and 3-bit copies of the same model.
why: Serving fleets keep 2–4 quantized copies per model; one progressive copy saves ~2–3× across a model zoo and cuts bytes read for low tiers.

title: Learned models plus Elias–Fano offsets replace pointer-heavy indexes
idea: Box: representation shrink × database engine × index × build time × piecewise-linear model + succinct leaf offsets. B-tree inner nodes and hash-index pointers become small learned position models with Elias–Fano coded offsets queried by rank/select.
why: Indexes take 20–50% of in-memory database DRAM; learned plus succinct encodings shrink them 10–100×.
note: Learned/PGM indexes and succinct structures are known.

title: Idle inference GPUs lend free HBM as host swap
idea: Box: harvest × installed GPU fleet × 2 MB page × idle windows × PCIe/NVLink peer access. A kernel driver exposes unused HBM on idle or lightly loaded GPUs as a fast swap device for CPU hosts and reclaims it within milliseconds when a large kernel needs it.
why: Off-peak, 30–60% of fleet HBM sits empty; borrowing already-fabricated memory replaces new DIMMs and needs no new fluorinated fab chemistry.

title: Retired FPGA SmartNICs host retired DDR4 as memory expanders
idea: Box: reuse × decommissioned FPGA boards × DIMM × redeployment × PCIe-attached memory-controller bitstream. Retired FPGA cards are reprogrammed as memory controllers for tested DDR4 RDIMMs harvested from retired servers and exposed as a warm tier for page cache and KV spill.
why: Both parts already exist: zero new wafer starts and so zero new fluorinated chemistry, while a near-free warm tier absorbs 20–30% of a host's capacity demand.

title: Po memory that forgets on purpose: refresh-free ephemeral pages
idea: Po: 'memory that forgets on purpose.' Extracted: the OS and compiler tag pages whose data will be overwritten or discarded within the retention window (AI activations, KV-cache chunks, network buffers) as ephemeral; the controller skips refresh on those rows and stores an expiry timestamp so a late read faults instead of returning corrupt data.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb): on AI servers where much of DRAM holds short-lived tensors, refresh energy and bandwidth loss on those rows go to zero.
note: Ephemeral-page refresh skipping resembles prior refresh-aware OS/controller work; expiry-fault is a nice twist.

title: Resistor weights from Minnesota: ReRAM compute tiles on SkyWater 130
idea: Po: the resistor is the weight. ReRAM integrated into SkyWater's Bloomington (MN) 130 nm flow stores edge and agent-model weights as multi-level conductances in crossbars that do matrix-vector products in place with on-chip ADCs, so weights never touch DRAM.
why: A DUV-only, trusted U.S. fab with no EUV runs small models DRAM-free, removing weight-fetch energy and DRAM footprint for edge fleets.

title: Per-row polarity flag parks most cells in hammer-immune state
idea: Worse: store data so the maximum number of cells sit in the charged state that hammer-induced leakage attacks. Flip: add one flag bit per 64B chunk and write the data or its inverse, whichever leaves more cells in the discharged orientation for their true/anti-cell type, so most victim cells have no charge to lose.
