why: Fact 9: hammer flips are strongly directional; halving the average number of charged cells roughly halves flippable bits per victim row and also lowers retention-failure exposure, for ~0.2% capacity.

title: Checksum-carrying matrix math replaces ECC for AI weights
idea: Worse: insist every bit of weight memory is perfect before compute touches it. Flip: keep weights in HBM regions with no on-die ECC and relaxed refresh, and use algorithm-based fault tolerance (row/column checksums embedded in GEMM tiles) to detect corrupted tiles at compute time and reload them from a host copy.
why: On-die ECC costs ~6-12% area and adds refresh pressure; ABFT detection costs ~1-2% extra FLOPs while enabling ECC-free, relaxed-refresh HBM for read-mostly weights.
note: ABFT well known; applied to ECC-free HBM.

title: Train models with bit-flip injection to tolerate 1e-4 BER
idea: Worse: train networks so fragile that one exponent flip derails inference. Flip: inject DRAM-realistic bit flips (directional, clustered by row) during training and use bounded activations and clipped exponents, so models run correctly from memory with raw BER up to 1e-4 and can be served from unprotected, refresh-relaxed DRAM.
why: Fact 3: inference memory can refresh 10x less often and weaker, cheaper cells qualify, cutting idle memory power 15-30% for inference fleets.
note: Widely studied (EDEN etc.).

title: Recompute-over-retain: regenerate KV caches instead of storing them
idea: Worse: store every intermediate tensor in DRAM just in case. Flip: schedulers keep only compact seeds (tokens, sparse checkpoints) in SRAM and recompute KV caches and activations on demand with spare FLOPs.
why: Zero refresh because nothing sits in DRAM; trades surplus compute for scarce memory, cutting memory per request ~5-10x.
note: Known compute-memory trade (vLLM recompute, checkpointing); full recompute cost grows with context.

title: Haiku poet's compression: distill long system prompts into gist tokens
idea: A haiku holds a scene in 17 syllables. A deployment's fixed 2-10k-token system prompt or tool manifest is distilled into 16-64 learned soft 'gist' tokens. Only those embeddings are trained, to match the model's outputs under the full prompt. The GPU cost is hundreds of dollars per deployment.
why: Agentic apps carry huge fixed prompts on every request. Gisting cuts per-request prefix KV and prefill by ~100x.
note: Gisting is known; shared prefix caching already amortizes fixed system prompts.

title: Self-boosting gain cell drives a plain inverter, no sense amp
idea: $1 IoT chips cannot afford precision analog: a 3T gain cell whose read wordline couples its storage node upward yields a near-rail bitline swing, so a skewed inverter replaces the cross-coupled SA and reference generator, all drawn at relaxed DUV rules.
why: SA area -70% and no offset trimming; periphery simple enough for 40-90 nm U.S. fabs, trading some cell area.

title: Zero-extra-mask eDRAM from stacked metal-finger capacitors in logic BEOL
idea: Extreme user: $1 MCUs that need 1-32 MB on-die. Store charge in interdigitated metal-oxide-metal fringe capacitors stacked through 6-8 standard logic metal layers, read by a 2T gain cell, so any logic flow gets DRAM without a single added mask or tool.
why: Capital: offloads small-memory demand to every logic fab at zero added masks; no EUV and no capacitor module.

title: Search-engine Bloom filter skips DRAM row activations
idea: Web search engines consult tiny Bloom filters before touching shards. Keep compact locality-sensitive-hash signatures of KV pages and embedding rows in logic-side SRAM; the controller activates a DRAM row only when its signature predicts relevance, so most rows are never opened.
why: Row activation is a third or more of access energy; skipping ~90% of activations in retrieval, attention and recsys gives ~10x lower energy per useful access with no memory-side change.

title: Deep-space image downlinks: ECC bits spent only on high-order bits
idea: Space probes protect image headers and coarse coefficients far more heavily than fine detail. The host controller repurposes the standard 8 ECC bits per 64-bit beat into a double-error-correcting code over only the sign, exponent and high bits of BF16/INT8 values, leaving low bits unprotected. The DIMM or HBM still stores 72 bits per beat; only the encoder changes.
why: For AI data, low-bit errors are harmless, so concentrating parity roughly triples correction where it matters and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER (relaxed refresh, weak bins) at no capacity cost (fact 3).
note: UEP for AI data studied.

title: KV-cache card that decays precision of aging tokens
idea: Extreme user: million-token-context AI. A 10-person team builds an FPGA CXL card that holds fresh KV entries at FP8 and requantizes entries older than N tokens to FP4, then 2-bit, in place, repacking pages to free capacity without host involvement.
why: 2-3x effective KV capacity per GB, relieving HBM and DDR demand.

title: Retention-binned salvage turns reject dies into usable capacity
idea: Time-scale binning: dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen because of a few weak rows are profiled per row. The map is stored in module SPD flash, and the controller refreshes weak rows at 16-32 ms while the rest run at 256 ms.
why: Recovers ~3-8% of existing wafer output that is scrapped today and cuts refresh energy on the strong rows, all from existing fabs.
note: RAIDR-style profiling; variable retention time makes per-row maps unreliable.

title: Harvest timing guard bands: cut tRCD and tRP 40% at 1% BER
idea: Shift the access timescale below the worst case: timings set so the slowest cell at the hottest corner never fails are cut ~40%, letting a few slow cells mis-sense and the row code absorb them.
why: ~30-40% lower random-access latency and higher bank throughput, so fewer stacks deliver a target bandwidth.

title: x32 ABI, fixed: automatic per-heap 32-bit pointer compression in LLVM
idea: The x32 ABI (32-bit pointers on x86-64) died because every library and distro had to be rebuilt for a new ABI. Instead, an LLVM pass plus allocator places each data structure in a 4 GB 'pointer island' and rewrites interior pointers as 32-bit base-relative offsets (like Java compressed oops / V8 pointer compression), leaving the external ABI untouched.
why: Pointer-heavy workloads (graphs, B-trees, KV stores, compilers) shrink 20-40% in DRAM footprint without an ABI break.
note: Lattner and Adve's pointer compression, plus V8 practice.

title: Backside-illuminated photoelectrochemical etch digs 150:1 trench capacitors in n-silicon
idea: Effect: photoelectrochemical macropore growth (Lehmann). In n-Si under anodic bias in HF, only holes photogenerated by backside light reach the pore tips, so pores grow straight to AR 150:1 from pits printed by i-line litho. A ~$40k PTFE cell with an LED array and potentiostat on 150 mm wafers demonstrates deep-trench DRAM capacitors within 24 months.
why: Fact 1: reaches AR far beyond 115 with a $40k tool instead of a $10M cryo etcher; fits embedded, legacy-node and chiplet DRAM at >=200 nm pitch, a niche the U.S. can manufacture.
note: Lehmann macropores are known; limited to >=200 nm pitch niche.

title: Supermarket expiry dating places perishable data in unrefreshed banks
idea: OS/runtime allocators tag buffers with a use-by time, as a supermarket dates perishables. Activations, KV-cache pages, packet buffers and staging tensors go to banks with refresh permanently disabled whose certified retention (e.g., 250 ms at 85 C) exceeds the tag. Expired data is recomputed or re-fetched.
why: Zero refresh power for the perishable share of capacity, often a large fraction of AI accelerator memory. It recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth there.
note: Refresh-off for short-lived data is widely explored (e.g., retention-aware accelerator buffers).

title: Felting: superpose many key-value pairs into one hypervector mat
idea: Felt mats thousands of fibers into one sheet with no single point of failure. Associative stores (retrieval caches, semantic caches, feature stores) bind each key and value into a 10k-bit hypervector and bundle hundreds of pairs into one stored vector by majority sum. A lookup unbinds with the key and cleans up against a small codebook, and the representation survives even 10% bit flips.
why: Holds hundreds of approximate associations per 1.25 KB vector, 5-20x denser than hash tables for approximate-lookup workloads, and natively immune to 1% BER.
note: HDC bundling capacity is limited; well-known.

title: Count-sketch compressed Adam moments for large-model training
idea: IFR: optimizer state takes no memory. Closest without new chips: Adam's first and second moments live in a count-sketch with heavy-hitter correction; exact moments are kept only for the top 1% of parameters by gradient magnitude, the rest use sketched estimates.
why: Optimizer state is 8-12 bytes per parameter; sketching cuts training DRAM/HBM 2-3x for large models.

title: Data that dies young gets no refresh: lifetime-tagged no-refresh banks
idea: Limit: refresh only bits that will outlive the retention window. The runtime tags allocations with a time-to-live and places short-lived ones (activations, attention scratch, gradient buffers overwritten every few ms) in banks with refresh disabled. A hardware lease timer raises an error if any data is read after its window.
why: Fact 3: a large share of AI training and inference DRAM traffic is short-lived. Taking those banks out of refresh recovers their share of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and of idle power.

title: No fab, only an FPGA: per-row refresh via ACT/PRE
idea: 10-person constraint: we cannot touch the die, so we own the controller. An FPGA CXL memory expander profiles every row of commodity DDR5 at boot. It then replaces blanket auto-refresh with targeted ACT->PRE restores scheduled per row from a retention table: 64 ms for the weakest ~0.1%, 1-4 s for the rest, plus a VRT guardband.
why: Fact 3: 90%+ of refresh operations are spent on strong rows. This recovers most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and cuts refresh energy ~5-10x on unmodified DRAM, using only an FPGA board, firmware and a CXL IP license.

title: Timing knobs only: extended restore time for weak rows
idea: 10-person constraint: only controller timing registers. Weak rows often fail because tight tRAS/tWR truncates their restore and leaves them at ~85-90% charge. The controller flags weak rows from profiling and gives only those activations and writes an extra 5-10 ns of restore, so the cell charges fully and its retention clears the slow-refresh threshold.
why: Fact 3: 10-20% more stored charge raises weak-row retention ~1.5-2x, which lets the global refresh tier relax a notch at under 0.1% performance cost.
note: Restore-truncation work (HPCA 2016) is close prior art; SoftMC demo is cheap.

title: Shake out the liars: VRT provocation profiling with thermal and voltage cycling
idea: 10-person constraint: make cheap profiling trustworthy. Before any relaxed-refresh deployment, run a 6-hour provocation routine on the FPGA tester: 25-95 C thermal cycling (chamber or heat gun), VPP/VDD corners and worst-case neighbor data patterns. This makes variable-retention-time cells toggle into their leaky state so they get caught.
why: Fact 3: VRT is the reason profile-based refresh is unsafe. Catching 99%+ of VRT cells makes 4-16x refresh relaxation safe, and the test recipe is something a small lab can sell.

title: Idle-RAM leasing agent across colocation tenants
idea: Within $1M/24 months: ship an open-source hypervisor agent that exposes each server's idle DRAM as encrypted RDMA-backed remote swap to neighboring tenants through a spot-price market, starting in one colo with 500 servers.
why: Typical clusters strand ~30-50% of installed DRAM; renting it out displaces new-DIMM purchases with zero new materials.

title: CCD fused into 3D NAND-style string: vertical shift-register DRAM
idea: Combine a charge-coupled device with a 3D NAND gate stack: 200 tier gate planes wrap one vertical oxide-semiconductor channel, and clocking the gates shifts charge packets held in surface wells toward a floating-diffusion sense node at the top. Each gate is both 'capacitor' and transfer switch, so there is no per-cell capacitor, contact or access transistor.
why: No 3D cell (fact 2) and charge wall (fact 1): ~0.1 fF wells suffice because the floating diffusion has gain; one hole etch stores 200 bits. Serial latency ~100-200 ns, hidden by striping each cache line across 512 strings.
note: No per-bit capacitor or transistor; doubts are transfer efficiency, dark current and clock speed in deposited channels.

title: Minify $/m2 3000x: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted memory foil
idea: Run steel or polyimide foil webs through R2R UV-nanoimprint at ~100 nm half-pitch with sputtered IGZO channels and anodized-aluminum high-k capacitors, making 0.4 um2 gain cells on kilometers of foil, then laminate and slit into memory ribbons.
why: At ~$20-40/m2 processed and ~300 GB/m2 (~1/80 DRAM density), cost lands at ~$0.07-0.13/GB, about 100x cheaper, trading speed (~200 ns), refresh energy and module size.
note: Multilayer 100 nm overlay on flexible foil is the killer; if solved ~10x cost/bit for a slow tier.

title: Eliminate cells: vertical charge-coupled shift-register strings
idea: Delete the per-bit capacitor, transistor and staircase: each vertical hole through 128 tiers is a CCD whose tier gates are tied to only 3 clock phases, so charge packets shift up to a single sense node at the top (128 ns worst-case serial access, pipelined bursts).
why: Water: one hole etch plus one channel deposition serves 128 bits with no capacitor module or tier contacts, so wet cleans and CMP per bit drop by >10x; also removes capacitor charge-wall limits.
note: ~10x density with no capacitor; doubt: charge-transfer efficiency over 128 stages in poly channels, dark current, serial latency.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge atop compute
idea: Eliminate both the interposer and TSVs: route top-metal lines to a polished, metallized die edge carrying ~2 um-pitch pads, stand dozens of DRAM dies vertically on the GPU's top surface and hybrid-bond their edges; the gaps between the standing dies become microfluidic coolant channels, so the memory doubles as a heat-sink fin array.
why: A 10 mm x 100 um edge offers ~250k contacts per die (more than a whole HBM stack) with zero TSV area and no interposer; vertical wire length <100 um targets <0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM and attacks the TSV tax.
note: Huge edge contact count with no TSVs; polished-edge 2 um pads and mechanical stability are major unknowns.

title: Tree-ring shells: coaxial gain cell in every tier-hole crossing
idea: Etch one array of vertical holes through a 100-layer wordline/oxide stack, then grow concentric shells like annual rings: an outer IGZO write-channel ring, a metal storage ring cut into per-tier segments by a selective recess, and an inner read-channel 'heartwood' that the storage ring gates. Each hole-tier crossing becomes a capacitorless 2T0C cell.
why: One hole litho and etch serves all tiers, as in 3D NAND; at ~100 nm hole pitch and 100 tiers that is ~100 nm2 per bit, ~8-10x planar DRAM bits/mm2 at roughly flat wafer cost, with no capacitor (facts 1, 2).
note: One hole litho for all tiers, ~8-10x bits/mm2; doubt: per-tier storage ring segmentation and reading floating-gated series channel.

title: Delay-line recirculating 3D string refreshes data by circulation
idea: As in mercury delay lines and drums, data in a vertical 3D DRAM string never sits still. The tiers are charge-coupled gates, and charge packets shift one tier per clock past a single regenerating sense amp at the string base, which restores each packet as it passes. No lateral access transistor is needed per tier, and refresh comes free with the circulation.
why: Attacks fact 2 (the lateral transistor blocks 3D) and fact 3 (refresh). One sense amp serves a 64-128-tier string. Random-access latency rises, so it fits capacity or streaming tiers.
note: Capacitor- and lateral-transistor-free 3D string with free refresh; doubts: transfer efficiency, serial latency.

title: Vertical CCD strings: 3D NAND geometry clocked as charge-coupled DRAM
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory inside a 3D-NAND-like stack: a vertical gate-all-around oxide-semiconductor or poly channel with 128 wordline tiers is clocked in three phases to shift charge packets up and down, with one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot. There is no per-cell contact, capacitor or access transistor, and bidirectional shifting halves average latency.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 7: cell area approaches 3D NAND bit density (~10x DRAM per mm2) and one sense amp serves 128 bits; ~60-130 ns access fits the DRAM-class window for streaming data.
note: ~10x density via contactless vertical CCD; doubts: transfer loss over 128 poly/IGZO stages, serial not random access.

title: Colors pick the layer: wavelength-addressed 3D stacks without staircases
idea: Inverts 'each 3D tier needs its own wired wordline contact': give each tier a photoconductive access element made of quantum dots tuned to a distinct absorption band (16 tiers, 16 wavelengths) and run a light pipe per column, so choosing the wavelength selects the tier and all tiers share their electrical lines with no staircase or tier-specific masks.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier wiring (fact 2), allowing 16-64 tiers at single-tier mask count, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: optical crosstalk, us-class access, dot stability.
note: Removes staircase/per-tier wiring if 16-band QD photoswitches work; crosstalk, dot stability and slow optical access are big doubts.

title: Retrofit US flexible-packaging converting lines into memory-foil fabs
idea: Partner with U.S. label and flexible-packaging converters, whose vacuum web metallizers, slot-die coaters and gravure units already run at km per hour, add enclosed ISO-5 web paths plus nanoimprint and spatial-ALD modules, and sell memory foil per square metre under a tolling model.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: a converted line costs ~$20-100M versus $15B+ for a DRAM fab, uses no EUV, no Czochralski wafers (no quartz-crucible chokepoint) and little helium, and can start within ~18 months in existing U.S. plants.
note: Converted web lines slash capex; doubt: web-processed devices reaching DRAM density, speed and particle-free yield.

title: Single carbon nanotubes coated as 1-micron coaxial storage capacitors
idea: Coaxial capacitance per length is 2*pi*eps/ln(r2/r1): a 1 nm-radius nanotube with 2 nm ZrO2 and a TiN shell gives ~2 fF/um, so a 1 um tube suffices at 10 nm pitch. Grow vertical tubes by methane CVD from Fe catalyst dots on each vertical-transistor drain.
why: ~100 nm2/cell vs 864 = ~9-10x density with an AR-100 pillar that is grown rather than etched (no fluorocarbon HAR etch), from carbon and iron. Catalyst contamination and tube placement are the risks.
note: Grown not etched AR-100 coax caps; doubt: single-tube placement at 10 nm pitch, CVD temperature, leakage of 2 nm ZrO2 at 1 nm radius.

title: Rotating nanostructured glass platter streams weights to batch inference
idea: In throughput-oriented batch inference the weight pass is a sequential scan of read-only data, which rotating media serve at the lowest cost per bit. A spinning fused-silica platter with laser-written multilevel nanostructures is read by a 10,000-element VCSEL/photodiode head array (~1 Gb/s each, ~10 Tb/s total), streaming a 70B FP8 model every ~60 ms, amortized over a batch of hundreds of sequences.
why: Weights leave DRAM entirely for batch jobs; the glass medium costs <$0.01/GB and needs no power to retain data.
note: Read-only glass at <$0.01/GB removes weights from DRAM for batch jobs; aligning a 10 Tb/s head array on a spinning platter is the big doubt.

title: Nanoimprinted oxide-TFT memory built into glass package substrates
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus ~$70,000/m^2 for finished DRAM wafers, a ~300x area-cost gap. Use nanoimprint lithography at 40-50 nm half-pitch on Gen-8 panels to pattern oxide-TFT gain cells, then cut the panel into glass-core package substrates carrying the memory directly under the chiplets.
why: At ~1/3 DRAM density, cost per bit ~100x lower and U.S.-manufacturable in display/glass lines; trades speed, retention and density.
note: Doubt: 40 nm NIL overlay and IGZO variability on Gen-8 glass; display $/m2 won't hold at that resolution.

title: Photomultiplier dynodes: electron-multiplying gain register on every bitline
idea: Forced connection to a photomultiplier/EMCCD dynode chain: between cell and sense amp insert a short serial register of 8-10 high-field transfer gates in the SA strip, each adding ~1.2x impact-ionization gain, so a 1 fF cell's ~3,000 signal electrons arrive at the latch as ~15,000-20,000. The register is clocked only during the sense phase.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-6x pre-latch gain lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF, cutting pillar AR from ~70:1 toward ~20:1 or making small-cap 3D tiers viable; risks are excess gain noise and the high clock voltage.
note: 5x pre-latch gain would ease the capacitor wall, but EMCCD gain needs high clock voltages and adds excess noise.

title: Vertical CCD charge-shift columns with one floating-diffusion sense node
idea: Box: potential-well storage in poly-Si/IGZO channel x CCD transfer gates x floating-diffusion source follower x 3D vertical stack x Si x CMOS image-sensor fab. Bits are charge packets that shift up one tier per clock to a single sense node at the top, like an image sensor's vertical register, so tiers need no individual wordline decoders or staircase contacts.
why: 3D DRAM blocker plus periphery: per-tier decoders and staircases vanish; uses U.S. CIS fabs; suits page-oriented ~100 ns access.
note: Charge shifts through tiers to one sense node, removing per-tier decoders; doubt: transfer efficiency, dark generation, serial access.

title: Gain-cell NAND string with dual-gate bypassable read transistors
idea: [Box: storage-node gate | dual-gate IGZO 2T0C | series-string current sense | monolithic vertical string | Si | 3D-NAND hole-and-plate deposition] Build 2T0C gain cells along a vertical macaroni string like 3D NAND; each read transistor has a back word-plate that, driven high, forces it on regardless of its stored node, so unselected cells act as pass gates and only the selected cell's storage node modulates string current. Write transistors hang off a second vertical write-bitline in the same hole.
why: Attacks 'no manufacturable 3D cell' (fact 2) and the capacitor wall (fact 1): no capacitor at all, reuses 3D-NAND tier economics; 64-128 cells per hole could give ~5x bits per footprint vs 6F2 at F=12 nm.
note: NAND-like 2T0C string with bypassable read FETs; doubt: series IGZO string current too low for 10-100 ns reads.

title: Po: memory printed like a newspaper — roll-to-roll nanoimprinted oxide cells
idea: Po: memory is printed like a newspaper. Extracted: roll-to-roll nanoimprint 50 nm features onto steel or polyimide foil, with spatial-ALD oxide channels and planar capacitors, making 1T1C arrays on a 1 m web; the slower cells sit behind a small silicon cache.
why: Processed DRAM silicon costs on the order of $100k/m2 vs ~$10-50/m2 for R2R, so even at ~17x lower density cost per bit can fall 100x+. Overlay accuracy on a moving web is the key risk.
note: Huge area-cost leverage if 50 nm overlay on a moving web works; that is far from shown.

title: Po: a wafer is a napkin — remote-epitaxy peel-and-stack floating-body tiers
idea: Po: a wafer is a napkin you can peel. Extracted: grow 50 nm single-crystal Si films by remote epitaxy through graphene on a reusable donor wafer, peel and laminate 64 of them; each membrane carries capacitor-less floating-body cells defined by one imprint step, and each donor is reused ~100 times.
why: Avoids Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy and high-AR etch and amortises crystal cost over 100 reuses; 64 tiers with no EUV aims at ~100x $/GB. Trade-offs: bonding yield and tier-to-tier alignment.
note: Reusable-donor peel-and-stack could slash $/GB; doubt: remote epitaxy of nonpolar Si and 64-tier alignment yield.

title: Mail carrier's local post offices: a sense amp every 32 cells
idea: Mail goes out from local post offices, not one central depot. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array so every 32 cells get their own sense amp on a ~0.05 fF micro-bitline, which cuts the charge a cell needs from ~5 fF to ~0.3 fF. The capacitor becomes a shallow planar MIM, the array shrinks to 4F^2, and 6 array decks share one sense wafer.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 vs 6F^2 times 6 decks is ~9-10x/mm^2. Dropping the 60-75:1 pillar etch saves ~20% of wafer cost, which pays for the bonding, and the periphery leaves the array die.
note: Tiny bitline cuts needed cell charge; doubt: one SA per 32 cells needs SA area and bond pitch (~200 nm) far below today's.

title: 3D-NAND-like vertical CCD strings as capacitor-less DRAM
idea: Scale-and-time jump back to 1970s CCD memory, rebuilt as a 3D-NAND-style vertical string: each of 100+ stacked gate tiers holds a charge packet in an IGZO channel potential well, and a read clocks packets down the string (~10 ns per tier) into one floating-diffusion sense node at the bottom, then recirculates them to the top. No per-tier capacitor or lateral transistor exists; there is one sense amp per string.
why: Bypasses both 3D DRAM blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2), and amortizes periphery over 100 tiers (fact 7); 5-10x the density of 6F2 if charge-transfer efficiency stays >0.9999, with wide-gap IGZO keeping dark current low.
note: IGZO CCD transfer efficiency over 100 tiers unproven; microsecond serial latency makes it a capacity tier.

title: Gigahertz CCD loops: one floating-diffusion amp per 64 bits
idea: Failure mined: 1970s CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on millisecond serial latency and charge-transfer loss. Fix: 64-stage buried-channel CCD loops with imaging-grade transfer efficiency (>99.9999%), 2-phase clocked at 4 GHz (worst-case 16 ns rotation), each sensed and re-injected by one floating-diffusion amplifier. Packets hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and there are no per-bit contacts, capacitors or wordline drivers.
why: 10x at the same cost: ~2F^2 per packet vs 6F^2 (3x) x 2 bits per packet (2x) x periphery shrinking from 49% to ~10% (~1.7x) = ~10x. Built with CMOS-image-sensor masks (no capacitor module, little EUV) in U.S. image-sensor fabs.
note: Revives CCD loops with CIS-grade transfer; clocking every gate at 4 GHz costs huge CV^2f power, and GHz transfer efficiency is unproven.

title: Core-memory sense weaving cancels sneak current in selectorless 3D crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: core memory's sense wire zig-zagged through the cores so half-select noise cancelled, a trick lost in the move to semiconductors, while selectorless vertical crosspoints died on sneak current. Fix: pair each data pillar with a woven twin pillar that crosses the same word planes, with its half-selected cells biased in mirror image. A differential sense amp subtracts the matched sneak currents and leaves only the selected cell's current.
why: 10x at the same cost: without a selector, 32 deposited word planes stack under one pillar etch (4F^2 per tier, roughly 1.5 tiers' worth of patterning cost), ~10-20x bits/mm^2. The twin pillar doubles pillar count, not cost.
note: Sneak currents depend on stored data in both pillars, so mirror cancellation needs matched data; element endurance not DRAM-class.

title: Electron-beam-addressed charge film (EBAM) with field-emitter arrays
idea: Failure mined: 1970s EBAM/BEAMOS (GE, Control Data) stored bits as charge written and read by an electron beam on a MOS target, and died on vacuum, beam deflection and slow serial access. Fix: replace the deflected beam with a CMOS-driven Spindt field-emitter array in which each tip covers a 64x64 patch at 8 nm spot pitch through a small electrostatic microlens. Bits are charge in a nitride film, read by beam-induced current to a common backplate.
why: 10x at the same cost: no per-bit access transistor, wordline or bitline. An 8 nm bit pitch on an unpatterned film is ~13x DRAM density, and the only patterning is the emitter array at a relaxed ~200 nm pitch (no EUV).
note: Transistor-free 8 nm-pitch charge film could beat DRAM density ~13x; doubts: 8 nm spots via microlenses, vacuum packaging, nitride endurance, serial access latency.

title: Plated-pillar magnetic memory: coincident-current writes, inductive non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: plated-wire memory (UNIVAC, Apollo era) read magnetic bits non-destructively with no per-bit transistor but died on hand-assembled wire. Fix: build it monolithically by ALD-coating vertical pillars with a soft magnetic film inside a stack of deposited word planes. Coincident currents in a plane and a pillar write one intersection, and a plane pulse rotates the film so the pillar picks up an inductive or AMR signal without erasing the bit.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistorless 4F^2 cell per tier and 32 tiers from one hole etch, with unlimited magnetic endurance and no refresh, ~15x bits/mm^2. Periphery scales per plane and per pillar, not per bit.
note: Transistorless 3D magnetic cell with unlimited endurance; doubts: nm-film inductive/AMR signal is tiny, half-select disturb, high write currents.

title: CCD memory fixed: vertical bucket-brigade strings feeding one base sense amp
idea: 1970s CCD memory died because serial charge shifting made access slow. Keep its strength, no per-cell contact, but cap strings at 8 vertical tiers. Charge packets in gated wells along a vertical channel are clocked down into one sense amp at the base, the whole string is latched into SRAM in about 20 ns, and it is written back in reverse order. This removes per-tier staircase and bitline contacts.
why: Attacks the contact/staircase cost of 3D DRAM (fact 2). Because DRAM already overfetches 128x (fact 8), a serial burst costs little. Target is 8 bits per 4F2 pillar footprint.
note: 8 bits per pillar with no per-cell contact; doubt is charge-transfer efficiency and dark leakage in deposited vertical channels.

title: 1970s CCD memory flipped vertical inside a 3D NAND stack
idea: CCD memories (Intel 2416, Fairchild) died because serial shifting lost to DRAM's random access. Turn a 3D NAND stack into vertical CCD shift registers: 2-phase clock its 300 word-line layers to push 4-level charge packets along an IGZO channel whose low generation current preserves packets for seconds, with one sense amp per string top and no storage transistor or capacitor per bit.
why: Meets 100x: NAND fab cost structure with no per-bit device, 2 bits per packet; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: ~150 ns average shift latency for random words, best for streamed AI weights and KV pages.
note: No per-bit device on NAND cost base; doubt is charge-transfer efficiency over hundreds of IGZO stages and serial latency.

title: Charge-gated Mott channel amplifies a few hundred stored electrons
idea: Effect walk: filling-controlled Mott transition. The storage node gates a 3-nm channel of a correlated oxide (strained NdNiO3 or electron-doped Sr2IrO4) poised at its metal-insulator boundary, so a few hundred stored electrons (~0.1-0.3 e per unit cell under a 100 nm2 gate) swing channel resistance ~100x for a gain read.
why: Cuts required storage charge ~100x (5 fF to ~0.03-0.05 fF), removing the high-AR capacitor (fact 1) and shrinking the cell toward 4F2; risks are retaining so few electrons against the leakage tail and Mott-channel variability.
note: Big charge cut if it works, but gating ~1e14 cm-2 electrostatically needs near-breakdown fields; 3 nm Mott-oxide variability.

title: Parametric charge pumping on common plate regenerates all cells continuously
idea: Effect: parametric amplification via a nonlinear C(V). Each storage node is a nonlinear MOS varactor plus a rectifying junction; a shared AC drive on the common plate pumps charge with a voltage-dependent sign, creating two stable fixed points, so every cell continuously restores itself toward its nearer rail with no row-by-row refresh. Reads compare node charge against a mid-level reference.
why: 10x density: cells tolerating ~1000x more leakage can be 2-terminal crosspoint varactor-diode stacks at 4F^2 in 8 BEOL layers (~10x); refresh counters, timers and restore-heavy sense periphery (fact 7) disappear, holding cost.
note: Parametron-like bistability via plate AC pump; doubts are drive power, crosspoint sneak paths and variability.

title: Four-pocket mirror-bit storage on both faces of channel sheets
idea: IFR: one gate crossing holds four bits. Each wordline crossing of a thin vertical oxide-semiconductor sheet stores charge in four spatially separate nitride-nanodot pockets (source-side and drain-side on front and back faces, with independent front and back gates), read by swapping source/drain direction as in mirror-bit NROM.
why: Constraint: 4 bits per crossing x 8 cheap tiers is ~20x bits per footprint versus 6F^2, leaving margin for ≥10x per dollar after process overhead.
note: NROM-style charge trapping has ~1e5 endurance and slow program; fails DRAM-class endurance even if density gain holds.

title: Series-gated shared read channel: NAND-string gain cells
idea: IFR: many bits, one read transistor. Make 8-16 storage nodes the consecutive gate segments of a single vertical read channel; to read node k, plate lines capacitively boost every other node above threshold so the string current reports only node k's charge, while tiny vertical oxide write devices fill each node.
why: Constraint: per-bit read transistors and contacts disappear and 16 bits share one hole footprint, ~10x density at 3D NAND-like cost; non-destructive read also removes fact 8's restore writeback.
note: Sixteen storage gates on one read channel remove per-bit read FETs; per-node write devices and 3D wiring are unsolved.

title: Coaxial nested capacitor shells: four cells in one hole
idea: IFR: one hole holds many cells. Conformally deposit four concentric storage electrodes separated by high-k and plate shells in one deep hole, each ending at a different height so a ring-shaped oxide-TFT access device wraps each shell's exposed top edge at its own level; one etch plus depositions makes four cells per hole.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per 4F^2 hex hole is ~6x versus 6F^2 planar, and a second hole tier reaches ~12x with mostly deposition steps; ultralow-leak ring TFTs offset the smaller per-shell capacitance.
note: Four shells per hole could give ~6x density; per-shell capacitance and staggered ring TFTs are the doubts.

title: Wound-film memory: roll-to-roll TFT DRAM coiled like a film capacitor
idea: Ideal: memory sold by the meter. Closest: imprint and print oxide-TFT DRAM arrays on 10 um aluminum/polyimide web at ~10 m/min, wind the web into a cylinder like a metallized-film capacitor, and connect every turn's wordline/bitline buses at the web edges via flame-sprayed 'schoopage' end metallization plus laser-cut edge decoders into parallel banks.
why: 100x: R2R processing ~$2-10/m2; a 1 m x 1000 m roll at 50-100 GB/m2 holds 50-100 TB for ~$10k -> ~$0.1-0.2/GB. Trades volume (a can-sized multi-TB brick), latency and thermal limits.
note: R2R at ~1-2 um2/bit with usable yield, plus per-turn edge bussing, is the doubt; volumetric bricks not dies.

title: Endohedral ion-in-cage dipole: one molecule, one bit
idea: Scarcity rule: the bit gets one molecule of space. A metal ion inside an elongated fullerene or nitride-cluster cage (Li+@C70-type) sits in one of two off-center wells, a gate field flips it, and the dipole shifts the threshold of an underlying 2D transistor. No bond breaks, and the cage is chosen for a ~0.8 eV barrier giving ms-s retention.
why: Self-assembled monolayer density near 1 nm2 per bit bypasses the litho wall (fact 4) with attojoule writes and unbounded cycling; barrier engineering and single-molecule readout are speculative.
note: ~1 nm2 bits would be huge, but sensing a single molecule's dipole via a transistor at that pitch needs a miracle.

title: GPU-owned sense amps: array stack bonded straight onto accelerator
idea: Limit: no base die and no DRAM-process periphery. Array-only layers with 8:1 bitline muxes are hybrid-bonded at fine pitch directly onto the accelerator die. Sense amps, decoders and controllers are built in the accelerator's 3 nm logic, at about 1/4 the area of DRAM-process periphery.
why: Facts 5 and 7: removes the HBM PHY and base die; data movement drops toward 0.3 pJ/bit and array dies become near-100% cells.
note: Building DRAM periphery in accelerator logic removes base die; 3 nm devices cannot drive boosted wordline voltages.

title: Nanoimprinted via-ROM weight tape laminated onto a readout die
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): frozen model weights are encoded as present or absent conductive vias in a roll-to-roll nanoimprinted passive crossbar (~200 nm pitch, ~25 Tb/m2) with printed Schottky contacts to block sneak paths, laminated face-to-face onto a small silicon sense-amp die that reads whole rows in parallel. Nothing active is printed; only the bit pattern is.
why: Weights are the largest frozen block in inference DRAM; moving them into printed ROM costing dollars per m2 could cut accelerator DRAM per model 2-5x with no EUV and no DRAM fab capacity.
note: TB/m2 ROM at $/m2 would slash weight storage cost; 200 nm R2R crossbar yield and alignment doubtful.

title: Panel-level 3D oxide memory [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Deposit 64-128 tier stacks on 620x750 mm glass using display-industry PECVD and sputter tools; pattern channel holes by step-and-repeat nanoimprint at ~100 nm features (large-area imprint is proven at 100-200 nm pitch for wire-grid polarizers); one HAR etch per tier group; spatial-ALD oxide channels. Each tile (a few mm) is self-contained, with complementary-oxide local sensing (B2-08), so there is no cross-panel overlay requirement; tiles are diced and bonded to small Si I/O chiplets. This revives ram-venture A1-03 (display-glass memory, killed at 2 um rules) by getting density from tiers rather than pitch.
why: F=100 nm, 3 b x 64 tiers -> 0.96 Gb/mm2 (2.1x 1-beta) on 6.6x the substrate area -> ~45 TB per panel; capital from display-class tools.
note: Display-glass capital with tier-based density; doubt: HAR etch, ALD and yield of 64-128 tiers on Gen-8 panels.

title: Sandwich stack: Smart-Cut single-crystal sense layers every 16 oxide tiers
idea: Build oxide-channel 3D DRAM tiers (horizontal or vertical-channel 1T1C or 2T0C) in groups of 16, then bond a ~50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top by Smart Cut (H-implanted donor, low-temperature bond, split) and build n- and p-channel transistors in it at <=400 C, as CEA-Leti showed with full 2.5 V n&p SOI MOSFETs at 400 C (IEDM 2025, nanosecond laser anneal plus solid-phase regrowth). That layer holds the local sense amps, tier decoders and muxes for the 16 tiers below; the next 16 tiers go on top. Each vertical bitline is only 16 cells tall (~2-4 fF), so a 1T1C cell needs only ~0.3-0.6 fF, which fits in a ~30-60 nm lateral capacitor inside the tier, shrinking the per-tier footprint from A1's ~0.03 um2 base case to ~0.01 um2. Global bitlines run up to a bonded or top-level periphery.
why: In-tier capacitor 600 nm -> 31-59 nm; per-tier footprint ~3x smaller; 64 tiers -> ~4.5 Gb/mm2 (10x 1-beta) and ~5-7x bits/$ before yield.
note: Grouped 16-tier short bitlines with repeated single-crystal sense layers; doubt: cost and thermal/H budget of repeated Smart-Cut layers erodes bits/$.

title: Swap inert TiN electrode for pseudocapacitive MXene intercalation electrode
idea: Coat the storage node with a Ti3C2 MXene film against a thin solid proton conductor. Proton intercalation between MXene layers adds Faradaic pseudocapacitance (hundreds of uF/cm2 in bulk) to the double layer, and MXenes are among the fastest-rate pseudocapacitive materials known.
why: Over 10x areal capacitance (fact 1) from abundant Ti and C, unlike RuO2, which needs scarce Ru; a planar or shallow cap at DUV pitch can store DRAM-level charge.
note: Faradaic MXene charge could give >10x areal Cs; doubt: ns redox, leakage, and unlimited endurance of intercalation.

title: Replace transistor with two-terminal punch-through selector: cross-point DRAM
idea: Substitute the 3-terminal access transistor with a 2-terminal n+/p-/n+ punch-through (or back-to-back Schottky) selector stacked on an MIM capacitor at every wordline/bitline crossing (1S1C). Idle lines sit at mid-level so each selector sees near-zero bias, and writes use V/2 half-select.
why: A stackable 4F^2 cross-point cell with no lateral transistor (the 3D DRAM blocker): denser per layer, with many layers. Retention needs a selector nonlinearity of >1e9 between V and V/2.
note: Stackable 4F2 1S1C would be a 3D DRAM; required 1e9 V/2 selector nonlinearity is far beyond known selectors.

title: Vertical charge-coupled columns replace per-bit access transistors
idea: Substitute the per-cell access transistor with CCD-style transfer gates: each 4F² footprint hosts a vertical column of 16-32 potential wells (one per tier, formed by tier gate-planes wrapped around a shared single-crystal Si pillar), and a 3-phase clock shifts the column's charge packets up to one sense node at the top and writes them back down. Only that top node needs a transistor and contact.
why: Attacks fact 2 (lateral transistor blocks 3D DRAM) and per-tier contact count: N bits per 4F² with 1/N the transistors, ~8-10x bits/footprint at 32 tiers; column access ~20-40 ns suits page/stream tiers.
note: CCD-style shift columns give many bits per 4F2 hole; multi-phase gates, transfer efficiency and clock power are the doubts.

title: Substitute silicon access transistors with nanoelectromechanical contact relays
idea: Each cell's access device is a sub-100 nm NEM relay (TiN cantilever over a vapor-HF-released air gap) that physically disconnects its capacitor; off-leakage is zero, so a 0.3 fF planar BEOL capacitor and a ~0.4 V pull-in design suffice, built with a 180-90 nm MEMS toolset above logic.
why: Constraint: zero leakage, tiny C and 0.4 V give >=10x lower cell and bitline energy and remove refresh; facet: no EUV, mature-node MEMS fabs. Contact wear versus unlimited endurance is the big risk.
note: Zero-leakage relay removes refresh and shrinks C; contact wear ~1e9-1e12 cycles far below DRAM-class endurance is the killer doubt.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric 2D bilayers from solid-lubricant hBN
idea: Adapt hBN, sold as a solid lubricant because its layers slide: in AB/BA-stacked bilayers a one-row interlayer slide flips out-of-plane polarization, so 1 nm bilayers serve as storage films in 20 tiers read through 2D MoS2 channels.
why: 10x at same cost: a 1 nm storage film lets 20 tiers fit in a 3D-NAND-like stack, with fatigue-free sliding switching; ~10-15x bits per footprint.
note: 20-tier stacked sliding-FE storage; wafer-scale parallel-stacked bilayer growth and endurance unproven.

title: Avalanche-photodiode charge multiplier at the bitline foot
idea: Borrowed from avalanche photodiodes and photomultipliers: a gated impact-ionization junction at the sense node multiplies the few thousand electrons dumped by the cell 10-30x before the latch fires, the way an APD amplifies single photons. A ~1 ns bias pulse limits dark current to the sensing window.
why: Charge wall (facts 1-2): a 0.3-0.5 fF capacitor at AR ~15:1 gives today's signal, removing the 60-75:1 pillar etch and making stackable 3D capacitors viable.
note: APD-style 10-30x charge gain would permit 0.3-0.5 fF low-AR cells; dark current, gain variance and bias control are unproven.

title: Leaky flash: 3D NAND fabs build volatile charge-trap DRAM
idea: Adapted from 3D NAND (already ~$0.05/GB): keep the 200+ tier charge-trap string but thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5 nm direct-tunneling so writes take ~10-50 ns at ~4 V, retention drops to ~1 s and endurance rises beyond 10^12; read through NAND page buffers and refresh each second, fronted by an SRAM cache.
why: Inherits NAND's per-bit cost (~100x below DRAM) and U.S.-buildable toolsets; trade-offs: 100-300 ns page-random reads and page-granular access.
note: Inherits 3D NAND cost/bit; doubt: endurance 1e12+ with direct tunnelling and 100-300 ns page access.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift-register strings replace per-cell transistors
idea: MAGNIFY charge transfer and MINIFY contacts: bits are charge packets clocked along vertical poly-Si CCD channels formed in 3D-NAND-style holes with 64 gate tiers; each string has one inject/sense contact at the top, so storage sites need no access transistor or capacitor.
why: 3D stacking with a NAND-like process (fact 2) and much less periphery (fact 7); average latency ~32 shifts x 0.5 ns = 16 ns, needs charge-transfer inefficiency < 1e-5.
note: Same 3D CCD string idea; CTI <1e-5 in poly-Si channels is the key doubt.

title: Minify displacement to sub-angstrom: sliding-ferroelectric bilayer access gate
idea: Use bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2 whose ~0.1 nm interlayer stacking slide flips out-of-plane polarization as the gate stack of a 2D-channel transistor, setting Vt non-volatilely. Switching is interlayer sliding with no ion motion or bond breaking, so there is no wake-up, fatigue or imprint mechanism.
why: Non-volatile 1T cell with potentially unlimited endurance, sub-1 V write, no capacitor and no refresh.
note: Capacitorless NV 1T cell with high endurance; wafer-scale stacking-domain control and read disturb are the doubt.

title: Minify the access device to nothing: self-rectifying ferroelectric diode crossbar
idea: Use Sc-doped AlN or BiFeO3 ferroelectric layers whose polarization flips the Schottky barrier at one electrode, producing a diode whose forward direction encodes the bit; the cell rectifies itself, so a passive crossbar needs no transistor and stacks in many BEOL layers with non-destructive current read.
why: Removes the access transistor and its leakage; 4F^2 per layer times stacking; non-volatile; avoids destructive read (fact 8).
note: Self-rectifying FE diode crossbar stacks transistor-free; DRAM-class endurance and speed of AlScN/BFO are the main doubts.

title: Magnify levels 256x: 8-bit analog cells with neural sensing
idea: Store 8 bits per gain cell as an analog charge level written by closed-loop program-verify and read by a tiny on-chip learned ADC that tracks drift and leakage, built as 8 stacked BEOL oxide layers in a depreciated 200 mm fab.
why: 8 bits/cell x 8 layers = 64x bits per area on ~10x cheaper wafers, targeting ~100x lower $/GB while trading latency (~0.5-1 us) and energy.
note: 256 levels against kT/C noise and leakage drift is near-miraculous; 2-3 bits/cell more realistic; latency leaves DRAM class.

title: Minify tool cost 30x: open-source fab equipment kits
idea: Fund open-hardware designs for the ALD, sputter, plasma-etch, anneal and nanoimprint tools needed for oxide-semiconductor memory, built from commodity vacuum parts and FPGA controllers at ~1/30 of OEM price, serviced locally, with a shared recipe library.
why: Tools are ~75% of fab capex; ~30x cheaper tools plus ~3x cheaper buildings with litho-free arrays push capital per GB down ~100x and grow a U.S. tool base.
note: Tool BOM is not the main cost; production uniformity, particles and uptime make a 30x cut doubtful.

title: Eliminate capacitor and access transistor: vertical 3D CCD charge-packet memory
idea: Eliminate both the per-bit capacitor and the per-bit access transistor: store bits as charge packets in the potential wells of a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel wrapped by 64-128 stacked gate tiers (3D-NAND-style), and clock them like a CCD to one sense node at the top of each string. A 4-phase clock at 2-4 GHz moves a packet one tier per phase, so a 64-tier string gives ~10-30 ns average access plus burst streaming.
why: Attacks fact 2 (no manufacturable 3D cell) and fact 4 by reusing the mature 3D-NAND channel-hole process with no capacitor and one transistor per string; potential 5-10x bits/mm2 at 64+ tiers; retention set by well dark current, refresh happens naturally as packets recirculate.
note: 3D-NAND holes as CCD shift strings remove capacitor and access FET; doubt: GHz CTE in oxide/poly channels.

title: Eliminate the access transistor: ALD tunnel-diode crossbar storage capacitors
idea: Eliminate the transistor: put each storage capacitor at a crossbar intersection behind an asymmetric metal-insulator-metal tunnel diode (ALD Al2O3/Ta2O5/TiO2 nanolaminate with barrier heights tuned for a >1e8 current ratio between 1.5 V and 0.3 V), so half-selected cells see too little bias to leak; lines are ALD TiN plus electroplated Cu, with no argon sputtering, and the 4F2 cell stacks in 8+ BEOL layers.
why: A stacked 4F2 crossbar attacks density and capital (facts 2, 4) and removes the leaky transistor; risk is holding diode leakage near fA, or refresh returns at a slower rate.
note: Stacked transistor-free 1D1C tiers could multiply density; doubt: MIM diodes far short of 1e8 nonlinearity and fA hold.

title: Eliminate the access transistor: 1-selector-1-capacitor cross-point decks
idea: Replace the transistor with a two-terminal threshold switch (Mott NbO2 or ovonic chalcogenide) in series with a planar MIM capacitor at every wordline/bitline crossing, stacked in 4-8 decks like cross-point memory; the selector snaps on above Vth to charge/read and blocks below it.
why: Density and capital: 4F2/deck with no epitaxial transistor per tier; trade-off is selector leakage, so targeted as a short-retention (ms) last-level working tier with fast refresh.
note: Selector-free density 6-12x if it works; doubt: OTS/NbO2 subthreshold and half-select leakage far exceed fA needed for even ms retention.

title: Eliminate the capacitor: volatile charge-trap strings with ultrathin tunnel oxide
idea: Build a vertical NAND-style string, but with a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide so electrons enter and leave a nitride trap layer by direct tunnelling in tens of ns (retention of seconds, refreshed like DRAM), avoiding Fowler-Nordheim wear-out.
why: Water: reuses the 3D NAND flow, where one deep-hole litho and clean sequence covers 100+ tiers; wet steps per bit fall >10x versus 1T1C DRAM. Endurance at 1e15 cycles is the key risk.
note: NAND cost with refresh; doubt: 1.5 nm tunnel oxide retention/endurance balance and slow page reads.

title: Crested van der Waals tunnel barrier: thick at hold, thin at write
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: write the storage node through an hBN/MoSe2/hBN 'crested' tunnel stack whose barrier peak collapses under write field (current up ~10^8x per volt) but stays thick at hold bias. Dangling-bond-free vdW interfaces generate far fewer traps than oxide flash, targeting >10^15 cycles.
why: Fact 3: a two-terminal selector with negligible hold leakage replaces the leaky access transistor, enabling 4F2 crosspoint charge cells.
note: Likharev crested barrier in vdW; ~1e10 nonlinearity needed for 4F2 stackable charge crosspoint.

title: Intermediary: threshold-switch selector capacitor crossbar with edge-only periphery
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: an ovonic threshold switch in series with each capacitor (1S1C) lets the capacitor charge or discharge only when the full row-column voltage exceeds the switch threshold, while half-selected cells stay isolated; arrays become transistor-free crossbars stacked 8 decks high in BEOL, with decoders and sense amps only at array edges.
why: 100x path: zero transistors in the array, ~2 masks per deck and periphery amortized over 8 decks on a mature-node base; trade-offs: sub-threshold selector leakage limits retention to ~ms (frequent refresh), selector endurance ~1e10-1e12 and higher read energy. Attacks Facts 2 and 4.
note: Transistor-free stacked 1S1C decks; doubt: OTS endurance 1e10-1e12 and selector leakage far below DRAM needs.

title: Vertical CCD columns shift charge through 3D NAND-style gate stacks
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: through a 192-layer deposited (not patterned) gate stack, clock three-phase pulses along a vertical single-crystal channel so charge packets march down the column like a CCD. A base amplifier reads and regenerates every packet on each lap, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: Fact 2 and 4: ~64-192 bits per lithographic hole with no capacitor or per-bit contacts (~10x bits per litho layer); access is serial (~50-100 ns average per 64-position column).
note: Same as I-00139 through a deposited gate stack; serial access and clock energy are the doubts.

title: Synaptic-vesicle quantal storage: count charged ferritin dots per cell
idea: Synapses signal in discrete vesicle quanta; dip-coat 15 ferritin-derived 7 nm oxide cores as separate islands over a 1.5 nm tunnel oxide on each oxide-semiconductor channel, charge 0-15 islands by direct tunnelling (ns writes, high endurance, ~100 ms retention, refreshed like DRAM) and read the step-quantized channel current as 4 bits.
why: 4 bits per cell in a capacitorless cell about 2.5x smaller than 6F2 gives ~10x bits/mm2; the dots self-assemble in a dip step, so wafer cost is nearly unchanged (facts 1, 4).
note: 4 bits/cell from counting ferritin dots would be ~10x density; dot-count variability and 16-level read in a tiny cell are doubtful.

title: Thylakoid grana: atom-thin 2D channel tiers stacked at 10 nm
idea: Chloroplasts stack thylakoid membranes into dense grana; alternate low-temperature MOCVD MoS2 monolayers with ~8 nm ALD insulator to build a 60-tier stack only ~0.6 um tall, then form vertical wordlines and bitlines once through it so each tier is a lateral gain-cell layer with a 0.7 nm channel and almost no off-state leakage.
why: A 10 nm tier pitch (vs ~50-60 nm for Si/SiGe) puts 60 tiers in the height of 10, so one shallow hole etch yields ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat cost and low refresh (facts 2, 3).
note: 60 tiers in 0.6 um; low-temperature MoS2 quality and edge contacts are the doubts.

title: Wood-frog torpor: capacitorless vertical cells run cold to stretch retention
idea: Wood frogs survive freezing by slowing their chemistry; build capacitorless floating-body cells in a 3D-NAND-like vertical channel stack and run the memory in a sealed -40 C enclosure, where junction and GIDL leakage drop ~100-1000x so millisecond room-temperature retention becomes seconds.
why: Removes the capacitor (the costliest, highest-AR module) and borrows NAND-style stacking; trades cooling energy and enclosure cost for a target ~100x lower cost per GB at rack level.
note: Insight: -40 C cuts junction leakage ~100x; doubt: poly-channel floating-body cells and enclosure cost.

title: Optical rectenna MIM diodes: transistor-free diode-isolated storage node
idea: Optical rectennas rectify THz signals with metal-insulator-metal tunnel diodes whose work-function asymmetry gives strong rectification; isolate each storage capacitor with two back-to-back asymmetric MIIM diodes (e.g., Nb/Nb2O5/Al2O3/Pt), so the node charges only when row and column voltages exceed turn-on, enabling 4F2 crosspoint decks with no silicon transistor.
why: Facts 2 and 4: transistor-free 3D stacking where each deck is deposition plus relaxed litho, all with sputter, ALD and evaporation; diode off-current at hold must reach ~1e-18 A per cell, ~1e4 below published MIIM diodes.
note: Transistor-free deposited capacitor decks would collapse 3D cost; MIIM hold leakage must improve ~1e4, near-miracle.

title: Antiferroelectric imprint crosspoint revives Bell's 1952 BaTiO3 matrix memory
idea: Bell Labs' 1952 passive BaTiO3 crosspoint memory died from half-select disturb; revive it with imprint-shifted, ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO whose double hysteresis loop gives a sharp switching threshold that V/3 half-select cannot reach, stacking 8 selectorless decks of 20 nm lines at <=400 C.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: effective ~0.5F2 per bit with no transistor or capacitor tower; AFE cycling (>1e12) plus wear leveling approaches DRAM endurance needs.
note: Imprinted AFE threshold could make selectorless stacked crosspoint ~0.5F2; doubt: half-select disturb, imprint drift, destructive read.

title: Core-style low selection ratio crosspoint that accepts and scrubs disturbs
idea: Core memory lived with a 2:1 selection ratio; build a 16-deck passive crosspoint of plain ferroelectric capacitors driven by a simple V/2 scheme, let each write flip up to 1% of half-selected cells, and have a write-then-scrub engine sweep the touched lines with a strong code before errors accumulate.
why: Facts 2 and 7: drops selectors and multi-level V/3 drivers (simpler periphery), enabling 16 decks of transistor-free cells at an effective ~0.25F2 per bit.
note: 0.25F2 effective if it works; doubt: half-select disturb accumulation, destructive FE read and HZO endurance versus DRAM traffic.

title: Reed-relay access DRAM: NEMS switches with zero off-leakage
idea: Revive the reed relays of the 1965 Bell No.1 ESS as BEOL NEMS contact switches that connect each storage capacitor to its bitline. When the switch is open, an air gap gives effectively zero leakage, so a small planar MIM capacitor holds charge for hours.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): refresh nearly disappears, so the capacitor can shrink to ~1 fF in flat MIM instead of high-aspect-ratio pillars (fact 1); BEOL at DUV pitch with no EUV; TiN/SiC materials, no Hf.
note: Air-gap off state kills leakage and refresh; doubt: relay endurance ~1e10 vs >1e15 DRAM access cycles, stiction.

title: Diode-capacitor crossbar DRAM using NiO/Ga2O3 heterojunction diodes
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-capacitor store (a rectifier per capacitor, no transistor) as a BEOL crossbar: each crossing stacks a p-NiO/n-Ga2O3 heterojunction diode (4.8 eV gap) on a MIM capacitor, written by forward-biasing the diode and read by charge sharing with a lowered row. Layers repeat at ~2 masks each above CMOS periphery.
why: Capital and Fact 2: 4F2 per layer with no FEOL array transistor and ~2 masks per stacked layer instead of 5-7 EUV layers; ultra-wide-gap reverse leakage could stretch retention ~100x (Fact 3). Risks are diode ideality and half-select disturb.
note: Transistor-free diode-capacitor decks; reverse leakage and half-select disturb likely kill retention.

title: Vertical CCD strings on 3D-NAND tooling as capacitorless 3D DRAM
idea: Invert 'every bit needs its own capacitor and access transistor at a fixed site' -> bits are charge packets that march. A vertical oxide-semiconductor or epitaxial channel threads 64-128 word-plane tiers clocked as a 3-phase CCD, so each pillar holds dozens of packets shifted to one sense/regenerate node at its top.
why: A 3D DRAM with no capacitor and no lateral transistor (fact 2) built in depreciated 3D-NAND fabs; area per bit ~pillar pitch^2/tiers gives >5x DDR5 density, refresh happens automatically every lap; latency ~tiers x shift time (~30-60 ns).
note: Same vertical CCD 3D DRAM; built on 3D-NAND tooling; transfer efficiency and lap latency are the doubts.

title: Two-terminal threshold-switch gated capacitors in crosspoint arrays on glass
idea: Invert 'every capacitor needs a three-terminal access transistor' -> gate it with a two-terminal ovonic threshold switch. A GeSe-class OTS in series with each MIM capacitor stays off below ~1.5 V and snaps on in <1 ns above it, forming a stackable 4F^2 1S1C crosspoint built at low temperature on glass, foil or ceramic.
why: Removes the access transistor (facts 2, 4) so tiers stack like 3D crosspoint without crystalline silicon; OTS off-current must reach ~fA or retention collapses to milliseconds, and threshold drift limits endurance.
note: Stackable 1S1C crosspoint DRAM would be big; doubt: OTS off-current is nA not fA, killing retention.

title: Volatile flash: a 2 nm tunnel oxide that forgets in seconds
idea: Inverts 'a charge-trap cell that loses data in seconds is a failed flash cell': on standard 3D NAND tools, thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5-2 nm so programming uses low-field direct tunneling (~3-4 V, ~100 ns) that barely damages the oxide, accept seconds-scale retention, and refresh in large background bursts.
why: Direct tunneling targets 10^12+ endurance for a capacitor-free, transistor-free 3D cell at NAND-like cost (~100x cheaper per GB); trade-off: ~100 ns writes, us page reads, ~1 s refresh.
note: Thin-tunnel-oxide volatile SONOS revisits known art; 1e12 endurance and microsecond page reads are doubts.

title: Two-terminal DRAM cells at crossings of spacer gratings
idea: Inverts 'every cell needs a three-terminal access transistor'. Stack a vertical n+/p-/n+ punch-through selector on a planar MIM capacitor at each crossing of two orthogonal spacer-defined gratings; the selector conducts only above ~1.5 V, so half-select biasing reads and writes a 4F2 cell with no per-cell gate or contact.
why: Per-cell patterning collapses to two self-aligned line layers, 4F2 from 1990s tools; selector sub-threshold leakage sets refresh (fact 3) and is the risk.
note: Punch-through selector leakage sets refresh; likely too leaky for DRAM retention.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche sense node gives digital output from 100 electrons
idea: Bias a tiny junction just above breakdown with a quench resistor; a '1' cell injects hundreds of carriers that trigger avalanche with near-unity probability, a '0' injects none, so the sense node outputs a full-rail digital pulse with no linear amplifier. Dark-count false triggers are handled by a short gated window plus ECC.
why: Cs could fall ~100x (fact 1) and the SA collapses to a quench + latch; strong density and periphery-area gain if dark counts can be tamed.
note: Same as I-02889: ~100x smaller Cs if dark counts and quench recovery can be tamed within DRAM pitch and timing.

title: Sugar-based block copolymers self-assemble 4.5-nanometer DRAM grids without EUV
idea: Self-assembly pitch is set by the Flory-Huggins parameter (chi*N >= 10.5); carbohydrate-polystyrene block copolymers have chi ~10x that of PS-b-PMMA, reaching ~9 nm pitch. Pattern a 4F2 vertical oxide-channel gain-cell array at F~4.5 nm (81 nm2/cell) with DUV chemical prepatterns guiding the assembly.
why: 81 vs 864 nm2 = ~10.7x density; replaces 5-7 EUV layers (single supplier, MW-class tools) with spin-coat and anneal using a bio-derived polymer. Defectivity is the risk.
note: Sugar-BCP 9 nm pitch known; DSA defectivity and a working 4.5 nm oxide gain cell both need miracles.

title: Zinc-oxide/cuprous-oxide diodes enable eight-deck selector-capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: Retention only needs reverse leakage below ~1e-4 A/cm2 at a 400 nm2 cell (Q~5e-16 C over 64 ms), within reach of wide-gap oxide heterojunctions. Stack a ZnO/Cu2O diode on a small MIM capacitor at each 4F2 crosspoint, deposited below 300 C, 8 decks high.
why: 4F2 x 8 decks = ~12x density with no per-cell transistor, using only Zn, Cu, Al and O. Forward current for 10 ns writes and half-select disturb are the risks.
note: 1D1C crosspoint stacks 8 decks without transistors; oxide diode rectification, destructive read and half-select disturb are the doubts.

title: Little's-law deep-queue byte interface over cheap NAND
idea: Bandwidth = bytes in flight / latency, so a 20 us medium delivers 1 TB/s if 20 MB are in flight. A controller chiplet beside the GPU exposes load/store addresses over SLC NAND with a 64k-entry tagged queue and 64 B read reassembly, while GPU warps hide the latency and an SRAM log absorbs writes.
why: Working memory at NAND cost (~100-200x cheaper per GB than 2026 DRAM); trades latency and write endurance.
note: Doubt: 64 B random reads from 16 KB NAND pages need ~1e10 IOPS; read amplification kills bandwidth.

title: Complementary Cu2O/ZnO oxide periphery lets entire memory live in BEOL
idea: Periphery (~49% of the die) is what pins memory to single-crystal silicon. Pair p-type Cu2O and n-type Zn-Si-O TFTs into low-temperature CMOS sense amps and decoders so both array and periphery deposit at <=400 C, allowing 10+ complete memory layers on any substrate.
why: Density and capital: monolithic 3D memory without 26-tier lateral Si transistors; the risk is Cu2O hole mobility (~1-5 cm^2/V-s) limiting periphery speed.
note: All-BEOL array plus periphery enables many monolithic layers; p-type oxide mobility and matching likely too weak for sense amps.

title: Line-only crossbar 1S1C DRAM: OTS selector plus capacitor, SAOP-patterned
idea: Box: MIM charge x ovonic threshold switch (two-terminal) x current-pulse sensing x stackable crossbar decks x Si x self-aligned octuple patterning of lines only. Each cell is a vertical OTS in series with a small capacitor at a WL/BL crossing, so a deck is just two orthogonal line/space layers from DUV+SAOP etched into self-aligned pillars; the OTS snaps on above Vth to charge/read and its off-state holds the charge.
why: Removes hole and contact layers, the ones that force EUV (fact 4); 4F2 with two masks per deck and decks stack like cross-point so density grows without litho; risk is OTS sub-threshold leakage and threshold drift capping retention.
note: Two-mask stackable 4F2 decks with no EUV; OTS off-state leakage likely caps retention at ms or less.

title: Po: memory that forgets on purpose — millisecond selector-capacitor crosspoint
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Extracted: drop the transistor and accept ~1-10 ms retention: a steep two-terminal tunnel selector in series with a planar MIM capacitor at every crossing of DUV-patterned lines, 32 layers deep at 2 bits per cell, refreshed by a background engine that sweeps an entire layer in parallel.
why: 4F2 x 32 layers x 2 bits with no EUV and no transistors gives roughly 100x more bits per wafer dollar than 6F2 1T1C. Trade-offs: high refresh energy and selector leakage, offset by parallel layer-wide refresh.
note: Crosspoint bitline loading gives tiny MIM signal; ms retention across 32 layers makes refresh energy dominant.

title: Transistorless crosspoint DRAM: threshold switch in series with capacitor
idea: Po: the array has no transistors. Each 4F2 crosspoint holds a MIM capacitor in series with an ovonic threshold switch that snaps on above ~1.5 V and is near-insulating below; half-select biasing writes and reads one cell, and the selector-capacitor pillar stacks in 4-8 decks like 3D XPoint but stores charge instead of phase.
why: Facts 2/4: 4F2 crosspoint with no lateral transistor sidesteps the 3D-DRAM transistor blocker; ~2 masks per deck gives ~3-5x bits per litho step. Risks: selector off-leakage sets retention and selector endurance must exceed 1e15.
note: Stackable charge crosspoint at ~2 masks/deck; OTS off-leakage (pA-nA) gives us-scale retention, needs ~1e-17 A miracle.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 300-tier holes without plasma
idea: Worse: push million-dollar cryogenic plasma etchers past 75:1 one wafer at a time. Flip: pattern a thin Au/Ag catalyst mesh and let metal-assisted chemical etching (HF/H2O2) sink it straight down through a Si/SiGe superlattice in a wet batch bath, producing holes and slits at AR >200 for ~300 tiers.
why: Etch aspect ratio stops capping tier count (facts 2, 4) and a batch wet step costs a fraction of plasma etch, so a 300-tier stack lands near today's wafer cost; at ~60F2 per tier-cell that is ~30 nm2/bit, comfortably >10x.
note: Plasma-free AR>200 could uncap tier count; doubts: catalyst wander in Si/SiGe and epi strain limit for 300 tiers.

title: Thousand-thread barrel cores make NAND the main memory
idea: Worsen: put all data on slow media and make the core stall on every access. Flip: build barrel processors with 1,000+ hardware threads per core (Tera MTA style) that switch every cycle, so 20-50 us SLC/TLC NAND reads are hidden and flash becomes byte-addressable main memory behind a small DRAM line buffer.
why: Cost: NAND at $0.05-0.15/GB vs DRAM at about $10+/GB, so 70-200x cheaper per GB; trades single-thread latency for throughput on graph, database and analytics work.
note: 70x cheaper bits if it works; 20-50 us needs ~10^4 outstanding requests per core and page-granular reads amplify heavily.

title: One shared latent per token across all layers, VQ-coded
idea: Worsen: store separate K and V for every head of every layer at fp16. Flip: train models to emit one small latent per token that all layers up-project from (cross-layer multi-head latent attention), then vector-quantize that latent to a 1-2 byte codebook index.
why: Cost and capacity: 100-300x smaller KV per token; trades retraining and some quality.
note: Stacks MLA, cross-layer sharing and VQ; 1-2 bytes per token for all layers likely destroys long-context recall.

title: Musician's harmonics: lensless Talbot EUV from a tabletop source
idea: A musician knows a string repeats its pattern at harmonic lengths. Light a periodic array mask with a compact coherent EUV source (laser-driven high harmonics or a compact FEL); the mask self-images at Talbot distances, and achromatic Talbot lithography prints the hole/line lattice at half the mask pitch through a ~100 um gap, with no projection optics.
why: Removes the $100M+ reflective projection optics; tool cost could fall ~10x for periodic layers, opening EUV-class periodic patterning to new suppliers. Risks: source power (throughput) and gap control.
note: Lensless achromatic Talbot removes projection optics for periodic layers; tabletop HHG source power is orders short of production throughput.

title: Squatter claims airspace: memory tiers in the BEOL above logic dies
idea: An urban squatter occupies unused airspace. Foundries sell a 'memory roof' option: 20 tiers of low-temperature (<400 C) ALD In2O3 2T0C gain cells built in the BEOL above accelerator and CPU logic, so die area already paid for by logic also carries DRAM-class memory and foundries become DRAM suppliers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: at ~20F^2 per cell with F=20 nm, each tier holds ~15 MB/mm^2, so 20 tiers give ~300 MB/mm^2, ~10x a DDR5 die. The only cost is BEOL deposition, roughly one DRAM wafer's worth per logic wafer, and no separate die, package or PHY is needed.
note: Gain-cell tiers above logic; each of 20 tiers needs ~20 nm patterning, so cost per tier, not density, is the doubt.

title: Child counting on fingers: 4-bit gain cells multiply existing fabs
idea: A child counts past ten by using more fingers per hand. Each non-destructive gain cell stores 16 current levels, read by a shared 4-bit flash ADC per 64 bitlines with per-row reference cells, and 3 tiers are bonded. A fabless memory-IP startup licenses it so existing DRAM fabs make ~4x the bits per wafer without new tools.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4 bits/cell times 3 tiers is ~12x bits/mm^2. Multi-level sensing adds ~10% periphery while wafer cost stays put; level margin against leakage drift is the risk.
note: 16 levels in a leaky gain cell with drift and noise is the doubt; 3-tier bonding adds risk.

title: Plumber's check valve: two-terminal thyristor crosspoint decks on ex-Optane tools
idea: A plumber thinks in valves. A two-terminal vertical poly-Si p-n-p-n thyristor latch at each crosspoint holds a bit by regeneration, with no access transistor and no capacitor. Eight 4F^2 crosspoint decks are built in the BEOL with the process flow and tool set of the retired 3D XPoint (Optane) lines.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 8 decks at 4F^2 vs 6F^2 is ~12x bits/mm^2. Two masks per deck on idled crosspoint tooling keep wafer cost near DRAM's; latch standby current and disturb are the risks.
note: Key doubt: BEOL poly-Si thyristors have poor latch margin, standby current and disturb; Kilopass VLT tried similar.

title: Pastry chef's mille-feuille: 64 tiers of 2D-semiconductor gain cells
idea: A pastry chef folds dough into hundreds of layers. Grow wafer-scale MOCVD MoS2/WSe2 monolayers (0.7 nm thick) and stack 64 transistor tiers separated by 10 nm hBN or oxide. Each tier's storage node is the gate of an ultralow-leakage 2D-channel 2T0C cell, and the whole stack is ~1 um tall. U.S. 2D-material growers become a new supply chain.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density is ~12x/mm^2. The thin tiers keep via etch aspect ratio under 20:1, so per-tier cost is small and wafer cost stays near DRAM's.
note: Key doubt: BEOL-temperature 2D growth/transfer and yield across 64 tiers.

title: Chemist's electron sponges: polyoxometalate molecules as 2-bit storage nodes
idea: A chemist sees molecules that soak up electrons like sponges. Graft polyoxometalate clusters (~1 nm, reversibly holding 0-3 extra electrons at distinct potentials) as the storage node on the gate of a vertical oxide-semiconductor read transistor, so one molecule stores 2 bits with no capacitor. U.S. specialty-chemical makers supply self-limiting monolayer inks.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: no capacitor plus 2 bits per cell lets a 4F^2 vertical cell in 3 tiers reach ~9-12x bits/mm^2 at about today's wafer cost. Electron transfer is fast, but retention and stability at 85 C are unproven.
note: POM charge-storage nodes (cf. Busche 2014 flash proposal); doubts: single-molecule charge sensing, variability, 85 C retention.

title: HPE memristor sneak paths cured by self-closing diffusive access
idea: HPE's TiO2 memristor crossbars died on sneak currents because they had no selector. Turn that failure around with an Ag-doped SiO2 diffusive memristor: it grows a filament only while a wordline pulse is applied, and the filament dissolves by itself within ~0.1-1 us. Used as a two-terminal volatile access switch in series with a stacked MIM capacitor, it gives >1e10 on/off with sub-fA off-current.
why: A two-terminal 4F2 access device that can be stacked in BEOL tiers, enabling 3D DRAM with no lateral transistor. Off-leakage far below the 13 fA tail cuts refresh 10-100x.
note: Diffusive Ag memristors show ~1e10 on/off, which is promising for stacked 1S1C; doubts: 1e15 endurance, Ag contamination, ns turn-on.

title: Delay-line regenerator: one fast sense amp services 64 dynamic bitlines
idea: Failure mined: mercury and magnetostrictive delay-line memories used one regenerating amplifier for thousands of bits and died only on serial access. Fix: in a 3D DRAM, the vertical bitlines hold their charge-shared signals dynamically for ~30 ns while one 20 GHz-class sense amp visits 64 of them through a fast mux, latching and restoring each in 0.4 ns. Row access stays random; only the sensing is serialized.
why: 10x at the same cost: SA area falls ~64x, so 3D DRAM breaks even at ~6-8 tiers instead of 26 (fact 2), and 48-64 tiers from shared etch steps give ~10x bits/mm^2.
note: Serial sensing could make 3D DRAM pay off at few tiers; restoring each vertical bitline in 0.4 ns is doubtful.

title: Snap-through buckled-beam NEMS crosspoint: bistable, contactless, self-selecting
idea: Failure mined: the first-generation NEMS memories from Cavendish Kinetics and Nantero died on stiction and contact wear. Fix: a pre-buckled 40 nm nanobeam over each crosspoint snaps between two stable shapes without touching anything. Snap-through has a sharp voltage threshold, so half-selected cells never flip, and the state is read as differential capacitance to the row and column electrodes.
why: 10x at the same cost: transistorless 4F^2 cells with built-in selection, unlimited contactless endurance and zero leakage (no refresh). Four sacrificial-release decks sharing lines, plus minimal periphery, give ~10x bits per wafer cost.
note: Contactless snap-through beams avoid stiction; doubt is aF capacitive readout and 40 nm beam stress control at scale.

title: IBM racetrack grown in anodized-alumina pores with zero bit-scale lithography
idea: IBM's racetrack memory died because nobody could fabricate its vertical 3D magnetic nanowires. Anodize aluminium into self-ordered 30-60 nm pores tens of um deep, pulse-electroplate Co/Ni-Cu modulated nanowires whose composition steps act as domain-wall pinning notches (~100 bits per wire), and read pore clusters holding majority-voted copies through a coarse MTJ crossbar underneath.
why: Meets 100x: no lithography at bit scale, only anodizing and plating baths, ~100 bits stacked per pore; est. <$0.05/GB vs ~$5-10/GB DRAM. Trades: 50-500 ns shift latency and sequential bias (good for streaming AI weights), redundancy overhead.
note: Bath-made modulated nanowires give ~100 bits per pore without bit litho; stochastic wall pinning and bottom-only readout are major doubts.

title: Nanoimprint's overlay killer neutralized by alignment-free stacked crossbars
idea: Canon's nanoimprint for NAND stalled on overlay error and defects. Perpendicular line arrays need no overlay because every crossing is a cell wherever lines land, so imprint 15 nm half-pitch lines from daughter templates replicated off one e-beam master, stack 16 decks of amorphous-carbon sp2/sp3 switching cells with shared lines, and absorb random offsets with a per-array line calibration map.
why: Meets 100x: no EUV, imprint tools ~1/5 scanner cost, 16 decks of 4F2 cells; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: carbon-cell endurance and write energy, template wear, defect mapping.
note: Overlay-free crossbars echo HP's NIL crossbar work; carbon-cell endurance far below DRAM-class.

title: FeRAM read fatigue removed by sub-coercive nondestructive capacitance readout
idea: Ramtron-era FeRAM's destructive read made every read a write, fatiguing cells and costing restore energy. Fix: read with a small sub-coercive AC probe that senses the polarization-dependent asymmetry of the capacitor's C-V curve (piezo/dielectric nonlinearity), leaving the domain state untouched.
why: Nonvolatile and refresh-free; reads consume no endurance, so ~1e10-cycle HZO acts as effectively unlimited endurance for read-heavy data, and no restore cycle is needed (fact 8).
note: Nonvolatile refresh-free 1T1C with no read fatigue; C-V asymmetry signal at small bias is tiny at DRAM scale.

title: Avalanche-multiplying sense junction gives charge gain before latch
idea: Effect: impact-ionization avalanche multiplication. Transfer cell charge into a small guard-ringed n+/p junction biased just below breakdown in linear mode; injected carriers are multiplied ~10-30x, then the packet is quenched and integrated on the SA node, so gain comes before any transistor offset.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): ~10x charge gain would allow ~0.5-1 fF cells and faster sensing.
note: Pre-latch avalanche gain could allow sub-fF cells; gain spread near breakdown, excess noise and temperature drift across millions of junctions.

title: Active negative-capacitance bitline cancels bitline load for 0.4 fF cells
idea: Effect: Miller feedback and negative impedance conversion. Each bitline pair gets a small cross-coupled negative-impedance converter, enabled only during charge sharing, that cancels ~85% of bitline capacitance; the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cb) rises ~6x, so a 0.4 fF cell develops the same ~100 mV signal a 5 fF cell gives today.
why: 10x density: 0.4 fF planar caps enable a 4F^2 vertical-gate cell (1.5x) stacked 8 tiers at ~0.8x per tier (~10x). Same cost: the NIC replaces part of the sense amp, and the high-AR capacitor module is eliminated.
note: Cancelling 85% Cb would remove capacitor module; doubt NIC stability, mismatch, offset.

title: NEMS relay access switches give zero-leakage tiny storage nodes
idea: Effect: electrostatic actuation of nano-electromechanical relays.
