The access transistor becomes an electrostatically actuated beam with a ~10 nm gap, and the air gap in the off state means no subthreshold or junction leakage, so a 0.1 fF parasitic node holds data far beyond 64 ms; the relays are metal-only and low-temperature, so they stack in BEOL.
why: 10x density: about 10 BEOL layers of 4F^2 crosspoint relays over CMOS periphery give ~10x. Same cost: metal deposition and no EUV. The reliability risk is contact wear against DRAM-level endurance (~1e15 cycles).
note: Air-gap off-state kills leakage and stacks in BEOL; 1e15-cycle contact endurance and ns switching are unsolved.

title: Co-decaying reference cells enable 16-level DRAM storage
idea: IFR: decay does not matter if the ruler shrinks with the data. Each row carries 15 reference cells written at the level boundaries together with the data; they leak through identical access devices at identical temperature, so a ramp-ADC sense amp compares against references that drift exactly as the data does, allowing 4 bits per gain cell.
why: Constraint: 4x bits for a few percent array area and no added masks; combined with three cheap deposition tiers or a 4F^2 vertical cell it reaches ~10x bits at near-equal wafer cost.
note: Leakage varies cell to cell, so row references cannot track each cell; 16 levels on fC charge lacks margin.

title: One-second dynamic NAND: leakage tuned to just-enough retention
idea: IFR: the barrier leaks exactly as much as the job allows. Build 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with a 2-2.5 nm tunnel oxide instead of ~6 nm so charge-trap cells write by direct tunneling at ~3-4 V in 10-50 ns, endure >1e14 cycles without Fowler-Nordheim damage and retain ~1 s; short 8-16-cell strings and SLC sensing aim reads near 100 ns.
why: Constraint: inherits 3D NAND's ~15x per-wafer bit density at NAND wafer cost, and 1 s retention means refresh 16x rarer than DRAM.
note: Direct-tunneling charge trap could be dense 3D DRAM; doubts: charge per 10-50 ns write, 1e14 endurance, poly-Si read speed.

title: Ultrawide-gap oxide gate storage removes capacitor, 32 deposited tiers
idea: IFR: the switch leaks so little that a transistor gate is the whole capacitor. An ALD ZnGa2O4/Ga2O3 write transistor (4.5-4.9 eV gap, off current ~1e-22 A) lets the ~0.1 fF gate of the read transistor hold charge for hours; with no capacitor each 2T0C layer is ~25 nm tall, so 32 tiers share one staircase and slit etch.
why: Constraint: removes the fact-1 capacitor and fact-3 refresh; 32 tiers at ~2x planar wafer cost and no EUV per tier give ~10x bits per dollar.
note: 3D 2T0C is widely pursued; 25 nm tiers, 0.1 fF read margin and usable Ga2O3 mobility are big doubts.

title: Crosspoint 1S1C with wide-gap punch-through selector, eight layers
idea: IFR: the cell needs no third terminal. Stack eight DUV-patterned crosspoint layers, each cell a MIM capacitor in series with a symmetric n-p-n punch-through selector in a wide-gap oxide engineered for <1e-19 A at V/3 half-select bias and steep turn-on above ~1.5 V; reads are destructive with write-back, as in DRAM.
why: Constraint: 4F^2 per layer x 8 layers versus 6F^2 is ~12x density, and each layer needs ~2 non-EUV masks, holding wafer cost near today's EUV-heavy DRAM.
note: Needs <1e-19 A half-select and a quality p-type wide-gap oxide; both unproven.

title: Area-selective deposition self-aligns every tier's access gate
idea: IFR: each tier's transistor assembles itself where it belongs. Inhibitor SAMs that bind everywhere except exposed oxide-semiconductor edges inside the slit let area-selective ALD grow gate dielectric and gate metal only on channel edges, in all tiers at once, with no per-tier lithography or overlay.
why: Constraint: removes the per-tier patterning that makes 3D DRAM costly (facts 2 and 4), so ~30 tiers cost mostly deposition time, about 2.5x planar cost for ~10x bits per dollar.
note: Per-tier gates without litho is a real 3D DRAM cost lever; ASD selectivity across 30 tiers in high-aspect slits is unproven.

title: SiGe quantum wells inside 3D tier stack hold the bit
idea: Ideal: the 3D DRAM's own epitaxial layers are the memory. Closest: in the Si/SiGe superlattice used to build 3D tiers, leave a thin SiGe well inside each Si channel layer as a hole pocket (~200 meV valence-band offset), turning every lateral transistor into a floating-body 1T cell so the lateral capacitor is never built.
why: Fact 2: removes the lateral-capacitor module that blocks 3D DRAM; each tier is one transistor tall, so >26 tiers come with roughly half the steps per tier.
note: Removes the lateral capacitor in 3D DRAM; floating-body retention and margin have historically failed at scale.

title: Transistorless cross-point capacitors: two line masks per stacked tier
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: replace the access MOSFET with a two-terminal wide-gap punch-through selector (AlN/SiC heterojunction) whose barrier keeps hot leakage tiny, giving a 4F2 one-selector-one-capacitor cross-point that needs only two line/space masks per tier and stacks monolithically.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 4F2 per tier and ~2 masks per tier vs ~25; cost per bit could fall several-fold if the selector holds fA-class leakage at 125 C.
note: Two-mask stacked 4F2 tiers could cut cost several-fold, but fA off-current at 125 C with ns write current and half-select disturb is unproven.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric 2D gain channel (fatigue-free polarization)
idea: In AB/BA-stacked bilayers, an out-of-plane polarization flips when one layer slides by a fraction of a lattice constant. No ions move, so there is no oxygen-vacancy migration and no charged-defect build-up. A semiconducting 3R-MoS2 bilayer can serve as both channel and ferroelectric, or a bilayer-hBN gate ferroelectric can sit on a MoS2/IGZO channel. Polarization ~0.7 uC/cm2 (~4e12 e/cm2) shifts Vt by 0.16-0.30 V per state at EOT 0.8-1.5 nm, a 0.3-0.6 V window. The cell is non-volatile with a non-destructive gain read, written at <1 V in ns.
why: [SPECULATIVE at array scale] A ferroelectric 1T DRAM-class cell with endurance on a path to >=1e12-1e15 (1e11 shown), zero refresh, and sub-1 V ns writes: closes the 1e8x endurance gap that kills hafnia FeFETs.
note: Ion-free sliding polarization could close FeFET endurance gap; doubt: wafer-scale stacking-domain control and tiny Vt window.

title: Restaurant cook-to-order: store token IDs, recompute KV on demand
idea: Borrowed from kitchens that cook to order instead of holding a buffet: long contexts are kept as token IDs (2 bytes/token) and the KV for any needed span is re-prefilled in compute-dense bursts into SRAM tiles just before attention, with only a small recent window kept resident.
why: At rest, per-token state drops from ~100 KB-1 MB of KV to 2 bytes; no long-lived volatile state means nothing to refresh, trading spare FLOPs for capacity.
note: Same token-ID recompute core as I-08597; re-prefill compute for long spans is the doubt.

title: Compiler-scheduled deterministic streaming replaces random access
idea: Transformer inference has a static access order per layer, so cache misses are a choice. The compiler emits a cycle-exact fetch schedule, and a stream engine pulls tensors from QLC NAND exactly one schedule-window ahead into a 64 MB SRAM; DRAM holds only what the compiler cannot predict.
why: Removes DRAM for static tensors (often >90% of bytes); cost per GB tracks NAND (~100x cheaper); trades generality to static-graph workloads.
note: Doubt: NAND bandwidth and QLC read-disturb under per-token full reads; if solved, ~100x cheaper weight storage. Close to FlexGen/LLM-in-flash.

title: Tiny hypernetwork generates layer weights on the fly
idea: Worsen: store every weight of a large network explicitly. Flip: store a small hypernetwork plus per-layer embeddings, and generate each layer's weight tiles in SRAM just before use, never materializing the full model in DRAM.
why: Cost: 50-200x smaller model footprint; trades extra compute and some accuracy (requires training for generation).
note: Hypernetwork weight generation is known; 50-200x compression without quality loss is unproven at LLM scale.

title: Substitute passive silicon interposer with DRAM-filled active interposer under GPU
idea: The ~2,500 mm2 CoWoS interposer is mostly empty 65 nm-class silicon; build deep-trench-capacitor eDRAM arrays into it (deep trenches are already etched there for decoupling caps) so the GPU's hot working set sits ~50 um below the logic through hybrid bonds instead of across an HBM PHY.
why: Constraint: vertical access ~0.2-0.4 pJ/bit versus HBM 3-4 pJ/bit (>=10x); capital: reuses interposer wafer starts and trench tools already in the packaging flow, adding a few GB without TSV stacks.
note: 65 nm trench eDRAM capacity is sub-GB per interposer.

title: Substitute one-time fab grants with a per-bit production tax credit
idea: Swap CHIPS-style lump capex grants for a solar-style production tax credit paid per Gb shipped from U.S. fabs, with a 10-year schedule that steps down.
why: Rewards output rather than groundbreaking; makes U.S. DRAM cost-competitive at ~$0.0x/Gb credit and tilts siting decisions toward volume.
note: Pays for yield/output; 45X-style credits exist for other sectors.

title: National open 3D-DRAM pilot line fused with shared PDK at Albany
idea: Combine the Albany NY public R&D fab with an open, licensable 3D-DRAM process design kit: startups and universities tape out cell and array variants on shared multi-project wafers, and CHIPS money buys tier-stack and bonding tool sets whose recipes transfer to US production fabs.
why: Capital and time (fact 4): entry cost for a new US memory architecture drops from ~$1B to ~$1-5M per experiment, speeding the 3D cell search (fact 2).

title: LNG-style take-or-pay project finance for DRAM fabs
idea: Combine the LNG-terminal project-finance structure, where 20-year take-or-pay offtake contracts serve as collateral, with DRAM fabs. Hyperscalers pre-buy fixed-price bit capacity, federal loan guarantees cover construction, and the fab SPV borrows at infrastructure rates instead of memory-cycle equity.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4). Cutting WACC from ~12% to ~6% and stretching depreciation lowers wafer cost ~15-20% and de-risks U.S. builds.

title: Open-standard base die enabling multi-vendor DRAM stacks
idea: Combine a royalty-free, open-source HBM base-die design (released like RISC-V) with a U.S. OSAT stacking line that buys known-good DRAM core wafers from any maker, including smaller and second-source DRAM fabs, so stacks can be assembled without the big three's TSV lines.
why: Usable supply and U.S. manufacturability: decouples HBM stacking capacity from three vendors, raising supply and creating domestic stacking capacity.

title: Take-or-pay capacity prepay notes modeled on LNG contracts
idea: Combine 20-year LNG take-or-pay contract structures with fab project finance. Hyperscalers and OEMs sign bit-delivery contracts with floor and ceiling pricing that become bankable collateral for non-recourse debt on a new fab, the way LNG trains are financed.
why: Attacks capital intensity and cyclicality, the reason fabs aren't built until shortages hit. It could lower cost of capital by 3-5 points on $15B+ fabs.

title: SpaceX rideshare: multi-project shuttle wafers on a DRAM pilot line
idea: Like rideshare launches that carry dozens of satellites, a national DRAM pilot line offers quarterly multi-project shuttle runs: startups and universities buy part of a wafer on a standard access-transistor and periphery flow and drop in their own capacitor or cell module.
why: Capital barrier to new cells: a cell experiment falls from $100M+ for a private line to ~$0.1-1M per shuttle slot, filling the U.S. pipeline of DRAM-class cells.

title: Car platform sharing: one DRAM core die, swappable interface chiplets
idea: Adapted from VW's shared MQB platform: fabs make one memory-array core die with a dense hybrid-bond face, and a separate interface chiplet turns it into DDR5, LPDDR, GDDR or HBM. Capacity moves between markets by changing only the cheap chiplet.
why: Capital and periphery (facts 4, 7): fewer mask sets, periphery moved to a cheaper logic node, and wafer starts reallocated in weeks, not quarters, during HBM/DDR shortages.

title: Pharma-style CDMO for fabless DRAM cell designers
idea: Adapted from biologics CDMOs like Lonza: a memory CDMO offers a qualified DRAM front end (capacitor module, buried wordline, periphery transistors) on which fabless memory startups tape out their own array and cell designs under tech-transfer contracts and pay per wafer.
why: Separates memory innovation from owning a $15B fab and does for memory what TSMC did for logic; cuts an entrant's capital need ~100x and widens the supplier base (capital intensity).

title: Strategic DRAM reserve modeled on the petroleum reserve
idea: Adapted from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve: a government or buyer consortium buys known-good dies in price troughs and stores them in nitrogen-purged, humidity-controlled vaults. It auctions them when contract prices pass a trigger (e.g., 2x the trailing average).
why: Damps the 4x price swings that freeze downstream production; buying in downturns also props up maker utilization and encourages counter-cyclical capex (supply stability).
note: Damps price swings; DRAM generation obsolescence limits shelf life of stored product.

title: LNG take-or-pay offtake financing for a DRAM fab SPV
idea: Adapted from LNG export trains financed on 20-year take-or-pay contracts: a fab sits in a special-purpose vehicle whose debt is secured by hyperscalers' 10-year commitments to buy fixed bit volumes at a cost-plus formula, so project-finance lenders can fund ~70% debt.
why: Cuts the weighted cost of capital from ~10-12% to ~6-7%; since depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, cost per bit falls ~15-20% and new fabs become bankable through the cycle (capital intensity).
note: Lower WACC via hyperscaler offtake; DRAM prepayment deals exist, SPV structure is the twist.

title: Generic-drug pathway: open off-patent DRAM process recipe
idea: Adapted from generic pharmaceuticals copying off-patent molecules: assemble a public reference DRAM flow from expired patents (stacked capacitor, recessed-channel array transistor at 2x-nm class), with an open PDK and published process windows that new entrants can run on DUV without licenses.
why: Removes the know-how barrier that keeps entrants out; serves mature segments (auto, industrial, IoT, ~15-20% of bits) and frees leading makers' capacity for advanced parts (capital intensity, supply).
note: Recipes need heavy fab tuning; validating without a line is hard.

title: American Tower model: neutral-host fab-shell REIT for memory startups
idea: Adapted from tower REITs that lease vertical space to several carriers: a REIT owns U.S. cleanroom shells, ultrapure water, gases, power and abatement, and leases bays per square meter to several memory entrants who bring only their tools.
why: Cuts an entrant's capex ~30-40% (shell plus utilities) and taps cheap, patient REIT capital for long-lived infrastructure, multiplying the number of U.S. entrants (capital intensity).
note: Cross-tenant contamination and shared utilities qualification are the doubts.

title: Frozen periphery platform wafer reused for three array generations
idea: Hybrid-bond each new array wafer onto a standardized 28 nm periphery wafer whose bond interface and protocol are frozen for 6+ years, so a new node needs only array masks: MAGNIFY the periphery's lifetime, MINIFY per-node mask and EUV spend.
why: Facts 4 and 7: per-node capex -30-40%; periphery wafers can come from existing U.S. trailing-edge fabs, raising U.S. content.
note: Xtacking/CBA-style split with frozen interface; array scaling may force periphery changes anyway.

title: Container fab: kill the ballroom cleanroom
idea: Minify the cleanroom from a 100,000 m2 ballroom to sealed mini-environments around each tool inside standard shipping containers, linked by sealed-pod conveyors, so the building is an ordinary warehouse.
why: Fab construction capital: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab cost and years of build; target 3-4x faster capacity add.

title: Reticle-stitched mega-DRAM wafer-bonded to logic
idea: MAGNIFY die size by stitching the DRAM array across 4+ reticles into one ~3,000 mm^2 die, bonded wafer-on-wafer to a logic wafer, with no dicing, no package I/O and no TSVs; row/column redundancy absorbs defects.
why: Packaging cost and data movement: removes the PHY and bumps; claims ~0.05 pJ/bit and terabytes per second per die.

title: Magnify 3D tier count 30% and fuse off failed tiers
idea: Fabricate 3D DRAM with ~30% more tiers than the sold capacity, giving each tier its own select line and BIST. Tiers with low capacitor or transistor yield are fused off at test and in the field.
why: Fact 2: 3D becomes economic at ~90% per-tier yield instead of near-perfect yield, so the 26-tier break-even becomes a yield-tolerant target.
note: Spare tiers trade density for yield; needs 3D DRAM fab to prove.

title: Magnify the buyer: a credit-union-style memory cooperative fab
idea: Fifty mid-size OEMs, clouds and automakers co-own a DRAM fab; each share carries a pro-rata wafer allocation at cost plus a reserve fund, governed one-member-one-vote.
why: Removes the boom-bust margin behind the ~4x price spike and guarantees offtake; members pay ~30-50% less over a cycle and small buyers get supply security.
note: Shifts capex to buyers; governance among competitors is the doubt.

title: Magnify the stockpile: a Strategic DRAM Reserve
idea: Government buys known-good DRAM dies and wafers at glut prices, stores them in nitrogen-purged vaults (bare dies are stable for decades), and releases them through packaging partners during shortages.
why: Gives fabs a price floor to invest against and caps spikes like the 4x rise; secures supply for defense and critical industry.
note: Same reserve concept as I-01341.

title: Thirteenth-die hot spare rescues HBM stack yield
idea: Eliminate 'one bad die scraps the stack': build 12-high stacks with a 13th identical spare die and a vertical channel crossbar in the base die; after final stack test, a failing die's channels are steered onto the spare.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: with 97% per-die post-bond survival, stack yield rises from ~69% (0.97^12) to ~94% with one spare, cutting effective cost/bit ~25%.

title: Cross-gated 2T1C: select one cell, not a whole row
idea: Rearrange selection from row-wide to cross-point: in a retired 2x/3x nm DRAM line, give each cell two series access transistors, one on the row wordline and one on a column-select line, so only the cell at the crossing connects. In hold, leakage must cross two off devices in series, and opening a row no longer disturbs its unselected cells.
why: Leakage ~10x lower via stack effect (fact 3), half-select and row-hammer disturbance largely gone (fact 9), 128x page overfetch removed (fact 8); ~1.5-2x density loss is paid in old fabs with spare capacity.

title: Array-only fab: sell bare DRAM arrays to logic foundries
idea: Rearrange the value chain: a U.S. fab makes only array wafers with no periphery, and sells them for bonding to periphery wafers made in an existing logic foundry, like a memory 'fabless in reverse'.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: the array fab needs about half the masks and none of the logic transistor modules, cutting startup capex ~40% and speeding U.S. entry.

title: Sell DRAM as bondable wafers and let customers stack
idea: Reverse the HBM value chain: memory makers sell finished DRAM wafers with a published hybrid-bond pad standard, and foundries, OSATs and accelerator firms do the thinning, stacking and base-die integration themselves, creating many parallel HBM assembly lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: the HBM bottleneck moves from three memory makers' packaging lines to any advanced packager, including U.S. OSATs.

title: Strategic DRAM reserve: government buys gluts, releases in shortages
idea: Reverse the market cycle, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve: a federal agency buys standardized DRAM (tested dies or wafers stored in nitrogen) at price troughs and releases it in shortages. Fabs keep running at full utilization through downturns.
why: Smooths supply, and full utilization lowers fixed cost per bit. It also prevents the downturn capex cuts that cause the next shortage.
note: Same reserve concept as I-01341.

title: Self-aligned dual-workfunction gate tames storage-side GIDL in lateral 3D cells
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: in each lateral 3D access transistor, recess the gate metal laterally from the storage-hole side and refill that ~5 nm edge with a low-workfunction metal, keeping a high-workfunction gate on the bitline side for drive. Field at the storage junction drops and the leakage tail shrinks, with no new mask because the storage hole itself defines the recess.
why: Fact 3: ~10x lower tail leakage -> ~4-8x longer refresh interval, recovering most of the 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth spent on refresh.
note: Port of production dual-workfunction buried-WL GIDL fix to lateral 3D cells, self-aligned via the storage hole.

title: Vaccine-style advance market commitment for new DRAM entrants
idea: A vaccine primes immune memory before the pathogen arrives. Hyperscalers and government sign a binding advance purchase at a guaranteed price floor for the first N exabits from any qualified new U.S. DRAM entrant, priming capacity years before the next shortage.
why: Removes the demand risk that blocks $15B fab financing; could cut entrants' cost of capital by several hundred bp and pull in 1-2 new fabs (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Steel minimill playbook: EUV-free DRAM on used DUV plus stacking
idea: Borrowed from Nucor's electric-arc minimills, which beat integrated mills starting with low-end rebar: build a $2-3B U.S. DRAM minimill on used ArF-immersion scanners at ~18-20 nm half-pitch with SAQP and no EUV, close the density gap by hybrid-bonding several array wafers over one periphery wafer, and sell first into industrial and auto DDR4/LPDDR4 that incumbents are exiting.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: ~5x less capex per wafer start than an EUV fab, with density recovered by stacking; enter low, move up.

title: Liberty-ship DRAM: frozen open design built by many fabs
idea: Borrowed from WWII Liberty ships, one frozen simplified design built in 18 yards by non-specialists: a 10-person federal program office freezes a royalty-free 8 Gb DDR4-class 1T1C design on ~25 nm DUV with documented recipes and test programs, and licenses it with qualification support to any U.S. fab or foundry.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes the ~$500M+ design and IP barrier that keeps foundries out of commodity DRAM and creates surge capacity for critical supply.

title: Vaccine-style advance market commitment for refresh-free 125 C memory
idea: Like the pneumococcal vaccine AMC, governments and automakers pre-commit to buy 100M units at a fixed price from whoever first delivers byte-addressable memory meeting <100 ns access, no refresh at 125 C, and 10-year life.
why: Pulls private capital into a hard technology by guaranteeing demand, targeting the refresh/leakage wall at its worst case (125 C).

title: Wafer-scale DRAM: bond whole undiced array wafer onto logic wafer
idea: Inverts 'the die is the product unit.' Hybrid-bond an undiced 300 mm DRAM array wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer, route around bad reticles in the logic, and ship the bonded pair as a ~2 TB memory slab with no scribe lines, pads, packages or TSVs.
why: Facts 5-6: kills HBM's ~3x area TSV tax and the package, gives ~PB/s internal bandwidth at <1 pJ/bit, and recovers ~10% wafer area lost to scribe and pads.

title: Abundant-elements-only zero-refresh memory prize
idea: Inverts 'industry picks materials, then finds supply': a federal staged prize ($50M/$250M/$1B) for a memory cell with >=10-year retention, >=1e15 endurance, <=50 ns access and DRAM-level cost per bit, built only from a whitelist of US-sourceable elements (no He, W, Hf, Ga, In, PGMs or PFAS) and judged on wafer-level arrays.
why: Pulls many teams toward chokepoint-free, zero-refresh cells while paying only for results; seeds a domestic manufacturing base.

title: Treat DRAM fabs like dams: 30-year public depreciation
idea: Inverts 'fab capital must be repaid in five years'. A public infrastructure authority owns shell, utilities and long-lived tools (furnaces, wet benches, CMP), depreciated over 25-30 years, and leases capacity at cost to memory makers who own only the short-life leading-edge tools.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4); moving ~half of capex to 30-year life cuts wafer cost ~20-25% and speeds U.S. siting.
note: Policy is executable but cost-of-capital, not just book life, sets the real saving.

title: HBM base-die reroute layer swaps in a spare core die
idea: Inverts 'all stacked dies are essential': one redistribution mask on the base die adds a channel crossbar so a 9-high stack can map out any core die that fails after stacking and route its channels to the spare.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) drops toward ~5%; one RDL mask on a mature-node base die.
note: Spare core die costs ~11% capacity; helps die fails, not bond/TSV opens.

title: Milestone prize ladder for printed DRAM foils reaching $1/GB
idea: Fund a federal prize ladder paid on independent testing: about $10M for a 1 Gb printed foil with 64 ms retention, $50M for under-100 ns access with 1e15-cycle endurance, and $200M for packaged modules under $1/GB built on U.S. R2R lines.
why: Targets the physics gates (retention, speed, endurance) rather than picking a technology, pulling many teams into the area-is-cheap regime that bypasses EUV (fact 4) and fab capital; money flows only on measured results.
note: Executable policy; printed DRAM reaching 1e15 endurance and <100 ns is the real doubt.

title: Strategic DRAM Die Reserve stored in dry-nitrogen vaults
idea: Unpowered, unpackaged known-good die hold no state and degrade negligibly in dry N2, so storage cost is essentially shelf space (<$0.01/GB-year). A government reserve buys die during gluts and releases them to domestic packagers during shortages, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
why: Supply resilience: a buffer of ~5% of annual demand flattens price spikes and counter-cycles the market at trivial carrying cost relative to fab capex.
note: Die storage is stable but generation obsolescence erodes reserve value.

title: Buyer cooperative co-owns a fab and takes bits at cost
idea: Electricity co-ops proved users can own capital-heavy plants. OEMs, clouds and automakers buy equity in a memory co-op fab in proportion to their offtake and receive bits at cost-plus, removing the producer margin that balloons during shortages.
why: Cost per bit in shortages: members pay depreciation plus opex instead of 4x contract prices, and guaranteed offtake de-risks the financing.

title: Ballroom-free fab: wafers travel only through sealed nitrogen tubes
idea: Particles kill yield only at the wafer surface, so cleanliness need exist only in the few liters around the wafer, not in a 10,000 m^2 class-1 ballroom. Connect tools with sealed N2-purged wafer conveyor tubes and FOUP-docked load ports so the building needs only gray-space HVAC.
why: Capital and energy: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and >40% of fab energy; removing the ballroom cuts both sharply.

title: National capacitor-module line where startups drop in new storage elements
idea: Box as infrastructure: a government-anchored 300 mm U.S. line runs standard domestic periphery and access-transistor wafers to the capacitor level, then lets startups insert their own storage-element module (AAO, CNT, rutile TiO2, AlBN and others) and finishes BEOL. Teams pay per wafer and keep their IP.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): proving a new storage element costs ~$50M instead of a $15B fab and shortens lab-to-1-Gb proof from ~8 years to ~3.
note: Lowers cost of proving new storage elements; needs government 300 mm line, not a $1M proof.

title: Open DRAM multi-project wafer shuttle service
idea: Box[Owner=national lab + incumbent fab x Fab=quarterly MPW runs of DRAM process x Finance=subsidized per-slot pricing]: like MOSIS for memory, startups and universities buy slots on real DRAM front-end flows to test new cells, capacitors and access devices.
why: Innovation rate: cuts the cost of a DRAM test chip from ~$10M+ to ~$100k, speeding new cell concepts to market.
note: Depends on an incumbent DRAM fab opening its flow; enabler rather than direct gain.

title: Advance market commitment for EUV-free domestic DRAM
idea: Po: the government buys DRAM that does not exist yet. Like vaccine advance market commitments, the U.S. guarantees to buy a set volume (e.g., 1 EB/year for federal and defense fleets) at a fixed price from any domestic producer whose process uses no EUV, paying only on delivery of qualified parts.
why: Removes demand risk for new entrants and hedges the single EUV supplier, paying only for results; attacks capital risk and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Periphery sandwich: mature-node CMOS bonded to arrays on both faces
idea: Worse: give every array a private periphery built in the expensive DRAM process. Flip: fabricate a 28 nm-class CMOS periphery wafer with hybrid-bond pads on both faces (via backside nTSVs), bond one cell-only array wafer above and one below, and time-share each sense amp between the upper and lower bitline through an isolation switch.
why: Periphery moves to cheap depreciated nodes and is amortized over two arrays: periphery area per bit -50% and the array wafer becomes cell-only (fact 7, fact 4 capital).

title: Open tier-stack standard on a shared U.S. pilot line
idea: Worse: keep every company's 3D DRAM base stack secret so each one separately relearns 100-tier deposition, slit etch and staircase. Flip: a U.S. consortium standardizes the base stack (superlattice, slits, staircase, bond interface) as a foundry PDK on a shared pilot line, and members differentiate only on the cell module inserted into it.
why: Splits the $15B+, 3-5 year learning curve (fact 4) across members and builds U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.
note: Executable consortium model; still needs a $100M+ pilot line to matter.

title: Sixteen-high hybrid-bonded SRAM cube in the HBM footprint
idea: Worsen: accept that SRAM is too sparse to matter. Flip: thin 16 mature-node SRAM dies to ~20 um and hybrid-bond them face-to-back at ~1 um pitch with dense through-vias, so a cube in the HBM footprint holds ~1-2 GB of nanosecond, refresh-free memory.
why: Capacity tier without capacitors: ~2 GB at ~0.1 pJ/bit and 5-10x lower latency than HBM, buildable in mature U.S. fabs.
note: Cost per bit stays high; latency tier, not capacity.

title: Alien asks why the basement is empty: eDRAM inside the interposer
idea: An alien sees that the huge interposer under every AI package is passive silicon. A 10-person team designs an active mature-node interposer with deep-trench 1T1C cells, which interposers already carry as decoupling capacitors, and has a foundry build it.
why: ~2000 mm2 of otherwise wasted silicon holds ~1-2 GB of near-logic memory per package, at ~1 pJ/bit (Fact 5), with no EUV.
note: Deep-trench eDRAM in active interposers is plausible; full-size interposer run exceeds $1M.

title: Privateer's letter of marque: advance market commitment for U.S. DRAM
idea: Governments once licensed privateers with guaranteed prize money. Here the U.S. issues an advance market commitment: federal datacenters and DoD will buy the first 2 EB of U.S.-made DRAM that meets a spec, at a guaranteed $/GB floor for 5 years, from any entrant.
why: Demand-side de-risking for U.S. manufacturability: guaranteed offtake makes new entrants bankable without the government picking technology winners.

title: Strategic DRAM wafer reserve stored in nitrogen, diced on demand
idea: Copy the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the 30-year-industrial 'die bank' practice. Government buys finished, probed DRAM wafers in slack quarters, stores them in N2 cabinets where they keep for decades, and releases them to U.S. packagers during price spikes, so surge supply arrives in weeks instead of fab-years.
why: Damps 4x price swings and secures defense surge supply; ~$1-2B buys a months-long national buffer.
note: Same reserve concept as I-01341.

title: Lattice stepper: a single-pattern projection tool built domestically
idea: Because array layers are one repeating motif, build a stripped-down U.S. DUV projection tool with a permanently mounted mask, no reticle exchange and relaxed stitching, exposing only that motif while periphery runs elsewhere.
why: Tool cost ~$10-20M vs $70-200M, and simple enough for a domestic optics base (fused silica, lens grinding, U.S. excimer lasers).
note: Immersion optics, not reticle handling, dominate scanner cost; still needs multipatterning.

title: Pre-built cleanroom shell bank leased to any memory entrant
idea: Time shift of construction: the government builds standardized 300 mm cleanroom shells with power, ultrapure water and gas yards years before anyone needs them, then leases them turnkey to the first memory maker that commits tools.
why: Cuts time to first wafer from ~4 years to ~18 months and removes ~30% of fab capex from the entrant's balance sheet. Directly raises U.S. manufacturability.

title: HMC logic die justified by per-subarray negative-wordline tuning
idea: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube died because bandwidth alone did not pay back the cost of its logic base die. Make the logic die earn its keep through leakage control. It holds per-subarray DACs and canary cells, measures the retention tail continuously, and sets each subarray's negative wordline voltage and refresh rate through hybrid-bond vias.
why: Leakage tails are local, so per-subarray NWL and refresh tuning is claimed to cut refresh energy and GIDL 2-4x versus one chip-wide setting. It also moves control logic off the DRAM die, where periphery takes 49% of the area.

title: Anamartic's wafer-scale memory returns as uncut DRAM wafer blades
idea: Anamartic's 'Catt spiral' wafer-scale memory shipped in 1989 but died on weak 1980s yields and cheap boards. Today's dies carry redundancy, so skip dicing, known-good-die test and packaging: one redistribution layer daisy-chains good dies via a self-configuring spiral bus mapped at wafer test, and whole 300 mm wafers (~2 TB) mount as AI-rack memory blades.
why: Removes dicing, packaging, substrates and per-die final test (~10-20% of DRAM cost) and sidesteps the advanced-packaging capacity bottleneck.

title: Wide I/O reborn on backside-power SoCs: memory bonded to freed frontside
idea: JEDEC Wide I/O died because ~1,200 TSVs had to pierce the hot, expensive SoC die, and phone vendors refused the yield, area and test hit. With backside power delivery (PowerVia/A16-class), the SoC's power and I/O exit through its back, so a thinned DRAM die can be hybrid-bonded face-to-face onto the SoC frontside at 3-9 um pitch with zero TSVs in either die, with refresh rate set from the logic die's thermal sensors.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): face-to-face bonds at ~0.05 pJ/bit vs ~4-5 pJ/bit for LPDDR5X, roughly 50-100x less I/O energy; removes the TSV tax (fact 6) and the package PHY area.
note: Insight: backside power frees SoC frontside so DRAM bonds F2F with zero TSVs; needs leading-edge logic access.

title: US Memories 2.0: binding take-or-pay buyers for a U.S. HBM-stacking plant
idea: The 1989 U.S. Memories consortium (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed in January 1990 because members would not sign purchase obligations once DRAM prices fell. Re-run it for the back end only (TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, base-die attach and test of HBM/CXL modules from known-good DRAM wafers bought globally), with binding 7-year take-or-pay contracts under a price collar and a federal buyer of last resort feeding a strategic memory reserve.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: a stacking/test plant costs ~$2-4B vs $15B+ for a front-end fab and captures the HBM TSV/packaging bottleneck (fact 6); the contracts remove the price-cycle risk that killed the original.

title: US Memories reborn: take-or-pay consortium with escrowed exit penalties
idea: US Memories (1989; IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed before breaking ground because members walked away when DRAM prices fell. Fix exactly that: members sign 10-year take-or-pay offtake contracts for capacity units (wafer starts per month) with a price collar, and post exit penalties equal to their share of unrecovered capex into escrow, so a price dip cannot dissolve the fab.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: pre-selling ~60-70% of output cuts the cost of capital for a $15B+ fab by several points and keeps a U.S. DRAM fab financeable through a downturn.

title: Inmos killed by impatience: statutory 15-year memory charter
idea: Britain's state-backed Inmos (founded 1978) was sold to Thorn EMI in 1984, mid-ramp, when political patience ran out. Fix: a statutory memory charter funded in pre-legislated tranches over 15 years, released on technical milestones (yield, bits shipped) rather than quarterly profit, and run by an independent trust that cannot be sold during the term.
why: Capital intensity and time: DRAM needs 3-5 years to build and ~5 more to learn yield; matching funding to that horizon removes the political cancellation risk that killed earlier national programs.
note: Milestone-tranched statutory trust; execution hinges on legislative will.

title: Repurpose automotive embedded-PCM lines as U.S. weight-memory chiplets
idea: Ge-rich GST embedded PCM, whose crystallization temperature has been raised for 150 C automotive MCUs at 28/18 nm, is sold as stand-alone read-mostly weight chiplets. They are built on underused mature-node lines without EUV and hybrid-bonded under NPUs, and DRAM is reserved for activations and KV.
why: Moves read-mostly bits off scarce DRAM onto mature, U.S.-capable capacity, at far lower capital per bit than a DRAM fab (fact 4).

title: Inline photoluminescence maps each tier's defects before stacking the next
idea: Effect: photoluminescence (band-edge versus defect-band emission). In monolithic 3D DRAM, after each crystalline tier forms, a wafer-scale PL scan maps trap density per subarray region; the map goes into a per-die non-volatile sparing table so defective tier regions are logically spared, and the process tool receives feedback for the next wafer.
why: 10x density: 50 tiers at 99% yield each is only 60% stack yield, which kills cost parity; PL-driven region sparing lifts effective yield above 90%, making a ~50-tier (~10x) stack cost-competitive.

title: Ti: getter-pumped vacuum wafer highway so wafers never see air
idea: Link etch, deposition and anneal tools with a titanium-getter/NEG-pumped vacuum transport spine and sealed vacuum carriers, so native oxide and airborne contamination never form and most cleans disappear; cleanroom air shrinks to tool-scale vacuum.
why: Water: attacks the two biggest users at once, cleans and cleanroom HVAC (humidification and chilled water), toward a 10x fab-level cut; also shrinks cleanroom capex.
note: Cleans also remove etch residues and particles, not just native oxide.

title: Dairy-cooperative fab owned by its biggest memory buyers
idea: Like Land O'Lakes, where farmers co-own the creamery. Hyperscalers, automakers and PC OEMs buy equity units in a DRAM fab, and each unit carries a take-or-pay right to a pro-rata share of output at cost plus a fixed margin. The fab runs a licensed process from a minority technology partner.
why: Financing and supply security: shifts $15B of capex onto the buyers hurt most by 4x price spikes. Members get bits at cost through the cycle.
note: Same buyer co-op fab as I-01806.

title: Shared EUV hub exposes critical layers for many small DRAM fabs
idea: Ideal: EUV is free for small makers. Closest: a central EUV hub exposes only the 5-7 critical layers of wafers shipped in sealed N2 FOUPs from several smaller DRAM fabs that do all DUV, deposition and etch locally, with tolling priced per layer.
why: Fact 4 and capital: $200-380M scanners are pooled at high utilization; a new entrant skips EUV capex, roughly -30% entry capital.

title: Wafer-scale capacitorless memory bonded face-to-face onto compute wafers
idea: Ideal: memory with no package, dicing or interposer. Closest: a full 300 mm wafer of logic-process gain-cell memory is hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer onto a wafer-scale accelerator; defective memory tiles are routed around by the compute wafer's network and test happens once per wafer pair.
why: Facts 5 and 6: removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x area/bit) and interposer/packaging capex; data movement <0.5 pJ/bit; yield loss handled by architecture.
note: Big energy gain but limited to wafer-scale accelerators; gain-cell capacity low.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve of nitrogen-vaulted known-good-die wafers
idea: Ideal: a shortage that never reaches users. Closest achievable: the government buys tested DRAM wafers during gluts, stores them diced on tape in dry-nitrogen vaults (unpowered die keep for decades), and releases them to OSATs for packaging whenever contract prices pass a trigger.
why: Price spikes and pig cycle: a 60-90 day bit buffer could cap 4x spikes, and smoother prices lower the cost of capital for all fabs.

title: $1B 3D-DRAM prize judged on a public test vehicle
idea: Ideal: infinite inventors working for free. Closest achievable: a Longitude-style prize paid for the first 3D DRAM stack hitting 26+ tiers, 64 ms retention and 1e15 cycles on an open test vehicle, with winning IP licensed into a common pool.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): prizes typically draw 10-20x their value in private R&D.

title: Copy-exact fab franchising licensed by an incumbent
idea: Ideal: a new fab appears as easily as installing software. Closest achievable: an incumbent franchises a frozen, copy-exact DRAM process plus fab design to sovereign or partner builders for royalties and equity, McDonald's style, with incumbent teams running the ramp.
why: Time to capacity and talent: ramp falls from 3-5 years to ~2, and the number of builders multiplies.

title: Kit fab: shipyard-built cleanroom modules on pre-permitted pads
idea: Ideal: a fab built in a week. Closest achievable: standardized cleanroom and sub-fab modules with pre-integrated AMHS, utilities and exhaust are built in shipyards, barged in and bolted onto pre-permitted pads.
why: Capital and time: construction drops from ~3 years to ~14 months, with 20-30% lower construction capex.

title: HBM-pin-compatible core dies built in U.S. logic fabs with deep-trench cells
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): drop into existing HBM3E stacks and controllers. Fabricate core dies in U.S. logic foundries on their deep-trench eDRAM process (bulk-Si trench caps of ~30-40 fF), stack them on a standard HBM base die, and sell them as lower-density but available HBM for inference tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4; U.S. makes 1-2% of DRAM): reuses depreciated logic capacity with no new DRAM fab; ~1/3 DRAM density but viable at 4x prices.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells trigger refresh on physical decay
idea: Substitute timer-driven refresh with physical sensing: each mat carries replica canary cells with ~30% smaller Cs and a longer-leakage access device, read by a dedicated sense amp. A mat refreshes only when its canary flips, so the interval follows the real temperature and leakage.
why: Refresh (fact 3): at typical datacenter temperatures retention is far above the 32/64 ms worst case, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss drop 50-80%.

title: Per-tier pulsed plates replace the static half-VDD common plate
idea: Substitute the global static plate at VARY/2 with tier-segmented plates driven by periphery: during restore the plate is pulsed -0.5 V so a 0.6 V bitline swing stores today's 1.1 V-equivalent charge, and during read it is bumped to boost signal into the SA; in 3D each tier's plate is naturally a separate film.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): VARY ~1.0 -> 0.6 V cuts array CV² energy ~2.5x and lowers wordline boost (~3 -> 2.4 V).

title: Fluorine-free-release nanoimprint replaces EUV on periodic array layers
idea: Substitute EUV exposures of the strictly periodic array layers (active, buried WL, BL, landing pad) with jet-and-flash nanoimprint, replacing the fluorinated anti-stick template silane (FDTS/FOTS) with a self-releasing siloxane-methacrylate resist plus a renewable water-soluble PVA release film and radical (PAG-free) UV cure.
why: EUV is one supplier and DRAM needs 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4): NIL is ~1/3-1/5 the capex per layer, buildable in the U.S., and the PFAS-free release removes NIL's own fluorine dependence.
note: NIL for DRAM already pursued; PFAS-free release chemistry is the twist.

title: Bonded diamond spreader tiers replace silicon spacers under stacked DRAM
idea: Substitute passive silicon spacers in memory-on-logic stacks with bonded polycrystalline CVD diamond tiers (CH4/H2 growth, mechanical thinning, O2-plasma activation, laser-drilled Cu vias) between GPU and stacked DRAM, spreading heat ~10x better than Si so DRAM can sit directly on compute.
why: Data movement (fact 5): DRAM-on-logic cuts ~3-4 pJ/bit (HBM) to <0.5; diamond keeps DRAM <85 C so refresh rate does not double (fact 3); no fluorinated coolants.

title: Substitute TSVs and microbumps with face-to-face capacitive proximity coupling
idea: Stack DRAM dies face-to-face or in a staircase so top-metal plates on neighboring dies form coupling capacitors across a ~1 um dielectric gap; data crosses as small-swing capacitive pulses with no through-silicon vias or bumps, and dies self-register with etched pits and balls.
why: Constraint: ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit versus HBM 3-4 pJ/bit (>=30x); facet: removes TSV etch/fill/reveal and microbump steps with their 20-30% yield hit and 3x area tax (fact 6).

title: Swap HBM-resident KV for attention-computing commodity DDR PIM DIMMs
idea: Substitute expensive HBM bits with cheap DDR bits. The KV cache moves to DDR5 DIMMs whose buffer chips hold bank-group dot-product and softmax units; the GPU sends only the query vector and gets back the attention output, so KV bytes never cross the bus.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6). Moving KV, often more than half of HBM demand, to DDR PIM halves HBM per accelerator, needs ~3x less wafer per KV bit, and cuts data-movement pJ (fact 5).
note: AttAcc/NeuPIMs/AxDIMM prior art.

title: Open chiplet memory socket standard to admit new DRAM makers
idea: Substitute vendor-dominated JEDEC HBM interfaces with a CHIPS-funded, royalty-free chiplet memory protocol on UCIe plus open reference base-die IP, so any new U.S. memory die maker can attach to any accelerator without building a full HBM PHY.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes $100M+ of PHY/interface development from a new entrant's path, diversifying supply.

title: Substitute ownership with leased bits that cascade down tiers
idea: Swap buying DRAM for Memory-as-a-Service: the memory maker keeps title to every module, leases it to cloud first, then recalls and re-leases it to enterprise, edge and consumer tiers, with RFID/serial telemetry tracking wear and retention.
why: Each bit serves 2-3 lifetimes instead of 1, multiplying effective supply per wafer by ~1.5-2x and turning capex into an annuity that smooths the price cycle.

title: Column-gated local wordline drivers activate one-eighth rows
idea: AND each sub-wordline driver enable with a column-segment signal decoded from the column address, so an ACT opens only the ~1 kb segment holding the requested data; the gate fits in existing SWD strips on old processes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~5-8x lower activation energy per random access, and ~8x less hammer coupling per activate (fact 9).

title: Capacitor-boosted 2T1C gain cell for thin lateral 3D tiers
idea: In each lateral 3D tier, combine a 0.5-1 fF short horizontal capacitor with a separate read transistor whose gate is the storage node; the capacitor only has to hold that gate's charge between refreshes, not drive a bitline.
why: Charge wall and 3D blocker (facts 1-2): lateral capacitors 5-10x shorter, tiers ~40 nm thick so 100+ tiers are plausible; read is nondestructive (fact 8).
note: Gain cells for 3D tiers widely pursued (imec IGZO); shorter capacitors ease tier pitch.

title: Photonic HBM base die from a US silicon-photonics foundry
idea: Merge the HBM logic base die with optical transceivers built at a US photonics fab (e.g., GF Fotonix, Malta NY): DRAM cores stack on a base die that speaks WDM over fiber, so the stack needs no 2.5D interposer beside the GPU and can sit centimeters to meters away.
why: Removes dependence on offshore CoWoS interposers and frees placement for more stacks per accelerator; ~1-2 pJ/bit links versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM (fact 5).

title: Liquid-nitrogen-cooled 3D DRAM with 1 fF lateral capacitors
idea: Fuse rack-scale LN2 cooling (US air-separation plants, no imports) with a 3D lateral array designed for 77 K: leakage falls by >10^6, so 1 fF short horizontal capacitors still retain for seconds, tiers become ~5x thinner and refresh nearly disappears.
why: Facts 1-3: capacitor wall sidestepped, refresh (46 fJ/bit) near zero, and wire resistance ~5x lower at 77 K (fact 5); cryo plant cost amortized per rack.

title: Polysilicon plant SiCl4 waste becomes synthetic silica crucible liners
idea: Combine the Siemens polysilicon byproduct stream with crucible making: flame-hydrolyze waste SiCl4 into ultra-pure synthetic silica soot, fuse it as the melt-contacting 3-5 mm inner layer, and build the outer bubble-composite body from ordinary quartz sand.
why: Breaks the Spruce Pine >80% high-purity-quartz chokepoint by turning a waste (~10+ kg SiCl4 per kg poly) into the scarce input, sited at U.S. polysilicon plants.

title: Log-structured SLC NAND tier with DRAM as write absorber
idea: Combine log-structured file-system writes with a CXL memory device built from SLC 3D NAND (DUV-made) plus a small DRAM buffer: evicted dirty pages are appended sequentially into erase blocks, DRAM holds the hot set and log head, and a 28 nm controller cleans segments during idle time so random writes never hit NAND directly.
why: NAND is roughly 1/10 the cost per bit and needs no EUV; moving the cold 60-70% of memory onto it cuts DRAM per server 2-3x while respecting endurance.

title: DRAM and NAND dies in one stack with self-tiering base die
idea: Combine a few older-node DRAM dies and several NAND dies in one bonded/TSV stack over a 28 nm logic base die that tracks page heat and migrates 4 KB pages between DRAM and NAND internally at TSV bandwidth, presenting one flat byte-addressable space.
why: Gives ~4-8x capacity per package from mostly DUV NAND bits; in-package migration avoids host-side tiering overhead and channel traffic.

title: Circular DRAM leasing with manufacturer take-back and re-binning
idea: Fuse equipment-leasing finance with memory. Makers lease DIMMs and HBM cards by GB-month and keep ownership. At end of lease they recover the modules, re-bin them by measured retention and speed, and redeploy them down a tiered ladder: hyperscale, then enterprise, then edge.
why: Doubles or triples each bit's productive life and gives makers annuity revenue that smooths cycles. Effective supply rises with no wafer starts.

title: Cold-chain DRAM: 77 K operation shrinks storage node height
idea: Borrow LNG/cryogenic logistics: run DRAM in liquid-nitrogen immersion, where leakage falls ~1e6x, then redesign the storage node to ~0.5 fF (a short AR ~8 cup) because retention becomes minutes.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 4: deletes the HAR capacitor module and refresh; cryocooling is amortized at datacenter scale.
note: Cryogenic DRAM already studied; 77 K cooling overhead of ~10 W per W offsets much of the gain.

title: ISO shipping-container standard for interchangeable memory tiers
idea: Like the ISO container standard, publish an open 'memory brick' spec: fixed 1 um hybrid-bond grid, power/signal pin map, test hooks and thickness, so any vendor's array tier or logic base stacks with any other.
why: Breaks HBM's vertically integrated stack (fact 6), lets U.S. fabs make bases or tiers separately, and pools capacity across many fabs; stack NRE down ~50%.

title: Optical-fiber soot deposition makes synthetic-silica crucible inner walls
idea: Adapted from outside vapor deposition (OVD) used to make optical-fiber preforms. SiCl4-derived silica soot is deposited on a rotating crucible-shaped mandrel and sintered into a 3-5 mm fully synthetic inner layer. That layer is backed with ordinary lower-grade fused silica, so no Spruce Pine HPQ ever touches the melt.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint. SiCl4 is a cheap polysilicon by-product, and a synthetic liner lowers metal contamination and may lengthen crucible life.

title: Solar project finance: offtake-backed DRAM fab special-purpose vehicles
idea: Finance each fab like a utility-scale solar farm: a special-purpose vehicle owns the fab, hyperscalers sign 10-year take-or-pay bit offtake contracts at indexed prices (like PPAs), and the transferable advanced-manufacturing investment credit is sold to tax-equity buyers, so the fab borrows non-recourse debt at infrastructure rates.
why: Cost of capital: WACC from ~10-12% to ~6-7% cuts the capital charge in wafer cost by ~25-30%; offtake removes the boom-bust risk that stops fabs from being built.

title: Repurpose LCD glass-panel lines to make giant memory interposers
idea: Adapted from display makers' Gen-8 (2.2 x 2.5 m) glass TFT lines with ~1.5 um lithography: pattern copper RDL and through-glass vias at panel scale. The panels become interposers that hold dozens of memory stacks around accelerators.
why: Silicon interposers are reticle-limited and capacity-bound; panels amortize over ~70x a 300 mm wafer's area, cutting interposer cost per area ~5-10x and freeing CoWoS capacity.
note: Panel-level glass packaging already pursued widely.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM with a tenfold smaller capacitor
idea: MINIFY temperature to 77 K: subthreshold and junction leakage drop >1e6, so retention reaches minutes even with Cs = 0.5 fF; capacitor AR falls from ~70:1 to ~7:1 and refresh nearly disappears, deployed as LN2-immersed rack sleds.
why: Hits facts 1 and 3 together: fewer high-AR steps (~20-30% cheaper cell process), refresh energy ~0; cooling overhead amortized at datacenter scale.
note: Cryo DRAM widely studied; smaller cap and no refresh real, but cooling overhead eats system gain.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K for pooled rack memory
idea: Put CXL-attached memory pools in a liquid-nitrogen dewar shelf: at 77 K subthreshold and generation leakage fall ~10^6x so retention reaches hours and refresh essentially stops, while lower wire resistance lets VARY drop to ~0.6 V. One cryocooler serves terabytes shared by a whole rack.
why: Removes refresh's 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth tax; CV^2 energy ~2.5x lower; cryo overhead amortized across the pool.

title: Magnify leakage on purpose: canary cells set refresh pace
idea: Seed every subarray with replica canary cells built 5-10x leakier (shorter channel, deliberate defect implant) that are sensed cheaply on a slow timer; a subarray is refreshed only when its canaries decay. Refresh then tracks real temperature, voltage and aging instead of a worst-case 85 C spec.
why: Real leakage is usually 10-50x below worst case, so refresh energy and bandwidth drop ~10x on average.
note: Replica/monitor cells for refresh tracking appear in patents; canary must bound VRT tail cells, not just median.

title: Minify the page: 512-bit sense slices with local wordline drivers
idea: MINIFY the activated page from 8 Kb to 512 bits: split each master wordline with local wordline drivers every 512 cells and gate sense-amp enable per slice using column address bits sent with ACT, so only the needed slice is charge-shared, sensed and restored.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): activation energy per useful bit drops ~10x and fewer bitlines swing near victims; cost ~3-4% area for extra local drivers.

title: Half-size canary capacitors trigger subarray refresh on demand
idea: MINIFY a few sentinel cells on purpose: each 512-row subarray carries 8 canary cells with half-size capacitors and deliberately leaky access devices; a low-power comparator polls them and refreshes the subarray only when a canary decays below threshold.
why: Fact 3: refresh tracks actual retention instead of the 13 fA worst-case tail, cutting refresh operations 4-10x at typical temperatures.

title: Minify the page to 64 bits with AND-gated wordline slices
idea: Split each wordline into 64-bit slices, each with a local AND gate that combines the row decode with a column-group select, so a random 64B access fires only 512 cells instead of 8 KB of cells.
why: 128x overfetch and the 5.9 pJ per useful bit of a random read: activation energy per useful bit could fall by 10-16x, and row-hammer disturbance is limited to the active slice.

title: Laser-free DRAM via retro-modulated light from host
idea: MINIFY the photonics on the memory side to passive reflective microring modulators: the host's comb laser sends continuous-wave light to the DRAM base die, which modulates and reflects it back on the same fiber.
why: Data movement and thermals: no laser or SerDes PLL on the DRAM side; claims <1 pJ/bit off-package links and a cooler, cheaper memory module.
note: External laser and reflective modulators are known; DRAM-process photonics integration is the gap.

title: Million-wire DC memory with no SerDes or PLL
idea: MAGNIFY wire count to ~10^6/cm^2 with 1 um hybrid bonds and MINIFY each wire's rate to ~10 Mb/s: unterminated, unclocked CMOS levels with no SerDes, DLL or training, yet 10 Tb/s per cm^2.
why: Data-movement energy and PHY area: claims ~0.01-0.02 pJ/bit and deletes most of the DRAM I/O periphery.
note: Interface energy drops greatly but array energy remains; wide-slow bonding widely pursued.

title: Coarse pitch with 224G SerDes on organic substrate
idea: MAGNIFY bump pitch back to ~150-400 um and MAGNIFY lane speed to 224 Gb/s PAM4, attaching commodity LPDDR/DDR chiplets to accelerators on plain organic substrate with no silicon interposer.
why: Capital intensity and CoWoS bottleneck: memory bandwidth from abundant substrate capacity; claims ~5x cheaper packaging per GB at ~3-5 pJ/bit.
note: Eliyan-style substrate PHYs already pursue this; pJ/bit higher than HBM interposer links.

title: Eliminate room temperature: 77 K liquid-nitrogen DRAM tier
idea: Run a DRAM pool immersed in liquid nitrogen, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall >1e6x so refresh disappears, and redesign access transistors with low Vt so the wordline drops from 3 V to ~1 V. Pair with cryo-CMOS controllers; LN2 is cheap and helium-free.
why: Refresh eliminated, wordline energy ~9x lower, relaxed Vt allows smaller devices; avoids the helium chokepoint. Cooling overhead (~10 W per W removed) limits it to large pools.

title: Eliminate refresh logic and wordline segmentation in a 77 K memory tier
idea: Run a liquid-nitrogen-cooled DRAM tier at 77 K, where access-transistor leakage collapses (retention of hours) and copper resistivity drops ~7x. That permits deleting the refresh controller, the sub-wordline driver stripes (4x longer wordlines) and half of the SA stripes (lower noise and mismatch).
why: Facts 3 and 7: removes refresh power and bandwidth loss, and the periphery area falls ~10-15%; LN2 cooling energy is partly offset by lower I/O resistance.

title: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: sealed-pod mini-environment fab
idea: Wafers never meet room air: every tool docks sealed nitrogen pods and the building is held only at ISO 8, so HVAC is sized for people, not particles, enabling small modular U.S. memory fabs.
why: Cleanroom HVAC is ~30-50% of fab electricity and a large share of shell capital; cuts both and shortens build time.

title: Eliminate the 8-kilobit page: activate only 512-bit wordline slivers
idea: Split each master wordline into 16 locally gated segments with per-segment sub-wordline drivers so an activate charges only the 512 bitlines that hold the requested burst.
why: Attacks the 128x overfetch (fact 8): ~5.9 pJ per useful bit falls to ~0.4 pJ, >10x per random access, and fewer aggressor rows for row hammer.
note: Partial/segmented row activation is well published (SBA, half-DRAM); sub-WL driver area is the cost.

title: Eliminate the data highway: dot-product units in each mat's sense-amp stripe
idea: Put an 8-bit column-serial MAC tree in every mat's sense-amp stripe so weights stay in the row buffer, activations are broadcast in, and only partial sums leave the bank.
why: Data never crosses the die or the I/O: ~4 pJ/bit effective drops to ~0.3 pJ/bit, and fewer HBM stacks (TSV copper, 3x area) are needed for the same throughput.

title: Eliminate ESD and I/O drivers: protection-free hybrid-bonded memory pins
idea: When DRAM is wafer-bonded to logic and never handled as a bare die, delete the ESD diodes, thick-oxide drivers and termination on every data pin and drive ~50 fF bond pads at 0.4 V from core devices.
why: ESD and pad capacitance dominate I/O energy; pin energy falls from pJ to ~10-50 fJ per bit (>10x), and I/O periphery area (fact 7) shrinks.
note: Die-to-die interfaces already relax ESD; gain real but confined to bonded stacks.

title: Eliminate silicon interposers: glass-core panel interposers put DRAM 2 mm away
idea: Mount memory dies on glass-core panel interposers (abundant borosilicate, 2 um lines, through-glass vias) within ~2 mm of the processor, driving unterminated low-swing links in place of CoWoS silicon interposers and ABF substrates.
why: Link energy falls to ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 for DDR5 (>10x), escaping the silicon-interposer and ABF chokepoints.
note: Glass substrates widely pursued (Intel and others); link energy gains mostly vs DDR, not HBM.

title: Eliminate hydrogen: hydrogen-free deposition plus titanium getters for oxide channels
idea: Hydrogen is a shallow donor in oxide semiconductors and the main source of their off-current tail and drift. Deposit the channel, gate dielectric and passivation below 350 C using hydrogen-free PVD/ALD (O3 or plasma O2, non-hydride precursors), and embed Ti/TiN getter islands that trap any residual H.
why: Tightens the leakage tail and drift of BEOL access devices, raising worst-case retention ~10x and shrinking ECC and refresh margins; no high-temperature anneal needed.
note: H control in IGZO actively pursued.

title: Column-first activation: CAS before RAS opens one row segment
idea: Reverse the RAS-then-CAS order: the column address arrives first and enables only the sub-wordline drivers and local SAs of the 1/16 row segment containing it, so ~512 bits are activated, sensed and restored instead of 8 Kb.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch): activation energy per useful bit ~5.9 pJ -> ~0.6 pJ; unopened segments also escape row-hammer stress. Costs ~3% area for segment-enable gating.

title: Sell tiers, not dies: overbuild tiers, fuse bad ones out
idea: Build early 3D DRAM with deliberately overprovisioned tiers (e.g. 40 built, 32 sold), test each tier through its own staircase contact, and map defective tiers out with tier-level fuses. This reverses the yield model from 'one defect kills the die' to 'a defect costs one tier'.
why: 3D break-even (fact 2): lifting die yield from ~40% to >90% for immature processes at 25% extra tier cost cuts cost per good bit ~45%, pulling 3D in years earlier.

title: One perfect donor, many cheap handles: layer-transfer DRAM wafers
idea: Reverse the substrate role: hydrogen-implant and cleave only the top 1-2 um of a prime CZ wafer onto low-grade polycrystalline or solar-grade handle wafers with a buried oxide barrier, then re-polish and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts prime-grade crystal (and therefore HPQ crucibles, polysilicon and furnace energy) per DRAM wafer by ~10x; the handle can come from abundant metallurgical-grade sources.

title: Inside-out fab: the cleanroom is a tube, not a ballroom
idea: Reverse which volume is clean: wafers never leave sealed N2/vacuum tube transport and docked tools, while people and the building air stay at ordinary grade.
why: Cleanroom HVAC/HEPA is a large share of fab energy and capital; shrinking the clean volume ~100x could cut fab facility energy ~30-40% and building capex.
note: Extends FOUP and Minimal Fab logic; tool maintenance openings are the practical doubt.

title: Content-addressed physical memory: the hash picks the address
idea: Flip address->content into content->address: the controller hashes each 64 B line and stores it in a slot chosen by the hash, with a reference count; page tables map virtual lines to content IDs, so identical lines (zeros, shared libraries, the same weights across tenants) physically exist once.
why: Line-granular dedup with no software scanning; multi-tenant cloud and VM hosts typically gain 1.3-2x effective capacity.

title: Wire-rich, clock-poor: 100k-wire interface at 200 MHz
idea: Push narrow-fast to the opposite extreme, wide-slow: hybrid-bond 100,000+ data pads between memory and logic at 3 um pitch, each a plain full-swing CMOS wire at 0.4 V and ~200 MHz with no SerDes, DLL, termination or equalisation.
why: Fact 5: ~0.02-0.05 pJ/bit and 20+ Tb/s per stack, with PHY area near zero (fact 7).

title: DRAM futures exchange to break the boom-bust capex cycle
idea: Reverse when risk is taken: a cleared futures market trades a standard contract (e.g., 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent delivered per quarter). Fabs sell output 2-3 years forward to finance capex, and buyers hedge price spikes.
why: Capital intensity: forward-sold output lowers financing risk and keeps capex steady through downturns, damping 4x price swings like the current one.

title: Point-of-use water: tool-level micro-UPW loops replace central plant
idea: Reverse centralization: each wet tool gets a compact closed-loop polishing skid (UV, ion exchange, ultrafiltration). The skid recaptures and repolishes the tool's rinse water before it mixes with other drains.
why: Unmixed rinse water is easy to repurify, so tool-level loops reach ~95% recovery. Fab intake falls ~10-20x and the central UPW plant shrinks.
note: POU reclaim exists; 10-20x intake cut is optimistic.

title: Run memory at 150-200 K and redesign the access device for it
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: change temperature instead of geometry. Cooling DRAM to ~150-200 K on a shared refrigerant loop cuts thermal leakage by many orders so retention reaches minutes; then exploit it by lowering the access-transistor Vt and shortening its channel for a smaller, faster cell at lower wordline voltage.
why: Refresh practically disappears (Fact 3) and lower Vt enables lower VPP (Fact 10): claim >50% memory energy reduction net of cooling at rack scale.

title: Other way round: column-first activation fires only requested wordline segments
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of row-first (open 8 KB, then pick 64 B), the column address arrives first and is AND-ed with the main wordline at each sub-wordline driver, so only the 1-2 segments and local sense-amp groups under that column fire.
why: Fact 8: overfetch drops from 128x to ~2-4x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.3-0.6 pJ per useful bit; fewer opened cells also reduces row-hammer stress per access.
note: Close to selective bitline activation (SBA, ISCA 2010).

title: Clamped-bitline charge-transfer sensing makes bitline capacitance irrelevant
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: hold each long bitline at a constant potential with a local cascode transistor so the bitline never swings; the cell's charge flows through the cascode into a ~0.5 fF sense node. Signal then scales with Qcell/Csense rather than Qcell/Cbitline.
why: Fact 1 and 7: ~4x more cells per sense amp (less periphery) or ~half the cell capacitance at equal margin; bitline CV2 energy ~5x lower.
note: Bitline-clamped charge-transfer presensing is 1990s DRAM art.

title: Wordline breakers resize the activated row to each request
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: insert a tiny switch transistor every 64 columns along each local wordline (or at each mat of a 3D wordline plane). Column address bits decide how many segments connect, so a 64 B random request opens ~512 bits instead of an 8 KB page while streaming requests still open the full row.
why: Fact 8: activation energy per useful bit falls from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.5-1 pJ for random access (5-10x), and fewer cells are disturbed (helps row hammer).
note: Fine-grained activation is known art (Half-DRAM, partial row activation).

title: Excessive action: 65,536-bit ultra-wide, ultra-slow hybrid-bonded bus
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: make the bus 32x wider than HBM3 using 3 um hybrid-bond pitch, but run each pin at only 200-400 Mb/s with unterminated 0.4 V inverter drivers and no SerDes, DLL or training.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit IO at HBM3E-class bandwidth, and the PHY shrinks because its circuits are trivial.
note: Wide-slow hybrid-bonded buses are the mainstream custom HBM/SoIC direction.

title: Asymmetry: read-mostly weight tier on legacy NAND with wide parallel reads
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: model weights are written once and read billions of times, so store them in a tier built on 64-layer-era NAND lines. A 28 nm controller reads thousands of planes in parallel, streaming each layer ahead into a small DRAM staging buffer to hide ~30 us read latency, while writes stay slow and rare. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less DRAM: moving weights out of HBM/DRAM frees 30-70% of memory for KV cache, at NAND cost per bit (~1/10 of DRAM) from depreciated lines.
note: Essentially high-bandwidth flash, already in development.

title: Nesting: legacy DRAM dies embedded inside the organic substrate under the GPU
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: use existing embedded-component substrate lines (already used for power modules and phone substrates) to bury thinned LPDDR/DDR4 dies inside the organic package core directly beneath the accelerator. The dies connect upward through ~100 um laser vias. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement (fact 5) and capacity: adds 16-64 GB per package without shoreline or an interposer, at ~1-2 pJ/bit versus ~10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 DIMMs.

title: Wood-frog freeze-tolerant memory pools at 77 K
idea: Wood frogs survive freezing with metabolism halted; run disaggregated CXL memory pools immersed in liquid nitrogen where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse, switch refresh off, and use access FETs re-targeted to lower Vt using the ~15-20 mV/dec cryogenic slope.
why: Retention grows from 64 ms to hours, removing refresh energy and bandwidth entirely, and VPP can drop ~30-40%; cooler overhead is amortized at rack scale for AI memory.

title: Lichen symbiosis: convert display-glass TFT lines into memory interposer fabs
idea: A lichen joins a fungus and an alga that pool their strengths. Glass makers team with idle Gen-6 to Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED TFT lines, which already pattern oxide and metal on huge glass sheets, to make glass-panel interposers and IGZO routing layers for memory packages, adding only laser via drilling and copper plating.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-capacity: reuses depreciated display tooling at panel scale (~10x wafer area per tool); a U.S. variant pairs domestic glass producers with new panel lines for packaging capacity in under 2 years.

title: Pantry kitchen: per-mat reduction engines in a bonded logic tier
idea: Cook where the food is stored: a logic tier bonded beneath each 3D DRAM mat carries one bit-serial adder/comparator per 64 sense amps, so dot-products, top-k and sums over a row finish in place and only the reduced result, 1/64 of the bits, leaves the mat.
why: Data movement and overfetch (facts 5, 8): bits moved per useful result drop ~64x; claims 10-30x lower energy per AI access such as attention scoring.
note: Near-bank PIM (HBM-PIM, AiM, UPMEM) is crowded; bonded logic tier is an incremental twist.

title: Vinyl pressing: frozen model weights stamped into via-programmed ROM
idea: Like pressing millions of records from one master, burn a released model's weights into via- or metal-programmed ROM chiplets (mature node, one custom mask, no EUV) bonded beside the accelerator; weights are inherently non-volatile and DRAM holds only KV and small LoRA patches.
why: ROM needs no capacitor or refresh and is several times denser than DRAM at mature nodes; removes weights from DRAM entirely and is U.S.-manufacturable on existing fabs.
note: Hardwired-model chips already pursued; mature-node ROM is not denser than DRAM.

title: ETA-10 liquid-nitrogen memory tier using U.S. air separation
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 ETA-10 supercomputer, which ran CMOS boards immersed in liquid nitrogen: put DRAM and HBM modules in LN2 baths made on site by U.S. air-separation units. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by >1e6, so refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms to minutes, and lower Vt allows lower wordline voltage.
why: Nearly eliminates refresh (fact 3), and lower voltages cut CV2 (fact 10); nitrogen comes from air, so the cooling needs no helium and has no Qatar exposure.

title: Williams-tube margin raster: scrub weak charges, stretch refresh 16x
idea: Williams tubes kept their spots alive by continuous raster regeneration; revive it as a base-die scrub engine that sweeps 3D tiers with a three-level sense (strong-1, weak-1, 0), rewrites only weak cells, and lets the refresh interval stretch until ~1% of cells have leaked, which the code then corrects.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~10x (64 ms toward ~1 s) by tolerating the leakage tail instead of designing for it.
note: Similar to ECC-based refresh relaxation; three-level sensing in SAs is the new piece.

title: Sun proximity-communication revival: capacitive face-to-face HBM with no bumps
idea: Revive Sun Microsystems' abandoned proximity communication: memory and logic dies overlap face-to-face with 10-20 um pads coupled capacitively across a 1-3 um plain SiO2 gap, clamped mechanically, with electronic pad steering cancelling misalignment.
why: Constraint: no underfill, fluoropolymer adhesive, plating or fluorinated etch; dies stay reworkable so known-good stacks replace bad ones (fact 6 yield), at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit and 10k+ channels/mm^2.

title: Word-Organized Core Revival: 64-Byte Rows Kill DRAM Overfetch
idea: Revive the 1950s linear-select word-organized core memory, where one drive line touched exactly one word: re-architect DRAM mats with segmented local wordlines gated by column select so an activation charges only the 512 cells of one cache line instead of 65,536.
why: Overfetch: activation energy scales with cells opened; 128x fewer cells gives ~10x lower energy per access after periphery, on mature lines with one extra metal layer and no new litho.
note: Known art: selective bitline activation, Half-DRAM, SALP.

title: IBM Thermal Conduction Module Revival: Planar Ceramic DRAM-Compute Modules
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s Thermal Conduction Module, which packed 100+ bare chips on a 33-layer ceramic substrate: place standard non-TSV DRAM dies millimeters from the accelerator on a multilayer glass-ceramic substrate with short, unterminated, wide buses, made by ceramic-package suppliers.
why: Energy per access: unterminated mm-length links at 0.2-0.5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ for DDR5 (>=10x) without HBM's 3x area-per-bit TSV tax; opens a U.S. ceramic-substrate supply route.

title: Liquid-nitrogen 77 K DRAM pods with planar capacitors
idea: Invert 'memory runs at room temperature' -> run DRAM at 77 K in liquid-nitrogen pods (nitrogen is abundant, unlike helium). Junction, GIDL and subthreshold leakage fall by >1e6, so a planar 0.3 fF capacitor retains for seconds, and steeper subthreshold slope allows ~0.6 V array and wordline swings.
why: Removes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3) and cuts CV^2 ~3x (fact 10); the ~10x cooling overhead at 77 K must be repaid by density and system energy gains.
note: Cryo DRAM studied by IBM and Rambus; cooling overhead offsets gains.

title: Persistent-current flux bits cooled by cryocoolers, not helium
idea: Invert 'bits must live in charge or polarization of matter' -> store them as a quantized persistent current. NbN or MgB2 nanowire loops hold one flux quantum clockwise or counter-clockwise with zero dissipation, written by kinetic-inductance switching and read by a nanowire cryotron, cooled by closed-cycle cryocoolers instead of liquid helium.
why: Zero static power, unlimited endurance and ~10 aJ switching (fact 10), fitting cryogenic AI accelerators; avoids the Qatar helium chokepoint; density and ~400 W/W 4 K overhead (MgB2 at 20 K cuts it ~10x) are the risks.

title: Canary cells: deliberately weak cells decide when to refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh is scheduled for the worst cell at the worst temperature': each mat carries a few canary cells built with a 2-3x wider access device (predictably leakier than any real cell) and a continuous-time comparator; a mat is refreshed only when its canary crosses threshold, tracking local temperature, voltage and aging.
why: Most mats retain >=10x longer than spec (fact 3); local triggering cuts average refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~4-8x without per-row profiling tables.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM: shrink capacitors 10x since leakage vanishes
idea: Inverts 'DRAM runs at room temperature.' Operate memory slabs at 77 K in LN2 made from air on site (no helium), where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse, so capacitors can be ~10x smaller (AR ~7:1) and refresh essentially stops.
why: Facts 1 and 3 plus the helium chokepoint: refresh power ~0 and the capacitor wall removed; cryocooler power of ~10x the heat removed is the honest cost.
note: Cryo-DRAM is well studied; cooling overhead offsets refresh and capacitor gains outside special systems.

title: Thread migration to the memory stack instead of data fetch
idea: Invert 'data moves to the compute': when a warp's next N accesses hit one HBM stack, the GPU ships the warp's register context (~2-8 KB) to a small SIMT island on that stack's base die and runs it there, migrating back when locality ends.
why: Moves kilobytes of state instead of megabytes of operands for pointer-chasing, graph and sparse-embedding kernels; 5-20x less off-stack traffic on those kernels, attacking the 20-25% data-movement share of accelerator power.
note: TOM (2016) and execution-migration work cover GPU-to-stack offload.

title: Selector-only chalcogenide: threshold-voltage polarity stores the bit
idea: A single RT-sputtered GeAsSe ovonic threshold switch is both selector and memory. A write pulse of one polarity shifts its threshold voltage by ~1 V through field-driven defect and ion redistribution without crystallizing, and the read uses the opposite polarity.
why: Removes the separate storage layer, giving a one-layer 4F2 cross-point stackable at <=350 C, with no melt (energy, endurance beyond PCM) and no capacitor (fact 1).
note: SOM already pursued by imec/SK hynix; endurance below DRAM class.
