title: License a BEOL memory tier into existing U.S. logic interconnect lines
idea: Package a <=400 C storage element as a foundry PDK option: 2-4 memory tiers inserted between upper metal layers on logic wafers already running in Arizona, Oregon and New York, built with the existing ALD/PVD/etch tools. The foundry earns revenue per wafer on bits added above the logic die.
why: Turns idle BEOL capacity into memory supply without a $15B DRAM fab (capital), puts memory on-die to cut data movement (fact 5), and raises U.S. manufacturability.
note: Embedded BEOL memory options (eMRAM, IGZO) already pursued; storage element unspecified.

title: Charge-transfer pre-sensing lets cells lose 80 percent of charge
idea: Today the cell's ~30,000 electrons are diluted onto a ~50 fF bitline to give ~100 mV, yet the kT/C noise of a 2 fF node is only ~1.4 mV. Hold the bitline at a fixed potential with a transfer gate biased at threshold, so the cell's charge is funneled onto a ~2 fF sense node. This revives the 1970s charge-transfer amplifier with modern offset cancellation and multiplies the signal ~20x.
why: If 20% of the original charge is enough for a reliable read, retention = dQ/I grows ~4-5x with no change in leakage. Refresh energy and bandwidth fall in proportion (facts 1, 3).
note: 1970s CTA revival; offset and speed within tRCD are doubts.

title: Sixteen-cell local bitlines cut required storage charge tenfold
idea: Derive Cs from the charge-sharing equation dV=(V/2)*Cs/(Cs+Cbl) instead of accepting a 30-40 fF bitline: split each vertical bitline into 16-cell local segments (~0.3 fF, ~1 um tall) that each drive one local gain transistor onto the global bitline. The cell capacitor then only has to swing a sub-femtofarad node.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and 3D blocker (fact 2): Cs=0.5 fF still yields ~300 mV of signal versus ~5 fF today, so lateral or planar capacitors in 3D tiers become sufficient; ~10x less charge per cell also cuts restore energy.
note: Hierarchical bitlines with local gain are known; local amp area per 16 cells is the cost.

title: Waste silicon tetrachloride becomes synthetic-silica crucibles beside polysilicon plants
idea: Crucible purity is set by metal content, not geology: Siemens polysilicon plants co-produce ~10-20 kg SiCl4 per kg Si, which flame hydrolysis (SiCl4 + 2H2 + O2 -> SiO2 + 4HCl, HCl recycled) turns into ppb-metal synthetic silica grain. Arc-fuse crucibles from it with a Ba-devitrified crystalline outer shell for 1450 C creep strength.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine HPQ dependence using a US waste stream next to existing polysilicon plants; synthetic grain is ~10x purer than natural HPQ.
note: Synthetic-lined crucibles exist; SiCl4 sourcing is the twist.

title: Maskless interference lithography prints DRAM array lattices without EUV
idea: A cell array is a perfect 2D lattice whose information content is a few numbers, not a mask; three-beam 193 nm immersion interference writes the hexagonal hole lattice using ~100% of the photons, spacer pitch division shrinks it, and a relaxed DUV cut mask defines array edges.
why: Replaces 2-4 EUV array layers (single supplier, ~1 MW per scanner) with low-cost interference optics; array litho capex down ~5x.

title: Offset-cancelled sense amps shrink the capacitor to AR 20:1
idea: First principle: a cell must store only enough charge to beat the sense amp's offset, dV = (Vdd/2)*Cs/(Cs+Cbl) > ~3 sigma_offset. Put auto-zeroed, offset-cancelling sense amps under the array (bonded CMOS) and cut bitline length 4x so Cbl falls; then a ~1.5 fF cell built at AR ~20:1 with standard etch replaces the AR 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor wall and etch capex (facts 1, 4): removes the hardest high-AR etch and mold module; ~10-15% fewer process steps and higher yield.

title: Laserless memory dies via optical backscatter modulation
idea: The irreducible optical cost is photons, not a laser on every die. The host sends continuous-wave light into the memory package; each DRAM base die carries only ring or electro-absorption modulators with a retroreflector, encoding read data onto reflected light like RFID backscatter, so the memory side spends ~10 fJ/bit and temperature-sensitive lasers stay at the host.
why: Optical memory links at ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit over meters let DRAM leave the hot accelerator package and decouple capacity from shoreline (facts 5, 6).

title: Spatially pipelined chiplet mesh: activations never land in memory
idea: Intermediate buffers exist only because producer and consumer run at different times. Map each layer group onto its own chiplet in a panel-scale mesh and chain them with FIFOs sized to pipeline skew, so activations flow directly chiplet to chiplet and activation DRAM goes to near zero.
why: Activation memory falls >100x; trades reconfigurability and needs many chiplets.

title: Canary in coal mine: leaky sentinel cells set refresh pace
idea: Place 8 canary cells per mat whose access transistors are drawn ~15% shorter so they leak ~3x faster than the worst real cell; during idle the SA checks them every few ms and the mat is refreshed only after a canary flips, so the refresh period tracks real temperature and process instead of a fixed 32-64 ms worst case.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth): typical dies and temperatures retain far longer than spec, so mat-level adaptive refresh can stretch intervals 2-4x safely.

title: Tweezers: 64-cell micro-row activation ends page overfetch
idea: Pick one item with tweezers instead of scooping the tray: split each wordline into 64-cell micro-rows with a 2-transistor local AND driver (global wordline x column-group select), so an access opens and senses only the 64-512 cells requested, not an 8 kb page.
why: Destructive read with 128x overfetch (fact 8, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): sensing energy per useful bit falls ~16-100x, so total access energy drops >10x; costs ~5-8% array area for local drivers.

title: Igloo: 77 K memory tier runs sensing at half voltage
idea: Keep memory cold like an igloo: put a capacity-tier DRAM in a liquid-nitrogen bath at 77 K, where access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude (refresh nearly vanishes), wire resistance drops ~5x and threshold voltages can be retargeted, so VARY runs at ~0.5 V and VPP at ~1.5 V with periphery at 0.4 V.
why: CV2 terms fall ~4x, wordline ~4x, refresh ~100x, and lower wire resistance shrinks drivers; net ~10x per access at the device even after amortized cryocooler overhead at data-centre scale is debated.
note: Cryo-DRAM studied; cryocooler overhead largely erases device-level gains.

title: Rubber stamp: electroformed nanoimprint stamper families replace EUV for capacitor holes
idea: Random stimulus 'rubber stamp' -> one e-beam-written master for the hexagonal storage-node hole array is copied, the way CD and DVD presses make stamper families, into father/mother/son nickel and quartz daughter templates. Jet-and-flash UV imprint then prints the periodic hole and landing-pad layers, and a 193i scanner handles only the aperiodic periphery.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): the most periodic layers are the ones that carry most of the 5-7 EUV passes. Imprint tools cost ~$10-20M versus $200M+ for EUV, so the patterning cost of those layers could fall 3-5x; daughter templates spread the master's cost over millions of wafers.

title: Bonsai pruning: memory-side unit trims never-attended KV tokens
idea: Prune what never sees light: the accelerator streams per-token attention-mass sums to a small memory-side 'bonsai' unit that keeps exponentially decayed importance per KV block and evicts or downgrades blocks below threshold in the background, off the decode critical path.
why: Most long-context tokens get negligible attention; 3-8x KV reduction at small quality loss with zero decode stall.
note: H2O/Scissorhands known; memory-side unit is the twist.

title: Weak canary bitlines trigger refresh only when decay is real
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x dedicated canary comparator x per-mat monitor x bulk Si x standard flow. Each mat carries a column of deliberately leaky cells (narrowed access gate) whose decay a reference comparator watches; that mat is refreshed only when the canaries cross threshold, tracking temperature and process automatically.
why: Refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) cut 3-5x at typical temperatures; bandwidth loss down.

title: Gain cell split across tiers: IGZO write above, silicon read below
idea: [Box: storage-node gate | IGZO write FET + Si read FET | current sense | sequential BEOL over FEOL | Si | ALD IGZO over 28 nm CMOS] Put the ultra-low-leakage IGZO write transistor in a BEOL tier directly over a high-drive Si read transistor in the substrate, with the vertical via between them as the storage node, giving each cell IGZO retention and Si read current in ~4-6F2.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capacitor wall (fact 1): retention >1 s, no capacitor, Si-speed read; refresh energy down ~10x.

title: 77 K cryogenic DRAM stacks with tenfold smaller capacitors
idea: [Box: small planar MIM | Si or poly-Si FET | charge-share SA | many-tier monolithic | Si | relaxed DUV] Run memory racks at liquid-nitrogen temperature where leakage falls by 1e4 or more and retention climbs to minutes; cells use 0.5-1 fF low-AR capacitors and leakier thin-film transistors, so tiers stack cheaply.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1), refresh (fact 3) and wire energy (fact 5, Cu resistance ~6x lower): near-zero refresh, simple cells; cooling cost amortized in AI datacenters.
note: Cryo DRAM widely studied; cooling overhead limits net gain.

title: Block-copolymer cylinders multiply ArF guide patterns into pillar lattices
idea: [Box: MIM charge | Si VCT | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | ArF-immersion guide trenches + PS-b-PMMA DSA, 4x density multiplication] Print coarse ~80 nm guide trenches with ArF immersion and let a block copolymer self-assemble into ~20 nm-pitch hexagonal cylinders inside them; the PMMA domains become the hard mask for VCT pillars and capacitor holes.
why: No EUV (fact 4): polymer thermodynamics multiplies density, replacing EUV on the 2-3 densest array layers at roughly a third of the litho cost per layer.

title: Liquid-nitrogen-cooled DRAM pools shrink capacitors fivefold
idea: Box [1 fF stub cap, AR ~15:1 | Si access at 77 K | low-noise voltage SA | LN2-immersion rack shared over CXL | Si | standard]: at 77 K, subthreshold and junction leakage fall by >1e6, so retention exceeds hours and 1 fF suffices; cooling uses LN2 from air separation, which needs no helium (unlike sub-20 K cryogenics).
why: Capacitor wall, refresh and materials: ~5x less capacitor stack, near-zero refresh, and ~5x lower Cu wire resistance; the cryocooler overhead means it pays off only for dense pooled racks.
note: Cryo-DRAM (77 K) well studied; cooling overhead limits net gain to dense pooled racks.

title: MicroLED imaging-fiber links make cheap DDR act like HBM
idea: Box: commodity DDR5 die x standard access x standard SA x 300-lane microLED/CMOS-photodiode array x coherent imaging fiber bundle x flip-chip GaN-on-Si chiplet. Each lane is a blue microLED at ~2 Gb/s imaged pixel-to-pixel through the bundle, so a buffer chip next to commodity DRAM delivers HBM-class aggregate bandwidth at <1 pJ/bit over 1-5 m.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): substitutes DDR (about 1/3 the wafer area per bit of HBM) for HBM while keeping bandwidth, and lets memory live outside the hot package.
note: Very close to Avicena LightBundle microLED links.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory packages kill refresh and wire resistance
idea: Box: 1T1C x cryo-optimized high-Vt access x SA retuned for 77 K x copper interposer at 77 K x cryostat-integrated package x standard fab. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude so retention stretches from 64 ms to hours, and copper resistance drops ~6x so links run at lower swing.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and data movement (fact 5): near-zero refresh energy and bandwidth loss, ~3x cheaper wires; cryo-cooling overhead partly offsets.
note: Cryo-DRAM researched; 77 K cooling overhead (~10x heat-removal power) offsets.

title: Run legacy-node U.S. DRAM at 77 K to erase tails
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar at 77 K | sense: standard | integration: liquid-nitrogen-cooled memory sled | substrate: bulk | fab: 25-30 nm DUV legacy process]. Junction and GIDL leakage fall >1000x at 77 K, so retention moves from 64 ms to minutes and weak tail cells become strong; older, EUV-free nodes with bigger, cheaper cells then serve disaggregated LN2-cooled memory racks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: no EUV, refresh (16-33% of idle power) nearly disappears; cooling overhead offsets about half of the energy gain.

title: Po: never open a full row — column-gated sub-wordlines
idea: Po: a row that is never fully opened. Merge ACT and RD into one command carrying row and column address, and AND the column-group select into each sub-wordline driver so only the ~1 kb segment containing the requested line is activated and sensed.
why: Overfetch (#8): 128x overfetch falls to ~16x for random access, ~5x lower activate energy per useful bit; fewer opened cells also cut aggressor activity (row hammer #9).

title: Bits travel to the sensor: CMOS bucket-brigade loop memory
idea: Worsen: give every bit its own transistor, contact and wire so periphery and contacts eat the die. Flip: store bits as charge packets in buried-channel CCD potential wells clocked around short 256-bit loops with one sense and regeneration stage per loop; no per-cell transistor, contact or capacitor etch, so a cell is ~2-4F2 of gate electrodes.
why: Density and capital (no high-AR capacitor, fewer EUV contact layers, fact 4) and a smaller periphery share (fact 7); latency held under ~100 ns by many short parallel loops.
note: 1970s CCD memory revived with short loops; continuous clocking energy is the doubt.

title: Liquid-nitrogen bathed memory pools nearly eliminate refresh
idea: Worsen: run DRAM hot (85-95 C) in air-cooled racks, so leakage forces 32-64 ms refresh. Flip: immerse pooled DRAM sleds in liquid nitrogen made from air on site. Junction leakage falls by orders of magnitude and retention stretches to minutes or hours, so refresh drops toward zero and VARY can come down.
why: Refresh energy (16-33% of idle power), row hammer margin and the voltage floor: memory power could fall ~3-5x, offsetting cryocooler cost, with no scarce coolant.
note: Same LN2-immersed DRAM pools as I-08926.

title: Rack-level content-addressed line store for shared weights
idea: Worsen: every tenant on every host holds its own copy of the same model weights and runtimes. Flip: a CXL memory appliance hashes each 4 KB block on write and stores it once in a content-addressed table; hosts map their pages to the hash, and copy-on-write breaks sharing only on mutation.
why: Capacity: 5-20x less DRAM for replicated read-mostly data (weights, libraries, VM images) across a rack.

title: Line-granular copy-on-write for forked inference workers
idea: Worsen: fork model servers and copy whole 4 KB or 2 MB pages on the first write. Flip: the controller tracks copy-on-write per 64 B line, so forked zygote workers share everything except the exact lines they mutate.
why: Capacity: 5-50x less memory duplication when spawning many workers from one warmed process (inference, serverless, browsers).

title: Quantize-on-write base die stores KV at 4 bits transparently
idea: Worsen: store every KV value at FP16 although attention tolerates far less. Flip: the HBM base die applies per-block scaled 4-bit quantization with outlier side tables on write and dequantizes on read, so the host still sees FP16 while the array holds ~3.5x more tokens.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~3-4x more KV per GB and ~3x fewer array bits moved per token.

title: Store tokens, not KV: base-die engines recompute keys and values
idea: Worsen: hold gigabytes of KV cache per long conversation in capacitors. Flip: keep only token IDs (2 bytes per token) plus sparse activation checkpoints, and let matrix engines in the memory base die regenerate K and V for evicted spans on demand, trading cheap FLOPs for scarce bits.
why: Capacity: KV per token (~100 KB+ in large models) collapses to bytes plus checkpoints, 10-100x less memory for long contexts at some recompute energy.

title: High-bandwidth flash plus SRAM appliances replacing DRAM for weights
idea: Worse: keep entire models resident in DRAM because flash is 'too slow'. Flip: stack many-plane NAND on a logic die for high-bandwidth parallel reads and prefetch weight tiles into on-die SRAM ahead of the layer schedule, so the only memories are static SRAM and NAND that retains data unpowered.
why: Zero refresh, and the bulk store comes from abundant NAND at ~5-10x lower cost per bit.

title: Chef's vinaigrette separation: block-copolymer hexagonal pillar masks
idea: Oil and vinegar separate on their own. Spin-coat high-chi PS-b-PDMS, anneal it into hexagonal cylinders at 16-24 nm pitch, and guide them with a coarse 248 nm pattern (graphoepitaxy). The result is transferred into a hard mask for a 4F2 vertical pillar array.
why: Sub-20 nm pillar patterning with a spin coater, hotplate and etcher. That is EUV-free and within a 10-person team's tool budget (Fact 4).
note: DSA defectivity, not resolution, has stalled adoption.

title: Alien with no CPU/memory split: attention computed in HBM logic die
idea: An alien that never separated thinking from remembering would score attention and accumulate values in the HBM base die. KV is stored in a 2-bit grouped format that only the in-stack PIM reads: dequantization and softmax happen beside the banks, and only the attended output vector leaves the stack.
why: KV capacity per stack rises 4-8x and KV traffic leaves the interposer, attacking both data-movement energy (3-4 pJ/bit) and capacity.

title: LN2 memory pods with 4x wordlines and 2x bitlines
idea: Design a die only for 77 K immersion pods: copper resistivity drops ~6x so each sub-wordline driver can serve 4x more cells, and lower thermal noise plus near-zero leakage allow 2x longer bitlines with a longer sense window. SWD and SA stripes shrink to roughly a third of their usual area.
why: Periphery 49% -> ~25-30% of die, refresh eliminated (fact 3), ~1.4x bits per wafer; cost moves into cryo infrastructure.

title: Satellite-lot nanoimprint tiers: periodic arrays without excimer or EUV
idea: Space programs build memory in lots too small to amortize EUV, and EUV and ArF sources consume neon, helium, krypton or argon; a DRAM array layer is a perfectly periodic line or hole lattice, so print it by jet-and-flash nanoimprint cured with UV LEDs and write only the small non-periodic periphery with a multi-beam electron writer. Every tier reuses the same template, and transfer etches run on HBr/O2 chemistry with no argon dilution.
why: Removes 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) and the neon/helium supply risk; template ~10x cheaper than an EUV mask set and tool capex ~$30M vs $200M+.
note: Canon/Kioxia NIL known; defectivity is the doubt.

title: Insect-swarm forking: cache-line copy-on-write for thousand-agent fan-out
idea: From swarms where thousands of agents share nearly identical state: the memory controller supports 64-byte-granular copy-on-write through an indirection table, so forking an agent, VM or KV prefix shares every identical line and allocates only the lines that actually diverge.
why: Page-level CoW wastes 4 KB per changed line; line-level sharing makes 1,000 forks cost ~1.1 copies, cutting DRAM, and its fab water, 10x+ for fan-out workloads.
note: Close to Page Overlays (Seshadri 2015).

title: Display-fab chip-on-glass panels as giant memory interposers
idea: Display driver ICs are bonded to glass with anisotropic conductive film for pennies per chip. Use depreciated Gen-6/8.5 LCD lines to pattern 2 um Cu RDL on glass panels, then bond DRAM and logic chiplets with fine-pitch ACF or microbumps, making half-meter interposers that hold dozens of memory stacks.
why: Bypasses the CoWoS silicon-interposer chokepoint and its reticle limit; panel cost per mm2 ~10-20x below silicon and uses idle display capacity plus US glass makers.

title: Endoscope imaging-fiber bundle carries 10,000 slow microLED memory lanes
idea: Medical endoscopes pipe whole images through coherent bundles of ~10k fiber cores. Couple a microLED array on the memory module to a photodiode array on the processor through an imaging fiber bundle, each pixel-lane at ~1-2 Gb/s with no SerDes, DSP or lasers.
why: Off-board memory links at ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit vs DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit (>10x), so cheap DRAM can sit meters away in pooled racks; avoids laser and EUV scarcity.
note: Closely matches published microLED/imaging-fiber wide-and-slow link work.

title: Million-token agents: attention scoring inside the HBM base die
idea: Million-token agent contexts make decode almost pure KV reads. The base die streams keys internally at full TSV bandwidth, computes low-precision q.k scores, and returns only the top-k keys' values plus a residual over the PHY.
why: For long contexts only ~1-5% of values need to cross the interface; PHY energy per logical token access drops 10-20x and HBM bandwidth stops bounding decode.
note: Widely pursued (AttAcc, NeuPIMs, HBM-PIM); top-k accuracy trade-off.

title: Contactless smartcard coupling: unbonded face-to-face capacitive memory links
idea: Contactless smartcards exchange data across air gaps. Place memory and logic dies face-to-face across ~1 um of dielectric with arrays of 5 um capacitor plates, signaling with low-voltage pulses and no metallurgical bond or ESD structures.
why: No ESD, no bumps and ~1-5 fF per channel give ~10-50 fJ/bit (>10x below HBM I/O); dies can be tested and swapped before final assembly, avoiding known-good-die losses.
note: Sun proximity communication prior art; pitch and coupling limit density vs hybrid bonding.

title: Solar-calculator near-threshold: 100,000 slow lanes at 0.3 V
idea: Solar calculators run for decades at near-threshold voltage by being slow. Use fine-pitch hybrid bonding to give memory 50-100k lanes at only 200-400 Mb/s each, so drivers and receivers run at 0.3 V with no equalization, termination or SerDes.
why: Switching energy scales with V2: 0.3 V lanes vs ~1.1 V I/O give ~13x lower energy at equal aggregate bandwidth; parallelism replaces frequency.

title: Cryo-control DRAM: shallow capacitors because 77 K kills leakage
idea: Quantum-computer control electronics run at 4-77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by ~10^6 and retention stretches to hours. Design a die that only runs in liquid nitrogen, with 0.5-1 fF capacitors (AR ~10 or planar) and no refresh circuitry, for sealed LN2-immersion AI racks. Reliability comes from temperature instead of capacitor height.
why: Removes the AR 60-75 capacitor and refresh (facts 1, 3): a ~5-6x shorter capacitor etch and fewer steps. The cost is LN2 cooling energy, partly offset by lower wire resistance and leakage.

title: Canary-cell event-driven refresh replaces the fixed clock
idea: Time shift from clock-driven (fixed 64 ms) to event-driven refresh: each subarray carries a row of deliberately weakened canary cells (smaller capacitor, slightly lower Vt) whose leakage tracks 2x the true array tail; a comparator watches them and the bank refreshes only when a canary crosses threshold, automatically tracking temperature, voltage and aging.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): removes the 4-8x worst-case guardband baked into fixed intervals; at 45 C refresh ops fall ~4x.
note: Same canary-cell refresh pacing.

title: 77 K floating-body 3D array with hour-scale retention
idea: Shift the thermal timescale: at 77 K (LN2 immersion at rack scale) thermal-generation leakage falls by >10^6, so a capacitorless floating-body cell in stacked thin silicon tiers holds charge for hours. The array is designed only for cryogenic racks and needs neither a capacitor nor refresh.
why: Removes the capacitor wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3); enables capacitorless 3D at ~4F2 per tier.

title: Crucible liners made from polysilicon plants' silicon tetrachloride waste
idea: Jump from chemical-plant scale to crucible scale: flame-hydrolyze the SiCl4 byproduct of U.S. polysilicon plants into synthetic silica soot. Plasma-fuse it as the 2-3 mm inner crucible layer that touches the melt, backed by ordinary-grade quartz sand.
why: Cuts Spruce Pine high-purity quartz needed per crucible by ~70% using an existing domestic waste stream. Synthetic silica also lowers metal contamination in the ingot.

title: Nanoimprint the periodic array, DUV the periphery: mix-and-match
idea: Exploit that a DRAM mat is a perfect crystal: one e-beam master is replicated into imprint templates that stamp the whole array layer (holes or lines) at 12-16 nm half-pitch per field, while ArF scanners pattern only the irregular periphery.
why: Replaces the most expensive EUV array layers; an imprint tool is ~1/5 the cost and ~1/10 the energy of EUV per layer (Fact 4).

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM: minutes of retention shrink the capacitor tenfold
idea: Time-shift retention via temperature: at 77 K leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention grows from ms to minutes; design the cell around a ~0.5 fF capacitor, delete the high-AR capacitor module, and deploy in U.S. datacenters cooled with domestic LN2 (no helium).
why: Removes the most expensive capacitor steps (Facts 1, 4) and nearly all refresh energy (Fact 3); cooling overhead is absorbed at rack scale.

title: HBM base die evicts KV tokens by accumulated attention
idea: This adds zero DRAM masks; the change lives in the HBM4 custom logic base die. The base die snoops attention-score writes, keeps each token's accumulated attention in SRAM, and on its own demotes low-scoring tokens' KV to a compressed far tier while pinning attention-sink tokens. The memory itself decides what to forget, on a microsecond timescale.
why: KV footprint is 3-8x smaller at matched accuracy, and the GPU spends no cycles on eviction policy.

title: Ultra-wide 200 MHz near-threshold interface with 64k wires per stack
idea: Shift the link's timescale 30x slower and its width 30x wider: with 3 um hybrid bonds a stack exposes 64k data pads clocked at 200 MHz with 0.2 V swing, driven by plain CMOS inverters with no SerDes, DFE, PLL or termination. Bandwidth matches HBM4 while each bit only charges ~20 fF of micron-length wire.
why: Interface energy falls from 3-4 pJ/bit to ~0.03-0.05 pJ/bit (fact 5) and PHY area on base and host dies shrinks ~5x.

title: National phone trade-in harvest of LPDDR into datacenter modules
idea: Time-and-scale mismatch: phones retire after ~3 years, but their LPDDR lasts 10+. Robots desolder LPDDR packages from billions of traded-in devices using nitrogen reflow, retest them, and rebuild them into CAMM/CXL modules for cloud tier-2 memory.
why: A flagship phone holds 8-16 GB. Recovering 10% of yearly smartphone retirements adds tens of exabytes, with no fab and no rare gases.

title: STT-DRAM's shrinking-Delta killer fixed with tall shape-anisotropy free layers
idea: Samsung and Hynix STT-MRAM DRAM-replacement efforts stalled because interfacial anisotropy cannot keep Delta >= 60 at sub-20 nm diameters and 125 C. Make the free layer a 20-40 nm tall CoFeB/FeCo cylinder (aspect ratio >1.5), so perpendicular shape anisotropy, which falls only slowly with temperature, supplies the stability.
why: 125 C/10 y retention at ~10-15 nm diameter: 2-4x density over interfacial-PMA MTJs.
note: Perpendicular shape-anisotropy MTJs already pursued (Tohoku, Spintec).

title: IBM Josephson lesson: run DRAM at 77 K, not superconducting
idea: IBM's 1980s Josephson computer program died largely for lack of a dense cryogenic memory. Instead of superconducting memory, run 3D DRAM tiers at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention stretches to hours, and the capacitor can shrink about 10x.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and the charge wall (fact 1), allowing short, cheap capacitors in many tiers. LN2 cooling avoids helium.

title: ETA-10 lesson: liquid-nitrogen-immersed DRAM pods that need no refresh
idea: ETA Systems' LN2-cooled supercomputer died on per-board cryostat logistics, frost and service cost, not physics. Fix exactly that with sealed rack-scale LN2 immersion tanks fed by an on-site air-separation reliquefier (closed loop, no venting); at 77 K DRAM leakage falls ~1e6x so refresh disappears, and new cells can use ~4x smaller capacitors (~20:1 aspect ratio, plain Al2O3/SiO2 dielectric).
why: Kills refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) and lets capacitors drop high-k Zr/Hf and 60-75:1 etching; coolant is nitrogen (78% of air) instead of Qatar-exposed helium; cooler, faster wires partially repay the cryo energy.
note: Cryo DRAM is well studied; 77 K cooling overhead offsets much of refresh savings.

title: Z-NAND's failure fixed: erase-free 64-byte sub-page flash over CXL
idea: Samsung Z-NAND and Kioxia XL-Flash failed to win DRAM sockets because 4 KB pages and block erases left them neither cheap nor fast enough. Build an SLC die with 512-byte mini-page sense amps per plane, append 64 B cachelines as log writes into pre-erased blocks, erase in idle planes, and absorb rewrites in a 1% DRAM front, exposed as CXL.mem.
why: Meets ~50-100x: ~$0.1-0.15/GB SLC-class cost serving warm DRAM data. Trades: 1-3 us misses, ~1e5 SLC endurance hidden by the DRAM front and wear-leveling.
note: Samsung CMM-H already pairs NAND with DRAM cache over CXL.

title: Virtual Channel SDRAM revived: sector caches and sub-row activation in base die
idea: NEC's VC-SDRAM put SRAM channel buffers in each DRAM to cut row conflicts, but died because its 3-5% die-area cost was too much for a commodity part and controllers ignored it. In HBM/CXL stacks the logic base die offers cheap area: give it per-bank 64 B sector caches and drive segmented wordlines so only the 1/8 row segment holding the requested sector activates, returning sectors instead of whole pages.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): 8x fewer cells activated per random access, cutting the ~5.9 pJ per useful bit by ~3-5x, and fewer full-row activations ease row hammer (fact 9).
note: Known art: FGDRAM, Half-DRAM, partial row activation.

title: Charge-transfer pre-sensing resolves half-decayed cells within tRCD
idea: Effect: charge transfer through a subthreshold-biased MOSFET (CCD floating-diffusion style). A charge-transfer preamplifier between bitline and sense amp funnels bitline charge onto a small sense node, multiplying signal ~5-10x by C_BL/C_sense, so cells that have lost ~70% of their charge still resolve. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Retention criterion (facts 1, 3): time-to-fail lengthens 2-3x for the same leakage, so internal refresh halves.

title: Liquid-nitrogen immersion DRAM pods eliminate refresh and cut wire energy
idea: N: run pooled CXL memory sleds immersed in 77 K liquid nitrogen made on site from air (no helium); subthreshold and junction leakage fall >10^6 so refresh can be disabled, Vt variation tightens, and copper resistance drops ~5x, enabling lower-swing I/O.
why: Kills refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and lowers data-movement energy (fact 5); cryocooling costs ~10 W per W at 77 K, so the net win targets capacity pools where DRAM idle power dominates.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM pools: let 77 K shrink the capacitor
idea: Periodic-table walk, N (7): run rack-scale memory pools at 77 K in LN2 or cryocooled sleds, where access-transistor leakage falls >1e6x and retention rises from 64 ms to hours, so cells can be designed with a 1-1.5 fF capacitor (AR ~15) and no refresh.
why: Deletes the most tool- and material-intensive steps (deep mold etch, high-k stacks) and refresh energy (46 fJ/bit); nitrogen comes from air.

title: Zircon fossil weights: frozen model hardwired into via-programmed ROM
idea: Zircon crystals lock elements in place for billions of years; a production 1-8B-parameter model's 4-bit weights are fossilized into via-programmed mask ROM on several accelerator dies (one via mask per model version) and read from macros next to the MAC arrays with no DRAM involved.
why: ROM reads at ~0.01-0.05 pJ/bit versus ~3-15 pJ/bit from HBM/DDR are a >100x energy-per-access cut, and weight DRAM goes to zero for that model, leaving DRAM only for KV (energy, cost/bit).

title: Ba: barium-titanate Pockels modulators for femtojoule memory optics
idea: Bond thin-film epitaxial BaTiO3 (r42 ~900 pm/V, ~30x LiNbO3) onto silicon microrings so memory-link modulators switch with ~0.5 V and ~10 fF, driven directly from DRAM-process logic without driver amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): optical memory I/O with ~50-100 fJ/bit modulator energy, making off-package memory cheaper per bit moved than HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit.
note: BTO-on-Si modulators already commercialized (Lumiphase, IBM work).

title: Newspaper-press model ROM: reprint inference weights each release
idea: Store frozen inference weights in via- or imprint-programmed mask ROM printed on mature U.S. nodes, reprinted per model release like a newspaper edition. It is byte-addressable at ~10-20 ns behind the accelerator.
why: Zero refresh: printed vias never leak. It removes the largest read-only consumer of HBM/DRAM capacity at a fraction of the cost per bit, with no EUV.
note: Hardwired-weight inference silicon already pursued; mature-node ROM density per bit is the doubt.

title: Float-glass panel interposers made in idle display fabs
idea: Retool underused Gen-6 LCD/OLED backplane lines (each panel ~40 wafers of area) to make 2 um line glass-core interposers and redistribution panels for memory-logic packages, using their existing steppers, sputter and plating, and replacing silicon CoWoS-style interposers for HBM/LPDDR stacks.
why: Fact 6 and capital: unlocks interposer capacity that gates HBM shipments using amortized panel fabs at ~1/5-1/10 the cost per area of 300 mm silicon interposers.

title: Spot-color fifth plate: one-mask IGZO gain cell in logic BEOL
idea: Treat a logic flow as a four-color press and add exactly one spot-color plate: one mask patterns an ALD IGZO island between Mn and Mn+1, the existing Mn line serves as bottom gate, and redrawn (not added) via masks form source/drain and read contacts, making a 2T0C gain cell any logic foundry can offer.
why: U.S. manufacturability/capital: DRAM-class embedded memory on existing logic capacity for +1 mask (~3% wafer cost), with no capacitor module and no EUV.

title: 3D-printed photonic wire bonds tying HBM base die to GPU
idea: Use two-photon 3D printing (like additive manufacturing at 100 nm voxels) to write freeform polymer waveguides plus printed micro-lenses between silicon-photonic ports on the HBM base die and the accelerator. Because optical loss hardly depends on length, stacks can sit centimetres away.
why: Attacks data-movement energy and shoreline limits: <1 pJ/bit links and 2-3x more stacks per accelerator because placement is not reach-limited.

title: LCD panel fab repurposed to print glass memory interposers
idea: Run 2 um redistribution layers on Gen-8.5 display lines (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, i-line steppers built for TFTs), the way TV panels are made, and dice them into memory interposers. No EUV and no silicon wafer is involved.
why: Huge idle display capacity yields interposer area at ~10x lower cost per mm2, relieving the 2.5D bottleneck that throttles HBM supply.

title: Decal transfer printing of lasers onto mature-node base die
idea: Use an elastomer stamp, like a water-slide decal, to pick thousands of InP lasers and photodiodes per stroke from their native wafer and print them onto a 28-65 nm HBM base die. The memory stack then gets optical I/O.
why: Optical memory I/O at ~1 pJ/bit with no advanced node; distance-free links decouple memory from compute shoreline.
note: Micro-transfer printing of InP lasers is established (X-Celeprint).

title: Reusable mother wafer: grow, use, and peel thin epi films
idea: Ideal: a wafer that is never consumed. Closest: grow a 10-20 um epitaxial device layer on a porous-silicon double layer of a premium Cz mother wafer, build the DRAM, bond it to a cheap reclaimed/metallurgical-grade carrier, cleave at the porous layer, re-polish and reuse the mother 10-20 times.
why: Cuts Cz crystal growth, HPQ crucibles, polysilicon and puller energy per wafer ~10x; de-risks concentrated wafer supply chains.

title: Superword tokenizer halves tokens and halves KV per conversation
idea: IFR: a whole thought fits in one KV slot. Closest with no hardware: retrain tokenizers with ~1M-entry multi-word vocabularies (frequent phrases as single tokens), moving cost into a larger embedding table that is stored once while every live sequence carries ~2x fewer tokens.
why: KV memory scales with token count; ~40-50% KV cut fleet-wide for a one-time embedding cost.
note: SuperBPE-style; needs model retraining.

title: Panel-scale glass interposers replacing reticle-stitched silicon
idea: Ideal: interposers as cheap as window glass. Closest achievable: build redistribution layers and through-glass vias on 510x515 mm glass panels with LCD-style lithography, giving ~6x the area per process pass of a 300 mm wafer with flatness good enough for 2 um lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: reuses display tools and domestic glass supply; interposer cost per package falls ~3-5x and the reticle-size limit disappears, allowing more HBM sites per GPU.

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard to admit second-source DRAM makers
idea: Ideal: any memory die works with any processor. Closest achievable: define an open die-to-die DRAM chiplet interface (UCIe-based, with a standard base-die command set, thermal limits and test protocol) so new or smaller U.S. memory fabs can sell bare array chiplets into anyone's package without building their own base die or PHY.
why: Supply concentration and U.S. manufacturability: lowers the entry ticket from full HBM stacks to bare arrays and widens the supplier base beyond three companies.
note: UCIe/BoW memory and HBM4 custom base die efforts already underway.

title: Nitrogen-immersed DDR5 DIMMs with sub-femtofarad cryo-optimized cells
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same DDR5 edge connector and protocol, so move the whole DIMM into the LN2 or cold-plate loop of an AI rack. At 77 K access leakage falls >1e6, so a redesigned array uses ~1 fF planar capacitors with half-length bitlines to keep Cs/Cbl and holds data for hours, while the PHY is retuned for 77 K thresholds but signals per spec.
why: Removes the HAR capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3), and higher mobility allows lower voltages (fact 10); nitrogen is abundant (no helium), cooling energy is the tradeoff.
note: Same 77 K DRAM with shrunk capacitors; cooling energy offsets.

title: 64-cell vertical bitlines let 1.5 fF capacitors suffice
idea: Limit: Cs may not exceed 1.5 fF. Make every bitline vertical and only as long as the tier count (64 cells, about 2 um), so bitline capacitance falls to about 3 fF versus about 50-80 fF planar. The transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cb) jumps about 5x, and a lateral capacitor that fits inside a tier gives enough signal.
why: Facts 1 and 2: breaks the 4.5-5.4 fF requirement that blocks 3D lateral capacitors and keeps about 150 mV of read signal.
note: Dup of short local bitlines lowering required Cs.

title: Retired LCD fab lines reborn as panel-level memory interposer foundries
idea: Scarcity: CoWoS silicon interposer capacity is sold out. Retool depreciated Gen-6/Gen-8 TFT-LCD lines (1.5-2 um steppers, large-area sputter and CVD already installed) to pattern copper RDL interposers on 1.5 m glass panels, cutting ~100 interposers per panel instead of ~15 per 300 mm wafer.
why: Capital intensity and the HBM packaging chokepoint: fully depreciated tools and ~5-8x more interposer area per exposure, targeting 3-5x lower $/mm2 of interposer.

title: No silicon wafer: federal guaranteed offtake for first non-Si memory
idea: Forced limit: the first buyers must be guaranteed. Federal agencies pre-commit to buy a fixed volume of qualified non-Si memory modules at a set price for five years, as Operation Warp Speed did for vaccines.
why: Removes demand risk that stops investors funding unproven substrates; brings first capacity forward by years.

title: Sidewall-wired DRAM cube with adaptive (die-position-corrected) side-face lithography
idea: Thin DRAM dies to 30-50 um, stack them with 2-5 um adhesive and no TSVs, then polish one or two faces of the cube to expose edge pads that each die routes to its edge. Pattern the vertical bus on the face with maskless laser direct imaging that first measures each die's actual position and adapts the wiring (adaptive patterning, as in fan-out packaging), so several um of die misplacement do not matter. Plated Cu stripes ~10 um thick carry power along the same face, and a base logic die at the bottom connects to the side bus.
why: TSV-free HBM-class stack: removes TSV keep-out and TSV/bond yield loss (HBM tax 3x -> ~2x [ESTIMATE]); 2,500-5,000 bus wires on two faces; 20-high stacks in under 1 mm.

title: Erasure-coded memory stacks: 16+2 dies, any two may fail
idea: Treat the dies of an HBM-class (or 3D wafer-bonded) stack like disks in RAID-6. Data channels are striped across dies with rotating parity computed in the logic base die. When a die fails (at stack test or in the field), the base die reconstructs its channels from the others in degraded mode, or remaps them to a spare die (simpler, preferred at test). Signal paths crossing a failed bond are protected by redundant TSV/bond pads with per-layer bypass, or by contactless inductive-coupling links, so one die's failure does not sever the chain. Power gets per-layer isolation switches. This lets stacks use non-known-good dies and imperfect bonds.
why: At 95% per-die-in-stack yield, 16-high stack yield rises from 44% to 94% with 16+2: 1.9x fewer dies per good stack-bit. At 90% yield the gain is 3.5x; at 98%, 1.2x.

title: Eliminate per-layer KV caches by sharing one KV across layer groups
idea: Train models where groups of 2-4 adjacent layers query one shared K/V projection stored once, with small per-layer query adapters for quality.
why: KV memory drops 2-4x architecturally, stacking with quantization and paging.
note: Cross-Layer Attention / YOCO already published.

title: Copper-style overlay sequencer streaming model layers from parallel flash
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a compiler precomputes a full 1980s-style overlay schedule of which weight tiles are needed when, and a 180 nm microcoded DMA sequencer (like the Amiga Copper) executes it, streaming tiles from 16-32 parallel NAND channels into a small DRAM ring one or two layers ahead of compute.
why: Deterministic batch inference needs only ~2 layers resident; 5-20x less weight DRAM, using only old-node control logic.

title: Triple-barrier resonant-tunneling III-V charge node on GaAs substrates
idea: Invert 'a retention barrier must be thick so writes need high voltage' -> make it thick but resonantly transparent at one voltage. An InAs/AlSb triple-barrier stack on GaAs or InP lets electrons enter an InAs storage well only when ~2.5 V aligns quantized levels, while the ~2.1 eV AlSb offset holds charge for years at zero bias.
why: Non-volatile charge with ~100x lower write energy than flash and high endurance (no oxide trap generation), usable as refresh-free DRAM (facts 3, 10) on U.S. III-V RF/optoelectronic lines; builds on ULTRARAM-type prior art.
note: This is ULTRARAM (Lancaster); III-V substrate cost and density are the scaling question.

title: Inductive-coupling die stacking replaces Bosch-etched TSVs in HBM
idea: Extreme user: AI HBM stacks, whose TSVs are etched with SF6/C4F8 Bosch cycles. Pass data between stacked dies through on-chip coil pairs (near-field inductive links) and deliver power with a few large through-mold or edge conductors, so no fluorinated via etch is needed.
why: HBM TSV tax: frees the TSV keep-out area (much of the ~3x area penalty) and removes TSV yield loss and the fluorinated Bosch process.

title: Check-valve bottling: resonant-tunnel barrier seals a quantum-well charge
idea: Like a bottle with a one-way valve cap, an InAs quantum well holds charge behind an InAs/AlSb triple barrier. The barrier is opaque at rest (~2.1 eV AlSb offset) and turns resonantly transparent only near 2.5 V, filling or emptying the well in ns.
why: Fact 3: retention of hours to years nearly removes refresh while writes stay fast and low-energy. It also gives U.S. III-V fabs a memory product.
note: Same ULTRARAM mechanism.

title: Puff-pastry laminated HfO2/ZrO2 tuned to the morphotropic boundary
idea: Laminate like puff pastry folds dough: ALD supercycles stack 0.5 nm HfO2/ZrO2 leaves whose interface strain pins the film at the tetragonal-orthorhombic morphotropic phase boundary. There, field-induced polarization rotation peaks permittivity at k~60-70 without full ferroelectric switching.
why: Fact 1 directly: k~70 is the stated alternative to AR 115. Cs rises 2-3x at the same AR, and since the film never fully switches, endurance stays effectively unlimited.

title: Kelvin curb-sending write pulses that cancel high-k dielectric soakage
idea: Revive Lord Kelvin's 1860s 'curb sender' for the transatlantic cable and the analog designers' dielectric-absorption compensation: each write or restore pulse gets a calibrated overshoot followed by a short reverse curb, pre-charging the slow Curie-von Schweidler polarization of the ZrO2/HfO2 storage capacitor. The apparent charge loss in the first milliseconds after a write, which today eats retention margin, goes away.
why: High-k relaxation removes a few percent of signal after each write and shows up as lost retention margin (facts 1, 3); recovering 5-10% of signal could stretch the refresh interval ~1.5-2x with only driver-timing changes.
note: Novel: pre-charge slow high-k polarization at write; doubt: relaxation is a small share of retention margin.

title: Substitute hours-long retention bakes with infrared photo-stimulated screening
idea: Substitute multi-hour hot-bake retention tests with sub-bandgap (~1.3-1.6 um) LED illumination at wafer sort. The light photo-ionizes the deep traps behind tail cells and speeds up only defect-assisted leakage, so a scan of a few seconds yields retention maps per row and per mat.
why: A cheap, gas-free test step that makes retention-aware refresh and binning practical at volume: more usable supply and 4-8x refresh cuts.
note: Sub-bandgap light may speed trap-assisted leakage; doubt: correlation with thermal tail and VRT behavior.

title: CDMA Walsh-coded wordlines read many gain cells at once
idea: Borrowed from cellular CDMA: N nondestructive gain cells on one bitline are activated together, each wordline modulated by an orthogonal Walsh code across N short read slots. One integrating sense block despreads the summed bitline current into N bits.
why: Periphery per bit: one sense block serves 8-16 cells per access with ~sqrt(N) noise processing gain, cutting sense amps ~4-8x in gain-cell arrays.
note: Walsh-coded multi-cell reads on nondestructive gain cells; real gain is noise averaging, not fewer SAs than sequential reads.

title: Fiber-drawing towers produce thousand-wire flexible memory ribbons
idea: Adapted from optical-fiber drawing: a macroscopic polymer preform embedded with copper rods is heated and drawn 100x thinner into kilometers of ribbon. Each ribbon holds thousands of insulated micro-wires at ~20 um pitch and links processor to memory away from the package.
why: Interposer area and adjacency limit: more DRAM can surround a processor through dense wide-slow buses at ~1 pJ/bit and very low cost per wire-meter.

title: Light-powered self-refreshing photo-latch cell under an LED flood
idea: MAGNIFY the refresh source from a controller to photons: each cell adds a tiny photodiode feeding its storage node through a transistor gated by that node, so under uniform LED illumination '1' nodes keep topping themselves up while '0' nodes stay shut, a bistable cell needing no refresh commands; built on a CIS MPW.
why: Removes refresh commands and the 10-20% bandwidth tax (fact 3); the photocurrent needed only has to beat ~13 fA, so LED power is negligible.
note: Clever photocurrent self-refresh; extra photodiode and transistor per cell make it SRAM-like in area.

title: Minify substrate, magnify layers: fold one memory sheet 32 times
idea: Make one long thin-film memory array on 10 um polyimide through a flexible-TFT foundry shuttle, then fold it accordion-style 32 times, with fold lines carrying edge interconnects to a controller.
why: Layer count by folding instead of tier deposition: tests a no-bonding 3D path for under $300k. Density per layer is low, so it is a moonshot demo.

title: Test first, wire last: liquid-metal rewiring of good dies
idea: Reverse wire-then-test: mount dies on a substrate under PDMS microchannels, and after electrical test inject gallium-indium liquid metal only into channels that join good dies and good channels to the host, then seal, so defective dies are simply never connected.
why: Yield and capital for multi-die memory modules, without known-good-die test cost; PDMS soft lithography is basic, best for wide buses at <=1 GHz.
note: Test-then-wire avoids KGD cost; liquid-metal channels limit speed and density.

title: Client-held encrypted session state for idle conversations
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the server holding idle users' KV cache, ship a compressed (low-rank plus INT4), encrypted, integrity-tagged KV snapshot to the user's device after each turn and have the client return it with the next request; servers keep KV only for sessions that are generating right now.
why: Most chat sessions are idle >95% of wall time; moving idle KV onto client devices cuts server KV residency by roughly an order of magnitude for long-context chat.
note: Novel twist, but multi-GB KV uploads per turn and server-side SSD offload as an alternative limit the gain.

title: Spectral Goertzel detector spots periodic hammer patterns cheaply
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration/resonance: per-bank Goertzel filters run on hashed activation-address streams; a hammer loop shows up as a sharp spectral line at the attacker's loop frequency and triggers targeted neighbor refresh for the hashed rows.
why: Detects hammering with a few thousand gates instead of KB-scale per-row counter tables (~10x less area than per-row-counter tracking); a tiny counter covers aperiodic attacks.
note: Aperiodic or jittered patterns evade spectral peaks; still needs counter backup.

title: Cochlear Hopf-bifurcation sense amplifier reads deeply decayed cells
idea: Hair bundles poise near a Hopf bifurcation for huge gain on tiny stimuli; bias each bitline sense amp as a cross-coupled latch with tunable negative resistance held at the edge of oscillation, so a few-mV bitline signal sets its oscillation phase before latching.
why: Cells can lose ~75% of their charge rather than ~50% and still read correctly, so refresh intervals grow ~2-3x, or a smaller capacitor works at today's interval, which also eases the charge wall.
note: Biasing latch at Hopf edge for high gain on tiny signals is fresh; noise and metastability may eat the margin.

title: Barn-owl Jeffress delay-line coincidence decoder on one wire pair
idea: Barn owls localize sound with counter-propagating axonal delay lines and coincidence-detector neurons. Pulses launch from both ends of a tapped delay-chain select wire, with their relative launch time encoding the row address. Only the driver where they meet sees both pulses inside its coincidence window and fires.
why: Fact 7: one wire pair plus a programmable launch delay replaces a multi-level decoder tree and predecode buses for 64-256 drivers, cutting decode area ~40% and decode energy.

title: Otoacoustic diagnostics: supply-current spectra reveal DRAM sense margin
idea: Healthy cochleae emit faint sounds that allow non-invasive hearing tests. Standard activate/read bursts run while a fast shunt samples DIMM supply current. The spectral shape of sense-amp and restore transients exposes weak banks, timing margin and aging without vendor test modes. A $20k scope plus an ML classifier trained on 1,000 DIMMs, ~$400k in 18 months.
why: Supply axis: grades used and salvaged DRAM in seconds instead of hours of pattern testing, and sets per-DIMM refresh/timing.

title: Spider-silk droplet bumping: Rayleigh-Plateau instability forms mask-free solder bumps
idea: Spider capture threads bead into evenly spaced glue droplets by Rayleigh-Plateau instability. A thin liquid-metal or solder line is printed along each pad row on a glass substrate and left to break up, with patterned pad wettability pinning exactly one droplet per pad at a pitch set by the line diameter.
why: Capital intensity: bumping without photomasks, plating lines or silicon wafers, aiming at 10-20 um-pitch bumps on glass panels for memory chiplets at very low cost.
note: Rayleigh-Plateau breakup pinned by wettability; volume uniformity is the risk.

title: Herd-immunity fleet broadcast of row-hammer attack signatures
idea: When any server's memory controller fires a row-hammer mitigation, it extracts a compact 'antigen' (hashed bank/row-delta/ACT-interval fingerprint) and gossips it fleet-wide within seconds; every other controller pre-loads a matching detector before the attacker reaches it, so the fleet gets vaccinated instead of each chip being infected and learning alone.
why: Row hammer (~1k-activation flips): each die can ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation (fewer tracker entries) because novel patterns are learned once and immunized everywhere; target 5-10x less mitigation area and victim-refresh overhead than per-chip worst-case provisioning.
note: Adversaries can craft novel patterns; cannot safely shrink per-chip trackers.

title: Thymic negative selection: random detectors that never match normal traffic
idea: The thymus deletes T-cells that react to self; at boot the controller generates thousands of random detector templates over (bank, row-delta, ACT-interval) features, deletes any that match the profiled benign workload, and keeps survivors in a tiny CAM, so traffic that triggers a survivor is flagged as non-self and throttled.
why: Row hammer: catches novel patterns (half-double, many-sided) without per-row counters, ~10x less SRAM than counter trackers with tunable false-positive rate.

title: Back-EMF flush: fan and PSU inertia power the persistence dump
idea: As hard drives use spindle back-EMF to park heads on power loss, harvest the rotational energy of server fans (~10-15 J each) and PSU bulk capacitors through a boost converter to flush a bounded dirty set from DRAM to on-board NAND (~3 J per GB).
why: Makes DRAM-as-cache-over-flash power-safe without batteries or supercaps, so DRAM can shrink to a dirty-bounded cache over cheap persistent flash.
note: Fan rotor energy (~10 J) is real but small; it bounds the dirty set to tens of GB.

title: Tuned-mass-damper resonance detector: spectral hammer detection without counters
idea: A tuned mass damper targets one resonant frequency of a building. Hammering is periodic, so each bank runs a few Goertzel/autocorrelation bins over a hashed row-address stream. Aggressor sequences that recur at a fixed lag, including many-sided TRRespass patterns, stand out using about 10-20 registers. The detected aggressors get neighbour refresh.
why: Tracking SRAM could shrink ~90% compared with per-row counters (PRAC) while catching patterns that sampling TRR misses (facts 7 and 9).
note: Blacksmith-style non-uniform patterns and hash collisions may evade bins.

title: Nanocryotron sense amps for 4-kelvin DRAM
idea: Revive Buck's 1956 cryotron in its modern form, the superconducting nanowire nTron. At 4 K a DRAM cell retains data for hours, and an NbN nanowire biased near its critical current switches to the normal state when the bitline's charge-sharing current adds to it, giving >1,000x gain at zero static power. Decoders become nTron trees, which removes CMOS periphery heat from the cold stage.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and slashes sense energy for quantum and superconducting computers, which lack dense cold memory today. Niche, but no incumbent holds it.

title: Hourglass: retention-failed dies hold only millisecond-lived data
idea: Sand runs out on a known schedule: bin dies that fail 64 ms retention (normally scrapped or downbinned) into 'hourglass DIMMs' with refresh disabled, and let the allocator place only data with guaranteed lifetimes under 5 ms there (activations, pipeline and staging buffers) via a lifetime tag in the allocation API.
why: Recovers several percent of wafer output lost to retention fallout and removes refresh energy (fact 3) for that data; supply gain at zero fab capex.
note: Clever lifetime-bounded use of retention rejects; guaranteeing data lifetimes and few-percent supply gain limit impact.

title: Double-angle shadow evaporation sets 20 nm channels without fine lithography
idea: Box: oxide-node charge x lateral oxide TFT whose source-drain gap is set by evaporation angle x current sensing x 2D x glass or Si x Dolan resist bridge plus two tilted e-beam evaporations, borrowed from superconducting-qubit junction fab. The gap equals bridge height times the tangent difference of the two angles, so a ~200 nm optical feature yields a ~20 nm self-aligned channel.
why: Sidesteps litho-bound scaling (fact 4): the critical dimension comes from angle and film thickness, not resolution; any university evaporator with a tilt stage works; risk is wafer-scale angle uniformity.

title: Reflash SSDs to zoned mode, lend freed FTL DRAM via CMB
idea: Box: repurpose × installed NVMe SSDs × controller DRAM (~1 GB per TB) × firmware reflash × NVMe Controller Memory Buffer. Switching drives to zoned/host-managed mapping frees the controller DRAM that held the FTL table, which firmware then exposes to the host as a PCIe-mapped CMB for I/O buffers, queues and spill of warm data.
why: Every installed 30 TB SSD carries ~30 GB of DRAM; reclaiming it adds host-usable memory with zero new wafers, so no new fluorinated etch gases, PFAS resists or fluoropolymer parts are consumed.
note: Needs vendor firmware; CMB latency and size limit usefulness, but zero new wafers.

title: Spectral activation listener detects hammer rhythms without row counters
idea: Po: the attacker sings, so listen for the song. A few Goertzel/sliding-DFT filters per bank analyze the time series of activated row-address bits; hammering shows up as sharp periodic peaks, which trigger targeted refresh of rows matching the peak's address hash, replacing large per-row counter tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) at ~1k thresholds, where counter SRAM becomes prohibitive: mitigation logic area down ~10x versus per-row counters.

title: Discarded phones repurposed as networked RAM nodes
idea: Worsen: landfill over a billion phones a year, each holding 4-12 GB of LPDDR. Flip: wipe and flash phone motherboards with a minimal RDMA-over-USB/Ethernet memory server, rack them as a remote-memory tier, and erasure-code across them for reliability.
why: Cost: near-zero marginal cost per GB from sunk-cost LPDDR, over 100x cheaper; trades latency (about 10 us), management effort and density.
note: Sunk-cost LPDDR is cheap, but per-GB power, latency and fleet management likely erase the savings.

title: Blind demand ledger using multiparty computation to kill double-ordering
idea: Worse: every OEM orders 1.5x from every supplier because nobody sees real demand. Flip: buyers submit encrypted orders to a secure multiparty-computation ledger that reveals only aggregate true demand and flags the same need ordered from several suppliers, without exposing any firm's plans.
why: Damps the bullwhip that turns ~10% real demand shifts into multi-x price spikes; existing supply gets allocated to real need.
note: Privacy-preserving aggregation exposes double-ordering; adoption by competing OEMs is the doubt.

title: Space-CCD bakeout: on-die heaters anneal leakage traps in field
idea: Space telescopes periodically heat their CCDs to anneal radiation-induced traps. Embed resistive heaters in the package or under each bank and, after migrating data away, bake the array at ~150-200 C for minutes a few times a year to anneal variable-retention-time traps and re-passivate interface states.
why: Fact 3: the VRT and tail population that forces refresh guardbands grows with age; periodic anneal resets it, keeping refresh intervals long over life and cutting guardband ~2x.
note: Cheap to test on commodity DIMMs; VRT anneal response unknown.

title: Film-capacitor self-healing: clearing electrodes rescue thin high-k capacitors
idea: Industrial power film capacitors last 30 years because a thin metallization vaporizes around any breakdown spot and isolates it. Build MIM capacitor arrays with a 3-5 nm Al or Ti top-electrode skin that burns back locally under a forming pulse, healing weak spots before a TiN cap goes on, and measure yield versus dielectric thickness in a university fab.
why: Lets ZrO2 stacks thin ~20-30% (higher Cs or shorter pillars) without leakage-tail failures, meaning fewer Zr precursors and less high-AR etch per bit.

title: Rack-level erasure coding lets DIMMs refresh ten times slower
idea: Scale jump from on-die ECC to cross-server parity: a CXL memory pool stripes each cache line plus parity across 10+2 memory nodes, each node refreshes only every ~0.5-1 s, and any decayed row is reconstructed from the other nodes and rewritten, so the rack, not the cell, guarantees retention.
why: Refresh energy at datacenter scale (fact 3): 8-16x fewer refreshes for ~20% parity overhead, plus reuse of retention-weak dies otherwise scrapped.

title: Decay-as-weight-decay memory for training master weights
idea: Time-shift the meaning of leakage: master weights and optimizer moments are rewritten every training step (~1 s), so they sit in refresh-free DRAM where MSBs use double-size robust cells and low mantissa bits use tiny cells whose 1->0 decay acts as stochastic rounding toward zero, a built-in weight decay.
why: Zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and ~30% more bits per area for low-order bits (fact 1).

title: Deferred linear correction: compute on raw weights, subtract error product later
idea: Exploit matmul linearity to shift correction in time: the accelerator multiplies immediately with raw 1%-BER weights (exponent bits ride in a protected lane), while the decoder later emits a sparse error matrix E, and the output is fixed by subtracting E*x at ~1-2% of the original work.
why: Removes ~10-20 ns of decode latency from every HBM read and lets cheap 1%-BER cells feed accelerators at full speed.
note: Matmul linearity lets correction trail compute (ABFT-like); E may be denser than 1-2% at 1% BER.

title: KV-cache precision decays with token age in leaky cells
idea: Time shift (data age = allowed precision): store the LSBs of older KV-cache tokens in unrefreshed weak cells and their MSBs in refreshed cells, so old context loses precision over seconds the way attention already discounts it. New tokens get full refresh.
why: Removes refresh for ~40-60% of KV bits and allows lower-grade cells for long-context inference memory.

title: Compliant nano-pillar chuck that cools wafers without helium backside gas
idea: Scale shift from gas conduction to solid contact: the electrostatic chuck surface carries a forest of compliant metal-coated nano-pillars that conform to the wafer's backside roughness and conduct heat directly, replacing helium backside gas in etch and deposition tools.
why: Helium backside cooling is a major fab helium use. A gas-free thermal contact removes it and also ends helium leak-related wafer loss.
note: Solid-contact nanopillar thermal interface; particles, uniformity and backside contamination are doubts.

title: Core memory's hand-threading killed it; print planar ferrite cores
idea: Ferrite core memory died because the cores had to be threaded by hand. Print soft-ferrite nanoparticle rings in planar form on a web, with screen-printed silver X, Y and sense windings, and read them by coincident-current half-select. There is no access transistor, so there is no leakage and no refresh.
why: A transistor-free, refresh-free, radiation-hard working-memory tier made roll-to-roll from abundant iron oxide. Density is low (~1 Mb/cm2), so the targets are edge and defense uses and supply diversity.

title: Photostructurable glass revived: laser-written trench capacitors inside the substrate
idea: Photostructurable glasses (Foturan, APEX) died in MEMS because UV exposure gave coarse, rough features. Femtosecond laser-induced deep etching (one pulse train modifies a line that then etches ~100x faster) writes ~1 um wide, 20-50 um deep trenches into plain alkali-free display glass; line them with ALD TiN/Al2O3-TiO2/TiN so every TFT cell sits over its own in-glass trench capacitor.
why: The substrate becomes the capacitor: no plasma high-AR etch (no C4F8/SF6), no Hf/Zr, and picofarad-scale charge budgets let tiny, weak TFTs work; trenches are direct-written, maskless.
note: Laser-etched trench caps in glass; cell pitch limited to microns, so density is weak.

title: EnerJ approximate storage fixed with age-aware asymmetric soft decoding
idea: EnerJ-style approximate storage never caught on because developers had to annotate types and accept silent errors. Fix: no refresh at all for buffers with a declared lifetime (activations, gradients, KV blocks); each write is time-stamped, and the decoder feeds elapsed age and the known 1-to-0 leakage direction as soft priors into an LDPC decode, recovering data exactly until the age limit.
why: Zero refresh power with exact, not approximate, results for data living under ~1 s, saving 16-33% of idle power (fact 3) and admitting weaker cells.

title: CCD memory reborn in idle sensor fabs for weight streaming
idea: CCD shift-register memory (Fairchild, Intel, 1970s) lost to DRAM because of serial access, and CCD sensor fabs are idling as CMOS image sensors won. Serial access is now a feature: AI inference streams weights and KV blocks in fixed order, so many parallel CCD loops built on 0.35-0.18 um CCD lines can stream blocks at full rate with no row decoders and little periphery.
why: Density and periphery: CCD storage is ~4F^2 with almost no periphery (vs ~49% of a DRAM die), giving a cheap streaming tier from stranded fabs; random access stays poor.
note: At 0.18-0.35 um, CCD density is ~100x below modern DRAM, so cost per bit likely worse.

title: Marangoni flow planarizes 3D DRAM tiers without chemical-mechanical polishing
idea: Effect: thermocapillary (Marangoni) flow. Spin a flowable siloxane and scan a laser line that sets up a surface-tension gradient, so liquid flows from hot high spots into cooler trenches and levels the topography before UV cure. A ~$250k scanned-laser coater on 100 mm wafers tests planarity over 26-tier stair topography within 24 months.
why: Fact 2: 3D DRAM tier stacks need many CMP steps ($5M tools, slurry, defects); thermocapillary leveling could replace a share of them.

title: Knudsen-regime hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in etch chucks
idea: Wafer-to-chuck heat transfer at 5-20 Torr is gas-kinetic conduction set by molecular speed and accommodation coefficient, where H2 matches or beats He. Feed chucks with on-site electrolytic H2 at sub-flammable volumes, and texture chuck surfaces to raise H2 accommodation.
why: Backside cooling is one of the largest fab helium uses; switching cuts He demand for etch and implant tools while Qatar's ~30% is offline.
note: H2 backside gas is rarely used; low accommodation coefficient, plasma leakage and safety are the doubts.

title: Supercritical-CO2-swellable mold compound frees bare dies for repackaging
idea: Encapsulant is a thermoplastic designed for high CO2 solubility that swells and loses adhesion in scCO2 at 31 C and 74 bar. Retired packages are soaked and rapidly depressurized, delaminating to release intact dies without acids.
why: Bare-die recovery enables re-binning into new packages and stacks, unlike acid decapsulation that destroys dies.
note: Design-for-disassembly mold compound released by scCO2; must still pass moisture, CTE and reliability quals.

title: N: liquid-nitrogen memory pods revive dies rejected for margin
idea: Sell 77 K immersion-cooled memory pods for data centers populated with DRAM dies that failed hot sense-margin or retention bins; at 77 K, MOS mismatch and leakage collapse, so these rejects run at full speed with almost no refresh.
why: Turns 5-15% scrap into product (more usable supply), cuts refresh power (fact 3) to near zero and widens SA margin; nitrogen is abundant, unlike helium.

title: Nitrogen-rich strained SiN bilayers roll planar arrays into memory scrolls
idea: Build a planar oxide-TFT DRAM array with i-line litho on a stress-graded SiNx bilayer over a sacrificial layer; releasing it makes the membrane self-roll into a 10-20-winding Swiss roll, turning the 2D array into a 3D cylinder with ~15 effective tiers per footprint, wired out through the unrolled tail.
why: Gets 3D layer count from 2D lithography with zero high-aspect etching (facts 2, 4); rolled-up nanomembranes are an established university technique, so a prototype memory scroll is buildable now.

title: Ge: sacrificial germanium self-erases as GeO vapor
idea: Use pure Ge sacrificial layers in tier stacks; after the slit opens, lightly oxidize the exposed Ge and anneal at ~500-600 C so Ge + GeO2 -> 2GeO(g) volatilizes, propagating laterally and erasing the layer selective to Si and SiO2 with no etchant gas or liquid.
why: Fact 2 plus water: lateral sacrificial removal with no wet etch, rinse or stiction (~100% module water cut) in a batch furnace.

title: Plywood cross-grain laminated channels break grain-boundary leakage paths
idea: Build the poly channel of 3D/BEOL access transistors as 3-5 ultrathin plies with rotated texture and amorphous seams between them, so grain boundaries never line up through the film. This copies the way plywood crosses its grain to stop through-splits.
why: Off-state tail in poly-Si or poly-oxide channels is set by the worst percolating GB path. Misaligned plies could cut the tail ~10x while on-current still flows along the plies.
note: Cross-ply textured channels break percolating grain-boundary leak paths; cheap to test in TFT runs.

title: Andon cord: fast raw reads, full decode only when confidence drops
idea: Toyota workers pull the andon cord to stop the line only when they see a defect. Weights sit in 1%-BER memory under a systematic LDPC whose data bits are usable as-is, so the fast path reads only the data bits and skips parity. When the model's token entropy or logit margin crosses an anomaly threshold, the step is re-run on parity-decoded weights.
why: Gives cheap-cell capacity with no decode latency on more than 99% of steps, and limits quality loss to rare anomalous steps, at about 12% parity instead of duplicate copies.
note: Entropy may miss silent weight corruption; bf16 exponent flips at 1% BER are severe.

title: Printing-house proofreader: language-model prior corrects flipped token streams
idea: Proofreaders fix typos from context. Stored token streams (prompt histories kept in place of KV, chat logs, RAG document caches, tokenized corpora) live in 1%-BER memory with only about 3% parity. On read, a small language model does joint source-channel decoding: for each corrupted 16-bit token it scores the roughly 17 one-flip candidates by LM likelihood times channel likelihood, subject to the parity, so the redundancy in the text itself corrects the errors.
why: Text carries about 1 bit of entropy per stored character byte, so using that redundancy as the code removes most ECC overhead; combined with storing token IDs instead of KV it supports 100x memory savings for long-context serving.
note: Joint source-channel decoding of token streams with an LM prior; useful only if 1%-BER memory is truly cheaper.

title: Ion-track membranes: particle-drilled pores averaged into capacitor cells
idea: IFR: 'pores drilled by particles, with no lithography.' Backward: irradiate a polyimide or glass sheet with swift heavy ions (~1e10-1e11 tracks/cm2), etch the latent tracks into ~20 nm pores 1-2 um deep, ALD-coat electrode/high-k/electrode, and bond a periodic TFT pad grid on top so each pad collects ~10 random pores whose capacitance averages statistically.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): tens of fF per cell with no etch tool, enough for 2-3 bits per cell; randomness is handled by averaging, not alignment.

title: Low-distortion codes: weights stored so any bit flip barely matters
idea: Combine source coding with error tolerance: each 8-bit quantized weight is mapped to a 10-bit codeword chosen by a Gray/lattice-style assignment so that any single flip moves the decoded value by at most one quantization step; the code itself, not an ECC decoder, absorbs weak-cell errors with zero decode latency.
why: Weak cells for AI (facts 1, 3): allows raw BER ~1e-4 storage with no ECC engine, enabling relaxed refresh or lower-Cs cells for inference memory at 25% overhead.
note: Exact 1-step bound with 10-bit codes is near Hamming-bound infeasible; approximate version fine.

title: Permute weight channels so neighbors compress, then delta-code
idea: Rearrange the order of rows and channels inside each weight matrix (with the matching permutation folded into the next layer) so similar channels sit side by side, then store each channel as a low-bit delta from its predecessor.
why: Adds ~1.3-2x near-lossless compression on top of quantization for weights held in existing DRAM; the permutation is free at runtime and needs no new hardware.
note: Weights are near-noise; delta coding gains on top of quantization uncertain.

title: Frequency-domain KV: DCT along sequence, drop high bands
idea: Rearrange the KV cache from time order to frequency order: blocks of 64 tokens are transformed per channel with a DCT along the sequence axis, high-frequency coefficients are quantized hard or dropped, and attention reads the inverse-transformed block.
why: KV channels change slowly across neighboring tokens, so 3-6x compression beyond token quantization is plausible, as a kernel on existing GPUs with no new silicon.
note: RoPE-rotated keys are not smooth along sequence; easy GPU kernel test.

title: Magnetosome-chain ordering aligns embedding rows for delta compression
idea: As magnetotactic bacteria align magnetosomes into a chain along the field, a one-time pass sorts embedding-table rows along a learned principal axis or space-filling curve so neighbors are similar, then stores each row as an entropy-coded delta from its predecessor; a small index maps original IDs to chain positions.
why: Recommendation embeddings occupy terabytes of DRAM; 2-4x compression decodable at line rate.

title: Companion planting: pair hammer-heavy pages with self-healing neighbours
idea: Gardeners plant companions that protect each other. A kernel page allocator uses the reverse-engineered DRAM address map to put physically adjacent rows next to frequently activated pages. Those adjacent rows are filled with data that rewrites itself every few ms anyway (ring buffers, network and DMA rings, scratch), or with guard and free pages. Hammer victims therefore heal on their own.
why: Raises the effective hammer tolerance with no hardware change (fact 9), as a pure kernel patch within budget.
note: Victims rewritten every few ms may still flip within ~1k activations (~50 us).

title: Bounded-error number encoding makes bit flips harmless
idea: Inverts 'binary place-value storage': KV-cache and activations are stored in a code where any single flipped cell moves the value by at most one quantization step (split-unary or Gray-coded mantissa, exponent stored twice), so errors become tiny noise instead of exponent blowups.
why: Removes ECC need for >50% of AI memory traffic and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER, enabling refresh-starved or weaker cells.

title: Sacrificial canary rows give closed-loop refresh margin
idea: Profile each channel's 64 weakest rows at boot, fill them with known patterns, and refresh them 1.5x less often than data rows. Poll them every interval, so the first canary flip (from a temperature spike or VRT jump) immediately tightens the refresh rate for data rows. Controller firmware and validation cost under $300k.
why: Worst-case guardbanding becomes feedback, so data runs near its measured retention (2-4x the spec interval) on commodity parts (fact 3), at a cost of a few rows per channel.
note: VRT cells jump randomly; canaries may not track the worst data cells.

title: Shortened-tRCD reads act as a non-destructive charge gauge
idea: A cell's remaining charge sets how fast its bitline develops, so reading a row with a deliberately shortened tRCD fails first on the cells that have leaked most. The sense amplifier still restores the row correctly. Probe rows this way periodically, then re-read at nominal timing for the real data, to build a live per-row charge-margin map and give each row its own refresh interval. FPGA controller work, ~$250k.
why: Online profiling that preserves data gets around the VRT problem that makes static profiles unsafe, enabling per-row refresh at 2-4x the average interval (fact 3).

title: Etch-free, lift-off-only 2T0C gain cell from evaporated ultrathin oxides
idea: Box: gate-node charge x ultrathin (3-4 nm) evaporated In2O3 write FET plus p-type SnO read FET x current sensing x 2D/BEOL x any substrate x additive lift-off only, no plasma etching. Every layer is evaporated or sputtered through patterned resist and lifted off, with an oxygen-plasma-free ozone anneal setting carrier density, so the flow needs an aligner, evaporator and sputterer only.
why: Process capital: removes etch tools and their gases from the flow while giving a complementary gain cell whose ultrathin channel keeps off-current low; risk is lift-off resolution and SnO stability.

title: Game texture artist: store tensors in GPU texture compression formats
idea: Game artists have shipped fixed-rate block-compressed textures (BC/ASTC) for decades, and GPU texture units decode them for free. Weights and cached activations are packed as 4x4 blocks in an ASTC-like fixed-rate tensor format and read through the otherwise idle texture-sampling path, which decompresses at line rate with random access and no indirection tables.
why: This gives a fixed 3-6x compression with random access and no ALU cost, using silicon already on every GPU. HBM capacity and bandwidth per model shrink by the same factor.
note: BC/ASTC exploit spatial image correlation that weights lack; little gain over 4-bit quantization.

title: Doppelganger cache, fixed: approximate dedup of near-identical KV blocks
idea: The Doppelganger approximate cache (2015) mapped similar-valued blocks to one copy but died because general programs need exact data. LLM KV caches tolerate it: LSH-hash each 16-token KV block and map blocks within cosine >0.995 across requests and layers to one physical block plus a small residual.
why: Shared-context and templated workloads see 1.5-3x KV footprint reduction, and KV dominates inference DRAM/HBM.
note: Exact prefix caching already captures shared contexts.
