title: tRCD-sweep charge spectroscopy predicts per-row retention in seconds
idea: Effect: RC kinetics of charge sharing. A small team's FPGA DDR5 controller reads each row repeatedly while shortening tRCD in 0.5 ns steps; the step where bits flip shows how far the stored charge sits from the sense trip point after a known wait. Fitting the decay gives each row's leakage rate without hour-long pauses, and rows are binned into 64/128/256/512 ms refresh classes.
why: Refresh (fact 3): multi-rate refresh can cut refresh operations ~60-75%, and profiling drops from hours to seconds per DIMM, so it can run in the field.
note: Reduced-tRCD profiling on an FPGA is easy to demo; VRT cells limit how safe the binning is.

title: Trap-noise fingerprints certify reclaimed DRAM in an open provenance ledger
idea: Each die's map of variable-retention-time cells, caused by random telegraph trapping in access transistors, is a stable physical fingerprint. Recyclers read it in seconds at retirement and register it with grade data, and buyers re-measure it to verify identity and history.
why: Counterfeit risk and unknown history suppress the secondary market; trusted provenance could return ~10% of yearly bit supply from retired servers.
note: Retention PUFs known; VRT cells are unstable by nature, so fingerprint robustness over aging is the doubt.

title: Firefly anti-phase coupled oscillators that self-spread refresh bursts
idea: Pulse-coupled fireflies with inhibitory coupling settle into anti-phase. Each bank's local refresh oscillator senses neighbors' refresh current on a shared line and delays itself when they fire, so refresh bursts spread evenly in time across banks with no central scheduler.
why: Peak refresh current sets power-grid metal, decap area and IR-drop margin. Spreading cuts peak current 4-8x, letting grid and decaps shrink (~2-3% of die).
note: Central schedulers already stagger refresh trivially.

title: Liver-style compensatory compression covers modules out for repair
idea: The liver regrows mass to keep function after losing tissue; when modules are pulled for repair the memory manager raises compression levels on the remaining DRAM to hold logical capacity constant, then relaxes it after reinsertion, so maintenance never shrinks jobs.
why: Removes 5-10% maintenance headroom and makes hot repair routine.

title: Pool memory over polyolefin twinax and acrylate-coated fiber, no FEP
idea: Box: pool × rack interconnect × rack × deployment × foamed PE/PP-insulated twinax + Ge-core silica fiber with urethane-acrylate coating. CXL memory-pooling fabrics are cabled with fluorine-free dielectrics and connectors, and retimers equalize the slightly higher loss so a PFAS ban does not block pooling.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM 10–25% fleetwide, but default high-speed cables use FEP/PTFE; a fluorine-free cable bill of materials keeps that saving deployable.

title: Weaver's warp and weft: codewords across nozzles, never along web
idea: A weaver knows faults run along the warp: inkjet nozzle failures and roller scratches leave long streaks in the machine direction, so the address mapping spreads each ECC codeword's bits across different nozzle tracks in the cross-web direction, and a dead nozzle costs at most one bit per codeword.
why: Correlated streak defects that would overwhelm ECC become independent single-bit errors that SECDED or BCH handles; required ECC strength for printed memory could fall ~2-4x.

title: Li: lithium-6 rack neutron monitor drives space-weather scrubbing
idea: A 6Li-glass scintillator neutron counter per row of racks (no scarce He-3), plus public neutron-monitor feeds, lets the fleet raise scrub rates and ECC modes during solar particle events or at high-altitude sites and relax them otherwise.
why: Soft-error rate tracks neutron flux (~2x over the solar cycle, several x with altitude), so the fleet stops paying worst-case scrub energy all year.
note: Niche scrub-energy saving.

title: Franchise recipe book: one certified memory process for every university fab
idea: Franchises win with an exact operations manual. Freeze an open 'franchise' process for a memory test vehicle, an oxide-channel 1T1C/2T0C array on 150/200 mm using i-line, ALD and sputter, with fixed recipes, golden wafers and inline metrics. Participating nanofabs certify on it and swap wafers mid-flow.
why: Strategy and time: creates a distributed U.S. memory pilot-line network with interchangeable data that speeds materials and cell qualification, at ~$1-2M per site.

title: Hydrogen tracer replaces helium for hermetic optics leak tests
idea: Substitute helium mass-spectrometer leak testing of hermetic optical-interconnect and memory packages with 5% hydrogen-in-nitrogen forming gas and low-cost MEMS palladium hydrogen sensors in a sniffer chamber.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps optical memory interconnect packaging running on a non-scarce gas; tester <$20k.
note: H2/N2 sniffer leak testing is already commercial; small helium saving.

title: Eliminate RMA scrapping: bad-row map stored in module SPD
idea: Eliminate discarding DIMMs with a few failing rows: an open firmware/Linux patch learns failing rows from correctable-error telemetry and writes a compact retirement map into spare SPD EEPROM bytes, so every future host offlines those pages; ~$300k, 12 months, upstreamed to Linux and coreboot.
why: Most fleet DIMM replacements (~1-3%/year) are few-row faults; keeping them in service saves petabytes per hyperscaler.

title: Retired DRAM reborn as unclonable-identity and true-random chips
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the retention-decay map of worn storage cells is random, unique and hard to clone. Recertify end-of-life DRAM dies as PUF identity chips and decay-based true-random generators for IoT security, priced above scrap value.
why: Recyclability and economics: a second life for dies otherwise shredded; raises the residual value of every wafer start.
note: DRAM PUF/TRNG well studied; small residual-value niche.

title: Ant-colony optimizer for spare row and column repair allocation
idea: Ants find short paths with depositing and evaporating pheromone. Ant-colony optimization solves the NP-hard redundancy-allocation problem (which spares fix a fail bitmap) on tester-side GPUs, approaching optimal repair. Two engineers plus partner fail bitmaps, ~$500k in 24 months.
why: Fact 7: spares, fuses and compare logic are several % of the die. Equal repair with ~25% fewer spares, or +1-3% repair yield on today's spares, cuts cost/bit directly.

title: Henneman size-principle recruitment of charge-pump units
idea: Muscles recruit small motor units first and large ones only under heavy load (Henneman's size principle). Each VPP/VBB pump is split into binary-weighted units (1x, 2x, 4x, 8x) enabled in order by a load monitor, so light loads run on small units at peak efficiency. Validated on a 65/130 nm MPW test chip and licensed, ~$700k in 24 months.
why: Fact 10/idle power: pumps are 20-40% efficient at light load. Recruitment roughly doubles that, cutting VPP/VBB standby and refresh power ~30-50%.

title: Power-transformer ester oil: single-phase immersion keeps DIMMs cold, PFAS-free
idea: Grid transformers moved to biodegradable natural-ester oils for safe, fire-resistant cooling. Immerse memory modules, heat spreaders removed, in a forced-flow single-phase synthetic-hydrocarbon or natural-ester bath, replacing the fluorocarbon two-phase fluids now being phased out, and hold every DRAM die at a uniform ~40 C.
why: Uniform low temperature removes hot-spot-driven worst-case refresh and the 2x refresh mode above 85 C (fact 3), with no PFAS fluid.

title: HVAC hydrogen-tracer leak testing eliminates helium mass-spec checks
idea: Refrigeration and automotive A/C lines are leak-checked with non-flammable 5% H2 / 95% N2 tracer and solid-state sniffers. Requalify fab vacuum-chamber, gas-line and package-hermeticity testing to H2 tracer with residual-gas analyzers tuned to mass 2; nothing changes in the DDR/HBM product.
why: Leak checking is a significant non-cooling helium use; switching removes it entirely using forming gas made anywhere, easing the helium chokepoint.

title: Anti-lock-brake pulsed row-open time cap against RowPress
idea: ABS pulses the brakes so the wheels never lock. The open-source FPGA controller caps continuous row-open time (tAggON) at ~200 ns. A row being held open for hits has its buffer copied to a controller-side row cache and is closed early. That defeats RowPress, which multiplies flips 10-100x when rows stay open long.
why: Keeps ACT-count-based protection valid without 10x over-provisioning mitigation (fact 9). It is a policy change demonstrable on DDR5 within budget.

title: Washing machine: endpoint sensors stop rinses when wafers are clean
idea: Stimulus 'washing machine' (rinse cycles run fixed times regardless) -> a 10-person team builds retrofit in-line resistivity/TOC sensors and controllers for wet benches that end each rinse when effluent matches incoming UPW, replacing fixed-time recipes.
why: Wet benches are the largest UPW users; endpoint rinsing cuts UPW and UPW-production energy ~25-40%.

title: UV-LED retrofit kits strip rare-gas lamps from legacy steppers
idea: Box [product: drop-in 365/385 nm LED illuminator | target: installed i-line steppers | layers: non-critical DRAM masks (implant blocks, pads, periphery) | model: per-layer service fee]: replace Hg arc lamps, whose bulbs carry Xe/Ar fill, with long-life LED arrays that switch instantly.
why: Removes rare-gas consumables and mercury from the ~30-40% of DRAM mask layers that are non-critical and cuts their litho energy ~60%; also sells to 200 mm fabs.

title: Repurpose installed Optane PMem as read-only weight and index tier
idea: Box: reuse × installed persistent-memory DIMMs × 256 B block × deployment × DAX-mapped read-mostly data. Fleets still holding discontinued 3D XPoint DIMMs map read-mostly data (model weights, inverted indexes, embedding tables) straight into the address space, sparing DRAM for write-heavy state.
why: Byte-addressable ~300 ns capacity already sitting in racks absorbs read-mostly working sets; no new production, so no fluorinated chemistry.
note: Installed base of discontinued PMem is small and shrinking.

title: Die-transplant repair rebuilds DIMMs with one failed die
idea: Box[Source=RMA'd DIMMs x Transform=localized hot-gas rework swapping single failed DRAM packages x Integration=standard DDR5 DIMM x Owner=repair depot]: most failed DIMMs lose one of 10-20 packages; replace just that package with a harvested good one and requalify, instead of scrapping 19 good dies.
why: Raises yield of the installed base: recovers ~95% of bits in failed modules; unchanged DDR interface.

title: Corn farmer's biochar supercapacitor lets DRAM survive outages
idea: Persona: a farmer who turns corn stover into biochar. Mount KOH-activated stover-carbon supercapacitors (~2000 m2/g) on each DIMM or HBM module, storing ~100-300 J. That is enough to flush DRAM into an on-module NAND shadow when power fails and restore it on boot: non-volatility by architecture.
why: Persistent memory at DRAM speed and cost with no lithium, cobalt or tantalum capacitors. It also replaces rack lithium-ion backup units.

title: Farmer's seed bank: OS donates pages as a growing spare-row pool
idea: A farmer keeps a seed bank instead of a fixed spare field: the memory controller's small CAM remaps failing lines found in the field into a pool of pages the OS donates (0.1-0.5% of capacity), and the pool grows as the module ages instead of relying only on the fixed spare rows fused at the factory.
why: Lets fabs ship dies with fewer on-die spares and lets weaker cells survive field aging; cuts scrap and DIMM RMAs.

title: Child's ice pack: printed phase-change wax pads keep DRAM below 85C
idea: A child puts an ice pack on a fever: thermal pads loaded with microencapsulated paraffin or salt-hydrate phase-change material are screen-printed or roll-to-roll coated onto DIMM heat spreaders and HBM lids; they absorb workload heat bursts as latent heat, so dies stay below the 85 C threshold that forces 2x refresh.
why: Fact 3: avoids double-refresh mode during bursts (refresh costs 10-20% of bandwidth at high density), and gentler thermal cycling slows solder and TSV fatigue.

title: Spider's web: printed ladder-mesh lines survive any single break
idea: A spider's web keeps working when a strand breaks: word- and bitlines are printed as two parallel rails cross-linked every few cells (a ladder or mesh), so a coffee-ring gap, satellite-drop void or crack in one rail is bypassed through the rungs, and the second rail also lowers line resistance.
why: Line opens dominate printed-array yield; the ladder makes yield depend on p2 rather than p, taking a Mb array from near zero to above 95% yield at ~15% area.

title: HVAC-technician tracer gas: hydrogen/nitrogen leak checks replace helium
idea: HVAC and automotive leak technicians use 5% H2 in N2 with palladium sniffers because it is cheap and needs no helium. Requalify vacuum-tool leak checking in a university fab using forming-gas tracer, H2-selective sensors and an RGA tuned to mass 2, and document a minimum detectable leak of ~1e-7 mbar-L/s.
why: Removes a recurring helium use at near-zero cost while supply is disrupted, with a procedure fabs can copy.

title: Legacy-socket emulator: one modern chip impersonates four obsolete ones
idea: 30-year industrial and avionics users hoard obsolete SDRAM and EDO. A 10-person firm builds pin-compatible carrier boards where a small FPGA plus one modern LPDDR4 chip emulates the old parts' timing exactly, releasing hoarded die banks and mature-node wafer starts.
why: Removes legacy demand on mature capacity; the lesson that generalizes is to decouple the interface from the die.

title: Depot-level single-chip repair for failed DIMMs
idea: Military depots repair boards rather than replacing them; data centers scrap a DIMM when one of its 18-36 chips fails. A 10-person depot uses X-ray, IR rework and an inventory of harvested chips to replace the single failed package, retest and return the module.
why: Recovers ~95% of each failed module's bits; a large share of RMA'd DIMMs become supply again.
note: Proven rework technique; RMA volumes are tiny relative to supply.

title: Qualification by kinetic-crossover hunting, not single-Arrhenius extrapolation
idea: Several dead memories (early PCM, CBRAM) passed high-temperature bakes but failed in the field because a second, lower-activation-energy failure path dominated at use conditions. Require bakes at five temperatures (125-250 C) plus Kissinger ramp analysis to detect kinetic crossover, and design storage elements with at least 0.3 eV margin between competing mechanisms.
why: Prevents the late qualification failures that kill ventures and makes the 125 C/10 y guarantee credible early in development.
note: Multi-temperature Arrhenius/Kissinger qualification is standard practice.

title: Pointer residues: self-healing data structures on unprotected memory
idea: Ideal: data structures that heal themselves. Closest: runtimes put a 16-bit residue code of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits and keep redundant back-links, so a corrupted pointer is detected on dereference and rebuilt from its partner; it runs on 1990s-class CPUs with no new silicon.
why: Fact 3: protects the control state that makes bit flips fatal, so bulk memory can run without ECC or at relaxed refresh.

title: Convert idle 3D-NAND lines to vertical floating-body DRAM strings
idea: Worse: insist new DRAM capacity needs new $15B DRAM fabs. Flip: toll existing 200+-layer 3D NAND lines (same oxide/nitride stack, channel-hole etch, staircase) to build vertical-channel capacitorless floating-body cells by swapping the charge-trap film for a thin gate oxide and adding a hole-reservoir body contact, then sell DRAM-class strings under take-or-pay tolling contracts.
why: At NAND-class wafer cost, 200 tiers at 1 bit/cell gives ~5-7 Gb/mm2 versus ~0.5 Gb/mm2 for 2D DRAM (>10x) and reuses tools already paid for (fact 4: 3-5 years, $15B); floating-body retention and refresh load are the main risk.
note: Paid-for NAND lines could give >10x density; close to NEO X-DRAM; floating-body retention and refresh load are the doubt.

title: Curvature: wound film memory roll with edge-metallized bitline contacts
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: like a film capacitor, a 5 um polymer strip carrying nanoimprinted oxide-TFT DRAM arrays is wound into a 1000-turn cylinder; bitlines of every turn run to one edge, where sprayed and laser-patterned end-cap metallization connects them to a CMOS reader disk, so all periphery sits on the circular end face.
why: 100x path: roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~0.5 um aims at ~80 GB/m2 per layer for ~$5-10/m2 (~$0.1/GB), with the reader disk amortized over 1000 turns; trade-offs: us-ms access, retention needs very low-leakage TFTs and end-cap registration is unproven. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.
note: Film-capacitor winding for ~$0.1/GB bulk tier; doubts: end-cap contact registration over 1000 turns, TFT retention, us-ms access.

title: Ferroelectric tunnel door sealing a capacitor's charge
idea: Combine a ferroelectric tunnel junction with a storage capacitor: the only path into the node is a 2-3 nm ferroelectric barrier whose polarization toggles it between transparent and opaque (tunneling ratio >1e5). The door is switched open for a write and closed to lock the charge, while a separate gain transistor reads the node without opening it.
why: Zero refresh while keeping charge storage (unlimited reads); the ferroelectric switches only on writes; closed-state tunneling must reach sub-aA levels.
note: Write-in-ns needs ~100 nA on; 1e5 ratio leaves pA off-current, so retention is ms, not years.

title: OFDM-style time-constant coding of eight nodes behind one transistor
idea: Borrow multicarrier telecom decoding: connect eight storage nodes to one access transistor through tunnel barriers of graded thickness (tau = 1, 2, 4 ... 128 ns); a read records the discharge transient and a matrix-pencil decoder recovers each node's charge.
why: 10x at same cost: 8 nodes share one transistor and contact, barriers are deposition-defined, so ~6x from sharing x 2 tiers with no extra masks.
note: Nodes share charge through barriers when idle, and exponential decoding is ill-conditioned at kT/C noise.

title: Protonic double-layer storage node packs tenfold charge per area
idea: The charge wall assumes a dielectric; an electric double layer (Debye length ~1 nm) stores ~10-20 uF/cm^2, ~10x a ZrO2/Al2O3 stack. Fill a shallow storage node with a hydrated nanoporous silica proton conductor between TiN electrodes so a planar or AR ~10:1 cell holds ~5 fF, with proton hops charging in nanoseconds.
why: Capacitor wall and capital: removes high-aspect-ratio etch and deposition tools, the biggest fab cost driver; charging speed and faradaic leakage are unproven.
note: EDL gives ~10x areal capacitance; doubt: proton RC ~microseconds and faradaic leakage kill ns access and retention.

title: T-RAM rebuilt as stacked back-end oxide thyristors
idea: T-RAM's thyristor cell died needing SOI and fighting temperature-sensitive leakage in silicon. Build the p-n-p-n latch from low-temperature deposited oxides (p-type SnO or Cu2O over n-type IGZO) in back-end layers, where wide bandgaps cut thermal leakage by orders of magnitude, using one via-sized mask per tier and stacking 8 tiers above the periphery.
why: Removes SOI and front-end area; a bistable latch needs no refresh (recovers ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth); 8 BEOL tiers give ~8x bits per mm2 without any EUV layer.
note: No-refresh stacked tiers; trap-dominated oxides lack the bipolar gain a thyristor needs.

title: Megasonic in-package anneal heals interface traps in cheap poly channels
idea: Effect: acoustically stimulated defect reconfiguration (ultrasound-induced interface-trap reduction in MOS structures). A transducer in the module periodically injects MHz acoustic energy into the 3D die, reordering and passivating traps in low-cost polysilicon thin-film access transistors and narrowing their leakage tail in the field (self-healing).
why: 10x density: poly-Si tiers cost far less per layer than single-crystal but have ~100x worse tails; healing them makes 40-tier poly-Si 3D DRAM (~10x) viable at the same cost.
note: Key doubt: ultrasound trap passivation is small and transient; 100x poly-Si tail narrowing needs a miracle.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM bonded whole to wafer-scale logic
idea: IFR: 'no dicing, no packages, no interposers.' Backward: never dice the DRAM wafer; stitch a redundant mesh across reticle boundaries, disable bad reticles at test, and wafer-to-wafer bond the whole DRAM wafer onto a wafer-scale processor.
why: HBM tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): no base dies, interposers or stack yield loss; ~3-4 TB of memory at <0.5 pJ/bit on one bonded pair.
note: Duplicate of I-08421: whole-wafer DRAM bonded to wafer-scale logic; yield/redundancy is the crux.

title: High-bandwidth flash stacks feed read-mostly weights through SRAM staging
idea: Worsen: keep weights written once a month in memory built for endless writes. Flip: stack charge-trap NAND dies with many small planes in the HBM footprint, read them wide and in parallel into a base-die SRAM staging buffer, and serve weights from there, leaving DRAM only for KV and activations.
why: Cost per bit: NAND is ~10-20x cheaper per bit than HBM; endurance is irrelevant for weights and deterministic streaming hides flash latency.
note: Essentially SanDisk/SK hynix High Bandwidth Flash (2025); real cost win for read-mostly weights, read latency/disturb are doubts.

title: Substitute idle wafer backsides with backside memory tiers
idea: Swap the bare thinned backside of logic or DRAM wafers, already processed below 400 C for backside power delivery, for a surface carrying oxide gain-cell tiers linked by nano-TSVs.
why: Nearly doubles the usable area per processed wafer; adds memory bits to every logic wafer without new substrate.

title: Shared oxide preamp in capacitor layer per eight cells
idea: Place one vertical IGZO or poly-Si source-follower in the BEOL capacitor layer for every 8 stacked-capacitor cells: the selected cell dumps charge onto a ~1 fF local node instead of a 60-80 fF bitline, and the preamp drives the long bitline. This combines plain 1T1C storage with gain-cell-style amplification at the cell-group level, not per cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): ~10x better transfer ratio lets Cs fall from 5 fF to ~1 fF and capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~15:1, a large etch and capex relief.
note: A BEOL IGZO follower per 8 cells shrinks the sensed node, letting Cs and aspect ratio fall; restore path and Vt spread are open questions.

title: DRAM bonded onto processor backside, sharing its backside power network
idea: Combine backside power delivery (BSPDN, arriving at 2 nm logic) with memory stacking: hybrid-bond a thinned DRAM die onto the logic die's backside PDN layer and reuse the same nano-TSV process that brings power in to carry memory signals, keeping the front side for signals and cooling.
why: Data movement: ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, no interposer, no HBM base die, reuses backside steps already paid for in logic fabs.
note: Reuse of BSPDN nano-TSVs for memory signals is novel; thermal and process clash unresolved.

title: VCSEL arrays on HBM top die, fibers routed inside cold plate
idea: Combine the liquid cold plate already sitting on HBM stacks with optical I/O: bond VCSEL and photodiode arrays on the top core die (fed by TSVs from the base) and embed glass waveguide bundles inside the cold plate so light exits vertically through the plate to rack-scale memory or peer GPUs.
why: Package beachfront and pooling: adds Tb/s per stack from the top surface at ~1-2 pJ/bit over meters without consuming interposer edge.

title: Cold-chain use-by dates: TTL-typed memory in refresh-free banks
idea: Borrowed from perishable-food logistics where every pallet carries a use-by date: allocations carry a time-to-live (malloc_ttl, compiler-known tensor lifetimes), and the controller places sub-retention lifetimes in banks with refresh permanently disabled, built with ~5x smaller capacitors that only need ~10 ms retention; long-lived data goes to SRAM or non-volatile tiers.
why: Zero refresh power for the ephemeral majority (activations, request heaps, packet buffers); small-capacitor ephemeral cells sidestep the 60-75:1 charge wall for denser, cheaper bits.
note: Small-cap short-retention banks for ephemeral data; leakage tail and custom DRAM die are doubts.

title: Magnify Spruce Pine leverage: quartz-for-fabs trade policy
idea: The U.S. supplies >80% of high-purity crucible quartz; tie long-term HPQ export allocations to memory makers' U.S. capacity commitments on a sliding scale of tons per domestic wafer-start.
why: Turns a U.S.-held chokepoint into a lever for U.S. manufacturability; could pull 10-20% of global DRAM capacity onshore within a decade.
note: Trade-law limits and emerging non-U.S. HPQ sources weaken the lever.

title: Vertical CCD pillars: bits climb a 100-gate stack instead of being addressed
idea: Reverse addressing: rather than moving the sense amp to the bit, clock charge packets up and down a 180 nm channel hole lined with polysilicon through 100 LPCVD-deposited gate layers (hole etched with 1990s deep-trench AR ~40); a sense node at the pillar top reads packets in sequence, ~50 bits per pillar.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): one 180 nm mask defines holes while film thickness sets vertical pitch, ~0.003 um2/bit footprint (near 12 nm DRAM) with zero EUV; ~50 ns average shift latency; risk is transfer efficiency in poly channels.
note: Charge-transfer efficiency over 100 poly-Si gates is the killer doubt.

title: Phyllotactic offset leaves halve the tier pitch of 3D DRAM
idea: Leaves alternate around a stem so they never shade each other; build the lateral 3D stack from two alternating SiGe compositions (A, B) and etch two interleaved hole sets, the first recessing only A tiers and the second only B tiers, so capacitor 'leaves' of neighbouring tiers sit half a cell offset rather than stacked. Coupling and leaning loads fall, so tier pitch can shrink from ~60 nm to ~30 nm.
why: Two masks serve every tier; doubling tiers per micron of stack lets an 80-tier stack fit where 40 did, reaching ~10x planar bits/mm2 at near-equal wafer cost (fact 2).

title: Moore-Shannon quadded relays revived as stacked series access transistors
idea: Moore and Shannon (1956) built reliable switching networks from crummy relays by series-parallel quadding. Build each vertical-channel access device as two gate segments stacked along the same pillar and driven by one wordline; a cell leaks only if both segments carry tail defects (trap-assisted GIDL, junction traps), which squares the tail probability, and in 4F2 vertical cells the second gate costs height, not area.
why: Access-leakage tail (fact 3): tail fraction ~1e-5 to ~1e-10, so refresh is set by the bulk distribution (~1 s instead of 64 ms), saving most of the 16-33% idle refresh power; on-current falls ~2x, recovered with pillar height.
note: Series gates square channel-leak tail, but junction/GIDL leakage to the body bypasses them.

title: Universal pre-patterned array blanks bought like SOI wafers
idea: Inverts 'every DRAM maker patterns its own array front end'. One mega-line with EUV makes standardized 'array blanks' (honeycomb active area plus buried wordlines, the first ~20 critical steps) for all customers; DRAM makers buy blanks like SOI wafers and finish capacitors, periphery and BEOL on DUV-only lines.
why: Concentrates the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) in one fully loaded line, so the rest of industry needs no EUV; scale and utilization could cut litho capital per bit ~30%.
note: Later storage-node contacts still need tight overlay, so DUV-only finishing is doubtful.

title: Odd and even buried wordlines at different depths
idea: Inverts 'all wordlines sit at the same depth': the single added mask covers even rows during an extra recess etch so odd buried wordlines sit ~15-20 nm deeper, staggering aggressor gates vertically away from neighbor storage-node junctions without changing pitch.
why: Weakens passing-gate and neighbor coupling, the dominant hammer paths at F~12 nm (fact 9); estimated 3-5x higher hammer threshold.
note: Depth stagger alters Vt of alternate rows; hammer gain unverified, needs fab.

title: Passive optical splitters copy one weight stream to many accelerators
idea: Copying a bit electrically costs CV^2 at every receiver; an optical 1:N splitter copies light passively, down to a shot-noise floor of ~100 photons per bit per receiver. Serve weights from a single pooled memory through polymer waveguides laminated into the organic board with 1:16 splitters, and synchronize the replicas so all of them read the same layer at the same moment.
why: Data-parallel replicas stop holding private weight copies, so weight memory per replica falls up to 16x; each extra receiver costs ~0.1 pJ/bit vs ~1-3 pJ/bit electrically.
note: Insight: passive optical fan-out lets lockstep replicas share one weight copy; doubt: splitter loss and TB/s per receiver.

title: Croissant lamination: binary-tree bonding of tested half-stacks for 3D DRAM
idea: Random stimulus 'croissant' (fold dough, layers double) -> 3D DRAM tiers are built as single-crystal SOI-like silicon layers by smart-cut transfer, merged pairwise in parallel (1+1 -> 2, 2+2 -> 4, ... -> 32). Every sub-stack is e-beam- and probe-tested before merging, so bad half-stacks are discarded early instead of poisoning a finished 32-tier wafer.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): bonded layers give perfect lateral-transistor silicon without Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy. Tree merging cuts serial cycle time from N to log2(N) bond steps and turns multiplicative tier-yield loss into screened yield.
note: Pre-testing and log2(N) pairwise merging is a nice yield insight; inter-tier wiring and orientation flips unclear.

title: Interposer made of DRAM: memory inside the substrate
idea: Box: planar 1T1C at relaxed F~25 nm x planar access x local SA x face-to-face hybrid bond x the interposer itself x DUV-only fab. The 2.5D interposer, today dead silicon, is fabricated as a reticle-stitched DRAM array with routing channels, and GPU/CPU chiplets hybrid-bond on top so each chiplet reads the gigabytes directly beneath it.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and data movement (fact 5): DUV-only node with zero EUV layers, reuses area already paid for, ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical access, ~10-20 GB per 2,500 mm2 interposer.
note: Planar-cell charge and stitched-array yield are doubts; reuses paid-for interposer area.

title: Open-source DRAM process kit built from expired patents
idea: Po: the fab is open source. A consortium assembles a full 30-40 nm-class stacked-capacitor DRAM process flow and array/periphery design from patents that have expired, publishes it under an open license, and qualifies it at a U.S. specialty foundry for legacy DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4.
why: Removes the IP and know-how barrier that keeps DRAM a three-firm market; legacy grades still ship billions of units to auto/industrial; attacks U.S. manufacturability and supplier diversity.
note: Expired patents omit the tacit yield know-how that is the real barrier.

title: Passive optical multicast feeds one weight copy to many accelerators
idea: Worsen: give each of 8-72 GPUs its own private HBM copy of the same model weights. Flip: keep one copy in a pooled memory appliance and broadcast weight streams through passive 1:32 optical splitters, so every accelerator receives the same layer at once and holds only activations and KV locally.
why: Usable supply: weight replication (often 50-80% of inference HBM) shrinks by the fan-out factor, freeing HBM for KV cache.
note: Needs lockstep GPUs and TB/s optical receive per device; split loss limits fan-out.

title: Military logistician: containerized sub-400 C memory micro-fabs shipped to sites
idea: A logistician ships capability in boxes. Because a <=400 C flow needs no furnaces, epi or implanters, pack a complete memory-tier line (sputter, PE-ALD, imprint stepper, etch, wet clean, metrology) into ~20 mini-environment 40-ft containers that deploy beside packaging plants or logic fabs and add tiers to purchased CMOS wafers.
why: Mass-produced modules could bring capex to ~$200-500M per 10k wafers/month, deploy in 6-12 months and spread U.S. manufacturing. Risks: contamination control and yield at container scale.

title: Alien asks why three companies own memory: open DRAM PDK
idea: An alien surveying Earth finds a three-vendor oligopoly. The U.S. buys a full mature-node DRAM process (or requires one through CHIPS conditions): 1y-nm 8 Gb cell, sense amp, redundancy and test flow. It publishes this as a licensed open PDK with a reference die, so any foundry (GF, Intel, SkyWater, TI) can run DRAM wafers on spare 300 mm capacity.
why: U.S. manufacturability and the know-how chokepoint: existing logic foundries could add DRAM output in ~2 years instead of 5; 20k wafers/month adds ~3-4% to world supply.
note: Know-how is the real chokepoint; transferring DRAM cell/capacitor modules to logic foundries is a large unknown.

title: Hibernation-latch ferroelectric gate: Vt parked high in deep idle
idea: Rosetta's spacecraft slept 31 months. Add a thin ferroelectric layer to the buried-wordline gate stack that is polarized only when a bank enters or leaves a long idle state (minutes to hours), shifting access Vt up ~0.4 V while hibernating and back when active; flips happen per hibernation, not per access, so ~1e6 cycles suffice.
why: Fact 3: idle banks of cold data (most server memory at any moment) get ~1e4 lower leakage and almost no refresh, without the endurance wall that ruled out per-access ferroelectric switching.

title: One hybrid-bond pad mask bolting a compressor onto every bank
idea: A single added Cu hybrid-bond pad mask on top of a standard DRAM wafer exposes each bank's internal data bus. A face-to-face bonded logic die compresses and decompresses per bank at internal bandwidth, so the capacity gain costs no external bandwidth. Compression moves from the CPU, centimeters away, to the bank, micrometers away.
why: About 2x effective capacity at bank-level bandwidth, with no TSVs and one mask.

title: Harvest HBM stacks from retired AI accelerators into CXL memory
idea: Time-scale mismatch: AI accelerators retire after ~3 years, but their HBM stacks keep working for 10+. Laser-debond each stack from its retired interposer, remount it on an HBM-to-CXL bridge carrier, and deploy it as a pooled near-memory tier.
why: Every HBM bit cost ~3x the wafer area of DDR5. Reclaiming even 30% of retired HBM adds exabytes of usable memory with no new wafers.
note: Debonding underfilled HBM from interposers and bridging 1024-bit PHY to CXL is hard but new.

title: Periphery foundry shuttle: the DRAM fab access startups never got
idea: Failure mined: Z-RAM, T-RAM and Nantero each died partly because they could never prove their sensing or cells inside a real DRAM flow. Fix: a for-profit multi-project-wafer service on a U.S. DRAM pilot line that sells 1 mm^2 slots next to a standard array. Startups drop in new sense amps, decoders or cells and get silicon back in 10 weeks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: a periphery experiment drops from ~$50M to ~$100k, and learning cycles run ~5x faster.

title: Shuttered Gen-10 LCD fabs reborn as stacked oxide-TFT memory fabs
idea: Giant LCD fabs are closing (Sharp's Sakai panel line halted in 2024) because TV panels commoditized, stranding PECVD, sputter, stepper and wet lines. Convert one into a glass-memory fab: 3-6 stacked oxide-TFT gain-cell tiers per ~9 m2 Gen-10 sheet, singulated into memory slabs, with only the host interface on a small chiplet.
why: Capital: reuses a ~$5-10B sunk fab at cents on the dollar; no Cz silicon, quartz crucibles, helium-cooled chucks or EUV; ~10 GB/m2 per tier at 1.2 um gives ~300+ GB per sheet, competitive as a capacity tier if sub-um patterning lands.
note: Sunk-capital reuse is clever; micron-scale TFT patterning gives poor density per area.

title: MAPPER revived for arrays: all beamlets write one shared tile
idea: MAPPER's 13,000-beam maskless e-beam went bankrupt in 2018 because its data path (petabits per wafer) and throughput never closed. Memory arrays repeat one cell billions of times, so drive every beamlet from one shared on-chip blanking pattern broadcast to all, collapsing the data path ~1e6x, and use it only for the 3-5 array layers while periphery stays on DUV.
why: EUV dependence and mask cost: replaces EUV scanners and masks on array layers with a ~$30M maskless tool; saves ~$10M+ mask sets per node and removes the single-supplier EUV chokepoint for those layers.
note: Broadcast pattern kills the data-path problem; current/throughput and beam reliability remain.

title: Tax credit for certified bytes-per-task software reductions
idea: IFR: saving a byte is valued like making one. Constraint: no materials at all, so make it policy: a federal credit pays firms per GB-year of DRAM demand avoided, measured against a standardized bytes-per-task benchmark suite and audited like energy-efficiency incentives.
why: Creates a market for compression, dedup and KV-efficiency software; a 10% demand cut equals a fab's output without the $15B.
note: Counterfactual bytes-avoided is hard to audit and easy to game.

title: Column-gated double-gate access: only requested 64 cells ever open
idea: Limit: never disturb a cell you did not ask for. Give each vertical-channel access transistor a back gate tied to a column-enable line running orthogonally to the wordline, so a cell connects only when wordline AND column-enable are high; only the 64-bit target slice charge-shares, and only its 64 sense amps fire and restore.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): ~5.9 pJ per useful bit could fall to ~0.3-0.5 pJ, sense energy -95%, and partial activations reduce row-hammer exposure (fact 9).
note: Extra back-gate line per column at 4F2 pitch is hard.

title: Power-fail dump: every sense amp owns a vertical NV backup string
idea: Constraint: DRAM data must survive power loss without giving up DRAM endurance. Under each SA stripe, a hybrid-bonded layer gives every sense amp its own short FeFET or charge-trap string; on power-fail detect, all banks open rows in lockstep and ~2M SAs per die program their bits in parallel, dumping 32 Gb in ~1 ms from on-package capacitors, then restore through the same SAs at power-up.
why: NV DRAM with no NVDIMM flash controller or battery; backup parallelism ~1000x NVDIMM-N, and the NV layer sees one write per power cycle, so its endurance is irrelevant.

title: Backside-BEOL DRAM on backside-power logic wafers
idea: Under 400 C, in the backside metal stack that backside-power-delivery logic processes already build, insert two to four oxide 1T1C tiers between power rails, directly under the logic transistors and about 1 um away.
why: Fact 5: GB-class memory at about 0.1 pJ/bit with no added wafer, package or bonding step.

title: Mirror-VCT: 4F2 oxide cells above and below one shared bitline plane (2F2 effective)
idea: Build a 4F2 vertical-channel 1T1C array (deposited IGZO/IGO pillars, ring wordlines) over a buried bitline plane, with capacitors on top, as in Samsung's VCT. Bond that face to the periphery wafer (the periphery-under-cell flow already flips the cell wafer), remove the handle down to the back of the bitline plane, and build a mirror-image 4F2 VCT array plus capacitors from the backside at <=400 C. Each bitline now connects cells above and below it, so one bitline layer, one set of bitline contacts and one periphery wafer serve two cell layers: 2F2 effective per bit. The backside module is all-deposited (ALD oxide channel, ALD ZrO2 MIM), so it never exceeds BEOL temperatures.
why: 2x density over single-sided 4F2: 0.88 Gb/mm2 (1.96x 1-beta) at F = 20 nm with DUV multipatterning only, or 1.62 Gb/mm2 (3.6x) at F = 14.7 nm; ~1.4-1.5x bits/$ vs single-sided VCT.

title: Memory interposer: oxide gain-cell tiers built into the silicon interposer
idea: Large AI packages use a silicon interposer that carries only wires and TSVs. Build 8 tiers of BEOL oxide gain cells (B3-04 coax cells, or A3-style vertical 2T0C) into the interposer's metal stack at <=400 C on the 65 nm-class line that makes interposers, with stitched periodic arrays under the GPU and HBM footprints and keep-outs around TSVs and bump fields. The GPU reads this memory straight down through its existing micro-bumps or hybrid bonds, adding a capacity tier between on-die SRAM and HBM with no extra footprint. Oxide cells hold >200 s at 95 C (imec), so the hot interposer is acceptable.
why: +21-145 GB per package on a 2,700 mm2 interposer (up to ~250 GB on 4,700 mm2) at ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3.5 for HBM, for ~$100-240 of added tier cost per interposer.

title: Swap ionic ferroelectric for sliding-stacking ferroelectric tunnel barrier
idea: Use parallel-stacked bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2 as an atomically thin tunnel barrier whose out-of-plane polarization flips when the layers slide by one-third of a unit cell. No ions move and no bonds break, so the cell should be fatigue-free, and the polarization modulates the tunnelling current for non-destructive read.
why: Turns endurance-limited ferroelectric memory into DRAM-endurance memory (>10^15 cycles targeted) at ~0.5 V (fact 10), and non-volatility removes refresh (fact 3).
note: Sliding ferroelectric endurance results promising; wafer-scale 2D integration is the gap.

title: Swap EUV hole patterning for guided anodic-alumina self-ordered pores
idea: Deposit 2-3 um of aluminum over DUV-made access transistors and imprint shallow DUV-defined pits at the landing-pad positions. Anodizing then nucleates pores at the pits, which self-order into ~25 nm holes with AR above 100:1, and ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN lines them as storage capacitors.
why: Exceeds the 60-75:1 pillar AR wall (fact 1) without EUV or a high-AR plasma etch (fact 4). The wet electrochemical step costs a few dollars per wafer and uses tools from the aluminum-capacitor industry.

title: Substitute silicon channel with beta-Ga2O3 ultrawide-gap access transistor
idea: Substitute the crystalline-Si access channel with a 4-6 nm beta-Ga2O3 (Eg 4.8 eV) gate-all-around channel built as a tier over the CMOS periphery and crystallized by local anneal. Its intrinsic carrier density is ~1e-22 that of Si, and because it contains no indium it avoids the indium supply that IGZO depends on.
why: Leakage tail/refresh: off-current below 1e-20 A per cell stretches retention from 64 ms to >100 s, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss by >99%. It goes beyond the IGZO prior work with a wider gap and no indium.
note: Ga2O3 beyond IGZO; crystalline thin-film quality at low temperature is the doubt.

title: Mass-transfer printing of pre-tested micro-tiles replaces monolithic stacking
idea: Substitute TSV die stacks or monolithic tiers with microLED-style elastomer-stamp mass transfer: 60x60 um DRAM sub-array micro-tiles (array + local SAs, ~3 um thick, released by sacrificial undercut) are tested on the source wafer and printed layer by layer onto a logic host with planarized redistribution vias between layers.
why: Yield and data movement (facts 5-6): bad tiles discarded at 60 um granularity instead of whole dies; memory sits within um of compute; tool base already exists in microLED fabs.
note: MicroLED mass transfer for DRAM sub-array tiles; ~1 um placement accuracy limits inter-tier via density.

title: Edge-standing bookshelf die stacks replace TSV vertical stacking
idea: Substitute horizontal TSV stacking with dies standing on edge like books: each thinned 30 um DRAM die routes I/O along its face to fine-pitch edge pads (exposed by dicing through scribe Cu bars), and 32-64 dies are laminated and bonded edge-down onto the base logic die, with heat leaving through full die faces to a top cold plate.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSVs, so no 3x area per bit or via yield loss; ~1-2k edge pads per die at 10 um pitch supports HBM-class width.
note: Edge-standing stacks remove TSVs; fine-pitch edge pad yield and lamination flatness are the doubts.

title: Crystal-plane KOH trenches on (110) silicon replace plasma deep etch
idea: Substitute fluorocarbon/Bosch deep etching with crystallographic wet etching: on (110) Si, KOH/TMAH etches trenches bounded by vertical {111} planes at AR >100:1 with atomically smooth walls; a dedicated bonded (110) capacitor wafer carries fin-shaped trench plates lined with TiCl4-ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN, its SiN hard mask opened with hot H3PO4.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): crystalline AR >100 from a wet bench costing ~1/20 of a HAR etcher, no fluorinated chemistry; line-shaped plates resist the pillar leaning that limits AR today.
note: (110) KOH gives very high AR cheaply; bonded capacitor wafer needs cell-pitch hybrid bonding.

title: Substitute ordinary US quartzite for Spruce Pine pegmatite via chlorination
idea: Upgrade widespread domestic quartzite and glass sand to crucible grade: microwave thermal-shock decrepitation opens fluid inclusions, hot Cl2/HCl gas leaching at 1100-1200 C volatilizes Al, alkali and Fe as chlorides, and vacuum fusion yields bubble-free high-purity silica.
why: Breaks the single-district HPQ chokepoint for crucibles, furnace ware and mask blanks by turning dozens of common US deposits into feedstock.

title: Substitute lithographic critical dimensions with sidewall-deposited film thicknesses
idea: Lay the cell on its side: gate length, channel thickness and capacitor dielectric are all set by ALD film thickness on sidewalls of coarse DUV-defined steps, so atomic-precision deposition replaces nm-precision lithography. Each tier needs only one coarse block mask because F no longer sets channel length.
why: Fact 4: breaks litho-bound scaling, since feature size follows ALD (+/-0.1 nm) instead of EUV; could remove 4-5 EUV layers per wafer.

title: Substitute bulk silicon with back-gated FD-SOI for dynamic-threshold cells
idea: Build the array on ultra-thin-body SOI with a buried back-gate plane held at deep negative bias during retention (high Vt, low leakage) and pulsed toward zero only under the activated mat, so the front wordline needs only a ~0.8 V swing; the recessed-channel BCAT etch module and VPP pumps go away.
why: Constraint: wordline energy ~14x lower (0.8 V vs 3 V) and lower bitline voltage give ~8-12x per access; facet: deletes the recessed-gate litho/etch module.

title: Substitute dissipative line charging with adiabatic resonant charge recovery
idea: Drive bitline precharge and wordlines from LC resonant rails using high-Q spiral inductors in a thick-copper redistribution layer borrowed from RF BEOL, ramping lines over ~5 ns so most of their CV2 energy returns to the tank instead of heating drivers.
why: Constraint: adiabatic recovery of 80-90% of line energy gives ~5-10x per access on the dominant line-charging term; facet: no new array lithography, only one mature thick-metal layer.

title: Substitute random-access cells with short-loop charge-coupled shift-register memory
idea: Store bits as charge packets in 64-stage CCD loops built only from parallel gate lines (no per-cell contacts, capacitors or access transistors), ideal for SAQP or self-assembled line/space patterning; a read clocks the loop past its single sense node using ~0.3 V three-phase clocks.
why: Constraint: a packet transfer costs ~fJ per stage, ~0.1 pJ/bit versus 5.9 pJ per useful bit; facet: line/space-only lithography, no HAR etch, 2-3 critical masks. Latency (~32-64 ns) and dark-current refresh are the risks.

title: Substitute copper die-to-die wires with microLED free-space optical links
idea: Each DRAM die face carries arrays of mass-transferred GaN micro-LEDs and silicon photodiodes (1-2 Gb/s per lane, thousands of lanes) that talk across the stack or to the processor through short imaging optics, replacing TSV/microbump buses and SerDes.
why: Constraint: ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit versus 3-15 pJ/bit (>=10x); facet: no TSV etch/fill and no microbump yield loss (fact 6), using display-industry microLED transfer.

title: Femtosecond-laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers
idea: Substitute copper interposer RDL with optical waveguides written in 3D inside a fused-silica interposer by femtosecond-laser index modification, evanescently coupled to grating ports on the GPU and HBM base die; waveguides cross in 3D without crosstalk, collapsing many routing layers into one glass volume.
why: Fact 5: interposer hop from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~1 pJ/bit, and HBM can sit 20-50 mm away, breaking the shoreline limit on stack count.

title: Origami flex interposer folds memory stacks around the processor
idea: Substitute the flat interposer with a 2 um-line polyimide flex bonded at the GPU edges and folded up and over, so HBM stacks mount on vertical walls and above the GPU, tripling the number of stacks within 5 mm of the die edge.
why: Shoreline limit (Facts 5/6): ~3x more stacks per processor without longer wires; memory capacity per accelerator up 2-3x.

title: Substitute DRAM fabs with idle display panel fabs making oxide memory
idea: Swap new DRAM fabs for under-used Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED lines, whose IGZO backplane processes already stay below ~350-400 C, upgraded with sub-um panel steppers to make 2T0C oxide gain-cell memory dies on glass.
why: Uses tens of billions of dollars of depreciated capacity for slower-capacity memory tiers; density per area is far lower, so the gain is capital and time-to-supply, not cost per bit.

title: Substitute DRAM-only supply with an open IP pool for foundry memory tiers
idea: Swap memory vendors' monopoly for a licensing pool that gives every logic foundry a qualified recipe for 4-8 tiers of oxide gain-cell memory built in BEOL at <=400 C above their logic.
why: Turns all U.S. logic capacity into memory capacity without new front-end tools, attacking U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity at once.
note: Oxide gain cells widely pursued; open IP pool for logic foundries is the twist.

title: Charge-active, polarization-parked hybrid capacitor rows
idea: Combine a DRAM capacitor and a FeRAM capacitor in one ZrO2/HZO bilayer: rows in active use run as fast volatile charge cells, and when a row sits idle past ~10 ms the controller issues one plate pulse that copies its charge state into the ferroelectric polarization and powers the row down. Idle rows cost zero refresh, and the first access restores them to charge mode.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy on idle data (most of capacity) goes to zero with no change to active performance; ferroelectric wear is spent only per park (~1e6 parks/year).
note: Parking idle rows into polarization cuts idle refresh; NVDRAM-like hybrids exist.

title: Silicon carbide cell array hybrid-bonded to silicon periphery
idea: Build the access transistors and storage junctions in 4H-SiC (Eg 3.26 eV) and hybrid-bond the array to a Si CMOS periphery wafer.
why: Junction generation leakage scales with intrinsic carrier density, which is ~1e-8 cm^-3 in SiC against ~1e10 in Si. That allows refresh-free, hour-scale retention, and SiC substrate supply is expanding in the U.S. through EV demand.
note: Hour-scale retention from SiC ni is real (Purdue); doubt is SiC MOS interface quality at DRAM pitch.

title: Antiferroelectric capacitor that switches to nonvolatile mode for sleep
idea: Use a ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric capacitor: high-k and non-remanent in DRAM mode. On sleep, a plate-line offset bias (as in work-function-engineered AFE memory) parks the loop so two polarization states hold with no power, and wake reads them back.
why: Removes self-refresh in standby (16-33% of idle power) and gives instant wake, while active-mode endurance stays unlimited.

title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout with correlated double sampling
idea: Adopt CMOS image-sensor pixel readout: a transfer gate moves cell charge onto a ~0.5 fF floating diffusion read by a source follower, sampled before and after transfer (correlated double sampling) to cancel kTC noise and offset at ~2 electrons rms. A cell then needs only ~1,000 electrons (~0.15 fF at 1 V).
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs ~30x smaller, removing high-AR capacitor etch; the cost is a slower ~30-50 ns read, acceptable for a capacity tier.

title: Open array-periphery bond standard plus CHIPS grants
idea: Publish an open die-to-die standard that fixes the bitline-group, wordline and power pinout between DRAM array wafers and periphery wafers, and use CHIPS-style grants to have U.S. trailing logic fabs (90-22 nm) build the periphery tier for any array maker.
why: U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share): moves about half of each die's function into existing U.S. capacity without a new DRAM fab.

title: Subarray sense amps fused with micro-ring optical modulators
idea: Bond a photonic wafer over the DRAM array so every subarray's local sense-amp row drives silicon micro-ring modulators directly; the latched bit biases the ring's PN junction, and global bitlines, I/O muxes and SERDES become one WDM waveguide bus running over the mats.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and overfetch (fact 8): claimed <1 pJ/bit array-to-processor versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, and bank-level parallel optical channels.

title: Vertical bitline pillar with built-in preamp transistor at its base
idea: Merge the local sense preamp into each vertical bitline of a 3D DRAM: a gain transistor whose gate is the short vertical bitline converts the charge-share signal to current before it reaches the long global bitline.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): with ~0.2 fF vertical bitline, a 1 fF cell transfers ~83% of its signal, so cells need ~1 fF instead of 5 fF; enables short lateral capacitors and 100+ tiers (fact 2).

title: Nanoimprint template also prints the self-assembly guide pattern
idea: Combine nanoimprint and directed self-assembly: one imprint stamps sparse 40-80 nm guide posts plus a chemically patterned brush, then a high-chi block copolymer fills in 4-8x denser features and heals imprint defects for capacitor-hole and active arrays.
why: Replaces 2-3 EUV/ArF multi-patterning layers with an imprint tool ~1/10 the cost of an EUV scanner, cutting single-supplier dependence and ~1 MW/tool energy.

title: Excimer-laser crystallized silicon tiers for monolithic 3D DRAM
idea: Combine LTPS-display line-beam laser crystallization with 3D DRAM: amorphous Si tiers are deposited one at a time over the finished lower tiers, and each is melted and crystallized by a nanosecond laser that heats only the top ~50 nm. This replaces Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattices.
why: Avoids strain-limited epi superlattices and the selective SiGe removal etch, so tier count is not capped by epitaxy and stays within BEOL thermal budget (fact 2).

title: DRAM dies embedded in glass-core substrate cavities under processor
idea: Combine the glass-core package substrates now arriving for AI packages with embedded-die technology: laser-form cavities in the glass core, embed thinned commodity DRAM/LPDDR dies face-up, and connect them with through-glass vias straight up into the GPU bump field so memory sits ~300 um below compute instead of beside it.
why: Data movement and CoWoS/HBM bottleneck: ~1-2 pJ/bit vertical links vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, no silicon interposer, no TSV stack (avoids 3x HBM area tax), uses commodity DRAM wafers.

title: Double-sided interposer with HBM mounted directly beneath the GPU
idea: Combine double-sided module assembly with 2.5D packaging: mount HBM stacks on the underside of a thin interposer directly under the GPU, connected by ~100 um through-interposer vias instead of 5-10 mm lateral wires, with the package substrate cavity-milled to receive them.
why: Data movement and interposer area: 50x shorter links (~0.5 pJ/bit), 8+ stacks without beachfront limits, ~40% smaller interposer.
note: Heat and GPU power delivery must pass through the memory region.

title: Leaky-bucket hammer counter: IGZO TFT integrator on each wordline
idea: Combine the networking leaky-bucket with the wordline driver: each activation pumps a fixed charge quantum through an IGZO TFT onto a small MIM capacitor, while a subthreshold TFT drains it with a ~32-64 ms time constant; crossing a threshold triggers neighbor refresh. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputtered IGZO, ALD gate oxide and MIM at <=350 C.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): replaces per-row SRAM counters/CAMs in the periphery (fact 7) with an analog device whose decay matches the refresh window, at near-zero storage cost.

title: Solar-cell recombination layer between cells absorbs hammer electrons
idea: Combine the defect-rich recombination junctions of tandem solar cells with DRAM isolation: line the gap between adjacent storage nodes with a thin, deliberately defective a-Si or heavily doped poly film that recombines electrons injected from the hammered row before they reach the victim node. Buildable in a university nanofab: PECVD/LPCVD film on paired-node test structures.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the charge-migration mechanism directly, potentially raising the flip threshold ~10x with no controller logic.

title: Dual-mode HZO/ZrO2 capacitor: volatile bit with ferroelectric safety copy
idea: Combine a DRAM capacitor with a ferroelectric backup in one ALD stack: a paraelectric ZrO2 layer holds the normal volatile charge, while a thin Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 layer is polarized only by an occasional higher-voltage backup pulse; if charge decays or ECC flags the row, the FE polarization is read to restore it. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD plus <=400 C anneal.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): enables very long refresh intervals with FE as fallback, while rare switching limits FE fatigue.

title: Anodized alumina pore arrays as self-organized capacitor molds
idea: Fuse industrial aluminum anodizing (oxalic/phosphoric acid, guided by an imprinted seed pattern) with DRAM capacitor fabrication. Self-ordered hexagonal AAO pores with AR over 100:1 become the storage-node mold, lined by ALD TiN, ZrO2 and TiN.
why: Delivers AR of about 115 (the Cs wall), skips EUV and fluorocarbon etch for the capacitor layer, and uses anodizing tools that cost pennies per wafer.
note: Self-ordered pores do not register to storage-node contacts; alignment is the key doubt.

title: MLCC-style interdigitated plate stack inside each storage node
idea: Copy multilayer ceramic capacitor construction at nanoscale: fill a wide shallow trench with 12 alternating metal/high-k layers, then use selective lateral recess on opposite sidewalls (as MLCC end terminations alternate) so odd plates tie to the storage node and even plates to the plate line.
why: Fact 1: capacitance scales with deposited layer count, not etch aspect ratio; 12 plates at 3 nm high-k reach ~6 fF at AR <10, deleting the 60-75:1 etch.

title: Snap-through nanodome bit copied from thermostat snap disks
idea: Fabricate a prestressed 20 nm SiN/TiN dome over each cell that, like a bimetal snap disc or keyboard tactile dome, has two stable buckled states; an electrode pulse snaps it up or down in ns and the gap change is read capacitively.
why: Facts 3 and 8: retention is mechanical, so no leakage and no refresh, and the capacitive read is non-destructive, removing restore energy.
note: Snap-through dome per cell; nm-scale thermal stability and ns actuation are open.

title: DVD replication: molded substrates carry all cell topography
idea: Adapted from DVD/Blu-ray replication (a nanostructured disc molded every ~3 s from one nickel stamper): mold glass-ceramic or high-Tg substrates that already contain capacitor wells, gate trenches and contact steps, then conformally coat electrode, high-k, IGZO and metal and planarize, so array geometry needs no lithography.
why: Collapses 5-7 EUV layers and their etches (fact 4) into one molding amortized over ~10^5 parts, ~100x lower patterning cost per GB; trade-offs: ~40 nm features, low-temperature materials, slower cells.

title: Engine remanufacturing: harvest and restack DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like remanufactured engines and toner cartridges: buy scrapped server DIMMs by the ton, debond and retest the dies, then edge-stack or hybrid-bond 8-16 known-good dies onto a new logic base die with fresh interface and strong ECC, sold as certified 'reman' capacity memory.
why: Harvested die cost approaches scrap value (~$0.05-0.2/GB), so restacked modules can be ~30-100x cheaper per GB than new 2026 contract DRAM; trade-offs: older densities, mixed speed bins, shorter warranty.
note: Debonding packaged dies for hybrid restack is impractical; DIMM/CXL reuse is the realistic path.

title: Telephone line concentrators: one sense amp serves 1024 bitlines
idea: Adapted from telephone line concentrators where many subscribers share few trunks: a tree of oxide-TFT pass switches inside the array tiers lets 1,024 bitlines share one CMOS sense amp, and each cell is an active gain cell so it can drive the long shared path instead of sharing tiny charge.
why: Sense-amp and periphery area fall ~95% (fact 7), collapsing CMOS area per GB so arrays stack on a cheap base, ~100x cost cut with tier stacking; trade-off: ~1 us per full row, fine for bulk capacity.

title: Cultured quartz from oscillator industry crushed into crucible sand
idea: The quartz-oscillator industry grows ultra-pure cultured quartz in hydrothermal autoclaves, using low-grade quartz as nutrient. Run large autoclaves purely for crucible feedstock, then crush and acid-leach the cultured bars into <10 ppm-impurity HPQ sand.
why: Turns abundant low-grade quartz into Spruce Pine-equivalent purity, ending dependence on a single deposit. The risk is autoclave throughput and cost.

title: Coca-Cola bottler franchise for a portable capacitorless memory module
idea: Coca-Cola ships concentrate and lets local bottlers add abundant local water. Adapt this by licensing a capacitor-free BEOL memory concentrate (PDK, recipes, precursor specs, test IP) that any CMOS fab, including US 28-65 nm and MEMS fabs, bottles onto its own wafers with local, non-chokepoint materials.
why: Spreads memory supply across dozens of existing fabs with no new $15B fab. It uses only BEOL-temperature steps that are light on Hf, W and He, and could lift the US share well above 2%.

title: Holographic-grating interference lithography for the periodic cell lattice
idea: Adapt diffraction-grating and security-hologram production: print the strictly periodic array layers with three-beam 193 nm interference or displacement Talbot lithography (one periodic phase mask scanned in z), which writes hexagonal hole lattices across a full field with near-unlimited depth of focus and no projection lens; a cheap KrF trim exposure clears the array edges.
why: EUV dependence and scanner capex (fact 4): interference tools cost ~$5-15M versus $200M+ for EUV, need no product reticle, and with one spacer pitch split reach array pitch; claim ~3 EUV layers removed.

title: MicroLED mass transfer: printing known-good DRAM array tiles
idea: Borrow microLED micro-transfer printing: build ~200 um DRAM array tiles on a donor wafer, test them, then elastomer-stamp only known-good tiles onto periphery wafers at the sense-amp interface; failed sites are re-printed as microLED repair does.
why: Yield and capital: die yield becomes tile yield (~99%+), letting new fabs run aggressive cells profitably at low yield, shrinking redundancy and fuse area, and letting several small fabs feed one assembler.

title: Accumulative roll bonding: 3D DRAM tiers from repeated layer transfer
idea: Metallurgy builds nanolaminates by repeatedly rolling and folding; build 3D DRAM tiers by hydrogen-implant smart-cut transfer of 30-50 nm single-crystal Si sheets onto an oxide-bonded stack, then bond stack to stack to double tiers each round (8 to 16 to 32 to 64), instead of growing a 100+ layer Si/SiGe superlattice.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): avoids the strain-relaxation limit on epi stack height, gives monocrystalline channels in every tier, and reaches 64 tiers in ~6 bond rounds.
note: Doubling cuts serial rounds but not total bonds (63 for 64 tiers).

title: Fiber-to-the-home splitter broadcasts model weights to many accelerators
idea: Adapted from passive optical networks (PON): a shared weight-memory pool transmits each layer's weights once on an optical channel, and a passive 1:32 splitter delivers the same stream to 32 accelerators at the same moment. Each accelerator keeps only KV-cache and activations in local HBM, not its own copy of the weights.
why: Replicated weights across data/pipeline-parallel GPUs waste scarce HBM; broadcast removes up to Nx duplication (30-60% of HBM freed per GPU) and replaces N reads with one.
note: 1:32 split loss and lockstep layer sync across GPUs are key doubts.

title: Deep-space soft-decision decoding inside the DRAM sense amp
idea: Adapted from deep-space telemetry (Voyager/Mars links decode near the noise floor with soft-decision LDPC): each sense amp reports the bit plus a 2-bit confidence derived from its latch time-to-decision (measured by a shared counter), and an on-die LDPC decoder over 512-bit codewords uses those soft values. Ambiguous bits from half-charge cells are flagged and corrected rather than guessed.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reading ~2-2.5 fF cells instead of 4.5-5.4 fF lets capacitor aspect ratio drop from 60-75:1 toward ~35:1, cutting etch/deposition cost; soft decoding buys ~2-3 dB effective margin over hard SECDED.

title: pH-buffer storage node: antiferroelectric plateau resists leakage droop
idea: Adapted from chemical buffer solutions, which hold pH nearly constant by drawing on a reservoir as acid is added: add an antiferroelectric layer (Zr-rich HfZrO tuned so its field-induced transition sits just below VARY) in the storage capacitor, so leakage first drains the stored polarization reservoir while node voltage stays flat near the plateau, delaying the fall below the sense threshold.
why: Retention tail and charge wall (facts 1, 3): an effective Q-V plateau could give 3-5x more charge per volt near the operating point, extending retention 3-5x or allowing a much shorter capacitor.
note: AFE fatigue under per-cycle switching conflicts with unlimited endurance.

title: Nanometre proton-intercalation channel bit with nanosecond writes
idea: MINIFY the ion path to ~2 nm: a gain-cell read channel of MoO3 or Nb2O5 sits on a sub-5-nm solid proton reservoir; a 1-2 V, 5 ns gate pulse moves protons in or out, shifting channel conductance ~10x for non-destructive reads, with retention set by reservoir barrier thickness.
why: Capacitor-free (fact 1), non-destructive read (fact 8), tungsten-free; endurance must clear ~1e12 cycles to play the DRAM role.
note: Protonic ns switching shown; endurance to 1e12+ and retention are unknowns.

title: Magnify the dielectric's job: linear high-k by day, ferroelectric at shutdown
idea: Make the DRAM capacitor dielectric a ZrO2/HfZrO2 morphotropic blend that acts as a k~50 linear dielectric under normal +/-0.5 V operation, and only when a power-loss detector fires a 2.5 V plate pulse is stored charge converted into remanent polarization; a power-up pulse converts it back.
why: DRAM-class endurance during operation plus survival of power loss; ferroelectric fatigue spent only once per power cycle; higher k also helps Cs (fact 1).
note: Dual-mode DRAM/FeRAM HZO capacitors are being researched (cf. NVDRAM); field-induced conversion reliability uncertain.

title: Minify the switch to two terminals: OTS selector plus FE capacitor
idea: Pair each ferroelectric capacitor with an ovonic threshold switch selector in a 1S1C stack: half-select voltages stay below the OTS threshold so unselected cells see no disturb, while the selected cell gets the full switching pulse; 4-8 layers stack above CMOS periphery.
why: Eliminates planar access transistor area and epitaxial silicon per layer; non-volatile 3D density multiplication.
note: FE endurance below DRAM-class; OTS threshold variability vs destructive read.

title: Magnify sense time: integrating time-to-digital sensing for 1.5 fF cells
idea: MAGNIFY the sensing window from ~2 ns to 20-40 ns: after charge sharing, a constant-current integrator per bitline pair races both lines to a threshold and a shared counter (TDC) records which crosses first and by how much, resolving 5-10 mV differences a latch cannot.
why: Fact 1: tolerating ~3x less signal lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1.5 fF, so pillar AR can fall from ~70:1 to ~25:1; added latency is hidden behind a row-buffer/SRAM tier for hot data.

title: Sense-amp resolution time becomes soft information for row LDPC
idea: MINIFY sense margin almost to zero and MAGNIFY the code: each SA's latch-resolution time (slow = low confidence) is captured as a soft bit, and an 8 Kb row-level LDPC codeword (~3% parity) is decoded in the periphery, tolerating raw BER up to 1e-4.
why: Facts 1 and 10: permits VARY ~0.65 V (CV2 array energy -55%) and ~30% smaller Cs; soft information roughly halves parity versus hard-decision codes.

title: SiGe HBT preamps exploit bipolar matching for tiny signals
idea: MAGNIFY matching precision by switching device physics: one SiGe heterojunction-bipolar differential preamp per 16 bitlines (Vbe mismatch ~1 mV versus 10-20 mV for minimum MOS) amplifies the signal before a CMOS latch.
why: Facts 1 and 10: resolves ~10 mV in ~1 ns, allowing ~3x smaller Cs or VARY ~0.6 V; BiCMOS DRAM died on cost, but periphery on a separate bonded wafer removes that penalty.

title: Switched-capacitor bitline doubler magnifies signal before latching
idea: After charge sharing, switches reconnect the two halves of each bitline pair in series (a switched-capacitor voltage doubler), MAGNIFYING the differential signal ~1.8x before the latch fires, which lets VARY MINIFY to ~0.5-0.6 V.
why: Fact 10: CV2 array energy -65%; alternatively relaxes Cs ~40% (Fact 1).

title: Minify DRAM die to 0.5 mm2 confetti, self-assembled onto logic
idea: Make DRAM as tiny 0.5 mm2 micro-dies, whose small area gives near-100% yield, and deposit thousands at once onto logic wafers by fluidic self-assembly into shaped receptor wells, followed by hybrid bonding.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: avoids the 20-30% stack yield loss and the 3x area per bit, with a microLED-style mass-transfer cost.
note: FSA placement accuracy vs hybrid bonding pitch.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching digs 150:1 capacitor holes without plasma
idea: Magnify aspect ratio while shrinking gas use to zero: a perforated Ag or Pt catalyst film immersed in HF/H2O2 sinks vertically into silicon, carving 150:1 holes with no fluorocarbon plasma, RF power or helium-cooled chuck. The silicon walls are then oxidized into the capacitor scaffold.
why: Removes C4F6/C4F8 PFAS etch gases and the hardest etch tool from the cell. AR 150 vs 70 roughly doubles Cs (fact 1).
note: Catalyst registration and wall roughness at 20-30 nm holes unproven.

title: Minify the page: 64-byte cache-line-granular paging
idea: Minify the paging unit from 4 KB to 64 B: the memory controller keeps per-line access bits and a line-level remap table, evicting never-touched lines inside 'hot' pages to a compressed CXL/flash tier while the page stays mapped. A miss to an evicted line is refilled by hardware in ~1 us without an OS fault.
why: Attacks page overfetch at the capacity level: 30-60% of lines in resident 4 KB pages are typically cold, so the DRAM needed shrinks ~1.5-2.5x for the same working set.
note: Per-line remap metadata and microsecond stalls on misses are the doubts.

title: Memory dust: fluidic self-assembled micro-DRAM chiplets
idea: MINIFY chiplets to ~0.5 mm^2 (128 Mb each) and place thousands of them into etched receptor sites on the compute wafer by shape-matched fluidic self-assembly, borrowing microLED mass-transfer methods.
why: Data movement and yield: memory is sprinkled within ~1 mm of every core, and known-good tiny dies yield >99%.

title: Eliminate destructive read: erasable conductive ferroelectric domain walls as bits
idea: Eliminate charge-sharing readout: in single-crystal LiNbO3 thin-film nanocells, a field pulse writes or erases a charged, conducting domain wall bridging two side electrodes in ns; reading is a small current through the wall (on/off ~1e3) that leaves the polarization undisturbed.
why: Non-destructive read removes the 128x overfetch and restore cost (fact 8) and refresh (fact 3); risks are scaling below 20 nm and wall-pinning variation.
note: Same conductive-wall mechanism.

title: Eliminate the storage-node conductor: retention-designed charge traps in nanolaminate dielectrics
idea: Eliminate the conductive storage node and its capacitor: store charge in a band of engineered traps (e.g., Ti dopants in Al2O3 tuned to ~1.0 eV depth) behind a 1.5-nm direct-tunneling oxide, so writes take ~10 ns at under 2 V and thermal emission gives seconds-to-minutes retention, a deliberately leaky flash sized for DRAM duty.
why: Removes the pillar capacitor (fact 1) and cuts refresh 100-1000x (fact 3); direct tunneling avoids Fowler-Nordheim wear; risk is trap generation capping endurance below 1e12.
note: Direct-tunnel memory known; engineered trap depth for minutes retention; endurance is key doubt.

title: Eliminate capacitor-hole etching: self-ordered anodic alumina pores become storage nodes
idea: Eliminate the HAR plasma etch, which needs helium backside cooling and argon-diluted plasmas: CVD aluminum from dimethylaluminum hydride (not argon sputtering), then anodize it in oxalic acid, guided by nanoimprinted dimples aligned to the transistor grid, to grow straight 20-30 nm pores at AR 100+. ALD with N2 purge and electroless Ru turn each pore into one capacitor.
why: Attacks fact 1 (AR 115 becomes cheap because pore depth is just anodizing time) and fact 4 (removes the costliest etch tool) using abundant materials; risk is pore registration to transistors at 30 nm pitch.
note: AAO pores give cheap AR>100, but registering self-ordered pores to a 30 nm transistor grid is unproven.

title: Eliminate the leakage tail in place: on-die electrothermal annealing of weak cells
idea: Eliminate retention-weak tail cells without furnaces or forming-gas and argon anneals: drive a short high current through selected wordline segments so Joule heating takes the local access transistors to ~300-400 C for microseconds, annealing the interface and junction traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells; the controller targets the cells its retention profiler flags.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x, using no process gases at all; risks are thermal disturb of neighbors and wordline electromigration.

title: Eliminate sensing during refresh: node-gated broadcast recharge pulse
idea: Add a small second transistor whose gate is the storage node, linking the node to a shared restore line; a bank-wide pulse on that line tops up every node holding '1' (transistor on) and leaves '0' nodes untouched (transistor off). Refresh becomes one global pulse with no row activation, sense amplifiers or bitline swing.
why: Refresh energy drops from ~46 fJ/bit to a few fJ/bit (no bitline CV^2, no sensing) and refresh no longer blocks banks, recovering 10-20% bandwidth; costs ~30% cell area.

title: Eliminate silicon periphery footprint: n-only oxide-TFT dynamic logic above array
idea: Drop PMOS entirely and build decoders, wordline drivers and column logic from n-type oxide-semiconductor TFTs in the BEOL directly over the cell array, using bootstrapped domino-style NMOS-only logic with capacitive self-boost loads. Sense amps stay in silicon.
why: Moves ~30-40% of the periphery off the silicon footprint, shrinking the die ~25-35% (fact 7). Oxide-TFT leakage near 1e-19 A/um lets dynamic nodes hold for milliseconds.

title: Eliminate the page: AND-gated two-transistor pillar cells
idea: In a vertical-bitline 3D array, each cell has two series access gates, a tier wordline and a pillar-select gate, so a cell connects only when both are high; one activation opens a single 64-tier pillar instead of an 8 Kb row.
why: 128x overfetch: activation energy per useful bit falls ~10-50x and row hammer shrinks because no full row is opened; the stack absorbs the second transistor's area.
note: Fine-grained activation known (half-DRAM, SALP); 3D stack absorbs the second gate's area.

title: Interposer that remembers: BEOL non-volatile memory inside it
idea: Eliminate the interposer's passivity: the ~2500 mm2 silicon interposer (65 nm-class, cheap, U.S.-fabbable) becomes an active interposer with BEOL MRAM or HZO FeRAM arrays and simple peripheral CMOS under and between chiplets, stacking 3-4 BEOL array layers.
why: Adds ~5-8 GB of NV capacity 1-2 mm from compute without extra dies, packages or EUV, reusing area that is today pure wiring, at ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Ferroelectric content-addressable KV store returns matches, not data
idea: Eliminate scanning KV caches over the bus: store quantized key signatures in 2-FeFET ternary CAM cells so a query is broadcast into the array and only matching token addresses come out; the index survives power cycles.
why: For sparse retrieval and long-context attention, interface traffic falls ~100x and persistent RAG indexes need no reload after power events.

title: Grid-flexible datacenters: non-volatile memory lets racks drop at peaks
idea: Eliminate the 'stay powered to keep state' requirement: with NV working memory, racks cut to zero power within milliseconds on utility demand-response signals and resume exactly where they were; policy lets utilities fast-track interconnection for certified interruptible NV-equipped load.
why: Grid power is now the binding constraint on new AI capacity; interruptible load connects years sooner and needs far less UPS battery, freeing capital and energy.
note: Depends on DRAM-class NV memory that does not yet exist; policy half is executable.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: panel-fab memory sold by good-gigabyte
idea: Build oxide-TFT DRAM on Gen-8 glass panels with existing display tools, all at <=400 C. Tile it into ~1 cm2 tiles, each with its own tile router, and map dead tiles at test. Modules are sold by the panel's verified good capacity, and software only ever sees good tiles.
why: Panel fabs cost far less per m2 than a DRAM fab and need no EUV; tolerating 20-30% dead tiles makes their defect density viable, for perhaps 3-5x lower capital per bit at relaxed density (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Phase not charge: parametric-oscillator bits sustained by their own pump
idea: Turn refresh from a tax into the storage itself: each bit is a high-Q nanomechanical or LC resonator pumped at 2f by a shared row line, oscillating in one of two phases (0 or pi) that the pump keeps alive; read by phase comparison, write with a brief seed pulse (a modern Goto parametron).
why: Refresh and row hammer (facts 3,9): no static charge to leak or disturb; at Q ~1e4 the shared pump costs ~fW per bit versus 46 fJ/bit refresh; risk is resonator density (~100 nm NEMS).
note: Nanomechanical parametron memory demonstrated; resonator area and pump distribution limit density.

title: Make refresh opt-in in the JEDEC standard
