Backward: run 8 stacked tiers of 2T0C oxide-semiconductor gain cells at ~1 um rules on 2.9 x 3.4 m LCD glass panels in under-used display fabs, accepting ~100x lower areal density because processed panel area costs hundreds of dollars per m2 versus tens of thousands for DRAM wafers.
why: Capital and cost per bit (fact 4): ~50-100 GB/m2 at roughly $5-10/GB with no new fab, as a 50-100 ns far-memory tier that offloads DRAM demand.
note: Same display-fab oxide memory panel mechanism.

title: Refresh-free silicon-carbide DRAM in existing U.S. SiC power fabs
idea: Ideal: memory that never refreshes, made of silicon and carbon. Closest: 4H-SiC 1T1C cells (3.26 eV gap, generation leakage ~1e-19 of Si; 1990s demos showed multi-year room-temperature retention) built on 200 mm SiC lines in North Carolina/New York idled by the power-SiC glut.
why: Removes refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth, Fact 3) using only Si, C and common dopants and idle U.S. capacity; density lags (larger F), so targets always-on low-power tiers.
note: Purdue showed SiC DRAM retention in 1990s; large F, poor SiC MOS interface and wafer cost limit it to niche tiers.

title: Square-meter laser interference lithography for perfectly periodic memory arrays
idea: Ideal: one flash of light patterns a whole panel. Closest: two- or three-beam interference of a 266/213 nm solid-state laser writes periodic lines or hexagonal dots (pitch >=0.12 um) over Gen-8 panels or R2R webs in seconds with no reticle or projection optics; only periphery and staircases use cheap panel steppers.
why: 100x: memory arrays are periodic, so they need no imaging optics; tool capex per m2 is ~1000x below EUV, enabling the ~0.25 um-F panel/foil tiers needed for ~$0.1/GB. Trades 5-10x larger F and stitching/overlay risk.

title: Kerfless epitaxial lift-off wafers end high-purity quartz crucible dependence
idea: Ideal: wafers without crucibles. Closest: grow 50-100 um epitaxial Si on a porous-Si release layer of a reusable parent wafer, peel and bond it to a cheap carrier, and reuse the parent 30-50 times, so one Czochralski crucible supports ~50x more wafers.
why: Resource chokepoint (Spruce Pine HPQ >80%): DRAM uses only the top few um of silicon; also cuts polysilicon energy per wafer.

title: One logic die multiplexes periphery for four bonded array dies
idea: Ideal: periphery costs nothing. Closest: leave only bitline sense amps and local drivers on array dies, and move decoders, I/O, DLL, refresh and ECC logic to one 28 nm logic die that time-multiplexes four stacked array dies through fine-pitch hybrid bonds.
why: Fact 7: periphery is ~49% of the die; sharing it 1:4 cuts total silicon per bit ~30-35% and moves logic to cheaper non-DRAM fabs.

title: Single-mask vertical thyristor pillars cut from blanket p-n-p-n epitaxy
idea: Ideal: a cell patterned by one exposure. Closest: grow a blanket p-n-p-n Si/SiGe epitaxial stack, cut it into 4F2 pillars with one DSA-assisted hole pattern, and form a self-aligned spacer gate on the p-base; the regenerative thyristor latch stores the bit with no capacitor.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: deletes the capacitor module (~25% of DRAM steps), 4F2 instead of 6F2, ~1 critical array mask; uA read currents simplify sensing.
note: T-RAM physics known; standby current and temperature sensitivity sank it before.

title: Film-thickness-defined vertical gain cells need only immersion lithography
idea: Ideal: every critical dimension set by deposition, none by light. Closest: vertical write-over-read transistors in one pillar whose channel lengths equal deposited spacer thicknesses and gate lengths equal ALD metal thicknesses; only pillar placement uses 193i at ~40 nm half pitch, giving a ~4F2 capacitorless 2T gain cell.
why: Fact 4: zero EUV layers and angstrom-level CD control from ALD; with no capacitor the cell is ~300 nm tall instead of ~1.5 um, so fewer deep etches.
note: Deposition-defined CDs remove EUV; vertical 2T gain cells under research.

title: Charge-coupled shift-register memory revived with spacer-patterned gates
idea: Ideal: a memory with no per-cell transistor and no capacitor. Closest: rebuild 1970s CCD memory as many short (32-64-bit) recirculating loops of overlapping gate electrodes formed by self-aligned double patterning on DUV; charge packets in surface potential wells are clocked past one shared sense/restore amplifier per loop.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4, 7: removes access transistors and capacitors, makes refresh part of recirculation, ~2-3F2 per bit at DUV pitch; ~20-30 ns average latency at GHz clocking, with clocking energy as the main risk.

title: Resonant interposer bus that recycles line charge every cycle
idea: Ideal: moving a bit costs zero energy. Closest achievable: integrate spiral inductors in the interposer so each memory data line resonates with its own capacitance; bits are encoded as the phase of a resonant swing and 60-80% of the CV2 energy sloshes back each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Fact 5 and fact 10 voltage floor: link energy falls 3-5x without lowering voltage, beating the CV2 wall by recovery rather than scaling.

title: Field-programmed antifuse stacks: burn weights through the memory interface
idea: Ideal: a memory you write once at deployment and never maintain. Closest achievable: multi-layer antifuse crosspoint dies (gate-oxide breakdown with diode select, 4F2 per layer) are programmed in place through the accelerator's own memory channels when a model is deployed, then served read-only with no refresh and no standby power.
why: Zero refresh and no per-model masks; stacked crosspoint OTP on mature nodes reaches DRAM-competitive density, and endurance is irrelevant for frozen weights.
note: 3D OTP crosspoint existed; models change often and HV programming through memory channels is hard.

title: Per-row trimmed negative wordline for tail rows only
idea: Ideal: zero off-state leakage. Closest: each row gets a 2-bit trim register set at test that picks its standby wordline voltage from -0.2/-0.4/-0.6 V, so rows holding tail cells get deep negative bias (~10x lower subthreshold leakage) while healthy rows stay shallow and avoid the GIDL penalty of deep bias.
why: Fact 3: cuts the leakage of the rows that set refresh by ~10x; refresh interval 2-4x longer at ~1% area.

title: Gen-8.5 display fabs printing stacked IGZO gain-cell memory sheets
idea: Ideal: memory printed by the square meter like wallpaper. Closest achievable with no new fab: idle LCD/OLED TFT fabs (2.2x2.5 m glass, IGZO already in production) build 3-4 stacked layers of 2T0C IGZO gain cells at 2 bits per cell, diced into slow-tier memory tiles (~100 ns-1 us) behind a controller.
why: Uses the world's largest idle lithography area with no EUV: ~10 GB per panel per layer at 1.5 um rules, maybe $3-8/GB with stacking; density and speed are the risk.
note: More modest than 32-tier variant: 1.5 um rules, slow tier; density and speed are the risk.

title: III-nitride resonant-tunneling floating well: ns write, hour retention
idea: Scarcity rule: refresh is banned. Store electrons in a GaN quantum well clad by AlN barriers (~2 eV offset) so thermionic leakage is negligible, and write through an AlN/GaN/AlN double-barrier resonant-tunneling stack that conducts only when the gate aligns its resonant level near 1 V. Read through the HEMT channel that the stored charge depletes.
why: Kills the leakage-tail refresh tax (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); cold resonant tunneling avoids hot-carrier damage for DRAM-class endurance; moves the ULTRARAM idea to wide-gap GaN-on-Si.
note: GaN port of ULTRARAM; nitride polarization and trapping complicate RTDs.

title: Contactless snap-through nanomembrane: bistable mechanical bit, vacuum-insulated
idea: Scarcity rule: vacuum is the only insulator allowed. A pre-buckled SiN or few-layer-graphene membrane over a sealed 20 nm cavity has two stable shapes; an electrostatic pulse from a bottom electrode snaps it up or down, and one access transistor senses the capacitance difference. It never touches anything, so there is no stiction or contact wear.
why: Zero leakage and zero hold power (fact 3) at GHz mechanical resonance for sub-100 nm membranes; elastic bending below 1% strain gives effectively unlimited cycles.

title: Gallium-oxide access transistor plus refresh-rate register cuts refresh 4x
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): keep the pins and protocol, and change only what the die reports. Replace the Si access transistor with a 4.8 eV beta-Ga2O3 vertical channel whose off current is ~1e-6 of Si so 5 fF holds for minutes, and have the die permanently report the slowest refresh-rate code already defined in the MR4 temperature/refresh register, so unmodified controllers issue 4x fewer REFs.
why: Uses an existing spec field to monetize retention: refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down ~75% with zero controller change; Ga2O3 crystal quality at BEOL thermal budget is the risk.
note: Clever MR4 refresh-code reuse; BEOL-compatible Ga2O3 channel quality is the doubt.

title: Racetrack rows: ACT shifts a domain-wall track, tRCD hides it
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): keep DDR's ACT-then-READ page model. Map each row address to a shift position of perpendicular domain-wall racetracks under a line of read/write heads; ACT drives a current pulse that moves the tracks to that position within tRCD (~14 ns at ~500 m/s covers ~64 bits at 100 nm spacing), the heads latch the row into sense amps, and PRE writes it back.
why: One head per 64 bits instead of a transistor per bit gives ~10x cell-area density (facts 4, 7), magnetic storage needs no refresh and has no wear; domain-wall pinning variability sets the risk.
note: At 100 nm bit spacing horizontal tracks are not denser than DRAM cells; pinning variability remains.

title: Crested-barrier floating node written by DRAM's existing 3 V wordline rail
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): no new supply pins, so reuse the ~3 V VPP rail DRAM already has. Store charge on a floating node behind a crested SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2 barrier whose peaked profile collapses under high field for ns writes but stays thick at hold fields for hours of retention; reads sense the storage transistor's threshold shift.
why: The existing wordline rail powers a quasi-nonvolatile 1T cell with no capacitor (facts 1, 3); endurance under repeated tunneling writes is the unknown.
note: Crested barriers known (Likharev); reuse of VPP rail is a practical twist; tunneling endurance unknown.

title: Wordline-swing ceiling of 1 V: band-to-band tunnel FET access device
idea: Limit: the access device may swing only 1 V yet must still cut off by 10 decades. Use a vertical p-i-n tunnel FET (SiGe source pocket, Si channel, n+ storage-side drain). It turns on by band-to-band tunneling at sub-60 mV/dec and has no thermionic subthreshold tail, so off-current is set by the reverse-biased p-i-n diode (aA range). Asymmetric doping blocks ambipolar leakage from the storage side.
why: Facts 3 and 10: lets VPP drop from 3 V toward ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV2) and removes the thermionic tail that forces refresh. A low on-current (~1 uA) still charges 5 fF in under 10 ns.

title: Refresh fixed at one second: sense amps flag low-confidence bits
idea: Limit: the refresh interval is forced to 1 s and the cell cannot improve. Add a dual-reference margin check to the sense amp (a second sense against a shifted reference) so cells whose signal sits near the decision point are flagged as erasures. The ECC decoder can then correct about twice as many errors, because an erasure costs half a correction.
why: Fact 3: knowing where the weak bits are doubles effective correction power, making 1 s refresh tolerable and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth ~15x.

title: Bitline capped at 10 fF: segment amplifiers inside the array tier
idea: Limit: no bitline may exceed 10 fF. Every 32 cells, a 2-transistor local amplifier (gate on the local bitline, drain on a global bitline) is built in the same vertical-channel tier as the access transistors, turning charge sharing into current gain on a global line.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): with a 4x smaller C_BL, Cs can drop to ~1.5-2 fF (planar or low-AR capacitors), which unblocks the 3D DRAM capacitor (fact 2).
note: Local amplifiers in vertical-channel tier; their Vt variation is the key doubt.

title: Dual-mode HZO: linear dielectric daily, ferroelectric only at shutdown
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, without ferroelectric fatigue. The capacitor runs as a sub-coercive high-k DRAM cell during operation; at power-fail, bipolar plate-line drivers pulse +/-Vc row by row so each cell's stored charge sets its polarization, and at power-up a destructive ferroelectric read with a dual-reference SA reloads the charge state.
why: NV plus unlimited daily endurance, since the ferroelectric switches once per power cycle; HZO's k (~30-40) also eases the capacitor wall (fact 1).

title: BEOL oxide-TFT sense amps above NV crossbar: die equals array
idea: Constraint: NV crossbar cells (BEOL-compatible MRAM/ReRAM/FTJ). Build the sense amps, column muxes and local drivers from complementary oxide TFTs (n-IGZO plus p-SnO or Te) in the BEOL directly above or between crossbar tiers, so the front-end silicon under the array holds only global logic.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): die area per bit approaches the array area (~2x density); BEOL processing at <=400 C suits U.S. legacy fabs.

title: Coarse-litho tall stack: 48 ArF-dry tiers beat EUV density
idea: Because nothing exceeds 400 C, oxide 4F2 cross-point tiers can be stacked sequentially without disturbing lower tiers. Each tier uses only two ArF-dry masks at 65 nm, and density comes from tier count instead of litho.
why: Fact 4: 48 tiers at 65 nm 4F2 give about 350 nm2/bit (2.5x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV; capital moves to cheap litho.

title: Spatial-ALD nanolaminate replaces Si/SiGe epitaxy for 128 tiers
idea: Under 400 C, deposit 128 alternating 8 nm IGZO (or indium-free ZTO) channel layers and 20 nm AlOx sacrificial layers in one spatial-ALD run, then build lateral 3D DRAM cells by hole/slit recess as in Si/SiGe flows.
why: Fact 2: removes about $5M epi tools and strain limits; tier deposition cost per wafer about 1/5 and tier count is not limited by strain.
note: Removes strain limit; IGZO vs AlOx etch selectivity and low mobility are open.

title: Known-good-tier lamination: binned two-tier oxide modules
idea: Under 400 C, fabricate two-tier oxide DRAM modules on cheap glass carriers, test and bin each one, then laminate only good modules by 250 C Cu-Cu hybrid bonding into 16-tier stacks. Modules are made in parallel, not in series.
why: Fact 2 and capital intensity: decouples stack yield from tier count and cuts cycle time about 8x versus sequential tier processing.

title: Packaging houses become DRAM fabs using 400 C tool sets
idea: Under 400 C, advanced-packaging and OSAT plants already run PVD, plating, ALD, steppers and hybrid bonders. They add oxide DRAM tier modules on purchased CMOS periphery wafers, with no furnaces or EUV.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: about 1/5 the capex per wafer start and uses existing U.S. packaging sites in 12-18 months.

title: Self-ordering anodic alumina pores as lithography-free capacitor molds
idea: Imposed scarcity: zero EUV and zero plasma for the capacitor layer. Deposit thick aluminum over the storage-node contacts, nanoimprint shallow pits on the contact grid, and anodize in sulfuric or oxalic acid so pores self-organize at the pits and grow straight to AR >100; open the barrier oxide at the bottom and fill with electrode and dielectric.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV or multipatterning masks and the hardest dry etch with a room-temperature electrochemical step using abundant aluminum; capacitor AR is set only by film thickness.

title: Display-fab memory: stacked oxide-TFT DRAM on Gen-8.5 glass
idea: Constraint: no silicon wafers at all. Repurpose idle Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines to build 1T1C capacity memory at ~1 um rules on 5.5 m2 glass, about 100 GB per TFT tier and 8 stacked tiers per panel, sliced into CXL capacity modules with ~200 ns access.
why: Glass area costs ~100x less than silicon and the capex is stranded and depreciated; target <$2/GB capacity tier with zero crucible quartz and no EUV.

title: Open tall-stack die standard turns memory dies into auctioned commodity
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. A JEDEC-style open spec fixes die size, thickness, pad maps and test interface for stackable DRAM dies so any vendor's dies drop into 32-64-high stacks; buyers reverse-auction dies and independent stackers compete separately.
why: Unbundling die-making from stacking lets tall stacks use the cheapest qualifying dies and opens many stacking houses (including U.S.), holding price flat at 10x dies per package.

title: Half the voltage: 0.5 V array rescued by on-die BCH
idea: Imposed limit: half the array voltage. Run VARY at ~0.5 V with offset-cancelling sense amplifiers and accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced sense margin. A low-latency on-die BCH(t=2) code per 128 bits, decoded in parallel with column select, cleans up the result.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: CV^2 array energy falls ~4x at ~6% check-bit overhead and ~1-2 ns decode latency.
note: Halving VARY cuts bitline energy but SA margin at 0.5 V may give far worse than 1e-5 BER.

title: Charge-transfer pre-sense on a long bitline: sub-fF cells without shortening the bitline
idea: Conventional sensing divides the cell charge by Cs + Cbl (35 fF), so only ~7 mV survives from a 0.5 fF cell. In charge-transfer pre-sensing (Arimoto/Mitsubishi lineage) the bitline is precharged through its own transfer gate, which therefore self-biases at its own threshold and cancels Vt mismatch. When the cell dumps charge, the bitline moves a few mV, the transfer gate conducts in subthreshold, and the charge flows onto a small sense node. Gain = Cbl/C_sn. The twist is pairing this with an IGZO access device (1 aA), so a 0.3-0.5 fF cell still retains 45-75 s, and using offset-cancelled latches. The capacitor becomes a ~120 nm stub (AR ~6) or even the gate-plus-junction capacitance of a vertical channel.
why: 10x smaller storage capacitor (5.4 -> 0.5 fF; pillar 1,300 -> ~120 nm) at today's 512-cell bitline. Signal on the sense node 155 mV vs 7.5 mV conventional.

title: 2-bit/cell 1T1C on an oxide access device
idea: Write one of four levels (0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 x VARY) through a vertical IGZO access transistor (OCTRAM/Samsung VCT style). Read by successive approximation: charge-share onto a short bitline, decide the MSB against a mid reference, then the LSB against a reference chosen by the MSB (or a time-domain ramp), then restore all four levels. A silicon cell cannot do this, because its 13 fA tail leaks a full level in milliseconds. At 1 aA the droop is 0.18 mV/s, so a 15 mV level budget lasts ~80 s. Combine with 128-cell bitlines (bonded periphery) or charge-transfer pre-sense (B1-04) for margin.
why: 2x bits per cell -> 1.8-2.8x die density at the same F, depending on array efficiency (0.89-1.23 Gb/mm2 vs 0.447), with no new lithography.

title: Vertical oxide semi-floating-gate 1T1D gain cell (4F2, capacitor-less, stackable)
idea: A vertical ALD In2O3/IGZO channel pillar is wrapped by a metal floating gate (FG), which is wrapped in turn by a control-gate wordline. A Schottky or MIS diode (Pt/IGZO, p-NiO/IGZO heterojunction, or a thin Al2O3 tunnel diode) links the FG to the drain/bitline at the pillar top. Write: the wordline couples the FG below the bitline, the diode forward-biases and the FG charges to the bitline level. Hold: raise the wordline so the diode is reverse-biased. Read: the FG charge sets the channel current, non-destructively. The reverse current of the diode sets retention, and the cell fits in the footprint of one vertical transistor. Fudan's Si SFG (Science 2013) showed ns writes at <2 V, but its embedded TFET/diode made it large; oxide BEOL lets the diode sit vertically on top.
why: 2.5x per-tier density vs 10F2 2T0C: at F = 20 nm, b x N for 1b parity falls from 3.7 to 1.5; at F = 40 nm (single-exposure ArF, no EUV) from 14.9 to 6.0 (e.g., 2 bits x 3 tiers).

title: Capacitive-NDRO ferroelectric gain cell for a read-mostly DRAM tier
idea: An HZO (or Zr-rich) capacitor with asymmetric electrodes has a zero-bias capacitance that differs between its two polarization states (imec reports a capacitive window ~8.7 at 0 V). The capacitor is the coupling element of a read transistor gate (1T-1C_FE or 2T-nC with n<=4). A small read pulse (below coercive) on its plate couples more or less charge onto the gate, and the read transistor converts that to current. Reads are non-destructive and never switch polarization; writes are full switching pulses. The memory is non-volatile, so there is no refresh and no restore, and pages need not be activated wholesale. Small n is essential: capacitive coupling dilutes as 1/n.
why: Refresh -> 0 and restore -> 0 for read-mostly data. Read endurance >1e11 (shown) vs ~1e7 write; read energy ~CV2 of a ~1.5 fF node (~0.1-0.4 fJ) instead of a 10 KB page restore (~5.9 pJ per useful bit random).

title: VCMA crosspoint MRAM with deliberately relaxed (refreshed) retention
idea: Each crosspoint is an OTS selector plus a perpendicular CoFeB/MgO MTJ with a high VCMA coefficient. A ~0.5-1 ns voltage pulse lowers the anisotropy so the free layer precesses half a turn, with no write current through a transistor, so there is no access transistor and the cell is 4F2. Thermal stability Delta is chosen for refreshed operation (Delta ~44-48 for 1 s to 1 min, vs ~64 for 10-year non-volatility), allowing a smaller or thinner free layer and lower write voltage. A 'refresh' is a TMR read plus conditional rewrite, done rarely. Four BEOL decks stack over CMOS.
why: 2.9x 1b density (4 decks, F = 20 nm) or 1.3x (F = 30 nm, no EUV); write energy 6-20 fJ vs a 46 fJ refresh plus pJ-class activation; refresh 15x+ less frequent than DRAM.

title: Protonic gain cell (H+ in WO3 behind a PSG electrolyte)
idea: Three terminals: a WO3 channel between source and drain; a nanoporous PSG electrolyte (2-5 nm) above it; a Pd (or PdHx) gate that serves as the proton reservoir. A gate pulse at ~1 V/nm drives H+ into or out of WO3 in ns; each inserted proton is charge-compensated by an electron, which raises channel conductance. At read voltages the field is too low to move protons, so the state is non-volatile and the read is non-destructive. Multi-level storage is natural (analog conductance). The 'protonic nano-supercapacitor stub' variant, which uses the same chemistry as a 2-terminal capacitor holding ~18x today's charge per area, is rejected: its charge cannot be extracted at low field in ns (see notes).
why: Non-volatile 2-4 b/cell gain cell with 5 ns writes; refresh -> 0. Density per tier similar to a 2T0C (~10F2) but multiplied by bits per cell. Unproven endurance.

title: 2D-barrier quasi-volatile 1T cell (seconds-to-minutes retention traded for endurance)
idea: A graphene or MoS2 channel sits over an hBN tunnel barrier (2-4 layers) and a floating gate or charge-storage layer (HfO2/Al2O3 or graphene). Fudan's PoX showed 2D-enhanced hot-carrier injection programming in 400 ps at 5 V, with 5.5e6 cycles. Fudan's 2D semi-floating gate showed 10 s retention with ~15 ns writes. The twist is to tune barrier thickness and injection mechanism (direct tunnelling vs hot-carrier) for a DRAM point: retention 10-100 s at 85 C, writes <=10 ns at ~2-3 V, and endurance as the optimisation target rather than retention. The read is non-destructive (gain cell). The cell is 1T, 4F2, BEOL-stackable if 2D films grow on wafers.
why: Refresh 156x (10 s) to 1,562x (100 s) less frequent; 1T 4F2 at F = 20 nm = 0.30 Gb/mm2 per layer (0.67x 1b), multiplied by layers or bits per cell. Endurance must rise 1.8e5x to reach 1e12.

title: Capacitor-first inverted flow with perovskite super-k
idea: On a bare carrier or Si wafer, deposit a conductive-oxide bottom electrode (LaNiO3, Nb:SrTiO3 or doped SnO2), sputter/ALD 10-12 nm (Ba,Sr)TiO3 or SrTiO3 into short pillars or cups, and RTA at 650-750 C to crystallize (k 100-250); add the top electrode and planarize. Then build vertical IGZO/ZTO access transistors directly on the capacitor top contacts at <=400 C (the OCTRAM-style transistor-over-capacitor arrangement), and finally hybrid-bond the logic periphery wafer on top. Because the capacitor comes first, no transistor, metal or gate stack ever sees the perovskite anneal. The bit is a normal 1T1C charge sensed through a short bitline.
why: 3-4x shorter capacitor at equal charge: k 150 (EOT 0.26 nm) gives 4.6 fF from a 0.5 um stub (vs 5.4 fF from 1.3 um today), AR ~23 instead of 60-75; a 0.3 um stub gives 1.8-3.8 fF, enough for 64-128-cell bitlines.

title: In-tier complementary-oxide sense amplifiers (no-bond short bitlines)
idea: Build complementary oxide TFT latch sense amplifiers (n-IGZO/ZTO + p-TeSeOx, mobility ~15 cm2/Vs, on/off 1e6-1e7) in a dedicated BEOL tier above or below the memory tier(s), connected by short vias to 64-cell local bitline segments. Short bitlines (Cbl ~8 fF instead of ~35 fF) cut the needed storage capacitance to ~1.2 fF and allow VARY ~0.4 V; the local SA restores the cell and drives a global bitline to the Si periphery. In 3D stacks one SA tier serves N memory tiers, so bitline capacitance no longer grows with tier count. Offset-cancelled (auto-zero) SA topology absorbs oxide Vt mismatch.
why: ~27x lower bitline CV2/2 energy per sense (17.5 -> 0.64 fJ) and ~4.5x lower Cs requirement (5.4 -> ~1.2 fF), monolithically, without a second bonded wafer.

title: Maskless interference lithography for an all-periodic cell wafer
idea: Two (or four) coherent 193 nm beams interfere in water immersion to write a fringe pattern at half-pitch ~34.5-36 nm; two crossed exposures give post or hole lattices at ~70 nm pitch, and one SADP halves that to ~35 nm. Scanning-beam interference lithography (Doppler writing) phase-locks the fringe to wafer marks for overlay and covers 300 mm continuously. Array edges and the few non-periodic features are cut by a coarse KrF/i-line trim exposure whose overlay is not critical. Possible only because bonded periphery has removed all random logic from the cell wafer.
why: No masks and no EUV for array layers; 4F2 at F~17-18 nm with one SADP; litho tool capex estimated ~10x below an ArF immersion scanner and ~50-100x below EUV [ESTIMATE: no projection optics].

title: BEOL-only cell mini-line on reusable glass carriers, bonded to trailing-node periphery
idea: Oxide gain-cell or oxide 1T1C stacks (8-32 tiers) are deposited and patterned on a 300 mm CTE-matched glass carrier with a laser-release layer, using only PVD/ALD/PECVD, dry etch, ArF/NIL, CMP, cleans and a hybrid bonder: no >450 C furnaces, implanters, epitaxy or EUV. The finished stack is hybrid-bonded face-down to a periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from a trailing-node foundry at 1-2 um pitch, which A3's model says is enough for litho-light oxide pitches. The glass is laser-debonded through its transparent back and reused.
why: Cell-side capex ~$44-68k per wafer-start-per-month vs $145-170k for a DRAM greenfield (2.5-3.3x lower) [ASSUMPTION: BEOL-only tool set = 30-40%]; prime-Si demand of dual-wafer (periphery-under-cell) DRAM -45-49% by reusing the cell carrier 10-50x.

title: Trailing-node fab reuse: CMOS-under-array deep-tier MLC oxide memory at F=65 nm
idea: Run the fab's 65 nm CMOS flow to build sense amps, decoders and write-verify DACs, then stack 16-24 tiers of vertical IGZO/ZTO 2T0C cells over them (CMOS-under-array, as in 3D NAND CuA), with one hole etch per tier group at F=65 nm, ALD channels and recessed gates. Each cell stores 3-4 bits by write-verify; long oxide retention gives the level stability that MLC needs. No bonding, no immersion, no EUV.
why: 1.8-2.7x 1-beta density and 1.7-3.5x 1-beta bits per wafer-dollar (before yield) at F=65 nm, in existing depreciated fabs with no new litho tools.

title: Coaxial 4F2 2T0C: the storage node is the core gate of a read-channel shell
idea: Each cell is one pillar on a 2F x 2F grid. The core is a metal storage node (~20 nm diameter, ~150 nm tall) wrapped by a gate dielectric and an ALD IGZO/IGO shell; the shell is the read transistor's channel and the core is its gate (an inverted channel-all-around device), contacted by a source plane at the bottom and a read-bitline ring at the top. Above the core sits the write transistor: a short vertical oxide channel gated by a write-wordline ring, linking the write bitline at the pillar top to the core. Four line levels (source rows, read-bitline columns, write-wordline rows, write-bitline columns) each run at 2F pitch at different heights, so the 2T0C occupies 4F2 per tier. Tiers stack monolithically at <=400 C over CMOS-under-array.
why: Per-tier density 2.5-3.4x better than A3's 10F2 vertical 2T0C: 1-beta parity at bits x tiers = 4.1 at F = 40 nm (no EUV, no multipatterning) vs 14; 2 bits x 8 tiers at F = 40 nm = 3.9x 1-beta density and ~2.5x bits per wafer-dollar before yield.

title: Ge-free dopant-contrast superlattice (Si / Si:B) for 3D silicon DRAM
idea: 3D silicon DRAM (Samsung VS-DRAM, SK hynix, imec) starts from an epitaxial Si/Si0.8Ge0.2 superlattice whose SiGe layers are later etched out to free horizontal Si channels; imec's 120-bilayer stacks still show dislocations because the 0.84% mismatch accumulates strain, and A2 puts fleet-scale Ge demand at 6-38% of refined supply. Instead grow intrinsic Si alternating with heavily boron-doped Si (1-3e20 cm-3, optionally carbon co-doped, or with ~1-4% Ge to null the small lattice contraction) by the same low-temperature RPCVD. Remove the sacrificial layers through the slit with dopant-selective chemistry: an HF/HNO3/CH3COOH etch that attacks heavily doped Si far faster than intrinsic Si, or selective electrochemical porosification of the p+ layers followed by a fast porous-Si strip. The intrinsic layers become channels; boron tails matter only until the sacrificial layers are gone.
why: Misfit 0.84% -> 0.05-0.16% (strain energy 30-260x lower), so tier count is no longer strain-limited; Ge per wafer 5-16x lower, or zero.
note: HNA/porous-Si selectivity known; boron outdiffusion and lateral etch uniformity through 100+ tiers are the doubts.

title: Approximate 4-level DRAM for low-order planes and 2-bit KV
idea: A 2-bit DAC-driven write driver writes one of four levels (0, 0.35, 0.70, 1.05 V). Reads use charge sharing followed by a 3-threshold successive sense, with extra reference levels from split reference bitlines as in the 1997 4-level 4 Gb DRAM. Gray coding makes an adjacent-level error a +/-1 LSB error of the 2-bit field. MLC rows hold only data classes that tolerate ~1e-3 level error: KIVI-style 2-bit KV (one element per cell), the low mantissa planes of BF16 (with B4-04), and MX/FP4 element codes whose shared scales stay protected. Exact data stay single-level. On short bitlines (128 cells, e.g., with sense amps under the array) the same scheme becomes exact.
why: 2x bits per cell for approximate data on the existing 1-beta array: KV capacity x2 vs single-level 2-bit storage, and BF16 with the B4-04 split x2.28 vs ECC'd BF16. At 128-cell bitlines the same circuit reaches exact-grade error rates (6.5e-15).

title: BitNet-native charge-sharing popcount PIM in commodity 1T1C
idea: Ternary weights {-1, 0, +1} are stored as two bit-masks (positive and negative) in 1T1C rows, and activations are bit-sliced (INT8 into 8 binary planes). For each activation plane, the controller first RowClones the selected weight rows, ANDed with the activation mask (Ambit-style), into dedicated compute rows. It then activates 8 compute rows at once on the same bitlines. Charge sharing gives a bitline voltage proportional to the number of charged cells (0-8), which a 3-bit flash ADC shared by 8-16 bitlines in the SA stripe digitises. A small near-bank adder shifts and accumulates the partial sums. Weights never leave the bank.
why: 12-35x lower energy per decode GEMV than reading ternary weights over HBM (0.39 J vs 0.011-0.033 J per token for a 70B ternary model), plus ~8x internal bandwidth.

title: Seconds-ULTRARAM: a resonant-tunnelling floating gate retuned from 1,000-year retention to DRAM-class speed
idea: A floating gate above a III-V (or 2D) channel is isolated by a triple-barrier resonant-tunnelling stack. Two quantum wells of different thickness sit between three barriers and line up only at the programming bias (~2.5 V today), so electrons pass resonantly with no hot-carrier damage; off resonance the stack blocks. The read is a non-destructive channel-conductance measurement, making this a gain cell with no capacitor. The DRAM retune thins the barriers and wells, which lowers the retention target from 1,000 years to seconds or days, pulls the resonance voltage toward ~1-1.5 V and raises current density for ns writes. A 2D van der Waals version (graphene/hBN/MoS2 resonant barriers) could be transferred onto Si BEOL.
why: Refresh energy falls 1e3-1e6x (1 s to 1 day retention); writes cost ~1e-17-1e-16 J, against fJ-class DRAM cells plus periphery; crystalline barriers make 1e15-cycle endurance plausible.

title: Myelinated bitline: vacuum-sheathed bitline segments with non-latching 2T 'nodes of Ranvier'
idea: Bitlines are enclosed laterally in a sealed vacuum or air cavity, extending today's air spacers to the full bitline sidewall and the bitline-to-landing-pad gap. Every 32-64 cells the bitline breaks at a 'node': a BEOL IGZO 2T amplifier (source follower plus reset, non-latching) stacked above the array. The node turns the local segment's charge-sharing voltage into a current on a global bitline, and the main sense amp sits at the end as it does today. Unlike a local sense amplifier, the node neither latches nor restores, so it fits in BEOL above the array; restore runs through the global path.
why: The Cs requirement falls from 3.65 to 0.6-0.8 fF (32-64-cell segments), so the capacitor is ~150-200 nm tall instead of ~1.3 um. The vacuum sheath alone lowers Cbl by only 1.5-1.7x.

title: Swap linear dielectric for antiferroelectric charge-burst capacitor dielectric
idea: Replace the ZrO2/Al2O3 linear cap dielectric with a field-induced antiferroelectric (ZrO2-rich HfZrO or Pb-free NaNbO3-based) whose AFE-to-FE transition sits just below the write voltage, so writing a '1' adds the released polarization (~15-25 uC/cm2) to the linear charge. At zero field the film relaxes back to the non-polar phase, so there is no remanent imprint and the cell stays a volatile DRAM cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 2-3x stored charge per pillar at today's AR ~60:1, or the same 5 fF at AR ~25:1, which also makes 3D tiers easier.

title: Swap stored charge for conducting ferroelectric domain wall presence
idea: In thin-film LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 mesa cells, the bit is whether a charged, conducting domain wall bridges two side electrodes. Writing creates or erases the wall in ns, and reading senses wall conduction (on/off >10^4) without switching polarization.
why: Non-destructive read cuts the restore share of the ~5.9 pJ/bit destructive read (fact 8); non-volatile, so no refresh (fact 3); cycling above 10^10 has been reported.
note: Widely pursued (Fudan, Belfast); LNOI wafers make device demos cheap.

title: Substitute plasma-etched capacitor holes with self-ordered anodic alumina pores
idea: Deposit 1-2 um of aluminum over the cell transistors, pre-dimple it with a coarse DUV pattern registered to the landing pads, then anodize in oxalic acid: pores self-order into a hexagonal lattice at a pitch set by voltage (~2.5 nm/V) with AR >100:1 in minutes. Open the pore bottoms, ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN inside, and keep the alumina as the mechanical support.
why: Facts 1 and 4: deletes the HAR etch (the slowest, costliest DRAM module) and the support-mesh patterning; AR 100-150 comes free, lifting Cs toward ~8 fF; wet anodization benches cost ~1/20 of HAR etch chambers.

title: Substitute plasma etch with metal-assisted chemical etching for vertical silicon pillars
idea: Pattern a Pt or Au catalyst mesh (lift-off or block-copolymer), then immerse the wafer in HF/H2O2: silicon under the catalyst dissolves and the mesh sinks straight down, carving vertical-channel-transistor pillars or buried-wordline trenches at >100:1 with no ion damage and no bowing; the catalyst is stripped and reclaimed.
why: Facts 2 and 4: a 50-wafer wet batch replaces $5-10M cryo/HAR etch chambers; damage-free sidewalls also shrink the GIDL leakage tail (fact 3). Metal contamination control is the main risk.

title: Substitute zirconia capacitor dielectric with templated rutile titania near k=100
idea: Grow rutile-phase TiO2 (k ~80-120) by ALD at <=400 C on a RuO2 bottom electrode whose lattice templates the rutile phase, with Al doping to block leakage, so the same ~5 fF fits in a hole of AR ~25:1 instead of 70:1.
why: Facts 1 and 4: shallower holes cut HAR etch and ALD time ~3x and remove support-mesh steps (or keep AR and double Cs). Ru is itself a scarce metal and leakage is the risk.
note: Long-studied (RuO2-templated rutile); leakage at low EOT is the blocker.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain walls in thin-film lithium niobate
idea: Combine the thin-film lithium niobate photonics platform with domain-wall nanoelectronics: a voltage writes or erases a charged domain wall between two electrodes, and the wall conducts 1e3-1e6x more than the bulk crystal. Read is a small non-destructive current through the wall, and the polarization holds the bit with no refresh.
why: Zero refresh plus non-destructive read (fact 8); LiNbO3 domain walls show >1e10-cycle endurance and fast switching; U.S. TFLN foundries exist.

title: Ferroelectric semiconductor channel: alpha-In2Se3 holds bit in itself
idea: Fuse channel and storage element: alpha-In2Se3 is a 2D semiconductor whose own lattice is ferroelectric, so switching its polarization changes the channel conductance directly. A one-transistor cell with no gate ferroelectric and no capacitor stores the bit in the channel and reads it non-destructively.
why: Zero refresh in a 1T 4F2 cell without the interface-trap fatigue of FeFET gate stacks; indium supply and 2D growth uniformity are risks.

title: Molybdenum-dioxide electrodes template rutile TiO2 for short lateral capacitors
idea: Combine a rutile-structured MoO2 storage electrode (from Colorado molybdenum) with ALD TiO2 so the dielectric grows in its rutile phase (k ~80-100) below 400 C, with light Al doping to curb leakage, replacing imported Ru/RuO2 templates and k~40 ZrO2.
why: Charge wall (fact 1, needs k~70): ~2x k makes lateral 3D capacitors ~2x shorter for thinner tiers; element chain Mo/Ti/Al is fully domestic.
note: Rutile templating on MoO2 is published; rutile TiO2 leakage remains the doubt.

title: Anodic aluminum oxide pores serve as the capacitor mold
idea: Combine electrochemical anodization (self-ordered AAO reaches aspect ratios above 200 in wet baths) with the DRAM capacitor. Al is deposited over the landing pads and imprint-textured so pores nucleate over each pad, anodized at room temperature into 15-20 nm pores 2-3 um deep, and the electrodes and dielectric are then ALD-coated inside.
why: Replaces the most capital-intensive DRAM tool, high-aspect-ratio plasma etch of the 60-75:1 mold, with bath processing. AR ~115 becomes reachable (fact 1) for ~+50% Cs, and module capex falls ~5x.

title: Store context as entropy-coded tokens, regenerate KV on demand
idea: Combine the model's own next-token probabilities with arithmetic coding: cold context is evicted from the KV cache and kept only as token IDs coded at ~1-2 bits per token, and when attention needs a span a burst prefill kernel recomputes its K/V. A tiny per-span key summary decides when recompute is worth it.
why: A token's KV is ~50-300 KB in large models versus under one byte as coded text, so long-context DRAM drops by orders of magnitude, paid for with abundant compute.
note: Recomputing a mid-context span needs causal prefix states; entropy coding IDs is irrelevant.

title: Switch multicast streams one shared weight copy to all GPUs
idea: Combine a pooled weight store (CXL/NVLink memory node) with switch-level multicast: data-parallel replicas run in lockstep and the switch broadcasts each layer's weights just in time to every GPU, which keeps only a two-layer ring buffer instead of a full replica in HBM.
why: HBM spent on duplicated weights falls by the replica count (8-64x), freeing it for KV cache or allowing smaller-HBM parts (fact 6).

title: Anodized aluminum pores self-assemble the capacitor forest without etch
idea: Borrowed from architectural aluminum anodizing: sputter 3 um of Al over the access-transistor array, imprint shallow dimples at cell sites, and anodize so hexagonal pores self-align to them at ~100:1 aspect ratio; line the pores with TiN/high-k/TiN to form every capacitor without plasma etch or EUV.
why: A wet bath replaces the hardest high-AR etch module and its masks (facts 1,4), capacitor module cost ~-95%; with a relaxed ~30 nm EUV-free periphery it is a core piece of a 100x cost path.

title: Optical-disc error correction lets arrays ship with 1% dead cells
idea: Borrowed from CDs and Blu-ray, which ship with defects and rely on interleaved Reed-Solomon/LDPC: design arrays with soft-decision sensing and ~25% parity so up to 1% dead or weak-retention cells are absorbed, eliminating laser repair and per-cell screening.
why: The enabler that makes 100x-cheap processes (panels, imprint, 200+ tiers) sellable: effective yield on 100-tier stacks rises from ~30% to ~95%, a ~3x lever inside the 100x stack-up.

title: Aerospace anodizing: aluminum-oxide nanopore templates for capacitors
idea: Instead of EUV plus deep plasma etch of 60-75:1 holes, deposit thick aluminum, nanoimprint shallow seed pits, and anodize it in oxalic or sulfuric acid (aircraft anodizing chemistry) so ordered vertical pores grow 1-3 um deep, then line them with TiN/ZrO2-Al2O3/TiN. Elements: Al, O, S, C, Ti, Zr, N only.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and etch capex (fact 4): AR ~115 is trivial for anodization; a ~$1M wet bath replaces $5-10M high-AR etchers; no W or Ru.

title: Sleep consolidation: idle-time compression of agent memory into gist tokens
idea: Borrowed from hippocampal sleep replay and spaced repetition: when an agent session idles, a background pass replays older context through the model to distill each chunk into a few learned gist tokens, keeping full-fidelity KV only for items retrieved repeatedly (high recall strength) and dropping the rest.
why: Long-lived agent contexts are mostly parked KV; consolidation claims 10-50x less resident KV for idle sessions.

title: Court-stenographer chords: bigger tokens shrink KV until it fits SRAM
idea: Borrowed from stenotype machines that write whole words in one chord: the model uses latent multi-byte patch tokens (dynamic 8-16-byte patches) so each KV entry covers ~4x more text, and with latent low-rank KV projection a 32k-character context fits in on-die SRAM.
why: About 4x fewer KV entries times 4-8x smaller entries gives 16-32x less KV memory, small enough to live in SRAM with zero refresh.

title: Anodized-alumina 1000:1 pore capacitor forest on foundry CMOS
idea: MAGNIFY aspect ratio to ~1000:1 with a beaker: sputter Al onto finished foundry CMOS wafers, anodize it into self-ordered 20-40 nm pores, then ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN inside; each 250-nm landing pad catches ~30 pores so no pore-to-cell alignment is needed. Tools: an anodization bath, one ALD tool and one contact litho.
why: Cs > 5 fF per cell without plasma high-AR etch (fact 1) and with tiny capital (fact 4); turns mature-node logic into embedded DRAM.

title: Sputtered complementary-oxide SRAM layer stacked over any chip
idea: MINIFY the fab to a sputter tool: room-temperature sputtered p-type SnO and n-type ZnSnO thin-film transistors form cross-coupled 6T latches above finished foundry CMOS; repeat the 4-mask module to stack several memory layers.
why: Static, refresh-free memory in monolithic 3D without EUV (facts 2, 4), all-U.S. tools; p-oxide mobility limits access to ~10-50 ns.
note: p-SnO stability and 6T TFT area limit density; oxide CMOS SRAM previously shown.

title: Magnify endurance with antiferroelectric ZrO2 given a built-in bias
idea: Antiferroelectric ZrO2 survives 1e12+ cycles but has no remanence; asymmetric electrodes (TiN vs RuO2 work-function offset) plus a fixed-charge dipole interlayer shift the double loop so one AFE loop straddles zero field, creating two stable remanent states.
why: Non-volatile cells with endurance 100-1000x beyond HZO FeRAM; refresh-free.

title: Tin-oxide seed grows hafnium-free rutile titania with k near 100
idea: Magnify k ~2.5x: a 2 nm SnO2 seed (rutile lattice) on the bottom electrode makes ALD TiO2 crystallize as high-k rutile below 450 C, with Al doping to tame leakage. It replaces ZrO2/HfO2 and the Ru-oxide templates used before.
why: Same Cs at aspect ratio ~30 instead of 70 (fact 1), removing hafnium and zirconium and halving the hardest etch; Sn and Ti are abundant.

title: Indium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cell keeps data minutes at 125 C
idea: Magnify bandgap, minify chokepoints: build 2T0C gain cells from amorphous Zn-Sn-O (Eg ~3.3 eV), whose off-current stays below 1e-19 A/um at 125 C, with no indium, no gallium and no high-AR capacitor.
why: Seconds-to-minutes retention at 125 C vs ~32 ms refresh for silicon DRAM above 85 C (fact 3). Removes In/Ga (China-dominated) and the deep capacitor etch; ZTO has no phase change below 300 C.
note: In-free twist on widely pursued IGZO 2T0C.

title: Self-ordering anodic alumina templates for capacitor holes
idea: Minify capacitor-hole lithography to zero: anodize a deposited aluminum film so it self-organizes into a hexagonal nanopore lattice (aspect ratio >100), then line pores with electrode and high-k by ALD.
why: Capacitor charge wall and EUV layers: electrochemistry in a beaker replaces the hardest EUV and high-AR etch step; pores naturally reach AR ~115+.

title: Minify KV vectors to 16-byte global product-quantized codes
idea: Minify each 128-dim FP16 key/value head vector (256 B) to a 16-byte product-quantization code against fleet-trained codebooks kept in on-chip SRAM. Attention scores are computed directly from lookup tables (asymmetric distance), never dequantizing.
why: 16x KV density on existing HBM and DRAM. The codebooks are shared by every session, so the overhead amortizes to zero.
note: PQ/VQ KV compression already published (PQCache etc.); 1 bit/dim accuracy doubtful.

title: Minify resident weights to a 3-layer ring streamed from NAND
idea: Minify weight residency to a ring buffer of 2-3 layers: weights stream from a 64-channel NAND array at >=100 GB/s per accelerator while large-batch compute hides the streaming time, layer by layer.
why: DRAM for weights drops 10-40x, and NAND bits cost ~1/15 of DRAM. Capacity per dollar rises >=10x at roughly equal system cost.

title: Minify weights to seeds: on-chip PRNG regenerates weight blocks
idea: Minify stored weights to an LFSR seed plus a few coefficients per block. On-chip PRNG units regenerate a pseudo-random basis and combine it into the weights at matmul time, after a seed search at compression time.
why: ~10x weight compression (16 bits down to ~1.5 effective bits) by converting memory into cheap on-die logic and FLOPs.
note: SeedLM-style; 1.5 effective bits likely loses accuracy.

title: Minify host memory: attention computed inside the SSD
idea: Minify host memory for long-context KV by keeping it on SSDs whose controllers include attention engines. The host sends queries and receives only softmax-weighted outputs (KBs), so the bulk KV never crosses PCIe.
why: Long-context KV moves to NAND at ~1/15 the cost per bit: >=10x capacity at the same cost, and data movement drops too.

title: Magnify the cache ratio 128:1: flash-backed DRAM-class memory
idea: Present SLC 3D NAND as byte-addressable memory through a controller with a DRAM cache 1/128 of capacity, write coalescing, hot-page prediction and terabyte-wide wear leveling; NAND is written only on eviction, so endurance holds by architecture.
why: Blended cost ~ NAND ~$0.06/GB + 0.8% DRAM = ~$0.15/GB, ~100x cheaper, trading tail latency (microseconds on misses) for capacity.
note: Known (CMM-H, IMDT); microsecond misses and write amplification break DRAM-class claims.

title: Eliminate the separate capacitor: ferroelectric-semiconductor channel stores the bit itself
idea: Eliminate both the capacitor and the gate stack: make the channel from a ~3-nm ferroelectric semiconductor (alpha-In2Se3) whose locked in-plane/out-of-plane polarization modulates its own conductance by 1e3-1e5, so one device is both storage and access, with a non-destructive read.
why: Collapses 1T1C into one ~4F2 device, removing the capacitor wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3); stackable in BEOL below 400 C; risk is retention and endurance beyond 1e12 cycles.

title: Eliminate plasma etch and PFAS gases: catalyst-drilled capacitor holes
idea: Define a silver nanodot catalyst array by block-copolymer self-assembly on a thick sacrificial silicon mold, then immerse in HF/H2O2 so each dot sinks vertically (metal-assisted chemical etching), drilling 15-20 nm holes beyond 100:1; build electrodes in the holes, strip the mold, and recover the silver from the bath.
why: The 60-75:1 capacitor etch burns C4F6/C4F8 (PFAS, high-GWP) in the costliest etchers; room-temperature wet drilling reaches the AR~115 that fact 1 asks for with a fraction of the capital.

title: Eliminate the high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch with anodized alumina pores
idea: Deposit 2-3 um of aluminium over the landing pads, pre-dimple it with a shallow DUV-defined seed lattice, and anodize it so self-ordered hexagonal nanopores grow straight down onto each pad; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN then lines the pores. No resist, no hard mask and no HAR plasma etch are used for the storage node.
why: Facts 1 and 4: electrochemical pores reach AR >150:1 in a wet bath, enabling Cs ~8 fF, and remove the slowest, costliest etch module and its hard-mask stack; capacitor-module capex down an estimated ~40%.
note: Barrier layer at pore bottom must be opened.

title: Eliminate minority carriers: hole-free oxide channels make row hammer impossible
idea: Build arrays from wide-bandgap n-type oxides deposited at <=350 C, with no body contact and essentially no holes. The substrate charge-pumping and electron-migration mechanisms behind silicon row hammer then have no carrier population to act through. Qualify with hammer tests at 1M activations.
why: Could eliminate row hammer (fact 9) by physics, removing TRR and counter logic and their refresh bandwidth and simplifying the periphery (fact 7).
note: IGZO DRAM widely pursued; hammer immunity plausible but passing-gate coupling remains; easy to test.

title: The wall is the bit: conducting domain walls in insulating ferroelectric
idea: Rearrange which part stores the data: in LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 films a domain wall conducts while domains insulate; a write creates or erases a wall across a 20 nm electrode gap, and a sub-coercive read senses the wall current without disturbing it.
why: Destructive read and refresh (facts 3,8): nonvolatile NDRO with uA read current and no restore write; 1-2 nm walls make density litho-limited, not charge-limited.

title: Metal digs the hole: catalyst-assisted chemical etching
idea: Reverse plasma-from-above into catalyst-from-below: put Au/Ag catalyst dots (patterned by DUV or dewetting) on silicon and let metal-assisted chemical etching sink them downward, carving 200:1 vertical trench capacitors at room temperature in a wet bench.
why: Capacitor charge wall and etch-tool capex: AR 200:1+ without cryo plasma tools or EUV, giving ~2-3x Cs per cell.

title: Per-block local losses discard activations before next block runs
idea: Reverse the training order from forward-all-then-backward-all to forward-and-learn per block: each block gets an auxiliary head or a forward-gradient estimate, updates at once, and frees its activations before the next block executes.
why: Stored activations are often 60-80% of training memory; per-block learning makes them O(1 block) instead of O(depth), a 10-50x cut in activation memory if accuracy holds.

title: Ferroelectric/paraelectric superlattice in stabilized negative capacitance, effective k ~80
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: stack ~1-nm HZO ferroelectric layers between Al2O3/ZrO2 paraelectric layers sized so the ferroelectric sits on its stabilized negative-capacitance branch, making the series stack capacitance larger than either layer alone, with no hysteresis. Contradiction resolved: thick (low-leakage) dielectric vs. high capacitance.
why: Fact 1 asks for k~70: reaching k_eff 60-90 at ~6 nm physical thickness cuts tunneling-leakage tail ~10x versus equal-EOT ZrO2.
note: HZO/ZrO2 superlattice capacitance boost actively pursued; stabilization without hysteresis is the gap.

title: Equipotentiality: clamped motionless bitlines with charge-transfer sensing
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: each bitline is held at a constant potential by a cascode clamp; the cell's charge flows through the clamp onto a ~0.5 fF sense node, amplified by the capacitance ratio, and restore injects charge back through the same clamp, so the large bitline never swings.
why: Facts 5, 8 and 10: bitline swing energy (~60% of activation energy) drops ~10x and bitline-to-bitline coupling noise nearly vanishes.
note: Restore through clamp still swings cell; 10x energy claim overstated.

title: Antiferroelectric-boundary dielectric biased for a giant effective permittivity
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: tune a ZrO2-rich HfZrO film to sit at its field-induced tetragonal-to-polar transition, and offset the plate voltage so the storage window rides the steep part of the P-E curve. The local dQ/dV gives k_eff ~80-120 without full ferroelectric switching.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k~70 target so a 40:1 capacitor holds what a 75:1 holds today; shorter capacitors shrink 3D tier pitch ~40%.

title: Hafnium-free antiferroelectric zirconia boosts charge near switching field
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: tune pure tetragonal ZrO2 so its field-induced transition to the polar orthorhombic phase sits just above the array voltage. The plate is biased at the edge of that transition, where steep dP/dE gives ~1.5-2x charge per area over linear ZAZ.
why: Raises Cs at the same pillar aspect ratio (fact 1) using only Zr, Al, Ti, N and O. Operating short of full switching avoids hysteresis and keeps endurance at DRAM levels.
note: MPB/AFE ZrO2 for DRAM Cs widely pursued.

title: Hemoglobin cooperativity: antiferroelectric window multiplies effective capacitance
idea: Hemoglobin releases most of its oxygen inside a narrow pressure window by cooperative switching. Bias the cell plate of an antiferroelectric ZrO2-rich capacitor so the 0 and 1 node voltages straddle its field-induced AFE-to-FE transition. The transition releases extra polarization charge, giving k_eff ~80-150 within the 1 V swing.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): reaches the k~70 target with no new elements, for 2-3x Cs at the same AR or half the AR. It does not store in ferroelectric hysteresis, so endurance stays near DRAM.

title: GC-rich bonds: ultra-wide-bandgap Ga2O3 channels let capacitors shrink below 1 fF
idea: Thermophile genomes are GC-rich (three hydrogen bonds per pair) for a higher melting point; likewise use ALD Ga2O3 (Eg ~4.8 eV) as the vertical channel in each tier, whose thermally generated off-current stays ~1e-21 A even at 125 C, so a sub-1 fF planar MIM capacitor per tier holds data for seconds.
why: Capacitor wall plus 3D blocker at 125 C: removes the tall capacitor entirely, flat ~30 nm tiers make 100+ tier stacks feasible, and refresh drops ~1000x versus Si at 125 C.
note: ALD Ga2O3 off-current is defect-limited, not thermal; overlaps IGZO 2T0C work.

title: Honeycomb anodic alumina self-orders capacitor holes at extreme aspect
idea: Bees build hexagonal comb from local wall rules; sputter aluminum over the landing pads and anodize it, so pores self-organize into a hexagonal lattice whose pitch is set by voltage (25-60 nm) and whose sites are pinned by shallow DUV-printed dimples on the pads; pores grow 5-10 um deep in a wet bench, then get ALD electrode and dielectric.
why: Replaces the capacitor-hole exposure and hardest plasma etch (facts 1, 4) with a ~$100k anodization bench; aspect ratio becomes nearly free, removing the charge wall.

title: Deck of cards: sliding-ferroelectric bilayer stacking flips store bits
idea: Shuffle cards by one atom: in parallel-stacked bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2, AB versus BA stacking gives opposite out-of-plane polarization, switched by ~1 V across ~1 nm as one layer slides a third of a lattice spacing; build cells from exfoliated or CVD bilayers with e-beam-defined gates and read the polarization as a threshold shift in a stacked MoS2 channel.
why: Endurance and voltage floor (Fact 10): sliding ferroelectricity shows little wake-up/fatigue because no ions or vacancies move, giving non-volatility at ~1 V with potentially >1e12 cycles; a transfer stage, e-beam and evaporator are the whole toolset.

title: Diatom biomineralization: DNA-origami templates place 10-nm storage nodes
idea: Diatoms grow silica shells on protein templates; adsorb DNA-origami tiles carrying metal seeds on a 10-nm grid onto shape-matched landing sites defined by relaxed e-beam litho, then grow storage nodes or floating islands from the seeds by ALD or electroless plating, burning off the origami afterward.
why: Fact 4: sub-12-nm feature placement without EUV using wet chemistry plus one relaxed-pitch e-beam step, all university-buildable; placement yield (~95-99% today versus >99.9999% needed) requires spare rows and ECC.
note: Kershner 2009 placement on landing sites is prior art; yield is far from needed.

title: Black-silicon MacEtch: catalytic wet etching of 100:1 capacitor holes
idea: Borrowed from solar black-silicon texturing, where Ag/Au catalyst sinks into silicon in HF/H2O2 and drills vertical pores: deposit an amorphous-Si capacitor mold, pattern a thin gold mesh on the hole lattice, immerse so the catalyst etches straight down to AR >100 at room temperature, strip the gold and line with electrode and dielectric; a small team runs it on a wet bench.
why: Facts 1/4: replaces a $10M+ high-AR plasma etcher with a ~$100k wet bench and has no aspect-ratio-dependent slowdown; gold contamination and verticality control are risks.

title: Seed bank weights: PRNG seeds plus low-rank corrections in NV
idea: Like a seed vault storing seeds instead of forests, store each weight block as a 32-bit PRNG seed selecting a random basis, a few coefficients and a low-rank residual in on-package NV; a hardware LFSR regrows the block in SRAM at compute time.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight-equivalent, zero DRAM for weights, native persistence; trades cheap logic for scarce memory.

title: Foldable-phone Z-fold flex memory stack
idea: Foldable phones bend circuits on polyimide. Mount thinned DRAM dies along one long polyimide flex (cured ≤350 C) carrying fine Cu traces, test every die flat, then Z-fold the strip accordion-style into a stack. Tier-to-tier signals travel over the folds instead of TSVs.
why: No TSV processing, and each die is tested before folding, which gives known-good stacks. It trades some wire length for 30-50% lower stacking cost.

title: Telegraph codebook KV: position-free phrase blocks shared rack-wide
idea: Like 1880s commercial telegraph codes that replaced common phrases with five-letter codewords, frequently reused segments (system prompts, tool schemas, popular documents) get codewords whose KV is computed once in a position-independent form and kept in rack-pooled memory. Sessions store only codeword references, and RoPE re-rotation plus a small boundary-correction pass place the phrase at any offset at read time.
why: Unlike prefix caching, reuse works anywhere in the context; for agent/RAG workloads where 50-90% of tokens are repeated chunks, per-session KV drops 2-10x.
note: Overlaps CacheBlend/EPIC-style position-independent caching.

title: Briggs log-table interpolation for cross-layer KV cache
idea: Henry Briggs printed logarithms only at anchor points plus difference columns for interpolation. Store full KV only for anchor layers (every 4th) and, for in-between layers, a per-head low-rank correction to the linear interpolation of the neighbouring anchors' KV, reconstructed on the fly in the read path.
why: KV capacity 2.5-3.5x smaller with the correction term holding accuracy, and stackable with quantization.

title: IBM 650 SOAP Revival: Time-Placing Tensors so Flash Replaces DRAM
idea: Revive the 1955 Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each instruction on the drum so it arrived under the read head just when needed: a compiler for static AI graphs lays out every weight and KV block across NAND/SSD stripes so it streams in just in time through a small DRAM staging ring.
why: Usable supply: replaces most resident-weight DRAM with flash at ~10-20x lower cost per bit; DRAM per served model can drop 5-10x.
note: Flash bandwidth limits decode-heavy inference; similar to LLM-in-a-flash and ZeRO-Infinity work.

title: Swiss-cheese tiers: stack defective layers, remap holes in base die
idea: Inverts 'every cell in a die must work.' Accept 3D tiers with up to ~5-10% dead cells, map defects at wafer probe into a per-stack CAM/remap table held in the logic base die, and drop per-tier redundancy rows/columns, so tier yields no longer multiply into stack yield.
why: Fact 2: lowers the yield-driven break-even tier count (26+) and recovers ~3-5% redundancy area; makes 100-tier stacks economically yieldable.

title: Copper-catalyzed MacEtch drills 100:1 holes without plasma tools
idea: Inverts 'high-aspect-ratio holes need plasma etch with W or carbon hard masks.' Use metal-assisted chemical etching with a patterned Cu catalyst in HF/H2O2 so silicon dissolves only beneath the catalyst, driving vertical holes and pillars past 100:1 at room temperature.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR 115 becomes reachable on a wet bench instead of ~$10M etch tools, using Cu, H, F and O.

title: Grow the holes: anodized alumina pores as capacitor molds
idea: Inverts 'deep capacitor holes must be plasma-etched': deposit thick aluminum over the array and anodize it; self-ordered hexagonal pores with aspect ratios above 100:1 (pitch set by anodization voltage, registration seeded by a shallow imprint) become the capacitor mold, lined with electrode and dielectric by ALD.
why: Removes the hardest high-AR fluorocarbon etch (C4F6/C4F8, fluorspar and PFAS supply chain) and its hardmask stack; room-temperature aqueous electrochemistry reaches the AR~115 needed for more charge.

title: Nitrogen-cooled racks freeze leakage, switching refresh off
idea: Inverts 'memory runs at room temperature': immerse DRAM modules in liquid nitrogen from air-separation units (no helium), where junction and subthreshold leakage fall by >1e6 and retention stretches from 64 ms to hours or days; firmware disables refresh for working sets whose lifetime is below the cryogenic retention.
why: Zero refresh power and bandwidth, wire resistance falls ~5x; nitrogen is the most abundant gas and LN2 costs cents per liter.
note: Same LN2 cryo-DRAM mechanism as I-02504; adds refresh-off firmware.

title: Anodized-alumina pores as a ready-made capacitor forest
idea: Inverts 'storage nodes must be individually patterned'. Anodize sputtered aluminium in oxalic acid so it self-orders into hexagonal pores (~25-60 nm pitch, AR >100:1); a 180 nm stepper only fences cell groups, and atomic-layer-epitaxy reactors of the 1990s TFEL-display type line the pores with electrode/dielectric/electrode, several pores in parallel per cell.
why: Self-assembled high-AR template from an electrochemistry bath; ~30x capacitor area per footprint so a 180 nm-rule cell gets ample Cs in a thin layer (fact 1).
note: AAO MIM nanocapacitor arrays are well published; registration to cells is the issue.

title: Catalytic gold-mesh wet etching drills 200:1 nanoholes
idea: Inverts 'deep holes require plasma'. Metal-assisted chemical etching: a perforated Au film (stepper-defined then spacer-shrunk) sinks into Si in HF/H2O2, drilling straight pores or freeing pillars at AR 100-200:1 at room temperature, then the Au is stripped in iodide before any thermal step.
why: Replaces the most expensive high-AR dry etchers (facts 1, 4) with wet benches, with no bowing; serves capacitor holes or vertical-channel pillars.

title: Lensless interference lithography with 1990s excimer lasers
idea: Inverts 'lithography needs a lens and a mask'. Interfere two or three line-narrowed 248/193 nm excimer beams (Lloyd's-mirror geometry) at the wafer to expose ~110-130 nm-pitch gratings or hexagonal arrays over a whole 200 mm wafer in one flash, then halve with one spacer step.
why: A ~$1M optical bench replaces a $100M+ scanner for every periodic array layer (fact 4); coherence over full-wafer area is the risk.

title: Canonicalized document KV shared across all tenants
idea: Inverts 'each request owns its KV cache': RAG chunks, tool schemas and system prompts are normalized into canonical position-independent KV blocks (re-rotated to the needed position at use) and stored once per cluster under a content hash, so any tenant that retrieves the same document reuses the same KV blocks.
why: In RAG and agent workloads 60-90% of context is shared documents, so KV memory per active user drops 5-20x.
note: CacheBlend/EPIC-like; cross-chunk attention loss needs blending.

title: Local-loss training lets each block free activations immediately
idea: Inverts 'backprop must store every activation': blocks train on local objectives (per-block predictive or contrastive heads, plus a periodic short global sync), so each block's activations are freed as soon as its local update finishes.
why: Activation memory, often 50-80% of the training footprint at long sequence lengths, shrinks to about one block's worth: a 10-30x cut in activation memory.

title: Charge-recycling bus: stacked voltage domains reuse every transition
idea: Invert 'each bit transition dumps its charge to ground': split the bus into N series-stacked voltage domains so charge discharging a line in domain k charges a line in domain k-1, with a small balancing regulator closing the loop.
why: Cuts I/O CV2 energy roughly by N (2-4x) despite the ~1 V floor, attacking the voltage floor and data-movement energy.
note: Stacked-domain charge recycling is decades-old art; balancing regulator and data-dependent imbalance limit gains.

title: Ferroelectric-semiconductor channel that stores and reads its own bit
idea: Use alpha-In2Se3, whose locked in-plane/out-of-plane polarization sets its own band bending and conductance, as the transistor channel. A gate pulse writes the polarization, and the read is a non-destructive channel conductance with no separate capacitor or ferroelectric gate stack.
why: Storage and gain merge in one 2D layer, removing the capacitor (fact 1) and destructive read (fact 8). Enables a vertical 4F2 cell with no capacitor etch.
note: In2Se3 FeS-FET demonstrated (2019); retention suffers from in-channel depolarization.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM: freeze out leakage, then shrink the capacitor
idea: Run the array at 77 K, where thermally activated leakage (junction generation, subthreshold, trap-assisted) falls by >1e6 because it scales as exp(-Ea/kT). Design out the weakly temperature-dependent GIDL with a lower wordline-off bias, so a 0.3 fF planar MIM holds data for hours and refresh is dropped. Racks are LN2-cooled at ~10x wall-power overhead on the much smaller memory heat.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and the capacitor charge wall (fact 1). Planar caps can approach 4F2 with no pillar etch, and bitline resistance falls ~5x.

title: Erasable conducting domain walls as non-destructive ferroelectric bits
idea: In thin-film z-cut LiNbO3-on-insulator, a field pulse injects a charged head-to-head domain wall between two electrodes that conducts ~uA, and a reverse pulse erases it. The read senses the wall current and never switches the polarization.
why: Read current is uA rather than fC, so reads are fast and non-destructive (fact 8). Walls are nanometers wide, so density is not capacitor-limited (fact 1), and nothing leaks (fact 3).
note: LiNbO3 domain-wall memory actively researched; wall pinning, speed and density at scale open.

title: Antiferroelectric back-switching plateau acts as a constant-voltage charge reservoir
idea: Add a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 film in parallel with the storage dielectric. Size it so the written '1' voltage is above its field-induced polar switching and its back-switching edge sits just above the sense threshold. As leakage drains the node, the AFE back-switches and releases ~10-20 uC/cm^2 of polarization charge at a nearly constant voltage, pinning the node like a clamped reservoir.
why: Usable charge above the sense threshold rises several-fold without taller pillars. That attacks fact 1 and the retention equation t = dQ/I (fact 3), for 3-5x retention at equal leakage.

title: Johnsen-Rahbek solid-contact chuck conducts heat with zero backside gas
idea: Contact conductance h ~ 1.25 k_s (m/sigma)(P/H)^0.95 grows with true contact area; a Johnsen-Rahbek chuck gives ~10x the clamp pressure of a Coulomb chuck, and a compliant 50 um pyrolytic-graphite skin raises true contact from ~0.1% to a few percent, reaching gas-gap-class 500-1000 W/m2K with no gas.
why: Removes helium entirely from chucks, including cryogenic etch where He cooling is critical; backside particle and carbon contamination control is the risk.

title: Tin-oxide rutile template grows k~90 TiO2 capacitors without Ru
idea: Rutile TiO2 has k~90-170 but only forms rutile at DRAM temperatures on a rutile-structured template, today RuO2 (Ru ~90% South Africa). Use conductive Sb:SnO2 or metallic MoO2 (rutile family, ~2-3% mismatch) as bottom-electrode template and 2-5% Al-doped TiO2 to raise the leakage barrier.
why: Fact 1 asks for k~70: doubling k from ZrO2's ~40 halves the 60-75:1 aspect ratio for the same Cs, and removes Zr/Hf ALD and ruthenium; Sn, Mo, Ti are diversified or US-sourced.

title: Catalyst-assisted wet etching digs 100:1 capacitor holes without fluorocarbon plasma
idea: Silicon dissolves only beneath a noble-metal catalyst in HF/H2O2 (metal-assisted chemical etching), so holes sink straight down at room temperature with no ion angular spread limiting depth. Pattern a catalyst mesh at storage-node pitch, sink 100:1 holes into silicon to revive trench-capacitor DRAM, then strip the catalyst in iodide etch.
why: Replaces the C4F6/C4F8 high-aspect-ratio plasma etch (PFAS-class gases, $10M+ tools, high energy) with a wet bench and pushes Cs past the 60-75:1 wall.

title: Regenerate weights from PRNG seeds in the HBM base die
idea: A trained weight block can be approximated as a few coefficients times pseudo-random basis vectors. Store, per 8x8 block, a 16-bit LFSR seed and 4 low-bit coefficients; an LFSR array in the HBM logic die regenerates the basis and the weights at read bandwidth, replacing stored bits with deterministic computation.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight effective (4-5x smaller than FP16); spare logic-die compute becomes virtual capacity.

title: Position-free KV storage for cross-user chunk dedup
idea: The same RAG documents and system prompts recur across users at different offsets, which defeats prefix caching. Store each chunk's keys before RoPE, under a content hash; apply the rotary rotation for the real position at read time, and run a small learned correction pass over the first few tokens of each chunk to restore cross-chunk attention.
why: In RAG-heavy serving, KV for shared corpora is stored once per cluster instead of once per request: 5-20x less KV capacity.

title: Garden hose: conductive ferroelectric domain wall opened or kinked off
idea: Stimulus 'garden hose' (flow on, or kinked off) -> in a thin LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 mesa, a write pulse creates or erases a charged head-to-head domain wall bridging two electrodes; the wall conducts ~1000x more than the bulk, so read is a small nondestructive current and the wall stays put without power.
why: Nondestructive read with no restore (fact 8), no refresh (fact 3), and current-mode read that suits vertical stacking (fact 2).
note: LiNbO3 domain-wall memory demonstrated by several groups; CMOS integration and scaling remain.

title: Honeycomb: anodized alumina pores template 500:1 capacitors, no plasma
idea: Stimulus 'honeycomb' -> anodize an aluminum film in oxalic acid so it self-organizes into hexagonal pores (40-60 nm pitch, AR up to 500:1), guided by a nanoimprinted pre-dent, then ALD TiN (from TiCl4/NH3) and ZrO2/Al2O3 into the pores. The electrolyte digs the holes: no fluorocarbon etch, no NF3 chamber clean.
why: Breaks the 60-75:1 AR wall toward >115:1 (fact 1) and removes the capacitor-hole EUV/etch step (fact 4); ~2x Cs or half the footprint, fluorine-free.
note: Same AAO pore capacitor; registration to the access device.

title: Honeycomb: anodic alumina pores self-register on landing pads as capacitor molds
idea: Random stimulus 'honeycomb' -> an aluminum film deposited over the landing-pad array is anodized at ~10-12 V, so pores nucleate at the pad-induced topographic dimples and grow straight down as a self-ordered hexagonal array with aspect ratio >100. The pores serve as the storage-capacitor mold, which needs no lithography and no high-AR plasma etch.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 115 needed) and capital (fact 4). The mold litho and the most expensive etch step become a wet electrochemical bench costing <$1M, and AR rises from 70 to 120+ for ~1.7x more Cs.

title: Dynamic copper-filament crosspoint memory refreshed like DRAM
idea: Box = {medium: volatile nanoscale Cu filament in SiO2 that dissolves over ~1 s | access: none (self-rectifying stack) | sense: filament on/off current ~1e3 | integration: 4F2 crosspoint stacked 8 layers | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: sputtered Arizona copper + PECVD SiO2}. Filaments are kept deliberately thin so they relax on their own, which allows low compliance current and longer endurance, and a 1 s refresh rewrites the ones.
why: Density (4F2 x 8 layers) and capital: a crosspoint with no access transistor, built from only Cu, Si and O.

title: Refresh interval set by 1% failure point, scrubbed by ECC
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x SA plus decode-on-refresh x controller scrub x bulk Si x standard. Retention is specified where 1% of cells fail instead of at the 1e-9 tail, which stretches refresh ~16-30x; each refresh pass reads through the decoder and writes back corrected data so errors never pile up.
why: Refresh energy (16-33% of idle) and bandwidth loss (10-20%) cut >90%; the ~13 fA leakage tail stops mattering.
note: 1% raw BER needs heavy codes; decode-on-refresh energy is the doubt.

title: Calcium titanate perovskite capacitors from earth-abundant elements
idea: Box [CaTiO3 (k~150) cap | Si access | voltage SA | pillar | Si | thermal ALD from a Ca cyclopentadienyl + Ti amide + O3 with N2 purges]: grow perovskite CaTiO3 on a conductive Nb:TiO2 bottom electrode that seeds crystallization near 450 C, with no Sr, Ru or Hf.
why: Capacitor charge wall (needs k~70) and scarce-element intensity: Ca and Ti are abundant and US-available, and k~150 lets AR fall to ~25:1; crystallization temperature and leakage are the risks.

title: Low-aspect-ratio capacitor from ALD rutile-TiO2/SrTiO3 on Ru, k~100
idea: Box: k 100-150 dielectric charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x ALD on Ru/RuO2 electrodes that template rutile or perovskite growth below 450 C. With k~100 vs ~40 today, the same ~5 fF fits in an AR ~25 pillar, so the module drops the cryo-etch, the support mesh and two hardmask layers; leakage is held by Al doping and a thin wide-gap interface layer.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) attacked through process: AR 70 to 25 removes the hardest etch and its helium-cooled tools, ~5-8% wafer cost; risk is leakage of narrow-gap high-k at ~0.4 nm EOT.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as 100:1 capacitor molds on chip
idea: Box: MIM charge x sputtered IGZO TFT x voltage sense amp x BEOL test chip x Si/SiO2 x two-step Al anodization in oxalic acid. A sputtered Al film is anodized into hexagonally ordered pores (~60-100 nm pitch, AR >100) with positions seeded by a light EBL pre-pattern, then ALD TiN/HfO2/TiN coats the pores, so the capacitor mold forms in a beaker, not a cryo-etcher.
why: Capacitor module capital (fact 1): a ~$2k anodization bath replaces a $5M+ high-AR etcher, with AR 100-500 possible (10-30 fF/cell); every step uses university sputter, EBL, ALD and wet benches.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching carves 100:1 capacitor trenches without plasma
idea: Box: Si trench charge x planar Si MOSFET access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x MacEtch with an EBL-patterned noble-metal mesh in HF/H2O2. The catalytic film sinks vertically into Si at room temperature, carving smooth high-AR holes in a wet bench; the catalyst is stripped and holes are lined by ALD.
why: Highest-AR etch with no plasma tool or helium-cooled chuck (AR >100 shown in research); capex <$10k; risk is catalyst contamination in a DRAM-grade flow and verticality below 50 nm.

title: Lloyd's-mirror crossed interference exposures print maskless pillar lattices
idea: Box: Si charge x vertical pillar transistor x standard sensing x 2D x Si x 266/325 nm laser Lloyd's-mirror interference lithography, two exposures at 90 degrees. Interference fringes print a perfectly periodic dot lattice over the wafer in seconds with no mask, and array-edge cuts plus periphery are added with a contact-aligner exposure.
why: Mask and EUV dependence for periodic arrays: a ~$50k optical table vs a $150M+ scanner; 100-150 nm pitch today, path below 40 nm with 193 nm immersion interference; risk is overlay of later layers to the lattice.

title: Po: the bit is a border — conductive ferroelectric domain-wall memory
idea: Po: the bit is not the country but its border. Extracted: in thin LiNbO3 or BiFeO3, write or erase a charged domain wall across a nano-gap; the wall conducts 1e3-1e6x more than the bulk, so the bit is wall present/absent, read non-destructively by a small current.
why: Non-destructive read removes restore energy (fact 8) and refresh (fact 3). Wall pinning and drift reliability are the risks.
note: Same conductive domain-wall bit.

title: Anodized aluminum pores as self-drawn capacitor molds
idea: Po: the metal draws its own circuit. Deposit thick Al, pre-dent it with a coarse DUV hexagonal guide grid, and anodize: self-ordered alumina pores form at 25-40 nm pitch with aspect ratios >150:1 in minutes; ALD TiN/high-k/TiN into the pores makes the capacitors with no high-AR plasma etch and no capacitor-hole EUV.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus etch/litho capex: AR >115 reached chemically for ~1.5-2x Cs; deletes the costliest etch step and a SAQP/EUV hole layer.

title: Forward-only training: learn without storing the forward pass
