idea: Inverts 'a database must cache pages in DRAM to be fast': filters, projections and aggregations run inside SSD controllers next to the flash, so only qualifying rows reach host memory and the buffer pool is sized for results instead of the working set.
why: Analytical databases give 50-80% of server DRAM to buffer pools; pushdown can shrink that 3-10x for scan-heavy work.

title: DIMM reincarnation: retired DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL bridges
idea: Inverts 'retired DIMMs are e-waste': hyperscalers pull DDR4 from decommissioned servers, retest it and mount it on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller is made on existing 28 nm logic lines. The result is a slow but large tier for cold pages and KV spill.
why: Millions of DDR4 DIMMs retire each year; reusing them adds 10-25% fleet capacity at near-zero cost per bit with no new DRAM wafers.
note: Already pursued by Azure/Meta (Pond-style DDR4 on CXL).

title: Tool-level cryogenic helium recapture closes the fab helium loop
idea: Helium is never consumed chemically in a fab; it is simply vented. Fit each wafer-cooling and purge exhaust with a membrane plus cryo-adsorption recovery skid that recompresses and repurifies to 5N, reaching >90% recycle.
why: Scarce resource: cuts fab helium draw ~10x while Qatar (~30% of supply) is offline; payback under 2 years at current prices.

title: Pool chlorine tablet: MoCl5-grown molybdenum electrodes replace WF6 tungsten
idea: Stimulus 'pool chlorine tablet' -> deposit storage-node contacts, landing pads and plate electrodes as molybdenum by ALD/CVD from MoCl5 or MoO2Cl2 plus H2 instead of tungsten from WF6; Mo has lower resistivity in narrow features and needs no TiN barrier. Molybdenum is mined in Colorado and Arizona.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 from the cell (scarce-resource axis); barrier-less contacts free ~2 nm per side for a larger capacitor (fact 1).
note: Industry already adopting Mo ALD for contacts and wordlines.

title: Immune memory: VRT suspects remembered forever via controller Bloom filter
idea: Variable-retention-time cells toggle good/bad and evade one-shot profiling; any address that ever yields a correctable error enters a counting Bloom filter (the 'memory T-cells'), and rows holding suspects get permanent 2x refresh or a stronger code.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: neutralizes VRT, the main reason profile-guided refresh is distrusted, unlocking safe 4x+ refresh relaxation.

title: Display-scrap indium and gallium loop feeding oxide-semiconductor memory
idea: Box [feedstock: spent IGZO sputter targets + end-of-life panels | refining: acid leach + solvent extraction | product: targets and ALD precursors | buyer: BEOL oxide-memory fabs]: contract recyclers to recover In/Ga from spent targets (only ~30% of a target is consumed) and scrapped panels, and recast them as dedicated memory-grade feedstock.
why: In/Ga chokepoints (China ~60% In, ~98% Ga): spent targets alone return ~70% of purchased indium, securing feedstock if oxide-semiconductor DRAM scales.
note: Spent ITO/IGZO target recycling is already standard practice.

title: Retrain tokenizers for fewer tokens per document, shrinking KV
idea: Box: fewer tokens × tokenizer × token × next model refresh × larger multilingual/code-aware vocabulary with frequent multi-word merges. New model generations adopt tokenizers that encode the same text in 20–30% fewer tokens, and KV size scales with token count.
why: 20–30% less KV per context at long context, outweighing the larger embedding table; software only, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Organ-donor program: retired DIMMs reborn as a CXL cold tier
idea: Po: dead memory comes back to life. Hyperscalers route decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 through a retest line that builds per-die weak-row maps, then mount the modules behind CXL controllers with strong ECC and map-based row retirement as a cold memory tier for VMs and caches.
why: Supply: reuses millions of DIMMs a year; 10-20% of server capacity demand could be served by second-life parts at <30% of new-part cost during the shortage.
note: Azure already reuses DDR4 behind CXL.

title: Heavy-water reactor engineer: deuterium-cured access transistor interfaces
idea: A CANDU operator has tonnes of heavy water on hand. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a 10-20 atm deuterium anneal so Si/SiO2 and junction dangling bonds are capped with Si-D bonds, which resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation ~10x better than Si-H and so stop traps from growing into variable-retention cells over life.
why: Narrows the end-of-life leakage tail, letting refresh intervals relax ~1.5-3x and improving yield; deuterium comes from Canada and the U.S., not a chokepoint.
note: High-pressure D2 anneal already in production use.

title: Ham radio operator's near-field link: coil-coupled stack without TSVs
idea: Ham operators talk without wires. Put 30-60 um inductive coils in the top metal of every die, glue thinned dies into a stack, and send data die-to-die by near-field magnetic coupling at ~1-8 Gb/s per coil and ~0.1-1 pJ/bit. Power comes in on edge wire bonds, and the design can be taped out on an MPW.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV area and yield tax (Fact 6) and moves data at under 1 pJ/bit (Fact 5), with packaging a small team can do.
note: ThruChip inductive coupling already demonstrated with DRAM stacks.

title: Deep-sea pressure: high-pressure deuterium anneal heals stacked-tier traps
idea: Deep-ocean hardware shows how pressure drives gas into solids; anneal finished 3D DRAM tier stacks in 20-50 atm deuterium/nitrogen at <=400 C so deuterium penetrates many tiers and passivates the channel and interface traps behind the leakage tail, staying within the stack's thermal budget. Deuterium bonds resist hot-carrier and activation-stress depassivation.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tail traps cut ~2-5x, lengthening refresh; trap-assisted row hammer (fact 9) reduced; no argon or helium ambient.

title: MRI-style closed-loop helium recovery across DRAM fabs
idea: Hospitals cut MRI helium loss ~90% with recondensers. Fabs, designed around the case of Qatar's supply offline, capture helium from wafer backside cooling, leak checks and purge lines with membrane-plus-cryo purifiers and recycle it on site.
why: Removes a chokepoint input (~30% of supply offline) and the tool downtime that shortages cause.

title: Fab-wide helium recapture loop with membrane and cryogenic polishing
idea: Scale jump from tool to fab: collect helium exhaust from chuck backside cooling, leak checking and purges into a fab-wide return header, then purify it with polymer membranes plus a small cryo-polisher and reinject it.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium supply has been offline since March 2026. Recapturing 80-90% makes fab helium demand ~5-10x less exposed to that chokepoint.

title: Helium reserve sell-off answered: closed-loop helium recapture per tool
idea: The 1996 Helium Privatization Act sold off the U.S. federal helium reserve, and Qatar's outage now starves fabs. Fix: fit recapture skids to every helium-using tool (backside wafer cooling in etch and implant, purge, leak check) that collect helium from the exhaust, purify it with membranes and pressure-swing adsorption, and feed it back to the tool.
why: Scarce resources: ~80-90% less helium bought per wafer, turning a geopolitical chokepoint into a small top-up.

title: Deuterium anneal hardens access transistors against tail and hammer damage
idea: Effect: the giant isotope effect in Si-H/Si-D desorption. The final H2 forming anneal is replaced by a high-pressure D2 anneal; Si-D interface bonds are ~10-50x more resistant to hot-carrier and hammer-cycling desorption, so the interface-trap generation that grows VRT tails and hammer susceptibility over life slows sharply.
why: Lifetime reliability: keeps time-zero retention and hammer thresholds over years, so end-of-life guard bands shrink (~1.5-2x refresh relaxation). It is a drop-in process change.
note: Deuterium and high-pressure D2 anneals are known since 1996 and used in production.

title: N: cryogenic nitrogen aerosol lifts particles with zero liquid
idea: Sweep an expanding jet of N2/Ar cryogenic aerosol (frozen micro-particles) across the wafer so momentum transfer lifts nanoparticles, after which the aerosol sublimes with no residue; use it wherever megasonic DI scrubs are used today.
why: Water: particle-removal scrubs drop to zero water, and the gentle dry action avoids toppling fragile capacitor pillars.

title: Aluminum remelt: retired DDR4 recast as a CXL far tier
idea: Aluminum is infinitely recyclable; likewise decommissioned servers' DDR4 DIMMs are tested, binned and mounted on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller adds stronger ECC and page compression, then deployed as the cold tier under new DDR5 hosts.
why: Hyperscalers retire millions of good DIMMs a year; reuse supplies ~25-40% of a host's capacity from sunk-cost silicon, cutting new DRAM purchases and scarce-resource intensity at near-zero fab capital.
note: Same retired-DDR4-on-CXL mechanism as I-04900.

title: Neon closed shells: zero and constant lines never touch DRAM
idea: Neon's full electron shell makes it inert; the controller keeps a 2-bit tag per 64 B line (zero, repeated byte, repeated word, real) in a 0.4%-overhead table cached in controller SRAM, so writes of trivial lines only update the tag, reads are synthesized on chip, and the unused backing lines join a free pool.
why: ReLU/sparse activations, fresh allocations and padded tensors are 30-80% trivial lines; those accesses cost ~0.05 pJ/bit of SRAM tag lookup instead of 10-20 pJ/bit, averaging >=10x lower energy per access on sparse workloads and freeing the same share of capacity (energy, density).

title: K: potassium-40 half-life tags skip refresh for short-lived data
idea: Allocator APIs tag buffers with an expected lifetime, like a radioisotope half-life; the controller tracks per-row last-write time and suppresses refresh for rows whose data will be rewritten or freed before retention expires (activations, KV caches, DMA buffers).
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) in AI training memory, where most data lives under 64 ms.

title: Brewery-style recapture: closed-loop helium recovery inside every fab
idea: Breweries capture fermentation CO2 and reuse it. Fit fabs with point-of-use helium capture on etch-chuck backside cooling, litho stage cooling and leak-check exhausts, then purify back to 6N with membrane plus PSA and recompress on site.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): 70-90% recovery cuts fab helium purchases 3-5x and de-risks wafer output.

title: Hot-swap CXL memory bricks with erasure-coded striping
idea: Rule: any memory unit must be removable for repair while the system runs. Pages are striped with RS(8+2) across 10 CXL memory bricks, so any brick can be pulled live, repaired or replaced, and rebuilt in the background onto a hot spare.
why: Tolerates whole-device failure at 20% overhead. Lets cheap, unqualified or second-life DRAM serve production pools, raising usable supply.
note: Close to IBM RAIM and distributed memory RAID.

title: Pinned-photodiode storage well from 180 nm image-sensor fabs
idea: Fuse the CIS 4T pixel with a DRAM cell. Charge sits in a fully depleted buried n-well whose surface is pinned by p+, away from the Si/SiO2 interface, and is read by a transfer gate onto a floating diffusion and source follower. This is built on existing 180 nm CIS lines.
why: Pinned-well dark current is ~10 e-/s against ~1e5 e-/s for DRAM junctions, so retention runs seconds to minutes with no refresh. The read is gain-based and non-destructive.
note: Pixel-scale 4T cells are ~1000x larger than DRAM cells; retention is real but density kills it.

title: LCD active-matrix backplane repurposed as bulk dynamic memory
idea: An LCD pixel is already a 1T1C DRAM cell refreshed at 60 Hz. Depreciated Gen-2/3 a-Si or LTPS lines (2-4 um rules) could pattern huge TFT-capacitor arrays with on-glass sense amps, and very wide rows offset the microsecond row time.
why: Attacks capital intensity, since those lines cost ~1/100 per area, and avoids EUV entirely. Density and latency are far below DRAM, so it fits only as a wide, slower bulk tier.
note: Reuse depreciated LCD lines as 1T1C arrays; cost/area falls 100x but density falls far more, so cost/bit worsens.

title: Dedup-as-redundancy: duplicate pages become free mirrors for weak rows
idea: Combine page deduplication with mirroring: when the hypervisor finds identical pages it keeps two copies in different banks only if one sits on weak cells, using the twin as a recovery mirror; all other duplicates are merged, so net memory still shrinks.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) and supply: reuses the 10-30% natural duplication in VM/AI fleets as free redundancy, letting weak rows hold data without extra parity.

title: Curie-point magnetic taggants encode material recipe for automated recycling
idea: Mold compound and substrates carry a few mg of ferrite microparticles with chosen Curie temperatures (e.g. 60/90/120/150 C). A recycler sweeps magnetization against temperature to decode the bill of materials and die grade, then routes each part to reuse or the right refinery.
why: Manual sorting caps recovery; machine-readable composition raises reuse and recovery rates.
note: Clever Curie-point barcode, but sorting is a niche lever on supply.

title: Wire-in-resin printed packages stack commodity memory BGAs
idea: Substitute substrate layers and TSVs with a printer-robot that embeds insulated fine copper wire inside 3D-printed resin frames as it prints, routing 3D connections between stacked commodity LPDDR packages and the host board.
why: Capital and density: dense memory modules without new silicon or substrate fabs; prototypes in days by a small team.

title: Murray's-law tapered power-tree generator for DRAM periphery
idea: Blood vessels and leaf veins follow Murray's law (parent radius^3 = sum of children's), minimizing transport cost per volume. An open-source EDA plugin synthesizes periphery VDD/VPP/VSS distribution as Murray-tapered trees instead of uniform meshes, with IR-drop sign-off on a test layout. Two engineers plus licenses, ~$600k in 24 months, then licensed to DRAM/eDRAM teams.
why: Fact 7 + tungsten chokepoint: ~20-30% less periphery power metal at equal IR drop frees routing tracks and cuts W/Cu usage in the lower levels.

title: Physarum flux-reinforcement floorplanner for global data and command buses
idea: The slime mould Physarum thickens tubes that carry flow and prunes the rest, finding near-optimal networks. Its flux-reinforcement model drives the routing of a DRAM die's global data, command and test buses, weighted by real access traces. Software only, ~$400k over 18 months, released and licensed.
why: Fact 5/7: trace-weighted Physarum topologies can cut weighted global wirelength ~10-20%, with similar savings in internal data-movement energy and bus area.

title: Lateral-line sensor tape maps helium leaks along every gas line
idea: Fish sense flow along the body with a lateral line of tiny neuromasts. Print a tape of thermal-conductivity microheater sensors every 5 cm (helium conducts heat ~6x better than air) with printed NFC readout, and wrap it along gas sticks, VCR fittings and chuck feeds to locate helium leaks in real time.
why: Leaks and over-flows are a large share of fab helium loss; continuous mapping could cut it 10-20% for a few dollars per metre.

title: Qubit-fab double-angle evaporation: self-aligned AlOx overlap storage capacitors
idea: Superconducting-qubit labs make Al/AlOx/Al junctions with one resist bridge and two angled evaporations plus in-situ oxidation; use this Dolan-bridge method to form the storage capacitor and its node contact in one e-beam exposure: first Al leg, controlled O2 dose for a 1.5-3-nm AlOx dielectric, then a second leg at a different angle whose overlap area, not the lithography, sets capacitance.
why: Capital and step count: capacitor plus contact in one exposure with zero overlay error, using an e-beam writer and angle evaporator; low-k AlOx limits charge, so it pairs with gain-cell or avalanche-sensed low-charge cells.
note: E-beam throughput and low-k AlOx limit it to a lab curiosity.

title: Bain-marie phase-change heat buffer clipping DIMM temperature spikes
idea: A bain-marie holds food below 100 C. A paraffin or salt-hydrate PCM pouch melting at ~78-80 C is bonded into the DIMM heatspreader. During load bursts it absorbs latent heat and holds the dies below 85 C, so the 2x refresh rule never triggers. Off-the-shelf PCM, a thermal chamber and qualification fit in under 12 months and under $300k.
why: Avoiding 2x refresh in hot servers saves ~10% bandwidth and 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and it keeps the retention tail in its nominal regime.

title: 48-hour printed test sockets for orphan salvaged packages
idea: Formula 1 teams iterate parts overnight. A 10-person shop uses high-resolution resin and two-photon printing plus pogo pins to make a BGA test socket for any orphan DRAM package in 48 hours instead of 8-12 weeks, so refurbishers can test whatever arrives.
why: Removes a hidden bottleneck in the reuse and micro-fab supply chains.

title: Retired AI GPUs reborn as networked HBM memory appliances
idea: Ideal: HBM never leaves service. Closest achievable with no new fab: when A100/H100 fleets retire, keep the boards in chassis as networked HBM servers (80 GB at TB/s each) that export KV-cache and embedding tables over RDMA to new accelerators.
why: Reuse of the costliest bits (3x wafer area per bit): billions of dollars of HBM stay in use 3-5 more years.
note: Network links cut HBM bandwidth to ~50 GB/s and idle GPU power per GB is poor.

title: Wafer-scale processor bonded face-to-face to a whole DRAM wafer
idea: Combine wafer-scale compute (one 300 mm logic wafer) with wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding of an entire undiced DRAM wafer on top; defect-tolerant routing maps out bad DRAM tiles the same way wafer-scale engines map out bad cores. No dicing, TSV stacks or package.
why: Data movement and HBM tax: on the order of ~1 TB of DRAM directly above compute at <0.1 pJ/bit per bond hop, ~30x bandwidth density vs HBM.
note: TB-class DRAM bonded over wafer-scale logic at sub-0.1 pJ/bit; doubts: thermal path, compound yield, fab-scale bonding.

title: DRAM bonded onto the backside of compute
idea: MINIFY vertical distance to ~10 um by hybrid-bonding DRAM to the back face of a backside-power-delivery logic wafer, with nano-vias interleaved with the power grid, so memory sits directly under every compute core.
why: Data-movement energy (HBM 3-4 pJ/bit): claims ~0.1 pJ/bit and removes the interposer entirely.
note: ~0.1 pJ/bit claim plausible; power must traverse DRAM layer and needs BSPDN wafers.

title: The DRAM wafer is the interposer; logic chiplets sit on it
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a passive interposer beside compute': fabricate an uncut DRAM wafer whose top metal levels double as interposer routing, then hybrid-bond GPU/CPU chiplets face-down onto it so every logic tile has gigabytes directly beneath it.
why: Eliminates the separate silicon interposer and TSV stacks; 1-5 um bond pitch gives ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit and TB/s per mm2 versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, while DRAM redundancy absorbs defects at wafer scale.
note: Uncut DRAM wafer as active interposer under logic chiplets; needs custom DRAM wafer and thermal solution.

title: Convert idle 3D-NAND fabs into vertical-stack DRAM lines
idea: Box[Source=glut-idle NAND fab x Transform=reuse 60-100:1 channel-hole etch and staircase tools x Medium=horizontally stacked 1T1C x Integration=CXL x Owner=NAND incumbent x Finance=downturn hedge]: NAND makers in a glut redirect their deep-etch, ALD and staircase toolsets to tiered lateral-capacitor DRAM, selling it as a CXL tier while the interface matures.
why: Attacks capital intensity and the 3D-DRAM tooling gap by reusing ~$20B-class depreciated NAND tool fleets instead of new fabs; turns NAND's glut cycle into DRAM supply.
note: Reuses NAND deep-etch fleets for 3D DRAM; doubt: lateral-capacitor 3D DRAM is unproven at yield.

title: Swap litho-defined cells for thickness-defined annular capacitors in stacks
idea: In a 64-pair Si/SiGe stack, etch one DUV hole per cell column and selectively recess the SiGe laterally into ring cavities whose height is set by film thickness (~8 nm). ALD fills them as ring capacitors, each wired to the lateral transistor in its tier.
why: Solves the 3D capacitor blocker (fact 2): deposition thickness, not lithography, sets the critical dimension, so 64 tiers need one DUV litho step (fact 4).
note: Thickness-defined 3D DRAM caps; widely pursued by majors, so little novelty.

title: Retune idle 3D NAND lines into quasi-volatile charge-trap DRAM
idea: Substitute NAND's ~5 nm FN-programmed tunnel oxide with a ~1.5-2 nm direct-tunneling oxide in a 3D NOR-organized charge-trap stack: writes in ~10-50 ns at <4 V, retention seconds-hours (refreshed), low-field tunneling for very high endurance, on existing 200+ layer NAND tools with mask changes only.
why: Capital and supply (fact 4): converts underused 3D-stacking capex into DRAM-class capacity with ~5-10x fewer refreshes and NAND-like cost per bit.
note: Essentially Sunrise Memory's quasi-volatile NOR; thin-oxide charge-trap endurance (~1e10-1e11) falls short of DRAM-class.

title: Relax F to 38 nm, magnify tiers to 300
idea: Minify lithography demand by freezing lateral pitch at a DUV-immersion 38 nm and magnify vertical tiers to 300 using NAND-style alternating deposition, one hole etch per 50 tiers, and a vertical-channel gain cell, so deposition and etch replace EUV.
why: Litho-bound scaling and EUV dependence: zero EUV layers; density grows with deposition tools costing ~1/4 of an EUV scanner per wafer-pass, targeting >2x bits per wafer at lower capex per bit.
note: Trade EUV for tier count; 3D DRAM is widely pursued, but 300 tiers via NAND-style stacks is a real density lever.

title: Grow up, not shrink down: relaxed-pitch 3D DRAM at F~38 nm
idea: Reverse the scaling vector: freeze lateral pitch where single ArF immersion exposure works (F~38 nm) and get density from 48-64 monolithic tiers whose shared vertical wordline is patterned once per stack, not once per tier.
why: No EUV; litho cost per bit falls with tier count; at 48 tiers density ~5x today's 2D at ~1/3 litho cost.
note: Same F~38 nm DUV-only multi-tier trade as I-01613.

title: Nacre brick-and-mortar: ALD-stacked capacitorless oxide tiers
idea: Nacre gets its strength from hundreds of thin mineral tiles bonded by organic layers. Monolithic stacks of 50-100 tiers of capacitorless oxide-TFT cells are deposited by low-temperature ALD, then patterned once with a staircase and vertical access holes, like 3D NAND with no capacitor in any tier.
why: Density comes from tiers rather than EUV, on more available NAND-style tooling; gets around the 3D DRAM capacitor blocker.
note: Capacitorless IGZO tiers would break the 3D DRAM blocker, but retention, tier variability and the approach are widely pursued.

title: Tier-for-litho: 64 BEOL tiers on DUV beat EUV density
idea: Bits/area = tiers / cell area. Pattern a <=400 C capacitorless cell at 4F2 with F = 45 nm on immersion DUV (no EUV), deposit 64 monolithic tiers as a blanket stack, and cut them with one 3D-NAND-style high-AR etch, reaching ~127 nm2/bit versus ~864 nm2 for 6F2 at 12 nm.
why: Removes EUV (fact 4) and much of the 55% depreciation burden. Thermal budget is what blocks monolithic stacking, and the 400 C limit is exactly what unlocks it.
note: 3D-NAND-style blanket stack plus one etch removes EUV; widely pursued; low-temp capacitorless cell retention and per-tier access are the doubts.

title: Flash-on-logic hybrid bonding reads 100,000 planes in parallel
idea: NAND bandwidth is limited by narrow package pins, not the array: each plane senses 16 KB per ~20 us. Hybrid-bond a 3D NAND array wafer face-to-face with a compute wafer so 10^5 planes each get their own bonded bus, giving ~80 TB/s from a medium priced like flash.
why: HBM-class bandwidth at ~100x lower cost per GB for read-mostly weights; trades write endurance and 20 us latency.
note: SanDisk HBF and Kioxia CBA pursue this; read disturb, 20 us latency, heat limit to read-mostly weights.

title: Volatile flash: ultrathin-tunnel charge-trap cells built on 3D-NAND lines
idea: Box = {medium: electrons in a SiN trap layer behind a 1.2 nm direct-tunneling oxide | access: the storage FET itself, NOR-wired | sense: nondestructive threshold read | integration: 200-layer vertical string rewired as NOR | substrate: Si | fab: unchanged 3D-NAND tool set}. Thinning the tunnel oxide trades 10-year retention for ~1-10 s and lets 4-5 V direct-tunneling writes finish in ~10 ns without the Fowler-Nordheim stress that wears out flash, with refresh every second instead of every 64 ms.
why: Facts 2, 3, 4: turns idle, depreciated 3D-NAND capacity into 3D DRAM-class memory with 15x less refresh and 200+ layer density.
note: If endurance holds, 200-layer DRAM-class density; but Sunrise Memory's 3D NOR QVM is prior art and tunnel wear persists.

title: Minutes-retention trap-charge cell with age-stamped scrubbing
idea: Box [medium: charge in SiN trap layer behind ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide | access: 1T gate-coupled storage | sense: Vt current sense | integration: 3D vertical stack | substrate: bulk | fab: NAND-style tools, no EUV]. Bits are written by low-voltage direct tunneling in nanoseconds and retained for minutes; reads sense transistor Vt without disturbing charge, and each block carries an age stamp so only blocks nearing their retention budget are scrubbed.
why: Constraint: a read is a small current pulse on a short line with no restore, ~10x below ACT+restore; refresh ~1000x rarer.
note: Close to Sunrise Memory quasi-volatile 3D NOR; thin-tunnel-oxide endurance toward 1e15 cycles is the key doubt.

title: Weights as wires: models compiled into fixed logic on 18A
idea: Po: the weights are welded into the chip. A frozen model is synthesized into constant-coefficient multiplier/adder trees (weights folded into gates, shared partial products via canonical-signed-digit recoding) on Intel 18A or Samsung Taylor (TX) 2 nm and packaged in the U.S.; only KV and activations need DRAM.
why: Removes weight storage and weight fetch entirely: DRAM per inference node drops by the weight share (50-90%) and energy per token ~10x, using U.S. logic fabs instead of foreign DRAM.
note: Gate area per weight far exceeds a DRAM bit; Taalas-style efforts already pursue this.

title: Core-and-cavity casting: radial 3D DRAM from one hole mask
idea: Like sand casting where core prints define internal cavities, deposit a 40-tier stack on the periphery wafer, punch one mask of vertical bitline holes (larger openings on the same mask act as slits), and build each tier's ring IGZO transistor and coaxial capacitor by successive selective lateral recesses and ALD fills from that hole.
why: Facts 2 and 4: array patterning costs one critical mask regardless of tier count, giving a 3D NAND-like cost curve and ~4-8x bits per mask vs 2D.
note: One-mask radial 3D cell gives NAND-like cost curve; closely tracks existing IGZO/3D X-DRAM programs.

title: Direct-tunnel charge-trap '3D AND' DRAM built with 3D-NAND tools
idea: Vertical channel holes (poly-Si or ALD IGZO/IGO) with vertical source/drain lines pass through stacked word planes (3D AND/NOR topology, as in SunRise 3D NOR and Macronix-style 3D AND). Gate stack: ~1.5-2 nm bandgap-engineered SiO2/SiON tunnel layer, SiN trap layer and Al2O3 blocking layer. Low-field direct tunnelling (few V) avoids the hot-carrier and FN damage that limits NAND endurance; retention falls to seconds-minutes, which is the trade: quasi-volatile. Each cell is read individually with ns-class parallel sensing on short vertical bitlines; refresh is 16-1,500x less frequent than DRAM.
why: 2.7-7.2x 1b density at 64-256 tiers on a NAND-class (EUV-free) line; refresh energy and time 16x (1 s) to 1,562x (100 s) lower.
note: Close to SunRise 3D NOR; density gain real on NAND lines but direct-tunnel endurance (~1e11) far short of DRAM.

title: Accelerator ion tracks etched into ultra-deep capacitor holes
idea: Accelerator users make track-etch membranes where each swift heavy ion leaves a straight damage trail that etches into an AR >1000 pore; irradiate a thick oxide or polymer mold through a registered silicon stencil with gold or bismuth ions (not xenon or krypton beams) and etch the tracks into one ultra-deep hole per cell. Several tracks per stencil opening merge to beat Poisson placement statistics.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): AR 200-500 gives 3-6x Cs with no plasma etch and no rare-gas ion species.
note: Track-etch gives AR>200 holes without plasma; doubt: registering one track per ~40 nm cell and beam throughput.

title: Swap lithography for thermal fiber drawing of capacitor preforms
idea: Build a cm-scale preform of coaxial metal/glass capacitors and thermally draw it 10^4x into fibers with sub-50-nm features. Stack and redraw the fibers into an ordered bundle (as in fiber-optic faceplates), then slice it into capacitor wafers bonded onto DUV access-transistor arrays with oversized landing pads.
why: Makes nanoscale storage capacitors with no lithography at all (fact 4), at drawing rates of km per hour, using furnaces instead of fabs (capital axis).
note: Thermal drawing reaches nm features, but glass k is low and registering slices to transistors is unsolved.

title: Swap big capacitor for small charge plus electron-multiplying readout
idea: Store only ~500 electrons on a shallow capacitor at DUV pitch. At read, the packet passes through a short EMCCD-style impact-ionization gain register on the bitline (gain ~20-100) before the sense amplifier.
why: Needs ~10x less Cs (fact 1), so planar or AR <8:1 caps work without EUV or a high-AR etch (fact 4); EMCCD gain registers already reach sub-electron noise.
note: EMCCD gain needs high-voltage multi-stage CCD clocking, too slow and large per bitline.

title: Swap one-physics capacitor for dual polarization-plus-charge two-bit cell
idea: Use a ferroelectric-dielectric capacitor that stores two independent bits: the polarization direction (non-volatile) and the linear charge magnitude (volatile). The read has two phases: a sub-coercive pulse senses the linear charge first, then a switching pulse with write-back senses the polarization.
why: 2 bits per DUV cell offsets the pitch loss from skipping EUV (fact 4), and the polarization bit survives power loss, so it can hold checkpoints.
note: Two bits per ferroelectric cap; linear and switching charge likely interfere.

title: Move drain high-field region into wide-gap heterojunction contact
idea: Substitute the n+ Si storage-node junction with a heterojunction: the gate-drain overlap and storage contact are n+ ZnO or TiO2 (Eg ~3.3 eV) grown on the Si channel. The conduction bands align so electrons pass, while a ~2-3 eV valence offset blocks holes. The high-field region where GIDL and SRH generation occur now sits in a material with ~1e-20 lower intrinsic carrier density.
why: Leakage tail (GIDL + junction): targets a 10-100x drop in the <=13 fA tail, extending tREF by 10x or more and cutting refresh energy ~90%.
note: Moving GIDL/SRH high-field region into a wide-gap contact is clever; heterointerface traps may simply relocate the leakage.

title: Strain-release rolls planar arrays into vertical Swiss-roll micro-tubes
idea: Substitute deposited tiers with rolled turns: build a planar thin-film array (oxide-semiconductor 2T0C cells plus wiring) on a strained SiNx/SiNx bilayer over a sacrificial Ge layer; release makes the membrane self-roll into a 10-20-turn tube standing on edge contacts, so one planar litho flow yields 10-20 effective tiers per footprint.
why: 3D bit density without a 26+ tier deposition/etch stack (fact 2) or high-AR etch; capex per bit near a planar thin-film line; ~5-10x bits per footprint for capacity memory.
note: Rolled-up nanomembranes exist; contacting inner turns, tube pitch and thermal budget limit real density.

title: Substitute shared row activation with dual-gate coincident-select vertical cells
idea: Give each vertical-channel access transistor two independent gates, the wordline on one face and a column-select line on the other, created by splitting the gate-all-around ring with one self-aligned spacer cut; a cell opens only where both lines are high, so only the requested 64-512 bits are sensed instead of an 8 KB row.
why: Constraint and fact 8: removes ~16-128x overfetch for ~10-30x lower energy per useful bit; facet: the added select needs no new lithography layer because the split is self-aligned.
note: Coincident double-gate AND select cuts overfetch; achieving clean AND behavior in a thin body is the doubt.

title: Lid-as-interposer: the heat spreader carries memory signals
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with the package lid: a copper/AlN ceramic lid with embedded multilayer redistribution bonds face-down onto GPU and HBM tops and carries die-to-die signals, while the organic substrate below handles only power and external I/O.
why: Fact 6/5: deletes a >2,500 mm2 silicon interposer, frees the bottom side for power, and pulls heat out of taller stacks directly.
note: Ceramic lid RDL density and bonding to uneven die heights are doubtful.

title: Quarter-dose EUV exposures quadruple scanner throughput, stochastics absorbed
idea: Combine EUV exposure with error-tolerant cells: the contact and capacitor-hole layers are exposed at ~15 mJ/cm2 instead of ~60, and the resulting photon-shot-noise missing or merged features (~0.1-1% of cells) are accepted as cell errors handled by the code layer.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited, so ~3-4x more wafers per scanner-hour cuts EUV cost per layer ~60% and the number of scarce single-supplier scanners needed (fact 4).

title: Plate-line popcount probe checks row health without activating it
idea: Combine popcount checksums with segmented plate-line charge sensing: pulsing a row segment's plate and integrating the displaced charge gives its total stored charge (about the count of '1's); comparing it with a stored popcount detects leakage or hammer flips non-destructively, so only drifted rows are refreshed or scrubbed. Buildable in a university nanofab: segmented-plate MIM arrays with an off-chip integrator.
why: Destructive read and refresh (facts 3, 8, 9): refreshing only drifted rows could cut refresh activations >5x.
note: Plate charge from floating nodes barely depends on stored charge; per-segment fC resolution is doubtful.

title: Hard-disk TDMR detection lets storage nodes crowd and crosstalk
idea: Adapt two-dimensional magnetic recording: shrink node pitch until neighbors couple ~25% (no isolation spacers), read each row together with its two neighbors, and decode jointly with a 2D Viterbi/MAP equalizer in the sense-amp stripe, at 2 levels per node.
why: 10x at same cost: ~2.5x from pitch, 2x from levels, 2x from a second deposited tier; no new litho node, because crosstalk is cancelled rather than prevented.

title: Li-ion battery staging quantizes multi-level ionic storage
idea: Borrow graphite intercalation staging, where ions order into discrete stages with flat voltage plateaus: intercalate protons into few-layer MoS2/graphene hosts so each node rests on one of four stage plateaus read by open-circuit potential, in 3 stacked tiers.
why: 10x at same cost: plateau-quantized 2 bits/node robust to small self-discharge, x3 tiers, x~1.7 smaller node with no capacitor, ~10x.
note: Staging plateaus quantize multilevel states; ionic speed, self-discharge and endurance doubtful.

title: Millefiori glass canes: thermally draw a macro preform into nanocells
idea: Borrowed from millefiori glass and optical-fiber preform drawing: assemble a centimeter-scale preform whose cross-section holds semiconducting glass, metal and dielectric regions forming a cell row, thermally draw it ~10,000x into kilometers of fiber, then slice, bundle and bond cross-sections as arrays with no lithography.
why: Pattern is made once at mm scale and replicated at km/hour; capital per bit ~1/100 of a fab; trade-offs: chalcogenide/oxide-glass devices, ~1 us access, coarse yield.

title: Battery jelly-roll winding: wind single-tier DRAM foil into cylinders
idea: Adapted from Li-ion jelly-roll cells: imprint a single-tier oxide-TFT array on a 5 um polyimide web at roll speed, then wind ~1,000 turns into a cylinder whose battery-style edge tabs bring segmented bitlines and wordlines out to a bonded controller.
why: Volume density comes from winding, not tier deposition; web processing at ~$5-10/m2 x 1,000 turns gives TB per cylinder near $0.05-0.1/GB; trade-offs: microsecond access, module-sized form factor.
note: Per-turn edge contacts and microsecond access make it a capacity tier, not DRAM-class.

title: Grid surge-arrester zinc-oxide varistors select crossbar DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from power-grid metal-oxide surge arresters, whose ZnO grain boundaries conduct ~10^10x more above a knee voltage: stack 8 decks of 1-selector-1-capacitor crossbars where a nanograin ZnO-Bi2O3 varistor film isolates each capacitor below half-select voltage, 2 masks per deck.
why: Transistor-free crossbar decks reach ~4F2/8 per bit at a fraction of DRAM process cost, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-offs: ~ms retention needing aggressive refresh, high write voltages.
note: Varistor leakage below knee likely too high for retention.

title: Magnify Vt shift to latch the access device permanently off
idea: Insert a thin HZO ferroelectric in each access-transistor gate stack; on power loss one global wordline pulse flips every access gate into a +1.2 V Vt-shifted deep-off state, trapping capacitor charge behind <1e-21 A leakage until power returns and a reset pulse restores normal Vt.
why: Turns conventional 1T1C into a power-loss-surviving memory with one FE switch per power cycle; also reduces refresh in operation.

title: Eliminate the latch: impact-ionization gain diode on each bitline
idea: Replace the cross-coupled latch with one p-i-n diode per bitline biased just below breakdown, in a gated Geiger mode. The ~30-100 mV charge-share signal shifts its avalanche delay, so a '1' fires a rail-to-rail pulse within ~0.5 ns while a '0' does not, and a quench transistor resets it.
why: Replaces a 6-transistor SA with 1 diode and 1 quench device (SA area -70%), and the sense charge is only a few fC. Dark counts, jitter and temperature drift are the risks.

title: Read ferroelectric bits by strain, never by switching
idea: Flip FeRAM's read path from electrical to mechanical: each HZO or AlScN ferroelectric capacitor sits on a piezoresistive channel; a small sub-coercive voltage makes up- and down-polarized cells expand or contract (opposite piezo sign), modulating channel resistance, so polarization is read without being switched.
why: Destructive read and fatigue (fact 8): removes the read-switch-restore cycle, cutting read energy ~5-10x and limiting wear to writes only.

title: Let the crystal draw the lines: vicinal step templates
idea: Rearrange mask and substrate: use miscut silicon annealed into regularly bunched atomic steps at a set pitch, then selectively oxidize step edges to template wordline pitch without printing it with EUV.
why: Removes one or more EUV layers (single-supplier tool, ~55% of wafer cost is depreciation) by letting the lattice provide the pitch for free.

title: Colloidal-crystal capacitor holes, addressed after they form
idea: Reverse design-then-build: self-assemble a hexagonal monolayer of silica nanospheres as the capacitor-hole template (no lithography), accept ~1% vacancies and dislocations, and build a per-die address translation map after formation, the cell array following the crystal.
why: Removes EUV and immersion layers from capacitor patterning; nanosphere lithography uses abundant silica and cheap spin/dip coating tools.

title: Surface-acoustic-wave wordline gates 2D channels on piezoelectric substrate
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: on lithium niobate or AlScN-on-sapphire, a GHz surface acoustic wave launched along a row carries a piezoelectric potential that momentarily opens MoS2 access channels as it passes, so the 'wordline' is a travelling wave, not a charged metal line. Between waves the channels sit deeply off with no static gate bias; row latency is transit time (~30 ns per 100 um).
why: Eliminates wordline CV2 and negative-bias pumps (Facts 7, 10) and row-hammer coupling (Fact 9) while keeping off-state leakage minimal (Fact 3); coupling strength is speculative.
note: GHz acoustic wavelength (~µm) and weak piezo coupling clash with nm-pitch cells.

title: Periodic action: lock-in readout of varactor cells, no destructive read
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: each storage element is a floating MOS varactor whose small-signal capacitance depends on its stored charge (accumulation versus depletion); a ~10 MHz small excitation on the wordline and a lock-in demodulator shared by 256 bitlines read that capacitance without moving the stored charge, so reads are non-destructive.
why: 100x path: deletes restore/write-back circuits and per-bitline sense amps (256:1 sharing) and allows planar cells stacked in 8+ BEOL tiers on mature or display-class lines; trade-offs: ~1 us reads and lower density per tier. Also removes Fact 8's destructive read.

title: Overlay-free bonded capacitor extension through a sub-pitch nanorod carpet
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split the capacitor across two wafers, and split the bond interface into a random carpet of 8 nm TiN-cored, high-k-coated nanorods at 1/4 cell pitch embedded in a common plate. When this wafer is bonded onto the array wafer's isolated storage pads, each pad statistically catches ~10 rod tips while the pad gap (> rod diameter) prevents bridging, so no cell-pitch overlay is needed.
why: Fact 1: adds ~3-5 fF per cell from an independently made wafer (doubling Cs without deeper etch) and decouples capacitor fab from transistor fab (capital, U.S. second source).
note: ACF-like statistical contact at nano scale; bridging and leakage risks.

title: Hydrogen-terminated diamond access transistor doped by vanadium oxide
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change (raise the bandgap from 1.1 to 5.5 eV): grow nanocrystalline diamond at <=500 C, hydrogen-terminate it, and cap it with V2O5, whose deep electron affinity pulls a 2D hole gas into the surface (surface-transfer doping), sealed under Al2O3. The channel needs no dopants and its off-state leakage is negligible.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3). Retention could stretch from 64 ms to seconds or more, cutting refresh energy (16-33% of idle power) by >90%, using only C, H, V, Al and O.

title: Nested conductive-core insulating-shell nanograins give colossal effective k
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: build the dielectric from ~3 nm semiconducting reduced-TiO2 grains, each wrapped by ALD in a 0.5 nm Al2O3 shell. The field drops only across the thin shells (an engineered version of CaCu3Ti4O12's internal barrier layers), so effective k could reach several hundred.
why: Targets fact 1's k ~70 requirement with Ti, Al and O only. The risk is that Maxwell-Wagner relaxation is too slow for ns access and that leakage percolates through the cores.

title: Butterfly-scale gyroid capacitor from block-copolymer self-assembly
idea: Green hairstreak butterfly scales grow a single-gyroid photonic network. Spin a double-gyroid block-copolymer film (~20 nm period) as a sacrificial template, ALD-fill one network with TiN, strip the polymer, coat with high-k, and fill the second network as the counter-electrode. The two interpenetrating continuous electrodes give a 3D capacitor with ~30-60x area per footprint in a 300 nm layer.
why: Charge wall and capital (facts 1, 4): spin-coat self-assembly replaces the AR-70 pillar etch and the support-mesh steps. Each cell is isolated by a shallow cut, not a deep etch.

title: Potassium-filter storage node sealed by a resonant tunneling gate
idea: K+ channels pass ions near diffusion speed yet block others because the filter is energy-matched. Put the storage node behind a double-barrier hBN/graphene/hBN resonant tunneling contact: during write the gate aligns the resonant level and current flows freely. During hold the gate detunes it by >0.3 eV, and transmission drops >10^6 because of energy mismatch rather than barrier thickness, so leakage depends weakly on geometric variation.
why: Leakage tail and refresh (fact 3): an energy-filtered off state could cut the <=13 fA tail 100-1000x and stretch refresh from 64 ms to seconds, saving most of the 16-33% idle refresh power.
note: Off-resonance transmission is phonon/inelastic limited; 1e6 suppression unlikely at room temperature.

title: Sodium-potassium pump ratchet: AC-powered in-cell self-refresh
idea: Neurons hold their resting potential against leaks with a local ion pump, not a central refresh. Couple every storage node to a shared global AC pump line through a tiny asymmetric MIM tunnel diode in series with a node-gated diode. Each clock cycle pumps a few electrons toward whichever rail the node is nearer, so 1s are topped up and 0s drained without opening any wordline or bitline.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes refresh activations, recovering the 10-20% of bandwidth and most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy. The pump current is pA per mat.
note: Per-node AC ratchet removes refresh activations; doubt: diode asymmetry, area and pump disturb.

title: Cytochrome P450 spin-switch bit held at 85C mid-hysteresis
idea: Heme enzymes like P450 flip the iron spin state when a substrate binds. Fe(II)-triazole spin-crossover films have a 30-40 K wide thermal hysteresis that can be tuned to centre near the DRAM junction temperature (~85 C). Hold the die at mid-loop, write with a local 20 ns heat or field pulse, and read the 5-10% dielectric or resistance difference between the high-spin and low-spin states.
why: Removes the capacitor and refresh, because the state is bistable while the die is warm. The molecular film is solution-processed with no EUV, and die temperature becomes a resource instead of a leakage enemy.
note: Holding die mid-hysteresis is clever; ns switching, endurance and small signal are doubts.

title: Chiral-molecule spin filter writes magnets with voltage, not current
idea: DNA and other chiral molecules spin-polarize the electrons that move through them (chiral-induced spin selectivity). Put a monolayer of helical oligopeptides on a thin perpendicular magnet. A gate voltage charge-polarizes the molecules, briefly creating a spin-polarized interface that tips the magnetization, so writing uses only displacement current.
why: Non-volatile magnetic bit written at fJ level, with no heavy-metal SOT lines (no W/Pt) and no MTJ breakdown. The molecules are cheap and solution-deposited.
note: Chirality-induced spin selectivity switching reported but gate-driven write is unproven.

title: S4 voltage-sensor gate: tethered ions flip between two sites
idea: Ion-channel S4 segments carry charged arginines that slide ~1 nm through the membrane field but never leave the protein. Make a gate dielectric with covalently tethered cationic groups (ammonium on short siloxane chains anchored to the oxide) that sit at one of two sites across a 1-2 nm layer. Their position shifts the transistor Vt, and the tether stops drift.
why: Non-volatile ionic bit whose endurance is not limited by ion loss or filament wear, because there are no free ions. Writes take ~10-100 ns at <2 V in a BEOL-compatible molecular layer.
note: Two-site bistability barrier and charge density for useful Vt shift unproven.

title: Prion-templated martensite variants: compatible-lattice ferroelastic flip for endless cycling
idea: Prions convert their neighbours by templating their fold. Use a shape-memory-alloy film (TiNiCu-type) tuned so its martensite twin variants meet at geometrically compatible interfaces, the condition that let such films survive 10^7+ transformation cycles. A piezoelectric strain pulse switches a 20 nm cell between two variants, a remaining seed of the target variant templates fast growth, and the variants' anisotropic resistivity reads the bit.
why: Non-volatile, diffusionless switching (ns, low energy, with no melt as in PCM), with endurance limited only by lattice compatibility. No chalcogenides and no EUV.
note: Compatibility-condition SMA films for endurance is a non-obvious memory insight; nm-scale variant switching unproven.

title: Entatic-state inversion: copper complexes whose geometry change locks electrons
idea: Blue copper proteins tune their geometry (the entatic state) to make electron transfer fast. Invert the trick: choose Cu(I)/Cu(II) complexes whose tetrahedral-to-square-planar change puts a ~1 eV reorganization barrier on spontaneous back-transfer, and place a dense monolayer between channel and gate. A gate pulse overcomes the Marcus barrier in ns, and the trapped charge shifts Vt non-volatilely.
why: Molecular-scale non-volatile charge storage whose retention comes from nuclear reorganization rather than thick tunnel oxides. Writes need low fields, endurance avoids oxide wear, and per-molecule storage could scale density.
note: Entatic barrier twist on molecular memory (ZettaCore lineage).

title: Photosynthetic self-refresh cells restored by a global light pulse
idea: Leaves turn light into stored energy without wires; put a tiny photodiode under each storage node, tied to VARY through a restore transistor gated by the storage node itself, so a periodic chip-wide backside flash at ~1.1 um tops up only cells holding '1' while '0' cells' restore path stays off.
why: Refresh needs no row activation, bitline swing or command slots, so the 10-20% bandwidth loss goes to ~0 and refresh energy can fall >5x if photo-efficiency and light isolation hold.
note: Per-cell photodiode and restore transistor cost area; light isolation at 1.1 um weak.

title: Channelrhodopsin-style optically gated access with waveguide wordlines
idea: Optogenetics opens ion channels with light; replace the electrically gated access device with a wide-gap a-SiC:H photoconductor (PECVD at 250 C) between bitline and storage node, lit row by row through SiN waveguide wordlines fed by an on-package laser and modulator.
why: In the dark the wide-gap film has almost no thermal generation and there is no gate at all, so GIDL and electrical wordline coupling vanish: off-current approaches 1e-20 A (refresh-free), the 3 V wordline CV2 is gone, and row hammer coupling disappears.
note: Wide-gap photoconductor in dark; doubts: persistent photoconductivity, ns switching, optical energy per row.

title: S-layer protein crystals pattern uniform sub-10-nm access gates
idea: Bacteria coat themselves in self-assembling S-layer protein lattices with 5-15 nm periodicity; recrystallize an S-layer on the BEOL wafer and harden it by sequential infiltration synthesis (ALD alumina at ~90 C) into a perfectly periodic mask that defines access-gate or channel arrays.
why: Molecular periodicity removes the width variation that drives the Vt and leakage tail and replaces 1-2 EUV layers, lowering both tail leakage and capital per wafer.
note: Protein-lattice masks hardened by SIS could replace EUV layers; doubt: defect density and registration to underlying array.

title: Chromatin-style folded thin-film memory sheet stacked by origami
idea: As DNA packs 2 m into a 6 um nucleus by folding, fabricate one long planar oxide-TFT DRAM sheet (a single cheap litho tier) on a releasable 2 um membrane with thinned Miura-ori hinge creases carrying metal traces, then pleat it accordion-style onto the CMOS die so each fold becomes a tier and fold edges land on a bond-pad strip.
why: 3D layer count and capital: N tiers for one tier's lithography and no high-AR stack etch, so array capex per bit falls roughly as 1/N.
note: Micron-radius folds, hinge trace reliability and tier contacts are big unknowns; TFT density per tier is low.

title: Butterfly-wing gyroid electrodes replace 70:1 capacitor pillars
idea: Copy the gyroid networks in butterfly wing scales: spin a gyroid-forming triblock copolymer into a 400 nm layer over the storage contacts, remove one network, ALD TiN/high-k/TiN through the periodic 3D labyrinth, then cut it per cell with a coarse self-aligned grid so each storage node owns a gyroid block.
why: Capacitor charge wall: a 20 nm-period gyroid has ~10x the area per volume of a cylinder, giving ~5 fF in a 400 nm-tall structure (AR ~20:1 instead of 70:1) and ending pillar collapse.
note: MIM stack ~12-15 nm cannot conformally fit a 20 nm-period gyroid.

title: Spider-silk fiber drawing shrinks a coax-capacitor preform to nanoscale
idea: As spiders and tendons build hierarchy by drawing and bundling fibres, draw a glass preform containing metal-insulator-metal coaxial rods down ~1000x, bundle and redraw (as for photonic-crystal fibre) to ~50 nm coax pitch, then slice perpendicular into 1-2 um wafers that are dense coax-capacitor arrays to bond onto access-transistor wafers.
why: Capacitor charge wall and EUV: capacitors of any length/AR made with no etch or lithography, Cs set by slice thickness; bit cost falls if fibre-draw throughput scales.
note: Multimaterial fiber draw to ~50 nm coax with intact thin glass wall is unproven; geometry gives ~1.5 fF/um, enough.

title: Silicatein-catalysed titanate dielectric grown inside capacitor holes
idea: Marine sponges grow glass spicules with the enzyme silicatein, which also turns titanium and barium alkoxides into crystalline oxides at room temperature. Immobilize a silicatein-mimetic serine-histidine catalytic monolayer on the TiN bottom electrode so a water-borne Sr/Ba-Ti precursor bath deposits conformal SrTiO3 (k~100+) only on catalytic surfaces, then crystallize it with a short anneal.
why: Replaces Hf/Zr metalorganic ALD (Hf is a nuclear-Zr byproduct; precursors are <10% utilized) and pushes k toward the ~70 needed to beat the ~5 fF charge wall at a lower aspect ratio.
note: Biomimetic catalytic SrTiO3 deposition is novel; thin-film k collapse and crystallization anneal are doubts.

title: Fiddlehead-rolled foil memory: square metres coiled into a cartridge
idea: Ferns pack a large frond into a tight coil. Print indium-free Zn-Sn-O TFT gain-cell arrays (~10 um2 cells) roll-to-roll on 25 um polyimide, then coil ~30 m2 into a 1 L cylinder with edge-bonded flex taps every 10 cm feeding a silicon controller behind a CXL port.
why: At ~$30-50 per processed m2 this could reach ~$3-5/GB with no EUV, no Cz wafers and no helium-intensive etch; ~100 ns-1 us latency suits a capacity tier and opens a new supply line.
note: Coiling square metres of printed gain cells into a CXL cartridge is new; printed TFT yield and $/GB doubtful.

title: Butterfly-scale gyroid electrodes grown inside lipid cubic-phase templates
idea: Butterfly scales grow gyroid networks from folded cell membranes; fill a shallow ~300 nm capacitor well with a monoolein lipid cubic phase (a self-forming gyroid with 5-10 nm water channels), electrodeposit Ru through the channels, wash out the lipid and ALD-coat the bicontinuous electrode with high-k and plate. Surface area per volume rises ~15-20x.
why: Reaches ~5 fF in a 4-5:1 well instead of a 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1), deleting the costliest high-AR etch and support layers; est. ~10% lower wafer cost and less etch-tool capex.

title: Synaptic plasticity trimming tunes each access transistor after fabrication
idea: Synapses are wired roughly and then tuned by use; after fab, apply controlled field pulses that drift mobile hydrogen in the gate stack (or hot-carrier pulses) to raise each leaky transistor's threshold until its leakage passes a target, using the array's own sense amps as the meter.
why: Fixes the leakage tail post-fab (fact 3), cutting refresh 4-8x, and widens process windows so less inline metrology and rework is needed; est. 3-5% lower fab cost.
note: Hydrogen or hot-carrier trims may relax over time and degrade reliability.

title: Fiddlehead roll-up: printed foil memory coiled a hundred turns
idea: Ferns pack a large frond into a tight coil; roll-to-roll imprint a 2T0C oxide-TFT memory array on 2 um polyimide foil at ~1 um rules (processing cost per m2 ~1/100 of a silicon wafer), route bus lines to one edge, then wind the foil 100+ turns into a dense cylinder whose edge contacts bond to a CMOS controller.
why: Low planar density is offset by 100x volumetric stacking: ~10x bits per board footprint at equal or lower cost per bit, using printing lines instead of EUV fabs (fact 4).

title: Single-photon avalanche diode logic: Geiger-mode read of a 300-electron node
idea: Treat the storage node as a gate over a tiny Geiger-mode avalanche junction: the stored charge shifts local breakdown by ~0.3 V, and the read biases between the two breakdown voltages for ~2 ns so a self-quenched avalanche (a large digital pulse) fires only for one state, as in SPAD pixels.
why: Fact 1: digital-gain sensing needs ~0.2-0.5 fF instead of ~5 fF, collapsing capacitor height 10-20x; dark-count false fires (~1e-7 per ns window) and afterpulsing demand ECC and are the risk.
note: Digital avalanche sensing of a tiny node; weak breakdown modulation, dark counts and SPAD area are doubts.

title: Gold-leaf electroscope: suspended graphene leaf holds charge in vacuum
idea: Store the bit as charge on a suspended graphene (or 20-nm SiN/Al) leaf in a sealed cavity, touching nothing but its clamp on thick thermal oxide; electrostatic repulsion deflects it a few nm, sensed capacitively by an underlying electrode without discharge, and charge is written or erased by field emission across a 5-nm vacuum gap to a sharp tip.
why: Facts 3 and 8: no junction or thin dielectric sits in the leakage path, so retention is set by negligible low-field emission, and read is non-destructive (no restore energy); built with graphene transfer, e-beam and critical-point drying; ns sensing of nm deflection is the risk.
note: No leakage path, nondestructive read; ns sensing of nm deflection and cavity area limit density.

title: Moire silk patterns: twist-angle-defined trap lattices as litho-free storage sites
idea: Moire fabric shows a large pattern from two fine weaves; twisting WSe2/WS2 bilayers by ~1-3 degrees creates a lattice of deep potential minima at ~8-10 nm pitch, each able to trap a hole; a 50-nm e-beam gate over a patch writes trapped-hole occupancy that shifts an underlying channel threshold, a floating-gate-like bit whose sites come from the twist, not lithography.
why: Density and litho: sub-10-nm storage sites with zero patterning, built with a twist-transfer stage, e-beam and hBN encapsulation; moire trap depths (~100-200 meV) give only ms-scale retention at room temperature unless deeper heterostructures are found.

title: Low-self-discharge battery separator: crested tunnel barrier in storage-node contact
idea: Low-self-discharge NiMH cells won with a separator that blocks slow parasitic currents while passing charge current. Insert a crested (triangular-profile SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2-type) tunnel barrier in the storage contact: at write/read bias the crest collapses and current flows, while at the few hundred mV seen in retention tunneling falls exponentially, starving the off-transistor leakage path.
why: Adds a >10^4 current nonlinearity between ~1 V and ~0.3 V in series with the subthreshold path (fact 3); could raise retention ~100x while keeping 10-20 ns access if the barrier stays thin.
note: Crested barrier in storage contact adds bias-dependent nonlinearity; doubt: series resistance at 10 ns write currents.

title: Fiber-draw nanocapillary scaffold grown on a draw tower, not etched
idea: Use the optical-fiber draw tower: stack a centimetre preform of glass rods with soluble cores, draw it down ~10,000x into a fused bundle with ~40 nm channels and >1000:1 aspect ratio, slice 3 um wafers, bond them onto the transistor wafer, and ALD electrodes plus high-k into the channels to form the capacitor forest.
why: Capacitor wall and etch capital (facts 1, 4): AR far beyond the 115 target with zero deep plasma etch; replaces cryogenic high-AR etch tools with draw towers costing a few $M.

title: Tabless jelly-roll battery: rolled thin-film memory cylinder
idea: Cylindrical cells roll a long electrode sheet, and tabless designs collect current along the whole edge. Deposit IGZO gain-cell arrays (≤350 C) on a thin polyimide sheet, roll it into a jelly-roll, and bring the bus out every few mm along the edge to an end-cap logic die.
why: Gets volumetric density by rolling instead of lithographic 3D stacking, with almost no EUV or front-end capex per bit. Speculative: winding yield and bus latency are open questions.
note: Display-litho density and winding yield are open; bus latency along a roll.

title: Armstrong superregenerative sensing to read deeply decayed cells
idea: Revive Armstrong's 1922 superregenerative receiver: replace the single latch with a quenched regenerative sense stage whose exponential build-up time encodes the initial bitline differential, read by a time-to-digital comparator. It resolves signals 5-10x smaller than today's ~100 mV margin.
why: If sensing works at 10-20% of nominal charge, cells can decay far longer before refresh (fact 3) and a smaller Cs becomes usable (fact 1), giving 3-5x longer refresh intervals.
note: Gain is not the limit; sense-amp offset and noise still bound the resolvable signal.

title: Superregenerative quench latch converts bitline signal into time
idea: Borrow Armstrong's 1922 superregenerative receiver. The sense latch is biased just past instability and quenched every cycle, so the tiny bitline differential grows exponentially and its time-to-threshold is proportional to ln(signal). A 6-bit time-to-digital counter at the mat edge decodes 2-bit-per-cell levels from one latch, with no ADC ladder.
why: Enables multi-level DRAM (2 bits/cell) at existing sense-amp pitch: ~2x bits per capacitor and half the sense amps per bit (fact 7 periphery share, fact 1 charge wall).
note: MLC DRAM margins historically insufficient.

title: Ferroelectric coercive-edge capacitor avalanches tiny bitline signals
idea: 1950s ferroelectric memories failed because switching was too easy to trigger; this turns that flaw into gain. One block mask keeps an HZO capacitor at each sense node, biased just below its coercive voltage. A 30-50 mV bitline signal tips it into switching, which dumps ~20 µC/cm² of polarization charge into the latch, and the capacitor is reset each cycle. Wear is spread across redundant capacitors.
why: ~10x charge gain at the sense node lets Cs fall toward 1-2 fF (fact 1 charge wall) with no new cell physics.
note: Coercive-voltage spread exceeds 30-50 mV and per-activation switching exceeds HZO endurance.

title: Transfluxor-inspired split-electrode ferroelectric cell with non-destructive read
idea: Revive the transfluxor, where the flux state around a major aperture blocked or freed switching around a minor one: a vertical ferroelectric capacitor has a large write electrode and a small adjacent read electrode, and the stored major domain's depolarizing field biases the minor region. Reading toggles only the minor region, which springs back, sensing state without disturbing the stored domain.
why: Fact 8: non-destructive read removes write-back energy and read fatigue; ~3-5x lower read energy, and ferroelectric endurance is spent only on real writes.

title: Flood-gun self-restoring cells: global diode pump refreshes every bit
idea: Revive the Tektronix bistable storage tube, whose flood gun held every spot at one of two stable potentials without reading it: each cell gets a tiny vertical diode plus coupling-capacitor pump driven by a global AC 'flood' line, so leaked '1' cells are recharged and '0' cells clamped low, all in parallel without activating rows or sense amps.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth loss) with an array-wide, sense-free restore; refresh energy down ~5-10x.
note: A diode pump cannot tell leaked 1 from 0 without a per-cell nonlinearity; effectively needs bistable cells.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers woven like core planes into memory
idea: Revive hand-woven core planes with fiber drawing: a macroscopic preform holding metal, dielectric and semiconductor features is drawn ~1000x down into kilometers of fiber with ~50-100 nm internal cell structures, then fibers are woven or bundled and sliced into dense 3D arrays. Patterning happens once in the preform, not per wafer.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: no EUV or per-wafer masks, built in fiber plants; cost per bit could drop >3x if drawn features stay uniform.

title: Bloch-line memory: bits smaller than the lithography defining them
idea: Revive NEC and JPL's 1980s Bloch-line memory, where bits are pairs of vertical Bloch lines inside the walls of litho-defined stripe domains, using modern ferrimagnetic garnet or PMA multilayer films and spin-orbit-torque pulses to shift the lines along the walls. Lithography only draws stripes at ~100 nm; the film's exchange length (~10 nm) sets bit pitch along each wall.
why: Litho-bound scaling (Fact 4): a ~10x density multiplier over drawn pitch, so arrays could be patterned with i-line/KrF on 200 mm tools instead of EUV. Risks are speed (historically microseconds) and Bloch-line stability at 10 nm.

title: Drawn coaxial-fibre bundles sliced into capacitor wafers
idea: Revive 1960s microchannel-plate and fibre-optic faceplate manufacturing: draw a preform of metal-core / high-k glass / metal-shell coaxial fibres in a nitrogen-purged tower, bundle and redraw three times to ~60 nm pitch, then slice the boule into 5 um wafers, each holding billions of parallel coaxial capacitors at AR ~80-100. Bond the slice to the transistor wafer so each landing pad catches several capacitors, averaging out random placement.
why: Facts 1 and 4: aspect ratio is set by slice thickness, not by etch, so AR 100+ needs no plasma, no litho and no rare gas, from ~$5-10M draw towers. Risks are metal/glass co-drawing below 100 nm and bond yield.
note: Metal/glass co-draw below 100 nm hits capillary breakup; no high-k drawable glass.

title: Rajchman laminated ferrite memory built on MLCC production lines
idea: Revive Jan Rajchman's 1960s RCA laminated-ferrite memory, where conductors were screen-printed between ferrite green sheets and co-fired into a solid block, on today's MLCC lines that already stack ~1,000 thin tape layers: X and Y conductors on alternate NiZn-ferrite sheets, laser-punched vias for layer selection, all fired in air. Each conductor crossing is a ferrite bit switched by coincident current.
why: Capital, scarcity and the constraint: MLCC lines make trillions of parts a year with no litho, no vacuum and no rare gas; 1,000 layers at ~1 Mb/cm2 each give ~1 Gb per cm2 of footprint at materials cost of cents. Risks are ferrite switching speed (tens of ns at small volumes) and drive current.

title: Holographic page memory revived as optical attention-key correlator
idea: Revive 1970s Bell/RCA holographic page memory as a correlator: a context's key vectors are written as superimposed Fourier holograms in a rewritable photorefractive crystal, and illuminating it with the query on an SLM produces every query-key dot product at once on a photodetector array. Only the top-k value rows are then fetched from DRAM.
why: Keys are half the KV cache and every key is read every token; optical key storage halves KV DRAM and cuts key-read energy 10-100x at long context.
note: Photorefractive SNR and crosstalk with many superimposed keys, plus slow rewrites, are the doubt.

title: Goto's parametron revived: parametric bitline pumping senses tiny charges
idea: Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron stored a bit as the phase of a parametrically pumped oscillation. Pump the bitline pair's MOS varactor at twice the sense frequency during sensing, so the cell's small charge seeds the phase of an oscillation that grows exponentially, with gain set by matched capacitors instead of threshold-mismatched latch transistors.
why: Capacitor charge wall and voltage floor (facts 1, 10): latch offset (~10-20 mV) dominates margin; parametric sensing could tolerate ~2x smaller signal, allowing Cs near 2.5 fF or longer retention.
note: Matched-capacitor gain sidesteps latch offset; pumping thousands of bitlines at GHz within a ns window is the doubt.

title: Mercury Delay Line Reborn as a Fiber Loop Broadcasting Weights
idea: Revive EDSAC's 1949 mercury delay line as a recirculating optical-fiber loop: a model's weights circulate as WDM pulses in a ~100 km fiber spool (100 wavelengths at 400 Gb/s hold ~2.5 GB, one lap every 0.5 ms) with an amplifier-regenerator, and dozens of accelerators tap the loop through passive splitters, each reading every weight once per lap, matching per-token decode cadence.
why: Replaces N per-accelerator DRAM weight copies with one in-flight copy and amortizes each weight access over N readers: ~10-50x lower energy per access at N>=32; built from telecom optics supply chains, not DRAM fabs.
note: Receivers at tens of Tb/s per tap, splitter loss and ~2.5 GB loop capacity versus model size undercut energy claims.

title: RCA Continuous-Sheet Superconducting Memory Revived in YBCO at 77 K
idea: Revive RCA's 1960s continuous-sheet cryoelectric memory, which stored bits as persistent current vortices in an unpatterned superconducting film at the crossings of drive lines, using high-Tc YBCO films (as made for HTS power cable) at liquid-nitrogen 77 K, so no helium and no cell lithography are needed.
why: Energy per access aJ-fJ, >=10x lower even with LN2 overhead; the storage film is unpatterned so density is set by drive-line pitch on cheap litho; avoids the helium chokepoint.
note: Flux creep at 77 K decays persistent currents in YBCO; cryo overhead and sensing unresolved.

title: Electric double layer storage: ions replace the solid dielectric
idea: Inverts 'the storage dielectric must be a solid insulator': use a nanometre-thin solid polymer or ionogel electrolyte between ion-blocking electrodes so the electric double layer gives ~10-30 uF/cm2 (3-6x high-k ZrO2); blocking electrodes keep DC leakage low and nanoscale thickness keeps the ionic RC short.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 60-75:1 -> ~15:1) and buys retention margin against access leakage (fact 3); risk is ionic switching speed at ns scale.
note: Ionic double-layer charging at ns speed and electrolyte leakage are doubtful.

title: Carousel memory: rows stream past a reader, decoders deleted
idea: Inverts 'refresh is a background chore and random access needs decoders': read, regenerate and rewrite every row in a fixed cyclic order every ~1 ms using simple counters (no row/column decoders, no refresh controller), with a small SRAM front buffer catching requested rows as they pass; 1000 parallel carousels cut the wait to ~1 us.
why: Removes most of the 49% periphery (fact 7) and makes refresh the data path, so cells with 1000x worse leakage become usable; with relaxed-cell 3D builds, ~100x cost/GB for latency-tolerant bandwidth tiers.
note: Full-array restore every 1 ms multiplies refresh energy ~64x, and ~1 us waits are not DRAM-class latency.

title: Sodium beta-alumina double-layer nanocapacitors in flat 3D tiers
idea: Inverts 'cell capacitance comes from a dielectric's permittivity.' Sandwich a 2-3 nm Na-beta-alumina solid electrolyte between TiN electrodes so the electric double layer gives ~20-40 uF/cm², 3-6x a high-k film, allowing flat lateral capacitors in each tier.
why: Facts 1-2: flat capacitors remove the 3D capacitor blocker using Na, Al, O, Ti, N only; ns ion response and self-discharge are the open questions.
note: Double layers in 2-3 nm solid electrolytes likely respond in us-ms, not ns, with self-discharge.

title: Vacuum-gap floating gate: flash physics without oxide wear
idea: Inverts 'a floating gate needs an oxide tunnel barrier, which wears out': suspend the floating node over a sealed 2-3 nm vacuum gap and charge it by Fowler-Nordheim field emission across vacuum with ~8 V local pulses; vacuum holds no traps to damage, so endurance is effectively unlimited, and at read fields emission is nil, so retention lasts years.
why: Zero refresh, nonvolatile, unlimited-endurance cell from Si, SiO2 and TiN only, with no high-k or Hf.
note: Trap-free vacuum barrier is the insight; sealed 2-3 nm gaps, stiction and 8 V writes are doubts.

title: Ionogel double-layer capacitors replace 70:1 dielectric pillars
idea: Inverts 'the storage dielectric is a solid insulator'. Fill shallow cups with a confined solid-polymer ionogel so charge sits in a nanometre electric double layer (~20-40 uF/cm2 vs ~7 for ZrO2), meeting 5 fF at AR ~15:1, with blocking electrodes to suppress Faradaic leakage.
why: Removes the hardest high-AR etch and ALD fill (fact 1) with 3-5x charge per area; must prove ns-scale ion response in sub-10 nm confinement.
note: Ion response time and self-discharge vs fA-level leakage budget are doubtful.

title: Thermally drawn fibers shrink a macro-preform into memory
idea: Inverts 'small features need lithography'. Machine a centimetre-scale preform with interleaved metal, glass and semiconductor channels laid out as a capacitor-plus-channel array, then draw it in a fiber tower (~10,000x cross-section reduction) to 50-100 nm features over kilometres; slice into chiplets and stack.
why: Litho-free nanoscale features from 1970s-90s fiber towers; extreme capital efficiency if channel crystal quality and contacts can be solved.
note: Drawn-fiber devices exist; crystal quality and per-slice contacts are the unknowns.

title: Single-proton tautomer molecules as one-nanometer dipole bits
idea: Self-assemble a monolayer of porphycene-type molecules whose inner hydrogen pair hops between two nitrogen sites, with substituents tuning the proton double-well barrier to ~0.8 eV for >=1 s retention. A gate pulse flips the ~100 tautomers under a 10x10 nm electrode, and their collective dipole shifts the threshold of a 2D-channel read transistor.
why: From first principles, the smallest object with a room-temperature-grade barrier is one proton in a double well (~1 nm3). Storage density is then limited only by addressing, at aJ switching energy, with no capacitor (fact 1) or charge leakage (fact 3).
note: Collective dipole of ~100 molecules may give too little Vt shift.

title: Vacuum-gap tunneling floating node: oxide-free, wear-free charge storage
idea: Separate a floating metal node from its write electrode by a 2-2.5 nm vacuum gap, made by ashing a sacrificial ALD carbon layer in O2 plasma at <=250 C. Write by direct or field-emission tunneling through vacuum (~ns at 2-3 V); retention is set by gap width because tunneling is exponential in it (2.5 nm gives >1 s).
why: Oxide wear-out needs a lattice to damage and vacuum has none, so this targets unlimited endurance for a floating-node store. No capacitor pillar (fact 1), and the cell stacks in BEOL tiers (fact 2).
note: 2.5 nm vacuum gap collapse and exponential gap variability.

title: Bonded 4H-SiC film access transistors erase the refresh leakage tail
idea: Generation leakage scales with intrinsic carrier density ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT); 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has ni ~1e-9 cm-3 versus 1e10 for Si, collapsing the 13 fA junction tail by many orders. Activate implants in a SiC wafer at 1600 C first, Smart-Cut a 100 nm film onto the DRAM wafer, and build access transistors in it under the capacitor process.
why: Fact 3: retention moves from 64 ms toward hours, deleting ~46 fJ/bit refresh and 10-20% bandwidth loss; SiC is Si+C and US-made. SiO2/SiC interface traps and mobility are the risk.
note: Smart-Cut SiC film under the cap is a new combo; low-temperature SiC gate interface and cap leakage cap retention.

title: One zinc-oxide film serves as channel, wordline and electrode via hydrogen
idea: ZnO conductivity spans ~1e-6 to 1e3 S/cm depending on hydrogen donors; deposit one ZnO film per tier and convert wordline/electrode regions into degenerate conductor with self-aligned H-plasma through the slit, leaving the masked channel semiconducting.
why: Each tier needs 2 depositions (ZnO + Al2O3) instead of ~4, cutting tier cost ~40% so 100+ tiers fit the same budget (~10x density) with no W, Mo, In or Ga. Hydrogen diffusion stability is the risk.
note: Self-aligned hydrogen conversion of one film to conductor and channel is clever; H diffusion destroys contrast over thermal budget.

title: Display-glass oxide-TFT warm tier priced by area, not wafer
idea: Cost per bit is area x cost per area, and processed display glass costs ~100-1000x less per cm^2 than a DRAM wafer. Build 1T1C arrays on Gen 8.5 glass on existing IGZO backplane lines, with large planar capacitors (no high-aspect-ratio etch) and ~1e-19 A/um leakage for minute-scale retention, packaged as a CXL warm tier at ~200 ns-1 us.
why: Even with a cell 100x larger than silicon DRAM, cost per bit can be ~5-10x lower. Warm pages move there, so silicon DRAM shrinks to the hot set (30-50% less), using idle LCD capacity.
note: Display design rules make cells ~10^4x larger than DRAM, not 100x; cost/bit claim likely fails.

title: Air-gap NEMS relay as zero-leakage gain-cell write switch
idea: The retention tail comes from access-device leakage, and a 10-20 nm gap electrostatic nano-relay has truly zero off-current. Use it only as the write switch of a gain cell, so reads never cycle it and contacts see ~1e10-1e12 cycles over life. The storage gate then holds for hours, limited only by gate tunneling.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially removed and the access-transistor tail eliminated, without a capacitor.
note: Relay stiction, size and 1e12-cycle limit clash with DRAM density and write counts.

title: Series ferroelectric layer makes storage gate self-restoring
idea: Add a thin series ferroelectric to the gain cell's storage gate so the node's charge-voltage curve becomes S-shaped with two wells. Small leakage drifts are resisted until the coercive field, so the node stays latch-like. The bit remains charge-based, unlike a FeFET, which requires full polarization switching.
why: Capacitorless retention: aims for 100x rarer refresh and tolerance of leaky access devices.
note: S-shaped node CV for latch-like retention; negative-capacitance stability doubtful.

title: Cobalt-free manganese-nitride magnetic cells for refresh-free working memory
idea: Today's MTJs need Co, Ru, Ir and Pt; ferrimagnetic Mn4N has perpendicular anisotropy and low magnetization, and spin-transfer switching current scales with Ms x Hk. Build Mn4N/MgO/FeB tunnel junctions (Mn, N, Mg, O, Fe, B only) with no synthetic antiferromagnet, targeting ~10 ns switching and >1e15 endurance.
why: Refresh and scarce resources: nonvolatile DRAM-class memory on any logic BEOL with no listed elements; risks are TMR ratio and thermal stability at small sizes.
note: Scarce-element-free MTJ; low TMR and thermal stability at small size are key doubts.

title: Champagne fizz: electrolytic nanobubble toggles nanochannel resistance
idea: Stimulus 'champagne bubble' -> a 15 nm nanochannel holds dilute aqueous electrolyte between two carbon electrodes; a short pulse electrolyzes a few thousand molecules into an insulating H2 nanobubble that pins in a hydrophobic pocket (bit 1), and a reverse pulse recombines and dissolves it (bit 0). Read is a 0.1 V resistance probe with >100x contrast.
