why: Targets k ~70-150 (fact 1 needs k ~70), raising Cs without more AR, in a wet bath rather than anneal tools, and suits stacked tiers. High risk: crystallinity below 8 nm, leakage, and carbonate contamination.
note: Thin-film dead layer, volume change and carbonate likely cap k and raise leakage.

title: Femtosecond self-organized surface ripples pattern bitline gratings without resist
idea: Extreme user: a fab with no resist chemistry at all. Scan a femtosecond laser over a thin carbon or silicon hardmask so laser-induced periodic surface structures form self-organized ripples at ~lambda/4 pitch, locked into order by a seed grating, then transfer with Cl2/O2.
why: Litho: chemical-free, maskless 1D grating patterning at high throughput; could remove both resist and masks from array line layers.

title: GPU tensor cores decode memory codewords so the base die stays dumb
idea: Move error correction across scales, from a small base-die ASIC to the accelerator's idle matrix engines: stacks ship raw 1%-BER codewords with parity, and the GPU runs batched min-sum LDPC decoding on tensor cores in the shadow of other loads. The stack's base die can then be built on the DRAM process with no logic node.
why: Lets cells run at 1% BER while removing the costly logic-process base die (fact 6, capital); decoding costs ~1-3% of GPU throughput.
note: Tensor cores suit min-sum poorly; decode latency on every read.

title: Ramtron FeRAM without lead or platinum: aluminum-boron-nitride ferroelectric capacitors
idea: PZT FeRAM died on lead, Pt/Ir electrodes, 600 C anneals and a failure to scale below ~130 nm. Replace PZT with wurtzite Al(1-x)B(x)N (ferroelectric near x~0.07-0.15), sputtered below 400 C onto TiN or Mo electrodes, as a 1T1C cell whose ~100+ uC/cm2 remanent polarization needs only a short ~3:1 cup instead of a 60-75:1 pillar, refreshed only on power-down.
why: Removes Pb, Pt, Ir and the hafnium of HZO; Al, B and N are effectively unlimited and U.S.-producible; nonvolatile so standby refresh vanishes; ~20x shallower capacitor etch. Endurance of nitride ferroelectrics is the open risk.

title: Fermented masks: bacterial S-layer protein crystals as nano-etch templates
idea: Grow S-layer-bearing bacteria (e.g., Sporosarcina, Deinococcus) in a fermenter, harvest the S-layer proteins, and recrystallize them on wafers as 2D lattices with 10-13 nm periodic pores. Infiltrate them by ALD to make a hard mask for dense hole and pillar arrays: a lithography template brewed in a vat.
why: Litho capital: sub-15 nm periodic patterning for the price of a fermenter, scaling by volume like brewing. Runs in a nanofab plus a bio lab.
note: S-layer templates studied for decades; small domains, defects and no registration to devices.

title: Papermaking nanosheets: Langmuir-Blodgett perovskite films with k near 200
idea: Paper forms by settling fibers out of a slurry. Exfoliate layered perovskites (Ca2Nb3O10, Sr2Nb3O10) into 1.5 nm nanosheets in solution and tile them onto wafers layer by layer by Langmuir-Blodgett transfer. This builds capacitor dielectrics with k ~100-200 at near-room temperature.
why: Charge wall needs k~70: ~3x ZrO2's k lets short, cheap capacitors hold 5 fF, with the dielectric made in beakers and no ALD precursor supply chain.

title: Self-assembled nanopillar composites multiply capacitor area in one deposition
idea: Ideal: an electrode that sprouts its own forest. Closest: co-sputter a phase-separating film (conductive TiN or NiO-type pillars in an Al2O3/MgO matrix) that spontaneously forms ~5 nm vertical pillars at ~10 nm spacing, etch back the matrix and coat with ALD dielectric and top electrode for 10-30x area gain with no patterning or HAR etch.
why: 100x enabler: gives cheap planar/panel cells pillar-class capacitance for ~$1/m2, deleting capacitor-module masks and fluorocarbon HAR etch on the ~$0.1/GB path. Trades pillar uniformity and tip leakage.
note: 5 nm pillars at 10 nm spacing leave no room for dielectric plus electrode.

title: KV cache kept as tokens; idle tensor cores recompute it
idea: IFR: the KV cache costs zero bytes. Closest achievable: store only token IDs plus a residual-stream checkpoint every 8th layer; during memory-bound decode the otherwise idle tensor cores re-derive K/V for the seven intervening layers block by block, overlapped with the weight fetch.
why: Attacks HBM capacity and the HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): KV footprint down ~6-8x for ~15-25% extra FLOPs that decode leaves unused anyway.
note: Rebuilding 7 skipped layers needs full-layer compute over all context tokens each step, far beyond decode slack.

title: Procedural weights: generator at the interposer synthesizes tensors from seeds
idea: Ideal: weights that take no storage because they are computed on demand. Closest achievable: train models whose weight matrices are a small stored core plus pseudo-random projections regenerated at line rate by a hash/PRNG engine in the base die or interposer, so only seeds and cores (~5-10% of bits) live in static storage.
why: Zero refresh because the stored state fits in SRAM or ROM, and 10-20x fewer bits moved; trades abundant logic for scarce DRAM capacity and bandwidth.

title: Statistical capacitors: unaligned anodic-alumina pores caught by oversized pads
idea: Constraint: no lithography and no plasma etch for the capacitor mold. Anodize a deposited aluminum film into self-ordered ~30 nm-pitch pores (AR >100 for free), deliberately unaligned to the cells; each oversized landing pad catches 3-5 pores, pores straddling gaps are sealed by a selective ALD cap, and the per-cell capacitance spread is trimmed out at test.
why: Facts 1 and 4: swaps the hardest high-AR cryo-etch and its mask for a wet bath; AR 100-200 gives ~1.5x Cs; capacitor-module capex -60-70%.

title: AFE-reservoir stub capacitor (Hf-free antiferroelectric ZrO2)
idea: Tetragonal ZrO2 films 5-7 nm thick show a pinched double hysteresis loop: above ~1-1.5 MV/cm they turn polar, below a lower field they snap back. Write '1' to ~1.3 V (polar state, storing induced polarization plus linear charge); write '0' to 0 V (never crosses the forward field). Precharge the bitline low (~0.35 V, below the backward switching voltage) instead of VARY/2, so a '1' dumps its polarization onto the bitline as the film relaxes while a '0' gives only linear charge. The backward branch is a near-constant-voltage plateau: leakage drains polarization before the node voltage droops, a built-in charge reservoir. Electrode work-function asymmetry (TiN/W or TiN/Mo) or fixed charge shifts the loop to tune the plateau voltage. Same ALD ZrO2/TiN tool set as today, applied to a much shorter pillar or a short horizontal capacitor in a 3D tier.
why: 3-6x signal charge per um2 of capacitor wall -> capacitor height 1,300 nm -> 210-420 nm (AR 62 -> 10-20) at equal signal; up to ~3x retention stretch from the plateau; horizontal 3D capacitor 3-6x shorter.

title: Temperature-hardened negative-capacitance stub (FE/DE superlattice)
idea: A ferroelectric biased in the unstable middle of its Landau double well has negative differential capacitance C_FE < 0. In series with a dielectric (C_DE) and with |C_FE| > C_DE, the total capacitance C_DE/(1 - r) exceeds C_DE, where r = C_DE/|C_FE|. The stack is an ALD superlattice of Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (or Zr-rich HZO) with ZrO2/Al2O3 layers on TiN, deposited in the same pillar or short horizontal capacitor. The twist is designing r against temperature: |C_FE| follows Curie-Weiss behaviour, so r is set to ~0.85 at the cold corner and falls to ~0.6 at 125 C. The capacitor then never crosses into hysteresis and still gives >=2.5x at the hot corner.
why: 2.5x (125 C) to 4.7x (25 C) capacitance per area -> pillar 1,300 -> ~430-650 nm for equal Cs; or the same height with a ~2.5-4x bigger signal at 1c/1d cell sizes.

title: Fab necromancy: restart mothballed fabs on depreciated used tools
idea: Reverse the newest-node instinct: buy idle 300 mm shells and used ArF-immersion toolsets from retired 2x-nm DRAM/logic lines. Run a frozen 20-25 nm DRAM process for capacity-tier DDR4/LPDDR4 and CXL expanders, which need gigabytes rather than speed.
why: Capital intensity: used tools cost ~10-20% of new, and depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) is near zero. Cost per bit can rival the leading edge despite 2-3x lower density, with capacity in 12-18 months instead of 3-5 years.
note: Depreciated tools cut wafer cost; well-trodden path, needs fab-scale capital.

title: Holographic superposition stores many pairs per vector
idea: Worsen: give each key-value pair its own exclusive memory slot. Flip: bind keys to values in 10k-dimensional hypervectors and superpose hundreds of pairs into one vector, retrieving by unbinding plus a clean-up codebook, for associative caches and semantic memory.
why: Cost: 100x+ more pairs per stored bit for approximate associative recall; trades exactness and capacity-dependent noise.
note: HDC superposition for associative memory; same core as I-07650, capacity-limited noise.

title: Rectangular glass panels replace round silicon interposers
idea: Invert 'interposers are cut from round silicon wafers': build large memory-plus-logic interposers on 510x515 mm Corning glass panels with through-glass vias and 2 um redistribution lines at the Absolics plant in Georgia.
why: ~3.7x more area per substrate than a 300 mm wafer with no edge waste, low-loss glass for fast links, an all-U.S. alternative to CoWoS; target 2-3x lower interposer cost per mm2.

title: Layer-sharded wafer-scale SRAM: weights stay put, activations flow
idea: Worsen: give every chip a full model copy in external DRAM. Flip: assign each transformer layer's weights to the SRAM of one chiplet on a wafer-scale glass panel and pass activations chip-to-chip over millimeter wires, so weights never move and no external DRAM holds them.
why: Data movement: weights are stationary and only activations move (~100x less traffic); removes DRAM for weights using mature SRAM processes.

title: RDRAM lesson: move the whole periphery to a bonded logic wafer
idea: Rambus RDRAM died largely because fast I/O built in slow, leaky DRAM transistors cost die area, heat and price. Split the die: the array wafer carries only cells, bitlines and wordlines, and a separate logic-node wafer with the sense amps, decoders and PHY is hybrid-bonded underneath at about 1 um pitch. Each wafer is made in its best process.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7), so array efficiency rises to ~85%, and fast low-voltage logic cuts I/O energy. About 1.6x bits per array wafer.

title: Open-hardware 1990s stepper cloned by U.S. machine shops
idea: Inverts 'litho tools come from two or three vendors'. Publish an open design for a 248 nm, 0.6 NA, 5x-reduction stepper (expired patents, catalog excimer lasers, fused-silica lenses ground by U.S. optics shops) buildable for ~$2-3M each in volume.
why: Removes the scanner chokepoint for every non-critical layer and for spacer/BCP pitch-multiplied flows; creates a domestic tool base.

title: Substitute row-level refresh with mat-local segmented refresh for weak cells
idea: Substitute full-row (8 KB) refresh with sub-row refresh: hierarchical wordlines already have per-mat local drivers, so add a per-mat enable. Only the ~512-cell mats that hold profiled weak cells get the fast refresh rate; the rest of the row runs at a 4-8x longer interval.
why: Weak cells are sparse, so refreshing only their mats cuts tail refresh energy 16-64x versus row-granular retention-aware refresh, for a few gates per mat.

title: Self-timed sense completion replaces worst-case DRAM timing margins
idea: Substitute fixed worst-case timing (tRCD/tRAS guard bands) with asynchronous completion detection. Each sense latch drives dual-rail outputs, and a C-element tree over a mat raises 'row sensed' as soon as the slowest latch has actually resolved, so column access starts at the real finish time.
why: Latency and bandwidth: typical rows resolve 25-35% faster than the worst corner, recovering tRCD time and part of the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: MTJ-shadowed sense latches give a nonvolatile row buffer
idea: Substitute the purely volatile sense latch with a latch shadowed by a pair of MTJs written on precharge. Periphery can then be hard power-gated between bursts, and open rows reload from the MTJs in nanoseconds without reactivating the array.
why: Idle energy: periphery leakage dominates idle power at advanced nodes; power-gating plus instant row-buffer recall cuts idle power by ~30-50% and avoids re-activate energy.

title: Cast or reclaimed silicon replaces prime CZ wafers under BEOL arrays
idea: When the array is built in BEOL-temperature tiers and the periphery is bonded from another wafer, the array wafer's substrate is only a flat carrier: substitute prime CZ silicon with reclaimed wafers, cast multicrystalline silicon (lower-purity Si3N4-coated crucibles, not Spruce-Pine-grade liners) or glass carriers.
why: Quartz-crucible chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): roughly halves prime-wafer demand per bit for bonded array/periphery products and cuts substrate cost ~$50-100 per wafer.
note: Only valid for bonded array/periphery products; eases quartz-crucible risk, modest cost effect.

title: Burn-out amorphous-carbon tiers replace nitride sacrificial layers in 3D
idea: Substitute sacrificial nitride/oxide tiers with PECVD amorphous-carbon tiers alternating with Si or IGZO channel tiers: cut slits with Cl2 (channel) and O2 (carbon), keep support pillars every ~2 um, then laterally ash the carbon with remote O2/H2 plasma (selectivity >1000:1) to open horizontal cavities for lateral capacitors.
why: Solves the lateral-capacitor cavity step of 3D DRAM (fact 2) with a dry release needing no HF or NF3; propylene-derived carbon is cheap and non-scarce.

title: Substitute phosphate-fertilizer fluorosilicic acid for imported fluorspar
idea: Recover fluorosilicic acid already scrubbed at Florida and Idaho phosphate plants, convert it to anhydrous HF through the ammonium bifluoride route, then distill to electronic-grade HF and NF3 feedstock.
why: Fab fluorine chemistry (HF cleans, NF3 chamber cleans, etch gases) rests on Chinese/Mexican fluorspar; this domestic byproduct stream could cover most US fab fluorine demand.

title: Substitute per-gigabit water allowances for volumetric fab water permits
idea: State permits and CHIPS-style grant terms meter fabs in liters per Gb shipped rather than total gallons, with a published ratchet to 10x lower within 8 years and tradable credits for fabs that beat the curve, funding dry-tool retrofits.
why: Makes water a per-step design target that pulls the dry technologies into production and lets more DRAM capacity fit in water-stressed US sites such as Arizona and Idaho.

title: Swap DRAM-blind procurement for mandatory memory-per-workload efficiency labels
idea: Substitute 'buy more RAM' with buyer pressure on software. Government and large-enterprise procurement require a measured GB-per-active-user or GB-per-transaction label under a standard benchmark (an Energy Star equivalent), give preference points to the top quartile, and require shared runtimes instead of a bundled browser engine per app.
why: Software bloat drives DRAM demand. Pressure on a few large vendors could cut client and server footprints 10-30% within one refresh cycle, with zero hardware change.

title: Twelve volts into the stack, per-die switched-capacitor converters
idea: Substitute hundreds of low-voltage power/ground TSVs with a few TSVs carrying 12 V; each DRAM die steps down locally with a switched-capacitor converter built from the DRAM process's own high-density trench capacitors.
why: Fact 6: power/ground TSVs are often >50% of all TSVs; cutting them ~10x shrinks TSV area, lifts stack yield and cuts IR drop for 16-24-high stacks.

title: Substitute zero-error spec with a JEDEC relaxed-BER memory grade
idea: Define a standard 'DDR-R/HBM-R' grade with a guaranteed raw BER (e.g., 1e-6) and mandatory host-side strong ECC, letting fabs sell high-BER dies into AI and cache tiers under a common spec and price.
why: Supply and cost per bit: unlocks downbinned output across all vendors and lets future nodes trade reliability for density (fact 4) ~10-20%.

title: Substitute new bits with negabytes bought through memory demand response
idea: Swap adding supply for paying data centers to free memory, as utilities pay for negawatts: an exchange pays per freed GB-month verified by telemetry (compression, dedupe, tiering), and the freed modules return to market.
why: Creates virtual supply from the ~30-50% of server DRAM that is stranded or idle, potentially adding the equivalent of a fab's output with zero capex.

title: Substitute vendor lock-in with a standard memory-tier socket interface
idea: Swap ad-hoc integration for a JEDEC/SEMI standard that sets the thermal budget (<=400 C), hybrid-bond pitch, power rails and protocol for a memory tier, so any vendor's tier fits any foundry's logic wafer.
why: Creates a competitive multi-vendor market for memory tiers, lowering price and letting new U.S. entrants sell into every foundry.

title: Convert U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs to spin-memory element lines
idea: Combine the hard-drive industry's thin-film head wafer fabs in Minnesota, which already deposit and pattern TMR stacks at sub-30 nm, with back-end memory integration: contract them to make refresh-free magnetic storage-element wafers that are bonded onto CMOS periphery made elsewhere. As head volumes decline, the tools and TMR know-how convert to memory.
why: U.S. manufacturability and zero refresh: domestic, depreciated magnetic thin-film capacity instead of a new $15B fab.
note: Executable reuse of TMR fabs; MRAM still not DRAM-class on write energy/endurance.

title: Recirculating CCD loops hold streamed model weights
idea: Buried-channel CCD loops built on 350-180 nm CCD lines hold weights that circulate continuously past a regenerating sense-and-restore stage. Each pass taps the stream out to compute at fixed cadence.
why: Refresh is intrinsic to circulation and there are no row decoders (periphery is 49% of the die, fact 7). The cell is ~4F^2 CCD gates, suiting sequential weight streaming.

title: Second-reference sense amp flags decaying cells during refresh
idea: Each refresh fires an extra comparator with a tighter reference (~60% of a full 1). Rows with cells below it go to a small fast-refresh list, and the base rate slows until flags appear.
why: Online, self-calibrating multi-rate refresh that catches VRT cells, with 60-80% fewer refreshes, using circuits from the 1990s.
note: Online retention profiling (AVATAR-like) via second reference; overhead per SA is the cost.

title: Detector-grade float-zone silicon cuts generation leakage and quartz dependence
idea: Build DRAM on crucible-free float-zone wafers of the kind used for radiation detectors, with ms-scale minority lifetime and very low metal content, nitrogen-doped for strength. FZ tops out at 200 mm, which suits 1990s tool sets.
why: SRH generation current scales with ni/tau, so junction leakage falls 3-10x. It also bypasses the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucible chokepoint (>80%).
note: Tail leakage is field/trap driven, not bulk lifetime; FZ caps at 200 mm.

title: Gate-on-array shift register walks refresh through wordline strips
idea: Borrow the LCD gate-driver-on-array (GOA) shift register: a ring of two-transistor shift stages embedded in each sub-wordline driver strip passes a refresh token row to row, so refresh activates rows without powering the refresh address counter, the predecoders or the global row bus.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): strips decode and global-wire energy (~30-40% of per-refresh energy) out of every refresh, sharply lowering self-refresh power.

title: Window-comparator sense amps flag uncertain bits as erasures
idea: Add a pair of offset-shifted comparators on the secondary sense path that flags bits whose sensed value fell inside a narrow uncertainty window; on-die ECC treats them as erasures, and erasure decoding corrects about 2x more bits than errors at unknown positions.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tolerating ~2x more weak bits stretches refresh intervals ~2-4x using circuits old nodes already build.

title: Bosch-etched TSVs and deep-trench storage cells in one etch
idea: Combine MEMS Bosch deep-reactive-ion etching with eDRAM-style deep-trench capacitors on 200 mm MEMS/power fabs. One DRIE step cuts both the stack TSVs and 40 um-deep trench capacitors (Cs >100 fF) for a relaxed-pitch, near-refresh-free buffer DRAM die.
why: Uses abundant, depreciated U.S. 200 mm capacity. Huge Cs cuts refresh ~100x (fact 3), and the TSV step becomes a shared step rather than an added tax (fact 6). Density is low, so this is a buffer/cache tier.
note: Low-density niche buffer on depreciated 200 mm fabs.

title: Half-height capacitors: 2.5 fF cells sensed with code-assisted margin
idea: Combine a 30:1 capacitor mold, half today's height, with an offset-cancelling sense amp and the 1% error budget. Cs halves to ~2.5 fF, and the weakest ~1% of cells that mis-sense are left to the code.
why: Halves HAR etch time on the costliest tool fleet, removes one or two support lattices and reduces mold collapse; ~8-10% wafer cost and ~2x etch throughput (facts 1, 4).

title: Burn-in deleted; field scrubbing absorbs infant-mortality bits
idea: Combine the patrol-scrub engine with infant-mortality physics: DRAM ships without 125 C multi-hour burn-in, because early-life weak bits (well under 1% of cells) surface as correctable errors that the scrubber remaps in the first weeks of service.
why: Burn-in ovens, boards and floor space are a notable share of test capex and cycle time; removing them cuts back-end cost ~3-5% and cycle time 1-2 days.
note: Customer acceptance and gross-defect escapes are the risk.

title: Row-hammer activation counters double as page-hotness telemetry
idea: Combine DDR5 per-row activation counting (PRAC, built for row-hammer defense) with OS memory tiering: expose a decayed counter summary through a mode-register/sideband read so the kernel knows exactly which rows are cold without page-table access-bit scanning, and demotes them to CXL, compressed or flash tiers.
why: Accurate, free hotness data lets 30-50% of resident pages move to cheaper tiers with little slowdown, cutting top-tier DRAM per server by about a third; reuses silicon already paid for (fact 9).
note: Row counters do not map cleanly to pages under interleaving; CXL hotness units already exist.

title: Coaxial TSV whose liner doubles as on-die decoupling capacitor
idea: Combine the HBM power TSV with a deep-trench MIM capacitor: build each power via as a coaxial stack (Cu core / ZrO2-Al2O3 high-k liner / doped-Si or TiN outer shell) so the ~50 um via sidewall supplies roughly 5-10 pF of decap. Thousands of power TSVs then become the stack's decoupling bank and the periphery's planar MOS decap arrays are deleted.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and HBM TSV keep-out tax: reclaims ~3-6% die area and lowers PDN noise so VDDQ margin and I/O energy drop ~5-10%; keep-out zones do double duty.
note: Coaxial/TSV capacitors studied; modest area gain.

title: E-beam-personalized interposer routes around each stack's bad channels
idea: Combine post-stack HBM test maps with direct-write multi-beam e-beam lithography (vacuum only, no laser gas): after each stack is tested, one custom top routing layer is written per interposer that maps out defective channels/TSV lanes and wires in spares, so partially failing stacks ship at full capacity.
why: HBM yield (down 20-30%): recovering about half adds ~10-15% usable supply with no new DRAM wafers and no neon.

title: Row-buffer XOR tree: every activation doubles as full-row scrub
idea: Combine the activation path with patrol scrubbing: a hard-wired XOR tree under the sense-amp stripe computes parity over each 1 KB segment of the opened row and compares it with parity bits stored in that row, so every ordinary activate checks the whole 8 KB page rather than only the 64 B fetched. Mismatching segments are flagged to a background corrector before errors accumulate.
why: Retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9) and overfetch (fact 8): ~128x more bits checked per activate at no extra activation energy, so refresh can stretch 2-4x because weak-cell flips are caught early.
note: Whole-row parity check per activate is clever cheap scrub; area of XOR trees in SA stripe.

title: One codeword from CPU core to capacitor: fused link-storage ECC
idea: Combine link CRC/retry with on-die and rank ECC into one end-to-end Reed-Solomon codeword generated in the CPU, carried unchanged over the bus and stored as-is; the DRAM die drops its own ECC engine and the module drops separate ECC chips, while the host decoder corrects both channel and cell errors.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and cost: removes duplicated on-die ECC logic and parity (~6% of die) plus x4 ECC devices while giving weaker cells stronger protection.

title: HBM base-die SRAM patch cache retires failing rows at runtime
idea: Combine a CPU victim cache with post-package repair: a small CAM+SRAM in the HBM logic die intercepts addresses of rows that start failing in the field and serves them from SRAM, removing fused spare rows from each DRAM die and allowing unlimited, reversible repairs.
why: Self-healing and yield (facts 6, 7): moves redundancy from 8-16 DRAM dies into one logic die on cheaper logic area, extending stack life and accepting dies with more defects.
note: Logic-die SRAM remap for failing rows; plausible, modest benefit.

title: Actuarial memory: price DRAM capacity by insured error budget
idea: Combine insurance actuarial models with ECC tiering: cloud providers sell memory at certified uncorrectable-error rates (e.g., 1e-17 vs 1e-14 per bit-hour) based on measured fleet data, with an insurance pool paying out on rare failures, so cheap weak-cell capacity is sold wherever the priced risk is acceptable.
why: Creates demand and a price signal for weaker, cheaper dies, enlarging usable supply; turns reliability margin into a priced product rather than a fixed spec.

title: Carbon-cluster proximity gettering beneath every storage junction
idea: Borrow the image-sensor wafer makers' C3H5 cluster-ion implant: bury a carbon-rich gettering layer ~1 um below the array so Fe, Ni and Cu deep-level contaminants diffuse to it and lock away from storage junctions during anneals.
why: Fact 3: many tail bits are metal-induced generation centres; CIS white-pixel counts fell >10x with proximity gettering, so the 13 fA tail could shrink and refresh intervals stretch 2-4x at near-zero cost.
note: CIS gettering transfer to DRAM tail bits; gain depends on how many tail bits are metal-induced.

title: Solar PERC passivation: negative-charge AlOx liner around storage junctions
idea: Adapted from the PERC solar cell's field-effect passivation: line the buried-wordline trench and storage-node contact sidewalls with 2-5 nm ALD Al2O3, which carries ~1e12-1e13 cm^-2 fixed negative charge. The charge accumulates holes at the p-type surface, starving interface traps near the storage-node junction of the depletion they need to generate leakage current.
why: Solar makers cut surface recombination 10-100x this way; aimed at the access-device junction it targets the trap-dominated leakage tail (fact 3), plausibly doubling worst-cell retention with one extra ALD step and no EUV.

title: Class-D amplifier efficiency for wordline supplies: inductive switched VPP
idea: Adapted from the class-D audio amplifier's switch from linear to switched-mode conversion: replace the on-die Dickson charge pumps that make VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline voltage with an inductor-based buck-boost converter using package-embedded inductors, at 70-85% efficiency instead of ~25-35%.
why: Every refresh activation draws wordline charge from VPP; generating that charge 2-3x more efficiently cuts refresh and standby power substantially (facts 3, 10) without touching the cell.

title: Circuit breakers, not fuses: resettable row repair held in MRAM
idea: Adapted from the move from one-time fuses to resettable breakers: replace laser-blown repair fuses with a small on-die MRAM remap table that can be rewritten without limit, so rows whose retention degrades or turns VRT are remapped, and later un-mapped, over the whole product life and through refurbishment.
why: Fuse and post-package repair are limited and mostly one-shot, so modules with drifting retention tails get scrapped; resettable repair keeps tail rows out of the refresh budget for life (fact 3) and makes refurbishment cheap.

title: Jet-engine power-by-the-hour: vendors sell retained gigabyte-hours
idea: Adapted from Rolls-Royce's power-by-the-hour model: DRAM vendors lease modules and are paid per GB-hour of error-free service, keep ownership, watch retention telemetry remotely, and swap, anneal or re-grade modules before leakage tails cause errors.
why: Gives the maker a profit motive to design repairable, long-lived access devices and to refurbish (fact 3), turning installed DRAM into a reused fleet asset rather than a disposable part.

title: Catalytic-converter-style smelting recovers tungsten from fab chamber waste
idea: Adapted from autocatalyst PGM recycling, which combines a collection network, assay-based pricing and smelt-and-refine. Collect W-coated chamber shields, spent W sputter targets and WF6 abatement scrubber sludge, oxidize them, refine via ammonium paratungstate and refluorinate to WF6 domestically.
why: Tungsten is ~80% Chinese, and CVD W uses only a small fraction of the delivered WF6; the rest ends up in abatement. Recovering 30-50% of fab tungsten flows creates a domestic secondary supply.

title: Phosphate-fertilizer fluorosilicic acid becomes domestic electronic-grade HF
idea: Florida phosphate plants scrub fluorosilicic acid (H2SiF6) out as a waste stream. Adapt the fertilizer industry's FSA-to-fluoride routes to crack FSA into anhydrous HF, then distill it to ppt-grade for wafer etch and for NF3/WF6 synthesis.
why: HF depends on fluorspar (China ~60%). US phosphate by-product fluorine could cover domestic fab HF demand, removing a mining chokepoint.

title: Solar porous-silicon lift-off: reusable seed wafers for DRAM substrates
idea: Adapt the PV kerfless process: anodize a porous-silicon double layer on a reusable 300 mm CZ seed, grow a 10-20 um device-grade epitaxial Si film, bond it to a cheap handle (reclaimed or multicrystalline Si), and cleave along the porous layer; the seed is re-polished and reused 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resources (high-purity quartz crucibles, polysilicon, CZ pullers): prime CZ silicon per wafer drops ~20x. Risk: epi defect density versus the retention tail.
note: PV kerfless lift-off; epi defect density vs retention tail unproven.

title: Fiber-optic soot deposition: fully synthetic silica crucibles
idea: The fiber industry makes 9N silica by flame hydrolysis of SiCl4 (VAD/OVD soot) on a mandrel; deposit soot on a crucible-shaped mandrel and sinter it into a fully synthetic crucible with a crystallization-promoting outer layer for hot strength, made from chlorinated metallurgical silicon instead of mined quartz.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes the Spruce Pine dependency for wafer supply using Si, O, Cl, H only; U.S. fiber makers already run the process.

title: Street-sweeper routes: LLM weight reads double as refresh
idea: Borrowed from municipal sweeper routes that cover every street on a fixed cycle: during decode every weight row is read once per token (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight fetches as a route covering every row inside the retention window and disables explicit refresh for weight banks; when the server idles the banks may decay and are reloaded from flash on wake.
why: Weights are the largest DRAM region on inference servers; zero refresh power and 10-20% bandwidth recovered, so fewer or smaller stacks deliver the same throughput.
note: Smart Refresh idea applied to LLM weight scans; needs per-bank refresh skip in DRAM.

title: Appliance energy labels: 'R0 zero-refresh' procurement class for memory
idea: Borrowed from ENERGY STAR and EU appliance labels: U.S. federal and CHIPS-funded datacenter procurement adopts an 'R0' rating for servers whose memory hierarchy spends no power on refresh (SRAM, ROM, NVM or refresh-free ephemeral tiers), with a 10-15% price preference and published watts per idle GB.
why: Creates a guaranteed early market for refresh-free, less-DRAM architectures; refresh is 16-33% of idle memory power across the fleet it targets.

title: Display mura compensation for sense-amp offset to shrink periphery
idea: Adapted from OLED/LCD panels, which measure per-region non-uniformity at the factory and apply stored correction constants at runtime: each sense amp's offset is measured at test or boot and stored as a 3-bit trim in a dense one-time-programmable array, which injects a small compensating charge before sensing so sense-amp transistors can be drawn at minimum size.
why: Periphery at ~49% of die (fact 7): sense amps oversized for mismatch are a big periphery block; offset trimming could shrink them ~30-40%, cutting die area ~5-8% while keeping read margin for weaker cells.

title: TLC-NAND strategy: relaxed-window DRAM on idle trailing DRAM lines
idea: Adapted from the NAND industry's move to TLC/QLC, which accepted far worse raw cells because controllers could correct them: older 2x/1x-nm DRAM lines run with loosened process windows (fewer capacitor rework loops, short retention screens, minimal fuse repair) to produce raw-grade dies sold only into ECC-heavy CXL controllers.
why: Capital intensity and supply (fact 4): idle or fully depreciated trailing DRAM capacity becomes productive; relaxed screens and repair raise yield and throughput 10-20% and cut test cost, feeding a cheap controller-corrected tier.

title: Power-by-the-hour memory leasing with vendor-owned cascading DIMMs
idea: Adapted from Rolls-Royce TotalCare jet-engine contracts: the DRAM maker keeps ownership of modules installed in data centers and bills per GB-hour. When a hyperscaler upgrades, the vendor pulls the modules, retests them and cascades them to tier-2 clouds, then enterprise and edge, then consumer refurb.
why: The vendor now profits from lifetime bit-hours instead of unit sales, so module service life stretches from ~5 to 10+ years; installed usable bits rise ~30-50% without new wafers (supply, capital intensity).
note: Vendor-owned GB-hour leasing aligns incentives to extend module life.

title: Auto-parts core charge on DIMMs and soldered memory boards
idea: Adapted from alternator and starter core charges: every server memory purchase carries a refundable $/GB deposit, paid back when the module or board goes to an authorized remanufacturer. The remanufacturer retests at speed bins, replaces failed packages, rewrites SPD and resells with warranty.
why: Raises collection of decommissioned DRAM from an estimated <20% to >80%; recovered DDR4/DDR5 could cover ~10-15% of demand during a shortage with near-zero capex (supply, scarce resources).

title: Offshore-wind contract-for-difference for new DRAM bits
idea: Adapted from UK offshore-wind CfDs: the government auctions 15-year contracts that pay new memory producers the gap between a strike price per Gb and a market index, and claws money back when prices exceed the strike.
why: Removes the boom-bust risk that blocks capex so new capacity can be financed at utility rates; in shortages like 2026 the clawback makes the net public cost near zero (capital intensity).

title: Airline rotable-parts pooling for critical fab tool components
idea: Adapted from airline rotable pools where carriers share engine and avionics spares: memory fabs join a regional pool of pre-qualified RF generators, electrostatic chucks, robots and EUV source modules with 4-hour delivery, billed per tool-hour.
why: Unplanned downtime eats several % of capacity; pooling lifts tool availability ~2-4 points, which adds a few % of wafer output without new fabs (capital intensity, supply).
note: OEM spares pools exist; a few % output gain.

title: Transit Buy America ramp applied to federal data-center memory
idea: Adapted from FTA Buy America rules that ramped U.S. content in rail cars: memory in federally funded data centers and AI programs must rise from 10% to 70% U.S.-made content (wafer, assembly and test) over 8 years on a published schedule.
why: Gives domestic fabs a predictable demand base worth several EB per year, enough to justify capex, and counts wafers and packaging, not just final assembly (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Biosimilar interchangeability: fast-track qualification for U.S.-made DRAM
idea: Adapted from the FDA biosimilar pathway: a NIST-run reference test suite and shared reliability datasets let a new U.S. maker earn an 'interchangeable' designation proving JEDEC equivalence, which OEMs accept in place of 12-18 months of bespoke qualification.
why: Qualification delay is a hidden entry barrier; cutting it to ~4-6 months gets U.S. bits to market about a year sooner (U.S. manufacturability, supply).

title: Orphan Drug Act incentives for U.S. legacy DRAM production
idea: Adapted from orphan-drug exclusivity and tax credits: give a U.S. maker 7-year exclusivity on federal procurement plus a 25% production credit for end-of-life DRAM types (DDR3/DDR4, LPDDR4, SDR) used in defense, auto, medical and industrial systems.
why: Secures parts for long-lived U.S. systems, lets incumbents move capacity to the leading edge, and gives a U.S. entrant a protected DUV starter market (U.S. manufacturability, supply).

title: Half-inch Minimal Fab runs a full 1T1C process on desks
idea: MINIFY the fab: run a planar or trench 1T1C process on 12.5-mm wafers with desk-sized Minimal Fab tools (maskless litho, per-tool local cleanroom, ~$5-20M total), so a 10-person team iterates storage-element materials in days instead of waiting for foundry lots.
why: Capital intensity ~1000x lower for R&D and small-batch defense or rad-hard memory (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).
note: Speeds materials iteration; product-scale impact is indirect.

title: Printed memory prize: 1 GB per square meter
idea: Minify entry capital with a US milestone prize (target: 1 GB per m2 at under $5/m2 and 100 ns latency) tied to a shared open roll-to-roll pilot line where teams rent web time by the meter.
why: US manufacturability and capital: dozens of teams can try printed DRAM approaches without each building a line.

title: Magnify dedup scope to the whole rack's CXL pool
idea: Magnify deduplication from one host to a whole rack: the CXL pool controller hashes every 4 KB page and 256 B chunk from all attached hosts and keeps identical content (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) once, as copy-on-write. The hash index sits in the switch ASIC, so hosts see ordinary loads.
why: Cloud racks run hundreds of near-identical guests. Rack-scope dedup recovers ~1.3-3x more capacity than per-host KSM, at almost no CPU cost.

title: Magnify bit-level ops: hardware rank/select for succinct structures
idea: Magnify ISA support for succinct data: single-cycle rank/select and wavelet-tree access instructions, plus a near-memory FM-index unit, make compressed bitvector tries, suffix arrays and indexes as fast as pointer-based ones.
why: Indexes, tries and genomic search structures shrink ~3-8x toward their information-theoretic minimum.
note: ISA support for succinct structures; modest segment.

title: Minify app bloat with a 'Memory Star' efficiency label
idea: Minify client DRAM demand through policy: an Energy-Star-style label rates apps by resident MB per standard task. Federal and enterprise procurement and the OS app stores require it, and OSes cap unlabeled background apps.
why: Bloated runtimes (Electron, browser tabs) use 5-10x the memory of native code. Industry-wide pressure could cut PC and phone DRAM demand ~20-40% and release supply.

title: Minify the billed byte: pay-per-hot-byte cloud memory pricing
idea: Minify what customers pay for and so what clouds must provision: memory is billed by the measured hot working set (hardware access-bit sampling), and cold allocations drop automatically to a compressed/flash tier priced at 1/10.
why: Allocated memory is often 3-10x the hot set. Aligning incentives lets providers back ~10x more allocated GB with the same DRAM.

title: Glass micro-bridges with copper and laser-written waveguides
idea: MINIFY the interposer to small ~1x2 mm glass bridges placed only where die edges meet, each carrying fine copper lines plus femtosecond-laser-inscribed optical waveguides for longer hops.
why: Interposer cost and capital (CoWoS capacity): ~95% less silicon interposer area, with optics on the same bridge.
note: Glass bridges plus fs-written waveguides; incremental on EMIB/CoWoS-L.

title: Full-row dump to a base-die SRAM row cache
idea: MAGNIFY transfer size to an entire 8 KB row: on activation, the row crosses an 8K-bit hybrid-bonded bus into a base-die SRAM row cache, the DRAM row closes at once, and random sub-reads are served from SRAM.
why: 128x overfetch and row hammer: the activated row is used fully and opened only once; claims ~3x less energy per useful bit.

title: Magnify charge only on weak rows via targeted overdrive writes
idea: Rows profiled as weak are written with boosted wordline and restore voltages (+10-15%) so they store as much charge as strong rows. The whole die then runs at the strong bin's refresh interval.
why: Fact 3: refresh is set by the retention tail, not the median. Lifting the worst ~0.1% of rows can double the die-wide refresh interval for a tiny write-energy cost.
note: Per-row write boost; reliability stress on boosted rows.

title: Magnify threshold only for leaky rows via per-row back-gate bias
idea: Dual-gate oxide TFTs, standard on glass, share a back-gate line per row. Rows with leaky cells get a few hundred mV of negative back-gate bias from a small DAC table set at test and updated in the field, shifting Vt up only where needed.
why: Fact 3: pulls in the leakage tail without slowing every cell, which could stretch refresh 4-10x for tail-limited arrays.

title: Borrow LCD laser line repair to fix shorts and opens on panels
idea: Apply the display industry's routine laser repair to memory panels, guided by the test map: laser-cut shorts and CVD-write metal across opens on bitlines and wordlines that would otherwise use up redundancy.
why: Yield and fact 7: panel memory yield rises toward ~99% without large spare arrays, cutting periphery and redundancy area.

title: Eliminate single-device isolation: stacked series access transistors exploiting stack effect
idea: Replace the single access FET with two series vertical FETs sharing one gate; in the off state the middle node floats up, giving the upper device negative Vgs and reduced Vds (the logic stack effect) and cutting subthreshold leakage ~10x. Vertical stacking keeps the 4F^2 footprint.
why: ~10x lower leakage gives ~10x longer refresh period with known silicon processing (fact 3).
note: Stack effect cuts subthreshold leakage only; storage-node junction/GIDL tail is untouched.

title: Eliminate the on-die command decoder: host drives raw array timing
idea: Remove the DRAM's command state machine, mode registers and timing counters. The die exposes raw controls (wordline enable, SA enable, precharge, column strobe) on a hybrid-bonded wide port. The host controller issues every edge with row-specific timing from a per-row strength map built by boot-time profiling.
why: Removes ~2-3% of area in command logic and cuts per-row tRCD/tRAS ~20-35%, since most rows are far from worst case. A new array generation also needs no new on-die logic.

title: Eliminate high-k metal-gate periphery: slow, wide internal buses with poly/SiON
idea: Make the internal datapath 8x wider at 1/8 the clock (a 4,096-bit, 400 MHz bonded port), so periphery transistors can be plain poly-Si/SiON at 65-90 nm-class speed. Gates are etched with HBr/Cl2 and spacers are Al2O3 etched with BCl3, removing gate-last HKMG, dual work-function metals and their fluorinated steps.
why: Periphery masks -4-6 and steps ~-20%, buildable on legacy U.S. tools; wide-slow I/O also cuts interface energy ~3x (fact 5).
note: Wide-slow bonded port lets poly/SiON periphery return; plausible mask savings.

title: Eliminate the row decoder: token-ring sequential wordlines for weights
idea: For AI weight memory that is read in fixed order, replace random row decoders with a shift-register token chain along the mat edge that activates wordline n+1 after n; random access falls back to a small seek-and-stream jump table per bank.
why: Periphery ~49% of die: row decode/predecode area and energy drop by most of their share, giving ~10-15% die area and lower activation energy for streaming workloads.

title: Eliminate thick-oxide I/O masks: co-packaged legacy-node DDR5 PHY chiplet
idea: Strip the I/O transistors, ESD and DLL from the DRAM die so its process needs only one gate oxide, and put the DDR5 PHY on a tiny 40 nm chiplet stacked face-to-face in the same FBGA package. Module pinout and timing stay JEDEC DDR5.
why: Removes ~3-5 masks (dual oxide, I/O implants, thick metal) and ~5-8% die area from the array process, cutting wafer cost per bit.

title: Eliminate the decompressed copy: load units decode compressed formats natively
idea: CPU/GPU load-store units gain decoders for dictionary, delta and bit-packed columnar encodings, expanding values into registers, so DRAM only ever holds the compressed form and no decompressed working copy exists.
why: Analytics and columnar workloads get 2-4x effective DRAM capacity and proportionally less data-movement energy.
note: Decoders in load path; ISA and pipeline cost.

title: Bond-level non-volatile repair switches heal failed hybrid bonds
idea: Eliminate scrapping stacks for a few bad vertical connections: place tiny ReRAM/antifuse crosspoint switches beside every 16 hybrid-bond pads plus 2 spares, programmed after post-bond test to route around opens and shorts; routing persists without power or e-fuse reload.
why: At 1-3 um pitch with millions of bonds, bond defects dominate stack yield; per-group sparing pushes vertical-link yield >99.9%, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss.

title: Eliminate retention binning on testers; characterize in the field instead
idea: Ship DRAM after only a short gross-defect test, skipping hours of ATE retention and burn-in screens. At every boot and in idle windows, an on-die BIST plus the controller maps weak rows, VRT cells and timing margins into a persistent profile stored in SPD/flash, and the system routes around them.
why: ATE time, burn-in and guard-bands are ~5-10% of DRAM cost; field profiling also recovers chips scrapped for marginal retention, adding several % sellable yield.

title: Eliminate one-shot reads: NAND-style read-retry for nondestructive BEOL gain cells
idea: A low-temperature 2T/3T gain cell reads without destroying its charge. So when ECC fails, the controller re-reads at shifted reference levels from a per-region table learned from drift history until the codeword decodes, as NAND read-retry does.
why: Tolerates the wider threshold distributions of cheap <=400 C transistors at a tiny average latency penalty (retries are rare), relaxing device uniformity requirements several-fold.
note: NAND read-retry ported to nondestructive gain cells; sensible enabler for cheap BEOL transistors.

title: Eliminate the fixed sense reference: pilot cells set each row's threshold
idea: Each row carries a few pilot cells written to known 0/1 values at every write. On read, the sense amp's reference comes from the pilots' current levels, the way wireless receivers use pilot symbols, so it tracks decay, temperature and drift of the <=400 C devices.
why: Removes drift and leakage guard-bands for low-thermal-budget transistors, extending effective retention ~2-4x and lowering read errors with no extra reads.

title: Eliminate DIMM ownership: cascade leasing priced per GB-month
idea: Eliminate end users buying DIMMs: a lessor owns modules, bills per GB-month, recovers them at each refresh, re-tests and cascades them down tiers (cloud, enterprise, edge, schools), financing the fleet with asset-backed securities.
why: Cascading keeps each bit in service 10-15 years instead of 5, cutting new-bit demand ~15-25% in mature segments.
note: Leasing exists; cascade plus ABS financing is the twist.

title: Capacitor first, transistor last: bonded perovskite capacitor wafer
idea: Reverse fabrication order: build a planar BST/SrTiO3 capacitor array first and crystallize it at 700 C (k ~300, the 1990s gigabit-DRAM dielectric), then smart-cut bond (1995) a pre-implanted thin silicon layer on top and finish 180 nm access transistors below 450 C so the perovskite never sees transistor hazards.
why: Charge wall and capital (facts 1,4): planar 0.2 um2 x ~100 fF/um2 ~ 20 fF with no deep etch; tiers repeat by further bonds; risk is hydrogen damage to the perovskite and bond overlay.
note: Planar BST at 0.2 um2 cell is far from DRAM density.

title: Store the majority in the leak-sink state with row inversion flags
idea: Flip data polarity per row: at each write, on-die logic counts the bits and stores the row inverted whenever that places more bits in the discharged state the cells leak toward, recording one flag bit per 1 KB row. Zero-heavy real data then keeps 80-90% of bits in a state that cannot decay.
why: Refresh (fact 3): only charged cells can fail, so per-row failure probability drops 5-10x and the refresh interval stretches ~2-4x at the same ECC strength; <0.1% bit overhead.

title: Refresh by relocation shuffles row-hammer adjacencies every window
idea: Reverse refresh from restore-in-place into move: each refresh slot copies one row into a spare row in the same subarray (in-array row copy through the shared sense amps) and updates a small remap table, so within each window every row is both refreshed and physically relocated. An attacker can no longer keep hammering the same physical neighbors, so extra target-row refreshes become unnecessary.
why: Merges regular and mitigation refresh (facts 3, 9), recovering ~10-30% of refresh-related bandwidth at ~1k hammer thresholds for ~1 spare row per subarray.
note: Close to randomized row-swap (RRS/SRS) mitigations; folding swap into refresh slots is the twist.

title: Power-switch fabs make memory switches: SiC-access DRAM tier
idea: Reverse the role of a power transistor: run underused 150/200 mm 4H-SiC MOSFET lines (idle after the EV slowdown) at their finest ~0.35-0.5 um rules to make 1T1C cells with SiC access transistors and trench capacitors. SiC's 3.3 eV gap gives intrinsic carrier density ~1e-9 cm-3, so off-current is low enough that retention reaches minutes to hours, as 1990s SiC DRAM demonstrations showed.
why: Uses existing SiC fabs (several in the U.S.) with no EUV to make a near refresh-free DRAM-class tier (fact 3); density is ~100x below leading DRAM, so it serves idle-dominated capacity, not bulk.
note: SiC DRAM shown in the 1990s; density ~100x lower limits it to an idle tier.

title: Sell the leaky dies: short-retention DRAM SKU for rewrite-heavy buffers
idea: Reverse the binning logic: dies that fail the 64 ms retention spec but pass at 8-16 ms, today scrapped or downgraded, become a 'fast-turnover' SKU for buffers that rewrite every row within milliseconds (AI activation and KV staging, video frames, packet buffers). The controller enforces a per-row touch deadline instead of refresh.
why: Raises usable supply from existing fabs by recovering retention-fallout yield (a few % of output) with no new tools, and drops refresh where it is wasted (fact 3).

title: Pitch-split: off-pitch periphery moves to U.S. 200mm chiplets
idea: Rearrange periphery by pitch-criticality: only bitline SAs and sub-wordline drivers stay on the array die from a U.S. memory fab; pumps, regulators, DLL, I/O, ESD, command logic, test and fuses move to a chiplet from U.S. 200mm/130-65 nm lines, attached face-to-face at a U.S. OSAT such as Amkor Arizona.
why: Fact 7 and capital: ~20-25% of die area returns to cells; the off-pitch half runs on fully depreciated U.S. fabs with zero EUV.
note: Off-pitch periphery onto depreciated U.S. 200mm chiplets via F2F bonding; bonding cost vs 20% area.

title: CHIPS-funded open DRAM periphery IP for every U.S. fab
idea: Reverse the IP model: a government-funded consortium publishes silicon-proven SA, decoder, pump and PHY hard macros with layouts for U.S. mature and memory fabs as open IP, so periphery becomes public infrastructure and companies compete on arrays.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery is ~40-50% of new-DRAM design cost; lowers entry for U.S. memory startups.

title: Counter-phase wordline drive on adjacent tiers cancels coupling
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, whenever a tier's selected wordline ramps up, drive an unselected wordline segment in each neighboring tier down by a matched step (deeper off-state), so vertical capacitive kicks into the neighbors' bitlines and storage nodes cancel instead of accumulating.
why: Inter-tier disturb and row hammer (facts 2,9): 2-4x less vertical coupling lets tier pitch shrink (more tiers per um of stack) and lowers disturb-driven refresh.

title: Stationary wafer, moving process heads
idea: Reverse which part moves: the wafer stays fixed on one chuck while a gantry carries in turn spatial-ALD, plasma-clean and anneal heads over it, so one station does several steps with no robot handoffs.
why: Fewer tools and transfer chambers per module, ~30% smaller footprint and higher throughput for the many deposition steps in DRAM capacitor and spacer modules.

title: DUV-first domestic DRAM incentive
idea: Reverse subsidy logic from 'most advanced node' to 'least chokepoint exposure': give U.S. tax credits per good bit made without EUV or China-sourced tungsten, rewarding fabs built on available DUV tools and alternative metals.
why: Redirects CHIPS-style capital toward faster, cheaper, chokepoint-free capacity; fabs can be built with tools available today.

title: Fewer, faster TSVs: serialize 16:1 inside the stack
idea: Reverse HBM's many-slow-wires rule inside the stack: each TSV carries a 16:1 serialized 25-32 Gb/s stream from compact injection-locked transceivers on each die, cutting signal TSVs from thousands to a few hundred at a relaxed 40-50 um pitch.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV area and keep-out shrink ~80% and the relaxed pitch raises stack yield; costs ~0.3 pJ/bit of SerDes energy, so it suits capacity-oriented stacks rather than peak-bandwidth ones.

title: Spare-free dies: host controller owns all row repair
idea: Reverse who owns redundancy: DRAM dies carry no spare rows, fuse banks or address comparators; failing rows found at test go into a signed manifest and the host memory controller remaps them through an on-SoC 64 KB CAM into a host-reserved pool, one remap fabric serving dozens of dies.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: removes ~3-5% die area of redundancy/fuses plus fuse-blow test time; yield loss becomes a small capacity haircut.

title: Skip fab retention test; profile retention in customer racks
idea: Reverse the test order: dies ship after a short functional test, skipping the hours-long hot retention screen and burn-in; on first boot and weekly thereafter the controller runs retention-pattern sweeps during idle and bins each row into refresh classes stored in module NVRAM.
why: Test capex and cycle time cut ~30-50%; per-row refresh binning cuts refresh energy ~50-70% vs worst-case refresh.

title: Field error telemetry tunes chlorine etch recipes back at the fab
idea: Reverse the information flow: modules stream anonymized per-row error and retention telemetry tagged with die IDs to the fab, where it trains recipe corrections for the less mature Cl2/HBr and O2 etches replacing fluorocarbon steps, closing the yield loop in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Speeds yield learning for a PFAS-free process ~2-3x, making the constraint economically survivable.
note: Telemetry for PFAS-free etch learning.

title: PFAS-free certified DRAM grade paired with system-level ECC
idea: Flip the constraint into a market: define a certified PFAS-free DRAM grade for public buyers and hyperscaler sustainability targets, specified at relaxed raw BER and retention and sold with mandatory system-level ECC and per-row refresh, so new fabs without fluorinated steps can sell from day one.
why: Raises supply from simpler new fabs, pre-empts the proposed EU universal PFAS restriction and strengthens US manufacturability.

title: Memory-as-a-service: vendor owns the DIMMs, customers rent GB-hours
idea: Reverse ownership: the memory maker keeps title to the CXL memory pools in customer racks and bills per GB-hour. It moves capacity between tenants as demand shifts, and at each server refresh it redeploys the modules to new customers instead of letting them be scrapped.
why: Usable supply: fleets strand 25-50% of the DRAM they buy. Vendor-run pooling pushes utilization toward 80%+, so each bit produced serves ~1.5x more demand.
note: Same vendor-owned leased memory as I-02267.

title: Expired-patent DRAM: litigation-free process from public-domain IP
idea: Turn the patent wall into a commons: mine DRAM patents filed before ~2006 (now expired), covering stacked and trench capacitors, recessed-channel transistors and 6F2 layouts. Build a royalty-free 30-40 nm-class flow from them, staffed by former Elpida, Qimonda and Inotera engineers.
why: U.S. manufacturability: removes newcomers' biggest legal risk. On used tools, the flow delivers capacity-tier bits fast.

title: Ephemeral 1 fF cells for millisecond-lifetime AI activations
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: build sub-arrays whose cells hold only ~1 fF and keep data ~1-5 ms with no refresh at all, reserved for activations and KV tiles that are written once and consumed within a millisecond. The compiler tags data lifetimes, and the controller rejects stale reads by timestamp.
why: Facts 1 and 3: capacitor 4-5x smaller (AR ~15:1), zero refresh energy, ~2x density for transient data.
note: Skip refresh for ms-lived activations; density gain modest since retention-limited cap still needs margin.

title: Sixty-four independently biased plate segments isolate shorted capacitor blocks
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: break the array's common capacitor plate into 64 switch-fed segments per bank. A plate-to-node short, today a die-killer because the plate is shared, is isolated in the field by floating that segment and remapping its 1/64 of the bank to spare rows, so the die is repaired rather than scrapped.
why: Yield and repairability: recovers dies lost to plate shorts (est. several % yield) and keeps aging parts in service.
note: Yield recovery of a few percent; switch area overhead.

title: Mono-family silicon storage element recyclable straight to solar-grade silicon
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: build the storage element only from Si, SiO2, Si3N4 and doped poly-Si (ONO dielectric, poly electrodes, no Hf/Zr/Ru/W/TiN) and accept the low k by reading with a gain cell instead of charge sharing. Shredded end-of-life dies go straight to silicon refining after an HF strip, with no heavy-metal contamination.
why: Scarce resources and recyclability: removes tungsten (China ~80%), Ru and Hf; gain readout tolerates ~0.5 fF storage.
note: Recyclability niche; low-k gain cell costs density.

title: JEDEC heal command and storage-cell health telemetry standard
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: standardize a host-visible cell-health report (per-mat retention-tail percentiles) plus a REJUV command class (thermal, detox pulse, spare swap), so the OS can schedule storage-element repair the way SSDs schedule TRIM and garbage collection; CHIPS-funded buyers require it in procurement.
why: Repairability at fleet scale: turns per-device heal mechanisms into a usable ecosystem, extending module life.
note: Standards adoption slow; value depends on heal mechanisms existing.

title: Back-to-back refresh rows hand their wordline charge to each other
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging (in time): refresh is the only DRAM operation whose next row is known in advance, so merge the falling edge of row i with the rising edge of row i+1. A charge-sharing switch between the two local wordline drivers dumps about half of row i's ~3 V wordline charge into row i+1 before the VPP pump tops it up, and bitline precharge charge is likewise recycled across consecutive refreshes in a mat.
why: Attacks refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, Fact 3) and the wordline CV^2 floor (Fact 10): ~30-45% less VPP pump energy per refresh, amplified because charge pumps run at only ~30% efficiency.
note: Two-step charge sharing; saves pump energy on refresh only.

title: Age-tracking sense reference counterweights expected charge decay
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: oppose the 'weight' of leakage with a counter-force. Because retention failures are overwhelmingly charged-to-discharged, the sense-amplifier reference (reference-cell charge or bitline precharge offset) is stepped down according to the known age of each row since its last restore (derived from the refresh counter), following the measured decay curve, so a partly drained '1' still reads and restores correctly.
why: Extends the usable refresh interval 2-4x (Fact 3) by spending the unused margin on the '0' side; costs a small reference DAC per sense-amp group.

title: Refresh only live sub-row segments using gated local wordlines
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: do only as much as needed. Split each row's local wordline into eight sub-row segments with per-segment 'live' bits set by writes and cleared by OS free/zeroing commands; refresh activates only live segments, so refresh energy and bandwidth scale with resident data rather than capacity.
why: Refresh energy (Fact 3) and overfetch (Fact 8): 2-5x lower refresh energy in partially used memories, far finer than bank-level partial-array self-refresh.

title: Sacrificial hydrogen getter keeps oxide-TFT leakage tail low for life
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: oxide-semiconductor access devices on glass drift leaky as hydrogen, a shallow donor, diffuses in from passivation and packaging. A buried Ti/Zr getter film patterned around each memory tile absorbs that hydrogen over the product life, cushioning the off-current tail before it can move.
why: Holds sub-1e-19 A leakage stable over ten years so refresh can be set in seconds (Fact 3); one cheap sputter step.

title: Self-service: refresh bursts double as sense amp offset self-calibration
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: during each refresh burst one sense amp per mat reads an equalized (shorted) bitline pair and the result steps a 4-bit successive-approximation trim register that back-biases or capacitively offsets that amp; over one refresh window every amp re-trims itself, tracking aging and temperature.
why: Facts 1 and 7: effective offset sigma ~3x lower, so cells need ~30% less signal or amps can be minimum-size, and wafer-level trim test time is removed.

title: Skipping: read-once scratch memory omits restore and refresh circuits
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: for streaming activations and KV-cache spills written once and read once within milliseconds, the cell is read destructively and restore and refresh are skipped entirely; the periphery loses write-back drivers, refresh counters and the restore VPP budget, and cells need only ~5 ms retention, so a ~0.5 fF planar capacitor is enough.
why: 100x path: no high-aspect-ratio capacitor, periphery ~30% smaller and BEOL-stackable planar cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: each datum is consumed by its read (re-reads need a host copy) and data expires after milliseconds. Attacks Facts 1, 3 and 8.

title: Graded-thickness tiers pre-compensate etch taper in deep 3D stacks
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: model the vertical hole's taper before deposition and grade each tier's Si/SiGe (or oxide) thickness so tiers near the narrow bottom are thicker. Lateral channel width and capacitor area then stay matched (Ion and Cs within ~3%) across 100+ tiers from a single etch.
why: Fact 2: ~2x tiers per single-deck etch instead of multi-deck stacking, saving a full deck of masks/etch/alignment per ~64 tiers and tightening the retention tail.

title: Merchant pre-grown superlattice starter wafers for capacitorless 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: a U.S. epitaxy house pre-grows and sells standardized 64-tier in-situ-doped Si/SiGe superlattice 300 mm wafers with certified defect maps, the way SOI wafers are sold today. Capacitorless 3D cell makers (floating-body, thyristor, gain-cell) start from a finished stack instead of owning epi reactors.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: entrants skip ~$1B of epitaxy capex and months of tier-growth cycle time; creates a new domestic supply-chain node.

title: Fast-track qualification protocol for abundant-element material swaps
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: a consortium pre-builds shared JEDEC test vehicles, accelerated-stress datasets and failure-physics models for each abundant-element substitute (TiSi2 for W, Mg-Zn-Si-O for IGZO, spinel for yttria). A fab can then qualify a swap with a ~6-month delta test instead of a 2-3 year full requalification.
why: Qualification time, not chemistry, is the real barrier to dropping Hf, W, Co, Ru, Ta, In and Ga. Cutting it ~4x de-risks supply shocks and favors U.S. Earth-abundant supply chains.

title: Helium-free etch: hydrogen backside cooling plus closed-loop recapture
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out separates the needed property (wafer-to-chuck heat conduction) from the scarce substance: switch electrostatic-chuck backside gas from He to H2 or H2/Ar where process-tolerant, and fit remaining He users with membrane plus cryogenic recapture loops reclaiming >90% of backside and purge flow.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium has been offline since March 2026; fab He use drops 70-90%, removing a shutdown risk for etch and ALD tools (scarce resource, throughput).

title: Producer-side compression: NICs and SSDs write memory pre-compressed
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: publish the memory controller's compressed-line format as a standard and let NICs, SSD controllers and accelerators DMA data already in that format, so the uncompressed copy never occupies DRAM; the CPU's controller decompresses only when a core actually touches the line.
why: I/O buffers, page cache and receive rings are 10-30% of server DRAM; storing them compressed from birth gives ~1.5-2x on that slice and saves write bandwidth.

title: Binaries ship heap-trained compression dictionaries loaded at context switch
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: at build/profile time, train a 4-16 KB dictionary on representative heap snapshots of each application and embed it in the ELF; the OS loads it into a dictionary slot in the memory controller on context switch, so line-granular compression is application-specific from the first write.
why: Generic line compressors reach ~1.3-1.6x; app-trained dictionaries give 2-3x on structured heaps (protobufs, JSON, strings).

title: Asymmetry: read-wide, write-narrow memory links for inference
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: inference reads weights and KV cache 10-50x more than it writes. So ~90% of HBM data lanes become one-way DRAM-to-GPU lanes with open-drain low-swing drivers and receiver-only GPU ends, and a narrow bidirectional lane group handles writes and commands.
why: Data movement (fact 5): read lanes need no ODT or driver pairs and have no turnaround, so PHY energy and area per read bit fall ~25-35% and usable bandwidth rises ~10%.

title: Blessing in disguise: crosstalk-coded TSV arrays using coupling as signal
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: instead of shielding densely packed TSVs, group them in sets of 4-6 and send chordal vector codes (ENRZ-style). Common-mode coupling cancels while the coupled differential modes carry data, so crosstalk becomes part of the signaling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 2x denser TSV pitch at ~1.3-1.5 bits per wire, for ~40% less TSV area per bit.

title: Segmented sub-wordline refresh restores only weak-cell segments
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation (contradiction: refresh often for the tail vs rarely for the bulk): reuse existing sub-wordline-driver boundaries so each 8 Kb row is 16 independently fired segments; a fuse-loaded 2-bit retention tag per segment lets the refresh engine fire only segments holding sub-256 ms cells at 64 ms while the rest refresh at 1 s.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: ~85-90% fewer segment restores, ~60% less refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth loss recovered at 32-64 Gb; marginal dies pass without row sparing.
note: Partial row activation plus retention binning; VRT still threatens profiled refresh.

title: Unused repair spares reborn as hammer-shadow and parity rows
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the 30-60% of redundant rows/columns left unused after repair get a second job; an on-die table exposes them so the controller migrates hammered hot rows into them and stores extra parity there for a stronger code.
why: Reclaims ~2-4% of die area already paid for as a live reliability resource; raises the effective hammer threshold and correction strength at zero extra silicon.

title: ECC-tracked adaptive negative wordline off-level per bank
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: the fixed wordline-off voltage becomes a per-bank 4-bit DAC; when on-die ECC sees correctable retention errors rise (hot, aged or weak bank) it drives VNWL deeper (-0.2 to -0.5 V) to cut subthreshold leakage, then relaxes it to save pump energy and GIDL.
why: Leakage-tail suppression on demand: ~2-4x retention in the worst banks without a global worst-case setting; ~30% less refresh energy.
note: ECC-driven per-bank VNWL; modest refresh gain.

title: Close wordline early, keep row buffer latched to cap RowPress
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping/rushing: wordline-on time is decoupled from row-open time; the wordline drops as soon as restore completes while the isolated sense amps keep serving reads as a row buffer, and writes trigger a brief re-raise.
why: Aggressor-on time (RowPress) is capped near minimum tRAS regardless of open-page policy, cutting press-induced flips ~10-100x while keeping open-page hit performance.

title: ECC-cluster feedback trims individual sense-amp offsets
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: when correctable errors cluster on one bitline, the controller writes a per-sense-amp offset trim (small capacitor or back-bias DAC loaded from a trim RAM), fixing the weak-sense-amp part of the tail instead of sparing the column.
why: Much of the effective retention tail is SA offset, not cell leakage; trimming lets ~10-20% smaller signal (smaller Cs) be sensed reliably and saves spare columns.

title: Feedback: field-to-fab telemetry loop relaxes over-conservative test guardbands
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: hyperscalers stream anonymized per-die correctable-error and retention telemetry back to the fab, which uses it to retune sort guardbands per lot and safely pass dies currently rejected by worst-case margins.
why: Yield: ~3-8% more passing dies, with less over-test time.

title: Countercurrent charge recycling between consecutively refreshed wordlines
idea: Fish gills and bird legs recover heat by countercurrent exchange; during refresh bursts a local switch links the falling wordline of row n to the rising wordline of row n+k so about half of the ~3 V VPP charge transfers before the pump tops up, and bitline restore charge is shared between subarrays refreshed in antiphase.
why: Wordline and bitline energy per refresh falls ~35-50% (~46 to ~25-30 fJ/bit), and the inefficient VPP pump load roughly halves, shrinking pump area in the periphery.

title: Octopus-arm self-timed mats with replica-bitline handshakes
idea: Octopus arms run local reflex loops with little central control. Each mat generates its own sense-enable, restore-done and precharge-done events from replica bitlines (bundled-data asynchronous handshake). The bank logic sends only 'go' and receives 'done', with no worst-case global timing chains.
why: Typical mats finish 20-30% before worst-case tRCD/tRP. Self-timing raises bandwidth and cuts latency, and removes timing-generator wiring and margin (~10% of periphery power).

title: Slime-mould via mesh: training pulses burn out shorted bond paths
idea: Bond memory dies through an over-provisioned mesh of 2-4 redundant micro-vias per signal, each with a thin series fuse link (like Physarum's initial diffuse network); a post-bond training current sequence blows the fuse on any via drawing excess current through a bridging short, leaving the reinforced healthy paths as the final network.
why: HBM TSV/bond yield tax (20-30% loss): turns bridging and single-via defects into self-repaired links; could recover ~10-15 points of stack yield without spare dies.

title: Pheromone-trail hash marks let tenants converge on shared pages
idea: A CXL switch keeps a decaying 'pheromone' table of content hashes recently written by any VM; when another tenant writes a page whose hash hits a strong trail, the switch maps it copy-on-write to the existing physical page. Trails evaporate, so only popular content (OS images, model weights, libraries) is deduplicated, without full memory scans.
why: Multi-tenant capacity: 15-40% dedup across VMs and inference replicas at negligible scan cost.
note: Decaying popularity table avoids full scans; twist on cross-host dedup.

title: Homeostatic plasticity: sense reference self-trims to keep 50% ones
idea: Neurons scale their synapses to hold average firing constant; because bus data is scrambled, each mat's reads should average ~50% ones, so a per-mat counter tracks the running ones-fraction and nudges the sense reference/precharge level to restore balance, cancelling temperature, aging and leakage drift before it becomes errors.
why: Voltage floor (VARY ~1 V) and retention tail: recovers ~10-20% of signal margin otherwise spent as guard-band, enabling lower array voltage or smaller Cs.
note: Ones-count dynamic reference is known in flash; new for DRAM.

title: Xylem pit valves: self-isolating subarrays contain shorts and defects
idea: Xylem pit membranes seal an embolized conduit so water reroutes; give each subarray a small isolation switch and current monitor on its local wordline supply and precharge rail, so a wordline-bitline short or gross leaker trips and seals that subarray (remapped to a spare) instead of collapsing the whole bank's voltage.
why: Yield and capital: shorts that poison entire banks are a major yield killer at aggressive pitch; containment turns bank kills into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield several points per wafer.

title: Heterochromatin silencing: ship dies with no repair, OS silences bad regions
idea: Cells silence unusable genome stretches as heterochromatin instead of repairing them; design ultra-cheap-process dies with zero spare rows/columns, no fuse banks and no repair test step, store a boot-time silence map, and let the OS never allocate silenced regions, selling each die by its actual capacity.
why: Repair test time and redundancy scale with defect density and would kill a ~100x-cheaper high-defect process; removing them (plus ~3-5% spare area and fuse periphery) keeps such processes economic.
note: Value hinges on a high-defect cheap process existing.

title: Paddlefish stochastic resonance: dithered multi-reads of non-destructive cheap cells
idea: Paddlefish electroreceptors use ambient noise to detect sub-threshold prey fields; for non-destructive-read cheap gain cells whose signal sits near the sense threshold, inject a known dither on the reference and take 8-16 rapid comparator samples, averaging to resolve signals ~5x below single-shot noise.
why: Lets the cheapest cells (tiny storage nodes, mature-node or printed transistors with wide Vt spread) be read reliably by spending ~8x read latency; enabler for ~100x cheaper stacked cheap tiers.
note: Dithered averaging beats random noise but not fixed Vt offsets that dominate cheap cells.

title: Scatter-hoard strategic DRAM reserve with rotating stock
idea: Jays and squirrels scatter caches across many sites and eat the oldest first. A national or consortium reserve buys DRAM in price troughs, holds it in many distributed bonded warehouses, and rotates stock into government and education systems every ~18 months so it never goes obsolete; releases trigger automatically when contract prices pass a set multiple.
why: Damps 4x price spikes and secures critical supply; rotation limits holding cost to inventory carry instead of write-offs.

title: Solar MPPT perturb-and-observe loop tunes each bank's negative wordline
idea: Solar inverters find the maximum-power point by nudging voltage and watching the response. Off-state leakage versus negative wordline voltage has a minimum (subthreshold falls while GIDL rises), so an on-die loop nudges each bank's VNWL by +/-25 mV, reads a replica-transistor leakage integrator, and settles at that bank's minimum for its current temperature and age.
why: Fixed VNWL is set for worst-case corners; tracking the true minimum could cut tail leakage 2-3x across temperature and aging (fact 3) for negligible area.
note: Closed-loop VNWL at subthreshold/GIDL minimum; replica may not track tail cells.

title: Astrophotography dark-frame subtraction: sense reference that tracks predicted decay
idea: Astronomers subtract a dark frame because dark current is predictable. Store a 2-bit leakage class per row from test, and lower the sense amplifier's reference (dummy-cell level) with time-since-refresh according to that class, so a partly decayed '1' still resolves against a reference that has 'decayed' alongside it.
why: Reclaims roughly half the sensing margin now spent on decay, giving 2-3x longer refresh intervals (fact 3) with no cell change.

title: Window-frame thermal break: keep HBM 25C cooler than its GPU
idea: Aluminum window frames got a polymer thermal break so cold never bridges to the warm side. Cut a low-conductivity trench (porous oxide or sealed void) through the interposer between the GPU and HBM footprints and give HBM its own colder coolant branch, holding DRAM near 60 C instead of 85-95 C.
why: Leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C and refresh doubles above 85 C; 25 C cooler cuts refresh ~4-6x and frees bandwidth (facts 3, 5).

title: Ugly-produce program: sell retention-failing dies with in-system refresh grades
idea: Grocers turned misshapen fruit from waste into a discounted product line. Bin DRAM dies by measured retention (32/64/128/256 ms grades at 85 C) instead of scrapping those that miss 64 ms, and sell low-retention grades to hyperscalers whose controllers apply per-module refresh rates read from SPD.
why: Retention fallout is real yield loss at advanced nodes; recovering even 3-8% of dies adds bit supply without new fabs (capital intensity, supply).

title: California 'One Watt' standby rule, applied to DRAM self-refresh power
idea: Standby-power regulation (the One Watt Initiative, California Title 20) pushed the appliance industry to redesign idle circuits within a few years. Propose an Energy-Star-style data-center label capping self-refresh/idle power per GB (e.g. <=0.5 mW/GB at 45 C), making low-leakage access devices and adaptive refresh a procurement criterion.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power at 32-64 Gb (fact 3); a standard turns that into a purchasing metric and funds the access-device R&D the market underprices.
