idea: Scale shift from statistical dopant atoms (~10-20 randomly placed per channel at F=12 nm) to one deterministic atomic sheet: a ~0.3 nm AlOx layer at the gate-dielectric/SiO2 interface forms a dipole shifting nFET Vt by +0.2-0.4 V, so the access channel can be left undoped; lower doping lowers the storage-junction field and collapses the trap-assisted tunnelling and GIDL that form the tail.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): random dopant fluctuation and high junction fields cause the <=13 fA tail; expect a 3-10x tighter tail using only Al and O.

title: Ring-counter time-slot addressing for streaming weight mats
idea: Replace the address with time: mats dedicated to streamed AI weights use a shift-register token that walks the wordlines in fixed order, one per clock, so a row's address is simply its time slot; random access remains only at mat level and row decoders shrink to one token flop per row.
why: Row-decoder area falls ~70-80% in streaming mats (fact 7) and address energy disappears; weight-sweep workloads lose nothing.

title: Open-source CHIPS-funded DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: Scale up from company to nation: a federally funded, silicon-proven, royalty-free library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps, sub-wordline drivers, pumps, PHYs) on U.S. 28 nm processes, so a new U.S. entrant only has to develop arrays.
why: Cuts entrant design time ~2-3 years and ~$0.5B of cost (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Strategic DRAM reserve banks wafers during gluts for shortages
idea: Time shift across the 3-4 year memory cycle: in glut years such as 2023, a government or consortium buys finished DRAM wafers and known-good dies from existing fabs near cost. They sit in nitrogen-purged dry cabinets (dies are stable for a decade) and are released to existing packaging lines in shortages like 2026.
why: Adds supply without any fab and keeps existing fabs at full load in downturns. A 5% annual-output buffer would have damped much of the 4x 2026 price spike.

title: Gen-8.5 display fabs print gain-cell memory on meter-scale glass
idea: Scale jump from the 300 mm wafer to 2.2 x 2.5 m glass: idle LCD/OLED backplane lines build 2T oxide-TFT gain cells (indium-free ZnSnO or IGZO) at 1.5 um rules. That gives ~3 GB per m2, or ~15 GB per sheet, diced into modules behind an SRAM/DRAM cache.
why: Uses oversupplied existing display capacity with no EUV, no buried tungsten and no HPQ crucibles. At ~$300-600 per sheet, raw cost is ~$20-40/GB, and ~100 ns-1 us latency makes it a far tier.
note: Gen-8.5 oxide-TFT memory is a real capacity pool but ~$20-40/GB does not beat DRAM.

title: Existing U.S. solar ingot pullers make carrier wafers for bonded DRAM
idea: Scale shift across industries: bonded and stacked DRAM uses full prime CZ wafers as mechanical carriers and handles. Existing solar M12 ingot lines already pull ~300 mm-diameter ingots with lower-purity crucibles, so they can be sliced and polished into handle and monitor wafers.
why: Moves ~30-50% of DRAM's silicon wafer demand (carriers, handles, dummies) off prime CZ and HPQ crucibles onto existing capacity.
note: Solar-grade ingots for handle/dummy wafers is plausible; carrier share of demand overstated.

title: 5 mm2 DRAM dielets tolerate dirtier fabs via exponential yield
idea: Shrink the die from ~70 mm2 to ~5 mm2 dielets: under Poisson yield a 3x higher defect density still yields >90%, so the line can run looser particle control and fewer inline inspections; dielets are assembled by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding onto a logic base.
why: Cuts cleanroom-class and inspection capex (~10-15% of a fab) and lifts yield 20-30% on immature lines (Facts 4, 6).

title: Regulated-utility fab shells depreciated over thirty years
idea: Split the fab's timescales: buildings, utilities and UPW plants (~40% of capex) become a regulated-utility asset with 30-year recovery and a capped return, leasing space to U.S. DRAM makers whose tools stay on short cycles.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (Fact 4); stretching the slow-aging 40% cuts wafer cost ~10-15% and lowers entry capital.

title: Follow-the-night DRAM provisioning across continents
idea: The global fleet is treated as one memory pool over 24 hours. Deferrable memory-heavy jobs (embedding rebuilds, batch inference, index builds, ETL) are routed to whichever region is in its diurnal trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for the flattened global curve, not for its local evening peak.
why: Fleets provision DRAM for peak, and diurnal peak-to-trough is 1.5-2x. This means 15-30% fewer DIMMs fleetwide with zero new silicon.

title: Memory-efficiency label: GB-hours per transaction disclosure standard
idea: This adds zero masks. A federal cloud procurement rule, plus an Energy-Star-like label, requires software vendors and cloud services to report resident GB-hours per standard transaction or per inference token, with bid credits for each halving.
why: A years-scale incentive shift toward lean software, with 10-30% memory demand reduction across public procurement during the shortage.
note: Energy-Star-like disclosure for GB-hours; slow, modest effect.

title: Cloud instances discounted by measured page compressibility
idea: This adds zero masks. The provider measures each tenant's compressibility and dedup ratio over a month, places compressible tenants on compressed-memory hosts, and passes back a discount. That creates a market incentive for compressible data layouts.
why: 1.5-2x effective capacity on participating hosts, lowering fleet DRAM demand 15-25%.

title: DRAM in the socket cavity on the CPU package underside
idea: Use the package's other face: LPDDR packages mount on the land side of the CPU substrate inside a cavity in the socket and motherboard, putting memory ~2 mm under the die instead of 5 cm away on DIMMs. The top side stays free for cooling.
why: The short channel runs unterminated at ~1-2 pJ/bit vs 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 (fact 5) while keeping DRAM out of the logic die's heat path.
note: Socket cavity costs CPU land pins; channel shortening is real.

title: Two-threshold sensing exports erasure flags over a side channel
idea: Shift from binary to graded certainty at the cell-to-wire boundary: sense amps resolve twice with offset references, marking gray-zone cells as erasures, and a sparse erasure bitmap travels beside the data. Erasure decoding corrects ~2x more than blind errors, so a 1% raw BER needs only ~8% parity.
why: Halves ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells, preserving density while enabling lower VARY (fact 10).

title: B-grade die recapture: weak-cell DRAM fallout into heavy-ECC stacks
idea: Move the pass/fail line from zero unrepairable bits to <=1% weak cells: dies that fab test would scrap or down-bin are stacked on a heavy-LDPC base die and sold as full-capacity memory, with a buyer contracting for fab fallout at scrap-plus prices.
why: Raises usable bit supply from existing wafers ~5-15% (typical DRAM yield loss) with zero new fab capex.
note: Post-repair DRAM yield loss is smaller than claimed; heavy LDPC adds latency.

title: Sell capacity-years: DIMMs that shrink gracefully as rows retire
idea: Time shift (time-zero spec -> lifetime contract): ship modules with weaker cells that the OS retires row by row as they degrade, and price them per guaranteed GB-year with a declining capacity curve (e.g. 100% -> 92% over 5 years). Today those weaker cells are screened out at the factory.
why: Lets fabs sell lower retention bins (an estimated 5-15% more good bits per wafer) and moves reliability from screening to contract.

title: Federal reliability-graded memory standard creates demand for DUV parts
idea: No EUV: a U.S. procurement standard defines 'graded memory' (module-level ECC plus row retirement plus telemetry) so federal and hyperscale buyers can buy DUV-made, weaker-cell DRAM at full qualification. Policy shifts demand toward non-EUV domestic supply.
why: Creates a guaranteed market that de-risks new U.S. DUV DRAM fabs (US share now ~1-2%).

title: 1 Gb UCIe DRAM tiles so many small fabs feed one package
idea: Scale jump from die to package: define a tiny standard DRAM chiplet (1 Gb, UCIe-like edge interface, fixed footprint). Small or legacy fabs anywhere make tiles, and packaging houses tile dozens of them, possibly from different makers, onto a base die.
why: Small dies yield far better (yield falls exponentially with area) and let sub-scale fabs contribute bits. Creates a distributed supply base instead of three vendors.

title: Consortium defect-map commons that pools years of yield learning
idea: Time compression by pooling: member fabs upload anonymized, federated defect and wafer-map data, and shared models flag excursions that one fab alone would need years of wafers to recognize.
why: Yield ramp time is cost. Cutting a new node's ramp by ~6-9 months raises cumulative bit output 10-15%.

title: LTS-DRAM: freeze one interface for 15 years so old fabs never retire
idea: Decade time shift of standards: JEDEC freezes a long-term-support DRAM interface (DDR4-compatible) guaranteed for 15 years, so fully depreciated legacy fabs keep running and platforms keep accepting their parts.
why: Once depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) reaches zero, legacy bits get very cheap. Keeping that capacity alive instead of scrapping it preserves ~10-15% of world wafer starts.

title: Maskless DMD diode-laser exposure for all non-critical DRAM layers
idea: Scale shift of the mask: micromirror arrays steer 375-405 nm diode lasers to expose implant, pad, redistribution and bump layers digitally, retiring the KrF excimer scanners and photomasks those layers use.
why: Removes krypton and neon from ~30-40% of exposure layers and cuts mask spend ~20%. Design changes take a file swap instead of a mask.

title: Noble-gas intensity credit: CHIPS bonus for rare-gas-free fabs
idea: Time-bounded policy: production credits scale with a fab's measured liters of helium, neon, argon and xenon per wafer, falling to zero by 2032, so every procurement decision pushes toward substitute processes.
why: Makes U.S. DRAM capacity immune to the Qatar-style and Ukraine-style gas shocks while sharing the substitution cost. It also builds a U.S. market for the tools in ideas 24-42.

title: Hot-zone beachhead: launch where silicon DRAM hurts most
idea: Nantero, Optane and early MRAM died without a market where they beat DRAM on day one. Launch a 125 C-native storage element first in Grade-1 automotive and industrial LPDDR sockets, where silicon DRAM must refresh ~8x faster and derate, and pre-sell to Tier-1s with 10-year supply contracts that fund the fab ramp.
why: Turns the constraint into a price premium (~1.5-3x $/bit tolerated), funds capital intensity from early revenue and builds U.S. volume.

title: IBM's cryogenic dream made cheap with LNG terminal cold
idea: IBM's cryogenic Josephson computer died on refrigeration cost. At 77 K, DRAM access-transistor leakage drops by ~1e5-1e6 and refresh effectively vanishes. Site memory-heavy racks at LNG regasification terminals, which normally dump ~0.8 MJ of cold per kg into seawater, and use a nitrogen loop to hold DRAM pools at 77-100 K.
why: Eliminates refresh power and the refresh bandwidth tax, and lets access transistors use a lower Vt for speed. Cooling comes from waste cold, and leakier dies scrapped today become usable supply.
note: Cryo DRAM known; LNG waste cold siting is the twist but geographically niche.

title: Canon ELTRAN porous-silicon donor wafers reused for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Canon's ELTRAN layer transfer (epitaxy on porous Si, split at the porous layer) lost to Smart Cut. It suits bonded 3D DRAM tiers well: grow each tier epitaxially on porous Si, bond, split, re-porosify the donor and repeat about 20 times.
why: Cuts crystal growth per tier ~20x, and with it demand for Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (a resource chokepoint), making many-tier bonded 3D DRAM affordable (fact 2). Donor wafers are recycled by design.

title: Optane write-off lesson: universal second-life interface on every DRAM die
idea: Intel's Optane exit ended in a large inventory write-down, partly because the dies worked only with one CPU interface. Put a small standardized test-and-reuse port (JTAG-like self-test plus a slow generic protocol) and a wear log on every DRAM die. Dies harvested from retired HBM and DDR modules can then be retested and repackaged into CXL capacity modules.
why: Adds usable supply from retired dies, perhaps 10-20% more bits per year at today's server refresh rates, without new fabs (capital intensity, scarcity).
note: Retired DRAM reuse already happens in CXL; standard port needs vendor/JEDEC adoption.

title: Undo the helium reserve sell-off: a chip-grade helium strategic stock
idea: The U.S. sold its Federal Helium Reserve (completed 2024), so Qatar's 2026 outage hit fabs with no buffer. Re-create a fab-dedicated stock: require 80-90% recapture of chuck-backside and leak-check helium (membrane plus cryogenic recovery) and bank recovered surplus and U.S. field helium in the Cliffside storage under a strategic-stock lease.
why: Helium is small in mass but irreplaceable for wafer cooling; recapture plus a reserve gives multi-year cover against single-region outages that otherwise cost weeks of DRAM output.

title: Buy bankrupt DRAM makers' patent portfolios to arm a U.S. entrant
idea: Qimonda's buried-wordline and 4F2 vertical-channel work, plus Elpida, Z-RAM, T-RAM and Kilopass portfolios, ended up with patent-assertion entities or in drawers after failure. A U.S. entrant (or a DOE-backed pool) buys or exclusively licenses them to gain freedom to operate for buried-wordline, vertical-channel and capacitorless designs on a low-EUV older node.
why: U.S. manufacturability and entry barrier: removes the litigation and royalty stack that blocks new fabs; buys ~20 years of process R&D for well under $1B, shortening time-to-first-wafer by years.
note: Many Qimonda/Elpida-era patents expire around now, eroding value.

title: Pay memory subsidies per gigabyte shipped, not per fab dollar
idea: Capex-first support such as Solyndra's loan guarantee failed by funding plants that never reached competitive cost. Restructure U.S. memory support as a production tax credit per Gb of DRAM-class memory shipped from U.S. fabs, decaying over 10 years, with a bonus per Gb made without EUV layers.
why: Capital efficiency and U.S. manufacturability: money flows to whoever reaches volume and low cost, rewards low-EUV processes, and grows U.S. share from 1-2%.

title: Diablo Memory1 lesson: royalty-free patent pool for memory tiering
idea: Diablo's Memory1 (flash on a DIMM used as memory) died largely from a Netlist patent suit and single-platform qualification. Form a defensive, royalty-free OIN-style patent pool covering flash/CXL memory tiering, page promotion and DIMM buffering so tiering vendors and hyperscalers can ship without existential lawsuit risk.
why: Removes the legal risk that killed tiered-memory products, accelerating adoption of 2-5x cheaper capacity tiers.

title: Approximate MLC storage, fixed: precision-tiered flash cells for KV
idea: Sampson et al.'s approximate MLC storage never shipped because general files cannot tolerate errors. KV caches can: write sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits to SLC-mode pages and low-mantissa bits to QLC-mode pages with relaxed program-verify, raising density and cutting program time for the error-tolerant bits.
why: Offloaded KV in flash at ~2x density with faster writes, so no DRAM is needed for cold KV beyond a small working window.

title: MCM known-good-die curse fixed: contactless near-field wafer test
idea: 1990s multichip modules died of the known-good-die problem, and HBM repeats it because hybrid-bond pads cannot be touched by probe needles (scratches ruin bonding), so dies are bonded half-tested. Add a field of tiny capacitive/inductive near-field couplers in top metal and test each DRAM wafer at full speed, including burn-in and retention, through a matching contactless probe card before any bonding.
why: HBM stack yield (fact 6) and capital: full at-speed known-good-die screening could recover most of the 20-30% stack loss and the scrapped base dies, for <0.5% die area.

title: Cu-Mn self-forming barrier, failed in fine lines, revived for TSVs
idea: Cu-Mn alloy seeds that self-form a MnSiO barrier on anneal were dropped from advanced BEOL because residual Mn raised resistivity in 20 nm lines, a penalty that vanishes in 2-10 um TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and contact plugs. Use Cu-0.5%Mn seed in HBM TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and base-die contact plugs to eliminate Ta/TaN barriers and W plugs; the 2-3 nm self-formed barrier also frees TSV diameter.
why: Removes Ta (conflict-region supply) and W (China ~80%) from the memory interconnect stack and cuts PVD steps (capital) and TSV stress; Cu and Mn only.

title: Silicon-on-AlN failed on bonding; AlN as hybrid-bond dielectric spreads heat
idea: Silicon-on-aluminum-nitride SOI, meant to cure self-heating, died because rough AlN bonded poorly. Hybrid-bond interfaces need only a few hundred nm of dielectric: deposit smooth amorphous AlN (~10-30 W/m-K vs ~1.4 for SiO2) capped with 10 nm of SiCN for bonding chemistry, so every HBM tier gets a lateral heat-spreading plane at each bond line.
why: Thermal limits on taller, faster stacks: claimed 10-20 C lower core-die peaks, fewer refresh-rate doublings (fact 3) and room for more tiers; Al, N, Si and C only.

title: Optane distrust fixed by endurance-as-a-service telemetry warranties
idea: Part of what killed Optane was buyers' fear of wear-out and an opaque, single-vendor reliability story. Fix: sell nonvolatile CXL memory by the write, not the module, with devices streaming per-region wear and corrected-error telemetry, a per-petabyte-written warranty, and pre-emptive module swaps before the uncorrectable rate crosses a contract threshold.
why: De-risks refresh-free nonvolatile tiers for hyperscalers, removing refresh power from the bulk of capacity and moving reliability risk to the party with the data.

title: Richmond fab clause: reversionary option keeps closed fabs warm
idea: When Qimonda's 300 mm fab near Richmond, Virginia closed in 2009, its tools were sold off and the U.S. lost a DRAM fab for good. Fix: every subsidized fab carries a reversionary option, so on closure the government can buy the cleanroom, utilities and tools at depreciated book value, keep them at minimum burn (purge, utilities, skeleton crew), and lease them to a new operator.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: restarting a warm shell takes ~12-18 months and ~30% of greenfield capex, versus 3-5 years and $15B+ for a new fab.

title: Carbon-cluster proximity gettering borrowed from image-sensor dark current
idea: Effect: impurity gettering. C3H5 molecular-ion clusters implanted ~1 um below the array (the CMOS image-sensor technique that cut dark current) form a dense sink that traps Fe, Cu and Ni during thermal steps, pulling midgap metal generation centres away from storage junctions. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 2-5x lower junction leakage tail, the same physics as CIS dark current; one substrate step.
note: Proven CIS technique; DRAM tail is largely GIDL/TAT, so metal gettering gain may be limited.

title: Antifuse weight ROM banks rotate through over-the-air model updates
idea: Freeze automotive perception weights into oxide-breakdown antifuse arrays with in-array MAC. Ship 8 banks and burn one per model release, so each OTA update takes a fresh bank. A broken-down oxide filament is permanent at 125 C.
why: ECUs need no DRAM for weights. Antifuse is 28 nm logic-compatible, U.S.-manufacturable and needs no EUV (fact 4).
note: Antifuse density low; 8 banks of model weights costly area; automotive niche.

title: Random-telegraph-noise dither enables unbiased 2-bit KV caches
idea: Quantize KV values to 2 bits with stochastic rounding, which keeps the expectation unbiased. The random bits come from single-trap random telegraph noise in minimum-size transistors. Trap switching speeds up at 125 C, so the entropy source gets better with heat over the 10-year life.
why: 2-bit KV with near-4-bit accuracy cuts KV memory 8x versus FP16.
note: RTN entropy source unnecessary; 2-bit KV known.

title: Capillary wicking: roll-embossed two-phase cooling film laminated onto memory stacks
idea: Hot-emboss micro-pillar wicks and vapor channels into copper-clad polymer film on R2R lines, then seal and laminate it as an ultra-thin vapor chamber over HBM; capillary pumping returns condensate with no pump.
why: Thermal height limit and refresh (facts 3, 6): 10-20 C lower hot spots allow taller stacks; replaces machined vapor chambers at a fraction of cost.
note: R2R embossed wick laminate; cheaper HBM heat spreading, incremental thermal gain.

title: Thin-oxide tunneling canary cells set each row's refresh interval
idea: Effect: direct/Fowler-Nordheim tunneling plus subthreshold leakage, made deliberately stronger. Each row carries 2-4 canary cells whose access device has a thinner gate oxide and shorter channel, so they fail ~4x earlier than the weakest real cell with the same temperature and voltage dependence. Rows refresh at a long default interval (256 ms+) and drop to a shorter interval only when a periodic check finds a flipped canary.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): ~99% of rows run 4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% bandwidth tax ~3-4x; the canaries track temperature and aging automatically, so no profiling database is needed.

title: Per-tier Seebeck thermopiles let 100-tier stacks refresh by tier
idea: Effect: Seebeck thermoelectric voltage. In a ~100-tier 3D DRAM whose inner tiers run 10-20 K hotter than outer ones, thermocouple pairs formed in the staircase contacts read each tier's temperature with zero bias power; the controller assigns per-tier refresh intervals (cool tiers ~4x longer) and steers hot data to cool tiers.
why: 10x density: without per-tier refresh the hottest tier sets refresh for all 100, a 30-40% bandwidth tax at 3D densities; keeping it under 10% makes a ~100-tier (~10x) stack viable, with thermocouples added to existing staircase steps at near-zero cost.

title: Na: big-capacitor LTPS DRAM on soda-lime glass in idle LCD fabs
idea: Build 1T1C DRAM with low-temperature poly-Si transistors and large planar capacitors on soda-lime glass (SiN barrier against Na+) in depreciated Gen-6/8 LCD lines at 1-2 um rules; a 2.8 m2 Gen-6 panel holds ~1e11 cells (~10 GB after periphery), and panel defect densities that would kill logic are fine because <=1% bad cells are mapped and coded out.
why: Uses already-paid-for display capital instead of $15B fabs (capital intensity) with no high-AR etch (fact 1) and no EUV (fact 4); a bulk-capacity tier for AI servers.
note: ~10 GB per Gen-6 panel implies far above DDR5 $1.48/GB cost; LTPS speed limits it to slow tier.

title: Helium nanocavity gettering layer beneath every storage-node junction
idea: He: implant a low-dose helium layer ~200 nm below the buried-channel access transistors and anneal it into nanocavities whose inner surfaces chemisorb Fe, Cu, Ni and Au, so a gettering sink sits within diffusion range of every storage junction instead of at the wafer backside; the helium used is grams per fab-year, immune to the Qatar outage.
why: Metal deep levels drive the SRH generation behind junction-leakage tail cells (fact 3); proximity gettering could pull the tail in ~1 decade, giving 2-4x longer worst-cell retention.

title: Silicon-on-nothing pocket removes the storage-node junction's bottom area
idea: Si: use an empty-space-in-silicon process (etch a hole array, hydrogen-anneal so silicon migrates and seals a void) to place a vacuum pocket beneath each storage-node diffusion, leaving the junction floating with only its sidewall touching the body.
why: Junction generation leakage scales with depleted area/volume (fact 3); deleting the bottom face cuts that component ~2-5x and stops substrate minority-carrier collection that disturbs neighbor cells.

title: Chlorination plus ligand-exchange thermal ALE for 3D DRAM lateral recess
idea: Periodic-table walk, Cl (17): recess TiN, ZrO2 and Al2O3 laterally inside 3D DRAM tiers by cyclic thermal atomic-layer etching, chlorinating with SOCl2 or BCl3 then removing the surface with TiCl4 or trimethylaluminum ligand exchange, avoiding the HF step of standard thermal ALE.
why: Self-limiting, isotropic, angstrom-precise cavities across 100+ tiers (fact 2 blocker), fluorine-free.

title: Sn: tin-oxo resist doubles as hardmask, leaves as stannane
idea: Vapor-deposit a Sn-oxo-carbon resist, dry-develop it, keep the remaining SnOx as the etch hardmask, then remove it with an H2 plasma that converts tin into volatile SnH4 (the trick used to clean EUV collectors).
why: Water: no spin solvent, TMAH develop, rinse or wet strip on each patterned layer (>10x litho-module water cut) and one fewer hardmask deposition per layer.

title: Helium leak test for heaps: tracer-tagged allocations expose bloat
idea: Borrowing the industrial helium leak test, the allocator stamps each allocation with a 12-bit call-site tracer in spare pointer/tag bits (MTE-style), and a memory-controller sniffer samples which tracer IDs are written but never re-read for N minutes. The fleet-wide profile auto-shrinks caches, caps pools and frees leaked objects at those call sites.
why: Production heaps carry 20-40% never-reused or leaked bytes; finding them by call site with hardware sampling instead of heap dumps recovers ~15-25% DRAM per service at negligible overhead (cost/bit).

title: Cesium clock TTL memory: allocations that expire in hardware
idea: Using a cesium-clock-style global timestamp, allocations made with a TTL (session state, request buffers, cache entries) carry an expiry field in line/page metadata, and the controller sweeps expired lines into a free list with no GC or free() call, faulting cleanly if a stale pointer touches them.
why: Services keep expired session and cache data for minutes to hours because sweeping is costly; hardware expiry trims resident memory 20-40% for TTL-heavy workloads (cost/bit).

title: Xenon strobe multicast: one weight read lights up all chiplets
idea: A xenon flash lights a whole room at once; the HBM base die gets a multicast fabric so one row read of a weight tile is delivered simultaneously to every compute chiplet in the package, and to all batched tenants of the same model, replacing per-chiplet weight copies with one shared copy.
why: With 8-16 consumers per read, DRAM energy per consumed weight bit falls 8-16x, and package weight DRAM shrinks by the replica count (energy, density).

title: S: Sb2S3 phase-change photonic crossbar pools memory across accelerators
idea: Use low-loss antimony-sulfide (Sb2S3) phase-change cells on silicon-nitride waveguides as non-volatile 2x2 switches in a 64x64 optical crossbar between accelerators and memory sleds; a route is set by one heater/laser pulse and then holds with zero static power, reassigning memory capacity per job.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: pooling typically recovers 20-40% of stranded provisioned DRAM; zero hold power makes per-job remapping cheap vs electrical switch fabrics.

title: Si: die-agnostic DDR5 buffer builds RDIMMs from any surplus die
idea: Put a silicon bridge buffer (extended RCD plus data buffers) on a standard DDR5 RDIMM that speaks JEDEC DDR5 to the host but drives LPDDR4X/LPDDR5, DDR4 or downbinned dies behind it, translating timing and bank structure, so modules can be assembled from whatever DRAM die is in surplus.
why: Usable supply with host interface unchanged: mobile and legacy DRAM inventories and mature DDR4 lines become server DDR5 capacity, adding several % of bits to the tightest market segment.

title: Au: right-to-reuse rule stops shredding retired server DIMMs
idea: Policy: require hyperscalers and IT-asset recyclers to route retired DDR4/DDR5 server DIMMs through certified re-test and resale before any gold-recovery shredding, with a per-GB reuse tax credit; reused modules drop into existing DDR slots unchanged.
why: Usable memory supply: retired fleet DRAM is a large stranded pool currently destroyed for grams of gold; reuse could add several % of annual bit supply at near-zero capex.

title: C: carbon co-implant getters point defects at storage-node junctions
idea: Add a shallow substitutional-carbon co-implant (~1e20 cm^-3) at the storage-node contact junction; carbon traps Si interstitials and binds Fe/Cu, preventing the deep-level clusters that create trap-assisted-tunneling hotspots in the depletion region.
why: Attacks the junction-leakage share of the retention tail (fact 3) with an abundant element already used for diffusion control in logic; target 3-10x fewer tail cells at equal Cs.

title: Cu: copper conductive-bridge antifuses give unlimited in-field row remapping
idea: Replace one-time fuses in the repair block with Cu-ion conductive-bridge cells programmable at ~1.5 V in the field, so the controller can remap hundreds of failing rows and columns over life (and undo them), instead of DDR5's handful of post-package-repair slots.
why: Self-healing repair makes weaker arrays acceptable: less test guardband, higher yield and fewer DIMM replacements.
note: Soft PPR plus controller remaps already give field repair; CBRAM integration adds cost.

title: H: Electrolytic hydrogen replaces helium as electrostatic-chuck backside gas
idea: Use on-site PEM-electrolyzed H2 (thermal conductivity 0.18 vs 0.15 W/mK for He) as the low-pressure backside cooling gas in etch and deposition chucks, with leak sensing and dilution exhaust, and deuterium blends where plasma chemistry requires.
why: Eliminates the largest helium use in DRAM fabs using only water and electricity, available anywhere.
note: H2 conductivity comparable; safety and plasma-chemistry interaction need qualification.

title: Au: Gold-finger DIMM deposit-refund law drives memory take-back
idea: Levy a $3-10 refundable deposit per DIMM/SODIMM, like bottle bills, redeemable at certified harvesters whose gold-finger and DRAM resale value fund the program and feed reballing lines.
why: Raises end-of-life memory return rates from <20% toward 70%, creating a steady secondary DRAM supply.
note: Same bottle-bill deposit as I-05037.

title: Zr: Open-source zirconia trench-capacitor DRAM PDK for U.S. foundries
idea: Publish an open PDK and macro compiler for a ZrO2/TiN deep-trench 1T1C DRAM cell on 130-90 nm U.S. foundries, so defense, auto and industrial buyers source companion DRAM domestically.
why: Mature fabs cost ~1/20th of leading-edge; moves legacy demand off scarce leading-edge bits and seeds U.S. DRAM skills.

title: Ga: Abundance-screened bill-of-materials procurement rule for memory
idea: Learning from China's 2023 gallium and germanium export controls, a federal procurement rule scores memory by mass-weighted element supply concentration and gives price preference to non-volatile memories built only from abundant elements.
why: Steers demand and venture money toward chokepoint-free non-volatile memory, cutting systemic supply risk.

title: Solar-cell fixed-charge passivation spacer on the storage junction
idea: Borrow PERC/TOPCon solar-cell field-effect passivation: put a SiNx/AlOx spacer with engineered fixed charge (positive next to the n+ storage node) over the storage-junction surface. The surface stays accumulated, so surface SRH generation and the GIDL fringe field are suppressed.
why: The solar industry cut surface recombination velocity ~100x this way. Here it targets the surface-generation share of junction leakage, aiming for a 3-5x tail reduction with tools already in high-volume solar fabs.
note: Surface generation is only part of the tail; CIS uses similar passivation.

title: Bearing-style selective assembly pairs leaky arrays with tight sense amps
idea: In a CMOS-bonded-array flow, map each array wafer's retention and each periphery wafer's sense-amp offset before hybrid bonding. Then pair dies by measurement, as bearing makers match graded balls to races, so the leakiest arrays get the lowest-offset sense amps.
why: Retention spec equals charge loss vs sense margin. Matched pairing could lift the worst-case refresh interval ~1.5-2x and raise sellable yield without any process change.

title: Cleanroom-airlock double gate splits voltage across two stacked channels
idea: Put two independent gates on the same vertical pillar with a floating middle node, like a cleanroom airlock with two doors. In hold, the middle node settles mid-rail, so each channel sees half the Vds.
why: Subthreshold (DIBL) and GIDL leakage are exponential in Vds. The stack effect gives 10-100x lower off-current at zero added footprint in a vertical cell.

title: Pre-printed forms: sea-of-gates periphery personalized by two i-line metal masks
idea: Like printers who stock pre-printed letterhead and add only the name, fab one universal 180 nm periphery master with gate-array sites for pumps, decoders and control. Interface width, protocol (DDR/LPDDR/CXL-lite) and redundancy are personalized with just two metal masks, the 1990s ASIC gate-array method.
why: Cuts per-variant mask sets and NRE ~80-90%, so small U.S. fabs can serve many memory SKUs from one wafer inventory.

title: Tailor's marker nesting: shape dies to harvest wafer-edge silicon
idea: Garment cutters nest pattern pieces to minimize scrap; design mature-node memory as small self-contained hexagonal banks that plasma dicing can cut in any outline, so partial wafer-edge regions yield sellable small dies.
why: Recovers ~5-10% more bits per wafer from existing capacity with zero new fab, raising usable supply.

title: Inventory carrying cost: bill cold resident memory like warehouse stock
idea: Manufacturers price inventory by its carrying cost. Clouds and internal chargeback bill memory by touched versus untouched GB-hours (taken from page access bits): untouched pages cost 3-5x more, and pages released to a compressed tier earn a credit. Teams finally get a price signal to shed cold memory.
why: Flat per-GB pricing hides the cold-page fraction (often 30-50%); a carrying-cost price signal could cut fleet DRAM 20-30% through behavior rather than hardware.

title: Double-stitched hot rows halve activations per physical copy
idea: Tailors double-stitch seams at stress points; for read-hot rows the controller keeps a duplicate in a distant subarray and alternates or randomises activations between copies (writes go to both), so each physical row sees 1/k of the activation rate.
why: Raises the effective hammer threshold k-fold for read-mostly hot data such as weights and page tables without counters or neighbour refresh (fact 9); the twin also backs up a retention-failed copy.

title: Kintsugi spares: repair rows built from a stronger cell technology
idea: Kintsugi mends pottery with gold so the repair is the strongest part; instead of spare rows from the same weak array, put repair capacity as SRAM or oxide gain-cell rows on the hybrid-bonded base die, so failed or weak rows remap to cells with no retention tail and no hammer sensitivity.
why: Frees the 2-5% of array area spent on in-array redundancy and gives repairs that never fail again, so more retention-tail rows can be retired (fact 3).

title: Power-by-the-hour: lease memory bits, take modules back, redeploy
idea: Rolls-Royce sells engine thrust-hours, not engines. Memory makers keep ownership of modules and bill per GB-hour, with telemetry from the SPD/CXL controller. Modules are reclaimed, re-screened and redeployed across customers as one fleet over 2-3 service lives.
why: Usable supply: lifetime bit-hours per wafer rise ~1.5-2x and shortages smooth out. Makers gain aftermarket revenue that funds new capacity.

title: Two-threshold sensing turns every read into a retention health check
idea: Ideal result: refresh only the bits that are truly about to fail. Every Nth activation, the SA stripe fires against a second, offset reference that flags cells whose signal is within 30% of failing; the controller logs those rows for faster refresh and stretches refresh for the healthy majority.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3): measures the leakage tail in the field instead of guarding for it; 60-80% fewer refreshes, reclaiming most of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Short local wordlines so abundant TiN replaces tungsten fill
idea: Ideal: a wordline with zero resistance. Work backward: make resistance irrelevant by splitting each buried wordline into 64-cell segments driven by local sub-wordline drivers placed under the array (CMOS-under-array), so all-TiN or doped-poly gates suffice and WF6 tungsten fill disappears.
why: Tungsten ~80% China, WF6 also consumes fluorine; segment RC falls ~16-64x (L squared), tolerating a 5-10x more resistive abundant conductor for ~3-5% driver area under the array.

title: Ashable carbon capacitor mold removed dry, ending pillar collapse
idea: Ideal: the capacitor mold vanishes without touching the pillars. Closest: build the pillar mold from amorphous carbon instead of oxide, so after electrode ALD it is removed by an O2/N2 plasma ash rather than an HF dip-out, eliminating capillary pillar collapse, supercritical-CO2 drying and the nitride support-mesh lithography.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR can rise from ~70 toward ~100 without collapse (Cs +30-40%), deletes one mask (support mesh) plus wet/dry steps, and removes a top yield-excursion source.

title: Hardware interning engine stores each string or record once
idea: IFR: every distinct value exists once. Closest with mature-node Al/Ti logic: a memory-side engine hash-conses immutable strings, JSON nodes and tuples at allocation, returning a refcounted handle to an existing copy, with 64-bit hash probes done near memory.
why: String and record duplication is 10-30% of heap in web, log and analytics services.

title: Ephemeral-memory cloud SKU: cheap RAM that forgets after 50 ms
idea: Ideal: users pay only for memory during the instant they use it. Closest achievable: a cloud instance class exposes a large never-refreshed 'ephemeral memory' region whose contents are guaranteed only 50 ms after the last write, priced ~40% lower, with SDKs for streaming ETL, video, AI activations and network buffers that fit the contract.
why: Zero refresh power on the ephemeral tier, and providers can fill it with DRAM dies that fail standard retention bins, salvaging 5-10% more usable supply from existing output.
note: 50 ms guarantee is below the 64 ms refresh window, so little salvage of weak dies; refresh savings modest.

title: Hot-row SRAM shock absorber caps physical activations
idea: Ideal: no physical row is ever activated more than a few hundred times per window. Closest: each bank holds a 4-8 row SRAM buffer that captures any row activated more than 64 times in a window; later hits are served from SRAM, so the physical row is never re-opened and cannot hammer its neighbors.
why: Fact 9: removes hammering at the source and cuts hit latency; ~1% die area and no TRR refresh overhead.
note: 4-8 entries per bank are defeated by many-sided hammer patterns.

title: ML-grade memory class with declared raw BER
idea: Ideal: fabs build cells exactly as weak as the workload can tolerate. Closest: JEDEC/OCP define an ML-grade memory class that declares raw BER and retention distribution and mandates host-side strong ECC, so fabs can relax the capacitor target from ~5 fF to ~3 fF and ship parts that today fail retention screens.
why: Fact 1: relaxing Cs ~40% lowers pillar aspect ratio from ~70:1 toward ~45:1, cutting etch difficulty and yield loss while adding supply.

title: 180 nm RAS hub chip lets leading-edge dies ship raw
idea: Ideal: the DRAM die is pure array and all reliability logic is free. Closest: a buffer chip built in a fully depreciated 180 nm US fab sits on each DIMM and performs page-level BCH, a bad-row remap CAM and hammer tracking for 8-16 dies, so memory makers can drop on-die ECC and ship dies through relaxed retention screens.
why: Facts 7 and 3 plus U.S. manufacturability: moves ~5-10% of die area off leading-edge silicon onto 180 nm tools and raises sellable yield.

title: Hammer-proof legacy tier for page tables and keys
idea: Ideal: hammering cannot hurt what matters. Closest: page tables, kernel structures and crypto keys live in a small 180 nm DRAM or SRAM tier whose wide cell spacing makes it physically immune to row hammer, so the dense main memory can drop costly TRR to cheap probabilistic neighbor refresh backed by ordinary ECC.
why: Fact 9: removes the privilege-escalation risk that forces aggressive mitigation; recovers ~5-10% of main-memory bandwidth and refresh energy.
note: Protects privilege structures but not user-data integrity attacks.

title: RAM-mileage standard: GB-per-request ratings in public procurement
idea: Ideal: software that needs no memory at all. Closest achievable: an Energy-Star-style rating of memory footprint (GB-seconds per transaction or per token) required in government and hyperscaler procurement, with annual CAFE-like improvement targets.
why: Usable supply from the demand side: 15-30% footprint cut from software bloat equals a new fab's output.

title: Digital-twin DRAM fab flight school for process engineers
idea: Ideal: experienced fab engineers available instantly. Closest achievable: a national academy runs a full-fab simulator that replays real, anonymized excursion data from partners and certifies yield engineers in 6 months, the way pilots train on simulators.
why: Talent bottleneck for U.S. fabs: roughly halves the learning curve of a ramp.

title: Freedom-to-operate DRAM built only from expired patents
idea: Ideal: technology with no owner. Closest achievable: design a DDR4/LPDDR4-compatible part using only expired-patent cell, stacked-capacitor and sense-amp techniques, backed by a formal freedom-to-operate audit, so an entrant faces no royalty stack or injunctions.
why: Entry barrier and cost: removes a ~3-5% royalty stack and injunction risk at some performance cost.
note: Design-around using only expired art; JEDEC-essential patents and performance gap remain.

title: Significance-aware HBM lanes: compact cells for bf16 mantissa bits
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): DQ lanes and bursts stay identical. Because inference stacks lay out bf16/fp8 tensors with fixed bit positions per DQ lane, build core dies whose arrays behind sign/exponent lanes keep full-size capacitors while arrays behind low-mantissa lanes use half-height capacitors with relaxed retention (raw BER ~1e-4), enabled by an existing mode-register write and defaulting to full reliability.
why: ~25-35% less capacitor height/area per stack for AI inference where LSB errors are tolerable (density, cost per bit) with an identical interface; depends on controller address and lane mapping.
note: Approximate DRAM for DNNs known; cutting capacitor height yields well under 30% cost per bit.

title: Idle power budget of 1 mW per GB: in-DRAM compaction before self-refresh
idea: Limit: in self-refresh the die may refresh only the rows it truly needs. On self-refresh entry, an on-die engine applies zero, pattern and base-delta compression to each subarray, packs the data into fewer subarrays with in-DRAM row copy, and stops refreshing the vacated subarrays. It decompresses on exit.
why: Fact 3: AI and server data compress ~2-3x, so self-refresh energy falls ~50-65% for idle devices.

title: No column decoder: CCD-style shift-out of the latched row
idea: Limit: no column decoder and no global column-select lines. After sensing, the sense amps are linked by two pass transistors each into a dynamic shift register that clocks the row out serially toward taps placed every 256 bits at the bank edge, like a CCD image sensor; random column access becomes 'shift N from the nearest tap'.
why: Periphery (fact 7): column decoders plus CSL wiring take ~5-8% of the die and one metal layer; streaming readout suits AI tensor fetches.
note: Random column access pays shift latency.

title: Ferroelectric-imbalanced sense latches keep open rows across power loss
idea: Constraint: open pages must survive an instant power cut with zero dump time. Two small HZO capacitors on each SA's internal nodes are polarized by the latched value in a ~10 ns pulse on power-fail detect (not on every activation, to spare endurance); when power returns, their remanent imbalance biases the latch so it re-resolves to the same value, recovering ~256 kB of open-row state.
why: Zero-latency persistence for in-flight rows (nvSRAM idea at row-buffer scale); complements a slower full-array backup.

title: Microwatt refresh island: coin cell keeps IGZO memory alive for years
idea: Constraint: data survives mains loss, with no NV material. Pair hour-retention IGZO DRAM with a tiny always-on periphery island (a ~2 uW clock, counter and row walker) that refreshes one row every ~1 ms from a 20 mAh lithium cell or harvested trickle, while all other periphery is cut off.
why: Quasi-NV with full DRAM endurance and speed; a 32 Gb die needs only ~0.4 uW of refresh, so the cell lasts ~2 years without ferroelectric wear or backup dumps.

title: Brownfield DRAM fabs on retired coal plants
idea: Imposed scarcity: no new water rights, no new transmission and no greenfield permit time. Site fabs on retiring coal plants that already hold industrial water allocations, cooling reservoirs, high-voltage interconnects and rail, and convert boiler halls into utility buildings.
why: Fab water (~10-20 ML/day) and 100-300 MW of power are often the binding permits; reuse could cut 1-2 years and ~$1B in utilities from a U.S. fab schedule.

title: Helium-free fab: hydrogen-neon chuck cooling and hydrogen-tracer leak checks
idea: Constraint: zero helium deliveries. Switch electrostatic-chuck backside cooling in high-AR etch and deposition from He to H2/Ne blends with redesigned micro-groove chucks that restore gas conductance, replace He leak testing with 5% H2/N2 tracer sniffers, and membrane-recapture any legacy He.
why: Removes exposure to the Qatar helium outage (~30% of supply) that can idle etch-heavy DRAM lines; mainly supply-risk removal, ~1-2% gas cost saving.
note: Supply-risk removal, small cost gain.

title: Revive IBM-heritage deep-trench eDRAM as hot-rated standalone memory
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: license the existing SOI deep-trench eDRAM process (~25-40 fF cells) held by a U.S. foundry and productize it as standalone 125 C DRAM in its New York fabs, with no new tool or process development.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: large-Cs trenches meet hot retention immediately, near-zero new capex, months not years to first product.

title: Line-level page meshing in the memory controller
idea: Imposed limit: no physical page may be less than 90% occupied. The controller keeps a 64 B-line indirection table, so two half-empty pages whose live lines do not overlap merge into one physical page without any change to virtual addresses; this brings Mesh-style compaction to unmanaged C/C++ heaps.
why: Fragmentation wastes 15-30% of heap memory in long-running services; meshing in hardware recovers most of it transparently.
note: Hardware Mesh: 64B indirection table costs metadata/TLB-like lookups; known Mesh allocator art moved into controller.

title: Memory insurance: fleets sized for median, peaks covered by pooled policy
idea: Imposed limit: servers are bought with P50 memory, not P99. Tenants buy 'memory insurance' units; on a peak, a rack-level compressed far-memory reserve plus eviction of preemptible jobs pays out, priced actuarially from fleet telemetry so the operator carries the statistical risk.
why: Provisioning for peak leaves 30-40% of DRAM idle; insurance-style pooling can cut installed DRAM ~20-30%.

title: The sensor is the frame buffer: pixel charge held for on-demand readout
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a large-area printed oxide-TFT backplane, like those in flat-panel X-ray detectors, integrates each frame and holds it as pixel charge for tens of milliseconds. The host reads out only the regions it wants; pixels it never requests are never digitized or written to DRAM.
why: Removes the ingest frame buffer in high-resolution scanners and in document, industrial and X-ray imaging; DRAM per channel drops ~5-20x.
note: X-ray flat panels already integrate and hold charge; ROI readout is known. Niche scanner segment.

title: Contactless inductive probing qualifies every die before stacking
idea: Scarcity: nothing may touch the die before bonding, since probe marks ruin hybrid-bond surfaces. Each die carries an on-die coil array and test controller; a coil probe card powers it inductively and runs full-speed tests wirelessly, so only pristine known-good dies enter the stack.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6, 20-30%): stack yield is the product of die yields; complete KGD screening with no pad damage recovers most of it.

title: Partial-good HBM: channel-isolated stacks sold and run degraded
idea: Rule: a dead channel must not kill a stack. Each HBM pseudo-channel gets independent power gating and fuse-isolatable TSV groups, so stacks with failed channels ship as 75% or 50% capacity SKUs, and channels that fail in the field are fenced off instead of retiring the stack.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss as sellable bits and lengthens field life.

title: Every GB sold must come back: DRAM module deposit-refund
idea: Self-imposed limit: no DRAM leaves the loop. A per-GB deposit at sale is refunded when modules are returned to certified reclaimers, which guarantees feedstock for die harvesting and cascade reuse.
why: Reuse supply: return rates rise from under 20% to over 80%, turning e-waste into a steady secondary bit supply.
note: Same bottle-bill deposit as I-05037.

title: No silicon wafer: substrate-neutral CHIPS grants paid per verified bit-capacity
idea: Forced limit: subsidies cannot favour Si. A grant tranche pays per verified Gb of monthly capacity added per dollar of capex, open to glass, foil, SiC and disk lines, with milestones audited by third-party benchmark.
why: Capital: steers public money to the cheapest bits per dollar rather than incumbent process paths.

title: No silicon wafer: multi-project panel shuttles for memory startups
idea: Forced limit: startups cannot afford a wafer lot. A panel foundry runs shared Gen 6 glass shuttles where 100 or more startups each get a tile of oxide-memory process, at about 1/100 of a mask set and lot.
why: Capital: cuts prototype cost from millions to tens of thousands of dollars and speeds non-Si memory innovation.

title: Etch-compensated graded tier stack: uniform lateral recess by composition grading
idea: 3D DRAM sets each cell's channel and capacitor length by a lateral recess from a vertical hole or slit, and Lam notes that recess sizes vary along the stack because the etchant depletes with depth. Instead of fighting that with chemistry, pre-compensate at deposition: ramp each tier's sacrificial composition with depth (Ge fraction in SiGe, Si/N ratio and hydrogen content in SiN, or boron level in B3-06 layers) so the intrinsic etch rate rises where etchant supply falls. Calibrate the profile once per stack recipe from per-tier TEM; the only tool knob is a gas-flow ramp. Finish with a few tens of lateral atomic-layer-etch cycles to trim the last nanometres uniformly.
why: Recess spread +-12.5% -> +-2.5%: 8% smaller cell pitch along the recess and 11% higher worst-case Cs at 64 tiers; or ~2x taller deck (~130 vs ~66 tiers) per hole etch at equal uniformity, halving decks and HAR etches.

title: Hydrogen-lean batch-furnace mold for oxide 3D DRAM
idea: NAND-style oxide 3D DRAM needs a 32-128-pair SiO2/SiN mold; single-wafer PECVD films carry ~3-25 at.% hydrogen, and hydrogen drives IGZO Vt drift (H-doping under PBTI, which imec cut ~30x with an H+O anneal). With the periphery on a separate bonded wafer, the cell wafer's mold can be made hot: deposit the alternating stack in a batch LPCVD furnace (100-150 wafers per load, ~4% H in LPCVD SiN, <1% in high-temperature oxide), then out-gas it at 800-900 C before any oxide channel is deposited (for example by Kioxia-style SiN->IGZO replacement). Add per-tier ALD Al2O3 hydrogen barriers around the replacement channels and finish with an O-rich anneal instead of forming gas.
why: Hydrogen reservoir next to each channel 4-8x smaller (PECVD SiN 4.8e16 -> LPCVD 1.1e16 H/cm2 per 30 nm tier, or 5.9e15 for oxide), relaxing the fraction allowed to reach the channel for a 20 mV (3-bit) budget from 3 ppm to 13-24 ppm; mold deposition at ~11 wafer-minutes per 64-pair stack.

title: Adiabatic refresh: recycle bitline and wordline charge with stepwise tanks or piezo-MEMS resonators
idea: During refresh (and optionally background activates), the VARY and VPP rails feeding a bank are ramped rather than fixed. The ramp comes from either (a) N-step tank-capacitor banks (stepwise charging) or (b) a resonant LC whose inductor is a compact AlN piezoelectric MEMS resonator or a package inductor, as in adiabatic or reversible logic. The sense amplifier makes its regenerative decision with a small non-adiabatic kick, then the bitline swing to VARY or 0 follows the ramped rails, and precharge returns charge to the tanks instead of shorting it. Wordlines (3 V, pumped at ~45% efficiency) are ramped the same way. No cell change is needed.
why: Refresh energy per bit falls 2.4-3.2x (refresh-only 29.8 fJ to ~9-13 fJ), from ~12 mW to ~4 mW per 16Gb die, with no new cell and no new materials.

title: 77 K oxide MLC gain-cell stage for cryogenic and superconducting computers
idea: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain cells (no capacitor) sit in BEOL tiers on a 77 K cryo-CMOS periphery wafer. At 77 K, oxide-cell leakage collapses (8,000 s reported for IGZO 2T0C) and threshold drift (PBTI, hydrogen motion) is thermally frozen. Si subthreshold swing falls to ~15-20 mV/decade, so periphery and wordlines run at ~0.4 / 1.0 V, and Cu resistance drops several-fold. Together these make 3-4 bits/cell with write-verify realistic. The stage links to 4 K superconducting logic through the thermal-break link in imec's architecture.
why: Array energy x0.13 (0.78 vs 5.9 pJ per useful bit); refresh cut ~1e5x; 3-4 bits/cell gives 1.2-1.6x 1-beta density per tier, ~17,000x the density of the best 4 K superconducting memory array.

title: Superconducting kinetic-inductance memory with frequency-multiplexed readout (4 K)
idea: Each cell is a NbN (or similar) nanowire loop whose kinetic inductance (~70 pH per square) holds a persistent current; one flux quantum is one bit. Heater cryotrons (hTrons) or nanocryotrons drive a branch normal to write and to read. Row-column arrays exist (MIT and NIST). The twist: each column's sense element is a superconducting resonator at its own frequency on a shared feedline (MKID-style), so thousands of columns read out through one coax and 4 K wiring heat drops sharply.
why: Intrinsic energy per operation is ~1e-20-1e-17 J (I*Phi0 ~2-6e-20 J), against ~fJ for CMOS. Density, however, is only 2.6e-5 Gb/mm2 today (1/17,000 of DDR5) and ~0.005 Gb/mm2 at best (1/90): an L1/L2-class memory for SFQ logic, not a DRAM replacement.

title: Swap capacitor electrons for flux quantum in kinetic-inductance nanowire loop
idea: At 4 K, a NbN or NbTiN nanowire loop whose kinetic inductance is ~100x its geometric inductance stores one flux quantum in under 1 um2. It is written and read by nanocryotron (nTron) gates instead of large Josephson junctions.
why: Zero static power, ~aJ writes and no refresh for superconducting and quantum processors, which then need no room-temperature DRAM; ~10x denser than SFQ memory built on geometric inductance.
note: Same KI nanowire loop memory.

title: Substitute raw data storage with leakage-minimizing per-row polarity coding
idea: Substitute raw data with a per-row inversion flag chosen at write time so most cells sit in their discharged, non-leaking state (true-cell/anti-cell layout included). The row's charged-cell count is stored, and rows with few charged cells are refreshed at a relaxed rate.
why: On average halves the number of cells exposed to leakage; with ECC margin, 1.5-2x less refresh from a pure controller/DRAM-logic change.

title: Substitute beamline implant with self-assembled monolayer doping on 3D channels
idea: Substitute ion implantation (whose plasma flood guns run on argon or xenon) with monolayer doping. Phosphorus- or boron-bearing molecules self-assemble on exposed Si sidewalls from solution, are capped with oxide, and are driven in by semiconductor diode-laser spike heating, forming a conformal, damage-free, sub-5 nm junction even on the lateral channels of 3D DRAM tiers.
why: No implant damage, which removes a main source of tail-leakage traps, and conformal doping of stacked lateral transistors, a 3D DRAM blocker.

title: Substitute hydrogen-passivated oxide channels with HF-vapor fluorine passivation
idea: Substitute hydrogen, a shallow donor and instability source in oxide semiconductors, with fluorine: oxide-channel access transistors are annealed in anhydrous HF vapor diluted in N2 instead of CF4/Ar plasma. The fluorine fills oxygen vacancies and replaces mobile hydrogen.
why: Fewer subgap states and no hydrogen drift give low, stable off-current (~10x less drift-induced leakage), allowing longer refresh intervals for oxide-channel cells.

title: Controller-side remap tables replace on-die fuse redundancy
idea: Substitute on-die laser/e-fuse banks and redundancy address comparators with a per-device bad-row/bad-column table held by the memory controller (like an SSD FTL), filled at test and refreshed during field scrubbing.
why: Periphery area and yield: removes ~3-5% of die area for fuses and compare logic, and finer-grained repair raises yield on immature nodes.
note: ArchShield-style controller fault maps are prior art.

title: Keyed Feistel scrambler in decoder randomizes physical row adjacency
idea: Substitute the fixed logical-to-physical row map with a tiny keyed Feistel permutation in the row predecoder, re-keyed each refresh epoch with background migration, so attackers cannot know which physical rows neighbor their aggressors.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): defeats targeted many-sided hammering at a few hundred gates per bank instead of large counter tables.

title: Sputtered IGZO thin-film decoders stacked above the cell array
idea: Substitute crystalline-silicon row decoders with sputtered IGZO TFT decoders built at <=350 C on top of the array (ALD HfO2 gate, Mo source/drain). A university nanofab can demonstrate a 64-row decoder over a MIM-cap test array with i-line lithography.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): moving decode above the array reclaims ~10-15% of die; low-temperature BEOL process, no EUV.
note: Oxide-TFT periphery above array is actively researched.

title: Infiltrated block-copolymer dots replace EUV pillar-hole patterning
idea: Substitute EUV contact/pillar patterning with self-assembly: PS-b-P2VP cylinders form a hexagonal lattice at 20-28 nm pitch inside coarse ArF-dry guide trenches, 3 cycles of sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O) turn P2VP domains into AlOx hard-mask dots, PS is O2-ashed and the pattern transferred with Cl2/HBr.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): sub-20 nm dense pillar arrays without EUV; SIS supplies fluorine-free etch selectivity (silicon-containing BCPs would need CF4).
note: BCP DSA with SIS hardmasks is demonstrated research; defectivity has blocked adoption.

title: Water-droplet self-alignment with alkylsilane rings replaces precision die placement
idea: Substitute high-precision pick-and-place for die-to-wafer DRAM stacking with capillary self-alignment: a water droplet on each hydrophilic bond site pulls the coarsely dropped die into ~0.2 um registration, the surrounding hydrophobic ring made from octadecyltrichlorosilane or plasma-polymerized HMDSO instead of the usual fluorinated FDTS.
why: Stacking capital and throughput (fact 6): parallel, tool-light alignment for thousands of dies per minute, enabling finer hybrid-bond pitch per dollar.

title: Substitute robotic pick-and-place with capillary fluidic self-alignment for die bonding
idea: Dispense a water droplet on a hydrophilic bond site ringed by hydrophobic SAM; a roughly placed DRAM die (+/-50 um) is pulled into <0.5 um alignment by surface tension in milliseconds, the water evaporates, and oxide/Cu hybrid bonding follows. Precision comes from physics, so a coarse gantry can drop >10,000 dies per hour.
why: Fact 6 (HBM stacking tax): hybrid bonders run ~1-2k UPH at $3-5M each; 5-10x throughput cuts stacking capex and misalignment yield loss.
note: Water-droplet die self-alignment already demonstrated (Tohoku, CEA).

title: Substitute ion implanters with molecular monolayer doping and in-situ epitaxy
idea: Replace most of DRAM's ~20-30 implant steps with self-assembled dopant-bearing molecular monolayers (boron or phosphorus esters) that are capped and spike-annealed, plus selective in-situ-doped epitaxy for source/drain. Dose is set by the molecular footprint and coats 3D pillars that line-of-sight implants cannot reach.
why: Capital: removes many implanters and implant masks; conformal, damage-free junctions narrow the junction-leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Substitute litho-etch pairs with area-selective bottom-up deposition
idea: Use small-molecule or SAM inhibitors that adsorb only on dielectric so ALD grows metal (or dielectric) only where wanted, forming landing pads and capacitor bottom contacts self-aligned to underlying features without a lithography and etch pair. Selectivity loss is reset with periodic deposition-etch supercycles.
why: Removes 2-4 edge-placement-limited masks and their etch/clean steps per wafer and raises overlay yield in the dense 6F2 contacts (fact 4).

title: Swap replicated cluster datasets for threads that migrate to data
idea: Substitute moving data with moving computation. On a remote access, a thread's ~200-byte context hops to the node that owns the data instead of the data being fetched or cached locally, so graph and sparse datasets are stored exactly once across the cluster.
why: Distributed graph analytics keeps 2-5x ghost and replica copies. Single-copy storage cuts cluster DRAM 2-3x for those workloads.

title: Swap small tokenizers for vocabulary transplants that shrink KV per text
idea: Substitute a 32k-token vocabulary with a 200k+ one tuned to code and multilingual text: new embeddings are initialized from compositions of old-token embeddings, then a short fine-tune follows. The same document becomes fewer tokens, so fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory scales with token count; 25-40% fewer tokens for code and non-English text cuts the KV cache proportionally on every request.

title: Swap declared field widths for profile-narrowed fields with overflow escape
idea: Substitute programmer-declared widths with observed widths. A profile-guided compiler pass finds struct fields and arrays whose values fit fewer bits (64-bit ints below 2^16, integral doubles), re-lays them narrow with hot/cold structure splitting, and adds an escape bit that boxes rare outliers into a side table.
why: Data-heavy C/C++/Rust services often waste 30-50% of struct bytes, so heaps shrink 1.3-1.8x on unchanged DDR.

title: Swap regional peak provisioning for follow-the-sun memory-heavy scheduling
idea: Substitute local peaks with a global flat curve. Memory-hungry, latency-tolerant jobs (batch analytics, embedding builds, offline inference, evals) are checkpointed and moved to regions in their local night, when interactive services leave DRAM idle.
why: Diurnal swings leave 30-40% of DRAM idle at night. Filling those troughs lets fleets buy ~15-25% less DRAM for the same work, with no hardware change.
note: Data gravity and migration cost limit gains; carbon-aware variants exist.

title: Charge-recycling bus: adjacent lines trade charge instead of dumping it
idea: Substitute rail-to-rail drivers with series-stacked voltage domains across a wide HBM bus: charge dumped by a falling line in one domain recharges a rising line in the next, and resonant LC tanks recycle clock-line energy.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: interface CV^2 energy down 2-4x at the same swing, shrinking HBM PHY share of accelerator power.

title: Silicon-core vias: trench-isolated die silicon replaces copper TSV fill
idea: Substitute copper-filled TSVs with pillars of the die's own heavily doped silicon, isolated by an oxide-filled annular deep trench, so there is no copper CTE mismatch and the stress keep-out around each via largely disappears.
why: Fact 6: keep-out zones are a big part of TSV area; removing Cu stress shrinks them several-fold and drops Cu plating/CMP steps; suited to many slow parallel lanes.
note: Known (Silex Sil-Via); high resistance limits to slow lanes.

title: Substitute laser fuse repair with in-field cuckoo remap in HBM base die
idea: Replace one-shot fuse row repair with a 64-byte-granular cuckoo-hash remap table in the HBM logic base die, backed by spare rows, that is rewritten in the field whenever ECC sees a recurring error, so dies with 10x more defects than today's repair budget still ship.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): recovering half of the lost stacks raises effective HBM supply ~10-15% with no new wafers.

title: Substitute hours of factory retention testing with in-field learning
idea: Ship dies with only basic test and fast-refresh guard bands; the controller profiles retention per row over the first weeks of service at real temperature and then relaxes refresh row by row.
why: Capital/test cost (fact 4): retention test is a large share of DRAM test time and tester capex; removing it cuts back-end cost ~5-10% and frees tester capacity for supply.

title: Substitute victim refresh with an in-die hot-row cache absorbing aggressors
idea: Replace 'refresh the neighbors' with 'stop hammering': a small SRAM row cache per bank catches rows activated more than N times in a window, so further accesses hit the cache and the array wordline stops toggling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) plus energy: removes hammer stress at the source and saves activation energy on hot rows ~20-30%.

title: Substitute fixed-rate ECC with time-since-write graded ECC for NV
idea: NV data is first stored with a light code; as a line stays unwritten (cold), a background engine re-encodes it with stronger codes because retention loss grows with time and unpowered periods; an orderly shutdown re-encodes all lines to the strongest tier.
why: Allows low-barrier, fast, low-energy NV cells (weak retention) with ECC overhead paid only on cold data; ~2x write-energy savings on hot data.
note: Retention-aware ECC known from NAND/PCM.

title: Substitute blocking ECC decode with speculative use of raw NV data
idea: Let the CPU consume raw NV read data immediately while a strong ECC decoder (needed for weak NV cells) checks in parallel; on a detected error the pipeline rolls back like a branch mispredict.
why: Hides 5-20 ns of strong-ECC latency so weak, cheap NV cells meet the 10-100 ns DRAM-class target.

title: Substitute new dies with remanufactured dies from retired server DIMMs
idea: Swap virgin DRAM for remanufactured DRAM: robotic de-soldering lines pull dies off decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs, re-ball them, run retention/row-hammer/BIST screens and re-mount them on new PCBs sold in warranty tiers.
why: Raises usable supply without wafers; hyperscalers retire ~tens of EB of DDR4/DDR5 yearly, and recovering even 20% adds several % of annual bit supply at ~30-50% of new cost per bit.

title: Substitute proprietary cell IP with an open DRAM PDK for mature foundries
idea: Swap closed DRAM cell know-how for OpenDRAM: a government-funded open-source eDRAM/gain-cell library, sense amps and compilers qualified on mature U.S. foundry nodes (90-22 nm), so any foundry can sell memory.
why: Attacks U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share) by turning existing logic fabs into memory suppliers for embedded and edge demand, freeing commodity DRAM for servers.

title: Logic-fab BEOL finger capacitors as DRAM storage nodes
idea: Combine the metal-oxide-metal finger capacitors that every logic back-end already offers with BEOL oxide-semiconductor access transistors, so a standard logic interconnect stack (interdigitated M3-M8 lines) becomes the storage capacitor field. No special capacitor module, high-AR etch or memory fab is needed: any U.S. logic fab can print DRAM-class memory above its own logic.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: uses existing domestic back-end tooling with zero new capex; density is ~1/3 of commodity DRAM but the memory sits on-die (fact 5).
note: MOM capacitors give only fF per um2, so density is ~100x below DRAM, not one third.

title: Work-function-imprinted antiferroelectric ZrO2 nonvolatile cell
idea: Combine antiferroelectric ZrO2's double hysteresis (fatigue-resistant, 1e11+ cycles) with asymmetric electrodes, a TiN bottom and a high-work-function MoO3-capped top, whose built-in field shifts one AFE loop to straddle 0 V. The film then holds two remanent states at zero bias like a ferroelectric but switches through the gentler field-induced AFE transition.
why: Zero refresh with endurance beyond HZO FeRAM; a nonvolatile 1T1C at DRAM-like ~1 V using no tungsten, ruthenium or platinum.
note: Work-function-shifted AFE loops for nonvolatility already published (NaMLab); still destructive read.

title: Liquid-nitrogen immersed DRAM racks where retention outlasts data
idea: Combine LN2 immersion cooling (already used for HTS cables and extreme overclocking) with commodity DRAM pools: at 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by many orders of magnitude, stretching retention from 64 ms to hours, so refresh is simply switched off. Cryo also speeds transistors ~20% and cuts wire resistance several-fold.
why: Zero refresh power and 10-20% bandwidth recovered; cooling overhead (~10 W input per W removed at 77 K) must be amortized at disaggregated memory-pool scale.

title: Compressed packing fills freed rows with leak-aligned padding
idea: The controller compresses pages, packs them into fewer rows, and writes the freed rows entirely with each cell type's leak-direction value (0 for true cells, 1 for anti-cells). A per-row flag marks those rows refresh-exempt until reallocated.
why: With ~2x compressibility, 40-50% of rows need no refresh, cutting refresh energy ~40%, and the same packing also yields capacity.

title: Compiler tensor liveness wired into per-row refresh skip
idea: The ML compiler already knows every tensor's lifetime. It tags buffers whose last read comes within the guaranteed retention window (activations in the decode loop, gradient staging, temp scratch), and the controller sets per-row no-refresh bits until they are freed.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy fall in proportion to the ephemeral share of the footprint, often 30-60% in training and inference.
note: Close to RANA-style lifetime-aware refresh for accelerators.

title: Retention-binned page allocator matches data lifetime to row strength
idea: Profile each row's retention class at test and store the map in SPD. The OS places frequently rewritten data in weak rows and long-lived data in strong rows, each class refreshed at its own rate.
why: Multi-rate refresh is normally capped by weak rows holding long-lived data. Matching them removes that cap and cuts refresh operations 70-80%.

title: Oscillator timed by real DRAM cells clocks refresh
idea: Build a relaxation oscillator whose timing element is a group of real array cells (same capacitor and access transistor) discharging to a threshold; its period tracks actual retention across temperature, voltage and process and directly sets each bank's refresh interval.
why: Refresh (fact 3): replaces the worst-case 64 ms plus temperature bins with tracked retention, typically 2-4x fewer refreshes for most dies and conditions.
note: Replicas track the mean, not the VRT tail.

title: Charge-transfer presensing doubles cells per bitline
idea: Revive 1990s charge-transfer presensing: a Vt-compensated transfer transistor between a long bitline and a small sense node amplifies the signal by the capacitance ratio, so 1,024 cells per bitline work and the number of SA stripes halves.
why: Periphery (fact 7): SA stripes are ~20-25% of die; halving them saves ~10% die area on existing processes.
note: 1990s charge-transfer presensing revival.

title: Nanotwinned copper pads enable 150 C bonding of heat-sensitive memory tiers
idea: Fuse (111)-oriented nanotwinned copper, electroplated from US-mined copper on US-built plating tools, into hybrid-bond pads; its fast surface diffusion forms Cu-Cu bonds at ~150 C, so finished AFE-capacitor or thin-film-transistor memory tiers can be stacked repeatedly without retention-damaging 300-400 C anneals.
why: 3D tier count (fact 2): cumulative thermal budget no longer caps bonded stacks; enables 8-16 bonded memory wafers per stack with domestic inputs.

title: Skip hafnium-zirconium separation: qualify natural-ratio zirconium precursors
idea: Combine the two elements nature already combines: electronics needs no nuclear-grade Hf/Zr separation, so qualify ALD precursors made directly from unseparated zircon (~2% Hf) for ZrO2 capacitors and specify periphery dielectrics as natural (Zr,Hf)O2.
why: Deletes the costly solvent-extraction separation step (a large share of precursor cost) and makes hafnium non-critical for DRAM.

title: Polymer-copper hybrid bond whose bonding polymer becomes the underfill
idea: Combine HBM die bonding and underfill: the one added mask patterns a photo-definable BCB/polyimide around Cu pads; at bonding, Cu-Cu interdiffuses while the polymer flows and cures into a void-free underfill, eliminating SnAg microbumps and capillary underfill.
why: Removes tin and silver from HBM stacks, shrinks bond pitch ~40 to ~10 um for more TSVs, and raises stack yield against the 20-30% TSV-tax loss.
note: Known hybrid-bonding variant.

title: Compression-funded inline ECC eliminates the dedicated ECC chips
idea: Combine lossless cache-line compression (base-delta / frequent-pattern) with error correction: any 64 B line that compresses by at least 8 B stores its own strong ECC in the freed bits, so the 9th/10th ECC DRAM device on each server rank is dropped. Rare incompressible lines spill to a small overflow region flagged by a pointer bit.
why: Removes the 12.5-25% of DRAM bits that servers spend on ECC devices while keeping chipkill-class protection.
note: Close to the published COP (compress-and-protect) work.

title: Tidal memory: scheduler pairs anti-correlated job footprints
idea: Combine the cluster scheduler with per-job memory-phase profiles: co-locate jobs whose peak footprints alternate in time (nightly ETL vs daytime serving, train vs eval phases) and shuttle the idle job's pages to a CXL/compressed tier at each phase boundary.
why: Servers are provisioned for each job's peak; sharing peaks across time cuts installed DRAM 25-40% fleet-wide.

title: RAID-5 parity across DIMMs replaces per-rank chipkill
idea: Combine RAID-5 striping with main memory: one parity DIMM covers a group of 4-8 data DIMMs, a per-line CRC carried in burst metadata detects errors, and reconstruction from parity runs only when a CRC fails, replacing per-rank ECC devices.
why: Reliability overhead drops from 12.5-25% of bits to ~6-12% at similar device-failure tolerance.

title: Succinct filters plus on-flash learned index shrink key-value indexes
idea: Combine ribbon/cuckoo filters with a learned on-flash index: a DRAM-resident filter (~1 byte per key) answers whether a key exists and in which segment, and a learned model stored on the SSD locates the record in one read, replacing full in-DRAM hash indexes.
why: Index DRAM falls from ~16-40 bytes per key to ~1-2 bytes per key for billion-key stores, using only commodity DUV-made SSDs.

title: Real-time memory exchange fused with VM balloon drivers
idea: Combine spot-market pricing with hypervisor ballooning: tenants post idle guest memory as sell orders, the balloon driver reclaims it within seconds when bought, and the buyer receives it through a CXL pool or same-host remapping.
why: Cloud memory utilization often sits under 50%; trading idle gigabytes raises effective supply 20-30% with no new silicon.

title: Base-die line compressor storing size tags in spare ECC bits
idea: Combine the HBM base die with a hardware cache-line compressor (base-delta plus shared FP8/BF16 exponents) whose per-line size tag lives in spare ECC/metadata bits, so two compressed lines pack into one slot transparently and the host sees normal addresses.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: 1.3-2x effective capacity and bandwidth on AI tensors with no host software change.
note: Compresso/Attache-style metadata compression known.

title: Single LED-cured nanoimprint defines via and trench for interposers
idea: Combine nanoimprint lithography with dual damascene: a two-tier stamp imprints via and trench together into a UV-curable dielectric cured by 365 nm LED arrays, followed by electroless seed and Cu plating. No scanner, no excimer laser, no argon PVD.
why: Interposer capital and neon exposure: 0.5-1 um L/S interconnect without DUV, halving lithography steps per metal level.
note: Dual-damascene NIL studied since 2000s; defectivity is the issue.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory vault: 77 K DRAM pool with near-zero refresh
idea: Combine rack-scale CXL memory pooling with liquid-nitrogen immersion (N2 is 78% of air, unlike helium cryogenics): at 77 K access-transistor leakage collapses so retention stretches to hours, refresh nearly stops, wires are ~6-7x less resistive and commodity DRAM runs at reduced VDD.
why: Refresh (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) goes to ~0 and racks pack 2-3x denser; net win for idle-heavy capacity tiers after ~10 W/W cryo-lift overhead.
note: Cryo DRAM studied; 10 W/W lift eats refresh savings.

title: Chip-first printed fan-out: interconnect printed directly onto placed dies
idea: Combine pick-and-place die embedding with aerosol-jet printing: DRAM and controller dies sit face-up in a molded panel and Ag/Cu nanoparticle inks plus polyimide dielectric are printed across die edges at 10-20 um lines, then sintered with near-IR diode lasers instead of xenon flash lamps.
why: Packaging capex and rare-gas exposure: zero masks, vacuum or rare gas; 3-5x lower capex for LPDDR/CXL memory modules on U.S. soil.
note: 10-20 um printed lines limit to LPDDR-class densities.

title: Retired-server DRAM harvesting line feeding CXL expander cards
idea: Combine e-waste DIMM recovery with CXL memory expansion: an automated line desolders DDR4/DDR5 packages from retired DIMMs, reballs and characterizes each chip for retention and speed, bins them, and remounts them on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller maps weak rows and applies per-chip adaptive refresh. No new wafers, so no new rare gas.
why: Usable supply: millions of retired DIMMs per year become capacity at ~10-20% of new cost/bit during the shortage.
note: Adds package-level harvest and reball; extra cost versus whole-DIMM reuse.

title: Bit-plane-transposed tensors: exponent planes refreshed, mantissa planes left drifting
idea: Combine approximate computing with bit-plane storage: the controller transposes BF16/FP8 tensors so each DRAM row holds one bit-plane; sign/exponent planes go to normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes to rows refreshed 8-16x less often, so any flip lands at a known, low significance.
