title: Olfactory combinatorial 3-of-24 constant-weight wordline decoder
idea: About 400 olfactory receptor types encode trillions of odors combinatorially. Replace one-hot predecode with a constant-weight code: each local wordline driver connects to a unique triplet of 24 shared select lines (2,024 triplets) through a vertical 3-gate stacked transistor. Only the triplet with all three lines high fires, and every other triplet has at most two high.
why: Fact 7: about 2-3x fewer predecode lines and decoder transistors than tree decoders, so row-decode area falls ~30%.
note: m-of-n decoding is known art; 3-gate stack is the twist.

title: Cuckoo strategy: host raises the on-die ECC and hammer logic
idea: Cuckoos let other birds raise their chicks. Write a JEDEC-style proposal plus open reference RTL in which the host controller does what each die's periphery does today (on-die ECC, refresh-management counters, thermal refresh) using metadata in ordinary rows, so 'lean' dies can omit those circuits. Three engineers, FPGA demo and standards work, ~$900k in 24 months.
why: Fact 7: on-die ECC alone adds ~6% array plus logic. Moving it and hammer counters to the host could reclaim ~6-10% die area per bit.

title: Retinal light adaptation: sense references track hot cells' decay
idea: The retina adapts by referencing each photoreceptor to its neighbourhood average; in each 3D mat keep a few reference cells per row written with 1 and 0 alongside the data, and derive the sense reference from their live average so the threshold drifts down with the same temperature-driven leakage as the data cells.
why: At 125 C the '1' level decays fast toward a fixed mid-rail reference; an adaptive midpoint roughly doubles tolerated decay, doubling the refresh interval for <2% area.

title: Hydra stem-cell renewal: retire rows as they age at temperature
idea: Hydra avoids ageing by continuously replacing worn cells from stem cells; profile every row's retention in the background at 125 C and progressively retire rows whose retention or variable-retention-time behaviour degrades into a 2-3% spare-row pool, updating a per-bank remap table over the decade.
why: Retention tails widen over 10 yrs at 125 C (aging, VRT); continuous renewal keeps refresh at a tail-free rate instead of guard-banding for end-of-life tails, ~2x refresh savings.
note: Online retention profiling and row retirement echo RAIDR/AVATAR; niche at 125 C.

title: Aquaporin-studded roll-to-roll membranes for ultrapure water reclaim
idea: Aquaporin channels pass about a billion water molecules per second while rejecting ions. Embed aquaporins or synthetic pillar[5]arene water channels in roll-to-roll-cast polyamide reverse-osmosis films for the UPW reclaim loop, running at about half the pressure of standard RO.
why: Cuts UPW energy ~30-50% and pushes water reclaim toward 90%, easing water intensity and drought siting for US fabs.

title: Kidney countercurrent membrane cascade recovers helium from tool exhaust
idea: The loop of Henle multiplies concentration with countercurrent flow across selective membranes. Put roll-to-roll-cast polymer membrane sheets (polyimide or PIM films) in a countercurrent cascade on etch and CVD exhaust, concentrating dilute helium stage by stage to >99.999% for reinjection.
why: Recovers 70-90% of fab helium while Qatar (~30% of supply) is offline, using printable films at a fraction of cryogenic recovery capital.

title: Bone-remodeling deposit-and-resorb supercycles self-align contacts without masks
idea: Bone is laid down and resorbed continuously, with net growth only where signals favor it; run ALD supercycles that deposit a dielectric everywhere and then a short etch that removes the thinner nuclei on metal but not the faster-grown film on oxide, repeated ~30x, so an isolation mask grows only on dielectric and contacts self-align.
why: Deletes 1-3 critical contact/via masks and their overlay budget (fact 4); est. 5-8% lower wafer cost.

title: Epigenetic methylation bits trigger heterochromatin-style in-place page compaction
idea: Each 4 KB page carries 2 'methylation' bits set by the OS or ML runtime; methylated pages are packed by the controller into dense heterochromatin form (entropy-coded, 3-4x) inside the same DIMM while acetylated pages stay open and uncompressed. Marks are inherited by forked or copied pages, like epigenetic inheritance through cell division.
why: Capacity: software-hinted compression tier without a separate far-memory device; 30-50% fewer DRAM bits per server.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve erodes low-order bits of aging data
idea: Tagged tensors (cached activations, retrieval embeddings, KV) lose least-significant bits on a forgetting schedule unless re-accessed, with each access acting as rehearsal that resets the clock; the controller periodically repacks eroded lines into denser formats.
why: Capacity: 2-3x density for approximation-tolerant aging data, with loss concentrated on rarely used items.

title: Quorum sensing decides when shared pages get local replicas
idea: Bacteria act only when autoinducer concentration crosses a threshold; each host counts remote accesses to a pooled page from its cores, makes a local replica only when demand crosses a quorum, and dissolves it when the signal decays, otherwise serving the page from the shared CXL pool.
why: Replication overhead: 30-60% fewer duplicate copies of shared data in pooled racks.

title: Fly mushroom-body hashing finds near-duplicate pages for delta storage
idea: Fruit flies tag odors via random sparse expansion then winner-take-all; the controller applies the same FlyHash to sampled page contents to bucket near-duplicates, storing each as a delta against a bucket representative (checkpoints, VM snapshots, model replicas with slight drift).
why: Capacity: catches near-duplicates that exact-hash dedup misses, a further 1.3-2x.
note: Difference Engine did similarity-based page patching.

title: Salmon-run return: retired GPUs serve their HBM as KV pools
idea: Salmon die upstream and fertilize the forest; aging training GPUs are redeployed as dedicated KV-cache and expert-weight memory nodes over NVLink or RDMA, running only memory-serving firmware, so their HBM keeps supplying fast capacity to new accelerators instead of being shredded.
why: HBM supply: recovers 80+ GB of HBM per retired GPU, reducing new HBM needed for inference growth.

title: Genome-like health ledger travels with every memory module
idea: Each module stores a tamper-evident lifetime record (hours, temperature, ECC events, hammer counts, repairs) in extended SPD, like DNA carrying heritable history, readable by any buyer or recycler to price and place the module in its next life; mandated in procurement standards.
why: Secondary-market liquidity: makes used DRAM trustworthy, raising reuse rates and lowering new-bit demand.

title: Myelinated interposer links with nodes-of-Ranvier regenerators
idea: Long GPU-to-memory interposer wires are cut into insulated segments wrapped in a thick low-k 'myelin' sheath, with tiny sense-and-restore 'nodes' every ~1 mm that regenerate a ~100 mV low-swing signal, as in saltatory conduction. Energy is spent only charging short low-capacitance segments, so memory stacks can sit 10-20 mm from the logic instead of 1-2 mm.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~2-3x lower capacitance per mm plus low swing targets <1 pJ/bit at longer reach, so more stacks can ring one accelerator beyond today's edge (shoreline) limit.

title: Penguin-huddle rotation: migrate hot data so no stack overheats
idea: Emperor penguins take turns between the cold edge and the warm centre of the huddle. Likewise the memory controller tracks per-stack temperature and periodically moves the hottest pages from stacks next to the GPU hotspot to cooler edge stacks, keeping every stack below the 85 C point where refresh doubles.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh on hot stacks, recovering ~5-15% bandwidth and idle power for under 1% migration traffic.
note: Thermal-aware memory management is prior art.

title: Lesion-wiring: fine-tune each model on its own DIMM's fault map
idea: Like a developing brain rewiring around a lesion, an accelerator profiles its own HBM's weak-cell map at a relaxed 1 s refresh, then runs a short fine-tune in which exactly those weight bits are clamped to their decayed values, so the deployed model stops depending on them and weight regions run permanently at the relaxed refresh.
why: Refresh bandwidth/energy (10-20% bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) and retention tail: weights are most of inference HBM capacity; ~16x longer refresh there with <0.1% accuracy loss frees bandwidth and idle power.
note: Similar to EDEN and Matic error-aware retraining.

title: Deinococcus polyploidy: scattered multi-copy for the critical 1% only
idea: Deinococcus radiodurans survives shattered chromosomes by keeping 4-10 genome copies and reassembling; replicate only page tables, kernel and allocator metadata 3-4x across banks with different physical neighbours and TSV columns, repairing by consensus on read, so the other 99% of memory runs with much lighter ECC.
why: ECC overhead and crash rate: crashes come mostly from corrupted metadata; strong protection of 1% lets bulk data drop from ~12.5% to ~3% check overhead.
note: Selective protection of critical data is known; modest ECC savings.

title: Wolff's-law remodeling: hot rows migrate into guard-flanked bunkers
idea: Bone reinforces where it is loaded; keep a small pool of 'bunker' rows in each bank that are physically flanked by unused guard rows, and when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold the controller swaps it into a bunker, where hammering has no victims.
why: Row hammer: guarantees zero victims for the hottest rows at ~1-2% capacity cost instead of victim-refresh overhead that explodes as thresholds approach 1k.

title: Muller's-ratchet recombination: two error-riddled copies make one clean page
idea: Sexual recombination breaks Muller's ratchet by mixing genomes with different mutations; store each page twice in very cheap cells with only an 8-bit CRC per 8-byte chunk (detect, not correct), assemble reads chunk by chunk from whichever copy passes, rewrite the failing chunk, and fall back to a rare third copy on double hits.
why: Cost per GB: replaces correction logic with detection plus duplication, so media at raw BER ~1e-5 (a 100x-cheaper class) works at ~2.25x bit overhead with trivially cheap decode.
note: Mirroring plus checksums is ZFS-style known art; 2.25x overhead eats most of the cheap-media gain.

title: Hermit-crab vacancy chains for synchronized DIMM cascade resale
idea: Hermit crabs queue by size and swap shells all at once, so every crab upgrades in one event. A marketplace pre-matches hyperscaler refresh dates with tiers of second-life buyers (enterprise, edge, education, embedded), so tested DIMMs move down a pre-arranged chain within days instead of being shredded.
why: Extends DRAM service life 2-3x; recovering even 20% of decommissioned server DRAM adds several % of annual bit supply at near-zero capital.

title: Epigenetic binning: deploy sub-spec dies with workload-matched refresh
idea: One genome is expressed differently in different environments. Dies that fail retention or speed bins go to workloads that tolerate them, such as AI inference caches, with per-row retention profiling and controller-managed higher refresh, instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises effective yield by a few % to ~10%, adding bits at zero wafer cost.

title: Ant-trail data-in-motion: activations stream, never parked in DRAM
idea: Ant trails hold information in moving traffic and evaporating pheromone, not in a warehouse. Accelerators are scheduled so intermediate activations circulate through chip-to-chip pipeline links and are consumed before they ever need to be parked in DRAM.
why: Cuts DRAM/HBM capacity per AI inference system by ~30-50%, with no capacitor anywhere.
note: Activations are a small share of inference memory versus weights and KV.

title: Plywood veneer slicing: film-thickness-defined 5-nm electrode combs
idea: Veneer exposes the edges of thin layers: grow 40 alternating 5-nm ALD TiN/Al2O3 layers on a sidewall (or MBE GaAs/AlGaAs, then cleave) and use the exposed edge as a stamp or mask (SNAP-style) to transfer a 10-nm-pitch line array; cross two such arrays with ultrathin ZrO2 so each intersection is a storage capacitor for gain-cell or diode-isolated arrays.
why: Fact 4: 10-nm-pitch lines defined by film thickness rather than lithography, beyond EUV resolution with an ALD tool; fits a university fab; line fan-out contacts and crossbar sneak paths are the risks.
note: SNAP prior art; fan-out contacts and crossbar access devices remain unsolved.

title: Cold-chain time-temperature indicator cells trigger refresh by accumulated thermal dose
idea: Vaccine shipments carry time-temperature indicators that integrate Arrhenius dose rather than trusting a schedule. In each subarray keep a few canary cells deliberately built leakier than the 6-sigma tail (wider junction implant); rewrite them at each refresh, poll them cheaply, and refresh the subarray only when a canary flips.
why: Spec refresh assumes 85 C worst case, but devices often run 45-65 C, so tracking real thermal dose cuts refresh 4-10x and most of the 16-33% idle refresh power (fact 3).

title: Foveated rendering for memory: refresh low-order mantissa bit-planes far less
idea: VR headsets render full detail only where the eye looks. Store AI weights and KV caches bit-plane-wise so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits live in normally refreshed rows, while the lowest 3-5 mantissa bits of BF16/FP8 sit in rows refreshed 8-16x less often and are allowed rare flips.
why: For LLM-dominated DRAM, 30-50% of stored bits tolerate occasional errors; cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~30-45% at 32-64 Gb (fact 3).

title: Let out-of-the-money options expire: recomputable data receives no refresh
idea: Traders let options expire when exercising costs more than they are worth. Tag regions holding recomputable data (KV-cache blocks rebuildable from tokens, cached embeddings, prefetch buffers) as 'expire-allowed': they get long or no refresh, ECC flags any decayed line, and the runtime recomputes it on demand.
why: KV caches are a growing share of inference DRAM; dropping their refresh and accepting rare recompute saves refresh power and lets weaker-retention, cheaper dies serve them (fact 3, cost per bit).
note: Same skip-refresh-and-regenerate mechanism.

title: Roundabout traffic: self-timed completion detection per mat
idea: Like a roundabout letting cars go as soon as the way is clear instead of waiting for a fixed signal cycle, each SA latch drives a dual-rail done signal, and a per-mat completion tree releases column access when that mat's slowest SA resolves, not after the chip's worst-case tRCD.
why: Latency/bandwidth: average tRCD falls ~25-35% by reclaiming PVT guard-bands.

title: Turbogenerator hydrogen cooling replaces helium as electrostatic-chuck backside gas
idea: Large power-plant generators are cooled with hydrogen because its thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/m-K) beats helium (~0.15). Use onsite PEM-electrolysis H2, or a sub-flammable H2/N2 blend at the ~10 Torr backside pressure, as the wafer-to-chuck heat-transfer gas in etch and CVD chucks, treating the small leak into the plasma as a known minor process species.
why: Removes the largest single helium use in a DRAM fab with equal or better wafer temperature control during high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch; ~100% helium substitution for chuck cooling using gas makeable anywhere in the U.S.

title: Phosphate-fertilizer fluorine recovery turns fab waste into synthetic fluorspar
idea: Phosphate plants recover fluorosilicic acid and convert it to AlF3 and HF instead of mining fluorspar. Precipitate fab HF, chamber-clean and abatement fluoride as acid-grade synthetic CaF2, or route it into fluorosilicic-acid-to-HF conversion, closing the fluorine loop behind the HF, NF3 and WF6 a DRAM fab buys; the DDR/HBM product is identical.
why: Fluorspar is a critical mineral (China ~60%) underpinning every fluorine chemical in the fab; target 40-60% of fab fluorine demand from recycled feed and avoid wastewater fluoride limits.

title: Regenerative braking for wordlines: charge recycling between successive row activations
idea: EVs and elevators recover braking energy instead of burning it as heat. Inside the die, when a row is precharged its ~3 V wordline dumps charge into a local reservoir capacitor that then pre-charges the next activated wordline and feeds the VPP pump, recovering ~40-50% of wordline CV^2 energy; commands and timings at the DDR/HBM pins are unchanged.
why: Fact 10: the ~3 V wordline locks CV^2 energy; recycling cuts activate energy and VPP charge-pump power and area, lowering energy per bit without a new interface.
note: Charge recycling in DRAM circuits has prior art; 40-50% recovery is optimistic given reservoir losses.

title: Holographic grating writer: mask-free interference lithography for array lattices
idea: Borrowed from holographic diffraction-grating production, which uses interfering laser beams instead of masks. Because DRAM array layers (active, buried wordline, capacitor lattice) are strictly periodic, expose them with 3-6-beam 193 nm immersion interference at ~70 nm pitch, spacer-double to ~35 nm, and use one coarse trim exposure to cut array edges.
why: Fact 4: array critical layers become maskless and EUV-free; interference optics are simple (~1/10 scanner cost) with very high throughput.

title: Pressure-cooker deuterium anneal to upgrade leaky DRAM wafers
idea: Borrowed from pressure cookers, which speed cooking with pressure: a small team runs a 20 atm deuterium furnace at ~400 C on retention-fallout DRAM wafers, driving D into the Si/SiO2 interface traps behind the leakage tail (Si-D bonds resist breaking far better than Si-H), then re-tests and re-bins them.
why: Fact 3: shrinking the leakage tail can stretch refresh 2-4x and rescue otherwise scrapped die; a high-pressure anneal vessel is a modest, small-team-buildable tool.

title: Display demura for DRAM: ship per-die retention maps, relax specs
idea: Borrowed from OLED panels, which are cheap only because every pixel's mura is measured and a correction table is burned into the driver: at wafer probe, record each die's weak-row retention map (a few KB), store it in module SPD/flash, and have the controller refresh weak rows fast and strong rows 4-8x slower, so fabs can ship die with looser leakage specs; firmware and test software fit a small team.
why: Facts 3/4: a relaxed leakage-tail spec raises yield and skips process tightening; refresh energy drops ~50-70%.
note: RAIDR-style art; variable retention time undermines probe-time maps.

title: Pointer dehydration: hardware shrinks 64-bit pointers on eviction
idea: Like dehydrating food for storage, the memory controller detects 64-bit pointers in evicted cache lines (high bits match a region-base register) and stores them as 32-bit region offsets, packing a 64 B line into 32-40 B; rehydration on fill is a single add.
why: Pointer-heavy workloads (graphs, JVM, Python, databases) are 30-50% pointers; transparent 1.3-1.6x capacity without software changes.
note: Base-delta compression already captures pointer redundancy.

title: Drop-shipping data: zero-inventory host memory for AI servers
idea: Like retailers that hold no stock and let suppliers ship direct, enforce a single-copy I/O path: storage DMAs straight into accelerator memory, page-cache and pinned bounce-buffer copies are eliminated, and the host keeps only metadata.
why: AI servers ship with 1-2 TB of host DRAM largely used as staging copies; could cut host DRAM 50-70% per node.
note: Largely GPUDirect Storage; host DRAM sizing has other drivers, 50-70% cut optimistic.

title: Android lifecycle for servers: killable services with saved state bundles
idea: Like Android killing background apps after they save an instance-state bundle, a server framework requires each service to serialize its minimal semantic state (not its heap) to persistent memory on a trim signal, so the OS can kill idle services aggressively and rehydrate them later.
why: Semantic state is often 100-1000x smaller than the heap; reclaims DRAM from idle microservices and makes their state power-safe.

title: Latent image writes: retention-tuned NV programming for short-lived data
idea: Like exposed-but-undeveloped film, data predicted short-lived is written to NV (SLC NAND, MRAM, ReRAM) with weak fast pulses giving days of retention, enough to survive outages, and is 'developed' with full-strength pulses only if it lives long; a lifetime predictor picks the mode.
why: Lets non-volatile media absorb DRAM-tier write traffic with 3-10x less write energy and wear, shrinking the DRAM tier while staying persistent.

title: Lending library: rack-wide shared read-only NV pages mapped in place
idea: Like a public library replacing private bookshelves, OS images, shared libraries, container layers and model weights live once in a rack-level persistent CXL memory appliance mapped read-only (DAX) into every host, so no host spends DRAM caching its own copy.
why: Removes per-host duplicates of identical read-mostly data (often 10-30% of DRAM) across 32-64 hosts.

title: ER triage at malloc: lifetime-predicted placement into DRAM or NV
idea: Like emergency rooms triaging on arrival, a profiler tags each allocation site with predicted object lifetime and write intensity, and the allocator places long-lived read-mostly objects directly in persistent memory at birth while only short-lived write-hot objects get DRAM.
why: Avoids later migration cost; most bytes are long-lived and read-mostly, so DRAM footprint shrinks 2-3x and long-lived state is durable.
note: Lifetime-predicted allocation (LLAMA, memkind/PMem placement) is known; NV tier availability is shrinking post-Optane.

title: Spot-market auction allocating weak rows to error-tolerant buyers
idea: Markets price goods of different quality. The OS sorts profiled rows into reliability grades and runs an internal auction. Each process declares how much error it tolerates: kernel structures none, video frames, KV-cache and activations some. Weak rows that would otherwise be retired or refreshed 4x go to the tolerant bidders at relaxed refresh.
why: The retention tail stops setting the global refresh rate (fact 3) and becomes a priced resource. Refresh could fall 20-40%, and the ~1-3% of weak cells stay usable.

title: Fishing zones and quotas: tenant-exclusive subarrays with boundary ACT limits
idea: Fisheries combine exclusive economic zones with catch quotas instead of tracking each fish. The FPGA/CXL controller gives each tenant (VM/ASID) exclusive subarray zones, so hammering inside a zone harms only its owner. Only boundary rows, about 1-2% of all rows, carry small ACT counters with strict quotas.
why: Cross-tenant hammer protection with ~50x less tracking SRAM, and it scales to thresholds of ~100 (fact 9). It needs only controller logic and kernel allocation.

title: Minimum-equipment-list grading: ship partial-good dies with signed fault maps
idea: Airliners dispatch legally with documented inoperative equipment. Draft a JEDEC-style SPD extension that carries a signed fault map (dead mats, weak rows). Write reference BIOS and CXL firmware that route around the mapped faults, and pilot 100 modules built from partial-good dies that are scrapped today. All of it fits in $1M.
why: Effective die yield up 5-15% at advanced nodes means more sellable bits per wafer and lower capital per bit (fact 4).

title: CD-style cross-interleaved two-level code across banks
idea: CDs survive 2.5 mm scratches with CIRC: two Reed-Solomon codes plus delay interleaving. In the FPGA controller, an inner RS code per 64 B burst detects and flags errors. An outer RS code spans 28 lines that address-mapping skew places in different banks and subarrays. A hammered row or dead wordline, the 'scratch', then corrupts at most one symbol per outer codeword.
why: Survives whole-row and wordline failures at ~12% overhead, so chips can ship with fewer row spares and weaker hammer margins (fact 9).

title: Fractional-reserve parity: one XOR row backs many detection-only rows
idea: Banks hold reserves for only a fraction of deposits because withdrawals are rare. Each line keeps only a detection CRC-8. One XOR parity row in another bank backs each group of 32 rows. On a detected error, the line is rebuilt from the other 31 plus parity on a slow path. A controller write cache coalesces the parity read-modify-writes.
why: ECC storage overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3-6% while still correcting whole-line errors (cost per bit). It can be implemented in FPGA controller logic.

title: Pharma accelerated-stability Arrhenius screening to shorten retention test
idea: Pharma predicts two-year shelf life from short accelerated aging. Short retention tests at three elevated temperatures, combined with Bayesian extrapolation of each die's retention tail and VRT probability, replace long nominal-temperature retention loops. The method is validated on 10k dies with a partner test house.
why: Test time and cost down 30-50%, and fewer false rejects raise yield. It is a methods and statistics project well within $1M.
note: Hot retention testing already standard; Bayesian extrapolation of VRT is the twist.

title: Frequency-hopping row remap with rotating secret keys
idea: Spread-spectrum radios hop channels on a secret sequence to defeat jammers. The FPGA controller applies a keyed small-Feistel permutation from logical to physical rows within each bank. It re-keys gradually, one row-pair swap per refresh interval, so an attacker never learns adjacency and aggressor ACTs spread over many victims.
why: Removes targeted hammering and raises the effective threshold about 10x (fact 9) with controller logic only.
note: Same keyed Feistel remap.

title: Airline overbooking: statistically overcommitted DRAM with bump pool
idea: Like airlines selling 105% of seats, cloud providers sell VMs with 130% of physical DRAM, backed by an actuarial model of peak co-usage and a 'bump pool' of compressed and CXL-attached memory that absorbs overflow, with credits paid when a tenant is bumped.
why: Buyers purchase 20-25% less DRAM per sold GB; the bump-pool tier costs far less per bit.

title: Crowe-cell persistent-current loops with nanocryotron readout for cryogenic AI
idea: The 1957 Crowe cell stored bits as clockwise or counter-clockwise supercurrent in a thin-film loop. Build it from 100-nm NbN kinetic-inductance loops read by the nTron (the modern three-terminal cryotron), stacked with cryo-CMOS or SFQ accelerators in dedicated AI pods.
why: Zero static dissipation, zero refresh, ~1e-19 J switching (Facts 3, 10); only pays at pod scale after ~400 W/W 4 K cooling overhead; target 10x system energy per bit including cooling.
note: MIT nanowire/nTron memory exists; value limited to cryogenic systems after cooling overhead.

title: CCD-era pinned storage well as a DRAM cell in image-sensor fabs
idea: Interline CCDs and the 1980 pinned photodiode held charge in fully depleted, surface-pinned buried wells with dark current near 1 e-/s. Use existing 65/45-nm CMOS-image-sensor flows (pinned well, transfer gate, floating diffusion, source follower) to store a bit as ~1000 electrons in a contactless pinned well, read by transfer to a shared floating diffusion with in-cell gain.
why: Retention of seconds to minutes instead of 64 ms (Fact 3: ~100x less refresh) and gain readout sidesteps the capacitor wall (Fact 1); CIS fabs are mature, EUV-free, with idle capacity; ~10x less dense than DRAM, so a refresh-free tier.

title: Widrow memistor reborn as a protonic WO3 three-terminal BEOL gain cell
idea: Widrow's 1960 memistor stored a value as electroplated copper thickness on a resistive film read through separate terminals. Build a three-terminal protonic cell (WO3 channel, ZrO2:H electrolyte, Pd gate) in the BEOL of an existing 180/130-nm fab; write pulses move H+ in or out and the channel conductance is read without disturbing it.
why: Separated read path means no read disturb (Fact 8), hour retention (Fact 3), fJ writes below 1 V (Fact 10); ~1e9 endurance makes it a weight/state tier rather than general DRAM; BEOL-only on U.S. 200-mm fabs.
note: Known IBM/MIT ECRAM; endurance limits it to a weight tier.

title: Relay-computer revival: NEM pull-in hysteresis latch at zero current
idea: Relay and neon-lamp memories held bits inside a hysteresis window between pick-up and drop-out. In existing MEMS foundries or 180-nm BEOL, build TiN or poly-Si cantilever relays biased between their pull-out (~1.5 V) and pull-in (~3 V) voltages, so a pulled-in beam stays in and a released beam stays out at zero DC current.
why: Static storage with zero leakage through an air gap (Fact 3), abrupt selector-like on/off, no capacitor; ~1 um2 cells make a low-power state store built entirely in existing MEMS capacity.
note: Relay hysteresis memory known; ~1 um2 cells, low density.

title: Diagonal sense-wire bitline twisting across tiers for 4F2 open arrays
idea: Copy core memory's diagonal sense wire, which crossed cores in alternating polarity so half-select pickup cancelled: in a vertical-channel 4F2 array, each bitline pair swaps tier position and coupling polarity every 8 cells, so wordline kick and neighbor coupling arrive as common-mode at the sense amp. This gives folded-bitline noise immunity at open-bitline area.
why: Facts 1 and 4: ~30-40% less coupling noise lets Cs drop from ~5 fF toward ~3.5 fF (lower capacitor aspect ratio) while keeping 4F2 (33% less area than 6F2).

title: Bubble-memory boot-loop map lets 3D tiers ship with dead strings
idea: Bubble chips shipped with several percent of minor loops defective plus a boot loop telling the controller which to skip; do the same in 3D DRAM: each mat stores a triple-replicated map of bitline segments whose cells fail, and column logic skips them at full speed. Up to 1% failing cells per mat are masked at test and remapped in the field.
why: Facts 2 and 4: tolerating 1% bad cells lets low-quality poly/oxide channels and 100+ tiers yield, cutting capital per good bit and the 3D break-even tier count.
note: Column redundancy/bad-block maps are standard; tolerating 1% bad cells per mat is the twist.

title: Gaines stochastic bitstreams multiplied by ANDing vertical tier strings
idea: Revive Gaines' 1960s stochastic computing: weights and activations are stored as random bitstreams laid along vertical strings, so multiplying two values is a single AND of two strings sensed together in the array, and a 1% cell BER shifts a value by only ~1%.
why: Fact 5: avoids moving operands off-die for low-precision ops (>=5x less data-movement energy) on cheap, error-prone tiers.
note: In-DRAM stochastic computing exists; long bitstreams inflate storage.

title: Saturn-V voting plus Whirlwind marginal checking per tier band
idea: Revive Whirlwind's marginal checking (stressing voltages to expose weak parts) and the Saturn V LVDC's triple voting: at boot and periodically the controller lowers array voltage per tier band to measure margin, then runs strong tiers raw at up to 1% cell BER under the normal code and weak top/bottom tiers in 3-way voted mode.
why: Fact 2: no tier is discarded, so a 128-tier stack with uneven etch still yields; density loss <10% versus scrapping wafers.
note: Margin testing and region-adaptive ECC are known; TMR costs 3x on weak tiers.

title: Telephone-exchange Erlang trunking for memory: optical circuit-switched DRAM pools
idea: Revive Bell System Erlang traffic engineering and crossbar exchanges: size rack memory like phone trunks, to the 99.9th-percentile aggregate demand rather than each server's peak, and connect servers to pooled DRAM through MEMS optical circuit switches carrying CXL over optics.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: about 25-30% of cloud DRAM sits stranded, and Erlang provisioning cuts purchased DRAM 20-30% with no new fabs and no EUV.
note: CXL pooling with statistical provisioning already studied (e.g., Pond); optics adds novelty modestly.

title: Transformer-coupled die stacking replaces TSVs, reviving IBM TROS
idea: Revive IBM's 1960s transformer read-only store, where data crossed between conductors by magnetic coupling, as inductive die-to-die links: each die in a DRAM stack carries top-metal coils that talk vertically through thinned silicon, so signals need no TSVs and power arrives by edge or wire bonds. Coils need no extra masks.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV module (deep Si etch, liner, Cu fill, reveal; ~5-8 steps and a big yield hit) and TSV keep-out area, potentially halving HBM's area-per-bit penalty; risks are power delivery and coil area at 1-2 Tb/s per stack.

title: Audio-RAM revival: partially defective DRAM for error-tolerant data
idea: In the 1980s DRAMs with bad bits were sold as 'ARAM' for answering machines. Revive it: dies and HBM stacks that fail test get a stored fault map and are sold for error-tolerant data, with the allocator putting activations, gradients and low-order weight bits on faulty regions and sign/exponent bits on clean ones.
why: Supply: turns part of the 20-30% HBM/DRAM yield loss into usable cheap capacity, adding several percent to world bit supply with no new fab.

title: Goodman shadow-casting optical multiplier with laser-written weight masks
idea: Revive Goodman's 1978 incoherent optical matrix-vector multiplier: an LED/microLED row carries the input vector, light passes through a grayscale weight mask written by the university laser writer or e-beam, and a photodiode column sums each row; swapping masks swaps models.
why: Weights become a photomask instead of DRAM bits and are read by photons in parallel, so fixed edge models need no weight memory or weight bandwidth.

title: Gaines stochastic computing: noise-driven rounding removes FP32 master weights
idea: Revive Gaines' 1967 stochastic computing by putting true-random noise sources (university-fabbed avalanche diodes or RTN transistors) in the memory write path, so every weight update into a bf16/fp8 store is stochastically rounded in hardware at no compute cost.
why: Unbiased stochastic rounding lets training drop FP32 master weights and FP32 optimizer copies, ~2-4x less training memory.

title: Cray-2 immersion revival with ester fluids enables taller HBM stacks
idea: Revive the Cray-2's total-immersion cooling but swap Fluorinert for natural or synthetic ester dielectric fluid, with micro-jets aimed through the gaps between stacks and a passive thermosiphon loop, removing heat through stack sidewalls.
why: Constraint: no PFAS coolants (Fluorinert/Novec production has been exited); side-cooling relieves the thermal cap on stack height so 16-24-high stacks run unthrottled, ~50% more GB per footprint.

title: Bell WT4 revival: polyethylene millimeter-wave waveguides carry rack memory traffic
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1970s WT4 millimeter waveguide as HDPE or polystyrene dielectric waveguides (not PTFE) at 130-300 GHz, driven by CMOS mm-wave transceivers on CXL memory sleds and linking pooled memory 1-5 m to compute.
why: Constraint: avoids PTFE dielectric and fluoropolymer cable jackets; ~1-2 pJ/bit and lower cost than optics at rack reach makes memory pooling cheap enough to raise utilization.

title: Whirlwind marginal checking reborn: live voltage-margin sweeps retire weak rows
idea: MIT Whirlwind and SAGE found dying tubes before they failed by deliberately lowering supply voltages during maintenance ('marginal checking'). The controller does this online: one subarray at a time is copied aside and exercised at VARY -60 mV, 4x stretched refresh and a skewed sense reference; any cell that fails under margin is logged and remapped before it can fail at nominal settings.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): catching marginal cells early lets the nominal refresh interval stretch 2-4x (refresh energy -50-75%) and lets vendors screen less aggressively at test; ~5-10% cost per bit from yield.
note: Close to REAPER/AVATAR reach profiling.

title: Apollo restart protection: phase-table rollback survives uncorrectable DRAM errors
idea: The Apollo Guidance Computer survived its 1202 alarms because software recorded restart-phase waypoints and resumed from the last one after a hardware restart. Runtimes keep per-task phase points with a small undo log of dirty lines in a strongly protected region; when the controller reports an uncorrectable error, only the affected task rolls back to its last phase and recomputes.
why: Error tolerance for cheaper memory: turns DUEs from node outages into millisecond recomputes, so fleets can accept 10-100x higher raw DUE rates from relaxed refresh, lighter ECC or lower-binned dies; ~10-20% lower cost per usable bit.
note: Checkpoint/rollback (ReVive, SafetyNet) is known art.

title: 1970s ceramic hermetic packaging revived: corrosion-proof memory for free-air cooling
idea: Military DRAMs of the 1970s sat in hermetic ceramic (CERDIP) packages that kept moisture and sulfur out. DIMMs and HBM packages get ALD alumina/parylene stacks or glass-frit hermetic lids plus silver-free, sulfur-resistant contacts, so memory survives unconditioned outside air (high humidity, sulfur creep corrosion) and facilities can cool with direct outside air without humidification.
why: Water: direct free-air cooling without evaporative humidity control uses ~0 L/kWh (>10x vs evaporative), and corrosion plus humidity-driven leakage are the memory failure modes that block it today.

title: Irvine Sensors Edge-Cube: Side-Metallized Die Stacks Instead of TSVs
idea: Revive Irvine Sensors' 1990s 'memory cube': thin 16-32 known-good DRAM dies, glue them into a block, lap one face to expose pads rerouted to the die edge, and pattern the interconnect directly on that side face with laser direct-write metallization, giving a high-capacity stack with no through-silicon vias at all.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: no TSV keep-out area or TSV process (recovering much of the ~3x area-per-bit penalty), KGD tested before stacking; lets U.S. defense and OSAT packagers make capacity stacks.
note: 3D-Plus/Irvine edge stacking already commercial for space; edge I/O limits bandwidth.

title: FB-DIMM AMB Reborn: Adapter Lets Reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 Join Modern Servers
idea: Revive the abandoned 2007 Fully-Buffered DIMM Advanced Memory Buffer as a cheap serial/CXL buffer chip on refurbished boards that host reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 chips, translating timing, voltage and protocol so decommissioned memory becomes a second-life capacity tier in new servers.
why: Supply and scarce resources: hundreds of millions of GB sit in retired servers; reuse at ~10-20% of new-bit cost can cover 10%+ of cold-data demand.
note: Same reclaimed-DRAM behind buffer/CXL controller as I-00423.

title: Intel 1103 Strategy: 3T Gain-Cell DRAM on Idle Mature Logic Fabs
idea: Revive the capacitor-free three-transistor cell of Intel's 1970 1103 on idle 28-65 nm 300 mm logic lines, using a standard logic flow plus a raised-Vt write device, and sell it as 'commodity-lite' DRAM chiplets for capacity tiers, letting a startup ramp the way Intel did with the 1103.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: no capacitor module or EUV, uses depreciated fabs (depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost); cost per bit ~2-3x higher than 1a DRAM but available now from existing U.S. capacity.
note: Gain cells at 28-65 nm are ~50-100x larger than 1a DRAM cells; cost/bit claim optimistic.

title: Complementary oxide-TFT static latch cells on cheap glass panels
idea: Invert 'working memory must be 1T1C DRAM' -> go static where area is cheap. Pair n-type IGZO with p-type SnO or Cu2O TFTs into a 4T loadless or 6T latch on glass whose feedback holds data with zero refresh, while oxide-level leakage keeps standby to ~pW per Mb.
why: No capacitor, no refresh and no destructive read (facts 1, 3, 8) with display tooling; density ~10x below DRAM but panel area makes it a cheap capacity or AI-scratch tier; p-type oxide mobility limits cycle time to ~100 ns.
note: Complementary oxide TFT SRAM shown; low density.

title: Thin-film magnetic core memory with zero transistors in the array
idea: Invert 'modern memory must be built from semiconductor transistors' -> revive coincident-current magnetic cores in thin film. Sub-micron permalloy rings electroplated around crossing X/Y/sense lines on glass or ceramic switch only when two half-currents coincide, storing the bit as flux direction with nanosecond thin-film switching and no transistor per cell.
why: Unlimited endurance, non-volatile, radiation-hard, uses only Ni, Fe and Cu (no tungsten, EUV or silicon wafer); ~1 um^2 cells make it a niche or capacity tier, and destructive read plus half-select margins are the risks.

title: Let only ones fall: unidirectional-error codes replace frequent refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh must stop every bit from decaying': charge leakage only flips true-cells 1->0 (anti-cells 0->1), so store each row with a Berger-style count code (~10 check bits in opposite-polarity cells) that detects any number of unidirectional errors plus a Z-channel code that corrects them, and stretch refresh until the code margin is nearly consumed.
why: Refresh interval 64 ms -> ~0.5-1 s by tolerating tail-cell decay (fact 3) at ~2-4% storage overhead, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth and refresh energy.

title: Lazy restore: defer write-back after destructive reads
idea: Inverting 'every read must immediately restore full charge': the sense amp releases the row once cells are ~70% restored and logs the row in a small weak-row table; the refresh engine tops those rows up within their shortened retention window, or immediately if the row is re-activated.
why: tRAS -30-40%, higher bank throughput and ~15% lower row-cycle energy with little added logic.
note: Known as restore truncation (HPCA 2016).

title: Self-timed tiers: replica bitlines replace global worst-case timing
idea: Inverts 'the array runs to one synchronous timing spec.' Each tier/subarray carries a replica bitline whose sense completion fires a ready signal, so fast tiers return data early and slow tiers no longer set tRCD for the whole stack or cause scrap.
why: Facts 2 and 4: tier-to-tier variation in 3D becomes latency variance instead of yield loss; ~15-30% average latency gain and higher stack yield.

title: Edge-wired stacks: plated copper down die edges replaces TSVs
idea: Inverts 'vertical signals must pass through the die.' Stack thinned DRAM dies with staggered setbacks and plate or print Cu/Al traces down the stepped edges to the base die, so no TSV keep-out zones or TSV liners are needed.
why: Fact 6: removes much of HBM's TSV area tax and TSV yield loss, using Cu/Al only with no W or Ta.

title: Helium-free plasma tools: hydrogen backside gas, textured chucks
idea: Inverts 'etch and deposition chucks need helium backside cooling'. Use low-pressure H2 or H2/Ne backside gas (thermal conductivity ~1.2x He) with a micro-textured AlN chuck face and closed-loop recapture of all purge gas.
why: Helium is a live chokepoint (Qatar offline since March 2026); substitution plus recapture could cut fab helium use >90% at low capex.

title: Crystal planes do the etching: KOH slot capacitors
idea: Inverts 'high-aspect-ratio etch needs plasma tools'. In (110) silicon, KOH/TMAH wet etching stops on vertical {111} planes, giving atomically smooth slots >100:1 deep from stepper-defined (spacer-narrowed) openings; lined with dielectric they form deep slot capacitors that share walls between neighbouring cells.
why: Hits AR ~115 (fact 1) on a ~$200k wet bench instead of $5M+ etchers; density still needs sub-litho line pitch from a companion trick.

title: Self-limiting oxidation carves 10 nm channels from 180 nm lines
idea: Inverts 'channel width is printed'. Pattern 180 nm Si lines and use stress-retarded thermal oxidation, which self-limits as the core shrinks, to thin them to uniform ~10 nm wires in a 1990s furnace; strip and wrap with gate for gate-all-around access transistors.
why: Thin all-around channels tighten the leakage tail (fact 3) and cut refresh; sub-litho channels from a furnace, though cell pitch stays litho-bound.

title: Internal GB-second market where memory-hungry jobs must bid
idea: Inverts 'memory is free once the server is bought': the cluster scheduler prices resident memory per GB-second at a spot price set by scarcity. Elastic consumers (caches, JVM heaps, prefetch buffers) register demand curves and shrink automatically when the price rises.
why: Fleets strand 25-40% of DRAM in over-requested allocations; price signals reclaim much of it with no new hardware.

title: Hardware base-relative 32-bit pointers in every load unit
idea: Inverts 'pointers are 64-bit absolute addresses': an ISA extension lets loads and stores take a 32-bit offset plus a per-region base register, so graphs, trees and object heaps store half-width pointers natively with no software decode cost.
why: Pointer-dense heaps shrink 25-45% (as JVM compressed oops show in software), across every language.

title: Clockless self-timed DRAM interface with no PLL or DLL
idea: Invert 'memory is synchronous': replace the DLL/PLL and forwarded clocks with delay-insensitive 1-of-4 handshake signaling between base die and host, so links idle at zero power and run as fast as local voltage and temperature allow.
why: Clock trees and DLLs burn much of DRAM I/O idle power and need retraining; self-timed links take idle I/O power toward zero and drop training latency, ~20-30% interface energy saved at low utilization.

title: Printed staircase sidewalls replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Invert 'vertical interconnect must be drilled through the die': stack DRAM dies offset like stairs and print fine conductive lines down the exposed steps with U.S.-made aerosol-jet printers (New Mexico), linking each die's edge pads to the base.
why: No TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones and no 30 um thinning; removes much of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax using domestic tools.
note: Edge-pad count at 10-20 um printed pitch falls short of HBM wire counts.

title: Tin-free joints: sintered copper bonds from domestic copper
idea: Invert 'packages need tin-silver solder': join dies and stacks with sintered copper-nanoparticle paste or direct Cu-Cu thermocompression, using U.S.-mined copper and no tin, silver or indium.
why: The U.S. mines no tin; copper joints remove that import, conduct better, tolerate higher temperatures and reach finer pitch (<20 um) than solder microbumps.

title: Exponent bits in strong rows, mantissa LSBs in weak rows
idea: Inverts 'all bits are equally important': rows are ranked by retention at test; the controller's address swizzle uses the fused ranking so sign/exponent bytes of BF16/FP8 words land in top-retention rows and low mantissa bits in the weakest rows, which are refreshed 4-8x less often.
why: The retention tail (fact 3) no longer sets the refresh rate for most bits; ~50-70% refresh energy cut with <0.1% accuracy loss on weights.
note: Retention-binned placement of tolerant bits known (RAIDR/EDEN/Sparkk).

title: Known weak cells decoded as erasures, halving ECC parity
idea: Inverts 'errors are random and unknown': the weak-cell map from test and in-field scrub is held by the controller and fed to a Reed-Solomon decoder as erasure locations; RS corrects two erasures per unknown error, so the same parity tolerates twice the weak cells, or the same cells with half the parity.
why: Refresh can be set by the 1e-6 instead of the 1e-9 retention quantile (~4x longer interval), or ECC overhead drops from 12.5% to ~6%.
note: Same erasure-map decoding.

title: Elastic parity that grows as the chip ages
idea: Inverts 'ECC strength is fixed at design time': pages start with a light code (CRC+SEC); when a page's syndrome rate rises the controller allocates extra parity from a pooled spare region and re-encodes it with a stronger LDPC, spending protection only where wear and tail cells appear.
why: Average ECC overhead ~3% instead of 12.5% while weak or aged regions get >4x stronger protection; extends module service life.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-hosted as CXL memory via package harvesting
idea: Inverts 'DRAM retires with its server': automated depopulation lines desolder DDR4/DDR5 packages from decommissioned DIMMs, re-characterize each package at speed and temperature, and re-mount them on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller still speaks the old DRAM protocol.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit: reuses silicon whose fab capex is already sunk; at hyperscaler retirement volumes this could add roughly 5-10% of annual server DRAM bits at ~25% of new cost.
note: Whole-DIMM CXL reuse already shown; package-level harvest adds rework cost.

title: Open-source DRAM macro compiler for mature logic foundries
idea: Inverts 'DRAM know-how lives inside three companies': publish an open bitcell, sense-amp, refresh-controller and deep-trench/MIM capacitor kit plus compiler for 22-28 nm logic processes so any logic foundry can sell DRAM-class capacity as a standard product.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: taps idle mature-logic capacity with no new tools; density is 5-10x below commodity DRAM, but it diverts embedded and edge demand that today consumes commodity parts.

title: Resell retention-reject die as 1%-tolerant memory instead of scrapping
idea: Inverts 'a die that fails 64 ms retention is scrap': die whose weak-cell tail is too long for standard refresh go to controllers that map and code around up to 1% leaky cells while keeping the normal refresh rate.
why: Yield and cost: retention is a top fallout mode at 1a/1b nodes; recovering those die adds a few percent of bits per wafer at near-zero cost.

title: BER-certified secondary market prices used memory by error grade
idea: Inverts 'used memory is either good or junk': an exchange tests every returned module, issues a raw-BER certificate (0.001%, 0.1%, 1%), and lists it by grade, so 1%-tolerant controllers set a floor price for even badly aged modules.
why: Reuse supply: turns the whole secondary stream into priced, tradable bits instead of scrap; price discovery raises return rates.

title: Consumer frame buffers on noisy DRAM, freeing clean bits for servers
idea: Inverts 'consumer devices need server-grade integrity everywhere': phones, consoles and TVs put frame buffers, texture caches and media pipelines on a 1%-tolerant memory partition with light parity, where an occasional pixel error is invisible.
why: Supply allocation: graphics and media buffers are a large share of consumer DRAM; moving them to error-tolerant grade frees perfect bits for servers.

title: Nanomechanical parametron storing the bit as oscillation phase
idea: Pump a ~1 um GHz nanomechanical or contour-mode AlN resonator at 2*f0 so it oscillates in one of two degenerate phases, 0 or pi. Write by briefly injecting a small f0 signal of the chosen phase, read by homodyne phase detection, and share one pump line across many frequency-multiplexed resonators.
why: The symmetry-broken phase ignores amplitude noise and has no charge-leakage tail (fact 3). Density is weaker, which suits radiation-hard or cryogenic niches.
note: Electromechanical parametron memory demonstrated (Mahboob 2008); density limits it to niches.

title: Retention-reject die salvage with per-row refresh controller cards
idea: A die that fails a 64 ms retention screen usually fails because of a few hundred rows, not the whole die. Buy retention-downbinned DRAM at scrap prices and profile every row at 85 C on ~$50k FPGA testers. Sell CXL or DIMM cards whose controller refreshes the weak ~0.1% of rows at 16 ms and the rest at 64 ms. $1M covers testers, the controller FPGA image and first inventory within 24 months.
why: Adds usable bits from existing fabs at near-zero capital, recovering perhaps 1-3% of output that is scrapped or sold into low-grade markets today (supply, capital intensity, fact 3).
note: Same downbinned-die salvage.

title: Polarity-aware scrambling keeps most cells in the uncharged state
idea: Only charged cells decay, and 'charged' means '1' in true cells and '0' in anti-cells. Learn each row's true/anti layout with a one-time retention test. Then XOR each 64 B line with that map, plus a per-line inversion bit chosen to minimize charged cells, so zero-heavy data leaves most capacitors empty. Firmware and FPGA work, <$300k.
why: The charged-cell fraction drops from ~50% to ~10-40% depending on data. Decay-error rate falls in proportion, so ECC-backed refresh intervals can stretch further (fact 3).

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal of purchased finished DRAM wafers
idea: Interface and dangling-bond traps near storage junctions drive SRH tail leakage, and Si-D bonds resist depassivation better than Si-H. Buy finished DRAM wafers or known-good-die lots, run 20 atm D2 anneals at 350-400 C in a rented high-pressure furnace, and measure the retention-tail shift against control wafers. ~$300-500k including test, 15 months.
why: If the tail compresses even 2x, vendors can adopt a single back-end anneal step for 2x longer refresh (fact 3).
note: High-pressure H2/D2 anneal is already used by memory makers.

title: JEDEC retention-class mode register lets controllers trust each die
idea: Propose and fund a JEDEC ballot that adds a mode-register field where each die reports its own tested retention class per bank (64, 128, 256 or 512 ms at 85 C) from production test. Add a 'relaxed refresh permitted' bit tied to the vendor's warranty. $1M funds reference characterization data, a compliant FPGA controller and two years of standards work.
why: Vendors already measure retention but throw the result away into a worst-case spec. Exposing it lets every controller run at the die's real interval, a fleet-wide 2-4x cut in refresh overhead (fact 3).

title: Zero-entropy token row selection for AI weight streaming memory
idea: AI inference reads weights in a fixed order, so the address entropy per access is ~0 bits; a full row decoder supplies log2(N) bits of random choice that are wasted. Replace decoders with a pitch-matched shift-register token that walks rows sequentially, keeping only coarse random access at mat level.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and energy: row decode area ~70-90% smaller in a streaming tier, plus predictable access removes most precharge/activate overhead.

title: Leakage-replica analog refresh timer built from access transistors
idea: Make the refresh clock a capacitor discharged by a bank of access transistors identical to the array's (same doping, GIDL and junction), so its period follows the true leakage physics: ni ~7x up from 85 to 125 C and aging included, without temperature tables.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes 2-4x worst-case guardband, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss at hot.

title: Hot-mode dynamic twin-cell row pairing trades capacity for margin
idea: When a die or region runs hot, the controller pairs rows on complementary open bitlines into twin-cell mode (both wordlines fire, cells store opposite data), doubling differential signal and extending retention ~4-10x. Capacity halves only where and when needed.
why: Avoids designing all cells for worst-case 125 C retention (fact 1); refresh at hot drops sharply (fact 3).
note: Close to CLR-DRAM (ISCA 2020) dynamic capacity-latency twin-cell mode.

title: Self-referencing double read cancels printed transistor threshold scatter
idea: Read each printed cell, write a known '1', read again through the same bitline and sense amp, compare the two samples, then restore the original data, so the cell's own capacitor and TFT threshold become its reference.
why: Printed TFT Vt scatter (~100-300 mV) and +/-20% capacitor variation would collapse a fixed-reference sense margin; self-reference turns cell variation into common mode, tolerating ~10x worse variability at ~2x read time (~40-60 ns).

title: Capacitively coupled pads signal between laminated foils without vias
idea: Print 50x50 um pads facing each other across the 2 um adhesive between laminated foils and drive them with pulse signaling into a receiver, so tier-to-tier signals cross by AC coupling instead of drilled vias.
why: C=eA/d gives ~33 fF per pad pair against ~10 fF of receiver load, about 75% signal coupling, and pads tolerate the ~25 um registration of R2R lamination, removing via drilling, fill and their yield loss from foil stacks (the foil analogue of fact 6).

title: Microgram hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in every wafer chuck
idea: Kinetic theory: free-molecular gas-gap conductance scales ~P/sqrt(m), so H2 (m=2) moves ~1.4x more heat per Torr than He (m=4). An on-tool PEM electrolyzer feeds 5-10 Torr H2 into the ~1 cm3 chuck backside volume (~2 ug inventory, orders below any ignition hazard), with interlocked N2 purge.
why: Chuck backside cooling is a dominant fab helium use and Qatar (~30% of supply) has been offline since March 2026; removes He from etch/CVD chucks at near-zero consumable cost.

title: Fab waste heat drives ceramic membrane distillation for zero discharge
idea: Separating pure water from brine has a thermodynamic minimum near 1 kWh/m3 while a fab rejects ~100 MW of 30-45 C process-cooling heat; use that temperature difference to drive vacuum membrane distillation of RO reject and CMP effluent through silane-hydrophobized alumina/SiC membranes instead of PTFE/PVDF.
why: Raises water recovery from ~60-70% to >95% on free heat, cutting withdrawal ~30-50% at drought-prone US sites with PFAS-free membranes.

title: Molecular-monolayer doping replaces arsine, phosphine and ion implanters
idea: A junction needs ~1e13-1e15 dopant atoms/cm2, roughly one molecular monolayer; graft phosphonate or boronate monolayers from solution with dose set by ligand footprint, cap with oxide and spike-anneal. It is conformal, so it dopes 3D sidewalls that implanters cannot reach.
why: Removes toxic, concentrated dopant gases (AsH3, PH3, B2H6) and ~100+ kW implanters per tool, and enables doping of buried 3D tiers.

title: Electrochemically regenerated wet chemistry: etchants as closed loops
idea: First principle: in most cleans the oxidant is consumed but the acid matrix is not. Regenerate sulfuric-peroxide (SPM) on site as electrochemical persulfate, recover HF/HNO3 by membrane distillation, and electrowin dissolved metals, so wet benches run closed-loop.
why: Water, chemicals and opex: ~70% less chemical purchase and much less UPW; eases U.S. permitting.

title: Electrorefine wafering kerf back into crystal feedstock
idea: First principle: diamond-wire slicing turns ~100-150 um of 11N Si per cut into sludge, yet the Si atoms are still pure. Collect the kerf, separate abrasive and coolant, strip the surface oxide, and electrorefine and remelt it into polysilicon feedstock for the next boule.
why: Scarce resource and polysilicon cost: recovers ~15-25% of crystal mass now lost per wafer; recycled by design.

title: Content-hashed singleton cache for model weights across a rack
idea: Inference hosts each keep 10-30 model checkpoints in host DRAM for fast swapping, mostly the same popular open weights. Hash each 2 MB weight page and keep one physical copy in a rack CXL appliance, mapped read-only into every host; LoRA adapters and private fine-tunes stay local.
why: Host-side model caches shrink 10-30x per rack (N identical copies down to 1), freeing hundreds of GB per server for KV offload or cutting host DRAM purchases.

title: Approximate-grade DRAM bins sold for error-tolerant tensors
idea: Dies that fail retention binning or exceed their redundancy still hold 99.999% good bits. Bin and sell them as approximate-grade modules with a published bad-cell map; the OS maps only error-tolerant pages there (NN activations, media, sketches), and the map steers sign and exponent bits onto known-good columns.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering 5-15% of dies that are now scrapped or down-binned, with no new fab capital.

title: Pulse-position one-hot coding: one wire toggle carries eight bits
idea: Interconnect energy is paid per transition, not per bit. On wide hybrid-bond buses where wires are cheap, send each byte by toggling exactly one of 256 wires (position = value), or 1 of 16 wires in 1 of 16 time slots; edge-detecting receivers decode. Random NRZ spends ~4 transitions per byte, this spends 1.
why: ~4x fewer charge events per bit on die-to-die links (fact 5); multiplies with low-swing gains.

title: Delta-merge-on-read lets thousands of fine-tunes share one base
idea: A fine-tuned model differs from its base by a low-rank delta under 1% of parameters. A delta-merge unit in the memory base die applies each tenant's LoRA or sparse delta as base weights stream out, so 100+ tenants each appear to own a full model while memory holds one base plus tiny deltas.
why: Memory per served model ~100x lower; trades a few % quality versus full fine-tunes and adds base-die compute.
note: Software multi-LoRA serving (S-LoRA, Punica) already shares one base; base-die merge adds little.

title: Poisson-tail-derived scrubbing replaces 64 ms refresh
idea: Fit the measured retention distribution and compute the expected failures per 1 KB row at a 1 s interval (~0.5). Choose BCH t=6 per row so P(uncorrectable) < 1e-18, then replace blanket refresh with a read-correct-writeback scrub every 1 s.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~15x less refresh energy and bandwidth, and tail cells become acceptable rather than repaired.
note: Known (Hi-ECC, ECC-based refresh extension); VRT is the doubt.

title: One end-to-end code replaces on-die ECC, link CRC, host ECC
idea: DDR5 pays separately for on-die SEC (6.25%), link CRC and host SECDED/chipkill. Shannon does not care where the noise enters. Encode once at the host with one long code, store it raw, and decode at the host using soft information from the link.
why: Periphery/overhead (fact 7): recovers ~6% die area and energy while correcting more errors.

title: Licensed gain-cell PDK plus scrub controller for U.S. logic fabs
idea: U.S. logic foundries have no capacitor module but can build BEOL gain cells. A company licenses them a bundle: gain-cell bitcell PDK, drift-compensation/scrub controller IP and a qualification report, for a per-wafer royalty. That turns underused 28-16 nm capacity into capacitorless memory dies.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: no new DRAM fab, so supply comes from existing tools within ~2 years.
note: Gain-cell IP for logic fabs exists; density far below commodity DRAM.

title: Lawnmower-pattern weight streaming makes inference itself the refresh
idea: Random stimulus 'lawnmower': one planned pass covers the whole lawn. The inference runtime lays out weights so every token's weight sweep visits every HBM row in the refresh counter's order within tREFW; because activation restores the row, the base die verifies the sweep and suppresses explicit refresh for every row it covered.
why: LLM decoding reads all weights every ~20-50 ms, so explicit refresh can drop >90%; refresh energy and its embedded generation and cooling water fall >10x for inference HBM (fact 3).
note: Same inference-sweep-as-refresh mechanism.

title: Tuning fork: analog trim cell retunes every sense amp offset
idea: Like filing a tuning fork to pitch, each SA gets one DRAM-style trim capacitor on its tail node; at power-up and then every refresh window the bitlines are shorted and a calibration loop pumps charge onto that cap until the latch flips at zero input, so the offset correction is stored as analog charge and refreshed like data.
why: Periphery area: SA devices are upsized only to beat Pelgrom mismatch; nulling ~80% of offset lets them shrink ~4x in area (SA strip ~25-35% smaller) or halves the bitline signal needed, easing the capacitor wall.
note: Dynamic offset-cancellation sense amps already in production DRAM.

title: Post-it notes: module controller remaps bad rows, fuses removed
idea: Instead of burning fixes into each die, stick notes on the module: dies ship without e-fuse banks or redundancy-steering comparators, and the CXL/buffer controller keeps a remap table of bad rows and columns found at test (stored in SPD flash) that redirects to spare rows pooled across every die on the module.
why: Periphery area and yield: fuse banks and spare-steering logic are ~3-6% of die; pooling spares at module level also lifts usable-die yield by a few percent.

title: Tin-can telephone: 60 mV ground-referenced global data lines
idea: A tin-can telephone carries a voice on a whisper of energy. Drive the mm-long on-die global data lines with ground-referenced ~60 mV swings from capacitively divided drivers and receive with clocked offset-trimmed sense amps, instead of full 1.1 V CMOS swings.
why: Global data-line energy scales with swing x supply: 60 mV vs ~1 V cuts it ~10-15x; global I/O is ~20-30% of DRAM access energy.

title: Impressionist painting: low-swing lossy sensing for low-order bit planes
idea: An impressionist painting only needs the broad strokes right. Store AI tensors so the low-order bit planes live in dedicated mats that run at VARY ~0.4 V and short sense times with an allowed raw bit error rate of ~1e-4, while sign and exponent planes run at full margin with ECC.
why: ~6x less CV2 energy on the 50-75% of bits that are low-order, about 10x on those mats, with negligible model-accuracy loss from LSB flips; a precision-aware access mode is needed in the controller.

title: Shingled roof: TSV-free 3DS DDR5 via printed staircase edge traces
idea: Roof shingles overlap in steps: stack 4-8 DDR5 dies offset by 150 um in a staircase, and aerosol-jet or EHD-print 10-20 um silver traces down the exposed step edges to link each die's pads to the substrate in place of TSVs. The result is a standard 3DS DDR5 RDIMM device with an unchanged interface.
why: TSV tax (fact 6) for high-capacity server memory: no TSV area, keep-out or TSV yield loss; claim die area -6-8% and 3DS stack cost -20%.
note: Edge-interconnect shingled stacks known (VIC-style).

title: Tea bag: chelating cartridges leach hafnium, ruthenium, tantalum from shields
idea: Stimulus 'tea bag' (steep, then lift out the goodness) -> steep used PVD/ALD chamber shields and target backing plates in mild oxidizing baths and pass the leachate through selective chelating-resin cartridges (hydroxamate for Hf/Zr, thiourea for Ru) to recover metal for target and precursor remanufacture.
why: 60-80% of sputtered or ALD metal ends up on shields and targets, not wafers; closing the loop could halve primary Hf/Ru/Ta demand.
note: Shield and target reclamation exists; selective resin recovery is incremental.

title: Velcro: capillary self-alignment for massively parallel die-to-wafer HBM bonding
idea: Random stimulus 'Velcro' (rough placement, self-locking) -> dies are dropped roughly onto hydrophilic bonding sites wetted with a water film, and surface tension pulls each die to sub-micron alignment before direct hybrid bonding. Thousands of dies are placed in parallel instead of one at a time by precision bonders.
why: HBM TSV tax and capital (fact 6): high-accuracy D2W bonders run ~$3-5M each at low throughput. Fluidic placement could raise stacking throughput ~10x and allows yield-sorted known-good dies.

title: Pawn shop: internal market where idle gigabytes are pledged
idea: Tenants pawn idle memory: a broker daemon pays credits for GB released through a balloon driver, guarantees redemption within 50 ms from a compressed/CXL reserve, and clears prices by auction every minute so memory flows to the highest-value job.
why: Prices reveal and recover idle allocations (often 30-50%); 15-25% fewer DIMMs per fleet and a direct lever during the 4x price spike.

title: Firefly anti-sync: scheduler de-phases co-located memory peaks
idea: Fireflies synchronize; we do the opposite: the cluster scheduler profiles each job's periodic memory peaks (optimizer steps, checkpoints, GC, batch spikes) and shifts their phases so peaks on a shared pool never coincide, then sizes the pool for the sum of averages. Pure scheduling, nothing fabricated.
why: Shared-pool DRAM falls 20-35% for periodic workloads.

title: Sushi conveyor: time-slotted page carousel ring for shared reads
idea: Memory chiplets put pages onto a circulating, time-slotted ring bus like dishes on a sushi belt; every accelerator snoops the passing slot and takes what it needs. Shared data such as batched-inference weights is read from DRAM once and consumed by N devices.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth for broadcast data: N-fold fewer DRAM reads of shared weights, so fewer HBM stacks are needed per cluster.
note: Ring-bus broadcast of shared weights; lockstep consumption required.

title: Tide: lanes reverse direction as read/write traffic ebbs and flows
idea: Like tides: memory link lanes are bidirectional and are reassigned between read and write direction every microsecond from traffic counters, so read-heavy inference gets nearly all the lanes.
why: Bandwidth per wire, about 1.6x effective read bandwidth for inference, so fewer pins, TSVs or stacks are needed.
note: DDR/HBM DQs are already bidirectional; only SerDes links gain.

title: Thrift store: buy fab-reject DRAM dies, remap bad rows in controller
idea: Like a thrift store selling flawed goods: buy partial-good DRAM dies that fail fab repair budgets at scrap prices, package them conventionally, and pair them with a controller (FPGA or CXL ASIC firmware) that holds large per-die bad-row and weak-cell remap tables.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer already produced, perhaps 2-5% more effective supply, at very low cost per bit.

title: Metronome: compiled deterministic DRAM schedule for AI inference
idea: Like a metronome: compile a model's entire memory access stream ahead of time into a fixed tape of activate, read, refresh and precharge commands that avoids bank conflicts and refresh collisions. An FPGA-with-HBM controller plays the tape back.
why: Raises HBM bandwidth utilization from ~60% to ~90%, about 1.5x more work per stack, so fewer stacks are needed.

title: Kaleidoscope: link-level cache-line dedup dictionary at both ends
idea: Like a kaleidoscope's repeated patterns: small matched dictionaries at the memory controller and in the CXL device remember recently sent 64B lines, and a repeated line crosses the link as a 10-bit index. Prototyped in FPGA RTL.
why: Link bandwidth and pJ/bit: 1.3-2x effective bandwidth on zero-heavy or duplicate-heavy traffic.
note: Same as matched-dictionary link dedup.

title: Abacus: accumulate-on-write memory-side atomics halve gradient traffic
idea: Like beads sliding on an abacus: the memory controller on an FPGA card adds incoming partial sums into stored values, so writes are atomic accumulate operations and no read-modify-write round trip is needed.
why: Halves link traffic for gradient accumulation and histograms; saves both energy and bandwidth.
note: Same accumulate-on-write mechanism, FPGA demo.

title: Firefly: burst-mode memory link wakes from off in 10 ns
idea: Like a firefly blinking: the memory PHY powers fully off between bursts and relocks in under 10 ns by keeping a forwarded clock and stored equalizer state, prototyped first on FPGA transceivers and then on a cheap MPW test chip.
why: Idle and low-utilization link power: energy per bit at 20% utilization falls 3-5x.

title: Paperclip: clip-on backside LPDDR module with pressure contacts
idea: Forced 'paperclip': a spring-clip frame presses an LPDDR module onto pads on the back of the processor substrate, directly behind the die, through compliant pogo/elastomer contacts. Traces get millimeters long, and the module stays field-replaceable.
why: I/O energy and capacity flexibility; near-PoP energy with upgradability, so less memory is overprovisioned at purchase.
note: Close to LPCAMM compression-attached modules; backside placement is the twist.

title: Tuning fork: resonant LC clocking for low-power memory PHY
idea: Like a tuning fork ringing at its natural frequency: on-die LC tanks resonate the forwarded clock distribution of a memory PHY, recycling clock charge instead of burning it, demonstrated on one ~$150k MPW shuttle.
why: Clocking is often 30-40% of PHY power; 20-30% lower interface pJ/bit.

title: Insurance pool: rack-level erasure coding across CXL memory devices
idea: As insurers pool risk, a CXL switch stripes each 4 KB page across 10+2 memory devices with Reed-Solomon parity computed in the switch, so individual devices can drop on-die ECC, chipkill and most spare rows and may even lose whole banks.
why: Removes ~12% ECC plus spare area per device and admits lower-grade dies; 20% pooled parity covers device-level failures across the rack.
note: Similar to Carbink/Hydra far-memory erasure coding; write parity updates costly.

title: Jazz wrong notes: bit-plane retention tiers for AI weights and KV-cache
idea: In jazz a wrong note resolves into the next; BF16/FP8 tensors are stored transposed by bit-plane, with sign/exponent/high-mantissa planes in normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes in rows with 8-16x longer refresh and no ECC, where flips dissolve into model noise.
why: Fact 3: roughly half of AI bits tolerate 1e-4 BER, cutting refresh power and ECC overhead on half the capacity.

title: Tattoo map: weak-row map inked into on-die OTP, standardized in JEDEC
idea: The fab's retention and hammer test map is permanently burned into on-die antifuse OTP in a standard JEDEC 'weak map' register format, so any controller can read it and apply targeted refresh, ECC placement or remapping.
why: Fabs over-design because controllers are blind; a standard map lets them ship lower-Cs, higher-variability dies for ~10% density/yield gain.
note: Same standardized weak-row map idea.

title: Hotel keycard: polarity encoding minimizes charged cells; empty rows skip refresh
idea: Like lights cutting off when the keycard leaves, each line stores a polarity bit chosen to minimize physically charged cells, and rows whose cells are all discharged (zeroed or free pages) set a per-row flag that skips refresh entirely.
why: Only charged cells leak: at 125 C halving the charged population and exempting empty rows (often 20-40% of memory) slashes hot refresh energy and exposure over 10 years.

title: Pothole map: temperature-binned weak maps convert errors into erasures
idea: Like a road crew's pothole map, the controller keeps compact weak-cell maps per temperature bin (85/105/125 C) learned in-field; at the current temperature those positions are decoded as erasures, which cost half as much as unknown errors in RS/BCH.
why: At 125 C the weak set is large but predictable; roughly doubles effective ECC strength and allows 2-4x longer hot refresh across the 10-year life.

title: Carpool: broker stranded datacenter DRAM as RDMA far-memory blocks
idea: Random stimulus 'carpool' -> empty seats in cars already driving. A cross-tenant broker inside a cloud region measures stranded DRAM (cores sold out, memory left over) and leases it as RDMA/CXL-over-fabric far-memory blocks to memory-hungry tenants with eviction SLAs.
why: Stranded memory is often 20-35% of installed DRAM; reclaiming half of it raises usable supply ~10-15% without one new die.

title: Lego: idle 28-40nm logic fabs make UCIe DRAM brick chiplets
idea: Random stimulus 'Lego brick' -> small standard bricks build anything. Underused 28-40 nm logic fabs make 1-2 Gb DRAM chiplets using BEOL MIM/trench capacitors and a standard UCIe edge, which are stacked and tiled into larger memories.
why: Low density (~0.1-0.2 Gb/mm2) but zero EUV, available today in US and allied mature fabs; adds surge supply for embedded and edge buyers to free leading-edge DRAM.

title: Origami: fold-stacked thinned DRAM die on printed flex, no TSVs
idea: Random stimulus 'origami crane' -> one sheet folded into 3D. Thinned DRAM die are mounted on R2R-printed polyimide flex carrying fine traces; the flex is folded zig-zag so the die stack vertically with wiring around the folds instead of through-silicon vias.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) for capacity-oriented stacks; bandwidth below HBM but bits per wafer ~2x higher.
note: Fold-over flex stacks (Tessera uZ) are known; bandwidth below TSV stacks.

title: Coffee filter: R2R-coated membranes recover fab and low-grade helium
idea: Random stimulus 'coffee filter' -> a cheap sheet that passes one thing. Roll-to-roll coated mixed-matrix membranes, rolled into spiral modules, recover helium from tool exhaust (He in N2/Ar) and extract it from 0.1-0.5% helium US natural-gas streams.
why: Closes the fab helium loop (>80% recapture) and taps domestic gas, removing the Qatar chokepoint from DRAM output.

title: SiC deep-depletion inversion-charge cell with hour-long retention
idea: Box = {medium: minority-carrier inversion charge under a SiC MOS gate | access: lateral SiC transfer gate | sense: charge transfer to a floating diffusion + source follower | integration: dedicated SiC memory die bonded to Si logic | substrate: U.S.-made 200 mm 4H-SiC (North Carolina/New York) | fab: U.S. SiC power-device lines}. SiC's 3.26 eV bandgap cuts thermal generation by ~1e-18 relative to silicon, so a deep-depletion well holds charge for hours at 85 C; it is the original inversion-layer 1T DRAM concept, minus refresh.
why: Fact 3: refresh disappears (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth), using U.S. SiC capacity that swings with power-device demand.
note: SiC DRAM long retention shown in 1990s (Purdue); low density.

title: Gated-diode amplifying storage node that boosts its own signal
idea: Box = {medium: charge in a Si gated-diode (MOS varactor) node | access: one Si FET | sense: on read the gate is pulsed so the varactor drops from inversion to depletion capacitance (~5x lower), raising node voltage ~5x before charge sharing | integration: planar 2T-class cell | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: standard domestic CMOS with no high-k capacitor}. The storage element amplifies itself (Q fixed, C collapses), so the cell needs only ~1 fF and no pillar.
why: Fact 1 and capital: removes the high-AR capacitor and its dielectric, so the cell can be built on existing domestic logic lines.
note: Same gated-diode self-amplifying node.

title: Liquid-nitrogen CXL memory sleds with refresh switched off
idea: Box: unmodified 1T1C dies x standard access at 77 K x standard SA x CXL memory sled immersed in LN2 x Si x no fab change, LN2 piped from on-site air separation. At 77 K junction and subthreshold leakage drop >1e6x so refresh is disabled, and lower wire resistance trims I/O energy.
why: Removes refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) and permits lower Vt/VPP (fact 10) for pooled capacity; helium-free cryogen. Cryocooling overhead limits it to dense pooled tiers.

title: Refresh-free transient zones for AI KV-cache and activations
idea: Box: standard DRAM/HBM x standard access x standard sense x controller tags rows as transient with a write timestamp x system x Si x firmware. Accelerator runtimes guarantee activation and KV-cache blocks are rewritten or freed within 32 ms, so the controller skips refresh on rows written within tRET and on freed rows.
why: Much of HBM holds data younger than tRET; skipping its refresh recovers 10-20% bandwidth and refresh power (fact 3) on the scarcest memory.
note: Skip refresh for recently written rows (Smart Refresh-style); needs runtime guarantees.

title: Bit-significance mats: AI weight LSBs on cheap unprotected mats
