idea: Box: mixed caps x Si access x two SA grades x bit-plane-split mats x bulk Si x standard. Model weights are stored bit-plane-sliced: MSB planes go to mats with full ECC, while LSB planes go to long-bitline, small-SA, rarely refreshed mats where 1% flips move a value by <0.4% of range, which inference ignores.
why: Unequal error protection: ~60% of bits live on mats with ~40% less periphery and ~10x less refresh.

title: Truncated restore: shorten write-back, accept 1% under-restored cells
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x early-terminated restore x standard x bulk Si x standard. After the destructive read the SA stops restoring at ~70% of full level, cutting tRAS/tRC ~30%; the few cells left too weak for the next read fall inside the code budget, and refresh tops them up.
why: Destructive-read cost: row cycle time ~-30%, higher bank throughput, less energy per activation.
note: Restore truncation is published art; using ECC budget for under-restored cells is a mild twist.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal trims the access-transistor leakage tail
idea: Box [standard cap | Si access with deuterium-passivated gate oxide and junction | standard | standard | Si | 10-20 atm D2 anneal at 400 C replacing Ar/forming-gas anneals]: Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation ~10x better than Si-H, so the trap sites behind trap-assisted GIDL stay passivated.
why: Leakage tail (13 fA) and refresh energy: pushing tail retention out 2-4x lets the refresh interval double or quadruple, roughly halving refresh power (16-33% of idle), using D2 rather than any rare gas.

title: Hydrogen-backside electrostatic chucks free etch and deposition from helium
idea: Box: unchanged cell x fab-method axis set to backside thermal gas. Replace helium backside cooling on electrostatic chucks (capacitor cryo-etch, CVD, ALD) with low-pressure H2 or forming gas, whose thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/m-K) matches helium, inside a closed recirculating plenum with on-site electrolytic H2, catalytic recombiner and leak sensors.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): backside cooling and leak check are the main fab helium uses; removing them de-risks wafer output; risk is safety qualification and edge-plasma interaction.

title: Block-copolymer holes hardened by sequential infiltration for deep etch
idea: Box: Si trench charge x planar access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x PS-b-PMMA cylinder graphoepitaxy in EBL-written guides, ALD sequential infiltration (TMA/H2O) turning PMMA into an AlOx hardmask, then cryo-DRIE. This yields 20-30 nm holes at ~40 nm pitch with a self-made inorganic mask robust enough for AR >30 silicon etch.
why: EUV-free sub-40 nm hole arrays (fact 4) from a spin coater, ALD and ICP; risk is DSA defectivity (needs ~1/cm2) and placement error.

title: Controller dictionary stores the 4,096 commonest lines as 12-bit handles
idea: Box: dictionary dedup × memory controller × 64 B line × on write × epoch-learned value table. The controller keeps a hardware dictionary of frequent full-line values (zeros, fill patterns, padding, one-hot rows) and stores matching lines as 12-bit handles in compact pages, refreshing the dictionary at epoch boundaries.
why: Zero and pattern lines are 10–30% of memory in many workloads; holding them at 12 bits per line gives 1.15–1.4× capacity for a few mm² of logic.

title: Scheduler anti-phases jobs' memory peaks, provisioning for p95 not peak
idea: Box: time-multiplex × cluster scheduler × job × forecast-triggered × small CXL burst pool. Each job's footprint curve is forecast (shuffle phases, eval passes, nightly batches) and jobs are packed so peaks interleave; rare collisions borrow from a small rack burst pool.
why: Servers are sized for peak and peak-to-mean ratios run 1.5–3×; anti-phase packing can cut installed DRAM 20–35%.

title: Internal exchange leases stranded server DRAM by the GB-minute
idea: Box: share × datacenter market × GB-minute × auction-triggered × CXL switch or RDMA delivery. Each server offers its idle DRAM on an internal exchange; jobs bid for GB-minutes delivered over the pooled fabric and owners' budgets are credited.
why: 25–40% of fleet DRAM sits idle at any moment; recapturing it cuts new DRAM purchases 10–25%.
note: Memtrade-style idle memory markets exist.

title: Single coherent copy shared by CPU, GPU and NIC kills bounce buffers
idea: Box: eliminate copies × coherent fabric × buffer × allocation time × one physical copy over CXL.cache or chip-to-chip links. Pipelines that hold the same tensor in pinned host memory, GPU memory and NIC staging use one coherent allocation with zero-copy DMA.
why: Staging and bounce buffers occupy 10–30% of host DRAM in AI servers; removing two of three copies frees most of it.

title: Sense-amp XOR delta encoding transmits only flipped bits
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x SA with XOR against a shadow latch holding the last-sent word x transition-coded TSVs x Si x standard. Each column remembers what it last sent; the SA outputs the XOR so a wire toggles only when a bit changed, and the receiver re-integrates.
why: Data movement energy: switching activity on correlated AI tensor streams falls 40-60%, cutting TSV and interposer I/O energy proportionally.

title: Bit-significance routing across strong and derated memory pools
idea: Box [medium: recycled or derated DRAM dies | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: CXL memory pool | substrate: reclaimed DIMMs | fab: legacy]. A CXL controller bit-slices bf16/fp8 tensors so sign and exponent bits land in a chipkill-protected pool while low mantissa bits land in end-of-life or out-of-spec dies with no ECC and 4x relaxed refresh.
why: Supply: returns retired and downbinned DRAM to service; ~30-50% of AI memory capacity can tolerate flips with <1% accuracy impact.

title: Po: the bit runs forever — kinetic-inductance fluxon nanowire loops
idea: Po: the bit is a current that runs forever. Extracted: ~100 nm NbN nanowire loops whose kinetic inductance (~100x geometric) lets one flux quantum be held in a tiny loop at 4 K; the bit is the direction of the persistent current, read by a shunted nanowire switch, as working memory for cryogenic AI racks.
why: Zero leakage and aJ-scale switching for cryo compute; loop area far below classic SQUID memory cells. Needs 4 K and NbN film uniformity.
note: Kinetic-inductance nanowire memories demonstrated (MIT); cryo niche.

title: Compress rows and pad with discharged cells that cannot decay
idea: Po: most memory is empty. The controller compresses each row, writes the payload into the fewest cells, fills the rest with the discharged state (which in true cells cannot leak into an error) and picks per-row polarity so most bits sit in the safe state; rows flagged all-safe skip refresh.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh; with ~2x compressibility and polarity choice, 50-70% of charged cells vanish and many rows skip refresh entirely.

title: Po: let the sense amp guess — early fire plus ECC
idea: Po: a sense amp allowed to be wrong. Fire the latch at ~40% of the normal signal-development time and accept raw bit errors ~1e-5, then correct with a strong on-die BCH code over 512-bit words computed in the periphery during the column access.
why: Capacitor wall (#1): either tRCD falls ~30% or Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~3 fF at today's timing, avoiding AR-115 pillars; the ECC logic costs ~3% die, far less than a capacitor-etch generation.

title: Po: weakest cousins schedule refresh — canary-cell mats
idea: Po: memory that is told when to refresh by its weakest relatives. Each mat holds one row of canary cells with deliberately shrunk capacitors (~60% Cs), sensed by the normal SAs at each refresh; the mat's refresh interval doubles while all canaries hold and halves on the first canary failure, tracking process and temperature automatically.
why: Refresh (#3): most mats can run 2-4x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss at <0.2% area, with per-mat rather than per-die worst-case margins.

title: Po: grade chips like diamonds — per-bank sense-margin timing
idea: Po: memory graded stone by stone. At test, measure sense margin and retention per bank and write per-bank tRCD/tRAS/tREFI tables into SPD; controllers run each bank at its own timing, so dies that miss a single global spec on a few banks are sold instead of scrapped.
why: Usable supply: recovers ~5-10% of dies that fail global bins and gives ~15% average latency gain on strong banks with no fab change.

title: Identical tiers self-number at power-up for stack-to-order capacity
idea: Po: tiers don't know who they are. Design every tier from one mask set with no tier-specific wiring; a daisy-chained token climbs the stack at power-up and each tier latches its address, so one assembly line builds 4- to 64-tier parts from the same wafers to match weekly demand.
why: Masks and capital: one mask set instead of per-tier variants; build-to-order capacity raises usable supply during shortages.

title: AI decode sweep doubles as free refresh by layout
idea: Po: the workload is the refresh controller. Stripe LLM weights so each token's matrix-vector pass activates every row of every bank and tier exactly once, guaranteeing a full sweep every 20-40 ms; row-open counters (already present for row-hammer tracking) certify coverage and the device issues zero refresh commands.
why: Refresh (fact 3): for inference memory, refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax drop to zero because activation already restores charge.

title: Po helium is a fab export: closed-loop recapture at every tool
idea: Po: 'the fab exports helium instead of importing it.' Extracted: hood every helium user (ESC backside cooling exhaust, leak checkers, load-lock purge, carrier gas) with point-of-use recovery manifolds feeding a central compressor, a polymer-membrane pre-concentrator and a cryogenic purifier back to 6N, so purchases shrink to make-up for leakage.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% of supply offline since March 2026): 85-95% recovery cuts purchased helium ~10x and makes the fab immune to spot shortages; payback likely under 2 years at 2026 prices.

title: Po dies stacked without touching: inductive-coupled TSV-free HBM
idea: Po: 'stacked dies that never touch.' Extracted: replace thousands of copper TSVs with on-die spiral-coil inductive transceivers that couple data through 20-50 um thinned dies, and bring power in through edge-plated pads, so DRAM dies need no TSV keep-out zones and no via-reveal process.
why: HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area per bit vs DDR5, yield down 20-30%): recovers most TSV area plus copper fill and reveal steps; coil arrays sit in top metal over the array.
note: ThruChip-style inductive coupling known; power delivery without TSVs limits HBM-class stacks.

title: Po chips talk through their sides: edge-metallized DRAM die cube
idea: Po: 'dies speak through their edges, not their faces.' Extracted: lap 180 nm DRAM dies to ~100 um, laminate 32-64 of them with adhesive, polish one face of the stack, and sputter and photo-pattern sidewall bus lines that join edge-routed pads (the 1990s Irvine Sensors memory-cube approach).
why: HBM TSV tax and density: 32-64x bits per footprint with no TSVs, no hybrid bonding and no copper via fill, all on U.S. 200 mm-era tools.

title: Po light digs the holes: electrochemical macroporous silicon trench capacitors
idea: Po: 'let light dig the holes.' Extracted: seed pits with a KrF stepper, then anodize n-type silicon in HF under backside illumination so pores grow straight to aspect ratios of 100-250 with no plasma; line them with thermal oxide/nitride and fill with doped poly to form trench storage capacitors.
why: Capacitor charge wall (AR ~115 needed) reached without plasma etch or high-k: at ~0.4 um pore pitch and AR ~200, Cs of 30-60 fF with ONO, which relaxes refresh; no Hf, Zr, W or fluorocarbon gas.

title: Fab in reverse: harvest DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Po: the fab runs backwards. Industrialize de-population of retired server DIMMs and boards: desolder packages, re-ball, test and rebin them into CXL memory expanders for tier-2 workloads, with a controller that tolerates mixed speed grades.
why: Capital intensity: ~1/100 of new-fab capex per GB; hyperscalers retire tens of petabytes per year, a few percent of global bit supply available within months.
note: Die-level variant of retired-server memory reuse in I-03937.

title: Hash joins without hash tables: in-bank PIM probe units
idea: Po: the CPU lives inside the RAM. Compare-and-gather units beside each DRAM bank scan the build-side relation in place and stream out only matching tuple IDs, so analytical joins and group-bys never materialize multi-GB hash tables in main memory.
why: Intermediate hash tables can be 1-3x input size in analytics; in-bank probing removes them and cuts data-movement energy (facts 5, 8).
note: Demonstrable on UPMEM; PIM joins already studied.

title: Replay paging: record once, then run forever with oracle prefetch
idea: Po: memory arrives from the future. Recurring batch jobs (ETL, training epochs, nightly simulations) record their exact page-access trace on the first run; later runs replay it as a deterministic prefetch/evict schedule from SSD or CXL-flash, so DRAM holds only the lookahead window.
why: Repetitive jobs can run with 20-30% of peak working set in DRAM at near-zero stall, freeing capacity for interactive work.
note: Record/replay prefetching known; trace divergence limits gains.

title: Three-life DIMMs: cascade U.S.-made modules from AI to edge
idea: Po: the same 42 mg of silicon is sold three times. U.S.-made modules are leased with take-back: first life in AI servers, then re-tested and re-binned (speed, ECC margin, row-hammer threshold) in U.S. facilities for web tiers, then remounted on CXL cards for cold-tier and edge use, stretching service life from ~5 to ~10-12 years.
why: Roughly halves new-DRAM demand per unit of deployed capacity over a decade and keeps scarce domestic bits in service.

title: Shingled staircase HBM wired by printed edge traces
idea: Po: holes in silicon are forbidden. Offset each DRAM die ~200 um like a NAND staircase and connect the exposed edge pads with aerosol-jet-printed copper traces running down the steps to the base die, giving a TSV-free stack with a few thousand edge links.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss), letting core dies cost like DDR5 dies while keeping a wide stacked interface.
note: Same staircase printed-trace mechanism.

title: Descriptor-driven HBM: send access programs, not addresses
idea: Po: the processor never names an address. The GPU sends compact tensor access descriptors (base, strides, tile shape) to an address generator on the HBM base die, which walks rows in bank-friendly order and streams data back without per-line commands.
why: Frees command/address pins and link energy, and lets the stack fetch full rows usefully, cutting overfetch energy per useful bit.
note: Same descriptor-driven base-die address generation.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs with one top-metal mask
idea: Po: dies talk by magnetism. One added thick top-metal mask forms coil arrays on each DRAM die; dies are stacked face-to-back with no TSVs, data crosses by near-field inductive coupling through the thinned silicon, and power arrives by edge wire bonds.
why: Removes TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal steps (HBM TSV tax) for a single mask; ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vertical links.

title: Bit-plane transposition gives each bit significance its own refresh
idea: Po: low bits don't deserve to be remembered. The controller transposes bf16/fp8 tensors into bit planes in separate rows; sign/exponent planes refresh at 64 ms, upper mantissa at 256 ms, and the bottom three mantissa planes at 2 s or never (they are regenerated by the next training step).
why: Refresh (fact 3) for AI tensor regions: ~50-60% fewer refreshes; weak-tail rows can be assigned to LSB planes instead of being repaired.

title: Leak-aligned inversion encoding keeps most cells discharged
idea: Po: memory that refuses to store ones. Retention errors only hit charged cells, so per 64-bit word the controller inverts the word (1 flag bit) whenever it would charge more than half the cells, respecting true-cell/anti-cell layout; sparse ML data then leaves only ~10-20% of cells charged.
why: Retention exposure (fact 3): halves or better the number of vulnerable cells, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~1.5% overhead.
note: Bus-invert style data inversion for retention.

title: Compression-funded strong ECC lets marginal dies pass
idea: Po: ECC bits that cost nothing. The controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta or zero-run); most real lines free 8+ bytes, which hold a strong BCH code, while incompressible lines fall back to standard SECDED and are steered to the strongest rows.
why: Yield: dies with higher weak-cell counts, previously scrapped, can ship, raising usable output ~5-10% with no extra ECC chips.

title: Triple-row majority refresh votes critical data clean in-DRAM
idea: Po: the sense amp is the judge. Page tables, kernel text and model metadata are kept as three copies in one subarray; at refresh the DRAM does a triple-row activation whose charge sharing yields the bitwise majority, written back to all three rows, so scrubbing happens with no data movement.
why: Protecting the few critical bytes in-array lets the bulk of the device run looser refresh/ECC; scrub energy ~100x lower than reading out to the controller.

title: Unequal protection for KV caches: guard exponents, expose mantissas
idea: Po: memory that forgets the details but keeps the gist. LLM KV-cache tensors are split so sign and exponent bits sit in a strongly coded region while mantissa bits sit raw in 1%-BER cells; softmax averaging turns sparse mantissa flips into a negligible perplexity change.
why: KV cache is a fast-growing share of inference DRAM; ~70% of its bits move to cheap, rarely refreshed cells with ~2% total code overhead.

title: Short-retention DRAM bins sold for ephemeral AI data
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16 or 32 ms are no longer scrapped; they are marked R16/R32 in SPD, priced lower, and paired with controllers that refresh 2-4x faster or host only data that lives <10 ms (activations, KV-cache scratch, network buffers).
why: Retention-tail failures are a major yield-loss bin; recovering them could add several percent sellable bits per wafer at zero capex; attacks cost per bit and supply.

title: Electromechanical parametron: bit stored as oscillation phase
idea: Worsen: store bits as static levels that drift and leak. Flip: store each bit as the 0 or pi phase of a parametrically pumped high-Q NEMS resonator (Goto's parametron revived mechanically); the shared pump line continuously sustains whichever phase was seeded, so the state cannot leak away.
why: Replaces refresh with continuous low-power pumping (fact 3), needs no capacitor (fact 1), and phase coding is noise-robust so voltages can drop (fact 10).
note: Duplicate of mechanical parametron.

title: Nanosecond protonic three-terminal bit with non-destructive channel read
idea: Worsen: use two-terminal cells where read and write fight over one path. Flip: store the bit as proton concentration in a 10 nm WO3 channel, moved through a phosphosilicate-glass electrolyte by ~5 ns gate pulses and read by channel conductance on a separate path at <0.1 V.
why: Non-volatile, non-destructive read (facts 3, 8) and sub-volt reads (fact 10); hydrogen is not a scarce resource.
note: Nanosecond protonic PSG/WO3 devices exist (MIT); retention and ~1e15 endurance unproven for working memory.

title: Rescue reject-bin DRAM die by remapping only the weak cells
idea: Worsen: scrap dies because a few thousand storage cells leak too fast. Flip: buy fail-bin and downgraded dies cheaply, run a 24-month retention census on an FPGA tester to map weak cells, and ship modules whose controller remaps those cells or refreshes them more often.
why: Raises usable supply now; salvaged dies cost ~30-50% of new per bit, and the program needs ~$1M of capital.

title: Image-sensor pinned photodiode as an ultra-low-leakage storage well
idea: Worsen: store charge right at a trap-filled Si/SiO2 surface. Flip: a CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode buries charge in a fully depleted well with ~1 e-/s dark current and lossless charge transfer; spend 24 months running blacked-out commercial sensors as memories, then a CIS-foundry shuttle for a compact 'dark pixel' memory cell.
why: Leakage ~1e4 below DRAM (fact 3), using the large CIS fab base instead of DRAM capacity.

title: Leak-direction encoding stores most cells in the discharged state
idea: Worse: store data so many cells hold leaky charge. Flip: a per-64-bit invert flag picks the polarity that maximizes cells in the non-leaking state (true or anti cell aware); rows whose vulnerable-cell count stays below an ECC-covered threshold get 4x longer refresh.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down 2-4x for ~1.5% capacity overhead.

title: OS-visible retention map steers long-lived pages to strong rows
idea: Worse: hide retention variation from software. Flip: the DIMM or CXL device reports per-region retention classes through a mailbox; the kernel puts page cache and cold heap in strong regions refreshed rarely and high-churn data in weak regions whose own write rate covers retention.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down 50%+ with no device change.

title: Hot-mode compression consolidates data before partial-array self-refresh
idea: Worse at 125 C: refresh every bank at the 4-8x hot rate even when half the data is compressible. Flip: when the die crosses 105 C, the controller compresses cold pages 2-3x into a subset of banks and power-gates the rest, so hot refresh covers fewer rows.
why: Hot self-refresh energy (fact 3) down 50-65%.

title: All-zero row tags let periphery answer reads without activation
idea: Worse: sense and restore 8 KB of zeros exactly like useful data. Flip: keep a per-row pattern tag in a small SRAM in the bank periphery; rows tagged all-zero or repeated-pattern are answered by the column logic without activating the row and skipped by refresh until written.
why: Refresh and overfetch (facts 3, 8): zero or duplicate pages are often 10-30% of memory; their refresh and activation energy goes to ~0.

title: Aerosol-jet printed edge wiring connects staircase-stacked memory dies
idea: Worse: drill TSVs through every HBM die. Flip: stack dies in an offset staircase with printed insulating ramps and aerosol-jet-print signal and power traces down the exposed edges, connecting pads tier to tier with no through-silicon vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area or TSV yield loss; cheaper stacking for capacity tiers.

title: Printed thermistor film maps hotspots for per-bank refresh rates
idea: Worse: refresh every bank at the hottest corner's rate. Flip: laminate a printed thermistor array film (NTC oxide or carbon ink) over each die or under the lid, read by the controller to set each bank's refresh from its true local temperature.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention roughly halves every ~10 C, so cool banks can refresh 2-4x less, cutting refresh energy ~20-40%.

title: Hydrogen backside gas frees etch chucks from Qatari helium
idea: Worse: keep helium backside cooling on every etch and deposition chuck while Qatar's supply is offline. Flip: switch electrostatic chucks to hydrogen backside gas (thermal conductivity ~1.2x helium, already plumbed in fabs) or a compliant CNT thermal pad for clean chambers, and requalify cryo high-AR etch uniformity.
why: Scarce resource: removes a ~30%-Qatar-dependent input from every plasma tool and prevents shortage-driven tool downtime.

title: Repurpose idle SiC power fabs for ultra-low-leakage DRAM
idea: Worse: let EV-slowdown SiC fabs idle while DRAM is scarce. Flip: build 1T1C DRAM on 150/200 mm 4H-SiC wafers in existing SiC fabs. The 3.2 eV bandgap cuts generation leakage by orders of magnitude (1990s SiC DRAM cells held charge for hours), so refresh nearly vanishes, and the lower density is accepted for capacity tiers.
why: Refresh (fact 3) plus capital: reuses sunk U.S. SiC capacity (NC, NY) and needs no Si crucibles.

title: Zero-word bitmaps so DRAM never stores a zero
idea: Worsen: burn full DRAM cells on the zeros that fill 20-40% of real heaps. Flip: the memory controller keeps a per-line 8-bit zero-word bitmap in a small tag store and packs only the non-zero words into variable-size slots, so an all-zero line costs no DRAM at all and a mostly-zero line costs a fraction.
why: Capacity: 15-35% fewer GB on sparse heaps, tensors and freshly allocated pages, with no software change; also less refresh and fewer activations.

title: Learned noise-floor zones that truncate float mantissas
idea: Worsen: store every float mantissa bit even below the data's noise floor. Flip: a per-allocation precision tag, set by profiling how many mantissa bits change the output, lets the controller store only the top k bits of each float in packed form and zero-fill on read.
why: Capacity: 1.5-3x for simulation fields, gradients and sensor data where low-order bits are noise.

title: Rank/select instructions for compressed-domain data structures
idea: Worsen: decompress everything into fat structures before touching it. Flip: add popcount-rank, select and wavelet-access instructions so succinct structures (wavelet trees, Elias-Fano lists, FM-indexes) are queried directly in compressed form at near-native speed.
why: Capacity: 3-10x smaller indexes, graphs and genomics data kept resident and queried without expanding them.

title: Recycled DIMM memory reefs behind CXL bridges
idea: Worsen: shred millions of retired DDR3/DDR4 DIMMs every year. Flip: test, bin and mount retired DIMMs on CXL expander boards with per-DIMM ECC and redundant spares, creating a pooled far-memory tier priced near e-waste value.
why: Cost: hardware at about $0.05-0.2/GB (bridge plus labor) vs new DRAM at $10+/GB, roughly 50-200x; trades power, bandwidth and floor space.

title: Codec-native memory keeps media as compressed bitstreams
idea: Worsen: decode video, images and textures to raw pixels in DRAM. Flip: keep media as AV1/HEVC tile bitstreams in memory and decode tiles on demand in a controller-side codec block, so only the touched macroblocks are ever expanded.
why: Cost: 50-200x effective capacity for media pipelines, vision training and rendering; trades decode latency and lossy fidelity.

title: Event-sourced memory rebuilt by deterministic replay
idea: Worsen: keep every intermediate state of a long computation resident. Flip: store periodic checkpoints and the input log on cheap storage, and rebuild any needed state by deterministic replay on cheap cores, with DRAM holding only the live frontier.
why: Cost: state that is 100x larger than its log costs storage prices, not DRAM prices; trades recompute time.

title: Progressive-precision bit-plane streaming of tensors
idea: Worsen: always send all 16 bits of every weight even when the low bits barely matter. Flip: store tensors transposed into bit planes and stream MSB planes first; the accelerator ends the transfer per tile once its error budget is met, so low-order planes move only when needed.
why: Data-movement energy and effective bandwidth: 1.5-3x fewer bits fetched for error-tolerant inference and training tensors; cold low-order planes can live in cheaper memory.

title: Self-timed delay-insensitive memory links with zero idle power
idea: Worsen: keep PLLs, DLLs and termination burning power while the link idles. Flip: use dual-rail or level-encoded self-timed signaling on short interposer links where each transfer is acknowledged by a handshake, so there is no clock tree, no training and near-zero power when no data moves.
why: Average link energy at real utilization (links idle 50-80% of the time): 2-4x lower; removes DLL/PLL periphery area.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory packages with minute-long retention
idea: Worsen: run DRAM hot so leakage forces 32-64 ms refresh. Flip: immerse memory packages and interposers in liquid nitrogen, where junction leakage falls by orders of magnitude (retention of minutes) and copper resistance drops ~6x, so refresh nearly vanishes and long links get cheaper.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and data movement: refresh power near zero, lower wire energy; LN2 is made from air anywhere, unlike scarce helium.
note: Cooling overhead at 77 K offsets refresh savings outside cryo datacenters.

title: Inline compute in CXL switches streams flash data, never landing
idea: Worsen: copy every dataset from SSD into DRAM, then to the GPU, then back. Flip: put streaming engines (decompress, filter, tokenize, embedding lookup) inside the PCIe/CXL switch so data flows flash to switch to accelerator SRAM at line rate and never lands in DRAM bounce buffers.
why: Data movement and DRAM demand: removes bounce buffers (tens of GB per server) and 2-3 copies per byte.
note: DPUs and GPUDirect Storage already bypass bounce buffers.

title: Gold and bronze subarrays split AI words by bit significance
idea: Worse: protect a weight's least-significant mantissa bit as fiercely as its sign and exponent. Flip: transpose bfloat16/FP8 words into bit planes; store sign+exponent in a 'gold' subarray (64 ms refresh, ECC) and low mantissa bits in a 'bronze' subarray refreshed every 1-2 s with no ECC, where rare flips cost <0.01% accuracy.
why: Facts 3 and 7: ~60% of AI bits move to relaxed refresh with no parity, cutting refresh power ~50% and ECC area for AI-dominated capacity.

title: Refresh-free mode for data that dies before it decays
idea: Worse: refresh activation buffers and KV blocks that will be overwritten within milliseconds anyway. Flip: add a per-bank 'ephemeral' mode in which the controller declares regions whose data lives shorter than retention time (training activations, streaming buffers) and refresh is skipped; dies with poor retention tails are binned and sold for exactly these accelerator streaming roles.
why: Fact 3 refresh energy and yield: removes refresh on 30-60% of accelerator memory and turns retention-reject dies into sellable product.
note: Flikker/RANA-style refresh skipping for short-lived data is known; retention-reject binning adds a supply angle.

title: Approximate-memory SKU letting AI data decay without refresh
idea: Worse: insist every bit is perfect for neural nets that tolerate noise. Flip: run unrefreshed DRAM for activations and gradients, where the controller maps sign and exponent bits to the strongest-retention rows (from a per-die retention map) and low mantissa bits to weak rows, accepting ~1e-5 bit errors.
why: Zero refresh power, and weak-retention dies become usable, with accuracy loss <0.1% in tolerant models.

title: Europa alien: kinetic-inductance nanowire persistent-current loop
idea: An alien from icy Europa assumes memory lives in the cold. A superconducting NbN nanowire loop holds a persistent current, clockwise or counter-clockwise, as a trapped flux quantum. Kinetic inductance lets the loop shrink to ~100 nm, and a nanocryotron reads it.
why: Zero leakage and femtojoule switching for cryogenic AI and quantum datacenters (facts 3, 5, 10).
note: Same KI nanowire loop memory.

title: Martian colonist: biased antiferroelectric ZrO2 bit in one vacuum tool
idea: A Mars colonist has no water, only vacuum. Asymmetric TiN/RuO2 electrodes give an antiferroelectric ZrO2 film a built-in bias, so one of its two field-induced polar states persists at zero volts. The whole electrode-dielectric-electrode stack is deposited in one cluster tool without breaking vacuum, with in-situ atomic-hydrogen cleans in place of wet RCA cleans.
why: A quasi-non-volatile AFE cell (fact 3) with AFE endurance above 1e12. Avoiding air breaks removes ~8 wet clean and rinse steps from the cell module and cuts its UPW use by more than 10x.
note: Work-function-biased AFE nonvolatility already proposed; single-tool vacuum flow is incremental.

title: Child's empty cups: minority-charge encoding with zero-row refresh skip
idea: A child notes that empty cups cannot spill. Each 64-bit word is stored with one invert bit chosen so at most half its cells sit in the charged (leak-prone) state, respecting true-cell/anti-cell polarity; a per-row 'all-safe' flag set on write lets the refresh engine skip rows that hold only discharged states.
why: Retention failures come only from charged cells: halving them halves tail exposure, and zero-filled or sparse rows (often 20-40% of server pages) skip refresh entirely; ~1.5-2.5x refresh energy cut for ~1.6% storage overhead.

title: Pumped-hydro operator: stepwise tank-capacitor wordline charging
idea: A pumped-hydro plant lifts water in stages and recovers it on the way down. Each wordline driver steps its line through 8 intermediate rails held by shared on-die tank capacitors (0, VPP/8 ... VPP) and steps it down the same way, returning charge to each tank.
why: Stepwise charging divides the CV^2 dissipation by the step count; 8 steps plus fewer pump-supplied coulombs cut wordline energy ~8-12x per access using standard transistors.
note: Stepwise charging known; wordline energy is a modest share of total.

title: Stethoscope on a whole mat: aggregate leakage sets refresh
idea: A doctor listens to the whole chest, not one cell. A dedicated idle sentinel mat ties millions of storage junctions to an integrating amplifier that measures aggregate leakage (nA scale) in real time, and the refresh interval tracks that measured leakage rather than worst-case temperature tables.
why: Most hours run far from the worst corner; measured-leakage refresh cuts refresh 2-4x in typical operation, part of the 16-33% idle power (fact 3).

title: Ant-colony refresh: per-mat thermal sensors with neighbor gossip
idea: Ant colonies act on local quorum, not central command. Each mat gets a tiny ring-oscillator thermometer; mats share readings with neighbors over a 1-bit chain and each sets its own refresh interval, so cool mats far from hot spots refresh less.
why: On-die gradients of 5-15 C mean most mats over-refresh; local scheduling cuts refresh operations ~30-50% (fact 3).

title: Child's tidy toy box: refresh skips rows holding only safe values
idea: A child knows toys already on the floor cannot fall. During refresh the SA stripe computes a wired-OR of bits stored in the leak-vulnerable charged state (using the die's own true/anti-cell map); rows with none, common for zeroed pages, are flagged in an on-die bitmap and skipped until next written.
why: Zeroed and sparse pages are often 20-40% of memory; skipping them cuts refresh energy proportionally (fact 3) with no controller change.
note: Zero-content refresh skipping is published; on-die bitmap is a twist.

title: Watchmaker's water drop: capillary self-aligned die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Make the bond sites hydrophilic and their surroundings hydrophobic, and dispense a water droplet on each site. A die dropped within +/-50 um self-centers to <0.5 um by surface tension as the water evaporates, then direct oxide/Cu bonding is annealed.
why: Memory-on-logic hybrid bonding with a ~$200k pick-and-place instead of a $5-10M precision bonder, within reach of a small team (Facts 5, 6).
note: Fluidic self-assembly D2W bonding widely published (Tohoku, imec, CEA).

title: Child watching dew form only on grass: area-selective ALD self-alignment
idea: Dew forms on grass, not on rock. Block the oxide with a self-assembled monolayer inhibitor so ALD Ru grows only on exposed metal. Capacitor bottom electrodes and landing pads then self-align to the contacts beneath, with no litho or overlay step.
why: Removes 1-2 critical masks and overlay-limited steps per tier (Fact 4). It needs just one ALD tool and a vapor-prime oven.
note: Area-selective ALD is widely pursued industry-wide; selectivity defects are the known limiter.

title: Librarian's bookshelf: memory dies standing upright on logic
idea: The librarian stores books on edge, not in flat piles. Stand 50 um thinned memory dies upright on a logic die, joined through half-via castellations made by dicing through plated vias at the die edge and soldered to the base. Coolant or air flows between the dies.
why: ~20 dies per mm of base. No TSVs and no stack-height thermal penalty (Fact 6). Dicing, plating and reflow are small-team tools.
note: Edge stacking is old art (Irvine Sensors); edge I/O count limits bandwidth.

title: Child's magnifying glass: green-laser crystallized silicon tiers over CMOS
idea: A child focuses sunlight to burn a spot without heating the whole table. Deposit a-Si at 350C on finished foundry CMOS, melt-crystallize it with a short-pulse 532 nm line laser so the transistors below stay cool, and build 2-4 tiers of top-gate poly-Si gain-cell TFTs.
why: Monolithic memory tiers over logic with a ~$1M laser and a PECVD tool (Fact 2, capital). Poly-Si leakage needs ms refresh, so it suits cache-like use.

title: Child asks why helium is allowed to float away
idea: Persona: a child asks 'why do you let the balloon go?' Put a cryo-sorption trap on each turbo-pump foreline and a small PSA/membrane purifier on each tool. Together they recover backside-leak and purge helium at >95% purity and refill a local manifold, closing the loop tool by tool.
why: Helium chokepoint: recovers 70-90% of the He consumed, with a payback of months at 2026 prices.

title: Bronze-age metallurgist: zinc-tin oxide replaces gallium and indium
idea: Persona: a Bronze Age smith who built a civilisation on tin and zinc. For oxide-semiconductor access transistors and gain cells, use ALD amorphous zinc-tin oxide (ZTO) instead of IGZO, hydrogen-gettered under an Al2O3 cap. Indium and gallium are removed entirely.
why: Gallium is ~98% Chinese and export-controlled. Indium is a concentrated byproduct. ZTO keeps the ultra-low off-current needed for refresh-free cells.
note: ZTO TFTs are mature in displays; off-current parity with IGZO is the question.

title: Embargo improvisation: helium-free wafer chucks and closed-loop helium recovery
idea: With Qatar's helium offline, a Soviet-style engineer redesigns the etch/deposition chuck: hydrogen-argon backside gas, a micro-channel liquid-cooled ceramic puck and a higher-clamp Johnsen-Rahbek chuck to close the gap, plus per-tool membrane capture that recycles >90% of the helium still used for stage cooling and leak checks.
why: Cuts fab helium use ~80-95%, removing a concentrated-supply chokepoint that can idle tools. Risks: H2 safety, and the lower thermal conductivity of argon demands tighter wafer-to-chuck gap control.

title: Chef's pressure cooker: supercritical CO2 metal electrodes for deep holes
idea: A pressure cooker reaches where dry heat cannot. Deposit Ru, Cu or Ni electrodes from organometallic precursors dissolved in supercritical CO2 at ~150-250 C and ~15 MPa, reduced by H2 at the surface; the zero-surface-tension fluid coats the bottoms of 100:1+ holes and trenches evenly.
why: Gives conformal electrodes at AR >100 without high-temperature CVD TiN, enabling taller capacitors and fewer steps; scCO2 reactors are simple pressure vessels, cheaper than ALD clusters. Risks: precursor purity, carbon pickup, throughput.

title: Quilter's patchwork: collective nanotwinned-copper die bonding at 200 C
idea: A quilter sews all the patches at once. Stack memory dies on (111)-oriented nanotwinned copper pads, which bond by fast surface diffusion at 150-200 C: tack-place a whole wafer of die stacks quickly, then bond them all in one batch press.
why: A lower bond temperature reduces warpage and allows thinner dies; batch bonding raises stacking throughput ~5-10x and cuts bonder count, attacking the HBM stacking cost (fact 6). Risks: pad planarity and voids at <5 um pitch.

title: Jugaad engineer: indium-free zinc-tin oxide channels from abundant metals
idea: A jugaad engineer builds from what is plentiful. With indium supply concentrated in China, swap IGZO for indium- and gallium-free amorphous zinc-tin oxide (or Zn-Sn-Si-O) sputtered at room temperature from cheap targets, annealed at 300-350 C, and capped with a Si-rich back-channel layer that suppresses the off-current tail.
why: Removes indium and gallium supply risk from every oxide-semiconductor memory tier and cuts target cost ~3x. Risks: lower mobility (~10 cm2/Vs) and bias-stress stability.

title: Homeric bard's formulas: fleet-trained compression dictionaries in memory controllers
idea: Oral poets held whole epics in memory as reusable formulas ('rosy-fingered dawn'). A hyperscaler mines fleet memory for recurring 16-64 B fragments (object headers, vtable pointers, UTF-8 strings, protobuf tags) and trains a shared dictionary per workload class. Memory-controller compressors load it and replace the fragments with short codes.
why: On small 64 B lines, shared dictionaries beat per-line compressors by about 1.5-2x. That is +30-60% effective DRAM capacity fleet-wide.
note: SC2-style statistically trained cache compression exists; fleet dictionaries are an incremental extension.

title: Artist's negative space: VM pages stored as diffs against rack-golden images
idea: Painters define a shape by what is missing. One golden copy of each common OS and runtime image lives in rack-shared CXL memory. Each VM page is stored as a sparse XOR or byte-diff delta against its matching golden page, found by content hash at boot and by background scanning.
why: VMs share 70-90% near-identical pages that differ by a few bytes, which exact dedup misses. Delta storage reclaims 15-30% of host DRAM in VM-dense racks.
note: Difference Engine (OSDI 2008) did sub-page patching.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: compiler narrows struct fields to observed ranges
idea: A tailor cuts cloth to the body, not a standard size. An LLVM plugin profiles field value ranges in production and rewrites hot structs with bit-packed narrow fields (int64 to int20, enums to 3 bits, pointers to 32-bit indices). A cheap overflow check migrates an object to a wide spill layout if a value ever exceeds its range. Three compiler engineers can do it in 24 months.
why: Typical C++/Rust structs are 30-50% padding and over-wide fields, so this cuts the heap 20-35% on data-structure-heavy services.

title: Teen texter's abbreviations: superword tokenizer adapter shrinks KV per document
idea: Teens write 'brb' for 'be right back'. An open model's tokenizer gains ~50k frequent multi-word tokens, and only the new embedding rows plus a light LoRA are trained (~$200k of compute). The same text then needs 25-35% fewer tokens, so it needs 25-35% fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory and prefill scale linearly with token count, so a 30% token cut is 30% less KV at any context length, and it stacks with quantization.
note: SuperBPE-style multiword tokens known; ~30% gain.

title: Postal sorting office in the HBM base die
idea: A postal worker sorts mail by street before delivery: a 2k-entry CAM in the HBM base die holds incoming random 64 B requests for a few hundred ns, sorts them by bank/row and issues one activation per row batch, then scatters the replies back.
why: Attacks destructive read and 128x page overfetch (5.9 pJ per useful bit): claimed 3-6x fewer activations on graph and KV-cache traffic and ~40% lower energy per useful bit.
note: Extends FR-FCFS scheduling with a larger window in the base die.

title: Thermophile biologist: fully intermetallic TLP microbumps that cannot age
idea: Thermophilic archaea survive 120 C by using bonds that are already at equilibrium: convert every Cu/Sn microbump completely to Cu3Sn during bonding (transient liquid phase), so no further intermetallic growth or Kirkendall voiding can happen in 10 years at 125 C.
why: Removes the main wear-out mode of memory microbumps at high temperature; lets 25-40 um microbumps survive automotive Grade 0/1 life without hybrid-bonding capex.

title: Japanese swordsmith's folded steel: nanotwinned copper TSVs and bonds
idea: Folded steel is tough because of its layering: plate all TSVs, pillars and hybrid-bond pads as (111) nanotwinned copper, whose twin boundaries block vacancy flow and allow 150-200 C direct bonding.
why: Electromigration life about 10x that of normal Cu at 125 C, and lower bonding temperature limits DRAM retention damage during assembly; this enables 125 C/10 year stacks.

title: Rope-maker's triplet: three distant weak cells fired as one bit
idea: A rope-maker twists three weak strands into a rope stronger than one thick strand: three small-capacitor cells at different physical positions on the same bitline are fired together (three wordlines driven at once) so their charges sum; a single leaky tail cell then removes only a third of the signal, and the sigma of the summed charge shrinks by sqrt(3).
why: Facts 1 and 3: each capacitor can drop to ~1.7 fF at far lower aspect ratio (easier etch), and tail-cell failures fall by orders of magnitude; density-neutral only if the smaller capacitors shrink the cell footprint.

title: Siberian engineer: sub-zero memory halls let leaky reject cells pass
idea: A Siberian engineer uses the climate as a component: run DRAM-heavy racks in -30 to -40 C glycol-immersion blocks that are free-cooled in cold regions; junction leakage falls ~2x per 10 C, so retention rises ~30-100x, and dies are tested and binned at that temperature so cells that fail at 85 C ship as 'cold-grade' parts.
why: Fact 3: refresh (16-33% of idle power) nearly vanishes, and low-temperature binning raises good-die yield and supply while slowing retention aging; condensation and cold start are the risks.

title: Painter's underlayer: MSB bit-planes in strong rows, LSB planes in weak
idea: A painter spends care on the underdrawing and lets the glaze be loose: the controller transposes numeric tensors into bit-planes, puts sign, exponent and high-order planes in ECC-protected rows on the normal refresh schedule, and puts low-order mantissa planes in tail-prone rows refreshed 8x less often and without ECC.
why: Fact 3: an estimated 30-40% refresh-energy cut on AI workloads, and tail rows are used rather than repaired or fused out.
note: Flikker-style approximate refresh.

title: Mail carrier's redelivery: detect-only CRC for clean pages, refetch on error
idea: A mail carrier doesn't repair a damaged parcel but asks for another copy: pages with a clean backing copy (model weights, file cache, code) carry only a short CRC, and a detected error triggers a re-fetch from flash or a peer node; the parity bits saved go to capacity or to stronger codes for dirty pages.
why: ECC storage overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3% for read-mostly AI weights, so the same dies hold more weights.

title: Archaeologist's fragments: profiled weak bits decoded as erasures, doubling correction
idea: An archaeologist reconstructs a pot knowing which shards are missing: online profiling keeps a map of the weak cells (retention- and hammer-prone), and the decoder treats those positions as erasures; a distance-d code corrects d-1 erasures but only (d-1)/2 unknown errors.
why: With the same parity budget, about twice as many weak cells can be tolerated, so marginal dies are accepted and more cells pass test.
note: Erasure decoding of mapped defects known; VRT cells evade static maps.

title: Economist's congestion pricing: per-process activation budgets metered by controller
idea: An economist prices congestion instead of building more roads: the controller counts row activations per address-space ID in each 64 ms window and throttles any process that exceeds its activation budget, with the OS able to buy extra budget for legitimate streaming workloads.
why: Fact 9: dies with low hammer thresholds stay safe without per-row counters, and the costs fall on the offending process.
note: Per-thread activation throttling (BreakHammer-like) already published.

title: Doctor's vaccination: stress-test mirrored subarrays to find weak cells early
idea: A doctor vaccinates before the disease arrives: the DRAM rotates through its subarrays, mirroring one into a spare and challenging the original with lower array voltage, a 4x refresh interval and hammer patterns, so cells about to fail are found and the refresh bins and remap tables are updated before user data sees an error.
why: Retention and hammer tails drift with age; online challenge-profiling lets cells ship with ~10-20% less Cs guardband.
note: Online profiling (REAPER-like) with mirrored spares.

title: 2050 engineer: every printed word carries its own reference pair
idea: A 2050 engineer assumes devices vary by 30% and designs around it: each 32-bit printed word includes a '1' and a '0' reference cell written in the same pulse, and on read the comparator uses the midpoint of those two local references, cancelling device-to-device Vth spread, drift since write and temperature to first order.
why: Printed TFT variation (sigma Vth ~0.2-0.5 V) defeats global references; local self-referencing cuts the required signal margin ~3x at 6% bit overhead.

title: Musician tunes to the instrument: train models on each foil's error fingerprint
idea: A musician adapts to the quirks of one particular instrument: each printed memory foil's measured error statistics (which bits flip, in which direction, how often) feed a short fine-tuning pass of the neural network whose weights it will hold, so the model becomes robust to that foil's BER of 1e-3 to 1e-2 and needs no ECC.
why: The cheapest printed cells, with no ECC and minimal redundancy, can hold read-mostly AI weights; removes the 12.5% ECC overhead and most test cost, with an expected accuracy loss below 0.5%.

title: Survivalist's go-bag: printed battery keeps memory alive through power faults
idea: A survivalist always keeps a go-bag packed: a thin-film zinc or lithium battery printed onto the DIMM or HBM carrier powers self-refresh for minutes after a PSU or rack power fault, so in-memory state (KV caches, in-memory databases) survives instead of being lost and recomputed.
why: Availability: avoids costly recomputation and checkpoint traffic and reduces the need for NVDIMM capacity, for cents per module.
note: Battery/supercap NVDIMM-N exists; printed thin-film battery energy is marginal for minutes of self-refresh.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina nanopores multiply capacitor area for embargoed fabs
idea: A fab cut off from EUV, tungsten and helium can still anodize aluminum: one mask defines array regions in a BEOL Al layer that anodizes into self-ordered 20-30 nm pores at >100:1 aspect ratio, which are ALD-coated with TiN/ZrO2/TiN to form massive storage capacitors above the transistors. Self-assembly replaces HAR plasma etch and EUV patterning.
why: >=10 fF per cell without HAR etch tools (facts 1, 4) using abundant Al (scarce-resource intensity, U.S. manufacturability); registering pores to cells is the risk.

title: ReLU-sparsity polarity mapping: zeros stored in the non-leaking state
idea: AI activation tensors are 50-90% zeros after ReLU. Map the dominant value to the cell state that cannot leak (discharged node, using true/complement bitline placement plus a per-row invert bit) and keep a per-row all-discharged flag so the controller skips refresh for rows holding no charged cells.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh, so for sparse AI data refresh energy drops by roughly the sparsity fraction (2-5x).

title: SEU-style bit interleaving turns clustered weak rows into random errors
idea: Rad-hard memories interleave codeword bits across distant cells so one particle strike flips at most one bit per word. Spread each codeword over the chips and subarrays that are activated together, so a weak row, a VRT cluster, a bad access-transistor column or a hammered row adds at most one bit per codeword, keeping errors iid at the 1% cell BER the code is sized for.
why: Facts 3 and 9: a cheap code handles 1% raw BER without being beaten by correlated failures, and row-hammer flips are absorbed without per-row counters, saving periphery area.
note: Chipkill-style interleaving already standard.

title: Insect-drone hyperdimensional memory in rarely refreshed banks
idea: Tiny drones use hyperdimensional computing, where items are 10,000-bit random vectors that stay recognizable with 10-30% bit flips. Hold the associative item and class hypervectors in banks refreshed only when raw BER reaches ~1%, re-bundling vectors from recent samples now and then.
why: Fact 3: for HDC workloads refresh energy and ECC almost vanish and 1% cell BER costs no accuracy, so cheaper, leakier cells can be used.
note: Approximate/refresh-relaxed storage for error-tolerant data is known (Flikker); niche workload.

title: Satellite data-carousel memory: detect, then refetch the golden copy
idea: Broadcast satellites loop data so receivers fill gaps. Treat DRAM as a 1%-BER cache of data that also lives in NAND or CXL far memory: each 4 KB block has a CRC plus a light code that fixes most errors, uncorrectable blocks are refetched from the golden copy, and DRAM refreshes only at its 1% age.
why: Fact 3: for read-mostly data (weights, page cache, embeddings, roughly half of server DRAM) refresh falls ~10x and parity stays ~3-5%, since rare failures cost a refetch, not a stronger code.
note: Same refetch-golden-copy mechanism.

title: HFT-overclocker truncated restore: cut tRAS, let weak cells fail
idea: High-frequency traders overclock and accept margins others refuse. Shorten the restore phase of activate and refresh (tRAS and tWR ~30-40% shorter) so slow tail access transistors leave cells partly charged; the code absorbs the resulting ~1% errors, and partly restored rows are queued to refresh first.
why: Facts 3 and 8: lower access latency and ~30% less refresh time and restore energy, recovering refresh bandwidth and row-cycle time with no device change.
note: Restore truncation already published.

title: Space cold-welding: atomic-hydrogen activated room-temperature Cu-Cu bonding
idea: In orbit, clean metals cold-weld on contact; reproduce this by reducing copper and SiCN bond surfaces with atomic hydrogen from a hot-filament H2 cracker in vacuum, instead of argon fast-atom beams or argon plasma, then pressing die to wafer at room temperature. No anneal is needed, so bonded DRAM tiers never see the 350-400 C that degrades retention.
why: Room-temperature bonding protects the leakage tail (fact 3), allows sub-0.5 um pitch with no copper expansion, and supports more bonded tiers (facts 2 and 6) without argon.
note: H-radical surface reduction for Cu bonding known; dielectric bond strength without anneal is the doubt.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling for cryogenic high-aspect-ratio etch, helium-free
idea: Etch tools cool wafers with helium between wafer and chuck; hydrogen conducts heat slightly better than helium, so run cryogenic (-110 C) SF6/O2 etch of capacitor holes and tier stacks with low-pressure H2 backside gas, using liquid-hydrogen rocket practice for sensors and inerted lines. Cryo etch passivates sidewalls with SiOxFy and needs no argon, giving vertical profiles at high AR.
why: Removes helium from every etch chamber; AR 100+ cryo etch for capacitors (fact 1) and tier stacks (fact 2) with better chuck uniformity.

title: PCB-shop vacuum-free metallization for TSVs and through-tier vias
idea: Circuit-board shops metallize millions of vias with no vacuum; replace argon-sputtered Ta/Cu seed in TSVs and through-array vias with an electroless Ni-B barrier and an electroless copper seed grafted on a silane monolayer, then fill by bottom-up superconformal plating. The whole via flow runs at atmospheric pressure on wet benches.
why: HBM TSV cost (fact 6) and argon PVD removed; wet tools ~5x cheaper, and conformal seeds allow 20:1+ TSVs, shrinking TSV diameter and keep-out ~2x.

title: Dental-resin chemistry for fluorine-free photoacid generators
idea: Dental composites are cured in human mouths with non-fluorinated photoinitiators because PFAS is unacceptable there. Synthesize non-fluorinated PAGs (sulfonium salts of camphorsulfonate or bulky sulfonated aromatic anions that limit acid diffusion) and benchmark sensitivity, LER and diffusion length on i-line and e-beam in a university fab.
why: The EU universal PFAS restriction threatens PFBS/PFOS-type PAGs in DRAM resists; a drop-in non-PFAS chemistry keeps the lithography supply legal and secure.
note: Non-fluorinated PAGs are actively pursued by resist makers.

title: Satellite-optics CO2-snow and supercritical CO2 cleaning replaces RCA rinses
idea: Spacecraft optics are cleaned with CO2 snow jets because liquids leave residues in vacuum. In a university fab, replace selected post-etch and pre-deposition SC1/SC2 cleans with CO2-snow particle removal and supercritical CO2 with co-solvent for residue strip, measuring particle adders and metals by TXRF.
why: Each RCA clean uses tens of liters of UPW plus acids; CO2 is a recycled industrial byproduct; target ~30% fewer wet steps and UPW use.

title: Space-shower mist rinse: megasonic aerosol rinses with one-tenth the water
idea: Astronauts wash with mist and no-rinse methods because water is precious. Replace overflow-bath rinses with megasonic-atomized UPW mist and an in-line resistivity endpoint that stops rinsing when the drain returns to 18 MOhm-cm, prototyped on a university spin-rinse-dryer.
why: Rinsing is most of a fab's UPW use; endpoint-controlled mist rinsing could cut rinse water ~70-90%.

title: Solar PERC spatial ALD: atmospheric-pressure dielectrics at 10x throughput
idea: Solar lines deposit Al2O3 passivation by spatial ALD, moving wafers under separated precursor zones at atmospheric pressure. Build a bench spatial-ALD head in a university fab for ZrO2/Al2O3 capacitor and liner films, and measure precursor utilization and conformality in 10:1 trenches.
why: Conventional ALD wastes most of its precursor and needs vacuum; spatial ALD could cut Zr/Hf organometallic use, pump energy and tool capital per wafer ~2-5x.

title: MEMS-release vapor HF replaces wet buffered-oxide etch and rinses
idea: MEMS makers release structures with anhydrous vapor HF and an alcohol catalyst, using no liquids. Replace wet BOE/DHF oxide strips with vapor HF in a university fab, recovering HF in a closed cylinder loop, and quantify selectivity to nitride and residues.
why: Cuts HF wastewater, rinse UPW and fluoride sludge per wafer, which matters most at water-scarce U.S. sites.

title: Garage-fab DMD maskless printers expose DRAM's non-critical layers
idea: Extreme user: hobbyist and university garage fabs that cannot afford masks. Use digital-micromirror maskless exposure (like PCB direct imaging, upgraded to ~150 nm with 4x reduction optics) for the ~40% of DRAM layers above 200 nm (implants, pads, thick metals, periphery wells).
why: Masks: cuts ~$3-6M of mask-set cost per product, enables same-day design spins and SKU variants without mask lead times.

title: (110)-silicon TMAH crystallographic etch makes 100:1 plasma-free trench capacitors
idea: Extreme user: MEMS inertial sensors for missiles, which etch vertical {111} walls in (110) silicon wet. Lay the cell array along <111> directions on (110) wafers and etch atomically smooth trenches in TMAH through an ALD Al2O3 mask, with no plasma and no fluorine.
why: Capacitor wall/capital: batch wet etch replaces single-wafer HAR plasma etchers (~$10M each) and gives AR >100:1 with smooth walls for reliable ALD.
note: (110) {111} walls known from MEMS; non-orthogonal planes constrain DRAM layout.

title: LHC-style hardware trigger decides which records deserve DRAM
idea: From the CERN trigger, which keeps about 1 event in 40,000 within microseconds: telemetry, log and clickstream records land in an SRAM ring on the NIC or memory controller, where a programmable L1 classifier (match-action tables plus a tiny model) promotes only 'interesting' records to DRAM and folds the rest into count-min and HyperLogLog summaries.
why: Observability, ad and security pipelines buffer 10-100x more data in DRAM than is ever queried; trigger-style early discard cuts ingest-tier DRAM 5-20x.

title: HFT zero-copy ownership: one physical buffer for the whole stack
idea: From high-frequency traders who never copy a packet: NIC, kernel, application and GPU pass capabilities to one physical buffer through IOMMU-enforced ownership transfer (move semantics in hardware), abolishing socket buffers, page-cache copies and GPU staging buffers.
why: Data is often held 3-5 times across the I/O stack; single-copy cuts I/O buffer DRAM 3-5x and the copy energy (fact 5).

title: Exascale memory futures market inside the cluster scheduler
idea: From exascale centers where bytes-per-flop keep falling: jobs bid for GB-hours in a real-time internal market with futures contracts, jobs that release memory early earn credits, and the scheduler auctions stranded DRAM to preemptible opportunistic jobs.
why: Fleets strand 20-40% of DRAM through static reservations; pricing exposes it so operators can buy 20-30% fewer DIMMs.

title: Mainframe-style rack-wide content-addressed page sharing over CXL
idea: From mainframes that pack thousands of guests on one box: a CXL memory appliance hashes 4 KB pages from every host in a rack, keeps one copy of identical pages (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) and maps it read-only into each host, breaking sharing with copy-on-write.
why: Cross-host duplication is 10-30% in VM and container fleets and far higher for replicated weights; rack-wide dedup recovers it.

title: One-dollar MCU trick: decompress weights inside the MAC pipeline
idea: From $1 microcontrollers that run neural nets from compressed flash: accelerators keep weights entropy-coded (ANS over exponents plus clustered mantissa palettes) in HBM and decode them in a stage fused into each MAC array, so uncompressed weights never exist in memory.
why: Lossless exponent coding saves 25-40% of BF16/FP8 weight bytes and palettes 2-4x, gaining capacity and bandwidth at once.

title: Satellite onboard latents: models compute directly on codec output
idea: From Earth-observation satellites that downlink only learned-codec latents: cameras and NICs emit learned-codec latent tensors and vision/analytics models are trained to consume latents directly, so raw frames are never decoded into DRAM anywhere in the pipeline.
why: Latents are 20-100x smaller than raw frames, so per-stream DRAM falls 20x+ and the embedded fab ultrapure water for those bits falls proportionally (>10x).

title: Follow-the-night memory: shift DRAM-heavy work to wherever it's cold
idea: From polar stations that schedule heavy work into the cold dark: a global scheduler migrates DRAM-heavy batch jobs, with CXL-flash snapshots of their memory, to whichever region is currently in cold night, so each region's DRAM serves local interactive load by day and global batch load by night, always on dry or free-air cooling.
why: One DRAM pool serves two workloads (~2x fewer bits), and running memory-heavy work only in cold ambient lets sites drop evaporative cooling, cutting water >10x.

title: Cryo-EM style LN2 memory drawer at 0.4 V and 50 mV swing
idea: Cryo-EM and magnet labs already handle LN2 routinely. Immerse whole memory drawers in liquid nitrogen: at 77 K subthreshold swing ~20 mV/dec lets periphery run at ~0.4 V and links at ~50 mV, copper resistance falls ~7x, and access-transistor leakage collapses so refresh nearly stops.
why: CV2 per access ~8-10x lower and refresh (~46 fJ/bit idle) vanishes at the memory; cryocooler overhead (~3-10 W/W) eats much of it, so net only wins with cheap industrial LN2 (~1.5-3x).
note: Cryo-DRAM studied (Rambus, CryoRAM); net gain only 1.5-3x after cooling overhead.

title: E-paper shelf-label stepwise charging of memory buses
idea: Electronic shelf labels last a decade on a coin cell partly by driving lines in small steps from tank capacitors. Charge each long column-datapath and interposer line through a ladder of N tank-capacitor rails; each step dissipates ~1/N of the CV2 and the tanks recapture charge on discharge.
why: With N=8-10 steps line energy falls ~8-10x, at the cost of ~N-times slower edges, which suits wide-slow buses.

title: CERN trigger-buffer logic: declared-lifetime rows skip refresh entirely
idea: LHC trigger buffers hold data for microseconds and discard 99.99% of it, so nobody refreshes them. Add a NOREF(range, lifetime) command: the OS or runtime marks rows whose data will be overwritten or discarded within ~30 ms (activations, framebuffers, network rings, attention scratch), and the DRAM leaves them out of internal refresh. Reading a row past its declared lifetime returns a poison flag.
why: In AI workloads a large share of the footprint is short-lived. Skipping its refresh cuts refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth at 32-64 Gb) in proportion, and lets those regions use weak-retention cells (fact 3).

title: Red-team defense: keyed, re-randomized row scrambling inside the DRAM
idea: Treat the row-hammer attacker as the extreme user. Inside each subarray, the DRAM maps logical rows to physical rows through a lightweight keyed permutation (a 4-round Feistel on the row bits). The key is re-drawn at each boot and rotated gradually by background migration during self-refresh, so attackers cannot learn which rows are physical neighbours. External addressing and timing stay standard.
why: Targeted hammering depends on knowing the neighbours. Randomizing them turns attacks into low-odds guessing, so vendors can tolerate cells that flip near 1k activations without heavy per-row counters (fact 9).
note: Close to RRS/SHADOW row-shuffling defenses.

title: $1-IoT free ECC: compress each line to make room for parity
idea: Cheap IoT and phone LPDDR has no ECC pins. The host controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta, zero and FP-pattern schemes succeed on ~70-90% of lines) and stores a SEC-DED or BCH code in the freed bits, tracked by one marker bit per line in a small metadata table. Standard non-ECC x16 parts gain protection on most lines.
why: Brings ECC to billions of non-ECC devices without the 12.5% extra chips, so phone and IoT DRAM can tolerate weaker cells and longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Desert solar thermal swings: thermal-cycling screen flushes out VRT cells
idea: Desert electronics see 50 C daily swings that expose latent defects. Add a fast package test that cycles dies between -10 C and 95 C several times while repeatedly retention-testing them, pushing variable-retention-time cells into their leaky state so they are repaired before shipment. Nothing at the interface changes.
why: VRT cells escape single-pass tests and later force fleet-wide conservative refresh. Catching them early cuts field errors and supports ~1.5x looser refresh guardbands (fact 3).

title: Cold-boot attacker insight: store each line in its discharge-safe polarity
idea: Cold-boot attackers know DRAM decays toward each cell's ground state. The host controller learns each row's true-cell or anti-cell polarity with a boot-time decay scan, then inverts each 64 B line so most cells hold the discharged state, which cannot leak away. One flag bit per line rides in spare ECC or metadata bits.
why: Real data is zero-heavy. Minimizing charged cells cuts retention and hammer error exposure by ~2-4x on the same silicon (facts 3, 9).

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly patterns capacitor holes without EUV
idea: Scale shift from polymer molecules to wafer patterns: use high-chi block copolymers that self-assemble into hexagonal cylinders at 16-20 nm pitch, guided by a coarse ArF template, to define the storage-node hole array.
why: Capital intensity: removes 1-2 EUV layers per cell array; molecules define the pitch for free.
note: DSA contact holes widely pursued; defectivity has blocked adoption.

title: Rack-scale erasure codes let cells skip most refreshes
idea: Jump from the cell to the rack: extend refresh to 1 s and accept that weak-tail cells flip, because data is striped with LDPC/erasure codes across 64 DRAM chips on several DIMMs; a rack scrubber repairs flips well before they accumulate.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth: ~15x fewer refreshes recovers 10-20% bandwidth and most idle refresh power.
note: Extends known ECC-based refresh relaxation to rack scale; decode latency across DIMMs.

title: Time-to-live allocations: never refresh data that dies first
idea: Time shift from the fixed 64 ms refresh clock to software data lifetimes: allocators (malloc, PyTorch caching allocator, NIC buffers) tag buffers with a TTL, and the memory controller keeps a per-row 'expires-at' timestamp, skipping refresh for rows whose contents will be overwritten or freed before their retention bin runs out and stopping refresh on freed rows entirely.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): in AI training/inference 50-80% of DRAM bytes are short-lived tensors living <30 ms, so refresh operations drop ~2-4x and refresh's share of idle power falls from ~25% to <10%.

title: Bit-plane split: mantissa low bits live in relaxed-refresh banks
idea: Scale shift down to the bits inside a number: the controller transposes FP16/BF16 tensors so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits sit in normally refreshed banks while low mantissa bits sit in banks refreshed every 2-4 s, where occasional decay only perturbs the 4th-7th significant bit.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): ~40-50% of weight/activation bits get 30-60x fewer refreshes with <0.1% accuracy impact in tolerant layers.

title: Bookshelf stacking: dies on edge with sidewall wiring, no TSVs
idea: Scale up from die to cube, reviving the 1990s Irvine Sensors cube: thin DRAM dies to 50 um, laminate 64 face-to-back, lap the stack edge, and metallize the exposed edge pads with 180-nm-class litho. The bus runs across the cube face to a logic die mounted perpendicular to the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims ~30% of die area and the yield loss, using old tools in U.S. back-end lines.
note: Irvine Sensors revival; edge bandwidth limited vs area TSVs.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging recycles the 3-volt swing
idea: Time-stretch the ns wordline edge into 4-8 small voltage steps fed from on-die tank capacitors held at intermediate levels. When the wordline closes, charge flows back into the tanks, recovering ~60-75% of the CV2 energy for a ~1-2 ns penalty.
why: Attacks the voltage-floor energy: ~3x lower wordline energy and smaller VPP charge pumps, so less periphery area and less power drawn per bit.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal lengthens retention in existing furnaces
idea: Isotope-scale fix with a year-scale payoff: a final 10-20 atm D2 anneal in existing high-pressure furnaces passivates access-transistor interface and GIDL trap sites with Si-D bonds, which resist breaking and leak less than Si-H over the product's life.
why: Tightens the <=13 fA leakage tail. If retention doubles, refresh energy (16-33% of idle power) halves. Deuterium comes from abundant heavy water.

title: Rack-level remapping lets fabs ship dies without laser repair
idea: Move repair up from the die (fuse banks, spare rows, laser repair station) to the rack: each die ships with an OTP defect map and the CXL memory-pool controller remaps around bad 1 MB regions in its page tables, accepting dies with up to ~3% dead capacity.
why: Eliminates laser-repair tools and most redundancy area (~3-5% of die), shortens test, and lifts effective yield 10-20 points on a new node (Facts 4, 7).

title: Supercritical CO2 drying lets capacitors stand without support lattices
idea: Scale insight: at the nanoscale, capillary forces from the final rinse topple tall pillars, which is why a nitride support lattice (extra deposition, litho, etch) is needed; drying in supercritical CO2 from domestic industrial gas (zero surface tension) lets freestanding pillars reach ~100:1.
why: Removes 1-2 masks and ~6 support-lattice steps; taller pillars add ~30% Cs (Fact 1).

title: Sub-second rack memory spot market over CXL
idea: Every 100 ms, the servers in a rack bid for 256 MB slices of pooled CXL memory. Each bid uses a price derived from that server's page-fault rate and SLO slack. An auctioneer in the switch reassigns slices, so stranded DRAM flows to whoever values it most at that instant.
why: Stranded or idle DRAM is 25-50% in clouds. Reallocating it every fraction of a second lets racks provision 20-30% less.

title: GOP-style delta frames for in-memory replicas
idea: This is video-codec thinking applied to replication. Hot-standby replicas of in-memory databases, caches or VMs keep one full I-frame replica per rack. The other replicas hold only periodic P-frame write deltas against it plus a log, and rebuild a full copy only on failover, which takes seconds.
why: In-DRAM replication factor drops from 3 to about 1.2, saving 40-60% of DRAM in replicated stores in exchange for failover time.

title: Pod-wide HBM borrowing over the scale-up fabric
idea: In a 72-GPU NVLink-class domain, each GPU exposes its idle HBM through the fabric. KV overflow and cold weights spill to a neighbor's HBM at about 1 TB/s, so no single GPU has to be provisioned for worst-case context length. Provisioning moves from the chip scale to the pod scale.
why: Provisioning for the pod average instead of each GPU's peak needs 25-40% less HBM per accelerator at the same SLOs.

title: Bit-significance-partitioned refresh for approximate tensors
idea: This adds zero masks. The allocator lays out tensors so that sign, exponent and high-mantissa bits sit in different rows from low-mantissa bits. The controller refreshes high-significance rows normally and low-significance rows 8-16x less often, using per-row directed refresh. Refresh time is matched to the importance of each bit.
why: It recovers 50-80% of refresh energy and bandwidth on tensor regions (fact 3), with errors confined to LSBs: approximate memory with no new cells.

title: Nanotwinned-copper 150 C bonding stacks DRAM without retention loss
idea: Shift the bonding time-temperature budget down an order of magnitude: (111)-oriented nanotwinned Cu pads diffuse fast enough to bond at ~150 C in minutes, avoiding the 300-400 C anneals that degrade access-transistor leakage. DRAM can then be bonded onto finished logic without a retention penalty.
why: Protects the retention tail (fact 3) during 3D stacking, raising stack yield and trimming refresh guard bands.
note: Nanotwinned Cu low-temperature bonding is well-published.

title: Z-channel codes exploit leakage's one-way arrow of time
idea: Time-direction shift: true-cells only decay 1->0 and anti-cells only 0->1, so the error channel is asymmetric. Encode with asymmetric (Z-channel/Berger-style constant-weight) codes, matched to the true/anti layout, that spend parity only on the one possible flip direction.
why: Corrects about 2x more retention errors per parity bit than symmetric SECDED/BCH, permitting ~30% lower Cs or a longer refresh interval at equal reliability.

title: Rack-scale erasure-coded CXL pool accepts dies with dead banks
idea: Scale jump (bank -> rack): stripe pooled CXL memory with a 14+2 erasure code across 16 memory devices on different sleds, with lazy reconstruction of any failed bank. Dies with whole dead banks or high raw BER, now scrapped, are sold into the pool because the failure domain becomes the rack, not the die.
why: Raises sellable die yield by an estimated 5-10 points and lets the parity overhead (~12.5%) replace per-die repair area.

title: Lifetime-typed allocation maps short-lived buffers to unrefreshed regions
idea: Timescale matching (data lifetime vs retention): the compiler/runtime tags each allocation with an expected lifetime (<1 ms, <64 ms, persistent) and the allocator places it in regions binned by retention. Short-lived buffers go to refresh-disabled or weak-cell regions that only have to hold data until it dies.
why: Cuts refresh energy (~16-33% of idle power) in AI workloads where most activations live under 10 ms, and gives weak-retention bins a use.

title: Training-cluster checkpoints replace ECC for bulk activations
idea: Scale jump (bit -> datacenter job): large training runs already checkpoint every few minutes, so activation and optimizer memory on non-ECC, denser, cheaper DRAM accepts silent-error risk. Cross-replica gradient checksums detect corruption and the job rolls back.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% ECC capacity and lets accelerators use lower-binned parts; converts reliability into a time-rollback budget.

title: Dynamic guard rows flank hot aggressors by migrating neighbors
idea: Scale/time shift (fixed layout -> runtime layout): when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold within a refresh window, the controller migrates its two physical neighbors' data elsewhere so the hot row is temporarily flanked by empty guard rows; the rows are re-filled when it cools.
why: Neutralizes hammer for the hot set at near-zero refresh cost, tolerating thresholds below 1k without per-row victim refresh storms.

title: Leakage-twin RC oscillator clocks each bank's refresh
idea: No EUV: build a tiny relaxation oscillator whose timing capacitor leaks through a replica access transistor drawn on the same DUV process. Its period tracks process, temperature and aging leakage directly, and it clocks refresh for its bank.
why: Refresh tracks real leakage instead of the worst-case 64 ms spec, saving an estimated 30-60% of refresh energy on wide-variation DUV silicon.

title: Rotating per-epoch scramble keys break pattern-dependent failures
idea: No EUV: mature-node arrays show data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling failures. Time shift: re-scramble each row with a new key every few refresh epochs during scrubbing, so no worst-case pattern stays in place long enough to fail and errors become random and ECC-friendly.
why: Narrows the pattern-dependent tail ~2-3x, letting DUV cells with more coupling pass spec.
note: Same scrambling mechanism with rotating keys.

title: Patent-expiry DRAM: open PDK built only from 20-year-old patents
idea: Decade time shift of IP: assemble a full cell, sense-amp and periphery design kit using only techniques from patents that expired more than 20 years ago, then publish it as an open PDK so new U.S. entrants have freedom to operate on day one.
why: Removes the licensing and litigation barrier that keeps entrants out of DRAM. Cuts years of legal risk and IP cost, enabling cooperative or startup fabs.

title: Rack-scale content-addressed page store for shared weights and OS images
idea: Scale jump from server to rack: a CXL switch hashes 4 KB pages and keeps a single physical copy of identical pages (model weights, container layers, kernels) for 32 hosts, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Inference fleets replicate the same weights on every host. Rack dedup frees 20-40% of DRAM, which counts as new supply.

title: Dead body-bias trick revived via printed back-gate planes
idea: Dynamic body biasing (DTMOS) died in bulk CMOS because the body-effect coefficient shrank and wells are huge capacitors. In a printed double-gate oxide TFT array, a printed global back-gate plane couples strongly to the thin channel. Hold the plane at -3 V during retention (high Vt, ultralow leakage) and swing it to 0 V only on the tile being accessed (low Vt, fast).
why: Decouples speed from leakage, so access devices can be fast and still retain for seconds. Cuts refresh ~100x on foil memory.

title: NVDIMM-N failure fixed with printed zinc battery self-refresh
