idea: NVDIMM-N modules died on the cost of their flash, supercapacitors and backup controller. Laminate a printed zinc-manganese battery film onto the DIMM that keeps the DRAM in self-refresh through a power loss for minutes to an hour, with no copy to flash.
why: Makes DRAM survive outages for pennies per module, so servers can drop a separate persistence tier. Refresh is carried by stored energy instead of a flash backup.

title: Irvine Sensors edge-stack revived: printed sidewall buses instead of TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors' 1990s 'loaf-of-bread' cubes routed signals to die edges and metallized the stack's side, but died on thinning yield and coarse wiring. Route each DRAM die's I/O to edge pads, stack the dies, polish the side, and laser-direct-write or aerosol-print fine-pitch copper buses down the sidewall. No TSV pierces the array.
why: Removes the TSV area and yield tax (fact 6). Edge buses at 10 um pitch carry wide I/O. Claims ~2x bits per wafer area vs HBM.

title: Zinc-tin-oxide gain cells: indium- and gallium-free, fixing ZTO's display failure
idea: ZTO lost to IGZO in displays because it resisted wet etching selectively against source-drain metals and its bias-stress threshold drift shifted pixel gray levels. In a 2T gain cell on glass neither matters: pattern ZTO by chlorine dry etch, and since every cell is rewritten each refresh interval, threshold drift is erased; off-currents near 1e-19 A/um give seconds-to-minutes retention.
why: Removes gallium (China export controls since 2023) and indium from oxide memory; zinc and tin have diversified supply; long retention cuts refresh energy ~100x versus silicon DRAM.
note: ZTO is a known IGZO alternative; gain cell use is a reasonable application.

title: Sun Rock scout threads, fixed: compiler helper threads hide far memory
idea: Sun's Rock used hardware 'scout' threads to run ahead and prefetch but was cancelled for power and complexity. Do it in software: the compiler emits a stripped address-generation slice that runs on an SMT sibling ahead of the main thread, prefetching from a slow CXL/NAND tier into cache so most data can live off-DRAM.
why: Lets 60-80% of capacity move to a 5-10x cheaper, 3-10x slower tier while hiding most of its latency for irregular code.
note: Helper-thread prefetching is well studied; cannot hide NAND latency.

title: Feature-phone NOR XIP, fixed: profile-clustered execute-in-place, DRAM-less SoCs
idea: Execute-in-place from NOR flash ran feature phones with little DRAM but was abandoned as code bloated and random fetches stalled. Profile-guided linking clusters hot code and read-only data into contiguous flash pages fronted by a 32-64 MB on-die SRAM cache, so edge AI devices, IoT and controllers ship with zero DRAM.
why: Removes DRAM entirely from billions of low-end devices, freeing supply for servers.
note: Low-end devices hold small DRAM share; MCUs already XIP.

title: ACF failed at fine pitch; magnetically aligned iron-nickel columns fix shorts
idea: Anisotropic conductive films lost to solder at fine pitch because randomly dispersed particles bridged neighbors or missed pads. Disperse Ni-coated Fe microspheres in epoxy and cure under a vertical magnetic field so they self-assemble into isolated columns at ~10 um pitch, giving a solderless, reworkable vertical interconnect for attaching memory stacks or tiles to substrates.
why: Solder-free (no Sn, Ag, In or Au) and reworkable: a bad memory stack can be replaced instead of scrapping a $1,000+ accelerator package, attacking HBM assembly yield (fact 6).

title: Flikker's annotation burden removed by hardware bit-plane splitting of tensors
idea: Flikker-style approximate refresh failed because programmers had to hand-mark non-critical data. Fix: the memory controller transposes words on pages whose dtype (bf16/fp8/int8) is known from the ML allocator, so sign/exponent bits land in fully refreshed rows while low mantissa bits land in rows refreshed 16x less often that tolerate ~1e-4 BER.
why: ~50-60% of AI tensor bits move to relaxed rows: ~45% refresh energy cut (fact 3) and rows of weaker cells become sellable, with negligible accuracy loss.

title: FeRAM imprint cancelled by scheduled whole-row polarity inversion
idea: Ferroelectric RAM (PZT, now HZO) fails by imprint: cells left in one state shift their coercive voltage until they will not switch or sense. Fix: a per-row inversion flag, so whenever a row is written its data is stored inverted with the flag toggled and every capacitor spends about half its life in each polarization, cancelling imprint.
why: Widens sense margin at high temperature, allowing thinner, lower-voltage HZO (voltage floor, fact 10) and longer retention.

title: STT-MRAM asymmetric write errors absorbed by Z-channel codes
idea: STT-MRAM lost the DRAM-replacement race partly because write error rate demands high current, and failures are strongly one-directional (P to AP). Fix: deliberately lower write current until errors are almost purely in that direction, then protect with asymmetric Z-channel codes (Varshamov/Constantin-Rao style) that correct only that direction.
why: ~30% lower write current/energy or ~40% less parity at equal uncorrectable rate; a smaller access transistor raises density.

title: Williams-tube read-around ratio revived as per-die fused hammer threshold
idea: Williams-tube memories lost to core, but had a working discipline: each tube's measured 'read-around ratio' set how many neighboring reads were allowed before regeneration. Fix today's worst-case row-hammer design the same way: test each die's real hammer threshold per bank, fuse it into a mode register, scale controller mitigation per bank, and price dies by threshold grade.
why: Stops sizing every die's mitigation for the worst die (~1k ACT, fact 9): typical dies run 3-10x less mitigation, and low-threshold dies are sold rather than scrapped.
note: DDR5 RFM thresholds already vendor-set in mode registers.

title: Optane endurance shielded by MMU write-budget traps and page migration
idea: 3D XPoint never displaced DRAM partly because ~1e7-1e8-cycle media wore out under hot writes. Fix: the MMU keeps a per-page write-budget counter, and a page exceeding its budget traps and migrates to a small SRAM-backed write log, so only read-mostly data (weights, code, indexes) ever lives in the nonvolatile tier.
why: Zero refresh for the bulk tier (read-mostly data is often >70% of AI-server bytes) with a guaranteed 5-year wear life; cuts DRAM bits needed.

title: Optane's App Direct trap fixed: transparent tiered memory with SLA
idea: Optane DIMMs disappointed because the best mode (App Direct) needed rewritten software and Memory Mode had poor tail latency. Fix: sell any cheaper tier (dense, slow-bin or NAND-backed memory) only behind a CXL controller that migrates hot 4 KB pages into local DRAM in hardware, priced against a contractual DRAM-equivalent latency SLA, with zero code changes.
why: Lets data centers cut fast DRAM per server by ~30-50% at the same delivered performance, which frees bits for AI.
note: Hardware tiering (Intel flat memory mode, Samsung CMM-H) already exists; SLA pricing is the twist.

title: SoftRAM fraud made real: rack-wide content-addressed page deduplication
idea: SoftRAM 95 promised doubled memory and did nothing, and RAM Doubler died as operating systems absorbed it. Fix with a real mechanism: a CXL memory node hashes 4 KB pages from every server in a rack and stores identical pages (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) once, mapped copy-on-write back to each host.
why: Cuts physical DRAM ~15-40% in VM and container fleets where pages repeat across hosts, not only within one host.

title: ETA10's cryo bet revisited: LN2-cooled legacy-node memory pools
idea: ETA Systems' liquid-nitrogen-cooled CMOS supercomputer (ETA10) died in 1989 from cost and timing, not physics. Fix with cryo for memory only: 180 nm DRAM dies at 77 K leak orders of magnitude less (refresh nearly disappears) and switch ~1.5-2x faster, so pooled LN2-cooled shelves of old-node memory approach modern latency and idle power.
why: Makes depreciated-fab memory performance-competitive (refresh cost near zero, faster transistors); density stays low and cooling overhead is the risk, so it suits pooled capacity tiers.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods run DRAM at 77 K, refresh off
idea: Effect: Arrhenius freeze-out of generation and subthreshold leakage. DIMMs/HBM sit on closed-loop LN2 cold plates; at 77 K subthreshold slope is ~15-20 mV/dec and generation ~exp(-Eg/2kT) collapses, so retention exceeds hours, refresh is disabled and Vt/VDD are retuned for cold operation.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth to ~0 (fact 3), wire resistance ~6x lower (fact 5), lower VDD (fact 10); cooling cost amortized at rack scale.
note: Cryo-DRAM studied (Rambus, CryoRAM); LN2 cooling overhead offsets refresh savings.

title: MOS-varactor capacitance collapse amplifies bitline signal before latching
idea: Effect: parametric amplification (voltage-dependent capacitance). After charge sharing, drive the bottom plate of an accumulation-mode MOS varactor on each bitline into depletion so bitline capacitance falls ~3x; charge is conserved, so the differential voltage grows ~3x (V=Q/C) with no DC current before the latch fires.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): ~3x signal allows 2x longer bitlines (half as many SA stripes) or ~2x smaller Cs.

title: Capacitive self-bootstrap wordlines eliminate the VPP charge pump
idea: Effect: capacitive bootstrap coupling. Revive the NMOS-era trick: the selected wordline driver's gate node is isolated, then kicked by its own rising output through gate-channel capacitance plus a small MOS cap, lifting the wordline to ~2xVDD for the access with no global VPP pump. Proven by a small team on a mature-node MPW macro.
why: Periphery area/energy (facts 7, 10): removes the VPP pump (~3-5% of die, ~30% efficient) and its grid, cutting activation energy ~20%.
note: NMOS-era bootstrap revival; device stress at 2xVDD and negative wordline needs remain.

title: Leakage-replica decay timer sets refresh interval automatically
idea: Effect: junction/GIDL leakage tracking in replica cells. Each mat holds a few replica storage cells with ~4x smaller capacitance, charged at every refresh and watched by a comparator; because they leak through the same physics as data cells, their threshold crossing marks a self-timed refresh deadline that follows process, voltage and temperature.
why: Refresh (fact 3): typical dies can refresh ~2-4x less often than the fixed worst-case spec; fits a small team's gain-cell/eDRAM macro on MPW.

title: Asymmetric-leakage data inversion keeps most cells in non-leaking state
idea: Effect: one-sided leakage (only charged cells decay toward error). An FPGA/CXL controller inverts each row's data whenever that leaves more cells discharged, using the module's true/anti-cell map learned once by a retention scan, and stores one inversion flag per row in spare metadata bits; zero-heavy data leaves ~70-90% of cells uncharged.
why: Refresh/reliability (fact 3): fewer charged cells means fewer retention failures, enabling ~2x longer refresh intervals at the same error rate; pure controller work.

title: AlScN wurtzite ferrodiode makes self-rectifying 3D ferroelectric cross-points
idea: Polarization-modulated Schottky barrier: in CMOS-compatible ferroelectric AlScN, deposited at ≤400 C, switching polarization raises or lowers the interface barrier. Each cell is therefore a non-volatile diode that both stores and rectifies, so selector-free cross-point tiers stack over logic.
why: Gives non-volatile 4F2 stacked arrays with very long retention and no access transistor (facts 2 and 4); claim 4-8 tiers in BEOL over periphery.
note: Already published; AlScN endurance far below DRAM-class.

title: Capacitive deionization loops recycle dilute fab rinse water cheaply
idea: Effect: electric-double-layer electrosorption. Activated-carbon electrodes pull ions out of dilute rinse streams with energy that scales with the ions removed, unlike RO, which scales with water volume. Cascade CDI and EDI to return >90% of rinse water to the UPW plant, and recover energy on discharge.
why: Water and energy intensity of DRAM fabs: 2-3x lower purification energy for dilute streams and a large cut in fresh-water draw.

title: Deuterium kinetic-isotope passivation trims the leakage tail at 400 C
idea: Effect: the kinetic isotope effect. Si-D bonds at access-transistor interfaces and STI corners desorb 10-50x slower than Si-H because the heavier isotope couples to Si phonons. A final 400 C high-pressure D2 anneal, or a deuterated SiN cap, keeps tail traps passivated, suppressing the trap-assisted tunneling that sets refresh.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 2-4x longer tail retention halves refresh energy; deuterium comes from abundant water.

title: Moire-fringe overlay upgrade lets used contact aligners reach 5 nm alignment
idea: Effect: moire magnification. Pairs of slightly mismatched gratings on mask and wafer produce fringes that magnify misalignment ~1000x; a $5k camera reads them and drives a closed-loop piezo stage retrofitted to a ~$100k used proximity aligner or imprint tool, giving sub-5 nm overlay for array layers. $1M funds two retrofits and 24 months of overlay qualification.
why: Fact 4: overlay is the barrier to cheap patterning; ~$250k per tool versus $50-200M scanners.

title: Solid-state laser interference prints 38 nm half-pitch gratings on a benchtop
idea: Effect: two-beam optical interference. Build an immersion Lloyd's-mirror interferometer with a ~$120k 213 nm fifth-harmonic Nd:YAG and a high-index prism; the fringes give about 38 nm half-pitch over a cm2 field, stepped and stitched across 100 mm wafers, and a double exposure at 60 degrees gives honeycomb arrays. $1M covers optics, resist and university fab access.
why: Fact 4: shows array layers can be printed by a <$300k tool, the first step toward a dedicated interference array-layer printer for U.S. fabs.

title: Home-built atmospheric spatial ALD deposits capacitor high-k without vacuum
idea: Effect: self-limiting chemisorption separated in space. A gas-bearing head keeps precursor and oxidant zones apart with N2 curtains, so the ALD half-reactions happen as the wafer moves under it at atmospheric pressure, depositing ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 at ~10x the rate of temporal ALD. $1M funds two heads, precursors and 24 months of electrical tests on capacitor molds.
why: Capital: vacuum ALD tools cost $3-5M; an atmospheric tool at ~$300k with higher throughput cuts deposition cost of ownership. Conformality in HAR holes is the risk.

title: Hydrogen backside gas replaces helium for wafer cooling in etch chucks
idea: Effect: gas-gap thermal conduction, set by molecular speed and the accommodation coefficient. H2 carries heat about as well as or better than He at the same low pressure, so retrofit a refurbished etch chamber's electrostatic chuck with a low-pressure H2 backside line, leak detection and N2-diluted exhaust, then qualify wafer-temperature uniformity. $1M covers the chamber and 24 months of tests.
why: Helium chokepoint: Qatar's ~30% of supply has been offline since March 2026, and backside cooling is a major fab helium use; H2 can be made on site by electrolysis.

title: Capillarity: water-droplet self-alignment speeds die-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Pattern hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surrounds, dispense a nanoliter water droplet, and drop DRAM dies coarsely; surface tension pulls each die to <200 nm alignment before direct bonding, so placement tools run 10x faster at coarse accuracy.
why: HBM assembly capital and throughput (facts 4, 6): hybrid bonders are slow and costly; capillary alignment cuts bonder capex per stack.

title: Shape-memory polymer: printed thermally releasable underfill makes chiplet modules reworkable
idea: Print an underfill made of shape-memory epoxy that is rigid and stress-relieving below 120 C but softens and contracts past a 160 C transition, so a failed memory chiplet can be lifted off a printed interposer and replaced.
why: Chiplet package yield and scrap (fact 6): reworkability saves the whole module; thermal-cycling reliability must be proven.

title: Self-focusing photopolymerization: light writes its own waveguide from fiber to chiplet
idea: Dispense photosensitive resin between a flex-waveguide or fiber end and a memory chiplet's grating coupler; light launched through the fiber self-focuses and polymerizes a bridging waveguide along its own path, giving automatic sub-um alignment.
why: Fiber attach is the cost and throughput bottleneck of optical memory links (fact 5); a printable resin step replaces $1M active-alignment stations.

title: Aerodynamic focusing: aerosol-jet printed staircase edge wiring replaces stack TSVs
idea: Stack DRAM dies offset like a staircase and aerosol-jet print conductive traces over printed dielectric ramps down the exposed edges, so every die connects to the base die without a single TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims TSV area and yield loss and removes via etch/fill tools; lower edge bandwidth suits capacity-optimized (CXL) stacks.

title: Replica-node relaxation oscillator times refresh from real leakage
idea: Effect: Arrhenius thermally activated generation current. Each subarray has a replica storage node built from the same cell transistor and capacitor that discharges to a comparator threshold, resets and repeats; its frequency tracks that subarray's actual leakage versus temperature, voltage and aging, and it clocks the refresh counter with a fixed guard factor instead of a fixed 64 ms timer.
why: Removes fixed worst-case temperature guard bands: at typical 45-60 C operation, refresh rate falls ~4-8x versus 85 C worst-case timing.
note: Replica-leakage refresh timing; temp-compensated self-refresh exists.

title: Molecular-sieve silica membranes recapture fab helium at every tool exhaust
idea: Helium's 2.6 A kinetic diameter lets it permeate amorphous-silica or carbon molecular-sieve hollow fibers ~1000x faster than N2/Ar. Put membrane skids on tool exhausts and load locks, recompress and repurify on site, and back it with a 'helium return credit' for fabs recycling >80%.
why: Cuts fab helium purchases 70-90% and insulates supply from single-region outages.
note: Helium recovery skids already sold to fabs.

title: Carrier freeze-out at 77 K lets old fabs build tiny-capacitor memory pools
idea: At liquid-nitrogen temperature junction and subthreshold leakage fall >10^6x, so a 1 fF planar capacitor on a 65 nm transistor holds data for minutes. Build cryogenic memory pools in LN2-immersed racks from cells made on depreciated 65-40 nm lines.
why: Bypasses the charge wall and refresh and uses idle mature capacity; LN2 is cheap and domestically abundant.

title: Capacitive-deionization loops regenerate rinse water with reusable carbon electrodes
idea: Rinse effluent flows between charged porous-carbon electrodes whose electric double layers adsorb ions; reversing the voltage releases a small brine stream and regenerates the electrodes, returning low-TDS water to UPW polishing with no chemical regenerants.
why: Reclaims >85% of dilute rinse water at low energy, opening water-capped sites.
note: Capacitive deionization is known; fab rinse reuse is incremental.

title: Oxygen pinch-off of Bosch scallops yields stacked nanowire tiers
idea: Etch tall Si fins with a deliberately scalloped Bosch (SF6/C4F8) cycle, then dry-oxidize at ~1000 C so the narrow necks between scallops oxidize through first, leaving vertically stacked, oxide-isolated horizontal Si nanowires, one per scallop, as lateral access-transistor tiers.
why: Crystalline stacked lateral channels (fact 2) from bulk Si using only DRIE and a furnace; scallop period sets tier pitch (~100-200 nm) for 4-10-tier university demonstrations.

title: Sulfur-anchored monolayers enable mask-free self-aligned contacts in stacked tiers
idea: Dip the wafer in an alkanethiol solution so a self-assembled monolayer binds only to exposed Cu lines, then ALD Al2O3 grows only on the dielectric (area-selective deposition); strip the SAM to leave metal exposed and perfectly self-aligned for the next tier's vias.
why: Each self-aligned level removes a critical alignment mask and its overlay budget (fact 4) and allows tighter via pitch in 3D stacks; a thiol bath and ALD are standard university equipment.
note: Thiol-SAM inhibited ALD on Cu is published ASD art.

title: Argon-activated room-temperature bonding stacks finished oxide-TFT memory tiers
idea: Fabricate oxide-semiconductor memory tiers on separate 100 mm wafers, activate both bonding faces with an Ar fast-atom beam or Ar plasma, bond in vacuum at room temperature, then grind/etch away the donor substrate; repeat for 4-8 tiers on IR-aligned keys.
why: Stacks fully processed tiers with zero thermal budget so each is optimized independently (fact 2) and tests a known-good-tier yield model; argon is abundant (0.93% of air) and SAB bonders exist in many universities.

title: Copper spiral coils link stacked dies wirelessly instead of TSVs
idea: Pattern 20-40 um Cu inductor coils by lift-off or plating on each thinned memory die and stack the dies with adhesive; inductive coupling carries Gb/s data per coil pair through 4-8 dies, while power arrives through a few coarse TSVs or edge wires.
why: Cuts the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): less keep-out area and TSV yield loss, and adhesive stacking replaces fine-pitch bonding; coils are single-mask university builds.
note: ThruChip-style; power still needs vias.

title: Zinc-oxide sacrificial release lets PDMS stamps transfer-print memory tiers
idea: Build thin-film memory tiles (oxide TFTs plus capacitors) on a ZnO sacrificial layer, undercut it in dilute acetic acid while tethers hold the tiles, pick them up with a PDMS stamp and print them onto logic or the previous tier, stacking only known-good tiles.
why: Known-good-tile stacking breaks the yield multiplication across tiers (fact 2) without wafer-scale bonders; micro-transfer printing needs only a stamp stage that universities have or can build.
note: Microtransfer printing of known-good TFT tiles; university-demoable.

title: C: closed-loop supercritical CO2 removes post-etch residues
idea: Replace aqueous/semi-aqueous post-etch residue removal and its DI rinse with supercritical CO2 carrying a few percent chelating co-solvent in a pressure cell; the CO2 is recompressed and recycled >95%.
why: Water: post-etch cleans recur dozens of times per DRAM flow, and their water drops >10x; zero surface tension also protects high-AR pillars and 3D tiers.

title: Xe: 172 nm excimer photons clean wafers inside load-locks
idea: Mount Xe2* excimer VUV lamps inside tool load-locks so every wafer gets a ~30 s photolysis in N2 that breaks organic and airborne molecular contamination before each deposition, replacing routine wet pre-cleans between steps.
why: Water: removes dozens of inter-step wet cleans with zero added queue time; those steps' water falls ~100%.

title: Hydrogen isotopes: near-duplicate pages stored as base plus neutron delta
idea: Like protium vs deuterium (same element, one extra neutron), the memory controller finds pages that differ from an existing base page in only a few bytes (forked VMs, container images, agent sandboxes, model replicas with patched metadata) using 64-bit similarity sketches, and stores them as a base pointer plus a <=256 B XOR delta. Reads rebuild lines in a delta-apply unit; writes that grow the delta past a threshold trigger a copy-on-write split.
why: Exact dedup (KSM) only catches identical pages (~5-15% in clouds); near-duplicate capture adds ~15-30% more effective capacity on VM/container/agent fleets, about 1.3-1.6x less DRAM per host (cost/bit).

title: Silicon logic is cheap: mature-node dedup die under DRAM stacks
idea: Because a 28 nm logic die costs a fraction of DRAM per mm2, the base die of a DRAM stack runs a content-addressed dedup engine: every 64 B write is hashed (CRC64, second hash on collision), unique lines are stored once with a reference count, and a translation table maps logical lines to physical lines inside the stack.
why: Line-granular exact dedup finds 1.3-2x redundancy in VM, container and inference-replica memory where page-level dedup finds little; it trades cheap logic area for scarce DRAM bits (cost/bit).
note: HICAMP-style line dedup on a base die; 1.3-2x gain with translation-table overhead.

title: Calcium bone remodeling: collections reshape themselves to their observed load
idea: Bone remodels to the loads it carries (Wolff's law); the runtime watches each large collection's access mix and swaps a read-mostly boxed HashMap (~48 B/entry) for an open-addressing primitive array (~12 B/entry) or a sorted static array, switching back when write bursts appear.
why: Boxed collections in Java/Python/JS hold 3-5x more bytes than their data; automatic remodeling saves ~30-50% heap on cache-heavy services (density).
note: CoCo/Brainy collection switching known.

title: Selenium trace: SRAM sketches replace DRAM hash tables until certain
idea: Selenium is essential in trace amounts; big DRAM hash tables for counting, dedup, joins and membership are replaced by SRAM-resident sketches (count-min, HyperLogLog, cuckoo filters) that answer most queries, and the exact table, kept compressed in DRAM or flash, is consulted only on sketch-positive or close-call results.
why: Sketches are 10-100x smaller than exact tables and SRAM costs ~50x less energy per bit than DRAM, so typical lookups fall >10x in energy and the index footprint in DRAM shrinks sharply (energy, density).
note: Sketch-first lookups are standard practice.

title: Boron icosahedra: succinct indexes with near-memory rank/select fit in SRAM
idea: Boron packs into compact 12-atom icosahedra; database and search indexes are rebuilt as succinct structures (Elias-Fano lists, wavelet trees, rank/select bitvectors) at 1-2 bits per element above entropy, and a near-memory unit adds single-cycle popcount-based rank/select so lookups stay fast.
why: Indexes shrink 5-20x so most fit in on-die SRAM or LLC, cutting energy per lookup >10x versus DRAM and freeing the DRAM they occupied (energy, density).

title: Iodine clock reaction: hold requests, then serve whole rows at once
idea: In the iodine clock reaction nothing happens until a threshold, then everything at once; the controller holds latency-tolerant reads (prefetches, bulk KV, GC, DMA) for up to ~2 us in per-row bins and issues one activation when a bin holds 16+ requests or times out, pooling requests across all tenants sharing the device.
why: Sharing one activate/precharge across 16+ accesses cuts activation energy per access ~10x or more and raises effective bandwidth, so systems that buy DRAM channels for bandwidth (HBM especially) need fewer stacks (energy, capital).

title: Ag: maskless inkjet-silver RDL for low-volume memory interposers
idea: Print redistribution layers with nano-silver ink sintered at ~150 C and inkjet-printed polyimide dielectric directly on glass or organic interposers at 5-10 um lines, so custom memory-chiplet interposers need no photomasks, steppers or plating lines.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): removes ~$100k-1M mask sets per interposer design and litho tools; lets small U.S. firms build HBM-style packages in weeks.

title: Cu: copper-pillar bare DRAM dies soldered straight onto motherboards
idea: Flip-chip unpackaged DRAM dies with Cu pillars directly onto a motherboard region beside the CPU (chip-on-board, glob-topped), eliminating the BGA substrate, DIMM PCB and connector so memory traces shrink from ~10 cm to ~2 cm.
why: Cost per bit and energy: package/module overhead is ~10-15% of DIMM cost and long traces dominate DDR's 10-20 pJ/bit; ~2x lower I/O energy and no substrate supply dependency.

title: N: liquid-nitrogen memory sled where refresh nearly disappears
idea: A small team builds a dewar-cooled, CXL-attached 1U memory sled running commodity DDR5 at ~77-120 K, where junction leakage freezes out so retention stretches to seconds and refresh is throttled ~100x; an FPGA controller re-tunes timings.
why: Eliminates the refresh tax and leakage-tail errors (fact 3) using off-the-shelf DRAM; cryocooler power is partly offset by lower wire resistance.
note: Cryo-DRAM well studied; cryocooler overhead offsets refresh savings.

title: Zn: zinc sacrificial-anode rows absorb hammer flips beside hot rows
idea: Like zinc galvanizing steel, the OS page allocator and controller place only recomputable content (clean page-cache copies, parity, prefetch buffers) in rows physically adjacent to detected hot rows, so flips land where they are harmless and heal on re-fetch. Software plus firmware.
why: Turns row hammer (fact 9) from a correctness failure into a small cache-miss cost with no new hardware.
note: ZebRAM-like guard rows via allocator.

title: Au: gold rows hold critical data in best-retention cells
idea: Boot-time firmware profiling ranks rows into gold, silver and bronze retention bins; the hypervisor maps kernel, page tables and model weights to gold rows at relaxed refresh and puts streaming and cache data in bronze rows with faster refresh.
why: Matches data criticality to cell quality instead of uniform worst-case refresh; ~30-50% refresh reduction (fact 3).

title: Fe: let the mantissa rust while exponent bits stay protected
idea: Like a thick iron beam that tolerates surface rust, a model-loading library splits bf16/fp8 weights so sign and exponent bits live in ECC-protected, normally refreshed rows while low mantissa bits sit in rows with 4x relaxed refresh and no ECC.
why: Neural nets tolerate mantissa flips, so ~60% of weight bits get cheaper storage and refresh, letting weaker cells serve inference.

title: Sn: tin-can preservation compresses cold pages to fund ECC
idea: The controller compresses cold pages (typically 1.5-2x) and fills the freed bits with a strong Reed-Solomon code in place, so these pages tolerate 8-16x relaxed refresh in a low-refresh region with no capacity loss. Firmware plus RTL.
why: Cuts refresh energy (fact 3) for the cold majority of memory and makes weak cells tolerable.

title: Sn: Bismuth-tin low-temperature reballing harvests DRAM from retired servers
idea: An automated line desolders DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards below 170 C with Bi-Sn solder and laser selective reflow, tests each die for retention and hammer threshold, reballs and remounts them as graded modules.
why: Hyperscalers retire exabyte-scale DRAM after 4-6 years; harvesting 30% of it adds several percent to annual supply at near-zero capital.

title: Na: Sodium-ion rack batteries make DRAM durable, deleting database replicas
idea: Rack-level Na-ion batteries hold servers up long enough to flush DRAM to NVMe on power loss, certified as durable, so in-memory databases and caches drop one of their 2-3 durability replicas.
why: Saves 33-50% of DRAM in replicated in-memory clusters; Na-ion avoids Li and Co.

title: Conveyor-belt CCD loops: charge packets recirculate, no capacitor per bit
idea: Treat memory as an assembly line. Bits are charge packets clocked around closed buried-channel CCD rings of 64-256 wells, and each ring has a single sense/regenerate station, so every lap is a refresh. No bit has its own access transistor or capacitor, only overlapping gates.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 7: the capacitor and access-transistor leakage are gone. A bit costs ~4F2 of gate and the periphery is shared across a whole ring. Fits streamed pages such as KV cache, with <=64 ns rotation latency.
note: Commercial CCD memories existed in the 1970s; serial latency and dark current limit it.

title: Andon-cord canary cells trigger refresh only when truly needed
idea: Each subarray carries a few deliberately weak canary cells (thinner Cs or a leakier spacer), sensed continuously by a tiny comparator. Like a Toyota andon cord, a tripped canary pulls refresh for that subarray only, tracking real temperature and VRT state.
why: Fact 3: replaces the fixed 64/32 ms guardband with measured need, plausibly 2-4x fewer refreshes and matching recovered bandwidth.

title: Assembly-line takt sweep: every row restored by normal reads
idea: Set the memory controller's address mapping and scheduler so streaming workloads (LLM weight sweeps, frame buffers) activate every row within a takt time below tREFW. Disable refresh and verify coverage with a per-row activation bitmap.
why: Zero refresh power: restore happens as a free side effect of reads that occur anyway. Fits HBM in inference, where weights are swept every token.
note: Smart Refresh skip-on-access known; only fits strictly streaming workloads.

title: Darkroom dodge-and-burn: per-mat precharge level trimmed at test
idea: Like a printer dodging and burning areas of a photograph, measure each mat's '0' and '1' bitline signal distributions at wafer sort. Then program a 4-bit offset on that mat's precharge voltage with 1990s laser-fuse repair tools, so the reference sits midway between the real, leakage-skewed distributions.
why: Leakage pulls stored '1's down asymmetrically; re-centering recovers ~20-30% of margin, which becomes ~1.5-2x longer refresh intervals or a smaller capacitor.
note: Per-mat precharge trim; global VBLP trims exist, fuse area per mat adds cost.

title: Wire-bonder pin forest: bond-via arrays link legacy dies to logic
idea: Use installed wire bonders as 3D printers to stand dense forests of vertical 25 um copper wires on a logic die, mold and grind them flat, and face-down-bond mature DRAM dies on top as an HBM-like wide bus with no TSV process.
why: Sidesteps the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) entirely in existing OSAT lines (~10-20k wires per stack) and places memory adjacent to compute to cut I/O energy toward ~2 pJ/bit (fact 5).
note: Invensas BVA-style wire forests are known; 25 um wires give far lower bandwidth than HBM.

title: Veneer-peel tiers: spall device layers instead of grinding wafers away
idea: Veneer mills peel thin sheets from a log instead of sawing it; after front-end processing on mature lines, deposit a stressed nickel layer and controlled-spall the top 10-20 um device layer for stacking, then repolish and reuse the parent substrate 5-10 times.
why: Backgrinding for stacking discards ~97% of each wafer; spalling cuts wafer and Spruce Pine crucible consumption per stacked tier ~5x and makes thin tiers with only a spall station added.
note: IBM controlled spalling is known; resource gain is incremental.

title: Jacquard loom lithography: Texas-made DLP mirrors write periphery layers
idea: The Jacquard loom replaced fixed patterns with programmable punched cards; build maskless exposure engines from Dallas-made DLP micromirror chips with reduction optics and expose DRAM periphery, pad, redistribution and upper-metal layers straight from data.
why: Removes masks and blanks for ~20-30 non-critical layers per product and foreign stepper dependence on those layers, and lets each wafer carry its own repair and redundancy wiring; ~0.3-1 um resolution suffices there.

title: Dry-cleaner wafer benches run on ethanol-plant CO2
idea: Dry cleaners wash clothes in liquid CO2 without water; replace post-etch residue removal and rinse-dry steps with supercritical CO2 plus co-solvent chambers, fed by fermentation CO2 captured at Midwest ethanol plants and recycled in a closed loop.
why: Cuts ultrapure water and IPA on cleaning steps ~50-80%, prevents pattern collapse of 70:1 capacitors, and turns a domestic waste gas into a process fluid.

title: Die-cast slabs: address bits imply object type, headers vanish
idea: Parts from one die-casting mold are identical, so they need no label. The runtime allocates every object of a class (a 'mold') in a 2 MB cast slab whose address bits encode the mold ID. That removes per-object headers, vtable pointers and type tags, and 64-bit references become 32-bit slab-relative offsets decoded by a hardware base register.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Python, JS, Go) spend 20-40% of memory on headers and fat pointers, so removing them gives about 1.3-1.6x effective capacity for the biggest DRAM users in cloud fleets.
note: BIBOP plus compressed oops; known runtime techniques combined.

title: SPC control charts per row: data classes follow measured cell quality
idea: Statistical process control tracks each machine against control limits. The memory controller keeps a CUSUM chart of corrected and detected errors for every row (from scrub and parity) and classifies rows as A (<0.01%), B (<0.3%) or C (up to 1%). Pages are remapped so precise data lives in A rows, approximate tensors in B rows, and noise-tolerant data (KV tails, activation stash, low bit-planes) in C rows.
why: Cell quality varies about 100x across a die; matching data tolerance to measured row quality lets whole modules run at relaxed refresh or voltage with 1% worst-case rows instead of paying for guard bands.
note: Heterogeneous-reliability memory work covers this.

title: Ripstop weave: error-contained compression for media and sensor buffers
idea: Ripstop fabric has a heavy thread every few mm so tears cannot spread. Compressed video frames, images and sensor streams kept in memory use fixed-length transform-coefficient codes and reversible variable-length codes, with a resync point every 32 symbols. A flip then corrupts one coefficient in one block instead of the rest of the stream, and the decoder conceals damaged blocks from their neighbors.
why: Camera, video-analytics and vehicle-log buffers can stay compressed 5-20x in 1%-BER memory instead of being decompressed into perfect DRAM.
note: RVLC/resync codecs are known; applying them to approximate memory is a twist.

title: Co-extruded micro-coax ribbon cables for memory shelves
idea: Co-extrude polymer and copper (like making cable sheathing) into 50 um shielded micro-coax ribbons with 64 lanes each, terminated straight onto memory and compute packages. The low-loss, low-crosstalk path lets 30 cm links run near HBM energy.
why: PCB traces cost 5-10 pJ/bit; micro-coax claims ~1-2 pJ/bit at rack-shelf distances, enabling disaggregated memory without optics.
note: Close to existing flyover twinax cabling.

title: Coin-struck dual damascene: via and trench in one press
idea: Make a nanoimprint stamp with two relief heights, like a coin die, so one press forms both the via and the trench of an interposer wiring level in resist. One etch and fill then replaces two litho and two etch passes.
why: Halves the BEOL step count and mask count for interposer and base-die RDL, cutting capital per interconnect layer.

title: Printing-plate kiss contact capacitive coupling for clip-on memory
idea: Place 20 um pitch electrode arrays made in 40 nm on memory and logic faces, pressed in kiss contact across 1 um of dielectric like an offset plate on a blanket. Data crosses capacitively with no metal joint, so memory clips on and off.
why: Reworkable, upgradeable memory attach with no bonding yield loss, at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, all in non-EUV nodes.

title: Vinyl-record hot-embossed polymer optical couplers for memory links
idea: Hot-emboss V-grooves, waveguides and 45-degree mirrors into cyclic-olefin polymer in seconds, as vinyl records and DVDs are replicated from a nickel master. Fiber arrays then align passively to memory photonic dies.
why: Optical coupler cost and alignment time drop ~10x, making optical memory links affordable at volume.
note: Polymer replicated couplers widely pursued in CPO.

title: Juice-concentrate links: compress in the base die before shipping
idea: Like shipping juice concentrate, a compression engine in the 12-28 nm HBM base die squeezes AI tensors 1.5-2x (exponent dedup, base-delta) before the bus; the GPU decompresses on arrival.
why: Cuts pJ per useful bit and raises effective bandwidth and capacity ~1.5x with no new memory silicon.

title: Triaxial-weave parity: row, column and diagonal threads catch clusters
idea: Triaxial fabrics weave threads at 0, 60 and 120 degrees so tears cannot run; overlay three interleaved parity families on each subarray mat (rows, columns, 60-degree diagonals), updated by on-die XOR trees at write-back, so a particle defect, a dead wordline segment or a hammered neighbourhood is located where three failing parity threads intersect and is corrected during scrub.
why: 2D clusters defeat on-die SEC; three-direction parity corrects them for ~3% overhead versus 6-12% for strong symbol codes, letting clustered-defect dies ship and absorbing hammer bursts (fact 9).

title: Adaptive-infill ECC: code strength varies page by page
idea: 3D printers vary infill density where stress is high; classify every 4 KB page at test and in the field by measured weakness and store it with a matching code rate (none, SEC-DED, or ~12% BCH), tracked in a page-attribute table, so strong pages hand their parity bits back as capacity.
why: Uniform worst-case ECC wastes ~12.5% of bits; adaptive rate recovers ~6-9% capacity on typical dies while still tolerating weak tails (cost per bit).

title: Sous-vide chilled DRAM using absorption chillers, not cryogens
idea: Sous vide holds food at an exact temperature; hold memory modules at a precise 5-10C with waste-heat-driven lithium-bromide/water absorption chillers (no helium cryogenics) and program refresh from measured temperature, since retention roughly doubles per 10C drop.
why: Refresh can relax ~8x versus 85C, cutting refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) by ~85% and letting weak tail cells pass, powered by data-centre waste heat.

title: Tire-retread playbook: remanufacture retired server DRAM into CXL pools
idea: Like tire retreading, take DDR4/DDR5 packages from decommissioned hyperscale servers and run a high-temperature retention and row-hammer screen. Reball the good packages and rebuild them onto CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controller applies per-device refresh profiles. Sell them as warrantied 'retread' tier-2 capacity, the way remanufactured auto parts are sold.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~15-25% of installed DRAM retires each year still working. Recovering half adds ~5-10% effective bits at <30% of new cost, with zero wafer, EUV or helium intensity.

title: Patchwork-quilt modules stitched from partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Quilters make full blankets from remnants. Dies that fail full spec because of a few dead banks or subarrays are scrapped or sold as junk today; instead, mount them on an organic substrate. A small 'quilting' controller holds each die's bad-region map and presents one contiguous address space by interleaving across the surviving banks.
why: Cost per bit and yield: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output that is lost today. That is like getting a free mini-fab per large fab with no new capex.

title: Loom-woven flex interposers: polyimide-copper bolts replacing silicon CoWoS
idea: Weave a multilayer polyimide/copper redistribution 'cloth' on a carrier wafer by spin-coat, i-line lithography and semi-additive plating at 2 um line/space, then release it. Like woven tape, it can be cut to length to wire 1024-bit HBM-class buses between memory and logic with no silicon interposer.
why: HBM interposer tax and the CoWoS capacity chokepoint: silicon interposer area goes to zero, and the line costs ~10x less. Spinner, aligner and plating bath suffice.

title: Self-assembled honeycomb: block-copolymer holes for storage-node capacitors
idea: Cylinder-forming PS-b-PMMA packs hexagonally on its own, the same honeycomb DRAM capacitor arrays use. Coarse i-line guide posts register the polymer, which self-assembles 4-9x denser hole arrays. Those holes are etched into the mold oxide as storage nodes.
why: Litho capital: replaces 1-2 EUV or quad-patterning layers with spin-coat, bake and RIE, all nanofab-standard.

title: Rotary-press ALD: spatial gas-zone heads for capacitor high-k
idea: A rotary press inks paper as it runs past fixed rollers. A spatial-ALD head with alternating precursor and purge slots, machined and assembled in a university shop, sweeps wafers under fixed gas zones at atmospheric pressure. It deposits ZrO2/HfO2/Al2O3 capacitor stacks 10-50x faster than temporal ALD.
why: Capital and tool count: high-k ALD is a large tool-count item, and spatial heads cut ALD capex per wafer start several-fold. An open design spreads to micro-fabs.
note: Spatial ALD is commercial in solar/display; open design for wafers is the twist.

title: Batik wax-resist: self-assembled monolayers steer where films grow
idea: Batik dyers wax areas so dye takes only elsewhere. Stamp or vapor-pattern alkylsilane/thiol SAM inhibitors so ALD metal and dielectric grow only on landing pads, self-aligned contacts and bottom electrodes. Deposition self-aligns, removing 2-4 litho/etch steps per flow.
why: Mask count and capital: each removed litho/etch layer saves ~3-5% of wafer cost. SAM-based area-selective deposition runs on any nanofab ALD.
note: Widely pursued AS-ALD; selectivity defectivity limits.

title: Refresh cycles double as in-DRAM scrub, zeroing and copy
idea: IFR: refresh does useful work. Each refresh already opens a row into the sense amps, so a small per-bank engine uses that open window to run ECC scrub, bulk zeroing of freed pages and RowClone-style copies queued by the OS, costing no extra activations.
why: Fact 3: turns the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh into productive work, giving back equivalent channel bandwidth and energy now spent on scrub and zeroing traffic.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory sleds where refresh switches off
idea: IFR: leakage frozen out. Put DRAM sleds in sealed 77 K LN2 baths fed by a shared data-center cryo plant, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall by many orders of magnitude so refresh is disabled and wire resistance drops ~5x.
why: Fact 3 and 5: removes refresh energy and bandwidth and lowers I/O energy; cryo overhead (~10 W per W removed) must be beaten by the lower heat produced, best for dense cold-data tiers.

title: Right-to-repair rule exposing spare rows to operators
idea: Ideal result: owners fix memory themselves. Require DRAM to expose a standard post-package repair command set, spare-row counts and repair logs to the OS, so data centers repair faults in place rather than return modules.
why: Usable supply: fewer discarded modules; a low-cost policy lever during the shortage.
note: DDR4/DDR5 already define hPPR/sPPR commands.

title: Retired sense-amp stripes reborn as bit-serial compute engines
idea: Ideal result: periphery that finds a second job. Design SA stripes with a bit-serial logic mode (multi-row activation for AND/OR plus a latch-side XOR), so dies retired for poor retention are reused as in-memory compute engines with short data lifetimes.
why: Recyclability: a second-life market for degraded dies, and fewer data-movement joules (fact 5) for bulk bitwise work.
note: Ambit/ComputeDRAM-style bitwise compute applied to second-life retired dies.

title: Laser-written cube-face bus replaces HBM through-silicon vias
idea: IFR: 'the stack has full bandwidth and no TSVs.' Backward: stack DRAM dies with all I/O routed to one edge, mold the stack, polish that face, and laser-direct-write then electroplate ~2,000 copper lines at 5 um pitch down the cube face to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers TSV keep-out area and TSV-related yield loss, part of HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield penalty.

title: Birth-tiering allocator places objects by predicted lifetime and heat
idea: IFR: DRAM holds only bytes about to be touched. Closest: allocation call-site, type and stack-hash features feed a tiny on-CPU model that predicts each object's heat; predicted-cold objects are born directly in CXL or flash-backed memory and never migrate, so hot and cold objects never share a page.
why: Page-granular tiering strands 30-50% of near DRAM on mixed hot/cold pages; object-level birth placement cuts near DRAM 30-40%.

title: Regenerable pages: kernel drops pages tagged with rebuild functions
idea: IFR: memory holds only information that cannot be rebuilt. Closest: applications tag pages with a regenerator (re-decode image, re-decompress file, re-JIT, rebuild index) plus a cost hint; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and a userfaultfd handler rematerializes them on fault.
why: 15-30% of client and server RSS is derived data; reclaims it with no swap I/O and no new hardware.

title: Hot-field arenas: garbage collector splits objects so rows carry hot bytes
idea: IFR: every fetched byte gets used. Closest: a managed runtime profiles per-field access and, during compaction, moves hot fields into dense hot arenas in near DRAM and cold fields into a far-memory arena reached by a compressed offset.
why: Objects average 20-40% hot fields; near-tier footprint drops 1.5-2x and row overfetch (fact 8) falls with it.

title: Revocable leases sell stranded VM memory to caches and batch jobs
idea: IFR: no installed DRAM bit is ever idle. Closest: hypervisors lease allocated-but-untouched guest memory (30-50% in public clouds) to caches and batch jobs under a 50 ms revocation contract; leased contents must be regenerable, so revocation simply drops them.
why: Recovers 20-40% of fleet DRAM with zero new chips.

title: DRAM-less SSDs via learned-index flash translation held in host
idea: IFR: storage needs no DRAM. Closest: host-managed/zoned SSDs whose logical-to-physical map is a piecewise-linear learned index 50-100x smaller than a page-level FTL table, kept in host DRAM, so SSD controllers ship without their ~1 GB/TB DRAM.
why: SSD-embedded DRAM is several percent of global DRAM bits; deleting most of it frees that supply for compute.

title: Exponent-plane storage: base die dedups bf16 exponents
idea: Ideal: store only information, never redundancy. Closest achievable: the HBM base die transparently splits bf16/fp8 tensors into sign-mantissa planes and an exponent plane, entropy-codes the low-entropy exponents (~2.5 bits instead of 8) and reassembles them at line rate on read.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~25-30% more effective HBM capacity and interface bandwidth for AI tensors with no host changes; fewer bits moved per useful value (fact 5).

title: Uploaded access programs delete the DRAM command bus
idea: Ideal: no requests at all, data simply arrives on time. Closest achievable: compilers for static AI graphs emit a timed access program (tile addresses, strides, bank schedule) once per layer, and a tiny sequencer in the base die replays it so the per-access command/address bus and controller queues vanish.
why: Facts 5 and 7: command/address bumps (~20% of HBM signal bumps) become data bumps, GPU controller area and energy shrink, and conflict-free schedules push bandwidth utilization toward 95%.
note: Same uploaded-access-program mechanism.

title: Bit-significance tiering: mantissa LSBs live in unrefreshed soft rows
idea: Ideal: errors that cost nothing because they do not matter. Closest: the memory controller splits each bf16/fp8 tensor word, storing sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in refreshed ECC rows and the low mantissa bits in 'soft rows' with 1 s refresh and no ECC, where rare decays add noise below quantization noise.
why: Facts 3 and 1: ~40% of AI tensor bits need no fast refresh or ECC; refresh power ~-35%, ECC overhead removed on that fraction, and soft rows can use smaller Cs.

title: Bit-flip-hardened training so AI memory runs at relaxed refresh
idea: Ideal: the application does not care about memory errors. Closest: train and fine-tune models with injected bit-flip noise matching a 1e-6 raw BER profile, protect only optimizer state and index tensors with CRC, then deploy weights and activations in DRAM running at 8x the normal refresh interval.
why: Fact 3: AI memory (the main demand driver) gets ~80% lower refresh energy and ~10% more bandwidth with <0.1% accuracy loss.
note: Close to EDEN (2019) error-tolerant DNN on approximate DRAM.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM vault where cells never forget
idea: Ideal: memory that never forgets. Closest: run 180 nm-era DRAM dies immersed at 77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by many orders so retention reaches hours, refresh disappears and the tail vanishes; the vault serves as a large refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Fact 3 and supply: refresh-free and tail-free on legacy fabs; cryocooling cost is partly offset by the removed refresh and relaxed cell design.

title: Leakage-clocked refresh: a diode array runs the refresh oscillator
idea: Ideal: refresh exactly as often as the physics demands, never more. Closest: a large reverse-biased diode array of the same junction type as the storage nodes discharges a timing capacitor that clocks the refresh counter, so the refresh rate follows temperature, process and aging automatically with plain 1990s analog parts.
why: Fact 3: removes the worst-case temperature guard band; ~2-4x fewer refreshes on average.
note: Same replica-leakage oscillator.

title: Fabric-wide content-addressed page dedup across many hosts
idea: Ideal: every unique byte is stored exactly once in the world. Closest achievable: a CXL pool controller hashes 4 KB pages and keeps one copy of duplicates (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) across dozens of hosts, with hardware copy-on-write.
why: Usable capacity: 20-40% fewer physical bits in multi-tenant clouds.

title: Retention-reject DRAM regraded with a weak-row fast-refresh buffer
idea: Ideal: every die that works at all gets sold. Closest achievable with no new fab: dies failing 64 ms retention because of the leakage tail are binned as a 16 ms grade, and a 40 nm module buffer refreshes only the profiled weak rows, using a map stored in on-module flash at test.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): recovers 2-5% of wafer output for a small refresh-energy cost.

title: Buy the rejects: harvest downbinned DRAM with remap firmware
idea: 10-person constraint: we cannot make bits, so we rescue them. Buy retention-failing or downbinned DRAM dies, plus decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs that fail the 64 ms/85 C screen, at scrap prices. Re-grade them on an FPGA tester and sell them on CXL cards whose controller combines weak-row remap, extra refresh for only the weak rows, and spare capacity.
why: Scarce-resource and cost axes: a few percent of global output that is now scrapped or downbinned becomes usable supply at under 30% of contract price, with no fab.

title: Ground-precharge charge-transfer preamp triples bitline length
idea: Limit: no VDD/2 precharge or equalizer devices. Bitlines precharge to ground, and a charge-transfer transistor biased at its threshold pumps the cell's charge from the big bitline into a ~1 fF sense node, giving a voltage gain of about C_BL/C_SN (~10x) before a small latch.
why: Periphery: 3x longer bitlines (1,536 cells per BL) mean 3x fewer SA stripes (die -8-10%). An old trick revived for the long vertical bitlines of 3D DRAM (fact 2).
note: Known CTPS circuit; applying it to 3D vertical bitlines is the twist.

title: No in-house analog team: open memory-periphery compiler for startups
idea: Limit: a new-memory startup gets zero analog designers. A CHIPS/DARPA-funded open-source periphery generator (sense amps, decoders, pumps, BIST) qualified on 28 nm and 22FDX U.S. processes lets array-technology teams design only the cell and tile it.
why: Capital and time-to-market: cuts ~18 months and ~$30-50M per new memory entrant, which widens U.S. supply diversity.

title: Tungsten-free plated copper staircases with self-forming barriers
idea: Under 400 C, fill all staircase contacts and vertical straps by room-temperature electroplated CuMn. A 300 C anneal self-forms a 2 nm MnSiOx barrier, so no W CVD is used anywhere in the 3D array.
why: Tungsten chokepoint: removes W from 3D wiring with about 3x lower contact resistance for tall stacks.

title: Diamond-wire kerf recycled into Czochralski recharge feedstock
idea: Within $1M/24 months: bench-pilot recovery of silicon kerf from 300 mm wafering (30-40% of the ingot) using froth flotation to strip coolant and diamond, an HCl leach for Fe/Ni, and induction melting with slag refining into recharge rods that meet CZ spec.
why: Returns about a third of every ingot to feedstock, cutting polysilicon demand and Siemens energy per wafer by up to ~30%.

title: Cold-trap recovery of unreacted zirconium ALD precursors
idea: Within $1M/24 months: insert a temperature-staged cold trap between capacitor ALD chambers and their pumps to condense unreacted Zr/Hf amide precursors (often >90% of dosed mass), then fractionally distill and re-certify them; validate on one ZAZ tool.
why: Cuts Zr/Hf precursor purchases ~3-5x and abatement load, easing both precursor cost and nuclear-chain Hf/Zr supply.

title: Fab consortium pre-buys helium from small U.S. wells
idea: Within $1M/24 months: form a buyers' consortium that signs 10-year forward offtake with small helium developers in Kansas, Montana and Wyoming, using the $1M for diligence, legal setup and escrow seed while member fabs supply the volume commitment.
why: Small helium projects stall for lack of offtake; guaranteed demand unlocks new domestic supply and removes Qatar exposure.

title: Assay campaign for second-source U.S. quartz pegmatites
idea: Within $1M/24 months: core and assay candidate pegmatites (Black Hills, Maine, Georgia) for low-Al/Ti/alkali quartz, run hot-chlorination and flotation purification trials, and make test crucible billets with partner crucible makers.
why: One qualified second U.S. HPQ source breaks the single-valley (>80%) chokepoint; the budget covers drilling and lab purification.

title: Supercritical CO2 drying lets capacitors grow taller without support meshes
idea: Constraint: cut ultrapure water use 80%. Replace post-etch wet cleans and spin-dry with supercritical CO2 plus co-solvent cleaning; with zero surface tension, 100:1 capacitor pillars no longer collapse, so the support-lattice (MESH) films and their masks can be dropped.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes 1-2 masks and lets AR rise from ~70 to ~100 (+40% Cs); fab water -80%.

title: Block copolymer quadruples a sparse capacitor-hole lattice
idea: Constraint: print only one in four capacitor holes. Sparse ArF guide posts at twice the pitch template a cylinder-forming block copolymer by graphoepitaxy, which self-assembles the missing hexagonal holes at ~24 nm pitch; the minority cores are removed and transferred into the mold.
why: Fact 4: replaces EUV or SAQP for the densest hole layer; 4x density multiplication from a cheap mask, about one fewer EUV layer.
note: DSA hole multiplication for DRAM honeycomb is widely pursued.

title: Hydrogen-sink liners stabilize oxide-semiconductor cells at 125 C
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: a same-chamber ALD sandwich of AlOx barrier plus Ti/TiOx absorber islands traps hydrogen that would otherwise diffuse into the oxide channel and turn it conductive, so standard hydrogen-rich SiN passivation and forming-gas anneals stay in the flow.
why: Fact 3 and capital: keeps BEOL oxide-channel memory stable for a decade at 125 C without special hydrogen-free tools or materials.

title: approx-tagged allocations silently stored at reduced precision
idea: Imposed limit: a bit earns DRAM only if it changes an output. Programmers or compilers tag allocations approx(bits=8); the memory controller transparently stores fp32 data as 8-bit block floating point with shared exponents and expands it on read, so caches and code still see fp32.
why: Graphics, ML activations, sensor data and scientific intermediates tolerate truncation; tagged regions shrink 2-4x with no code rewrite.

title: One nested weight set serves every model size
idea: Imposed limit: a provider may store one weight set per model family. Transformers are trained matryoshka-nested, so each smaller model is a prefix (a subset of neurons, heads and layers) of the largest, and the 8B, 30B and 120B tiers are all served from one resident copy by masking.
why: Providers keep several model sizes resident; nesting removes the duplicates and cuts weight DRAM ~1.5-2x across a model family.
note: MatFormer/Flextron known.

title: Foveated framebuffers stored at eye-tracked resolution
idea: Imposed limit: an AR headset frame may occupy one eighth of its pixel count in DRAM. Eye tracking picks the foveal tile; the display pipeline stores only that tile at full resolution and keeps the periphery as low-resolution mip levels, upsampling in the display controller during scan-out.
why: Framebuffers and render targets dominate XR memory; foveated storage cuts them 4-8x and also saves bandwidth energy.

title: DRAM-free enterprise SSDs via learned flash translation layers
idea: Imposed limit: an SSD may hold zero DRAM. The page-level mapping table (1 GB of DRAM per TB) is replaced by a learned piecewise-linear index of logical-to-physical runs plus a small SRAM delta log, exploiting the fact that most writes are sequential.
why: Enterprise SSDs carry ~0.1% of their capacity as DRAM; at hundreds of exabytes of NAND a year, removing it frees on the order of 1% of global DRAM bits.

title: Printed battery laminate makes DRAM durable, killing write buffers
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a printed thin-film zinc battery laminated onto each module powers a flush to onboard flash on power loss, making the DRAM itself durable. Databases and filesystems can then drop their separate write-ahead-log buffers and duplicate caches, because the primary copy in DRAM is already safe.
why: Durable DRAM removes duplicate buffering (WAL buffers, page cache alongside app cache) worth ~10-20% of database host memory, with no supercap bank.

title: Delay-insensitive self-timed link deletes DRAM DLLs and training
idea: Scarcity: no forwarded clock and no DLL on the DRAM. Send data in a level-encoded dual-rail (1-of-4 transition) code so every symbol carries its own timing; the DRAM side drops DLL/PLL, link training and per-pin deskew.
why: Periphery and idle power (fact 7): DLLs and training logic burn mW per channel at idle; targets 20-30% lower I/O power and near-instant power-state exit.

title: Line-rate exponent-sharing and ANS codec inside the base die
idea: Scarcity: no redundant bit may cross the link. The HBM base die carries a block-floating-point repacker (shared exponent per 32 values) plus an asymmetric-numeral-systems entropy coder that losslessly compresses BF16/FP8 tensors at line rate; the GPU memory controller decodes.
why: Data movement (fact 5): BF16 exponents hold ~2.5 bits of entropy in 8, giving 1.3-1.6x effective bandwidth and capacity without touching cells.

title: Plastic sub-terahertz waveguide ribbons link memory without lasers
idea: Scarcity: no lasers, and copper cannot reach beyond 10 cm. 140-300 GHz CMOS transceivers couple into polymer dielectric waveguides (PTFE/HDPE ribbons) linking memory modules to processors over 0.1-2 m at 50-100 Gb/s per strand.
why: Disaggregation energy (fact 5): pooled memory at ~1-3 pJ/bit with plastic media and CMOS-only transceivers, no III-V lasers.

title: One flag bit: polarity coding keeps weak cells discharged
idea: Imposed limit: one extra bit per 64-bit word. Retention failures happen only when a leaky cell holds its charged state. Using a boot-time weak-cell map, the controller stores either the data or its inverse, whichever puts the known weak cells of that word in their discharged, safe state, and records the choice in the flag bit.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: most weak-cell errors are eliminated at 1.6% overhead, so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x past the weak tail.

title: No external sensors: ECC syndrome servo trims bias and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no added test or sense hardware. On-die ECC correction counts per bank feed a closed-loop controller that continuously adjusts the negative wordline voltage, VARY trim and refresh interval to hold a target corrected-error rate (~1e-9). The ECC syndromes are the sensor.
why: Removes worst-case guardbands set for corner temperature and the worst die. Average refresh interval ~2x longer and wordline stress lower.
note: VRT cells can jump faster than the loop reacts.

title: One retention test only: per-row data whitening kills worst patterns
idea: Imposed limit: testers may screen retention with just one pattern. All data is XORed with a per-row keyed pseudo-random whitening sequence, so worst-case neighbor and bitline-coupling patterns become statistically rare. Refresh and test margins are then set for typical patterns rather than worst-case ones.
why: Cuts retention test time and the pattern-dependent guardband, recovering ~1.5-2x refresh interval and test cost per die.
note: Controller scrambling already standard.

title: Zero new dies for 24 months: robotic chip-level DIMM reclamation
idea: Self-imposed limit: no fresh dies allowed. Robotic lines desolder DRAM packages from retired hyperscaler DIMMs, reball, retest and speed-bin each die, then remount them on CXL Type-3 expanders whose controller trains per-die timing so mixed-speed reclaimed DDR4/DDR5 dies run as one pool.
why: Supply/reuse: retired fleets discard tens of millions of working GB a year; recovering 30-50% of it adds several percent to usable bit supply at ~$1/GB rework cost with zero wafer starts.

title: Every failed die must ship: salvage-grade DRAM with controller sparing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no die is scrapped. Fabs sell dies that fail speed or have more bad rows than fuse repair covers as a 'salvage grade'; a host or CXL controller with large row-remap tables and spare-die striping uses them for KV-cache and cold tiers that tolerate lower speed.
why: Recovers part of the 10-20% wafer yield fallout as usable bits; +3-8% effective supply with no new capex.

title: No server may own its RAM: spot market per GB-second
idea: Self-imposed limit: memory is only rented. A CXL-switched rack pool runs an internal exchange where VMs bid for capacity by the GB-second. Stranded memory, which is 25-50% of provisioned DRAM in clouds, is auctioned back within milliseconds via page migration.
why: Do the job with less: cuts the DRAM provisioned per server by 10-25% fleet-wide through price signals rather than static sizing.

title: Helium at zero for a year: recapture-and-substitute retrofit leasing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no helium deliveries. Leased retrofit kits recover helium from etch-chuck backside cooling and load-locks with membrane and cryogenic recovery (>90%), and switch tolerant chucks to hydrogen or argon backside gas. They are priced per wafer, not as capex.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: keeps fabs running through the Qatar helium outage (about 30% of supply) and cuts helium per wafer by about 10x.

title: Every byte must be borrowed: off-peak HBM lending over scale-up fabric
idea: Self-imposed limit: no new memory for batch jobs. The cluster scheduler lends idle HBM on lightly loaded inference GPUs at night as remote memory over NVLink-class fabric for training checkpoints and KV spill.
why: Raises HBM utilization from diurnal lows of about 30-40%, which avoids buying extra capacity.
note: Same idle-memory lending mechanism as I-04098, applied to HBM over scale-up fabric.

title: Off-silicon creates an indium chokepoint: switch to indium-free ZTO channels
idea: Forced limit, plus a second one: no Si and no indium. Gain-cell channels use zinc-tin oxide and Ga-free amorphous oxides deposited by ALD, avoiding indium, whose refining is concentrated in China.
why: Scarce resources: keeps a non-Si memory industry from trading the quartz chokepoint for an indium one; Zn and Sn supply is widely distributed.

title: Gallium-free, indium-lean oxide channels (ZTO / SnO2 / ITZO) for gain cells and VCT
idea: Deposit amorphous Zn-Sn-O (ZTO), SnO2, or In-lean In-Sn-Zn-O / In-W-O channels by ALD (or PVD for planar) at <=350 C, with the gate insulator and channel grown in one ALD chamber without a vacuum break (UMich) and Al2O3/SiO2 passivation (Hf-free, unlike the HfO2 used for the SJTU record). Cells are the same 2T0C/3T0C gain cells or 4F2 VCT access transistors now built with IGZO. Zn and Sn suppress oxygen-vacancy carriers less strongly than Ga, so thin (3-5 nm) channels, Al or Si doping, and O3 anneals set the threshold voltage. The bit is stored on the read transistor's gate (gain cell) or on a capacitor (VCT).
why: 100% Ga-free (and In-free for ZTO) oxide DRAM supply chain at >=1500 s demonstrated retention (~23,000x a 64 ms refresh interval), with 2-6 ns single-bit read on a 64-cell read bitline.

title: DSA honeycomb: block-copolymer self-assembly for the capacitor/channel hole lattice
idea: Coat PS-b-PMMA (or a high-chi BCP for <30 nm) whose cylinder lattice period L0 (~28-40 nm) matches the 1-beta (35 nm) or 1c (32 nm) capacitor honeycomb. A single-exposure ArF immersion guide pattern (or chemical pre-pattern) at 2-3x the pitch registers the lattice and DSA multiplies density 3-4x, rectifying CD and placement noise. Sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O into PMMA) hardens the pattern into an AlOx mask for transfer into the mold (SiO2 or the carbon mold of B2-10). For 4F2 square lattices, chemo-epitaxy with a square guide is used.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers in the array: $165-330 per wafer (3.8-7.7% of a $4.3k 1c wafer) before netting DSA cost; the hole lattice comes from polymer physics rather than wavelength.

title: Cold-bond stack: room-temperature surface-activated hybrid bonding for oxide memory
idea: Standard hybrid bonding needs a post-bond anneal above ~350 C to close the Cu pads, and every sequential bond re-anneals everything below it. For oxide-channel memory wafers that cumulative heat (8-16 h at 350 C for an 8-layer stack) shifts Vt and redistributes hydrogen, which multi-level storage cannot tolerate. Use surface-activated bonding instead: Ar fast-atom-beam cleaning in ultra-high vacuum lets Cu-Cu (and, with Si nano-adhesion layers, dielectric) surfaces bond at room temperature without anneal. Memory layers can then be bonded after multi-level calibration and after hydrogen-sensitive steps, and heterogeneous layers (ferroelectric, photonic, organic) can join without a thermal limit.
why: Post-bond thermal budget 8-16 h at 350 C -> 0, removing a thermal dose equal to ~5-37 years at 85 C of activated drift kinetics per stack.

title: Procedural weights: seeds plus coefficients, regenerated in the memory path
idea: Each block of ~8 weights is approximated as a linear combination of 3-4 pseudo-random basis vectors. An LFSR generates them from a 16-bit seed, weighted by 4-bit coefficients (SeedLM-style). Only seeds and coefficients (~3-4 b/weight) are stored in DRAM. A generator array in the GPU memory partition (or the HBM base die) expands them to BF16/FP8 on the way to the tensor cores. The LFSR and MACs cost ~0.3 pJ per weight, against ~14-56 pJ to fetch 4-16 bits over HBM.
why: 4-5.3x fewer stored bits than BF16, but only 1.0-1.33x vs FP4. The step is real only if accuracy at ~3 b/weight beats plain FP4/INT3 quantisation.

title: Reversible layers fused with backprop eliminate activation storage
idea: Combine reversible (bijective) residual blocks with training: activations are reconstructed exactly from layer outputs during the backward pass instead of being stored, using fixed-point coupling functions so reconstruction never drifts.
why: Activation memory, often the largest training footprint, becomes constant in depth, cutting training DRAM/HBM 3-10x on any hardware including mature-node accelerators.
note: RevNet/Reformer prior art; checkpointing captures most of the gain.

title: HPC algorithm-based fault tolerance for AI weight matrices
idea: Adapted from ABFT in scientific computing, where matrices carry row and column checksums so errors are found from the math itself: weights are stored with one checksum row and column per 128x128 tile, verified as a side effect of each matmul (output checksum vs checksum-vector product), and corrected by locating the intersecting failing row and column; DRAM ECC is turned off for those regions.
why: Capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6): ~1.5% checksum overhead replaces 12.5% ECC, freeing ~11% HBM capacity and allowing lower-grade stacks, with no hardware change.

title: Magnify model tolerance: train networks on measured DRAM error maps
idea: Fine-tune networks with bit-flip injection that copies measured DRAM error maps: retention-tail positions, hammer patterns and true/anti-cell decay direction. Deployed weights then tolerate 1e-4 raw BER with no ECC and 10x longer refresh.
why: Fact 3: inference memory runs nearly refresh-free on cheaper bins and frees ~10% ECC capacity.
note: EDEN (2019) already retrains DNNs on DRAM error models.

title: Tensor checksums replace DRAM ECC for model weights
idea: Flip error checking from memory to compute: weight matrices carry row/column checksums (algorithm-based fault tolerance), the GEMM verifies them, and a mismatch re-fetches that tile from a peer GPU or flash; the weight region in DRAM drops ECC entirely.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC overhead for AI's largest data class and tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER weak cells; checksum cost <1% of FLOPs.

title: Reversible layers reconstruct activations instead of storing them
idea: Box: invertibility × model architecture × layer activations × backward pass × additive coupling blocks. Training uses invertible residual blocks whose inputs are recomputed exactly from outputs during backpropagation, so per-layer activations are never kept.
why: Activation memory becomes constant in depth, 5–10× less training memory; mathematics only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Leakage-balanced loadless node that holds its own bit
idea: Worsen: let leakage only ever drain the storage node toward zero. Flip: design a 4T loadless cell on a ~$50k shuttle where the access transistors' off-current deliberately trickles charge into the high node while cross-coupled pull-downs sink the low node, so leakage itself holds the bit.
why: Eliminates refresh (fact 3) with 4 transistors instead of 6T SRAM and no capacitor; cheap to prove within 24 months.

title: VMware page sharing, fixed: timing-equalized dedup with uniform write faults
idea: Transparent Page Sharing was disabled by default after Flush+Reload and Dedup-Est-Machina exploited copy-on-write timing. Re-enable cross-VM dedup but force every write to any merge-candidate page through an identical pre-allocated fault path (shared or not) and flush shared lines on cross-domain access, so the timing oracle disappears.
why: Restores the 20-40% DRAM savings TPS gave dense VDI/cloud hosts, cutting DRAM per VM at ~1-2% write-path overhead.
note: VUsion (2018) already proposed uniform fault behavior for secure page fusion.

title: Electrocaloric heat-pump layer makes 0.3 fF stacked cells refresh-viable
idea: Effect: electrocaloric cooling. A 64-tier monolithic stack of thin-film cells with only ~0.3 fF planar MIM caps (no high-AR pillar) sits on a P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) or PST electrocaloric film; field cycling of the film pumps heat solid-state toward the sink, holding the stack ~20 K below its neighbors, which cuts thermal-generation leakage ~4-6x so 0.3 fF cells still retain ~16 ms.
why: 10x density: 64 tiers at ~0.2x per-tier density is ~13x bits/mm^2. Same cost: the 5-7 EUV layers and AR-75 capacitor etch are traded for repeated deposition, with the electrocaloric film as a cheap package layer.
note: Electrocaloric films give a few K, not a sustained 20 K; the real lever is an unsolved 64-tier stack.

title: Swap 3D NAND thick tunnel oxide for direct-tunnel volatile trap
idea: Run existing DUV 3D NAND lines with a ~1.5-2 nm direct-tunnelling oxide under the nitride trap. The cells write in ~10-50 ns at <4 V, keep data for seconds to minutes (refreshed like DRAM) and avoid Fowler-Nordheim damage, aiming at >10^14 cycles.
why: Puts 200+-layer 3D NAND capacity, which needs no EUV, to work as volatile working memory at DRAM-class density or better (facts 2, 4). The fabs and tools already exist, including in the U.S.
note: Repurposes 200+ layer NAND fabs as DRAM-density memory; doubt: string resistance gives slow reads and 1e14 endurance unproven.

title: Deposition-defined 3D DRAM patterned only with US micron-scale steppers
idea: Combine 3D NAND's thickness-defined geometry with a DRAM cell: gate length, capacitor gap and tier pitch are all set by film thickness on US-built ALD/CVD/etch tools, and the only lithography is a ~1 um hole/slit grid from US-made i-line steppers, halved by one spacer pitch split. Density comes from ~300 tiers in 3 decks and 4 cells around each hole, not from imported EUV or immersion scanners.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4) and US manufacturability: zero EUV; 0.25 um2 per hole / (4 cells x 300 tiers) is ~2e-4 um2/bit, about 4x 1-beta density.
note: i-line-only thickness-defined 300-tier stack, ~4-6x density; doubt: cell plus capacitor must fit within 0.25 um hole radius.

title: Vertical CCD charge column stacked like an automated warehouse
idea: Combine image-sensor CCDs with AutoStore's stacked bins: deposit a 128-layer gate stack with 3D NAND tools, etch one channel hole, and store ~60 charge packets per hole that are clocked up or down to a single sense amp at the top, recirculating through it to self-refresh.
why: 10x at same cost: 60 bits per ~60 nm hole pitch is ~60 nm2/bit vs 864 nm2 today (~14x) on NAND-class non-EUV tooling; no capacitor and unlimited endurance; latency hidden by bidirectional shifting and bank interleave.
note: ~14x bits/area on NAND tooling if charge transfer efficiency and retention survive many shifts.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobby bitlines enable 0.3 fF nodes in tall stacks
idea: Adapt sky lobbies, where express elevators stop at lobbies and local cars serve 16 floors: split each vertical bitline every 16 tiers with a local deposited-oxide sense amp, so each tier's node needs only ~0.3 fF against a short local bitline.
why: 10x at same cost: tiny capacitor-free nodes keep 128-tier stacks sensible; ~12x bits per footprint because the long-bitline capacitance problem is removed.
note: Local sense amps every 16 tiers enable tiny nodes; doubt: deposited-oxide sense-amp offset and area per tier.

title: Used-ship market: depreciated 200 mm fabs build deep tier stacks
idea: Like shipping firms buying used vessels, acquire fully depreciated 65-180 nm 200 mm fabs and run only deposition-heavy 256-tier vertical stacks at ~90 nm pitch (one KrF/i-line litho per 64 tiers), bonding a thin modern logic base later.
why: Depreciation (~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) goes to ~zero while 256 tiers at 90 nm still give ~8 Gb/mm2; ~30-100x lower cost per bit; trade-offs: big die, ~200 ns latency.
note: Density from tier count on depreciated 200 mm fabs; doubts: 256-tier etch and a working 3D cell, ~200 ns latency.

title: Magnify cells per transistor: vertical CCD shift-register string
idea: Stack 8 storage nodes along one vertical channel and clock the tier gates as CCD phases, so charge packets shift down bucket-brigade style to a single access transistor and sense node at the bottom. This is 1970s planar CCD memory turned 3D.
why: Density and the access-transistor problem: 8 bits per access device and bitline contact, cutting 3D transistor count about 8x, with serial latency of about 20-40 ns.
note: Same 3D CCD string; 8 bits per access device, CTE in vertical channel unproven.

title: Eliminate long bitlines: 16-cell micro-bitlines over a hybrid-bonded sense layer
