idea: Fabricate the cell-array wafer and a CMOS sense-amp wafer separately and hybrid-bond them at ~0.5 um pitch so every 16-cell bitline segment lands on its own sense amplifier below.
why: Bitline C drops from ~40-60 fF to ~3 fF, >10x lower activation energy, and Cs can shrink to ~1 fF, removing the 70:1 capacitor (facts 1 and 7).
note: 10x lower bitline C and tiny Cs; doubt: a sense amp cannot fit under 16 cells' footprint at 0.5 um bond pitch.

title: Eliminate the fab's lithography: DNA-origami templated nanoscale memory assembly
idea: DNA origami tiles bind to a coarse DUV-patterned wafer and place carbon-nanotube transistors and metal-oxide nanoparticle capacitors with ~5 nm precision, after which ALD locks and metallizes the assembly; the cell layout is coded in DNA sequence, not masks.
why: Ultimate litho elimination: sub-10 nm cells from a fab of wet benches, coarse litho and ALD; speculative, but would cut capital per bit by >10x.
note: DNA-placed CNT FETs/capacitors bypass litho; doubt: yield, contamination and interconnect at 5 nm across 300 mm.

title: Brain-fold gyrification: build cells on deep corrugated wafer sidewalls
idea: The cortex triples its area by folding; etch the wafer once into 1.2 um tall fins at 120 nm pitch (ArF plus spacer doubling), then build cells on both sidewalls using only conformal ALD and horizontal bands defined by repeated deposit-fill-recess cycles, so every band along the fin height is a row of cells.
why: Sidewall area is ~20x the footprint; even at half the planar cell efficiency that is ~10x bits/mm2, with the extra area coming from cheap deposition/recess cycles rather than EUV (fact 4).
note: Sidewall area gives ~10x bits/mm2; addressing many recess-defined bands per fin is unresolved.

title: Retinal filling-in: panel-scale nanoimprinted memory tolerating dead pixels
idea: Nanoimprint 2T oxide-semiconductor gain cells at F~100 nm onto Gen-10.5 display glass (~9 m2 per sheet); like the brain filling in the blind spot and dead photoreceptors, a power-up scan builds a defect map and a long Reed-Solomon erasure code reconstructs dead cells, so 1-3% dead pixels from imprint particles are acceptable.
why: Cost per GB/capital: display TFT area costs ~$50-150/m2 vs ~$100k/m2 for DRAM wafers; ~2 TB/m2 per layer gives ~$0.05/GB, ~100x below 2026 DRAM, trading latency (~100-300 ns) and areal density.
note: ~100x capital-cost cut if 100 nm imprint over 9 m2 glass with multilayer overlay works; that patterning step is the miracle.

title: Coral colony tiers: build 120 monolithic tiers, keep the best 100
idea: A coral colony thrives though individual polyps die; deposit ~120 monolithic oxide-semiconductor memory tiers by low-temperature ALD/sputter with shared vertical wordline contacts, test each tier after deposition, and permanently bypass dead tiers with tier-select transistors, so ~85% tier yield still yields a full stack.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers to break even; at ~100 EUV-free tiers cost per GB falls ~30-100x, and tier sparing removes the compound-yield wall (0.99^100) that kills deep stacks.
note: Tier sparing defeats 0.99^N compound yield; doubt: mid-fab per-tier test access and IGZO cell leakage at 100 tiers.

title: Two-stage synaptic consolidation in NAND-fab charge-trap strings
idea: Synapses hold new memories in fast, fragile early-LTP and consolidate stable ones into protein-synthesis late-LTP; build DRAM-class memory on 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with ultrathin tunnel oxide (us writes, seconds retention, refreshed), and in the background 'consolidate' cold pages with a stronger pulse into deep traps that hold for hours, switching their refresh off.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-style fabs make bits at ~$0.03-0.08/GB vs ~$5-10/GB DRAM (~100x); consolidation tames refresh and wear by applying high-stress writes only to cold data.
note: NAND cost leap if real, but us writes, string-serial access and trap endurance conflict with DRAM-class needs.

title: Vertical CCD charge columns: 3D DRAM without per-tier transistors
idea: Revive 1970s serial CCD memory vertically: the tier word planes of a 3D stack act as CCD transfer phases around a vertical crystalline-Si or IGZO channel, so charge packets march up the column to one sense/regenerate node at the top. Three tiers per bit and 240 tiers give 80 bits per column.
why: Removes the lateral transistor and capacitor that block 3D DRAM (Fact 2) with 3D-NAND-style one-etch tiers; full column shift at ~1 ns/step gives ~80 ns access; ~10x bits per area.
note: Key doubt: charge-transfer efficiency over ~240 shifts in poly/IGZO channel and serial latency.

title: Bubble-memory major/minor loop organization for stacked skyrmion tiers
idea: Reuse the bubble chip's architecture: in each tier of a sputtered magnetic multilayer stack, skyrmions circulate in hundreds of parallel minor loops driven by spin-orbit current, and a block-transfer gate swaps a whole page into one major loop read by a single MTJ. One etch defines the loops through all tiers, so tiers are added by deposition, not masks.
why: Facts 4 and 7: one reader per ~1e5 bits collapses periphery and extra tiers cost deposition only; a dense second-tier working memory at ~100 ns page access.
note: Bubble-memory loop architecture with deposition-only skyrmion tiers; pinning, small-size thermal stability and readout are the doubts.

title: Hundred-electron bits read by room-temperature single-electron transistors
idea: Invert 'a bit needs ~30,000 stored electrons' -> store ~100. Each node is a ~20 aF floating island sensed by a single-electron transistor built from a ~1.5 nm metal cluster or molecule, whose Coulomb oscillations turn +/-100 electrons into a large current swing.
why: Eliminates the capacitor (fact 1) and cuts write energy to ~1.6e-17 J (~1000x, fact 10) at ~4F^2; room-temperature SET uniformity is the speculative part.
note: Room-temperature SET uniformity and background-charge noise have defeated this since Yano's 1990s work.

title: Dynamic-mode 3D NAND: hold charge in the channel, not the trap
idea: Inverts 'NAND lines can only make nonvolatile flash': operate existing 300-layer 3D NAND strings as capacitorless floating-body cells, injecting holes by GIDL into the poly channel under a selected wordline (neighbors biased as barriers), sensing the Vt shift through the string and refreshing every ~1-10 ms; the trap layer is never programmed, so endurance is unlimited.
why: Taps existing, depreciated NAND fab capacity and flow, ~50-150x cheaper per GB than DRAM; trade-off is ~1-5 us latency, page-granular access and heavy refresh.
note: Close to 3D X-DRAM-type floating-body work; poly-channel retention and microsecond latency limit it to a capacity tier.

title: Recirculating vertical bucket-brigade string without cell capacitors
idea: Inverts 'every bit is randomly addressable in place.' A 64-128-gate vertical channel string stores charge packets in potential wells under its gates and clocks them tier-to-tier like a CCD to one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot, which rewrites each packet as it recirculates; random access is per string (~30-60 ns) and refresh comes free with circulation.
why: Facts 1-3: 3D with no capacitor and no lateral transistor; density scales with tier count; separate refresh energy folds into the shift itself.
note: Dup of vertical CCD string; transfer efficiency over 64-128 stages and channel dark current are key doubts.

title: Deposition sets density: 128-tier DRAM strings from 180 nm holes
idea: Inverts 'density comes from lithography'. Deposit 128 alternating oxide/poly (or Si/SiGe) tiers, punch 180 nm channel holes with a KrF stepper and 1990s deep-trench RIE (AR ~36:1), and form one ring-gate transistor plus lateral-recess capacitor per tier per hole, with staircase contacts made by repeated resist-trim etching.
why: Each 0.13 um2 hole holds 128 cells, ~1,000 nm2 per bit versus ~860 nm2 for a 6F2 cell at 12 nm, with no EUV; capital moves to cheap deposition tools (facts 2, 4).
note: EUV-free density via tiers; per-tier lateral capacitor in a ring gives tiny Cs, likely unsensable.

title: Panel-scale memory on Gen-8.5 glass using nanoimprint
idea: Because nothing exceeds 400 C, build a planar oxide or ferroic storage array on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in display-type panel lines, patterned by roll-to-plate nanoimprint at ~30 nm with ~4 stacked tiers. Each panel has ~78x the area of a 300 mm wafer.
why: Panel cost per m2 is ~10-20x below wafer cost, attacking capital intensity and cost per bit. Panel lines can be built in the U.S. faster than DRAM fabs.
note: Panel area is cheap, but 30 nm overlay-aligned imprint across 2.5 m glass is far beyond any display line.

title: Volume holographic page memory steered by silicon-photonic phased arrays
idea: A hologram stores a megabit page per angle in a cheap photopolymer block and reads it in one flash onto a detector array, so bandwidth comes from page parallelism, not fast cells. Replace slow angle addressing with silicon-photonic optical phased arrays switching in ~100 ns, and hybrid-bond the detector array to an SRAM page buffer.
why: Medium cost could make read-mostly working sets ~100x cheaper per GB; trades write speed, latency and alignment robustness.
note: Page-parallel reads could cut read-mostly cost/GB ~100x; decades of holographic failure, photopolymer endurance doubts.

title: Sushi conveyor: vertical charge-packet shift string replaces per-cell capacitors
idea: Forced connection to a sushi belt: in a NAND-like stack of 64 gate tiers around a low-leakage IGZO or poly-Si vertical channel, bits are stored as charge packets in gate-induced potential wells and clocked along the string CCD-style to one sense node at the base. There is no capacitor or access transistor per bit, only a gate electrode over a shared channel, and reads stream in order like plates passing a diner.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): bit cost tracks NAND-like tier cost (claim ~5-10x below 2D DRAM at 64+ tiers) with unlimited endurance; latency 20-70 ns by position, suited to streaming rows such as KV caches.
note: Dup of vertical CCD string; IGZO mobility limits clocking speed and latency claims.

title: Beach metal detector: back-end capacitive key-sketch array picks tokens
idea: Sweep a detector before digging: keep 1-bit sketches of all keys in a back-end HZO/MIM capacitive compute-in-memory array (crystallized <=400 C) on the accelerator; a query is broadcast as charge, the array returns top-k token indices in one shot, and only those full K/V blocks are fetched from a cheap CXL/flash tier.
why: Full KV leaves HBM entirely (10-50x less DRAM for long context) because only ~1-5% of tokens are fetched per step.
note: Insight: a 1-bit key sketch in BEOL CIM picks the tokens. Doubts: sketch top-k accuracy, per-layer flash fetch latency.

title: Few-electron planar cells with local two-transistor segment preamps
idea: Box: 0.3 fF planar MIM cap x IGZO access x local 2T gain preamp per 16 cells x monolithic BEOL x Si x no high-AR etch. Each cell stores ~1,800 electrons on a flat capacitor, a local preamp at each 16-cell segment amplifies it, and the ~1% errors from shot noise and leakage scatter are corrected by the code.
why: Capacitor charge wall: removes the 60-75:1 pillar entirely and can be stacked in BEOL tiers for 3D.
note: Planar BEOL tiers could enable stackable 3D DRAM; doubts: 1% raw BER, preamp variation, IGZO leakage tail.

title: Plate wordlines and hole bitlines: one-mask annular 3D DRAM
idea: [Box: annular lateral capacitor | annular IGZO channel | charge-share SA | 3D-NAND-like plate stack | Si | blanket stack + one ArF hole mask + isotropic recesses] Each tier is a blanket wordline plate; one hole etch through all tiers forms vertical bitlines, and isotropic recesses carve an annular IGZO channel and ring capacitor around every hole in every tier, so a cell is (tier, hole) and mask count is independent of tier count.
why: No EUV + 3D (facts 2, 4): ArF holes at ~80 nm pitch x 100 tiers give ~64 nm2 per bit, ~13x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm; small ring Cs is the risk.
note: Same hole-plus-recess annular cell as I-11175; ~13x density claim hinges on small ring Cs.

title: Po: the capacitor lies down and sleeps — flat pseudocapacitive tiers
idea: Po: the capacitor lies down and sleeps. Extracted: use a 5 nm MnO2 or Nb2O5 pseudocapacitive film (surface redox, 100s of uF/cm2) so a flat ~30x30 nm pad holds a few fF with no pillar; with each tier reduced to deposition plus one imprint, stack 32-64 tiers.
why: Removes the 60-75:1 etch (fact 1) and makes tiers cheap (fact 2); 64 flat tiers at relaxed pitch aim at 100x lower $/GB. Trade-offs: self-discharge, us redox kinetics, more frequent refresh.
note: Cheap flat tiers could cut $/GB greatly, but us redox kinetics and self-discharge undermine DRAM-class use.

title: Vertical charge-coupled strings: bits march through 128 gate tiers
idea: Worse: give every bit its own access transistor, capacitor and contact. Flip: store bits as charge packets in a vertical CCD channel threaded through a 128-tier stack of 3-phase clocked gate plates, shifting them to one sense/regenerate node at the base, which also refreshes each packet as it recirculates.
why: A bit costs ~3 gate tiers in one hole with no capacitor or per-bit transistor: ~42 bits per 60 nm-pitch hole ~74 nm2/bit versus 864 nm2 for 6F2 at F=12 nm (~11x) with a 3D-NAND-like flow at similar wafer cost; refresh is built in, and 32-stage segments keep latency in the 10-100 ns range.
note: Same vertical CCD; recirculating refresh and segmenting help latency, but CTE in poly channels is the doubt.

title: One hole, a hundred capacitors: tier-segmented storage rings
idea: Worse: etch a separate deep hole for every capacitor. Flip: in a lateral-transistor 3D stack, etch one vertical hole per cell column, recess each tier's channel end into a ring-shaped storage node, line the hole with one high-k film and fill it with a single common plate core, so every tier's capacitor is a segment of the same hole.
why: Capacitor etch, dielectric and plate are paid once for N tiers: 100 tiers at ~60F2 footprint per tier-cell gives ~86 nm2/bit (~10x) at deposition-dominated cost similar to today's wafer; the ~1 fF rings require short segmented bitlines (high risk).
note: Capacitor etch and plate paid once per hole for N tiers; ~1 fF rings demand short segmented bitlines.

title: Atomically thin channel tiers: 250 tiers in the same etch depth
idea: Worse: make each tier 50-70 nm thick so 100 tiers already need a 6 um etch. Flip: shrink tier pitch to ~20 nm by using 1-3 nm channels (ALD In2O3-class oxide or CVD MoS2), 5 nm gate dielectric and thin metal gates, so ~250 tiers fit into the 5-6 um depth that 3D NAND already etches.
why: ~3x more tiers per unit etch depth: 250 tiers at ~60F2 per tier-cell is ~35 nm2/bit (>10x even with 50% array efficiency) at an unchanged etch budget (facts 2, 4).
note: 20 nm tiers leave no room for a capacitor; needs gain cell or capacitorless with 2D/oxide channels.

title: Epitaxial thyristor cross-point decks: no capacitor, no access transistor
idea: Worse: build a capacitor plus a transistor for every bit. Flip: grow p-n-p-n layers and self-align-etch them into cross-point pillars between orthogonal word and bit lines so each crossing is a gated bistable thyristor cell, and stack 12 decks where every line layer serves the deck above and below.
why: 4F2 per deck at F=16 nm (DUV SAQP) across 12 decks is ~85 nm2/bit (~10x), patterned with ~13 DUV line masks, roughly the cost of the 4-5 EUV layers it replaces (fact 4).
note: 12-deck 4F2 thyristors ~10x density; doubt: no single-crystal epi over buried lines, standby current and variability.

title: Grandparents' fabs: depreciated lines make thin array layers for bonding
idea: Retirees still work, and cheaply. Fully depreciated 300 mm fabs (28-40 nm) make array-only wafers with just 3 ArF masks and no periphery. These are thinned to 5 um and hybrid-bonded 16 deep onto one leading-edge wafer that carries all sense amps and decoders.
why: Toward the 10x constraint: 16 array layers at ~0.6x areal density each is ~10x bits per footprint. Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost and is gone in written-off fabs, so the full stack costs ~1.5x one conventional wafer for 10x the bits (~6x lower $/bit). This misses strict same-cost, but it makes a new business for old fabs.
note: 16-deep bonded array-only layers need per-bitline vertical links to bottom sense amps; old logic fabs lack capacitor process.

title: Fishmonger's fresh catch: 1 ms 'ephemeral DRAM' grade for AI
idea: A fishmonger sells today's catch, not frozen stock. A JEDEC 'ephemeral DRAM' grade for AI activations and KV caches, whose data lives under 1 ms, specifies 1 ms retention instead of 64 ms. Each cell can then drop from 5 fF to ~0.1 fF, a planar gate-capacitance node with no pillar, so cells shrink to 4F^2 and stack 6 thin tiers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: capacitor-free 4F^2 cells times 6 tiers is ~9-10x/mm^2. Deleting the high-aspect-ratio capacitor module (~25-30% of process cost) pays for the tiers, and most rows are rewritten before they need refresh.
note: 1 ms retention lets tiny storage nodes work; doubt: 0.1 fF needs gain-cell readout and 6-tier stacking is unproven.

title: QLC-SSD poly-channel stacking: 3D DRAM tiers on NAND's process
idea: 3D NAND reaches 300+ layers with leaky, variable poly-Si channels because controllers absorb ~1e-2 raw BER. Build vertical-bitline 3D DRAM with poly-Si lateral access devices deposited in the stack, accepting grain-boundary leakage and variability as ~1% raw BER handled by page LDPC.
why: Fact 2: existing NAND fabs (depreciated tool sets, some in the U.S.) could make 3D DRAM tiers without single-crystal Si/SiGe epitaxial stacks, making the ~26-tier break-even reachable.
note: 3D DRAM on depreciated NAND fabs would be a step change; poly-Si leakage likely gives sub-ms retention.

title: Cheapest-bit market: convert idle 3D NAND lines to vertical-string DRAM
idea: Design for the buyer of the cheapest possible bits (the $50 laptop market): 3D NAND fabs already run 200+ tier staircase, channel-hole and replacement-gate tools on DUV only, so retool idle NAND lines to build vertical-string DRAM at relaxed F~40 nm with 64 tiers. License a cell that keeps the NAND tool set and swaps only the channel and storage modules.
why: Capital intensity and EUV dependence (fact 4): reuses $10B+ of installed tools, no EUV, and capacity in ~1-2 years instead of 3-5.
note: Hinges on a NAND-tool-compatible 3D DRAM cell that does not yet exist; if found, idle NAND capacity is a huge lever.

title: Hot-stack: DRAM bonded straight onto a 1 kW GPU at 125 C
idea: Shift the thermal scale: retention collapses at high temperature, which is why DRAM is kept off hot logic, but with 1% tolerance and row-scale codes DRAM dies can be hybrid-bonded directly on the GPU die at 115-125 C with refresh only modestly raised.
why: Deletes the interposer and HBM PHY (facts 5, 6): memory-on-logic at ~0.1 pJ/bit in the tightest possible package.
note: Retention at 125 C needs ~8x more refresh, not modest; ECC tolerance is the enabling bet.

title: Vertical NAND-structured DRAM strings with shadow-page sequential read
idea: Failure mined: Toshiba's 1993 NAND-structured DRAM put cells in series to eliminate contacts, but died because cells had to be read and restored in strict order. Fix: build 64-cell vertical strings in a 3D-NAND-style stack (word planes deposited and etched once, a thin capacitor at each tier) and treat each string as one burst. A shadow latch page in bonded periphery reads it out sequentially and restores it in reverse order.
why: 10x at the same cost: 64 tiers from one channel-hole etch (3D NAND cost structure, ~1 EUV layer), with one contact and one sense amp per string, give ~10-15x bits/mm^2 at similar wafer cost. A 64-bit string matches cache-line bursts.
note: 3D NAND cost structure for DRAM strings; each tier's thin capacitor hits the charge wall and series read/restore adds latency.

title: Vernier decoders address sub-lithographic spacer wires, learned after fab
idea: Failure mined: the HP and Caltech nanowire/molecular crossbars died because nothing could address 5 nm-pitch wires from 50 nm-pitch lithography. Fix: pattern array lines by quadruple spacer pitch-splitting to ~6 nm half-pitch, and cross them with coarse gate lines drawn at a slightly different pitch so each coarse pair coincides over exactly one fine wire, like a vernier scale. A power-up calibration records the actual coincidences in a small remap table.
why: 10x at the same cost: the array reaches ~6 nm half-pitch with zero EUV (spacers are cheap depositions), (12/6)^2 = 4x, times 1.5x for a 4F^2 crosspoint and ~1.7x for decoders that stay at coarse pitch, ~10x bits per cost.
note: Vernier coincidence is clever, but coarse gates cannot isolate one 6 nm wire, and no DRAM-class cell works at that pitch.

title: IBM racetrack made buildable: horizontal tracks from blanket stacked films
idea: IBM's racetrack memory died because its vertical U-shaped nanowires could not be built and domain walls pinned at etched edges. Deposit magnetic multilayer tracks as blanket films in a 3D-NAND-like layer stack, cut them with one vertical slit etch so each tier becomes a horizontal track, and put write and MTJ read heads on a vertical pillar. Short 16-domain tracks keep shifts under ~20 ns.
why: Density without a transistor per bit (fact 4), with mask count independent of tier count (fact 2). Targets ~16 bits per pillar per tier.
note: Slit-etched track edges still pin domain walls; if shifting works, ~16 bits per pillar per tier is a real density jump.

title: Nanosolar's non-vacuum dream fixed for memory: an atmospheric-pressure fab
idea: Nanosolar and spatial-ALD solar startups died because non-vacuum films lost on efficiency to cheap crystalline silicon. Memory arrays do not need photovoltaic-grade films, so build a fab with no vacuum chambers: damascene electroplated lines, spin-on and atmospheric spatial-ALD dielectrics, anodized memory oxide, imprint patterning, and only periphery chiplets bought from a conventional fab.
why: Meets 100x with stacked decks: vacuum PVD/CVD/etch is ~40% of fab capex and atmospheric tools are ~5-10x cheaper and faster; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: film quality, defect density, coarser features.
note: Atmospheric tools for array tiers slash capex; doubt: memory-grade leakage/defects from non-vacuum films; $0.1/GB unsupported.

title: Room-temperature Coulomb-blockade electrometer reads half-femtofarad cells
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. Put one single-electron transistor with a sub-2 nm Si or metal-nanocluster island (charging energy >10 kT) at each local bitline as an electrometer; its drain current swings full scale for a gate-charge change of e/2, so a storage capacitor 10x smaller (~0.5 fF) still gives a readable swing that then drives a conventional latch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 10x less Cs lets pillar aspect ratio fall from ~70:1 to ~10:1, removing the hardest etch and deposition steps.
note: Would break the capacitor wall, but random background charge and sub-2 nm island uniformity make per-bitline room-temperature SETs implausible.

title: Few-electron Coulomb-blockade nanodot strings along vertical pillars
idea: Coulomb blockade: a ring of ~2 nm Si nanodots in a thin tunnel oxide along each vertical channel pillar stores 3-10 electrons per bit. Charging energy quantizes the charge state and helps it resist leakage, while the thin barrier allows ~10 ns low-voltage writes. The layout follows 3D NAND, but the low fluence aims at high endurance.
why: Gives a non-volatile 3D cell at DRAM-like speed and lower voltage (facts 2 and 10); claim 3D NAND-class density with 1e10+ cycles, given the tiny charge moved.
note: Speed-retention dilemma: thin tunnel oxide for 10 ns writes undermines non-volatility; Coulomb blockade alone unlikely to rescue.

title: Random nanowire crossbars addressed by post-fab calibrated stochastic decoder
idea: Effect: stochastic self-assembly. Sub-10 nm-pitch Si nanowire crossbars are grown or transfer-printed with gain cells at the crossings and no litho at cell scale; each wire carries a randomly doped code region, a post-fab discovery pass learns which address code activates which wire and stores a translation table, and defective wires are simply never mapped.
why: 10x density: 4F^2 crossbars at F ~5 nm without EUV give >10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: error tolerance turns disorder into a feature, so no precision patterning is paid for.
note: Echoes DeHon-era stochastic decoders; litho-free 4F2 at 5 nm would be 10x, but gain cells at crossings and access speed unproven.

title: Photographic latent-image bit: few silver atoms hold a few electrons
idea: Silver-halide film keeps a stable 4-atom Ag cluster as the latent image, which development later amplifies. Here sub-3 nm Ag clusters self-assembled in an oxide each hold 1-5 electrons behind a Coulomb-blockade barrier. An integrated single-electron transistor 'develops' the latent charge on read.
why: Fact 1: about 5 electrons replace 5 fF (~30k electrons), cutting write charge and CV2 energy ~1000x. The high charging energy makes tunneling-out, and so refresh, rare.
note: ~1000x less charge per bit; RT Coulomb blockade needs sub-3 nm uniformity, and offset charges plague SETs.

title: Plywood veneer: Smart-Cut array laminates share one periphery base
idea: Like plywood glued from thin veneers, transfer thin 180 nm array layers (cells and bitline selects only, no periphery) one at a time onto a periphery base wafer using 1995 Smart-Cut hydrogen splitting and oxide bonding. Each veneer's bitlines drop through vertical vias to the shared SA/decoder base.
why: Periphery is built once for 8-16 layers, so array efficiency nears 90% and density scales with layer count instead of lithography: a U.S. 200 mm-fab path to dense memory.
note: Shared periphery under 8-16 transferred array layers; doubt is per-layer thermal budget for access devices and capacitors, and compounding bond yield.

title: Vertical CCD loops in channel holes with built-in refresh
idea: IFR: no cell needs a switch because the bit travels to the switch. 3D-NAND-style channel holes with 64-128 tier gates are clocked as a charge-coupled device; packets circulate around ~32-position loops and pass one regeneration/sense amplifier at the top every lap, so refresh is inherent and there is one transistor per loop.
why: Constraint: each bit is one gate crossing in a deposited stack, giving >10x density at 3D NAND cost per wafer; ~32 ns per lap keeps latency DRAM-class if loops stay short.
note: Short vertical loops claim DRAM-class lap time; same transfer-efficiency risk as I-04670.

title: 2D heterojunction thyristor crossbar: bistable bits without capacitors
idea: IFR: the bit holds itself and needs only two wires. Each crosspoint is a vertical p-n-p-n van der Waals stack (WSe2/MoS2) acting as a thin-film thyristor that latches on or off; a sub-100 pA holding bias keeps '1', '0' draws nothing, and a reverse pulse resets it, so there is no capacitor and no refresh.
why: Constraint: nanometer-thin two-terminal layers allow 8-16 cheap stacked 4F^2 layers, >10x density versus 6F^2, with refresh eliminated if holding current stays below ~100 pA per cell.
note: Stacked two-terminal latching cells could exceed 10x density; doubt: pA holding current and multilayer 2D transfer yield.

title: SiGe quantum-well hole pocket replaces capacitor in each tier
idea: IFR: the transistor body is itself a leak-proof bucket. In epitaxial Si/SiGe/Si superlattice tiers, holes are stored in a buried compressively strained Ge-rich quantum well under each lateral channel; the ~0.3-0.5 eV valence-band offset confines them and their charge shifts channel Vt for non-destructive reads.
why: Constraint: capacitorless 1T cells at ~30 nm tier pitch allow ~100 epi tiers with NAND-like per-tier cost, aiming >10x density per wafer.
note: 0.3-0.5 eV valence offset implies microsecond-scale thermal hole emission at room temperature; retention doubtful.

title: Quadrant-gated pillars: four lateral storage pockets per tier
idea: IFR: one bitline pillar serves every direction. Around each vertical bitline pillar, split the tier wordline into four independently driven quadrant gates, each gating a short lateral oxide channel to its own storage pocket, so each pillar holds four cells per tier.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per pillar per tier across ~16 tiers is ~64 bits per pillar footprint, >10x density per wafer, while bitline contacts drop 4x.
note: Four pockets per pillar per tier multiplies 3D density; tiny per-pocket storage and quadrant gate control are doubts.

title: Shipping-container micro-fabs printing DRAM arrays by nanoimprint
idea: Ideal: a fab that fits anywhere and costs as much as a house. Closest achievable: 40-ft containerized minienvironments use jet-and-flash nanoimprint for the dense, regular array layers (honeycomb capacitor holes, bitlines) and dry ArF for periphery, ganged into $200-500M micro-fab clusters.
why: Capital intensity, EUV avoidance and U.S. manufacturability: claimed ~10x less capex per wafer-start module; imprint defectivity is the main risk.
note: NIL defectivity and overlay for DRAM plus containerized-fab capex claims are unproven; Minimal Fab precedent.

title: Two-mask array: hole-and-slit concentric annular 3D DRAM cells
idea: Limit: the whole array may use only two critical masks. One hole mask through 96 Si/SiGe tiers defines vertical bitlines, and a timed lateral recess from each hole carves a concentric ring per tier (BL core, then an annular channel gated by the tier plates above and below, then an outer ring capacitor). One slit mask cuts the plates into wordline regions, so a cell is the crossing of one hole and one tier-region.
why: Facts 2 and 4: about 10,000 nm2 per tier-cell at 100 nm hole pitch gives about 104 nm2/bit over 96 tiers (8x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV array layers.
note: 8x density with zero EUV; doubt: tiny ring Cs and multi-ring timed lateral recess uniformity.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift columns with zero transistors per bit
idea: Limit: no access transistor per bit. Each 4F2 column is a stack of 3-phase clocked gate tiers forming CCD potential wells. Charge packets shift down the column at about 2 GHz to one sense node at its base, giving page access in about 10-30 ns.
why: Facts 1-3: about 20 bits per 4F2 footprint with no capacitor or transistor per bit; endurance is unlimited because the storage is charge.
note: Dup of vertical CCD string; 2 GHz shifting in deposited channels is implausible.

title: Porous-silicon release layers recycle donor wafers across forty tiers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Build DRAM on a porous-silicon cleave layer (ELTRAN-style), transfer only the 2 um device film into the stack, then re-epi and reuse the donor substrate 10-20 times; 40+ films fit in the height of three normal dies.
why: Silicon and quartz-crucible chokepoint plus wafer cost: substrate cost per tier falls ~90%, paying for the extra tiers, so ~10x bits per footprint at similar package cost.
note: Donor reuse makes 40-tier film stacks affordable; capacitor height, thermal budget and multiplicative bond yield are the doubts.

title: No silicon wafer: panel-scale nanoimprint to sub-100 nm rules
idea: Forced limit: glass panels must reach DRAM-like density without EUV. Step-and-repeat nanoimprint templates are pattern-stitched across Gen 6 glass to print sub-100 nm gain-cell features, with die-by-die alignment correcting glass distortion.
why: Density and capital: at 100 nm a Gen 6 panel holds about 1-2 TB, similar to one or two DRAM wafers, with no scanner.
note: A 100 nm imprint makes a Gen-6 panel worth 1-2 wafers; glass distortion, overlay and defectivity are doubts.

title: No silicon wafer: monolithic oxide tiers multiply panel density
idea: Forced limit: panels cannot shrink to DRAM litho. Stack 8-32 monolithic IGZO gain-cell tiers on glass at 350 C or below, each tier self-aligned to the one below with shared staircase contacts.
why: Density: tiers instead of nodes multiply bits per panel by up to 32x, reaching the roughly 26-tier break-even on cheap glass.
note: Tiers replace nodes on cheap glass; per-tier yield compounding and panel-litho cell size make 8-32 tiers a big doubt.

title: Minify tunnel oxide to 1.5 nm: leaky 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: Take a 200+ layer charge-trap 3D NAND flow and thin the tunnel oxide to about 1.5 nm, so cells write by direct tunneling in about 10-50 ns and leak in about 1-10 s. The controller refreshes them like DRAM, and direct tunneling may avoid hot-carrier wear.
why: Reuses the cheapest per-bit 3D process in the world for working memory, with density about 5-10x DRAM. Endurance is unproven.
note: NAND density for working memory; doubt: string-read latency, byte access, and 1e15+ cycle endurance.

title: Minify the litho tool to a spin coater: block-copolymer arrays
idea: Spin-coat high-chi block copolymers that phase-separate into 12-16 nm pitch hexagonal dot arrays, use them as etch masks for vertical pillar cells, align domains to wordlines with coarse i-line trenches (graphoepitaxy), and absorb assembly defects with redundancy.
why: Coater + bake plate + i-line stepper instead of EUV gives ~20x lower capex per wafer, and sub-15 nm pitch packs ~4x more cells than 6F2 at F=12 nm: ~80-100x lower cost per GB.
note: DSA removes EUV; doubts: decades-old defectivity problem and capacitor at 12-16 nm pitch hits charge wall.

title: Eliminate the three-terminal transistor: threshold-switch selector 1S1C crosspoint DRAM
idea: Isolate each capacitor with a two-terminal volatile threshold switch (OTS or NbO2 Mott selector) stacked directly on it in a crosspoint, addressed by V/2 biasing; no wordline transistor and no lateral device, so tiers stack like 3D crosspoint.
why: Removes the 3D DRAM lateral-transistor blocker (fact 2) and enables 4F^2 stacking; half-select leakage must reach <1e-15 A for even millisecond retention, hence high risk.
note: Would remove the lateral-transistor blocker for 3D, but OTS/Mott selector off-leakage is orders above the needed sub-fA.

title: Reverse the charge wall: 50-electron bits read by single-electron transistors
idea: Instead of fighting for ~30,000 electrons in a 5 fF pillar, store ~50 electrons on a 0.01 fF planar node and move all the gain into the reader: a 3-5 nm room-temperature silicon Coulomb island coupled to the node swings its current by decades per few electrons.
why: Charge wall and capacitor process (facts 1,4): the tall capacitor vanishes (planar ~4F2 cell) and CV2 write energy drops ~100x; risks are RT single-electron uniformity and keeping 50 electrons from leaking.
note: Few-electron node with SET gain removes the capacitor; doubt: room-temperature SET variability, Yano-style prior art.

title: Optane's abandoned threshold-switch stack reused for capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: Revive the shelved 3D XPoint selector process: pair an Ovonic threshold switch with a tiny MIM capacitor (1S1C) in stacked crosspoint decks so the selector replaces the access transistor; OTS threshold scatter and leakage cause ~1% cell errors that tile-level codes correct.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: stackable charge cells with no transistors, built on existing deck-process know-how; 4 decks give ~4x bits per mask set.
note: Same OTS+MIM crosspoint; codes cannot fix pA-scale selector leakage limiting retention.

title: Transistorless 1S1C crosspoint: threshold switch guards each capacitor
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM cell needs an access transistor.' Put a volatile ovonic threshold switch in series with a small MIM capacitor at every crosspoint of stackable 4F² line layers; full-select pulses exceed threshold to read/write, half-selected cells stay off, and decks stack like 3D XPoint.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 4F² per deck times N decks with no lateral transistor; OTS off-leakage (~pA) forcing ms-scale refresh is the honest risk.
note: Same OTS+MIM crosspoint; pA off-leakage forces sub-ms refresh.

title: Vertical CCD charge-packet strings replace per-bit transistors and capacitors
idea: Box = {medium: charge packets in buried-channel potential wells | access: three-phase clocked ring gates, no per-bit FET | sense: floating-diffusion source follower at the string end | integration: vertical 32-bit CCD strings in deep holes | substrate: Si | fab: 3D-NAND-style hole etch + conformal gate stack}. Each vertical hole is a 32-stage CCD; a random access shifts the string past one amplifier in <30 ns, and every access recirculates and re-amplifies the packets, so refresh happens as a side effect of normal shifting.
why: Facts 2, 4, 7: ~2F2 per bit with no capacitor and no access transistor; density scales with string length rather than lithography, and one amplifier per 32 bits shrinks the periphery.
note: Duplicate vertical CCD; charge-transfer efficiency over 32 stages in hole channels is the doubt.

title: 3D NAND strings retuned for DRAM retention and endurance
idea: Time-shift flash from 10-year retention to ~1 s: thin the tunnel oxide to 1.5-2 nm direct tunneling so charge traps in a 200-tier vertical string write in ns with 1e15 cycles, refreshed like DRAM, using existing 3D NAND fabs.
why: Capital intensity and density: 200 stacked tiers built with mature NAND tools and no EUV, multi-x bits per mm2.
note: Claims ns writes and 1e15 cycles from charge traps; overstated.

title: Ten-electron quantum-dot storage node read by a single-electron transistor
idea: Jump down to the electron count: store a bit as ~10 electrons on a 3-nm silicon quantum dot behind an engineered double tunnel barrier, whose Coulomb blockade gives ms-to-s retention. An adjacent single-electron transistor reads it, its current swinging fully per electron, so cell capacitance is ~1 aF instead of 5 fF.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) by trading charge quantity for charge sensitivity: ~1000x less stored charge, enabling 3D cells under 20 nm.
note: Yano-style SET memory known; doubt: room-temperature variability and background charge.

title: Optane's selector, not its PCM: OTS-gated capacitor crosspoint DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's real breakthrough was the ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selector; what killed it as a DRAM substitute was slow, wearing phase-change material (PCM). Pair the OTS with a MIM capacitor (one selector, one capacitor) in stacked crosspoint decks. The OTS snaps on above threshold to charge or discharge the cap in nanoseconds and blocks under half-select, giving transistor-free DRAM cells of 4F2 per deck.
why: Removes the access transistor and EUV-patterned cell (facts 2, 4). Four to eight decks with shared litho could give ~4x density. Endurance is unlimited because no material changes state; shorter retention is the main risk.
note: Same OTS+MIM crosspoint; retention set by selector leakage is the blocker.

title: Band-offset Ge quantum wells store holes behind a heterobarrier
idea: Effect: heterojunction band offset. Charge is stored as holes in a buried SiGe/Ge quantum well under each access channel; the ~0.5 eV valence-band offset confines them so thermionic loss falls ~exp(-0.5 eV/kT), giving seconds of retention with no capacitor, and reads sense the threshold shift of the overlying channel (built-in gain-cell amplification).
why: 10x density: a capacitorless 1T cell at 4F^2 stacked 32 tiers by Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy gives >10x. Same cost: the capacitor module and its EUV steps are removed.
note: Capacitorless stackable 1T would be big; doubt retention vs GIDL/tunnelling, QW 1T-DRAM known.

title: Ni: Ni(OH)2 pseudocapacitive storage node stores tens of times more charge
idea: Coat the storage electrode with 2-3 nm of Ni(OH)2 and a thin solid proton conductor so a write drives faradaic Ni2+/Ni3+ redox, whose pseudocapacitance (hundreds of uF/cm2) is tens of times a high-k dielectric (~7 uF/cm2); the charge dumps onto the bit line like a normal DRAM read.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): a planar or low-AR node holds 5+ fF; nickel is widely available; redox rate at ~10 ns and electrolyte leakage are the risks.
note: Redox charge would break charge wall; doubt: 10 ns faradaic kinetics, self-discharge, 1e15-cycle endurance.

title: Transistorless crosspoint DRAM with wide-bandgap Schottky selector and capacitor
idea: IFR: 'no access transistor, so cells stack like crosspoint.' Backward: replace the transistor with a two-terminal back-to-back Schottky selector in a wide-bandgap oxide (e.g., Ga2O3 with Pt contacts) targeting ~1e-19 A half-select leakage, in series with a small MIM capacitor, stacked as 1S1C crosspoint decks of only word and bit lines.
why: 4F2 and 3D without lateral transistors (facts 2, 4): ~2 masks per deck and ~4x density at the same F, if the selector's ~1e12 on/off ratio holds.
note: Schottky selector needing 1e12 on/off and 1e-19 A leakage is the miracle required.

title: Embrace random wiring: self-assembled crossbars mapped after fabrication
idea: Ideal: wiring that costs nothing because nobody designs it. Closest: grow dense random or partly ordered nanoline crossbars (dewetting, DSA) with a cell wherever lines cross; reach lines through a coarse-litho stochastic decoder (randomly doped address wires, Lieber/DeHon style) and run a one-time BIST discovery pass that writes a per-chip address-translation table.
why: 100x: shifts cost from lithographic precision to cheap logic and test time; if 30-50% of random cells are usable, $/GB falls ~100x versus precision-patterned arrays. Trades ~1-3% map overhead and variable capacity per die.
note: Revives DeHon/Lieber stochastic decoding; doubt is a fast per-crosspoint cell with selector, and usable yield.

title: Backside-power flow repurposed to build capacitors behind the transistors
idea: Combine backside-power-delivery/BSI wafer thinning with the 1T1C cell: access transistors and bitlines are built on the front, the wafer is bonded to a carrier and thinned to the channel bottoms, and the storage capacitors are formed on the exposed backside drains, so bitline and capacitor no longer compete for one plane.
why: Decouples capacitor thermal budget and geometry from bitline routing, enabling a 4F2 cell at relaxed F (~15 nm rather than 12 nm) and removing ~2 EUV-critical self-aligned contact steps; ~30% density at the same litho (facts 1, 4).

title: Steel mini-mill disruption: EUV-free DUV mini-fabs for mature DRAM
idea: Nucor beat integrated mills by entering at rebar with cheap electric-arc mini-mills; build 10-20k wafer-starts/month fabs using refurbished 193i scanners and SAQP to make 1y/1z-class DDR4, LPDDR4 and CXL-expander dies, sell into the commodity tier the HBM-focused majors are abandoning, then climb node by node.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~$3-5B per mini-fab versus $15B+; zero EUV; DUV tools are available on the secondary market; adds supply in under 3 years.

title: Memory-only 450 mm wafers with a stripped-down tool set
idea: The G450C 450 mm program died around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund ~$20B of development against uncertain orders from three logic giants. DRAM uses far fewer distinct tool types than logic, so a memory-only 450 mm consortium with government cost share qualifies only ~40 tool types and pre-commits volume.
why: Throughput and capital per bit: 2.25x area per wafer pass; past wafer-size transitions cut cost per die ~30%; fewer, larger tools per bit lower fab capex per Gb.

title: Merchant-foundry periphery wafers bonded to array-only DRAM wafers
idea: Substitute DRAM-process periphery with periphery made on depreciated 28/22 nm merchant-foundry logic lines and wafer-bonded to array-only wafers. DRAM fabs then spend all their EUV and DRAM-specific tool time on cell arrays, and periphery is bought by the wafer.
why: Capital intensity and capacity: with periphery at ~49% of die, array-only wafers yield ~1.8x more bits per DRAM-fab wafer start; idle mature-node US foundry capacity becomes DRAM supply.

title: Substitute EUV with nanoimprint for periodic DRAM array layers
idea: Replace EUV exposure of the repetitive storage-node-contact, landing-pad and bitline layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (UV-cured resist pressed by a 1x quartz template replicated from an e-beam master); keep EUV/ArF only for irregular periphery. Imprint defects are absorbed by row/column redundancy mapped to each template's defect map, and templates rotate through a replica line.
why: Fact 4 (litho capital, single EUV supplier): an imprint tool is ~1/10 the price and power of an EUV scanner; moving 3-4 of the 5-7 EUV layers could cut litho depreciation per wafer ~30-40%.

title: Substitute monolithic DRAM die with array wafer bonded to logic periphery
idea: Fabricate the cell array on an array-only wafer (no periphery transistors and no dual/triple gate-oxide modules, roughly half the masks) and the sense amps, decoders and I/O on a 28-16 nm logic wafer, then hybrid bond the two wafer-to-wafer at ~1 um pitch.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery (~49% of die) moves under the array to existing logic foundries; die area -30-40% and array-wafer process steps about -35%.

title: Substitute ballroom cleanrooms with sealed tool-to-tool mini-environments
idea: Build the fab as a sealed transport network where pods dock tool-to-tool under nitrogen, with ISO-1 cleanliness only inside tools and AMHS tubes, so the building itself is an ordinary ISO-8 warehouse.
why: Capital: cleanroom construction, HVAC and make-up air are ~20-30% of fab capex and a major energy/water load; could cut building capex ~2/3 and build time by about a year.

title: Photonic base die turns HBM into a fiber-attached appliance
idea: Substitute the HBM base die's electrical PHY with a silicon-photonics base die (microring modulators, Ge detectors, fiber V-grooves), so a stack talks over fiber at ~1 pJ/bit and can sit anywhere on a board or rack.
why: Facts 5/6: frees GPU shoreline and interposer area; memory scales independently of compute and can be pooled for higher utilization.
note: Celestial AI and Ayar Labs pursue optical memory attach.

title: Substitute monolithic DRAM fabs with split array fab plus logic-foundry periphery
idea: Swap making periphery in the DRAM fab for buying periphery wafers from idle U.S. mature-logic foundries and hybrid-bonding them face-to-face onto array-only wafers made in a lean array fab.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; moving it to existing logic capacity frees ~40% more array area per DRAM wafer and lets the U.S. use fabs it already has.
note: Xtacking-style cell-on-periphery bonding is already pursued for 3D DRAM.

title: Substitute boom-bust cycles with a Strategic DRAM Reserve
idea: Swap the free-running DRAM cycle for a petroleum-reserve analogue: a government buys tested wafers and dies in gluts at floor prices, stores them in dry-nitrogen vaults, and auctions them in shortages.
why: Damps the 4x price swing and guarantees fabs a demand floor, which lowers capital risk and makes new U.S. fabs financeable.

title: Substitute integrated memory makers with a pure-play DRAM foundry
idea: Swap the three vertically integrated DRAM makers for a TSMC-style pure-play DRAM foundry offering a cell-array process plus design kits, so fabless memory companies and hyperscalers tape out custom DRAM.
why: Opens DRAM to new entrants and custom parts, spreading fab capital over many customers and raising utilization through cycles.

title: Passing-gate trenches become shield lines that back-bias neighbors
idea: Combine row-hammer shielding and leakage control in one buried trench: every passing-gate buried wordline is replaced by a line held at about -0.5 V that both screens active rows from aggressor coupling and back-gates the adjacent access channels into deeper off-state.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and leakage tail (fact 3): removes the passing-gate hammer path (threshold up >10x) and cuts GIDL/subthreshold tail ~10x for ~4-8x longer refresh; area cost offset by deleting hammer-tracking logic.

title: Mature U.S. foundry periphery wafers hybrid-bonded under array-only wafers
idea: Combine Xtacking-style wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with idle U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundry capacity. The DRAM wafer carries only cells, bitline sense amps and wordline drivers; decoders, I/O, DLL, charge pumps and test logic are made on mature logic wafers and bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7). The array wafer becomes nearly all cells and drops ~8-12 HKMG periphery masks, and depreciated U.S. fabs supply half the silicon, so array-fab wafer starts per bit fall ~25-35%.

title: Active interposer merging HBM base dies with GPU memory controllers
idea: Combine the HBM logic base die and the GPU-side memory controller/PHY into one active interposer in a 12-16 nm logic node: DRAM core stacks bond directly onto it with controllers right underneath, so both ends of the PHY pair vanish and the GPU reaches memory over on-chip-style wires.
why: Data movement and GPU beachfront: removes ~1-1.5 pJ/bit of the 3-4 pJ/bit HBM cost and ~10% of GPU die area spent on PHYs/controllers.
note: Converges with HBM4 custom base dies.

title: Buyer-owned memory cooperative fab, Ocean-Spray style
idea: Combine agricultural co-op ownership with a DRAM fab. Tier-2 clouds, automakers, PC OEMs and defense primes buy member shares in proportion to their volume and receive output at cost plus a reserve, with patronage dividends when prices spike.
why: Members swap price exposure for capex ownership. It aligns long-term demand with supply and opens a new buyer-funded U.S. capacity channel outside the three incumbents.

title: Pure-play foundry model with an open DRAM cell PDK
idea: Borrow TSMC's split of design from manufacturing: a DRAM foundry runs one qualified cell process with an open process design kit (cell, sense amp and redundancy libraries), and many fabless memory designers tape out custom DRAMs (AI-tuned page sizes, CXL, in-memory compute) on shared capacity.
why: Capital utilization and innovation: pooled demand keeps the fab full across cycles, and new memory products need design budgets (~$20-50M) instead of a $15B fab.

title: Automotive microcontroller fabs: hafnium-free poly-SiON periphery wafers
idea: Carmakers' MCUs run on 40/28 nm poly-gate SiON processes in underused U.S. fabs; move row decoders, wordline drivers, I/O and control onto such a Hf-free wafer (contacts in TiN-lined Al, not W) and hybrid-bond it to the array wafer, which keeps only pitch-matched sense amps.
why: Hf-free, EUV-free periphery (facts 4, 7): much of the ~49% periphery leaves the costly array wafer, cutting array-wafer area per bit ~30-40% and putting idle U.S. mature capacity to work.

title: Magnify die to the full wafer: wafer-scale DRAM
idea: Make a 300 mm wafer one memory, with no dicing: tiles are linked by an on-wafer mesh with spare-tile rerouting. Bond it face-to-face to a wafer-scale compute wafer, so there are no packages, PHYs or scribe lines.
why: Data movement and packaging: about 1 TB per wafer pair at about 0.1 pJ/bit, recovering about 5-8% of wafer area lost to scribe lines and edges.
note: Cerebras-style wafer-scale with WoW memory; well-trodden direction.

title: Periphery on legacy 200 mm US fabs, bonded to array
idea: Minify what needs a leading-edge fab to only the dense cell array; make the 49% periphery (sense amps, decoders, I/O) on underused 200/300 mm mature-node US fabs, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond the two.
why: Periphery die area and capital: frees ~half of expensive DRAM wafer area for bits (~1.8x density per DRAM wafer) and reuses depreciated US fabs for the logic half.

title: Eliminate periphery from the memory wafer: subarray-granular hybrid bonding
idea: The memory wafer carries only cell arrays with 16:1 bitline muxes at each subarray edge; sense amps, decoders and I/O sit on a separately made logic wafer joined by ~400 nm pitch hybrid bonds at subarray granularity.
why: Periphery ~49%: array efficiency rises toward ~85-90%, and periphery moves to a cheaper or better-suited logic node; ~1.6x bits per memory wafer.
note: CBA/periphery-on-separate-wafer is widely pursued for 3D DRAM and NAND; 400 nm subarray bonding is aggressive.

title: Eliminate die-by-die thermocompression bonders: wafer-on-wafer HBM core stacking
idea: Hybrid-bond whole core-die wafers on top of each other and dice finished stacks, replacing hundreds of slow pick-and-place TCB bonds per wafer with one bond per layer; the base die still speaks standard HBM3E/HBM4.
why: Fact 6 and capital: removes the TCB bonder bottleneck that limits HBM output, with ~10x stacking throughput per tool; best paired with spare-die repair to offset compounded yield.

title: Periphery wafer on top in leading-edge logic, array beneath
idea: Rearrange the stack: an array-only wafer is hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~0.5 um pitch to a periphery wafer made in a 3 nm-class GAA logic process, so SAs and sub-wordline drivers are ~5x denser than DRAM-process periphery.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery footprint fits under the array, die area -35-45%, array wafer drops ~20 masks. Known in NAND as CBA; new with logic-node periphery.

title: Merchant periphery wafers: U.S. array startups build only arrays
idea: Reverse vertical integration: one U.S. fab sells known-good periphery wafers with a standard hybrid-bond map, while startups and national labs fabricate only array wafers (~20 fewer masks) in small U.S. fabs and bond them domestically.
why: Capital intensity: an array-only line could cost ~1/3 of a full DRAM fab, multiplying U.S. supply sources.
note: CMOS-bonded arrays already pursued (Xtacking, VCT DRAM); bond pitch vs bitline density is key.

title: Rotate the page vertical: one cell per tier, 64-bit activation
idea: In 3D DRAM, reverse the activation axis: a short vertical word-pillar gates exactly one cell in each of 64 tiers, and each tier senses on its own horizontal bitline, so one activation opens a 64-bit vertical column instead of an 8 kb row.
why: Overfetch and row hammer (facts 8,9): activation energy per useful bit drops ~50-100x; an aggressor pillar disturbs only its few neighbors, not a whole row.

title: Ship periphery to logic fabs: array-only DRAM wafers bonded to CMOS
idea: Rearrange array and periphery: the DRAM fab builds only cell arrays, and a mature-node logic foundry builds the sense amps, decoders and I/O on a separate wafer. The two are hybrid-bonded wafer to wafer, as Xtacking does for NAND.
why: Fact 7: periphery is ~49% of the die. Moving it out nearly doubles the bits each DRAM-fab wafer yields and draws on abundant logic capacity.

title: Taking out: periphery made in U.S. mature fabs, bonded to arrays
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out pulls the ~49% periphery off the EUV array wafer: sense amps, decoders, pumps and I/O are made on 28-40 nm logic wafers in existing U.S. fabs and hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch onto array-only wafers. A national 'periphery foundry' program qualifies one bonding interface that several array suppliers can use.
why: Facts 4 and 7 plus U.S. manufacturability: array die area per bit ~-45%, array wafer masks ~-20-30%, and about half of each DRAM's value-added silicon moves onshore without building an EUV fab.

title: Array-only wafers bonded to U.S. mature-node periphery wafers
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: pull all periphery (sense amps, decoders, charge pumps, I/O) off the DRAM wafer onto a 28-40 nm logic wafer from a U.S. foundry, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond at ~1 um pitch. The DRAM fab runs only the array flow, so its EUV and high-AR tools spend all their time on bits.
why: Fact 7 and U.S. manufacturability: array efficiency rises from ~51% to ~85% of die area (~1.6x bits per array wafer) and roughly half the process steps move to existing U.S. fabs.
note: CBA/Xtacking for DRAM widely pursued.

title: Segmented fab: array-only line plus mature-node periphery wafer
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'leading-edge cells vs cheap periphery': run only the ~25 array-critical layers in a slim array fab, build sense amps, drivers and I/O on a 28-40 nm logic wafer bought from idle U.S. foundry capacity, and join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding under the mats. The array fab no longer needs high-voltage, multi-Vt or logic-metal modules.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and ~15-20 masks; splitting cuts array-fab tool types ~30-40%, frees die area for cells (+40-60% bits/wafer) and lets U.S. foundries supply half the silicon (facts 4, 7; capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Disposable nanoimprint daughter templates for periodic array layers
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying plus #27 Cheap short-living objects: write one master template by e-beam, replicate hundreds of daughter templates by imprint, and run each daughter for ~1-5k wafers on jet-and-flash imprint tools for capacitor-hole and landing-pad layers, discarding it when defects accumulate while array redundancy absorbs the rest.
why: Imprint tools cost ~1/5-1/10 of an EUV scanner and ~1/10 the power; moving 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers to NIL cuts the litho cost of those layers ~40-60% (fact 4).

title: Segmentation: per-tile 2-high DRAM micro-stacks bonded over compute
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation, resolving 'more bandwidth vs. limited die-edge shoreline': replace 6-8 edge-mounted 12-high HBM stacks with ~64 two-high DRAM micro-stacks hybrid-bonded on top of each compute tile at ~9 um pitch. Each micro-stack feeds only the tile beneath it, and the logic NoC handles sharing.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): wire length drops from ~5 mm to <0.1 mm, so ~3.5 falls to ~0.3 pJ/bit. 2-high stacks avoid compound 12-high yield loss, and shoreline stops limiting bandwidth.
note: DRAM-over-compute widely pursued; thermal coupling to hot logic is the main doubt.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM that routes around dead tiles on-wafer
idea: TRIZ separation by scale: a whole 300 mm wafer is left undiced at a U.S. fab; 1,000+ DRAM tiles join through a stitched on-wafer mesh and at power-on a route table skips dead tiles and reticle-stitch faults, yielding one ~1-2 TB memory slab with no packaging, TSVs or foreign OSAT.
why: Defects become routing problems instead of scrapped dies: nearly all good tiles used, packaging and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) avoided, fully domestic.
note: Anamartic wafer-scale memory (1980s) did exactly this route-around.

title: Taking out: move DRAM periphery to foundry wafers, hybrid-bond back
idea: TRIZ #2 Extraction: strip sense amps, decoders and I/O off the DRAM wafer so the scarce DRAM fab prints only cell arrays, while plentiful logic foundries build the periphery wafer; the two are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at 1-2 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: ~1.6-1.9x more bits per scarce DRAM wafer start, and periphery gets faster logic transistors.
note: Cell-on-periphery bonding is already widely pursued for 4F2/3D DRAM.

title: V(D)J recombination: mix-and-match array and periphery chiplets
idea: Immune cells generate diversity by recombining gene segments. Capacitorless array chiplets from many fabs (gain-cell, floating-body, crosspoint) are hybrid-bonded to periphery and controller chiplets from logic fabs through one standard interface, so any fab that can make one segment adds to supply.
why: Unbundling moves the ~49% periphery to cheaper logic nodes and widens the supplier base.

title: Cell-to-pack memory: unsingulated DRAM wafers bonded onto compute wafers
idea: Like EV cell-to-pack removing the module layer, skip die singulation, packages and DIMMs: wafer-bond whole yield-mapped DRAM wafers (with spare-tile rerouting) onto whole compute wafers so memory meets compute through millions of bonds at full wafer scale.
why: HBM TSV tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): removes TSVs, interposer and package; claims ~3x area efficiency vs HBM and ~100 TB/s per wafer pair.
note: Widely pursued (SoIC, wafer-scale); compound yield issue.

title: Prefab-housing utility cores: periphery wafers from mature U.S. logic fabs
idea: Modular housing builds the plumbing and electrical core in a factory and drops it on site. Split DRAM into an array wafer (DRAM fab) and a periphery CMOS wafer built on 28-40 nm logic lines at U.S. foundries with spare capacity, then hybrid-bond them face-to-face; the bonded die presents the same DDR5/HBM pins and timing.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) and needs no EUV; moving it to depreciated mature fabs frees ~40% of DRAM-fab wafer capacity and raises bits per DRAM wafer.

title: TSMC-for-memory pure-play DRAM foundry with open shuttles
idea: Copy the logic-foundry model that unlocked fabless design: a DRAM-only foundry publishes a cell-array PDK and runs multi-project shuttles so startups can tape out custom periphery, HBM base dies and domain-specific DRAM without owning a fab.
why: Breaks the 3-firm design monopoly; adds design diversity and new demand-specific products, and lets a U.S. fab sell capacity to many customers, raising utilization 10-20 points.

title: Core-stack business model: periphery wafers from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Core memory was sold as a woven stack from one vendor and a driver/sense chassis from another. Split DRAM the same way: array-only wafers (cells and bitlines, no periphery) from existing DRAM fabs are hybrid-bonded to periphery wafers built on depreciated 28-40 nm U.S. logic lines, creating a merchant market for memory periphery.
why: Array dies gain ~1.6x bits per leading-edge wafer by shedding the 49% periphery (fact 7), and more of the value is made in the U.S. on existing tools (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Array-only DRAM wafer with periphery bonded from US 28nm logic
idea: Inverting 'cells and periphery share one wafer process': the DRAM fab builds wafers with only access devices, bitlines and capacitors (no periphery transistors, fewer implants and masks), while sense amps, decoders and I/O are made on a 28nm logic wafer in a US foundry and hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch along every subarray edge.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) leaves the expensive EUV DRAM wafer, so bits per DRAM wafer rise ~1.7-1.9x, periphery moves onto depreciated US logic capacity, and sense amps get faster logic transistors.

title: Buried back-gate plane per tier: negative hold bias, low-swing wordlines
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor threshold is fixed.' Give every tier a doped-Si back-gate plane under its channels, biased strongly negative during hold to raise Vt and crush leakage, then relaxed per bank on access, so wordlines swing ~1.5 V instead of ~3 V.
why: Facts 3 and 10: leakage tail cut ~10-100x and wordline CV² energy ~4x lower, with Si only.

title: Hyperscaler joint venture owns a cost-plus DRAM fab, Airbus-style
idea: Inverts 'buyers and makers of DRAM are adversaries over margin': 4-6 large buyers form a joint-venture entity that owns a U.S. fab running a licensed process from a second-tier vendor, sells at cost, and splits output pro rata to equity.
why: Cost per bit: strips the 40-60% peak-cycle vendor margin and guarantees offtake that de-risks $15B capex; also adds a U.S. source.

title: Array-only fabs bond to US logic-foundry periphery wafers
idea: Split the business: a new entrant builds an array-only fab (capacitors and access devices, no periphery CMOS), and buys periphery wafers from US 22-28 nm logic foundries, joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with periphery under the array.
why: Capital intensity and US manufacturability (fact 4): array fab capex and mask count drop, periphery uses existing US capacity; ~30-40% lower entry capex.

title: One sense amplifier per vertical stack, multiplexed across 32 tiers
idea: Because only one tier of a bank is activated at a time, give each vertical column of 32 tiers a single sense amplifier reached through a per-tier select transistor at the column foot, instead of one sense amp per bitline per tier.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): sense-amp area per bit divides by the tier count, pushing periphery toward ~5-10% of footprint and making the 26-tier break-even (fact 2) reachable with cheaper tiers.
note: Vertical-bitline 3D DRAM already puts one SA per column; known architecture.

title: Periphery from depreciated U.S. logic fabs, hybrid-bonded to array
idea: First principle: the array needs the finest pitch, but the periphery (~49% of the die) only needs ~28 nm-class CMOS. Make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab and the periphery on fully depreciated 28-65 nm U.S. logic fabs, then join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: up to ~1.8x bits per expensive DRAM wafer, using idle U.S. mature-node capacity.
note: CBA/Xtacking known; mature-fab sourcing twist.

title: Relocatable fab pods: containerized modules with high resale value
idea: First principle: fab capital is expensive partly because it is stranded: a fab building cannot be moved or resold. Factory-build fab segments as sealed clean pods with minienvironment tools inside, bolt them together in months, and move, refurbish or resell them later, which lowers the risk premium on capital.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity (3-5 years today): ~12-18 month deployment; redeployable by design.

title: Bank-level attention PIM moves KV from HBM to LPDDR
idea: An HBM bit costs ~3x the wafer area of a DDR5 bit (TSVs and yield loss), yet the KV cache only needs bandwidth for one dot product. Put q.k and softmax-weighted v accumulation units at each LPDDR bank, so the KV cache lives in commodity DRAM and only scores and results cross the bus.
why: The same KV capacity for ~1/3 of the wafer area, freeing HBM for weights; internal bank bandwidth exceeds the HBM interface.

title: Seed bank: national shuttle wafers for wild storage-element candidates
idea: Stimulus 'seed bank' -> a CHIPS-funded 300 mm back-end shuttle where any lab drops a candidate storage stack into a standard 1T1X 1 Mb test array four times a year, with shared ns-pulse testers, 10^15-cycle endurance rigs and open retention-tail data. One-off device papers become array statistics in 6 months.
why: Cuts the time and capital to qualify a new bit element from years and ~$50M to months and ~$100k (capital/time chokepoint), seeding U.S. memory manufacturability.

title: Ice-cream sandwich: U.S. mature-node periphery wafers bonded to arrays
idea: Split every die into an array-only wafer (cells, bitlines, capacitors) and a periphery wafer (SAs, decoders, pumps, I/O) built on existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic lines, joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with one bond per bitline staggered along its length (a ~50 um bitline has ~1.5 um2 of footprint, room for a 1 um-pitch pad).
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: the ~49% periphery needs no EUV and moves to depreciated U.S. fabs, freeing ~40% of scarce DRAM-fab wafer area per bit and letting new array-only fabs skip most logic steps (~30% less capex).

title: Ship in a bottle: cell wafer bonded onto 28nm periphery wafer
idea: Build the ship outside, then slide it in: make a cell-only wafer (arrays, bitline sense amps and local column mux in the cell process) and a separate periphery wafer in a mature 28 nm logic fab carrying decoders, data paths and the standard DDR5 PHY, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond at ~0.5 um pitch with one bond per 16 bitlines. The bonded die is a normal DDR5 x8 part with the same pinout, commands and timing.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and EUV capital (fact 4): cell-wafer area per bit about -40%, and periphery moves to depreciated U.S. 28 nm fabs (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Food truck: periphery-as-a-service from U.S. mature-node logic fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'food truck' (cook elsewhere, serve on site) -> the array wafer, which carries the EUV and capacitor steps, is made in a lean array-only fab. The CMOS periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) is bought from existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundries and hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) yet needs no DRAM-specific tools. Moving it to depreciated U.S. logic capacity cuts DRAM-fab capex per bit ~30-40% and creates a U.S. supply path without a $15B fab.

title: Mosaic: wafer-scale DRAM-on-logic with defective tiles mapped out
idea: Forced 'mosaic': a whole undiced DRAM wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer, and tiles found bad at test are fused out of a mosaic address map. The result is one wafer-scale memory with no packaging, no PHYs and no dicing between memory and compute.
why: Interface energy and packaging cost; removes PHY/SerDes per die and gives TB/s-class bandwidth per mm of wafer.
note: Wafer-on-wafer bonding plus tile map-out; Cerebras-style redundancy is known, matched wafer yields and thermals are the doubt.

title: Orchestra: US logic fabs build periphery wafers bonded to imported arrays
idea: Random stimulus 'orchestra' -> sections rehearse separately and play together. The cell array wafer (capacitors, WL/BL) comes from existing Asian DRAM fabs; the periphery (~49% of die) is built as a separate CMOS wafer in US logic fabs and joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, Xtacking-style.
why: Array wafers lose the periphery so bits per array wafer rise ~1.6-1.9x; about half the die value becomes US-made using idle FinFET capacity with better transistors for sense amps.
note: CMOS-bonded-array is already on every DRAM maker's roadmap; US-periphery angle is the twist.

title: Sequential smart-cut stacking of single-crystal planar 1T1C tiers
idea: Box = {medium: charge on a planar trench-free MIM | access: lateral single-crystal Si FET in each transferred film | sense: SA on the base die | integration: 16-32 tiers by repeated hydrogen-implant layer transfer below 400 C | substrate: reusable donor wafers | fab: low-temperature bonding + splitting}. Each tier is a thin crystalline Si film with near-bulk access transistors, avoiding the poor poly or oxide channels that hurt monolithic 3D.
why: Fact 2: single-crystal channels in every tier remove the lateral-transistor blocker, and reused donor wafers keep substrate cost per tier small.
note: Sequential smart-cut 3D known (CoolCube-like); cost per transferred tier high.

title: Hafnium-free periphery: array bonded onto mature SiON-poly CMOS wafer
idea: Box [standard 1T1C array | Si access | sense amps on bottom wafer | Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded CMOS-bonded-array | array wafer + 28-40 nm SiON/poly periphery wafer | split fab]: build sense amps and decoders on a mature node with no HfO2/La high-k metal gate and no EUV, then bond the array wafer on top.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and DRAM's only HKMG/Hf user: moves half the die to depreciated, EUV-free tools and removes Hf/La from DRAM while shrinking the array die ~40%.

title: Pure-play DRAM array foundry for fabless memory designers
idea: Box[Owner=foundry x Medium=standard 1T1C array PDK x Integration=customer periphery/logic x Business=wafer-per-month service]: a DRAM fab sells array wafers with a PDK and IP library, the way TSMC sells logic, so fabless firms design custom DRAMs (AI, automotive, CXL) without owning a fab.
why: Industry structure: opens DRAM to many designers, raising fab utilization and innovation; could support new entrants with zero capex.

title: Buyers' cooperative co-owns a U.S. DRAM fab via take-or-pay
idea: Box[Owner=cooperative of hyperscalers, automakers and OEMs x Finance=prepaid take-or-pay offtake x Operator=contract manager x Scale=megafab]: members prepay 10-year offtake pro rata to equity and receive bits at cost-plus, with an operator running the fab.
why: Capital intensity: prepayment covers ~40-60% of a $15B fab, and members get allocation insulated from 4x price spikes.
note: Same buyer co-op plus take-or-pay offtake as I-01806.

title: Po: an array die that cannot decode
idea: Po: an array die that knows no addresses. Row/column predecoding, redundancy CAMs, refresh counters and command logic move to a hybrid-bonded logic-node base die, which drives pre-decoded one-hot group selects through ~1 um-pitch bonds; the array die keeps only sub-wordline drivers, SAs and final pass gates.
why: Periphery (#7): array-die periphery drops from ~49% to ~25-30%, ~35% more bits per array wafer, while the moved logic is ~5x denser on a logic node.

title: Periphery outsourced to idle 28 nm logic wafers, bonded under array
idea: Po: half the chip is missing. Existing DRAM fabs make array-only wafers (cells, bitlines, minimal local sense) while idle 28-40 nm logic fabs make periphery wafers (decoders, sense amps, I/O); the two are hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer with periphery under the array.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): ~1.6-1.9x more bits per existing DRAM wafer start using surplus mature logic capacity; no new fab.

title: Hyperscaler take-or-pay SPVs that own DRAM fab lines
idea: Po: the customer owns the fab. Like LNG trains financed by 20-year take-or-pay contracts, 3-5 hyperscalers fund a special-purpose vehicle that owns a DRAM line run by an incumbent or new entrant, receiving output at cost-plus in proportion to equity.
why: Contracted offtake lets fab debt be priced like infrastructure (~5-6%) instead of chip equity (~12-15%); with depreciation ~55% of wafer cost, a lower WACC cuts cost per bit ~15-25%; attacks capital intensity.

title: Array wafer plus foundry periphery wafer joined by hybrid bonding
idea: Po: one chip is two chips from two countries. A DUV-only DRAM fab makes array-only wafers, while a U.S. 28/22 nm logic foundry makes the periphery wafer; the two are wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonded so the ~49% periphery sits under the array.
why: Uses idle mature logic capacity, shrinks DRAM die area up to ~40%, and lets the array fab skip high-performance transistor steps; attacks periphery overhead, capital and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Hybrid-bonded area pads above each bank replace the global datapath
idea: Worse: haul every bit across the die through global I/O lines and serializers to edge pads. Flip: place hybrid-bonded area-array pads directly above each bank's column logic so a logic die below reads each bank locally, deleting global I/O buses and most serializers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery area (fact 7): <1 pJ/bit access and ~8-10% of die freed.

title: U.S. mature logic fabs build control dies; DRAM fabs only arrays
idea: Worse: build control periphery on scarce, EUV-laden DRAM wafer starts. Flip: contract control, I/O, pump and test dies to U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundries and hybrid-bond them to array-dense dies from DRAM fabs that keep only bitline sense amps and spend the rest of the wafer on bits.
why: Capital intensity and supply: ~30-40% more bits per DRAM-fab wafer start, using underused U.S. logic capacity.

title: Unsawn wafer-scale memory slab bonded to a logic wafer
idea: Worse: dice, package and TSV-stack small dies, losing kerf, pads and 20-30% stack yield. Flip: hybrid-bond an entire array wafer face-to-face onto a logic wafer, keep it whole, and route around failed tiles with a programmable on-wafer mesh, so no dicing, packaging or HBM TSVs are needed.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, fact 6) and package cost, recovers ~10% area from kerf and pads, and gives <0.5 pJ/bit links versus 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Vacuum-continuous fab where wafers never meet cleanroom air
idea: Worsen: build ever-bigger ballroom cleanrooms where huge air handlers filter air around wafers 24/7. Flip: link tools with sealed vacuum or N2 tunnels and maglev carriers so the wafer's environment is always a tool interior, letting building air drop to industrial grade.
why: Energy (cleanroom HVAC is ~30-50% of fab energy) and capital: also cuts yield loss from airborne molecular contamination.
note: Mini-environments and Minimal Fab already exist.

title: Mature-node SiON periphery wafers bonded under the array
idea: Worsen: build the 49% of the die that is periphery in the same leading-edge flow, with Hf/La high-k metal gates and EUV. Flip: make the periphery logic on 28-40 nm SiON-gate wafers in existing U.S. mature fabs and hybrid-bond it beneath an array-only wafer, so hafnium, lanthanum and EUV appear only where the cell needs them.
why: Hf/La and EUV intensity, periphery area and U.S. manufacturability: the array die shrinks ~40%.
note: CMOS-bonded-array widely pursued; mature-node periphery must still meet SA pitch and I/O speed.

title: Periphery from U.S. mature foundries bonded to array-only wafers
idea: Worse: build sense amps and logic in the same costly DRAM process that compromises both. Flip: make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab, buy the periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from a 28/22 nm U.S. foundry, and hybrid-bond the two wafer-to-wafer at sub-micron pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): DRAM fab bit output per tool rises ~1.6-1.9x, using underused U.S. mature-node capacity.
note: Bonded-periphery DRAM is already on industry roadmaps.

title: Pure-play DRAM foundry with open PDK for fabless designers
idea: Worse: keep the DRAM process locked inside three IDMs. Flip: a DRAM foundry offers an array PDK (cell, capacitor, sense-amp macros) and multi-project wafers, so fabless startups and hyperscalers can tape out custom PIM, wide-I/O or CXL-native DRAM.
why: Capital: spreads utilization over many customers, unlocks designs that do DRAM's job with fewer bits, and opens a U.S. entry path.

title: Bank-under-tile: each compute tile owns the DRAM bank beneath it
idea: Worsen: route every bit across a shared bus to a DIMM 10 cm away. Flip: hybrid-bond DRAM face-to-face onto logic at ~1 um pitch so each compute tile talks only to the bank directly below it through thousands of vertical wires, with no PHY, no shared bus and no SerDes.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): wire length drops from cm to <50 um, ~3 pJ/bit to ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit; PHY periphery area removed from both dies.

title: Farmer's co-op grain elevator: shared toll-EUV hub for new fabs
idea: Farmers don't each own a grain elevator. A neutral co-op owns a cluster of 4-6 EUV scanners sited among several new U.S. memory fabs (start-ups, IDMs, national labs); sealed FOUP shuttles carry wafers to the hub for their EUV layers only, members pay per exposure, and capacity shares are owned like co-op stock.
why: Takes the ~$1B EUV ticket off each new entrant, so a 20k wafer/month fab can start with DUV-only capex, and lifts EUV utilization from ~70% to >90%. Risks: logistics, contamination, and ~1-2 days of queue time per pass.

title: Downhole-grade FD-SOI periphery wafer bonded under array via bitline mux
idea: Without EUV, put SAs and decoders on a 22-65 nm DUV FD-SOI wafer (the substrate downhole and space chips use for heat and radiation) and hybrid-bond it to an array wafer that holds only cells plus an 8:1 bitline select mux, matching ~0.5 um bond pitch to 30-40 nm bitlines. FD-SOI back-bias trims SA offset per mat.
why: Array die gets ~2x bits per mm2 (fact 7) and periphery moves to a cheap DUV node, removing EUV layers from periphery entirely.

title: Trusted-packaging-first US strategy: stack imported wafers domestically
idea: DoD trusted-foundry users secure supply through trusted assembly. Fund US memory OSATs that buy commodity DRAM wafers from several countries and do base-die integration, stacking, test and HBM/CXL module assembly onshore, with tariff exemptions on wafers and offtake from federal AI programs.
why: Packaging capex is ~1/10 of a DRAM fab with a 1-2 year ramp; moves the highest-value, scarcest step (HBM assembly) onshore years before a US fab could.
