idea: Inverting 'one sense amp per bitline pair': four bitline pairs charge-share simultaneously, are isolated, and hold their analog signals while a single sense amp resolves and restores them one after another in ~2 ns slots.
why: Sense-amp count -75%, freeing ~10-15% die area for a few ns of activation time; risk is signal decay and coupling during the hold.
note: Held bitline signals resolved sequentially by one SA; coupling during hold is the risk.

title: Constant-weight coding with winner-take-half rank sensing
idea: Inverting 'a reference must come from a dummy cell or twin bitline': rows store data in a constant-weight code (exactly 8 ones per 16-cell group), and a winner-take-half circuit declares the 8 highest bitlines of each group to be ones, so no reference voltage exists at all.
why: Removes reference/dummy circuitry, is immune to common-mode drift and leakage, and tolerates ~2x smaller signals for robust open-bitline 4F^2 sensing, at ~15% code overhead.
note: Constant-weight codes with rank sensing remove references; WTA circuit area and 15% overhead.

title: In/Ga-free ZnMgO:Al BEOL access transistors for stacked arrays
idea: Inverts 'oxide-TFT DRAM needs indium and gallium.' Use Mg-alloyed ZnO (band gap up to ~4 eV, Al-doped contacts) as the BEOL access channel and stack capacitor-cell tiers above the logic at <400 C.
why: Facts 2-3 and In/Ga chokepoints: the wide gap aims for leakage far below the 13 fA tail, stretching refresh toward seconds with abundant elements only.
note: Polycrystalline ZnO grain boundaries likely worsen the tail versus amorphous IGZO.

title: Dirty bulk, clean skin: metallurgical silicon substrate under thick epi
idea: Inverts 'the whole wafer must be 11N electronic grade': use upgraded-metallurgical-grade (5-6N) seed-cast mono silicon as the substrate, add a buried phosphorus/aluminum gettering layer and a carbon-doped epitaxial diffusion barrier, then grow a 10 um high-purity epitaxial skin from silane where all devices live.
why: UMG silicon needs ~15-20 kWh/kg vs ~50-70 kWh/kg for Siemens polysilicon (~3x lower embodied energy per wafer) and can come from US/Norway metallurgical plants instead of concentrated polysilicon makers.

title: Fab that breathes with the grid: buffer WIP to follow cheap power
idea: Inverts 'a fab runs flat out 24/7': size work-in-progress buffers in front of the most energy-hungry steps (epitaxy, furnaces, CVD, abatement burners, chillers) so they run hard during curtailed solar/wind hours and idle at peaks, add chilled-water thermal storage, and schedule with a cycle-time vs $/MWh co-optimizer.
why: Shifting ~30% of fab load to curtailed power cuts electricity cost ~20-30% and makes renewable-rich US regions viable fab sites.

title: Back-end oxide CMOS latches: static memory stacked over logic
idea: Inverts 'static memory must live in the silicon substrate': build cross-coupled latches from n-type amorphous ZnO and p-type SnO/Cu2O thin-film transistors in the metal stack at <350 C, several tiers high, with wide-gap leakage below 1e-18 A per device.
why: Zero refresh with standby ~1000x below silicon SRAM; abundant Zn, Sn and Cu; no substrate area or capacitor materials.
note: p-type SnO/Cu2O are leaky; the 1e-18 A standby claim holds only for n-type oxides.

title: Sixteen-fold spacer multiplication on a 1990s KrF stepper
idea: Inverts 'resolution belongs to the scanner'. Print 360 nm-pitch lines on a KrF stepper and run four rounds of sidewall-spacer transfer (LPCVD nitride/oxide spacers plus RIE), each halving pitch, to reach ~22 nm-pitch array lines with no overlay-critical steps.
why: Modern array pitch from fully depreciated litho; ~5-10x lower litho capex per dense layer (fact 4); line-edge roughness and cut layers are the limiters.

title: Dewetted metal nano-islands roughen electrodes into area
idea: Inverts 'the capacitor needs an ordered geometry'. Anneal a 5 nm sacrificial Sn film so it dewets into ~15-25 nm random islands, use them as an RIE mask to texture the poly-Si storage node into nanopillars (the 1990s hemispherical-grain trick taken ~10x further), strip, then coat with dielectric.
why: 5-10x electrode area per footprint from a furnace and an etcher (fact 1), letting thin planar-ish 180 nm-rule caps hold >20 fF.

title: Time-coded analog tensor links instead of binary symbols
idea: Invert 'link symbols are digital bits': for weights and activations each wire carries a pulse whose width/edge timing encodes a 6-8-bit value, generated by a delay line and decoded by a time-to-digital converter, accepting ~1 LSB noise that AI numerics tolerate.
why: One edge pair per value instead of up to 8 bit transitions: 3-5x fewer transitions and lower CV2 on in-package links, targeting <0.5 pJ per bit-equivalent.
note: 6-8-bit timing resolution at speed is jitter-limited.

title: Anodized-aluminum substrates with copper-filled pores replace ABF film
idea: Invert 'package dielectric must be polymer build-up film': anodize thick U.S. aluminum sheet into porous alumina whose self-ordered vertical pores are electroplated with copper to form dense vias, then pattern RDL on top.
why: Drops dependence on single-source Japanese ABF; self-forming via fields give ~1e8 vias/cm2, better thermal conduction and closer CTE match to silicon.
note: AAO interposers researched; thick AAO brittleness is the doubt.

title: Interference-lithography buses: the memory bus is a grating
idea: Invert 'interconnect needs mask-based photolithography': memory buses are thousands of identical parallel lines, so pattern them with maskless two-beam laser interference lithography (U.S.-buildable tool), then cut and connect line ends with coarse lithography.
why: Sub-micron bus pitch on interposers without masks or scanners; very low capital and fully U.S. tooling.

title: Laser decap and rebump LPDDR die mined from e-waste phones
idea: Inverts 'e-waste recycling means shredding for gold': robotic lines laser-decapsulate package-on-package stacks from recycled phones, extract the LPDDR die, re-bump and retest them, and package them for IoT, automotive and edge boards.
why: Scarce resource and supply: billions of retired phones hold exabytes of working LPDDR silicon; even 10% recovery adds meaningful low-end supply at near-zero wafer cost.

title: Balanced-code words generate their own mid-level sense reference
idea: Encode each 64-bit word as a 68-bit constant-weight code (exactly 34 ones), so the average of the word's own bitlines is exactly halfway between its decayed '1' and '0' levels. A charge-sharing copy of the word's bitlines becomes the SA reference, tracking leakage at 125 C automatically.
why: Cells can decay much further before failure: ~2-4x longer refresh at hot for 6% bit overhead (fact 3).
note: Average reference does not rescue tail cells that decay fastest.

title: Inductor ping-pong moves charge from closing to opening wordline
idea: Connect the wordline being closed to the next wordline being opened through a shared on-die or interposer inductor for one LC half-cycle, so the 3 V charge transfers almost entirely instead of being dumped to ground, then top off the remainder from the pump.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): direct charge sharing between equal capacitors recovers at most 50%, but a resonant half-cycle recovers ~80% of CV^2; with a ~3 V wordline swing, pumped wordline energy and charge-pump losses fall several-fold.

title: EHD jet-printed pillar capacitors grown upward, never etched
idea: Use multi-nozzle electrohydrodynamic jet printing to stack silver nanoparticle droplets into 0.5 um-wide, 5 um-tall pillars on each cell's storage pad, then coat them with spatial-ALD AlOx and a conformal printed counter-electrode.
why: Additive growth escapes the aspect-ratio-dependent etch limit behind the charge wall (fact 1): C=eA/d over a 0.5x5 um pillar with 8 nm AlOx is ~80 fF, ~15x today's Cs, allowing ~10x longer bitlines and far fewer sense amps per foil.
note: Additive printed pillars give large Cs but only at micron pitch; foil-scale niche.

title: Sol-gel gallium oxide printed channels give day-scale retention
idea: Inkjet or slot-die print Ga2O3 sol-gel channels (Eg ~4.8 eV), densify them by deep-UV photo-annealing below 250 C, and use them as access transistors in foil arrays with 4k-cell bitlines, since refresh traffic disappears.
why: Leakage scales as exp(-Eg/2kT), so at 4.8 eV intrinsic generation is negligible; with defect-limited off-current ~1e-21 A an 8 fF cell loses 10% only after ~days, removing refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and going beyond the IGZO already studied.
note: Printed Ga2O3 gives long retention but very low density; foil niche.

title: Inverse-opal printed electrodes multiply capacitor area twentyfold
idea: Convectively assemble 200 nm polystyrene spheres into embossed cell wells, infill electroless nickel, burn out the spheres, then coat spatial-ALD AlOx and infill a conductive-polymer counter-electrode, forming a sponge capacitor per cell.
why: Interface area per volume of an FCC inverse opal is ~2.2/r, about 2e7 per metre, so a 2 um-thick cell holds ~40x its footprint in plate area; even derated, ~20x more capacitance per um^2 with no etch (fact 1).

title: Nickel-aluminide intermetallic buried wordlines replace tungsten below 15 nanometers
idea: At sub-15 nm widths line resistivity scales with rho0*lambda (bulk resistivity x electron mean free path), not rho0, and ordered B2 NiAl has a few-nm mean free path so its size penalty is small. Fill buried-wordline trenches with Ni/Al ALD nanolaminates and anneal to NiAl, which self-passivates with Al2O3 and needs no TiN barrier.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 fluorine chemistry from DRAM's largest W use; barrier-free fill gives ~20-30% more conductor cross-section and lower wordline RC.

title: Gallium-free zinc-tin-silicon oxide channels for low-leak gain cells
idea: Oxide gain cells leak little because Eg>3 eV makes intrinsic carriers ~1e-25 cm-3 and holes immobile; mobility comes from overlapping metal ns orbitals, which Sn4+ 5s supplies as well as In3+, while Si (strong Si-O bond) takes Ga's carrier-suppressing role. Deposit amorphous Zn-Sn-Si-O by ALD as read and write channels.
why: Removes gallium (China ~98%, export-controlled) and indium from IGZO gain-cell roadmaps while keeping sub-aA off-current; Zn and Si are abundant and US-sourced.

title: One ALD chemistry family builds every layer of the cell
idea: First principle: tool count scales with the number of distinct materials in the flow. Make the channel (IGZO), electrodes (degenerate In2O3:H/ITO), dielectric (Ga2O3/HfO2 laminate) and passivation from one In/Ga/Zn/Hf precursor set in one multi-station ALD cluster, changing only cycle ratios and oxidant.
why: Capital and tool set: ~5 tool types collapse into one platform, with a simpler U.S. tool supply chain.

title: Thermoplastic, solvent-release packages make DRAM dies recoverable
idea: First principle: epoxy molding compound is a thermoset that cannot be undone, so it traps the die forever. Package DRAM in a high-Tg thermoplastic (e.g., liquid-crystal polymer) with a solvent-releasable underfill, so a low-temperature solvent bath frees bare, intact dies for retest and redeployment.
why: Recyclability: die-level reuse plus gold/copper recovery; feeds reverse-fab supply.

title: Zinc-silicon-oxide BEOL gain cells replace IGZO without indium or gallium
idea: Leakage physics depends on bandgap and trap density, not on indium: amorphous Zn-Si-O (~3.5 eV gap, with Si suppressing oxygen vacancies the way Ga does in IGZO) can give 2T0C gain cells with sub-1e-18 A off-current. Build them in the BEOL of any U.S. CMOS foundry, using only Zn, Si and O.
why: Refresh wall and scarce resource: In/Ga-free oxide memory with >100 s retention cuts refresh energy ~1000x and turns every logic fab into a potential memory fab.
note: Zn-Si-O TFTs exist; mobility and off-current at gain-cell scale unproven.

title: Seashell nacre: titania nanosheets self-stack into a k~125 dielectric
idea: Stimulus 'nacre' (layered bricks of mineral) -> exfoliate Ti0.87O2 nanosheets in water with tetrabutylammonium hydroxide and deposit them layer by layer by Langmuir-Blodgett at room temperature, giving a ~5 nm dielectric with k~125 and low leakage; no plasma, no fluorinated surfactants.
why: k~125 exceeds the k~70 needed (fact 1), letting capacitor AR fall to ~40:1; room-temperature aqueous deposition lowers tool capex (fact 4).

title: Seashell roar: chopped, dithered comparator voting senses sub-offset signals
idea: A seashell turns random noise into a perceptible 'ocean': use stochastic resonance. After charge sharing, sample the bitline onto a small isolated cap, then fire a minimum-size comparator 8 times against a reference dithered by an on-die junction-noise source, swapping inputs on alternate firings (chopping) to cancel offset, and majority-vote in a 3-bit counter before restore.
why: Sense-amp area: minimum-size comparators with ~30 mV offset can resolve ~10 mV signals statistically, so SA transistors shrink ~4x in area (SA strips are a large share of the ~49% periphery), at a cost of ~2-3 ns latency.
note: Chopping plus majority voting resolves sub-offset signals; latency and sampling-cap charge loss.

title: Spider web: MOF cartridges catch and recycle fluorocarbon etch gases
idea: Stimulus 'spider web' (a net tuned to its prey) -> put metal-organic-framework adsorbent beds, pore-tuned to C4F8, C4F6, NF3 and SF6, on etch exhausts instead of burn-box abatement; temperature-swing regenerate, purify and return captured gas to cylinders.
why: Fluorocarbons are PFAS-classified, high-GWP (NF3 ~17,000) and few-supplier; 70-90% recapture cuts purchases and emissions together.

title: Pearl: one seeded ferroelectric grain per cell kills variability
idea: Random stimulus 'pearl' (one crystal grows around one seed) -> a self-aligned nucleation seed (a ZrO2 or TiN facet) is planted at the bottom of each ferroelectric capacitor, so the HZO crystallizes as a single orthorhombic grain per cell instead of random multigrain.
why: Non-volatile FeRAM is currently sized for grain-induced variation of Pr and Ec. Single-grain cells could shrink 2-3x at the same litho (relaxed DUV instead of EUV) and cut wake-up and fatigue spread.

title: Tetris: memory-controller line compaction collapses fragmented heaps
idea: Like Tetris rows clearing once full, a controller-side engine migrates live 64 B lines out of sparsely occupied pages into dense pages during idle cycles, tracked by an SRAM-cached line-remap table so software pointers never change; fully emptied pages are handed back to the OS.
why: Allocator fragmentation strands 15-40% of heap DRAM in long-running services and Python/AI runtimes; reclaiming half of it is ~1.1-1.25x capacity.

title: Zipper merge: approximate cross-request KV block deduplication
idea: Two lanes zip into one: hash every 16-token KV block with locality-sensitive hashing; when a new block lies within epsilon of a canonical block from any request (same RAG passage at a different offset, near-identical prompts), store a pointer plus a sparse int4 residual, applying a RoPE offset correction at read.
why: Exact prefix sharing misses non-prefix repeats; in RAG/agent fleets 30-70% of KV is near-duplicate, giving 2-4x KV capacity relief.

title: Fridge magnet: magnetic self-alignment for low-cost chiplet assembly
idea: Like a fridge magnet snapping into place: dies get patterned Ni/Co pads and are dropped onto a substrate over a patterned magnet fixture that pulls each die to sub-micron alignment, then bonded in a batch oven, with no $5M placement tool.
why: Packaging capital intensity; fine-pitch memory-logic assembly on cheap equipment and a U.S.-friendly assembly route.

title: Junkyard: harvest retired-phone LPDDR into CXL inference memory modules
idea: Random stimulus 'junkyard' -> phones are memory scrap heaps. Automated desoldering lines at e-waste recyclers pull LPDDR4X/5 packages from ~0.5-1B retired phones a year, test and reball them onto carrier boards behind a CXL controller as KV-cache/far-memory for inference racks.
why: Raises usable supply with near-zero fab capex: ~700M phones x 6 GB x 30% recovered x 80% pass is roughly 1 EB/yr, a few % of world DRAM bits, and it is US-local scarce-resource-free supply.

title: Gold assay: karat-graded salvage DRAM with per-row refresh maps
idea: Random stimulus 'gold assay' -> grade by purity, price by karat. Decommissioned server DIMMs are assayed with a per-row retention histogram, graded (e.g. 18k/14k/10k), and the grade's row map is loaded into a CXL expander that refreshes weak rows often and strong rows rarely.
why: Extends second-life DRAM to modules that fail uniform refresh, raising reuse yield from maybe ~60% to ~90% and cutting their refresh energy 50-70%.
note: RAIDR-style per-row refresh on salvage; VRT makes profiles drift.

title: Parametric varactor amplification boosts bitline voltage after charge sharing
idea: Box: stacked cap x Si access x parametric amplification x MOS-varactor bitline segments x bulk Si x standard. After the cell shares charge onto the bitline, a pump pulse drives MOS varactors on the bitline pair into depletion, shrinking capacitance so V = Q/C and the differential rise 3-5x before the latch fires: low-noise gain from capacitance modulation.
why: 3-5x more signal without more Cs: shrink the capacitor or lengthen bitlines.
note: MOS varactor capacitance pumping raises signal, but added varactor capacitance erodes net gain.

title: Multi-row OR-sensing reads sparse zero blocks in one activation
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x threshold-OR sensing x 8-wordline simultaneous activation x bulk Si x standard. For sparse activations and pruned weights, eight rows open at once and the SA only asks whether any charge is present (group testing); all-zero groups are confirmed with one sense instead of eight, and the extra multi-row disturb (<1%) is tolerated.
why: Sense energy and overfetch for sparse data cut up to 8x, spending the 1% budget on multi-row disturb.
note: OR-sensing of 8 rows to confirm zero blocks; true/anti-cell encoding and disturb complicate it.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching carves single-crystal VCT pillar forests
idea: [Box: MIM charge | single-crystal Si VCT | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | DSA-patterned Pt/Au catalyst mesh + HF/H2O2 MacEtch] A perforated noble-metal mesh sinks into Si in HF/H2O2 and leaves straight, plasma-damage-free 20 nm pillars at AR >50, which become the vertical channels.
why: No EUV (fact 4) and leakage tail (fact 3): damage-free sidewalls trim the trap-assisted leakage tail, and wet tools cost far less than plasma etch.

title: Germanium-free 3D DRAM using porosified p+ silicon sacrificial tiers
idea: Box [lateral cap | lateral Si access per tier | voltage SA | 3D stacked tiers | CZ Si | all-Si epi + electrochemical porosification]: grow alternating p++ (B 1e20) and lightly doped Si epi tiers instead of Si/SiGe, then after slit etch anodize only the p++ layers into porous Si and remove them laterally, leaving suspended single-crystal channels.
why: Removes germane/Ge (China dominates refined Ge, export-licensed since 2023) from 3D DRAM, and avoids the SiGe strain-relaxation cap on tier count so >100 tiers become possible.
note: Boron diffusion from 1e20 tiers and lateral anodization contact through slits are the doubts.

title: ALD alumina nano-topcoat replaces fluorinated immersion-litho topcoats
idea: Box [any | any | any | any | Si | ArF immersion]: after resist coat, grow 2-3 nm of 60 C ALD Al2O3 from TMA/H2O as the leach barrier, cap it with a fluorine-free hydrocarbon monolayer for water receding angle, and let the TMAH developer dissolve it.
why: PFAS: immersion topcoats and topcoat-free additives are fluorinated and face EU restriction; removes fluorinated chemistry from ~10-15 immersion layers per DRAM flow.

title: Beaker-grown anodic Nb/Ta/Hf oxide as the capacitor dielectric
idea: Box: barrier-type anodic oxide charge x EBL-patterned IGZO access x standard sensing x 2D test array x Si x room-temperature electrochemical anodization of a sputtered valve metal. The bottom electrode's surface is anodized at ~1.5-2 nm/V into a dense dielectric (Nb2O5 k~40, Ta2O5 k~25) whose thickness is set by a voltage and whose pinholes self-heal during growth.
why: Removes the ALD tool from the dielectric step and self-heals defects for yield; buildable with a potentiostat and wet bench; risk is anodic-oxide leakage below 5 nm and contacting the electrode during anodization.

title: Spin-coated, UV-cured indium-zinc oxide access transistors in BEOL
idea: Box: MIM charge x solution-processed InZnO TFT x voltage sense amp x BEOL x Si or glass x sol-gel spin coating plus deep-UV photo-annealing below 250 C. A nitrate precursor coats the topography and 185/254 nm UV generates ozone and radicals that condense the oxide network, reaching 5-20 cm2/Vs with no vacuum deposition.
why: Removes sputter/ALD clusters from the access-device module (capital); uses only a spin coater and UV lamp; risk is trap density widening the leakage tail and thickness control in 3D topography.

title: Glancing-angle-deposited nanohelix electrodes multiply capacitor area, maskless
idea: Box: MIM charge on a 3D nanocolumn electrode x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x glancing-angle e-beam evaporation at ~85 degrees with substrate rotation. Self-shadowing grows isolated TiN or Ru columns or helices of set height on EBL-seeded storage pads, then ALD dielectric and top electrode coat them for 5-20x area with no high-AR etch.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) by additive self-shadowing instead of etching; needs only an evaporator with a motorized stage; risk is column porosity raising leakage and fill conformality.

title: Direct nanoimprint of sol-gel high-k: pattern the dielectric itself
idea: Box: imprinted metal-oxide charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x thermal imprint of a ZrO2/HfO2 sol-gel with a PDMS replica of an EBL master. The functional film acts as the resist: imprinting forms corrugated 3D capacitor shapes and a cure converts it to oxide, deleting the resist-etch-strip sequence.
why: Collapses ~4 steps per layer and avoids high-AR plasma etch for capacitor area enhancement using a university imprint press; risk is shrinkage cracking and leakage of solution-derived oxide.

title: Bosch scallop-engineered corrugated capacitor walls double area
idea: Box: Si trench charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x time-multiplexed DRIE with deliberately deep, tuned scallops. Etch/passivation cycle times are set to cut 30-50 nm periodic corrugations, then conformal ALD TiN/high-k/TiN coats them, giving a fixed-depth trench ~1.5-2.5x sidewall area from a recipe timing parameter.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) at lower AR as a recipe-only change on any DRIE; risk is field crowding at corrugation tips raising leakage and scaling scallops below 50 nm holes.
note: Works for large-pitch Si trench caps; 30-50 nm scallops can't fit sub-50 nm holes.

title: Pulse-position DRAM I/O encodes three bits per edge
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x time-to-digital receiver x pulse-position-modulated TSV and interposer lanes x Si x standard. Each lane sends one edge per unit interval whose position among eight timing slots encodes 3 bits, so wires toggle 3x less often for the same data.
why: I/O energy (fact 5): ~2-3x lower switching energy per bit at modest TDC area cost.

title: Laser-forward-transferred copper redistribution on glass, no plating bath
idea: Box: LPDDR dies x standard x standard x fan-out RDL x glass panel x laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) of Cu nanoparticle ink plus laser sintering. 8-15 um RDL lines are written digitally from a donor ribbon and sintered in place, replacing resist coat/develop, seed sputter, electroplating, strip and etch and the rinse after each.
why: Water: semi-additive plating lines use hundreds of litres per panel; dry digital additive writing cuts >10x and maskless writing removes photomasks.

title: Copper wires ultrasonically embedded in thermoplastic form the interposer
idea: Box: LPDDR or HBM-lite x standard x standard x wire-scribed routing x hot-embossed thermoplastic carrier x ultrasonic embedding of 15 um insulated Cu wire. A CNC head lays and embeds insulated wires into the polymer like a multiwire board, with laser-ablated ends forming pads: no etch, no plating, no rinse.
why: Water: substrate fabrication is packaging's main water user; wire scribing is dry, >10x less, and yields an ultra-cheap carrier for memory-dense packages.

title: Po: memory made of molasses — thermally selected glassy-electrolyte crossbar
idea: Po: memory made of molasses. Extracted: print a crossbar of polymer electrolyte that is glassy (ions frozen) at operating temperature but softens above Tg; a coincident current pulse heats only the selected crossing above Tg so ions drift to set its conductance, then it re-freezes, making heat the selector.
why: Transistorless, solution-printed stacked layers aim at a 100x cost cut. Trade-offs: us thermal writes, thermal crosstalk, lower endurance.
note: Heat as selector; us thermal writes and low endurance keep it out of DRAM class.

title: Lazy refresh with LDPC resurrection across row groups
idea: Po: let bits die, then resurrect them. Refresh 8x less often and protect each group of 8 rows with a soft-decision LDPC code whose parity sits in a spare row; sense amps report a soft confidence level, and the decoder rewrites corrected data on read, treating decay as a noisy channel.
why: Fact 3: an 8x longer interval cuts refresh energy ~85% and returns 10-20% bandwidth for ~6% capacity overhead.

title: Po: memory trims its own readers via dummy cells
idea: Po: memory that calibrates the circuits that read it. At power-up each SA's offset is measured by repeatedly sensing balanced bitlines, and a correction charge is written into a dedicated dummy cell on that bitline pair; before every sense the dummy wordline fires and pre-biases the bitline by exactly that offset, refreshed alongside normal refresh.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): cancels ~80% of SA Vt mismatch, so SA devices can be ~3x smaller or Cs ~30% lower; trim storage costs one row per subarray instead of fuses or analog trim DACs.
note: Offset storage as dummy-cell charge; trim precision limited by dummy-cell Cs variation and leakage.

title: Let bits decay and recover them with cross-tier erasure codes
idea: Po: memory that is allowed to rot. Disable refresh and stripe each 64 B line across 12 tiers with an 8+4 Reed-Solomon erasure code plus weak-cell location maps from test, so the retention tail is corrected at read while the median cell holds data for minutes, longer than most working sets live.
why: Refresh zero by converting the leakage tail into a coding problem; 50% parity overhead is offset by cheap tiers and removed refresh periphery.
note: Cross-tier erasure codes for retention errors; 50% parity offsets refresh savings.

title: Po the chuck is a hairbrush: gas-free nanofiber thermal contact
idea: Po: 'the wafer is cooled by a hairbrush, not a gas.' Extracted: replace helium backside gas in electrostatic chucks with a dense, vertically aligned boron-nitride-nanotube or carbon-nanotube forest capped with a thin alumina skin, whose millions of compliant tips conduct heat under electrostatic clamping as well as ~10 Torr of helium.
why: Removes backside-cooling helium, one of a fab's largest helium uses, from etch, implant and CVD tools; zero per-wafer helium on those steps.

title: Po the crystal draws the pattern: facet-defined sub-litho fins
idea: Po: 'the crystal is the lithographer.' Extracted: on (110) silicon, TMAH wet etch stops on vertical {111} planes, so a coarse 40 nm DUV pattern yields atomically flat vertical walls; self-limiting oxidation then thins fins to 8-10 nm, giving access-transistor fins and buried-wordline trenches without EUV.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint (5-7 EUV layers): replaces 2-3 EUV layers with DUV plus wet chemistry, and the wet etch avoids fluorinated plasma gases.

title: Wet crystal-plane etch carves vertical trenches in (110) silicon
idea: Po: the crystal is the mask. On (110) wafers, align line-type array features to <112> so KOH/TMAH etching stops on vertical {111} planes, giving atomically smooth slits with AR >200:1 in a wet bench for trench capacitors or line-type 3D DRAM slits.
why: Etch capex and capacitor AR (fact 1): extreme aspect ratio at near-zero tool cost, no bowing.

title: Client-carried KV cache: the user's device holds the server's memory
idea: Po: the user remembers the conversation, not the server. Between turns the server quantizes, entropy-codes, encrypts and MACs a session's KV cache and ships it to the user's phone/laptop/browser storage; the next request uploads it back, so the server holds zero KV for idle sessions.
why: Idle chat/agent sessions dominate KV residency; parking KV on billions of client devices cuts server DRAM/HBM for KV 5-20x, practical for contexts up to ~32k tokens on modern links.

title: Single-metal-layer bridge enabled by mirrored crossing-free ballouts
idea: Po: an interposer with only one wiring layer. Co-design HBM and GPU bump maps as mirror images so every connection routes without crossings, then build the bridge die with just one patterned 1 um copper layer in a mature fab.
why: Cuts bridge or interposer masks from 4-6 to one, slashing 2.5D cost and letting U.S. mature fabs make the parts.

title: Liquid-metal microwell interconnects that never freeze
idea: Po: the solder stays liquid forever. One mask patterns microwells in a polymer layer, a gallium alloy fills them by squeegee, and the mating die's pads dip into the wells, giving fine-pitch joints that absorb thermal mismatch and can be reworked.
why: Removes solder-fatigue and warpage yield loss in large HBM packages and allows reuse of stacks; no reflow heat on DRAM.
note: Ga alloys attack Cu/Al and migrate; long-term reliability is the doubt.

title: Refresh-by-relocation: every refresh moves data to a new row
idea: Po: data runs away from the hammer. Instead of restoring a row in place, refresh copies it (RowClone-style, inside the subarray) to a free spare row and updates a small in-DRAM indirection table, so each logical row wanders across physical rows every window and no victim keeps the same neighbors for long.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): an aggressor's disturbance is spread over many short-lived residents; effective threshold x8-16 with ~1-2% spare rows.

title: Activation-rate billing makes row hammer an economic problem
idea: Po: hammering is legal but expensive. Cloud hypervisors meter each VM's per-row activation density from memory-controller counters, bill activation bursts beyond a budget, and throttle or live-migrate tenants whose activation pattern looks adversarial.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) in shared clouds: lowers reliance on costly in-DRAM mitigation, letting cheaper low-threshold dies be deployed safely.
note: Per-row activation counts are not exposed by controllers today.

title: Diagonal codeword interleaving makes row hammer statistically harmless
idea: Po: let the rows flip. Each codeword's bits are spread diagonally across 16-32 physical rows in several subarrays, so a fully hammered victim row contributes at most 1/16 of any codeword's errors; with 1%-capable codes an attacker must flip dozens of bits in many rows at once.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): effective threshold x10-100 with no per-row counters; mitigation logic area largely removed.
note: Spreading codewords over 16-32 rows multiplies activations per access; energy cost undercuts the gain.

title: Die-level DRAM harvesting from retired server DIMMs
idea: Po: chips are fruit you can pick twice. Retired hyperscaler DIMMs are depackaged at die level (laser ablation of mold compound plus selective wet etch of wires/RDL), dies are re-probed and re-binned as known-good-die, then restacked into new 4-8-high fan-out packages with fresh SPD and ECC profiles.
why: Turns millions of retired DDR4/early-DDR5 modules a year into supply with near-zero wafer capex; harvest cost per bit ~20-30% of new silicon if post-decap die yield >70%; attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability (harvest plants can be domestic).
note: Decap and re-stack retired dies; post-decap pad damage and yield set economics vs reusing whole modules.

title: GaN polarization well that holds charge behind 3.4 eV walls
idea: Worsen: store charge in silicon, whose 1.1 eV gap invites thermal leakage. Flip: use a GaN-on-Si power-foundry shuttle (~$80k per run) to build AlGaN/GaN cells whose built-in polarization well stores electrons behind wide-bandgap barriers, aiming to show ~1000x lower leakage within 24 months.
why: Refresh (fact 3): hours of retention, using existing US and allied GaN fabs instead of DRAM fabs.
note: Cheap GaN shuttles enable demo, but density and CMOS integration are poor.

title: Co-aging reference cell that leaks in lockstep with data
idea: Worse: compare every leaking cell against a fixed VDD/2 reference so margin shrinks every millisecond. Flip: each row carries a few reference cells written to a half level at the same instant as the data, through identical access transistors, so the reference droops with the data and the sense amp compares against a co-aged threshold.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): most '1' margin loss is common-mode droop; tracking it could stretch retention 2-4x and cut refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~50-75%.
note: Tracks common-mode droop, but the refresh-setting tail cells are outliers.

title: Electrohydrodynamic-jet printed nano-copper microbumps for memory stacking
idea: Worse: run lithography, seed, plating and etch steps to form every microbump. Flip: EHD-jet-print copper nanoparticle pillars at ~10 um pitch directly onto pads and sinter them in a maskless additive bumping step.
why: HBM cost and capital (fact 6): removes bump masks and plating lines, with denser I/O at lower capex.

title: Indium-free MgZnO wide-gap channel for gain-cell DRAM
idea: Worsen: build every next-generation oxide gain cell from indium and gallium that are refined mostly in China and subject to export controls. Flip: use amorphous Al-doped MgZnO deposited by spatial ALD as the channel. Its bandgap (~3.8-4.2 eV) is wider than IGZO's (~3.2 eV), which suppresses off-state leakage further.
why: In/Ga chokepoint and refresh energy: all-abundant elements with a U.S. supply. Longer retention could cut refresh ~10x if mobility of ~5-15 cm2/Vs is enough.

title: Thermally reversible Diels-Alder adhesive lets HBM stacks be unstacked
idea: Worsen: lock HBM dies together with permanent underfill and Cu-Cu bonds, so one bad die scraps the whole 12-high stack. Flip: bond the core dies with a Diels-Alder polymer underlayer and low-melting Sn-Bi microbumps that release at ~150 C, so a failed die can be heated out and replaced and the stack rebonded.
why: HBM yield loss (20-30%) and the wafer-area tax: recovering 11 good dies per failed stack could lift effective HBM output ~15-25%.

title: Vitrimer mold compound lets packages reflow open for die harvest
idea: Worsen: encapsulate dies in thermoset epoxy that can only be burned or acid-dissolved. Flip: mold with a silica-filled vitrimer whose exchangeable covalent bonds soften at ~200 C, so packages can be reflowed open, dies lifted out intact and the compound remolded.
why: Die reuse and package material recovery: intact known-good dies could be re-packaged at a fraction of the cost of new silicon.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 100:1 capacitor holes wet
idea: Worse: push plasma etch to AR 115:1, with ever slower rates, bowing and twisting. Flip: pattern a perforated catalytic metal mesh and let metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2 sink the catalyst straight down at room temperature. This gives bow-free holes beyond 100:1 on a wet bench, followed by catalyst strip and clean.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus capital: replaces the costliest high-AR etch chamber-hours with wet benches and makes AR~115 (~1.5x Cs) reachable.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing makes mask-free personalization layers on glass
idea: Worse: buy a new mask set for every memory variant. Flip: on standard glass-panel memory arrays, write the variable layers (wordline strapping, redundancy routing, I/O fan-out) with multi-nozzle e-jet printing of nanoparticle inks at ~100 nm, so one array panel serves many products.
why: Masks/capital: zero mask cost per variant makes low-volume specialty memory viable.

title: Idle consumer RAM leased as an erasure-coded remote cache
idea: Worsen: let a billion PCs sit with gigabytes of unused RAM. Flip: a client leases idle consumer RAM to a cloud remote-memory service, striping cache data with erasure codes across many homes so it survives churn, and pays owners per GB-hour.
why: Cost: idle RAM has near-zero marginal cost, giving 100x+ cheaper cache GB; trades latency (ms), privacy engineering and churn.

title: Cryo-salvage: retention-reject dies run refresh-free in 77 K pods
idea: Worse: scrap dies that fail retention at 85 C. Flip: route them into liquid-nitrogen memory pods where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse by many orders, so cells hold data for days and refresh is switched off entirely.
why: Zero refresh power; turns a few percent of scrap output into supply, with cooling cost amortized over large pooled memory.

title: Well-digger farmer lets chemistry dig: metal-assisted wet etch capacitor holes
idea: The farmer digs wells with water, not drills. Put a patterned Au/Pt catalyst mesh on silicon and immerse it in HF/H2O2: the silicon under the metal dissolves straight down, giving 100-200:1 smooth holes at room temperature in a beaker. ALD then lines them into trench capacitors.
why: Reaches Fact 1's AR ~115 without $50M high-AR plasma etchers, and a 10-person team can run it on a wet bench.
note: MacEtch reaches high AR cheaply, but Au/Pt catalyst contamination creates deep traps that worsen leakage.

title: Astronomer's bucket brigade: CCD charge chains instead of capacitor cells
idea: An astronomer stores charge in CCD potential wells and reads single electrons at one output amplifier. Build 8-stage buried-channel charge-coupled chains in a 22-40 nm image-sensor foundry, via MPW. Each bit is ~100 electrons under one gate with no contact or capacitor, and a floating-diffusion amplifier serves every 8 bits.
why: Removes capacitor, cell contacts and most sense amps. CCD dark current gives seconds of retention (Facts 1, 3, 7), and the whole thing is made in a US/Israel CIS foundry with a fabless 10-person team.

title: Jeweler's plating bath: electroless cobalt wordline fill replaces tungsten
idea: The jeweler grows metal from a bath. Activate the lateral wordline cavities of a 3D stack with a Pd seed and fill them bottom-up with electroless Co-B or Ru at <=70C on a ~$100k wet bench.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and the $5M CVD-W chamber from array metallization. A 10-person team can qualify the bath chemistry.
note: Bottom-up electroless fill of deep lateral cavities is transport-limited.

title: Vacuum-world alien clamps wafers on carbon bristles, no gas
idea: Persona: an alien from an airless world has never used gas to move heat. Coat the chuck with a vertically aligned carbon-nanotube or graphite-flake micro-bristle carpet capped with 20 nm AlN. Electrostatic clamping then presses the wafer into thousands of compliant solid contacts per mm2, which conduct ~1-5 kW/m2K with no backside gas.
why: Eliminates helium backside gas and its plumbing entirely, and removes backside-gas arcing as a failure mode.
note: Particle shedding and conductance at ESC pressures.

title: Painter's Prussian blue pigment becomes a non-volatile ionic memory
idea: Persona: a painter whose Prussian blue (iron hexacyanoferrate) is also a sodium-ion battery cathode. Build a three-terminal ECRAM in which gate pulses shuttle Na+ between a Prussian-white reservoir and a Prussian-blue channel, setting its conductance. Read is separate from write and non-destructive.
why: Non-volatile and lithium-free, made of Fe, C, N and Na. The non-destructive read avoids DRAM's destructive read (fact 8).
note: Ion shuttling is slow with limited endurance; not DRAM-class working memory.

title: Child's toothpaste squeeze: liquid-metal-printed atomically thin oxide channels
idea: A child squeezes toothpaste onto glass. Touch a droplet of low-melting In-Sn or gallium alloy (<160 C) to the wafer and wipe: its self-limiting 1-3 nm oxide skin transfers as a continuous InOx or Ga2O3 channel sheet with no vacuum sputter tool, and a <=300 C anneal sets carrier density.
why: Makes ultra-thin, low-leakage oxide channels for gain cells at ~1% of sputter-tool cost, and thinner channels improve off-state. High risk: uniformity at 300 mm, and metal-droplet residue.

title: Battery chemist: room-temperature electrochemical ALD electrodes in capacitor holes
idea: A battery chemist grows metal one atomic layer at a time. Use electrochemical ALD: deposit an underpotential monolayer (Cu or Pb), galvanically swap it for Pt or Ru, and repeat, so electrodes grow conformally in 200:1 capacitor holes from aqueous solution at room temperature.
why: Gives conformal electrodes without vacuum ALD chambers (~$4M vs ~$0.5M electrochemical cell), enabling deeper capacitors at lower capex. High risk: minutes per nm, and uneven potential deep in holes.
note: Potential drop deep in holes and seeding on oxides are risks.

title: Jazz musician plays by ear: self-timed delay-insensitive memory link
idea: A jazz band follows the music, not a metronome: replace the clocked, trained HBM/LPDDR interface with a quasi-delay-insensitive encoding (1-of-4 with acknowledge) whose timing is correct at any temperature, voltage or ageing state, so no retraining is ever needed.
why: Removes timing margin wasted on worst-case 125 C and end-of-life drift, about 20-30% of the link's cycle budget, and skips periodic recalibration stalls over 10 years.

title: Farmer's companion planting: cluster hot rows so neighbors self-refresh
idea: A farmer plants crops that protect each other: the OS or hypervisor uses per-page activation counters to put frequently activated pages in physically adjacent rows, because each activation restores a row's own charge; hot rows then hammer only other hot rows that are constantly restored, and rarely touched data is kept out of hot neighborhoods.
why: Fact 9 row hammer: removes most vulnerable aggressor-victim pairs without TRR logic or extra refreshes; matters most once thresholds fall below 1k activations.

title: Old radio repairman: self-clearing printed electrodes isolate capacitor shorts
idea: Old metallized-film capacitors heal themselves: storage-capacitor top electrodes are printed as ultrathin (~20 nm) metal films, and a one-time clearing pulse at test vaporizes the electrode around any pinhole short in the printed dielectric, isolating it with negligible capacitance loss instead of killing the cell or the whole line.
why: Dielectric pinholes are the main shorting defect in printed high-k capacitors; self-clearing turns hard shorts into ~1% capacitance loss and allows thinner, higher-capacitance printed dielectrics.

title: Stacked antiferroelectric staircase capacitor stores three charge levels
idea: Downlink-limited imaging satellites value capacity per gram; the capacitor dielectric becomes a bilayer of two antiferroelectric films with different switching fields (ZrO2 and Hf-doped ZrO2), yielding a staircase charge-voltage curve with three flat plateaus, so each cell holds 1.58 bits with wide margins. The only added mask restores the old dielectric for periphery decoupling capacitors.
why: ~1.5x bits per pillar (density, cost per bit); plateaus give better multi-level margins than linear analog levels.
note: Hysteretic plateaus complicate charge-share multi-level reads.

title: Spacecraft residue-number codes for error-tolerant numeric storage
idea: Fault-tolerant spacecraft arithmetic used redundant residue number systems. Store integers and quantized weights as residues modulo small coprimes plus two redundant moduli in rows running at 1% BER; a corrupted residue is located and corrected via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and add/multiply run on residues without decoding.
why: Facts 3 and 5: refresh drops to the 1% quantile and the same redundancy protects in-memory arithmetic; ~25-35% overhead, competitive with ECC because compute stays carry-free.
note: At 1% BER, two redundant residues miss multi-residue errors too often.

title: Skipper-CCD repeated non-destructive sampling of gain-cell charge
idea: Borrowed from dark-matter Skipper CCDs that measure one charge packet hundreds of times: a gain cell's storage node gates a floating-gate sense transistor that a column-parallel integrator samples 16-64 times without disturbing the charge, averaging noise down by sqrt(N). Cells holding only ~200-500 electrons (0.03-0.08 fF) become reliably readable.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): required storage charge drops 10-50x, freeing planar or capacitor-less cells from 60-75:1 pillars; cost is ~5-15 ns extra read latency.

title: Lock-in detection of gain-cell current via modulated read wordline
idea: Gravitational-wave and lock-in instruments pull nanovolt signals out of 1/f noise by modulation; the read wordline is toggled at ~2 GHz for 8-10 cycles and the sense amp synchronously demodulates the bitline current with a mixer-integrator, so static offset and 1/f noise of the periphery cancel. Gain cells with read currents of only ~100 nA become sensible.
why: Lets weak, ultra-low-leakage gain cells (refresh-light, fact 3) work without big read transistors; SA offset requirement relaxed ~5x.

title: Voltage-stacked mats recycle bitline charge through series domains
idea: Space and implant power systems stack loads in series: two mats sit between 2 V and ground with a 1 V mid-rail, so charge that discharges the upper mat's bitlines then charges the lower mat's. A scheduler pairs activations to keep the stack balanced.
why: Bitline energy drawn from the supply roughly halved (fact 10), with simpler regulators and only DUV circuitry.

title: Hearing-aid origami: fold one thinned DRAM strip into eight-high stack
idea: Hearing aids fit electronics by folding flex circuits; thin a strip of 8 DRAM die segments to ~10 um so the silicon flexes, pattern polymer-copper hinge interconnects between segments, and fold it accordion-style into a stack bonded with thin adhesive. The fold edges carry hundreds of wires per mm and replace TSVs for capacity-oriented stacks.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV keep-out area and TSV yield loss (20-30%) removed, and stacking becomes a back-end assembly step.

title: Transient-implant chemistry: cleavable-crosslink underfill frees good dies from bad stacks
idea: Biodegradable implant electronics are designed to come apart on cue. Formulate stack underfill and mold compound with acid-cleavable acetal/ketal crosslinks that survive reflow but dissolve in a mild acid bath, so a stack with one bad die is taken apart and its good dies are re-stacked. Test bond strength, warpage and debond in a university packaging lab.
why: HBM stack yield loss (fact 6: 20-30%) throws away fully processed good dies; reclaiming them cuts wafer starts and all materials per good stack ~10-20%.

title: Cryogenic-etch silicon mold builds capacitor holes without fluorocarbon gases
idea: Extreme-cold etching (-110 C SF6/O2 DRIE) carves 50:1+ holes in silicon behind an SiOxFy passivation that evaporates on warm-up, with no C4F6/C4F8 polymer. Replace the oxide capacitor mold with amorphous Si, etch the holes cryogenically in a university ICP tool, deposit TiN/ZrO2/TiN, then strip the Si mold with XeF2 vapor behind a SiN support lattice.
why: Removes PFAS-class, high-GWP fluorocarbon gases from DRAM's highest-AR step (fact 1) and uses faster, cheaper Si etching.

title: Spacecraft thermal straps: gasless nanotube chucks remove helium backside cooling
idea: Spacecraft move heat across vacuum joints with compliant metallic and CNT interfaces. Grow a vertically aligned CNT or Cu-nanowire forest on the chuck surface (university CVD or electroplating) so electrostatic clamping alone gives >2000 W/m2-K contact conductance without backside gas, and test particle shedding.
why: Removes helium from etch and deposition chucks entirely (Qatar risk) and simplifies chuck gas hardware.

title: Photo-patternable metal-oxo films become the cell dielectric, no etch
idea: Extreme user: $1 printed-electronics IoT, where photo-curable sol-gel oxides are routine. Spin a Hf/Zr oxo-cluster film with carboxylate ligands, expose it so exposed areas crosslink, develop in a non-fluorinated solvent and anneal it into the final high-k dielectric: no resist, no PAG, no etch.
why: Process steps: collapses coat/expose/etch/strip into coat/expose/develop for dielectric layers (~4 fewer steps per layer) and removes PFAS photoacid generators.
note: Spin-on films cannot coat 3D holes; film quality vs ALD.

title: Self-unzipping polyphthalaldehyde resist enables dry, PAG-free development
idea: Extreme user: thermal-scanning-probe nanolithography, which writes polyphthalaldehyde by local unzipping. Use PPA as a high-resolution resist that depolymerizes to volatile monomer under exposure-triggered heat or weak non-fluorinated acid, so it develops by evaporation with no solvent or developer.
why: PFAS/process: removes PFAS photoacid generators and wet develop/rinse (no pattern collapse at high AR), ~3 fewer steps per litho layer.

title: Lensless displacement-Talbot printing of cell arrays with metal-oxo resist
idea: Extreme user: an EUV-less regional fab. Self-image a single cheap grating mask onto the wafer by displacement-Talbot proximity printing at 193 nm, which halves the pitch with no projection lens, into a fluorine-free tin/hafnium-oxo resist.
why: Litho capital: a ~$5M tool prints periodic DRAM array layers in place of ~$200M EUV exposures; no PFAS photoacid generators.
note: 193 nm DTL minimum period ~100 nm; still needs multipatterning for DRAM pitch.

title: Pacemaker compressive sensing: store random projections, not samples
idea: From microwatt implants that store ECG as sparse projections: sensor and telemetry streams are written to memory as compressive-sensing measurements (random +/-1 projections computed in the NIC), and a sparse-recovery engine reconstructs a window only when it is actually queried.
why: Sparse signals (vibration, network flows, sensor feeds) need 4-10x fewer measurements than samples and most stored windows are never read, so buffering DRAM drops 4-10x.
note: Niche sensor workloads.

title: Bee-brain superposition: hyperdimensional associative storage for approximate lookups
idea: From insects that store rich associations in about a million neurons: many key-value pairs are bundled into one hyperdimensional vector by binding (XOR and permutation) and superposition; lookups unbind and clean up against a small codebook, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: For approximate caches, feature stores and candidate sets, superposition packs 5-20 associations per slot, cutting DRAM 3-10x where exactness is not required.

title: One-dollar MCU lesson: SRAM-only microservers for tiny serverless functions
idea: From $1 IoT chips that have no DRAM at all: serverless functions whose working set WebAssembly static analysis proves to be under 4-8 MB run on many-core chips with only on-die SRAM and code streamed from flash; only the minority of large functions land on DRAM servers.
why: Most functions are allocated 128 MB+ but touch a few MB; running them DRAM-free cuts DRAM bits per invocation >10x, and the fab water with it.
note: Working-set proofs via static analysis are unreliable; SRAM costs far more per bit.

title: Camel's hump storage: model-codec page compression for text heaps
idea: From camels that carry dense reserves and metabolize them on demand: cold pages of text-heavy heaps (JSON, logs, documents, prompts) are compressed by a small learned language model plus arithmetic coder on the memory controller (~10x versus ~3x for LZ) and expanded into a staging area only on touch.
why: Cuts resident DRAM for text-heavy services ~10x; fewer manufactured bits means proportionally less fab ultrapure water.
note: LM-based text page compression; same learned-codec core as I-01663; controller compute heavy.

title: Sky-survey neural fields: datasets stored as tiny networks
idea: From astronomy surveys drowning in petabytes of images: large read-mostly arrays (images, volumes, simulation snapshots, maps) are fitted into compact hash-grid neural fields and queried by evaluating the network at coordinates on the accelerator, with a residual store only where error exceeds the bound.
why: Neural fields reach 10-100x compression on smooth data, so resident DRAM per dataset falls 10x+ and fab water with it.
note: Only smooth data; query compute heavy.

title: Stretchable-electronics liquid-metal bumps for warpage-free giant panels
idea: Stretchable wearables connect rigid chips with gallium alloy that never fatigues. Attach memory dies to large glass or organic panels with encapsulated eutectic gallium-indium microbump wells (30-50 um pitch) at room temperature, absorbing CTE mismatch and allowing rework by warming.
why: Warpage and reflow mismatch cap interposer and package size; room-temperature compliant joints allow 100-stack panels and rework, raising assembly yield.
note: Gallium attacks Al and alloys with Cu; long-term joint reliability is the doubt.

title: Deep-space PPM: one pulse carries four to six bits
idea: NASA's deep-space optical link uses pulse-position modulation because photons are scarce. Encode each 4-6-bit symbol as the position of a single short current pulse within a 16-64-slot frame on each memory lane; one transition per symbol replaces several NRZ transitions, and idle lanes send nothing.
why: Transitions per bit fall ~4-8x; with low-swing pulsed drivers, link energy ~10x below DDR5/HBM PHYs, at the cost of a faster slot clock and tighter timing.

title: Pacemaker hibernation: stop refresh, decode the decay on wake
idea: Implants live on microwatts by sleeping. In deep sleep, turn refresh fully off for seconds to minutes and let the retention tail decay. On wake, a page-level BCH/LDPC code (6-8% overhead, sized for the expected tail at that sleep length and temperature) reconstructs every page before use, so no backing store is needed.
why: Refresh and self-refresh are 16-33% of idle power (fact 3). Zero-refresh sleep plus decode-on-wake removes most of it for phones, laptops and parked servers.
note: Fail fraction grows fast beyond seconds; payoff bounded by sleep length.

title: Die-level urban mining: decap, thin and restack salvaged dies
idea: Old low-density packages have no buyers. Plasma-decap retired DRAM packages, recover the bare dies, thin them to ~50 um, retest, and stack 8-16 into new staircase wire-bond packages, building high-capacity parts from scrap dies.
why: Recovers dies the package-level resale market cannot use and multiplies their density per slot 4-8x.
note: Old low-density dies give poor power/bandwidth; reliability after decap uncertain.

title: Polyglot CXL card that accepts any mix of harvested DRAM chips
idea: Extreme user: GPU-mining and phone e-waste full of orphaned DDR3, DDR4, LPDDR4 and GDDR5 chips. A 10-person team designs an FPGA-based CXL Type-3 card with swappable daughterboards and per-channel PHY profiles, so any tested mix of harvested chips becomes one pooled memory device; boards go through contract SMT, and the team owns firmware and test.
why: Opens a stream of orphan chip types that no module standard can absorb, at perhaps $1-2/GB effective.

title: Croconic acid proton-transfer ferroelectric bit
idea: Scale down to one hydrogen bond: in croconic acid crystals polarization flips by protons hopping between oxygens, giving room-temperature ferroelectricity at low coercive field from an organic, non-tungsten, low-temperature film.
why: Scarce resources and process: solution-processable bit layer near room temperature, sub-1 V target.
note: Croconic acid RT ferroelectric known; endurance and speed unproven.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor cells: anodize a porous niobium sponge for conformal dielectric
idea: Scale the electrolytic capacitor down to a cell: sputter a columnar, porous Nb film by glancing-angle deposition onto each 180-nm storage node, then anodize it so conformal Nb2O5 (k~40) grows inside every pore, with thickness set by voltage at ~2 nm/V. Surface area rises ~20x without any high-AR lithographic etch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): >5 fF in a short structure from beaker anodization, avoiding tantalum and AR-75 etches.

title: Doping-selective porous-silicon anodization carves all tier cavities at once
idea: Use a wafer-scale electrochemical bath on every tier in one step: grow alternating p+/p- silicon layers in a 1990s epi reactor, open one 180-nm slot, and anodize. Only the p+ layers turn porous and dissolve, leaving lateral cavities for capacitors and gates in every tier at once, with no SiGe and no high-AR selective dry etch.
why: Lateral-cavity formation is a key 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2): one wet step replaces a lateral etch per tier, cheap and U.S.-manufacturable.

title: Langmuir-Blodgett perovskite nanosheets as a k~200 room-temperature capacitor dielectric
idea: Work at the molecular scale with a 1930s Langmuir trough: float exfoliated Ca2Nb3O10 perovskite nanosheets and transfer 5-10 monolayers onto storage electrodes at room temperature. That gives k~200 in ~10-nm films with no high-temperature anneal.
why: The capacitor charge wall needs k~70 (fact 1); k~200 cuts the required AR ~3x and suits low-temperature stacking of 3D tiers.
note: LB transfer is planar only; cannot coat 3D capacitor cavities.

title: Follow-the-sun memory lending across hemisphere datacenters
idea: Day-night time shift at planetary scale: memory-heavy batch jobs (checkpoint merges, analytics, embedding builds) migrate each evening to whichever region's daytime interactive load has fallen. The fleet then provisions DRAM for the planetary average rather than each site's peak.
why: Cuts installed DRAM an estimated 10-20% for the same work, with no new fab and no new wafers.

title: Bit-plane progressive memory with mantissa tails in flash
idea: Numeric arrays are stored transposed into bit-planes. DRAM holds the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes. The low-order planes live in CXL-attached flash and stream in only for operations flagged as precision-critical, such as optimizer updates. It is progressive JPEG for working memory, shifting from the bit scale to the tier scale.
why: BF16/FP32 tensors need 2-3x less DRAM when most kernels run on 6-8 effective bits. It also lowers the bandwidth spent per useful bit.
note: Overlaps with quantization; flash tail latency for precision-critical ops.

title: Predictive link sends only surprises, leaving sub-1% residual errors
idea: Shift from sending bits to sending surprises: identical predictors (previous value plus learned delta) run at both ends of the memory link and only mispredicted bits are sent; since consumers already absorb 1% cell errors, the predictor may be lossy and residual mismatches are simply not retransmitted.
why: ~2-4x effective link bandwidth for smooth tensor streams (fact 5), cutting pJ per useful bit proportionally.

title: Vertical product codes striped through the stack's TSV columns
idea: Rotate part of the codeword 90 degrees: each die keeps a horizontal row code for its 1% cell errors, and a vertical Reed-Solomon code places one symbol per die along the same TSV column, so a dead TSV or an entire failed die becomes a correctable erasure in the same structure.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (fact 6, -20-30%) toward ~95% while tolerating 1% cell BER and removing redundancy rows and repair fuses from periphery (fact 7).

title: Two-timescale ECC: light inline code plus strong background scrub
idea: Time split (ns access path vs seconds scrub path): reads use only a cheap SEC code, while a scrubber walking memory every few seconds checks and repairs it against a heavy erasure parity computed over 1 MB regions. The strong code never slows the critical path.
why: Tolerates ~100x higher accumulating retention error rates at ~4% total overhead, enabling longer refresh intervals.
note: Related to multi-tier ECC (VECC, LOT-ECC); 1 MB parity update per write is costly.

title: Move burn-in and retention screening into the first weeks of deployment
idea: Time shift of testing: ship DRAM after a short wafer sort. On-module BIST and the host memory controller run retention, row-hammer and burn-in sweeps during each server's first 2 weeks in service, and parts that fail are mapped out or swapped.
why: Test equipment and burn-in ovens are a capacity chokepoint. This frees ~30-50% of test capacity and cuts test cost per bit ~5%.

title: 1952 BaTiO3 crossbar redone in AlScN: square loop, Tc >1000 C
idea: Bell Labs' 1952 BaTiO3 matrix memory failed because its rounded loop let half-select pulses disturb neighbours, and its ~120 C Curie point sits right at 125 C. Wurtzite Al0.7Sc0.3N switches through nucleation-limited, very square loops (Ec ~3-5 MV/cm), so a passive V/3 crossbar is disturb-free, and its polarization is safe far above 125 C because its Tc exceeds 1000 C.
why: Transistor-free stackable crosspoint FeRAM that qualifies at Grade 1 (125 C/10 y); ~4F2 per layer; lead-free, sputtered with CMOS-compatible tools.

title: Optane's 85 C ceiling raised by a tensile cage around amorphous GST
idea: Optane-class PCM was rated for only ~85 C retention because amorphous GST crystallizes when hot. The amorphous phase is ~6-8% less dense than the crystal, so wrap each cell in a pre-stressed SiN/TiN liner that holds its volume in tension; tension penalizes the denser crystal and should raise the effective crystallization barrier by ~0.2-0.4 eV.
why: Pushes 10-year retention past 125 C without Ge-rich alloys that slow writes, keeping ~100 ns PCM speed for automotive and industrial memory.
note: Tension may raise the barrier modestly; PCM endurance stays far from DRAM class.

title: CBRAM's hot-retention killer fixed by intermetallic-compound filaments
idea: Adesto/Crossbar Ag and Cu filaments dissolved at 125 C because a few-atom metallic chain has high surface energy and diffuses away. Switch in an amorphous Ge-Te or Si-Te matrix where injected Cu reacts into a Cu2Te or Cu3Ge compound filament, a thermodynamic minimum rather than a metastable chain, and reset it by field-driven decomposition.
why: Moves CBRAM retention from ~85 C to Grade 1 while keeping ns low-voltage writes in a dense crosspoint.
note: A thermodynamically stable filament may also resist reset; CBRAM endurance stays far below DRAM class.

title: Resistive-load 4T SRAM revived with printed oxide TFT loads
idea: The 4T SRAM with polysilicon load resistors died because its TOhm loads would not scale and drew standby current. Oxide semiconductors lack a good p-type, so they cannot make CMOS SRAM, but they make superb loads. Print a cross-coupled pair of oxide TFTs whose loads are oxide TFTs in deep subthreshold, sized so the load current (~1e-15 A) exceeds pull-down leakage (~1e-18 A).
why: A static, refresh-free, n-type-only printed cell with ~fW standby per bit, which gets around oxide electronics' missing p-type.

title: Lock-in AC tone read buries memristor sneak currents
idea: Failure mined: HP's TiO2 memristor crossbar died on sneak-path currents and line leakage that swamped the selected cell. Fix: put a small 200 MHz tone on the selected wordline only, hold all other lines at AC ground, and read the bitline through a mixer and integrator locked to that tone. DC bias leakage, half-select currents and 1/f noise all fall outside the detection band.
why: Selectorless 1k x 1k tiles can be read with >30 dB rejection of the background. That removes selector layers and makes tiles 4-16x larger, so decoders and sense amps take a smaller share of die area.

title: HMC logic base die made detachable with liquid-metal microbumps
idea: HMC died partly because its logic base die tied the DRAM stack to one controller generation. Join the base die to the DRAM core stack with gallium-indium liquid-metal microbumps held in polymer cups. Warming slightly releases the joint, so a stack can move to a new base die (for example a new CXL/UCIe PHY) and a failed base die can be replaced.
why: DRAM core dies outlive 2-3 controller generations, about doubling the useful life of scarce bits, and repair needs no stack scrap (fact 6).

title: Socketed DRAM chips return as MEMS micro-spring die sockets
idea: Socketed DIP DRAM was abandoned because of contact reliability and size. Use lithographically defined MEMS micro-springs, as in probe cards, as a permanent fine-pitch die socket on the interposer. A lid holds the HBM stack down, and it can be lifted out, retested and replaced.
why: Fixes HBM's irreparability and yield scrap (fact 6). Good stacks and interposers are reused instead of scrapped with the assembly.

title: BCB polymer bonding repurposed as debond-on-demand tier interlayer
idea: BCB adhesive wafer bonding was abandoned for 3D stacking because it degrades above ~350C. Make that a feature: bond DRAM tiers with a thin, thermally decomposable polymer pierced by short copper nails for signals. At end of life a bake separates the tiers for retest and reuse, or for clean copper and silicon recovery.
why: Makes multi-tier stacks (facts 2, 6) recyclable into reusable dies or clean material streams instead of mixed shredder waste.
note: Recyclable stacks via decomposable polymer; fine-pitch copper nail reliability is the doubt.

title: Anodized-aluminum nanopores as lithography-free capacitor molds on aluminum sheet
idea: Anodic-alumina nanopore MIM capacitors reached very high capacitance in university labs but never shipped because pore-ordering defects made single pores unreliable. Use the aluminum sheet as substrate: anodize self-ordered 30-60 nm pores 1-2 um deep, line with ALD TiN/Al2O3/TiN, and define each cell as a bundle of ~50-100 pores so defects average out, with oxide TFTs on the planarized alumina above.
why: 30-60:1 capacitor holes with no lithography, no EUV and no fluorocarbon plasma (oxalic-acid anodization at room temperature); ~100 fF/um2; aluminum is abundant and smelted in North America.

title: Flikker, fixed: auto byte-plane split, MSBs in DRAM, LSBs offloaded
idea: Flikker/EnerJ approximate memory died on programmer annotation burden. The memory controller splits pages tagged as FP tensors by the ML framework's allocator (no annotations) into byte-planes: exponent/high-mantissa planes stay in DRAM, low-mantissa planes go to a CXL flash tier and are fetched only when a kernel requests full precision.
why: Most kernels run on the high planes, so weights/activations/optimizer state need ~50% of the DRAM: ~1.5-2x effective capacity.

title: Value prediction, fixed: store only predictor residuals off critical path
idea: Load-value prediction never entered CPUs because mispredictions cost pipeline flushes. Reuse stride, context and small learned predictors as a memory codec: on write store only the residual from the prediction in SRAM or flash, on read run the predictor and add the residual, so a misprediction costs only extra bits.
why: Smooth data (sensor streams, counters, indices, embeddings) compresses 2-5x, letting SRAM/flash-only devices hold working sets that used to need DRAM.

title: Charge-recycling buses failed on imbalance; balanced coding fixes voltage-stacked HBM lanes
idea: Charge-recycling (voltage-stacked) buses from 1990s research failed because data-dependent current imbalance between stacked lane groups collapsed the mid-rail. Split a 1,024-bit HBM bus into two stacked groups (0-0.4 V and 0.4-0.8 V) so charge spent by the upper group powers the lower, and apply DC-balanced 8b/9b-style coding per group so transitions match each cycle, leaving only a tiny mid-rail regulator.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~2x lower I/O energy by reusing each coulomb, and balanced current shrinks the decoupling needed (fewer Ta/Hf decaps); plain Si CMOS and Cu.

title: Computational sprinting's wax died; salt-hydrate buffers let HBM burst bandwidth
idea: Computational sprinting (UPenn, 2012) proposed paraffin heat buffers but never shipped because wax conducts poorly and re-solidifies slowly. Fill the spacer and dummy-die volumes beside HBM stacks with magnesium nitrate hexahydrate (melts ~89 C, ~160 J/g) infiltrated into sealed copper foam, which soaks up heat right at HBM's throttle point so stacks can run 20-40% higher bandwidth for tens of seconds and re-freeze during idle phases.
why: Thermal throttling and temperature-doubled refresh (fact 3) during AI bursts, letting a smaller memory system meet peak demand; Mg, N, O, H and Cu only.

title: IBM RAIM moved inside the bank: parity rows rebuild hammered victims
idea: IBM's RAIM (RAID across memory channels) protects against whole-DIMM loss but never addressed row-level bursts such as hammer victims, which exceed per-line ECC. Fix: on-die logic maintains one XOR parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray, updated on writes, so any single row corrupted beyond ECC is rebuilt from its siblings.
why: Converts row-hammer and single-row retention bursts into recoverable events, letting mitigation thresholds relax ~2-4x (fact 9) at ~3% capacity cost.

title: TRRespass fixed off-die: exact hammer counters on 180 nm chip
idea: In-DRAM Target Row Refresh was broken in 2020 (TRRespass) because its small sampler could not track enough aggressor rows. Fix: a 180 nm companion chip on the module keeps exact per-row-group activation counts (Misra-Gries tables in SRAM) and issues neighbor refreshes, so dies that flip at ~1k activations, now down-binned or scrapped, can be sold safely.
why: Row hammer and yield: recovers hammer-weak dies as standard parts and protects scaled DRAM without spending advanced-die area on counters.
note: Module-level exact counting needs vendor row-remap knowledge; DDR5 PRAC/RFM and controller trackers overlap.

title: Domain-inverted lithium niobate microrings store bits as optical resonance shifts
idea: Effect walk: Pockels effect sign inversion. In thin-film LiNbO3, poling a segment of a microring flips the sign of its electro-optic coefficient; under a small DC bias the ring resonance moves left or right depending on the domain, so a WDM probe reads 32 rings in parallel non-destructively and a 5-V electrode pulse rewrites the domain.
why: Puts memory directly on the optical interconnect, deleting O-E-O conversion energy (fact 5) for photonic switches and CPO buffers; area per bit is um2, so it is a photonic buffer tier rather than a DRAM substitute.
note: TFLN MPW accessible; um2 per bit restricts to photonic buffers.

title: Backside 1064 nm illumination accelerates DRAM retention screening
idea: Effect: photoconductive carrier generation. A benchtop station floods bare dies (or windowed package backs) with calibrated 1064 nm light, which passes through silicon and adds a uniform, dose-set generation current to every storage junction. A known added leakage turns a long retention wait into minutes, and the dose-response slope separates leaky cells from merely marginal ones.
why: Test capital/time (fact 4): 5-10x shorter retention screens cut tester capex per bit and enable fine retention binning for low-refresh SKUs; one optics bench plus an existing tester.

title: Triple-row charge sharing detects duplicate pages for in-DRAM dedup
idea: Effect: multi-row charge-sharing majority. On commodity DDR4/DDR5, an FPGA controller issues back-to-back ACTs (the timing-violation trick from ComputeDRAM) to open a candidate page, a complement copy of the suspected twin and an all-zero reference together; the result equals the reference wherever the pages agree. Duplicate 8 KB rows are found at sense-amp bandwidth and mapped to one physical copy.
why: Usable supply: VM and AI-serving memory often holds 10-30% duplicate pages (zero pages, shared weights, KV prefixes); cheap in-DRAM comparison enables continuous dedup worth ~+10-25% effective capacity.

title: Storage-node-controlled ring-oscillator readout stores two bits per gain cell
idea: Effect: voltage-controlled oscillation frequency. In a 2T gain cell, the storage node gates the current source of a short current-starved ring oscillator shared per column group; a read counts oscillations for ~10 ns, so four charge levels map to clearly separated counts. The count is digital and immune to bitline offset.
why: Density/cost per bit: 2 bits per cell doubles gain-cell macro density on mature U.S. nodes, and counters replace analog SAs; MPW-feasible.

title: LC-resonant adiabatic driver chiplet recycles command/address bus energy
idea: Effect: LC resonance energy recovery. A small mature-node chiplet drives the DRAM command/address and clock nets as part of an LC tank (on-package inductor plus net capacitance), so energy sloshes between the inductor and the wires instead of being dumped as CV^2 on every toggle; commands are encoded by pulse position on the resonant waveform.
why: Data-movement/periphery energy (fact 5): CA and clock bus energy cut ~60-75%; MPW plus OSAT only.

title: Photoacoustic isotope-tracer leak detection retires helium mass spectrometers
idea: Effect: photoacoustics. A modulated mid-IR laser absorbed by a 13CO2 tracer gas creates pressure waves that a resonant MEMS microphone detects at ppb levels. 13CO2 has almost no background, so it replaces helium spraying for leak-checking vacuum chambers, gas lines and EUV/etch tools.
why: Helium: leak testing is a top-3 fab helium use; equivalent sensitivity is reached with a recyclable, abundant tracer.

title: Stress-limited oxidation self-equalizes pillar diameters from sloppy cheap litho
idea: Effect: stress-retarded oxidation at high curvature. Pattern Si pillars with relaxed, high-LWR ArF or imprint litho, then wet-oxidize at ~850 C: compressive stress at small radii slows oxidation, so all pillars converge to a uniform 8-10 nm core whatever their starting diameter. Strip the oxide to get uniform vertical channels.
why: Facts 3 and 4: channel-diameter spread feeds the leakage tail; a physics-based CD equalizer lets patterning with 3x worse CD control still reach tight Vt distributions.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal heals leakage tails in downgraded DRAM wafers
idea: Effect: isotope-hardened dangling-bond passivation. Buy downgraded or scrap DRAM wafers from brokers before dicing and anneal them at ~400 C in a used 10-20 atm D2 furnace (~$400k): deuterium passivates the interface and GIDL trap centers behind the leakage tail, and Si-D bonds are ~10x more stable than Si-H. Re-test and resell recovered dies; the rest of the $1M funds test and 24 months of qualification.
why: Fact 3: trims the <=13 fA tail that sets refresh failures; recovered dies add supply with no new fab.

title: Hot-wire sweep zone-anneals block copolymers into defect-free arrays
idea: Effect: directional ordering in a moving thermal gradient (zone annealing). A heated wire or line-focused IR lamp crosses a BCP film at um/s, and domains order like a directional solidification front that pushes defects to the edge, reaching long-range order in minutes instead of hours in an oven. A $40k sweeper plus ~$600k of university fab time tests 14 nm half-pitch bitline gratings.
why: Fact 4: defectivity kept DSA out of DRAM; below 0.01 defects/cm2, DSA could replace SAQP passes at ~1/5 the cost.

title: Ultrasonic piezo excitation speeds nanoimprint resist fill several-fold
idea: Effect: piezoelectric ultrasonic excitation (acoustic streaming and shear thinning). A transducer behind the imprint template drives 20-100 kHz vibration that speeds capillary filling of nanoscale cavities and dissolves trapped gas, cutting fill time per field from ~1 s to ~0.2 s. A ~$400k retrofit of a used imprint tool plus a 24-month defect study.
why: Fact 4: NIL throughput (~25 wafers/hour per head) and bubble defects limit it as an EUV substitute; faster fill raises throughput and cuts litho cost per layer.

title: Peltier-cooled DRAM island inside a 125 C module
idea: Mount one small LPDDR die on a thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier cooler held at 85 C, and keep the rest of the working set in heat-tolerant NVM (AlScN FeFET or Ge-rich PCM). The cooled island holds only the hottest 10-15% of data, so cooling costs just a few watts.
why: Most data avoids 4x refresh and retention failure at 125 C, and DRAM per ECU drops 5-10x.

title: Pyroelectricity: self-powered per-bank thermal telemetry drives fine-grained refresh
idea: Deposit thin AlScN pyroelectric patches over each DRAM bank in the stack; temperature changes generate charge with no bias, integrated and read via spare sideband lanes, so the controller refreshes each bank at its true temperature instead of the stack worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): most banks run far cooler than the hottest spot; 20-40% fewer refreshes and recovered bandwidth.

title: Displacement current: printed high-k nanocomposite pinless capacitive memory connectors
idea: Print a BaTiO3-polymer high-k layer over connector pads on module and motherboard flex so signals couple capacitively across a thin gap with no metal contact, decoded by pulse-mode receivers; modules slide in with no pins to wear or corrode.
why: Module cost and signal integrity (fact 5): removes stubs and pin capacitance, enabling cheap hot-swap memory expansion; DC power still needs contacts.

title: Magnetostrictive underfill shakes memory packages free from retired boards
idea: Underfill and solder mask under DRAM packages carry Fe-Co or Ni-ferrite magnetostrictive microparticles; a kHz alternating field makes them strain and heat locally, cracking the interface and softening solder. Packages lift off intact for re-balling without cooking the rest of the board.
why: Today >90% of retired soldered DRAM is shredded; intact harvest adds second-life supply in seconds per board.

title: Self-limiting oxidation sharpens DUV pillars into sub-10 nm access channels
idea: O: pattern ~40 nm silicon pillars with DUV and thermally oxidize them; compressive stress in curved oxide retards oxidation as the core shrinks, so it self-terminates at a nearly uniform ~8-10 nm core regardless of starting CD, which becomes a gate-all-around vertical access channel after oxide strip.
why: Converts DUV CD variation into a self-limiting physical endpoint, giving thin uniform channels (low leakage, tight Vt) below EUV dimensions without EUV (facts 3, 4).

title: Cerium-oxide redox buffer pins oxide-channel stoichiometry for years-stable Vt
idea: Ce: cap DUV-patterned zinc-tin-oxide access transistors with a few-nm CeOx layer whose reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ couple absorbs or releases oxygen and hydrogen, buffering the channel's oxygen chemical potential so bias-stress and hydrogen-driven Vt drift, which raises off-current over life, is suppressed with no added lithography.
why: Oxide access devices deliver ultra-low leakage only if Vt stays put; stable Vt preserves seconds-scale retention (fact 3) over product life and makes relaxed-pitch BEOL DRAM viable without EUV.
note: Ce-doped oxide channels studied for stability; capping-layer redox buffer is a twist.
