title: Al: anodic alumina nanopore forests as litho-free die-to-die vias
idea: Anodize an aluminum layer to self-order 20-40 nm pores, electroplate Cu into them, and use the vertical wire forest as a dense random interconnect between a stacked periphery die and the array; a calibration pass learns which pores join which pads.
why: Gives ~1e9-1e10 vertical connections per cm2 without EUV/ArF or tight bond alignment, enabling periphery-on-top stacking (fact 7) cheaper than TSVs (fact 6).

title: Zinc-tin oxide channels give indium-free 64-tier BEOL DRAM
idea: Use ALD amorphous Zn-Sn-O at ~250 C as the lateral access-transistor channel of each BEOL tier, stacked 64 high over CMOS; Sn 5s orbitals carry mobility in place of In while keeping wide-gap off-current near 1e-19 A/um.
why: Keeps the oxide-semiconductor leakage advantage (fact 3) and BEOL stackability (fact 2) while removing indium supply risk, so high-tier oxide 3D DRAM can reach commodity volume.

title: Aluminum layer exchange crystallizes each tier's silicon below 450 C
idea: For each stacked tier, sputter Al, let a thin oxide membrane form, sputter a-Si on top and anneal at ~425 C so Si diffuses through the Al and crystallizes beneath it as large-grain (>10 um) (111)-textured poly-Si; etch away the displaced Al, counter-dope the Al background and build lateral transistors in the grains.
why: Near-crystalline lateral channels for every 3D tier (fact 2) inside BEOL thermal budget over finished periphery, using only sputter, furnace and wet etch.
note: ALILE poly-Si is known from solar; heavy Al doping and grain boundaries threaten leakage.

title: Titanium angle-evaporation forms self-aligned half-gates on pillar arrays
idea: Tilt the wafer 60-75 degrees in an e-beam evaporator so Ti lands only on one face and a set height band of each pillar (neighbors shadow the rest), then nitride it; rotating between evaporations writes wordlines and contacts at self-aligned heights with no lithography.
why: Shadow-defined wordlines on 4F2 pillars remove critical masks (fact 4) and set gate length by geometry, and the gate-free face lowers GIDL (fact 3); a tilt-stage evaporator is ubiquitous in university fabs.

title: Bismuth-tin capillary injection fills through-tier vias at 150 C
idea: As the final back-end step, evacuate the wafer, flood it with molten Bi58Sn42 (melts at 139 C) and apply gas pressure so liquid metal is forced into 50:1 through-tier vias and staircase contacts in seconds; wipe and polish the excess for void-free vertical connections.
why: Removes tungsten and slow CVD fills from deep contacts (resource and capital) at a temperature compatible with oxide-TFT tiers; a vacuum chamber and hotplate suffice in a university lab.

title: Rutile TiO2 dielectric templated by antimony-doped tin-oxide electrodes
idea: Periodic-table walk, Ti (22) with Sn (50): SnO2 is isostructural with rutile, so a conductive Sb:SnO2 bottom electrode templates rutile TiO2 (k~90-110) at <=350 C ALD, replacing Ru/RuO2 templates and Hf/Zr high-k; a 1 nm Al-doped TiO2 cap holds leakage.
why: Hits the k~70 target from fact 1 with Ti and Sn only: ~2x Cs at the same aspect ratio or AR 70->~35; Hf-free, Ru-free.

title: KOH-on-(110)-silicon crystal-plane trenches for capacitor fins
idea: Periodic-table walk, K (19): on (110) wafers, alkaline etchants cut near-perfect vertical {111} walls at 100-600:1 plane selectivity, so one DUV line mask along <112> yields atomically smooth deep trench/fin capacitors; TMAH substitutes for KOH where alkali contamination matters.
why: Swaps EUV-pitch plasma HAR etch for wet crystal anisotropy, fluorine-free, at roughly 1/20 the etch-tool capital.

title: Al: self-ordered anodic alumina pores replace EUV capacitor-hole patterning
idea: Deposit Al over the storage-node landing pads, pre-texture with a coarse DUV guide pattern, then anodize so pores self-organize at a voltage-set pitch (~2.5 nm/V) and grow straight to AR >100:1 with no plasma etch; line the pores with TiN/ZrO2/TiN to form the capacitors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the EUV hole layer and the slowest high-AR dry etch while reaching AR beyond 115 for more Cs; ~30-40% capacitor-module cost cut claimed.

title: Sn: liquid-tin skin printing of 2D SnO p-channel periphery
idea: Touch a wafer to a liquid Sn-Ga alloy under controlled O2 so its self-limiting, atomically thin SnO surface skin transfers in one stroke over 300 mm; pattern it into p-type TFTs stacked above the array to host part of the decoder and sense-amp periphery.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49% of die): stacking periphery in BEOL layers made by a vacuum-free heated-bath tool (vs a ~$5M CVD) could reclaim 20-30% die area; complements n-type oxides from prior work.

title: C: diamond-armored nanoimprint templates for repetitive array layers
idea: Coat nanoimprint replica templates with a thin conformal CVD-diamond skin so they survive >10x more imprints and resist particle damage, then use step-and-repeat nanoimprint for the 3-4 most periodic array layers (holes, lines) instead of EUV.
why: Fact 4: NIL tools cost ~1/5-1/10 of EUV in capital and energy; template wear and defects are NIL's blocker for DRAM, which diamond's hardness and inertness attack.

title: O: oxidation volume expansion halves pitch instead of SAQP
idea: Print poly-Si lines at relaxed pitch, then thermally oxidize: SiO2 occupies ~2.2x the volume of the Si consumed, so the growing sidewall oxide narrows each gap by a kinetically controlled amount, producing sub-litho trenches that are filled with the second line set.
why: Replaces spacer deposition/etch loops of SAQP with a 100+-wafer batch furnace step; ~30-50% fewer patterning steps on those layers at a fraction of the tool capital.

title: Na: epitaxial NaCl release layers for single-crystal tier transfer
idea: Grow epitaxial NaCl on a reusable crystalline donor, grow single-crystal oxide channel or ferroelectric films on the salt, bond them to the CMOS wafer and dissolve the salt with a small water mist to release the film; the donor is reused hundreds of times.
why: Facts 2 and 4: high-quality stacked tiers without high-temperature processing on the CMOS wafer and without buying a new single-crystal substrate per tier; donor cost amortized ~100x.

title: Te: thermal-threshold chalcogenide resist writes sub-diffraction imprint masters
idea: Use phase-transition mastering: a Ge-Sb-Te or incomplete-oxide resist changes phase only above a sharp temperature threshold, so a cheap 405 nm laser writer prints features ~1/4 of its spot size; selective development yields DRAM array masters for nanoimprint.
why: Master writing today needs multi-million-dollar e-beam tools and days per plate; thermal-threshold writing (Blu-ray mastering heritage) cuts master cost and time ~10x.

title: Al: anodic-alumina nanowire film replaces aligned microbumps for stacking
idea: Anodize aluminum into a 20-40 um AAO membrane with ~1e10 pores/cm2, electroplate Cu into the pores, and laminate it between dies as a z-axis-only conductor: any pad overlap conducts while lateral neighbors stay isolated, so die stacking needs only coarse (+/-5 um) placement yet reaches ~2-3 um effective pitch.
why: HBM bump/TSV tax and capital (fact 6): replaces multi-$M hybrid-bond aligners and CMP-critical surfaces with a wet anodization film; ~10x microbump density at a fraction of tool cost from abundant, US-sourced Al.

title: Fe: magnetite-loaded underfill enables induction rework of one HBM stack
idea: Load HBM underfill and joint regions with Fe3O4 nanoparticles so a localized RF coil heats only the failing stack's joints to reflow, lifting and replacing it while the GPU and seven neighbors stay below ~100 C; package and interface are unchanged.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): rework instead of scrapping very expensive multi-stack packages; recovers the ~10-20% of packages that fail final test because of a single stack.
note: RF also heats Cu traces; magnetite conductivity risks bump leakage.

title: H: high-pressure deuterium anneal of finished stacks tightens retention
idea: Anneal completed HBM/3DS stacks in ~20 atm D2 at 250-300 C (within microbump limits) so deuterium diffuses to passivate Si/SiO2 interface traps in access transistors that drive trap-assisted leakage; the heavier isotope resists later hot-carrier depassivation.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): fewer weak cells means more stacks pass 32/64 ms retention at 85-95 C and fewer repair elements consumed, ~3-5% yield gain with interface unchanged.
note: SiN capping layers block D2 diffusion in finished stacks; high-pressure anneals are known.

title: Na: rock-salt lattice data inversion picks least-hammerable neighbor pattern
idea: Like Na+ and Cl- alternating in a crystal, controller RTL XORs data with a physical-row-parity mask (learned from the DIMM's address scramble) chosen per module after profiling which neighbor charge relation (same or opposite) flips least, so adjacent rows mostly hold the benign pattern. FPGA/RTL only.
why: Row hammer flips (fact 9) are strongly data-pattern dependent; enforcing the benign relation claims ~2-5x higher effective threshold.
note: XOR mask only helps if data correlates; pattern dependence varies per row.

title: Si: silicone microcapsule underfill self-heals cracks in memory stacks
idea: Formulate an underfill with PDMS healing-agent microcapsules and a tin catalyst (no platinum); a growing microcrack ruptures capsules and seals itself before moisture and stress concentrate on microbumps. A small formulation and dispensing line suffices.
why: Thermal-cycle cracking drives opens in HBM/3DS stacks (fact 6); target ~2x thermal-cycle life.

title: Cu: Copper conductive-bridge memory released as zero-new-material open IP
idea: Release royalty-free CBRAM IP that uses a fab's own Cu BEOL and SiCN/SiO2 dielectric as the switching electrolyte, adding one mask and no new tools.
why: Every Cu-BEOL logic fab becomes a non-volatile memory supplier for persistence and capacity tiers.
note: CBRAM endurance far below DRAM-class; persistence tier only.

title: Ripstop Z-channel codes let decayed ones be woven back
idea: Like ripstop nylon's reinforcing threads stopping tears, encode rows with asymmetric Z-channel / constant-weight codes built for one-way 1->0 decay. Leaked ones become known-direction erasures that are corrected and rewritten on read.
why: Zero refresh for data read within the extended window: the usable unrefreshed lifetime grows from ~64 ms to several seconds, covering most transient AI data with no refresh energy.

title: Hydrogen-cooled chucks borrowed from turbo-generator cooling
idea: Large power-plant generators are cooled with hydrogen because it conducts heat better than helium; use 1-20 Torr hydrogen as electrostatic-chuck backside gas in etch, CVD and implant tools, with sealed-band chucks, leak-rate interlocks and hydrogen from on-site electrolysis.
why: Backside cooling is the largest fab helium use, and Qatar's ~30% is offline; H2 thermal conductivity (~0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K for He) gives equal or better wafer temperature control at ~1% of helium cost, removing most fab helium demand.

title: Mist-CVD humidifier grows indium-free zinc oxide channels
idea: Like an ultrasonic humidifier or a spray gun, nebulize aqueous zinc acetate with silicon or aluminum dopant precursors and carry the mist in air onto ~300 C wafers to grow amorphous Zn-Si-O channels for BEOL access transistors, using zinc smelted in Tennessee.
why: Gives a wide-gap (3.3 eV), low-leakage, indium- and gallium-free channel for stacked gain cells with no vacuum, no organometallics and ~1/10 the energy of sputter or ALD lines.
note: Mist-CVD known for Ga2O3; electronic-grade amorphous films without vacuum need validation.

title: Two-angle stencil spraying: one mask, two self-aligned features
idea: Like a painter spraying one stencil from two angles to get two offset strokes, pattern one resist-bridge mask and perform double-angle directional deposition (Dolan-bridge style) so each opening yields two offset, self-aligned features, e.g. access gate plus storage contact, or two cells per opening.
why: Fact 4: halves critical masks for paired features and removes their overlay; ~2x pattern density from one DUV mask.

title: Lego-key bonding: etched studs self-align dies without precision bonders
idea: Use the single added mask to etch tapered studs on the DRAM die and matching sockets on the base wafer; a cheap micron-accurate placer drops dies and gentle vibration seats them so the mechanical keys pull overlay below 100 nm before hybrid bonding.
why: Capital/Fact 6: replaces ~$5M sub-200 nm hybrid bonders with pick-and-place at ~1/5 the cost and several times the throughput.

title: Cored casting: coarse skeleton protected, fine interior repaired by physics
idea: Cored castings are hollow, with metal only where strength is needed. Simulation state is stored as a coarse multigrid level in protected memory plus fine-level residual corrections at 4-8 bits in 1%-BER cells. On each load, a local PDE-residual check flags any cell whose residual jumps (the signature of a bit flip), and only those cells are re-solved from their neighbors and the coarse level.
why: Fine meshes dominate scientific DRAM use; storing them as low-bit residuals cuts footprint 4-8x, and the physics itself detects and corrects errors at 1% BER.

title: Gravure-offset printed fan-out redistribution layers on panels
idea: Borrow gravure-offset printing from printed electronics: an engraved cylinder inks silver/copper nanoparticle lines at 5 um width onto a blanket and transfers them to fan-out panels at about 1 m/s. Use it for the coarse layers that route memory base dies to the package.
why: Cuts capital and step count for the coarse RDL that makes up most layers; claims ~10x lower capex per layer.

title: Stalactite bonding: electroless copper grows across the gap
idea: Hold two dies face to face with a 2-5 um gap in an electroless copper bath; metal grows from both pads like stalactite and stalagmite until they fuse. No bonding force is needed.
why: Warp-tolerant, low-temperature stacking that preserves DRAM retention and lifts yield; parallel across whole wafers.
note: Electroless bumpless bonding has research precedent; plating uniformity across wafers is the risk.

title: Micro-Velcro hook-and-loop reworkable memory die attach
idea: Plate copper mushroom hooks through i-line resist on one die and loop arrays on the other; pressing them interlocks hundreds of thousands of contacts at room temperature. A stack can be peeled off and swapped.
why: Reworkable stacks raise effective yield and enable field-upgradeable memory; no solder reflow and no EUV.
note: Contact resistance and density of plated hooks versus hybrid bonds is the doubt.

title: Lost-wax cast microfluidic cooling around taller memory stacks
idea: Print sacrificial polycarbonate lines around and between HBM stacks, mold over them, then burn them out like investment casting so coolant channels remain inside the encapsulant.
why: Heat limits stack height; in-package cooling enables 16-24-high stacks, raising density per footprint.

title: Lost-wax casting: anodic-alumina molds for 200:1 capacitors
idea: Anodize a sputtered aluminum layer above the bitline level so it self-organizes hexagonal nanopores at 40-60 nm pitch with AR >200:1. Coat the pores conformally by ALD with TiN/ZrO2-HfO2/TiN, then dissolve the alumina 'wax' (or keep it as a scaffold), leaving a cast forest of tall capacitors.
why: Capacitor charge wall (needs AR ~115): electrochemistry reaches AR 200+ with no deep-RIE tool, for ~1.5-2x Cs per footprint. An anodization bath and ALD are in any nanofab.

title: Halftone printing: grayscale-litho staircases for many-tier 3D DRAM
idea: Halftone printing makes continuous tone from dot density. An e-beam-written sub-resolution-dot grayscale mask defines the whole wordline staircase of a 3D DRAM in one exposure, and a proportional etch transfers it. This replaces ~N/2 trim-etch loops for N tiers.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers: one-shot grayscale cuts staircase litho/etch steps ~10x, lowering capex and cycle time. Grayscale litho is routine in nanofabs.
note: Proportional etch landing on each of 26+ thin tiers is the doubt.

title: Analog activation integrators in wordline drivers stop row hammer
idea: Ideal result: a row that knows when its neighbors are in danger. Each sub-wordline driver adds a fixed charge quantum to a tiny leaky capacitor per activation; crossing a comparator threshold flags a targeted neighbor refresh, and the leak resets it at the refresh-window rate.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2% driver area instead of counter SRAM or 10-15% bandwidth for probabilistic schemes.
note: Leak rate must track the refresh window across temperature.

title: Fluidic self-assembled memory-tile carpet on a glass panel
idea: IFR: 'memory chips place themselves.' Backward: make 100 um oxide-on-glass memory tiles with shape-coded keys and solder-coded faces, pour them as a slurry over a glass panel with matching wells, and let capillary and solder self-alignment seat millions in minutes, then wire them with panel redistribution layers.
why: Packaging and HBM tax (fact 6): tiny known-good tiles give ~99% effective yield; ~1e6 tiles/hour assembly without pick-and-place.
note: FSA of chiplets is known; panel RDL wiring limits bandwidth.

title: See-through substrate: backside flood exposure self-aligns every tier
idea: IFR: 'every tier aligns perfectly with no extra masks.' Backward: because glass is transparent, pattern the opaque wordline grid once, then expose each later tier's photoresist with UV flood light from the back of the panel, using the buried metal as an automatic mask so every tier's features self-align with zero overlay error.
why: Litho capital (fact 4) and 3D overlay: masks per tier fall toward zero and the overlay budget vanishes, allowing tighter pitches on cheap panel steppers.
note: Known TFT-LCD trick; only reproduces shadows of buried metal, so few tier features can use it.

title: Gasless chuck: solid-contact thermal coupling replaces backside gas
idea: Ideal: wafer cooling with no gas at all. Closest: an electrostatic chuck whose surface is a dense field of compliant micro-pillars capped with AlN/graphite composite; Johnsen-Rahbek clamping presses the wafer into intimate solid contact (>1000 W/m2K), and a replaceable pillar film handles wear.
why: Eliminates helium from chuck cooling plus He leak-check/recovery hardware; drives fab helium exposure for etch/CVD toward zero with roughly flat tool cost.

title: One-metal cell: aluminum conductors with anodized-alumina dielectrics
idea: Ideal: one cheap material does everything. Closest: deposit a single aluminum film and convert chosen regions into dense barrier-type Al2O3 by room-temperature electrochemical anodization through a soft mask (thickness set at ~1.3 nm/V), so the same film supplies wordlines, plate electrodes and capacitor/gate dielectric.
why: Replaces W, TiN, Hf/Zr ALD and several vacuum steps with U.S.-abundant aluminum and wet benches; suits low-temperature oxide-TFT tiers; k~9 gives modest Cs but zero scarce inputs.
note: Anodized-Al TFT dielectrics known in displays; k~9 and through-mask lateral spread limit cell use.

title: Self-restoring keeper transistor makes gain cell quasi-static, refresh-free
idea: Ideal: a dynamic cell that refreshes itself. Closest: add to a 2T gain cell a minimum-size keeper transistor gated by the read node, whose subthreshold current tops the storage node up toward its own stored rail faster than the access device leaks it away, so the capacitorless cell holds data without refresh.
why: Fact 3 and Fact 4: no refresh and no leakage-tail screening, which relaxes implant/anneal control and cuts retention test time (a major test cost).

title: Bit-plane storage with learned LSB synthesis on read
idea: IFR: store only the bits that matter. Closest: error-tolerant arrays (activations, images, sensor data) are stored as bit planes, MSB planes in DRAM and LSB planes dropped or parked in flash; on read a tiny predictor in the memory controller synthesizes dithered LSBs from neighbouring values within a programmer-declared SNR budget.
why: 1.5-2.5x capacity for media and ML activations at controlled error.

title: Retention-binned stacks with weak-row exile and sub-second rewrite cadence
idea: Ideal: every cell holds charge as well as the best cell. Closest achievable: at stack test, measure each row's retention and remap the weakest ~0.1% (the 13 fA tail) to base-die SRAM spares so the stack guarantees >=2 s retention, then dedicate it to training jobs whose optimizer step rewrites all weights, gradients and moments in under 1 s, with refresh switched off.
why: Fact 3: retention is set by the tail; exiling it lifts guaranteed retention ~30x so the natural rewrite cadence removes refresh power and the 10-20% bandwidth tax.
note: VRT cells defeat one-time retention binning.

title: Gated-diode self-restoring cell refreshed by one global pulse
idea: Ideal: every cell refreshes itself at once with no sensing. Closest: add a small transistor whose gate is the storage node, in series with a poly diode from a global pulse line; when the line pulses high, cells holding '1' turn the transistor on and top themselves up while '0' cells stay off, so the whole array refreshes in one pulse.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (bandwidth loss, ~46 fJ/bit) with a global pulse of a few fJ/bit; buildable at 180 nm.

title: Die-level LPDDR harvesting from scrapped phones into CXL modules
idea: Ideal: every bit ever manufactured keeps working forever. Closest achievable: an automated laser-debond, clean and reball line pulls LPDDR4X/5 packages from the ~1.2B phones retired each year, retests them at speed, and mounts 16-32 packages per CXL Type-3 card behind a RAS-heavy controller.
why: New supply without wafers: retired phones hold several EB of DRAM; 5% recovery adds roughly 1% of annual bit supply at ~1/3 the cost per bit.
note: PoP/underfill removal and part heterogeneity hurt yield; CXL controller can mask variation.

title: Pulse-width-weighted reads: one integrator resolves four NV bits
idea: Constraint: non-volatile cells with ON/OFF ratio above 50x (ReRAM/FTJ). Four cells on one bitline are read at once with wordline pulse widths of 1:2:4:8, so their currents integrate on one capacitor as a binary-weighted charge, and a 4-bit SAR converter returns all four bits.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp count and read energy per bit fall ~4x; the read is non-destructive so it needs no restore.

title: Registration-free anodic alumina capacitor forest at room temperature
idea: Under 400 C, anodize a sputtered 3 um Al film over the transistor tier at room temperature to self-form 25 nm pores (AR over 100) with no litho or plasma etch. Each storage-node pad is wider than the pore pitch, so it captures 2-3 pores. ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN at 300 C lines the pores.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR over 100 without a high-AR etch tool; Cs above 6 fF with no capacitor mask.
note: Registration-free AAO pores are clever, but TiN/ZrO2/TiN stack nearly fills 25 nm pores; known in silicon capacitors.

title: Capacitor-first substrate: MacEtch forest with the wafer as plate
idea: Under 400 C, metal-assisted chemical etching (Au mesh in HF/H2O2 at room temperature) drills 20 nm holes at AR about 150 into a doped Si wafer. After an ALD MIM liner at 300 C, the oxide transistor tier is built on top, and the bulk wafer itself is the common cell plate.
why: Fact 1: breaks the 60-75:1 etch limit with a wet bench instead of a $10M+ etcher; Cs 8-10 fF.
note: Cheap wet etch for high-AR holes; uniformity, Au contamination and hole-transistor registration are doubts.

title: Barium-armored crucibles from non-Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Within $1M/24 months: coat the inner wall of crucibles made from lower-grade Norwegian or U.S. quartz with a barium-hydroxide wash that nucleates a dense, uniform cristobalite skin at melt-in to act as an impurity diffusion barrier; validate on a 4-6 inch lab puller with lifetime and oxygen metrology.
why: If the skin blocks alkali and Al outdiffusion, crucibles no longer need Spruce Pine (>80%) HPQ; lab pullers make the test affordable within the budget.

title: Procedural memory: store generator seeds instead of predictable cache lines
idea: Imposed limit: any cache line that a 16-instruction program can regenerate gets zero DRAM bytes. The memory controller detects arithmetic sequences, strided pointers, timestamp runs and repeated structs, stores a small generator descriptor in an on-die table, and synthesizes the line on read.
why: Index arrays, page tables, sparse-matrix metadata and freshly initialized buffers are highly procedural; this could save 10-30% of footprint on such workloads, beyond what zero-page detection gets.

title: Phase-interleaved co-tenancy: two jobs time-share the same physical bytes
idea: Imposed limit: every byte must be live more than 90% of the time. A scheduler pairs jobs whose memory-phase curves complement each other (prefill vs decode, forward vs backward, map vs reduce), and the compiler emits deterministic memory timetables so job B's peak lands in pages that job A has provably freed.
why: Accelerators provisioned for peak leave 30-50% of DRAM-time idle; timetabled sharing raises utilization and cuts installed DRAM 1.3-2x.

title: Capability-tagged immutable buffers enforce zero-copy across services
idea: Imposed limit: serialized copies of the same message are banned. Microservices pass read-only buffers through hardware capabilities (CHERI-style tagged pointers) that grant read rights across process boundaries, so RPC payloads, deserialized protobufs and caches all point at one physical buffer instead of 3-5 copies.
why: Copying and serialization take a sizable share of datacenter memory footprint and bandwidth; one-copy semantics could trim service heaps 10-25%.

title: Printed diffractive 4f layer convolves images in light
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll embossed phase mask in the Fourier plane of a 4f lens system applies a fixed bank of convolution kernels to incoming camera light, so the first CNN layers' feature maps, the largest activations, form on the sensor and are never stored in DRAM.
why: Early feature maps are the biggest activation buffers in vision models, often over half of activation memory; doing the first layers optically removes them.

title: Chip-on-glass display bonding builds memory cassettes for pennies
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Bond bare DRAM dies face-down onto 0.3 mm glass sheets with anisotropic conductive film exactly as LCD driver ICs are bonded (cents per bond, 1e5 bonds/day per line), then stack 20 sheets into a cassette with a flex edge connector.
why: Package substrate and socket cost (~$0.5-1 per die) disappears; sheets stack at ~0.4 mm pitch vs ~10 mm DIMM pitch, ~10x+ bits per volume at equal $/GB.
note: Display ACF bonding; volume density is rarely the binding constraint.

title: LED-strip memory tape spools gigabytes into empty chassis space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount DRAM dies every 5 mm along a flat polyimide ribbon with a shared differential serial bus, built on reel-to-reel LED-strip SMT lines, and coil or fold the tape into chassis voids alongside cooling ducts.
why: Uses volume DIMM slots cannot reach at LED-strip assembly cost (fractions of a cent per placement): ~10x bits per chassis liter vs DIMMs.
note: Long shared serial bus adds latency; chassis volume rarely the limit.

title: No silicon wafer: 300 mm glass wafers through existing BEOL lines
idea: Forced limit: no CZ silicon. Run oxide-semiconductor memory stacks on 300 mm borosilicate glass wafers in existing BEOL-only tool sets (all steps at or below 400 C). The process needs no crystal pulling, quartz crucibles or FEOL implant and anneal.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and CZ chokepoints, and substrate cost drops by 5-10x. It uses idle BEOL capacity at mature foundries.

title: Ru-free rutile: SnO2-templated TiO2 short-stub capacitor
idea: Cap the TiN bottom electrode with 3-5 nm of ALD Ta-, Nb- or F-doped SnO2 (conductive, rutile/cassiterite structure, a=4.74 A vs rutile TiO2 a=4.59 A). ALD TiO2 (optionally lightly Al-doped to suppress leakage) nucleates epitaxially in the rutile phase on the SnO2 grains at 250-340 C, giving k ~60-100 without the >800 C anneal or the Ru/RuO2 template used in earlier rutile work. A doped-SnO2 top electrode makes the stack symmetric and keeps the high-work-function contact. At 7 nm physical thickness the EOT is 0.34-0.40 nm. The capacitor is used either to shorten the 1-beta pillar from 1.3 um to 0.8-0.95 um, or as a 0.30-0.35 um stub holding ~2 fF for short-bitline, 4F2 or 3D-tier cells.
why: 1.4-1.6x more capacitance per area than ZrO2-based stacks (EOT 0.40/0.34 vs 0.55 nm): equal Cs from a capacitor 27-38% shorter (AR ~39-45 instead of 62), or 2 fF from a 0.30-0.35 um stub; zero Ru and zero Hf.

title: Errors set the refresh rate: ECC-feedback refresh loop
idea: Reverse the control direction: instead of a fixed worst-case tREFI, the controller lengthens each bank's refresh interval stepwise while watching DDR5 on-die ECC error-check-and-scrub counts and its own ECC syndromes, and backs off as soon as corrected errors per row exceed a threshold far below correction capacity. The memory reports its real retention instead of the datasheet predicting it.
why: Most dies retain 4-10x longer than spec at real temperatures, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50-75% (fact 3); firmware on existing DDR5.

title: Stock reduction: simmer near-duplicate tokens into weighted KV entries
idea: As a chef reduces stock to concentrate flavour, a background pass merges runs of KV entries whose keys are near-duplicates into one centroid entry carrying a count that adds log(count) to its attention logit, preserving attention mass.
why: Long contexts are full of repetitive tokens; 2-5x fewer stored KV entries for documents and code with attention mass conserved on merged clusters.
note: KV merging (CaM, D2O) already published.

title: Solar MPPT perturb-and-observe tuning of per-bank refresh
idea: Solar inverters wiggle their operating point to track maximum power. Firmware in an open FPGA/CXL controller periodically lengthens one bank's refresh interval by a step and watches patrol-scrub correctable-error counts for a window. It keeps the step while errors stay flat and backs off when they rise, so it tracks each bank's true minimum refresh as temperature and aging drift.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth 40-70% (fact 3) using only controller firmware, which fits a 24-month, $1M scope.
note: Error-feedback adaptive refresh known; VRT cells make backing off on observed errors risky.

title: Hardware video encoders compress parked KV caches as 10-bit frames
idea: Box: lossy compression × existing GPU video engines × per-head KV tensor × session parked × HEVC 10-bit with channel-reordered frames. Parked KV caches are reordered so tokens become frame time and channels become pixels, then encoded by idle on-die video engines and decoded on resume.
why: If token-to-token correlation holds, parked KV shrinks 5–10× using fixed-function engines already shipped; no new silicon, no fluorinated chemistry.
note: Close to LLM.265 (video codecs as tensor codecs).

title: Backprop activations stored as random-projection sketches
idea: Worsen: keep every layer's full activation tensor for the backward pass. Flip: store a seeded random projection (sketch) of each activation at 1/8 to 1/16 size and compute weight gradients from the sketch, regenerating the projection matrix from its seed.
why: Capacity: 8-16x smaller activation memory in training with small, unbiased gradient noise.

title: Sparse 1-bit activation memory for inference
idea: Worsen: store activations as dense fp16. Flip: train networks whose stored activations are binary and 90% sparse, keeping them as run-length-coded bitmaps, so activation buffers shrink by 16x times 10x.
why: Cost: about 160x less activation memory; trades retraining and accuracy on hard tasks.

title: Space-AI noise training: models learn to ignore 1% weight flips
idea: Satellite AI on commercial hardware is trained with fault injection. Fine-tune LLM and vision models with random 1% bit flips injected into stored weights (with exponent clamping at load), producing weights that run from unrefreshed, ECC-free DRAM at 1% cell BER with negligible accuracy loss.
why: Fact 3 and supply: weights are 50-80% of inference memory; dropping 12.5% ECC and most refresh frees capacity and energy with no hardware change.
note: Similar to EDEN-style error-injection retraining; 1% BER is aggressive.

title: Noise-trained models let inference memory strip all ECC
idea: Shift the error budget from access time (ns) to training time (hours): models are trained with injected 1% bit flips on stored weights and KV entries, with exponent clamping, so inference memory runs with zero parity, zero decode latency and unprotected cheap cells.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% capacity and bandwidth spent on ECC bits and lets inference memory use 1%-BER cells with relaxed refresh (fact 3).
note: EDEN-style approximate DRAM known; 1% BER on weights is very aggressive.

title: Chemostat refresh holds corrected-error population at a setpoint
idea: A chemostat holds a culture at steady density by tuning its dilution rate; let each bank's refresh interval float under closed-loop control that targets a fixed rate of ECC-corrected errors seen by patrol scrubbing, lengthening refresh until corrections appear and shortening it when errors or temperature rise.
why: Most cells retain for seconds; tracking actual behaviour instead of the worst case could cut refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) by 50-80%, with ECC as the safety net.

title: Closed-loop refresh servo from DDR5 error-check-and-scrub counters
idea: 10-person constraint: no silicon, only firmware listening to the die. Read DDR5's built-in ECS (error check and scrub) counts and the on-die ECC error reports per bank. A PI controller stretches each bank's refresh interval until the corrected-error rate reaches a set target (e.g. 1e-12 per bit-hour), and backs off as temperature rises.
why: Fact 3: refresh follows actual leakage instead of the worst-case datasheet, typically 2-4x fewer refreshes at the same reliability. It ships as BMC or memory-controller firmware.

title: A patch table on the FPGA: weak bits live in SRAM
idea: 10-person constraint: no die changes. The CXL controller keeps a small CAM/SRAM table (~1 MB per 64 GB) with the address and correct value of every profiled weak bit. Reads are patched on the fly and writes update the table, so the DRAM runs at a refresh interval set by its strong-cell population.
why: Fact 3: the ~0.001% of weak bits stop setting refresh, which can move from 64 ms to over 1 s, at a cost of ~1 MB of SRAM per 64 GB.

title: Wafer-position-aware ECC strength fused per die
idea: Scale jump (wafer map -> die config): edge and notch-region dies show worse retention tails, so at sort each die's ECC mode (SEC vs DEC vs chipkill-lite) is fused based on its wafer radius and measured margin. Strong dies ship more user capacity and weak dies ship more parity.
why: Turns marginal edge dies into sellable parts and reclaims ~3-6% capacity on center dies.

title: Substitute mined indium with indium recovered from scrapped LCD panels
idea: Swap primary indium (China ~60% of refining) for indium leached from e-waste LCD/ITO glass by acid recovery and electrowinning, feeding IGZO/ITO sputter targets for <=400 C oxide memory tiers.
why: Removes an emerging chokepoint for oxide-semiconductor memory; e-waste displays hold enough indium for many fabs' targets.

title: DRAM's own capacitor forest replaces package decoupling MLCCs
idea: Combine the cell-capacitor process with power-delivery decoupling: the one added mask shorts blocks of storage capacitors in periphery gaps and die corners into on-die decaps (>1 uF/mm2, since 5 fF per ~900 nm2 cell), deleting most BaTiO3/Ni MLCCs and tantalum capacitors on HBM and DIMM substrates.
why: Sidesteps recurring MLCC and tantalum (DRC) shortages; quieter supply lets VDD margin drop ~5%, a direct CV2 energy cut.
note: Cell-capacitor decaps already common in DRAM periphery.

title: Formic-acid vapor oxide reduction built into the Cu-Cu bonder
idea: Combine the solder industry's formic-acid oxide reduction with Cu-Cu micro-pillar thermocompression: dies and wafer are exposed to formic-acid vapor in nitrogen at ~200 C inside the bonder, reducing Cu2O, then pressed immediately in the same oxygen-free atmosphere, replacing argon plasma cleaning.
why: Rare-gas-free fine-pitch bonding at lower thermal budget (DRAM retention degrades with hot anneals); enables 3-10 um Cu-Cu memory stacking without argon.

title: Theatre understudy: on-module spare die shadows the riskiest die
idea: Adapted from theatre understudies who rehearse the lead's part so the show goes on: an RDIMM carries one extra die whose data path is steered by a trailing-node mux; firmware watches per-die correctable-error trends and continuously mirrors whichever die is degrading fastest into the understudy, swapping it out with no data loss when it crosses a threshold.
why: Field failure and screening cost: modules can be built from lower-bin dies because the single most likely failure is pre-mirrored; one spare per 10 dies (~10% capacity) can replace stricter and costlier screening.
note: Similar to existing DDDC/ADDDC chip sparing.

title: Eliminate yield loss from retention: sell short-retention dies to streaming customers
idea: Bin dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass 8-16 ms and sell them at a discount into weight-streaming inference appliances whose firmware runs 4-8x refresh or proves per-pass re-reads. Dies now scrapped or patched with redundancy become supply.
why: Raises usable DRAM bit supply a few percent up to ~10% per wafer during a 4x price shock without new fabs (capital intensity).

title: Eliminate the zero-defect requirement: DIMMs from downgraded DRAM dies
idea: Buy DRAM dies that failed full-spec binning, assemble them into modules at a contract manufacturer with an on-module SPD map of bad rows, and have a Linux memmap/badram driver retire those pages at boot.
why: Recovers supply that fabs scrap or sell for scrap, at deep discount: 5-15% more usable bits from existing wafer output.
note: Downgraded dies already sell as lower-grade parts; small supply gain.

title: Eliminate small-buyer spot premium: purchasing cooperative pools OEM demand
idea: Eliminate spot-market exposure for small OEMs: a ~$500k-funded purchasing co-op aggregates 50-200 small hardware makers' forecasts into contract-size volumes, holds a shared rolling buffer, and allocates by commitment.
why: Small buyers pay spot premiums of 30-100% in shortages; pooling wins contract pricing and allocation.

title: Eliminate external DRAM from low-end devices: MCU redesign service
idea: Eliminate the DRAM chip from products that never needed Linux: a consultancy with an open template library ports low-end routers, thermostats and HMIs from 128-512MB DDR boards to MCU, on-chip SRAM and XIP flash designs; $1M seeds ten conversions.
why: Billions of IoT units carry legacy DDR; removing it frees legacy-node supply for critical uses.

title: Reverse the airflow: DIMMs breathe first, processors second
idea: Rearrange server layout so cold inlet air, or the first segment of the liquid cold-plate loop, crosses the DRAM before the CPUs/GPUs: DIMM banks move to the chassis front and accelerators sit downstream. DRAM hot spots drop from ~85-95 C to ~50-60 C.
why: Exits the >85 C double-refresh range and halves leakage per ~10 C, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~2-8x (fact 3); a chassis change, no fab.

title: Buy retention-reject DRAM and qualify it for cooled datacenters
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: dies binned out for leakage-tail failures at 85 C / 64 ms are not dead, only heat-intolerant. A business buys these rejects, re-screens them at 25-40 C with a 16-32 ms refresh contract, and sells them as qualified modules for immersion- or liquid-cooled racks, with controller firmware enforcing each module's refresh profile.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering a few percent of output from existing fabs with zero new capex; buyers get bits well below 4x contract prices.

title: Dead-bank harvesting turns partial DRAM dies into lower-capacity SKUs
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: instead of scrapping dies whose repair redundancy runs out in a few banks, fuse those banks off. Sell the dies as 3/4- or 7/8-capacity parts with a mode register the controller maps around, as CPU makers do with harvested cores.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer ~2-6% at zero capital. The gain is largest for HBM, where one bad die scraps an entire stack.

title: Lizard-tail autotomy: salvaging fab-reject dies by amputating failed mats
idea: Lizards shed a tail to survive. Buy DRAM dies that fail final test on a few unrepairable mats or a dead sense-amp stripe, map those regions out with post-package repair plus a controller remap table, and sell them as odd-capacity modules (e.g., 14 GB) for caching tiers. $1M covers a used-tester test flow and first lots within 24 months.
why: Supply axis: turns several % of yield fallout into sellable bits at a fraction of new cost/bit, with no fab capex.

title: Margin-binned short-refresh SKU rescues dies failing JEDEC
idea: Dies that fail JEDEC sense margin at 85 C are binned (not scrapped) into a datacenter SKU whose controller runs 2x refresh and stronger ECC, with the measured margin written into SPD.
why: Raises usable supply by converting yield loss into product; few-percent more bits per wafer at zero capex.
note: Derated datacenter SKU from margin-failing dies; few-percent supply gain.

title: Jam jar: precursor ampoule heel recovery and repurification service
idea: Stimulus 'jam jar' (the last scrape left in the jar) -> a 10-person team collects returned ALD/CVD ampoules still holding 10-25% unused Hf, Zr, Ru or Mo precursor heel, fractionally sublimes or distills it to spec and refills the ampoules.
why: Recovers scarce-metal precursors otherwise incinerated; cuts precursor demand ~15-20%.

title: Po memory from four common elements: HSG polysilicon ONO capacitor
idea: Po: 'the cell contains only silicon, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus.' Extracted: revive the late-1990s stacked capacitor with hemispherical-grain rugged polysilicon electrodes (2-2.5x area), a thin nitrided oxide-nitride dielectric and doped-poly plugs, removing TiN, Ru, Zr, Hf and W from the cell.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: zero chokepoint metals in the array, fully U.S.-manufacturable on 200 mm tools; density is modest but material supply risk falls to ~0.
note: Known late-1990s HSG/ONO cell; works only at large nodes.

title: Smart-valve rinse segregation feeds matched water regeneration trains
idea: Worsen: mix every rinse stream into one waste line so nothing can be reclaimed. Flip: install conductivity/TOC-sensing smart valves at each wet bench that split rinse water into ~5 contaminant classes, each piped to a matched regeneration train (EDI, UV-ozone, RO), reaching ~90% water reuse by design.
why: Water intensity: ~90% reuse versus ~40-60% typical, making fabs viable in water-stressed U.S. sites.

title: Conductor's staggered entries: sense amps fire by section
idea: A conductor brings sections in one after another. Each row's sense amps are split into four groups fired ~300 ps apart within tRCD, flattening the peak current that bounces local ground and corrupts late-resolving SAs.
why: Cuts peak SA current ~4x and the ground-bounce share of the noise budget, letting SA devices shrink ~20% (fact 7).

title: Voyager engineer's lane sparing with lifetime eye-margin remapping
idea: Voyager has run for 49 years on redundancy: add 10% spare lanes, have the base die measure every lane's eye margin weekly and move traffic off lanes that are degrading before they fail, keeping a wear map in on-die fuses.
why: Turns 10 year/125 C bump and TSV wear-out from a fatal event into graceful degradation, which allows fewer, finer-pitch lanes without needing big margins.
note: Lane repair and sparing already exist in HBM and server memory.

title: Small-lot known-good-die brokerage for IoT SiP makers
idea: $1 IoT and medical SiP designers need 1k-10k bare DRAM dies, but suppliers sell only huge lots. A 10-person firm buys whole wafers, runs wafer-level probe, dicing and KGD sort, and sells tested dies in small lots.
why: Opens supply to fragmented demand and spreads buying across more suppliers.
note: Small-lot die banks already exist.

title: Weak-retention dies resold as short-refresh AI memory
idea: Time-shift the binning: rather than scrapping dies that fail 64 ms retention, bin them by tail and sell them qualified at 16-32 ms refresh for AI accelerators that refresh aggressively anyway.
why: Scarce supply: recovers a few percent of wafer output as sellable bits with zero new fab capacity.
note: Recovers only a few percent of output.

title: Forming-gas hydrogen tracer replaces helium leak checking fleet-wide
idea: Time-and-scale shift of a maintenance routine: every vacuum tool and gas line in the fab is leak-checked with 5% H2/N2 forming gas and networked MEMS hydrogen sensors that log trends continuously instead of once per shift.
why: Leak checking is a top helium sink. This saves ~10-20% of fab helium, and continuous monitoring catches leaks days earlier.

title: On-site electrochemical persulfate regeneration closes the sulfuric loop
idea: Periodic-table walk, S (16): electrolyze spent sulfuric acid on boron-doped-diamond anodes to regenerate peroxydisulfate continuously, so the cleaning oxidant is remade on-site rather than consuming fresh H2SO4 and H2O2.
why: ~90% less sulfuric/peroxide purchase and wastewater; fluorine-free; uses only S, O, H and C/B electrodes.
note: Electrolytic sulfuric/persulfate regeneration is already sold to fabs.

title: Ca: dry lime beds turn fab fluorine into resaleable fluorspar
idea: Replace water-fed local wet scrubbers on etch/CVD exhaust with a plasma abatement front end plus heated CaO/Ca(OH)2 granular beds that capture HF and fluorine as CaF2, sold back to HF producers as synthetic fluorspar.
why: Water: wet scrubbers are ~5-10% of fab water and drop to ~0; it also closes the loop on fluorspar, a critical mineral.

title: Fe: iron-boron pair photodissociation screen bins wafers for retention
idea: A benchtop laser plus photoconductance tool measures minority-carrier lifetime before and after a flash that splits Fe-B pairs, giving interstitial iron per wafer; a 10-person company sells it as incoming-wafer screening that routes iron-rich wafers away from retention-critical products.
why: Iron is a top retention-tail culprit (fact 3); early binning lifts yield and lets fabs qualify wafers grown in non-Spruce-Pine crucibles safely.
note: Fe metrology via Fe-B dissociation is standard fab QC.

title: Ti: titanium-airframe damage tolerance schedules DIMM replacement from error growth
idea: Borrowing aerospace titanium inspection logic (Paris-law crack growth), fleet software fits each DIMM's correctable-error growth curve and predicts time to first uncorrectable error, scheduling replacement or regrading at planned maintenance.
why: Keeps weaker modules safely in service longer and avoids crashes; cuts premature replacements ~30%.

title: Reclaim retention-failed dies for short-lived AI buffers
idea: IFR: no die is scrap. Dies that fail 64 ms retention screening are binned by measured retention (8-32 ms) and sold as accelerator scratch modules, where the controller refreshes faster or the runtime guarantees the data (activations, KV spill) dies sooner.
why: Scarcity: recovers a few percent of wafer output with zero capex; at 4x contract prices each recovered percent is worth billions in supply.

title: ECC syndromes trigger background column remapping
idea: Ideal result: a memory that fixes faults before anyone notices. On-die ECC logs syndromes per column in a small nonvolatile table; repeat offenders are remapped to spare columns online, with data copied during refresh idle time.
why: Keeps parts in service and cuts module returns; periphery repair happens continuously in the field.

title: Scribe-line sensors replace blanket monitor wafers
idea: Within $1M/24 months: put film-thickness, sheet-resistance and particle test structures in product scribe lines and pair them with tool-sensor virtual-metrology models, so process qualification uses product wafers instead of blanket monitor wafers; pilot with one fab partner.
why: Monitor and dummy wafers consume ~10-20% of prime-wafer starts; halving them frees silicon, crucibles and helium for real DRAM.

title: Substitute in-place NV writes with ping-pong shadow-row versioning
idea: Map each logical row to two physical NV rows and write updates alternately with a version and CRC, so a write cut by power loss leaves the old row valid and wear is spread across both copies.
why: Power-fail atomicity with no logging software and 2x wear spreading; doubles endurance of FeRAM/ReRAM-class cells at 2x raw bits for hot regions only.

title: Lego: partial-good DRAM dies stitched into reduced-capacity modules
idea: Stimulus 'Lego' (odd bricks still build things) -> a 10-person assembly shop buys wafer-sort rejects with one dead bank or sub-array, maps bad regions on an FPGA tester and builds modules whose controller firmware fences the bad addresses, sold as reduced-capacity memory.
why: Recovers silicon whose helium, energy and water were already spent on scrapped dies; adds several percent to effective supply.
note: Downbinned partial-good memory is long-standing practice.

title: Glass blower: refurbish quartz chamber parts instead of buying new
idea: Stimulus 'glass blower' -> a 10-person shop strips etch deposits from quartz focus rings, bell jars and furnace tubes, re-fuses eroded zones with a hydrogen-oxygen torch, fire-polishes and recertifies them, extending part life 2-4x.
why: Fab quartzware draws on the same high-purity quartz as crucibles; refurbishment roughly halves that consumption and spare-part cost.
note: Quartzware refurbishment services already exist commercially.

title: Compost: e-waste DRAM package reclamation and reballing line
idea: From 'compost': a small line desolders DRAM packages from scrapped boards with IR rework tools, reballs them, screens them on a low-cost FPGA-based tester, and bins them by speed and retention for secondary markets. Equipment fits well under $1M.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit; recovers bits already manufactured and avoids helium, quartz and EUV use entirely.

title: Turn off memory mirroring and rank sparing; checkpoint in software
idea: Box: remove redundancy × BIOS RAS settings × channel/rank × fleet policy × application checkpoint and replication. Servers configured for mirroring (50% of capacity lost) or rank sparing (12–25%) are switched to full capacity, with reliability provided by software checkpoints and service-level replication.
why: Reclaims stranded capacity on installed hardware immediately; configuration only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Hot-air rework refurbishes failed DIMMs at chip granularity
idea: Ideal: no DRAM chip is ever wasted. Closest: decommissioned and failed server DIMMs pass through 1990s-era BGA rework stations and memory testers; the single faulty package is swapped for a harvested good one and the module is re-certified with a lower-speed or extra-scrub profile.
why: Supply: returns ~70-80% of failed DIMMs to service (most failures are one chip), adding capacity at a fraction of new cost.

title: Bistable e-paper display as its own framebuffer
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): electrophoretic and cholesteric display films are made roll-to-roll and hold an image at zero power, so signage, shelf labels, dashboards and e-readers push partial updates straight from the compositor to the pixels and drop the DRAM framebuffer entirely.
why: Billions of low-end displays carry a DRAM/SRAM framebuffer; the bistable film stores the picture itself, removing that memory and its refresh energy.
note: E-paper and memory-in-pixel displays already hold images without a framebuffer.

title: Optical-fiber stack-and-draw: sliced silicon-core fiber capacitor plates
idea: Draw a preform of doped-silicon rods in silica (molten-core fiber method), restack and redraw until cores are ~20-30 nm at cell pitch, fuse the bundle into a boule, slice it like an ingot into wafers of vertical Si electrodes in SiO2, recess the silica to expose 1-3 um Si pillars as bottom electrodes, and bond onto the transistor wafer through oversized landing pads that absorb lattice misregistration. Elements: Si, O, B, P.
why: Removes deep etch and EUV for the capacitor layer (facts 1, 4): aspect ratio set by slice thickness, not etch; fiber draw is cheap, continuous and U.S.-strong.
note: Draw-ratio replaces litho and HAR etch; 25 nm Si cores break up (Rayleigh) and cannot register to transistors at cell pitch.

title: Eliminate the wafer fab entirely: thermally drawn fiber DRAM
idea: Assemble a macroscopic preform of semiconductor, glass and metal stripes encoding capacitor-transistor cross-sections, thermally draw it into kilometres of fiber with thousands of parallel nanoscale cells, then cut, align and tile fiber segments into planks addressed at their ends.
why: Capital intensity: replaces lithography with fiber-draw towers costing millions instead of billions; density and access speed are open questions.
note: Fiber devices exist at micron scale; nanoscale gated transistors with end-addressing over km fibers need a miracle.

title: Swiss-roll DRAM: one planar array rolled into forty tiers
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality/curvature: build a single planar 1T1C array (thin trench capacitors) on a strained SiNx/Si bilayer over a sacrificial layer, then release it so the strip self-rolls into a 40-turn tube. All bitlines exit along the strip's leading edge, which stays flat and is hybrid-bonded to a logic die, so 40 effective tiers come from one mask set.
why: Fact 2 and 4: ~40x bits per litho pass without tier-by-tier processing; capital per bit could drop several-fold if roll registration, thermal path and contact yield can be solved.
note: 40 tiers per litho pass, but spiral bitlines, registration, contacts and heat need miracles.

title: Coral strain-templating: each tier self-assembles directly atop the last
idea: New coral polyps settle on the old skeleton; use the vertical correlation seen in stacked quantum dots: tier N's buried metal nodes leave a periodic strain and surface-energy imprint through a ~10 nm spacer that pins the block-copolymer or nanoparticle self-assembly defining tier N+1's features exactly above them. Only the first tier is lithographed.
why: If replication fidelity holds, 12-16 tiers cost one critical litho plus a cheap coat/anneal per tier, ~10x bits/mm2 at near-planar wafer cost and no EUV beyond tier 1 (fact 4).
note: Would give 12-16 tiers from one litho; error accumulation and 10 nm strain-pinning fidelity unproven.

title: DNA-brick 3D crystals cast an entire multi-tier cell array
idea: Grow micron-thick 3D DNA-brick crystals (programmed voxel lattices at ~2.5 nm resolution) on the CMOS wafer from anchor pads, with designed voids forming the channel, wordline and bitline network of a 6-tier gain-cell array; infiltrate by sequential ALD (In2O3, HfO2, TiN/Ru) and burn out the DNA to leave a ceramic-metal cast.
why: All tiers are patterned at ~8 nm pitch by one self-assembly step and no masks; 6 tiers x ~2x lateral shrink is ~10x+ bits/mm2, at flat cost if enzymatic DNA synthesis reaches <$50 per wafer (fact 4).
note: One self-assembly step patterns all tiers at ~8 nm; defectivity, CMOS registration and wire resistance need miracles.

title: Moire superlattice traps self-assemble a ten-nanometer bit lattice
idea: Invert 'cells must be lithographically patterned' -> let a twist angle draw them. A twisted hBN/WSe2 stack on glass forms a moire potential with ~10 nm period, each minimum a trap holding a few electrons; relaxed-pitch crossbar gates address blocks and an adjacent 2D charge sensor reads occupancy.
why: Lithography-free ~1e12 sites/cm^2 (density, EUV elimination, fact 4); room-temperature retention needs >100 meV moire depth and single-site addressing is unsolved.
note: Moire potentials are tens of meV: no room-temperature retention, and single-site addressing is unsolved.

title: Po: the bit is a rattle — ion-in-cage endohedral fullerene dipole
idea: Po: the bit is a rattle in a box. Extracted: a Li+@C60 endohedral molecule has two off-centre sites for the lithium ion; a field pushes the ion to one side, forming a molecular dipole that shifts the threshold of an adjacent 2D-channel transistor, while the cage stops the ion from ever migrating.
why: ~1 nm bits with no lattice ion migration (no wear). The room-temperature barrier between sites is speculative.
note: 1 nm molecular dipole bit; Li+ likely rattles freely in C60 at RT, so retention is doubtful; placement is unsolved.

title: Naturally layered crystal grows the 3D tier stack itself
idea: Po: chips are grown like minerals, not built. Epitaxially grow a Ruddlesden-Popper layered oxide whose unit cell alternates a semiconducting perovskite sheet with an insulating rock-salt spacer, so one PLD/MBE growth yields hundreds of perfectly registered channel/dielectric tiers; gate and bitline holes are then etched vertically through the crystal.
why: Fact 2: hundreds of superlattice deposition steps collapse into one epitaxy; atomically flat spacers give near-identical Vt in every tier.
note: Hundreds of registered tiers in one epitaxy; nm-thin channels and per-tier contacts need miracles.

title: Femtosecond-laser-written volumetric memory inside a glass block
idea: IFR: 'the array is written in the volume with no layers at all.' Backward: focus femtosecond pulses inside a doped glass block to precipitate conductive nanowire lines, laser-crystallized high-k capacitor voxels and oxide-semiconductor channel segments, writing word lines, bit lines and cells in 3D at ~0.5-1 um voxel pitch in one machine.
why: Capital (fact 4): a ~$1M laser writer instead of a fab; ~1e9 cells per mm3 if laser-formed devices switch reliably.
note: Distinct device materials cannot be precipitated from one glass; serial voxel writing is far too slow.

title: Vertical tier-column pages replace 8 kb horizontal rows
idea: Substitute the horizontal row as the unit of activation with a vertical slice: one activation opens N tiers x a 16-bitline group (e.g., 32x16 = 512 bits, one 64 B line); tier-select lines act as the row address and the vertical bitline pillar group is the page, each pillar landing on its own sense amp in a bonded CMOS wafer.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): 8 kb -> 512 b page cuts activation energy ~10x toward ~0.6 pJ per useful bit; activations spread over many small pages dilute hammer counts.
note: Tier-column pages cut overfetch ~10x; small-page sensing area overhead is the cost.

title: Spare-wafer remapping replaces known-good-die testing in wafer-on-wafer stacks
idea: Substitute die-level HBM stacking (TSV + microbump + known-good-die test) with wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding of 9 full DRAM wafers, one a spare; every bank has a fuse-programmable vertical bypass in the base logic so a failed bank on tier k is remapped to the same footprint on the spare tier.
why: HBM TSV tax and 20-30% yield loss (fact 6): one bond step per wafer instead of per die; stack yield rises from ~0.92^8 = 51% to >85% for 12.5% area overhead.
note: Wafer-on-wafer DRAM with a spare wafer and bank remap; through-wafer vias still needed.

title: Swap DRAM KV cache for an append-only log on write-once NVM
idea: Substitute DRAM with endurance-limited NVM by matching the workload: KV entries are written once and read thousands of times, so an HBM-style stack of dense PCM/RRAM dies holds them as an append-only log. The accelerator prefetches the next layer's KV into SRAM while the current layer computes, which hides the ~100-300 ns NVM reads. A conversation's whole region is erased at once when it ends, so each cell sees only ~1e5-1e6 writes in its lifetime.
why: KV cache is 30-70% of HBM demand in long-context serving. The write-once pattern sidesteps NVM's endurance limit, so 2-3x fewer DRAM bits are needed per served token.
note: Write-once KV matches NVM; prefill write bandwidth and RRAM endurance over many conversations are doubts.

title: Substitute new fabs with bolt-on memory-tier upfit shops
idea: Swap greenfield fabs for independent BEOL-only upfit shops (no implant, no furnaces above 400 C) that receive customers' finished logic or DRAM wafers and deposit extra memory tiers on top, like a paint shop for wafers.
why: Capex ~$1-2B versus $15B+, buildable in ~18 months; adds bits to wafers that already exist.

title: Vertical CCD charge-packet strings using 3D NAND tier stacks
idea: Fuse 1970s CCD memory with 3D NAND's stacked-gate vertical channel: 128 wordline tiers around a vertical poly-Si or IGZO channel are clocked in three phases to shift charge packets up and down, so bits live as packets in potential wells with no per-bit capacitor or lateral transistor. A sense amp at the string top reads packets as they arrive: serial within a string, massively parallel across millions of strings.
why: Fact 2: a 3D storage element with no capacitor and no lateral transistor, reusing NAND tooling; 5-10x bits per mm2 at block-sequential latency of a few hundred ns.

title: Si/SiGe superlattice selectively oxidized into 100-plate stacked capacitor
idea: Combine GAA nanosheet epitaxy with selective conversion: grow 100 alternating Si/SiGe layers, cut a slit, replace the SiGe with high-k through Ge-selective etch and ALD refill, and silicide alternate Si sheets contacted from two opposite staircases to form an interdigitated stack. Horizontal plates become stacked storage capacitors for 3D DRAM tiers with no vertical high-AR hole.
why: Facts 1 and 2: capacitance grows with tier count instead of AR, and one epi stack serves both transistor and capacitor tiers, aiming at the 26+ tier break-even.
note: Mainstream 3D DRAM already uses Si/SiGe stacks; ganging tiers into one capacitor trades away bits per tier.

title: TFET gatekeeper fused in series with a MOSFET access channel
idea: One wordline gates a single channel with a p+ tunnel-junction segment next to the storage node and a conventional n+ MOSFET segment toward the bitline. In the off state the band-to-band tunnel junction blocks with a steep (<40 mV/dec) turn-off, and in the on state the MOSFET segment supplies the drive current.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): about 100x lower off-current at the same on-current. The refresh interval goes from 64 ms to seconds, cutting refresh energy by ~90%.
note: Hybrid tunnel-junction segment for steep turn-off; ambipolarity and drive tradeoffs.

title: Back gate merged as a second, slow wordline
idea: Build the array on UTBB FD-SOI with a ground plane per row group. Hold the plane strongly negative while the group is retaining (Vt +0.3-0.5 V) and swing it toward neutral only for the group being activated.
why: Decoupling on-current from off-leakage gives ~100x less subthreshold leakage. It also lets the wordline boost fall from 3 V toward 2 V, about 55% less CV^2 (fact 10).
note: Back-plane swing energy and FD-SOI array density are costs.

title: Sub-wordline driver doubles as row-wise back-gate bias generator
idea: Build access transistors with a buried back gate patterned per row, and merge the back-gate driver into the existing sub-wordline driver: idle rows sit at about -1 V back bias to choke the leakage tail, and the activated row flips to forward bias for stronger drive. One driver serves two gates, so no extra decoder is needed.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): a 150-200 mV effective Vt shift on idle rows could cut tail leakage ~10x (refresh 64 to ~512 ms); forward bias on the open row allows lower wordline voltage (fact 10).

title: Tier-select transistor at each staircase step for 3D DRAM
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, put a vertical oxide transistor at each staircase landing that acts as a tier decoder switch, so a few shared vertical wordline drivers fan out to N tiers through local selects; staircase contacts drop from N x rows to rows + N.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM (fact 2): staircase contacts and decoder area grow with tier count; this keeps periphery area nearly flat from 26 to 100+ tiers.

title: Coaxial hole: capacitor sheath below, gate-all-around transistor above
idea: One high-AR hole per 4F2 site does both jobs: the lower ~80% is lined as a cylinder capacitor (plate/high-k/storage shell), and the top ~20% passes through a deposited wordline plane where a channel-all-around transistor joins the storage shell to a top bitline. Gate length is set by wordline-plane thickness, so capacitor and transistor share one etch and one alignment.
why: Facts 1 and 4: 4F2 (about 33% less area than 6F2) with full-height capacitor and no storage-node contact or landing pad, deleting ~2 critical litho layers.

title: DRAM tiers and NAND tiers sharing one CMOS-under-array stack
idea: Combine a 3D DRAM tier block and a 3D NAND tier block above the same CMOS-under-array die, sharing staircases and page buffers, so pages migrate between DRAM and NAND tiers internally at TB/s without crossing an I/O pin.
why: Do DRAM's job with less DRAM: cold pages demote in-die, so a system needs maybe 30-50% fewer DRAM bits; data movement (fact 5) for swap traffic nearly eliminated.

title: Vertical wordline makes each activation span tiers, not rows
idea: Combine tier count with page size: in a 3D array with vertical wordlines and per-tier horizontal bitlines, an activate opens one pillar's cells in all 64-128 tiers, each tier landing on its own sense amp at the staircase edge, so a page is 64-128 bits by construction.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~64-128x less activation per useful bit (activate share <0.1 pJ/bit); row hammer (fact 9): logically adjacent rows are separate pillars, not coupled neighbors.

title: Silicon-skull cold crucible pulls Czochralski ingots without quartz
idea: Combine induction skull melting with Czochralski pulling: a segmented water-cooled copper crucible plus RF induction holds a frozen silicon skull so the melt only touches silicon; oxygen for internal gettering is supplied by controlled O2/N2 gas doping instead of crucible dissolution.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucible (>80% concentration) and its consumable cost from DRAM wafer supply; tunable oxygen improves wafer uniformity (trade: +20-40% melt energy).
note: Dislocation-free growth in skull melt with high heat loss unproven at 300 mm.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM routes around dead mats and bits
idea: Combine Cerebras-style wafer-scale integration with DRAM: the wafer is never diced but hybrid-bonded whole to a wafer-scale compute or interposer wafer. Mat-level crossbar routing disables dead mats, and a code layer covers 1% cell BER.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packaging, KGD sorting and the HBM TSV/microbump tax, giving ~2-3x bandwidth per edge-mm and ~20% back-end cost avoided (facts 5, 6).

title: Interposer fabbed as a mature-node DRAM capacity tier
idea: Combine the passive silicon interposer (2,500+ mm2 of idle silicon under every AI package) with a 2x-nm-class trench-capacitor DRAM array built into the same wafer in depreciated 300 mm lines, wired to the GPU by mm-scale interposer traces as a near tier between HBM and CXL. Arrays are tiled with stitched redundancy so a bad block is fused off instead of scrapping the interposer.
why: Capacity and capital intensity: ~10-30 GB extra per package at mature-node cost/bit with zero added footprint and ~2-4 pJ/bit access; shifts bits off scarce EUV-node wafers.

title: Hub-and-spoke periphery die time-shared by four array dies
idea: Borrowed from airline and parcel hub-and-spoke networks: four periphery-free array dies (cells and local latches only) stack on one logic-process hub die holding decoders, pumps, refresh, I/O and test, linked by hybrid bonds; the hub serves whichever array is active.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): amortizing periphery over four arrays lifts array efficiency from ~51% to ~80%+ and moves periphery to EUV-free mature logic.
note: Only the bonded die is directly attached; others need TSVs and pitch-matched SAs.

title: Skyscraper sky lobbies: tier-local sense amps every 16 tiers
idea: Adapted from supertall-building sky lobbies (express elevator to a lobby, local elevators onward): long vertical bitlines in a 3D DRAM stack are cut into 16-tier segments, each ending at a 'sky lobby' tier holding oxide-TFT local sense amps that drive a low-swing express global bitline down to CMOS.
why: Bitline capacitance seen per sense drops ~8x, so Cs can shrink from ~5 fF to <1 fF with the same margin (fact 1) and stacks can exceed 100 tiers without a high-AR capacitor (fact 2).
note: Hierarchical bitlines with oxide local SAs every 16 tiers; known in 2D, new in 3D.

title: Precast concrete: test each crystalline tier before stacking it
idea: Like precast panels cured and inspected off-site, each single-crystal DRAM tier is built on a donor, wafer-tested, and only then transferred by hydrogen smart-cut onto the stack, with bad sub-arrays remapped before the next tier is added.
why: Monocrystalline lateral transistors in every tier (facts 2,3: tighter leakage tail) and stack yield that does not compound per tier, making 26+ tiers economic.
note: Testing a tier before transfer conflicts with implant-through-devices; needs bond-and-thin flow instead.

title: Power-electronics snubber: slew-shaped wordline edges cut hammer disturbance
idea: Adapted from snubbers and slew-rate control that suppress ringing and EMI in power converters: wordline drivers use a programmable current-starved two-segment edge (fast to ~70%, then slow ramp, and a slow falling tail), reducing dV/dt coupling and the abrupt trap-assisted electron emission at wordline fall that drives row hammer and RowPress flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturbance scales with edge rate and injection at wordline fall; shaped edges may raise flip thresholds 2-4x at a ~1-2 ns tRAS/tRP cost, shrinking mitigation-refresh overhead.

title: Regulated-utility rate base for a domestic memory utility
idea: Adapted from electric utility regulation: a public commission grants a U.S. DRAM fab a regulated ~8-9% return on its rate base, with guaranteed offtake by federal and critical-infrastructure buyers at cost-of-service prices.
why: Lowers the cost of capital and removes cyclicality for one or two U.S. baseline fabs, cutting cost per bit ~10-20% against merchant financing while guaranteeing domestic supply (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Minify the fab: 400 C-only periphery add-on lines in U.S.
idea: Build $1-2B BEOL-only lines (no furnaces, epi, implanters or EUV) near U.S. packaging sites that add IGZO periphery, row-buffer and repair tiers onto array wafers bought from any supplier, capturing roughly half of die value domestically.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~1/8 the capex of a full DRAM fab and ~18-month build versus 3-5 years.

title: Magnify wafer use: double-sided cells around a mid-height bitline
idea: Bury the bitline at mid-height in the wafer. An upper vertical transistor and capacitor are built on the front side; after bonding and thinning, a second vertical transistor and capacitor are built on the backside, both hanging from the same bitline. Two storage cells then share each 4F2 footprint, for 2F2 effective.
why: Density and litho: doubles bits per mm2 without a smaller F, so the same EUV layer count buys about 2x the bits.
note: Backside second cell layer doubles density; backside thermal budget harms front-side cells.

title: Cold-wall skull crucible pulls 300 mm silicon without quartz
idea: Minify the crucible to nothing: melt silicon in a water-cooled, segmented copper induction crucible so a frozen silicon skull holds the melt, and pull Czochralski crystals from it. Electromagnetic stirring and partial levitation keep the melt off the cold wall.
why: Removes Spruce Pine high-purity quartz (>80% share) from ingot growth entirely and lowers interstitial oxygen; attacks the scarcest crystal-growth consumable.

title: Bitline-direct bonding: one bond per 16 bitlines
idea: MAGNIFY interface width down to the subarray: hybrid-bond each subarray's local I/O lines (one 1 um pad per 16 bitlines) straight to compute-die pads, deleting global I/O lines, column muxes, the DDR PHY and most of the DRAM periphery.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and data-movement energy; claims ~30-40% more bits per DRAM wafer and <0.1 pJ/bit transfers.

title: Policy: glass-memory fabs qualified on raw BER plus mandated host ECC
idea: Fund new U.S. glass-substrate memory lines next to domestic glass makers, and back a JEDEC-style class that qualifies such memory on raw BER and retention with mandatory host-side ECC, instead of demanding near-perfect dies.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: weaker cells are accepted by standard, bringing memory onshore without EUV or silicon wafers.

title: Magnify the die to a whole undiced wafer slab
idea: Skip dicing, packaging and per-die final test: ship whole 300 mm DRAM wafers with fuse-mapped redundancy, face-to-face bonded to a wafer-scale logic or interposer wafer as a rack 'memory slab'.
why: Packaging, test and singulation are ~15-25% of DRAM cost and HBM TSV yield loss is 20-30%; a wafer slab avoids both while giving huge bandwidth.

title: Magnify module lifetime to 25 years: a memory utility
idea: A regulated-utility-style company owns optically attached CXL memory racks on 25-year books, decoupled from 4-year server refreshes, and rents GB-hours; fleet pooling (~85% utilization), compression and dedup stack on top of the long amortization.
why: 25/5 lifetime x ~2x utilization x ~2x compression x ~2.5x dedup = ~100x lower cost per used GB-year.
note: Stacked 100x multipliers are overclaimed; old DRAM energy and interface obsolescence.

title: Magnify the prize: $0.10/GB advance market commitment
idea: Governments and AI buyers pledge an advance market commitment to buy the first 10 exabytes of DRAM-class memory (<=100 ns, unlimited endurance via any architecture) at $0.10/GB, plus milestone prizes, modeled on the pneumococcal vaccine AMC.
why: Aims the whole startup and academic ecosystem at exactly 100x cheaper; guaranteed demand de-risks capex for radical processes (panels, R2R, NAND conversion).

title: Magnify cumulative volume: solarize memory with one open SKU
idea: Define one open-standard memory brick (fixed interface, form factor, capacity) and pay a declining per-GB feed-in subsidy for 10 years that steps down with each doubling of cumulative output, like German PV feed-in tariffs, forcing ~7 volume doublings on cheap processes.
why: Solar fell ~100x per watt through standardization plus guaranteed, declining support; a ~25-30% learning rate over ~7 doublings on a radical low-cost process yields ~100x.
note: DRAM already rides steep learning; subsidy unlikely to create new 100x curve.

title: Eliminate periphery and product layout from array wafers: universal lattice wafers
idea: Fabricate wafers that hold nothing but an endless, product-agnostic cell lattice (no decoders, sense amps or I/O), then hybrid-bond them wafer-to-wafer onto separately made logic wafers that define product, banking and die boundaries; die size is chosen at dicing.
why: Facts 4 and 7: the array fab needs ~40% fewer masks and no product-specific reticles, runs one recipe at full utilization, and periphery moves to a cheaper logic process; ~20-30% cost-per-bit gain.

title: Append-only KV log on NAND bonded beneath HBM
idea: Eliminate the flash translation layer and the SSD path for KV-cache spill: bond 3D NAND under the HBM base die and write KV caches as append-only logs aligned to erase blocks, erasing whole blocks when conversations expire, which matches NAND's native semantics so no mapping table, GC or write amplification is needed.
why: KV spill to SSD crosses PCIe at ~10-30 pJ/bit; in-stack NAND gives ~10x capacity per package at NAND cost/bit with only one fresh write per token.
note: Close to High Bandwidth Flash efforts; append-only KV fits NAND semantics.

title: Eliminate the front-end fab: US BEOL-only lines deposit memory on bought logic
idea: Buy finished mature-node CMOS logic wafers (including from U.S. foundries) and deposit memory tiers on them in retrofitted U.S. BEOL-only lines (MEMS, packaging or display fabs) that never exceed 400 C. On-die ECC and remap in the purchased logic absorb those lines' higher defect density.
why: Cuts new-capacity capital ~5x vs a DRAM fab and time-to-capacity to ~18 months, raising U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.

title: Eliminate the boom-bust cycle: allied strategic DRAM reserve
idea: Eliminate the price cycle that suppresses investment: a US/allied agency buys packaged DRAM and wafers in gluts, stores them in dry nitrogen, and releases them inside a price band in shortages, like a petroleum reserve.
why: A 2-3 month reserve would blunt 4x price spikes and let makers commit capex counter-cyclically.

title: Capacitor-first, transistor-last cell with high-temperature dielectric anneal
idea: Reverse the process order: build and crystallize the storage capacitor first (rutile TiO2 or SrTiO3 annealed at 700-800 C for k~70-100), then bond a thin single-crystal Si layer on top and form the access transistor with laser or microwave anneal so the capacitor is never reheated. The transistor never sees the capacitor's thermal budget, and the capacitor never has to tolerate the transistor's.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) and retention (fact 3): k~70+ gives ~2x Cs at today's aspect ratio, and a top-side transistor has no storage-node-to-substrate junction; ~2-4x longer refresh interval.
note: Perovskite dielectric leakage and bond alignment to dense pads are doubts.

title: Spend periphery to buy back the capacitor: 16-cell bitlines
idea: Reverse the classic trade of long bitlines to save sense amps: use 16-cell bitlines (Cbl ~0.4 fF) with SAs placed under the array, so a planar or shallow ~1 fF capacitor gives the same transfer ratio a 5 fF pillar gives today.
why: Fact 1: eliminates the 60-75:1 pillar etch and exotic high-k; capacitor module steps -30-40%. Requires SA-under-array at ~4x today's SA density.

title: SiGe bipolar global sense amps on a U.S. BiCMOS chiplet
idea: Reverse the amplifier family: local bitlines pass their signal through one array-side gain transistor onto global bitlines at 8x relaxed pitch, which cross hybrid bonds to SiGe HBT sense amps on a chiplet from a U.S. BiCMOS line (e.g., Vermont); HBT Vbe matching (~1 mV) beats MOS (~10-15 mV), and the milligrams of germanium per wafer can come from U.S. zinc refining.
why: Facts 7 and 1: ~10x lower offset allows 4x longer bitlines (SA count /4) or ~40% smaller Cs, all built domestically.

title: Interference lithography for arrays, multibeam e-beam for periphery
