idea: Reverse which region gets premium patterning: perfectly periodic array lines are printed by simple laser interference lithography (buildable in the U.S.) and pitch-split with U.S.-made deposition/etch, while the sparse, irregular periphery layers are written maskless by U.S.-built multi-column e-beam.
why: Fact 4: replaces 5-7 EUV layers and mask sets with an all-U.S. toolchain, removing the single-supplier EUV dependency.
note: DRAM cells need 2D honeycomb patterns plus cuts; multibeam e-beam throughput unproven at volume.

title: Pattern first, stack later: DUV tiers bonded into 3D
idea: Reverse 3D's 'stack then pattern through all tiers': each tier is a complete relaxed-pitch (F~35 nm, DUV-only) 2D DRAM-lite layer built on its own donor wafer, tested, then ion-cut transferred onto the stack with a coarse inter-tier via; repeat 8-16 times. Density comes from tier count, not EUV pitch.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): zero EUV layers; 16 tiers at ~1/8 the density per tier still give ~2x 2D density, using depreciated DUV fabs and known-good-tier yield control.

title: Vertical capacitor column segmented per tier, lateral transistors
idea: Swap the usual 3D orientation: keep transistors lateral in each tier but etch one deep vertical capacitor trench per cell column through all tiers; each tier's storage-node layer is exposed as a ring on the trench wall (isolated from neighbors by the inter-tier dielectric), a scalloped recess enlarges it, then one conformal high-k and a common plate fill finish every tier's capacitor at once.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): one HAR etch makes N tiers of ~0.7-1.5 fF capacitors without lateral capacitor recess; viable with short bitlines, aiming at break-even below 26 tiers.

title: Invert the supply chain: U.S. makes periphery, bonds arrays
idea: Use the CMOS-bonded-array split to reverse where value sits: periphery wafers come from existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic fabs, array-only wafers come from a lean new U.S. array fab or allied DRAM fabs, and hybrid bonding plus test happen domestically.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): an array-only fab skips ~40% of process steps; underused U.S. mature-node fabs supply periphery; capacity in ~2 years versus 5.
note: Array/periphery wafer split is known CBA; supply-chain inversion is the twist, but array fab still capital-heavy.

title: Nanoimprint DRAM: let the code eat the template defects
idea: Pattern critical DRAM layers by nanoimprint (no EUV, no light source) and stop fighting its defect density: imprint-induced particle and pinch defects (~1% of cells at worst) are mapped at test and corrected by on-die ECC.
why: NIL failed for DRAM mainly on defectivity; tolerating 1% BER removes that blocker and replaces EUV ($200M+ tools, one supplier) with ~10x cheaper, lower-power imprint tools.
note: Template defects repeat and cluster; overlay, not only defectivity, limits NIL for DRAM.

title: Open DRAM PDK: royalty-free cell, periphery and process recipes
idea: Reverse IP from secret to open: a federally funded consortium publishes a full 1x-nm-class DRAM process recipe, cell and sense-amp library and test programs under a royalty-free license, backed by a defensive patent pool. New fabs then license nothing from incumbents.
why: Lowers the entry barrier of years of process learning and litigation risk. Time from start to first good wafer for a new U.S. entrant could fall from ~5 years to ~2.

title: Tool vendors paid per good wafer, not per tool
idea: Reverse the capex flow: litho, etch and deposition vendors install tools in a new DRAM fab with no upfront charge and are paid a fee per good wafer pass, like aircraft-engine 'power by the hour'. Vendors share yield risk and keep the tools upgraded.
why: Capital intensity: ~70% of fab capex moves off the entrant's balance sheet, so a $15B+ barrier becomes an operating cost that scales with output.
note: Power-by-the-hour for fab tools; vendors' balance sheets and yield-risk sharing are the barrier.

title: Time-shared EUV: consortium scanners rented by the hour
idea: Rearrange ownership of the scarcest tool: a consortium fab hosts EUV scanners and tracks. DRAM startups send sealed lots in for the 5-7 EUV critical layers only and do every other step in their own lower-cost fabs.
why: EUV has one supplier and costs $200M+ per tool. Entrants avoid buying scanners, cutting entry capex by ~$1-2B and raising scanner utilization.

title: Segmented gate: negative retention finger guards the storage junction
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'strong on-current vs. tiny off-leakage': split the buried wordline into a long drive segment on the bitline side and a short, independently driven 'retention finger' over the storage-node junction. The finger sits at about -1 V except during the ~20 ns activation, so the drain field and trap-assisted tunnelling at the storage node are borne by a deeply-off segment while the drive segment can use a lower Vt.
why: Attacks Fact 3 (<=13 fA tail, GIDL/TAT dominated): target 10-50x lower tail leakage, stretching refresh from 32-64 ms toward ~1 s and recovering most of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss, at the cost of a second wordline driver per row.
note: Independent negative finger over storage junction; cost is second driver per row; related to dual-WF BCAT.

title: Per-row programmable Vt via charge-trap layer in the wordline stack
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: make a fixed property adjustable. A thin SiN charge-trap layer in the buried-wordline gate stack lets each row's access-transistor Vt be programmed by Fowler-Nordheim pulses at test and retrimmed in the field: leaky rows get ~+200 mV of Vt, strong rows keep low Vt for speed.
why: Compresses the retention distribution so refresh is set by a trimmed tail (Fact 3): 3-5x longer refresh interval without a global speed penalty.
note: Charge-trap Vt drift; row-level trim misses cell-level tail.

title: Prior action: commodity periphery base wafers sold for array build-up
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a merchant foundry pre-manufactures standardized periphery base wafers (sense amps, decoders, pumps and I/O on a fixed grid at 40 nm) in very high volume, and low-capex array companies add only BEOL memory tiers on top, as with gate arrays and structured ASICs.
why: 100x path: array entrants skip ~$15B front-end fabs and periphery design cost, base wafers aim at <$1500 at volume, and BEOL tier lines cost ~$0.5-1B; trade-offs: a fixed periphery limits array flexibility. Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability.
note: Merchant base wafers let low-capex entrants add tiers; hinges on an unproven BEOL DRAM cell.

title: Amplifier tiers interleaved every eight storage tiers
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: every 9th tier of the 3D stack is built from the same lateral transistors but wired as single-ended pre-amplifiers (gated source followers). Each one buffers an 8-tier local vertical bitline segment before it drives the long global bitline to the sense amp below.
why: Fact 1 and 2: cell needs ~1/4 the charge because the local segment capacitance is tiny, so lateral capacitors can be short and thin, making 26+ tiers practical.

title: Electromagnetic cold-crucible Czochralski eliminates the quartz crucible
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution (a field replaces the vessel): hold the melt in a segmented water-cooled copper crucible where induction currents heat and partly levitate it inside a frozen silicon skull, so silicon touches only silicon. Gettering oxygen is added deliberately through O2/H2O partial pressure, and nitrogen doping restores wafer strength.
why: Removes the HPQ crucible chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%) and crucible-borne metal contamination, using only Si, Cu, O and N.

title: Vertical-channel 6T SRAM built on the 4F² DRAM transistor process
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: reuse the vertical-channel transistor module being developed for 4F2 DRAM, add a complementary p-type pillar, and wire six vertical transistors as a cross-coupled latch in ~24-30F2, skipping the capacitor module entirely.
why: Bistable, so zero refresh; ~5x denser than logic SRAM (~0.004 vs ~0.021 um2/bit) and built in DRAM fabs without the capacitor module (~20-25% fewer steps); ~4x less dense than DRAM, so it targets hot refresh-heavy tiers (facts 3, 4).

title: Legacy-fab conversion fund for drop-in zero-refresh memory
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: a CHIPS-style program pays conversion costs plus a 5-year offtake for U.S. 200/300 mm legacy fabs (65-180 nm lines with idle tools) to run a standard refresh-free memory PDK (asymmetric-electrode AFE capacitor or self-selecting crosspoint), keeping depreciated tools productive instead of building new $15B fabs.
why: Conversion ~$0.2-0.5B per fab vs $15B+ greenfield; adds U.S. zero-refresh memory supply in ~18-24 months and offloads refresh-hungry DRAM (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Vertical XOR parity tier rescues defective layers in 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: in a monolithic 3D DRAM with N tiers, one tier per vertical string stores XOR parity of the bits above it, so a whole failed tier, string segment or leaky-tier tail can be rebuilt by reading the column.
why: Fact 2: tier yield compounds (0.98^26 = 59%); tolerating one bad tier per string lifts yield to ~90% and makes 26+ tier break-even reachable with weaker lateral transistors.

title: Anti-weight: DRAM fab financed as regulated 30-year infrastructure asset
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: counter the crushing depreciation weight by financing fab shells and long-life tools through pension/sovereign infrastructure bonds at ~4% over 30 years with a regulated return, leaving only short-life tools on the maker's balance sheet.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost: halving WACC on long-lived assets cuts cost per bit ~15-20%.

title: Partial action: Lego-fab adding 2,500-wafer modules as demand appears
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: rather than one $15B mega-fab, build containerized prefab cleanroom modules each sized for ~2,500 wspm of a fixed mature DRAM flow, adding modules in 9-month increments.
why: Capital intensity and cycle risk: lowers entry ticket to ~$1-2B and avoids overbuild at cycle peaks.

title: Thermophile compact core: 2 nm silicon sheets raise bandgap, shrink leak volume
idea: Hyperthermophile proteins keep compact cores with few exposed loops; make the 3D lateral access transistor a quantum-confined 2-3 nm epitaxial Si nanosheet, which raises the effective bandgap to ~1.5 eV and cuts the depleted generation volume ~20x versus a bulk junction, with a metal storage node silicided directly to the sheet.
why: At 125 C SRH generation in depletion regions dominates leakage; wider effective gap plus tiny volume could cut the 125 C leakage tail ~50-100x and keep 64 ms refresh at grade-1 temperature.
note: Confinement raises gap, but DRAM tail is trap-assisted; mobility and variability penalties.

title: Cuttlebone chambers: air-gap tiers on pillars cut coupling and height
idea: Cuttlebone is thin floors separated by gas-filled chambers and tiny pillars; after the tier stack is patterned, dissolve sacrificial carbon or SiGe isolation layers through the slits, leaving air gaps (k=1) held by self-aligned oxide pillars at the bitline holes, then pinch-off seal the slits.
why: Air gaps cut inter-tier coupling ~4x so isolation shrinks from ~30 nm to ~8 nm, about doubling tiers per stack height; with a 50-tier-class process that is ~10x bits/mm2 for one extra wet etch (fact 2).

title: Glial potassium buffering: buried sink lines soak up hammer electrons
idea: Astrocytes mop up excess K+ so neighbouring neurons do not fire spuriously; add a buried, positively biased n+ 'glial' collector line in the isolation between adjacent access transistors that captures electrons emitted by the aggressor wordline's trap-assisted charge pumping before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: a physical root-cause fix; raising the threshold even 10x removes most tracker and victim-refresh overhead.

title: Coral-polyp fab growing bay by bay from revenue
idea: Coral reefs grow one self-sufficient polyp at a time. A DRAM fab is built from sealed cleanroom pods, each with its own mini-environment, utilities and material handling; the first pods make legacy parts and each quarter's revenue funds the next pod, so capacity accretes without $15B upfront.
why: ~10x less capital at risk at start; first wafers in ~18 months; capacity tracks demand (capital intensity).

title: Coelacanth revival: restart crosspoint lines for selector-only memory
idea: The coelacanth was thought extinct until it reappeared. Shuttered 3D crosspoint tooling is restarted for chalcogenide selector-only memory, which stores the bit as a threshold shift in the OTS itself, as a cheap DRAM-extension tier.
why: Reuses existing U.S. crosspoint know-how and tools; stacked 4F2 with no capacitor, at ~1/3 the cost per bit of DRAM.

title: SOI-wafer supply model: capacitor arrays shipped under transferred silicon
idea: Copy the engineered-substrate business behind SOI wafers: a specialist supplier fabricates the deep-trench/ high-k storage-capacitor array (with alignment marks) on depreciated 65-nm-class tools, then layer-transfers a thin crystalline Si film on top by Smart-Cut bonding; the DRAM fab aligns and builds access transistors and periphery in that film.
why: Fact 4 capital: moves the high-AR capacitor module out of the leading-edge DRAM fab, decouples capacitor thermal budget from transistors (allowing >900 C crystallization for higher k), and creates a U.S. supplier tier; overlay through the transferred film is the main risk.

title: Lift-slab tier manufacturing across idle mature fabs
idea: Like lift-slab construction where floors are cast on the ground and jacked into place, run each tier of a bonded 3D DRAM stack as a simple array-only wafer (1-2 critical layers) in under-used U.S. 65-28 nm fabs, then ship tier wafers to one bonding hub that hybrid-bonds and thins them into 8-16 tier stacks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4, resources): reuses depreciated fabs instead of $15B greenfield; claims U.S. DRAM capacity without EUV at ~3-4x lower capex per wafer-tier.

title: Basement-and-rooftop sandwich: periphery split across two bonded wafers
idea: Copy buildings that put plant rooms in the basement and on the roof: a three-wafer stack with row decoders and wordline drivers bonded below the array wafer and sense amplifiers plus column logic bonded above it, each at line pitch, leaving the middle array wafer 100% cells.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): array efficiency rises toward ~90%; claims ~1.7x bits per array-wafer area with periphery on cheaper logic nodes.
note: Twist on cell-over-periphery bonding; two fine-pitch bonds and thermal budget.

title: Mobile-shelving sense amps: one aisle serves eight stacked mats
idea: Like compact library shelving that opens one aisle at a time, put one sense-amp stripe at the base of eight vertically bonded subarrays sharing a vertical bitline through isolation switches, so only the opened subarray connects to the amplifiers at a time.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): sense-amp area amortized 8x instead of today's 2x shared-SA; claims ~25-30% smaller die.

title: Reusable foundry molds: nitride crucibles pull many ingots each
idea: Metal foundries replaced one-shot sand molds with permanent molds for volume castings. Make dense reaction-bonded or CVD-coated silicon nitride crucibles that molten silicon does not wet and that survive cooldown, so one crucible serves 10+ pulls; the slight nitrogen pickup doubles as the intentional N-doping DRAM wafer makers already use to engineer vacancy defects.
why: Quartz crucibles devitrify and crack on cooldown and are single-use; a 10x reusable crucible cuts HPQ demand per ingot ~90% and turns a scarce consumable into durable capital.

title: Puff-pastry lamination: bond-thin-flip cycles double 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Borrowed from croissant dough, which gets 2^n layers by fold-and-roll: build a short 4-tier 3D DRAM block, hybrid-bond two such wafers face to face, thin one down to its tiers, and repeat on the doubled stack, so 4 to 8 to 16 to 32 tiers takes three bonding cycles instead of one 32-tier etch.
why: Fact 2: avoids the deep multi-tier etch and cumulative bow; every cycle reuses the same short process, so capex scales with bonders (~$5M) not high-AR etchers. Compounded bond yield is the risk.

title: Seismic base isolation: grounded shield rail buried between wordlines
idea: Base isolation decouples a building from ground shaking. A thin grounded TiN or doped-poly rail is buried in the isolation trench between adjacent buried wordlines. It terminates the fringing fields and collects the electrons injected by the aggressor before they reach the victim storage-node junctions.
why: It could raise the row-hammer threshold about 10x, from ~1k to ~10k ACTs (fact 9), removing most counter area and RFM bandwidth. The cost is a small increase in pitch.
note: Needs process integration; benefit depends on whether coupling or substrate electron migration dominates hammer flips.

title: Advance market commitment for element-agnostic trailing-node working memory
idea: A CHIPS-funded advance market commitment buys ~1 exabyte over 5 years of byte-addressable working memory from existing >=28-nm U.S. fabs at a fixed $/GB and spec (<=100 ns, >=1e15 endurance or architectural equivalent), open to any revived storage element.
why: Guaranteed demand lets revived elements (pinned wells, T-RAM, MNOS, micro-magnetics) fill idle 200/300-mm trailing capacity now instead of waiting 3-5 years for a DRAM fab; capital intensity and U.S. share.

title: Plated-wire revival: coated bitline wires with strap-defined junctionless access
idea: Revive Univac's plated-wire memory, in which crossing word straps addressed a continuous film on a wire: coat vertical bitline wires conformally (ALD) with a thin junctionless semiconductor shell. Each horizontal wordline strap wraps the wire and gates, all around, a shell segment linking the wire to an adjacent ring capacitor, so transistors are defined by strap crossings rather than per-cell lithography or doping.
why: No implanted junctions means no junction leakage and no GIDL hot spots (fact 3); strap-defined devices suit multi-tier 3D (fact 2) and need fewer EUV layers (fact 4).

title: Core-memory coincident selection from one shield-strip cut mask
idea: Core memory switched only the bit where X and Y half-currents coincided. One added cut mask splits the inter-channel shield (back-gate) plate of a vertical-channel array into strips that run along the bitline direction, one strip per 1/16 of a row. A cell turns on only when its row wordline and its segment strip are both raised, and each alone is subthreshold.
why: Only the addressed 1/16 of a row dumps charge and is sensed, cutting the 128x overfetch to ~8x (fact 8) and activation energy ~10x, and it shrinks the row-hammer blast radius (fact 9).

title: Toshiba chain FeRAM stood vertically as 3D ferroelectric strings
idea: Revive Toshiba's 1997 chain FeRAM, where each cell's transistor shunts its own ferroelectric capacitor in a series chain: build it as a vertical string of 32 shunted capacitors per pillar, 3D-NAND style, and accept ~1% read-disturb flips in neighbours that a per-string code corrects on write-back.
why: Facts 2 and 4: a 3D ferroelectric cell with one channel hole per 32 bits; error tolerance lets mismatched shunt devices and thin HZO work.
note: Ferroelectric endurance ~1e10-1e11 falls short of DRAM-class; read disturb in chains.

title: SAGE-style federal anchor order for error-tolerant U.S. memory stacks
idea: SAGE's huge core-memory order drove core prices down ~100x and built U.S. core factories; revive it as a multiyear federal purchase commitment for 'grade-T' 3D memory specified at up to 1% raw cell BER with on-stack correction, made in U.S. mature-node fabs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: guaranteed volume justifies cheaper tolerant fabs without EUV, raising domestic share from ~1-2%.

title: Core-memory inhibit winding revived as anti-hammer neighbour counter-pulse
idea: Coincident-current core planes drove an 'inhibit' current through cores that must not switch, cancelling the half-select field. Each time a wordline rises, the drivers of its two physical neighbours apply a brief matched negative counter-pulse (~-0.3 V for the rise time) that cancels the capacitive kick and suppresses electron injection from the aggressor channel into neighbouring storage nodes, the mechanisms behind hammer flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aims to push the flip threshold from ~1k to 10k+ activations, cutting mitigation refresh and counter overhead; costs ~5% extra wordline-driver energy.

title: Bell Labs SEED Smart-Pixels: Free-Space Optical Memory-to-Processor Links
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1980s-90s self-electro-optic-effect device (SEED) smart-pixel arrays: flip-chip a 2D array of quantum-well modulators onto the DRAM die so thousands of bits of an open row beam in parallel through a microlens array onto a photodetector array on the processor, with no SerDes or PHY.
why: Data movement: fJ-class modulators and detectors versus 3-20 pJ/bit electrical I/O, >=10x lower energy per access, and no TSV/HBM base die.
note: SEED needs III-V hybridization, external laser power and microlens alignment; laser wall-plug erodes 10x claim.

title: One sense die multiplexed across four headless array dies
idea: Inverting 'every array owns its periphery': four stacked array dies carry only a one-transistor local preamp per bitline group, and a single logic die underneath holds the latching sense amps, decoders and I/O, selecting which die's preamps drive the shared vertical hybrid-bond column buses like a bank select along the z-axis.
why: Amortizes the ~49% periphery over four arrays so array dies are ~90% cells; stack-level cost per bit -30-40% and only one die needs logic-grade transistors.

title: US periphery foundry-as-a-service for capacitorless memory startups
idea: Inverting 'each memory maker owns its fab end to end': a CHIPS-funded shared 28nm line runs standard sense/decode wafers and bonding for any capacitorless cell startup, paid per wafer, with guaranteed government purchase of first products.
why: Cuts a startup's capital need from $15B+ to array-only lines, builds US manufacturability and diversifies away from three incumbent DRAM makers.

title: Pillar-as-page: activation opens one vertical column, not a row
idea: Inverts 'a page is a long horizontal row.' In a 3D array with per-pillar vertical wordlines and per-tier horizontal bitlines, one activation opens exactly one cell on each of 64 tiers, each sensed by its own tier's sense amp, so the activated page is 64 bits (one cache line) instead of 8 kb.
why: Fact 8: removes the 128x overfetch; ~5.9 pJ per useful bit could fall toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also confines row-hammer coupling to one pillar.

title: Array-logic-array sandwich: one periphery wafer serves two faces
idea: Inverts 'periphery sits beside or beneath one array.' Hybrid-bond array wafers to both faces of a thinned periphery wafer so each sense amp senses an open bitline above and its reference bitline below, halving periphery per bit and giving a naturally matched reference.
why: Fact 7: the ~49% periphery share can drop to ~25% effective; symmetric above/below bitlines improve noise immunity.
note: Arrays bonded to both faces of a periphery wafer share sense amps with a matched reference bitline.

title: Pitch-relaxed 30-tier DRAM in existing U.S. 28-65 nm fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM density comes from the smallest pitch.' Design a 3D DRAM at ~40 nm pitch (cell ~11x larger than at F=12 nm) with ~30 tiers, so density is bought with deposition and etch steps that mature U.S. logic fabs already own instead of EUV.
why: Fact 4 and U.S. manufacturability: zero EUV, depreciated tools, U.S. capacity in ~2-3 years instead of 5; cost/bit parity if tiers stay cheap.

title: Wavelength-addressed banks: color selects the bank, not a decoder
idea: Invert 'addresses are decoded electrically in the periphery': each bank group gets a microring drop filter tuned to its own wavelength on a base-die waveguide bus, so a request on lambda-7 physically reaches only bank 7 and data returns on the same color; bank select becomes optical routing with no global address decode tree.
why: Attacks periphery (~49% of die) and global-wire energy; with comb lasers, 16-32 colors x 32 Gb/s per stack at ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM.

title: Active interposer swallows DRAM periphery; arrays go periphery-light
idea: Invert 'periphery lives on the memory die': make the interposer in a U.S. 65-90 nm fab carrying upper decoder levels, refresh control, ECC and repeaters, while hybrid-bonded DRAM dies keep only sense amps and local drivers.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die; moving half onto cheap mature silicon lifts array efficiency toward 70-75%, ~1.4x bits per DRAM wafer.
note: Wordline drivers and SAs stay local; interposer bond density limits how much periphery moves.

title: Diamond interlayers let DRAM sit directly on the hot GPU
idea: Invert 'memory must sit beside the hot compute die': bond thin single-crystal diamond plates grown in Washington state between GPU and stacked DRAM to spread heat sideways, with through-diamond vias carrying signals.
why: Diamond's ~2000 W/m-K lets memory go on top of logic without overheating: face-to-face 3D bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit and no interposer.

title: Exchange-traded multi-year DRAM futures that pre-fund fab construction
idea: Inverts 'DRAM is sold spot or by quarterly contract': list standardized 1-5 year bit futures (Gb-equivalent, DDR5 delivery) so new fabs can pre-sell output and post hedged revenue as collateral for construction loans.
why: Capital intensity: lowers cost of capital by several points and breaks the boom-bust underinvestment cycle that produced the 4x spike.
note: Liquidity and standardization are hard; prior memory spot exchanges stayed thin.

title: Federal tool-loan bank inserts DRAM tool sets into idle U.S. logic fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM needs a purpose-built DRAM fab': a federal bank buys and loans DRAM-specific tool sets (capacitor etch, high-k ALD, cell implant) to underused U.S. 300 mm logic fabs that run a licensed 1x-nm DRAM flow.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: reuses existing cleanroom shells and utilities at roughly 1/3 the capex and 2-3 years faster than greenfield.

title: Monolayer WSe2 channel wrapped around the capacitor pillar sidewall
idea: Thermal generation scales with depleted semiconductor volume times n_i. A 0.7 nm monolayer has almost no volume and a gap of ~1.6-2 eV. Grow MOCVD WSe2 or MoS2 conformally (<500 C) on the outer sidewall of the vertical storage pillar with a ring wordline. The result is a gate-all-around vertical access device with no silicon body and a 4F^2 footprint.
why: Leakage drops ~1e6 from n_i and ~10x from volume, removing the junction and TAT tail sources (fact 3). It also gives a vertical, stackable cell (fact 2) with no lateral transistor.

title: Sandwich bonding: sense wafer below, wordline-driver wafer above array
idea: Fabricate the cell array on a wafer with no peripheral transistors, hybrid-bond a matched low-voltage logic wafer carrying sense amps to its bitline face and a thick-oxide wafer carrying 3 V wordline drivers to its wordline face, each at ~0.5-1 um pitch.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and voltage floor (fact 10): each function gets its ideal process, the array wafer drops its periphery masks, and array efficiency rises toward ~90%, with periphery built on depreciated logic lines.
note: Twist on CMOS-bonded array; pitch-matched sense amps need fan-out finer than 0.5-1 um bond pitch.

title: Two-nanometer silicon channels widen the bandgap to starve leakage
idea: Thin the access channel to ~2 nm by oxidation-trimming epitaxial nanosheets so quantum confinement raises the effective bandgap by ~0.3-0.5 eV; drive current remains adequate because each cell holds little charge.
why: Leakage physics: generation and band-to-band leakage scale roughly as exp(-Eg/2kT), so +0.4 eV gives ~3 decades less tail leakage (fact 3), moving silicon refresh from 64 ms toward ~1 min without exotic oxides.
note: Same 2 nm confinement idea; mobility and thickness-variability exponentials.

title: Deep trench capacitors etched into the thinned wafer backside
idea: First principle: frontside capacitors compete for height inside a ~2 um back-end stack, while the substrate below the transistor is idle volume. After frontside transistors are made and bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer to ~1.5 um and etch single-crystal Si trenches (AR ~40, which etches more uniformly than oxide/nitride molds) from the backside, aligned to the storage nodes with backside-power-delivery alignment tools.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): decouples the capacitor from frontside wiring and reuses the BSPDN tooling now being installed for logic.
note: Uses BSPDN tooling; backside contact to storage node is hard.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM with fault-mapped mesh; no dicing or packages
idea: First principle: dicing, packaging and final test are ~15-25% of DRAM cost, and a wafer can stay one device if defects are routed around. Keep the 300 mm wafer as one memory with a reconfigurable on-wafer mesh network and per-tile power gates, so defective or worn tiles are mapped out at test and in the field, and the wafer goes back for tile-level reclaim.
why: Cost per bit and capital (packaging, test, TSVs): ~2 TB per wafer as one repairable unit.

title: Glass-panel interposer lets accelerators share one memory set
idea: Weights are replicated per GPU only because off-package bandwidth is too poor to share them. A 510x515 mm glass-core panel interposer with 2 um RDL and through-glass vias places 8 accelerators around one common ring of memory stacks at near-local bandwidth, so tensor- and data-parallel groups read a single physical copy of the weights.
why: Weight replicas per 8-GPU group drop from 8 to 1-2, cutting HBM bits per deployment 30-60%; glass is low-loss and uses no silicon interposer wafers.

title: Advance purchase commitment for US-made glass memory tiers
idea: Federal buyers (DOE labs, DoD, GSA cloud) pre-commit to buy, for example, 500 PB over 5 years of CXL warm-tier memory built on non-silicon substrates at a target of <$1/GB, paid on delivery. This lets US glass makers and idle display lines finance conversion without silicon fab capital.
why: Removes demand risk from a substrate path that needs no EUV, no helium-intensive crystal pulling and no Spruce Pine quartz crucibles, and builds US memory supply outside the DRAM oligopoly.

title: Logic-die wordline segment drivers kill 128x page overfetch
idea: Overfetch exists because global wordlines are long and drivers are costly in DRAM process. Hybrid-bond a logic die whose fine-pitch bonds drive each 512-cell local wordline segment directly, so a 64 B read activates 64 B of cells instead of an 8 KB row.
why: Cuts random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.2 pJ (fact 8) and shrinks row-hammer aggressor exposure (fact 9).
note: Per-wordline segment bonds exceed hybrid-bond pitch; sub-row activation itself is known art.

title: Read-only charge-trap chiplets programmed once at wafer sort
idea: A deployed model's weights never change, and storage with no write path is the cheapest physics allows. Program 3D charge-trap arrays with weights at wafer sort via massively parallel probe cards, then ship dies with the program/erase pumps stripped, thicker retention oxide, and read-in-place sensing bonded beside compute.
why: Bit cost at or below 3D NAND (~100x+ cheaper than DRAM) with smaller periphery; trades flexibility (new model means new chips).

title: Buried high-SRH recombination layer absorbs row-hammer electrons
idea: Part of the hammer disturbance is electrons injected by the aggressor that diffuse through the substrate to victim junctions. Implant a carbon- or gold-doped layer deep below the storage-junction depletion region, where short minority lifetime (<1 ns) kills the migrating electrons. Keeping it out of the depletion region avoids raising SRH generation leakage.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): could push the flip threshold from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs, with no controller logic.

title: Coffee pod: storage-element wafers sold as bondable consumables
idea: Stimulus 'coffee pod' -> a dedicated, EUV-free line makes only the storage-element layer (dense capacitor or bit-element array on a thin carrier) and ships it as a consumable that logic or periphery fabs hybrid-bond face-to-face onto their CMOS wafers. Each layer runs on the cheapest line suited to it.
why: Splits DRAM capital: the bit-element fab needs no EUV transistor layers (fact 4) and the ~49% periphery runs in logic fabs (fact 7); claimed 30-40% capex per bit reduction and a U.S. entry point.
note: Splits capex, but needs hybrid bonding at near cell pitch, far beyond today.

title: Dam: GaN/AlGaN potential well holds stored charge for days
idea: Stimulus 'hydro dam' (water held behind a tall wall) -> store the bit as electrons in an AlGaN/GaN 2DEG pocket behind a 3.4 eV-gap barrier and read it through a gain transistor; leakage falls exponentially with bandgap, so retention reaches hours to days. GaN is grown by MOCVD and etched with Cl2/BCl3, with no fluorine.
why: Shrinks the leakage tail >1000x vs silicon (fact 3) so refresh becomes rare; capacitorless gain-cell read (fact 1).
note: GaN 2DEG gain cell; integration with Si periphery is the barrier.

title: Skyscraper sky lobby: sense-amp tier every 16 cell tiers
idea: Like express elevators that feed sky lobbies, a 128-tier vertical-bitline 3D DRAM inserts a layer-transferred single-crystal Si sense-amp tier every 16 cell tiers. Each local vertical bitline spans only 16 cells, and sensed data rides 'express' global vertical lines down to the base die.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2) and capacitor wall (fact 1): bitline capacitance per sense ~8x lower, so a 1-1.5 fF lateral capacitor gives the signal of today's 5 fF pillar, which makes lateral 3D capacitors good enough.
note: Low-temperature layer-transferred SA tiers (CoolCube-like) plausible; process complexity high.

title: Thermos flask: sealed vacuum gaps between wordlines block hammer coupling
idea: A thermos insulates with vacuum: after the buried wordlines are formed, recess the isolation dielectric between passing wordlines and neighbor active areas and seal it with a pinch-off cap, leaving vacuum gaps (k=1). Capacitive kick and charge migration from aggressor to victim fall, and the DDR5/HBM interface is untouched.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): coupling ~3x lower, aiming at a 3-5x higher flip threshold; lower wordline capacitance also trims wordline CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Parking garage: idle 3D NAND lines build vertical 1T-nC ferroelectric stacks
idea: Random stimulus 'multi-storey parking garage' -> one access transistor at ground level with n HZO ferroelectric capacitors stacked as floors along a vertical plate pillar. It is built with the staircase, channel-hole and replacement-gate tools of 3D NAND fabs that sit idle in NAND down-cycles.
why: Non-volatile, ~1e12-1e15 endurance, ~10-50 ns. It reuses depreciated NAND capex, so near-zero new tools are needed, and 8-16 bits per transistor footprint gives a step change in density per litho layer.

title: Storage layer on the backside power network of U.S. logic
idea: Box = {medium: charge on BEOL MIM capacitors | access: low-temperature Zn-based oxide TFTs | sense: SAs in the front-side logic | integration: memory tier built on the wafer backside after backside-power processing, plate tied to the backside power mesh | substrate: U.S.-made leading-edge logic wafers (Arizona/Oregon) | fab: <400 C backside ALD}. The thinned backside otherwise carries only power rails; a 1T1C tier there puts several MB per mm2 directly under the compute with sub-micron vertical paths.
why: Fact 5 data-movement energy (~10x below HBM) and U.S. manufacturability: memory capacity from domestic leading-edge logic fabs that already exist.
note: Needs leading-edge backside-power wafers; thermal budget and access.

title: Series lock gate: second gate per channel shared by subarray
idea: Box: cap x vertical channel with two stacked gates (row wordline + a subarray-wide lock gate nearest the storage node) x SA x in-array 3D x Si x second gate tier deposited in the same trench. The lock gate stays deeply negative except when its subarray is active, adding a series stack that multiplies isolation.
why: Stack effect plus deeper off-bias cuts leakage 10-100x in idle subarrays (most of the chip), extending their refresh (fact 3) and blocking hammer coupling into them (fact 9).
note: Subarray-shared lock gate; same series negative gate near storage node.

title: Vertical bitlines climb bonded array tiers to one shared sense amp
idea: [Box: 1T1C charge | buried-channel Si FET | sense amp multiplexed across tiers | 8-tier stack of array-only wafers | thinned Si | hybrid bond + sub-um through-tier vias] Stack 4-8 thinned array-only wafers (no periphery) on one periphery wafer and drop every bitline segment through through-tier vias to a sense amp time-shared among tiers, so sense amps and decoders are amortized over 8x the cells.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): periphery share falls toward ~10%, ~1.6-1.8x bits per processed silicon area, and HBM-class capacity without per-die TSV keep-outs (fact 6).
note: Through-tier vias cannot reach bitline pitch without muxing; amortizing periphery over 8 bonded array wafers is the insight.

title: Universal array-tile consortium: one shared mask set across vendors
idea: Box: business axis set to shared mask and process. U.S. and allied fabs standardize a 1T1C array tile (cell pitch, sub-array size, BL/WL interface) whose ~20 array masks and process module are developed once and licensed per wafer, so new entrants and foundries only design periphery.
why: Capital and time to enter (U.S. ~1-2% share): removes ~$50-100M of mask and module development and ~2-3 years per entrant; risk is IP and competitive reluctance.
note: Array and periphery are co-optimized; vendor reluctance high.

title: Backside capacitors: storage nodes etched into the thinned wafer back
idea: Box: deep-trench charge x vertical-channel access x standard sensing x front/back split x thinned Si on carrier x backside trench etch self-aligned to buried drains. After front-side transistors and bitlines, the wafer is bonded face-down and thinned, and capacitor trenches are etched from the back into bulk Si landing on each transistor's buried drain, so capacitors no longer compete with bitlines for front-side space.
why: Removes storage-node-contact and landing-pad layers (2-3 masks incl. ~1 EUV) and gives free capacitor height (Cs >8 fF); reuses backside-power tools now entering logic fabs.

title: One-hole cell: capacitor and vertical oxide transistor share one hole
idea: Box: MIM charge at hole bottom x vertical IGZO channel lining the hole top x voltage sense amp x BEOL over periphery x Si x single etched hole with sequential ALD fill and recess. One hole receives bottom electrode and high-k, is recessed, then gets a lined IGZO channel and gate-all-around wordline fill, so storage-node contacts, landing pads and their overlay steps disappear.
why: Mask count and overlay (fact 4): removes 3-4 masks including EUV contacts, natively 4F2, and sits over periphery (fact 7); risk is IGZO quality on the hole sidewall and series resistance.

title: Split buried wordline turns passing gate into negative shield
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: buried-channel transistor | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: EUV + split-gate etch]. The buried wordline is split so the segment that passes beside a neighbour's storage junction becomes a separately biased shield held at about -0.4 V, so toggling the aggressor no longer gates the victim's junction (the passing-gate hammer path).
why: Fact 9: removes the dominant passing-wordline hammer mechanism physically; ~10x higher hammer threshold claimed with no refresh overhead.

title: Exchange-cleared DRAM bit futures fund capacity expansion
idea: Box[Finance=standardized futures on a 16 Gb DDR5-equivalent bit contract x Owner=exchange + clearing house x Channel=delivery against graded dies]: list 12-36 month DRAM bit futures so fabs can presell output and bank-finance new lines against hedged revenue, while buyers lock price.
why: Capital intensity and cycle risk: hedged revenue lowers cost of capital several points, making counter-cyclical fab builds bankable.
note: Grading standardization and liquidity are hard; CFTC listing needed.

title: Module micro-fabs: one plant per process module, wafers travel
idea: Po: a fab is spread across a country. Split the DRAM flow into module plants (transistor FEOL, capacitor module, BEOL/TSV) each sized to its bottleneck tool and linked by sealed-pod wafer logistics, so capacity grows one $1-3B module plant at a time instead of a $15B integrated fab.
why: Capital lumpiness and time (fact 4): smaller capex steps, faster ramps, U.S. siting of individual modules, higher tool utilization.

title: Image-sensor wafer-bond lines put capacitors on the backside
idea: Po: the wafer has two front sides. Use existing backside-illuminated image-sensor lines (wafer bonding, thinning to a few microns, backside litho) to flip a 40-65 nm transistor array and build tall capacitors on the freed backside, contacting drains through the thinned silicon so bitlines and capacitors stop competing for one side.
why: Capacitor wall and cell area (facts 1,7): front carries bitlines and periphery, back carries capacitors; near-4F2 layouts in trailing fabs with existing CIS tools.

title: Expose commodity DDR5 internal wide bus through one pad mask
idea: Po: the inside of the chip becomes the outside. On a standard DDR5 die, one added pad mask brings the wide internal global I/O lines up to hybrid-bond pads so a logic die bonded face-to-face reads them directly, skipping the DDR serializer and PHY.
why: Turns high-volume DDR wafers into HBM-like wide memory without TSVs or a new die design; ~3-5x lower pJ/bit than DDR5 I/O.
note: Internal DDR5 datapath is only a few hundred bits wide; needs DRAM-vendor pad and bond process.

title: Hot-stacked DRAM bonded straight onto accelerators at 115 C
idea: Po: memory that loves the heat. DRAM dies are hybrid-bonded directly onto accelerator logic with no thermal derating; at 105-125 C leakage rises roughly 8-30x, and refresh is set so the hot-spot raw BER stays at or below 1%, which the code corrects.
why: Data movement (fact 5): logic-on-DRAM stacking cuts movement energy from 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit and removes the thermal objection to it.
note: A 1% raw BER implies heavy ECC overhead and latency.

title: Airbus-style allied DRAM company with stage-hosting by member nations
idea: Po: the factory belongs to many nations. Allied governments (e.g., U.S., Japan, EU, India) co-own one DRAM company in which each hosts a stage (front-end fab, test, packaging, stacking) and receives allocation proportional to equity, Airbus-style.
why: Splits the $15B+ fab ticket across sponsors and creates a fourth supplier outside today's three; attacks capital intensity and chokepoint concentration.

title: Shipyard-built fab modules assembled on site in 18 months
idea: Po: a fab is built in a year. Cleanroom bays, sub-fab utility skids and chemical distribution are built as standardized transportable modules in shipyards and factories (as LNG trains and offshore platforms are), then stacked on site under one frozen copy-exactly design.
why: Cuts fab construction from 3-5 years to ~18-24 months and construction cost ~20-30% through repetition; attacks the time and capital bottleneck.
note: Vibration and utility integration at fab scale are doubts; LNG analogy apt.

title: Turnkey EUV-free DRAM fab franchise
idea: Po: a fab is a burger franchise. A franchisor packages a frozen EUV-free DRAM process (DUV plus self-aligned patterning), tool list, recipes, yield-learning database, training academy and a qualification brand; regional franchisees (states, sovereign funds, consortia) build identical fabs and pay royalties per wafer.
why: Copy-exactly replication shrinks yield ramp from years to months and lets capacity grow in parallel without EUV allocation; attacks capital, time and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Line-tunneling TFET access device exploits DRAM's tiny on-current need
idea: Worse: use a thermionic MOSFET whose off-state is set by kT. Flip: DRAM writes need only ~5-10 uA for ~10 ns, so use a vertical line-tunneling Si/SiGe TFET whose only injection path is band-to-band tunneling, giving sub-aA off-current when the gate is low.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 100x+ lower; refresh interval in the seconds range at 85 C.

title: AlScN shadow layer parks idle rows non-volatilely when hot
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep refreshing idle data at the 4-8x hot refresh rate, or use HZO backup that depolarizes. Flip: put a wurtzite AlScN ferroelectric capacitor layer (Curie point >1000 C) under each mat; rows idle beyond N ms are copied into it and their DRAM refresh stops, so the low AlScN endurance is spent only on rare parks.
why: Hot idle refresh energy (fact 3) down 10x+; retention guaranteed over 10 years at 125 C.
note: AlScN coercive field high; nvDRAM concepts exist.

title: Backside-built sense amplifiers connect through bitline-pitch nano-vias
idea: Worse: lay periphery beside the array where it eats half the die. Flip: after the front-side array, bond to a carrier, thin to under a micron as in backside power delivery, and layer-transfer low-temperature transistors for sense amps and sub-wordline drivers onto the backside, contacting bitlines through nano-vias at bitline pitch.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): folding periphery under the array shrinks die ~35-40% and raises bits per wafer without litho scaling.

title: Second array on the wafer backside sharing one periphery
idea: Worse: use only one face of the wafer and grind 700 um of silicon to dust. Flip: after building the front array and bonding to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, build a second low-thermal-budget array on the exposed backside, and tie both arrays to the same sense amps through nano-TSVs so every periphery block serves two arrays.
why: ~2x bits per wafer start and half the periphery area per bit (fact 7: periphery ~49% of die); halves quartz-crucible wafer demand per bit.

title: Micro-row 3D activation: per-tier wordline stubs open 64 bits
idea: Worse: open an 8 KB row for every 64 B request. Flip: in a vertical-wordline 3D array, split each vertical wordline into per-tier stubs behind a local select device at the tier edge, so one activation energizes only one tier of one subarray stripe (64-512 bits).
why: Overfetch falls from 128x to ~1-8x and random-read energy from 5.9 pJ per useful bit to <1 pJ (fact 8); fewer activations also shrink row-hammer exposure (fact 9).
note: Same core as tier-column small pages; per-tier select devices add area.

title: Per-tier back-gate plane biased negative during retention
idea: Worse: let one worst-case leaky cell among billions set the refresh period. Flip: embed a thin conductive back-gate plane under each channel tier as part of the deposited stack and pump it negative during retention to suppress tail leakage, releasing it during access for full drive.
why: Pushing the <=13 fA tail toward ~1 fA could stretch refresh ~10x, cutting the 46 fJ/bit refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax (fact 3).
note: Negative back-gate may raise GIDL; 10x refresh stretch is optimistic.

title: One wordline plate gates two channel tiers: shared double-gate stack
idea: Worse: give every channel tier its own wordline tier and isolation, so each bit costs ~3 films of stack height. Flip: build repeating channel/gate/channel/isolation units where each metal wordline plate gates the channel above and the channel below, with upper and lower channels routed to alternate vertical bitlines so the two cells stay independently addressable.
why: Stack height per bit falls ~35%, so ~1.5x more tiers fit the same etch: a 100-tier-depth etch holds ~150 effective tiers, enough for ~10x at unchanged etch and similar deposition cost.
note: Each wordline plate gates channels above and below; ~1.5x tiers per etch depth.

title: Replacement capacitor: 200 placeholders swapped for high-k through the slit
idea: Worse: finish each tier's capacitor before building the next, so early tiers suffer every later anneal and every tier pays its own dielectric step. Flip: leave a sacrificial SiN placeholder at each tier's capacitor site, complete the whole stack, then through the slits exhume all placeholders and deposit electrode, high-k and plate into all 200 tiers in one ALD sequence, like NAND gate replacement.
why: Capacitor cost becomes ~O(1) in tier count and thermal budget stops accumulating (facts 1, 2), letting ~200 tiers reach 10x at near-2D wafer cost.

title: Mass-produced fab modules: build factories like ships, not cathedrals
idea: Worse: build each fab as a bespoke 5-year megaproject. Flip: design a 5k-wafer/month DRAM fab module where tools sit in sealed N2 minienvironments linked by enclosed transport, so no ballroom cleanroom is needed. Build identical modules on an assembly line and drop them onto prepared pads.
why: Capital/time: the cleanroom shell (~25-30% of fab capex) goes away, time to first wafer falls from ~4 to ~1.5 years, and replication drives the module learning curve.

title: Nanoimprint mask-ROM tier for immutable weights and code
idea: Worsen: store frozen model weights and libraries in rewritable, refreshed DRAM. Flip: burn frozen artifacts into ultra-dense 3D mask ROM patterned by nanoimprint (no EUV, no capacitor, no refresh) on swappable cartridges, keeping DRAM for mutable state only.
why: Cost: ROM bits at NAND-like or lower cost give 100x cheaper per GB for read-only data; trades immutability (a new cartridge per model version).
note: Nanoimprint 3D ROM twist; 100x cost claim optimistic.

title: Take-or-pay offtake converts idle U.S. mature fabs to memory chiplets
idea: Worsen: let U.S. 65-28 nm fabs sit underused while memory is short. Flip: government and hyperscaler consortia sign 7-year take-or-pay contracts for capacitorless memory chiplets from those fabs, funding hybrid-bond and stacking add-ons (~$0.3-1B per site) instead of $15B DRAM fabs.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. share: adds bit capacity on depreciated tools with no EUV and no tungsten-heavy capacitor stack.
note: Capacitorless memory chiplets on 65-28 nm are not yet product-ready or bit-competitive.

title: Buried n+ collector rails sweep hammer-injected electrons away
idea: Worse: let electrons emitted from an aggressor's repeatedly switching channel wander through the silicon into neighbor storage nodes. Flip: implant a phosphorus-doped collector rail (Si dopant only, no W fill) beneath the isolation between wordlines, biased to sink migrating minority electrons before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Fact 9: physically blocks the charge-migration part of row hammer, raising the flip threshold several-fold without metal shields or counters.
note: Addresses electron-migration hammer path only; capacitive/passing-gate paths remain.

title: EV power engineer's SiC access tier bonded beneath the capacitors
idea: An EV inverter engineer reaches for 4H-SiC, now mass-produced on 200 mm wafers for cars, including in U.S. fabs. Build high-temperature-activated SiC access MOSFETs first, layer-transfer the 1 um SiC film onto the DRAM wafer, then build capacitors above; SiC's intrinsic carrier density (~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 for Si) removes thermal generation as a leakage path.
why: Junction and generation leakage drop by many decades, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes, so refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) nearly vanishes; low SiC mobility is acceptable for an access switch.

title: Gardener's graft: transistor-last access devices on transferred crystal silicon
idea: A gardener grafts a healthy scion onto rootstock. Build the capacitor array first at its full thermal budget, then bond and smart-cut a pristine 50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top and form access transistors at <=500 C with in-situ-doped, laser-activated junctions, so no capacitor anneal ever crosses the junctions and no implant damage seeds traps.
why: Implant damage and thermal cycling seed the leakage tail; a damage-free low-thermal-budget junction could improve tail retention 3-10x, and decoupling capacitor and transistor processes also eases the 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2).
note: CoolCube-style sequential integration applied to DRAM; low-thermal-budget junction quality is the doubt.

title: Club bouncer's guest list: cold-source energy-filter access FET
idea: A bouncer admits only the guests on the list. The access transistor gets a 'cold source': a semimetal or superlattice source whose density of states cuts off above a narrow energy window, filtering out the hot Boltzmann-tail electrons behind subthreshold leakage, so slope reaches ~30-40 mV/dec at room temperature.
why: Same leakage at ~0.4 V lower threshold lets a ~1 V wordline run without a pump, ~10-15x lower wordline energy per access, with no ferroelectric or moving parts.

title: Toll-road banker: U.S. merchant periphery foundry for bonded DRAM
idea: A banker sees a shared toll road. Build a U.S. merchant foundry that makes only CMOS periphery wafers for bonded DRAM (periphery-under-array, wafer-on-wafer) for every DRAM maker and array startup, who still ship standard DDR5 and HBM.
why: Spreads periphery capex across vendors and brings half of DRAM die function onshore without a full $15B fab (capital, U.S. manufacturability).
note: Shared U.S. periphery-wafer foundry for bonded DRAM; makers may refuse to outsource co-designed periphery.

title: Child's two-sided paper: memory arrays on both wafer faces
idea: A child asks why we only draw on one side of the page. Build the cell array on the front over the periphery, bond to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, then build a second array on the backside, wired to the same sense amps and decoders through nano-TSVs (as in backside power delivery).
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; two arrays sharing one periphery layer gives ~1.6-2x bits per mm2 with no extra litho shrink.
note: Same core as I-04751: arrays above and below one periphery layer; nano-TSV per bitline group is the hard part.

title: Glassmaker's float line: continuous linear fab instead of cluster tools
idea: Pilkington made glass as a continuous floating ribbon instead of cast sheets. Build the DRAM front end as a linear tunnel where wafers move nose-to-tail on carriers through in-line deposition, etch and clean stations (spatial-ALD heads, linear plasma sources) set by takt time, with litho as the only off-line island, so in-line segments have no FOUPs, stockers or overhead hoists.
why: Cuts AMHS, buffers and floor space (~15-20% of fab cost) and cycle time from ~90 to ~40 days; in-line stations run near 100% utilization, so fewer tools are needed. Risks: one station stalls the line (needs bypass loops), and recipe flexibility.

title: Chef's mise en place: bank generic array wafers, personalize later
idea: Chefs prep ingredients before the orders arrive. Build one standard cell-array-only wafer (capacitors, access transistors, bitlines, no periphery) in huge volume on a stripped-down array fab, stockpile it, then hybrid-bond it to a periphery wafer made in any CMOS foundry, choosing a DDR5, LPDDR or HBM-base personality at bonding time.
why: The array fab needs ~1/3 fewer tool types and no high-performance periphery transistors; the periphery (~49% of die, fact 7) moves to cheaper logic capacity; the wafer bank absorbs demand swings. Risks: ~1 um bond pitch per sense-amp group, and paying for two wafers.

title: Real-estate developer's Fab REIT leases cleanroom bays monthly
idea: A REIT owns the cleanroom shells, utilities and depreciating tools (scanners, deposition, etch) and leases 'bays' with shared metrology to DRAM startups and university spinouts on 3-36 month terms. A team can then run a 2k-wafer/month line without owning a $15B building.
why: Capital intensity and entry barriers: turns capex into opex and cuts a startup's entry cost from billions to ~$50-200M, so more DRAM approaches can reach volume.
note: DRAM flows are not modular bays; contamination and integration issues.

title: Retention-tiered monolithic stack with minutes-retention tiers for KV data
idea: Serve the AI KV-cache user whose data lives seconds to minutes: in one monolithic 3D stack the lower tiers use a thicker tunnel barrier around a charge-storage gate (minutes retention, slower write) while the top tiers keep fast capacitor cells, and the controller places each KV block by expected lifetime. The tier recipes differ in a single dielectric thickness, so it remains one process flow.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) vanishes for the long-lived bulk of KV data and capacitor-free tiers are denser (fact 1); ~2-4x capacity per die at similar cost.

title: Stacked-sensor sandwich: wordline drivers bonded above, sense amps below
idea: Three-layer stacked camera sensors showed a thinned die can be bonded on both faces; thin the DRAM array wafer to ~3 um, hybrid-bond a wordline-driver wafer to its top face and a sense-amp wafer to its bottom face, so wordlines exit upward and bitlines exit downward. The two peripheries never compete for one routing plane, the array die is ~100% cells, and both periphery wafers use logic processes.
why: Periphery and routing congestion (fact 7): array efficiency ~51% to ~95%, ~1.6x lower bit cost, and low-voltage logic periphery cuts energy (fact 10).

title: Wafer-scale DRAM hybrid-bonded whole onto wafer-scale AI engines
idea: Extreme user: wafer-scale AI processors that starve for on-wafer memory. Fabricate a full DRAM wafer with row/column redundancy and route-around and hybrid-bond it face-to-face to a logic wafer, skipping dicing, packaging, TSVs and per-die test.
why: HBM tax/capital: removes HBM packaging, TSV area and stack-yield loss; ~10x bandwidth per watt and no interposer.

title: DRAM wafer-start futures market lets AI labs pre-fund fabs
idea: Extreme user: AI labs whose memory demand swings 4x in a year. Create a standardized exchange-traded contract for 'wafer starts in year+3', so buyers lock capacity and fab builders raise construction capital against sold futures instead of balance sheets.
why: Capital intensity: shifts ~30-50% of fab financing risk to buyers who value certainty; smooths boom-bust and speeds new capacity.
note: Liquidity and standardization are the barriers; prepay deals already exist.

title: Inference fleet single copy: optically multicast weights to many GPUs
idea: From the extreme of serving one giant model on thousands of GPUs: instead of replicating weights in every replica's HBM, a pooled weight memory streams each layer once per step over an optical multicast fabric to 32-64 accelerators that consume it in lockstep, so HBM holds only KV and activations.
why: Weight replication is often 10-60x across replicas; single-copy streaming cuts fleet HBM bits ~10x, and with them the most water-intensive bits the industry makes.
note: Lockstep streaming needs HBM-class optical bandwidth per accelerator.

title: Airbus-style multinational DRAM fab consortium with offtake shares
idea: Mid-size sovereign users (India, EU states, Canada, Gulf states) each lack scale. A treaty consortium funds one shared fab with offtake rights pro rata to equity, as Airbus and CERN do, sited away from the helium, tungsten and EUV chokepoints.
why: Splits $15B+ capital across 5-8 states and adds a new independent supplier.
note: Treaty politics and offtake governance are the hard part; adds an independent supplier.

title: Two-faced wafer: capacitors built on the thinned backside
idea: Borrow the wafer-scale backside-power trick: after front-side transistor and bitline processing, bond to a carrier, thin to 1 um and build the capacitor stack on the backside, connected by nano-vias through vertical access transistors, so capacitors no longer compete with bitlines and contacts.
why: Density and process: frees ~30-40% of front-side cell area and lets capacitors use full-cell footprint; enables 4F2 vertical-channel cells.
note: Wafer-bonded 4F2 VCT approaches already in industry roadmaps.

title: Pixel-style bonded sense amps on every 256-cell bitline
idea: Scale jump from stacked CMOS image sensors (one bonded readout per pixel) to DRAM: hybrid-bond the array wafer to a 28 nm periphery wafer at 0.5 um pitch so every ~9 um (256-cell) bitline gets its own sense amp directly beneath it, instead of 1024-cell bitlines ending in edge SA stripes. The array die becomes pure cells; SAs, sub-wordline drivers and decoders all sit on the cheap wafer below.
why: Cbl drops ~3-4x so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~1.5-2 fF (capacitor AR ~60:1 -> ~25:1, fact 1), and the ~49% periphery leaves the expensive array die (fact 7); est. 25-35% lower cost per bit.

title: Array sandwiched between two CMOS wafers: double-sided periphery
idea: Jump from one die face to a wafer-pair sandwich: hybrid-bond a CMOS wafer to both the top and the bottom of a thinned memory-array wafer, with wordline drivers on one side and sense amps on the other. That doubles the periphery area under the array and allows mats half as large with shorter lines.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): moving all of it off the array plane approaches ~90% array efficiency, ~1.7x bits per array-wafer area.

title: Rotate the page vertical: one activation reads one cell per tier
idea: Use 3D geometry to shrink the page from an 8-KB row to a single vertical word: run the wordline as a vertical gate pillar through 64 tiers and give each tier its own short lateral bitline to a local sense amp. One activation touches exactly the 64 cells of one word.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): targets ~5.9 pJ falling to <0.5 pJ per useful bit, and large shared rows that invite row hammer disappear (fact 9).

title: Wafer-scale memory plate: one undiced wafer per rack sled
idea: Shift the product unit from die up to whole wafer: stitched identical array fields with redundant inter-field links, no dicing, no per-die packaging; the 300 mm wafer is mounted on a cooled sled board with edge connectors as a ~1-2 TB rack memory plate that routes around dead fields at boot.
why: Deletes dicing, packaging and per-die known-good-die test (~15-25% of finished DRAM cost) plus ~5% scribe area; I/O periphery is shared across fields.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve buys gluts and sells shortages
idea: Time-shift demand risk: a federal reserve buys U.S.-made DRAM wafers at a floor price in gluts and releases them in shortages, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, storing unpackaged wafers for years in nitrogen vaults.
why: Damps the boom-bust cycle that makes DRAM capital expensive; a lower risk premium could cut the cost of capital several points.
note: Stored wafers go obsolete within 2-3 generations.

title: RDL side-port lets HBM time-slice between tenants in milliseconds
idea: One added redistribution-layer mask on the interposer routes a wide side-port from each HBM base die to a co-packaged flash/LPDDR tier. A tenant's entire 24 GB HBM context then swaps in about 5 ms without crossing the GPU, so HBM is time-shared among 3-4 low-duty inference tenants like CPU time slices.
why: HBM is allocated in time instead of space, so bursty low-duty serving needs 2-3x less HBM.

title: Liner-free ruthenium nano-TSVs at 300 nm through 5 um dies
idea: Shrink the TSV ~20x in diameter: ruthenium needs no diffusion barrier and keeps low resistivity at small cross-sections, so dies thinned to 5 um get 300 nm Ru vias at 1 um pitch instead of 5-10 um Cu TSVs with large keep-out zones. Vias drop into the array region instead of a dedicated TSV stripe.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV plus keep-out area falls >90%, moving HBM area per bit from ~3x toward ~1.3x DDR5, and lower via capacitance trims pJ/bit.

title: National EUV scanner-hour utility shared by memory startups
idea: Time-slicing a $200M asset: a national center owns EUV scanners and sells exposure hours. Startups' DRAM wafers travel in sealed FOUPs by courier, get their 5-7 EUV layers, and return to the startups' smaller DUV-only fabs.
why: Removes the single largest capex item from entrants and keeps scanners near 100% utilized. Entrant fab capex falls ~40%.

title: T-RAM fixed: electrostatically doped thyristor erases dopant variability
idea: T-RAM Semiconductor's thin-capacitively-coupled thyristor died on the spread of its latch and holding voltages, caused by random implanted p-n-p-n doping. Build the thyristor in an undoped silicon nanosheet and induce its four regions with split gates (electrostatic doping). The controller trims the latch threshold per bank after test by setting gate voltages. Run the cell in dynamic mode, so data is stored as base charge rather than as holding current.
why: Removes both killers of thyristor RAM, variability and standby current. The result is a ~1-2 ns gain-read cell with no capacitor (attacks the capacitor wall), and base-charge refresh is claimed to be needed ~100x less often than DRAM refresh.
note: Z2-FET/FB-FET known; base-charge retention and disturb remain risks.

title: Tezzaron's split periphery fixed with in-array 16:1 preamp multiplexing
idea: Failure mined: Tezzaron's DiRAM moved sense amps onto a separate logic die but was capped by TSV pitch and lack of capital. Fix: give each bitline a 2-transistor gain preamp in the array wafer and time-multiplex 16 preamps onto one 1 um hybrid bond. Latching, write-back and ECC run on a bonded logic wafer from a mature U.S. node.
why: The array wafer becomes ~85-90% cells vs ~51% today (fact 7), ~1.7x bits per array wafer. The periphery wafer uses cheap non-EUV logic, which lowers blended capital intensity.
note: In-array 2T preamps plus 16:1 bond multiplexing serialize restore.

title: HMC's SerDes replaced by sense amps driving TSVs directly
idea: Failure mined: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube lost on SerDes power and cost. Fix: each bank's secondary sense amps drive their TSV with a 100-150 mV charge-domain swing straight to a strobed latch on the base die. This deletes the DRAM-side global I/O lines, data buffers, serializers and DQ drivers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~0.5-1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, and ~8-10% of the DRAM die's periphery is deleted.

title: Wide I/O fixed: thermal-break bond layer under DRAM-on-SoC
idea: JEDEC Wide I/O (DRAM stacked on mobile SoCs) died because SoC hot spots doubled DRAM refresh and because nobody wanted the TSV yield liability. Insert a porous low-k bonding layer with copper pillars that cuts heat flow into the DRAM about 5x. Add refresh zoning driven by a live SoC thermal map, so only rows above hot cores refresh fast.
why: Brings back 3D DRAM-on-logic for data-movement energy (fact 5: from 10-20 pJ/bit to under 1 pJ/bit) while capping refresh overhead (fact 3).
note: Thermal break forces SoC heat elsewhere; temperature-zoned refresh is known.

title: U.S. Memories redone: take-or-pay offtake plus chokepoint-free bill of materials
idea: U.S. Memories Inc. (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) died in 1990 when PC makers refused binding purchases once prices fell. Re-form it with 10-year take-or-pay contracts from hyperscalers, a price collar (floor and ceiling), and a charter requiring at least two non-chokepoint sources for every input (Mo for W, recaptured helium, non-Spruce-Pine crucibles).
why: The U.S. makes ~1-2% of DRAM; offtake de-risks a $15B+ fab while the material charter removes exposure to helium, quartz and tungsten shocks.

title: Z-RAM revived on GAA nanosheets: free floating bodies, no SOI
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died on costly SOI wafers and a floating-body signal that shrank with scaling. Gate-all-around nanosheet stacks, already standard in logic fabs, are naturally floating bodies: write holes into 3-4 stacked sheets per cell by gate-induced drain leakage and sense the summed current shift, giving capacitorless DRAM with ~2 extra masks in any GAA foundry.
why: Deletes the capacitor module (AR 60-75 mold etch, high-k ALD, ~5-7 litho/etch steps) and the SOI premium; multi-sheet summing restores the margin that killed Z-RAM; lets U.S. GAA logic fabs build DRAM-class macros. Claimed ~30-40% fewer array process steps.

title: X-ray lithography's mask killer dodged with interference-only array exposure
idea: Proximity X-ray lithography died mainly because 1x masks could not be made or inspected. DRAM arrays are periodic, so print line/space and hexagonal hole lattices by mask-free interference of 2-4 coherent EUV/soft X-ray beams split from one compact free-electron-laser source feeding 10+ exposure stations, trimmed by cheap DUV cut masks.
why: Removes EUV scanners from ~4 of the 5-7 EUV layers; one source amortized over many stations and huge depth of focus cut cost per array layer several-fold.

title: Graphcore IPU, fixed: hybrid-bonded MRAM weight die under SRAM
idea: Graphcore's SRAM-only IPU faded because 900 MB on-chip could not hold modern models and its DDR streaming was slow. Hybrid-bond a read-optimized STT-MRAM die (weights are written rarely, so slow high-energy writes and limited endurance do not matter) directly under the compute die at >10 TB/s.
why: Gigabytes of weights per package with no DRAM or HBM; MRAM is capacitorless, nonvolatile and ~3-4x denser than SRAM.

title: FB-DIMM fixed: passive WDM optical bus, each module drops its own color
idea: FB-DIMM died because every Advanced Memory Buffer had to retime and re-drive all downstream traffic (4-6 W per DIMM, plus latency per hop). Replace the daisy chain with a motherboard waveguide carrying one wavelength per module: a passive ring filter on each module drops only its own wavelength and adds replies on a paired one, so no module repeats another's traffic and every slot sees the same latency.
why: Capacity per channel beyond DDR5's 1-2 DIMMs-per-channel electrical limit: 8-16 modules per channel at constant latency with ~5x lower buffer power than AMB, raising usable memory per socket.

title: Xeon Phi capacity limit fixed: DRAM stacks on package underside too
idea: Knights Landing's on-package MCDRAM was abandoned largely because 16 GB was too small, a ceiling set by package beachfront beside the die. Use a glass-core substrate with 25-50 um through-glass vias to mount a second ring of memory stacks on the package underside, directly beneath the processor's I/O edge, with a board cutout and bottom cold plate, doubling the stacks within ~5 mm of the PHY.
why: Breaks the beachfront limit on stacks per accelerator: ~2x on-package capacity at the same short-reach pJ/bit, delaying the need for far memory.

title: T-RAM temperature failure fixed by replica-thyristor closed-loop gate biasing
idea: T-RAM stalled at GlobalFoundries because thyristor holding current swings by orders of magnitude from 0 to 105 C, losing data hot and writing slowly cold. Fix: every mat carries a replica thyristor whose holding current an on-die loop servos by adjusting the shared gate-assist voltage, keeping all cells a fixed margin above holding across temperature and aging.
why: Makes a capacitor-less one-device cell robust across corners, removing the capacitor wall and much sensing periphery (facts 1, 7).

title: 450 mm died on toolmaker risk: tools paid per wafer pass
idea: The 450 mm transition (G450C) was abandoned around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund development without guaranteed volume. Fix the risk split: toolmakers own and maintain tools inside the fab and are paid per wafer pass with uptime guarantees, so fab capex becomes opex and toolmakers profit from throughput and yield.
why: Capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost; per-pass pricing could cut an entrant's upfront capital ~50-70% and align toolmakers with uptime.

title: 1.5 nm quantum-confined silicon access sheet widens effective band gap
idea: Effect: quantum confinement. Thin the vertical access channel to ~1.5 nm Si so subband confinement raises the effective gap from 1.12 to ~1.6-1.8 eV, cutting band-to-band GIDL and SRH generation (proportional to ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT)) by up to ~10^4 at the storage junction.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 10-100x retention, compatible with 4F2 vertical-channel cells. Risk: Vt variation ~1/t^2 and mobility loss.
note: Vt variation ~1/t^2 is severe.

title: Charge-trap flash computes attention over cold tokens in place
idea: KV tokens older than a recency window are programmed by Fowler-Nordheim tunneling into charge-trap NAND strings as analog conductances. The query is applied as wordline voltages, and bitline currents sum the dot products, so the array returns only the attention-weighted value sum. DRAM keeps just the last few thousand tokens.
why: KV for 1M-token contexts lives in NAND bits that are ~10x cheaper, and the DRAM KV footprint drops 10-100x (facts 4, 5).
note: Analog CT-NAND precision and programming slowness are doubts.

title: Recombination-sink grid absorbs hammer electrons at much tighter pitch
idea: Effect: minority-carrier recombination in engineered short-lifetime silicon. A self-aligned buried carbon-doped or p+ grid runs between adjacent active rows; electrons injected by aggressor activation recombine inside this short-lifetime strip before reaching victim nodes, while storage junctions stay in long-lifetime silicon.
why: 10x density: tighter rows would otherwise drop hammer thresholds below ~100 and mitigation refresh would erase the gain; the sink allows ~40% row and tier pitch shrink, which with 16-tier stacking gives ~10x at the cost of one implant or epi step.

title: Dairy-cooperative periphery foundry co-owned by rival DRAM makers
idea: Like farmer co-ops that share one creamery, DRAM vendors jointly own a U.S. fab that makes only periphery/CMOS-under-array logic wafers to a common bond interface. Each vendor bonds its proprietary array wafers on top and buys periphery at cost.
why: Pools capex for the ~49%-of-die periphery function, frees each vendor's DRAM-node capacity for cells (~1.5x bits per DRAM wafer), and puts a large memory fab in the U.S.

title: Pop-up-book sense amplifier: vertical-channel latch fits bitline pitch
idea: Like a pop-up book that stands flat art upright, build the SA cross-coupled pair and equalizer from vertical-channel transistors in a two-tier stack (n-latch below, p-latch above). One complete SA then fits under a single 2F bitline pitch instead of a 4-6F-wide strip.
why: Shrinks SA-strip footprint ~3-4x (SA strips are ~10-15% of die) and enables open-bitline 4F^2 arrays without an SA-pitch crisis.

title: Arsenal conversion: retool legacy 3D-NAND lines for vertical oxide DRAM
idea: Like WWII car plants converted to bombers, fund conversion of 48-96-layer 3D NAND lines, which need no EUV and already own deep-hole etch and staircase tools, to make vertical-string oxide-channel gain-cell DRAM under a Defense Production Act Title III style program with offtake guarantees.
why: Fastest route to 3D DRAM tiers (fact 2) without a $15B, 3-5 year fab; reuses depreciated deep-etch capacity and policy can unlock it in months.
note: Underlying vertical oxide gain-cell DRAM still unproven.

title: Contract-brewing program: idle U.S. fabs add BEOL memory layers
idea: As craft brewers rent others' tanks, a federal tolling program buys finished CMOS periphery wafers from foundries and pays idle U.S. 200/300 mm fabs per wafer to add DUV-only, <=350 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory layers, with 5-year guaranteed offtake.
why: U.S. manufacturability/capital: reuses depreciated tools and staff with no EUV and no new shell; output in ~18 months vs 3-5 years for a new fab.

title: Duplex printing: memory stacks on both faces of compute
idea: Like printing both sides of a page, make DUV nano-TSVs through the thinned logic die so HBM-like stacks bond to both its top and bottom faces.
why: Doubles memory shoreline and bandwidth per compute die without EUV; shorter wires cut pJ/bit.
note: Thermal path conflict: one compute face normally carries the heat sink.

title: Synthetic-rubber program: government-owned, contractor-operated memory plants
idea: In 1942-44 the U.S. built 51 synthetic-rubber plants in about two years as government-owned, contractor-operated (GOCO) sites with pooled process licenses. Do the same for DRAM: government-owned shells and tools, operators who bid to run them under pooled-IP agreements, and privatization after a decade.
why: U.S. manufacturability: removes private capital risk for moving from 1-2% to 10%+ U.S. share, and pooled licenses allow a fast build cadence.

title: Split-gate vertical access device with floating mid-node stack effect
idea: IFR: leakage finds no voltage to push it. Split the vertical access channel into two gate segments driven by the same wordline with a short doped mid-node between them; in the off state the mid-node floats to an intermediate voltage so each segment sees small Vds, negative Vgs on the upper segment and no DIBL.
why: Fact 3: the series stack effect cuts subthreshold and GIDL leakage ~10-30x with no footprint cost in a vertical cell, extending refresh interval proportionally.
note: Floating mid-node stack effect; dual-gate vertical cells partly explored.

title: Wafer-scale memory board with pick-and-place replaceable cell tiles
idea: Ideal result: memory as a field of interchangeable tiles. A periphery interposer wafer carries all decoders and sense amps in repeated sockets; small cell-array tiles are compression-bonded, tested in place, and bad tiles are lifted and replaced.
why: Yield and capital (facts 4, 7): tiny tiles yield ~99%, and the periphery wafer can be built at 28-40 nm in the U.S.

title: Cold-side memory: DRAM tiers face the cold plate
idea: IFR: 'memory sits at coolant temperature even on a 1 kW chip.' Backward: flip the 3D stack so DRAM tiers touch the cold plate with logic beneath, and carry logic heat up through dense copper or diamond-like-carbon thermal pillars that pass through dedicated keep-out columns in the array.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention roughly doubles per 10 C; holding DRAM 30-40 C cooler cuts refresh ~8x and makes memory-on-logic stacking viable.
note: Thermal pillars through array cost area; enabling memory-on-logic is the payoff.

title: Capacitor-first wafer with transferred silicon film for transistors on top
idea: Ideal: the capacitor never competes with the transistor for space or heat. Closest: etch and fill deep capacitors in a bulk wafer first, anneal the high-k at >1000 C for its highest-k phase, then Smart-Cut-bond a thin single-crystal Si film on top and build access transistors aligned to the buried capacitor contacts.
why: Facts 1 and 4: capacitor depth is no longer limited by stack height or thermal budget, high-k phase gives Cs gains, and the capacitor module can run in a separate, less advanced line.

title: Fifteen-day cycle-time capacitorless line sells memory build-to-order
