idea: Ideal: memory made on demand, with no inventory or price swings. Closest: a ~30-mask capacitorless flow on single-wafer tools only (RTP instead of furnaces, no 12-hour batch ALD) targets 15-20-day fab cycle time versus ~90, and sells capacity as monthly build-to-order contracts.
why: Capital and supply: far less WIP (~$1B per fab tied up today) and supply that tracks AI demand monthly, damping 4x price spikes.

title: Glass-interposer LPDDR fan-out replaces HBM stacks
idea: IFR: bandwidth without the TSV tax. The constraint drives toward Si/Al/O/Na/Ca glass: aluminosilicate glass interposers with fine Cu/Ti redistribution wiring fan out 16-32 standard LPDDR dies around the accelerator at wide I/O, with no TSVs and no Ta barriers.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR (fact 6); delivering similar capacity with planar LPDDR needs about one third of the DRAM wafers.

title: Mat-granular bond clusters for 64-byte, zero-overfetch activation
idea: Ideal: fetch exactly the byte asked for and nothing else. Closest achievable: give every 512x512 mat its own cluster of hybrid-bond pads for local wordline enable and data, so the logic die activates a single mat segment instead of an 8 KB page spread across 16 mats.
why: Fact 8 overfetch: 128x overfetch falls to ~8x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.6 pJ; fewer cells disturbed per ACT also eases row hammer (fact 9).
note: Per-mat hybrid-bond activation extends fine-grained DRAM work; needs DRAM fab access.

title: Backside deep-trench storage capacitors under a frontside transistor array
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): same die footprint and pinout. After frontside transistors and periphery are built and bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer and etch storage trenches into crystalline Si from the backside (Bosch/cryo Si etch reaches 100:1), contacting each access transistor drain through the thinned body, which frees the frontside for periphery and bitline routing.
why: AR >100 in silicon (fact 1) decoupled from the transistor stack, with periphery congestion relieved (fact 7); reuses backside-power-delivery process know-how.
note: Backside Si trench caps decouple from transistor stack; needs full fab process.

title: Tier-multiplexed sense-amp layer shared by sixteen bonded array layers
idea: Limit: 0% periphery on any array die. Sixteen thin array layers are hybrid-bonded onto one bottom sense-amp layer. Each layer's bitline group reaches the sense amps through a per-layer select transistor in a vertical bond-via column, so one sense-amp row serves 16 layers in turn.
why: Fact 7: periphery is about 49% of the die; amortizing sense amps over 16 layers cuts periphery per bit about 16x and lifts array efficiency toward 90%.

title: Stack-of-stacks: hybrid-bonded sixteen-tier superlattice modules
idea: Limit: strain allows no more than 20 Si/SiGe pairs per epi run. Grow strain-safe 16-tier modules on separate wafers, process their lateral cells, then hybrid-bond eight modules face-to-face and back-to-back with vertical bitline vias crossing each bond.
why: Fact 2: reaches 128 tiers without epi relaxation defects, and module yield is binned before stacking.
note: Bitline vias crossing each bond need sub-100 nm bond alignment; module binning is the clever part.

title: LNG regasification cold runs refresh-free cryogenic memory racks
idea: Imposed scarcity: no power budget for refresh. Site memory-heavy data halls at LNG import terminals and use the ~-160 C cold released during regasification, through a nitrogen loop, to hold DRAM at ~100-120 K, where access-transistor leakage collapses and refresh intervals can stretch >1000x.
why: Refresh (16-33% of idle DRAM power) and most cooling energy disappear using free waste cold, with no helium; higher carrier mobility at low temperature also trims access time.
note: LNG waste cold as heat sink is a siting twist on cryo-DRAM; requires co-located data halls.

title: Frozen cell: decade-long nanoimprint templates replace node chasing
idea: Constraint: one cell geometry for ten years. Pattern every array layer by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from e-beam masters replicated into hundreds of daughter templates; R&D money shifts to stacking, periphery and sensing while array litho cost collapses to template wear.
why: Fact 4: a node buys only 10-20% cost per bit; freezing it avoids ~$1-2B of litho reinvestment per node and cuts array litho cost ~80%.

title: Five-mask array wafer: sense amps live on bonded logic wafer
idea: Constraint: the array wafer gets five masks (active, wordline, bitline, capacitor, bond pad). Sense amplifiers, decoders and all upper metal sit on a separately made CMOS wafer hybrid-bonded face-to-face, with a 16:1 local bitline-select device formed in the same wordline step so bond pitch can stay near 0.5 um.
why: Fact 7: the ~49% periphery moves to a cheap logic node and stops occupying DRAM-process area; array wafer cost -50%, array die density ~1.8x.

title: ISO-6 ballroom fab survives on 4,096 self-repairing tiles per die
idea: Constraint: a cleanroom one to two classes dirtier than today. Wafers stay only in sealed minienvironments, and each die is 4,096 independently testable 1 Mb tiles with 20% spares and a boot-time self-test controller that remaps dead tiles, tolerating ~10x defect density.
why: Capital and time: fab shell/HVAC is ~20-25% of fab capex; halving it and cutting build time ~1 year helps U.S. manufacturability while spares hold yield.

title: Open DRAM PDK lets idle U.S. foundries run memory lots
idea: Constraint: no access to incumbent DRAM IP. A public consortium develops and releases a royalty-free 1T1C process kit (recipes, cell, sense amp, redundancy) at a 20-28 nm class on standard logic toolsets, qualified at several U.S. foundries so spare capacity can produce DRAM.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: activates depreciated fabs with ~zero new fab capex and breaks the three-company know-how wall.

title: Prefab cleanroom pods add DRAM capacity in $500M steps
idea: Constraint: capital may arrive only in $500M increments. Factory-built cleanroom pods, each a complete array-only line for ~2k wafer starts/month, are shipped and plugged into shared utilities and a partner logic fab for periphery, going from order to output in ~12 months.
why: Capital intensity and time: replaces $15B, 3-5-year lumpy bets with demand-matched modules, lowering financing risk and speeding a U.S. ramp.

title: Inverted fin capacitor: storage discs between continuous plate sheets
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: deposit a ~20-layer stack of continuous plate metal sheets alternating with sacrificial layers, etch one hole per cell, laterally recess the sacrificial layers into rings and fill dielectric plus storage metal, giving a stack of storage discs interleaved with the plates.
why: Facts 1 and 4: ~3-6 fF at AR ~15 instead of 70, so the extra charge for 125 C retention comes from deposition, not from the hardest etch.

title: Downturns may not kill capex: revenue-floor insurance for builders
idea: Self-imposed limit: no fab plan may be cancelled because of the cycle. A government-backed insurer guarantees a per-bit revenue floor to makers who keep building through troughs, funded by premiums and clawbacks at peak prices.
why: Capital intensity: removes the cyclical underinvestment behind today's shortage and keeps 3-5-year fab timelines from restarting.
note: Moral hazard and fiscal exposure are key doubts.

title: MSB-DRAM: hierarchical 64-cell bitlines with sense amps bonded under the array
idea: Keep a conventional 1T1C cell (Si BCAT, or an oxide 4F2 VCT) but break each bitline into 64-cell local segments. Eight local segments in a column each connect through one pass transistor (built in the cell process) to a short global bitline that drops through a single Cu-SiCN hybrid bond to a sense amplifier on a separately made logic periphery wafer bonded face-to-face (Samsung's periphery-under-cell scheme, but at sense-amp granularity). Only the segment holding the activated wordline is switched on, so the sense amp sees ~9 fF instead of ~35 fF. By the A1 sense criterion the capacitor needed falls from 5.4 fF to ~1.4-1.8 fF, a 335-445 nm stub instead of a 1.3 um pillar; alternatively keep the tall capacitor and drop the array voltage toward ~0.4 V. Sense amps, sub-array decoders and I/O leave the cell wafer, lifting array efficiency from ~0.51 to ~0.70.
why: Capacitor aspect ratio 62 -> 16-21 (3-4x shorter, no AR-60 capacitor etch); bitline energy per sensed bit 3.9x lower at today's VARY, or ~22x lower at VARY ~0.4 V with the tall capacitor; 1.37x density from array efficiency; bond pitch 0.74-1.05 um instead of 0.26-0.37 um. Cost per bit ~1.1-1.3x 1-beta in 2D (an energy and capacitor win, not a cost win, until stacked).

title: Photonic periphery wafer: every bonded DRAM die is born with optical I/O
idea: Samsung's 4F2 DRAM builds the periphery on a separate wafer bonded under the cells. Make that periphery wafer in a monolithic photonics-CMOS process (microring modulators, Ge photodetectors, waveguides and 45 nm-class transistors on one wafer) so every DRAM die has optical I/O built in. The memory die connects to compute over fibers or a photonic interposer at metre scale, so capacity is not limited by the 8-12 HBM stacks that fit around a GPU or by TSV stacks. Closed-loop heaters keep the rings locked as DRAM die temperature moves.
why: DRAM at a distance at ~3.4 pJ/bit (HBM parity) instead of ~10-20 pJ/bit for off-package DDR [UNVERIFIED], ~500 GB/s per die, and unlimited capacity per accelerator; no TSVs or HBM stacking on the memory side. Energy is NOT better than HBM today.

title: Sequential periphery-over-cell for Si DRAM: lithographic vias instead of hybrid bonds
idea: Keep a conventional high-temperature Si 1T1C array (1-beta-class cell with a short capacitor), finish it including its capacitor, cap it with oxide, and transfer a ~50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top by Smart Cut. Build the sense amplifiers, sub-wordline drivers and decoders in that layer with CEA-Leti-style 400-500 C n&p CMOS. Connect each 64-128-cell bitline segment to its sense amp with a lithographically aligned via (~100-200 nm, overlay ~5-10 nm) instead of a hybrid-bond pad (>=300-400 nm pitch, ~50-100 nm overlay). This delivers A1 white space 1 (one sense amp per short bitline) at 1-beta pitch without the bond-pitch wall and without the second periphery wafer of bonded periphery-under-cell.
why: Capacitor 1.3 um -> 226-376 nm (AR 62 -> 11-18) with no mux; one wafer instead of two (vs bonded PUC); array efficiency ~0.51 -> ~0.7 (1.37x density).

title: Swap ferromagnet for antiferromagnetic Neel-vector bit with zero stray field
idea: Store the bit in the Neel vector of a non-collinear antiferromagnet (Mn3Sn, Mn3Pt) or of Mn2Au. Neel spin-orbit torque switches it in picoseconds, and it is read through an all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junction (tunnelling magnetoresistance was shown in 2023).
why: Non-volatile, so no refresh (fact 3); immune to field and row-hammer disturbance (fact 9); ps writes. With no dipolar crosstalk, cells pack at litho pitch, which FM MRAM cannot do.
note: Widely pursued (CuMnAs, Mn3Sn, all-AFM TJ 2023).

title: Swap stored charge for snap-through state of buckled nanobeam
idea: A compressively prestressed SiN or diamond-like-carbon nanobeam (~15 x 150 nm) clamped over a recess has two mirror-image buckled states. A 1-2 ns electrostatic pulse from a side electrode snaps it over, and the state is read capacitively without disturbing it.
why: No leakage path, so no refresh (fact 3); non-destructive read removes restore energy (fact 8); immune to radiation and row hammer (fact 9).
note: NEMS bistable beam memory is known; density ~20-50F2 and 1e15-cycle fatigue are unproven.

title: Swap gate-dielectric polarization for ferroelectric semiconductor channel (alpha-In2Se3)
idea: Use a 2D ferroelectric semiconductor such as alpha-In2Se3, where the polarization lives inside the channel itself. Flipping it shifts the band bending and so the channel conductance, with no ferroelectric/dielectric interface to trap charge or depolarize.
why: Gives a capacitor-less 1T cell with non-destructive read and no refresh (facts 1, 3, 8), and avoids the endurance loss that limits HZO FeFETs.

title: Swap silicon storage node for 4H-SiC junction-isolated node
idea: Build the 1T1C or gain-cell storage node in 4H-SiC, whose 3.26 eV bandgap cuts junction generation leakage by >10^15 versus Si. SiC DRAM test cells in the 1990s already held data for hours to years at room temperature.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3: ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth). SiC boules grow without Spruce Pine quartz crucibles, and U.S. SiC fabs (NC, NY) already exist, which helps U.S. manufacturing.

title: Swap leaky capacitor for series resonant-tunnelling-diode latch (TSRAM)
idea: Two vertically stacked resonant-tunnelling diodes (Si/SiGe, InGaAs/AlAs or graphene/hBN) in series form a bistable latch held at valley current (<10 pA). With one pass transistor for access, it is a static cell about the size of 1T1C.
why: Refresh-free static storage (fact 3) at ~10 mA standby per Gb, no tall capacitor (fact 1) and non-destructive read (fact 8).
note: TI TSRAM precedent; standby valley current ~mW/Gb rivals refresh power.

title: Substitute per-word SECDED with row-wide LDPC in sense stripe
idea: Substitute 64-bit Hamming with a 4 KB-row LDPC code: parity sits in spare columns and the decoder in the sense-amp stripe. Tail-cell retention failures become correctable erasures, so tREFI can be set at a ~1e-5 raw bit error rate instead of zero failures.
why: 8-16x longer refresh interval (refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss recovered) for ~6% parity overhead.
note: Hi-ECC-style prior art; 8-16x refresh relax at ~6% parity.

title: Substitute logic ALUs with bit-serial adders drawn from DRAM array masks
idea: Reserve every 64th mat edge for a strip of 1-bit full adders and latches built only from the array's own access transistors and capacitors as dynamic logic, on the same pitch, so no periphery masks are added; tensors are reduced bit-serially along the sense-amp row and operands never leave the mat.
why: Constraint: skips I/O and global-bus energy (most of DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit) for >10x lower energy per elementwise or reduction operation; capital: zero new process steps.

title: Substitute high-temperature epitaxy with laser-crystallized silicon above logic
idea: Deposit amorphous silicon over finished logic BEOL and melt-crystallize it with nanosecond excimer or green laser pulses that heat only the top ~100 nm (BEOL stays below 400 C), seeding grains through small vias; then build silicon access transistors and capacitors in this layer directly over compute.
why: Constraint: memory ~1 um above logic gives ~0.1 pJ/bit access (>20x below HBM) with silicon-like leakage; capital: excimer annealers are commodity tools from LTPS display lines.
note: Grain boundaries add leakage tail incompatible with DRAM retention.

title: Substitute one-bit cells with analog charge levels and charge-domain MAC
idea: Use larger DUV-defined capacitors (~4x area, no EUV) holding 16 charge levels (4 bits) for AI weights or KV cache; on access, selected cells dump charge onto a summing line weighted by input voltages, so a whole dot product is read with one ADC conversion instead of streaming every bit out.
why: Constraint: one result moves instead of N operands, ~10-50x lower energy per MAC-equivalent access; facet: equal bit density with ~2x coarser lithography and no EUV.

title: Substitute oversized cell capacitors with power-up offset-trimmed sense amplifiers
idea: Store each sense amplifier's Vt-mismatch correction in a trimmed capacitor bank calibrated at power-up, so the bitline needs only ~25 mV of signal instead of 100+ mV; cells then need ~1-1.5 fF and bitline swing can be reduced.
why: Constraint: ~4x less cell charge plus reduced swing on shorter bitlines gives ~10x lower array energy per access; facet: capacitor AR from ~70:1 to ~20:1, shrinking the HAR etch/ALD module (fact 1).

title: Swap all-DRAM main memory for a DRAM cache over SLC NAND
idea: Substitute most DRAM capacity with low-latency SLC NAND on a CXL device. A hardware-managed DRAM cache of about 1/8 of capacity sits in front, with page-level hot/cold tracking and a sector write-back buffer to protect endurance.
why: Most server memory is cold at any instant, so DRAM per server falls 4-8x for in-memory databases, caches and VM hosts, replaced by non-EUV NAND bits.
note: DRAM cache over SLC NAND; same core as I-09015.

title: Sub-terahertz plastic waveguide ribbons replace DDR copper channels
idea: Substitute PCB DDR traces with PTFE/HDPE dielectric ribbon waveguides carrying 140-300 GHz carriers from CMOS transceivers in the memory controller to modules up to 1 m away; each ribbon moves 50-100 Gb/s with no equalization and no connector stubs.
why: Fact 5: DDR5 10-20 pJ/bit to ~2-3 pJ/bit; distance freedom enables rack-scale pooled DRAM, recovering the ~20-30% stranded memory.

title: CVD-diamond interlayers replace silicon spacers in tall stacks
idea: Substitute dummy silicon spacers and mold compound between DRAM dies with 20 um polycrystalline diamond wafers carrying laser-drilled vias, so every bond layer is a lateral heat spreader (k ~1,500 vs ~150 W/mK).
why: Heat limits HBM to 12-16 high: 24-32-high stacks (about 2x GB per stack) at the same junction temperature.

title: Bookshelf DRAM: dies standing on edge in slotted carriers
idea: Substitute vertical stacking with edge mounting: dies with pads redistributed to one edge stand upright in a laser-machined or 3D-printed ceramic slotted carrier, like books, with each edge soldered to substrate pads at 50 um pitch; ~50 dies per cm of shelf.
why: Near-HBM density per footprint without TSVs or thinning, and each die is independently reworkable so stack-yield coupling (Fact 6) disappears.

title: Substitute contact-based NEMS switches with non-contact buckled-beam bistable cells
idea: Store bits as the up/down state of a nanoscale buckled beam held by mechanical bistability and toggled electrostatically, with no contact closure, so there is no stiction or contact wear.
why: NV with high endurance and no charge leakage tail; radiation-immune; avoids scarce materials.
note: Same buckled-beam cell.

title: Substitute EUV array patterning with block-copolymer self-assembly at 250 C
idea: Swap EUV for directed self-assembly of block copolymers (annealed at ~250 C) guided by coarse DUV templates, which naturally forms the periodic hexagonal and line arrays memory tiers need.
why: Breaks the single-supplier EUV chokepoint for array layers and cuts patterning cost per layer ~3x.

title: Substitute water-hungry wet cleans with supercritical CO2 dry processing
idea: Swap ultrapure-water wet benches for supercritical CO2 cleaning, resist strip and drying at ~40-80 C plus dry plasma cleans, allowed by the low-temperature tier flow, so a memory fab can sit in water-scarce Arizona.
why: Cuts fab water use ~70-90% and ultrapure-water capex, removing a water constraint on siting.
note: scCO2 cleaning studied for decades; full wet-clean replacement unproven.

title: Ultra-wide-bandgap Ga2O3 or diamond access transistor locks charge
idea: Combine power-electronics materials with the DRAM cell: a thin-film beta-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) or hydrogen-terminated diamond access transistor built in BEOL has thermal-generation and band-to-band leakage far below 1e-21 A, so a 1-5 fF node keeps its charge for years. Bits are written like DRAM and held like flash, with unlimited endurance because nothing tunnels through an oxide.
why: Fact 3: refresh power goes to zero and 10-20% bandwidth returns; goes past IGZO's ~3.2 eV gap that prior work studied.
note: Oxide-semiconductor access already pursued; leakage is trap-limited, not bandgap-limited; BEOL diamond infeasible.

title: Strain-coupled piezo layer flipping a magnetostrictive nanomagnet
idea: Combine a thin AlScN piezoelectric pad with an elliptical magnetostrictive FeGa nanomagnet on top: a voltage pulse strains the magnet and rotates its easy axis by 90 degrees, and a timed pulse pair completes a 180-degree flip. A tunnel junction stacked above reads the state; writing draws almost no current, and the magnet holds the bit indefinitely.
why: Zero refresh, ~1 aJ writes (about 100x below STT-MRAM), effectively unlimited magnetic endurance; AlScN is CMOS-compatible.
note: Straintronics well studied; nanoscale strain transfer, clamping and 180-degree switching reliability are open.

title: Antiferromagnetic Mn3Sn bit written by spin-orbit torque
idea: Combine the noncollinear antiferromagnet Mn3Sn with a BiSb topological-insulator spin-orbit-torque write line and a tunnel-magnetoresistance read: the antiferromagnetic order switches in picoseconds, produces no stray field so cells pack at pitch without crosstalk, and ignores external fields. The order is stable at zero power.
why: Zero refresh, dense packing with no stray-field spacing, ps switching and effectively unlimited endurance; small read signal is the risk; avoids W and Pt write lines.
note: Widely pursued; small read signal and high-temperature epitaxy hinder integration.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric bilayer hBN: fatigue-free interlayer shift bit
idea: Combine 2D-material stacking with ferroelectric memory: in parallel-stacked bilayer hBN, sliding one layer by a fraction of a lattice constant flips an out-of-plane dipole, and an adjacent MoS2 channel senses the dipole as a threshold shift. Because no bonds break and no ions migrate, switching is reported nearly fatigue-free.
why: Zero refresh with endurance approaching unlimited and sub-ns switching; wafer-scale aligned stacking is the risk.
note: Sliding ferroelectricity shown 2021; wafer-scale aligned stacking is the barrier.

title: Junctionless gate-all-around access continuous with the storage electrode
idea: Channel and storage node are one uniformly n+ doped nanowire, turned off by full depletion from a gate-all-around wordline. There is no metallurgical pn junction at the storage node.
why: Removes junction leakage and the abrupt-junction GIDL hotspot, which may give a 10-100x lower tail at sub-10 nm wire diameters.
note: Heavily doped junctionless channels have their own BTBT leakage; studied for DRAM.

title: Antifuse redundancy sized for one-second retention binning
idea: Run deep retention tests on 1990s ATE to find rows failing a 1 s retention target. Antifuses remap them to an enlarged spare pool (3-5% spare rows), and the part ships with a 1 s refresh.
why: Refresh energy falls ~94% for a few percent of area.
note: At 1 s many rows fail plus VRT; 3-5% spares likely insufficient.

title: Two bits per cell using old nodes' fat capacitors
idea: Trailing 2x-3x nm DRAM nodes have ~15-25 fF cells; pair that surplus charge with time-domain multilevel sensing, where a ramped reference and a counter in the SA stripe quantize four charge levels per cell.
why: Density and cost per bit (facts 1, 4): ~1.8x bits per wafer after ECC overhead, from fully depreciated old fabs with no new lithography.

title: Cell layout co-designed with block-copolymer hexagonal lattice
idea: Combine directed self-assembly and the vertical-channel cell: put transistors and capacitors on the natural hexagonal lattice of a cylinder-forming block copolymer, with zig-zag wordlines and 60-degree bitlines matched to that symmetry, so one coarse guide exposure plus self-assembly defines the array.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): replaces 2-3 EUV layers; hex packing at pitch 2F gives ~3.5F2 per cell versus 6F2 (~40% denser).
note: DSA for DRAM hole arrays was evaluated industrially; defectivity is the blocker.

title: Pulsed-laser-crystallized silicon tiers stacked monolithically above periphery
idea: Combine the display industry's laser crystallization with 3D DRAM: deposit amorphous Si for each tier and melt-crystallize only its top ~100 nm with nanosecond pulses from US-made laser sources, keeping lower tiers and CMOS below 400 C and giving near-single-crystal access channels tier by tier.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): monolithic tiers without wafer bonding or Si/SiGe epitaxy (no imported germanium); crystalline mobility for lateral transistors at the cost of one deposition plus laser pass per tier.

title: Copper-free capacitive hybrid bond: dielectric bond doubles as signal coupler
idea: Combine oxide-oxide direct bonding with AC-coupled proximity signaling: each die-to-die signal is two overlapping metal plates separated only by the ~0.5 um bond oxide, driven with edge/pulse signaling, so no Cu pads must touch. Only a sparse grid of coarse TSVs carries DC power.
why: HBM stacking yield and alignment: removes Cu dishing/protrusion defects and tightens nothing beyond plate overlap (~+/-1 um) at 2-3 um signal pitch; <0.05 pJ/bit per hop; claims to recover most of the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: Resonant adiabatic memory bus recycles wire charge via LC tank
idea: Combine resonant clocking's on-chip LC tank with the wide data bus: interposer/HBM data lines become part of a resonant network where transitioning lines swing sinusoidally through an inductor and hand their CV2 energy back to the tank instead of dumping it to ground; steady bits park.
why: Data movement and the voltage floor: recovers ~50-70% of bus switching energy at interposer lengths without lowering voltage.

title: CCD bucket-brigade column shifts charge to one amplifier
idea: Borrowed from astronomical CCDs: in streaming banks, clocked gates along each column shift every cell's charge packet down to a single floating-diffusion source follower at the column end instead of dumping it onto a heavy bitline. The packet arrives undivided, so the signal is Cs/Cfd instead of Cs/Cbl.
why: Charge wall: signal gain ~20-50x versus charge sharing, permitting sub-fF cells; fits sequential AI weight streaming at ~1 ns per shift stage.
note: CCD serial memories existed; transfer efficiency and leakage over many stages are concerns.

title: LNG cryogenic logistics: 77 K racks enable capacitor-less tiers
idea: Borrowed from LNG handling: memory sleds run immersed in liquid nitrogen, where subthreshold leakage falls by many orders of magnitude, so a bare floating node in a 3D tier holds charge for seconds to hours with no capacitor at all.
why: Removes the capacitor (facts 1-2) and nearly all refresh (fact 3); wire resistance drops ~6x; cooling overhead ~10-20% of saved power.
note: Cryo-DRAM is active research; 77 K cooling costs ~10x removed power, not 10-20%.

title: Dry-lubricant molybdenite monolayers as a domestic-supply gain-cell channel
idea: Molybdenite (MoS2) is mined in Colorado mainly for lubricants and steel. Adapt CVD monolayer MoS2 (1.8 eV gap, no dangling bonds) as the write transistor of a capacitor-free gain cell, where the 2D channel's tiny off-current lets the read transistor's own gate hold charge for seconds or longer.
why: Capacitor-free and indium-free, built on a US-mined element. Retention could cut refresh energy >100x (Fact 3).

title: RF SiGe quantum wells hold holes in a floating-body cell
idea: Adapt the bandgap-engineered SiGe base of RF heterojunction transistors by burying a thin SiGe quantum well below a vertical-channel transistor. Holes generated by band-to-band tunneling collect in the well and shift the threshold, and the valence-band offset stretches retention far beyond plain floating-body cells.
why: A capacitor-free bit in bulk silicon plus a few % germanium, avoiding the capacitor etch and dielectric. The germanium can come from US zinc-smelter residues.
note: Bandgap-engineered SiGe-well 1T-DRAM is published; retention and disturb remain the gap.

title: CD-stamping nanoimprint patterns capacitorless arrays without EUV
idea: Optical-disc plants stamped nanoscale pits from nickel masters by the billion. Adapt jet-and-flash nanoimprint with replica templates for the repetitive array layers of a capacitor-free vertical-transistor cell, where there is no landing-pad-to-capacitor overlay chain to break, and keep DUV only for periphery.
why: EUV has one supplier, draws ~1 MW per scanner and consumes tin and hydrogen. Imprint uses ~1/10 the energy and no EUV, and removing the capacitor removes the hardest overlay stack.
note: NIL for memory already trialed; defectivity/overlay.

title: Vinyl-record stamper replication for nanoimprint DRAM array layers
idea: Adapted from record pressing, where electroformed father-mother-son stampers multiply one lacquer master: write one master with U.S. e-beam, electroform many daughter imprint templates, and pattern DRAM's periodic array layers (active, bitline, storage node) by UV nanoimprint in U.S.-built tools.
why: Imprint tools cost ~1/10 of EUV and draw little power; replication amortizes the expensive master, and array redundancy absorbs imprint defects, so array patterning becomes EUV-free and all-U.S. (capital, energy).

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode latch storing bits at a quarter volt
idea: MINIFY hold voltage to ~0.25 V: two series Esaki band-to-band tunnel diodes grown as a vertical Ge/Si or GaSb/InAs stack form a bistable midpoint node (Goto pair) behind one access transistor, holding a static bit with ~10 pA standby and no refresh.
why: Escapes the ~1 V VARY / CV2 floor (fact 10) and refresh (fact 3); vertical diode stacking keeps area near 1T1C.
note: Tunneling SRAM (TI, 1998) failed on valley current and peak-to-valley variability.

title: Noncollinear antiferromagnet tunnel junction switched in picoseconds
idea: MAGNIFY switching speed to ~10 ps exchange timescales and MINIFY stray field to zero: the bit is the octupole order of Mn3Sn/Mn3Pt in an all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junction, written by spin-orbit torque and read by its tunnel magnetoresistance.
why: Unlimited magnetic endurance, no refresh, and no dipolar crosstalk so cells pack at ~2F spacing; DRAM-class latency with nonvolatility (facts 3, 9).
note: All-AFM tunnel junctions demonstrated 2023; TMR and SOT write currents open.

title: Minify the swing with a band-to-band tunneling access FET
idea: Make the access device a vertical heterojunction TFET (SiGe source at the bitline, Si channel, drain into storage node) whose off-state has no thermionic Boltzmann tail, so off-current is set by tunneling (~1e-18 A). Its low on-current is offset by short local bitlines.
why: Off-current decoupled from kT: refresh interval ~10x longer, and wordline swing can fall from ~3 V to ~1.5 V (fact 10).
note: TFET access studied; real TFET off-current is trap-assisted, not ideal BTBT.

title: Magnify bandgap to 3.3 eV: SiC-junction DRAM holding charge for decades
idea: Build the storage junction and access transistor in 4H-SiC, whose intrinsic carrier density (~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 for Si) cuts thermal generation current by ~18 orders of magnitude, so a charged node holds >10 years at 85 C with the access device off. The read/write scheme stays DRAM-like and U.S. SiC power-device lines can host it.
why: Data survives power loss and refresh disappears (fact 3); reuses domestic SiC fabs; MOS interface traps and density are the risks.

title: Magnify mechanical inertia: bistable buckled nanobeam bit
idea: Store each bit as the up/down state of a pre-compressed, snap-through-bistable 100 nm SiN nanobeam; electrodes above and below snap it in ns and its position is read capacitively by a gain transistor. No charge is retained, so nothing leaks, and elastic flexing has no oxide-breakdown wear mechanism.
why: Non-volatile, zero refresh, abundant materials; elastic endurance targeted >1e15.

title: Magnify the domain wall into the switch: LiNbO3 conductive-wall cells
idea: In thin-film LiNbO3 nanofins a write pulse nucleates or erases a charged domain wall across the fin; the wall conducts ~1e6x better than bulk, so the cell reads on/off non-destructively and has no leakage path when the wall is absent. Walls are stable indefinitely at room temperature.
why: Non-volatile, non-destructive read (fact 8), no stored charge to leak; LiNbO3 thin films already run in photonics fabs.

title: Minify write voltage to 100 mV: magnetoelectric BiFeO3-gated nanomagnets
idea: Couple a multiferroic BiFeO3 layer to a CoFe nanomagnet so a ~100 mV field reverses BFO polarization and, via exchange coupling, flips the magnet; an MTJ stacked on top reads it. Write current is capacitive only, so the access transistor can be minimum-width.
why: Non-volatile, aJ-class write, escapes the CV^2 voltage floor (fact 10); FE endurance in BFO is the limit.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K, minify capacitor to 0.5 fF
idea: Run whole memory sleds immersed in liquid nitrogen. At 77 K, junction and subthreshold leakage fall by more than six orders of magnitude, so a planar 0.5 fF capacitor holds data for hours, and a 4F2 cell needs no high-AR pillar at all.
why: Capacitor wall and refresh: refresh disappears, the capacitor process collapses to planar, and density could reach about 1.5x 6F2. The cost is cryocooling at datacenter scale.
note: Dup of 77 K capacitor-less/planar memory.

title: Minify litho to zero EUV: block-copolymer hex-lattice 4F2
idea: Let block-copolymer cylinders self-assemble into a hexagonal lattice at about 24 nm pitch, guided by one coarse DUV template, to define the vertical-channel pillars and caps of a hexagonal 4F2 array.
why: Litho capital: could replace 3-5 EUV layers with a spin-coat and bake, cutting array patterning cost about 5x.
note: Same BCP hex-lattice pillar definition.

title: Polysilicon-plant waste chlorides recast into synthetic silica crucibles
idea: Magnify a waste stream: hydrolyze the SiCl4 byproduct of Siemens polysilicon reactors into ultra-pure soot or sol-gel silica, then fuse it into crucible bodies and inner liners, so crucibles no longer need natural Spruce Pine quartz.
why: Breaks the >80% HPQ chokepoint with a US-domestic feedstock that is already purified and is currently a disposal cost; purity exceeds natural quartz.

title: Talbot self-imaging lithography for perfectly periodic arrays
idea: Exploit that the DRAM array is a perfect lattice: minify the optics to zero by using lensless Talbot/interference self-imaging of a periodic grating, magnifying the coherent print area to the full wafer for all array layers.
why: Litho capital: lens-free optics cost <5% of a scanner; 193 nm interference can print ~40 nm pitch lattices with infinite depth of focus, and periphery stays on cheap DUV.

title: Minify duplicates: one copy per rack replaces cache tiers
idea: Minify the 6-10 copies a hot byte has in a web stack (Redis/memcached tier, DB buffer pool, OS page cache, replicas): database pages live once in rack-shared, coherent CXL memory that app servers read directly with loads, and the separate cache fleets are retired.
why: Total DRAM per unit of hot data drops ~6-10x, with no new memory technology.

title: Magnify reuse: mine e-waste DRAM with a polyglot CXL controller
idea: Robotic lines desolder LPDDR/DDR3/DDR4 packages from discarded phones and PCs, test them, and mount them on carrier boards behind a 'polyglot' CXL controller that speaks every legacy protocol, absorbs mixed speeds and adds strong ECC, producing pooled memory sleds.
why: Input cost is near scrap value; at ~$0.05-0.15/GB automated handling, memory comes out ~100x cheaper than new contract DRAM, and billions of discarded GB per year rival annual production.
note: Polyglot multi-protocol controller is the twist; 100x cost claim ignores test/handling.

title: Eliminate stored electrons: nanosecond protonic channel bits in tungsten-free oxides
idea: Eliminate stored electrons: the bit is the proton content of a 10-nm oxide channel (WO3, or MoO3 to avoid tungsten), pumped in or out of a phosphosilicate-glass electrolyte by nanosecond pulses, as protonic programmable resistors have shown; the result is a nonvolatile conductance read with tiny current.
why: Nonvolatile and refresh-free (fact 3), BEOL compatible, writes under 2 V (fact 10); risks are endurance toward 1e15 and ionic drift.

title: Eliminate the oxide capacitor: band-offset germanium quantum-well hole pocket
idea: Eliminate the external capacitor: grow a 5-nm SiGe or Ge quantum well beneath a vertical Si access channel so its ~300-500 meV valence-band offset traps holes as the stored bit, shifting the channel threshold; a heterobarrier rather than a junction sets retention, 10-100x longer than plain floating-body cells.
why: Capacitor-less ~4F2 cell with retention near the 64 ms spec (facts 1, 3), epitaxial with no HAR capacitor etch; risk is band-to-band generation in Ge.
note: Quantum-well 1T-DRAM studied; capacitorless cells repeatedly failed on retention spread and disturb.

title: Eliminate refresh: bistable tunnel-diode pair holds each bit statically
idea: Eliminate refresh: put two Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes in series on each storage node, so their negative-differential-resistance curves cross at two stable node voltages (a Goto-pair latch) with ~pA standby current per cell, while one access transistor reads and writes as in DRAM. The diodes are grown by RPCVD in hydrogen carrier with in-situ B/P delta doping, so no rare gases are used.
why: A static cell with a 1T footprint plus a vertical diode stack drives refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) to zero and needs only a small capacitor (fact 1); risk is peak-to-valley ratio uniformity at nm scale.
note: TI tunneling-SRAM (TSRAM) prior art; nm-scale PVR uniformity is the risk.

title: Eliminate current-driven writes: magnetoelectric bismuth ferrite flips electroplated nanomagnets
idea: Eliminate write current and the tunnel junction: a BiFeO3 layer grown from solution or by PLD in O2 switches its coupled ferroelectric and antiferromagnetic order at sub-volt bias and drags an exchange-coupled electroplated CoFe nanomagnet with it; the bit is read from the CoFe's anomalous Hall voltage, so no MgO barrier or fixed layer is sputtered with argon.
why: aJ-scale writes break the CV2 floor through low voltage (fact 10), nonvolatile (fact 3), rare-gas-free stack; risks are BFO switching endurance and ns speed at scale.
note: MESO-style BFO switching widely pursued; endurance and ns speed open.

title: Eliminate refresh with bistable Goto-pair tunnel-diode cell
idea: Make silicon interband tunnel diodes with spin-on dopants and rapid thermal anneal, and series-connect two of them (a Goto pair) at the storage node so their NDR curves create two stable voltages; one access FET writes the node. The cell holds state statically at nA standby current, so refresh is eliminated.
why: Static retention near DRAM density (three devices, vertical diodes) removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3); standby current must stay <1 nA/cell.

title: Eliminate thermionic injection: Ge/Si heterojunction tunnel FET access device
idea: Build a vertical tunnel FET with a CVD-grown p+ Ge source on an n-type Si channel so carriers enter only by band-to-band tunneling; at hold bias the tunneling window closes and there is no thermionic tail, giving ~1e-18 A/um off current. The low on current is fine because one cell needs only microamps.
why: Leakage 100-1000x below MOSFET access devices at equal gate bias, enabling ~10x longer refresh intervals; university CVD plus RTA.

title: Eliminate EUV in the array: maskless DUV interference lithography lattices
idea: The cell array is a perfectly periodic lattice, so expose the wordline, bitline and capacitor-hole layers with a three-beam 193 nm immersion interference tool (no reticle, no projection optics), then halve or quarter the pitch with ALD spacers. One coarse DUV trim mask removes the lattice at array edges, where conventional DUV patterns the periphery.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): replaces 5-7 EUV exposures with a reticle-free tool costing ~$10-20M vs ~$200M per EUV scanner; estimated 15-25% wafer-cost cut and no single-supplier EUV dependence.

title: Eliminate garbage-collector heap headroom with compile-time memory management
idea: Managed languages switch from tracing GC, which needs 2-5x heap headroom, to region inference plus precise reference counting with in-place reuse (Perceus-style) chosen by the compiler.
why: Heaps of Java/Go/C#-class services shrink 2-3x at equal throughput.

title: Solderless nano-velcro interconnect makes HBM socketable and reworkable
idea: Eliminate solder and permanent bonding: grow interlocking copper nanohook forests on memory and logic pads (~5 um pitch) that mesh mechanically at room temperature under clamp pressure and can be unclipped; a failed or outgrown stack is swapped instead of scrapping a $30k GPU package.
why: HBM package yield loss (20-30%) compounds over 8 stacks; reworkability recovers most of it and lets memory be sold/upgraded separately from compute, claimed ~15-25% lower effective cost/bit.
note: Resembles Cu nanowire 'Klett-welding' work; contact reliability at speed unproven.

title: Eliminate domain switching: antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor biased at transition edge
idea: Anneal ALD ZrO2 at <=400 C into its antiferroelectric phase, and DC-bias the plate just below the field-induced AFE-to-FE transition, where small-signal permittivity peaks (k~50-70). Read and write swings stay inside the linear region, so domains never fully switch.
why: Reaches the k~70 needed to break the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) at low AR; avoiding switching removes ferroelectric fatigue, wake-up and imprint; BEOL-compatible capacitor for stacked arrays.
note: MPB/AFE ZrO2 high-k work exists; full storage swing leaves the linear region near the transition.

title: The channel is the bit: ferroelectric-semiconductor transistor, no capacitor
idea: Merge storage and access roles into one layer: an alpha-In2Se3-type ferroelectric semiconductor forms the transistor channel itself, and its own polarization bends the band to set high or low current; there is no capacitor and no separate gate ferroelectric to fatigue.
why: Capacitor and 3D blockers (facts 1,2): 1T 4F2 thin-film cell stackable in tiers, nonvolatile so refresh disappears; risk is polarization screening by channel carriers.
note: FeS-FET (alpha-In2Se3) widely studied; screening and retention are known problems.

title: A magnet with no magnetization: Mn3Sn Weyl antiferromagnet bits
idea: Reverse ferromagnet thinking: store the bit in the chiral spin order of a noncollinear antiferromagnet (Mn3Sn) with ~zero net moment, toggled by spin-orbit torque and read through its large Berry-curvature anomalous Hall voltage rather than through magnetization.
why: Density, speed and refresh (fact 3): zero stray field lets cells pack below 20 nm pitch without coupling, ps-scale dynamics, nonvolatile; risk is small Hall signal at tiny sizes.

title: Remove defects, not add capacitance: hBN-sealed 2D gain cell
idea: Reverse retention strategy from bigger capacitor to zero trap states: a WSe2 or MoS2 monolayer write transistor fully encapsulated in hBN (no dangling bonds) charges an hBN-isolated graphene storage gate, so the trap-assisted tunneling behind the 13 fA leakage tail has no sites to use.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 1.5-2 eV-gap channels with clean interfaces target <1e-19 A, i.e., minutes-to-hours retention and >100x less refresh energy; thin-film tiers stack (fact 2).
note: Clean hBN interfaces help, but 2D gain-cell DRAM is actively pursued.

title: Sliding ferroelectric bits: polarization set by atomic-layer registry
idea: Flip the direction of motion: in bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2, sliding one layer in-plane by one bond length reverses the out-of-plane polarization (AB to BA stacking); write with a vertical field pulse, read by tunnel-current asymmetry, with no ion displacement or oxygen vacancies to fatigue.
why: Endurance and density: sliding ferroelectrics switch essentially fatigue-free in 0.6 nm films, enabling nonvolatile no-refresh cells stacked by layer transfer; risk is wafer-scale stacking-order control.
note: Active research topic; wafer-scale stacking-registry control is the blocker.

title: Turn GIDL into the switch: band-to-band tunnel-FET access device
idea: Reverse the role of the worst leakage mechanism: GIDL is band-to-band tunneling at the gate edge, so make that the ON mechanism with a p-i-n tunnel-FET access device (SiGe/Ge source pocket at the bitline end). The off state has no thermionic path, giving aA-level off current and sub-60 mV/dec swing, and DRAM tolerates the TFET's low on-current because a 5 fF cell needs only ~1-5 uA to write in a few ns.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): off current 100-1000x below the ~13 fA tail could stretch retention from 64 ms to seconds; the smaller wordline swing also eases the voltage floor (fact 10).

title: Move the data, not the amplifier: circulating CCD ring memory
idea: Reverse the access pattern: store bits as charge packets in short rings (32-64 positions) of buried-channel charge-transfer gates, so each packet passes a regenerating sense amplifier once per lap (~20-30 ns at 2 GHz during traffic, slowed to a crawl when idle). Refresh happens on every lap, random access waits at most one lap, and the buried channel under each gate is the storage well, so no capacitor pillar is needed.
why: Makes refresh intrinsic (fact 3) and removes the capacitor (facts 1, 2); latency stays in the 10-30 ns DRAM class; clocking energy and ~2-3 gates per bit are the risks.
note: Essentially 1970s CCD memory with short regenerating loops; no density gain at 2-3 gates per bit.

title: Turn idle display fabs into oxide-TFT memory foundries
idea: Rearrange industries: run oxide-TFT gain-cell memory arrays on Gen-8.5 glass panels in under-utilized LCD/OLED backplane lines, then dice and hybrid-bond the panels onto small CMOS periphery chiplets.
why: Uses glass (no crystal silicon, no HPQ crucibles, no EUV) and already-depreciated tools; Gen-8.5 panel area is ~25x a 300 mm wafer, attacking capital intensity and time-to-capacity.
note: Same display-fab oxide-TFT memory as I-06624.

title: Cold memory: nitrogen-cooled racks make leaky abundant cells work
idea: Reverse the temperature assumption: run DRAM-class arrays at 77 K in liquid-nitrogen racks (N2 is abundant, unlike helium), where leakage falls by orders of magnitude, so small capacitors with simple Al2O3/SiO2 dielectrics hold charge.
why: Removes the need for high-k ZrO2/HfO2 and tall capacitors; retention rises ~10^3-10^4x, cutting refresh energy and capacitor process steps.
note: Cryo-DRAM well studied; LN2 cooling overhead ~10x wall power limits it to niche racks.

title: Two bits per cell: multi-level DRAM with 1% level errors
idea: Rearrange the cell's voltage range into four charge levels sensed by a successive-approximation sense amp, accepting ~1% level misreads corrected by Gray-coded symbol ECC.
why: Halves wafers, crucibles, helium and tungsten per bit (~2x density) at a modest periphery cost.
note: MLC DRAM known since 1990s; sense margin and refresh at 4 levels are the doubt.

title: Octuple spacer patterning from KrF-printed mandrels
idea: Reverse 'print at the final pitch': print fat mandrels at ~160 nm pitch with KrF and multiply them 8x through three nested ALD spacer cycles (SAOP), reaching ~20 nm pitch on the array.
why: No EUV and no ArF immersion needed for the array; KrF tools cost about 1/10 of ArFi and 1/30 of EUV, trading litho for cheap deposition and etch.

title: Flash serves reads, DRAM only absorbs writes in inference
idea: Reverse the tier order for read-only data: model weights stream on a fixed layer schedule (so they can be prefetched perfectly) from a many-channel high-bandwidth NAND stack straight into accelerator SRAM, and DRAM/HBM is kept only for the mutable KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are often 50-80% of inference HBM; taking them out of DRAM cuts DRAM bits per served model 2-4x and sidesteps the HBM TSV tax (fact 6).
note: High-bandwidth flash and LLM-in-a-flash are actively pursued; NAND bandwidth for decode is the doubt.

title: Attention computed inside SSD controllers, only outputs returned
idea: Reverse data-to-compute for KV: the host sends the query vector to computational SSDs whose controllers run dot-products and softmax-weighted sums over KV stored in NAND, returning only the partial output vector and its normalizer.
why: KV never enters DRAM: KV capacity moves to NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit, and PCIe traffic per step falls from GBs to KBs.
note: Close to InstInfer; limited by internal NAND bandwidth.

title: Adiabatic resonant links that recycle wire charge every cycle
idea: Reverse dissipate-and-replace signalling: each interposer line's capacitance forms an LC tank with an on-die spiral or package inductor, and data is encoded by phase or selective clamping of the resonant swing, so most of the CV^2 energy sloshes back instead of burning in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data-movement energy (facts 5, 10): 3-5x lower energy on long interposer and substrate lines (~0.5 vs ~2 pJ/bit), at the cost of fixed-frequency operation.

title: Row overfetch turned into row-wide LDPC in sense-amp stripe
idea: Reverse the 128x overfetch from waste into an asset: every ACT already senses a full 8 Kb row, so an XOR-tree LDPC check (~3% parity over the whole row) runs in the sense-amp stripe at activation, instead of SECDED per 64 b at the I/O. The row-wide code corrects 40+ bit errors per row, so cells with raw BER ~1e-4 (smaller Cs, longer refresh) become shippable.
why: Capacitor charge wall + refresh: tolerating 1e-4 raw BER allows ~30-40% smaller Cs or ~4x refresh interval; parity overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3%.
note: Same row-codeword LDPC mechanism.

title: Clean with snow: cryogenic aerosol and supercritical CO2 replace wet cleans
idea: Reverse cleaning from liquid to dry: argon/CO2 cryogenic aerosol jets remove particles, and supercritical CO2 with cosolvents strips residue and resist. The CO2 is recaptured and recycled in a closed loop.
why: Wet cleans and rinses (100+ per DRAM flow) are the largest UPW use. Moving most of them to dry methods cuts UPW >10x and lets fabs site where water is scarce.
note: Same dry-clean water substitution as I-00456.

title: Circulating CCD loop memory with refresh built into the motion
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: store bits as charge packets marching around short (64-256 stage) buried-channel CCD loops at ~2F gate pitch with no per-bit transistor; one floating-gate amplifier per loop regenerates each packet as it passes, so refresh is inherent and there is no capacitor or access device.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 7: ~2-3F2 per bit with no capacitor; GHz loop rotation gives tens of ns average latency, best for streaming AI weights.
note: 1970s CCD memory revived; GHz high-CTE transfer at 2F pitch is hard.

title: Non-collinear antiferromagnet Mn3Sn bit with zero stray field
idea: TRIZ #13 Other way round: instead of a ferromagnet (MRAM, already examined), store the bit in the octupole order of a non-collinear antiferromagnet (Mn3Sn) switched by spin-orbit torque from an underlying heavy-metal or topological line and read by its large anomalous Hall or tunnel magnetoresistance. Zero net moment means no stray-field coupling and ~10-ps switching.
why: Facts 3 and 9: nonvolatile with no refresh, immune to row-hammer-style neighbor coupling, and packable at 2-3F2 because there are no stray fields.

title: Silicon-carbide 1T1C DRAM with hours-long native retention
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change (bandgap): build 1T1C cells on 4H-SiC wafers (Eg 3.26 eV, intrinsic carrier density ~1e18x lower than Si), where 1990s SiC DRAM test cells already showed hours-to-years room-temperature retention. A buried-channel SiC MOS access device at relaxed 40-90 nm rules serves as a refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Refresh eliminated (Fact 3); SiC boules grow by sublimation, sidestepping Spruce Pine quartz crucibles; existing U.S. SiC wafer capacity improves domestic manufacturability. Density is lower, so it targets capacity/standby tiers.

title: Keep the sacrificial SiGe as hole-storage wells in each tier
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: 3D DRAM flows grow Si/SiGe superlattices and then spend effort removing the SiGe; instead keep a thin SiGe layer under each Si channel as a valence-band quantum well. Holes written by impact ionization or GIDL sit in the well and shift the overlying channel's Vt via body effect, giving a capacitorless 1T cell in every tier.
why: Fact 1 and 2: removes both 3D blockers (capacitor and its lateral integration); ~4F2 per tier and the ~0.2-0.3 eV band offset could extend floating-body retention ~10-100x.
note: Quantum-well capacitorless 1T-DRAM already published (Saraswat group).

title: Self-latching lateral thyristor in each superlattice tier
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: dope each tier's lateral Si strip in situ as p+/n/p/n+ during epitaxy and gate the p-base with the vertical wordline, so the cell latches itself into a regenerative ON or blocking OFF state. It holds that state on ~pA standby current with no refresh and no capacitor, and reads with a large current ratio.
why: Fact 3 and 8: no refresh (saves 16-33% idle power), non-destructive read (no restore energy), ~6F2 per tier, stackable to 32+ tiers.

title: Direct-tunneling hBN floating gate for van der Waals quasi-volatile tiers
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping (rush through the harmful stage): charge a graphene floating gate through a 3-layer hBN barrier by pure direct tunneling in ns, never entering the Fowler-Nordheim/hot-carrier regime that creates traps. The dangling-bond-free barrier keeps endurance DRAM-like with seconds of retention, and MoS2-channel tiers stack as transferred 2D films.
why: Fact 3: capacitorless 1T cell with ~100x longer retention than DRAM (refresh energy -99%) built in low-temperature tiers stackable on logic.

title: Resonant-tunneling InAs/AlSb floating gate from compound-semiconductor fabs
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: a triple-barrier InAs/AlSb heterostructure is opaque at rest (AlSb ~2.1 eV conduction offset) but turns transparent when ~2.5 V aligns its resonant level, letting electrons enter or leave an InAs floating gate fast and at low energy while retention is non-volatile (ULTRARAM-type), grown on Si by MBE/MOCVD.
why: Zero refresh; switching energy per area ~100x below flash and demonstrated endurance >1e7; uses U.S. III-V epitaxy capacity instead of DRAM fabs and needs no HAR capacitor; the endurance gap is covered by write buffering (facts 3, 4).

title: Anti-weight: microfluidic cooling interlayer lifting heat between compute and DRAM
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight (counter a harmful load with a force from the environment): put a 100 um silicon interlayer between a hot accelerator and the DRAM stacked on it. The interlayer has through-vias and two-phase dielectric coolant microchannels that carry compute heat sideways, keeping the DRAM below 85 C.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): memory-on-logic stacking (~10x lower pJ/bit than HBM) becomes possible without the 2x refresh rate required above 85 C.

title: Continuity of useful action: full-duplex simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: add hybrid echo-cancelling receivers to every DQ TSV so reads and writes flow on the same wire at the same time. This removes read-write turnaround bubbles and the idle direction.
why: Data movement and HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): recovers the 10-20% lost to turnaround and gives up to 2x bandwidth per TSV, so half the DQ TSVs deliver the same bandwidth.
note: SBD signaling known; echo cancellation at TSV speeds adds power.

title: Continuity: government buyer-of-last-resort keeps DRAM fabs at full utilization
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: during downturns a national memory reserve buys known-good die at cost-plus, keeping tools at 100% loading; the stored die (dry-nitrogen cabinets) are released into the market during shortages.
why: Capital efficiency: idle tools waste depreciation; continuous loading plus a strategic buffer flattens price spikes.

title: Discarding and recovering: one RDL mask stitches good dies into wafer-scale slabs
idea: TRIZ #34 Discard and recover: after wafer sort, a single per-lot RDL mask routes across scribe lines to connect only good neighbouring dies into wafer-scale memory slabs, discarding bad dies in place without dicing.
why: Packaging cost and yield: removes dicing, substrates and per-die packaging for memory appliances.
note: Anamartic wafer-scale memory precedent.

title: Allosteric strain relay: piezo pulse precesses a magnetostrictive nanomagnet
idea: Allosteric enzymes switch an active site through a distant binding event transmitted mechanically. Put an elliptical magnetostrictive FeGa nanomagnet on a US-made, CMOS-compatible AlScN piezoelectric layer. A timed voltage pulse strains the magnet and rotates its easy axis, so the magnetization precesses 180 degrees in ~0.5 ns, and a tunnel junction reads the state.
why: Non-volatile magnetic bit written by voltage at ~1 fJ instead of ~100 fJ of STT current, with no SOT heavy metals (avoiding the tungsten chokepoint) and unlimited endurance.

title: Mitochondrial proton-gradient storage node immune to electron leakage
idea: Mitochondria store energy as a proton gradient across an electron-insulating membrane; store the bit as protons shuttled between two nanometric proton-hosting layers (WO3/HxWO3) through an electron-blocking proton electrolyte, and read it as the conductance of an oxide channel modulated by proton concentration, all deposited near room temperature.
why: The stored state has no electronic leakage path, so retention moves from ms to hours (refresh removed), with ~10-100 ns writes if the electrolyte is a few nm thick; endurance beyond 1e12 is the key risk.

title: Dendritic-spine IGZO gain stage every 32 cells on short bitlines
idea: Dendritic spines amplify input in a tiny isolated compartment. A BEOL oxide-semiconductor 'spine' transistor every 32 cells takes the cell's charge from a very short local bitline (~1/16 the capacitance) and drives current onto the global bitline. A separate transfer gate writes back.
why: Fact 1/2: the Cs/Cbl transfer ratio improves ~10x, so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF with AR ~15:1 capacitors. That breaks the capacitor wall and makes 3D tiers practical.

title: Honeycomb anodic pores grow litho-free 300:1 capacitor arrays
idea: Like bees and corals that self-organize hexagonal cells, anodize a thick Al (or Ta) film over the access-transistor array so self-ordered hexagonal pores (25-40 nm pitch, AR >300:1) form spontaneously, registered to imprinted dimples over each storage contact; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN then lines the pores after field-assisted barrier-layer thinning opens the pore bottoms.
why: Capacitor charge wall and litho capital: AR 200-300 capacitors with no EUV and no high-AR plasma etch; ~2-3x Cs per footprint and 1-2 fewer EUV layers.

title: Transcription cascade: roll-to-roll daughter stamps replace EUV array layers
idea: Cells copy DNA into many disposable mRNAs instead of reading the master directly. Write one e-beam master per periodic array layer, replicate it roll-to-roll into thousands of polymer daughter nanoimprint stamps, and imprint each wafer with a fresh daughter used only a few times before discarding it.
why: Disposable daughters solve nanoimprint's defect build-up and remove EUV (one supplier, ~$200M per tool) from 2-3 DRAM array layers with imprint tools costing ~1/10 as much.

title: Firefly-lantern microLED arrays on sapphire for wide-and-slow memory optics
idea: Fireflies get light out efficiently through a nanostructured cuticle. GaN microLEDs grown on sapphire get firefly-like tapered light-extraction structures and are bonded to glass interposers, where they drive hundreds of parallel 2-5 Gb/s fiber-bundle or waveguide channels to memory with no lasers.
why: Interface energy and reach (fact 5): ~0.3-1 pJ/bit at meter reach for pooled memory racks, using mature GaN-on-sapphire lines outside silicon fabs.

title: Exonuclease excision: per-row skip masks for 5%-defective cheap cells
idea: DNA polymerase proofreads each base and excises misincorporations; every write is read back, cells that fail are 'excised' by setting a bit in a short per-row skip mask kept in the row header, and the row's data is shifted past them on all later accesses, so a random point defect costs one cell, not a row or column.
why: Makes ultra-cheap high-defect processes (solution-processed oxide tiers, relaxed cleanroom, no laser repair) with 1-5% random dead cells usable at ~6-8% overhead, a prerequisite for ~100x cheaper media.
note: NAND-style column skipping at cell granularity; shifter latency.

title: Chemotactic co-aged references: multilevel cheap cells read against twins
idea: E. coli chemotaxis compares the present with a methylation-held memory of a moment ago rather than absolute levels; each row of 2-3-bit-per-cell cheap storage includes reference cells written at the same instant to each level, which leak and drift alongside the data, so sensing compares data to co-aged references and drift cancels.
why: Multiplies bits per cheap cell 2-3x where leak and drift normally forbid multilevel storage; a multiplier toward ~100x with stacked cheap tiers.
note: Drift-tracking reference cells are standard in MLC flash; cancels mean drift, not cell-to-cell leakage spread.

title: Holographic interference exposes periodic storage-node arrays mask-free
idea: Holograms record perfectly periodic fringes without a mask. Because DRAM arrays are strictly periodic, expose the honeycomb storage-node and landing-pad lattice by three-beam 193 nm interference or achromatic Talbot lithography, then trim array edges with a coarse DUV exposure; the die stays a standard DDR/HBM part.
why: Removes EUV and multi-patterning passes for 1-3 array layers using commodity DUV lasers; interference tools cost ~1/20 of an EUV scanner and need no lattice photomask.

title: HDD bit-patterned-media block copolymers quadruple capacitor hole density
idea: Borrowed from HDD bit-patterned-media R&D, which made 1 Tdot/in2 hexagonal dot arrays by guiding PS-b-PDMS block copolymers on sparse e-beam patterns. DRAM's storage-node array is the same hexagonal honeycomb: print a 4x-sparse guide with 193i, let a high-chi BCP fill the missing holes in each unit cell, then transfer by etch.
why: Fact 4: deletes the EUV or quad-patterning step for capacitor holes and gives a near-perfect lattice with low CD variation; needs defectivity below ~0.01/cm2.

title: Ethernet hybrid echo cancellation for simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: Gigabit Ethernet runs both directions on one pair with a hybrid and an echo canceller. Do the same in HBM: each TSV/microbump carries read and write data at once, and a replica-driver hybrid subtracts the die's own transmitted signal.
why: Doubles bandwidth per TSV or bump, or halves the data-TSV count at the same bandwidth. Either way it directly cuts HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax.
note: Same hybrid echo cancellation idea.

title: Cable-TV head-end laser with polymer modulators on DRAM
idea: A cable head-end broadcasts a carrier to every home. Here a remote CW laser feeds light to the memory packages. The DRAM base die carries electro-optic polymer ring modulators (poled and cured ≤200 C) and sputtered low-temperature Ge photodetectors, so no laser or III-V growth enters the memory flow.
why: Optical memory links at <1 pJ/bit over meters allow disaggregated DRAM pools with no interposer. That cuts movement energy 3-10x against DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit.
note: EO polymer rings on DRAM base die; polymer stability is the extra risk.

title: Core memory reborn as vortex-chirality nanorings threaded by crosspoint lines
idea: Shrink the 1950s ferrite core to a 40-nm CoFeB/NiFe nanoring whose bit is the clockwise/counter-clockwise flux-closure vortex, exactly the core's circumferential flux. Write by coincident half-currents in an X and a Y line threading the ring hole (the core's square-loop half-select), and read non-destructively through a small MTJ patch on one ring segment instead of the core's destructive sense wire.
why: Removes capacitor and access transistor (Facts 1, 3); flux closure has no stray field so rings pack at ~4F2 and stack in decks; zero refresh and ~zero standby; claims 2-3x density per area at equal F with 4 decks.
note: Ring MRAM explored ~2000s; threading lines through 40 nm ring holes is hard.

title: MNOS revival: direct-tunnel nitride-trap one-transistor cell on SONOS lines
idea: The 1967 MNOS stored charge in nitride traps behind a thin oxide. On existing 40/28-nm embedded SONOS lines, thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5 nm so writes are pure direct tunneling at +-3 V in ~20 ns, giving hour-scale retention ('dynamic flash') without hot-carrier or FN damage.
why: 1T cell with no capacitor (Fact 1), refresh every ~10 minutes instead of 64 ms (Fact 3: ~10,000x fewer refreshes), non-destructive read; endurance projected 1e12+ because direct tunneling avoids oxide wear, still to be proven DRAM-class.
note: Same direct-tunnel volatile charge-trap 1T concept; endurance at 1e15 unproven.

title: Magnetostriction reused: piezo-strain-written nanomagnets on FRAM PZT lines
idea: The magnetostriction behind 1950s delay lines can write bits: place elliptical Galfenol or Terfenol-D nanomagnets on a PZT film using existing 130-nm FRAM PZT tooling, flip them with a voltage-driven strain pulse plus small bias field, and read with an AMR/GMR stack sputtered in the same BEOL.
why: aJ-class current-free writes break the CV2 floor (Fact 10), non-volatile (Fact 3), no capacitor (Fact 1); uses existing PZT and magnetic sputter tools.
note: Straintronics well explored; reusing FRAM PZT tooling is the twist.

title: GE's SCR revived as thyristor RAM cells on U.S. thin-SOI
idea: Revive GE's 1957 silicon-controlled rectifier and the thin-silicon thyristor RAM abandoned around 2012: a gate-coupled pnpn thyristor in thin silicon latches on at a picoamp holding current to store a 1 and stays blocked for a 0, switched by a gate-coupled pulse. Build it on an existing U.S. FD-SOI line.
why: The bistable latch removes refresh (fact 3) and needs no capacitor (fact 1), at near-1T density on a U.S. fab with no EUV; the trade is ~pA-per-bit holding power instead of refresh power.

title: Anodic alumina pores self-assemble litho-free 3D cell arrays
idea: Revive the 1950s Keller anodic aluminum oxide pore process used in electrolytic capacitors: anodize thick aluminum into self-ordered ~25-40 nm pitch vertical pores that template capacitor and channel pillars without lithography, accepting ~1% irregular or merged pores as failed cells.
why: Fact 4: removes EUV/immersion litho layers from the cell array, cutting capital per bit with abundant aluminum.

title: Interference lithography with neon-free solid-state lasers for array lines
idea: Revive 1970s holographic-grating interference lithography for the periodic DRAM array: two or four beams from a 213 nm fifth-harmonic solid-state laser print dense line/space and hole arrays without masks, with DUV steppers used only for trims and periphery.
why: No EUV, no array masks and no neon (ArF/KrF excimer lasers need neon, concentrated in Ukraine); claims 60 nm-pitch arrays for ~10% of an EUV scanner's capital.

title: Vertical thyristor RAM revived inside the 4F² pillar
idea: Revive T-RAM and Kilopass's vertical-layered thyristor RAM (abandoned ~2010-2017): build a pnpn latch in the same vertical silicon pillar that 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM already etches, with a gated base for fast set and reset. The bistable thyristor holds data with a small standby current, so no storage capacitor is formed.
why: Fact 1 and capital: deletes the capacitor module (high-AR etch, high-k ALD, top plate) for ~15-20 fewer steps and about one EUV layer. Risks are standby current and temperature sensitivity.

title: Revive BST, the abandoned gigabit-era DRAM dielectric, by N2-ALD
idea: Revive (Ba,Sr)TiO3, the k~200-300 perovskite the 1990s gigabit DRAM programmes abandoned because it could not be deposited conformally: grow it by ALD with nitrogen purge and ozone, crystallize it with a solid-state-laser spike anneal instead of a xenon flash lamp, and use SrRuO3 electrodes to suppress the interfacial dead layer. An effective k of 70-100 at 8 nm already meets Fact 1's target.
why: Fact 1 and capital: k ~70+ lets the capacitor drop from AR 60-75 to ~30, halving the hardest etch time, easing pattern collapse and deleting support-lattice steps. Risks are thin-film leakage and thermal budget.

title: MITI 3D-IC laser recrystallization stacks single-crystal DRAM tiers
idea: Revive Japan's 1981-90 MITI 3D-IC programme, which made stacked single-crystal silicon by laser zone-melting through seed windows: deposit amorphous silicon for each 3D-DRAM tier and melt it with a scanned green Nd:YVO4 solid-state laser (no excimer, no neon) so it regrows epitaxially from seed holes to the tier below, giving crystalline lateral access transistors tier by tier.
why: Fact 2: single-crystal lateral transistors without a thick Si/SiGe superlattice epi and its thermal budget; solid-state lasers cost ~$1-3M and need no rare gas. Risks are heat reaching lower tiers and grain boundaries far from seeds.

title: Talbot self-imaging with solid-state deep-UV lasers prints periodic arrays
idea: Revive Talbot's 1836 self-imaging effect: a periodic mask under coherent light reproduces itself at fixed distances, and averaging over one Talbot period (displacement Talbot) prints half-pitch features with nearly unlimited depth of focus. Use a 193-213 nm all-solid-state frequency-multiplied laser, with no ArF excimer and no neon buffer gas, for DRAM capacitor and active-area grids.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: a lens-free proximity tool at ~$5-10M versus ~$60M immersion scanners for periodic layers, with free pitch halving. Risks are solid-state DUV power and defects in regular arrays.

title: Burroughs B5000 segment descriptors carrying a per-object codec
idea: Revive B5000 descriptors and presence bits: every allocation gets a hardware descriptor with exact length, presence bit and codec ID (zero, constant, delta, dictionary, bf16-exponent entropy), and touching an absent or compressed segment traps to a decompress engine in the memory controller. Segments are stored at their compressed byte size, so there is no 4 KB/2 MB page rounding.
why: Capacity: removes page-granularity fragmentation (10-30% in KV block pools and heaps) and adds 1.5-2.5x typed compression, about 2-3x effective server DRAM.
note: Zippads/Hotpads did object-based compressed hierarchies; ISA change is costly.

title: Cordwood-module revival: edge-standing DRAM dies plug into logic like books
idea: Revive Apollo-era cordwood construction: thinned DRAM dies with I/O routed to one edge stand perpendicular to the logic die like books on a shelf, their laser-diced edge pads finished with PFAS-free electroless Ni/Au and joined to a grid of landing pads.
why: Constraint: no TSV etch or fluorinated plating additives; each die gets its own full-edge I/O (10 mm x 25 pads/mm = 250+ signals) instead of sharing through-stack vias, and coolant can flow between the 'books'.
note: Same edge-on die mounting.

title: Toshiba's forgotten 4-level DRAM, Gray-mapped like Frank Gray's tube
idea: Toshiba (1989) and NEC (1996) demonstrated 2-bit/cell DRAM and then dropped it; Frank Gray's 1947 PCM coding tube used reflected-binary code so a beam landing between zones made only a one-bit error. Store 2 bits per cell as four charge levels with Gray mapping, read by a two-step charge-sharing sense amp, so leakage drift into the adjacent level costs one bit, which a light per-word BCH repairs.
why: Density and cost per bit (fact 4): ~1.8x bits per area without a litho node; Gray mapping converts the dominant MLC failure (one-level drift) into single-bit errors; needs ~2x refresh and much tighter sensing.

title: Lithium-niobate domain-wall conduction gives non-destructive ferroelectric reads
idea: Invert 'ferroelectric bits must be read destructively by switching' -> read the walls, not the domains. In thin-film lithium niobate on insulator, a written nanodomain creates charged conductive domain walls between two lateral electrodes; the bit is presence or absence of wall current (on/off >1e4), read without switching polarization.
why: Non-destructive read removes the write-back half of every access (fact 8) and read fatigue; non-volatile so no refresh (fact 3); LNOI wafers come from the photonics supply chain, not silicon; write endurance and sub-30 nm wall stability are the risks.

title: Voltage-written magnetoelectric chromia bits grown epitaxially on sapphire
idea: Invert 'magnetic bits need current to write' -> write with voltage alone. Cr2O3 grows epitaxially on corundum sapphire; its antiferromagnetic order is reversed by an electric field in a small magnetic bias (magnetoelectric switching), and its boundary magnetization is read by anomalous Hall voltage in a 2 nm Pt overlayer.
why: Non-volatile, effectively unlimited endurance (no ion motion or barrier wear), write energy ~fJ capacitive instead of MRAM's ~100 fJ-pJ (fact 10), no silicon or tungsten; the ~307 K Neel point needs boron doping and the read signal is small.
note: Boron-doped Cr2O3 ME switching already studied; read signal small.

title: Insulating garnet racetracks shift magnetic domains without Joule heating
idea: Invert 'magnetic memory needs metallic magnets on silicon' -> use an insulating ferrimagnet. Thulium-iron-garnet nanowires, sputter-crystallized on glass or grown on garnet, carry dozens of domains each, driven at >1 km/s by spin-orbit torque from a Pt underlayer, so one read/write junction per track replaces one access transistor per bit.
why: 32-64 bits per access device shrinks periphery and raises density (fact 7); non-volatile, unlimited endurance and 10-100x lower damping than metal magnets; domain-position errors and gadolinium in GGG substrates (favor glass) are the risks.
note: TmIG fast DW motion known; shift latency and position errors hurt random access.

title: Atom-thin channel: 2D semiconductor access with no bulk to leak
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor is carved from bulk silicon': grow or transfer monolayer WSe2/MoS2 channels into a BEOL vertical gate-all-around access device; the 0.7 nm body has no junction volume, a 1.6-2 eV gap and full gate control, putting Ioff around 10^-19 A/um and allowing stacking above CMOS.
why: Retention 64 ms -> minutes (fact 3), near refresh-free, and stackable 3D tiers without a lateral silicon transistor (fact 2).
note: 2D-channel DRAM access widely pursued (imec etc.).

title: Thyristor columns where an inverter replaces the sense amp
idea: Inverting 'the cell signal is millivolts': vertical npnp thyristor cells latch on with ~10-30 uA read current versus pA off, so bitlines swing to the rail within ns and each column is read by a skewed inverter with a keeper; reads are nondestructive, so the restore phase disappears.
why: Periphery ~30% smaller (no latch sense amp, no half-VDD precharge, no restore) and tRC ~5 ns, with no capacitor to scale.
note: T-RAM precedent; standby current and variability stalled it.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain walls give nondestructive reads
idea: Inverting 'ferroelectric reads are destructive': in thin-film lithium niobate cells, switching creates a conducting domain wall between electrodes, so the state is read as a 1e3-1e5 current ratio without switching the polarization.
why: Nondestructive, high-margin reads remove restore circuitry and refresh; uses a non-tungsten, non-EUV material stack; endurance of wall motion (~1e10+) must be proven.
note: LiNbO3 domain-wall memory widely published; endurance unproven.

title: 4H-SiC vertical-pillar DRAM: wide gap kills refresh, shrinks capacitor
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must be built in silicon.' Make 4F² vertical-pillar access transistors and trench capacitors in 4H-SiC (3.26 eV gap), where thermal leakage falls by many orders of magnitude, so retention runs to minutes and Cs can shrink ~10x.
why: Facts 1 and 3: refresh nearly vanishes and capacitor AR collapses from ~70:1 to ~7:1; taps U.S. SiC wafer capacity built for power devices.
note: SiC DRAM with hour retention shown in 1990s; defects, mobility and 4F2 SiC processing limit density.

title: Laser-crystallized silicon tiers stacked in BEOL above logic
idea: Inverts 'crystalline access transistors require front-end epitaxy.' Deposit amorphous Si on each tier and crystallize it with an excimer-laser super-lateral-growth pulse whose heat stays in the top ~100 nm, building dozens of near-crystalline Si access-transistor tiers over finished logic with Si only.
why: Facts 2 and 7: array tiers over the periphery with no In/Ga oxides, using display-industry laser tools and no EUV.
note: Grain-boundary leakage hurts DRAM access devices.

title: Silicon carbide access transistor: retention outlives the server
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor must be silicon': build 1T1C cells on 4H-SiC (3.26 eV gap, intrinsic carriers ~1e-9 cm^-3) so junction and subthreshold leakage drop by many orders of magnitude and a 5 fF node holds its level for years at 85 C; refresh circuits are deleted and lines run in idle US 150/200 mm SiC power fabs.
why: Zero refresh power (16-33% of idle power) and no refresh bandwidth loss; Si and C are abundant; adds US capacity from existing SiC fabs.
note: Same SiC 1T1C in SiC fabs as I-10782.

title: Gate-coupled thyristor: a self-latching pure-silicon bit
idea: Inverts 'a cell is passive and must be topped up from outside': a vertical PNPN thyristor with a gate-coupled base latches on or off by its own regenerative gain; a low-gain design holds 'on' cells at sub-pA holding current and 'off' cells draw nothing, so no refresh cycle exists.
why: Zero refresh power; no capacitor, no high-k, fewer metal layers; a pure-silicon 4-6F2 cell buildable in older US fabs.
note: T-RAM was commercialized then abandoned on variability and holding current.

title: DRAM on glass: repurpose idle Gen-10.5 display fabs
idea: Inverts 'memory needs a semiconductor fab'. Run 2.9 x 3.4 m display lines to build 8 sequential tiers of low-leakage oxide-TFT 1T1C cells at ~1 um rules, giving ~0.5 TB of slow-tier DRAM-class memory per panel for CXL far memory.
why: A Gen-10.5 panel has ~120x a 300 mm wafer's area on built, under-used capital; competitive per GB only if 8-tier panel cost stays under ~$1,500, so it is a capacity-tier hedge with near-zero new fab capital (fact 4).

title: Revive the 1990s BST bet: planar k~250 capacitors
idea: Inverts 'more charge needs taller capacitors'. Deposit (Ba,Sr)TiO3 by MOCVD or sol-gel on Pt/Ru electrodes, the material of the 1990s Gbit-DRAM programs, with compositional grading to cut leakage; at k ~250 a 44 nm planar film stores 5 fF in 0.1 um2.
why: Takes fact 1's k~70 escape route with ~3x margin and no high-AR etch, using only 1990s deposition tools.

title: Laser-grown single-grain silicon tiers stacked over finished arrays
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must live in the wafer'. Deposit a-Si over the previous tier, etch 180 nm grain-filter holes, and melt it with a 1990s XeCl excimer pulse so each transistor sits in one location-controlled grain (micro-Czochralski), then repeat for 8-16 tiers below a 450 C substrate budget.
why: Monolithic 3D without bonding or epi, with one cheap mask set reused per tier (facts 2, 4); grain-boundary-free channels keep leakage near bulk.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge in a silicon comb
