idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: deposit Mo by ALD/CVD from MoO2Cl2 (no WF6) directly in the buried-wordline trench. Without fluorine there is nothing to attack the gate oxide, so the 2-3 nm TiN barrier that W needs can be removed, and at 10-15 nm widths Mo's shorter electron mean free path gives lower resistance than TiN/W.
why: Takes China-dominated tungsten (~80%) and WF6 out of the cell array, for ~20-30% lower wordline RC or a ~2 nm narrower trench at the same RC.

title: Deuterated-drug kinetic isotope effect hardens access-transistor interfaces
idea: Deuterated drugs slow metabolism because C-D bonds break more slowly than C-H. Replace the forming-gas H2 anneal with high-pressure D2 from Canadian heavy-water stocks so Si-D bonds passivate the access-transistor and STI-edge interfaces and resist hot-carrier and GIDL-stress depassivation; DDR/HBM refresh commands are unchanged, on-die refresh management simply tracks fewer weak rows.
why: Fact 3: the leakage tail forces refresh (16-33% of idle power); a tighter, longer-lived tail lets retention bins relax ~1.5-2x and cuts burn-in screening loss.
note: Deuterium anneal is known and already used.

title: Scuba rebreather loop recycles excimer-laser neon in DUV scanners
idea: Closed-circuit rebreathers scrub contaminants and recirculate the diluent gas. Put a getter and cryo-purification loop on every ArF/KrF excimer laser to strip fluorine-reaction contaminants (HF, CF4, O2) from the ~96% neon buffer and re-inject it, topping up F2 from onsite electrolysis; only litho tools change, DDR/HBM products do not.
why: Neon came mostly from Ukrainian and Russian steel-plant air separation; DRAM runs many DUV immersion layers, and recirculation cuts neon purchases ~90%.
note: Excimer neon recycling is already offered by laser vendors.

title: 1970s molybdenum-gate MOS revived to replace tungsten wordlines
idea: Revive molybdenum-gate MOS, and the WWII practice of substituting molybdenum for tungsten: fill buried wordlines and bitline contacts with barrier-thin Mo deposited from MoCl5/MoO2Cl2 instead of WF6, sourced from US mines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and fluorine use (WF6): Mo's short electron mean free path lowers narrow-line resistance; claims near-zero tungsten per wafer.

title: Adaptive patterning wires each module to measured die positions
idea: Invert 'wiring masks are fixed before chips are placed': place DRAM and logic dies loosely, measure each die's true position and write custom redistribution per package with maskless lithography (Arizona adaptive-patterning lines).
why: Cheap placement plus maskless wiring gives fine-pitch memory links without CoWoS-class bonders or masks; lower capital per unit and an all-U.S. flow.
note: Deca adaptive patterning already commercial.

title: Tungsten-free DRAM: ALD molybdenum wordlines plus Cu-Mn bitlines
idea: Box [ZrO2 cap | buried-channel Si RCAT | voltage SA | planar 1T1C | CZ Si | thermal ALD + electroplating]: fill buried wordlines with liner-free ALD Mo from MoO2Cl2/H2 and replace W bitlines, contacts and periphery plugs with electroplated Cu wrapped in a self-forming MnSiOx barrier.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): removes essentially all W from the flow; Mo comes largely from US/Chile copper by-product, and dropping the TiN liner cuts wordline resistance ~30% at 10 nm width.

title: Tungsten-free retrofit: molybdenum precursors in existing CVD chambers
idea: Po: memory needs no tungsten. Swap WF6 for MoO2Cl2/MoCl5 precursors in existing W CVD/ALD chambers (minor heater and delivery changes) for buried wordlines, contacts and plugs, gaining lower resistance in narrow lines.
why: Scarce resource (China ~80% of tungsten): removes W dependence with tool retrofits, no new fab; lower wordline RC as a bonus.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten in buried wordlines
idea: Worse: keep 80%-China tungsten in every buried wordline, contact and plug. Flip: switch to fluorine-free, barrierless Mo CVD sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines; Mo has lower resistivity than W at thin dimensions.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint removed; ~20-30% lower wordline RC also permits thinner, denser lines.
note: Mo replacing W is already being adopted.

title: Trusted-foundry molybdenum wordlines from Colorado ore replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Defense trusted-foundry users must avoid adversary-sourced metals. Molybdenum is mined in the U.S. (Climax, Henderson) and has a shorter electron mean free path than W, so it beats W resistivity in <20 nm trenches. Deposit Mo by ALD/CVD from MoO2Cl2 into buried wordlines and bit-line contacts with thin or no TiN liner.
why: Removes ~80%-China tungsten and WF6 from the cell array and lowers wordline RC ~20-30% thanks to liner-less fill.

title: Defense-trusted DRAM uses chloride-precursor molybdenum wordlines, no WF6
idea: Extreme user: defense buyers who must avoid Chinese tungsten and fluorinated gases. Replace WF6-CVD tungsten buried wordlines and contacts with molybdenum from MoO2Cl2/H2, barrier-less, and run a chlorine-only metal stack.
why: Scarce resource: removes the ~80% China tungsten exposure and WF6; barrier-less Mo also cuts wordline resistance ~30% for finer pitch.

title: Deuterium isotope passivation trims the access-transistor leakage tail
idea: Scale down to the isotope: anneal in D2 instead of H2 so interface traps are capped with Si-D bonds, which resist desorption and trap-assisted tunneling more strongly over years of operation, shrinking the GIDL tail.
why: Leakage tail and refresh: if the worst tail drops 2-4x, refresh can be 2-4x rarer at 32-64 Gb; cheap drop-in.
note: High-pressure D2 anneal is known and already commercial.

title: Drop-in molybdenum precursor swap in existing tungsten CVD chambers
idea: Molecule-level substitution: replace WF6/H2 with fluorine-free MoO2Cl2 in the same CVD chamber hardware on existing trailing lines. Contacts and periphery lines fill with Mo, whose ~11 nm mean free path needs no TiN barrier at small widths.
why: Cuts tungsten (China ~80%) in contacts. Mo supply is diversified (U.S., Chile, Peru), and removing fluorine ends oxide attack.

title: Idle 65 nm back-end lines make interposers replacing glass-cloth substrates
idea: Scale shift from PCB laminate to wafer BEOL: existing 65-130 nm copper back-end lines pattern 2-4 metal-layer passive silicon interposers and bridges for DRAM packages and HBM-lite stacks. These replace BT/ABF laminates built on T-glass cloth.
why: Bypasses the T-glass/ABF substrate bottleneck and gives finer wiring for wider, lower-energy buses, using existing mature-fab capacity.

title: 1970s molybdenum-gate MOSFETs revived as fluorine-free buried wordlines
idea: Mo-gate MOS of the 1970s was abandoned because molybdenum oxidized and etched badly next to polysilicon. A buried wordline entombs the metal: deposit Mo by ALD from MoO2Cl2 (chlorine, not fluorine) directly on a thin barrier, recess it, and seal it with SiN so oxidation never occurs.
why: Replaces TiN/W buried wordlines: Mo has lower narrow-line resistivity than W, the U.S. mines roughly a quarter of world Mo (Colorado) versus ~80% China for W, and WF6 is eliminated; ~20-30% lower wordline RC.

title: Mo: molybdenum-chloride CVD replaces tungsten in periphery contacts
idea: Fill periphery contacts and wordline straps with Mo from MoO2Cl2 and H2 CVD (H2 carrier, N2 purge, no argon) instead of WF6 tungsten; Mo's short electron mean free path lowers resistance in narrow lines.
why: Lower resistance lets drivers shrink (fact 7) and removes the China-dominated tungsten chokepoint from periphery metallization.

title: Gallium harvested from alumina-refinery Bayer liquor
idea: Periodic-table walk, Ga (31): install amidoxime ion-exchange columns on Bayer liquor (~100-200 ppm Ga) at U.S. and allied alumina refineries, turning a waste stream into tens of tonnes per year for oxide channels and GaN periphery power.
why: China holds ~98% of primary Ga under export controls; this route could cover U.S. semiconductor demand.
note: Bayer-liquor recovery is how nearly all primary gallium is already made.

title: Fluorine-free molybdenum buried wordlines from oxychloride ALD
idea: Periodic-table walk, Mo (42): deposit buried-channel wordlines by ALD Mo from MoO2Cl2 + H2 (chloride, no WF6); Mo's ~11 nm electron mean free path beats W's ~15.5 nm in 10 nm trenches, and without fluorine attacking the gate oxide the TiN barrier can be thinned or dropped.
why: Kills W (~80% China) and WF6; the U.S. is a top-two Mo producer (Colorado); ~20-30% lower wordline resistance.

title: Mo: Climax molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten in DRAM wordlines
idea: Switch buried-wordline fill and bitline contacts from WF6-CVD tungsten to barrierless MoO2Cl2/MoCl5-CVD molybdenum under long-term offtake from Colorado's Climax and Henderson mines plus a U.S. precursor plant.
why: Removes most exposure to ~80% China tungsten supply; barrierless Mo also lowers narrow-line wordline RC ~20-30%.

title: Deuterium passivation of junction traps to shrink leakage tail
idea: IFR: no trap ever helps an electron hop. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a high-pressure deuterium anneal so access-device interface and junction dangling bonds are capped by Si-D bonds, which resist thermal and hot-carrier dissociation far better than Si-H (kinetic isotope effect).
why: Fact 3: trap-assisted tunneling forms the retention tail and variable retention time; a cleaner, more stable tail could double the refresh interval for one anneal change.
note: High-pressure deuterium anneal already used/studied for DRAM retention.

title: Gold-free, glass-cloth-free DRAM packaging via fan-out redistribution
idea: Ideal: a package that is just the chip. Closest: replace board-on-chip gold-wire FBGA packages on BT laminate (near-monopoly T-glass cloth) with wafer-level fan-out: copper RDL plated directly over a reconstituted mold wafer, solder balls on the RDL.
why: Removes gold wire and BT/T-glass substrate chokepoints, shortens I/O paths (lower pJ/bit), ~20-30% lower package cost per GB.

title: Molybdenum wordlines from Colorado mines to sidestep Chinese tungsten
idea: Ideal: DRAM made only of domestic elements. Closest achievable: replace tungsten buried wordlines and contacts with barrier-less ALD molybdenum, which has lower resistivity at thin dimensions, sourced from U.S. Climax/Henderson mines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) plus ~20-30% lower wordline resistance.

title: Constraint-tool debottlenecking with refurbished secondary-market tools
idea: Ideal: an existing fab produces 2x with no construction. Closest achievable: simulate each DRAM fab's queue network to find the 2-3 constraint tool groups (often high-AR etch, ALD, ArFi) and fill cleanroom whitespace with refurbished copies of only those tools.
why: Capacity: +8-15% wafer outs at ~5% of greenfield capex per added wafer.

title: Getter-coated chamber walls replace helium-loop cryopumps
idea: Combine the chamber liner with the vacuum pump: sputter a TiZrV non-evaporable getter film on PVD chamber liners that pumps H2, CO and H2O at room temperature and reactivates during normal bake/seasoning, with small turbo pumps handling argon.
why: Retires helium-compressor cryopump loops and their makeup helium and ~7 kW compressors per tool; fewer regeneration downtimes.
note: Cryopump helium is closed-loop; real helium saving small.

title: Aluminum-doped zinc oxide top plate replaces germanium SiGe fill
idea: Combine the plate electrode and pillar-forest gap fill (zero added masks, same plate mask): replace the boron-doped poly-SiGe plate fill over the TiN top electrode with ALD/CVD ZnO:Al, which fills conformally at ~200 C and conducts ~1e-3 ohm-cm.
why: Removes germanium (China-dominated, export-controlled) and GeH4 from every DRAM wafer; low temperature protects the dielectric.

title: On-die moisture sensor replaces helium leak testing of cavity packages
idea: Combine package sealing with an on-die interdigitated capacitive moisture sensor and micro-heater read out through DRAM test-mode registers: after sealing optical/mm-wave cavity memory packages, a short heat-soak and capacitance trend gives each unit's leak rate, and the sensor keeps monitoring in the field.
why: Rare-gas dependence of packaging QA: removes helium leak detection for cavity and photonic memory packages and adds field reliability telemetry at ~zero area.

title: Rare-gas content ledger in packaging PDKs and CHIPS grants
idea: Combine the packaging process-design kit with a per-step bill of gases: each OSAT/fab step declares its He/Ne/Ar/Kr/Xe consumption, EDA flows total it per product, and CHIPS-style packaging grants pay a per-stack bonus for products built on rare-gas-free flows.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and resilience: makes rare-gas exposure visible and pays for substitution across U.S. memory packaging, hedging Qatar-type outages.

title: LCD polarity inversion cancels oxide-TFT bias stress
idea: Borrowed from LCD dot inversion, which keeps liquid crystal from DC drift: the periphery stores each row inverted on alternate refresh epochs, tracked by a per-row polarity bit, so IGZO access and sense transistors see near-zero average bias stress.
why: Removes oxide-TFT threshold drift (often 100+ mV over life) from the sensing budget, so glass-panel sense amps can run tighter margins for longer.

title: Organic-food certification model for PFAS-free capacitor-free memory
idea: Copy USDA Organic's audited-label model. Certify memory made in flows free of perfluorinated etch gases, PFAS photoacid generators and fluoropolymer wetted parts, which becomes achievable because a capacitor-free cell drops the 60:1 fluorocarbon etch, and sell it at a premium to EU buyers facing PFAS restrictions.
why: Turns the EU PFAS squeeze into market pull for a resource-light flow. PFC emissions per wafer fall ~50%+.

title: Eliminate open-bitline dummy edge mats: self-referenced double sampling
idea: Replace reference-from-neighbour-mat sensing with a sense amp that samples its own bitline before and after charge sharing on a small on-SA capacitor, so the half-used dummy mats at array edges disappear.
why: Periphery/area: edge dummy mats waste ~3-5% of array area in open-bitline 6F2/4F2 designs; also gives better offset cancellation.
note: ~3-5% area only.

title: Crucible-free memory: laser-crystallized silicon gain cells on glass
idea: Reverse the substrate dependency: deposit amorphous silicon on glass or metal-foil panels and excimer-laser-crystallize it (1990s LTPS display process, >=1 um rules) into 2T gain cells, so the storage tier needs no Czochralski ingot, no high-purity quartz crucible and no 300 mm wafer.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine quartz >80%) and capital: capacity from display-class lines priced per m2, though LTPS leakage needs ~10 ms refresh; a bulk-capacity tier strategy.

title: Cache becomes main memory: DRAM-less servers for small-state services
idea: Reverse the hierarchy: services whose working set fits in large stacked caches (DNS, firewalls, routing, rate limiters, lookup services under ~256 MB across sockets) are rewritten to run entirely from 3D-stacked L3/SRAM with flash as backing, and their servers ship with one minimal DIMM or none.
why: Removes tens to hundreds of GB of DRAM per such node using CPU SKUs already in production, so no new DRAM bits and no rare-gas fab demand.

title: Fluorescent tracers encode storage-stack chemistry for automated recycling sorting
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: dope each die's passivation with distinct carbon-dot or Mn:ZnS emission signatures that encode its storage-stack chemistry (Ru vs TiN electrodes, Hf vs Zr dielectric); shredder lines sort fragments optically into chemistry-matched streams for metal recovery.
why: Recyclability and scarce resources: higher-purity recovered Ru/Hf/Zr at low sorting cost.
note: Recycling niche with small memory impact.

title: Precursor cryo-trap recovery returns hafnium and ruthenium to suppliers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: ALD uses only ~1-10% of its metal-organic precursor, so fit each ALD/CVD exhaust with a cold trap or adsorbent cartridge that captures unreacted Hf, Zr, Ru and Mo compounds, shipped back to the supplier for re-purification in a closed loop.
why: 50-80% metal recovery lowers precursor cost and Ru supply risk and lightens abatement load (scarce resource, cost).

title: Camel-nose countercurrent water recovery from fab exhaust
idea: Camels recover water from exhaled breath with cooled, hygroscopic nasal turbinates. Put cyclically cooled, desiccant-coated turbinate heat exchangers in wet-scrubber and cooling-tower exhausts that capture vapour on the way out and release it as condensate during reverse-flow regeneration, feeding the UPW reclaim plant.
why: A DRAM megafab uses tens of ML of water a day and loses much of it as vapour; recovering 20-30% of evaporative loss eases siting in dry US states such as Idaho and Arizona.

title: Nacre-stacked titania nanosheets printed as hafnium-free capacitor dielectric
idea: Copy nacre's brick-and-mortar layering: exfoliate layered titanate into 1 nm Ti0.87O2 nanosheets (k~125) and lay them down roll-to-roll by Langmuir-Blodgett transfer, interleaved with sub-nm polymer mortar that blocks leakage paths at sheet edges. Use the film as the storage capacitor of printed oxide-TFT memory cells or as decoupling sheets on DRAM modules.
why: Titanium is abundant and US-sourced; k ~100+ at ~10 nm without Hf/Zr or vacuum ALD lets printed cells hold ~fF in um2 footprints.

title: Stencil spray-paint: shadow-mask deposition of periphery pads and power
idea: Like a graffiti stencil, deposit the periphery's wide top-level features (pads, power straps, redistribution at >=2 um) through a reusable silicon-nitride MEMS stencil held in proximity during sputtering or evaporation. No resist, develop, strip or post-etch clean.
why: Water: top-metal/pad litho, etch and clean sequences (~30-50 L UPW per layer) fall ~10x, and those layers cost a fraction to pattern.

title: OLED fine-metal-mask evaporation: resistless shadow patterning of thick metals
idea: Borrowed from OLED fabs, which pattern pixels by evaporating through fine metal masks with no photoresist: pattern DRAM's coarse top-metal, power grid and redistribution layers (>3 um lines) by depositing through reusable Invar shadow masks on a small-team-built aligner, deleting coat, expose, develop, etch and strip for those levels.
why: Fact 4: removes 3-5 litho loops per wafer on non-critical layers, roughly 5-8% of process steps and their tools.

title: LCD polarity inversion: per-row epoch flip of stored data
idea: LCDs invert pixel polarity every frame so that DC stress does not cause image sticking. Each row stores its data XORed with a per-row epoch bit that toggles on every scrub pass, so no cell or access transistor holds the same charge polarity for months. The controller decodes with the flag bit.
why: This balances BTI and data-pattern-dependent charge trapping, which drive aging and VRT, and it defeats hammer patterns tuned to particular data. It could shrink aging guardbands and data-dependent retention outliers by an estimated ~2x.

title: Reinsurance pool: rack-level CXL spare memory absorbing failing pages
idea: Reinsurers pool rare risks across many insurers. Each rack keeps a shared CXL-attached spare pool of about 2% of rack capacity. The hypervisor live-migrates pages from any DIMM whose correctable-error rate rises into the pool, so individual DIMMs ship with thinner margins and fewer on-die spare rows.
why: Pooled spares scale with sqrt(N) instead of N. That recovers ~3-5% of die area spent on redundancy and raises yield, so cost per bit falls.

title: Hollow-core fiber widens memory-pooling radius by 45 percent
idea: Remote-memory latency is bounded by the speed of light in the medium: ~5 ns/m in solid glass, ~3.4 ns/m in hollow-core fiber. Wire memory pools with hollow-core fiber so a 300 ns round-trip budget reaches ~47% farther, roughly doubling the floor area, and so the number of servers, that one pool can cover.
why: Pool headroom scales roughly as 1/sqrt(N), so doubling the servers per pool trims another ~5-10% of provisioned DRAM.
note: Propagation is a minor share of pool latency; the DRAM gain is a few percent.

title: Zipper pairing: interlock weak and strong columns across chips per codeword
idea: Zipper teeth alternate: at module test each chip's retention-weak column groups are profiled and a per-DIMM permutation table in the RCD/buffer reroutes column bits so every ECC codeword pairs one chip's weak column only with other chips' strong columns, guaranteeing at most one weak bit per codeword.
why: A SEC code that dies at two weak bits now tolerates dies with ~10x the weak-cell density; marginal dies get binned into ECC DIMMs, ~5% more sellable bits.
note: ~5% sellable-bit gain via buffer-chip remap.

title: Hibernating bear: hot-triggered compaction parks cold pages in strong rows
idea: Above ~105 C the controller or OS compresses cold pages 2-3x, packs them into the strongest-retention subarrays, and turns refresh off for the emptied subarrays (partial-array self-refresh).
why: Refresh power at 125 C is 4-8x room temperature; refreshing ~40% of the array cuts hot refresh energy ~60% and lowers self-heating over 10 years.

title: Tea-kettle whistle: ECC error rate, not temperature, drives thermal throttling
idea: Per-bank on-die ECC correction counters feed the SoC power manager; when corrected-error rate crosses a budget, adjacent compute is throttled or cooling boosted, replacing fixed 85/95 C thresholds that assume worst-case cells.
why: Most parts survive 125 C with margin; closing the loop on the real failure signal removes conservative 2x refresh and throttling guard-bands while holding the 10-year error budget.

title: Luggage tag: printed NFC history label for second-life DIMMs
idea: Random stimulus 'luggage tag' -> the bag carries its own itinerary. A roll-to-roll printed passive NFC tag with printed nonvolatile memory, laminated on each DIMM, logs power-on hours, peak temperature, row-hammer counters and retest results, signed by the operator.
why: Verified history removes the lemons problem in used DRAM; resale price and reuse rates rise, extending each bit's service life ~1.5-2x.

title: Interposers made from reclaimed monitor and reject wafers
idea: Po: fab garbage is the interposer. Collect test, monitor and scratched prime wafers, re-polish them, laser-drill vias with no mask, and add one thick copper redistribution layer with a single mask for simple HBM-to-logic routing.
why: Removes demand for new silicon and crucible-grown wafers in interposers, cutting cost and quartz-crucible exposure.

title: Bulk acoustic delay-line loop memory from RF filter fabs
idea: Worsen: build bits only in scarce DRAM fabs. Flip: store bits as acoustic pulses circulating in short AlN/ScAlN bulk-acoustic delay lines made by RF-filter foundries, with a CMOS regenerator per loop; a $1M, 24-month prototype targets 100 ns loops as a refresh-free buffer.
why: U.S. manufacturability (RF filter fabs are large and US-based), with no capacitor and no refresh; density is modest but capital is tiny.
note: Delay-line density is tiny (~mm per kbit).

title: Magnetite-core ceria abrasives recaptured and reused tenfold
idea: Worsen: use ceria abrasives once and send rare-earth-laden slurry to wastewater. Flip: make the abrasives as a thin ceria shell on magnetite cores, so spent slurry passes a magnetic separator and the abrasives are washed, reclassified and reused ~10 times.
why: Ce chokepoint and slurry cost: ceria demand falls ~90%.

title: Deep-eutectic solvent cascade recovers metals from designed-open packages
idea: Worsen: incinerate memory boards and lose Ru, Hf, Ta, Au and Pd to slag. Flip: design packages with solvent-accessible layers, then dissolve them in a sequence of choline-chloride deep-eutectic solvents that selectively leach Au/Pd, then Cu, leaving Ru/Ta/Hf residues for electrowinning.
why: Precious and critical metal recovery at low temperature with little water: turns scrap DRAM into a domestic mine.

title: Procedural memory lines that store a generator, not data
idea: Worsen: store huge regular arrays (index ranges, constant fills, strided tables, LFSR masks) byte by byte. Flip: a line tag marks a line as procedural, holding a 16-byte micro-program (base, stride, affine coefficients or LFSR seed) that a tiny ALU in the controller expands on read; writes that break the pattern fall back to a normal line.
why: Capacity: 10-100x for pattern-heavy data such as position tables, masks, and initialization buffers; small gains overall but zero-cost when unused.

title: Communal-kitchen row pre-decoders shared across banks
idea: A Soviet communal apartment shares one kitchen because residents cook at different times. JEDEC's tRRD and tFAW guarantee activates arrive several ns apart, so one fast global row pre-decoder, latched into each bank's local decoder on its ACT, replaces the per-bank pre-decoders.
why: Removes ~75% of row pre-decode logic and its wiring (fact 7), invisible to the controller.

title: Tailor's darning: aerosol-jet ink jumpers swap in spare memory chips
idea: A tailor darns a garment instead of throwing it away: modules are laid out with a spare DRAM footprint and open jumper pads; after burn-in, an aerosol-jet printer writes silver-nanoparticle traces that route the spare chip's lanes in place of a failing chip, followed by laser sintering and a conformal coat.
why: Raises module-level yield and lets marginal dies ship without BGA rework; an estimated 1-3% more supply from parts that would be scrapped.
note: Printed jumpers to swap in spare chips; tiny supply gain.

title: Demoscene procedural page faults: regenerate data from seeds
idea: From 64 KB demoscene intros that synthesize whole worlds from code: the runtime tags buffers whose content is a deterministic function (RNG-initialized tensors, positional tables, lookup tables, dropout masks, synthetic test data) and stores only a seed plus generator ID. A page-table miss raises a 'procedural fault' that a small generator engine on the memory controller fills on the fly.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes; removes 10-30% of footprint in training and simulation jobs whose bulk state is regenerable, and eliminates the write traffic for it.
note: Most seeded buffers are overwritten after step one; regenerable share is small.

title: Voyager's 69 kilobytes: compact bytecode tier for cold server code
idea: From Voyager's tiny memory and threaded interpretive code: toolchains emit server binaries as dense bytecode for the ~90% of code that is cold and native code only for profiled hot paths; a threaded interpreter runs the cold code, shrinking resident text segments.
why: Cold code is 5-10x smaller as bytecode; for microservice fleets with hundreds-of-MB binaries, code DRAM falls ~10x with matching fab-water savings.

title: Nitrogen-sealed DIMM canisters, Project Natick style
idea: Microsoft's undersea data center saw about 1/8 the failure rate in dry nitrogen. A 10-person firm builds hermetic N2-filled memory canisters in the CXL E3.S form factor that exclude humidity, sulfur corrosion and oxygen, roughly doubling module service life.
why: Halves replacement demand at harsh and edge sites; supply through longevity.

title: Tungsten recovery skid for WF6 exhaust and chamber shields
idea: Design for a zero-import fab while China holds ~80% of tungsten. A 10-person company builds skid-mounted units that capture unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust as tungstate in alkaline scrubbers and strip W from chamber shields, returning tungsten to precursor makers.
why: Could cut virgin tungsten per wafer 30-60% and hedge the chokepoint.
note: Plausible chemistry; tungsten volume per fab is small relative to market.

title: Aerosol-jet printed rewiring for salvaged bare dies
idea: Satellite one-offs use additive interconnect. A 10-person shop prints silver traces and dielectric ramps by aerosol jet to rewire salvaged bare DRAM dies onto new substrates without masks or substrate tooling, so any die mix becomes a custom module.
why: Removes the $50k+ substrate NRE that blocks reuse of small die lots.
note: Niche small-lot reuse.

title: Qimonda trench resurrected in MEMS DRIE fabs: 100 fF cells
idea: Qimonda's deep-trench DRAM lost because trenches could not shrink below ~50 nm. At 180 nm and above, shrinking does not matter: Bosch deep reactive-ion etch in 200 mm MEMS fabs cuts 100:1 trenches, giving ~100 fF cells (vs ~5 fF today) that hold data ~20x longer for the same leakage.
why: Refresh and supply: long retention allows low-refresh buffer DRAM built in MEMS capacity outside the memory oligopoly; density is low, so it targets refresh-light buffer roles, not bulk bits.

title: Single-poly floating-gate CAM stores repair addresses without fuses
idea: Effect: Fowler-Nordheim tunneling onto a floating gate. In a standard-logic MPW macro, repair and trim addresses live in single-poly floating-gate cells programmed through the thin gate oxide with no extra masks, arranged as a CAM that compares incoming row addresses directly. No laser fuses, no boot-time fuse broadcast, and field re-programmable for post-package repair.
why: Periphery area/yield (fact 7): fuse banks (~2% of die) removed and in-field repair raises effective yield; zero added mask cost suits a fabless team.
note: Single-poly FG CAM for repair; fuse area is small and PPR antifuses exist.

title: Seebeck heat-flux sensors predict die temperature to drop refresh guardbands
idea: Effect: Seebeck thermopile heat-flux sensing plus package thermal lag. Laminate off-the-shelf thin-film Bi2Te3 heat-flux sensors between DRAM packages and the heat spreader; heat flux leads die temperature by tens of ms through the package's thermal RC, so the controller forecasts temperature ~50 ms ahead and runs relaxed refresh until a real rise is coming.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removing a static ~10 C guardband gives ~2x longer refresh at typical temperatures (~30-40% refresh energy) with module-level parts.

title: Borrow solar photoluminescence imaging tools for cheap substrate screening
idea: The solar industry maps wafers with band-to-band photoluminescence cameras in under a second per wafer on <$500k tools. Adapt them to map lifetime-killing defects and metal contamination in incoming DRAM substrates and after key thermal steps.
why: Cuts metrology capital for micro-fabs, where $10-50M inspection tools are a barrier.

title: Electrochromic coulometer stripe shows each module's lifetime wear at a glance
idea: A tiny Prussian-blue electrochemical cell on the DIMM receives a current proportional to temperature-weighted ON-time, and its colored front advances along a printed scale like a coulometer. Recyclers grade modules visually with no tester or power.
why: Grading cost and uncertainty dominate second-life economics; passive and tamper-evident.

title: Eddy-current susceptor pads reflow only memory packages for harvest
idea: Boards carry thin Ni-Fe susceptor layers under DRAM land patterns; a tuned induction coil heats only those sites to reflow in ~5 s. Packages are vacuum-lifted while CPU, passives and laminate stay cool.
why: Fast, selective, low-energy harvest that avoids the thermal damage that ruins packages in whole-board rework.

title: Al: aluminum-polysilicon thermocouple mesh sets per-subarray refresh rates
idea: Lay Al / n+ poly-Si Seebeck junctions (Al by thermal evaporation, poly by LPCVD, no argon sputter) across the die; their uV/K outputs feed a shared chopper ADC so each subarray's refresh interval follows its own local temperature instead of the hottest spot.
why: Refresh is sized for worst-case temperature; hot-spot-aware refresh can cut refresh ops ~30-50% in cooler regions (fact 3) with near-zero-power sensors.

title: B: boron-10 hBN coating shields DIMMs from thermal neutrons
idea: A small coating line sprays an epoxy loaded with 10B-enriched hexagonal boron nitride flakes over DRAM packages on DIMMs and HBM modules; 10B absorbs thermal neutrons before they reach residual 10B in die dielectrics, and hBN spreads heat. Needs only mixing, a spray booth and a cure oven.
why: Cuts the thermal-neutron share of soft errors (large near concrete and water-rich datacenters), letting operators relax scrub rate or ECC strength.

title: Putting-out system: idle academic cleanrooms do paid value-add steps
idea: Under the 18th-century putting-out system, merchants sent cloth to cottage workshops. Memory makers ship die-banked or reclaimed dies to U.S. university nanofabs for off-hour value-add work that needs only aligners, evaporators and bonders (redistribution layers, micro-bumping, re-sort), paying per finished piece.
why: Capacity and U.S. manufacturability: ~100 U.S. academic cleanrooms run at ~30-50% utilization. Selling idle hours adds specialty packaging supply and funds the fabs.

title: Solvent-releasable spare-die patch site on every DIMM
idea: Ideal result: a module that repairs itself by accepting a spare part. Each DIMM has an empty die site using anisotropic conductive film; when a die fails, a depot bonds a spare there and the register clock driver remaps that die's chip-select to it, and the film later dissolves for reclaim.
why: Usable supply: keeps 95%+ of module bits in service instead of scrapping whole DIMMs during a shortage.

title: Park KV caches in network-switch SRAM across the rack
idea: Ideal: storage that already exists and sits idle. Closest achievable: modern switch ASICs carry ~100-200 MB of SRAM packet buffer that is mostly empty at moderate load; reserve part of it as a rack-wide static parking lot for KV pages of paused conversations, addressed by RDMA-like verbs and evicted under congestion.
why: Zero refresh power for parked state and new capacity from silicon already deployed (dozens of switches per pod at 100+ MB each), relieving HBM pressure from idle sessions.
note: 100-200 MB per switch is negligible next to HBM.

title: Lazy restore after power-up: rows restored on first touch
idea: Constraint: data survives power loss via a backup layer, but boot restore must not take milliseconds. A per-row 'restored' bitmap in the periphery, cleared at power-up, lets the memory accept requests immediately; the first touch of a row triggers its restore from the backup layer through the SAs, while a background walker finishes the rest.
why: Instant availability (us instead of ms to s of restore), so NV-backed DRAM suits fast-failover servers and edge devices.

title: Printed resistive crossbar compresses e-skin signals before digitization
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): on a printed tactile skin with thousands of taxels, a co-printed resistor-ladder crossbar applies a fixed learned projection to the analog taxel signals by Kirchhoff current summing, so only a 32-64-value embedding per frame is digitized and buffered instead of every taxel.
why: Robot hands and smart-surface arrays buffer raw high-channel streams; analog projection at the source cuts buffer DRAM and ADC count 20-50x.
note: Niche sensor-side compression.

title: Field-patchable row-hammer defense in an embedded FPGA buffer
idea: Rule: a new attack must never force a recall. Row-hammer mitigation runs in a small eFPGA or microcode engine in the RCD/CXL buffer, so new defenses against new attack variants can be patched over the air instead of discarding vulnerable modules.
why: Fact 9: avoids fleet-wide module replacement when thresholds drop or new attacks appear, keeping deployed DRAM in service.

title: Magnify the 3D array 20x to measure parasitics cheaply
idea: Build 3D tier stacks at 20x feature size with contact lithography but identical aspect ratios and materials, and measure their tier-to-tier and BL-BL coupling and RC directly. Calibrate 3D DRAM design models for about $150k.
why: Speeds up 3D array design: capacitive coupling scales geometrically, so a cheap magnified twin gives real parasitic data years before nm tiers exist.

title: Genetic-programming evolved sense-amp netlists proven on SkyWater 130 shuttle
idea: Sense-amp netlists are treated as genomes and evolved by mutation and recombination in open-source SPICE on cloud CPUs, selecting for Monte-Carlo offset, area and energy. The top 10 survivors tape out on an open SkyWater 130 shuttle next to a classic latch. Compute $100k plus shuttle/test $150k plus 2 engineers, ~$750k in 24 months.
why: Fact 1/7: may find sense amps with ~30% less area or 2x lower offset per area, licensable to DRAM makers.
note: Evolutionary analog design on open shuttle; modest expected gains.

title: Termite-mound chimney DIMM shroud enabling refresh downshift
idea: Termite mounds hold steady temperatures with passive convection chimneys. 3D-printed DIMM shrouds with mound-like chimney and tunnel geometry use existing server airflow to keep DRAM under ~45 C. A BIOS policy, keyed to the on-DIMM temperature sensor, leaves 2x refresh mode and stretches refresh when the sensor confirms cool operation. CFD plus prototypes, ~$300k in 12 months.
why: Fact 3: retention roughly doubles per ~10 C. Running ~15 C cooler avoids 2x refresh and cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~50%.

title: Elephantnose-fish impedance spectroscopy fixture catching counterfeit DRAM
idea: Elephantnose fish identify objects by how they distort a self-made electric field. A low-cost fixture sweeps tiny AC signals (10 kHz-1 GHz) across each DRAM package's pins and matches the impedance spectrum to genuine-die references, flagging remarked, recycled or wrong-die parts in seconds. VNA-based fixture plus reference database, ~$350k in 12 months.
why: Supply axis: in a 4x price spike, grey-market fakes surge. Trusted screening lets OEMs safely tap secondary supply.

title: Retention-map fingerprints certify provenance of reused DRAM
idea: Box[Sensing=read-back after controlled refresh pause x Transform=weak-cell retention map as physical unclonable fingerprint x Owner=neutral registry x Channel=secondary market]: each die's retention-failure map is a unique fingerprint, readable through standard DDR commands, logged in a registry to defeat counterfeit and remarked used DRAM.
why: Enables trusted second-life supply at scale; no interface change.

title: Printed-electronics aqueous cluster inks replace organometallic ALD precursors
idea: Roll-to-roll printed-electronics makers spin aqueous inorganic clusters (Al13 hydroxo clusters, zirconium oxo-nitrate clusters) that densify into dense oxide films at ~300 C. Spin-coat AlOx/ZrOx dielectrics from water-based inks in a university fab and compare leakage, k and step coverage with ALD.
why: Removes costly, supply-concentrated organometallic precursors and vacuum tools from some dielectric layers; material use ~90% versus ~10-30% for ALD.

title: O: lambda-sensor loop tunes DDR5 PMIC voltages to error rate
idea: Like an engine O2 sensor trimming fuel, DIMM firmware closes a loop on corrected-error and hammer-alert rates and nudges the on-DIMM PMIC's VPP and VDD within spec, lowering VPP to reduce hammer susceptibility and raising it if retention errors climb.
why: Finds each module's reliable minimum-energy point, cutting wordline CV2 energy (fact 10) and hammer flips (fact 9) using existing I2C-programmable PMICs.

title: Use the spare rows already inside: host-driven PPR for weak rows
idea: 10-person constraint: only JEDEC commands. DDR5 exposes host-initiated soft and hard post-package repair. Firmware runs the retention profile, then uses hPPR to fuse the worst row in each bank onto the die's own spare rows (and sPPR for temporary fixes), so the weakest rows physically leave the array before refresh is relaxed.
why: Fact 3: one worst row often sets each bank's refresh interval. Removing it raises the bank minimum by ~1.5-2x with firmware alone.
note: Too few spare rows; weak cells are spread across thousands of rows, so gain likely small.

title: Pitch-for-tiers trade: 200-tier DRAM on depreciated DUV fabs
idea: Worse: chase F~12 nm with 5-7 EUV layers on new, fully depreciating tools. Flip: relax the lateral pitch to F~20 nm, which DUV immersion SAQP prints in already-depreciated logic or NAND fabs, and buy density back with ~200 tiers whose added cost is only deposition and a shared etch.
why: A ~40F2 lateral cell at F=20 nm is 16,000 nm2 per tier, so 200 tiers give ~80 nm2/bit (~11x versus 6F2 at 12 nm); with depreciation (~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) mostly gone and no EUV, wafer cost holds flat despite the extra deposition.
note: Mainstream 3D DRAM thesis; doubt: 200 lateral tiers far beyond demos, deposition and etch cost not flat.

title: Trade lithography node for tier count: ArF-only 3D DRAM
idea: Shift density from the litho-bound x-y plane to the deposition-bound z axis: a horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM drawn at F~38 nm with ArF single exposures only, reaching bit-density parity at ~120-150 Si/SiGe epitaxial tiers patterned by one high-AR slit plus staircase per block.
why: Zero EUV layers and ~40% fewer masks; deposition/etch passes cost ~5x less per wafer than EUV exposures, so capex per bit falls even with many tiers (Facts 2, 4).
note: ArF-only horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM at 120-150 epi tiers; same trade as I-01613.

title: Vertical farmer grows 64 crystal tiers in one epitaxy season
idea: A vertical farmer grows many layers in one season instead of buying more land. One epitaxy run deposits 64 Si/SiGe pairs; a single slit mask lets the SiGe be removed selectively, freeing 64 single-crystal Si channel tiers that are wrapped in ALD gates, with lateral ZrO2 capacitors in the space the SiGe left. U.S. epi-tool makers and a DRAM startup co-own the flow.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density each gives ~12x bits/mm^2. The tiers come from one epi run and one etch rather than 64 litho cycles, so wafer cost stays near a planar DRAM wafer's.
note: Same core path imec, Samsung and SK hynix pursue; strain, selective etch and lateral caps keep wafer cost well above planar.

title: Substitute passive glass interposers with memory-bearing glass cores
idea: Swap passive glass-core package substrates for glass cores that carry oxide gain-cell memory tiers deposited at <=400 C under the accelerator, so the package substrate itself is a memory.
why: Turns substrate makers (e.g., U.S. glass companies) into memory suppliers and cuts HBM demand plus data-movement energy (~3-4 pJ/bit to <1 pJ/bit).
note: Gain-cell tiers on glass cores: density, yield coupling to the package are big unknowns.

title: WDM optical readout of quantum-dot charge storage cells
idea: Fuse silicon-photonic wavelength multiplexing with charge storage: each cell is a quantum dot coupled to a micro-ring whose resonance shifts through the quantum-confined Stark effect when the dot holds charge. One waveguide carrying 64 wavelengths reads 64 cells at once, non-destructively, with no bitline or sense amp.
why: Facts 5, 7, 8: no destructive read or page overfetch, data leaves the array as light at ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit, and the sense-amp periphery shrinks.
note: A few dot charges barely shift a microring resonance; ring footprint far exceeds a DRAM cell.

title: Wide-gap oxide drain pocket on a silicon access transistor
idea: The storage-node contact is an IGZO or Ga2O3 landing pad that forms the drain extension, so the high-field drain edge where GIDL is generated lies in >3 eV-gap material while the channel stays silicon for mobility.
why: Band-to-band GIDL dominates the leakage tail under negative-wordline bias, and a wide gap suppresses it exponentially. That could push the 13 fA tail below 0.1 fA, about 10x longer retention.
note: Oxide/Si heterointerface traps may add leakage offsetting GIDL gains.

title: Electrowetting liquid-metal nanodroplet toggling between two chambers
idea: Adapt electrowetting displays and liquid lenses: seal a ~10 nm gallium-alloy droplet in a dual-chamber cavity with hydrophobic dielectric walls; voltage on one chamber electrode wets and pulls the droplet there, surface-tension pinning holds it, and a capacitance difference reads it.
why: Fact 3: state is held by interfacial energy rather than stored charge, so no refresh; non-destructive capacitive read removes restore energy (fact 8).
note: 10 nm Ga droplet electrowetting: oxidation, speed, sealing doubtful.

title: Quantum-cascade-laser superlattice as a charge ladder per pillar
idea: Adapt QCL epitaxy: grow 8 coupled quantum wells with engineered barriers in each vertical pillar; each well's subband aligns with the injector at a unique bias, so resonant tunneling loads or senses one well at a time.
why: 10x at same cost: 8 wells x 2 levels in one 20 nm pillar footprint is ~16 bits, all defined by layer thickness in one epitaxy run rather than litho.
note: Room-temperature charge retention in wells is short.

title: Type-II superlattice storage separates electrons from holes
idea: Adapt infrared-detector InAs/GaSb type-II superlattices (in Si/SiGe or oxide analogues): electrons and holes sit in spatially separated adjacent wells, so each site holds an independent electron bit and hole bit with recombination suppressed by the gap, in 5 tiers.
why: 10x at same cost: 2 bits per site x epitaxially defined tiers is ~10x per footprint; ambipolar read through separate n and p sense paths.
note: Room-temperature carrier retention in separated wells for ms is doubtful.

title: Pipe-organ multimode nanomechanical parametron with many bits per membrane
idea: Like one organ wind chest feeding many pipes, a single 100 nm membrane has ~100 vibrational modes; pump each mode parametrically at twice its frequency from a shared comb so each mode holds a 0/pi phase bit, read by heterodyne detection.
why: 10x at same cost: ~100 bits per 100x100 nm element is ~100 nm2/bit (~9x), and phase states never leak; pump-comb energy is the risk.
note: Pump-comb energy and mode crosstalk.

title: Silicon-on-Nothing cavity tiers from MEMS pressure sensors
idea: Borrow MEMS pressure-sensor empty-space-in-silicon: H2-anneal trench arrays so silicon migrates into sealed buried voids, repeat to form 20 single-crystal Si membranes separated by voids, then fill the voids with ALD high-k/TiN as plate capacitors under single-crystal lateral transistors.
why: 10x at same cost: single-crystal tiers without SiGe superlattice epitaxy remove the 3D lateral-transistor quality blocker (fact 2); 20 tiers at relaxed DUV pitch, ~10x.
note: Stacking 20 SON membranes repeatedly is unproven.

title: Photocopier-drum physics: optically gated photoconductor access switch
idea: Adapted from xerography, where a photoreceptor holds surface charge for minutes in the dark and discharges only where light hits: the access element is a wide-bandgap photoconductor (e.g., ZnO or a-SiC) switched by light pulses from an on-chip silicon-nitride waveguide 'wordline'. With no gate electrode there is no gate-induced drain leakage and no wordline CV^2.
why: Wide-bandgap photoconductor dark resistivity can exceed 1e14 ohm-cm, giving sub-aA hold leakage (fact 3) and removing the 3 V wordline swing (fact 10); the trade-offs are optical power budget and nanosecond photoconductor speed.
note: Persistent photoconductivity, waveguide pitch versus 4F2 cells and optical power budget make this very hard.

title: Cross-laminated timber: each conductor plane serves two tiers
idea: Like CLT boards glued with alternating grain, conductor planes alternate X/Y orientation: each plane is the bitline of the tier below and, through a thin gate dielectric, the gate/wordline of the tier above, with an oxide-semiconductor cell at every crossing.
why: Halves deposition/etch layers per tier (~4 to ~2), cutting stack height and per-tier cost ~40% and pulling the 26-tier break-even (fact 2) toward ~15 tiers.

title: Auto-parts remanufacturing for HBM: harvest, re-bump, redeploy stacks
idea: Adapted from the alternator/starter core-return model: HBM stacks from retired accelerators are thermally debonded, tested, re-bumped and mounted on CXL memory cards or low-cost interposers for inference and cache tiers.
why: Raises usable supply with no wafers: each retired 8-GPU node holds ~1-1.5 TB of HBM that is now shredded; reclaiming half adds supply at near-zero capital.
note: Debonding underfilled CoWoS stacks and re-bumping microbumps is hard; reuse needs an HBM-PHY CXL controller.

title: Minify oxide damage: write floating gates with photons, not fields
idea: Program floating-gate cells by internal photoemission: an on-chip waveguide delivers ~3.5 eV photons that lift electrons over a thick 8 nm SiO2 barrier at low field, so the oxide never sees the high-field stress that limits flash to ~1e5 cycles; hole photoemission erases. The thick oxide gives 10-year retention.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free, potentially 1e12+ endurance; write speed set by optical power per row with full-row parallel writes.
note: Photoemission yield implies watt-class optical power per row write; on-die UV waveguides.

title: Magnify the barrier to vacuum: field-emission-written floating islands
idea: Suspend a metal storage island in a sealed 5 nm vacuum nanocavity, write it by field emission from a sharpened tip electrode (1-2 V across nm gaps), and read it by capacitive coupling to a gain FET. Vacuum has no traps to wear out and essentially no zero-bias conduction.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free, endurance not limited by oxide damage; uses common metals (Mo, Ti).

title: Eliminate the solid channel: vacuum nanogap field-emission access transistor
idea: Isolate each storage node with a 10-20 nm vacuum gap between a sharpened emitter tip and collector, gated by a surrounding electrode; electrons cross only by field emission when the gate thins the barrier. With no semiconductor there is no thermal generation, GIDL or subthreshold conduction.
why: Off current ~1e-21 A lets the capacitor dielectric set retention (minutes+); temperature-immune, ideal for hot AI packages where Si leakage doubles every ~10 C.

title: Eliminate silicon wafers for periphery: LTPS-on-glass panels from display fabs
idea: Build DRAM periphery as laser-crystallized LTPS CMOS on Gen-6 glass in underused LCD/OLED fabs converted to wet etches (H3PO4/HNO3/acetic, oxalic) and Cl-only dry etch, with fluorine chamber cleans replaced by Cl2/O2. Dice the panels into tiles and bond them face-to-face over array dies at 2-5 um pitch through mux-concentrated bitline groups.
why: Display-fab area costs ~1/10 of silicon fab area, and LTPS mobility (~100 cm2/Vs) handles 200-400 MHz periphery, so periphery capital and cost per die fall sharply.
note: LTPS periphery on glass bonded to array dies; pitch matching and CTE-mismatched fine-pitch bonding are severe doubts.

title: Eliminate the separate memory die: DRAM on the logic backside
idea: Use the silicon freed by backside power delivery under a logic die to build a trench-capacitor DRAM array, connected to the frontside cache controllers by nano-TSVs at ~1 um pitch.
why: Data movement: memory sits 10 um under the cores, giving <0.5 pJ/bit access and removing a separate die, package and interposer for the first few GB.
note: BSPDN thins away backside silicon; capacity limited to ~GB.

title: Resonant bitline reads the stored bit as a frequency shift
idea: Reverse voltage sensing into frequency sensing: each bitline forms part of a resonator; turning on the access transistor loads it with the cell's state-dependent MOS-varactor capacitance, and one wideband counter reads the detuning of 64 bitlines tuned to separate tones.
why: Facts 7 and 8: one reader replaces 64 SAs, and a probe amplitude far below the stored voltage makes the read non-destructive, eliminating restore energy.
note: Femtofarad detuning against tens-of-fF bitlines at ns timescales is a big ask.

title: Capacitor holes extended into nano-TSVs inside the array
idea: Repurpose the capacitor lattice: in HBM core dies thinned to ~3 um, one added mask selects every 64th capacitor site for an extended etch through to the backside, turning those holes into ~30 nm nano-TSVs spread through the array instead of large TSVs in dedicated keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes most TSV keep-out area and gives thousands of vertical links per mat, a large step toward DDR5-like area per bit for HBM.

title: Access transistor nested inside the capacitor's hollow pillar
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: use the hollow core of the tall cylinder capacitor as the body of a vertical access transistor. An ALD channel lines the upper inner wall and a gate electrode fills the core, so the device gets a 150-300 nm channel length (killing DIBL and short-channel subthreshold leakage) without using any lateral area.
why: Breaks the 'smaller cell vs. longer, less leaky channel' contradiction (Facts 2, 3): ~10x lower subthreshold leakage and a route to 4F2 without a separate transistor tier.
note: Long ALD channel inside capacitor core gives low on-current; clever 4F2 path.

title: Memory arrays fabricated inside the glass-core package substrate
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge memory with a part every accelerator already needs, the package substrate. Glass-core substrates entering production for large AI packages get panel-processed oxide-TFT 1T1C memory layers in their build-up stack directly under the die shadow, connected by fine-pitch vias, so a slow-refresh capacity tier rides beneath each processor without separate dies or TSVs.
why: Data-movement energy (Fact 5) and the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6) for a capacity tier; panel processing cuts capital per bit; ultralow-leakage TFTs allow ~1 Hz refresh (Fact 3).

title: Local quality: graded-threshold tiers replace the 3D staircase decoder
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: each tier of a 3D stack is deposited with its own in-situ doping so its select-transistor pair (one n-type, one p-type in series) has thresholds stepped ~150 mV per tier, forming a voltage window; a single vertical gate rod driven by one precision DAC level opens exactly one tier, with no staircase contact etch.
why: 100x path: deletes the staircase (~10-20% of 3D die area and dozens of trim/etch steps) so tiers can scale cheaply; trade-offs: threshold control limits each window band to ~16-32 tiers, and selection is slower. Attacks Facts 2, 4 and 7.
note: Vt-stepped tiers replace staircase; 150 mV windows across many tiers need very tight doping control.

title: Two-faced wafer: front and back arrays form each differential bitline pair
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: build array plus sense amps on the front, carrier-bond, thin to ~5 um and build a mirror array on the backside at low temperature, joined by nano-TSVs at each sense amp. Each sense amp compares a front bitline with the geometrically identical back bitline, so open-bitline noise mismatch disappears and both faces share one periphery.
why: Fact 7 and resource axis: ~2x bits per wafer start and per quartz-crucible-grown wafer with one set of sense amps; periphery share per bit falls from ~49% toward ~30%.
note: Low-temperature backside access transistors are the blocker.

title: Merchant EUV template wafers sold to DUV-only memory fabs
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action resolves 'need EUV pitch but cannot afford EUV': a central hub pre-patterns the three densest periodic layers (active islands, buried wordlines, capacitor-hole hardmask) into a durable SiN/carbon hardmask stack on blank wafers and ships them to small fabs that finish every coarse layer on DUV, aligning to marks embedded in the template.
why: Each small fab avoids $200M+ per EUV scanner and most of the 5-7 EUV layers; the hub runs scanners at >90% utilization across customers, letting several U.S. memory fabs start at ~1/3 the capex (fact 4).
note: Pre-patterned hardmasks cannot sit above layers not yet built; becomes a shuttling litho foundry.

title: Vacuum-gap floating gate: field-emission writes, no oxide to wear
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere (vacuum): replace a floating gate's tunnel oxide with a sealed ~3-4 nm vacuum gap formed by sacrificial-layer release; writes use Fowler-Nordheim field emission across vacuum at a few volts, and with no dielectric there are no traps to generate, while the ~4.5 eV vacuum barrier keeps charge non-volatile.
why: Zero refresh with endurance no longer oxide-limited; a planar 1T cell with no HAR capacitor, using MEMS-style release and sealing already common in U.S. MEMS fabs (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Mitochondrial nano-battery bit: emf read by a high-impedance gain transistor
idea: Mitochondria store energy as an electrochemical gradient, not as free charge. Put a 20 nm solid-state micro-battery (LixTiO2 | thin solid electrolyte | LixMnO2) on each gain-transistor gate. The bit is the electrode state of charge, which sets an open-circuit voltage ~0.3-0.5 V apart, read with no current drawn.
why: Non-volatile like a battery (months), yet read non-destructively in ns. Chemical potential replaces capacitance, so there is no capacitor wall, and writes below 1 V attack the voltage floor (fact 10).
note: 20 nm solid-state battery with ns read and fast ionic write is far beyond demonstrated kinetics.

title: Hin-invertase dipole rotor: molecular rotor crystal flips orientation
idea: Bacteria toggle genes when Hin invertase flips the orientation of a DNA segment, and the inversion persists through division. Use an amphidynamic crystal of dipolar molecular rotors (fluorinated phenylene rotors in rigid stators) with the rotation barrier engineered to ~1 eV. A gate field turns the dipoles 180 degrees in ns, and their collective dipole shifts an FeFET-like channel threshold.
why: Non-volatile ferroelectric-like bit from rotation inside a rigid framework, so there is no oxygen-vacancy fatigue or wake-up as in HZO. Deposited at low temperature from solution or vapor.
note: A 1 eV rotation barrier needs ~10 V/nm fields to flip a few-debye dipole.

title: Blood-clotting self-heal pulses seal leakage paths in the field
idea: Platelets clot only at the wound; put an oxygen-rich reservoir film (over-stoichiometric HfO2+x or CeO2) next to the access junction and gate dielectric, and when profiling flags a leaky cell, send a localized heal pulse whose Joule heat is confined to the conductive defect chain, driving oxygen from the reservoir to fill the vacancy cluster.
why: Gives a cell-local in-situ anneal while the chip stays below 400 C, removing variable-retention and tail cells after fabrication and during aging, so the array runs nearer median retention (10-100x the tail) with 5-10x less refresh.
note: fA leakage paths cannot self-heat; needs forced current and oxygen-reservoir chemistry at cell scale.

title: Gap-junction tiers: adjacent bonded array dies share sense amplifiers
idea: Array dies are hybrid-bonded face-to-face at bitline-group pitch so that one sense-amplifier and column layer sits between them and serves bitlines from the die above and the die below, like gap junctions joining the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. Each pair of array dies carries one periphery instead of two.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): sharing sense-amp and column circuits across two arrays halves periphery per bit, roughly 25% more bits per mm^2 of stack.
note: Bitline pitch (~40 nm) far below hybrid-bond pitch; per-bitline sharing across dies infeasible today.

title: Hydra conveyor: charge shifts continuously up vertical CCD strings
idea: Hydra tissue flows endlessly from body column to tentacles and is shed; use a 3D-NAND vertical string as a charge-coupled shift register, stepping charge packets along 200+ gate layers and regenerating them at a sense amp at the top of each loop, so no packet sits long enough to leak and transfer errors are reset at every regeneration.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-fab cost structure (~100x cheaper per bit), no capacitor, refresh replaced by circulation itself; trade is serial access (~us to first byte), fit for capacity tiers and streaming.
note: Charge transfer efficiency through trap-rich poly channels over 200 stages is doubtful; microsecond serial access is not DRAM-class.

title: Optical Bragg mirror for electrons: superlattice blocks hold-state leakage
idea: Insert an epitaxial Si/SiGe (or AlGaN/GaN) superlattice into the storage-node leakage path designed so electrons at hold bias fall in a minigap and are Bragg-reflected, while at write bias a miniband aligns and transmits resonantly, making an electron energy filter that acts as a check valve.
why: Fact 3: suppresses band-to-band and trap-assisted tunneling (GIDL) at hold by ~100-1000x while keeping ns writes; coherent miniband transport through ~10 periods at room temperature is the physics risk.
note: Coherent miniband transport at RT through 10 periods is unlikely.

title: Photoconductive switch from pulsed-power labs as an optically gated access device
idea: Pulsed-power and THz labs use photoconductive switches: wide-bandgap semiconductors that insulate in the dark and conduct when illuminated. Make the access element a GaN or ZnO photoconductive bridge under an on-chip SiN waveguide 'optical wordline'; dark off-current is set by a ~3.4 eV bandgap (sub-aA) and a ~1 ns light pulse opens it for read/write.
why: Removes the ~3 V wordline swing (fact 10) and the bandgap-limited leakage tail (fact 3); optical wordlines have no RC, allowing longer rows with fewer drivers (fact 7).
note: Per-cell optical gating density and persistent photoconductivity are major doubts.

title: Wavelength-addressed tiers: color-coded phototransistor tier select
idea: Like wavelength-division multiplexing in fibre, give each tier's select transistors a different absorber bandgap (graded SiGe or tuned quantum dots) and light the stack through an in-plane waveguide grid at one wavelength, so only that tier's selectors turn on and no staircase or per-tier decoder is needed.
why: 3D staircase and periphery (facts 2, 7): staircase area goes to zero for 16-32 tiers and tier decoding moves off-die into a tunable laser.
note: Bandgap absorbers are edge filters, not band-pass; deeper tiers absorb all shorter wavelengths.

title: Decal capacitors: high-temperature forest transferred onto transistors
idea: Like a water-slide decal, build the capacitor forest on a donor wafer at 600-800 C, allowing crystalline rutile TiO2 or SrTiO3 (k ~80-150), then bond it upside-down onto a finished access-transistor wafer and remove the donor, so the dielectric never meets the transistor's thermal limit.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): k ~100 directly meets the k ~70 requirement; claims 2x Cs at half the aspect ratio (AR ~35).
note: Bonding capacitor forest to cells at ~40 nm pitch exceeds bond overlay; rutile TiO2 leaky.

title: Plasma-panel wall-charge memory shrunk to sealed field-emission nanogaps
idea: AC plasma displays (PLATO, 1964) had inherent memory: wall charge left on the dielectric keeps a fired cell firing under a common sustain wave while unfired cells stay dark. Replace the gas discharge with field emission across 20-nm sealed dielectric-coated nanogaps; a global sustain AC re-deposits wall charge each half-cycle only in 'on' cells, and X/Y address pulses add or erase wall charge.
why: The hysteresis itself is the selector, so the crosspoint is 4F2 and stackable; the global sustain is built-in refresh with no row activations, which also removes row hammer (Facts 3, 8, 9).
note: Field emission lacks the avalanche threshold that gives plasma-cell bistability.

title: Vertical Bloch line memory revived with DMI-tuned stripe domains
idea: NEC's 1983 VBL memory stored bits as pairs of vertical Bloch lines inside the walls of stripe domains, features far smaller than bubbles. Revive it in [Pt/Co/Ir] multilayers whose interfacial DMI is tuned near the Neel-Bloch crossover so Bloch-line pairs are stable at ~10-nm pitch, shifted along walls by in-plane current pulses and read where the wall end meets an MTJ.
why: Bits defined by topology, not litho: ~10x skyrmion-track density potential (Tb/in2 class) with no transistor or capacitor per bit (Facts 1, 2, 4).

title: Twistor reborn: helical-anisotropy nanowires read by Wiedemann torsion pulses
idea: Bell's twistor wound magnetic tape helically on a copper wire. Electroplate vertical Cu-core/CoFe-shell nanowires under applied torsion so the shell has a helical easy axis, write helical domain segments by coincident axial current plus a tier strap, and read by the Wiedemann effect: a core current pulse twists each domain, launching a torsional acoustic echo sensed by an AlN piezo pad at the wire top.
why: A vertical wire is a 3D string with no transistor per tier (Fact 2); a mechanical readout signal sidesteps resistance-variation tails; ~64 bits per 20-nm wire.

title: Selectron flood-holding: global photocurrent keeps nodes bistable, no refresh
idea: Revive RCA's 1948 Selectron and the Tektronix bistable storage tube, in which a continuous electron flood held each element at one of two stable potentials: a weak backside IR flood lets each storage node's photodiode supply a tiny current that balances leakage. A per-node negative-differential-resistance element gives the node two stable points (0 and VDD), so cells self-latch at picowatt levels instead of decaying.
why: Removes refresh as an operation (fact 3); standby power becomes flood power, targeted at under 1/10 of refresh power for 32-64 Gb dies.
note: Needs nm-scale NDR with tiny valley current and uniform photocurrent balance.

title: Skipper-CCD multi-pass sensing reads sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Revive 1970s CCD memory together with the skipper output amplifier. After the access gate opens, the cell's charge packet is clocked back and forth between two transfer gates under a floating-gate electrometer and read non-destructively 16-64 times, then averaged. Noise falls by sqrt(N), so a 1 fF storage node (~6,000 electrons at 1 V) still resolves cleanly.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and destructive read (fact 8). Cs can drop ~4-5x, so pillar aspect ratio can fall from 60-75:1 toward ~20:1. Multi-pass reads add latency, so this suits capacity tiers.
note: Averaging fixes noise, but SA offset and transfer efficiency dominate.

title: Twistor helical-anisotropy nanowires that write and sense through every tier
idea: Revive Bell's twistor (magnetic tape wound helically on a wire): grow vertical nanowires whose magnetic shell has a helical easy axis set by a twisted strain field, so an axial bitline current plus one tier strap's field switches only the crossing, and readout uses the inverse-Wiedemann voltage pulse induced along the same wire.
why: Facts 2 and 7: transistor-free vertical array where each pillar is both write and sense line for all tiers; per-cell device count and periphery drop sharply if the twist works below 50 nm.

title: Vertical Bloch-line memory revived in stacked synthetic antiferromagnet films
idea: Revive Konishi's 1983 vertical Bloch-line memory: store bits as pairs of Bloch lines inside the domain walls of stripe domains in stacked perpendicular synthetic-antiferromagnet films, stepping them along the walls with in-plane pulse fields. The domain wall itself is the track, so no lithographic cell exists.
why: Density and capital intensity: bits at wall-internal scale (~10-20 nm) with tiers added by sputtering; a mask-light bulk working memory candidate.
note: Revival in SAF stacks is fresh; stepping Bloch lines reliably at 10-20 nm and serial access are unproven.

title: Vertical Bloch-line memory revived in rare-earth-free barium hexaferrite
idea: Revive Konishi's 1983 vertical-Bloch-line memory, which stores bits as pairs of Bloch lines inside stripe-domain walls, in perpendicular BaFe12O19 hexaferrite (Ba and Fe are abundant) instead of gadolinium-gallium garnets. A 1 um i-line pattern hosts bits about 10x finer than itself.
why: No EUV, yet bit density below the lithography limit; nonvolatile; no Gd, Ga, Hf or W; claims 10-30x density over the litho node used, as a nonvolatile memory tier.
note: VBL never worked commercially even in garnets; hexaferrite damping and speed likely too slow for DRAM class.

title: Selectron holding-beam revival: global flood pulse re-latches every cell
idea: RCA's Selectron kept every bit stable with a flood of 'holding' electrons that pushed each eyelet to the nearer of two stable potentials. Give each storage node a weak bistable element (an ovonic threshold switch to a shared flood line plus a high-resistance leak) so one flood pulse every ~64 ms tops up every node still above threshold while discharged nodes stay low, restoring the whole array at once with no row activation and no bitline swing.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (facts 3, 9): replaces ~46 fJ/bit row-by-row refresh with one array-wide pulse (goal ~5x less energy), returns 10-20% of bandwidth and removes refresh activations that add to hammer stress.

title: Contact-free buckled nanotube bit clamped inside a BEOL via
idea: Invert 'storage is electronic' -> store the bit as which way a beam bows. A nanotube or nanowire clamped top and bottom in a BEOL via under compressive pre-strain buckles left or right; side electrodes flip it electrostatically and read the asymmetric capacitance, with no contact ever made, so no stiction or wear.
why: Non-volatile with zero leakage (fact 3), elastic bending can survive >1e15 cycles in principle, and it stacks in BEOL with no silicon transistor per bit (fact 2); thermal stability below 20 nm is the risk.
note: Thermal stability and switching voltage at sub-20 nm buckled beams are doubtful.

title: Woven memory: crossbar cells where drawn fibers cross in a textile
idea: Inverts 'memory is lithographed on a flat wafer': thermally draw multimaterial fibers (metal core with Schottky-diode shell, or metal core with dielectric shell) down to ~1 um by the kilometre, then weave or align-lay them orthogonally so every crossing is a diode-capacitor cell, and stack woven sheets into blocks.
why: Fiber drawing makes km of device per hour at material cost, so a 100-layer block reaches ~$0.1/GB-class (~100x cheaper); trade-off: low areal density, slow high-capacitance lines, contact variability.
note: Cheap km-scale fiber devices, but density, line capacitance and speed fall far short of DRAM class.

title: Wafers stay put; process heads travel like print heads
idea: Inverts 'wafers travel between tools'. Clamp each wafer once on a precision carrier for its whole front end; spatial-ALD, atmospheric-plasma etch and DUV/imprint heads sweep over a moving row of carriers like a printing press, so chucking, alignment reference and load-lock overhead are paid once.
why: Removes ~30-40% of non-productive tool time (pump-down, transfer, re-chuck, re-align) and most automated material handling; ~20% less capital per wafer start (fact 4).

title: Reusable capacitor-forest template: grow once, transfer-print many times
idea: First principle: the costly high-AR etch only defines a shape, and a shape can be reused if the mold separates cleanly. Etch one master Si template with high-AR pores, grow capacitor electrodes plus high-k inside a release liner, transfer-bond the capacitor forest onto the storage-node contacts, and lift the template off for 50-100 reuses.
why: Capacitor etch capex (fact 1): the hardest etch is amortized over many wafers; the template is reused by design.
note: Clean release of a 70:1 forest and cell-pitch bonding are both unproven.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel broadcasting one copy to a hall
idea: Decode reads every weight once per step in a fixed order, so weights need sequential access, not random access. Circulate one copy of a model's weights in a multicore WDM glass-fiber loop (InP lasers, thin-film lithium-niobate modulators, erbium amplifiers, periodic optical regeneration), and let every accelerator tap the passing stream through a passive coupler instead of holding the weights in HBM.
why: One copy in flight serves hundreds of accelerators, so weight HBM per GPU falls toward zero (weights are ~50-70% of inference HBM). Honest cost: per bit-second the loop burns more power than refresh (~0.1 nW vs ~0.7 pW per bit), and a 70B FP8 model at 100 Tb/s needs ~1,100 km of fiber, so it only wins through massive fan-out.
note: One in-flight weight copy fanned to many accelerators; per-accelerator Tb/s receivers and loop power are doubts.

title: Charge-domain KV attention in glass capacitor arrays
idea: Attention needs dot products, not exactly stored bits. Store each key as analog voltages on TFT capacitors on glass (3-4 effective bits per cell), compute q.k by switched-capacitor charge sharing along the columns, digitize only the top-k scores, and fetch the values for those tokens digitally.
why: The KV cache moves off silicon DRAM into cheap glass area as approximate storage: ~4x fewer bits than FP16, and no KV traffic during the score phase.

title: Photorefractive crystal associative memory prefilters attention keys
idea: Attention is a correlation search, and optics does correlation natively. Record the keys as holographic gratings in an iron-doped lithium-niobate crystal; a query beam diffracts into correlation peaks whose brightness ranks the keys, and only the top-k token positions are fetched from a compressed KV store for exact attention.
why: Full-precision KV no longer has to sit in fast DRAM, because only the top-k (<5%) is read. The KV store can then be compressed or tiered, ~10x less DRAM for million-token contexts.
note: Photorefractive recording is slow and decays on read; per-token key appends are a doubt.

title: Uncut DRAM wafer serves as the interposer for chiplets
idea: An interposer is just wires on silicon, and a DRAM wafer is already silicon with metal. Leave the DRAM wafer uncut, add a top RDL, and hybrid-bond logic chiplets face-down so each sits on its own memory field; boot-time self-test maps out bad dies and routes around them through the wafer RDL.
why: Deletes interposer, dicing, KGD handling and HBM TSVs: wafer-scale bandwidth at <0.2 pJ/bit and ~30-40% lower packaged cost per bit for HBM-class memory (facts 5, 6).
note: DRAM BEOL has few coarse metal layers; wafer-scale defect routing and thermal from bonded logic are big doubts.

title: State-dependent gate capacitance enables global read-free refresh pulse
idea: Gate capacitance differs 2-3x between inversion ('1') and depletion ('0'). A global ratchet pulse train on the read-transistor source couples more charge into '1' nodes than into '0' nodes, and the write device's subthreshold conduction acts as the rectifying pawl. Every row is then refreshed at once with no sensing.
why: Refresh (fact 3): no activates, no sense amps, no bandwidth loss. Energy approaches the leaked-charge minimum.

title: Thermos vacuum-gap field-emission access switch
idea: Random stimulus 'thermos flask': its vacuum blocks heat, so a sealed 4-6 nm vacuum gap blocks charge. The access device is a wordline-gated nano-emitter (low-work-function LaB6 or Cs-dosed tip) facing the storage node; off-state current is Fowler-Nordheim-limited to essentially zero, and raising the gate field opens a ~uA emission pulse for read/write.
why: Removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction leakage paths at once (fact 3): retention limited only by capacitor dielectric, refresh interval 100x+ longer, ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy nearly eliminated.
note: Field emission is one-way and emitters degrade; a per-cell switch must write both states over 1e15 cycles.

title: Alignment-free hybrid bonding onto a statistical nanocapacitor carpet
idea: Box = {medium: charge on a carpet of isolated 8 nm DSA-defined nanopillar capacitors | access: transistor wafer with 40 nm landing pads | sense: standard SA | integration: wafer-to-wafer bond with no cell-level alignment | substrate: separate capacitor wafer | fab: block-copolymer DSA + ALD, high-temperature anneal before bonding}. Each pad lands on ~10 random nanocapacitors in parallel, and because each capacitor is smaller than the gap between pads, none bridges two cells; the capacitor wafer can take thermal budgets the transistors could never survive.
why: Facts 1 and 4: separates the capacitor and transistor processes, removes the cell-level overlay requirement and needs no EUV on the capacitor wafer.
note: Statistical many-caps-per-pad removes overlay; but 40 nm hybrid-bond pitch and AR>100 8 nm pillars are far beyond state of art.

title: Display-fab glass panels manufacture DRAM periphery at Gen-8.5 scale
idea: Box: Si array die x Si access x LTPS/IGZO sense amps x panel-level bonding x glass substrate x display fab. Sense amps, decoders and pumps are made as high-variability LTPS/oxide TFT circuits on large glass panels in under-used display fabs and bonded to array-only dies; the 1% budget absorbs TFT Vt scatter.
why: Capital intensity: display area costs ~1/50 of 300 mm logic per m^2; frees DRAM-fab capacity and adds a new supply base.
note: TFT Vt scatter and bond pitch make SAs on glass doubtful.

title: Bond interface doubles as a shared bitline for mirrored arrays
idea: [Box: 1T1C charge | 4F2 VCT | differential cross-interface sensing | face-to-face mirror bond | Si | Cu-Cu hybrid bond] Two mirror-image VCT arrays are finished with bitline half-lines on top and bonded face-to-face so the Cu halves fuse into one bitline serving cells above and below; the sense amp compares a cell on one side with the idle half on the other, giving folded-bitline noise rejection in a 4F2 open layout.
why: Density at fixed F: two cell layers per bitline layer (2x bits per footprint), and differential sensing recovers margin lost when Cs is capped (fact 1).

title: Periphery wafer sandwiched between two array wafers, cross-face sensing
idea: [Box: 1T1C | VCT | open-bitline SA with true line above and complement below | front hybrid bond + backside bond | thinned periphery Si | hybrid bonding + nano-TSV backside contacts] Bond one array wafer to the periphery wafer's front and another to its thinned backside, so every sense amp serves an open bitline from the top array and its complement from the bottom array.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): one periphery layer per two arrays halves periphery cost per bit, and balanced top/bottom pairs cancel array noise.

title: Wavelength-addressed banks: the address is the light colour
idea: Box: 1T1C sub-arrays x wordline fired by a ring-filter photodiode x bitline read by microring modulator x WDM bus x SiN waveguides deposited below 400 C on DRAM BEOL x back-end photonics. Each bank owns one wavelength; a request is a pulse at that colour that only its filter absorbs, firing the wordline with no global row/column decoder tree, and data returns on a modulated carrier.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): removes much of the global decode and long electrical I/O; speculative ~30% die-area saving and <1 pJ/bit off-die.
note: Ring filters far larger than the decoders they replace; thermal tuning cost.

title: Mirror lid reflects free-space light between memory and logic
idea: Box: DRAM chiplet x standard x photodiode array x upward-facing microLED arrays bounced off a molded aspheric mirror lid x dry-laminated power-only carrier x injection molding. Chiplets need only a few power layers below; all memory data travels as light up to the lid and back down to the processor.
why: Water: removes the interposer and high-layer-count signal substrate (the wet-heavy parts), ~10x less water; bandwidth no longer tied to shoreline.

title: Photoconductive access switch opened by waveguide light pulses
idea: Po: the switch is opened by light.
