idea: Po: the hole digs itself. Place Pt or Ag nanodots by imprint or self-assembly and run metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2: each dot sinks straight down, giving AR >100:1 holes in a wet bench; strip catalyst and line with high-k for trench-type storage capacitors.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and etch capex: wet bench ~1/20 the cost of a high-AR plasma etcher; AR >100 without bowing for Cs >8 fF.

title: Quantum-paraelectric capacitor whose k explodes in cold pods
idea: Worsen: keep the dielectric constant fixed near 40 and keep etching deeper. Flip: run memory in 40-77 K pods and use quantum-paraelectric SrTiO3 or KTaO3 as the cell dielectric, whose k climbs from ~300 to several thousand on cooling, so a planar or shallow-cup capacitor reaches 5 fF at 4F2.
why: Destroys the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: the k ~70 target exceeded >10x) and removes high-AR etch tools (capital, fact 4).

title: FD-SOI buried-oxide back-gate cell on a 22nm shuttle
idea: Worsen: spend the whole budget inventing a capacitor process. Flip: on a ~$100k 22FDX multi-project wafer, use an isolated per-cell back-gate under the thin buried oxide as the storage node (the BOX is a free capacitor) and read the bit as a front-gate threshold shift; 24 months covers two tapeouts and retention characterization.
why: Proves a capacitor-free, non-destructive-read cell in a US-fab logic process; U.S. manufacturability with near-zero capital.

title: Sputtered AlScN ferroelectric cap with 20x hafnia's charge
idea: Worsen: depend on ALD precursors and hafnia wake-up cycling. Flip: use a used reactive-sputter tool (~$400k) to deposit 10 nm wurtzite AlScN on 200 mm CMOS back-end test chips and use its ~100 uC/cm2 polarization as a planar storage capacitor with no deep trench; 24 months maps endurance and scaling.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): ~20x charge per area versus a linear dielectric in a planar cap at low capital; endurance is the risk to retire.

title: Hafnium-free AlBN ferroelectric capacitors from abundant elements
idea: Worse: build all nonvolatile capacitor memory on hafnium, a nuclear-zirconium byproduct with few refiners. Flip: use boron-substituted aluminum nitride, a wurtzite ferroelectric, sputtered at back-end temperatures as the nonvolatile capacitor dielectric.
why: Zero refresh from abundant Al, B and N on ubiquitous sputter tools, which helps U.S. manufacturability; high coercive field and endurance are the risks.
note: AlBN/AlScN widely studied; high coercive field and poor endurance vs DRAM needs.

title: Jazz drummer's frozen groove: hidden charge-density-wave state in 1T-TaS2
idea: A jazz drummer can hold a groove after the band stops. In 1T-TaS2 a single ~30 ps electrical pulse switches the electrons' charge-density-wave pattern into a hidden metallic order that persists, and a second, longer pulse restores the insulating order; the bit reads as a ~10x resistance change.
why: ps switching at fJ energy and non-volatile storage (facts 3, 10).
note: 1T-TaS2 hidden/CDW switching actively studied; room-temperature stability and integration are open.

title: Radar pulse-forming inspired internal-barrier nanolaminate with giant permittivity
idea: Radar pulse-forming networks prize giant-permittivity dielectrics; a nanolaminate of 0.5 nm insulating Al2O3 barriers between 2 nm semiconducting TiO2-x layers shows Maxwell-Wagner giant effective k (~1000), deposited blanket into pillars with one mask protecting periphery. Tuning sublayer conductivity pushes the relaxation frequency above ~1 GHz so the high k survives ns charge sharing.
why: k_eff 10x+ over ZrO2 (fact 1) could cut pillars to AR ~10:1; leakage vs relaxation speed is a fundamental trade, hence speculative.
note: Al2O3/TiO2 giant-k nanolaminates reported; relaxation-leakage trade.

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric layer amplifies cell capacitance
idea: Scale down to the domain level: insert a thin ferroelectric layer in series with the linear high-k so the ferroelectric operates in its negative-capacitance region, raising total stack capacitance above that of the high-k alone.
why: Capacitor wall: target 1.5-2x Cs without higher AR; hysteresis-free design keeps endurance unlimited.
note: Same NC series-stack mechanism.

title: Hafnium-free antiferroelectric zirconia capacitor storing switched charge
idea: Periodic-table walk, Zr (40): use pure tetragonal ZrO2's field-induced double hysteresis loop, biasing the plate at the loop midpoint so each write swings through one antiferroelectric loop and releases ~20-30 uC/cm2 instead of ~5-8 uC/cm2 linear charge; zero-field relaxation avoids ferroelectric imprint.
why: 2-3x effective Cs at AR<=40 with Zr (~100x more abundant than Hf, whose world output is ~70-80 t/yr).

title: Negative-capacitance HZO layer amplifies cap density in series
idea: Scarcity rule: stay inside today's capacitor footprint, no taller pillar. Add a thin HZO layer in series with the ZrO2, matched so the HZO is stabilized on its negative-capacitance branch; the series stack's capacitance then exceeds ZrO2 alone, raising stored charge 1.5-3x at the same aspect ratio.
why: Raises Cs from ~5 to 8-15 fF without AR 115 (fact 1), or drops AR to ~40:1; must stay non-hysteretic at ns speeds.
note: Same NC series-stack mechanism.

title: No silicon, no litho: self-ordered anodic alumina capacitor templates
idea: Forced limit: no wafer and no capacitor lithography. Aluminium foil from electrolytic-capacitor plants is anodized into self-ordered nanopores (AR 100+), lined by ALD with high-k and electrodes as storage capacitors, then bonded to TFT access arrays.
why: Capacitor charge wall: AR beyond 115 with no lithography or EUV; reuses the capacitor-foil industry.

title: Substitute fab-owned tools with an aircraft-style lithography leasing bank
idea: Swap each fab buying its own scanners and etchers for a sovereign-backed lessor (AerCap-style) that owns tool fleets, leases them by wafer-hour and moves them between fabs as the cycle turns.
why: Attacks capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; higher fleet use and cheaper lessor capital could cut tool cost per wafer ~15-25% and let new entrants start without $15B.

title: Revive deep-trench SOI eDRAM as U.S.-made memory chiplets
idea: Combine the deep-trench SOI eDRAM process once used in IBM POWER and z processors with chiplet and hybrid-bond stacking: a U.S. fab builds dense eDRAM-only chiplets on existing 14-22 nm SOI lines and stacks them into HBM-like cubes. Trench capacitors (~20-40 fF) are proven, and the lines are already depreciated.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: domestic, EUV-free supply; large trench Cs also eases refresh; density ~1/4 of commodity DRAM but sovereign.
note: Proven tech, but 1/4 density and line revival exceeds $1M.

title: Silicon interposer fused with deep-trench DRAM banks
idea: Combine the passive 2.5D interposer under GPU+HBM with memory: fill its 2,000-3,000 mm2 with 40-65 nm deep-trench eDRAM (AR ~80) plus interposer-native refresh and sense logic, so the wiring substrate is also a multi-GB near-memory tier.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and HBM shortage: uses depreciated legacy fabs, no EUV; ~2,500 mm2 at ~0.06 um2/bit gives ~3-5 GB per package at mm-scale wire lengths (fact 5).

title: Backside power network fused with DRAM periphery
idea: Borrow logic backside power delivery for DRAM: move VPP/VARY/VDD rails and charge-pump capacitors to the wafer backside through nano-TSVs, freeing frontside metal for 2x bitline/local-IO tracks and letting row-decoder strips tuck under the mats.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and voltage floor (fact 10): periphery area -20-30%, lower IR drop allows tighter VARY margins; die area per bit -10-15%.

title: Dual-damascene fusion of storage-node contact and landing pad
idea: Combine BEOL dual-damascene with the DRAM buried-contact module: the storage-node contact hole and the landing-pad trench are etched into one stacked dielectric in a single trench-first/via-last sequence, then filled with one Ru or Mo deposition and planarized with one CMP.
why: Removes one critical EUV/SAQP patterning layer, one metal fill and one CMP from the 5-7 EUV-layer flow (fact 4), ~3-5% wafer cost; the Ru/Mo fill also cuts tungsten (China ~80%) exposure.

title: Nuclear-plant co-located DRAM fab with utility rate-base financing
idea: Fuse an existing nuclear plant (or new SMR cluster) with a DRAM fab on the same site. Firm 24/7 carbon-free power comes in at cost, and condenser waste heat preheats ultrapure water and HVAC makeup air. The utility finances the power and water infrastructure as a regulated asset.
why: Fab power is about 5-10% of wafer cost and the shell and utilities about 20% of capex. This cuts both by an estimated 20-40% and de-risks U.S. siting.

title: DoD procurement preference fusing PFAS-free and Buy-American rules
idea: Combine the NDAA's PFAS-procurement restrictions with Buy-American content rules into one weighted preference for domestic F-free memory in defense and federal purchasing, with 10-year volume guarantees.
why: Creates anchor demand that de-risks the first U.S. F-free memory fab and turns two existing policy levers into one demand signal.
note: Policy fusion; depends on an F-free process existing.

title: Solar junction-box bypass: power-gate and replace leaky mats in the field
idea: Adapted from the bypass diodes that route current around a shaded or cracked solar cell: each memory mat gets its own power gate and well switch plus a remap entry, so a mat whose leakage rises (seen in its refresh-error rate) is switched fully off and replaced by a spare mat in the same bank.
why: One leaky mat today forces the whole device to refresh faster or be scrapped; mat-level bypass repairs it in the field, removes its standby leakage, and keeps the rest of the die at a relaxed refresh rate (fact 3).

title: Hong Kong high-rises: 8-high hybrid-bonded SRAM as sole memory
idea: Borrowed from dense cities that build upward when land is scarce: eight thinned, capacitor-free SRAM dies on a mature node are hybrid-bonded onto an edge inference SoC for 0.5-1 GB of sub-5 ns on-package SRAM, and 2-bit weights let small models and their KV fit entirely, removing DRAM from the bill of materials.
why: Zero refresh and zero DRAM purchase for edge devices; stacking mature-node SRAM avoids EUV and the HBM TSV yield tax.
note: SRAM cost/bit ~50x DRAM and 8Gb leakage; hybrid bonding mature-node dies is feasible.

title: Grid fault-current limiters islanding shorted wordlines per mat
idea: Adapted from power grids that use fault-current limiters and islanding so one short does not black out a region: each mat's local wordline-driver supply has a self-tripping current limiter (a small overcurrent-sensing latch), so a WL-to-BL or WL-to-plate short isolates its own mat instead of collapsing VPP for the whole bank; the mat is then marked out and its addresses remapped.
why: Yield (facts 4, 7): hard shorts are among the few defects that kill whole banks or dies; islanding turns a die-killer into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield on large-die parts by several percent.

title: Catastrophe bonds hedging DRAM price spikes to fund capacity
idea: Adapted from reinsurance cat bonds: buyers sponsor notes that pay investors a coupon in normal years. When the DRAM contract index passes ~2.5x baseline, principal is released to the sponsors, who must spend it on pre-negotiated capacity reservations.
why: Turns shortage risk into a tradable instrument; buyers get price certainty and a pre-funded pool to reserve buffer capacity, which is cheaper than holding inventory (supply stability, capital).

title: Shale DUC wells: front-end-complete U.S. wafer bank for surges
idea: Adapted from drilled-but-uncompleted shale wells that wait for prices to rise before fracking: U.S. fabs park wafers in nitrogen stockers once the array and capacitor are done but before final metal and personalization, then finish them in ~3-4 weeks when prices spike.
why: Supply responds ~4x faster than a ~4-month full cycle, and one inventory can serve DDR or LPDDR personalizations, damping price spikes (supply, capital efficiency).

title: MOSIS-style multi-project shuttle on a U.S. DRAM pilot line
idea: Adapted from MOSIS, which shared CMOS wafers among university designs: run quarterly DRAM-process shuttles at a U.S. pilot line where dozens of startups and universities share reticles to test new cells, capacitors and sense amps at real array density.
why: New DRAM cell ideas currently have nowhere in the U.S. to be built; shuttles cut cost per experiment from ~$5-10M to <$100k and speed up the domestic innovation pipeline (U.S. manufacturability, density).
note: Needs an existing US DRAM-capable pilot line willing to host.

title: Magnify HBM stack by one spare die, disable the worst
idea: Build HBM stacks 9-high to sell 8-high. After bonding and stack test, the base die disables the worst core die or failed TSV group through redundant TSV routing.
why: Fact 6: stack yield losses of 20-30% shrink to a few percent; a 12.5% silicon adder pays for itself when bonding yield is the limiter.

title: Slow the depreciation clock: 15-year frozen-node vintage memory
idea: Commit a fully depreciated 1x/1y-nm DRAM line to a frozen node for 15 years, with products (heritage DDR5, LPDDR5 capacity parts) designed for that node, sold on a cash-cost-plus basis instead of retiring tools after 5 years.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; a depreciation-free line cuts cost per bit ~2x and keeps capacity in the market instead of scrapping it.

title: Eliminate whole-stack scrap: a hot-spare core die inside each HBM stack
idea: Bond 13 core dies for a 12-high HBM3E stack; the base die tests each layer after bonding and steers a failed die's channels to the spare through a crossbar, so the GPU sees a standard 12-high device.
why: Fact 6: stack losses of 20-30% (one bad die kills the stack) fall to a few percent, worth far more than the ~8% extra die cost.

title: NIC inside the HBM base die for direct remote writes
idea: Eliminate the GPU hop for network data: put a co-packaged optical RDMA engine in each HBM base die so remote nodes write KV caches, gradients and activations directly into the target stack without crossing the GPU's PHY and NoC twice.
why: Removes ~2 extra interface crossings per byte (~6-8 pJ/bit saved) and frees GPU beachfront from network SerDes for more memory.

title: Dual-ported HBM shared by neighboring GPUs ends stranded capacity
idea: Eliminate fixed one-GPU ownership of HBM: a base die with two PHYs links a stack to two adjacent GPU packages via a bridge, so capacity flows to whichever GPU needs it (KV cache on one, weights on the other).
why: Fleet HBM utilization is often 50-70%; pairwise pooling recovers ~15-25% capacity, so fewer DRAM bits are bought per useful bit.

title: Retention-first respin of a legacy DRAM node
idea: Reverse the optimization target on a fully depreciated 2x/3x nm DRAM line: give up ~30% density and spend the area on a longer recessed channel, thicker gate oxide at the storage-node overlap and a fatter capacitor, so the leakage tail drops ~10x and Cs rises ~1.5x. The part ships with ~1 s refresh as a low-idle-power LPDDR or CXL capacity tier.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3) falls ~15x, and a paid-off line (depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) keeps cost per bit competitive despite lower density.

title: Decoding moves to the controller; DRAM receives one-hot row lines
idea: Reverse where address decoding happens: a logic base die performs row predecode and sends one-hot group-select lines through dense hybrid-bond pads to each array tile; the DRAM die keeps only the final AND gates at the wordline drivers.
why: Fact 7: row/column decoder and address-latch area (~6-8%) leaves the DRAM die; logic-node decode is faster and lower power.

title: Face-to-face HBM pairs halve the TSV count
idea: Rearrange HBM from face-to-back stacking to face-to-face pairs: two core dies are hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch with no TSVs between them, and only pair-to-pair interfaces use TSVs, with one die's TSVs serving both.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV count and keep-out area halve; dense face-to-face bonds let two dies share I/O and repair logic; ~10-15% more bits per wafer and better stack yield.
note: F2F pairs halve TSVs; ~10-15% bits per wafer.

title: Recess only passing-wordline segments with one mask
idea: Rearrange the buried wordline: one added mask exposes only the segments where wordlines cross isolation (the passing gates) and recesses them deeper, moving their field away from the neighboring cell's storage junction while active-crossing segments stay at normal depth.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): passing-gate coupling drives the ~1k-activation threshold; a deeper passing segment could raise it several-fold with zero cell-area cost.
note: Targets the passing-gate row-hammer mechanism at zero area; needs a DRAM fab to prove.

title: Rotate the crystal under the layout for quieter channels
idea: Zero added masks: rotate the 4F2 vertical-channel array 45 degrees relative to the wafer notch (or start from (110) wafers) so channel sidewalls become {100} planes, which have ~3x lower interface-trap density than {110}.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): the trap-assisted tail sets refresh, so fewer interface traps can shift the ~13 fA tail down and stretch refresh intervals for the price of a layout rotation.
note: Tail is set mostly by GIDL and bulk traps, not interface Dit alone.

title: Mirror tier pairs to share bitline layers
idea: Flip every second tier upside down so tiers 2k and 2k+1 face each other and share one bitline/contact layer between them (the 3D NAND mirror trick applied to 3D DRAM). It is done by deposition order alone, with zero added masks.
why: Stack height and 3D cost (fact 2): ~25-30% fewer layers per bit tier means more tiers within the same HAR etch budget.
note: Mirror sharing of contact layers is a modest, plausible stack-height saving.

title: Sell the ramp: defect-tolerant early-yield wafers
idea: Reverse 'ship only mature yield': during a new fab's ramp, sell lower-bin dies with published defect maps to AI training customers whose software already tolerates row retirement, so the ramp earns revenue instead of scrap.
why: Brings forward ~6-12 months of revenue on a $15B fab, which cuts net capital at risk and payback time for new U.S. capacity.

title: Pay per good bit: vendor-owned DUV litho as a service
idea: Reverse the purchase: the scanner vendor installs and runs DUV tools in the fab and is paid per good die or bit that leaves the litho step, not for the tool.
why: Capital intensity: the fab avoids litho capex and the vendor's incentives match yield; it lowers the entry barrier for no-EUV U.S. fabs.

title: Parity mat per bank absorbs particle killers from NF3-free cleans
idea: Flip yield from fab to array: chambers are cleaned with remote H2/O2 or Cl2 plasma instead of NF3, accepting more particle killers, and each bank adds a parity mat equal to the XOR of its 16 data mats in the same activation, so a particle-killed mat is reconstructed on the fly without fuse repair.
why: Removes NF3 while holding yield; tolerates one dead mat per bank for ~6% area.

title: Resurrect IBM trench eDRAM at GlobalFoundries as U.S. memory chiplets
idea: Rearrange a logic foundry's role: restart the deep-trench-capacitor eDRAM modules GlobalFoundries inherited from IBM (used in POWER/z chips at 32/22/14 nm). Use them to make standalone DRAM-class cache and memory chiplets in New York as a domestic second source.
why: U.S. manufacturability: trench capacitors (~20 fF class) are already proven and no new fab capex is needed. The chiplets serve L4/near-memory demand that now consumes HBM and DRAM.
note: eDRAM density ~10-20x worse than commodity DRAM; niche cache tier.

title: Unbundled HBM: independent U.S. stacker buys dies, builds stacks
idea: Rearrange the HBM value chain: DRAM makers sell known-good core dies, and a U.S. OSAT does TSV reveal, hybrid bonding and stack test. The stacks pair with a foundry-made base die from any customer, as in the logic chiplet market.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): a specialist stacker can raise stack yield and creates onshore HBM output with no DRAM front end. Supply widens beyond the three integrated vendors.

title: Cleanroom REIT: separate fab shells from tool capital
idea: Reverse the capital stack: a real-estate investment trust builds and owns the cleanroom shells, utilities, UPW and power plants. It leases them on 20-year terms to DRAM operators, who buy only tools.
why: Capital intensity: the shell and facilities are ~20-30% of fab cost. Financing them at REIT cost of capital (~6-8%) instead of chipmaker equity (~12%+) lowers the depreciation and finance charge per wafer.

title: DRAM shuttle: shared wafer runs for new cell inventors
idea: Rearrange who goes to the fab: an existing DRAM line sets aside spare lots each month for multi-project wafers. Startups and universities test new cells on a real DRAM flow for ~$100-300k instead of building a line.
why: Shortens the path from new memory concept to supply, and turns idle capacity into a cell incubator.
note: Needs incumbent willing to expose its flow.

title: Water-gated subsidies: full award only at one-tenth liters per bit
idea: Reverse incentive design: memory subsidies and permits are tiered by verified liters of fresh water per GB shipped, with the full award only at 10% of today's industry baseline. Overperformers earn tradable water-per-bit credits.
why: Water turns from a siting obstacle into a competitive axis. The rule pulls dry processes and reuse into new U.S. fabs and targets a 10x cut in industry water intensity.

title: Nesting: sub-wordline drivers built inside the array's vertical-transistor process
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: sub-wordline driver transistors are made as vertical-channel devices in the same pillar and buried-wordline steps as the cells, nested in a dummy-row band inside each mat, so the separate SWD stripes of planar logic transistors and their array-to-periphery boundary rules vanish.
why: Fact 7: SWD stripes are ~8-10% of die; nesting removes ~70% of that area and its extra masks, about a 6% die shrink per node with no lithography change.

title: Continuity: wide-IO DRAM redesigned for fully depreciated legacy DRAM lines
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: keep retiring 2x/3x-nm DRAM lines running by taping out a new 512-bit-wide, low-speed DRAM die for them, designed for fan-out packaging beside accelerators. The wide, slow interface hides the older node's lower density. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital (fact 4): depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so fully depreciated lines make bits at about half the wafer cost, adding supply with zero new fab capex.
note: Depreciated wafers are cheaper but older nodes have 3-4x lower density, so cost/bit may not improve.

title: N+1 hot-spare die in U.S.-assembled memory stacks
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: every domestically assembled 8-high stack carries a ninth die; base-die BIST tracks per-die error rates and, when one degrades, migrates its contents in the background and switches its channel to the spare.
why: Stack yield and field life no longer hinge on the worst of 8 dies; recovers part of the 20-30% stacking yield loss (fact 6) and permits more aggressive cell designs.

title: Borrow image-sensor dark-current tricks: pinned STI sidewall implant
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: DRAM retention leakage and CMOS-image-sensor dark current are the same generation physics, so copy the sensor playbook: a p+ pinning implant along the STI sidewall keeps storage-node depletion off interface traps, plus a carbon-co-implanted gettering layer in domestically grown epi wafers.
why: Image sensors cut dark current 10-100x this way; even 3-5x lower tail leakage stretches refresh ~4x using U.S. wafer and process capability.
note: Pinning implants cut dark current; DRAM already uses related isolation engineering.

title: Variable-pitch hammer-hardened row zone for page tables and kernels
idea: TRIZ separation by condition: each bank has a ~3% zone laid out at wider wordline pitch with larger capacitors on the same U.S. process; the OS places page tables, kernel and security metadata there while the dense 6F2 zone holds ordinary data with lighter mitigation.
why: Hammer attacks that matter (privilege escalation) hit the hardened zone, so the dense zone can accept lower thresholds and simpler trackers; suits a trusted domestic defense supply.

title: Asymmetry: hyperscaler capex prepay for capped-price capacity call options
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry in risk-sharing: hyperscalers prepay ~30% of a new fab's capex and in return hold call options on 50% of its output at a capped price for 10 years, while the maker keeps all upside on the other half and all downside protection on the first.
why: Capital intensity and 3-5 year fab lag: de-risks greenfield builds so they start 1-2 years earlier during shortages.

title: Blessing in disguise: failed HBM stacks rebinned as HBM-lite via TSV bypass
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: build redundant TSV bypass lanes in every core die so a 12-high stack with one or two dead layers is re-addressed and sold as an 8-high 'HBM-lite' instead of scrap.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30%: converts much of that loss into sellable capacity.

title: Lichen pairing: DRAM fab fused with a domestic helium gas plant
idea: Lichen fuses an alga and a fungus into one organism that thrives where neither could alone. Site a DRAM fab beside a U.S. natural-gas helium separation plant (e.g., Hugoton field), taking captive helium by pipeline and using the plant's cryogenic cold for fab chillers in exchange for long-term offtake.
why: Removes exposure to Qatar helium (~30% of supply, offline) and cuts chiller energy ~10-20%.

title: Cicada-cycle capacity bank investing only in price troughs
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime-numbered cycles so predators cannot synchronize with them. A public-private capacity bank buys tools and builds shells when DRAM prices crash and incumbents cut capex, then leases the capacity to operators when prices rise.
why: Breaks the boom-bust cycle behind 4x spikes; trough-priced tools cost ~20-30% less.

title: Pollinator nectar credit: per-bit tax credit for capacitor-free memory
idea: Flowers pay pollinators per visit, not upfront. A production tax credit pays per shipped gigabit of U.S.-made, capacitor-free, DRAM-class memory (<=100 ns, >=1e15 cycles), tapering as volume grows.
why: Rewards output rather than announcements and steers capital to cells that mature fabs can build.

title: Kalundborg-style fab symbiosis with neighboring heavy industry
idea: Borrowed from the Kalundborg industrial park, where plants trade steam, water and byproducts: site a DRAM fab beside a chlor-alkali plant (byproduct H2), a steel-mill air-separation unit (N2/O2/Ar), a data center that absorbs fab waste heat and a municipal water-reclaim plant, with pipelines replacing on-site gas yards and UPW pretreatment.
why: Capital, energy and water: on-site utilities are ~15-20% of fab capex; sharing could cut that by a third and shorten fab build time by months.

title: Precious-metal streaming finance for DRAM wafer starts
idea: Borrowed from royalty-streaming firms like Franco-Nevada, which fund mines upfront for a fixed share of future metal at a fixed low price with a small staff: a 10-person fund pays ~20% of a DRAM line's capex in exchange for 10% of its wafer output for 15 years at cash cost, and resells the bits on long-term contracts to hyperscalers.
why: Capital intensity: non-dilutive, non-debt capex lowers the cost of capital for new fabs and gives buyers a hedge against 4x price spikes.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobby relay dies for 32-high stacks
idea: Skyscrapers use sky lobbies so elevators run in short segments. Put a thin logic 'sky-lobby' die every 8 DRAM tiers. It re-times signals, runs local ECC and refresh control, and splits TSV chains into short, low-capacitance segments.
why: TSV load and yield get worse as stacks grow. Segmenting lets stacks reach 24-32 tiers with flat TSV energy per bit and confines faults to one segment, for ~2x capacity per package footprint.

title: Core-memory thermistor compensation: servo the off-wordline to leakage minimum
idea: Revive core memory's thermistor-compensated drive currents: a replica access transistor in each bank continuously measures total off-leakage (subthreshold plus GIDL), and a small dither loop holds the negative wordline voltage at the leakage minimum, which shifts with temperature and aging.
why: Fixed negative-wordline levels are set for the worst case and leave 3-10x leakage on the table across temperature (fact 3); tracking the minimum could double refresh intervals at hot corners.

title: Intel-AMD 1982 Second-Source Rule Applied to DRAM Designs
idea: Revive the IBM and DoD rule of the 1970s-80s that every critical chip have a licensed second source: federal buyers and a hyperscaler purchasing consortium qualify a DRAM product only if it is licensed, with design-kit and process escrow, to a second, geographically separate fab.
why: Supply resilience and U.S. manufacturability: creates guaranteed demand for a second U.S. fab and spreads know-how; the x86 second-source deal is what created AMD's fab business.
note: Proven historical lever; DRAM makers resist licensing.

title: Zero-vent fab: noble gases treated as leased capital, not consumables
idea: Inverts 'process gases are bought, used once and vented': a fab-wide exhaust spine with cryogenic fractional distillation and membranes recovers He, Ne, Kr, Xe and NF3 from every tool exhaust before abatement, repurifies to 6N and returns them to gas cabinets; the gas vendor keeps ownership and bills only for grams lost.
why: Targets >85% recovery of helium and neon (Qatar, Ukraine/Russia chokepoints), turning a supply shock into a small make-up stream; the lease model aligns the vendor with recovery.

title: Deuterium chimneys through the nitride over the array
idea: Inverts 'barrier layers must seal everything': the single added mask opens small windows in the hydrogen-blocking nitride over the array so a final deuterium anneal reaches storage-node junctions and gate interfaces, passivating dangling bonds with harder-to-break Si-D bonds.
why: Shrinks the trap-driven VRT and retention tail (fact 3) ~2-3x and hardens cells against hammer-induced trap generation; one non-EUV mask.

title: Wafer-form strategic DRAM reserve packaged into whatever is short
idea: Inverts 'stockpiles are finished goods': a national reserve buys known-good DDR5/LPDDR5 wafers during gluts, stores them in nitrogen cabinets, and contracts OSATs to package them into whichever form factor (DIMM, LPDDR, CXL) is scarce during a spike.
why: Price stability and supply: a 2-3 month buffer that damps 4x price swings; wafers are compact, cheap to store, and avoid locking bits into a form factor that may not be the one in shortage.

title: Grounded shield film between every wordline tier, deposition-defined
idea: In horizontal-wordline 3D stacks, insert a 5-10 nm grounded metal or doped-poly film between adjacent wordline tiers so aggressor field lines terminate on ground instead of on the victim's storage node or channel.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) is driven by capacitive coupling and carrier injection across wordline spacing; in 3D the vertical spacer costs one deposition, not lithographic area, so coupling can drop >10x, raising flip thresholds from ~1k toward >50k activations and retiring TRR/RFM bandwidth overhead.

title: Pay depreciated DRAM lines to keep running instead of converting
idea: A fully depreciated line's wafer cost is ~45% of a new one because depreciation is ~55% of cost. Governments or buyer consortia pay fabs to keep old 1x/1y-nm lines producing for 5 more years rather than converting them to HBM or scrapping tools, with guaranteed offtake covering the opportunity cost.
why: Cost per bit and supply: preserves the cheapest bits on Earth, adding ~10% supply at ~50% of new-node cost.

title: Irrigation-ditch water-rights swap funds dry access-module retrofits
idea: Random stimulus 'irrigation ditch': water is a tradable right, not just a pipe. A DRAM fab in a western U.S. water-rights state retrofits its access-device module to dry cleans and area-selective deposition, then leases the freed allocation to farms or cities under a long-term contract; the water utility co-finances the retrofit because it is cheaper than a new supply source.
why: Turns a 10x water cut in the most clean-heavy module into revenue and a permitting advantage, which speeds new U.S. capacity (U.S. manufacturability, capital intensity).

title: Recipe card: open national NV-memory process kit for 200mm fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'recipe card' -> a federally funded lab line publishes a complete, licensable FeRAM/MRAM-on-CMOS process module (recipes, PDK, test and reliability data) designed for 200 mm and 300 mm mature tools. Any U.S. fab can then add a non-volatile memory product.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: it lowers the barrier from billions in development to tens of millions in module tools and spreads NV capacity across ~20 existing U.S. fabs.

title: Inline e-beam voltage contrast maps junction leakage before capacitor
idea: Box: standard cell x access transistor probed at storage-contact level x e-beam voltage-contrast imaging of charge decay per contact x inline metrology x Si x fab method. Charging each exposed storage contact and imaging its decay over ms maps the leakage distribution on every wafer, feeding implant/anneal recipes in days rather than months of electrical test.
why: Faster learning on the leakage tail (fact 3) shortens yield ramps for new nodes and new US fabs, reducing capital time (fact 4).

title: Neutral-beam etch of wordline recess removes plasma-induced traps
idea: Box: standard cap x recessed access x SA x in-array x Si x neutral-beam (charge-free, VUV-free) etch replacing RIE for the recess trench, zero masks. Neutral beams avoid the charging and VUV photon damage that seed interface traps on the trench walls forming the channel and storage-junction edge.
why: Fewer interface traps shrink the subthreshold/TAT tail and Vt spread (fact 3), targeting ~2x retention on the same mask set.

title: Neighbor wordlines driven deeper negative while a row is open
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x sub-wordline drivers given a second negative rail selected for rows N+-1 during row N activation x in-array x Si x zero masks. The extra ~-0.3 V on adjacent wordlines cancels coupling and passing-gate effects that transiently open neighbor access transistors.
why: Cuts activation-induced leakage that erodes neighbor retention and drives row hammer (facts 3, 9): ~2x retention under heavy traffic, higher hammer threshold.

title: CHIPS packaging grants gated on litres-per-gigabyte water budgets
idea: Box: any memory x any access x any sensing x any packaging route x U.S. sites x dry toolsets required. Federal packaging incentives require metered packaging water intensity of 0.1 L/GB or less, with bonus credit for dry steps such as laser dicing, SAB, ACF and dry resist.
why: Water and U.S. manufacturability: lets packaging plants get permits in water-stressed Arizona and Texas, forces 10x cuts and creates a U.S. market for dry tools.

title: Pay-per-exposure EUV scanners as securitized tool-as-a-service
idea: Box[Finance=scanner owned by lessor SPV, metered per wafer-layer exposure x Owner=tool vendor + asset managers x Scale=any fab]: lithography scanners are owned by an asset-backed vehicle and billed per exposure, moving ~$200M-per-tool capex off DRAM makers' balance sheets.
why: Capital intensity and depreciation (~55% of wafer cost): turns fixed cost into variable cost and lowers new-entrant barriers.

title: Grounded shield tiers interleaved so no row has a neighbor
idea: Po: no row has a neighbour. In a stacked 3D DRAM, insert a grounded doped-Si or metal shield tier between active tiers and route wordlines so laterally adjacent cells belong to rows separated by a grounded wall; deposition tiers are cheap, so spending one tier in three on shielding buys electrostatic isolation.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aggressor-victim coupling cut >10x, raising the threshold from ~1k toward 100k activations and removing mitigation refresh traffic.

title: Revive defunct DRAM makers' process IP in idle 300 mm lines
idea: Po: dead companies make memory. License documented flows from defunct DRAM makers (e.g., buried-wordline 4x-nm processes) and transplant them into idle U.S. 300 mm logic/foundry lines whose 193i, ALD and CMP tools already exist, producing mature DDR4/LPDDR4 parts.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: skips ~5 years of process development; output in 2-3 years at a fraction of greenfield capex.

title: Dual-ported HBM stack serving two GPU chiplets
idea: Po: the memory has two front doors. One added redistribution mask on the base die creates a second bump field on the opposite edge, so one stack sits between two GPU chiplets and both read the same data without copies.
why: Shared weights and KV cache need no duplicate copy; effective capacity per GPU pair up 30-50%.
note: Arbitration and coherence between two hosts; needs a DRAM vendor base-die change.

title: Face-to-face DRAM pairs halve TSVs in HBM stacks
idea: Po: dies kiss in pairs. One hybrid-bond pad mask lets two DRAM dies bond face-to-face, so each pair needs TSVs in only one die and an 8-high stack needs TSV processing on 4 dies.
why: Half as much TSV processing and keep-out area, easing the HBM TSV area and yield tax.

title: Bottle-deposit refunds on every gigabyte of DRAM
idea: Po: memory has a bottle deposit. A refundable deposit (e.g., $0.50/GB) is charged on DRAM-bearing devices and modules and refunded when they are returned to a certified harvester; unclaimed deposits fund harvest-plant capex.
why: Bottle-bill regions see 70-90% return rates versus ~20% e-waste collection; guarantees predictable feedstock so die/package harvesting can be financed; attacks scarce-resource intensity and supply.

title: Co-site fabs on domestic helium fields with closed-loop recapture
idea: Po: the fab sits on a helium well. New DRAM fabs are sited at U.S. helium-bearing gas fields (Kansas/Texas Hugoton, Wyoming) with a dedicated cryogenic extraction plant, and every helium-using tool (backside cooling, leak check, purge) exhausts into a membrane-plus-PSA recapture loop.
why: Removes exposure to the Qatar outage (~30% of supply) and recaptures ~80-90% of fab helium; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: Capacity cascade moving legacy DRAM to depreciated DUV fabs
idea: Po: the oldest fab cures the newest shortage. Auto, industrial and set-top demand for DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 is contractually migrated to fully depreciated 25-38 nm ArF fabs (including revived shuttered lines) under swap agreements: the advanced-node maker gets the freed wafer starts, the old-fab operator gets long-term qualified volume.
why: Legacy grades still occupy a meaningful share of advanced wafers; freeing them for DDR5/HBM adds capacity with no new EUV tools, and depreciated fabs sell bits near cash cost; attacks capital intensity.

title: RAID-5 HBM stack: parity die survives a dead core die
idea: Worse: let one bad core die or TSV column kill an entire 12-high HBM stack. Flip: build stacks with N+1 core dies where the base die stripes each burst across dies with XOR parity, so any single failed die or bad TSV group is rebuilt on the fly and the stack still ships.
why: Fact 6: stack yield loss of 20-30% compounds with height; die-level erasure coding could recover most failed stacks for ~8% extra silicon, netting 10-20% more good HBM bits per wafer.
note: Related to Citadel-style 3D-stack RAS; needs HBM base-die redesign.

title: Closed-fab knowledge escrow licensed to new DRAM entrants
idea: Worse: when a DRAM maker dies (Qimonda, Elpida) let its recipes, defect libraries and engineers scatter. Flip: a national escrow buys recipes, tool settings and yield-learning logs from any exiting memory fab, retains key engineers on paid retainer, and licenses the bundle to qualified new entrants.
why: Cuts years off new U.S. lines' yield ramp; attacks the time chokepoint and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Base-camp pumps: HBM core dies take rails from base die
idea: Mountaineers leave heavy gear at base camp. Move VPP, VBB and VBLP charge pumps and regulators from every HBM core die into the logic base die, built as efficient switched-capacitor converters on better transistors, and deliver the rails up dedicated power TSVs.
why: Frees ~4-8% of each core die and roughly doubles pump efficiency (facts 6, 7, 10); the HBM PHY is untouched.

title: Mycologist's fungal network: package-level HBM pooling crossbar
idea: Mycelium lends nutrients between trees: route a switched crossbar through the interposer so that, in a multi-die package, any compute die can borrow idle capacity in a neighbour die's HBM stacks with a one-hop ~5 ns penalty.
why: Reduces stranded HBM (often 20-30% idle per device), so fewer stacks are bought per unit of useful capacity.

title: Split-fab DRAM with U.S. capacitor-and-BEOL completion of imported arrays
idea: Extreme user: defense 'trusted foundry' programs that already split fabrication. Import transistor-level array wafers from allied fabs, then complete the capacitor, metallization, test and packaging in a U.S. back-half fab costing ~1/4 of a full fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability: domestic value-add and trust for ~25% of the capital and about 2 years to build.
note: Trusted-foundry split exists; modest capital gain.

title: Climate-model halo links: memory stacks talk directly to neighbors
idea: Weather codes are dominated by halo exchange between neighboring domains. Add short serial side-links from each HBM base die to the nearest stack of the adjacent GPU, so halos, KV pages and pipeline activations migrate memory-to-memory without crossing either GPU's PHY and NoC.
why: Halves PHY crossings for inter-GPU transfers (each ~1-5 pJ/bit) and frees GPU I/O for compute traffic; lets neighboring GPUs pool capacity instead of duplicating it.

title: QLC-flash logic for DRAM: half-height capacitors plus LDPC
idea: QLC NAND ships cells with raw BER around 10^-2 because LDPC corrects them. Build DRAM with capacitors at half the height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) and a raw BER near 10^-5, and put a 10-15%-overhead quasi-cyclic LDPC decoder, with a fast hard-decision first pass, in the HBM or CXL logic die so the external error rate meets spec.
why: Halving capacitor aspect ratio cuts the hardest etch and deposition steps and allows a tighter pitch (fact 1). Expect ~15-25% lower cost per bit after paying for parity and the decoder.
note: Half-height caps plus base-die LDPC; ~20% cost gain.

title: Downhole-and-orbit beachhead funds a domestic DRAM learning curve
idea: Extreme users at 200 C downhole and in rad-hard space and defense pay 50-200x commodity $/bit, so a small U.S. 90-65 nm SOI trench-DRAM line can be profitable at a few thousand wafers a year. Margins fund a planned descent through nodes toward commercial sockets, the way GaN moved from radar to phone chargers.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share): premium niches pay for the learning curve instead of a $15B+ upfront bet.

title: Revive deep-trench eDRAM at a U.S. logic fab as merchant chiplets
idea: Mainframe CPUs, extreme users of on-die memory, used deep-trench eDRAM in 14 nm SOI made in New York. Restart that process module to sell merchant DRAM chiplets to AI accelerators, using an existing U.S. logic line and trench-capacitor know-how instead of a dedicated DRAM fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: reuses a paid-for logic fab; trench caps reach 20+ fF without 70:1 pillars (fact 1).

title: Ten-person 150 mm DRAM shuttle line for researchers
idea: University cleanrooms run on about 10 staff. Dedicate one to a multi-project DRAM shuttle with a frozen 180 nm trench-cap baseline, where startups and labs drop in new capacitor dielectrics, selectors or cell layouts and get working arrays back in 8 weeks.
why: Shrinks the time and capital of DRAM innovation cycles so more cell ideas reach pilot; a long-run supply lever.

title: Fleet-wide weak-cell atlas predicts new dies' failures from lot genealogy
idea: Scale jump (one cell -> global fleet): aggregate ECC-corrected-error addresses from millions of deployed DIMMs, keyed by fab lot, wafer XY and die coordinate, into a Bayesian prior; a new die's likely weak rows are predicted from its genealogy and pre-mapped before boot. In-field profiling drops from hours to seconds and the prior catches rare tails that factory tests miss.
why: Retention/VRT tail coverage without long factory bakes; targets a ~5-10x reduction in uncorrected-error escapes and in test time per die.
note: Needs fleet-scale data from hyperscalers; genealogy prior is plausible but access-limited.

title: ECC compresses the yield-learning curve from years to months
idea: No EUV: a new DUV DRAM line normally needs 18-24 months of yield learning before it can ship. Time shift: ship from month 3 with heavy on-die ECC plus OS row retirement covering immature defect density, then relax ECC by firmware as the line matures.
why: Brings new fab revenue and supply forward by about a year, which matters more than density during a 4x price spike.

title: Counter-cyclical tool bank: buy lithography and etch tools in downturns
idea: Time shift of tool procurement: a cooperative buys DRAM process tools while vendors discount them in a downturn, keeps them crated in bonded climate-controlled warehouses, and leases them out when the upturn comes.
why: Tool lead times of 12-24 months are a hidden ramp bottleneck. A tool bank cuts ramp time by ~1 year and tool cost by 15-30%.

title: Campus-scale HBM stack-and-test micro-lines inside datacenter parks
idea: Scale jump from the global back-end supply chain to the campus: put small TSV-stacking, hybrid-bonding and test lines inside datacenter campuses, so known-good DRAM wafers arrive and finished HBM goes straight to accelerator boards on site.
why: HBM back-end capacity and a 20-30% yield loss are bottlenecks. Local lines add capacity, cut weeks of logistics, and let failed stacks be reworked instead of scrapped.

title: DRAM bit futures exchange to end memory-cycle bankruptcies
idea: Qimonda (2009) and Elpida (2012) were killed by price troughs, not technology. Create exchange-cleared monthly futures per Gb of DDR5-equivalent bits so fabs hedge 2-3 years of output and banks lend against hedged revenue as with oil producers, while buyers hedge shortages.
why: Capital: removes the boom-bust risk premium that inflates financing and causes over/under-build; a few points lower cost of capital and steadier utilization worth ~10-15% of wafer cost.

title: Lehi fab lesson: swing fab toggling new memory and DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's dedicated Lehi fab ran far below capacity, and its fixed cost helped kill Optane. Fix: launch any new memory in a swing fab whose toolset is ~80% shared with a DRAM flow, with a dual-qualified recipe library, so wafer starts move between DRAM and the new memory each quarter as demand changes.
why: Capital intensity: a new memory rides DRAM's utilization (keeping the fab ~85%+ loaded) instead of carrying an empty fab, and in shortages the same tools make DRAM.

title: Nantero's contamination wall: bolt-on BEOL annex for exotic memory
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM spent more than a decade on adoption because fabs would not let CNTs (or other exotic materials) into their lines. Fix: a small back-end annex beside a logic or DRAM fab receives finished CMOS wafers in sealed pods, deposits and patterns the new memory layers in its own cleanroom, and returns sealed wafers, so the host line never touches the material.
why: Removes the main adoption barrier for new memory materials; an annex costs ~$0.3-1B versus $15B for a fab and lets new memories use existing CMOS capacity.
note: Post-CMOS annex model; sealed-pod logistics plausible, capital still large.

title: Per-mat segmented back-bias wells tuned to measured leakage tail
idea: Effect: MOSFET body effect. The array p-well is split into per-mat wells isolated by deep n-well rings, each fed by a tiny local charge pump; mats with leakage tails get an extra -0.3 to -0.8 V reverse body bias (+60-100 mV Vt), while healthy mats stay at nominal bias and avoid the extra junction-field GIDL penalty.
why: Retention tail: ~5-10x leakage reduction on the worst mats without penalizing the whole die, so the refresh interval is set per mat, not by the die's worst cell.
note: Reverse body bias worsens junction/GIDL tail cells.

title: Argon cluster-ion beam trims access-gate CD map die by die
idea: Ar: measure wordline-recess and fin CDs across each DUV-patterned wafer by scatterometry, then scan an argon gas-cluster ion beam whose local dwell time removes exactly the excess material, flattening the CD map before gate formation (location-specific processing).
why: Across-wafer CD variation widens Vt and the leakage tail (fact 3); flattening it lets DUV arrays approach EUV-grade uniformity, extending refresh ~1.5-2x.

title: Al: Shuttered aluminum smelters become fast-track memory fab sites
idea: Acquire idled aluminum smelter sites whose 300-700 MW firm grid interconnects, industrial water permits, rail spurs and heavy-industry zoning already exist, and drop in modular back-end first, then front-end shells.
why: Grid queues and permitting are 2-4 years of fab lead time; reuse cuts time-to-bits by ~1-2 years and avoids grid capex.
note: Reuse of firm-power interconnects and permits; saves time, not cost per bit.

title: Na/Cl: Salt-cavern strategic helium reserve for semiconductor fabs
idea: Store purified helium in leached Gulf Coast salt caverns, as done for oil and hydrogen, funded by a per-wafer industry levy, with automatic release triggers on supply shocks like the 2026 Qatar outage.
why: Replaces the privatized Federal Helium Reserve; buffers 1-2 years of U.S. semiconductor helium demand.
note: Salt-cavern helium storage feasible; buffers supply, no cost change.

title: Ge: Shared silicon-germanium superlattice epi foundry for 3D DRAM
idea: A U.S. epi-as-a-service foundry grows 30-100-tier Si/SiGe superlattices, the starting stack for lateral 3D DRAM, on customer wafers using SiGe BiCMOS epi know-how, so new entrants need no epi capex.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers and epi uniformity is a bottleneck; pooled tools cut entry capital and accelerate many 3D DRAM teams.

title: Hot-isostatic-press deuterium loads buried channels of deep 3D stacks
idea: Borrow HIP, which closes casting voids: 20-100 atm D2 at ~350 C forces deuterium through 26+ tiers to passivate dangling bonds in buried lateral channels that ordinary forming gas never reaches. Deuterium's mass also resists hot-carrier depassivation.
why: Fact 2/3: equalizes the leakage tail between top and bottom tiers of 3D DRAM, plausibly 2-5x in deep tiers.

title: Steel-minimill DRAM: small DUV-only fabs on a frozen node
idea: Copy Nucor's electric-arc minimills, which beat integrated mills by being small, flexible and fed on cheap inputs. Build 5k-wafer/month DRAM fabs frozen on a 1y-class (~17 nm) 6F2 process that uses only ArF-immersion SAQP, with no EUV. Depreciate them over 10+ years and sell into the commodity DDR4/LPDDR4 tiers the leaders abandon.
why: Capital intensity and the EUV chokepoint: ~$2-3B vs $15B+, and the depreciation share collapses on a long-frozen node. This frees leading-edge wafers for HBM.

title: Trim storage on the cell die makes periphery dies generic
idea: Ideal result: the periphery die carries no identity. Store all array-specific trims (redundancy map, reference offsets) in a small ferroelectric block on the cell die instead of periphery e-fuses, so periphery dies are tested generically and can be re-bonded to any array.
why: Enables periphery rebonding and recycling and removes fuse banks from the periphery die (fact 7).

title: Backside bitlines free the front side for capacitors alone
idea: IFR: 'bitlines occupy no space between capacitors.' Backward: build vertical-channel transistors and front-side capacitors, bond to a carrier, thin to the transistor bottoms and form bitlines on the wafer backside (borrowing backside-power-delivery flows), so no bitline contact threads between capacitor pillars.
why: Density and litho (facts 1, 4): 4F2 with relaxed capacitor spacing, ~30-40% lower bitline coupling, and one fewer EUV contact layer.

title: Shield-tier interleave makes row hammer geometrically impossible
idea: IFR: 'no wordline has a neighbor to disturb.' Backward: in a 3D horizontal-cell stack, insert a grounded metal shield tier between active tiers and stagger in-plane adjacent rows into alternating tiers, so every row's nearest neighbors are shields or idle tiers; spend cheap extra tiers to buy isolation.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): >10x lower aggressor coupling removes TRR/RFM refresh overhead (~5-10% bandwidth); the price is tiers, the cheap axis in 3D.
note: Spending tiers on grounded shields is sound but costs density; hammer mechanisms in 3D differ.

title: Substrate-agnostic memory credit to convert existing non-silicon fabs
idea: IFR: 'new memory capacity appears in months, not 3-5 years.' Backward: extend the 48D advanced-manufacturing credit plus DoD/DOE guaranteed-offtake contracts to memory made on glass, foil or SiC substrates, and fund conversion kits (oxide ALD, panel steppers) for existing U.S. display, thin-film-PV and power-semiconductor lines.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): uses already-built non-silicon fabs; conversion at ~5-10% of a DRAM fab's cost per unit of capacity.

title: N-plus-one HBM: a spare die rewired in after stacking
idea: Ideal: stacking never wastes a good die. Closest achievable: build 13-high stacks sold as 12-high, with a crossbar of redundant TSV lanes in the base die so any one failing core die or TSV column is mapped out at final test.
why: Fact 6: converts 20-30% stack yield loss into a fixed ~8% capacity overhead; stack yield rises toward 90%+, cutting HBM cost per good bit ~15-20%.

title: Universal die: one DRAM die, fuse-selectable DDR5, LPDDR5 or GDDR
idea: Ideal: any wafer becomes whatever bit type is short. Closest achievable on existing lines: a die with a multi-protocol PHY and fuse/firmware-selectable bank organization is configured at packaging, so fabs stop guessing product mix 6 months ahead.
why: Mix-mismatch shortages: ~5-10% more effective supply through fungibility for ~3-5% die-area cost.

title: Leakage must be a product, not a sum: stacked double-gate pillar
idea: Limit: no single gate may hold off the full voltage. In a vertical-channel 4F2 pillar, split the gate into two stacked electrodes that are driven together to turn on. When off, the mid-channel node floats to an intermediate potential, so each segment sees about half the Vds, and DIBL and GIDL drop superlinearly (the stack effect) at zero added footprint.
why: Fact 3: the stack effect cuts off-current ~10x in logic. In a vertical cell the second gate costs height, not area, so the refresh interval could rise ~5-10x.

title: Backside bitlines buried under a 4F2 vertical-channel array
idea: Limit: the front side may carry only capacitors and wordlines. After the 4F2 pillars are formed, flip-bond the wafer, thin it, and pattern bitlines on the exposed pillar bottoms from the backside. This removes bitline contacts and buried-bitline doping steps from the front.
why: Fact 4: true 4F2 (vs 6F2, about 1.5x density) with fewer front-side critical layers and lower bitline resistance.

title: Buyer carries the inventory: DRAM wafer tolling contracts
idea: Self-imposed limit: the fab owns no product risk. A hyperscaler buys raw wafers, chemicals and masks, owns the work-in-process, and pays the fab a fixed conversion fee per wafer, the way oil refineries are paid under tolling contracts.
why: Capital intensity: moves price risk and working capital off the maker, making new lines financeable at lower cost of capital.
note: Close to existing foundry/consignment models.

title: Weight-streaming DRAM die: few banks, wide rows, no refresh
idea: HBM4 dies carry 256 banks and wide internal datapaths to serve random access from many pseudo-channels. A weight stream instead reads the same addresses in the same order every decode step. A streaming die uses ~16 large banks whose full rows are latched into a row-wide output FIFO and shifted onto TSVs, and a programmable sequencer replaces command decoding and per-bank state machines. It has no REF logic or refresh timers, because use refreshes every row (B4-03), with only a minimal self-refresh for idle. Mats and bitlines can be longer wherever the stream hides latency. It keeps the HBM base-die and TSV interface, so it stacks or sits beside HBM4 and HBF.
why: ~1.3-1.5x less silicon per bit than HBM for the weight-holding share of accelerator memory (array efficiency ~0.36 -> 0.45-0.55), plus zero refresh. It lands between HBM (3x DDR5 wafer/bit) and HBF.

title: Substitute oxygen-precipitate gettering with implanted nanocavity gettering layer
idea: Substitute intrinsic oxygen-precipitate gettering with a buried band of nanocavities 1-2 um under the cell array, made by light-ion implant and anneal. Cavity walls bind Fe, Cu and Ni far more strongly than precipitates do, pulling the deep-level metal centers that create tail cells away from the storage junctions.
why: A few defect-bearing junctions dominate the retention tail; cleaning them pulls it toward the main distribution (2-4x tREF) and relaxes wafer-quality needs, so less depends on Cz quartz crucibles.
note: Implanted-cavity proximity gettering is 1990s art.

title: Substitute helium backside cooling with hydrogen for cryogenic implants
idea: Substitute the helium backside gas in the implanter chuck with low-pressure H2, which conducts heat even better than helium, to hold wafers at -100 C during storage-node junction implants. The cold implant fully amorphizes the region, which then regrows by solid-phase epitaxy without end-of-range dislocation loops.
why: End-of-range defects sit inside the storage-junction depletion region and drive SRH junction leakage; removing them cuts tail leakage ~3-10x.

title: Substitute plasma channel thinning with thermal atomic-layer etching
idea: Substitute argon-ion or plasma recess of ultrathin channels with thermal atomic-layer etching (oxidation/fluorination plus ligand-exchange cycles, N2 purged). It removes ~0.1 nm per cycle with no ion damage and sets channel body thickness to within one monolayer.
why: Body-thickness variation is a leading source of Vt scatter in thin channels; monolayer control halves sigma-Vt and shrinks the leakage tail ~10x.

title: Dopant-free undoped nanowire channels shrink sense-amp mismatch
idea: Substitute doped-channel sense transistors with undoped SOI nanowire gate-all-around devices whose Vt is set by gate work function (TiN/TaN), removing random dopant fluctuation. Oxidation thinning and e-beam patterning are university-standard.
why: Periphery area: sigma-Vt drops ~3x, so pitch-matched SA area shrinks up to ~5-9x (area scales with 1/sigma^2).

title: Sawtooth multilayer mold replaces smooth capacitor cylinder walls
idea: Substitute the uniform oxide capacitor mold with a 10 nm-period SiO2/SiN nanolaminate; after the hole etch, recess SiN laterally ~5 nm in hot phosphoric acid so the ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN conforms to a sawtooth sidewall with ~1.7x surface area, a deterministic successor to 1990s hemispherical-grain poly.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs 5 -> 8 fF at today's 60:1 AR, equivalent to AR ~100 without the harder etch; corrugations stiffen pillars against leaning.

title: All-epitaxial Si/SiGe stack etched only with HBr/Cl2 chemistry
idea: Substitute the oxide/nitride stack of 3D DRAM (etched with C4F6/C4F8/CH2F2) with an all-semiconductor Si/SiGe epitaxial stack whose slits and holes are etched only with HBr/Cl2/O2 at cryogenic chuck temperature (SiOxBry sidewall passivation), deferring every dielectric to non-fluorinated fills (aminosilane ALD SiO2, TMA Al2O3) planarized by CMP instead of etch-back.
why: Builds the 26-100 tier stacks 3D DRAM needs (fact 2) without fluorocarbon gases (GWP up to ~9,000) or their abatement, keeping single-crystal channels for a tight leakage tail.

title: Argon fast-atom activated Si-Si bonding replaces HF-last tier bonding
idea: Substitute HF-dip hydrophobic bonding and oxide-interface bonding with room-temperature surface-activated bonding: an Ar fast-atom beam in UHV strips the native oxide and two single-crystal Si tiers are pressed into a conductive, oxide-free junction, so vertical bitline/channel pillars run continuously through layer-transferred tiers.
why: Monolithic-quality 3D tiers (fact 2) with dry, fluorine-free surface prep; conductive bonds remove one via per tier per pillar (~10-20% fewer steps per tier).
note: Ar-FAB surface-activated bonding is established (Suga).

title: One CZ donor wafer supplies twenty tiers via repeated layer splitting
idea: Substitute 'one CZ wafer per device layer' with 'one CZ donor per ~20 layers': H/He co-implant a donor, bond to the growing stack, split at ~400 C, restore the donor with touch CMP and H2 anneal (no HF), re-implant; each transferred 50-200 nm single-crystal Si layer becomes a partially pre-processed array tier.
why: Quartz-crucible chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): CZ wafers per bit fall 10-20x for stacked tiers; single-crystal tiers beat deposited channels on leakage tail.

title: Substitute US wellhead membrane helium for Qatari LNG helium
idea: Deploy skid-mounted multistage membrane plus PSA units at US gas wells holding only 0.3-1% helium (too lean for cryogenic plants) and ship 99.999% helium in tube trailers on long-term contracts to fabs.
why: Replaces the offline Qatar ~30% share with distributed domestic supply; semiconductor demand is small relative to the reachable lean-well volume.

title: Substitute laser cold-splitting for wire-saw wafering and lapping
idea: Focus a pulsed laser to write a subsurface damage plane inside the ingot, cleave a 300 mm wafer off with a polymer stressor or thermal shock, then use dry plasma stress relief instead of slurry lapping, wet etch and multi-step wet polish.
why: Wafer manufacturing spends hundreds of liters per wafer on saw coolant, lapping and cleaning; laser splitting cuts that >10x and saves ~40% kerf silicon, so each quartz crucible yields more wafers.

title: Substitute fab-heat membrane distillation for fresh-water intake
idea: Route RO reject and rinse effluent through membrane-distillation modules heated by 40-70 C process-cooling return water, polish the distillate back to UPW, and crystallize the brine for zero liquid discharge.
why: Raises site water recovery from ~60% to >95%, cutting fresh intake >10x using waste heat rather than extra electricity.

title: Substitute photoresist patterning with block-copolymer self-assembly for capacitor honeycomb
idea: Cylinder-forming PS-b-PMMA (or high-chi PS-b-PDMS) packs naturally into the same hexagonal lattice as DRAM storage nodes; a sparse ArF guide pattern (one post per 3-4 sites) registers the film and the polymer fills in the rest, then PMMA cores are removed and transferred into the hard mask. One DUV exposure plus spin-coat and 250 C bake replaces a double-EUV or SAQP hole sequence.
why: Fact 4: 3-4x density multiplication from one cheap exposure; removes 1-2 EUV layers and the hex-array LELE overlay budget.
note: DSA for DRAM holes widely pursued; defectivity limits.

title: Substitute sawn bulk wafers with reusable porous-silicon donor layer transfer
idea: Anodize a parent wafer to form a double porous-silicon release layer, grow 30-50 um of device-grade epitaxial silicon, bond it to a low-cost polysilicon carrier and split at the porous layer; the parent is re-polished and reused 20-50 times. DRAM front-end only needs the top few microns of single crystal.
why: Cuts ingot, polysilicon and quartz-crucible demand per DRAM wafer ~20x and lets U.S. epi reactors supply substrates.

title: Swap fixed DIMM ownership for optically re-patched memory blades
idea: Substitute static wiring with a reconfigurable optical patch panel. Memory blades connect to servers through optical circuit switches, which reassign blades to servers every few minutes or hours following scheduler forecasts, so capacity physically follows demand.
why: Clouds strand ~25-35% of DRAM because each server is sized for its own peak. Moving capacity between servers cuts installed DRAM ~20% at equal service.

title: Swap raw bf16 in HBM for ANS-coded tensors decoded at load
idea: Substitute raw storage with entropy-coded storage. An asymmetric-numeral-system decoder in the GPU's L2-to-SM path, driven by a per-tile offset table, lets weights and KV live entropy-coded in HBM and expand transparently on load. bf16 exponents carry only ~2.6 bits of entropy, and activation tiles are often sparse.
why: A lossless 1.3-1.6x capacity gain on weights, more on sparse tensors, plus fewer pJ per useful bit moved (fact 5).
note: Software analogs (DFloat11, ZipNN) exist; hardware decoder is the twist.

title: Swap uncompressed line storage for controller compression with ECC-hidden metadata
idea: Substitute raw line storage with compressed lines whose compression tag hides in unused ECC code-space encodings. The SoC controller compresses each 64 B line (zero, base-delta, frequent-pattern) and packs compressible pages 2:1, with no separate metadata lookups. Standard DDR5 RDIMMs, JEDEC commands and timings stay unchanged, and the OS sees elastic capacity with a balloon for overflow.
why: Server memory typically compresses 1.5-2x. Hiding metadata in ECC removes the metadata-cache penalty that held back earlier schemes, giving 30-60% more effective capacity on existing DIMMs.
note: Attache/CRAM hide compression metadata already.

title: Air-gap suspended interposer wires: vacuum dielectric instead of oxide
idea: Substitute the oxide/polyimide around long interposer lines with air: a sacrificial polynorbornene layer is thermally decomposed after RDL build, leaving copper lines suspended on periodic posts and cutting line capacitance ~3x.
why: Fact 5/10: wire CV^2 drops ~60%, taking the interconnect share of HBM energy from ~3-4 toward ~1.5-2 pJ/bit.

title: Sidewall-written stack wiring replaces TSVs in DRAM cubes
idea: Substitute TSVs with wiring on the stack's faces: dies route pads to their edges, the stacked cube's sides are planarized, then copper traces are laser-direct-written down each sidewall; four faces give ~4,000 lines per cube at 10 um pitch.
why: Fact 6: removes TSV area tax and the TSV process module (~30% of HBM packaging cost), allowing near-standard dies to be stacked.
note: Sidewall interconnect done by Irvine Sensors/Vertical Circuits.

title: Memory lives in the top-of-rack switch, not in servers
idea: Substitute per-server DIMMs with DRAM co-packaged inside the rack switch ASIC module and exposed over existing Ethernet/CXL ports as a shared pool with line-rate atomics; servers keep only small local DRAM.
why: Stranded memory (~20-30% idle in clouds): pooling at the switch cuts DRAM bits purchased by ~15-25%.

title: Substitute static twin-cell mode with on-the-fly pairing of weak rows
idea: Rows flagged weak by profiling switch into differential twin-cell mode (two adjacent cells per bit on complementary bitlines) under a mode bit, while healthy rows stay single-cell, so capacity loss is only local.
why: Retention tail: twin-cell mode gives ~4x retention margin to the worst ~1% of rows, letting the rest of the die run 4x slower refresh (fact 3).
note: Close to CLR-DRAM reconfigurable twin-cell.

title: Substitute verified strong MRAM writes with sloppy writes plus BCH
idea: Write STT-MRAM at ~0.6x critical current with no write-verify, accepting ~1e-4 write error rate, and correct with BCH-6 per 512 bits; the smaller write current allows a ~40% smaller access transistor.
why: Energy per bit and density: ~3x lower write energy and ~25-35% smaller cell while staying non-volatile.

title: Substitute single write strength with weak working writes and power-fail consolidation
idea: Write ReRAM/MRAM cells weakly (low compliance current or short pulse) during operation for speed, low energy and high endurance, tracking 'weakly written' lines in a table; at power-fail or idle, a consolidation pass rewrites only those lines with strong retention pulses.
why: Endurance and energy: weak writes give ~10x endurance and ~3x lower energy, while only a small dirty fraction needs strong writes.

title: Substitute vented helium with closed-loop recapture and hydrogen backside cooling
idea: Swap once-through helium in etch-chuck backside cooling and furnace purges for on-tool cryogenic recapture loops plus H2/Ar backside gas on chucks that tolerate it, so a fab's helium draw drops to make-up losses.
why: Attacks the Qatar helium chokepoint (offline since Mar-2026); targets >90% helium-use reduction per wafer and removes a supply-outage shutdown risk.
note: On-tool He recapture plus H2/Ar backside; recovery loops already common in labs/MRI, resilience gain not memory step change.

title: Substitute Spruce Pine quartz crucibles with synthetic sol-gel silica crucibles
idea: Swap natural high-purity quartz sand for crucibles cast from synthetic silica made by hydrolysing SiCl4 (a polysilicon by-product), with a Si3N4 inner coat to extend pulls per crucible.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine dependence for CZ wafer crucibles; uses an existing waste stream, and longer crucible life cuts consumable cost per ingot ~20-30%.
note: Synthetic inner-layer crucibles already exist.

title: Substitute single-use donor wafers with ion-cut layer reuse
idea: Swap consuming a full prime CZ wafer per device layer for Smart-Cut-style hydrogen-ion splitting that peels ~1 um single-crystal films onto handle wafers, re-polishing the donor 10+ times.
why: Cuts prime-wafer and quartz-crucible demand per device layer ~5-10x, attacking the Spruce Pine chokepoint and wafer cost in stacked/bonded DRAM.
note: Smart Cut donor reuse is standard SOI practice.

title: Substitute factory burn-in ovens with in-host self-burn-in
idea: Swap long ATE/oven burn-in for shipping modules after short screens and running a 72-hour on-board BIST burn-in inside the customer's server at first boot, reporting telemetry and remapping weak rows before production use.
why: Burn-in/test capacity bottlenecks output; shifting it to the host frees ~30-50% of test-floor capacity and shortens cycle time by days.

title: Substitute vacuum ALD clusters with atmospheric spatial ALD lines
idea: Swap vacuum ALD tools for atmospheric-pressure spatial ALD heads (oxide channels and dielectrics at 150-250 C) that move the wafer under gas curtains, built by U.S. tool makers.
why: Deposition tool cost ~3-5x lower with ~10x throughput, cutting BEOL memory-tier capex and the dependence on a few foreign tool vendors.

title: Substitute in-house HBM TSV lines with OSAT low-temperature Cu hybrid bonding
idea: Swap memory makers' captive TSV/micro-bump stacking for nanotwinned-Cu hybrid bonding at <=250 C licensed to U.S. OSATs, so packaging houses stack standard DRAM dies into HBM-class stacks.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax and 20-30% stack yield loss, and frees memory makers' wafers by moving the stacking step elsewhere.

title: Substitute CVD tungsten lines with electroplated copper in memory tiers
idea: Swap WF6-based tungsten wordlines and bitlines in BEOL memory tiers for electroplated copper with ALD barriers at <=400 C, using U.S.-sourced copper and the logic BEOL plating supply chain.
why: Removes China-dominated tungsten and WF6 from memory tiers and gives ~3x lower line resistance for longer, cheaper arrays.

title: Substitute furnace polysilicon with excimer-laser LTPS periphery tiers
idea: Swap furnace-crystallized silicon for display-industry excimer-laser annealing that melts a-Si into high-mobility polysilicon in nanoseconds while the substrate stays below 400 C, giving fast periphery transistors in upper tiers.
why: Reuses the display ELA supply chain, gives ~100 cm^2/Vs periphery transistors in BEOL and enables multi-tier memories with local decoders.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly patterning hexagonal capacitor arrays
idea: Combine directed self-assembly of PS-b-PMMA cylinders, which form hexagonal close-packed arrays at 20-28 nm pitch, with the DRAM capacitor array, which is already hexagonal: a coarse DUV prepattern guides the cylinders, which are transferred into a hard mask to define capacitor holes. Spin-on chemistry replaces one or two EUV or quad-patterning layers.
why: Fact 4: removes EUV from the capacitor level; ~5-8% wafer cost reduction and less dependence on the single EUV supplier.
note: DSA for DRAM holes widely pursued; defectivity is the barrier.

title: Thin-film flux-closure nanorings: magnetic core memory reborn
idea: Combine 1960s ferrite core memory with thin-film lithography: each bit is a 50-100 nm CoFeB ring whose vortex magnetization circulates clockwise or counterclockwise, switched by a current pulse through a central via and read by a TMR sensor at the ring edge. Closed flux means no stray field between neighbours and no refresh.
why: Zero refresh and unlimited endurance (no tunnel barrier in the write path), radiation hard, 6-10F2 cells.
note: Vortex MRAM rings proposed around 2000 (Zhu, Prinz).

title: Floating-gate shadow block behind each DRAM subarray
idea: A double-poly EEPROM block behind each subarray acts as a nonvolatile shadow (nvSRAM fused with DRAM). Before power-down, rows stream through the sense amps into the shadow and refresh stops; on wake the shadow restores them, and shadowing can be limited to an OS-state slice.
why: Standby refresh energy falls to zero for edge devices that sit idle for hours, and a 1990s EEPROM flow is enough.

title: Canary rows with undersized capacitors gate refresh timing
idea: A mask change gives a few rows per subarray ~70% of normal capacitance, and they are written with a known pattern. A background sampler issues refresh only when canaries start to flip, so the rate tracks real temperature, voltage and aging.
why: 64 ms is a worst-case guardband while typical retention is seconds, so 4-10x fewer refreshes are possible safely.
note: Canary cells track temperature but not the random VRT tail.

title: SIMOX buried oxide under the storage diffusion
idea: Build cells on 1990s SIMOX SOI so the storage n+ sits directly on buried oxide, shrinking its pn junction to a thin sidewall. A body tie suppresses floating-body bipolar leakage.
why: Junction leakage area falls ~90%, giving a 5-10x longer retention tail for the same cell.

title: Thin p-epi on p+ substrate with buried sink drains leakage
idea: Fuse the CCD vertical-overflow-drain design with DRAM. Storage nodes sit in thin, lightly doped epi over a heavily doped, short-lifetime substrate, plus an n-buried layer biased as a carrier sink that removes thermally generated charge before it reaches storage nodes.
why: The diffusion leakage component, which dominates at 85 C, falls ~10x, giving 3-5x hot retention.

title: Liquid-nitrogen racks with cryo-CMOS periphery and no refresh
idea: Combine datacenter immersion-cooling infrastructure with 77 K operation: access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude so retention reaches hours, and periphery gains ~2x mobility with lower wire resistance; redesign the periphery for 77 K with higher Vt and VDD near 0.6 V.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially eliminated and voltage floor (fact 10) relaxed; system energy per bit perhaps ~3x lower even after ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead.
note: Cryo DRAM studied; cooling overhead erodes energy gains.

title: Array cell capacitors as flying caps for on-die converters
idea: Wire blocks of spare and edge DRAM cell capacitors (very high density at ~5 fF each) into a multi-phase switched-capacitor converter that generates VPP, VBB and VARY at ~80-85% efficiency instead of ~30-40% for Dickson charge pumps.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): pumps take ~5% of die and waste power; doubling pump efficiency cuts wordline and refresh supply energy ~15-20%.
note: Cell-type reservoir caps already used in DRAM periphery; SC converter twist.

title: DIMM PMIC takes over VPP and VBB generation
idea: Extend the existing 180/130 nm BCD power-management chip on DDR5 modules with two more rails (VPP ~3 V and a negative VBB) delivered through dedicated balls, so DRAM dies delete their charge pumps and pump decap; inductor-based BCD converters run at ~90% versus ~30-40% for on-die pumps.
why: Periphery area (~5% of die) and energy (fact 10); trailing BCD capacity is plentiful.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs in trailing-node stacks
idea: Stack 8 trailing-node DRAM dies with no TSVs: data and commands move vertically through on-chip coils drawn in existing top-metal layers (ThruChip-style inductive coupling), while power arrives through staircase wire bonds at OSATs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): avoids TSV processing and its ~20-30% yield loss, giving ~1 Tb/s stacked bandwidth from legacy fabs plus wire-bond capacity.

title: Boot-calibrated dummy cells cancel each sense amp's offset
idea: At power-up, measure each SA's offset by sweeping a reference on a dummy bitline cell, then write a compensating charge into a per-bitline dummy cell that is charge-shared with the real cell on every read and refreshed with the row.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): 3-4x lower effective offset allows 2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes, ~8-10% die area) on existing processes.

title: Display-fab panel interposers for wide-IO memory modules
idea: Use idle Gen-6 LCD lines (1.5-2 um lithography on large glass panels) to pattern multilayer redistribution interposers for wide, slow DRAM-to-processor links, replacing scarce silicon interposers.
why: Data movement (fact 5): wide-IO links at ~1 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5, and relief for the advanced-packaging bottleneck, using existing display capacity.

title: Bit-significance placement with per-subarray voltage and refresh
idea: Give each subarray its own VARY tap and refresh rate set by mode register; the memory controller places AI tensors' sign and exponent bits in strong, often-refreshed subarrays and low-order mantissa bits in low-voltage, rarely refreshed ones.
why: Refresh and voltage (facts 3, 10): ~40% lower array energy for weights and KV caches with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Bootstrapped wordline drivers revive 1980s self-boost, shrinking pumps
idea: Use per-driver-group MOS bootstrap capacitors to self-boost the wordline above VDD at activation, as early NMOS DRAMs did, so only a tiny VPP pump remains to hold leakage.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): removes most charge-pump area and energy (~3-5% of die and a notable share of activation power).

title: Shingled die staircase with vertical bond-via wires replacing TSVs
idea: Fuse NAND-style offset die stacking with free-standing vertical copper wire arrays (US-developed bond-via-array): each DRAM die is shifted to expose an edge pad row and molded ~50 um-pitch vertical Cu wires rise from the substrate to every die, built on Arizona OSAT lines.
