idea: Like canaries in a mine combined with bacterial quorum sensing, each bank carries a few rows built with ~30% smaller capacitance; the controller lengthens the refresh interval until a quorum of canaries across the die begins to flip and then backs off, so the main array always runs at the largest safe interval for its real temperature and age.
why: Refresh is set by worst-case datasheet margin (64 ms at 85 C); live canary feedback could run typical parts at 4-8x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Hermit-crab reuse mandate: thymus-screened retired DIMMs into CXL pools
idea: Hermit crabs live in shells others discard; a federal right-to-reuse rule plus procurement credit routes hyperscalers' decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 into CXL memory pools instead of shredders, after an automated 'thymic' stage that stress-tests each DIMM and maps out weak rows before reissue.
why: U.S. supply and cost per GB: retired server DRAM is sunk-cost capacity; reuse costs test plus CXL controller (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~50-100x below new 2026 contract DRAM.

title: Loop-of-Henle countercurrent helium concentrator for fab exhaust
idea: The kidney's countercurrent multiplier concentrates solutes from dilute flows through cascaded exchange. Countercurrent cascades of helium-selective membranes pull dilute helium from wafer-cooling, leak-check and purge exhausts and re-concentrate it to 5N purity for reuse on site.
why: Cuts fab helium purchases 80-95%, neutralizing the Qatar helium chokepoint.
note: Membrane cascade helium recovery is established practice; countercurrent framing is a twist.

title: Aquaporin membranes turn brackish groundwater into fab ultrapure water
idea: Aquaporin channels pass water near the diffusion limit while rejecting ions. Membranes with embedded biomimetic aquaporins treat brackish aquifers in the U.S. Southwest into UPW feed at lower pressure, and close the loop on fab wastewater.
why: Opens water-scarce sites and cuts water-treatment energy ~20-30%, removing a siting barrier for new U.S. fabs.

title: V-formation consortium rotating the costly node-development lead
idea: Geese take turns flying at the front of the V, where drag is worst. In a U.S./allied DRAM consortium, members take turns funding and running pathfinding for each new node or cell concept, and every member licenses the result at cost.
why: Splits ~$2-4B per-node R&D across members so smaller players keep pace, raising the number of suppliers.

title: Endosymbiont memory-as-organelle: royalty IP inside every accelerator die
idea: Mitochondria live inside cells but keep their own genome. A memory company licenses a capacitorless on-die memory macro, with its own test and repair firmware, to AI accelerators and SoCs for per-bit royalties, so the bits are made on logic wafers instead of in memory fabs.
why: Memory supply grows with logic capacity, and data-movement energy falls.

title: Solar-wafer gettering sinks buried under arrays to vacuum up tail metals
idea: Multicrystalline solar silicon became usable through phosphorus-diffusion and cavity gettering that pull Fe, Cu and Ni out of the active volume. Build a sacrificial gettering band 2-3 um under each DRAM array (carbon co-implant plus a hydrogen-implanted cavity layer, no scarce helium) and add a late low-temperature 'gettering soak' so transition-metal deep-level traps migrate away from storage junctions.
why: Retention-tail and VRT cells cluster at metal/defect sites; shrinking the tail 3-10x moves the refresh-limiting cell population and raises yield of 32-64 Gb dies (fact 3).
note: Gettering already standard in DRAM wafers; incremental tail gain.

title: Regenerative braking for bitlines: recycle refresh charge into the next subarray
idea: Electric vehicles recover braking energy instead of burning it in friction brakes. After a subarray's refresh, before equalization, connect its high-side bitlines through a charge-sharing switch matrix to the next subarray's bitlines so the next refresh starts part-charged, recovering a further ~25-40% of bitline CV^2 beyond normal equalization.
why: Bitline swing dominates the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy (fact 3); recycling could cut refresh energy 25-40% with no cell change.

title: Pressure-cooker deuterium anneal replaces fluorine interface passivation of access gates
idea: Pressure cookers cook through at lower temperature by raising pressure. Instead of fluorine implants or F-containing gate stacks, run a 20-25 atm pure-D2 anneal at ~350 C after capacitor and BEOL so deuterium penetrates deep buried-wordline and vertical-channel interfaces that forming gas cannot reach; Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation better than Si-H.
why: Lower, more stable interface-trap density narrows the GIDL/trap-assisted tail (fact 3) by ~1.5-3x with zero fluorinated chemistry.

title: District-heating supply of wordline high voltage from base die
idea: Like a district heating plant replacing a boiler in every house, generate VPP (~3 V) and negative back-bias in one efficient inductive or switched-capacitor converter on the HBM base die or DIMM PMIC, and deliver them to every core die through dedicated TSVs/pads instead of many small on-die charge pumps.
why: Periphery area (~5-7% of die in pumps and pump caps) and energy: pump efficiency rises from ~30% to ~85%, halving wordline supply energy.

title: Grid capacitor banks: dummy cell capacitors become pumps and decap
idea: Like a utility's capacitor bank, gang the edge/dummy rows of the cell array, whose high-AR capacitors are already built (~50 fF/um2), in parallel as charge-pump flying capacitors and on-die decoupling, replacing large planar MOS capacitors in the periphery.
why: Periphery area: MOS pump and decap area (~3-5% of die) shrinks ~10x by borrowing the densest capacitor on the chip.

title: Insurance pool: hashed global spare columns replace per-mat redundancy
idea: Like insurers pooling risk instead of every household holding reserves, remove the redundant columns from each subarray and give each bank a shared pool of spare column segments addressed by a small CAM keyed on (subarray, column), mapped in at the column path.
why: Periphery overhead: redundancy and fuse area (~3-6% of die) roughly halves, because statistical multiplexing needs ~5x fewer spares for the same yield.

title: Radio aperture synthesis: twin mini-cells summed on one bitline
idea: Like an interferometer combining small dishes into one big aperture, store each bit in two half-size capacitors on different tiers/wordlines that fire together onto one bitline; their charges add, so each capacitor needs only ~2.5 fF.
why: 3D DRAM capacitor blocker: lateral capacitors need half the charge, at the cost of 2x cells, which are cheap in 3D; this may lower the 26-tier break-even.

title: Liquid-CO2 garment dry-cleaning for periphery post-etch residue
idea: Dry cleaners replaced perchloroethylene with liquid CO2. Clean every periphery post-etch and post-ash step with supercritical CO2 plus 1-3% alcohol/amine cosolvent in a pressure chamber that recaptures >95% of the CO2, keeping one short single-wafer UPW rinse only before the gate.
why: Water: ~30-40 periphery residue cleans each drop from ~10-20 L UPW per wafer to near zero, ~10x less for the module; relaxed periphery pitch makes scCO2 penetration easy.

title: Canal-lock water-saving basins for bitline precharge
idea: German canal locks store emptied water in side basins at intermediate heights and reuse it to refill; give each mat 8 on-pitch reservoir capacitors at VDD/8 steps so bitlines discharging after a row closes dump charge stepwise into the basins and the next subarray's bitlines refill from them, taking only the final step from the supply.
why: Bitline CV2 (facts 8, 10): stepwise charging with N basins cuts supply energy roughly N-fold; claims ~6-8x lower bitline energy per access.
note: Stepwise/adiabatic charge recycling is known; on-pitch reservoir area and timing eat most of the claimed 6-8x.

title: Lithium-from-brine playbook: membrane skids harvest helium from U.S. gas streams
idea: Like Salton Sea direct-lithium-extraction plants that pull a minor element out of brine already being pumped, DRAM makers fund containerized hollow-fiber membrane plus pressure-swing-adsorption skids at U.S. nitrogen-rejection units, CO2 wells and small gas fields carrying 0.3-1% He, under fab offtake contracts that pay per liter delivered.
why: Turns dozens of stranded, sub-economic U.S. helium sources into a distributed domestic supply sized for fabs, so U.S. DRAM capacity no longer depends on Qatar or one large plant.

title: Optical-fiber preform chemistry builds synthetic crucible inner walls
idea: Optical-fiber preforms are made by flame-hydrolyzing SiCl4 (VAD/OVD) into ultra-pure soot that is sintered into glass. Deposit a 3-5 mm VAD-soot synthetic-silica inner layer onto a crucible shell made of ordinary non-Spruce-Pine quartz sand, then vacuum-sinter it bubble-free so the melt only ever touches synthetic silica.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine dependence by needing ultra-high purity only in a thin liner; SiCl4 is a by-product of polysilicon production. HPQ demand per crucible falls ~80%.

title: MP3 bit reservoir: fixed compressed slots with borrowed bits
idea: MP3 frames borrow unused bits from a shared reservoir to hold a constant bitrate; likewise every compressed page gets a fixed 2 KB slot (address = index x 2 KB, no translation table) and pages that overflow borrow 256 B chunks from a per-region reservoir located via a tiny overflow bitmap.
why: Variable-size memory compression needs translation tables and fragmentation handling that add latency; fixed slots plus a reservoir keep O(1) addressing while capturing ~1.8-2x capacity.
note: Close to Linearly Compressed Pages with exception region.

title: Bullwhip damping: cache each block in exactly one stack layer
idea: Like supply chains where every tier hoards safety stock, the app cache, runtime, OS page cache, hypervisor and storage controller each cache the same block; a cross-layer exclusive-caching protocol passes block ownership tokens on eviction so each block lives in exactly one layer.
why: Duplicate caching wastes 20-40% of server DRAM in database and AI data-loading stacks.
note: Exclusive caching protocols (Wong-Wilkes) known.

title: Sushi conveyor: weights circulate a ring, each chip grabs its plate
idea: Model layers circulate continuously on an optical/SerDes ring of accelerators like plates on a kaiten-sushi belt; each chip computes on the layer passing it and holds only a 2-3 layer window locally instead of a full or gathered copy.
why: Per-chip weight memory drops by roughly the ring size while ring bandwidth, not HBM capacity, sets throughput; attacks the HBM capacity tax.
note: Weight streaming and FSDP-style rings are known; needs large batches.

title: Flight recorder: MRAM intent journal makes DRAM a crash-safe cache
idea: Like an aircraft black box logging only essential parameters, a small MRAM ring records memory-tier metadata (page-map updates, dirty-line intents, epoch markers) so a flash-backed memory can treat DRAM purely as a volatile cache and rebuild consistent state after power loss.
why: Lets cheap NAND carry capacity with DRAM shrunk to the working set and no NVDIMM batteries; MRAM needed is ~0.1% of capacity.
note: Small NV journal for tier metadata is known practice.

title: Tidal-flow reversible lanes matched to read/write mix
idea: Reversible highway lanes follow the commute. HBM data lanes are split into groups, and the controller sets each group's direction per epoch (for example 15 read : 1 write during decode). This replaces symmetric bidirectional bursts and the turnaround bubbles they cause.
why: LLM inference is about 90% reads. Asymmetric lanes remove turnaround penalties and idle write capacity, for ~10-20% more effective read bandwidth per pin and per TSV.

title: Vinyl-pressing nanoimprint stamped RDL trenches and vias
idea: Records are pressed from a master. Likewise, UV-nanoimprint a reusable master into polymer dielectric at room temperature to form 0.5-1 um RDL trenches and via cups in one stroke. Electroplate Cu, then CMP, with a final cure ≤250 C.
why: A stamp replaces several litho exposures per RDL layer. That cuts interposer patterning capex ~3-5x and gives sub-um lines for wider memory buses.

title: Post-tensioned-concrete stress films enabling 15 um dies
idea: Post-tensioned concrete is pre-loaded to resist sagging. Deposit tuned compressive and tensile PECVD SiN/SiO2 films at ≤350 C on die backsides to cancel warpage, so 15 um core dies bond flat.
why: Thinner dies fit 24+ tiers within the 720 um JEDEC height and shorten TSVs, lowering capacitance and pJ/bit. That is ~1.5-2x capacity per stack.
note: Backside stress-compensation films are standard practice.

title: OFDM pilot cells that calibrate each row's sense reference
idea: OFDM inserts known pilot tones to estimate the channel. Each row stores a few pilot cells holding known 1s and 0s, rewritten at every restore. At sense time the pilots' developed bitline voltages set a row-specific sense reference. The reference therefore tracks how far that row has decayed since its last restore, and its temperature.
why: This recovers ~30% of sense margin, so Cs can drop toward ~3.5 fF (fact 1) or refresh can run 2x longer (fact 3).

title: Apoptotic rows: autonomous self-test and soft repair during self-refresh
idea: Cells that detect their own damage trigger programmed death (apoptosis). During self-refresh, an on-die BIST samples rows at extended retention. Rows that fail retire themselves and swap in spare rows through soft-PPR registers, which persist in a small OTP block. The die reports the swaps to the host through mode registers.
why: The die heals VRT and aging failures in the field without host ECC escalation. Factory retention test time can shrink (test cost), and fewer DUEs reach the host.

title: Power-by-the-hour DRAM leasing with manufacturer take-back
idea: Like Rolls-Royce leasing jet-engine thrust-hours, memory makers keep ownership of modules, bill per GB-hour from on-module telemetry, and take modules back at end of term for retest and redeployment in lower tiers.
why: Aligns the maker with lifetime utilization, closes the reuse loop and smooths revenue; extends average module service life from ~4 to ~8 years.

title: Aircraft-MRO industry for used DRAM tools plus mothball fab reactivation
idea: Like airline MRO shops that keep 30-year-old jets flying and the Navy's mothball fleet, a U.S. remanufacturing industry overhauls used DUV scanners, etchers and furnaces to as-new spec, paired with a national registry of idle fab shells that can be reactivated for mature DRAM in 18 months.
why: Cuts tool capex 50-70% for mature-node DRAM and reuses existing shells, adding U.S. capacity fast.

title: Svalbard-style shared die vault replacing last-time-buy hoarding
idea: Like a seed vault, an industry cooperative stores Grade-1 qualified DRAM wafers sealed in dry nitrogen at low temperature, then packages and 125 C-screens die on demand for members, so OEMs stop each holding 5-10x over-buys for 10-year programs.
why: Pooling long-life inventory across OEMs cuts hoarded industrial/automotive DRAM 50-70%, releasing that supply to the market.

title: Shipping-container standard footprint for hot automotive memory
idea: Like the ISO container that made all ships and cranes interchangeable, automakers adopt one solder-down memory footprint, pinout and 125 C/10-year thermal profile for all ECUs, so any qualified supplier's parts drop in without board redesign.
why: Makes automotive memory fungible across vendors and programs, so shortages at one supplier no longer halt car lines (as in 2021).

title: RAID-style base die makes commodity DRAM 125 C-capable
idea: Like RAID making cheap disks reliable, stack ordinary commodity DRAM die on a logic base die with symbol-level ECC, a per-row refresh map measured at 125 C, and spare-row remapping, so ordinary die meet 10 years at 125 C.
why: Ends the split between commodity and automotive die, so any DRAM wafer can serve either market and supply becomes fungible.

title: Contiguous-disk bubble tracks driven by one global rotating field
idea: Late-1980s bubble chips used ion-implanted contiguous-disk tracks that moved sub-lithographic bubbles under a global rotating in-plane field. On existing 200-mm lines, deposit perpendicular CoTb films, define tracks by ion implantation through a 0.5-um mask (no magnetic etch), drive every track at once with a package-level rotating-field coil, and detect with same-fab magnetoresistive bridges.
why: Bit size set by material (~100 nm) not litho; per-track drivers vanish so periphery shrinks (Fact 7); non-volatile; ~us latency at 10 MHz field makes a capacity tier that offloads DRAM.
note: us latency; a capacity tier, not DRAM-class.

title: Bell Labs CCD memory revived: charge rings with one regenerator
idea: Revive the 1970s CCD serial memories (invented at Bell Labs in 1969, later sold as CCD RAMs): store bits as charge packets in gated MOS potential wells with no per-bit contact or junction, arranged in short rings that pass one regeneration amplifier. Build them at relaxed nodes on U.S. CCD and imager fab processes.
why: There is no per-bit access transistor or junction leakage path (fact 3), refresh happens naturally as charge circulates, and few contacts means lighter lithography (fact 4). Latency of ~100 ns to 1 us makes it a capacity tier.
note: Serial latency limits it to a capacity tier; dark current still forces regeneration.

title: Molybdenum-gate MOS revived: graded-work-function wordlines that cut GIDL
idea: Revive the refractory molybdenum-gate MOSFETs of the 1970s: replace tungsten buried wordlines with Colorado-mined molybdenum whose nitrogen content is graded with depth, so the gate work function is high over the channel (good Vt) and low where the gate overlaps the drain (less band bending), suppressing GIDL.
why: GIDL is a dominant tail mechanism (fact 3), targeted at ~10x lower; also removes dependence on China's ~80% share of tungsten.
note: Dual-work-function buried wordlines already ship; Mo replacing W widely pursued.

title: Stepwise wordline charging from cell-capacitor tank banks
idea: Revive 1990s adiabatic stepwise charging. Each wordline rises to 3 V in 6 steps through switches to tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages and falls back through them, recovering most of its CV² energy. The tanks are dummy DRAM cell-capacitor arrays reused in the periphery, so the only added mask is a block mask that opens the storage-node module there.
why: Wordline switching energy falls ~4-6x despite the 3 V floor (fact 10). Area cost is near zero because cell capacitors give ~100 fF/µm².

title: ThruChip inductive coupling revived to strip signal TSVs from HBM
idea: Revive Kuroda's abandoned ThruChip Interface: replace the thousands of signal TSVs in an HBM stack with on-die spiral coils that couple data inductively between thinned dies, keeping only a few coarse, wide-pitch power TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees TSV keep-out area and copper fill and removes a major yield detractor; claims 1.5-2x more HBM bits per wafer.

title: Wartime tungsten scrap reclamation feeds domestic fab tungsten chemistry
idea: Revive 1940s cemented-carbide scrap reclamation (the zinc process) and capture tungsten from WF6 exhaust and chamber cleans, converting both into fab-grade WF6 and W targets inside the US for DUV-only memory lines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): closes the loop on fab tungsten; claims 50%+ of fab W from recycled sources.

title: IBM-style memory leasing: makers own bits, reclaim and redeploy
idea: Revive IBM's 1950s practice of leasing core memory instead of selling it: DRAM makers lease modules by the GB-month, keep ownership, and are paid to reclaim, retest and redeploy them into second-life tiers.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: aligns incentives to stretch module life from ~5 to ~10 years, effectively raising supply; no EUV; claims 10-20% more bit-years per wafer.

title: Tape-automated-bonding revival: folded polyimide tapes stack DRAM without TSVs
idea: Revive 1970s reel-to-reel TAB: DRAM dies are inner-lead-bonded to non-fluorinated PMDA-ODA polyimide tape with 20 um-pitch copper leads, and the tape is accordion-folded so 8-16 dies stack with their leads converging on a base die.
why: Constraint: copper/polyimide/gold TAB uses no PTFE, fluorinated polyimide or fluorine etch and no TSVs; roll-to-roll throughput gives HBM-like stacks at near-LPDDR cost (~10x cheaper per stack, lower bandwidth).

title: IBM TCM revival: glass-ceramic cofired substrates replace silicon interposers
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s thermal conduction module substrate: 30-60-layer cofired glass-ceramic/copper panels, screen-printed with Cu paste and mechanically punched 50 um vias, carrying many HBM-class stacks plus logic over 100-150 mm.
why: Constraint: punching, screen printing and cofiring use no photoresist PAGs, HF or fluorinated plasma; breaks the CoWoS chokepoint on US-buildable 1980s-class tooling, with 15-20 um lines fine for wide, slower memory channels.
note: 15-20 um lines give low bandwidth density versus 2 um interposers.

title: IBM EL-1 revival: maskless e-beam RDL in non-fluorinated PMMA resist
idea: Revive IBM's 1970s EL-1 direct-write e-beam personalization: multi-beam writers pattern interposer RDL and base-die customization layers directly in PMMA or HSQ, with no PFAS photoacid generators, giving per-product memory interface variants without masks.
why: Constraint: removes chemically amplified resists with PFAS PAGs; capital: no $1-5M mask sets for low-volume custom HBM base dies and interposers, and throughput suffices for a few coarse layers.
note: Multi-beam maskless writing exists; value limited to low-volume custom base dies.

title: Air-bridge revival: suspended interposer wires via polynorbornene thermal burnout
idea: Revive 1970s GaAs MMIC air-bridges: pattern interposer signal lines over sacrificial polynorbornene that decomposes at ~400 C and diffuses out through a thin SiN cap, leaving lines suspended in air (k~1).
why: Constraint: replaces fluorinated low-k (FSG) and HF-vapor release; wire capacitance falls ~3-4x, cutting interposer link energy ~2-3x (fact 5) and extending HBM reach.

title: Chappe optical-telegraph revival: steerable free-space links to memory pools
idea: Revive Chappe's line-of-sight optical telegraph inside the data hall: MEMS-steered free-space optical transceivers on rack tops form a reconfigurable mesh to pooled memory racks and are re-aimed in milliseconds as jobs move.
why: Constraint: no fluoropolymer (FEP) plenum cable jackets or fluorine-doped fiber; direct reconfigurable circuits to memory pools with no packet switches, raising pooled DRAM utilization ~20-30%.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop: self-stored subarray defect map replaces fuse banks
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with up to ~10% dead minor loops, listed in an on-chip 'bootloop' read at power-up. Design DRAM dies with ~12% spare subarrays and store the bad-subarray map in a few DRAM rows spread over several banks with 15x repetition coding, loaded into the address translator at boot and appended in the field as new failures appear.
why: Yield, periphery and capital (facts 4, 7): removes laser-fuse banks and lets aggressive cells or 3D tiers ship with clustered defects; ~15-25% more sellable dies per wafer at risky nodes.

title: Drum clock-track revival: leaky canary columns time each subarray's refresh
idea: Magnetic drums carried a dedicated clock track that timed everything else on the drum. Each subarray gets one canary column of cells built deliberately at the leaky tail (shorter gate, extra junction implant) that is rewritten at every refresh; the subarray is refreshed only when canaries start failing sensing, so the interval tracks local temperature, voltage and aging instead of a fixed 64 ms.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): most subarrays most of the time could run 3-8x longer intervals; area ~0.2%.
note: Canaries track temperature/aging, not random VRT tail cells; largely overlaps temperature-compensated refresh.

title: Core-stack thermistor compensation revived: temperature-tracking negative wordline bias
idea: Core memories put thermistors in the stack to retune drive currents as ferrite properties drifted with temperature. Each subarray sets its negative wordline-low voltage and body bias from a local temperature sensor and replica leakage cells that find, in real time, the minimum of subthreshold leakage plus GIDL (which moves with temperature), instead of using one worst-case bias.
why: Water and leakage tail (fact 3): holding the hot leakage tail ~3x lower lets DRAM run 10-15 C hotter at the same refresh rate, removing the need for chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers).

title: Federal Helium Reserve Reborn, With Fab Priority and Recapture Mandates
idea: Re-create the Bush Dome Federal Helium Reserve sold off in 2024 as a strategic semiconductor helium bank: buy North American helium in normal years, re-inject it at Cliffside, release it to fabs under priority rules in shocks, and pair it with grants for closed-loop helium recapture on litho, wafer-cooling and leak-check tools.
why: Scarce resources: Qatar (~30% of supply) offline since March 2026; recapture cuts fab helium use 50-90% and the reserve buffers multi-year disruptions.

title: Dual-Port VRAM Revival: Serial Access Port Streams Entire DRAM Rows
idea: Revive the 1980s video RAM serial access memory (SAM) port: each bank gets a row-wide shift register that captures a full 8 KB row in one activation and streams it out through a narrow low-swing port, so weight and KV streams use 100% of each opened row instead of one 64 B burst.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): a random read costs ~5.9 pJ per useful bit because of 128x overfetch; consuming whole rows cuts activation energy per useful bit 50-100x and total access energy ~10x; buildable on existing DDR4/DDR5 lines with periphery changes only.
note: Open-page streaming already amortizes activations; gain mostly for random-ish access.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM pods with four-times-longer bitlines
idea: Inverting 'DRAM runs at room temperature': operate memory racks at 77 K, where sense-amp transistors gain ~2-3x drive with less mismatch and access-transistor leakage nearly vanishes, then redesign mats with 4x longer bitlines (fewer sense amps) and refresh effectively off.
why: Sense-amp count -50-75%, refresh energy ~0 and ~15-25% density gain from freed area; cooling overhead amortized in hyperscale pods.
note: Cooling overhead at 77 K erodes the energy gain; close to CLL-DRAM work.

title: Complementary MTJ voltage divider readable by an inverter
idea: Inverting 'MRAM needs a sensitive sense amp': each bit is two MTJs written to opposite states and stacked as a voltage divider, so the mid-node swings ~0.3 V between states and a plain skewed inverter at the column replaces the current-mode sense amp.
why: Removes reference cells and analog sense amps, cutting column periphery ~25% and read latency to a few ns; capacitor-free.

title: Three-terminal SOT cells give read-while-write banks
idea: Inverting 'reads and writes share one path': spin-orbit-torque cells have separate write (heavy-metal line) and read (MTJ) terminals, so each bank gets an independent read sense path and write driver and can serve a read and a write in the same cycle.
why: Removes write-to-read turnaround and bank conflicts, raising effective bandwidth ~20-40% without more banks; capacitor-free with unlimited endurance.

title: Capacitive tier vias: AC-coupled signaling with no metal plugs
idea: Inverts 'tier-to-tier connections need metal vias (W plugs).' Separate tiers by thin SiN and pass signals through overlapping Al pads acting as ~1-5 fF coupling capacitors driven by pulse-mode transceivers, with power on a few large Al vias.
why: Fact 6 and W chokepoint: no TSVs or W plugs, and tiers bond without fine metal-to-metal alignment.

title: Plate-pulsed sensing doubles signal so low-k capacitors suffice
idea: Inverts 'the capacitor plate is a static common electrode.' Segment the plate per sub-array row and pulse it during sensing so stored charge is pumped onto the bitline with ~2x signal, letting abundant-element dielectrics (Al2O3/TiO2 laminates, k~30-40) meet sense margin with ~half the Cs.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: compensates by architecture for losing Hf/Zr/Ru high-k; Cs requirement drops ~2x.
note: Driven-plate sensing is known (FeRAM, boosted DRAM schemes); segmenting the plate costs area.

title: One Czochralski boule, fifty tiers: repeated hydrogen-cut exfoliation
idea: Inverts 'each stacked tier consumes a wafer.' Split ~100 nm single-crystal Si films from one donor wafer again and again by hydrogen implant and cleave, re-polishing between cuts, so a single crucible-grown wafer supplies ~50 tiers.
why: Quartz-crucible chokepoint: ~50x less CZ silicon (and Spruce Pine quartz) per tier, using only Si and H.
note: Smart Cut donor reclaim is already standard; quartz share of wafer cost is small.

title: Waterless cleans: supercritical CO2 replaces ultrapure-water rinses
idea: Inverts 'cleaning means water': run post-etch residue removal, particle cleans and resist strip in supercritical CO2 with small co-solvent doses (alcohols, amine chelators), recompressing and recycling the CO2; near-zero surface tension also stops 70:1 capacitor pillars from collapsing during drying.
why: Cuts ultrapure-water use across DRAM's 100+ wet steps by an estimated 40-60% and removes pillar-collapse yield loss; feedstock can be captured industrial CO2.

title: Urban-mined tungsten: carbide scrap to domestic WF6 loop
idea: Inverts 'tungsten comes from mines (China ~80%)': dedicate US cemented-carbide scrap recycling (zinc-process and oxidation routes) to APT and then WF6 for fabs, and feed fab chamber scrapings and spent targets back into the same loop under long-term offtake contracts.
why: A few hundred tonnes per year of domestic scrap can cover US fab WF6 demand, insulating DRAM from tungsten export controls and price shocks.

title: No-refresh DDR standard lets non-DRAM fabs supply main memory
idea: Inverts 'main memory is defined by the DRAM cell': publish a JEDEC-style NR-DDR/CXL interface with no refresh commands, fixed read/write windows and a nonvolatile-capable flag, so SiC, oxide, ferroelectric or magnetic dies from power, display and 200 mm fabs drop into existing sockets.
why: Zero refresh power by specification and new supply from underused US fabs without DRAM-specific capacitor tools; widens the supplier base beyond three companies.

title: Reuse each Czochralski wafer ten times via porous-silicon lift-off
idea: Inverts 'the silicon substrate is consumed'. Anodize a double-layer porous Si film on a prime wafer, grow 2-5 um device-quality epi on it, build the DRAM array, bond to a cheap carrier and split at the porous layer; the prime wafer is repolished and reused ~10x (ELTRAN-style).
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand 5-10x and with it the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint; also hands bonding flows a ready backside.
note: ELTRAN-style reuse is known art.

title: Rack-wide content-hash page fabric: one physical copy per rack
idea: Inverts 'memory is private to each host': a CXL 3.x switch keeps a hash-indexed page directory so identical 4 KB pages (OS images, shared libraries, model weights, zero pages) across every server in a rack map to one physical copy in a pooled tier, with copy-on-write on store. Hashing runs in the switch ASIC at line rate, so no host CPU scans pages as per-host KSM does.
why: Capacity: cloud VM fleets show 20-40% cross-VM duplicate pages, and inference fleets holding identical weights collapse N replicas to ~1 per rack, so DRAM per rack drops 1.3-3x.

title: Wire-bonded 16-high stacks of trailing-node DRAM, no TSVs
idea: Inverts 'dense memory needs TSV stacking': staircase wire-bonded stacks of 16 thinned dies from mature DRAM nodes, built on existing OSAT lines, form capacity-only packages for CXL modules, where GB per slot matters more than bandwidth per package.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV area and yield tax and delivers high GB per module from existing fabs and packaging lines.
note: Wire-bonded stacks routine for NAND and DRAM QDP.

title: SiGe bipolar PHY chiplets deliver fast I/O from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Invert 'fast memory I/O needs leading-edge CMOS': build the memory SerDes/PHY as a separate chiplet in U.S. SiGe BiCMOS (GlobalFoundries Vermont/New York) whose HBTs exceed 300 GHz fT, while DRAM base logic stays on a mature node.
why: 64-112 Gb/s lanes without foreign leading-edge nodes; cheaper base dies and domestic I/O supply.

title: MEMS-mirror optical switches rewire memory pools per job
idea: Invert 'memory-to-compute wiring is fixed at build time': use U.S. micromirror fabs (Dallas DLP heritage) to build optical circuit switches that reassign fiber links from memory sleds to accelerators per job within milliseconds.
why: Fixed configurations strand 20-40% of fleet DRAM; reconfigurable pooling raises utilization so fewer bits must be bought.

title: Royalty-free wide-slow memory interface for mature U.S. nodes
idea: Invert 'memory interfaces are written by incumbents for leading-edge PHYs': publish a federally sponsored open spec for a 2048-bit, ~2 Gb/s-per-pin unterminated memory interface that any U.S. 28-90 nm fab and glass/organic packager can build.
why: Lowers entry barriers for new U.S. memory makers and packagers; wide-slow short-reach links are cheaper and ~0.5 pJ/bit.
note: Overlaps BoW, OpenHBI and UCIe efforts.

title: Open-bitline twin-cell mode for hot and weak rows
idea: Inverts 'one bit, one cell, single-ended read': in open-bitline arrays the controller switches a row pair (row i in mat A and the mirror row in mat B, which share sense amps) into differential mode, writing true and complement and activating both, so the sense amp sees ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance (hammer, coupling, VARY noise) cancels.
why: Hammered or weak rows survive ~10x more activations and ~4x longer retention, costing half capacity only in those rows (<2% of the die).

title: Maskless per-die repair layer written after test
idea: Inverts 'every die gets identical masks': the one added litho step is maskless direct-write (e-beam or laser), personalized per die from its wafer-test map, writing a few hundred repair links that reroute weak rows and columns to spares far beyond fuse-bank capacity.
why: Repair is no longer capped by fuse area in the periphery (fact 7); a few % yield and much heavier weak-tail tolerance, with no physical mask to buy.
note: Laser-fuse repair is already per-die personalization.

title: Low-leak isolation switch halves bitlines for weak rows
idea: Inverts 'every row sees the full bitline capacitance': one Vt-adjust implant mask creates a low-leakage isolation transistor mid-bitline; near-half rows are read with the far half cut off, halving Cbl, and the controller maps weak or hot data to those rows.
why: ~2x sense signal and faster tRCD for mapped weak cells (facts 1, 3); extends tiered-latency DRAM into a reliability tier.

title: Colocation memory exchange auctions idle DRAM between neighboring tenants
idea: Inverts 'a server's memory belongs only to that server's owner': colocation operators lay CXL-over-optics links between tenant cages and run an exchange that auctions stranded DRAM (often 25-40% idle) in 15-minute leases with per-lease hardware encryption.
why: Usable supply from the installed base: recovering half of stranded DRAM gives ~10-20% more usable capacity with zero new wafers, at ~300-600 ns far-memory latency.

title: Mandatory RAM-footprint efficiency labels for operating systems and apps
idea: Inverts 'software memory demand is a given': an Energy-Star-style rating (resident memory per standardized task) required for government procurement and shown in app stores, plus OEM incentives to ship with less installed RAM.
why: Demand side: a 20% cut in DRAM per phone and PC across ~1.5B units/yr frees an estimated several percent of world bit supply for servers.

title: Socketed-memory mandate so laptop and server RAM can be harvested
idea: Inverts 'memory is soldered for life': require CAMM/DIMM-style sockets in laptops and servers above a size threshold, plus a standard test interface, so modules can be removed, retested and redeployed at end of device life.
why: Reuse/recycling: soldered LPDDR is shredded today; making it harvestable could feed a second-life stream of several percent of annual bits.

title: LC-resonant adiabatic refresh spends refresh's spare time, not energy
idea: A normal restore dissipates ~CV^2 because bitlines and wordlines are slammed in ~10 ns, yet refresh has a 64 ms window. Drive refresh-only activations with ~1 us ramps from an on-package LC tank or N-step tank capacitors. Dissipation then follows (RC/T)*CV^2, and most of the charge returns to the supply.
why: With T/RC ~50-100, the switching part of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy drops ~10x. That attacks refresh's 16-33% share of idle power (fact 3) without touching the cell.

title: Thin p-well with deep minority-carrier sink beneath the array
idea: Above ~70 C, diffusion current from carriers generated in the neutral p-well (Ea ~ Eg ~1.1 eV) overtakes depletion generation, and any electron generated within a diffusion length can wander into a storage node. Thin the array p-well to ~0.3 um and place a strongly biased buried n+ collector plane just below. Thermally generated electrons are swept away vertically before they reach storage nodes, the image-sensor vertical-overflow-drain trick.
why: The generation volume feeding storage nodes shrinks ~10-30x. This matters most in hot HBM stacks at 85-95 C, where refresh doubles. Expect a 2-5x retention gain at high temperature (facts 3, 6).
note: DRAM arrays already sit in triple wells with deep n-wells; incremental.

title: Carbon-cluster proximity gettering pulls metal traps from storage junctions
idea: Mid-gap metal impurities (Fe, Cu, Ni at ~1e10 cm^-3) are ideal SRH generation centers, and image sensors remove dark-current hot pixels with buried carbon-cluster gettering layers. Implant a C3H5 molecular cluster layer ~1 um under the array before the well anneals, so metals precipitate there, away from storage-node depletion regions.
why: SRH generation scales with trap density in the depletion region. Cutting metallic traps 10x compresses the leakage tail that sets the 64 ms interval (fact 3), for one implant step and no lithography.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging with on-die tank capacitors
idea: Charging C through a switch to V always dissipates CV^2/2; charging in N equal steps from N-1 tank capacitors dissipates ~CV^2/(2N). Drive the 3 V wordlines and bitline restore in 4 steps from tank capacitors built in the array's own capacitor process.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline/restore energy ~3-4x lower; charge-pump load and area drop too.

title: 77 K re-architected array: longer bitlines, halved wordline voltage
idea: Redesign the array for liquid-nitrogen operation: copper resistivity drops ~5x and subthreshold swing falls to ~15-20 mV/dec, so bitlines can be 2-4x longer with fewer sense amps, Vt can drop ~0.3 V and wordline boost shrinks from ~3 V to ~1.5 V.
why: kT physics: retention grows by many decades (refresh nearly vanishes, fact 3), CV^2 falls ~4x (fact 10) and sense-amp count halves (fact 7); honestly net-positive only after ~10x cryocooler overhead, so it targets large pooled-memory racks.
note: Cryo DRAM studied (CryoRAM, Rambus); cryocooler overhead eats most gains.

title: Logic-on-top stacking keeps DRAM tiers cool, with per-tier refresh
idea: Flip the HBM-style stack so the hot logic die sits against the heatsink and DRAM tiers hang below it, and embed a thermal diode in every tier that sets that tier's own refresh interval.
why: Leakage is Arrhenius (Ea ~0.6 eV), about 2x per 10 C, so running DRAM 15-20 C cooler cuts refresh rate 3-4x (fact 3), and per-tier refresh stops the whole stack refreshing at the hottest tier's rate.

title: Anhydrous HF vapor and atomic hydrogen replace ultrapure-water cleans
idea: Clean targets are ~1e9-1e10 contaminant atoms/cm2, nanograms per wafer, yet each wafer consumes thousands of litres of UPW. Convert pre-deposition cleans to anhydrous HF/NH3 vapor oxide removal, remote atomic hydrogen for carbon and UV/O3 for organics, keeping one megasonic water rinse per module for particles.
why: Cuts UPW per wafer ~40-60% plus the energy of making it, and shrinks HF-laden wastewater.
note: HF vapor and remote-H cleans exist; particle removal still needs water.

title: Mine the fab's own WF6 exhaust as tungsten ore
idea: Tungsten CVD deposits only ~20-40% of delivered WF6, so scrubber streams carry W far richer than ore (~0.5% WO3). Trap exhaust in alkaline scrubbers as sodium tungstate, ion-exchange to ammonium paratungstate, calcine to WO3 and re-fluorinate with on-site F2 back to WF6.
why: Cuts new tungsten demand per wafer ~50-60% and turns the remainder into a US-domestic loop against China's ~80% share.
note: Same fab WF6 exhaust recovery as I-09861.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in etch and deposition chucks
idea: First principle: helium is used under wafers only for heat transfer (0.15 W/m-K), and H2 conducts heat better (0.18 W/m-K) and can be made from water anywhere. Re-engineer electrostatic chucks to run 5-15 Torr pure-H2 backside gas with millimole-scale inventory, hydrogen sensors and catalytic recombiners on the chamber exhaust.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline since March 2026): removes one of the largest fab uses of helium and protects uptime from price spikes.

title: Fab-scale noble-gas fractionation recovers helium, neon and xenon
idea: First principle: helium, neon, krypton and xenon are chemically inert, so consuming them is a design choice. Route every tool exhaust to a fab-level cryogenic separation and membrane plant that recovers >90% of the noble gases and reinjects purified gas, with tools standardized to closed-loop gas ports.
why: Helium chokepoint and neon risk: 80-90% less purchased He; protects uptime and price.

title: Range-proven bit-precise fields with hardware bitfield load/store
idea: A field holding 0-100 needs 7 bits but is stored in 32 or 64. The compiler proves value ranges (abstract interpretation plus runtime guards) and packs struct fields at bit granularity; new bitfield load/store instructions with extract/insert at the memory side keep access single-cycle and trap on overflow so the layout can widen.
why: 20-40% smaller record-heavy data (in-memory databases, game state, ad features) with no change to algorithms.
note: Adds hardware bitfield load/store to struct narrowing.

title: MicroLED-on-sapphire parallel links make pooled memory nearly free
idea: Pooling saves DRAM only if remote access costs nearly as much as local. GaN microLED and photodiode arrays grown on sapphire, coupled into glass imaging-fiber bundles, carry CXL traffic across a rack over hundreds of slow parallel lanes (~2 Gb/s each, no SerDes) at ~1 pJ/bit and low latency.
why: Makes rack-scale pooling viable even for latency-sensitive tiers, so operators provision ~20-30% less DRAM per server by reclaiming stranded memory.
note: Wide-slow microLED links already pursued (Avicena, MOSAIC).

title: Piezo-steered fiber switches re-home memory blades by demand
idea: Static wiring between memory and servers forces each server to carry its own peak. Fiber cross-connects steered by piezoceramic actuators (no silicon MEMS) rewire whole memory blades between servers every few seconds to minutes, following the scheduler's demand forecast, with the optical path carrying CXL over fiber.
why: Capacity follows demand at rack-to-row scale, so provisioned DRAM per server drops 20-35%, and an attached blade still delivers local latency and full bandwidth.

title: Mandated e-waste DRAM harvest re-hosted behind CXL adapter chiplets
idea: Millions of working DDR4 DIMMs from retired servers are shredded yearly, and their manufacturing cost is already sunk. A procurement/ITAD rule requires federally funded and hyperscale decommissions to route DIMMs to re-hosting, where a CXL card with a protocol-translation chiplet, strong ECC and per-chip retirement masks pools 32-64 old DIMMs as a far-memory tier.
why: Bits cost only test plus adapter (~$0.05-0.2/GB), ~50-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades energy, density and bandwidth; supply bounded by decommission flow.
note: CXL reuse of DDR4 already done by hyperscalers.

title: Adaptive twin-cell pairing retires weak cells into differential bits
idea: When test or field ECC finds a weak cell, a fuse pairs it with its neighbor as a 2T2C differential bit sensed on complementary bitlines. Differential sensing doubles the signal and cancels common-mode leakage, so the tail cell stops limiting refresh. The cost is about 0.1% of capacity.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): refresh is set by the 0.1% tail rather than the 1e-9 tail, for ~2-4x longer intervals.
note: Twin-cell / CLR-DRAM style switchable 2T2C is known art.

title: High-field leakage fingerprint screens tail cells in seconds
idea: Tail cells are single traps with field-enhanced (Poole-Frenkel/trap-assisted tunneling) emission, so their leakage climbs steeply with junction field while normal cells barely change. At sort, write '1', raise the plate/substrate bias for 10 ms and read back. Failing cells are the would-be 64 ms tail and get mapped for repair or binning.
why: Test capital/time: replaces hours of retention bake with seconds per die and yields a per-row retention map for relaxed refresh.

title: Pilot cells in every row calibrate multilevel gain-cell reads
idea: This borrows pilot tones from wireless. Each 512-cell row carries 8 pilot gain cells written to known levels together with the data, and on read their currents reveal that row's decay, temperature and read-transistor drift. The ADC thresholds are interpolated from the pilots.
why: Density/reliability: 2 bits/cell in capacitorless gain cells despite drift, for 1.5% overhead.
note: Reference cells are standard in MLC flash.

title: Just-enough-barrier volatile MRAM scrubbed every second
idea: Retention is tau = tau0*e^Delta, and write current scales with Delta. Nonvolatile MRAM over-pays at Delta ~60 kT. Size pMTJs for Delta ~38-40 kT: the per-cell flip probability is ~1e-8 per second, a 1 s ECC scrub catches the rare flips, and the smaller free layer packs denser.
why: Capacitorless, refresh-like scrub at 1 s. Write current -35%, write energy ~-50%, and lower barrier stress gives near-unlimited endurance.
note: Known relaxed-nonvolatility STT-RAM (Smullen 2011).

title: Microsecond memory exchange auctions stranded DRAM across tenants
idea: Measured cloud DRAM utilization averages ~50% because memory is provisioned per server for peak. A rack-scale CXL switch runs a continuous double auction that leases 256 MB segments between hosts with microsecond reassignment and hardware isolation, so idle bits are sold rather than stranded.
why: Usable supply: raising effective utilization from ~50% to ~75% is equivalent to ~50% more usable DRAM with zero new wafers.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordline using all-TiN fill at sub-10 nm widths
idea: Below ~10 nm width, electron surface and grain-boundary scattering raise W's effective resistivity toward ~30-40 uOhm-cm while its barrier eats the cross-section; mean-free-path math shows a barrierless TiN or Ti-Al-N full fill lands within ~1.5x. Qualify a W-free buried wordline with all-TiN fill and a thin n+ poly-Si cap for work-function tuning.
why: Scarce resource: removes China-sourced tungsten (~80%) from DRAM's most W-intensive layer, at a small RC penalty offset by shorter wordline segments.
note: TiN-filled buried wordlines already common in DRAM; resource angle only.

title: Chokepoint index printed per gigabit steers procurement off banned elements
idea: Compute each die's mass of every element per Gb, weight it by supply concentration (HHI) and geopolitical risk, and print an elemental chokepoint index on the datasheet. Federal and hyperscaler procurement scores bids on cost x (1 + index), so designs built only from Si, Al, Ti, Zr, Cu, O, N and C win.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: converts invisible supply risk into a price signal, pushing W, Co, Ru, Hf, Ta, In and Ga out within one product cycle.

title: Synthetic crucible silica from any beach sand via chloride distillation
idea: Purity is a chemistry problem, not geology: carbochlorinate ordinary sand to SiCl4, fractionally distill to 9N, flame-hydrolyze to fused silica soot, and form crucibles by slip casting plus arc fusion. Inputs are only Si, O, C, Cl and H.
why: Scarce resource: breaks Spruce Pine's >80% hold on HPQ crucibles, and fully synthetic walls lower metal contamination in ingots.

title: Supercritical CO2 cleaning slashes fab ultra-pure water demand
idea: Wet cleaning uses water only as solvent and particle carrier; supercritical CO2 (31 C, 74 bar) with alcohol cosolvent has near-zero surface tension, so it rinses high-aspect-ratio capacitor holes without pattern collapse. Replace most post-etch and pre-deposition wet rinses with closed-loop scCO2 recycled at >95%, using only C, O and H.
why: Water/energy and yield: cuts UPW use by >50% at fabs drawing ~10 ML/day and removes stiction-driven collapse of 60-75:1 pillars.

title: Sourdough-starter replica cells clock each mat's refresh
idea: Random stimulus 'sourdough starter': you feed it when it looks hungry, not on a fixed clock. Each mat holds 64 deliberately weakened replica cells (shorter gate, thinner spacer) written high at every refresh; a comparator fires that mat's refresh only when the median replica sags past threshold, so the interval tracks real temperature, aging and process instead of a worst-case 64 ms at 85 C.
why: Most mats retain for seconds; replica-gated refresh cuts refresh operations and their 16-33% idle-power share by ~70-90% while the deliberately weaker replicas guarantee coverage (fact 3).

title: Cactus clean: anhydrous in-situ surface prep for access gates
idea: Random stimulus 'cactus': it thrives on almost no water. Replace the HF-last/SC1/SC2 wet sequences before the access-transistor gate oxide, buried-wordline liner and storage-contact epi with a cluster-tool chain of anhydrous HF/NH3 vapor etch, atomic-hydrogen radical clean and in-situ ALD, with no air break, so no native oxide ever needs a wet strip.
why: The access-device module carries ~20 pre-clean steps at ~20-50 L of UPW per wafer each; dry in-situ prep cuts that module's water >10x and lowers interface-trap density, which also trims the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Snowball CO2 aerosol and supercritical rinse for wordline trenches
idea: Random stimulus 'snowball': a frozen projectile cleans, then disappears. Post-etch particle removal in high-AR buried-wordline trenches and vertical-channel pillars uses cryogenic CO2 snow jets followed by a supercritical-CO2 rinse/dry with a little cosolvent, replacing DI megasonic rinses and IPA drying; the CO2 is recaptured and recycled.
why: Removes DI-rinse and IPA-dry water from the access module (>10x less on those steps) and eliminates capillary collapse of 60:1 structures, a yield loss that falls on leakage-critical pillars.

title: Lego bottom-up ruthenium wordlines with no CMP
idea: Random stimulus 'Lego': pieces snap on only where they belong. Grow the buried wordline by area-selective ALD/CVD of Ru (or Mo) from a seeded trench bottom, with the oxide top surface blocked by a vapor-dosed small-molecule inhibitor, so metal fills bottom-up to the exact recess height: no overburden, CMP, wet recess etch or post-CMP brush clean.
why: Deletes the slurry and post-CMP clean water of the wordline loop (>10x for that module) and removes tungsten (China ~80%); a lower-resistance wordline also allows a lower boosted voltage (fact 10).
note: Bottom-up Ru/Mo ASD fill is widely pursued; water and W savings real but module-local.

title: Tear-off notepad: reusable donor wafer for transferred access layers
idea: Random stimulus 'tear-off notepad': many sheets from one block. Form the single-crystal silicon access-transistor layer by repeated hydrogen-split layer transfer from one thick donor wafer (10-20 transfers per donor, plasma touch-up between splits) onto a capacitor-first array wafer, instead of consuming a fresh polished prime wafer as the access substrate.
why: Prime-wafer making (CZ growth in Spruce Pine quartz, slicing, lapping, polishing, cleaning) carries large embedded water; reusing the donor cuts substrate-attributable water per access layer >10x and enables capacitor-first stacking toward 3D (facts 2, 3).

title: Motion-sensor porch light: clockless periphery wakes only on command
idea: A porch light stays dark until someone walks up. Remove the always-on DLL and replace it with source-synchronous strobes, bias command receivers only when chip-select toggles, and replace idling charge pumps with reservoir capacitors recharged right after each burst, so the periphery draws near zero between accesses.
why: At 10-30% utilization, background power (DLL, receivers, pumps) is 40-60% of energy per access; making it event-driven cuts energy per access ~3-10x for lightly loaded memory tiers.

title: Sourdough starter: one reusable donor wafer seeds every single-crystal tier
idea: Keep one starter and bake many loaves: grow porous-Si plus epi-Si on a premium Czochralski donor, split off a 50 nm single-crystal layer for each 3D DRAM tier, then re-polish and regrow the donor 10-20 times. Each stacked tier uses only a fraction of a newly pulled wafer.
why: Scarce resources: Spruce Pine quartz crucibles (>80%) and CZ wafer supply; claim ~10x fewer pulled wafers per tier, plus thin, high-quality channels for 3D (fact 2).

title: Rubber stamp: nanoimprint replaces EUV on the periodic array layers
idea: A rubber stamp copies a pattern with no optics: because the cell array is perfectly periodic, pattern the capacitor-hole, bitline and active layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (one master, many replica templates), and keep EUV or DUV only for the irregular periphery. The die and its interface match standard DDR5.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): 3-5 of the 5-7 EUV layers move to imprint tools at ~1/5 the cost; claim wafer cost -10-15% and less dependence on the single EUV supplier.
note: NIL for periodic layers is under evaluation by memory makers; defectivity and overlay limit it.

title: Sourdough starter: reusable donor wafer feeds epitaxial DRAM layers
idea: Stimulus 'sourdough starter' (keep a mother culture, bake only a portion) -> keep a mother Cz wafer and 'bake' only a thin epitaxial slice from it. Grow a porous-Si release layer plus device-grade epi (or the Si/SiGe superlattice for 3D DRAM) on the donor, bond to a low-grade carrier, split at the porous layer, re-polish and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts Cz crystal pulls, high-purity quartz crucibles and polysilicon per wafer by up to ~10x; carriers can be recycled or low-purity silicon.
note: ELTRAN/Smart Cut reuse known; substrate is small share of DRAM cost.

title: Ice cube tray: freeze crystallization reclaims fab rinse water
idea: Stimulus 'ice cube tray' (ice freezes out pure and rejects solutes) -> run RO reject and spent rinse water through an indirect-contact freeze crystallizer; pure ice crystals are washed and melted back into the UPW feed while brine concentrates for zero liquid discharge. Latent heat is 334 J/g versus 2,260 J/g for evaporation.
why: Water intensity: lifts fab water recovery from ~60-80% to >95% at ~1/5 the energy of thermal evaporators, opening water-stressed U.S. sites.

title: Snowflake: 77 K DRAM shrinks capacitor and drops high-k
idea: Stimulus 'snowflake' (cold preserves delicate structure) -> run DRAM arrays in liquid-nitrogen-cooled racks where junction and subthreshold leakage fall by >10^4, so retention stays long with Cs ~1 fF; that permits a short, low-AR capacitor with plain Al2O3/SiO2 dielectric instead of ZrO2/HfO2.
why: Removes high-k (Hf/Zr) and the deepest fluorocarbon etch and nearly eliminates refresh energy; LN2 comes from air, with cooling energy as the trade-off.

title: Seltzer: supercritical CO2 drying saves tall pillars and rinse water
idea: Stimulus 'seltzer' (CO2 dissolved under pressure) -> after capacitor-mold removal, exchange the rinse liquid for supercritical CO2 with a co-solvent so no liquid-vapor meniscus can topple tall pillars, and use scCO2 plus chelator cleans for post-etch residue.
why: Pillar leaning caps aspect ratio; zero capillary force allows >100:1 pillars while cutting UPW and IPA per clean ~80%, with CO2 recycled.

title: Mail sorting: NV array stores its own repair map, fuse-free
idea: Random stimulus 'mail sorting room' (routing table kept on site) -> because the cells are non-volatile, redundancy maps, trim codes and sense-amp offsets are written into reserved rows of the array itself. This eliminates the laser-fuse repair step, the e-fuse banks and their test-floor tools, and allows in-field re-repair.
why: Periphery (fact 7) shrinks ~2-4% of die area, laser repair tools leave the back-end, and test cost falls. Field self-repair raises effective yield.

title: Railway switch: MEMS optical circuit switching pools rack memory
idea: Like railway points: memory sleds connect over fiber through a MEMS optical circuit switch that re-routes whole sleds to whichever accelerator needs capacity, reconfiguring on ms timescales.
why: Stranded memory (often 20-30% in clusters) becomes usable supply, raising effective DRAM per dollar with no new wafers.

title: Slinky: helical micro-spring bonds absorb CTE mismatch
idea: Forced 'slinky': electroplated helical micro-springs at 10 um pitch connect silicon DRAM dies to large glass or organic panels and flex to absorb CTE mismatch, so large panels do not crack or warp joints.
why: Panel-level packaging cost; lets cheap large substrates replace silicon interposers for memory-rich modules.
note: Close to Georgia Tech G-Helix compliant interconnects.

title: Canary cells: deliberately weakened sentinels set per-subarray refresh
idea: Forced connection to the coal-mine canary: each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with ~60% of normal Cs (truncated pillar or partial plate), written to '1' and sensed every window; their first failures set that subarray's refresh interval through a tiny on-die state machine instead of a global worst-case 32/64 ms.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: typical subarrays run 4-8x longer intervals while the weakened canaries bound tail risk; ~60-75% less refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Piano tuner: in-field sense-amp offset auto-zeroing during refresh idle
idea: Like periodic retuning, each sense amp samples its own offset against a shorted dummy bitline pair in spare refresh slots and stores a correction on a small trim capacitor or 3-bit DAC, cancelling both mismatch and aging drift.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: cutting effective SA offset ~20-30 mV lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3.5 fF (or AR from ~70:1 to ~50:1) at the same error rate.
note: Offset-cancellation sense amps already published by major vendors.

title: Recycling sorter: sell retention-binned 'harvest grade' DRAM with mandated controller ECC
idea: Dies failing JEDEC 64 ms retention but passing at 16 ms or under stronger ECC are graded into a new SKU for AI KV-cache and cold-tier buyers whose controllers run 4x refresh or LDPC, with a standard grade label and warranty model so the parts are bankable.
why: Recovers ~5-15% of wafer output now scrapped or downgraded; pure supply gain without new fabs, helium or EUV.

title: Thermostat wordline: off-voltage tracks temperature to the leakage minimum
idea: At each temperature the access transistor's total leakage (subthreshold vs GIDL) has a minimum at a specific negative wordline voltage; an on-die sensor and table steer VNWL from about -0.2 V at 25 C to about -0.5 V at 125 C, re-trimmed yearly to follow aging.
why: Fact 3 under 125 C for 10 years: ~2-4x lower hot leakage than a fixed VNWL, halving hot refresh while avoiding the constant GIDL field that accelerates oxide wear.

title: Chameleon cells: auto-switch 1T1C to twin-cell 2T2C above 105 C
idea: Wordline decoders support a paired mode where two adjacent rows store complementary data on one sense amp (differential twin cell); above 105 C the OS shrinks the hot region and the controller migrates its pages into paired mode, doubling signal margin.
why: Twin cells tolerate ~4-10x more leakage, so parts survive 125 C for 10 years while cooler deployments keep full 1T1C density - no cell designed for worst case.
note: Temperature trigger for the same switchable twin-cell mode.

title: Pressure cooker: high-pressure deuterium anneal plus nitride reservoir hardens interfaces
idea: Cook wafers in ~20 atm D2 at ~400 C so access-transistor and storage-node interfaces are passivated with Si-D (several times more resistant to depassivation than Si-H), capped by a deuterium-rich SiN reservoir that re-passivates bonds broken during 10 years at 125 C.
why: Interface-trap growth drives retention-tail drift at high temperature; ~3-10x slower drift keeps refresh constant over life.
note: High-pressure D2 anneal is established practice; reservoir adds little novelty.

title: Warehouse receipt: exchange-traded DRAM bit futures with bonded physical delivery
idea: Random stimulus 'pawnshop warehouse receipt' -> metals trade on LME warrants. List standardized DDR5 16 Gb component futures, deliverable from bonded warehouses, so producers hedge 3-5 years forward and banks lend against hedged output to finance fabs.
why: Lowers cost of capital for capacity (fact 4: depreciation ~55% of wafer cost) and gives small buyers price certainty; est. 1-3 pts lower WACC on fab debt.

title: Hermit crab: shuttered mature fabs make HBM interposers and bridges
idea: Random stimulus 'hermit crab' -> move into an empty shell. Underused 65-130 nm 200/300 mm fabs make passive silicon interposers and local silicon bridges (only thick metal and TSV, no transistors), unblocking the advanced-packaging queue that throttles HBM.
why: Interposer capacity, not DRAM die, often gates HBM output; idle fabs add it at a fraction of new CoWoS-class capex and onshore it.
note: Passive interposers in old fabs already made (UMC); real onshoring lever.

title: Cookie cutter: printed long-lead fab tool parts cut ramp time
idea: Random stimulus 'cookie cutter' -> shape on demand from stock. Regional additive-manufacturing farms print showerheads, gas manifolds, ESC bases and ceramic chamber liners by laser powder-bed fusion and binder-jet ceramics on demand.
why: Tool lead times of 12-18 months gate fab ramps; printed parts cut months off tool delivery and spares, pulling new DRAM capacity in earlier.

title: Helium nanocavity gettering layer beneath DRAM arrays
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x array-wide buried layer x Si x MeV He implant + anneal forming nanocavities ~1 um below junctions. Cavity walls trap Fe, Cu and Ni that create mid-gap generation centers in storage junctions, the origin of many tail cells.
why: Shrinks the retention tail (fact 3) 2-5x; uses milligram-scale helium, negligible against the Qatar-constrained supply.

title: One-mask selective reoxidation thickens storage-side gate edge
idea: Box: standard cap x recessed access with asymmetric gate dielectric x SA x in-array x Si x one mask exposing only storage-side recess tops to an extra radical oxidation. Thicker dielectric only where the gate overlaps the storage junction lowers the field driving GIDL while channel oxide stays thin for drive.
why: GIDL is exponential in field; ~30% thicker edge oxide can cut it ~10x, extending refresh (fact 3) for one mask.
note: Gate-edge reoxidation for GIDL is established practice.

title: Deep boron barrier implant blocks substrate diffusion leakage
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x one high-energy implant mask placing a p+ layer ~0.5-1 um below the array. Its built-in field reflects electrons diffusing from the substrate and periphery (including sense-amp hot-carrier emission) away from storage nodes.
why: Diffusion current dominates at 85-95C; blocking it gives ~2x hot retention (fact 3) and less periphery-induced disturb for one mask.

title: Zero-majority row encoding plus refresh skip for empty rows
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA with per-row invert flag and all-discharged flag x in-mat logic x Si x zero masks. Rows are written inverted when that leaves fewer charged (leak-vulnerable) cells, and rows flagged all-discharged are skipped by refresh since discharged true cells cannot decay.
why: Zero pages and sparse AI tensors are common; skipping them and halving charged cells elsewhere cuts refresh energy 20-50% and retention-failure exposure (fact 3).

title: One-mask BEOL thermistor grid sets refresh per subarray
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x vanadium-oxide thin-film thermistor grid patterned by one added mask above the arrays x per-subarray refresh timers x Si. Each subarray's refresh rate follows its local temperature instead of the hottest die sensor.
why: On-die gradients reach 10-20C in HBM/3D stacks; local rates cut average refresh 30-60% (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Bank-to-bank bitline charge recycling during refresh bursts
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x charge-transfer switches linking bitlines of two banks refreshed in antiphase x in-array design x Si x zero masks. When bank A finishes restore, its high-side bitline charge is shared into bank B's bitlines before discharge, reusing up to half the swing charge.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, fact 3) and VARY supply current cut ~30-40% with only switches and timing.
note: Bitline charge-recycling schemes are published art.

title: Solar-cell Al2O3 negative-charge liner passivates isolation sidewalls
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x ALD Al2O3 STI liner carrying ~-5e12 cm-2 fixed charge (the PERC solar-cell trick) replacing the oxide liner, zero masks. The negative charge accumulates holes on the trench sidewall next to the storage junction, field-effect passivating edge interface states.
why: STI-edge generation is a known tail source; this passivation cut solar surface recombination ~10x, so expect 2-5x tail reduction (fact 3).

title: One wordline metal gates IGZO tiers above and below
idea: [Box: lateral 1T1C | top- and bottom-gated IGZO pair | standard SA | monolithic 3D | Si | ALD stack, ArF hole/slit patterning only] Order each repeat as IGZO / gate oxide / wordline / gate oxide / IGZO so a single wordline gates two cell layers, removing one metal layer per pair of tiers.
why: 3D tiers (fact 2): ~30% thinner stack per bit means shallower high-AR etches for the same bit count; density comes from deposition, not lithography.

title: Supercritical CO2 and ozone dry cleaning replaces most UPW rinses
idea: Box [any | any | any | any | Si | single-wafer scCO2 + co-solvent + dissolved O3 cleaner with CO2 recompression loop]: strip post-etch residue and particles inside high-AR capacitor holes with supercritical CO2, which has no surface tension and so causes no pattern collapse, recovering >95% of the CO2.
why: Water and pattern collapse at AR 70+: could cut wet-clean UPW ~50-70%, eliminate IPA drying and allow taller capacitors without stiction.

title: Water-vapor plasma activated hybrid bonding for HBM stacks
idea: Box [HBM DRAM dies | standard | standard | bumpless Cu-SiCN hybrid-bonded HBM | Si | H2O/N2 low-power plasma activation + formic-acid vapor Cu-oxide reduction + 250 C anneal]: hydroxyl-terminate the SiCN with water-vapor plasma and reduce Cu oxide chemically instead of using Ar/N2 plasma activation or Ar sputter cleaning.
why: HBM TSV/microbump tax (3x area, 20-30% yield loss): bumpless bonding cuts pitch ~10x and removes underfill, with no argon in the flow.
note: Minor process twist on established hybrid bonding.

title: Crucible-free kerfless DRAM substrates via porous-silicon epitaxial lift-off
idea: Box: any cell x any access x any sense x 2D monolithic x epitaxial Si foil on a reusable seed x CVD epitaxy. One CZ seed wafer is anodized into double-layer porous Si and sealed by H2 anneal; a 50-100 um device-grade epi layer is grown, bonded to a recycled-Si or glass carrier and lifted off, and the seed is reused 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resources: cuts Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible use and CZ pulling per wafer by ~20-50x and eliminates slicing kerf; substrate is ~5-10% of DRAM wafer cost.

title: Electroless ruthenium wordlines and plugs escape tungsten and WF6
idea: Box: standard cell x buried-wordline access with Ru gate fill x standard sensing x 2D x Si x seedless electroless or ALD-seeded Ru plating. Buried wordlines and contact plugs, today CVD W from WF6, are filled bottom-up by barrier-free Ru (short electron mean free path keeps resistivity low in 10 nm trenches).
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and fluorine chemistry removed; barrier-free fill gives ~30% lower WL RC or allows a thinner WL that lowers GIDL; Ru needed is micrograms per die.

title: Line-granular copy-on-write for forks, snapshots and VM clones
idea: Box: share × MMU plus memory controller × 64 B line (not 4 KB page) × first write × per-page 64-bit diverged-line mask. Cloned pages keep pointing at the parent frame; a write copies only the touched line into a small overlay frame, and the controller merges parent and overlay on reads using the mask.
why: Serverless snapshots, VM clones and forked workers duplicate a full 4 KB page to change a few bytes; line CoW cuts post-fork memory growth 5–20×, packing more instances per GB.
note: Page Overlays (MICRO 2015) proposed this.

title: Shingled LPDDR staircase on glass panel replaces TSV stacks
idea: Box: 1T1C LPDDR die x planar access x on-die SA x offset-staircase edge pads x glass-core panel x panel-level RDL. Eight LPDDR dies are shingled with 0.4 mm offsets so every die's edge pads stay exposed, then a single panel-level RDL plus through-glass vias wires all eight to a 1024-bit bus without one TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area and no 20-30% stack yield loss; uses commodity LPDDR wafers at roughly half the wafer area per bit of HBM, at about half HBM's bandwidth density.
note: Similar to vertical-post fan-out LPDDR stacking; RDL over staircase topology is the hard part.

title: Photonic wire bonds written in place link memory and compute
idea: Box: DRAM chiplet with SiN grating couplers x standard x Ge photodiodes x free-form polymer waveguides x organic carrier x two-photon direct laser writing with closed-loop recycled solvent developer. 3D polymer waveguides are written in situ between memory and compute chiplets after placement, so no interposer and no active optical alignment are needed.
why: Water: eliminates silicon-interposer fabrication (many wet clean and plating loops) for ~10x less water per package; ~1 pJ/bit over centimetres.

title: Extruded polymer waveguides replace water-hungry memory PCB traces
idea: Box: DDR/LPDDR modules x standard x standard x 140 GHz CMOS transceivers into PTFE dielectric waveguide cables x extruded polymer x dry extrusion. Memory channels leave the motherboard entirely as 100 Gb/s mm-wave links through plastic waveguides, so boards shrink from 20+ to ~8 layers.
why: Water: every PCB layer pair adds wet etch, plating and rinse; memory-channel interconnect water falls >10x when plated layers become extruded cable; also enables memory at rack distance.

title: Molten-salt ion exchange writes waveguides inside glass interposers
idea: Box: DRAM chiplets with grating couplers x standard x photodiodes x buried graded-index waveguides x glass interposer x dry molten KNO3/AgNO3 ion exchange through a laser-ablated metal mask. Waveguides form by ion exchange in a molten salt bath, with no water anywhere, and carry memory traffic across the package.
why: Water: replaces wet silicon-interposer processing, >10x less; optical package links at <1 pJ/bit.

title: Shingled overlap: memory die hangs over logic die edge
idea: Box: DRAM die x standard x standard x 2 mm overlap strip bonded face-to-face by Cu-Sn transient-liquid-phase thermocompression x no interposer x dry formic-acid-vapor oxide reduction. The memory die extends over the logic die's edge so a 2 mm strip of each faces the other, forming a direct bridge with no interposer or bridge chip.
why: Water: deletes the wet-heavy interposer and uses fluxless dry bonding, >10x cut; links ~0.2 pJ/bit.

title: On-die segment cache absorbs repeat activations and caps hammering
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard | integration: 256 KB SRAM segment cache per bank group | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Recently activated 64 B segments stay in an SRAM cache beside the bank; repeat accesses hit SRAM instead of re-activating, and any row that hits the cache N times is pinned there so it can never be hammered past N.
why: Constraint: for AI/KV workloads with >80% segment reuse, average access energy ~5-10x lower; Fact 9 bounded by construction.

title: UCIe memory chiplet marketplace for small-fab memories
idea: Box[Integration=UCIe die-to-die memory chiplet profile x Medium=any (eDRAM, oxide, MRAM) x Owner=open standards body x Channel=certified chiplet catalog]: define a memory-chiplet protocol so small fabs can sell interchangeable working-memory chiplets to any SoC maker.
why: Supply diversification: opens a channel for many smaller fabs and new media to add bits outside the big three.

title: Fuse 32 Gb partial-good dies down to JEDEC 24 Gb density
idea: Box[Source=dies with a defective bank group x Transform=e-fuse remap to the standard 24 Gb address map x Integration=standard 24 Gb DDR5 die in 48/96 GB DIMMs x Owner=DRAM maker]: dies with defects beyond row and column repair have the bad quarter fused off and present as a legal JEDEC 24 Gb device.
why: Raises good die per wafer by an estimated 2-5% on new nodes, using the non-binary densities DDR5 already allows.

title: Synthetic-silica crucibles and new quartz sources for wafers
idea: Box[Material=sol-gel synthetic fused-silica inner crucible liner x Source=non-Spruce-Pine quartz outer body x Owner=U.S. crucible maker x Finance=DPA]: line crucibles with synthetic silica made from SiCl4 so lower-purity quartz suffices for the outer body.
why: Removes the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz chokepoint for CZ wafers that feed standard DRAM.
note: Synthetic inner layers already used by crucible makers.

title: LPDDR5X dies redeployed into DDR5 RDIMMs behind a bridge buffer
idea: Box[Source=LPDDR5X die oversupply from phones x Transform=bridge buffer translating DDR5 protocol to LPDDR x Integration=standard DDR5 RDIMM form factor x Owner=module maker]: when phone demand softens, route mobile die into server RDIMMs where a buffer chip presents a JEDEC DDR5 interface to the host.
why: Supply fungibility across die families; lets mobile capacity cover server shortfalls; host interface unchanged.

title: Po: the bit is trapped light — photonic nanocavity buffer RAM
idea: Po: the bit is light that cannot leave. Extracted: an InP or Si photonic-crystal nanocavity with Kerr/thermal bistability holds on or off light under a shared ~10 nW bias beam; placed at co-packaged optical I/O as buffer memory so in-flight data never converts to charge.
why: Removes O/E/O conversion and data-movement energy (fact 5) for packet and activation buffers. Low density limits it to buffers.
note: NTT-style PhC bistable RAM already demonstrated; buffer niche.

title: Deliberately low-barrier MTJs as refreshed fast spin DRAM
idea: Po: a magnet that is supposed to forget. Design MTJ free layers with only ~25 kT energy barrier so bits flip spontaneously after ~10-100 ms; the low barrier cuts write current ~10x, so a minimum access device suffices, and bits are scrubbed on a DRAM-like refresh schedule.
why: Facts 1 and 10: no capacitor, low write voltage, ~10 fJ writes and effectively unlimited endurance since the barrier is never stressed; beyond prior nonvolatile MRAM.
note: Volatile STT-MRAM known; MgO tunnel barrier still wears under writes.

title: Po: biased sense amps that favor the decaying state
idea: Po: a sense amp that is deliberately unfair. Because only the charged state leaks (true cells toward '0', anti cells toward '1'), give every SA a designed offset (asymmetric device sizing or a shifted bitline precharge) toward the leaky state, with the skew direction flipped per mat to match true/anti-cell layout in open-bitline arrays.
why: Refresh (#3): the full-swing non-leaking state has margin to spare, so lending it to the decaying state extends the retention tail ~1.5-2x, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Po: wordlines on springs — stepwise adiabatic charge-recycling drivers
idea: Po: a wordline that bounces back for free. Drive each global/main wordline through a stepwise adiabatic charger, 4-6 on-die tank capacitors switched in sequence, so the ~3 V wordline rises and falls in small steps and returns most of its charge to the tanks instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Voltage floor (#10): wordline CV^2 energy falls ~60-75%, which also unloads the VPP charge pump and shrinks it (periphery #7).
note: Stepwise charging is known art; wordline energy is a modest share of activate energy.

title: Po: rows only know 'next' — token-ring subarray refresh
idea: Po: a decoder that only knows 'next'. Add a display-style shift-register gate-driver chain (2-3 transistors per row, like gate-on-array in LCD panels) beside each subarray that passes a refresh token row to row, so idle subarrays refresh independently of the address decoder while others serve accesses.
why: Refresh (#3): hides the 10-20% bandwidth loss at 32-64 Gb through subarray-parallel refresh with ~1-2% area and no decoder contention.

title: Po: the charge pump is a magnet — NiFe inductor boost
idea: Po: a charge pump replaced by a magnet. Generate VPP with an on-die inductive boost converter using thin-film permalloy (NiFe)-cored spiral inductors in the top Al/Cu level, switched at ~100 MHz by thick-oxide silicon devices.
why: Voltage floor (#10) and periphery (#7): ~75-85% efficient vs ~30-40% for charge pumps, halving VPP energy and freeing pump capacitor area; Ni and Fe are abundant.

title: Po: the chip forgets its repairs — off-die repair maps
idea: Po: a chip that does not remember where it is broken. Delete on-die e-fuse/antifuse banks and their HV programming; store row/column repair maps in module SPD flash or the controller, upload them at boot over a sideband into a small CAM per bank, and update them in the field as weak rows appear.
why: Periphery (#7) and usable supply: frees ~2-4% of die, removes silicide fuse links, and field-updatable repair raises effective yield and lifetime.

title: Po: half the transistors missing — NMOS-only bootstrapped sense amp
idea: Po: a sense amp without PMOS. Use an NMOS cross-coupled latch for sensing and restore the high side through a capacitive bootstrap that lifts an NMOS pull-up gate above VDD for a few ns, eliminating the n-well, PMOS implants and well-to-well spacing in the SA strip.
