why: Periphery (#7) and capital (#4): SA strips lose ~30% width from well spacing and drop a couple of implant masks; Si, B, P, SiO2 only.
note: NMOS-era DRAMs used bootstrapped NMOS restore; saves well spacing but adds bootstrap caps and timing.

title: TSV-free memory stacks with inductive coupling between dies
idea: Po: the stack has no wires through it. Stack thinned DRAM dies with power fed by edge wraps and move data through on-die spiral coils at ~30 um pitch that couple inductively through 5-10 dies, placing coils over array area with no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims TSV area and the 20-30% yield loss from TSV processing.

title: Po the fab drinks no water: supercritical CO2 clean and dry
idea: Po: 'the fab is built in a desert with no water.' Extracted: replace post-etch residue removal, rinse and spin-dry on most cleaning steps with supercritical CO2 plus alcohol and chelating co-solvents, recaptured and recompressed in a closed loop; the zero surface tension of scCO2 also stops tall capacitor pillars collapsing during drying.
why: Water intensity (large fabs draw millions of gallons per day; cleaning is the biggest use) cut by perhaps 30-50%, and the capillary-collapse limit on capacitor aspect ratio (fact 1) is lifted.
note: scCO2 drying for HAR collapse is known and in use.

title: Po every gas well is a helium well: fab-anchored membrane extraction
idea: Po: 'every gas well near the fab is a helium mine.' Extracted: install modular hollow-fiber membrane plus PSA skids on U.S. pipeline gas streams with only 0.1-0.5% helium, normally uneconomic, co-located near fabs in Arizona, Texas and New York, and justify them with fab waste heat and long-term offtake contracts.
why: Helium supply security: many low-helium streams are vented or ignored; fab-anchored micro-extraction could cover a fab's net make-up need from domestic gas.

title: Po memory made of sandpaper: silicon-carbide refresh-free DRAM
idea: Po: 'memory made of sandpaper.' Extracted: build 1T1C cells in 4H silicon carbide (carborundum) on 150 mm SiC lines with >=0.5 um tools; the 3.2 eV bandgap cuts thermal generation leakage so cells hold charge for hours to years at room temperature, as 1990s SiC DRAM experiments showed.
why: Refresh eliminated (fact 3) and U.S. manufacturability (SiC fabs in NC and NY); density is low but energy per bit for refresh-free working memory drops sharply.

title: Po the crucible is brewed in a test tube: sol-gel silica liners
idea: Po: 'the crucible is brewed in a test tube.' Extracted: for 150-200 mm pullers, whose crucibles are small, cast the melt-contact liner from synthetic silica made by sol-gel hydrolysis of silicon alkoxides (or flame hydrolysis of SiCl4) and sinter it onto a lower-grade quartz back wall, ending reliance on Spruce Pine natural quartz.
why: Breaks the >80% high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint for 200 mm legacy-memory wafers on 1990s pullers; synthetic silica is purer than natural quartz.
note: Synthetic-silica inner-layer crucibles are already sold.

title: Po the transistor stands up: vertical surrounding-gate 4F2 cells
idea: Po: 'the transistor stands on its head.' Extracted: etch silicon pillars with a KrF stepper, wrap each in a gate by conformal LPCVD poly and spacer etch (Toshiba's 1988 surrounding-gate transistor), with buried diffused bitlines below and the capacitor on top, giving a 4F2 cell.
why: Density at old pitch: 4F2 vs 8F2 halves cell area, so a 180 nm U.S. line gets ~2x bits per wafer without any litho upgrade.

title: Universal half-finished wafers finished regionally as DDR, LPDDR or HBM
idea: Po: memory is finished at the customer's door. Freeze a common front end through the capacitor module, bank those wafers, and let regional back-end lines apply product-specific metal, TSV and test, so supply swings between DDR, LPDDR and HBM in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Capital efficiency: less capacity mismatch and inventory write-down, ~5-10% more usable bits from the same capex.

title: Reusable seed wafers via porous-silicon layer lift-off
idea: Po: the ingot needs no crucible. Grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a reusable seed wafer in existing epi reactors, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier and lift off, reusing the seed 10-20 times.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine quartz >80%): cuts Czochralski wafer demand ~5-10x per wafer start using existing epi capacity.

title: Inductive coil links stack trailing DRAM dies without TSVs
idea: Po: the stack is wireless. Stack thinned DRAM dies from existing lines and pass data vertically through near-field inductive coils drawn in standard top metal (no TSV etch, fill or reveal), with power delivered by edge wire bonds or a few large vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes the TSV module and much of its area/yield tax, enabling HBM-like stacks from trailing fabs at ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Planet-once pages: content-addressed dedup inside the CXL memory switch
idea: Po: every byte exists only once on Earth. The rack's CXL switch hashes each 4 KB page written to pooled memory and maps identical pages (OS images, container layers, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) to one physical copy with copy-on-write, across all hosts rather than inside one hypervisor as KSM does.
why: Cross-host duplication in VM/container fleets is 15-40%; switch-level dedup recovers most of it with no per-host CPU scanning.

title: Stranded-memory exchange: hourly auction of idle DRAM across tenants
idea: Po: your memory belongs to your neighbor. Cloud hosts expose DRAM left stranded when cores sell out first (typically 25-50%) into a CXL pool, and an exchange auctions it hourly to tenants' elastic caches under preemption contracts with posted prices.
why: Turns stranded capacity into supply; recovering half the stranded share raises usable fleet memory ~15-25% with zero new wafers.

title: Half-size pointers: base-relative 32-bit addressing in the ISA
idea: Po: addresses cost nothing. An ISA extension adds region-base registers and load/store forms taking 32-bit (or 24-bit) offsets with hardware base addition, so C/C++/Rust programs and runtimes use compressed pointers everywhere, not only in JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; halving them cuts footprint 15-25% and raises cache density.

title: Manassas-plus: compressing CXL expander for domestic mature-node DRAM
idea: Po: America only makes yesterday's DRAM, so make yesterday's DRAM hold twice as much. A CXL Type-3 expander pairs Micron Manassas (VA) mature-node DRAM with a GlobalFoundries Malta (NY) 12LP+ controller doing inline LZ-class and zero-line compression with variable-size line mapping, assembled on U.S. EMS lines.
why: 2-3x effective capacity lets domestic older-node DRAM match imported leading-edge DIMMs on cost per usable bit, raising U.S.-only supply with no new fab.

title: Rack memory commons: a domestic CXL switch pools all DRAM
idea: Po: servers own no memory. A CXL 3.x switch ASIC fabbed at GlobalFoundries Malta links 16-32 hosts to shared drawers of U.S.-made DRAM; hosts keep small local DIMMs and borrow the rest at ~250 ns, with the pool sized for the rack's aggregate peak, not the sum of per-host peaks.
why: Statistical multiplexing cuts provisioned DRAM 20-30% per rack, stretching scarce U.S.-made bits.
note: Pond-style pooling well known; domestic switch ASIC exceeds $1M.

title: Blurry numbers: error-bounded compression of live simulation state
idea: Po: numbers are blurry on purpose. DOE-lab error-bounded lossy compressors (SZ/ZFP class) run inline in the memory path of U.S.-built supercomputer nodes, keeping field data compressed under a user-set pointwise error bound and decompressing per tile on access.
why: Scientific floating-point fields compress 5-20x within physics-acceptable error, so domestic HPC fits larger problems in the same DRAM.

title: Live-set-sized heaps: hardware read barriers for pauseless compaction
idea: Po: the heap is exactly as big as the live data. A load-barrier ISA extension (colored-pointer check and forwarding in hardware) on a U.S.-designed core fabbed at Intel Arizona makes concurrent compacting GC nearly free, so managed heaps run at 1.1-1.2x live set instead of 2-3x headroom.
why: Java/Go/.NET heaps are routinely provisioned 2-3x live data to keep GC cheap; hardware barriers could cut managed-heap DRAM ~40%.

title: PCB-shop panel packaging with one stepper mask for die field
idea: Po: the memory package is made in a print shop. Large panels are patterned by maskless laser direct imaging for all coarse layers, and only the fine-pitch die-attach field uses one stepper mask, so U.S. PCB fabs can build HBM-class packages.
why: Onshore packaging capacity at lower capital per unit, easing the U.S. manufacturability gap.
note: Panel-level packaging with LDI is broadly pursued.

title: Air-gap interposer wires halve memory link capacitance
idea: Po: the best insulator is nothing. One mask defines where a sacrificial fill between interposer lines is later removed, leaving air gaps around long HBM-to-GPU wires.
why: Wire capacitance falls 2-3x, so CV2 energy on interposer links drops the same amount; ~1.5 pJ/bit saved on 3-4 pJ/bit HBM links.

title: Thick-copper superhighway layer for low-swing bank-to-PHY transport
idea: Po: wires thicker than transistors are tall. One added mask lays a 10-20 um thick copper top layer that carries global data from far banks to the I/O with very low resistance, so data can move at 100-200 mV swing.
why: Cuts on-die data movement energy (a large part of the 5.9 pJ per useful bit) ~2x without new transistors.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells set each subarray's refresh
idea: Po: memory that fails on purpose to warn you. Each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with a thinned capacitor or an extra junction-leakage implant so they fail at ~0.6x the retention of the worst real cell; the in-DRAM scheduler slows refresh until canaries start to flip, then backs off one step.
why: Refresh (fact 3): each subarray runs at its true retention instead of the global worst case, ~2-4x fewer refreshes at normal temperatures.

title: Hammer-absorbing row cache intercepts repeated activations
idea: Po: the hammer hits a pillow. A small SRAM cache of 8-16 row buffers per bank inside the DRAM holds rows activated more than N times in a window; further ACTs to those rows are served from SRAM without raising the array wordline at all.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and activation energy: attackers cannot toggle the hot wordline; also cuts ACT energy for hot rows ~30%.

title: Delete repair: no spare rows, fuses, or laser repair
idea: Po: the chip arrives broken and that's fine. Redundant rows and columns, fuse banks, and the laser-repair and re-test steps are removed; every manufacturing defect up to 1% of cells is handled by the code as an erasure or error.
why: Periphery and test capital (facts 4, 7): ~3-5% die area and ~10-15% of test/repair cycle time removed.

title: Ship imperfect dies with a standardized bad-row map
idea: Po: every chip is broken. A JEDEC-style 'fault map in SPD' lets fabs ship dies with up to ~0.5% bad rows beyond on-die repair; BIOS/OS reads the map at boot and retires those physical pages, so dies now downgraded or scrapped become full-price product.
why: Raises good-die yield at leading nodes by an estimated 3-10%, i.e., free wafer capacity; attacks cost per bit and capital intensity.

title: Exchange-traded DRAM bit futures for long-dated hedging
idea: Po: bits are traded like wheat. A standardized cash-settled contract (e.g., 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent per quarter against a published contract-price index) lets fabs sell output 3-5 years forward and buyers hedge, so a greenfield fab can be project-financed against hedged revenue.
why: Hedged revenue opens project finance to new entrants and cuts the risk premium over the 3-5-year build gap; attacks capital intensity.

title: Synthetic fused-silica crucibles replacing Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Po: crucibles are made, not mined. Czochralski crucibles are slip-cast from synthetic silica made by flame hydrolysis of domestic SiCl4 (a polysilicon byproduct), with a barium-doped inner layer that mimics natural high-purity quartz devitrification behavior.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine chokepoint for the wafers DRAM is built on and recycles a polysilicon waste stream; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: Molybdenum wordlines and contacts mined in Colorado replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Po: tungsten is illegal. Buried wordlines, bitline contacts and periphery plugs switch from W to ALD/CVD molybdenum (lower resistivity at narrow widths, barrier-free on some layers), sourced from U.S. mines such as Climax and Henderson.
why: China supplies ~80% of tungsten while the U.S. is a top molybdenum producer; also trims wordline RC; attacks scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Gridded one-direction layouts for every DRAM layer
idea: Po: the chip only has straight lines. Array and periphery are redesigned so every critical layer is unidirectional lines on a fixed pitch made by self-aligned quadruple patterning, with shapes defined only by DUV cut masks; a gridded 1D periphery cell library replaces 2D shapes.
why: 1D patterns print reliably at ~18-20 nm half pitch with ArF immersion, recovering most of EUV's density; mask count rises modestly while ~$150-380M per avoided EUV scanner is saved; attacks capital and single-supplier risk.

title: Ultra-short local bitlines trade sense margin into retention
idea: Worse: hang 1,024 cells on a bitline so the signal is tiny and any leakage kills the bit. Flip: hierarchical bitlines with 32-cell local segments and a local gain transistor raise the charge-transfer ratio from ~0.2 to ~0.8, so a cell can lose 3x more charge before failure.
why: Retention about 3x, refresh down about 65%, and the same trick relaxes the Cs wall (fact 1).

title: Series-stacked access transistors on one pillar exploit stack effect
idea: Worse: trust one transistor to isolate the bit. Flip: stack two gate-all-around segments in series on the same vertical pillar; in the off state the intermediate node floats up and reverse-biases the upper device, cutting subthreshold leakage about 10x at zero footprint cost.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 10x lower; also helps 3D tiers where a long channel cannot be laid laterally (fact 2).

title: Pump-less VPP: refresh wordlines fed from a board GaN rail
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline supply with on-die charge pumps at ~30% efficiency. Flip: deliver VPP from a high-efficiency GaN point-of-load converter on the module through dedicated balls, removing the pumps and their area.
why: Refresh and activation energy (facts 3, 10) down ~25-30%; frees periphery area (fact 7).

title: Deuterium-only process plus hydrogen barrier for oxide-channel access devices
idea: Worse at 125 C: leave process hydrogen free to diffuse into an oxide-semiconductor channel and shift Vt. Flip: run every deposition with deuterated precursors (D2O, SiD4), seal the array with ALD Al2O3/SiN and a Ti getter ring, so the remaining isotope moves slower and binds more strongly.
why: Makes oxide-channel low-leakage devices (fact 3) survive 10 years at 125 C with less than 50 mV drift.

title: Buried minority-carrier collector layer sweeps substrate electrons
idea: Worse at 125 C: let thermally generated electrons in the hot substrate diffuse up into storage nodes. Flip: implant a biased buried n+ collector plane a few microns below the array that sweeps diffusion current away before it reaches the storage junctions.
why: Removes the diffusion component of hot leakage (fact 3), which dominates above ~100 C; ~3-5x retention at 125 C.

title: Ten-year-equivalent stabilization bake plus per-die Vt trim fuses
idea: Worse at 125 C: ship access devices that will drift for years as defects relax. Flip: run a hot-bias stabilization bake equivalent to 10 years at 125 C during the BEOL anneal, then measure each die's leakage and blow eFuses that set its wordline-low and refresh trim to the post-drift value.
why: Removes lifetime drift guard-bands on leakage and refresh (fact 3), roughly 1.5-2x refresh savings.

title: Hot-mode twin-cell switch trades half the capacity for 4x retention
idea: Worse at 125 C: keep single-ended cells that fail as the leakage spike eats the signal. Flip: above 110 C the controller remaps selected banks to differential twin-cell mode (a bit and its complement on adjacent cells), doubling signal and cancelling common-mode decay.
why: Retention ~4x and refresh 4x lower in the hot regime (fact 3), with no new device.

title: Shared physics-of-failure qualification fast-tracks new hot access devices
idea: Worse: make every new access-device material wait 3 years of 125 C HTOL before anyone buys it. Flip: fund a consortium test house with standardized 200 C accelerated stress and model-based 10-year extrapolation so wide-gap and novel access devices qualify in ~9 months.
why: Cuts time-to-market for low-leakage devices (fact 3) and lowers U.S. entrant barriers.

title: Ruthenium buried-wordline gate replaces tungsten and channel doping
idea: Worse: use tungsten wordlines (China ~80%) with heavy channel doping to set Vt, adding random-dopant leakage tails. Flip: use a high-work-function Ru buried gate (~4.8 eV, electromigration-robust at 125 C) to set Vt with a near-undoped channel, removing random-dopant fluctuation.
why: Tightens the leakage tail (fact 3), removes a tungsten chokepoint, and stays stable over a 10-year 125 C life.

title: Module PMIC supplies wordline high voltage, deleting on-die charge pumps
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline rail and negative back-bias on every die with ~30%-efficient charge pumps. Flip: supply VPP and VBB from GaN or switched-capacitor converters on the module PMIC through dedicated bumps and package planes, deleting on-die pumps and their reservoir capacitors.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and voltage-floor energy (fact 10): frees ~4-6% of die and lifts VPP efficiency from ~30% to ~85%.

title: Segmented sub-wordline gates activate only the requested 512-byte slice
idea: Worse: open an entire 8 KB row to read 64 bytes. Flip: insert segment-select transistors in the sub-wordline drivers so only the cells and sense amps of one 512 B slice connect and fire, leaving the rest of the row untouched.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): activation energy per useful bit drops ~10-16x and row-hammer exposure per activation shrinks.
note: Close to Half-DRAM and fine-grained activation.

title: Roll-to-roll polymer waveguide flex carries memory traffic optically
idea: Worse: push every bit through lossy copper with power-hungry SerDes equalizers. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-embossed polymer waveguide flex between memory stacks and the processor package, coupled to micro-LED or VCSEL transmitters on the memory base die.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): sub-pJ/bit links over centimeters, letting memory sit farther from the accelerator and escape interposer area limits.

title: Printed micro-heater film for fast wafer-level retention binning
idea: Worse: profile retention with slow chamber bakes so rows are never binned individually. Flip: laminate a printed resistive heater film at the probe-chuck interface that steps each die through precise temperatures in seconds while BIST logs per-row retention, storing bins for retention-aware refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3): cheap per-row retention bins enable 2-4x longer refresh for most rows.
note: Retention-aware refresh known; VRT limits one-time bins.

title: Origami chip-on-flex stack folds dies around a printed shared bus
idea: Worse: stack dies rigidly with TSVs and microbumps. Flip: mount thin dies at intervals along a roll-to-roll-printed flex tape carrying a shared command and data bus plus printed passives, then fold it accordion-style into a 3D stack bonded at one edge.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and capital: no TSVs and known-good-die assembly on roll-to-roll lines, giving cheaper capacity stacks.
note: Fold-stack packaging is known; bandwidth far below HBM.

title: Spare tiers with post-stack tier-remapping fuses
idea: Worse: stack tiers or dies blindly so one bad layer scraps the whole stack (yield^N). Flip: build every stack with 1-2 spare tiers and a tier-map fuse ROM in the base die, test after stacking, and logically swap failed tiers out exactly as spare rows are swapped today.
why: HBM stack yield loss is 20-30% (fact 6): 0.97^12 ~69% becomes >95% with two spares at ~15% bit overhead; the same scheme makes 100+ tier monolithic stacks yieldable.
note: Dup of spare-tier redundancy; ~15% overhead buys large stack-yield gains.

title: Smart-cut tier films with donor-wafer reuse
idea: Worse: consume a full CZ wafer, grown in a Spruce Pine quartz crucible, for every bonded layer and then grind it away. Flip: hydrogen-implant and split a 100-200 nm single-crystal Si film from a donor for each tier, bond it onto the stack, pattern after bonding so alignment is litho-limited, and re-polish and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
why: Single-crystal access transistors in every tier keep the leakage tail low (fact 3) while wafers and crucibles consumed per tier fall ~10-20x (resource chokepoints).
note: Smart Cut and donor reuse are established; resource benefit real but incremental.

title: Corrugated capacitor walls from multilayer selective recess
idea: Worse: etch smooth cylinder walls so electrode area grows only with height. Flip: etch capacitor holes through an alternating oxide/nitride (or Si/SiGe) mold and selectively recess every other layer before electrode deposition, giving fin-like corrugated walls that multiply area 2-3x at the same aspect ratio.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall without AR 115 or k 70 (fact 1): ~5 fF at AR ~30-40, which also eases mold collapse.

title: Spatial-ALD carousel deposits ten tiers per wafer pass
idea: Worse: deposit 200 tiers sequentially in chamber-based ALD/CVD so deposition time becomes the new cost wall. Flip: run wafers through rotary spatial-ALD carousels with gas-separated precursor zones that lay down alternating channel/dielectric/sacrificial films at ~10x the throughput per tool, with in-line ellipsometry closing the loop on each tier's thickness.
why: Keeps per-tier deposition at ~0.1-0.2% of wafer cost, so the ~150-200 tiers needed for 10x density add <30% to cost and less capex than chamber tools (fact 4).
note: Spatial ALD is commercial; 3D stacks are mostly PECVD already, so gain is modest.

title: Synthetic crucibles cast from polysilicon-plant SiCl4 waste
idea: Worsen: require Spruce Pine natural quartz for the inner layer of every Czochralski crucible. Flip: hydrolyze SiCl4, the main byproduct of Siemens polysilicon plants, into sol-gel silica and sinter it into the crucible's inner wall, keeping ordinary sand only for the outer structural shell.
why: High-purity quartz chokepoint (>80% Spruce Pine): turns a waste stream into crucible feedstock and takes HPQ demand for crucible inner layers toward zero.
note: Same synthetic-silica crucible liner as I-06658, SiCl4 feed.

title: Tungsten closed loop from chamber shields and scrubber residues
idea: Worsen: let 70-90% of WF6 tungsten end up on chamber walls, in scrubbers and in sludge. Flip: line W CVD chambers with removable collection shields, oxidize the shield and scrubber tungsten into soluble tungstate, refine it to ammonium paratungstate and re-fluorinate it to WF6 domestically.
why: Tungsten (~80% China) and low CVD utilization: the loop could cut virgin W demand ~50-70%.

title: Memory-as-a-service: makers keep ownership and take modules back
idea: Worsen: sell DRAM outright, so makers profit from short lives and scrap. Flip: makers lease memory capacity to data centers by the GB-month, keep ownership, and take modules back for re-binning, repair and redeployment, so durability becomes the maker's profit lever.
why: Usable supply per wafer and capital intensity: each fabricated bit serves 2-3 deployments.

title: Rotary spatial ALD conveyor for capacitor dielectric stacks
idea: Worse: deposit ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor stacks by slow pulse-purge temporal ALD. Flip: carry wafers on a rotating platen under gas-curtain-separated precursor zones (spatial ALD from solar passivation), so each revolution is one cycle at ~10x throughput and higher precursor utilization.
why: Throughput/capital: capacitor dielectric/electrode tool count falls ~60-80% and Zr/Hf precursor use drops.

title: Reusable porous-silicon seed wafers slash crucible-quartz demand
idea: Worse: consume one Czochralski crystal slice, and its share of a Spruce Pine crucible, per wafer. Flip: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial device layer on a porous-Si release layer, transfer it to a cheap carrier or the bonded periphery wafer, and reuse the seed wafer 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource: high-purity quartz crucible use per wafer falls 90%+ and substrate cost drops.

title: Near-memory collectives eliminate per-GPU staging buffers
idea: Worsen: allocate large send/receive staging buffers in every GPU for all-reduce and all-gather. Flip: execute reductions inside the CXL or NVLink-attached memory pool, so each GPU writes once into the pool and reads the reduced result back, with no per-GPU staging copies.
why: Capacity: frees 5-15% of HBM per accelerator used today for communication buffers, and cuts redundant traffic.

title: Microfluidic interposer channels hold DRAM cool to cut refresh
idea: Worsen: put the hottest logic directly under DRAM so retention collapses and refresh doubles every ~10 C. Flip: etch microfluidic coolant channels in the interposer and base die between logic and memory so DRAM runs at ~45 C instead of ~90 C, stretching refresh intervals 4-8x.
why: Refresh (fact 3): refresh overhead falls from 10-20% to ~2-4% of bandwidth and idle power drops; also unblocks memory-on-logic stacking.
note: Interlayer microfluidics widely researched (IBM, Georgia Tech).

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard lets any logic fab make memory
idea: Worsen: let memory supply depend on three firms because only they can build the capacitor. Flip: publish an open memory-chiplet standard (UCIe-based protocol, bump map, test and thermal envelope) for capacitorless dies such as SRAM, gain-cell, ROM and flash, so mid-size logic fabs can sell interchangeable memory chiplets.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: brings dozens of logic fabs into memory supply and makes them compete on cost per bit.
note: Capacitorless chiplets cost far more per bit than DRAM.

title: Sacrificial canary cells trigger refresh only when needed
idea: Worse: refresh every row at the worst-case 64 ms forever, blind to real temperature and aging. Flip: plant ~0.1% deliberately weakened canary cells (half-depth capacitor, leakier junction) in every subarray; a tiny comparator polls them and refreshes that subarray only when canaries start to decay, so refresh tracks actual physics instead of a datasheet guardband.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: typical retention is 10-100x the 64 ms spec, so canary-paced refresh can cut refresh energy/bandwidth loss 4-10x, and weaker main cells can ship because the canary tracks their real decay.

title: Base-die patch cache repairs any core die's weak cells
idea: Worse: give each core die a fixed, fused spare-row budget, so one unlucky die runs out of spares while its neighbors waste theirs. Flip: put a small SRAM patch cache plus address CAM on the HBM base logic die that serves correct data for weak rows of any core die, loaded at boot from a stored repair map and updatable in the field.
why: Facts 6-7: pools repair resources across the stack, raising stack yield and allowing core dies with fewer on-die spares and smaller periphery.

title: Ship-then-learn: dies finish retention testing inside customer servers
idea: Worse: hold every die in hours-long, worst-case retention testers. Flip: ship after a short screen with conservative 32 ms refresh, then let the module's own BIST profile each row's retention during its first weeks of idle time and gradually relax refresh to measured values, uploading the map to the controller.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): retention test is a large share of test-floor capital and cycle time; moving it into the field could cut test cost 30-50% and shorten time to market.

title: Weak rows auto-morph into differential twin-cell pairs
idea: Worse: store a weak row's bits in single cells and hope. Flip: when a row's retention or margin drops below threshold, the DRAM pairs it with its neighbor row in a twin-cell (2T2C) mode where the two cells hold complementary charge on both bitline halves, doubling the sense signal at half capacity for just those rows.
why: Facts 1 and 3: converts the weak tail (~0.1-1% of rows) into reliable storage instead of spares or fuses, allowing smaller Cs at an affordable capacity cost.

title: Closed-loop helium recapture and hydrogen-argon backside cooling
idea: Worse: vent all fab helium and rely on Qatar. Flip: capture helium from wafer backside cooling, leak checking and chamber purges with cryogenic and membrane recovery for >90% recycle, and switch backside cooling in etch and deposition to H2/Ar blends where conductivity suffices.
why: Cuts per-wafer helium demand ~80-90%, removing the Qatar chokepoint from DRAM output.
note: Same recapture mechanism as I-03645 plus H2/Ar backside substitution.

title: Synthetic-silica crucibles from ordinary sand via chloride purification
idea: Worse: depend on Spruce Pine quartz for every crystal puller. Flip: convert common silica sand to SiCl4, distill it, and hydrolyze it into synthetic fused-silica grain for crucible inner layers, then regenerate used crucibles by stripping and re-lining only the inner layer.
why: Breaks a >80% single-mine dependency for crucibles; scarce-resource intensity of wafers drops.
note: Synthetic-silica crucible liners already exist commercially.

title: Tungsten urban mining from spent sputter targets and chamber shields
idea: Worse: buy fresh Chinese tungsten for every wordline and contact. Flip: collect spent W targets, CVD chamber kits and WF6 scrubber residues across U.S. fabs and refine them electrochemically back to WF6 feedstock in a shared regional plant.
why: Spent targets keep ~70% of their tungsten; a closed loop could cover a large share of fab demand and cut China dependence.

title: National tool bank leasing recertified 300 mm tools to micro-fabs
idea: Worse: make every new fab wait 18-24 months for new tools. Flip: a public-private bank buys used 300 mm DUV scanners, etchers and ALD tools from closing or upgrading fabs, refurbishes them, and leases them on 5-year terms to memory startups and pilot lines.
why: Cuts startup capex ~60-70% and tool lead time to months.

title: Lighthouse keeper: photonic-crystal nanocavity optical bistable bit
idea: A lighthouse keeper stores the message in the beam itself. Each bit is an InP photonic-crystal nanocavity held in one of two optically bistable states by a shared ~uW holding laser; femtojoule pulses on a waveguide write and read it, as a buffer co-packaged with optical I/O.
why: Attacks data-movement energy (fact 5) by keeping data optical between links, with no electrical charge to leak.
note: NTT showed PhC RAM; holding power and density limit.

title: Bonsai minimal fab: half-inch dry pilot lines for exotic cells
idea: A bonsai master grows a forest on a tray. Build storage-element pilot lines on half-inch wafers with sealed, shuttle-based minimal-fab tools: only a local cleanroom, dry processes and no UPW plant. Each new bit physics can then be tested for ~$5M instead of ~$500M.
why: Cuts the capital and learning time behind fact 4. A line with no UPW plant uses more than 10x less water per experiment.

title: Farmer's soil probe: replica-leakage sensor triggers refresh per mat
idea: A farmer irrigates when the soil probe reads dry, not by the calendar. Each 512-row mat gets a 'probe' of 256 minimum-Vt, maximum-GIDL replica access transistors in parallel discharging a 50 fF reference node; a comparator fires that mat's refresh when the replica node crosses the sense limit, so the interval follows real temperature, voltage and aging instead of the 85 C worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): servers typically run at 40-60 C, where retention is 4-16x the spec point; a tracking interval cuts refresh energy and lost bandwidth 3-8x for ~0.1% probe area.

title: Mechanic's torque wrench: per-row fused negative wordline level
idea: A mechanic torques each bolt to its own spec. At test, each row's leakiest cell is measured and a 3-bit fuse sets that row's off-level from 0 to -0.6 V, applied by its local sub-wordline drivers; strong rows sit near 0 V (low GIDL, low stress) and only weak rows get deep negative bias.
why: A single global negative wordline trades subthreshold leakage against GIDL; tuning per row lifts worst-case retention ~2-4x and reduces the large wordline swings that aggravate row hammer.
note: Per-row fused VNWL; same tuned-off-level mechanism.

title: Glissando wordlines: stepwise adiabatic charging from tank capacitors
idea: A musician slides through notes instead of jumping. Ramp each wordline to 3 V in four steps from a ladder of on-die tank capacitors (built from spare cell capacitors) and return the charge to the tanks on the falling edge, instead of switching straight from the pump.
why: Stepwise charging cuts wordline CV^2 loss ~4x and avoids ~30%-efficient pump conversion, attacking the 3 V wordline energy floor (fact 10).

title: Plumber's backflow: hand restored bitline charge to the next mat
idea: A plumber never dumps hot water that could preheat the next tank. When one mat closes, its bitlines still at VDD are briefly shorted to the rising bitlines of the next mat being sensed, handing over about half their charge before the supply finishes the restore.
why: Cuts bitline restore energy ~20-30% per activate, a large part of the ~5.9 pJ per useful bit random read (fact 8).

title: Homeostatic body bias: replica latch steers sense-amp wells
idea: Living cells hold their internal state steady by feedback. A replica sense amp per bank measures its own offset continuously, and a slow loop adjusts the NMOS and PMOS well bias of the whole SA stripe to null systematic drift from temperature and NBTI aging.
why: Systematic drift is ~30-40% of the SA guard band; nulling it lets SA devices shrink or bitlines lengthen (fact 7).

title: Triage-nurse refresh: in-die retention classes skip strong rows
idea: A triage nurse checks the sickest patients most often. At wafer test each row's retention is classed by timed SA reads after reduced restore; the class map sits in a small on-die table, and the internal refresh engine skips strong rows on most REF commands, with a guard class for variable-retention cells.
why: Cuts internal refresh operations ~50-70% and their energy (fact 3) while REF commands stay unchanged.

title: Shipbuilder's reusable donor hull: fifty Smart-Cut tiers per wafer
idea: Shipyards reuse the same slipway. Implant hydrogen into one thick bulk donor, bond it, cleave a 60 nm single-crystal Si tier, CMP the donor and repeat ~50 times. Each tier gets its transistors at <=450C.
why: Gives single-crystal channel tiers for 3D DRAM, and one Czochralski wafer feeds 50 tiers, cutting high-purity quartz crucible demand per bit ~50x.

title: Braille embosser's dual-relief stamp: one-imprint wordline and contact
idea: A blind reader's world is embossed, not projected. Pattern the perfectly periodic array with nanoimprint lithography from a master carrying two relief heights, so wordline trench and contact depth are defined in one dual-damascene imprint.
why: Per-layer patterning cost falls to ~1/3-1/5 of EUV, and two litho steps merge into one (Fact 4). The master can be repaired because the array has no randomness.
note: Dual-relief imprint for dual damascene has prior art; core is NIL replacing EUV on periodic arrays.

title: Gleaner's leftover grain: restacking fab-rejected DRAM dies
idea: Gleaners collect the grain harvesters leave behind. A 10-person team buys binned-out DRAM dies (partial-bank fails, weak retention, slow bins) at scrap prices, thins them, and stacks 8 on a small base ASIC that maps out dead banks and sets per-die refresh. The stacks are sold as capacity modules for AI KV caches.
why: Turns ~5-10% of scrapped fab output into usable supply with no new wafers. Capex is a die bonder and a wire bonder.
note: Same binned-die restacking with remap base die.

title: Sourdough baker keeps the starter: porous-silicon wafer printing
idea: Persona: a baker who keeps the starter and bakes many loaves. Anodize a parent wafer into a double-porosity porous-Si layer and grow a 50-100 um DRAM-grade epitaxial film on it. After processing or bonding, split at the weak porous layer and reuse the parent wafer 10-20 times.
why: One crucible-grown wafer yields 10-20 device substrates, so polysilicon, quartz crucibles and crystal-growth energy per bit fall ~5-10x.

title: 2050 engineer's reusable parent wafer: kerfless porous-silicon lift-off
idea: A 2050 engineer laughs that we melt polysilicon in a quartz crucible and saw it for every slice. Grow DRAM-grade epitaxial silicon on a sintered double-layer porous-silicon release layer over a parent wafer, run the front end, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier, cleave at the porous layer, and re-polish the parent for ~10-20 more cycles.
why: Cuts prime-wafer and high-purity-quartz crucible demand ~10-20x (Spruce Pine chokepoint) and leaves a thin device layer ready for stacking. Risks: epi defects driving the retention tail, and porous-layer stability through 1000 C steps.

title: Railroad standard gauge: open memory-brick footprint any fab can supply
idea: Railroads boomed once gauge was standard: define an open, royalty-free 'memory brick' footprint (bump map, PHY, thermal envelope, test hooks) so DRAM dies from any fab, including U.S. mature-node lines, drop onto any vendor's interposer the way containers fit any ship.
why: Raises usable supply by breaking HBM's three-vendor lock-in and qualification lag: second-source memory chiplets could add capacity within 18-24 months, not 3-5 years.

title: Core-memory technician's threaded coil column broadcast bus
idea: Like wires threaded through a stack of ferrite cores: a single vertical column of aligned on-die spiral coils runs through all 16 dies of a stack, so the base die broadcasts commands and addresses to every die at once inductively, with no command TSVs.
why: Removes command/address TSVs and their keep-out area, so the per-die TSV tax drops and stacks with mismatched dies can be mixed; ~0.1 pJ/bit for broadcast.
note: ThruChip Interface inductive stacking is well published.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: maskless late-binding RDL after die test
idea: A tailor cuts after measuring: mount mass-produced memory chiplets loosely, test them, then write the interposer RDL wiring per package with direct-write laser lithography, routing around dead dies and binning good banks into full channels.
why: Removes interposer mask sets and rescues partially failing dies (HBM yield loss 20-30%); claimed 10-15% more usable bits per wafer.
note: Deca Adaptive Patterning already does per-package maskless RDL.

title: Navy signalman's heliograph: optical retromodulator backscatter from memory
idea: A signalman flashes a mirror instead of carrying a lamp: the cool-side controller shines a beam onto the memory chiplet, which sends data back by switching an electro-absorption retroreflector, so the hot memory side has no laser and very little transmit power.
why: No laser in the 125 C package and almost no transmit heat on the memory side; claimed ~0.2 pJ/bit on the memory end of the link.
note: External-laser modulator links are standard silicon photonics practice.

title: Soviet salvage grade: sell retention-binned reject dies with refresh maps
idea: A Soviet engineer under embargo wastes nothing: dies that fail 64 ms retention or have a few dead subarrays are binned into 16 ms and 32 ms classes and packaged as 'salvage-grade' modules whose SPD carries a compressed per-row refresh/remap table, which an open controller-firmware specification honors.
why: Supply strategy: raises usable output by an estimated 3-8% of wafer starts with zero new fab capex.

title: Chef tastes and adjusts: in-line probing retunes ink chemistry mid-roll
idea: A chef tastes the sauce while it cooks: test structures printed every few meters of web are probed in-line (Vth, off-current, capacitance), and a feedback controller adjusts the next meters' oxide-precursor ink composition (e.g., Ga/Zn ratio), drop volume and flash-lamp energy, narrowing the device distribution in real time.
why: Variation, not mean performance, sets the ECC and redundancy overhead; halving sigma could halve spare and ECC overhead on printed memory and raise yield.

title: Biologist's apoptosis: sell dies with dead banks as smaller parts
idea: Cells die in a controlled way so the organism survives. Likewise, fuse off the failed banks or subarrays on DRAM dies that miss full spec and ship them as 12 Gb or 8 Gb 'harvested' parts, with a JEDEC capacity descriptor so controllers map only the live banks (GPU binning applied to memory).
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers the ~5-15% of dies scrapped at wafer sort and burn-in, adding supply without a single new wafer.
note: GPU-style binning applied to DRAM; DDR5 non-binary densities make it practical.

title: Error-tolerant AI cells with half-height capacitors and BER budget
idea: LLM weights and activations survive ~1e-5 bit error rates in low-order mantissa bits, so an 'approximate' DRAM grade uses 2-2.5 fF capacitors at AR ~30:1 with longer refresh, while sign and exponent bits live in a few full-charge rows of the same mat. The storage element is deliberately under-built where the extreme user does not care.
why: Halves capacitor aspect ratio (fact 1), cutting HAR etch/deposition cost and refresh power ~2x for the ~70% of AI bits that tolerate noise: roughly 15-25% cost-per-bit gain.

title: Photonic-crystal nanocavity bistable bits for optical router packet buffers
idea: Optical packet routers want buffers that stay in the optical domain; InP or Si photonic-crystal nanocavities with carrier-induced bistability hold a bit at ~30-100 nW while light circulates and switch with fJ optical pulses. Placed beside co-packaged optics they cache data in flight without O-E-O conversion.
why: Targets data-movement energy (fact 5) in interconnect-heavy AI fabrics; density is low (~um2/bit), so it is a small fast tier, not bulk DRAM.
note: NTT showed PhC nanocavity optical RAM; low density niche.

title: LN2-immersion memory pods with 77K-retuned low-Vt access transistors
idea: Borrowing from cryo-CMOS built for quantum-computer control, retune the access transistor for 77 K: subthreshold slope steepens from ~80 to ~20 mV/dec, so Vt can drop ~0.4 V and the wordline from ~3 V to ~1.5 V while off-current still falls >1000x. DIMMs run immersed in boiling liquid nitrogen (made from air, no chokepoint) with refresh stretched from 64 ms to minutes.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh tax (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) goes to near zero and wordline CV^2 roughly quarters; cryoplant overhead must stay below the saving, which favors large AI memory pods.
note: Cryocooler overhead ~10x at 77 K erodes savings.

title: Pacemaker-style adiabatic refresh recycling charge between subarrays
idea: Implants live on nanowatts by never dumping charge to ground. During refresh, pair a subarray whose bitlines must rise with one whose bitlines must fall and move charge between them through a stepwise switched-capacitor ladder, so each refresh recovers roughly half of the bitline CV^2 instead of discarding it.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) could drop ~40-60% and self-refresh standby power with it, for a few % more periphery area.

title: Particle-detector correlated double sampling: decay-tracking reference cells
idea: Detector front-ends subtract a reference sample taken under identical conditions. Each subarray keeps reference cells written with 1 and 0 at the same moment as the data rows and refreshed with them; the sense reference is set at the midpoint of the decayed reference pair instead of a fixed VBL/2.
why: Fact 3: as stored ones droop the reference follows, so cells stay readable down to much lower residual charge, plausibly a 2-3x longer refresh interval and better temperature tolerance.

title: Trusted-foundry domestic metals: tungsten-free TiN or poly buried wordlines
idea: Defense trusted foundries prize domestic materials. Replace tungsten in buried wordlines with TiN-only or heavily doped polysilicon; the higher RC makes far-end access devices turn on late and leaves some cells partly restored (~0.5-1% raw BER near row ends), which the code absorbs instead of finer wordline segmentation.
why: Resources: removes a China-~80% tungsten dependency from the array (contacts can move to U.S.-mined molybdenum) at no density cost, with a modest throughput hit at row ends.

title: Fleet-learned per-bank sense timing and voltage from hyperscaler telemetry
idea: Hyperscalers are extreme users with millions of DIMMs: expose per-bank trim registers for tRCD, sense delay, VARY and refresh rate, and let a fleet model trained on correctable-error events and temperature push tuned settings to each die over its life.
why: Recovers ~15-25% latency and energy margin designed for worst-case silicon, and raises usable supply by keeping marginal dies in service.
note: Adaptive-latency DRAM known; needs hyperscaler cooperation.

title: Lunar-fab materials: molybdenum periphery contacts and helium-free processing
idea: Design periphery for a fab with no tungsten or helium, as on a Moon base: periphery contact plugs and wordline straps use ALD molybdenum or ruthenium instead of W/WF6, and wafer backside cooling uses hydrogen-argon blends instead of helium, all at DUV rules.
why: Removes chokepoints (tungsten ~80% China, Qatari helium offline) from periphery and lowers small-via resistance.

title: NMOS-only bootstrap wordline drivers revive 1970s DRAM tricks
idea: Early DRAM designers had no PMOS and drove wordlines with self-bootstrapped NMOS gates; reusing this, sub-wordline drivers need no PMOS or n-well, which removes well spacing from the SWD stripe and gives a uniform NMOS pitch printable with DUV.
why: SWD stripe area -25-35% (fact 7) and fewer masks.

title: Hot-spare tiers from 30-year industrial controllers raise stack yield
idea: An industrial controller must run 30 years unserviced, so each 3D array carries two spare tiers and a per-mat tier-remap table in the bonded logic layer; a failing tier is retired in the field and its data copied to a spare. In the fab the same mechanism lets a 64-tier stack ship with any two bad tiers.
why: Tier-count yield blocks 3D DRAM (fact 2): 0.99^64 = 53% compound tier yield rises to ~97% with two spares, ~1.5x lower cost per bit.
note: Spare tiers with remap table; monolithic tier defects are local, so mat-level remap matters more.

title: Fiber-optic preform silica lines CZ crucibles, ending Spruce Pine dependence
idea: Optical-fiber makers need ppb-pure silica and synthesize it by flame hydrolysis of SiCl4 instead of mining it. Polysilicon plants produce SiCl4 as a byproduct: turn it into synthetic silica soot and sinter a 3-5 mm bubble-free inner liner onto a crucible shell made from ordinary non-Spruce quartz sand.
why: HPQ crucibles are >80% Spruce Pine: a synthetic inner layer could cut HPQ per crucible ~70% and turns a polysilicon waste stream into a strategic input.
note: Synthetic-silica inner-layer crucibles already commercial.

title: Space-station water loop: 98% UPW recovery with vapor-compression distillation
idea: The ISS recycles ~98% of its water with vapor-compression distillation and catalytic oxidation. Build fab reclaim the same way: segregate rinse streams by contamination class, send low-TOC rinses straight back through UV/RO/EDI, and push high-TOC streams through mechanical-vapor-recompression distillation, targeting 90-98% reuse.
why: Water limits Arizona and Texas fabs: cuts withdrawal ~5-10x and opens water-scarce U.S. regions for siting.

title: Constellation-style field self-repair replaces hours of DRAM burn-in
idea: Extreme user: satellite constellations that fly tens of thousands of COTS parts and repair in orbit. Ship DRAM with on-die BIST plus repeatable post-package repair of spare rows at every power-up, and screen infant mortality in the field instead of multi-hour high-temperature burn-in.
why: Test capital: burn-in ovens and testers are ~10-15% of DRAM cost; cutting burn-in time ~70% removes a large tester fleet and floor space.

title: Helium-free wafer backside cooling for a helium-blockade fab
idea: Edge case: Qatar's helium offline since March 2026. Replace helium backside gas in etch/CVD electrostatic chucks with hydrogen-argon mixes or compliant solid thermal-interface chuck surfaces, and switch leak detection to hydrogen-tracer sniffers.
why: Scarce resource: removes the main helium dependence of a DRAM fab with minor recipe retuning; avoids shutdowns.

title: Block-copolymer hexagonal holes with alumina infiltration replace EUV capacitor layer
idea: Extreme user: an EUV-less fab. Self-assemble non-fluorinated PS-b-PMMA into a hexagonal hole lattice at ~24 nm pitch on a guide pattern, harden the PMMA with sequential-infiltration Al2O3 (TMA/H2O) or remove it with UV + acetic acid, and transfer with Cl2/HBr.
why: Litho: replaces 1-2 EUV exposures for the capacitor array with a coat-and-bake step; the infiltration hardmask survives chlorine transfer.

title: HCl-vapor lateral SiGe recess builds fluorine-free stacked 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache racks that need capacity density above all. In Si/SiGe superlattice 3D DRAM, cut the lateral cavities for capacitors and transistors with HCl vapor at ~600C, which etches SiGe selectively, instead of CF4/O2 or HF/H2O2 etches.
why: 3D DRAM: makes the ~26+ tier lateral-recess module fluorine-free and epi-compatible, removing a key process blocker.
note: HCl vapor SiGe etch is known in GAA flows; incremental process enabler.

title: Thermally decomposable polynorbornene air-gap bitlines boost sensing margin
idea: Extreme user: 0.5 V energy-harvesting IoT that needs a large sense signal. Fill between bitlines with a sacrificial polynorbornene that decomposes cleanly at ~425C through a porous cap, leaving air gaps with no fluorinated low-k or HF release.
why: Capacitor wall: bitline capacitance falls ~30-40%, so the same signal needs ~30% less Cs, allowing shorter pillars and an easier capacitor etch.

title: PFAS-free fab plumbing using polyolefin, PEEK, metal seals and dry pumps
idea: Extreme user: implant-device makers demanding fully PFAS-free supply chains. Replace PFA/PTFE/PVDF wetted parts with high-purity HDPE/PP, PEEK, quartz and electropolished stainless, FFKM o-rings with metal/EPDM seals, and PFPE-oil pumps with dry screw pumps.
why: Policy-proofs the fab against EU/US PFAS bans that could otherwise stop a line; small cost, large continuity value.

title: UNIVAC delay lines reborn: fiber loops as packet buffers
idea: From 1950s mercury delay-line memory: switch and NIC packet buffers are replaced by recirculating DWDM fiber loops where data is stored as light in flight and regenerated each lap by a semiconductor optical amplifier, with an SRAM index recording which time slot holds which packet.
why: Buffer DRAM/SRAM holds data that is only waiting; a 20 km loop at 1.6 Tb/s holds ~20 MB with no capacitor and no refresh.
note: Optical packet-switch fiber delay buffers are well studied; sequential access only.

title: Sparse-HPC zero elision: pattern lines stored as metadata only
idea: From sparse-matrix HPC where most memory lines are zero: the controller keeps a per-line 2-bit pattern tag (zero, repeated byte, repeated word, real data) in ECC-adjacent metadata, so patterned lines consume no data storage and backing pages are reclaimed dynamically.
why: Sparse tensors, fresh allocations and padded buffers are often >90% patterned lines; eliding them cuts DRAM, and fab water, ~10x for those workloads.
note: Zero/pattern line compression known; large gains only in niche workloads.

title: XIP-style narrow serial DRAM chiplets for a bulk capacity tier
idea: $1 microcontrollers execute in place from 12-pin Octal-SPI/HyperRAM parts. Define a 12-16-pin high-speed serial DRAM chiplet for accelerator capacity tiers, ringed on cheap substrate, with a large logic-side cache hiding latency.
why: Pins and PHY area per GB drop ~5-10x vs DDR/HBM, so many cheap older-node DRAM dies add capacity without HBM's TSV and interposer costs.

title: Mars-rover autonomy: on-die repair agent remaps rows without the host
idea: Mars rovers repair faults on their own because Earth is 20 light-minutes away. Put a tiny state-machine agent and a 1-4K-entry CAM in the DRAM periphery or HBM base die. The agent watches on-die ECC syndromes, judges when a row or column is degrading, copies it to a spare during refresh slots and redirects its address. Repairs are reversible and continue for the whole life of the part, not just once at test.
why: In-field degradation (VRT, aging, hammer damage) turns into silent sparing. Dies with marginal rows can ship, giving ~2-5% yield and a several-fold cut in field DIMM replacements (facts 3, 9).

title: Fleet-proven spec: JEDEC grade with percentile error limits and mandatory ECC
idea: Hyperscaler field studies show real DRAM errors come from a small minority of cells. Create a JEDEC grade that states retention and hammer specs as percentiles (e.g., at most 1e-6 of cells may fail at 64 ms and 85 C) and requires system ECC, instead of demanding that every cell meet the worst case.
why: The worst 1e-6 tail sets refresh and capacitor height today. Percentile specs let vendors ship dies that are now scrapped or downbinned and trim guardbands: ~5-10% yield plus capacitor relief (facts 1, 3).

title: Hyperscale error fingerprints: a CVE-style exchange for DRAM failure signatures
idea: The largest fleets log billions of DIMM-hours. Create an industry exchange where operators and vendors share anonymized correctable-error spatial fingerprints (bank, row and column patterns per die lot). Host controllers use them to predict which pages will go uncorrectable and retire them early, and vendors adjust screening by lot.
why: Predictive retirement makes dies with higher raw error rates safe to deploy and could cut DIMM replacements ~30-50%, lifting usable supply and tightening yield feedback to fabs (facts 3, 9).

title: Trusted-memory advance market commitment for U.S.-made DRAM
idea: Defense, the extreme price-insensitive user, signs a Warp-Speed-style 10-year take-or-pay commitment for U.S.-fabbed DRAM at a ceiling price, with surplus resold commercially, so a domestic line becomes bankable before it ships.
why: U.S. manufacturability from 1-2% share; turns policy demand into financeable offtake.
note: Same guaranteed-purchase mechanism as I-00893, defense-targeted.

title: Low-barrier magnetic tunnel junction refreshed like DRAM
idea: Time-shift the magnet's retention from 10 years to ~1 s by designing thermal stability near 25 kT; a small STT pulse writes it and a DRAM-like controller refreshes every few hundred ms, so the bit is held in spin, not charge.
why: Energy and endurance: write current ~5x lower than nonvolatile MRAM, essentially unlimited endurance, and a cell with no capacitor at ~20 F2.
note: Same relaxed-retention MTJ idea.

title: Kinetic-inductance nanowire loops hold persistent-current bits
idea: Pair cell scale with datacenter cryogenics: NbN nanowire loops 100-200 nm across store a fluxon as circulating supercurrent with indefinite retention at 4 K, read by a nanowire cryotron; deployed in cryo pods next to superconducting accelerators.
why: Energy: zJ-class writes and no refresh; kinetic inductance shrinks the loop well below magnetic-inductance limits.
note: Known nanocryotron memory work; 4 K helium-dependent niche.

title: Deuterium-hardened access stack starves variable-retention traps
idea: Scale jump down to the atomic nucleus: replace hydrogen with deuterium in the final forming-gas anneal and in SiN/SiO2 precursors around the access transistor and storage junction; the heavier Si-D bond resists breaking, so fewer interface and junction traps form over life and fewer metastable defects toggle, which is the source of variable retention time.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): VRT and trap-assisted GIDL dominate the <=13 fA tail; the isotope effect cuts hot-carrier trap generation 10-50x in logic, so a 2-4x tighter retention tail and longer refresh interval are plausible.
note: Deuterium passivation is known art for hot-carrier and DRAM retention.

title: Graded work-function wordline flattens the GIDL hotspot
idea: Scale shift into a nanometre composition profile: deposit the buried wordline as a laterally graded TiN-to-TiAlN stack (composition changing over ~10-20 nm) so the gate work function is lower facing the storage node and higher at the channel centre, reducing the gate-to-drain field that drives band-to-band tunnelling while keeping Vt high.
why: GIDL tail (fact 3): ~20-30% lower peak field gives ~10x lower GIDL and permits a smaller negative wordline bias (fact 10).
note: Dual work-function buried wordlines are already used to cut GIDL.

title: Carbon co-implant gettering scrubs iron from storage junctions
idea: Scale shift to ppb impurities: a single mid-gap Fe or Ni atom in a depletion region can create a 1e-9 tail cell, so carbon is implanted a few hundred nm below the array (with an oxygen-precipitate denuded zone) and C-related complexes getter transition metals away from storage junctions throughout the thermal budget.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tail cells are often single-defect; gettering targets 2-5x fewer tail cells and longer refresh bins using only carbon.

title: HBM stack thermal gradient: long-lived data sinks to cooler dies
idea: Scale shift to the stack: HBM layers run at different temperatures (top dies 5-15 C hotter), so the controller sets a per-die refresh interval from on-die sensors and migrates long-lived, rarely accessed pages to the coolest layers while frequently touched (naturally refreshed) data lives in the hottest ones.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): retention halves per ~10 C, so per-die binning and placement cut refresh ~30-50% in unmodified Si/Cu HBM.

title: Slow-tier thick-oxide cell trades 30 ns for ten-second retention
idea: Time trade inside the access device: a capacity-tier DRAM built with 5-6 nm SiO2, long-channel, high-Vt access transistors at relaxed pitch accepts tRCD ~30-40 ns in exchange for ~10 s retention, with wide parallel interfaces hiding latency for bulk AI weights.
why: Refresh (fact 3) nearly eliminated, and capital (fact 4): the tier can run on depreciated 28-40 nm DUV fabs in the U.S. using only Si, SiO2, TiN, Al and Cu.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging from a tank-capacitor ladder
idea: Time-stretch the wordline edge from ~1 ns to ~5 ns and charge it in 6 voltage steps from a ladder of deep-trench tank capacitors on the periphery wafer that recapture the charge when the wordline falls, so each 3 V wordline is charged quasi-adiabatically instead of straight from the VPP pump.
why: Wordline CV^2 at ~3 V plus ~30-40%-efficient pumps are stuck at the voltage floor (fact 10); stepwise charging cuts wordline+pump energy ~4-5x, about 10-15% of activation energy, for a few ns of tRCD.

title: Size sense amps for 3.5 sigma, repair the tail by columns
idea: Time-shift the design decision to wafer test: SA input pairs are sized for 3.5-sigma Pelgrom offset instead of ~6 sigma, and the ~0.02% of SAs whose offset fails at sort are mapped out once, for the chip's years-long life, with extra spare columns.
why: Matching-device area scales with the square of the sigma target, so SA input pairs shrink ~3x, SA stripes ~25-35%, about 5-8% of die area (fact 7).

title: 77 K drawer in each rack holds long-lived data refresh-free
idea: Scale jump to rack infrastructure: one liquid-nitrogen-cooled drawer per rack hosts DRAM whose leakage at 77 K gives hours-to-days retention, with sense amps re-centered for cryogenic Vt and lower offset; warm DRAM keeps hot data while the cold drawer holds embedding tables and long-lived state with refresh disabled.
why: Zero refresh power (fact 3) and faster cryo periphery; the ~10 W-per-W cooling overhead restricts it to capacity-heavy, low-access data.

title: One mandrel, eight spacers, punched through 32 tiers
idea: Amortize one sub-litho pattern across many tiers: print 180-nm mandrel lines with KrF, run three rounds of sidewall-spacer doubling to reach ~22-nm lines, and transfer that pattern once through a 32-tier stack. One patterning sequence serves 32 tiers, so litho cost per bit falls ~32x.
why: Litho capital and EUV dependence (fact 4): sub-25-nm pitch from 1990s steppers, amortized across tiers.
note: Spacer multiplication amortized over tiers is inherent to 3D stacks.

title: Taper-aware tiers: size each tier's cells to match the hole taper
idea: Accept the 88-89 degree taper of 1990s RIE instead of buying new tools, and design for the depth variation tier by tier: deeper tiers get thicker deposited gate layers, so a narrower hole at depth still yields matched transistor drive and capacitance.
why: High-AR etch is a 3D blocker (fact 2): a tool limit becomes a design parameter, letting old etchers handle 32+ tiers.

title: Spatial ALD converts precursor pulses in time into zones in space
idea: Time-to-space shift: rather than seconds-long pulse/purge cycles that send >90% of the Zr/Hf/Ti precursor to the exhaust, wafers rotate under a gas-bearing head. There, each precursor is confined by N2 curtains and pulled back through a cold-trap return loop for reuse.
why: Raises precursor utilization from ~5-10% to >50%, cutting hafnium/zirconium chemical and energy per wafer 5-10x and raising throughput 3-5x. Conformality in deep holes must be proven.

title: Supercritical CO2 cleans and dries tall capacitor pillars without water
idea: Jump from wafer scale to pillar scale: capillary forces during water/IPA drying topple 70:1 pillars, which is why support lattices and extra films are added. Replace post-etch wet clean, rinse and dry with scCO2 plus chelating co-solvents, which have zero surface tension.
why: Cuts ultra-pure water per capacitor module ~30-50% and removes the collapse limit, allowing taller unsupported pillars for higher Cs.

title: Machine-shop carbide scrap becomes domestic tungsten hexafluoride
idea: Scale jump from industrial tooling to semiconductor gas: collect U.S. cemented-carbide scrap (drills, inserts; thousands of t/yr) and recover tungsten by the zinc process or oxidation to WO3. An existing U.S. chemical plant then fluorinates it to electronic-grade WF6.
why: Builds a domestic closed loop around the ~80%-Chinese tungsten chokepoint. Fab WF6 demand is only hundreds of tonnes, far below the scrap available.

title: Molecular self-assembly prints the capacitor lattice instead of EUV
idea: Scale shift from scanner optics down to molecular length: a high-chi block copolymer (PS-b-PDMS or PS-b-PMMA) self-assembles into a hexagonal cylinder lattice that matches the honeycomb capacitor array, registered by an ArF-immersion guide pattern at 4x pitch; sequential infiltration synthesis turns one block into an alumina hardmask for the hole etch.
why: Removes 1-2 EUV exposures (capacitor hole, landing pad) from Fact 4; ~15-25% lower array litho cost per wafer because the molecule, not the scanner, sets the pitch.

title: Shift burn-in from oven hours to fleet weeks
idea: Time-shift the reliability screen: skip factory burn-in ovens and long retention tests, ship dies with on-die BIST that runs adaptive stress patterns during the first weeks of server idle time, and retire weak rows through the host before data is trusted.
why: Burn-in and test are ~10% of DRAM cost and heavy capital; cutting them ~70% saves ~5-7% per bit and frees tester capacity.

title: Colorado molybdenum replaces Chinese tungsten from mine to monolayer
idea: Vertical integration across scales: Colorado molybdenite is refined domestically into MoO2Cl2/MoCl5 ALD precursors, and molybdenum replaces tungsten in buried wordlines and contacts, where its shorter electron mean free path gives lower resistance below 20 nm width.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint; ~20-30% lower wordline resistance permits longer wordlines and less periphery.

title: Kerfless epitaxial wafers: one seed crystal reused fifty times
idea: DRAM uses only the top few microns of a 775 um wafer: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial Si film on a porous-Si release layer atop a reusable seed wafer, lift it off onto a low-cost domestic carrier, and re-polish the seed for ~50 reuses.
why: Cuts Czochralski pulling, quartz crucibles and polysilicon per wafer by ~10-30x; Michigan polysilicon and U.S. epi reactors suffice.

title: Thin sol-gel synthetic liner so crucibles need 10x less HPQ
idea: Scale jump from bulk to skin: build the crucible body from lower-grade quartz and line only the 1-2 mm surface that touches the melt with synthetic sol-gel silica made from chemical precursors.
why: Spruce Pine supplies >80% of high-purity quartz. Confining high purity to the melt-contact layer cuts HPQ demand per crucible ~10x.

title: Hydrogen ion-cut: one donor wafer becomes 15 device layers
idea: Scale shift from 775 um wafers to 1.5 um films: implant hydrogen (an electron flood gun replaces the Ar/Xe plasma flood), split off thin Si films, and bond them onto cheap carriers for DRAM front-end processing. The donor is repolished and reused 10-20 times.
why: Crystal, polysilicon and Spruce Pine crucible demand per DRAM wafer falls ~10x, removing argon-purged crystal pulling from most of the supply.

title: Monolayer molecular doping instead of ion implanters
idea: Scale jump from beamline accelerator to molecule: self-assembled monolayers of phosphorus- or boron-bearing molecules coat the silicon, and a spike anneal drives the dopant in, replacing implanters and their Ar/Xe flood guns for shallow source/drain and periphery junctions.
why: Implanters are high-capex and rare-gas-dependent. Molecular doping is a wet bench process at ~1/10 the capex, with sharper junctions for periphery transistors.

title: Mid-process wafer bank: park front-end wafers, finish during spikes
idea: Time shift inside the fab: during gluts, process wafers through the capacitor module and store them in nitrogen stockers. When a shortage hits, run only the back-end layers, cutting fab-out time from ~3 months to ~3 weeks.
why: Turns slack fab time in a glut into ready supply for a shortage. The cycle-time cut lets output follow demand spikes; needs only N2 purge.

title: Delay-line regeneration reborn as a self-timed refresh wave
idea: Mercury delay-line memories died on serial latency, but they refreshed themselves by recirculating every bit through a regenerator. Make refresh a travelling wave in the same way: each subarray refreshes one row locally, then hands a token to its neighbor, so refresh ripples continuously across the die. There are no global REF commands or all-bank stalls; the controller only sees a known 1-of-N subarray busy.
why: Recovers most of the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh at 32-64 Gb and flattens peak refresh current. Scheduling moves on-die with negligible periphery.

title: Automata Processor salvaged as a sense-amp key-match GET engine
idea: Failure mined: Micron's Automata Processor put state machines next to DRAM arrays and died on an alien programming model. Fix: add one XOR plus wired-NOR comparator per 64 sense amps and expose a single command, GET(key). A broadcast key is matched against every key in the open row (one hash bucket), and only the matching value leaves the chip.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and overfetch (fact 8): hash and key-value lookups move 64 B instead of 8 KB, ~100x fewer bits on the bus, for ~1-2% of SA-stripe area.
note: Close to Sieve-style in-DRAM matching.

title: TSV-free HBM: ThruChip inductive links plus power-only vias
idea: HMC's power-hungry SerDes and Keio's ThruChip inductive-coupling interface both stalled, and HBM won while paying a large TSV tax. Stack DRAM dies with on-die spiral coils carrying data over near-field links (~0.1 pJ/bit). Keep only a sparse ring of large power TSVs at the die edge, so about 90% of TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: 3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss). Targets ~1.5x area per bit and recovers most of the yield loss.
note: ThruChip known; power vias remain.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop map applied to 3D DRAM strings
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with defective minor loops masked by an on-chip loop map, then died on speed. Give every 3D DRAM die a rewritable defect map at the vertical-string level. Firmware retires defective or worn strings in the field, and the map's health record grades the die for second-life reuse.
why: Tolerating ~5% bad strings brings yield of 26+ tier 3D DRAM (fact 2) to economic levels, extends service life, and makes regrading and reuse possible.
note: Redundancy and post-package repair are standard DRAM practice; extension to strings is incremental.

title: Supercritical CO2 cleaning, abandoned in 2000s, revived for capacitor rinse-dry
idea: Supercritical CO2 wafer cleaning was abandoned on particle redeposition and slow high-pressure single-wafer chambers. Aim it at the one place it wins: replace the repeated wet clean and IPA dry of 60-75:1 pillars with SC-CO2 plus amine/alcohol cosolvent residue removal and stiction-free drying, recirculating >95% of CO2 captured from ammonia or ethanol plants.
why: Cleaning is a large share of a fab's ultrapure water; claim ~30% water cut on array steps and removal of pattern-collapse yield loss, which also permits taller, thinner pillars.

title: Purdue's 1990s silicon-carbide DRAM rebuilt on EV-glut SiC wafers
idea: Purdue built 4H-SiC DRAM cells in the 1990s with retention of hours or longer at room temperature, killed by expensive, micropipe-riddled SiC wafers. EV power electronics has since driven 200 mm SiC to low defect density and falling prices; build a planar or trench 1T1C cell on 4H-SiC whose 3.3 eV bandgap makes junction and GIDL leakage negligible.
why: Refresh essentially eliminated (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); SiC boules grow by sublimation in graphite crucibles, so no high-purity quartz; U.S. SiC capacity already exists; trades density (~28-40 nm rules) for energy and supply security.

title: ThruChip inductive coupling replaces HBM's through-silicon via tax
idea: Keio's ThruChip Interface (inductive coils in standard metal layers) never displaced TSVs because coil area and link power looked worse at 2010 bandwidths. Put 30-50 um coils in the DRAM top metal under each channel, thin dies to ~20 um, stack with adhesive only and bring power through edge wirebonds, so no via etch, fill, reveal or keep-out zones remain.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes ~10+ TSV process steps, keep-out area and much stacking yield loss; claims ~1.5-2x more stacked bits per wafer.

title: HP The Machine, minus memristor: rack single-copy read-only data
idea: HP's The Machine died because its memristor never shipped, orphaning a sound idea: fabric-attached memory shared by many nodes. Use CXL 3 shared memory with commodity DRAM to hold exactly one rack-wide copy of read-only data (model weights, reference genomes, dictionaries, container layers) mapped read-only into every host.
why: Eliminates N per-host copies; for a 16-host rack serving the same models, weight DRAM drops ~10x.
note: CXL 3 shared memory widely discussed; GPU HBM copies remain.

title: Global Memory Service, fixed: a spot market for idle fleet DRAM
idea: UW's 1990s Global Memory Service paged to idle workstations' RAM but died on 10 Mb/s networks and owners' lack of incentive. With 400G RDMA, run an internal spot market where hosts post unused DRAM at a price, borrowers bid for 1 GB revocable leases, and the scheduler packs elastic jobs onto borrowed memory.
why: Clouds strand 25-50% of provisioned DRAM; pricing it unlocks that supply without buying new chips.

title: Transparent huge pages, fixed: per-4KB valid bitmap stops bloat
idea: Databases disable THP because 2 MB pages physically back untouched memory and bloat RSS. Give each 2 MB TLB entry a 512-bit valid bitmap read by the page-table walker so only touched 4 KB frames are physically backed, keeping TLB reach without the bloat.
why: Recovers the 10-30% of DRAM lost to huge-page bloat on memory-heavy services.
note: Partial-subblock TLBs (Talluri-Hill) and Ingens/HawkEye cover this; needs CPU changes.

title: Everspin MRAM, fixed: MRAM write-combining journal makes NAND workable memory
idea: Everspin MRAM never reached Gb density, so it never replaced DRAM. Use a small MRAM as a nonvolatile write-combining journal in front of NAND: random 64 B stores land in MRAM at ns latency, are coalesced into full NAND pages in the background, and reads check the MRAM index first.
why: Lets NAND serve as main memory for write-active data, not just read-only data, with no DRAM buffer and no capacitor-backed power-loss protection.
note: MRAM write caches in SSDs already shipped.

title: Connection Machine, fixed: bit-serial compute inside cache SRAM arrays
idea: Thinking Machines' CM-1 used 65,536 bit-serial processors with private memory and died on cost and programmability. Do bit-serial compute inside existing SRAM subarrays by activating two wordlines and sensing bitline AND/NOR on transposed data, so each bitline is a processor and activations are processed where they sit.
why: Activations never leave SRAM, so DRAM staging buffers between layers disappear for small and mid-size models.
note: Neural Cache / Compute Caches prior art.

title: RDRAM's royalty trap fixed: royalty-free open memory-PHY commons for newcomers
idea: Rambus RDRAM lost partly because per-chip royalties, litigation and costly at-speed test made it pricier than SDRAM. Create a RISC-V-style foundation that funds, silicon-proves and licenses royalty-free DRAM-side PHYs, TSV/hybrid-bond I/O cells and controller IP, backed by a defensive patent pool of CHIPS-Act buyers, so a U.S. memory or packaging startup can tape out a base die without a $10-30M IP bill.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: removes tens of $M and months from entry, and blunts the litigation risk that killed earlier memory-interface startups.

title: Sub-THz plastic waveguides lost to optics; In/Ga bans flip that
idea: Polymer dielectric waveguides carrying 100-300 GHz carriers lost to optical cables because lasers were cheaper at volume. With In/Ga-based lasers ruled out, use solid polyethylene or PTFE ribbons fed by CMOS sub-THz transceivers to connect compute sleds to memory sleds at 1-3 m, carrying 100+ Gb/s per ribbon at ~1-2 pJ/bit with no lasers.
why: Rack-scale memory pooling reclaims the 20-30% of server DRAM that sits stranded, without lasers that need In or Ga; materials are C, H, F, Si and Cu.

title: MLC PCM resistance drift neutralized by co-written in-line reference cells
idea: Multi-level phase-change memory was abandoned largely because amorphous resistance drifts as t^0.1, collapsing level margins. Fix: each line writes three reference cells at the intermediate levels in the same pulse train, and reads compare data cells against those references, which drift identically, so thresholds track automatically.
why: Restores 2 bits/cell PCM (2x density) without periodic reprogramming.

title: Samsung's withdrawn PRAM fixed by checkerboard thermal-phase write scheduling
idea: Samsung's mobile PRAM never scaled partly because RESET heat partially crystallizes neighboring cells (thermal disturb). Fix: the write scheduler splits each array into four checkerboard phases and never writes adjacent cells within one thermal time constant (~100 ns), so each phase's idle neighbors act as heat sinks.
why: Permits ~30% tighter pitch (density) without disturb-induced retention loss.

title: GaAs memory's cost death revisited: junction-storage DRAM in RF fabs
idea: GaAs memories (Gigabit Logic, Vitesse SRAMs) died on cost against silicon in the late 1980s-90s. But GaAs's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^4x lower than silicon's, so thermal leakage falls by orders of magnitude: a JFET- or HEMT-access junction-storage DRAM cell built on 6-inch RF GaAs lines (0.25-0.5 um, 1990s-class, largely U.S.-based) could hold charge for very long times with almost no refresh.
why: Refresh and U.S. manufacturability: taps a compound-semiconductor fab pool outside DRAM's chokepoints for low-density, near-refresh-free working memory; density and wafer cost are the main risks.
note: GaAs DRAM with hours of retention was shown in the 1990s (Purdue); density and wafer cost limit it.

title: nCHIP silicon MCMs revived as 180 nm HBM interposers
idea: Early-1990s silicon-substrate multichip modules (nCHIP and others) died for lack of a product valuable enough to pay for them. HBM is that product: run thin-film silicon interposer and bridge lines (0.4-2 um wiring, Bosch-etched through-silicon vias, a 1994 process) in idle 200 mm, 180 nm-0.5 um fabs to add capacity beside the CoWoS-class packaging bottleneck.
why: Packaging capacity limits HBM output as much as DRAM wafers do; 1990s tools can draw interposer-scale lines, adding U.S. supply at a fraction of advanced-fab capex.

title: Irvine Sensors cubes: edge-wired DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Irvine Sensors stacked bare memory dies into edge-wired cubes for military use in the 1990s, and the method never went mainstream. Fix: laminate 8-16 thinned standard DDR dies, route their pads to the cube's side face, and pattern the side wiring with 1990s thick-film lithography, giving high-capacity stacks for CXL and server modules without TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax: capacity (not bandwidth) stacks avoid TSV area (~3x wafer area per bit) and its 20-30% yield loss, leaving HBM-grade wafers for AI.

title: Wafer-level burn-in revived with 1990s-made full-wafer contactors
idea: Full-wafer DRAM burn-in (tried in the 1990s-2000s, e.g. Aehr's WaferPak) stalled because full-wafer contactors were costly. Make the contactors with 1990s tools: MEMS spring-probe arrays and polyimide flex membranes patterned at 1-5 um on old 200 mm lines, so every HBM core-die wafer is burned in and screened before stacking.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% partly because weak dies get stacked; wafer-level screening raises stack yield and relieves test-floor capacity, a bottleneck alongside TSVs.

title: Orbital Hall torque from chromium writes magnets without tungsten or platinum
idea: Effect walk: orbital Hall effect. Replace W/Pt/Ta spin-Hall write lines in SOT magnetic cells with light 3d metals (Cr, Ti, V) whose orbital Hall conductivity is predicted ~10x Pt's spin Hall conductivity, converting the orbital current to torque through a 1-nm Ni or Gd conversion layer under the free layer.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and platinum from the write path and may cut write current 2-5x, making SOT-class DRAM-replacement cells cheaper in scarce-resource terms.
note: Orbital Hall torque is an active research field.
