why: Charge wall and 3D blocker: ~20 fF planar capacitor in a ~0.005 um2 folded footprint, built flat with mature tools and no high-AR etch.
note: Fold planar caps upright via stressed hinges; doubt: nm-registered folding of interconnected arrays is a miracle step.

title: Edinburgh-rock fiber draw: slice prebuilt vertical cell arrays from preforms
idea: Borrow optical-fiber drawing and seaside rock-candy making: assemble a macroscopic preform of doped-Si-core rods clad in gate glass, metal-glass gate sleeves and capacitor shells, co-draw it ~1000x, bundle and redraw to ~40 nm cell pitch, then wafer-slice the boule crosswise so every slice is a ready-made 4F2 vertical-transistor array needing only top and bottom wiring.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): array pitch is set by draw ratio, not EUV, and one draw-tower run yields thousands of slices; claimed 5-10x lower array capex. Molten-core Si fiber draw exists, but device-grade co-drawn junctions are unproven.
note: Pitch set by draw ratio, not litho, is genuinely new; device-grade junctions surviving co-draw at 40 nm needs a miracle.

title: Shingled-recording discipline: overlapping cells written in sequential bands
idea: Adapted from SMR hard drives, which overlap tracks and require sequential zone writes: adjacent storage nodes along a row share partially overlapping electrodes with no isolation, and a band is written in order so each write fixes the trailing cell's charge; reads remain random.
why: Removing isolation spacing gives ~2-3F2 cells, ~2-3x density (fact 4); stacked in tiers this is a 100x path for read-mostly AI weights and KV cache; trade-off: band-granular writes.
note: Overlapping storage nodes without isolation share charge; random reads would disturb neighbors.

title: Self-stratifying paint: one coat separates into fifty tier layers
idea: Borrowed from self-stratifying industrial coatings that split into primer and topcoat in one application: spin a block-copolymer plus metal-oxide-precursor blend that phase-separates into ~50 parallel lamellae, then UV-ozone convert and anneal it into alternating conductive-oxide and insulating-oxide tiers for a vertical gain-cell stack.
why: One coat-and-bake replaces ~100 CVD steps for a 50-tier stack, aiming at ~100x lower stack cost; trade-off: oxide-electrode resistance limits access to hundreds of ns.

title: Magnify layers to 1000: MLCC-style tape-cast laminated memory
idea: Borrow the multilayer ceramic capacitor industry (tape casting, gravure-printed 2 um electrodes, 1000-layer lamination, co-firing at trillions of parts a year) to build 3D crosspoint dynamic cells: a sub-micron dielectric tape capacitor in series with a co-fired oxide threshold selector.
why: Very low per-layer cost times 1000 layers offsets coarse lateral pitch, aiming at ~$0.1/GB (~100x), accepting slow access and large modules.
note: Novel borrowing of MLCC lamination, but per-layer addressing and selector leakage are unsolved; not DRAM-class access.

title: Neural pruning: over-grown random nanowire mesh carved into addressable cells
idea: Brains over-wire and then prune; solution-grow a dense random mesh of ~10 nm oxide-semiconductor nanowires between two orthogonal coarse electrode grids, then use electroforming pulses to burn out shorts and weak paths, characterize the surviving junctions on-die and address them through a learned map stored in a small SRAM table.
why: Self-assembled junctions far denser than the coarse lithographed grids give ~10x bits/mm2 using only relaxed ArF masks, if surviving-junction yield stays above ~30% (fact 4).
note: Addressable bits can't exceed coarse-grid crosspoints; density claim is flawed.

title: Kitchen sponge: gyroid block-copolymer electrode fills each capacitor well
idea: A sponge hides huge internal surface: spin a gyroid-forming block copolymer into each capacitor well, remove one block, and ALD-coat the continuous 3D network with TiN/high-k/TiN so the electrode becomes a triply periodic minimal surface. At a 20-25 nm period the internal area is about 10x that of a plain cylinder.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 5 fF at AR ~15:1, or 20+ fF at today's aspect ratio for much longer retention.
note: At DRAM pitch the well is only ~1-2 gyroid periods, and TiN/high-k/TiN cannot fit a 20 nm network.

title: Neuroscientist's ion bath: printed ion-gel double-layer storage node
idea: Neurons hold state in ion gradients, not in dielectrics: the storage capacitor is replaced by a printed ion-gel electric-double-layer capacitor (~10 uF/cm2, about 100 fF/um2), so a planar 0.1 um2 node holds ~10 fF, twice a 70:1 pillar, and the charge margin is large enough that leaky, variable printed access transistors still meet retention.
why: Facts 1 and 2: the charge wall is broken without high-aspect-ratio etch, and the margin makes weak devices acceptable; the open question is whether ionic response in sub-100 nm films can reach ~10 ns.
note: EDL charging and self-discharge are microseconds or slower; 10 ns is implausible.

title: Glass-fiber draw tower: thermally drawn nanolayer capacitor fibers
idea: Build a centimeter preform of interleaved conductive and high-k glass/polymer layers, then thermally draw it ~10,000x in a fiber tower so the layers thin to ~10 nm. Chop the fiber and stand the pieces in etched wells as pre-built capacitor cores.
why: Charge wall and capital: the capacitor stack comes from a ~$1M draw tower instead of ALD in deep holes, and 1 km of fiber yields billions of cores. University fiber labs can build it.
note: Drawn fibers end up ~1 um across, far above cell pitch; placing and contacting billions of chopped cores is unsolved.

title: Vacuum-free tier stacks grown by pulsed-electrodeposition superlattices
idea: Ideal: a 3D memory stack poured from a bath. Closest: pulse-electroplate 100+ periods of Ni or Cu conductor layers alternating with cathodically deposited ZnO semiconductor/dielectric layers (~20-40 nm each, <90 C, aqueous) to replace CVD/PVD tier depositions for 3D gain-cell stacks.
why: 100x path: plating tools ~$1-3M vs $10-30M vacuum clusters, no helium or vacuum pumps, abundant Zn/Ni/Cu; tier cost falls ~10-30x, which with self-patterned holes targets ~$0.1/GB. Trades film quality and interface traps (more refresh).
note: Transistor-grade plated ZnO superlattices are speculative.

title: Core-shell nanocrystal barrier-layer film giving colossal-k planar capacitor
idea: Box = {medium: interfacial (Maxwell-Wagner) polarization in a film of 5 nm conducting doped-TiO2 cores with 1 nm Al2O3 shells | access: Si FET | sense: charge share | integration: planar or very-low-AR capacitor | substrate: Si | fab: colloidal dip coat + ALD shell infill}. Each conducting core acts as a floating plate, so the film behaves like hundreds of series-parallel nanocapacitors with effective k of 300-1000, provided core conductance keeps the relaxation frequency above ~100 MHz.
why: Fact 1: an effective k far above the k~70 target lets the pillar flatten to AR <10:1 and removes the deepest etch steps.
note: At 5 nm cores in ~6 nm film, MW effective k stays ~30, not 300-1000.

title: Array-only DRAM fab plus U.S. mature-node periphery foundry, hybrid-bonded
idea: Substitute the monolithic DRAM die with a two-wafer product: the DRAM fab makes an array-only wafer (cells, bitlines, WL straps, ~40% fewer masks) and an existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic fab makes a periphery-only wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) with sub-array-edge pads at ~1 um pitch; the two are hybrid-bonded.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): ~1.8x bits per DRAM-fab wafer, better periphery transistors, and half of each chip made in U.S. fabs that already exist.
note: Cell-on-periphery hybrid bonding is widely pursued by majors.

title: Wafer bonding fused with monolithic tiers: four wafers of 32
idea: Combine both 3D routes: each wafer carries a 32-tier monolithic memory stack (aspect ratio manageable in one etch), and four such wafers are hybrid-bonded to one periphery wafer, giving 128 tiers without a 128-tier etch.
why: 3D break-even (fact 2, ~26+ tiers): reaches 128 tiers with 4 moderate etches; etch AR stays <40:1, raising yield and cutting high-AR etch tool time.

title: Minify the IDM: pure-play DRAM foundry for fabless designers
idea: Create a DRAM-process foundry that sells array and capacitor modules to fabless memory design houses, separating design innovation (custom HBM base dies, AI-tuned arrays) from $20B capex as TSMC did for logic.
why: Raises the number of memory designers ~10x, fills capacity across many customers, and speeds novel products to market.
note: PSMC/Winbond already offer DRAM foundry; needs a fab.

title: Eliminate EUV entirely: 4F2 vertical-channel cells at relaxed DUV pitch
idea: Move to a 4F2 vertical-channel-transistor cell but hold F at ~15 nm, which matches the bit area of today's 6F2 at 12 nm and is reachable with immersion DUV plus self-aligned quadruple/octuple patterning. Output is an ordinary DDR5/HBM core die.
why: Fact 4: zero EUV layers at bit-density parity, removing ~$1B+ of scanners per 100k wafers/month and the single-supplier dependency.

title: Customers become owners: hyperscaler memory co-op fab at cost
idea: Reverse buyer and seller: the largest DRAM buyers form a cooperative that owns a fab, run under contract by an incumbent or licensee, and take output at cost plus depreciation in proportion to their equity. Members put in capex as equity instead of paying shortage premiums.
why: Capital intensity and supply: at 4x contract prices, buyers already pay for a fab in premiums. The co-op turns that premium into owned capacity (~100k wafer starts/month) and cuts members' long-run cost per bit ~30-50%.
note: Like JV fabs and prepay LTAs; capex scale is the barrier.

title: Inversion: pure-play DRAM foundry with open PDK for fabless designers
idea: TRIZ #13 Inversion: instead of three IDMs designing and fabbing their own DRAM, a pure-play DRAM foundry publishes a cell/array PDK and accepts designs from fabless memory startups, hyperscalers and universities, like TSMC did for logic.
why: Industry structure: unlocks new entrants and specialized memories without each building a $15B fab.
note: Same pure-play DRAM foundry as I-01816.

title: Flip the wafer: build capacitors on the backside
idea: Inverts 'capacitors sit above bitlines on the front'. After front-side transistors and bitlines, bond to a carrier, thin to ~0.5 um and open storage-node contacts from the back directly onto source/drain, building capacitors over the full cell footprint with no bitlines in the way.
why: Removes the buried-contact and landing-pad layers that snake past bitlines (1-2 EUV layers) and gives ~1.5x capacitor footprint, so AR can drop ~30% (facts 1, 4).

title: Ghost kitchen: pure-play DRAM foundry serving fabless memory designers
idea: Random stimulus 'ghost kitchen' -> one kitchen cooks for many brands. A DRAM foundry offers a 1-beta-class cell and capacitor process as a PDK; fabless firms design custom HBM base dies, AI-specific DRAM and niche parts on it, and the foundry aggregates demand to stay full.
why: Unbundles design from capital; brings startup innovation into DRAM like TSMC did for logic; keeps fabs >90% utilized across cycles.

title: Pastry chef's croissant lamination: stack-on-stack doubling of tiers
idea: Laminated dough doubles its layers with every fold. Make wafers with 8 monolithic tiers, hybrid-bond two face-to-face, thin and open vias; then bond 16-tier pairs to 16-tier pairs, mirroring orientation so the bitlines align.
why: Tier count doubles with each bond cycle: 3 cycles take 8 to 64 tiers, past the 26-tier break-even of Fact 2 without 64 sequential monolithic tiers.

title: Two-scale stacking: 32 monolithic tiers per wafer times eight bonded wafers
idea: Combine nm-scale monolithic tiers with um-scale wafer bonding: build 32-tier 3D arrays per wafer, thin each to 5 um, and hybrid-bond eight wafers with one inter-wafer via per mat at 1-um pitch, reaching 256 tiers without any 256-tier etch.
why: High-AR etch and tier yield (fact 2): yield compounds over 32 tiers instead of 256, giving 256-tier density at 32-tier process risk.

title: Periphery wafer from U.S. legacy fabs bonded onto cell array
idea: Combine image-sensor wafer bonding with DRAM: build sense amps, decoders and I/O on 28-40 nm logic wafers in existing U.S. mature fabs and only the array on the DRAM wafer; the array wafer adds exactly one mask (hybrid-bond pads) and drops its periphery masks.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; moving it to EUV-free, depreciated U.S. fabs cuts DRAM-fab area per bit ~40% and frees the array from periphery thermal budget.
note: CMOS-bonded-array DRAM is on major vendor roadmaps already.

title: Bond a mature-node periphery wafer under the array
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: move sense amps, decoders and I/O (~49% of the die) to a separately processed 28-40 nm CMOS wafer that is hybrid-bonded beneath the cell array. The array wafer then needs no Hf-based HKMG and fewer metal layers.
why: Raises bits per array wafer ~1.6-1.9x, removes Hf HKMG from the array fab, and lets periphery run in existing U.S. mature-node fabs (capital and U.S. manufacturability).
note: CMOS-bonded-array DRAM is on major makers' roadmaps.

title: Glass-panel interposers break the silicon-interposer packaging bottleneck
idea: Worsen: make every HBM attach depend on a reticle-stitched silicon interposer from one supplier's line. Flip: build interposers on 510x515 mm glass panels with 2 um semi-additive copper lines and laser through-glass vias, giving ~8x more interposer area per panel than a 300 mm wafer and a lower-loss dielectric.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~3-5x lower cost per interposer mm^2, lower insertion loss trims pJ/bit; panel and PCB supply chains exist in the U.S. and allies.
note: Widely pursued (Intel, Absolics).

title: Onshore HBM stacking hubs using imported known-good DRAM wafers
idea: Worsen: keep all HBM stacking and advanced packaging in one region so one disruption halts AI memory. Flip: fund U.S. packaging hubs that import known-good DRAM wafers and do TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, stacking and test domestically, since a packaging line costs ~$1-3B versus $15B+ for a fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply security within ~2 years instead of 5; captures ~20-30% of HBM value-add and seeds a later fab.

title: Cu: hybrid-bond DRAM arrays to periphery from depreciated US fabs
idea: Make only the cell array in the leading-edge DRAM fab and fabricate the periphery (~49% of die) on 28-40 nm logic wafers in existing, depreciated U.S. foundries, joining the two with Cu-Cu hybrid wafer bonding.
why: Facts 4 and 7: roughly doubles array bits per expensive DRAM wafer and uses idle U.S. capacity with near-zero new capex for the periphery half.

title: Hybrid-bond pads double as sense-amp coupling capacitors
idea: In a wafer-on-wafer DRAM (array wafer face-bonded to a CMOS wafer), leave a 2-3 nm oxide in the Cu-Cu bond pads that carry 16:1-muxed local bitlines, so each pad is both the interconnect and the coupling capacitor of a charge-transfer preamp on the logic wafer. The bond needs no DC continuity, and the logic-side sense amp runs at 0.5 V.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7) and voltage floor (fact 10): sense amps leave the array wafer; low-voltage sensing claimed ~2x lower sensing energy and ~25% smaller array die.

title: Refresh cycles fused with page fingerprinting for in-DRAM dedup
idea: Combine the mandatory refresh operation with content hashing: a tiny CRC/hash unit at each subarray's sense amplifiers folds every row into a 32-bit signature as it is refreshed and writes it to a reserved signature row. The controller reads the signature table every 64 ms, verifies candidate matches and merges duplicate pages by remapping, replacing CPU-driven KSM scanning.
why: Dedup recovers 10-40% of capacity on VM/container hosts but today costs CPU and bandwidth to scan; piggybacking on refresh (fact 3) makes always-on dedup nearly free, so fewer DRAM bits per host.
note: Pages interleave across chips/banks, so row-level hashes at sense amps map poorly to pages.

title: Refresh-piggybacked mirroring into a bonded non-volatile twin layer
idea: Eliminate the separate backup flush: a ferroelectric or MRAM twin layer bonded under each bank receives a row copy whenever that row is refreshed and its dirty bit is set (the row is already open, so only the vertical transfer is paid); at power loss only rows dirtied since their last refresh are flushed, within the PSU's existing ~10 ms hold-up energy.
why: Gives DRAM speed and endurance with full non-volatility, removing NVDIMM batteries/supercaps and 30-s serial flushes; copying rides on refresh activations, so no extra ACT energy or row-hammer exposure.
note: Piggybacking NV copies on refresh is clever; full-row vertical transfer and NV write energy are costs.

title: Rotate alternate 3D tiers 90 degrees to split staircases
idea: In a lateral 3D DRAM stack, rotate every other tier's cell orientation 90 degrees so odd-tier bitlines run X and even-tier bitlines run Y. Odd tiers stair-step on the east/west edges and even tiers on north/south, so each staircase is half as tall, and vertically adjacent bitlines only cross at points instead of running parallel.
why: 3D blockers (fact 2): staircase footprint per edge halves (~20-30% array-efficiency gain at 64+ tiers) and inter-tier bitline coupling drops ~5-10x, allowing thinner tiers.
note: Clever staircase split; vertical shared lines must align across rotated, non-square lateral cells.

title: DRAM-bridge: the chiplet bridge die is itself memory
idea: Rearrange the bridge's role: the small embedded silicon bridges (EMIB/LSI-style) that link adjacent GPU chiplets are fabricated as DRAM dies whose top metals carry the die-to-die wires and whose array area is dual-ported to both neighbouring chiplets' edge bumps. Silicon that today only carries wires becomes a shared buffer between neighbours.
why: A 16 mm2 bridge at ~0.3 Gb/mm2 holds ~0.6 GB, so 8 bridges add ~5 GB of on-package shared memory at <0.5 pJ/bit with zero extra package area; chiplets exchange tensors through memory instead of the link (fact 5).

title: Local quality: tapered TSV stacks, fewer TSVs in each higher tier
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: in a uniform HBM stack every die carries the full TSV farm, though the top die needs none. One common front-side mask lays out the TSV farm region as spare subarrays, and a cheap i-line backside mask per tier etches only the TSVs that die needs for the dies above it. In upper tiers the unetched subarrays are fused on as extra capacity.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): average TSV area per die drops ~45% in a 12-high stack, for ~5-10% more bits per stack with the same front-side masks.

title: Mercury delay-line revival: recirculating photonic loop broadcasts streaming weights
idea: Replace the 1940s mercury tank with a ~2 m low-loss silicon-nitride spiral on the interposer (~10 ns, 64 wavelengths x 50 Gb/s) closed by an SOA regenerator; a weight tile read once from HBM recirculates for N laps and 8-16 compute chiplets tap it each lap via ring drop filters.
why: Facts 5/8: each weight byte crosses the HBM PHY once instead of once per consumer or per micro-batch step, cutting DRAM reads and pJ/bit on broadcast/expert-shared traffic ~4-8x; loop holds only ~32 kbit so it is a broadcast medium with temporal reuse, not a store.

title: Woven tiers: alternate bitline direction 90° to dilute row hammer
idea: Inverts 'a row's neighbors are fixed parallel rows.' Rotate line orientation by 90 degrees on alternate tiers so a hammered row's nearest neighbors above and below are orthogonal lines that each share only one cell with it, spreading aggressor coupling over many victims.
why: Fact 9: disturbance per victim per activation drops ~16-64x, lifting the effective hammer threshold well above 1k.
note: Alternating line direction conflicts with shared vertical bitlines across tiers.

title: Ferroelectric sanctuary rows hold weak data during idle
idea: Inverts 'volatile data must stay volatile': one mask swaps the capacitor dielectric to HZO in a few rows per bank, forming FeRAM rows on the same sense amps; before self-refresh the controller parks data from mapped weak rows there so the weakest rows need no refresh.
why: Self-refresh rate is set by the 1e-4 rather than the 1e-9 tail (fact 3), ~4x lower idle refresh energy.
note: FeRAM sensing needs plate pulsing; remapping weak rows to strong rows may suffice.

title: Ant pheromone trails: refresh operations decay per-page hotness counters
idea: Ant trails fade unless re-walked: keep a 3-bit hotness counter per page in spare on-die ECC/metadata bits; accesses increment it and the DRAM's own refresh, which already opens every row, decrements it for free, giving the controller hardware-aged heat maps to drive tiering with zero sampling overhead.
why: Tiering accuracy limits how much DRAM cheaper tiers can replace; free precise hotness lets 30-50% of footprint leave DRAM versus ~15-20% with page-table scanning.
note: Refresh restoring rows could decay counters for free; needs on-die logic changes.

title: Camera pixel: pinned storage-node junction suppresses 125 C generation leakage
idea: Automotive image sensors beat 125 C dark current with a p+ surface pinning layer; the same shallow pinning implant over the storage-node junction surface plus an STI-sidewall passivation liner removes surface-state generation, the dominant hot leakage term.
why: Sensors cut dark current ~10x this way; the cell leakage tail at 125 C could fall 3-10x, allowing normal 64 ms refresh at 125 C through 10 years.

title: Halve the EUV dose; stochastic misprints become erasures
idea: Po: print the chip blurry. EUV dose on critical DRAM layers is cut 40-50%, raising scanner throughput ~1.5-1.8x, and the resulting rise in stochastic missing or bridged contacts (~0.1-1% of cells) is mapped at test as stuck cells, which as erasures cost about half the redundancy of random errors.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital (fact 4): the same scanner fleet patterns ~50% more wafer layers; ~5-8% lower cost per bit and less dependence on new scanners.

title: Orthogonal-per-tier cells cut by two alternately opened slit families
idea: Worse: point every tier's cells the same way so adjacent bitline columns must sit a full cell length apart. Flip: alternate two sacrificial materials by tier and open X-slits and Y-slits at different times, each selectively recessing one material, so even tiers' cells run along X and odd tiers' along Y and neighboring columns interleave into each tier's vacant quadrants.
why: Packs ~1.5x more cells per footprint per tier with no extra masks beyond the second slit, so 10x is reached at ~80 tiers instead of ~120 at the same cost (fact 2).

title: Harvest working SRAM from reject CPU/GPU dies as memory chiplets
idea: Worse: scrap processor dies whose cores fail although their L2/L3 SRAM tests good. Flip: fuse off the logic, expose the surviving SRAM over the die's existing die-to-die or I/O link, and package the dies as static memory chiplets.
why: Zero refresh and zero new wafers; each large reject accelerator die carries 50-200 MB of good SRAM.
note: Failed dies often fail in fabric too; small total capacity.

title: DRAM test-mode compare reused as in-chip dedup verifier
idea: This adds zero masks. The parallel-test compare circuitry that already sits on every DRAM die for production test is exposed as a runtime command. A candidate duplicate page is then verified bit-exact inside the DRAM in one operation, instead of streaming both copies to the CPU. A factory-time feature becomes a runtime one.
why: It removes the 2 x 4 KB of bandwidth and energy each dedup verification costs, which makes continuous fine-grained dedup cheap: 10-25% capacity savings on VM hosts.

title: Thin-provisioned DRAM die with on-die row indirection
idea: This adds zero masks. A latch-based row indirection table in the periphery lets a die advertise about 1.5x more logical rows than it has physical rows. A physical row is allocated on the first non-zero write, and rows that are freed or zeroed through a TRIM-like command return to the pool. Virtual memory moves down to the die scale.
why: Zero or never-written memory is 10-30% of allocated footprint. Die-level thin provisioning reclaims it transparently, for 1.2-1.4x effective capacity.

title: Latching vertical-thyristor sub-wordline drivers from Kilopass VLT
idea: Failure mined: Kilopass's vertical layered thyristor (VLT) DRAM was abandoned over cell variability and the lack of a fab partner. Fix: use the VLT device where variability is harmless, as the sub-wordline driver. One anode pulse latches it on to drive the 3 V wordline and a cathode pull resets it, so each driver is a single ~4F^2 vertical device with no static decoder hold state.
why: Sub-wordline driver and local decoder strips are ~8-10% of the die. A vertical latching driver cuts them ~3x and removes static hold power, giving back ~5-6% of die area.

title: Spin-Hall stochastic writes keep an attention-weighted KV reservoir
idea: When a token's KV arrives, a spin-Hall (beta-W) current pulse tries to switch a low-barrier MTJ, with amplitude set by the token's running attention score. The switching probability equals the keep probability, so the KV buffer becomes a hardware importance-weighted reservoir sample of the context. Only switched tokens are written to the fixed-size KV store; dropped ones are compensated by unbiased reweighting.
why: Caps KV memory at a fixed budget (4-10x smaller) while keeping attention estimates unbiased. One device per token replaces digital PRNG and sort logic.
note: The KV saving comes from reservoir sampling itself; a spintronic coin flip adds little over a digital PRNG.

title: Pyroelectric film senses heating transients and gates refresh rate
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A Sc-doped AlN patch per bank (CMOS-compatible and pyroelectric) outputs current proportional to dT/dt, giving a zero-bias, microsecond heating-event detector; refresh steps up only during and after thermal ramps (for example a GPU power spike), and banks sit at the slow rate while temperature is steady and cool.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3): today's slow polled thermal sensors force ~10 C guard bands and a blanket 2x refresh above 85 C; transient-aware refresh removes the guard band, giving ~2x longer average refresh intervals.

title: Convert U.S. silicon-carbide power fabs into refresh-free SiC DRAM lines
idea: C (as SiC): retool 150/200 mm 4H-SiC power-device fabs in NC, NY and TX with existing DUV steppers to build SiC MOS 1T1C cells, whose 3.26 eV gap gave early research SiC DRAM cells orders-of-magnitude longer room-temperature retention than silicon, and sell them as a big-cell, refresh-free working-memory tier behind DRAM on CXL.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturable memory supply (U.S. ~1-2% share) with tools already installed and no EUV (fact 4), and removes refresh (fact 3); lower density means it wins on capital per usable GB, not on die density.

title: Basket-weave buried wordlines dive and rise to starve passing-gate leakage
idea: Route each buried wordline over-and-under like basket weave: it runs deep beside one storage node and shallow beside the next. No storage node then sits beside a full-depth passing gate whose toggling pumps electrons into it.
why: Facts 3 and 9: passing-gate-induced charge loss is a leakage mechanism behind row hammer. Weave geometry could raise the hammer threshold ~5-10x and remove most targeted-refresh overhead.

title: Capacity-market retainers for DRAM lines that can swing from HBM
idea: Ideal: memory capacity that moves instantly to wherever the shortage is. Closest achievable: as in electricity capacity markets, the government pays a per-wafer-start retainer to keep lines qualified for both HBM and DDR/LPDDR and to switch within 60 days when called during commodity shortages.
why: AI crowding of commodity DRAM: a fast surge lever that avoids 4x price spikes.
note: HBM vs DDR lines differ in back end and TSV; swing capability limited to front end.

title: Swap ZrO2 for cryogenic quantum-paraelectric SrTiO3 storage dielectric
idea: Operate the array at 20-77 K and use SrTiO3 or KTaO3, whose permittivity climbs toward 10^3-10^4 as quantum fluctuations suppress the ferroelectric transition. A planar or AR<5:1 MIM cap then reaches 5 fF in a 12-nm-class cell footprint, aimed at cryo-cooled AI and quantum-computing racks.
why: Removes the 60-75:1 pillar etch (facts 1, 4). Planar caps cut capacitor process steps by ~50%, and leakage freeze-out also cuts refresh (fact 3). The honest cost is cooling power.

title: Substitute biased well with buried fixed-charge Al2O3 back-gate
idea: Substitute the charge-pumped negative body bias (VBB) with a 3-5 nm ALD Al2O3/SiO2 liner on the back side of each buried or vertical channel. Its built-in negative fixed charge (~-5e12 cm^-2) permanently depletes the body near the storage junction and raises off-state Vt by ~150-250 mV at zero standby power.
why: Leakage + periphery: ~10-30x lower subthreshold leakage for tail cells, and the VBB pump and its idle power (part of the 16-33% idle budget) go away.

title: Substitute hard-switched refresh with LC resonant charge recovery
idea: Substitute CV^2-dissipating drivers with adiabatic resonant drive: an inductor on the package or interposer resonates with wordline and bitline capacitance. Two subarrays refresh in antiphase, so energy swings back and forth between them instead of burning in drivers.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and voltage floor: recovers ~50-70% of refresh-burst CV^2. Refresh is periodic and schedulable, which suits resonant drive.
note: Adiabatic LC drive works physically, but refresh is a modest energy share; inductor area and ns ramps limit recovery.

title: Substitute sputtered IGZO with N2-curtain spatial-ALD gallium-tin oxide
idea: Substitute argon/oxygen-sputtered IGZO with amorphous Ga-Sn-O deposited by atmospheric-pressure spatial ALD, in which nitrogen gas curtains rather than argon separate the precursor zones. The result is an indium-free wide-gap channel with angstrom thickness control at high throughput.
why: Indium-free oxide-semiconductor access devices (~1e-19 A/um off-current class) made without rare gases or vacuum tools: a cheaper BEOL tier for refresh-light gain cells.
note: Spatial ALD oxide channels and GTO TFTs known; combination aimed at supply chain.

title: Substitute amorphous oxides with MBE-grown BaSnO3 perovskite channel
idea: Substitute amorphous oxide channels with La-doped BaSnO3 grown by MBE on a SrTiO3 buffer on Si (ultra-high vacuum, ozone oxidant, no carrier or sputter gas). It is a 3.1 eV-gap perovskite with film mobility above 100 cm^2/Vs, so on-current and off-leakage stop trading against each other.
why: At least 5x the on-current of IGZO at similar sub-aA leakage: shorter write times and refresh-light cells without large transistors.

title: Substitute VDD/2 idle bitline with trimmed leakage-balance parking voltage
idea: Substitute the fixed VDD/2 standby bitline level with a parking voltage trimmed per subarray by an on-die DAC at test. It is set where channel leakage into the storage node offsets junction and GIDL leakage out of it for the weakest profiled cells.
why: Cuts the weakest cells' net leakage ~2-5x, extending the tail-limited refresh interval with existing devices and no new process step (so no rare gases).
note: One parking voltage helps one stored polarity and hurts the other.

title: Substitute static cell plate with idle-lowered plate voltage
idea: Substitute the constant cell-plate voltage with one that drops ~0.2-0.3 V while a bank is idle. That couples every floating storage node down and shrinks the storage-to-gate field that drives GIDL on '1' cells; the plate returns before activation, and the negative wordline tracks it to keep '0' cells off.
why: GIDL-dominated tail leakage drops ~3-5x, lengthening the self-refresh interval accordingly; a circuit-only change needing no gas-consuming process step.
note: Idle plate lowering cuts GIDL on ones; risks forward bias on zeros and plate settling energy.

title: Analog leaky-capacitor activation integrator replaces row-hammer counter tables
idea: Substitute digital SRAM activation-counter tables with a per-row analog integrator: each activate dumps a fixed charge packet onto a small leaky capacitor in the wordline driver, and when a Schmitt detector trips, the neighbors are refreshed. The leak rate itself sets the time window.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row instead of large CAM/SRAM trackers, which fail at 1k-activation thresholds.
note: Per-row cap in SWD stripe area; PRAC already counts per row.

title: Pulsed back-plate biasing replaces 3 V thick-oxide wordline drivers
idea: Substitute the boosted ~3 V wordline with a buried back plate under each mat that is pulsed during access to lower the access-transistor Vt and held negative during retention. Wordlines then swing only ~1.2 V through thin-oxide drivers.
why: Voltage floor and periphery area (facts 7, 10): drivers shrink ~3x, charge-pump load drops sharply, and wordline CV^2 falls ~6x.

title: Ferroelectric HZO polarization stores per-amp offset trim
idea: Substitute large matched sense transistors with minimum-size FeFETs whose ALD HZO gate polarization is partially switched at test to null each amp's offset, so the trim is stored as analog polarization. HZO ALD, TiN sputter and RTA are standard nanofab tools.
why: Periphery area: offset-limited SA area shrinks ~3-5x once mismatch is trimmed instead of sized away.

title: Thin-film AlN piezoelectric transformer replaces wordline charge pumps
idea: Substitute switched-capacitor VPP charge pumps with a released thin-film AlN contour-mode piezoelectric transformer that steps 1.1 V to ~3 V at resonance. AlN sputtering, XeF2 release and e-beam electrodes are university-fab processes.
why: Periphery energy and area: piezo transformers can reach >80% conversion efficiency against ~30-50% for multi-stage pumps, cutting wordline supply energy ~2x.

title: Shadow-evaporated single-electron transistor electrometers sense cryo-DRAM bits
idea: Substitute the CMOS sense amp with an Al/AlOx single-electron transistor (double-angle shadow evaporation, e-beam resist bridge) whose island couples to the bitline, reading sub-attofarad charge for 4 K memory beside quantum processors.
why: Charge wall: cell capacitance could shrink ~100x for cryogenic memory, making a planar cell possible with no high-AR capacitor.

title: NbN nanocryotron sense amplifiers with superconducting niobium bitlines
idea: Substitute both the copper bitline and the CMOS latch with superconductors: zero-resistance Nb bitlines feed an e-beam-patterned NbN nanocryotron (nTron) whose choke switches the channel normal when the bitline current exceeds its threshold.
why: Energy per bit: superconducting sensing costs aJ per event and has no bitline RC, enabling multi-thousand-cell bitlines and ~10x fewer sense amps for cryogenic computing.

title: Thin-film Schottky diode-matrix passive row decoder
idea: Substitute transistor NAND decode trees with a 1950s-style diode-matrix decoder made of thin-film Pt/IGZO Schottky diodes at address-line crossings, so only the selected row line stays high. It needs two masks plus sputtering.
why: Periphery area: decode moves into a passive crossbar layer that can sit over the array, and the transistor count of decoders drops ~5x.

title: One-time ReRAM-programmed crossbar decoder routes around defects
idea: Substitute hard-wired decoders with a crossbar of HfOx ReRAM switches programmed once at test to connect each address code to any healthy physical row. Decoding and redundancy repair merge into one reconfigurable layer.
why: Yield and periphery: removes separate redundancy decoders and lets any spare row replace any failed row, raising yield on low-cost processes.

title: Stencil-indexed deposition builds the 3D staircase, replacing trim-etch loops
idea: Substitute the staircase made by dozens of resist-trim + oxide/nitride fluorocarbon etch loops with deposition-defined steps: sputter an oxide-semiconductor/Mo/Al2O3 tier stack through a stepper-indexed stencil whose aperture edges move inward ~0.5 um per tier at each staircase site, so every tier terminates at its own offset; stencils are swapped and stripped in oxalic acid/H2O2.
why: 3D DRAM staircase cost (fact 2): eliminates ~N/2 litho-trim-etch cycles and all their fluorocarbon use; staircase becomes native to deposition.
note: Shadow-mask penumbra at 0.5 um steps is the doubt.

title: Carbon-mandrel, titania-alumina spacers replace fluorocarbon quadruple patterning
idea: Substitute oxide-spacer/fluorocarbon SAQP with an ashable/chlorinable set: amorphous-carbon mandrels (O2 ash), ALD TiO2 first spacers and ALD Al2O3 second spacers etched with Cl2/BCl3 at >20:1 mutual selectivity, printed with a non-fluorinated PAG (sulfonium camphorsulfonate) resist, so ~16 nm pitch uses only O2, Cl2, BCl3 and HBr.
why: Litho capital and fluorine dependence (fact 4): ArF + SAQP array lines without EUV, fluorocarbon spacer etches, or PFAS photoacid generators.

title: Substitute amorphous-carbon molds and ashing for oxide mold HF dip-out
idea: Build the capacitor mold from amorphous carbon etched with O2/COS (no fluorocarbons), form the pillars, then remove the mold by O2/H2 plasma ash instead of a buffered-HF full dip-out followed by rinses and IPA drying.
why: Deletes the wet dip-out, cutting capacitor-module water >10x; with no liquid meniscus, pillars can exceed AR 100 without leaning (charge wall), and the etch is PFAS-free.

title: Substitute thermophoretic particle shielding for after-the-fact wafer cleaning
idea: Hold wafers a few kelvin above ambient on heated carriers and stages and add biased electrostatic guard grids, so thermophoretic and electric forces repel sub-100 nm particles before they land, then skip cleans whose only job is particle removal.
why: Prevention instead of washing removes much of the particle-clean step count, cutting that water >10x; the same physics already protects EUV reticles.

title: Substitute tester-based burn-in with on-die BIST and contactless wafer test
idea: Embed a programmable march/retention test engine and near-field RF coupling coils in every die so whole wafers are tested in parallel by a wafer-scale wireless tester without probe cards; weak cells are repaired by on-die eFuses during the same pass.
why: DRAM test and burn-in equipment is ~10% of capex and a throughput bottleneck; massively parallel contactless test could cut test cost ~5x and free cleanroom floor.

title: Infrared light through silicon replaces vertical TSV signal lanes
idea: Substitute signal TSVs with bonded 1310 nm micro-LED / Ge photodiode pairs: silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so each die shines data straight up through thinned neighbours, with Fresnel zone lenses etched in backside oxide to focus; only a few fat TSVs remain for power.
why: Fact 6: ~90% fewer signal TSVs and their keep-out area; contactless vertical signalling decouples bond yield from data integrity; ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit.
note: BEOL metal in every tier blocks light; needs optical windows per die.

title: Flood-lit optical comb clock replaces per-channel forwarded clocks
idea: Substitute every channel's forwarded clock, DLL and PLL with one mode-locked laser that floods the backside of all chiplets at 1.3 um through the silicon; on-die photodiodes recover a common low-jitter clock so data lanes run source-synchronous with no CDR or link training.
why: Fact 7 periphery and Fact 5: removes clock lanes (~10% of pins) and DLL/PLL area and power (~15-20% of PHY power).

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory racks with YBCO superconducting backplanes
idea: Substitute copper backplane traces with YBCO coated-conductor striplines in a 77 K memory enclosure: DRAM leakage collapses at 77 K so refresh nearly vanishes, and lossless lines carry 100 mV low-swing signals for meters without equalization.
why: Fact 3 refresh (-90%+) and Fact 5 link energy (~5x lower), traded against cryocooler power amortised over a large pooled memory.
note: YBCO lines add little versus cryo overhead.

title: On-package antenna mesh replaces address and command wiring
idea: Substitute command/address wiring to every DRAM die with a ~300 GHz on-chip antenna broadcast network inside the package: the controller transmits each command once, all dies receive it simultaneously, and only data stays wired.
why: Facts 6/7: C/A pins and TSVs (~20-30% of HBM signals) disappear; more ranks per channel without electrical loading.
note: 300 GHz on-package antennas for C/A; wireless NoC art exists.

title: Substitute voltage-level sensing with time-to-threshold soft readout
idea: Replace the latch-type sense amp decision with a bitline discharge timer: the time for the bitline to cross a reference is digitized to 3 bits, giving soft reliability info per cell that a soft-decision LDPC decoder uses to fix marginal cells hard-decision ECC cannot.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): soft decoding gains ~2-3 dB, which allows ~30-40% less stored charge per cell or longer refresh intervals.

title: Substitute supercapacitor hold-up with DRAM-process energy capacitors flushing dirty rows
idea: Keep a bounded dirty budget (e.g., 3% of rows) in a write-back policy and pair the DRAM with an on-die MRAM persistence tile; spare high-AR capacitor array area, filled with antiferroelectric ZrO2 energy-storage caps, powers the dirty-row flush on power fail.
why: Persistence at DRAM speed without NVDIMM supercaps/NAND: removes module BOM and makes HBM/DRAM persistent at ~3-5% area.
note: Niche persistence feature.

title: Substitute UPS spend with NV-memory datacenters selling instant demand response
idea: Business model: datacenters with persistent working memory can drop to zero power within milliseconds and resume exactly, so they sell fast frequency/demand-response capacity to grid operators; the revenue subsidizes the NV memory premium.
why: Energy and capital: grid services revenue (~$50-150/kW-yr) can offset NV memory cost and shrink UPS/battery capex.
note: Grid services revenue small relative to memory premium; UPS savings real but modest.

title: Substitute one stable large MTJ with analog majority of tiny unstable MTJs
idea: Store each bit in 5 sub-15 nm MTJs in parallel, each with low thermal stability (fails ~1e-3/hour alone); reading the summed parallel resistance gives the majority, so the bit fails only if 3 of 5 flip (~1e-8/hour) and periodic scrub restores flips.
why: Write energy and density: low-barrier MTJs switch with ~5x less current and tiny transistors; retention comes from redundancy, not barrier height.

title: Substitute single-crystal wafers with crucible-free amorphous carrier substrates
idea: Because <=400 C memory tiers need no crystalline silicon, swap prime CZ wafers for reclaimed test wafers or glass carriers that hold only memory tiers, later bonded to a small periphery die.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and prime-wafer dependence from most of the memory area; substrate cost per wafer drops ~5-10x.

title: Substitute bonded silicon dies with memory decals from reusable glass carriers
idea: Swap whole-die stacking for building thin oxide-memory tiers on reusable glass carriers at <=400 C, then laser-debonding and laminating them as ~2 um decals onto any target die or wafer, with the carrier reused many times.
why: Decouples memory manufacture from the target wafer's fab; carrier reuse cuts substrate cost and thin decals avoid TSVs.
note: Laser lift-off known; dense alignment of transferred decals to target die is the doubt.

title: Separate capacitor wafer hybrid-bonded to transistor wafer at cell pitch
idea: Combine deep-trench decoupling-capacitor manufacturing (mature, DUV-only) with sub-500 nm pitch wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding: one wafer carries only dense trench capacitors, the other carries access transistors and periphery, and each cell's storage node is joined by a Cu-Cu pad. Each wafer is optimized and yield-screened separately, and the capacitor wafer can come from a low-capital U.S. MEMS or passive-component fab.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability (facts 4, 7): no EUV in the capacitor flow and parallel fabs; claimed 20-30% wafer cost cut; bond pitch and overlay are the risks.
note: Sub-500 nm bond pitch is ~10x coarser than DRAM cell pitch, so density falls far short.

title: Split-pillar complementary capacitor in one etched hole
idea: Etch a single capacitor hole, then split its bottom electrode lengthwise into two half-shells separated by a dielectric fin, so one hole holds a true and a complement storage node sharing one plate. Complementary charges give a differential 2x signal that cancels plate and coupling noise.
why: Fact 1: 2x sense margin per hole lets each half carry ~40% less charge (shorter pillar); differential sensing also improves row-hammer tolerance (fact 9).
note: Same split-pillar complementary nodes.

title: Gen-10.5 display-glass fabs building IGZO capacitor memory panels
idea: Combine display-panel manufacturing (Gen-10.5 glass, 2-3 um lines, IGZO backplanes already in volume) with 1T1C memory: pattern memory arrays across square meters of glass at roughly a cent per cm2, then cut them into large capacity-tier panels attached by flex to CXL controllers. It trades density for ~1000x cheaper area and zero EUV.
why: Capital and scarce tools (fact 4): uses idle display capacity outside the EUV supply chain; cost per bit could approach parity for capacity tiers; latency, RC and physical size are the risks.

title: High-entropy fluorite oxide dielectric suppressing crystallization leakage paths
idea: Combine the high-entropy-alloy concept with the storage dielectric: an ALD supercycle mixes five cations (Hf, Zr, Ti, Ce, Sn) into one oxide so configurational entropy stabilizes a single fine-grained high-k phase and blocks the grain-boundary leakage paths that cripple pure TiO2 or ZrO2 at k>50. Target: k~50-60 with ZrO2-class leakage.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~1.5x Cs at equal leakage and a tighter leakage tail; avoids scarce Ta, Nb and Ru.
note: Entropy stabilization in 5 nm ALD films is unproven.

title: Floating negative wordlines replace standby charge pumps
idea: In self-refresh, a single capacitive kick (domino-precharge style) drives all idle wordlines to about -0.6 V, after which they float and their own capacitance holds the bias, topped up rarely by a tiny timer.
why: Keeps the 10-100x leakage benefit of a negative wordline without the static power of an always-on negative pump, cutting standby current 20-30%.

title: Sense amp fused with time-to-digital converter as retention canary
idea: Combine every sense-amp stripe with a shared 6-bit time-to-digital converter that timestamps how long each bitline pair takes to cross the latch threshold during ordinary activations; slow-resolving (low-charge) rows are logged in a small per-bank table and refreshed at 64 ms while all others drop to 256-1024 ms. Normal reads become free, continuous retention measurements, which also catches variable-retention cells that offline profiling misses.
why: Refresh (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); in-field margin tracking could cut refresh operations ~4x.
note: Sense-time as a retention canary; SA offset may swamp the timing signal.

title: Per-stripe adaptive array voltage regulated by sensed margin
idea: Put a micro-LDO in every SA stripe and close the loop with a replica sense pair on a programmable reference: the regulator lowers that subarray's VARY until measured margin reaches target, so strong subarrays run near 0.7 V while weak ones stay at 1.0 V.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~20% average VARY drop gives ~35% lower array CV^2 energy, with per-region guardbands instead of one worst-case guardband per die.

title: Wordline drivers built on the 3D staircase steps
idea: Combine the 3D contact staircase with the X-decoder: deposit thin-film transistors directly on each staircase tread so every tier's wordline driver and pre-decoder sits on its own step, turning dead staircase area into periphery.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and 3D cost (fact 2): removes decoder strips and long fan-out wires; ~8-12% die area recovered.
note: TFT drive current marginal for fast high-voltage wordlines.

title: Series-stacked array voltage domains recycle bitline charge between tiers
idea: Combine two arrays (bonded tiers) in series between 0 and 2xVARY: the upper array swings VARY-2VARY and its restore current returns through the lower array swinging 0-VARY, recycling charge like stacked-voltage logic, with the scheduler balancing activations.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~40-50% of array CV2 supply energy recycled without lowering VARY; fewer pumps shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: CTE-matched molybdenum TSVs dropped inside the cell array
idea: Fill TSVs with domestic molybdenum, whose ~5 ppm/K expansion nearly matches silicon, so stress keep-out zones shrink from ~10 um to <1 um and TSVs can sit inside the subarray grid (in sense-amp gaps) instead of dedicated TSV channels.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims ~5-10% die area, avoids China-dominated tungsten and Cu-pumping yield loss, and allows more channels per stack.

title: HBM die thinning by layer splitting so parent wafers recycle
idea: Combine HBM's mandatory 30-50 um die thinning with porous-silicon layer transfer: build core dies on epi above a buried porous-Si cleave plane, split the 40 um device layer off after carrier bonding instead of grinding ~700 um to slurry, then re-polish and re-epi the parent for 10+ reuses.
why: HBM grinds ~95% of each wafer's silicon away; reuse cuts prime wafer, polysilicon and crucible demand per HBM bit ~80-90% and removes grinding water.

title: Molybdenum dioxide electrode replaces ruthenium and templates rutile TiO2
idea: Combine the capacitor bottom electrode with the dielectric's crystal seed: metallic, rutile-type ALD MoO2 plays the templating role RuO2 plays in lab stacks, nucleating rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100) at <=400 C, with an Al-doped TiO2 interface layer to cut leakage.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (needs k ~70) without ruthenium (South Africa ~85-90%); Mo is U.S.-mined; ~1.5-2x Cs at the same aspect ratio.

title: All-carbon capacitor mold etched with oxygen instead of fluorocarbons
idea: Combine mold material and strip chemistry: replace the oxide/nitride capacitor mold with amorphous carbon, etch holes in O2/N2/COS plasma with sulfur sidewall passivation, deposit electrodes, then remove the mold in the same O2 ash rather than an HF wet strip.
why: Removes C4F6/C4F8/CHF3 (high-GWP, PFAS-adjacent) from DRAM's hardest etch and the HF strip; dry removal ends pillar collapse; carbon etches 2-3x faster, so fewer etch tools.

title: ALD exhaust cold-trap reclaims precursors for on-site repurification
idea: Combine the ALD foreline trap with a precursor refinery: a staged cryogenic trap captures the >90% of Zr/Hf/Ti metal-organic precursor that passes unreacted during purge pulses, and an on-site fractional distillation unit repurifies it to 6N for re-feed.
why: Cuts metal precursor consumption 3-5x and abatement energy; the capacitor stack burns the most ALD cycles in the fab.

title: Deuterated nitride supporter doubles as an interface-passivation reservoir
idea: Combine the capacitor's existing SiN support lattice with trap passivation (zero added masks): deposit it from SiD4/ND3 so it stores ~20 at.% deuterium, which diffuses down during later anneals and passivates access-transistor interface/GIDL traps with stronger Si-D bonds.
why: Trims the <=13 fA leakage tail that sets refresh; halving it doubles the refresh interval (~23 fJ/bit saved, 5-10% bandwidth back) and replaces high-pressure H2/D2 anneals.

title: One block mask lets capacitor ZrO2 double as periphery gate
idea: Combine the cell-capacitor ZrO2 ALD with the periphery high-k gate: periphery moves to a gate-last module whose trenches are opened by the single added mask, so the same ZrO2 run coats capacitor and periphery gates, with La/Al dipoles setting Vt.
why: Removes hafnium entirely and one full HKMG dielectric module (~6-8 steps); ALD tool demand per wafer start down ~10%.

title: Silicon-on-nothing voids isolate cells using only silicon and hydrogen
idea: Combine isolation and body insulation via the empty-space-in-silicon effect: the one added mask etches arrays of deep holes under active-area ends, and a high-temperature H2 anneal lets silicon surface-migrate to seal them into buried voids that cut leakage paths beneath the access transistor.
why: Cuts the junction leakage tail (refresh energy ~30-50% lower) and replaces part of the STI fill oxide and its CMP with nothing but silicon and hydrogen.

title: Temporary-bond tester wafer probes every die in one touch
idea: Combine temporary direct bonding with wafer probing: a reusable tester wafer carrying BIST controllers and power delivery is bonded face-to-face to the DRAM wafer through the fine-pitch pads later used for stacking. It runs all die tests in parallel and then debonds.
why: Probe cards and ATE are ~10% of DRAM capex. Whole-wafer parallel test cuts tester count and test time ~10x and makes known-good die for HBM cheaper (fact 6).

title: Kerfless porous-silicon lift-off reuses each crystal-grown wafer tenfold
idea: Combine solar-industry epitaxial lift-off (porous-Si release layer under 20 um epitaxy) with DRAM. The memory is built in the epi layer, bonded device-side to a carrier or logic wafer, cleaved at the porous layer, and the CZ parent wafer is re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand ~10x and with it the Spruce Pine (>80%) high-purity quartz crucible dependence. Wafer cost (~5-8% of DRAM cost) falls, and HBM thinning comes free (scarce resources, fact 6).

title: Spatial ALD-ALE supercycles sculpt capacitor holes in one tool
idea: Combine spatial (rotary-platen) atomic layer deposition with atomic layer etching on one platen. Alternating sectors deposit a protective liner at the hole top and quasi-isotropically etch the bowed and tapered zones, reshaping each high-aspect-ratio hole into a straight cylinder in one pass.
why: Replaces separate etch-deposit-etch profile-correction loops across 3-4 tools. Straight walls give ~20% more Cs at the same AR (fact 1) and ~15% fewer chamber-hours.

title: Heat-vanishing polymer capacitor mold eliminates the support lattice
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap sacrificial polymers (thermally decomposable polycarbonate/polynorbornene) with the capacitor mold. Holes are etched in the polymer and low-temperature PEALD electrodes are formed, then the mold is removed by dry burnout rather than an HF wet strip, so no capillary forces topple the pillars.
why: Wet-strip capillary leaning is why 1-3 SiN support lattices are needed. Dropping them removes ~2 masks and ~12 steps and allows AR beyond 75 (facts 1, 4).
note: Polymer mold limits electrode thermal budget; HAR polymer etch plausible.

title: Array buried-channel transistor reused as the only periphery transistor
idea: Combine the array's recessed-channel buried-wordline transistor with periphery logic: decoders, sense control and I/O are built only from the same BCAT-style devices (upsized, paralleled, dynamic logic styles), and the separate HKMG planar periphery module is deleted.
why: The HKMG periphery module adds ~8-12 masks plus integration complexity. Deleting it removes ~10-15% of mask count and periphery-specific tools, and more bank parallelism absorbs the speed cost.

title: Delete retention-tail implants and anneals; codes absorb the leakers
idea: Combine the cell recipe with system coding: the halo and compensation implant masks and the extended hydrogen anneal, which exist only to tame the 13 fA leakage tail, are removed. The ~1% of cells that then fall below 64 ms retention are absorbed by scrub plus code.
why: Drops ~2-3 implant masks and a long furnace step (~3% wafer cost) and the multi-hour hot retention-screen test (fact 3).

title: Sort-time error syndromes replace most inline metrology
idea: Combine code-layer syndrome counters with advanced process control: every probed die reports spatial maps of corrected bits, which are decoded into virtual metrology (CD, overlay, etch depth inferred from error signatures). Inline CD-SEM/OCD sampling can then drop ~70%.
why: Metrology and inspection are ~10-12% of fab capex. The 1% budget makes the slower feedback loop acceptable (capital intensity, throughput).

title: Lower-grade crystals from recycled-quartz crucibles, leakers absorbed by codes
idea: Combine cheaper crystal growth (crucibles with thin synthetic liners over recycled or non-Spruce-Pine quartz, several pulls per crucible) with error tolerance. Higher oxygen-precipitate and metal densities lengthen the leakage tail, and the extra retention-weak cells are absorbed within the 1% budget.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint and cuts wafer cost ~20-30% (scarce resource).

title: DIMM data-buffer chip doubles as a base-delta decompressor
idea: Combine the MRDIMM/LRDIMM data-buffer and RCD chips (already made on 28-40 nm DUV processes) with a base-delta-immediate compression engine and a small remap table, so a DIMM built from older 1y/1z DUV DRAM dies presents ~1.6-2x its raw capacity to the host.
why: Lets non-EUV DRAM nodes match EUV-node logical density per module, skipping the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) while all added logic stays on mature, U.S.-available nodes.
note: Real BDI ratios are ~1.5x; adding indirection to timing-critical buffers is hard.

title: Fiber delay-line carousel circulates weights past pipelined accelerators
idea: Combine 1950s delay-line memory with WDM optics: model weights circulate continuously in a 10-20 km amplified fiber loop at ~25 Tb/s aggregate, and each pipeline-stage accelerator taps the wavelengths carrying its layer exactly when they pass, so weights are stored in flight instead of in DRAM.
why: Holds ~150-300 MB per loop with zero lithography; fits strictly sequential weight streaming, though the ~50-100 us lap latency rules out random access.

title: Sense-amplifier row latch reconfigured as on-die serializer
idea: Combine the bitline sense-amp row (an 8-16 kb latch already holding the opened page) with a SerDes shift register: add a segment-level pass chain so the latched row shifts directly into a local high-speed serializer next to the mat, bypassing column decoders, global I/O lines and the central datapath for streaming reads.
why: Overfetch and periphery: for streaming AI weight reads the 'overfetched' 128x row is actually used; cuts internal data-movement energy ~30-50% and column/global-I/O periphery area.

title: Electroplated copper-manganese alloy that grows its own barrier
idea: Combine TSV electroplating with barrier formation: plate Cu-0.5%Mn from a non-aqueous or ionic-liquid bath onto an electroless seed; a 350 C anneal drives Mn to the oxide liner forming a few-nm MnSiO3 barrier and leaves pure Cu, deleting the argon-sputtered Ta/TaN barrier.
why: TSV cost and HBM area tax: removes a rare-gas PVD tool and enables thinner, higher-aspect TSVs with smaller keep-out zones.
note: Cu-Mn self-forming barriers are known BEOL art; plating Mn alloy from non-aqueous bath is the hard, unproven step.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in TSV plasma etch
idea: Combine the electrostatic chuck's backside gas cooling with hydrogen, whose thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/m-K) beats helium's (~0.15), using a low-leak sealed chuck with H2 sensing and interlocks so TSV DRIE and other plasma steps keep wafer temperature control with no helium; H2 is made domestically by electrolysis.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps HBM TSV etch lines running independent of helium supply.

title: Soft-decision sensing plus NAND LDPC to read tiny capacitors
idea: Combine the DRAM sense amp with NAND flash soft-read: the bitline is compared against 3-7 shifted references (a mini flash-ADC sharing one regenerative latch) to give per-bit confidence, and a short-latency LDPC decoder at the bank uses those log-likelihoods. Cells with roughly half today's charge (~2.5 fF, AR ~35) then read at acceptable error rates.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): halving required Cs cuts capacitor aspect ratio ~2x, saving etch/deposition steps and easing 3D tiers; costs ~6-10% parity and a few ns.

title: Three-tier charge-summing majority vote on a shared vertical bitline
idea: Combine triple modular redundancy with charge sharing: three cheap stacked oxide-TFT/capacitor tiers on one vertical bitline are written together and read by opening all three gates at once, so the bitline sees the analog sum and one fully leaked or shorted cell cannot flip the bit. Buildable in a university nanofab: three sequential low-temperature IGZO/MIM tiers.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): makes low-yield, leaky tiers acceptable because each bit tolerates a bad tier, enabling cheap BEOL stacking despite 3x cells.

title: Test-then-write: maskless e-beam final metal routes around defects
idea: Combine wafer test with maskless lithography: after electrical test of the cell array, a per-die e-beam (or laser direct-write) exposure of the final metal layer is computed so bitline/wordline straps bypass defective cells and segments, giving every die custom wiring. Buildable in a university nanofab: e-beam writer plus probe-station test.
why: Yield and redundancy area (facts 4, 7): replaces built-in spare rows and fuses with per-die wiring; with multi-beam writers in production it raises yield of immature 3D or new-material arrays.

title: Federated university fab relay with baton-passed wafer lots
idea: Fuse a network of university and national-lab 200/300mm cleanrooms with a MOSIS-style shuttle. Each site certifies 1-2 module steps (implant, capacitor ALD, metallization), and lots travel in sealed nitrogen FOUPs on a scheduled courier loop.
why: Uses $10B+ of stranded, underused U.S. tool sets to make pilot and defense DRAM and to train the workforce, with no new fab.

title: UCIe memory die bank: interchangeable known-good DRAM chiplets
idea: Fuse a standard die-to-die interface (UCIe/BoW) with a commodity exchange. Any qualified small maker sells known-good DRAM chiplets with a common footprint, pinout and test spec through a brokerage that warrants interchangeability, the way a grain elevator does.
why: Lowers entry barriers for new memory makers (no package or brand ecosystem needed) and diversifies supply beyond three firms.

title: Nanoimprint memory litho with siloxane-brush non-fluorinated release
idea: Fuse Canon-style nanoimprint lithography (already qualified for memory pitches) with a PDMS/siloxane polymer-brush or graphene release layer on the quartz template, replacing the fluorinated FOTS anti-stick monolayer.
why: Gives an EUV-free, PFAS-free patterning route at about 1/10 the litho capex of EUV for DRAM array layers.

title: Polysilicon capacitor mold etched with HBr and stripped by TMAH
idea: Combine a thick doped-polysilicon storage-node mold (etched to high AR with HBr/O2 cryogenic etch) with ALD electrode and dielectric deposition and a wet TMAH mold strip, replacing the C4F6/C4F8 high-AR oxide mold etch.
why: Removes the costliest fluorocarbon etch step in DRAM while keeping 1T1C capacitors, and silicon etch may reach higher AR than oxide.

title: Chlorine-etchable spacer materials for EUV-free quadruple patterning
idea: Combine self-aligned quadruple patterning with spacer and hard-mask materials chosen to etch in BCl3/Cl2 (TiO2, ZrO2, HfO2) on carbon mandrels removed by O2 ash, replacing SiN and SiO2 spacers that need fluorocarbon etchback.
why: Enables F-free pitch division to 12-14 nm half-pitch without EUV, attacking the EUV and capex bottleneck.

title: Solar-cell field-effect passivation shell around the storage junction
idea: Adapt PERC/TOPCon solar passivation: wrap storage-node junction sidewalls in ALD Al2O3 carrying ~-5e12 cm-2 fixed negative charge, and replace the implanted node contact with a 1.2 nm tunnel-oxide/poly-Si passivating contact, removing implant damage and repelling carriers from interface traps.
why: Fact 3: the leakage tail comes from a few trap-rich junctions; solar data show ~10x lower surface recombination, aiming at 3-10x longer tail retention and proportionally fewer refreshes.
note: Tail leakage is GIDL/trap-assisted at high field; solar passivation gains may not transfer to 15 nm junctions.

title: Tesla-valve graded barrier that ratchets charge into the node
idea: Borrow the no-moving-parts Tesla fluidic diode: build a compositionally graded oxide barrier (InGaZnO to Ga2O3 to Al2O3) between access channel and storage node so the write-direction barrier collapses under field while the retention-direction barrier stays >1.5 eV.
why: Fact 3: an asymmetric barrier decouples write speed from retention, targeting ~10 ns writes with seconds of retention and ~10x fewer refreshes.
note: Graded barrier asymmetry; IGZO already gives long retention.

title: MLCC core-shell grain engineering for 5 nm high-k films
idea: Adapt the BaTiO3 core-shell grains MLCC makers use to flatten k versus field: grow nanolaminated rutile TiO2 grain cores with Al/Nb-doped shells via ALD supercycles, so k ~80-100 survives at 5 nm while grain-boundary leakage is blocked.
why: Fact 1: k ~70 is the stated escape route from the charge wall; ~1.6x Cs at the same AR, or today's Cs at AR ~45.
note: Incremental Cs gain; leakage at 5 nm likely limiting.

title: Canal-lock access: series switches with an equalized middle chamber
idea: Adapted from canal locks, which equalize a chamber before opening a gate: put two access transistors in series and drive their middle node with a minimum-size follower whose gate is the storage node, so the inner transistor always sees ~0 V drain-source. Both gates open together for read/write; in hold, the storage-side device has almost no Vds to drive leakage.
why: Subthreshold leakage scales with (1 - exp(-Vds/kT/q)); holding Vds near 0 on the inner device cuts its leakage 10-100x and removes it from the retention tail (fact 3), at the cost of extra vertical transistors that 3D tiers could hide.

title: Electret-microphone charge sets the access-transistor threshold permanently
idea: Adapted from electret microphones, whose fluoropolymer holds implanted charge for decades: implant a stable sheet of fixed charge into a deep-trap dielectric layer beside the access channel so its threshold is raised permanently, letting the wordline rest at 0 V instead of a negative voltage when off.
why: The negative off-wordline adds gate-drain field that drives GIDL and needs always-on charge pumps; an electret-set threshold keeps subthreshold leakage low while cutting GIDL and removing the negative pump's standby power (facts 3, 10).

title: Pipeline cathodic protection: guard junctions intercept stray carriers
idea: Adapted from cathodic protection, where a sacrificial anode takes corrosion current instead of the pipe: run a shallow, reverse-biased n+ guard stripe between storage-node rows, tied to a collector rail, so minority electrons generated in the bulk or injected by hammered neighbor rows are collected before reaching a storage node.
why: Part of the leakage tail and much row-hammer charge loss is carrier diffusion through the substrate; a collector that grabs it could cut bulk-generated leakage several-fold (fact 3) and raise row-hammer thresholds (fact 9).

title: Self-cleaning oven: wordline Joule heating anneals away the leakage tail
idea: Adapted from pyrolytic self-cleaning ovens and Macronix's self-healing NAND: during maintenance windows, drive a controlled current through selected buried wordlines to heat local cells to ~250-400 C for milliseconds, annealing traps and re-passivating interfaces that hot-carrier and hammer stress created over the module's life.
why: Repairable in place: rather than guard-banding refresh for end-of-life growth of the leakage tail (fact 3), the tail is periodically reset, extending service life and keeping refresh margins tight.
note: Macronix self-healing NAND precedent; heating neighbors and metallization risk.

title: Self-healing concrete capsules: buried hydrogen reservoir re-passivates interfaces
idea: Adapted from self-healing concrete, which embeds capsules that release healing agent into new cracks: deposit a deuterium-rich SiNx reservoir film above the access-device level, capped by a barrier with a controlled leak rate, so D slowly re-supplies the Si/SiO2 interface and re-passivates dangling bonds as they form over a 10-year life.
why: Interface-trap generation drives leakage-tail growth with age (fact 3); a built-in healing supply keeps retention stable for longer and makes modules fit for second-life reuse instead of scrap.

title: Plumbing unions for 3D stacks: reworkable low-temperature microbump joints
idea: Adapted from plumbing unions that let one pipe section come out without cutting the rest: bond HBM-style stacks with low-melting In or Sn-Bi microbumps at defined 'union' levels, so a die whose retention fails burn-in or ages in the field can be removed near 150 C and replaced without scrapping the stack.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% (fact 6), often from one weak die; reworkable unions recover the other dies and let leaky dies (fact 3) be swapped instead of guard-banding refresh for the whole stack.

title: Solar PID-recovery box: nightly reverse-bias de-trapping of access devices
idea: Adapted from the PID-recovery boxes that undo potential-induced degradation in solar parks with a night-time counter-voltage: during idle windows the controller applies reverse gate and well bias to blocks of rows for seconds, emptying charge trapped in access-transistor gate dielectrics and spacers by wordline and hammer stress.
why: Trapped charge raises leakage and causes drift over life (fact 3); routine recovery undoes it, keeping retention near day-one values and delaying replacement.

title: Resonant gate drive recovers wordline CV-squared energy
idea: Borrowed from resonant gate drivers in MHz power converters: groups of wordline drivers share an LC tank (inductor in the package or interposer), so each wordline charges along a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank on close instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of the ~3 V wordline swing energy and shrinks the VPP charge pump that feeds it.

title: Noise-cancelling headphone loop on the cell plate
idea: Borrowed from active noise cancellation and ECG driven-right-leg amplifiers: dummy bitlines in each mat pick up common-mode noise (plate bounce, wordline kick, substrate), and a fast amplifier drives the inverse onto the plate and reference lines during sensing.
why: Sensing margin: removes ~10-20 mV of correlated noise (~25% of today's budget), allowing smaller Cs or longer bitlines.
note: Driving the large plate node at ns speed needs a big amplifier.

title: RFID backscatter turns DRAM output into reflection
idea: Borrowed from passive RFID backscatter: the processor sends a continuous carrier down each data line, and the DRAM die only switches a small termination impedance to modulate the reflection, so it needs no output drivers or their supply current.
why: Data movement (fact 5): DRAM-side I/O energy down ~60-80% and I/O driver periphery shrinks; transmit power moves to the cheaper logic-node host.
note: Resembles POD signaling; carrier separation at multi-Gbps.

title: X-ray flat-panel charge integrators read centimeter-long bitlines
idea: Borrowed from flat-panel X-ray detectors, which read ~1 fC pixel charges down 40 cm data lines: each glass-panel bitline is held at virtual ground by a switched-capacitor charge-integrating amplifier, so the cell's full charge transfers to a small feedback capacitor whatever the line capacitance.
why: Charge wall on glass: the signal is set by Cs/Cfb instead of Cs/Cbl, so bitlines can be ~10x longer and sense amps per bit fall ~10x.

title: Touchscreen mutual-capacitance sensing reads cells nondestructively
idea: Borrowed from projected-capacitive touch controllers: each cell is a coupling capacitor at a wordline-bitline crossing on glass whose value is shifted by a trapped-charge or ferroelectric layer; a TX pulse on the wordline and charge sensing on the bitline read it without discharging any storage node.
why: Destructive read (fact 8): no restore write-back on read and far less refresh, roughly halving read energy, built from thin films on any substrate.

title: Ion-exchanged glass waveguides form the panel's global data bus
idea: Borrowed from ion-exchange waveguides used in planar fiber couplers: optical waveguides are written into the glass substrate itself, with microLED emitters at each mat and thin-film photodiodes at the panel edge replacing centimeter-long metal global I/O lines.
why: Data movement on large panels: long-wire CV2 energy becomes ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit optical links, with no extra wiring layers since the waveguide is inside the substrate.
note: Assumes glass-panel memory; microLED/TFT photodiode speed and energy.

title: ARM-style IP licensing of thin-film periphery to display fabs
idea: Borrowed from ARM's licensing model: develop a validated library of oxide-TFT sense amps, decoders and pumps (with process recipes) and license it to underused Gen-6/8.5 display fabs for a royalty per square meter, so memory supply grows with existing panel capacity.
why: Supply and capital: taps tens of millions of m2 per year of display capacity without new fabs and turns periphery design into a reusable asset.

title: Event-camera address-event bus for self-requested refresh
idea: Borrowed from neuromorphic event cameras' address-event representation: each row on a glass panel has a sentinel cell with a deliberately weaker capacitor and a thin-film comparator that fires the row address onto an arbitrated event bus when it decays, so only rows that need refresh get it.
why: Refresh (fact 3): oxide-TFT cells rarely leak, so event-driven refresh cuts refresh operations 100x+ versus timed sweeps and removes the refresh counter.

title: Hard-disk TDMR: joint bitline sensing cancels neighbor crosstalk
idea: Adapted from two-dimensional magnetic recording, where multiple readers cancel inter-track interference: sense amps resolve neighboring bitline pairs jointly and subtract a calibrated coupling term, letting bitline pitch go below today's coupling limit.
why: Bitline pitch ~25-30% tighter at the same litho (fact 4), cost per bit ~-20%, and tolerance for denser 3D pitches.
note: Joint detection needs ADC-like sensing per bitline, inflating periphery.

title: Coaxial cable: grounded sleeves around every vertical bitline
idea: Adapted from coax: each vertical bitline in a 3D array is wrapped in a thin grounded metal sleeve over low-k, trading ~20% more self-capacitance for near-zero coupling to neighbor bitlines and plates.
why: Coupling noise ~-80% allows open-bitline 4F2 3D arrays without folded/twisted schemes and smaller sense margins (fact 1).

title: Gemstone-style cleaving recovers backside slabs from thinned memory wafers
idea: Stacked and HBM DRAM dies are ground from 775 um down to ~30-50 um, so >90% of the crystal becomes sludge. Adapt gemstone cleaving: after the front side is bonded to a carrier, an IR laser writes a buried damage plane ~60 um deep, and a thermal-stress pulse splits off a ~650 um slab that is repolished into a new wafer.
why: Each pulled wafer yields a second wafer, roughly halving crystal, quartz-crucible and energy per HBM bit. It also eliminates grinding sludge and grinding water.

title: LCD panel fabs build capacitor-free memory on Gen-8 glass
idea: Display fabs pattern oxide TFTs on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass at a tiny fraction of wafer cost per area. Adapt idle Gen-6/8 oxide lines to make capacitor-free gain-cell memory sheets that are diced into tiles and bonded as a capacity tier behind CXL controllers.
why: No Czochralski crystal, quartz crucible, EUV or helium-intensive deep etch. It suits bulk far-memory capacity where density per area matters less than cost per area; density at ~0.5-1 um rules is the main limit.

title: Data-center 48-volt distribution brought inside the memory stack
idea: Adapted from the 48 V rack transition: the HBM stack is fed at ~12 V through a few TSVs, and integrated switched-capacitor converters on each die step it down. This replaces hundreds of low-voltage power TSVs.
why: Power/ground take a large share of HBM TSVs and bumps; 10x less current frees ~30-50% of them for data or area and cuts IR-drop loss (fact 6).
note: 12 V conversion on DRAM-process devices is hard.

title: Power-line communication sends data over HBM power TSVs
idea: Adapted from home power-line networking: modulated high-frequency data is superimposed on the stack's many power/ground TSVs and planes through simple 180 nm couplers, so power vias also carry control, refresh and sideband traffic.
why: TSV count (fact 6): frees signal TSVs now spent on command and sideband, ~10-20% fewer TSVs, or more data lanes in the same footprint.

title: Laptop heat pipes etched into silicon spacers cool tall stacks
idea: Adapted from laptop heat pipes: the 1994 Bosch DRIE process etches sealed micro heat-pipe channels with wicking grooves into silicon spacer dies inserted in the memory stack. Filled with water or methanol, they carry heat sideways to the lid passively.
why: Thermal limits on stack height and hot refresh (fact 3): ~2-5x lower stack thermal resistance, allowing taller stacks and halving high-temperature refresh.
note: Spacer dies add height and TSV length; micro heat pipe capacity at mm scale is small.

title: NAND-style read-reference tracking keyed to time since refresh
idea: Adapted from NAND flash controllers that shift read thresholds as charge drifts: each mat holds a few dummy cells rewritten at every refresh; at read time a small comparator samples their decayed voltage and shifts the sense-amp reference so the decision threshold follows the leakage curve instead of sitting at a fixed VARY/2.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): a moving reference recovers ~30-40% of signal margin late in the refresh window, allowing 2-4x longer tREFI and cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.
note: Dummy cells track typical decay, not the tail cells that set refresh.

title: SerDes decision-feedback equalization across neighboring bitlines
idea: Adapted from high-speed SerDes receivers, which subtract known inter-symbol interference using already-decided bits: even-column sense amps resolve first, and their decided values drive a small coupling-cancel capacitor onto the adjacent odd bitlines before those resolve, removing the data-dependent bitline-to-bitline coupling that eats margin.
why: Charge wall and pattern-dependent failures (facts 1, 8): bitline coupling consumes ~15-25% of sense margin at tight pitch; cancelling it restores margin worth ~1 fF of storage capacitance and removes worst-case data-pattern errors.

title: Solar epitaxial lift-off: reusable porous-silicon donor for DRAM wafers
idea: Adapted from U.S. kerfless solar startups: grow 20-50 um epitaxial silicon on a porous-Si release layer over one CZ donor wafer, bond it to a U.S.-made polysilicon carrier, lift it off, and reuse the donor 10-20 times.
