idea: A pheromone released once reaches the whole colony. Likewise a passive polymer-waveguide star coupler on an organic board broadcasts each memory read of model weights to 4-8 accelerators at once, so tensor-parallel GPUs stop keeping replicated weight copies in their own HBM.
why: Usable memory supply: weight replication wastes ~30-60% of HBM capacity in some deployments; broadcast deduplication frees that capacity with waveguides that need no silicon.
note: Tensor parallel shards rather than replicates weights; benefit narrower than claimed.

title: Leaky integrate-and-fire capacitor as per-row hammer sentinel
idea: Give each small row group an analog 'membrane' capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaks with a time constant matched to the refresh window; when it crosses a comparator threshold it fires a targeted neighbour refresh and resets, replacing SRAM counter tables with one array-device capacitor plus comparator per group.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: digital per-row counters cost ~1-4% die area and grow as thresholds fall; an LIF integrator gives continuously decaying counts that cannot be gamed by window resets, at ~10x less area.
note: Leaky analog activation counter replaces SRAM tables; accuracy and aliasing per row group.

title: Kinetic-proofreading sense amp that flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Hopfield's kinetic proofreading gains accuracy by adding a dissipative delay step; add a second timed sensing stage in which the bitline differential must survive a controlled bleed, marking cells whose signal collapses as 'erasures' rather than guesses, so the ECC decoder (which fixes two erasures for the cost of one error) repairs them.
why: Capacitor charge wall (Cs ~5 fF at AR 60-75:1): roughly doubling effective correction lets designs accept ~30-40% less cell signal, i.e. shorter, cheaper capacitors at equal failure rate.

title: Retinal lateral inhibition between sense amps cancels coupling noise
idea: Retinal neurons subtract a fraction of their neighbours' signals to sharpen edges; add weak, calibrated cross-coupling between adjacent bitline sense amplifiers that subtracts a set fraction of each neighbour's developing signal, cancelling the bitline-to-bitline capacitive coupling that grows at every pitch shrink.
why: Capacitor wall and pattern-dependent errors: coupling eats ~10-20% of sense signal at 12 nm-class pitch; cancelling it lets Cs shrink or bitlines lengthen (fewer sense amps, less of the 49% periphery).

title: Stigmergic open DRAM periphery IP with pheromone bounties
idea: Termites build mounds by reacting to marks left by others, with no central planner. An open-source DRAM periphery and controller repository (sense amps, decoders, PHY, BIST) where each unresolved design issue carries a buyer-funded bounty 'pheromone' that grows over time, so foundries with no DRAM heritage can tape out commodity parts.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and the deepest IP barrier; open IP could let 2-4 new entrants skip a decade of design learning.

title: Quorum-sensing escrow that auto-triggers fab expansion at threshold
idea: Bacteria act together only when signal-molecule concentration crosses a threshold. Buyers deposit refundable commitments into an escrow; when committed volume for a fab phase crosses the preset level, the funds release as prepayment and construction starts automatically.
why: Turns fragmented demand into bankable capex and removes years of deliberation from capacity response.

title: Pan-genome patent pool for capacitorless DRAM-class cells
idea: Bacterial species share an accessory gene pool that any strain can draw on. A FRAND patent pool with a reference open PDK covers gain cells, floating-body and selector-only cells, and any CHIPS-funded fab can license it for a flat per-wafer fee.
why: Clears the IP thicket that keeps entrants out; capacitorless cells avoid incumbents' capacitor patents.

title: Long/short hedge: split-pillar dipole bit cancels common-mode leakage
idea: Like a market-neutral long/short position, store each bit as +Q/-Q on two halves of one pillar capacitor split by a vertical dielectric fin, accessed by twin transistors in the same active area; leakage and temperature drift hit both halves almost equally, so the difference decays far slower, and the sense amp compares the halves with no reference.
why: Facts 3 and 10: differential read doubles signal per pillar and tolerates ~3-5x more common-mode leakage, stretching refresh 4-8x; half-swing operation allows ~30% lower VARY for ~2x CV2 savings, at ~20% area cost versus 6F2.
note: Twin-cell differential sensing in one pillar; area cost offsets refresh gain.

title: Dam spillways: self-limiting overflow barriers quantize multi-level charge
idea: Borrow the image sensor's anti-blooming drain and a dam's spillway: each storage node gets a gate-controlled lateral overflow barrier whose height, set by the write voltage on the spill gate, caps stored charge at 1/3, 2/3 or full; writing deliberately overfills and the excess spills, so each cell lands on the exact level without a program-verify loop.
why: Cost per bit: 2 bits per cell with self-calibrated levels removes the cell-to-cell variation that kills DRAM MLC, ~1.6-2x bits per mm2 at the same lithography; needs a 3-threshold sense amp and somewhat larger node.
note: Spill-gate levels self-calibrate, but leakage shrinks per-level margin and refresh rises.

title: Croissant lamination and MLCCs: multilayer electrodes inside a shallow hole
idea: Copy multilayer ceramic capacitors and laminated pastry: in a shallow AR~15 hole, ALD-deposit four alternating TiN/ZrO2 layers, then tie odd electrodes to the node and even ones to the plate using a selective recess etch and self-aligned sidewall contacts at the rim, so capacitance multiplies by the number of dielectric interfaces.
why: Fact 1: three parallel dielectric layers give ~3x capacitance per footprint, allowing ~20:1 instead of 70:1 pillars and shorter lateral capacitors for 3D DRAM; contacting alternate layers is the process risk.
note: Alternate-layer contacting inside ~30 nm hole consumes the hole; modest net gain.

title: Vacuum flask isolation: NEMS relay access switch with zero off-current
idea: A thermos blocks heat by removing the medium; block leakage the same way: connect the storage capacitor to the bitline through a ~200-nm TiN or poly-SiC cantilever relay in a sealed nanocavity, closed electrostatically by the wordline and open (vacuum gap) at rest, built with e-beam litho, sputtered TiN, sacrificial SiO2 and HF-vapor release.
why: Fact 3: off-state current is truly zero, so only capacitor dielectric leakage (~aA) remains and refresh nearly vanishes, and VARY is no longer tied to transistor Vt; contact wear and stiction (~1e10 cycles shown) are the risk for DRAM endurance.
note: Zero off-current but relay endurance far below DRAM cycling needs.

title: UNSW light-steered hydrogenation re-passivates deep access-transistor traps
idea: UNSW's 'advanced hydrogenation' for solar cells shines intense light during a 200-400 C anneal to set hydrogen's charge state (H0/H-), letting it diffuse far and bond to otherwise unreachable defects. Apply a flash-lamp or LED-illuminated hydrogenation step after capacitor formation so hydrogen reaches buried-wordline gate-oxide and channel traps hidden under the capacitor stack.
why: Interface traps under the buried gate drive GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling in the tail (fact 3); deeper, charge-state-controlled passivation could halve Dit and shrink tail leakage 2-5x.
note: Light-steered hydrogenation from UNSW solar; reaching buried-gate traps unproven in DRAM.

title: Time-release capsule: buried hydrogen reservoir re-passivates traps over product life
idea: Extended-release drugs meter an active ingredient for years from an embedded reservoir. Embed a hydrogen-rich silicon nitride layer, sealed above by a dense diffusion barrier, a few hundred nm below the cell array so it slowly releases hydrogen at 85 C operation and keeps re-passivating dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and VRT activity.
why: The retention tail drifts with aging and in-field VRT (fact 3); a self-replenishing passivant keeps the tail tight for 10 years and removes the ~2x end-of-life refresh guardband.

title: Subsea pressure-compensated housings: park standby bitlines at the leaky state's level
idea: Deep-sea electronics survive by equalizing pressure instead of resisting it. During self-refresh, park bitlines at the stored-'1' voltage instead of VDD/2 so '1' cells (which also suffer junction leakage) see zero drain-source voltage and no subthreshold loss, while robust '0' cells' small upward subthreshold leak is partly offset by their own downward junction leak.
why: Targets the weakest state in the tail; could extend worst-case retention 2-4x in idle, where refresh is 16-33% of power (fact 3).

title: Water-utility pressure management: store a lower '1' level during standby
idea: Water utilities cut leaks by lowering night pressure because crack flow rises faster than linearly with pressure. On self-refresh entry, rewrite rows with a '1' of ~0.75 VARY instead of full VARY; GIDL and trap-assisted junction leakage fall super-linearly with storage-node voltage, so tail cells lose charge more slowly than the signal shrinks, and full levels are restored on exit.
why: Net retention gain of ~1.5-3x for GIDL-dominated tail cells plus lower CV^2 per standby refresh (facts 3, 10).
note: Gain only if leakage falls faster than halved sense signal.

title: Batik wax-resist: hydrocarbon-inhibited selective deposition self-aligns GIDL offset spacers
idea: Batik artists block dye with wax so color lands only where intended. Use long-chain alkylsilane or alkanethiol inhibitors (no fluorinated SAMs) to block ALD on the gate metal while a SiN/SiOC offset grows only on the junction side, self-aligning a 2-3 nm gate-to-storage-junction underlap that weakens the field driving band-to-band GIDL.
why: Self-aligned underlap without extra lithography cuts GIDL, often the dominant tail mechanism, 3-10x (fact 3) and removes an overlay-limited step (fact 4).

title: Shop-door air curtain: electrostatically doped storage junction with no dopant atoms
idea: An air curtain separates indoors from outdoors with no physical door. Form the storage-node 'n+ region' electrostatically: a low-workfunction metal contact (hafnium- or yttrium-based) on an undoped silicon tip induces an electron layer by workfunction difference, so there is no implanted junction, no dopant clusters and no BF2 or fluorine co-implant.
why: Without implanted dopants and their damage, generation sites and random-dopant Vt variation shrink, narrowing the leakage tail (fact 3) and removing implant steps (fact 4).

title: Battery active balancing recycles bitline charge between subarrays
idea: Like a BMS shuttling charge from full cells to empty ones, a switched flying-capacitor bus links subarrays: when subarray A equalizes its full-swing bitlines, its surplus charge is dumped into subarray B, which is mid-restore. About 40% of restore charge is recycled from the previous activation.
why: Energy per bit/voltage floor: bitline CV2 dominates activation; activate energy falls ~30-40%, as does charge-pump load.

title: Battery coulomb-counting: dual-threshold reads flag weakening rows
idea: Like a battery gauge estimating health on every cycle, each SA gets a second small comparator at a raised '1' threshold; normal reads flag cells that have lost >40% of charge, and the row goes into a per-bank weak-row table refreshed at 4x while all other rows refresh at 1/4 rate.
why: Refresh (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power): ~60-70% fewer refreshes, driven by live in-field retention data instead of one-time profiling.

title: LTPS display demux: one sense amp serves four bitlines
idea: Like the 1:3 demultiplexers that let one display source driver feed several columns, bitlines develop in parallel and hold their signal on their own capacitance while a BEOL switch tree steps one SA across four bitlines in ~1 ns slots, restoring each before moving on.
why: Periphery area: SA count falls 4x (SA stripe ~15% to ~5% of die) for ~+3 ns tRAS; nanosecond holding fits the leakage budget.

title: Options trading: speculative early latch with cancellable confirmation
idea: Like buying an option, a small fast SA latches at ~40% signal development and ships data early; the main SA finishes at full development and, on the rare disagreement, sends a cancel/replay token on the data bus, like exercising the option.
why: Latency: ~30% faster tRCD on most reads, with replays rare (<1e-4) when references are centred.

title: Helical parking-ramp tier contacts instead of a staircase
idea: Like a spiral parking ramp reaching every level without stairs, deposit the tier stack conformally over a pre-etched helical ramp in a ring trench; after one planarization every tier surfaces at a different angular position on a flat ring, contacted by a single litho of radial vias.
why: 3D staircase cost and area (facts 2, 7): N trim-etch cycles become one ramp etch plus CMP; claims ~5x smaller contact region for 64+ tiers.

title: Garage-door spring: tier back-plate bias lowers wordline swing
idea: A torsion spring carries most of a garage door's weight; give the lateral access transistors of each 3D tier a shared back-gate plate held at a retention-safe negative bias, and switch only the tier being served to a Vt-lowering bias for a batch of accesses, so front wordlines need only a ~0.9 V swing.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline energy ~ V2 drops ~11x from 3 V to 0.9 V; plate switching is amortized over hundreds of accesses per tier dwell.

title: Catalytic-converter metal recovery: onsite tungsten hexafluoride regeneration loop
idea: Like precious-metal refiners that recover platinum from spent catalytic converters, trap unreacted WF6 and W-bearing byproducts in CVD exhaust, recover W from CMP slurry and chamber-clean residue, and directly fluorinate the recovered tungsten with onsite electrolytic F2 back into WF6 for the same tools.
why: Tungsten is ~80% Chinese and much of the WF6 fed to CVD never becomes film; a closed loop could cut virgin tungsten purchases ~50-70% and shrink HF/fluoride waste.

title: Catastrophe bonds finance second sources for single-point chokepoints
idea: Insurers use parametric cat bonds that pay out on a measurable trigger. DRAM makers and hyperscalers pool premiums into a 'chokepoint bond' that pays automatically if Spruce Pine output, Qatari helium shipments or WF6 import prices cross thresholds, while the standing premium pool funds qualification of alternates (Norwegian quartz, synthetic crucibles, U.S. helium).
why: Prices tail risk so second sources that look uneconomic in calm years get funded; cuts expected lost DRAM output from single-region chokepoints.

title: Lab-grown diamond glut repurposed as HBM thermal interlayers
idea: Lab-grown jewelry diamonds have crashed in price as CVD reactor capacity floods the market. Point those reactors at thin polycrystalline diamond wafers (~1,500 W/m-K) bonded to the HBM base die and top core die as lateral heat spreaders, with extra die thinning to keep the standard stack height; JEDEC HBM pinout and protocol are untouched.
why: Lowers peak stack temperature ~10-15 C so more of the stack stays below 85 C and avoids 2x refresh (refresh costs 10-20% of bandwidth), using spare non-chokepoint diamond-grower capacity.

title: Solar-cell spatial ALD multiplies hafnium and zirconium precursor utilization
idea: PERC solar lines deposit Al2O3 by spatial ALD, moving wafers under separated precursor zones instead of filling and purging a chamber. Adapt rotary-platen spatial ALD for DRAM ZrO2/HfO2/Al2O3 capacitor dielectrics and TiN electrodes and capture the unused metal-organic stream for re-synthesis; the capacitor stack and DDR/HBM interface stay identical.
why: Temporal ALD often uses only a few percent of costly precursor; spatial ALD can exceed ~30-50% utilization with 5-10x throughput, cutting Hf/Zr/Ti precursor demand and tool count.
note: Spatial ALD struggles with conformality in 60:1+ holes due to short exposure times.

title: Two-level nanoimprint stamp, like CD replication, for node and pad
idea: Borrowed from CD/DVD plants, which mold multi-depth pit structures in one shot: make a two-level quartz imprint template carrying both landing-pad and storage-node levels, so one jet-and-flash imprint replaces two critical exposures and their overlay step, the way dual damascene merged via and trench.
why: Fact 4: removes 1-2 EUV/193i-multipatterning layers per die from the array; NIL tool ~1/3 the price of EUV and self-aligned levels eliminate one overlay error budget.

title: Controlled spalling from PV: peel device layers, reuse substrates tenfold
idea: Borrowed from IBM's solar controlled-spalling work, which peels 10-20 um silicon layers by plating a stressed nickel film and starting a crack: a small team spalls blank device layers off 300 mm substrates for epi or bonding, mounts them on cheap carriers and re-polishes the donor wafer for 5-10 reuses.
why: Scarce resource: cuts crystal growth, HPQ crucible and polysilicon demand per bit 5-10x and yields thin dies for stacking; surface roughness and crack control are risks.

title: Blast chiller: compress lines at LLC eviction straight into NV log
idea: Like blast chillers freezing food before ice crystals form, a 'chiller' engine at the last-level cache compresses evicted lines predicted cold and appends them directly to a persistent NAND/MRAM log on CXL, bypassing DRAM; reads of chilled lines return through a small decompress buffer.
why: Cold data never occupies DRAM even briefly and is durable on arrival; claims a 2-3x smaller DRAM tier with persistence included.

title: Bipolar-battery voltage stacking of HBM core dies
idea: Bipolar battery stacks put cells in series so the same current flows straight through every cell. Do this with four groups of HBM core dies across a ~4.4 V rail: each group sees ~1.1 V and the same current is reused in every tier. Small switched-capacitor balancers on the base die absorb load mismatch between tiers.
why: Cuts supply current, and with it the count of power TSVs/bumps and PDN IR loss, by about 4x. That shrinks HBM's TSV tax and could return 10-15% of die area or allow taller stacks.

title: Lego-stud reworkable press-fit sockets for HBM stacks
idea: Like Lego studs, electroplated Cu micro-pillars (~40 um pitch) on the interposer cold-press into compliant plated cups on the stack. A clamp frame holds them instead of solder, so stacks can be swapped, upgraded or harvested at room temperature.
why: One bad stack no longer scraps a $20k+ package, and memory can be reused across generations. Package yield and effective memory supply rise 10-20%.
note: Thousands of cold-press contacts at 40 um pitch: contact resistance and reliability doubtful.

title: Organ-transplant harvesting of HBM from retired accelerators
idea: Like organ donation, debond HBM stacks from end-of-life GPUs below 300 C, using local laser reflow and a solvent-swellable underfill. Retest and re-bump them, then transplant them into low-cost organic-substrate inference cards.
why: Millions of HBM stacks retire with 3-5 year-old accelerators. Reusing even 30% adds supply with no new wafer capacity.

title: Newspaper-press roll-to-roll interposer ribbons for memory rings
idea: Like a rotary newspaper press, make polyimide ribbons with 2-5 um semi-additive Cu lines roll-to-roll at ≤250 C. Use them to connect HBM-class stacks placed in a ring 2-5 cm around the compute die.
why: Ribbon cost per mm² is ~10x below silicon interposers, and the ring lifts the shoreline limit. That allows ~2x more stacks per accelerator at a modest pJ/bit penalty.
note: 2-5 cm wide parallel lanes cost energy and signal integrity; 2-5 um R2R lines aggressive.

title: OLED burn-in ledger that trims subarray wordline voltages over life
idea: OLED drivers count the cumulative on-time of each pixel and boost the aged pixels. The DRAM would accumulate the activation-time integral of each subarray in a small counter. Local regulators then trim that subarray's VPP and negative-wordline level to track the access-transistor Vth drift from BTI/HCI, so the full end-of-life guardband is not applied from day one.
why: This recovers ~100-200 mV of lifetime guardband against the voltage floor (fact 10): about 10-15% wordline energy, or a tighter leakage tail early in life.

title: Adaptive-optics guide-star canary cells in every subarray
idea: Adaptive optics measures the atmosphere with a bright guide star. Each subarray holds about 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (smaller cap, closer spacing) that fail at ~1/2 the retention time and ~1/2 the hammer count of normal cells. A comparator scan during refresh catches canary flips and locally doubles refresh or restores the neighbours.
why: Nominal refresh can then be set for typical conditions while canaries give in-situ early warning. That cuts refresh 40-60% (fact 3) and adds a hammer tripwire (fact 9).

title: HDR exposure bracketing: double sensing that flags erasures
idea: HDR photography brackets exposures to capture the marginal tones. A replica latch senses each line again with +delta and -delta reference offsets. Bits whose answers disagree are flagged as erasures, and the on-die RS/BCH decoder runs erasure decoding, which corrects about twice as many flagged symbols as unknown errors with the same parity.
why: Effective ECC strength roughly doubles, so the raw weak-cell rate can be 10-100x higher. That allows smaller capacitors or longer refresh (facts 1 and 3).
note: Parallel offset comparators before latching could work; area cost of replicas.

title: Chocolate-tempering anneal cycles for capacitor dielectric phase purity
idea: Chocolatiers cycle temperature so that only the stable Form V crystals survive. The ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor dielectric would get a cycled RTP profile: above the phase transition, cooled to nucleate, then reheated just below the melt point of the unstable phases. This dissolves the minority monoclinic and amorphous pockets and the vacancy-rich grain boundaries that make up the leakage tail.
why: A narrower leakage distribution could mean ~10x fewer weak cells and possibly k toward 45-50. Both relax the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the retention tail.

title: Water-hammer arrestor: transient deep-negative clamp on neighbour wordlines
idea: Plumbing arrestors absorb pressure spikes. While wordline i rises and falls, the sub-wordline drivers of i+-1 and i+-2 pulse deeper negative (about -0.5 V instead of -0.2 V), but only for the edge window. That damps capacitive coupling and electron injection into victims without the GIDL penalty that a constant deep negative bias would carry.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold 3-10x (fact 9) without counters, using only sub-wordline driver timing.

title: Pick-n-pull robotic DRAM package harvesting from consumer e-waste
idea: Copying the auto-junkyard 'pick-n-pull' model at component scale, a robotic line X-rays scrapped phones and laptops, selectively reflows only the LPDDR/DDR packages with a hot-gas nozzle, reballs them, and mounts them on standard CXL carrier cards with a small controller that hides package heterogeneity.
why: Turns e-waste (billions of devices, ~8 GB each) into a U.S. domestic memory source; scarce-resource and capital intensity near zero, cost per usable bit maybe 25-40% of new.

title: Repurpose idle Gen-6 LCD lines into glass-substrate oxide memory
idea: Following China's LCD overcapacity, retool mothballed Gen-6 display fabs (1.5 x 1.85 m glass, IGZO TFT capable) to pattern 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays at ~0.5-1 um rules on glass, sold as panel-scale 'memory tiles' for far-memory CXL shelves.
why: Uses fully depreciated display capital (near-zero capex) and m2-scale substrates; bits are low density but cost per area of glass is ~100x lower than 300 mm silicon, targeting cold-but-byte-addressable tiers.
note: At ~1 um rules density is ~1000x below DRAM; glass cost/area advantage likely does not close cost/GB.

title: Downhole-oil HT-SOI lines retooled for hot automotive DRAM
idea: Like the 200 C SOI electronics used in oil wells, put DRAM cells on thick buried oxide so the storage-node junction has no bulk leakage path, made on existing 200 mm HT-SOI fabs that already qualify parts for 10 years at 125-175 C.
why: Junction-leakage-limited retention at 125 C improves ~5-10x, cutting hot refresh, while moving auto bits onto otherwise niche U.S./EU lines.

title: Vehicle-to-cloud memory lending from parked ADAS computers
idea: Like vehicle-to-grid batteries, parked EVs on smart chargers lend their 32-128 GB Grade-1 (125 C, 15-year) ADAS DRAM and compute to an edge cloud over a fiber or ISO 15118 link in the charge cable, with an attested sandbox that wipes on unplug.
why: Cars sit idle ~95% of the time; tens of millions of high-memory EVs form a stranded memory fleet of tens of PB that can absorb edge inference demand.

title: Camel-mode chiller-free data centers enabled by 125 C memory
idea: Like camels that let body temperature rise rather than sweat away water, specify memory and modules qualified for 10 years at 125 C junction so halls can be air-cooled with 50 C intake in deserts with no evaporative towers; temperature-aware refresh keeps data intact.
why: Opens cheap-power, water-scarce sites (e.g., Arizona, Gulf) without water permits and removes 20-40% of cooling energy, making new AI capacity and its memory deployable faster.

title: Nordic district-heating revenue from 125 C-rated memory racks
idea: Like CHP plants that sell waste heat, run memory and compute at junction temperatures near 115 C so the coolant leaves at 90-95 C, high enough to sell to district-heating or industrial-process loops; heat revenue is contracted to subsidize memory purchases.
why: Heat sales can offset 10-20% of memory TCO and give municipalities a reason to host DC capacity; requires parts qualified for 10 years at 125 C.
note: Refresh rate and leakage climb above 85 C; energy penalty offsets heat revenue.

title: Tire-retreading: re-package harvested die into 125 C packages
idea: Like retreading a sound tire casing, laser and plasma decapsulation strips the consumer-grade mold compound and bond wires from harvested DRAM, die that pass a 125 C retention screen are re-bumped and re-packaged in high-Tg, low-chloride mold compound rated for 10 years at 125 C.
why: Upgrades the good fraction of e-waste die into the scarce, premium automotive/industrial grade, adding a recycled supply of high-temperature parts.

title: Whisky-warehouse thermal seasoning during inventory dwell
idea: Like whisky aging in a warehouse while it waits to be sold, wafers and die already held in buffer inventory sit in 150 C bake chambers that double as burn-in, so weak retention cells reveal themselves and are mapped out before packaging; parts ship pre-screened for 10 years at 125 C.
why: Converts idle inventory time into free HTOL screening, raising yield of 125 C-grade parts and removing a separate burn-in step from the supply chain.

title: Debond-on-demand packaging designed for multiple die lives
idea: Like smartphone battery stretch-release adhesives and cradle-to-cradle furniture, package memory in an encapsulant that stays stable for 10 years at 150 C but debonds cleanly at 260 C under a chemical trigger, so die can be recovered intact and repackaged at end of product life.
why: Makes every high-temperature memory die harvestable for 2-3 lives, multiplying effective supply per wafer over decades.

title: Atanasoff capacitor drum as transistorless capacitors swept by MEMS brushes
idea: The 1942 ABC stored bits on capacitors mounted on a rotating drum, read and regenerated by brushes, with no switch per capacitor. Fabricate a field of isolated nano-capacitors (10-nm dielectric, no junction, no transistor) under a 2D MEMS array of conductive probe tips, each tip scanning a 50x50 um field with its own sense amp.
why: Without an access transistor leakage is dielectric tunneling only, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours (Fact 3 refresh ~0); ~2F2 cells with no wordline; microsecond 'drum tier' that needs a DRAM cache.
note: Millipede-style probe storage gives micro-to-millisecond access and tip wear; not working memory.

title: Zuse Z1 sliding-plate memory as nanomechanical detented shuttles
idea: Zuse's 1938 Z1 held bits as the position of sliding metal plates with pins. Fabricate 200-nm Si or TiN shuttles in BEOL cavities with a buckled-beam double-well detent, set left or right by an electrostatic comb pulse and read by differential capacitance to a sense line.
why: Bit is a mechanical position: non-volatile, zero leakage, contact-free so effectively unlimited endurance (Fact 3); ~10 ns switching at this size; ~20F2 cell but zero refresh energy.
note: Mechanical detent bit, nonvolatile but ~20F2 and slow.

title: Dekatron glow-stepping counter revived as a multi-position domain-wall cell
idea: The Dekatron stored a decimal digit as the position of one glow among ten cathodes. Store 4 bits as the position of a single domain wall among 16 notches in a 400-nm magnetic strip, stepped by current pulses and read by an MTJ whose free layer overlaps a wedge so resistance tracks wall position.
why: 4 bits per cell instead of 1 gives density without a litho shrink (Fact 4), non-volatile with no capacitor (Facts 1, 3); risk is separating 16 resistance levels.

title: Magnetostrictive delay line reborn as recirculating spin-wave registers
idea: 1950s calculators stored bits as acoustic pulses in magnetostrictive nickel wire. Store bits instead as ~5 GHz spin-wave packets in permalloy/CoFeB waveguide loops patterned on an existing 180-nm line, with inductive antennas and a CMOS amplifier regenerating each loop every pass.
why: Bit is a wave in flight: no cell, no capacitor; ~1-um bit spacing gives ~0.1-1 Mb/mm2 and 10-50 ns latency in short loops for FIFO/KV-cache streaming buffers; regeneration energy is the open risk.

title: Plated-wire space heritage: sell rad-hard magnetic memory first, then scale
idea: Plated wire flew on Voyager and the Shuttle because radiation cannot upset it. Launch a revived plated-wire-style magnetic memory on existing U.S. 200-mm trailing-node fabs into space and defense, where rad-hard memory sells at ~1000x DRAM $/bit, and use the margin to fund density learning toward commodity parts.
why: Funds a new storage element without a $15B fab, builds U.S. manufacturing know-how, and de-risks the physics on paying customers.
note: Plated wire scales poorly; rad-hard MRAM already owns this niche.

title: Static induction transistor revival as an oxide-free access switch
idea: Revive Nishizawa's 1950s static induction transistor: a vertical pillar whose current is pinched off by buried p+ junction gates, with no gate dielectric and no gate-drain overlap, so the off state is a pure electrostatic potential barrier. With no MOS overlap there is no gate-induced drain leakage and no oxide-trap-assisted tunnelling, the two mechanisms behind the DRAM tail.
why: Attacks the GIDL and trap-assisted tail (fact 3), with a claimed 10x tail reduction; junction gates swing ~1-1.5 V instead of a ~3 V wordline, so wordline CV2 drops 2-4x (fact 10).

title: Twistor helical vertical bitlines cancel 3D coupling noise
idea: The twistor wound magnetic tape helically around a wire to define its sensing path. Shift each vertical 3D DRAM bitline a quarter pitch at every tier step, so it climbs in a staircase helix and spends equal length beside each neighbor. Coupling then becomes common-mode, which the differential sense amp rejects.
why: Cuts inter-bitline coupling noise ~3-5x in 3D stacks (fact 2), allowing smaller signals and more tiers per sense amp.

title: Widrow memistor trims sense-amp offset in one via
idea: Revive Widrow's 1960 memistor, a three-terminal electroplated resistor. One added via mask fills a Cu/GeSe electrolyte plug in each sense amp's tail leg, which is plated up or down at test (and retouched in the field) to null that amp's measured Vt offset.
why: With offset trimmed out, sense transistors can shrink to near minimum size because mismatch no longer sets W·L: ~2-3x smaller sense stripes (fact 7) and ~40% less required signal (fact 1).

title: Delay-line wave-pipelined data bus on one thick RDL layer
idea: Mercury delay lines stored bits as pulses in flight. One added thick-copper redistribution layer, which reuses existing pad openings as vias, carries low-loss global data lines with 3-4 bits in flight at once (wave pipelining, used in 1960s IBM machines) and no intermediate pipeline latches or repeaters.
why: Triples global-bus throughput per wire, removes repeater and latch stripes (fact 7) and cuts global-data energy ~30% (fact 5).

title: Chopper-measured sense offsets stored in a per-stripe trim row
idea: 1940s chopper-stabilized amplifiers swapped their inputs to cancel drift. During refresh slots each sense amp's inputs are shorted and swapped and its decisions counted, giving a 2-bit offset estimate per amp. The estimates are kept in a dedicated trim row and loaded into per-amp dynamic trim capacitors, which are rewritten with each refresh. Zero added masks.
why: Mismatch-driven sense-amp area halves (fact 7) and margin improves ~30 mV, extending bitlines or shrinking Cs (fact 1).

title: Core-memory coincident-current selection with dual-gate 3D cells, no tier decoders
idea: Revive core memory's X/Y coincident-current selection: each 3D cell's access device is a dual-gate thin-film transistor that conducts only when both its tier strap and its vertical pillar gate are at half-select level, so N tier straps plus M pillars address N x M cells with only N+M drivers. Half-selected cells see one gate on and stay off, exactly as half-selected cores stayed below coercive force.
why: Facts 2 and 7: removes per-tier word drivers and most staircase decode, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% and lowering the tier count needed to break even below 26.

title: Atanasoff capacitor-drum brushes: sense amps commutated across mats
idea: Revive the Atanasoff-Berry Computer's capacitor drum, where a few brushes served thousands of capacitors: mats carry no local sense amps, and a small pool of sense amps is commutated across 8 mats through a low-capacitance charge-transfer bitline multiplexer that pre-amplifies before switching.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp count and pitch-matched area shrink ~8x, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% at a modest bank-parallelism cost.

title: MgB2 persistor arrays: niobium-free cryogenic memory without liquid helium
idea: Revive the 1957 persistor (a persistent supercurrent loop) and Buck's cryotron in magnesium diboride (Tc 39 K): bits are clockwise or counterclockwise currents in MgB2 loops switched by thermal cryotron gates. The arrays run at 20-25 K on sealed pulse-tube coolers rather than liquid-helium baths.
why: Avoids consuming helium (Qatar outage) and the niobium chokepoint of SFQ memory (~85% from one Brazilian producer); zero-resistance loops need no refresh; claims 10-100x lower energy per access for cryogenic AI and quantum controllers.
note: Cryogenic niche; MgB2 thin-film loops and cryotron switching density far from DRAM scale.

title: Atanasoff capacitor-drum regeneration on Gen-10.5 display glass panels
idea: Revive the 1942 Atanasoff-Berry 'jogged' capacitor memory as huge-area arrays on 3 m display glass: LTPS TFTs and metal-insulator-metal capacitors at 1.5 um design rules, with ABC-style continuous regeneration by row-parallel sense circuits at the panel edge.
why: No EUV, no Czochralski wafers or quartz crucibles (glass is made from sand), and it reuses idle panel fabs; ~9 m2 per substrate offsets the low density; claims 5-10x lower capex per bit for bulk, slower tiers.
note: 1.5 um panel rules give very low density; LTPS leakage is high; capex per bit gain doubtful.

title: CCD serial memory revived in idle CMOS image-sensor fabs
idea: Revive Fairchild/Intel's 1975 CCD memory: build buried-channel two-phase CCD loops, where data recirculates and is regenerated every lap, at 65-90 nm on image-sensor lines, as a sequential tier for weight streaming and KV-cache scans.
why: No EUV, no capacitor pillars, no Hf or W; uses mature 300 mm sensor capacity at ~4F2 per bit at relaxed F; claims 3x cheaper per bit than DDR for streaming access.
note: Serial access and slow shift rates make it a streaming tier at best.

title: Apollo rope memory reborn: laser-programmed inductive ROM for frozen weights
idea: Revive Apollo core-rope ROM, where each bit is whether a sense wire threads or bypasses a shared core: on a mature-node die with ferrite micro-transformers, a laser-cut or inkjet last-metal layer sets the threading choice after fab, so one die type can store any frozen model's weights.
why: No EUV, no per-model masks, no refresh, and no DRAM bits spent on weights; uses only Fe, Ni and Cu; claims to free 50-80% of inference DRAM capacity for KV cache.
note: Ferrite rope density far worse than via-ROM or flash.

title: Crystallographic KOH etching on (110) silicon for vertical trenches
idea: Revive 1970s anisotropic wet etching of (110) silicon, where KOH or TMAH attacks {110} ~100x faster than {111}, leaving atomically vertical {111} walls: align DRAM active-area and isolation trenches to <112> so a wet bath cuts 50:1 vertical walls with no plasma, using hard masks printed by LED or Talbot exposure. The crystal lattice becomes the CD reference.
why: Constraint and capital: replaces Ar/He-assisted STI and buried-wordline plasma etches with ~$1M wet benches; smooth {111} walls cut interface traps feeding the retention tail (Fact 3). Risks are a two-direction layout and lower nMOS mobility on (110).

title: CDC 6600 Extended Core Storage rebuilt on fully depreciated DRAM fabs
idea: Revive ECS, the CDC 6600's huge, slower, block-transfer-only memory: build a wide (1-4 KB block), ~1 us bulk tier from 2x-nm-era DRAM lines whose tools are fully depreciated, reached only by a block-copy instruction with no load/store and no coherence. Compilers and runtimes explicitly stage tiles from ECS into a much smaller fast DDR5/HBM.
why: Fact 4 (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost): zero-depreciation old-node bits with relaxed timing approach leading-edge cost per bit without EUV; keeping only the hot 20-30% in fast DRAM roughly halves premium DRAM demand.
note: Old-node bit density is 2-3x lower, so zero depreciation only partly closes the cost-per-bit gap.

title: Differential-analyzer integrators hold sequence state instead of KV cache
idea: Revive analog computers, where state lived as voltage on integrators: state-space or linear-recurrent layers run on arrays of switched-capacitor integrators whose capacitor voltages are the recurrent state, updated per token and digitized only at layer outputs. Context length no longer grows memory.
why: For SSM/hybrid models a fixed few hundred KB of analog state per sequence replaces a KV cache that reaches tens of GB at 1M tokens, and state read/write energy disappears.

title: Core-memory read-modify-write: accumulate inside the restore cycle
idea: Core memories rewrote every word they read, and machines like the PDP-1 used that rewrite to increment memory in place. Do the same on destructive-read arrays: a sense amplifier with an adder/XOR in its writeback path folds an incoming gradient or count into the data during restore, demonstrated on a university-fab 1T1C or gain-cell test array.
why: Gradient accumulation and embedding/histogram updates dominate training memory traffic; accumulating during restore removes double-buffered accumulators and halves read-plus-write traffic.
note: Adder in sense-amp writeback at bitline pitch is the hard part; bit-serial needed.

title: Holographic-memory optics revived: volume-hologram lid routes chiplet beams
idea: Revive 1960s-70s holographic page-memory optics as interconnect: memory dies emit page-wide micro-LED/VCSEL arrays upward and a volume hologram in the package lid diffracts each beam to a fixed photodiode on any of several compute chiplets, giving all-to-all fan-out without waveguide routing.
why: Facts 5/6: thousands of 5-10 Gb/s optical channels per mm^2 with no interposer wiring, ~1 pJ/bit, and broadcast fan-out for free.

title: Setun balanced-ternary revival: end-to-end trits for ternary-weight models
idea: Revive the 1958 Setun balanced-ternary computer as a data path: store {-1,0,+1} weights as three charge levels (VDD/2 +/- dV) in DRAM cells, ship them over PAM-3 lanes without binary conversion, and sense them with a ternary sense amplifier.
why: Density/movement: 1.58 bits per cell versus 2-bit packing that wastes ~21%, and ternary-weight LLMs cut traffic ~10x versus FP16; end-to-end trits capture it with no unpack logic.
note: Three-level sense margin shrinks; PAM-3 already in GDDR7.

title: Xerography revival: electrophotographic copper-toner printing of package wiring
idea: Revive Carlson's 1938 xerography: a laser-imaged photoconductor drum picks up charged copper-nanoparticle toner and transfers it to the package substrate, followed by sintering and electroless copper thickening, giving maskless, resist-free 10-20 um RDL.
why: Constraint: no photoresist at all, so no PFAS PAGs or fluorosurfactants; a printer-class tool (~$1M) replaces lithography for package redistribution, cutting capital and enabling distributed US packaging.

title: Ferreed-switch revival: magnetically latched crosspoints circuit-switch pooled memory
idea: Revive Bell's 1960s ferreed (remanent-magnet-latched reed switch from No. 1 ESS) as MEMS crosspoint arrays with semi-hard magnetic latches that connect any server's copper lanes to any memory sled and hold with zero power.
why: Constraint: glass-sealed NiFe reeds need no fluorinated chemistry or fluoropolymer insulation; circuit switching adds no per-access latency or energy (just a wire) versus 100+ ns and several pJ/bit through CXL packet switches.

title: Spark-gap revival: impulse radio broadcasts between chiplets inside package cavity
idea: Revive spark-gap carrierless transmission as on-chip impulse UWB: memory chiplets radiate 20-50 ps pulses from on-die antennas into the metal-lid cavity, and compute chiplets receive with crystal-set-style envelope detectors (no PLL or LO).
why: Constraint: wireless links need no TSVs, no fluorinated etch and no PTFE high-frequency substrate; broadcast fan-out of weights is free at ~1-3 pJ/bit and 10-20 Gb/s per channel.
note: Cavity multipath and envelope-detector sensitivity limit rate.

title: Geiger ratemeter diode pump: one extra cell integrates row activations
idea: 1950s Geiger-counter ratemeters used a diode pump that added a fixed charge packet per pulse to a leaky capacitor, giving a time-windowed count with no logic. Each row gets one extra 'hammer cell' that receives a fixed charge quantum through a diode-connected device whenever its wordline fires, while natural leakage drains it; at refresh, a threshold sense reveals rows activated more than ~500 times recently and triggers neighbour restores.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): windowed activation counting for one cell per row (~0.01% area) instead of SRAM or in-array counters, with no timing penalty.

title: Dolby pre-emphasis writes overdrive leaky rows from recycled-water fabs
idea: Dolby noise reduction boosted quiet signals when recording and cut them on playback. Rows profiled as leaky are written with ~+150 mV boosted array voltage and a longer write time (pre-emphasis) and read with a matching reference shift (de-emphasis) from a row-class table, so cells with extra junction leakage still hold enough charge across a normal refresh interval.
why: Water: lets the fab run a ~90-95% closed rinse loop at 1-5 MOhm-cm instead of once-through 18 MOhm-cm ultrapure water (~10x less fresh water), whose trace metals widen the leakage tail (fact 3); pre-emphasis recovers ~2x retention on affected rows.
note: Boosted writes stress dielectrics; water-saving link speculative.

title: Core-stack parity plane revived: XOR row rebuilds any killed wordline
idea: Many core memories carried an extra parity plane computed across all bit planes. Each subarray gets one XOR parity row, kept up to date in a small per-subarray SRAM latch on every write and written back at refresh, so a whole wordline lost to a particle short, a hammer burst or a stuck driver is rebuilt from the other rows and remapped in the field.
why: Water: whole-wordline kills are the dominant yield loss from particles left by dry cleaning; rebuilding them lets an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water flow hold yield for ~0.2% extra rows plus latch area.
note: Parity row rebuild of whole wordlines; write-update overhead and water claim tenuous.

title: Arsenal Conversion: Idle Gen-8 LCD Lines Make Oxide Memory Panels
idea: Revive the WWII conversion of car plants into bomber plants: buy shuttered Gen-8.5 LCD TFT fabs and convert their IGZO backplane process to build 2T0C oxide gain-cell memory arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass panels, diced into low-cost capacity chiplets.
why: Capital: one glass panel has ~70x the area of a 300 mm wafer at a fraction of the cost per area; repurposes stranded display capex instead of building fabs.
note: Same LCD-fab IGZO gain-cell panels as I-04100.

title: Esaki Diode Revival: Goto-Pair RTD Memory on Phone RF GaAs Fabs
idea: Revive the 1958 Esaki tunnel diode and Goto's tunnel-diode-pair memory as resonant-tunneling-diode bistable cells (two series RTDs plus one HEMT access device) running at 0.3 V, made on the GaAs/InP lines that build smartphone RF front ends in North Carolina, Massachusetts and Oregon.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower via 0.3 V swing and static, refresh-free storage with nW standby; adds memory supply from underused III-V RF fab capacity.

title: Parametron phase bits held by a shared resonant pump
idea: Invert 'a bit is a static stored quantity' -> the bit is the phase (0 or pi) of a sustained sub-harmonic oscillation. On-die high-Q LC or AlN bulk-acoustic parametrons are pumped at 2f by one shared resonant clock tree; each locks into one of two phases, written by a tiny seed injection and read by mixing against a reference phase.
why: Removes the capacitor charge wall and refresh entirely (facts 1, 3): the pump regenerates every bit every cycle and the resonant tree recycles most pump energy; standby cost scales with 1/Q rather than leakage tails.
note: LC/BAW resonators are micron-scale; density far below DRAM.

title: Rank-order charge encoding survives common-mode leakage drift
idea: Invert 'each cell's charge level carries data absolutely' -> encode data in the relative order of charges in a group. Four cells written to four distinct analog levels encode one of 24 permutations (4.58 bits per 4 cells); because leakage drags all levels down together, the rank order survives long after fixed thresholds fail, and a read is a local comparator sort.
why: Stretches refresh interval ~4-10x (fact 3) and adds ~15% bits per cell (cost/bit); tail cells that break order are handled by a light outer code.
note: Rank modulation known from flash; DRAM tail cells leak individually, not common-mode, and analog sensing costs area.

title: Airlock isolation: a second hold gate that closes only in idle
idea: Inverts 'one access gate must serve both speed and isolation': split the vertical access pillar into a fast low-Vt segment driven by the wordline and an ultra-high-Vt 'hold' segment that is statically on during active periods and driven to about -1.5 V when a bank enters idle/self-refresh. The hold segment switches only on mode changes, so its slowness costs nothing.
why: Idle leakage drops 100-1000x (fact 3), cutting self-refresh power (16-33% of idle) by ~10x while active timing is unchanged; ~1 extra gate layer.

title: Breathing cell plate: park stored charge at the leakage minimum
idea: Inverts 'the cell plate sits at a fixed VDD/2': in idle, ramp the common plate down ~0.3 V so '1' nodes sit lower (shrinking the GIDL and junction fields where the trap-assisted tail lives) while '0' nodes stay just short of forward bias, then ramp back before access; the stored difference is untouched because the plate shifts both states equally.
why: The tail's exponential field dependence (fact 3) gives ~3-10x longer idle retention, cutting self-refresh power proportionally with only a plate-driver change.

title: Delete the junction: dielectric-isolated junctionless storage node
idea: Inverts 'the storage node is a doped pn junction': build the access device as an accumulation-mode junctionless transistor in layer-transferred thin silicon on buried oxide, with the capacitor contacting a uniformly doped n+ segment wrapped in dielectric, so there is no depletion region where trap-assisted generation (the dominant tail mechanism) can occur.
why: Cuts the junction/GIDL-driven leakage tail (fact 3) 10-100x, pushing refresh toward seconds, and removes floating-body coupling that aids row hammer (fact 9).

title: Scout comparators forward speculative data before the sense amp settles
idea: Inverting 'data is valid only after the latch fully resolves': a tiny scout comparator on each selected column taps the bitlines through high-impedance gates at ~60% of tRCD and forwards data early, while the main sense amp keeps developing and restoring normally; a parity check on the scout word triggers a replay from the main latch on mismatch.
why: First-data latency -25-30% for ~1% added periphery area, because only the 64-512 selected columns get scouts; replay rate is tuned by scout timing.

title: Twin-FeFET race: first-to-conduct wins, no reference needed
idea: Inverting 'sensing compares a cell against a reference': each bit is stored as opposite polarizations in two FeFETs; their shared gate is ramped and a tiny arbiter latches whichever drain current crosses first, so the decision needs no reference voltage and the read is nondestructive.
why: Eliminates reference generators and restore, rejects common-mode Vt drift and temperature, and drops read energy to the arbiter's few fJ; 2 cells/bit offset by vertical 4F^2 FeFETs.
note: FeFET endurance ~1e10 falls short of DRAM-class.

title: Universal programmable sense front-end die for any capacitorless array
idea: Inverting 'periphery is designed for one cell type': a merchant logic die with sense channels configurable in current, voltage, or time mode is hybrid-bonded to any capacitorless array (thyristor, FeFET, floating-body, MTJ), so new cell startups only build arrays.
why: Removes ~2-3 years and most periphery design cost from each new memory technology and gives a volume product for US logic fabs.

title: Nano-MLCC cells: deposited multilayer capacitor with side terminations
idea: Inverts 'capacitor plate area is set by etch depth.' Deposit N alternating electrode/dielectric films, cut cells, and contact alternate electrodes from two side vias like a ceramic MLCC termination, so plate area grows with layer count on a flat footprint.
why: Fact 1: a 10-layer stack gives ~10x plate area per footprint with no high-AR etch; capacitance scales with deposition cycles instead of AR 115.
note: 10 plates give ~10x footprint area, below a 70:1 pillar's ~70x.

title: Fe/MgO/Fe junctions pinned by FeMn: chokepoint-free MRAM cells
idea: Inverts 'STT-MRAM needs Co, Ta, W, Ru and Pt.' Build stacked MTJs as TiN seed / FeMn antiferromagnet pin / Fe / MgO / Fe free layer / TiN cap, reviving the original high-TMR Fe/MgO/Fe system in place of CoFeB, Ta, W and Ru synthetic antiferromagnets.
why: Scarce resources: removes chokepoint metals from a ~10-30 ns, high-endurance cell and may lower stack cost.

title: Capacitor-first DRAM: anneal the dielectric before transistors exist
idea: Inverts 'transistor first, capacitor last'. Etch and fill the storage-capacitor array into a bare carrier wafer, anneal the dielectric at 800-1000 C to crystallize ultra-high-k phases (rutile TiO2, SrTiO3, k 80-150) that a finished transistor could never survive, then Smart-Cut-transfer a thin single-crystal Si film on top and build access transistors aligned to the buried capacitor marks.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): k~100 lets pillar AR fall from ~70:1 to ~35:1, removing the slowest high-AR etch/fill steps and their tool count; ~10-15% fewer process hours per wafer.

title: Grow capacitor pillars upward instead of etching 70:1 holes
idea: Inverts 'deep features are carved top-down'. Pattern only a thin hard mask of seed openings, then grow single-crystal Si or TiN-clad nanopillars upward by selective-area epitaxy/CVD to 2-3 um (AR >100:1) and wrap them with ALD dielectric and plate; height becomes a growth-time knob instead of a plasma-selectivity limit.
why: Removes the deepest, slowest plasma etch and its bowing/twisting yield loss (facts 1, 4); AR ~115 reached with no extra litho, ~25% more charge per cell.
note: Selective growth uniformity at 2-3 um and thermal budget after transistors.

title: Twin landing pads let EUV expose at half dose
idea: Inverts 'one printed feature per electrical function'. Give every storage node two parallel, slightly offset contact/landing-pad features so a stochastic missing or bridged print of one is electrically harmless, then expose those stochastics-limited layers at ~50% EUV dose.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited; halving dose on 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers raises scanner wafers/hour ~40-60% (fact 4) for a few-to-10% cell-area cost.
note: Twin pads help missing prints, not bridges to neighbours.

title: One universal grating reticle prints every array layer
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own critical mask'. Lay out all array layers (active, wordline, bitline, storage node) on a single gridded honeycomb lattice so one ultra-high-quality periodic reticle prints the dense lines for every layer by rotation/offset, and only coarse DUV-printable cut/keep masks are layer-specific.
why: ~60-70% fewer critical reticles and qualification cycles, and a path to replace 3-4 EUV layers with DUV cut layers (fact 4).

title: Test storage nodes mid-flow through a sacrificial wiring layer
idea: Inverts 'electrical test happens at the end'. Right after capacitor formation, deposit a temporary metal grid that ties storage nodes into addressable test groups, map shorts and leakers with a probe card in minutes, strip it, and feed the map to redundancy planning and scrap/rework before the costly BEOL.
why: Stops spending ~40% of remaining process cost on doomed wafers and cuts yield-learning loops from ~3 months to ~1 (fact 4 capital efficiency).

title: Garbage collector living inside the memory expander
idea: Inverts 'GC is a host-CPU job that needs 2-3x heap headroom': a CXL Type-3 expander runs a concurrent copying/compacting collector next to its DRAM, with hardware forwarding pointers serving as the read barrier. Because it compacts continuously, managed heaps run at 1.1-1.3x live data.
why: Java/Go/.NET fleets reserve large heap headroom; shrinking it frees 30-50% of the DRAM those services occupy.
note: Hardware/near-memory GC is published; allocation still needs headroom.

title: Bytes-per-transaction disclosure standard for federal software procurement
idea: Inverts 'memory efficiency is a private engineering choice': a public benchmark and label, like Energy Star, reports peak and average DRAM per transaction for cloud services and enterprise software, and federal procurement favors top-quartile products.
why: Creates market pull for memory-lean software; cutting software footprint 20-30% equals years of new fab output, without a fab.

title: Clamped unbonded die stacks with inductive coupling and swappable layers
idea: Invert 'stacks are permanently bonded': DRAM dies are stacked with no microbumps or TSVs, held by a spring clamp, talking through on-die inductor coils with power fed through edge contacts; a die that fails burn-in is popped out and replaced before final encapsulation.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax and 20-30% stack-yield loss: die-level rework turns a scrapped 12-high stack into a one-die swap, and coil area replaces TSV keep-out area.

title: Molybdenum TSVs: CTE-matched vias from Colorado ore
idea: Invert 'TSVs are copper and contacts tungsten': fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum mined and refined in the U.S. (Colorado), whose CTE (~4.8 ppm/K vs ~17 for Cu) sits close to silicon's 2.6.
why: Shrinks TSV stress keep-out zones several-fold for denser TSVs and a smaller HBM area penalty, while avoiding the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint.
note: Mo resistivity ~3x Cu and slow CVD fill of high-aspect TSVs.

title: Flex-wrapped memory: DRAM ribbons folded around the compute package
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a flat plane next to compute': mount thinned DRAM dies on U.S.-made polyimide (Ohio) flex with fine-line wiring and fold it around the four sides and top of the accelerator module.
why: Uses five faces instead of one plane: ~3-4x memory contact perimeter and shorter links than 2.5D in the same footprint.

title: Dual-threshold sense amps feed soft-decision LDPC
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM read is a hard 0/1 decision': each sense amp gets a second offset comparator that flags weak-0/weak-1 when bitline signal is near the reference, giving NAND-style soft information; a soft-decision LDPC uses it to correct ~2x more errors per parity bit.
why: Cells can run with 30-40% less signal margin (smaller Cs, longer refresh; facts 1, 3) for a small periphery cost.

title: Completion-detecting sense amps: weak cells read slow, not wrong
idea: Inverts 'memory timing is synchronous and fixed': each sense-amp group asserts a done signal once its latch resolves past a full-rail threshold; the bank uses this asynchronous handshake, so a low-charge weak cell simply takes 2-3 ns longer instead of being mis-sensed at a fixed tRCD.
why: Turns the charge/retention tail (facts 1, 3) from an error source into a small latency tail; strong cells finish ~15% faster than the worst-case timing.
note: Signal below sense-amp offset resolves wrong, not slow.

title: Slew-limited wordlines reduce hammer coupling per activation
idea: Inverts 'faster wordline edges are always better': one mask adds a high-sheet-resistance poly resistor in each sub-wordline driver path, shaping a slower rise and fall that reduces the capacitive kick and hot-carrier injection each activation delivers to neighbors.
why: Hammer disturbance per ACT cut ~2-4x (fact 9) for ~1 ns of tRAS, with no counters.
note: Slower edges trade tRAS for less coupling; capacitive and trap paths partly addressed.

title: Contactless RF test coils make every die's retention map cheap
idea: Inverts 'test requires probe needles': one top-metal mask adds an on-die inductive coil and rectifier so whole wafers are powered and read wirelessly in parallel inside a heated chamber for hours of retention mapping without probe cards.
why: Cuts test cost (~10-15% of DRAM cost) and gives every die the full weak-cell map that tolerance schemes need.

title: Helium-free fabs via hydrogen-neon backside cooling and recapture membranes
idea: Inverts 'wafer chucks and leak checks need helium': retrofit electrostatic chucks in etch/CVD tools to run closed-loop low-pressure hydrogen or neon backside gas, and recover residual helium from tool exhaust with on-site membrane purifiers.
why: Scarce resource: Qatar's ~30% helium share is offline; cutting fab helium purchases >90% removes a supply-stop risk for every DRAM line.

title: Recycle tungsten from WF6 exhaust and spent targets on-site
idea: Inverts 'tungsten is a consumable bought from China': cryo-traps capture unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust and an on-site fluorination cell converts chamber scrapings and spent sputter targets back into WF6 feedstock.
why: Scarce resource: China supplies ~80% of tungsten; closing the loop could roughly halve virgin tungsten demand per wafer.
note: WF6 capture from exhaust plausible; volume recovered per fab is modest.

title: Sell bits during a node's immature yield ramp
idea: Inverts 'a new node ships only after defect density matures': with up to 1% cell faults absorbed by controller codes, vendors sell error-tolerant parts from the first months of a ramp instead of waiting 12-18 months for near-zero-defect yields.
why: Time to capacity: pulls 6-12 months of saleable output forward on each node and pays down ramp costs sooner.
note: 1% cell-fault tolerance needs heavy ECC overhead; ramp-phase volume is modest.

title: Delete spare rows, fuses and laser repair from the die
idea: Inverts 'arrays need redundancy and repair': design die with no spare rows or columns, no e-fuse banks and no repair test insertion; scattered faults up to 1% are handled by a host-side defect map and coding.
why: Periphery area and test capital: frees ~3-5% of die area and a full tester insertion, raising die per wafer and tester throughput.

title: Half-height capacitors: cut aspect ratio, accept weak-cell sensing errors
idea: Inverts 'Cs must stay near 5 fF': etch storage nodes at ~35:1 instead of 60-75:1 for ~2.5-3 fF; codes keep the weak-sense tail under 1% while each high-AR etch chamber processes about twice as many wafers.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital: halves the slowest, most tool-hungry etch, a major capacity bottleneck.
note: Sense margin at 2.5-3 fF needs short bitlines and strong ECC.

title: Breathing mat back-plate lowers wordline swing to 1.3 V
idea: The 3 V wordline exists only because Vt must be high for retention. Make Vt dynamic: a mat-shared back-gate plate sits at -1 V in standby (deep off, leakage tail suppressed) and steps to 0 V only for the accessed mat, so the wordline needs ~1.3 V and its drivers become thin-oxide core devices.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): wordline CV^2 energy ~5x lower ((3/1.3)^2), driver area ~3x smaller, charge pump eliminated or shrunk.
note: Plate switching energy and coupling disturb to storage nodes.

title: BEOL oxide-TFT sub-wordline drivers stacked over the array
idea: Move sub-wordline driver strips out of silicon into a back-end thin-film transistor layer directly above the mats (wide-bandgap channel, high off-resistance suits 3 V switching), so the substrate under the array returns to cells or sense amps.
why: Periphery footprint (fact 7): ~10-15% die area freed without hybrid bonding.

title: Self-referenced double read only for test-flagged weak cells
idea: MRAM-style self-reference: read the cell, write a known '1', read again and compare both levels on the same SA input, cancelling per-cell Cs variation and SA offset. Applied only to the ~0.1% weak cells flagged at test via a small address table.
why: Lets the bulk population run with ~2x thinner margins (smaller Cs, longer refresh) while the tail is rescued (facts 1, 3).

title: Metal-contact NEMS relays power-gate mats and steer redundancy
idea: Mechanical relays have zero leakage and no oxide or junction to degrade at 125 C; their endurance limit (~1e10 cycles) is only a problem for fast paths. Use BEOL NEMS relays for mat power gating and redundancy steering, which switch only at boot or idle transitions.
why: Periphery standby leakage at hot -> ~0; relays sit above silicon, freeing area (fact 7).
note: BEOL relays for rarely switched gating; stiction and contact reliability remain open.

title: MIM-feedback charge amplifier sense with geometry-set gain
idea: Hold the bitline at virtual ground with a compact cascode integrator whose gain is Q/Cf, set by a MIM capacitor ratio rather than transistor Vt or mobility, so the output is independent of Cbl, temperature and aging.
why: Cbl no longer divides signal (fact 1): ~3-5x more output per electron, stable over 10 y at 125 C; longer bitlines cut SA count.
note: Per-stripe CSA area/power and speed versus latch SA.

title: Hexagonal close-packed vertical cells reach the 3.46F2 packing limit
idea: Use cylinder-forming block-copolymer self-assembly over a coarse ArF guide pattern to place vertical channels on a hexagonal lattice, routing wordlines and bitlines along two of its three 60-degree axes so each cell occupies 2*sqrt(3)*F^2 instead of 4F^2.
why: Geometry is a hard minimum: hexagonal packing (0.907) beats square (0.785), giving ~13% more bits per area at the same F, while polymer chain length rather than EUV sets the 20-30 nm pitch, removing several of the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4).
note: Only ~13% density gain; DSA defectivity remains the barrier.

title: Millimeter mat-lets fluidically self-assembled onto logic base wafers
idea: Dice DRAM arrays into ~1 mm^2 tested mat-lets and flow them in a carrier fluid over a logic wafer with shape-matched recesses, where they self-align and solder at millions per hour, so only known-good mats enter a stack or 2.5D tile.
why: Yield follows Y=exp(-D*A): at D=0.1/cm^2, 1 mm^2 parts yield ~99.9% versus ~90% for 1 cm^2 dies, compounding across 12-16 die HBM stacks, so the 20-30% HBM yield loss (fact 6) falls to a few percent.

title: Stepwise adiabatic bitline restore using spare-tier capacitors as reservoirs
idea: Dedicate a few cell rows per tier as reservoir capacitors held at V/4, V/2 and 3V/4; during restore and refresh, bitlines step through these reservoirs before the final rail connection, and falling bitlines replenish them.
why: Charging a capacitor in N equal steps dissipates CV^2/(2N) instead of CV^2/2, so four steps cut bitline restore loss ~4x; with refresh at ~46 fJ/bit (fact 3) and restore dominating activation energy (fact 8), this is a direct cut using cells already in the stack.
note: Reservoir cells are tiny versus bitline capacitance; half-VDD precharge already recovers much of the charge.

title: Mirror-twin tiers interleave bitlines so the idle twin provides reference
idea: Fabricate tiers in mirrored pairs above and below one shared bitline layer whose lines alternate between serving the top tier and the bottom tier; when the top tier fires, each neighbouring bitline belongs to the idle bottom tier and acts as a perfectly matched reference.
why: Recovers folded-bitline noise rejection (~2x effective signal) inside a 4F^2 open geometry, lowering required Cs (fact 1), and halves bitline layers and sense-amp rows per tier pair (fact 7) at no area cost.

title: Micro-transfer-printed silicon sense amplifiers dot a printed array foil
idea: Make 50x50 um sense-amp and decoder chiplets on a depreciated logic line, release them by undercut etch, and pick-and-print thousands per elastomer-stamp cycle onto the foil, one chiplet per ~1k x 1k printed sub-array.
why: Puts the speed- and matching-critical periphery (49%, fact 7) in silicon while the array stays at R2R cost; since transistor matching sets sense margin, silicon sense amps let printed cells hold less charge and reach ~10-30 ns access.

title: DUV photo-annealed printed oxide memory tiers atop finished logic dies
idea: Nanoimprint and inkjet-print metal-oxide TFT DRAM tiers directly on a finished logic wafer's passivation, converting sol-gel films with 185/254 nm UV below 150 C so the 400 C back-end budget is never approached, in an advanced-packaging house.
why: Data movement (fact 5): memory sits micrometres above the compute it feeds, so wire energy for the hot working set falls ~10-30x versus HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit, without hybrid bonding or a DRAM fab.

title: Grayscale nanoimprint cuts the 3D staircase in one etch
idea: A staircase carries one piece of information, a depth profile, yet costs N resist-trim/etch cycles; imprint a single tapered resist profile from a grayscale NIL master and transfer it with one 1:1-selectivity etch, exposing every tier's landing pad at once.
why: Removes ~N/2 litho-etch cycles for 150+ tiers, so tier count can grow ~10x without added staircase cost, while cutting resist (PFAS PAG) and etch gas per bit.

title: Dose-coded grayscale exposure defines three depths in one shot
idea: First principle: a mask carries 2D information, but exposure dose is a free third channel. A halftone grayscale reticle plus a resist with linear dose-to-depth contrast prints the buried-wordline trench, bitline-contact and isolation recess as three depth levels in one exposure, and a single etch with ~1:1 resist-to-substrate selectivity transfers all three.
why: Masks and steps (fact 4): 3 litho-etch modules become 1, saving ~2 critical masks and their overlay budget; ~5% lower wafer cost.

title: BEOL-only oxide DRAM built in packaging-class back-end fabs
idea: First principle: channels only need high-temperature processing if they are single-crystal Si; amorphous oxide channels, ALD high-k and MIM capacitors all form below 400 C. Build the whole cell array (oxide-channel gain cells plus MIM capacitors) as back-end layers on cheap logic wafers in advanced-packaging/back-end fabs, which cost about 1/3 per wafer-pass of front-end fabs.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: runs on U.S. advanced-packaging lines being built under CHIPS, with no implanters, diffusion furnaces or EUV.

title: Purity only where electrons live: epi device layer on cheap substrate
idea: First principle: retention-critical leakage depends on defects within ~1 um of the surface, so 11N Czochralski purity in the other ~774 um is wasted. Grow a 3 um high-purity epitaxial device layer on substrates made from upgraded metallurgical-grade Si by directional solidification (no quartz CZ crucible), with a buried oxygen-precipitate getter to trap metals.
why: Scarce resources and cost: less dependence on Spruce Pine quartz crucibles and electronic-grade polysilicon; ~40-60% lower substrate cost.

title: Capture and regenerate the 95% of ALD precursor that misses wafers
idea: First principle: ALD uses one monolayer per cycle, so ~95-99% of Hf, Zr and Ru precursor flows to the exhaust or the chamber walls. Fit each ALD exhaust with a cold-trap or sorbent cartridge that captures unreacted metal-organic precursor, and return the cartridges to the precursor maker to be regenerated into fresh precursor.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (Hf, Ru) and opex: ~5x less precursor purchased; recycled by design.

title: Memory-controller-assisted marking lets GC heaps run near live size
idea: Garbage-collected heaps are sized at 2-3x live data because marking is slow and must stay ahead of allocation. The memory controller keeps a hardware mark bit per 16 B granule in spare ECC metadata and traces references in the background with a pointer-chasing engine, so the runtime can collect continuously and set headroom near 1.2x live.
why: Java, Go, .NET and JS heaps are a large share of cloud DRAM; cutting headroom from ~2.5x to ~1.2x frees 30-50% of that memory.

title: Laser-written diffractive glass embodies frozen network layers
idea: A fixed linear transform needs no stored bits if it is built into geometry. Write the frozen embedding projection or the early layers of vision and speech models as stacked phase plates in fused silica (femtosecond direct write); a microLED array encodes the inputs and photodiodes read the outputs, so those weights occupy no DRAM and need no refresh.
why: Weights and activations of frozen front-end layers leave DRAM in edge devices and high-volume serving, and energy per MAC is near zero because propagating light does the work.

title: Series voltage-stacked DRAM dies slash power-TSV current
idea: Power TSVs and bumps exist to carry current, and I^2R loss and electromigration scale with current, not power. Run four stacked dies in series from a 4.4 V rail, each floating in its own 1.1 V domain, with small switched-capacitor balancers absorbing activity mismatch, so the stack draws one quarter of the current through one quarter of the power vias.
why: Frees ~30-50% of HBM TSVs (much of the array is power/ground) for data or area savings and cuts PDN loss ~16x per via (facts 6, 5).

title: Single-flux-quantum superconducting interposer for cryogenic memory links
idea: An SFQ pulse costs Ic*Phi0 ~ 2e-19 J, about 10^4 below CMOS link energy. For 4 K cryo-AI and quantum-control systems, route memory traffic on passive niobium microstrip lines in the interposer that carry SFQ pulses ballistically without dispersion, with CMOS-to-SFQ converters at the cryo-DRAM edge.
why: aJ-scale data movement with zero resistive loss, and cryo-DRAM needs almost no refresh (facts 5, 3).

title: Diamond interleaf wafers make DRAM-on-logic thermally survivable
idea: The shortest data path is DRAM directly on logic, but heat raises leakage and refresh rate. Bond 30 um polycrystalline CVD diamond wafers (k ~1500 W/mK) between logic and DRAM tiers with laser-drilled Cu vias, spreading hotspots sideways before they reach the cells.
why: Lets DRAM sit ~50 um from compute (~0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4) while holding cells <=85 C so refresh does not double (facts 5, 3).

title: ESD-free die-to-die pads via laser-cut sacrificial shorting ring
idea: ESD diodes often contribute over half of an I/O pad's capacitance, yet they only matter during handling. Tie all bond pads to a metal shorting ring through dicing and stacking, then laser-ablate or fuse the ring after bonding, leaving bare pads at ~1-2 fF instead of ~100 fF.
why: 2-4x lower CV^2 per bit on chiplet and HBM links and smaller I/O area (facts 5, 7).
note: Pad cap claims inflated; ESD-light D2D already industry trend.

title: Molybdenum CTE-matched TSVs: no keep-out zone, no tungsten
idea: Keep-out zones exist because copper (17 ppm/K) fights silicon (2.6 ppm/K). Fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum (4.8 ppm/K) so thermal stress drops ~5x, allowing transistors right next to vias and avoiding tungsten, which China supplies at ~80%.
why: Shrinks TSV area overhead ~30-50% and removes a chokepoint metal from the stack (fact 6, resources).

title: Terahertz in-package broadcast: one transmission feeds every chiplet
idea: A wire costs energy per destination; a radiated wave costs once for N receivers. Put 300 GHz on-chip antennas on the HBM base die and every compute chiplet inside a metal-lidded package cavity acting as a waveguide, broadcasting weights or shared activations to all chiplets simultaneously.
why: For multi-chiplet weight broadcast, energy per delivered bit falls ~N (4-16x) versus point-to-point copies (fact 5).
note: 300 GHz link energy today exceeds wire energy, eroding the broadcast advantage.

title: E8 lattice coding packs 3 bits/cell in noisy gain cells
idea: Slicing each multilevel cell independently is a cubic lattice and wastes ~3 dB of packing gain. Group 8 gain cells and map 24 bits onto E8 lattice points, the densest packing in 8D, decodable with a few hundred gates. The Voronoi decision regions give 1.5-3 dB more margin against drift.
why: Density: 2 to 3 bits/cell (+50%) with the same capacitorless cells and retention drift.

title: Junctionless storage transistor removes high-field junction leakage tail
idea: In conventional cells the tail is trap-assisted tunneling/GIDL at the high-field n+/p junction. A uniformly doped junctionless thin-body write transistor in a gain cell has no metallurgical junction, so peak field falls 3-5x, and field-enhanced trap emission, which is exponential in field, drops by orders of magnitude.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10x longer refresh in a capacitorless cell.

title: Kirchhoff current-sum parity check scrubs eight rows per read
idea: Gain-cell reads are non-destructive current sources. Opening 8 read wordlines on one bitline sums their currents, and a small ADC returns that column's Hamming weight across 8 rows. Its LSB is checked against a stored column parity.
why: Capacitorless reliability: 8x less scrub energy and bandwidth, so weak cells can be checked often enough.

title: Data-lifetime-matched retention grade: short capacitors for AI working memory
idea: Retention only has to exceed the data's lifetime, and AI activations and KV-cache are rewritten every ~1-10 ms, not held for 64 ms. Define a JEDEC short-retention grade with a 4 ms guarantee; since required charge scales with leakage x hold time, Cs can drop ~40% (with shorter bitlines to keep Cs/Cbl), allowing AR ~30-35:1 capacitors built with fewer high-aspect-ratio etch and deposition steps.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital: halving cylinder height removes the hardest HAR steps, lifts yield and frees etch-tool capacity; ~15-25% lower cost per bit for the AI tier.
note: Sense margin, not retention, often sets Cs; weights are long-lived, limiting AI fit.

title: Silicon-carbide access transistors make refresh-free DRAM in U.S. power fabs
idea: Junction and off-state leakage scale with intrinsic carrier density n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT); 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has n_i ~1e-9 cm^-3, about 1e18 below Si, so retention moves from milliseconds to hours. Build 1T1C arrays on 200 mm SiC lines (already operating in the U.S.) using only SiC, SiO2, Al, Zr and TiN.
why: Refresh wall and U.S. manufacturability: eliminates refresh (16-33% of idle power) using domestic SiC capacity; risks are SiC/SiO2 interface traps, low channel mobility and ~3x wafer cost.
note: SiC DRAM retention shown in 1990s; low density, interface traps and wafer cost limit it to niche.

title: Grow oxide memory arrays on cheap cast-silicon carriers, not prime wafers
idea: A BEOL oxide-TFT array needs only a flat, insulating, thermally stable carrier, not a dislocation-free crystal. Core 300 mm rounds from cast multicrystalline solar ingots, polish and oxidize them as carriers for Zn-Si-O memory stacks, then hybrid-bond onto a thin CMOS periphery wafer.
why: Scarce resource and cost: removes HPQ crucibles and CZ pulling from the array half of the die; carrier cost per wafer falls up to ~100x.

title: Pencil lead: carbon mold capacitors released by dry ash, no HF
idea: Stimulus 'pencil lead' -> build the capacitor mold from amorphous carbon instead of oxide, etch holes with O2/SO2 plasma, deposit the electrodes, then remove the mold by oxygen ashing. Today the oxide mold is stripped in liquid HF whose capillary forces topple tall cylinders; a dry ash has no capillary force at all.
why: Removes the pattern-collapse limit so pillars can reach the ~115:1 AR needed for more charge (fact 1); eliminates HF and C4F8 from the capacitor module with existing tools.
note: Carbon mold etch at AR >100 and mechanical support still needed; incremental.

title: Bamboo forest: grow capacitor pillars upward instead of etching them
idea: Stimulus 'bamboo forest' (tall shoots grow up, nobody carves them) -> pattern a thin Al2O3 mask with BCl3/Cl2, then grow vertical Si/SiGe nanopillars by selective-area epitaxy (SiH4/HCl) to 100:1 and convert them into bottom electrodes with chloride-ALD TiN. Height comes from growth time, not a deep fluorocarbon etch.
why: Decouples pillar aspect ratio from etch physics (fact 1) and drops the hardest etch/EUV layer (fact 4); fluorine-free end to end.

title: Breathing lung: brownmillerite oxide inhales oxygen to switch whole-volume
idea: Stimulus 'lungs' -> a 10 nm SrFeO2.5 brownmillerite layer topotactically 'inhales' oxygen from an adjacent Ta2O5 reservoir under +1 V to become metallic SrFeO3, and exhales it at -1 V; the whole volume switches (not a filament), giving ~1000x resistance change with tight cell-to-cell spread.
why: Volume switching removes the variability tail of filamentary ReRAM while staying nonvolatile with no refresh (fact 3); iron-based oxides deposited without fluorine.
note: Ionic switching endurance far below DRAM needs.

title: Airlock two-gate pillar using stack-effect isolation
idea: Random stimulus 'airlock': two doors that are never open together.
