Split the vertical access pillar's gate into two independently driven segments (upper/lower wordlines, no added footprint); in retention both are off and the floating mid-channel node self-biases, giving the storage-side segment negative Vgs and near-zero Vds (the stack effect), while both open together within ~1 ns for access.
why: Stack effect cuts subthreshold leakage ~10-30x and suppresses DIBL on the storage side, pulling the <=13 fA tail toward ~1 fA so the refresh interval rises 8x+ (fact 3) at zero footprint cost in a vertical-channel cell.

title: Tailor-trimmed access transistors: charge-trap Vt fix for tail cells
idea: Random stimulus 'tailor': alter only the garments that do not fit. Add a thin nitride trap layer to the access gate stack; after retention screening at wafer test, the ~1 ppm leaky cells get a one-time Fowler-Nordheim program pulse that adds ~150 mV of Vt, pulling them back into the main distribution.
why: The refresh interval is set by the worst-ppm tail, not the median; trimming it lets refresh go from 64 to ~512 ms (8x) for all cells (fact 3). Risk: trapped-charge retention over 10 years at 85 C.

title: Bubble-wrap void beneath each storage-node junction
idea: Random stimulus 'bubble wrap': air pockets isolate whatever sits on top. Form a silicon-on-nothing cavity (Si/SiGe epi, SiGe removed laterally, top Si sealed by H2 anneal) under the storage-node junction only, so the junction has no bottom area facing the substrate while the channel stays body-tied.
why: Removes bottom-area junction generation leakage and substrate-injected minority carriers (fact 3), aiming at 5-10x lower junction leakage without floating-body effects in the channel.

title: Pressed-flower 2 nm silicon channel widens the bandgap
idea: Random stimulus 'pressed flower': flatten it and its properties change. Thin the vertical access channel to a 2-3 nm sheet by self-limited oxidation and strip, where quantum confinement raises silicon's effective bandgap by ~0.2-0.3 eV and gives near-ideal gate control.
why: A wider effective gap suppresses band-to-band GIDL and generation current exponentially, and swing approaches 60 mV/dec: tail leakage down ~10x (fact 3). Risk: mobility and on-current loss, sheet-thickness variation.

title: Fridge-magnet doping: dopant-free charge-plasma access transistor
idea: Random stimulus 'fridge magnet': it holds by field, not glue. Make the array access transistor junctionless and implant-free: low-work-function metal contacts (e.g., Er/Hf silicide) electrostatically induce n-type source/drain in undoped silicon ('charge plasma'), and channel Vt comes from the gate metal work function rather than halo/well implants.
why: Each array implant needs litho, an SPM resist strip and a wet clean; deleting ~6 of them cuts array-FEOL UPW >10x, and with no metallurgical junction there is no junction leakage and the GIDL field is softer (fact 3).
note: Fermi-level pinning at metal/Si contacts and residual BTBT GIDL limit the leakage benefit.

title: Bonsai pillars: grow vertical channels instead of etching them
idea: Random stimulus 'bonsai': shape the growth rather than carve the wood. Form vertical access channels by selective epitaxy upward from bitline-contact seeds through a patterned oxide template made with one low-AR etch, so there is no 60:1 silicon etch, no etch-polymer wet strip and no damaged sidewall.
why: Deletes the high-AR etch-clean-rinse loop (>10x less water for the pillar module) and yields damage-free channel sidewalls with fewer interface traps, attacking the leakage tail at its source (fact 3).
note: Template sidewall defects and facet/merge control are the doubt.

title: Camel HBM rated to 125 C enables waterless warm cooling
idea: Random stimulus 'camel': built to tolerate heat instead of drinking to stay cool. Rate a hot SKU of HBM to 125 C junction by combining an elevated-Vt array (+150 mV gate work function), base-die refresh that scales with temperature and hot-screened dies, so accelerator coolant loops can run 45-50 C inlet and reject heat through dry coolers all year with no evaporation.
why: HBM's ~85-95 C ceiling often forces cold coolant and evaporative towers; dry cooling takes memory-attributable cooling water from ~1.5-2 L/kWh to near zero, far more than 10x, with the extra leakage at temperature (fact 3) absorbed by design.

title: Pendulum resonant wordline drivers recycle 3 V swing energy
idea: Random stimulus 'pendulum': energy swings back and forth instead of being thrown away. During refresh bursts, wordlines are driven as part of an LC resonant tank (integrated inductors on the HBM base die), so each 3 V wordline rise and fall returns most of its charge to the tank instead of burning CV^2 through inefficient pumps.
why: Wordline pumps run at ~30-40% efficiency and the 3 V swing is stuck (fact 10); recovering ~80% of wordline energy cuts the wordline share of refresh energy ~10x, and the generation and cooling water embedded in that energy falls by the same factor.
note: Single selected wordlines are poor resonant loads; integrated inductor area large.

title: Noise-cancelling headphones: cross-neutralization capacitors cancel bitline coupling
idea: Like active noise cancellation, inject anti-noise: each SA gets small neutralization capacitors from both neighbours' complementary latch nodes, so as an adjacent bitline develops its signal, an equal anti-phase charge is injected, nulling bitline-to-bitline coupling at 24 nm pitch.
why: Signal margin (fact 1): coupling from opposite-data neighbours steals ~20-30% of read signal; recovering it is worth ~1 fF of Cs or ~25% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.

title: Suspension bridge: mid-span regenerator towers double bitline length
idea: A suspension bridge spans far with a few towers. Insert a stripped-down 4-transistor single-ended regenerator (no column switch, equalizer or I/O, compared against a shared mid-rail reference) at the midpoint of each bitline, so bitlines can be 2x longer while the full SA sits only at the end.
why: Periphery area: halving the number of full SA strips (~20% of die) while towers cost ~1/3 of an SA saves ~6-8% die area.

title: Hourglass flip: precharge-free sensing starts from last value
idea: An hourglass is never reset, just flipped. Skip bitline equalization: each bitline starts from whichever rail its last sensed value left it at, a 1-bit tag per bitline group tells the SA to use a high-side or low-side reference, and a cell matching the rail moves no charge, so bitlines toggle only when data changes.
why: Precharge and equalize charge per activation becomes proportional to data change rate; for correlated or zero-heavy data (50-90% unchanged) bitline energy falls ~3-10x.

title: Rubik's cube: transposable 3D cell with orthogonal row and column access
idea: A Rubik's cube twists along either axis: each storage node connects to two access transistors in different tiers, a lower one gated by an X-wordline onto Y-bitlines and an upper one gated by a Y-wordline onto X-bitlines. The array can open a row or a column, so matrix transposes and column-wise tensor reads need no overfetch.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): claim 2-4x less energy per useful bit on transposed or strided AI access, at ~1.3x cell area that tiers absorb.

title: Three-way road junction: sense amps shared by three hexagonal mats
idea: Forced connection from a three-way junction: tile the die with hexagonal mats so each sense-amp cluster sits where three mats meet, and multiplex one sense amp across bitlines from three mats instead of the two of open-bitline sharing. Sub-wordline drivers line the hex edges and serve the two mats on either side.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): one-third fewer sense amps per bit; claim periphery ~49% to ~40% of the die and ~15% more bits per wafer.

title: Puff pastry: exponential lamination reaches 128 tiers in seven bonds
idea: Fold-and-roll multiplies pastry layers exponentially: build a 2-tier single-crystal cell stack, bond it face-down onto an identical stack and split off the donor to get 4 tiers, then repeat 4-on-4 and 8-on-8. 128 tiers take 7 bonding steps instead of 128 depositions, and every tier keeps a single-crystal channel.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): single-crystal lateral transistors far beyond the 26-tier breakeven with log2 process steps; claim cost per bit -40% versus 2D.
note: Doubling bonds still consumes 2^n tier builds; cost argument does not hold.

title: Lighthouse: infrared beams through silicon replace TSV fields between dies
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm the way air is to a lighthouse beam: put micro-LED or VCSEL emitters and Ge photodiodes at matching metal-free windows on thinned stacked dies, so each link beams straight through several dies to its receiver. Hundreds of wide optical channels replace thousands of TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no metal vias through cell dies; claim 10-15% less die area per bit and +10 points stack yield, at ~1 pJ/bit link energy.

title: Kangaroo pouch: spare-subarray chiplet carried beside the HBM base die
idea: A pouch carries a spare: co-package a small 'spare' DRAM chiplet bonded under or beside the HBM base die, and give the base die a CAM that redirects any failed core-die subarray to spare subarrays within the tRCD budget. Hosts see a standard HBM3E stack, and failures found after stacking are repaired instead of scrapped.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): claim stack yield above 90% and cost per good HBM bit -15 to -25%.
note: Stack yield loss is largely bonding/TSV, not subarray faults; PPR already covers some.

title: Aquarium glass: core dies framed in glass carry HBM channels
idea: An aquarium holds its contents in a glass frame: embed each thinned, TSV-free DRAM core die in a glass frame with laser-drilled, Cu-filled through-glass vias, and stack the frames so the vertical HBM channel wiring runs through the glass around the dies, with short RDL fan-in to edge pads. The base die and the HBM3E/HBM4 interface do not change.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): core dies shed TSV area and keep-out (~10-15% of die) and become standard thin dies; glass is cheap and not a chokepoint.
note: Fan-out with through-glass vias is known; perimeter via count and RDL length limit HBM-class width.

title: Bread slicer: laser-slice HBM backgrind silicon into reusable wafers
idea: Stimulus 'bread slicer' -> before HBM core dies are thinned to ~50 um, focus an IR laser ~100 um below the device side to write a subsurface cleave plane (stealth-slicing style), lift off the ~650 um remainder intact, polish it and recycle it as a reclaim or donor wafer instead of grinding it to dust.
why: ~90% of each HBM wafer's silicon is ground away; recovering it cuts Cz pulls, crucibles and polysilicon per HBM bit by ~40-50%.

title: Crime-scene fingerprint: hybrid-bonded dedup base die under DRAM
idea: Fingerprints expose duplicates: a logic die hybrid-bonded (Cu-Cu anneal ~250-300 C) beneath a DRAM stack hashes every written line, keeps the fingerprint table in on-die SRAM and transparently stores duplicate lines once, exposing more logical than physical capacity to the host.
why: Virtualized and AI fleets show 20-40% duplicate lines; module-level dedup multiplies capacity 1.2-1.6x with assembly entirely below 400 C.

title: Melting snowman: MoS2 back-end scratchpad for transient activations
idea: A snowman only needs to last the afternoon: transfer monolayer MoS2 transistors (<=300 C) into the accelerator's back-end as 2T gain-cell scratchpads whose ultra-low leakage holds charge 1-10 s without refresh, sized for inter-layer activations that live only milliseconds.
why: Activations stop round-tripping through HBM; activation DRAM drops 2-5x and refresh disappears for that data.
note: MoS2 2T0C cells are researched; BEOL scratchpad capacity is small and IGZO is more mature.

title: Lighthouse: lid-mirror free-space optical broadcast inside the package
idea: Forced link to a 'lighthouse': a VCSEL array at the center of the logic die beams upward to a curved, mirror-coated package lid, which reflects the beams down onto photodiode arrays on memory chiplets placed in a ring several cm away. No waveguides and no interposer traces are needed; each beam is a lane.
why: Escapes the shoreline/beachfront limit so 2-3x more memory chiplets fit around compute at ~1 pJ/bit over cm distances; removes large interposers.
note: Lid warpage and alignment over cm and VCSELs on hot logic are doubts.

title: Choir: frequency-multiplexed mm-wave carriers share each TSV
idea: Like a choir singing different notes on one stage: each TSV carries 4 mm-wave carriers with on-die mixers and filters, so one via does the work of four.
why: HBM TSV count and keep-out area cut about 4x, recovering part of the ~3x area-per-bit HBM tax.
note: Multi-band RF-interconnect known; mixer/filter area may exceed saved keep-out.

title: Umbrella: package lid delivers backside power, freeing TSVs
idea: Forced 'umbrella': the metal lid becomes a power/ground plane with spring contacts onto the backside of each stack die (through backside metal), so power comes down from above and the power TSVs, often a third of the total, are freed for data or deleted.
why: HBM TSV tax and IR drop; ~30% fewer TSVs or 1.3x more data TSVs at the same area.

title: Ant pheromone: analog decaying charge counters track row activations
idea: Each ACT deposits a fixed charge packet on a tiny per-row 'pheromone' capacitor beside the wordline driver; it leaks with a designed time constant near tREFW and a comparator fires a neighbor refresh at threshold, so the trail's evaporation is the sliding window for free.
why: Fact 9 (flips at ~1k ACTs): exact per-row tracking for ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row, <0.3% area versus 1-3% for SRAM/CAM counters.

title: Fire sprinkler: margin-sniffing sense amps trigger local auto-repair
idea: A second, offset-biased comparator per sense-amp group flags any activate whose bitline differential is under ~40 mV; flagged rows are immediately re-restored and logged on-die, and repeat offenders are remapped through soft PPR with no host involvement - a sprinkler that fires only where the heat is.
why: Catches weakening cells (retention, VRT, hammer) before they flip, making every read a free audit; supports ~2x longer refresh and smaller Cs margins.

title: Bamboo septum: buried electron-sink implant between adjacent storage nodes
idea: Like bamboo's node walls that stop splits, a narrow grounded n+ sink implanted in the isolation between a buried wordline and the neighbor storage node collects electrons injected when the aggressor toggles, before they reach the victim.
why: Fact 9: attacks the charge-migration hammer mechanism directly; could raise flip thresholds from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs at <3% cell area.
note: Process-level hammer mitigation; similar barrier engineering pursued by vendors.

title: Kitchen sponge: oxygen-vacancy scavenger laminate stabilizes hot capacitor leakage
idea: A 0.3-0.5 nm oxygen-reservoir layer (e.g. partially oxidized Ru/RuO2 or SrO) at the top electrode of the ZrO2/Al2O3 stack donates oxygen to refill vacancies that migrate under field at 125 C, halting the barrier lowering that raises dielectric leakage over years.
why: Hot leakage drift blocks qualifying thinner, higher-k dielectrics; stabilization lets k~40+ stacks pass 125 C/10 years, giving more charge per area (Fact 1).

title: Ticket scalper: non-transferable allocation tokens to kill shortage double-ordering
idea: Random stimulus 'ticket scalper' -> named tickets stop scalping. During allocation, a clearinghouse issues non-transferable bit tokens tied to verified installed-base telemetry and past consumption, so buyers cannot double-order or hoard phantom inventory.
why: Bullwhip hoarding amplified the 2021 chip shortage; removing phantom orders frees est. 5-15% of shipped bits to real demand during spikes.

title: Balloon: hydrogen backside wafer cooling replaces helium in fab tools
idea: Random stimulus 'party balloon' -> helium vs hydrogen lift. H2 conducts heat better than He (0.18 vs 0.15 W/m-K), so low-pressure (~10 Torr) H2 or forming-gas backside cooling on electrostatic chucks, with ppm-level flows and H2-tracer leak checks, replaces helium.
why: Cuts fab helium use est. 60-80% while Qatar (~30% of supply) is offline; keeps DRAM output from being gated by helium allocation.
note: H2 in plasma chambers raises safety and process-chemistry concerns.

title: Wallpaper: roll-to-roll fine-line polyimide interposers for HBM
idea: Random stimulus 'wallpaper' -> patterned rolls laminated onto walls. Roll-to-roll semi-additive copper on 25 um polyimide at 2/2 um L/S (flex-display-style R2R photolithography) is laminated on a glass stiffener as the HBM-to-GPU interposer.
why: Bypasses the silicon-interposer bottleneck; interposer cost est. 5-10x lower and capacity scales with web lines not 300 mm fabs, so more HBM ships per year.

title: Seed tape: fluidic self-assembly of known-good die onto moving web
idea: Random stimulus 'garden seed tape' -> seeds pre-spaced on paper. Tested DRAM die suspended in liquid fall into shape-matched recesses embossed in a moving polymer web (Alien-RFID-style fluidic assembly), then R2R printing adds RDL and solder to form fan-out packages.
why: Packaging throughput ~10x a pick-and-place or wafer-level fan-out line at a fraction of capex; back-end stops gating memory output.

title: Pottery wheel: 3D-print crucibles from polysilicon-byproduct synthetic silica
idea: Random stimulus 'pottery wheel' -> shape clay, then fire it. SiCl4 byproduct from polysilicon plants is converted to synthetic fumed silica, robocast or SLA-printed into crucible green bodies, and sintered to bubble-free fused silica.
why: Takes Spruce Pine natural HPQ out of the loop using a waste stream US polysilicon makers already have; secures DRAM wafer supply.

title: Aluminum-boron-nitride ferroelectric FeFET built from U.S. borax and aluminum
idea: Box = {medium: wurtzite AlBN polarization | access: Si FET whose gate dielectric is the AlBN film | sense: nondestructive threshold shift | integration: BEOL plus an SRAM write-coalescing buffer that keeps each cell below 1e9 cycles in 10 years | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: reactive sputtering with boron from Boron, California}. AlBN switches like AlScN but needs no scandium (imported), so every element in the stack (Al, B, N, Si, Mo) is mined and refined in the U.S.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability: nonvolatile and refresh-free with a fully domestic element list; the architecture covers the endurance gap.
note: High coercive field and FeFET endurance limit DRAM use; value mainly supply-chain.

title: Indium- and gallium-free zinc-silicon-oxide gain cell from domestic zinc
idea: Box = {medium: charge on the gate node of a read transistor | access: amorphous Zn-Si-O write TFT (wide gap, ultralow off-current) | sense: gain-cell read current | integration: 4-8 monolithic BEOL tiers | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: ALD with zinc from Alaska + U.S. silane}. Si suppresses oxygen vacancies in ZnO the way Ga does in IGZO, aiming for aA-level off-current without indium (mostly imported) or gallium (~98% Chinese).
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: removes In and Ga from oxide-semiconductor DRAM while keeping long retention and 3D tiers.
note: Supply-chain win; ZnSiO off-current and mobility likely below IGZO.

title: Rare-earth-free Fe16N2 nanomagnet SOT cell from Minnesota iron nitride
idea: Box = {medium: high-anisotropy alpha''-Fe16N2 free layer | access: Si FET | sense: TMR with MgO from Michigan brine | integration: BEOL 3-terminal SOT cell | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: sputter + low-temperature nitridation from the U.S. Fe16N2 magnet industry}. Fe16N2's high magnetization and anisotropy keep a bit stable at ~15 nm without Pt, Co or rare earths, and spin-orbit-torque writes keep current out of the tunnel barrier for DRAM-class endurance.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Co, Pt, Ir, Ru and rare earths; nonvolatile and refresh-free.
note: Fe16N2 thin-film phase stability is hard; value is resource substitution.

title: Elemental-tellurium dynamic phase-change cell that self-erases
idea: Box = {medium: metastable amorphous vs crystalline elemental Te in a 10 nm confined pore | access: Si FET | sense: ~1e3 resistance ratio | integration: BEOL with Mo heater | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: evaporated Te recovered at Utah copper refineries}. Confined amorphous Te recrystallizes on its own in ~seconds at 85 C, so the cell is deliberately dynamic: a ~10 ns quench writes a one, decay plus refresh handles the rest, and no Ge or Sb is needed.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: a one-element storage medium from a domestic byproduct, with retention set by crystallization kinetics rather than transistor leakage.
note: Melt-quench write energy and PCM endurance far below DRAM duty.

title: Silicon-on-nothing void under every storage junction
idea: Box: cap x recessed access x SA x in-array x bulk Si with empty-space-in-silicon cavities x shallow trench array + high-temperature H2 anneal that migrates Si to seal a void beneath each storage diffusion. The junction bottom, usually the largest generation volume, now faces vacuum instead of depleted silicon.
why: Junction leakage (fact 3) cut 3-5x by area removal; lower junction capacitance also improves charge-transfer ratio.

title: Leakage-balanced bitline standby voltage cancels junction loss
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x retuned SA precharge generator x in-array x Si x zero masks. In self-refresh the bitlines park slightly above VDD/2 so subthreshold current flows into 1-nodes and offsets their junction/GIDL loss, while 0-nodes absorb the small extra leak from their larger margin; the park voltage is trimmed per die at test.
why: Balancing the two failure tails extends worst-case retention ~1.5-2x (fact 3) with only a trimmable regulator.

title: Segmented cell plate dips during idle to relax junction field
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x one mask that cuts the common cell plate into per-subarray segments. Idle subarrays lower their plate ~0.2-0.3 V, coupling all storage nodes down and reducing reverse bias and gate-edge field on 1-nodes; the plate is restored before activation.
why: GIDL/TAT fall exponentially with field: ~3-5x retention in idle subarrays (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Supercritical CO2 deuterium passivation at 250C, no masks
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x whole-wafer post-BEOL treatment x Si x supercritical CO2 carrying D2/D2O at ~250C and >100 bar. The supercritical fluid penetrates dense metal stacks to reach junction and gate-oxide traps that forming-gas anneals miss, and Si-D bonds resist thermal/hot-carrier depassivation better than Si-H.
why: Shrinks and stabilizes the tail, including variable retention time (fact 3), with zero masks on cheap US-buildable tools.
note: Supercritical-CO2 delivery of deuterium; same Si-D passivation core.

title: Self-referenced slow sensing during refresh rescues decayed cells
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA run in two-step self-reference only during refresh (read and hold bitline level, write a known 1, read again, compare) x in-mat x Si x zero masks. Comparing the cell with itself removes capacitor and offset mismatch, so cells decayed to ~25% of signal still resolve; normal reads stay fast.
why: Refresh need only catch cells before ~75% decay instead of ~50%, allowing ~2x longer intervals (fact 3); the extra latency hides in background refresh.
note: Destructive read complicates self-reference; needs analog hold per bitline.

title: Time-domain bitline sensing with shared TDCs on bonded logic wafer
idea: Box: pillar 1T1C x buried-channel access x time-domain sensing x CMOS-under-array x bulk Si x 28 nm logic wafer bonded. Each bitline's post-charge-share voltage starves a tiny inverter so the bit becomes a delay, and one time-to-digital converter serves 16 bitlines through a delay-line race, replacing 16 latch SAs with 16 inverters plus 1 TDC.
why: Periphery (~49% of die): SA stripe area -50-60%; time-domain gain stays cheap at low voltage, easing the voltage floor.

title: Spare array mats double as flying capacitors for wordline charge pumps
idea: Box: pillar caps x array access FETs as switches x no sensing x in-array power conversion x bulk Si x zero added masks. A few mats per bank wire their millions of 5 fF cell caps into parallel groups clocked as a switched-capacitor VPP/VBB pump, replacing the large planar MOS pump capacitors in the periphery.
why: Pump and decap area (several % of die) shrinks ~80% because cell caps are ~100x denser than MOS caps.

title: IGZO-isolated charge-transfer preamp enables 2048-cell bitlines
idea: Box: 1T1C x Si access x charge-transfer preamplifier x local isolation x bulk Si x BEOL IGZO switch. A gate-biased transfer transistor holds the bitline at a fixed potential while the cell charge is pushed onto a tiny sense node (gain ~Cbl/Csn ~10x), and an ultra-low-leakage IGZO switch isolates that node so the signal survives.
why: Bitlines 4x longer and SA count /4 (periphery ~-15% of die); bitline swing energy also drops.

title: Tall silicon pillar as inversion-layer capacitor, no MIM mold
idea: [Box: MOS inversion charge | VCT on the same pillar | charge-share SA | monolithic | single-crystal Si | deep Si pillar etch + ALD high-k/metal plate wrap] Extend each VCT pillar ~1 um downward and wrap the lower section with a high-k/metal plate at fixed bias, so electrons in the sidewall inversion layer form the cell capacitance (~4 fF for a 20 nm pillar at 0.5 nm EOT); single-crystal dark generation (~few e-/s) is negligible against ~25k stored electrons.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): one etched Si feature is both transistor and capacitor, replacing the 70:1 oxide mold + MIM module and cutting masks.

title: Carbon-mold capacitors etched with oxygen instead of fluorocarbons
idea: Box [ZrO2 cylinder cap | Si access | voltage SA | pillar | CZ Si | O2/SO2 plasma + ash]: build the capacitor mold from amorphous carbon with nitrogen-doped carbon support bands, etch the 70:1 holes with O2/SO2 instead of C4F6/C4F8 on oxide, deposit TiN/ZrO2/TiN, then ash the mold away (no HF wet strip).
why: PFAS/PFC intensity: oxide capacitor-hole etch is one of the largest fluorocarbon users (GWP 6,000-9,000); swapping it could cut fab PFC emissions ~20-30% and the carbon etch is faster.

title: Cold-trap recapture and re-purification of unreacted ALD precursors
idea: Box [any | any | any | any | any | ALD]: insert a condensation trap plus sorbent bed between each ALD chamber and pump to capture the Zr/Hf/Ti amide and Al alkyl precursor that passes unreacted, then redistill it centrally and requalify it by NMR and ICP-MS.
why: Hf/Zr/Ti precursor and energy intensity: ALD precursor utilization is often <10%, so recapture could cut precursor purchases ~5x for the high-k steps that dominate DRAM ALD.

title: Slot-die sol-gel zinc-tin-oxide gain cells patterned on logic BEOL
idea: Box [charge on read-TFT gate | 2T0C ZnSnO TFTs | current sense | BEOL monolithic over CMOS | logic wafer | aqueous nitrate sol-gel slot-die coat + NIL patterning + 265 nm UV-LED assisted 300 C cure in air]: coat ZnSnO channel and AlOx gate-dielectric inks at atmospheric pressure, with no vacuum, no sputter targets and no lamps.
why: Ga/In-free (Zn and Sn are abundant) and sputter-free oxide gain cells: leakage <1e-18 A gives seconds of retention, so refresh falls ~100x, with no IGZO targets or Ar plasma.

title: Three 60-degree line exposures intersect into honeycomb capacitor holes
idea: Box: Si capacitor charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x triple sidewall-image-transfer at 0, 60 and 120 degrees. Three spacer line arrays are stacked as hardmasks and the etch opens only where all three gaps coincide, giving a hexagonal hole lattice at ~18 nm half-pitch from DUV line exposures, self-aligned to active lines set by the 0-degree array.
why: Removes the EUV or LELE hole layer for storage-node contact and capacitor (fact 4), since line/space is far easier than holes for DUV; ~1-2 EUV layers saved; risk is compounded LER and hexagonal hole CD uniformity.

title: Sub-terahertz waveguides inside glass core link memory chiplets
idea: Box: HBM-lite stack x standard x standard x 300 GHz on-die patch launchers x glass-core substrate with laser-written dielectric waveguides x panel process. Instead of thousands of interposer wires, 32 sub-THz channels at 100 Gb/s each ride rectangular waveguides formed inside the package glass core, so memory can sit 20-50 mm from logic.
why: Interposer cost and shoreline: removes the 2.5D silicon interposer and decouples memory count from logic perimeter, targeting ~1 pJ/bit with 3-4x more attachable stacks.
note: 32 x 100 Gb/s is below one HBM stack; sub-THz transceiver energy is several pJ/bit today.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops tiny DRAM dielets into panel wells
idea: Box: 0.5 mm2 DRAM dielets x standard x on-dielet SA x shape-keyed wells plus panel RDL x 600 mm organic panel x fluidic self-assembly. Asymmetric trapezoid dielets tumble in a carrier fluid until they lock into matching wells, then one RDL pass wires thousands of dielets into wide memory channels.
why: Yield and assembly capital: tiny dies yield >95% even at aggressive rules, and parallel assembly replaces millions of pick-and-place moves; cost per good bit -15-25%.
note: Tiny DRAM dielets pay heavy periphery/IO overhead; DRAM yield already high via redundancy.

title: Memory scroll: dielets on flex coiled around the processor
idea: Box: DRAM dielets x standard x standard x fine-line polyimide ribbon x flexible substrate x roll-to-roll assembly. Dielets are bonded along a 2 m flex ribbon that coils around the processor package like a scroll, so attachable memory grows with the number of turns instead of the die's shoreline.
why: HBM shoreline limit: 3-5x more attachable capacity per package at DDR-like cost per bit.
note: Meter-scale ribbon forces serial links with DDR-class latency/energy.

title: Laser-sliced active layers replace backgrinding and save donor wafers
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x hybrid-bond stack x reusable donor wafer x dry laser subsurface slicing. A laser-focused cleave plane 40 um under the device layer lets the finished DRAM layer split off dry, skipping water-cooled backgrinding and polish; the remaining wafer is plasma-smoothed and reused for another DRAM layer.
why: Water: backgrind/polish coolant and rinses are a top packaging water draw; dry cleave plus plasma cuts that >10x. Also cuts virgin silicon and quartz-crucible demand (Spruce Pine chokepoint) by reusing donors 5-10x.

title: Diamond fly-cut planarization enables CMP-free hybrid bonding
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x standard x Cu-Cu surface-activated bonding x Si x single-point diamond fly-cutting plus Ar fast-atom-beam activation in vacuum. Bond surfaces are flattened by dry ultra-precision fly-cutting and activated in UHV, eliminating CMP slurry, post-CMP scrubbing and DI rinses.
why: Water: CMP and post-CMP cleans are among the largest UPW users in hybrid bonding; the dry route cuts >10x and removes slurry chemistry supply.

title: Supercritical-CO2 electroplating fills TSVs with no rinse steps
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x Cu TSV x Si x electroplating in a supercritical CO2/electrolyte emulsion. The low-viscosity emulsion penetrates high-aspect TSVs void-free and depressurizes to leave wafers dry, so the multi-stage DI rinses and spin-dries vanish; CO2 is recompressed and reused.
why: Water: plating plus rinse is a large share of TSV water, cut >10x; better high-aspect fill also lifts stack yield (fact 6).

title: Elastomer stamps mass-transfer memory dielets dry, microLED-style
idea: Box: 0.3 mm DRAM dielets x standard x standard x transfer-printed onto RDL x panel x laser release from carrier plus kinetically controlled PDMS stamp mass transfer. Borrowed from microLED fabs, one stamp stroke picks up 10,000 dielets and prints them onto the panel.
why: Water: replaces water-sprayed blade dicing and wet release with laser release and dry transfer, >10x cut; small dielets raise yield and allow fine-grained memory placement.

title: Magnetic self-alignment snaps dielets into place on vibrating tables
idea: Box: DRAM dielets with patterned NiFe pads x standard x standard x self-aligned direct bonding x substrate with matching micromagnets x dry vibratory assembly. Dielets scattered on the substrate are pulled into +/-0.5 um registration by magnetic forces and then bonded, with no liquid (unlike capillary or fluidic assembly).
why: Water: dry self-assembly replaces fluidic/capillary methods and post-placement wet cleans, >10x cut; enables low-cost massive-dielet memory.

title: Laser-debonded HBM reclaimed from retired accelerators and remounted
idea: Box: used HBM3 stacks x existing x existing x laser debond, laser solder-jet re-bump, remount on new carrier x reclaimed package x dry laser rework. Retired GPU modules have their HBM stacks lifted by IR laser heating, tested, re-balled with jetted solder spheres and reused on inference cards.
why: Water: a reused stack needs zero fab water (vs thousands of litres per wafer), >100x cut per reused GB; adds supply with no new wafers.
note: Damage-free debond and re-bump at microbump pitch is hard.

title: Twin-cell glass-panel DRAM with invalid-pair erasure decoding
idea: Box [medium: capacitor charge | access: LTPS planar TFT | sense: differential twin-cell | integration: chiplet | substrate: Gen-6 glass panel | fab: i-line/DUV panel litho]. Each bit is a complementary cell pair on cheap panel-made arrays; a pair that senses 00 or 11 (one cell leaked or dead) is flagged as an erasure, and a Reed-Solomon code over 32-pair symbols corrects ~2x more erasures than unknown errors.
why: Fact 4 capital: lets panel fabs with ~1e-3 raw cell failure ship usable working memory; ~2x cell area but ~10x lower capex per m2 of array.
note: Panel-litho cells are orders of magnitude larger; capex per m2 savings do not win cost/bit.

title: Discharge-slope telemetry from normal reads builds live retention map
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: time-to-digital sense amp | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: EUV]. Each sense amp records the picoseconds the bitline takes to cross a threshold, which encodes the cell's remaining charge; the controller turns these free samples from ordinary reads into a continuously updated per-row retention class and adapts each row's refresh period.
why: Fact 3: retention profiling with no test downtime that also catches variable-retention-time cells live; ~4x fewer refresh operations.

title: Analog leaky integrator capacitor counts hammers per row
idea: Box [medium: per-row MOS integrator capacitor | access: charge-packet injection on each ACT | sense: threshold comparator | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Every activation dumps a fixed charge packet onto a tiny per-row integrator that leaks with a time constant matched to the refresh window; crossing threshold triggers neighbour refresh, giving an exact per-row counter for about one cell's area.
why: Fact 9: deterministic tracking at hammer thresholds of 1k and below with <1% area, versus 5-10% for SRAM counter tables.

title: Carbon-doped gettering liner between rows traps migrating electrons
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: vertical channel | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk with carbon-implanted isolation liner | fab: DUV implant]. The isolation between adjacent rows is lined with carbon-doped silicon that creates recombination centres >50 nm from storage junctions, so electrons injected by a toggling aggressor recombine before reaching the victim node.
why: Fact 9: raises hammer threshold ~5-10x passively; the risk is adding retention tail, controlled by keeping the liner away from junctions.

title: Resonant adiabatic wordline drivers recycle charge and soften hammer edges
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard | integration: monolithic + in-package LC tank inductor | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Wordlines are swung by a shared resonant LC tank with a ~2 ns sinusoidal ramp, returning most wordline charge to the tank instead of dumping it, and the slower dV/dt cuts capacitive coupling and electron injection into neighbour rows.
why: Constraint: wordline plus ~30%-efficient VPP-pump energy falls ~5-10x; Fact 9: smoother edges raise the hammer threshold modestly.
note: Wordline energy is a minor part of activation energy; 2 ns LC resonance hard in package.

title: Golden-copy flash backing replaces ECC and refresh for weights
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: low-swing | integration: DRAM + NAND in one package | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Immutable inference weights live in a 0.4 V, ECC-less, refresh-relaxed DRAM region with a 16-bit CRC per 256 B; a CRC failure refetches that line from the packaged NAND golden copy and rewrites it.
why: Constraint: ~6x lower CV^2 plus near-zero refresh gives ~10x amortized energy per access; reliability comes from the backing store, not margin.
note: 0.4 V array operation and 10x energy claim are doubtful.

title: Po: the bit is a shrug — sliding van der Waals ferroelectric
idea: Po: the bit is a shrug of the shoulders. Extracted: in bilayer hBN or rhombohedral MoS2 the bit is AB vs BA stacking; a field slides one layer by one bond length without breaking bonds, flipping polarization with almost no fatigue, read as a threshold shift of an underlying 2D channel.
why: Effectively unlimited endurance (no bond breaking, unlike HZO wake-up/fatigue) plus non-volatility. Wafer-scale stacking-controlled growth is the risk.
note: Wafer-scale stacking control and small threshold shift are the risks.

title: Po: memory you read by listening — piezo-sensed AlScN ferroelectric bit
idea: Po: memory you read by listening to it. Extracted: store the bit in wurtzite AlScN polarization and read it non-destructively with a small sub-coercive AC drive; the sign of the piezoelectric response (charge or acoustic phase) reveals the polarization without ever switching it.
why: Non-destructive ferroelectric read removes restore energy and read-induced fatigue (fact 8). Nanoscale signal size is the risk.

title: Per-cell threshold trimming via charge-trap layer in access gate
idea: Po: every access transistor is custom-made. Add a thin SiN charge-trap film inside the buried-wordline gate stack; at wafer test, cells in the leakage tail receive a one-time Fowler-Nordheim program pulse that raises their Vt ~150 mV, tightening the Vt distribution until the tail disappears.
why: Fact 3: a 10x tighter off-current tail lets refresh run 4-8x less often and permits a shallower negative wordline, saving refresh energy and charge-pump area (fact 7).

title: Pulsed-hold thyristor array refreshed blindly without sense amplifiers
idea: Po: refresh without reading. Use vertical gated thyristor latches (no capacitor) but power their anode lines only in short pulses; between pulses an ON cell's base charge decays slowly, and each pulse re-latches every ON cell in the array at once while OFF cells stay off.
why: Fact 3: refresh needs no activate, sense or restore, so it uses no bitline charge or bandwidth, and duty cycling cuts thyristor standby power 10-100x.

title: Read-restoring gain cell where every read tops up storage node
idea: Po: reading is refreshing. In a 2T capacitorless gain cell, add a diode-connected feedback from the read path so read current through a 1 cell briefly pulls its storage gate back toward full level, while a 0 cell draws no current and stays low; any row read regularly never needs a separate refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: hot rows refresh themselves for free and reads stay nondestructive; with typical access patterns 50%+ of refreshes vanish.

title: Po: sense amps take turns — 1:8 charge-parked sensing
idea: Po: a bank with one-eighth of its sense amps. After activation, isolation gates park each bitline's charge-shared signal on the bitline itself; one SA serves 8 bitlines through a mux, sensing and writing back group by group in ~2 ns slots, with the requested column group always sensed first.
why: Periphery (#7): SA+equalizer strips (~15-20% of die) shrink ~7/8, ~10% better cost per bit; first-access tRCD unchanged, only tRAS grows. Parked charge decays over microseconds, so the 16 ns window is safe.
note: Parked ~100 mV signals must survive coupling from neighbors swinging full rail.

title: Po: wordlines count themselves — analog hammer integrator cell
idea: Po: a wordline that keeps its own tally. Each sub-wordline driver gets one extra DRAM-style cell coupled to its wordline through a tiny capacitor so every activation deposits a fixed charge quantum; when that integrator crosses a threshold during the row group's refresh, its neighbors are flagged for targeted refresh and the integrator is reset.
why: Row hammer (#9) at ~1k activations: exact per-row counting at roughly one cell per row instead of SRAM counter tables or controller tracking, and it keeps working as thresholds fall further.
note: Analog per-row counter vs JEDEC PRAC; charge-quantum precision over ~1k steps is hard.

title: Po: no reference — read, write midlevel, read again
idea: Po: a sense amp with no reference. Charge-share the cell onto the bitline and hold the result on sample cap A, write VDD/2 into the cell, re-open the wordline and hold the second result on cap B, then compare A vs B; both samples traverse the identical path, so wordline kickback, bitline-pair imbalance and open-bitline layout mismatch cancel.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): removes ~10-20 mV of systematic offset, allowing ~30% lower Cs or 2x longer bitlines (half the SA strips); the extra latency suits a density-optimized capacity tier.

title: Po: bitlines never precharge — rail-held transition sensing
idea: Po: bitlines that never return to VDD/2. Each bitline stays at the full rail left by the last restore; on the next activation an AC-coupled detector sees either no step (new bit equals held rail) or a full charge-sharing step, and the latch, knowing the held rail, decodes 'same/different' into the new bit.
why: Destructive read (#8) energy: removes equalization and tRP (~14 ns), and bitlines only swing when consecutive rows differ, ~50% bitline energy saving on random data and more on correlated data.
note: Needs a per-bitline reference tied to held rail; margin similar to single-ended.

title: Po: wordlines latch themselves — vertical Si thyristor drivers
idea: Po: a wordline driver that needs only a nudge. Replace each sub-wordline driver's high-voltage CMOS pair with a vertical p-n-p-n silicon thyristor at wordline pitch: a small decoder pulse triggers it, it regenerates and holds the wordline high through a shared weak bleed, and a common reset pulse turns all off.
why: Periphery (#7): sub-wordline driver strips (~10% of die) shrink ~3x because vertical thyristors need no thick-oxide PMOS or well spacing; Si, B, P only.

title: Po: decoders woven into wiring — a-Si diode matrix
idea: Po: a decoder made of wire crossings. Build the row predecoder as a 1960s-style diode matrix, with hydrogenated amorphous-silicon p-i-n diodes deposited at the crossings of two BEOL aluminum levels above the array, so decoding uses metal-layer space instead of silicon area.
why: Periphery (#7) and capital (#4): moves ~3-5% of die (predecode) off silicon using Si and H deposited below 350 C on cheap tools.

title: Po: gate from underneath — Hf-free back-gated FD-SOI periphery
idea: Po: transistors controlled from underneath. Build the periphery on thin-BOX FD-SOI with SiON front gates and TiN or doped-poly electrodes (no HfO2), using the back gate through the buried oxide for Vt control, and give each SA pair its own back-gate island biased to null its offset.
why: Scarce resources and capacitor wall (#1): avoids hafnium while recovering Vt tuning via body bias; per-SA back-bias trim cuts required signal; Si, O, N, Ti only.
note: Per-SA FD-SOI back-gate islands for offset nulling; hafnium is not a real chokepoint.

title: Po: periphery made in a TV factory — LTPS glass chiplets
idea: Po: memory periphery from a display fab. Fabricate slow periphery (pumps, test, fuse/repair, ESD, power gating) as laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT circuits on Gen-6 glass panels, dice them into chiplets and bond them beside or under array dies.
why: Capital (#4) and U.S. manufacturability: panel lines process ~50x the area per tool-hour at a fraction of the cost per cm^2, and LTPS uses silicon only.

title: Bonded nonvolatile shadow tier dumps idle banks before power-off
idea: Po: memory that sleeps with its eyes shut. Pair each DRAM tier with a hybrid-bonded thick-oxide charge-trap shadow tier sharing its vertical bitlines, so an idle bank copies out in parallel in ~10 us and is power-gated; dumps are rate-limited to one per bank per 5 minutes, so 1e6-cycle endurance lasts ~10 years.
why: Refresh and idle power to zero for idle banks (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) without slowing active banks.

title: Photoresist that stays: patternable oxide becomes the device layer
idea: Po: the resist is the product. Use hafnium/zirconium oxo-cluster photoresists that, after exposure and anneal, densify into HfZrO dielectric or hard mask left in place, eliminating the deposit-coat-expose-etch-strip chain for those layers.
why: Process steps and tool count: ~3-4 fewer steps per affected layer, ~5-10% shorter cycle and fewer etch tools.

title: Memory by the square meter in idle display-panel fabs
idea: Po: RAM is made in TV factories. Idle Gen-6/8.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines already run IGZO transistors; pattern 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays at ~1-1.5 um rules on glass (a ~5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 panel holds on the order of 20 GB), dice into tiles and bond them to 28 nm controller dies.
why: Capital intensity and non-EUV supply: zero new fab, no EUV, no quartz crucibles; ~$10-20/GB slower capacity tier from idle capacity, with IGZO's low leakage cutting refresh.

title: Laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers link HBM optically
idea: Po: wires are written, not printed. Femtosecond lasers write buried 3D waveguides inside a glass interposer that connect edge-coupled micro-ring transmitters on the HBM base die to the GPU, routing hundreds of WDM channels in 3D with zero lithography.
why: Lets HBM sit 5-50 mm away, breaking the GPU shoreline limit (more stacks per GPU) at ~1 pJ/bit and with no interposer masks.

title: Power fed from the lid into the top of HBM stacks
idea: Po: power falls from the sky. One backside mask adds power landing pads on the top die of each stack; a copper lid with compliant pins injects current into the top of the existing power TSV columns, so power enters from both ends.
why: Halves stack IR drop and frees about half of the bottom power bumps for extra signal channels, raising bandwidth per stack ~1.3-1.5x.

title: Stress-metal microsprings for socketed, re-testable HBM
idea: Po: the bumps are springs. A single mask patterns stress-graded MoCr fingers on the DRAM pad field; a release etch lets them curl up into microsprings that press-contact the interposer, so stacks can be tested at speed and swapped before final lock-down.
why: Fixes the known-good-stack problem: bad stacks are caught and replaced instead of scrapping a whole package; 10-20% package yield gain.

title: Sacrificial shorting bar removes ESD circuits from bonded links
idea: Po: memory with no protection. One top-metal mask adds a shorting bar that grounds every die-to-die pad during handling and bonding, then is laser-cut after assembly, so the I/O needs no ESD diodes.
why: ESD structures add area and pad capacitance; removing them cuts PHY area and per-bit link energy 20-40%.
note: LCD shorting-bar trick; bar is buried after hybrid bonding, so needs electrical fuse.

title: Self-assembled block-copolymer capacitor holes replace EUV layers
idea: Po: chips grown, not made. Capacitor hole arrays are patterned by directed self-assembly of a cylinder-forming block copolymer guided by a coarse DUV template; DSA's ~0.1-1% missing or merged holes, which kept it out of production, become dead cells that the code treats as erasures.
why: Capital/EUV (fact 4): removes 1-2 EUV layers (~5-10% wafer cost) while reaching ~10 nm-class hole pitch by self-assembly.
note: DSA for DRAM holes is known; 0.1-1% erasures need heavy code overhead.

title: Low-Vt access transistors cut the wordline swing to 2 V
idea: Po: let the transistor leak. The access-transistor threshold is lowered ~0.3 V, so the wordline boost drops from ~3 V to ~2 V and the negative standby bias shrinks; the leakage tail grows until ~1% of cells fail retention within the window, which the code absorbs.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline CV^2 energy down ~55%, smaller charge pumps (periphery, fact 7) and lower gate-oxide stress.

title: Tiny unbalanced sense amps with offsets mapped as erasures
idea: Po: the sense amp is allowed to guess. Sense amplifiers are shrunk to minimum-size devices with no offset cancellation; the ~1% whose static offset exceeds the bitline signal are found at test and their columns treated by the decoder as known-position erasures.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~30-40%, total die area down ~6-10%.
note: Offsets drift with temperature and aging, so a static map is incomplete.

title: Dirty-silicon DRAM grown in non-Spruce-Pine crucibles
idea: Po: memory made from dirty sand. Wafers come from ingots grown in synthetic-silica or lower-purity quartz crucibles, accepting more oxygen and trace metals; the extra generation-recombination centers fatten the junction-leakage tail to ~1% retention failures, which the code tolerates.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz): removes a single-point chokepoint and trims wafer cost ~5-10%.
note: Synthetic-silica crucible layers already used; leakage-tail cost.

title: Cross-tenant memory exchange points in colocation campuses
idea: Po: memory is a utility traded between strangers. Like an Internet exchange point, a neutral CXL 3.x switch fabric in each colo lets tenants post idle DRAM and others lease it by the GB-hour, with per-lease memory-encryption keys and bandwidth QoS enforced in the switch.
why: Fleet studies show ~25-50% of server DRAM stranded; turning 10% of it into tradeable supply equals a new fab's annual output; attacks effective cost per bit and capital.

title: Move DRAM burn-in from the factory into the server
idea: Po: never test a chip in the factory. Factory test shrinks to wafer sort plus a fast package screen, and the long retention/burn-in screens run in the customer's server at first boot via on-die MBIST and post-package repair, with anonymized telemetry streamed back to the fab.
why: DRAM test and burn-in take hours per part and test floors are a large back-end capex; halving them frees test capacity and cuts cycle time by days; attacks capital intensity and time-to-supply.
note: Customers bear escapes; partial in-field MBIST/PPR already exists.

title: Repurpose LTPS display backplanes as giant 1T1C memory sheets
idea: Worsen: make memory only on 300 mm silicon at ~$10/cm2. Flip: an AMOLED backplane is already a 1T1C array, so re-mask an existing LTPS display line (3 um cells, storage caps, access TFTs) into memory sheets; $1M buys a re-spun driver IC and a 24-month cost-per-bit study for cold bulk-capacity tiers.
why: Capital and cost per area (~100x cheaper per cm2) using idle display-fab capacity; 100 ns-1 us latency fits a capacity tier.
note: 3 um cells are ~5000x less dense than DRAM; LTPS leakage high; cost per bit unlikely below DRAM.

title: Decay-clock sensing: reference voltage tracks time since last restore
idea: Worse: assume worst-case decayed charge on every read so the margin is gone early. Flip: keep a coarse per-row refresh-epoch counter and set the sense-amp reference from a replica cell aged the same amount, so a stored '1' can decay to ~30% instead of ~60% before misreading.
why: Leakage-limited retention (fact 3): 2-3x longer refresh interval without touching the access transistor.
note: Reference tracks average decay; fast-decaying tail cells still fail.

title: Aerogel thermal-break trench between accelerator and HBM
idea: Worse: bolt the DRAM onto the hottest chip in the system. Flip: cut a silica-aerogel-filled trench in the interposer between GPU and HBM footprints and give HBM its own top heat-pipe path, holding the stack 20-25 C cooler than the logic die.
why: Leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh rate (fact 3) drops ~4x and HBM can drop from 2x to 1x refresh mode.

title: Built-in electret charge in gate stack replaces negative wordline
idea: Worse: run a negative-wordline charge pump all through standby to hold Vt up. Flip: embed a fixed negative charge layer (Al2O3/SiO2 interface dipole or implanted electret) on the storage-node side of the access gate so the device carries a built-in +Vt shift only where leakage matters.
why: Removes negative-wordline pump energy and area (facts 3, 7) and cuts GIDL at the storage node.
note: Gate-stack dipole/electret near storage node; similar to dual-WF buried gates.

title: Ultra-thin fully depleted body shrinks thermal generation volume
idea: Worse at 125 C: give the access device a large depleted silicon volume that generates carriers at mid-gap traps. Flip: thin the vertical channel to a 4-5 nm shell on an oxide core so the generating volume is ~50x smaller and quantum confinement widens the effective gap.
why: Generation leakage, the dominant term hot (fact 3), down ~20-50x at 125 C.

title: Reduced-field storage levels when hot: low '1', raised plate
idea: Worse at 125 C: store '1' at full array voltage so field-enhanced generation and GIDL explode with heat. Flip: in hot mode store '1' at ~0.7 V and raise the cell plate to cut junction field, then recover signal with an offset-cancelled sense amp; leakage falls exponentially while charge falls only linearly.
why: Hot leakage (fact 3) down 5-10x and CV2 energy (fact 10) down ~40% in the hot regime.

title: Near-miss flagging sense amps drive traffic-based adaptive refresh
idea: Worse: refresh every row at worst-case 64 ms because nobody knows which cells are weak. Flip: add a cheap offset-biased secondary latch per sense-amp group that flags reads whose signal landed near the trip point during normal traffic; flagged rows enter a small refresh-priority table while all other rows run 4-8x longer refresh intervals.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): retention-aware refresh with no offline profiling; ~50-70% refresh reduction at 32-64 Gb.

title: Resonant LC tank charges wordlines adiabatically and recycles energy
idea: Worse: slam 3 V wordlines up from ground and dump their charge to ground on every activation. Flip: drive the selected wordline group from a package-level inductor in a resonant loop that ramps it up sinusoidally and swings the charge back into the tank, or into the next wordline, on deactivation.
why: Voltage floor and activation energy (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of wordline CV^2 energy and offloads the VPP pumps.

title: Isolated early-latch sensing with parity-checked deferred restore
idea: Worse: wait for every bitline to fully develop under worst-case corners before latching. Flip: latch at half the usual development time with isolation gates cutting the latch off from the bitlines, ship data out, and write back only after a per-burst parity check passes; on a rare mismatch the still-intact shared bitline charge is re-latched with more time.
why: Latency, bandwidth and read energy: ~30% lower tRCD at typical corners while keeping worst-case correctness.

title: Per-segment adaptive negative wordline bias tames the leakage tail
idea: Worse: hold every unselected wordline at the same off level so the leakiest 0.01% of cells set refresh for all. Flip: give each wordline segment a test-programmed negative off level (-0.2 to -0.4 V) from a small local bias generator, applying deep negative bias only where the tail lives.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): ~10x tail suppression in hot spots stretches refresh 2-4x while sparing gate stress elsewhere.
note: Deeper NWL can worsen GIDL, which drives part of the leakage tail.

title: Threshold-coded tier select replaces the staircase
idea: Worse: carve a giant staircase so every tier gets its own contact, with area and trim steps growing linearly with tier count. Flip: dope each tier's built-in select transistor to one of several thresholds during in-situ deposition and drive a few shared vertical select gates with a voltage code that turns on exactly one tier, i.e., a binary decoder embedded in the stack.
why: Tier contacts drop from N to ~2*log2(N) lines; saves ~5-10% die area and dozens of trim/etch steps at 64+ tiers (facts 2, 7).

title: Memory on the cold side: thermal-break 3D DRAM beneath logic
idea: Worse: stack DRAM directly on a 700 W accelerator so it bakes at 95 C and refreshes 4x more often. Flip: hybrid-bond the DRAM tiers to the logic through a low-thermal-conductivity bonding interlayer that only signal vias cross, and cool the DRAM from its own backside cold plate while logic heat exits the opposite face.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C; holding DRAM at ~55 C instead of 95 C cuts refresh ~10x (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) while keeping on-logic data-movement savings (fact 5).
note: Double-sided cooling with thermal break is plausible; vias and thin interlayers leak heat.

title: Floating-plate differential capacitor shared by two stacked cells
idea: Worse: give each cell its own plate electrode, plate contacts and a single-ended half-signal. Flip: place one capacitor dielectric directly between a storage node in tier k and a storage node in tier k+1 so the two access transistors write complementary charge across it, storing one bit differentially with no plate line at all.
why: Doubles sense signal per fF so Cs can roughly halve (fact 1) and removes plate-line wiring and contacts from the 3D stack (fact 2).

title: Ge-fraction-coded superlattice: chemistry, not overlay, cuts every cell part
idea: Worse: align each tier's transistor, gate and capacitor regions with separate masks whose overlay drifts tier by tier. Flip: grow all tiers in one epitaxy run with sublayers of different Ge fraction, then from a single vertical slit run composition-selective lateral etches whose recess depth scales with Ge content, so capacitor cavity, gate recess and spacer of every tier are cut in a few etches, self-aligned by chemistry.
why: Per-tier masks and overlay error go to zero (facts 2, 4), so added tiers cost only epitaxy time.

title: Long lateral capacitors storing two bits per cell
idea: Worse: hold to 1 bit/cell because 5 fF barely yields one clean sense level. Flip: exploit the fact that a 3D lateral capacitor's length is set by a cheap timed recess, make ~20 fF capacitors whose 4x signal supports 4-level (2-bit) storage, and read them with a successive-approximation charge-sharing sense amp under the array.
why: 2 bits/cell halves the tiers needed for 10x: ~60 tiers x 2 bits reaches ~10x density with half the deposition and etch depth (facts 1, 2), keeping wafer cost flat.

title: Contactless whole-wafer self-test keeps test cost flat at 10x bits
idea: Worse: probe-test 10x more bits per die serially so test time and probe-card capex scale 10x. Flip: power every die on the wafer inductively or through on-die photovoltaic pads, run built-in self-test of all tiers in parallel, read pass/fail maps through an optical or RF backchannel, and program tier and row spares in the same pass.
why: Test (~5-10% of DRAM cost) stays flat while bits per die grow 10x, so the density gain is not eaten by test capex (capital intensity).

title: Separable-liner quartz crucibles recycled into new inner layers
idea: Worsen: break and landfill every CZ crucible after one pull. Flip: design crucibles with a separable high-purity inner liner, then crush spent liners, strip the devitrified cristobalite and metal-rich skin by hot chlorination and HF leach, and re-fuse the purified grain into new liners.
why: HPQ Spruce Pine chokepoint: recovering ~50-60% of liner mass roughly halves virgin HPQ need.

title: PCB-free all-silicon memory module as a two-material recycling stream
idea: Worsen: mount DRAM on brominated FR-4 boards full of glass fiber, copper and gold that are costly to separate. Flip: build memory modules on a silicon or glass-core interposer card with only Cu and Al metallization, so the whole module is a two-material recycling stream and the chips can be re-bonded.
why: Recyclability and scarce-resource intensity: removes brominated flame retardants and Au finishes and shortens the signal path, which saves I/O energy.

title: CVD diamond substrates remove the thermal ceiling on stacking
idea: Worse: stack memory on a substrate that traps heat, so retention collapses and refresh doubles above 85 C. Flip: build tiers on thin polycrystalline CVD diamond plates (~1500 W/mK) that hold stacked arrays near coolant temperature. Leakage roughly halves for each ~10 C of cooling, so stacks of 16-24 tiers stay viable.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and HBM thermals: ~2-4x retention and more tiers per stack; diamond is grown from methane in U.S. reactors.

title: Hardware page meshing merges half-empty pages
idea: Worsen: let fragmentation leave thousands of pages 10-30% full. Flip: the controller adds a sub-page remap table so two virtual pages whose live objects do not overlap share one physical frame, and a background engine finds mesh candidates from allocation bitmaps without moving objects.
why: Capacity: 15-40% less resident memory for fragmented heaps (Redis, browsers, Python) without a compacting GC.
note: Hardware version of Mesh allocator.

title: Reduce-on-the-wire: interposer repeaters sum partial results in flight
idea: Worsen: write every partial sum to memory and read it back at each all-reduce step. Flip: put small adder-repeaters at segment boundaries of long active-bridge wires so gradients and partial dot products accumulate as they travel between chiplets, and only the final sum is written to memory.
why: Data movement: all-reduce memory traffic cut by ~N contributors, shrinking HBM bandwidth and gradient-buffer capacity needs.

title: Display fabs build IGZO gain-cell memory into glass interposers
idea: Worsen: allow only memory fabs with 75:1 capacitor etch to make working memory. Flip: Gen-8.5 display fabs already pattern billions of IGZO TFTs on 2.2x2.5 m glass, so build 3T gain cells (charge held on a read transistor's gate, no capacitor) in the glass interposer's layers, turning the substrate under the chips into seconds-retention memory.
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity: uses surplus display-fab capacity instead of DRAM fabs; IGZO leakage <1e-19 A/um nearly kills refresh. Density is low (tens to hundreds of MB per interposer).

title: Optically bistable microrings buffer packets inside photonic interposers
idea: Worsen: convert every optical packet to electrons and park it in DRAM for microseconds. Flip: use carrier- or thermo-optically bistable silicon microrings, where a holding beam keeps each ring in one of two transmission states, as nanosecond photonic latches that buffer packets in the optical domain.
why: Data movement: avoids the O-E-O plus DRAM round trip (~10-20 pJ/bit) for switch and link buffers; no capacitor, small capacity.
note: Tiny capacity and holding-beam power limit it to switch buffers.

title: Fleet error telemetry sold back to fabs to shave guardbands
idea: Worse: hyperscalers hoard corrected-error logs while DRAM makers set guardbands blind. Flip: a data-exchange business in which cloud operators sell anonymized per-die error and temperature histories, keyed to die IDs, to manufacturers, who use the field evidence to relax test limits and requalify borderline bins.
why: Yield and test cost: real field-failure data can justify recovering several percent of dies now scrapped for guardband margin, adding supply with zero capex.

title: Ephemeral DRAM: refresh-free SKU for data that dies young
idea: Worse: refresh every bit, even KV caches and packet buffers the host rewrites every few ms. Flip: sell a die variant with refresh counters, refresh timing and refresh-based row-hammer logic removed, warranted only for data rewritten within the measured retention window, for activations, network and frame buffers.
why: Zero refresh power, 10-20% bandwidth recovered and a few percent less periphery area, so more bits per wafer for a large buffer market.
note: Retention tail over temperature and dropping row-hammer defenses are risks.

title: Orphan-IP rescue fund relaunching thyristor static RAM
idea: Worse: let dead startups' memory IP, such as T-RAM thyristor cells, rot in patent portfolios. Flip: a fund buys orphan memory IP and relaunches thyristor RAM, a bistable negative-differential-resistance cell that holds state statically, on spare foundry SOI capacity.
why: No refresh at roughly 10-15F2 versus ~120F2 for 6T SRAM; revives a proven concept without new invention.

title: Mongolian yurt: dry-peeled single-crystal BaTiO3 membranes, reusable substrate
idea: A herder carries a yurt in pieces and pitches it anywhere, dry. Grow single-crystal BaTiO3 on graphene-coated substrates by remote epitaxy, peel the membrane off mechanically with a dry stamp, and laminate it onto CMOS as the storage layer; the substrate is reused hundreds of times.
why: A single-crystal ferroelectric storage layer with low fatigue (facts 1, 3) without high-temperature steps on CMOS. There is no sacrificial wet etch or CMP, a more than 10x water cut.
note: Membrane lamination cannot coat 3D structures; mainly a water and fatigue improvement.

title: Colorado River water lawyer: liters-per-gigabit permits for memory cells
idea: A water-rights lawyer prices every acre-foot. Make CHIPS-type grants and state water permits conditional on a certified 'liters of UPW per gigabit' figure for the storage-cell module, with a bonus tier for a 10x reduction, so that dry cell technologies win the funding.
why: Makes US manufacturing viable in water-stressed states (Arizona, Texas, Idaho) and turns the 10x water constraint into market pull for dry storage elements.
note: Water use is fab-level, not cell-level; pull for dry cells is indirect.

title: Child's take-turns sense amp: one latch scans eight bitlines
idea: A child asks why every bitline needs its own teacher. After charge sharing, isolation switches freeze each bitline's signal on its own bitline capacitance (it survives tens of ns), and one offset-cancelled latch visits 8 bitlines in ~1 ns steps, sensing and writing each back to full level in turn.
why: Periphery (fact 7): bitline sense-amp transistors drop ~6-8x, a ~10-15% die shrink; row cycle grows ~6-8 ns, acceptable for capacity tiers.

title: Retina lateral inhibition between neighboring sense amplifiers
idea: Copying the retina's horizontal cells, each sense amp gets weak cross-coupled 'inhibition' transistors to its two neighbors, so a disturbance common to the region (wordline kick, plate bounce, aggressor-bitline coupling) is subtracted before latching while the true local difference survives.
why: Cancels the correlated noise that eats ~30-40% of the sense budget, allowing 1024 cells per bitline (half the SA stripes, ~7% die) or ~30% less cell charge (facts 1, 7).

title: Rod-cell cascade: vertical bipolar preamp at every bitline segment
idea: A rod cell turns one photon into a million-fold cascade from a tiny first stage. Build a vertical n-p-n transistor under each short bitline segment, with the segment driving its floating base, so a few-fC cell dump becomes a 10-30x larger collector current onto a global sense line before any MOS latch.
why: Bipolar current gain lets one global SA serve 4-8 segments and tolerate smaller Cs, roughly halving SA count (facts 1, 7).

title: 2050 trim: ferroelectric offset memory inside every sense amp
idea: A 2050 engineer would never accept factory-random mismatch. Insert a ~30 nm HZO capacitor at each SA latch node, programmed once at wafer test to a polarization that cancels that SA's measured offset and retained for years.
why: Offset drops from ~15 mV to ~3 mV, so bitlines can double (half the SA stripes, ~7% die) or Cs can shrink ~40% (facts 1, 7).

title: Embargoed engineer's tungsten-free wordline: doped epitaxial gate tiers
idea: Without Chinese tungsten, the embargoed engineer grows the wordline in the same epi run as the channel. A degenerately boron-doped SiGe layer in each tier is the gate, wordlines are segmented every 512 cells and strapped to copper at each segment end.
why: Removes W replacement metal from 3D arrays (tungsten chokepoint) and also drops a CVD-W module and its fill-void yield loss.

title: Nose-to-tail butcher saves the silicon ground off HBM wafers
idea: Persona: a nose-to-tail butcher who wastes nothing. HBM core dies are thinned from 775 um to ~40 um, which grinds ~95% of each prime wafer into slurry. Instead, while the wafer sits on its carrier, focus an IR laser 60 um below the devices to make a cleave plane (stealth slicing). Split off the ~700 um back slab and polish it for reuse as a test or prime wafer.
why: Recovers ~0.9 wafer-equivalent of silicon per HBM wafer. Halves the crystal growth, crucibles, polysilicon and energy behind HBM bits, and cuts grinding water and consumables.
note: Laser slicing Si under live devices; silicon value small vs wafer.

title: Frugal homesteader: implant-free junctionless fab with no furnaces
idea: A homesteader without tractors designs around the missing tool. Make every transistor in the memory tiers junctionless or Schottky-contacted (as-deposited doped oxide or poly channels thinned for off-state, metal-silicide contacts), so no dopant-activation anneal is ever needed and the fab owns no ion implanters, diffusion furnaces or RTP.
why: Implanters and furnaces are ~10-15% of front-end capex and many steps; a <=400 C, implant-free tool list (~25 vs ~45 tool types) cuts capital and opens the market to non-semiconductor tool vendors. Risk: junctionless off-current tail vs refresh (fact 3).
note: Sense amps need high-performance CMOS; oxide channels lack good p-type.

title: Parent reading food labels: memory-footprint labels in software procurement
idea: Parents compare nutrition labels. An open 'Memory Facts' label (peak RSS, steady-state RSS per 1k users, bytes per stored record) is measured by a reference harness, and the campaign gets federal and large-enterprise procurement (GSA, state CIOs) to require it, as Energy Star did for power. Costs: standards work, the harness and outreach.
why: Buyer pressure pushes memory efficiency across the software supply chain, and 5-10% footprint cuts per procurement cycle compound.

title: Bridge engineer's expansion joints: islands-and-meanders segmented interposer
idea: Long bridges need expansion joints: split a large interposer into rigid silicon islands, one per memory stack and logic die, joined by meandering copper-on-glass bridges that flex, so warpage and CTE stress stay small.
why: Very large memory-rich packages would otherwise warp and crack over 10 years at 125 C; this allows reticle-busting interposers carrying many more stacks.
note: Flexible meander bridges lose wiring density; CoWoS-L already segments.

title: Alien coder's view: soft-decision LDPC fed by 3-bit sense amps
idea: An alien who sees DRAM only as a noisy channel would never throw away analog information: keep the latch sense amp but add 7 shared flash comparators per 8 columns that grade each bit's margin into log-likelihood ratios, and decode 512-byte pages with an on-die soft-decision LDPC that tolerates a raw BER of ~1e-3.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: cells with ~30% less capacitance (or a 4x longer refresh interval) become acceptable; soft decoding gains ~2 dB over hard SECDED.
note: LDPC decode latency on 512 B pages conflicts with DRAM access time.

title: Navigator's dead reckoning: sense reference shifted by time-since-refresh
idea: A navigator estimates position from elapsed time and speed: the controller knows each row's time since last refresh and the temperature, and before sensing it shifts the bitline precharge or reference-cell level by the expected decay, so a sagging '1' still resolves correctly.
why: Fact 3: roughly doubles effective retention of tail cells, halving refresh at near-zero area cost.
note: Reference tracking elapsed decay helps one polarity; tail cells decay unpredictably.

title: Farmer overplants then thins: printed spare columns plus printed WORM map
idea: A farmer sows extra seed and then thins it: gravure- or inkjet-printed oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays on foil carry ~40% spare columns; an in-line probe on the web tests each tile and writes its bad-column map into a printed write-once (electrochemical-fuse) ROM on the same foil, which the attached CMOS controller reads at boot.
why: Printed TFT device yield of 99-99.9% gives near-zero yield for Mb-scale arrays; redundancy plus an on-foil map raises array yield above 90%, the precondition for any printed memory tier.

title: Soviet scrapyard: transfer-print good tile dielets from defective DRAM wafers
idea: A Soviet engineer under embargo salvages everything: DRAM dies are laid out as mosaics of ~1 mm2 tiles, each with local periphery and scribe lanes; wafers with clustered defects are thinned and diced into tiles, and only known-good tiles are mass transfer-printed with elastomer stamps onto a roll-to-roll-made polyimide interposer with printed redistribution and a small CMOS controller.
why: A defect cluster kills a whole ~100 mm2 die but only a few 1 mm2 tiles, so good silicon from defect-limited lots is recovered (~10-25% yield gain on those lots).
note: Yield gain only on defect-clustered lots; transfer-print interconnect cost.

title: Child writes bigger where paper is rough: quality-adaptive bits per cell
idea: A child writes bigger on bumpy paper: the controller reads a per-region print-quality map (device sigma, leakage) for a printed memory foil and configures each region for 2 bits/cell where devices are tight, 1 bit/cell where they are average, and one bit across two ganged cells where they are poor, exposing whatever capacity results.
why: Variation becomes a capacity variable instead of a yield loss: nothing is scrapped, and average density can beat a worst-case design by ~1.5x.

title: Artist's new canvas: DRAM-class gain cells on display-fab glass
idea: An artist sees the world's underused Gen-8.5 display fabs as huge, cheap canvases. Pattern IGZO 2T0C gain-cell arrays at 1-2 um rules on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass, dice the glass into tiles and stack them as low-cost capacity modules for warm data.
why: Capital intensity: a whole new non-semiconductor source of capacity in fabs that process glass for ~$100-300/m^2; areal density (~3 GB/m^2) and speed at TFT rules are the weak points, so it suits bulk tiers.
note: Same LCD-fab IGZO gain-cell panels as I-04100.

title: Venus-grade NEMS relay access gives charge node zero off-current
idea: Designed for 460C Venus landers where any junction leaks, the access transistor is replaced by a SiC/TiN nanoelectromechanical contact relay whose open vacuum gap passes literally zero current. The storage node becomes a small MIM or the gate of a read transistor and holds charge for hours to days at room temperature.
why: Removes the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3), so refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) and the refresh bandwidth tax go to ~0; also hot and rad-hard. Contact endurance (~1e10-1e12 shown) must be pushed toward 1e15 with low-force contacts.
note: Relay area and contact endurance toward 1e15 are the limits.

title: Polarization-bound GaN quantum-well charge storage for 200C downhole tools
idea: Oil-well logging tools need memory at 200C; an AlN/GaN/AlN double heterostructure forms a 2DEG well bounded by 6.2 eV AlN barriers and fixed polarization charge, so an injected electron sheet barely emits thermally. The stored sheet modulates an adjacent HEMT channel for non-destructive read, built in existing U.S. 200 mm GaN-on-Si power fabs.
why: Ultra-wide barriers cut leakage >1e6x vs Si junctions, giving seconds-to-hours room-temperature retention (fact 3) without a capacitor (fact 1), on U.S.-available GaN capacity (manufacturability).

title: Deep-level dopant pocket memory from cryogenic dopant freeze-out
idea: Quantum-computer controllers at 4-40 K watch shallow dopants freeze out and hold their charge state for hours; the room-temperature analog implants, with one mask, a pocket of deep-level dopants (S, Se or Zn in Si, 0.3-0.6 eV) under the access device so captured electrons take milliseconds to minutes to re-emit. Pocket occupancy shifts the device threshold as the stored bit.
why: Capacitorless storage governed by emission-time physics rather than leakage paths (facts 1, 3); one implant mask; capture speed and uniform trap density are the risks.
note: Few traps per nanoscale device give large threshold variability; emission-time spread is the risk.

title: Silicon-on-nothing vacuum-isolated membrane holds charge at 300C
idea: For hot users such as Venus probes and jet-engine controllers, one trench-array mask followed by a hydrogen anneal migrates silicon to seal an empty cavity under a thin Si membrane (empty-space-in-silicon process); the membrane is the storage body, isolated below by vacuum instead of junctions. Charge in the membrane modulates the overlying channel.
why: Removes the substrate-junction leakage component (fact 3) for 10-100x retention in a capacitorless cell (fact 1); one mask; membrane thickness uniformity is the risk.
note: Niche high-temperature market; vacuum-isolated membrane body is plausible.

title: Photodiode storage node written by co-packaged laser light
idea: Laser-crosslink satellites receive data as light, so one implant mask turns storage nodes into Si photodiode junctions under a transparent plate; rows are precharged to '1' and a modulated micro-LED/VCSEL array discharges the '0' cells optically in parallel, while reads stay electrical. Write drivers and write bitline swings largely disappear.
why: Cuts write data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery (fact 7) for streaming-write workloads; optical alignment and neighbor crosstalk are the risks.

title: Leaky-integrator analog counters catch row hammering at activation rate
idea: Design for the extreme user, the attacker: each activation dumps a fixed charge packet onto that row's ~2 fF integrating capacitor in the SWD stripe, which self-leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a shared comparator checks it on every activation and triggers neighbor refresh past threshold. An analog rate detector replaces SRAM counter tables.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9) tracked for every row with ~0.5% area instead of megabits of counters, and with no counter aliasing.

title: Ring-oscillator time-domain sensing at 0.4 V array voltage
idea: Energy-harvesting IoT tags have no voltage headroom, so they sense in time: the bitline voltage starves a tiny ring oscillator per column group, and a counter compares its edge count over a fixed window against a reference column. It works at VARY ~0.4 V, where latch SAs fail.
