idea: During refresh-idle windows the array applies brief reverse-polarity, sub-breakdown bias across cell capacitors (plate and bitline swapped) that drifts oxygen vacancies back off the electrode interface, resetting the trap-assisted leakage that grows with time under bias.
why: Makes thinner, higher-k ZrO2/HfO2 stacks (more fF per pillar, fact 1) survive lifetime leakage creep; claim ~2x dielectric lifetime or ~15% more Cs at the same lifetime.
note: Bipolar stress recovery seen in HfO2 reliability; gain modest.

title: Al: Al2O3 negative charge passivates storage junction surfaces, solar-style
idea: Line STI sidewalls and the buried-wordline trench top near the storage node with ALD Al2O3, whose ~-5e12 cm^-2 fixed negative charge accumulates holes at the p-type surface and pushes the depletion region off the defective interface (the field-effect passivation used in PERC solar cells).
why: Suppresses surface-generation leakage, a major retention-tail contributor (fact 3), with abundant Al and existing ALD; target 2-5x tail reduction.

title: Zn: indium-free zinc-tin-oxide TFT layer hosts ECC logic above array
idea: Fabricate a BEOL ZnSnO thin-film-transistor logic layer (Zn and Sn are abundant; no In or Ga) over the cell array to hold on-die ECC syndrome decoders and row/column repair muxes, wired down by vias to local sense amps.
why: Moves reliability logic out of the ~49% periphery (fact 7) so stronger on-die ECC costs no die area; ~3-5% die shrink or 2x ECC strength at equal area.

title: Ar: argon-implanted recombination layer annihilates stray carriers below cells
idea: Implant argon deep below the active cell region to form a thin damaged layer with short minority-carrier lifetime (the IGBT lifetime-control trick), placed outside junction depletion regions, so substrate electrons recombine before diffusing to storage nodes.
why: Cuts substrate-mediated row hammer (fact 9) and alpha/neutron charge collection; claim ~3x lower soft-error rate, letting weaker Cs pass.

title: Ti: Rutile TiO2 on tin-oxide seed breaks the capacitor charge wall
idea: Replace ZrO2-based capacitor dielectrics with rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100) crystallized at low temperature on an isostructural rutile SnO2 seed instead of scarce RuO2, with Ti precursor from U.S. ilmenite sands.
why: k ~90 meets the fact-sheet k~70 target, allowing ~40:1 instead of 75:1 pillars (cheaper etch, more cell headroom) and less Hf/Zr reliance.

title: W: Closed-loop WF6 recovery from CVD exhaust and target scrap
idea: Cryotrap unreacted WF6 from CVD exhaust (typical utilization 20-30%) and re-fluorinate tungsten chamber scrapings and sputter-target remnants back to WF6 in an on-site loop.
why: Cuts virgin tungsten demand ~50-70% in a supply chain ~80% controlled by China.

title: O: Atmospheric spatial-ALD micro-fabs for ferroelectric oxide memory
idea: Vacuum-free spatial-ALD heads deposit HZO and oxide electrodes at ~10x throughput on mature-foundry 200 mm CMOS wafers, finishing a FeRAM BEOL in a $50-100M micro-fab.
why: Distributed non-volatile memory manufacturing at ~1/50th the capital of a DRAM fab.

title: Galvanized sacrificial hydrogen reservoir re-passivates traps over lifetime
idea: Place a hydrogen-rich SiNx:H liner next to the access channel as a galvanizing-style sacrificial layer. It slowly releases H to re-passivate interface traps as they depassivate in service, much as zinc corrodes first to protect steel.
why: Lifetime retention drift and VRT growth: keeps the tail near time-zero quality, avoiding end-of-life refresh-rate derating.

title: Jacquard warp-weft coincident wordline selection replaces tree decoders
idea: Borrow the Jacquard loom, where a hook lifts only where card and lifting bar coincide: each sub-wordline driver is a two-input threshold switch at the crossing of a 'warp' line (high address bits, sqrt(N) lines) and a 'weft' line (low bits, sqrt(N) lines). Each line supplies only half the boost charge, so half-selected drivers stay below threshold and only the doubly-selected wordline fires.
why: Cuts decoder transistors per wordline from ~6-10 to ~2 and predecode routing from O(log N) tracks per row to O(sqrt N) per mat: ~40-60% row-decoder area reduction.
note: Half-select threshold switching for wordline drivers; threshold variability sets margin.

title: Miura-fold bitlines: true and complement stacked vertically, not side by side
idea: Fold the bitline pair like Miura-ori: the true bitline runs on tier 1 and its complement directly above on tier 2, swapping tiers every 64 cells through a zig-zag via 'crease'. Both lines see identical wordline and neighbor coupling, giving folded-bitline noise rejection in the lateral footprint of an open bitline.
why: Open-bitline cell density with folded-bitline common-mode immunity, and each sense amp gets 2x the lateral pitch; ~30% less signal margin needed and an easier SA-pitch wall.

title: Braided trio bitlines with permutation-coded, reference-free sensing
idea: Like a three-strand braid, route three bitlines that rotate positions every few cells so all see identical coupling. Store data as the rank order of three distinct charge levels across three cells (6 permutations = 2.58 bits per 3 cells) and read it with three pairwise comparators and no mid-rail reference.
why: Common-mode leakage shifts all three cells together, so rank order survives ~2-4x longer: refresh power drops and reference-generation circuits leave the periphery, at a ~14% raw density cost.
note: Rank modulation known for flash; new DRAM application.

title: Permanent-mold sense amps: ferroelectric gate nulls each amplifier's offset forever
idea: Like a permanent metal mold that is set once and reused for thousands of castings, give one transistor of each SA input pair an HZO ferroelectric gate layer. At wafer test a binary search programs its polarization to cancel that SA's measured offset, and it stays trimmed for life with no fuse area.
why: Residual offset falls from ~15-20 mV sigma to ~3-5 mV, so bitline signal can drop ~3x: 2-3x longer bitlines (SA strip area -50%) or Cs reduced to ~2 fF.
note: FeFET trim; polarization disturb from SA swings is a doubt.

title: Pin-factory split: tiny per-pair preamps, shared high-voltage restore drivers
idea: Adam Smith's pin factory split one job into specialized steps: split the SA into a minimal thin-oxide preamp per bitline pair that only decides and holds the bit, plus one strong restore driver shared by four pairs. The shared driver writes full-swing values back in four ~3 ns phases within tRAS.
why: Restore devices are the largest part of the SA; sharing them 4:1 cuts SA-strip area ~30-40% and lets the preamp use smaller, better-matched devices.

title: Burn-in tempering: stress each sense amp until its offset vanishes
idea: Like tempering steel with controlled heat, use the 1990s wafer-level burn-in oven to apply asymmetric hot-carrier stress to the stronger transistor of each SA pair, chosen by a built-in offset measurement. The stress shifts its Vt until the pair matches, and the trapped charge makes the shift permanent.
why: SA offset sigma drops ~2-3x with zero added area, allowing ~2x more cells per bitline (SA strips -50% of their ~12% die share) using only legacy burn-in equipment.
note: HCI-trimmed offset; recovery and drift over life.

title: Core-rope weaving: diode-matrix row decoder with no PMOS
idea: Like Apollo's core-rope memory, where each wire threaded through or around a core encoded a bit, encode each wordline's address by placing or omitting a Schottky diode where it crosses the predecoded lines (one implant mask at 180 nm). The result is a dynamic diode-AND decoder.
why: Diodes are ~4x smaller than a CMOS NAND stack and need no well spacing: decoder area -50-60%, buildable at i-line rules.
note: Diode-AND wordline decode; Schottky diodes not native to DRAM flow.

title: Selective assembly: pick the best-matched transistor fingers per sense amp
idea: As engine plants pair pistons with bores by measured size, build each SA input side from four half-width candidate fingers. At test, e-fuse switches keep the finger pair whose Vts match best, the way 1990s analog chips trimmed matched pairs.
why: Best-of-4x4 selection cuts offset sigma ~2-3x without advanced litho, so bitlines can double in length; net SA area falls ~20-30% even at 180 nm.

title: Kiln witness cones: in-array cells integrate activation heat-work for row hammer
idea: Like pyrometric cones that slump after enough cumulative kiln heat, each row has a witness cell that gets a small charge kick through a weak device on every activation and leaks it away over time. Refresh reads the witness column and schedules neighbor refresh wherever a witness has slumped past threshold.
why: Replaces megabits of SRAM row-hammer counters in periphery with ~0.1% extra array cells; analog decay tracks hammer physics at ~1k-activation thresholds.

title: Accordion-folded die strip: one thinned strip folded into sixteen tiers
idea: Map-folding origami: fabricate a long strip of 16 array segments on one wafer, thin to ~10 um, replace the silicon between segments with polyimide hinges carrying the bus wiring, then Z-fold the strip into a stack held by die-attach film, so every tier is electrically continuous without TSVs or tier-to-tier alignment.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: ~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) and bond-alignment failures; claimed ~2x bits per wafer area versus HBM with stack yield set by per-segment repair.

title: Crystal-pulled nanowire forest as 4F2 vertical access transistors
idea: Borrow crystal growth: place SiGe seed nubs at 4F2 sites with spacer-defined dots and grow vertical single-crystal Si nanowires by self-catalysed selective epitaxy, then backfill gate-all-around wordlines and land capacitors on top, so the access transistor is grown rather than etched.
why: 4F2 vertical channels are ~33% smaller than 6F2 (fact 4), and etch-damage-free gate-all-around channels tighten the 13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3); self-catalysed growth avoids gold contamination.

title: Running-bond brick stacking: each chiplet straddles two below
idea: Lay DRAM chiplets like bricks in running bond: each upper die is offset by half a die and hybrid-bonded to two lower dies, so vertical links form a 3D mesh with two paths to every die instead of a single TSV column.
why: One bad TSV column kills an HBM stack today (fact 6: 20-30% yield loss); path diversity tolerates failed links and spreads heat; claimed +15-20 points of stack yield.

title: Roll-to-roll memory book: one hundred laminated oxide-TFT foils
idea: Print-shop analogy: produce oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays roll-to-roll on 5 um polyimide or steel foil, cut sheets, and laminate 100 of them into a book whose spine is edge-bonded with anisotropic conductive film to a CMOS controller.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability: R2R lines cost ~1% of a DRAM fab; bits per sheet are low, but 100 penny sheets could give a ~$1-2/GB capacity tier; access may sit at 100 ns-1 us rather than 10-100 ns.

title: Nano-velcro reworkable stacking: unhook and replace bad tiers
idea: Template-electroplate copper nanowire hook fields on stack pads in existing bump lines so mating fields interlock at room temperature like Velcro; test the stack, peel off any bad die, press in a good one, then anneal to make the joints permanent.
why: Turns the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss (fact 6) into a repairable step, so stack yield approaches die yield, with no bonding thermal budget.

title: Crepe-paper electrodes: controlled buckling doubles capacitor area
idea: Like crepe paper or pleated filters gaining area through wrinkles, deposit the bottom electrode on a compliant sacrificial underlayer with compressive mismatch so it buckles into 20-40 nm-wavelength wrinkles before dielectric and top-electrode ALD on mature tools.
why: +1.5-2x area per footprint permits lower aspect ratio or trailing-node cells (fact 1) without new high-AR etchers.

title: Overspray recovery: capture and re-refine ALD precursors from exhaust
idea: Paint booths reclaim overspray; fit ALD and CVD forelines with cold-finger condensers and chelating sorbent cartridges that capture unreacted Zr, Hf, Ru, Mo and W organometallics and halides, then return the cartridges to a precursor refinery that strips and redistills them.
why: ALD sends 90-99% of metal precursor to the abatement burner; closing the loop could halve new hafnium, zirconium and ruthenium demand and cut abatement fuel.

title: Copper heap-leach playbook: bacteria mine tungsten and gallium domestically
idea: Copper mines pull metal from low-grade heaps with acidophilic bacteria; apply engineered bioleaching heaps to Nevada tungsten-skarn tailings, Appalachian coal fly ash and alumina red mud to dissolve W, Ga and Ge, then recover them by solvent extraction and ion exchange.
why: Supplies U.S. fabs with tungsten, gallium and germanium (all China-dominated and export-controlled) from existing waste piles at low capital; semiconductor demand is small in tonnage, so modest heaps suffice.

title: Porcelain enameling: borax-glaze BCN barrier replaces tantalum liners
idea: Enamelers fuse borax glazes to steel as impermeable barriers; deposit a ~1-2 nm amorphous boron-carbon-nitride 'glaze' from precursors made from California borax as the copper diffusion barrier and liner in DRAM metal layers, replacing Ta/TaN.
why: Tantalum comes from conflict-mineral regions; a thinner barrier also frees conductor cross-section for ~20-30% lower line resistance at tight pitch.
note: Amorphous BN/BCN barriers researched; 1-2 nm pinhole-free coverage is the doubt.

title: Veneer peeling: controlled spalling yields thin dies and reusable substrates
idea: Like rotary-peeling veneer from a log, deposit a tensile Ni stressor on finished DRAM wafers and peel off a 10-20 um device layer on handle tape for stacking, then reclaim-polish and re-epi the 700 um parent substrate for up to ~5 more uses.
why: Capital and scarce resources: skips backgrind and thinning CMP and cuts quartz-crucible-dependent CZ silicon per bit several-fold.

title: Movable-type reticles: tile-stepped array masks shared across products
idea: Like Gutenberg composing pages from reusable type, write a small defect-free array-tile reticle (one mat) and step it repeatedly inside a bladed field, then expose periphery from a type case of standard sense-amp, decoder and I/O tiles; new densities are composed from existing tiles instead of new full reticles.
why: Mask cost/cycle time: small tiles are cheaper and higher-yield to write; derivative mask-set cost falls ~50-70% and tape-out-to-wafer shrinks by weeks.

title: Plywood cross-lamination cancels warp in many-tier stacks
idea: Copy plywood's alternating grain: rotate each tier's line orientation (and its anisotropic film stress) 90 degrees relative to the tier below and alternate tensile/compressive liner recipes, so wafer bow cancels instead of accumulating through the stack.
why: Fact 2/yield: warp and overlay drift cap tier count; cancellation could allow ~2x more tiers before bow exceeds scanner and bonder chuck limits.

title: Planed wood-grain staircase: one sloped trough exposes every tier
idea: Use the single added mask to open a wide trough at the array edge and etch it through reflowed resist into a 5-10 degree ramp; deposit the tier stack conformally, then CMP flat so each tier surfaces as its own ~400 nm stripe, like grain on a planed board, giving wordline contact landings for all tiers.
why: Capital/throughput: replaces the multi-mask staircase with dozens of trim-etch loops by one mask plus one CMP for 3D DRAM.

title: Embossed relief: one grayscale mask prints three cell levels
idea: Like a relief-embossing die that presses several heights at once, use one grayscale multi-transmission mask on a multi-threshold resist to print landing-pad, bitline-contact and storage-node patterns as three resist heights, then transfer them by sequential etch-back so each level opens self-aligned to the others.
why: Fact 4: adds one mask yet retires two to three critical exposures and their overlay budget; ~5-8% wafer cost reduction.

title: Hoffmann kiln: compute wave rides the refresh sweep across banks
idea: In a Hoffmann ring kiln the fire travels around the stationary bricks. Refresh already opens every row on a schedule, so simple bank-level ALUs work on each row while it is open: scans, popcounts, zero-detection, dedup hashing, entropy measurement and scrubbing. Memory-saving services thus ride a 'fire zone' that marches through DRAM at no extra activation cost.
why: Background services such as dedup hashing and choosing cold pages to compress currently take host bandwidth; riding on refresh activations (about 46 fJ/bit already paid) makes them nearly free.
note: Bank ALUs during refresh; same core as I-03058.

title: Ribbon-grown silicon interposer blanks without quartz crucibles
idea: Pull interposer-grade silicon as continuous ribbon through a graphite die (edge-defined film-fed growth) instead of Czochralski boules from Spruce Pine quartz crucibles. Interposers do not need prime crystal quality, and ribbon growth avoids sawing kerf.
why: Cuts reliance on high-purity quartz (>80% one source) and ~40% kerf loss for the large passive silicon used in HBM packaging.

title: Plywood cross-laminated thin-glass interposer fused in one bake
idea: Laser-drill and print orthogonal routing onto 50 um glass sheets, alternating direction like plywood grain, then stack and fuse them at ~600 C into one monolithic interposer. Each sheet is tested before lamination.
why: Mask-free multilayer interposer with glass's low loss and flatness; claims ~3x lower cost than silicon interposers and higher yield from known-good layers.

title: Knitted micro-spring interposer layer absorbing warpage
idea: Knit 10 um copper-alloy wire into a loop fabric; each loop becomes a compliant vertical spring contact between a giant panel interposer and the board. The knit soaks up thermal-expansion mismatch.
why: Warpage limits package size; compliant knit lets >100 cm2 memory-plus-compute panels survive, putting far more DRAM within short reach.

title: Tire-retreading remanufacture of DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Harvest DRAM dies from retired server DIMMs, decapsulate them chemically, retest and bin them, then re-stack them into new CXL or inference-tier modules in U.S. remanufacturing plants, like retreading tires.
why: Raises usable supply from installed base; U.S.-located, no wafer capacity needed; low capital intensity.

title: Self-folding micro-origami antennas for sub-THz wireless memory links
idea: Strain-mismatched metal bilayers on a 130 nm SiGe die curl up into 3D vertical dipoles and horn antennas when released, like self-folding origami. Memory chips then broadcast to compute across the board without package pins.
why: Wireless memory buses cut pin count and package cost and allow one-to-many broadcast; all mature-node.
note: Wireless buses lack bandwidth density and energy efficiency vs wires.

title: Swiss-roll self-rolling capacitors enabling low-swing memory I/O
idea: Strained nanomembranes roll themselves into Swiss-roll capacitors embedded in the interposer, giving ~10x decoupling density. The quieter power delivery lets memory I/O drop to ~0.2 V swing.
why: I/O energy scales with V^2, so the claimed cut in link pJ/bit is ~3-5x.
note: I/O swing is limited by noise, crosstalk and receivers, not only PDN decap.

title: Registration-mark pilot cells recalibrate sense references for every row
idea: Like the registration marks that align a press's colour plates, write 2-4 known pilot cells (one charged, one discharged) into each row at every restore; on activation a small comparator measures the pilot bitline swings and shifts that row's sense-amp reference and sensing delay on the fly, so rows whose cells have drifted (leakage, temperature, ageing) still sense correctly.
why: Turns marginal retention-tail reads into recoverable margin, allowing ~2-4x longer refresh or cells with ~30% less Cs (facts 1, 3) for ~0.5% cell overhead.

title: Letterpress fingerprint remap: nanoimprint template defects fixed once for all dies
idea: Worn letterpress type repeats the same blemish on every page; pattern critical array layers by nanoimprint cured with 365 nm UV-LEDs (no ArF/KrF excimers, which burn neon, argon and krypton), map the template's defects once, and burn one shared fuse remap into every die that template stamps, since its defects land at identical coordinates.
why: Removes neon-dependent litho and turns NIL's main weakness, repeating template defects, into a one-time characterisation instead of per-die yield loss; litho capex could fall by half (fact 4).

title: Felted fountain-coded pages for UV-LED-printed defect-dense arrays
idea: Felt is strong because random fibres overlap; store each 4 KB page as fountain-coded fragments across 18-20 subarrays so any 16 rebuild it, letting arrays patterned by 365 nm UV-LED lithography with self-aligned spacer pitch division (no Hg-Xe lamps or excimers) carry whole dead subarrays without spare mapping.
why: Defect-dense, cheap rare-gas-free litho becomes usable for a capacity tier behind cache, tolerating ~15-20% subarray loss (capital, scarcity).
note: 365 nm UV-LED patterning yields low density even if defects are tolerated.

title: Willow Run conversion: idle LCD fabs build oxide gain-cell memory
idea: In WWII, Ford's Willow Run auto plant was converted to build bombers. Convert shuttered Gen-6/Gen-8.5 TFT-LCD fabs, which already have IGZO sputter, PECVD and large-area litho, to print 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays on glass at 1-2 um rules (~20 GB per Gen-8.5 sheet). Dice them into slow-tier CXL capacity tiles.
why: Supply and capital: dozens of idle panel fabs are sunk capex. They can yield low-density but huge-area bits for a capacity tier that offloads DRAM, with no EUV, CZ silicon or quartz.
note: Same LCD-fab IGZO gain-cell panels as I-04100.

title: Glass-cullet loop: re-fuse spent quartz crucibles into new ones
idea: Glass furnaces run on recycled cullet. Crush spent CZ crucibles, which today are single-use and landfilled. Strip devitrified cristobalite and metals by hot chlorination and plasma-torch refining, then arc-fuse the purified grain into new crucible inner layers.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz): a closed loop could replace ~40-60% of virgin high-purity quartz per ingot.
note: Re-purifying devitrified spent crucibles to inner-layer grade is the doubt; alkali/metal removal must reach ppb.

title: Bolt-of-cloth die: seamless tile fabric diced to any capacity
idea: Textile mills weave continuous bolts that are cut to any length. Lay out the wafer as a seamless sea of self-contained memory tiles, each with local periphery and a bus that crosses scribe lines. The saw then cuts any rectangle, so wafer-edge and defect-adjacent regions become smaller-capacity parts instead of scrap.
why: Usable area: recovers ~5-8% of the wafer lost to edge exclusion and partial dies, and one mask set serves many capacities.

title: Kintsugi rework: rescue HBM stacks from failed CoWoS packages
idea: When a GPU die or interposer fails after assembly, the good HBM stacks are scrapped with it. Turn breakage into value like kintsugi: thermally debond the stacks, plasma-clean them, and re-form SnAg microbumps by evaporation through a lithographically made silicon shadow mask. Then re-bond them to a new interposer with a flip-chip bonder.
why: HBM supply: a few % post-assembly loss wastes the most expensive bits, and recovering them adds HBM with no wafers. Aligner, evaporator and bonder are standard nanofab tools.
note: Same debond-and-reuse core as I-08709, sourced from assembly fallout.

title: Blacksmith tempering: high-pressure deuterium re-anneal rescues retention-failed wafers
idea: Smiths re-temper steel to restore toughness. Wafers that fail retention binning at sort, before bumping, get a 20-atm deuterium anneal at 400-450 C that re-passivates interface and junction traps in the access transistors. The weak-cell tail shrinks and the wafers are re-sorted into higher bins.
why: Leakage tail, refresh and yield: if the tail shrinks even 2x, 1-3% of wafers and many low bins are recovered. High-pressure anneal furnaces exist in nanofabs.

title: Memory wallpaper: square metres of printed foil DRAM
idea: IFR: memory as cheap per area as a solar panel. Closest achievable: print 1T1C oxide-TFT cells at 2 um pitch on PV-grade foil (~2.5e7 bits/cm^2, ~30 GB per m^2 at ~$50/m^2) and mount panels as a capacity tier behind HBM/DDR.
why: Cost per bit (~$2/GB) and capital (PV-class lines) at the price of us-class latency; adds supply outside DRAM fabs.

title: Per-module retention passport in SPD, standardized by JEDEC
idea: IFR: each module is refreshed exactly as fast as it needs, no faster. Testers already measure retention, so JEDEC adds an SPD retention passport (per-bank retention histogram at three temperatures) plus a controller rule that stretches tREFI to match, and vendors sell 128/256/512 ms bins.
why: Fact 3: most dies retain far longer than the 64 ms worst-case spec; fleet-wide refresh power and bandwidth could drop 2-8x with no new silicon.

title: Ferroelectric-stored offset trim lets sense amps resolve 5 mV
idea: Ideal result: a sense amp with zero offset. At wafer test, each latch's mismatch is measured and written as a polarization state into a small FeFET in its tail or body-bias path, so the offset stays cancelled with no trim registers, fuses or periodic calibration.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): required bitline signal falls from ~20 mV to ~8 mV, allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines, cutting SA stripes (fact 7) by up to 40%.

title: Socketed HBM base die rescues good DRAM dies from failed stacks
idea: Ideal result: a stack that is never scrapped. Join the periphery/base logic die to the DRAM stack with low-temperature indium micro-bumps and a removable clamp frame instead of underfill, so a failed base die or bad bottom joint is swapped at ~160 C and the good DRAM dies are reused.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss; the base die becomes a field-replaceable part.

title: Defect-tolerant self-assembled lattice with a learned per-die address map
idea: IFR: 'the array patterns itself and defects do not matter.' Backward: form storage-node pillars by block-copolymer directed self-assembly (hexagonal cylinders at ~12-14 nm pitch guided by coarse DUV prepatterns), accept ~1e-4 dislocation rates, and electrically map each die at test into a compact defect-to-spare translation table in on-die fuses.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): replaces the capacitor-landing EUV layers; remapping makes DSA defect levels, which killed it before, acceptable.

title: Spalled device-layer stacking: one wafer yields twenty memory tiers
idea: IFR: 'the substrate is consumed zero times.' Backward: after front-end processing, lift off a ~10 um device layer by stressor-induced spalling (or hydrogen-implant splitting), bond it onto the growing stack, re-polish the parent wafer and repeat ~20 times.
why: Scarce resources and capital: ~20x fewer ingots (and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles) per stacked bit; wafer cost amortized over tiers.

title: Silicon-carbide EV fabs make hot, near-refresh-free trench DRAM
idea: IFR: 'memory never refreshes and runs at 125 C.' Backward: use the 150/200 mm 4H-SiC lines overbuilt for EV inverters to make trench-capacitor 1T1C arrays whose 3.3 eV bandgap gives leakage orders below silicon (hours of retention at 125 C), sold as hot-side memory next to accelerators.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and U.S. manufacturability: refresh energy and bandwidth loss near zero; U.S. SiC capacity (NC, NY) is under-loaded, though first-generation density is ~20-50x below DRAM.
note: SiC leakage is tiny but MOS interfaces are poor and density is 20-50x lower; niche hot memory.

title: Paper-stack tiers laminated with z-axis anisotropic conductive film
idea: IFR: 'stacking tiers is as easy as stacking paper.' Backward: build each memory tier on a reusable glass carrier over a laser-release layer, peel it off as a 5 um polyimide film, and laminate dozens of films with anisotropic conductive film whose particle chains conduct only vertically through aligned pads.
why: 3D tiers and HBM tax (facts 2, 6): known-good films are tested before lamination; no TSVs or hybrid-bond tools, and carriers are reused.

title: Scarce-input substitution credits verified by digital material passports
idea: Ideal: a market that rewards memory made from nothing scarce. Closest: a U.S. per-GB production credit scaled by the share of the bill of materials free of designated chokepoints (helium, natural HPQ, Chinese-origin W/Ge/Ga/In, PFAS), verified with lot-level material passports (supplier attestations plus isotopic/trace fingerprints).
why: Creates demand pull for He-, W-, HPQ- and PFAS-free processes, pulling their time-to-volume in by years and shifting adoption risk from fabs to policy.

title: Two-height nanoimprint template prints wordline trench and contact together
idea: Ideal: one stamp prints the whole cell. Closest: an e-beam master is replicated into two-height nanoimprint templates that imprint buried-wordline trenches and bitline-contact recesses in one resist step (dual-damascene in resist); array layers imprint only, periphery stays on DUV.
why: Fact 4: replaces 2-3 EUV exposures in the array with one NIL step at ~1/10 the tool capex, and the self-registered two-level pattern deletes one overlay budget; ~15-20% litho cost cut.

title: Selective-area ALD grows storage contact and bottom electrode as one
idea: Ideal: contact and capacitor are one object made in one step. Closest: inhibitor SAMs on oxide let TiN or Ru ALD/CVD nucleate only on doped-Si landing pads and grow bottom-up through the mold, forming the storage-node plug and the capacitor bottom electrode continuously with no CMP or recess.
why: Facts 4 and 7: deletes one litho layer, one CMP, one etch-back plus metrology; removes an interface that adds contact resistance; ~3-5% fewer steps.

title: Fully silicided polysilicon buried wordlines eliminate tungsten fill
idea: Ideal: wordlines that need no imported metal. Closest: fill the buried-wordline trench with in-situ-doped amorphous Si and fully convert it with a self-limiting Ni silicidation anneal (FUSI, as in fully silicided gates), skipping WF6 CVD, W etch-back and W CMP.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and Fact 4: removes W deposition tools and steps; NiSi ~15 uOhm-cm is competitive with thin W in narrow trenches.

title: Halve EUV dose by designing arrays to absorb stochastic defects
idea: Ideal: EUV throughput doubles for free. Closest: expose array layers at ~30 mJ/cm2 instead of ~60, accepting more stochastic micro-bridges and missing contacts, and absorb them with column/row spares, per-sub-array ECC and a repair map designed in from day one.
why: Fact 4: EUV is the bottleneck tool; ~1.6-1.8x scanner throughput means fewer $150M+ scanners per 10k wafer starts.
note: Defect rate rises steeply at half dose; spares/ECC may not absorb it.

title: Prestressed buckled nanobeam stores bits as mechanical states
idea: Ideal: a bit that needs no charge at all. Closest: a 200 nm compressively stressed SiN or amorphous-carbon beam released over a BEOL cavity buckles up or down; side electrodes snap it in ~10 ns (GHz resonance) and a non-contact capacitive sense reads position, so the state is held mechanically with zero leakage and no wear.
why: Facts 3 and 4: no capacitor, no refresh, zero standby power; BEOL-only on any logic wafer with 3-4 DUV masks plus a release step.
note: Beam footprint far above DRAM cell; stiction/fatigue risk.

title: Self-amplifying floating-base bipolar cell needs no sense amplifiers
idea: Ideal: a cell loud enough that the periphery disappears. Closest: a vertical npn whose floating p-base stores holes; on read, the stored charge switches on bipolar gain (beta ~50-100) for uA-level bitline current, so simple inverter sensing replaces pitch-matched differential sense amps, with no capacitor anywhere.
why: Fact 7 and Fact 4: periphery is ~49% of the die; relaxed sense-amp pitch rules shrink it and let it move to a cheaper process; reads need no charge sharing.
note: Floating-body retention issues; periphery saving partial.

title: Blow-away ESD shunts after bonding to strip I/O capacitance
idea: Ideal: die-to-die wires with zero parasitic load. Closest achievable: replace each inter-die pad's ESD diode stack (~0.2-0.5 pF) with one shared sacrificial shunt network that protects only during handling and bonding, then laser- or electrically fuse it open after the stack is sealed, leaving ~10 fF bond loads.
why: Facts 5 and 6: link energy scales with C, so removing ESD load cuts per-bit energy 5-10x on hybrid-bond and TSV lanes and shrinks pad area so more lanes fit per mm2.
note: Hybrid-bond D2D ESD is already minimal (tens of fF), so gains are smaller than claimed.

title: On-die micro-heaters anneal leaky access-transistor traps in the field
idea: Ideal: weak cells repair themselves. Closest: polysilicon heater lines under each mat drive local 250-350 C pulses lasting milliseconds (after migrating that mat's data) to anneal the interface and junction traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells, resetting them to their low-leak state.
why: Fact 3: could shrink the leakage tail and VRT population 3-10x so refresh slows proportionally; also extends field life.

title: Sense-settling timer flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Ideal: knowing exactly which bits are wrong without storing extra bits. Closest: a per-column comparator times how long each sense amp takes to resolve; bits that resolve slowly (small signal) are flagged to the decoder as erasures, and since an erasure costs half an error, a code fixing t errors now fixes 2t marginal bits.
why: Facts 1 and 3: doubles effective ECC strength at no parity cost, allowing ~2x weaker cells or 2-4x longer refresh.

title: Leaky-capacitor integrators count hammer activations automatically
idea: Ideal: hammer counting that needs no counter memory. Closest: a 180 nm companion chip holds an array of MOS capacitors, one per row group, each receiving a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaking with a time constant equal to the refresh window, so each voltage is a free sliding-window activation count; a comparator fires neighbor refresh at threshold.
why: Fact 9: analog decay implements the sliding window that digital trackers spend kilobytes of SRAM on; ~10x less area than counter tables.

title: Bitline charge recycling between paired subarrays during refresh
idea: Ideal: refresh costs zero energy. Closest: at the end of each refresh, the high bitlines of one subarray dump half their charge through a 180 nm transfer switch into the bitlines of the next subarray to be refreshed, so each refresh reuses roughly half of the previous one's CV2.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy ~-40% without lowering the voltage floor.
note: Cross-subarray transfer wiring and timing eat much of the claimed 40% refresh-energy gain.

title: Conveyor memory: data circulates so refresh and scrub are inherent
idea: Ideal: memory that is always being read, so always fresh and always checked. Closest: a 180 nm shift-loop DRAM in which every row's data circulates through a sense-and-ECC station every few milliseconds, so refresh and scrubbing happen as a side effect of motion, with many short loops keeping average access near 100 ns.
why: Fact 3: no separate refresh scheduling and errors are corrected before they accumulate; suits a bulk refresh-tolerant tier.

title: OpenDRAM patent pool with FRAND royalties and reference PDK
idea: Ideal: DRAM know-how that is free to everyone. Closest achievable: gather licensable cell, sense-amp and buried-wordline patents from defunct-maker estates and universities into a FRAND pool bundled with an open reference PDK and test chips, so an entrant pays one fixed royalty instead of facing lawsuits.
why: Barrier to entry: removes multi-$B litigation risk and cuts years of design time for new makers.

title: Via-last HBM TSVs etched in existing MEMS fabs
idea: Ideal: the DRAM fab spends nothing on TSVs. Closest achievable with no new fab: TSV etch, liner, fill and thinning move from DRAM fabs to existing 200/300mm MEMS and power fabs that already run Bosch DRIE, using a via-last flow with landing pads designed into the periphery.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees DRAM-fab tool time and can shrink keep-out area, using idle trailing capacity.

title: Anodized-aluminum nanopores grow capacitor holes instead of etching them
idea: Scarcity rule: no high-aspect-ratio etch tool. Deposit an Al film over the cell transistors, imprint dimples at the storage-contact pitch, and anodize so self-ordered pores grow straight down at AR >150:1 by electrochemistry alone; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN lines the pores as cup capacitors after the pore-bottom barrier is thinned to open each contact.
why: Reaches the AR ~115 needed for more charge (fact 1) without HAR dry-etch tools and hardmask stacks, cutting capital intensity (fact 4); pore-to-contact registration is the main risk.
note: AAO nanocapacitor arrays known; registration to storage contacts is the crux.

title: Planar 1.5 fF capacitor rescued by stronger invisible on-die ECC
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): the host must see ordinary DDR5 data. Shrink the capacitor to a low-AR 1.5 fF cup that tolerates raw BER near 1e-5, and replace DDR5's internal SEC(136,128) with a hidden double-error-correcting code over 256-bit internal words (same ~6% parity) plus offset-cancelled sensing inside tRCD.
why: Spends invisible ECC and sense-time slack to delete the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and several HAR/EUV steps (fact 4), ~20% lower wafer cost; partial-write read-modify-write must fit in tWR.
note: Stronger hidden ECC trades for smaller caps; ~20% cost gain.

title: Charge-plasma junctionless storage node kills GIDL leakage tail
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): unchanged timings and voltages. Remove the doped n+ storage-node junction: the access channel is undoped and the storage-node extension is electrostatically doped by a low-work-function metal (charge plasma), so no metallurgical pn junction remains for junction leakage or GIDL band-to-band tunneling.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) ~10x, stretching retention and cutting refresh via the existing refresh-rate register, while removing implant and anneal steps.
note: Charge-plasma doping of node; benefit on GIDL tail uncertain.

title: Ban all implants: fixed-charge dielectrics electrostatically dope the access transistor
idea: Limit: no dopant atom may be implanted near the storage node. Fixed charge in the spacer dielectric induces the source/drain extensions instead: positive-charge SiNx for n-type, negative-charge Al2O3 for p-type. The result is an atomically abrupt, damage-free 'junction' with no random dopant fluctuation and no end-of-range defects to act as SRH generation centers.
why: Fact 3: implant damage and dopant clusters seed the high-leakage tail. Removing them could pull worst-cell leakage from ~13 fA toward the median, ~10x, and the refresh interval would stretch accordingly.
note: Electrostatic/charge-plasma doping known in research; DRAM-tail application is new.

title: Intrinsic carriers below one per chip: amorphous Ga2O3 access channel
idea: Limit: the channel's intrinsic carrier density must make thermal leakage physically negligible. Use ALD amorphous Ga2O3 (Eg ~4.8 eV, no indium) as a BEOL access-transistor channel, with source/drain doped by oxygen vacancies from a local H2 plasma. The theoretical off-current floor is ~1e-24 A/um, orders of magnitude below IGZO.
why: Fact 3 and resources: refresh-free retention of hours or more at 85 C, no exposure to indium supply concentration, and the device stacks in BEOL for 3D tiers (fact 2). Risk: mobility below 5 cm2/Vs demands a short channel.

title: Rent a furnace: high-pressure deuterium anneal of purchased DRAM wafers
idea: 10-person constraint: one tool, no fab. Buy known-good DRAM wafers before dicing and run a high-pressure (10-20 atm) deuterium anneal at 350-400 C, which drives D through the BEOL stack to passivate residual Si/SiO2 dangling bonds at the access transistors. Re-sort the results into long-retention bins and sell them as low-refresh parts.
why: Fact 3: high-pressure anneal studies show large interface-trap reductions, which could compress the leakage tail ~2-5x. A 10-person shop with one HP anneal tool creates a premium grade. Risk: BEOL thermal budget.
note: Vendors rarely sell unsorted wafers; nitride liners block D diffusion through BEOL.

title: No charge pumps: neighbor-wordline bootstrap boosts selected wordline
idea: Limit: no VPP charge pumps on the die. Local wordline drivers self-boost: a precharged, deselected neighbor segment's capacitance is coupled through a MIM capacitor to kick the selected wordline from VDD to ~3 V (like NAND channel boosting), and the charge is recycled back into the neighbor when the row closes.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): deleting VPP pumps (~3-4% of the die, 30-40% conversion loss) cuts wordline energy ~30-40%.

title: Switching-time sensing: read FeRAM by when the current peaks
idea: Constraint: non-volatile 1T1C ferroelectric cells shrunk until switching charge is tiny. Sense the time of the current spike rather than its charge: a peak detector plus time-to-digital converter on each bitline tells a switching cell (delayed nucleation peak) from a non-switching one (immediate displacement only), with no reference cell.
why: Immune to capacitor-area variation and fatigue-induced charge loss, so 3D FeRAM cells can shrink until switching charge is ~1 fC; no reference columns (periphery -5%).

title: Persistence-domain DRAM standard: mandatory per-die power-fail dump pin
idea: Constraint: data survives power loss in every server, by standard. Propose a JEDEC/OCP 'DDR-P' profile in which each die has a power-fail pin, an energy-budget register and an in-die backup engine, so hosts can drop batteries, NVDIMM-N modules and flash-backed caches; seed it via U.S. federal procurement of persistent memory.
why: Strategy: creates a market for NV periphery IP in which U.S. firms can lead, and removes ~$50-100 of backup hardware per server.

title: One crucible wafer seeds twenty monocrystalline tiers by donor reuse
idea: Limit: at most one CZ (quartz-crucible) wafer per 20 tiers. Smart-cut transfers 60 nm single-crystal Si films from one donor onto the stack one tier at a time, with refinishing CMP between transfers. The donor is reused about 20 times before it is sliced into test wafers.
why: Resource chokepoint: Spruce Pine high-purity quartz; cuts crucible-grown Si per tier-bit about 20x while keeping crystalline access transistors.

title: Maskless three-beam interference lithography for hexagonal cell arrays
idea: Limit: no photomask for the array. Expose the whole cell field with three-beam laser interference, which prints a perfect hexagonal pillar lattice in one shot. Periphery is defined separately by cheap i-line or ArF litho and stitched at mat edges.
why: Fact 4: replaces several EUV array layers with a tool costing about 1/50 as much, and hex packing gains about 15% over square.
note: Same as three-beam interference array patterning; mat-edge stitching and pitch limits.

title: In-plane side-gated tiers: wordline silicided from the tier itself
idea: Limit: zero tungsten. Next to each tier's lateral channel, a parallel strip of the same Si tier, across a narrow ALD-dielectric-filled slit, is converted to NiSi and becomes an in-plane side-gate wordline. No metal fill goes into deep recesses.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China about 80%) and Fact 2: removes W replacement-gate fill and its void and stress problems in high-tier stacks.
note: Single side-gate across a slit gives weak channel control and higher leakage.

title: Ion-cut prime silicon films onto cast metallurgical carriers
idea: Imposed scarcity: one CZ wafer must feed ten DRAM wafers. Hydrogen-implant and split a 1.5 um prime silicon layer from a reusable CZ donor, bond it over a thin oxide-nitride diffusion barrier onto a cheap cast upgraded-metallurgical silicon carrier (made in graphite or Si3N4 molds), and build the array in the transferred film.
why: ~10x less CZ crystal and HPQ crucible per wafer; the carrier costs ~$5-10 vs ~$100+ for prime 300 mm; the buried barrier can also serve as a back-bias plane for leakage control.

title: Thin-kerf, thin-wafer diet: more wafers per crucible
idea: Imposed scarcity: ingot output frozen at today's crucible count. Slice 300 mm ingots with 35 um diamond wire into 450 um wafers (vs 775 um wafers with ~150 um kerf), and carry each thin wafer through FEOL on a reusable bonded glass or silicon handle that is debonded before backgrind.
why: Ingot consumed per wafer drops from ~925 um to ~490 um, so ~1.8x more wafers per ingot; the same Spruce Pine crucible and polysilicon supply feeds ~60-80% more DRAM wafers.

title: Fully silicided nickel wordlines replace tungsten fill
idea: Imposed scarcity: no W and no WF6. Fill the wordline trench with doped amorphous silicon, cap it with Ni(Pt) and anneal so the whole trench converts to NiSi (full silicidation); the work function is tuned by dopant pile-up at the gate interface.
why: Removes tungsten and fluorine from the cell; work-function engineering by dopant segregation can cut GIDL and so the leakage tail that forces refresh; NiSi at ~15 uOhm-cm competes with narrow W lines.

title: Oxygen-ashable carbon mold capacitors with no HF dip-out
idea: Imposed scarcity: no fluorocarbon gases and no HF. Build the capacitor mold from amorphous carbon etched in O2/N2/COS plasma, deposit TiN/ZAZ at <=400 C, then remove the mold by O2 ashing instead of an HF wet dip-out.
why: Removes PFC etch gases and the wet capillary forces that topple tall pillars, so AR can rise from ~70 toward ~100 for more Cs; also cuts PFAS-regulated chemistry and UPW per wafer.

title: Superlattice edge stamps print 16 nm wordlines without optics
idea: Constraint: pitch must come from deposition thickness, never from light. Grow a Si/SiGe superlattice of 8 nm layers, cleave and selectively recess its edge into a ridge master, metallize the ridge tips and transfer them as wordline/bitline gratings (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer), each master printing thousands of wafers through daughter stamps.
why: Fact 4: sub-20 nm pitch set by epitaxy with zero scanner time; critical-layer litho capital -50-80%.

title: Pre-patterned back-gate SOI wafers give temperature-tracking threshold voltage
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: the substrate supplier delivers SOI wafers with a buried back-gate grid under a thin BOX, so planar fully depleted access transistors raise their threshold by back bias as the die heats, holding 125 C leakage at 85 C levels while the fab skips its buried-wordline trench module.
why: Facts 3 and 4: moves ~10 front-end steps to a relaxed-pitch substrate process; leakage tail at 125 C cut ~10x by bias.

title: Roll-to-roll assembled memory ribbons with a compressor per die
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): flexible-hybrid-electronics lines place thinned DRAM dies and tiny compression/decompression chiplets alternately on a printed-interconnect flex ribbon, so every DRAM die gets its own inline compressor, and the ribbon is sold by effective (compressed) GB.
why: Inline compression per die at negligible board cost gives ~2x effective capacity, while roll-to-roll assembly lowers module cost and avoids rigid-substrate bottlenecks.

title: Vapor-chamber dies interleaved every eighth tier cool tall stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Every eighth tier is a 50 um silicon vapor-chamber die (micro-wick etched into reclaimed wafers, water-filled, hermetically bonded) that carries heat sideways to the package edge, keeping 64-high stacks below 85 C.
why: Heat, not wiring, caps tall stacks; reclaimed-silicon cooling dies cost little, enable 10x tiers, and stop refresh rates (fact 3) from exploding.

title: Reworkable HBM: low-melt indium bumps let bad dies be swapped
idea: Rule: an HBM stack must be repairable at die level. Core dies are stacked with indium or Sn-Bi microbumps that reflow at ~120-140 C instead of permanent hybrid bonds, so a die that fails at stack test or in the field can be desoldered and replaced at a repair station.
why: Fact 6: much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss becomes a die swap rather than scrapping 8-12 good dies.

title: Diels-Alder reversible mold compound for intact die recovery
idea: Rule: the package must open without damaging the die. DRAM is encapsulated in a mold compound with thermally reversible Diels-Alder crosslinks that de-crosslink at ~150 C, so dies can be lifted intact from failed or retired packages for failure analysis, repair or repackaging.
why: Makes die-level recycling and failure analysis cheap. Recovered good dies add supply, and the root-cause loop for reliability shortens.

title: No proprietary IP: open DRAM design kit for trench foundries
idea: Self-imposed limit: everything must be open. A consortium releases an open-licensed DRAM macro kit (trench or stacked cell, sense amp, redundancy, DDR/CXL PHY RTL) qualified on foundry processes that already have deep-trench capacitors, so any logic foundry can make commodity-interface DRAM.
why: Breaks the three-maker oligopoly and the IP barrier; adds foundry capacity to DRAM supply. Density is lower, but U.S. manufacturability improves.

title: No silicon wafer: idle SiC power fabs build refresh-free retention memory
idea: Forced limit: the substrate must not be Si. Overbuilt 200 mm SiC fabs, idle after the EV slowdown, make 1T1C cells whose 3.3 eV-bandgap access transistors leak orders of magnitude less than Si, giving refresh intervals of minutes to hours for standby tiers.
why: Removes refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) for standby tiers and uses stranded SiC capacity. Density is modest.
note: SiC DRAM with long retention shown in 1990s; poor density and SiC interface traps limit it.

title: No silicon wafer: laser-lift-off memory foils laminated onto packages
idea: Forced limit: no thick substrate. Oxide-TFT memory tiers are built on polyimide on a reusable glass carrier, released with flexible-OLED laser lift-off, and laminated as micron-thin memory foils onto logic packages.
why: Uses the large flexible-OLED LLO base. The carrier is reused, and thin foils stack without TSVs, avoiding the HBM TSV tax.

title: No silicon wafer: all-on-glass LTPO memory with LTPS periphery
idea: Forced limit: periphery cannot sit on a Si wafer. Laser-crystallized LTPS CMOS forms decoders and sense amps, and IGZO forms the low-leakage storage cells, all on one glass sheet with the LTPO process phones already use.
why: A complete memory chip with no wafer; reuses LTPO capacity at display makers, and the low-leakage cells allow long refresh intervals.
note: Full chip on glass removes Si, but density and LTPS periphery speed limit it.

title: Row-RAID: in-bank XOR parity rows built by triple-row activation
idea: For read-mostly regions (weights, and KV after it is written), the controller issues in-DRAM bulk-bitwise sequences that accumulate one parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray. These are Ambit-style triple-row activation for AND/OR plus a dual-contact-cell NOT, composed into XOR. Group membership is interleaved so physically adjacent rows (the +/-1 and +/-2 victims of any aggressor) fall in different groups. Per-line ECC (on-die SEC or B4-01's BCH) detects a damaged row. The controller then XORs the other 31 rows and the parity inside the subarray and writes the reconstruction back. A write to a protected row updates parity with two in-DRAM XORs (old ^ new).
why: Row-hammer and weak-row tolerance for read-mostly data at ~3% capacity, instead of PRAC's <13% performance overhead today and up to 94% for future chips. Any single row per group may lose all its bits.

title: Swap voltage-amplitude sensing for time-to-digital bitline sensing
idea: Substitute the voltage-amplitude latch with a time-domain sensor: the shared bitline charge sets the bias of a current-starved delay cell, and one 8-way time-to-digital arbiter shared by 8 bitline pairs decides which edge arrives first. Signal margin becomes picoseconds of delay instead of millivolts on a latch.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): pitch-matched latches shrink about 4x because the TDC sits off-pitch and is shared; tolerates 30-40% lower bitline swing, easing the Cs charge wall (fact 1).

title: Substitute rutile TiO2 on MoO2 electrodes for zirconia capacitor stacks
idea: Replace ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor dielectric with ALD rutile TiO2 templated below 400 C by a lattice-matched MoO2 bottom electrode (instead of scarce RuO2), with Al doping and a thin Al2O3 interlayer to suppress leakage.
why: Rutile k ~80-100 hits the k~70 target from the capacitor charge wall without going to AR 115; ~1.5x Cs at today's AR using only Ti, Mo and Al, removing Zr/Hf dependence.
note: Rutile templating known (RuO2); TiO2 leakage from ~3 eV gap is the doubt.

title: Substitute zinc-tin oxide for indium-gallium oxide in gain cells
idea: Build 2T gain cells with amorphous Zn-Sn-O (or Si-doped ZTO) channels by ALD, controlling oxygen vacancies with N2O plasma and Al2O3 capping to reach ~1e-19 A/um off-current.
why: Keeps the ultra-low-leakage, near-refresh-free benefit of oxide gain cells while removing indium (China-dominated refining) and gallium (China ~98%), the scarce elements in IGZO.

title: Swap word-granularity tiering for bit-plane significance tiering
idea: Substitute the word with the bit-plane as the unit of placement. Tensors are stored transposed into bit-planes: the memory controller keeps the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes in DRAM and the low-order planes in CXL flash. Kernels compute first on the coarse planes and fetch low planes only for rows where an error-bound or confidence check fails.
why: Most ML reads need only 4-6 of 16 bits. Full values stay recoverable while DRAM-resident bits drop 2-3x for weights and activations, which improves cost per bit and energy per useful bit.

title: Magnet-aligned nickel-chain film replaces solder microbumps
idea: Substitute microbumps with an anisotropic conductive film whose nickel microspheres are pulled into vertical columns by a permanent magnet during cure, conducting only vertically at 15-20 um pitch; a hot press and a magnet are the whole bonding line.
why: Capital and process: no bumping or reflow line, so a small team can build wide-IO memory-on-logic assemblies cheaply.

title: Projector micromirror chips switch light between memory and hosts
idea: Substitute the electrical CXL switch with a free-space optical crossbar built from a commodity DLP micromirror array that steers fiber-collimated beams between memory sleds and servers; kHz reconfiguration is enough for circuit-switched memory pooling.
why: Utilization: memory reassignable across 32-64 hosts over passive, low-energy optical paths built from cheap consumer parts.

title: Liquid-metal micro-wells make chiplet memory reworkable
idea: Substitute solder joints with laser-etched micro-wells in the substrate filled with gallium-indium alloy over a nickel barrier; die pillars plunge into the wells for contact, and a failed memory die lifts out cold and is replaced.
why: Yield and cost: rework instead of scrapping multi-die packages, run with dispensing and lamination equipment a small team owns.
note: Ga alloys attack metals; reliability of liquid contacts doubtful.

title: Substitute refresh for retention-noise-aware model training on mantissa planes
idea: Store AI weights bit-sliced so sign/exponent bits sit in normally refreshed rows and low mantissa bits sit in never-refreshed 'leaky planes'; models are fine-tuned with injected DRAM-decay noise matching measured retention statistics so accuracy holds with mantissa bits decaying.
why: Refresh energy and density (facts 1,3): ~50% of weight bits need no refresh and can use cheaper, smaller-capacitor cells, cutting effective cost per weight-bit ~25-35%.

title: Substitute TSVs with inductive coupling coils for die stacking
idea: Swap through-silicon vias for on-chip inductor coils patterned in BEOL at <=400 C, giving TSV-free wireless die-to-die links (ThruChip-style) so ordinary thinned DRAM dies can be stacked by any packager.
why: Removes the TSV keep-out area and process (HBM ~3x area per bit) and saves ~10-20% of die area per stacked bit.
note: ThruChip known; power delivery still needs vias, so TSVs not eliminated.

title: Predecoder XOR key rotates the row map each epoch
idea: Add a 16-bit XOR stage to the row predecoder whose key is re-randomized every refresh window, migrating data row by row during the refresh walk that already reads and restores every row, so an attacker's physical neighbors change unpredictably and hammer counts never accumulate on fixed victims.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): defeats targeted ~1k-activation attacks without large counter tables; a gates-only change any old node can build.

title: Registering clock driver stores weak-row map, targets refresh
idea: Load a per-row retention profile (from test or in-field scrubbing) into a small SRAM in the DIMM's registering clock driver, which is already a trailing-node chip; it lowers auto-refresh frequency and inserts targeted ACT/PRE refreshes only for the ~0.1% weak rows.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~3-4x fewer refresh operations, reclaiming ~10% bandwidth and ~20% idle power on DDR5 modules without changing the DRAM die.
note: RAIDR-style; VRT makes static weak-row maps unreliable.

title: Antiferroelectric zirconia biased near its field-induced transition boosts charge
idea: Combine paraelectric storage with antiferroelectric switching (zero added masks): tune ALD ZrO2 thickness and Si/Al doping so its tetragonal phase sits just below the field-induced polar transition at the storage voltage, giving an effective k ~50-60 across the operating window.
why: ~1.5x stored charge per capacitor without higher aspect ratio or hafnium, or equal charge at lower VARY (CV2 energy).
note: Morphotropic-boundary HZO/ZrO2 for DRAM k boost is widely pursued.

title: Anodized aluminum oxide film as litho-free vertical interconnect interposer
idea: Combine cookware-style anodization with z-axis interconnect: anodize a 50-100 um aluminum sheet into a rigid self-ordered nanopore template (~10^9 pores/cm2), electroplate Cu into every pore and polish both faces, giving a ceramic film that conducts only vertically and connects any pad above to the pad below with no lithography or plasma.
why: Interposer capital and alignment: wet-only, rare-gas-free memory-on-logic interposer, pitch-agnostic so placement tolerance relaxes; ~10x cheaper than TSV interposers.
note: Cu-filled AAO anisotropic conductors already studied.

title: Phone e-waste LPDDR harvest reballed into LPCAMM modules
idea: Fuse an e-waste smartphone/laptop dismantling line with an automated package-rework cell. It hot-air-removes LPDDR4X/5 packages, laser-cleans and reballs them, tests each package on a socketed ATE, and mounts bins of matched speed onto new LPCAMM or soldered edge-device boards.
why: Recovers 4-16 GB per scrapped premium phone (billions in the waste stream) as new-equivalent supply for edge and IoT devices. Cost per bit is about 30-50% of new and needs zero fab capital.

title: Keyboard snap-dome physics as a contactless bistable nanobeam bit
idea: Keyboard snap-domes and pressure-relief discs use buckled shells with two stable states. Adapt this as a pre-stressed silicon-nitride nanobeam per bit that snaps up or down under electrostatic pulses and is read without contact through piezoresistive strain or a MOS gate underneath.
why: No capacitor, no leakage path and no refresh, using only Si and SiN (no Hf, W or In). A contactless snap avoids stiction, so endurance could exceed 1e15, and GHz-scale nanobeams switch in ~1-10 ns.
note: Buckled-beam NEMS bits known; DRAM-class density unlikely.

title: Gas-storage MOF chemistry: zinc-imidazolate vapor-deposited photoresist
idea: Borrow zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIF-8) from gas separation: grow the resist by vapor-phase conversion of an ALD ZnO film into ZIF-8 (Zn, C, H, N), which decomposes under EUV, DUV or e-beam and develops in vapor, replacing Sn-, Hf- or Zr-based metal-oxide EUV resists and spin tracks.
why: EUV throughput (fact 4): Zn absorbs EUV far better than organic resists, so lower dose and more wafers per scanner-hour; solvent-free conformal coating; no Hf.

title: Pre-printed forms: frozen base weights, only adapters live in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from pre-printed forms where only the handwritten fields vary: models are split into a frozen base held in non-volatile storage and per-tenant low-rank adapters plus normalization deltas (a few MB each) held in on-die SRAM; the scheduler batches requests by adapter so mutable state never exceeds SRAM.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving needs no DRAM for per-tenant weights and no refresh; 100+ tenants per accelerator instead of one full copy each.
note: S-LoRA/Punica known; base weights still need bandwidth from NV.

title: Double-entry ledgers: derive state from an append-only NVM journal
idea: Borrowed from accounting, where balances are derived from an immutable journal: services keep only an append-only event log in non-volatile memory and compute derived views (indexes, aggregates, session state) on demand into SRAM scratch, caching only results whose reuse distance is under a millisecond.
why: Eliminates large DRAM-resident materialized views and session caches in transactional systems; no long-lived volatile state, so zero refresh power.

title: Humbucker twin-cell mode on commodity DRAM for critical data
idea: Adapted from humbucking guitar pickups that pair two opposite-polarity coils to cancel hum: the controller uses the simultaneous multi-row activation already demonstrated on off-the-shelf DDR chips to write a row and its complement into a paired row on the opposite bitline side, so the sense amp sees a differential signal; critical pages (kernel, page tables, keys) run in this twin mode at half capacity.
why: Retention and row hammer (facts 3, 9): differential twin cells give ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance rejection, potentially extending retention 10x+ and resisting hammering for the few percent of memory that needs it, with no new silicon.

title: Cybersecurity honeypots: decoy rows tripwire hammering in real time
idea: Adapted from honeypots and canary tokens in network security: the OS seeds each bank with decoy pages holding known patterns physically adjacent to rows owned by untrusted tenants; a high-rate scrubber reads only the decoys, and any flip in a decoy pinpoints the aggressor rows for migration and tenant throttling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): deterministic detection on existing DRAM without counters, spending ~1% capacity on decoys and focusing scrub bandwidth on <1% of rows.

title: Lithium-niobate domain-wall conduction bit on purchased LNOI wafers
idea: MINIFY the readout to a domain wall: on commercial thin-film lithium-niobate-on-insulator, a ~1-2 V pulse between surface electrodes nucleates a nanoscale inverted domain whose charged walls conduct ~nA; read non-destructively at sub-coercive voltage, erased by reverse pulse. Needs only a stepper, metal lift-off and an etcher.
why: Non-destructive read (fact 8), nonvolatile so no refresh (fact 3), LN wall cells have shown >1e10 cycles; minimal tooling.

title: Leaky floating gate with direct-tunneling oxide for unlimited writes
idea: MINIFY the tunnel oxide to ~2.5 nm so writes use direct tunneling at ~2 V in ~10 ns instead of damaging Fowler-Nordheim injection, accepting seconds-to-hours retention; a 10-person team runs it on a 180-nm university or MPW-compatible flow with a poly floating gate.
why: Quasi-volatile memory refreshed ~1000x less than DRAM (fact 3), capacitor-free (fact 1), endurance >1e12 because direct-tunnel stress is low; U.S. mature-node manufacturable.

title: Self-boosting MOS varactor capacitor doubles read charge
idea: MAGNIFY the signal with a nonlinear capacitor: the storage capacitor is a MOS varactor whose inversion threshold sits between the '0' and '1' levels, so a stored '1' is in high-capacitance inversion and a '0' in low-capacitance depletion; a plate pulse at read delivers ~2-3x the bitline charge difference of a linear capacitor of equal area.
why: Smaller capacitor for the same sense margin (fact 1) in any mature foundry eDRAM; smaller CV2 swing.

title: Magnify capacitor sidewall area 2.5x with corrugated superlattice mold
idea: Deposit the capacitor mold as an alternating SiN/SiO2 (or Si/SiGe) superlattice, etch the hole, then selectively recess every other layer, so the pillar sidewall becomes a corrugated bellows that the ALD electrode and dielectric coat conformally.
why: Charge wall: about 2.5x more electrode area, and so Cs, at the same AR of 60-75. This could avoid the jump to AR 115.
note: Little room for corrugation in ~30 nm holes; 2.5x optimistic.

title: Minify sense-amp offset by trimming each amp after fab
idea: Add a fuse- or antifuse-programmed binary capacitor trim to every sense-amp pair, set during wafer test, to cancel measured offset below 5 mV. Prove it on a 28 nm MPW and license to second-tier DRAM makers.
why: Charge wall: smaller offset allows about 30% smaller Cs or lower VARY. The IP plus test chip fits in $1M.
note: Offset-cancelling SAs in production; per-SA trim caps don't fit at pitch.

title: Magnify bus width 8x on a cheap glass interposer
idea: Place four bare commodity LPDDR dies side by side on a panel-made glass interposer with 2 um lines, giving a 1024-bit bus to an FPGA or ASIC without TSVs or a silicon interposer, built through glass-panel vendors for about $300k.
why: HBM TSV tax: HBM-like bandwidth from LPDDR bits, without HBM's 3x wafer area per bit or stack yield loss.
note: Commodity LPDDR dies cannot supply a 1024-bit bus.

title: Helium-free chucks using liquid-metal backside contact
idea: Minify helium use to zero: replace helium backside cooling in etch and deposition chucks with a thin gallium-alloy film or compliant metal pads that conduct heat to the wafer.
why: Scarce resource: helium supply (Qatar ~30%, offline) currently gates fab output; removes a chokepoint for every wafer step.

title: One microcontact stamp sets surface energy for every ink
idea: Minify patterning to a single microcontact-printed self-assembled monolayer pattern; every following functional ink is blade-coated and de-wets into the matching wells by surface energy, self-aligned across layers.
why: Process steps and alignment: one stamp replaces several print-align steps, and cuts material waste by >90%.

title: Electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 ink for low-leakage access devices
idea: Magnify off-state resistance by printing electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 nanosheet inks (1.8 eV gap) as the access transistor channel, so leakage is low enough for long retention.
why: Refresh: wide-bandgap printed channels cut leakage far below the 13 fA tail, stretching refresh intervals on cheap printed arrays.

title: Rolling film masks printed for pennies
idea: Minify mask cost from ~$300k to under $100 by roll-printing flexible photomasks and using rolling near-field contact lithography to pattern non-critical DRAM layers.
why: Masks: disposable printed masks for periphery and BEOL layers cut mask-set spend and lead time.

title: Elastomer micro-socket for HBM on the interposer
idea: MINIFY socket pitch to ~100 um with an anisotropic conductive elastomer, so HBM stacks are clamped (not soldered) onto the interposer and can be swapped in the field.
why: HBM yield and lifetime: a bad stack no longer scraps a ~$30k accelerator; failed stacks go back for repair and reuse.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: re-mateable room-temperature interconnects
idea: MINIFY bonding heat to zero: dense interdigitated Cu nanowire arrays on both faces interlock at room temperature like nano-velcro, giving electrical contact that can be pulled apart and re-mated several times.
why: Removes solder and tin and allows rework of memory chiplets; claims ~20 um pitch with 5+ re-mating cycles.

title: Eliminate indium and gallium: zinc-tin-silicon oxide channels for gain cells
idea: Replace IGZO with amorphous Zn-Sn-Si-O deposited by ALD or sputtering: Si binds oxygen and suppresses vacancies for a very low off-current, while Sn 5s orbitals carry ~15-20 cm2/Vs mobility, all from widely mined elements.
why: China holds ~98% of primary gallium under export controls and indium is a concentrated zinc by-product; this de-risks every oxide-semiconductor DRAM path at no loss in leakage.

title: Eliminate resist and etch: imprinted inhibitor molecules steer area-selective ALD
idea: Nanoimprint a monolayer of ALD-inhibitor molecules (e.g., alkylsilane SAMs) in the negative pattern, then grow the film only where it is uninhibited, so the layer is patterned additively in one deposition with no resist coat, exposure, develop, etch or strip.
why: Collapses a ~5-tool, 8-12 step patterning loop into 2 steps for semi-critical layers; applied to ~15 layers it trims fab tool count ~10% and cuts chemistry and water per layer.
note: Microcontact-printed inhibitor ASD is known art.

title: Eliminate stored weights: regenerate weight blocks from PRNG seeds
idea: Each weight block is replaced by a seed plus 4-8 coefficients that combine LFSR-generated pseudo-random basis vectors; banks of on-chip LFSRs regenerate the block at use time, so DRAM holds only seeds and coefficients.
why: 3-5x weight compression with no DRAM bandwidth for the regenerated part; attacks capacity and data-movement energy.
note: SeedLM (2024) known; accuracy at 3-5x uncertain.

title: Eliminate object headers and pointers by compiling graphs into arenas
idea: A compiler pass converts pointer-linked object graphs into struct-of-arrays arenas addressed by implicit 32-bit indices, deleting per-object headers, 64-bit pointers and alignment padding.
why: Pointer-heavy heaps shrink 30-50%, and denser arrays also cut cache-line overfetch.

title: No-TSV shingled staircase stack with printed edge ramps
idea: Eliminate TSVs: offset each DRAM die ~200 um like roof shingles so every die exposes a ledge of fine-pitch pads, then plate or aerosol-jet-print copper 'ramps' down the stairs to the base die at 10-20 um pitch, using several ledge rows for a 1024-bit bus. No via etch, no via reveal, no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% yield loss): recovers the ~10-15% of die area spent on TSV arrays and keep-out, removes via-reveal steps and their yield loss; claimed ~20-30% lower HBM cost/bit.

title: Imprint as a feature: work-function-biased antiferroelectric bistable cell
idea: Reverse a reliability defect into the design: asymmetric electrodes (~1 eV work-function gap) or a fixed dipole layer around antiferroelectric ZrO2 shift one of its double-hysteresis loops to straddle 0 V, making the AFE bistable at zero bias while keeping AFE's high endurance (no FE domain pinning, target >1e15 cycles).
why: Refresh and voltage floor (facts 3,10): nonvolatile zero-bias storage written at ~1 V by a field-induced transition, removing refresh energy.

title: Voltage strains a magnet: PZT-Galfenol magnetoelectric bit
idea: Reverse magnetics' write path from current to voltage: a 180 nm elliptical Galfenol (FeGa, U.S. Navy 1998, rare-earth-free) nanomagnet on a PZT film is strained by a ~1 V pulse that rotates its easy axis and toggles magnetization, read non-destructively by a GMR stack.
why: Write energy and refresh (facts 3,10): ~fJ current-free writes, nonvolatile, all from 1990s sputtering, PZT and GMR-head processes with no rare earths; risk is deterministic 180-degree switching.
note: Straintronics known; 180-degree deterministic switching and 180 nm density limit it.

title: Shadow deposition: existing topography replaces the next mask
idea: Reverse etch-to-define into deposit-to-define: tilt the wafer and evaporate or sputter at grazing angles so the tall lines already on the wafer shadow precise gaps, forming self-aligned contacts and gate offsets with no litho step.
why: Replaces 1-2 critical DUV/EUV layers with a cheap directional deposition tool; overlay errors go to zero because shadowing is self-aligned.

title: Rotate the stack: film thickness becomes linewidth
idea: Rearrange the axes: deposit a 100-layer superlattice of alternating conductor/dielectric films with atomic-scale thickness control, then slice it and bond it on its side so each film edge becomes a 5-15 nm line on the new surface.
why: Sub-10 nm periodic lines without any lithography; line pitch is set by ALD/epitaxy thickness with angstrom precision.
note: SNAP-style edge patterning known; limited to um-wide patches.

title: Test in the field: ship lightly tested dies, repair at boot
idea: Rearrange where testing happens: cut wafer and package test time ~70%. In-system BIST, post-package-repair fuses and runtime ECC telemetry then find and repair weak cells at first boot and over the product's life.
why: Testers are a capacity bottleneck and a large cost. Moving test into the field frees tester capacity and raises output ~5-10%.

title: Cryogenic helium bank filled from the fab's own exhaust
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: pipe He-bearing exhaust from leak-check stations, load locks and chuck fore-lines into a header, upgrade it with a polymer membrane, and adsorb it on activated carbon chilled by the fab's existing LN2. The fab builds a 3-6 month He buffer and releases it during supply shocks.
why: Turns helium from a just-in-time import into a buffered resource that is ~70-90% recycled, so wafer starts are insulated from events like the Qatar outage.
note: Activated carbon at 77 K adsorbs little helium; storage needs compression instead.

title: Self-oxidized TiN skin seeds rutile titania capacitor dielectric
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: oxidize the top 1-2 nm of the TiN bottom electrode with a controlled O3/plasma pulse into rutile TiO2 that serves as its own template, then grow Al-doped TiO2 by ALD so it crystallizes as rutile (k ~80). The whole stack is Ti, Al, N and O.
why: Breaks the 'smaller cell but more charge' contradiction without Ru templates or Hf/Zr. k ~2x ZAZ gives ~2x Cs, or the pillar aspect ratio can fall from ~70:1 to ~40:1.

title: Single aluminum film anodized into lines and dielectric together
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: deposit one blanket Al film and convert the spaces between future lines into anodic Al2O3 by through-mask electrochemical anodization. One material then serves as wire, via, dielectric and pad, with no metal etch and no damascene CMP.
why: Removes Ta/TaN barriers, Co liners, W vias and Cu plating from DRAM's relaxed-pitch upper metal layers, along with several etch/CMP tools. Uses only Al, O, Ti and N.

title: Conducting domain-wall memory in lithium-niobate-on-insulator wafers
idea: TRIZ #32 Changing properties: in thin-film LiNbO3 (made by smart-cut for photonic modulators) a voltage pulse writes a nanodomain whose inclined wall conducts while the bulk insulates; reading measures wall current non-destructively and the domain persists without power.
why: Zero refresh and non-destructive read (no restore energy, cf. fact 8); a planar two-electrode cell patterned by DUV in a dedicated back end reuses the LNOI photonics supply chain, with 1e10-class endurance reported (facts 3, 4).
note: Known research; high write voltage, 1e10 endurance.

title: Three nested codes sized to relax cell BER to 1e-6
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting (Matryoshka): inner on-die SEC per 128 bits fixes scattered bits, a middle cross-device symbol code per cache line fixes dead mats/chips, and an outer controller-side XOR erasure code across each 4 KB page group (invoked only on rare uncorrectables) rebuilds whole lines; budgets are co-designed so raw cell BER can be 1e-6 instead of ~1e-12.
why: A ~10^6x relaxed raw error target permits ~25-35% smaller Cs (attacks the 4.5-5.4 fF charge wall) or 4-8x longer refresh at ~15% total parity.

title: Rice-husk biogenic silica reduced magnesiothermically to polysilicon feedstock
idea: Rice and horsetail plants biomineralize nanoporous, low-metal silica. Acid-leach rice-husk ash to >99.9% SiO2, reduce it with magnesium at ~650 C (recycling the MgO electrolytically) and refine it by the Siemens or FBR route, replacing carbothermic reduction of quartzite in arc furnaces.
why: Uses an agricultural waste (US rice states produce millions of tonnes of husk) as silicon feedstock, cutting metallurgical-silicon energy ~50% and avoiding concentrated quartzite and silicon-metal supply.

title: Mushroom-body sparse wide access hides slow printed cells
idea: Insect mushroom bodies get fast recall from ~200k slow Kenyon cells through sparse, very wide parallel coding. Organize printed memory sheets as 64k-bit-wide rows read at once into an on-silicon SRAM landing buffer with prefetch, so ~1 us printed cells supply the bandwidth while the SRAM serves 10-100 ns hits.
why: This architecture lets abundant printed memory do DRAM's job for streaming and AI-weight workloads without fab capital, EUV or Cz wafers.

title: Gecko-setae thermal pads replace helium backside wafer cooling
idea: Gecko feet make intimate contact through millions of compliant setae. Hot-emboss roll-to-roll a replaceable chuck-top film of copper-flake-filled polyimide micro-pillars that conform to the wafer backside under electrostatic clamping and carry heat by solid contact instead of helium gas.
why: Eliminates helium backside cooling in etch and CVD, one of the biggest fab helium uses, with pads made by the kilometre as cheap consumables.

title: Pea-pod DIMMs with socketed packages replaced one at a time
idea: Like peas pulled from a pod, DRAM packages sit in low-profile LGA micro-sockets on the module, so one failing package is swapped in minutes and firmware remaps its range, instead of scrapping a 64-128 GB DIMM for one bad chip.
why: Repair: cuts DIMM scrap by ~80%, shrinking replacement DRAM demand.

title: Magnetosome chains: field-aligned nanoparticle vias without drilling
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria line magnetite crystals into chains. Here a polymer underfill loaded with gold-shelled Ni/Fe3O4 nanoparticles is cured under a vertical magnetic field, so the particles self-assemble into conductive columns at 1-3 um pitch between stacked dies, with no TSV etch, no microbump and no fine-pitch alignment.
why: Capital intensity and TSV tax (fact 6): removes deep-etch and bumping steps; aims at ~10x denser vertical I/O than microbumps at a fraction of hybrid-bonding tool cost.

title: Osteoclast lines: robotic die harvesting and repackaging of retired DRAM
idea: Bone is continuously dissolved by osteoclasts and rebuilt from the same minerals. Automated lines de-solder retired modules, laser-debond packages, retest bare dies at probe level, and re-bond known-good dies onto new substrates as warrantied modules.
why: New-module supply at ~10-20% of the cost of fresh bits, using no wafers, helium or EUV (capital intensity, scarce resources).

title: Soma floating-body cells on domestic FD-SOI lines
