idea: A neuron's soma integrates charge in its body. Capacitorless floating-body cells store holes in the thin SOI body and hold them with FD-SOI back-gate bias, made in existing U.S. 22 nm FD-SOI capacity.
why: 1T cell at ~4-6F2 with no capacitor module, on domestic lines (U.S. manufacturability, capital).

title: CMOS image-sensor pinned photodiode as a near-zero-dark-current storage well
idea: Copy the 4T image-sensor pixel: hold the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, moved in and out through a transfer gate with complete charge transfer, so the stored charge never touches the Si/SiO2 interface where SRH generation lives. Image sensors routinely reach <1 e-/s dark current per pixel (~1e-19 A) versus the ~13 fA DRAM leakage tail.
why: Fact 3 refresh: leakage 3-5 orders lower stretches retention from 64 ms to minutes, removing most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh and 10-20% bandwidth loss; trade is a smaller full-well (~2-5k e- at 100 nm) that needs a more sensitive sense amp.

title: Pulse-power antiferroelectric capacitors: ZrO2 biased at its field-induced transition
idea: Pulse-power capacitors exploit antiferroelectric ceramics whose permittivity peaks at the AFE-to-FE transition; ALD a ZrO2-rich Hf(1-x)Zr(x)O2 film (x~0.7-0.9) and shift its transition field into the cell's 0-to-VARY window with asymmetric TiN/RuO2 electrodes (work-function offset plus interface dipoles), so operation rides the steep P-E segment where k_eff reaches ~60-100.
why: Fact 1: k~70 is exactly what stops AR growth, letting AR fall from ~70 to ~35:1 at 5 fF; provable with university ALD, sputter and RTA; hysteresis loss and fatigue near the transition are the risks.
note: ZrO2-rich MPB/AFE high-k widely explored; hysteresis and charge return limit.

title: Coral and stalagmite growth: VLS nanowire forests grown as capacitor electrodes
idea: Grow the electrode instead of etching it: place Al, Sn or Cu catalyst dots (CMOS-friendlier than gold) by dewetting or e-beam litho, grow 1-2-um vertical Si or SnO2 nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid growth in a university LPCVD furnace, where 100:1 aspect ratios come for free, then ALD-coat the dielectric and top electrode.
why: Fact 1: AR >=100:1 electrodes with no 70:1 plasma etch or its EUV-defined mask, removing the hardest capacitor process; nanowire leaning, collapse and catalyst contamination are the risks.

title: Drip irrigation: ground-precharged bitlines with sparsity-maximizing encoding
idea: Water only the plants that need it: precharge bitlines to 0 V instead of VDD/2 and store each 64-bit word in whichever polarity has fewer ones (plus a flag bit), paired with zero-skewed tensor formats, so only bitlines that read a 1 draw charge.
why: Bitline energy proportional to ones (facts 8, 10): with ReLU/quantized tensors at 5-15% ones after encoding, claims 5-10x lower bitline energy per access.

title: CZTS solar lesson: indium- and gallium-free oxide channels for gain cells
idea: Thin-film PV swapped scarce indium/gallium (CIGS) for earth-abundant Cu-Zn-Sn-S. Do the same for oxide-semiconductor gain cells and vertical 3D-DRAM access transistors: amorphous Zn-Sn-O or Si-doped SnO2 n-channels replace In-Ga-Zn-O, paired with p-type SnO or Cu2O for complementary gain cells.
why: Gallium is ~98% Chinese and export-controlled and indium is a China-dominated zinc by-product; this keeps oxide gain-cell ultra-low leakage and long retention while removing both chokepoints.

title: Kitchen microwave volumetric heating anneals capacitors at low thermal budget
idea: Microwave ovens heat the water in food rather than the oven walls. Use 2.45-5.8 GHz variable-frequency microwave annealing that couples selectively into doped silicon and ZrO2 dipoles to activate junctions and crystallize the tetragonal high-k phase at a substrate temperature ~150-200 C lower than RTP or furnace, with no change to the DDR/HBM die interface.
why: Preserves TiN/high-k interfaces (higher k, lower leakage) and abrupt junctions (less GIDL), cutting thermal-process energy ~50% and enabling higher Cs from existing materials.

title: Shingled-roof staircase stack with aerosol-printed silver wires
idea: Offset dies like roof shingles so each die's pad row is exposed on a staircase. Then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the steps and sinter them at ~200 C, replacing both TSVs and wirebonds.
why: TSV-free stacking at low capex. Printed 10-20 um lines give far more connections than wirebonds and avoid TSV yield loss, which suits capacity-tier memory.

title: Goto parametron revived as phase-bistable NEMS resonator bits
idea: Goto's 1954 parametron stored a bit as the 0 or pi phase of an oscillator pumped at twice its frequency. Use arrays of ~1 GHz AlScN or SiN NEMS beams pumped by a shared 2 GHz line; a bit is the vibration phase, written by a small seed pulse, read by phase-sensitive piezo detection, and majority-voted in place.
why: Holding set by mechanical Q, not junction leakage, so no leakage tail (Fact 3); a shared pump replaces per-row refresh; in-place majority logic trims data movement (Fact 5); needs <1 fW pump per bit.
note: Mahboob/Yamaguchi NEMS parametron memory precedent; pump power and density vs DRAM unclear.

title: Hitachi single-electron polysilicon memory revived on 130-nm lines
idea: Hitachi's 1990s Yano memory stored a few electrons in a polysilicon nanograin that gated a percolation channel. Reproduce it with 3-nm poly-Si or Si-nanocrystal films on existing 130/90-nm lines, where ~10 stored electrons shift the channel threshold enough to read in a 1T gain structure.
why: Few-electron storage removes the capacitor wall (Fact 1) and the Coulomb-blockade barrier extends retention to seconds or more (Fact 3); the storage grain self-assembles, so old-node litho suffices.

title: 1968 zinc-oxide TFT revived as indium- and gallium-free access device
idea: Revive Boesen and Jacobs' 1968 ZnO thin-film transistor with modern ALD: an amorphized nitrogen/Mg-alloyed ZnO channel, using zinc from Alaska and Tennessee, forms BEOL access transistors with ultralow off-current from its 3.3 eV gap. It avoids IGZO's indium and gallium, both refined mostly abroad.
why: Oxide-semiconductor-level leakage gives multi-second retention (fact 3), with an all-U.S. element supply and BEOL stacking (fact 2).
note: ZnO/ZnSnO TFTs well studied; supply-chain angle only.

title: Si-only Esaki tunnel-diode latch replaces the DRAM capacitor
idea: Revive TI's 1990s tunneling SRAM, descended from Esaki's 1957 diode: stack two delta-doped, silicon-only interband tunnel diodes (no germanium) on the storage node of a single access transistor. The negative-differential-resistance pair latches the node at two stable voltages, giving a static cell with pA-level standby current and no capacitor.
why: Removes the high-aspect-ratio capacitor (fact 1), its ZrO2/HfO2 and its TiN/W electrodes, and refresh (fact 3); claims a static cell with a 1T footprint of ~8F2.
note: Si ITD peak-to-valley ratio and valley current limit standby and margins.

title: Adiabatic resonant wordline drivers recycle charge, reviving 1990s reversible computing
idea: Revive 1990s adiabatic switching (Younis/Knight) for DRAM periphery: drive wordlines and plate lines from shared on-die LC tanks with slow sinusoidal ramps, so each activation's charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers 50-70% of the 3 V wordline CV2 energy, and energy is a scarce data-center resource; needs no new materials.

title: Intel 1103 three-transistor cell rebuilt in indium-free zinc-tin oxide
idea: Revive the 1970 Intel 1103 3T dynamic cell in BEOL-stacked amorphous zinc-tin-oxide transistors, with no indium and no gallium. The wide bandgap gives ultra-low off-current, so the gate node holds charge for seconds and the gain transistor reads it non-destructively.
why: The prior work's IGZO depends on indium and gallium, both concentrated in China, while ZTO uses Zn and Sn; the gain read removes the capacitor (fact 1), slashes refresh (fact 3) and stacks over the periphery (fact 7).

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops DRAM dielets into glass interposers
idea: Revive Alien Technology's 1990s fluidic self-assembly, where shaped micro-chips in a slurry settle into matching wells: dice DRAM into ~0.3 mm keyed trapezoidal dielets that self-orient into wells on a large glass interposer next to an accelerator, then wire them with one panel RDL layer. Thousands of dielets assemble in seconds without pick-and-place or TSV stacking.
why: Fact 6 and capital: replaces HBM's TSV stack (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) with planar known-good dielets at ~10 um RDL pitch; an assembly bath costs <$1M versus $50M+ hybrid-bonding lines.

title: Self-rolling nanomembrane Swiss-roll capacitors on polymer foil
idea: Invert 'a 3D capacitor must be etched deep into a substrate' -> deposit it flat and let strain roll it up. A strained bilayer (SiNx stress layer plus TiN/HfZrO/TiN stack) patterned on a sacrificial polymer releases and curls into a 5-10 turn micro-tube, multiplying electrode area 10-20x per footprint; whole arrays roll in parallel on polyimide or glass.
why: Reaches fact-1 capacitance from planar deposition plus one release step (EUV-free, low capex) on any substrate; roll diameters below ~200 nm are hard, so it suits a cheap capacity tier.

title: Superconducting nanowire-loop memory with single-flux-quantum sensing
idea: Inverting 'memory sensing is analog voltage at room temperature': bits are clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent currents in kinetic-inductance nanowire loops at 4 K, read by a single-flux-quantum comparator that switches only for one current direction, for cryogenic AI and quantum-control racks.
why: Read energy ~1e-18 J with no leakage and no refresh; periphery in SFQ logic. Density and cooling cost make it speculative.

title: Rutile TiO2 on MoO2 electrodes: k~90 without hafnium or ruthenium
idea: Inverts 'DRAM high-k must be ZrO2/HfO2 stacks on TiN or Ru': oxidize a molybdenum liner into a rutile MoO2 bottom electrode that templates low-temperature (<450 C) rutile TiO2 (k 80-110), with an Al-doped interfacial layer to suppress leakage.
why: Hits the k~70 requirement of the capacitor charge wall with Ti and US-mined Mo instead of Hf/Zr/Ru; ~2x capacitance at the same aspect ratio, or AR dropped from ~70:1 to ~40:1, cutting etch time and fluorocarbon gas use.

title: Proton shuttle in phosphosilicate glass: nanosecond nonvolatile resistor
idea: Inverts 'memory state is held by electrons': drive protons under strong short field pulses through a few-nm phosphorus-doped SiO2 electrolyte into and out of a MoO3 or TiO2 channel, changing its conductance 10-100x; the proton stays put without power.
why: Zero refresh; materials are Si, P, O, H and Mo/Ti (abundant, US-available), at BEOL temperatures so it can stack over logic.
note: Close to published PSG protonic resistors; endurance unknown.

title: Superlattice cleave-edge master stamps sub-20 nm DRAM lines
idea: Inverts 'line pitch comes from optics'. Grow a Si/SiGe or GaAs/AlGaAs superlattice by 1990s MBE, cleave and selectively etch its edge into a nanoimprint master whose line pitch equals layer thickness (~16-20 nm), then thermally imprint wordline/bitline gratings with a 1995-style imprint press, using a >=180 nm stepper only for coarse layers.
why: Sub-20 nm dense lines with zero EUV/ArF (fact 4); master replication makes a dense layer cost a few dollars.

title: Block copolymer turns 180 nm trenches into 12 nm lines
idea: Inverts 'every line must be exposed'. Spin PS-b-PMMA into 180 nm stepper-defined trenches (graphoepitaxy), anneal so it self-assembles into ~12 nm lamellae aligned to the walls, remove the PMMA and transfer by RIE, a ~15x pitch multiplication from a hot plate.
why: Bitline/wordline gratings at modern pitch with 1990s steppers; materials cost cents per wafer (fact 4).

title: Four-level cells read by time-to-threshold sensing
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM cell stores one binary bit'. Store four charge levels per large 180 nm-rule cell (~30 fF) and read by timing how long the bitline takes to cross a reference, with a ramp and counter shared per mat and reference cells rewritten each refresh to cancel leakage drift.
why: Doubles bits per mask step at fixed litho; big old-node capacitors give MLC the margin modern 5 fF cells lack (facts 1, 4).

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops keyed chiplets into substrate wells
idea: Invert 'chiplets must be placed by precision bonders': give memory and logic chiplets unique keyed shapes that settle into matching wells of a glass carrier in a liquid bath, with surface tension giving final alignment before batch bonding.
why: Removes dependence on imported high-precision bonders, assembling thousands of chiplets per minute on a low-capital U.S. line.
note: Shape-keyed FSA is Alien Technology/eLux prior art.

title: Tungsten-free BiSb topological spin-Hall write line for nanomagnet bits
idea: Write perpendicular nanomagnets with a BiSb topological-insulator line (spin Hall angle ~10) sputtered at <=250 C after the 350 C MTJ anneal, instead of W/Ta/Pt. The large spin Hall angle cuts the required current density ~10x.
why: ~10x lower SOT write energy and no tungsten (China ~80% chokepoint), in a fully BEOL-stackable magnetic bit.

title: Electrostatic pull-in hysteresis latch held at zero static current
idea: A sputtered TiAl nanobeam over a dielectric-capped electrode is bistable at any hold voltage between its release and pull-in voltages. A small up or down pulse sets the state, the capacitive hold draws no DC current, and the read senses the ~2x capacitance change; process is <=400 C BEOL MEMS.
why: Static storage held by electrostatics, with no leakage-driven refresh (fact 3), no capacitor charge requirement (fact 1) and no ohmic contact to wear. Dielectric charging and stiction are the risks.
note: Contact-mode NEMS memory known; dielectric charging and stiction limit endurance.

title: Time-domain sensing via bitline-starved delay elements
idea: Convert the tiny bitline difference into a delay difference: the true and complement bitlines each set the current of a starved inverter chain, and a digital arbiter decides which edge arrives first, with a vernier for extra resolution. The SA becomes digital logic that scales with logic nodes.
why: Periphery area and voltage (facts 7, 10): SA shrinks and runs at core voltage; delay averaging over several stages reduces offset ~sqrt(N).

title: Multi-height imprint stamp encodes all cell layers, zero web overlay
idea: Imprint one resist layer with a 4-5 level stamp whose heights encode gate, channel, via and capacitor patterns, then pattern each layer by successive etch-backs that expose the next height, so every level is self-aligned by the stamp itself.
why: First principles: PET expands ~20 ppm/C, so 1 C across a 30 cm web is ~6 um of misregistration, making overlay the true R2R density limit; encoding overlay in the stamp enables sub-um cells with one stamp instead of a mask set (fact 4).

title: Zig-zag folded printed sheet: continuous traces cross folds, no vias
idea: Print one long sheet of 64 array panels separated by fold lines, encapsulate the traces at the bending neutral plane, and accordion-fold it into a 64-tier stack whose tier buses run continuously across every fold.
why: Bending strain e=y/R vanishes at the neutral plane, so 12 um films can fold at ~50 um radius without cracking traces; 64 tiers (above the 26-tier break-even, fact 2) need zero vias, zero bonding and zero alignment steps.

title: Core-shell BaTiO3-alumina ink: printed high-k with leakage-blocking shells
idea: Formulate an ink of ~30 nm BaTiO3 nanoparticles each wrapped in a 2 nm Al2O3 shell, then print and compact a 60 nm dielectric, so high-k cores raise capacitance while continuous shells block grain-boundary leakage paths.
why: C=eA/d: a composite k of ~40-60 approaches the k~70 called for in fact 1 with a printable, low-temperature dielectric, letting foil cells shrink ~5x in area at equal charge.

title: Air-bridged interposer wires: vacuum dielectric cuts wire capacitance
idea: Wire capacitance per mm scales with permittivity, so oxide or polyimide (k 3-4) costs 3-4x the energy of vacuum. Build RDL lines over a sacrificial polymer and release it, leaving lines suspended on periodic posts in a sealed cavity like MEMS air bridges.
why: ~3x lower CV^2 for every interposer and chiplet bit, and faster lines allow lower swing (fact 5).
note: Air gaps known; long suspended RDL lines face mechanical reliability limits.

title: Drop array voltage to 0.6 V, buy margin with ECC
idea: Restore energy goes as CV^2, so the true optimum is minimum (restore + decode) energy, not zero raw errors. Run VARY at 0.6 V (2.8x less CV^2), accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced signal, and correct with a 2-error code in the base die.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~2x lower array and refresh energy.
note: Voltron-like voltage scaling.

title: Laser-decap and reball LPDDR die from discarded phones and laptops
idea: A GB of DRAM is ~42 mg of silicon whose value is entirely in its pattern, and discarded phones carry working LPDDR. Automated lines X-ray-locate PoP packages, laser-ablate mold compound, extract die, test them on a carrier, and rebuild them as fan-out packages for embedded, IoT and low-end PC markets.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2 billion phones/yr x 4-8 GB is several EB of DRAM entering e-waste (~20% of annual output); recovering 10% adds ~2% global supply with little capital.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly writes capacitor lattices with carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
idea: A symmetric diblock copolymer at its free-energy minimum forms hexagonal cylinders at a pitch set by chain length (~20-30 nm), exactly the storage-hole lattice. Guide PS-b-PMMA with a coarse DUV prepattern, harden it by sequential Al2O3 infiltration, and etch storage holes through the alumina mask.
why: Capital and EUV: replaces 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers with spin-coat and bake; defectivity must reach <0.01/cm^2 for full adoption.
note: DSA hole arrays long pursued; defectivity target is the blocker.

title: Sticky note: stiction itself becomes the bit in fluorine-free NEMS
idea: Stimulus 'sticky note' (sticks, peels, re-sticks) -> a TiN nano-cantilever is either stuck to its pad by van der Waals adhesion (1) or freed by a thermal-bimorph or repulsive electrostatic kick (0), read by contact current. MEMS normally fights stiction with fluorinated anti-stiction monolayers and releases with HF vapor or XeF2; here an amorphous-carbon sacrificial layer is ashed in O2 and stiction is the feature.
why: Zero-power nonvolatile mechanical bit with no leakage (fact 3), no capacitor (fact 1), stackable in BEOL (fact 2); no fluorinated release or coating chemistry.
note: Close to Nantero NRAM and TiN NEMS NVM; speed, density and contact wear limit DRAM use.

title: Rubik's cube: re-keyed permutation shuffles physical row neighbors
idea: Twist the cube so neighbours change: put a 3-round keyed Feistel shuffle on the 6 low row-address bits in front of each mat's decoder and re-key it incrementally, swapping one row pair per refresh command, so logically adjacent rows map to unpredictable physical neighbours that keep moving.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attackers cannot aim aggressors at a victim, removing most per-row counter area; cost is a few hundred gates per bank plus one row swap per refresh slot (~1% bandwidth).
note: Close to Randomized Row-Swap (RRS/SRS); hammering still flips physical neighbors.

title: Chess clock: time-domain race arbiter replaces voltage latch sense amp
idea: Turn voltage into time like a chess clock: the bitline and reference each set the current of a starved inverter discharging a node, and a mutual-exclusion arbiter (first press locks out the other) latches whichever crosses first before a restore driver writes back.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and SA area: delay gain turns ~20 mV into ~100 ps and keeps working at 0.5-0.6 V where cross-coupled latches fail; the arbiter is ~4 transistors plus 2 delay cells.

title: Velcro: press-fit nanowire forests make stacked memory dies reworkable
idea: Forced connection to hook-and-loop: grow 2 um Cu nanowire or CNT forests on both die faces at 10 um pad pitch, so dies interlock by room-temperature press-fit with low contact resistance. A die that fails stack test is pulled and replaced before the final anneal and underfill lock the stack.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) becomes rework: claim stack yield ~70% to ~95% and cost per HBM bit about -20%.
note: Nano-velcro Cu nanowire bonding is commercial (NanoWired); rework helps stack yield.

title: Pottery glaze: sol-gel synthetic silica lining on ordinary-quartz crucibles
idea: Stimulus 'pottery glaze' (a thin perfect layer on a rough pot) -> a 10-person shop sprays TEOS-derived sol-gel synthetic silica onto crucibles made from lower-grade, non-Spruce-Pine quartz and fuses it with a plasma torch into a bubble-free 1-2 mm inner liner.
why: Only the melt-contact layer needs ultra-high-purity quartz; a synthetic liner removes the Spruce Pine chokepoint for that layer at small capital.

title: Rice terraces: bevel-polish exposes all tiers for one-mask contacts
idea: Random stimulus 'rice terraces' -> instead of a 3D NAND-style staircase (many trim-etch loops) for a multi-tier ferroelectric or MRAM stack, a tilted-pad CMP or ion-beam bevel cuts a shallow ramp through all tiers at once, and every plate line is contacted on the ramp in a single lithography step.
why: For non-volatile 3D FeRAM and FeFET stacks, it replaces 10-30 staircase litho/trim cycles with one bevel plus one mask, cutting ~5-10% of wafer cost and much of the cycle time.

title: Piezo lighter: sputtered AlScN ferroelectric made in U.S. RF-filter fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'piezo lighter' -> ferroelectric AlScN (Pr >100 uC/cm2) is deposited by plain reactive sputtering at <400 C, as in the BAW filter fabs of U.S. RF companies. It is used as the storage element of 1T1C non-volatile cells, and its giant Pr gives enough signal charge from a planar, non-pillar capacitor.
why: Non-volatile. It eliminates the high-AR capacitor mold and the ALD tools (facts 1 and 4) and reuses U.S. RF sputter capacity. Endurance (~1e7 today) needs a DRAM cache front and materials work.
note: 1e7 endurance is far from DRAM; AlScN FeRAM is widely studied.

title: Bicycle gears: one ferroelectric capacitor shifts between DRAM mode and NV mode
idea: Random stimulus 'bicycle gears' -> a near-antiferroelectric HZO cell runs as a fast linear high-k (k~40) DRAM capacitor during operation, with unlimited endurance because the polarization does not switch. On a power-fail signal, a plate-line pulse shifts every row into remanent polarization, so the polarization flips only at power events.
why: Non-volatile when it matters and unlimited endurance in normal use. One capacitor module replaces separate DRAM plus NVDIMM/flash backup, and high k eases the charge wall (fact 1).
note: Close to Micron NVDRAM-style dual-mode hafnia; k gain minimal vs ZrO2.

title: Orrery: orbital-current torque in light metals replaces heavy-metal SOT lines
idea: Random stimulus 'orrery' (orbits drive the motion) -> SOT-MRAM write lines use the orbital Hall effect in abundant light metals (Ti, Cr or oxidized Cu), with a Ni-based conversion layer that turns orbital current into torque on the free layer. This replaces beta-tungsten, Pt or Ta spin-Hall lines.
why: Non-volatile SOT-MRAM keeps unlimited endurance (no barrier current) and sub-ns writes. It removes tungsten and PGM dependence, and lower-resistivity lines cut write energy and driver area.

title: Coral reef: electroless copper grows bonds between facing pads
idea: Like coral growing into a reef: dies are held with a 2-5 um gap over the substrate, and an electroless Cu bath grows metal from both pad faces until they fuse, giving room-temperature, pressure-free interconnects. University-cleanroom feasible.
why: Capital intensity and thermal damage; no bonders or anneals, and potentially reworkable before passivation.

title: Comb: R2R-made polyimide spring-probe sheets multiply DRAM test capacity
idea: Random stimulus 'hair comb' -> thousands of teeth in one cheap strip. Roll-to-roll photo-patterned polyimide/copper cantilever probe sheets replace $100k+ probe cards, so cheap test cells can run massively parallel retention and speed testing of KGD and salvaged die.
why: Test time and capital gate known-good-die and second-life supply; probe cost per site down ~20x and test throughput up several-fold.

title: Anodized-aluminum pore template capacitors with domestic hafnium and molybdenum
idea: Box = {medium: charge on ALD HfZrO in self-organized anodic alumina pores | access: vertical Si FET | sense: charge share | integration: 1T1C | substrate: U.S.-grown 300 mm Si (Texas) | fab: anodization (no lithography) + U.S.-built ALD tools}. Pores self-order at a pitch set by voltage (~40 nm at ~16 V) and are registered to the transistors by pre-indent dots from a U.S. multibeam e-beam writer; Hf and Zr come from Oregon zircon processing and Mo electrodes from Colorado.
why: Capital/EUV (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability: replaces EUV plus high-AR plasma etch for the capacitor layer with a wet electrochemical step at a fraction of the tool cost, and uses no tungsten.
note: AAO nanocapacitors known; long-range order and registration on 300 mm unproven.

title: Pinned-photodiode-style buried well storing 200 electrons, image-sensor readout
idea: Box = {medium: ~200 electrons in a buried n-well pinned by a p+ surface layer | access: transfer gate | sense: high-conversion-gain floating diffusion (~150 uV per electron) shared by 4 cells | integration: 4-shared cell like a CMOS image-sensor pixel | substrate: U.S. Si | fab: image-sensor implant flow on U.S. lines (e.g., Idaho)}. Surface pinning suppresses interface generation so dark current is a few electrons per second, and low-noise image-sensor readout resolves 200 electrons where DRAM stores ~15,000, so the well itself is the capacitor.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no stacked capacitor and refresh intervals of seconds, using domestic image-sensor process know-how.

title: Time-interleaved high-speed sense amp serves eight bitlines
idea: Box: stacked cap x Si access x ADC-style time interleaving x analog mux plus isolation x bulk Si x FinFET periphery. After charge sharing, eight bitlines are isolated and hold their signals on their own parasitic capacitance while one fast, well-matched SA resolves them in ~1 ns slots through an analog mux and restores each in turn.
why: SA count /8 and SA stripe -60%; one large matched SA also lowers offset.

title: Drop row-hammer counters; let flips land inside ECC budget
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x standard SA x no TRR or counter logic x bulk Si x standard. Target-row-refresh trackers and per-row activation counters are removed; a randomized background scrub plus the 1%-capable code absorb hammer flips, and a simple activation-rate cap keeps them under 0.1% of a codeword.
why: Periphery: row-hammer tracker SRAM and logic (growing as the threshold falls to ~1k) removed, with code margin as the defense.

title: Run DRAM hot at 105 C without double-rate refresh
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x temperature-aware soft SA x dense hot packaging x bulk Si x standard. The array may run at 105 C on base refresh; thermally accelerated leakage pushes raw BER up to ~1%, the code absorbs it, and packages can sit closer to accelerators.
why: Energy: removes refresh doubling and some cooling; tighter co-packaging cuts data-movement pJ/bit.

title: Antimony-tin-oxide electrodes template rutile TiO2 high-k capacitors
idea: Box [rutile TiO2 cap, k~90 | Si access | voltage SA | pillar stack | CZ Si | thermal ALD]: use ALD SnO2:Sb, which is conductive and rutile-structured, as the bottom electrode so ALD TiO2 crystallizes directly as rutile below 400 C instead of low-k anatase; a 0.5 nm Al2O3 interlayer at the top electrode suppresses leakage.
why: Capacitor charge wall (needs k~70) plus Hf/Zr/Ru intensity: k~90 vs ~40 lets aspect ratio fall from ~70:1 to ~35:1 at equal Cs, halving deep-etch time and fluorocarbon use, with no Ru (the usual rutile template) and no Hf.

title: Edge-printed sidewall interconnects replace TSVs in HBM stacks
idea: Box: standard DRAM die x standard access x standard sensing x die stack wired on its edge x thinned Si x aerosol-jet plus laser-sintered metallization on the polished stack face. Pads routed to die edges are exposed on one face of the stack and 5-10 um pitch vertical lines are printed down that face, with capacitive face-to-face coupling carrying the fastest lanes.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV etch, fill, reveal and keep-out zones that drive ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss; claims 20-40% HBM area back; risk is edge I/O density and signal integrity.

title: Reusable silicon-nitride nanostencils pattern memory layers resist-free
idea: Box: MIM charge x evaporated oxide TFT x standard sensing x 2D x any substrate x deposition through EBL+DRIE-made SiN membrane stencils. Metals, oxides and semiconductors are evaporated through aligned membrane apertures, skipping resist, develop, etch and strip, and the stencil is cleaned and reused hundreds of times.
why: Process steps and chemicals: 4-5 steps per layer collapse to one, suited to low-capex BEOL memory layers; risk is aperture clogging and edge blur below ~50 nm.

title: Molecular-ruler multilayers define 10 nm gaps between electrodes
idea: Box: oxide-node charge x lateral nanogap TFT x current sensing x 2D x Si x molecular-ruler lithography. Alternating phosphonate/metal-ion layers self-assemble on a parent electrode to a thickness counted in molecules (~1.5 nm per layer), a second metal is deposited and lifted off, and dissolving the ruler leaves a precise gap for a channel or dielectric.
why: Critical dimension from self-assembly count, not litho resolution (fact 4), with beakers, an evaporator and a contact aligner; risk is wafer-scale uniformity and ruler defects.
note: Published molecular-ruler technique; wafer uniformity doubtful.

title: Phone LPDDR harvested and rebuilt into LPCAMM2 modules
idea: Box[Source=retired flagship phones x Transform=separate discrete LPDDR5 packages, reball, retest x Integration=standard LPCAMM2 for laptops and edge servers x Owner=e-waste refurbisher]: billions of phones hold 8-16 GB of LPDDR; recover the discrete packages and assemble them into standard LPCAMM2 modules.
why: Large untapped reuse pool (an estimated multi-EB of LPDDR retired per year) feeding standard LPDDR5 interfaces.

title: Po photoresist from shrimp shells: water-developed chitosan resist
idea: Po: 'photoresist is made from seafood waste.' Extracted: use a chemically modified chitosan or cellulose resist with non-fluorinated photo-crosslinkers that develops in plain water, applied to the non-critical DRAM layers (implants, pads, periphery), which are the majority of mask steps.
why: PFAS (fluorinated PAGs and surfactants facing EU restriction) and TMAH developer removed from most litho steps; renewable feedstock; lighter wastewater load.

title: Po holes arrange themselves: anodic-alumina template with anodized-titanium dielectric
idea: Po: 'holes that arrange themselves.' Extracted: anodize a sputtered aluminum film so it self-organizes into a hexagonal array of 30-60 nm pores microns deep, sputter or CVD titanium into the pores and anodize it into a conformal TiO2 dielectric; the self-ordered pores give each 180 nm cell many sub-litho capacitor tubes.
why: Charge wall and litho-bound scaling: ~10-20x capacitor area per cell footprint without EUV, ALD or hafnium; aluminum and titanium are abundant and U.S.-produced.

title: Po transistors from solder metals: indium-gallium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain cells
idea: Po: 'the transistor is made from melted solder.' Extracted: RF-sputter amorphous zinc-tin oxide channels for 2T gain cells patterned with i-line/KrF tools at <=350 C, replacing IGZO's indium and gallium (gallium refining ~98% Chinese) with abundant zinc and tin while keeping very low off-current.
why: Scarce-resource intensity for oxide-semiconductor memory; low-temperature gain-cell layers can be stacked over 180 nm CMOS to add density without new litho.

title: Po energy is borrowed, never spent: resonant inductor wordline drivers
idea: Po: 'the memory borrows energy and gives it back.' Extracted: drive wordlines and bitline precharge from resonant LC tanks built with thick top-metal on-die inductors (easy in 180 nm aluminum processes), ramping lines slowly and returning their charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Voltage floor (CV2 stuck at ~1 V array and ~3 V wordline): 50-70% energy recovery on wordline and bitline swings; 180 nm thick-oxide devices handle the swings natively.

title: Masks grown from wafers: electroformed nickel imprint stamps
idea: Po: the mask is the product. Pattern one perfect array-layer wafer once (EUV or e-beam), electroform nickel replicas of its etched topography, and use the Ni shims (thousands per master, like CD stampers) as nanoimprint templates for the periodic capacitor and bitline layers on production wafers.
why: Litho capex and EUV dependence (fact 4): replaces 2-3 EUV array exposures with NIL at ~1/5-1/10 the tool cost; templates become cheap consumables; ~15-25% wafer-cost cut if imprint defectivity is controlled.

title: Vacuum-free spatial ALD heads for capacitor dielectrics
idea: Po: the fab runs at room pressure. Replace vacuum ALD chambers with atmospheric spatial ALD: wafers rotate under gas-bearing heads with alternating precursor zones, depositing ZrO2/HfO2 and TiN ~10x faster with no load locks or pumps.
why: Tool cost and throughput in the capacitor module: ~3-5x lower cost per wafer pass and lower energy.

title: Magnetically chained conductive film replaces microbumps
idea: Po: the glue is the wire. Only one pad-opening mask is used; an adhesive film loaded with nickel particles is cured in a vertical magnetic field so the particles line up into columns that conduct only along z at ~5 um pitch.
why: Removes bump plating, reflow and underfill steps, lowering assembly cost and thermal stress on DRAM.

title: Nanoimprint-stamped capacitor pillar array instead of EUV
idea: Worsen: buy EUV exposures for every capacitor layer. Flip: because the capacitor array is a perfectly periodic hex lattice, write one master template by e-beam (~$150k) and replicate it by nanoimprint on a rented tool, demonstrating 30 nm-pitch capacitor holes on 200 mm test wafers within 18 months.
why: Capital and EUV intensity (fact 4): imprint is ~1/10 the cost per layer and removes the single-supplier EUV dependency for the storage array.
note: NIL for memory already pursued by Kioxia/Canon; defectivity is the issue.

title: Stiction-latched graphene nanorelay held by van der Waals force
idea: Worsen: hold the bit with a charge that leaks. Flip: hold it with adhesion: an exfoliated few-layer graphene cantilever snaps onto a contact and stays stuck by van der Waals force until a reverse pulse peels it off; build 100 devices in a university lab in 12 months and spend the next 12 on cycling.
why: Zero leakage, zero standby power, no refresh (fact 3), for under $500k.

title: Time-domain sense amps race delay lines at 0.6 V arrays
idea: Worse: insist on full 1 V voltage swings and amplitude margin on every bitline. Flip: let the bitline differential set the bias of two current-starved delay stages and resolve which edge arrives first with a time comparator, so a ~0.6 V array supply still yields a clean decision.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline CV^2 energy drops ~60% if VARY goes from 1.0 to 0.6 V, with less access-transistor stress.

title: Resistless patterning via UV-written monolayers and selective ALD
idea: Worsen: depend on fluorinated photoacid generators and PFAS surfactants in every resist and developer. Flip: coat a self-assembled monolayer inhibitor, write the pattern by DUV-induced decomposition of the monolayer, and grow the hard mask by area-selective ALD only where the monolayer is gone, skipping resist coat and develop.
why: PFAS phase-out risk and resist supply concentrated in Japan: removes resist chemistry and track tools on non-critical layers, ~20-30% fewer chemicals per layer.

title: Beveled-sidewall printed wiring replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Worsen: drill thousands of TSVs per die so each via eats area and yield. Flip: stack thinned dies in a slight staircase with beveled edges and laser-direct-write or aerosol-jet-print the vertical bus down the sidewalls, so no die area goes to TSVs or keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers ~5-10% of die area and removes TSV-related yield loss; uses OSAT-class tools. Edge-limited wire count caps bandwidth per stack.
note: Staircase stacks are known in NAND; bandwidth capped by edge.

title: Geologist's fault lines: conductive ferroelectric domain-wall bits in LiNbO3
idea: A geologist knows fluids flow along faults, not through solid rock. In thin-film single-crystal LiNbO3, writing a nanoscale reversed domain creates a charged domain wall that conducts ~1e4x better than the bulk; the bit is 'wall present or absent' and is read non-destructively as a current.
why: Non-destructive read (fact 8), non-volatile storage (fact 3), and ferroelectric switching endurance above 1e10 with no high-AR capacitor (fact 1).

title: Farmer grows memory: croconic-acid proton-tautomer ferroelectric storage layer
idea: A farmer asks why memory can't be grown. Croconic acid, a small organic molecule, is ferroelectric at room temperature (Pr ~20 uC/cm2) because its protons hop between oxygen atoms; vapor-deposit it as the storage layer of a 1T1C cell instead of using mined Hf/Zr.
why: Removes the Hf/Zr dependence and allows low-temperature BEOL deposition; per area, the switched polarization charge is ~20x what a dielectric capacitor holds (fact 1).

title: Fire-stick land manager: Ge-doped VO2 hysteresis latch, laser processed
idea: Aboriginal fire-stick land management uses controlled heat, not irrigation. A Ge-doped VO2 nanobridge (transition near 90 C) is biased inside its insulator-metal hysteresis window, where it holds a 0 or 1 phase on nW of standby power. Pulsed-laser shock cleaning and laser annealing replace wet cleans and furnaces.
why: ~1 ns, low-voltage switching (fact 10) in a compact two-terminal cell (fact 4). Laser processing makes the storage module dry, a more than 10x water cut.
note: VO2 hysteretic memory known; needs a regulated ~90 C die and narrow nanoscale loops; laser-processing claim is incidental.

title: 2050 quantum engineer: superconducting loops with nanowire-cryotron access
idea: A 2050 quantum-computing engineer already has 4 K space to spare. Each bit is a persistent current in a NbN loop, selected by a nanowire cryotron (nTron) that a small gate current drives normal; loops hold current indefinitely, so there is no leakage or refresh, and switching costs attojoules.
why: Device-level access energy drops 100-1000x and refresh is zero; fits as working memory next to cryogenic processors where cooling already exists.
note: Nanowire/nTron superconducting memories published; cryogenic niche.

title: Alien race-to-latch: delay-domain sensing with shared arbiters
idea: An alien that measures everything in time converts each bitline pair's small differential into a delay difference through two current-starved inverters, and a 4-transistor mutual-exclusion arbiter decides which edge arrived first; one arbiter serves 4 bitlines by staggered firing.
why: Delay-domain comparison keeps working at low supply, enabling VARY ~0.6 V instead of ~1 V (fact 10) with fewer analog transistors per bitline (fact 7).

title: Origami artist's accordion: dies folded on flexible hinges
idea: Leave N memory dies in a row on a wafer strip and thin it to 20 um. Laser-ablate the silicon between dies so polyimide/Cu flex hinges carrying the shared bus remain, then fold the strip accordion-style in a jig into an N-high stack.
why: No TSVs, no die-to-die bonding and no interposer. The bus runs through the hinges, and a 10-person team can build an 8-high stack with thinning, a laser and a fixture (Fact 6).

title: Burdock-burr walker's velcro: copper nanowire room-temperature stack bonding
idea: Velcro came from burrs caught on a walker's clothes. Electroplate copper nanowire forests through track-etched polymer membrane templates on both bonding faces, then press them together at ~10 MPa so the wires interpenetrate into electrical and mechanical joints at room temperature.
why: Stacks memory on logic without nm-flat CMP, a high-temperature anneal or a precision bonder (Fact 6). A 10-person team can do it with plating and a press.
note: Cu nanowire room-temperature bonding is published; fine pitch risks shorts.

title: Borax geologist builds FeRAM from boron-aluminum nitride
idea: Persona: a geologist at the borax pit in Boron, California. Use wurtzite Al(1-x)B(x)N (x ~0.07-0.15), sputtered below 400 C, as the ferroelectric in 1T1C FeRAM. Its square hysteresis, with Pr above 100 uC/cm2, switches far more charge per area than a DRAM dielectric.
why: Non-volatile, with ~10x the charge density, which shrinks capacitor aspect ratio sharply. No Hf, Zr or Sc, and boron and aluminum are abundant in the U.S. Risk: the ~5 MV/cm coercive field needs fatigue engineering.

title: Coal miner's carbon memory: sp2 versus sp3 bond switching
idea: Persona: a coal miner who knows soot and diamond are both carbon. Store bits by field-driven conversion between insulating sp3 and conducting sp2 bonding in 5 nm tetrahedral amorphous-carbon films between carbon electrodes. A DRAM write-coalescing cache in front keeps each cell to 1e8 writes or fewer.
why: Non-volatile cell made of carbon only: no Ge, Sb or Te (PCM) and no Hf or Ta (ReRAM).

title: Watchmaker's click spring: snap-through nanomechanical bistable memory
idea: Persona: a watchmaker who relies on bistable click springs. A pre-stressed SiC or SiN nanobeam buckles either up or down, the two stable states. An adjacent electrode snaps it electrostatically and a capacitive sensor reads it, with no contact or stiction.
why: Non-volatile mechanical memory with no wear limit, made of Si, C and N. Leakage is essentially zero and ~10 ns switching is possible.

title: Cartographer: the border is the bit in barium titanate
idea: Persona: a cartographer who knows borders carry the traffic. Write and erase charged conductive domain walls in thin BaTiO3. The bit is whether a wall bridges two electrodes, read non-destructively by its conductance.
why: Non-volatile with non-destructive read (fact 8). Barium comes from Nevada barite, and no Li, Nb, Hf or Pb is needed.

title: Jeweler's plating bath: tungsten-free electroless cobalt or ruthenium wordlines
idea: A jeweler plates gold in a beaker at 60 C. Replace CVD TiN/W buried and stacked wordlines with seed-activated, bottom-up electroless Co or Ru fill from aqueous baths at <90 C, densified at <=350 C.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 chemistry, swaps ~$5M CVD chambers for wet cells, and lowers line resistance, since Co and Ru scale better than W below 20 nm. Risks: void-free fill and electromigration.

title: 2050 engineer laughing at boxed integers: unboxed CPython containers
idea: A 2050 engineer finds 28-byte Python ints absurd. A CPython extension, later an upstream PEP, gives lists and dicts lazily specialized storage: a container holding only ints, floats or short ASCII strings switches to a packed unboxed array or arena and boxes values only on access, invisibly to user code. Two core developers, 24 months.
why: Python data-processing heaps are 4-10x the raw data size. Specialized containers cut DRAM 2-5x in ETL jobs, ML data loaders and web caches.

title: Chef's mise en place: command-less, compiler-scheduled streaming DRAM
idea: A chef preps every ingredient before service: for static AI dataflows, the compiler preloads a whole row schedule into the HBM base die, which then streams data open-loop with no per-access command bus, and the freed command/address pins are repurposed as data lanes.
why: Removes command-bus overhead and scheduling bubbles: ~15% more data pins, ~10% more bandwidth efficiency and lower controller periphery power.

title: $1-IoT zinc-tin-oxide gain cells, indium and gallium free
idea: Disposable $1 IoT tags push oxide transistors toward the cheapest metals. Sputter amorphous Zn-Sn-O (ZTO) as the channel of 2T0C gain cells with ALD Al2O3 gate dielectric and Al or Mo electrodes, annealed below 350 C in a university fab.
why: IGZO gain cells (prior work) depend on indium (China ~60%) and export-controlled gallium; ZTO uses abundant Zn and Sn while aiming for the ~1e-19 A off-current needed for long retention (fact 3).

title: Low-budget-fab block copolymers print the honeycomb capacitor array without EUV
idea: Fabs that cannot buy EUV (universities, developing nations) can use directed self-assembly. High-chi block-copolymer cylinders (PS-b-P2VP) guided by a sparse e-beam or i-line template, hardened by sequential infiltration synthesis of AlOx, print the hexagonal capacitor array at ~30 nm pitch.
why: Replaces one of DRAM's 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) with spin-coat and bake, cutting dependence on the single EUV supplier for that layer.
note: DSA for DRAM hole arrays widely pursued (imec, majors).

title: Fluidic self-assembly of tiny DRAM confetti dies raises yield
idea: Extreme user: smart dust and RFID tags assembled in fluid. Dice DRAM into 0.2 mm^2 'confetti' chiplets by plasma dicing, then let them settle by shape into recesses on an interposer in a liquid bath, assembling thousands per minute without pick-and-place.
why: Yield/capital: tiny dies have near-100% yield at immature processes, so new fabs sell output in months; assembly cost per die falls ~10x.
note: Tiny dies pay heavy periphery/IO overhead; FSA known from Alien/microLED.

title: Wake-once sensor: clockless delay-insensitive memory link
idea: Seismic and wildlife sensors that wake once a minute cannot afford PLL/DLL lock power. Replace forwarded clocks, DLLs and link training with a delay-insensitive 1-of-4 code: each 2-bit symbol is one transition on one of four wires plus a completion acknowledge, so energy is spent only per symbol.
why: Clocking, DLLs and idle termination are often half or more of DRAM interface power; removing them plus one transition per two bits cuts energy per access ~5-10x at typical 20-40% utilization.

title: Scratched-CD codes: cross-interleaved 2D product codes over each mat
idea: Car CD players survived scratches through CIRC, two Reed-Solomon codes crossed by interleaving. Apply a row-by-column product code over each 512x512 mat, so a whole failed wordline or bitline (a burst) is corrected by the orthogonal code during scrub instead of needing a fused spare.
why: Wordline and bitline defects and hammer clusters use up repair resources and yield. A 2D code corrects whole-line failures for ~6% overhead, cutting redundancy area and raising yield (facts 7, 9).

title: Contactless bistable buckled nanobeam snaps between two shapes
idea: Shrink the hair-clip snap-through to a 100 nm single-crystal SiC beam pre-buckled by film stress: the bit is up or down buckling, flipped electrostatically and read by piezoresistance, and it never touches a contact so it avoids stiction.
why: Endurance and leakage: nonvolatile, zero standby power, 1e12+ fatigue cycles in single-crystal SiC.
note: Bistable buckled-beam memories known; large footprint.

title: Access-scheduled refresh: OS rotates hot pages across every row
idea: Scale jump from DRAM rows to OS page tables and time shift to workload access intervals: the kernel and a controller indirection table periodically re-place frequently touched pages so natural activations sweep every physical row within its retention window, and rows activated recently are logged and skipped by refresh.
why: Refresh ops/bandwidth (fact 3): in bandwidth-heavy AI serving, explicit refresh is cut 40-70%; spreading activations also lowers per-row hammer counts (fact 9).

title: Refresh locked to the rhythm of AI training steps
idea: Time shift by synchronizing two clocks: AI accelerators run near-periodic steps (forward, backward, all-reduce) with predictable memory-idle phases; the runtime publishes a phase schedule and the memory controller bunches refresh bursts into compute-bound and all-reduce windows on plain silicon DRAM with no new elements.
why: Refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) is >90% hidden with zero material change; the constraint pushes the gain into timing instead of chemistry.
note: JEDEC postponement limits (~8 tREFI) cap how much refresh can be bunched into ms phases.

title: Roving sense amp visits sampled bitlines in picosecond turns
idea: Time jump inside one row cycle: each bitline gets a tiny isolation switch that freezes its charge-shared signal, then one fast SA on a ~100 ps cycle visits 8 bitlines in turn, resolving and writing back each, like the column-shared ADCs of image sensors. SA count falls 8x for ~4 ns of added serial latency per segment.
why: SA stripes are a large slice of the ~49% periphery (fact 7); 8x fewer SAs cuts SA-stripe area ~60-70% net of switches, roughly 8-12% of die area.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 200:1 capacitor holes in a beaker
idea: Let a nanoscale metal catalyst do a plasma tool's job: pattern a perforated gold mesh with 180-nm litho plus spacer shrink, then immerse it in HF/H2O2. The metal sinks into the silicon and carves vertical holes at aspect ratios >200:1 for deep capacitors or vertical bitlines, with no plasma tool.
why: The capacitor charge wall wants AR ~115 (fact 1); MACE reaches it on a wet bench and slashes etch capital.

title: High-chi silicon block copolymers self-assemble the capacitor honeycomb
idea: Scale jump: the chain length of a PS-b-PDMS copolymer sets a ~24 nm hexagonal lattice, so one sparse ArF guide pattern plus a minutes-long anneal writes billions of capacitor holes. The silicon-rich block becomes its own etch hardmask.
why: Removes one or two EUV layers and their fluorinated photoacid-generator resists from the array, about 5-8% of wafer cost and a share of PFAS use. Defectivity must reach <0.01/cm2.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive DRAM interface eliminating DLLs and PLLs
idea: Abandon the global nanosecond clock: data moves with dual-rail or level-encoded handshakes so each transfer completes when it completes, and the DRAM drops its DLL, which burns power even when idle. Bus speed tracks voltage and temperature automatically.
why: Removes DLL/PLL standby power and worst-case timing guard bands: ~20-30% lower interface energy at low utilization.
note: Same clockless interface idea.

title: IBM TrueNorth, fixed: delta-event storage of token activations
idea: TrueNorth's event-driven spiking design faded because spiking nets could not be trained to state of the art. Keep its useful trick of storing only changes: hidden states across adjacent tokens or frames are kept in SRAM as sparse thresholded deltas against the previous step, with periodic keyframes like a video codec.
why: Streaming inference (video, audio, agents) cuts activation/KV memory 3-10x where inputs change slowly.

title: Cryogenic DRAM revived where cooling already exists: 77 K no-refresh tier
idea: Cryogenic memory efforts (IBM's Josephson program, later cryo-DRAM studies) died on the cost of dedicated cooling. Fix: place a DRAM tier inside LN2 loops already present in immersion-cooled AI pods or HTS power distribution, where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse and retention stretches far beyond typical data lifetimes; refresh is disabled and data older than the qualified retention is poisoned and restored by software.
why: Zero refresh power plus lower wire resistance; the leakage tail (fact 3) effectively vanishes, allowing smaller capacitors (fact 1).
note: AI immersion pods use warm dielectric fluid, not LN2; cryo-DRAM is known.

title: Z-RAM retargeted: floating-body bits from underused FD-SOI foundries
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died because standalone DRAM makers found the floating-body cell's margin too thin for commodity parts, and the startup had no fab. Fix: target FD-SOI logic foundries (22/28 nm, often underused) that already run SOI wafers, offering a standard macro that uses thin-BOX back-gate bias to widen the sense margin, and build memory chiplets there that bond to processors.
why: Adds DRAM-class bit supply from logic capacity outside the three DRAM makers, with no capacitor module and no EUV.
note: Floating-body cells on FD-SOI (A2RAM, Z2-FET) studied; ms retention and margin remain weak.

title: FB-DIMM's hot buffer fixed: off-path refresh-brain rescues weak dies
idea: FB-DIMM's advanced memory buffer died of heat (several watts) because it sat in the data path. Fix: keep a 180 nm buffer off the data path and use it only for control: it profiles each row's retention at boot and drives multi-rate refresh (RAIDR-style), refreshing strong rows rarely and weak rows often.
why: Refresh: cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss by ~50-75%, and lets dies rejected for a few short-retention rows ship as standard parts.
note: Variable retention time makes boot-time profiling unreliable; RAIDR-class idea.

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor bitline charging cuts precharge energy several-fold
idea: Effect: adiabatic stepwise charging. In a small team's MPW macro, bitlines charge and discharge through 3-4 intermediate voltage steps supplied by on-die tank capacitors, so each step dissipates only ~C(V/N)^2; the tanks self-balance because rising and falling lines exchange charge through them.
why: Energy per bit (facts 8, 10): bitline CV^2 energy falls ~N-fold (2-3x in practice) without lowering VARY, at the cost of ~1-2 ns per step.
note: Bitline equalization already recycles charge, so the extra gain is small.

title: Lithium-moved Schottky barrier makes selector-free cross-point tiers
idea: Ion migration: a field-driven Li-ion shift at a LixTiO2/metal interface moves a Schottky barrier, so the same junction stores a non-volatile resistance state and rectifies current. Self-rectifying cells allow 4F2 BEOL cross-point tiers with no separate selector layer.
why: Gives 4F2 stacked non-volatile cells without a transistor or selector (facts 2 and 4); claim 2x fewer layers per tier than 1S1R cross-point and cheap BEOL stacking.

title: Indium- and gallium-free zinc-tin oxide gain cells under 350 C
idea: Effect: conduction through overlapping spherical Sn 5s / Zn 4s orbitals keeps amorphous Zn-Sn-O a good semiconductor, and its ~3.3 eV gap suppresses thermal generation to ~1e-19 A/um. Sputter ZTO at room temperature and anneal it at <=350 C to build 2T0C gain cells stacked in BEOL.
why: Scarce-element intensity of oxide memory: removes In (China ~60%) and Ga (China ~98%), with retention >100 s for ~1000x lower refresh energy.

title: Autocatalytic electroless plating fills contacts at 80 C without WF6
idea: Effect: autocatalytic reduction. A DMAB-reduced Ni-B film nucleates directly on TiN and acts as a liner for bottom-up electroless Cu, filling high-AR contacts and buried lines void-free in aqueous baths at <90 C, replacing CVD tungsten from WF6.
why: Tungsten (China ~80%), fluorine chemistry and CVD tool cost; ~5x lower line resistivity than W at contact dimensions, with a bath far below 400 C.
note: Cu near FEOL junctions is a contamination risk.

title: Deep-UV photochemical activation forms oxide dielectrics at 150 C
idea: Effect: photolysis. 185/254 nm UV breaks sol-gel ligands and makes ozone and atomic oxygen in situ, condensing dense M-O-M networks of AlOx and ZrOx from spin-coated or inkjet precursors at <=150 C. This replaces furnace and ALD steps for storage-node and gate dielectrics in stacked tiers.
why: Energy and vacuum-tool capital; removes the thermal budget that drives quartz furnace consumables; printable dielectrics cut capital intensity for oxide memory tiers.

title: High-chi block copolymers plus vapor infiltration draw 12 nm arrays
idea: Effect: thermodynamic microphase separation. A high-chi block copolymer anneals at <=250 C into 12-20 nm hexagonal dots or lines, guided by a coarse ArF graphoepitaxial template. Sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O at 90 C) turns one block into an AlOx hard mask for array etches.
why: EUV chokepoint and PFAS-containing photoacid generators: 3-5 array EUV exposures replaced, with every step <=250 C.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing wires staircase DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Effect: electrohydrodynamic Taylor-cone jetting. Stack standard DDR dies in an offset staircase and e-jet print 1-2 um silver or copper nanoparticle traces down the stepped edges, forming hundreds of wide-I/O channels per die without through-silicon vias. $1M buys a commercial e-jet printer (~$200k), dies and 24 months of reliability work.
why: Fact 6: TSVs drive HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit and its yield loss; edge-wired stacks reuse ordinary DDR wafers and add high-bandwidth supply without TSV capex.

title: Superionic silver-sulfide stamps electrochemically etch metal lines without resist
idea: Effect: solid-state ion migration in a superionic conductor. A Ag2S stamp patterned once is pressed onto a Ag or Cu film under bias, and Ag+ ions move into the stamp only at contact points, removing metal with ~10 nm fidelity with no resist and no plasma etch. $1M demonstrates bitline-pitch metal patterning on 100 mm wafers.
why: Fact 4 and capital: one stamp station replaces coat, expose, develop, etch and strip for metal layers; Cu or Ag lines also avoid tungsten (~80% from China).
note: Solid-state superionic stamping (S4) already published.

title: Fused-silica diffractive plate performs the first vision layers optically
idea: Etch a learned phase mask into fused silica, which is stable far above 125 C, in front of each camera sensor. The first convolutional layers then happen as diffraction before photons reach the pixels, and the sensor outputs feature maps directly. Neither those weights nor their large early activations ever touch DRAM.
why: Early layers create the largest activation tensors, so removing them cuts ADAS vision DRAM 3-5x.

title: Melting-point depression: low-temperature sintered copper nanoink printed redistribution layers
idea: Inkjet/EHD-print 3-5 um Cu nanoparticle lines whose size-depressed melting point lets them sinter below 200 C under photonic flash, forming fan-out RDL on molded memory panels without lithography, sputter or plating tools.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): replaces litho+plating for fan-out lines; no silver; low thermal budget protects retention; 2-3x bulk resistivity is acceptable for fan-out.

title: Magnetic dipole chaining: field-aligned nickel-particle printed films for fine-pitch z-interconnect
idea: Print a curable polymer loaded with nickel microparticles on R2R film; an applied magnetic field chains the particles into vertical columns at ~5 um pitch before UV cure, giving an anisotropic z-conductor that attaches memory dies to printed interposers without bumps.
why: Packaging cost and pitch (fact 6): bumpless, solderless die attach on R2R lines at 5-10x finer pitch than conventional ACF.

title: Al: self-ordered anodic alumina pores replace EUV for capacitor holes
idea: Deposit a thick Al film over the cell array and two-step anodize it so the oxide self-organizes into a hexagonal nanopore lattice (pitch ~25-40 nm set by anodizing voltage, AR >100), registered by shallow pre-indents from the bit-line grid; the pores become the capacitor holes and the Al2O3 is the mold.
why: Hits the AR~115 needed for more charge (fact 1) with a wet electrochemical bath instead of an EUV layer plus a deep dry etch (fact 4); aluminum is abundant and U.S.-sourced.
note: Duplicate AAO pore capacitor.

title: Atomically thin junctionless sulfide access switch with no p-n junction
idea: S: make the access device a uniformly doped bilayer SnS2 or MoS2 ribbon with no source/drain junctions; the ~1.3 nm body is fully depleted by the gate in the off state, so there is no junction volume for SRH generation and no drain-overlap region for band-to-band tunnelling.
why: Removes both junction leakage and GIDL (fact 3), the two dominant tail mechanisms of recessed silicon access transistors; off-current is limited to thermionic emission over a 1.5-2 eV barrier.

title: Silicon-nitride retention canary cells trigger refresh only when needed
idea: N: in every row, build one canary cell with the same DUV process but a deliberately trap-rich nitride liner at its storage contact so it leaks ~3x faster than the worst data cell; a small comparator flags when the canary drops below threshold and refreshes that row only, so refresh follows real temperature, aging and process.
why: Most rows retain >10x longer than the 64 ms spec (fact 3); hardware-ground-truth refresh could cut refresh operations 4-10x with no new litho capability.

title: Si: silicon delay-line sensing tolerates variable rare-gas-free transistors
idea: Convert bitline voltage into delay by letting it bias the footer of a 16-stage current-starved Si inverter chain, then race it against a reference chain in a time-to-digital arbiter; averaging across 16 stages tolerates the larger device variation of periphery patterned with gas-free LED or solid-state-laser lithography.
why: Allows ~0.6 V sensing (fact 10) and relaxed periphery patterning; claims ~2x lower offset sensitivity than a single latch.

title: Silver-catalyzed chemical etch drills 200:1 vertical silicon pillars
idea: Pattern a perforated Ag film by e-beam lift-off, immerse in HF/H2O2 so the Ag sinks into the Si, and carve smooth vertical pillars or holes at aspect ratios >200:1 with no plasma, used as vertical channels and deep capacitor electrodes.
why: Breaks the capacitor aspect-ratio wall (fact 1 needs AR ~115) with a beaker-cost wet etch and no plasma damage to worsen the leakage tail (fact 3); Ag use is nanograms per wafer.

title: Indium- and gallium-free zinc-tin-oxide gain-cell transistor
idea: Periodic-table walk, Zn (30): replace IGZO in 2T0C gain cells with amorphous Zn-Sn-O (Zn:Sn ~2:1) by ALD (diethylzinc + TDMA-Sn), with Si or Al doping to pin oxygen vacancies for <1e-19 A/um off-current.
why: Removes Ga (~98% China primary) and In (~60% China) from capacitor-less oxide DRAM; two abundant metals only.

title: Barrierless copper-aluminum intermetallic local interconnect
idea: Periodic-table walk, Cu (29) with Al: use ordered intermetallics such as CuAl2, whose short electron mean free path keeps resistivity flat down to ~10 nm and which do not diffuse into dielectrics, so no TaN/Ta or Co liners; deposit by co-sputter plus 400 C anneal or subtractive Cl2 etch.
why: Removes W, Ta, Co and Ru from the tightest DRAM pitches; ~2x lower line resistance than W at 12 nm.

title: Zn: vapor-grown zinc MOF films as dry-developed resist
idea: Convert an ALD ZnO film into a ZIF-8 metal-organic framework by exposure to 2-methylimidazole vapor; e-beam/EUV exposure alters the framework so a reactive gas removes exposed or unexposed areas, giving a solvent-free, water-free, metal-rich resist.
why: Water: removes the wet track (spin, develop, rinse) from each litho layer, >10x water and solvent reduction for that module, with higher etch resistance than organic resists.

title: Al: aluminum-infiltrated block copolymers pattern capacitor holes dry
idea: Thermally anneal a block copolymer into a hexagonal hole lattice matched to cell pitch, infiltrate one block with trimethylaluminum/ozone vapor pulses to make AlOx, then O2-plasma away the polymer to leave a dry hardmask.
why: Water and litho: replaces the EUV hole layer and its wet track with self-assembly plus vapor infiltration that uses negligible water (>10x cut for that layer).

title: P: vapor phosphonate monolayer doping replaces implant-and-strip loops
idea: Form a phosphorus-bearing self-assembled monolayer from the vapor phase on Si exposed through a reusable hardmask (not resist), cap it and spike-anneal to drive a shallow conformal dopant profile, even inside 3D tunnels that implant beams cannot reach.
why: Water: each implant layer (10+ in DRAM) normally needs resist coat, strip and clean; vapor doping removes that water (>10x for the doping module) and enables doping of lateral 3D cells.

title: F: PTFE-laminate channels enable full-speed two-DIMMs-per-channel DDR5
idea: Route server DDR5 channels and DIMM risers on PTFE/fluoropolymer laminate (Df ~0.001 vs ~0.01-0.02 for FR-4 class) so two-DIMMs-per-channel topologies keep DDR5-6400 instead of derating to ~4400.
why: Capacity per socket at unchanged interface: doubles DIMM count per channel without a speed penalty, so lower-density, more available DIMMs can meet capacity targets.

title: Chocolate-tempered rutile TiO2: seed crystals select the k~100 polymorph
idea: Chocolatiers add Form-V cocoa-butter seed crystals to force the right crystal form. Here a 2 nm rutile-structured beta-MnO2 (or F:SnO2) seed on a TiN electrode, plus a tempering anneal cycle, forces TiO2 to crystallize as rutile (k~90-110) instead of anatase (k~40) at <=450 C, with no RuO2 template.
why: Fact 1: about 2-2.5x today's ZrO2 k using only Ti, Mn and O. Removes the Ru dependence of rutile-TiO2 DRAM capacitors.

title: Bell-cast parametron: AlN nano-resonator stores bits as oscillation phase
idea: Revive Goto's parametron using a bell-founder's resonator. A shared 2f pump drives an AlN/Si nanobeam, which rings at f in one of two phases (0 or pi), and that phase is the bit. A small seed signal writes it, phase comparison against a reference reads it, and one global pump powers millions of cells.
why: Facts 10 and 3: energy recirculates in a high-Q (~1e4) resonance, escaping the CV2 floor. No leakage tail, and only Al, N and Si.
note: Same parametron resonator mechanism.

title: Wire-drawn superconducting persistent-current loops for cryogenic working memory
idea: Use superconducting wire-drawing know-how (NbTi/Nb3Sn) as thin-film Nb micro-loops where the bit is a circulating persistent current. Josephson-junction access switches write and read it at 4 K, next to quantum computers and cryo-CMOS.
why: Zero refresh: persistent currents never decay and junction-based access has no leakage, so refresh and hold power are both zero. This serves cryogenic compute without a warm-DRAM round trip.

title: Fractional-distillation sensing: one timed comparator reads multi-level cells
idea: Like a distillation column where each fraction boils off at its own temperature, each 2T gain cell's stored level sets how fast its read bitline discharges, and a single comparator timestamps the threshold crossing. Early/mid/late/no crossing yields 2 bits per cell from one comparator and a shared counter instead of three SAs per bitline.
why: Enables 2-bit/cell DRAM-class arrays (2x density) without tripling SA area; sensing periphery per bit roughly halves.

title: Roof-shingle HBM: offset die stacks with 3D-printed edge traces
idea: Stack legacy DDR4/LPDDR dies offset like roof shingles so each die's edge pad row is exposed, then aerosol-jet 3D-print 20 um-pitch copper traces down the staircase to a logic base die, giving a wide bus without TSVs.
why: Removes TSV area and yield tax (fact 6) with installed OSAT tools; ~1-2k traces per edge gives HBM2-class bandwidth from mature dies.
note: Legacy x8/x16 dies lack wide IO; edge trace pitch caps bus width well below HBM.

title: Half-tone staircase: grayscale mask forms all tier steps at once
idea: Half-tone printing renders gray by dot density; use a sub-resolution dot grayscale reticle on an i-line/KrF stepper to form a stepped resist profile, then a proportional etch transfers all N staircase steps for a 3D array in one litho+etch instead of N trim-etch cycles.
why: Staircase cost and time scale with tier count (fact 2); one exposure on a depreciated scanner cuts staircase loops >10x for 32-64 tiers.

title: Resin-vat recoating: spin-on liquid oxide tiers cured by UV
idea: SLA 3D printers recoat liquid resin and cure layer by layer; stack tiers by spin-coating solution In-Zn-O semiconductor and spin-on high-k, curing each with deep-UV photochemical activation below 250 C on existing coat/track tools, patterned with KrF masks.
why: Vacuum-free tier deposition slashes per-tier capex and lets old track tools add oxide gain-cell tiers on logic BEOL (facts 2, 4), avoiding new ALD and sputter capacity.

title: Interchangeable parts: snap near-duplicate float lines to standard gauges
idea: Interchangeable parts came from making every part to a gauge tolerance. A line-level 'gauge dedup' engine hashes float lines after rounding to a per-region tolerance, using a locality-sensitive hash on the top mantissa bits. Lines within tolerance map to one canonical stored line, while regions flagged as precise get exact dedup only.
why: Model checkpoints, ensembles, fine-tune variants, simulation snapshots and gradient histories hold many near-identical lines that exact dedup misses, so tiers holding them gain 1.5-4x capacity.

title: Template-grown compliant copper nanowire forest replaces hybrid bonding
idea: Grow vertical copper nanowires by electroplating through anodic-alumina pores, like crystal whiskers in a mould, on every die bond face. Each 1 um pad touches dozens of springy wires, so stacks bond at low force while tolerating 1-2 um of warp that would break hybrid bonding.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (attacks the 20-30% loss) and removes the need for CMP flatness at sub-10 nm; keeps ~1 um interconnect pitch.

title: Magnetorheological chained-particle z-axis film for alignment-free bonds
idea: Mix nickel-cored silver particles into an adhesive film and cure it under a vertical magnetic field, so particles chain into 1-2 um pitch conductive columns. Any pad lands on several columns, so no precision alignment is needed.
why: Lowers die-to-die bonding cost and boosts yield at near-hybrid-bond density, which helps cheap memory stacking.

title: Miura-ori keyed fold scrambles physical row adjacency every boot
idea: A Miura-ori fold sends sheet neighbours far apart; add a tiny programmable mapping layer in each subarray's row decoder that applies a per-boot secret keyed permutation, so logically adjacent rows are physically distant and an attacker cannot tell which rows sandwich a victim; correlated physical faults are also spread across codewords.
why: Targeted double-sided hammering (fact 9) needs adjacency knowledge; a keyed fold makes it probabilistically infeasible without per-row counters.
note: A per-boot static key can be learned by probing flips.

title: Mirror-silvering chemistry: electroless ruthenium replaces tungsten wordlines
idea: Mirrors are silvered by electroless reduction from solution. Fill buried wordlines, contacts and plugs by Pd-seeded electroless Ru (or Co) with bottom-up superfill additives, at low temperature on a wet bench, instead of WF6 CVD tungsten.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): removes W from the cell and gives lower line resistance at narrow widths. Ru is needed only in milligrams per wafer. Wet-bench nanofab process.
note: Ru/Co wordline replacement widely pursued; electroless superfill is the twist.

title: Hysteretic Mott latch: niobium dioxide cell held inside its loop
idea: IFR: a cell that latches itself with no transistor and no capacitor. Closest achievable: bias a nanoscale NbO2 device through a series resistor at a hold voltage inside its insulator-metal hysteresis window so either phase is stable; a short over- or under-voltage pulse flips it and reading senses the ~10^3 resistance ratio.
why: Facts 1 and 7: a one-element 4F^2 volatile latch with no capacitor, ns switching and no filament wear-out.
note: Hold current in metallic state gives large static power.

title: Printed metal-insulator-metal tunnel diode replaces access transistor
idea: IFR: an access device that is only a sandwich. Closest achievable: use a printed Ta2O5 or Al2O3 MIM diode, as in early active-matrix LCDs, as a two-terminal nonlinear access device for each printed storage capacitor; strong I-V nonlinearity isolates half-selected cells.
why: Facts 7 and 4: two-terminal printed access removes TFT gate layers, giving a printable 4F^2 crosspoint cell.
note: Diode-access crosspoint DRAM proposed before; retention and sense margin weak.

title: Paired banks swap bitline charge instead of dumping it
idea: Ideal result: bitline swings cost nothing because charge is borrowed and returned. When a bank precharges, its high bitlines connect through a shared bus to a second bank's bitlines that are about to precharge, so half that bank's charge comes from the first bank's discarded charge.
why: Energy (facts 8, 10): recovers ~25-40% of bitline activation energy, the largest term in random-access energy.

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor charging cuts wordline drive energy
idea: Ideal result: wordlines that swing 3 V for free. Drive each global wordline through 4-6 staircase steps from on-die tank capacitors at intermediate voltages, so each step dissipates only (dV)^2 and charge returns to the tanks on the falling edge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline swing energy drops ~3-5x and charge pump load falls accordingly.

title: Vapor-deposited zinc-imidazolate MOF dry resist without fluorinated photoacids
idea: Ideal: a resist made from zinc and a common organic, deposited like a gas. Closest: grow ZIF-8-type zinc 2-methylimidazolate films by vapor-phase MOF-CVD; exposure breaks Zn-N links and the image develops in mild solvent or vapor, with no PFAS photoacid generators, fluorinated surfactants or spin-coat waste.
why: Resist PAGs/surfactants are a top fab PFAS use; dry deposition also cuts resist consumption ~10x and solvent wastewater; zinc is abundant.
note: ZIF e-beam/X-ray patterning already published.

title: Indium- and gallium-free zinc oxynitride channels for gain cells
idea: Ideal: an oxide transistor built only from zinc, oxygen and nitrogen. Closest: sputtered or ALD amorphous ZnON (mobility 50-100 cm2/Vs) stabilized with a few % Si or Al to suppress anion vacancies, replacing IGZO in 2T0C and 3D gain cells while keeping wide-gap ultra-low off-current.
why: Removes China-concentrated indium and export-controlled gallium from the lead capacitor-less candidate; higher mobility than IGZO (~10-20) gives faster writes.

title: Self-assembled nanocrystal monolayer forms storage nodes without patterning
idea: Ideal: storage nodes that place themselves. Closest: a spin- or Langmuir-Blodgett-assembled monolayer of 5 nm Ru nanocrystals over a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide on the transistor channel; each cell gate overlaps ~20 dots that hold charge (ms retention, ns direct-tunneling write at ~1.5 V), with no lithography for the nodes.
why: Facts 1 and 4: no capacitor; storage-node formation is a single coating step; direct tunneling instead of Fowler-Nordheim avoids oxide wear and targets high endurance.
note: Nanocrystal memory known (Tiwari); few electrons per small cell gives a weak signal.

title: Prediction-residual codec for simulation fields and time series
idea: IFR: memory stores only surprise. Closest: a memory-controller codec stores HPC fields and telemetry as entropy-coded residuals from a predictor (previous timestep, neighbour stencil), like video P-frames, decoded losslessly on access.
why: 3-10x footprint reduction for smooth physical fields in climate, CFD and sensor workloads.
note: FPC/fpzip-style lossless prediction gives ~1.5-2x on floats, not 3-10x; random access breaks predictor chains.

title: Seed-generated weights from LFSR banks in mature-node logic
idea: IFR: weights that occupy no memory. Constraint: memory chips need W, Hf and Ta but plain logic need not, so trade memory for logic: each 8x8 weight block is stored as a 16-bit LFSR seed plus four small coefficients, and thousands of LFSR+MAC units regenerate weights at line rate in 65-130 nm CMOS wired in Al-Cu with Ti/TiN barriers and TiSi2 contacts.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight cuts weight DRAM 4-5x versus BF16 using only Si, Al, Cu, Ti, N and O.
note: Close to SeedLM; gain over INT4 is small.

title: Moving-target rows: keyed rolling remap defeats hammering
idea: Ideal: hammering is pointless because the aggressor never stays next to its victim. Closest: the DRAM keeps a secret keyed permutation of logical to physical rows and migrates one row per refresh slot to a new physical position, so any logical aggressor's physical neighbors change before ~1k activations can accumulate.
why: Fact 9: makes falling hammer thresholds irrelevant without per-row counters; costs one extra row copy per refresh slot (~1-2% bandwidth).
note: Close to RRS/SRS; one migration per refresh slot is too slow against ~1k activations.

title: Image-sensor pinned well as capacitorless DRAM storage node
idea: Scarcity rule: no capacitor at all. Borrow the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: a buried n-well under a p+ surface pin stores the bit as a few hundred electrons, and a transfer gate dumps it onto a floating diffusion read by a source-follower gain transistor (3T cell), so tiny charge still swings the bitline. The p+ pin keeps interface traps filled with holes, cutting generation leakage to a few electrons per second.
why: Removes the 60-75:1 capacitor pillar (fact 1) and its HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); pinned-well dark current implies seconds of retention vs 64 ms, cutting refresh energy (fact 3) ~10x, using image-sensor process steps U.S. fabs already run.

title: Only one sense amp per 16 bitlines: bitline charge queue
idea: Self-imposed limit: one sense amp per 16 bitlines. After the wordline fires, each bitline holds its charge-shared signal on its own ~40 fF capacitance behind an isolation switch, and one offset-compensated sense amp resolves and writes back the 16 bitlines one after another in ~2 ns slots while the wordline stays open; the requested slice is resolved first and the rest are restored in the background.
why: Periphery (fact 7): the sense-amp stripe is ~15-20% of the die, and sharing cuts its area ~8-10x (die area -10-12%). The cost is a longer tRAS for full-row restore, which hides behind fine-grained access.

title: No matched analog pairs: delay-chain arbiter sense amps
idea: Limit: the sense amp must be synthesizable from standard digital cells. BL and BLB each set the supply of a short starved inverter chain, the cell's +/-dV becomes a ps-scale delay difference, and an SR-latch arbiter at the end decides; mismatch is trimmed by digitally tuned delay taps calibrated at power-up.
why: U.S. manufacturability and periphery cost: sense amps that port to any logic fab or node, with digital calibration replacing matched-pair area (SA area -30-40%).

title: Controlled-spalling wafer multiplication demo
idea: Within $1M/24 months: electroplate a stressed nickel layer on 300 mm prime wafers, start a crack to peel 20 um single-crystal films onto low-cost carriers, re-polish the parent and repeat ~20x; prove gate-oxide integrity and junction leakage on the spalled films.
why: Each CZ wafer (and its share of HPQ crucible and polysilicon) yields up to 20 device substrates; spalling is room-temperature and needs few tools, unlike ion-cut.
note: Same controlled-spalling wafer multiplication as I-10313.

title: MOF cartridges capture neon, krypton and xenon from exhaust
