idea: Within $1M/24 months: package selective metal-organic-framework adsorbents (Xe/Kr-selective SBMOF-type beds plus a Ne-capture stage) into swappable cartridges on excimer-laser and etch exhausts, regenerate them offsite by temperature swing, and resell the rare gases.
why: Ne/Kr/Xe supply is tied to Russian and Ukrainian air-separation byproducts; cartridges target ~70-90% recovery for DUV lasers and etch at cartridge rather than plant capex.
note: Neon adsorbs weakly on MOFs; excimer neon recycling already exists.

title: Metal-assisted wet etching carves 150:1 buried trench capacitors
idea: Constraint: no high-AR plasma etcher in the fab. A patterned Pt catalyst mesh sinks into single-crystal silicon in HF/H2O2 (MacEtch), carving 150:1 trenches at room temperature on a wet bench; the catalyst is stripped and reclaimed and the trenches become buried capacitors under the access transistors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR 150 in crystalline silicon gives ~10 fF cells; a ~$2M wet bench replaces an $8-10M etcher; the top surface is freed for wiring.
note: Buried trench variant of MacEtch.

title: Sidewall-printed vertical buses replace TSVs in offset die stacks
idea: Scarcity: TSVs banned. Stack thinned DRAM dies with a 20 um staircase offset so every die exposes an edge pad row, then aerosol-jet print 10 um copper/silver traces down the stepped sidewall (with printed polymer dielectric between traces) to tie every tier to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV-driven 20-30% yield loss, recovering ~25-30% of die area per bit; printing tools are cheap and U.S.-available.

title: Interlocking copper nanowire velcro makes cold-welded reworkable die joints
idea: Scarcity: no solder reflow and no bump pitch above 2 um. Template-electroplate dense 100 nm Cu nanowire forests on facing pads; pressing at room temperature interlocks and cold-welds them into 1-2 um-pitch joints that can be pulled apart and re-pressed.
why: HBM micro-bump pitch and yield (fact 6): no warpage from reflow, a bad die is reworked instead of scrapping the stack, and I/O density rises ~25x vs 10 um bumps.

title: Package magnet quenches spin-dependent trap-assisted leakage in VRT cells
idea: Effect: spin-dependent recombination/hopping. Trap-assisted tunneling via paramagnetic defect pairs needs spin-pair conversion; a ~0.3-1 T ferrite or SmCo magnet in the package lid polarizes defect and carrier spins, slowing the hop rate of the dominant variable-retention-time trap pairs.
why: Targets the VRT component of the leakage tail (fact 3); honest gain unknown (known effects 0.1-10%), large only if a giant-effect defect class exists; zero die change.
note: Spin-dependent TAT quench via package magnet is novel and trivially testable; expected effect likely tiny.

title: Substitute end-of-life solar panels for virgin polysilicon feedstock
idea: Thermally delaminate retired solar panels, chemically strip silver, aluminum and AR coatings, then hydrochlorinate the recovered silicon to trichlorosilane and redeposit it as 11N polysilicon for DRAM ingots.
why: Tens of Mt of panels retire by 2050; recovered silicon skips carbothermic quartz reduction (~11 kWh/kg) and imported poly, creating a domestic, low-energy feedstock loop.

title: Substitute dry plasma abatement and sorbents for wet exhaust scrubbers
idea: Replace burn-wet point-of-use abatement with atmospheric microwave plasma that decomposes PFCs and NF3, followed by regenerable dry Ca(OH)2/CaO beds that capture HF and F2 as calcium fluoride for resale.
why: Wet scrubbers need continuous water streams; dry abatement cuts scrubber water >10x and closes a fluorine loop that offsets the fluorspar chokepoint.

title: Partial-good DRAM dies salvaged via controller remap
idea: Combine wafer-sort binning with controller-side sparing: DUV-node DRAM dies that fail spec in a few banks or subarrays (normally scrapped) are sold as reduced-capacity parts with a fuse map that the memory controller reads at boot to remap around bad regions.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by several percent with no new tools, which matters when every non-EUV wafer counts.

title: Laser-coded material tags plus memory take-back policy
idea: MINIFY sorting cost: every memory package carries a laser-etched material bill of Cu/Sn/Si/Au, read by automated shredder lines, under an extended-producer-responsibility rule for DRAM.
why: U.S. scarce-resource recovery: makes recycled Cu, Sn and Au streams economic and gives domestic secondary supply.

title: Disulfide-staple pillars stitch all tiers against 125 C creep
idea: Thermophile proteins add disulfide bonds and salt bridges to stay folded when hot; add dense SiCN 'staple' plugs etched through all tiers every few microns in dummy regions and anchored into the substrate, mechanically clamping the stack so CTE mismatch at 125 C cannot drive delamination or slow creep of contacts over 10 years.
why: 3D stack integrity at high temperature: suppresses delamination and creep-driven contact drift so 100+ tier stacks can meet grade-1 life for <1% area.

title: Ice-storage building cooling shifts fab chiller load off-peak
idea: Office towers make ice at night to cool by day. Add stratified chilled-water and ice thermal storage to the fab process-cooling plant, and modulate upstream polysilicon reactors and abatement heaters like aluminum smelters' 'virtual battery' potlines, shifting 15-25% of electric load into cheap off-peak or curtailed-renewable hours.
why: Lowers energy cost per bit and lets ~0.5-1 GW-class memory fabs site on constrained U.S. grids without new peak generation.

title: Dry-developed metal-oxide resist patterns all redistribution layers
idea: Box: DRAM chiplets x standard x standard x fan-out RDL x Si or glass x vapor-deposited tin-oxide resist with plasma dry development and dry metal etch. Every lithography step in the RDL/interposer flow runs with no spin coat, aqueous develop or wet strip.
why: Water: develop, strip and rinse are a major litho water draw; dry resist plus dry etch cuts >10x for RDL layers and resist chemical use ~5x.

title: Foreign-trade-zone DIMM assembly lines at hyperscale campuses
idea: Box[Source=imported KGD wafers x Fab=U.S. SMT, test and burn-in x Scale=campus-adjacent line x Finance=FTZ duty deferral x Integration=standard RDIMMs built to order]: assemble and test DIMMs at the data-center gate in configurations each cluster needs, holding wafers rather than finished modules.
why: U.S. manufacturability of back-end; cuts inventory and lead time weeks to days; standard DDR5 output.

title: Mise-en-place decoding: arm wordline drivers on ACT's first cycle
idea: A chef preps before the full order arrives. DDR5's ACT spans two command cycles; the die decodes bank and upper row bits from the first cycle and pre-boosts the selected mat's wordline-driver group, finishing the lower bits on the second cycle.
why: Frees ~1-2 ns of internal tRCD slack, spent on smaller, lower-leakage decoder devices or lower VPP (facts 7, 10).

title: Downhole drilling engineer: FD-SOI PHY with temperature-tracking back-bias
idea: Oil-well tools run for years at 175 C on SOI: build the memory interface PHY and base logic on FD-SOI and let an on-die temperature loop set the back-gate bias so threshold voltage, leakage and delay stay constant from -40 C to 150 C.
why: Junction leakage disappears with SOI, and back-bias holds timing and I/O power flat at 125 C, so links run at full speed with no hot derating.

title: Diode-laser array millisecond annealing replacing xenon flash lamps
idea: Time-scale-matched heating: tiled high-power near-IR/green diode bars scan the wafer with 0.1-10 ms dwell, reproducing flash-lamp and XeCl excimer anneal profiles with no xenon fill gas.
why: Removes xenon, among the scarcest gases, from activation anneals. Diode arrays last 10x longer than flash lamps and use less energy per wafer.
note: Laser spike anneal with diode/CO2 lasers is already used.

title: Back to polycide: tungsten-free legacy-node memory flow
idea: Polycide (WSi, CoSi2) wordlines were abandoned for tungsten because their resistance scaled badly in narrow lines, which now ties DRAM to tungsten (China ~80%). At 180 nm and above that problem does not exist: run legacy-node memory and companion chips with poly/CoSi2 wordlines, Al-Cu interconnect and Ti/TiN-lined Al-reflow plugs (a 1990s technique) instead of W plugs.
why: Scarce resources: removes tungsten from the old-node memory and companion-chip flow, shielding that supply from a single-country chokepoint.

title: Paint-pigment TiCl4 refined into electronic capacitor electrodes
idea: As sugar refiners turn table sugar into pharmaceutical sucrose, add a fractional-distillation and adsorber polishing train beside U.S. chloride-process pigment plants in Tennessee and Mississippi to make 6N TiCl4 for TiN capacitor electrodes, gate liners and barriers.
why: TiN is in every DRAM capacitor and wordline; this gives a domestic electrode supply at commodity cost, removing imported TiCl4/TDMAT and the pull toward scarce ruthenium electrodes.

title: Spare subarray swap triggered by ECC error-trend detection
idea: Rule: big defects must be fixable in place. Each bank holds one spare subarray (~1/64). When ECC logs show a subarray's error rate trending upward (for example, a failing sense-amp stripe), it is copied into the spare with in-DRAM bulk row copy and remapped live.
why: Repairs large-area defects that spare rows cannot cover at ~1.5% area, so fewer modules are retired.

title: Spare cell-capacitor pillars serve as charge-pump flying capacitors
idea: Substitute planar MOS capacitors in the VPP/VBB charge pumps with blocks of ordinary high-aspect-ratio array capacitor pillars, placed in dummy mats and wired in parallel as flying and reservoir capacitors.
why: Periphery area: array caps store ~50-100x more charge per um^2 than gate-oxide caps, shrinking pump area ~80% (pumps are several % of die) with zero new process steps.
note: Cell-capacitor decap is common practice.

title: Substitute CVD silicon carbide for quartz furnace ware and chamber rings
idea: Replace quartz diffusion tubes, wafer boats, liners and etch focus rings with CVD-SiC, sintered Y2O3 or single-crystal-silicon parts that are re-coated in place by plasma spray or CVD when eroded, so parts are refurbished rather than scrapped.
why: Quartzware is the second-largest high-purity-quartz draw after crucibles; 5-10x longer part life cuts quartz demand and particle-driven yield loss.

title: Substitute cryogenic argon aerosol jets for megasonic water rinses
idea: Expand chilled argon/nitrogen through a nozzle to form frozen micro-solids that knock 20 nm particles off the wafer by momentum transfer and then sublime, so no liquid ever touches the wafer.
why: Particle-removal passes use ~10-30 L UPW per wafer each; aerosol cleaning uses none (>50x cut) and avoids water-induced pattern collapse.

title: Substitute stealth laser dicing and dry polish in HBM stacking
idea: Thin HBM wafers by mist-cooled grinding plus fixed-abrasive dry polishing, and singulate them by internal stealth-laser modification plus tape expansion instead of water-flooded blade dicing.
why: Blade dicing and wet grinding run continuous litres-per-minute flows; the dry route cuts back-end water >10x and reduces chipping that contributes to HBM's 20-30% yield loss.

title: Eliminate laser fuse repair: on-die BIST and BIRA blow antifuses
idea: The die runs its own march test and built-in redundancy analysis at wafer sort and programs repair electrically into antifuses, so the laser-repair tools, their test insertion and external repair-analysis servers disappear. The host sees an ordinary DDR5 or HBM3E die.
why: Test capital: removes laser repair and a repair-test insertion (~5-10% of back-end test cost) with zero interface change.
note: On-die antifuse self-repair and PPR are already standard.

title: Pre-plasma wet etching returns for non-critical DRAM layers
idea: Revive 1970s wet chemical etching (hot phosphoric acid for nitride, buffered HF for oxide, aqueous metal etches with recycled etchant) for coarse layers, replacing fluorocarbon plasma steps that also need helium backside wafer cooling.
why: Cuts PFAS/fluorinated greenhouse-gas use and helium consumption, with no EUV; claims 20-30% fewer plasma steps per wafer.

title: Aquarium filter: electrodialysis skid recycles TMAH developer
idea: Stimulus 'aquarium filter' (water cycles while waste is pulled out) -> a 10-person team builds bipolar-membrane electrodialysis skids that split spent TMAH developer back into pure TMAH concentrate and clean water for reuse.
why: Cuts TMAH purchases ~80% and wastewater toxicity, easing the fab's water-treatment load.

title: Smoke detector: hydrogen-tracer sniffers replace helium leak detectors
idea: Stimulus 'smoke detector' (a cheap solid-state sniffer) -> a 10-person team builds Pd-alloy thin-film hydrogen sniffer leak detectors that use non-flammable 5% H2/95% N2 forming gas as tracer for gas lines, chambers and packages instead of helium mass-spectrometer detection.
why: Removes helium from routine leak testing, a top fab helium use, at ~1/5 the tool cost.

title: Navigator's chart: printed thermistor skin sets refresh per die
idea: A navigator wants a detailed local chart, not one compass: an array of NTC thermistor-ink pads and silver traces is screen-printed onto the DIMM PCB or interposer next to every DRAM die or bank region and read by the module PMIC, so the controller sets each die's refresh interval from its local temperature rather than from the hottest sensor.
why: Fact 3: dies in real racks differ by 10-20 C, so per-die refresh saves an estimated 15-30% of refresh energy for pennies of ink.
note: DDR5 dies already report on-die temperature.

title: Uranium-enrichment fluorine plants: on-site F2 replaces NF3 and fluorocarbons
idea: Uranium enrichment has made elemental fluorine electrolytically at ton scale for 80 years. Put modular KF-2HF electrolyzers at each fab: F2 replaces NF3 (GWP ~17,000) for chamber cleans and serves as a carbon-free fluorine-radical source, fed by HF recovered from fab fluoride wastewater.
why: Cuts PFC/PFAS-class gas use and GHG emissions; recycling wastewater HF eases fluorspar dependence (China ~60%).

title: CVD silicon-carbide tubes and boats replace high-purity quartz furnaceware
idea: Time-shift consumable life: quartz tubes, boats and liners in existing furnaces devitrify and are swapped every few months. Drop-in CVD-SiC parts made from abundant Si and C (methyltrichlorosilane) last 5-10x longer and tolerate higher temperature.
why: Removes Spruce Pine high-purity quartz from furnace consumables in existing trailing fabs and cuts downtime.

title: Tin-copper solid-liquid interdiffusion bonds stack tiers without remelting earlier joints
idea: Bond each memory tier with thin Sn on Cu pads at ~250 C; the Sn fully converts to Cu3Sn/Cu6Sn5 intermetallic that melts above ~600 C, so later bonding steps never reflow earlier joints, allowing sequential 8-16-high stacks on a simple flip-chip bonder.
why: A low-cost, particle-tolerant alternative to hybrid bonding for stacked memory (fact 6) using abundant Sn and Cu, buildable in university packaging labs.
note: SLID/TLP bonding is mature; does not address fine-pitch TSV tax.

title: Boron cluster molecules for fluorine-free p-type doping
idea: Periodic-table walk, B (5): replace BF3/BF2+ implants with octadecaborane (B18H22) cluster implantation or monolayer doping from boronic-acid esters plus spike anneal, with no fluorine co-implant and no BF3 gas cabinets.
why: Removes a major fluorinated implant gas; cluster beams give ~10-20x effective low-energy dose rate, so fewer implanters.

title: Si: plasma dicing and dry thinning for HBM die
idea: Finish thinning HBM DRAM wafers with high-rate SF6 plasma instead of wet polishing, and singulate with deep reactive-ion plasma dicing instead of water-cooled blade sawing; die edges come out chip-free.
why: Fact 6 (HBM yield -20-30%): chipping and microcracks fall; grinding/sawing water and slurry for the module fall >10x.
note: Plasma dicing already commercial.

title: C: graphene-hex interleave spreads clustered flips across codewords
idea: Map codeword bits onto physical columns and chips in a honeycomb pattern, so bits that are physical neighbors (which fail together from shared defects or hammer hot zones) always fall in different codewords, each seeing at most one bad symbol. A remap table in controller RTL.
why: Turns clustered multi-bit failures (facts 8-9) into single-symbol errors that existing SEC or chipkill corrects; claim ~10x fewer uncorrectable events.
note: Interleaving and chipkill already spread clustered faults.

title: Aircraft-brake carbon composites become crystal puller hot zones
idea: U.S. aircraft-brake plants make carbon/carbon composites by winding PAN fiber and densifying it by chemical vapor infiltration from natural gas; use those lines for CZ heaters, susceptors, heat shields and crucible supports, replacing imported isostatic graphite.
why: Isostatic graphite comes mainly from Japan and China; C/C parts last ~3-5x longer and cut hot-zone heat loss ~15-25%, lowering crystal-growth energy per wafer with an all-domestic chain.
note: C/C composite heaters and supports already standard in CZ pullers.

title: Silicon-carbide furnace ware removes the second quartz dependency
idea: Imposed scarcity: zero HPQ anywhere in the fab, not just in crucibles. Replace quartz diffusion tubes, boats, injectors and bell jars with CVD-SiC-coated or recrystallized SiC, plus single-crystal silicon parts machined from ingot tops and tails.
why: Fab quartzware also depends on Spruce Pine-grade sand; SiC parts last ~3-5x longer at high temperature and survive HF cleans, cutting consumable volume and chokepoint exposure.

title: Po: the bit is a knot — 3D hopfion storage, chiral magnets
idea: Po: the bit is a knot that cannot untie itself. Extracted: in a thick chiral magnetic film a hopfion (3D knotted magnetization soliton) is topologically protected; bits are hopfion present/absent at pinning sites stacked through the film thickness, nucleated by local spin-orbit torque and read by MTJ.
why: Volumetric non-volatile storage without per-tier transistors (fact 2). Room-temperature hopfion stability is speculative.
note: Volumetric magnetic bits without per-tier transistors; doubt: room-temperature hopfion control and reading buried bits.

title: One-run van der Waals superlattice: 100 monolayer channels, 100 tiers
idea: Treat the crystal lattice as the tier stack: grow 100 alternating MoS2/hBN monolayer pairs by wafer-scale MOCVD in one run, with a tier pitch of ~1.5 nm instead of ~60 nm. Then cut vertical slots and contact each monolayer edge as a lateral access-transistor channel; the whole 100-tier stack is ~150 nm tall.
why: The high-AR etch through 26+ tiers is a 3D blocker (fact 2); 40x thinner tiers make 100 tiers etchable at AR <10.
note: Growing 100 uniform MoS2/hBN pairs and edge-contacting each 1.5 nm-pitch monolayer individually both need miracles; storage element unaddressed.

title: Single-electron electrometer sense amps make 300-electron cells readable
idea: Failure mined: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano) died because the SET was too variable as a storage device. Fix: use the SET only as the sensor, a 3 nm silicon-island electrometer per 32-cell local bitline with charge sensitivity near 0.01 e, auto-calibrated on every access. Cells then need only ~300 electrons (~0.05 fF), which planar thin-film storage nodes can hold.
why: 10x at the same cost: a 100x smaller capacitor removes the 70:1 pillar and allows a 3D-NAND-style stack of 32+ tiers of lateral planar cells from deposited layers, ~10x bits/mm^2 at similar litho cost.
note: A 100x smaller cell would allow stacked planar tiers; doubts are room-temperature SET variability and 300-electron retention below a fA.

title: Single-electron transistor electrometer senses attofarad cells
idea: Borrow spin-qubit readout: couple a silicon single-electron transistor capacitively to each micro-cell storage node and read it by RF reflectometry with frequency multiplexing, so cells storing only ~100 electrons can be read.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): Cs ~50x smaller (~0.02 fF), allowing planar cells and many cheap 3D tiers (fact 2); needs room-temperature SET operation, which is very hard.
note: SET readout would allow 50x smaller Cs; room-temperature SET and per-cell RF readout are near miracles.

title: Bacterial S-layer protein crystals pattern the array at 9 nm
idea: Many bacteria coat themselves in S-layers, 2D protein crystals that recrystallize on surfaces in minutes; engineer a square-lattice S-layer (~9 nm period) with a metal-binding loop, recrystallize it over the array region guided by DUV-printed edge anchors, mineralize the pores into a Pt/Al2O3 hardmask and etch one vertical-channel gain cell per lattice site with self-aligned spacer wordlines.
why: ~80 nm2 per cell vs ~860 nm2 for 6F2 at F=12 nm gives ~10x bits/mm2 with no EUV in the array; the protein costs cents per wafer, so wafer cost stays flat (fact 4).
note: ~10x density claim; doubt: a vertical gain cell per 9 nm site plus defect-free protein lattice registration.

title: Spider-spinneret thermal drawing shrinks a macro preform into nanocell arrays
idea: Spiders draw nanoscale fibers from a gland; assemble a centimetre-scale preform of chalcogenide-glass channel, low-melting metal electrodes and polymer dielectric in the exact cell pattern, thermally draw it ~10^4x like optical fiber to ~20 nm features, then bundle, fuse and slice the fibers crosswise into thin 'memory wafers' that are hybrid-bonded onto CMOS.
why: Feature size comes from draw ratio, not lithography; one cheap preform yields kilometres of fiber, so slices can reach ~10x bits/mm2 at bulk-material cost with zero masks (fact 4).
note: Thermal draw sets features without masks; 20 nm multimaterial cores, uniformity and registration to CMOS are unproven.

title: V(D)J clonal selection: wire random nanowire meshes, then select working cells
idea: The immune system generates random receptors and keeps the ones that work; spray self-assembled nanowire/nanotube networks over a coarse CMOS grid with no fine lithography, probe at test time which random junctions behave as good storage cells, and record their addresses in an on-chip translation table, discarding the rest.
why: Capital/EUV: eliminates fine patterning of the array (5-7 EUV layers, ~55% depreciation share); even at 30% junction yield plus table overhead, cost per GB could fall ~100x because the array costs almost nothing to form.
note: 100x cost claim assumes random junctions form fast, high-endurance storage cells; no known random junction meets DRAM speed/endurance.

title: Optical-fiber preform drawing: coaxial capacitors drawn, bundled, sliced
idea: Borrowed from telecom fiber drawing and multimaterial fibers, which shrink a 10 cm preform 10,000x: draw a preform of packed coaxial metal/glass-dielectric/metal rods to ~50 nm cores, bundle and redraw, then slice the bundle into 1-5 um discs; each disc is a ready-made capacitor array, with aspect ratio set by slice thickness, bonded onto a transistor wafer.
why: Facts 1/4: zero lithography and zero high-AR etch for the capacitor, AR 100+ for free; core uniformity and registration to transistors are speculative.
note: Same draw-and-slice concept; 50 nm coaxial cores and registration to transistors remain unproven miracles.

title: Single-molecule tautomer switch: one hydrogen hop stores a bit
idea: Effect walk: proton tunneling in tautomerization. A porphycene or naphthalocyanine molecule anchored in a nanogap flips which nitrogen atoms hold its inner hydrogens when a 0.2-0.4 eV tunneling electron excites it, and its two tautomers give distinct junction conductance read at 10 mV.
why: Switching costs one vibrational excitation (~0.1 aJ) and a 10-mV, ns read through one molecule is ~10^-17 J: >=100x below DRAM, at molecular density; room-temperature stability and contact reproducibility are speculative.
note: Tautomer switching is shown only by cryogenic STM; RT stability and nanogap reproducibility are unsolved.

title: Charge-coupled circulating loops refresh by recirculation, no access transistors
idea: Effect: charge-coupled transfer. Bits are charge packets in short 64-stage CCD loops of gate-only electrodes over a buried channel (2F^2 per bit, no capacitor, no per-cell contact); packets circulate at ~2 GHz, and each lap passes a regenerator that restores packet size, so leakage and transfer inefficiency are corrected every ~30 ns. Many parallel loops give bandwidth, with ~16 ns average access.
why: 10x density: 2F^2 versus 6F^2 is 3x per layer, and 4 stacked thin-film CCD tiers give ~12x. Same cost: gates-only arrays need no capacitor module and no cell contacts.
note: Key doubt: clocking every electrode at GHz costs roughly kW per GB; thin-film transfer inefficiency.

title: Thousand-tier monolithic stack of atom-thin transistor sheets
idea: Po: tiers are counted in thousands, not tens. Grow wafer-scale MoS2 monolayers by MOCVD on sapphire, dry-stamp each 0.7 nm channel plus 3 nm high-k plus 5 nm metal as one 10 nm 'tier sheet', and pattern all tiers with one deep vertical-gate etch (3D NAND style) to get ~1000 lateral 1T1C tiers per 10 um of height.
why: Fact 2 (break-even at 26+ tiers): 1000 tiers at relaxed F~40 nm without EUV gives ~10x bits/cm2 of 2D DRAM; transfer yield per tier is the dominant risk.
note: 1000 tiers would give ~10x density, but transfer yield^1000 and step count kill cost/bit.

title: Another dimension: stacked CFET sense amp fits a single bitline pitch
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: the cross-coupled latch is built as complementary FETs stacked vertically (nFET pair under pFET pair with shared gates), so each sense amp fits one bitline pitch instead of two to four, letting every bitline of a 4F2 open-bitline array have its own amp.
why: Facts 4 and 7: sense-amp strip area ~-50% and 4F2 vertical-channel cells become usable, since their pitch cannot host today's planar sense amps.

title: Liberty-ship mini-fabs: identical DUV-only DRAM fabs from used tools
idea: Revive the WWII Liberty-ship approach: freeze one standardized no-EUV DRAM design and fab layout (10k wafers/month, second-hand ArF-immersion scanners, refurbished etch and deposition tools) and have the same crews replicate it quickly across many US states.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity: no EUV, ~1/5 the capex of a leading-edge fab, built in 18 months; claims to raise the US share of bits from 1-2% to ~5%.
note: DUV-only DRAM fabs lag on cost per bit; replication speed is a strategy claim, unprovable for $1M.

title: Second-source HBM core dies on a standard foundry base die
idea: Box[Source=core dies from smaller DRAM makers x Integration=HBM4 stack on a JEDEC-compliant foundry base die x Owner=base-die vendor as integrator x Finance=multi-sourced KGD contracts]: a neutral integrator buys core-die wafers from second-tier DRAM fabs and stacks them on its own HBM4 base die, delivering standard HBM to GPU makers.
why: Breaks the three-supplier HBM bottleneck: adds second-tier DRAM capacity to HBM supply without changing the HBM interface.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM bonded onto wafer-scale compute
idea: Po: memory has no die edges. Keep the 300 mm DRAM wafer whole, stitch reticles with redundant cross-reticle wiring, map bad blocks at test, and bond it wafer-to-wafer onto a wafer-scale accelerator so every compute tile has its own DRAM directly above.
why: Data movement (fact 5) <0.3 pJ/bit vertically; no dicing, packaging or HBM TSV tax (fact 6); harvests every good block instead of scrapping dies.

title: Copy-exactly DRAM micro-fab franchise replicated across states
idea: Worse: build one $15B gigafab every five years in one place. Flip: design a standardized ~10k wafers/month DRAM module (fixed tool set, recipes, building) and franchise it to regional operators who pay royalties while the franchisor runs centralized yield engineering and tool spares.
why: Entry ticket falls to ~$2-3B per site, capacity arrives in small staggered steps and U.S. manufacturing spreads out.
note: 10k wpm DRAM modules lose scale economics; franchising tacit yield know-how is the real doubt.

title: Substitute excimer and EUV lithography with nanoimprint for wordline trenches
idea: Substitute ArF scanners (argon/neon gas laser) and EUV (CO2 drive laser with helium in its gas mix) with UV-LED-cured nanoimprint from e-beam-written masters for the buried-wordline and active layers. The periodic DRAM array suits imprint, which reproduces the master's ~1 nm line-edge roughness.
why: Lower line-edge roughness gives tighter access-transistor Vt and leakage spread (sigma-Vt down ~30%), shrinking the tail that sets refresh, while cutting litho capex and rare-gas use.

title: Coincident row-and-column-group selection borrowed from core memory
idea: Substitute single-wordline activation with core-memory coincident selection: the access transistor is dual-gated, with the top gate on the row line and a buried back gate on a column-group line, and it conducts only when both are high. Only a 512-bit segment of the row opens.
why: Destructive-read overfetch (fact 8): activated bits drop from ~8K to 512, cutting energy per useful bit up to ~16x on random access, and less charge disturbance also eases row hammer.

title: Swap HBM weight storage for read-only stacked NAND beside smaller HBM
idea: Substitute HBM with high-bandwidth stacked NAND for the read-only tier. Inference weights do not change for months, so a wide, many-plane NAND die stack on the same interposer streams them into SRAM in 4-16 KB pages, and HBM shrinks to KV cache and activations. Endurance does not matter because weights are written only at model deployment.
why: Weights are 40-70% of accelerator memory. NAND is ~10x cheaper per bit and needs no EUV for capacity, so HBM per accelerator falls ~2x, and the HBM TSV tax falls with it.
note: Close to SanDisk HBF.

title: Substitute passing-gate coupling with a buried negative-biased shield plate
idea: Insert a thin conductive shield line, held at a negative bias, between each buried wordline and the neighboring storage-node junction, so hammering electrons and coupling from the aggressor gate end on the shield instead of the victim node.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aims to push flip threshold from ~1k back to >50k activations, removing most mitigation refresh and periphery logic.
note: Same buried biased line between aggressor and victim as I-03610.

title: HBM base die absorbs all core-die periphery
idea: Make HBM core dies array-only (cells plus wordline straps), hybrid-bond each one face-to-face to a logic-process periphery tier holding the SAs and decoders, and merge the base-die functions into the same periphery design, so the duplicate IO and TSV drivers on each core die disappear.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): array efficiency ~50% to ~85% (~1.6x bits per array wafer), with lower-power logic-process SAs.
note: CBA applied to HBM; industry already exploring.

title: Old-node DRAM arrays bonded to 40nm periphery in CIS fabs
idea: Strip the periphery from 2x-nm DRAM array designs still running in depreciated lines, and hybrid-bond those wafers face-to-face to 40/28 nm logic periphery wafers using the wafer-to-wafer bonding lines that image-sensor fabs already run at volume; SAs connect through ~1-2 um pitch pads per bitline-pair group.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): ~1.6x bits per wafer from old DRAM lines with no new fab, using idle 28-40 nm logic and existing CIS bonding tools.

title: Array-only DRAM wafers bonded to one shared logic periphery tier
idea: Combine CMOS-bonded-array (Xtacking-style 3D NAND) with multi-tier DRAM: fabricate array-only wafers with no sense amps or decoders, then bond 2-4 of them through vertical bitline/wordline vias at ~2 um hybrid-bond pitch onto a single advanced-logic wafer carrying all sense amps, decoders and I/O.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) and masks: array wafers need fewer masks and cheap transistors while periphery gets fast logic; claims 30-45% lower cost/bit and 1.6-2x bits per footprint.

title: Vertical-farming stacks memory tiers on logic, deleting separate wafers
idea: Vertical farms grow many crop tiers on one footprint. Adapt this by depositing 8-16 tiers of capacitor-free BEOL memory directly over the accelerator's logic die, replacing HBM's separate DRAM dies, base die and TSV stack.
why: HBM consumes ~3x the wafer area per bit plus 8-12 separate CZ wafers per stack. Monolithic tiers use no extra crystal or quartz crucible per bit and remove the TSV tax (Fact 6) and much of the data-movement energy (Fact 5).
note: BEOL oxide tiers over logic are widely pursued; capacity per die area falls far short of HBM.

title: Player-piano rolls: stream weights from NAND page buffers to compute
idea: Borrowed from player pianos reading music straight off a moving roll: NAND dies with wide internal page buffers stream compressed weights over a short die-to-die bus directly into the NPU's SRAM line buffers, with dozens of planes interleaved so the read rate matches decode throughput and no DRAM staging exists.
why: Weights sit in NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit of DRAM with zero refresh; DRAM shrinks to KV/activations, cutting capacity per inference server 5-10x.

title: Seismic base-isolation shield lines buried between wordlines
idea: Adapted from base-isolated buildings that decouple a structure from ground shaking: insert a grounded buried shield line (a dummy recessed gate held at slight negative bias) between every pair of active buried wordlines, so aggressor wordline swings and hot electrons injected into the substrate are absorbed by the shield rather than the victim storage node.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): blocks both electrostatic coupling and trap-assisted charge pumping, potentially raising flip thresholds 10x+ at ~15-25% array-area cost (6F2 to ~7.5F2), trading density for deleting counters, RFM and victim-refresh overhead.

title: ISO shipping-container standard for bare memory dies
idea: Adapted from the 1956 intermodal container: define a fixed die footprint, hybrid-bond pad grid, power map and self-test port so any fab's DRAM die, of any cell technology, drops into any HBM/CXL stack or package without requalifying the package.
why: Breaks vendor lock-in and lets small fabs and new cell types sell into high-value stacks; widens the supplier pool and shortens qualification (supply, capital intensity).
note: Chiplet and HBM base-die standards widely pursued (UCIe, JEDEC).

title: Ocean Spray-style buyer cooperative owning a DRAM fab
idea: Adapted from agricultural cooperatives: PC, phone, auto and server OEMs buy co-op shares in a jointly owned fab. Each member gets wafer allocation in proportion to equity, pays cost-plus, and gets surplus back as patronage dividends.
why: Guarantees members supply through shortages and strips out the oligopoly margin (~30-60% at peak), lowering effective cost per bit (cost, supply security).

title: Tesla gigacasting adapted: wafer-scale DRAM slabs skip packaging entirely
idea: Adapted from gigacasting, where one casting replaces ~70 stamped parts: keep each 300 mm DRAM wafer whole as a ~1 TB memory slab with on-wafer redundancy routing, and mount it on a U.S.-made glass or silicon backplane with bonded CXL controllers, skipping dicing, packaging and offshore OSAT steps.
why: Removes the Asian packaging/test dependence, recovers scribe area (~5-8%) and gives TB-class pooled-memory appliances made entirely in the U.S. (U.S. manufacturability, cost per bit).

title: Minify the channel to one atomic layer: MoS2 vertical access
idea: Shrink the access-transistor body to a 0.65 nm MoS2/WSe2 monolayer wrapped gate-all-around on the pillar sidewall; with no bulk volume and no doped junctions, subthreshold and junction-generation leakage both collapse. Semimetal Bi/Sb contacts keep on-current above ~20 uA.
why: Leakage tail (<=13 fA) targeted below 0.1 fA; retention 64 ms -> ~10 s, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss by >90%.

title: Minify transistors per bit: VCMA-gated spin-orbit strip with 8 MTJs
idea: Place 8 MTJs on one tungsten-free (Pt-alloy or BiSb) spin-orbit-torque write strip with a single access transistor; a voltage on each MTJ's top electrode lowers its anisotropy (VCMA) so only that MTJ flips when strip current passes, and reads use the same per-MTJ electrode.
why: One transistor per 8 bits, non-volatile, unlimited MTJ endurance, ns writes; ~3x SOT-MRAM density; sidesteps the tungsten chokepoint.

title: Minify die to 4 um thick: 64-high nano-TSV stack
idea: Use wafer-on-wafer bonding and grind each DRAM wafer to an etch stop at about 4 um, then link layers with 0.5 um nano-TSVs instead of 40 um microbumps, stacking 64 dies in about 300 um.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV keep-out area could fall 10-50x and stack height capacity rise 4-5x.
note: W2W thin stacking with nano-TSVs known; 64-high W2W compounds yield.

title: Minify weight replicas: one copy per rack, optically broadcast
idea: Minify the full weight replica each GPU node holds to one copy per rack: weights live once in a pooled memory appliance and are broadcast layer by layer over an optical memory fabric to 72 accelerators in lockstep.
why: Aggregate weight DRAM falls 9-72x, so HBM can go almost entirely to KV and activations.

title: Wafer-scale memory carpet replaces stacked HBM
idea: MAGNIFY the interposer to a full 300 mm passive silicon wafer and MINIFY stack height to one: ~200 single DRAM dies tile the wafer flat around ~20 accelerator dies, so every die is within ~5 mm of compute and needs no TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): uses DDR-cost dies at HBM-class bandwidth; claims ~2-3x lower cost per GB/s.

title: Magnify the die to a whole panel; mesh routes around defects
idea: Never dice: pattern a glass panel as ~10,000 memory tiles joined by a redundant mesh and served as many channels from edge connectors. A panel-level test writes a defect map, and the router fabric bypasses dead tiles, as in wafer-scale processors.
why: Facts 4 and 7: display-fab defect densities stop mattering, and per-die dicing, packaging and known-good-die test disappear; usable panel yield nears 100%.

title: Eliminate periphery from the DRAM fab: array-only wafers bonded per 32 bitlines
idea: Build the DRAM wafer with only cells, vertical access transistors and a 32:1 bitline mux made from the same vertical-channel devices. Each mux output lands on a 0.5-0.8 um hybrid-bond pad to a mature-node CMOS wafer that holds every sense amp, decoder, pump and I/O circuit.
why: Fact 7: the ~49% periphery area leaves the expensive DRAM wafer, and the DRAM flow drops its HKMG periphery and ~6-8 masks. Periphery can be built in U.S. 28-40 nm fabs; cost per bit -25-35%.
note: Xtacking/CBA-style split for DRAM; already on vendor roadmaps.

title: Eliminate immersion water and develop: nanoimprint for periodic layers
idea: Pattern the highly periodic array layers (active, wordline, bitline, capacitor holes) by UV nanoimprint with a master template; there is no immersion water film and no aqueous develop, and only the irregular periphery uses optical litho.
why: Water and capital: removes immersion UPW and developer rinses on array layers and avoids EUV for perfectly periodic patterns; ~5-10x lower litho water combined with dry cleans.

title: Eliminate EUV from periodic array layers: one-master nanoimprint templates
idea: Wordline, bitline, landing-pad and storage-node layers are perfectly periodic, so write one e-beam master per layer, replicate imprint templates from it, and pattern by jet-and-flash nanoimprint, keeping DUV only for the aperiodic periphery.
why: Removes 5-7 EUV exposures (fact 4) from a single-supplier tool drawing ~1 MW each; NIL tools cost and consume roughly a tenth as much.
note: NIL for DRAM already pursued by Canon and memory makers; overlay and defectivity block it.

title: Eliminate the memory package: oxide memory built in the logic die's BEOL
idea: Deposit 4-8 tiers of indium/gallium-free oxide 2T0C cells in the upper metal stack of the accelerator die itself at <=400 C, wired by vias a few microns from the compute that uses them.
why: Removes the PHY, TSVs, interposer, separate wafer and package; access energy falls from 3-4 pJ/bit (HBM) to ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit.
note: Same BEOL oxide 2T0C tiers over logic as I-01148.

title: Eliminate deposited channels in 3D tiers: ion-cut transfer of single-crystal films
idea: For each 3D tier, bond and Smart-Cut a 20-50 nm single-crystal Si film from a donor wafer onto the finished tier below, build the lateral transistors at <=500 C with laser anneal, and reuse the donor dozens of times.
why: Fact 2: gives 3D DRAM a crystalline lateral transistor without Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy and its 26+ tier stack etch, cutting epi tool count and stack-etch risk.
note: Sequential smart-cut monolithic 3D is known (CoolCube); per-tier bond cost and <=500C transistor quality are the doubts.

title: Eliminate TSVs and microbumps: memory tiers deposited directly on HBM base die
idea: Instead of thinning, TSV-drilling and bonding DRAM dies, deposit <=400 C memory tiers monolithically on the HBM logic base die and connect them with ordinary BEOL vias at ~1 um pitch. The stack has no bumps, underfill or die-to-die misalignment to fail.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss, fact 6) and bump fatigue under thermal cycling; via density is ~100x higher.

title: Swap 3D NAND roles: depreciated NAND lines build 3D DRAM
idea: Reverse 3D NAND's roles in a depreciated 64-96-layer NAND line: deposit alternating thin poly-Si and oxide planes as usual, but fill the vertical hole with metal as a wordline gate wrapping each plane, so each plane segment becomes a lateral access transistor whose far end is recessed and filled with a lateral MIM capacitor. The <=5 nm poly planes are fully depleted, and laser anneal enlarges grains to cut leakage.
why: Attacks 'no manufacturable 3D DRAM' (fact 2) and capital intensity (fact 4) on depreciated NAND tools with no EUV; poly-channel leakage limits retention, so it suits a dense short-refresh tier.
note: NAND-process 3D DRAM is actively pursued (e.g., floating-body 3D X-DRAM); poly leakage limits retention.

title: Periphery sandwiched between two array wafers, bitline pairs across bonds
idea: Reverse the CMOS-under-array order: thin the periphery wafer and hybrid-bond array wafers to BOTH faces (one face-down above, one face-up below). Each sense amplifier takes its true bitline from the upper array and its complement/reference bitline from the lower array, so one SA stripe and one decoder set serve two arrays.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): periphery silicon per bit halves (~1.6-1.8x bits per periphery-wafer area); arrays get unrestricted thermal budget; mirrored open-bitline pairs see matched noise.

title: Never dice: wafer-scale DRAM module
idea: Reverse the singulate-then-assemble order: keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory object with on-wafer redundant mesh routing that maps around dead reticles, mounted directly as a rack-level memory sled.
why: Eliminates dicing, per-die packaging, per-die test handlers and substrate cost (~15-25% of DRAM COGS) and HBM-style TSV stacks for capacity tiers.

title: Coaxial cell: capacitor shells wrapped around the vertical transistor pillar
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: in a 4F2 vertical-channel cell, extend the pillar's lower n+ drain upward as a thin outer electrode shell, coat it with high-k, and fill the inter-pillar space with the common plate, while the upper part of the same pillar carries the gate-all-around wordline. Capacitor and transistor live inside one pillar, so there is no storage-node contact or landing-pad layer.
why: Fact 4: 6F2 -> 4F2 (-33% area) and one fewer critical mask; the full pillar sidewall gives ~3-4 fF at AR ~40.
note: Resembles Toshiba's 1988 surrounding-gate-transistor DRAM cell with capacitor around the pillar.

title: Thermally trimmed wafer distortion for cell-pitch wafer-to-wafer bonding
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: map both wafers' in-plane distortion, then heat the top-wafer bond chuck with a zoned IR array so each region expands by exactly the ppm needed just before contact. Residual overlay falls from ~100 nm to <20 nm, enough to bond a separately built capacitor wafer onto ~40 nm-pitch storage pads.
why: Fact 1 and 4: makes capacitor fab and transistor fab separable (different tools, sites, even companies), each with a simpler, cheaper flow.
note: Bonders already compensate distortion; <20 nm overlay is a stretch.

title: Pillar-word organization: one vertical wordline opens exactly one word
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: segment the page vertically instead of horizontally. In a 64-tier capacitorless stack, one vertical wordline pillar gates exactly one cell per tier, and each tier has its own short bitline and latch, so one activation delivers a single 64-bit word up the column.
why: Fact 8 and 9: overfetch drops from 128x to ~1x (energy per useful random bit ~5-10x lower) and only 64 cells are disturbed per activation.

title: Plane-wide charge-pumping refresh restores millions of cells per pulse
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: instead of read-and-rewrite refresh, apply a periodic gate/source pulse pair to an entire 3D wordline plane. Impact ionization adds holes only in bodies already above a threshold potential (the 1s) while 0s recombine slightly, so every cell on the plane is restored at once without being read.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~100x because ~10^6 capacitorless cells refresh per pulse with no sense-amp cycles.
note: Close to known bistable floating-body holding schemes (Zeno-style) restoring whole arrays via bias pulses.

title: Self-selecting chalcogenide crossbar on a former 3D XPoint toolset
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out removes both the separate selector and the phase change: a single amorphous chalcogenide layer whose threshold voltage memorizes the polarity of the last pulse acts as selector and bit at once, built with 2 DUV masks per deck on a toolset like the one that ran 3D XPoint in Lehi, Utah.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; 4F2 per deck with stacked decks, no transistor or capacitor per bit and no EUV, reusing U.S. crosspoint know-how; ~1e9-1e10 endurance needs write buffering (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Taking out: periphery moved to a bitline-pitch bonded logic wafer
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the harmful part: the DRAM wafer keeps only cell mats and bitlines. Sense amps, decoders, refresh logic and the HBM PHY sit on a logic-process wafer hybrid-bonded at ~0.7 um pitch, one bond per bitline pair, so data goes from cell to PHY without crossing a slow DRAM-process wire.
why: Periphery (~49% of the die, fact 7) is recovered for cells, giving ~1.7x bits per DRAM wafer. Logic-speed sense amps and wires cut on-die movement energy ~40% and let VARY drop.

title: Constant-bias shield line between adjacent buried wordlines
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: a narrow buried line held at a fixed negative potential sits between neighboring wordlines where the passing gate used to face the storage node, so the victim never sees the aggressor's 3 V swing or its trap-mediated electron flow.
why: Targets the passing-gate path behind the ~1k hammer threshold, aiming at 10x higher thresholds and lower GIDL for ~6F2 to 6.5F2 area.

title: Horticultural grafting of a crystalline silicon film onto the capacitor array
idea: Grafting joins a separately grown scion to a rootstock; dope and activate a crystalline Si layer on a donor wafer at high temperature, bond it onto the finished capacitor array with a <=350 C Smart-Cut split, and only then pattern access transistors aligned to the landing pads below, using pre-activated or junctionless doping.
why: Gets FEOL-quality low-leakage channels above capacitors made with materials that cannot see >400 C (k~70 perovskites, Ru electrodes), separating the transistor and capacitor thermal budgets and enabling 3D tiers.

title: Ommatidial columns: every vertical bitline gets its own bonded sense amp
idea: As each insect ommatidium wires its photoreceptors to a dedicated neural cartridge, hybrid-bond the 3D array wafer face-to-face to a CMOS wafer at ~0.4 um pitch so every vertical bitline column (64-128 tiers) lands on its own sense amplifier directly beneath, with no global bitlines or column muxes.
why: Periphery 49% and data movement: bitline length equals stack height (~5 um), CBL drops ~10x, periphery leaves the array plane; density +40-60%, read energy ~3x lower.
note: Vertical bitline over bonded CMOS is known art; 0.4 um bond pitch exceeds bitline pitch, few cells per SA.

title: Pearl-oyster self-crucible: silicon melt held in its own frozen skin
idea: An oyster seals an irritant inside its own nacre. Grow Cz ingots in a segmented, water-cooled cold crucible with electromagnetic levitation, so the melt touches only a frozen skull of its own silicon and never quartz.
why: Eliminates high-purity quartz crucibles (Spruce Pine >80%) and lowers oxygen in the crystal; the higher RF energy is offset by a reusable crucible and recycled skull.

title: Dendritic subarrays compute attention scores where the keys live
idea: Neurons integrate synaptic inputs on dendrites before the soma; DRAM subarrays likewise perform bit-serial dot products of a broadcast query against stored keys using charge-sharing logic beside the sense amplifiers, and only top-k indices leave the bank, so no staging copy of the KV cache is needed in HBM.
why: HBM capacity and data movement: removes duplicate KV staging and cuts attention read energy 5-10x.

title: Drip-irrigation valves: column-gated local wordlines stop overfetch
idea: Like drip lines watering only the plants that need it, split each 8 kb row into 32 segments whose local wordline is gated by a BEOL vertical select transistor driven from the column address, so an activate opens only the 256 bits being read.
why: Overfetch/destructive read (~5.9 pJ per useful bit, 128x overfetch): random-access activate energy falls ~10-20x, and row-hammer exposure falls too.

title: Fiber-to-the-mat: photonic waveguide layer replaces TSV I/O
idea: Like fibre-to-the-home replacing copper last miles, put a silicon-nitride waveguide layer in the 3D DRAM base die with micro-ring modulators per mat cluster, carrying data at ~30 fJ/bit straight from local datalines to an off-stack optical link with no global copper datalines, TSV drivers or SerDes.
why: Data movement (facts 5, 6): ~2-3 pJ/bit of global dataline, TSV and PHY energy replaced by ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit optical path; claims ~10x lower energy per bit delivered.

title: Double-stack railcars: memory stacks on both interposer faces
idea: Double-stack container trains double what a track can carry. Mount HBM stacks on both the top and bottom faces of a thin interposer. Dense through-interposer vias link the underside stacks to the compute die's PHY edge, and a two-sided cold-plate sandwich cools them.
why: HBM count is capped by the compute die's shoreline. Using both faces puts ~2x the stacks within the same wire reach, so capacity per accelerator roughly doubles without longer links.

title: Water-slide decal transfer of thin DRAM layers by laser lift-off
idea: Like water-slide decals, build DRAM layers on a sacrificial release film and bond them to a logic wafer with ≤250 C adhesive or hybrid bonding. Laser lift-off then frees the carrier, avoiding Smart Cut's ~500 C split anneal. Repeat for multiple layers.
why: Layers 2-5 um thick allow ~1 um via pitch, versus ~40 um for TSVs: ~100x denser vertical interconnect and far lower pJ/bit than HBM.
note: DRAM front-end temperatures limit release films; similar to W2W bond-thin.

title: PJM-style capacity market for DRAM wafer starts
idea: Like electricity capacity auctions that pay generators 3 years ahead to exist, a cleared exchange sells standardized forward contracts for 'Gb delivered in quarter Q+12'; fabs post the auction-cleared revenue as collateral to finance tool orders, and buyers hedge 4x price swings.
why: Attacks capital intensity and the boom-bust cycle that delays fab builds; forward revenue visibility could cut cost of capital by 3-5 points and pull capacity forward 12-18 months.

title: Vinyl-record stamping: nanoimprint masters for repetitive array layers
idea: Like pressing records from one master, use nanoimprint templates for the highly periodic bitline, storage-node and landing-pad layers, keeping EUV only for irregular periphery layers; templates are cloned from an e-beam master in a domestic mask shop.
why: Removes 3-4 of 5-7 EUV layers, easing the single-supplier EUV chokepoint and cutting litho capex and energy per wafer by ~30-40%.
note: NIL for DRAM already explored; overlay and defectivity are the gate.

title: Catt-spiral wafer-scale DRAM that routes around bad tiles
idea: Revive Anamartic's 1989 Wafer Stack, built on Ivor Catt's self-organizing spiral: every DRAM tile on an uncut wafer tests itself at power-up and links to a good neighbour, forming a chain that skips bad tiles, while a wafer-level redistribution layer brings out wide buses to a host. No dicing, die test, packaging or TSVs.
why: Fact 6 and capital: avoids HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax and 20-30% stack yield loss plus packaging and test lines (~15-25% of DRAM cost); tolerates lower yield, so depreciated 300 mm lines can make bandwidth-rich memory.

title: Compact-synchrotron X-ray proximity lithography for DRAM array layers
idea: Revive the 1990s IBM/NTT X-ray proximity lithography programme, dropped in favour of optics, with compact storage-ring sources (~1 nm wavelength) and 1:1 membrane masks at a few um gap, combined with spacer pitch division to print DRAM's periodic arrays. One ring can feed 10-20 exposure ports.
why: EUV single-supplier risk and capital (Fact 4): a ring plus several X-ray steppers built from U.S. accelerator know-how could print the 5-7 critical layers for less than the ~$200M+ per EUV scanner; risks are 1:1 mask making and overlay.

title: SCALPEL electron projection prints DRAM arrays without EUV or neon
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1990s SCALPEL, which projected a 4x-reduced image of a scattering-contrast membrane mask with 100 keV electrons: modern high-brightness cathodes, aberration-corrected optics and fast resists let it expose DRAM's repetitive array layers in vacuum. Its source is a hot cathode, so there is no excimer neon and no EUV drive-laser helium.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: replaces 5-7 EUV layers with tools targeted at ~$30-50M versus $200M+ for EUV. Risks are space-charge blur and throughput (~20-40 wafers/hour).
note: Space-charge throughput limit killed SCALPEL; still unsolved.

title: VLSI Research Association Redux: U.S. Cooperative for EUV-Free DRAM
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where five rivals shared one joint lab and built the steppers and e-beam tools that won DRAM: a time-boxed U.S. cooperative of a memory maker, tool vendors, hyperscalers and national labs co-develops patent-pooled DUV/nanoimprint DRAM process modules, then disbands so members compete on products.
why: Capital and litho: shares the ~$5B R&D for a non-EUV DRAM flow; Japan's version helped move its DRAM share to a majority within a decade.
note: Sematech/NSTC-style cooperatives exist; non-EUV DRAM focus is the angle.

title: Fair-Market-Value Floor Revived: Offtake Price Corridor for New DRAM Fabs
idea: Revive the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement's fair-market-value price floors as a 10-year price corridor: hyperscalers and the government sign take-or-pay contracts with new-entrant fabs at a floor and a cap per Gb, and a stabilization fund pays the difference during gluts and is refilled during spikes.
why: Capital intensity: the bust half of the cycle is what kills new fabs; a floor cuts the cost of capital by several points and makes a $15B fab bankable.

title: Coincident row-and-column select with dual-gate access transistors
idea: Inverting 'the wordline alone opens a cell': each access transistor gets a back gate tied to a column-group select line so a cell conducts only where the wordline and its column-group line are both high (like core memory's X-Y coincidence), so an activate opens 64-512 bits instead of 8 KB.
why: Cuts the 128x page overfetch toward 2-8x, lowering random-read energy ~5x from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit, and shrinks the set of rows a hammering pattern can disturb.

title: Nanoimprint-patterned array tiers: templates replace EUV exposures
idea: Inverts 'DRAM pitch requires EUV.' Pattern the repetitive cell-field layers of each tier by nanoimprint lithography with C/H/O/Si resists and silica templates, keeping optical litho only for the irregular periphery.
why: Fact 4 and the EUV single-supplier chokepoint: removes 5-7 EUV layers from the array and cuts litho capex per wafer ~50%+.

title: Multi-beam electron writing for DRAM's critical layers
idea: Inverts 'critical layers must be printed by EUV from one supplier': use ~100k-beam electron direct write with silicon field-emitter tip arrays and blanking apertures, dedicated to DRAM's highly repetitive cell layers where pattern data compresses to a small repeat unit.
why: Removes EUV (single supplier, tin source) and masks for 5-7 layers; array regularity makes throughput tractable; target ~3x lower capital per critical layer.
note: MAPPER/IMS-style multibeam; throughput for high-volume DRAM is the historic killer.

title: Bond a sense amp under every 64 cells; shrink capacitors
idea: Inverts 'bitlines must be long and capacitive'. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array at ~250 nm pitch so each local bitline serves only ~64 cells, cutting bitline capacitance from ~60 fF to ~8 fF; the cell then needs only ~1-1.5 fF, a stubby AR ~10:1 capacitor.
why: Breaks the charge wall (fact 1) by changing the transfer ratio, not the charge; removes the deepest etch, ~4 masks and much of the fill tool set.
note: 250 nm hybrid-bond pitch is aggressive.

title: Photonic base die: stacks talk to GPUs by fiber
idea: Invert 'the HBM base die is electrical logic beside the GPU': build the base die on a U.S. monolithic silicon-photonics process (GlobalFoundries Fotonix, New York) so all stack I/O leaves as light on fiber and stacks can sit centimeters to meters away.
why: Removes the silicon interposer and its reticle limit on stacks per GPU; ~1-2 pJ/bit with capacity scaling past 8 stacks.

title: Wafer-scale memory panels: no dicing, defects mapped and coded
idea: Inverts 'memory must be cut into small die for yield': keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory with stitched interconnect, mapping out dead regions and coding around 1% faulty cells, mounted on a cold plate with optical I/O.
why: Cost and packaging: removes dicing, scribe area, per-die packaging and test; ~1-2 TB of memory per wafer for rack-scale pools.

title: AND-gated cell activates only the addressed 64-bit segment
idea: Stack a column-gated vertical transistor in series with each cell's lateral access transistor so a cell reaches its bitline only when both its wordline and its column-select line are high; a random read then disturbs only the 64 addressed cells instead of the 8 kb row.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): activation energy scales with bitlines swung, so ~5.9 pJ per useful bit falls toward ~0.05 pJ; the extra device lives in Z, preserving 4F^2, and fewer opened cells also slows row hammer (fact 9).

title: Five-micron DRAM tiers with bitline-pitch nano-TSVs
idea: TSV diameter is set by copper fill aspect ratio (~10:1) times die thickness, so the TSV tax is really a thickness tax. Thin each DRAM wafer to 5 um on a temporary carrier and stack wafer-on-wafer, allowing 0.5 um vias at ~1 um pitch tucked into subarray gaps instead of a dedicated TSV region.
why: Removes most of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit penalty and keep-out zones while raising vertical bandwidth ~100x (fact 6).

title: Array-only fabs: bond simple cell wafers to foundry-made periphery
idea: From first principles the array is a few periodic layers (wordline, bitline, capacitor) while periphery is generic logic. Split them: specialized array fabs with ~1/3 of a DRAM fab's tool set make cell wafers, logic foundries make periphery wafers, and wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding joins them (as CBA does for 3D NAND).
why: Capital and density: array-fab capex drops ~50%, die area per bit falls up to ~40% with periphery under the array, and each half runs on its optimal process.

title: Layer cake: lateral capacitors carved by HCl vapor in Si/SiGe stacks
idea: Stimulus 'layer cake' -> grow a 32-tier Si/SiGe superlattice, cut one vertical slot with Cl2/HBr, recess the SiGe layers sideways with highly selective HCl vapor to form horizontal pockets, and line each pocket with chloride-ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN to make lateral capacitors stacked like cake layers.
why: Delivers the 26+ tiers needed for 3D DRAM breakeven (fact 2) with one litho step for many tiers (fact 4), with no fluorocarbon etch and no HF.
note: This is mainstream 3D DRAM process flow pursued by all majors.

title: Turtle-shell back plate that retracts the channel during retention
idea: Random stimulus 'turtle shell': pull in when idle, come out to act. A thin-body access channel sits on a buried per-mat back plate; idle mats drive the plate to -1.5 V, raising Vt ~250 mV (about 3.5 decades of subthreshold current), and an activate command returns the plate to 0 V within ~5 ns through a local driver.
why: Gives retention-time high Vt without paying the on-current penalty of a permanently high-Vt device; subthreshold tail down ~1000x, letting refresh run 10x+ slower (fact 3) and shrinking negative-wordline pumps.

title: Reference-only reading room: back-end ReRAM layer holds model weights
idea: Reference books are read but never checked out: deposit HfOx/TaOx ReRAM crossbars (<=400 C) in the accelerator's upper metal stack to hold inference weights written once per deployment (needing only ~1e3-1e4 endurance), leaving DRAM/HBM for KV and activations only.
why: Weights are 40-70% of inference HBM; monolithic back-end storage frees that capacity while sidestepping the unlimited-endurance requirement that killed ReRAM as DRAM.
note: BEOL ReRAM capacity per die (a few GB) is far below model sizes; read bandwidth is unproven.

title: Laundromat: pay-per-wafer-pass tool leasing inside memory fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'laundromat' -> pay per load, never own the washer. Litho, etch and deposition vendors own and maintain tools inside the fab and bill per wafer-pass; they can redeploy tools across fabs as cycles shift.
why: Cuts the memory maker's upfront capex ~40-60%, moves depreciation risk to whoever can redeploy tools, and lowers the entry bar for new DRAM entrants.

title: Bond array-only wafers to US mature-node periphery wafers
idea: Box: 1T1C x vertical-channel access x SA on a separate wafer x wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at ~0.4 um pitch x two Si substrates x US 22-28 nm foundry. The memory fab builds pure arrays with no periphery or HV devices, and an existing U.S. logic foundry builds all SAs, decoders and pumps on a second wafer bonded face-to-face per bitline group.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery's ~49% moves to depreciated U.S. fabs; array die area ~-40%, DRAM-fab capex per bit down, domestic content up.
note: CMOS-bonded-array is industry roadmap; U.S. foundry sourcing is the twist.

title: Nanoimprint plus block-copolymer DSA prints DRAM arrays without excimer lasers
idea: Box [ZrO2 cap | buried-WL Si | voltage SA | standard | CZ Si | jet-and-flash NIL cured by 365 nm LEDs + PS-b-PMMA DSA annealed in N2 + O2/HBr/N2 transfer etch with no Ar dilution]: imprint guide patterns at 2x pitch from e-beam-written masters, then let the block copolymer split them into 12 nm honeycomb holes and lines.
why: Neon (ArF laser buffer gas) and EUV (whose CO2 drive laser runs on a helium mix): removes all array-layer excimer and EUV exposures; NIL tool capex is ~1/4 of EUV and power ~1/10.

title: Nanoimprint-only array layers, DUV periphery: EUV-free 1T1C DRAM
idea: Box: Si-capacitor charge x buried-channel access x voltage sense amp x 2D monolithic x 300 mm Si x jet-and-flash nanoimprint. The strictly periodic array layers (active, buried WL, BL, storage-node contact, capacitor holes) are imprinted from e-beam-written masters into jetted resist, while the irregular, relaxed-pitch periphery stays on DUV immersion; overlay is held by a magnification-actuated template chuck and in-situ moire alignment marks.
why: Litho-bound capital (fact 4): replaces 5-7 EUV layers with imprint tools at roughly 1/4-1/5 of EUV capex and ~90% less litho energy; claims 20-30% lower wafer cost if imprint defectivity reaches <0.1/cm2.

title: Cold repeated ion-cut tier stacking with microwave dopant activation
idea: Box: gain-cell or capacitor charge x planar single-crystal Si transistor per tier x standard sensing x 8-16 tiers via layer transfer x Si x hydrogen ion-cut plus microwave anneal below 450 C. Each tier is a single-crystal film transferred from a reusable donor onto the previous patterned tier, exposed with the same DUV masks, and activated by microwaves that couple to dopants without cooking lower tiers.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) with single-crystal channels and reused masks, so bits/area scale with tiers at flat mask count; risk is per-tier yield and reaching the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Per-bitline hybrid bonds move all sense amps to logic
idea: Box: vertical-channel 1T1C array x VCT access x sense amplifiers on 5 nm logic wafer x 0.8 um-pitch Cu-Cu bonds per bitline pair x Si x wafer-to-wafer bonding. The memory wafer becomes ~95% array because every bitline pair lands on its own bond pad and is sensed, decoded and repaired on a separate logic wafer stacked face-to-face.
why: Periphery 49% of die (fact 7): roughly doubles bits per memory-wafer area and puts periphery on fast logic transistors, also shortening the data path to ~0.1 pJ/bit.
note: Industry already moving to CMOS-bonded-array DRAM; bitline-level bond density is aggressive.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM slab with redundancy routing fabric
idea: Box: 1T1C DRAM x standard x standard x on-wafer mesh network with spare-tile routing x whole 300 mm wafer x no dicing. The entire DRAM wafer serves as one memory, with a reconfigurable mesh that routes around bad tiles, face-to-face bonded to a wafer-scale compute or optical I/O wafer.
why: Packaging cost and data movement: no dicing, bumping or per-die packaging; ~1-2 TB per wafer at ~0.3 pJ/bit; yield handled by redundancy instead of scrap.

title: Split-fab: periphery on legacy partner wafers, arrays on DRAM wafers
idea: Box[Integration=wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond x Fab=array-only DRAM wafer + periphery on depreciated 28-40 nm logic fab x Owner=two-company tolling x Scale=distributed]: the DRAM fab patterns only cells, and partner logic fabs (including U.S. 300 mm legacy lines) make sense amps, decoders and I/O that are bonded face-to-face.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die; moving it off DRAM wafers frees ~40% more leading-edge DRAM wafer area for bits and moves value to U.S. legacy fabs.

title: Every vertical bitline bonded down to its own generous sense amp
idea: Po: the sense amp is bigger than the cells it serves. Fabricate only arrays on a litho-light 'array wafer' with vertical bitlines spanning 64+ tiers, and all sense amps and decoders on a separate logic wafer, hybrid-bonded at ~0.5 um pitch so each bond carries one vertical bitline to a large, low-offset sense amp.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and capital: array fab drops logic-transistor steps (~30% fewer masks); larger matched sense amps (offset <5 mV) let Cs shrink, easing the charge wall.

title: Retired 3D NAND lines prototype 3D DRAM via replacement-gate recess
idea: Po: a NAND fab is a DRAM fab. Older 64/96-layer 3D NAND lines already run oxide/nitride stacks, high-AR hole etch, lateral nitride recess and metal fill; reuse that replacement-gate recess to carve lateral capacitor cavities and channel slots for horizontal-cell 3D DRAM, filling with Mo instead of W.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM yet (fact 2): paid-off tools already proven beyond 26 tiers; no new fab and less tungsten.

title: Whole-wafer memory from an old DRAM line, never diced
idea: Po: the chip is the wafer. Run a 2x-nm DRAM flow with reticle stitching and per-reticle redundancy, keep the 300 mm wafer whole (~0.5-1 TB of bits), and bond it face-to-face to a wafer of compute or switch chiplets, skipping dicing, packaging and per-die test.
why: Packaging/test and data movement (fact 5): removes ~15-25% of cost in packaging and test; wafer-level links <1 pJ/bit; uses a depreciated fab.

title: DUV quad-patterning with a doubled overlay budget in mature fabs
idea: Po: make leading-edge memory in a trailing-edge fab. U.S. 28-40 nm-class fabs with immersion DUV run SAQP for the cell layers with overlay tolerances relaxed 2x; the resulting systematic misaligned contacts (~0.5-1% of cells) are mapped and corrected as erasures.
why: U.S. manufacturability and EUV independence (fact 4): ~16-18 nm-class cell density from existing U.S. tooling at roughly a third of an EUV DRAM fab's capex.
note: CXMT-style DUV multipatterning is known; overlay misses cluster rather than scatter randomly.

title: Nanoimprint stamps for DRAM array layers, DUV for periphery
idea: Po: masks are rubber stamps. The highly periodic array layers (active, buried wordline, bitline, storage-node contact) are patterned by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from e-beam-written master templates, while irregular periphery stays on ArF immersion with mix-and-match alignment.
why: Imprint tools cost a fraction of EUV and use ~10x less power; array redundancy absorbs NIL's isolated defects; attacks capital intensity and energy.

title: Multi-beam e-beam direct write for cut and contact layers
idea: Po: a million pens instead of one camera. Mask-writer-class multi-beam e-beam columns (~250k beamlets) write only the sparse cut and contact layers directly on wafers while dense lines come from spacer patterning; no masks are needed, so micro-fabs and fast design spins become economical.
why: Cut/contact layers are the ones that otherwise force EUV; writing them maskless avoids EUV and multi-million-dollar mask sets, with throughput suited to ~5-10k wafers/month micro-fabs; attacks capital and U.S. micro-fab viability.

title: Pay-per-wafer-pass equipment leasing from toolmakers
idea: Po: the toolmaker owns the fab. DUV scanner, etch and deposition OEMs keep ownership of their tools inside the DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass with uptime guarantees; the operator carries only building, people and materials.
why: Moves depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) off the entrant's balance sheet and ties OEM revenue to yield and uptime; cuts the entry ticket for a 20k-wafer fab by billions; attacks capital intensity.

title: Vertical-channel 4F2 cells at relaxed DUV pitch
idea: Po: density comes from area, not pitch. A vertical-channel transistor with buried bitline and surrounding-gate wordline gives a 4F2 cell; at F=18 nm (reachable by SAQP on ArF immersion) the cell is 1,296 nm2, equal to a 6F2 cell at ~14.7 nm, a node that otherwise needs EUV.
why: Matches next-node density using DUV only; attacks litho capital and EUV dependence.

title: Charge-redistribution SAR sensing stores three levels per cell
idea: Worse: spend all margin storing a single bit per cell. Flip: share the bitline charge onto binary-weighted reference capacitors in a two-step successive-approximation sense amp that resolves three charge levels (1.58 bits/cell), Gray-coded so a one-level slip becomes a single-bit ECC-correctable error.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per cell area if the signal margin holds.

title: Sideways cell: film thickness, not lithography, sets every dimension
idea: Worse: make every critical dimension depend on optical resolution. Flip: rotate the access transistor 90 degrees so gate length, channel thickness and capacitor dielectric are ALD films grown on the sidewalls of coarse 80 nm DUV trenches. Litho only cuts trenches; Angstrom-precise deposition 'prints' the sub-10 nm features.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): scaling continues by deposition without EUV, toward ~4F2 at relaxed F.

title: UCIe DRAM chiplet standard making any fab's die package-fungible
idea: Worse: make every HBM a bespoke co-design locked to one GPU vendor. Flip: define an open DRAM chiplet footprint and protocol over UCIe so a qualified DRAM die from any maker drops into any accelerator package and packagers can mix suppliers per lot.
why: Makes AI memory supply fungible, lets second-tier and U.S. fabs sell into AI packages, and offers lateral chiplets that avoid the TSV tax.

title: Embargo periphery: 65 nm US wafers bonded under the array
idea: A Soviet engineer denied EUV builds what the old fab can make. Put all sense amps, drivers and decoders on a separate 65-40 nm DUV wafer from an existing U.S. trailing-edge fab, relax their pitch with 4:1 bitline multiplexers on the array wafer, and hybrid-bond the two at ~1 um pitch.
why: Takes periphery off the EUV wafer (fact 4), uses depreciated idle U.S. capacity (U.S. manufacturability), and returns ~49% of array-wafer area to cells (fact 7).

title: 2050 engineer's memory utility: optical DDR pools metered like electricity
idea: In 2050 memory is a metered utility: put commodity DDR dies on co-packaged optical chiplets in a memory sled 1-2 m away and reach it over WDM links at ~1 pJ/bit and ~20 ns of flight time, which replaces most HBM with cheap DRAM shared by many accelerators.
why: Escapes HBM's 3x area/bit and TSV yield loss: claimed 2-3x cheaper bits for capacity-bound AI workloads, plus pooling that cuts stranded memory 25%+.

title: Fisherman's net: passive optical multicast of shared weights
idea: One net catches many fish: one memory chiplet's optical transmitter feeds a passive 1:8 splitter, so a shared weight tensor read once from DRAM reaches eight accelerators together instead of being duplicated in eight HBM stacks.
why: Cuts duplicated model copies across GPUs (common in inference serving): claimed 3-8x less DRAM capacity for weights, and one read's energy serves many consumers.

title: Farmer's grain co-op: OEMs jointly own a take-or-pay DRAM fab
idea: Thinking like a Midwest grain cooperative, mid-size OEMs (PC, auto, telecom, tier-2 cloud) form a member-owned memory co-op that signs 7-year take-or-pay offtake for a 40k-wafer/month fab and pledges those contracts as collateral for project-finance debt. Members get bits at cost-plus with patronage dividends instead of paying spot prices.
why: Capital intensity and price volatility: turns $15B of equity risk into contract-backed debt at a cost of capital ~2-3 points lower, makes a new U.S. fab bankable, and shields members from 4x price spikes.
note: Same pooled-offtake shared-fab mechanism as I-08252, with project-finance framing.

title: Quilter uses whole cloth: undiced wafer-scale memory cassettes
idea: A quilter works with whole cloth. Skip dicing, packaging and DIMM PCBs: ship whole 300 mm DRAM wafers with wafer-level redundancy routing and edge contacts, stacked 20 deep in a liquid-cooled cassette that plugs into a rack CXL switch.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: one wafer holds ~1.5-2 TB, so a 20-wafer cassette is ~35 TB in ~4 L, versus hundreds of liters of server DIMM slots. Packaging, PCB and per-die test savings (~15-20% of module cost) pay for the redundancy.

title: One hole mask defines every tier's annular capacitor in 3D
idea: Exascale machines need TB-class capacity; borrowing 3D NAND punch-and-plug, a single deep-hole mask through a 48-tier Si/SiGe stack is followed by lateral recess etches that carve an annular storage node and gate in every tier self-aligned to the hole, all tied to a shared vertical bitline.
why: Beats fact 2's 26+ tier break-even with only one critical mask for all tiers, collapsing litho cost per bit (fact 4); recess-etch uniformity across 48 tiers is the risk.
note: Similar to industry vertical-bitline 3D DRAM concepts.

title: Rad-hard SOI trick: buried plate swung negative in standby
idea: Satellite SOI chips tune transistors through the substrate; build the array over a buried plate (SOI or deep n-well) under all access channels and drive it to about -2 V whenever a subarray idles, raising Vt ~150-200 mV, then to 0 to +0.5 V when the bank opens to boost drive current.
why: Fact 3: ~10-50x lower subthreshold leakage in idle subarrays lengthens refresh intervals by a similar factor, and active-mode forward bias lets the access device shrink; cost is the plate charging energy per bank open.

title: Trusted-foundry legacy fabs supply U.S. DRAM periphery dies
idea: Defense programs already fund trusted 90-45 nm U.S. fabs; a policy program pays these lines to make DRAM periphery and base dies (SAs, decoders, I/O) for hybrid bonding to array wafers, backed by offtake guarantees from federal and hyperscaler buyers.
why: U.S. manufacturability: roughly half of DRAM die function made domestically with no EUV, using existing capex.

title: Pixel-detector bonding: every 16 bitlines get their own sense-amp bond
idea: Particle-physics pixel detectors bond each sensor pixel to its own readout channel; hybrid-bond the DRAM array wafer at ~0.4 um pitch so every group of 16 bitlines, muxed by an in-array selector, lands on its own sense amplifier on a separately made logic wafer. The array wafer then holds no sense amps, decoders or I/O at all.
why: Periphery ~49% of the die (fact 7) moves to a cheap logic wafer: ~2x array-wafer area per bit, and logic-process sense amps run faster at lower voltage (fact 10).
note: CMOS-bonded-array / cell-over-periphery is already pursued for 4F2 DRAM.

title: Whole DRAM wafer bonded onto a wafer-scale accelerator
idea: Wafer-scale computers already route around defects; hybrid-bond an undiced 300 mm DRAM wafer face-to-face onto a wafer-scale accelerator with bonds at every compute tile and map out bad mats in the routing fabric. Each tile reads the DRAM directly above it over millimeter-scale wires.
why: Data movement (fact 5): 3-4 pJ/bit HBM to ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit; HBM TSV tax (fact 6), dicing and packaging removed; ~1 TB at multi-TB/s per wafer.

title: Irvine-style edge-metallized die cubes replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: 1990s military/space 'cube' memories laminated thinned dies and wired them along a ground, metallized side face. Stack 16-32 thinned DRAM dies with edge-routed RDL fans, polish and metallize the cube face at ~10 um pitch, then turn the cube on its side and hybrid-bond that face to a logic base die or interposer.
why: Eliminates TSV keep-out area, TSV etch/fill tools and TSV yield loss (behind HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield hit); dies can be near-standard DDR dies with an edge RDL.
note: Irvine Sensors cubes are prior art at coarse pitch.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM plane with stitched redundancy routing
idea: Wafer-scale engines built for national labs never dice. Leave a DRAM wafer whole, add a stitched cross-reticle RDL mesh, laser-fuse out bad dies and route around them, then face-bond it to a wafer of logic tiles or use it as a 1-2 TB memory board with on-wafer wiring.
