why: Removes dicing, per-die packaging and handling (~15-25% of back-end cost) and gives terabyte-scale memory over on-wafer links at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit instead of board traces.

title: Stacked-image-sensor split: DRAM sense amps live on logic wafer
idea: Sony's stacked image sensors keep only pixels on top and put ADCs on a logic wafer below, joined by per-block hybrid bonds. Build a DRAM wafer with only cells and bitlines, and hybrid-bond each subarray's local I/O at ~1 um pitch to sense amps, decoders and datapath on an advanced logic wafer underneath.
why: Removes the DRAM global datapath and off-chip I/O (wires shrink from mm to um) and moves periphery (~49% of die) to efficient logic; ~10x lower energy per access if bond capacitance stays below ~1 fF.

title: Contact-lens monolithic memory tiers grown directly over logic
idea: A smart contact lens must fit a whole system in ~1 mm2, which forces monolithic 3D. Grow low-temperature memory tiers sequentially in the BEOL above logic, linked by 100 nm inter-layer vias at 1e7-1e8 per mm2, so each mat has its own micron-length vertical path to compute at ~0.3 V swing.
why: Micron wires and per-mat parallelism give ~10-30 fJ/bit movement, >10x below HBM; via density ~1e4x TSVs removes the bandwidth/beachfront limit.

title: Two gates in series on one pillar: stack-effect leakage suppression
idea: Scale jump that folds logic's standby 'transistor stacking' trick into one vertical-channel access pillar with two independently driven gate segments (upper and lower wordline); both turn on for access, but in hold the intermediate node floats up a few hundred mV, putting the upper device at negative VGS with reduced DIBL.
why: Subthreshold leakage tail (fact 3): the stack effect cuts off-current 10-30x, enabling 4F^2 vertical cells with ~1 s retention.

title: Retool idle 3D-NAND channel-hole lines into oxide gain-cell strings
idea: Shift the time horizon to the NAND glut cycle: 3D-NAND fabs already etch 200+ tier channel holes and staircases. Swap the charge-trap ONO for an ALD oxide-semiconductor channel and use the word-plane stack as write and read gates of 2T0C gain cells strung vertically, so existing $10B+ lines can run DRAM-class memory during NAND downturns.
why: Capital intensity and 3-5-year fab lead times (fact 4): converts existing tier-stacking capacity to DRAM-class memory in ~12-18 months.
note: NAND-like 3D DRAM pursued (NEO X-DRAM, Macronix); series-string gain-cell read path is problematic.

title: Mixed-use zoning: a compute tier after every eight memory tiers
idea: Copy urban mixed-use zoning into monolithic 3D: add a thin-film logic tier (adders, popcount, comparators) after every 8 memory tiers, so reductions happen within ~1 um of the data and only results travel down the stack.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): moving a bit 1 um costs fJ, versus pJ to reach HBM; targets 10-30x less energy for reduction-heavy AI kernels.
note: Monolithic 3D compute-in-memory (N3XT) known; thin-film logic is weak and n-type only.

title: Rent idle U.S. logic back-end lines for monolithic memory layers
idea: Turn spare back-end-of-line capacity at U.S. logic fabs into memory capacity: after the logic interconnect, add 6-10 oxide-semiconductor gain-cell layers at <400 C using existing BEOL tools and ArF litho, so memory rides on logic wafers already in production.
why: Near-zero new capex adds supply without a DRAM fab; memory directly above compute cuts data movement (Fact 5).

title: Sense-amp-direct bonding: data exits each bank vertically, skipping global I/O
idea: Jump the data path from millimeter global I/O lines to micrometer vertical hops: each bank's sense-amp stripe carries its own fine-pitch hybrid-bond field to the logic die above, so column data leaves exactly where it is sensed. Column muxes, global data lines and the center-strip I/O block disappear.
why: On-die global data movement is a large slice of the 3-4 pJ/bit (fact 5) and of periphery (fact 7); ~40-60% lower access energy and ~10-15% die area returned to cells.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory racks permit 1 fF capacitors
idea: Scale+temperature jump (cell -> rack-level cryostat): at 77 K junction and GIDL leakage fall by orders of magnitude, so retention runs from hours to days. Size cells for ~1 fF (shallower, AR ~20:1 pillars) and operate whole LN2-cooled memory racks almost refresh-free.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall and the refresh tail together: capacitor etch depth drops ~3x and refresh energy almost vanishes; cooling overhead is amortized at rack scale.
note: Same 77 K retention mechanism.

title: Continuous Czochralski: one crucible pulls 8 ingots instead of one
idea: Time shift of crucible life: adapt solar-industry continuous CZ (granular polysilicon fed in while pulling) to 300 mm prime wafers, so one crucible survives several ingot pulls over ~2 weeks.
why: Crucible consumption, and the Spruce Pine quartz it embodies, falls ~5-8x per wafer, and puller utilization rises ~20%.

title: 1T-8C ferroelectric stack: plate-line selection and twin-plate reference sensing
idea: Failure mined: Ramtron's FeRAM never shrank because each bit needed its own transistor (1T1C, often 2T2C). Fix: stack 8 HZO capacitors vertically on one access transistor's storage node, each on its own plate line, and read one by pulsing its plate while the other 7 float. A twin dummy plate provides a matched reference that cancels coupling from the unselected capacitors on the shared node.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 bits per transistor on a ~4F^2 vertical-channel footprint = ~12x bits/mm^2, with all 8 capacitors made from one deposition stack and one hole etch.

title: Nantero NRAM, fixed: BEOL-only CNT fab hybrid-bonded to logic
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled because fabs feared CNT contamination of front-end lines and integration took a decade. Fabricate the CNT switching layer in a dedicated BEOL-only fab on wafers carrying only select transistors, then hybrid-bond them to logic, so no mainline fab ever touches nanotubes.
why: A nonvolatile, refresh-free, capacitorless tier replacing part of DRAM, buildable in small, cheap U.S. BEOL fabs.
note: NRAM already BEOL-compatible; density and speed, not contamination, are the real blockers.

title: Mapper's throughput death fixed: e-beam writes only cuts on gratings
idea: Mapper's massively multi-beam e-beam lithography went bankrupt in 2018 because writing whole layers was too slow (~10 wafers per hour). Fix: use multibeam only for the sparse cuts and contact holes on top of self-aligned quadruple-patterned gratings (DRAM arrays are highly periodic), so the beams expose ~1-2% of the area and effective throughput rises ~50x.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: replaces 2-4 of DRAM's EUV layers with tools costing a fraction of a $200M scanner, ending single-supplier lock-in for those layers.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO gate stack buys 0.3 V higher access Vt
idea: Effect: ferroelectric negative capacitance. Insert a 3-4 nm HZO layer capacitance-matched to the buried-channel access transistor's gate oxide so the stack amplifies surface potential and swings below 60 mV/dec in the switching window; raise Vt ~0.3 V (up to ~5 decades less subthreshold current) while keeping on-current at equal or lower wordline voltage.
why: Leakage tail and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): 10-100x retention, or wordline from 3 V to ~2.2 V (~45% less wordline CV2).
note: Steady-state NC benefit contested.

title: Ba: barium-titanate Pockels modulators replace DRAM DQ SerDes
idea: Bond epitaxial BaTiO3 electro-optic ring modulators at the DRAM periphery edge so each data group modulates light directly from the column data bus at 25-50 Gb/s, eliminating high-swing DQ drivers, termination and most SerDes logic.
why: DDR5 I/O at 10-20 pJ/bit (fact 5) could fall to ~1 pJ/bit and pad area shrinks; barium is abundant (barite).

title: Si: laser-crystallized silicon pre-amp per bitline segment, excimer-free
idea: Deposit a-Si (SiH4 in H2) over the bitlines and crystallize it with a diode-pumped solid-state 532 nm laser instead of a XeCl excimer (xenon plus neon fill) to form a source-follower pre-amp on every 32-cell bitline segment, which then drives a long global bitline.
why: Hierarchical gain lets 4x longer bitlines share each SA stripe, cutting SA count ~4x (fact 7) and decoupling the needed Cs from bitline length (fact 1).
note: Laser-crystallized poly-Si preamp variability over the array is the doubt.

title: Hydrogen ion-slice stacking of 32 single-crystal silicon tiers
idea: Implant H+ into a pre-doped donor Si wafer, oxide-bond it onto the growing stack at <=350 C, cleave at the hydrogen plane, CMP, pattern only the lateral access transistors, and repeat ~32 times, reusing each donor ~10x; all capacitors are then formed by one vertical etch through every tier.
why: Removes the 3D-DRAM lateral-transistor blocker (fact 2) by giving every tier bulk-grade mobility and a tight leakage tail (fact 3), without the strain limit of Si/SiGe epi stacks; targets 26+ crystalline tiers and ~3-4x bits per wafer vs planar 1z.
note: Sequential smart-cut known (CoolCube); 32 bond/cleave/CMP cycles cost is the doubt.

title: Copper hybrid bonds: stacked SRAM working set, DRAM demoted to cold store
idea: Cu-Cu hybrid bonding at <5 um pitch stacks four ~2 GB SRAM dies directly on the accelerator, so the hot working set (activations, hot KV, hot weights) is served at ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit over vertical bonds; DRAM becomes a compressed write-back cold tier that can be cheaper LPDDR or flash-backed.
why: Most accesses drop from 3-15 pJ/bit to ~0.2 pJ/bit (15-50x lower energy per access), and per-device DRAM shrinks because DRAM no longer has to supply bandwidth, only capacity (energy, cost/bit).

title: Tantalum charge wells: matrix-vector products by DRAM charge sharing
idea: Tantalum capacitors pack charge densely; weights sit in DRAM subarrays as charge, and activating several wordlines at once while bitlines are driven with input-coded pulses sums charge on each bitline in proportion to a weighted sum, read by a 4-bit ADC per column group, so GEMV happens in the array and only results leave it.
why: Only outputs cross the I/O and no row is read out bit by bit, so energy per MAC-equivalent access falls 10-30x, and low-precision analog weights need fewer cells per weight (energy, density).

title: Cold-source access transistor halves wordline voltage
idea: IFR: a switch that turns off infinitely sharply. Put a semimetal or graphene cold source on the bitline side of a vertical access transistor so injected carriers have a truncated thermal tail, giving ~30-40 mV/dec; the same on/off ratio then needs about half the gate swing.
why: Facts 3 and 10: VPP drops from ~3 V to ~1.5 V for ~4x less wordline CV^2 and smaller charge pumps, or at the same VPP the leakage tail drops ~100x and refresh becomes rare.

title: Material-contrast self-alignment lets each layer inherit the one below
idea: Ideal: one lithography step for the whole cell stack. Closest: after the active area is defined, each later layer (wordline cap, bitline, storage contact) is placed by selective deposition and selective etch chemistries keyed to the material contrast of the layer beneath, so only line-cut masks remain.
why: Fact 4: critical masks per cell ~7 to ~3, zero edge-placement error between inherited layers, ~50% less EUV dependence.

title: Resonant-tunneling-diode latch makes the DRAM cell bistable
idea: Ideal: a capacitor cell that never needs refresh. Closest: a pair of series resonant tunneling diodes on each storage node forms a negative-differential-resistance bistable that holds the node at '0' or '1' against leakage with picoamp standby current, while the cell is still read and written through its single access transistor.
why: Fact 3: eliminates refresh entirely (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) if RTD peak-to-valley ratios can be made uniform across billions of cells.
note: Tunneling SRAM (TI, 1990s) did this; RTD uniformity and standby current killed it.

title: Magnetoelectric BiFeO3 voltage-written magnet with TMR read
idea: Scarcity rule: no current may cross any insulator during a write. Ferroelectric switching of a BiFeO3 layer rotates its antiferromagnetic order, which exchange-couples to the CoFe free layer of an MTJ, so a ~100 mV gate pulse writes and TMR reads; charge only moves capacitively.
why: Attojoule-class nonvolatile writes (facts 3, 10) with no barrier stress; BiFeO3 fatigue and switching speed must reach 1e15 cycles and ns.
note: Same BFO voltage-written magnet.

title: Same capacitor, +58% bits: tri-level cells with stepped-reference sensing
idea: Limit: no new cell and no new litho, only periphery. Store three charge levels (0, 1/2, 1) and sense in two steps: first against a +1/3 reference, then against a -1/3 reference created by coupling a small trim capacitor, packing 3 bits into 2 cells.
why: Density and cost per bit: +58% bits from the same array, paid for by ~20% more SA area and tighter margins, so it works best paired with offset trimming.

title: Wafer-scale stitched DRAM plane bonded to wafer-scale compute
idea: Limit: no reticle boundary and no dicing. Stitch array tiles across a full 300 mm wafer with redundant tile routing, then hybrid-bond the whole memory wafer face-to-face onto a wafer-scale compute wafer.
why: Facts 5 and 6: tens of PB/s of vertical bandwidth at sub-0.5 pJ/bit with no package, interposer or TSV overhead.

title: Zero-EUV array: one grating mask plus spacer cascade
idea: Constraint: no EUV anywhere in the array. Print a single ~80 nm-pitch ArF-immersion grating per direction and derive active, buried wordline, bitline and storage-node contacts by self-aligned spacer quadrupling with tone inversion at the crossings, leaving only two relaxed-pitch cut masks at the array edge.
why: Fact 4: removes the 5-7 EUV exposures and ~60% of array masks; est. -25-35% wafer cost and no dependence on the single EUV supplier.

title: Array-only DRAM wafer bonded to periphery wafer at subarray IO
idea: Scarcity: the DRAM die may contain zero periphery. Build a wafer of only cell mats plus local sense amps, expose each subarray's local I/O lines and wordline-driver inputs as ~0.5 um-pitch hybrid-bond pads, and bond it face-to-face to a cheap logic wafer carrying decoders, column logic, DLL and I/O.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): ~1.6-1.8x bits per DRAM wafer, and periphery moves to faster, cheaper logic with shorter on-die data paths.

title: Undiced wafer-scale memory slabs with route-around redundancy
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Never dice the DRAM wafer: add a top metal mesh that routes around bad reticles, then mount whole 300 mm wafers as a stack of 10 slabs with edge connectors and liquid cooling between slabs.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packages, test sockets and module PCBs (~15-30% of module cost); a 10-wafer slab holds ~10x the bits per rack U of DIMMs at similar cost.
note: Same never-dice route-around core as I-05862; whole-wafer warp, cooling and connectors are hard.

title: No private stockpiles: Strategic DRAM Reserve buying known-good die
idea: Self-imposed limit: only the state may hoard. A federal reserve buys wafers and known-good dies during price troughs, stores them under nitrogen, and releases them in spikes under a price-trigger rule, as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve does.
why: Damps the 4x price swings and gives makers a buyer of last resort in downturns, which supports steady capex.

title: Photonic periphery wafer bonded under the DRAM cell array
idea: 4F^2 VCT and 3D DRAM programmes (Samsung 10a VCT, VS-DRAM, SK hynix VG) all wafer-bond the periphery to the cell array. Here that periphery wafer is a monolithic CMOS + silicon-photonics process: 45 nm-class SOI with microring modulators, Ge photodiodes and WDM filters. It carries the global periphery (command decode, SerDes, ECC and codecs from B4-01/07) plus 8-16-wavelength microring transceivers. Sense amps and local drivers stay on the cell wafer, bonded to the photonic wafer at 1-10 um pitch. Each die exits through 2-4 waveguides edge-coupled to fibre or a photonic interposer, with an external laser source. Memory can then sit 1-10 m away on cool sleds (B4-13) or in pools. For capacity tiers, HBM's silicon interposer and TSV I/O tax disappear.
why: ~2-3 pJ/bit at metre reach (vs HBM 3.4-3.5 pJ/bit at millimetre reach and DDR5 ~10-20 pJ/bit), using DDR-density dies at ~1x DDR5 wafer per bit instead of HBM's 3x.

title: Wireless-charger resonance recycles memory-bus switching energy
idea: Adapted from resonant inductive phone chargers: a wide HBM-style bus is driven as part of an LC tank with on-interposer spiral inductors. Line capacitance charges and discharges sinusoidally, and most of the CV^2 energy returns to the tank instead of being burned in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data movement (facts 5, 10): resonant drive can recover 50-80% of switching energy on wide, clock-like buses.

title: Eliminate thermal generation leakage: wide-bandgap SiC or GaN storage junctions
idea: Eliminate silicon's thermal generation current: build the storage node and access junction in 4H-SiC or GaN (3.3-3.4 eV), where intrinsic carrier density is ~1e-8 cm-3 vs ~1e10 in Si, so junction and GIDL leakage fall by many orders of magnitude; 1990s SiC DRAM test cells already held charge for hours or more at room temperature.
why: Stretches retention from 64 ms to hours (fact 3), letting Cs drop to ~1 fF and the pillar to AR ~15 (fact 1); leans on the U.S.-strong SiC power-device supply chain; risk is SiC lithographic scaling and defect density.

title: Make flash leak on purpose: direct-tunnel nanocrystal storage
idea: Reverse flash's priorities: grow silicon nanocrystals on a 2 nm tunnel oxide in a 180 nm logic flow (Tiwari-style, 1996) so electrons enter and leave by direct tunneling in ~10-100 ns at +/-2-3 V with no Fowler-Nordheim damage, trading retention (seconds to hours) for near-unlimited endurance; the bit is a threshold shift read non-destructively.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3,8): 1T capacitor-free cell with >=1000x DRAM retention and NDRO; risk is Vt window and endurance beyond 1e12.
note: Tiwari 1996 nanocrystal memory prior art; Vt window and endurance the issues.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC-tank data bus recycling switching energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: make each wide-bus line part of an LC tank with an inductor in the interposer, so the line rings sinusoidally at the clock rate and data is encoded by conditional phase injection. Energy swings between L and C instead of being dumped on every toggle.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): 3-5x lower IO energy on capacitive 1-2k-bit buses.

title: Nanoconfined monatomic antimony phase-change cell that cannot segregate
idea: Fill 5 nm TiN-lined pores with pure Sb by RT sputtering; confinement stabilizes the amorphous phase, and melt-quench of ~100 nm3 costs ~10 fJ. A single element cannot phase-separate, which removes the composition drift that kills Ge-Sb-Te endurance.
why: Attacks PCM's endurance failure mode at its root (no elemental migration), with fJ writes in a stackable cross-point (density).

title: Resonant LC adiabatic signaling on interposer memory wires
idea: First principles: abrupt switching burns CV^2/2 per transition no matter the driver, but adiabatic charging over time T burns only (RC/T)*CV^2. Pattern thin-film spiral inductors in the interposer RDL so each HBM lane group forms an LC tank with its own wire capacitance, ringing at the bus rate; data selects which wires join the resonant phase, and their charge returns to the tank instead of to ground.
why: Attacks data-movement energy (fact 5): with RC/T~0.05 on a 5 mm interposer wire, link energy could fall from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit (5-10x).

title: Po the cell latches like a light switch: implanted vertical thyristor
idea: Po: 'memory that holds itself like a light switch.' Extracted: build a p-n-p-n thyristor vertically in bulk silicon with stacked high-energy implants under a 180 nm pillar, gated by one wordline; the cell latches on or off with no capacitor or high-k and holds data with a tiny standby bias instead of refresh.
why: Removes capacitor materials (Hf, Zr, TiN) and the charge wall; a ~4F2 vertical cell lets a 180 nm line reach useful density, with refresh replaced by low hold current.
note: T-RAM/VLT tried; variability and hold current.

title: Resonant LC tank bus recycles CV2 energy every clock cycle
idea: Match the bus to a resonant timescale: inductors integrated in the interposer let the wide bus's wire capacitance swing inside an LC tank, with data encoded on an adiabatic sinusoidal clock-power line. Charge sloshes back between L and C each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Breaks the CV2 floor on interface energy (facts 5, 10): ~50-70% lower energy for wide parallel memory buses.

title: Strain-switched magnetostrictive nanomagnets written by a piezo voltage
idea: Effect walk: inverse magnetostriction (Villari effect). An elliptical 50x40 nm Co-Fe nanomagnet on an AlScN piezo layer receives a 0.2-V strain pulse that rotates its easy axis 90 degrees; releasing the strain at the precessional half-period toggles magnetization, and an MTJ reads it.
why: Capacitive strain write costs ~1 aJ-1 fJ with no current, versus ~100 fJ STT and ~10 fJ DRAM cell+bitline: >=10x lower, non-volatile so no refresh; uses Co-Fe instead of Ga- or rare-earth magnetostrictors.

title: Adiabatic ramped access recycles bitline charge through resonant LC tanks
idea: Effect walk: adiabatic charging, where dissipation scales as (RC/T) x CV2. Make the cell-plus-bitline part of an LC tank using 3D BEOL inductors and drive wordlines and bitlines with a resonant sinusoidal clock over 5-10 ns instead of ~0.1-ns steps, returning ~90% of the bitline charge to the tank after each access.
why: Bitline charging dominates DRAM access energy (facts 5, 8, 10); ramps with T~20 RC cut dissipation ~10x at the cost of a slightly longer row cycle, with standard materials.

title: Piezo-resonant tier select replaces 3D staircase contacts
idea: Piezoelectric effect: each tier of a 3D DRAM stack gets a thin AlScN bulk-acoustic resonator in its local wordline-driver enable path, with a tier-unique film thickness (tier-unique resonance). One shared vertical RF drive line carries the frequency of the target tier, so only that tier's resonator builds enough piezo voltage to enable its drivers.
why: Removes the staircase and per-tier decoders that grow with 26+ tiers (periphery ~49%, fact 7; 3D blocker, fact 2); claim 30-50% less tier-addressing area and one shared via instead of N staircase contacts.
note: Frequency-division tier addressing via thickness-tuned BAW is unseen; doubt: resonator size, Q, and per-tier rectification.

title: Substitute 77 K with 4 K quantum-paraelectric SrTiO3 planar capacitors
idea: Beside quantum computers and cryogenic accelerators, exploit SrTiO3's dielectric constant rising to ~10^4 at 4 K to make planar (AR ~1) 5 fF capacitors, with superconducting NbN bitlines and 0.2 V cryo-CMOS sensing.
why: Constraint: 0.2 V swing on lossless lines gives >=25x lower switching energy per access; facet: no HAR etch, no EUV. 4 K cooling overhead (~500-1000 W/W) means it fits only where 4 K already exists.
note: Thin-film STO k is strongly suppressed versus bulk; 4 K niche.

title: Ultrasound replaces TSVs: GHz acoustic links through thinned stacks
idea: Substitute copper TSVs with ScAlN bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on each die's backside: data rides 5-10 GHz ultrasonic bursts through ~30 um of thinned silicon to a receiving transducer on the die above, so the stack itself becomes an acoustic waveguide. No TSV etch, liner, fill, reveal or keep-out zones.
why: Fact 6 HBM TSV tax: removes signal-TSV area and TSV-related yield loss; claim ~20-30% lower stack cost if per-link energy stays under ~1 pJ/bit.
note: Transduction loss and lateral crosstalk threaten pJ/bit.

title: Substitute mains power with betavoltaic trickle power for long-retention DRAM
idea: Pair long-retention cells (hours) with a power-gated self-refresh controller and an on-module Ni-63 betavoltaic source: refreshing 1 GB hourly at ~46 fJ/bit needs only ~0.1 uW, inside betavoltaic output, so contents survive outages for years.
why: Turns 'volatile' memory into effectively non-volatile with no new memory physics; the retention tail sets the energy budget.
note: Needs hours-retention cells and sub-uW controller standby; periphery leakage dominates.

title: Substitute die scrap with a low-temperature repair tier on top
idea: Swap scrapping dies with too many failing rows for depositing a <=400 C tier of spare oxide gain-cell rows above the finished array and rerouting failed addresses to it with a one-time programmable map.
why: Recovers dies beyond fuse redundancy; a ~3-5% yield gain on a 4x-priced commodity is a large supply gain.
note: Thermal budget on finished DRAM and timing mismatch of oxide spares are doubts.

title: Light-gated photoconductive switch isolating a dark capacitor
idea: Combine a wide-bandgap GaN thin-film photoconductor as the access switch with a storage capacitor: in the dark the switch is an insulator (~1e-20 A), and a nanosecond pulse from a row waveguide or micro-LED makes it conduct for write and read. With no electrical gate on the access path, the node holds charge for days without refresh.
why: Zero refresh and no 3 V wordline (fact 10), since the wordline is delivered as light; persistent photoconductivity is the risk.
note: Light-gated access novel; per-row optics and persistent photoconductivity are severe.

title: Defect charge-state memory in silicon carbide color centers
idea: Combine quantum-sensing color centers with memory: divacancies in 4H-SiC switch between stable charge states when an electrical pulse injects carriers in a p-i-n structure, and the charge state persists for hours to years in the dark. Read is electrical, through the defect ensemble's effect on junction capacitance, at ns speed.
why: Zero refresh, radiation hard, on a material with U.S. production (SiC power wafers); signal per cell and density are speculative.
note: Per-cell ensemble capacitance signal is tiny; density and ns electrical read unproven.

title: On-die microheaters anneal variable-retention-time defects in situ
idea: Borrow PCM-style TiN heaters under each subarray. After migrating the subarray's data, pulse it to 300-400 C for microseconds to milliseconds to re-passivate hydrogen-related traps behind the VRT and leakage tail.
why: VRT forces a 2-4x refresh guardband. Periodic healing shrinks the tail so the refresh interval can grow 2-4x over the part's life.

title: Capacitor plate electrode doubles as an in-field annealing heater
idea: Combine the common top plate with a Joule heater: the one added mask cuts the plate into serpentine segments with two contacts each, so during idle maintenance the controller pulses a sub-array to ~150-200 C for seconds to anneal out variable-retention (VRT) trap cells.
why: Recovers retention-tail cells in service, extending module life and usable yield ~1.5-2x and reducing demand for scarce new bits.
note: Plate-as-heater for in-service anneal is novel, but 150-200 C rarely cures VRT traps and wipes data.

title: Shadow-evaporation self-alignment places bitline and storage contacts without masks
idea: Combine the angled shadow deposition used for Dolan-bridge qubit junctions with the 6F2 cell. The buried-wordline trench topography acts as a built-in stencil, and two directional depositions at +theta and -theta drop the bitline-contact and storage-contact metals on opposite sides of each active pillar.
why: Eliminates 1-2 contact-defining masks and their overlay budget (fact 4); contacts are self-aligned by geometry, giving ~5% cost reduction plus yield gain.
note: Line-of-sight angles vary across 300 mm; ~20 nm topography stencil fidelity doubtful.

title: FOUPs that pre-clean wafers while traveling between tools
idea: Combine overhead automated transport with a vapor-phase process chamber: smart FOUPs with onboard N2 purge, HF-vapor native-oxide removal and UV dehydration run queue-time-critical pre-clean steps in transit. Time-linked sequences then no longer need dedicated tool clusters.
why: Queue-time constraints idle ~5-10% of DRAM tool capacity and force tool duplication; in-transit processing reclaims it (capital intensity, throughput).

title: Backscatter chiplet links: memory dies reflect a shared mm-wave carrier
idea: Combine RFID backscatter with in-package interconnect: the host radiates one 60-300 GHz carrier into a shielded package cavity and each memory die switches the impedance of a small on-die antenna to reflect its data; memory dies need no oscillator, PA or bump field for data.
why: Data-movement energy and assembly: transmit energy at the memory die ~0.1 pJ/bit; dies can sit unbonded/swappable in the cavity, removing TSV/bond yield loss for capacity tiers.
note: Unbonded dies still need power; cavity multipath limits bandwidth.

title: Voltage-stacked HBM: dies wired in series to recycle supply current
idea: Combine voltage stacking (charge recycling) with die stacking: power a 12-high HBM from ~12 V with each die in its own 1 V domain in series, small on-die push-pull regulators balancing mismatch and level-shifting signal TSVs crossing domains. The same current is reused by every die.
why: PDN and TSV tax: supply current falls ~12x, cutting power TSV/bump count (about half of all TSVs) and IR drop; ~5-10% die area recovered and interposer PDN losses reduced.

title: Dielectric-absorption reservoir: slow polarization refills leaking storage node
idea: Combine dielectric absorption (soakage, normally a capacitor flaw) with DRAM: a bilayer of fast linear dielectric plus a slow-relaxing defect-dipole layer (Nb- or La-doped ZrO2) releases polarization charge back onto the node over milliseconds after a write, offsetting junction leakage and flattening the decay curve. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD doping supercycles.
why: Charge wall and retention (facts 1, 3): adds effective storage at long timescales without fast capacitance; speculative ~2x retention.

title: Qubit dynamical decoupling applied to variable-retention-time traps
idea: Adapted from the dynamical-decoupling pulse trains that protect qubits from noise: VRT cells toggle between low and high leakage when one defect near the junction changes charge state, so short periodic pulses on the plate or well bias (every few microseconds, ~10 ns wide) reset that defect into its low-leakage state before it can switch.
why: VRT forces vendors to guard-band refresh 2-4x above static profiles because weak cells cannot be found reliably; pinning the traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh (fact 3) run safely, cutting refresh 2-4x.

title: Battery direct recycling for dies: harvest and re-bond onto new base dies
idea: Adapted from direct cathode recycling, which restores battery material instead of smelting it: debond DRAM dies from retired modules, thin and retest them, then hybrid-bond them onto a new logic base die that holds a per-row retention map and issues row-specific refresh, so dies with drifted leakage run again behind a smarter refresh engine.
why: Reuses the most capital-heavy part, the EUV-patterned array (fact 4), and compensates aged access devices (fact 3) with new logic; each reused die avoids new fab capacity.
note: Commodity dies have wire-bond pads, not hybrid-bond surfaces; reclaim cost likely exceeds the ~$1.5/GB cost of a new bit.

title: Film-capacitor self-clearing: a pulse burns out each leakage path
idea: Adapted from self-clearing metallized film capacitors, whose thin electrode vaporizes around a breakdown spot to isolate it: make the storage-node top electrode an ultrathin film and apply a controlled clearing pulse to cells that test leaky, so the electrode opens or oxidizes locally at the leakage path while the rest keeps most of the capacitance.
why: Turns dielectric leakage defects in the tail (facts 1, 3) into repairable events at test or in the field rather than row replacement or faster refresh; a cleared cell keeps working with slightly lower capacitance.

title: Pulse electroplating grows a 200-layer wordline stack in one bath
idea: Borrowed from compositionally modulated multilayer electroplating: plate a 200-period Cu/Ni superlattice from one bath by switching potential, selectively recess one metal and backfill oxide, forming the 3D wordline stack without CVD tungsten.
why: Plating costs ~1/100 of CVD/ALD per layer and avoids tungsten (China ~80%); stack deposition cost ~-95%; trade-offs: barrier liners, uniformity at the wafer edge.
note: Cu/Ni stack cannot be plasma-etched for holes.

title: Solar chemical-bath deposition grows channels in thousand-wafer tanks
idea: Borrowed from thin-film solar, where CdS/ZnO buffer layers grow from warm aqueous baths in huge batches: grow the ZnO/InZnO channel and Al2O3 gate liner inside 256-tier vertical holes by self-limiting chemical bath deposition, ~1,000 wafers per tank instead of single-wafer ALD.
why: ALD/CVD dominates 3D memory capex; a ~$1M bath line replaces ~$100M of ALD, cutting the channel module ~100x and pulling total cost per GB toward the 100x target; trade-offs: lower mobility, more refresh.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor forming: anodically grown TiO2 dielectric that self-heals
idea: Electrolytic capacitors anodize ('form') their dielectric at a set voltage and 're-form' to heal weak spots; deposit a Ti/Al storage electrode, turn on every wordline so each cell is biased through its own access transistor, and anodize the electrode surface in a borate electrolyte to a voltage-set TiO2 thickness (~2 nm/V), re-forming after the crystallization anneal.
why: Hf/Ru-free dielectric without ALD (facts 1, 4): thickness is set by voltage, not precursor diffusion, so it is conformal at any AR; a wet bench costs ~10x less per pass than ALD; TiO2 k ~40-90.
note: Biasing cells through live transistors in electrolyte; anodic TiO2 leakage.

title: Metallized-film capacitor self-clearing: aluminum plates that isolate shorts
idea: Film capacitors survive breakdowns because their thin Al electrode vaporizes around a fault; make the DRAM cell plate a thin Al-Ti film and apply a wafer-level clearing pulse, so a plate-to-node pinhole short burns open locally and becomes one dead cell (handled by ECC) instead of a shorted plate that kills a whole mat or chip.
why: Yield, redundancy and periphery (fact 7): lets dielectrics thin for more Cs without mat-level yield loss and cuts repair rows; Al replaces W/TiN plate fills.
note: Local clearing energy in nm cells risks neighbour damage; Al hard to deposit conformally.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: KV cache that evicts by natural decay
idea: Borrowed from human memory, where recall strengthens traces and neglect lets them fade: KV entries live in refresh-free DRAM where every attention read restores the row's charge, so attended tokens persist and ignored tokens decay; a per-row parity bit flags decayed entries, which attention masks out as forgotten.
why: Both the eviction policy and refresh disappear: zero refresh power, and the KV footprint self-limits to the actively attended set (often 10-30% of tokens).
note: Doubt: dense attention reads every KV row each step, so nothing decays; cell-level retention is random, not per-row.

title: Jacquard-loom woven wire interposer for memory buses
idea: Adapted from programmable textile looms: 15-25 um insulated copper wires are woven into a fabric of crossing warp and weft. Insulation is laser-stripped at programmed crossings and welded to form a custom X-Y routing grid, which is embedded in epoxy as the processor-memory substrate.
why: Replaces lithographic interposers with loom automation plus a laser; capital-light and U.S.-manufacturable, with thick copper giving low-loss long buses.
note: Novel loom-woven routing; 15-25 um wires far too coarse for memory buses.

title: CDMA code-division storage across simultaneously activated rows
idea: Adapted from CDMA cellular radio, where users share a channel through orthogonal spreading codes and despreading averages out noise: k data bits are stored across N cells on one bitline with Walsh-coded charge levels written by N simultaneously activated wordlines; on read the same multi-row activation sums charge on the bitline and a code-matched sense sequence recovers each bit with processing gain, so any single leaky or dead cell only adds noise.
why: Capacitor wall and retention tail (facts 1, 3): processing gain of ~10log(N/k) dB lets individual cells shrink to ~1-2 fF and makes isolated leaky cells irrelevant, removing most row/column repair and relaxing refresh.
note: Destructive multi-row reads give one analog sample; recovery of k bits is unclear.

title: Minify refresh to nanowatts and feed it with a betavoltaic cell
idea: Pair hour-retention cells with a sleep-mode refresh interval of ~1 h and integrate a Ni-63 or tritium betavoltaic film on the package supplying microwatts for decades, so the module keeps its data alive after mains loss with no battery to wear out.
why: A 16 Gb die refreshed hourly needs ~0.2 uW (46 fJ/bit); volatile cells become effectively non-volatile with zero grid idle power.
note: Needs hour-retention cells; periphery standby far exceeds betavoltaic power.

title: Iron-nitride magnetic tunnel junction RAM free of platinum-group metals
idea: Minify rare metals: replace MRAM's CoFeB/Pt/Ir/Ru/Ta stack with strained tetragonal Fe16N2 free and pinned layers, an MgO barrier and an Fe-Mn synthetic antiferromagnet, keeping thermal stability above 80 kT at 125 C.
why: Byte-addressable working memory with 1e12+ endurance built only from Fe, N, Mg, O and Mn; removes platinum-group metals and cobalt while meeting 10-year retention at 125 C.

title: Magnify light through glass: backside LEDs reset oxide-TFT threshold drift
idea: On a transparent glass substrate, a backside micro-LED/UV array illuminates idle tiles on a schedule to photo-detrap charge and reset bias-stress threshold shifts in the oxide access TFTs, followed by a mild thermal step. Dose and wavelength are tuned to avoid light-induced negative drift.
why: Self-healing: keeps the access-transistor Vt, and so the leakage tail, near day-one values for life, relaxing aging guardbands ~2x.
note: Glass-substrate niche; light-induced drift risk.

title: Eliminate the decoder tree: colliding-pulse time-of-flight row selection
idea: Launch pulses from both ends of a slow-wave RC delay line that runs past 512 wordline taps. The relative launch delay encodes the address and sets where the two pulses meet, and only at that tap does the summed amplitude exceed a threshold inverter that fires its wordline.
why: Replaces predecoders and decoders (~4-6% of die, ~13 address wires per mat) with 2 wires and one threshold device per row. Needs ~10 ps/row timing accuracy with PVT calibration.

title: Magnetic stray-field vias couple stacked MRAM dies
idea: Eliminate TSVs in a non-volatile stack: each die carries 'transmitter' nanomagnet columns switched by spin-orbit torque, and the die above senses their stray field with TMR sensors across a thinned-die/bond gap of a few um; the vertical link itself holds state with zero power.
why: Removes TSV area tax and via reveal; vertical signalling at ~fJ switching energy. Field decays steeply over microns, so this is a long shot.

title: Eliminate static storage: data circulates as a regenerated delay line
idea: Use leaky, capacitor-light cells (~1 ms retention) and keep moving data from row to row with in-array copy (RowClone-style). Each hop re-senses and re-amplifies like a repeater, so a row holds data for only one circulation slot. Reads are timed to the slot or served from the ring head.
why: Removes the retention-tail requirement entirely (fact 3) and lets Cs drop several-fold (fact 1); copy energy replaces refresh, and the density gain comes from the smaller capacitor.

title: Eliminate permanent breakdown: self-clearing nanometal electrodes on MIM capacitors
idea: Borrow the metallized-film power-capacitor trick: sputter a ~3-5 nm top electrode (Al or Zn alloy) at room temperature. The discharge at a dielectric breakdown spot then vaporizes or oxidizes the electrode around it, isolating the defect at a cost of <1% of the cell's area instead of killing the bit.
why: Lets capacitors run thinner high-k films at higher fields (more fF, fact 1) because TDDB events isolate themselves; extra margin for low-temperature films, which carry more defects.

title: Eliminate permanent vacancy damage: oxygen-reservoir layer re-oxidizes channel defects
idea: Place an over-oxidized cap (IrOx or oxygen-rich HfO2 deposited at <=300 C) next to the oxide channel. A periodic low-voltage 'heal' bias drives oxygen ions back into the vacancy sites that formed under stress, electrochemically restoring off-current and threshold.
why: Makes aging-induced growth of the leakage tail reversible, holding retention for life and allowing cheaper, less stable low-temperature films.

title: Idle sense amps run backward as distributed charge pumps
idea: Reverse the latch's job: during standby and refresh gaps, two extra switches per SA reconfigure the cross-coupled latches plus bitline capacitance into a distributed switched-capacitor doubler that tops up VPP/VBB right beside the wordline drivers.
why: Facts 7 and 10: central charge pumps and their decap (~5-8% of die) shrink, and local generation removes IR drop on the 3 V wordline rail.

title: Germanium-free 3D DRAM tiers via porous-silicon sacrificial layers
idea: Rearrange the 3D DRAM superlattice: instead of Si/SiGe epitaxial stacks, grow Si with alternating boron-doping layers and selectively anodize the doped layers into porous Si as the sacrificial layers for lateral cell formation.
why: Removes germanium (China-concentrated) and SiGe epi from 3D DRAM, and enables 26+ tiers from plain silicon.
note: Lateral anodization deep in stack slits needs current paths; doping-selective porosification.

title: Power by light, data by wire: photovoltaic-fed memory dies
idea: Swap delivery roles: a laser delivers power through a window or fibre onto photovoltaic cells on the top die of a memory stack, so the power TSVs that today outnumber signal TSVs can be repurposed for data.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): frees ~40-60% of TSVs; only viable for low-power capacity stacks (<=0.5 W) because PV conversion is ~50%; PV cells and windows are uni-fab buildable.
note: Lower dies still need power vias; PV heat and windows in stack; only tiny-power stacks.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes burn away dielectric weak spots
idea: Borrow film-capacitor self-healing and reverse what fails: the top electrode is ultrathin TiN from TiCl4/NH3 ALD (no WF6, no NF3 cleans), and a controlled overvoltage pulse at test vaporizes electrode around any leakage spot in the ZrO2, isolating the defect while ~99% of the capacitor stays active.
why: Retention tail from dielectric weak spots (higher with fluorine-free chamber cleans): converts leaky cells into good ones, shrinking the tail ~3-10x.
note: Clearing needs local energy; ultrathin plate TiN raises resistance; DRAM tail is mostly junction, not dielectric.

title: Re-meltable tin-bismuth plate fill replaces tungsten and drains out
idea: TRIZ #29 Hydraulics + #36 Phase transition: pressure-infiltrate molten Sn-Bi eutectic (139 C) over a wetting liner to fill capacitor interiors and the common plate instead of CVD W/TiN. It is solid in service, can be reflowed to heal voids, and is melted out at end of life for direct reuse.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and recyclability; avoids WF6 fluorine damage; ~100 MPa Laplace pressure for 10-nm pores is the risk.
note: 139 C melt conflicts with later 400 C BEOL steps; 10 nm infiltration pressure is extreme.

title: Wavelength-coded absorber tiers enable stack-first, anneal-later 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: give each tier an absorber with a distinct optical resonance (SiGe of graded Ge %, tuned-thickness TiN, plasmonic nanodisks), deposit the whole stack cold, then crystallize or activate each tier's channel with a laser tuned to that tier. Neighboring tiers are transparent at that wavelength and stay cool.
why: Fact 2: removes the thermal-budget conflict of monolithic tiers; one-pass deposition cuts cycle time and capital per tier ~30-50%.
note: Heat diffuses across ~40 nm tier pitch in nanoseconds; tier-selective crystallization unlikely.

title: Mechanical vibration: GHz acoustic links replacing signal TSVs
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: ScAlN thin-film transducers on each die send 5-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses through the stacked silicon. Each tier's receiver resonates at its own frequency, so tiers are addressed by acoustic frequency instead of by TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): signals need no TSV keep-out or bond alignment, and contactless tiers can be tested and stacked at higher yield.

title: Diatom silaffin chemistry: liquid-phase high-k grown inside deep pores
idea: Diatoms grow nanostructured silica at room temperature from dilute silicic acid using silaffin peptides and polyamines. Coat the capacitor holes with a polyamine monolayer that catalyses local hydrolysis of Ti/Zr/Nb alkoxides from solution. This builds a conformal 4-5 nm high-k layer that stops growing once it buries the catalyst, deep inside AR >100 pores and without vacuum ALD.
why: Capital and AR (facts 1, 4): conformal dielectric at AR >100, where ALD purge times explode, on liquid tools costing ~1/5 of an ALD cluster. It also opens Nb2O5/TiO2 (k 40-80).
note: Bio-inspired catalysed growth is novel, but film quality and leakage vs ALD unproven; AR is etch-limited anyway.

title: Gecko peel-angle latch: adhesive nanoflap released by torque, not force
idea: Gecko setae grip by van der Waals force but release at once when peeled at ~30 degrees. Make the bit a hinged graphene or SiN nanoflap that sticks flat to either face of a V-shaped trench. A small electrode at the hinge applies peeling torque, so release needs ~10x less voltage than a straight pull-off, while adhesion holds the state with no power.
why: Non-volatile mechanical bit written at ~1 V instead of the 5-10 V of NEMS contact switches, which helps with the voltage floor (fact 10) and with stiction failure. Read by capacitance.

title: Hydrophobic-gating nanopore: wet or vapor-locked pore stores the bit
idea: Many ion channels open and close as water fills or empties a hydrophobic constriction. Seal an array of hydrophobic 1-2 nm nanopores to an electrolyte reservoir. An electric field wets a pore (electrowetting), the wet state persists inside a hysteresis window, and a reverse pulse triggers vapor-lock dewetting; ionic conductance differs by >10^3.
why: Non-volatile bistability with no lattice damage, because the liquid simply refills each cycle; simulations show ns-to-us switching. Built from SiN or graphene membranes.
note: Hydrophobic-gating hysteresis is real; liquid in the chip and slow ionic reads hurt.

title: Antifreeze-protein supercooled metal: liquid or solid nanodroplet bit
idea: Antifreeze proteins keep water liquid below freezing by blocking ice nucleation, and ice-nucleating proteins trigger it. Encapsulate a ~20 nm Sn-Bi alloy droplet in a nucleation-inhibiting oxide shell, so a melt pulse leaves it as a supercooled liquid that stays liquid at operating temperature. A second electrode with a seeding surface triggers crystallization on demand, and liquid and solid resistivity differ ~3-4x.
why: Non-volatile metallic phase change with no amorphous-chalcogenide drift, fast low-voltage metallic read, and abundant non-chokepoint metals.
note: Decade-scale supercooled metastability and small resistivity contrast are doubtful.

title: Beetle-cuticle ferroelectric nematic: fluid polar bit that cannot fatigue
idea: Beetle cuticles and cell membranes are biological liquid crystals. Fill 20 nm cells with a ferroelectric nematic liquid crystal (RM734-class, polarization ~6 uC/cm2) between electrodes whose polar surface anchoring makes both polarization directions stable. A field reorients the fluid to write, and the switching current reads the bit, as in FeRAM.
why: Non-volatile, with intrinsically unlimited endurance because a fluid has no lattice defects to fatigue. Switches below 1 V at 20 nm and is filled from solution.

title: Silicatein biocatalytic silica liners grown near room temperature
idea: Sponges grow flawless silica spicules in cold seawater with the enzyme silicatein; tether silicatein-mimetic catalysts (imidazole/amine-terminated monolayers or peptides) to the sidewalls of high-AR access-channel and storage-node trenches, then expose to silicic acid or alkoxysilane vapor so dense SiO2 grows conformally only where the catalyst is, at <80 C.
why: Provides a hydrogen-poor, low-trap passivation and spacer around BEOL access devices without the 600-800 C oxidation and anneals, aimed at a 2-5x narrower leakage tail with conformality at AR >60:1.

title: Schwann-cell spiral roll-up wraps gate-all-around around BEOL channels
idea: Schwann cells wrap axons in a compact spiral of membrane; deposit a strained bilayer (graded SiNx plus metal gate plus ALD dielectric) on a sacrificial layer beside each vertical oxide channel, then release it at room temperature so it rolls itself into a multi-turn gate-all-around shell.
why: Gives ideal GAA control (~62 mV/dec, low DIBL) on low-temperature channels without high-temperature conformal fills in narrow gaps, cutting off-current 10-100x at the same on-current.
note: Rolled-up nanomembranes work at µm diameters; nm-radius rolls need extreme strain.

title: Sunflower phyllotaxis pillar layout starves row-hammer aggressors
idea: Place vertical-channel cells in each mat on a golden-angle (137.5 deg) Fibonacci spiral tiling with wordlines following the parastichy spirals; because neighbours along irrational spiral directions never align, no victim has a single dominant parallel aggressor and coupling is split over 8+ weak neighbours, as sunflower seeds pack without aligned gaps.
why: Row hammer (~1k activations): spreading coupling could raise the hammer threshold ~4-8x and remove aggressor-counting logic, at near-optimal packing density.
note: Spiral wordlines break periodic litho; density loss.

title: Diatom-style peptide biosilica grows high-AR scaffolds at 25 C
idea: Mimic diatom silaffin peptides: graft polyamine catalysts onto sidewalls of a shallow patterned template so silica deposits only there from dilute silicic acid at room temperature, iteratively growing tall thin walls/tubes that serve as capacitor molds directly over finished CMOS.
why: Capital and thermal budget of 3D BEOL stacking: plasma-free room-temperature mold growth replaces thick oxide deposition plus 70:1 etch, cutting etch-tool time and energy.

title: Thermonastic capacitors: permittivity rises with heat to offset leakage
idea: Like flowers and pinecones that open in response to heat, tune the 3D cell dielectric to a ferroelectric-paraelectric transition near 140-150 C (e.g. Sn/Zr-doped BaTiO3 or a Zr-rich HfZrO superlattice) so permittivity climbs ~2-3x from 25 to 125 C, raising stored charge just as leakage accelerates.
why: Retention scales with Cs*dV/Ileak: a temperature-rising Cs partly cancels the leakage rise, cutting the 125 C refresh penalty ~2-3x at no area cost.

title: Lanmodulin-style protein splits hafnium from zirconium cheaply
idea: Lanmodulin binds rare earths about a billion times more tightly than calcium. Use directed evolution to engineer an EF-hand-like metal-binding protein that tells Hf4+ from Zr4+ by their tiny hydration and radius difference, then immobilize it on agarose columns to separate the two from US zircon-sand leachate in water at room temperature.
why: Hf/Zr separation now uses MIBK/thiocyanate solvent extraction and depends on nuclear-Zr output; a protein column could make US hafnium for high-k and HZO a primary product.
note: Hf4+/Zr4+ are near-identical chemically; protein selectivity is a long shot but cheap to test via directed evolution.

title: Antifreeze-protein mimics template high-k tetragonal zirconia without hafnium
idea: Antifreeze proteins bind specific ice crystal faces to steer growth. Dose face-selective small-molecule inhibitors between ZrO2 ALD cycles so they block the surface sites that favor the monoclinic phase, forcing pure tetragonal zirconia (k~40-45) without Hf or thick Al2O3 interlayers.
why: Raises effective k ~30% and drops hafnium from the capacitor stack, so the pillar aspect ratio could fall ~25% for the same charge.
note: Using surface inhibitors to select tetragonal ZrO2 phase is new; mechanism unproven.

title: Diatomaceous-earth frustules as printed 3D capacitor scaffolds
idea: Diatom shells are nanoporous silica lattices with huge surface area. Print a paste of size-sorted diatomaceous earth (mined in Nevada and California) onto foil, coat it roll-to-roll by spatial ALD with electrode-dielectric-electrode, and use each frustule cluster as a 20-50x area-enhanced storage capacitor.
why: Gives DRAM-like charge per footprint in printed memory without HAR etching or EUV, from a mineral that costs cents per kg.
note: Frustules are microns wide; area gain cannot reach DRAM charge per footprint.

title: Molting crucible: spray-printed silica cuticle on a reusable shell
idea: Crabs shed and rebuild a thin cuticle on the same body. Keep a reusable silicon-nitride-coated graphite or SiC crucible body and spray-print a fresh 1-2 mm synthetic silica cuticle inside it before each Cz pull, peeling it out with the residual melt after cooling.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz per ingot ~80-90% and makes synthetic silica practical for crucibles, attacking the Spruce Pine >80% chokepoint.

title: Diatom polyamine emulsions grow capacitor silica molds without lithography
idea: Diatoms build frustule pores by letting phase-separated polyamine droplets template silica precipitation; spin a long-chain polyamine/phosphate film that breaks into droplets pinned on each hydrophilic storage-node landing pad, then feed silicic acid so silica grows only in the continuous phase. Burning out the organics leaves a self-registered honeycomb mold of deep pores for the cylinder capacitor.
why: Deletes the capacitor-mold exposure, its hardmask stack and the 60-75:1 plasma etch (facts 1, 4) with a room-temperature wet step; est. one fewer critical litho layer and 8-12% lower wafer cost.
note: Biosilica templating will not yield registered 1 um deep pores at DRAM pitch.

title: Blood-clotting repair: current-triggered electroless plating heals weak lines
idea: Platelets clot only at an injury; before final passivation, flood the wafer with an electroless Co or Ru bath and drive test current along every wordline and bitline so constrictions and thin spots heat locally, accelerating thermally activated plating exactly there until resistance normalizes.
why: Repairs near-open and high-resistance defects, a top yield killer at ~12 nm half-pitch; est. +3-6% yield, which also permits more aggressive, cheaper patterning.

title: Decomposer line recovers known-good DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like fungi turning logs back into nutrients, a low-temperature depackaging and test line recovers known-good DRAM dies from scrapped phones, laptops and DIMMs and re-packages them on a passive organic interposer as heavily ECC-protected far-memory chiplets.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: domestic urban-mine bit supply with no front-end fab.
note: Yield after depackaging and the low density of old dies undercut the economics.

title: Wood nanocellulose paper interposer with silicon-matched thermal expansion
idea: The interposer core is transparent cellulose-nanofiber 'nanopaper' (CTE ~3-8 ppm/K, close to silicon), which copies the low-expansion fibril architecture of plant cell walls. It is made from wood pulp on roll-to-roll paper lines, laminated with a moisture barrier and metallized with semi-additive copper RDL.
why: Scarce resources and capital intensity: wood-derived and roll-to-roll, so it avoids the quartz-crucible and silicon-wafer chains for interposers and taps large U.S. pulp capacity.
note: Moisture uptake, reflow-temperature stability and fine RDL on nanopaper are major doubts.

title: Growth-cone interconnects: field-guided copper pillars find their pads
idea: Axon growth cones steer toward chemical cues. Here copper pillars are electrodeposited from pads on an organic panel substrate into a thin electrolyte gap, and the field from the biased pads of the chiplet above steers each growing tip so it meets its target even with several um of misalignment.
why: Capital intensity: removes high-precision bonders and silicon interposers; 5-10 um-pitch chiplet-to-substrate links on cheap organic panels with self-correcting alignment.
note: Electrodeposit steering tends toward dendrites; pitch and uniformity unproven.

title: Weaverbird woven interposer: copper and glass-fiber threads loomed into substrate
idea: Weaverbirds knot strong nests from simple strands. Memory-module substrates are woven on modified textile looms from insulated copper microwires and glass optical fibers, warp-weft crossings are laser-welded where vias are needed, and the cloth is resin-impregnated before DRAM packages are mounted.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: cheap domestic looms make high-capacity CXL memory boards with built-in optics at a fraction of PCB/HDI tooling cost.
note: Loomed microwire boards unlikely to meet high-speed impedance and via density needs.

title: Magnetosome chains: bacteria grow uniform nanomagnets for memory arrays
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria grow chains of uniform 40-50 nm magnetite crystals. Harvested magnetosomes, whose protein shells direct self-assembly onto patterned CMOS, serve as storage bits read by magnetoresistive or Hall sensors; they are grown in fermenters instead of deposited with Pt/Ir/Ru sputter stacks.
why: Swaps scarce precious-metal stacks and fine patterning for fermentation; non-volatile, no capacitor.
note: Novel bio-assembly, but write mechanism and ns readout of 40 nm magnetite bits unresolved.

title: Heat-assisted magnetic recording logic: heat-gated thermionic write barrier
idea: As HAMR writes high-coercivity media only while a laser heats the spot, isolate the storage node behind a ~1.0 eV conduction-band-offset barrier (Si node under an AlN or Ga2O3 spacer) that is opaque at 300 K, and write with a 2-ns pulse in an integrated TaN microheater that lifts the barrier region to ~600 K, where thermionic emission rises ~1e8x.
why: Fact 3: hold-state leakage over a 1 eV barrier is ~1e8 below the write-state current, enabling refresh-free retention; 50-nm heaters have ~1-5 ns thermal time constants, but heater energy (~10-100 fJ) must be shared row-wide to beat refresh savings.

title: Glow-in-the-dark phosphor traps: optically erased deep-trap charge bit
idea: Persistent phosphors (SrAl2O4:Eu,Dy) hold electrons in Dy-type traps for hours; dope a thin wide-gap film over a readout channel with one engineered deep trap (~1.0-1.3 eV), fill it electrically through a thin barrier, and empty it with a sub-ns pulse from an integrated micro-LED/waveguide (optically stimulated detrapping, as in OSL dosimeters) instead of high-field tunneling erase.
why: Fact 3: deep-trap retention of seconds to hours removes most refresh, and avoiding Fowler-Nordheim erase stress is the bet for flash-beating endurance (>=1e12); optical routing area and write speed are open questions.
note: Per-cell optical erase routing destroys density.

title: E-ink capsule shrunk: electrophoretic nanoparticle shuttles between nanowell electrodes
idea: Each cell is a 30-nm e-beam-defined nanowell sealed by ALD, holding one charged 5-nm Au or TiO2 nanoparticle in a low-viscosity dielectric fluid; a write pulse drives it to the top or bottom electrode (~10 ns over 15 nm at 1e8 V/m), where van der Waals adhesion holds it like E-ink pigment, and read is the capacitance change or tunneling current through the particle.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free and immune to row-hammer charge disturb, with no material fatigue; buildable with e-beam, ALD and colloid drop-casting; nanoscale liquid sealing and particle aggregation are the risks.

title: TOPCon passivating contact replaces the implanted storage-node junction
idea: Solar TOPCon contacts reach saturation currents of ~5 fA/cm^2 by placing a 1.5 nm tunnel oxide between crystalline silicon and heavily doped poly-Si, so the defective metallurgical junction sits outside the crystal. Form the storage-node contact as a tunnel-oxide/n+ poly stack on an undoped channel tip: by reciprocity, a contact with near-zero recombination J0 also has near-zero generation (leakage) current.
why: Junction generation is a core part of the <=13 fA tail (fact 3); a contact that gave solar cells 10-100x lower J0 could cut junction leakage ~10x and extend refresh 4-10x.
note: Reciprocity insight is clever, but tunnel-oxide contact resistance at ~20 nm area gives µs RC writes.

title: Self-clearing film-capacitor electrode isolates leaky capacitor defects automatically
idea: Metallized-film power capacitors survive dielectric flaws because a local breakdown vaporizes the ultrathin electrode around the flaw, isolating it. Make the DRAM top plate locally ultrathin (2-3 nm TiN or Ru) over the high-k so a forming pulse at test burns open a nanometric hole around any leakage hot spot, removing that path while losing <1% of the cell's capacitor area.
why: Dielectric leakage defects set part of the retention tail and block thinner/higher-k films (facts 1, 3); self-clearing converts defect-tail cells into normal ones and lets the film be thinned for more fF.
note: Nanoscale burn-out may damage neighboring cells in 3D cylinders.

title: Radar time-of-flight addressing with counter-propagating pulses
idea: Like a phased array placing energy where waves meet, launch two short pulses into opposite ends of a row-select transmission line; their launch delay sets where they overlap, and only there does the summed amplitude exceed the row-driver threshold. A 512-row decoder becomes two pulse generators and a digital delay.
why: Periphery area: decoders shrink ~10x, if ~10 ps on-die timing and dispersion can be controlled.
note: On-die lines are RC-dominated, so pulses diffuse instead of overlapping cleanly.

title: Cloud erasure coding lets periphery fabs skip particle cleans
idea: Backblaze runs cheap consumer disks reliably by erasure-coding across them. Group each bank's 16 subarrays with 2 parity subarrays and an on-die Reed-Solomon reconstruct engine in the column path, so a particle-killed subarray is rebuilt on the fly, and the fab removes ~80% of inter-step particle scrubs and megasonic rinses.
why: Water: ~10x higher killer-defect density is tolerated, so particle-removal rinses, a top UPW user, fall ~5-10x at constant yield; parity costs ~12% array area.

title: Charlieplexed wordline decode with bidirectional selector pairs
idea: Hobbyists drive N(N-1) LEDs from N pins by Charlieplexing with tri-state polarity. Hang each sub-wordline driver gate between an ordered pair of predecode lines through a polarity-sensitive diode-like BEOL selector, so 24 tri-state predecode lines address 552 drivers instead of a full NAND decoder per row.
why: Water via area: row-decode area falls ~10x (decoders ~8-10% of die to <1%), cutting the wafers, and hence the water, attributable to decoding ~10x; die area -8%.

title: Mars electrodynamic dust shield built into the wafer chuck
idea: Mars and lunar solar panels shed dust with a traveling-wave field from embedded electrodes. Build interleaved 3-phase electrodes into the electrostatic chucks and load locks of periphery dry tools, hopping charged particles off the wafer into a vacuum trap between steps instead of sending wafers to scrubber rinses.
why: Water: post-step brush/spray scrubs in periphery modules (~5-10 L each) fall ~10x, and particles are caught before they become defects.

title: CCD bucket-brigade charge transport from subarrays to I/O
idea: A CCD image sensor shifts pixel charge to a single amplifier. In the same way, sensed bitline charge packets are clocked along buried-channel CCD lanes to a few shared, high-quality sense/ADC stations at the I/O, in place of full-swing digital global buses.
why: The CV² of global data buses and repeated sense circuits makes up much of the 49% periphery and of on-die movement energy. Moving data as charge could cut on-die transport energy 3-5x.
note: Buried-channel CCD incompatible with DRAM process; transfer losses over mm.

title: Telephone switchboard: IGZO TFT patch panel inside the interposer
idea: An operator's switchboard re-patches calls by hand. Build ≤350 C oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) TFT pass-gate matrices into the glass or organic interposer RDL, so after test the routes between memory channels and compute PHYs can be re-patched around bad channels or re-allocated per workload.
why: Saves packages that have one bad memory channel and allows configurable memory-to-compute ratios. That is ~5-10% package yield and better use of scarce HBM.

title: Cryosar freeze-out barrier access device for cryogenic memory tiers
idea: Revive IBM's 1959 cryosar, which switched by impact ionization of frozen-out impurities: at 40-77 K, a lightly doped silicon region between storage node and bitline insulates because its dopants are frozen out. A wordline field pulse impact-ionizes the donors so the region conducts for nanoseconds, then it refreezes.
why: Off-state leakage is limited by frozen-out carriers and is effectively zero (fact 3); for memory co-located with cryogenic AI or quantum hardware, refresh disappears and the cell needs no MOS gate stack.

title: Grid-leak self-biased wordlines replace the negative wordline pump
idea: Revive vacuum-tube grid-leak bias, in which a capacitor and leak resistor made a negative grid bias from the signal itself: each local wordline driver ends every activation by coupling its falling edge through a small MIM capacitor to undershoot below ground. The negative off-level relaxes slowly through a high-resistance leak, so recently used rows (hammer aggressors and their neighbors) sit deepest off.
why: Removes or shrinks the negative-wordline charge pump and its distribution in the periphery (fact 7), and deepens off-bias exactly where leakage and disturbance are worst (facts 3, 9).
note: Idle rows relax to 0 V and lose negative bias, which most rows need continuously.

title: Neuristor Mott lines self-regenerate global wordlines
idea: Revive Crane's 1960 neuristor, an active line that propagates pulses without loss. NbO2 Mott-threshold elements with local shunt capacitors are spaced along long global wordlines and data lines, so the pulse re-fires at each element the way an action potential travels down an axon, and no CMOS repeaters are needed.
why: Removes repeater and buffer stripes (fact 7) and cuts energy on long global lines ~2x (fact 5).

title: Marx-generator local boost replaces the central VPP pump
idea: A 1924 Marx generator charges capacitors in parallel and switches them into series for a high-voltage spike. At each sub-wordline driver, three dummy cell capacitors charge to VDD in parallel during precharge and switch into series to deliver ~3 V only to the row being opened. The one added mask is a contact mask that strings them through existing array transistors.
why: Removes most of the central VPP charge pump and its global distribution (fact 7) and halves the VPP conversion loss (fact 10).
note: Series stack of few-fF cell caps cannot drive ~100 fF wordline; charge sharing collapses boost.

title: Williams-tube pickup plate: segmented cell plate becomes the sensor
idea: The Williams tube read every spot through one pickup plate over the tube face. One added plate-cut mask divides the common cell plate into tiles, each wired to a charge amplifier in the CMOS under the array. When a cell is accessed, its charge redistribution appears on its tile, so one amplifier per tile can read any cell for scrubbing, retention profiling and low-bandwidth reads without firing the bitline sense-amp row.
why: Background operations skip the 8 kb page activation, ~100x less energy per scrubbed bit (fact 8), and enable per-row adaptive refresh (fact 3).
note: Wordline activation still destroys row data; tile signal is tiny versus plate capacitance.

title: Lithium-niobate acoustic delay block streams KV cache in bulk
idea: Revive the 1950s mercury and quartz acoustic delay lines as a ~1 cm3 block of lithium niobate pulled by Czochralski in air (no argon), with a 2D array of evaporated transducers on one face launching 2-5 GHz bulk waves that reflect and recirculate; each transducer channel holds ~1-2 kbit per transit. LLM decoding reads the KV cache in fixed order every token, matching a delay line's access pattern.
why: Capital and the constraint: ~2 masks for transducers and no rare gas anywhere; 1e5-1e6 channels per block could hold ~1 Gb at >10 TB/s sequential bandwidth. Risks are GHz acoustic attenuation, transducer crosstalk and ~1-2 us worst-case latency.

title: 1970s SAW radar convolver computes long convolutions without buffers
idea: Revive surface-acoustic-wave convolvers from 1970s radar: on thin-film LiNbO3 or AlN, the input sequence launches as an acoustic wave past interdigital taps weighted by the filter kernel, and the summed tap output is the convolution, so neither the sliding input window nor the kernel ever sits in memory.
why: Long-convolution/SSM layers and audio/RF front ends need large sliding buffers and kernel reads; doing them in the acoustic domain removes those DRAM/SRAM buffers and their bandwidth.

title: Transfluxor multi-aperture cells as analog non-destructive weight multipliers
idea: Revive RCA's 1955 transfluxor as electroplated planar permalloy elements with two apertures: the flux set around the small aperture is an analog weight level that gates how much of an input read pulse couples to the output winding, without disturbing the stored flux. Arrays of them perform weight-times-input in place.
why: Compute-in-memory with nonvolatile, unlimited-read magnetic weights, so weights are never fetched from DRAM; litho plus NiFe plating only.
note: Planar multi-aperture magnetics scale poorly in density; analog flux levels are noisy.

title: Core-plane-sized memory sheets on display glass as cold tier
idea: Core planes were big, cheap, hand-woven panels; revive the form factor as large-area memory on glass: 2 um-rule oxide-TFT gain cells patterned on glass sheets (prototyped on 4-6 inch glass in a university nanofab) and read through edge-mounted silicon sense chips, giving ~30 GB per square metre at ~1 us.
why: Glass processing costs ~100x less per area than silicon; a microsecond cold tier shrinks DRAM to the hot set and draws on display fabs instead of DRAM fabs.
note: 30 GB/m2 at 2 um rules implies ~1F2 cells; realistic density ~20x lower, losing to flash on cost.

title: Core-rope wired-sum: shared magnetic cores reduce partial sums in-package
idea: Like Apollo rope memory threading dozens of wires through one core, route the current-mode outputs of 8-16 processing-in-memory chiplets through shared thin-film magnetic cores on the substrate, so one secondary winding carries the analog sum and a single host ADC reads the reduced value.
why: Fact 5: in-package accumulate/all-reduce of partial dot products moves one value instead of N (8-16x less reduction traffic) with zero active circuitry; precision ~6-8 bits, limited by core linearity and drive matching.
note: Plain current summation on a wire does the same; thin-film core linearity and bandwidth limit precision.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode repeaters turn passive interposers into regenerating links
idea: Deposit two-terminal Esaki/backward tunnel diodes every few mm along passive interposer wires; their negative-resistance bistability latches and re-sharpens 50-100 mV signals using only a shared bias line, with no transistors in the interposer.
why: Facts 5/10: permits ~70 mV signaling over 20-40 mm interposer runs (realistic 5-10x lower wire energy than full swing) while keeping the interposer a cheap passive part; extends HBM reach so more stacks fit per accelerator.
note: Deposited films unlikely to give good Esaki junctions.

title: Pupin loading coils make interposer wires distortionless Heaviside lines
idea: Add periodic thin-film CoZrTa-cored inductors along RC-dominated interposer and RDL wires, as Pupin loaded telephone lines, pushing them toward Heaviside's distortionless condition so pulses keep their shape without CTLE/DFE equalizers.
why: Facts 5/6: longer HBM-to-logic reach at low swing without power-hungry equalization, ~30-50% PHY energy savings and more stacks per package; inductor area and loss at GHz are the risk.
note: On-chip lines are R-dominated; the required inductance is impractically large.

title: Theremin passive cavity bug revived as backscatter memory chiplets
idea: Like the 1945 Great Seal bug that transmitted with no internal power, memory chiplets carry a resonant slot antenna loaded by a varactor; the host floods the package with a 140-300 GHz carrier and reads data from the modulated reflections.
why: Fact 5: link power moves to one efficient host-side source, memory-side transmit energy <0.05 pJ/bit, and read paths need no metallurgical bond, so chiplets become wireless and easily reworked.
note: Multi-chiplet backscatter interference and low data rates limit it.

title: Single-wire earth-return revival: bulk silicon as shared stack return path
idea: Revive the telegraph's single-wire earth return: use the heavily doped bulk of ohmically bonded dies as the common signal and power return, so the stack needs signal vias only, not paired ground vias.
why: Constraint: halving vertical via count halves the slower fluorine-free (HBr/laser) via process time, making it economic; shrinks the HBM TSV area tax (fact 6) ~30-40%, with substrate noise the main risk.

title: Tape AC-bias revival: dithered refresh pulses park VRT traps
idea: Magnetic tape needed a high-frequency AC bias to shake domains out of hysteresis and record linearly. Variable-retention-time cells toggle because one defect near the storage junction flips between configurations; a short high-frequency dither on the cell plate or wordline-low level during refresh, tuned to drive metastable traps into their low-leakage configuration, keeps VRT cells in the long-retention state most of the time.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): VRT defeats retention profiling and forces worst-case refresh; parking traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh work, giving ~2-4x longer average refresh intervals.
note: Speculative trap physics; dither may not bias defect configuration.

title: Metallized-film self-healing: clearing pulses isolate pinholes in dry-processed capacitors
idea: Bosch's 1930s metallized-paper capacitors healed themselves when a breakdown arc vaporized the thin electrode around the flaw. The DRAM capacitor's top electrode becomes an ultrathin segmented TiN film, and at wafer sort a controlled overvoltage clearing pulse drives current through any pinhole hard enough to oxidize the electrode locally, turning a shorted or leaky capacitor into a slightly smaller good one.
why: Water: capacitor modules cleaned dry (no wet cleans after high-aspect-ratio etch or between high-k layers) carry more particles and pinholes; self-clearing restores yield and the retention tail, enabling the all-dry ~10x water cut at a Cs loss of ~2-5% on healed cells.

title: Frequency-addressed nano-resonator cells read in parallel by FFT
idea: Invert 'addressing is spatial, one access transistor per cell' -> address by frequency. Each cell on a shared line is a nano-resonator with a unique designed frequency; the bit is charge parked on its electrostatic spring (shifting frequency ~1%), and a single broadband chirp plus FFT reads all 64 cells of a line non-destructively at once.
why: Removes access transistors and most row decoding (periphery ~49%, fact 7), and replaces destructive reads (fact 8) with parallel non-destructive ones; resonator footprint is the main risk.
note: Charge on resonator still leaks; resonator footprint and Q at scale limit density.

title: Bacterial magnetite crystals as uniform nonvolatile bit cells
idea: Inverts 'memory materials are deposited by vacuum tools': harvest monodisperse ~45 nm magnetite crystals grown by magnetotactic bacteria in water at room temperature, self-assemble them onto chemically patterned sites as magnetic bits, and write and read them with crossed current lines and a Hall-sensor stripe.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; fermentation and iron replace sputtered Co/Pt stacks, and biological size uniformity removes the bit-to-bit spread that limits magnetic memory.

title: Coolant channels that double as liquid-core waveguides
idea: Invert 'cooling and interconnect are separate systems': microfluidic channels etched between stacked dies are filled with a high-index dielectric coolant so each channel also guides light, carrying memory-logic data while removing heat.
why: Lets memory stack directly on hot logic and adds optical bandwidth with no dedicated waveguide layers; attacks data-movement energy and HBM placement limits.

title: Annular DRAM die with the GPU dropped into its hole
idea: Invert 'memory dies are rectangles with one beachfront edge': plasma-dice a DRAM die with a square hole in its center, drop the GPU die into the hole and bridge all four inner edges with short fan-out wiring.
why: Four inner edges give ~4x beachfront per memory die and uniform ~1 mm wires; ~2x bandwidth per package at lower pJ/bit than one-sided HBM placement.
note: DRAM dies are much smaller than GPU dies, so the ring would exceed reticle size and waste area.

title: Acoustic through-die links from U.S. FBAR piezo transducers
idea: Invert 'vertical data must flow as electrons': place AlN/ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers (made in a Colorado FBAR fab) on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses straight through bonded silicon to a receiver on the next die.
why: No TSVs, holes or optics; ~50 um transducers at ~1-5 Gb/s each let stacks skip the TSV tax with a fully domestic supply chain.
note: Bandwidth per area far below TSVs or hybrid bonds; interface scattering and crosstalk unknown.

title: Recombination-enhanced annealing pulses lock VRT defects in benign state
idea: Variable-retention-time cells come from metastable defects that flip between high- and low-generation configurations over a ~0.5-1 eV barrier. Periodically park a row's data in a spare row by in-DRAM copy, then pulse its bitlines ~0.3 V below the p-well for ~1 us to forward-bias the storage junctions, and write the data back. Injected minority carriers recombine at the defect, delivering ~1 eV per event to drive it into its low-leakage configuration (recombination-enhanced defect reaction).
why: VRT forces 2-4x refresh guardbands and makes retention profiling unsafe. Locking defects into the benign state would remove that guardband and make per-row refresh trustworthy (fact 3).
note: Recombination-enhanced defect reactions are real; whether VRT traps stay locked benign is unproven.

title: AlN piezoelectric transformer replaces VPP charge pumps
