idea: AlN is piezoelectric but not ferroelectric, so it cannot depolarize and works to >500 C. A thin-film AlN resonant piezo transformer steps 1.1 V up to 3 V at high efficiency, replacing multi-stage capacitive VPP/VBB charge pumps.
why: Periphery area and energy (facts 7, 10): pump area ~3-5% of die removed, conversion loss roughly halved.

title: Coextruded 500-layer polymer film forms stacked capacitor plates in one pass
idea: Use microlayer coextrusion (layer-multiplier dies proven on ~800-layer optical films) to make alternating conductive-polymer/dielectric-polymer laminates, imprint a trench grid that segments the stack into per-cell capacitors, and contact odd and even plates on opposite sidewalls after selective lateral recess.
why: Layer count is nearly free in coextrusion: C=N*eA/d with 500 layers of 50 nm, k=3 gives ~250 fF per um^2 footprint, so the tier count of fact 2 arrives in one extrusion pass rather than hundreds of deposition cycles.
note: Polymer leakage, 40 nm cell segmentation and odd/even plate contacting make DRAM retention implausible.

title: Etched-anodized aluminum foil substrate is the shared capacitor plate
idea: Borrow the electrolytic-capacitor recipe for the array substrate: tunnel-etch aluminum foil for ~50x surface area, anodize ~10 nm of Al2O3, then print each cell's conductive-polymer storage electrode and oxide TFT on top, with the foil itself as common plate, ground shield and heat spreader.
why: Low-voltage electrolytic foils already exceed ~10 uF/cm^2, i.e. ~100+ fF per um^2, so charge is abundant (fact 1) on a substrate made today by the kilometre, with anodization as a cheap wet R2R step.
note: Printed cells on tunnel foil give very low bit density.

title: Print coarse, heat-shrink fine: shrink-film substrates compress cells sixfold
idea: Print the array at 2.5 um features on biaxially pre-strained polyolefin or polystyrene shrink film, then heat it so the web contracts ~60% linearly, compressing cells to ~1 um while rigid oxide films buckle into controlled wrinkles that add capacitor area.
why: Cheap printing resolution sets density; a 2.5x linear shrink gives ~6x more bits per m^2 without finer tools, and wrinkling adds plate area for free (fact 1); the risks are cracking and registration under shrink.

title: Light-powered, contactless wafer-level DRAM test
idea: First principle: a retention test needs only power, a clock and a readout, and all three can be optical. Put a photodiode power island and a micro-LED or optical modulator on each die, flood-light the whole wafer so every die runs BIST march and retention tests in parallel, and read pass/fail maps with a camera, replacing probe cards and most testers.
why: Test capital and throughput: DRAM testers and probe cards are billions of dollars of capex; full-wafer parallel test in minutes.

title: Self-healing capacitor dielectric via in-field oxygen-vacancy anneal
idea: First principle: high-k leakage tails come from mobile oxygen-vacancy clusters, which field and heat can redistribute. Add an array-level reverse-bias plus on-die microheater pulse (~300 C for microseconds) during idle that disperses vacancy clusters in ZrO2/HfO2, repairing weak cells in the field so the fab can relax its leakage-tail screen.
why: Leakage tail and yield (fact 3): fewer weak bits scrapped or fused out; longer refresh intervals.
note: On-die 300C pulses risk disturbing neighbours; vacancy redistribution may worsen tails.

title: IGZO panel sums embedding rows in place by current mode
idea: Recommender inference gathers dozens of embedding rows only to sum them, so only the sum matters. Store the embedding tables in IGZO 2T gain cells on display glass and activate every row of a lookup batch at once, so read currents add on shared column lines and a column ADC returns the pooled vector directly.
why: TB-scale embedding tables move from silicon DRAM onto glass, and only one vector per lookup crosses the link (20-80x less traffic).
note: Display-glass gain cells need ~100+ m2 per TB; analog sum ADC precision is the doubt.

title: Oxide-TFT leakage as a built-in forgetting curve for KV
idea: For most heads, attention decays with distance, so old tokens can fade instead of being refreshed. Store low-priority KV heads on glass TFT capacitors whose leakage is tuned per bank (channel length, gate bias) to a chosen time constant, and have the sense circuit treat faded entries as zero.
why: Zero refresh energy and automatic eviction with no bookkeeping; these heads, roughly 30-50% of KV in long-context models, need no silicon DRAM at all.

title: Balloon on sweater: contact-electrified charge tapped onto a pad
idea: Stimulus 'balloon rubbed on a sweater' -> a biased nanocantilever taps a trap-rich dielectric pad (e.g., Si3N4) to deposit or strip a few hundred electrons by contact electrification; the trapped charge gates a sense FET below. No tunnel current crosses an oxide, so there is none of Flash's oxide wear.
why: Nonvolatile charge storage with years of retention and no refresh (fact 3), yet endurance is not limited by tunnel-oxide damage; no storage capacitor (fact 1).
note: Moving cantilever per cell is slow and wears; probe-storage lineage.

title: Ice sculpture: frozen ionomer double layer locks the gate charge
idea: Stimulus 'ice sculpture' (shape fixed while frozen) -> gate a gain-cell transistor with a nanodot of high-Tg sodium polystyrene-sulfonate ionomer instead of the usual TFSI/PF6/BF4 fluorinated ionic liquids; an embedded nanoheater softens it for ~20 ns while the gate field forms an electric double layer, then cooling freezes the ions, shifting threshold by >1 V.
why: Retention set by frozen ions rather than junction leakage (fact 3); large Vt signal allows tiny cells without a capacitor (fact 1); avoids every fluorinated electrolyte salt.
note: Per-cell nanoheater and 20 ns polymer softening are energy and thermal-crosstalk doubts.

title: Toothpaste without fluoride: hydroxyapatite OH-column dipole order stores bits
idea: Stimulus 'fluoride toothpaste', inverted -> use hydroxyapatite (the fluoride-free tooth mineral) thin films, whose columns of OH- ions can order head-to-tail into a polar state; a field pulse reverses the OH column orientation, read as a polarization or capacitance change. Calcium phosphate comes from Florida phosphate rock.
why: Earth-abundant, U.S.-sourced nonvolatile polar storage layer (scarce-resource axis) with low switching voltage from proton/OH reorientation (fact 10).
note: Abundant material, but polar order in thin films is debated.

title: Electrometer umbrella: bootstrapped guard lines erase bitline capacitance
idea: Electrometers hide cable capacitance under a guard 'umbrella' driven by a unity-gain copy of the signal. Route a guard trace in the metal level directly above each bitline (stacked, so no pitch cost) and drive it during charge sharing from a per-pair source follower that tracks the bitline, so the bitline-to-overlayer and contact coupling sees almost no voltage change.
why: Transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+C_BL): removing ~30-40% of effective bitline capacitance raises read signal ~1.5x, worth ~1.5 fF of Cs (lower capacitor AR) or ~50% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.
note: In COB DRAM the space above the bitlines is taken by capacitors and their contacts.

title: Zamboni: in-array microheater lines anneal leaky cells during self-refresh
idea: A Zamboni resurfaces the ice between periods: thread thin TiN heater lines under each mat, and during self-refresh or idle copy a mat's data to a neighbor, pulse the mat to ~150-200 C for milliseconds to de-trap the interface charges behind variable-retention and leakage-tail cells, then copy it back. The controller never sees it and keeps issuing normal REF commands.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): pruning the 13 fA tail 3-5x lets the die skip internal refreshes, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and idle power by 10-20%.

title: Pneumatic tube: coolant microchannels double as sub-THz waveguides
idea: Mail tubes carry capsules, so the interposer's dielectric-coolant microchannels are shaped as rectangular waveguides and carry 200-300 GHz modulated carriers between chiplets while also cooling the HBM stack. A single channel provides both heat removal and a multi-10 Gb/s data path.
why: Long-reach (2-5 cm) chiplet links at <1 pJ/bit without extra routing layers; lets memory sit farther from hot compute and still be cooled.
note: Sub-THz waveguides need ~0.4-0.9 mm cross-sections, far larger than microchannels; fluid loss too.

title: Origami: one folded thinned DRAM strip forms an 8-high stack
idea: Forced 'origami': instead of dicing and stacking 8 dies, a strip of 8 adjacent DRAM dies is left joined, thinned, and coated with polyimide redistribution that runs across flexible hinge zones; the strip is then folded accordion-style into a stack. Tiers connect through the hinges, so there are no TSVs and no die-to-die alignment.
why: HBM TSV tax and stacking yield; uses wafer-level RDL instead of TSV etch/fill and hybrid bonding tools, so capital intensity is lower.

title: Spaghetti: printed hybrid CNT-read IGZO-write gain cells on foil
idea: Random stimulus 'spaghetti' -> tangled noodles as carbon nanotubes. Electrohydrodynamic-jet printing at ~1-2 um puts down a sol-gel IGZO write transistor (ultra-low leakage) and a sorted-CNT read transistor (high mobility, fast sensing) per cell on R2R foil, using US-made CNT inks.
why: A printable, vacuum-free capacity tier at est. <$1/GB process cost, offloading cold pages from DRAM; density is far below DRAM, so it serves as a far-memory tier.

title: Puff pastry: fold one printed memory sheet into 64 laminated tiers
idea: Random stimulus 'puff pastry' -> folding dough makes hundreds of layers. A long R2R sheet of printed oxide-TFT memory is zig-zag folded and laminated N times, and a printed edge-spine bus contacts every fold, giving 3D tiers from lamination instead of monolithic deposition.
why: 64 folds give ~64x areal density with no high-AR etch and no per-tier thermal budget; a radically low-capex 3D route, if the fold interconnect works.
note: Fold interconnect is the doubt; base printed-TFT density is so low 64x still trails DRAM.

title: Bistable DX-center defect ensemble as charge store in AlGaN HEMT
idea: Box = {medium: electrons captured by DX centers (large lattice relaxation) in Si-doped high-Al AlGaN | access: the HEMT gate itself | sense: 2DEG density shift read as drain current | integration: GaN-on-Si memory tiles | substrate: GaN-on-Si | fab: MOCVD}. DX centers capture hot electrons in nanoseconds, but their lattice relaxation raises a ~0.6-1 eV emission barrier, so trapped charge stays for seconds to minutes; the defect's own physics acts as the capacitor.
why: Facts 1 and 3: a capacitorless store with engineered retention and 100x+ longer refresh intervals, using a defect normally treated as a nuisance.
note: Nuisance defect turned into storage; capture/emission barrier in AlGaN at speed is speculative.

title: GaP epitaxy in existing storage contacts puts field in wide-gap material
idea: Box: standard cap x access with a Si/GaP heterojunction storage drain x standard SA x in-array x Si x selective GaP MOCVD inside the already-opened storage-node contact holes (zero added masks). GaP is lattice-matched to Si (0.4%) with a 2.26 eV gap, so the gate-edge high-field region sits where band-to-band tunneling is negligible.
why: GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling dominate the tail (fact 3); a wide-gap drain could cut them >10x with no new mask. Antiphase defects and thermal budget are the risk.
note: Selective GaP MOCVD in nm contacts risks antiphase defects and Ga/P contamination.

title: Defective DRAM arrays recycled as flying capacitors for regulators
idea: Box: failed 1T1C sub-arrays x wordlines held on x no sensing (capacitor bank) x in-stack switched-capacitor converter x each DRAM die x fuse-programmed at test. Sub-arrays that fail test are fused into parallel banks (5 fF x millions = tens of nF) that act as flying caps for an on-die 4:1 converter, so the stack accepts 4 V input on far fewer power TSVs.
why: Yield and TSV tax (fact 6): turns scrap area into function, cuts power TSVs and bumps ~4x through higher input voltage, and lowers I2R loss.
note: Access-transistor ESR and cell voltage limits hurt converter efficiency; failed arrays may be shorted.

title: Ferroelectric remnant in capacitor gives LDPC a second opinion
idea: Box [medium: Hf/Zr-oxide capacitor with a tuned small ferroelectric remnant | access: standard | sense: dual-mode charge + polarization | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. The bit is stored as charge, but each write also nudges a weak, slowly relaxing polarization; when ECC fails, a second polarization read supplies a likelihood value per bit so LDPC soft decoding recovers words that hard decoding cannot.
why: Facts 1/3: a free, physically independent second copy lets smaller-Cs or leakier cells pass; ~10x lower uncorrectable rate at equal raw BER.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrode isolates dielectric leakage hot spots
idea: Box [medium: capacitor with MnOx/VO2-type top electrode | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. The top electrode is a conductive oxide that converts to an insulating phase where local leakage current heats it (as MnO2 does in tantalum capacitors), so a weak dielectric spot clears itself during a forming pulse instead of becoming a retention-tail cell.
why: Facts 1/3: allows thinner, higher-k, more defective dielectrics (more Cs at lower aspect ratio) by healing defects; ~10x tail shift claimed.
note: MnO2-style clearing in nm-scale DRAM electrodes unproven; may raise leakage elsewhere.

title: Per-row ferroelectric Vt trim of access transistors lowers wordline swing
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: FeFET access transistor with HZO gate layer | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. At test and periodically in the field, each row's access-transistor Vt is trimmed by partially polarizing its ferroelectric gate, pulling leaky-tail rows up and slow rows down, so the wordline can swing ~1.3 V instead of ~3 V without a leakage tail.
why: Constraint: wordline CV^2 ~5x lower and the VPP pump removed, ~10x on the wordline path; Fact 3: leakage tail compressed by trimming.

title: Po: memory that tops itself up — plate-pumped self-restoring cell
idea: Po: the memory refreshes itself. Extracted: add a two-terminal threshold switch and a diode in series between each storage node and the plate line; a global low-amplitude AC carrier on the plate tops up only nodes already above threshold (stored 1s) while 0s stay below it, making 1T1C self-restoring without extra transistors.
why: Removes row-by-row refresh commands and their bandwidth/power cost (fact 3). Per-cell threshold variability is the risk.
note: Series threshold switch and diode add leakage paths and variability; plate AC carrier disturbs every cell.

title: Po: memory is woven like cloth — drawn-fiber capillary-breakup storage nodes
idea: Po: memory is woven like cloth. Extracted: thermally draw a glass preform with a metal core and dielectric shell into km of fiber, then anneal so the core breaks into a chain of isolated nanospheres by Plateau-Rayleigh instability (each sphere a floating storage node); weave X and Y fibers so crossings capacitively address the spheres.
why: Fiber drawing yields km of nanostructure per hour with no lithography, cleanroom or EUV, targeting <1% of silicon's cost per area. Trade-offs: coarse addressing, us speed, a new interconnect scheme.
note: In-fiber Plateau-Rayleigh spheres as nodes is novel; addressing and speed weak.

title: Po: bitlines are the pump — idle-bank flying capacitors
idea: Po: a charge pump built from the memory's own wires. In idle banks, groups of bitlines (~100 fF each, millions available) are reconfigured through the equalizer switches plus a few added series switches into a switched-capacitor ladder that stacks charge up to VPP for the active banks' wordlines.
why: Periphery (#7): deletes most dedicated pump capacitor area by reusing capacitance already paid for; silicon only.

title: Alignment-free capacitor carpet: cells harvest random nanorod capacitors
idea: Po: the capacitor ignores the transistor. Make a dense random carpet of isolated vertical nanorod capacitors (diameter smaller than the gap between storage-node pads) in an insulating matrix laid over the transistor array; each landing pad simply collects whatever rods sit on it, so no capacitor litho or overlay is needed.
why: Capacitor litho/overlay (facts 1,4): removes the capacitor-hole patterning layer; summing ~10-50 rods per cell tightens the Cs distribution.
note: Rods under ~10 nm can't fit a full MIM stack.

title: Optical-disc mastering machines write imprint templates for old fabs
idea: Po: memory is mastered like Blu-ray discs. Repurpose idle optical-disc mastering machines (rotary phase-transition thermal lithography with sub-100 nm marks) to write large-area line/dot imprint templates, which feed nanoimprint tools placed in existing 2x-nm DRAM bays for array layers.
why: Template supply and EUV avoidance: template writing at ~1% of e-beam cost on idle equipment; NIL gives sub-20 nm periodic features in trailing fabs.
note: Rotary PTM marks are ~100 nm and spiral, far from 20 nm Cartesian array pitch.

title: Wireless in-package multicast of shared weights to many GPUs
idea: Po: memory that shouts instead of whispers. One weights-holding DRAM stack drives a 140 GHz antenna into the metal package lid cavity, which acts as a shared waveguide, so all eight accelerators in the package receive the same weight stream at once instead of each storing its own copy.
why: Model weights are replicated per GPU; de-duplication frees 30-60% of HBM capacity for KV cache, and one transmission serving N readers cuts energy per reader-bit ~N-fold.
note: One mm-wave link gives ~10s GB/s, far below HBM TB/s; bandwidth mismatch.

title: Metastable DX-centre traps with lattice-relaxation recapture barriers
idea: Worsen: trap charge behind thin barriers that tunneling defeats. Flip: store charge in an engineered layer of DX-like centres (Si-doped AlGaN or Ga2O3 defect complexes) whose large lattice relaxation creates a configurational barrier to recapture, giving persistent stored charge for hours at room temperature, written and erased by gate pulses.
why: Retention orders of magnitude beyond the 13 fA tail (fact 3) without a big capacitor (fact 1).
note: DX-center persistent charge decays quickly at room temperature in known systems.

title: Fill-then-freeze pulses pin telegraph traps in low-leak state
idea: Worse: let variable-retention-time traps flip randomly between high- and low-leak states. Flip: before each idle period apply a calibrated gate/drain pulse that charges the GIDL-enhancing border traps into their neutral configuration, which then persists for seconds because emission time is long.
why: Removes the VRT tail that forces ~2x refresh guard-banding (fact 3).

title: Joule self-anneal pulses heal leaky tail cells in the field
idea: Worse: ship cells whose leakage tail is frozen in by process traps forever. Flip: find tail cells with in-DRAM retention tests, then drive a microsecond high-current pulse through that wordline segment to self-heat it locally to ~400 C and anneal the responsible interface traps.
why: Shifts the <=13 fA tail (fact 3) about 2x tighter and recovers yield otherwise lost to retention.

title: Self-rolling Swiss-roll array: one patterned film becomes twenty tiers
idea: Worse: pay a full lithography and alignment cycle for every tier. Flip: pattern one long strained-bilayer (e.g., SiN on Si/SiGe or oxide-semiconductor) thin-film array once, then undercut a release layer so built-in strain rolls it into a tight multi-turn tube whose turns become tiers, with wordlines exiting at the tube ends and bitlines contacted along the outer seam.
why: Tier count is set by roll turns, not litho steps: ~20x footprint density from a single planar mask set; attacks EUV dependence and capital intensity (fact 4).
note: Rolling saves footprint, not wafer area per bit; inner-turn contacts are hard.

title: Photo-electrochemical planarization ends dependence on ceria slurries
idea: Worsen: make every oxide CMP step consume Chinese rare-earth ceria slurry and polyurethane pads. Flip: planarize by UV-activated photo-electrochemical etching in a thin electrolyte film under a TiO2-coated transparent platen. High points see more field and light and dissolve faster, so no abrasive is needed.
why: Rare-earth (Ce) chokepoint, slurry waste water and scratch defects: no ceria or abrasive slurry at all.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers woven into memory fabric
idea: Worse: build memory only by stacking films on flat plates. Flip: draw a macroscopic metal/semiconductor/insulator preform into kilometers of fiber whose cross-section holds a storage capacitor and an access junction. Weave orthogonal fibers into a crossbar fabric so every crossing is an addressable cell.
why: Capital: fiber towers cost ~$1M and run km/hour with no lithography, a speculative path to cheap bulk capacity.

title: Tunnel-etched electrolytic-capacitor aluminum foil becomes DRAM capacitor plate
idea: Worse: plasma-etch every capacitor hole into hard crystal. Flip: borrow the electrolytic-capacitor industry's DC tunnel etching, which in seconds drills straight crystallographic <100> tunnels above 50:1 into Al foil. Seed the tunnel sites with a pattern, coat them with ALD high-k and a top electrode, and use the foil itself as the common plate.
why: Capacitor wall plus capital: wet electrochemical etch at $/m2 cost replaces high-AR plasma etchers.
note: Al tunnels are 0.1-1 um and randomly sited; can't be seeded at DRAM pitch.

title: Curie-tuned barium strontium titanate gains capacitance as it heats
idea: Worse: use dielectrics whose capacitance stays flat while leakage doubles every 10 C, so hot chips lose data fastest. Flip: tune the Ba/Sr ratio of a (Ba,Sr)TiO3 capacitor so its permittivity peak sits near 85-95 C; as the die heats, Cs rises and partly offsets the faster leakage, flattening retention versus temperature.
why: Fact 3: hot-case refresh sets the spec; temperature-compensated Cs could cut worst-case refresh rate ~2x using Ba, Sr, Ti and O instead of Hf.
note: Thin-film BST permittivity peaks are broad and lossy; the compensation is likely weak.

title: Beekeeper's honeycomb: vapor-grown MOF crystal of dipolar molecular rotors
idea: A beekeeper fills a honeycomb one cell at a time. Convert an ALD ZnO film into a ZIF-type metal-organic framework by exposing it to linker vapor (no solvothermal bath), using linkers that carry dipolar rotors. A field aligns the rotors, a rotational energy barrier locks them, and the polar bit is read capacitively.
why: A molecular-scale, non-volatile dipole bit (facts 1, 3). The process is gas-phase and low-temperature with no solvent or UPW rinse, using more than 10x less water than a capacitor module.
note: Rotor barriers either too low for retention or too high to switch electrically.

title: Kalahari tracker: laser-crystallized improper-ferroelectric YMnO3 dots in blanket film
idea: A San tracker reads marks pressed into dry sand. Deposit a blanket amorphous YMnO3 film, then laser-crystallize only the cell sites into the hexagonal improper-ferroelectric phase; the amorphous remainder serves as isolation, so there is no etch or clean. Improper ferroelectrics keep their polarization at sizes where proper ones depolarize.
why: Lets a ferroelectric bit scale to tiny volumes (facts 1, 4). Write-by-light patterning needs no etch, strip or clean, a more than 10x water cut.
note: Laser-crystallized YMnO3 cells novel; high crystallization temperature and switching speed doubtful.

title: Microbiologist farms magnetotactic bacteria for ready-made magnetite bits
idea: Persona: a microbiologist whose magnetotactic bacteria grow chains of uniform 45 nm magnetite crystals at room temperature. Harvest the magnetosomes and align them by field into lithography-free pockets on a CMOS crossbar. Read each half-metallic Fe3O4 crystal by tunnel magnetoresistance through a thin ALD barrier.
why: Single-domain non-volatile bits made from iron and sugar water, with no Co or Pt sputter targets, at low fabrication energy.
note: No write mechanism given; placement and room-temperature Fe3O4 TMR are weak.

title: Pharmacist's zinc and magnesia: all-zinc-oxide ferroelectric transistor
idea: Persona: a pharmacist looking at zinc ointment and milk of magnesia. Grow ferroelectric wurtzite Zn(1-x)Mg(x)O epitaxially on a ZnO channel, which is the same crystal family and nearly lattice-matched. The result is a FeFET with none of the amorphous interfacial dead layer that limits HfO2 FeFETs to ~1e5 cycles.
why: Non-volatile 1T cell made only of Zn, Mg and O at BEOL temperatures. The coherent interface aims at >1e10 cycles.
note: Wurtzite ferroelectrics need ~3 MV/cm coercive fields near breakdown; coherent interface endurance is speculative.

title: Farmer's irrigation canals double as mm-wave signal waveguides
idea: A farmer digs one canal for both water and transport: etch microfluidic coolant channels into the interposer, fill them with low-loss dielectric fluid (fluorocarbon) and launch 300 GHz signals down the same channels as dielectric waveguides between memory stacks and logic.
why: Uses one structure for cooling and data movement; claimed 100+ Gb/s per channel over 2-5 cm at <1 pJ/bit, which frees interposer metal layers and lets memory sit farther from the hot die.
note: Fluorocarbon fluid loss and coupling at 300 GHz uncertain.

title: Weaver's loom: woven wire-and-glass-fiber interposer
idea: A weaver builds strong cloth from crossed threads: weave insulated 10 um copper warp wires and glass-fibre weft into a fabric, laser-weld chosen crossings to make vias, and embed the fabric in glass to form a large-area, lithography-free interposer for memory chiplets.
why: Replaces costly silicon or organic RDL interposers (which need masks and litho) with a textile process; claimed 5-10x cheaper interposer area per cm2 for wide, slow memory buses.
note: Weave registration far too coarse for chiplet bump pitch.

title: Submariner's sonar: GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded stack
idea: Sound travels well through solids: put ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses vertically through the bonded stack as a contactless data bus, with frequency-division channels assigned per die.
why: TSV-free vertical signalling with no drilled vias, which recovers the TSV area tax and yield loss; speculative 10-50 Gb/s per transducer site at sub-pJ energy.

title: Origami artist folds one thinned wafer into an accordion stack
idea: Fold rather than stack: process DRAM on a partial wafer thinned to 10 um on a polyimide carrier with continuous RDL running across score lines, then fold it into a zig-zag accordion of 8-16 layers so the inter-layer wiring runs around the folds.
why: No TSVs, no die-to-die bonding and no known-good-die stacking yield multiplication; claimed ~40% lower stacking cost per bit than HBM.
note: Bandwidth limited to fold-edge wiring.

title: Desert architect's double roof: thermal-break gap between memory and logic
idea: Desert dwellers use a ventilated double roof: suspend the DRAM stack over a 5-10 um vacuum gap above the 150 C+ logic die, couple signals across the gap by near-field coupling, and feed power from the board side through separate thermal-choke ribbons.
why: Keeps DRAM at the 125 C ambient instead of logic's 150-170 C junction, cutting refresh about 4-8x and ending retention-driven bandwidth loss.
note: Near-field signaling density across 5-10 um vacuum gap and mechanical support are doubtful.

title: Mars-ISRU gas whitelist as a rare-gas-free DRAM process kit
idea: A Mars fab could only use gases made from CO2, water and nitrogen; define a binding whitelist (N2, H2, O2, CO2, H2O, NH3, NF3, HF, HBr, Cl2, SiH4) and requalify every 3D-array step against it, publishing the recipes as an open process design kit. Make whitelist compliance a condition of federal fab grants so U.S. DRAM lines cannot be stopped by a helium, neon or xenon shock.
why: Helium (Qatar ~30% offline), neon and xenon chokepoints removed and U.S. manufacturability raised; a step change in supply resilience rather than cost.
note: ArF lasers need neon and sputtering needs argon; binding whitelist is impractical as stated.

title: Phase-change heat-sponge interlayers enable 24-high stacks for burst seconds
idea: Use the thermal timescale (seconds) as a design variable: thin sealed micro-cells of low-melt Bi-In alloy between DRAM dies melt during training bursts and refreeze during communication lulls. Peaks are buffered rather than conducted, so taller stacks stay within temperature limits.
why: Stack height is thermally capped; 24-high instead of 12-16-high raises GB per package footprint ~1.5-2x without more interposer beachfront (fact 6).
note: Thin alloy layers hold little latent heat; they melt in ms, not over training bursts.

title: Palladium-hydride reservoir re-passivates traps during monthly healing sleep
idea: Time/scale jump (atomic bond -> years): a thin PdHx film inside the package releases H2 when the stack is warmed to ~150 C during a scheduled monthly 'healing sleep', re-passivating Si/SiO2 dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and hammer stress. Years of trap-generation aging are undone in hours instead of being covered by guard-banded refresh.
why: Retention tail and row-hammer drift grow with age; resetting interface trap density could hold end-of-life retention at time-zero values, letting fabs ship cells with ~2x less retention margin.
note: Pb-center passivation needs ~400 C; in-package H2 harms high-k and ferroelectrics.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes isolate dielectric breakdown spots
idea: Scale borrow (metallized-film power capacitor -> nanoscale DRAM pillar): use an ultra-thin top electrode that locally vaporizes or oxidizes around a dielectric breakdown spot, so a defect becomes a detectable open cell instead of a leaking short that disturbs neighbors.
why: Lets fabs push high-k dielectrics thinner and higher-k (toward the k~70 target) despite weak spots, because failures turn into ECC-friendly erasures.
note: A breakdown spot is comparable to the whole cell; isolating it at <1% area is implausible.

title: Thinfilm polymer FeRAM fixed: proton-transfer organic ferroelectric crystals
idea: Thin Film Electronics' and Intel's PVDF polymer FeRAM died from microsecond switching, half-select disturb and a low Curie point. Grow croconic-acid-type hydrogen-bonded crystals in BEOL vias: they switch by collective proton transfer along H-bond chains (P ~20-30 uC/cm2) and deposit below 150 C, so many tiers can stack.
why: Lead-free nonvolatile layer with a tiny thermal budget for monolithic multi-tier stacks; fast proton switching makes FeRAM DRAM-class.
note: Croconic acid crystals in vias and ns switching unproven.

title: Straintronics unclamped: remanent ferroelastic strain read by MoS2 gauge
idea: Straintronic memories stalled because substrate clamping cut piezo strain to ~1e-4, too little to switch magnets reliably. Drop the magnet: store the bit as a 71/109-degree ferroelastic domain state in a BiFeO3 or PMN-PT island, which holds ~0.1-0.5% remanent strain, and read it through a monolayer MoS2 channel on top whose strain-shifted bandgap changes its current several-fold.
why: Nonvolatile, written by field (fJ-class charge) with a non-destructive read and no current through any storage barrier.
note: Clamped island remanent strain and MoS2 gauge sensitivity likely give small read margin.

title: Printed-electronics bust fixed by toll-printing memory foil on converters
idea: The 2008-2012 printed-electronics boom went bust because startups built their own lines to make low-value labels. Instead, license a memory-foil recipe (printed oxide access devices plus capacitors) to U.S. flexible-packaging converters whose roll-to-roll lines run below capacity, and pay them per m2 of good foil.
why: Near-zero capital per unit of capacity because it uses idle presses, so supply can scale fast. Low-leakage printed access devices make the foil refresh-light, so it ships with only a simple controller.
note: Printed devices far from DRAM-class density and speed.

title: Kovio printed silicon diode pairs as two-way crosspoint access
idea: Kovio's printed-silicon RFID died because printed tags had to undercut cheap silicon chips. Use its cyclopentasilane ink, crystallized by flash lamp, to print two opposing p-i-n diodes per cell, one to a write-1 line and one to a write-0 line. When idle, the storage node is isolated by two reverse-biased diodes, giving a transistor-free crosspoint 2D1C cell.
why: Printable access with no transistor, with leakage set by reverse diode current, and the cells can be stacked in printed tiers. Memory's value per m2 justifies the cost of printed silicon where RFID's did not.
note: Two printed diodes replace the access transistor; reverse leakage and micron pitch likely kill retention and density.

title: Plated-wire memory reborn as drawn multimaterial fiber woven into crossbars
idea: Plated-wire memory put the storage film on a beryllium-copper wire substrate and died on per-wire plating cost and coarse pitch. Thermally draw a glass/polymer preform containing conductor, charge-storage sheath and semiconductor layers into kilometers of 20-50 um fiber (multimaterial fiber drawing), then weave orthogonal fibers so each warp-weft crossing is a cell.
why: No wafer, lithography or EUV: a $1-2M draw tower makes km of device per hour from grams of preform; removes beryllium; ~1-2 GB/m2 of fabric, stackable in layers.
note: Fiber crossing pitch of 20-50 um gives ~50 MB/m2, far below the claim; cell physics unspecified.

title: Bell Labs ferroelectric matrix fixed by co-fired ZnO varistor selectors
idea: 1950s Bell Labs barium-titanate matrix memory died on half-select disturb because BaTiO3 has no sharp switching threshold. Co-fire a multilayer ceramic stack on the MLCC process (hundreds of ~0.5 um layers) where each BaTiO3 cell sits in series with a ZnO varistor layer (nonlinearity >30) that blocks half-select voltages.
why: MLCC lines already make trillions of BaTiO3/nickel parts a year with no wafer, EUV or helium; Ba, Ti, Zn, Ni are abundant; ferroelectric storage is nonvolatile; density limited by printed electrode pitch, offset by layer count.
note: MLCC co-fired FE plus varistor selector is novel; density at printed pitch is orders below DRAM.

title: CCD memory reborn as charge-packet data bus inside DRAM periphery
idea: 1970s CCD memories lost to DRAM because serial shifting made random access slow, yet moving charge packets down a buried channel is extremely cheap per hop. Use a short CCD-style bucket-brigade channel to carry the 128-256 bits fetched from a bank toward the I/O hub as charge packets clocked at ~0.3 V, instead of full-swing global I/O lines, serializing the data naturally as it moves.
why: On-die data movement (facts 5, 8): global I/O wiring is a large share of DRAM read energy; claimed 2-4x lower on-die transport energy per bit and fewer long metal lines in the periphery (fact 7).
note: Buried-channel CCD in DRAM process and transfer loss at GHz rates doubtful.

title: Iron-disilicide LED fizzled; Purcell microcavity makes it a 1.55-um source
idea: Surrey's 1997 beta-FeSi2 light-emitting diode on silicon faded because room-temperature emission was weak. Embed FeSi2 nanocrystals in a silicon photonic-crystal nanocavity (Q ~1e4) to Purcell-enhance the radiative rate 10-50x, couple straight into Si waveguides, and detect with divacancy-implanted silicon waveguide photodiodes, giving an in-package photonic memory link with no InP, GaAs, Ge or Er.
why: Data movement and scarce resources: replaces III-V lasers (Ga, In) and Ge detectors in co-packaged memory optics, targeting <2 pJ/bit with fully Earth-abundant photonics (Fe, Si, O).
note: Purcell boost of weak FeSi2 emission still far from laser-class efficiency.

title: Spectrum-sliced LED WDM failed in telecom; incandescent silicon sources suit packages
idea: Spectrum-sliced incoherent WDM (one broadband source cut into channels) died in telecom from excess intensity noise and low power per slice over km distances. Over 1-10 mm in-package paths, a microheated SiC/silicon photonic-crystal selective thermal emitter (W-free) can feed SiN waveguides whose silicon microrings slice and modulate dozens of channels, detected by Si photodiodes below 1.1 um, with no laser at all.
why: Removes III-V lasers (Ga, In), the dominant cost and failure item in co-packaged optics, from memory links; ~5 pJ/bit at first with a path toward ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Prussian-blue electrochromic bit read by light on a photonic bus
idea: Effect walk: electrochromism. Each bit is a 50-nm Prussian-blue (iron hexacyanoferrate, tungsten-free) patch on a silicon-nitride waveguide; inserting ~10^3 K+ or H+ ions from a thin solid electrolyte bleaches or colours it, changing optical absorption, so a passing light pulse reads the bit without electrical bitlines while the coloured state holds for hours.
why: Reads memory straight onto co-packaged optics, skipping bitline CV2 and SerDes energy (fact 5, 3-20 pJ/bit) for disaggregated memory pools, with abundant iron chemistry; ion kinetics are us-class unless patches shrink to ~10 nm.
note: Ion kinetics us-ms and electrochromic endurance far from DRAM duty.

title: Pyroelectric wordline layer auto-cancels hot-die leakage rise
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A poled AlScN film in the access gate stack generates bound charge equivalent to a more negative gate bias as temperature rises (~-2 to -4 mV/K), offsetting the access transistor's Vt drop that doubles leakage every ~10 C.
why: Refresh bandwidth (fact 3): flattens retention vs temperature so >85 C operation needs no 2x refresh (10-20% bandwidth); passive, zero power. Risk: pyro charge screening over long times.

title: Maxwell-Wagner bilayer capacitor back-fills leaked charge from interface reservoir
idea: Effect: interfacial (Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars) polarization, i.e., dielectric absorption. The cell capacitor is a high-k/low-conductivity bilayer engineered so interface charge accumulates over ms after a write and re-emerges as the node droops, like a capacitor's recovery voltage; a reset pulse on writes clears ghost charge from the previous value.
why: Retention x2-5 without a better transistor (fact 3). Risk: data-history ghosting and slow charging.
note: Absorbed charge leaks too and causes data-history ghosting.

title: Photon-emission retention mapping fuses per-row internal refresh bins
idea: Effect: junction and hot-carrier electroluminescence. At sort the array is biased to stress leakage paths and a cooled InGaAs camera images the faint NIR emission; leaky row segments glow, so a weak-row map is captured in seconds instead of hours of retention testing and burned into fuses; the die then refreshes strong rows only every 4th REF. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): -50-75%; optics resolve row segments, not single cells, which is enough for row binning.
note: fA leakage yields well under one photon per second per cell; seconds-scale mapping doubtful.

title: Power-up microheater pulses anneal variable-retention-time defects
idea: Effect: thermally activated defect reconfiguration. VRT cells toggle as a metastable defect switches configuration; TiN microheaters in thermally isolated mats deliver ~us pulses at ~250 C during the JEDEC initialization window (before data exists), biased with a gate field that favours the low-leakage configuration, pruning the VRT population each boot. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): fewer VRT escapes lets the die relax internal refresh ~2x. Risk: which defect state annealing favours is unproven.
note: Boot-time thermal pruning of VRT defects is new; whether anneal favours low-leak state, and on-die thermal isolation, are unproven.

title: NbO2 Mott-switch sense latch replaces cross-coupled sense amplifier
idea: Effect: Mott insulator-to-metal transition. Bias a ~20 nm NbO2 threshold switch just below its transition voltage between the bitline and a reference; the cell's ~60 mV charge-sharing signal tips it across threshold, its resistance collapses ~100x in <1 ns, and one restore FET writes the row back. One BEOL device plus 1-2 FETs replaces the 6-10 transistor latch and equalizer.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp stripes are ~15-20% of die; a 3-4x smaller SA, which could also sit in BEOL above the array, frees ~10% of die area.
note: NbO2 threshold variation far exceeds the ~60 mV signal.

title: Injection-locked oscillator pair turns bitline signal into phase decision
idea: Effect: sub-harmonic injection locking. Each SA stripe hosts a pair of tiny coupled ring oscillators pumped at their second harmonic, so they become phase-bistable (0 or 180 degrees, as in oscillator Ising machines); the bitline differential briefly biases the coupling, the pair locks into one phase, and a phase detector restores full swing. Gain comes from locking dynamics rather than transistor matching.
why: SA offset and area (facts 7, 10): a phase decision averages mismatch over many cycles, tolerating ~5x worse device matching and working near 0.5 V.

title: Magnetostrictive-piezo laminate receivers replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Magnetostriction: each thinned die carries micro-coils that transmit, and FeGa/AlN magnetoelectric laminate pads that receive. The stray AC field from the die below strains the magnetostrictive layer, and the piezo layer turns that strain into a mV-scale voltage. The laminate's high field-to-voltage gain allows smaller-pitch, higher-bandwidth contactless links than plain inductive coils.
why: Removes TSVs and their keep-out zones (HBM TSV tax ~3x area and 20-30% yield loss, fact 6); claim recovers 15-25% die area and stacks known-good dies with no through-silicon etch.

title: Pyroelectric heat-pulse non-destructive read of stacked ferroelectric tiers
idea: Pyroelectric effect: in a 3D-stacked HZO ferroelectric capacitor array, a nanosecond current pulse in a resistive heater line beside each row warms the cells by a few kelvin. Each cell then emits a pyroelectric current whose sign gives its polarization, so the read never switches the cell and the data is non-volatile with no write-back.
why: Removes the destructive read and write-back (fact 8) and the endurance drain of FeRAM reads; claim read energy cut ~5x, with cycling wear only on writes.
note: Pyroelectric charge at DRAM-scale cell area and few-K heating is a handful of electrons; unreadable.

title: Spin-crossover molecular tiers with room-temperature-straddling hysteresis loops
idea: Thermal hysteresis: Fe(II)-triazole spin-crossover films whose 30-40 K hysteresis loop is engineered to straddle 20-60 C hold either the high-spin or low-spin state with no power. A heater pulse writes high-spin, a field pulse writes low-spin, and the ~10% dielectric or resistance change is the read. The films can be evaporated at <200 C, so many cheap tiers fit in BEOL.
why: Gives non-volatile tiers from molecules with no critical minerals (resource axis, fact 2); claim very low capital per tier. Speed and endurance are unproven.
note: Writing low-spin needs cooling; slow, fatigue-prone, not DRAM-class.

title: Shape-memory NiTi microsprings close warped HBM gaps on heating
idea: Effect: martensitic shape-memory recovery with thermal hysteresis. Sputter NiTi micro-bumps trained as compressed springs; heating above the austenite finish temperature makes each bump extend 1-3 um to meet its pad and absorb die warpage, and the hysteresis keeps them extended at operating temperature. $1M covers the target, university MEMS line time and a 24-month reliability demo.
why: Fact 6: warpage forces costly TCB and CMP-flat hybrid bonding with 20-30% yield loss; compliant self-actuating bumps raise stack yield on cheaper bonders.

title: Tunneling-leak gain cells make old KV tokens fade like ALiBi
idea: Store KV entries in gain cells whose tunneling oxide is deliberately thin, so charge decays with a time constant of a few hundred tokens. Each read value is then naturally scaled by exp(-age/tau), which is exactly a recency-bias attention prior. Cells whose signal drops below the sense threshold are reclaimed as free slots, with no refresh or eviction logic.
why: Gives refresh-free KV memory (fact 3) that reclaims its own capacity. Expect a 3-8x smaller KV footprint for long contexts, where distant tokens are down-weighted anyway.
note: Multiplicative decay is not ALiBi; leakage tail variability makes decay non-uniform.

title: Magnetostriction: magnetoelectric nano-antennas give chiplet memory links without interposer wires
idea: FeGaB/AlN magnetoelectric antennas radiate at their GHz acoustic resonance rather than their electromagnetic wavelength, making them ~100x smaller than patch antennas; arrays on memory and compute chiplets talk wirelessly through mold compound with no interposer routing.
why: Removes silicon interposer (CoWoS capacity and cost) for low-to-mid bandwidth memory chiplets; packaging capex down; ~1-3 pJ/bit target.
note: Bandwidth and pJ/bit of ME antennas far from link needs.

title: Mott transition: NbO2 steep-threshold receivers enable 80 mV memory I/O swings
idea: Put NbO2 threshold-switch elements at the front end of DRAM I/O receivers; their abrupt insulator-metal transition acts as near-infinite-gain slicing so a 60-100 mV interposer swing switches cleanly, replacing 300-400 mV swings and biased sense amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): I/O CV^2 falls ~16x at 4x lower swing; HBM PHY from ~3.5 to <1 pJ/bit if sub-ns switching and endurance hold.

title: Direct tunneling: oxide tunnel-bond hybrid bonding without metal-to-metal contact
idea: Cap both Cu bond pads with 1-1.5 nm of bond dielectric so current crosses by direct tunneling (ohmic-like at mV) plus capacitive coupling for AC; pads no longer need to expand and fuse, so dishing tolerance loosens and anneal drops below 200 C, protecting DRAM retention.
why: HBM stacking yield and pitch (fact 6): relaxes CMP/dishing specs that drive hybrid-bond yield loss, enables sub-um pitch at low thermal budget; pad tunnel resistance must stay low.

title: Ion migration: electroformed silver filaments grow and repair vias after stacking
idea: Bond dies through a thin chalcogenide solid-electrolyte layer between coarsely aligned pads; a post-bond forming pulse drives Ag+ ions to grow filaments bridging whichever pads face each other, and any open or degraded bond found in field test is re-grown by another pulse.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): turns opens into repairable defects and relaxes alignment to a few um; filament current capacity and long-term stability are the risks.

title: Elastic buckling: roll-printed kirigami interposers pop up into 3D memory cages
idea: Print wiring on a pre-cut kirigami polyimide film; releasing pre-strain buckles it into a 3D cage that surrounds a processor with memory chiplets on all sides instead of along one edge.
why: GPU memory beachfront and interposer area (facts 5, 6): 3-4x more memory adjacency per processor from flat R2R manufacturing; thermal and mechanical robustness risk.

title: Oersted-pushed magnetic domain wall counts activations per row
idea: Effect: field-driven domain-wall motion. A short perpendicular-magnetized CoFeB nanowire with ~64 pinning notches runs alongside each wordline driver; each activation current pulse's Oersted field advances a domain wall one notch, and when the wall reaches the last notch a small MTJ senses it, requests neighbor refresh and a reverse pulse rewinds the wall. The count is exact and non-volatile, and it is built in BEOL over the driver.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row activation counts with zero SRAM area and no loss at power-down or self-refresh entry; avoids the 10-20% bandwidth cost of conservative probabilistic mitigations.
note: Wordline charge and discharge currents push the wall both ways; mA Oersted fields are near depinning thresholds.

title: AlScN piezo patches strain leaky mats to raise access Vt
idea: Effect: piezoelectric actuation plus deformation-potential band shift. AlScN piezo patches deposited over each mat are biased after retention test so that mats with leakage tails get uniaxial stress on their buried-channel access transistors, shifting band edges and Vt by ~20-40 mV and reducing junction band-to-band tunneling. The bias can be retuned in the field as the part ages.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and yield: worst mats see ~2-3x less tail leakage, so tail-limited mats are used instead of spared out, and their refresh relaxes ~2x with no new cell-array masks.
note: Thin piezo patches through BEOL transfer little stress to buried-channel devices.

title: Electrochromic contact images capacitor-dielectric defects across whole wafer
idea: Effect: electrochromism. After the capacitor dielectric step and before the top plate, a removable transparent electrolyte-plus-WO3 electrochromic contact is pressed onto the wafer and the bottom electrodes are biased through the substrate; cells whose dielectric leaks (pinholes, thin spots, pA-nA) color the film locally, and an optical scan maps millions of defect sites in seconds into a mat-level repair or rework map.
why: Capacitor leakage is a major retention-tail contributor (facts 1, 3): defects are caught at the step instead of after full flow and hours of multi-temperature retention test, raising yield and cutting test cost and scrap.
note: Optical resolution far coarser than cell pitch; electrolyte contact into high-AR electrodes is doubtful.

title: Ca: mayenite electride cages trap electrons as lattice-site anions
idea: Use a thin crystalline C12A7 (Ca12Al14O33) film, whose sub-nanometre cages host electrons as anions, as the storage layer of a gate stack; a gate pulse loads or empties cages near the interface and the caged electrons shift the read transistor's threshold.
why: Electrons sit in designed, identical lattice cages rather than random defects, aiming at trap-like retention without the oxide wear that limits flash endurance; all abundant Ca/Al/O; cage stability under cycling is speculative.
note: Charge-trap memory variant; still needs tunnel oxide, so flash-like wear and no clear DRAM win.

title: LiPON ionic back-gate puts idle subarrays into deep-Vt hibernation
idea: Li: put a thin-film-battery-style LiPON electrolyte plus Li reservoir under each subarray, separated from the silicon by an Al2O3 Li-blocking liner; a ~1 V, ~10 ms pulse builds an ionic double layer that shifts access-transistor Vt up ~0.3-0.5 V for subarrays idle for seconds, and is reversed before reactivation.
why: Idle refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3); a 0.4 V Vt lift cuts subthreshold leakage ~10^4-10^5, so cold pages need ~100x fewer refreshes on OS-idle timescales.
note: Lithium in a DRAM fab is a contamination hazard; only helps idle refresh.

title: Post-test oxygen-vacancy trimming raises Vt of leakage-tail cells only
idea: O: use an oxide-semiconductor access FET with an oxygen-exchange TaOx gate liner; at wafer test, locate the ~0.01% leakage-tail cells and apply a per-cell high-field gate pulse that pumps oxygen into the channel near the drain, annihilating donor vacancies and permanently raising that cell's Vt ~0.2 V.
why: The tail, not the median, sets refresh (fact 3); trimming the worst 1e-4 of cells could extend the refresh interval 4-10x without touching the rest of the array.

title: Polarization-doped AlGaN access channel eliminates random dopant fluctuation
idea: Al: build the access transistor in a compositionally graded AlGaN layer whose polarization gradient creates fixed 3D charge (polarization doping) instead of impurity atoms, so channel and junction 'doping' is set by a continuous Al-fraction grade identical in every cell.
why: Random dopant fluctuation in ~20 nm channels is a principal source of the Vt spread that makes the 13 fA tail (fact 3); dopant-free channels could tighten sigma-Vt ~2x and extend refresh 2-4x, if GaN-on-Si dislocation leakage is tamed.

title: Water-soluble salt release layer for stacking oxide memory tiers
idea: Periodic-table walk, Na+Cl (11,17): evaporate a NaCl film on a reusable carrier, seal it with ALD Al2O3, build an oxide-transistor DRAM tier at <=400 C (below NaCl's 801 C melt), bond it onto the stack, and dissolve the salt in water to release it.
why: Tier-by-tier 3D DRAM without HF/XeF2 sacrificial release and without consuming a Si wafer per tier; carrier reused indefinitely.
note: Sodium is a mobile-ion poison for oxide transistors; contamination control is the key doubt.

title: Fe: magnetically chained magnetite nanoparticles as wordline etch masks
idea: Spin a monodisperse Fe3O4 nanoparticle ink into coarse DUV guide trenches, apply an in-plane magnetic field so particles chain into parallel lines with spacing set by dipole repulsion, then sinter into an iron-oxide etch mask that strips in dilute acid.
why: Litho capital: field-directed assembly substitutes for SADP/SAQP on periodic array lines; each avoided multipatterning loop saves ~4-8 steps and an EUV pass. Defectivity is the risk.
note: Fe contamination is a retention killer.

title: Zn: ZnO piezo transducers send data acoustically through silicon stacks
idea: Sputter ZnO thin-film bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on every die so 1-5 GHz acoustic pulses carry data vertically through the bonded silicon stack (low acoustic loss in crystalline Si), with frequency-division channels per transducer; dies need a bonded acoustic path, not drilled and filled holes.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): hole-free stacking removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV yield loss; speculative ~0.5-1 pJ/bit links at modest per-channel rates.
note: GHz BAW data through Si; low per-channel rate and crosstalk unknowns.

title: O: IGZO-TFT active glass interposer hosts memory buffers and repeaters
idea: Fabricate InGaZnO oxide thin-film transistors (display-fab tooling, 1-10 um rules) directly on a glass interposer to implement repeaters, address buffers, ECC and power gating between logic and many DRAM dies, so the DRAM base die/PHY shrinks and the memory plane can span half a meter.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): moves logic onto Gen-8 display tools at ~1/100 the $/mm2 of silicon; enables panel-sized memory planes with distributed repeaters.
note: IGZO TFTs at 1-10 um rules cannot drive Gb/s repeaters.

title: Co: CoFeB spin-torque nano-oscillators as in-package memory radios
idea: Use CoFeB/MgO magnetic-tunnel-junction spin-torque nano-oscillators (~100 nm, 5-40 GHz, tuned by bias current) as frequency-agile transmitters and detectors, giving each DRAM die its own wireless channel inside a shielded package so dies can sit without TSVs or bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and packaging capital: each oscillator uses <1 um2 vs ~100 um2 for a TSV plus keep-out; speculative 1-2 pJ/bit.
note: STNO output power is nW-uW with broad linewidth; Gb/s links doubtful.

title: Ge: germanosilicate fiber delay loops hold model weights in flight
idea: Echoing mercury delay-line memory, circulate model weights as WDM light in a Ge-doped silica fiber loop (10 km ~ 50 us at 100 Tb/s ~ 600 MB in flight), re-amplified each lap and tapped at each accelerator exactly when the next layer needs those weights; the wire itself is the storage.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are read cyclically every token, so sequential delay storage fits the access pattern; replaces GBs of HBM with fiber at cents per meter, energy set by amplification per lap.
note: Lap amplification noise needs regeneration; 100 Tb/s transceivers cost more than the HBM replaced.

title: Sn: tin-bismuth microbumps self-reflow to heal opened HBM joints
idea: Use low-melting Sn-Bi (~139 C) microbumps with resistive heaters on the base die; when built-in self-test finds an open or high-resistance joint, the controller pulses local heat to re-melt and re-wet it, with spare TSV lanes as fallback.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) and field joint opens; recovering half the open-joint fallout adds ~10% usable HBM supply.
note: Local re-melt inside underfilled stacks risks neighbor joints; HBM moving to hybrid bonding.

title: One-drop-fill ferroelectric nematic: fluid polar bit that cannot fatigue
idea: Use LCD one-drop-fill manufacturing: dispense a ferroelectric nematic liquid crystal (RM734/DIO class: C, H, N, O, F) into sealed nano-cells whose antiparallel polar surface anchoring makes the ~5 uC/cm2 polarization bistable. A low-voltage pulse flips it in ns, and a capacitive charge read senses it.
why: Fact 10 and endurance: a fluid ferroelectric self-heals and does not wear out, with polarization comparable to solid ferroelectrics from commodity organics. The fill process is borrowed from the LCD industry.
note: Fluid polarization retention, ns switching and narrow N_F temperature range doubtful.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor 'forming': self-healing anodic Al2O3 kills leakage tail
idea: Copy the forming step of aluminum electrolytic capacitors: each cell has an anodic Al2O3 dielectric under a conductive polymer (PEDOT: C, H, O, S) counter electrode. A periodic forming voltage re-anodizes weak spots, and the polymer over hot spots de-dopes into an insulator, so leaky outlier cells cure themselves instead of setting the refresh rate.
why: Fact 3: refresh is set by the worst ~ppm leakage tail. Self-healing compresses that tail ~10x (refresh 64 ms -> ~0.5 s) using Al and organics only.
note: Novel, but the refresh tail is mainly junction/GIDL leakage, not dielectric.

title: Thermal-receipt printing: buried metal self-registers the next layer
idea: Like a receipt printer that marks only where heated, flash the wafer with near-IR that buried metal absorbs far more than oxide, so a thermally crosslinking resist hardens only above metal; this registers landing pads to contacts with zero overlay error and no mask, leaving the one allowed new mask for the cut layer.
why: Fact 4: overlay-critical layers without scanner time; overlay error near zero vs the ~2 nm budgets that push layers onto EUV.

title: Jacquard-loom woven micro-wire substrate with laser-fused crossings
idea: Weave 10 um insulated copper micro-wires (weft = signals) through glass-fiber warp on a Jacquard loom; a punched-card-style program decides which warp/weft crossings get laser-stripped and welded into vias. The result is a multilayer memory-to-compute substrate made with no lithography.
why: Cuts substrate capex and lead time; woven routing gives low-loss round wire (lower pJ/bit than flat traces) and ~10 um pitch without masks.
note: 10 um pitch via weaving with glass warp is implausible; loom-made substrate is a striking but doubtful idea.

title: Damascus-fold edge wiring: film thickness sets 40 nm pitch
idea: Deposit 100 alternating copper/oxide films 20 nm thick, or fold-laminate metal foil like Damascus steel, then slice the stack on edge and polish it. The face shows parallel wires whose pitch is set by deposition thickness, and this becomes a bridge die between memory and logic.
why: Sub-EUV wire pitch with no lithography at all; claims bridge densities beyond today's silicon bridges for HBM-class links.

title: Cast multicrystalline array wafers with grain-boundary-aware row retirement
idea: For the array wafer of a hybrid-bonded array/periphery split, replace argon-purged Czochralski pulling and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles with directional casting under vacuum/N2 in silicon-nitride-coated crucibles, as solar does; photoluminescence-image every wafer's grain boundaries and retire or remap the mats and rows that cross them, since boundaries mostly create leakage-tail cells.
why: Removes two chokepoints (argon, high-purity quartz) and cuts substrate cost several-fold, using reliability mapping to make imperfect silicon acceptable.
note: Intragrain dislocations and metal impurities in cast mc-Si likely ruin retention well beyond boundaries.

title: Jelly-roll memory: one patterned film rolled into a thousand tiers
idea: IFR: 'a thousand tiers for the price of one.' Backward: pattern one long polyimide ribbon with oxide-TFT memory mats and an edge bus, then wind it like a battery jelly-roll; each turn's exposed edge bus lands on a laser-patterned end-cap whose radius-coded traces act as the vertical interconnect, like battery tabs.
why: 3D tier count and capital (fact 2, 4): tiers come from winding, not deposition or bonding; 1,000 turns of a 10 um film make a 1 cm cylinder.
note: Winding adds volume density, not cost relief: the whole ribbon is still patterned.

title: MLCC-line ferroelectric block: one transistor, many plate-selected capacitors
idea: IFR: 'capacitor layers cost what a commodity chip capacitor costs.' Backward: use multilayer-ceramic-capacitor tape casting and screen printing to co-fire a block of thin doped-BaTiO3 layers where each layer is its own plate line, and bond an oxide-TFT glass lid giving one transistor per vertical column, a 1T-nC ferroelectric chain read by pulsing one plate at a time.
why: Capital (fact 4): runs on lines that make trillions of parts a year with near-zero new capex; low density (~10 Mb/mm2) and ferroelectric endurance must be proven.
note: ~10 Mb/mm2 is ~30x below DRAM; FE endurance and plate disturb unresolved.

title: Self-healing clearing electrodes burn out capacitor weak spots at test
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): the die must look like normal DDR5, so fix the leakage tail inside the cell. Make the capacitor top electrode an ultrathin clearable layer, as in metallized-film capacitors: a wafer-sort overvoltage pulse makes each dielectric weak spot conduct and locally oxidizes or vaporizes the electrode around it, isolating the defect so the dielectric can be thinned ~20%.
why: ~20% more Cs from a thinner dielectric (fact 1) and a tighter retention tail (fact 3) with no interface change; each cleared area must stay below ~5% of the electrode.
note: Clearing needs vented vaporization, which is hard inside high-AR holes; cleared cells lose capacitance.

title: Frequency-division wordline decoding with resonant driver gates
idea: Limit: zero logic gates in the row decoder. Each wordline-driver group is gated by a tiny resonant element (BAW or varactor tank) tuned to a unique frequency pair; the bank broadcasts two tones on one shared line, and only the group resonant at both rectifies enough voltage to fire, so address-to-frequency replaces the NAND decode tree.
why: Removes multi-stage decoder trees and predecode buses (~8-10% of the die) and frees one routing metal. Feasibility hinges on resonator size versus pitch, so it applies at subarray-select granularity, not per wordline.

title: Molten-salt electro-epitaxy grows wafers without Siemens or Czochralski
idea: Imposed scarcity: no polysilicon reactor and no crystal puller. Electrodeposit 300-700 um of single-crystal silicon from a KF-KCl-K2SiF6 molten salt at ~750 C onto a seed wafer capped with a weak porous-silicon release layer, then peel off the grown wafer and reuse the seed.
why: Collapses polysilicon (Siemens ~60-100 kWh/kg) and CZ (HPQ crucible, argon) into one low-temperature electrochemical step; a possible ~3x energy cut per wafer and zero crucible use.
note: Electrodeposited Si from fluoride melts is mostly polycrystalline; device-grade single-crystal wafers are a big leap.

title: Idle U.S. silicon-carbide power fabs build hot-proof DRAM transistors
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: 4H-SiC's 3.26 eV bandgap keeps off-state leakage negligible even hot, so build the access transistor (or gain-cell write device) in 200 mm SiC power fabs left underused by the SiC glut, then hybrid-bond a silicon capacitor/periphery wafer on top.
why: Fact 3 and capital: retention of seconds or more at 125 C (refresh ~1000x rarer) using existing U.S. SiC capacity instead of new DRAM fabs; density is limited by ~90 nm SiC litho.

title: No silicon: GaN-on-sapphire periphery from idle LED fabs
idea: Forced limit: no Si wafer for CMOS periphery. Idle LED MOCVD fabs grow AlGaN/GaN HEMT sense-amp and driver dies on sapphire (2DEG mobility about 1500 cm2/Vs), which are flip-bonded along the edges of glass oxide-TFT memory arrays.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die; putting it on fast GaN from stranded LED capacity lets cheap glass arrays reach about 50 ns access.

title: Self-assembled tier stack: parallel block-copolymer lamellae + sequential infiltration synthesis [SPECULATIVE]
idea: A lamella-forming BCP (L0 25-40 nm) with preferential wetting on both interfaces orders parallel to the substrate after annealing, giving 25-80 alternating layers in a 1-2 um film. Sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O) converts the PMMA layers into AlOx sheets; the PS layers remain as sacrificial carbon tiers (removed later by oxidation, as in B2-10). A single hole etch then opens all tiers; lateral recess and ALD oxide-channel/gate fills proceed as in B2-09. Tier thickness is set by polymer molecular weight rather than deposition time.
why: 25-80 tiers per coat vs one PECVD pair per tier: tier-formation tool time ~10-50x lower [ESTIMATE]; no SiN/SiGe stack.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous TiN sponge replaces smooth capacitor electrodes
idea: Substitute the smooth storage-node TiN with a nanoporous one: ALD a TiN/AlN nanolaminate electrode (TiCl4/TMA/NH3), selectively leach the Al phase in dilute NaOH/TMAH to leave a 3D sponge with 5-10 nm ligaments, then conformally coat with ALD ZrO2 and top TiN.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 2-3x electrode area in the same pillar (Cs 5 -> 10+ fF) without raising AR; no HF needed.
note: 5-10 nm pores leave no room for ZrO2 plus top TiN in a DRAM-pitch pillar; roughness raises leakage.

title: Mo wordline surface sulfurized into its own MoS2 channel
idea: Combine wordline and channel from one element: after each 3D tier's Mo wordline and an ALD HfO2 gate dielectric (Oregon hafnium), a thin Mo film on top is sulfurized below 450 C into 2-3-layer MoS2, giving a self-aligned, atomically thin access channel per tier.
why: Facts 2-3: ~1.6-1.8 eV few-layer MoS2 cuts off-leakage below Si and a 2 nm channel keeps tiers thin; all-US supply (Climax Mo, refinery sulfur, domestic Hf) and no indium/gallium.

title: NAND-grade LDPC replaces DRAM redundancy, fuses and laser repair
idea: Combine NAND flash's quasi-cyclic LDPC engine with DRAM. A rate-0.85 code in the base/buffer die absorbs a 1% raw cell BER, with a ~10 ns fast path for clean lines, so the DRAM die ships with no spare rows or columns, no fuse bank, no laser-repair pass and no repair-analysis test step.
why: Redundancy and fuses take ~5-8% of die area, and laser repair plus repair test take ~5% of back-end capex; together ~10% lower cost/bit (facts 4, 7).

title: Atmospheric mist-CVD oxide channels for error-tolerant gain cells
idea: Combine atmospheric ultrasonic mist-CVD, as used for Ga2O3 and solar TCOs, with 2T gain cells: the In-Ga-Zn-O-like channel is deposited without vacuum sputtering or ALD, and ~1% of cells with off-current outliers are absorbed by the code layer.
why: Vacuum tools cost $3-8M each, while mist-CVD tools are ~10x cheaper with higher throughput, cutting BEOL memory-tier capex (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Thermochromic-window vanadium dioxide as a Mott-transition latch cell
idea: Smart-window coatings switch VO2 between insulator and metal. Adapt a strain-tuned nanoscale VO2 element in series with an access transistor, using the transition's hysteresis window to hold two stable resistance states, with vanadium recovered from US steel slag and refinery residues.
why: A capacitor-free cell with a sub-ns transition, using vanadium from domestic waste streams instead of China/Russia. It trades refresh for a small hold bias.
note: Room-temp transition and hold-bias power.

title: Catalyst regeneration: in-field thermal anneal heals aged DRAM
idea: Adapted from refineries that regenerate fouled catalyst with heat instead of replacing it: DIMMs carry a thin-film PCB heater and thermistor (board-level and trailing-node parts) and, during scheduled windows with data evacuated, bake their dies at ~150-175 C for about an hour to anneal interface traps and restore hydrogen passivation degraded by hot-carrier and hammer stress.
why: Retention tail and aging (facts 3, 9): trap generation drives variable retention and rising error rates; partial recovery could extend module life and keep refresh rates low, stretching the installed base without new wafers.
note: 150-175 C bakes give little Si-H re-passivation, but cheap to test on aged DIMMs.

title: Self-assembled BaTiO3 nanocube ink as a spin-coated high-k
idea: MAGNIFY permittivity by printing it: hydrothermally synthesized 10-15 nm single-crystal BaTiO3 nanocubes self-assemble from ink into dense superlattices on the bottom electrode, then an ALD infill densifies the film without high-temperature sintering, targeting k ~100-200.
why: k well above 70 (fact 1) without perovskite MOCVD/ALD capital; the low-k infill in series is the risk.
note: 10-15 nm cubes exceed DRAM dielectric thickness; low-k infill drags k down.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing of maskless periphery wiring
idea: Minify the mask count of interconnect layers to zero: multi-nozzle EHD jets print sub-100 nm silver/copper lines for periphery routing straight from CAD, so every wafer can carry custom wiring or repair routes.
why: Masks and BEOL capital: removes metal masks and the litho-etch loop for those levels; gives instant design iteration.

title: Transistor-free crosspoint: printed threshold selector plus capacitor
idea: Minify the cell to 4F2 by printing crossed wordlines and bitlines, with a volatile Ag-filament threshold switch in series with a planar capacitor at each crossing as the access device.
why: Density and process steps: no transistor layers in the array, so 2-3 printed layers make a full array.

title: Single ink whose function is set by laser dose
idea: Minify materials from six inks to one: print one In-Zn oxide precursor everywhere, then a laser dose map sets each region as conductor, semiconductor or insulator by controlling oxygen-vacancy density.
why: Process steps and tool count: one print station plus one digital laser replaces multiple deposition-litho-etch loops.

title: Eliminate deposited tunnel oxides: ligand shells set nanocrystal storage barriers
idea: Eliminate the deposited tunnel oxide: spin-cast monodisperse 4-nm Si or InP nanocrystals as storage nodes whose organic ligand shell (C8 vs C12 alkyl chains) is the tunnel barrier, so barrier width is fixed molecularly to ~0.1 nm and retention from ms to s is chosen by ligand length; writes tunnel in ns at ~1 V, with no vacuum tool or gas.
why: Removes ALD/PVD steps and the capacitor (fact 1), and molecularly uniform barriers collapse the retention tail (fact 3); risks are ligand degradation under repeated tunneling and film packing defects.
note: Organic ligands degrade under repeated tunneling; packing defects widen the tail.

title: Eliminate CMP before bonding: in-vacuum atomic diffusion bonding
idea: Stack tiers by sputtering a few nm of Ti or Au-free metal onto both surfaces in the same vacuum and pressing them together at room temperature (atomic diffusion bonding), with no CMP to 0.5 nm roughness and no wet surface activation.
why: Water: hybrid bonding's CMP plus megasonic clean is repeated per bonded tier; vacuum bonding is dry, cutting bonding water ~10x and enabling cheaper multi-tier stacks.
note: Blanket metal films short hybrid interconnects.

title: Eliminate photoresist and PFAS: stamped-inhibitor area-selective deposition
idea: Microcontact-stamp a self-assembled inhibitor monolayer pattern from a reusable master onto the wafer; ALD then grows only on unstamped regions, forming hardmask lines directly with no resist, photoacid generator, developer or immersion topcoat.
why: PFAS photoacid generators and topcoats face EU restriction; removes coat/develop tracks and fluorinated chemistry from patterning.
note: Microcontact printing defectivity and overlay far from DRAM needs.

title: Porous materials: anodized macroporous capacitors in legacy 200 mm fabs
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: one mask opens a lattice of seeds and electrochemical anodization grows deep macropores (AR >100:1) for storage capacitors, letting legacy fabs without advanced high-AR plasma etchers produce DRAM.
why: Tool chokepoint and capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches high AR with a wet bath instead of a $10M+ etcher.
note: Anodized pores are disordered or micron-scale; registering ~30 nm pores to transistors unproven.

title: Electrocyte stack: parallel-store, series-read capacitor quartet
idea: Electric eels get high voltage by firing thousands of thin electrocytes in series. Each cell stores its bit on four small sub-capacitors charged in parallel, and at read three in-cell switches restack them in series so the bitline sees about 4x the voltage. Each sub-capacitor needs only ~1.3 fF at AR ~20, instead of one 5 fF pillar at AR 70.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): trades voltage gain for charge, so the signal per fF is ~4x and the AR-70 etch goes away. The cost is extra in-cell devices, so it fits best in BEOL/3D tiers where area is cheap.
note: Into a large bitline, series stacking delivers one sub-cap's charge; signal gain mostly vanishes.

title: Hopf-critical oscillator sense amp poised at edge of oscillation
idea: Cochlear outer hair cells sit near a Hopf bifurcation for huge gain on faint sound. A tiny oscillator is biased just below onset, so a few-mV bitline differential tips it into oscillation whose starting phase encodes the bit, captured by a flip-flop in ~2 ns. Proven on an open 130 nm shuttle with on-chip bitline/cell-cap replicas for <$1M in 24 months.
why: Fact 1/7: gain near criticality (>40 dB at microamp bias) could halve the required bitline signal, enabling longer bitlines with fewer sense amps or smaller Cs.

title: Silaffin-peptide biosilica as synthetic crucible-grade quartz
idea: Copy diatoms: silaffin-mimetic polyamine peptides (or cheap long-chain polyamines) precipitate amorphous silica at room temperature and neutral pH from silicic acid made by dissolving ordinary US industrial sand in base and purifying it by ion exchange first. The biosilica is sintered into the inner layer of fused-silica crucibles, so purity comes from solution chemistry instead of rare pegmatite quartz.
why: Attacks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz chokepoint for Cz crucibles; any sand becomes feedstock at ppb metal purity, decoupling crucible supply from one county.
note: Base dissolution adds alkali; ppb purity via ion exchange is the doubt.

title: Coral electro-accretion: electrodeposited capacitor dielectric from water
idea: Biorock reefs grow mineral on a cathode straight from seawater. Generate base electrochemically at the TiN storage-node surface in an aqueous zirconyl/titanyl bath, so a conformal ZrO2-TiO2 film precipitates evenly down 70:1 holes and stops itself as it becomes insulating, then densify it with an anneal.
why: Self-limiting electro-accretion grows only on electrodes with near-100% precursor use, versus <10% for ALD metalorganics, and needs no hafnium.

title: Chromatophore-shrink mastering makes nanoimprint templates without e-beam writers
idea: Squid chromatophores expand and contract pigment sacs elastically; write nanoimprint master patterns at 4x size with cheap i-line lithography on a resist atop a biaxially pre-stretched shape-memory polymer, release it so the relief shrinks 4x, then electroform a nickel or replicate a quartz daughter. Shrink distortion is measured once and pre-compensated in the 4x layout.
why: E-beam NIL mastering costs ~$0.5-1M and weeks per layer; this targets <$20k and days, making nanoimprint viable for DRAM layers that now need EUV (fact 4).

title: Mussel-foot catechol bonding of chiplets onto glass at room temperature
idea: Mussels stick to wet rock with DOPA catechol-metal coordination bonds. Memory chiplets are attached to a glass panel substrate with a catechol-functionalized adhesive that cures near room temperature, filled with conductive particles only over the pads, which avoids the CTE mismatch and warpage of 250-400 C bonding.
why: Packaging yield and cost: low-temperature bonding on glass removes warpage-driven yield loss in large multi-stack packages and the need for silicon interposers, and allows reworkable bonds.

title: Lock-in chopper sense amp doubles cells per bitline
idea: As in a lock-in amplifier, cross-switches chop bitline vs reference at ~4 GHz during signal development; the preamp works in the modulated band and a demodulator feeds the latch, so SA offset and 1/f noise fall outside the signal band. Resolvable signal drops from ~80 mV to ~25 mV.
why: Periphery area: 1024 instead of 512 cells per bitline halves the SA stripes (~10% of die); or the same margin with ~3x smaller Cs.
note: GHz chopping at bitline pitch adds charge-injection offset; offset-cancel SAs already exist.

title: Column-inversion storage cancels bitline coupling, like LCD panels
idea: LCD drivers alternate pixel polarity column by column to cancel crosstalk; store data in alternating true/complement polarity on adjacent bitlines and flip the pattern each row, so neighbour-swing coupling arrives common-mode at each sense amp and cancels, allowing tighter vertical-bitline pitch without shield lines.
why: Density in 3D arrays and signal margin (facts 1, 2): removes shield lines (~20-30% of bitline pitch) and recovers ~30% signal; claims ~1.25x density.
note: Data-dependent bitline swings stay random under fixed inversion; coupling does not become common-mode.

title: Delay-line recirculation with decode-and-correct at every string lap
idea: Mercury delay lines regenerated every pulse on each lap; revive that in shift-register 3D strings: as data pass the string-foot regenerator, a short BCH codeword is decoded and rewritten corrected every lap (~1 us), so per-transfer and leakage errors of up to 1% per cell never accumulate.
why: Facts 2 and 3: allows leaky, trap-rich channels and 128+ tier strings, while refresh becomes free scrubbing; near-NAND density for working memory.
note: Shifting every bit each ~1 us costs enormous energy at GB scale; ECC-per-lap concept is neat.

title: Apollo restart protection: recompute tensors instead of storing them perfectly
idea: Revive the Apollo guidance computer's restart groups, which recovered from faults by re-running from checkpoints: data in 1%-BER 3D memory carry a light detection code, and on a detected-uncorrectable error the runtime recomputes that tensor tile from its producer kernel instead of relying on heavy ECC.
why: Cuts code overhead to ~3% and admits marginal cells; recompute is cheap for activations and KV pages, raising usable capacity.
note: At 1% BER nearly every line has errors, so detection would trigger recompute almost always.

title: Anderson's 1952 crossbar ferroelectric memory revived in hafnium-free AlBN
