title: Po the test wafer is the product: reclaimed monitor-wafer substrates
idea: Po: 'the test wafer is the product.' Extracted: route the large stream of 200 mm monitor and dummy wafers used for tool qualification through CMP reclaim plus a thin epitaxial refresh layer, and run them as product substrates for 180 nm memory instead of virgin prime wafers.
why: Virgin polysilicon, crucible quartz and wafer energy per bit cut sharply for legacy memory; reclaim wafers cost roughly a third to a half of prime.

title: MRAM commit buffer: dirty pages leave DRAM the instant they are written
idea: Po: dirty pages are already safe. An Everspin (Chandler, AZ) STT-MRAM persistent write buffer on a domestic CXL card acknowledges database commits and redo records at byte granularity, so OLTP buffer pools no longer pin dirty pages or double-buffer log data while waiting for flush.
why: Write-heavy databases oversize buffer pools ~30-50% to absorb dirty pages and log buffers; persistent commit lets that DRAM shrink.

title: One-hot token ring steps refresh without waking address decoders
idea: Worse: run the full row decoder and predecode buses for every refresh command. Flip: a one-hot shift chain embedded in the wordline driver strip passes a token row to row during refresh and streaming scans, so decoders and global address buses stay power-gated.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): periphery share of refresh energy cut ~25-35%.

title: Cold-spray refill of eroded sputter targets on reusable backplates
idea: Worsen: scrap sputter targets when only ~30-40% of the metal has eroded. Flip: design targets with a reusable backing plate and refill the erosion groove by cold-spraying recovered Ru, Ti or W powder, then HIP and re-machine, instead of buying new targets.
why: Ru/W/Ta intensity: target material utilization rises from ~35% to >90%.

title: Strippable absorber mask blanks cycled through multiple reuses
idea: Worsen: scrap synthetic-quartz mask blanks at every DRAM node and every pattern ECO. Flip: design blanks with a sacrificial etch-stop under the absorber stack so it strips cleanly, then re-polish and re-coat the quartz substrate, cycling each blank 3-5 times.
why: Synthetic quartz and mask-shop capacity: DRAM uses ~60-80 masks per node, so blank demand falls ~3x.

title: Stonemason builds plasma chamber walls from local spinel, not yttria
idea: Persona: a medieval mason who builds with local stone. Replace yttria and YOF plasma-facing coatings with aerosol-deposited MgAl2O4 spinel or AlON. Both resist fluorine plasma and are made from U.S. magnesia and alumina.
why: Removes a rare-earth chokepoint (yttrium is >90% Chinese) from every etch chamber.

title: Cathedral builder's flying buttress: corner anchors carrying CTE strain
idea: Flying buttresses carry a wall's thrust outside it: place sintered-silver anchor pillars at the corners and edges of each memory die to take all shear from CTE mismatch, so the fine-pitch signal bonds in the field never see cyclic strain.
why: Fine-pitch signal joints survive 10 years of thermal cycling at 125 C, which allows denser, smaller bonds and so more bandwidth per mm of die edge.
note: Corner/dummy stress bumps already common.

title: Kintsugi conductor: liquid-metal microcapsules heal cracks in printed lines
idea: Kintsugi turns a crack into the strongest seam: microcapsules of gallium-indium liquid metal are blended into the printed silver interconnect ink of flexible memory foils and interposers, so when bending or thermal cycling cracks a line the capsules rupture and the liquid metal wicks into the gap, restoring conduction within milliseconds.
why: Line opens in printed and flexible circuits are a leading field failure; self-healing could cut them ~10x and allow cheaper, thinner foils.

title: Grocer's freshness label: printed time-temperature indicator predicts module aging
idea: Food labels change color with cumulative heat: a time-temperature-integrating indicator (enzymatic or diffusion-based ink, also readable electrically as a printed resistor) is printed on every DRAM module, and its integrated thermal dose predicts retention-tail and hammer-threshold degradation, so fleet software retires or re-bins modules before error rates rise.
why: Predictive retirement lets cells run on thinner margins safely and cuts DUE-driven outages, for less than a cent per module.
note: Onboard temp sensors already allow thermal-dose logging.

title: Naval-reactor hafnium trap avoided: zirconia-only periphery gate stacks
idea: Hafnium exists only as a byproduct of making Hf-free zirconium for naval and power reactors, so its supply is hostage to nuclear demand. Build DRAM-periphery HKMG transistors with ALD ZrO2 or La-doped ZrO2 on a SiON interlayer (TEMAZ precursor, standard in university ALD) and characterize EOT, mobility and PBTI against HfO2.
why: Removes hafnium from DRAM periphery using zirconium, which is roughly 20-50x more available, at similar k ~25-35.

title: Photonic curing: flash-lamp crystallizes zirconia in milliseconds, not furnace hours
idea: Plastic-substrate electronics that cannot exceed 150 C are cured with millisecond xenon flash lamps. Use flash-lamp annealing to crystallize ZrO2 into its high-k tetragonal phase and activate dopants in milliseconds instead of furnace anneals, tested on a university flash/RTA tool.
why: Furnaces are big energy and thermal-budget sinks: ms anneals cut anneal energy ~10x and can raise tetragonal fraction (higher k, more Cs).

title: Under-hood automotive: phase-change heat spreaders clip DIMM thermal spikes
idea: Automotive ECUs ride out engine heat soak with thermal mass. Fill DIMM and HBM heat spreaders with a phase-change material that melts near 80 C (paraffin blend or Ga-In-Sn alloy), so it absorbs workload bursts and keeps DRAM under the 85 C point where retention halves and 2x refresh kicks in.
why: Avoids doubled refresh (bandwidth and energy) and retention-tail failures during bursts, and lets marginal retention bins operate safely (fact 3).

title: ISS-style hot-spare dies that auto-swap in the field
idea: Space stations carry spares because resupply is rare. A 10-person team builds modules with one or two spare DRAM packages and a small mux controller that copies a degrading chip's contents and fails over automatically, so a module serves 12-15 years instead of being pulled at its first chip failure.
why: About doubles module service life and cuts replacement demand.

title: Datacenter fiber loops store bits as light in flight
idea: Jump to datacenter scale and to time of flight: coil 10-50 km of fiber per rack and circulate WDM pulse trains with amplification; a 20 km loop at 64 channels x 100 Gb/s holds about 0.6 Gb in transit for streaming tensors.
why: Scarce resources: memory capacity from mature telecom fiber and lasers, with no DRAM wafers, for sequential-access buffers.

title: Big old capacitor, many levels: 16-level charge in 180-nm cells
idea: Turn the coarse scale into resolution: 180-nm trench cells hold ~30-40 fF, enough charge for 16 levels about 60 mV apart, so a shared successive-approximation sense amp per mat reads 4 bits per cell. A 1990s-geometry cell stores 4x the bits.
why: Density without litho (fact 4): 4x bits per cell area by spending the surplus charge of older, larger cells.

title: Virtual metrology retires most monitor and dummy wafers
idea: Time shift from per-shift qualification to continuous checks: replace physical monitor wafers with models that fuse chamber RF, optical-emission and pressure traces with on-product scatterometry sites. Tools in existing trailing fabs are then qualified on product wafers.
why: Monitor and dummy wafers are 5-15% of wafer consumption. Cutting them ~70% frees CZ silicon, crucible demand and tool hours.

title: Elastic spare rows borrowed from user capacity on demand
idea: Time shift (fab-time redundancy -> lifetime redundancy): instead of fixed spare rows burned at the fab, all rows ship as user capacity, and the controller later converts address-remapped rows into spares through a firmware remap table as wear and weak cells appear.
why: Recovers the ~2-4% of array area spent on idle redundancy at time zero and spends it only when needed.

title: Garbage-collector compaction doubles as hardware refresh
idea: Timescale coupling (ms GC cycles <-> 64 ms refresh): managed runtimes rewrite live objects during compaction, so the controller exposes a 'freshly written' bit per row and skips refresh on heap regions rewritten within their retention window. Dead regions are never refreshed at all.
why: Cuts refresh operations on managed-heap memory by an estimated 30-70%, with weak-retention rows parked in high-churn nursery spaces.

title: Konarka's moisture death avoided via roll-to-roll spatial-ALD ultrabarrier
idea: Konarka's roll-to-roll organic PV died largely from water and oxygen leaking through weak barriers. Deposit a 20 nm Al2O3/ZrO2 nanolaminate by R2R spatial ALD (WVTR <1e-6 g/m2/day) directly over the oxide access TFTs. It also blocks in-diffusing hydrogen, which acts as a donor and raises off-current.
why: Stops the leakage tail from drifting in the field, the main reliability risk of printed oxide memory, so a long refresh interval set at test stays valid for years.

title: Thin-film magnetic memory on glass, read by cobalt-free permalloy spin valves
idea: 1960s thin-film magnetic memories deposited permalloy dots on glass but died on tiny inductive read signals and bulky drivers. Keep the glass and the permalloy, but read each dot with a NiFe/Cu/NiFe pseudo-spin-valve (thick and thin NiFe layers of different coercivity, ~5% GMR) and write with on-glass stripline current selected by oxide TFTs.
why: Removes Co, Pt, Ir, Ru, Ta and MgO from magnetic memory stacks; Ni, Fe, Cu are diversified; nonvolatile with unlimited endurance, so no refresh; cheap m2 glass substrate.

title: Copper-sinter pastes failed from oxidation; formate copper replaces indium TIM
idea: Copper nanoparticle sinter pastes lost to silver sinter because Cu oxidized and needed hydrogen furnaces. Use Cu-formate complex inks that decompose in situ at ~200 C into fresh, oxide-free Cu, sintering a 20-50 um porous Cu layer between HBM/accelerator dies and the lid in place of indium solder and gallium liquid-metal thermal interfaces.
why: Removes In and Ga from the TIM of >700 W accelerator packages; sintered Cu (~100-200 W/m-K vs ~80 for In) keeps memory stacks cooler for more bandwidth and less refresh.
note: Cu-formate sinter TIM; modest thermal gain, removes In/Ga.

title: Paraffin latent-heat buffer keeps DIMMs below the 2x refresh threshold
idea: Effect: latent heat and melt/freeze thermal hysteresis. Bond an encapsulated paraffin/graphite phase-change pad (melting ~75-80 C, ~200 J/g) between DRAM packages and the heat spreader; during load spikes it clamps die temperature below 85 C so the controller never enters JEDEC 2x refresh, and it re-solidifies in lulls.
why: Refresh bandwidth/energy (fact 3): ~10-20% bandwidth recovered on hot servers; off-the-shelf materials and a small hardware team.

title: Latent heat: printed phase-change heat buffers flatten HBM burst temperatures
idea: Screen-print a microencapsulated phase-change composite melting at ~75 C into a lid cavity over the HBM stack so AI burst heat is absorbed at constant temperature, keeping DRAM under the 85 C double-refresh threshold during peaks.
why: Refresh (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh rate in bursts with a cheap printed paste; buffers only seconds-scale transients.

title: Cold-spray refill of sputter targets keeps scarce metal in the loop
idea: W, Ru and Ta rotary targets are designed with a thick reusable backing tube; eroded racetracks are refilled by cold spray, where powder bonds through adiabatic shear instability at ~800 m/s without melting.
why: Raises effective metal utilization from ~35% to >90% and cuts tungsten purchases.

title: In-situ ALD recoating renews etch-chamber liners without teardown
idea: Chamber liners are designed with a plasma-tolerant base; during idle, self-limiting ALD cycles redeposit sacrificial AlF3/Al2O3 skins that the plasma erodes, so parts are renewed in place instead of swapped and shipped out.
why: Cuts chamber-part opex and rare-earth yttria coatings and raises tool uptime ~3-5%.
note: In-situ seasoning/precoat is common practice.

title: Mg: MgO magnetic-junction coin-flippers drive randomized row-hammer refresh
idea: Use the thermally stochastic switching of low-barrier MgO tunnel junctions as a true random bit source in every bank, so each ACT triggers a neighbor refresh with tunable probability p, with no LFSRs, counters or tables.
why: Probabilistic row-hammer defenses need fast, unbiased, attack-proof randomness; one ~0.01 um2 MTJ per bank replaces counter tables, cutting row-hammer logic area >10x at ~1k thresholds (fact 9).

title: O: electrochemically anodized gate oxides for room-temperature periphery transistors
idea: Anodize Zr or Al gate metal in an aqueous electrolyte so oxygen from water grows a self-limited ZrO2 or Al2O3 gate dielectric whose thickness is set by voltage (~1-2 nm/V), building BEOL periphery transistors without plasma ALD or argon sputtering.
why: Atomic-scale thickness control without vacuum tools enables cheap low-temperature periphery tiers over the array (facts 4, 7).

title: B: boron-doped diamond anodes close the rinse-water loop
idea: Pass spent rinse water through boron-doped diamond anodes that electrochemically mineralize organics and oxidizable species with no chemical dosing, then electrodeionize and return it to UPW grade at point of use instead of discharging it.
why: Water: raises recycle from ~40-60% to ~95%, cutting net withdrawal ~10x for the remaining wet steps.

title: Ga: GaN single-stage 48V-to-VDDQ regulation at the memory
idea: Mount GaN-FET hybrid switched-capacitor converters on the package substrate (and on DDR5 DIMMs in place of the 12 V PMIC) converting 48 V straight to VDD/VDDQ for the DRAM, eliminating an intermediate bus-conversion stage.
why: Energy per bit at system level: memory power delivery loses ~10-15% across two stages; single-stage GaN recovers ~5-8 points and cuts board copper, with DRAM interfaces unchanged.

title: Mg: polymerase-style proofreading verifies writes before row close
idea: Like DNA polymerase's Mg2+-dependent proofreading, controller RTL reads back freshly written columns before precharge while the row is still open and checks ECC; a mismatch triggers a rewrite with longer tWR or a remap.
why: Write-recovery failures grow as Cs shrinks (fact 1); verifying catches them before they become latent errors and allows aggressive tWR safely.

title: Ce: Closed-loop ceria CMP slurry recovery cuts rare-earth exposure
idea: Recover CeO2 abrasive from spent STI/ILD CMP slurry by flocculation, acid leach and recalcination, and qualify blended ceria-silica slurries using half the cerium.
why: China dominates rare-earth cerium refining; recycling and dilution cut a hidden chokepoint in DRAM CMP.

title: Anodized-aluminum pore forests become dense charge-pump capacitors
idea: Borrow the architectural-aluminum anodizing line: anodize a sputtered Al layer over the periphery so it self-assembles hexagonal pores ~150 nm wide and 2-3 um deep. Line the pores with a CVD TiN/Ta2O5/TiN stack (a 1990s DRAM capacitor stack) to make 3D capacitors stacked above the pump and decoupling circuits.
why: ~100-200 fF/um^2 vs ~10-20 fF/um^2 for MOS caps: VPP/VBB pump and decap area (several % of die) shrinks ~5-10x using only a wet bench and CVD.
note: DRAM periphery already reuses cell capacitors as reservoir caps.

title: Calculator-style chip-on-board DIMMs skip the package substrate
idea: Cheap calculators and LED boards bond bare dies straight to the board under a glob-top; mount known-good DRAM dies directly on the module PCB with copper-pillar flip-chip and one over-mold per module, eliminating per-die BT substrates, glass cloth and individual mold caps.
why: Package substrates and low-CTE glass cloth are a separate Japan-concentrated chokepoint; removing them cuts materials and package cost per GB ~10-20% and shortens traces for lower I/O energy.

title: Refinery stripping of chamber shields recovers tungsten and hafnium
idea: Gold refiners strip plated scrap electrochemically; instead of bead-blasting deposits off PVD, CVD and ALD chamber shields into landfill, strip them in selective anodic baths that redissolve W, Mo, Hf, Zr, Ru and Ta, then precipitate and calcine each metal as a pure salt for precursor makers.
why: Chamber kits accumulate a large share of deposited metal (PVD target utilization is only ~30-40%); recovery gives fabs a secondary supply of China-concentrated tungsten and scarce hafnium and ruthenium.

title: Foundry-sand reclamation for ceria: closed-loop Mountain Pass CMP slurry
idea: Foundries scrub and recalcine used casting sand; collect ceria CMP waste from trench-isolation and dielectric polishing, hydrocyclone and acid-wash it, recalcine to set crystallite size, and top up with ceria from Mountain Pass, California.
why: Ceria abrasive is a rare-earth product mostly from China; a 70-80% reclaim loop plus a domestic mine makes CMP fully domestic and cuts slurry waste and water.

title: Chlor-alkali cells on site: electrolytic ozone water replaces sulfuric-peroxide cleans
idea: Chlor-alkali plants make chemicals from brine with electricity; put diamond-electrode electrolyzers at each wet bench to generate ozonated water, hydrogen water and peroxide on demand, replacing piranha resist strips and RCA cleans.
why: Removes bulk semiconductor-grade sulfuric acid and H2O2 (short in the U.S. in 2021-22), their trucking and neutralization waste, and cuts chemical and rinse water ~30-50% using only domestic water and electricity.

title: Refresh stream doubles as a free read channel
idea: Ideal result: reading costs nothing because the row is already open. Route rows opened by refresh into an on-die staging buffer and serve queued reads to that row from it, while the scheduler reorders refresh to hit predicted hot rows first.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3, 8): turns part of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss into useful bandwidth, up to ~10% effective gain.

title: Error-correcting address codes keep decoders working after faults
idea: Ideal result: a decoder that cannot misfire. Encode each row address into a distance-3 code across the predecode lines, so a stuck predecode wire or broken gate still selects the correct row (or none, never two), and the fault is reported for repair.
why: Periphery reliability (fact 7): decoder faults become repairable events instead of yield or field killers.

title: Polarity-swapping latches spread transistor stress evenly
idea: Ideal result: transistors that never age unevenly. Periodically invert each mat's stored polarity, tracked by one inversion flag bit, so every SA cross-coupled pair sees balanced BTI stress and offset drift never accumulates.
why: Offset drift otherwise eats ~5-10 mV of margin over life; recovered margin allows smaller Cs and longer service.

title: Fuse-free die: redundancy map lives in the controller
idea: Limit: no fuse banks, antifuse arrays or laser repair on the die. At test, failing rows and columns are recorded in a signed table on the module SPD, and the memory controller remaps addresses before issuing them, with spare rows as ordinary rows.
why: Periphery area (-2-3% of the die), removes laser-repair tools (capital), and allows field repair at boot.

title: Glass-lined, SiC-coated wet benches replace fluoropolymer plumbing
idea: Within $1M/24 months: build one acid wet-bench loop with borosilicate-glass-lined stainless piping, CVD-SiC tank linings and ceramic valve seats instead of PFA/PTFE, and qualify metal-ion leaching to ppt levels over 12 months.
why: Fabs depend on PFA/PTFE wetted parts that pending PFAS restrictions threaten; a proven fluoropolymer-free path de-risks every U.S. fab.

title: Diamond-electrode loop regenerates sulfuric acid resist strip
idea: Within $1M/24 months: put a boron-doped-diamond electrolysis cell on the SPM resist-strip bath to oxidize spent sulfuric acid into peroxydisulfuric acid in situ, removing H2O2 dosing and recycling the acid instead of draining it.
why: SPM strips use large acid and peroxide volumes; closed-loop regeneration cuts ~80-90% of those chemical purchases and the wastewater neutralization load.

title: Recover ceria from spent CMP slurry
idea: Within $1M/24 months: bench pilot that concentrates spent STI CMP slurry by ultrafiltration, dissolves silica fines in dilute caustic, recovers ceria by flocculation, and re-calcines it to abrasive spec for reuse.
why: Cuts purchases of China-concentrated rare-earth ceria by ~50-70% and reduces slurry waste, on existing CMP tools.

title: No silicon: mine indium from scrapped LCD panels for oxide memory
idea: Forced limit: indium only from waste. Shred end-of-life LCD panels, leach the ITO with acid, and recover indium by solvent extraction into IGZO targets for oxide-memory lines.
why: Scarce resources: a secondary indium supply equal to a large share of primary output, sourced in the U.S. from e-waste.

title: Swimming-pool ozone chemistry replaces sulfuric-peroxide resist strip
idea: Pools and bottling plants sanitize with dissolved ozone instead of harsh chemicals. Strip photoresist and organics with high-concentration ozonated UPW (>80 ppm, with UV assist and CO2 spiking to protect surfaces) in a university wet bench, benchmarking against SPM on implanted resist.
why: SPM consumes large volumes of sulfuric acid, peroxide and rinse water; ozone is made from oxygen on demand, cutting chemical purchases and wastewater ~80%.

title: TSV-stacked read-optimized NAND beside the accelerator for weights
idea: Combine HBM-style TSV stacking and wide I/O on a mature-node base die with NAND dies tuned for massive read parallelism, dedicated to read-only inference weights; the accelerator's HBM keeps only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are read-only so NAND endurance is irrelevant; 8-16x capacity per stack versus HBM DRAM, with no EUV layer in either the NAND or the base die.
note: High Bandwidth Flash already announced; >10x capacity per stack for read-only weights.

title: Memory tier slipped into Intel 18A backside-power stack
idea: Fuse logic backside power delivery with memory: after the US PowerVia flow thins the wafer, deposit a low-temperature capacitor plus thin-film-transistor memory tier on the backside between the transistors and backside power rails, giving each logic die tens to hundreds of MB of DRAM-class memory microns from its cores.
why: Data movement (fact 5): <0.1 pJ/bit vertical access; absorbs cache/KV traffic so accelerators need fewer HBM bits; built in existing US leading-edge fabs.
note: Backside contacts land directly on S/D, leaving little room for a memory tier; needs a leading-edge fab.

title: Magnetostrictive-squeezed Mott switch from delay-line wire technology
idea: Revive the magnetostrictive nickel-wire delay line: wordline current through a Galfenol (Fe-Ga) strip strains an adjacent nanoscale piezoresistive Mott material (SmSe-class) into its metallic phase, opening the cell. With no current the material relaxes to its insulating phase, ~1e5x more resistive, and there is no semiconductor junction to leak.
why: Isolation comes from a band-gapped insulator at zero strain rather than a subthreshold MOSFET (fact 3); galvanic separation between wordline and channel also removes wordline-coupling row-hammer paths (fact 9).
note: Magnetostrictive strain at nm scale weak; SmSe piezoelectronic integration unproven.

title: Wafer stitching mask turning a DRAM wafer into shared pool
idea: One added top-metal stitching mask links reticle fields across the scribe lines, so an entire 300 mm DRAM wafer becomes one TB-scale memory fabric. Compute tiles bonded around it all read a single copy of the weights and shared KV prefixes, and defective fields are routed around.
why: Jumping from chip-scale to wafer-scale sharing collapses weight and prefix replication across 50-100 accelerators into one copy, cutting memory need 2-5x for large-model serving.
note: Bandwidth from one shared copy to many tiles and wafer-scale DRAM yield are the doubts.

title: Coulomb blockade: thousand-electron charge-packet signaling read by single-electron sensors
idea: Encode each interposer bit as a ~1,000-electron charge packet clocked down a short low-capacitance line and sense it with room-temperature single-electron transistors built from sub-2 nm silicon islands whose conductance swings per elementary charge.
why: Moves ~0.16 fC per bit instead of ~40 fC (100 fF x 0.4 V): ~250x less charge, attacking pJ/bit (fact 5) at the extreme; thermal noise and reliability make it speculative.
note: Room-temperature SETs and mV-level signals on real lines need near-miracle noise control.

title: Substitute electrical wordline with optical wordline and photoconductive access
idea: Substitute the metal wordline and gate with one silicon-nitride waveguide per row feeding a wide-gap (AlGaN or diamond) photoconductive switch at each cell. A pulse from an on-chip micro-LED makes the switch conduct; in the dark it is an insulator with attoampere-scale leakage.
why: Removes the 3 V wordline pump and the wordline RC delay and gives near-zero dark leakage (refresh-free retention); no wordline coupling for row hammer. Switching speed and persistent photoconductivity are the risk.

title: Swap electrostatic gating for piezoelectronic pressure-driven insulator-metal switch
idea: Substitute the gate field with mechanical pressure: a thin AlScN piezo actuator squeezes a pressure-sensitive insulator-metal transition layer (SmSe-type) between storage node and bitline. Under GPa-scale stress its resistance drops ~1e4-1e6; relaxed, it is a bandgap insulator.
why: Steep ~0.3 V switching breaks the wordline voltage floor, and the off state is a true insulator rather than a weakly-off transistor: ~10x wordline energy and long retention claimed.
note: IBM PET concept; GPa stress at cell scale and endurance unproven.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si repeaters amplify bitlines every 32 cells
idea: Substitute one long passive bitline feeding one end latch with a distributed bitline: excimer-laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT repeater stages every 32 cells regenerate the charge-shared signal locally, as display backplanes do.
why: Charge wall: each segment sees only 32 cells of bitline capacitance, giving ~8x higher signal per femtofarad and allowing much smaller Cs.
note: No room at array pitch for TFTs, and laser crystallization over capacitors is a thermal risk.

title: Substitute 300 mm silicon wafers with Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build a capacity-tier DRAM (oxide-TFT access devices plus stacked MIM capacitors) on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in converted LCD/OLED fabs, patterning 40-60 nm features with panel-scale nanoimprint. One panel equals the area of ~70 300 mm wafers and the line tools are largely depreciated or idle.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: panel fabs cost 5-10x less per m2 processed; even at 4-8x lower density than DDR5, cost per bit could compete for cold/capacity tiers. Overlay on glass and TFT leakage are the risks.
note: 40-60 nm imprint and overlay on Gen-8.5 glass is far beyond panel capability.

title: Substitute per-write ferroelectric switching with power-event-only polarization snapshot
idea: A DRAM capacitor gets a thin ferroelectric HZO liner that stays unpolarized-active in normal DRAM mode (charge only); a power-fail detector fires one global 'snapshot' pulse that writes each cell's charge state into polarization, and recall happens at power-up.
why: NV without the FE fatigue problem: the ferroelectric is cycled only per power event (~1e4 in life), so DRAM-mode endurance stays unlimited while refresh-on-idle can be fully powered off.

title: Bistable buckled nanobeam storing bits as mechanical position
idea: Combine a pre-compressed (buckled) SiC nanobeam, which has two stable shapes, with a capacitive-gap read: an electrostatic pulse snaps the beam up or down, and the beam's position sets the capacitance to a sense electrode. Mechanical bistability holds the bit with zero hold current and no refresh; nanoscale beams switch in ~10 ns.
why: Facts 3 and 9: refresh (16-33% of idle power) and row hammer both disappear because there is no charge to leak or disturb; SiC MEMS show >1e12-cycle fatigue life.
note: Same buckled-beam mechanism.

title: Vacuum nanogap field-emission access device
idea: Replace the semiconductor channel with a ~10 nm vacuum gap between a sharpened storage-node tip and the bitline electrode, gated by the wordline (a vacuum tube fused into the cell). It conducts only by gate-assisted field emission.
why: No junction, BTBT or diffusion current exists in the off state, so leakage is near zero and the cell is radiation hard.
note: Zero junction leakage, but 10 nm field-emission tips give poor, variable on-current; vacuum nanogap transistors known (NASA Ames).

title: Coincident X-Y selection with dual-gate access transistor
idea: Like core memory's coincident-current selection, give each access transistor two gates (row wordline plus a column-segment select line) so only cells where both are high open; activating a cache line opens 64-512 cells, not an 8 kb row.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): removes most of the 128x overfetch (~5.9 pJ to under 1 pJ per useful bit) and confines hammer exposure to a segment.
note: Fine-grained activation is known; a dual-gate access device in the cell costs area and half-select leakage.

title: Light-through-silicon vias: 1310 nm optical bus vertically through stack
idea: Combine silicon's transparency at 1310 nm with HBM die stacking: keep small metal-free windows in each ~30 um thinned die and place a wavelength-selective vertical grating coupler plus ring modulator/Ge detector at each window, so a single WDM beam injected from the base die rises through all 12-16 dies and each die drops/adds its own wavelength. Photons replace most data TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (~3x area/bit, 20-30% yield loss): replacing 1,000+ data TSVs with a few optical windows cuts stacking area overhead and TSV-related yield loss, enabling >16-high stacks.
note: Si emitters absent; windows through 16 metal stacks and per-die WDM drop filters are very hard.

title: Polyoxometalate multi-electron clusters as quantized storage nodes
idea: Adapt polyoxometalate catalysts, which reversibly accept 2-6 electrons at sharp molecule-defined potentials: graft a monolayer of W18-type POMs onto a buried node electrode so each node holds discrete charge states read through a gain transistor.
why: Density and fact 1: molecule-defined charge levels give 2 bits per node without analog trimming, and the node is ~1 nm thick instead of a ~1 um pillar.
note: POM molecular flash shown; ns redox kinetics and endurance unproven.

title: 3D XPoint selector film gating vertical sidewall capacitors
idea: Adapt Optane's threshold selector and vertical-RRAM geometry: a vertical bitline pillar crosses 48 word planes, and at each plane the sidewall carries a mixed-ionic-electronic selector film in series with a 4 nm MIM capacitor, making a transistor-free two-terminal 1S1C cell.
why: 10x at same cost: 48 planes share one hole litho, so even with ms retention bits per footprint rise ~15x; requires selector half-bias leakage below ~1 fA.

title: Matryoshka concentric storage shells nested in one hole
idea: Like nesting dolls, ALD alternating TiN node shells and grounded shield shells inside one 80 nm hole, then recess each shell to a different height so its rim lands on a different tier of thin-film access transistors; each shell is an independent capacitor.
why: 10x at same cost: a 20 nm-radius, 1 um-tall shell already holds ~15 fF, so 6 nested nodes x 2 bits/node gives ~12 bits from one hole etch.

title: Quanta-image-sensor jot stores each bit in twenty electrons
idea: Borrow Gigajot's pump-gate jot with ~0.2 e- rms read noise and ~400 uV/e- conversion gain: store a bit as 0 vs 20 electrons in a sub-aF buried node, read non-destructively by an in-cell source follower, and pack jots at 4F2 in stacked tiers.
why: 10x at same cost: ~20 e- instead of ~30,000 e- per bit shrinks the storage element ~1000x in charge, enabling 4F2 cells in 6 tiers, ~10x density.
note: In-cell source follower cannot fit 4F2; sub-electron read needs slow CDS.

title: Jelly-roll memory: roll a display-fab sheet into dense cylinders
idea: Adapt cylindrical Li-ion jelly rolls: fabricate a large thin oxide-TFT gain-cell array on a strained release layer at display-fab cost per area, then self-roll it into 100-winding micro-cylinders whose edge lines contact a CMOS base die.
why: 10x at same cost: display fabs make area ~100x cheaper per m2 than DRAM wafers, so 100 windings of a 1/10-density sheet give ~10x bits per footprint at equal cost.
note: Same self-rolling multi-tier concept.

title: UV-C LED AlGaN ultra-wide-bandgap capacitorless node in tiers
idea: Borrow AlGaN from UV-C LED fabs: a ~6 eV bandgap AlGaN channel transistor with near-zero leakage holds charge on its own gate node (no capacitor) for hours, enabling a 4F2 2T0C cell stacked in 8 low-temperature-deposited tiers.
why: 10x at same cost: no capacitor and no refresh, 1.5x from 4F2 x 8 tiers is ~12x; nitride tools are mature and present in the US.
note: Low-temperature AlGaN quality is poor.

title: Vacuum-tube revival: nano vacuum-channel field-emission access switch
idea: Adapted from vacuum tubes and the thermos flask: replace the silicon access transistor with a gated nano vacuum channel (sharp Si or Mo emitter tip, 10-20 nm sealed vacuum gap, gate ring) that conducts by field emission only when the wordline raises the tip field. With the gate low, electrons must tunnel through the full vacuum barrier, so there is no junction, no GIDL and no subthreshold diffusion path.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3): off-current set by vacuum tunneling could be <1 aA, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes and cutting refresh energy >100x; risks are emitter wear, drive voltage and hermetic sealing at cell pitch.
note: Field emission needs high fields; on-current, wear and hermetic sealing at cell pitch unresolved.

title: Stacked image-sensor Cu-Cu bonding gives every bitline segment a sense amp
idea: Borrowed from Sony's pixel-parallel stacked image sensors: the array wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer at ~1 um pitch so each 32-64-cell bitline segment connects to its own sense amp below, eliminating long bitlines.
why: Charge wall: bitline capacitance drops ~10x, so ~0.5 fF or capacitorless cells work, and sense-amp stripes leave the array die (~15% area).
note: Needs ~0.3 um bond pitch and a full SA per 32-64-cell segment area; geometry does not close.

title: Williams-tube revival: field-emitter arrays write charge on bare film
idea: Adapted from the 1940s CRT Williams-tube memory and field-emission displays: a CMOS-driven field-emitter tip array (one tip per ~1,000 bits) sits ~1 um above an unpatterned dielectric storage film in vacuum; each tip deflects its micro-beam to deposit charge spots and reads them by secondary-emission current.
why: The storage film costs cents per wafer and needs no transistors, wires or litho; only the tip array is patterned at relaxed pitch, ~100x lower cost per bit in principle; trade-offs: vacuum package, 100 ns-1 us access, spot drift needing refresh.

title: MRI-style cryostat with superconducting interposer for memory links
idea: Adapted from the MRI magnet and superconducting-wire industry: the accelerator+DRAM module runs in a 77 K closed-cycle cryostat on an interposer with YBCO high-temperature superconducting traces. Links become nearly lossless, and DRAM leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): near-zero resistive link loss and 100x+ retention at 77 K; this works only if cryocooler overhead stays below the energy saved.
note: YBCO needs epitaxial substrates; cryocooler overhead likely exceeds savings.

title: AlN-clad GaN quantum-well storage node with barrier-tilting write
idea: MAGNIFY the confining barrier from ~1 eV (Si junction) to ~2 eV by holding the bit as electrons in a 3-nm GaN well clad with AlN; a transfer gate transiently tilts the barrier with the help of the built-in polarization field (CCD-style transfer) to write in ~5 ns, and a HEMT channel beneath the well senses the stored charge non-destructively.
why: Thermionic escape falls by ~e^(-1 eV/kT) ~1e-17, so retention moves from 64 ms to hours and refresh (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) nearly vanishes; no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.
note: GaN on Si integration with dense CMOS is the main barrier, not the retention physics.

title: Four bits stacked in one pillar hole by depth segmentation
idea: MAGNIFY bits per etched hole 4x: form an AR-60 cylinder capacitor in an ONON-style mold, then interrupt the storage electrode with three ALD SiO2 plugs so four isolated segments sit at different depths, each reached by a ring-gate vertical-channel transistor patterned in the matching mold tier.
why: Reuses today's capacitor etch while placing 4 bits per hole, ~3x density without a 26-tier lateral 3D DRAM (fact 2); each ~1.2 fF segment needs a gain-cell or sensitive sense amp.

title: Minify bitlines for refresh: 16-cell local sense nodes
idea: Add a hierarchical micro-sense amplifier every 16 cells (placed under the array via bonded CMOS) used only for refresh, so each cell restores against a ~1 fF local bitline rather than a 50-100 fF global one. Normal reads still use the global path.
why: Bitline charge per refreshed bit drops >10x; all subarrays can refresh in parallel, hiding the 10-20% bandwidth loss.

title: One-mask cell array via self-aligned everything
idea: Minify array masks to one: a single DUV mandrel feeds self-aligned quadruple patterning in two orthogonal directions, and every later array layer (contacts, landing pads, capacitor holes) is defined by selective deposition and etch keyed to the prior topography, never by an overlay exposure.
why: Masks and EUV count: array EUV layers fall from 5-7 to 0 and array mask count drops roughly 80%, removing overlay error budgets and cutting litho share of wafer cost by about half.
note: Zero-overlay array relies on perfect selective deposition chains; defect accumulation likely.

title: Full-wafer single-shot nanoimprint of each array layer
idea: Magnify the imprint field from one 26x33 mm die to the whole 300 mm wafer: a flexible quartz-on-glass master imprints every array layer in a single press using thermal-expansion-matched chucks and in-situ moire alignment.
why: Lithography throughput and tool cost: one press per wafer replaces ~100 scanner shots; tool cost ~$15-30M versus ~$200M EUV, targeting >5x lower litho cost per wafer layer.

title: Diamond interlayers enabling 64-high cool stacks
idea: MAGNIFY stack height to 64 dies by bonding ~1 um polycrystalline-diamond heat-spreading films between DRAM layers in place of dummy thermal bumps, carrying heat sideways to the stack edge.
why: Density per package footprint and interposer area: 4x the capacity per HBM site without heat-induced refresh penalties.
note: Diamond CVD temperatures incompatible with DRAM; heat still exits at the edge.

title: Magnify the ECC codeword to an entire 8 KB DRAM row
idea: Every activation already latches the whole 8 KB row into the sense amps, so a row-wide quasi-cyclic LDPC decoder (~3% parity) in the bank periphery corrects the full row at activation/restore instead of using 128-bit SEC words. Raw BER up to ~1e-3 becomes acceptable versus ~1e-6 today.
why: Facts 1 and 8: turns 128x overfetch into a free ECC window; weaker cells are fine, so Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~2.5 fF (AR ~35:1 instead of 70:1) for ~3% parity overhead.

title: Eliminate up-down polarization: polar-vortex chirality bits in oxide superlattices
idea: Eliminate the up/down polarization picture: in PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices, polarization curls into vortices or polar skyrmions whose handedness is a topologically protected bit, written by a curl-shaped field from split electrodes and read through its chirality-dependent (gyrotropic) electrical response.
why: Topological protection gives nonvolatility with no net polarization reversal (low fatigue) and ~10-nm bits; attacks refresh (fact 3) and density; electrical chirality readout is unproven.
note: Electrical chirality readout is unproven.

title: Eliminate the metal storage node: polyoxometalate clusters as multi-electron reservoirs
idea: Eliminate the electrode-plus-dielectric capacitor: graft one molybdenum- or vanadium-based polyoxometalate cluster per cell (no tungsten), which reversibly accepts 2-8 electrons at discrete, well-separated redox potentials, gated by an oxide-semiconductor access transistor; each redox state is one level, giving 2-3 bits per cell.
why: A 1-2 nm molecular storage node breaks the capacitor wall (fact 1) and multi-level raises density 2-3x; risks are redox kinetics under 10 ns and cycle endurance.
note: Same POM mechanism.

title: Eliminate the solid channel: vacuum field-emission access to storage nodes
idea: Eliminate solid-state leakage: connect each storage node through a sealed 10-nm vacuum nano-gap with a sharp field-emission tip; at hold bias the Fowler-Nordheim current is effectively zero because there is no semiconductor and no generation, while a few-volt access pulse across the gap conducts uA in picoseconds.
why: Retention limited only by dielectric leakage (hours), so refresh disappears (fact 3); radiation hard; risks are tip wear, work-function drift and 3-5 V access voltage (fact 10).

title: Eliminate TSVs: infrared light links shining straight through thinned dies
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so bond InP micro-LEDs and place Ge photodiodes at the same x-y sites on every 30 um-thinned die, and each lane's beam passes vertically through a 12-high stack. Time slots or wavelengths pick which die speaks, so there are no TSV keep-out zones and no TSV yield loss.
why: Fact 6: attacks the TSV area tax and the 20-30% HBM yield loss and removes TSV etch and fill; target ~1 pJ/bit vertical links.
note: Each die's Ge photodiode and BEOL metal block the beam; 12-high pass-through implausible.

title: Eliminate the flat wafer surface: arrays built on trench sidewalls
idea: Etch 50-100 um-deep parallel trenches across the wafer and build DRAM cells on both vertical walls using tilted-implant and self-aligned spacer patterning, folding several square centimetres of array area into each square centimetre of footprint.
why: Density per footprint and per wafer: each wafer behaves like several wafers of area, cutting crystal-silicon and depreciation per bit if sidewall uniformity holds.

title: Eliminate the quartz crucible: electromagnetic cold-crucible silicon crystal growth
idea: Melt silicon in a water-cooled segmented copper crucible where RF induction heats the charge and pushes the melt off the wall (skull melting), so it never touches quartz, and pull 300 mm crystals from it under a magnetic field; oxygen is added only by controlled gas doping.
why: Removes the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz dependence outright and tightens interstitial-oxygen control (fewer slip and precipitate yield losses); cold-crucible casting already exists for solar silicon.

title: Rotate the array into depth: four capacitors stacked in one trench
idea: Rearrange the 2D array vertically: in a 1990s-style 0.25 um wide, 10 um deep trench, deposit alternating doped-poly electrodes and collar oxides to form four isolated storage capacitors stacked along the trench, each reached by its own buried strap and sidewall transistor at a different depth (depth-addressed wordlines).
why: Density without a litho shrink (fact 4): four cells per trench footprint, ~25 fF each (2 um2 of 5 nm ONO per segment); risk is forming straps and transistors at depth.
note: Transistors and straps at several trench depths are very hard; 0.25 um trench pitch erodes density gain.

title: Mechanical switch: vertical NEMS contact replaces the access transistor
idea: Reverse what moves: instead of gating electrons through a semiconductor, the wordline electrostatically pulls a ~10 nm-gap vertical nanocantilever (Ru- or TiN-coated) into contact with the storage node. When open the gap is vacuum or gas, so off-state leakage is essentially zero and retention is limited only by capacitor dielectric leakage (minutes to hours).
why: Eliminates the access-transistor leakage tail and refresh (fact 3) and allows a low actuation voltage via nanogap; contact endurance of ~1e15 cycles is the core risk.
note: 1e15 contact endurance and stiction at 10 nm unproven.

title: Inside-out cell: access transistor grown inside the capacitor's hollow core
idea: Rearrange inside and outside: form the cylindrical storage capacitor first as an open shell, then grow a vertical gate-all-around channel up its hollow core so the capacitor's inner electrode is the transistor's drain, with no landing pad or buried contact between them. The wordline wraps the channel inside the cylinder.
why: Removes the storage contact/landing pad, a dominant leakage and resistance site (facts 3, 7), and folds transistor into capacitor footprint (~4F2), improving both retention tail and area.

title: Negative-capacitance bitline element cancels parasitic bitline capacitance
idea: Reverse the sign of the parasitic: a ferroelectric HZO negative-capacitance element at the bitline foot subtracts from the effective bitline capacitance the cell sees, raising the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) from ~0.1 to ~0.3-0.4.
why: Facts 1 and 7: a 3x larger sense signal lets Cs drop to ~2 fF (AR ~25:1) or bitlines grow 3x longer (SA count /3). Hysteresis-free transient NC is the risk.
note: Stable ferroelectric NC cancellation is unproven.

title: Sense-amp latches drive silicon-photonic rings, skipping column decode
idea: Reverse the data path: instead of SA -> column mux -> global I/O -> PHY, groups of SA latches directly drive micro-ring modulators on a silicon-photonics layer from a U.S. photonics fab (e.g., New York), bonded over the array, with 64 wavelengths per waveguide carrying the row out.
why: Fact 5: data movement ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-20 pJ/bit; the global I/O tree (~5-8% of periphery) disappears.
note: Micro-rings cannot pitch-match sense amps; tuning power per ring.

title: Sense amps flipped beneath array, one per 128-cell bitline
idea: Move sense amplifiers from mat edges to a logic wafer hybrid-bonded underneath, with one ~0.4 um-pitch bond per 128-cell bitline segment (staggered so pads fit), giving every short bitline its own SA directly below. Bitline capacitance falls ~6-8x versus 1k-cell bitlines, so a ~1 fF capacitor delivers today's signal.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): capacitor AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~10-15:1, removing the hardest etch; shorter bitlines also cut sensing energy and latency.
note: Sense amp cannot fit in area of 128 cells; 0.4 um bond pitch frontier.

title: Capacitor first, vertical transistor regrown over it, bitline on top
idea: Reverse the 4F2 vertical-channel order: etch and fill storage capacitor trenches first in bulk silicon (annealed at ~1000 C for crystalline high-k), cap them, grow silicon laterally over them by epitaxial lateral overgrowth, form the vertical-channel transistor in the regrown silicon, and put the bitline on top. The notoriously hard buried bitline of 4F2 VCT disappears.
why: Density + capacitor wall (facts 1,4): 4F2 (+33% cells/area vs 6F2) with a capacitor not limited by BEOL height and a high-temperature dielectric (k~40+).

title: Inside-out flower cell: plate in the hole, transistors radiating
idea: Invert the lateral 3D DRAM cell: each through-stack hole holds a shared plate pillar; the tier's silicon around it is recessed into a ring capacitor, and 4-6 lateral access transistors radiate outward to per-tier horizontal bitlines. Built on a 3D NAND tool line reusing its hole and slit mask types, plus one added plate-contact mask.
why: 3D cell (fact 2) and capacitor (fact 1): each hole serves 4-6 cells per tier with capacitor area growing with hole circumference, roughly doubling bits per hole versus one-cell-per-hole lateral designs.
note: Ring capacitor plus 4-6 radiating transistors per hole per tier is geometrically very demanding.

title: Split the cell across two wafers: capacitor wafer bonded on
idea: Rearrange where the cell is made: build the capacitor array alone on a cheap, relaxed-tool wafer and the access transistors on a second wafer, then hybrid-bond them face to face at sub-100 nm pad pitch so each transistor lands on its capacitor.
why: Decouples the high-AR capacitor module (no thermal or litho limits from the transistor) and lets each wafer run on its own cheaper tool set; ~20% fewer steps on the expensive wafer.
note: Needs ~40 nm-pitch hybrid bonding, far beyond today's ~0.4-1 um.

title: Light is the wordline: photoconductive access switches on glass
idea: TRIZ #32 Changing optical properties: each cell's access switch is a high-dark-resistivity photoconductor (e.g., low-temperature-grown GaAs or amorphous-selenium-class film, >1e12 ohm-cm dark) on transparent glass, opened by a picosecond pulse from a row waveguide. Off leakage is set by dark conductivity, the optical wordline carries no CV2 charge, and wordline coupling disturbs vanish.
why: Removes the ~3 V wordline energy (Fact 10) and hammer coupling (Fact 9) with very low dark leakage for long retention (Fact 3); requires on-panel laser and waveguide integration.

title: Taking out: transistor-free array dies time-share one CMOS reader die
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: array dies hold only capacitor cells, oxide-TFT access devices and a TFT 1024:1 bitline multiplexer, built with ~10 masks on depreciated 65-90 nm lines; 16 such dies stack on one 28 nm CMOS reader die whose sense amps, decoders and I/O serve every die through vertical global bitlines, one die active at a time.
why: 100x path: no front-end CMOS on 15/16 of the silicon (~3x), mature tools (~4x), periphery amortized 16x (~2x) and cheap stacking (~4x); trade-offs: ~1/16 bandwidth per stack, ~us row cycle and thermal limits. Attacks Facts 4 and 7 and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Parameter change: 77 K operation lets junk polysilicon transistors stack 64-high
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: memory sleds run immersed at 77 K, where leakage of cheap low-temperature polysilicon access transistors falls by ~1e6 and kT/C noise by ~4x, so 64 BEOL tiers of poly-Si 1T1C cells with planar ~2 fF capacitors hold data for minutes and are read by small low-offset cryo-CMOS sense amps under the array.
why: 100x path: 64 cheap tiers on a 40 nm logic base (~30x more bits per dollar of area), refresh periphery deleted, sense amps ~2x smaller; trade-offs: liquid-nitrogen infrastructure and ~10 W of cooling per W dissipated, so it suits rack-scale memory pools. Attacks Facts 2, 3 and 4.

title: Double-sided wafers: memory arrays on both front and back faces
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: finish a front-side array plus periphery, bond face-down to a carrier, thin to a 1-2 um etch stop, then build a second transistor/capacitor array on the backside of the same active layer, reaching the shared front periphery through nano-TSVs.
why: Doubles bits per starting wafer, halving CZ silicon and high-purity quartz crucible use per bit and sharing one periphery for two arrays (~20-25% die-cost cut; scarce resource, capital).

title: Sixteen layer-transferred DUV tiers replace EUV shrink for density
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation moves density into height: transfer a ~50 nm single-crystal Si film per tier by smart-cut, build only an ~8-mask DUV array tier of planar nonvolatile cells (e.g., 6F2 at F~40 nm with asymmetric-electrode AFE capacitors) at <=500 C with laser dopant activation, and repeat 16 times above one shared periphery.
why: Zero refresh; 16 tiers at ~0.0096 um2/bit give ~0.0006 um2/bit effective, beating 1b-node DRAM (~0.00086) with zero EUV; capex shifts from scanners to cheap repeated DUV and bonding modules (facts 2, 4).

title: Nesting: DRAM dies set into pockets in the GPU backside
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: with backside power delivery the GPU substrate is thinned anyway. Etch ~30 um pockets into its backside and set thinned DRAM dies inside, wired through nano-TSVs into the backside network, so each DRAM die sits ~30 um from the logic it feeds.
why: Data movement (fact 5): the interposer and long wires disappear, for <0.3 pJ/bit and no shoreline limit, and capacity grows with no added footprint.

title: Another dimension: DRAM dies standing on edge, bonded at sidewalls
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: stand thinned DRAM dies upright like books on a logic base die. Route metal lines to the diced edge and open them as sidewall pads, then solder or hybrid-bond each die's edge to the base, so there are no TSVs and every die has its own path down.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV area and no 12-hop stacking yield cascade, attacking the ~3x area-per-bit penalty, and heat leaves along each die's full height.

title: Periodic action: staggered counter-cyclical capex rotation under antitrust safe harbor
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace synchronized boom-bust fab building with a published rotation where each maker adds capacity in assigned years, supervised under a government safe harbor and backed by offtake guarantees in its slot.
why: Pig-cycle volatility: smooths supply so 4x price spikes and loss years are both dampened.

title: DNA supercoil topology: polar-vortex chirality as a protected bit
idea: Supercoiled DNA keeps its linking number until an enzyme cuts and passes a strand. In lead-free BaTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattice nanodots, store the bit as the clockwise or counter-clockwise chirality of a polar vortex, which is topologically protected against thermal flips. Asymmetric electrodes supply a curled field to switch it, and in dots where axial polarization is locked to chirality, the sign of the switched charge reads it.
why: Non-volatile at ~10 nm, where ordinary ferroelectric domains depolarize, so ferroelectric storage can scale below the ~20 nm FeRAM limit.
note: Polar vortex memory proposed widely; electrical chirality write and read unproven.

title: Mechanosensitive-channel piezo-strain gated access switch
idea: Bacterial MscL opens only when membrane tension stretches it; build the access switch from a pressure-driven insulator-to-metal piezoresistor (SmSe or Cr-doped V2O3 film) squeezed by a ScAlN piezoelectric wordline actuator, so the channel is a true band insulator until the wordline strains it metallic.
why: Off-current is limited by insulator conduction, not the Boltzmann subthreshold tail (~1e-20 A), and piezo gain can let the wordline swing <1 V instead of ~3 V, cutting wordline CV2 energy ~9x.

title: Dendritic-spine cells sprout sideways from one vertical bitline shaft
idea: Each vertical bitline is a dendrite shaft; at every tier a selective SiGe recess in a Si/SiGe superlattice leaves a thin 'spine neck' nanowire channel gated by that tier's wordline plane, ending in a bulbous 'spine head' storage node lined by ALD dielectric, so a 64-tier cell column is made from a single hole.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell: self-aligned per-tier transistor+capacitor from one etch; the narrow neck gives high off-resistance; aims at 3D break-even near 30 tiers with 2-3 critical masks per 64 tiers.

title: Hemoglobin cooperativity: stacked GaN/AlN tunnel-diode pairs self-latch each bit
idea: Hemoglobin's cooperative binding gives a sharp two-state switch; give each 3D cell a vertically stacked Goto pair of AlN/GaN resonant-tunneling diodes (~2 eV band offset keeps negative resistance at high temperature) on the storage node, so the node is bistable and self-restores against leakage, read through one vertical access transistor.
why: Eliminates refresh at 125 C (tunnel-SRAM at near-DRAM density): refresh's 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth go to near zero, with standby set by RTD valley current.
note: Tunnel-SRAM revival; III-N epitaxy is not BEOL-compatible and per-cell valley current kills standby.

title: Tree-ring lamination: test each printed tier before stacking
idea: Trees add one growth ring per season on top of the last. Print one memory tier per foil, test each tier at speed in line, then laminate only known-good tiers (32+) with printed through-foil vias, so yield does not compound across tiers as in monolithic 3D DRAM.
why: Breaks the 26+ tier breakeven problem for 3D memory because each tier's yield is independent, using printing lines instead of a $15B fab and EUV.
note: Printed tiers cannot reach DRAM speed or density.

title: Electric-eel electrocyte stacks: shallow nanolaminate capacitors replace tall pillars
idea: Electric eels reach high output by stacking thousands of thin electrocytes; ALD-stack 8-12 alternating Ru/ZrO2 layers in a shallow ~150 nm recess and tie odd and even electrodes to node and plate through two self-aligned sidewall spacers, like a miniature multilayer ceramic capacitor.
why: Capacitor area multiplies by layer count without high-AR etching (fact 1); removes the 60:1 etch and support layers, est. 8-10% lower wafer cost and lower etch capex.

title: Imaginal-disc HBM lifts off via pressure contacts for next boards
idea: Insect imaginal discs survive metamorphosis into the adult; HBM stacks mount to the interposer through anisotropic conductive film or micro-spring pressure contacts instead of permanent microbumps, so stacks can be lifted off a dead or obsolete accelerator and placed on its successor.
why: HBM supply and TSV-yield tax: one stack serves 2-3 accelerator generations.
note: Pressure contacts at HBM microbump pitch are very hard.

title: Compound-eye infrared links shining straight through stacked dies
idea: Silicon is transparent above ~1.1 um, so each DRAM tier carries tiny bonded 1.3 um emitter and detector pixels under a microlens array, like an insect's ommatidia, that beam data vertically through the thinned dies above and below. Hundreds of vertical optical channels replace signal TSVs with no drilling and no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): signal TSVs and their keep-out area disappear and vertical bandwidth scales with pixel count; target <0.3 pJ/bit per vertical hop.

title: Williams tube reborn: field-emitter array writes charge spots on continuous film
idea: Revive the 1947 Williams tube (the first DRAM) with field-emission-display Spindt tip arrays: in a vacuum-sealed package each tip is electrostatically deflected over a 4x4 patch to write and read charge spots on an unpatterned SiO2 electret film over a sense grid, reading by secondary-emission contrast. The storage plane needs no per-bit transistor, capacitor or lithography.
why: Facts 4 and 7: the storage plane is a blanket film, so patterned features per bit drop ~16x (16 bits per tip); charge on high-quality oxide in vacuum leaks negligibly; vacuum packaging and tip lifetime are the risks.

title: Pumped-hydro twin reservoirs: fixed electron shuttled between paired quantum dots
idea: Like pumped hydro moving the same water between two reservoirs, each cell holds a fixed electron that never leaves the cell, only shifting between two coupled 2-4-nm Si nanodots (~0.3 eV charging energy) across a tunnel barrier; a write gate tilts the double well and an electrometer gate senses which dot is occupied.
why: Facts 3 and 8: with no path to a bitline there is no junction leakage to refresh, and read is non-destructive (no restore after 128x overfetch); RT operation needs sub-5-nm dots with uniform barriers, the key risk.
note: RT needs sub-5 nm uniform dots; QCA-like.

title: Thin-film battery plateau: two-phase lithium node holds voltage despite leakage
idea: A battery's flat voltage plateau barely moves as charge leaks, unlike a capacitor's linear droop; make each node a ~50-nm solid-state nanobattery (sputtered Li4Ti5O12 or LiFePO4 electrode, ~10-nm Li3PS4 or LiPON electrolyte) whose states are the charged and discharged plateaus, sensed by a gain transistor; ~1e5 stored Li+ outlast fA leakage.
why: Fact 3: at the 13 fA tail, 1e5 charges last ~1 s (~20x the refresh window) while the voltage stays digital, never drifting into the sense margin; buildable with sputter, evaporator and a glovebox; ionic write speed and cycle life are the risks.
note: Plateau insight is nice but ionic write speed and cycle life block DRAM-class use.

title: Pinch-valve access: piezo-squeezed channel that physically closes the conduction path
idea: Pinch valves seal by squeezing a tube flat instead of holding back pressure. Build the access element from a piezoresistive Mott material (SmSe-type) clamped by a thin relaxor piezoelectric driven by the wordline: strained, the material goes metallic; unstrained, it is a wide-gap insulator, so there is no gate-controlled subthreshold tail at all.
why: Replaces exponential subthreshold behavior with a pressure-driven insulator-metal transition switching at ~0.1-0.3 V, attacking both the voltage floor (fact 10) and leakage (fact 3).
note: Nanoscale PET unproven; SmSe gap too small for DRAM-grade off-resistance.

title: Apartment-tower shared lobby: one sense die serves eight array dies
idea: An apartment tower shares one lobby and elevator bank. Stack eight array-only dies whose short bitline segments drop through hybrid-bonded vertical vias into one shared sense/decode die, with a tier-select switch at each die's bitline foot so one die connects at a time.
why: Water/periphery: periphery wafers per bit fall ~8x and array dies need no CMOS module, so periphery-attributable water falls ~10x with no new chemistry; added via capacitance is the physics risk.
note: Via plus tier-switch capacitance on bitlines likely destroys signal.

title: Fire-brigade bucket chain: CCD charge transfer to a tiny sense node
idea: Like a bucket brigade passing water hand to hand, read a vertical 16-cell string CCD-style: 4-phase 0.5 V transfer gates clock the selected cell's charge along a buried channel to a ~0.3 fF floating diffusion with a source follower and correlated double sampling, and reverse clocking writes it back.
why: Energy per access (facts 8, 10): no bitline swing at all, only low-voltage transfer gates and a tiny high-gain node; claims >10x lower read energy and supports ~0.2 fF cells.
note: CCD readout of cell strings; same core as vertical CCD string.

title: Multilayer ceramic capacitor stacking for lateral 3D-DRAM storage nodes
idea: MLCC makers stack hundreds of BaTiO3 layers between nickel electrodes using abundant elements. In horizontal 3D-DRAM tiers, build each storage capacitor as an interdigitated lateral finger stack: recess the Si/SiGe superlattice sidewall, then ALD alternating TiN and paraelectric (Ba,Sr)TiO3 shells so each tier holds several parallel plates instead of one cylinder.
why: Attacks the 3D-DRAM capacitor blocker (fact 2) without 60-75:1 vertical pillar etches; thin-film BST (k ~200) can raise Cs per footprint ~3x using Ba, Sr and Ti, none of them chokepoint materials.
note: BST k collapses in sub-10 nm conformal films and needs high crystallization temperature.

title: Backside-power analogy: deep-trench capacitors etched from wafer backside
idea: Borrowed from logic backside power delivery and BSI image sensors: build transistors and bitlines on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, then etch deep-trench storage capacitors from the backside, landing on each transistor's source through nano-TSVs, so capacitors stop competing with bitline contacts for front-side space.
why: Facts 1/7: capacitor height is decoupled from front topology and the front area is freed for periphery; nano-TSV alignment at ~30 nm pitch is high risk.
note: Nano-TSV landing at ~30 nm pitch after thinning is the overlay killer.

title: Player piano: cold MoE experts computed inside 3D NAND
idea: Like a piano roll that plays the instrument directly, store rarely routed mixture-of-experts weights in 3D NAND with string-level analog multiply-accumulate (bitline current summing); the token vector goes to the NAND die and only the expert output returns, while hot experts stay in HBM.
why: MoE models leave 90%+ of parameters idle per token; computing the cold majority inside persistent NAND removes it from DRAM/HBM, ~5-10x less memory per model.

title: Williams tube 2.0: on-chip field-emitter arrays writing a charge mosaic
idea: Like the Williams-Kilburn CRT that stored bits as charge spots on a phosphor face, a vacuum-sealed micro-cavity holds a carbon-nanotube field-emitter array, each emitter electrostatically deflected over a 4x4 um patch of a nitride charge-trap mosaic. Bits are 20-nm trapped-charge spots written by beam dose and read by secondary-electron yield on re-scan, with write-back exactly like the Williams regeneration raster.
why: No wire, transistor or capacitor per bit: periphery is per-emitter not per-row (Fact 7) and bits are not litho-defined (Fact 4); ~40k bits per emitter gives ~5 Gb/cm2 per layer from old-node litho; beam slew ~20-50 ns.
note: Resembles HP field-emitter probe storage; vacuum packaging and emitter stability.

title: Bobeck bubble chip reborn: skyrmion minor loops with replicate gates
idea: Bring back the bubble chip's major/minor-loop organization (many short minor loops, transfer gates into a major loop) using 20-nm skyrmions in compensated ferrimagnetic GdFeCo stepped by spin-orbit-torque pulses. Keep the bubble chip's replicate gate, which splits a skyrmion and sends the copy to the detector, so reads are non-destructive.
why: At 40-nm pitch and ~1 bit/ns stepping a 32-bit minor loop gives <=32 ns access; only tracks are patterned so ~2F2 per bit, no capacitor or transistor per bit (Facts 1-4), non-volatile.
note: Reliable skyrmion replication and stepping at 20 nm unproven.

title: BEAMOS revival: electron-beam addressed storage with no access transistor
idea: Revive GE's 1970s BEAMOS: a MEMS-deflected array of molybdenum field-emitter microcolumns (one per ~64k-bit tile, in a vacuum cavity wafer-bonded over the die) writes and reads charge on fully floating MOS storage islands via secondary-emission balance, so no bit is ever tied to a transistor. Refresh becomes a slow background raster sweep, as on a Williams tube.
why: Removes the access transistor and its leakage tail (fact 3); a floating island leaks only through dielectric, so retention could reach hours and refresh energy drop >100x; periphery shrinks to beam drivers (fact 7). Open risk: 10-100 ns spot access with fast deflection.
note: BEAMOS worked at us access; 10-100 ns random access with microcolumn deflection is the doubt.

title: Purdue GaAs heterojunction storage well revived on silicon
idea: Revive the 1980s-90s Purdue AlGaAs/GaAs DRAM cells, which held charge for hours at room temperature because electrons sat in a well bounded by a wide-gap barrier: integrate a selectively grown heterostructure storage well (AlGaAs/GaAs, or GaP/AlP, which is lattice-closer to Si) on silicon, so stored charge can escape only by thermionic emission over 0.4-1 eV band offsets.
why: Storage-node leakage is set by the band offset rather than by junction or trap generation (fact 3); retention orders of magnitude longer would make refresh rare.

title: Nano vacuum-channel triodes as zero-leakage access switches in BEOL tiers
idea: Bring back the vacuum tube at 20 nm: each 3D cell's access device is a vertical field-emission triode etched into dielectric (metal tip, gate ring, storage-node anode), needing no crystalline channel and leaking essentially nothing when off. Cells stack in 50+ BEOL tiers because no epitaxy or high-temperature anneal is required.
why: Facts 2 and 3: removes the single-crystal lateral transistor blocker for 3D and the <=13 fA leakage tail, stretching retention from 64 ms to minutes and cutting refresh energy (16-33% of idle) by >90%.
note: Field emission is one-way, so a single triode cannot both charge and discharge the node.

title: Field-emitter array writes charge into an unpatterned storage film
idea: Revive the Williams tube and GE's 1970s electron-beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS): a carbon-nanotube field-emitter array, each emitter with micro-deflection plates, sits ~20 um above a blank MOS storage film in sealed vacuum and writes and reads charge spots by secondary-emission contrast, regenerating them as the Williams tube did. Bit pitch is set by beam spot (~20 nm), not by lithography on the storage film.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (Fact 4): the storage plane needs zero critical masks and no access transistor; one emitter sweeping a 50x50 um field addresses ~6M bits, moving complexity into a coarse emitter chip and cutting the 5-7 EUV array layers to none. Latency may land at 100 ns-1 us.

title: Mandated U.S. second-source licensing of DRAM designs, 1970s-style
idea: Revive the 1970s-80s rule, enforced by military and big buyers, that every memory part had a licensed second source (the Intel 1103 was second-sourced): require that DRAM bought in volume by federal agencies and subsidized hyperscalers has a licensed U.S. second source, with design, test programs and process recipes transferred under royalty.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: transfers proven designs instead of each new entrant spending 5+ years of learning; could seed ~5-10% domestic supply on existing logic or legacy lines within ~3 years.

title: Bubble major/minor loops in Co/Pt tracks rotate KV each token
idea: Revive the bubble chip's major/minor-loop layout with university-sputtered Co/Pt perpendicular films whose tracks are defined by ion irradiation: each minor loop holds one KV block as magnetic domains, all loops shift together under spin-orbit-torque current, and the whole KV cache passes the readout once per decode step.
why: Attention reads all KV every token, so a nonvolatile rotating store matches the access pattern with zero standby power and no refresh, moving long-context KV out of DRAM.

title: NEC 4-Level DRAM Revival With Setun Balanced-Ternary Storage
idea: Revive NEC's 1997 four-level 4 Gb DRAM and the Soviet Setun's balanced-ternary memory: store three levels (-, 0, +) around the VDD/2 bitline precharge so the 0 state needs no charge, sensed by a two-step sense amplifier with a reference half-cell, giving 1.58 bits per cell on an unchanged capacitor.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per wafer on existing fabs without new litho; only two thresholds are sensed, easing the 5 fF charge wall versus 4-level designs.
note: Halved sense margin on a charge-starved cell; retention tail worsens.

title: Contactless tunneling nano-relay isolates the storage capacitor in vacuum
idea: Invert 'the access device is a leaky semiconductor junction' -> isolate the storage node with a vacuum gap. A vertical electrostatic nano-relay in the BEOL never touches: it closes from ~5 nm to ~1 nm so charge tunnels in/out, and when open the vacuum gap has no junction, GIDL or trap-assisted leakage.
why: Kills the <=13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3): retention becomes dielectric-limited (hours), recovering 10-20% bandwidth and refresh energy; no contact means no wear, keeping endurance effectively unlimited.

title: Altermagnet bits read by spin-split tunneling with zero net moment
idea: Invert 'magnetic memory needs net magnetization to be read' -> store the bit in an altermagnet whose moments cancel. MnTe or RuO2-class altermagnets have zero net moment yet spin-split bands, so a tunnel junction reads Neel orientation by TMR and spin-splitter torque writes it; no stray field permits ~10 nm pitch and wear-free, THz-fast switching.
why: Non-volatile, unlimited endurance, dense without dipolar crosstalk and immune to row-hammer-style disturbance (fact 9); MnTe avoids ruthenium scarcity; room-temperature TMR magnitude is the risk.
note: Hot topic since 2022; RT TMR in altermagnets is unproven.

title: Polar-vortex handedness bits in oxide superlattices on scandate substrates
idea: Invert 'a ferroelectric bit is polarization up or down' -> store the chirality of a polar vortex. PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices grown on DyScO3 or SrTiO3 substrates form ~10 nm vortex tubes whose left/right handedness is a topologically protected binary state, switched by a curled field from twin gate electrodes and read by a chirality-dependent capacitance/piezo asymmetry.
why: Topological protection gives retention and disturb immunity at ~10 nm pitch (density, fact 9) with no capacitor; electrical chirality read/write at speed is unproven.
note: Same polar-vortex handedness bit.

title: Vacuum-channel field-emission access to vacuum-isolated storage electrodes
idea: Invert 'the storage node must sit in solid insulator next to a semiconductor' -> put it in vacuum. Each cell is a sealed nano-cavity on glass where a sharp emitter faces the floating storage electrode across a ~20 nm vacuum channel, gated so field emission charges or discharges the node; when off, vacuum conducts nothing.
why: Removes junction leakage and its refresh (fact 3), radiation- and temperature-immune, no silicon wafer; emitter uniformity, nano-cavity sealing and ~10 V emission fields are the risks.
note: ~10 V emission, emitter uniformity and surface leakage around node are the doubts.

title: Light is the wordline: photoconductor cells addressed by micro-LED rows
idea: Inverts 'the access device is a transistor on a metal wordline': a blanket wide-gap photoconductor film sits between capacitor dots and metal bitlines, insulating in the dark (retention set by very high dark resistivity), and a row is selected by flashing a stripe of a bonded micro-LED/waveguide array for ~10 ns. No transistors, no wordline drivers, two masks per layer.
why: Removes access transistors and much of the 49% periphery (fact 7) at film-coating cost, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off is optical power per access, 10-100 ns latency and photoconductor persistence.

title: Random-wired memory: nanowire mesh with addresses discovered, not designed
idea: Inverts 'every cell has a designed address': spray a random mesh of core-shell nanowires (each a gated-diode storage element) between coarse electrode grids, then let a self-test routine discover which electrode pairs reach a usable cell, store the map in on-chip flash, and address through stochastically doped decoder wires instead of patterned decoders.
why: No overlay or fine litho, so cost tracks coating plus coarse patterning (~100x cheaper per GB claimed), with refresh tuned per discovered cell; trade-off is ~30-60% usable sites and a lookup table.

title: Williams tube reborn: MEMS electron beams paint charge on film
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs a transistor': like the 1947 Williams-Kilburn tube, store bits as charge spots on a continuous unpatterned dielectric film, written and read by secondary emission from an array of ~10^4 microfabricated field-emitter beamlets each scanning a ~100 um patch; the beam re-scan doubles as refresh.
why: Cost per bit falls to film coating plus the amortized emitter array, ~100x cheaper per GB claimed; trade-off: us latency, vacuum packaging, emitter lifetime.

title: Threshold-graded tier select replaces staircase contacts in 3D
idea: Inverting 'each tier of a 3D stack needs its own staircase contact and driver': each tier's select transistor in a stacked capacitorless (floating-body or thyristor) array is given a different threshold voltage by graded work-function gates, so one shared vertical gate line picks the tier by voltage level.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier drivers, a major area and process cost of 26+ tier 3D DRAM; breaks the 3D break-even barrier sooner.
note: A single gate level turns on every tier with lower Vt; needs coded multi-line select (like 3D NAND LSM).

title: Ferroelectric ZnMgO shadow tier lets idle arrays stop refreshing
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must be refreshed while idle.' Pair each DRAM tier with a wurtzite ZnMgO ferroelectric twin tier on the same vertical bitline; when a bank idles, rows copy into the FE tier in parallel and refresh shuts off, restoring on wake, so FE endurance is spent only at idle transitions.
why: Fact 3: idle refresh power (16-33% of idle) falls to near zero without Hf-based HZO.
note: Wurtzite ZnMgO FE needs very high coercive fields; nvSRAM-style shadow backup applied to DRAM idle states.

title: Recombination barrier implant stops hammer electrons between wordlines
idea: Inverts 'the substrate is a passive bystander': one implant mask places a deep p+ or carbon-rich trap layer between adjacent buried wordlines so electrons injected from the aggressor channel recombine before reaching the victim storage node.
why: Raises the row-hammer threshold (fact 9) from ~1k to ~10k+ activations, shrinking mitigation SRAM and extra refresh; one implant mask.

title: Polar flux-closure vortex chirality as a sub-5 nm ferroelectric bit
idea: In PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattice nanodots, polarization curls into closed vortices that carry no surface bound charge, so the depolarizing field vanishes. Store the bit as vortex chirality (clockwise or counterclockwise), written by a curled field from an offset electrode pair and read through the chiral piezo or tunneling signal.
why: Ordinary ferroelectric bits fail below ~10 nm because depolarization energy beats the barrier; closure textures delete that term. Aims at a 3-5 nm polar bit (density) with no charge leakage (fact 3).
note: Same flux-closure chirality bit.

title: Atomically precise one-nanometer gold clusters as room-temperature Coulomb-blockade bits
idea: Derive the island from e2/2C >= 25 kT at 300 K: C <= 0.12 aF, a sub-1 nm island, which lithography cannot make but chemistry can (Au25(SR)18 clusters, ~1 eV charging gaps). Trap one cluster per cell between multiple tunnel junctions, store 0/1/2 electrons, and read with a single-electron-transistor electrometer, using the Coulomb staircase for 2 bits per cell.
why: Bits held as countable electrons need ~1 electron, not 31,000. Targets ~1e4x less stored charge, sub-aJ writes and multi-level density (facts 1, 10).

title: vdW-latched nanoparticle shuttle bit in a sealed nanocavity
idea: A 3 nm gold nanoparticle sits in a 7 nm sealed cavity between two electrodes, held against either wall by van der Waals adhesion (~2 eV, ~80 kT from the Hamaker estimate). A charge-plus-field pulse throws it across in ~100 ps, and the read senses tunneling current, which changes ~1e4x with particle position.
why: A rigid-body position bit has no leakage tail (fact 3), an exponentially sensitive non-destructive read (fact 8), and a cell volume of ~10 nm3.
note: 7 nm sealed cavity fabrication and impact wear are major unknowns.

title: Tunneling-mode NEMS access switch: vacuum gap replaces the leaky channel
idea: Start from the lowest-leakage switch physics allows: a vacuum gap, where off-current falls about 10x per angstrom of tunneling distance. Replace the access MOSFET with an electrostatically pulled 3 nm SiC nanobeam in a hermetically sealed cavity that moves from a 4 nm gap to a ~0.5 nm non-contact tunneling gap. It never touches, so there is no stiction or wear. Near-gap tunneling easily supplies the ~0.5 uA a 5 fF write in 10 ns needs, while the open-gap current is below 1e-21 A.
