why: Removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction leakage in one move, so the 13 fA tail (fact 3) disappears. Retention becomes limited by the capacitor dielectric (minutes to hours), cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax by >100x.
note: Sub-nm non-contact gap control at cell pitch fights vdW pull-in; NEMS DRAM explored before.

title: Lattice-matched GaP storage-node junction starves GIDL and SRH generation
idea: Silicon's 1.12 eV gap is what makes band-to-band tunneling at the gate-drain overlap easy. Regrow only the storage-node contact as 5-10 nm n+ GaP (2.26 eV, 0.37% lattice mismatch to Si) by selective MOCVD. The high-field overlap and the metallurgical junction then lie in wide-gap material, while the channel stays silicon for drive current.
why: BTBT rate ~ exp(-B*Eg^1.5/F), so doubling Eg multiplies the exponent about 2.9x and cuts GIDL by >1e5 at equal field. SRH generation in the GaP volume falls ~1e9 through n_i. Together they attack the GIDL/TAT-dominated 13 fA tail for an estimated 4-10x longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Monolayer MoS2 channels collapse 3D tier pitch to twenty nanometers
idea: Tier pitch = channel + 2x dielectric + gate + isolation; a 0.65 nm MoS2 monolayer (Eg 1.8 eV, no dangling bonds, low off-leakage) replaces a 10-20 nm Si channel, shrinking tiers from ~50 to ~20 nm. Grow MoS2 per tier by low-temperature MOCVD.
why: A fixed 5 um etchable stack holds 250 tiers instead of 100; with a relaxed lateral cell that is ~10x density at the same etch/litho cost. Mo and S are US-abundant; W-based TMDs avoided.
note: Per-tier MoS2 growth and contacts unproven; 10x density claim overstated.

title: Reusable sapphire carriers let hot-grown memory stacks laser-lift onto CMOS
idea: Thermal budget, not physics, forbids crystalline oxides above CMOS. Grow the 100-tier array stack on a sapphire carrier at 700-900 C (crystalline STO/ZnO/Si tiers), bond it face-down onto the periphery wafer, release it by UV laser lift-off as in microLED, and re-polish the carrier for ~1000 uses.
why: Unlocks high-temperature tier materials for ~10x density via 100 tiers while substrate cost per wafer approaches zero and no second CZ wafer or quartz crucible is consumed.
note: 100 crystalline tiers on sapphire plus wafer-scale face-down bonding is a stack of miracles.

title: Continuous-flow inline fab: wafers stream under spatial process heads
idea: First principle: a DRAM wafer is actually being processed for only ~5% of its 60-90 day cycle; the rest is queueing between batch tools. Build array-module lines where single wafers ride gas bearings continuously under spatial ALD heads, spatial plasma etch heads and inline litho, like a printing press, cutting cycle time ~5x.
why: Capital and time: WIP inventory and idle tools are hidden capital; 3-5x faster learning cycles speed yield ramps.

title: Fused-silica volume holograms hold cold MoE experts
idea: In a large MoE most experts are idle most of the time, yet they occupy HBM. Store them as page-oriented volume holograms in femtosecond-laser-written fused silica or photopolymer on glass, read by a fixed-angle laser array and a detector array that returns a megabit page in ~1-10 us; only experts routed for the next few tokens are staged into HBM.
why: Trillion-parameter MoE needs 3-10x less HBM because only active experts stay resident; glass media cost cents per GB and retain data with zero refresh energy.

title: Atomically uniform hBN barrier collapses gain-cell retention tail
idea: Retention tails come from thickness and trap variation in amorphous oxides, where one extra trap opens a trap-assisted tunneling path. Isolate a 2D storage node (graphene/MoS2) with 5-layer hBN, whose thickness is quantized at 0.33 nm per layer and nearly trap-free, so every cell sees the same barrier.
why: Refresh is set by the median cell instead of a 1e-9 tail cell, for ~100x longer intervals, capacitorless.
note: hBN uniformity real but 2D integration at DRAM density remains far off.

title: Repurpose idle LTPS display lines into silicon-only memory panels
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus >$10,000/m^2 for wafers; laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT gain cells at ~1 um rules, stacked 8-16 recrystallized layers deep on Gen-6 glass, can trade feature size for area cost. Build capacity-tier memory panels, diced into tiles, on idle LCD/LTPS lines using only Si, O, N, Al and Ti.
why: Capital and scarce resources: uses written-off display capacity with no EUV, HPQ crucibles or banned elements, targeting $/GB within ~2x of DRAM for capacity tiers.
note: Poly-Si TFT leakage hurts gain-cell retention; multilayer laser recrystallization on glass unproven; 2x DRAM $/GB doubtful.

title: Zipper NEMS contact closes at one volt, opens to air
idea: Random stimulus 'zipper': it closes progressively from one end with little force. A curved nano-cantilever contact anchored at the bitline zips onto the storage-node pad under a ~1 V wordline because the electrostatic gap at the zipping front is tiny; released, it springs back to a 10 nm gap, with Ru/RuO2 contact faces and a hermetic cavity to fight stiction.
why: A physical gap has no subthreshold or junction leakage, so refresh nearly vanishes, and low actuation voltage attacks the 3 V wordline floor (facts 3, 10). Risk: 1e15-cycle contact endurance.
note: Zipping actuation lowers voltage; same NEM contact endurance problem.

title: Snowshoe: wide flat multilayer-plate capacitor replaces the tall cylinder
idea: A snowshoe spreads weight wide instead of sinking deep: replace the tall cylinder with ~20 alternating TiN and ZrO2/HfO2 horizontal plates deposited as a blanket stack, patterned once per cell, with odd plates tied to a storage post and even plates to a shared plate post by sidewall-selective recess and fill (MLCC-style). Only the capacitor module changes; the die and its DDR5/HBM interface do not.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 4-6 fF from ~0.4 um of stack height with no high-AR hole etch and no pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: Kaleidoscope: tabletop EUV Talbot self-imaging for periodic array layers
idea: Random stimulus 'kaleidoscope' (repeating images from simple optics) -> achromatic Talbot lithography: a compact 13.5 nm source shines through a simple transmission grating mask, and the self-imaging effect reproduces the periodic line/hole pattern at a set gap with no projection optics. It is used only for the fully periodic array layers; DUV handles cuts and periphery.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint and capital (fact 4): a mirror-less exposure tool could cost ~1/10 of a scanner and needs no reflective-mask infrastructure. It suits DRAM's array layers, which are almost perfectly periodic.

title: Lighthouse beam: SiN photonic broadcast streams weights to accelerators
idea: One lighthouse serves many ships: a single weight memory broadcasts each layer over PECVD silicon-nitride waveguides (<=400 C) on a panel interposer to N accelerators at once using WDM, so each accelerator holds only a two-layer ring buffer instead of a full replica.
why: Replicas stop duplicating weights; weight DRAM per accelerator falls N-fold (8-32x).

title: Sushi conveyor: CNT logic over DRAM decodes compressed KV in place
idea: Dishes pass the chef on a belt: deposit carbon-nanotube FET logic (<=325 C) on top of the DRAM array's metal stack so 2-bit compressed KV rows passing the sense amps are decoded and dot-producted with the query right there, returning only scores and selected values.
why: KV can live at 2-bit density permanently (4-8x capacity) because decompressed copies never need buffer space; also cuts data movement (fact 5).

title: Drip irrigation: Esaki-diode trickle latch makes storage nodes self-sustaining
idea: Each storage node gets a vertical Si/SiGe interband tunnel diode to a bias line; its negative-differential-resistance curve against a matched load forms two stable voltages, so leakage is replenished continuously like drip irrigation rather than refreshed.
why: Eliminates refresh at 125 C if peak-to-valley ratio stays >~3 when hot (interband tunneling is weakly temperature dependent) and valley current stays <~10 fA/cell over 10 years.

title: Double-barrier resonant tunneling access acts as energy filter
idea: Box: InAs quantum-well storage node x AlSb/InAs/AlSb resonant-tunneling two-terminal access x current sense x 4F2 crossbar x GaSb-on-Si x MBE + bonding. Electrons pass only when wordline-bitline bias aligns the resonant level (target on/off >1e6 within ~0.3 V); off resonance the 2 eV AlSb barriers block, so no transistor is needed.
why: Transistor-free 4F2 cell (~1.5x density) with access at ~0.3-0.5 V (fact 10, CV2 ~4x lower) and leakage set by barrier height (fact 3). Valley current and sneak paths are the risk.

title: Mott NDR load-line bistable cell keeps data without refresh
idea: Box: small node cap x one access transistor plus one NbO2 Mott or Si/SiGe Esaki NDR element tied to a hold rail x SA x vertically stacked over the transistor x Si x ALD + anneal. The NDR load line intersecting the leakage line gives two stable node voltages, so leakage self-corrects instead of decaying (tunnel-SRAM idea at ~1T footprint).
why: Eliminates refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) entirely; standby set by NDR valley current (target <1 pA/cell). Needs high peak-to-valley ratio at nm scale.
note: Tunnel-SRAM revival; valley current and PVR at nm scale are doubts.

title: Room-temperature single-electron transistor electrometer per bitline segment
idea: Box: 0.5 fF planar MIM cap x IGZO access x SET electrometer x local segment sensing x SOI x e-beam/DSA-defined dots. A silicon-nanowire quantum-dot SET (dot <5 nm, charging energy >> kT) at each 32-cell bitline segment turns a few hundred electrons of signal into a large current swing, so the cell no longer needs a 60:1 pillar capacitor.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Cs can drop ~10x (5 fF to 0.5 fF), deleting the high-AR etch; local gain also shortens bitlines.
note: At room temperature, SET background charge and variability are unsolved.

title: Negative-capacitance film cancels bitline parasitic capacitance
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x NC-compensated bitline x in-line HZO capacitor x Si x ALD ferroelectric. A stabilized negative-capacitance HZO element on the bitline subtracts most of its parasitic capacitance during charge sharing, raising the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) from ~0.1 toward ~0.4.
why: 3-4x more signal from the same 5 fF cell, so Cs can shrink (AR 60:1 toward 20:1) or bitlines can lengthen; attacks the capacitor wall.

title: Dedicated deep-trench capacitor wafer hybrid-bonded onto transistor wafer
idea: [Box: single-crystal Si trench charge | Si VCT | charge-share SA | wafer-on-wafer hybrid bond, one pad per storage node | low-grade Si capacitor wafer | Bosch DRIE + ALD] Etch capacitors as 100:1+ trenches into a separate Si wafer (single-crystal Si etches deeper and straighter than oxide molds, and the doped wafer itself is the plate), then bond it face-to-face to the access-transistor wafer using oversized self-aligned Cu pads per storage node.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) plus process decoupling: Cs >10 fF possible and the high-AR mold module leaves the transistor wafer, so each wafer runs on its own optimized line.
note: Per-storage-node hybrid bonding needs ~40 nm pitch overlay; today's bonding is ~10x coarser.

title: Hydrogen-ambient Czochralski pulling in silicon-nitride crucibles
idea: Box [standard | standard | standard | standard | 300 mm CZ Si under recycled low-pressure H2 | Si3N4-coated SiC crucible + magnetic CZ]: sweep SiO and CO from the puller with H2 instead of argon (its higher thermal conductivity allows faster pulling) and hold the melt in a nitride-faced crucible that releases nitrogen, useful for void control, rather than oxygen.
why: Removes both the argon purge and the Spruce Pine HPQ crucible from wafer making; H2 heat extraction might raise pull rate ~10-20%.

title: Sixteen-subcell majority bits from nanoimprinted crossbars
idea: Box [medium: 16 nano-capacitors per bit | access: crossbar diode | sense: ensemble charge summing | integration: monolithic | substrate: glass | fab: nanoimprint lithography]. Each bit is a cluster of 16 sub-10 nm imprinted capacitors on one local bitline sensed as a summed charge, so up to ~5 dead or leaky subcells per bit change nothing.
why: Facts 1/4: swaps defect-free EUV patterning for defect-tolerant imprint; ~5x lower patterning cost per layer.

title: Bonded local sense amps per 32 cells rescue tiny capacitors
idea: Box [medium: 1 fF capacitor | access: vertical channel | sense: one sense amp per 32-cell bitline on a bonded logic wafer | integration: hybrid bonding at 0.5 um pitch | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Bitline capacitance drops ~16x, so a 1 fF cell gives more signal than a 5 fF cell does today while each sense event only charges a tiny bitline.
why: Constraint: ~10x lower bitline energy per access; Fact 1: capacitor aspect ratio can fall from ~70:1 to ~15:1, and weak cells gain margin.

title: Complementary tunnel-FET static latch with attoamp hold current
idea: Po: SRAM that costs nothing to hold. Build a 4T cross-coupled latch from complementary vertical tunnel FETs whose band-to-band off-current is ~1e-17 A, monolithically stacked in two tiers over the access tier so a bit occupies ~8F^2; data is held statically and refresh disappears.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh, with standby near mW per GB; risk is TFET on-current (read speed) and tier-stacking density.

title: Engineered single border trap per cell as atomic-scale bit
idea: Po: the defect that causes leakage is the memory. Place one deep border trap per minimum-size transistor by single-ion implantation and use its occupancy, which shifts Vt by tens of mV in a ~10 nm device just as random telegraph noise does, as the stored bit; write by gate-bias pulse, read by drain current.
why: Facts 1 and 3: the smallest conceivable capacitorless cell, with retention set by trap emission time (designable ms to s); speculative because single-trap placement and read margin are hard.

title: Corrugated substrate hosts planar arrays on both sidewall faces
idea: Po: the wafer is not flat. Etch the silicon into 20:1 parallel walls before front-end processing, then build planar-transistor DRAM conformally on both wall faces with tilted implants and conformal ALD gates, so 1 cm2 of footprint carries ~10-20 cm2 of active surface.
why: Density without tier deposition: ~10x surface at relaxed F with no EUV; capacitors can run long along the wall.
note: Tilted implants and gate patterning on 20:1 walls suffer shadowing and litho on vertical faces.

title: One scaffold printed, then every later layer self-aligns
idea: Po: lithography stops at the first layer. Print a single sacrificial lattice scaffold, then form word lines, bit lines, contacts and capacitor landing pads by successive spacer, selective-etch and selective-deposition steps referenced to it, so no later layer needs overlay.
why: Overlay budget and mask count (fact 4): critical masks from ~5-7 EUV to ~1-2; removes overlay-limited yield loss at F~12 nm.

title: Pinless DRAM die fed data by light through its backside
idea: Po: memory with no pins. A VCSEL array in the package lid shines modulated light onto Ge photodiode and micro-LED tiles on each thinned DRAM die's backside, so the bumps carry only power and ground and each die exchanges data with the logic die through free space.
why: Removes signal TSVs and microbumps (HBM TSV tax) and decouples die count from bump field; targets ~0.5 pJ/bit and 2x more dies per package footprint.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si tiers for cheap 3D DRAM
idea: Po: build 3D DRAM from bad transistors. Each tier's lateral access transistors use excimer-laser-crystallized polysilicon (a display-industry process) whose grain-boundary variability gives a ~1% weak-cell tail; codewords span all tiers so a weak cell or even a poor tier is just an erasure.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): a cheap deposited transistor that is good enough at 1% BER makes 26+ tiers plausible without epitaxial Si/SiGe stacks; ~2-3x lower cost per bit at 32+ tiers if it works.

title: Panel-fab DRAM on Gen-8.5 glass with oxide-TFT access
idea: Po: memory printed like television screens. Idle flat-panel lines pattern 1T1C arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass with oxide TFTs at sub-micron imprint rules; TFT variability gives ~1% BER, and the panels are diced into a near-DRAM capacity tier bonded to a logic decoder.
why: Capital: panel area costs ~100x less per m^2 than wafer area; ~$2-4/GB only if ~0.5 um rules are reached, with latency at the slow edge of DRAM-class (~100 ns+).
note: Sub-micron panel patterning unproven; $2-4/GB is above DDR5 make cost, so gain is capital intensity only.

title: Sequential layer-transfer tiers re-patterned with the same DUV masks
idea: Po: the wafer grows a new wafer every week. After a DRAM array tier is finished, a thin single-crystal Si sheet is transferred on top by ion-cut at <400 C and the same DUV mask set builds the next tier with laser-annealed low-temperature transistors; four tiers quadruple bits per area with no pitch shrink.
why: Density by tier count rather than lithography, reusing one mask set; attacks EUV dependence and cost per bit if per-tier yield exceeds ~95%.

title: Topological polar vortex chirality as an unleakable bit
idea: Worsen: hold bits as fragile scalar charge that any trap can steal. Flip: encode the bit as the handedness (left or right chirality) of a polar vortex or polar skyrmion in PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices, switched by a sub-volt field pulse with an in-plane bias and read by tunneling resistance or piezo-current; topology protects the state at ~10 nm size.
why: Density (sub-10 nm bits, no capacitor) and refresh elimination; the topological barrier gives non-volatility without diffusion-driven fatigue.
note: PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices need oxide substrates; deterministic chirality switching unproven.

title: Cold-source access FET filters the thermal electron tail
idea: Worse: accept the 60 mV/dec Boltzmann tail that sets off-current. Flip: build the bitline-side source as an n+/p+ superlattice whose density of states is cut off above the band edge, so only cold electrons inject and the slope reaches ~35-40 mV/dec.
why: Off-current about 1000x lower at the same Vt and wordline swing; attacks leakage (fact 3) and allows lower VPP (fact 10).

title: GaN/AlN deep quantum-well storage node with 2 eV barrier
idea: Worse at 125 C: store electrons in a shallow potential well they boil out of. Flip: hold the bit as a 2DEG charge packet in a GaN well clad by AlN barriers (~2 eV offset), written and erased by a gate pulse that lowers the barrier rather than by tunneling through oxide, so endurance is unlimited and thermionic escape is negligible at 125 C.
why: Retention hours to days at 125 C (fact 3), removing almost all refresh.

title: Micro-transfer-printed periphery dielets onto array-only wafers
idea: Worse: build every decoder, pump and I/O block in the same costly, EUV-heavy DRAM process. Flip: fabricate pre-tested periphery dielets on cheap logic wafers, release them, and elastomer-stamp transfer-print thousands per pass onto array-only DRAM wafers, then print or plate the short interconnects.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7) and capital: DRAM wafer area goes ~90% to cells and only known-good periphery is placed, raising bits per wafer ~1.6x.
note: Printed interconnect cannot reach bitline-pitch connection density.

title: Pillar-first stacking: grow tall nanowire bitlines, then deposit tiers
idea: Worse: drill ever-deeper holes through a finished tier stack until etch aspect ratio caps tier count. Flip: grow the vertical bitline/channel pillars FIRST by templated selective-area epitaxy (bottom-up AR >100 is routine for nanowires), then build the tiers around them with conformal deposition and one blanket CMP per tier, so stack height comes from growth and deposition and no deep etch ever happens.
why: Removes the high-AR etch that blocks manufacturable 3D DRAM (facts 2, 4); tier count no longer capped near 75:1, plausibly 150+ tiers with zero per-tier lithography.

title: Silicon carbide access transistors erase the leakage tail
idea: Worse: use narrow-bandgap silicon whose thermal generation and band-to-band tunneling create the leakage tail. Flip: bond a thin SiC layer (Si, C) as the access-transistor tier above a Si periphery wafer; its ~3.2 eV bandgap suppresses junction and tunneling leakage by orders of magnitude.
why: Fact 3: retention could rise from milliseconds to minutes, removing most refresh energy and making large, leaky abundant-element capacitors acceptable.

title: MiG-25 vacuum-tube engineer: floating island in sealed nano-vacuum
idea: A Soviet engineer under embargo trusts vacuum electronics because they shrug off radiation. The storage node is a metal nano-island suspended in a sealed 20 nm vacuum cavity with no dielectric and therefore no leakage path. Field emission from a sharp tip writes it, and the island's charge is read by how it modulates a neighbouring field-emission current.
why: Leakage-free storage removes refresh (fact 3) and the need for a high-k, high-AR capacitor (fact 1); a vacuum gap has no trap-assisted tunneling or dielectric wear, so endurance is effectively unlimited.
note: Sealed 20 nm vacuum cavities and field-emission write/read at array density are far from any fab flow.

title: Diamond cutter: hydrogen-diamond floating-island cell, dry plasma-polished
idea: A diamond cutter polishes stone on a dry scaife. Build the storage node on hydrogen-terminated CVD diamond (5.5 eV gap), where a MoO3 acceptor layer makes a hole-doped channel and the node has almost no thermal leakage, so charge stays for years. Dry plasma/ICP polishing planarizes the diamond.
why: Refresh-free (fact 3), radiation-hard, and made of carbon rather than a chokepoint material. Dry polishing and dry etch give more than 10x less water.
note: Surface transfer doping is fragile; diamond-on-CMOS integration is far off.

title: Venusian alien's diamond access transistors for hot, chiller-free memory
idea: An alien from 460 C Venus would never cool its memory. Grow boron-delta-doped or hydrogen-terminated diamond (5.5 eV gap) thin-film access FETs by low-temperature plasma CVD over the capacitors; leakage stays sub-fA even at 150-200 C, so DRAM can sit hot beside accelerators.
why: Today refresh doubles every ~10 C, which forces cooling; diamond access devices hold retention at 150 C, cutting refresh to near zero and removing memory-side chiller energy, and diamond needs only carbon.
note: Low-temperature diamond over capacitors is nanocrystalline; H-terminated conduction unstable.

title: Dam engineer's spillway: resonant-tunneling barriers isolate the storage node
idea: A dam spillway passes water only above a set level. Replace the access channel with a double-barrier quantum-well stack (AlN/GaN/AlN or SiO2/Si-well/SiO2) between bitline and storage node; the wordline shifts the well's subband into resonance for fast transfer, while off-resonance transmission through two barriers is exponentially suppressed.
why: On/off ratios of 1e15 or more with no doped junction remove refresh, and transfer happens at ~1 V; extends the UltraRAM barrier idea to DRAM speed and endurance.
note: RTD off-resonance leakage and PVR far from 1e15 on/off.

title: Archer's drawn bow: pre-stressed NEMS relay access at 0.2 V
idea: A drawn bow releases great energy at a finger's touch. Each access device is a lateral nanoelectromechanical relay whose beam is built pre-stressed near snap-through (a negative-stiffness bistable flexure), so a 0.2 V gate nudge closes the contact; open, it is an air gap with zero leakage.
why: Zero off-current removes refresh, and a 0.2 V actuation versus a 3 V wordline is ~200x less gate CV^2; key risks are 1e15-cycle contact endurance and ns-scale closing.

title: 2050 stacked periphery: four tiers of 2D-semiconductor sense amps
idea: A 2050 engineer builds periphery upward. Grow four monolithic BEOL tiers of MoS2 (n) and WSe2 (p) CMOS above the array; each tier hosts sense amps for one in four bitlines, relaxing SA pitch 4x and freeing the silicon footprint.
why: Moves most of the 49% periphery off the silicon footprint (fact 7) without hybrid bonding; relaxed pitch avoids EUV on periphery (fact 4).

title: Biologist's cortical minicolumns: 16-cell bitlines with private sense amps
idea: The cortex scales by repeating short minicolumns. Split the 3D array into 16-32-cell local bitlines; a 4x4 bundle of them is muxed in the array tier onto one hybrid bond to a sense amp in a CMOS wafer below.
why: Bitline capacitance falls to ~1-2 fF, so at the same signal margin Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~1 fF. That removes the 60-75:1 capacitor (Fact 1) and enables shallow 3D tiers.
note: Sense-amp area cannot fit under so few cells.

title: Skyscraper architect's sky lobbies: periphery tiers every 32 floors
idea: Tall towers use sky lobbies so no elevator runs the full height. Every 32 array tiers, insert a laser-crystallized Si or oxide CMOS 'lobby' tier holding local tier decoders and wordline drivers. Global lines only reach lobbies, and each staircase spans just 32 steps.
why: Removes the height limit on 3D DRAM (Fact 2) and shrinks staircase and periphery area (Fact 7), toward 128+ tiers.

title: TV maker's view: DRAM gain-cell tiles on idle Gen-10.5 display lines
idea: A display engineer notes that LCD/OLED fabs already process 9 m2 glass at <=350 C with oxide-TFT tools, and many sit idle. Add panel-scale nanoimprint for ~100 nm features, build 2T0C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays at <=350 C on Gen-10.5 glass, and cut them into memory tiles for CXL far memory, attaching periphery chiplets.
why: At F=100 nm and 8F2, one panel holds ~15 TB of raw cells, with capex per m2 ~50-100x below a wafer fab: a possible <$1/GB capacity tier. High risk: imprint overlay on large glass with thermal expansion, and speed of long panel wires.

title: Newspaper pressman: roll-to-roll gain-cell memory sheets on steel foil
idea: A pressman prints kilometers of paper per hour. Run planarized stainless or Invar foil through a roll-to-roll line of atmospheric spatial-ALD heads (<=250 C), roll-to-roll UV nanoimprint and web plasma etch to build oxide-semiconductor gain-cell sheets, then cut and laminate the sheets into memory slabs.
why: Continuous web processing at meters per minute could cut capex per bit ~10x for capacity memory, with no wafers, crucibles or EUV. High risk: imprint overlay on a moving, stretching web, and particle defects.

title: Alien's question: grow memory tiers on the processor wafer's backside
idea: An alien asks why memory and compute come from different factories. After a GPU wafer finishes its front side and backside power network, deposit 4-16 tiers of <=400 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory straight onto the backside, joined by nano-TSVs and built with the same backside tool set.
why: No separate memory wafer and no HBM stacking or interposer (facts 5, 6); wires ~10x shorter, maybe ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4, with memory capex riding on logic tools. High risk: hot logic below worsens retention.
note: Hot logic under the memory worsens OS gain-cell retention.

title: Child's floor carpet: TSV-free edge-bonded planar memory tiling
idea: As a child asks 'why stack the blocks when the floor is empty?': tile plain, TSV-free DRAM dies edge-to-edge in a ring around the accelerator on a glass panel and join neighbours by sidewall hybrid bonds at 2 um pitch on the polished die edges, forming a planar 'memory carpet' with die-to-die relay links.
why: Kills the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% stack yield loss): commodity-like dies with no TSV keep-out, claimed ~2x bits per wafer versus HBM at ~70% of its bandwidth.
note: Sidewall hybrid bonding at 2 um is unproven; relay hops add energy.

title: Embargo engineer's ruler: ALD film thickness, not EUV, sets pitch
idea: Denied EUV, a Soviet-style engineer measures with films instead of light. ArF-defined trenches get access transistors on both sidewalls, with gate length and wordline width set by ALD film thickness (~5 nm). The sidewall cell is repeated on 2 stacked trench levels, all in mature U.S. 28-40 nm fabs.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: an effective ~5 nm F on the sidewalls gives ~5x cells/mm^2 versus 6F^2 at 12 nm, times 2 levels, ~10x. Dropping all 5-7 EUV layers keeps wafer cost flat or lower.
note: ALD-defined 5 nm gates leak too much; capacitor area still limits density.

title: Dual-bit cell stores capacitor charge and floating-body charge together
idea: Million-token AI contexts are capacity-starved, so one counter-doping implant mask isolates a floating p-pocket under each access transistor; the cell keeps one bit as capacitor charge and a second as body holes that shift threshold. Reads first sense the body bit by current at an intermediate wordline level, then charge-share the capacitor bit.
why: Up to 2x bits per cell area on existing 6F2 arrays for one mask (density, cost per bit); body/capacitor disturb coupling and two retention clocks are the risks.

title: CCD charge-transfer bitline segments feeding a tiny sense node
idea: Astronomical CCDs move charge packets with 99.9999% efficiency instead of sharing them; each bitline is split into 8-16 clocked transfer gates that shift the cell's packet to a ~0.3 fF floating diffusion at the SA rather than dumping it onto a 50-100 fF bitline. The SA sees roughly 10x the voltage of conventional charge sharing.
why: Breaks the Cs/Cbl ratio rule behind fact 1: ~10x signal allows ~1 fF cells or 4x longer bitlines; the transfer adds ~3-8 ns.

title: Vertical CCD charge-shift strings as append-only KV-cache memory
idea: An AI KV-cache is written once in order and read back as a stream, so build a 3D-NAND-like vertical string but run it as a charge-coupled device: 128 stacked gate tiers around one channel pass charge packets along the string by 3-phase clocking to a single sense node at the top. There is no per-cell access transistor, capacitor or contact; a bit is just one gate crossing.
why: Density ~30-50x bits per mm2 vs planar 6F2, no capacitor (fact 1), periphery amortized over 128 bits per string (fact 7), and no per-bit bitline swing (fact 8); latency is sequential, which suits KV traffic.
note: Same vertical CCD string, framed for append-only KV cache traffic.

title: Mars-colony do-everything single chamber for regional DRAM minifabs
idea: Extreme user: a Mars colony that can land one tool, not 400. A reconfigurable plasma chamber with swappable gas manifolds and an in-situ ALD head runs etch, deposition, clean and anneal sequentially on one wafer; a minifab of 30 such chambers plus one scanner trades throughput for a 10x smaller tool count.
why: Capital/time: regional DRAM capacity for ~$1-2B and 12-18 months instead of $15B and 4 years; good for trusted/defense volume and fast ramp.

title: MRI-safe metal-free stack: optical vias through silicon at 1310 nm
idea: MRI-compatible implants must avoid metal paths. Silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so give each die in a stack aligned micro-emitter and germanium photodiode arrays and pass data vertically through the dies as light; only power needs vias.
why: Removes signal TSVs and their capacitance; sub-100 fJ/bit vertical links (~10x below TSV+PHY paths), looser die alignment, and less TSV area tax.

title: Venus-lander electronics: SiC access transistors for refresh-free cells
idea: NASA's SiC JFET circuits have run for weeks at 460 C because SiC's intrinsic carrier density is ~10^19 times lower than silicon's. Bond a thin 4H-SiC (or beta-Ga2O3) access-transistor layer onto a silicon periphery wafer, so each cell's off-state leakage is in the attoamps and retention lasts minutes to hours even at 125 C.
why: Attacks the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) beyond the IGZO prior work, and holds up at high temperature, where IGZO is weaker. Refresh nearly disappears and Cs could drop ~5x (fact 1).
note: SiC/Ga2O3 interface quality and layer transfer at DRAM pitch are big unknowns.

title: Cold-crucible Czochralski: grow DRAM wafers without Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Design for the edge case Hurricane Helene exposed, the >80% Spruce Pine crucible-quartz source going offline. Pull 300 mm silicon from an induction-heated, water-cooled segmented copper cold crucible where the melt forms its own silicon skull, using no high-purity quartz.
why: Removes the HPQ crucible chokepoint, and lower oxygen may help retention; strengthens wafer supply.
note: Dislocation-free 300 mm growth from cold crucible skull is unproven.

title: Heteroepitaxial 3C-SiC access pillar: retention from milliseconds to hours
idea: Time shift through bandgap: grow the vertical access-channel pillars as 3C-SiC (Si and C only, N/Al dopants) on the Si wafer; SiC's intrinsic carrier density (~1e-1 cm^-3 versus 1e10 for Si) suppresses generation and band-to-band leakage by >10 decades, so retention becomes limited by the capacitor dielectric instead of the transistor.
why: Leakage tail/refresh (fact 3): minutes-to-hours retention removes >99% of refresh; all elements Earth-abundant, no W or Hf in the device.
note: 3C-SiC on Si is defect-laden; traps would dominate generation, not ni.

title: Silicon charge racetrack: CCD loops that refresh by moving
idea: Time shift: rather than holding charge still and refreshing it, data circulates as charge packets in short buried-channel CCD loops (e.g., 16 bits per vertical pillar) clocked at ~1-2 GHz with a regenerative re-inject stage per loop, so every bit is restored each ~10 ns loop and random access waits <=8 ns on average; silicon replaces magnetic racetrack's Co/Pt.
why: Refresh disappears as a separate operation and density rises (~16 bits per footprint, an alternative route around fact 2); Si/O/TiN only; risks are charge-transfer inefficiency and clock power.

title: Gallium-oxide access-transistor arrays bonded onto silicon periphery
idea: Material jump with a time jump to years of retention: 4.8 eV-gap beta-Ga2O3 transistors, grown on native substrates and layer-transferred, form the cell array with off-currents below 10^-21 A, and the slower array is read through time-domain integrating sense amps on a bonded Si CMOS wafer; no refresh circuitry is built.
why: Retention beyond product life means zero refresh (fact 3) while fast Si periphery is kept; a crystalline wide-gap route distinct from IGZO.
note: Ga2O3 at DRAM pitch and layer transfer are unproven.

title: One-shot ferroelectric shadow freezes rows before charge leaks
idea: Time-shift between two storage physics: the capacitor stack has a thin HZO layer left untouched during DRAM-speed use, and when a row's age counter passes ~half its retention one pulse copies the charge state into polarization, after which charge may leak freely; the next read senses polarization switching current and returns the row to charge mode.
why: No periodic refresh (fact 3), and FE endurance is spent only once per long idle episode, sidestepping FeRAM's endurance limit.
note: Dual-mode HZO NV-DRAM is known art; copying charge to polarization needs coercive voltage at the cell.

title: Thermally isolated array tier cooled by microfluidics
idea: Scale-shift the thermal stack: the array wafer bonds to the hot periphery/logic wafer through sparse Cu pillars across a vacuum gap and is cooled from its own backside by microfluidic channels on 10 C rack chilled water, holding cells ~75 C below the logic; with leakage halving every ~10 C, worst-case retention goes from 64 ms to ~10 s and refresh is dropped for step- and token-scoped data.
why: ~150-200x retention deletes refresh (fact 3) and fixes heat-driven retention loss in memory-on-logic stacks.
note: Dense Cu pillars conduct heat well; holding a 75 C gap across a bonded interface is doubtful.

title: Vertical bucket brigade: charge hops tier-to-tier down to one sense tier
idea: Take the astronomy CCD and rotate its shift axis to vertical: stacked storage tiers linked by gated vertical channels clock charge packets down plane by plane to a single bottom tier of sense amps, so 64 storage tiers need no periphery of their own. Time split: dense tiers hold charge for ms, and a whole-plane shift takes ns per hop.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7), and per-tier wordline and sense wiring blocks 3D (fact 2); one sense tier for 64 storage tiers could cut periphery area per bit by >10x.
note: Charge-transfer efficiency over 64 hops in deposited channels is the doubt.

title: Micro-MLCC: nanolaminate multilayer capacitor inside each lateral 3D cell
idea: Scale the 1000-layer multilayer ceramic capacitor, a mm-size component, down to a 50-nm lateral cell: ALD a blanket nanolaminate of 8 electrode/high-k pairs inside each tier's capacitor cavity, then connect odd and even electrodes at opposite ends by selective recess etch. Eight plates in parallel give ~8x capacitance per footprint.
why: Capacitor charge wall in lateral 3D cells (facts 1, 2): reaches 5 fF in a capacitor ~8x shorter, which shrinks the lateral cell pitch and the footprint of the stack.

title: Panel-scale nanoimprinted oxide gain cells on depreciated display lines
idea: Jump from a 0.07 m2 wafer to 5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 display mother-glass: retired LCD/OLED lines run panel-scale nanoimprint at ~50 nm half-pitch to build 8 stacked low-temperature oxide-semiconductor 2T0C gain-cell tiers, which are diced into memory tiles and bonded to silicon periphery chiplets.
why: Capital intensity: display fabs are fully depreciated and processed area costs ~50-100x less per m2 than a DRAM wafer, so ~8 tiers at 50 nm can reach cost-per-bit parity for a capacity tier without new fab capex.

title: Fiber delay-line loop memory for strictly periodic weight streams
idea: This revives delay-line memory at datacenter scale. Weights that are read in the same order every decode step circulate in a 40 km dense-WDM fiber spool (100 wavelengths x 400 Gb/s gives about 1 GB in flight on a ~200 us loop), kept alive by optical amplifiers. Accelerators tap the stream as it passes, because sequential lockstep access never needs random addressing.
why: It replaces DRAM capacity for repeatedly streamed read-only data with roughly $5k of fiber: GB-scale capacity with no DRAM wafers.
note: Transceiver and amplifier cost far exceeds fiber cost.

title: Precision-resistor mask enabling charge-domain MAC inside commodity DDR
idea: One added thin-film resistor mask gives commodity DDR dies a calibrated charge-sharing reference, enabling bit-serial analog multiply-accumulate on the bitlines. Bandwidth-hungry decode GEMV runs inside the DDR, so weights can live in cheap DDR instead of HBM. Compute moves from the package scale to the bitline scale.
why: HBM costs about 3x the wafer area per bit (fact 6). Moving GEMV into DDR cuts HBM bits needed 2-4x and total memory wafer area per model by about 40%.
note: Analog precision and variation on commodity bitlines; requires DRAM-fab adoption.

title: Glass-panel substrate memory: multi-tier oxide TFT cells in package RDL
idea: Jump to display-panel scale: the 600 mm glass package substrate is built on LCD lines with 8 tiers of IGZO thin-film-transistor capacitor cells in its redistribution layers, giving a few GB per package of working memory; the ~1% BER from TFT variation is absorbed by row codes in the logic die.
why: Adds non-EUV, U.S.-buildable capacity on LCD-class capital (fact 4) right next to the logic die.

title: Qimonda trench reborn on a separate bonded capacitor wafer
idea: Qimonda's trench DRAM died because deep trenches competed with the transistor for area and thermal budget below 40 nm. Etch 100:1 trenches with porous-Si sidewalls (5-10x area) in a cheap blank carrier wafer, fill them with ALD high-k MIM, then hybrid-bond the carrier face-to-face onto the access-transistor wafer at cell pitch.
why: Decouples capacitance from the transistor process: 2-5x Cs (Fact 1), no pillar leaning, and the carrier needs no EUV (Fact 4). Risk: sub-100 nm bond pitch.
note: Trench capacitor wafer bonded at cell pitch; sub-100 nm bond pitch unproven.

title: Bubble memory's rotating field drives skyrmion loops, no transistors
idea: Magnetic bubble memory died because long serial loops made access slow. Keep its best trick, one global rotating field that moves every bit so no bit needs its own transistor, and fix the latency. Use 64-bit skyrmion loops in thin multilayer rings, each with one sense MTJ, clocked by an on-chip stripline field so that any bit arrives within 64 steps.
why: The array has no access-transistor leakage and needs no refresh because it is nonvolatile, and density comes from cell-free tracks. Step speed and drive energy are the speculative parts.
note: Global rotating-field drive is a twist on racetrack; not DRAM-class latency.

title: Servo-marked racetracks: hard-disk servo loop fixes domain-wall shift errors
idea: Failure mined: IBM's racetrack memory stalled on pinning-induced over- and under-shifting of domain walls. Fix: interleave a known servo pattern every 32 bits. The read MTJ's sense amp time-stamps each domain-wall arrival, and a per-track controller trims the next current pulse width, like hard-disk servo wedges.
why: Pushes shift error rates from ~1e-4 toward ~1e-12, so one read head can serve hundreds of bits and sense amps are shared over ~100x more bits (fact 7).

title: Skyrmion bubble memory: globally clocked major/minor loops, TMR detectors
idea: Failure mined: magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) died on micron-size bubbles, 100 kHz shifting and millivolt permalloy detectors. Fix: keep its best idea, one global drive that clocks every loop at once with no per-bit transistors, but use 25 nm skyrmions in Co/Pt multilayers pushed by a global spin-orbit current sheet. Data is read through block-replicate gates onto a major loop with one 200% TMR detector per 4096 bits.
why: 10x at the same cost: ~60 nm^2 per bit vs ~860 nm^2 per DRAM cell, with periphery amortized over 4k bits. The films are blanket sputtered layers with ~2 critical masks, no capacitors and no EUV.
note: Major/minor loop latency runs to microseconds, not DRAM-class random access; room-temperature skyrmion pinning is unsolved.

title: IBM trench capacitor revived from the wafer backside
idea: Trench DRAM (IBM, Infineon, Qimonda) lost to stacked capacitors because a deep trench competes with the transistor for front-side area. After building 4F2 vertical transistors on the front, thin the wafer and deep-etch (DRIE) trenches from the backside directly under each pillar's source. Trench depth is then limited by the 5-10 um wafer thickness rather than by front-side topology.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1). The backside trench is equivalent to AR >150 and gives Cs >10 fF without a k~70 dielectric, while the front side stays free for 4F2 cells.

title: MAPPER's bankrupt multibeam e-beam reborn as DRAM tile character projection
idea: MAPPER Lithography (13,000 beamlets, bankrupt 2018) died on throughput for random logic. DRAM arrays are ~95% identical cells: give each beamlet a stencil aperture of a full 8x8-cell tile so one flash writes 64 cells, exposing fluorine-free metal-oxide or HSQ resist.
why: Displaces EUV (one supplier, ~1 MW per tool, tin plasma, hydrogen) on 5-7 critical array layers at ~1/5 the capex; PFAS photoacid generators eliminated; 64x flash multiplication brings throughput to production class.
note: Stencil tiles per beamlet add character projection to multibeam; same mechanism as I-04806.

title: NASA's vacuum-channel transistor as a zero-leakage DRAM access switch
idea: NASA's nanoscale vacuum-channel transistor stalled because emitter tips eroded under continuous current. A DRAM access device conducts only nanoseconds per access, a duty cycle near 1e-6: form 50-100 nm sealed vacuum gaps with carbon or Mo tips on glass that connect a storage capacitor to the bitline by field emission only when the wordline gate field passes threshold.
why: Off-state current across a vacuum gap is essentially zero, so retention of hours and no refresh; no doped semiconductor or silicon wafer; materials are glass, carbon or Mo and SiO2.
note: Field emission at DRAM voltages needs extreme tip enhancement; tip uniformity across billions of cells doubtful.

title: Canon ELTRAN porous-silicon transfer builds 30-tier single-crystal 3D DRAM
idea: Canon's ELTRAN layer transfer (epitaxy on porous Si, split by water jet) lost to Smart Cut on cost for single SOI layers. For 3D DRAM needing 26+ single-crystal tiers its advantage returns: one donor is re-epitaxied and split repeatedly, each tier bonded below 400 C onto the growing stack with one coarse alignment litho per tier and no hydrogen implant.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): supplies single-crystal lateral-transistor tiers without Si/SiGe superlattice limits; donor reused ~50x; per-tier cost ~one bond plus split.

title: GE's BEAMOS reborn: microcolumn electron beams address unpatterned MOS film
idea: GE's 1970s beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS) wrote and read charge on a MOS target with an electron beam, but died on bulky vacuum tubes and slow deflection. Wafer-fabricate 10,000 MEMS microcolumns in a chip-scale vacuum package, each deflecting a 10-20 nm spot across a 100 um field of an unpatterned SiO2/Si target and reading bits by beam-induced current.
why: Meets 100x: the storage medium needs zero lithography and each column covers ~25 Mb; est. $0.02-0.1/GB. Trades: vacuum packaging, ~100 ns-1 us access, beam-induced oxide wear limits endurance unless run at low voltage.

title: SEL's IGZO DOSRAM built on glass in shuttered LCD fabs
idea: Semiconductor Energy Laboratory's IGZO DOSRAM never found a fab, while Gen-8 to Gen-10 LCD fabs such as Sharp Sakai are closing. Retool one closed line with roll-to-plate nanoimprint at 30 nm, stack 4 layers of IGZO 2T0C gain cells on 2.2x2.5 m glass with wide landing pads that absorb glass distortion, and bond CMOS periphery chiplets along the panel edge.
why: Meets 100x: panel capex per m2 is ~1/100-1/500 of wafer fabs and already written off; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: low IGZO mobility (100 ns+ access), slab form factor, panel-scale imprint yield.

title: InPhase holography, fixed: optical associative attention over KV keys
idea: InPhase's holographic disc died because tape and disk won archival storage. Use holography where it is unbeatable, parallel correlation: record key vectors as a volume hologram in a photorefractive crystal, shine the query as a beam, read correlation peaks on a camera to get top-k token indices, then fetch only those V vectors from flash.
why: Full keys never sit in DRAM/HBM; million-token attention fetches only top-k values, cutting KV memory >10x.

title: Altermagnet tunnel junction: spin-split readout without net magnetization
idea: Effect walk: altermagnetic spin splitting. Build a tunnel junction whose free electrode is an altermagnet (CrSb or MnTe, avoiding Ru) with momentum-dependent spin-split bands, so the Neel vector produces a TMR-like resistance change; write by spin-orbit or current-induced Neel switching.
why: Combines ferromagnet-grade electrical readout with antiferromagnet immunity to fields and THz dynamics, enabling magnetic cells below 20-nm pitch without dipolar crosstalk and with abundant elements.

title: Charge-order ferroelectric switches by electron hopping, not ion motion
idea: Effect walk: electronic ferroelectricity from charge ordering. Use a mixed-valence oxide (LuFe2O4-type, or a rare-earth-free charge-ordered ferrite or manganite) whose polarization comes from Fe2+/Fe3+ ordering, so switching moves electrons between sites rather than displacing ions, at ~meV per unit cell with no oxygen-vacancy fatigue.
why: Electron-only switching promises ~10x lower switching charge-voltage product and fatigue-free endurance for a polar storage cell; room-temperature electronic ferroelectricity in these materials is contested.
note: LuFe2O4 electronic ferroelectricity is disputed; RT switchable material not established.

title: Resonant-tunneling access diode opens only at wordline-tuned resonance
idea: Effect: double-barrier resonant tunneling. Replace the access transistor with a vertical AlN/GaN/AlN (or SiO2/Si-well/SiO2) stack whose quantized well level aligns with the storage-node Fermi level only when the wordline, acting as a gate on the well, pulls it into resonance; off-resonance transmission is 10^6-10^9 lower and fixed by barrier thickness rather than doping.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): a thin vertical film stack replaces the lateral transistor, so tiers stack without lithography of channels; leakage decoupled from channel length (fact 4).
note: Room-temperature peak-to-valley ratios far short of DRAM off/on needs.

title: Wordline-gated Coulomb-blockade nanodot valve in storage-node contact
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A ~1 nm Pt or Si nanodot between two tunnel barriers sits in the storage-node plug, capacitively gated by the same wordline: wordline-high moves the dot to its charge-degeneracy point (conducts), wordline-low leaves it deep in blockade with charging energy ~0.6 eV, above the 0.5 V node-to-bitline hold bias, so it blocks transistor leakage in series. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): claims 10x retention used for die-internal refresh skipping behind standard REF. Risk: on-current through dots vs tRCD/tWR (needs parallel dots).

title: Lattice-matched GaP storage-node contact blocks band-to-band tunneling
idea: Effect: heterojunction band offset. A few-nm epitaxial GaP layer (0.4% lattice mismatch to Si, Eg 2.26 eV) at the gate-overlapped storage-node contact forces GIDL tunneling across a wider gap (rate ~exp(-Eg^1.5/F)), cutting GIDL by up to ~10^3. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): GIDL dominates at negative wordline hold bias; claims 4x internal refresh skip. Risk: Ga cross-contamination in a DRAM line.
note: Ga contamination and GaP/Si interface quality.

title: Micro-ring modulators driven directly from sense-amp row skip SerDes
idea: Effect: electro-optic refractive-index modulation (Pockels in thin-film LiNbO3, or carrier plasma dispersion in Si). Put micro-ring modulators at the column-select outputs so each sense-amp group modulates its own WDM wavelength; light carries the page off-die in parallel, eliminating the serializer, DLL and long global data lines.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and periphery (fact 7): I/O energy falls from 3-20 pJ/bit to <1 pJ/bit, and ~10% of die area (I/O plus DLL) is removed.

title: Single-electron-transistor sense amp counts stored electrons directly
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A single-electron transistor with a ~2 nm Si island (charging energy well above kT at room temperature) capacitively coupled to the bitline acts as a sub-electron electrometer; its periodic current oscillation (Coulomb staircase) resolves signals of a few hundred electrons, with reference cells calibrating background-charge drift.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): the Cs requirement could drop from ~5 fF to ~0.5 fF, and heavily drooped weak cells still read correctly, removing the AR-75 capacitor.

title: Rank-modulated multi-level cells immune to common-mode leakage drift
idea: Effect: correlated (common-mode) leakage drift. Groups of 8 tiny cells are written with 4 charge levels, two cells each, and information is the permutation of charges (8!/2^4 = 2520 states, ~1.4 bits/cell), not absolute levels; neighbors sharing substrate and temperature leak together, so the ranking survives long after levels drift, and a winner-take-all comparator tree reads it.
why: 10x density: ~1.4 bits/cell tolerating ~5x retention drift, on 0.5 fF cells stacked 8 tiers (~7x), gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: the comparator tree is shared per bank.
note: Rank modulation known from flash; four levels on 0.5 fF cells leaves negligible signal.

title: Dithered multi-comparator sensing reads four-level cells reliably
idea: Effect: stochastic resonance and dithering. After charge sharing the bitline voltage holds for a few ns; three coarse comparators shared per 8 bitlines sample it several times with injected calibrated dither, and averaging resolves below comparator offset, reading 4 levels (2 bits) from a ~0.8 fF cell before a DAC-driven restore.
why: 10x density: 2 bits/cell times a 12-tier stack of ~0.8 fF cells (~5x) gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: comparators and DACs are amortized across 8 bitlines, with no capacitor module.
note: Four levels from 0.8 fF leave ~20 mV spacing; leakage and kTC noise, not comparator offset, dominate.

title: Na: Prussian-white nanocell stores bit as sodium electrochemical potential
idea: Each cell is a ~20 nm solid-state sodium couple of two Prussian-blue-analogue electrodes (Na, Fe, C, N) across a thin Na+ conductor; a write moves a few hundred Na+ ions, and the bit is the resulting ~0.3 V open-circuit voltage sensed on a read-transistor gate.
why: The bit is a thermodynamic potential, not a leaking charge, so electronic leakage does not erase it and refresh disappears (fact 3); all elements abundant; ion transit at ns and self-discharge are the risks.

title: Diamond inversion-channel access transistor with week-long retention
idea: C: build the access device as an inversion-channel diamond MOSFET (phosphorus-doped n-type diamond with an Al2O3 gate, p-channel inversion) grown as diamond-on-Si; the 5.5 eV gap makes intrinsic carrier density ~10^-27 cm^-3, so off-current is set only by defects and storage nodes could hold charge for days.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and frees capacitor margin so Cs can shrink (fact 1); retention margin ~10^5x larger, with cost hinging on heteroepitaxial diamond quality.

title: Lattice-matched GaP storage-node junction moves depletion into wide-gap material
idea: P (as GaP): selectively regrow a thin n+ GaP contact (2.26 eV gap, only 0.4% lattice mismatch to Si) on the silicon access transistor so the junction depletion region, where SRH generation happens, sits in GaP with ~10^7x lower intrinsic carrier density, while the channel stays silicon.
why: SRH junction leakage is proportional to n_i (fact 3); relocating even part of the depletion region into GaP could cut junction leakage by orders of magnitude while keeping silicon drive current.

title: Magnetically latched FeCo nanorelay gives true open-circuit access
idea: Fe: replace the access transistor with a vertical FeCo nanocantilever relay with Ru contacts, pulled closed electrostatically by the wordline and biased by a CoPt permanent-magnet film so it latches open or closed; the off state is a vacuum gap with zero subthreshold or junction leakage.
why: Retention becomes limited only by capacitor dielectric leakage (hours), removing refresh (fact 3); contact wear (~10^15 cycles needed) is the risk, so pair it with an SRAM/cache layer that limits per-cell switching.

title: MoS2 grown on trench sidewalls: channel geometry set by depth
idea: Mo: etch DUV-pitch trenches and grow monolayer MoS2 conformally by MOCVD on the vertical sidewalls; each sidewall becomes a vertical 2D access channel whose length equals the step height, and an ALD gate fills the trench, giving two cells per DUV feature.
why: Doubles effective cell density per DUV pitch without EUV (fact 4), while the 0.65 nm body suppresses short-channel leakage (fact 3).
note: Conformal monolayer MoS2 on sidewalls and contacts immature.

title: Mo: grounded molybdenum shield fins screen buried-wordline passing-gate coupling
idea: Insert a thin grounded Mo fin between adjacent buried wordlines, electrostatically screening the passing-gate field that modulates neighbor channels and storage-node junctions; Mo also replaces some tungsten (an 80%-China chokepoint) and is mined in the U.S.
why: Attacks the passing-gate row-hammer mechanism (fact 9) and GIDL tail (fact 3) at the source; target 5x higher hammer threshold.
note: No room for a grounded fin between buried wordlines at 6F2 pitch.

title: Williams-tube revival: field-emitter arrays write charge spots on dielectric
idea: The 1940s Williams tube stored bits as charge spots on a CRT face. Its nanoscale successor is a vacuum-sealed array of Spindt field-emission tips, each deflecting its beam over an 8x8 field of spots to write and read electron charge in a trap-rich dielectric film. The bit lives in the film, with no access transistor.
why: Facts 3 and 4: the storage medium is an unpatterned film, so no transistor or litho-defined capacitor is needed per cell. Vacuum-isolated traps cut refresh, and the cost moves into emitter arrays.
note: Like HP atomic-resolution storage; vacuum packaging, emitter stability and access speed are big unknowns.

title: Lost-wax helical channel packs a 60 nm gate into 12 nm footprint
idea: Deposit a sacrificial carbon helix in the pillar hole by glancing-angle spiral deposition, wrap it with gate dielectric and metal, burn the carbon out (lost-wax casting), then ALD-backfill the helical void with the channel. The result is a gate-all-around helix with L~60 nm in a vertical cell.
why: Fact 3: long L kills DIBL and short-channel subthreshold leakage by orders of magnitude, so VT can be lowered and wordline voltage dropped (fact 10) while retention rises ~10x. The cost is on-current, offset by the GAA helix width.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembled 3 nm nanowires widen bandgap by confinement
idea: Use block-copolymer self-assembly (no litho) to define 3-4 nm vertical Si nanowire access channels. Quantum confinement raises the effective gap to ~1.6-2 eV, exponentially suppressing BTBT/GIDL and intrinsic generation.
why: Facts 3 and 4: wider effective gap could cut junction/GIDL leakage 10-100x and removes an EUV layer. Series resistance and diameter variability are the risks.

title: Locksmith combination-lock access: resonant-tunneling barrier opens only at key bias
idea: Replace the gated transistor with a double-barrier resonant-tunneling stack (e.g., AlN/GaN wells) between bitline and storage well. Charge passes only when the bitline bias aligns the quantized level, like a key cut to one combination. Off-resonance, thick wide-gap barriers block flow.
why: Zero refresh: off-resonance transmission and thermionic leakage over ~2 eV barriers give retention of years, and energy-selective access needs no gate oxide or junction.

title: E-ink microcapsule bit: charged nanoparticle parked top or bottom
idea: Scale e-paper microcapsule manufacturing to a sealed ~10 nm cage holding one charged nanoparticle or ion cluster, held by image-charge adhesion to the top or bottom electrode. It is moved by a field pulse and read by capacitance difference.
why: Zero refresh: position is held by adhesion with no leaking charge and no hold power. The ns transit over 10 nm in vacuum is the speculative part.

title: Perfecting-press wafer: periphery printed on the backside of the array
idea: Like a perfecting press that prints both sides of a sheet in one pass, thin the finished array wafer to ~1 um and build low-temperature periphery transistors (laser-annealed Si or oxide FETs) on its backside. These connect to bitlines and wordlines through sub-um nano-TSVs directly beneath each mat.
why: Periphery stops consuming front-side area: array efficiency rises from ~51% to ~85%, ~1.6x bits per wafer without a litho shrink, and SA-to-bitline paths get shorter.
note: Low-temperature backside transistors are slow; industry chose bonded cell-on-periphery instead.

title: Duplex-printed pillar: one vertical channel serves front and back cells
idea: Like printing both sides of a sheet, build each vertical pillar with a buried bitline contacting it at mid-height, an upper gate linking it to a front-side capacitor and a lower gate linking it to a backside capacitor formed after bonding and thinning, so one 4F2 footprint stores two bits.
why: Doubles bits per footprint to an effective 2F2 without extra lithographic tiers (fact 4) and halves bitline contacts per bit; risk is two independent gates on one short pillar.

title: Swiss-roll capacitors: strained films self-roll into nano-scrolls
idea: Like a wound film capacitor or a jelly roll, deposit a TiN/dielectric/TiN stack on a strained bilayer over a sacrificial layer; releasing it makes the film curl into a tight multi-turn scroll above each cell, multiplying plate area 10-20x with no deep hole etch.
why: Gives 2-5x more Cs per footprint than 70:1 pillars while eliminating the high-AR fluorocarbon etch and its multilayer hard mask (PFAS gas, energy and critical litho for the hole layer).
note: Strained bilayers roll at 100s nm to um radii, far above DRAM cell pitch.

title: Puff-pastry fold-and-bond doubles 3D DRAM tiers each round
idea: Fabricate one complete planar 1T1C tier on thinned donors, then laminate like croissant dough: bond tiers face-to-back in pairs, thin, bond pairs to pairs, so N tiers need only log2(N) sequential bond-thin rounds (5 rounds = 32 tiers) and every tier reuses the proven planar mask set; oversized landing pads absorb ~100 nm bond overlay.
why: Fact 2: reaches the ~26-tier break-even with planar-proven cells, sidestepping the lateral transistor and lateral capacitor; one identical tier flow runs at full volume.
note: log2 bond rounds is neat, but yield compounds and cost/bit barely moves.

title: Fiducial marks: pilot-calibrated two-bit-per-cell DRAM with soft decoding
idea: Pick-and-place machines read fiducial marks to correct for drift. Each DRAM page embeds pilot cells with known values, read through the sense amp at several reference levels to track drift and leakage. That lets each cell hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and a soft-decision LDPC decoder uses pilot-calibrated likelihoods to turn a ~1% raw symbol error rate into reliable reads for a compressed or cold tier.
why: Doubles the bits per capacitor, giving 2x density on the same wafer area and EUV layers for page-granularity tiers where LDPC latency is hidden; the 1% error budget is what makes multi-level DRAM viable.

title: Lost-foam air gaps between buried wordlines via oxygen ash
idea: Lost-foam casting burns out a foam pattern to leave a cavity; deposit a carbon or polymer spacer between buried wordlines, cap it with porous oxide, then burn it out with an O2 ash (no argon sputter or plasma), leaving vacuum gaps that cut wordline-to-wordline and passing-gate coupling.
why: Lower coupling could raise the row-hammer threshold ~3-10x (fact 9) and cut wordline capacitance and energy (fact 10), all without rare gases.
note: Buried wordlines are separated by active silicon/STI, leaving little room for gaps.

title: Micro-Williams tube: field-emission beam addresses bare electret film
idea: IFR: no cell has an access device; one beam serves a million bits. Each 30x30 um tile has a gated field-emitter tip and electrostatic deflection plates in a vacuum-sealed MEMS cavity, writing and reading 10-15 nm charge spots on a continuous SiO2/Si3N4 electret film (read by secondary-electron yield, then rewrite).
why: Constraint: the medium is an unpatterned film at ~100-200 nm^2/bit versus 864 nm^2 for 6F^2 at 12 nm, and tiles need only coarse MEMS lithography, targeting 5-10x density at lower cost; electret charge in vacuum lasts years, so no refresh.

title: Negative-capacitance bitline dielectric makes the bitline vanish electrically
idea: Ideal result: a bitline with zero capacitance, so every femtofarad of cell charge becomes signal. Closest achievable: line the bitline-to-plate spacer with a thin stabilized HZO negative-capacitance layer in series with the parasitic, so effective Cbl drops 2-3x while staying hysteresis-free in the small-signal range.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) rises from ~0.1 to ~0.25, allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes, fact 7).

title: Microwave dispersive readout senses cells without draining them
idea: Ideal result: a read that costs nothing and leaves the bit untouched. Borrowing qubit readout, make each bitline segment part of a GHz resonator; a storage node gating a tiny varactor shifts the resonance, and a picowatt probe tone reflected from the line reveals the bit with no charge sharing and no restore.
why: Destructive read and CV^2 energy (facts 8, 10): no restore cycle and no full-swing bitline; target <0.5 pJ per useful bit versus ~5.9 pJ.

title: Neighbor bitlines form a SAR DAC for two-bit cells
idea: Ideal result: the bitline itself is the analog-to-digital converter. Store 4 charge levels per cell and resolve them by successive approximation, with adjacent precharged bitlines switched in binary-weighted groups acting as the DAC capacitors against the sensed line.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits/cell at ~1.3x periphery cost gives ~1.5x bits per wafer without a litho shrink (fact 4).
note: Neighbor bitlines are not free DAC caps: every bitline on the row is charge-sharing its own cell during activation.

title: Dual-ended mirror pillar stores two bits per 4F2 footprint
idea: IFR: 'two cells in the space of one.' Backward: build a vertical channel pillar with one capacitor on top (front side) and another at its bottom (after backside thinning), split the gate into independent upper and lower half-gates, and tap the shared bitline at the pillar midpoint.
why: Density (fact 4): ~2F2 effective cell without shrinking F, ~1.8x bits per wafer at the same litho.

title: Soft-decision re-sense with shifted bitline references
idea: Ideal: never lose a bit, even when the cell signal is nearly zero. Closest: when the fast decoder fails, the row is re-sensed twice more with the bitline precharge shifted by +/-15 mV, producing per-bit confidence (like NAND read-retry) that feeds a soft-decision decoder able to recover cells with only ~20 mV of signal.
why: Facts 1 and 3: roughly doubles usable cell margin, enabling smaller capacitors or longer refresh at the price of rare slow reads.
note: DRAM read is destructive: after first sense the restore overwrites charge, so re-sensing needs preserved signal.

title: Altermagnet tunnel junction: magnetoresistance without stray fields
idea: Scarcity rule: no net magnetization allowed, since stray fields set MRAM pitch. Store the bit in the Neel vector of an altermagnet (RuO2, MnTe or Mn5Si3) whose spin-split bands still give tunneling magnetoresistance, and flip it with spin-splitter or spin-orbit torque at THz-class dynamics.
why: 10 nm-pitch magnetic bits with no dipolar crosstalk, ps writes and unlimited endurance (density and energy axes); room-temperature TMR magnitude is unproven.

title: Charging-energy wall: Coulomb-blockade island as the leakage stopper
idea: Limit: leakage must be stopped by a quantum effect, not a barrier height. Put a sub-2 nm silicon or metal nanocrystal island in series with the access channel. Its charging energy (>0.5 eV) blocks single-electron transit until the wordline shifts the island level into resonance, and co-tunneling leakage is exponentially suppressed.
why: Fact 3: the off-state is set by the charging energy (~20 kT), not by doping or trap statistics, which could collapse the tail distribution. Speculative: island uniformity at room temperature.

title: Spin-orbit voltage readout: nanomagnets drive inverters, no sense amps
idea: Constraint: non-volatile magnetic bits. Instead of current-mode TMR sensing, pass a small supply current through the bit's spin-injection layer into a strong spin-orbit layer (Bi2Se3/Pt), where the inverse Edelstein/spin-Hall effect converts spin to a charge voltage whose sign follows magnetization (MESO-style); that voltage gates a local inverter directly, with no reference or SA.
why: Periphery (fact 7): deletes SAs and references. Risk: ~10-100 mV output and spin-to-charge efficiency.

title: Bond-then-drill: one etch wires a 64-tier wafer stack
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Fusion-bond 64 DRAM wafers thinned to 5 um each (oxide bonding, <100 nm alignment), then pattern once and etch/fill vertical buses through the whole stack like a 3D-NAND channel hole, so one litho step and one deep etch replace 63 separate TSV and bump steps.
why: TSV/bump cost (fact 6) is amortized across tiers: 64 thin tiers vs 8-12 in HBM gives ~10x bits per footprint and volume while per-tier interconnect cost drops ~50x.
note: 64-tier wafer stacking compounds yield catastrophically; density per footprint, not cost per bit.

title: No wafer at all: roll-to-roll steel-foil memory with drum nanoimprint
idea: Forced limit: no discrete substrates. Stainless-steel foil gets a planarizing dielectric, then sputtered oxide-semiconductor and drum-nanoimprinted gain-cell layers in a continuous web line.
why: Capital intensity: web processing cuts tool cost per m2 by about 10x versus batch wafers; foil is cheap and plentiful.

title: No silicon: roll-to-roll MoS2 memory grown on copper foil
idea: Forced limit: the channel and substrate must be non-Si. Monolayer MoS2 is grown by CVD on a continuous copper foil web, transferred to glass or polyimide, and patterned into gain-cell access transistors whose wide bandgap gives sub-fA leakage.
why: Lower leakage reduces refresh, and 2D channels allow scaling without a wafer; supply comes from the copper-foil battery industry.

title: Deep-level charge bit: QD-Flash physics shrunk toward an atom-placed single-defect cell
idea: Ensemble version (exists): self-assembled GaSb or InGaSb quantum dots in a GaP matrix give ~1 eV hole localisation. A gate bias floods the dots with holes (capture, ns), and a reverse field empties them by field-assisted emission (350 ns measured, ~10 ns predicted). The stored charge sits above a channel whose conductance is read non-destructively. Single-defect version (2040 tools): hydrogen-depassivation lithography or deterministic single-ion implantation places 1-3 deep-level dopants or engineered defects in a crystalline barrier under a 10-15 nm gate. Each trapped charge is a quantised threshold step, so the cell is natively multi-level (bits = number of charges). No amorphous tunnel oxide sits in the write path, so there is no oxide wear.
why: [SPECULATIVE] 2.7-5x density (4F2 at F = 10 nm, 1-2 bits/cell), ~3.5 aJ gate write energy, and a refresh interval anywhere from 1 s to 1 day by picking a 1.0-1.3 eV level.

title: Swap 30,000-electron capacitor for 200-electron node plus single-electron sensor
idea: Shrink the storage node to a ~0.03 fF gate island and read it with a room-temperature silicon single-electron transistor shared by a few cells. The transistor's sub-3-nm dot is formed by a dopant cluster or an oxidised nanowire constriction, and its Coulomb oscillation turns a few-electron change into a large current swing.
why: Breaks the charge wall outright (fact 1): the storage element needs no capacitor, so the cell is planar and easy to stack for 3D (fact 2).
note: Room-temperature SET memory known since Yano 1994; offset-charge noise and variability.

title: Swap current-driven magnet for voltage-flipped magnetoelectric BiFeO3 bit
idea: Exchange-couple a CoFe nanomagnet to multiferroic BiFeO3. A 100 mV field flips the BiFeO3 polarization and antiferromagnetic order, which drags the magnet with it, and the state is read through inverse Rashba-Edelstein charge output, as in MESO.
why: Breaks the voltage floor (fact 10): a ~100 mV write needs ~10-30x less CV2 energy than a 1-3 V DRAM write, and storage is non-volatile.
note: MESO-type physics; 100 mV deterministic BFO switching not yet achieved.

title: Swap binary charge for eight-level charge with shared SAR sensing
idea: At relaxed DUV pitch (F ~ 20 nm) the larger cell cap stores eight charge levels (3 bits). They are read by a charge-redistribution SAR sense amplifier shared across four bitlines, protected by a strong symbol ECC, and refreshed at a rate set by the narrowest level margin.
why: 3 bits per cell offsets the ~2.8x area loss of skipping EUV (fact 4), giving equal or better bits per mm2 with no EUV capex.
note: Leakage collapses 8-level margins; prior 4-level DRAM efforts stalled.

title: Substitute linear gate dielectric with antiferroelectric ZrO2 steep-switch stack
idea: Substitute the HfO2/SiO2 gate stack with antiferroelectric ZrO2. Its field-induced AFE-to-FE transition gives a transient negative-capacitance boost at turn-on, then relaxes fully to zero polarization at zero field: no remanence and none of the wake-up or fatigue of ferroelectric gates.
why: Sub-60 mV/dec turn-on allows a higher Vt and lower VPP: target ~10x lower leakage or ~1 V less wordline, without ferroelectric endurance limits.

title: Capacitor-DAC successive approximation sense for two-bit cells
idea: Substitute the single-threshold latch with a two-step successive-approximation comparison: switched trim capacitors on the reference bitline act as a capacitive DAC that steps the reference to resolve four stored charge levels, so each cell holds 2 bits.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~2x bits per cell area if sense resolution reaches ~25 mV steps, which is helped by soft-decision ECC.

title: Steep-slope tunnel-FET sense amps enable 0.5 V array voltage
idea: Substitute MOSFET sense pairs with heterojunction tunnel FETs (~30 mV/dec) used only in the latch, where low drive current matters less, so the array voltage drops from ~1 V to ~0.5 V while the latch still regenerates.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): array CV^2 falls ~4x; leakage at low VARY also falls.

title: Transferred 2D-crystal tiers replace deposited semiconductor tiers
idea: Substitute epitaxial/deposited tier stacks with wafer-scale dry transfer of MOCVD monolayer MoS2 channels plus hBN gate dielectric grown on reusable sapphire donors, stacked tier by tier with a non-fluorinated polymer handle (PPC); each cell tier including its gate is <10 nm thick.
why: Tier pitch ~60+ nm (Si/SiGe) -> ~20-30 nm, 2-3x more tiers per um of stack and lower slit/hole AR (fact 2); 1.8 eV channel pushes leakage orders of magnitude below the 13 fA tail (fact 3).

title: Substitute access transistors with BEOL two-terminal selectors in line-space crosspoints
idea: Build a 1S1C crosspoint: a threshold-switching selector (NbOx or OTS) in series with a planar MIM capacitor at each intersection of two perpendicular line arrays, which need only line/space patterning (SAQP or DSA, no contact holes, no EUV) and stack in BEOL; only the single selected intersection is charged or read.
why: Constraint: bit-granular access on short 4F2 lines gives ~0.2-0.5 pJ per useful bit versus 5.9 pJ (>=10x); facet: ~3 masks per layer, BEOL-stackable. Selector leakage forces frequent refresh.

title: Threshold-switch selector stacked on capacitor for cross-point 3D DRAM
idea: Fuse the ovonic threshold switch selector from 3D XPoint with a MIM capacitor into a two-terminal 1S1C stack at each wordline/bitline crossing, built in 8-16 decks with no transistor. Half-select bias stays below the OTS threshold to isolate the node; a full-select pulse snaps the OTS on to charge or sense it.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 4F2 per deck with no front-end transistor; 8 decks ~5x density per wafer; requires OTS sub-threshold leakage below ~1 fA.

title: Porphyrin redox monolayer giving multi-level charge per node
idea: Graft a monolayer of porphyrin or ferrocene molecules with 2-3 discrete oxidation states onto the storage-node electrode, combining molecular electronics with the DRAM capacitor so charge sits in molecular redox states at fixed potentials. Discrete states give quantized charge levels (2 bits/cell), and electrons must cross a molecular tether barrier to escape, stretching retention from 64 ms toward minutes.
why: Facts 1 and 3: 2 bits/cell plus up to ~1000x longer retention cuts refresh power; molecule stability over 1e15 cycles is the risk.
note: ZettaCore pursued porphyrin multilevel memory; failed on kinetics, stability and integration.

title: Tunnel-FET gain cell with steep-slope read amplification
idea: Combine a band-to-band tunneling FET (sub-30 mV/decade) as the read device with a small storage node in a 2T gain cell, so every 10 mV of stored voltage moves read current by about an order of magnitude. Storage nodes can be 0.5 fF or less at a 0.4 V swing, and reading never disturbs the node.
why: Facts 1, 8, 10: ~10x smaller Cs, 0.4 V operation for ~6x lower CV2 energy, and non-destructive read.
note: TFET steep slope rarely holds at useful current; low on-current slows reads.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO layer inside the buried-wordline gate stack
idea: Put a thin ferroelectric HZO film in series with the high-k gate dielectric of the buried-channel access transistor. Its negative capacitance amplifies gate-to-channel coupling and gives a sub-60 mV/dec subthreshold slope.
why: Allows Vt to rise ~200 mV at the same on-current, for 50-100x lower subthreshold leakage. Alternatively it lets the 3 V wordline boost drop (fact 10).
note: NC-FET steep slope widely pursued; hysteresis and speed remain unresolved.

title: Nanoelectromechanical contact in series with each access transistor
idea: A monolithic BEOL TiN or CNT cantilever relay sits between the access transistor and the storage node. The same wordline field pulls it in, and it springs open during retention to leave an air gap.
why: The off-state leakage path is a vacuum or air gap, so retention is limited only by capacitor-dielectric leakage and refresh is eliminated for most data. Nanosecond closure and contact wear are unproven.

title: Tunnel-FET input pair inside a conventional MOSFET latch
idea: Replace only the input pair of the DRAM sense amp with steep-slope tunnel FETs (sub-60 mV/decade) and keep MOSFETs for restore, so the latch begins amplifying at VARY ~0.5 V, where MOSFET-only latches barely turn on.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): halving VARY cuts bitline CV^2 energy ~4x, and refresh energy falls with it.

title: MEMS micromirror process fused with DRAM: nano-relay access switches
idea: Replace the access transistor with an electrostatic nano-cantilever relay built in a back-end sacrificial-gap MEMS flow like TI's Dallas DLP micromirror line; the open contact is a vacuum gap, so off-state leakage is essentially zero, and the relay sits above its capacitor in the same 4F2 footprint.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): no subthreshold or GIDL path, retention limited by dielectric leakage (minutes+), refresh almost gone; nm relays switch in ~10-50 ns, contact endurance (>10^15) is the risk.
note: NEMS DRAM was proposed before; 1e15 contact endurance and stiction are unsolved.

title: Two-bit-per-capacitor DRAM made viable by 1% sensing tolerance
idea: Combine NAND's multi-level-cell sensing with the DRAM capacitor: four charge levels per cell are read by a charge-sharing, two-step successive-approximation sense amp. The scheme historically failed on margin but works once the code absorbs ~1% level misreads.
why: 2x bits per wafer with the same masks, litho and capacitor, roughly halving capital per bit (facts 1, 4).

title: NEMS relay access switch: air-gap off-state ends leakage tail
idea: Combine a nanoelectromechanical relay with a storage capacitor: a released TiN or poly-Si seesaw relay replaces the access transistor, so the off-state is an air gap with essentially zero leakage and retention is limited only by the capacitor dielectric. Buildable in a university nanofab: sacrificial oxide released by vapor HF, e-beam defined gaps.
