idea: Scale down to the molecule: graft a monolayer of fast one-electron redox molecules (ferrocene/viologen derivatives) onto the TiN pillar surface so each cell stores charge Faradaically in molecular orbitals, not only in the dielectric field. Electron transfer at a tethered monolayer is sub-ns and the molecules add ~10-30 uC/cm2 of switchable charge at <0.5 V swing.
why: Capacitor charge wall: 3-10x stored charge per pillar area lets AR drop from 60:1 toward 15-20:1, cutting etch steps and enabling lower VARY.

title: Time-domain sensing reads two bits per cell
idea: Time-shift the read: instead of a single voltage comparison, record how long the bitline takes to cross a threshold after charge sharing using a per-sense-amp time-to-digital counter; four charge levels map to four crossing times, storing 2 bits per capacitor.
why: Cost per bit: ~1.8x bits per cell area after margin; reuses existing capacitor process.

title: Room-temperature single-electron box with electrometer readout
idea: Scale down to counting electrons: store tens of electrons on a sub-3 nm silicon or metal nanocluster whose charging energy exceeds kT at 300 K, read by an adjacent single-electron transistor whose current jumps with each electron.
why: Energy and density: write energy near aJ, cell footprint ~10 nm, attacking CV2 voltage floor.

title: Charge-density-wave hidden state in 1T-TaS2 flakes
idea: Jump to the picosecond timescale: a ps electrical pulse switches 1T-TaS2 into a metastable hidden CDW state with orders-of-magnitude different resistance, and a longer pulse restores it; the bit is a collective electron-lattice crystal phase.
why: Speed and energy: ps writes at fJ; no ion motion.

title: Polyoxometalate redox clusters as molecular gain-cell storage nodes
idea: Molecule-scale jump: a monolayer of polyoxometalate clusters, which hold discrete electrons in deep molecular orbitals, forms the storage layer in the gate stack of a gain FET; writes add or remove 1-2 electrons per cluster at low voltage and the deep levels keep the charge for hours, so no refresh is scheduled.
why: Hours of retention -> zero refresh (fact 3), no capacitor (fact 1), and self-assembly instead of EUV patterning (fact 4).
note: POM flash proposed in 2014; flash-like speed and endurance.

title: Charge-modulated bipolar gain cell from a 1990s BiCMOS line
idea: Scale the signal up by gain instead of capacitor size: store charge on the floating base of a vertical bipolar transistor stacked over the access device, so read current is ~beta (about 100) times what the stored charge alone would give. A ~0.5-fF node yields the read signal of a ~50-fF capacitor.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 100x current gain stands in for capacitor size, on depreciated 0.35-0.25 um BiCMOS lines.
note: Floating-base charge recombines and is drained by read base current; retention and disturb doubtful.

title: Redox polymer brushes store capacitor charge in shallow holes
idea: Scale jump from dielectric capacitor to molecule: a ~10 nm brush of poly(vinylferrocene) or porphyrin redox polymer grafted on a TiN electrode stores charge faradaically, roughly 100 uC/cm2 at 1 V, which is ~15x a ZAZ capacitor. A shallow 10:1 hole would then hold ~5 fF, with a solid polymer electrolyte cap.
why: Eliminates HAR etch and Hf/Zr dielectrics using Fe, C and H. Redox kinetics (ns vs us) and solid-state retention are unproven.

title: Pitch-octupling on old KrF scanners writes the DRAM array lattice
idea: Scale shift via spacer chemistry: the array is a perfectly periodic lattice. A 200 nm-pitch KrF line pattern in an existing 200 mm fab is divided by three spacer generations into 25 nm pitch, and the crossing hole lattice comes from two orthogonal passes. Periphery stays at native KrF resolution.
why: No EUV, no immersion and no new fab: unlocks idle 200 mm lines for 2-4 Gb DRAM. Accumulated CD variation is the risk.
note: SAOP from KrF accumulates CD variation; overlay for cuts and contacts is the doubt.

title: Grow capacitor pillars bottom-up instead of etching 70:1 holes
idea: Invert the length-scale problem: rather than etching 1.5 um-deep holes, grow vertical Si nanowires from CMOS-compatible catalyst dots (Al or Cu-silicide) placed on the capacitor lattice sites, then wrap them in ZrO2/HfO2 and a top electrode; aspect ratio becomes a function of growth time, not etch physics.
why: Breaks the AR 60-75:1 etch wall (Fact 1): AR ~150:1 for Cs >8 fF without cryogenic etch tools, removing the single costliest etch step.

title: Four charge levels per cell doubles bits without new tools
idea: Store 2 bits per 1T1C cell as four charge levels, read by a time-to-digital sense amplifier that measures how long the bitline takes to develop rather than its polarity; same fab, same masks, same node.
why: 1.6-1.8x bits per wafer net of larger sense amps with zero new capex (Fact 4); fights the charge wall (Fact 1), hence high risk.

title: Hard-drive flying heads become plasmonic lithography writers
idea: Borrow from storage at rack scale: a Minnesota-made HDD slider carrying a plasmonic ridge aperture flies ~10 nm above a spinning resist-coated wafer at ~10 m/s and writes ~20 nm features with near-field light; 100+ heads write the periodic array as concentric tracks.
why: Maskless sub-20 nm patterning from an all-domestic HDD supply chain at ~1% of EUV tool cost (Fact 4).

title: Liquid-metal micro-sockets let interposers outlive three DRAM generations
idea: Shift packaging lifetime from one product cycle to a decade: HBM stacks seat into polymer wells filled with gallium-indium alloy at ~20 um pitch, held by a clamp, so stacks lift out at room temperature for swap, upgrade or redeployment. The costly logic die and interposer persist while memory rotates.
why: Raises effective supply and cuts embodied capital: good HBM is no longer scrapped with the accelerator, giving ~2-3x more service years per stack.

title: Zettacore revived: solid-state redox monolayer multiplies capacitor charge
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin memory died because its redox molecules needed a liquid electrolyte. Tether a ferrocene/porphyrin monolayer to the DRAM storage-node electrode and cap it with an ALD solid ion conductor (LiPON-like): Faradaic charge of 1-4 electrons per molecule adds ~10-30 uC/cm2 of pseudocapacitance on top of the dielectric charge.
why: 3-10x storage charge per area breaks the capacitor wall (Fact 1) without AR 115; shorter pillars save etch steps and collapse risk. Risk: redox kinetics must reach <10 ns.

title: Spin-crossover molecular film stores bits in iron's spin state
idea: Effect walk: thermal hysteresis of spin crossover. A 5-nm film of an Fe(II)-triazole coordination polymer with a 20-40 K hysteresis loop straddling room temperature forms the dielectric of a small capacitor; a short heat or field pulse flips low-spin and high-spin, changing permittivity and volume ~10%, read as a capacitance difference with a small AC probe.
why: A bistable molecular state needs no refresh and no high-AR capacitor; solution-deposited BEOL layers stack without EUV (fact 4) and use only iron, carbon and nitrogen, no chokepoint materials; switching speed and cycling endurance are unproven at ns scale.
note: Same Fe-triazole spin-crossover storage.

title: Charge-density-wave order in 1T-TaS2 holds bits as electron-crystal phase
idea: Effect walk: charge-density-wave ordering. A 10-nm 1T-TaS2 film switches between a commensurate insulating CDW and a metastable metallic 'mosaic' CDW under a ~30-ps few-volt pulse, is read by its 10-100x resistance difference, and is reverted by a longer, weaker pulse.
why: Electronic ordering switches in picoseconds with fJ-class energy and no atomic migration, promising endurance and speed in a BEOL crosspoint; the hidden state is only long-lived at cryogenic temperatures, so room-temperature analogues are needed.
note: Same CDW hidden-state mechanism.

title: Single-electron Coulomb-blockade node read by an on-cell SET
idea: Effect walk: Coulomb blockade. Store the bit as 0 vs ~10 electrons on a 3-nm Si dot whose ~150 meV charging energy quantizes occupancy, written through a tunnel barrier at ~0.2 V and read by a co-integrated single-electron transistor whose current swings ~100x per added electron.
why: Moves ~10 electrons instead of ~30,000 (5 fF x 1 V) and the SET gain lets the bitline swing only ~50 mV: ~100x lower cell+bitline energy per access (fact 10), and the Coulomb gap suppresses leakage (fact 3); room-temperature SET variability is the risk.

title: Gate voltage flips interlayer magnetic order in a 2D magnet
idea: Effect walk: electrostatic doping-tuned interlayer exchange. In bilayer CrI3-class or room-temperature Fe3GaTe2 van der Waals magnets, a ~0.1 V/nm gate field shifts interlayer exchange between antiparallel and parallel, switching a spin-filter tunnel junction resistance by >10x with a purely capacitive write.
why: No current flows through the junction during write (~aJ at sub-volt) and spin-filter read has very large TMR, so access energy can be 10-100x below DRAM; Curie temperature and air stability are the risks.
note: Shown in CrI3 at cryogenic temperature; no room-temperature insulating vdW magnet exists.

title: Negative-capacitance boosted cell lets array voltage fall to 0.3 V
idea: Effect walk: ferroelectric negative capacitance. A thin, domain-stabilized ferroelectric layer in series with the storage dielectric raises the stack's effective capacitance ~3x inside the non-hysteretic NC window, so the cell stores the same signal charge at an array voltage of ~0.33 V and wordline ~1.2 V.
why: Breaks the voltage floor (fact 10): bitline CV2 scales with V2, so 1 V to 0.33 V cuts array energy per access ~9-10x while also easing the capacitor wall (fact 1); hysteresis-free NC at GHz rates is disputed.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode pair self-restores each bit without refresh
idea: Effect: interband tunneling negative differential resistance. Two nanoscale p++/n++ Ge (or SiGe) Esaki diodes stacked in series on the storage node form a Goto pair; a pA standby current biases them so the node has two stable voltages that actively restore against leakage, giving a refresh-free 1T2D cell barely larger than 1T1C.
why: Refresh eliminated (fact 3) at near-DRAM density; trade-off is pA/cell standby current, which must beat 46 fJ/bit refresh.

title: Ferroelectric negative-capacitance layer cancels bitline parasitic capacitance
idea: Effect: ferroelectric negative capacitance. Hang a stabilized HZO/dielectric NC capacitor in parallel on each bitline sense node, tuned so the net node capacitance stays positive but drops ~2x. The charge-transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+CBL) roughly doubles.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): halves the Cs needed (AR ~70:1 to ~40:1), or doubles cells per bitline so half the SA stripes are needed.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel latch stacked in one vertical pillar
idea: Interband tunneling (negative differential resistance): two series Si/SiGe Esaki tunnel diodes, grown epitaxially in one vertical pillar, form a bistable Goto-pair storage node. A single surrounding access gate connects that node to the bitline. The result is a static, capacitor-free 4F2 cell held by pA-level tunnel current.
why: Removes both the capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3); claim 4F2 static density at a few nW per Mb standby, with no refresh bandwidth loss.

title: Purely electronic Mott-avalanche switching in lacunar spinel cross-points
idea: Electric-field-driven Mott transition: GaV4S8-family lacunar spinel films switch by an electronic avalanche that collapses the Mott gap, with no ion motion, into a retained metallic filament. Cross-point tiers of these films aim at RRAM-like density without oxygen-vacancy wear.
why: Gives a non-volatile 4F2 stackable cell (fact 2) with ion-free switching for DRAM-class endurance; claim >1e12 cycles in principle. Room-temperature retention is the risk.
note: GaV4S8 electric-field Mott switching is an active research line; room-temperature retained filaments remain the doubt.

title: 1T-TaS2 charge-density-wave hidden-state switching in vdW tiers
idea: Charge density waves: picosecond electrical pulses drive 1T-TaS2 flakes into a metastable hidden CDW state whose resistance differs by orders of magnitude, and a longer pulse restores the ground state. Transferable van der Waals flakes can be stacked as many thin non-volatile tiers.
why: Gives ps-scale switching with non-volatile tiers of atomic thickness (facts 2 and 10); claim fJ writes. Room-temperature stability of the hidden state is speculative.
note: 1T-TaS2 hidden state is unstable at room temperature; actively researched.

title: VO2 hyper-FET access transistor gives sub-60 mV per decade switching
idea: V: place a Ge-doped VO2 film (insulator-metal transition raised above ~100 C) in series with each access transistor's bitline contact; once the gate turns on, current triggers the abrupt IMT, giving an effective subthreshold slope of a few mV/decade, so Vt can sit higher at the same on-current and wordline voltage.
why: Breaks the 60 mV/dec link between leakage and wordline voltage (facts 3, 10): either ~10^3 less off-current at the same VPP or ~0.5-1 V lower wordline boost.

title: Selenide threshold switch builds a crosspoint one-selector-one-capacitor DRAM
idea: Se: replace the three-terminal access transistor with a two-terminal Ge-As-Se ovonic threshold switch stacked on a vertical capacitor at 4F2 crosspoint pitch; selected cells see V above threshold (~1.5 V), half-selected cells see V/2, and Se-rich, N-doped compositions push sub-threshold leakage toward the fA regime.
why: 4F2 density and stackable decks without a lateral transistor (facts 2, 4); viability needs OTS off-current ~10^3 below today's, so physics risk is honestly high.

title: Nickel-seeded lateral crystallization makes single-grain transistors in every 3D tier
idea: Ni: in a stacked 3D DRAM, deposit amorphous Si for each tier and open one DUV-defined Ni seed window per row; a 500-550 C anneal sweeps a NiSi2 front laterally (metal-induced lateral crystallization), leaving long single-grain needles where lateral access transistors are placed, followed by Ni gettering.
why: Attacks the lateral-transistor blocker of 3D DRAM (fact 2) with near-single-crystal leakage at low thermal budget, without epitaxial superlattices or EUV; residual Ni is the leakage risk.
note: MILC is known and residual Ni raises TFT leakage, the exact metric DRAM needs.

title: Tin monoxide p-type transistors put sense amps above the array
idea: Pair p-type SnO (Sn2+, sputter/ALD at ~250 C) with n-type ZTO to build complementary oxide sense amplifiers, sub-wordline drivers and local decoders in a BEOL tier directly over each 3D-DRAM mat, so periphery tiles the mat footprint rather than flanking it.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7); stacking local periphery over the mat with low-temperature CMOS gives ~30-40% die shrink with no second wafer or hybrid bond, and no indium.
note: Same as I-04778 with SnO/ZTO; SnO is the better p-oxide but still weak for matched sense amps.

title: Swiss-roll capacitor: self-rolled film-capacitor winding inside each cell
idea: Copy how wound film capacitors are made, at nanoscale. Deposit a strained TiN/ZrO2/TiN/ZrO2 nanomembrane on a sacrificial layer and release it, so built-in stress rolls it into a 3-4 turn spiral tube standing in the cell. Each winding adds electrode area without etching a 70:1 hole.
why: Facts 1 and 4: a stress-driven roll replaces the costly high-AR capacitor etch. Target is 5 fF at an equivalent AR of ~20.

title: Electroplated pseudocapacitor bit: hydrous RuO2 stores charge as surface protons
idea: Use electroplating to fill each shallow cup with hydrous RuO2.xH2O. Charge is held by fast surface proton redox (pseudocapacitance) rather than a dielectric, ~10-50x a dielectric capacitor per real area. A thin solid proton conductor is the separator.
why: Fact 1: 5 fF from a cup of AR ~5-10, so no deep capacitor etch. The main risk is whether the redox kinetics reach ns.
note: Same pseudocap mechanism with Ru (scarce).

title: Paper-mill layered magnet: gated vdW ferromagnet spin-filter tunnel bit
idea: Like pressing paper sheets, stack a few layers of the room-temperature vdW ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2 with hBN. A gate pulse switches interlayer coupling between ferro and antiferro alignment, and spin-filter tunneling changes the current by >100x.
why: Fact 10: a magnetic bit set by voltage, not current, at aJ energy. The giant read signal allows small sense amps (fact 7), and it is nonvolatile, so no refresh.
note: Fe3GaTe2 is metallic: gating is screened and it cannot act as a spin-filter barrier.

title: Raney-nickel sponge electrode: dealloy Ni-Al to multiply capacitor area
idea: Use the way Raney nickel catalyst is made. Deposit Ni-Al alloy in each shallow cup and leach the Al out with NaOH, leaving a nanoporous Ni sponge with ~5 nm ligaments that ALD then coats with Al2O3/ZrO2 dielectric and a TiN counter electrode.
why: Fact 1: 10-20x internal area per footprint makes 5 fF at AR ~5. Ni, Al, Zr, Ti and O replace Ru, Hf and W electrodes and liners.

title: Softgel nanocapsule: sealed ionic-liquid double-layer capacitor per cell
idea: Use pharmaceutical softgel encapsulation: fill each cup with an imidazolium ionic liquid (C, H, N, O, S, F) and seal it under an ALD Al2O3 lid. Charge sits in the ~1 nm electric double layer at carbon or TiN electrodes, at ~15-20 uF/cm2 (10-20x an oxide dielectric) and ~ns RC at 10 nm scale.
why: Fact 1: 5 fF from an AR ~8 cup. Inside the electrochemical window there is no dielectric tunneling leakage, and the materials are commodity organics.
note: Ionic-liquid EDL in sealed cup; BEOL thermal budget and ns charging are the risks.

title: Veneer-peeled single-crystal foils give every 3D tier bulk-grade transistors
idea: Like a rotary veneer lathe peeling a log, repeatedly cleave 30-50 nm single-crystal Si foils from one reusable donor boule (H-implant plus stressor-controlled spalling) and bond them tier by tier, so each of 26+ tiers gets bulk-quality lateral access transistors with no Si/SiGe superlattice epi and no poly-Si.
why: Fact 2 (lateral transistor blocker): single-crystal channels avoid poly grain-boundary leakage (~100x lower tail) in every tier, and donor reuse keeps cost per tier to a bond plus cleave step.

title: Stamped snap-dome nanobeam stores bits as buckled up or down
idea: Like keyboard snap domes stamped from prestressed sheet, each cell is a prestressed nanobeam buckled up or down, flipped electrostatically in ns and read capacitively. Contact-free flexing avoids wear.
why: Zero refresh: the bit is mechanical shape, not charge, so nothing leaks. Zero standby and refresh power, with GHz-resonator-class flexures able to reach high endurance.
note: Buckled-beam NEMS memory proposed before; ns switching, endurance and density unproven.

title: Non-contact bistable buckled nanobeam as a mechanical bit
idea: IFR: a bit held by geometry that costs nothing to keep. Closest achievable: a ~50 nm compressively prestressed SiC or graphene beam buckles up or down (two energy minima), is flipped by a ns electrostatic pulse from side electrodes and read capacitively; it never touches anything, so there is no stiction or wear.
why: Zero retention energy and no refresh (fact 3), no capacitor charge wall (fact 1); GHz-class beams switch in ~1-10 ns; endurance effectively unlimited because there is no contact.
note: Same buckled bistable mechanical bit.

title: Air-gap NEMS relay replaces the leaky access transistor
idea: IFR: an access switch whose off-state is perfect emptiness. Closest achievable: a vertical nanoelectromechanical relay (TiN cantilever, ~5 nm air gap) gates each storage capacitor; off-state leakage is tunnelling through air (<1e-21 A), so today's 5 fF capacitor holds charge for minutes to hours.
why: Fact 3: removes the <=13 fA tail and refresh power; with retention solved, Cs can fall 5-10x and break the aspect-ratio wall (fact 1). Contact endurance is the main risk.

title: Polar skyrmion topological charge as an unforgettable bit
idea: IFR: a bit that thermal noise cannot flip because it is topologically protected. Closest achievable: in PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices, nucleate or annihilate a ~10 nm polar skyrmion with a local electrode field and read its presence through its distinct local permittivity or piezoresponse.
why: Density (~10 nm bits, below 4F^2) and retention without refresh (fact 3); no ion motion so endurance is effectively unlimited; sidesteps capacitor scaling (fact 1).

title: Superionic nanolayer pseudocapacitor packs 30x charge per pillar
idea: IFR: a capacitor with infinite charge density that charges instantly. Closest achievable: line the pillar with a ~3 nm superionic conductor (alpha-AgI or Cu2Se class, ionic diffusivity ~1e-5 cm^2/s) between blocking electrodes so ions cross the film in ~25 ns, storing pseudocapacitive charge 10-30x that of a dielectric of equal area.
why: Fact 1: delivers the Cs that AR 115 or k 70 would, at AR ~10-20; fewer deep-etch steps lower capital (fact 4).
note: alpha-AgI and Cu2Se are superionic only above ~150-400 C; blocking electrodes make it EDL, not pseudocapacitive.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode pair that self-refreshes the storage node
idea: IFR: a charge bit that pulls itself back when it leaks. Closest achievable: hang two series interband tunnel diodes (Si/SiGe or oxide heterojunction) on the storage node so their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages fed by a pA standby current, turning the 1T1C into a static cell.
why: Fact 3: refresh (46 fJ/bit, bandwidth loss) eliminated while keeping near-1T1C area.

title: Charge-density-wave hidden state in tantalum disulfide as bit
idea: IFR: a bit stored in the electron crystal itself. Closest achievable: in thin 1T-TaS2 a ps-to-ns voltage pulse switches the commensurate charge-density wave into a metastable mosaic metallic state and a longer pulse restores it; read is the ~10x resistance change.
why: fJ-scale switching with no capacitor (fact 1) and no ion migration, so endurance is high; needs the hidden state stabilized at room temperature.
note: Room-temperature hidden state needed.

title: Nested triple-coaxial cylinder capacitor like an MLCC in a pillar
idea: IFR: every bit of cell volume is capacitor plate. Closest achievable: build three concentric electrodes inside one pillar hole by alternating ALD electrode, dielectric and sacrificial layers, tying alternate shells together at top and bottom as an MLCC interdigitates its plates.
why: Fact 1: ~2.5-3x Cs per pillar vs a single cylinder, so AR can fall from ~70 to ~30.
note: Duplicate of nested coax capacitor.

title: Self-rolling Swiss-roll nanomembrane capacitors printed flat
idea: IFR: a capacitor that folds itself into 3D. Closest achievable: print a strained bilayer carrying dielectric and electrode layers on a sacrificial film; releasing it makes the stack roll into a multi-turn tube, multiplying plate area 10-50x per footprint.
why: Fact 1: high Cs from planar printing, no high-AR etch and no EUV.
note: Same self-rolling nanomembrane capacitor.

title: Vacuum-gap NEMS relay as the leak-free access switch
idea: IFR: the off-switch is empty space. Replace each access transistor with a vertical nanoelectromechanical relay (TiN/Ru beam, ~5 nm sealed vacuum gap) pulled in electrostatically by the wordline; when off there is no conductor between storage node and bitline, and a 1 nm carbon contact coating fights stiction and wear.
why: Fact 3: off-leakage falls from fA to tunneling-limited <1e-21 A, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the ~46 fJ/bit refresh plus 10-20% bandwidth tax disappear; contact endurance toward 1e15 cycles is the gamble.

title: Langmuir-assembled silica-sphere monolayers replace array lithography masks
idea: Ideal: a mask that assembles itself on water. Closest: self-assemble a close-packed monolayer of 40-60 nm Stober silica spheres on a Langmuir trough, transfer it to wafer or panel, shrink the spheres by O2/ion trimming, and use it as a hexagonal hard mask for capacitor-node or vertical-channel arrays; only coarse periphery uses conventional litho.
why: 100x: hexagonal DRAM arrays match a sphere lattice, so a cent of TEOS-derived spheres replaces an EUV exposure; with cheap multi-tier stacks array patterning cost per GB drops >100x. Trades grain-boundary defects needing spare rows and defect-tolerant mapping.
note: Nanosphere lithography is old; grain-boundary and vacancy defect densities are orders above DRAM tolerances.

title: Redox-molecule monolayers store several-fold more charge in planar capacitors
idea: Ideal: a capacitor where every molecule holds electrons. Closest: self-assemble multi-state redox molecules (porphyrin/ferrocene tripods with phosphonate anchors, ZettaCore-style) on a TiN or doped-oxide electrode with an ionic-gel counter electrode; ~1e14 molecules/cm2 x 1-2 electrons gives ~16-32 uC/cm2 vs ~5-7 for a 1 V planar ZrO2 cap.
why: 100x enabler: lets cheap planar cells on panels/legacy fabs hold enough charge, collapsing the capacitor module (HAR etch, Zr/Hf ALD, several masks) into one dip-coat on the path to ~$0.1/GB. Trades molecule stability (needs >1e15 cycles) and redox speed.

title: Stacked resonant-tunneling-diode latch replaces the storage capacitor
idea: Ideal: a cell that holds its state forever with one transistor. Closest: grow two series resonant-tunneling diodes (Si/SiGe or InGaAs/AlAs) as blanket epitaxy over the access-transistor contact (a Goto pair); their N-shaped I-V gives two stable storage-node voltages held by valley current, patterned with the same contact mask.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor and no refresh (saves ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% bandwidth); one epi step replaces ~20 capacitor steps; needs peak-to-valley >10 at nA levels.

title: Wafer vendor ships memory substrates with buried back-gate planes
idea: Ideal: the memory maker buys a wafer that is already half a memory. Closest: a bonded Smart-Cut substrate with a buried n+ back-gate plane under thin BOX and a 10 nm Si film; the fab runs a plain planar logic flow and gets double-gate floating-body 1T cells whose negative back-gate holds stored holes, with no capacitor.
why: Facts 1, 4, 7: removes ~25-30% of DRAM front-end steps and shifts that work to cheap substrate-bonding lines; lets FD-SOI-style logic fabs make 1T memory.

title: Solid-ionic double-layer nanocapacitor replaces the high-k pillar
idea: Scarcity rule: no high-k dielectric allowed. Store the bit in an electric double layer: a 3-5 nm solid ionic conductor (LiPON or a proton-conducting oxide) between ion-blocking electrodes gives Helmholtz capacitance of ~10-20 uF/cm2, about 10x a ZrO2 stack, so a planar or <=5:1 cup reaches 5 fF. Sub-redox voltages keep it purely capacitive (no faradaic reaction), so each write only displaces ions by a few angstroms.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 10x areal capacitance turns a 70:1 pillar into a 5:1 cup, deleting the hardest etch and dielectric ALD steps; requires ion response under 10 ns at nm length scales.
note: Duplicate EDL capacitor.

title: No-conduction-path rule: NEMS relay as the cell access switch
idea: Self-imposed limit: the off state may contain no solid conduction path at all. Replace the access MOSFET with a vertical nano-electromechanical relay sitting on the capacitor: a 10 nm gap with a low-adhesion Ru- or Pt-coated contact that the wordline pulls in electrostatically. When open, the vacuum/air gap leaks less than an attoamp, so retention is set only by capacitor dielectric leakage.
why: Fact 3: removes the <=13 fA subthreshold, GIDL and junction tail entirely. Refresh goes from 64 ms to minutes or hours, and the 16-33% idle refresh power nearly vanishes. Risk: contact endurance (~1e15 cycles needed) and ns switching at nanoscale.

title: Zero refresh energy from the supply: Esaki tunnel-diode latch storage node
idea: Limit: holding data may cost no refresh cycles at all. Hang a pair of series Esaki tunnel diodes from each storage node to a standby rail. Their negative-differential-resistance load line gives two stable node voltages. Picoamp tunnel current continuously compensates leakage, so the cell latches like static memory in a DRAM footprint.
why: Fact 3: turns ~46 fJ/bit of refresh energy into a static picoamp hold current and frees the 10-20% of bandwidth refresh consumes. Risks: diode peak-to-valley ratio at nm scale and standby current density.

title: Monolayer MoS2 tiers at 15 nm pitch: 256 tiers per 4 um
idea: Under 400 C, wafer-scale MOCVD grows monolayer MoS2 (0.7 nm channel) for each tier. With an ALD gate stack, each tier is about 15 nm thick, and the atomic-thin body plus 1.8 eV gap gives aA-level leakage.
why: Facts 2 and 3: about 3x more tiers per stack height than Si tiers (about 45 nm), and refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms toward minutes.

title: Laser interference lithography exposes the periodic cell lattice maskless
idea: Constraint: no litho tool may cost over $5M. A DRAM array is a perfect lattice, so expose it with 193 nm immersion four-beam interference that writes 40 nm-pitch hexagonal hole or line lattices over the full field in one flash; a conventional dry-ArF mask exposure only trims the non-periodic array edges and periphery.
why: Fact 4 capital: interference tools ~$3-5M vs $200M+ for EUV, >150 wafers/hour, no reticles for array layers; litho cost per array layer -80%.
note: 40 nm pitch exceeds the ~70 nm 193i interference limit without pitch splitting.

title: 1T + 2 tunnel-diode latch: a refresh-free static cell at near-DRAM density
idea: The storage node of a 1T cell sits between two series NDR diodes (resonant tunnelling or interband Esaki) tied to the supply and ground rails. Their I-V curves cross at two stable points near the rails, so the node self-restores against leakage, with no refresh, no tRFC and a non-destructive read. Van der Wagt's III-V RTD/HFET gain cell proved the latch at ~50 nW/cell. The new part is BEOL-stackable, ultra-low-current-density NDR diodes stacked on the capacitor/storage contact in ~8F2. Candidates: oxide double-barrier (Al2O3/ZnO/Al2O3 quantum well) or MIIM diodes, Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes, or vdW graphene/hBN resonant tunnelling.
why: Refresh energy and refresh time -> 0 (7.6% availability at 16 Gb, ~20% at 64 Gb recovered). Static standby set by valley current: break-even with today's refresh power at J_valley ~0.23 A/cm2 (25 nm diodes).

title: Redox-molecule pseudocapacitor with natural multi-level plateaus (ZettaCore revival)
idea: ZettaCore's cell is a standard DRAM 1T cell whose capacitor is replaced by a porphyrin self-assembled monolayer between electrodes, an electrochemical cell. Charge is held in the molecules' discrete redox states, which appear at fixed potentials (e.g., +0.5 and +0.8 V), so voltage levels quantize naturally: multi-level storage without analog trimming. Retention of minutes was reported, vs tens of ms for DRAM. The twist: tether the SAM to a TiN pillar wall, fill the gap with an ALD-compatible solid ion conductor (or confined ionic liquid) for counter-charge, and read through an IGZO access device with 3-level sensing.
why: 2.4-4.9x signal charge per area -> pillar 1,300 -> 270-540 nm at equal charge per state; 1.6-2 bits/cell from discrete plateaus -> up to ~2x density at the same cell.

title: Gutenberg's fixed type: a single-pattern scanner that prints only arrays
idea: A printer would not buy a universal press to print one page forever. Build a stripped-down ArF or EUV exposure tool with a hard-mounted periodic array mask (no reticle handler or library, fixed dipole illumination, smaller fixed-field optics) that only steps the array pattern die to die, leaving periphery to flexible scanners.
why: Dropping reticle-stage dynamics, pupil flexibility and reticle logistics could cut tool price ~50-70% and raise array-layer throughput ~30%, and is easier for a second supplier to build. Risk: an EUV version still needs the EUV source.

title: Substitute spatial light modulators for photomasks on non-critical layers
idea: Expose periphery, implant and pad layers with maskless DUV lithography in which MEMS tilt-mirror or LCoS modulators write the pattern through a 248/193 nm projection lens, so synthetic-quartz mask blanks and mask-shop lead times disappear for those layers.
why: DRAM uses ~60-80 masks; dropping 30-40 physical masks saves scarce synthetic quartz, ~$10-30M of mask capital per product and weeks per design spin.
note: Throughput of SLM writers is the limiter; mask cost small share.

title: Substitute sealed nitrogen carriers for humidified ballroom cleanrooms
idea: Keep wafers in N2-purged sealed pods and tool mini-environments end-to-end so the building needs only ISO-8 air with no tight humidity control; steam humidifiers and most chilled-water coil load disappear.
why: Cleanroom make-up air is a major water (humidification and cooling-tower load) and energy user; a mini-environment-only fab cuts HVAC water >10x and HVAC energy ~50%.

title: Substitute continuous vacuum for air between front-end process steps
idea: Link deposition, etch, anneal and inspection into long vacuum-transfer cluster lines where a wafer stays under vacuum for ~30 consecutive steps, so native oxide never grows and airborne particles never land, deleting the pre-clean before most steps.
why: Pre-cleans are the most frequent wet steps; a vacuum-continuum front end removes most of them for >10x less UPW in those modules, and cleaner interfaces shrink the leakage tail.

title: Substitute bank capital with take-or-pay bit offtake contracts
idea: Swap debt/equity fab financing for LNG-style 10-year take-or-pay bit contracts: hyperscalers prepay 30% of a fab's capex against guaranteed Gb/month at a cost-plus formula, and the contracts are securitized as tradable capacity notes.
why: Attacks capital intensity and 3-5 yr risk; derisking lowers WACC by ~3-5 points, cutting depreciation-heavy wafer cost ~10-15%.
note: Hyperscaler prepays already happen; securitization is a modest WACC lever.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM fused with bonded defect-routing mesh
idea: Never dice: keep a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer, hybrid-bond a router-mesh wafer above it (Cerebras-style), and route around bad mats, so the wafer, package and module become one ~1 TB memory plane fed by edge optical links.
why: Removes dicing, packaging, TSVs and KGD test (fact 6); ~100% of good mats usable after sparing; cost per bit claimed -20-30% and ~1 pJ/bit on-wafer transport.
note: Anamartic wafer-scale memory and Cerebras precedent; needs DRAM wafers from a maker.

title: Reconstituted known-good array dies bonded wafer-to-wafer onto periphery
idea: Combine fan-out wafer reconstitution with wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding: tested good array dies are placed into a reconstituted 300 mm carrier at a US advanced-packaging center (e.g., SkyWater Florida), planarized, then bonded in one step to a periphery wafer.
why: 3D/HBM yield (fact 6): W2W throughput without compounding yield loss, since bad array dies never kill good periphery; ~15-25% more good stacks per wafer pair.

title: Tin-oxo dry resist converts itself into the etch hardmask
idea: Combine EUV photoresist and hardmask: vapor-deposited tin-oxo-cluster resist is exposed and dry-developed, then an in-situ O2/H2O plasma densifies the remaining pattern into SnO2 that serves directly as the etch hardmask, deleting fluorinated-PAG resist, spin-on carbon and SiON layers.
why: Drops PFAS-bearing photoacid generators and 2-3 film depositions per critical layer; dry develop cuts solvent waste ~5-10x; lower dose frees scarce EUV scanner time.

title: HBM base die merged into an active interposer bridge
idea: Combine the HBM logic base die and the silicon interposer: the interposer region under each stack carries the PHY, ECC and TSV landing logic, so core dies hybrid-bond straight onto it and the separate base die and its microbump layer disappear.
why: Saves ~100 mm2 of silicon per stack (~10-15% of package silicon) and one SnAg bump layer, and removes one assembly yield loss from the HBM TSV tax.
note: Custom HBM base die integration already pursued.

title: Subtractive molybdenum bitlines with self-aligned air-gap spacers
idea: Combine bitline patterning with spacer formation (zero added masks, existing bitline mask): blanket Mo is etched subtractively in Cl2/O2, then a non-conformal cap pinches off over the gaps, leaving k=1 air spacers.
why: Tungsten-free bitline from U.S.-mined Mo; ~30% lower bitline capacitance gives more sense signal or longer bitlines (fewer sense amps) and lower CV2 energy per access.

title: Helium gas-field membrane plant feeding a fab recapture loop
idea: Fuse a U.S. helium-rich natural-gas field (Kansas/Wyoming/Arizona) membrane separation unit with a fab that captures and re-liquefies backside-cooling and purge helium on site. The fab buys only makeup gas at a fixed price.
why: Helium supply lost about 30% when Qatar went offline. A 90% recapture loop plus domestic sourcing removes helium as a fab-stopper.
note: Domestic gas-field membrane supply plus fab recapture; plant scale beyond $1M demo.

title: Molybdenum roasting loop: tungsten-free, recoverable dual-work-function wordline
idea: Adapted from the molybdenum industry's purification route (roast to MoO3, which sublimes near 700 C and recondenses pure): make the buried wordline and contacts from Mo with a lower-work-function cap near the storage junction to cut GIDL, so the only refractory metal on the die is one that end-of-life roasting recovers cleanly.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) from the access device, lowers GIDL through the dual work function (fact 3), and gives scrap dies a simple metal-recovery route; Mo is mined in the U.S.
note: Mo wordlines and dual-WF gates already in industry roadmaps.

title: Pharmaceutical isolators: a ballroom-free DRAM fab
idea: Pharma replaced Grade-A cleanroom suites with sealed isolators; keep ISO-1 air only inside FOUPs, EFEMs and tool minienvironments, run the building at ISO-8, and give every tool maintenance access through pharma-style rapid-transfer ports (alpha/beta double doors) so the tool interior is never exposed to room air.
why: Fab capital, energy and build time: cleanroom shell plus HVAC is ~15-25% of fab construction cost; claim 10-15% capex and 20-30% facility-energy reduction and a faster build.
note: Minienvironments/FOUPs already do most of this; incremental.

title: Shipyard block construction: prefabricated fab modules built in parallel
idea: Shipyards build fully outfitted hull blocks in parallel halls and join them at the dock; build a DRAM fab as ~300 factory-made blocks (subfab utility skids, pre-piped tool pads, ceiling cassettes with fan filters, abatement modules) made off-site in a U.S. yard while foundations are poured, then craned in and bolted together.
why: Time-to-capacity and capital (fact 4): build time 3-5 years toward ~18-24 months, cutting capitalized interest; repeated block designs give a learning curve across multiple U.S. fabs.
note: Prefab skids already used; schedule gain incremental.

title: Wartime auto-plant conversion: idle U.S. 200 mm fabs make interposers
idea: Adapted from Willow Run's conversion from cars to bombers: shuttered or underused U.S. 200 mm/180 nm fabs are retooled to make passive silicon interposers, RDL and DRIE TSVs, all of which need only 0.5-2 um features.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: packaging capacity in months at ~10% of new-fab cost, easing the CoWoS-class bottleneck that gates HBM.
note: Mature-fab interposer production already pursued; retooling exceeds $1M.

title: Prefab-hospital modules: factory-built cleanroom bays from U.S. shipyards
idea: Adapted from prefab COVID hospitals and SMR module yards: build cleanroom bays, sub-fab utility racks and gas pads as transportable modules in U.S. shipyards and modular plants, then barge or truck them in and plug them together on a pre-poured slab.
why: Cuts fab construction from 3-5 years to ~18-24 months and construction cost ~20-30% with U.S. steel and labor; capacity can grow in ~5k-wafer steps (capital intensity, time).

title: Minify trap density: millisecond laser anneal of storage junction
idea: After the storage-node implant, apply a sub-millisecond laser/flash anneal that heals end-of-range implant defects without diffusing dopants, then high-pressure deuterium sintering to passivate remaining mid-gap traps that create trap-assisted tunneling and variable retention time.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA tail population ~10x; minimum retention up 2-4x.

title: Minify front-side clutter: move 4F2 bitlines to wafer backside
idea: In a vertical-channel 4F2 cell, form the bitlines on the backside after wafer thinning to about 300 nm, contacting the bottom of each vertical channel, as backside power delivery does. The front side is then free for a full-height capacitor, and the buried-bitline coupling and resistance problem goes away.
why: Makes 4F2 manufacturable: 33% less area than 6F2, lower BL-BL coupling (about 30% less sense noise), and a wider BL metal (about 3x lower resistance).

title: Fifteen ingots per crucible with continuous-feed Czochralski
idea: Magnify crucible life 10-15x: feed granular FBR polysilicon continuously during the pull and devitrify the crucible's inner wall with a barium coating, so one HPQ crucible yields 10-15 prime 300 mm DRAM ingots instead of 1-2.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz per wafer ~10x, along with puller downtime and argon per wafer; reuses solar-industry CCZ know-how for prime wafers.

title: Frozen-node DRAM: depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: Minify node changes to zero: design a DRAM generation that never shrinks and is upgraded only by stacking more dies per package, so tools run 15 years instead of a 5-year depreciation schedule.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; tripling tool life cuts wafer cost roughly 30-35%, while a node only buys 10-20%.

title: Nano-TSVs through 5 um thinned DRAM dies
idea: MINIFY die thickness to ~5 um with backside-power-style wafer thinning so TSVs shrink to 0.5 um diameter, the size of ordinary vias, and the keep-out zone shrinks about 100x.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV area overhead falls from ~5-10% to <0.5% and stress-related yield loss falls; claims ~15% more bits per stack wafer.

title: Hot-spare die plus empty bond site per stack
idea: MAGNIFY redundancy to the whole die: each HBM stack ships with one spare DRAM die and base-die bypass switches that logically replace a failing die in the field, plus an open top site for a later add-on die.
why: Field repair and HBM yield: a dead die no longer kills the stack; claims +10-15% shipped yield and longer life.

title: Minify cycle risk with exchange-traded DRAM bit futures
idea: List standardized DRAM futures (per Gb-month, DDR5 and HBM contracts, physically settled at bonded warehouses) so fabs hedge future output and buyers hedge spikes.
why: Price risk drives underinvestment and 4x swings; hedging lowers fabs' risk premium and enables counter-cyclical capex.

title: Eliminate air breaks: never-break-vacuum linear cluster for tiers
idea: Deposit all channel, dielectric and electrode films for 32+ tiers in one linear vacuum cluster with in-situ remote-plasma hydrogen cleaning between steps, so there is never a native oxide and never a wet pre-clean.
why: Water: pre-deposition wet cleans are a large share of a fab's UPW; doing a whole tier stack in vacuum replaces dozens of rinses with one, per stack.

title: Eliminate NF3 cleans: closed fluorine loop with on-site electrolytic F2
idea: Scrub HF from fab exhaust and wet benches, electrolyze it as KF-2HF on site to regenerate F2 for chamber cleaning, and retire purchased NF3 (GWP ~17,000).
why: Cuts dependence on fluorspar (China-dominated) and on concentrated NF3 makers, and removes a potent greenhouse emission.
note: On-site F2 generators already supplied to fabs.

title: Eliminate ion implantation: junctions set by in-situ doped epitaxy and work functions
idea: Form access-transistor and periphery source/drains by selective in-situ doped epitaxy and set thresholds with gate-metal work-function stacks and dipole layers, so the flow needs no implanter and no implant masks.
why: Removes ~8-12 non-critical masks plus implanters and activation anneals, shortening cycle time ~10% and lowering tool capex; also removes random dopant fluctuation from the leakage tail.

title: Eliminate two EUV contact layers: self-aligned selective-epi bitline contacts and pads
idea: Grow bitline contacts and storage landing pads by selective Si/SiGe epitaxy only on exposed active silicon between spacer-defined lines, so they self-align to active areas instead of being printed with EUV contact masks. Output is an ordinary DDR5/HBM core die.
why: Fact 4: removes the two most overlay-critical EUV layers of current flows; self-aligned contacts tolerate DUV-grade overlay.

title: Eliminate greenfield fabs: convert shuttered 300 mm shells to DUV DDR4/DDR5
idea: Re-equip idle or shuttered US 300 mm shells with refurbished DUV-era DRAM tools to make 1x-nm DDR4, DDR5 and LPDDR4 for industrial, auto and PC markets, freeing leading-edge capacity for HBM. Parts are standard JEDEC devices.
why: Capital and time: ~1/3 the capex and ~1/2 the time of a greenfield fab, with no new interface for customers to qualify.

title: Eliminate leading-edge wafers for legacy demand: restart mothballed DUV lines
idea: Eliminate serving DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 demand from leading-edge fabs: acquire mothballed or exiting 300mm lines and run 2x-nm DUV-only DRAM (zero EUV) for auto, industrial and networking, so leading fabs stop diverting wafers to legacy parts.
why: Legacy parts are rising fastest in price; a depreciated DUV line costs ~10-20% of greenfield per wafer start and avoids the single-supplier EUV chokepoint.

title: Eliminate equity-funded fabs: take-or-pay prepayments collateralize fab bonds
idea: Eliminate funding fabs from equity at the cycle top: hyperscalers sign 7-10-year take-or-pay bit contracts that, like LNG offtake agreements, collateralize project-finance bonds for a dedicated US fab SPV.
why: Lowers cost of capital ~3-5 points on a $15B fab where depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost.

title: Bottom-up Mo fill from Colorado moly replaces periphery tungsten
idea: Reverse fill direction and metal: periphery contacts, wordline straps and local interconnect are filled bottom-up by area-selective molybdenum CVD nucleating on the contact floor (no liner, no seams), with precursor refined from U.S.-mined molybdenum.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) removed; Mo's lower narrow-line resistance (~30-50%) speeds wordline drivers and drops liner steps.
note: Mo fill widely pursued by tool vendors; U.S. sourcing is the twist.

title: Wide-and-slow periphery lets U.S. 65 nm logic drive DRAM
idea: Reverse speed for width: the array die exposes 8x more data bonds at 1/8 the clock (e.g., 4096 bits at 800 MT/s) to a face-bonded base die from a U.S. 65-90 nm fab; serialization happens only on the host link.
why: Facts 5 and 7: high-speed periphery that forces advanced nodes disappears from the DRAM; I/O energy ~0.5 pJ/bit.
note: Wide I/O / HBM-base-die concept on a mature node.

title: Bitlines on the backside, wordlines on the front
idea: Rearrange the routing planes: after front-side transistor and capacitor formation, flip and thin the wafer and form bitlines on the backside contacting the bottom of each vertical channel, so bitlines and capacitors never compete for the same front-side layers.
why: Layout congestion and signal margin (facts 1,4): bitlines become wide low-R lines with air gaps (~30% less bitline capacitance = proportionally smaller Cs) and the front side can pack capacitors at 4F2.
note: Backside/buried bitlines with wafer bonding already used in VCT DRAM development.

title: Bring the fab to the helium: co-locate on U.S. gas fields
idea: Reverse siting logic: place the next U.S. DRAM fab beside helium-rich gas processing (Wyoming/Kansas) and firm nuclear/hydro power, with direct pipeline helium and on-site recapture.
why: Shields from the Qatar outage and makes helium a local input; improves U.S. manufacturability through cheap firm power and supply security.

title: Node-freeze fab with 15-year depreciation
idea: Reverse the roadmap: freeze one mature node and run it 15+ years, drawing cost-down from yield, cycle time and tool reuse instead of shrinks; tools are depreciated straight-line over 15 years, not 5.
why: Depreciation share of wafer cost falls from ~55% to ~20-25%, giving 30-40% cost-per-wafer cut, larger than a node shrink's 10-20% per-bit gain.

title: Cleanroom inside the carrier, no ballroom fab
idea: Reverse the cleanliness boundary: each wafer moves in a sealed, purged micro-pod that docks directly to tool load ports, so the building only needs ISO-8 air instead of a class-1 ballroom.
why: Fab building and HVAC is ~20-30% of fab capex and much of its energy; a sealed-pod fab cuts shell cost and lead time, and suits modular U.S. sites.

title: Grown, not implanted: epitaxial n-p-n wafer for vertical cells
idea: Reverse implant-after-pattern into dope-before-pattern: grow the source/channel/drain as an in-situ doped epitaxial stack, etch the pillars with ArF plus SADP, and wrap the wordline gate as a self-aligned spacer, so every critical length is a film thickness.
why: Gives a 4F2 vertical cell without EUV and removes several implant masks; channel length is set within 1 nm by epitaxy, which tightens the leakage tail.

title: Rows switch to twin-cell mode when HF-free cleans leave leaky cells
idea: Rearrange two single cells into one differential cell on demand: wafers cleaned without HF (ozone water, SC1/SC2, H2 bake) show more leaky-tail cells, so at boot the controller switches only rows containing tail cells into 2T2C mode, pairing them with a neighbor row storing the complement on BL/BLB.
why: Differential pairs tolerate ~10x more leakage; applied to only ~1-3% of rows, capacity loss stays small while enabling a fully HF-free front end.

title: Etch slow to leak less: chlorine atomic-layer channel recess
idea: Reverse the throughput priority: the recessed-channel access transistor trench is cut by self-limiting Cl2/Ar atomic-layer etching, one monolayer per cycle, instead of fast fluorine plasma, flattening channel depth variation to ~1 nm.
why: Tighter Vt and lower trench-corner field compress the leakage tail ~2x so refresh can relax; slower etch adds tool time but zero fluorine.

title: Ballroom-free fab: mini-environments end cleanroom humidification
idea: Rearrange cleanliness from the room to the wafer: wafers live only in nitrogen-purged FOUPs and sealed tool mini-environments, and the building around them runs as ordinary grey space. That removes most make-up air humidification and the cooling-tower load for HVAC.
why: Shrinking the controlled air volume ~10-50x cuts HVAC humidification and cooling water ~10x and lowers fab shell capex.

title: Harvest helium and neon from the fab's own nitrogen plant
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a mega-fab's on-site air-separation unit already processes ~100k Nm3/h of air for nitrogen. Add a non-condensable stripping column and a small cryo-adsorber that co-produce crude Ne (18 ppm in air) and He (5 ppm), then purify both on site, so rare-gas production merges into a plant the fab already runs.
why: Makes neon (litho lasers, a Ukraine-exposed supply) and part of the helium a domestic byproduct: a few thousand Nm3/yr of He and ~10k Nm3/yr of Ne per fab ASU, covering laser gas and leak checking.

title: Continuous-recharge Czochralski stretches one crucible across many ingots
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: grow 300 mm DRAM-grade crystal by continuous CZ. Granular polysilicon feeds through a weir-partitioned double crucible while a magnetic field (MCZ) holds oxygen and melt height constant, giving 5-10 ingots per crucible instead of 1-2.
why: Crucibles per wafer fall 3-5x, which eases the HPQ chokepoint. Flatter axial oxygen and dopant profiles add ~15% usable ingot length.

title: 1D-only design rules: every critical layer is lines and cuts
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: make the cell tight in one direction only - active, wordline and bitline are pure line/space gratings by self-aligned quadruple patterning on DUV, all 2D information comes from cut masks at 3-4x pitch, and storage nodes are segments formed where two SAQP gratings intersect.
why: 1D gratings print on DUV at 20-24 nm pitch with high yield; removes EUV holes and pads (~5 EUV exposures) at ~10% cell-area penalty (fact 4).

title: Ballroom-free fab: ISO-1 microenvironments inside an ISO-7 shell
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter changes moves cleanliness from the building to the wafer: sealed FOUPs, nitrogen-purged EFEMs and tool-integrated ISO-1 microenvironments carry all contamination control, while the building is a cheap ISO-7 warehouse with ordinary HVAC.
why: Cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction cost and set much of the 3-5 year build; could cut shell capex ~50% and time-to-first-wafer by ~1 year (capital).

title: Rounded trench and junction corners to clip GIDL tail
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality/curvature: a hydrogen anneal reflows silicon so buried-wordline trench bottoms and storage-node contact edges reach radii of 3 nm or more, lowering the peak junction field that drives trap-assisted tunnelling in the worst cells.
why: Fact 3: 20-30% lower peak field can cut tail leakage ~5-10x (exponential in field), stretching refresh ~4x.

title: Nesting: fab-in-fab DRAM lines inside idle logic, solar and LED shells
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: insert a compact 10-20k wspm DRAM module line into existing idle cleanroom bays (shuttered 300 mm logic, solar-cell, LED or MEMS fabs) reusing their utilities, gas yards and permits.
why: Capital and time: cuts greenfield cost ~30-40% and time-to-wafer by ~2 years; boosts U.S. manufacturability.

title: Segmentation: multi-project DRAM shuttle with one custom mask per startup
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation applied to the reticle: a DRAM foundry runs a frozen base flow and splits one reticle among many startups, each allowed exactly one custom mask layer to test new cell, capacitor or array ideas.
why: Innovation throughput: ~100x cheaper experiments for new DRAM entrants than private lots.

title: Asymmetry: one-mask asymmetric halo implant shrinks access-transistor leakage tail
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: one added implant mask places a halo only on the bitline side of the access transistor, keeping the storage-node junction graded and lowering GIDL, so far fewer dies fail the 13 fA retention tail.
why: Retention yield and refresh (fact 3): more passing dies per wafer and longer refresh intervals.

title: Termite-mound fab: sealed mini-environments plus passive stack-effect ventilation
idea: Termite mounds hold a steady climate with chimneys and earth thermal mass; build the fab as sealed tool mini-environments in an ISO 8 hall, pre-condition makeup air through buried earth tubes and exhaust it through solar-heated chimneys, eliminating most ballroom fan-filter units.
why: Cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-25% of fab construction and ~40% of facility power; est. 30% less shell capex and 40% less HVAC energy.

title: Zebrafish-heart regeneration: spare die and reroutable TSVs in HBM
idea: Zebrafish regrow damaged heart muscle; each HBM stack carries one spare core die and redundant TSV lanes, and field logic bypasses a failing die and reroutes broken TSVs, so the stack is repaired in place instead of the whole accelerator being scrapped.
why: HBM TSV yield tax (20-30%) and field failures: fewer scrapped stacks and GPUs per usable GB.
note: HBM already uses redundant TSVs; spare die adds cost.

title: Salmon-homing take-back: deposit-refund chip ID for DRAM modules
idea: Salmon return to the river they hatched in. Each module carries a cryptographic ID and a deposit built into its price, refunded when it comes back through the vendor's reverse-logistics network, which routes it to test, redeployment or die harvesting.
why: Raises module recovery from <20% to >80%, as bottle bills do, feeding second-life supply.

title: Drywall prefab: array wafers plus dry-bonded periphery chiplets
idea: Construction cut on-site water by moving from wet plaster to factory drywall. Keep only pitch-matched SAs on the array wafer and move the non-pitch-matched periphery (pumps, global decode, control, DLL, I/O) to 40 nm logic chiplets, bonded fluxless with formic-acid-vapor reflow and plasma activation, both dry steps.
why: Water: the array wafer skips the high-metal-count logic module, and the chiplets use few wet steps on ~1/3 the area, so water for that periphery falls ~10x; it also takes periphery off EUV.
note: Water saving applies only to the periphery share.

title: Vinyl record pressing: nanoimprint all periphery-only layers
idea: Like pressing vinyl from a master stamper, pattern periphery-only layers (implant blocks, periphery contacts, metals at >=40 nm half-pitch) by jet-and-flash nanoimprint: drop-dispensed UV resist, imprint, cure, and descum the residual layer by plasma. No wet develop, no BARC rinse, no EUV.
why: Water: each periphery litho module loses its develop/rinse (~10x less UPW per layer); litho capital per periphery layer is ~3-5x lower.

title: Strategic Petroleum Reserve model for helium, crucibles and WF6
idea: Copy the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the Defense Logistics Agency stockpile: a federally chartered Semiconductor Materials Reserve holds 6-12 months of helium (re-using the Cliffside storage formation), HPQ crucible blanks, WF6/tungsten powder and neon, releasing them at pre-set price triggers and selling to fabs at cost in a disruption.
why: Turns shocks like the March-2026 Qatar outage or Hurricane Helene's 2024 Spruce Pine shutdown into non-events for U.S. DRAM and caps input spikes that feed the 4x price rise.

title: Grid protective relays isolating shorted mats at runtime
idea: Power grids open relays to isolate faulted segments and keep the rest live. Each mat's VPP/VBLP feed gets a tiny current monitor and pass gate. A wordline-bitline or capacitor short drawing excess current trips isolation for that mat alone, and its addresses remap to a spare mat. Today such a short kills the bank or the die.
why: Shorts are a top yield killer on large dies, so this could add ~3-8% yield. It also makes the die resilient to hard shorts that appear in the field.

title: BASF Verbund shared-utility campus for multiple memory fabs
idea: Like chemical parks where one plant's byproduct is another's feedstock, co-locate 3-4 fabs from different firms with a shared air-separation unit, ultrapure-water plant, acid regeneration, wafer reclaim and on-site power, owned by a neutral utility company.
why: Utilities and subfab are ~25-30% of fab capex; sharing cuts that 15-25% and shortens each new fab's build by a year.
note: Science parks already share some utilities; neutral ownership is the twist.

title: Utility-style long-tenor bonds backed by 10-year auto contracts
idea: Like regulated utilities financing dams with 30-year bonds, a fab dedicated to 125 C-qualified memory signs 10-year take-or-pay contracts with automakers and securitizes them into investment-grade bonds at ~5% instead of ~15% equity.
why: Long-life parts create long-life contracts; a 10-point drop in cost of capital cuts wafer cost ~20% since depreciation and financing dominate.

title: Linux-LTS frozen DRAM process sold by subscription
idea: Like long-term-support kernel releases, a fab commits a 125 C-qualified DRAM process to a copy-exact freeze for 15 years, with industrial customers paying annual subscriptions that fund spare tools and parts, so products never need requalification.
why: Ends the forced EOL churn that wastes capacity on requalification and hoarding, and monetizes depreciated tools.

title: Manhattan Project parallel paths for a refresh-free access device
idea: Revive the Manhattan Project's parallel uranium-enrichment strategy: fund four competing access-device routes (SiC, vacuum nano-gap, NEM relay, zinc oxide) at four U.S. sites against one fixed spec (>=10 s retention at 85 C, <=30 ns access, >=1e16 cycles), with shared test vehicles and a hard down-select at 18 months.
why: De-risks the physics of fact 3 in parallel and shortens time to a solution, concentrating domestic capital on the access device, the biggest refresh lever.
note: Standard parallel-path funding; far beyond $1M.

title: Re-establish the Federal Helium Reserve with mandatory fab helium recapture
idea: Reverse the 2024 sale of the Amarillo Bush Dome reserve: restore a federal helium reserve with semiconductor priority, and revive the 1960 Helium Act's conservation intent by requiring fabs to recapture backside-cooling and leak-test helium with on-site purifiers and liquefiers.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar's ~30% offline since March 2026): recapture cuts fab helium purchases 70-90% and the reserve buffers outages.

title: Trench-capacitor eDRAM revived inside idle U.S. logic fabs
idea: Revive IBM/Siemens/Qimonda deep-trench DRAM, abandoned by commodity DRAM in 2009 but kept in IBM POWER eDRAM down to 14 nm: license the deep-trench module to U.S. logic fabs so they can sell multi-GB memory chiplets from idle 14-28 nm capacity. The trench is formed before transistors, so it fits logic flows without a dedicated DRAM line.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: no new fab dollars and only ~4 extra masks on depreciated 300 mm logic lines; trench Cs ~20-40 fF eases refresh; density is ~3-5x below 1-beta DRAM, so the gain is fast domestic supply at low marginal capex.

title: VLSI-Project-style consortium builds non-EUV DRAM patterning tools
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where rival DRAM makers co-funded lithography and tool R&D and then competed: form a U.S. DRAM tool consortium funded per wafer start that develops e-beam projection, imprint and X-ray tools aimed at DRAM's periodic arrays, with IP pooled among members.
why: Capital intensity and EUV single-supplier risk: shares ~$2-4B of tool R&D across members and targets the 5-7 EUV layers behind depreciation's ~55% share of wafer cost.
note: Similar to SEMATECH and the VLSI Project.

title: Core-sorting bins: grade dry-process DRAM into tiers, sell every die
idea: Core-memory makers tested every ferrite core and sorted them into hysteresis grades for different products. A DRAM maker running an all-dry, water-lean fab tests each die for retention and defect class and sells three grades with their own pricing and warranties: server ECC, AI-tensor (relaxed retention handled by the controller) and edge (reduced capacity, soft-formatted).
why: Water and cost per bit: the dry flow's wider defect spread becomes a product mix instead of a yield loss, which pays for converting a fab to ~10x less ultrapure water; ~95% of dies sold instead of ~85%.

title: Ever-Normal Granary for Bits: Strategic DRAM Wafer Buffer Stock
idea: Revive the 1930s ever-normal granary and the Cold War National Defense Stockpile for memory: a government corporation buys finished, tested DRAM wafers in die-bank form (stored under dry nitrogen) during gluts at floor prices and sells them into shortages, holding about three months of national demand.
why: Supply volatility: shaves 4x price spikes and keeps fabs at full utilization in busts, lowering cost per bit ~10-15% over the cycle.

title: Cleanroom-free fab: wafers ride sealed nitrogen tunnels between tools
idea: Inverts 'the whole fab must be an ISO-class cleanroom': wafers stay permanently inside sealed N2-purged carriers that dock to sealed tools through an overhead N2/vacuum tunnel network, so the building itself is ordinary ISO-8 air and HVAC moves ~10x less air.
why: Cleanroom HVAC and makeup air are ~30-50% of fab electricity and drive humidification water; lowers shell capital and build time, easing US siting.

title: Packaging inside the DRAM fab: wafers never leave the building
idea: Invert 'packaging is a separate offshore back end': run wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding of DRAM array wafers to base-logic wafers inside the U.S. DRAM fab (Idaho/New York) using its cleanroom, metrology and yield data.
why: Removes Asia OSAT round trips, cuts weeks of cycle time and unifies front/back-end yield learning; U.S. HBM-class memory becomes a single-site product.
note: Micron already plans US HBM packaging; needs fab-scale capital.

title: Backside-powered base die frees the whole front for signals
idea: Invert 'power and signals share the same face': build the HBM base die on a U.S. backside-power process (Intel 18A PowerVia, Arizona) so power enters from the back and every front-side bond carries data.
why: Signal bond density roughly doubles, ~2x I/O per base die, with cleaner power delivery for faster stacks.

title: One mask grows deliberately weak sentinel cells that call refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh runs on a timer': the single added mask partially blocks the mold etch for a few sentinel cells per subarray so their capacitors are shorter and fail first; a sentinel flip, found by a cheap probe read, triggers refresh of only that subarray.
why: Refresh follows actual local temperature and leakage instead of worst-case 32/64 ms timers; ~50-75% refresh cut (fact 3).

title: Thin-film thermometer per mat drives local refresh rates
idea: Inverts 'one temperature sensor per die': the single added mask patterns a TaN thin-film resistor meandering over each mat, read by the periphery to scale each mat's refresh to its own temperature, since mats under hot compute dies differ by 10-20 C.
why: Most mats refresh at their cooler local rate; 30-50% refresh cut in HBM and 3D stacks with thermal gradients (facts 3, 6).

title: Pure-play DRAM foundry for fabless memory designers
idea: Inverts 'whoever designs DRAM must own the fab': a foundry offers a frozen DRAM cell/capacitor platform with an open periphery design kit so fabless firms tape out custom interfaces, logic-in-periphery and niche densities.
why: Supply diversity and utilization: lets startups enter without $15B, keeps the foundry full across cycles, and creates specialty parts that relieve commodity demand.

title: Undoped channel with workfunction-set Vt shrinks the random-dopant tail
idea: A 12 nm access channel holds only ~50-100 dopant atoms, so Poisson fluctuation (sigma ~ sqrt(N)) gives sigma-Vt ~30-50 mV and a fat low-Vt tail. Remove channel doping and set Vt with a dipole-tuned workfunction metal (TiN with La or Al dipoles) in the buried wordline, as logic did with FinFETs. Sigma-Vt drops to ~10-15 mV, limited by metal grain granularity.
why: The refresh interval is set by the ~6-sigma cell. A 3x smaller sigma moves that cell ~150 mV closer to the median Vt, for ~100x less tail leakage and a 2-4x longer refresh interval using only logic's toolkit (fact 3).

title: Pre-permitted fab-ready federal sites cut construction interest by a third
idea: Time is capital: on a $15B fab every year of construction costs ~$1B in interest and lost output. Pre-certify federal sites with completed environmental review, water recycling, 500 MW interconnects and gas lines so a fab can break ground in weeks and run in ~24 months.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-supply: shaves 1-2 years off the 3-5 year lead time and ~30% of interest during construction.

title: Ice-sculpture cryogenic etch leaves no residue to wash
idea: Random stimulus 'ice sculpture': carved cold, and the shavings sublime away. Etch buried-wordline trenches and vertical channels at about -100 C in SF6/O2 or HF-based plasma, where sidewall passivation is a condensed SiOxFy film that sublimes as the wafer warms, so the post-etch polymer wet strip and its rinses disappear.
why: Removes the wet residue-removal loop after each access-module etch (>10x less water there) and gives smoother, less damaged sidewalls with fewer interface traps (fact 3).
note: Cryo etch already in production for 3D NAND channel holes.

title: Bamboo nodes: two-deck capacitor stitched at a conductive landing node
idea: Bamboo grows tall in segments joined at nodes: etch the capacitor hole as two ~45:1 decks with a TiN landing 'node' and SiN support ring between them, as 3D NAND does for two-deck channel holes, then form the electrode and dielectric continuously through both decks. The effective aspect ratio reaches ~90-110:1 without one extreme etch.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1, needs AR ~115): ~1.6-2x capacitor area, so Cs 8-10 fF or today's Cs at a smaller F.
note: Two-step mold etch with supports is close to current practice.

title: Iceberg: bitlines built from the wafer backside under 4F2 cells
idea: Most of an iceberg is underwater: build a 4F2 vertical-channel array with capacitors on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to the channel bottoms, and form low-resistance Cu or Ru bitlines on the backside, the way logic now does backside power. No buried bitline has to survive the full front-end thermal budget.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): makes 4F2 practical, a cell 33% smaller than 6F2, without buried-bitline resistance or thermal limits; claim ~30% more bits per wafer at the same F.

title: Double helix: vertical bitline pairs twist between tiers, cancelling noise
idea: Like DNA strands swapping sides, true and complement vertical bitlines in a 3D array swap positions every 8 tiers through crossover vias, so coupling from neighbor bitlines and wordline steps lands equally on both and cancels in the sense amp. Vertical bitlines can then pack at minimum spacing without shields, inside a standard DDR5/HBM die.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2) and capacitor wall (fact 1): bitline coupling noise ~5x lower, allowing smaller sense signals (lower Cs) and ~20% tighter vertical bitline pitch.
note: Twisted bitlines are standard in 2D DRAM; 3D crossover vias add cost.

title: Toll booth: HBM base-die-as-a-service, disaggregated stack supply chain
idea: The 'toll booth' is the gate at the road's entry, and the HBM base logic die is the gate to the stack. Standardize the base die-to-core die interface so a logic foundry makes base dies and any vendor's core DRAM dies can be stacked on them at a U.S. OSAT. The base die becomes a separately sourced, competitively bid part.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supplier concentration; opens HBM assembly to new entrants and moves the logic-heavy periphery onto cheaper logic wafers.

title: Pit crew: hot-swap process chamber modules refurbished off-site
idea: Random stimulus 'F1 pit crew' -> swap the tire, fix it later. Etch and deposition chambers become kinematic-mount cartridges; at preventive maintenance a pre-seasoned spare cartridge is swapped in in about an hour while the used one is cleaned at a regional depot.
why: PM downtime falls from ~8-24 h to ~1 h, tool availability rises ~5-8%, and existing fabs ship ~5% more wafers with no new building.
note: Quick-swap process kits exist; full chamber cartridges need OEM redesign.

title: Sourdough starter: transplant retired ArF DRAM toolsets into US legacy fab
idea: Random stimulus 'sourdough starter' -> a proven culture moved to a new kitchen. Buy whole ArF-immersion DRAM toolsets that Korean and Taiwanese fabs retire as they move to EUV, license the matching 1y/1z process, and re-erect them in the US for DDR4/LPDDR4 for auto, industrial and defense.
why: ~25% of greenfield capex, no EUV, 18-24 month ramp; frees leading-edge capacity for HBM and adds US manufacturing share.
note: Process licensing from incumbents is the blocker.

title: Wordline topography shadows tilted halo implant, zero added masks
idea: Box: standard cap x asymmetric access transistor x SA x in-array x Si x high-tilt implant in which the existing wordline/hardmask stack shadows the storage side. Only the bitline side receives the halo dose, so the storage junction stays lightly doped and low-field while short-channel control is kept.
why: Lower storage-junction field cuts TAT/GIDL tail 3-5x (fact 3) without the usual dedicated asymmetric-implant mask.

title: Two-deck capacitor molds joined like 3D NAND channel decks
idea: [Box: MIM | VCT | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | two sequential 50:1 mold decks + self-aligned conductive inter-deck plug] Etch the capacitor mold as two stacked 50:1 decks joined by a self-aligned plug, building electrodes in each, for ~100:1 effective height from ArF-resolvable holes and production-proven etches.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): ~100-115 effective AR without new etch physics or EUV.
note: 3D NAND multi-deck approach applied to capacitors; inter-deck overlay at ~40 nm pitch.

title: JEDEC relaxed-retention DRAM grade with mandatory host chipkill
idea: Box [policy layer over medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: DIMM | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Standardize a DRAM grade with 16 ms base retention, readable per-bank retention-class registers and mandatory host chipkill, so fabs can ship dies that fail the 64 ms spec as standard parts.
why: Supply and yield: +5-10% usable output per wafer and a faster yield ramp for new U.S. fabs.

title: Closed-loop helium recapture plus regional helium bank
idea: Box[Resource=He x Transform=on-tool membrane recapture of backside-cooling and leak-check He x Owner=fab cooperative x Finance=shared reserve storage]: retrofit etch and implant tools with point-of-use He capture and purification (target ~90% recovery) and pool fab He into a regional cryogenic reserve that buffers outages like Qatar's.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: ~10x lower net helium draw and outage insurance keep DRAM lines running during He shocks.

title: Domestic molybdenum wordlines replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Box[Material=Mo buried wordline and contacts x Source=U.S. Mo mines (by-product of Cu/Mo mining) x Fab=ALD Mo fill x Owner=mine-to-precursor offtake x Finance=DPA Title III]: qualify Mo (lower resistivity at narrow widths, no TiN liner) for buried wordlines and plugs, with a U.S. precursor supply chain under long-term offtake.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint and lowers wordline RC; U.S. manufacturability of a critical material.
note: Mo metallization already being adopted by industry; supply-chain angle is the twist.

title: 45X-style per-gigabyte domestic DRAM production tax credit
idea: Box[Policy=production tax credit per GB of domestically fabricated DRAM x Finance=transferable credits x Owner=any producer]: pay a declining $/GB credit for U.S.-made DRAM bits, so support follows output instead of one-time capex grants.
why: U.S. manufacturability: closes an estimated 20-40% U.S. cost gap per bit and rewards yield and density.

title: Dual DDR4/DDR5 PHY server CPUs to keep DDR4 in service
idea: Box[Source=installed DDR4 fleet x Integration=CPU memory controller supporting both standards on separate boards x Owner=CPU vendor + hyperscaler]: ship next-gen server CPUs with a combo PHY (as consumer chips did) so retired-platform DDR4 RDIMMs move into new servers unchanged.
why: Extends ~100% of DDR4 fleet life by a server generation; cuts new-DIMM demand without changing either interface.

title: Substrate removal by back-side thinning eliminates junction leakage paths
idea: Po: the chip has no floor. After front-end processing, bond the DRAM wafer face-down to a carrier and remove the bulk silicon so access transistors sit in a fully depleted thin body on oxide, deleting the storage-node-to-substrate junction and the substrate holes that feed leakage.
why: Fact 3: junction and substrate-driven tail mechanisms disappear (3-10x tail reduction); the exposed back side also hosts a bias/power plane, freeing periphery area (fact 7).

title: Po cleanroom the size of a wafer: sealed nitrogen tool tunnels
idea: Po: 'the cleanroom is no bigger than the wafer.' Extracted: drop ballroom ISO-class cleanrooms and connect tools with sealed, nitrogen-purged carrier tunnels and tool-mounted mini-environments, so only ~2% of the building volume is ultraclean and the rest uses ordinary industrial HVAC.
why: Energy and capital: cleanroom air handling is roughly 30-40% of fab electricity and the shell is a large share of the $15B+ capex; cutting ultraclean volume ~50x could halve facility energy and shrink building cost.

title: Po the chip is the whole wafer: 200 mm wafer-scale memory slab
idea: Po: 'one chip per wafer.' Extracted: on a fully depreciated 200 mm, 180 nm fab, pattern one wafer-scale DRAM with 4-8% redundant mats and 1990s laser-fuse rerouting, stitch a global bus with the stepper, and mount the slab with edge connectors; no dicing, bumping or packaging.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) goes to ~0; ~6 GB per slab (8F2 cell ~0.26 um2, ~50% array efficiency) of cheap, domestic capacity-tier memory with packaging and test cost per bit far lower.

title: Cleanroom-free fab: sealed wafer mini-environments in plain warehouse
idea: Po: the fab has no cleanroom. Keep every wafer in nitrogen-purged sealed pods and tool-integrated ISO-1 mini-environments docking through gasketed ports, so the building is an ordinary ISO-8 warehouse into which modular tool pods are trucked and plugged.
why: Fab capital and time (fact 4): cleanroom shell, makeup air and subfab are ~25-35% of construction cost and 1-2 years of schedule; ~20-30% lower fab $ and faster time to output.
note: Mini-environments already standard; incremental capex cut.

title: Bit-forward securities pre-sell future DRAM to finance fabs
idea: Po: the fab is paid for with memory not yet made. Issue tradable forward contracts on standardized gigabit deliveries 3-5 years out, bought by hyperscalers, OEMs and funds, financing ~50% of capex before groundbreaking and settling physically or against a price index.
why: Capital intensity and cyclicality: moves capex risk to buyers who need supply, lowers cost of capital ~3-5 points and breaks boom-bust underinvestment.

title: Capacity-elastic twin-cell mode for deep sleep
idea: Po: memory that doubles itself to fall asleep. When a device idles, the controller compacts live data into half the rows and rewrites each bit into two cells on complementary bitlines; twin-cell differential sensing doubles signal, so self-refresh stretches from 64 ms to ~1 s.
why: Idle power (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle): self-refresh power down ~10x during idle periods, at a temporary 2x capacity cost.
note: CLR-DRAM/twin-cell known; idle-only benefit.

title: Tool bank of displaced immersion scanners leased to new entrants
idea: Po: the scanner nobody wants is the treasure. A fund buys ArF immersion scanners and multi-patterning track/etch sets displaced as logic fabs migrate to EUV, refurbishes them to spec, and leases them to new DRAM entrants with guaranteed service contracts.
why: Used immersion tools cost a fraction of new and skip allocation queues, turning a 2-3-year tool lead time into months; attacks capital and time.

title: Revive deep-trench eDRAM as standalone memory chiplets
idea: Po: the logic foundry already makes DRAM. Deep-trench capacitor eDRAM, proven on 32-14 nm SOI logic lines without EUV, is turned into standalone 4-8 Gb capacity chiplets with simplified periphery, built on existing U.S. logic lines and sold via CXL or UCIe.
why: Taps idle mature U.S. logic capacity for DRAM-class memory; ~10+ fF trench caps extend retention; attacks U.S. manufacturability and supplier diversity at some density penalty.

title: Asymmetric gate oxide: thick on storage side, thin on bitline side
