why: Cuts prime silicon, crucible quartz and polysilicon energy per DRAM wafer by ~10x; handles come from abundant solar supply chains already scaled to hundreds of GW.
note: ELTRAN-style transfer known; materials saved are a small share of wafer cost, so step change is modest.

title: Substitute supercritical CO2 for ultrapure-water wet cleans
idea: Run post-etch residue and particle cleans in single-wafer supercritical CO2 chambers (100-200 bar, 40-60 C) with 1-5% amine/alcohol chelant co-solvent, recompressing and recycling >95% of the CO2 on-tool; no DI rinse and no spin dry.
why: Wet cleans plus rinses are ~40-50% of fab UPW; this module drops its water >20x and removes capillary collapse of high-AR capacitor and wordline features.
note: sCO2 cleaning researched since 2000s; particle removal and throughput limited adoption.

title: Substitute gas-cluster ion beams for slurry chemical-mechanical polishing
idea: Planarize with location-specific gas-cluster ion beams (Ar/NF3 clusters of ~1000 atoms) steered by an in-line thickness map, combined with spin-on planarizing film plus selective plasma etch-back, replacing CMP slurries and post-CMP brush and megasonic cleans.
why: CMP plus post-CMP cleaning is ~15-30% of fab UPW; dry planarization cuts that >10x and removes ceria/silica slurry waste.
note: GCIB is too slow for global planarization; useful only for trim.

title: Substitute vapor-phase chelation for SC2 metal-contamination cleans
idea: Remove Fe, Cu and Ni contamination by exposing wafers to formic acid or acetylacetone vapor at 150-250 C, forming volatile metal formate or acac complexes that are pumped away, replacing HCl/H2O2/H2O SC2 baths and rinses.
why: Metal cleans are a major recurring wet step; dry chelation drops their water >20x and removes hydrogen peroxide and HCl supply from the step.
note: Vapor-phase hfac/formic metal removal studied since 1990s; incomplete removal of some metals.

title: Substitute distillable organic solvent for water in final rinses
idea: Use a low-boiling non-PFAS solvent such as electronic-grade isopropanol or PGME as the rinse fluid in closed single-wafer tools, with on-tool vacuum distillation recovering >99% per cycle and a metal-scavenger resin bed.
why: Replacing water as the rinse carrier with a recirculated solvent cuts UPW in those steps >10x, and lower surface tension reduces drying collapse of tall structures.
note: Solvent rinses do not remove ionic residues like water; IPA drying already common.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: room-temperature interlocking die bonds
idea: Substitute solder microbumps and thermocompression with electroplated copper nanowire forests grown through porous-alumina templates on both mating pads; pressed together at room temperature they interlock and cold-weld at 5 um pitch.
why: Fact 6 and Fact 3: no thermal budget hit to DRAM retention, a simple press replaces a ~$2M TCB tool, bond yield improves.
note: Cu nanowire interlocking bonds published; yield at 5 um pitch unproven.

title: Substitute refresh timer with same-process canary cells that flip first
idea: Swap the fixed 64 ms refresh clock for a few deliberately undersized 'canary' capacitors per subarray, built in the same litho/etch steps so they track the local leakage tail and temperature; when a canary flips (checked by a cheap read every few ms), only that subarray is refreshed.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3): most subarrays hold data 4-10x longer than the worst-case guard band, so canary gating cuts refresh energy/bandwidth loss 60-80% and lets tail-limited dies pass bin.

title: Substitute SRAM hammer counters with analog activation-integrating witness cells
idea: Replace per-row digital activation counters with one tiny floating-node 'witness' cell per row pair that gets a fixed charge packet pumped onto it each time a neighbor wordline fires (capacitive coupling pump); crossing a threshold flags a victim refresh, and normal refresh resets it.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): removes the SRAM/CAM counter area and power from periphery (fact 7) while tracking every row exactly, not just sampled ones.
note: Same leaky integrator.

title: Substitute EUV with nanoimprint for honeycomb capacitor array layers
idea: Swap EUV exposure on the perfectly periodic storage-node and landing-pad layers for nanoimprint lithography with e-beam-written masters, funded as a second-source litho program so array layers no longer depend on one EUV supplier.
why: Removes 2-3 of 5-7 EUV layers; NIL tools are ~1/3-1/5 the price of EUV with ~90% less power, cutting litho capex per wafer start by ~25%.

title: Four-level DRAM cell using flash-style program-and-verify
idea: Combine NAND flash's incremental-step program-and-verify loop with DRAM charge storage: the write driver applies short pulses and senses the node between pulses until it lands in one of four charge windows, storing 2 bits per cell. A gain read device and a reference ladder resolve the levels, and refresh re-centers each level.
why: Density and cost per bit (fact 4): 2x bits/cell without a node shrink, worth several nodes of 10-20% scaling; write latency roughly doubles.
note: Multi-level DRAM proposed since 1989; margin shrinks with leakage.

title: NEMS parametron storing bits as oscillation phase
idea: Revive Goto's 1950s parametron with GHz nanomechanical resonators: each cell is an AlN or SiN nanobeam pumped at twice its resonance, so it oscillates in one of two phases (0 or pi) that encode the bit. A shared pump line drives thousands of resonators, and phase is read by capacitive pickoff against a reference without destroying it.
why: Facts 3, 8, 9: no charge leakage tail, non-destructive read, no row hammer; high-Q (>1e4) resonators keep shared pump power low; density is the risk.

title: Flash charge-trap layer for per-cell access-transistor Vt trimming
idea: Add a thin nitride charge-trap film to the access-transistor gate stack (SONOS fused with DRAM). At wafer test, retention-profile every cell, then Fowler-Nordheim program electrons into only the leakiest access devices to raise their Vt by 0.2-0.4 V permanently.
why: Refresh rate is set by the top 0.01-0.1% leakage tail. Trimming those cells lets the whole array refresh at median retention, 64 ms to ~1 s, cutting refresh energy ~90%.

title: Adiabatic resonant charging for refresh wordlines and bitline restore
idea: Fuse adiabatic logic with refresh bursts. A stepwise or LC-resonant supply ramps the 3 V wordlines and restore drivers, and charge from the row being closed is recycled into the next row opened.
why: Recovers 50-70% of refresh CV^2 energy, roughly 46 to 20 fJ/bit (facts 3 and 10).
note: Charge recycling in DRAM arrays studied; refresh share limits system gain.

title: Vertical NPN gain cell with storage on the floating base
idea: A BiCMOS cell puts the storage node on the floating base of a vertical bipolar transistor under the MOS access gate. A read pulses the emitter so collector current amplifies the stored charge by beta, roughly non-destructively.
why: A gain of 50-100 lets sub-fF residual charge be sensed, tolerating ~10x more decay before refresh, and it removes most restore energy.

title: Tunnel-diode latch pair inside a one-transistor cell
idea: Two series resonant or Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes on the storage node (a Goto pair, after TI's late-1990s TSRAM) create two stable voltages held by picoamp current. Access uses a standard DRAM transistor.
why: Refresh-free at near-1T1C area, since the diodes stack vertically, costing ~1 mW per Gb of holding power.
note: TSRAM prior art; ~1 mW/Gb holding power rivals self-refresh.

title: Sense amp with nonvolatile ferroelectric offset trim
idea: Integrate a tiny HZO ferroelectric capacitor in each sense amp and program its polarization at wafer test so it couples a compensating charge onto the weak side of the latch, permanently trimming offset from ~15 mV to ~3 mV with no runtime calibration.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): lower offset allows ~40% smaller SA devices, or ~2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes), or smaller Cs.

title: Oxide-TFT predecoders and test logic built over the array
idea: Move slow, low-drive periphery (row predecoders, fuse latches, test-mode logic, mode registers) into BEOL IGZO thin-film transistor layers built over the cell array, leaving only the sense amps and fast IO in silicon.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): moving ~15-20% of die area into the space over the array gives ~1.2x bits per wafer without wafer bonding.

title: Cymer-laser interference lithography plus Multibeam e-beam cuts for arrays
idea: Combine maskless two-beam 193 nm interference lithography (ArF lasers built in San Diego) for the perfectly periodic wordline, bitline and pillar gratings with US multi-column e-beam direct-write (Multibeam, Santa Clara) for the sparse cuts, contacts and periphery, plus one spacer doubling to reach ~20 nm half-pitch.
why: Fact 4: removes 5-7 EUV layers and the photomask set; interference tool estimated <$10M; e-beam writes only the ~5% irregular features, so throughput stays workable for an all-US flow.
note: Gratings plus e-beam cuts is known CEBL; dense DRAM contacts overwhelm e-beam throughput.

title: Laser-polymer spalling slices ingots into wafers without kerf
idea: Combine subsurface IR laser modification with polymer stress spalling: a focused 1.3-2 um laser writes a damage plane 775 um deep, and a chilled polymer film bonded on top cracks the wafer off along it, replacing multi-wire sawing that turns ~40% of the ingot into kerf.
why: ~40-60% more wafers per ingot, so proportionally fewer quartz crucibles, less polysilicon energy and no saw slurry water.

title: Two-pass Czochralski purifies upgraded metallurgical silicon, then grows prime
idea: Combine purification and crystal growth (zero masks): a fast sacrificial pull from low-B/P upgraded metallurgical silicon dumps metals into the melt tail by segregation (k ~1e-5 to 1e-8 for Fe, Cu, Ni); the clean section is crushed and repulled as a slow prime ingot.
why: Skips most of the Siemens process (~50-100 kWh/kg, chlorosilane chemistry), roughly halving polysilicon energy; B/P must be removed upstream by slag refining.

title: Nanoimprint guide plus block-copolymer multiplication for EUV-free capacitor holes
idea: Combine J-FIL-style nanoimprint, which prints a 4x-relaxed hexagonal guide pattern, with high-chi block-copolymer self-assembly that subdivides each guide cell into a 12 nm-scale honeycomb. The densest DRAM layer, the capacitor holes, then needs no EUV and no SAQP.
why: Takes the capacitor-hole layer off EUV: an NIL tool costs ~$30-40M against ~$200M for EUV, roughly halving litho cost for that layer and easing the single-supplier chokepoint (fact 4).
note: Both NIL and DSA widely pursued for DRAM holes.

title: Area-selective ALD merges wordline-module patterning and deposition
idea: Combine area-selective ALD (inhibitor monolayers that block growth on SiN/SiO2) with the buried-wordline module. The gate dielectric grows only on exposed trench silicon and the Mo/TiN wordline grows only on that dielectric, so recess, cap and isolation self-align without block masks.
why: Cuts ~2 masks and ~15 dep/etch/clean steps in the wordline module, ~4% fewer tool-hours per wafer (fact 4).
note: ASD widely pursued; selectivity defects remain.

title: NOR flash analog arrays compute FFN layers in place
idea: Combine 40 nm embedded NOR flash cells with analog matrix-vector multiplication: transformer feed-forward weights (~2/3 of parameters) are programmed as cell conductances and compute in place, while attention and KV stay digital in a small DRAM.
why: FFN weights never occupy DRAM; 40-55 nm NOR is DUV-only and domestically fabbable, though accuracy is limited by analog noise and drift.

title: CXL switch holds a rack-wide page dedup table
idea: Combine the CXL switch's address-routing tables (mature-node switch silicon) with a global content-hash index: identical pages across every host in a rack (OS images, runtimes, model weights) are stored once in pooled memory and mapped read-only into each host, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Cross-host duplication in a rack far exceeds per-host duplication, so 20-40% of pooled capacity could be saved.

title: Magnetically aligned nanowire underfill replacing microbumps
idea: Combine anisotropic conductive film with magnetic-field assembly: Ni-cored, Au-shelled nanowires dispersed in a curable underfill chain into vertical columns between pads under a field applied during bonding, then cure, giving 2-5 um pitch z-axis interconnect with no microbump plating or Cu CMP.
why: HBM stacking cost and warpage tolerance: claims 30-50% lower stacking cost and reworkable joints.
note: Magnetically aligned ACF published; 2-5 um pitch bridging risk.

title: Final CMP step doubles as bond activation, no plasma
idea: Combine CMP with surface activation: a tailored final-polish slurry (colloidal silica plus OH/amine terminating chemistry) leaves the SiCN or oxide bond face densely silanol-terminated and particle-free, and dies bond in-line within minutes, skipping the argon/N2 plasma activation chamber.
why: Hybrid-bond cost and rare-gas independence: removes a tool and queue-time limit, ~15-25% lower hybrid-bond module cost, enabling argon-free die-to-wafer HBM stacking.

title: Sacrificial-polymer air gaps between wordlines cut hammer coupling
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap interconnect with DRAM wordlines: fill wordline gaps with a thermally decomposable polymer (polynorbornene or polycarbonate), cap with PECVD oxide and bake so the polymer diffuses out, leaving air gaps that cut line-to-line capacitance ~50%. Buildable in a university nanofab: spin-coat, PECVD and bake.
why: Row hammer and wordline energy (facts 9, 10): reduces capacitive disturbance coupled into neighbor rows and CV^2 wordline energy.

title: Block copolymer DSA plus infiltration synthesis for honeycomb capacitors
idea: Combine PS-b-PMMA cylinder-forming block copolymer (hexagonal, matching DRAM's honeycomb capacitor layout) with sequential infiltration synthesis of Al2O3 into PMMA to make a hard mask, followed by BCl3/Cl2 transfer etch. There is no fluorine at any step.
why: Self-assembles the densest DRAM array layer without EUV or fluorocarbon etch, cutting a 5-7 EUV-layer bill.

title: Inductive-coupling stacked DRAM eliminating SF6 Bosch TSV etch
idea: Fuse thinned-die stacking with ThruChip-style inductive or capacitive near-field links between layers, plus wire-bonded or edge-plated power delivery. That removes the SF6/C4F8 Bosch TSV etch and the TSV keep-out area.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (about 3× area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) and fluorinated deep-Si etch, raising HBM-class bits per wafer.

title: Thermos-style sealed vacuum isolation around each storage node
idea: Borrow vacuum-flask insulation: replace STI oxide next to each storage node with sealed vacuum cavities (sacrificial carbon ashed out, then capped by non-conformal deposition), so no oxide traps or bulk paths remain between adjacent nodes.
why: Facts 3 and 9: removes trap-assisted leakage and the electron-migration path behind row hammer; aims at ~10x higher hammer threshold and lower node-to-node coupling.
note: Air gaps already used in DRAM spacers; tail leakage is mostly junction/GIDL, not via STI.

title: LIDAR time-to-digital converter turns bitline voltage into delay
idea: Borrowed from automotive LIDAR TDCs: the bitline voltage starves a short inverter chain so a 20 mV difference becomes ~30 ps of delay, and a digitally calibrated arbiter flip-flop decides the bit from arrival order. No large matched cross-coupled latch is needed.
why: Periphery area and voltage floor (facts 7, 10): sense-amp area down ~2x and sensing at 0.6 V, since time-domain resolution does not shrink with supply.

title: Laser-trimmed op-amp offset trim for minimum-size sense amps
idea: Borrowed from precision analog trimming: sense-amp transistors are drawn at minimum size (accepting large mismatch), and each SA gets a 3-bit trim capacitor array whose code is measured by power-up BIST and held in a small nonvolatile register per 8 SAs. Matching comes from digital trim instead of area.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~2.5-3x; stripes are ~10-15% of the die, so ~6-8% die per bit is saved.

title: Differential-GPS reference cells broadcast decay corrections
idea: Borrowed from differential GPS base stations: a few reference cells per mat, written at known levels, are sensed alongside each row to measure how much charge has leaked since refresh at the current temperature, and that correction trims the mat's shared sense reference.
why: Refresh (fact 3): sense amps correctly read half-decayed cells, stretching the refresh interval ~2x with negligible area.
note: Reference cells track average decay, but refresh is set by tail cells.

title: AMOLED threshold-compensation sense amp on glass
idea: Borrowed from AMOLED 7T1C pixel compensation: in each IGZO or LTPS sense amp on a glass panel, the input transistors are first diode-connected so their own threshold is stored on a gate capacitor, then the bitline signal is applied on top, cancelling +/-300 mV thin-film threshold scatter.
why: Makes thin-film periphery on glass usable at ~30-50 mV margins, unlocking memory on Gen 8.5 panels (~60x a 300 mm wafer's area per substrate) with no EUV and no silicon.

title: Downhole-oil-tool SiC electronics make refresh-free hot memory
idea: Borrowed from SiC electronics in oil-well logging tools and EV inverters: cells and CMOS periphery are built on 4H-SiC wafers (bandgap 3.26 eV), whose intrinsic carrier density is ~1e16x lower than silicon's, so junction leakage stays negligible at 150-200 C beside accelerators.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention of minutes to hours removes refresh engines and cooling needs, using U.S. SiC wafer capacity built for EVs.
note: SiC DRAM demonstrated at Purdue in 1990s; density and MOS interface limits.

title: LTPS display lasers crystallize silicon for every 3D tier
idea: Borrowed from LTPS phone-display backplanes: each 3D tier receives low-temperature amorphous Si that is melted and recrystallized by line-beam excimer laser pulses too short to heat the tiers below, yielding large-grain lateral transistors tier by tier.
why: Silicon-class mobility (~10x IGZO drive) for monolithic 3D lateral transistors without high-temperature epi (fact 2); the laser tools already exist at Gen-6 scale.

title: Termite-mound chimneys: heat-pipe pillars threaded through the stack
idea: Adapted from termite-mound ventilation shafts: every 64th vertical bitline slot in a DRAM-on-logic stack becomes a Cu/diamond 'chimney' pillar tying all tiers to a top heat spreader, holding every tier within ~5 C of the coolant.
why: Retention roughly halves per ~10 C, so cooler tiers cut refresh power ~2-4x (fact 3) and allow DRAM stacked directly on hot accelerators (fact 5).

title: HVDC thyristor valves shrunk into a capacitor-free bulk-silicon latch
idea: Grid HVDC valves hold state as latched pnpn thyristors that stay on at minimal holding current. Adapt a vertical pnpn thyristor per bit in plain bulk silicon, gated by the wordline to latch or unlatch, with a sub-uA hold current only on active rows and a slow-decay off state elsewhere.
why: Deletes the whole capacitor module: Zr/Hf ALD dielectric, TiN electrodes, nitride support lattice, and the 60:1 fluorocarbon etch with its helium-cooled chucks. That is ~20-30% fewer process steps and ~35% less PFC gas per wafer.

title: Microwave tunnel-diode latch makes a refresh-free one-transistor SRAM
idea: Microwave oscillators exploited the negative resistance of Esaki tunnel diodes. Adapt two series Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes as the bistable load on a single access transistor (1T-2TD), forming a static latch at roughly 2x DRAM-cell area with no capacitor.
why: Eliminates both capacitor and refresh (Fact 3) using only Si, SiGe and dopants. It needs a room-temperature peak-to-valley ratio >3 at very low valley current.
note: TSRAM concept from 1990s; PVR/valley current.

title: PCB direct metallization replaces tungsten plugs in shallow cells
idea: PCB makers coat through-holes with a graphite colloid and then electroplate copper directly. Adapt this with a conformal CVD amorphous-carbon seed plus electroplated Co or Cu fill for cell contacts, made feasible because a capacitor-free cell has only shallow ~5:1 contacts instead of deep storage-node plugs.
why: Eliminates WF6 CVD (tungsten plus fluorine) for contacts and uses aqueous plating with abundant chemistry.

title: Airport baggage CT: inline X-ray laminography for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Adapt CT and laminography from airport scanners and BGA inspection into an inline compact-source X-ray laminography tool that reconstructs tier-by-tier recess depth, channel thickness and capacitor fill in 100-tier 3D DRAM stacks on every lot without cross-sectioning.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) and ramp speed: replaces slow destructive TEM; cutting ramp by months is worth ~$1B on a $15B fab.
note: X-ray metrology for 3D NAND exists; nm resolution needs flux.

title: Printing-press plates: one copy of model weights serves many hosts
idea: Borrowed from printing, where one plate prints a whole run: a CXL 3.x multi-host shared-memory appliance holds a single read-only copy of popular model weights mapped into 8-32 servers, each of which keeps only KV and activations locally; a hot-row SRAM cache in the switch absorbs repeated reads.
why: Every inference host now stores its own copy of the same 100-800 GB of weights; sharing cuts weight DRAM 8-32x across a pod.
note: CXL bandwidth far below HBM; only host-side staging copies can be shared.

title: Wine-cellar racking: match data lifetime to each row's retention
idea: Borrowed from cellars that put long-aging vintages in the coolest, most stable racks: a boot-time and online profiler bins every row by measured retention (most rows hold 1-10 s, only a tail is near 64 ms), and the OS places each page by its predicted rewrite interval into a row that outlasts it; pages with uncertain lifetimes go to a non-volatile shelf.
why: Removes refresh by exploiting the retention distribution instead of designing for the 13 fA tail; recovers 16-33% of idle power and keeps weak-retention dies in service, raising usable supply.
note: RAPID/RAIDR prior art; VRT undermines profiling.

title: Cable-TV frequency division: many DRAM dies share one RF line
idea: Adapted from DOCSIS cable-TV plant: each DRAM die on a stack or interposer gets its own RF carrier (e.g., eight carriers spread over 10-80 GHz) on one shared transmission line, using tiny on-die mixers instead of dedicated wires. Dies tune in and out like set-top boxes on a multi-drop coax-like trace.
why: Attacks interposer/TSV wiring tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): ~4-8x fewer wires per GB/s and more dies per channel for capacity, targeting <1 pJ/bit at short reach.
note: Echoes UCLA multiband RF-interconnect work; mixer power and area are the doubt.

title: Turbine-blade internal cooling channels inside HBM spacer layers
idea: Adapted from jet-engine blade cooling: serpentine microchannels are etched into thin silicon spacers placed every few dies and carry pumped dielectric coolant through the stack. Heat leaves from the stack interior instead of conducting up through 16 dies.
why: Thermal limits cap stack height and force 2x refresh above 85 C (fact 3); internal cooling could allow 24-32 high stacks and halve hot refresh.
note: Interlayer microchannel cooling is well studied; TSV routing through channels is the hard part.

title: RFID fluidic self-assembly drops memory dielets into interposer wells
idea: Adapted from 1990s fluidic self-assembly used by RFID tag makers: millions of small DRAM dielets suspended in liquid flow over an interposer with etched, shape-matched wells. The dielets settle into place by gravity and shape and are then bonded by reflow.
why: Small dielets yield far better (yield ~ e^-AD), and assembly runs massively in parallel, cutting pick-and-place cost and large-die yield loss.

title: Supermarket holographic scanners inspire free-space optical memory interconnect
idea: Adapted from the holographic optical elements in 1990s barcode scanners: a single cast hologram plate above the board redirects hundreds of VCSEL beams from memory packages to photodiodes on the processor, replacing board traces.
why: Board-level data movement and pin count: no copper trace loss, and routing is set by a cheap replicated hologram, so memory can be placed in 3D around the processor.
note: 1990s free-space optical board interconnect revisited; alignment/thermal drift issues.

title: Transit-card inductive coupling powers and talks to glued stacks
idea: Adapted from contactless smart cards: each DRAM die gets on-die spiral coils in 180 nm-era metal, used both for near-field data links and for resonant power transfer like a card reader. The dies are simply glued together, with zero TSVs and zero bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): bad dies are swapped before gluing, and there is no via-related yield loss; no DRIE or hybrid bonding needed.
note: Inductive die-to-die data (ThruChip) known; wireless power to DRAM stacks is inefficient.

title: Phone-refurbisher robotic harvesting of soldered LPDDR and GDDR
idea: Adapted from smartphone refurbishing lines: scrapped laptops, GPUs, consoles and phones are X-ray mapped, memory packages are freed by laser-assisted selective reflow and picked, robots reball them, and high-parallel testers burn them in before they are rebuilt into LPCAMM/SODIMM modules.
why: Hundreds of millions of devices with soldered DRAM retire each year; recovering ~10% of them could add a few % of annual bit supply with almost no fab capital (scarce resources, supply).

title: Hard-disk bit-patterned-media self-assembly for DRAM capacitor honeycombs
idea: Adapted from the HDD industry's block-copolymer work on bit-patterned media: a coarse guide pattern from a U.S.-built stepper plus a high-chi block copolymer from U.S. chemistry makers self-assembles the hexagonal storage-node hole array at ~20 nm pitch.
why: The capacitor array is the periodic hexagonal lattice BCPs form naturally, so this removes 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers with no ASML dependence for that layer (litho capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Display-fab DRAM panels: magnify area, minify cost per area
idea: MAGNIFY substrate area ~1000x and MINIFY cost per m2: a 10-person team designs 1T1C arrays of oxide or LTPS TFTs at ~3 um pitch and buys Gen-8.5 glass runs from idle LCD fabs; a 5.5 m2 sheet of ~10 um2 cells holds ~70 GB raw, diced into slabs bonded to logic by panel-level fan-out.
why: Zero EUV and uses depreciated display capital (fact 4), ally-sourced capacity; at ~$10-20/GB it serves a slower 100-ns tier, not the hottest DRAM.
note: Same display-fab panel memory strategy.

title: Magnify refresh duration, minify energy: adiabatic resonant refresh
idea: Refresh whole banks slowly with microsecond ramps driven by an on-package LC resonator that swings wordlines and bitline precharge sinusoidally and recovers charge each cycle, so dissipation scales as (RC/T)*CV^2 instead of CV^2. Refresh has no latency requirement, so stretching it costs nothing.
why: Refresh energy ~46 fJ/bit -> ~5-10 fJ/bit (5-10x lower).

title: Magnify isolation: storage node floats on buried oxide, no junction
idea: Form the storage-node contact region on a local buried-oxide pocket created by Si/SiGe selective etch-and-fill, so the storage node touches no p-n junction or substrate and the only leakage paths left are the gated channel and the capacitor.
why: Junction generation and trap-assisted tunneling are a large share of the tail; removing them targets ~10x longer minimum retention.

title: Zero-kerf laser slicing: thinner wafers on reusable carriers
idea: Magnify wafers per ingot ~2.5x: split ingots along a laser-modified subsurface plane (zero kerf) into 300 um wafers, temporarily bonded to reusable carriers for processing, instead of wire-sawing 775 um wafers and losing ~150 um of kerf each.
why: DRAM dies are thinned below 50 um anyway, so over 90% of today's wafer becomes slurry. Silicon, polysilicon energy and crucible quartz per bit fall ~2.5x.

title: Area-selective deposition ends blanket metal plus CMP
idea: Minify metal to only where it stays: self-assembled inhibitor monolayers on dielectric surfaces make Mo/TiN ALD nucleate only in contacts and lines. This eliminates the overburden and the CMP step that today removes 80-95% of the deposited metal.
why: Cuts metal precursor use 5-10x and removes ceria slurry (rare earths, China-dominated), slurry water and pad waste on several layers.
note: ASD is a heavily pursued research field.

title: Two-beam interference lithography prints the cell grid maskless
idea: Magnify one exposure to the whole periodic array: pattern the perfectly periodic DRAM cell grid with interfering 193 nm beams (standing-wave lithography), and use a cheap DUV trim mask only at array edges.
why: Replaces several EUV or multi-patterning steps, cutting EUV electricity (~1 MW per tool), tin and hydrogen use, and capital (fact 4).

title: Silicon-on-sapphire DRAM removes substrate leakage at 125 C
idea: Minify the leakage path to zero: grow thin silicon on Kyropoulos sapphire (alumina from bauxite, pulled in molybdenum crucibles) so storage nodes have no junction to a substrate; only the channel can leak.
why: Junction leakage, which doubles every ~10 C, disappears, and the substrate needs no quartz crucible. SOS is a proven high-temperature, radiation-hard technology.
note: SOS defect density raises leakage; GIDL still dominates.

title: Inductive coupling replaces TSVs in stacked DRAM
idea: Minify die-to-die vias to zero: thin each die to 10 um and pass data through on-chip inductor coils stacked over each other, with power delivered through a single edge-plated rail, removing TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes the TSV process module and its 20-30% yield loss, recovering area spent on TSV keep-out zones.

title: High-chi block copolymer multiplies DUV hole density fourfold
idea: Magnify density without new optics: coarse DUV guide posts direct a high-chi block copolymer to self-assemble 4 cylinders per guide at ~12 nm, used for landing pads and storage-node contacts.
why: Lithography: removes 1-2 EUV layers per die; DSA tooling is a track, not a scanner.

title: Rotary spatial ALD at atmospheric pressure
idea: Magnify deposition throughput 10x by spinning wafers under fixed precursor zones separated by gas curtains (spatial ALD) at atmospheric pressure for capacitor high-k and liners, instead of slow pulsed vacuum ALD.
why: Throughput and tool cost: ALD is a bottleneck in capacitor and 3D flows; 10x fewer chambers per wafer start.

title: Programmable photomask for periphery layers
idea: Minify mask-set cost to zero for non-critical layers by exposing through a 193 nm-compatible spatial light modulator (micromirror array) that reprograms its pattern per layer and per product.
why: Masks: a DRAM mask set costs millions of dollars; periphery variants and test chips become free to iterate.

title: Micro-banks: sixteen cells per printed bitline
idea: Minify the bitline to 16 cells and magnify the bank count to millions, each tiny sub-array with its own printed sense amplifier, so printed-wire RC drops about 64x.
why: Latency of printed memory: brings slow printed arrays toward ~100 ns access, trading area for speed on cheap area.

title: Minify GC heap headroom with a hardware collector
idea: Minify the 2-3x heap headroom that Java, Go and JS runtimes need for throughput. A memory-side co-processor in the controller does concurrent mark and compaction using read barriers in hardware, so heaps run at 1.1-1.2x live size without GC thrash.
why: Managed-language fleets are a large share of server DRAM. Tighter heaps cut that DRAM ~1.5-2.5x for those services.

title: Edge-standing die library: DRAM dies stood upright
idea: MAGNIFY dies per footprint by standing 100 thin DRAM dies upright like books, each bonded on one polished edge to the substrate through edge pads, with coolant flowing in the gaps between them.
why: Removes TSVs entirely and multiplies capacity per footprint about 10x versus a flat layout, with cooling built in.
note: Edge-interconnect cubes known (Irvine Sensors); edge pad bandwidth is limited.

title: Capacitive proximity tiles aligned by micro-magnets
idea: MINIFY the gap to a ~1 um dielectric: memory tiles clamp face-to-face with compute and signal through capacitive coupling pads at 10 um pitch, aligned by patterned micro-magnets; unclamp to replace.
why: No TSVs, bumps or solder; ~0.1 pJ/bit links, with full disassembly for repair or recovery.

title: Magnify vertical link count: over-provisioned laser-drilled through-glass vias
idea: Stack thin glass memory layers using laser-drilled through-glass vias at ~4x the needed count, with any of four vias able to carry each signal through a switch. Open or high-resistance vias never kill a stack.
why: Fact 6: TSV-type yield loss (20-30% in HBM) shrinks to ~1%, and glass vias cost far less per hole than silicon TSVs.
note: TSV redundancy schemes are well known; glass stacking adds unknowns.

title: Magnify HBM life: debond retired stacks and remount them
idea: Laser-release and thermally debond HBM stacks from retired AI accelerators, re-bump them, and mount them on fresh low-cost silicon or glass interposers for inference cards binned at lower bandwidth.
why: HBM pays a ~3x wafer-area-per-bit TSV tax up front; a second life amortizes that tax, roughly halving effective wafer area per HBM-bit-year.

title: Minify crucible dependence: kerfless epitaxial wafers peeled from templates
idea: Grow 300 mm device-grade silicon by fast epitaxy on a porous-silicon release layer over a reusable template, peel it off, and reuse the template 50x+ with no Czochralski ingot, quartz crucible or wire saw.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and ingot-pulling chokepoints, halves kerf silicon waste, and enables domestic wafer supply.

title: Eliminate static states: nanomechanical parametrons store bits as oscillation phase
idea: Eliminate the static bistable well: each cell is a high-Q nanomechanical or LC resonator pumped at 2f by a shared line, which forces it to oscillate at f in one of two phases (0 or pi), reviving Goto's 1950s parametron at GHz. A small injection seeds the phase on write, a mixer reads it, and the pump continuously restores amplitude so the bit cannot decay.
why: Replaces refresh (fact 3) and destructive read (fact 8) with continuous parametric regeneration; hold energy is the shared pump (~nW per kbit for high-Q resonators); risks are resonator density and pump crosstalk.

title: Eliminate excimer lithography: block-copolymer cylinders template every storage node
idea: Eliminate ArF and EUV exposure for the cell array, since excimer lasers need neon, argon and krypton and EUV drive lasers use helium: a high-chi block copolymer on a sparse UV-LED-exposed chemical guide self-assembles into a hexagonal 24-nm-pitch cylinder lattice. Sequential infiltration synthesis (TMA/H2O, N2 purge) turns the cylinders into AlOx hard masks for the storage nodes.
why: Removes 2-3 litho layers from the cell array (fact 4: 5-7 EUV layers today), and hexagonal packing fits ~15% more nodes per area; risk is reaching defect density under 1/cm2.
note: DSA for DRAM holes long pursued; defectivity remains the blocker.

title: Eliminate deposited dielectrics: Bi2O2Se channel with native Bi2SeO5 gate oxide
idea: Grow 2D Bi2O2Se by CVD and partly convert it with UV-ozone or O2 plasma into its native high-k (k~20) Bi2SeO5, forming a Si/SiO2-like clean interface on an atomically thin body; the access device reaches near-60 mV/dec swing with full depletion. All steps are tube-furnace and plasma steps.
why: Atomically thin, trap-free channel shrinks GIDL and trap leakage and is vertically stackable (facts 2-3).
note: Bi2O2Se/Bi2SeO5 already demonstrated (Peking U.); access-device use is incremental.

title: Eliminate bulk thickness: 2 nm quantum-confined silicon body widens bandgap
idea: Thin SOI by repeated thermal oxidation and HF strip to a 2-3 nm body, where quantum confinement widens silicon's effective gap by ~0.3-0.5 eV and suppresses intrinsic carrier density 1e3-1e4x; build the access device in this film over a thick buried oxide. Only furnace oxidation and wet etch are needed.
why: Leakage drops ~1000x from bandgap widening while staying all-silicon and U.S.-manufacturable; mobility loss is tolerable because a cell needs only microamps.

title: Eliminate heat-driven leakage: thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier cooler under array
idea: Sputter or co-evaporate thin-film Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 thermoelectric couples into the substrate or interposer beneath the memory array, pumping the cell region 15-25 C below the surrounding logic. Since leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C, cooling only the array extends retention 3-6x.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall 3-6x in hot HBM stacks beside GPUs; thin-film thermoelectrics are university processes; costs some Peltier power.
note: Thin-film TEC heat plus pumping power may cancel savings in hot stacks.

title: Eliminate the solid gate dielectric: air-gap suspended-gate FET
idea: Fabricate a suspended metal gate over the channel on a sacrificial amorphous-Si layer released by XeF2; the gate pulls in electrostatically for access with abrupt switching and springs back to a large air gap in hold, deepening the off state and removing gate-oxide traps. Unlike a contact relay, current still flows through a semiconductor channel.
why: Steep switching cuts wordline voltage and leakage together (facts 3, 10); sacrificial MEMS release is routine in university fabs; stiction and speed are risks.

title: Eliminate per-bitline latches: shared time-to-digital bitline sensing
idea: Remove the cross-coupled latch from every bitline pair. After charge sharing, each bitline gates a single discharge transistor onto a shared ramp, and one time-to-digital converter, time-interleaved over 32 bitlines in about 4 ns, records which bitlines cross threshold first. A global restore bus then rewrites the cells through one-transistor restore switches.
why: Periphery (fact 7): SA stripes are ~10-15% of the die; replacing 6-8 matched transistors per pair with 2 small devices cuts SA area ~50-60% (die -5-8%). Costs +2-4 ns latency.

title: Eliminate VDD/2 precharge: plate-pulsed sensing from grounded bitlines
idea: Hold bitlines at ground and delete the equalizer transistors and the VBLP generator. To read, pulse the segmented cell plate of the selected 512-cell sub-array upward (FeRAM-style plate-line drive). A '1' cell pushes more charge onto the floating bitline than a '0', against a half-plate-pulse dummy reference, and a ground-referenced NMOS stage resolves it.
why: Removes precharge/equalize current (~15-20% of activate energy) and the VBLP regulator (~1-2% area); a ground-precharged bitline also eases low-voltage operation (fact 10).

title: Eliminate multi-patterning in sense-amp stripes via block-copolymer self-assembly
idea: SA and column-select transistor arrays are periodic at bitline pitch, so define their gate and active lines by directed self-assembly of PS-b-PMMA guided by coarse KrF chemical prepatterns. Remove the PMMA with UV plus an acetic acid rinse and transfer with HBr/Cl2/O2, eliminating fluorocarbon SADP spacer etches and PAG resists.
why: Pitch-matched SAs below 30 nm without EUV or SADP (fact 4); SA-stripe patterning cost ~-40-60%.

title: Eliminate the high-AR capacitor etch: anodic alumina pore templates
idea: Skip plasma-etching capacitor holes; deposit thick aluminium over the transistor array, pre-dent it at each storage node, and anodize so self-ordered pores with aspect ratios above 500:1 grow straight down onto each node; line them with high-k and electrode.
why: Capacitor charge wall: the AR 115:1 needed for more charge comes from electrochemistry instead of a hard mask and etch, giving a ~2x Cs headroom with no hard mask.
note: AAO nanocapacitors are known; self-ordered pore pitch (~60 nm) and registration to storage nodes are the doubts.

title: Eliminate binary storage: three-level cells paired across adjacent tiers
idea: Store three charge levels per cell and pair cells vertically across two tiers so 9 states encode 3 bits in 2 cells; a shared vertical reference ladder in each pillar tracks temperature and leakage drift.
why: Density/cost per bit: +50% bits per cell pair with no extra lithography; needs ~2x sense margin, which short vertical bitlines provide.

title: Eliminate etch-fill-polish cycles: flat-by-construction conversion patterning
idea: Define isolation and channels by locally converting silicon rather than removing it: patterned oxygen or nitrogen implant plus anneal (SIMOX-like) turns selected regions into insulator, so the surface stays planar and no gap-fill or CMP is needed.
why: Water: STI etch, fill, CMP and their cleans are among the heaviest UPW users per layer; a planar conversion flow removes them for the array, cutting array-module water ~10x.
note: LOCOS/SIMOX-like; volume expansion and implant dose costs.

title: Eliminate implant masks: junctionless in-situ doped access channels
idea: Grow channels in-situ doped during epitaxy or deposition and use junctionless accumulation-mode access transistors, removing source/drain and well implant masks with their resist strips and post-implant wet cleans.
why: Water: each implant layer costs resist develop, ash plus wet strip and rinse; removing 6-10 implant layers in the array cuts a major water block and also avoids junction leakage tails.
note: Junctionless devices struggle to turn off and add GIDL; oxide channels already junctionless.

title: Eliminate TSVs: through-silicon optical links at 1310 nm
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so stacked thinned dies talk vertically through the bulk with micro-LED or VCSEL emitters and Ge photodiodes aligned in columns, with no drilled or plated vias.
why: Water and HBM tax: no TSV etch, wet clean, ECD or reveal CMP, and no keep-out zones; each optical column can carry tens of Gb/s.

title: Eliminate ceria CMP: flowable oxide plus atomic-layer etch-back planarization
idea: Replace ceria-slurry oxide CMP steps with spin-on polysilazane fill cured to SiO2, then planarize by quasi-atomic-layer etch-back that stops on a SiN etch-stop detected optically, so no slurry or pad is used.
why: Ceria abrasive is a rare-earth product dominated by China, and CMP is a top ultrapure-water and waste consumer; removes ~5-10 CMP steps per DRAM flow.

title: Eliminate the wafer fab: oxide gain-cell memory on idle display-glass lines
idea: Build 2T0C oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays on Gen-8.5 glass (~5.5 m2, ~75x a 300 mm wafer) in under-used LCD fabs with 1-1.5 um lithography, then dice tiles for a high-capacity, slower CXL memory tier.
why: Repurposes depreciated capacity with no crucible quartz, no EUV and a <400 C process; ~1/50 the processing cost per m2, offsetting much lower areal density.

title: Eliminate vacuum pumps: atmospheric spatial ALD for capacitor dielectrics
idea: A gas-bearing spatial ALD head separates precursor zones with N2 curtains at atmospheric pressure while the wafer moves beneath it; pulsed-pressure dwell cycles push precursor down high-AR holes.
why: Drops dry pumps (a major share of deposition-tool energy), raises throughput 5-10x and cuts precursor waste; conformality at 70:1 is the open question.

title: Eliminate the binary bit: ternary-charge cells give 58% more bits per mask
idea: Store three charge levels per cell (0, half and full VBLH) and read them with a two-reference successive-approximation sense amplifier; pairs of cells hold 9 states and encode 3 bits.
why: Litho and capital: ~50% more bits from the same mask stack and wafer, a 'free node' without EUV, paid for with sense margin and a higher refresh rate.

title: Eliminate the capacitor-hole mask: block-copolymer self-assembly guided by landing pads
idea: Coat a cylinder-forming block copolymer over the landing-pad topography so it self-assembles into a hexagonal hole array registered to the pads, and use it directly as the hard-mask template for capacitor holes. The die and its DDR5/HBM interface are unchanged.
why: Replaces one EUV or 2-3 DUV multipatterning exposures with a spin and bake, and tightens hole-CD uniformity, narrowing Cs variation.

title: Eliminate per-die probe touchdowns: scribe-line test bus, one contact per wafer
idea: Wire every die to a shared power and serial test bus routed through the scribe lines to a few large edge pads; one touchdown powers all dies, each runs BIST and reports over the bus, and a fuse isolates shorted dies. Dicing cuts the bus away, leaving standard DDR5/HBM dies.
why: Replaces fine-pitch probe cards and multi-touchdown sort with one cheap contact; ~10x sort throughput and no probe marks on hybrid-bond pads.

title: Eliminate duplicate lines with content-addressed main memory in CXL expanders
idea: A CXL memory expander stores 64B lines by hash in a deduplicated store with reference counts; host physical addresses map to hash entries, so identical lines across VMs and containers are stored once.
why: VM and container fleets have 20-50% duplicate content: 1.25-2x capacity per installed bit.

title: ESD-free hybrid-bond IO for wafer-level-only stacks
idea: Eliminate ESD protection on internal die-to-die pads: hybrid-bonded faces are never touched by humans or probes after bonding, so drop ESD diodes and use a sacrificial wafer-level discharge grid that is severed during bonding, shrinking pad capacitance from ~200 fF to ~10 fF.
why: IO energy is CV^2 dominated by pad capacitance: vertical-link energy/bit falls ~5-10x and smaller pads allow 2-3x more vertical channels in the same area.
note: Same sacrificial ESD grid concept.

title: Photonic phase-change memory read by light without conversion
idea: Eliminate O/E/O conversion at disaggregated memory: store bits in GST or Sb2Se3 patches on silicon-nitride waveguides whose phase state sets transmission, and read them with WDM light pulses arriving directly from compute.
why: Read is just attenuation with no modulator or photodiode at the memory, cutting link-plus-access energy toward ~1 pJ/bit; ~1e8-1e12 endurance limits it to read-mostly data.

title: Eliminate controller refresh timers: per-row canary cells trigger refresh
idea: Add one deliberately weakened canary cell to each row (smaller capacitor, leakier transistor) and write it to '1' at every restore. A low-power background sense polls the canaries, and only rows whose canary has decayed get refreshed, so refresh tracks actual temperature and leakage.
why: Most rows retain data for seconds; demand-driven refresh could cut refresh count ~5-10x and the bandwidth loss (fact 3) in proportion, with a self-calibrating guard-band.

title: Eliminate interface traps: transferred 2D-semiconductor channels with van der Waals gates
idea: Grow MoS2/WSe2 monolayers on a sacrificial wafer, transfer them onto the memory tier at <=300 C, and gate them through hBN or another vdW dielectric with no dangling bonds. That removes the interface-trap population behind random telegraph noise and variable retention time.
why: Attacks VRT and the leakage tail (fact 3); atomically thin channels also give ultra-low off-current, potentially seconds-level retention in BEOL-stacked cells.
note: Widely pursued; wafer-scale transfer is unsolved.

title: Eliminate helium from the DRAM fab bill of materials
idea: Eliminate helium: replace He backside cooling in etch/CVD electrostatic chucks with H2 or H2/Ar mixes (H2 conducts heat ~1.2x better than He) with chuck seal redesign, and membrane-recapture any residual He at tool exhaust.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium supply is offline since March 2026; removing He from the critical path protects wafer starts.
note: H2 conducts heat well; seal, safety and chemistry compatibility are the real unknowns.

title: Eliminate one-ingot-per-wafer: reusable donor wafers via porous-silicon transfer
idea: Eliminate consuming a full prime wafer per lot: grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a donor, bond it to lower-grade handle wafers, cleave, and reuse each donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts prime polysilicon, crucible and ingot demand ~5-10x per wafer start; DRAM arrays need only the top tens of microns of perfect silicon.

title: Leakage as the keeper: Si/SiGe tunnel-diode latched storage node
idea: Reverse leakage from enemy to holder: two series Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes (1990s low-temperature CVD) on a 180 nm cell's storage node cross their negative-resistance curves at two stable points, so tiny diode currents continuously restore '0' or '1' against junction leakage; one access FET reads and writes (tunneling SRAM).
why: Refresh (fact 3): static retention in a ~2-device footprint with pW-scale valley-current standby; no capacitor needed; risk is peak-to-valley ratio uniformity.
note: Same tunneling-SRAM latch; Si RITD PVR known.

title: Junctionless storage node removes the leakage-tail junction
idea: Reverse the doping layout: make the access device a uniformly n-doped ultrathin (<=5 nm) junctionless channel that turns off by full depletion under a wraparound gate, so there is no n+/p metallurgical junction at the storage node. Trap-assisted junction leakage and junction-field GIDL, the main sources of the retention tail and variable retention time, lose their high-field region.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): removing the storage-node junction field could cut tail leakage ~10x and shrink VRT, relaxing refresh ~4-8x.

title: Thin to widen: quantum-confined 2 nm channel raises effective bandgap
idea: Reverse the scaling instinct of keeping a thick body for less variability: thin the access-transistor body to ~2 nm Si (vertical fin or nanosheet), which raises the effective bandgap ~0.2-0.3 eV by quantum confinement. Band-to-band tunneling and thermal generation currents fall exponentially with the gap, and DRAM's modest on-current need absorbs the mobility loss.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10-100x lower GIDL/generation current stretches retention several-fold at the same Cs.

title: Store less charge to keep more: low-field hold during self-refresh
idea: Reverse the instinct to store maximum charge: in self-refresh, restore '1's to ~0.7 V instead of ~1.0 V and set plate and negative wordline so the gate-to-storage-node field is minimal. GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling fall exponentially with field while charge falls only ~30%, so GIDL-limited tail cells hold longer; one full-swing pass restores normal margin on wake.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3, 16-33% of idle): if tail leakage drops >3x for 30% less charge, the interval can double while each refresh costs ~50% less CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Reference cells that decay alongside their row
idea: Flip the sensing reference from a fixed VARY/2 to a moving one: each row carries a '1' and a '0' reference cell written at the same instant as the data and leaking through identical devices, and their charge-shared average becomes that row's sense threshold. As stored '1's sag, the threshold follows them down instead of waiting for them to cross a fixed midpoint.
why: Retention (fact 3): tracking common-mode decay tolerates ~2x more charge loss, giving ~1.5-2x longer refresh for ~0.03% area (2 cells per 8k).

title: Resonant wordline tank recycles refresh wordline energy
idea: Reverse the energy flow of refresh: because refresh activates rows in a fixed, known sequence, drive the boosted wordlines from an on-die LC tank (thin-film inductor in top metal) that swings each wordline up and returns its charge to the tank on the way down, instead of dumping pumped VPP charge to ground every row.
why: Refresh energy (facts 3, 10): wordline and charge-pump losses at VPP~3 V are a large share of refresh energy; recovering ~50-70% of them cuts refresh energy ~20-30% and shrinks VPP pump area (fact 7).

title: Resist-free periphery via area-selective deposition, no imported photoresist
idea: Reverse subtractive patterning: periphery contacts and vias are formed by depositing only where wanted, using area-selective deposition with self-assembled inhibitor monolayers from U.S. chemical suppliers and one coarse e-beam template, eliminating several resist-litho-etch loops.
why: Supply chokepoint: advanced photoresist is ~90% Japanese; also removes ~3-5 litho steps from the periphery flow.

title: Capacitor first, IGZO transistor last, perovskite dielectric
idea: Re-sequence the flow: build the capacitor array first in the silicon wafer and crystallize a SrTiO3 dielectric (k~100+) at 700 C, then build low-temperature (<400 C) IGZO vertical access transistors on top by re-using the existing active/wordline/bitline masks; the only added mask is the via from capacitor top to transistor drain.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and leakage tail (fact 3): reaches k~100 with no 1000 C anneal hitting the transistor; IGZO off-current (<1e-19 A/um) shrinks the leakage tail.
note: Capacitor-first with IGZO vertical transistor on top resembles Kioxia OCTRAM; k~100 STO thin-film doubtful.

title: Castellated kerf vias: TSVs moved to die edges
idea: Move vertical interconnect from die interior to edge: one added mask etches via trenches in the dicing streets, and sawing through their centers leaves half-vias on each die's sidewall. After stacking, the aligned sidewall half-vias are connected vertically by plating or printed redistribution.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees interior TSV keep-out area for cells and avoids TSV-induced stress and yield loss.
note: Edge/sidewall die stacking (Irvine Sensors, Vertical Circuits) is known; perimeter limits IO.

title: Move purity from the quartz to a sacrificial inner liner
idea: Rearrange where purity lives: make crucibles from ordinary non-Spruce-Pine fused silica and spray an inner barium-doped devitrifying coat plus CVD Si3N4 liner that crystallizes into a dense cristobalite skin in the first hour, so the melt only ever sees the engineered liner.
why: Breaks the >80% HPQ chokepoint by letting any 4N quartz source qualify; target crucible cost down ~40% and supply base widened to dozens of quarries.

title: Waterless fab: supercritical CO2 replaces ultrapure water rinse
idea: Reverse wet to dry: replace most UPW rinse and post-etch clean steps with supercritical CO2 plus co-solvent cleaning in closed recycle loops; this also prevents capillary collapse of high-AR capacitor pillars.
why: Water and energy intensity drop ~50-70%, the pillar-collapse yield loss that limits AR goes away, and fabs can sit at water-stressed U.S. sites.

title: Interference-printed array: the light itself is the mask
idea: Reverse the role of mask and light: print the periodic cell array with maskless two- or four-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (~40 nm pitch, shrunk by one spacer step), and use only a cheap KrF trim exposure to cut array edges.
why: No EUV and no critical reticle for array layers; interference tools are simpler and cheaper than scanners, cutting array litho capex ~50%.

title: Chemistry is the mask: area-selective deposition of landing pads
idea: Reverse 'litho decides where material goes': passivate oxide with self-assembled monolayer inhibitors so ALD metal only nucleates on exposed contact plugs, growing storage-node landing pads in place with no lithography.
why: Removes the landing-pad layer, one of the critical EUV layers in leading DRAM, and its overlay budget.

title: Fluidic self-assembly of shape-keyed memory tiles
idea: Reverse pick-and-place: diced memory tiles with keyed asymmetric outlines tumble in a fluid over a logic wafer etched with matching recesses, and the capillary pull of molten low-temperature solder in each recess drags tiles into ~1 um alignment, assembling thousands in parallel.
why: Capital intensity of placement and bonding tools; parallel assembly makes many small, high-yield memory tiles economical.
note: Fluidic self-assembly known (Alien Technology, Tohoku).

title: Cool from inside: microchannels etched into memory die backsides
idea: Reverse the heat path so memory can sit on top of compute: DRIE ~100 um microchannels into the back of each die, seal them with the next bonded layer, and circulate dielectric coolant through the stack so heat leaves sideways instead of through the hot logic.
why: Removes the thermal limit on memory-on-logic stacking and HBM stack height, enabling 16+ high stacks with vertical links (facts 5, 6).
note: Interlayer microchannel cooling is a long-studied approach.

title: Microspring sockets for reworkable, upgradable memory dies
idea: Reverse permanent bonding: sputter stress-graded metal fingers that curl up off the interposer into 20 um-pitch microsprings, and clamp memory dies onto them, so dies can be tested, swapped or carried to the next compute generation after assembly.
why: Yield and supply: bad or worn dies are replaced instead of scrapping a whole ~$10k package, and DRAM is reused across compute generations; stressed-metal springs need only sputtering and a release etch.
note: Same reworkable socket mechanism (PARC stressed-metal springs).

title: Silicon ribbon sub-THz waveguides between memory and compute
idea: Reverse 'metal for wires': DRIE-etch high-resistivity silicon ribbons on the interposer as dielectric waveguides for 150-300 GHz carriers, with tapered couplers at each chiplet, giving low-loss 100+ Gb/s channels over several centimetres without copper skin-effect loss.
why: Memory can sit 5-20 cm away for capacity beyond beachfront at ~1 pJ/bit (fact 5); the waveguides are plain silicon etch.

title: Planarize nothing: area-selective growth eliminates CMP slurry water
idea: Reverse blanket-then-polish into growing only where needed: area-selective ALD/CVD with inhibitor monolayers fills trenches and contacts from the bottom up to the target height. That removes CMP, its slurry and the post-CMP clean.
why: CMP and post-CMP cleans are a large share of fab UPW. Removing several CMP steps cuts that share >10x and also eliminates slurry waste.

title: Wafer as a stamp: layer-transfer arrays, reuse the donor wafer
idea: Reverse the wafer from consumable to reusable template: grow a crystalline device layer on a porous-Si or ion-cut donor and transfer it to a cheap carrier. The donor is re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Cuts the water for crystal pulling, slicing and polishing ~10x per wafer. Reusing donors also cuts demand for Spruce Pine quartz crucibles.

title: Image-sensor pinned well with source-follower readout replaces the capacitor
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality + #2 Taking out: borrow the CMOS image sensor 4T pixel and store the bit as ~500-2,000 electrons in a buried n-well under a p+ pinning layer (dark current ~aA, since the surface traps are pinned), transfer it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate and read it through an in-cell source follower. Gain readout, not charge sharing, senses it, so no tall capacitor is needed; the shrink target is a vertical pinned pillar of ~40 nm.
why: Facts 1 and 3: removes the 60-75:1 capacitor and drops leakage ~1,000x (refresh every seconds), at the cost of 3-4 transistors per cell; today's 0.5-um pixels are far too large, which is the main risk.

title: Resonant LC drivers sweep refresh wordlines adiabatically
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration / resonance: refresh is perfectly periodic and predictable, so drive it with a resonance. Package-level inductors form an LC tank with a bank's refresh wordline and bitline load, so lines rise and fall as sine half-cycles and their energy is recovered rather than dissipated through the ~3 V VPP pump.
why: Attacks the CV^2 floor (Fact 10) and refresh energy (Fact 3): claim 40-60% lower refresh energy without changing the cell.

title: Wafer-scale monolayer WSe2 on sapphire: junction-free atomically thin switch
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells and thin films: use a 0.7 nm monolayer channel grown by MOCVD directly on c-plane sapphire and double-gated so the gate controls every atom of the channel; with no bulk, no pn junction and a ~1.6-2 eV gap, junction generation leakage vanishes and short-channel leakage stays suppressed at ~10 nm gate length.
why: A small, low-leakage access device (Facts 2, 3) on a non-silicon, crucible-free substrate; risks are contact resistance and defect-assisted leakage.
note: Same 2D monolayer access channel.

title: Modulation-doped In2O3/Ga2O3 superlattice channel resolves mobility versus leakage
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: build the channel on glass as an ALD superlattice of ~1 nm In2O3 wells and Ga2O3 barriers, so electrons in the wells give high mobility when the gate fills them, while in the off state the wide-gap Ga2O3 barriers set the leakage floor and trap out oxygen-vacancy donors.
why: Breaks the drive-vs-leakage contradiction of single-composition oxides (Fact 3): target >30 cm2/Vs with <1e-20 A/um off-current, enabling 10-100 ns access on glass.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC wordline drive recycles boost energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: wordlines are driven from a resonant tank formed by an interposer inductor and the selected wordline capacitance, so the ~3 V boost arrives as a half-sine and its charge returns to the tank when the wordline falls, bypassing most of the ~30%-efficient VPP charge pump.
why: Fact 10: wordline/VPP energy ~-60% and charge-pump area in the periphery ~-50%.

title: Zirconium disulfide channel with its own oxide as gate dielectric
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: 2D ZrS2 (bandgap ~1.7 eV) oxidizes easily, which is normally a defect. Here a controlled O2 plasma deliberately converts the top layers into amorphous ZrO2 (k ~20) that serves as a perfect-interface gate dielectric, giving a 2-3 layer ZrS2 write transistor for a 2T0C gain cell.
why: Replaces IGZO (In, Ga) in capacitor-less gain cells with Zr, S and O only. An atomically thin channel with native high-k targets sub-aA leakage at <=400 C, compatible with stacking 3D tiers.
note: Native high-k oxide on ZrS2/HfSe2 is published; wafer-scale 2D growth remains the barrier.

title: Plasma-deposited organosilicon resist converts to glass under exposure
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes (exposure switches the film's chemistry): plasma-deposit a solvent-free methylsilane film whose exposed areas photo-oxidize into SiO2-like glass, then dry-develop the unexposed film in a Cl2 plasma.
why: Removes PFAS photoacid generators, spin solvents and developer water, and avoids tin-oxo EUV resists. Uses only Si, C, H, O and Cl.

title: Supercritical CO2 with ozone replaces water rinse-and-dry cycles
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: clean and dry wafers in pressurized supercritical CO2 carrying dissolved ozone and a little alcohol co-solvent, then recompress and reuse the CO2.
why: Cuts UPW and IPA use. Zero surface tension also ends pillar collapse, so taller capacitors become possible (fact 1); only C, O and H are involved.

title: Three-beam interference lithography for all dense hexagonal array layers
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: one maskless tool interfering three 193 nm beams at 120 degrees prints the honeycomb lattice for active islands, capacitor holes and landing pads by only changing phase and rotation; spacer doubling brings it to ~40 nm hex pitch and a cheap DUV block mask trims the array edges.
why: No reticle and simple optics: tool cost perhaps 1/20 of EUV and 1/5 of an immersion scanner, and ~3-4 masks disappear from the flow (fact 4).

title: 180 nm TCAM dedup engine for constant-time page fingerprint lookup
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: borrow the 1990s router TCAM; a 180 nm ternary CAM holds partial fingerprints of pages, each newly written or newly cold page is looked up in one cycle, and only hits are byte-verified, making dedup a continuous hardware service instead of a CPU scan.
why: KSM-style scanning costs CPU and finds duplicates late; continuous dedup recovers 10-30% of memory in VM/container hosts.
note: 180 nm TCAM cannot hold fingerprints for hundreds of millions of pages; DRAM hash tables suffice.

title: Self-describing paired lines with header-in-slack, no metadata table
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: when two adjacent 64 B lines each compress to 30 B or less, they are packed into one 64 B slot whose first bits describe the encoding, and the freed buddy slot goes to a free list; a decoder simple enough for 180 nm reads the header in-line, so no separate metadata table, metadata cache or extra DRAM access is needed.
why: Removes the metadata-access penalty that kills line compression; 1.3-1.8x capacity with decode logic small enough for old nodes.
note: Similar to LCP/buddy-style compressed layouts.

title: Universality: coaxial TSV acting as signal, decap and heat pipe
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: build each signal TSV as a coax with a Cu core, a 20 nm high-k ZrO2 liner and a grounded Cu sleeve. The shielded core carries data at tight pitch, the sleeve-to-substrate stack acts as distributed decoupling capacitance, and the extra copper conducts heat up the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax and power integrity (fact 6): 2x tighter TSV pitch without crosstalk, and no separate decap or dummy thermal TSVs, for a ~20-30% smaller TSV region.

title: Microfluidic channels etched in U.S.-made stack base die
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics/hydraulics: coolant microchannels are etched into the domestically fabbed logic base die and capped with a bonded silicon lid, so liquid flows directly under the stack and holds DRAM dies at 60 C or below instead of 85-95 C.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C drop, so ~4x longer refresh and no hot 2x-refresh mode; retention-weak dies pass, raising U.S. stack yield.

title: Nesting: oxide-TFT memory nested in logic BEOL reusing existing masks
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: a memory layer is nested between two existing logic metal levels, reusing the via mask as the TFT gate contact and metal mask as source/drain, so the only new mask defines the oxide channel island.
why: Capacity: every logic wafer gains a memory layer for buffers, with one mask of added cost.

title: Another dimension: embedded-die PCB DIMMs doubling module density
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bare DRAM dies are embedded inside the module PCB core and connected with one added laser/litho via layer, while the surfaces carry more packaged dies, doubling GB per DIMM slot.
why: Slot-limited server capacity: more memory per socket without new dies or a new die node.

title: Physarum oscillation-phase bit: nanomechanical parametron storing 0 or pi
idea: Slime mould encodes information in the phase of its cytoplasmic oscillations. Store each bit as the 0 or pi phase of a parametrically pumped ~1 GHz AlScN nanomechanical resonator: a 2f pump sustains either phase indefinitely, and a weak seed signal chooses which. Read by mixing with a reference phase on a shared line; many resonators share one pump line.
why: Replaces stored charge with phase, so there is no leakage tail, no refresh and no destructive read (facts 3, 8). AlScN is US-made and needs no EUV; energy scales with resonator Q (10^3-10^4).
note: Same pumped-resonator phase bit.

title: CaMKII avalanche chain: small trigger magnet flips a stable cluster
idea: CaMKII holoenzyme subunits phosphorylate their neighbours, so one activated subunit switches the whole ring and keeps it switched. Make each bit a chain of 6-12 exchange-coupled nanomagnets. A short SOT pulse switches only the low-barrier 'trigger' magnet at the end, and the reversal runs down the chain as a domain wall; the chain's collective barrier (>60 kT) sets retention.
why: Decouples write current from retention: write energy is set by the small trigger (~5-10x lower), while retention scales with chain size. Non-volatile, with MRAM-like unlimited endurance.
note: Resembles exchange-coupled composite media; a chain of magnets enlarges cell area.

title: Hippocampal sleep consolidation: in-cell ferroelectric backup at power-fail
idea: The brain stores new memories quickly in the hippocampus and consolidates them into cortex during sleep. Coat each DRAM capacitor's inner electrode with 3-4 nm HZO and run it below the coercive field as a linear DRAM cap. On a power-fail interrupt, energy from a package hold-up capacitor drives all rows to write each cell's charge into polarization within ~10 ms, and the state is restored at power-up.
why: Data survive power loss while normal operation keeps DRAM speed and unlimited endurance. The ferroelectric switches only at power events, so ~10^5 lifetime cycles are enough.

title: NiFe-hydrogenase proton loading: hydrogen-doped nickelate Mott switch
idea: Hydrogenase enzymes shuttle protons and electrons in and out of a Ni-Fe active site. Gate a thin SmNiO3 or NdNiO3 channel through a solid proton conductor: a write pulse injects hydrogen, which dopes electrons into the nickelate and drives it from metal to insulator (resistance change >10^3). The hydrogen stays put when unpowered and is pulled back out by reverse bias.
why: Non-volatile, multilevel-capable Mott switch read at low voltage, with large on/off ratio and rare-earth nickelates instead of chalcogenides. Proton moves of a few nm aim at ~100 ns writes.
note: Known H-doped SmNiO3 work (Ramanathan).

title: Hibernating banks with on-die thermoelectric torpor cooling
idea: Like hibernators that drop body temperature to slash metabolism, place thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier elements under each bank/HBM die region, pump heat from idle banks into active ones' sinks to hold idle banks 15-25 C cooler, and let the refresh controller stretch tREFI per bank from its temperature sensor.
why: Leakage roughly halves every 8-10 C, so idle banks get 2-4x longer refresh intervals, cutting refresh power (16-33% of idle) by ~50-75%.

title: Leaky-integrate-and-fire timestamps let sense references track decay
idea: Neurons integrate with a known membrane time constant; store a 3-4 bit coarse refresh timestamp per row in a sidecar column, and have the sense-amp reference DAC slide with elapsed time to follow the expected droop of '1's and creep of '0's, so a half-decayed cell still resolves.
why: Tracking margin over time stretches usable retention ~1.5-2.5x, cutting refresh rate ~50%.
note: Time-based sliding reference; same decay-tracking reference core.

title: Pneumatized bird-bone air-gap spacers isolate wordlines from storage nodes
idea: Bird bones are hollowed by air sacs; in vertical-channel BEOL DRAM, fill the gaps between adjacent wordlines and storage-node contacts with sacrificial polynorbornene that decomposes at 350-400 C through a porous cap, leaving sealed air gaps (k=1).
why: Cuts wordline-to-node coupling ~3x, so the passing-gate row-hammer threshold rises ~3-5x and neighbor-field GIDL falls; wordline capacitance and CV2 drop ~30%.
note: Same air-gap spacer concept via sacrificial polymer.

title: Plasmodesmata junctionless access channels need no dopant activation
idea: Plant cells connect through continuous plasmodesmata channels that callose closes by squeezing; build the access device as a junctionless, uniformly n-doped 3-5 nm channel (in-situ doped In2O3 or poly-Ge:P deposited at 350 C) that a wrap gate fully depletes to turn off.
why: With no p-n junctions there is no >900 C activation anneal and no junction GIDL or trap-assisted junction leakage, often the dominant tail component, so tail leakage drops ~10x within 400 C.
note: Same junctionless access concept with low-temp oxide channel.

title: Synaptic-vesicle charge packets shifted by bucket brigade to edge amplifiers
idea: Instead of a sense amp on every bitline pair, the activated row's charges move as discrete packets (like vesicles to a release site) through CCD-style transfer gates under each bitline. They reach a few high-quality correlated amplifiers at the mat edge, which digitize and write back by reverse transfer.
why: Fact 7: one amplifier per ~32 bitlines cuts sense-amp stripe area ~70% (~12-15% of the die). Random latency gets worse, so it suits streaming/AI-weight memory tiers.

title: Stomatal back-gate planes seal every 3D tier when idle
idea: Give each tier of a lateral-transistor 3D DRAM a buried conductive back-gate plane under its channel layer, driven strongly negative when that tier's banks are idle and relaxed during access, like stomata closing at night, using the plane's large capacitance as a slow low-power control.
why: Leakage tail and refresh: deep back-bias trims the off-current tail 10-100x in idle tiers, stretching refresh 10x+ and cutting refresh's 16-33% share of idle power.

title: Hornbeam-leaf fold stacking replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Hornbeam leaves fold along pleats inside the bud and open intact. Mount thinned DRAM dies on a roll-to-roll printed polyimide flex with fine copper wiring and fold it accordion-style so each die connects through the fold edge, giving an 8-16 die stack with no TSVs.
why: Avoids the TSV tax (~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss in HBM); wide fold-edge buses can give HBM-class bandwidth at lower cost.
note: Folded-flex die stacking is old packaging art; fold-edge I/O density far below TSV/hybrid bond.

title: Nephron countercurrent coolant loops through stacked DRAM tiers
idea: Microchannels in alternating DRAM tiers carry coolant in opposite directions, like the loop of Henle, so the hot outlet of one layer sits beside the cold inlet of the next and every die sees nearly the same temperature. The whole stack stays below 85 C, the point where DRAM refresh rate doubles.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and stack height: avoids 2x refresh in hot upper tiers and allows 16-24-high stacks beside 1 kW accelerators; ~10-20% refresh energy and bandwidth recovered.

title: Electric-eel series stack: voltage-stacked HBM tiers
idea: An electric eel sums voltage by stacking thousands of electrocytes in series. Likewise HBM tiers are wired in electrical series: the package supplies ~8-12 V, the same current passes down through each tier at ~1.1 V each, and small on-die push-pull regulators balance the tiers. Supply current, and with it the power TSV count and IR drop, falls about N-fold.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and power delivery: power TSVs and bumps fall ~8x for an 8-high stack, freeing area, raising yield and cutting package I^2R loss.

title: Pluripotent wafer bank: hold half-processed wafers to differentiate later
idea: Stem cells stay undifferentiated until signals commit their fate. Fabs run wafers through common front-end steps (isolation, buried wordline, periphery transistors) and bank them, then finish them as DDR5, LPDDR or HBM core dies once demand is clear.
why: Cuts response time from ~12 weeks to ~4 weeks and reduces misallocated bits during shortages by ~10%.
note: Different products differ in floorplan from early masks; only works within a shared die design.

title: DNA-replication templating: nanoimprint masters replace EUV for cell arrays
idea: DNA copies itself by templating from a master strand. Capacitorless cell arrays are laid out on regular gratings that nanoimprint lithography reproduces from e-beam-written masters cloned into daughter templates, removing EUV from the array layers.
why: Removes the single-supplier EUV dependency and 5-7 EUV layers; imprint tools cost ~1/3 as much.

title: Hodgkin-Huxley NDR bistable cell: transistor plus tunnel-diode pair
idea: Sodium channels give the membrane an N-shaped I-V curve, which makes it bistable. A Goto pair of tunnel or resonant-tunneling diodes latches a node into one of two stable states behind one access transistor, using an Esaki-junction module added to a logic process.
why: SRAM-like unlimited endurance and no refresh with 2-3 devices per cell instead of 6, and no capacitor; standby current is the risk.
note: Echoes 1990s TI tunneling SRAM; standby current versus speed tradeoff and Si Esaki PVCR are the doubts.

title: Goto's parametron revived: bits as oscillation phase in pumped nanoresonators
idea: The 1950s parametron stored a bit as the 0 or pi phase of a parametrically pumped resonator; build rows of ~200-nm GHz NEMS beams (or compact LC tanks) driven at 2f by one shared row pump, so parametric bistability holds the phase while pumped and reading is a nondestructive phase comparison against a reference tone.
why: Facts 1 and 3: the bit is a dynamical state, not stored charge, so there is no capacitor and no refresh; pump power (~nW per high-Q resonator) beats 46 fJ/bit refresh only for Q>1e4, so it suits hot-buffer tiers rather than bulk capacity.
note: Same parametron revival.

title: Vacuum-flask isolation: hydrogen-anneal voids float storage junctions above nothing
idea: A thermos keeps heat in by surrounding it with nothing. Etch a dense array of tiny holes with Cl2/HBr plasma beneath each storage-node region and anneal in H2 at ~1100 C so silicon surface migration seals them into a continuous buried void ('empty space in silicon'); the storage junction sits on vacuum, with no HF release etch or fluorinated gas.
why: Eliminates most of the junction's bottom-area depletion volume and its generation leakage toward the substrate (fact 3): ~2-5x lower junction leakage.

title: MEMS bulk-micromachining: TMAH crystallographic etch makes atomically smooth access pillars
idea: MEMS fabs carve mirror-flat silicon walls along slow-etching crystal planes with alkaline TMAH, no plasma. Define vertical access pillars with an amorphous-carbon hard mask opened in O2 plasma, rough-etch with Cl2/HBr, then finish sidewalls in dilute TMAH so channel faces terminate on crystal planes, replacing SF6/fluorocarbon etch and its damage and polymer residue.
why: Plasma-damaged, rough sidewalls set Dit in 4F2 vertical transistors; crystallographic faces could cut Dit 3-10x and tighten Vt spread, shrinking the leakage tail (fact 3) while dropping PFAS-class etch gases.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: nanoimprint wordline gratings with diamond-like-carbon release, not fluorosilanes
idea: Records are stamped from a master in seconds instead of each being cut. Pattern dense wordline and active-line gratings by UV nanoimprint from a master mold coated with hydrogenated diamond-like carbon as the anti-stick layer, using a PFAS-free acrylate resist, O2 plasma descum and Cl2/HBr transfer etch in place of fluorosilane release layers and PFAS photoacid generators.
why: Cuts EUV/immersion passes and capital (fact 4); master-replicated lines avoid stochastic EUV line-edge roughness, narrowing the access-transistor Vt and leakage tail (fact 3).
note: NIL for memory already pursued; defectivity and overlay limits.

title: Microwave oven annealing: low-temperature regrowth of storage junction damage
idea: Microwave ovens heat what absorbs, not the whole kitchen. Activate storage-node dopants and regrow amorphized silicon by 2.45/5.8 GHz microwave annealing at 400-500 C, where dipole-assisted solid-phase epitaxy avoids the end-of-range loops and diffusion of spike anneals, replacing the fluorine co-implants used to suppress those defects.
why: Fewer end-of-range dislocation loops near the junction shrinks the generation-leakage tail (fact 3); the low temperature also suits monolithically stacked tiers (fact 2).

title: MicroLED mass transfer of known-good DRAM micro-tiles
