title: Locksmith's deadbolt: separate per-row hold gate on vertical channels
idea: A locksmith throws the deadbolt only when the house is empty. Each vertical access pillar gets a second gate on its back face, tied per row: idle rows hold it at -1.5 V for a very high threshold, and it is released to 0 V ~2 ns before that row activates, so the front wordline needs no negative off level and its GIDL disappears.
why: Separates 'hold' from 'switch': ~0.3 V higher idle threshold (about 5 decades less subthreshold leakage) without the GIDL penalty, cutting refresh ~5-10x and permitting a lower wordline high level.
note: Back-gated vertical-channel DRAM already explored by major vendors.

title: Pendulum maker's LC-resonant wordlines recycle their own swing
idea: A pendulum keeps swinging because energy trades between height and speed. Each bank's wordline drivers share an interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the selected wordline's capacitance; the wordline rises and falls on a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground, with the pump only topping up losses.
why: A ~3 V wordline fed by ~30%-efficient pumps is a large share of activate energy (fact 10); 85-90% recovery with no pump loss cuts wordline energy ~10x per access.

title: Canal-lock charge transfer between local and global bitlines
idea: A farmer moves water uphill with locks, not pumps. A short 64-cell local bitline gets a high charge-share ratio, then a clocked PMOS charge-transfer gate (the 'lock') moves that packet onto a pre-biased global bitline in two staged transfers, multiplying voltage by the capacitance ratio before one shared SA latches.
why: Raises effective signal 3-5x without a bigger capacitor, letting one SA serve 8 local segments and easing the ~5 fF Cs requirement (facts 1, 7).

title: Chef's early taste: column read from half-resolved sense amps
idea: A chef tastes before the dish is done. A small comparator on the local I/O pair reads the SA nodes once they split by ~150 mV and sends data down the column path while the main latch keeps restoring cells; a late-flip detector cancels the burst in the rare disagreement.
why: Trims ~3-5 ns (~25%) off tRCD and lets SA transistors be weaker and smaller because restore leaves the critical path (fact 7).

title: Canary rows for row hammer: deliberately weak sentinel cells
idea: Miners carried canaries because they faint first. Every 32 rows include a sentinel row with smaller capacitors holding a known pattern; the SA stripe checks the sentinels when their neighbors activate, and a sentinel flip triggers targeted refresh nearby before real data can flip.
why: Senses real disturbance instead of counting activations, adapting to each die's actual ~1k hammer threshold (fact 9) at ~3% area, transparent to the bus.

title: Termite mound chimneys: convective cooling shafts through tall stacks
idea: Termites cool their mounds with vertical chimneys. Etch dummy vertical shafts every ~200 um through the 3D array stack and fill them with a sealed two-phase working fluid (micro heat pipes) that carries heat to a top cold plate.
why: Retention roughly doubles for every ~10C cooler. Holding inner tiers ~20C cooler cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~4x and allows taller stacks (Fact 3).
note: In-chip microfluidics studied (ICECool); shaft area and sealing two-phase fluid in stacks are costs.

title: Potter fires a reusable silicon nitride crucible for twenty pulls
idea: Persona: a potter who reuses kiln furniture. Replace single-use fused-quartz crucibles with dense reaction-bonded Si3N4 crucibles that carry a renewable sprayed Si3N4/SiO2 release coat, each reused for 10-20 pulls. Dose oxygen into the melt on purpose from a small sacrificial silica rod instead of relying on crucible dissolution.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz use per wafer 10-20x and decouples oxygen control from crucible wear.

title: Waterless-planet alien cleans DRAM wafers with no liquid at all
idea: Persona: an alien from a dry world. Replace RCA and SPM wet cleans with a dry sequence: anhydrous HF/alcohol vapor oxide strip, UV-ozone organics removal, and cryogenic argon/nitrogen aerosol jets for particles. Dry the high-AR capacitor arrays with supercritical CO2 so they do not collapse.
why: Cuts ultrapure water ~50-60% and wet chemicals. Supercritical drying also removes stiction collapse of 70:1 pillars, a yield gain.

title: Rice farmer refines husk ash into crucible-grade silica
idea: Persona: a rice farmer whose husk ash is ~90% amorphous silica. Acid-leach the ash, then hot-chlorinate it at ~1200 C to volatilize alkali, Fe, Al and B as chlorides. Vacuum-fuse the purified powder into HPQ-substitute crucible sand, sourced from U.S. rice states (~1 Mt of husk per year).
why: Quartz chokepoint: an agricultural waste stream replaces Spruce Pine sand, if purity reaches <10 ppm metals.

title: Child says rust holds the magnet: hematite pins MRAM, not iridium
idea: Persona: a child notices that rusty nails still stick. Replace the IrMn antiferromagnetic pinning layer in MTJ stacks with an epitaxial alpha-Fe2O3 (hematite) or NiO film, deposited by reactive sputtering. Its exchange bias pins the reference layer.
why: Non-volatile MRAM without its scarcest element: world iridium supply is ~7 t/yr. The insulating pin layer also reduces shunting.
note: NiO/hematite exchange bias used in early spin valves; thermal stability in scaled MTJs is the question.

title: 2050 engineer drives MRAM with orbital currents in titanium
idea: Persona: a 2050 engineer who sees heavy-metal spin-Hall layers as a detour. Write SOT-MRAM with the orbital Hall effect of the light metals Ti and Cr, converting orbital current to torque through a 1 nm Ni insertion layer. The beta-W, Pt and Ta underlayers disappear.
why: Non-volatile SOT-MRAM without tungsten (China ~80%) or Pt. Low-resistivity Ti also cuts write energy.

title: Venusian alien builds silicon-carbide DRAM that remembers for years
idea: Persona: an alien from scorching Venus picks wide-bandgap silicon carbide. Build a 4H-SiC access transistor and buried capacitor. Intrinsic carrier density in SiC is ~1e-8 cm-3, so leakage falls many orders of magnitude below silicon's and charge persists for years unpowered. Uses U.S.-made SiC wafers.
why: Refresh-free, quasi-non-volatile DRAM that removes refresh energy (fact 3). Made from abundant Si and C. Risk: SiC/SiO2 interface traps.

title: Hibernation zoologist: server memory that sleeps with the grid
idea: Persona: a zoologist who studies hibernation. With non-volatile main memory, whole racks drop to zero power in seconds and resume instantly when renewable supply returns. Datacenters then follow solar and wind curves and sell demand response instead of holding batteries and diesel.
why: Energy input: less firmed power is needed, along with fewer Li and Pb UPS batteries, and the 16-33% idle refresh power disappears.
note: Depends on a non-volatile main memory that does not yet exist.

title: Child's LEGO stamp: nanoimprint the three most periodic array layers
idea: A child asks why you photograph the same honeycomb billions of times instead of stamping it. Replace EUV on the most periodic array layers (active-area lines, buried wordline, storage-node landing-pad holes) with jet-and-flash UV nanoimprint fed by a master-daughter template tree (one e-beam master spawns ~1,000 replicas, each good for ~10k wafers); DUV keeps the periphery.
why: Removes ~3 of 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4); an imprint tool is ~1/5 the price and ~1/10 the power of an EUV scanner; claim ~8-12% lower wafer cost and less single-supplier exposure. Risks: defectivity and overlay at 12 nm.
note: Canon J-FIL with replica templates is the known approach.

title: 2050 engineer's bottom-up fab: area-selective deposition replaces cut masks
idea: From 2050, deposit-everywhere-then-etch looks wasteful. Use area-selective ALD with inhibitor monolayers (aminosilane SAMs or small-molecule inhibitors that block dielectric so films grow only on metal) to grow landing pads, caps and self-aligned vias only where the layer below already defines them, deleting separate cut/block masks and their overlay budget.
why: Removes ~6-10 of ~60 mask steps and their overlay error, giving lower litho capex and ~10% fewer process days. Risk: selectivity is lost beyond ~5-10 nm of growth, so periodic etch-back cycles are needed.

title: Cell biologist's membranes: block-copolymer self-assembly below 250 C
idea: Cell membranes self-organize into 4 nm bilayers with no instructions. Coat a high-chi silicon-containing block copolymer (e.g., PS-b-PDMS) into coarse DUV guide trenches; a 200-250 C thermal or solvent-vapor anneal self-assembles 8-10 nm half-pitch hole and line arrays, which transfer as hard masks for array layers.
why: Replaces 2-3 EUV or quad-patterning passes with a ~$2M coater and hotplate, all inside 400 C. Risks: defect density (target <0.01/cm2) and placement error.

title: Bedouin water reuse: resonant LC charge recovery on memory buses
idea: A desert nomad never pours water away: place spiral inductors on the interposer that resonate with each memory bus's capacitance, so energy sloshes back and forth between bit transitions instead of being dumped to ground at every edge.
why: Recovers ~60-70% of CV2 bus energy on HBM/DDR links (3-20 pJ/bit today); this is the voltage-floor problem solved in the interface instead of the cell.
note: Same resonant bus charge-recovery mechanism.

title: Honeybees fan the hive: thin-film thermoelectric cooler under DRAM
idea: Worker bees fan to cool the brood: embed a thin-film Bi2Te3 thermoelectric cooler in the interposer directly under the DRAM stack only, pumping it 15-20 C below the 125 C package while the logic runs hot.
why: DRAM at ~105 C instead of 125 C has about 4x longer retention, so it needs about 4x less refresh energy and loses less bandwidth; the TEC power is spent only on the memory footprint.

title: Ant pheromone counter: analog leaky integrator tracks hammering per row
idea: Ants mark trails with pheromone that evaporates: each row gets one extra capacitor that a charge pump tops up by a fixed quantum per activation and that leaks with a designed 10-60 ms time constant; when its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the neighbor rows are refreshed, so the hammer rate is measured physically with no SRAM counters.
why: Fact 9 row hammer: about one cell's worth of area per row instead of large counter tables, and it scales to 1k-activation thresholds.
note: Same leaky integrator.

title: Field-immune antiferromagnetic Neel-vector bit for EMP-hardened military memory
idea: EMP-hardened systems need storage unaffected by external fields, so the bit is the Neel vector of a noncollinear antiferromagnet such as Mn3Sn, switched by spin-orbit torque in ~10-100 ps and read through its anomalous Hall or tunnel magnetoresistance. Zero stray field lets cells pack at minimum pitch without dipolar crosstalk.
why: Unlimited endurance, non-volatile, picosecond writes potentially below DRAM CV2 energy (fact 10); removes refresh entirely; small readout signal is the main risk.
note: Same Mn3Sn SOT bit framed for an EMP-hardened niche.

title: Reactor surveillance-capsule canary cells that age ahead of the array
idea: Reactor vessels carry test specimens placed to age faster than the vessel itself. Put canary cells in every bank with deliberately weakened isolation (shorter gate, thinner spacer, higher junction field) so they lose data and wear 3-5x faster; the controller sets refresh from when canaries fail, tracking a 30-year industrial life.
why: Fact 3: replaces a worst-case-plus-margin 64 ms schedule with a measured, aging-aware one, typically 2-4x less refresh early in life while staying safe as traps accumulate.

title: Phone-sleep charge overdrive: boosted restore before self-refresh
idea: Phones spend >90% of their time in standby. When memory enters self-refresh, write back every row once with the array voltage boosted ~1.3x (and wordline boost to pass it), storing ~30% more charge so cells take longer to droop to the sense threshold, then self-refresh at a proportionally slower rate.
why: Fact 3: ~1.5-2x lower self-refresh rate in standby, the phone's biggest DRAM energy term; dielectric stress and higher leakage at high stored voltage limit it to sleep only.

title: Hearing-aid tunnel-FET access device with sub-60 mV/dec switching
idea: Zinc-air hearing aids run near 1.2 V, which pushes designers toward band-to-band tunneling switches. Use a vertical heterojunction TFET (Ge source, Si channel in the pillar) as the access device: its modest on-current still charges 5 fF in ~10 ns, and its steep slope lets the wordline swing shrink while off-current falls to sub-fA.
why: Facts 3 and 10: wordline swing ~3 V to ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV^2) and ~10x smaller leakage tail; drain-side ambipolar leakage must be suppressed with asymmetric doping.

title: Implant-free Schottky source/drain access devices from flexible electronics
idea: Flexible electronics cannot use high-temperature implant anneals, so they rely on Schottky metal contacts. Build the DRAM access transistor with silicide Schottky source and drain (no junction implants, no activation anneal), accepting its higher thermionic off-leakage and a 1% raw BER from the weakest cells.
why: Facts 2 and 4: drops implant and anneal steps and allows low-temperature access devices in stacked 3D tiers, easing a 3D DRAM blocker; refresh at the 1% quantile keeps refresh near today's level.
note: Schottky MOSFETs known; higher thermionic leakage works against retention.

title: Particle-detector charge amplifier holds bitline at virtual ground
idea: Like LHC pixel ASICs that read ~1000-electron hits in 25 ns, each sense stripe uses a folded-cascode charge-sensitive amplifier that clamps the bitline at virtual ground and integrates the full cell charge onto a ~1 fF feedback capacitor, so the output is Qcell/Cf instead of Qcell/(Cs+Cbl). Bitline capacitance drops out of the signal equation.
why: Charge wall and periphery area: a signal independent of Cbl lets bitlines be 2-4x longer (2-4x fewer SAs, ~10-15% die saved) or Cs ~3x smaller.

title: Telegraph-style regenerative repeaters halve effective bitline capacitance
idea: Undersea telegraph cables used repeaters to regenerate signals along long spans; a 4-transistor regenerative latch at each bitline's midpoint isolates the far segment, amplifies the near-segment signal, then drives the far segment, so each cell sees half the bitline capacitance.
why: Doubles cells per SA or doubles signal, so relaxed-pitch DUV arrays stay viable with 2x longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Thermal-cycling satellite stack with doped-silicon vias, no copper or tungsten
idea: Satellites cycle -150 to +120 C and copper vias crack silicon through CTE mismatch; build through-tier and through-die vias from degenerately doped epitaxial or poly silicon and fusion-bond Si to Si, so the whole stack is one CTE-matched material. Vias are fat but short because tiers are thinned to a few um.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) from vias and Cu-pumping keep-out zones, shrinking the TSV area tax (fact 6) ~2x and raising stack reliability.
note: Poly-Si vias exist in MEMS; resistivity ~600x Cu limits power delivery.

title: $1-IoT block-copolymer pillar arrays guided by UV-LED exposure
idea: A $1 IoT memory needs dense pillars at near-zero patterning cost; spin a cylinder-forming block copolymer that self-assembles into a hexagonal ~22 nm pitch lattice of vertical-channel transistor sites, registered by coarse 200 nm guide posts printed with a 365 nm UV-LED stepper instead of a mercury-xenon lamp or excimer laser. Hexagonal packing gives slightly better than 4F2 density.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4) without EUV or rare-gas light sources; 4F2-class pillar arrays at <10% of EUV patterning cost.

title: 300-layer NAND edge case: area-selective ALD molybdenum wordlines
idea: The tallest 3D NAND stacks already fill wordlines by CVD; take this further for 3D DRAM tiers with area-selective ALD molybdenum (MoCl5/H2 with nitrogen purge) that nucleates only on exposed seed edges in recessed lateral cavities while a self-assembled inhibitor blocks the oxide. No argon-sputtered liner, no tungsten and no wordline-isolation patterning step.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and argon PVD; void-free low-resistance lateral wordlines allow thinner tiers and more of them (fact 2).
note: Mo ALD wordlines already shipping in NAND; area-selective twist is minor.

title: Giant-display lesson: blue diode lasers crystallize silicon for stacked tiers
idea: Gen-10 display fabs crystallize silicon over square meters with XeCl excimer lasers that consume xenon and neon; replace them with line-scanned 450 nm GaN diode-laser arrays to melt-crystallize thin amorphous silicon (PECVD in SiH4/H2) on top of each finished DRAM tier. The heat stays in ~100 nm, so lower tiers stay below 400 C while the new tier gets large-grain channels for its access transistors.
why: Monolithic tier stacking (fact 2) without a bond per tier and without xenon or neon; ~200 cm2/Vs channels for 3D cells.

title: Rocket regenerative cooling: microchannels between bonded tiers allow 32-high
idea: Rocket nozzles survive by pumping coolant through channels in their own walls; wet-etch (TMAH, no plasma) 20 um microchannels into the backside of every fourth thinned DRAM die and bond with nitrogen-plasma-activated oxide instead of argon activation, so dielectric coolant flows through the stack and pulls heat from inside. Stacks grow to 24-32 high while staying below 85 C.
why: Layer count is thermally limited: cooler DRAM cuts refresh 2-4x (fact 3) and doubles capacity per stack, with argon-free bond activation.

title: Sanctioned-fab rule: film-thickness-defined cell replaces litho-defined pitch
idea: Design for a country cut off from EUV, ArF and neon: rotate the cell so every critical dimension is a deposited film thickness (channel length is an epitaxial layer, gate length a wordline film, cell pitch the tier pitch), and the only lithography is a 0.5 um UV-LED step that cuts slits and staircases. The cell is a lateral transistor plus lateral capacitor in each tier, like a rotated 3D NAND page.
why: Removes litho-bound scaling and EUV capital (fact 4): density comes from 64-100 tiers at 0.5 um lithography, roughly halving the 55% depreciation share.

title: Kerfless-solar epitaxial lift-off: crucible-free crystalline tiers from reusable parents
idea: Kerfless solar startups grow epitaxial silicon on porous-silicon release layers and peel it, reusing the parent wafer many times; grow 1 um device-grade epi in H2-carrier trichlorosilane on a porous parent, bond it onto the finished DRAM stack, cleave at the porous layer to form the next tier, and re-porosify the parent for ~50 reuses. This replaces smart-cut, whose co-implants often use helium.
why: Spruce Pine quartz-crucible dependence cut ~50x per tier, crystalline bonded tiers for 3D DRAM (fact 2), helium-free.
note: ELTRAN-style porous Si transfer is known art; per-tier bonding cost remains.

title: Hurricane-proof quartz: chlorination-upgraded vein quartz from five countries
idea: Hurricane Helene's 2024 shutdown of Spruce Pine is the extreme edge case: design crucible supply to survive it. Upgrade ordinary hydrothermal vein and pegmatite quartz (Norway, Brazil, India, Quebec, Arizona) by 1200 C Cl2/HCl gas leaching plus electrodiffusion 'sweeping', the field-driven alkali removal used for oscillator-grade quartz, to reach <10 ppm total impurities.
why: Second-sources the >80% single-region HPQ chokepoint through geographic diversity instead of reliance on one ore body.

title: Kerfless solar trick: epi DRAM wafers lifted off reusable porous-silicon parents
idea: Kerfless solar firms grow epitaxial wafers on porous-silicon release layers and reuse the parent wafer dozens of times. For DRAM, grow a 20-50 um device-grade epi layer on double-porous Si, bond it to a cheap carrier (UMG or recycled Si), split it off, and repolish the CZ parent for 10-20 reuses.
why: Only the top few um of a DRAM wafer are active: cuts prime CZ silicon, HPQ crucibles and polysilicon per bit ~10x.

title: Satellite-lidar solid-state 193 nm source frees lithography from neon
idea: Spaceborne UV instruments cannot carry gas bottles, so they use frequency-multiplied solid-state lasers. Build a 193 nm source from a high-power Yb fiber laser and an OPO mixed through a CLBO sum-frequency cascade, sized for non-critical ArF-dry and periphery layers.
why: Excimer lasers depend on neon and krypton, historically ~50% from Ukraine/Russia: this removes rare-gas consumption and laser-gas refill downtime.

title: Deposit-only cell flow by area-selective ALD with alkyl inhibitors
idea: Extreme user: an ISS-style orbital fab with almost no etch gases. Grow lines and plugs only where wanted, using non-fluorinated alkyl-silane or aminosilane inhibitor monolayers that block ALD on the dielectric, with brief Cl-based atomic-layer etch-back to clean stray nuclei.
why: Litho/capital: self-aligned additive growth removes ~2 etch+litho loops per level and fixes overlay error at critical contacts.

title: Mars-perchlorate Cl2/O2 cyclic deep etch revives silicon trench capacitors
idea: Extreme user: a Mars fab where perchlorate soil yields chlorine but not fluorine. Etch deep trench capacitors into crystalline silicon with alternating HBr/Cl2 etch and O2 sidewall-oxidation passivation cycles (a chlorine Bosch process), then line them with ALD ZrO2/TiN.
why: Capacitor wall: the trench uses silicon depth under the cell (AR 80:1 possible) instead of a tall oxide mold, freeing surface for 3D stacking with no fluorocarbon gas.

title: Desert-fab supercritical CO2 cleans replace ultrapure-water wet benches
idea: Extreme user: an Arizona fab with almost no water. Replace RCA/SPM wet cleans with supercritical CO2 plus alcohol/amine co-solvents and cryogenic CO2-aerosol particle removal, with residues stripped dry and CO2 recaptured.
why: Water/capital: cuts ultrapure-water demand ~50% and the UPW plant capex; no fluorinated surfactants or HF; no wet-drying pattern collapse.

title: Implant body-channel trick: send memory data over power planes
idea: Implants use the body itself as the wire (intra-body communication). Superimpose low-amplitude multi-GHz carriers on the stack's power/ground TSV network and separate them on each die with on-die band-pass filters, so power TSVs double as data channels.
why: Power and ground take a large share of HBM TSVs and bumps; reusing them adds ~1.5-2x signal capacity without more TSVs, easing the TSV tax.

title: Qubit-fridge FDM: dozens of memory channels on one trace
idea: Quantum computers frequency-multiplex qubit readout because fridge wires are precious. Carry 16-32 memory channels as QAM subcarriers on one wideband line with integrated mm-wave mixers at both ends, so a far memory module needs a few lines instead of hundreds of pins.
why: Cuts pin, beachfront and routing cost ~10x for capacity tiers, letting memory sit on cheap remote boards; the trade is mixer power.

title: Put SiC fab overcapacity to work on wide-bandgap, near-refresh-free DRAM
idea: Downhole and EV users built SiC fabs that now have spare capacity. 4H-SiC's 3.2 eV bandgap cuts storage-node leakage so far that 1990s SiC DRAM cells held charge for hours; build SiC-MOS 1T1C arrays on underused U.S. SiC lines for refresh-free memory tiers.
why: Attacks refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and U.S. supply with idle 150/200 mm SiC lines; density is far lower, so it starts in niche or slow tiers.

title: Gen-10.5 display fabs print 1T1C memory panels
idea: Scale up from wafer to 3 m glass: every LCD pixel is already a TFT plus storage capacitor, so retool display fabs to print oxide-TFT 1T1C arrays at ~1 um rules across whole panels, diced into far-memory tiles.
why: Capital intensity and US manufacturability: panel cost ~$100-300/m2 makes a slower capacity tier at single-digit $/GB with no EUV and no Spruce Pine crucibles.
note: Same display-fab memory idea; single-digit $/GB claim optimistic.

title: Nanomechanical parametron stores bits as oscillation phase
idea: Revive Goto's 1954 parametron at nanoscale and GHz: a doubly clamped SiC beam pumped at twice its resonance oscillates in one of two phases (0 or pi), which is the bit; the pump sustains it every cycle and neighboring beams couple to shift data.
why: Endurance and leakage: no charge to leak and no wear-out; logic and memory share one element.
note: Same parametron phase memory.

title: Photonic-crystal nanocavity bistable bits held by bias light
idea: Shift storage into photon lifetime: an InP photonic-crystal nanocavity with carrier-plasma bistability sits on a shared continuous bias beam, and the bit is the high or low intracavity energy state; a pulse flips it.
why: Data movement: memory lives in the optical domain beside photonic interconnect, with ~fJ switching.
note: NTT demonstrated photonic-crystal nanocavity RAM; continuous bias power and density limit it.

title: Magnetic core memory reborn as 100 nm nanorings
idea: Shrink 1950s ferrite cores from mm to nm: CoFe nanorings store the bit as clockwise or counterclockwise vortex chirality, written by coincident current pulses in vertical through-wires and read by an embedded MTJ.
why: Endurance and stray-field-free density: flux-closure chirality is immune to neighbors; no capacitor and nonvolatile.
note: Vortex-ring MRAM proposed in the 2000s; coincident-current write limits density.

title: Resonant LC wordline drivers recycle refresh energy
idea: Time shift that exploits refresh's metronome-like periodicity: because refresh activations arrive on a fixed cadence, refresh wordlines and sense-amp enables are driven from an on-package LC tank tuned to that cadence, swinging the ~3 V wordline adiabatically and returning ~60-70% of the CV^2 charge to the tank instead of dumping it from a charge pump.
why: Refresh energy and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): wordline boost pumps are ~30-40% efficient, so adiabatic driving cuts refresh wordline energy ~3x, borrowing resonant clocking from CPUs.

title: Charge-plasma junctions: abundant-metal work functions replace implanted dopants
idea: Scale shift from implanted dopant atoms to an electric field: the access transistor's source/drain are induced electrostatically by low-work-function Mg- or Al-capped contacts (~3.7-4.1 eV) beside an undoped Si channel gated by a NiSi/TiN gate, so no metallurgical p-n junction sits at the storage node, which is the main seat of junction and trap-assisted leakage.
why: Junction leakage tail (fact 3): removes implant damage and dopant-related traps, ~5-10x lower junction leakage; no Hf, W or Co.

title: Floating-diffusion charge-transfer readout for sub-femtofarad slow tier
idea: Scale-shift the image-sensor floating diffusion into DRAM and slow it down: a gated transfer transistor moves the bitline's charge onto a ~0.05 fF sense node over ~200-500 ns, giving voltage gain of ~Cbl/Cfd, which makes 0.3-0.5 fF planar cells readable as a ~1 us capacity tier.
why: No high-AR capacitor (fact 1) and fewer HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); ~2-3x bits per mask set for a capacity tier behind HBM.
note: Slow capacity-tier twist; kT/C on 0.05 fF node and transfer-device Vt variation.

title: Twenty-nanosecond excimer pulses crystallize each tier without cooking those below
idea: Shift the thermal timescale from hour-long furnace anneals to 20-ns XeCl excimer pulses, a 1990s LTPS display tool: deposit amorphous Si for each new tier and melt-recrystallize it in nanoseconds so heat never reaches the tiers below. Stack 16-32 poly-Si 1T1C tiers this way.
why: Thermal budget blocks sequential 3D (fact 2): monolithic tiers become possible with display-era tools.
note: LTPS-grade poly-Si leakage is poor for DRAM retention.

title: Porous-silicon template wafers spawn fifty epitaxial DRAM wafers each
idea: Scale shift from the 775 um wafer to the ~5 um a DRAM array actually uses. Anodize a reusable CZ template to form a double-porosity seam, grow 10-20 um of epitaxial Si on it, bond to a low-grade carrier, and lift off along the seam. Re-polish the template and reuse it 50 or more times.
why: Cuts prime CZ silicon and high-purity quartz crucible use per DRAM wafer by ~10-50x. Oxygen-lean epi silicon may also tighten the retention-leakage tail.

title: Surface chemistry inherits one mask through four self-aligned layers
idea: Shift patterning from the reticle to the monolayer: after a single bitline exposure, small-molecule inhibitors (aminosilanes on oxide, thiols on metal) bind to only one surface type, so area-selective ALD grows plugs, landing pads and caps exactly on prior features with no new masks.
why: Removes 3-4 masks and their overlay budget per array (~10% fewer litho passes) and cuts edge-placement failures (Fact 4).

title: MicroLED-style mass transfer of 100 um DRAM micro-tiles onto panels
idea: Borrow microLED mass transfer: release 100 um DRAM micro-tiles from the wafer by undercut etch and pick 10,000 at once with elastomer stamps onto large panels carrying RDL and logic chiplets.
why: Panel-scale assembly cuts packaging cost per bit 3-5x and harvests good tiles from every wafer at near-100% (Fact 6).

title: Arizona panel-level fan-out replaces TSV stacks for HBM bandwidth
idea: Scale from wafer to 600 mm panels: thin DRAM dies are placed face-down side by side on panels with ~1.5 um-line RDL made on domestic 1X panel steppers, routing ultra-wide buses laterally to the accelerator instead of through TSV stacks.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6: 3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss); square panels use ~90% of area vs ~60% for round wafers.

title: Free in-DRAM row copy unlocks aggressive copy-on-write sharing
idea: In-subarray row copy (RowClone-style back-to-back activation) breaks copy-on-write in about 90 ns instead of a microsecond page copy over the bus. With the time cost of unsharing 10x lower, the OS shares far more aggressively: fork-heavy servers, VM clones, database snapshots, and pages with short expected sharing lifetimes.
why: When unsharing is nearly free in time, sharing pays off even for short-lived pages. That adds 10-30% to dedup savings.

title: Single-mask polymer waveguide backplane for rack memory pooling
idea: One lithography mask patterns polymer optical waveguides directly into the rack backplane PCB. With existing co-packaged transceivers, they link 32 compute sleds to a shared memory sled. That makes rack-scale pooling cheap enough for each sled to ship with half its local DRAM.
why: Pooling recovers 25-50% stranded memory, so racks need 30-40% fewer DIMMs.
note: Polymer backplanes researched for decades; pooling gain unchanged by medium.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory backplane: 77 K copper for passive 2 m links
idea: Shift the temperature scale to change wire physics: memory sleds and backplane sit in LN2, where copper resistivity drops ~7x, so passive 2 m memory channels need no retimers or heavy equalization, and DRAM retention stretches to seconds so refresh nearly vanishes.
why: Rack-scale pooled-memory link energy drops ~3-5x and refresh (fact 3) nearly disappears, traded against cryocooling overhead.

title: Sacrificial-etch air gaps isolate adjacent wordlines from hammer
idea: No EUV: at DUV pitch, a sacrificial carbon or oxide fill between buried wordlines is removed through DUV-defined vents and sealed, leaving air gaps (k=1) that cut aggressor-victim capacitive and trap coupling.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold ~3x and lower wordline capacitance (and CV2 energy) ~20%.
note: Air gaps known in NAND and DRAM bitline spacers; hammer is mostly carrier-mediated, not capacitive.

title: Optane endurance fix: monatomic antimony that cannot segregate
idea: Optane cells wore out after ~1e7-1e8 cycles as Ge, Sb and Te segregated and voids formed during repeated melt-quench. Use pure Sb confined to a 3-4 nm film inside a carbon/SiN pore: a single element has nothing to segregate, and nanoconfinement keeps the amorphous phase stable.
why: Endurance pushed toward 1e12+ with lower reset energy from the thinner film, keeping the 4F2 stacked crosspoint density.
note: IBM showed monatomic Sb PCM; endurance still short of DRAM class.

title: Cavendish NEMS fixed: contactless bistable buckled nanobeams
idea: Cavendish Kinetics' MEMS memory died from contact stiction and wear. Use a compressively pre-stressed SiN or TiN nanobeam (~1 um x 20 nm) that Euler-buckles up or down: side electrodes snap it between the two stable shapes without it touching anything, and a capacitive or piezoresistive pickoff reads which way it bows.
why: No contact means no stiction or wear (endurance 1e15+ plausible); nonvolatile mechanical state with zero leakage or refresh; GHz-class nanobeams switch in ~ns.
note: Bistable buckled-beam NEMS memories demonstrated; micron beams limit density.

title: Optane without melting: MnTe crystal-to-crystal polymorph switching
idea: Optane's melt-quench writes burned energy, and its amorphous state drifted and recrystallized when hot. Switch MnTe between its NiAs-type and wurtzite-type crystalline polymorphs through a displacive transition with no melting: both states are crystals, so neither drifts nor crystallizes at 125 C, and the polymorphs show a large reported resistance contrast.
why: 10-year retention above 125 C with an estimated 3-10x lower write energy than melting and no resistance drift, so multi-level storage becomes viable.
note: MnTe polymorph switching already reported (Tohoku).

title: Nanocrystal variability ended: atomically identical molybdenum polyoxometalate charge nodes
idea: Freescale's silicon-nanocrystal memories and Hitachi's few-electron PLEDM died from dot-to-dot size and charge variability. Graft monodisperse Mo- or V-based polyoxometalate clusters, every one atomically identical, multi-electron redox-active and stable above 400 C, as discrete storage nodes over a 2-3 nm tunnel oxide; choosing Mo/V instead of the usual tungsten POMs dodges the W chokepoint.
why: Zero size variability with quantized multi-bit charge levels and 125 C robustness; ~1e13 nodes/cm2.
note: POM molecular flash already published (2014); thin tunnel oxide gives flash-like, not DRAM, behavior.

title: HPE memristor's wandering vacancies ordered: brownmillerite-perovskite topotactic switching
idea: TiO2 memristors failed hot because disordered oxygen vacancies diffused and filaments relaxed. Use an SrFeO2.5 brownmillerite film whose vacancies sit in ordered channels: a field converts a nanoscale region topotactically to conductive perovskite SrFeO3-d, so the two states are distinct crystal phases separated by a structural barrier rather than a diffusing cloud.
why: Phase-distinct states give 125 C/10 y retention with area-type, non-filament switching and low variability.

title: Charge-trap-trimmed sense amps: offset fixed once, transistors minimum size
idea: Failure mined: MRAM ventures such as Spin Memory could not shrink their arrays because low-TMR signals needed huge low-offset sense amps (offset scales as 1/sqrt(area)). Fix: put a nitride charge trap in each sense-amp input transistor's gate stack and program it at wafer test, with field recalibration, to null the offset. SA devices can then be minimum size, and the same trick works for DRAM sense amps.
why: Halves to quarters SA area, or lets the cell signal fall ~3x for a smaller capacitor (fact 1): ~5% of die area or a shallower capacitor.

title: HP memristor sneak paths cancelled with mirrored complementary decks
idea: HPE's memristor crossbars stalled partly because sneak currents through unselected cells swamped reads in large passive arrays. Stack two decks on one shared bitline and store each bit as complementary states in the upper and lower deck. A differential read subtracts the common-mode sneak current, so selector-less arrays can grow to 4k x 4k.
why: Larger mats spread the periphery cost (fact 7) and remove selector cost, at passive 4F2 per deck. Claims array tiles ~10x larger than selector-less crossbars allow today.

title: Forcefill revived: high-pressure aluminum extrusion replaces tungsten contact plugs
idea: Trikon's Forcefill pushed sputtered aluminum into vias with ~700 atm argon and died only because copper damascene took over logic wiring. DRAM still fills every contact and bitline plug with CVD tungsten from WF6; fill the plugs formed after the capacitor anneals with Al-Si-Cu by high-pressure extrusion over a thin TiN liner.
why: Removes tungsten (~80% China) and WF6 fluorine chemistry from back-end plugs; aluminum is abundant and smelted in North America; Al's lower resistivity in narrow plugs trims RC ~30%; argon pressure gas is plentiful.

title: Directed self-assembly confined to DRAM's honeycomb capacitor array
idea: Directed self-assembly was abandoned for logic because defect density stalled and logic layouts are not periodic. DRAM's storage-node array is a hexagonal lattice, the native pattern of cylinder-forming block copolymers, so DUV-printed guide trenches (graphoepitaxy) multiply hole density 4-7x and residual defects are absorbed by existing row/column redundancy.
why: Replaces 1-2 EUV exposures with a ~$1M coat/anneal track; cost per patterned layer down ~5x; defect spec relaxed from logic-grade to repairable-grade.

title: Asynchronous logic fixed: clockless 1-of-4 links inside the HBM stack
idea: Asynchronous design (Fulcrum, Handshake Solutions) failed because whole-chip async needed tools nobody had. Confine it to one hard IP block: the vertical links between HBM core dies and the base die use delay-insensitive 1-of-4 encoding with completion detection, so the stack needs no clock TSVs, DLLs or per-die clock trees and each die runs as fast as its process corner allows.
why: Data movement (fact 5): clock distribution and DLLs are ~20-40% of DRAM I/O power and standby current; removing them and their timing margins claims 25-35% lower in-stack I/O energy and better yield across corners.

title: TRR tracker overflow fixed with per-row analog hammer integrators
idea: Target Row Refresh died to TRRespass/Blacksmith because its few-entry aggressor table overflowed under many-sided patterns. Fix exactly that: each wordline driver gets a tiny leaky MIM capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT, a shared comparator fires a neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold, and the leak rate matches the refresh window, so there is no table to overflow or game.
why: Row hammer at ~1k ACT (fact 9): deterministic, pattern-independent protection for ~1-2% array area versus digital per-row counters and their tRC penalty; lets denser, more hammer-prone cells ship.
note: Same leaky integrator.

title: Z-RAM retention tail cancelled by differential twin floating bodies
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died when floating-body retention and disturb variability blew up at 45 nm and AMD walked away. Fix: store each bit as complementary hole charge in two adjacent floating bodies sharing a well and sense them differentially, so common-mode junction leakage and temperature-driven loss cancel and only mismatch decays.
why: Capacitor-free cell (attacks the charge wall, fact 1) with ~10x tighter retention tail at 2 transistors per bit, still smaller and simpler than 1T1C with a 70:1 pillar.
note: Twin-cell differential floating-body cells were explored by Toshiba and others.

title: HP memristor variability averaged by five-device vertical voting pillars
idea: HP's TaOx memristor program died on device-to-device variability and random forming. Fix: build five tiny switching layers in parallel along one vertical pillar so the sense amp reads their summed conductance; variability shrinks by ~sqrt(5) and one dead device costs margin, not data.
why: Tolerates ~30%-sigma devices without verify loops; in 3D the extra tiers are cheap, so density barely drops while yield rises sharply.
note: Parallel averaging known; ReRAM endurance not DRAM-class.

title: Macronix self-healing heater idea reborn as wordline Joule annealing
idea: Macronix's 2012 self-healing flash (on-chip heaters annealing oxide traps) never shipped because dedicated heaters cost area and power. Fix: use the existing buried wordline itself as the heater, so rows that ECC or scrubbing flag for rising leakage get millisecond high-current pulses that anneal the access-transistor interface traps driving the leakage tail.
why: In-field self-healing of retention and hammer-induced trap damage; shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) over life instead of letting it grow, enabling longer refresh intervals.
note: KAIST gate-electrode electro-thermal annealing is close prior art.

title: FeFET retention loss cured by capacitance-matched floating-metal MFMIS stacks
idea: 1T FeFET memory stalled because the depolarization field and interface charge trapping erase stored polarization in hours to days at temperature. Fix: insert a floating metal gate and size the ferroelectric area at 1/4-1/10 of the MOS area (MFMIS) so the ferroelectric sees almost no depolarizing field, and replace the SiO2 interlayer with a thin high-k layer to cut trapping.
why: Nonvolatile, zero-refresh 1T cell with no capacitor (fact 1); the retention tail is removed by electrostatic design rather than refresh.
note: MFMIS well studied; FeFET endurance far below DRAM-class.

title: Crossbar Inc. ReRAM stuck faults self-healed by ECC-triggered reforming
idea: Crossbar Inc. and other ReRAM ventures lost DRAM-class ambitions to stuck-at-set/reset cells that accumulate with cycling. Fix: when the decoder corrects the same bit twice, the controller fires a reverse-polarity 'reforming' pulse that dissolves the overgrown or ruptured filament and re-forms it, returning the cell to service instead of retiring it.
why: Nonvolatile and zero refresh; in-field self-healing extends usable endurance ~10x and tolerates cheaper, less uniform films.

title: Bubble memory's slowness fixed: current-driven domain-wall shift lines
idea: Bubble memory (Intel Magnetics, TI) was killed by slow field-driven bubble motion (~100 kHz) and a separate garnet process. Fix: pattern Co/Pt or CoFeB multilayer nanowires at 250 nm and above with 1990s steppers and HDD-media sputter tools, move domain walls with spin-orbit-torque current pulses (~100+ m/s), and reuse bubble memory's major/minor-loop layout and bad-loop map.
why: A non-volatile, refresh-free warm tier that takes cold pages off DRAM, built on old lines; ~10-100 ns per shift step makes block access practical.
note: Racetrack memory widely pursued; old-line build is the twist.

title: Dopant-free charge-plasma access transistor removes implant-driven leakage outliers
idea: Effect: work-function-induced charge plasma. Source/drain are induced electrostatically in an undoped channel by low-work-function (Hf-based) contacts, so there is no implanted metallurgical junction: no implant damage, no end-of-range defects and no random-dopant clusters that create the 13 fA outliers.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): narrows the retention distribution so refresh is set near the median, not the 1-ppm cell; claims 4-8x less refresh.

title: Resonant LC wordline driver recycles refresh switching energy
idea: Effect: LC resonance and adiabatic charging. During internal refresh bursts, wordlines swing through an interposer or RDL spiral inductor resonating with the wordline capacitance, returning charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground; the burst still fits inside today's tRFC. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Voltage floor and refresh energy (facts 3, 10): recovers 50-70% of 3 V wordline CV2, cutting refresh energy ~25-40%.

title: Thin-film Peltier layer in HBM base die cools the array
idea: Effect: Peltier thermoelectric cooling. Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 superlattice pads between the base logic die and the lowest DRAM die, plus over hotspot columns, pump heat to the lid only when the stack exceeds ~80 C, holding array temperature ~10 C lower (retention roughly doubles per 10 C). DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh bandwidth (fact 3): avoids the 2x refresh regime above 85 C (10-20% bandwidth); costs some pump power.

title: Nanosecond laser melt regrows defect-free storage junctions
idea: Effect: liquid-phase epitaxial regrowth. After the storage-node implant, a ~50 ns UV/green laser pulse melts only the top ~20 nm, regrowing the junction epitaxially and dissolving end-of-range dislocation loops that act as generation centres, while the short thermal budget spares buried wordlines. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 2-3x tail compression, translated into internal refresh relaxation.

title: Hot-carrier-injection trimming nulls sense-amp offset permanently at test
idea: Effect: hot-carrier charge trapping. At wafer test, a built-in ramp measures each SA's offset, then short high-Vds pulses inject hot carriers into the stronger transistor's gate oxide to raise its Vt until the pair balances within ~3 mV; the trapped charge holds for years, with an optional field top-up.
why: SA area (fact 7): offset sets SA sizing (Pelgrom), so cutting sigma from ~15 mV to ~3 mV allows ~4-10x smaller SA devices or 2x cells per bitline.

title: Zero-stray-field Mn3Sn antiferromagnetic bits packed at sub-ferromagnetic pitch
idea: Anomalous Hall effect in noncollinear antiferromagnets: Mn3Sn bits switched by spin-orbit torque are read by their large anomalous Hall or tunneling signal. Because antiferromagnets emit no dipolar stray field, neighboring bits and stacked tiers can be packed far tighter than ferromagnetic MTJs without crosstalk.
why: Gives denser non-volatile 3D packing with ps-scale switching (facts 2 and 5); claim ~2x tighter pitch per tier than ferromagnetic MRAM and field-immune bits.
note: Mn3Sn SOT switching widely pursued; small readout signal is the doubt.

title: Interfacial phase-change superlattices on vertical-bitline hole sidewalls
idea: Interfacial phase change: an ALD-deposited GeTe/Sb2Te3 superlattice switches by flipping Ge atoms at the interfaces, not by melting, cutting energy ~10x. The superlattice lines the sidewalls of vertical bitline holes crossing horizontal wordline plates, making a VRRAM-style 3D array with a single-mask hole etch.
why: Gives dense non-volatile 3D cells (fact 2) with low capital (fact 4); claim tier count scales like 3D NAND, with 10x lower switching energy than PCM.

title: Low-temperature ferroelectric tier licensing for idle US logic fabs
idea: Low-temperature orthorhombic-phase crystallization: HZO and AlScN become ferroelectric at ≤400 C, so non-volatile memory tiers can be added on top of finished logic wafers. A business would license a 'memory-tier kit' (process recipe, compiler, test IP) to US 28-65 nm fabs, turning underused capacity into memory output without a new DRAM fab.
why: Attacks US manufacturability (1-2% share) and capital intensity (fact 4); claim memory output at <10% of greenfield DRAM capex per wafer.
note: Ferroelectric endurance falls short of DRAM-class unlimited.

title: Orbital Hall torque from titanium and oxidized copper, no heavy metals
idea: Effect: the orbital Hall effect makes orbital angular-momentum currents in light metals (Ti, Cr, Cu/CuOx) with Hall conductivity rivaling Pt spin Hall. A Ti or Cu/CuOx channel plus a thin Ni orbital-to-spin conversion layer switches an MTJ free layer, building SOT-MRAM working memory with no Pt, W or Ta.
why: Scarce-metal intensity (W China ~80%, Ta conflict mineral, Pt): SOT-MRAM gives ~1-5 ns, no refresh and >1e14 endurance; if orbital torque efficiency reaches ~0.5, switching current is ~3-5x lower than with W.
note: Same orbital-torque light-metal SOT mechanism as I-07568.

title: Supercritical CO2 rinsing eliminates surface tension and ultrapure water
idea: Effect: above its critical point (31 C, 74 bar) CO2 has zero surface tension and liquid-like solvating power. Post-etch residue removal and drying of 70:1 capacitor pillars runs in recycled sCO2 with a cosolvent instead of UPW rinse and IPA dry, so capillary forces cannot collapse the pillars.
why: Water intensity (several m3 UPW per wafer) and the pillar-collapse limit on capacitor aspect ratio (fact 1), allowing taller capacitors.

title: NbO2 Mott threshold switch replaces the access transistor in BEOL crosspoint
idea: Effect: insulator-metal (Mott/Peierls) transition. An NbO2 two-terminal selector in series with a MIM capacitor is stacked in crosspoint arrays above logic at 2 masks per layer; a sub-threshold hold bias limits leakage and refresh runs in bursts.
why: Capital: no front-end transistor per bit, 4F2 per layer, and 8 layers on cheap BEOL tools. Honest trade: Mott selector off-current is far above 13 fA, so retention is us-ms and this fits a cache or buffer tier.
note: Honest us-ms retention makes it a buffer tier.

title: Magnetostrictive actuators correct nanoimprint template distortion in situ
idea: Effect: magnetostriction. Galfenol or Terfenol-D thin-film actuators along the imprint template frame are driven by a coil array under the chuck, deforming the template by nanometers without contact to correct magnification and trapezoid errors field by field, with hysteresis compensation in the controller.
why: Fact 4: overlay is what keeps NIL from replacing EUV on DRAM layers; sub-2 nm overlay would move 2-3 layers to NIL at ~1/3 the EUV cost of ownership.

title: Hard-disk flying heads carry plasmonic lenses for near-field array lithography
idea: Effect: surface-plasmon near-field focusing. Bowtie plasmonic apertures on surplus HDD air-bearing sliders fly 10-20 nm above a spinning 100 mm resist-coated wafer and squeeze 355 nm light into ~25 nm spots; 16 heads write periodic cell arrays in parallel. Budget: ~$400k mechanics and lasers, $300k university fab time, $300k team over 24 months.
why: Fact 4: shows sub-30 nm patterning built from mass-produced HDD parts costing dollars each, versus a $200M EUV tool; scaling to thousands of heads is the follow-on.
note: Flying plasmonic lens demonstrated ~2008; wafer throughput is the doubt.

title: NbO2 Mott spiking encoders store activations as sparse events
idea: NbO2 Mott threshold-switch oscillators convert layer activations into spike trains. The insulator-metal transition sits near 800 C, so devices stay stable at 125 C ambient. Only spike addresses (typically 5-10% density) are written to memory as event lists, not dense tensors.
why: Activation memory drops 10-20x for sensor-processing networks.
note: The memory gain comes from sparse coding; NbO2 hardware adds little.

title: Superconductivity: liquid-nitrogen memory pool with YBCO lossless backplane traces
idea: House pooled DRAM at 77 K where YBCO-coated tape traces carry signals with near-zero resistance and dispersion, while cold DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude so refresh nearly disappears and the leakage tail collapses.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3, 16-33% idle power) and data-movement loss (fact 5); the ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead must be beaten by refresh and I/O savings at pool scale.

title: Peltier effect: thin-film thermoelectric base die cools taller HBM stacks
idea: Embed thin-film Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 Peltier couples in the HBM base die under hot spots, actively pumping heat out of the DRAM core layers into the cold plate, so 16-24-high stacks stay within thermal limits at the normal 64 ms refresh rate.
why: HBM height ceiling (density per footprint, fact 6) and refresh (fact 3): spends a few W of TEC power for 30-50% more bits per stack.

title: Dielectrophoresis: fluidic self-assembly drops memory chiplets onto roll-to-roll interposers
idea: Flow shaped DRAM chiplets in a carrier fluid over a printed polyimide interposer web whose electrodes form dielectrophoretic traps matching the chiplet outline; chiplets lock into sites at tens of thousands per minute, then printed solder joins them.
why: Packaging capex and throughput (facts 4, 6): replaces serial pick-and-place, making many-small-die memory modules (higher die yield) cheap; site-fill yield is the risk.

title: Open-IP block-copolymer phase separation recipes for capacitor-hole multiplication
idea: A pre-competitive consortium publishes high-chi block-copolymer directed self-assembly flows in which microphase separation quadruples storage-node hole density inside DUV-printed guides. Members license royalty-free and pool defect data.
why: Removes 1-2 EUV layers and the IP barrier for second-source DRAM makers and micro-fabs.
note: DSA for DRAM holes long studied; defectivity is the blocker, open IP the twist.

title: Inductive-coupling stacks need no bonds, so memory towers disassemble
idea: Stack DRAM dies with on-chip coil pairs for data (inductive through-chip links) and edge-delivered power, held by a mechanical clamp frame instead of TSVs and hybrid bonds. Failed dies are swapped and stacks reassembled.
why: Removes much of the HBM TSV area tax (~3x area per bit) and makes stacks repairable instead of scrapped.

title: O: topotactic oxygen shuttle toggles CaFeO2.5 insulator and CaFeO3 metal
idea: Place a ~5 nm brownmillerite CaFeO2.5 layer against an oxygen-reservoir oxide; a field pulse fills or empties its pre-ordered vacancy channels so the whole film converts topotactically to metallic perovskite CaFeO3 and back, read as a 10-100x resistance change.
why: Uniform phase conversion through ordered channels avoids the random filaments of ReRAM, removing forming and most variability; all Ca/Fe/O; ns switching and endurance are unproven.

title: Ni: permalloy vortex-core polarity flipped by gigahertz pulses
idea: Store the bit as the up/down polarity of the vortex core in a 50-100 nm Ni80Fe20 disk, switched in ~100 ps by a short resonant in-plane current pulse and read by a tunnel junction over the core; ~1% of disks that nucleate a wrong state or chirality are absorbed by the code.
why: Topologically protected, non-volatile spin bit from abundant Ni and Fe without Co or Pt, fast enough for DRAM-class access (facts 3, 10); disk size limits density.
note: Vortex-core switching known; core read via MTJ and disk size limit density.

title: Fluorinated alumina electret plane gives every access transistor built-in back bias
idea: F: bury a fluorine-implanted Al2O3 layer under the active area; Al2O3:F holds a stable negative fixed charge (~5e12 cm^-2) that acts as a permanent negative body bias, raising Vt and suppressing subthreshold leakage without a pumped VBB rail or heavy channel doping.
why: Deletes the body-bias charge pump from the periphery (fact 7) and lowers the channel doping that sharpens junction fields and GIDL (fact 3); ~2-3x lower leakage at equal on-current.
note: Same buried negative fixed-charge back bias.

title: XeF2-carved vacuum gap isolates storage node from passing wordline
idea: Xe: deposit a sacrificial Si or Ge spacer between the storage-node contact and the adjacent passing buried wordline, then release it with XeF2 vapor (near-infinite selectivity to oxide/nitride) through a small vent, leaving a sealed k=1 vacuum gap that weakens passing-gate field and coupling at the storage junction.
why: Passing-wordline fields drive GIDL and row-hammer charge pumping (facts 3, 9); a k=1 gap versus nitride (k~7) cuts coupling ~5x, plausibly 3-10x lower passing-gate leakage and a higher hammer threshold.

title: Strontium titanate capacitor turns relaxed DUV pitch into 10x retention
idea: Sr: since a DUV-only cell is larger, spend the extra footprint on a planar or shallow-trench MIM capacitor of ALD SrTiO3 (k~100-200) instead of 60:1 pillars, storing 10-30 fF so the same fA leakage takes 3-6x longer to cross the sense margin.
why: Turns the no-EUV area penalty into charge (fact 1) and longer refresh intervals (fact 3) while avoiding extreme-aspect pillar etch; STO leakage and crystallization temperature are the risks.

title: Al+N: aluminum-nitride piezoelectric transformer generates wordline boost voltage
idea: Replace the multistage capacitive VPP charge pump with a Rosen-type AlN thin-film piezoelectric transformer driven at mechanical resonance from the 1.1 V rail; its 3-5x voltage gain plus a small rectifier gives the 3 V wordline supply without large flying capacitors.
why: Charge pumps occupy notable periphery area at ~30-40% efficiency; piezo step-up could cut pump area ~3x and raise efficiency toward 60%+, trimming the energy of the stuck 3 V wordline swing (fact 10).

title: Ti: titanium-oxide BEOL ROM stores per-row retention class
idea: At wafer test, measure every row's retention and write a 2-bit class into a TiOx resistive crosspoint ROM printed above the row decoder; the refresh counter reads the class inline and refreshes strong rows at 128-512 ms instead of 32-64 ms.
why: The leakage tail forces worst-case refresh (fact 3); multi-rate refresh cuts refresh operations ~70-80%, recovering 10-20% bandwidth and much of idle power with ~zero silicon area.

title: S: thiol monolayers self-align periphery contacts without lithography
idea: Use alkanethiol (C, H, S) self-assembled monolayers that bind only to exposed metal and block growth there, so dielectric grows only on dielectric in N2-purged area-selective ALD and vias self-align, removing via-litho layers and argon-sputtered liners.
why: Saves 2-3 masks per periphery stack (fact 4) and reduces contact-to-gate shorts so decoders pack tighter (fact 7), all without rare gases.

title: Ba: sol-gel barium titanate decoupling capacitors stacked over pads
idea: Spin-coat and cure sol-gel BaTiO3 (thin-film k ~200-500) MIM decoupling capacitors in top metal over pads and buses, processed in air or N2 with no argon sputtering, replacing the MOS decaps that fill periphery white space.
why: Decaps take several percent of die; moving them up frees ~3-5% area (fact 7).
note: Crystalline high-k BaTiO3 needs anneals beyond the BEOL thermal budget.

title: Iron-nickel magnetic pads self-align dies for fine-pitch hybrid bonding
idea: Pattern soft-magnetic FeNi pads at die corners and matching hard-magnetic pads on the target wafer; dies placed by a coarse pick-and-place onto a thin water film self-register to <200 nm via magnetic plus capillary forces before Cu/SiCN hybrid bonding.
why: Die-to-wafer bonding throughput and aligner capital choke HBM stacking (fact 6); magnetic self-assembly could run ~10x faster on cheaper tools, enabling known-good-die stacks with fewer TSV-heavy wafer stacks.
note: Capillary self-assembly for hybrid bonding is active research; FeNi in bond interface a contamination risk.

title: Iron-catalyzed carbon nanotube bundles form vertical through-tier bitlines
idea: Evaporate ~1 nm Fe catalyst on Al2O3 at the bottom of vertical holes through a tier stack and grow dense multi-walled CNT bundles by thermal CVD at 550-650 C, filling each hole with an electromigration-immune vertical bitline or plate line contacted by every tier.
why: Replaces tungsten fill in deep holes (resource chokepoint) where CVD metal voids at high aspect ratio (fact 2); Fe and C are abundant and CNT CVD furnaces are common in university labs.
note: CNT vias studied for decades; real bundle resistivity at small diameters exceeds W.

title: Carbon molds etched by oxygen with sulfur sidewall passivation
idea: Periodic-table walk, C+S (6,16): form capacitor holes in an amorphous-carbon mold using O2 plasma with COS/SO2 additive, whose sulfur-carbon sidewall film replaces fluorocarbon polymer passivation for straight ~80:1 holes; after electrode deposition the mold is simply ashed in O2.
why: Removes C4F8/CHF3 and HF mold strip; ashing instead of a wet release avoids pillar collapse and rinse water.

title: Molten calcium chloride electrolysis turns ordinary sand into silicon
idea: Periodic-table walk, Ca+Cl (20,17): electro-deoxidize pressed SiO2 pellets from ordinary sand at ~850 C in molten CaCl2 (FFC route), with the salt recycled, and feed the Si powder to zone refining and CZ recharge.
why: Bypasses the arc furnace (11-13 kWh/kg plus coke) and Siemens chlorosilane steps; any sand works, no fluorides, U.S.-sited.

title: Rice-husk biogenic silica feeds synthetic Czochralski crucibles
idea: Periodic-table walk, Si+O (14,8): acid-leach rice-husk ash (~90% amorphous SiO2) with HCl/citric acid, calcine it to high-purity silica, and slip-cast crucibles with an inner sol-gel synthetic-silica layer; U.S. rice states supply millions of tonnes of husk.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz chokepoint with a renewable domestic feedstock, purified without HF.

title: Supercritical-CO2 drying to push capacitor pillars past AR 100
idea: Periodic-table walk, C+O (6,8): perform post-etch rinse and dry in supercritical CO2 with a non-fluorinated co-solvent, removing the liquid meniscus whose capillary force topples 60-75:1 pillars, and recover CO2 from industrial streams.
why: Direct attack on the capacitor charge wall (AR ~115 needed), plus less water and IPA.

title: N: nitrogen-terminated surfaces steer ALD into self-aligned contacts
idea: Expose the wafer to an NH3 plasma chemistry that N-terminates the dielectric but not the Si/metal landing pads, then use precursors that cannot nucleate on N-terminated SiN so liner and contact metal grow only on the pads (area-selective deposition), deleting the contact litho and etch.
why: Fact 4: removes 1-2 mask layers per contact level and their overlay budget; ~3-5% wafer-cost cut and better contact yield at tight pitch.

title: H: hydrogen-blister peeling stacks tiers from one reusable donor
idea: Implant H into a donor Si wafer, bond to the target, split at the blister plane to transfer a 30-50 nm single-crystal tier, smooth by H2 anneal, then repeat 26+ times from the same donor with low-temperature device steps between transfers.
why: Fact 2: replaces long SiGe/Si epitaxial stacks with repeated layer transfer; tier quality equals bulk Si and one donor feeds many tiers.
note: 26+ bonds is costly; still needs per-tier patterning.

title: Ni: nickel-stressor spalling makes kerfless substrates without saw slurry
idea: Sputter a tensile Ni stressor film on an ingot face or reclaimed wafer and peel off a 20-50 um single-crystal Si layer by controlled spalling, then smooth it by H2 anneal and bond it to a carrier, skipping wire sawing, lapping and wet polishing.
why: Water and resources: substrate making drops >10x in water, and kerf-free use roughly halves silicon and quartz-crucible demand per wafer (Spruce Pine >80%).

title: Zinc sacrificial anode: hardware-droppable pages for regenerable data
idea: Zinc corrodes first to protect steel; software tags regenerable data (decompressed copies, JIT code, memo tables, page-cache clones) as sacrificial in the page table, and under pressure the memory controller zeroes and reassigns those frames in microseconds without OS swapping, raising a fault so the data is rebuilt if touched again.
why: Servers can run with 20-30% less DRAM headroom because the spare capacity lives inside regenerable caches that are reclaimed instantly (cost/bit, capital).

title: Ni: electroless-nickel sidewall wiring replaces TSVs in die stacks
idea: Route HBM core-die I/O to the die edge, stack the dies, then laser-pattern and electrolessly plate Ni/Cu/Au traces down the polished stack sidewall at ~10 um pitch (~4,000 lines on a 10 mm die perimeter) to the base die, which keeps the standard HBM PHY.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): core dies need no TSVs, keep-outs or backside processing, saving ~5-10% die area and improving stack yield.

title: Bi: Bismuth-antimony topological SOT-MRAM from HDD reader know-how
idea: Use sputtered BiSb, with a record spin Hall angle developed for HDD readers, as the spin-orbit-torque write line in MRAM instead of W, Ta or Pt.
why: ~10x lower write current than W-based SOT and avoids China-dominated tungsten and platinum.
note: BiSb SOT actively pursued; thermal stability and integration open.

title: Dye-bath ferrocene grafting: quantized multi-level molecular charge storage
idea: Copy textile mordant dyeing: dip the wafer so the cup walls graft a mixed monolayer of ferrocene and biferrocene derivatives (Fe, C, H). Their distinct redox potentials store charge in discrete plateaus (2 bits per cell), and leakage cannot drift a level until a whole plateau has emptied.
why: Fact 3: quantized levels tolerate the leakage tail, allowing ~10x longer refresh intervals and 2 bits per cell. Iron-based chemistry needs no scarce metals.
note: ZettaCore-style porphyrin/ferrocene memory precedent; BEOL thermal stability and ns kinetics doubtful.

title: Wordline hot-wire annealing heals retention in the field
idea: Periodically drive a calibrated current pulse through a wordline segment, as hot-wire annealing or blade tempering does, to flash-heat the gate stack to ~300-400 C for microseconds. The pulse re-passivates interface traps and resets VRT defects that grew during service.
why: Retention degradation over life and VRT: restoring the tail ~2x late in life avoids derating refresh rates and extends module service life.

title: Coin-minting nanoimprint strikes the access-pillar layer instead of EUV
idea: Write one master die by e-beam, replicate working stamps, and strike the access-pillar layer by nanoimprint like coin minting. A reverse-tone, self-aligned spacer step reaches sub-12 nm pillars.
why: Fact 4: removes 1-2 EUV exposures from the access device module. Imprint's low line-edge roughness tightens VT spread and so trims the leakage tail.
note: Canon/Kioxia already pursue NIL; defectivity and overlay at sub-12 nm pillars are the doubt.

title: Progressive-die cascade: three charge-transfer stages pre-amplify before latching
idea: Like a progressive stamping die that forms a part through several small stations, pass the bitline charge through three cascaded switched-capacitor charge-transfer stages, each dumping charge from a larger capacitor onto one ~3x smaller. The result is ~20-27x voltage gain before a relaxed latch fires.
why: A large signal at the latch tolerates small, high-offset SA devices (SA area ~-40%) and lets bitlines carry 2-3x more cells, or allows Cs to fall ~2x toward 2-3 fF.

title: Continuous-casting sensing: no precharge, sense against the previous state
idea: Like continuous casting that never stops to pour a new ingot, bitlines are never equalized to VDD/2: they keep the last row's resolved values. The SA chooses between two references (VDD-delta or delta) based on the bitline's held previous bit, so the next activate starts at once.
why: Removes tRP (~14 ns) and equalize/precharge energy (~20-30% of activate energy), raising effective random-access bandwidth ~15-25%.

title: Fruit-grading line: laser-fused refresh classes per mat
idea: Like a fruit packing line that grades every piece into bins, measure each mat's retention at wafer sort and blow two laser fuses that set its refresh multiplier (1x/2x/4x/8x). The on-die refresh counter then skips cycles for long-retention mats.
why: Most mats retain 4-8x longer than the worst one; refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~60-70% for two fuses per mat on 1990s laser repair tools.
note: Each mat holds tail cells and VRT moves them, so per-mat gains are likely far below 4-8x.

title: Pre-outfitted tier blocks with local sense amps for digital stacking
idea: Shipyards fit pipes and wiring into hull blocks before joining them; likewise give every bonded array tier its own thin-film IGZO sense amplifiers and latches, so inter-tier bonds carry latched digital data at relaxed pitch instead of one analog bitline per bond.
why: Bond pitch can relax ~10x with digital links, raising hybrid-bond yield, and short tier-local bitlines cut CV2 energy; distributes the 49% periphery (fact 7) and trims data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: Roll-formed corrugated tiers: long-channel lateral transistors in short pitch
idea: Roll-formed corrugated sheet gets length without footprint; deposit each tier over a pre-patterned sinusoidal base so the lateral access transistor's channel follows the wave, giving ~2x channel length (and extra flank width) inside the same cell pitch.
why: A longer effective channel suppresses short-channel leakage and the refresh-forcing tail (fact 3) by up to ~10x while keeping 3D cell pitch, making lateral transistors viable (fact 2).
note: Same principle as recessed-channel transistors in 2D DRAM; 10x leakage cut claim optimistic.

title: Post-tensioned tendons: one through-stack via fill for N tiers
idea: Precast bridge segments are stacked with aligned ducts and one tendon is threaded through; stack thinned tier wafers with pre-opened, tapered, aligned ducts made by relaxed trailing litho, then one electroplating step fills a continuous via through every tier.
why: Replaces N separate TSV reveal-and-fill sequences with one, cutting HBM TSV cost and yield loss (fact 6); tapered ducts tolerate misalignment.

title: Veneer peeling: slice twenty thin wafers from one crystal
idea: Plywood mills peel thin veneers from a log; peel 20-50 um device-grade silicon layers from a thick CZ donor by stress-induced spalling or porous-silicon lift-off, bond each onto a reusable or glass handle, and repolish the donor for the next peel, so one prime wafer yields 15-25 device layers.
why: DRAM uses only the top ~5 um of a 775 um wafer; this cuts CZ ingots, quartz crucibles, polysilicon and growth energy per wafer ~10x and removes wire-saw kerf (~40% of each crystal).
note: Spalling and porous-Si lift-off known; film quality, flatness and donor reuse yield are the doubts.

title: Tie-dye wicking: slit-fed lateral diffusion dopes every tier at once
idea: Like dye wicking into folded cloth, use the single added slit mask to cut through the 3D DRAM tier stack, fill slits with doped glass or vapor dopant, and drive a timed lateral diffusion that forms source/drain junctions in all tiers simultaneously, setting channel length by diffusion distance.
why: Fact 2: lateral-transistor junctions for 50+ tiers in one step, where per-tier implants are impossible; no per-tier masks.

title: Movable-type rack: lines typeset from a shared CXL slug case
idea: A print shop keeps one case of type and sets any page from it. Here a rack-level CXL memory appliance keeps one copy of each unique 64B line (a 'slug'), indexed by a 64-bit content hash. Each server's page table points to page 'formes', which are lists of slug IDs that the memory controller assembles at read time, with copy-on-write on stores. Read-mostly content (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) is then set once per rack instead of once per server.
why: Cuts capacity demand: rack-wide dedup at line rather than page granularity catches the near-identical pages that KSM misses, saving 1.3-3x footprint in VM, container and inference fleets that hold the same bytes in dozens of servers.
note: HICAMP-like; 8B slug ID per 64B line and indirection latency eat gains.

title: Glassblown microlenses for optical vias straight through silicon
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so stacked dies can talk vertically by light through the bulk: reflow polymer into surface-tension microlenses (as glassblowers rely on surface tension) and use reflective silicon plasma-dispersion modulators on each tier to answer a beam sent up from the base die.
why: Eliminates TSVs entirely for data; claims sub-pJ/bit vertical links and no TSV area tax.

title: Print-on-demand maskless interposers written straight from CAD
idea: Write each interposer's RDL directly with laser direct imaging plus electrohydrodynamic jet printing, so no masks exist, like print-on-demand books. Small-lot memory configurations become economic.
why: Removes mask cost and lead time, so custom memory-compute packages are cheap at low volume, all without EUV.

title: Bookbinding spine bus: plated sidewall links across die stacks
idea: Stack dies like book pages with routing pulled to their edges, grind the spine flat, and plate and laser-pattern conductors down the spine, like glue binding a book. The whole stack's bus lives on its sidewall.
why: No TSVs in the DRAM die, and works for commodity dies; removes TSV area tax with i-line-class patterning.

title: Kanban charge-bucket counters: analog leaky integrators per row group
idea: Kanban cards cap work in progress; give each row group a tiny capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a ~32 ms time constant, and a comparator fires neighbour refresh when the bucket crosses threshold, making an analog activation counter with built-in decay and no SRAM counter tables.
why: Per-row hammer counting costs counter bits and read-modify-write timing; analog buckets cost one capacitor and comparator per group and no bandwidth (fact 9) at under 1% area.
note: Same leaky integrator.

title: Micro-Czochralski seed dots grown with green solid-state lasers
idea: Copy crystal pulling at micron scale: etch seed holes in each 3D tier's oxide, deposit amorphous Si, and melt it with a 532 nm diode-pumped solid-state laser (not a XeCl excimer, which needs xenon and neon) so each grain grows from its own seed and every access transistor sits inside a single grain.
why: Grain boundaries drive the leakage tail of poly-Si tier transistors (facts 2, 3); location-controlled grains could let lateral 3D access transistors meet the <13 fA tail without rare-gas lasers.
note: Micro-Czochralski grain filter is known (Delft); green-laser variant incremental.

title: Spun-yarn bits: one bit's charge summed across several tiers
idea: Yarn spins many weak fibres into a strong thread; store each bit on 3-4 small capacitors in successive tiers sharing one vertical bitline and fired together, so a single leaky transistor from low-temperature, rare-gas-free tier deposition only shaves a fraction of the signal.
why: Averaging suppresses the leakage tail (fact 3) roughly by the fibre count and sums Cs across tiers to beat the charge wall (fact 1) without high aspect ratio; trades per-tier density for many cheap tiers.

title: Carbon-implant proximity gettering beneath bonded array tiers
idea: Gettering is the fab's filter press; implant carbon (not argon or xenon pre-amorphisation) a few microns beneath each bonded or layer-transferred array tier, creating sinks that pull Fe, Ni and Cu out of storage-node junctions during low-temperature anneals.
why: Metal contamination is a prime source of retention-tail junction leakage, worse in low-thermal-budget 3D flows (facts 2, 3); image sensors cut dark current ~10x this way.

title: Microwave kiln anneal heals implant damage in upper tiers
idea: Ceramic makers sinter in microwave kilns; activate dopants and heal implant damage in 3D tiers with 5.8 GHz microwave annealing at ~400-500C, replacing excimer melt-laser anneals (xenon/neon) and argon RTP, so end-of-range defects that cause junction leakage are repaired without cooking lower tiers.
why: Lower junction leakage tail in stacked tiers (facts 2, 3) at a rare-gas-free, low thermal budget; enables more tiers without retention loss.

title: Sourdough-starter template tree: nanoimprint masters cloned across micro-fabs
idea: Bakers pass on sourdough starter. One e-beam-written 20 nm-pitch master template is replicated by UV-NIL into daughter and granddaughter working stamps. Each micro-fab patterns DRAM array lines and holes by imprint plus self-aligned double patterning, with no EUV.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint: an imprint tool costs ~$10-20M vs a ~$200M scanner, and one master seeds thousands of stamps. University nanofabs have e-beam and NIL.

title: Acoustic recirculating delay-line memory: bits stored as phonons in flight
idea: IFR: memory with no cells at all. Closest achievable: store bit streams as GHz acoustic pulses circulating in thin-film LiNbO3 or AlN on-chip delay loops (sound is 10^5x slower than light, so 1 mm holds ~1000 bits at 4 GHz), regenerated each lap by a small amplifier; many short loops keep average latency near 100 ns.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): needs no capacitors and no fine lithography, only piezo films; fits streaming KV-cache and weight traffic that is accessed sequentially.
note: Duplicate of on-chip acoustic delay loop.

title: Vortex nanoring core memory threaded by word and bit lines
idea: IFR: core memory's unlimited endurance at nanoscale. Closest achievable: permalloy nanorings threaded by a vertical via hold clockwise or counter-clockwise vortex chirality, set by coincident current in the via and a bitline as in 1950s cores, and read by a small TMR stack on the ring.
why: Nonvolatile, unlimited endurance, closed flux means no stray field (row-hammer immune, fact 9) and no capacitor (fact 1).
note: Echoes Zhu's vertical nanoring MRAM; coincident-current write margins and density at scale uncertain.

title: Resonant LC wordline drive recovers refresh energy adiabatically
idea: IFR: refresh energy flows back into the supply. Drive refresh wordlines and the VPP rail from an on-die or interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the wordline capacitance, ramping over ~5-10 ns so the swing is quasi-adiabatic, then returning the charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Fact 10: the ~3 V wordline CV^2 and charge-pump losses dominate activation energy; recovering 50-70% of it cuts refresh energy ~25-40% and shrinks charge-pump area.

title: In-field electrothermal annealing heals leaky tail cells
idea: IFR: weak cells repair themselves. The controller locates tail cells by retention scan, then drives a controlled microsecond current pulse through that wordline segment (local ~300-400 C) so mobile hydrogen re-passivates the trap sites near the storage junction that cause trap-assisted GIDL.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail sets refresh for the whole chip; healing the worst ~0.01% of cells could stretch the refresh interval from 64 ms to 256 ms or more, ~4x less refresh energy and bandwidth.

title: Per-row canary cells request refresh when they fade
idea: IFR: memory refreshes only when it is about to forget. Add 2-4 canary cells per row written at ~70% charge, polled by a tiny comparator in the sub-wordline driver during low-power checks; a row is refreshed only when its canaries flip.
why: Fact 3: retention varies 10-100x by row and temperature; canary-driven refresh cuts refresh operations 4-10x and tracks VRT and temperature in situ.

title: Asymmetric air-gap underlap kills GIDL at the storage junction
idea: IFR: no field exists where the leak is born. Form an air-gap spacer and gate underlap only on the storage-node side of the access transistor (angled deposition and etch), removing the gate-to-storage-junction overlap field that drives GIDL while the bitline side keeps overlap for drive current.
why: Fact 3: GIDL dominates the tail under negative wordline bias; removing the overlap field could cut tail leakage ~10x and allow 256 ms+ refresh.
note: Asymmetric drain underlap for GIDL is known; angled air-gap at DRAM pitch is hard.

title: Time-domain sensing converts bitline signal into delay
idea: Ideal result: sensing that improves with digital scaling, not analog headroom. Each bitline drives a current-starved inverter whose delay depends on its voltage; a column-shared time-to-digital converter decides the bit and also reports margin or multi-level information in the same pass.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): time resolution improves each node while voltage headroom does not; works below 0.6 V supplies.

title: Coolant-in-substrate microchannel glass keeps stacked memory tiers cold
