idea: A radio operator listens for a tone instead of draining a bucket: the storage node is a MOS varactor whose capacitance depends on its stored voltage, read by sending a small RF tone down the bitline and detecting the phase shift; the read leaves the charge intact, so weak cells can be read several times and majority-voted, and no restore is needed.
why: Facts 8 and 1: no destructive-read restore energy or read disturb, and marginal cells are rescued by repeated reads (~3-5 dB SNR gain).
note: Non-destructive phase readout of a tiny varactor against large bitline parasitics is a weak-signal problem.

title: Frequency-tuned resonators select mats instead of decoder wiring
idea: Shift the address from space to frequency: each mat's local wordline-driver enable is gated by a micron-scale AlN film-bulk acoustic resonator tuned to a unique GHz tone, and one shared RF line selects a mat by broadcasting its tone; only a short local decoder picks the row inside the mat. Predecoders and the global address bus collapse into one line plus a frequency synthesizer.
why: Attacks decoder and global-routing periphery (fact 7) and address-bus wire energy; est. 3-6% die area saved and fewer routing metal layers.
note: FBARs are far larger than micron scale; per-mat resonators cost more area than the 3-6% decoder savings.

title: Sense amps that self-trim offset over months via charge trapping
idea: Time jump from nanoseconds to months: each SA input transistor carries a nitride charge-trap spacer, and whenever on-die ECC corrects an error on that SA's column a micro-pulse traps a little charge to null the offset, so offsets anneal toward zero over field life and track aging.
why: Recovers the ~10-20 mV offset budget, raising sense margin ~20-30% so Cs or tRCD can shrink (facts 1, 7) and aging margin loss is cancelled.

title: Refresh-as-scanner computing row fingerprints for free
idea: This adds zero masks. Every row is already sensed once per 32-64 ms refresh, so a tiny CRC unit at the sense-amp edge folds each refreshed row into a signature table. That gives the OS a continuously updated map of duplicate and zero rows. The DRAM's own refresh rhythm becomes the dedup scan cycle.
why: Refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, fact 3) now does useful work, and detecting duplicate and zero rows without CPU scans reclaims 10-30% of capacity.

title: Williams tube's ghost: vacuum-nanogap access switch for temperature-proof retention
idea: Tube memories died from heaters, size and drift, but vacuum isolates charge perfectly. Gate each storage node with a 10-20 nm vacuum-gap field-emission switch carved in the BEOL and sealed at wafer level: its off-current is Fowler-Nordheim tunneling, essentially temperature-independent, not thermionic or generation leakage, so the femtoamp tail does not grow at 125 C.
why: Temperature-flat retention removes the ~8x refresh penalty silicon DRAM pays at 125 C (Fact 3); no channel material means no PBTI drift.
note: FN off-current is near zero but on-state needs very high fields; niche high-temperature benefit.

title: ReRAM endurance failure fixed: strippable, re-coatable consumable memory layer
idea: ReRAM and PCM never replaced DRAM partly because the switching film wears out. Put the switching film as the top BEOL layer over a permanent CMOS base die, designed so a depot can plasma-strip and redeposit it. A worn die is then remanufactured instead of scrapped.
why: Lets cheap BEOL memories do DRAM's job despite finite endurance, while the expensive CMOS base (periphery, fact 7) is reused 3-5 times.
note: Depackaging and refab reprocessing likely cost more than new dies.

title: Williams tube on glass: field-emitter arrays read and refresh charge dots
idea: The Williams tube stored bits as charge spots on a CRT face and died on drift, bulk and constant regeneration; Candescent's field-emission display died on vacuum spacers and panel cost. Fuse them: a thin vacuum-sealed glass panel where gated carbon or Mo emitter arrays address an opposing grid of dielectric charge dots, reading by secondary-emission current and regenerating each frame.
why: Cells contain no transistor, no Hf/Zr dielectric and no tungsten plug; periphery is the emitter row/column matrix; built from glass, carbon or Mo and oxide films on retired FED/plasma panel lines.
note: Field-emission Williams tube on glass is novel; vacuum panel cost and drift are severe.

title: HPE memristor, fixed: stochastic switching as probabilistic optimizer counters
idea: HPE's memristor died because its stochastic, variable switching made it unreliable storage. Turn the flaw into the feature: store Adam moments as Morris-style probabilistic counters in memristor crossbars, where each pulse switches a cell with a known probability, giving unbiased stochastic rounding for free.
why: Optimizer state (8-12 B/param) dominates training memory; ~1 B/param probabilistic counters cut it ~8x with no capacitor and no DRAM.
note: Signed EMA moments do not fit monotonic counters; 8-bit Adam already cuts state.

title: Core memory's ferrite returns: transformer-coupled power through the stack
idea: Magnetic core memory died of hand-threaded cores, but its ferrites are cheap Earth-abundant flux guides. Spin-spray-plate thin-film MnZn-ferrite cores through ~30 um holes in each thinned DRAM die, with a primary winding in the base die and secondary spirals on each tier, and transfer power magnetically at ~50-100 MHz so power TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear; paired with contactless data links, the stack becomes TSV-free.
why: Removes the power TSVs that block TSV-free stacking (fact 6, ~5-10% die area) and isolates supply noise per tier; Fe, Mn, Zn, O and Cu only, no Co-based magnetics.
note: MnZn ferrite lossy at 50-100 MHz; still needs through-die holes.

title: DX-centre persistent photoconductivity: light writes, lattice barrier holds
idea: Effect walk: photoconductivity with large lattice relaxation. A waveguide photon pulse ionizes DX-type deep donors in a channel (AlGaAs:Si-like centres re-engineered in a wide-gap host with a >=0.9 eV capture barrier) into shallow donors, raising conductance; the configurational barrier keeps electrons free, and a hot-electron gate pulse recaptures them to reset.
why: Holds the bit in a lattice-relaxation barrier instead of leakage-limited charge, targeting refresh-free retention (fact 3) and an optical write path that bypasses wordline drivers (fact 7); known DX hosts only retain below ~100 K, so a new host is required.
note: Needs a new host with room-temperature DX barrier.

title: Acoustic-resonator frequency-division addressing replaces global predecoder buses
idea: Effect: mechanical (BAW/contour-mode) resonance. Give each subarray block an AlScN resonator tuned to a unique frequency (e.g., 64 tones from 1.0-2.6 GHz); the controller sends a tone burst on one shared line, and only the block whose resonator rings up past threshold enables its local wordline drivers. The address travels as a frequency instead of over dozens of routed wires.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): one RF line can replace ~20-40 global address/predecode wires and repeaters per bank.
note: Needs high-Q AlScN resonators per block and fast ring-up; saves only global wires.

title: Wavelength-addressed photoconductive wordlines through vertical light pipes
idea: Photoconductivity: SiN waveguides thread vertically through the 3D stack, and each tier taps them with a micro-ring drop filter tuned to that tier's wavelength. The dropped light switches photoconductive a-Si/IGZO access channels in place of gate metal. Choosing a wavelength picks the tier, and choosing a waveguide picks the row.
why: Removes the tungsten wordline metal (W chokepoint), the staircase and the high-voltage wordline drivers (facts 2, 7 and 10); claim tier count no longer limited by staircase area.
note: Micro-rings per tier kill density; photoconductive oxide channels are slow.

title: Electrochromic tiers with plasmonic readout for read-mostly AI weights
idea: Electrochromism: WO3 nanocells, colored or bleached by proton intercalation, keep their state with no power. Each cell sits on a plasmonic nanoantenna whose resonance shift a bonded photodiode array reads optically, a whole page in parallel. Writes are slow (µs) but reads are fast, which suits model weights that are written rarely.
why: Takes read-mostly AI weight capacity off DRAM and removes per-read data movement (facts 5 and 8); claim page-parallel optical reads at tens of fJ/bit with non-volatile storage.

title: Piezoacoustic recirculating delay loops stream decode weights, skipping DRAM
idea: LLM decode reads every weight in the same fixed order each token, so a bank of GHz LiNbO3 bulk-acoustic delay loops on the interposer holds weight shards as circulating phonon pulses. The pulses are re-amplified each lap and timed to arrive exactly when the systolic array needs them. Piezo transducers convert bits to acoustic packets at ~10 Gb/s per loop, and thousands of loops form a sequential 'weight carousel'.
why: Takes deterministic weight streams out of DRAM: no row activations and no overfetch (facts 5, 8). Target is 20-40% less DRAM for small-batch inference, but each loop holds only ~10-100 kb, so it suits on-package buffers.
note: GHz LiNbO3 acoustic loss and transducer energy per lap; kb-scale per loop limits value.

title: Charge sharing rebuilds rows from a base row plus deltas
idea: Store groups of similar rows (neighboring embedding vectors, image tiles) as one full-precision base row plus low-bit delta rows. On read, the subarray opens the base and delta rows together onto shared bitlines with binary-weighted capacitive coupling, so charge redistribution adds them in analog before sensing. Decompression happens inside the mat with no logic.
why: Gives 1.5-3x effective capacity for redundant data at zero periphery cost (facts 7, 8).
note: Doubt: analog charge sum of base+delta rows needs multi-level sensing/ADC, not a standard sense amp.

title: Microheater-gated zirconia ionic memory hosts shared read-mostly pages
idea: Store deduplicated read-only pages (shared libraries, model weights, map tiles) in yttria-stabilized zirconia cells. Their oxygen-ion motion is frozen at 125 C but fast at ~400 C, so writes use a local microheater pulse and the hot ambient cannot disturb the data. Reads are fast and resistive.
why: Thermal write gating gives 10-year retention at 125 C, and one shared physical copy serves all processes and VMs, cutting DRAM 20-40%.
note: 400 C microheaters in BEOL raise thermal crosstalk and energy; dedup claim is a separate effect.

title: Thermal hysteresis: NiTi shape-memory microcontacts make HBM stacks reworkable
idea: Replace permanent microbumps with NiTi micro-springs that clamp pads at operating temperature and release when the stack is heated through the austenite transition, so one failed DRAM die in a 12-high stack is lifted out and replaced instead of scrapping the stack and its GPU.
why: HBM compound yield and scrap (fact 6): converts a $1,000+ package loss into a single-die swap; contact resistance and ~20 um pitch limit it.
note: NiTi springs at ~20 um pitch with stable contact resistance across thousands of TSV-scale joints is doubtful.

title: Electrowetting liquid metal: Galinstan microchannel vias are stress-free and reconfigurable
idea: Fill vertical microchannels with gallium-alloy liquid metal instead of solid Cu, removing CTE stress and keep-out zones; electrowetting electrodes along spare channels move metal plugs to connect or disconnect lanes, giving in-field lane repair.
why: TSV keep-out area and stress-induced yield loss (fact 6); repair without heavy spare-TSV overprovisioning; Ga attack on Al/Cu needs barriers.
note: Ga embrittlement and electrowetting reliability in micro-vias are severe unknowns.

title: Acousto-optics: Bragg-cell beam steering time-shares one optical link across memories
idea: A surface-acoustic-wave acousto-optic deflector on a lithium niobate interposer steers a host's free-space beam among 32 memory chiplets in ~100 ns by changing the RF drive frequency, forming a solid-state switched memory fabric with no electrical crossbar.
why: Data movement and pooling (fact 5): one transceiver serves 32 memory targets, cutting SerDes count and stranded memory; switch time suits page migration, not per-access.

title: Pyroelectric crystal emitters power cheap multi-beam lithography in micro-fabs
idea: Thermally cycled LiTaO3 crystals build >100 kV/cm surface fields that field-emit electrons without high-voltage supplies. Tile thousands of gated micro-pyro emitters into a maskless multi-beam writer for DRAM periphery layers and low-volume masks.
why: Removes $5-15M mask sets and EUV for low-volume periphery, letting small fabs write custom memory.
note: Novel emitter, but pyroelectric emission is erratic and slow-cycling; litho-grade current stability doubtful.

title: Fe: bacteria-grown greigite magnetosomes self-assemble into magnetic bit arrays
idea: Harvest near-monodisperse 40-80 nm Fe3S4 (greigite) magnetosomes from magnetotactic bacteria and dock them by magnetic self-assembly into a pre-patterned spin-orbit-torque crossbar, one particle per site; the ~1% of sites left empty or doubly filled are mapped out as erasures.
why: Bio-fabricated storage elements grown at room temperature with no lithography for the bit itself (fact 4), from abundant Fe and S; docking accuracy and read speed are major unknowns.
note: Docking accuracy and SOT read speed on 40-80 nm particles make DRAM-class use doubtful.

title: Fe: electroplated permalloy domain-wall counters track row activations
idea: Electroplate Ni-Fe nanowire loops (no argon PVD) as magnetic domain-wall counters, as in multi-turn rotation sensors, per row group; each ACT current pulse advances a wall one notch by spin-transfer, and an anisotropic-magnetoresistance stripe flags when a threshold notch is reached.
why: Nonvolatile, leak-free row-hammer counters (fact 9) without SRAM tables, ~0.1 um2 each in BEOL.

title: Vanadium dioxide graded-threshold switches replace the tier staircase
idea: Run one shared vertical select pillar per block through all tiers with a VO2 insulator-metal-transition switch at each tier junction, its thickness graded so switching voltage steps ~0.15 V per tier; ramping this pillar against a counter-pillar opens exactly one tier using two contacts instead of 32.
why: The staircase and per-tier contacts grow in area and mask count with tiers (facts 2, 7); collapsing them into two pillars could save ~5-10% die area and many staircase litho/etch cycles.
note: VO2 is metallic above ~68 C and thresholds vary; 0.15 V per-tier discrimination is doubtful.

title: Ge-Sn: group-IV emitters beam data vertically through HBM dies
idea: Grow GeSn light emitters at ~2 um wavelength (where silicon is transparent) and matching GeSn photodiodes on each core die so bit lanes pass optically straight through the thinned stack, dropping signal TSVs; the base die converts to the unchanged HBM interface.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): optical vertical channels avoid TSV keep-out and alignment loss while staying CMOS-compatible; speculative ~1 pJ/bit.
note: Room-temperature GeSn emitters remain inefficient; optical through-silicon links unlikely to beat TSV energy.

title: H: hydride reservoir re-passivates hammer-aged access transistors in field
idea: Deposit a Pd-capped TiHx hydride strip in the BEOL over each bank, above a window in the SiN hydrogen barrier. A controller-scheduled maintenance pulse from on-die poly heaters (~250 C for seconds, bank taken offline) releases atomic hydrogen that diffuses to the recess-gate Si/SiO2 interface and re-caps dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and hammer stress.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) widens over life as interface traps form; periodic in-field re-passivation keeps weak-cell counts near time-zero, allowing ~2x longer refresh over product life and less test guardband.

title: N: nitride charge-trap sliver as per-row analog hammer dosimeter
idea: A thin SiN charge-trap strip (SONOS-like) under a dummy gate coupled to each wordline receives a small, repeatable charge injection on every activation, so its Vt shift integrates activation count non-volatilely; refresh logic compares it to a threshold, refreshes the neighbors and erases the strip.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) tracking with no SRAM/CAM counter tables, so per-row tracking at ~1k-activation thresholds costs almost no periphery (fact 7).

title: V: VO2 phase-change thermal integrator flags hammered subarrays
idea: A doped VO2 sliver (insulator-metal transition tuned near 70 C) is thermally coupled to each subarray's local wordline driver; sustained high activation rates heat it through the transition, its resistance drop trips a sense line that forces targeted neighbor refresh, while normal traffic never heats it enough.
why: Analog, counter-free hammer-rate detection (fact 9) that costs no logic area; complements fine-grained trackers.

title: Crimped weft capacitors: weave 3D DRAM's lateral capacitors over posts
idea: Borrow the crimp of woven cloth. In a stacked 3D DRAM tier, the horizontal capacitor is coated like a yarn (Ru core, HZO/ZrO2 sheath, TiN outer shell) and snakes over and under a comb of sacrificial vertical 'warp' posts that are removed afterward. The crimped path packs 1.3-1.6x more electrode length into the same tier footprint.
why: Fact 2: the lateral capacitor is what blocks 3D DRAM. ~1.5x Cs per cell cuts the tiers needed to break even from ~26 toward ~18.
note: Novel weave geometry but only ~1.5x Cs and very hard lateral processing.

title: Die-cast gallium droplet bit: liquid metal shuttles between two wells
idea: Borrow metal casting. A ~10 nm Ga-alloy droplet is sealed in a dumbbell-shaped nano-cavity, and electrocapillary pulses move it from one lobe to the other, where surface tension holds it (bistable). A sense electrode reads the position as a capacitance change.
why: Mechanical storage with no leakage, so no refresh (fact 3). A liquid cannot fatigue, so endurance is effectively unlimited and the state holds with no power.
note: Ga oxide skin and 10 nm droplet electrocapillary control are doubtful.

title: Zone-refined access pillars sweep deep-trap metals into a sacrificial cap
idea: Borrow ingot zone refining: scan a nanosecond-laser molten zone up each vertical access-transistor pillar topped with a sacrificial a-Si cap, so Fe/Cu/Ni deep-level impurities (segregation coefficient k<<1) ride the melt front into the cap, which CMP then removes.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail is set by rare cells hosting SRH deep traps; purging them could cut tail cells ~10x, pushing worst-case retention toward 0.5-1 s and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss by up to ~80%.

title: Parking-garage helicoid tiers via rotating glancing-angle deposition
idea: Thread-rolling and helical-ramp analogy: deposit the tier stack as one continuous helicoid ramp around a central pillar by glancing-angle deposition while rotating and slowly tilting the wafer, so each tier is one turn of a ramp and all tiers are reachable from the ramp edge without a staircase etch.
why: Staircase area and its many litho-trim loops grow with tier count (facts 2, 4); a helical ramp turns tier access into one contact row. Glancing-angle deposition makes 10-100 nm helices today, but not yet device-grade films.
note: GLAD films are porous; a continuous helicoid does not give electrically isolated tiers.

title: Lost-wax cast aluminum wordlines replace CVD tungsten
idea: Like investment casting: fill buried-wordline trenches with a carbon 'wax' placeholder through all high-temperature steps, burn it out with an oxygen-radical ash, then squeeze-cast molten Al-Si-Sc alloy into the voids at ~600 C and high pressure over the TiN gate liner and planarize.
why: Removes WF6 and tungsten (China ~80%) from the densest metal layer in the array and cuts wordline resistance ~1.5-2x, which allows thinner wordlines; uses the most abundant structural metal and no fluorinated precursor.
note: Squeeze-casting molten Al into ~10 nm trenches fights wetting and capillarity at nanoscale.

title: Printed molecular-rotor framework where dipolar guests store the bit
idea: IFR: a crystal of identical, frictionless dipole switches. Closest achievable: print a metal-organic framework film whose pores hold polar rotor molecules that align up or down under a field and stay pinned by tuned ~0.8 eV rotational barriers, read as polarization charge.
why: Facts 1 and 10: molecular-scale bit with low switching barrier, printed from MOF inks at low temperature; no defect migration so endurance is high.
note: Polarization charge from rotors likely too small to sense.

title: HBM buyback harvests base dies and good DRAM layers
idea: Ideal result: every die returns to service. Vendors pay a deposit-refund on HBM-equipped modules; returned stacks with reversible bonds are disassembled, dies retested, and good DRAM layers restacked onto new base dies.
why: Supply and capital: recovers bits at a fraction of new-wafer cost and offsets HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit (fact 6).
note: HBM bonds are not reversible; debonding thinned dies is hard.

title: Two-device sense amp: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto pair latch
idea: Limit: a sense amp may contain only two devices. Use a series pair of Si/SiGe Esaki tunnel diodes (a 1960s Goto pair) whose N-shaped I-V gives the shared node two stable points; a clocked bias ramp drives the node through its unstable point, and the +/-50 mV bitline nudge decides which stable state it falls into within ~50 ps.
why: Periphery area and speed: 2 devices instead of the 6-10 in an offset-compensated latch, which could cut the SA stripe by ~3x. Matching depends on peak current rather than Vt, so random dopant mismatch matters less; decisions cost sub-fJ.

title: Pyroelectric read: wordline heat pulse makes polarization announce itself
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, and the read must not flip domains. A ~1 ns current pulse through a resistive wordline strap heats one row of ferroelectric capacitors by ~10 K; each cell emits a pyroelectric current whose sign matches its polarization, and charge integrators on the bitlines read it without ever crossing the coercive field.
why: Non-destructive NV read with no reference cells (sign detection). Risk: ns thermal time constants and the ~fJ heating energy per bit.
note: Pyro charge at 10 K is ~tens of electrons per cell; far below sensing floor.

title: Embossed holographic film stores frozen prefix KV caches
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): the KV caches of high-traffic frozen prefixes (system prompts, popular documents, codebases) are mastered once per model release as computer-generated surface-relief holograms and copied by roll-to-roll embossing, the process used for credit-card holograms. An LED-addressed reader projects a whole KV page onto a photodiode array in one flash.
why: Shared-prefix KV is read-only yet duplicated across GPUs; moving it to film that costs pennies per copy frees DRAM/HBM for per-user KV, ~1.5-3x more sessions per accelerator.

title: Newspaper memory: reprint embedding-table snapshot daily on microdot film
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): each night a maskless electrohydrodynamic-jet printer writes the recommender's long-tail embedding rows as ~2 um microdots on PET sheets, read by lenslet-coupled CMOS image sensors. By day DRAM holds only hot rows plus a delta log of updates since the print, and yesterday's sheet is recycled.
why: Long-tail embeddings are terabytes and rarely updated; a daily printed snapshot at under $1/GB, with DRAM only for hot rows and deltas, could cut embedding DRAM 5-10x if millisecond tail reads can be hidden by session prefetch.
note: Daily printed optical snapshot; read latency and printer throughput are doubts.

title: Printed antifuse golden-page library for hardware dedup
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a cheap printed one-time-programmable antifuse sheet is burned at rack install with the fleet's most common read-only pages (kernel text, glibc, Python runtime, base container layers). Memory controllers map any matching page to the printed copy and keep only a small DRAM/SRAM cache of its hottest lines to hide the slow printed reads.
why: Common pages recur in every VM; a write-once printed library takes them out of DRAM (~5-15% per host) for almost no capex.
note: Printed antifuse density is orders too low to hold GBs of golden pages; reads too slow.

title: Million-lane printed scanner sheet filters cold data in place
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): the design trades area for speed: a square-meter printed sheet carries a million slow (~1 MHz) oxide-TFT comparators, each scanning its own patch of co-printed cold storage, for ~10^12 comparisons per second in aggregate. Filters and counts over cold datasets run in place, and only matches move into DRAM.
why: Analytics loads whole cold datasets into DRAM just to scan them; wide in-place scanning cuts DRAM staging 10-100x for selective queries.
note: Co-printed cold storage cannot hold TB datasets at printed densities; scanning idea sound, substrate not.

title: Roll memory like a film capacitor with sprayed end contacts
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Transfer DRAM device films onto a 10 um polyimide ribbon whose bus lines all exit at the two ribbon edges, wind it into a tight cylinder like a metallized-film capacitor, and arc-spray (Schoop) metal end caps that tie every turn's edge lines to power and a radial data comb.
why: Volumetric density with capacitor-industry roll-to-roll and winding tools that cost pennies per part; a 10 mm cylinder holds ~100x the silicon area of its footprint.
note: Footprint density is not cost/bit; transferred thin-film DRAM retention and roll contacts unproven.

title: Latent TSV stubs let retired DDR dies become HBM stacks
idea: Rule: every die must have a higher-value second life. DDR dies are designed with TSV keep-out zones and buried, unrevealed TSV stubs. Retired dies are thinned, revealed and stacked into low-cost HBM-like stacks for second-life inference memory.
why: Fact 6: turns retired commodity bits into scarce stacked bandwidth without new wafers.
note: Burdens all dies; retired DDR I/O unsuitable for HBM.

title: Altermagnetic tunnel-junction RAM: MRAM without stray fields
idea: The free layer is an altermagnet (RuO2, CrSb, MnTe or newer candidates) whose Neel vector sets spin-dependent tunnelling through an MgO-type barrier to a reference electrode. Writing uses spin-splitter or spin-orbit torque from an adjacent line, or the altermagnet's own current-induced torque; reading uses TMR. Zero net moment removes dipolar coupling to neighbours and to external fields, so crosspoint pitch can drop from ~2.5 to ~1.5 diameters, and exchange-enhanced switching could reach ps timescales. Endurance is magnetic, with no wear mechanism.
why: [SPECULATIVE] 2.8x denser than ferromagnetic MTJ crosspoints at the same diameter (900 vs 2,500 nm2 at d = 20 nm), ~1.2x 1-beta per deck; non-volatile; potential ps writes.

title: Swap solid dielectric for superionic RbAg4I5 electric-double-layer storage node
idea: Fill the storage node with a room-temperature superionic conductor (RbAg4I5, ~0.3 S/cm) against an ion-blocking electrode. The bit is held as a sub-nm Helmholtz double layer (~10-20 uF/cm2), and the high ionic conductivity keeps the RC charging time near ~10 ns at nanoscale.
why: Fact 1: 2-3x charge per area over an EOT-0.5 nm dielectric, multiplied by porous electrode area, so short pillars with AR ~20:1 can be used.
note: RbAg4I5 Ag contamination and moisture instability in CMOS.

title: Swap oxide ferroelectric for vapor-deposited molecular ferroelectric croconic acid
idea: Use a proton-tautomerism organic ferroelectric (croconic acid, Pr ~20 uC/cm2, or DIPAB) evaporated onto the cap electrode at <150 C. It switches by proton transfer, not oxygen-vacancy motion, so HZO's vacancy-driven wake-up and fatigue are absent.
why: A low-temperature BEOL storage layer for monolithic stacking above logic, with periphery under the array (fact 7), and no rare inputs; the target is FeRAM-class endurance beyond 10^12 cycles.
note: Croconic acid thin films have lower Pr and thermal stability concerns; still capacitor FeRAM.

title: Swap charge for ferroelastic twin variant read by piezoresistance
idea: Store the bit as which of two ferroelastic twin orientations a nanocrystal adopts (for example tetragonal-twin BiFeO3 or a NiTi martensite nanopillar). A strain pulse from an integrated AlN piezo layer switches it, and the read uses the anisotropic piezoresistance of an underlying channel.
why: Non-volatile with non-destructive read (facts 3, 8); voltage-driven at <0.5 V through piezo coupling (fact 10).
note: AlN piezo strain likely too weak to switch twin variants.

title: Swap tungsten/platinum spin-orbit layer for chiral-molecule spin filter
idea: Write a nanomagnet bit by chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS): a self-assembled monolayer of helical molecules (helicenes or alpha-helix peptides) spin-polarizes the write current, replacing heavy-metal W/Pt/Ta spin-orbit-torque layers.
why: Takes tungsten (China ~80%) and platinum-group metals out of non-volatile working memory, and the monolayer self-assembles with no lithography (scarce-resource axis).
note: CISS magnitude in solid-state devices remains contested.

title: Replace amorphous oxide liners with epitaxial CaF2 crystalline insulator
idea: Substitute the amorphous SiO2/SiN gate insulator and isolation liner around the access channel with epitaxial CaF2 (0.6% lattice mismatch to Si) grown by MBE on Si {111} facets. A crystalline insulator has orders of magnitude fewer border traps than an amorphous oxide.
why: Variable retention time (VRT) and random telegraph noise come from border and oxide traps; removing them shrinks the retention tail so refresh is set by the bulk distribution: 2-4x longer tREF.
note: CaF2 epitaxy needs Si(111) and MBE; conformal growth in DRAM trenches unlikely.

title: Resonant LC energy recovery for bitline precharge and restore
idea: Substitute dissipative CMOS precharge and restore with adiabatic swing: banks of bitlines are switched onto an in-package inductor so their charge rings sinusoidally between two bank groups instead of being dumped to ground and recharged from VDD.
why: Energy per bit (fact 10): bitline CV^2 dominates activate energy, and resonant recovery of 50-70% of that charge cuts activate/restore energy about 2x without lowering VARY.
note: In-package inductor timing and switch losses at ns cycles.

title: Dithered minimum-size comparator triplets replace large matched sense pairs
idea: Substitute one large, carefully matched sense pair with three minimum-size comparators per bitline pair, each fed an independent small dither offset, followed by a 3-input majority gate before the restore latch fires. Random offsets average instead of being sized away.
why: Periphery area: matching-driven transistor sizing is the main SA area cost; three minimum devices plus majority cost ~40% less area at equal bit-error rate.
note: At equal area, one larger matched pair beats a majority of three min-size comparators.

title: Self-referenced two-pulse sensing eliminates reference bitlines
idea: Substitute the external reference (dummy cell or VDD/2 twin bitline) with the cell itself: read once, inject a known small charge step into the same cell, read again, and let the sign of the difference give the data. This is the self-reference trick from MRAM applied to DRAM.
why: Density: makes open-bitline, near-4F^2 layouts tolerable without reference-mismatch errors, gaining ~1.3-1.5x cell density.
note: A linear capacitor gives no data-dependent difference after charge injection, unlike MRAM.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel-diode latch as sense amplifier
idea: Substitute the cross-coupled inverter latch with a Goto pair: two series Esaki tunnel diodes whose negative differential resistance forms a bistable node that the bitline signal tips one way. Degenerately doped Si or uni-MBE InGaAs junctions are within university reach.
why: Speed and energy: NDR latching switches in ps at ~0.3 V, cutting sense energy and allowing lower array voltage (fact 10).
note: Si Esaki PVCR and peak-current uniformity; Goto pairs never scaled.

title: Sputtered NbO2 Mott threshold switch as sense comparator
idea: Substitute the transistor comparator with a two-terminal NbO2 insulator-metal-transition device biased just below its threshold: bitline signal above the reference triggers abrupt (~ns) conduction that sets the restore driver. Reactive sputtering and e-beam pillars suffice.
why: Periphery area: a two-terminal device fits at bitline pitch in a via, shrinking sense strips ~2-3x.

title: Analog-voltage address bus with per-row window comparators
idea: Substitute the binary multi-wire address bus with two analog address lines (row-group and row-within-group voltages); each wordline driver carries a resistor-ladder window comparator that fires only when both voltages land in its window, which is coincidence decoding in the analog domain.
why: Periphery area: replaces ~16 address wires and NAND trees with 2 lines plus local comparators, simplifying routing in narrow sub-array gaps.
note: Window comparators cannot resolve ~1000 analog levels in the noise.

title: Selective SiGe oxidation converts sacrificial tiers into stacked buried oxides
idea: Substitute etch-and-fill tier isolation with in-place conversion: oxidize a Si/SiGe superlattice from its slit sidewalls at 750-850 C, where SiGe oxidizes 5-20x faster than Si, so each SiGe tier becomes buried insulator and the stack becomes multi-tier SOI; a thin Si:C barrier on each Si tier blocks rejected Ge from the channels.
why: Isolates stacked single-crystal channels (fact 2) without HF or fluorocarbon dielectric etch; fully depleted SOI body per tier tightens the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Substitute self-passivating MAX-phase conductor for tungsten bitlines and barriers
idea: Sputter Ti3AlC2/Ti2AlC nanolaminate bitlines and crystallize by laser anneal; aluminum in the lattice self-forms a ~1 nm Al2O3 sidewall skin that acts as liner and diffusion barrier, removing separate TiN barriers and WF6 chemistry.
why: Abundant Ti, Al and C replace tungsten; one conductor/barrier film with short electron mean free path suffers little size-effect resistivity rise, and a thinner liner lowers bitline capacitance and sense energy.
note: MAX phases need high crystallization temperature; thin-film resistivity unproven at scale.

title: Substitute tin-catalyzed grown nanowires for etched storage pillars
idea: Grow vertical, heavily doped silicon nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid growth from tin catalyst dots (not gold, which kills carrier lifetime) placed on each storage-node contact, then coat with high-k and TiN to form capacitors bottom-up.
why: Additive growth reaches AR >150 with no high-AR fluorocarbon etch and no EUV hole layer; tin is abundant and electrically benign in silicon.

title: Substitute manganese-aluminum and oxidized copper for platinum-group MRAM layers
idea: Build spin-orbit-torque memory from a perpendicular tau-MnAl free layer, an oxidized-copper (CuOx) spin-current source and a Mg-Al-O tunnel barrier, eliminating Pt, Ir, Ru, Ta and W from the stack.
why: Gives DRAM-class, refresh-free nonvolatile working memory from abundant elements only, removing the platinum-group metal inventory that limits MRAM scale-up.

title: Substitute permanent dielectric breakdown with self-healing anodizable capacitor dielectric
idea: Swap the static high-k stack for a high-k layer over an anodizable Al/Ta thin film inside a mild solid electrolyte layer, so a breakdown spot leaks current that locally re-anodizes the metal and seals the defect, like electrolytic-capacitor self-healing.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): self-healing allows a thinner, higher-field dielectric (~1.5x more charge per area) without killing yield on pinholes.
note: Electrolytic self-healing is polar; DRAM capacitor sees bipolar half-VDD stress.

title: Substitute NMOS access with PMOS access to blunt hammer charge injection
idea: Swap electron-carrier access transistors for hole-carrier (PMOS) ones in the array; holes have lower trap-assisted injection and weaker GIDL, so both the leakage tail and hammer-induced charge migration may shrink, at some cost in drive current.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and row hammer (fact 9): a speculative 3-10x hammer threshold gain and tighter retention tail if the hole-transport hypothesis holds.
note: Hole-transport hammer hypothesis speculative; drive current loss hurts density.

title: Substitute polycrystalline HZO with templated single-grain epitaxial ferroelectric cells
idea: Grow HZO on a lattice-matched seed layer (e.g., YSZ or perovskite template) patterned so each cell is one oriented grain, removing grain-to-grain variation in coercive field and polarization.
why: Variability is the main FE error source at small cells; near-uniform cells cut raw BER and ECC overhead and allow scaling below 20 nm.
note: Per-cell templated epitaxy in BEOL 3D structures is far beyond current HZO process control.

title: Substitute silicon DRAM in edge devices with roll-to-roll foil memory
idea: Swap silicon DRAM in IoT, wearables and appliance controllers for oxide gain-cell memory made on polyimide foil by roll-to-roll sputter/ALD lines at <=300 C, freeing silicon bits for servers.
why: Moves the low-density, high-unit-count share of demand off DRAM wafers; R2R capex per m^2 is ~100x lower than a fab.

title: Vacuum nanochannel field-emission valve as cell access device
idea: Fuse vacuum-tube electronics with the DRAM cell: each storage node reaches the bitline through a sealed 10-20 nm vacuum gap between a sharp emitter tip and a collector, gated by a ring electrode. Below the field-emission threshold no carrier exists in the gap, so the node cannot leak; raising the gate field emits electrons for ns-speed write and read.
why: Fact 3: refresh eliminated; the vacuum gap is temperature-insensitive, so hot (125 C) operation carries no retention penalty, and it is radiation hard.
note: Per-cell emitter uniformity and stability, plus low emission current for ns writes.

title: Idle bitlines parked at the subarray's majority stored level
idea: Write logic keeps a per-row inversion flag so most cells in a subarray hold the same level. In idle, bitlines park at that rail instead of VDD/2, so majority cells see Vds~0 and subthreshold current, proportional to 1-exp(-Vds/kT), collapses.
why: More than 80% of cells see near-zero leakage drive, extending retention 3-5x and cutting self-refresh energy proportionally.
note: Minority cells see full VDD drain bias, worsening the tail that sets refresh.

title: NEMS relay latch inside the sub-wordline driver
idea: Replace the sub-wordline driver's level shifter and pull-down with a nanoelectromechanical relay whose mechanical hysteresis both latches the wordline state and gives true zero off-leakage; low-voltage decode pulls it in and it switches the 3 V VPP line directly.
why: Voltage floor and periphery leakage (facts 10, 7): removes level-shifter area and the SWD leakage that dominates standby, and gives a perfectly held negative wordline on idle rows.

title: Polycrystalline diamond bond layer doubles as interlayer heat spreader
idea: Combine bonding dielectric and heat spreader: grow ~1 um CVD diamond (US-built reactors, methane/hydrogen feedstock) on DRAM wafers, polish it, and use it as the bond layer between a hot logic die and DRAM tiers so hotspots spread laterally before reaching the cells.
why: Enables logic-on-DRAM stacking (fact 5) while keeping DRAM below 85 C (refresh doubles per ~10 C, fact 3); diamond ~1,000 W/mK versus 1.4 for SiO2; all-domestic inputs.
note: CVD diamond temperatures exceed DRAM capacitor budget; 1 um film spreads little laterally.

title: Area-selective ALD self-aligns storage-node landing pads, deleting masks
idea: Combine area-selective deposition with the landing-pad step: inhibitor molecules adsorb on dielectric but not on contact plugs, so Mo/TiN grows only on plugs and mushrooms into self-aligned landing pads on US ALD tools, removing the landing-pad lithography.
why: Fact 4: deletes one of the 5-7 EUV layers and an overlay-critical step (~5-8% wafer cost), making a non-EUV US flow more viable.
note: Landing pad offsets BC grid to SN hex grid; mushroom growth cannot shift position and shorts at pitch.

title: Molybdenum wordlines double as in-field annealing heaters
idea: Combine the wordline with a micro-heater: during maintenance windows, pulse current through domestic Mo buried wordlines (replacing Chinese tungsten) to Joule-heat a mat to ~250 C for milliseconds to seconds, annealing hydrogen-related interface traps behind variable-retention-time leakage and weak cells.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): shrinking the <=13 fA tail could double or more the refresh interval (refresh energy halved) and heal hammer-induced trap damage (fact 9); thermal stress on neighbors is the risk.
note: 250 C likely too low to anneal H-related traps; neighbor stress.

title: Self-barrier CuMn bitline merges conductor and diffusion barrier
idea: Combine the bitline conductor and its TiN/WSix barrier into one Cu-0.5%Mn alloy fill; a post-fill anneal drives Mn to the dielectric interface where it forms a ~2 nm MnSiOx barrier in situ, replacing the W/TiN bitline stack (later capacitor anneals capped below ~500 C).
why: Removes bitline tungsten (China ~80%) and the barrier deposition; ~2x lower bitline resistance allows longer bitlines and fewer sense-amp stripes (~5-8% die area, periphery wall).
note: Cu in DRAM front-end and the <500 C cap clash with capacitor thermal budget.

title: Replacement buried wordline: sacrificial poly early, aluminum fill late
idea: Combine logic's replacement-metal-gate flow with the buried wordline: a sacrificial poly-Si plug sits in the trench through the hot activation steps, then is removed and the trench filled with Al-Cu by low-temperature CVD, with all later steps (low-temp ALD capacitor) kept <=450 C.
why: Removes the largest tungsten volume in a DRAM die using abundant aluminum; lower narrow-line resistance lets wordlines double in length, cutting sub-wordline drivers in the ~49% periphery.

title: Gray-tone mask and dual-tone resist merge two EUV layers
idea: Combine two critical layers in one EUV exposure: a gray-tone mask (partial-transmission absorber) gives two dose levels that a dual-tone resist resolves into two solubility states, developed sequentially (positive, then negative) into two stacked hardmasks; this removes a mask rather than adding one.
why: Cuts one of 5-7 EUV layers (~15-20% of per-wafer EUV time freed), easing the single-supplier chokepoint and ~1 MW/tool energy.

title: Reusable silicon-nitride crucible supplies the wafer's nitrogen doping
idea: Combine crucible and dopant source (zero masks): a dense, non-wetting Si3N4 crucible is reused across 10-50 melts, and its slow dissolution supplies the 1e14-1e15 cm-3 nitrogen DRAM wafers already need for void control, with oxygen added by gas.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine quartz crucible consumable entirely and a separate nitrogen-doping step; risk is nitride precipitate inclusions.

title: Mature-node fat capacitors enable tri-level DRAM for approximate data
idea: Combine NAND-style multi-level sensing with DRAM on a relaxed DUV node, where larger cells hold enough charge for three levels: a two-step sense amplifier resolves 0/half/1, storing 1.58 bits per cell for error-tolerant data such as activations, low mantissa planes or KV, with a binary mode for everything else.
why: +58% bits per cell without lithographic shrink, turning the absence of EUV (bigger cells, more charge, fact 1) into multi-level margin.

title: Liquid-metal microchannel interconnects for reworkable memory-on-logic stacks
idea: Combine microfluidic channels with interconnect: a thin glass spacer with fiber-laser-drilled holes filled with gallium-indium eutectic sits between electroless Ni-P/Au barrier pads on memory and logic, so joints form at room temperature without plasma or bonding gases and a memory die can be removed and replaced.
why: Stacking yield and lifetime: rework recovers nearly all stacking yield loss and makes memory field-upgradable; rare-gas-free assembly.
note: Ga alloys with Au/Ni-P over time; pitch and reliability doubtful.

title: Flash-style detrap pulses heal variable-retention-time cells in field
idea: Combine NAND erase-style detrapping with DRAM self-refresh: during idle, access transistors get brief negative-gate and reverse-junction bias pulses that empty the oxide/junction traps behind random-telegraph leakage, pushing VRT cells back into their low-leak state.
why: Leakage tail <=13 fA (fact 3): VRT cells force pessimistic refresh; pinning them low-leak could allow ~2x longer refresh and fewer field failures.

title: Wordline doubles as heater for periodic in-situ trap annealing
idea: Combine Joule microheaters with the array wordlines: in maintenance windows, after data is moved to another subarray, current through Mo or TiN wordline segments heats the local array to ~200-300 C for microseconds to milliseconds, annealing hydrogen-related and interface traps that create leakage tails. Buildable in a university nanofab: patterned Mo/TiN lines over IGZO or Si TFT arrays.
why: Retention tail and aging (fact 3): lifetime self-healing could tighten the tail 2-5x; also avoids tungsten wordlines (China ~80% chokepoint).

title: Etch-free printed oxide micro-fab using inkjet and laser sintering
idea: Fuse inkjet or electrohydrodynamic printing of In-Zn-O precursor inks with flash or laser sintering to build gain-cell memory tiles additively. Nothing is etched, so there is no fluorine and no masks, in containerized micro-fabs near customers.
why: Distributed, near-zero-capex (about $5M per pod) supply of low-density working memory for edge and defense, with no PFAS or EUV.

title: Photochromic-lens diarylethene switched electrically as the storage molecule
idea: Adapt Transitions-lens photochromics: diarylethene molecules ring-close or ring-open on a redox pulse, changing conductance ~100x; a monolayer between nanogap electrodes stores the bit as molecular conformation.
why: Fact 3 and density: conformation needs no stored charge, so retention is set by a ~1 eV isomer barrier rather than leakage, at molecular footprint.

title: LCD panel laser repair: spot-anneal the retention-tail cells
idea: Adapted from the laser repair stations that fix defective TFT pixels in LCD fabs: after retention test, or at a refurbisher, a nanosecond laser heats ~1 um spots containing weak cells through a thinned backside in forming gas, annealing the traps that cause their leakage.
why: Repairs the leakage tail (fact 3) of finished dies without spending spare rows; LCD fabs run such tools at high throughput, and repair can be repeated at end of first life before resale.

title: Railway wheel re-profiling: per-cell charge injection retunes leaky transistors
idea: Adapted from underfloor wheel lathes that re-profile train wheels without removing them: for each cell flagged as leaky, a high-field write sequence injects charge into that access transistor's drain-side spacer, relieving its gate-edge field or raising its local threshold until leakage meets spec; it can be repeated in the field.
why: Repairs individual tail cells (fact 3) without spare rows or global bias changes, so the tail is trimmed as it appears and the whole array refreshes at the strong-cell rate.
note: Uncontrolled spacer charge injection may damage oxide and lose charge at 85 C.

title: Telephone-exchange relay logic rebuilt with NEMS relays on glass
idea: Borrowed from relay telephone exchanges, rebuilt with nano-electromechanical relays (metal beam, air gap) made on glass: decoder trees and mat power gates use relays with zero off-current, switched one cycle ahead because addresses arrive early.
why: Idle power: periphery standby leakage goes to ~0, and a relay process needs only metals and oxides, no silicon wafer.

title: Display-fab turnkey lines for U.S. memory periphery
idea: Borrowed from the solar and display industries' turnkey-line model: buy standard Gen-6 glass toolsets (flat-panel i-line steppers, PECVD, sputter) and run memory panels with relaxed 1-2 um periphery rules, since glass area costs ~100x less than wafer area, sited in the U.S. within ~18-24 months.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: periphery capex per m2 ~10x below a DRAM fab, with no EUV and no quartz crucibles.
note: 1-2 um periphery rules inflate area far more than glass saves per m2.

title: Charlieplexed wordlines with thin-film bidirectional selectors
idea: Borrowed from LED charlieplexing: wordlines are selected by ordered pairs of N driver lines through back-to-back oxide Schottky-diode selectors on glass, so N drivers address N(N-1) rows (32 drivers select 992 rows).
why: Periphery: row-driver count per mat down ~30x, which matters on glass where thin-film drivers are large.
note: Sneak paths through half-selected rows undermine charlieplexing for wordlines.

title: Aerospace honeycomb: hex-packed cells with three 120-degree line sets
idea: Adapted from honeycomb sandwich cores: vertical-channel cells sit on a hexagonal close-packed lattice addressed by three line families at 120 degrees (wordline, bitline, plate-select), with a cell chosen by coincidence of two of them.
why: Hex packing gives ~3.5F2 vs 4F2 square and 6F2 today (fact 4), ~15% more bits per litho area, plus isotropic support that resists tall-pillar collapse.

title: Blu-ray layer focus: threshold-window gates select tiers by voltage
idea: Borrowed from multilayer optical discs where focus depth picks the layer: each tier's access transistor has two series gates on two shared vertical lines, with thresholds graded up the stack on one and down on the other, so voltage level k on both turns on only tier k, with no per-tier staircase contact.
why: Removes staircase contacts and per-tier drivers for ~8 tiers per gate pair (facts 2,7); staircase area ~-80%.
note: Resembles layer-selection-by-multilevel in 3D NAND; Vt variation limits tiers per gate pair.

title: Veneer slicing: deposit layers, slice block, get 10 nm lines
idea: Borrowed from wood-veneer slicing and nanoskiving: deposit 500 alternating 10 nm metal/oxide layers as a thick block, slice it perpendicular with a diamond microtome into thin slabs, and lay the slabs flat so the cut face exposes 10 nm lines whose pitch is set by deposition, not litho; cross two slabs for a crosspoint array.
why: Sub-10 nm wordline/bitline gratings without EUV (fact 4), patterning cost ~1/100; trade-offs: slab registration, needs a crosspoint-compatible gain cell or selector.

title: Rare-earth-free motor magnet chemistry for platinum-free MRAM
idea: EV-motor makers are replacing NdFeB with iron nitride (Fe16N2) and synthetic tetrataenite (L10-FeNi). Adapt these phases as the perpendicular free and reference layers of a spin-torque cell, removing Pt/Co multilayers, the Ir in the synthetic antiferromagnet and heavy Ta seeds.
why: MRAM is capacitor-free with very high endurance but leans on Pt, Ir, Ru and Ta (South Africa/Russia/DRC chokepoints). Iron and nitrogen are everywhere.

title: Planar ferrite inductors revive core memory at micron scale
idea: Power-supply makers now print MnZn/NiZn ferrite planar cores on silicon. Adapt this to bring back magnetic core memory: a 1-2 um ferrite toroid per bit, threaded by BEOL wordline, bitline and sense traces, with coincident-current writes and on-die restore-after-read.
why: Core was DRAM-class working memory before DRAM: no capacitor, no leakage, no refresh, unlimited endurance, all iron/manganese/zinc oxides. Density is the hurdle; the aim is ~10-20 F2 per tier across many stacked BEOL tiers.
note: Micron ferrite cores give poor density.

title: RF filter aluminum-boron-nitride ferroelectric in an endurance-shielded cell
idea: Phone BAW filters are sputtered aluminum nitride made in vast volume. Adapt boron-doped AlN (a ferroelectric wurtzite needing no Sc or Hf) as a ferroelectric-gated transistor bit on the same sputter tools, and shield its finite endurance with an SRAM write-back buffer that absorbs hot writes so each cell sees <1e9 cycles over its life.
why: A capacitor-free, Hf-free, Sc-free nonvolatile bit needs no refresh. The risks are the high coercive field (~4-6 MV/cm) and fatigue.
note: FeFET endurance far below DRAM-class; write buffer cannot fully hide it.

title: Parametron revival using MEMS-timing resonators storing phase bits
idea: MEMS timing chips (silicon resonators that replaced quartz crystals) meet Goto's 1950s parametron. Each bit is stored as the 0 or pi phase of a parametrically pumped nanomechanical resonator; one shared pump tone holds every bit, and reads use phase-sensitive detection.
why: No capacitor and no leakage tail, in all-silicon. Refresh is replaced by a continuous low-power pump, possibly ~fW per bit for high-Q resonators. Density and speed are unproven.
note: Phase-bit MEMS resonators demonstrated; density, vacuum Q and readout speed far from DRAM-class.

title: Solar-grade silicon plus RAID coding tolerates leaky capacitorless cells
idea: Solar uses cheaper upgraded-metallurgical silicon, and RAID tolerates failing disks. Combine both: build capacitor-free floating-body or gain-cell arrays on 6N-7N wafers and absorb the fatter leakage tail with row-level erasure codes that rebuild expired bits instead of refreshing everything faster.
why: Siemens polysilicon purification (~50-60 kWh/kg) and 11N purity are energy and supply chokepoints. Tolerating impurity-driven tails could cut substrate energy and cost ~20-30%.

title: Optical-disc stamper family tree for DRAM array nanoimprint
idea: Adapt CD/DVD/Blu-ray replication: one e-beam-written quartz master is electroformed into nickel 'father', 'mother' and 'son' stampers (each generation multiplies copies ~10x), and the sons serve as UV-nanoimprint working templates for the periodic array layers (capacitor holes, landing pads, bitlines). Each son is retired after a fixed imprint count, as disc plants do, so defects never accumulate; EUV is kept only for the periphery.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): replaces 3-4 of the 5-7 EUV array exposures with NIL tools at ~1/5 the cost and ~1/10 the power of an EUV scanner; claim 15-25% wafer-cost cut. Risks: overlay at 12 nm-class pitch and imprint defectivity.
note: Nickel stampers are UV-opaque and Si wafers too, so UV-NIL cure fails; overlay at 12 nm.

title: Bear hibernation: migrate idle rows to NVM before retention expires
idea: Borrowed from hibernating animals that drop to near-zero metabolism: the controller timestamps each row's last activation and, when an untouched row nears its retention deadline, moves it once into a dense non-volatile tier and marks it hibernating instead of refreshing it; a later access wakes it back into DRAM.
why: Periodic refresh becomes a one-time migration of cold rows; DRAM holds only the awake working set (often 20-40% of allocated), shrinking provisioned DRAM with zero refresh power.
note: Untouched-for-64ms describes most rows; migration would thrash.

title: Phone-filter piezo transducers send ultrasonic data vertically through stacks
idea: Adapted from AlN bulk-acoustic-wave filters in smartphones: thin piezo transducers on each die launch GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded silicon stack to receivers on other dies. Data TSVs are replaced by frequency- or time-multiplexed acoustic channels.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): could remove ~1-2k data TSVs per die and their keep-out zones, leaving only bonding and power vias.
note: Acoustic channel density and per-channel bandwidth far below TSVs; bond interfaces reflect.

title: Space-solar Miura fold turns one thin DRAM sheet into a stack
idea: Adapted from Miura-ori folding of satellite solar arrays: a strip of DRAM dies is built on an ultra-thin flexible bonded film with continuous copper traces across the fold lines. The strip folds accordion-style into a 16-high stack whose wires wrap around the folds instead of passing through TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSVs, their keep-out and per-tier bonding steps, targeting ~20% lower stack cost and higher yield.

title: Pupin loading coils make long interposer memory lines distortionless
idea: Adapted from the 1900 telephone loading coil: small thick-metal spiral inductors are added periodically along long memory traces to meet the Heaviside condition (L/C = R/G). A wide slow bus can then stretch 5-10 cm without equalizers.
why: More DRAM dies can sit around a processor (capacity) at near-HBM energy, and power-hungry equalization goes away.

title: Military fuzz-button connectors make solderless, reworkable memory stacks
idea: Adapted from fuzz-button (compressed gold-wire wad) interconnects in avionics: DRAM dies or packages stack in a clamped frame with fuzz-button arrays between them, so any failing die can be swapped after test with no reflow.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): one bad die no longer scraps a 12-16 die stack (~20-30% yield recovery), using 1990s machining and wire-forming tools.
note: Fuzz-button pitch ~0.5 mm cannot carry HBM-class I/O.

title: CRT degaussing: trap-reset pulses to tame variable-retention cells
idea: Adapted from degaussing coils that reset magnetized CRT masks with a decaying field: using existing vendor test modes on current dies, the controller periodically applies a short decaying-amplitude negative wordline and plate bias sequence to idle subarrays, trying to drive variable-retention traps into their low-leakage state and hold them there.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): variable-retention cells force pessimistic refresh because they toggle unpredictably; if trap states can be biased, the worst-case tail could shrink ~2x, allowing longer refresh on parts already in the field.
note: Whether VRT traps can be biased into low-leak state is unknown.

title: On-chip gigahertz phononic delay loop recirculating bits in flight
idea: MAGNIFY frequency and MINIFY wavelength of 1940s mercury delay-line memory: 20 GHz acoustic pulses travel ~4 km/s in thin-film LiNbO3 or AlScN waveguides, so a 1-mm spiral holds ~5 us x 20 Gb/s = 100 kbit, regenerated by a piezo transducer and comparator at each loop end.
why: ~1e8 bit/mm2 with no cell, no capacitor and no EUV (facts 1, 4); energy only spent regenerating; suits sequential tiers such as streaming KV caches.

title: Vanadium dioxide hysteresis bit parked inside its transition loop
idea: MINIFY the thermal window: hold a sputtered VO2 cell array at the midpoint of its ~5-10 K metal-insulator hysteresis with a chip thermostat; a forward current pulse through a VO2/Bi2Te3 junction Peltier-heats a 30-nm cell onto the metallic branch, and a reverse pulse Peltier-cools it back onto the insulating branch, read by resistance.
why: Static, refresh-free, non-destructive read (facts 3, 8) built with two sputter targets; local Peltier cooling strength is the weak point.

title: Ovonic threshold switch acts as one-device bitline comparator
idea: A room-temperature-sputtered chalcogenide OTS is biased just below threshold; the charge-shared bitline from a '1' pushes it over, and its snap-back delivers a large current pulse (near-infinite gain) captured by a 2-TFT latch, MINIFYING a ~12-transistor SA to ~3 devices.
why: Fact 7: SA area -70%; OTS threshold spread (~50 mV) must be trimmed per device, hence high risk.
note: OTS threshold spread (~50 mV) is comparable to the bitline signal; per-device trim needed.

title: Active glass interposer with IGZO switches routes around bad dies
idea: MAGNIFY redundancy from cells to whole dies: a glass interposer carries IGZO TFT switch matrices (<=350 C) that remap channels from a failing HBM die or TSV column to a spare die in the stack, configured at final test.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss; glass panel substrates are cheap and a U.S. manufacturing strength.

title: IGZO charge-coupled readout drains rows to few sense nodes
idea: MAGNIFY serialization: like a CCD image sensor, a row's charge packets are shifted bucket-brigade along BEOL IGZO transfer gates (<=350 C) to one floating-diffusion sense node per 64 columns, MINIFYING sense amps 64x for sequential tensor streams.
why: Fact 7: periphery area in stream banks -50%; IGZO's tiny leakage keeps packets intact during transfer, but transfer inefficiency is the risk.

title: Accumulative ferroelectric FET counts activations per row nonvolatilely
idea: Exploit accumulative partial switching in HZO/AlScN: each ACT applies a sub-coercive pulse to a per-row FeFET (<=400 C), nudging its threshold one step; after N steps it trips a neighbor-refresh flag and is reset, MINIFYING a row-hammer counter to one transistor.
why: Fact 9: exact per-row counts at ~0.5% area with no SRAM tables; FeFET endurance (~1e10 cycles) versus reset rate is the main risk.
note: Partial-switching fatigue under billions of activations on hot rows.

title: Minify speed to 1 us: 2-bit cells with shared ramp sensing
idea: Build a deliberately slow far-memory tier with 1 us access: cells store 2 bits (4 charge levels), and 64 bitlines share one slow, precise ramp-ADC sense circuit, time-multiplexed.
why: Cost per bit: 2x bits per cell and 64x fewer sense amps, for tiered memory holding cold KV-cache and pages at about 40-50% lower cost per bit.

title: Grain-roughened TiN electrodes let plain alumina replace hafnia capacitors
idea: Magnify electrode area ~2.5x by reviving 1990s hemispherical-grain roughening in TiN form (seeded nanocrystal nucleation inside the hole), so a robust Al2O3/TiO2 laminate (k ~20) stores the same charge as ZrO2/HfO2.
why: Alumina's wide bandgap and lack of phase transitions make 125 C/10-year TDDB and leakage easier to meet, and hafnium and zirconium leave the cell.
note: HSG roughening needs room inside the hole; sub-30 nm capacitors leave no space for grains.

title: Photo-electrochemical macropore capacitor wafer with thermal oxide-nitride dielectric
idea: Magnify a cheap old process: etch 100:1 macropores into n-type silicon by backside-illuminated HF anodization (no plasma, no EUV), line them with thermally grown ONO, and hybrid-bond this capacitor wafer to the transistor wafer.
why: ONO is among the most reliable dielectrics at 125 C, and capacitor wafers can come from depreciated U.S. 200 mm lines, with no hafnium, zirconium, PFAS or EUV in the capacitor.

title: Printed relaxor polymer dielectric hitting k near 60
idea: Magnify dielectric constant by slot-die coating P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) relaxor terpolymer (k~50-60) biased in its non-switching paraelectric regime as a planar storage capacitor dielectric.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Fact 1 needs k~70 to escape the pillar; a printed planar capacitor with k~60 approaches it at ~1/10 the process cost.

title: Inline print-test-repair loop with capacitive probe rollers
idea: Magnify test throughput by running the web past non-contact capacitive probe rollers that map bad blocks in real time; a downstream laser cuts and a printer reroutes around them before lamination.
why: Yield and test capital: testing at web speed removes probe-card floors and turns defects into reroutes, not scrap.

title: Print memory directly on package substrate panels
idea: Magnify memory placement onto 510x515 mm organic package panels: inkjet-print oxide gain-cell arrays beside the processor footprint during panel-level packaging, so memory and package are made in one line.
why: Data movement and capital: millimeters from the compute die, no separate memory wafer, and it uses existing panel-packaging lines.

title: Sacrificial backside allows one debond and re-thin cycle
idea: MAGNIFY reuse cycles: HBM dies keep a ~10 um sacrificial backside margin, so a debonded die can be re-thinned, re-polished and hybrid-bonded once more into a new stack.
why: Recovers known-good DRAM dies from failed or retired stacks, cutting wafer demand per shipped GB.
note: Hybrid-bonded dies cannot be cleanly debonded.

title: Eliminate charge storage: spin-crossover molecules hold bits in spin state
idea: Eliminate charge: a thin film of Fe(II)-triazole spin-crossover molecules switches between low-spin and high-spin states, with ~10% volume change and a large permittivity shift, inside a room-temperature hysteresis loop; a strain pulse from a piezoelectric gate flips it and capacitive sensing reads it.
why: Bistable at room temperature with no leakage-driven decay (fact 3) at molecular density; risks are electrical switching speed (ns shown only optically) and fatigue.
note: Electrical ns switching unproven; volume change fatigue.

title: Eliminate stored charge: 77-K YBCO persistent-current loops as bits
idea: Eliminate charge storage: the bit is the direction of a persistent supercurrent in a ~100-nm YBCO nano-loop broken by a grain-boundary Josephson junction, written by a current pulse and read by an adjacent nano-SQUID. YBCO superconducts at 92 K, so LN2 rather than helium is enough, and it is grown by MOCVD in O2 with no argon sputtering.
why: Zero static dissipation and ps switching (facts 3, 10) with no leakage at all; the ban on liquid helium forces high-Tc materials; risks are junction reproducibility and loop inductance limiting density to ~0.1 um2 per bit.
note: YBCO grain-boundary junction reproducibility and loop inductance limit density.

title: Eliminate holding energy: van der Waals stiction latches nanocantilever bits
idea: Eliminate any energy source for holding state: a 10-nm graphene or ALD-TiN cantilever is pulled electrostatically onto a pad where van der Waals adhesion keeps it stuck (bit 1) with zero power, and a second pull-off electrode peels it free (bit 0); contact resistance reads the state. The sacrificial ALD oxide is removed by vapor HF, so no rare gases are used.
why: Turns the classic MEMS failure, stiction, into the storage mechanism: nonvolatile, leak-free and refresh-free (fact 3); risks are adhesion variability and contact endurance.
note: Same stiction-latch mechanism.

title: Eliminate vacuum-deposited ferroelectrics: solution-grown croconic-acid proton-transfer bits
idea: Eliminate inorganic, vacuum-deposited ferroelectrics: grow the room-temperature organic ferroelectric croconic acid (Ps ~20 uC/cm2) from solution inside cell pores, where polarization reverses by collective proton transfer along hydrogen bonds, a light-particle switch that needs small fields and no oxygen-vacancy motion.
why: Nonvolatile storage at low coercive voltage (fact 10) made by solution casting with no process gases; proton transfer avoids the vacancy-driven fatigue of HZO; risks are thermal budget, thin-film quality and BEOL integration.

title: Eliminate sub-wordline drivers: resonant LC wordlines with energy recovery
idea: Delete the sub-wordline driver stripes by making master wordlines low-resistance Ru lines that a single pass switch per row connects to a bank-wide resonant LC rail. The switch closes at the sinusoid trough and opens at its peak, so the wordline charges adiabatically and most of its energy returns to the tank on discharge.
why: SWD stripes are ~8-10% of the die. Adiabatic charging recovers ~60-70% of wordline CV2 energy, which is stuck by the 3 V wordline (fact 10).
note: Single pass switch per row and sinusoid timing at ns access.

title: Eliminate probe pads and probe cards: optically powered contactless wafer test
idea: Give each die a 100 um coil and a small photovoltaic cell. Flood illumination powers whole wafers, and test patterns flow over near-field inductive links at ~1 Gb/s, so thousands of dies test in parallel untouched. Probe pads, their drivers and test-lane ESD disappear.
why: Test is ~8-12% of DRAM cost; massively parallel contactless test lifts tester throughput ~10x and frees ~1-2% of die area.
note: Flood-lit PV cells cannot supply DRAM test power per die.

title: Eliminate the sense amplifier via negative-capacitance bitlines
idea: Put a thin ferroelectric HZO layer in series between each bitline and its parasitic shield, biased so its negative capacitance cancels ~60% of bitline capacitance. The charge-share signal rises from ~100 mV to ~300 mV, enough for a plain skewed-inverter pair instead of a matched latch.
why: SA offset-matching area goes away (SA -40%), or Cs can drop 2-3x at the same margin, attacking the capacitor charge wall (fact 1). Negative-capacitance stability and hysteresis are unproven.
note: Same NC bitline-capacitance cancellation.

title: Eliminate the isolation trench: grow periphery isolation by area-selective ALD
idea: Skip the fluorocarbon STI etch and the HF liner and oxide strips. Non-fluorinated alkyl-aminosilane inhibitor SAMs mark the device islands, and repeated inhibitor-refresh cycles of area-selective ALD grow ~80 nm Al2O3 isolation ridges only between them. Selective Si epitaxy (dichlorosilane/HCl) then raises the active areas level.
why: Removes the whole STI module (trench etch, liner, fill, heavy CMP) and every fluorine step in isolation; periphery front-end cost ~-30%.

title: Eliminate transistor sense latches: carbon-released NEMS bistable beams
idea: Each bitline pair drives the two electrodes of a ~2 um buckled TiN nano-beam above it. The charge-share imbalance plus a common pull-in bias snaps the beam to one side, where its contact pulls that bitline to the rail. The cavity is cut by O2-ashing an amorphous-carbon sacrificial layer, which replaces HF-vapor or XeF2 release.
why: Gives a sense latch with zero leakage and no Vt mismatch, stacked in BEOL over the bitlines (SA area -30%) at ~fJ per sense. Mechanical speed (10-50 ns) restricts it to dense, slow tiers.
note: Mechanical asymmetry dwarfs mV signals; endurance and stiction.

title: Eliminate address buses: two-wire analog voltage row addressing
idea: Replace the ~13 predecoded address lines per mat with two analog wires (16 coarse and 32 fine levels) and a resistive ladder. Each wordline driver ANDs two 2-transistor window comparators tied to its ladder taps and fires only when both broadcast voltages fall in its window; the wiring is Cl-etched Mo.
why: Removes the predecoders (decoder area -40%) and the metal level that hosts the address bus; noise margin needs ladder calibration.

title: Eliminate the common plate: pairwise differential plateless capacitors
idea: Remove the shared top-plate electrode and its conformal TiN/poly fill; neighbouring pillar storage nodes face each other through the high-k film so each pair forms one capacitor written with complementary charge (+Q/-Q) and read differentially on a folded bitline pair.
why: Capacitor charge wall: differential read roughly doubles signal per unit Cs, so ~5 fF pillars behave like ~9-10 fF single-ended; deletes the plate deposition/etch module.
note: Two pillars per bit halves density; pillar-to-pillar crosstalk in hex arrays.

title: Eliminate the 3D staircase: contact tiers at the etched die sidewall
idea: Remove the NAND-style staircase entirely; terminate every tier at a deep-etched trench wall at the mat edge where all tiers are exposed edge-on, then a laser-written or tilted-deposition redistribution layer fans each tier out to the top surface.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM: the staircase costs area and N trim/etch cycles; edge contacting makes tier count nearly free in area, helping reach the 26+ tier break-even.
note: Resolving ~40 nm tiers on a sidewall with laser writing or tilted deposition is unrealistic.

title: Eliminate the capacitor hole: bottom-up nanowire capacitor electrodes
idea: Instead of etching a mold, grow a conductive nanowire (doped Si or silicide, using a CMOS-safe Al or Sn catalyst) vapour-liquid-solid straight up from each storage node to AR 200:1, then wrap it in ALD high-k and plate.
why: Water and charge wall: no mold deposition, hole etch, polymer clean or dip-out, so most capacitor wet steps vanish; free-standing high-AR wires give ~2x Cs.

title: Eliminate sacrificial SiGe: Si/CaF2 epitaxial insulator superlattice
idea: Grow 3D DRAM tiers as an epitaxial superlattice of silicon and lattice-matched CaF2 (~0.6% mismatch), so the inter-tier insulator is grown in its final form and no sacrificial layer needs wet lateral removal and refill.
why: Water: removes the wet lateral SiGe recess, its rinses, and the refill/etch-back cycles of 3D DRAM tier formation; helps reach 26+ tiers with ~10x fewer wet steps per bit.
note: Large CaF2/Si thermal mismatch and poor Si-on-CaF2 regrowth.

title: Eliminate wafers and wet benches: roll-to-roll vacuum web tiers
idea: Deposit oxide-semiconductor capacitor-transistor tiers on a moving stainless or polyimide web inside a vacuum roll coater, patterning with in-line laser ablation and shadow-roll masks, then laminate cut sheets into stacks.
why: Water and capital: vacuum web coating uses almost no process water and costs tens of millions per line; it suits slower, higher-capacity working-memory tiers.
note: R2R pitch (~um) yields bits/area orders below DRAM; cost per bit unlikely to win.

title: Eliminate charge pumps: monolayer MoS2 access transistors driven from 1 V
idea: Replace the buried silicon access device with a gate-all-around monolayer MoS2 channel (U.S. molybdenum, refinery sulfur) whose ~2 eV gap and 0.7 nm body give near-zero off-current at 0 V, so the wordline swings 0-1 V straight from VDD with no VPP pump or negative-wordline supply.
why: Wordline energy drops (3 V/1 V)^2 times ~2.5x avoided pump loss, ~20x; also removes the leakage tail behind refresh (fact 3) and the pump area.
note: MoS2 on-current/contact resistance at 1 V and wafer-scale GAA integration are the doubts.

title: Eliminate access-transistor lithography: grow vertical nanowire channels from catalysts
idea: Place catalyst dots with a block-copolymer lattice (no mask), grow vertical single-crystal Si nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid epitaxy with a CMOS-friendly catalyst (Al or Cu-silicide), then wrap them in ALD gate stacks to form 4F2 vertical access transistors.
why: Facts 2 and 4: removes the EUV-class active-area and channel etch masks; bottom-up wires have smooth sidewalls and low trap density, tightening the leakage tail.

title: Eliminate fragmentation slack with transparent hardware object compaction
idea: The memory controller keeps a small redirection table and relocates live small objects in the background into dense pages, updating mappings like a hardware copying collector, so malloc arenas stop wasting free holes.
why: Long-running allocators waste 15-30% of DRAM to fragmentation; reclaiming it is pure capacity gain without app changes.
note: Hardware lacks object boundaries; per-object redirection table would be huge.

title: Eliminate EUV and single capacitors: self-assembled redundant capacitor fingers per bit
idea: Pattern capacitor holes at sub-20 nm pitch by directed self-assembly of a block copolymer annealed at ~250 C, and wire four cylinders in parallel per cell. A DSA defect that drops or merges one cylinder then only reduces Cs ~25% instead of killing the bit.
why: Makes DSA defectivity tolerable and removes EUV layers at the capacitor level (fact 4); cell yield follows per-quad rather than per-hole statistics.
note: Sub-20 nm pitch holes cannot fit a full MIM stack per cylinder.

title: Inside-out capacitor: block-copolymer pore sponge replaces one tall pillar
idea: Flip the capacitor from a solid pillar into voids: inside each cell footprint a self-assembled block-copolymer template is etched into sacrificial oxide as ~10 nm pores (AR ~20 each), then coated TiN/ZrO2/TiN by ALD, so area comes from many shallow holes instead of one 70:1 pillar.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): ~2-3x electrode area at one third of the aspect ratio, reaching ~5 fF without AR 115 and removing pillar-collapse yield loss.
note: 10 nm pores cannot fit a TiN/ZrO2/TiN stack (~16+ nm); area gain doubtful at DRAM cell pitch.

title: One heavy-metal strip: forward to write, backward to read
idea: Rearrange the spintronic stack around one effect run both ways: a perpendicular nanomagnet on a Pt or Bi2Se3 strip is written by spin-orbit torque (charge to spin) and read by the inverse, a GHz pulse excites precession whose spin pumping yields an inverse-spin-Hall voltage whose sign is the bit; no MgO tunnel barrier.
why: Endurance and refresh (fact 3): nonvolatile with no barrier to break down, aiming at DRAM-like unlimited cycles; drops the tungsten-heavy MTJ stack; risk is a uV-scale read signal.
note: Dropping MgO for uV inverse-spin-Hall read worsens signal; endurance gain unclear.

title: Molecular spin-state bit: hysteretic Fe(II) spin-crossover film
idea: Instead of moving electrons in and out of a node, flip their pairing inside an ion: a thin film of a room-temperature-hysteretic Fe(II) spin-crossover complex toggles between low-spin and high-spin with ~10-20% dielectric-constant change; a field/charge pulse sets the state and a capacitive divider reads it.
why: Refresh (fact 3): a bistable molecular state needs no refresh and molecule-scale units (~2 nm) promise density; risks are solid-film switching speed and cycling.
note: Solid-film spin-crossover switching is slow, needs temperature bias, and permittivity contrast is small.

title: Write-first read infers old bit from charge the driver supplies
idea: Flip read and write order: a per-column-group write driver forces the opened cell to '1' while a charge integrator measures how much charge it delivered (~0 for a stored 1, ~Cs*VDD for a stored 0); the result is latched and 0s are written back. Latch-type sense amp and separate restore phase merge into one driver/integrator.
why: Facts 7 and 8: removes the cross-coupled SA and equalizer (~30% of SA strip area); the integrator sees full Cs*VDD rather than a ~100 mV charge-shared swing, so 2-3 fF cells suffice.
note: Integrator also sees large common-mode bitline charge; signal charge is still Cs*VDD, as with charge sharing.

title: High-voltage drivers on glass: TFT periphery on U.S. panels
idea: Reverse the substrate for high-voltage periphery: global wordline drivers, level shifters and pumps, which need 3-5 V rather than density, are built as TFTs on a U.S.-made glass interposer panel and connected to the array die through fine-pitch redistribution.
why: Fact 7 and capital: thick-oxide periphery (~8-10% of die) leaves the silicon; panel processing costs ~1/10 of silicon per area.

title: Grow capacitor walls up instead of etching holes down
idea: Reverse subtractive to additive: area-selective ALD grows the capacitor support lattice upward from seeded lines, so the 60-75:1 storage structure forms without a fluorocarbon high-aspect-ratio etch.
why: HAR capacitor etch is the heaviest user of PFAS-class fluorocarbon gases and NF3 chamber cleans; additive growth could cut those per wafer by >50% and relax the charge-wall aspect ratio limit.

title: Helium-off etch: edge dies carry extra parity
idea: Rearrange reliability by location: run etch tools without helium backside gas, accept the resulting radial temperature/CD drift, and assign stronger ECC to edge-zone dies or rows (from a known radial map) so their ~1% raw BER is absorbed.
why: Eliminates most fab helium demand (Qatar ~30% offline) with no new tool; costs ~5% extra parity on outer-ring dies.
note: Without backside gas, wafer temperature control fails broadly, not just radially; ECC may not absorb it.
