Existing wordline and dummy-gate conductors are driven as resistive heaters in maintenance windows (about 1 s pulses heating locally to ~250 C), passivating hydrogen-related interface traps and resetting variable-retention-time defects in the array.
why: Fact 3: shrinking the ≤13 fA tail could let the refresh interval stretch ~4x, plus self-healing of aging-induced leakage over the product's life.

title: Zero added disturb at tighter pitch: buried electron-sink layer
idea: Imposed limit: shrink wordline pitch without adding disturbance. A thin carbon-doped or SiGe trap-rich layer is implanted beneath the buried wordlines. It captures and recombines electrons injected by repeated aggressor activation before they diffuse to neighboring storage-node junctions.
why: Fact 9: could raise hammer thresholds several-fold and allow the 6F^2 pitch to keep shrinking without pushing thresholds below 1k.

title: No silicon wafer: phone display backplane doubles as standby memory
idea: Forced limit: the memory must ride on an existing non-Si substrate. Low-leakage oxide TFTs already in LTPO phone backplanes get a few hundred MB of gain-cell array in the bezel and backplane, used as frame buffer and standby memory so the LPDDR can sleep.
why: Supply: about 1.5 billion phones a year could each offload 0.25-0.5 GB of LPDDR demand, which frees wafers for servers.

title: No wafer consumed: remote epitaxy on a reusable donor
idea: Forced limit: the substrate may not be used up. Crystalline Ge or InGaZnO-class films are grown by remote epitaxy through graphene on a donor that is reused 50 or more times, peeled off, and laminated onto glass or metal carriers.
why: Substrate consumption per device drops by about 50x, which decouples memory output from wafer and crucible supply.

title: Voltage-clocked skyrmion shift register: magnetic bubble memory revived with gate clocks instead of currents
idea: A chiral multilayer (Pt/Co/MgO type, with perpendicular anisotropy and strong DMI) is patterned into tracks 2F wide. Gates at 2F pitch on 1.5 nm MgO modulate interface anisotropy through VCMA. Two-phase clocks with a built-in ratchet (an asymmetric gate profile) create a moving energy minimum that carries each skyrmion one bit-length per clock, like charge packets in a CCD. A skyrmionic MTJ at the track end reads the bit (20-70% contrast reported), and a VCMA/SOT nucleator writes it. The state is non-volatile between shifts. With no lateral current there is no electromigration or Joule heating, and thousands of tracks share each clock line.
why: [SPECULATIVE] Refresh goes to zero; ~47 aJ per gate toggle; no capacitor or access transistor per bit. Density is 1.34x WORSE than 1-beta per layer at F = 13.4 nm (parity needs F ~11.6 nm or two layers). This is an energy and volatility play, not density.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO layer fused onto ZrO2 storage capacitor
idea: Combine a thin ferroelectric HZO film, biased in its non-switching negative-capacitance regime, in series with the paraelectric ZrO2/Al2O3 cell dielectric so the ferroelectric's negative dQ/dV cancels part of the dielectric's inverse capacitance. Thickness-match the layers so the stack stays hysteresis-free while effective k reaches ~70-100 in the same 60:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): hits the k~70 target without going to AR 115; 1.5-2x Cs or 30-40% shorter pillars with fewer etch/deposition steps.
note: Stabilized NC enhancement contested; MPB ZrO2 already mainstream path.

title: Nanoporous dealloyed metal electrode inside storage capacitor
idea: Borrow dealloyed nanoporous metals from battery and catalyst electrodes: deposit a TiAl alloy in a wider, shallower capacitor hole, selectively etch out the Al to leave a sponge with 10-20 nm pores, then coat ALD dielectric and top electrode throughout. The sponge multiplies internal surface area 3-4x within the same footprint.
why: Fact 1: 3-4x area allows AR ~20:1 instead of 60-75:1 at the same Cs, cutting deep-etch time and tool count.
note: HSG-silicon precedent; 10-20 nm pores cannot hold dielectric plus electrode.

title: Jewelry lost-wax: sacrificial zinc-oxide layers for lateral 3D cavities
idea: Lost-wax casting relies on a filler that is easy to remove; build the 3D DRAM tier stack with sputtered ZnO sacrificial layers between Si or SiN tiers, then dissolve the ZnO in dilute acetic acid, which leaves Si, SiO2 and SiN untouched, carving micron-deep lateral capacitor cavities from one vertical slit.
why: 3D capacitor blocker (fact 2): replaces SiGe epitaxy and aggressive vapor etch with sputtering and a mild wet etch, cutting epi tool needs and recess variability; Zn and O are abundant.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina grows the capacitor mold
idea: Reverse etching a mold into growing one: deposit ~2 um of aluminum over the landing pads, use one added mask to imprint pore nucleation dimples aligned to the pads, and anodize so self-ordered pores grow straight down at AR >100; line the pores with TiN/high-k/TiN.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): AR 100-150 with no plasma HAR etch and no support-lattice masks; AAO pore AR >1000 is proven at larger pitch.

title: Nanosphere monolayer sets the capacitor lattice
idea: Reverse top-down patterning into bottom-up packing: spread a Langmuir-Blodgett monolayer of 40 nm silica spheres that close-pack into a hex lattice, shrink them by plasma, and use them as the etch mask for honeycomb capacitor holes.
why: Replaces the EUV/ArFi honeycomb capacitor-hole layer with a wet coating step; tool cost near zero.
note: LB sphere monolayers have domain defects and cannot register to landing pads.

title: Fully silicided titanium wordline grown inward from polysilicon fill
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of depositing metal into the buried-wordline trench, fill the trench with doped polysilicon and convert it in place, top-down, into C54 TiSi2 (Ti deposition, Si pre-amorphization, two-step RTA). The conductor is grown from what is already there.
why: Removes W, WF6 and the TiN liner from the array. TiSi2 (~15 uOhm-cm bulk) approaches W at these widths, survives ~850 C and uses only Ti and Si.
note: C49-to-C54 TiSi2 transformation is suppressed in narrow lines.

title: Holographic binding bundles low-priority tokens into superposed vectors
idea: Peripheral KV pairs are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations, akin to distributed cortical traces) and summed into a few bundle vectors per block; queries unbind to recover approximate values, cleaned up against a small codebook.
why: KV capacity: 8-16x compression on the long tail of context.

title: Keyboard snap-dome: buckled nanomembrane holds bits mechanically
idea: Snap-dome keys and Venus flytraps use buckling bistability: deposit a 20-nm PECVD SiN membrane tuned to ~1 GPa compressive stress over a 300-nm cavity so it rests buckled up or down; electrostatic pulses from top or bottom electrodes snap it within ns (tiny mass, GHz modes), and its position sets a 3-5x capacitance difference read by the sense amp.
why: Zero-power non-volatile bit that cannot leak and ignores row hammer or radiation, with no contact wear because nothing touches; buildable with PECVD stress control, e-beam and HF release; ~300-nm membranes limit density.

title: Traffic-jam phases: charge-density-wave domain states in 1T-TaS2
idea: Traffic flips between free flow and jams; in 1T-TaS2 electrons lock into commensurate or nearly commensurate charge-density-wave states with ~10x resistance contrast, and thin flakes switch between metastable states under short current pulses; build two-terminal cells from exfoliated ~10-nm flakes with e-beam contacts and hBN encapsulation.
why: A collective electronic state holds the bit with no ions or defects moving, so endurance could be effectively unlimited with fJ-scale switching; the narrow room-temperature metastability window threatens retention at 85 C.
note: Flake demo easy; 85 C retention doubtful.

title: Plasmonics nanosphere lithography: floated monolayer masks for capacitor arrays
idea: Borrowed from plasmonics labs, which float colloidal spheres into a close-packed monolayer on water and lift it onto a substrate: float 40 nm monodisperse silica spheres on a Langmuir-Blodgett trough over a wafer with shallow lattice guides, shrink them by plasma, and use them as the etch mask for the hexagonal storage-node array.
why: Fact 4: replaces an EUV layer with a ~$50k trough a small team can run; the honeycomb matches DRAM's capacitor lattice; grain-boundary defects are the high risk.

title: Shrinky Dinks lithography: pattern large, heat-shrink into imprint masters
idea: Borrowed from the Shrinky Dinks toy, whose pre-stretched polystyrene shrinks ~2.5x when baked: write DRAM array master patterns oversized on pre-stretched shape-memory polymer with cheap optical lithography, shrink thermally, electroform a hard nickel copy as a NIL master, and repeat for a second shrink stage, all in a garage-scale lab.
why: Fact 4: master fabrication without e-beam or EUV; edge roughness and non-uniform shrink below 50 nm make it speculative.

title: Lehmann photo-electrochemical macropores etch capacitors without plasma
idea: Revive Volker Lehmann's 1990 photo-electrochemical macropore etching (studied by Siemens for trench DRAM): n-type silicon anodized in HF under backside LED illumination grows pores only where photogenerated holes reach the pore tips, giving straight pores of AR >150:1 from shallow seed pits. Dielectric and electrodes go in by nitrogen-purged ALD, so no step uses argon, helium or neon.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: replaces the hardest Ar/He-diluted plasma etch with a ~$2-5M wet bench, and AR ~150 roughly doubles Cs or allows tighter pitch. Risk is pushing pore pitch below ~100 nm.
note: Macropore pitch tied to space-charge width; sub-100 nm pitch unproven.

title: Williams-tube interlaced raster: rotating row interlace starves row hammer
idea: Williams-tube memories limited the 'read-around ratio' (charge spill from reading neighbouring spots) by interlacing the raster so neighbours were regenerated before spill accumulated. Logical rows map to physical rows through an interlace whose stride and phase rotate every 1/16 of the refresh window, and the migration piggybacks on refresh (each refresh reads a row and writes it into its new slot), so no aggressor keeps the same physical victims long enough to reach ~1k activations.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturb per victim is capped per phase instead of per window, ~16x margin with no per-row counters; periphery cost is one address-permutation unit per bank.
note: Close to RRS/SRS; a 4 ms phase still allows ~80k ACTs, far above the threshold.

title: Planar sol-gel BST capacitor, flash-lamp crystallized, ends deep etching
idea: Box: paraelectric (Ba,Sr)TiO3 charge (k~300) x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x spin-on sol-gel plus millisecond xenon flash-lamp anneal. The flash crystallizes only the top ~100 nm into perovskite while the substrate stays below 400 C, so a near-planar 1:1 to 3:1 capacitor on Pt or SrRuO3 reaches ~5 fF.
why: Removes high-AR capacitor modules entirely (fact 1) with a spin coater and flash/RTP tool; risk is grain-boundary leakage and dead-layer k collapse in films under 20 nm.
note: k~300 planar cap at DRAM cell area gives well under 1 fF; BST was tried and abandoned.

title: Segmented cell-plate kick boosts read signal before charge sharing
idea: Worse: hold the cell plate at a static VDD/2 so the signal is only what Cs alone delivers. Flip: split the plate into per-mat segments and pulse the selected mat's plate by a few hundred mV during the read to couple extra charge onto the bitline, then return it before restore.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): ~20-30% more signal from the same ~5 fF, buying aspect-ratio relief or longer bitlines.
note: Plate kick shifts 0 and 1 equally, so differential signal does not grow.

title: Floating nanosphere monolayers mask capacitor holes without scanners
idea: Scale shift to colloids: U.S.-synthesized 25-30 nm silica nanospheres self-pack as a hexagonal monolayer on a Langmuir trough, transfer onto the wafer, are trimmed by plasma, and serve as the etch or lift-off mask for the capacitor lattice.
why: Removes the scanner from the capacitor layer; trough equipment is cheap and domestic.

title: ZFS dedup's RAM hunger, fixed: flash-resident delta store for fine-tunes
idea: ZFS dedup became notorious for needing ~5 GB of RAM per TB for its dedup table. Serve thousands of fine-tuned model variants by content-defined chunking of weight tensors into flash, with an SRAM cuckoo filter (~1 byte per chunk) to spot duplicate chunks and a flash-resident index, so each variant costs only its unique delta.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving without N copies in DRAM: 10-100x fewer bytes for near-identical variants.
note: Full fine-tunes perturb nearly every value, so exact chunk dedup finds little; LoRA already solves deltas.

title: Siloxane soft-stamp nanoimprint copies one e-beam master to every tier
idea: Write a single 4F2-pitch Si master by e-beam, cast hard-PDMS/PDMS stamps from it, and UV-nanoimprint the critical cell layer of every tier on every wafer at ~15 nm resolution, using the master only to replicate stamps and a mask aligner for overlay.
why: Capital per critical layer falls ~100x vs EUV (fact 4); imprint has been trialed by NAND makers and imprint tools are common in university fabs.
note: Soft PDMS stamps and mask-aligner overlay cannot meet DRAM overlay at 15 nm.

title: Rock-candy croconic acid: proton-hopping organic ferroelectric bit
idea: Like rock candy growing on a seeded string, croconic acid (C5H2O5) crystallizes from vapor onto seed lines between TiN electrodes. It is a room-temperature ferroelectric whose polarization flips by proton transfer along hydrogen bonds, read through a ferroelectric tunnel junction.
why: ~20 uC/cm2 polarization from C, H and O alone, with low coercive field (targets fact 10's voltage floor). Proton tautomerism has no oxygen-vacancy fatigue path.

title: Ball-bearing packing: colloidal monolayer masks for hex vertical-channel arrays
idea: Like ball bearings settling in a tray, float a Langmuir monolayer of 40-60 nm silica spheres onto wafers, shrink them in plasma to set hole size, and etch a hexagonal vertical-channel array with mature etch tools; periphery uses ordinary litho and colloid grain boundaries are mapped out as spare rows.
why: Dense hex arrays at ~50 nm pitch without immersion or EUV (fact 4); at roughly a quarter of leading-edge wafer cost, cost per bit approaches mainstream for capacity memory.
note: Nanosphere masks lack registration to underlying layers and semiconductor-grade defectivity.

title: Negative-capacitance superlattice dielectric hitting effective k of 100
idea: IFR: a dielectric with infinite permittivity. Closest achievable: stack 1 nm ferroelectric HZO with 1 nm Al2O3 in a superlattice tuned so the dielectric stabilizes the ferroelectric's negative-capacitance branch, multiplying net capacitance 2-4x without hysteresis.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k~70 target with existing ALD materials, letting AR fall from ~115 back to ~40.

title: Printed proton-transfer organic ferroelectric with low coercive voltage
idea: IFR: polarization that flips without moving heavy atoms. Closest achievable: solution-print croconic acid or diisopropylammonium bromide films whose polarization reverses by proton hopping along hydrogen bonds (P ~20 uC/cm^2) at low field, used as printed capacitors in a 2T nondestructive-read gain configuration.
why: Fact 10 and capital: organic ferroelectric printed below 150 C with remanent polarization comparable to HZO.

title: Printed alpha-indium-selenide ferroelectric semiconductor flake ink
idea: IFR: a channel that remembers by itself with no separate dielectric. Closest achievable: inkjet exfoliated alpha-In2Se3 nanoflakes, a 2D ferroelectric semiconductor whose locked in-plane/out-of-plane polarization modulates its own conductance, so each printed flake is a two-terminal or FET bit.
why: No capacitor (fact 1), low-temperature printing, sub-volt switching; no oxygen-vacancy wake-up as in oxide ferroelectrics.
note: Printed flakes add thickness and orientation variability to the In2Se3 bit.

title: Printed relaxor terpolymer dielectric reaching k of 50
idea: IFR: a printable dielectric with ceramic-class permittivity. Closest achievable: slot-die coat P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) relaxor terpolymer (k ~50 at room temperature, slim hysteresis) as the storage-capacitor dielectric, optionally loaded with BaTiO3 nanocubes to push higher.
why: Fact 1: approaches the k~70 target in a printable low-temperature film at cents per area.
note: Polymer k collapses at GHz and nm thickness; BEOL thermal budget incompatible.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrode multiplies capacitor area without height
idea: IFR: 'the capacitor has infinite area in a tiny height.' Backward: deposit the bottom electrode as an alloy (e.g., Ni-Al or Cu-Mn), selectively dissolve the sacrificial metal to leave a 3-5 nm ligament nanoporous sponge, then ALD high-k and a conformal top electrode, giving 4-8x the surface of a smooth pillar.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): 5 fF at ~15-20:1 aspect ratio instead of 60-75:1, cutting the hardest etch and pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: No tracking state: keyed rotating row permutation defeats hammering
idea: Imposed limit: no per-row tracking state. Each refresh window, the bank rekeys a lightweight Feistel permutation that maps logical to physical rows within a subarray, migrating a few rows per refresh command. An attacker cannot keep hammering the same physical neighbors long enough to cause a flip.
why: Fact 9: probabilistic hammer immunity at near-zero area; cost is ~1-2% extra row copies during refresh.

title: LED constant-lumen drivers: aging-compensated negative wordline trim per mat
idea: Adapted from LED drivers that raise current as LEDs age to hold light output constant: each mat carries a replica access transistor whose leakage is measured monthly, and a small trim DAC deepens that mat's off-wordline voltage step by step to hold replica leakage at its day-one value, logging the trim history for refurbishers.
why: Compensates access-device aging in place (fact 3), so factory refresh settings stay valid over a 10-year life and second-life modules need no slower refresh.

title: Merge-mask bridges landing pads into double-charge cells
idea: Inverts 'one cell, one capacitor': one added mask bridges pairs of adjacent storage-node landing pads in a designated region so two pillars act as one ~10 fF capacitor driven by two access transistors in parallel.
why: Creates a robust region (2x signal, ~4x retention, immune to single-pillar defects) for metadata and ECC parity, letting the rest of the die use cheaper, weaker cells.

title: Medieval guild: teaching fab whose apprentices ship real DRAM
idea: On the guild model, a state-chartered 200 mm teaching fab has apprentice technicians run a legacy DDR3/LPDDR2 product for automotive and industrial customers as their coursework, with certification after 18 months. Product revenue covers ~60% of operating cost.
why: The workforce chokepoint in U.S. manufacturability: a 40k-wafer/month fab needs ~3,000 technicians; the guild trains them while adding legacy supply that frees leading-edge capacity.

title: Substitute zirconium silicate for hafnium oxide in periphery gates
idea: Replace HfO2 in DRAM periphery high-k metal gates with ALD Zr silicate, using silicon incorporation to suppress ZrO2 crystallization and an Al2O3 dipole layer for threshold tuning.
why: Hafnium is a costly byproduct of nuclear-grade zirconium refining with very few producers; Zr is ~50x more abundant and US/Australia-sourced.

title: Substitute remote-plasma radicals for hot phosphoric acid nitride removal
idea: Remove sacrificial SiN (and lateral recesses for stacked 3D DRAM) with downstream NF3/O2/N2 radicals tuned for >100:1 SiN:SiO2 selectivity, replacing 160 C phosphoric acid baths that need continuous DI water spiking and heavy rinses.
why: Hot phosphoric baths are water- and energy-hungry; dry isotropic etch cuts the step's water >10x and gives the atomic-scale recess control 3D DRAM tiers need.

title: Swap scrapped retention-fail dies for an error-tolerant DRAM grade
idea: Substitute 'scrap' with 'approximate grade'. Dies that fail retention or margin screens are packaged as standard DDR5/LPDDR5 parts rated for a measured bit-error rate, and the OS and ML frameworks place only error-tolerant data on them (activations, media buffers, refetchable caches). DDR/HBM interfaces are unchanged.
why: Adds sellable bits with no new wafers by recovering several percent of test fallout, and loosens the leakage-tail screen (fact 3).
note: EDEN-style approximate DRAM; recovers only a few percent.

title: Retention rejects rewired as twin-cell half-density parts
idea: A fuse or metal-option mode pairs each cell with its bitline-pair neighbor storing the complement (2T2C). That doubles the sense signal and extends retention ~10x, so dies that would be scrapped sell at half density.
why: Raises usable supply from yield-loss wafers using only legacy fuse and test tools.

title: Pair partial-good dies behind a 65nm bank-remap bridge
idea: Instead of scrapping or down-binning dies with dead banks, package two partial-good dies with a small 65 nm bridge chip that presents one standard full-capacity die and routes each bank address to whichever die has it working.
why: Usable supply: recovers ~5-10% of wafer output now scrapped or sold as low density, using only trailing logic and OSAT capacity.

title: Reclaimed monitor wafers reborn under thick device-grade epitaxy
idea: Combine wafer reclaim with epitaxy (zero masks): repolish reclaimed monitor and prime-reject wafers, grow a 3-5 um device-grade epi layer, and add a backside polysilicon gettering layer to replace oxygen-precipitate gettering.
why: Monitor/test wafers are ~10-20% of fab wafer use; turning them into product substrates cuts virgin wafer, crucible and polysilicon demand ~10-15% and epi lowers the defect-driven leakage tail.

title: Thermoelectric-cooled HBM stacks traded for 4x longer refresh
idea: Combine an in-package Peltier stage between GPU and HBM stack with temperature-indexed refresh: holding the DRAM ~20 C cooler roughly quadruples retention (leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C), so the refresh interval stretches and weak cells pass.
why: Refresh costs 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3): recovers most of it in hot AI packages; Peltier power offsets part of the energy, but bandwidth gain is net.
note: Poor Peltier COP dumps extra heat into the package.

title: Piano tuning: periodic field re-trim of sense-amplifier offsets
idea: Adapted from routine piano tuning: each sense amplifier has a small offset-trim capacitor bank whose setting is stored in non-volatile cells, and a maintenance routine re-measures offsets with known test levels every few months and re-tunes them as transistors drift.
why: Sense-amp offset consumes a large share of the retention signal margin; keeping it trimmed for life allows perhaps 30-50% more decay, so refresh intervals stay long as parts age (fact 3), and refurbishers re-tune instead of scrapping.

title: Charge-pump capacitors move into six BEOL MIM levels
idea: ALD ZrO2/HfO2 MIM capacitors (250-300 C) stacked in six upper metal levels MAGNIFY pump capacitance per footprint ~6x, so pumps run at lower frequency with higher efficiency and their silicon area is freed for cells.
why: Facts 7 and 10: ~3-4% die area reclaimed and VPP efficiency +15-20 points.

title: Resonant clock grid with electroplated copper inductors
idea: Thick electroplated Cu spiral inductors (<=250 C) in top metal resonate with the periphery clock-grid capacitance, recycling clock energy each cycle instead of dumping it, MINIFYING clock and DLL power.
why: Fact 5: clock power -40%, worth ~5-8% of DRAM interface power; uses only mature low-temperature steps.

title: BEOL MTJ repair registers replace laser and eFuse banks
idea: MINIFY redundancy fuse area ~10x by storing repair addresses in BEOL magnetic tunnel junctions (annealed <=400 C) instead of laser fuses or eFuses, and MAGNIFY repair opportunities by reprogramming them in the field after aging or row-hammer damage.
why: Fact 7 (fuse banks and repair logic are several % of periphery) plus lifetime yield: weak rows can be swapped for spares over the product life.

title: Minify waste: bin panel zones into gold, silver, bronze memory grades
idea: Panel uniformity is best at the center and worst near the edges. Test tiles by zone and package them as gold (servers), silver (PCs) and bronze (AI inference with host LDPC) grades instead of scrapping marginal regions.
why: Usable bits per panel rise ~10-20% with no process change; bronze grades monetize weaker cells.

title: Eliminate the dual gate oxide with drain-extended cascode wordline drivers
idea: Build every 3 V wordline-driver device as a thin-oxide drain-extended or two-high cascode transistor, so one gate oxidation serves the whole die. This removes the thick-oxide mask and its HF strip; pre-gate cleans use SC1/SC2 plus an in-situ H2 bake instead of HF-last.
why: Removes one mask, the HF strip and a gate-stack variant from the periphery (fact 7), at a ~10% area cost in drivers.

title: Eliminate deep-trench decoupling capacitors with traveling-wave sense-amp firing
idea: Fire the 8k SAs of a row as a wave crossing the mat over ~2 ns, each SA enabling its neighbor through a delay cell, so the 1-2 A sensing spike becomes a flat ramp. Supply droop falls ~5x, so deep-trench decaps (which need SF6 Bosch etch) and most MOS decaps are deleted; the remaining flow uses Cl-based etches.
why: Removes ~2-4% of die in decaps, and the lower droop lets the array voltage margin shrink (fact 10); the first-needed column is fired first to hide latency.

title: Eliminate quartz furnace tubes: flash-lamp and microwave anneals
idea: Replace batch diffusion and anneal furnaces (high-purity quartz tubes and boats) with millisecond flash-lamp and volumetric microwave anneals in single-wafer chambers for dopant activation, dielectric crystallization and passivation.
why: Removes recurring Spruce Pine quartzware demand and long furnace thermal cycles; less dopant diffusion also helps the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Light-latched bits: self-electro-optic effect device memory planes
idea: Reverse light's role from signal to holder: arrays of symmetric SEEDs (GaAs quantum-well p-i-n pairs, 1990s Bell Labs, ~5 um pixels) latch a bit through photocurrent feedback under a uniform bias beam; pages are written and read by light in parallel with no electrical wires.
why: Data movement (fact 5): page-parallel optical I/O at fJ/bit and static retention while illuminated; low density (~25 um2/bit) fits optically linked buffers, not bulk capacity.
note: Bell Labs S-SEED known; ~25 um2/bit and hold-beam power make it a niche optical buffer.

title: Test brains live in the probe card, not every die
idea: Reverse where DFT lives: test-mode logic, BIST engines, compression and burn-in controllers are stripped from the DRAM die and implemented once on an ASIC in a U.S.-made probe card, reaching the array through a thin raw-access port.
why: Fact 7: ~2-4% die area recovered on every die; test logic is amortized over millions of dies and upgradable without a respin.
note: Test logic in probe card; loses package-level BIST and PPR.

title: Abatement fluoride captured as synthetic fluorspar for HF regeneration
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: run fluorine-bearing scrubber effluent through lime crystallizers that precipitate high-purity CaF2 pellets instead of sludge. The pellets go back to an acid plant that regenerates electronic-grade HF with H2SO4, closing the fab's fluorine loop.
why: Fluorspar is China-dominated (~60%). Recovering ~50-70% of fab fluorine cuts that dependence and sludge disposal, using only Ca, F, S, H and O.
note: Same CaF2-capture-to-HF loop as I-09865.

title: Small-die tile DRAM on depreciated U.S. lines plus erasure coding
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation under the U.S.-only rule: dies are split into 1-2 Gb tiles made on fully depreciated, EUV-free domestic DRAM nodes, and many tiles are packaged at a U.S. OSAT with a U.S. logic die that rides through a dead tile with tile-level erasure coding.
why: Small dies yield higher and depreciated tools cut wafer cost ~40-50% (depreciation is ~55% of cost), so domestic bits get cheaper without new EUV fabs.

title: Mechanics substitution: maskless multi-beam write for the single added layer
idea: TRIZ #28 Replace mechanical system: the one permitted extra litho layer is written by multi-beam e-beam direct write instead of a physical photomask, letting micro-fabs personalize DRAM (repair, config, customer ID) per wafer with no mask shop.
why: Capital: removes ~$1-3M mask cost and mask-shop lead time for small-volume DRAM fabs.

title: Bamboo-node diaphragms segment vertical lines below the Blech length
idea: Bamboo compartmentalizes its culm with periodic nodes; insert thin Ru/Co node diaphragms every ~0.5 um along vertical Cu/Mo bitlines and power pillars of tall stacks so each segment is shorter than the electromigration Blech length and atoms cannot migrate past a node.
why: 125 C electromigration in high-current vertical pillars of 100+ tier stacks: Blech-segmented lines are effectively immortal, allowing higher current density and thinner pillars (less metal, more density).

title: Bone remodeling rotates hot rows to equalize aging stress
idea: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts continuously rebuild stressed bone; the controller migrates hot pages across banks and ranks on a slow schedule so hammer exposure, BTI aging and thermal stress spread evenly, leaving each chip with uniform, predictable remaining life that makes reuse grading simple.
why: Longer first life and higher reuse yield; fewer modules scrapped early from localized wear.

title: RV absorption fridge: GPU waste heat chills memory without fluorinated refrigerants
idea: Absorption refrigerators in RVs and hotels run on heat, using water/lithium-bromide or ammonia/water instead of HFC/HFO refrigerants. Drive a rack-level LiBr/water absorption chiller with the 60-90 C accelerator coolant return to make chilled water dedicated to HBM and DIMM cold plates at ~30 C.
why: Memory 30-40 C cooler cuts leakage ~8x and allows long refresh intervals (fact 3) using heat that is otherwise rejected, with no fluorinated refrigerant or PFAS immersion fluid.

title: Sculptor carving: subtractive dry-etched ruthenium/molybdenum periphery wiring
idea: Damascene copper is casting: pour into a mold, then grind and wash (CMP). Carve instead, like a sculptor: blanket-deposit Ru or Mo, pattern, and plasma-etch the periphery's local/intermediate wiring and contacts, then gap-fill with flowable low-k. No barrier, plating, CMP or post-CMP scrub.
why: Water: CMP plus post-CMP cleans, among the biggest UPW users per layer, fall ~10x on periphery metal levels; Mo contacts (U.S.-mined) also replace tungsten, easing the China-80% chokepoint.
note: Subtractive Ru/Mo is already widely pursued; periphery metal is a small share of fab water.

title: Monument laser cleaning: shock-wave particle removal before periphery contacts
idea: Conservators clean cathedral stone with pulsed lasers and no water. A nanosecond laser flash-heats the wafer surface so thermal expansion and the gas-film shock wave lift particles from periphery contact/via openings, and a nitrogen cross-flow sweeps them into an exhaust, replacing megasonic DI-water scrubs.
why: Water: periphery particle scrubs (~10-20 L UPW each) fall ~10x, and dry removal has no capillary pattern-collapse risk.

title: Electric-arc-furnace scrap loop: wire-saw kerf remelted into wafer feedstock
idea: Steel's electric-arc-furnace route makes new steel from scrap. Recover the ~30-40% of each ingot lost as diamond-wire kerf, strip its surface oxide with HF vapor, densify it by induction melting, and purify it by directional solidification plus vacuum refining into feedstock for handle, test and dummy wafers.
why: Raises silicon yield per kg of polysilicon, crucible and argon ~1.4x for the non-device wafers that are 20-30% of fab wafer starts, freeing crystal-growth capacity and quartz for device wafers.

title: Kraft-mill recovery cycle regenerates sulfuric acid and peroxide cleans
idea: Pulp mills recover more than 95% of their cooking chemicals in recovery boilers. Treat spent sulfuric-peroxide and SC1/SC2 baths the same way: boron-doped-diamond electrolysis regenerates persulfate and peroxide in-line, and vacuum distillation restores H2SO4 to semiconductor grade for reuse; no change to the DRAM product or DDR/HBM interface.
why: Cuts sulfuric-acid and peroxide purchases and neutralization waste ~70-80%, with associated UPW and trucking, easing water and chemical permits for U.S. fab siting.

title: Catalytic-converter-style tungsten recovery from CVD exhaust and targets
idea: Like recovering platinum metals from scrapped catalysts, fab abatement adds cold traps that capture unreacted WF6 and W-bearing chamber deposits, which a regional refiner converts back to WF6 or APT together with spent sputter targets.
why: Cuts virgin tungsten demand 30-50%, reducing exposure to the ~80% China concentration.

title: Auto-parts core-charge loop for ECU memory remanufacturing
idea: Like alternator cores returned for a deposit, every ECU or ADAS board carries a core charge refunded when the scrapped unit returns; Grade-1 memory die are recovered, rescreened at 125 C, and used in spare-part ECUs that would otherwise force last-time buys of EOL DRAM.
why: Automakers must supply service parts for 10-15 years and hoard EOL DRAM to do so; a remanufacturing loop frees those hoarded bits and supplies long-tail parts.

title: Spark-plug ceramic suppliers make hermetic LTCC memory substrates
idea: Like spark plugs whose ceramics survive engine heat (made by firms that also make IC packages), use CTE-matched low-temperature co-fired ceramic substrates from U.S. technical-ceramics plants for memory packages and stacks rated for 10 years at 125 C.
why: Bypasses the ABF build-up film chokepoint (~95% one supplier) and improves high-temperature reliability, adding domestic substrate supply.
note: Memory packages mostly use BT not ABF; LTCC is known art.

title: Direct-view storage tube revived as bistable pixels without framebuffers
idea: Tektronix direct-view storage tubes held the image on the screen with no frame memory; revive it with university-fabricated bistable pixels (ferroelectric or cholesteric liquid crystal on a glass TFT backplane) that latch their state, so phones, laptops and thin clients send only changed regions and keep no scanout framebuffer or panel self-refresh RAM.
why: Removes 50-150 MB of scanout buffers per device plus display-refresh DRAM traffic; small per device, but LPDDR is about a third of world DRAM bits, so a 1-2% cut across billions of devices frees real supply.

title: Chemical autarky: make fab chemistries on site from air, water and salt
idea: Inverts 'chemicals are purchased from concentrated suppliers': on-site electrolyzers make H2, O2 and ozone from water, chlor-alkali cells make HCl and Cl2 from salt, H2O2 comes from electrochemical oxygen reduction and NH3 from a small Haber-Bosch unit, all distilled to electronic grade at point of use.
why: Removes multi-week logistics and single-country dependencies for the highest-volume wet and gas chemicals; strengthens US manufacturability and resilience.

title: Fusion-bond stacks of sixteen thinned 180 nm array layers
idea: Inverts 'one wafer makes one memory layer'. Build cheap 180 nm array layers on 200 mm SOI, then oxide-fusion-bond and etch back 16 of them (the 1990s BESOI technique), connected by 2 um through-oxide vias at mat edges to a single bottom periphery layer.
why: ~16x density per footprint with no litho shrink; each layer costs depreciated-tool prices (facts 2, 4).
note: 16 stacked 180 nm layers still less dense than one modern layer at 16x wafer cost.

title: AI-grade binning: sell failing DRAM dies to fault-tolerant workloads
idea: Inverts 'every die must pass full spec': dies from existing lines that fail retention screens or have clustered bad rows get a per-die bad-row map in a 40 nm controller's fuse table. They are sold as 'AI-grade' modules for weights and KV, where row remapping plus tensor-level checksums hide the defects.
why: Recovers several % of wafer output that is now scrapped or downbinned, so existing fabs yield more usable bits with no new capacity.

title: BTI-balanced sense latches through epoch-wise data polarity swapping
idea: At 125 C, NBTI/PBTI shifts Vt ~10-30 mV over 10 years, mostly on whichever latch half sees one data value more often, eating a ~50 mV signal. Store every row inverted on alternate refresh epochs (one polarity bit per row) and swap which SA half is 'true', so both halves age equally to within ~1 mV.
why: Keeps sense margin intact for 10 y at 125 C without guardband; lets Cs stay ~20% smaller than an aging-guardbanded design (fact 1).

title: FD-SOI periphery with PTAT back-bias flattens hot leakage
idea: Build periphery on fully-depleted SOI: buried oxide removes most junction area (generation leakage scales with ni and junction area), and a PTAT back-bias generator raises Vt ~1 mV/K as temperature climbs, holding standby leakage roughly flat from 25 to 125 C.
why: Periphery standby power at hot down ~5-10x; less self-heating feedback on retention.

title: Vt-tracking wordline high voltage relieves hot oxide stress
idea: Access Vt falls ~1 mV/K, so at 125 C the wordline needs ~100 mV less overdrive than at 25 C. Scale VPP down with temperature exactly by the Vt tempco, cutting oxide field when TDDB is most accelerated (~3x lifetime gain).
why: Enables thinner WL oxide and lower CV^2 energy at hot while meeting 10 y (fact 10).

title: Spider web: dual-end wordline drive tolerates mid-line opens
idea: Each wordline segment is driven from both ends, with a weak keeper at the far end, so a single open (void, CMP break) still leaves both halves driven - a web that holds after one strand snaps; only shorts consume spare rows.
why: Opens are a large share of row repairs; ~30-50% fewer spare rows needed, returning array area and raising yield.

title: Food freshness label: on-die Arrhenius dose integrator for life-aware derating
idea: Like time-temperature indicator labels on food, a tiny on-die structure (a floating node leaking through thermally activated oxide, cross-checked by a BTI ring oscillator) integrates cumulative thermal stress; firmware reads the 'age' and tightens refresh, VNWL and ECC mode as the dose nears 10 years at 125 C equivalent.
why: Parts in milder missions run ~2x relaxed refresh while hot ones are protected to the 125 C/10-year budget; cuts lifetime guard-band ~20-30%.
note: Silicon odometer sensors are known.

title: Move DFT and BIST logic onto an active probe-card ASIC
idea: Box: any cell x any access x any SA x test logic off-die x bulk Si x probe-card ASIC. Built-in self-test engines, test-mode decoders and compression logic leave each DRAM die and live on a reusable active probe card that drives a minimal raw test port.
why: Periphery -2-4% per die forever, paid once per probe card; faster test too.
note: Active probe cards known; DRAM keeps BIST for in-field repair.

title: Rescue scrapped dies with per-row refresh maps sold as SKU
idea: Po: the trash bin is a warehouse. Dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen because a few hundred rows are weak get a per-row refresh-class map burned into on-die fuses; the module controller refreshes those rows at 16-32 ms and the rest normally, and the parts ship as a mapped-refresh grade.
why: Usable supply: recovering 3-8% of output lost to retention fallout adds bits with no new fab, at <1% bandwidth cost.

title: Po: the charge pump lives in the package
idea: Po: a DRAM die with no charge pumps. Generate VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias in a package-level GaN or deep-trench-capacitor integrated-passive converter at ~85% efficiency and deliver them through dedicated bumps or hybrid-bond pads, deleting on-die pumps and their decoupling capacitors.
why: Periphery (#7) and voltage floor (#10): on-die pumps and decaps take ~5-8% of die and run ~30-40% efficient; moving them out frees area and roughly halves VPP energy.
note: DDR4 already supplies an external VPP pin.

title: Po: the barrier grows itself — CuMn wiring, no Ta/Co/Ru
idea: Po: copper wiring that makes its own diffusion barrier. Use a Cu-0.5%Mn seed; on anneal Mn migrates to the dielectric interface and forms a ~2 nm MnSiOx barrier, replacing PVD Ta/TaN and Co/Ru liners in all periphery metal levels, with plain Al for top global levels.
why: Scarce resources: removes Ta, Co and Ru from periphery BEOL; the thinner barrier also adds ~15-20% copper cross-section in narrow lines, cutting RC.
note: CuMn self-forming barrier is published art.

title: Po the fab never heard of helium: batch-tool gas-free flow
idea: Po: 'the fab has never heard of helium.' Extracted: build the 180 nm DRAM flow around batch vertical furnaces (LPCVD poly, nitride, oxide), wet etches and low-power batch plasma tools whose wafers sit on boats or mechanical clamps needing no backside gas; use hydrogen or argon for any leak checks and purges.
why: Helium (Qatar supply offline): zero helium in the bill of materials; batch tools also cost far less per wafer-pass.

title: Tungsten-free wordlines driven from both ends with mid-line repeaters
idea: Worse: keep buried wordlines dependent on tungsten, ~80% sourced from China. Flip: switch to supply-safe TiN or doped-poly fill and offset its higher resistance by splitting each local wordline into halves driven from both ends plus a mid-array boost repeater in the sub-wordline driver strip.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (tungsten chokepoint) while holding wordline RC within ~10% of today.

title: Triple-redundant Mn-barrier copper TSVs with majority voting
idea: Worse: build HBM TSVs with tantalum barriers and accept that one void kills a channel. Flip: use Cu TSVs with a self-forming MnSixOy barrier from a CuMn seed and route each critical signal through three TSVs with majority voting in the base die, so random defects of the cheaper barrier no longer cost the stack.
why: Fact 6 and scarce resources: removes Ta while raising TSV-related stack yield, for ~2x signal-TSV area on critical lines only.

title: Art restorer's field retouching: relaxed screening plus in-field PPR
idea: A restorer fixes cracks as they appear instead of discarding the painting. Ship dies screened at a looser sense-margin limit, and let the host's existing patrol scrub find weak rows and remap them with DDR5's existing soft and hard post-package repair commands.
why: Lowers test yield loss and burn-in time (+3-6% supply, lower test cost) using only JEDEC commands.

title: Fly-by-wire wordlines: per-mat VPP trimmed to the minimum
idea: A fly-by-wire jet trims each control surface on its own. Each mat gets a small LDO that drops its wordline high level from global VPP to the lowest value that passed that mat's test margin, stored in fuses.
why: Typical mats run 10-15% below worst-case VPP, cutting wordline energy ~20-25% and reducing GIDL and hammer coupling (facts 9, 10).

title: Librarian's central catalog: base-die NVM holds all repair maps
idea: A librarian keeps one catalog, not a card box on every shelf. Redundancy and trim data for every HBM core die live in nonvolatile memory on the logic base die (embedded RRAM or MTP) and are broadcast up the TSVs at power-up, deleting the fuse banks from each core die.
why: Fuse and antifuse banks cost ~2-4% of core die area; removing them adds density and lets repair be updated after stacking (facts 6, 7).

title: Grandmother saves the drippings: recapture fluorocarbon etch gases
idea: Persona: a grandmother who saves the bacon fat. Instead of burning C4F8, CF4 and NF3 in abatement, pass etch exhaust through a cold trap and fluorocarbon-selective membranes to recover >70%. Re-purify the gas by distillation at a regional plant and send the cylinders back.
why: Fluorocarbons are potent greenhouse gases, PFAS-adjacent and supply-limited. Recovery cuts purchases and CO2e by about half for the high-AR capacitor etch steps.

title: DIMM PMIC delivers VPP and VBB, deleting on-die charge pumps
idea: Automotive and industrial boards push high-voltage generation into 180 nm BCD PMICs; DDR5 already moved 12 V to 1.1 V conversion onto the DIMM, so extend it by supplying ~3 V VPP and negative VBB on dedicated balls and deleting on-die pumps (30-40% efficient), keeping only local switches.
why: Die area -5-8% (fact 7) and pump energy ~2x better; the PMICs come from U.S. legacy BCD lines with no EUV.

title: Data-polarity rotation balances sense-amp aging over 30 years
idea: Thirty-year industrial parts fail from slow asymmetric drift: the controller inverts stored polarity on alternate refresh epochs (tracked by a per-row flag bit), so both transistors of each SA pair see equal NBTI/PBTI stress and offset stays near zero. SAs can be sized for beginning-of-life margin.
why: SA width ~20% smaller at relaxed DUV rules (fact 7) with no end-of-life guard band.
note: Cell-flipping for BTI balance known from SRAM.

title: Package-level GaN switched-capacitor rails replace on-die pumps
idea: Scale shift from die to package: VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias come from a GaN switched-capacitor converter embedded in the package substrate through a dense bond/TSV grid, deleting the dozens of on-die charge pumps.
why: On-die pumps take several % of area at ~30-40% efficiency; ~90%-efficient package converters roughly halve wordline supply energy (fact 10) and free ~3-5% of die (fact 7).

title: Recover backgrinding swarf as feedstock-grade silicon
idea: Scale shift: a stacked DRAM die keeps 30-50 um of a 775 um wafer, so >93% of the silicon becomes sludge. Collect it unmixed from backgrind tools at existing OSATs, then centrifuge, acid-leach and remelt it as solar or carrier-grade feedstock.
why: Each HBM wafer discards ~120 g of silicon. Recovery cuts polysilicon demand and its ~50-70 kWh/kg energy for the carrier/solar loop.

title: Shift legacy DRAM orders onto 200 mm mature lines
idea: Market-scale shift: DDR3, LPDDR2 and low-density (<=2 Gb) DRAM for industrial, automotive and IoT still occupy 300 mm leading DRAM lines. Requalifying them on existing 200 mm 40-90 nm DRAM and specialty fabs lets leading lines convert those starts to DDR5/HBM.
why: Frees several percent of leading-edge DRAM starts for AI-class parts with zero new fabs, using mature lines that have spare capacity.

title: Thermal atomic-layer etch for capacitor-hole and recess steps
idea: Time shift from continuous plasma etch to self-limiting second-scale chemical cycles (fluorination, then ligand exchange): critical recess and trim etches remove one atomic layer per cycle, with no plasma and no argon dilution.
why: Removes argon from the precision etch steps and gives Angstrom control of wordline recess depth, which tightens the leakage tail. Tool capex is ~30% lower than high-density plasma.

title: Anamartic Wafer Stack redux: self-configuring wafer-scale memory slabs
idea: Ivor Catt's Anamartic wafer-scale memory (1989) chained good dies on an uncut wafer into a spiral but died because hand-assembled wafer stacks could not keep up with falling DRAM die prices. Fix with 1990s tools only: on fully depreciated 200 mm, 180 nm lines, pattern whole wafers of DRAM tiles with built-in self-test that fuses a spiral chain through good tiles, and ship each wafer as one memory slab with no dicing, die packaging or per-die sort.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: uses zero-book tools in idle 200 mm fabs and removes packaging and test (~25-35% of module cost); ~5-7 GB per 200 mm wafer, so it is surge capacity, not a cost-per-bit leader.

title: Phase-change repair registers replace laser-fuse banks and their latches
idea: Effect: thermal hysteresis of the amorphous/crystalline phase change. Store redundancy repair addresses in small GST or Sb2Te3-superlattice cells in BEOL, programmed once at test by an on-die micro-heater pulse and read directly by the decoder compare logic. This eliminates pitch-limited laser-fuse banks and the boot-time fuse broadcast latches.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: ~2-3% of die area recovered and the laser-repair tool step removed.

title: Cobalt-free Fe-B/MgO tunnel junctions crystallized under 350 C
idea: Effect: interfacial perpendicular anisotropy from Fe 3d-O 2p hybridization at the Fe/MgO interface. Drop Co entirely and use Mg or Al boron-sink caps instead of Ta/W, so Fe-B free and reference layers crystallize from the MgO template at <=350 C while keeping TMR >150%.
why: Cobalt (DRC ~70%), Ta and W removed from MRAM working-memory stacks; anneal stays inside the 400 C budget.

title: Strip-and-rewrite photomask blanks with plasma etch-stop layers
idea: Periphery masks put the absorber over a thin Ru etch-stop on low-expansion quartz; obsolete or damaged masks are stripped selectively in Cl/O2 plasma, re-coated and rewritten, reusing the costly blank many times.
why: Mask blanks come from few suppliers and mask sets cost millions; reuse lowers that barrier and quartz demand.

title: Closed fluorine loop: scrubber fluorspar back to on-site F2
idea: Periodic-table walk, F (9): capture HF and fluorocarbon exhaust in Ca(OH)2 scrubbers as synthetic CaF2, convert it back to HF, and electrolyze KF.2HF on-site to F2 for chamber cleans, replacing NF3.
why: Removes NF3 (GWP 17,200, few suppliers) and virgin fluorspar (China/Mexico) dependence; F2 has GWP 0.

title: O: downstream atomic-oxygen ash ends sulfuric-peroxide resist strips
idea: Strip implant and patterning resists with a remote O-radical plasma preceded by an H2/N2 radical crust-break step, eliminating hot sulfuric-peroxide (SPM) baths and their rinses.
why: Water and chemicals: SPM strips and hot rinses are heavy UPW and acid users; dry strip cuts that module's water >10x and removes sulfuric waste treatment.

title: Ti: rutile-TiO2 trench decoupling under the HBM PHY
idea: Line interposer and base-die deep-trench capacitors with rutile TiO2 (k~80-110, templated on RuO2) instead of HfO2/ZrO2 (k~25-40), tripling decap density directly under the HBM PHY and TSV power columns.
why: Speed-bin yield at an unchanged HBM interface: supply droop is a leading reason stacks miss top speed; ~3x decap cuts droop and could raise good-stack output ~5-10%.

title: Dropped-stitch knitting: token-chained subarrays replace fuse-compare redundancy
idea: Like a knitter passing over a dropped stitch, a token threads through every subarray at power-up (the Catt-spiral idea from 1989 Anamartic wafer-scale memory). A subarray that fails its built-in self-test simply passes the token on, so the chain itself builds the address map with no fuse banks or address comparators.
why: Removes most fuse arrays and redundancy comparators (~3-6% of die) and gives coarse subarray sparing that tolerates clustered defects, raising yield at 180 nm and above.
note: Anamartic revival; coarse sparing at legacy nodes.

title: Sprue-and-runner test periphery: built in scribe lanes, sawn off at dicing
idea: Like the sprues and runners trimmed off a molded part, put test-mode logic, compressed-test comparators, extra probe pads and fuse-programming drivers in the 80-100 um scribe lanes at 180 nm rules, linked across the seal ring by sacrificial connections. After wafer sort and repair, the dicing saw removes them.
why: Recovers the ~3-5% of die area spent on test-only periphery: a direct ~4% bits-per-wafer gain with no process change.

title: Optical-fiber soot process makes domestic photomask blanks, recycled like cullet
idea: Use New York flame-hydrolysis high-purity fused silica (the soot method behind optical-fiber preforms) as mask substrate, and add a cullet-style reclaim line that strips chrome, repolishes and recoats retired DRAM masks for reuse.
why: Mask blanks are concentrated in Japan; a U.S. source plus 3-5 reuse cycles per blank cuts synthetic-quartz demand and mask cost for the ~60-70 masks a DRAM product needs.

title: Steel minimill for silicon: remelt kerf and scrap wafers domestically
idea: Electric-arc minimills make new steel from scrap; build a U.S. silicon minimill that collects wire-saw kerf, broken and spent test wafers and off-spec ingot tops, acid-cleans and plasma-refines them, and directionally solidifies them into CZ recharge feedstock.
why: Kerf wastes ~40% of each crystal; recycling it reduces new polysilicon and its ~50-60 kWh/kg Siemens energy, giving a domestic loop independent of Chinese polysilicon.

title: Riveted hybrid bonds: redundant pads with nitrogen plasma activation
idea: Shipbuilders put several rivets in every joint so one failure is harmless; activate hybrid-bond surfaces with N2/O2 plasma (no argon) and give each critical vertical signal three parallel bond pads feeding a majority/OR receiver, so voids from the gentler activation never open a circuit.
why: Makes argon-free bonding yield-safe for HBM and 3D stacks (fact 6: 20-30% yield loss), turning single-pad voids into non-events.
note: Redundant TSV/pad schemes common.

title: Double-ended sub-wordline drivers survive any single driver failure
idea: Ideal result: a wordline that cannot be cut off. Drive each sub-wordline from both ends with drivers that can be disabled individually; if self-test finds one dead or a mid-line break, the other end drives the line.
why: Removes a top cause of row fuse-outs and halves wordline RC delay, enabling longer wordlines and fewer driver stripes (fact 7).

title: Reusable donor wafers supply periphery silicon via layer transfer
idea: Ideal result: silicon that is used ten times. Grow periphery device layers on a porous-silicon or SiGe release substrate, transfer the thin layer onto the bonded memory stack, then polish and reuse the donor wafer.
why: Scarce resources: cuts virgin wafer and Spruce Pine quartz crucible demand for periphery tiers ~5-10x.

title: Tungsten-free periphery metal designed for selective recovery
idea: Ideal result: periphery made only of materials you can get back. Replace W contacts and wordline straps with Mo and Ru using liner chemistries chosen for selective wet dissolution, so end-of-life dies yield separable Cu, Mo and Ru streams.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and recyclability by design.

title: Load-and-kill instruction frees memory at a value's last use
idea: IFR: memory frees itself the instant data is dead. Closest: a compiler-emitted load-and-kill instruction marks a line or page dead after its final read; the cache drops it without writeback and the OS reclaims fully dead frames immediately.
why: Cuts temporary-buffer footprint 10-20% in streaming and ML pipelines and removes useless writeback bandwidth.
note: Dead-block hints and invalidate-without-writeback exist; small gains.

title: Electrical healing: scheduled BTI recovery epochs for aged periphery
idea: Rule: repair by electricity, not replacement. The controller schedules recovery epochs that apply reverse gate bias and modest self-heating to sense-amp and wordline-driver transistors, reversing accumulated BTI threshold shifts that erode sense margin over years.
why: Keeps aged modules within margin for second and third service lives, so fewer are retired for slow parametric drift.
note: BTI recovery and circuit rejuvenation well studied.

title: Eliminate metal electrodes: degenerate epitaxial silicon plates replace TiN and tungsten
idea: Eliminate sputtered TiN and tungsten electrodes: form both capacitor plates and node contacts from in-situ phosphorus-doped (>1e21 cm-3) epitaxial Si or SiGe grown with hydrogen carrier, so there are no metal targets, no argon PVD and no tungsten; at that doping the depletion penalty is under ~5% of capacitance.
why: Removes a tungsten dependence (China ~80%) and argon PVD chambers (scarce-resource axis), and same-tool epitaxy cuts steps; risks are plate resistance slowing RC and depletion at high field.
note: Poly-Si SIS plates were abandoned for MIM because of depletion.

title: Cryogenic CO2-argon aerosol cleaning replaces wet rinse steps
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: replace selected post-CMP and pre-deposition wet-clean, rinse and dry steps with a cryogenic aerosol of solid CO2/Ar micro-crystals. The crystals knock particles off by momentum transfer and then sublime, leaving no liquid or residue.
why: Cuts UPW and IPA per wafer pass (~10-20% of fab UPW in the targeted steps) and removes capillary forces that collapse 60-75:1 capacitor pillars.

title: Paraffin phase-change lid keeps stacks under 85 C
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: a sealed U.S.-made paraffin/fatty-acid phase-change pack bonded to the memory-stack lid melts at ~70 C, absorbing AI burst heat so DRAM never enters the 85 C+ double-refresh range, and refreezes between bursts.
why: Avoids the 2x refresh rate and retention-fail spikes during bursts (~10-15% bandwidth recovered at peak) and lets retention-marginal dies pass, using domestic petrochemical material.

title: Kombucha: bioleaching vats recover metals from scrapped memory modules
idea: Stimulus 'kombucha SCOBY' (a living culture doing chemistry in a jar) -> a 10-person team runs Acidithiobacillus and cyanogenic Chromobacterium bioleaching vats on shredded DIMMs and memory boards, recovering gold, palladium, copper and tantalum at ambient temperature.
why: Turns e-waste into domestic strategic metals without smelters, feeding tantalum and gold back into memory packaging and targets.

title: Ozone-gas and UV dry stripping to cut ultrapure water
idea: Periodic-table walk, O (8): replace sulfuric-peroxide resist strips and organic cleans with UV-activated O3 gas and humidified-ozone single-wafer dry oxidation, keeping wet steps only for metal and particle removal.
why: Cuts DRAM-fab UPW use ~30-50% and acid consumption; fluorine-free.

title: Cell-pitch hybrid bonding of separate capacitor and transistor wafers
idea: Combine wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with the 1T1C cell: all capacitors are made on one wafer (free to use high thermal budget and high-k) and all access transistors on another. The wafers are bonded at ~40-60 nm pitch, and ~1% void-killed bonds are accepted as cell errors.
why: Each wafer flow sheds the other's constraints (~20% fewer steps, no capacitor-over-transistor thermal compromise), and the 1% budget makes sub-100 nm bonding yield-viable years earlier (facts 1, 2).
note: 40-60 nm hybrid-bond pitch is ~10x beyond state of the art.

title: Magnify sharing: eight array-only wafers on one periphery wafer
idea: Bond eight array-only wafers (cells, wordlines and bitlines; about 4 masks each, no periphery) onto one CMOS periphery wafer. Nano-TSV global bitline risers and a tier-select transistor let each sense amp serve all eight tiers.
why: Periphery takes 49% of the die: periphery area per bit falls 8x, and array wafers drop most critical and periphery masks.

title: Coulomb-blockade island chain as a leak-proof access channel on quartz
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation, taken to the extreme: segment the access channel into a chain of 1-2 nm nanocrystal islands self-assembled on a quartz or sapphire substrate (no silicon wafer). In the off state the single-electron charging energy (>> kT at room temperature for <2 nm islands) blocks transport exponentially with chain length; the wordline gate lifts the blockade for access.
why: Leakage is set by charging energy rather than doping or bandgap (Fact 3): theoretical off-current far below 1e-21 A for hours of retention; bottom-up assembly avoids EUV (Fact 4).

title: Dandelion franchise micro-fabs running a 25-mask capacitorless flow
idea: Dandelions spread identical seeds widely. Dropping the capacitor removes the high-AR etch, capacitor high-k stack and support lattice; the remaining ~25-mask flow ships as a turnkey containerized micro-fab kit franchised to regional operators who pay royalties and share a parts depot.
why: Micro-fab capital of ~$0.3-1B vs $15B; distributed U.S. production.
note: Capacitorless retention unsolved; containerized DRAM micro-fab at sub-$1B is speculative.

title: Onion-shell 3D access devices: one etch, one clean, many tiers
idea: Random stimulus 'onion': many layers around one core, peeled at once. In a vertical-bitline 3D DRAM the access transistors of all ~32 tiers are concentric gate-all-around shells around one bitline hole, defined by a single hole etch, one dry clean and one conformal channel/gate deposition, with each tier's wordline a lateral plane.
why: Wet steps per wafer are nearly tier-independent, so water per bit falls ~1/N: 32 tiers gives >10x less water per bit while attacking the missing manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2).

title: Piezoelectronic pressure switch replaces silicon access transistor
idea: Box: MIM cap x piezoelectronic transistor (PMN-PT actuator squeezing a SmSe piezoresistive layer through its insulator-metal transition) x SA x BEOL stack x Si x sputter + anneal. The wordline drives the piezo, pressure drops channel resistance >1e4x; unpowered, the channel is a gapped insulator with no junction to leak.
why: Off-state set by an insulating phase rather than a subthreshold tail (fact 3, ~100x retention) and switching at ~0.1-0.2 V breaks the 3 V wordline floor (fact 10).

title: Cell-stamp e-beam: a million shaped beamlets each write one cell
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x massively parallel e-beam with a programmable aperture plate shaped to the cell motif. Because the array is a lattice, each of ~1e6 beamlets is shaped into the same cell feature (parallel character projection) and the stage scan makes each beamlet write its own sub-array tile, so there are no masks and shot count falls by orders of magnitude vs pixel writing.
why: Mask cost and EUV dependence (fact 4); periodicity attacks e-beam's throughput problem; target 20-40 wafers/hour per column cluster at ~$30-50M; risk is beamlet uniformity and stitching.

title: NAND fab swing lines producing 3D vertical FeRAM
idea: Worse: let NAND fabs idle in every flash glut while DRAM is short. Flip: reuse NAND high-aspect-ratio etch and ALD lines to build 3D vertically stacked HZO ferroelectric capacitor memory, so lines swing between NAND and nonvolatile DRAM-class output with demand.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; converts existing capacity rather than building fabs.
note: HZO endurance ~1e10-1e12 falls short of DRAM-class; Micron NVDRAM shows feasibility but not swing economics.

title: Bubble memory, fixed: magnetic loop memory for sequentially-read KV
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) died on millisecond serial access through major/minor loops. Attention reads all K/V in order every decode step, so store KV in domain-wall racetrack loops that shift continuously in lockstep with the token loop, re-synced every lap by a marker domain so positioning errors never accumulate.
why: Capacitorless, transistor-sparse, refresh-free KV storage at potentially <4F^2/bit for the largest inference memory consumer.
note: Streaming KV access suits racetrack, but shift errors and bandwidth remain unsolved after decades.

title: Gate-triggered Mott-gap channel gives access device without subthreshold tail
idea: Effect: filling-controlled Mott transition. The access channel is a correlated oxide (e.g., electron-doped SmNiO3 or Ca2RuO4) where the wordline field adds ~0.1 carrier per site and collapses the Mott gap abruptly; below critical filling it is a gapped insulator whose leakage scales as exp(-Eg/kT) instead of following a gradual subthreshold slope.
why: Leakage tail and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): an abrupt switch allows wordline swing ~1.5 V instead of 3 V (~4x less wordline CV2) while holding <1 aA, removing most refresh.
note: 0.1 e/site needs ~1e14 cm^-2 gating, near dielectric limits.

title: Swap thermionic switching for heterojunction tunnel-FET access device
idea: Substitute the MOSFET's thermionic barrier with band-to-band tunneling: a p+ SiGe source on the bitline side, an intrinsic Si channel and a lightly doped n storage side. The device is asymmetric (it tunnels only when the wordline is high) and sub-60 mV/dec, and the lightly doped storage side suppresses ambipolar leakage.
why: Voltage floor + leakage: the steep slope lets VPP drop from ~3 V to ~1.5 V (~4x lower wordline CV^2 energy) while keeping fA-class off-current, so refresh activation energy falls too.
note: TFET DRAM access studied; on-current and ambipolarity remain hard.

title: Substitute periodic refresh with static Esaki tunnel-diode latch per cell
idea: Substitute capacitor decay plus refresh with a bistable hold: two series interband (Esaki) tunnel diodes at the storage node form a negative-differential-resistance latch with two stable voltages. A tiny valley current (target ~pA) holds the state continuously, and the access transistor still reads and writes it.
why: Removes refresh entirely (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) in exchange for a static current; viable if the valley current is engineered below ~10 pA per cell.
note: Tunnel-diode SRAM (TSRAM) explored in 1990s; pA valley current at DRAM cell area and PVR unproven.

title: Single-electron transistor sensing attofarad storage nodes
idea: Combine a room-temperature silicon single-electron transistor (sub-3 nm island) as the in-cell sense element with a 10-50 aF storage node, so a few hundred electrons, not ~30,000, encode a bit. The SET's Coulomb oscillations turn each few-electron change into a large current change, read through a gain path that never discharges the node.
why: Facts 1 and 10: the capacitor shrinks ~100x (no high-AR pillars) and storage swings can drop to ~0.3 V; write energy falls ~10x.
note: RT SETs need sub-3 nm islands with huge variability; Yano-type single-electron memory precedent.

title: Hollow TSVs that are also microfluidic coolant channels
idea: Make annular TSVs whose copper shell carries power/signal while the hollow core carries a two-phase dielectric coolant through the whole stack, combining vertical interconnect and cooling in one via field.
why: Lets compute sit on DRAM (fact 5) while holding DRAM <=60 C; retention roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh energy (fact 3) falls 2-4x and 24-32-high stacks become thermally feasible.
note: Microfluidic TSVs studied (Georgia Tech); two-phase flow in micron cores faces large pressure drop.

title: Image-sensor pixel bonding: one sense amp per 64 cells
idea: Borrowed from stacked CMOS image sensors with pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonds and per-pixel ADCs: bond the array wafer face-to-face to a logic wafer at sub-1 um pitch so every 64-cell micro-bitline lands on its own sense amp, eliminating long bitlines entirely.
why: Bitline capacitance falls from ~50-80 fF to ~2 fF, so Cs can drop to ~0.5 fF (no 70:1 pillar, fact 1), read energy ~10x lower, and periphery leaves the array die (fact 7).

title: Printing-press nanoimprint drum for continuous wafer streams
idea: Magnify lithography throughput 20x by passing wafers on a conveyor under a rotating nanoimprint drum carrying the array pattern, printing one layer per second like a newspaper press.
why: Litho tool cost and throughput: ~3600 wafer-layers per hour versus ~150 for EUV, from a drum tool costing a fraction of a scanner.

title: Minify leakage by decades with SiC-substrate wide-bandgap access transistors
idea: Build the 1T1C access device as a 4H-SiC MOSFET on SiC substrates, with capacitors deposited above. SiC's intrinsic carrier density is ~1e-8 cm^-3 versus ~1e10 in Si, so junction and band-to-band leakage almost disappear.
why: Fact 3: retention could reach hours at 85C, making refresh nearly vanish, and the U.S. has domestic SiC substrate capacity. SiC/SiO2 interface traps and mobility are the risks.

title: Magnify the substrate 100x: Gen-10.5 display fabs make memory
idea: Repurpose overbuilt Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines (2.9 x 3.4 m glass) to deposit 16-32 stacked layers of IGZO 2T0C gain cells at a 0.5-1 um rule, with periphery on small CMOS chiplets bonded along tile edges; panels are diced into memory tiles.
why: Processed panel cost is ~$100-300/m2 per layer stack vs ~$80,000/m2 for DRAM wafers; even at ~1/20 DRAM bit density, cost targets ~$0.1/GB (~100x cheaper), accepting ~100-300 ns access and frequent refresh.
note: Sub-um rules on Gen-10.5 glass and $0.1/GB both look off by several x.

title: Eliminate analog sensing: Coulomb-blockade dots hold quantized electron counts
idea: Eliminate the continuous charge level: store 0, 1, 2 or 3 extra electrons on a ~2-nm silicon or metal nanodot whose charging energy (>150 meV, ~6 kT) quantizes the stored charge, so each cell holds 2 bits as discrete states read by an integrated single-electron-transistor electrometer.
why: 2 bits per tiny cell (fact 1, density) with attojoule writes (fact 10); thick barriers make it refresh-free; risk is room-temperature operation needing sub-2-nm uniformity and offset-charge noise.

title: Eliminate the semiconductor channel: NEM contact relay access switch
idea: Remove the transistor channel altogether and isolate each storage node with a nanoelectromechanical cantilever relay whose off state is a 5-10 nm air gap. The wordline electrostatically pulls the beam into contact for read/write; once released there is no subthreshold, junction or GIDL path, only gap tunneling (<1e-24 A).
why: Attacks the 13 fA leakage tail and refresh (fact 3): retention is bounded only by capacitor dielectric leakage, so refresh interval moves from 64 ms to minutes, removing most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy and 10-20% bandwidth loss. Contact wear threatens unlimited endurance.

title: Eliminate leakage pathways: Coulomb-blockade-locked silicon nanodot storage node
idea: Store a small charge on a 2-3 nm Si nanodot (LPCVD-grown or e-beam defined) that gates a sense FET and is separated from the bitline by a tunnel barrier; the >100 meV Coulomb charging energy blocks single-electron escape at hold bias, exponentially suppressing leakage. A write gate lowers the barrier.
why: Retention could exceed seconds with non-destructive gain-transistor reads (facts 3, 8); room-temperature blockade needs sub-3 nm uniformity.
note: Room-temperature single-electron memory (Hitachi) known; sub-3 nm uniformity unsolved.

title: Eliminate the Boltzmann tax: all-silicon bilayer tunnel-FET periphery at 0.3 V
idea: Build decoders, sense control and datapath from electron-hole bilayer tunnel FETs in silicon (no Ge or III-V indium), whose band-to-band switching allows sub-60 mV/decade slopes and a 0.3 V supply.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and much of the access energy; 0.3 V versus 1.1 V cuts its CV2 ~13x.
note: TFET drive current remains too low for DRAM periphery speed.

title: Infrared through-silicon optical vias replace TSV stacks
idea: Eliminate copper vias: silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so each thinned die carries Ge photodiodes and micro-emitters in metal-free windows; beams pass straight through intervening dies to receivers on the target die, addressed by position or wavelength.
why: Removes TSV area, via reveal, stress keep-out zones and TSV-driven stack yield loss (HBM TSV tax); no capacitive load on vertical links, claimed <0.5 pJ/bit vertical.

title: Charge-coupled pillar: vertical shift-register DRAM, no capacitor
idea: Reverse 3D NAND's vertical string: store charge packets under each word-tier gate of an oxide-semiconductor channel pillar and clock them up the pillar CCD-style (three-phase gates) to one sense node at the top, so each pillar is a 64-bit vertical shift register with no per-bit transistor or capacitor.
why: Capacitor wall and 3D cell (facts 1,2): bit = one gate tier x pillar pitch on a 3D NAND-like line; IGZO's low leakage gives ms retention; ~1 ns/stage keeps a 64-bit block read under ~100 ns; charge has unlimited endurance.

title: Sense amps on the host: bitline-pitch bonding across dies
idea: Rearrange array and periphery: the DRAM die carries only cell arrays whose bitline segments end in hybrid-bond pads, and sense amplifiers, decoders and I/O live on a logic-process die bonded below at ~1 um pitch. The DRAM process loses its periphery steps, and fast logic transistors sense at lower voltage.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49% of die): the array die gets nearly 2x bits per mm2; logic-node sense amps lower VARY and energy (fact 10); one logic die can serve two array dies.
note: Bitline pitch far below bond pitch; bond-pad capacitance hurts sensing.

title: Vacuum-sealed storage node with field-emission nanogap access switch
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere (vacuum): suspend each storage node on thin oxide posts inside a sealed nano-vacuum cavity so no junction or dielectric film touches it, and access it through a gated vacuum-channel field-emission diode with a <50-nm gap that conducts only above its turn-on field. Vacuum has no traps or band tails, so hold leakage is set by Fowler-Nordheim at low field (aA-class).
why: Fact 3: refresh intervals of minutes to hours; the vacuum switch's extremely steep turn-on also helps fact 10.

title: Few-electron quantum-dot bit sensed by an adjacent single-electron transistor
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation taken to the limit: store each bit as ~5-10 electrons on a <3-nm Si or SnO2 quantum dot whose Coulomb charging energy (>100 meV) blocks leakage, and sense it non-destructively with an adjacent single-electron transistor whose current swings ~10x per electron.
why: Facts 1 and 10: ~1,000x less charge than a 5-fF cell, so CV2 write energy drops ~100x and no capacitor is needed; room-temperature dot uniformity is the risk.
note: Hitachi-era single-electron memory; room-temperature dot uniformity remains the blocker.

title: GaN/AlN tunnel-diode pair self-holds the bit without refresh
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: let the cell maintain itself. On GaN-on-sapphire, two room-temperature GaN/AlN resonant tunnelling diodes are stacked in series with the storage node at their midpoint; their negative-differential-resistance curves intersect at two stable points, so the node self-restores against leakage at pA standby current, accessed through one GaN HEMT.
why: Refresh eliminated (Fact 3) with non-destructive hold; risk is RTD peak-to-valley ratio and standby current per bit (needs <10 pA/bit for 1 Gb under 10 mW).
note: Same NDR latch concept with GaN RTDs.

title: Nanomechanical gap switch isolates the gain-cell storage gate
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution, used in reverse (field -> mechanics): replace the write transistor of a 2T0C gain cell with an electrostatically actuated vertical NEMS contact switch built in the tier stack. An open air gap has essentially zero leakage, so the read transistor's gate keeps its charge until gate-dielectric leakage alone drains it.
why: Fact 3: refresh interval from ~64 ms to minutes; ~10 ns mechanical write; requires contact endurance near 10^15 (graphene or Ru contacts), which is the main risk.
note: Same as I-00628; 1e15 contact cycles far beyond demonstrated NEMS relay endurance.

title: Antiferromagnetic Mn3Sn bits pack densely with no stray fields
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight (counterweight): each bit's antiparallel magnetic sublattices counterbalance, so cells emit no stray field and can sit edge-to-edge; spin-orbit torque from a heavy-metal line switches the noncollinear antiferromagnet in sub-ns, an antiferromagnetic tunnel junction reads it, and retention needs no power.
why: Zero refresh; the stack is ~4-6 sputtered layers vs ~15-20 for a perpendicular MTJ, with no pinned reference layers, easing deposition and etch and allowing DUV-pitch crossbars; small readout signal is the risk (facts 3, 4).

title: HZO nonvolatile shadow layer makes leaked cells recoverable
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: a thin ferroelectric HfZrO sublayer (hafnium and zirconium from U.S. refiners) sits in series with the linear capacitor dielectric; before long idle periods data is copied into polarization and refresh stops, and on wake a polarization read restores the charge.
why: Refresh vanishes for idle regions (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) and retention-tail losses become recoverable; limited ferroelectric endurance is spent only on idle/wake transitions.

title: Synaptic-vesicle quantal storage: Coulomb-staircase multilevel node
idea: Synapses release transmitter in fixed quanta. Make the storage node a sub-3 nm metal island (e.g. an Au cluster in SiO2) whose >100 meV charging energy quantizes stored charge into discrete electron-number plateaus. A single-electron-transistor sense node writes and reads four robust levels per cell, so the levels are set by physics rather than analog trimming.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits per cell from built-in quantization, and the tiny node removes the capacitor. The main risk is room-temperature background charge noise.

title: Shaker-channel ball-and-chain NEMS access gate
idea: Copying the K+ channel's N-type inactivation ball that plugs the pore, replace the access FET with a nanoelectromechanical gate: a conductive nanoball on a compliant SiN tether is pulled by the wordline field into a contact cavity bridging bitline and storage node, and the tether spring plus a self-timed 'inactivation' electrode retracts it, leaving a ~3 nm vacuum gap.
why: Off-state is vacuum tunneling (<1e-21 A vs the 13 fA tail), so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the ~46 fJ/bit refresh and 10-20% bandwidth tax disappear; zero subthreshold slope also removes the need for a ~3 V wordline overdrive.

title: Coin-counting purse: single-electron box stores countable electron numbers
idea: Count coins instead of weighing gold: couple a 3-5-nm Si or Pt island (e-beam litho plus oxidation thinning, or ALD nanoparticle) through one tunnel junction to a reservoir so Coulomb blockade (>150 meV charging energy) makes occupancy discrete; each cell stores 0-3 extra electrons (2 bits), read by a nearby single-electron transistor electrometer without disturbing the count.
why: Fact 10 and energy: writes of a few electrons at ~0.2 V are attojoule-scale and multi-level states are quantized rather than analog; RT operation needs sub-5-nm islands, and random background-charge offsets are the classic killer.

title: SF6 breakers to vacuum interrupters: nano vacuum-gap access switch
idea: The grid is replacing SF6 gas-insulated breakers with vacuum interrupters because vacuum insulates without fluorinated gas. Build a lateral 20-30 nm vacuum-gap field-emission switch, sealed by a PVD cap, whose emitter tip conducts only when the wordline gate thins the barrier; off-state current is Fowler-Nordheim limited and there is no substrate junction.
why: Removes junction and subthreshold leakage paths entirely (fact 3) with temperature-insensitive retention, and the cavity seal needs no fluorinated chemistry.
note: Same vacuum field-emission access device.

title: Light-switch air gap: NEMS relay access device in BEOL tiers
idea: A wall switch draws nothing when off because of its air gap; make each 3D cell's access device a laterally actuated ~10 nm-gap TiN/Ru NEMS relay built at BEOL temperatures, whose near-zero off-current lets the capacitor shrink to ~0.3 fF (signal-limited, not retention-limited) and removes refresh.
