title: Sub-critical stochastic MTJ writes with ECC absorbing misses
idea: Box [medium: perpendicular MTJ | access: spin-orbit-torque line | sense: TMR at 50 mV bias | integration: BEOL over CMOS | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Writes use a short pulse at ~60% of deterministic switching current so ~1e-3 of bits fail to switch; instead of write-verify loops, a BCH code over each 512-bit word absorbs them and background scrubbing rewrites only failed bits.
why: Constraint: write energy ~5-10x lower and low-bias reads keep read energy small; byte-addressable nonvolatile cell with no refresh.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM tiles sold undiced for rack memory
idea: Box[Integration=whole-wafer memory with on-wafer spare routing x Transform=no dicing or packaging x Owner=startup x Scale=rack appliance]: keep the DRAM wafer intact, route around defective dies via redistribution-layer switches, and mount it as a single ~300+ GB memory plane fed by a wafer-edge controller.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by using edge dies and skipping package losses; cuts packaging cost ~15-25% per bit.

title: Po: every bitline wears a shield — coaxial poly-Si bitlines
idea: Po: a bitline wrapped like a TV cable. Form bitlines inside a grounded conformal doped poly-Si sleeve separated by an SiO2/air liner, so neighbor-bitline coupling and wordline kickback terminate on the shield; Cb rises ~15% but pattern-dependent noise (up to ~30% of sense margin) disappears.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and density: ~15% net margin gain and tighter bitline pitch, using Si, O, N only.

title: Multibeam e-beam direct write replaces masks for irregular layers
idea: Po: masks don't exist. Use a ~250k-beam electron writer (today's mask-writer technology) directly on wafers for the irregular, low-area layers (periphery cuts, fuse/redundancy personalization, product variants) while periodic array layers use cheap patterning.
why: Mask cost and EUV dependence: removes $10M+ mask sets per product spin and EUV for irregular layers; product variants in days.

title: Fab in a tube: continuous vacuum track for capacitor module
idea: Po: the wafer never leaves the tool. Chain all ~40 capacitor-module steps (mold deposition, etch, clean, ALD, anneal) in a linear vacuum-linked track with single-wafer flow: no FOUPs, no queues, no air exposure between steps.
why: Cycle time and footprint: capacitor module from weeks to ~1 day, ~30% less WIP and floor area, fewer native-oxide cleans.
note: Vacuum-linked linear track, a module-scoped version of I-07598.

title: Self-aligned octuple patterning lets old 193i scanners print 1x-nm
idea: Po: the old scanner prints finer than its spec. Add three generations of spacer cascades (SAOP) to a 2x-nm DRAM line's existing 193i scanners so an 80 nm litho pitch becomes 10 nm lines for wordlines/bitlines; only extra ALD and etch chambers go into the existing building.
why: EUV dependence and capital: lifts an old fab ~1.5-2 nodes in density without EUV for ~10% of new-fab cost.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM slabs from mature DUV nodes
idea: Po: the wafer is the chip. A 25 nm-class DUV DRAM wafer is never diced: on-wafer redundancy, a wafer-level routing mesh and a bonded controller tile expose the whole wafer (~0.5 TB) as one memory slab for rack-level CXL pools, with bad mats mapped out at test.
why: Skips dicing, packaging and module assembly (~15-25% of cost) and lets older DUV fabs supply capacity-tier memory; attacks capital and cost per bit.
note: Wafer-scale memory tried before (Anamartic); thermal, yield and interconnect hurdles.

title: Retention-mode back-gate swing on double-gate vertical transistors
idea: Worse: use one fixed Vt that must stay low for speed. Flip: in 4F2 vertical-channel arrays, make the shared isolation plate a back gate driven to about -1.5 V in self-refresh (Vt +300 mV, subthreshold leakage about 100x lower) and to 0 V when the bank is active.
why: Idle power share of refresh (16-33%, fact 3); ~10x retention in standby with no speed penalty.

title: Laser-regrown epitaxial storage contact removes implant-damage leakage
idea: Worse: implant the storage-node junction and leave damage clusters that drive trap-assisted leakage. Flip: form the junction by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy followed by nanosecond laser melt-regrowth, giving a defect-free graded junction with no implant cascades.
why: Junction leakage tail (fact 3) about 10x tighter; longer refresh interval.
note: Selective epi contacts already standard; laser regrowth is the twist.

title: Solid-state 193 nm lasers eliminate neon and fluorine gas
idea: Worsen: make every immersion DUV scanner burn neon sourced from a war zone, plus fluorine-rich gas fills. Flip: replace ArF excimer lasers with fiber-laser-pumped solid-state sources that reach 193 nm by cascaded harmonic generation in CLBO-type borate crystals grown domestically, so no rare gas is needed.
why: Neon chokepoint (historically ~50% from Ukraine) and fluorine handling: DRAM uses ~15-25 ArF layers, so the gas dependency goes away entirely.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM panels for rack memory pools
idea: Worse: dice, package and test thousands of dies, each losing scribe and edge area. Flip: keep the whole wafer as one memory, with reticle-stitched interconnect and die/row-level redundancy routing. Mount it directly in a rack memory appliance behind a wafer-level CXL fabric.
why: Packaging, test and scribe are ~15-25% of cost; redundancy turns defects into lost capacity, not scrap; ~20% lower $/GB for pooled memory.

title: Silicon-on-sapphire cells eliminate substrate junction leakage tail
idea: Worse: keep the storage-node junction in a bulk crystal whose defects create the 13 fA tail. Flip: put thin epitaxial Si on Kyropoulos sapphire, so the node has no substrate junction and leaks only through the channel. Sapphire boules use molybdenum crucibles, not high-purity quartz.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes the junction/GIDL tail for ~10x retention, on a substrate independent of Spruce Pine.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM modules that never dice, test or package dies
idea: Worse: dice every wafer, throw out flawed dies and package survivors one by one. Flip: keep the 300 mm wafer whole as one memory module with defect-tolerant routing and spare-block remapping, bonded directly to a cold-plate carrier board.
why: Eliminates dicing, packaging and known-good-die loss so nearly all good area is used; cost per bit down perhaps 15-25%.

title: Legacy DRAM patent commons with fixed-fee entry licenses
idea: Worse: sue every entrant over DRAM patents. Flip: pool expired and soon-expiring DRAM patents plus contributed FRAND licenses into a commons that grants new fabs a fixed-fee entry license, with CHIPS-style grants conditioned on incumbents contributing.
why: Lowers legal risk and licensing cost of entry, so more suppliers can start.
note: Incumbent participation is the crux.

title: Submariner's bulkheads: grounded shield tiers isolate hammer coupling
idea: Submarines compartmentalize so one flood does not sink the boat. Interleave a 3 nm grounded conductive bulkhead film between active tiers, and grounded shield fins between adjacent lateral wordlines in 3D DRAM.
why: Cuts wordline-to-wordline and tier-to-tier capacitive coupling and trap-mediated disturb, aiming at a row hammer threshold above 10k activations (Fact 9). Costs one deposition per tier.

title: No-till farmer grows silicon without any quartz crucible
idea: Persona: a no-till farmer skips the plow, so skip the crucible. Run Czochralski growth from a cold, segmented, water-cooled copper crucible. Induction fields push the melt off the walls, so a frozen silicon skull is the only wall the melt touches. Add nitrogen co-doping to make up for the wafer strength normally supplied by oxygen.
why: Removes Spruce Pine high-purity quartz (>80% share) from DRAM wafer supply. Lower interstitial oxygen means fewer precipitate defects in the retention tail.

title: Stage magician hides magnetism: Mn3Sn antiferromagnetic tunnel junction memory
idea: Persona: a magician whose magnet is invisible. Store bits in the chiral antiferromagnetic order of Mn3Sn and read them with a Mn3Sn/MgO/Mn3Sn all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junction. Write by spin-orbit torque in picoseconds.
why: Non-volatile, immune to stray fields, and roughly 2x denser packing. No Co, Pt, Ir or rare earths.

title: Homesteader builds upward: memory-layer foundry on legacy logic wafers
idea: Persona: a homesteader who adds a floor instead of buying land. A U.S. business deposits non-volatile BEOL memory layers, such as nitride ferroelectric or MRAM below 400 C, directly on customers' finished logic wafers in existing lines.
why: Needs no extra crucible-grown silicon, no EUV and no helium-cooled high-AR etch. Puts memory next to compute (fact 5).

title: Prospector without Spruce Pine: reusable crucibles with continuous Czochralski
idea: A prospector cut off from the one quartz mine refuses to scrap a crucible per ingot. Grow DRAM-grade silicon by continuous Czochralski with granular-poly feeding in a long-life crucible: synthetic sol-gel silica made from fumed silica (any sand plus chlorination) inside a reusable silicon-nitride-coated graphite susceptor, pulling 5-10 ingots per crucible.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz per wafer ~5-10x and escapes >80% single-site supply; continuous CZ also evens out resistivity and oxygen. Risk: oxygen and contamination control for retention-sensitive DRAM.

title: Child asks why break the cookie: wafer-scale DRAM, no dicing
idea: A child asks why you bake one big cookie and then break it into crumbs. Keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory: redundant tiles with an on-wafer mesh that maps out bad tiles at test, wafer-level power planes and edge optical I/O, giving a ~1-2 TB rack memory slab per wafer.
why: Eliminates dicing, per-die packaging, per-die test handling and per-die I/O duplication (~10-20% of cost), with yield handled by redundancy instead of scrap. Risks: power delivery and heat across 70,000 mm2, and serviceability.

title: Commodity trader's forward curve: hyperscaler-funded DRAM capacity options
idea: Grain markets finance planting with forward contracts. Hyperscalers buy tradable 10-year wafer-start options on a new fab, prepaying 30-40% of capex at a strike price and keeping the right to resell on an exchange; builders get capital at near-sovereign cost while demand risk shifts to buyers who can hedge it.
why: Cuts the cost of capital, and the boom-bust risk premium in DRAM pricing, by maybe 3-5 points, making $15B fabs financeable sooner and damping 4x price swings. Risks: contract enforcement and antitrust.

title: Detector-grade crucible-free float-zone wafers for leak-free arrays
idea: Particle detectors use float-zone silicon grown without a quartz crucible, with ~100x less oxygen and few oxygen-vacancy traps. Develop 300 mm float-zone (or crucible-free pedestal-grown) substrates for DRAM array wafers so oxygen-precipitate generation centers near the access junction are gone.
why: Resources and fact 3: removes the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible dependency for array wafers and shrinks the retention tail; 300 mm FZ growth is unproven and oxygen-free wafers lose some mechanical strength.
note: 300 mm FZ unproven; loses oxygen-precipitate gettering.

title: Nanoimprint templates pattern decoder and sub-wordline-driver stripes
idea: Patterned-media hard drives and RFID makers imprint sub-20 nm features cheaply; the highly regular decoder and SWD stripes are imprinted from a master template at 15-20 nm half-pitch, while irregular logic stays on DUV at relaxed rules.
why: Pitch-critical periphery layers made without EUV at ~1/4 the tool cost (fact 4 capital intensity).

title: Deposition-defined vertical decoder transistors replace lithographic gate lengths
idea: Like MEMS and solar fabs that set critical dimensions by film thickness, decoder transistors are vertical channels whose gate length is an ALD film thickness and whose width is a spacer thickness; logic personalization is done with implants at relaxed DUV pitch.
why: 10 nm-class decoder devices with no EUV, keeping decoder area competitive (facts 4, 7).

title: Dumb-array DRAM: CXL controller absorbs refresh, ECC, repair, test
idea: Hyperscalers already own smart memory controllers, so strip the DRAM die to cells, SAs, decoders and a narrow I/O; refresh scheduling, row-hammer tracking, ECC, repair remapping, mode registers and BIST move into a CXL controller on a logic node. With no random logic left, the DRAM die needs no EUV.
why: Periphery 49% -> ~30% (fact 7), and the DRAM die can be made in DUV-only fabs.

title: Well-less satellite tiers: oxide-isolated array layers remove STI for 4F2
idea: Satellites dodge single-event upsets by putting transistors on buried oxide with no bulk well; build every DRAM array tier on transferred thin silicon over oxide so there is no substrate junction, no well contact and no shallow-trench isolation between cells. Gate-all-around vertical channels abut at true 4F2 because isolation comes from the oxide below, and the bulk charge-collection volume behind soft errors and junction leakage disappears.
why: Layout density 6F2 to 4F2 (~33% more bits per tier), removes the junction/GIDL part of the retention tail (fact 3), and gives inherent soft-error immunity.
note: SOI DRAM floating-body effects degrade retention; 4F2 via oxide isolation is known.

title: Containerless space-furnace logic: cold-crucible induction Czochralski for 300 mm
idea: Space crystal growers avoid containers altogether. On Earth, a segmented water-cooled copper cold crucible with induction heating makes silicon hold itself inside a frozen Si skull, so the melt never touches quartz. Controlled O2/Ar ambient or SiO dosing restores the oxygen needed for intrinsic gettering, and cusp magnetic fields steady the melt.
why: Eliminates quartz crucibles entirely (the HPQ chokepoint) and lowers metal contamination, at roughly 2x melt power, which is small next to crucible scarcity risk.

title: KV-cache-grade rows: full cells for exponents, cheap cells for mantissas
idea: AI KV-caches and weights survive flipped low mantissa bits but not flipped exponents. Build a 'BF16-graded' region where hard-wired bit-lane routing places sign, exponent and high mantissa bits in standard ~5 fF cells on normal refresh. The 8 low mantissa bits go in half-height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) capacitors on a relaxed 256 ms refresh with no retention guarantee.
why: Half of the bits avoid the AR 60-75 capacitor and most refresh: ~20-30% less refresh energy and a cheaper capacitor module for AI memory, at <0.1% accuracy loss (facts 1, 3).
note: Same graded capacitor mechanism.

title: DRAM futures exchange lets new fabs borrow against forward sales
idea: Airlines, extreme fuel users, hedge on exchanges. A cleared DRAM futures contract (per Gb of DDR5-equivalent, quarterly delivery) lets AI clouds and phone OEMs hedge, and lets new entrants pre-sell output and borrow against hedged revenue.
why: Lowers cost of capital for new capacity and damps the boom-bust underinvestment behind 4x price spikes.

title: Coaxial capacitor shell wraps the vertical access transistor
idea: Collapse two scales into one pillar: the vertical channel transistor sits in the core and the storage capacitor is a coaxial dielectric/electrode shell wrapped around its upper half, so a 4F2 footprint holds both.
why: Density: 6F2 to 4F2 (~33% area gain) without separate capacitor landing pads.
note: Modest 6F2-to-4F2 gain; coaxial shell capacitance small without tall pillar.

title: Bond eight DRAM wafers before dicing: TSV-free wafer-stacked HBM
idea: Replace die-by-die microbump stacking with sequential wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding of 8-12 DRAM wafers, using fine-pitch bonded vias through 5 um-thinned silicon instead of large TSVs, then dice the finished stack once.
why: Cuts the HBM TSV area tax (Fact 6) by 2-3x and deletes per-die microbump and underfill steps; throughput scales per wafer, not per die.
note: Compound wafer yield is the known blocker.

title: One vacuum cluster runs forty capacitor steps without queuing
idea: Collapse the wafer's timescale: a linear vacuum cluster integrates ~40 sequential deposition, etch and clean steps of the capacitor module, so the wafer never leaves vacuum or waits in a FOUP queue; the module goes from ~20 days to ~1 day of cycle time.
why: Cuts WIP inventory capital and queue-time defects; fewer transfers raise yield and total fab cycle time drops ~25%.

title: Domestic multi-column e-beam writes periphery and cut layers maskless
idea: Use thousands of parallel miniature e-beam columns built in the U.S. to direct-write only the sparse, irregular layers (periphery contacts, cut masks, chip IDs), while self-assembly or imprint handles the dense arrays.
why: Eliminates ~10-15 masks per product ($10-20M per node) and imported scanners on those layers; product variants turn in days.

title: Nanoimprint-first DRAM fab for repetitive array layers
idea: Molecule-to-wafer replication: a master template stamps the extremely periodic cell-array layers (bit lines, capacitor holes) into resist by UV nanoimprint, with no excimer laser and so no neon, argon or krypton. LED UV cures the resist.
why: Lithography capex for the array falls ~40-60% and rare-gas dependence of the array layers drops to zero. The array's regular pattern hides NIL's weakness with irregular layouts.
note: Canon NIL already evaluated for memory; defectivity and overlay limit.

title: Quartz-free crystal pulling: cold-crucible Czochralski from failed electromagnetic casting
idea: Electromagnetic casting held molten silicon in a water-cooled segmented copper crucible by induction, with no quartz, but died because it only made multicrystalline solar ingots. Combine that cold crucible with seed pulling and a cusp magnetic field so 300 mm dislocation-free crystals grow with zero quartz contact, and add nitrogen doping for gettering since the crystal is now oxygen-poor.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucible (>80% single site) from DRAM wafer supply; oxygen-free crystals avoid thermal donors; melt power rises ~30% but one consumable chokepoint disappears.

title: Canon nanoimprint for DRAM: repair maps absorb defects, fluorine-free resist
idea: Nanoimprint stalled on particle-induced defects and template wear. DRAM already repairs defects with spare rows and columns: imprint capacitor-hole and storage-node layers in UV-cure acrylate resist with a non-fluorinated siloxane release layer, map imprint defects by fast inline e-beam inspection, fuse them to redundancy, and replicate cheap daughter templates from one e-beam master.
why: Replaces EUV or SAQP on 2-3 array layers; imprint uses ~1/10 the energy and capex of EUV; resist and release chemistry are PFAS-free; ~10-15% wafer cost cut.

title: Ball Semiconductor's sealed-flow, cleanroom-free fab applied to flat memory wafers
idea: Ball Semiconductor proposed processing 1 mm silicon spheres in sealed tubes without a cleanroom and failed because lithography on spheres was poor. Keep the part that worked, sealed continuously flowing minienvironments, but carry flat wafers in nitrogen-purged pods through linked single-wafer modules so DRAM's repetitive flow needs no ballroom cleanroom.
why: Fab cost: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of capex and much of a fab's water and energy; claims ~25% capex cut and an 18-month build.

title: Cray's SRAM main memory revived at near-threshold with ECC-mapped Vmin failures
idea: Cray-1 and other supercomputers used SRAM main memory until DRAM's cost won. Fix the cost and power that killed it: CFET-stacked 6T SRAM in monolithic 3D tiers run at ~0.45 V, where leakage collapses but ~1e-4 cells fail, with a test-time row-sparing map plus SECDED absorbing the low-Vmin failures.
why: Static storage: zero refresh, no capacitor, buildable in U.S. logic fabs; ECC turns low-voltage unreliability into a ~4x leakage cut.
note: SRAM cell area keeps cost/bit roughly 10x+ above DRAM even with CFET tiers.

title: Air gaps between buried wordlines stop passing-gate leakage
idea: Effect: fringing-field coupling (passing-gate effect). The oxide between neighbouring buried wordlines and the storage-node junction becomes a sealed air gap (k~1), so a neighbour's 3 V swing no longer lowers the barrier of the passing cell, removing the activity-dependent leakage spikes that force conservative refresh. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) with row-hammer relief (fact 9): claims ~2x tail improvement; process drop-in.
note: Air-gap spacers already used in DRAM bitline isolation; modest tail and hammer gain.

title: Cold-crucible induction skull melting gives quartz-free Czochralski silicon
idea: Effect: eddy-current induction heats silicon inside a segmented, water-cooled copper crucible while the Lorentz force pushes the melt off the wall, so molten Si rests on its own frozen Si skull and never touches fused quartz; add a cusp magnetic field to damp convection while pulling 300 mm crystals.
why: High-purity quartz crucibles (Spruce Pine >80%): removes about one crucible per ingot and most oxygen contamination, at roughly +30-50% melt energy.

title: Pockels thin-film lithium niobate links make rack memory pooling viable
idea: Use thin-film LiNbO3 Pockels modulators (sub-pJ/bit, no carrier lifetime, ns latency) in CXL optical links so a rack-scale memory pool sits under 100 ns away. Servers keep a small local DRAM and borrow from the pool on demand, which removes per-server overprovisioning.
why: Stranded memory runs 25-35% in cloud fleets. Pooling recovers most of it, so each rack buys ~20% less DRAM.
note: Pool latency dominated by protocol/switching, not modulator; TFLN adds cost.

title: Carbon-nanotube van der Waals memory runs code and weights in place
idea: Use CNT-fabric memory, which switches by van der Waals contact and is projected to retain data over 10 years well above 125 C, as byte-addressable main storage. OS images, maps and model weights then execute in place, removing the duplicate copy that is loaded from flash into DRAM at boot.
why: Eliminates the storage-to-DRAM double copy, for 40-60% less DRAM in ECUs plus instant-on.

title: Heat-annealed self-healing flash becomes a write-tolerant DRAM extension
idea: Use the 125 C ambient plus brief on-die heater pulses to keep annealing trapped charge out of NAND tunnel oxide (the self-healing flash effect), pushing SLC endurance toward 1e8 cycles. Flash can then act as a swap tier for warm pages behind a small DRAM.
why: Turns heat from enemy into feature: DRAM can shrink 2-4x behind a high-endurance flash tier in hot environments.
note: Macronix showed heater-annealed flash with ~1e8 cycles.

title: Aluminum-doped zinc oxide shield planes stop vertical row-hammer coupling
idea: Insert a 5 nm ALD Al:ZnO conductive plane, grounded through the staircase, between each pair of 3D-DRAM tiers so an aggressor wordline in tier k couples into the shield instead of victim cells in tiers k+1 and k-1.
why: 3D stacking adds vertical hammer and crosstalk paths (fact 9); a grounded shield cuts inter-tier coupling ~90%, allowing tighter tier pitch without new hammer exposure, using only Al, Zn and O at 200 C.

title: F: fluorine-hardened recess-gate edge resists hot-carrier depassivation
idea: A tilted low-dose fluorine implant aimed only at the gate-to-storage-node overlap corner replaces Si-H with Si-F bonds (~5.7 eV vs ~3.1 eV), so hammer-induced hot carriers and GIDL fields cannot re-create the interface traps behind RTN and variable retention time.
why: Cuts VRT cells and lifetime growth of the leakage tail (fact 3) plus trap-assisted hammer coupling (fact 9); target ~2x fewer VRT cells.

title: U: Uranium-style take-or-pay contracts finance new non-volatile memory fabs
idea: Like utilities buying enrichment a decade ahead, hyperscalers sign 7-10-year take-or-pay contracts for MRAM/FeRAM wafer output at indexed prices, letting startups finance fabs with project debt.
why: Cuts cost of capital from ~20% equity to ~8% debt for a non-volatile memory industry that lacks scale.

title: MLCC-style multi-plate lateral capacitor for 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Copy multilayer-ceramic-capacitor construction: inside each tier's lateral capacitor recess, ALD 2N alternating TiN/high-k layers, then open one vertical slit where odd plates are recessed on one side and even plates on the other (like MLCC end terminations), so all plates connect in parallel between storage node and plate line.
why: The lateral capacitor blocks 3D DRAM (fact 2); parallel plates give Cs proportional to plate count instead of recess length, so 4 plate pairs cut lateral cell length ~4x, shrinking cell pitch and lowering the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Zoned newspaper editions: consortium base wafers, one personalization mask
idea: Like papers that print a common edition and swap one plate per zone, a consortium fab runs one standardized DRAM base wafer (array, sense amps, generic I/O) at maximum volume, and each buyer personalizes it with exactly one metal/via mask (density cut, interface, I/O width) on its own BEOL line.
why: Capital: hyperscale volume on one base flow lowers cost per bit, and new entrants need only a ~$0.5-1B BEOL line instead of a $15B fab.

title: Sacrificial-anode collector implants absorb hammer-injected electrons
idea: Galvanising protects steel with a zinc anode that corrodes first; add a shallow grounded n+ collector ribbon (or biased deep well) between adjacent active regions in the buried-channel array so electrons emitted by aggressor wordline traps and passing-gate charge pumping are collected before they reach a victim storage node.
why: Attacks a physical root cause of row hammer (fact 9), possibly raising the threshold 5-20x and removing counter and refresh overhead at a modest density cost.

title: Print-on-demand memory: maskless multibeam runs for niche DRAM SKUs
idea: Print-on-demand publishing killed minimum print runs. Write only the product-specific layers (periphery options, fuses, metal personalization) of automotive, defense and legacy DRAM SKUs with maskless multibeam e-beam, so 1000-wafer lots need no mask set. This moves the long tail off mainstream lines.
why: Masks, capital and supply mix: removes $5-15M mask sets for long-tail SKUs, frees mainstream capacity, and enables trusted U.S. legacy DRAM.

title: Sixteen-tier decks hybrid-bonded with stitched vertical bitlines
idea: IFR: 'unlimited tiers without an unlimited etch.' Backward: build 16-tier decks with modest 30:1 etches, thin each deck to ~3 um, and hybrid-bond decks face-to-back at ~200 nm pitch so each vertical bitline continues through bond pads; six bonds give 96 tiers.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): avoids 100:1+ etches for high tier counts and lets each deck pass known-good test before stacking.

title: Crucible-free 300 mm silicon via cold-crucible induction skull melting
idea: Ideal: a crystal grown from a melt that touches nothing. Closest: pull 300 mm Cz crystals from a water-cooled segmented copper cold crucible where induction heats and partly levitates the melt and a frozen silicon skull is the container; interstitial oxygen for gettering is dosed via a controlled O2/Ar ambient instead of dissolving quartz.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine (>80%) high-purity quartz crucible chokepoint and gives tighter oxygen control; costs ~1.5-2x melt energy.

title: Kerfless laser-split wafering of DRAM-grade silicon ingots
idea: Ideal: slicing with zero sawdust. Closest: focus an IR picosecond laser inside the ingot to write a sub-surface modified plane (KABRA-style, proven on SiC), then split each wafer off by thermal/ultrasonic stress; kerf drops from ~150 um to ~20 um and lapping shrinks.
why: ~30-40% more wafers per ingot, cutting polysilicon, quartz crucibles, puller energy, slurry and water per wafer proportionally.

title: Laser-crystallized silicon tiers stack refresh-free SRAM toward DRAM density
idea: Ideal: a static, refresh-free cell at DRAM density. Closest: monolithically stack 6-8 tiers of thin single-grain Si, crystallized by pulsed-laser melting of amorphous Si at <450 C wafer temperature, with n and p halves of each SRAM cell on alternate tiers, so bits per footprint multiply with no capacitor and DUV-friendly 28 nm rules.
why: Facts 1, 3, 4: no capacitor, no refresh, standard logic tools plus laser anneal; honestly still ~4-8x below DRAM per area today, so the target is cache and buffer tiers.
note: Still 4-8x below DRAM density; CFET-like split known.

title: Wavelength is the address: passive AWG-routed photonic memory pool
idea: Ideal: addressing that costs no logic and no switching energy. Closest achievable: the host tunes a comb line whose wavelength encodes the target bank, a passive arrayed-waveguide grating steers that light to the bank's receiver, and the reply returns on the same wavelength, so bank selection needs no electronic switch or decoder tree.
why: Facts 5 and 7: removes switch, arbiter and decoder energy and area for pooled memory; latency is time of flight (~5 ns/m), keeping a rack-scale pool within DRAM-class access.

title: Shaped wordline falling edge and capped row-open time
idea: Ideal: activating a row disturbs nothing. Closest: the wordline driver uses a slow, shaped falling ramp (~5 ns) instead of a sharp edge to cut electron injection and capacitive kick into adjacent rows, and the controller closes rows after <=36 ns to avoid RowPress-style long-open disturbance.
why: Fact 9: may raise the effective hammer threshold 3-10x at small latency cost, reducing mitigation refreshes.
note: RowPress tRAS capping already proposed; edge shaping gain uncertain.

title: SIMOX-isolated access transistors remove junction leakage tail
idea: Ideal: a storage node with no leakage path to the substrate. Closest: build the cell array on 1990s SIMOX silicon-on-insulator so the storage-node junction sits on buried oxide, eliminating the substrate junction area and deep-level-defect generation current that create most retention tail cells.
why: Fact 3: junction-leakage tail cut perhaps ~10x, tightening retention spread so refresh runs 4-10x less often.
note: SOI DRAM researched in the 1990s-2000s; cost and capacitor integration issues.

title: BiCMOS bipolar sense amps read half-charge cells
idea: Ideal: a sense amp that sees any charge. Closest: use 1990s BiCMOS processes to build the sense amps from bipolar differential pairs, whose Vbe matching (~1 mV offset versus 10-20 mV for MOS) lets cells that have lost half their charge still read correctly.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~2x signal margin lets refresh slow ~2x or Cs drop by about half.
note: BiCMOS DRAMs existed in the 1990s; pitch-matched bipolar pairs are costly.

title: Mid-size OEM memory cooperative owning a shared DRAM line
idea: Ideal: memory always available at cost. Closest achievable: auto, industrial, PC and console OEMs jointly fund a line as a cooperative (Airbus-GIE or farm-co-op style) and get allocation in proportion to equity at cost-plus during shortages.
why: Supply security for segments that AI demand crowds out, plus price neutrality.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM: RDL-stitched good dies on mature wafers
idea: Ideal: memory with no package, socket or dicing. Closest achievable with no new fab: existing OSAT redistribution-layer lines stitch every good die on a mature 2x-nm DRAM wafer into one wafer-scale slab with spare routing around bad dies; one wafer gives ~2 TB on a cold plate serving a rack over CXL.
why: Removes packaging, substrate and final-test cost (~20-30% of module cost) using only existing lines.

title: Multi-beam e-beam writes only cuts, making DRAM variants maskless
idea: Constraint: no new mask set per product. Print array gratings once with cheap periodic litho, then use a ~250k-beam electron writer only on sparse cut and via layers (<5% exposed area) to customize die size, ECC layout and bank count.
why: Mask sets cost $10-20M; cut-only exposure makes e-beam throughput viable (~10-20 wph) for specialty and low-volume DRAM lines.

title: Replaceable base die carries ECC and refresh logic upgrades
idea: Rule: reliability logic must be upgradable without scrapping arrays. In stacked DRAM, the ECC engines, refresh scheduler, hammer defense and repair logic live in a base die joined through a reworkable interface. When better algorithms appear, the base die is swapped and the array dies are reused.
why: Fact 7: periphery (~49% of die) moves to a cheap logic node. Arrays outlive several generations of reliability logic.
note: Custom HBM base dies already move logic to logic nodes; reworkable joints conflict with hybrid bonding.

title: Substitute area-selective deposition for resist-pattern-etch-strip loops
idea: Grow films only where wanted by first patterning inhibitor monolayers (UV-cleaved aminosilane SAMs or DUV-written carbon), then running ALD that nucleates only on uninhibited regions, deleting resist coat, develop, etch, strip and their cleans.
why: Each lithography loop carries ~5-8 wet steps; ASD-built layers cut water per patterned layer >10x and save ArF/EUV exposures.

title: Substitute stochastic filaments with deterministic proton intercalation cells
idea: Swap filamentary ReRAM (random breakdown, high variability) for nanosecond protonic electrochemical cells where a gate pulse shuttles protons through a solid electrolyte (e.g., phosphosilicate glass) into a WO3 channel, giving smooth, repeatable non-volatile conductance states.
why: Error tolerance: much lower cycle-to-cycle variability cuts raw BER and ECC overhead; abundant elements avoid chokepoints.
note: MIT protonic PSG/WO3 programmable resistors already demonstrated; not DRAM-class endurance.

title: Magnify nanotube count per transistor to average away leakage variance
idea: Build each access transistor from ~20 aligned semiconducting carbon nanotubes on quartz or glass instead of 1-3. Per-device variance falls ~1/sqrt(N), and any metallic tube is burned open by an electrical breakdown pulse at test.
why: Facts 3 and 4: CNT variability blocks CNT memory; averaging plus burn-off gives a low-temperature, non-silicon access device whose leakage tail approaches the 13 fA spec.

title: Nanomechanical parametron stores the bit as oscillation phase
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action + #15 Dynamics: revive Goto's 1954 parametron at nanoscale. Each cell is a high-Q nanomechanical resonator pumped at 2f by a shared wordline AC drive, ringing at f in one of two phases (0 or 180 degrees); phase is the bit, the pump continuously regenerates it, and a small injected signal picks the phase on write.
why: Facts 3 and 10: no transistor leakage tail and no refresh, plus native majority-logic in memory; pump power and density are the risks.

title: Spatial ALD carousel boosts dielectric deposition throughput tenfold
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: replace pulse/purge temporal ALD with wafers rotating under gas-curtain-separated precursor and oxidant zones, so every revolution is one ALD cycle; ZrO2/Al2O3 capacitor dielectrics and liners deposit ~10x faster near atmospheric pressure.
why: ALD is a large share of capacitor and 3D-module tool count; ~5-10x wafers/hour per tool cuts ALD capex and footprint proportionally (throughput, capital).
note: Spatial/rotary semi-batch ALD already commercial; HAR conformality limits gain.

title: Zebra stripes: superlattice edge transfer defines 8 nm bitlines without lithography
idea: Random stimulus 'zebra' -> an ALD/epitaxial superlattice of alternating materials (for example Si/SiGe) is cleaved and polished edge-on, selectively etched, metallized and stamped onto the wafer as a line array (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer). Film thickness, controlled to the angstrom, sets pitch and CD instead of optics.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): it enables sub-10 nm half-pitch bitline and wordline arrays with no EUV and near-zero CD variation, and the master superlattice is reusable.
note: Heath group SNAP, 2003.

title: Pacemaker heartbeat: NEMS parametron stores bit as oscillation phase
idea: A biologist sees life keeping information as a rhythm, like the heart's pacemaker. Each cell is a nanomechanical resonator pumped parametrically at 2f by a shared global pump; it settles into one of two phase states (0 or pi) that encode the bit, and it couples to a read line only when selected.
why: A shared pump supplies the energy, so there is no per-cell refresh; phase does not leak away like charge (fact 3) and is immune to row hammer (fact 9). It revives Goto's 1954 parametron at NEMS scale.

title: MLCC-style strontium titanate nanolaminate stretches pillar capacitors past k=70
idea: MLCC makers ship trillions of titanate capacitors made from abundant Ba, Sr and Ti. Grow ALD SrTiO3/TiO2 nanolaminates (Sr cyclopentadienyl + TTIP, two-step crystallization) inside TiN-lined pillars in a university fab, with Al2O3 interface doping to tame leakage.
why: Fact 1 says k ~70 is needed; STO reaches k ~100-150 below 10 nm, enabling ~2x Cs or ~40% shorter pillars (less high-AR etch and PFC gas).

title: NEMS parametron: bit as the phase of a vibrating beam
idea: IFR: a bit made of motion, free to keep if lossless. Closest achievable: a high-Q nanomechanical resonator pumped at twice its frequency oscillates in one of two degenerate phases (0 or pi); a small seed signal sets the phase (write) and phase-sensitive detection reads it, reviving Goto's 1950s parametron.
why: Facts 3 and 9: no charge to leak or hammer; one shared pump replaces per-cell refresh; near-reversible dynamics allow sub-fJ writes.

title: First-boot forming pulse punches through HF-free contact oxide
idea: Reverse a defect into an antifuse: without HF dips, contacts keep ~0.5-1 nm of chemical oxide that creates a resistance tail; at first power-up a controlled forming pulse breaks down that thin oxide only in contacts flagged as slow-writing, turning them ohmic.
why: Contact-resistance tails cause write and restore failures; a one-time electrical fix enables an HF-free front end.
note: Breakdown filaments are resistive and variable; per-contact targeting at billions scale doubtful.

title: Cochlear tonotopic row selection with frequency-addressed wordline groups
idea: Like the basilar membrane, where each position resonates at its own frequency, each local wordline-driver group gets a tiny on-die resonator (BAW/MEMS or LC) tuned to a unique frequency. The bank broadcasts one tone burst on a single shared line, and only the matching group rectifies it into a wordline enable, replacing predecode buses and one decoder level.
why: Fact 7: collapsing 64-way selection onto one wire could cut that decode level's area 30-50% and remove predecode bus switching energy.
note: MEMS/LC resonators dwarf decoder logic area; ring-up latency.

title: Triboelectric generators: contact-electrified charge patches store bits
idea: Triboelectric nanogenerators move a saturating charge between dissimilar surfaces on contact; let an e-beam-defined, electrostatically actuated Ti cantilever tap a PTFE- or Al2O3-coated pad above a sensing transistor, transferring a self-limiting ~50-500 e- charge per contact, and reverse it by tapping with an opposite-polarity material, the patch retaining charge with electret-grade stability.
why: Electret retention (years) removes refresh, and the self-limiting transfer tolerates actuator variation; buildable with e-beam, sputter and sacrificial release; small charge per contact, wear and ns actuation are the risks.
note: Mechanical tapping per bit is slow and wears; charge per contact is tiny.

title: Diatom biosilicification: room-temperature catalytic silica for gapfill and supports
idea: Diatoms build intricate silica shells at ambient temperature using polyamine/silaffin peptides that catalyze silicic-acid condensation. Use synthetic polyamine-catalyzed silica sols to conformally fill capacitor support lattices and shallow trenches below 100 C with a gentle cure, replacing high-temperature furnace TEOS and polysilazane steam anneals.
why: Cuts furnace energy and quartz furnace-ware wear for dielectric fill; the low thermal budget also protects TiN/high-k capacitor stacks, allowing higher-k phases.

title: Acoustic delay-line page buffer frees sense amps instantly
idea: A modern mercury delay line: an AlN surface-acoustic-wave track runs under each bank's I/O edge. A sensed row is launched as acoustic pulses that take ~100 ns to cross, during which the sense amps precharge and open the next row; a transducer at the far end recaptures the bits as they arrive and serves bursts in flight.
why: Hides precharge and row-cycle time and replaces SRAM row caches in the periphery, for ~1.5x effective bank bandwidth on streaming loads.

title: Marconi coherer revival: link receivers that latch arriving bits nonvolatilely
idea: Like the 1890s coherer whose filings fused under RF, end each die-to-die write lane with a filamentary Ag/Cu nanogap switch that forms a filament when a pulse arrives, so the receiver is itself a nonvolatile staging latch, reset later by a counter-pulse 'tapper'.
why: Facts 3/5: merges receiver and write buffer, removing an SRAM/register staging hop for write-mostly streams (checkpoints, KV-cache spill), ~30% data-path energy on those writes; endurance limits it to staging, not working memory.
note: Filament formation time and endurance make it a niche staging trick at best.

title: Core-weaving revival: robots thread insulated microwire through laser-drilled stacks
idea: Like core-memory weavers threading wires through ferrite rings, laser-ablate aligned 20 um holes through a stack of thinned dies or glass and robotically thread polyester-imide-enamelled (not PTFE) copper microwire through them, then press-contact it to pads on each tier.
why: Constraint: laser ablation plus threading replaces Bosch DRIE, PFAS resists and plating chemistry for vertical interconnect; suited to 4-8-tier power/ground and slower signals at very low capital.
note: Robotic threading of 20 um holes is impractical at volume.

title: Twistor revival: thermally drawn memory fibre, reel-tested, bad segments skipped
idea: Bell's twistor memory stored bits along woven magnetic wires. Thermally draw a multi-material preform (glass or polymer cladding, embedded metal wordlines, a ferroelectric or charge-storing core) into kilometres of memory fibre in a fully dry process; a reel-to-reel tester maps bad segments the way tape drives map defects, and good segments are woven into mats addressed like twistor planes.
why: Water and capital (fact 4): fibre drawing needs no ultrapure-water wet cleans (>10x less water than a wafer flow) and little capital, and segment mapping makes a crude process usable; density and speed are far from DRAM-class today.
note: Novel fibre-drawing route, but density and speed are far from DRAM-class.

title: Twistor Revival on Magnetic-Tape Coating Lines
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor (magnetic tape wrapped helically on a sense wire) as laminated sheets: surviving data-tape coating lines deposit high-coercivity barium-ferrite stripes on PET film over printed copper sense lines, then laminate crossed drive-line films roll-to-roll at km per hour.
why: Capital intensity: a roll-to-roll web line costs ~$50M versus a $15B fab and reuses the LTO tape industry; yields a non-volatile slow working-memory tier to absorb cold DRAM pages.
note: Twistor bits are mm-scale and microsecond-class; density orders of magnitude below DRAM.

title: Williams Tube 2.0: Field-Emitter Arrays From Abandoned FED Display Lines
idea: Revive the 1947 Williams tube (bits as charge spots on a dielectric written and read by an electron beam) using the field-emission-display tooling Candescent and Sony abandoned: each microtip emitter addresses a 1-4 um patch of unpatterned charge-storage film, read back by secondary-emission sensing, so cell density is set by beam focus rather than lithography.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital: the storage film needs no patterning or EUV, and mothballed display vacuum lines supply the emitter arrays.
note: Micron-scale beam-addressed spots are far less dense than DRAM; vacuum packaging too.

title: Po: banks chosen by pitch — AlN resonator select tones
idea: Po: a decoder that listens for its note. Each bank or subarray group enable is gated by an AlN thin-film acoustic resonator with a unique frequency on one shared RF select line; a single-tone burst wakes only the matching group through a rectifier, replacing trees of global decode wires and repeaters.
why: Periphery (#7): fewer global decode wires and repeaters and less routing congestion, using CMOS-compatible Al and N only.

title: Sacrificial printed fan-out exposes internal test nodes, then dissolves
idea: Worse: dedicate die area to hundreds of large probe pads and on-die test muxes. Flip: inkjet-print a temporary solvent-soluble polymer-and-silver fan-out over the wafer that connects tiny internal test points to large probe pads, test through it, then strip it before final passivation and bumping.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): probe-pad and test-mux area (~2-4% of die) shrinks, with deeper analog visibility into sense amps during test.
note: Inkjet resolution far coarser than internal test points.

title: Compressed-sensing reads of sparse tensors with fewer sense ADCs
idea: Borrow compressive sampling from MRI and radio astronomy and shrink it to the column: in non-destructive gain-cell mats holding ReLU-sparse activations, the read currents of 8 columns are summed onto one sense line through pseudo-random +/-1 select patterns, taking 3 measurements per 8 columns, and a small base-die solver reconstructs the (at most 1-of-8 nonzero) data. Dense data falls back to normal column reads.
why: Cuts sense circuitry ~2.7x and read energy per useful bit for sparse AI data (facts 7, 8); applies to the 50-90% sparse share of activation traffic.
note: Needs strict 1-of-8 sparsity and analog current summing accuracy; real activations rarely meet that.

title: Core memory rethreaded by lithography: microtoroids around through-glass vias
idea: Magnetic core memory died on hand-threading labor and millimeter cores, not on its materials (iron oxide ferrite and copper). On glass panels, laser-drill via arrays, electroplate copper X, Y and sense lines through them, and form 5-10 um ferrite or NiFe rings around each crossing by room-temperature aerosol deposition, writing by coincident current.
why: Only iron oxide, Zn/Mn/Ni, copper and glass: no chokepoint input; infinite endurance and nonvolatile, so no refresh; ~1 GB/m2 per layer at 10 um pitch, so best for rad-hard or infinite-write tiers unless rings shrink further.
note: Microsecond, ~1 GB/m2 density keeps it niche.

title: Sn: reflowable tin micro-links make field-reprogrammable repair fuses
idea: Replace one-time laser/e-fuses with Sn micro-links in sealed cavities: a Joule pulse melts a link so surface tension beads it open, and a second heater over wetting pads reflows it closed, so repair maps can be rewritten in the field as cells weaken.
why: Enables in-field repair of retention-weak rows (fact 3) and higher usable bits per wafer (~2-5%); reflow links pitch tighter than laser fuses.

title: Electrochromic rewritable optical pages host the LoRA adapter library
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll coated electrochromic film (WO3/PEDOT) is written electrically through a passive printed electrode grid and read optically in parallel by an image sensor. Serving clusters park thousands of rarely used fine-tune adapters on it and load a whole adapter into HBM with one optical page read when a request arrives.
why: Multi-tenant serving keeps thousands of adapters in DRAM; a bistable optical tier that is written rarely and read in bursts frees that DRAM at film cost.

title: Chill first, etch second: ride on thermal inertia, no helium
idea: Reverse when cooling happens: pre-chill wafers cryogenically in the load lock and run short etch/deposition steps on the wafer's own thermal mass, replacing continuous helium backside gas with a time-budgeted temperature window.
why: Helium supply lost ~30% (Qatar offline since March 2026); removing backside-He for short steps could cut fab helium use ~50-70%.

title: UV-transparent lid lets depots erase trapped charge in oxide storage layers
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution (optical for electrical): for back-end oxide-semiconductor storage tiers that sit at the top of the stack, package them under a fused-silica window like an EPROM; in a repair depot, deep-UV de-traps charge accumulated in the gate dielectric and channel, restoring threshold voltage and retention without electrical stress.
why: Fact 3 drift reversal and module reuse; turns threshold-voltage drift from a scrap cause into a serviceable condition.
note: UV often worsens oxide-TFT instability (NBIS); niche repair use.

title: Hair-cell stochastic resonance: dithered mini-latch with majority vote
idea: Cochlear hair cells use stochastic resonance, where added noise helps a threshold detector see sub-threshold input. An isolated mini-comparator hanging off the bitline pair gets a controlled zero-mean dither on its tail node and fires 3-5 times in ~4 ns. A majority vote sets the main latch, which then restores the cell.
why: Fact 1/7: tolerates ~40% smaller bitline swing (60 mV vs 100 mV), so bitlines can carry 1024 cells instead of 512. That halves the sense-amp count and its stripe area, roughly 5-8% of the die, or allows smaller Cs.
note: Dither plus voting reduces noise but not static offset.

title: Xylem-sap capillary wicking fills contacts without tungsten CVD
idea: Plants lift sap up narrow, hydrophilic, slightly tapered xylem vessels by capillarity. Make periphery and BEOL plug holes slightly tapered and plasma-hydrophilic, spin on a Cu-Mn nanoparticle ink that wicks to the bottom, then sinter at ~400 C so the Mn forms its own MnSiOx barrier while the copper densifies.
why: Replaces W CVD from WF6 in plugs (tungsten ~80% China, fluorine chemistry) with spin-on and furnace steps on cheap tools.

title: Blind-spot filling-in regenerates lost weight blocks approximately
idea: The visual cortex fills the retina's blind spot from its surroundings; weights are stored with a tiny per-layer predictor so if a recycled chip's bank dies, its weight blocks are regenerated from neighboring blocks plus a stored residual sketch, keeping the model serving until the part is swapped.
why: Lets cheap recycled DRAM hold weights without full mirroring; ~2x less redundancy overhead.

title: Electroless nickel-boron electrodes coat 100:1 capacitor holes conformally
idea: Box [MIM cap with Ni-B electrodes | Si | voltage SA | standard | Si | autocatalytic electroless deposition after molecular Sn/Ag activation]: seed the hole walls, grow 3 nm Ni-B autocatalytically (self-limiting by bath depletion), then nitridize its surface with NH3 for a stable interface to the dielectric.
why: Replaces slow TiCl4/NH3 ALD TiN with a wet, room-temperature process that is conformal at any aspect ratio, needs no vacuum or rare gases, and uses broadly sourced Ni.

title: Sous-vide chef: memory held isothermal at a constant 125 C
idea: Sous-vide works because the temperature never changes: instead of fighting heat, on-die heaters hold the memory stack at a constant 125 C at all times, so it never thermally cycles, and refresh and link timing are calibrated once for that single point.
why: Thermal-cycling fatigue of bumps and interposers, the main packaging failure mode, is eliminated; one-temperature tuning recovers margin that wide-range designs waste.
note: At 125 C retention collapses and refresh rises sharply.

title: Zinc solders abandoned for corrosion; Zn-Al fluxless joints inside sealed stacks
idea: Sn-Zn and Zn-Al solders were rejected in the 2006 lead-free transition because Zn oxidizes and corrodes in humid, flux-based board assembly. Inside an HBM-style stack the joint is never exposed: deposit Zn-Al eutectic caps on Cu pillars, reflow fluxless in formic-acid vapor and encapsulate immediately in molded underfill, replacing SnAg microbumps and In-based low-temperature solders.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Sn (~2 ppm of the crust, concentrated supply), Ag and In from the microbump layer of every stack; Zn-Al (381 C) also serves as a high-temperature first joint in the solder hierarchy.
note: 381 C reflow exceeds the DRAM assembly thermal budget.

title: Domestic molybdenum dual-work-function buried wordline replaces tungsten
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: tungsten (China ~80%) is replaced by molybdenum from U.S. mines in the buried wordline; Mo needs no thick TiN barrier, which frees room for a low-work-function lower segment next to the storage-node junction that softens the gate-to-drain field.
why: Removes the tungsten chokepoint, cuts GIDL in tail cells ~3-5x and lowers wordline resistance ~20-30% in narrow trenches: a refresh and supply-security win.
note: Mo wordlines and dual-work-function gates already pursued in industry.

title: Instant-photography dry resist and dry develop for periphery litho
idea: Like Polaroid replacing the wet darkroom, vapor-deposit a metal-oxide photoresist, expose, develop it in a plasma/thermal gas step and strip it dry on every periphery-only mask (implant blocks, contacts, metals), so these layers never touch developer, rinse or wet strip.
why: Water: track develop/rinse and post-implant wet strips (~15-25 L UPW per layer) fall ~10x on periphery layers; resist solvent supply chains shrink too.

title: Vacuum canning: no-air-break integration of periphery gate and contacts
idea: Canned food needs no preservatives because it never meets air. Run the periphery gate stack (interface, high-k, metal, cap) and the contact module (etch, liner, fill) each in one vacuum cluster with in-situ dry cleans, so wafers never grow native oxide or pick up airborne contamination, and queue-time wet re-cleans disappear.
why: Water: ~10-15 inter-step wet cleans per periphery flow are removed (~10x less water in those modules), along with queue-time scrap; cycle time also falls.

title: Molybdenum buried wordlines exploit shorter electron mean free path
idea: Effect: electron mean-free-path size effect (Fuchs-Sondheimer/Mayadas-Shatzkes). Replace TiN/W buried wordlines with barrierless Mo or Ru (mean free path ~11 and ~7 nm vs ~19 nm for W), cutting 10 nm-line resistance ~30-40% and freeing the barrier's trench volume; faster wordline edges shorten each internal refresh burst. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh time and resources (facts 3, resources): ~2x lower wordline RC, ~20-30% shorter refresh activity, and tungsten (China ~80%) removed from the array.
note: Mo/Ru replacing W is mainstream industry roadmap.

title: The wire is the memory: electron-position cells that store and route
idea: Erase the line between storage and interconnect: four-dot silicon dangling-bond or molecular cells hold a bit as which diagonal two electrons occupy, and the same cells chained in a line shift the bit to the array edge under a clocked field (quantum-dot cellular automata); no bitlines, no charge sharing.
why: Data movement and periphery (facts 5,7): moving a bit costs near-kT energy instead of pJ, cells are ~2 nm; risks are room-temperature margins and single defects breaking chains.
note: QCA serial memory is old idea; room-temperature margins and atomic-precision fabrication at scale need a miracle.

title: Molecular quantum-dot cellular automata loop memory
idea: Scale bits down to electron positions inside a 2 nm mixed-valence molecule: the bit is which diagonal pair of four redox sites holds two electrons, and a clocked ring of molecules circulates bits like a shift register.
why: Density and energy: THz switching with near kT energy, theoretical 1e14 bits/cm2.
note: Promises 1e14 bits/cm2, but molecular QCA has not been clocked or read at RT in 25 years.

title: Substitute one shared free-electron laser for many tin-plasma EUV sources
idea: Build an energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser producing ~10 kW of 13.5 nm light and split it by grazing-incidence mirrors to 10-20 scanners, replacing per-tool tin-droplet plasma sources from a single supplier.
why: ~3-5x lower EUV electrical power per wafer, no tin debris or collector consumables, and the scarce single-source module becomes shared infrastructure for the 5-7 EUV DRAM layers.

title: Synchrotron-style shared light source: free-electron laser feeds many scanners
idea: Cities replaced household generators with central power plants. Build one energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser per fab and split its multi-kW EUV beam to 10-20 scanners, replacing per-scanner laser-produced tin-plasma sources; wafers and DDR/HBM products are unchanged.
why: Cuts EUV wall-plug power per wafer several-fold (each tin-plasma source draws ~1 MW), adds a second EUV-source path beyond the single supplier, and higher dose reduces stochastic defects.

title: Shared energy-recovery free-electron laser feeds a whole EUV fab
idea: Tin-plasma EUV converts wall power at ~0.02%; an energy-recovery-linac FEL recycles the electron beam's energy and lases at 13.5 nm at ~0.1-1% wall-plug. One 10 kW source split by grazing-incidence optics feeds 10-20 scanners with no tin droplets and no hydrogen debris flow.
why: EUV electricity down ~5-10x and the tin-source/hydrogen chain removed, building on US national-lab accelerator expertise.
note: Shared ERL-FEL EUV already pursued by startups/labs; needs $100M+.

title: Po one lightbulb lights the whole fab: shared FEL EUV source
idea: Po: 'one lightbulb lights every scanner in the fab.' Extracted: drive 10-20 scanners from a single energy-recovery-linac free-electron laser at 13.5 nm, distributed by grazing-incidence beamlines, replacing per-scanner tin-droplet laser-produced-plasma sources.
why: EUV energy (~1 MW per LPP scanner) and tin/hydrogen consumption: several-fold lower wall-plug energy per exposed wafer and higher available dose, which permits lower-defect resists.

title: Inkjet-head e-beam writer: 10,000 beamlets pattern without EUV
idea: Inkjet heads fire thousands of nozzles in parallel; build U.S. multi-column electron-beam direct writers with MEMS beam-blanker arrays that write DRAM critical layers straight into resist, replacing EUV exposures with a mask-free step.
why: EUV has one foreign supplier and each tool draws ~1 MW with tin plasma and hydrogen; a domestic multibeam writer removes EUV, masks and pellicles and can write per-wafer redundancy maps.
note: MAPPER-style multibeam direct write pursued for decades; throughput never met fab needs.

title: Offset-trim implant enabling 2-bit cells only for millisecond-lived data
idea: One added halo/Vt implant mask tightens sense-amp transistor mismatch enough for 4-level sensing. Cells store 2 bits only for data that lives shorter than the shortened MLC retention of ~4-8 ms: in-flight activations and current-step scratch. Before that deadline, the allocator demotes any surviving data to 1-bit mode. Data lifetime is matched to cell retention.
why: Ephemeral data is 20-40% of accelerator working memory. Doubling its bits per cell gives 1.2-1.4x capacity per die.
note: Matching data lifetime to MLC retention is clever; 4-level sensing margin is the doubt.

title: Swap litho-patterned storage nodes for area-selective bottom-up growth
idea: Use area-selective ALD/CVD (inhibitor self-assembled monolayers on the dielectric, so growth occurs only on metal landing pads) to grow TiN storage-node pillars upward from each contact. The node layer copies the DUV-made contact pattern with no lithography or etch of its own.
why: Removes one or two critical litho/etch layers (fact 4) and the high-AR etch (fact 1); the pillars are self-aligned, so there is no overlay error.
note: ASD selectivity lasts nanometres, not tall pillars; mushrooming expected.

title: Replace semiconductor switch with non-touching tunneling-gap NEMS relay
idea: Substitute the channel with a vacuum-gap nanomechanical beam. When the wordline pulls it in, it stops ~1 nm from the storage electrode on an oxide standoff, so charge moves by electron tunneling and never by metal contact. When released (gap >5 nm), the only off-current is vacuum tunneling, effectively zero.
why: Leakage/refresh: off-leakage below an attoampere leaves retention limited only by the capacitor dielectric (hours). Because the contacts never touch, there is no wear (target >1e15 cycles).

title: Substitute argon-purged Cz crystal with hydrogen-ambient crucible-free silicon
idea: Substitute argon-purged Czochralski pulling in quartz crucibles with electromagnetic cold-crucible casting in a hydrogen/nitrogen ambient for the substrate. The access transistors live in a 3-5 um low-oxygen epitaxial layer grown by H2-carrier CVD, with nitrogen co-doping for gettering.
why: Removes the argon and Spruce Pine quartz chokepoints, and low-oxygen epi has fewer generation centers, so the leakage tail improves rather than worsens.
note: Cold-crucible cast Si is multicrystalline; epi inherits grain boundaries.

title: Backside-etched capacitors in the thinned bulk replace front-side cylinders
idea: Substitute the front-side capacitor stack with capacitors etched from the wafer backside: after front-end transistors and bitlines, bond face-down, thin to ~3 um and etch capacitor holes from the back into silicon directly beneath each access transistor's storage junction, then line with ALD dielectric/electrode.
why: Capacitor charge wall and layout (facts 1, 4): the capacitor no longer competes with bitline/contacts for front area, can use the full 4F² footprint (~1.5x cross-section), and frees the BEOL; Cs ~7-8 fF at today's AR.
note: Backside trench needs 90:1 AR in 3 um and a junction connection; gain modest.

title: Infrared through-silicon optical links replace Bosch-etched copper TSVs
idea: Substitute SF6/C4F8 Bosch-etched Cu TSVs with vertical free-space optics: silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so beams from bonded InP micro-emitters (Cl2/BCl3-etched) on the base die cross 30 um-thin DRAM dies to Ge-on-Si detectors (GeH4 epi) placed at a unique XY site on each die (position multiplexing).
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no via keep-out zones or via yield loss, which drive much of the 3x area per bit, and the stack is built with no fluorinated deep-etch gases.

title: Substitute quartz crucibles with electromagnetic cold-crucible silicon crystal growth
idea: Melt silicon in a water-cooled segmented copper crucible where induction currents push the melt off the walls (skull melting), and pull single crystals from the levitated pool under a cusp magnetic field. No fused-quartz crucible is consumed and oxygen from SiO2 dissolution disappears.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz chokepoint (>80%); oxygen-free crystals avoid oxygen precipitates that feed junction-leakage tails (fact 3).

title: Substitute megafabs with containerized low-temperature memory lines
idea: Swap $15B megafabs for ISO-container tool modules (sputter, spatial ALD, imprint, plating, metrology), possible because <=400 C flows need no diffusion furnaces or implanters, set up next to data centers.
why: Distributed U.S. manufacturing in modules of ~$50-100M, deployed in months; capacity scales with demand rather than in decade-long steps.

title: Bucket-brigade row buffer replaces column decoder and datalines
idea: Turn the sensed row into a CCD-style charge-transfer shift register: after sensing, bits march out of the stripe edge in parallel lanes at GHz rates straight into the serializer, so the column decoder, column-select lines and global I/O sense amps are gone. This combines CCD readout with the DRAM row buffer.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and overfetch (fact 8): the column path is ~10% of die; streaming full rows turns the 128x overfetch into useful data for AI/streaming, ~3-5x lower pJ per useful bit.

title: Solution-grown YBCO superconducting interposer lines cooled by liquid nitrogen
idea: Combine coated-conductor chemistry (TFA-MOD chemical solution deposition of YBCO on solution-deposited buffers, no argon ion-beam assist or sputtering) with interposer wiring operated in LN2, so memory-to-processor transmission lines have zero DC resistance and carry low-swing signals over 10-50 cm without repeaters; no helium cryogenics.
why: Data movement and beachfront: ~0.1 pJ/bit over long reach decouples memory capacity from package edge length.

title: Laser-trim healing: test, then locally anneal each leaky cell
idea: Combine laser trimming of analog resistors with retention test: after mapping tail cells, a focused laser pulse locally anneals each leaky cell's junction or channel to passivate the defect, or deliberately opens it so it is mapped out. Buildable in a university nanofab: laser writer plus probe-station retention map.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): targeted repair of the ~1e-5 tail could double the refresh interval; production needs fast galvo systems.
note: Cannot target ~15 nm buried cells through BEOL with a laser.

title: Minimal Fab half-inch wafers plus maskless direct-write lithography
idea: Combine Japan's Minimal Fab (0.5-inch wafers, desk-sized local-cleanroom tools) with multibeam e-beam or laser direct-write. The result is a mask-free micro-fab that makes small lots of radiation-hard or specialty DRAM inside defense or auto plants.
why: Cuts capital per site from billions to about $10-30M and removes masks, for secure, distributed niche supply that frees the big fabs for commodity bits.

title: Deposit-only patterning: area-selective ALD with chlorine silicon etch
idea: Fuse area-selective ALD (inhibitor SAMs that block growth on the masked areas) with HBr/Cl2 silicon etch, so dielectrics are only ever grown where wanted and never etched. That removes every CF4/C4F8/NF3 oxide-etch and chamber-clean step from the DRAM flow.
why: Removes fluorinated etch gases (and their supply and regulatory risk) and cuts the number of etch tools, a large share of DRAM capex.

title: Fluoride-free effluent enabling 95% water recycle in arid sites
idea: Combine a fully F-free process (no HF, no fluoride effluent, no CaF2 sludge) with reverse-osmosis plus EDI zero-liquid-discharge loops. With fluoride gone, the hardest RO-fouling and scaling ion is removed, so 95%+ of UPW can be recycled.
why: Water stops being a siting constraint for fabs in Arizona or Texas. Water and wastewater opex drops 30-50%.

title: Carbon credits for avoided NF3, SF6 and CF4 finance fab capex
idea: Fuse a fluorine-free DRAM flow with verified carbon-credit issuance. Avoided F-gases (NF3 GWP about 16,100, SF6 about 23,500, CF4 about 7,400) earn credits over a baseline fab's emissions, which are pre-sold as offtake to fund construction.
why: A typical fab emits about 0.5-1 Mt CO2e per year in F-gases. Credits could fund 5-10% of capex and lower $/bit.

title: Federal fast-track permitting for certified fluorine-free fabs
idea: Combine a NEPA categorical exclusion for the chemical and effluent review with mandatory PFAS-free certification. A fab that can show zero F inventory gets a 6-month permit track instead of 2-3 years.
why: Time is capital. Taking 1.5-2 years off a $15B project saves billions in carrying cost and brings U.S. bits forward.
note: Zero-fluorine DRAM fab is not yet technically possible.

title: Scanning-tunneling-microscope gap switch: non-contact NEMS access device
idea: Adapted from the STM, whose current changes ~10x per angstrom of gap: a nano-cantilever tied to the storage node is pulled by the wordline from a 3 nm gap to ~0.8 nm from the bitline contact so electrons tunnel across in the on state. It never touches, so there is no contact wear, and at full gap tunneling current is ~1e-9 of on-current.
why: Removes the semiconductor junction from hold entirely, so off-leakage is set by vacuum tunneling (far below 1 aA) and retention could reach hours (fact 3); non-contact motion sidesteps the contact-wear endurance problem that stalled NEMS relays.

title: DWDM wavelength-addressed wordlines through transparent glass
idea: Borrowed from telecom DWDM: each wordline driver on a glass panel is a photo-TFT under a thin-film Fabry-Perot filter tuned to one of 64 wavelengths, and a fast tunable laser beneath the transparent substrate selects a row by color, with 1-of-16 electrical predecode choosing the mat.
why: Periphery: optical selection replaces row decoders and global address wiring, cutting decoder area ~70% in exchange for an off-panel photonic source.

title: Foldable-phone flex hinge folds periphery behind the array
idea: Borrowed from foldable phones and flex-PCB folding: array and periphery are built side by side on polyimide, then the periphery strip is folded 180 degrees behind the array through a thin bent interconnect zone, so it takes no footprint and sits ~20 um under its mats.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): footprint array efficiency rises toward ~90% with short vertical links, without wafer bonding or TSVs.

title: Roof shingles: inclined lateral capacitors overlap neighbor footprints
idea: Like overlapping roof shingles, each lateral capacitor in a 3D stack is built on a slant, climbing one tier over its length, so it extends beneath the next cell's footprint without colliding; the slant comes from an inclined sacrificial ramp cut by tilted ion-beam etch.
why: Doubles capacitor length per lateral pitch in 3D DRAM (facts 1-2), ~2x Cs without raising tier pitch.
note: Tilted etch inside buried lateral cavities is not practical.

title: Multilateral oil wells: six lateral cells branch from one hole
idea: Borrowed from multilateral drilling, where one vertical well feeds many horizontal laterals: each vertical bitline hole in a 3D stack is recessed in six directions per tier by a crystallographic wet etch, forming six lateral cells in a star around one vertical line.
why: Vertical holes per bit fall ~3x vs two-sided designs, ~2x 3D bit density per footprint (fact 2).

title: Duplex printing: DRAM arrays on both faces of one wafer
idea: Adapted from duplex printing and logic backside power delivery: build the array on the front, bond to a carrier, thin, and build a second array on the backside of the same silicon, sharing periphery through nano-TSVs in the middle.
why: Roughly doubles bits per wafer start while sharing substrate and periphery, ~1.6x lower cost per bit.

title: Antifouling-paint copper oxide and varistor zinc oxide form oxide SRAM
idea: Marine antifouling paint consumes Cu2O by the kiloton, and surge arresters use ZnO. Adapt p-type Cu2O and n-type ZnO thin-film transistors into a complementary BEOL latch: a static 4T/6T cell stacked in multiple tiers over logic.
why: Refresh-free bits with no capacitor and no indium, from abundant Cu and Zn oxides; multi-tier stacking recovers density. The risks are Cu2O hole mobility and off-current.

title: PCB laser direct imaging: maskless DUV for low-volume periphery layers
idea: PCB makers dropped phototools for DMD laser direct imaging; apply a 193/248 nm micromirror-array maskless writer to DRAM's relaxed periphery layers (40 nm and up) and HBM base-die redistribution layers, so custom memory variants need no new reticle set.
why: Mask capital and agility: a DRAM mask set costs $10-30M+; custom low-volume AI memory becomes nearly mask-free; the throughput penalty is tolerable on a few layers.
note: DMDs at 193/248 nm and 40 nm resolution are unproven; mirror damage and throughput.

title: Titanium-industry cold crucibles: quartz-free Czochralski silicon
idea: Titanium and multicrystalline-silicon casting melt the charge inside water-cooled segmented copper 'cold crucibles' where induction fields hold the melt off the wall; adapt a cold-crucible induction Czochralski puller to 300 mm DRAM ingots, metering oxygen through a controlled SiO feed to keep the interstitial oxygen needed for gettering.
why: High-purity quartz chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): eliminates quartz crucibles entirely with only Cu and Si, and lowers crucible-dissolution contamination.
note: 300 mm dislocation-free growth from a cold crucible is unproven.

title: Dairy fresh-processing: consume activations in-DRAM before they decay
idea: Borrowed from dairies that process milk within hours rather than store it: activations are written into refresh-free DRAM subarrays and consumed within microseconds by charge-sharing multiply-accumulate in the same subarray (processing-in-memory), so no datum ever has to outlive milliseconds.
why: Combines compute-in-memory with ephemerality: zero refresh power, 3-20 pJ/bit of host data movement avoided, and capacitors sized for microseconds rather than 64 ms.
note: Analog charge-sharing MAC precision is limited.

title: Self-clearing film-capacitor electrodes for thin high-k DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from metallized polymer film capacitors, whose ultra-thin electrode vaporizes around a breakdown spot so the part survives with negligibly less area: use a 2-3 nm top electrode of a low-melting conductive oxide so a local dielectric breakdown burns a sub-10-nm hole in the electrode, isolating the defect instead of shorting the cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): dielectric thickness is set by breakdown and leakage tails; tolerating pinholes could allow ~20-30% thinner high-k and proportionally higher Cs or lower aspect ratio without yield loss to shorted cells.

title: Civil Reserve Air Fleet adapted: retainer-paid U.S. reserve fab fleet
idea: Adapted from CRAF, where airlines get peacetime contracts in exchange for lending aircraft in crises: U.S. logic, NAND and foundry fabs are paid retainers to keep a qualified DRAM-compatible module flow (capacitor and buried-wordline recipes, spare tool kits) that they can activate within 90 days of a declared shortage.
why: Creates latent U.S. DRAM capacity without idle fabs and can surge ~5-10% of domestic need (U.S. manufacturability, supply resilience).

title: NEMS relay wordline drivers with zero off-leakage
idea: Ruthenium-contact nanoelectromechanical relays are built in BEOL at <=350 C with a sacrificial release and used as mat-select and wordline-driver switches: they pass 3 V natively, need no level shifters or stacked high-voltage transistors, and leak nothing when open.
why: Facts 7 and 10: wordline-driver area MINIFIED 2-3x and standby leakage to ~0, tungsten-free; contact wear and ~10 ns mechanical delay are the risks.

title: SiN photonic H-tree replaces the die's global data wires
idea: PECVD silicon-nitride waveguides (<=350 C), electro-optic polymer ring modulators (cured <=200 C) and sputtered polycrystalline Ge detectors form an optical global bus from banks to I/O, MAGNIFYING bandwidth per wire ~20x.
why: Fact 5: on-die global data-movement energy from ~1 pJ/bit to ~0.2 pJ/bit with far fewer global wires; low-temperature poly-Ge responsivity is the risk.
note: On-die mm-scale links rarely favor optics over wires.

title: Retrofit idle web presses into printed-memory lines
idea: Minify fab capex to ~$20M per line by converting idle US newspaper and packaging web presses into memory lines, adding laminar-flow tunnels around the web path and inline photonic/laser stations.
why: US manufacturability and capital: reuses US industrial plants and skilled press workforce; capacity added in months.

title: YBCO superconducting interposer lines at 77 K
idea: MINIFY line loss to near zero: pattern YBCO superconducting traces on a sapphire interposer, cool the package with liquid nitrogen, and let memory sit centimeters away with lossless, low-swing transmission.
why: Data-movement energy: link energy limited only by drivers (~0.05 pJ/bit); cold DRAM also cuts leakage and refresh.
note: Cryocooler wall-power overhead and driver-dominated link energy erase most of the gain.

title: Minify replacement unit: swappable foil-memory cartridges with wear telemetry
idea: Make oxide-TFT memory roll-to-roll on polyimide or steel foil and package it as cheap hot-swap cartridges. Each reports ECC-correction and retention telemetry and is swapped like an ink cartridge when it crosses a threshold, so cells only need a 2-3 year life.
why: Capital and cost: roll-to-roll lines cost a sliver of a fab; the business model takes per-cell lifetime requirements out of the spec.
note: Oxide-TFT foil memory unlikely to meet DRAM-class latency.

title: Eliminate per-column sense amps: charge-coupled shift readout to edge amplifier
idea: Under each row of storage nodes, run a buried-channel CCD register. On read, all cell charges of the row dump into the CCD and are clocked sideways (4-phase, ~1 GHz) to one floating-diffusion amplifier per 1,024 columns, which digitizes them in series. Restore uses reverse clocking.
why: Removes the SA stripes (-10-15% of die) for a bulk sequential tier. At 0.99999 transfer efficiency per stage, ~1% of the charge is lost over 1,024 stages, and a full row takes ~1 us, which suits weights and checkpoints but not random access.

title: Eliminate CMOS sense latches: resonant-tunneling-diode Goto pairs
idea: Two series resonant tunneling diodes (SiGe/Si or InGaAs, grown on the bonded periphery die) form a MOBILE/Goto-pair bistable whose midpoint ties to the bitline. When the shared clocked bias rises, the pair snaps in ~10 ps to the state set by the bitline imbalance, and the same NDR logic can do column muxing.
why: Replaces 4-6 MOSFETs with 2 RTDs (SA area -50%, sensing ~10x faster), attacking the periphery share (fact 7). Integrating RTDs and keeping their peak current uniform is hard.

title: Eliminate the voltage-mode latch: selective-epitaxy bipolar pre-amp in bitline contact
idea: Form a vertical n-p-n inside each bitline contact by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy (DCS/HCl with PH3/B2H6, avoiding BF2 implants), with the bitline driving the base. The charge-share signal becomes a collector current (beta ~50) into one shared current comparator per 16 bitlines, and a shared write driver restores the cells.
why: Cuts SA latch count 16x (die -8-10%) with ~2 ns sensing, and drops fluorinated BF2 implant species from the periphery.
note: Base current drains the femtocoulomb charge-share signal.

title: Eliminate the landing pad: oxide capacitor grown self-aligned on channel
idea: Delete the storage-node contact and landing-pad litho layer; grow a conductive perovskite oxide (e.g. SrRuO3 or LaNiO3) by selective-area epitaxy only on the exposed top of each vertical channel, so the capacitor bottom electrode self-registers to the transistor with zero overlay margin.
why: Litho-bound scaling: removes one critical (often EUV) layer and its overlay budget, enabling true 4F2 without pad-to-pillar misalignment; ~10-15% cost/bit.
note: Selective perovskite epitaxy on Si pillar tops needs buffers and high temperature.

title: Eliminate ingots and wire saws: kerfless seeded direct-solidified wafers
idea: Freeze 300 mm wafers directly from a silicon melt onto a cooled, seeded template that imposes single-crystal orientation, then high-temperature anneal to drive out dislocations; there is no ingot, no wire saw and no kerf.
why: Kerf wastes ~40% of polysilicon and ingot pulling is energy- and crucible-intensive; halves silicon and energy per wafer if defect density reaches DRAM grade.

title: Eliminate refresh and capacitors: complementary oxide-TFT static latch cell
