note: Anamartic wafer-scale memory shipped c.1989; 180 nm density makes cost per bit uncompetitive.

title: No EUV: fat DUV cells drop on-die ECC and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no EUV layers. Use relaxed-pitch DUV cells with ~2x capacitor volume and very low raw BER. On-die ECC (6.25%) is removed and the refresh interval stretched 4x, reclaiming area and bandwidth that partly offset the density loss.
why: Fact 4: removes 5-7 EUV layers from the bill. The reliability margin is spent to claw back ~10% of effective density and ~15% of bandwidth.
note: Density loss far exceeds reclaimed ECC/refresh margin.

title: Substitute self-forming manganese silicate barriers for tantalum liners
idea: Plate periphery copper on a Cu-Mn alloy seed; on anneal Mn segregates to the dielectric interface and forms a 1-2 nm MnSixOy barrier, eliminating PVD TaN/Ta liners.
why: Removes conflict-mineral tantalum and frees ~3-4 nm of each narrow wire for copper, lowering periphery wire resistance and energy per bit moved.
note: Well-studied Cu-Mn self-forming barrier for BEOL copper.

title: Ozone radical healing of oxygen vacancies in capacitor dielectric
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: after the ZrO2-based capacitor stack is deposited (zirconium from U.S. refiners), a low-temperature ozone/oxygen-radical anneal fills oxygen vacancies that form leakage paths through the thin dielectric in the worst pillars.
why: Cuts the capacitor contribution to the leakage tail and allows ~10% thinner dielectric (more Cs per pillar), attacking fact 1 with domestic chemistry.

title: Millipede revived: thermomechanical probes on recyclable Diels-Alder polymer
idea: Revive IBM's abandoned Millipede: arrays of heated silicon cantilever tips write nanometer pits into a thermally reversible Diels-Alder polymer film and read them through the tip's thermal resistance change. The tip arrays are i-line patterned at 50 um pitch while the bits are 10 nm.
why: Density below the lithography limit without EUV; the medium is cheap organic polymer with no metals; a dense nonvolatile capacity tier that offloads cold DRAM pages; claims 1 Tb/in2 at microsecond access.

title: Cu-Mn self-forming barriers replace TaN in array and bond metal
idea: Inverts 'copper wiring needs a Ta/TaN barrier.' Deposit a Cu-Mn alloy seed so Mn diffuses to the dielectric interface and forms a ~1-2 nm MnSixOy barrier on anneal, used for array bitlines, hybrid-bond pads and stack vias alike.
why: Ta (and Co liner) chokepoints removed; the thinner barrier leaves more Cu cross-section for ~20-30% lower line resistance at 20 nm.

title: Wet-activated hybrid bonding for HBM stacks without argon beams
idea: Molecular-scale surface engineering: activate copper and oxide bond pads with a dilute chemical bath and water-vapor plasma instead of the argon fast-atom beams used for surface-activated bonding, then bond at room temperature.
why: Stacking 8-16 HBM dies multiplies argon-intensive activation steps. Wet activation makes the HBM back end rare-gas-free and cheaper per stack.

title: Capacitive-bootstrap wordline drivers retire the global VPP pump
idea: Effect: capacitive bootstrapping. Each wordline driver self-boosts: its gate node floats as the wordline rises and a coupling capacitor kicks it to ~2.8 V, so VPP is created locally from the transition rather than by a 30-40%-efficient global charge pump; timing fits normal ACT and REF. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): refresh energy -20-30% and pump area freed.
note: Bootstrapped wordline drivers were standard in NMOS-era DRAM.

title: Boron-carbon hardmask replaces tungsten-doped carbon for deep etches
idea: Periodic-table walk, B (5): PECVD boron-rich carbon (30-60% B from B2H6 plus C3H6) gives B-C bonds whose etch resistance rivals W-doped carbon in high-aspect-ratio etches, and it strips in O2/Cl2.
why: Removes W from hardmasks for capacitor and contact etches; the U.S. is a top-two borate producer.
note: Boron-doped carbon hardmasks already commercial.

title: Bistable photonic-crystal nanocavity holding a bit as trapped light
idea: IFR: a bit that moves at light speed with no resistive loss. Closest achievable: an InP or Si photonic-crystal nanocavity with Kerr or carrier bistability holds high or low intracavity intensity under a shared bias beam (~tens of nW hold), written by fJ pulses and read on a waveguide bus.
why: Fact 5: data-movement energy falls because the bit already lives on the optical interconnect; ps switching.
note: NTT PhC nanocavity memories demonstrated; hold power and density restrict to buffers.

title: Ten-million-beam maskless e-beam wafer writer
idea: Magnify the beam count of multibeam mask writers by 100x to 10 million individually blanked beams on a MEMS aperture plate, with array rasters stored as one repeated tile, so DRAM layers are written maskless at ~50 wafers/hour.
why: EUV single-supplier risk and mask cost: removes EUV and multi-million-dollar mask sets; a US-buildable electron-optics tool chain.

title: Eliminate gate electrostatics: piezoelectric transduction switch as access device
idea: Replace the FET with a piezoelectronic transistor: a relaxor piezoelectric (PMN-PT) actuator squeezes a thin piezoresistive SmSe layer, driving an insulator-to-metal transition with 1e4-1e5 resistance change at ~0.1 V. The off state is a wide-gap insulator rather than a thermally populated channel.
why: Sub-0.2 V switching attacks the 1 V/3 V voltage floor (fact 10) and the insulating off state could cut leakage by orders of magnitude; materials integration risk is very high.

title: Eliminate the 12-die HBM stack: one monolithic 3D-tiered die
idea: Replace 12 thinned DRAM dies bonded with TSVs by one die with 48-96 monolithic array tiers over periphery, so there is a single grind, no TSV reveal CMP and no 11 repeated bond-surface preparations.
why: Water and HBM tax: backgrinding, TSV reveal CMP, bond prep cleans and dicing are repeated per die today; one die removes >90% of them and the TSV area tax.

title: Monolithic stack whose vertical bitlines replace HBM's TSV die stack
idea: Worse: build 12 separate DRAM dies, each losing area to TSV keep-out zones and microbumps, and stack them. Flip: fabricate one monolithic many-tier array whose vertical global bitlines run through the tiers as native interconnect, bonded once to a logic base die, so the 12-high TSV stack becomes one die and one bond.
why: Removes the ~3x area-per-bit HBM TSV tax and the 20-30% stack-yield loss (fact 6): one bond instead of twelve.

title: Twin resonant-tunneling diodes form a static bit at DRAM pitch
idea: Effect walk: resonant tunneling negative differential resistance. Two stacked double-barrier RTDs (Si/SiGe or GaN/AlN) in series form a Goto pair with two stable midpoint voltages; one access transistor writes the midpoint, and holding draws only the RTD valley current.
why: Static storage without refresh (fact 3) or capacitor (fact 1) in a vertical ~6-8F2 stack; feasible only if valley current density falls to ~1 A/cm2 (pA per cell), i.e. peak-to-valley ratio >10^4 at room temperature.

title: RF reflectometry reads bitlines through on-chip LC resonators
idea: Substitute DC charge-sharing readout with RF reflectometry, as used for qubit readout: each bitline is part of a spiral-inductor LC tank whose MOS-varactor tuning depends on the cell charge, and a frequency-multiplexed probe tone reads many bitlines on one line from phase shifts.
why: Periphery area: frequency multiplexing lets one RF readout chain serve dozens of bitlines, replacing pitch-matched latches.

title: Watch-escapement multi-detent nanomechanical ratchet bits
idea: Adapt the escapement and pawl: a released 15 nm beam rests in one of four van der Waals detents along a serrated sidewall, is stepped by electrostatic pulses and read capacitively, with five sealed released layers stacked.
why: 10x at same cost: 2 bits per element x 5 deposited-and-released tiers; mechanical state needs no refresh and has no dielectric wearout.

title: MKID frequency multiplexing reads hundreds of segments per line
idea: Borrowed from astronomy's microwave kinetic inductance detector readout: on low-loss fused silica, each bitline segment gets a thin-film LC resonator at its own frequency whose Q is loaded by the selected cell's state, and one feedline carrying a frequency comb reads ~100-500 segments at once.
why: Periphery: one wideband receiver per feedline replaces hundreds of sense amps and column muxes; glass's low loss tangent makes inductors practical where silicon substrates kill Q.
note: Room-temperature thin-film resonator Q too low for MKID-style multiplexing.

title: OTDR reflectometry reads a whole column from one pulse
idea: Borrowed from optical time-domain reflectometers: a glass-panel bitline is built as a low-loss transmission line, each cell's state switches a small shunt impedance, and a ~20 ps pulse launched from one end returns reflections whose timing gives cell position and whose amplitude gives state.
why: Periphery: one fast receiver reads hundreds of cells per pulse instead of hundreds of sense amps; only practical on low-loss glass with centimeter lines.
note: fF cell shunts give tiny reflections at 20 ps; this is not practical.

title: Field-emission display tips become vacuum-channel sense amplifiers
idea: Borrowed from field-emission displays' nanogap emitters on glass: nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (sub-100 nm gaps, which work in air below the electron mean free path) serve as sense-amp input pairs whose transconductance does not depend on substrate crystal quality.
why: Gives glass substrates fast, high-gain sensing despite poor thin-film mobility, and is radiation-hard; a speculative path to periphery without silicon.
note: Field emission needs high fields; such voltages and emitter variability rule out sense amps.

title: Zipper teeth: capacitor meshes together at the hybrid-bond interface
idea: Like interlocking zipper teeth, each of two bonded wafers carries half of an interdigitated fin capacitor (storage-node fins on the transistor wafer, plate fins on the top wafer), both pre-coated with high-k; hybrid bonding meshes them into a capacitor of double height with no single high-AR etch.
why: Splits the 60-75:1 pillar etch (fact 1) into two ~35:1 etches; ~2x electrode area at equal etch difficulty, ~5-8 fF at relaxed aspect ratio.
note: Interdigitating per-cell fins needs ~10 nm bond overlay, far beyond wafer bonding capability.

title: Phased-array radar timing: colliding pulses select the wordline segment
idea: Borrowed from radar/ultrasound beam steering: a long tier wordline is driven as a transmission line from both ends with two sub-threshold pulses timed to superpose above threshold only at the target segment, selecting it without any per-segment decoder.
why: Deletes local wordline decoders and drivers in 3D stacks (fact 7, periphery ~49%), periphery area ~-30%; requires ps-level timing control.
note: Wordlines are RC-dominated, not transmission lines; pulses disperse.

title: Cable TV frequency multiplexing reads eight tiers on one line
idea: Borrowed from FDM in cable TV: each tier's cell group couples to a shared vertical line through an on-tier LC or ring resonator with a distinct frequency; a multi-tone read pulse interrogates 8 tiers at once and the sense chain separates them by frequency.
why: Cuts vertical bitlines and sense amps per footprint ~8x in 3D stacks (fact 7); signal levels are the open risk.
note: On-tier LC resonators impossible at cell scale; fC signals cannot be read by resonant coupling.

title: Eliminate electrical wordlines: optically gated photo-TFT access
idea: Replace metal wordlines and their 3 V drivers with a row-scanning micro-LED or waveguide grating that illuminates one row of photoconductive oxide-semiconductor access switches; dark switches have very low leakage, while lit ones conduct.
why: Voltage floor: the ~3 V wordline swing and its CV2 energy disappear, and row hammer from wordline coupling vanishes; switching speed is the open risk.

title: Eight-segment self-clearing capacitor survives dielectric defects at thinner EOT
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation + #25 Self-service: split each cell's capacitor into 8 parallel sub-capacitors, each tied in by a ~2-nm top-electrode neck that vaporizes like a metallized-film capacitor's self-clearing spot when a defect shorts it, so the cell keeps 7/8 of its charge instead of dying.
why: Fact 1 and yield: EOT can shrink 20-30% (Cs +25-40%) because tail defects no longer kill cells; fewer redundant rows needed.
note: Eight sub-capacitors with 2 nm fusible necks inside one cell is unfabricable; tail is soft leakage.

title: Copying: optical readout of stacked electro-optic charge films
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying replaces per-bit silicon sensing with an optical copy: bits are charge in a transistor-free photoconductor/electro-optic film stack (like optically addressed light modulators), written by a micro-LED projector and read by a CMOS image sensor that selects one of 32 films through wavelength-selective layers; refresh is re-projecting the captured image.
why: 100x path: the storage films cost cents per m2 and one image sensor plus micro-LED array serves 32 films and millions of bits per frame; trade-offs: 1-10 us frame latency, optical volume, ms retention requiring constant re-copy, and interlayer crosstalk. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Flying-spot optical wordline addressing replaces drivers and pumps
idea: Modernize the Williams-tube flying-spot scanner. A backside micro-LED or waveguide-grating array lights one row of photogated access-transistor gate lines, and a stacked photovoltaic diode string on each subarray gate line supplies the gate overdrive, replacing the VPP pump. The CMOS row decoder becomes a light-source driver on a separate cheap die.
why: Removes row decoders, sub-wordline drivers and VPP charge pumps (a large part of the 49% periphery, fact 7) and takes the 3 V wordline off the logic node (fact 10).
note: Diffraction cannot select ~40 nm-pitch rows; PV diode currents too slow for ns wordlines.

title: MEMS micro-drum with a thousand heads and unpatterned media
idea: Revive the 1950s magnetic drum as a 2 mm MEMS rotor on an electrostatic or gas bearing spinning at ~1M rpm, coated with continuous perpendicular magnetic media and served by 1,000 fixed thin-film heads around its rim, so a wanted bit arrives within ~60 ns. Bits are defined by head field, so the media needs no lithography at all.
why: Capital and litho (Fact 4): heads come from mature HDD-head wafer fabs (~100 nm rules) and the rotor from 1 um MEMS lines; at ~1 Tb/in2 media density a 3 mm2 face holds ~5 Gb; risks are bearing wear, shock and rotational latency.
note: 1M rpm rotor with nm head spacing and 1000 heads; wear, shock and capacity per device doubtful.

title: AM radio dial: frequency-multiplexed resonator readout of 64 bitlines
idea: Like superconducting-qubit dispersive readout or an AM dial, give each of 64 bitlines a tiny BEOL LC resonator at its own frequency, all coupled to one feedline; the post-charge-sharing bitline voltage tunes a varactor and shifts its resonance by a few MHz. One broadband comb probe plus a digital channelizer reads all 64 at once, and a minimal pass-gate driver writes the decoded value back.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): replaces 64 full latch sense amps with one wideband receiver plus 64 write-back switches, potentially 3-5x less SA-strip area if resonators fit in upper metal over the array.
note: Room-temp on-chip LC Q too low to resolve MHz shifts; resonators far larger than bitline pitch.

title: Pin-art toy: alignment-free bonding onto an unpatterned nano-capacitor forest
idea: Like a pin-art toy taking any shape, make a separate capacitor wafer as an unpatterned forest of isolated 8 nm-pitch nanopillar capacitors (separate bottom electrodes, common top plate), then hybrid-bond it to the transistor wafer. Each ~20 nm landing pad touches 4-6 pillars in parallel while pillars over the gaps touch nothing, so the capacitor needs no mask and zero overlay to the cells.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and litho capital (fact 4): the critical capacitor-hole EUV layer disappears and capacitors come from a cheap separate fab; claim -1 to -2 EUV layers and ~10% lower wafer cost.
note: 8 nm-pitch pillars cannot hold electrodes plus dielectric, and 20 nm bond pads are far beyond hybrid bonding.

title: Time-domain reflectometry reads a whole gain-cell column in one pulse
idea: Box: 2T gain cell (storage node gates read FET) x read-FET loading x TDR echo sensing x controlled-impedance transmission-line bitline x Si x standard BEOL. With all read wordlines of a column enabled, each '1' cell's conducting read FET adds a shunt load at a known position, so one picosecond pulse's echo profile encodes every bit in the column by time of flight.
why: One TDR receiver per column instead of per-segment SAs; 256+ bits per pulse cuts sense energy and periphery count.

title: Light-addressed wordlines with photoconductive access devices
idea: Box: stacked cap x photoconductive access (a-Si:H or MoS2) x electrical SA x bonded photonic layer x Si plus SiN waveguides x photonic foundry. Each row's access devices sit under a waveguide; a light pulse routed by an on-chip optical switch tree turns the row on, so no row decoders, 3 V wordline drivers or VPP pumps are needed, and dark access devices barely leak.
why: Periphery: row decode/drive area and wordline CV^2 energy removed; row hammer gone because there is no wordline coupling.

title: Wavelength-addressed optical wordlines open single row segments
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: Ge photo-FET | sense: standard | integration: SiN waveguide wordlines with ring filters | substrate: SOI | fab: DUV]. Each row is opened by light: a waveguide over the row carries several wavelengths and ring filters steer each wavelength to one 64-bit segment of photo-gated access devices, so there is no high-voltage wordline swing and no capacitive wordline-to-wordline coupling.
why: Constraint: removes ~3 V wordline CV^2 and pump loss and fetches only one segment, ~10x per useful bit; Fact 9: kills the wordline-coupling component of row hammer.
note: Micron-scale ring filters cannot address 64-bit segments at DRAM row pitch.

title: Optical waveguide wordlines with photoconductive access devices
idea: Po: rows are opened by light. Replace metal wordlines with SiN waveguides over each row and use wide-bandgap photoconductors (ZnO or Ga2O3) as access devices that conduct only under a UV row pulse; transparent oxide tiers let one pulse address a vertical column of tiers.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): removes wordline CV2 (~30% of activation energy) and 3 V drivers; dark photoconductor leakage can be sub-fA.
note: Waveguide pitch far above cell pitch; ZnO/Ga2O3 photoconductors are slow with persistent photoconductivity.

title: Waste-heat Seebeck read: cells report state with no applied bias
idea: Effect walk: Seebeck effect. A phase-state cell whose two states have very different thermopower (insulator ~400 uV/K vs metal ~10 uV/K, e.g. a correlated oxide) spans the natural 1-5 K vertical gradient of the BEOL stack; selecting it connects it to a high-impedance sense gate that sees ~1 mV vs ~10 uV of thermovoltage, so the read is powered by waste heat.
why: The read draws no charge from the supply, only the select and low-swing sense gate are charged, cutting read energy ~10x and avoiding destructive read (fact 8); gradient uniformity and mV-level sensing noise are the risks.

title: Light-addressed photoconductive access through silicon-nitride waveguide wordlines
idea: Effect: photoconductivity. A PECVD SiN waveguide grid (300 C) replaces metal wordlines, and each cell's access device is a microcrystalline-Si photoconductor (PECVD 250 C). A laser pulse into one row's waveguide turns its photoconductors on (on/off ~1e5) while dark cells isolate their storage nodes.
why: Tungsten wordlines, wordline-driver periphery (fact 7) and row hammer (fact 9, since there is no electrical wordline coupling); all layers are BEOL-compatible.
note: Waveguide pitch cannot reach DRAM cell pitch and 1e5 on/off is far too leaky for retention.

title: Li: lithium-ion drift trims threshold of weak access transistors
idea: Embed a LiPON-sealed Li+ pocket in the access-transistor spacer; after wafer-level retention test, a high-field program step drives Li+ away from the channel only on the weakest-leakage transistors, raising their effective Vt ~100 mV, then a low-temperature freeze locks the ions in place.
why: Fixes the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) cell by cell instead of guard-banding the whole array; could move tail-limited refresh from 32 ms toward 128 ms.
note: Mobile alkali ions are a classic MOS contaminant; stability over 10 years unlikely.

title: A battery per bit: LiPON nano-cell stores the bit as voltage
idea: Swap stored charge for stored chemistry: each 180 nm-patterned cell is a ~50 nm-thick LiCoO2/LiPON/Si thin-film battery (LiPON: Oak Ridge, 1992) whose state of charge is the bit, read non-destructively as open-circuit voltage by a high-impedance FET; self-discharge, not junction leakage, sets retention.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3,8): months of retention, no charge sharing, multilevel via voltage plateaus; risks are Li diffusion speed for ~100 ns writes and intercalation endurance.
note: Li intercalation is too slow for 100 ns writes and endures only ~1e4 cycles.

title: Venus-flytrap bistable nanoshells: refresh-free mechanical bits, nanoimprinted
idea: The flytrap snaps between two stable curvatures using little energy. Nanoimprint arrays of 200 nm pre-stressed metallic-glass domes roll-to-roll on foil that snap between two stable states under a gate pulse; the state is read capacitively and holds with zero leakage.
why: No charge leakage means no refresh (16-33% of idle power) and no storage capacitor; NEMS at this scale can switch in ~10-100 ns, but fatigue endurance is the open risk.
note: Same bistable-mechanical idea as I-06198; roll-to-roll 200 nm domes on foil is implausible for memory.

title: Mitotic-spindle field assembly places pre-grown nanowire access transistors
idea: The spindle lines chromosomes up at the metaphase plate with fibers and forces; grow single-crystal Si or oxide-semiconductor nanowire transistors in bulk off-wafer, suspend them in a dielectric fluid and use AC electrode arrays to pull one into each cell site by dielectrophoresis, then bond and contact them.
why: Takes transistor making off the array wafer, removing ~10 front-end masks and high-temperature steps and letting arrays be built on cheap substrates; est. 30% fewer wafer process steps.
note: Placing billions of nanowires per die by dielectrophoresis at near-100% yield needs a miracle.

title: Chain DRAM: Toshiba's chain-FeRAM topology with linear capacitors
idea: Failure mined: Toshiba's chain FeRAM (each capacitor in parallel with its transistor, 16 in series) died with Toshiba's FeRAM exit and its plate-pulse complexity. Fix: build the chain with ordinary DRAM linear capacitors. To read cell k, turn off only its transistor so its capacitor sits in series between the chain and the bitline; one bitline contact serves 16 cells and no plate pulsing is needed.
why: 16x fewer bitline contacts cut bitline capacitance ~40%, which raises the signal. Bitlines can then be 1.5-2x longer with proportionally fewer sense amps, and the cell gets denser without contacts.
note: Linear capacitors shunted by ON parallel transistors lose their charge; chain topology relies on ferroelectric remanence.

title: Resonant-capacitance read of varactor cells, after RCA's CED stylus
idea: Failure mined: RCA's Capacitance Electronic Disc read its signal as capacitance shifts in a 915 MHz resonant circuit, but its contact stylus wore out. Fix without contact: the storage node is the gate of a MOS varactor, and the cell is read by the resonant-frequency shift of a short bitline LC tank at a few GHz. The read draws no charge from the node, so no restore is needed.
why: Destructive read and restore (fact 8): removes write-back energy, so the same row can be re-read at ~1/3 the energy, and row-hammer exposure falls because reads stop disturbing neighbors.
note: GHz LC tank per bitline is area-prohibitive.

title: Heat-shrink film: relaxed-pitch mask halves pitch on release
idea: Like heat-shrink tubing, print the array at 2x pitch with the single added DUV mask onto a biaxially pre-strained polymer membrane on a carrier, release the strain so features shrink ~50% isotropically, then laminate the shrunken membrane onto the wafer as the etch hardmask.
why: Fact 4: relaxed-pitch printing on a cheap immersion mask replaces EUV or SAQP for one array layer; shrink uniformity across mats is the risk.
note: Laminating a shrunken membrane hardmask with array overlay is implausible.

title: Substitute new EUV scanners with refurbished DUV fleets and SAQP
idea: Swap buying EUV for a U.S. refurbishment corridor that buys retired 193i immersion scanners from upgraded fabs, rebuilds them, and runs an all-DUV self-aligned quadruple-patterning 1y-nm DRAM flow.
why: Bypasses the single EUV supplier and its lead times; refurbished DUV costs ~1/10 of EUV per tool, trading a ~10-15% cost-per-bit penalty for a fab online in ~2 years.

title: Tardigrade revival of mothballed fabs for legacy DDR3/DDR4
idea: Tardigrades dry into dormant 'tuns' and revive decades later. Shuttered 200/300 mm DRAM lines and secondary-market tools are re-hydrated to make legacy DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 for industrial, auto and IoT customers that incumbents are abandoning.
why: Frees leading fabs for HBM/DDR5; fully depreciated lines remove the ~55% depreciation share of wafer cost.

title: Woodworking glueless joinery: solder-free hybrid bonding for HBM stacks
idea: Fine joinery such as dovetails holds without nails or glue. Replace HBM's SnAg microbumps and molded underfill with direct Cu-Cu/SiCN hybrid bonds between core dies, keeping the standard HBM3E/HBM4 base-die PHY and JEDEC footprint.
why: Removes tin, silver and underfill polymer per stack, thins each layer so 16-high fits the same height, and improves heat removal ~20-30%, easing the HBM TSV tax (fact 6).

title: EUV-free 1y-class DRAM micro-fab built from refurbished immersion scanners
idea: Derive the cost floor from tool $ per patterned layer: a 6F^2 cell at F~17 nm needs only 193i SAQP, and a refurbished immersion scanner costs ~1/8 of an EUV tool. Build a 10k-wafer/month U.S. line on second-hand 193i, etch and ALD tools running a frozen ~17 nm process, accepting ~50% of leading density at ~25% of capex per wafer start.
why: Capital intensity, EUV chokepoint and U.S. manufacturability: roughly 2x bits per capex dollar versus a leading-edge greenfield, and a 2-3 year ramp with no single-supplier tool.

title: Refurbished ArF immersion scanners with SAQP for EUV-free DRAM
idea: Box[Fab=secondhand ArFi scanners + self-aligned quadruple patterning x Owner=new-entrant fab x Finance=used-tool leasing]: patterning 1a-class DRAM with refurbished ArFi tools and SAQP instead of EUV lets entrants make DDR5-compliant parts without a single-supplier EUV tool.
why: Capital and chokepoint: avoids EUV single-supplier dependence and cuts litho capex ~50-70% at some cost in steps.

title: Solar bypass diodes: segment switches replace column redundancy
idea: Adapted from photovoltaic panels, whose bypass diodes route current around a shaded or failed string instead of losing the panel: each bitline is split into 4 segments joined by small pass switches; a segment with a defect (short, leaky cluster) is opened and its cells skipped via a decoder offset, so only a quarter-column is lost instead of swapping in a full redundant column.
why: Periphery and repair area (fact 7): spare columns plus fuses and muxes cost several percent of area; segment bypass trades ~1-2% switch overhead for removing most column redundancy and lets arrays ship with more local defects.

title: Twin landing-pad contacts survive stochastic misses from PFAS-free resists
idea: Rearrange each storage-node contact from one landing pad into two half-size pads in parallel: tin-oxo metal-oxide EUV resists without fluorinated photo-acid generators print more stochastic missing contacts, but a cell now fails only if both pads miss, squaring the defect rate.
why: Contact stochastic failure falls from ~1e-7 to ~1e-14 per cell, allowing PFAS-free resists without yield loss for a few % area.
note: Half-size pads miss more often stochastically, so the squaring argument is optimistic.

title: Architectural-glass rotary magnetrons cut sputter-target metal waste
idea: Architectural glass coaters use rotating cylindrical targets that erode evenly to ~80-90% utilization versus ~30-40% for planar racetrack targets. Adapt dual rotary-cathode PVD with a scanning 300 mm pedestal for W/Mo, Ti/TiN and Ta liners and re-spray spent tubes; the film stacks are identical, so DDR/HBM dies are unchanged.
why: Cuts purchased tungsten, tantalum and titanium per wafer by roughly half with identical films, and fewer target swaps raise tool uptime.

title: Minimal-fab half-inch wafers with maskless writing for defense memory
idea: Box[Fab=12.5 mm wafer minimal-fab tool modules x Lithography=maskless direct-write x Medium=oxide gain cell chiplets x Owner=DoD x Finance=program funding x Scale=micro-fab]: build a <$50M micro-line that makes small lots of trusted memory chiplets for weapons and space systems, removing low-volume trusted demand from the commodity market.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: ~1000x lower capex for trusted low-volume memory; frees allocation fights over legacy DRAM.
note: Minimal Fab exists in Japan; trusted low-volume niche only.

title: Po no fab owns a whole chip: relay-fab consortium of 200mm sites
idea: Po: 'no fab makes a whole chip.' Extracted: split the 180 nm DRAM flow into modules (front-end transistors, capacitor module, metallization, test) assigned to under-used U.S. 200 mm analog and MEMS fabs, moving wafers between them in sealed carriers under a shared copy-exact spec and a pooled tooling fund.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: uses existing idle capacity instead of a $15B greenfield fab, with time to first supply measured in months.

title: Al-strapped TiN wordlines with per-row variable latency
idea: Worse: keep tungsten (China ~80%) buried wordlines because cheaper conductors are too resistive. Flip: build buried wordlines from TiN plus heavily doped Si, strapped every 256 cells with Al lines, and let the controller use per-row measured tRCD/tRAS so the few slow far-end rows get extra cycles instead of forcing global worst-case timing.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: removes W from the array while keeping average latency within ~5% via variable-latency timing.

title: Cobalt-free Fe/MgO junctions store a field-updatable repair map
idea: Worse: rely on one-shot laser or e-fuse repair, so cells that weaken after shipment can never be fixed. Flip: put a small array of Fe/MgO/Fe magnetic tunnel junctions (no Co, Ta or Ru) on-die as rewritable repair memory; their lower TMR is acceptable with write-verify and redundancy, and spares can be reassigned in the field indefinitely.
why: Self-healing and yield: in-field repair cuts returns and lets makers ship with tighter spare budgets, avoiding the Co/Ru/Ta that standard MRAM needs.

title: Rotating cylindrical tungsten and titanium targets triple sputter utilization
idea: Scale transfer from display-glass coaters to wafer tools: planar PVD targets erode in a racetrack groove and are scrapped at ~25-35% use. A compact rotary cylindrical magnetron adapted to 300 mm chambers erodes the target evenly to ~80%.
why: ~2.5x less tungsten, titanium and target-bonding material per wafer, plus fewer target-change downtimes.

title: Argon-free vacuum Czochralski with cold-trap SiO capture
idea: Shift the puller's gas regime from argon sweep to molecular flow: grow 300 mm ingots under high vacuum, or in a hydrogen/nitrogen ambient, using large cryo-pumped cold traps and a redesigned heat shield to remove SiO vapor.
why: Crystal growth is a large argon consumer. Ingot supply becomes rare-gas-independent, and crucible life may improve because SiO is removed faster.

title: Lumber-grade radial zones: extra redundancy designed into wafer-edge fields
idea: Sawmills grade heartwood and sapwood differently; when helium backside cooling is replaced by electrostatic chucks with hydrogen or conductive-elastomer contact, accept wider centre-to-edge CD drift and print two reticle designs, full-density centre fields and edge-ring fields with 2x spare rows/columns and stronger on-die ECC.
why: Makes helium-free thermal control yield-neutral by spending redundancy only where non-uniformity lives, keeping ~90-95% of the wafer at full density.

title: Convert U.S. packaging and label printing lines to memory-offload films
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a contract-manufacturing program uses the large U.S. base of flexo/gravure packaging, label and thin-film PV coating lines, which already run kilometers of film at 10-50 um registration, to make the offload films in this cell: holographic ROM, sensor masks, e-paper, RFID logbooks and waveguide harnesses.
why: The U.S. makes ~1-2% of DRAM but has a large roll-to-roll converting industry; offload films reduce DRAM demand with domestic capacity in months, not 3-5-year fabs.
note: Vague link from converting lines to DRAM demand reduction.

title: Flowable oxide fills and self-planarizes, ending ceria STI polish
idea: Combine trench fill and planarization (zero masks): flowable-CVD silazane oxide fills STI and levels like a liquid, then a timed dry etch-back endpointed on the pad nitride replaces the ceria CMP and post-CMP clean.
why: Removes rare-earth ceria slurry and hundreds of liters of UPW per wafer for CMP/cleans; flowable fill also voids less in 10 nm array trenches.

title: H2-bake and ozonated-water clean cluster replacing HF dips
idea: Fuse an epi-style in-situ H2 bake (800-850 °C, desorbing native oxide) with ozonated-UPW plus dilute-HCl megasonic cleaning in one vacuum-linked cluster, so wafers never see HF before gate oxide or contact formation.
why: Removes HF, the most common fluorinated fab chemical, along with CaF2 sludge treatment. It simplifies the waste plant and permitting.
note: High-temperature H2 bake conflicts with thermal budget at contact steps.

title: Squeeze casting: high-pressure forced aluminum fill replacing tungsten plugs
idea: Die casting pushes molten metal into fine cavities with pressure; replace CVD tungsten contacts and landing pads with PVD aluminum forced into TiN-lined openings by a 60-100 MPa argon anneal at 400-450 C, run in batch hot-isostatic-press chambers adapted from aerospace castings.
why: W-free metallization (constraint) and RC: removes WF6 CVD and W targets; Al ~3 uOhm-cm versus 10-20 for narrow W lowers contact resistance and allows smaller contacts; batch HIP is cheap per wafer.

title: Case hardening: fully silicided poly buried wordlines without tungsten
idea: Steel case hardening converts a surface in place by diffusion rather than depositing a coating; fill buried-wordline trenches void-free with doped poly-Si, then convert the upper part fully to NiSi or C54 TiSi2 by metal deposition and anneal, keeping a thin poly region near the drain for low GIDL.
why: W-free (constraint) with fewer steps (fact 4): poly fills sub-10 nm trenches without seams, needs no WF6 or nucleation barrier, and silicide reaches ~15 uOhm-cm, competitive with scaled W.

title: Building expansion joints: compliant spring microbumps for HBM stacks
idea: Adapted from expansion joints that let bridges and buildings move with temperature without cracking: replace rigid microbumps in HBM stacks with helical or serpentine copper micro-springs electroplated in a sacrificial resist mold, absorbing CTE mismatch and warpage during bonding and thermal cycling so TSVs and bumps do not crack.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): much of the 20-30% stack yield loss and early-life failure comes from bonding stress and warpage; compliant joints could recover ~5-10 points of stack yield and allow thinner dies.

title: Rotatable cylindrical targets and shield reclaim triple metal yield
idea: Magnify sputter-target utilization from ~30% to ~85%: move Ti, Mo, W and Ta PVD to rotating cylindrical cathodes, and recover metal from chamber shields by acid stripping and re-casting into new targets.
why: Cuts sputter-metal demand ~2.5x, including tantalum (a conflict mineral) and tungsten.

title: Magnify grain size so each LTPS access transistor sits in one grain
idea: Use sequential lateral solidification or seeded laser crystallization on glass to grow polysilicon grains longer than each access or periphery transistor, so no channel contains a grain boundary, the main source of LTPS leakage and Vt spread.
why: Facts 3 and 7: tightens LTPS leakage tails by about an order of magnitude, making glass-based periphery and access devices reliable.

title: Eliminate spare rows, columns and fuses: DDR5 on-die ECC absorbs defects
idea: Remove most row/column redundancy and fuse banks; single-cell hard faults stay in place for the existing DDR5 on-die SEC ECC and Error-Check-and-Scrub to correct, with a small spare pool kept only for cluster faults. The DDR5 interface and its ECS reporting are unchanged.
why: Frees ~3-5% of die area and removes fuse-programming test time, a few percent more bits per wafer at no tool cost.

title: NMOS-only sub-wordline drivers bootstrapped by cell capacitors
idea: Rearrange the sub-wordline driver: drop the PMOS and its N-well spacing and revive 1970s NMOS bootstrap drivers, using array-process cylinder capacitors as bootstrap capacitors so wordlines still reach ~3 V. Zero added masks: it is a layout change.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7): sub-wordline driver stripes shrink ~30-40% (well spacing dominates them), giving roughly 3-5% more bits per die.
note: 3-5% bits; NMOS bootstrap drivers are old art with speed and standby trade-offs.

title: Self-silicided titanium bitlines with column erasure coding
idea: Replace tungsten bitlines with TiSi2 formed in place from the bitline polysilicon (the conductor made from the material already there), accept the ~1% open/high-resistance columns from narrow-line agglomeration, and treat them as column erasures in the page code.
why: Removes W and WF6 from the bitline using abundant Ti; erasure decoding costs far less parity than random errors.

title: Ruthenium electrodes reclaimed as volatile RuO4 into ALD precursor
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: specify Ru electrodes (which template rutile TiO2 with k~80-100) and design the recycling route in from day one. Ozone-treat shredded dies at ~100 C so Ru leaves as volatile RuO4, trap it in a cold scrubber and convert it directly back to Ru ALD precursor, closing the loop for a metal mined at only ~30 t/yr.
why: Fact 1 via high-k rutile, without the supply risk of a South-Africa-concentrated metal; near-total Ru recovery.

title: Refrigerant HFO transition applied to high-aspect-ratio etch chemistry
idea: Air conditioning moved from high-GWP HFCs to short-lived hydrofluoroolefins (HFO-1234ze/yf). Requalify capacitor-hole and contact etches on unsaturated fluorocarbons (C4F6 isomers, HFO-1234ze, CF3I) whose C=C bonds deposit sidewall polymer at lower flow, combined with point-of-use plasma abatement.
why: Cuts the GWP of etch emissions >90% and pre-empts PFAS/F-gas restrictions that could choke C4F8/CF4 supply, while keeping HAR selectivity for 60-75:1 pillars.

title: Sail-reefing mode: elastic conversion to twin-cell under thermal stress
idea: Sailors reef sails when the wind is high. When die temperature exceeds 85 C or the error rate climbs, the OS can switch selected subarrays from 1T1C to 2T2C twin-cell mode: complementary data in paired cells with differential sensing. That halves capacity but doubles the signal and stretches retention about 4x. Memory hot-unplug absorbs the lost capacity.
why: This avoids the 2x refresh penalty at high temperature (fact 3) and lets nominal cells be built weaker, because they have a safe fallback mode.

title: EDSAC-style delay loops rebuilt as WDM light on photonics foundries
idea: Recirculate bits as light in low-loss SiN spiral loops on existing 45/90-nm silicon-photonics foundry lines (such as AIM Photonics), with 32 WDM channels at 50 Gb/s and an SOA plus clock-recovery regenerator per loop.
why: 1.6 Tb/s x 20 ns loop holds 32 kb with <=20 ns latency: DRAM-class access, no cells, and optical I/O straight to accelerators (Fact 5); energy per regeneration pass is the risk.
note: Meters of waveguide per 32 kb: hopeless density and regeneration power.

title: Plate-pulse charge boost during restore adds hot retention
idea: During restore, pulse the accessed mat's cell plate down by DeltaV, then release after the wordline closes: the storage node, now isolated, rises by ~DeltaV x Cs/(Cs+Cj), storing ~25% more charge without raising bitline voltage.
why: ~25% more charge = longer retention at 125 C or smaller Cs at equal retention (facts 1, 3).

title: Ceria-free, slurry-free planarization by photo-cured resin etch-back
idea: Box [any cell | any access | any sense | any | Si | spin-on self-leveling resin + UV-ozone conversion + uniform dry etch-back]: replace CeO2-slurry oxide CMP steps (STI, capacitor top, ILD) with a self-leveling photo-curable siloxane resin that is converted to SiO2 by UV-ozone and etched back 1:1 to the stop layer.
why: Cerium (rare earth, China-dominated refining) and water: removes 6-10 CMP steps per DRAM flow, together with their slurry waste and a large share of rinse UPW.

title: Roll-to-roll high-k decoupling film laminated onto the die
idea: Worse: fill periphery with MOS decoupling capacitors to keep supply noise down. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-coated thin-film decoupling sheet, such as a BaTiO3-polymer nanocomposite between foil electrodes, onto the die top or package through a printed bump array.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): on-die decap is several percent of die; moving it to a laminate frees area and adds lower-inductance bulk capacitance.

title: Printed passive equalizer networks replace on-die CTLE and FFE
idea: Worse: keep growing active equalizers and DFE taps inside every DRAM I/O. Flip: print resistor-capacitor-inductor equalization networks (gravure-printed thin-film R and C, printed spiral L) on the package or module flex at each lane to pre-shape the channel passively.
why: Periphery area and I/O power: removes ~10-20% of PHY power and area.

title: 2050 faith in codes: double-length bitlines guarded by on-die ECC
idea: A 2050 engineer accepts noisy sensing and corrects it. Double bitline length to 1024-2048 cells per sense amp, accept a raw sense error rate near 1e-6, and absorb it with DDR5's mandatory on-die ECC widened internally to longer codewords; the host still sees standard DDR5.
why: Halves bitline sense-amp stripes (~8-10% die area, fact 7) with an interface-transparent fix.

title: Jeweler's bench-sweep recovery for sputter targets and chamber shields
idea: Jewelers recover gold dust from bench sweeps, while fabs scrap sputter targets at ~30-40% utilization and bead-blast metal off chamber shields into waste. Move to rotating cylindrical targets (>80% utilization) and send shield and target residues to closed-loop hydrometallurgy that recovers Ti, Ta, Co and W, with chain of custody back to the target makers.
why: Cuts virgin tantalum (conflict mineral), tungsten and cobalt per wafer ~2x.

title: Space-SOI-inspired patterned oxygen implant replaces trench isolation
idea: Extreme user: radiation-hard space chips built on SIMOX silicon-on-insulator. Form cell isolation by masked high-dose O+ implantation and anneal, growing buried and lateral oxide islands in place of STI etch, oxide fill, CMP and HF deglaze.
why: Process/PFAS: removes ~8-10 steps of the STI module and every HF touch on it; also gives buried oxide that cuts junction leakage.

title: Adaptive twin-cell fusion of weak row pairs as cells age
idea: Time shift (static 1T1C -> on-the-fly 2T2C): when a row pair shows weak retention, the controller reconfigures them into a differential twin-cell pair (true and complement stored), halving that pair's capacity but doubling signal and cancelling common-mode leakage.
why: Rescues the weakest ~0.1-1% of rows at 2x local cost instead of discarding the die; a graceful-degradation path for aging.

title: N: silicon-nitride waveguide loop recirculates bits as light
idea: Hold 64 WDM channels x 100 Gb/s in a ~1.5 m spiral of ultralow-loss Si3N4 waveguide (~10 ns round trip, ~64 kbit per loop), regenerated by an on-chip amplifier every pass, so any bit is reachable from a loop tap within ~5 ns on average.
why: Sits beside co-packaged optical I/O of AI accelerators and avoids electrical data movement (fact 5) with only Si and N and no capacitor; density per mm² is low, so it fits as a bandwidth tier.
note: ~64 kbit per 1.5 m spiral; density and amplifier power make it a niche buffer.

title: Vapor-deposited zinc-imidazolate framework as a dry photoresist
idea: Periodic-table walk, Zn (30): grow ZIF-8-type zinc 2-methylimidazolate films by CVD/ALD; EUV or e-beam exposure changes linker bonding so films develop in vapor or non-fluorinated solvent, with no PFAS photoacid generator, no fluorinated surfactant and no spin-coat waste.
why: PFAS-free patterning; Zn has high EUV absorption (lower dose); eliminates the ~95% of spin-coated resist that is discarded.

title: Dairy-grade plumbing: electropolished stainless and polyolefins replace fluoropolymers
idea: Dairies and breweries run clean-in-place 316L electropolished stainless with passivated chromium-oxide skins; rebuild fab solvent, gas and ultrapure-water distribution from electropolished, ozone-passivated stainless and reserve high-purity polypropylene and polyethylene for acids, removing PFA and PVDF wetted parts.
why: Fluoropolymer piping, valves and tanks are the bulk of a fab's PFAS inventory and a supply risk as PFAS rules tighten; stainless and polyolefins are abundant, domestic and recyclable.

title: Manganese-for-nickel stainless playbook: lanthanum replaces hafnium high-k
idea: Steelmakers swapped scarce nickel for manganese in 200-series stainless; swap hafnium in periphery high-k metal gates and capacitor interlayers for lanthanum aluminate and La-doped ZrO2, made from Mountain Pass (California) rare-earth output and deposited by ALD from lanthanum amidinates.
why: World hafnium supply is only ~70-100 t/yr from a few zirconium refiners; lanthanum is the most abundant rare earth with a domestic mine and separation, and LaAlO3 (k ~25) matches HfO2.

title: On-die microheaters anneal aging sense amps back to health
idea: Ideal result: periphery that resets its own wear. Polysilicon microheaters under SA stripes and drivers heat local transistors to ~250 C for seconds during maintenance windows, recovering BTI and hot-carrier threshold shifts.
why: Lifetime and offset (facts 1, 7): keeps SA offsets near day-zero for years, allowing tighter margins and longer service life.

title: Off-die replaceable voltage-generation chiplet powers memory periphery
idea: Ideal result: the memory die holds no pumps or regulators that wear out. Move VPP, VBB and VARY generation to a socketed power chiplet on the module that feeds dies through dedicated rails; failing or outdated regulators are swapped, and the chiplet is reused on new modules.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): frees several percent of die area from charge pumps and makes the highest-stress periphery repairable.

title: Ceria-free shallow-trench planarization by selective dry etch-back
idea: Imposed scarcity: zero rare-earth ceria slurry and no CMP water. Fill isolation trenches with flowable oxide, then planarize with a self-limiting, nitride-stopping remote-plasma etch-back under optical endpoint control instead of ceria-slurry CMP.
why: Ceria is a China-concentrated rare earth and CMP is a major slurry and UPW consumer; dry etch-back also reduces dishing and particle defects, removing one chokepoint per STI layer.

title: Titanium-silicide strapped dual-work-function polysilicon wordline
idea: Combine the old poly gate with a self-aligned silicide strap (zero added masks): fill the buried-wordline trench with in-situ doped poly, recess it, then sputter Ti and anneal so TiSi2 forms only on exposed poly, leaving lower n+ poly near the channel and the strap for conduction.
why: Removes buried-wordline tungsten with abundant Ti and Si; work-function engineering of the poly reduces GIDL, lengthening refresh intervals.

title: PFAS-free DNQ-novolac resist revival for periphery layers
idea: Revive 1980s diazonaphthoquinone-novolac i-line resists, which contain no fluorinated photoacid generators, for every periphery and non-critical layer (about half the die), paired with second-hand i-line steppers.
why: PFAS phase-outs threaten chemically amplified resists, while DNQ is PFAS-free and cheap; no EUV; claims 50-60% of resist volume becomes PFAS-free at no cost penalty.

title: Vacuum-linked cluster runs the whole capacitor module airlessly
idea: Combine the cluster-tool concept with the full capacitor module (mold deposition, HAR etch, dry mold removal, electrode ALD, high-k ALD, top plate) on one vacuum transfer backbone. Wafers never see air, wet cleans or FOUP queues inside the module.
why: Removes ~5 wet cleans and their tools, eliminates native-oxide and queue-time losses, and shrinks the module's cleanroom footprint ~40% (capital intensity, water use).

title: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: wafers live inside a vacuum backbone
idea: Connect every process tool to a linear vacuum or nitrogen wafer highway so wafers never meet fab air from start to finish; the building becomes an ISO-8 warehouse without raised floors or giant make-up air handlers.
why: Capital and time: the cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction cost and a large energy share; could cut build time by about a year and total capex ~15%.

title: Eliminate the arms-length buyer: OEM cooperative co-owns a DRAM fab
idea: Eliminate the pure-buyer role: automotive, industrial and PC OEMs form a cooperative, like farm co-ops or airline fuel consortia, that owns a mid-size legacy-node DRAM fab and allocates output at cost by equity share.
why: Guarantees allocation in shortages and spreads capex across many balance sheets.

title: Resurrected-scanner fab: build on the industry's retired DUV tools
idea: Reverse the tool lifecycle: buy retired KrF/ArF dry scanners and older etchers on the secondary market, refurbish them, and pair them with a design rule set made only for spacer multiplication and self-alignment.
why: Litho capex falls ~90% compared with a new EUV fab and tools ship in months, not years; this suits a U.S. startup fab.

title: Ocean Spray-style OEM buyer cooperative that co-owns a fab
idea: Like cranberry growers' cooperative, mid-size OEMs (PCs, networking, auto Tier-1s) buy equity in proportion to committed GB/year, the co-op owns a fab run by a contract operator, and members get output at cost plus patronage refunds.
why: Gives mid-size buyers supply security that big hyperscalers already lock up via LTAs; co-op capital plus offtake makes a $5-8B fab financeable without a memory giant.

title: Vacuum-railway fab with no ballroom cleanroom
idea: Inverts 'a fab is a giant cleanroom building'. Link cluster tools with sealed sub-mTorr maglev tube conveyors so wafers never touch air from bare wafer to passivation; the building becomes an ordinary industrial shed with local maintenance enclosures.
why: Cleanroom shell, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy/water load; also removes queue-time oxidation limits.

title: Prefabricated copy-exact fab pods cut build time to 18 months
idea: Box[Fab=factory-built cleanroom and utility modules x Scale=10k wafers/month pods x Owner=modular fab builder x Finance=pod-by-pod project finance]: build DRAM capacity in identical shippable modules (cleanroom, sub-fab, utilities) that bolt together, so capacity is added in increments.
why: Capital and time: an estimated 18 vs 36-60 months to first wafer, smaller financing tranches; output is standard DDR5/HBM.

title: Cartridge-based fab tools refurbished across node transitions
idea: Worsen: scrap or export whole fab tool sets at every node transition. Flip: build process tools as standard frames with swappable process cartridges and open control interfaces, so older DRAM fabs refurbish chambers for new chemistries (gain cells, 3D) instead of buying new tools.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity: could cut new-node tool capex ~30-40%.

title: 2050 engineer's cleanroom-less fab: wafers travel only in sealed tubes
idea: A 2050 engineer finds it odd that we filter a stadium of air to protect a 300 mm disc. Link conventional tools with a sealed pod-in-tube network held at vacuum or ultra-dry N2, with load-lock interfaces on every tool, so wafers never meet room air from start to finish and the building becomes a plain ISO-8 warehouse.
why: The ballroom cleanroom, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction and a large energy load; removing them cuts build cost ~15-25% and build time. Risks: standardizing tool interfaces, and contamination inside the tubes.

title: War Production Board converts idle logic and NAND lines to DRAM
idea: As the 1942 War Production Board turned car plants into bomber lines, use the Defense Production Act to fund converting underused 300 mm logic or NAND lines (28-40 nm) to DRAM under licensed cell IP. Grants cover retooling of the capacitor and deep-etch modules.
why: Time and capital: conversion takes ~18 months at ~20% of greenfield cost because the shell, utilities and most tools already exist.
note: Logic lines lack capacitor and HAR etch modules; conversion cost understated.

title: Wake-shield-inspired all-vacuum DRAM line with no cleanroom
idea: Extreme user: orbital fabs that get free ultra-high vacuum behind a wake shield. Recreate that on Earth by linking deposition, etch, anneal and (already-vacuum) EUV/e-beam tools through a continuous maglev vacuum wafer tunnel so wafers never touch air; the building drops to a gray corridor and native-oxide cleans vanish.
why: Capital/energy: cleanroom, HVAC and ultrapure-water plant are ~15-25% of fab capex and a large share of energy; also removes ~10% of clean/strip steps and shortens cycle time.

title: Multi-beam e-beam direct-write line accepting slow, maskless cycles
idea: Time-for-capital trade at the tool scale: 250k-beam Schottky-emitter writers in ultra-high vacuum pattern the critical DRAM layers with no masks and no laser gas. Slower throughput is accepted through more writers working longer cycles.
why: Removes the EUV/excimer dependence and the ~$10M-plus mask sets for low-volume U.S. secure and specialty DRAM. A line with no rare gases at all.
note: MAPPER-style multibeam throughput was the failure mode; only niche secure volumes.

title: LaB6 multi-beam maskless writer prints only the access-gate cut layer
idea: La: deploy a massively parallel e-beam writer (LaB6 source split into ~10^5 beamlets) dedicated to the single cut/contact layer that isolates access transistors and lands storage contacts, while every other layer uses DUV pitch multiplication; no mask set and no EUV scanner are needed.
why: Removes the EUV dependency for the 1-2 layers DUV cannot pitch-split cleanly (fact 4) at a fraction of EUV capital; throughput limits it to a few layers per wafer.
note: Multibeam cut-layer writers known (MAPPER, Multibeam); building one far exceeds $1M.

title: Convert depreciated planar-NAND lines into DRAM lines
idea: Ideal: an idle fab that already prints 15 nm lines. Closest achievable with no new fab: old planar NAND lines (15-20 nm SAQP on ArFi) left idle by the 3D NAND shift add capacitor-module tools and run 1x-nm DDR4/LPDDR4, because litho, CMP and cleans already match.
why: Capacity in ~18 months with no shell build.
note: Planar NAND lines largely already converted.

title: No Si wafer: relocate retired Gen 6 display toolsets stateside
idea: Forced limit: no Si and no new tools. Buy complete Gen 6 backplane tool sets (PECVD, sputter, panel steppers) from retiring Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese LCD fabs and reinstall them in a U.S. brownfield to make oxide-TFT memory panels.
why: U.S. manufacturability: an onshore memory-substrate line for under $1B in about 2 years, where the U.S. today has almost no display fabs.
note: Relocation variant of LCD-fab IGZO panels in I-04100.

title: COCOM-embargoed engineer patterns DRAM without EUV using block copolymers
idea: Persona: an Eastern Bloc engineer denied Western lithography, who turns to chemistry. DUV immersion defines guide stripes. PS-b-PMMA, or high-chi PS-b-PDMS, block copolymers then self-assemble into 24 nm-pitch lines and holes that correct and multiply those stripes. This replaces the 5-7 EUV layers of a 1-beta-class DRAM with ArF plus directed self-assembly.
why: EUV comes from one supplier at ~$200M per tool. DSA uses commodity polymers and could cut litho capex per wafer start by ~40%.

title: Layer offload: non-critical DRAM layers exposed on KrF/i-line elsewhere
idea: Ideal: precious scanners print only the hardest layers. Closest achievable with no new fab: of ~40-60 mask layers, the ~25 coarse ones (implants, pads, upper metals) move to depreciated KrF/i-line scanners in a nearby trailing fab under a wafer-shuttle and overlay-matching protocol.
why: Frees ~30-40% of ArFi scanner time at the constraint tool, so more wafer starts.

title: Substitute battery ride-through rules with NV-state credits for telecom sites
idea: Policy: let cell sites and critical infrastructure meet backup mandates (e.g., multi-hour battery rules) with fewer battery hours if their compute uses certified non-volatile working memory that resumes state instantly.
why: Creates a guaranteed early market for U.S.-made NV DRAM-class memory and cuts lithium battery demand; drives volume and cost-down learning.
note: Logic weak: sites still need power during outages; NV memory does not replace ride-through energy.

title: Wavelength-addressed wordline decoding with silicon microring filters
idea: Broadcast the row address as a WDM optical comb on a waveguide running over each bank; each sub-wordline driver group has a microring tuned to one wavelength plus a photodiode that fires its driver. The predecoder tree and its long, repeated global wires disappear, because a photonic add-drop filter now does the row decoder's job.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): removes global decode wiring; ~30% lower decode energy and area in large banks, with optical I/O as a natural extension.
note: Microring tuning power per ring outweighs the decoder savings.

title: Radio-frequency tone addressing selects wordline groups via resonators
idea: MINIFY decoder wiring to a single line: the row address is broadcast as a sum of on-die RF tones, and each wordline-driver group has a tuned LC or MEMS resonator filter bank that fires only when its tone combination is present.
why: Fact 7: replaces predecode buses and NAND decode trees (several % of die) with one global line; selectivity and latency make this speculative.

title: Sushi-conveyor optical delay-line ring for hot broadcast data
idea: Copy the kaiten-sushi conveyor. A closed, low-loss SiN waveguide loop on the interposer keeps tiny, very hot structures (MoE routing tables, norms, sync flags) circulating as WDM pulse trains. Each compute chiplet 'picks a plate' with a thermally tuned microring drop filter as the block goes by, and an on-loop re-timer re-injects the train every lap.
why: Serves many readers with no DRAM activation and no contention at the HBM PHY. Capacity is only kilobits per meter of loop, so the gain is modest: fewer hot-spot conflicts and roughly 5-10% fewer small HBM reads.
note: Kilobit loop capacity; self-admitted 5-10% gain.

title: Core-rope weaving: per-die e-beam via layer hardwires repairs
idea: Apollo's core-rope ROM was woven by hand, each wire passing through or around each core. After wafer sort at the via-2 level, a maskless multi-beam e-beam writes one custom via layer per die that hardwires spare rows and columns into place. That layer is the one added 'mask', and no physical mask exists.
why: Deletes fuse banks, fuse latches and address-compare logic (~3-5% of die, fact 7) and power-up fuse loading, so repaired addresses take no extra latency.

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode CAM as hardware hash-cons index
idea: Revive the 1960s Goto pair, two series tunnel diodes that latch a bit with no transistor, as the storage element of a CAM cell: Esaki diodes made by degenerate spin-on doping in a university fab form a dense CAM that holds content hashes and answers 'is this block already stored?' in one cycle for inline memory dedup.
why: Inline dedup needs a huge, fast hash index that today eats DRAM; a native associative store makes dedup feasible at memory speed, 1.3-3x effective capacity on duplicate-heavy servers.
note: Tunnel-diode latches draw static current and are not dense; the index fits in SRAM/DRAM anyway.

title: Million slow TFT compressors on glass for cold pages
idea: Compressing cold pages is bound by throughput, not latency, so slow transistors suffice if there are enough of them. Tile a glass panel with ~1 million LTPS-TFT LZ/rANS engines at ~1-5 MHz each (aggregate >1e12 symbol operations/s), fed through optical I/O, which compress cold pages in the background and write them back to DRAM compacted.
why: Every server gets zswap-class 2-3x compression of cold memory without spending CPU cycles or silicon logic area.
note: Offloads only zswap CPU cost; feeding a million slow engines over optical I/O impractical.

title: Tree-ring radial tiers: concentric shells in one wide hole
idea: Rotate the stacking axis from vertical to radial: deposit 10 concentric semiconductor/dielectric/conductor shells in a 400-nm hole, each ring the channel and storage node of its own cell. A conical chamfer etched at the hole top exposes each ring for contact, like tree rings on a slanted cut.
why: Tier count without tall stacks (fact 2): 10 cells per hole without 26+ deposited tiers, ~5x density per hole versus a one-cell vertical channel.

title: Optical clock trees failed on alignment; a light shaft through the stack
idea: Free-space optical clock distribution (1980s-2000s research) failed because external optics could not stay aligned to chips. Etch one 20-50 um oxide-lined vertical hole through every die of a memory stack so it acts as a light pipe, put an n-ZnO/p-NiO UV LED in the base die at its bottom, and let a ring photodiode on each die's shaft wall tap the pulse, broadcasting clock and command strobes to all tiers with sub-ps skew.
why: Removes clock/strobe TSVs and per-tier deskew circuits (fact 6), shrinking in-stack timing margins and power; uses only Zn, Ni, O and Si.
note: ZnO/NiO UV LED weak; clock TSVs are a tiny share of the tax.

title: Quantum anomalous Hall edge chirality as a dissipationless cryogenic bit
idea: Effect walk: quantum anomalous Hall effect. In a MnBi2Te4 or Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)2Te3 micro-Hall cell at 2-10 K, magnetization sets which way the dissipationless edge channel circulates; read senses the Hall-voltage sign at sub-mV, and write uses the topological insulator's own giant spin-orbit torque.
why: Read dissipation approaches zero (quantized, backscatter-free), which matters where every nW at 4 K costs ~1 W at room temperature: >=10x lower system energy per access than shipping data to warm DRAM for quantum-control and cryo-compute stacks.
note: Cryogenic niche; very low temperature QAH and write mechanism immature.

title: Pyroelectric film images row heat to steer page tiering
idea: Deposit a thin LiTaO3 pyroelectric layer over each DRAM bank, patterned into per-subarray pixels. Activation bursts heat their rows by millikelvins; each pixel emits charge proportional to dT/dt, and a tiny integrator turns that into a hotness map. The OS keeps only the hottest 20-30% of pages in DRAM and pushes cold pages to compressed CXL or flash, with no SRAM access counters or page-table sampling.
why: Gives tiering hardware-free access tracking. Cuts DRAM per server 30-40% for <1% area and no extra periphery (fact 7).
note: Thermal diffusion blurs per-subarray signal; access tracking is already cheap (CXL hotness monitors).

title: Mott-oscillator phase locking flags duplicate pages for inline dedup
idea: Each page fingerprint drives a row of NbO2 threshold-switch relaxation oscillators through bit-weighted coupling resistors. Rows fed identical patterns injection-lock in phase within ~100 cycles, while different patterns stay incoherent. One phase detector therefore answers 'does this page duplicate any of N stored signatures?' in parallel, and a hit triggers copy-on-write page merging in the hypervisor.
why: Dedup across VMs and containers saves 15-40% of DRAM in cloud hosts. The all-to-all compare costs O(1) energy instead of hashing and searching on every write.
note: Hash lookup is not the dedup bottleneck; analog phase locking of page signatures is fragile.

title: AlN resonator spectra read hundreds of ROM bits per wire
idea: Encode tokenizer, embedding and activation lookup tables as the mass-loading of AlN bulk-acoustic resonators, each tuned to a distinct frequency. One RF sweep on a shared line reads hundreds of resonators at once from their spectral peaks, so no row decoders are needed. A reference resonator cancels the ~-25 ppm/C temperature drift, and frozen mass-loads do not change at 125 C.
why: A dense, decoder-free ROM for static lookup data attacks periphery (fact 7) and moves MB-scale tables out of DRAM in edge devices.
note: Spectral multiplexing limited by resonator Q and area; niche.

title: Frequency-addressed wordlines replace row decoders with tuned resonators
idea: Ideal result: no decoder at all; the address is broadcast and the right row answers. Each sub-wordline driver gets a tiny BEOL LC or bulk-acoustic resonator tuned to one of 64 frequencies; a global line carries a tone burst and only the matching resonator's rectifier fires its driver, with a 2-level predecode covering 64x64 rows.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): a decoder tree becomes one broadcast line plus passive filters stacked above the drivers; ~30% smaller row-decoder stripe.

title: Two-terminal ovonic threshold switches replace bitline equalize transistors
idea: Substitute the three-transistor precharge/equalize block with sputtered GeSe-class ovonic threshold switches between bitline pairs and the precharge rail, fired by a short overdrive pulse.
why: Periphery area: equalizers sit at bitline pitch in vias rather than in active silicon, freeing ~10% of the sense strip.
note: OTS holding voltage prevents precise equalization; threshold drift.

title: LCD array-tester voltage imaging replaces on-die test periphery
idea: Borrowed from the LCD fab's electro-optic array tester, a modulator plate that images every pixel's voltage without contact: after the array layer on glass is built, a pattern is written and all cell voltages are imaged to find dead or weak-retention cells before periphery and stacking.
why: Periphery and capital: removes test-mode and BIST circuitry (~2-3% area) and probe cards, and yields full retention maps for refresh binning.

title: Eliminate vias in decoder routing: capacitively coupled dynamic signal layers
idea: Decoder and predecoder signals are pulses, so let them cross metal levels through overlap capacitors with 5 nm ALD Al2O3 between the layers instead of vias, with a keeper on each node restoring DC level. Only power rails use vias, placed in a few relaxed landing zones etched with BCl3/Cl2, and the wiring is subtractive Cl-etched Mo.
why: Removes most periphery via etches (normally fluorocarbon), barrier and fill steps; periphery BEOL cost ~-20% and via-yield failures disappear.

title: Purity in the code, not the crystal: solar-grade DRAM wafers
idea: Reverse where reliability lives: build DRAM on solar-grade silicon grown in ordinary quartz crucibles, accept that ~1% of cells have contamination-shortened retention, and protect each 4 KB page with an on-die LDPC code (~12% parity) that corrects a 1% raw BER.
why: Removes the 11N polysilicon and HPQ crucible chokepoints; wafer cost down ~20-30% for ~12% bit overhead.

title: Skip the deuterium anneal; let ECC cover the trap tail
idea: Reverse the final passivation step: omit the high-pressure deuterium/H2 interface anneal, accept the ~1% of access transistors with extra trap-assisted leakage, and correct them with ECC.
why: Removes deuterium (heavy-water derived, few suppliers) and a high-pressure furnace step.
note: Skipping hydrogen passivation raises interface traps broadly, not just 1%; ECC cannot absorb the retention loss.

title: Honeycomb mat tiling sharing each sense-amp hub among three mats
idea: Bees' hexagonal comb shares every wall between neighbors. Mats are tiled hexagonally so each sense-amp hub sits where three mats meet and is time-multiplexed among their bitlines: one active, one as open-bitline reference, one idle. Conventional open bitline shares between only two.
why: Fact 7: sense amps per bit fall ~1/3, so the sense-amp stripe shrinks ~30% and the die ~5-7%. The cell array is already hex-packed, so lithography fits.
note: Directional SAQP/EUV line patterning cannot run bitlines at 120 degrees.

title: Jet-engine MAX-phase ceramics as tungsten-free buried wordline conductor
idea: Aerospace uses MAX phases (Ti3SiC2, Ti2AlC), layered carbides that conduct like metals yet tolerate heat like ceramics. Deposit nanolaminate Ti2AlC/Ti3SiC2 by ALD supercycles plus a front-end crystallization anneal as buried-wordline and contact fill, exploiting their layered in-plane conduction to dodge the grain-boundary resistivity penalty that hurts tungsten below 10 nm width.
why: Replaces tungsten (China ~80%) with Ti, Al, Si and C, all abundant and domestic; targets W-parity wordline resistance at 8-10 nm widths.

title: Gunn-domain delay line: travelling field domains as a shift register
idea: 1960s engineers proposed Gunn-effect domains as high-speed memories. Launch bits as high-field domains travelling ~1e5 m/s along a long n-GaN or GaAs channel, recirculate them through a regenerating trigger electrode, and tap them with capacitive pickups along the channel.
why: ~1-um bit spacing at 100 Gb/s per channel and ~10 ns per mm tap latency with no cell structure at all; domain stability at sub-um scale is very uncertain.
note: Micron bit spacing and high Gunn power dissipation make density and energy poor.

title: Eccles-Jordan flip-flop rebuilt from nanoscale vacuum-channel triodes
idea: Revive the 1918 vacuum-tube flip-flop at nanometer scale: cross-couple two field-emission vacuum-channel triodes (silicon tips, 50 nm sealed gaps, no gate dielectric) into a static latch. The vacuum gap has no dielectric leakage and no junctions, so the cell holds state without refresh and runs at 250 C.
why: Removes Hf/Zr dielectrics, implants and the leakage tail (fact 3); running hot lets data centers drop chillers, saving energy and water; claims refresh energy near zero.

title: Crowe persistent-current cells in YBCO at 77 K, no helium
idea: Revive the 1957 Crowe cell and Buck's cryotron, where a bit is a supercurrent circulating clockwise or counterclockwise in a superconducting loop, using YBCO films grown by reactive thermal co-evaporation (no argon sputtering, no KrF excimer) and cooled by liquid nitrogen made from air. A persistent current does not decay, so cells never refresh.
why: The constraint and Fact 3: liquid nitrogen replaces helium cryogenics, and loop arrays need ~4-6 masks at 0.5 um on depreciated fabs. Risks are loop inductance capping density at ~10-100 Mb/cm2 and YBCO junction reproducibility.

title: Magnetostrictive Delay Line Reborn as YIG Magnon Loops on Bubble-Memory Lines
idea: Revive the nickel-wire magnetostrictive delay lines of 1960s calculators as spin-wave (magnon) recirculating loops in yttrium-iron-garnet films grown by the liquid-phase-epitaxy garnet process of 1980s bubble memory: data rides as spin waves with no charge current and is regenerated by a parametric pump each lap.
why: Energy per access: spin-wave propagation costs aJ per bit versus pJ for charge-based bitlines, >=10x net; garnet LPE needs no EUV and little capital.
note: Delay lines are serial access, not byte-addressable random access; damping and pump power add doubt.

title: Thermal moat isolates the cool array from hot periphery
idea: Inverts 'the whole die shares one temperature': a single mask etches an air-gapped ring trench between the array and the hot periphery and I/O, forcing periphery heat to flow to the backside instead of laterally through the array.
why: Array runs ~8-10 C cooler, roughly doubling retention (fact 3) and halving refresh; also widens hammer margins.

title: Halve ultrapure-water rinses in water-scarce fabs, absorbing residue faults
idea: Inverts 'every rinse must be exhaustive': cut UPW rinse time and volume by ~40% on non-gate steps, accepting residue-induced isolated cell faults within the 1% budget.
why: Water and siting: lets fabs in water-stressed U.S. regions such as Arizona expand capacity within existing water permits.

title: Acoustic delay-line FIFOs buffer pipeline-parallel activations
idea: Pipeline-stage activations and switch packet buffers are strictly first-in-first-out, so they do not need random-access cells. Store them as surface acoustic waves on lithium-niobate or quartz: at ~3.5 km/s a 2 cm line holds ~6 us, and 1,000 parallel 5 GHz channels in recirculating, re-amplified loops hold ~30 Mbit.
why: Frees MB-scale HBM and DRAM buffers in deep-buffer switches and pipeline stages. The capacity is small, but every byte moved out of HBM also avoids its ~3x wafer tax.

title: Banknote press: security-printing intaglio lines print memory module substrates
idea: Random stimulus 'banknote' -> mints already print with micron registration 24/7. National security printers (BEP and allied mints) retool idle intaglio/gravure capacity with conductive and dielectric inks to print DIMM, CXL-module and coarse package-substrate layers as surge capacity.
why: Package substrates and module boards caused shortages in 2021; a government-owned printing base gives sovereign surge capacity for the non-silicon half of memory supply.

title: Analog syndrome bitlines compute parity by charge summation in-array
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x multi-level analog-sum sensing x dedicated parity bitline x bulk Si x standard. During activation, cells of a parity group also dump charge onto a shared parity bitline; a small multi-level comparator turns the summed charge into a count whose mod-2 is the syndrome, so only words with a nonzero syndrome go to the full decoder.
why: Decoder power and latency at 1% BER: most words skip decoding; periphery ECC logic ~-50%.
note: Multi-level charge-sum parity is fragile; at 1% BER many words have errors anyway.

title: On-site electrolytic hydrogen and nitrogen as the fab's only inerts
idea: Box [supply: PEM electrolyzers on reclaimed water + PSA N2 generators | uses: load-lock venting, carrier gas, PECVD dilution | leak test: 5% H2-in-N2 tracer with Pd-gate sniffers | storage: no rare-gas cylinders on site]: redesign the fab gas plant so N2 and H2 cover every inert role, and send the electrolytic O2 by-product to ozone generators.
why: Removes all He/Ne/Ar/Kr/Xe supply exposure for a DRAM fab using US-manufacturable equipment and renewable power.
note: Argon is hard to replace in PVD and plasma etch, so full rare-gas elimination is doubtful.

title: At-tool electrochemical synthesis of ALD precursors from bulk metal
idea: Worsen: rely on a handful of overseas suppliers for TEMAZ, TDMAT and other organometallic precursors shipped in hazardous cylinders. Flip: put a small electrochemical cell at each ALD tool that anodically dissolves Zr, Ti or Al metal into ligand solution, making precursor on demand at the purity the tool needs.
why: Precursor chokepoint and shipping hazards: ~2-3x lower precursor cost and less inventory, from commodity metals.

title: Cleaved mica substrates give atomic flatness without CMP
idea: Worse: add dozens of CMP steps and ceria slurry to flatten each layer. Flip: start on cleaved muscovite mica, atomically flat over cm2. Grow oxide-semiconductor and high-k films by van der Waals epitaxy, and keep later tiers flat by vdW-bonded transfer instead of polishing.
why: Process steps: removes ~10-20% of CMP steps and their ceria consumables, on an abundant U.S.-mined substrate.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel stores model weights as light in flight
idea: Worsen: park every weight in a leaky capacitor and drag it across a bus each token. Flip: inference reads all weights in the same order every token, so keep them circulating in a 64-wavelength fiber loop with in-line amplification and periodic electronic regeneration (a 100 km loop holds ~0.8 GB); accelerators tap each layer as it passes.
why: No capacitor or refresh for streaming weights; capacity scales with cheap fiber length instead of wafers, and latency equals loop period (~0.5 ms), acceptable for per-token weight streaming.
note: 100 km loop holds 0.8 GB; amps and regenerators cost far more than DRAM.

title: Beekeeper's honeycomb: hexagonal plasma-diced chiplets for more beachfront
idea: Bees tile with hexagons: plasma-dice compute and memory chiplets into hexagons so each compute die shares three or six full edges with memory dies in a honeycomb mesh, instead of a rectangle with only two usable sides.
why: Raises die-edge beachfront per mm2 by ~1.5-2x, so more memory channels attach per accelerator without TSV stacking: bandwidth per package goes up without HBM's area tax.
note: Hexagons have less perimeter per area than squares; beachfront claim doubtful.

title: Potter's kiln: co-fired AlN ceramic memory brick with copper lines
idea: Fired ceramics last millennia: co-fire an aluminium nitride carrier with copper conductors (no tungsten) to form a 'memory brick' that holds 4-8 DRAM dies around a logic die, with a silicon-matched CTE (~4.5 ppm/K) and 170 W/mK conductivity.
why: A rugged 125 C/10 year memory module that avoids China-dominated tungsten and organic laminates, with less thermal-cycle stress than FR-4.
note: AlN sinters far above copper's melting point; niche rugged market.

title: Kintsugi artist: liquid-metal microcapsules that heal cracked bonds
idea: Kintsugi fills cracks with gold: embed microcapsules of gallium-indium alloy, with a barrier shell, around microbump fields; when a fatigue crack forms, the capsules break and liquid metal wicks into the gap to restore conduction.
why: Self-repairs interconnect opens during 10 years at 125 C, which extends package life without big redundancy; risky because gallium embrittles Al and Cu.

title: Farmer's rain barrel: printed supercapacitor film steadies array voltage
